concepts.subsection: Weighted average cost of capital
concepts.statement: WACC weights each source of finance by its market value, not its book value, and uses debt's after-tax cost, not its quoted rate — the tax shield on interest is part of what debt actually costs the firm. Book-value weights or a pre-tax cost of debt both misstate the discount rate applied to project cash flows.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — real options
concepts.statement: A project's strategic value is its static NPV plus the value of the flexibility attached to it — options to expand, abandon or delay that ordinary discounting prices at zero. A negative static NPV can still be worth taking up when the option it carries is worth more than the shortfall.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Risk in capital budgeting — sensitivity, scenario and simulation
concepts.statement: Sensitivity analysis moves one variable at a time to find each one's break-even point. Scenario analysis moves several variables together in a few named, internally consistent bundles — best, base, worst. Simulation draws thousands of random combinations from each variable's probability distribution and builds the full outcome distribution, which the other two only sample at a handful of points.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation
concepts.statement: A one-step binomial model prices an option from the two possible next-period stock prices using the risk-neutral probability that makes the stock's own expected return equal the risk-free rate — not the real-world probability of an up move, which plays no part in a no-arbitrage price. The expected payoff under that probability is then discounted at the risk-free rate.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — Black-Scholes inputs
concepts.statement: Black-Scholes prices an option from five inputs: spot, strike, time to expiry, the risk-free rate and volatility. A call rises with spot, time, the rate and volatility, and falls with a higher strike; volatility raises both the call and the put together, since either option gains from a larger move and loses no more than its premium either way.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — convexity
concepts.statement: Duration prices the bond's yield sensitivity as a straight line; convexity is the curvature that line misses. Because the true price-yield curve bends away from the line, a positive-convexity bond gains more from a yield fall than duration predicts and loses less from an equal yield rise — the convexity term always adds back value that a duration-only estimate leaves out.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — yield measures
concepts.statement: Current yield is the annual coupon divided by the bond's market price, not its face value. For a bond trading below par, the order runs coupon rate < current yield < yield to maturity, because YTM also captures the pull to par at redemption that current yield ignores; above par the order reverses, and only a par bond has all three equal.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Risk Management — credit default swaps
concepts.statement: A credit default swap transfers a bond's default risk from a protection buyer to a protection seller: the buyer pays a periodic spread regardless of what happens, and the seller pays out only if the reference entity defaults, and then only the loss given default — the face value less whatever the recovery rate returns.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Rights issue — theoretical ex-rights price
concepts.statement: The theoretical ex-rights price weights the cum-rights price and the subscription price by the number of old and new shares, not by a simple average of the two prices. The value of the right attached to one existing share is the ex-rights price less the subscription price, divided by the number of old shares needed to subscribe for one new share.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Dividend policy — Walter's model
concepts.statement: Walter's model prices a share as P = [D + (r/Ke)(E − D)] / Ke and ties the optimal payout to how the firm's internal return r compares with its cost of equity Ke — retain everything when r exceeds Ke, since the firm compounds cash better than the market prices it; pay out everything when r is below Ke; payout is irrelevant only at r = Ke, the special case MM's irrelevance proposition generalises.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — leveraged buyouts
concepts.statement: A leveraged buyout funds most of the purchase price with debt secured on the target's own assets and cash flows, leaving the sponsor's equity a small slice of the deal. Returns come from paying that debt down over the holding period — and from any exit-multiple expansion — so the same flat operating performance produces a far larger percentage return on the sponsor's equity than on the deal as a whole.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — two-asset risk and correlation
concepts.statement: A two-asset portfolio's standard deviation equals the weighted average of the two assets' standard deviations only when they are perfectly positively correlated. At any lower correlation the covariance term in the variance formula is smaller than that limiting case, and the portfolio's risk falls below the weighted average — the diversification benefit correlation below one always buys.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — unequal lives and equivalent annual cost
concepts.statement: Two assets that do the same job over different lives cannot be compared on total present value of cost, because the shorter-lived one simply carries fewer years of cost. Each total is converted into an equivalent annual cost by dividing it by the annuity factor for its own life — not by the number of years, which would throw away the time value the annuity factor holds — and the lower annual charge wins.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — adjusted present value
concepts.statement: APV splits a project in two rather than folding financing into the discount rate: value it first as if it were all-equity funded, at the ungeared cost of equity, then add every financing side effect separately — the present value of the interest tax shield, less issue costs, plus any subsidised-loan benefit. The tax shield is the tax saved on the interest, not the interest itself, and a project can turn from reject to accept on the financing half alone.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — enterprise multiples and the bridge to equity value
concepts.statement: An EV/EBITDA multiple prices the whole enterprise, so what it produces belongs to lenders and shareholders together. Getting from there to a share price means walking the bridge — deduct the debt, add back the cash the buyer also acquires, then divide by shares outstanding. Deducting gross debt without crediting the cash, or skipping the bridge entirely, values the equity at the whole firm's worth.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — purchasing power parity and expected spot rates
concepts.statement: Relative purchasing power parity says the expected spot rate moves with the ratio of the two countries' expected inflation, so the higher-inflation currency is expected to depreciate. Quoting home currency per unit of foreign currency, the expected rate is the spot multiplied by one plus home inflation over one plus foreign inflation. Where interest rate parity works from interest rates and binds today's forward, PPP works from inflation and predicts a future spot.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — multilateral netting, leading and lagging
concepts.statement: Multilateral netting collapses every intra-group payable and receivable into one net position per company through a central desk, so only the net balances actually cross a border and only those bear conversion and transfer cost. Bilateral netting is the step before it and not a rival to it: each pair of companies first cancels what the two of them owe each other, and what survives that pass is what the central desk then nets across the whole group. ICAI has asked which method has to be applied before the multilateral one and the answer it gives is the pairwise method, so treat the two as consecutive stages of one procedure rather than as competing choices. What the group-wide stage adds is that it also strikes out flows no single pair could ever cancel, because those offset only once every company is looked at together. Leading and lagging is the companion timing tool — settle early in a currency expected to strengthen, delay in one expected to weaken.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — delta and the hedge ratio
concepts.statement: Delta is how much an option's value moves for a one-rupee move in the underlying — between zero and one for a call, between minus one and zero for a put — and it doubles as the hedge ratio. A written call position is neutralised by holding delta times the number of underlying shares the options cover. The hedge holds only locally, because delta itself shifts as the share moves, which is why a delta hedge must be rebalanced rather than set once.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Interest Rate Risk Management — swaptions
concepts.statement: A swaption is an option on a swap, not on a rate. A payer swaption gives its buyer the right, never the obligation, to enter a swap as the fixed-rate payer, so it protects a borrower against rates rising while leaving the gain if rates fall; a receiver swaption is the mirror, the right to receive fixed, which suits a lender or an investor fearing a fall. The buyer pays a premium and holds the right; the writer collects the premium and carries the obligation.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — rebalancing strategies and portfolio insurance
concepts.statement: The three rebalancing disciplines pull in different directions after a market move. Buy-and-hold does nothing. Constant mix restores a fixed percentage split, so it buys into a fall and sells into a rise. Constant proportion portfolio insurance sets the equity holding at a multiplier times the cushion — portfolio value less the floor — so a fall shrinks the cushion and forces selling, which is what keeps the floor intact.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — Sharpe's single index model and the cut-off rate
concepts.statement: Sharpe's single index model builds the optimal portfolio by ranking securities on excess return to beta — expected return less the risk-free rate, divided by beta — and admitting every security whose ratio exceeds the computed cut-off rate. The ratio, not the raw expected return, decides: a high-return security carrying a heavy beta can rank below a modest one that earns its return cheaply, and the cut-off is a threshold that admits several securities, not a contest the top name wins alone.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Corporate restructuring — demerger, sell-off and equity carve-out
concepts.statement: The three ways of separating a division differ in who ends up owning it and whether cash comes in. A demerger or spin-off hands shares in the new company to the parent's own shareholders in proportion to their holding — no buyer, no consideration, no cash. A sell-off sells the division outright to a third party for cash. An equity carve-out floats a minority stake in the subsidiary to outside investors, raising cash while the parent keeps control.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: International Financial Management — depository receipts and cross-market pricing
concepts.statement: A depository receipt is issued abroad by an overseas depository against a fixed number of home-market shares held by a domestic custodian, and that ratio is what makes the two prices comparable. Convert the receipt's foreign currency price at spot and set it against the ratio times the home share price: a gap either way is a premium or a discount, and it is measured against the underlying shares' value, since that is what the receipt is a claim on.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

concepts.subsection: Financial restructuring — share buyback and earnings per share
concepts.statement: A buyback funded from surplus cash cuts the share count, which lifts EPS, but it also surrenders the after-tax income that cash was earning, which lowers it. The net effect turns on which is larger, so the working must charge the earnings forgone net of tax — not gross — and divide by the reduced share count. Counting one side without the other guarantees the wrong answer, and in either direction.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — convertible debentures, conversion value and premium
concepts.statement: A convertible debenture has two values underneath it. Conversion value is the conversion ratio times the share price; straight bond value is what the same coupon and maturity would fetch without the conversion right. The floor is whichever of the two is higher, because the holder can always fall back on it. The conversion premium is the market price less the conversion value — measured from the price actually paid, not from face value, and expressed against the conversion value it exceeds.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — warrants and equity dilution
concepts.statement: A warrant is written by the company itself, which is what separates it from an exchange-traded call option written by another investor. Exercise brings the exercise price into the company in cash and makes it issue new shares, so the share count rises and existing holders dilute; an option merely moves existing shares between two outsiders. A detachable warrant is a security in its own right, separately listed and separately priced, and exercising it leaves the debenture it came attached to still outstanding — where a convertible debenture is extinguished on conversion.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — the abandonment option
concepts.statement: The option to abandon is exercised state by state, not once for the whole project: at the decision date, compare the abandonment value with the present value of continuing in that state and take the larger. Its worth is the expected gain over the states where abandoning wins, discounted back — never the raw abandonment proceeds, and never the gain in the worst state taken alone. A static NPV that discounts probability-weighted cash flows prices this flexibility at exactly zero, which is how a rejected project turns acceptable.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Currency swaps — comparative advantage and the quality spread differential
concepts.statement: The gain in a currency swap comes from comparative advantage, not absolute advantage. One party may borrow more cheaply than the other in both currencies and the swap still creates value, because what matters is that its edge is wider in one currency than in the other. Each borrows where its edge is widest and swaps into what it wants, and the total gain available — the quality spread differential — is the difference between the two spreads, never their sum.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — commodity futures and basis risk
concepts.statement: A buyer of a commodity hedges by going long futures, so a rise in the price he must pay is met by a gain on the futures leg that reduces his effective cost. The hedge does not lock the entry futures price: it locks that price plus the basis — spot less futures — prevailing when the hedge is lifted. Because the closing basis is unknown today, basis risk survives the hedge, and it is the whole reason the effective cost lands near the futures price rather than on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Risk Management — what a credit rating says and does not say
concepts.statement: A credit rating is an opinion on the likelihood that one specific instrument is serviced on time — so the same company's long-term facilities and its commercial paper can be rated differently, since tenure, security and structure all move the grade. It is not investment advice: it ranks default risk and is deliberately silent on whether the price or yield on offer compensates for that risk. It is not permanent either; the agency keeps the issuer under surveillance and rating migration, including to default grade, is ordinary.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — gamma, theta and vega
concepts.statement: Delta measures how much an option's price moves for a one rupee move in the share, but delta itself moves. Gamma measures that movement — the curvature — and it is why a delta-only estimate understates a bought option's gain in either direction. Theta measures what the option loses as a day passes, and it works against the buyer. Vega measures what it gains when volatility rises, and it works for the buyer of either a call or a put. A second-order estimate adds one-half of gamma times the square of the price move to the delta term.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — the minimum variance portfolio
concepts.statement: Among all the mixes of two assets there is one whose standard deviation is lowest, and its weights come from the variances and the covariance, not from the standard deviations taken alone. The weight of the first asset is the second's variance less the covariance, over the sum of the two variances less twice the covariance. Where correlation is below one this minimum sits below the risk of the safer asset held on its own, which is the whole reason a cautious investor still diversifies instead of holding the quietest asset by itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — exchange traded funds
concepts.statement: An exchange traded fund is bought and sold on the exchange through the day at a market price, where an open-ended scheme transacts only with the fund itself at the day's net asset value. What keeps the two numbers together is creation and redemption in large lots by authorised participants, usually against the basket of shares rather than cash — any gap between price and net asset value is an arbitrage they close. Units are created and cancelled continuously, which is what separates an exchange traded fund from a closed-end fund whose count is fixed.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — return to the unit holder
concepts.statement: What a unit holder earned over a year is the change in net asset value plus every distribution taken out during the year, over the net asset value he started with. The distributions belong in the numerator because they came out of the fund and are the reason the closing net asset value is lower than it would otherwise have been, and the opening figure belongs in the denominator because that is the money actually put to work. Dividing by the closing figure answers a different question and always flatters a rising fund.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Securitisation — pass through and pay through instruments
concepts.statement: A pass through certificate sells the investor a proportionate ownership interest in the pool itself, and whatever the borrowers pay in that month is passed on to him as it arrives — so an early repayment reaches him early and the timing risk is his. A pay through security is a debt obligation of the special purpose vehicle, which keeps ownership of the pool and uses its collections to service paper it has re-sequenced into tranches of different maturity and seniority. Ownership of the receivables, and who carries prepayment timing, separate the two.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.subsection: Startup finance — venture capital exit routes
concepts.statement: A venture investor makes his money by selling the stake, never by being repaid, because he holds equity and not a loan. Four routes are open — an initial public offering, a trade sale to a strategic buyer, a secondary sale to another financial investor, and a buy-back by the promoters or the company — and the fund's agreement is written around which of them can be forced and when. The route decides the price, the timing and how much of the holding can be sold at once, which is why the exit is negotiated at entry rather than at the end.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — market value added
concepts.statement: Market value added is the market's verdict on every rupee of capital the company has been given. It is the market value of the firm — the market capitalisation of the equity plus the value of the debt — less the total capital employed, and it is positive only where the market believes the company earns more than the cost of that capital. Capital employed means all of it, retained reserves included, since money kept back is money the shareholders were not given. Where EVA is one year's verdict, market value added is the verdict on the whole life.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Mergers and acquisitions — synergy and the maximum price payable
concepts.statement: Synergy is what the combination is worth over and above the two companies valued separately, and it is the only thing an acquirer can afford to pay a premium out of. The ceiling on the price is therefore the target's own standalone value plus the whole of the synergy; pay more than that and the acquirer's shareholders are worse off however good the business is. The premium actually paid is not the synergy — it is how the synergy is split between the two sets of shareholders, and anything the acquirer keeps back is its own gain.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: Corporate restructuring — financial reconstruction and capital reduction
concepts.statement: A financial reconstruction rearranges the claims on a company without changing the business underneath. Share capital is written down, lenders and preference holders agree to take less, assets are brought to realistic values, and the accumulated losses are wiped against what is surrendered. No cash enters the company from the exercise itself — that is why fresh money is almost always raised alongside it. Every party that sacrifices does so on one calculation: what the scheme leaves him against what a liquidation would actually have paid him.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: Mergers and acquisitions — takeover defences
concepts.statement: The defences against a hostile bid work by making the target dearer, less attractive or already spoken for. A poison pill lets every shareholder except the bidder buy new shares cheaply, so the raider's stake is diluted and the bid becomes too expensive to press. A white knight is a friendlier acquirer invited in to outbid the hostile one. Greenmail is the target buying the raider's block back at a premium to send him away. The crown jewel defence sells or options away the target's own best asset, so there is less left worth bidding for.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: International Financial Management — the effective cost of a foreign currency loan
concepts.statement: A foreign currency loan is never as cheap as its coupon. The borrower must buy the foreign currency to pay both interest and principal, so the effective cost in home currency compounds the foreign interest rate with the expected movement in the exchange rate rather than adding them. Adding the two understates the cost, because the currency's rise applies to the interest as well as to the amount borrowed. Only when that full cost is set against the home currency rate is the comparison honest.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — spot rates and implied forward rates
concepts.statement: A spot rate is the average return over the whole period to which it applies, not the return of its final year. The forward rate for that final year is what is left when the shorter spot rate is taken out of the longer one by compounding, not by subtraction — one plus the longer rate raised to its own number of years, divided by one plus the shorter rate raised to its years. It is the rate at which lending long and rolling a short loan give the same money, so any other rate would be arbitraged away.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — theories of the term structure
concepts.statement: Three explanations compete for the shape of the yield curve. The expectations theory says the long rate is the average of the short rates the market expects, so an upward slope is a forecast that rates will rise. Liquidity preference adds that a lender parting with money for longer must be paid a term premium, so the curve can slope up while rates are expected to stay flat. Market segmentation says each maturity has its own borrowers and lenders and its own rate. The same upward curve is evidence for all three, which is why the shape alone settles nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — the Fisher effect and the international Fisher effect
concepts.statement: The Fisher effect splits a nominal interest rate into a real return and expected inflation. Carried across two countries, it says the currency of the higher nominal interest rate is expected to weaken by roughly that interest difference, so a lender gains nothing by chasing the higher rate abroad. The expected future spot rate is today's spot times one plus the home rate over one plus the foreign rate. Where interest rate parity fixes the forward rate that can be contracted today, the international Fisher effect is a statement about the spot rate people expect, and the two can differ.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — replacement of an existing asset
concepts.statement: A replacement decision is an incremental one. The initial outlay is the new asset's cost less what the old one actually fetches, and less or plus the tax the sale itself triggers — a price above the written-down value is taxed, a price below it saves tax. Book value is not cash and never enters the outlay on its own. Thereafter only the differences count: the operating savings the new asset brings, the depreciation shield it earns net of the shield the old asset would have gone on earning, and the two salvage values at the end.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — decision trees and staged investment
concepts.statement: A decision tree is used where a project is taken in stages and the second stage is entered only if the first turns out well. It is solved backwards, from the far end towards today. At every chance node the branch values are weighted by their probabilities; at every decision node the best branch is taken and the others are dropped, because nobody is compelled to spend good money after a bad result. Averaging the branches at a decision node instead of choosing between them prices away the very flexibility the staging was arranged to buy.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — real cash flows and money cash flows
concepts.statement: Inflation may be handled in a project appraisal in either of two ways, and the only rule is that the numerator and the denominator must agree. Either inflate the cash flows to the actual rupees expected and discount at the money rate, or leave the flows in today's prices and discount at the real rate. The two rates are linked by compounding, not addition — one plus the money rate equals one plus the real rate times one plus the inflation rate. Mixing the two counts inflation twice or leaves it out altogether, and the second mistake makes every project look better than it is.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — asset beta and equity beta
concepts.statement: A quoted company's equity beta measures two things at once — the risk of the business it runs and the gearing it happens to carry. To borrow that beta for a differently geared company the gearing must be stripped out and put back. Stripping gives the asset beta, the equity beta divided by one plus the after-tax debt to equity ratio; putting it back multiplies the asset beta by one plus the new company's after-tax debt to equity ratio. The tax factor belongs in both steps, because interest is deductible and the taxman therefore carries part of the gearing risk.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management — active and passive strategies
concepts.statement: A passive strategy accepts the benchmark's return and competes on cost and faithfulness of tracking; it still trades, because an index changes its constituents and new money has to be put to work. An active strategy tries to beat the benchmark by choosing securities or by timing the market, and it carries higher research costs and higher turnover, so the honest test is whether it beats the benchmark after all of that, not before. Turnover is a symptom of the mandate, never its definition — what makes a strategy active is that a return above the benchmark is being sought at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — early exercise of American options
concepts.statement: An American option may be exercised any day up to expiry, but that right is worth having and rarely worth using. A call on a share paying no dividend should never be exercised early — selling it in the market fetches its intrinsic value plus whatever time value is left, so exercising throws that time value away. A dividend changes the case, because the option holder receives no dividend and exercising just before the share goes ex-dividend can be worth more than the time value surrendered. An American put can be worth exercising early on its own merits, since the strike money comes in at once and can be put to work.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — currency options and the range forward
concepts.statement: A range forward, or currency collar, hedges a payable by buying an option that caps the rate and selling one that floors it, with the strikes chosen so the premium paid and the premium received cancel. The importer therefore pays nothing for the protection and gives up the benefit of a large favourable move instead. The rate finally paid lives inside the band — at the cap if the currency runs above it, at the floor if it falls below it, and at the spot rate in between. The written option is the part beginners forget, because it is exercised against the hedger rather than by him.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Interest Rate Risk Management — hedging with interest rate futures
concepts.statement: An interest rate future is priced as one hundred minus the rate, so its price falls when rates rise. A borrower expecting to raise money later therefore sells futures — his loss on the loan is met by a gain on a short position — while a depositor expecting to place money buys them. The number of contracts is the exposure divided by the contract size, then scaled by the length of the exposure against the length the contract covers, because a three-month contract hedges only three months of interest however large the principal is.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

concepts.subsection: International Financial Management — project cash flows against parent cash flows
concepts.statement: A foreign project is worth to the parent only what the parent can actually get out of it. Two things stand between the project's cash flow and the parent's bank account — restrictions that block part of the money in the host country, and taxes the host country deducts on what is remitted. Blocked funds are not lost for ever, but they arrive later and are worth less, and cash left idle abroad is worth less still. The project view and the parent view of the same investment can therefore differ enough for one to be worth doing and the other not.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — bonds with half-yearly coupons
concepts.statement: Where a bond pays interest twice a year the whole calculation moves to a half-yearly period. The coupon is halved, the number of periods is doubled, and the quoted annual required return is halved to give the rate per period. Doubling the periods without halving the rate punishes the bond twice over; halving the rate while leaving the coupon annual flatters it, because the money is made to arrive later than it does. Half-yearly interest is worth more than the same annual total, since the first half arrives six months sooner.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — dividend discount model with non-constant growth
concepts.statement: Few companies grow at one rate for ever, so the dividend discount model is run in two parts. Each dividend of the high-growth phase is forecast and discounted on its own. At the end of that phase a terminal value is computed by capitalising the first dividend of the stable phase at the required return less the stable growth rate. That terminal value already stands at the end of the last high-growth year, so it is discounted for that many years and no more — a point that costs marks twice over, because the dividend inside it is the following year's, not the last one forecast.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — growth from retention and return on equity
concepts.statement: A valuation that takes the growth rate as given has assumed the hardest number in it. Growth that a company can fund out of its own profit is the retention ratio times the return on equity — the share of profit kept back, multiplied by what that kept-back money earns. Using the payout ratio in place of the retention ratio inverts the relationship and makes a generous dividend look like a source of growth. And the return on equity on its own is not the growth rate either, because a company that pays out anything at all grows more slowly than it earns.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — valuing an unlisted holding, control and marketability
concepts.statement: A value built from listed comparables describes a small parcel of shares that can be sold on any working day. Two adjustments carry it to an unlisted minority holding, and they answer different questions. A minority discount reflects that the holder cannot direct the dividend, the strategy or a sale. A discount for lack of marketability reflects that there is no ready buyer even at the right price. Because each bites on what is left after the other, the two are applied one after another on a shrinking base — adding the percentages together overstates the fall.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation — the net asset method against capitalised earnings
concepts.statement: The net asset method values a business at what its assets would realise less what it owes, and it is the natural measure for a company about to be broken up or for one whose value sits in property. The earnings method capitalises maintainable profit at a rate appropriate to the risk, and it is the measure for a going concern. The gap between the two is goodwill — what the business earns over and above what its assets alone would justify. Neither number is automatically the answer, and the lower of the two is not a rule.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Securitisation — internal and external credit enhancement
concepts.statement: Credit enhancement is what stands between the pool's losses and the investor, and it comes from inside the structure or from outside it. Internal enhancement uses the deal's own material — a pool larger than the paper issued, junior tranches that absorb loss first, the excess of pool interest over what the paper pays, and a cash collateral account. External enhancement is a third party's promise, such as a guarantee or a letter of credit, and it imports that party's own credit standing, so the enhanced paper can never be safer than the guarantor. Enhancement moves loss about; it does not remove it.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — systematic investment and rupee cost averaging
concepts.statement: Investing a fixed sum every month buys more units when the net asset value is low and fewer when it is high, so the average cost per unit comes out below the simple average of the net asset values used. That is arithmetic and it always holds where the prices differ. What it does not do is guarantee a profit — the average cost still has to be below the value on the day the units are sold. Buying a fixed number of units each month instead of a fixed sum reverses the effect and lands the investor on the simple average.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Mergers and acquisitions — cash consideration against a share exchange
concepts.statement: How an acquisition is paid for decides who carries the risk that the expected synergy never arrives. Cash pays the target's shareholders a fixed sum and ends their interest, so every rupee of disappointment falls on the acquirer's own shareholders. A share exchange gives the target's shareholders a fixed proportion of the combined company rather than a fixed amount, so they share both the gain if the merger works and the loss if it does not. The two look identical on the day the terms are agreed and diverge the moment the outcome differs from the forecast.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — fundamental and technical approaches
concepts.statement: The two approaches to security analysis differ in what they look at, not in how carefully they look. Fundamental analysis works from the economy to the industry to the company, estimates an intrinsic value, and buys where the market price sits below it. Technical analysis ignores the accounts entirely and reads price, volume and open interest on the belief that price already discounts everything, that prices move in trends, and that history tends to repeat itself. Fundamental analysis is aimed at long-term investing, technical analysis at short-term.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Risk Management — types of risk faced by an organisation
concepts.statement: An organisation faces four broad kinds of risk. Strategic risk is a strategy becoming less effective as the world moves — a new competitor, a technology shift, a change in customer demand. Compliance risk is the cost of failing the rules and regulations it must live under, which bites hardest on entering a new state or a new line of business. Operational risk is people and process going wrong in the day-to-day running. Financial risk is unexpected change in financial conditions — prices, exchange rates, interest rates, credit standing.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — open ended, close ended and interval schemes
concepts.statement: The functional classification of mutual funds turns on when an investor may leave. An open-ended scheme takes money in and buys units back at any time at a price based on NAV, so its capital is unlimited and its redemption period indefinite. A close-ended scheme has a fixed life and a fixed corpus; before maturity the only exit is a sale on the stock exchange at whatever the market offers. An interval scheme sits between the two, opening for both purchase and redemption only during pre-specified intervals at NAV-based prices.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Startup finance — innovative sources of funding
concepts.statement: Banks are the least likely benefactors of a startup, so the sources are non-bank and each one answers a particular shortage. Crowdfunding raises small amounts from a large number of individuals. Peer-to-peer lending pools a group who lend to each other. Microloans are small sums from individuals at low rates. Vendor financing stretches the supplier's payment terms. Purchase order financing advances money straight to the supplier so a large new order can be produced. Factoring turns an invoice already raised into cash. Matching the source to the shortage is the skill; naming them is not.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — the efficient market hypothesis and its three forms
concepts.statement: Efficient market theory says price already reflects the available information, and it comes in three nested levels. Weak form — price reflects everything in the record of past prices and volumes, so charting earns nothing. Semi-strong form — price also reflects all other publicly available information, so an announcement cannot be traded profitably once it is out. Strong form — price reflects private information too, so even insiders earn nothing extra. Each level contains the one below it, so a market cannot pass a higher test and fail a lower one.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — economy, industry and company analysis
concepts.statement: Fundamental analysis is three concentric circles worked from the outside in — economy analysis, then industry analysis, then company analysis. The economy sets growth, inflation and the monsoon; the industry adds its product life-cycle stage, its demand supply gap, its barriers to entry and the state of competition; only then does the company's own net worth, growth record, competitive advantage and quality of management decide anything. A good company inside a contracting industry inside a contracting economy is still a bad holding.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy — the advanced role of the CFO
concepts.statement: The traditional role — governance, compliance, controls and business ethics, in service of wealth maximisation — has not gone anywhere; it has been built on. Globalisation, the growth of information and communications and the pandemic pushed the CFO into four further areas: the organisation's whole risk management framework, the financial viability of the supply chain, mergers and corporate restructuring, and Environmental, Social and Governance financing. The objective held still while the range of responsibilities widened, which is what makes the CFO a leader in value creation rather than its bookkeeper.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — support and resistance levels
concepts.statement: When a price falls away from a peak, that peak becomes the resistance level, because everyone who failed to sell at the high wants out there. When it rebounds from a trough, that trough becomes the support level, because everyone who failed to buy at the low wants in there. The price is then expected to travel between the two. A breach of either is the signal that matters — a distinct departure from the status quo and an attempt to set newer levels.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Securitization — obstacles to growth in India
concepts.statement: Six things hold securitisation back in India and none of them is a doubt about the structure itself. Stamp duty on the transfer of a mortgage debt is charged under the Transfer of Property Act and runs high in some states, though a pass through certificate evidences a receivable rather than a debt and escapes it. Taxation is unsettled — no specific provision exists, and opinion divides between taxing the SPV in a representative capacity and taxing the investors. Accounting treatment in the originator's books is unsettled. Documentation is unstandardised, the debt market is thin, and foreclosure laws are weak.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.subsection: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy — levels of strategy
concepts.statement: Strategy exists at three levels and the level is a property of the question, not of who signs it off. Corporate level strategy selects which businesses to compete in and coordinates that portfolio, and is tested for suitability, feasibility and acceptability. Business unit level strategy builds and sustains competitive advantage for one strategic business unit's products. Functional level strategy sits in the operating divisions and departments and turns the level above into action plans. Senior management decides strategy, middle management tactics, line management operations.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — the Dow Theory
concepts.statement: The Dow Theory sorts market movement into three that run at once. The primary movement is the main trend, from a year to thirty-six months or longer, and it is what the words bull and bear name. The secondary movement is shorter — two weeks to a month or more — and runs opposite to the primary, which is what makes it a correction and not a reversal. The daily fluctuations are the narrow day-to-day moves and are no part of the theory's interpretation. The trend is up when successive highs and successive lows are both higher. The theory says where the market is going, never how far or how high.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — the head and shoulders pattern
concepts.statement: A head and shoulders top is a left shoulder, a higher head and a right shoulder, and it is the single most important pattern for signalling a reversal of trend. The neckline joins the points where the head and the shoulders meet. What matters is the price movement after the second shoulder: a fall below the neckline is the sell signal, and the drop expected equals the distance from the top of the head down to the neckline. The inverse pattern is the same shape upside down, and there it is a rise above the neck line that signals a purchase.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Risk Management — the categories of financial risk
concepts.statement: Financial risk is the unexpected movement in financial conditions — prices, exchange rates, credit standing, interest rates — and five categories are listed under that heading. Counter party risk is the other side not honouring its obligation, which covers credit default. Interest rate risk is a rate change moving assets and liabilities. Currency risk is exchange rate movement changing cash flows. Liquidity risk is being unable to meet liabilities as they fall due. Political risk is the fifth, and it carries a qualification the examiner asks for by name. Adverse action by a host government — confiscation, rationing of remittance, restriction on converting the local currency, price control, invalidation of patents — is not a financial risk in the direct sense; it is counted under the heading because an unexpected political change abroad creates country risk, and country risk ends in financial loss. When a question asks whether political risk is covered, the answer is that it is included, and the marks are for saying by what route rather than for the bare label. Filing any of the five under operational risk mistakes an outside movement for an inside failure.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Startup finance — the venture capital investment process
concepts.statement: A venture capital investment runs through six stages in a fixed order. Deal origination, where the fund sources the proposal directly or through intermediaries. Screening, the quick sort on what was sourced. Due diligence, the detailed verification of what the founder claimed. Deal structuring, where terms are negotiated only once the case has survived that verification. Post investment activity, where the fund nominates its nominee to the board. And the exit plan, which the fund makes the promoter spell out at the time of investing, not at the end.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — side pocketing
concepts.statement: Side pocketing separates the risky or doubtful assets in a scheme from its other investments and cash. Money linked to the stressed asset is locked until the fund recovers it, so the manager is not forced into distress selling of illiquid securities to meet redemptions, and the main scheme's NAV then reflects the actual value of the liquid assets. It protects the investor who stays. It has also been used abroad to keep investors from genuine returns, which is why it is watched rather than simply allowed.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — moving averages and trading signals
concepts.statement: A moving average is plotted against price to generate decisions, not to describe. The buy signals are the price line rising through the moving average line while that line is flattening out; the price line falling below an average that is still rising; and a price line above the average that dips but turns back up before touching it. The sell signals are the mirror image. A 200-day average traces the long-term trend, 60 days the intermediate, 10 days the short. An exponential average weights the latest price most heavily; an arithmetic one weights all periods alike.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Risk Management — scaling Value at Risk across a horizon
concepts.statement: A Value at Risk figure is built from three things — the holding's volatility, a Z score for the chosen confidence level, and a time horizon. Volatility in rupees times the Z score gives the one-day figure. Stretching it to a longer horizon multiplies by the square root of the number of days, not by the number of days, because independent daily moves partly cancel. Ten days therefore costs about three times one day. A VaR quoted without its horizon and its confidence level is not a number at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Securitization — stripped securities
concepts.statement: A stripped security splits the cash flows of the underlying pool into an Interest Only instrument and a Principal Only one. Their prices move in opposite directions with rates, because it is not only the discount rate that changes — the borrowers' behaviour changes too. When market yields rise, borrowers hang on to their cheaper existing loans, so principal arrives later and the PO price falls, while interest keeps accruing and the IO gains. When yields fall, borrowers repay early and the two reverse. Both are highly volatile, which is why investors prefer them least.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — testing the weak form empirically
concepts.statement: Three tests check the weak form of efficient market theory and they check the same claim by different arithmetic. The serial correlation test correlates the size of the price change in one period with the change in another. The run test throws the sizes away, marks each change plus or minus, and compares the number of unbroken same-sign stretches against a purely random series of the same size. The filter rule test buys after a rise of N per cent and sells after an N per cent fall from a subsequent high, then asks whether that beat buying and holding after costs. By and large all three support the random walk model.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy — growth beyond the sustainable rate
concepts.statement: The sustainable growth model assumes three things at once — a target capital structure held without issuing new equity, a target dividend payment ratio held, and sales growing as fast as conditions allow. Hold the first two and the third is no longer a choice: the only new equity is retained earnings, so assets and sales cannot outrun retained earnings plus the debt those earnings will carry. A board demanding growth above that rate must give up one of the three. Mature firms have the opposite problem — growth below the sustainable rate, and cash with nowhere productive to go.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

concepts.subsection: Portfolio Management
concepts.statement: Diversification removes unsystematic risk, the part specific to individual securities. What remains in a well-diversified portfolio is systematic risk, which beta measures and which no amount of diversification can remove.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation
concepts.statement: An option premium is intrinsic value plus time value. A put's intrinsic value is the excess of strike over spot (zero if spot is higher); whatever of the premium is not intrinsic value is time value.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.statement: Under interest rate parity, the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount and the lower-rate currency at a forward premium, by the interest differential — otherwise borrowing in one currency and depositing in the other would be a free profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation
concepts.statement: Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes. It rises with maturity and falls with coupon; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, the maximum for any bond of that term.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation
concepts.statement: To hedge a stock portfolio with index futures, the number of contracts is the portfolio's value multiplied by its beta, divided by the value of one futures contract. Ignoring beta hedges a different portfolio than the one held.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.statement: An importer with a foreign currency payable loses when that currency rises, so the hedge is to buy it forward or buy a call option on it. A forward locks the rate both ways; the option caps the cost while keeping the gain if the currency falls, at the price of the premium.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
concepts.statement: When mutually exclusive projects rank differently under NPV and IRR, NPV decides. IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself and can prefer a small project with a high rate over a large one that adds more value; NPV measures the wealth actually added at the real cost of capital.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Mutual Funds
concepts.statement: Net asset value per unit is the market value of the fund's investments plus other assets, minus liabilities and accrued expenses, divided by units outstanding. Entry and exit prices derive from NAV, and the expense ratio quietly drags it every day.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Business Valuation
concepts.statement: Under constant dividend growth, equity value per share is next year's expected dividend divided by the excess of the required return over the growth rate. The model runs on the coming dividend, not the one just paid, and dies where growth meets or beats the required return.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Interest Rate Risk Management
concepts.statement: A forward rate agreement fixes today the interest rate for a future borrowing or deposit period — a 6x9 FRA covers a three-month period starting six months out. The buyer gains when rates rise above the agreed rate and is compensated by a discounted settlement at the period's start; no principal ever moves.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation
concepts.statement: For European options on the same share, strike and expiry, the call price minus the put price equals the share price minus the present value of the strike. When market prices break that chain, a riskless arbitrage exists — buy the cheap side, sell the dear one, and lock the difference.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Portfolio performance measures
concepts.statement: Sharpe divides excess return by total risk (standard deviation); Treynor divides the same excess return by systematic risk (beta). For a fully diversified portfolio the two rank alike, because diversification has squeezed out the unsystematic part. Where they disagree, the fund is carrying diversifiable risk the market does not pay for.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: CAPM and the security market line
concepts.statement: CAPM's required return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. A security whose expected return sits above that line has positive alpha — it is underpriced, and the decision rule says buy; below the line, overpriced, sell. Alpha measures mispricing against systematic risk only.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Futures pricing — cost of carry
concepts.statement: The fair futures price is the spot price grown at the carrying cost — financing, storage, minus any yield the asset throws off. A traded futures price above fair value invites cash-and-carry arbitrage (buy spot, sell futures); below fair value, reverse cash-and-carry (sell spot, buy futures). The arbitrage, not opinion, is what pins the price to the formula.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Mergers — exchange ratio and EPS
concepts.statement: In a share-for-share merger, the acquirer's EPS rises when the price paid values the target at a lower price-earnings multiple than the acquirer's own, and falls when the target is bought at a higher multiple. The exchange ratio decides how the combined earnings spread over the combined shares; accretion is arithmetic, not evidence of a good deal.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — money market hedge
concepts.statement: A money market hedge manufactures a forward rate from the two interest rates: an exporter awaiting foreign currency borrows that currency today against the receivable, converts at spot, and invests at home; the foreign loan is repaid by the receivable itself. If interest rate parity holds exactly, the locked-in rate equals the forward rate and the choice is a matter of transaction cost and access, not principle.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Risk management — Value at Risk
concepts.statement: Value at Risk states the largest loss expected over a stated horizon at a stated confidence — a one-day 99 per cent VaR of ₹10 lakh means one trading day in a hundred should lose more than ₹10 lakh. It says nothing about how much worse that hundredth day gets, which is the measure's famous blind spot.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Capital market line and security market line
concepts.statement: The capital market line prices total risk (standard deviation) and holds only efficient portfolios — combinations of the risk-free asset and the market portfolio. The security market line prices systematic risk (beta) and holds every fairly priced asset, efficient or not. A single stock full of diversifiable risk plots on the SML yet below the CML.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Interest rate swaps
concepts.statement: In a plain vanilla interest rate swap one party pays fixed and receives floating on a notional principal that is never exchanged; only net interest differences change hands each period. A borrower with floating-rate debt who pays fixed on a swap has synthetically fixed its cost; the swap's value at inception is zero and moves as rates move.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — cross rates and triangular arbitrage
concepts.statement: Three currencies imply each cross rate from the other two; when a quoted cross rate strays from the implied rate, riding the three legs in the right circle returns more of the starting currency than was put in, risk-free. The direction matters — one way round the triangle profits, the other way loses — and the trade itself pushes the quotes back into line.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Corporate valuation — FCFF and FCFE
concepts.statement: Free cash flow to the firm belongs to all capital providers and discounts at the weighted average cost of capital to give enterprise value; free cash flow to equity — FCFF less after-tax interest and net debt repayments — belongs to shareholders alone and discounts at the cost of equity to give equity value directly. Mixing a flow with the other side's discount rate is the classic valuation error.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: Risk in capital budgeting — certainty equivalents
concepts.statement: The certainty equivalent approach shrinks each risky cash flow to the certain amount the decision-maker would accept instead, then discounts at the risk-free rate; the risk-adjusted discount rate approach keeps the expected flows and loads the risk into a higher rate. The rate route compounds the risk penalty with time even when risk does not grow; certainty equivalents price each year's risk on its own.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: International capital budgeting — currency consistency
concepts.statement: A foreign project can be valued two ways that must agree: discount foreign currency cash flows at the foreign discount rate and convert the NPV at spot, or convert each year's flows at expected forward rates and discount in home currency at the home rate. Mixing — foreign flows with the home rate, or forwards with the foreign rate — builds the currency premium in twice or not at all.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

concepts.subsection: Bond portfolio immunisation
concepts.statement: A bond portfolio is immunised against interest rate moves by matching its duration to the investment horizon: a rate rise then costs price but earns more on reinvested coupons, a fall does the reverse, and at the horizon the two effects offset. The match decays as time passes and rates move — durations drift at different speeds — so immunisation needs periodic rebalancing, not a one-time set-up.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Currency swaps
concepts.statement: A currency swap exchanges principal and interest in one currency for principal and interest in another — and unlike an interest rate swap, the principals are real: exchanged at the start (or notionally referenced) and re-exchanged at maturity at the original rate, which is where the currency risk transfers. Each party ends up servicing debt in the currency it wanted, having first borrowed where its comparative advantage lies — the market where its own borrowing spread against the other party is widest, which is not always the market where it borrows cheapest in absolute terms.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Arbitrage pricing theory
concepts.statement: APT prices assets from several systematic factors — industrial production, inflation surprises, interest rates, credit spreads — each with its own beta and premium, where CAPM compresses all systematic risk into one market beta. APT's discipline is arbitrage: two portfolios with identical factor exposures must earn identical expected returns, or the difference is picked up risk-free. It says nothing about which factors — that is empirical.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

concepts.subsection: Securitisation
concepts.statement: Securitisation sells a pool of receivables to a bankruptcy-remote special purpose vehicle that funds the purchase by issuing securities serviced by the pool's collections. True sale takes the assets off the originator's balance sheet; tranching splits the paper into senior, mezzanine and equity slices absorbing losses bottom-up; credit enhancement — overcollateralisation, subordination, guarantees — lifts the senior tranche's rating above the originator's own.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.subsection: Startup finance — funding stages
concepts.statement: Startup money arrives in stages priced to risk: bootstrapping and friends-and-family at the idea, angels at the prototype, venture capital in lettered rounds as revenue proves out, and strategic or public markets at maturity. Each round prices the company anew — pre-money plus new cash equals post-money — and earlier holders dilute unless they follow on. Venture investors buy convertible preferred with liquidation preference, anti-dilution and board rights, not plain equity.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

concepts.section: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.subsection: Types of foreign exchange exposure
concepts.statement: Transaction exposure is a booked receivable or payable awaiting settlement — hedgeable with forwards and options. Translation exposure is the accounting restatement of foreign subsidiaries' balances at consolidation — a reporting effect with no cash flow of its own. Economic exposure is the deepest: the effect of exchange rates on future competitiveness and cash flows, reaching even firms that never invoice abroad, and managed by operational choices more than by derivatives.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Mutual funds — costs and tracking error
concepts.statement: The expense ratio is deducted from the fund's assets daily, so investors earn the portfolio's return minus costs — a one-and-a-half per cent ratio on an eight per cent market compounds into a fifth of the wealth over decades. For index funds the second report card is tracking error: the volatility of the fund's return differences against its benchmark. Low fees with faithful tracking is the entire proposition of passive investing.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Futures — margins and marking to market
concepts.statement: A futures position opens with initial margin and is marked to market daily — losses are debited and gains credited to the margin account each evening at the settlement price. When the balance falls below the maintenance margin, a margin call demands topping back up to the initial level; failure triggers position closure. Daily settlement is why futures carry negligible counterparty risk and why they can bankrupt a trader long before expiry.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Interest rate caps, floors and collars
concepts.statement: A cap pays the borrower whenever the reference rate fixes above the strike — insurance against rising rates, bought for a premium; a floor pays the lender when rates fix below its strike. A borrower's collar buys a cap and sells a floor, financing the protection by surrendering the benefit of falls below the floor — at zero net cost when the strikes are chosen so the premiums offset. The borrower's rate then lives inside a band.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

concepts.subsection: Economic value added
concepts.statement: EVA charges profit for all the capital that earned it: net operating profit after tax minus the capital employed times its weighted average cost. A company can grow accounting profit every year while destroying value, if the new profit earns less than the capital's cost. Positive EVA — return on capital above WACC — is what accounting profit alone never certifies.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

concepts.subsection: SA 300 — Planning an Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: The overall audit strategy sets the scope, timing and direction of the audit and guides the development of the more detailed audit plan; the plan turns that strategy into named procedures with their nature, their timing and their extent settled — the risk assessment procedures first, and then the further audit procedures worked at the assertion level. The two remain interrelated after they are first set — changes discovered while developing the plan can send the auditor back to revise the strategy — and planning continues as an iterative process throughout the audit rather than ending as a discrete opening phase.

citation.ref: Overall audit strategy and the audit plan

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 402 — where the entity uses a service organisation, and what the report may say
concepts.statement: Where the auditor uses evidence from a service organisation's type 1 or type 2 report, the auditor's report on the user entity's financial statements does not refer to that service auditor's report — doing so could be misread as dividing responsibility, which the user auditor may not do. A reference is made only where law or regulation requires it, and even then the report states that the reference does not reduce the user auditor's own responsibility for the opinion expressed.

citation.ref: Reference to a service auditor in the auditor's report

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: The auditor accumulates every misstatement identified during the audit other than those that are clearly trivial — a threshold set well below materiality, catching only amounts that are inconsequential in size and nature, individually and in aggregate, beyond any reasonable doubt. Where there is any uncertainty about whether an item is clearly trivial, the auditor treats it as not clearly trivial and accumulates it.

citation.ref: The clearly trivial threshold

concepts.subsection: SA 500 — Audit Evidence
concepts.statement: A management's expert is an individual or organisation with expertise in a field other than accounting or auditing whose work is used by the entity to help prepare the financial statements. Before relying on that work as audit evidence, the auditor evaluates the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity; obtains an understanding of the expert's field sufficient to evaluate the work; and evaluates the appropriateness of the work, including the source data, methods and assumptions used, as evidence for the relevant assertion.

citation.ref: Using the work of a management's expert

concepts.subsection: SA 540 (Revised) — Auditing Accounting Estimates
concepts.statement: Accounting estimates sit on a spectrum of inherent risk: some carry low estimation uncertainty and complexity — a straightforward provision computed from a fixed formula — while others, such as an expected credit loss model or a goodwill impairment test, carry high estimation uncertainty, subjectivity and susceptibility to management bias. The auditor's response scales with where an estimate sits on that spectrum: the rigour applied to testing methods, data, assumptions and indicators of bias rises with the estimate's complexity rather than staying uniform across every estimate in the file.

citation.ref: Spectrum of inherent risk

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(i)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(i) covers property, plant and equipment: whether the company maintains proper records showing full particulars, including quantitative details and situation, of PPE and intangible assets; whether PPE is physically verified by management at reasonable intervals with discrepancies properly dealt with in the books; whether title deeds of immovable property are held in the company's own name, with details where not; and whether any revaluation was carried out, based on a registered valuer's valuation, with the quantum of change specified where the change is 10 per cent or more of the net carrying value.

citation.ref: Clause 3(i)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(vii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(vii) asks whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues — GST, provident fund, employees' state insurance, income tax and other applicable dues — with the appropriate authorities, stating what arrears stood outstanding at the balance sheet date having gone unpaid for over six months after they fell due; it separately asks for disputed statutory dues not deposited, with the amount involved and the forum where the dispute is pending.

citation.ref: Clause 3(vii)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(ix)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(ix) covers repayment discipline: whether the company defaulted in repayment of loans or other borrowings, or in payment of interest, to any lender, with the period and amount of default; whether the company has been declared a wilful defaulter by any bank, financial institution or lender; whether term loans were applied for the purpose for which they were obtained, with the amount and details of any diversion; and whether funds raised on a short-term basis were used for long-term purposes.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ix)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 3
concepts.statement: Clause 3 of Part I of the First Schedule stops a member in practice from taking a share of what somebody outside the Institute earns from professional work, and from agreeing to take one. The Council has carved a limited exception for prescribed reciprocal arrangements with certain other recognised professional bodies; outside that carve-out, sharing professional profits with a non-member is misconduct regardless of the non-member's own standing or the quality of the work referred.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 3

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 4
concepts.statement: Clause 4 of Part I of the First Schedule bars a member in practice from entering into partnership, in or outside India, with any person other than a chartered accountant in practice, unless that person belongs to a professional body the Council has notified as permitted — company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates enrolled with a Bar Council, architects and actuaries among them — subject to the Council's conditions for such multidisciplinary partnerships.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 4

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3)(i) — Internal financial controls reporting
concepts.statement: Section 143(3)(i) requires the statutory auditor's report to state whether the company has an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to the financial statements in place, and whether it operated effectively — a separate opinion from the opinion on the financial statements themselves. MCA notification G.S.R. 583(E) dated 13 June 2017 lifts that reporting for a private company which is a one person company or a small company, or whose turnover is less than ₹50 crore as per the latest audited financial statement and whose aggregate borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate at any point during the financial year are less than ₹25 crore. The notification as first published put an "or" between those two figures; a corrigendum dated 13 July 2017 replaced it with "and", so both must hold. The exemption is forfeited entirely if the company has defaulted in filing its financial statements under section 137 or its annual return under section 92.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i), read with entry 9A and paragraph 2A of MCA Notification G.S.R. 583(E) dated 13.06.2017 (amending G.S.R. 464(E) dated 05.06.2015, issued under section 462) and the corrigendum thereto dated 13.07.2017

concepts.subsection: Companies (Accounts) Rules — Audit trail
concepts.statement: Every company using accounting software to maintain its books must use software carrying an audit trail (edit log) feature that records every transaction, logs every change made to it, and cannot be disabled — mandatory from financial years commencing on or after 1 April 2023. The statutory auditor separately reports whether such software was used throughout the year, whether the audit trail feature operated for all transactions without being tampered with, and whether the audit trail has been preserved as required by the statutory record-retention period.

citation.ref: Audit trail requirement, Rule 3

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — materiality
concepts.statement: In an audit of consolidated financial statements the auditor computes materiality for the group as a whole, and uses that group materiality to assess whether the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments made by the parent's management are appropriate, and to judge which components are material enough to be scoped in. The principal auditor also computes materiality for each component and communicates it to the component auditor where he believes that is required for a true and fair view on the consolidated financial statements.
