Materiality for a component's own standalone opinion is computed component-wise on a standalone basis by that component's auditor, for a different opinion, and it does not become the group's materiality.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Materiality in the audit of consolidated financial statements

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — consolidation adjustments
concepts.statement: Permanent consolidation adjustments are made only on the first occasion of consolidation, or on a later occasion when the shareholding in a consolidated entity changes: determining goodwill or capital reserve, and determining the amount of equity attributable to the minority or non-controlling interests. The auditor pays particular attention to the pre-acquisition reserves and the dates of investment, and to whether pre-acquisition reserves have been allocated correctly between the parent and the minority. Current period consolidation adjustments are made in the period being consolidated and relate mainly to eliminating intra-group transactions and balances — intra-group interest and management fees, unrealised intra-group profits on assets transferred between components, deferred tax on those eliminations, intra-group indebtedness, harmonising different accounting policies, and adjustments for recognised subsequent events.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Permanent consolidation adjustments and current period consolidation adjustments

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — a component on a different framework
concepts.statement: Where a component prepares its financial statements under an accounting framework different from the parent's — a foreign subsidiary on US GAAP, IFRS or a local GAAP — the parent's management performs the conversion of the component's audited financial statements to the framework used for the consolidated financial statements, and the principal auditor audits those conversion adjustments so that the component's financial information is suitable for consolidation. The alternative route is for the component to report against the group accounting manual, in which case the principal auditor performs procedures to determine that the group accounting policies comply with the GAAP applicable to the parent. On the auditing side, for the parent auditor to rely on and refer to the component auditor's report, the component's financial statements should have been audited under a framework corresponding to Indian GAAS.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Component auditor reporting under an accounting or auditing framework different from the parent's

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — an unaudited component
concepts.statement: Where the financial statements of one or more components remain unaudited, the auditor reporting on the consolidated financial statements evaluates both the qualitative and the quantitative factors bearing on the amounts left unaudited, and considers a modification of the opinion under SA 705, because sufficient appropriate audit evidence has not been obtained for those consolidated balances. An unaudited component is not dropped out of the consolidation, and an Emphasis of Matter paragraph does not cure missing evidence.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Components not audited — evaluation of a possible modification under SA 705

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: SSAE 3000 — Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information
concepts.statement: SSAE 3000, Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information, issued by ICAI, is the umbrella standard for every assurance engagement on an entity's sustainability information, and it covers engagements giving either reasonable assurance or limited assurance. It applied on a voluntary basis to assurance reports covering periods ending on 31 March 2023, and on a mandatory basis to assurance reports covering periods ending on or after 31 March 2024. Assurance on a greenhouse gas statement is dealt with separately by SAE 3410, Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements.

citation.ref: Scope of the Standard and effective date of application

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: BRSR — essential and leadership indicators
concepts.statement: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report is mandatory from financial year 2022-23, having been voluntary in 2021-22, and SEBI has started with the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. It has three sections: Section A, general disclosures about the entity, its products, operations, employees and group companies; Section B, management process and policy disclosures covering governance, leadership and oversight; and Section C, performance disclosures taken principle by principle across the nine principles the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct lay down. Section C splits its key performance indicators in two — essential indicators, which are mandatory disclosures, and leadership indicators, which are optional.

citation.ref: Regulation 34(2)(f) read with the prescribed BRSR format, Sections A, B and C

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Climate-related risks in an audit of financial statements
concepts.statement: Climate-related risks belong inside the auditor's understanding of the entity, and matter more in some sectors than others — energy, materials and buildings, transportation, agriculture, food and forestry products, and banking and insurance. Before considering any reference to climate in the auditor's report, the auditor determines whether the entity has appropriately disclosed the relevant climate-related information in the financial statements under the applicable financial reporting framework, because a climate commitment is frequently evidence about an estimate already in those statements — a useful life, an impairment, a decommissioning provision. Where a climate disclosure in the financial statements is of fundamental importance to users' understanding, an Emphasis of Matter paragraph may be warranted; climate narrative sitting elsewhere in the annual report is other information, read for consistency, and carries no opinion.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — role of the auditor, consideration of climate-related risks

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SEBI LODR Regulation 18 — audit committee composition and meetings
concepts.statement: Every listed entity constitutes a qualified and independent audit committee of at least three directors, of whom two-thirds are independent directors; where the entity has outstanding superior rights (SR) equity shares, the audit committee comprises only independent directors. Every member is financially literate — able to read and understand a balance sheet, a profit and loss account and a statement of cash flows — and at least one member has accounting or related financial management expertise. The chairperson is an independent director and is present at the annual general meeting to answer shareholder queries, and the company secretary acts as secretary to the committee. The committee meets at least four times a year with not more than one hundred and twenty days between two meetings, and the quorum is two members or one-third of the members, whichever is greater, with a minimum of two independent directors present.

citation.ref: Regulation 18(1) and Regulation 18(2)

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: Certificate on compliance of conditions of corporate governance
concepts.statement: A listed entity obtains a compliance certificate on compliance with the conditions of corporate governance from either its auditors or a practising company secretary, and annexes it to the directors' report. The auditor's responsibility is the verification and certification of the factual implementation of the conditions stipulated in the LODR Regulations: it is neither an audit nor an expression of opinion on the financial statements, and it is neither an assurance as to the future viability of the company nor as to the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted the company's affairs. The work is carried out under the Guidance Note on Certification of Corporate Governance, with documentation under SA 230 and management representations under SA 580. Facts such as an audit committee that did not meet four times, or a chairman of the audit committee who is not an independent director, call for an adverse or qualified statement in the certificate.

citation.ref: Regulation 34(3) read with Schedule V — compliance certificate on conditions of corporate governance

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Section 143(6) — CAG supplementary audit of a government company
concepts.statement: In a government company the Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints the auditor under Section 139(5) or Section 139(7) and directs the manner in which the accounts are to be audited; the auditor then submits a copy of his audit report to the CAG, and that copy includes the CAG's directions, the action taken on them, and their impact on the accounts and financial statement of the company. Section 143(6) gives the CAG, within sixty days from the date of receipt of that audit report, a right to conduct a supplementary audit through persons he authorises and to comment upon or supplement the audit report; the comments or supplement are sent by the company to every person entitled to copies of the audited financial statements under Section 136(1) and are placed before the annual general meeting at the same time and in the same manner as the audit report. Section 143(7) separately allows the CAG to order a test audit.

citation.ref: Section 143(5), Section 143(6) and the proviso to Section 143(6), and Section 143(7)

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — retention of engagement documentation
concepts.statement: SQC 1 requires the firm to establish policies and procedures for the retention of engagement documentation, and on an audit engagement it fixes a floor: the file is ordinarily kept for seven years, counted from the later of two dates — when the auditor signed his own report, and when the group auditor signed his. This is a firm-level retention obligation running from a report date, and it is separate from the SA 230 requirement to complete the administrative assembly of the final audit file ordinarily within not more than sixty days after the date of the auditor's report.

citation.ref: para 83 — retention period for engagement documentation

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Advances — provisioning norms
concepts.statement: Provisioning follows classification. A substandard asset carries a general provision of 15 per cent of the total outstanding, made without any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover or securities available, and an unsecured exposure identified as substandard carries an additional 10 per cent — 25 per cent in all. On a doubtful asset the extent not covered by the realisable value of the security carries 100 per cent, and the secured portion carries 25 per cent where the asset has remained doubtful up to one year, 40 per cent for one to three years, and 100 per cent beyond three years. A loss asset should be written off, and if it is permitted to remain on the books, 100 per cent of the outstanding is provided.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on IRACP — paras 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Section 212 — investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office
concepts.statement: Under Section 212(1) the Central Government may, by order, assign an investigation into a company's affairs to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office on receipt of a report of the Registrar or an inspector under Section 208, on intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs are required to be investigated, in the public interest, or on a request from any Department of the Central Government or a State Government. Once a case is so assigned, Section 212(2) bars any other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government from proceeding with an investigation in that case in respect of an offence under the Act; an investigation already initiated is not proceeded with further, and the agency concerned transfers the relevant documents and records to the SFIO.

citation.ref: Section 212(1) and Section 212(2)

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: Two escapes exist from a requirement, and neither of them is discretion. A requirement binds unless the standard carrying it has nothing to do with the engagement at all, or unless the requirement is written conditionally and its condition never arose. Past those two, stepping away is open only where the circumstances are exceptional, and it costs the auditor substitute procedures that reach what the abandoned requirement was aiming at. SA 230 then refuses to let the step pass unrecorded: the file must show why the auditor left the stated route, and how the substitutes got him to the same place. Ordinary documentation carries three further facts about the testing — which items or matters were picked out and how a reader can trace them again, who did the work and the day it was finished, and who checked it, on what day, and how far that check went.

citation.ref: para 9 and para 12, read with SA 200 para 23

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: Satisfying himself about the competence, capabilities and objectivity of the auditor's expert is only the entry ticket. Adequacy is a second and separate test, and it is aimed at the work rather than at the person. Three things are weighed. The expert's findings or conclusions have to bear on the audit question, have to hold up as reasonable, and have to sit comfortably beside whatever else the file already contains. Where the work leans on assumptions and methods that matter, those are judged the same way — do they bear on the question, and do they stand up against this entity's own circumstances. Where it leans on source data that matters, that data is tested for relevance, for completeness and for accuracy. Work that comes out inadequate leaves exactly two roads, and acceptance is not one of them: settle with the expert what more he will do and how far it will go, or run further audit procedures of the auditor's own that suit the circumstances.

citation.ref: para 12 and para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: SA 510 separates the two reasons an opening balance damages the current opinion. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, the opinion is qualified or disclaimed, as appropriate. Where the opening balances contain a misstatement that materially affects the current period's financial statements and the effect is not properly accounted for or not adequately presented or disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse. The same qualified-or-adverse answer applies where the current period's accounting policies are not consistently applied in relation to the opening balances, or where a change is not properly accounted for, presented or disclosed. And where the predecessor auditor's opinion was modified and the matter remains relevant and material to the current period's financial statements, the auditor modifies his own opinion on the current period's financial statements — an Other Matter paragraph recording what the predecessor said does not discharge it.

citation.ref: paras 10, 11, 12 and 13

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures
concepts.statement: A predecessor's audit of last year's figures, where no law or regulation shuts the door on naming his report, has to be declared in an Other Matter paragraph: that somebody else audited the corresponding figures, what kind of opinion he gave, the grounds of any modification he made, and when he dated it. Where nobody audited the prior period at all, the same paragraph says the corresponding figures are unaudited. Neither declaration buys the auditor out of SA 510. He must still satisfy himself, on evidence that is enough and apt, that nothing is sitting wrongly stated in the opening balances on a scale that would bend this year's figures.

citation.ref: para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 520 — Analytical Procedures
concepts.statement: A substantive analytical procedure is only as good as four things the auditor must settle before it is run. First, is this particular procedure suited to the assertions in hand, given how risky those assertions were assessed to be and what tests of detail are already planned against them? Second, how dependable is the data the expectation will be built on — where it came from, what it can fairly be set beside, its nature, its bearing on the question, and how well its preparation was controlled? Third, the expectation of a recorded amount or ratio has to be sharp enough that a misstatement able to make the statements materially wrong would show through, whether standing alone or added to others. Fourth, before the comparison is made, the auditor fixes how wide a gap between recorded and expected he is willing to leave unexamined. Should the results then throw up movements or relationships that sit oddly beside what else he knows, or a gap wider than the one he allowed, he asks management, gathers evidence bearing on what management says, and runs whatever further procedures the situation calls for.

citation.ref: para 5 and para 7

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: An anomaly is a misstatement or deviation that is demonstrably not representative of misstatements or deviations in a population. The label is available only in extremely rare circumstances, and only where the auditor has obtained a high degree of certainty that the misstatement or deviation is not representative of the population — a certainty obtained by performing additional audit procedures sufficient to provide it, not by accepting management's explanation of the cause. An anomalous misstatement may then be left out when projecting misstatements from the sample to the population, but the misstatement itself does not disappear: its own effect, if uncorrected, is still added to the projected misstatement of the rest when the auditor evaluates the results of the sample.

citation.ref: para 5(e), para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: After the financial statements have been issued the auditor has no obligation to perform any audit procedures on them. But should a fact reach him afterwards which, had it reached him before he signed, would have sent him back to rewrite the report, he discusses the matter with management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance, determines whether the financial statements need amendment and, if so, inquires how management intends to address the matter. Where management amends, the auditor carries out the audit procedures necessary in the circumstances on the amendment, reviews the steps management takes to ensure that anyone in receipt of the previously issued financial statements together with the auditor's report on them is informed, and issues a new or amended auditor's report that includes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph or Other Matter paragraph referring to a note that more extensively discusses the reason for the amendment and to the earlier report. Where management does not take those steps and does not amend the financial statements, the auditor notifies management and those charged with governance that he will seek to prevent future reliance on the auditor's report, and if they still do not act, takes appropriate action to seek to prevent that reliance.

citation.ref: paras 14, 16 and 17

concepts.subsection: SA 580 — Written Representations
concepts.statement: Dating comes first. The letter carries a date as close to the auditor's report as can be managed and never a later one, and it reaches across every statement and every period that report speaks to. Should management hold back a representation that was asked for, the auditor raises it with them, asks himself afresh how far management can be trusted and what that does to the dependability of representations and of his evidence at large, and acts on the answer, the opinion included. Two situations are answered by withholding the opinion altogether rather than by qualifying it. One is where doubt about management's integrity runs deep enough that its representations about its own responsibilities cannot be relied on. The other is where those particular representations are simply not given — that management discharged its responsibility for preparing the financial statements, and that it handed the auditor every relevant piece of information and all the access promised when the engagement terms were agreed.

citation.ref: para 14, para 19 and para 20

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: A related party, or a significant transaction with one, that the auditor turns up himself while management's list and its note say nothing about it triggers six responses, and editing the disclosure is not one of them. Word goes to the rest of the engagement team without delay. Management is then asked to produce every transaction it has had with the party just surfaced, so that the auditor can weigh each of them. The auditor asks how the controls meant to catch related party relationships and their transactions let this one through, neither identified nor disclosed. Substantive procedures fitting the circumstances are run over the party and the dealings newly on the table. The earlier assessment is revisited, because if one was missed others may be sitting undisclosed as well, and further procedures follow as the answer demands. And a non-disclosure that looks deliberate is read as a pointer towards a risk of material misstatement from fraud, whose implications for the rest of the audit the auditor then works out.

citation.ref: para 22

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: A suspicion that the breach reaches management itself, or reaches those charged with governance, sends the communication upwards: the next rung of authority inside the entity hears it — an audit committee, a supervisory board — provided such a rung is there. Where none is, or where the auditor doubts his message will be acted on, or cannot see whom he should be addressing, legal advice is what he goes for. The opinion then answers whichever of two faults is in front of him. The first fault is a breach he judges material to the statements which those statements do not adequately reflect; that is met by a qualification, or by an adverse opinion. The second is being shut out — management, or those charged with governance, blocking the evidence he needs before he can judge whether a breach that could be material has happened or probably has. Being shut out narrows the audit's scope, so the answer there is a qualification or a disclaimer.

citation.ref: reporting to a higher level of authority and the implications for the opinion, read with SA 705; reproduced at section 3.6 of the ICAI Study Material chapter on general auditing principles and the auditor's responsibilities

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Litigation and Claims
concepts.statement: Suits and claims against the entity are hunted for rather than waited for, because any one of them can carry a risk that the statements come out materially wrong. Three roads do the hunting. The auditor asks management, and where it fits anybody else inside the entity who would know — the lawyers the entity employs on its own payroll included. He reads what the board and its committees minuted, together with the letters passing between the entity and the firm of lawyers it retains outside. And he goes through what has been spent on legal fees. Should a matter already found carry an assessed risk of material misstatement, or should the work so far hint that other material suits or claims are out there, the outside lawyer is approached directly. The mechanics of that approach are fixed: management drafts the letter of inquiry, the auditor is the one who sends it out, and the answer is asked to come straight back to the auditor. Permission refused by management, a lawyer who will not answer properly or is barred from answering, and alternative procedures that still leave the evidence short of sufficient and appropriate — that combination modifies the opinion.

citation.ref: paras 9, 10 and 11

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: A fraud the auditor has found, or information reaching him that says one may be there, starts a clock rather than a file note. Management is told promptly, and the ear it goes to sits ordinarily one rung at least above whoever looks to be mixed up in it. A second channel opens the moment the suspicion touches management itself, or staff holding significant roles over internal control, or anybody else whose fraud has left the statements materially misstated: then those charged with governance must be told, and told promptly too. Where a misstatement resulting from fraud or suspected fraud brings the auditor's ability to continue performing the audit into question, the auditor determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances, considers whether to withdraw where withdrawal is possible under applicable law, and if he withdraws, discusses the withdrawal and its reasons with the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance and determines whether there is a professional or legal requirement to report the withdrawal and its reasons to the persons who made the audit appointment or to regulatory authorities. The professional duty of confidentiality may be overridden by law, and the auditor may take legal advice on where that line falls.

citation.ref: para 38, para 40, para 41 and para 43

concepts.subsection: Section 143(12) with Rule 13 — the mechanics of reporting a fraud
concepts.statement: Fraud against the company by one of its own officers or employees, where a single offence carries — or looks set to carry — one crore rupees or more, puts the auditor on a fixed road to the Central Government the moment he has reason to believe in it, and it makes no difference whether the offence is finished or is still running. Step one stays inside the company. The Board, or the Audit Committee, is told at once and in no case later than two days from the auditor coming to know, and it is asked for its reply or its comments inside forty-five days. A reply that does arrive then travels onward beside the auditor's own report and his remarks on what the company said, reaching the Central Government within fifteen days of that reply landing. Silence lasting the whole forty-five days stalls nothing: the report still goes, carrying a note that sets out what was sent earlier and left unanswered. How it travels is prescribed as tightly as when. Its addressee is the Secretary of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs; its cover is sealed; the post is registered with acknowledgement due, or else speed post, and an email afterwards confirms it. The paper is the auditor's own letterhead, signed and sealed, carrying his membership number, and the statement takes the shape Form ADT-4 lays down. Under one crore rupees the road stops inside the company: the fraud is put to the Audit Committee constituted under section 177 or the Board, inside the same two days, and what is stated there is the nature of the fraud described, roughly how much is involved and who the parties are. Those details then surface in the Board's report.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) read with Rule 13(1), Rule 13(2) and Rule 13(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Sections 21A and 21B — the Board of Discipline and the Disciplinary Committee
concepts.statement: Which forum hears a case is decided by which Schedule the misconduct sits in, and the Director (Discipline) makes that routing after forming a prima facie opinion on the complaint or information. A case of misconduct falling under the First Schedule goes before the Board of Discipline. A case falling under the Second Schedule, or under both the Schedules, goes before the Disciplinary Committee. The powers differ with the forum. On holding a member guilty under the First Schedule, the Board of Discipline may reprimand the member, remove his name from the Register of Members for a period not exceeding three months, or impose a fine. On holding a member guilty under the Second Schedule or under both Schedules, the Disciplinary Committee may reprimand the member, remove his name from the Register of Members permanently or for such period as it thinks fit, or impose a fine. Permanent removal belongs to the Disciplinary Committee alone, and the Director (Discipline) punishes nobody.

citation.ref: Section 21A(3) and Section 21B(3), read with the routing under Section 21(3)

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: Planning communication and findings communication are two different requirements, and the second is a named list. Six things belong on it. How the auditor sees the entity's accounting choices sits at the top — its policies, its estimates, and how it discloses them, judged for whether each is a reasonable one for this business. Any difficulty the audit itself ran into belongs there too. So does a matter the audit turned up and put to management, discussed or argued over the course of the engagement — but only where governance is a separate body from the people running the entity; where the two overlap completely there is nobody left to tell. The representations the auditor still means to ask management for get a mention, and so does anything shaping how the final report will look and read. A catch-all closes the list for whatever else touches the oversight of financial reporting and does not fit the other five. Significant findings go down in writing whenever the auditor, weighing it on his own professional judgement, decides that saying them aloud would leave the communication short. None of it is conditional on the opinion turning out modified, and telling management is not telling those charged with governance.

citation.ref: para 16

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: A significant deficiency does not stop at those charged with governance. SA 265 sends it in writing to those charged with governance and, separately and also in writing, to management at an appropriate level of responsibility; other deficiencies of sufficient importance to merit management's attention go to management alone. The written communication of a significant deficiency has a prescribed content, built from two limbs. The first is substantive: what each deficiency is, and what could go wrong because of it. The second is orientation, so a reader is not left to guess what the letter is and is not saying — that the audit's purpose was an opinion on the financial statements, not on the control system; that looking at internal control was only ever a means of shaping which audit procedures fit the engagement, never an exercise producing its own opinion on internal control's effectiveness; and that the letter reports only what turned up during this particular audit and was judged significant enough to be worth reporting, nothing beyond that.

citation.ref: para 10 and para 11

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Relying on a Service Organisation's Controls
concepts.statement: A complementary user entity control is one the service organisation has built its own system around, on the assumption that the client's side will run it — the description of the service names it as necessary to reaching a stated control objective only when the client's own step is also in place. That client-side step never happens at the service organisation, so no service auditor ever tests it. A user auditor working off a type 1 or type 2 report must therefore go back to what the service organisation's description names as belonging to the client, decide whether each one actually matters to this client, and — for the ones that do — find out whether the client actually built and ran it, then test how well it worked in practice. A type 2 report earns reliance only after two more checks: does the period it covers suit what the user auditor needs, and does the stretch it tested, set against how much time has since gone by, still hold up.

citation.ref: para 8(a) defining a complementary user entity control, with the requirement, when a type 1 or type 2 report is used, to determine whether those controls are relevant and to test them at the user entity

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Audit evidence about the operating effectiveness of controls obtained in a previous audit may be carried forward, on conditions. The auditor first establishes the continuing relevance of that evidence by obtaining audit evidence about whether significant changes in those controls have occurred since, through inquiry combined with observation or inspection. Where the controls have changed, they are tested in the current audit. Where they have not changed, they are tested at least once in every third audit, and some controls from the rotating population are tested in each audit so that no year passes with none of them tested. The concession stops at a significant risk: where the auditor plans to rely on controls over a risk he has determined to be a significant risk, those controls are tested in the current period, every period he relies on them.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 15, with the continuing-relevance test in para 13

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Substantive procedures performed at an interim date leave a gap between that date and the period end, and SA 330 does not let it stay open. The auditor covers the remaining period by performing substantive procedures combined with tests of controls for the intervening period, or, where he determines that is sufficient, further substantive procedures only — either route having to provide a reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions from the interim date to the period end. And where misstatements that the auditor did not expect are detected at the interim date, the auditor evaluates whether the related assessment of risk and the planned nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures covering the remaining period need to be modified. Interim work is a way of spreading the audit, not a conclusion that survives contrary evidence found while doing it.

citation.ref: para 22 and para 23

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Before the evaluation of uncorrected misstatements begins, SA 450 sends the auditor back to materiality. The auditor communicates on a timely basis all misstatements accumulated during the audit with the appropriate level of management, unless prohibited by law or regulation, and requests management to correct them. Where management refuses to correct some or all of them, the auditor obtains an understanding of management's reasons for not making the corrections and takes that understanding into account when he judges whether the statements are, taken as a whole, free of material misstatement. Before he weighs the effect of what is still uncorrected, the auditor reassesses materiality determined in accordance with SA 320 to confirm whether it remains appropriate in the context of the entity's actual financial results. The planning figure was built on an expectation; by the end of the audit the year has actually happened.

citation.ref: para 8, para 9 and para 10

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: SA 701 states its own limits. Naming a matter as a key audit matter in the auditor's report does not stand in for anything else the standard requires — not for disclosures the applicable financial reporting framework already requires management to make in the financial statements, not for the auditor expressing a modified opinion where the engagement's circumstances call for one under SA 705 (Revised), not for reporting under SA 570 (Revised) where a material uncertainty relating to going concern exists, and not for a separate opinion on any individual matter. Follow that through and a matter that gives rise to a modified opinion, or a material uncertainty related to going concern, still counts as a key audit matter by its nature — it is simply kept out of the Key Audit Matters section itself, which instead carries a pointer to the Basis for Qualified (Adverse) Opinion section or to the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, wherever the matter was actually reported.

citation.ref: para 4 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A limitation management imposes only after the auditor has already accepted the engagement follows its own route, and that route starts well before any opinion is drafted. First the auditor asks management to withdraw the restriction; if management will not, the auditor tells those charged with governance about the refusal and works out whether alternative procedures could still get him to sufficient appropriate audit evidence. When that evidence still cannot be obtained, how serious the gap is decides what happens next. A gap whose undetected misstatements might affect the financial statements without spreading through them broadly — material, but not pervasive — earns a qualified opinion. A gap that could be both material and pervasive sends the auditor toward withdrawal, taken up wherever applicable law or regulation makes it practicable and possible, with a disclaimer of opinion reserved for cases where withdrawing before the report is issued cannot be done. An auditor who does withdraw first tells those charged with governance about any misstatement identified along the way that on its own would have called for a modified opinion.

citation.ref: para 11, para 12, para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — Going Concern
concepts.statement: SA 570 has three reporting outcomes and they are not interchangeable. Where management has used the going concern basis of accounting to prepare the financial statements yet, in the auditor's judgement, that choice of basis is inappropriate, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion — and a full and accurate note does not rescue it, because the basis of preparation runs through every figure rather than through one disclosure. Where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified with a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section; where that disclosure is not adequate, the opinion is qualified or adverse as appropriate. And where management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment when the auditor requests it, the auditor considers the implications for the auditor's report, the question being an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the appropriateness of the basis itself.

citation.ref: para 21, para 23 and para 24

concepts.subsection: SA 805 — Special Considerations: Single Financial Statements and Specific Elements
concepts.statement: SA 805 draws a line between a single financial statement and a specific element of a financial statement once the opinion on the complete set has gone wrong. Where the opinion on the entity's complete set of financial statements is adverse, or the auditor disclaimed an opinion on it, the auditor shall not, in that same report, express an unmodified opinion covering either a single financial statement drawn from that complete set or a specific element drawn from it, because the unmodified opinion would contradict the adverse opinion or disclaimer. A specific element may still carry an unmodified opinion in a separate audit, on three conditions that must all hold: the auditor is not prohibited by law or regulation from doing so, that opinion is expressed in an auditor's report that is not published together with the report containing the adverse opinion or disclaimer of opinion, and the specific element does not constitute a major portion of the entity's complete set of financial statements. A single financial statement never can, because the standard deems it to constitute a major portion of those financial statements.

citation.ref: para 17, para 18 and para 19

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 10
concepts.statement: Clause 10 catches any fee arrangement in which a member in practice ties what he charges, or offers to charge, or accepts, or offers to accept, for a professional engagement to either a share of profits or an outcome — a percentage-of-profits fee and a fee contingent on the findings or results of the work are both professional misconduct, and the clause reaches every kind of professional employment, not audit alone. The only escape is a regulation framed under the Chartered Accountants Act, and Regulation 192 is that escape: a receiver or liquidator may still be paid a percentage of what is realised or disbursed from the assets; a co-operative society's auditor may be paid at a percentage tied to its paid-up capital, its working capital, or its gross or net income or profits; someone valuing property for direct-tax purposes may be paid a percentage of the value placed on it; and the Council has separately cleared a percentage or contingent basis for named categories of work — certain management consultancy, fund raising, debt recovery and cost optimisation services. Nothing beyond that list is saved by how the engagement letter is worded.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xix)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xix) requires a going-concern-adjacent opinion of its own. Working from the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and how financial liabilities are scheduled to be paid, whatever else accompanies the financial statements, and what he knows of the Board's and management's plans, the auditor states his opinion on material uncertainty — specifically, whether the company can be expected to meet the liabilities it already carries at the balance sheet date, within one year measured from that date, as and when each one falls due. That opinion is dated to the audit report and goes stale the moment facts move on; the clause separately has him disclaim any guarantee or assurance that those same liabilities — due within one year counted from the balance sheet date — will actually be discharged as and when they fall due. Both the liabilities counted and the year measured run from the same anchor, the balance sheet date, and none of this is the SA 570 going concern conclusion.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xix)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xiv)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xiv) has two limbs and each is answered on its own. The first limb tests fit: does the company run an internal audit system that matches, in scale, the size and nature of its business — a question apart from section 138. A company outside the classes section 138 covers still attracts a negative answer if the function it does run is inadequate, and a company inside those classes still fails the limb if the coverage does not match the size and nature of its business. The second limb is about the statutory auditor's own conduct — did he take account of what the Internal Auditors reported for the period under audit. Considering those reports is not the same as adopting them: SA 610 (Revised) governs whether and how the internal audit function's work may be used at all.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiv)(a) and 3(xiv)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(1) — Right of access and the duty of inquiry
concepts.statement: Section 143(1) gives every auditor standing access, at any time, to the company's books of account and vouchers wherever they are kept, and lets him call on the company's officers for whatever information and explanation he needs to do his work. A proviso attached to that section then lists six things he must specifically look into. He checks security-backed loans and advances: were they properly secured, and do the terms on which they were made work against the company or its members? He checks book-entry transactions: do entries with no real movement behind them work against the company? He checks any sale of the company's shares, debentures or other securities — outside an investment or banking company — for a price below what was originally paid. He checks whether loans and advances the company has actually made have instead been entered as deposits. He checks whether expenses that are personal to a director or officer have found their way into the revenue account. And where shares are recorded as allotted for cash, he checks that the cash was truly received, and if it was not, whether the account books and the balance sheet still present the position honestly. Inquiring into all six is compulsory; saying anything about them in the report is not, unless one of the inquiries turns up something adverse.

citation.ref: Section 143(1) and its proviso, clauses (a) to (f)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 140(1) — Removal of an auditor before expiry of term
concepts.statement: An auditor appointed under section 139 may be removed from his office before the expiry of his term only by a special resolution of the company, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and the auditor concerned must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any action is taken. Rule 7 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 fixes the sequence: the Board passes a resolution; the application to the Central Government goes in Form ADT-2 with the prescribed fee within thirty days of that Board resolution; and the company holds the general meeting to pass the special resolution within sixty days of receiving the Central Government's approval. Approval first, special resolution second — the word in the section is previous approval. None of this is the resignation route under section 140(2), where the auditor leaves of his own motion and files a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within thirty days.

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with Rule 7(1), Rule 7(2) and Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clauses 5, 6, 8 and 9
concepts.statement: Four clauses of Part I of the Second Schedule punish the auditor for what his report does not say. Clause 5 catches a member who sits on a material fact he already knows — something missing from a financial statement he is professionally concerned with, where the statement needed that disclosure to be complete. Clause 6 catches him where he already knows a financial statement he is professionally concerned with carries a material misstatement and says nothing about it. Clause 8 catches him where his opinion is not backed by the sufficient information an opinion needs, or where the exceptions he has taken are themselves too material to let an opinion stand. Clause 9 catches him where a material departure from audit procedure generally accepted for the circumstances passes without any word from him. Clause 5 is about a fact absent from the statements, Clause 6 about a wrong figure present in them, Clause 8 about the evidence behind the opinion, and Clause 9 about the audit's own method. All four sit in the Second Schedule, which routes the case to the Disciplinary Committee.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clauses 5, 6, 8 and 9

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: A request to change the terms of an audit engagement is answered by asking why. SA 210 forbids the auditor to accept an altered engagement wherever the request rests on no reasonable justification whatever. A change in circumstances that affects the entity's requirements, and a misunderstanding as to the nature of the service originally requested, are reasonable justifications. A change sought because the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, or because he would otherwise have to modify his opinion, is not — an engagement downgraded to a review so that a qualification disappears is a change with nothing behind it. Where the terms are changed, the auditor and management shall agree on and record the newly agreed terms — set down in an engagement letter, or whatever other suitable written form the agreement takes. Where the auditor is unable to agree to the change and is not permitted by management to continue the original audit engagement, he withdraws from the engagement where possible under applicable law or regulation, and determines whether there is any obligation, contractual or otherwise, to report the circumstances to other parties, such as those charged with governance, owners or regulators.

citation.ref: para 14, para 16 and para 17

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: Overall responsibility for quality does not stop at a signature. SA 220 (Revised) makes the engagement partner responsible for the nature, timing and extent of the direction and supervision of the engagement team and the review of their work, and requires that direction, supervision and review be planned and performed on the basis that the work of less experienced engagement team members is directed, supervised and reviewed by more experienced engagement team members. The partner himself reviews the audit documentation relating to hard calls and contentious matters, the judgements behind them, and the conclusions those judgements led to. He will not let the auditor's report carry a date until he is satisfied that what has been gathered is enough, and of good enough quality, to back those conclusions and to justify issuing the report at all — and where an engagement quality review is required, that date waits further still, until he is told the review itself is complete. The extent of the review responds to the nature and circumstances of the engagement — a flat house rule that sends every file through the same review has stopped responding to anything.

citation.ref: the engagement partner's overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality at para 13, with the requirements on direction, supervision and review, on the partner's own review of documentation on significant matters and significant judgements, and on the completion of an engagement quality review before the auditor's report is dated

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Dividing the work does not make joint auditors strangers to each other. SA 299 (Revised) puts a writing duty on whichever joint auditor's own portion turns up something touching a colleague's territory during the audit — a matter deserving that colleague's attention, one needing disclosure, or one calling for discussion with him or a judgement call by him — and the finder puts it in writing to every other joint auditor, finishing that before the audit itself is finished. On reporting, the joint auditors ordinarily issue a common audit report. A split opinion gets no vote to settle it: whenever the joint auditors disagree, whether over what the audit report should say or over any matter it ought to cover, the dissenting one simply writes his own view into a report of his own, separate from the rest, and majority opinion carries no weight over him at all. Coordination is a duty owed in writing to all of them; agreement is not a duty at all.

citation.ref: covers the duty to write to every other joint auditor before the audit closes, what happens on the report when they disagree, and the division of responsibility fixed at para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 500 — Audit Evidence
concepts.statement: Appropriateness has two halves, and SA 500 puts both in front of the auditor when procedures are designed. Relevance is the connection between the procedure and the assertion being tested — selecting recorded sales and tracing them outwards tests occurrence, not completeness, and no quantity of that procedure answers the assertion it does not touch. Reliability is influenced by the source and the nature of the evidence, and the standard's generalisations run: evidence from independent sources outside the entity is more reliable than evidence generated internally; internally generated evidence is more reliable where the related controls are effective; evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly or by inference; documentary evidence is more reliable than oral; and an original document is more reliable than a photocopy or a facsimile. And where information produced by the entity is used as audit evidence, the auditor evaluates whether it is sufficiently reliable for his purposes — obtaining audit evidence about the accuracy and completeness of the information, and evaluating whether it is sufficiently precise and detailed for those purposes.

citation.ref: para 7 and para 9

concepts.subsection: SA 505 — External Confirmations
concepts.statement: Control of the external confirmation process belongs to the auditor — determining the information to be confirmed, selecting the appropriate confirming party, designing the requests so that they are properly addressed and ask for replies to be sent directly to the auditor, and sending the requests including any follow-up. When management refuses to allow the auditor to send a confirmation request, SA 505 treats the refusal neither as the end of the matter nor as automatically fatal. The auditor inquires as to management's reasons for the refusal and seeks audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness; weighs what the refusal does to his own reading of the relevant risks of material misstatement — the risk of fraud included — and to the nature, timing or extent of the other audit procedures he had planned; and turns to whatever alternative procedures will get him evidence that is both relevant and reliable, by some other route. If he concludes that the refusal is unreasonable, or if the alternative procedures do not produce relevant and reliable audit evidence, he communicates with those charged with governance in accordance with SA 260 and determines the implications for the audit and for the auditor's opinion in accordance with SA 705 (Revised).

citation.ref: para 7, para 8 and para 9

concepts.subsection: SA 540 (Revised) — Auditing Accounting Estimates
concepts.statement: An estimate can be defensible on its own and still be evidence of something. SA 540 (Revised) has the auditor evaluate, based on the audit procedures performed and the audit evidence obtained, whether the accounting estimates and related disclosures hold up against what the applicable financial reporting framework actually calls for, or whether they are misstated. It then makes a separate demand: the auditor evaluates whether the judgements and decisions made by management in making the accounting estimates, even if they are individually reasonable, are indicators of possible management bias. A provision set at the low end of a reasonable range, a useful life extended in the year profits fell, an impairment test deferred to the next period — each may pass alone; all of them leaning the same way is the finding. Where indicators of possible management bias are identified, the auditor evaluates the implications for the audit, and where the bias is accompanied by an intention to mislead it is fraudulent in nature and SA 240 follows. Indicators of possible management bias do not themselves constitute misstatements for the purpose of drawing conclusions on the reasonableness of individual accounting estimates.

citation.ref: the overall evaluation of whether the accounting estimates and related disclosures are reasonable or are misstated, and the separate evaluation of whether management's judgements and decisions are indicators of possible management bias, read with the retrospective review at para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: Before the report is written the opinion has to be formed, and SA 700 sets out what forming it involves. The auditor first reaches a conclusion on assurance: has he got enough of it, at the reasonable level, that the financial statements taken as a whole carry no material misstatement — a conclusion built on whether SA 330 has given him sufficient appropriate audit evidence and on whether SA 450 shows the uncorrected misstatements immaterial, alone and together. He then turns to compliance: does the set of financial statements, taken in all its material respects, meet what the applicable financial reporting framework actually asks of it — a question that folds in the entity's accounting practices at a qualitative level, bias in management's judgements included. Specifically he evaluates whether the financial statements adequately disclose the significant accounting policies selected and applied; whether those policies are consistent with the framework and are appropriate; whether accounting estimates made by management are reasonable; whether the information presented is relevant, reliable, comparable and understandable; whether adequate disclosures enable users to understand the effect of material transactions and events; and whether the terminology used, including the title of each financial statement, is appropriate. Where the framework is a fair presentation framework, he also evaluates whether the financial statements achieve fair presentation.

citation.ref: para 11 to para 15

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph clears only after two gates. Its purpose is narrow: pointing the reader toward something already on the face of, or already disclosed within, the financial statements — something the auditor's own judgement rates important enough that a user's grasp of the statements would be incomplete without seeing it. Gate one asks whether that matter would otherwise force a modified opinion under SA 705 (Revised); if it would, the paragraph is barred. Gate two, live only where SA 701 applies, asks whether the matter has already been classed as a key audit matter and routed to the auditor's report on that separate track; if so, the paragraph is barred again. An Other Matter paragraph answers to the same second gate, plus one of its own — law or regulation can rule it out outright. Where an Emphasis of Matter paragraph does go in, it gets its own section headed with the words "Emphasis of Matter", a clear pointer to the matter and to where its full disclosure can be found, nothing beyond what the financial statements themselves present or disclose, and an express line that the opinion stands unmodified on account of it. Reach for the device too often and its value to the reader erodes.

citation.ref: para 8(a) and para 8(b), with the content and placement requirements in para 9

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: Reading the other information is the start; SA 720 then says what happens when the reading turns something up. A suspected inconsistency, or other information that otherwise looks materially wrong, sends the auditor to management first, and if needed into further procedures — the destination being one of three conclusions: the other information itself carries a material misstatement, the financial statements do, or nothing is actually wrong except the auditor's own picture of the entity and its environment, which then needs updating. A finding that lands on the first of those three starts a chain: management gets asked to fix it; agree, and the auditor confirms the fix was actually made; refuse, and the next stop is those charged with governance, told plainly that a correction is still owed. Uncorrected other information that reached the auditor before his report was dated triggers action of a further kind — he weighs what it does to his report and tells those charged with governance how he means to handle the misstatement sitting inside it, right up to walking away from the engagement altogether wherever the law lets him. Other information that turns up only after the report's date gets a lighter but still real response: whatever steps, legal advice included, will get the matter properly addressed.

citation.ref: para 16 to para 19

concepts.subsection: SA 810 — Engagements to Report on Summary Financial Statements
concepts.statement: A summary financial statement is a smaller, condensed version of something already audited in full — less detail, but still a structured picture of what the entity owns and owes, or of how that picture moved, across the period. SA 810 puts one door in front of the auditor before he can report on it at all: somewhere in his own past, an audit — done to the Standards on Auditing — of the very financial statements the summary was built from; nobody reports on a summary of numbers he never audited himself. Acceptance also turns on the applied criteria being acceptable and on management agreeing its responsibilities, including making the audited financial statements available to the intended users. What the opinion delivers is not a fresh audit opinion on the summary — it is one of two possible verdicts instead: either the summary tracks the audited numbers, in all material respects, on the basis of the criteria applied, or it fairly sums them up on that same basis. Two warnings travel with either verdict. First, the summary is thinner than the source: whatever disclosures the applicable financial reporting framework demanded when the full set was prepared are not all here, so nobody should treat the summary as a stand-in for opening the audited financial statements themselves. Second, the report names its source precisely — which financial statements, and the date the auditor reported on them — and carries forward whatever that original report flagged: a modified opinion, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, or a material uncertainty tied to going concern. And the summary report can never be dated earlier than the report on the audited financial statements it summarises.

citation.ref: covers the precondition of having audited the source financial statements, the two possible verdicts a summary opinion can reach, and the warnings the report must carry about omitted disclosures and about not treating the summary as a substitute

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3402 — Assurance Reports on Controls at a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: Where a service organisation itself uses a subservice organisation, the description of its system deals with that subservice organisation by one of two methods, and the service auditor's report follows the choice. Under the inclusive method the description includes the nature of the services provided by the subservice organisation together with its relevant control objectives and related controls, and the service auditor's procedures — and his opinion — extend to those controls. Under the carve-out method the description identifies the nature of the services performed by the subservice organisation but excludes its control objectives and related controls, and the service auditor's procedures do not extend to them; the report then covers the service organisation's own controls alone, and a user auditor has to obtain assurance about the carved-out controls elsewhere. A carve-out is a permitted presentation, not a modification of the opinion. SAE 3402 also puts a written assertion in the service organisation's own hands — it has to speak to three things: that the description is presented fairly, that the controls were designed the way they should be, and, in a type 2 report only, that they actually operated that way across the specified period; refuse to give it, and the service auditor does not accept or continue the engagement unless law or regulation says otherwise. The service auditor must be independent of the service organisation; he is not required to be independent of the user entities.

citation.ref: covers how the description of the system handles a subservice organisation under each method, and what the service organisation's written assertion has to cover in a type 1 versus a type 2 report

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — The Examination of Prospective Financial Information
concepts.statement: SAE 3400 deals with numbers that look forward rather than back — built on assumptions about what might happen and what an entity might do about it, not on what has already happened. Two kinds of that forward-looking number exist. A forecast rests on management's best guess at what will actually happen and what it will actually do; a projection instead runs on one or more hypothetical assumptions — events and actions nobody necessarily expects to occur, sometimes mixed with best-estimate ones. Because none of it has happened yet and some of it may never happen, the auditor cannot say the figures shown will come true, and his opinion never promises that. What the standard asks of him instead is two things: negative assurance on whether the assumptions give those figures a reasonable footing to stand on, and a positive opinion on whether they were properly worked out from those assumptions and set out the way the applicable financial reporting framework requires — alongside a warning that the real numbers, once they arrive, will probably differ, because events rarely play out exactly as assumed and the gap can matter. And a gate sits in front of all of this: an engagement gets refused, or dropped partway, wherever the assumptions are plainly unrealistic, or wherever the auditor thinks the whole exercise will mislead whoever is meant to rely on it.

citation.ref: the definitions of a forecast and of a projection, the negative assurance on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis together with the opinion on preparation and presentation, and the circumstances in which the engagement should not be accepted

concepts.subsection: SRS 4400 — Engagements to Perform Agreed-upon Procedures
concepts.statement: An agreed-upon procedures engagement carries no assurance of any kind. The practitioner performs procedures of an audit nature to which he, the entity and any appropriate third parties have agreed, and reports the factual findings — what he did and what he found — leaving the users to assess those procedures and findings for themselves and to draw their own conclusions. Because the report means something only to those who know what was agreed, its distribution is restricted to the parties that have agreed to the procedures, and the report says so. The report of factual findings sets out the purpose and the agreed procedures in enough detail for a reader to understand the nature and extent of the work performed; states that the procedures performed were those agreed with the recipient; identifies the specific financial or non-financial information to which they were applied; states that the engagement was performed in accordance with SRS 4400; and carries a plain statement that none of this amounts to an audit or a review, so no assurance is being given at all. Independence is not a requirement for an agreed-upon procedures engagement; where the terms or objectives of the engagement, or national standards, require it, that requirement governs, and where the practitioner is not independent a statement to that effect is made in the report of factual findings.

citation.ref: the elements of the report of factual findings, the statement that no assurance is expressed, the restriction of distribution to the parties that have agreed to the procedures, and the position that independence is not a requirement with a statement to be made where the practitioner is not independent

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 139(2) — Rotation of auditors
concepts.statement: Rotation is a limit on tenure, not a comment on performance. No listed company, and no company belonging to the classes of companies prescribed under the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, shall appoint or re-appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive years. An individual who has completed his term is not eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of that term, and a firm that has completed two terms is not eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of those terms. The bar reaches past the outgoing firm itself: as on the date of appointment, no audit firm having a common partner or partners with the outgoing audit firm, whose tenure has expired in a company immediately preceding the financial year, shall be appointed as auditor of the same company for a period of five years. Rotation runs against the company, so a firm barred in one company may audit any other. And section 139(3) lets the members resolve, if they wish, that the audit partner and his team shall be rotated at such intervals as they may resolve, or that the audit shall be conducted by more than one auditor.

citation.ref: Section 139(2) with its provisos on ineligibility for re-appointment for five years and on a firm having a common partner with the outgoing audit firm, read with section 139(3)

concepts.subsection: Sections 145 and 146 — Signing the report and attending the general meeting
concepts.statement: Two short sections settle who signs and who has to show up. Section 145 hands the signing pen to one person only — whoever holds the office of auditor puts his name to the report, or to any other document of the company he certifies, and does so on section 141(2)'s terms: where the auditor is a firm, including a limited liability partnership, the pen stays with partners who are themselves chartered accountants, and nobody else in the firm may act or sign for it. That same section then turns to what gets read out: any qualification, observation or comment touching financial transactions or matters that harm how the company functions, once it lands in the auditor's report, has to be read aloud before the company in its general meeting, and every member of the company keeps the right to inspect it afterward. Section 146 covers the other half — every notice of a general meeting, and everything else about it, must reach the auditor, who then has to turn up himself or send a representative qualified in the same way an auditor would be, unless the company excuses him; and once there, he may be heard, but strictly on whatever part of the business touches him as auditor. That last phrase is the boundary — it buys him no wider platform to address the room.

citation.ref: Section 145 read with section 141(2), and section 146

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xviii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xviii) puts the spotlight on how the last auditor's exit gets handled by the one who follows. Two questions sit inside it: did the statutory auditors resign at all during the year, and, where they did, did the incoming auditor actually weigh whatever issues, objections or concerns the departing one raised. Both questions belong to the auditor now holding office, asked about a predecessor, and the clause is triggered by any resignation in the year regardless of whether a dispute sat behind it. Weighing those concerns is not the same as agreeing with them — the incoming auditor owes no duty to adopt the outgoing auditor's conclusions — and doing so does not let him off a separate hook: the Chartered Accountants Act's First Schedule, Part I, Clause 8 still treats it as misconduct to step into a seat an accountant already held without writing to him first. The person leaving carries a different duty again — section 140(2) has him file Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar inside thirty days of resigning, setting out his reasons and whatever else bears on the resignation.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xviii)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xx)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xx) reports on where unspent corporate social responsibility money went, and it splits by whether the project was an ongoing one. Clause 3(xx)(a) has the auditor report on the other kind of project — anything that is not ongoing — and whether the money left unspent on it made it into a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act, the clock for that transfer running six months from the close of the financial year, all of it measured against the second proviso to section 135(5). Under clause 3(xx)(b) he states whether any amount remaining unspent under section 135(5) pursuant to any ongoing project has been transferred to a special account in compliance with section 135(6) — the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account, into which the unspent amount goes within thirty days from the end of the financial year, to be spent by the company towards that ongoing project within three financial years, failing which it is transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days of the end of the third financial year. The two limbs have different destinations and different clocks, and the clause reports a transfer, not the quality of the spending.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx)(a) and 3(xx)(b), reporting compliance with the second proviso to section 135(5) and with section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xiii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xiii) has the auditor state whether all transactions with related parties are in compliance with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 where applicable, and whether the details have been disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards. Three things are reported at once and each can fail on its own: the audit committee's approval under section 177 where the company has an audit committee; the approval regime of section 188, which reaches the transactions that section specifies where they are not in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis; and disclosure under the applicable accounting standard. The words "where applicable" work in both directions — a transaction outside section 188 because it is in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length still has to be disclosed under the accounting standard, and a company with no audit committee still answers the section 188 and the disclosure limbs. The population the clause reports on is all transactions with related parties, which is wider than the list of transactions section 188 regulates.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiii), reporting compliance with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and disclosure as required by the applicable accounting standards

concepts.subsection: Section 132 — National Financial Reporting Authority
concepts.statement: The National Financial Reporting Authority is a statutory body constituted by the Central Government under section 132 to make recommendations on accounting and auditing policies and standards, to monitor and enforce compliance with them, to oversee the quality of service of the professions associated with ensuring that compliance, and to suggest measures for improvement. Its jurisdiction runs over the classes of companies and bodies corporate prescribed by the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018 — the listed and large end of the population, not every company. Within it, the Authority may investigate, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government, misconduct — professional or otherwise — committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants who carries registration under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949; and the proviso is the part that decides most questions: where the Authority has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct. Where misconduct is proved the Authority may impose a monetary penalty, and may debar the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for a minimum period of six months and up to a maximum of ten years. An appeal against such an order lies to the Appellate Tribunal.

citation.ref: Section 132(2) and section 132(4) with its proviso barring proceedings by any other institute or body, read with the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — the conceptual framework and threats to independence
concepts.statement: The Code of Ethics does not work by a list of banned acts alone.
