It sets out a conceptual framework requiring a professional accountant to identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, to evaluate whether the threats identified are at an acceptable level, and to address those that are not — by eliminating the circumstances that create the threat, by applying safeguards to reduce it to an acceptable level, or, where neither is possible, by declining or ending the professional activity. An acceptable level is the level at which a reasonable and informed third party would be likely to conclude that the accountant complies with the fundamental principles. Threats fall into five categories. A self-interest threat arises where a financial or other interest will inappropriately influence judgement. A self-review threat arises where the accountant will not appropriately evaluate the results of a previous judgement made, or activity performed, by himself or by someone in his firm, on which he will rely in forming a current judgement. An advocacy threat arises where he promotes a client's position to the point that objectivity is compromised. A familiarity threat arises from a long or close relationship making him too sympathetic to the client's interests or too accepting of its work. An intimidation threat arises where he is deterred from acting objectively by pressures, actual or perceived, including attempts to exercise undue influence. For an audit engagement the accountant must be independent both in mind and in appearance, and a threat that cannot be brought to an acceptable level ends the engagement rather than being disclosed away.

citation.ref: the conceptual framework — identify, evaluate and address threats to compliance with the fundamental principles — with the five categories of threats and the requirement of independence in mind and in appearance for audit and review engagements

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: Two things SA 200 says about what an audit cannot do are constantly turned into an excuse for what the auditor did not do. Every ethical requirement that touches independence binds him on every financial statement audit engagement, no exceptions written in. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but not absolute, because an audit has inherent limitations, with the result that most of the audit evidence on which the auditor draws conclusions is persuasive rather than conclusive. Those limitations arise from the nature of financial reporting, which involves judgement and estimates; from the nature of audit procedures, since management may not provide complete information, since a fraud can be built with elaborate care so that it hides itself from anyone looking, and the auditor is neither trained as nor expected to be an expert in the authentication of documents; and from the fact that an audit has to be finished in a reasonable time and at a reasonable cost. What the standard then refuses is the inference some auditors want to draw from all this. Evidence that falls short of persuasive is never excused by an audit's inherent limitations, and a procedure with no alternative is never skipped merely because it would take longer or cost more. Claiming compliance with the Standards on Auditing is only available where every SA relevant to the audit was actually followed.

citation.ref: para 14 on compliance with relevant ethical requirements, including those pertaining to independence, read with para 5 on reasonable assurance and para 15 on professional skepticism, and with the inherent limitations of an audit and the rule that they are not a basis for being satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Fraud is distinguished from error by intent, and SA 240 names three things generally present when it happens. Somebody has a reason to do it — a target, a covenant, a bonus riding on a number. Somebody has an opening — a weak control or a position that lets management override one. And somebody can talk themselves into it — an attitude or a habit of mind that makes the act feel justified. Together these are fraud risk factors: conditions pointing to a reason or an opening, and finding one is a flag to chase, not proof that anything has actually happened. What the auditor asks management is a set of topics rather than a single yes-or-no question — how management itself has assessed the danger of a material misstatement caused by fraud, how often and how thoroughly; what process management runs for spotting and reacting to fraud risks it finds inside the business, plus anything specific it has already flagged or been told about; whatever it has told those charged with governance about that process; and what it has told staff about its own stance on ethics and acceptable practice. He also asks management, and others in the entity as the situation calls for, whether they know of any fraud, suspected or alleged, affecting the entity — and he puts that same question to those charged with governance too, and asks how they oversee management's work on it, except in the one case where the board and management are the same small group of people. Governance and management carry the main duty to stop and catch fraud; assessing the risk of a material misstatement caused by it is the auditor's own job, and no answer he receives to an inquiry lets him hand that job back.

citation.ref: the three conditions generally present when fraud occurs — an incentive or pressure, a perceived opportunity and an ability to rationalise the act — and the required inquiries of management, of others within the entity and of those charged with governance, read with the presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition at para 26 and management override at para 31

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 begins by giving the duty away. Keeping the entity's operations inside the law is a management job, watched over by those charged with governance — that includes the rules that shape what gets reported and how it gets disclosed in the financial statements. The auditor answers to a narrower brief: he is not on the hook for stopping breaches, and nobody expects him to catch every one, across every law that touches the business. What he does answer for is reasonable assurance that the statements as a whole carry no material misstatement, fraud or error alike, judged against the legal and regulatory setting the entity actually operates in. A breach is harder to catch than an honest slip, for three reasons the standard gives: much of the law that binds a business shapes how it runs rather than what it reports, so none of it ever reaches the financial reporting systems at all; a breach is often dressed up on purpose — a collusive deal, a forged paper, a transaction nobody recorded, a control somebody overrode, a lie told straight to the auditor; and settling whether something actually was a breach is, in the end, a question for a court or another body with the power to rule on it, not for the audit file. That last point shapes the report: the auditor never signs off on the entity's compliance with the law, and a representation management gives him about it is one piece of evidence among others, never a conclusion he is entitled to repeat as his own.

citation.ref: the split between management's duty to run the entity lawfully, under governance oversight, and the auditor's narrower duty toward reasonable assurance on the financial statements; the express limits on what the auditor answers for regarding breaches of law generally; and the point that ruling on whether something was a breach at all sits with a court, not the auditor — read with the two categories of law at para 6

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: SA 260 opens with a question of identity, not content: who counts as those charged with governance? The standard's answer — the people or the body carrying the entity's strategic direction and its accountability obligations, financial reporting included. From that identification flows a practical task for the auditor: picking out, inside the entity's own governance structure, exactly which person or persons he should be talking to. A subgroup — an audit committee, or one individual — may be his contact point, in which case he must still work out whether the full governing body also needs to hear from him separately. One carve-out exists for the very small company where the same people manage and govern it: what was already said to them wearing their management hat need not be repeated in their governance hat, though the auditor still has to be sure they were properly informed either way. Beyond that single carve-out, talking to management is never a substitute for talking to governance. Form, timing, and expected general content are all things the auditor settles as he communicates, and at the close of the engagement he steps back and judges whether the back-and-forth with them did its job for the audit; a negative judgment feeds into how he weighs misstatement risk and his own evidence position, and calls for some response from him.

citation.ref: how the auditor works out exactly who to contact within governance, what he owes the full governing body when a subgroup is his usual contact, the single carve-out for an owner-managed entity, and how he judges at the end whether the exchange with them did its job — read with the planning communication at para 15 and the significant findings at para 16

concepts.subsection: SA 300 — Planning an Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Planning does not start with the strategy. Three things come first, every single year, and SA 300 names all three: the SA 220 work that checks the firm still wants this client and this job; a fresh look at whether the firm still meets the ethics rules, independence chief among them, again under SA 220; and pinning down, per SA 210, what the engagement is actually agreed to cover this time round. Note the emphasis on "this time round" — these three steps are not signed off once in year one and then carried forward unread. They repeat because what they are meant to catch is itself new each year: something that came up mid-year that would have made the firm walk away had it been known sooner, a fresh financial stake or non-audit assignment that has quietly cost the firm its independence, or a shift in the entity such that the old engagement letter no longer describes the actual job. A first-year audit adds one more layer: the SA 220 client-acceptance work itself, plus, if there was a prior auditor, an ethics-compliant exchange with them — a step that belongs to year one and nowhere else. Planning itself involves the engagement partner and the other senior members of the team, including a shared discussion among them.

citation.ref: why these three checks — wanting the client and the job, meeting the ethics rules, and pinning down what is actually agreed to be done — repeat every year rather than being signed off once, and what a first-year engagement adds on top of them

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: The auditor obtains an understanding of the entity and its environment, the applicable financial reporting framework and the entity's system of internal control, and that understanding is the basis on which risks of material misstatement are identified and assessed. The system of internal control is understood through its components — the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, the entity's process to monitor the system of internal control, the information system and communication, and control activities. What the standard asks of the auditor for the controls he identifies is precise and is routinely overstated: he evaluates the design of those controls and determines whether they have been implemented, by performing procedures in addition to inquiry of the entity's personnel. Inquiry alone establishes neither. Evaluating design asks whether the control, individually or with others, is capable of effectively preventing, or detecting and correcting, material misstatements; determining implementation asks whether the control exists and the entity is using it. Neither is a conclusion about operating effectiveness — whether the control operated as designed throughout the relevant period — which is tested under SA 330, and only when the auditor plans to rely on controls, or when substantive work by itself would leave a gap in the evidence needed at the assertion level. Risk assessment procedures on their own never supply enough of a foundation for the audit opinion.

citation.ref: the requirement to obtain an understanding of the entity's system of internal control through its components — the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, the entity's process to monitor the system of internal control, the information system and communication, and control activities — and the requirement to evaluate the design of identified controls and determine whether they have been implemented by performing procedures in addition to inquiry of the entity's personnel, read with the significant risk definition at para 12(l)

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: The materiality set when the audit was planned was set on an expectation, and SA 320 does not let it stand once the expectation is known to be wrong. Whole-statement materiality, and any lower figures set for particular transaction classes, balances or disclosures, both go back on the table the moment something learned mid-audit shows the original number would have come out differently had it been known at the start. A division sold, a business lost, a loss where a profit was budgeted, a benchmark that turns out to be unrepresentative — each is such information. Nor does one changed number end the exercise: a lower overall figure pulls performance materiality along with it, and the auditor has to go back and ask whether the further procedures already planned — their nature, their timing, how far they reach — still hold up against sample sizes computed on the old figure, scoping calls about which components or balances get tested, and analytical thresholds. What starts the whole exercise is new information arriving, never a date on a calendar, and it is a separate requirement from the reassessment SA 450 has the auditor carry out at the end, ahead of weighing uncorrected misstatements. What gets written down is the amounts settled on, the reasoning behind them, and any change made as the audit went along.

citation.ref: para 12 and para 13, read with para 9 and para 11

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations
concepts.statement: Segment information is the third specific item SA 501 singles out, after inventory and litigation and claims. The evidence-gathering route the auditor takes for how it is shown and broken out runs through management's own working method, not through the numbers directly: he gets to grips with how management arrived at the segment figures, weighs whether that method would sensibly land on disclosure that fits the framework being reported under, tests how the method was actually applied where that is warranted, and then backs all of that with analytical or other procedures suited to the case. Three parts of that method reward a closer look, because this is where a number is manufactured rather than simply read off: how sales, transfers and charges are priced between segments and how the inter-segment amounts get eliminated; how the figures stack up against budgets or other expectations, say, operating profit as a share of sales; and how assets and costs get divided among segments, costs shared by more than one segment included. And a limit sits right alongside the work: none of this obliges the auditor to do the extra work he would need to form an opinion on the segment figures as though they were a standalone set of accounts. Segment information stays a disclosure inside the financial statements he is reporting on — never a separate set of accounts, never other information.

citation.ref: para 13, read with the litigation and claims requirements at para 9 to para 11

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: Three decisions are made before a single item is examined, and a sample that fails any of them cannot be rescued afterwards. When designing an audit sample the auditor considers the purpose of the audit procedure and the characteristics of the population from which the sample will be drawn — the population has to be appropriate for the objective of the procedure and it has to be complete, and stratifying it or selecting a value-weighted approach is part of the design. He determines a sample size sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level; the size responds to the level of sampling risk he is willing to accept, to the tolerable misstatement or tolerable rate of deviation, and to the misstatement or deviation he expects to find. And he selects items in such a way that each sampling unit in the population has a chance of selection. Sampling risk is what a sample-based conclusion can get wrong purely by being a sample — it might not match what testing every single item in the population would have shown; non-sampling risk is any other route to a wrong conclusion, one that has nothing to do with the sample being partial. Of the selection methods, random and systematic selection and monetary unit sampling give every unit its chance; haphazard selection is acceptable because the auditor selects without following a structured technique while still avoiding conscious bias or predictability, though it is not available where a statistical evaluation is intended; and block selection of contiguous items is ordinarily not appropriate, because most populations are structured so that items in a sequence share characteristics with each other and differ from the rest.

citation.ref: para 6, para 7 and para 8, read with para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: Where management has made an assertion in the financial statements to the effect that a related party transaction was conducted on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the assertion. It is an assertion like any other and it is audited like any other; what makes it hard is that the support may not exist. There may be no identical or similar transaction with an unrelated party to compare with, the item may have no open market, and management's process for supporting the assertion may amount to an internal opinion recorded in a minute. The procedures available are to compare the terms of the transaction with those of an identical or similar transaction with one or more unrelated parties, or with known market terms for broadly similar transactions on an open market; to evaluate the appropriateness of management's process for supporting the assertion; and to verify the source of the internal or external data supporting the assertion and test the data for accuracy, completeness and relevance. Where the audit evidence contradicts the assertion, the disclosure is misstated. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about an assertion the applicable financial reporting framework requires to be disclosed, that is an inability to obtain evidence, with the consequences SA 705 (Revised) attaches. Management asserting it is not the auditor evidencing it, and this requirement is separate from the significant risk that a related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business creates.

citation.ref: para 24, read with para 23

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: Before any of the internal audit function's work may be used, the external auditor asks a threshold question, judged on three fronts: does where the function sits in the organisation, and the rules it works under, leave its people genuinely independent-minded; is the function good enough at what it does; and does it work to a disciplined, quality-controlled method rather than ad hoc. Each front is a gate on its own, so a failure on any one of the three shuts the door — weak standing that leaves the internal team unable to act independently, thin competence, or a loose, undisciplined method each rule out reliance on their own. Cleared that gate, the external auditor still has to size how much reliance is sensible, weighing the nature and reach of the internal work against his own plan, and weighing how much judgement that work called for against how risky the underlying assertion is — more judgement, higher risk, or shakier independence and skill all push the external auditor toward doing more of it himself. His own plan is built so every significant judgement in the audit stays his, and the more such judgements there are, the smaller a role the internal function plays overall. Before leaning on any of it he reads what was produced, checks it was properly planned, carried out, supervised, reviewed and written up, checks the evidence behind it actually supports its conclusions, checks those conclusions are sound and match what was reported, and runs his own sufficient procedures over the body of work, reperformance included. None of this trims his own sole ownership of the opinion. A separate and stricter set of conditions governs direct assistance, which is a different question entirely.

citation.ref: the three-front test for whether internal audit's work can be leaned on at all — standing and rules that support independent-mindedness, competence, and a disciplined method — the shutdown that follows a failure on any one front, and what the external auditor still checks before using the work, reperformance included — read with the direct assistance conditions at para 28, para 30 and para 33

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: SA 620 puts a written agreement between the decision to use an expert and the expert starting work. Four items need to be settled, in writing where that is the sensible thing: what the expert's own piece of work covers and is meant to achieve; who does what between auditor and expert; how and when the two of them will talk to each other, and what shape any report from the expert will take; and that the expert must keep entity information confidential. Whether the settling has to be on paper turns on things like whether the expert will see sensitive entity data, how the work is divided between the two of them, any legal or regulatory demand, how big and complicated the job is, and whether this is an in-house or an outside expert. That last item — confidentiality — is the one people forget: simply being engaged does not fold an outside expert into the auditor's own professional secrecy duty, which is exactly why the standard insists it be spelled out and agreed rather than assumed. Two more duties sit before any of the expert's own work begins — checking the expert is skilled, equipped and independent enough for the auditor's purposes, and getting enough grip on the expert's own field to be able to both define the job and later judge whether it was done well. Settling the scope is not steering the expert's judgement; it is simply what makes judging the finished work possible at all.

citation.ref: para 11, read with para 12 and para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: Past the Opinion and Basis for Opinion sections, SA 700 (Revised) prescribes elements that are routinely treated as formalities and are routinely got wrong. Naming the engagement partner is the default for a listed entity's full annual accounts — every one of them, not a sample — and the only way out is a real, rare threat to that partner's personal safety, and even then the auditor has to raise that intention with the governance side before dropping the name. Signing is not enough on its own; the report must also say where the auditor put pen to paper. And the date carries real weight, not paperwork weight: it can be no earlier than the day the auditor actually has enough of the right evidence behind the opinion — which folds in confirmation that the full set of statements, notes attached, actually exists in finished form, and that the people with the standing to do so have owned it as theirs. Put plainly, the date can never sit before the board's own approval of the accounts, and it is not simply whichever day fieldwork wrapped up. Beyond that, a title flagging this as an independent auditor's work, an addressee, a paragraph on what management (and governance, where relevant) owns, and one on what the auditor owns, round out the report; any further reporting duty under law sits in its own separate section, kept apart so it never muddies the opinion itself.

citation.ref: why naming the engagement partner is the default for a listed entity's full annual accounts, with a genuine safety threat as the narrow exception; why the place of signing matters alongside the signature itself; and why the date has to wait for both enough evidence and the board's own sign-off, not simply the end of fieldwork — read with the Opinion section at para 23 and the Basis for Opinion at para 28

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: Getting to a key audit matter takes three narrowing passes, each one a smaller set than the last. First pass: everything already raised with those charged with governance. Second pass: out of that pool, whatever genuinely pulled hard on the auditor's own attention while the work was being done — a higher-risk area or a significant risk under SA 315, a spot where management leaned heavily on judgement (an estimate with real uncertainty baked into it counts here), or a big event or transaction that shaped the audit during the year. Third pass, and the smallest set of all: whichever of those stood out above the rest as this year's audit unfolded — that final handful, nothing more, earns the label key audit matter. What gets written about each one is equally fixed. A subheading of its own inside a section titled Key Audit Matters, a pointer to wherever the financial statements themselves discuss it, and an explanation of both why it rose to that level and how the auditor actually dealt with it. The section's own opening lines have to say, in substance, that these are this year's standout items, that they were weighed as part of the audit taken as a whole rather than judged in isolation, and that none of them carries its own separate opinion. Size alone never earns a matter this label, and if the auditor lands on no key audit matters at all, the section says exactly that.

citation.ref: the write-up prescribed for each key audit matter, read with the three narrowing passes that get there — what governance already heard, what genuinely pulled the auditor's attention, and what stood out above the rest this year — and with para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: Choosing the modification is half the answer; SA 705 (Revised) then changes the report in several places at once, and a report that carries the right label over the wrong words is worse than one that carries neither. First, the heading itself flips to whichever of the three applies — Qualified, Adverse, or a Disclaimer. Then the wording of the opinion sentence tracks which of the two roads got the auditor there: a misstatement he knows about is carved out with one turn of phrase, an evidence gap he could not close is carved out with a softer one that allows for what he could not pin down. Where the whole thing tips over into adverse territory, the sentence flips from giving assurance to withholding it outright — the statements simply do not present fairly, full stop. And where the gap in evidence is too wide to opine at all, the report says plainly that no opinion is being given, and why: the shortfall in what could be gathered leaves nothing solid enough to opine on. The Basis heading changes to match, and that section spells out what drove the modification, putting a number on it wherever the misstatement is one that can be quantified — unless that itself cannot practically be done, in which case the report admits as much instead. Two changes are reserved for a disclaimer alone: the line claiming SA-compliant conduct of the whole audit gives way to a narrower claim of simply having been engaged to do the work, the responsibilities paragraph is reworded to match, and Key Audit Matters drops out of the report unless some other law forces it to stay in.

citation.ref: how the Opinion heading and its wording change with each of the three modifications, how the Basis section is reworded and quantified to match, and the two changes reserved for a disclaimer alone — read with para 11 to para 14 and with the requirements that apply where the auditor disclaims an opinion

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — Engagements to Review Historical Financial Statements
concepts.statement: A review is built for limited assurance and leans mainly on asking questions and running analytics — but that is only the starting toolkit, not a fence around it. The moment something surfaces that makes the practitioner suspect a material problem in the numbers, he has to build and run whatever further work gets him to a conclusion on it, or tells him a modified one is called for. That conclusion, once reached, is stated the way a review states things: nothing has come up that suggests the statements fail to present fairly or fail to follow the applicable framework in all material respects — a negative assurance, not a positive one. From there the modification choices mirror an audit's own two-by-two split. A misstatement that is real and material but contained pulls a qualified conclusion; one that is pervasive pulls an adverse one. A gap in evidence that is material but contained also pulls a qualification; one wide enough to be pervasive pulls a disclaimer instead. And where management itself blocks the work badly enough that a disclaimer looks likely, and nothing in law compels the practitioner to stay, he walks away from the engagement wherever that is actually workable. What marks a review off from an audit is everything it skips: no routine inspection, observation or confirmation of the accounting records themselves, no built understanding of internal control aimed at pinning down misstatement risk, no testing of controls, and never an audit opinion at the end of it. Ethics and independence still bind him throughout, and so does professional skepticism and judgement.

citation.ref: when the practitioner has to build further work beyond inquiry and analytics, how the negative form of the conclusion is worded, the four-way modification split mirroring an audit's own, the withdrawal option on a management-imposed limitation, and everything a review skips that an audit does not

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3420 — Reporting on the Compilation of Pro Forma Financial Information
concepts.statement: Pro forma financial information is a what-if picture: it takes the unadjusted numbers and asks what they would have looked like had some big event or deal already happened by some earlier date chosen purely to make the illustration work. It lives in a prospectus and it exists to illustrate, nothing more. SAE 3420 hands the practitioner a reasonable-assurance job, but a narrow one, and that narrowness is exactly what gets tested: he is opining on whether the responsible party put the pro forma figures together properly, against the stated criteria — not on whether the future will actually resemble the picture, and not on the unadjusted numbers themselves, which he neither re-audits nor refreshes. Three checks decide his opinion. Where the unadjusted numbers came from has to be clearly flagged. Each adjustment has to trace directly to the event or deal, has to be backed by fact rather than hope, and has to sit consistently with the entity's own accounting framework and policies. And the criteria being used have to be fit for purpose and properly disclosed. Since an illustration only does its job if the reader knows it is one, the practitioner also weighs whether the picture is presented and explained clearly, and scans the rest of the prospectus for anything that jars against it. An adjustment built on cost savings management merely hopes to achieve fails the fact-based test, however confident that hope is.

citation.ref: the narrow scope of the opinion — that the figures were properly compiled against stated criteria, not that the future will match the picture — and the three checks behind it: where the unadjusted numbers came from, whether each adjustment is fact-based and tied to the event, and whether the criteria used are fit for purpose and disclosed

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — audit data analytics
concepts.statement: Audit data analytics let the auditor examine an entire population rather than a sample — every journal entry, every sales invoice, every vendor payment — and they change what the auditor gets, not what he owes. Three limits hold, and each is where a file goes wrong. First, the output of an analytic is a set of items carrying the characteristic the auditor asked it to find; it is not a list of misstatements. Every exception is investigated, and most of them usually have an ordinary explanation. Second, an analytic is only as good as the data it ran on. Data extracted from the entity's systems is information produced by the entity, so the auditor obtains audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness — reconciling the extraction to the general ledger or to another control total, and checking the parameters the extraction was run with — and where the analysis depends on system-generated data he must first be satisfied about the general IT controls over that system, because a weak change-management or access control undermines everything the system produced. Third, testing one hundred per cent of a population removes sampling risk, which is the risk that a conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion on the whole population. It removes nothing else. A rule written to the wrong threshold, an analytic that tests the wrong attribute, and an auditor who accepts what the tool produced without a critical assessment are all non-sampling risk, and that is exactly where professional skepticism is still required. Analytics are used across the audit — in risk assessment, as substantive procedures, and in the overall review at the end — but they never make the significant judgements, which remain the auditor's.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance, read with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

concepts.subsection: Section 138 — Internal audit
concepts.statement: Section 138 puts a duty on whichever classes of companies get prescribed for it: bring in someone to internally audit how the company's own functions and activities are running. The section itself is generous about who can fill that seat, wider than the audit profession's own fence — a CA, a cost accountant, or whichever other professional the Board settles on. The point most students get backwards sits in the Explanation to the section: that person can just as easily be on the payroll as outside it, either is fine. Rules the Central Government may issue cover how often the work happens and how it gets reported up to the Board. Two lines run off this section worth keeping straight. One — the outside statutory auditor is barred from also being the internal one, because section 144 puts internal audit on the list of services that auditor may not sell to the company or to its holding or subsidiary companies, in any form. Two — having appointed someone under section 138 is a wholly separate question from whether CARO 2020 thinks the internal audit setup actually fits the company's size and type, which is what the statutory auditor reports on there; and neither of those settles whether the statutory auditor may actually rely on that internal work, which is SA 610 (Revised)'s call alone.

citation.ref: Section 138(1) with its Explanation that either an in-house or an outside professional can fill the role, and section 138(2), read with section 144

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: SA 720's work begins before there is anything to read. What counts as other information first needs pinning down: anything financial or otherwise that sits inside a company's yearly reporting package alongside — but separate from — the audited numbers and the auditor's own report on them. That yearly package itself is usually one document or a bundle of them, put out roughly once a year by whoever runs or governs the company, following whatever custom or rule applies, existing so owners can see how the business performed and where it stands, beyond just reading the raw statements. Getting hold of it starts with a conversation: the auditor and management work out together what actually makes up that package and when it is due to come out. From there the auditor has to chase the finished versions of those documents down early enough — ideally before he signs his own report — through whatever arrangement management agrees to. Where a piece of it genuinely will not exist until after his report is already dated, he gets a written promise from management instead: that the finished version will reach him once it exists, and before the company itself puts it out, so he can still do what the standard requires of him. None of this is triggered by mere proximity — a press release or an investor deck sitting near the annual report is not automatically part of it; what makes something other information is that it belongs inside the package, not that it was published around the same time — and whatever form it takes, the auditor never gives it an opinion or a conclusion.

citation.ref: what makes a document part of the entity's yearly reporting package rather than merely published near it, and the sequence of arrangement, chasing, and written promise from management the auditor works through to get finished versions in time — para 13, read with the reading requirement at para 14

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — verification of advances
concepts.statement: Advances are where a bank audit is won or lost, and the work on an advance runs on four questions that come before any question of classification. Is it within sanction — the drawing power recomputed by the auditor from the latest stock and book-debt statement, after deducting the margin stipulated in the sanction and after deducting creditors for goods, because a drawing power worked out on the gross value of stock is a limit the borrower never had. Is it properly secured — the charge created and, where the law requires it, registered; the security in existence, inspected and valued on a basis the auditor can see; the valuation not simply carried forward from the year before. Is the documentation complete and enforceable — the loan and security documents executed by persons authorised to execute them, stamped, and not time-barred, which is why acknowledgements of debt and revival letters are examined and why a document that has run out of time is a defect however good the borrower looks. And are the terms of the sanction being observed — the end use of the funds, the conditions precedent, the financial covenants, the periodicity of the statements the borrower is required to submit. Only then comes classification, and there the discipline is that the auditor tests the branch's identification of non-performing assets rather than accepting the list the system produced. That list is generated on parameters configured by the entity, so it is information produced by the entity: the auditor establishes its accuracy and completeness, and he independently examines accounts showing the symptoms the norms care about — no credits, credits insufficient to cover the interest debited, an outstanding persistently above the limit or the drawing power, a limit renewed on paper without a fresh appraisal, and a facility whose overdue position was cured by a fresh advance from the same bank.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — verification of advances: drawing power and the margin stipulated in the sanction, creation and registration of the charge, enforceability and limitation of the documents, and the auditor's own testing of the branch's identification of non-performing assets, read with the RBI Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning and with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — treasury operations
concepts.statement: Treasury is a small number of people moving very large sums very quickly, so the first control the auditor looks for is not a limit but a separation. The front office deals. The mid office measures exposure, monitors the limits and reports independently. The back office confirms with the counterparty, settles and accounts. No person straddles two of the three, and a dealer who confirms his own deals has removed the only independent check on what he says he did. From that structure the procedures follow. The auditor confirms deals against the counterparty's confirmation and the exchange or clearing corporation record rather than against the dealer's own slip. He tests that deals were struck inside the counterparty, currency, instrument and open-position limits sanctioned by the board, and that a breach was reported and approved rather than absorbed. He examines rates against the market rate ruling at the time of the deal, because a deal put through away from the market is how value is moved out of the bank or a loss is moved into another book. And he looks specifically for deals cancelled and rebooked with the same counterparty, for deals done outside dealing hours or outside the dealing room, and for a pattern of late confirmations, all of which are the recognised means of postponing a loss to a later period. Existence is verified from the bank's own account with the depository or from a confirmation obtained directly from the custodian, never from the front office's own record, and a security shown as sold is traced to delivery. Because the volumes are large and the period between statutory audits is long, treasury is one of the areas ordinarily covered by concurrent audit, and the statutory auditor reads the concurrent auditor's reports and the action taken on them rather than treating their existence as assurance.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — treasury operations: segregation of the front office, the mid office and the back office, independent confirmation of deals with the counterparty and the exchange, dealing within the limits sanctioned by the board, scrutiny of off-market rates and of deals cancelled and rebooked, and verification of the existence of securities from the depository or the custodian, read with SA 265 on communicating deficiencies in internal control

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations
concepts.statement: Two committee reports sit permanently in the bank auditor's checklist and students routinely swap them, so learn them by subject. The Ghosh Committee was on frauds and malpractices in banks, and what it recommended is anti-fraud housekeeping: rotation of staff holding sensitive positions and compulsory leave, so that no one seat is held by one person indefinitely; joint custody of cash, of security documents and of the keys; control over the issue, custody and record of security stationery such as demand drafts, cheque books and pay orders; verification of specimen signatures and of the powers under which an instrument is signed; prompt reconciliation of inter-branch accounts, of nostro accounts and of suspense and sundry accounts, since an unreconciled account is where a fraud lives undisturbed; and prompt reporting of frauds through the prescribed channel. The Jilani Committee was on the internal control and inspection or audit system in banks, and what it recommended is the machinery that checks: an independent inspection and audit department reporting to the top of the organisation rather than to the executives it inspects; coverage of every branch on a defined cycle, with the interval between inspections set by the risk and the size of the branch; a proper system of concurrent audit for large and sensitive branches and for treasury; a system for the rectification of the irregularities reported rather than the mere listing of them again in the next report; and a report to the audit committee of the board. The statutory auditor reports on the implementation of both sets of recommendations in the long form audit report, and what he reports is compliance and not recital: a recommendation not implemented is reported as not implemented, and a recommendation implemented on paper with no evidence that it operated is not implemented.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the Ghosh Committee on frauds and malpractices in banks and the Jilani Committee on the internal control and inspection or audit system in banks, and the reporting on the implementation of their recommendations in the long form audit report

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the memorandum of changes
concepts.statement: A branch auditor cannot alter the branch's books, so what he does with a figure he disagrees with is a memorandum of changes: a statement annexed to and forming part of his branch audit report setting out every change he considers necessary in the returns the branch has submitted, each change described, quantified, and grouped by its effect — on the profit and loss account, on the classification of advances, on provisioning, on the balance sheet heads, and on the asset classification returns the head office consolidates. It exists because the branch's figures are consolidated at the head office, and the central statutory auditors and the head office need each proposed change in a form they can apply without re-doing the branch audit. Two rules decide its contents and neither is about size alone. A change goes in whether or not the branch has accepted it, because the memorandum is the auditor's statement and not a negotiated one. And a change the branch has already carried out in its books before the report is not a change at all and does not go in, because it is already in the figures being reported on. The memorandum is a supplement to the report and never a place to park an opinion: where changes the branch has refused to make are material to the branch's own financial statements, the branch auditor qualifies his branch audit report and the memorandum quantifies what he has qualified. Where he proposes no change he states the memorandum is nil rather than omitting it, since a missing memorandum reads at the head office as one not yet received. Changes touching the classification of an advance are always set out with their consequence for the provision, because classification and provisioning move together and a reclassification carried without its provision is only half the change.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the memorandum of changes annexed to the branch audit report: changes proposed whether or not accepted by the branch, changes already carried out in the books excluded, a nil memorandum stated as nil, and the rule that the memorandum supplements the branch audit report and does not substitute for a qualification of it

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the auditor's report to the Reserve Bank
concepts.statement: The statutory auditor of a non-banking financial company carries a reporting duty the Companies Act alone does not give him. Under the directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies he makes an additional report to the Board of Directors of the company, separate from and in addition to his report under section 143 on the financial statements, on the matters those directions specify: whether the company is engaged in the business of a non-banking financial institution and holds a certificate of registration that section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 requires; whether, on the basis of its asset pattern and its income pattern as at the year end, it is entitled to continue to hold that certificate. Since 1 July 2026 the first of those has an answer the module does not carry: a company that takes no deposits, draws on no public funds and deals with no customer of its own is outside sections 45-IA and 45-IC altogether while its assets stay under a thousand crore rupees, and may ask to come off the register. For such a company the auditor's statement is that no certificate is called for, which is not the same statement as one being absent, and the exception route below is not engaged by its absence. Above that figure, and for any company that touches public funds or customers at any size, the certificate is required as before. Then: where the company does not accept public deposits, whether the board has passed the resolution the directions require to that effect and whether the company has in fact accepted any; whether the prudential norms that bind it — how income is recognised, the accounting standards, how assets are classified, and provisioning — have been observed; and, where applicable to the company, whether the capital adequacy ratio has been correctly determined and reported to the Reserve Bank. The examinable part is the exception route. Where any of those statements is in the negative or is unfavourable, the auditor does not stop at the Board. He reports the matter directly to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank in whose jurisdiction the company's registered office is situated, within the period the directions allow. That duty is the auditor's own; it does not depend on the Board agreeing with him, on the Board forwarding anything, or on the matter being material to the financial statements. And it stands alongside, not instead of, his duty under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, which is engaged once he has grounds to believe that officers or employees of the company are defrauding it or have already done so — a regulatory non-compliance is not by itself such an offence, and a fraud is not discharged by a report to the Regional Office.

citation.source: Reserve Bank of India directions to auditors of non-banking financial companies
citation.ref: the additional report to the Board of Directors on the matters specified, including registration under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, section 45-IA, and continued entitlement on the asset and income pattern, and the obligation to report a negative or unfavourable statement directly to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank in whose jurisdiction the registered office is situated, read with section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Sections 139(5) and 139(7) — appointment of the auditor of a government company
concepts.statement: In a government company — and in any other company that the Central Government owns or controls directly or indirectly, or that one or more State Governments do, or that the two of them hold between them — the appointment of the auditor does not run through the Board and the members in the ordinary way. Section 139(5) provides that the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India shall appoint an auditor duly qualified to be appointed as an auditor of companies under the Act within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, and the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting. Section 139(7) deals with the first auditor of such a company and sets out a cascade: the Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints the first auditor within sixty days from the date of registration of the company; if he does not appoint within that period, the Board of Directors appoints within the next thirty days; and if the Board also fails to appoint within those thirty days, it informs the members, who appoint the first auditor within sixty days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting. The cascade is the examinable part — it moves outward from the Comptroller and Auditor-General to the Board and only then to the members, and each step opens only on the failure of the step before, never by choice. This is the government-company track, and it is not the section 139(6) track under which the Board of any other company appoints the first auditor within thirty days of registration and, failing that, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. Reading one cascade into the other is the commonest way this question is lost.

citation.ref: Section 139(5) — appointment by the Comptroller and Auditor-General within one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year — and Section 139(7) with its cascade of sixty days for the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the next thirty days for the Board and sixty days for the members at an extraordinary general meeting, read against Section 139(6) for a company that is not a government company

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — comprehensive audit of a public enterprise
concepts.statement: A public enterprise is set up with public money for a stated purpose, and comprehensive audit is the Comptroller and Auditor-General's examination of whether the way it is being run is serving that purpose. It goes past the accounts and past the vouchers into management's decisions and their results: whether the capacity created is being used and, where it is not, why; whether projects were completed to time and to cost and what the overrun cost; whether the price at which the product or service is sold recovers what it should; whether inventory, receivables and idle assets are being carried far beyond what the operation needs; whether the return on the capital employed justifies the investment made; and whether the objectives for which the enterprise was created are being achieved at all. The areas are not fixed by any rule. They are selected after a study of the enterprise, its stated objectives, its published policy, the decisions of its board and the reports it makes to Government, and the criteria against which performance is judged are drawn from those sources rather than from the auditor's own preference — which is precisely what keeps the exercise from collapsing into an opinion about management. Two boundaries are examined. Comprehensive audit expresses no opinion on the financial statements and certifies nothing; it reports findings, the reasons behind them and recommendations, and its reader is Parliament through the Comptroller and Auditor-General's report. And it is not the transaction-level prudence test that propriety audit applies to a particular item of expenditure: comprehensive audit asks how the enterprise as a whole has performed against the objectives for which it was set up, not whether one payment was wisely made.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — comprehensive audit of a public enterprise: the areas examined, including capacity utilisation, project execution and cost overrun, inventory and receivables, pricing and return on capital employed; the selection of those areas after a study of the enterprise and its objectives; and the reporting of findings and recommendations rather than an opinion

concepts.subsection: Internal audit — scope, independence and reporting line
concepts.statement: Internal audit is an independent appraisal activity established within an entity to examine and evaluate its activities as a service to the entity, and the two words carrying the weight are "independent" and "within". Because the function sits inside the organisation, its independence cannot come from being an outsider; it comes from where it reports and from what it is kept out of. The function reports to the audit committee, or where there is none to the board or to the highest level of management able to act on what it finds, and it never reports to the head of the activity it audits. Its scope is settled by the audit committee or the board and not by the managers whose work it examines, and it has unrestricted access to records, to personnel and to premises. And the internal auditor does not design, install or operate the controls he later evaluates and owns no part of the process he reviews, because a person reviewing his own work is not appraising it. The scope reaches wherever the entity's risks are — the adequacy and the operating effectiveness of the internal control system, compliance with law and with the entity's own policies, the reliability and integrity of financial and operating information, the safeguarding of assets, and the economy, efficiency and effectiveness with which resources are used — which is wider than the financial statements the statutory auditor reports on. That difference in scope is why the two are not substitutes in either direction. The statutory auditor may use the internal audit function's work only on the conditions SA 610 (Revised) lays down, and using it never reduces his sole responsibility for the opinion; equally, having a statutory auditor does not relieve a company of appointing an internal auditor where the Act requires one, and a well-run internal audit function does not narrow the statutory audit.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — internal audit as an independent appraisal activity established within the entity; its reporting to the audit committee or the board rather than to the management it audits; the scope settled by the audit committee or the board and unrestricted access; the bar on evaluating controls the internal auditor himself designed or operates; and the relationship with the statutory audit, read with SA 610 (Revised) and section 138 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Due diligence — normalised earnings and hidden liabilities
concepts.statement: A financial due diligence does not verify last year's profit; it works out what the buyer is actually buying, and two numbers come out of it. The first is normalised or sustainable earnings — the phrase his own module uses for this is estimating future maintainable profits, and a question may put it either way: reported profit adjusted to strip out what will not recur and to put in what the seller's own arrangements have been suppressing. Out come one-off gains and losses — profit on the sale of an asset, the write-back of a provision no longer required, an insurance recovery, income from a business the seller is retaining. Out also come the effects of arrangements that end at completion: a proprietor's remuneration far below or above the market rate, rent paid to a related party at a concessional rate, a group service charge, a sale to a group company at a price nobody outside the group would pay. In come the costs the business will bear after completion and has not been bearing — a market rent, a full management team, the audit and compliance costs of a standalone company. The second number is net debt together with the working capital the business normally needs, because a price agreed on a multiple of earnings is settled in cash against a debt-free, cash-free position, and everything debt-like is pulled into net debt: unfunded gratuity and leave obligations, deferred consideration on an earlier acquisition, receivables factored with recourse, statutory dues in arrears. Then come the hidden liabilities, which is where the assignment earns its fee — disputed tax and duty demands and their likely outcome, guarantees given for group companies, undisclosed contingent liabilities, litigation, pending regulatory action, an onerous long-term contract, environmental obligations, disputed employee dues, and a lease or a borrowing carrying a change-of-control clause that the transaction itself will trigger. The reporting is not an audit's. A due diligence report states findings of fact, is addressed to the party who engaged it and for the purpose for which it was engaged, expresses no opinion on the financial statements, and feeds the price, the warranties and the indemnities rather than a report to members.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — financial due diligence: the normalisation of reported earnings for non-recurring items and for arrangements that end at completion, the computation of net debt and normal working capital against a debt-free cash-free price, and the identification of hidden liabilities including disputed demands, guarantees, onerous contracts and change-of-control clauses

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Sections 210 and 213 — investigation into a company's affairs
concepts.statement: Two sections open an investigation into a company's affairs and they differ in who moves. Section 210 is the Central Government's. It may order an investigation where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or of an inspector under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest; and where a court or the Tribunal, in any proceeding before it, orders that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall order an investigation. In every case the Central Government appoints one or more persons as inspectors to investigate and to report in the manner and within the period it directs. Section 213 is the Tribunal's, and it starts with an applicant rather than with the Government. The Tribunal may order an investigation on an application by members of the requisite number the section prescribes, or by any other person, on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest what the section lists: that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person, or for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive to any of its members, or that the company was formed for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose; that persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or that the members have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. The applicant is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and the Tribunal may require security for costs. Where the Tribunal so orders, the Central Government appoints the inspectors, and where the report makes out a case the section provides for action against those responsible. Neither section is a route a member takes by writing to the auditor, and neither is section 212, under which the Central Government assigns an investigation to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office.

citation.ref: Section 210 — investigation ordered by the Central Government on a report under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution, in the public interest, or on the order of a court or the Tribunal — and Section 213, under which the Tribunal may order an investigation on an application by the requisite number of members or by any other person on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest the matters the section lists, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — reporting on components audited by other auditors
concepts.statement: The parent's auditor signs one report on the consolidated financial statements and he alone is responsible for the opinion in it, however many other auditors audited the components inside it. What the report does is disclose the extent of what he did not audit himself. Where components have been audited by other auditors, the parent's auditor includes an Other Matter paragraph stating that he did not audit the financial statements of those components, giving the number of components concerned and the quantum they represent — total assets, total revenues and net cash flows, and the group's share of profit or loss for associates and joint ventures accounted for on the equity method — that those financial statements have been audited by other auditors whose reports have been furnished to him, and that where those components' own amounts and disclosures are concerned his opinion rests solely on what those other auditors reported. The paragraph is a disclosure of division and not a disclaimer. It does not qualify the opinion, it does not reduce the parent auditor's responsibility for the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and it does not excuse him from the work the framework requires of him on the consolidation itself — the uniformity of accounting policies across components, the consolidation adjustments and eliminations, the computation of non-controlling interests, and the treatment of a component whose figures are unaudited. Where a component auditor has modified his opinion, the parent's auditor evaluates whether the matter is material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole and modifies his own opinion only if it is; a matter material to the component but not to the group does not travel up. And an Other Matter paragraph is never the way to deal with a matter that requires a modification, exactly as an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not — a paragraph that describes a matter is not an opinion about it.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: the Other Matter paragraph in the parent auditor's report stating the number of components not audited by him, the total assets, total revenues and net cash flows they represent, and that his opinion on the amounts and disclosures in respect of those components is based solely on the reports of the other auditors, read with SA 706 (Revised) paras 8 and 10 on Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs and with SA 705 (Revised) on when a modification is required

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: Sections 177(4) and 177(5) — terms of reference of the audit committee
concepts.statement: Section 177(4) requires the Board to specify the audit committee's terms of reference in writing, and it lists what those terms include. The recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors of the company. Review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance, and of the effectiveness of the audit process. Examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report on it. Approval of, or any subsequent modification of, transactions of the company with related parties. Scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments. Valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary. Evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems. And monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers and related matters. Section 177(5) then gives the committee the means to do it: it may call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems, the scope of audit including the observations of the auditors, and review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board, and it may discuss any related issues with the internal and statutory auditors and the management of the company. Two consequences run off that list and both are examined. Because the committee recommends the auditor's appointment and reviews his independence and performance, the auditor's relationship with the company on those matters runs through the committee and not through the management whose figures he is auditing — which is what makes the committee, and not the finance function, the right addressee for a difficulty encountered during the audit. And because the committee approves related party transactions, a transaction entered into without its approval is an identified non-compliance with law, which the auditor treats as one under SA 250, communicates to those charged with governance, and considers for its effect on the financial statements and on his risk assessment.

citation.ref: Section 177(4) — the terms of reference of the audit committee specified by the Board, including the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors, review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance, examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report, approval of related party transactions, scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, valuation of undertakings or assets, evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers — and Section 177(5), read with Section 177(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 148 — cost records and cost audit
concepts.statement: Section 148(1) empowers the Central Government, by order, to direct that particulars relating to the utilisation of material or labour or to other items of cost be included in the books of account kept by such class of companies engaged in the production of such goods or providing such services as may be prescribed. Section 148(2) empowers it, where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, to direct by order that the cost records of such class of companies as may be prescribed, and which have a net worth or a turnover of such amount as may be prescribed, be audited. That audit is conducted by a cost accountant, appointed by the Board, and it is in addition to and not in place of the audit under section 143 — the two look at different books and answer different questions, and neither report is evidence that the other was not needed. Three limits are examined and all three are frequently missed. The cost auditor is not the statutory auditor: the proviso to section 148(3) provides that the auditor appointed under section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records. Students look for that bar in section 144's list of prohibited services and do not find it there, because it is not there — section 148(3) contains it in terms. The cost audit report goes to the Board of Directors of the company, and the company furnishes it to the Central Government together with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification contained in it, within the period the section allows. And the reservations in a cost audit report are not the statutory auditor's to disregard as a cost matter: they are audit evidence about the entity's costing, its inventory valuation, its capitalisation and its margins, and where they indicate a misstatement in the financial statements the statutory auditor deals with it in his own report. The company and every officer in default, and the cost auditor in default, are liable under the section's penal provisions.

citation.ref: Section 148(1) on the inclusion of cost particulars in the books of account, Section 148(2) on the direction that cost records be audited, the proviso to Section 148(3) that the auditor appointed under Section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, and Section 148(6) on furnishing the cost audit report to the Central Government with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification in it, read with Section 144

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — the elements of a system of quality control
concepts.statement: SQC 1 reaches every audit a firm performs, every review it performs of historical financial information, and its other assurance and related services work. What it demands of the firm is a quality control system built to give reasonable assurance on two things: that the firm and everybody in it are obeying professional standards and whatever the law and the regulator require, and that a report going out over the firm's name or an engagement partner's suits the circumstances it is issued in. The system is built out of six elements and the list is examinable as a list. Leadership responsibilities for quality within the firm — the chief executive officer or the managing partners take ultimate responsibility for the system, and the firm's business strategy is never allowed to let commercial considerations override the quality of the work performed. Ethical requirements, including independence, with written confirmation of compliance with the firm's independence policies obtained at least annually from all personnel required to be independent. Acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements — the firm takes on and retains only what it is competent to perform, where it can comply with relevant ethical requirements, and where it has considered the integrity of the client. Human resources — recruitment, capabilities and competence, career development, and the assignment of engagement teams and of an engagement partner whose identity and role are communicated to the client's key management and to those charged with governance. Engagement performance, which carries direction, supervision and review, consultation on difficult or contentious matters, the resolution of differences of opinion before the report is released, and the engagement quality control review. And monitoring — an ongoing consideration and evaluation of the firm's system, including the periodic inspection of a selection of completed engagements. The policies and procedures are documented and communicated to the firm's personnel, because a policy nobody has been told about is not a policy. SQC 1 is the standard in force for Indian firms: the quality management standards that would have replaced it were deferred by the Council in March 2026 and have not taken effect.

citation.ref: how far SQC 1 reaches — every audit, every review of historical financial information, and the firm's other assurance and related services work — the objective of the system of quality control, and the six elements — leadership responsibilities for quality within the firm, ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements, human resources, engagement performance, and monitoring — read with the retention period at para 83

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: ESG — the three pillars and the Sustainable Development Goals
concepts.statement: Two ideas sit underneath everything else in this chapter and students routinely blur them. Sustainable development, in the Brundtland report's own definition, means meeting today's needs in a way that leaves future generations just as able to meet theirs. Applied to a business, it rests on three pillars, and those three pillars are what the letters ESG stand for. Environment covers the entity's climate policies, its energy use, its waste and pollution, its conservation of natural resources and its treatment of animals — the resources it draws in and the carbon emissions, water discharges and electronic waste it leaves behind. Social covers the relationships the entity has and the reputation it builds with people and institutions in the communities where it does business and along its value chain, including labour relations, health and safety, product safety and privacy, diversity and inclusion. Governance is the internal system of practices, controls and procedures an entity puts in place so it can run itself well, decide where to invest, stay within the law and answer to everyone with a stake in it, and it carries board diversity, executive pay, business ethics, anti-competitive practices, corruption and tax transparency. The second idea is separate and belongs to the United Nations rather than to any company. In 2015 the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by all United Nations member states as a blueprint and a call for action by developed and developing countries alike, and there are seventeen of them — from no poverty and zero hunger through climate action and life below water to partnership for the goals. They are addressed to countries; a company contributes to them, and its ESG reporting is where that contribution becomes visible. ESG reporting itself may be qualitative, describing strategy and policy, or quantitative, carrying metrics and key performance indicators against goals, and a mixed approach adds the most to the quality of the disclosure.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — sustainable development as defined in the Brundtland report, the three pillars of Environment, Social and Governance and what each covers, and the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015 by all United Nations member states

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Integrated Reporting — the six capitals
concepts.statement: Integrated Reporting asks how an organisation creates value over the short, the medium and the long term, and it answers by tracking six stores of value rather than one. They are known as the six capitals, and the list is examinable as a list. Financial capital is the pool of funds available to the organisation for producing goods or providing services, obtained through debt, equity or grants or generated by its own operations and investments. Manufactured capital is the human-created, production-oriented equipment and tools available to it — buildings, plant, infrastructure such as roads, ports, bridges and water treatment plants. Natural capital is an input to production which the organisation's activities also affect for better or worse, and it includes water, land, minerals, forests, biodiversity and ecosystem health.
