Human capital is people's skills and experience, their capacity and motivation to innovate, their alignment with the organisation's governance framework and ethical values including its recognition of human rights, and their ability to understand and implement its strategy. Social capital is the institutions and relationships established within and between communities, stakeholder groups and other networks — common values and behaviour, the trust and loyalty built with customers, suppliers and business partners, and the organisation's social licence to operate. Intellectual capital is the key element in future earning potential, tied to investment in research and development, innovation, human resources and external relationships, and it is what determines competitive advantage. The reason the framework matters to an auditor is that an integrated report says something about resources no balance sheet carries, so it is a report about value creation and not a restatement of the financial statements — and a company already reporting on this basis may cross-reference those disclosures to the ones the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report asks for rather than writing them twice.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Integrated Reporting and its six capitals: financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and intellectual capital, and the cross-referencing of integrated reporting disclosures to those sought under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: BRSR — the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct
concepts.statement: Section C of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report asks for principle-wise performance disclosures, and the principles are the nine of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Two of the nine sit in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance, and although they are stated separately they interlock — environmental protection is bound up with stakeholder engagement and inclusive growth. Principle 1 is ethics, transparency and accountability: business decisions are open to disclosure and accessible to interested parties, policies and procedures keep ethics uncompromised, adverse effects are disclosed with more care rather than less, the value chain is encouraged to adopt the same principles, and the entity responds proactively to those who violate them. This is the principle under which an anti-bribery policy, the internal control mechanism behind it and the machinery for dealing with bribery and corruption complaints are disclosed. Principle 2 is safe and sustainable goods and services — design, production methods and technologies that minimise resource use, consumer education, and reduce, reuse and recycle. Principle 3 is the well-being of all employees including those in the value chain: no child, bonded or involuntary labour, freedom of association, living wages paid on time, a safe and harassment-free workplace, and skill development. Principle 4 is respect for stakeholders' interests and responsiveness. Principle 5 is respect for and promotion of human rights, read against the Constitution of India, national law and the International Bill of Human Rights. Principle 6 is protection and restoration of the environment across the whole life cycle of the product, with measurement of pollution, waste, energy and land use and a contribution to climate resilience in line with India's commitments including the Paris Agreement. Principle 7 is influence on public and regulatory policy, conducted so as to encourage fair competition and prevent human rights abuses. Principle 8 is inclusive growth and equitable development, including the impacts of land acquisition and of business-induced displacement. Principle 9 is providing value to consumers responsibly — reducing negative impacts, not restricting freedom of choice, disclosing adverse impacts accurately, and respecting the customer's right to privacy when handling customer data.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct against which Section C of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report seeks principle-wise performance disclosures, two of them in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Global sustainability reporting frameworks
concepts.statement: Sustainability reporting has no single global standard yet, and the examinable skill is telling the bodies apart by what each one publishes and who it is addressed to. The Global Reporting Initiative is the most widely used framework in the world — an independent international organisation based in Amsterdam, used in over a hundred countries, with ninety-three per cent of the world's largest two hundred and fifty corporations reporting through it. It helps organisations report their economic, environmental and social impacts, and its report is addressed to all the stakeholders of the entity. The Carbon Disclosure Project captures environmental performance data — greenhouse gas emissions, water, forests and the supply chain — and reports on climate change, forests and water security to investors, buyers and other stakeholders. The International Integrated Reporting Council's framework sets guiding principles and content elements for an integrated report covering organisational overview, governance structure, business model, risks and opportunities, strategy, performance and outlook. The Financial Stability Board set up the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures in 2015 to push companies toward consistent climate-related disclosures, and its audience is narrower than the Global Reporting Initiative's broad sweep — it speaks mainly to firms whose business is finance itself, banks and insurers among them. Separately, the Climate Disclosure Standards Board framework exists to help organisations put climate-related risks and opportunities into their disclosures. Then came consolidation: the Value Reporting Foundation was the result of the merger of the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council, and the IFRS Foundation Trustees, on 3 November 2021, unveiled a new body — the International Sustainability Standards Board — to build one comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards for investors and other capital market participants. In March 2022 the International Sustainability Standards Board launched a consultation on its first two proposed standards, one on general sustainability-related disclosures and one on climate-related disclosures, the climate one building on the Task Force's recommendations and incorporating industry-based requirements derived from the SASB standards.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — global trends in sustainability reporting: the Global Reporting Initiative, the Carbon Disclosure Project, the International Integrated Reporting Council framework, the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board, the Climate Disclosure Standards Board, the Value Reporting Foundation and the International Sustainability Standards Board announced by the IFRS Foundation Trustees on 3 November 2021

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Social Audit Standards — SAS 100 to SAS 1600
concepts.statement: Beyond the assurance standards on sustainability information, the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has issued a separate series called the Social Audit Standards, numbered SAS 100 to SAS 1600. They are not a form of financial audit and they are not a review of a report. Each one guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise working in a particular field, and each sets out the audit steps and procedures to be applied in conducting the social impact assessment. Each Standard states the minimum requirements to be followed, and where a law or a regulation establishes additional requirements those are followed as well, so the Standard is a floor and not a ceiling. The series follows the fields the enterprises work in: SAS 100 on eradicating hunger, poverty, malnutrition and inequality; SAS 200 on health care including mental health care, sanitation and safe drinking water; SAS 300 on education, employability and livelihoods; SAS 400 on gender equality and the empowerment of women and LGBTQIA+ communities; SAS 500 on environmental sustainability and climate change including mitigation and adaptation and forest and wildlife conservation; SAS 600 on national heritage, art and culture; SAS 700 on training for rural, nationally recognised, Paralympic and Olympic sports; SAS 800 on supporting incubators of social enterprises; SAS 900 on other platforms strengthening the non-profit ecosystem; SAS 1000 on livelihoods for the rural and urban poor including small and marginal farmers; SAS 1100 on slum area development and affordable housing; SAS 1200 on disaster management including relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction; SAS 1300 on financial inclusion; SAS 1400 on access to land and property assets for disadvantaged communities; SAS 1500 on bridging the digital divide and addressing misinformation and data protection; and SAS 1600 on the welfare of migrants and displaced persons. The board that issued them is the same one that carries the Institute's sustainability work generally, which is why the series sits in this chapter and not in the chapter on related services.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Social Audit Standards SAS 100 to SAS 1600 issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, guiding the Social Auditor in independent impact assessment engagements of Social Enterprises and setting the minimum requirements for a social impact assessment

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — accepting the engagement and setting the examination procedures
concepts.statement: Five things shape whether he accepts an engagement to examine prospective financial information, each one bearing on the work itself rather than just the fee: what the information will be used for; whether its distribution will be general or limited; the nature of the assumptions behind it, best-estimate or hypothetical; which elements the information is meant to cover; and what period it spans. He also weighs how far reliance on the entity's historical financial information is justified, and, as with any engagement, settles the terms in an engagement letter. Two situations rule the engagement out entirely: acceptance is refused, and an ongoing engagement is dropped, wherever the assumptions read as clearly unrealistic, or wherever he judges the prospective financial information unsuited to the use intended for it. Once he is in, seven factors fix how far the examination procedures reach and how they are timed: what he already knows from earlier engagements with the entity; how competent management is at preparing this kind of information; how likely a material misstatement is; how much management's own judgement shapes the figures; how solid the underlying data is and where it came from, management's sources included — third-party inputs such as industry statistics count here too; how stable the entity's business is; and how much experience the engagement team carries with this business, this industry, and reporting of this kind generally. Working through those procedures, he weighs where the evidence behind management's best-estimate figures originates and how dependable it is — budgets, debt agreements and industry publications are typical sources. Hypothetical assumptions bring their own discipline: every consequence that follows from one has to show up in the figures, so an assumed jump in sales past current plant capacity forces the added investment in capacity, or the cost of an alternative like subcontracting, into the picture as well. He also confirms those hypothetical assumptions fit the purpose the information serves and gives him no reason to call them unrealistic.

citation.ref: the matters considered before accepting an engagement to examine prospective financial information — the intended use, general or limited distribution, whether the assumptions are best-estimate or hypothetical, the elements to be included and the period covered — the obligation not to accept or to withdraw where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic or the information would be inappropriate for its intended use, and the matters determining the nature, timing and extent of the examination procedures

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — presentation and disclosure of prospective financial information
concepts.statement: A forecast is only as honest as the notes around it, so SAE 3400 gives the auditor a checklist for assessing the presentation and disclosure of prospective financial information and of the assumptions underneath it, over and above whatever a statute, a regulation or a professional pronouncement separately requires. The presentation must be informative and not misleading. The accounting policies must be clearly disclosed in the notes to the prospective financial information. The assumptions must be adequately disclosed in those notes, and it must be clear whether each one is a best-estimate assumption or a hypothetical one; where assumptions are made in areas that are material and subject to a high degree of uncertainty, that uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of the results must be adequately disclosed, because a reader shown a single number cannot see how far it moves. Disclosure must also fix the date the prospective financial information was prepared as of, with management confirming the assumptions still hold good as of that date — this holds regardless of how long a stretch the underlying figures were actually gathered over. Where the results are expressed as a range, the basis of establishing the points in the range must be clearly indicated and the range must not be selected in a biased or misleading manner — a range whose ends were chosen to flatter is worse than a single figure, because it wears the appearance of candour. And where the entity's accounting policy has changed from that disclosed in the most recent historical financial statements, the reason for the change and its effect on the prospective financial information must be adequately disclosed. The consequence of failing these tests is not a note in the file: where the auditor believes the presentation and disclosure are not adequate — for example where the information fails to disclose adequately the consequences of highly sensitive assumptions — he expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion, or withdraws from the engagement.

citation.ref: the assessment of presentation and disclosure — informative and not misleading presentation, accounting policies and assumptions disclosed in the notes with best-estimate assumptions distinguished from hypothetical ones, disclosure of uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of results, disclosure of the date as of which the information was prepared, the basis of establishing points in a range and the bar on a biased or misleading range, and disclosure of any change in accounting policy from the most recent historical financial statements

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — modifying the report on prospective financial information
concepts.statement: An examination of prospective financial information carries two conclusions in one report — a negative assurance statement on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, and an opinion on whether the information is properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions and presented in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework — so the ways it can go wrong are more than one and SAE 3400 pairs each fault with its own answer. Where the auditor believes the presentation and disclosure of the prospective financial information are not adequate, he expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion, or withdraws from the engagement; the example the standard gives is information that fails to disclose adequately the consequences of assumptions which are highly sensitive. A different fault gets a different answer: once he concludes one or more significant assumptions fail to give the prospective financial information a reasonable basis — regardless of whether those assumptions were best-estimate ones or hypothetical ones suited to the purpose the information was prepared for — a mere qualification will not do. What SAE 3400 requires instead is an adverse opinion, reasons stated in the report, or withdrawal from the engagement altogether. The logic is that the assumptions are the whole foundation, and information built on a foundation that does not hold cannot be partly relied on. And where the examination is affected by conditions that preclude the application of one or more procedures he considers necessary in the circumstances, he considers either withdrawing from the engagement or disclaiming the opinion and describing the scope limitation in the report. Two boundaries are worth holding on to. The auditor never expresses an opinion that the results shown will be achieved, so no modification is ever a statement about achievability; and the refusal at the acceptance stage — no engagement where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic or where the information will be inappropriate for its intended use — is a different rule from these, because it operates before any report exists.

citation.ref: the modification of the report on an examination of prospective financial information — a qualified or adverse opinion or withdrawal where the presentation and disclosure are not adequate, an adverse opinion setting out the reasons or withdrawal where one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis, and withdrawal or a disclaimer describing the scope limitation where conditions preclude a necessary procedure

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3402 — the description of tests of controls and the reporting of deviations
concepts.statement: What separates a type 2 report from a type 1 report in practice is not the opinion sentence but the attachment. A type 2 report carries something a type 1 report does not: a separate section after the opinion, or a stand-alone attachment, laying out which controls the service auditor tested and what those tests turned up. That write-up has to name the controls tested, say whether every item in the population was examined or only a sample of it, and describe the testing closely enough that a user auditor can work out what it means for his own risk assessment — the whole document exists so that a user auditor who cannot see what was tested is not left guessing. When deviations turn up, he discloses how much testing led him to them — the sample size, if sampling was used — along with how many deviations there were and what they looked like. The rule that settles most disputes here: a deviation gets reported regardless of whether the tests, taken as a whole, still supported a conclusion that the control objective was met. A deviation is not suppressed because it was survivable — the user auditor is entitled to know the population it came from and to reach his own conclusion about what it means for his entity. The report also carries a built-in audience restriction: it — and, for a type 2 report, the write-up of tests performed — is meant only for entities that use the service and their auditors, on the assumption that they understand it well enough to read it alongside other information, including their own knowledge of the controls they run themselves. Modification is separate again: the opinion is modified where the description does not fairly present the system as designed and implemented, where the controls were not suitably designed, where in a type 2 report the controls tested did not operate effectively, or where the service auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, and the report then contains a clear description of all the reasons for the modification.

citation.ref: the separate section or attachment to a type 2 report describing the tests of controls and their results, the requirement to state which controls were tested and whether the items tested were all or a selection of the population, the disclosure of the extent of testing including the sample size and the number and nature of deviations, the rule that deviations are reported even where the service auditor concluded the related control objective was achieved, the restriction of the report to user entities and their auditors, and the grounds on which the service auditor's opinion is modified

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3420 — engagement acceptance and a modified opinion
concepts.statement: Before he takes on an engagement to state whether a prospectus's pro forma financial information matches the applicable criteria, the practitioner works through a defined checklist. He determines that he has the capabilities and the competence to perform the engagement. Based on an early read of the circumstances and a discussion with the responsible party, he satisfies himself that the applicable criteria are suitable and that the pro forma figures are unlikely to mislead anyone relying on them for their intended purpose. He evaluates the wording of any opinion prescribed by law or regulation, to satisfy himself that he will likely be able to express that prescribed opinion on the basis of the procedures this standard specifies. Where the sources from which the unadjusted financial information or any acquiree or divestee information were extracted carry a modified audit opinion, a modified review conclusion or an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, he considers whether the relevant law or regulation permits their use, or a reference to them in his report. Where the entity's historical financial information — or an acquiree's, in an acquisition — has never been audited or reviewed, he considers whether he can obtain a sufficient understanding of the entity or the acquiree and of its accounting and financial reporting practices to perform the engagement at all. And he obtains the responsible party's agreement acknowledging its own responsibility for adequately disclosing and describing the applicable criteria to the intended users where these are not publicly available, for compiling the pro forma financial information on the basis of those criteria, and for giving him access to all relevant information, to any additional information he requests, and to the people within the entity, its advisers and the acquiree from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. The examined trap sits at the other end. Where the relevant law or regulation precludes the publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion and the practitioner nonetheless concludes that a modified opinion is appropriate, he discusses the matter with the responsible party; and if the responsible party does not agree to make the necessary changes, he withdraws from the engagement or considers seeking legal advice. He does not soften the opinion to fit the prospectus. Separately, he can add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph where something shown or disclosed in the pro forma figures or their explanatory notes is central to a user's understanding — but only once he has gathered enough evidence of the right kind to be sure that matter does not change whether the compilation itself meets the criteria, and the paragraph can point only to content that already sits in the pro forma information or its accompanying notes.

citation.ref: what the practitioner checks before accepting a prospectus pro forma engagement, the responsible party's acknowledgement of its own duties, what happens when law or regulation blocks a modified opinion in a prospectus, and when an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available

concepts.subsection: Sections 129(3) and 129(4) — when consolidated financial statements must be prepared
concepts.statement: A holding company with even one subsidiary — the Act treats an associate and a joint venture the same way — must go beyond its own standalone accounts and produce a consolidated financial statement covering itself and every subsidiary, built in the same form as its own statements (section 129(3)). Everything the Act requires of a holding company's own financial statements — how they are prepared, adopted and audited — carries over to the consolidated version too (section 129(4)); that is why the Board approves and signs the consolidated set before it goes to the annual general meeting alongside the standalone figures, and why its audit is a statutory audit rather than a courtesy exercise. A subsidiary-wise summary — the salient features of each subsidiary's financial statement — also gets attached, in Form AOC-1. Schedule III and the applicable accounting standards govern how the numbers are put together, and a company outside the accounting standards' own consolidation requirement can instead simply follow Schedule III's consolidation provisions. Escaping consolidation altogether needs all three of the following at once, not any one alone: the company is either wholly owned, or majority owned with its other members — even those without a vote — written to with proof of delivery and none of them objecting; none of its securities are listed or headed toward listing, in India or abroad; and its own parent, immediate or further up the chain, already files Registrar-compliant consolidated accounts. Separately, section 129(6) lets the Government carve out a whole class of companies by notification, in the public interest. No exemption exists, though, for control that is only temporary or for a subsidiary hemmed in by severe long-term restrictions on moving funds — consolidation tracks control itself, starting the day it is obtained and stopping the day it is lost, so a subsidiary bought and sold within the same year is still consolidated for however long it was actually controlled.

citation.ref: Section 129(3)'s duty to consolidate wherever a subsidiary, associate or joint venture exists, Section 129(4) extending the holding company's own preparation, adoption and audit rules to the consolidated set, the AOC-1 attachment, the three-part exemption test in the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, and Section 129(6)'s government carve-out — with Ind AS 110 confirming there is no exemption for merely temporary control

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xxi)
concepts.statement: CARO 2020 does not attach clause by clause to a report on consolidated financial statements. The Order applies to the auditor's report on the standalone financial statements of the companies it covers, and on consolidated financial statements only one clause operates: clause 3(xxi). Under it, the group auditor reports on whether any CARO report among the companies swept into the consolidation carries a qualification or an adverse remark from that company's own auditor, and if one does, he names the company and points to the paragraph number in that CARO report where the qualification or adverse remark sits. That is the whole of it, and the shape of the duty is the examinable part. He is not answering the twenty other clauses again for the group. He is not preparing a separate clause-by-clause CARO report covering the parent and every Indian subsidiary, nor annexing one, nor supplementing the standalone CARO report with additional information about the subsidiaries. He is pointing the reader of the consolidated statements at the places where a component's own CARO report already carries a qualification or an adverse remark, so that something reported at the component does not disappear inside the consolidation. Two consequences follow. Only companies included in the consolidated financial statements that are themselves covered by CARO produce anything to report, so a component to which the Order does not apply contributes nothing to this clause. And the clause is a signpost rather than an opinion: it is not a modification of the opinion on the consolidated financial statements, and a qualification in a component's CARO report is evaluated separately for whether it says anything material about the consolidated financial statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xxi) — the sole CARO clause reaching a report on consolidated financial statements, requiring the group auditor to flag any qualification or adverse remark carried in a component's own CARO report, naming the company and the paragraph where it sits

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — written representations
concepts.statement: SA 580 calls for written representations from management and, where it fits, those charged with governance; in a group audit these come from the parent's own management. Two representations are the familiar ones every audit takes, just adapted for a group: that the parent's management takes ownership of presenting the consolidated figures fairly under the framework the parent itself reports against, and that it has signed off on that consolidated set. Past those two, the auditor asks for representations on whatever else in the consolidated statements is material, and four recur as the standard set. Whether every component that belongs in the consolidation is actually in it — the one representation the auditor is worst placed to check unaided, since a component simply missing leaves no trace behind. Which segments have been picked out as reportable, for segment disclosure. Which parties count as related, and which transactions with them need reporting. And whether the adjustments made — both the ones carried forward and the ones made fresh this period, eliminating transactions between group companies — are complete and fit for purpose. None of this raises what a representation is worth on its own: it remains audit evidence, never enough by itself to stand as the evidence for any of these matters, and getting one never excuses the auditor from the completeness work, the consolidation-adjustment work or the related-party work he would otherwise have to do. What a representation is actually good for is pinning down, in writing, management's position on things only management can really know — and a refusal to give one is itself something to act on.

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — the parent-management representations a group audit obtains beyond the two universal ones: on completeness of components, reportable segments, related parties, and the adjustments that eliminate intra-group transactions, read with SA 580

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — the constitutional position of the Comptroller and Auditor General
concepts.statement: Government audit in India is performed by an independent constitutional authority, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, through the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, and the Constitution itself carries the provisions that protect that independence. Article 148 provides for the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General by the President, and for a special procedure for his removal, only on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity; his salary and other conditions of service are determined by Parliament. Article 149 provides that he leaves the actual content of his duties and powers over the accounts of the Union, the States and any other body open to Parliament to fill in by law — and Parliament did fill it in, through the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which spells out his functions in detail and fixes his term at six years or up to the age of sixty-five, whichever comes first, with resignation open to him at any time by letter to the President. Article 150 provides that the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept in such form as the President prescribes on his advice. Article 151 provides that his audit reports relating to the accounts of the Central or a State Government are submitted to the President or to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly. The bodies within his audit purview are wide: all Union and State Government departments and offices including the Railways and Posts and Telecommunications; public commercial enterprises controlled by the Union and the State Governments, meaning government companies and corporations; non-commercial autonomous bodies and authorities owned or controlled by the Union or the States; and authorities and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues. For the commercial audit of companies in which Government equity participation is fifty-one per cent or more, the auditors are firms of chartered accountants appointed by him, to whom he gives directions on the manner in which the audit is to be conducted, and he may comment upon their reports, conduct a supplementary audit and order a test audit. A unique feature of that work is the constitution of Audit Boards, which associate experts in the relevant disciplines, discuss their findings with the enterprise's management and the controlling ministry before finalisation, have no separate legal entity, and work under his supervision and control.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution on the appointment and removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General, his duties and powers, the form of the accounts and the laying of his reports; the term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971; and the Audit Boards constituted for comprehensive appraisals in commercial audit

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — the Parliamentary financial committees
concepts.statement: Parliament cannot itself scrutinise every annual account and every audit report, so it and the State Legislatures have constituted specialised committees to which those reports and accounts automatically stand referred, and telling the three apart is a standing question. The Public Accounts Committee checks that money went out lawfully, spent on the service or the purpose it was meant for, that the spending itself was properly authorised, and that any re-appropriation followed the rules laid down for it; it also looks at the accounts of autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies that the Comptroller and Auditor General audits, whether that audit happens on the President's direction or because a Parliamentary statute requires it. The Estimates Committee goes through the estimates to point out where economy, better organisation, efficiency or administrative reform is possible without disturbing the policy behind them, to put forward alternatives, to check that the money is being put to good use within its limit, and to recommend how the estimates ought to be laid before Parliament; policy itself, once Parliament has approved it, is off limits — but if the evidence shows a policy is not delivering or is running to waste, flagging that to the House becomes its job. The Committee on Public Undertakings does for public sector undertakings what the Public Accounts Committee does for Government departments — the same kind of financial control, applied to a different set of bodies. It goes through the undertakings' own reports and accounts, through what the Comptroller and Auditor General has reported on them, and through how much autonomy and efficiency they show and whether sound business judgement and prudent commercial practice actually run the show. Its examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal or evaluation of the performance of the undertaking, including its policies, its programmes and its financial working. The Comptroller and Auditor General is described as the friend, philosopher and guide of these committees: his reports generally form the basis of their working, though they are not precluded from examining issues he did not raise; he scrutinises the notes ministries submit and helps the committees check the correctness of the facts and figures in their draft reports. The committees report to the legislature with observations and recommendations, the ministries are required to inform them of the action taken, and Action Taken Reports are presented in turn. The object throughout is to focus not only on the individual irregularity but on the defect in the system that produced it.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Public Accounts Committee, the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings, their respective functions, the Comptroller and Auditor General's role as friend, philosopher and guide to the financial committees, and the Action Taken Reports presented to the legislature

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: PSU audits — the elements, and attestation against direct reporting engagements
concepts.statement: Every public sector audit is built out of the same three components, and the third is where financial, compliance and performance audit actually separate. First, three parties. The auditor — the role is filled by the Supreme Audit Institution of India, which is the Comptroller and Auditor General together with the Indian Audit and Accounts Department functioning under him, his senior functionaries in the States being the Accountants General. The responsible party, whose responsibilities are determined by constitutional or legislative arrangement, generally the auditable entity and those charged with its governance; its job can be producing the information about the subject matter, running the subject matter day to day, or acting on what recommendations say. Then the intended users: whoever the auditor is actually writing the report for. Second comes a trio that is easy to blur — subject matter, criteria, subject matter information. The subject matter is whatever gets measured or evaluated: an activity, a condition, a body of information. Criteria are the yardstick applied to it. Subject matter information is simply what comes out once that measuring happens. Third, and this is where the split matters most, the engagement takes one of two shapes. Attestation puts the measuring in the responsible party's hands — it does the work and hands over the resulting information, while the auditor's task is to gather enough of the right evidence to reach and support his own conclusion about it. Direct reporting flips that: here the auditor does the measuring and the evaluating himself, with no prior statement from anyone else to check against. A financial audit is attestation work through and through, since it starts from figures the responsible party has already put together; performance and compliance audits usually run the other way, as direct reporting, simply because there is rarely any existing claim by the entity about its own economy, efficiency or effectiveness for the auditor to test. That is why a performance audit report reads as findings, reasons and recommendations rather than as an opinion on something management prepared.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the basic elements of a public sector audit: the three parties of auditor, responsible party and intended users; the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information; and the two types of engagement, with financial audits always attestation engagements and performance and compliance audits generally direct reporting engagements

concepts.subsection: Section 138 with Rule 13 — which companies must appoint an internal auditor
concepts.statement: Section 138 requires such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed to appoint an internal auditor, and Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 is where the prescription lives. The appointee may be an individual, a partnership firm or a body corporate. Every listed company must appoint one, with no threshold at all. An unlisted public company falls under the requirement the moment any one of four numbers is crossed at any point during the preceding financial year: paid-up share capital reaching fifty crore rupees, turnover reaching two hundred crore rupees, loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions going past one hundred crore rupees, or deposits reaching twenty-five crore rupees. A private company answers to only two of those same numbers — turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more in the preceding year, or loans and borrowings from banks or public financial institutions crossing one hundred crore rupees at any point during it. Three details decide most questions on this rule. The tests are alternatives joined by "or", so meeting any one of them brings the company in, and a company that fails the capital test on a small paid-up capital is still caught by its turnover. A private company has only two tests — turnover and borrowings — so the paid-up capital and deposits limits that apply to an unlisted public company are not read into it. And where an existing company gets covered by any of these criteria, it must comply with the requirement within six months of the commencement of such applicability, rather than waiting for the next financial year. What Rule 13 settles is only whether the company must have an internal auditor. Who may be appointed is section 138 itself, and whether the statutory auditor may use the function's work is SA 610 (Revised) and nothing else.

citation.ref: which companies Section 138 with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 catches — every listed company automatically; an unlisted public company once paid-up capital hits fifty crore, turnover hits two hundred crore, bank or public-financial-institution borrowings pass one hundred crore, or deposits hit twenty-five crore; a private company on just the turnover and borrowings tests at those same two hundred crore and one hundred crore marks; and the six-month compliance clock that starts once any of these criteria is first met

concepts.subsection: SIA 370 — reporting the results of an internal audit
concepts.statement: SIA 370 governs only the first of two separate reporting stages for internal audit results. Once a single assignment wraps up, the internal auditor writes it up in an Internal Audit Report scoped to that particular area, function or part of the entity — describing how the work was carried out and what it found — and sends it to the auditee, copying local and executive management the way the planning phase had already settled. A second, separate report gathers everything up: periodically, usually every quarter, once a plan period closes, the Chief Internal Auditor (or the engagement partner, if the function has been outsourced) puts together one comprehensive account of every internal audit activity across the whole entity for that period, and sends it up to whichever body has ultimate authority over internal audit — typically the audit committee. SIA 370's remit stops at the first report; the periodic one is a separate duty. What the assignment-level report must be is clear and well documented, and it needs to cover: the objectives, scope and approach behind the assignment; a statement — only where the auditor can back it with actual evidence — that the work followed the Standards on Internal Audit; an executive summary zeroed in on the key observations; what management has agreed or been asked to do to correct each observation; and whatever level of assurance, if any, the observations support. Beyond that the Standard fixes no template and no checklist — format and content are left to the internal auditor's judgement, worked out together with the auditee. Two things, though, are not negotiable. A draft has to reach the auditee before any final version of the report goes out. And the final report has to follow reasonably soon after the fieldwork ends, not sit indefinitely. The conclusions drawn have to rest on the whole body of findings, not a handful of deviations, and controls that were found working properly get acknowledged just as much as the ones that were not — a report naming only failures paints a false picture. And should the internal auditor stumble on an actual or suspected fraud or other misappropriation, that does not wait for any report at all; it goes straight to management.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: the two-stage reporting structure — assignment-level and periodic — the required contents of the Internal Audit Report, the draft-before-final and reasonable-time rules, and the immediate escalation of a fraud finding

concepts.subsection: SIA 390 — monitoring and reporting of prior audit issues
concepts.statement: An internal audit finding that nobody closes is a finding repeated in next year's report, so SIA 390 makes the tracking of prior issues a duty with a named owner. The Chief Internal Auditor keeps a continuous watch over whether prior findings actually get closed, tracking whether the action plans from past audits are carried out on time, and does it through a formal monitoring process whose elements are pre-agreed with management and with those charged with governance rather than invented after the fact. Monitoring and reporting here means the periodic tracking of issues raised during prior audits, the evaluation of the corrective actions the auditee has undertaken to resolve them, and the reporting of any open and pending matters to management and to those charged with governance, generally the audit committee. In practice the internal auditor's responsibility takes the form of an Action Taken Report on previous audits. The line that decides most questions is the one about ownership: the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management. The internal auditor monitors, evaluates and reports; he does not implement, because implementing a control and then reviewing it are the two things one person cannot do. The rest follows from that. He reviews whether follow-up action has been taken on the basis of his report, and if no action is taken within a reasonable time he draws management's attention to it. Where management has not acted on his suggestions or not implemented his recommendations, he ascertains the reasons rather than simply recording non-compliance. And where management has accepted his recommendations and initiated action, he periodically reviews the manner and the extent of implementation and reports back, highlighting the recommendations that have not been implemented fully or in part.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 390, Monitoring and Reporting of Prior Audit Issues
citation.ref: who owns tracking prior-issue closure and how the monitoring process gets set up, what the Action Taken Report covers, why execution stays with management rather than the auditor, and how partial or unimplemented recommendations get flagged back

concepts.subsection: Internal audit — performing the engagement
concepts.statement: A typical internal audit engagement runs in five steps and they are performed in that sequence. Step one, obtain knowledge of the business and its environment: meetings with key stakeholders, the Board and key managerial personnel to understand the business environment, the operations, the organisation's vision and mission and what top management expects of the audit function, together with an understanding of the standard operating procedures and financial statements, of the information technology landscape, the applications, the enterprise resource planning system and the management information system, and of the regulatory landscape and the laws applicable to the organisation. Step two, perform audit planning, under SIA 310, Planning the Internal Audit Assignment — and the gate that sits here is that the audit scope must be approved by the audit committee and the Board, not by the management whose processes are to be examined. Only once approved does the internal auditor share the detailed audit plan with key managerial personnel, schedule the work in advance, hold an opening meeting with key stakeholders and state the information and system access he needs. The detailed work plan is prepared by the audit managers and approved with the Head of Internal Audit or Chief Internal Auditor, and it is prepared after evaluating the major risks in the process under review and deciding the audit checks that will assess whether the control environment mitigates them. Step three, gather the required information, obtained so far as possible directly from the source, with checks on its correctness and integrity and advance intimation for anything needed at an interim stage. Step four, perform the audit checks: collate the data and run analytical procedures to identify key trends and outliers under SIA 6, select samples where needed under SIA 5, collect and store evidence under SIA 320, document the work papers under SIA 330, and issue any interim report only after review under SIA 350. Step five, report the internal audit issues — a draft report covering the process reviewed against the scope, the coverage and any exclusions, the audit period, and the gaps found with their business implication and the recommendation to close each one. A management action plan is agreed with a named owner and a timeline, the status of actions agreed in previous audits is reviewed and reported, and the final report is circulated and the findings presented to the audit committee, under SIA 360 on communication with management and SIA 370 on reporting results.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — the five steps of an internal audit engagement performed in sequence: obtaining knowledge of the business and its environment, audit planning under SIA 310 with the scope approved by the audit committee and the Board, gathering the required information, performing the audit checks under SIA 6, SIA 5, SIA 320, SIA 330 and SIA 350, and reporting the internal audit issues with an agreed management action plan under SIA 360 and SIA 370

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Income recognition and asset classification
concepts.statement: A term loan turns non-performing when interest or principal stays overdue for more than ninety days; a cash credit when the account stays out of order. Once non-performing, the asset walks a ladder — substandard for its first twelve months as an NPA, doubtful once it stays substandard beyond twelve months, loss when identified as such — and income on it is recognised only on realisation, not accrual.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Long form audit report
concepts.statement: The LFAR is the RBI-prescribed questionnaire the bank auditor answers alongside the main report — advances, credit appraisal, NPA identification, internal controls, frauds — branch LFARs feeding the central auditor's consolidated one. It supplements the statutory report and does not dilute it: a matter grave enough to affect the true and fair view belongs in the main report, qualified, not parked in the LFAR.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 141 — Auditor disqualifications
concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(d) with Rule 10 draws money lines around the auditor's independence: a relative may hold securities of the company up to one lakh rupees face value; indebtedness to the company beyond five lakh rupees disqualifies; a guarantee for a third party's debt to the company beyond one lakh rupees disqualifies. The disqualification reaches the member, the firm and its partners, and one incurred during the term vacates the office.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d) read with Rule 10

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xi)
concepts.statement: CARO's fraud clause asks three things: whether any fraud by the company or on the company was noticed or reported during the year, with nature and amount; whether any section 143(12) report was filed in Form ADT-4; and whether the auditor considered whistle-blower complaints received by the company. The clause covers fraud on the company by anyone, not only by its officers and employees.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — Engagement quality control review
concepts.statement: SQC 1 requires an engagement quality control review — an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions reached — for audits of financial statements of listed entities, completed before the report is dated. The reviewer stands outside the engagement team, and the report cannot be signed past an unresolved difference with the reviewer.

citation.ref: Engagement quality control review requirements

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Due diligence, investigation and audit
concepts.statement: An audit expresses an opinion on financial statements against a framework; due diligence is a purchaser-side examination of a target's whole position — financial, legal, operational — to price a deal and surface hidden liabilities; an investigation is a deep, targeted probe into a suspected specific matter, going wherever the suspicion leads. Scope, purpose and the reporting audience differ across all three; assurance levels are not interchangeable.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — propriety
concepts.statement: Propriety audit asks questions regularity audit cannot: not only was the expenditure sanctioned and lawful, but was it wise, economical, and free of personal advantage — would a person of ordinary prudence have spent his own money so? The C&AG's audit of public undertakings runs on both rails, and a transaction can pass every rule yet fail propriety.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Peer review
concepts.statement: Peer review examines a practice unit's systems — whether its quality controls, documentation and compliance with technical standards for attestation services are adequate and were followed — through sample engagements. The reviewer evaluates the unit, not the clients: a review is not a second audit of any auditee, and its report speaks to the unit's systems, leading to a peer review certificate.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 139(6) — First auditor
concepts.statement: A company's first auditor (other than a government company) is appointed by the board within thirty days of registration; if the board fails, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor holds office until the conclusion of the first annual general meeting — and needs no ratification meanwhile.

citation.ref: Section 139(6)

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Forensic accounting and investigation
concepts.statement: Forensic engagements run under ICAI's Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards and differ from audit at the root: the mindset presumes the possibility of fraud rather than neutrality, procedures chase evidence that will stand in legal proceedings — chain of custody, corroboration, documentation to litigation grade — and the outcome states findings of fact, not an opinion or an assurance conclusion. Materiality thresholds do not excuse small frauds from a forensic scope.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — scale-based regulation
concepts.statement: RBI regulates NBFCs in layers by size and risk — base, middle, upper and a normally empty top layer — with regulatory intensity rising through the stack: the upper layer carries bank-like requirements. The auditor's concerns scale accordingly: income recognition and asset classification norms, the layer's specific prudential requirements, and the statutory auditor's own direct reporting duties to RBI on matters such as non-compliance with the RBI Act.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3) — The auditor's report
concepts.statement: Section 143(3) prescribes what every company audit report states: whether information and explanations sought were obtained, whether proper books were kept, whether the accounts agree with the books, whether the statements comply with the accounting standards, the section 164(2) director disqualification status, internal financial controls where applicable, and the rule-prescribed matters. Each is answered — a negative or qualified answer comes with reasons under 143(4).

citation.ref: Section 143(3)

concepts.subsection: Audit in an IT environment
concepts.statement: General IT controls govern the environment — access, change management, operations, backup — while application controls live inside each system, checking individual transactions: input validations, exception reports, interface reconciliations. Weak general controls undermine every application control running on that system, so the auditor tests the foundation before relying on what stands on it; automated controls tested once can be relied on across the period only if change management held.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Services an auditor may not render
concepts.statement: A company's auditor may not render, directly or indirectly, to the company, its holding or its subsidiary: accounting and book keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory and investment banking, outsourced financial services, and management services. "Directly or indirectly" reaches the auditor's relatives, connected persons and entities using the firm's brand or network. Permitted other services need audit committee or board approval.

citation.ref: Section 144

concepts.subsection: Review engagements and agreed-upon procedures
concepts.statement: A review gives limited assurance in negative form — "nothing has come to our attention" — built mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures; an agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance at all, reporting factual findings of the exact procedures the parties specified, for those parties alone to judge. An audit's reasonable assurance sits above both. Naming the engagement wrongly misleads every reader about what stands behind the numbers.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services (SRS 4400), read with Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2400)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part II — Members in service
concepts.statement: A member in employment commits professional misconduct by paying any person a share of the emoluments of his employment, or by accepting any part of the fees, profits or gains of a lawyer, chartered accountant, broker or agent engaged by his employer. The profession's fee-sharing discipline follows the member into service — kickbacks on either side of an employer's engagements are the mischief.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part II

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Tax audit — Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD
concepts.statement: Every tax audit report carries Form 3CD, the statement of particulars; what varies is its cover. Form 3CA is used where the accounts are already audited under any other law — a company under the Companies Act — and it references that statutory audit; Form 3CB is used where no other audit exists, and there the tax auditor himself expresses the true and fair opinion on the accounts. Picking 3CB for a company duplicates an opinion someone else owns.

citation.ref: Section 44AB with Rule 6G

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(ii)
concepts.statement: CARO's second clause covers inventory and borrowings against it: whether physical verification of inventory was conducted at reasonable intervals with material discrepancies dealt with in the books — and, where working capital limits above five crore rupees are sanctioned against current assets, whether the quarterly returns filed with the banks agree with the books of account, with disagreements detailed. Statements to bankers and statements to shareholders must be the same statements.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ii)

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — performance audit
concepts.statement: Performance audit examines the three Es — economy (spending less for the same inputs), efficiency (getting more output per input), and effectiveness (achieving the intended outcome) — of a programme or entity, against criteria agreed or derived, reporting findings and recommendations rather than an opinion. It differs from propriety audit's transaction-level prudence test: performance audit judges the scheme, not the voucher.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Interim reviews — SRE 2410
concepts.statement: The statutory auditor's review of a listed company's quarterly results runs under SRE 2410: inquiry of finance personnel and analytical procedures, sized for limited assurance, concluding in negative form. It is not a small audit — no control testing, no third-party confirmations by default — but the auditor who becomes aware of a possible material misstatement must extend procedures until the doubt resolves; the lighter vehicle carries no licence to drive past red flags.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2410)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Responding to NOCLAR
concepts.statement: On becoming aware of non-compliance or suspected non-compliance with laws and regulations at a client, the member's response runs in sequence: understand the matter, raise it with the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance, urge rectification and disclosure, then judge whether further action — up to withdrawal or disclosure to an authority — is needed in the public interest. Confidentiality does not bar a disclosure the framework calls for; walking away silently is the response the framework rejects.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(iii)
concepts.statement: Where a company has made investments in, given guarantees or security for, or granted loans or advances in the nature of loans to any parties, CARO asks: the amounts involved (with related-party loans separately shown), whether the terms are prejudicial to the company's interests, whether repayment schedules exist and repayments are regular, overdue amounts beyond ninety days and the steps taken, whether loans were renewed or fresh loans settled old ones, and loans repayable on demand or without terms — again with the related-party share disclosed.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)

concepts.subsection: Surcharge on individuals, HUFs, AOPs, BOIs and artificial juridical persons — the tiers, the 15% cap, and marginal relief
concepts.statement: For an individual, HUF, AOP, BOI or artificial juridical person paying tax under the default regime of section 115BAC, the income-tax computed under that section and under sections 111A, 112, 112A, 115BBE and 115BBJ is increased by surcharge at 10% where total income exceeds ₹50 lakh but does not exceed ₹1 crore, 15% where it exceeds ₹1 crore but does not exceed ₹2 crore, and 25% where it exceeds ₹2 crore. The 25% tier applies to the income-tax on the portion of income other than dividend income and capital gains chargeable under sections 111A, 112 and 112A; the surcharge on the income-tax attributable to that dividend and capital gains portion is capped at 15%. Outside the default regime a fourth tier survives: 37% where total income, excluding that dividend and capital gains portion, exceeds ₹5 crore, again with the 15% cap on the portion. Marginal relief accompanies every threshold: the increase in tax and surcharge caused by the income exceeding ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore or ₹2 crore cannot exceed the amount by which the income exceeds that threshold, worked as the lower of the tax-plus-surcharge on total income and the tax on the threshold plus the excess income. Health and education cess at 4% is added after the surcharge and after marginal relief.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule with section 115BAC
citation.ref: Surcharge at 10%, 15% and 25% on the default regime; 37% above ₹5 crore outside it; the 15% cap on dividend and section 111A, 112 and 112A gains; marginal relief at each threshold

concepts.subsection: Domestic company — 25% or 30% by the ₹400 crore test, the concessional regimes, surcharge stepped at 7% and 12% but flat at 10% under sections 115BAA and 115BAB, marginal relief
concepts.statement: A domestic company is taxed at 25% of total income where its total turnover or gross receipts in the previous year 2023-24 did not exceed ₹400 crore, and at 30% in any other case, with the special rates of sections 111A, 112 and 112A applying to its capital gains. A domestic company that has exercised the option under section 115BAA is taxed at 22% of total income, computed without the deductions the section lists and without set-off of losses attributable to them. A domestic company in manufacturing that was newly formed and registered from 1 October 2019 onwards, began to manufacture before 31 March 2024, and opted for section 115BAB pays 15% on income derived from or incidental to manufacturing. Surcharge then runs on two different plans, and which plan applies depends only on whether the option was exercised. For a company outside those two sections, surcharge is 7% of the income-tax once total income passes ₹1 crore and stays at or under ₹10 crore, and 12% above ₹10 crore, each with marginal relief: the tax with surcharge cannot exceed the tax on ₹1 crore (or the tax with surcharge on ₹10 crore) plus the income in excess of that threshold. The module's own worked case: on a total income of ₹1,01,00,000 at 30% plus 7% surcharge the tax would be ₹32,42,100, but is limited to ₹30,00,000 plus ₹1,00,000 = ₹31,00,000, a marginal relief of ₹1,42,100, before cess at 4%. A company that has opted into section 115BAA or section 115BAB is on the other plan: whatever its total income, the surcharge is a single flat 10% of the income-tax that the chosen section produces. It does not begin at ₹1 crore, it does not step up at ₹10 crore, and a company with a total income well under ₹1 crore still bears it. Because no threshold gates that 10%, there is no boundary for income to sit just above, and so marginal relief never arises at all for such a company — the relief only ever exists to soften a step, and here the surcharge has no step in it. Carrying the flat 10% and then cess at 4% through the arithmetic gives an all-in burden of 25.168% where section 115BAA has been chosen and 17.16% where section 115BAB has.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule with sections 115BAA and 115BAB
citation.ref: 25% or 30% by the ₹400 crore turnover test for the previous year 2023-24; 22% and 15% concessional rates; surcharge at 7% and 12% with marginal relief at ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore; the flat 10% surcharge on a company that has opted into section 115BAA or section 115BAB, which has no threshold and therefore no marginal relief, and the resulting 25.168% and 17.16% effective rates

concepts.subsection: Section 91 — unilateral relief where India has no agreement, at the lower of the two rates
concepts.statement: Where income arises to an assessee in a country with which India has no double taxation agreement, section 91 grants relief if six conditions are all met: the assessee is resident in India in the previous year in which the income is taxable; the income accrues or arises outside India; it is not deemed to accrue or arise in India; the foreign country has charged income-tax on it in the assessee's own hands; the assessee has paid tax on it there; and there is no agreement for relief between India and that country. The relief is a deduction from the Indian income-tax otherwise payable, worked out on the doubly taxed income at whichever is lower — India's own rate or the foreign country's rate — and at India's rate when the two come out equal. The Indian rate of tax is the Indian income-tax, after any relief due under the Act but before double taxation relief, divided by total income; the rate of tax of the foreign country is the income-tax and super-tax actually paid there after all relief due but before double taxation relief, divided by the whole income assessed there. Income-tax in relation to a foreign country includes any excess profits tax or business profits tax charged by its government, any part of it, or a local authority.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) with its Explanation — the six conditions, the deduction at the lower of the Indian rate and the foreign rate on doubly taxed income, and the definitions of both rates

concepts.subsection: Section 90(1) — the four purposes of an agreement; section 90(2A) — GAAR applies even where not beneficial
concepts.statement: Section 90(1) empowers the Central Government to enter into an agreement with the government of any country or specified territory for four purposes: granting relief in respect of income on which tax has been paid both in India and there, or of income-tax chargeable under both laws to promote mutual economic relations, trade and investment; avoiding double taxation under the two laws without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through evasion or avoidance, including treaty-shopping arrangements aimed at the indirect benefit of residents of a third country; exchanging information for the prevention of evasion or avoidance of income-tax under either law or the investigation of such cases; and recovering income-tax under both laws. Section 90A gives the same power to a specified association for a specified territory. Where such an agreement applies, the Act's own provisions govern only so far as they leave the assessee better off, which is section 90(2), but section 90(2A) makes Chapter X-A, the general anti-avoidance rule, apply to the assessee even where its provisions are not beneficial to him.

citation.ref: Section 90(1)(a) to (d) — relief, avoidance without non-taxation, exchange of information, recovery; section 90(2A) — the general anti-avoidance rule applies regardless of benefit

concepts.subsection: Section 245RR — once a resident applies for a ruling, no income-tax authority or Tribunal decides the issue
concepts.statement: Under section 245RR, once a resident applicant has put an issue before the Board for Advance Rulings for decision, neither an income-tax authority nor the Appellate Tribunal may decide that issue itself. The effect is that a resident assessee cannot pursue both remedies at once — an appeal or revision before an income-tax authority or appellate authority, and an application for an advance ruling — in respect of the same issue; the application to the Board freezes the issue everywhere else. This sits beside section 245R(2), under which the Board shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before an income-tax authority, the Tribunal or a court, except for a notified resident applicant: the two provisions together stop the same question from being argued on two roads. Section 245P adds that a proceeding before, or a ruling by, the Board is not invalid merely because of a vacancy or defect in its constitution.

citation.ref: Section 245RR — restriction on appellate authority once a resident's application is made; section 245R(2) — no ruling on a question already pending; section 245P — vacancies do not invalidate proceedings

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties — Articles 26 to 31, and India's position as a non-party
concepts.statement: Tax treaties are interpreted on the principles of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, in force from 1980, which codifies customary international law. India is not a party to it, but the Supreme Court in Ram Jethmalani v. Union of India held that its principles of interpretation, in particular Article 31, give a broad guideline for interpreting a treaty in the Indian context, and the Delhi High Court in AWAS Ireland read Articles 26, 27 and 31 with Article 51(c) of the Constitution as obliging a state to honour a treaty and not to cite internal law as a justification for failing to perform it. Article 26 is pacta sunt servanda — a treaty in force binds the parties to it, and they must carry it out in good faith. Article 27: a party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty — so a contracting state should not dishonour its commitment by retrospectively amending its domestic tax law. Article 28, non-retroactivity: unless a different intention appears, treaty provisions do not bind a party as to any act, fact or situation before the treaty entered into force for it. Article 29: a treaty binds each party in respect of its entire territory unless otherwise intended. Article 31 lays down the general rule — read a treaty in good faith, giving its terms the ordinary sense they carry in the setting they sit in, and reading them against what the treaty was made to do — ordinary meaning first, purpose only where that meaning is ambiguous or leads to illogical results — with the context comprising the text, preamble and annexes and any agreement made between all the parties in connection with its conclusion.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969
citation.ref: Articles 26 (pacta sunt servanda), 27 (internal law no justification), 28 (non-retroactivity), 29 (territorial scope) and 31 (general rule of interpretation); Ram Jethmalani v. Union of India; AWAS Ireland v. DGCA

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Article 32 and the extrinsic aids — protocols, subsequent agreement and conduct, parallel treaties, commentaries
concepts.statement: Article 32 of the Vienna Convention admits supplementary means of interpretation, including the treaty's preparatory work and the circumstances in which it was concluded. The module, following Starke, lists the extrinsic aids to which one may resort provided clear words are not thereby contradicted: interpretative protocols, resolutions and committee reports that record an agreed reading; any later agreement the parties reach on how the treaty is to be read or applied, which Article 31(3) brings into the context; the subsequent conduct of the state parties as evidence of their intention and their conception of the treaty; and other treaties in pari materia, relating to the same subject matter, in case of doubt. A parallel treaty of the same country whose language is the same but clearer may be referred to for the intention of the parties, though its interpretation is not binding, and the Indian courts are not consistent on the point. Commentaries — Kanga and Palkhivala and Sampath Iyengar in domestic cases, Philip Baker and Klaus Vogel on treaties — and international articles and reports are treated as extrinsic aids, as in CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust. A protocol is a supplement to the treaty that puts certain matters beyond doubt and forms part of it, so it is read with the treaty and not as an afterthought.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 with ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
citation.ref: Article 32 — supplementary means; Article 31(3) — subsequent agreement; Starke's four extrinsic aids; protocols, parallel treaties and commentaries; CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Sections 10(2) and 10(2A) — a member's receipt from the HUF, a partner's share of the firm, and Circular 8/2014
concepts.statement: A Hindu undivided family is a person and pays tax on its own income, so section 10(2) keeps the same income from being taxed twice: any sum a member receives from the family is exempt in his hands, but only where it is paid out of the income of the family or out of the income of an impartible estate belonging to the family. Section 10(2A) does the same for a partner: where a firm is assessed separately, a partner leaves his share of that firm's total income out of his own computation. The CBDT settled in Circular No. 8/2014 what the share is where the firm's own taxable income is nil because of an exemption under Chapter III or a deduction under Chapter VI-A — tax on a firm's profit falls on the firm alone, and no partner may be assessed on the same profit a second time, so the entire profit credited to the partners' accounts is exempt even though the firm paid nothing. The exemption also switches off clubbing: where a spouse's capital in a firm came from the other spouse's gift, section 64(1)(iv) clubs the proportionate interest on capital, but the share of profit is exempt under section 10(2A) and section 64 does not apply to income from a transferred asset which is itself exempt.

citation.ref: Sections 10(2) and 10(2A); CBDT Circular No. 8/2014 dated 31 March 2014

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 10(23C) — the 50% government-financing test, the ₹5 crore receipts ceiling, and the approved sub-clauses
concepts.statement: Section 10(23C) exempts income received on behalf of named funds — the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund and PM CARES, the Swachh Bharat Kosh, the Clean Ganga Fund, a Chief Minister's or Lieutenant Governor's Relief Fund — and of three tiers of universities, educational institutions and hospitals that exist solely for their purpose and not for profit.
