Sub-section (4) is the hardest of them — no deduction of any expenditure or allowance at all against winnings, whether they come from lotteries, crossword puzzles or races, from card games and games of every other sort, or from gambling and betting, so the cost of winning is simply not recognised.

citation.ref: Sections 57(i) to (iv), Section 58(1)(a), Section 58(2) and Section 58(4), read with the Explanation to Section 2(24)(ix)

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Sections 70, 71 and 74 — Setting off and carrying a capital loss
concepts.statement: A capital loss travels along one road and it is a narrow one. Section 70(2) lets a short-term capital loss be set off against income under the head capital gains in respect of any capital asset, so it may go against a long-term gain as freely as against a short-term one. Section 70(3) is the restriction, and it runs the other way — a long-term capital loss may be set off only against a long-term capital gain. Section 71(3) then closes the head off entirely: a loss under capital gains cannot be set against income under any other head, whatever is left of it, which is why a capital loss can never reduce salary, house property or business income. Whatever survives is carried forward under section 74 for eight assessment years immediately succeeding, and the same asymmetry follows it — a carried short-term loss may be set against any capital gain, a carried long-term loss only against a long-term gain. Section 80 puts one condition on the carry forward, that the loss be determined in a return furnished within the time allowed under section 139(1), and section 74 requires the same business or asset in no sense at all, which is where it differs from section 72.

citation.ref: Sections 70(2), 70(3), 71(3) and 74(1) and 74(2), read with Section 80 and Section 139(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(1) — Intimation and the adjustments it may make
concepts.statement: Processing under section 143(1) is not a scrutiny and it is not a rubber stamp either. The return is taken, the total income or loss is computed after a closed list of adjustments in section 143(1)(a), tax, interest and fee are worked out, and an intimation follows which is deemed to be a notice of demand under section 156 where any sum is payable. The list is what must be known. Clause (i) an arithmetical error in the return; clause (ii) an incorrect claim apparent from any information in the return itself; clause (iii) disallowance of a loss claimed where the return of the year in which the loss arose was furnished beyond the due date under section 139(1); clause (iv) an expense struck out, or income added, where the audit report says so and the return has ignored it; and clause (v) disallowance of a deduction claimed under section 10AA or under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A where the return is furnished beyond the due date. Nothing outside that list may be done, so no question of fact and no view about whether an expense was excessive belongs here. The first proviso bars any adjustment unless an intimation of it is given to the assessee in writing or electronically, and the second requires the response to be considered, the adjustment being made if none comes within thirty days. The intimation itself cannot go out later than nine months after the close of the financial year the return was filed in.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(a) clauses (i) to (v) with its first and second provisos, read with Section 156

concepts.subsection: Section 142 — Inquiry before assessment and the special audit
concepts.statement: Section 142(1) gives the Assessing Officer three powers before he assesses. Clause (i) is a notice requiring a person who has not made a return within the time allowed under section 139(1) to furnish one — no escapement need be alleged and section 148 is not involved. Clause (ii) is a notice to produce such accounts or documents as he may require. Clause (iii) is a notice to furnish information in writing, including a statement of assets and liabilities. Two provisos fence them. A statement of assets and liabilities not included in the accounts may be required only with the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner, and no accounts may be required relating to a period more than three years prior to the previous year. Section 142(2A) is the heavier power. Having regard to the nature and complexity of the accounts, the volume of the accounts, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions or the specialised nature of the business, and the interests of the revenue, the Assessing Officer may direct the assessee to get the accounts audited by an accountant whom the Principal Chief Commissioner, the Chief Commissioner, the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner names. It needs that authority's previous approval, and the proviso requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard for the assessee — his consent is nowhere in the section. Since 1 June 2007 the expenses of the audit are determined by that authority and paid by the Central Government under section 142(2D).

citation.ref: Section 142(1) clauses (i) to (iii) with provisos (a) and (b), and Sections 142(2A), 142(2C) and 142(2D)

concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Best judgement assessment
concepts.statement: Section 144(1) is triggered by any one of four failures — failure to make the return required under section 139(1) and no return under section 139(4) or 139(5) either, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 142(1), failure to comply with a direction for a special audit under section 142(2A), or, having made a return, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 143(2). On any of them the Assessing Officer shall, after taking into account all relevant material he has gathered, make the assessment to the best of his judgement. Best judgement means an honest estimate resting on some material, not a guess and not a punishment, and the assessment is appealable like any other. Two provisos govern the hearing. The first says no such assessment shall be made without giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard by serving a notice calling on him to show cause why the assessment should not be completed to the best of the officer's judgement. The second removes that requirement altogether where a notice under section 142(1) has already been issued before the assessment is made, on the footing that the assessee has already been asked and has already not answered. No approval of any superior officer is required — that belongs to section 153D, which governs a search assessment.

citation.ref: Section 144(1) with its first and second provisos, read with Sections 142(1), 143(2) and 153D

concepts.subsection: Sections 148 and 148A — The stage that comes before a reassessment notice
concepts.statement: Reassessment stopped being a matter of the officer's private reasons in 2021. Section 148 now permits a notice only where there is information which suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment, only after the procedure in section 148A has been followed, and only with the prior approval of the specified authority under section 151. Section 148A is the pre-notice stage. The Assessing Officer serves a show cause notice on the assessee setting out the information relied on and giving a period specified in the notice to explain why a notice under section 148 should not be issued; the assessee replies; and the Assessing Officer then passes an order under section 148A(3), on the material on record and that reply, deciding whether it is a fit case. This replaced the practice built on GKN Driveshafts, under which the assessee filed a return, asked for the reasons recorded and objected afterwards — the objection is now heard before the notice rather than after it. Cases where a search is initiated or books are requisitioned are outside section 148A and go down the block assessment route in section 158BA instead.

citation.ref: Section 148 with its provisos and Section 148A as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Sections 151 and 158BA

concepts.subsection: Section 154 — Rectification of a mistake apparent from the record
concepts.statement: Section 154 lets an income-tax authority amend any order it has passed, any intimation under section 143(1) and any intimation under section 200A(1) or 206CB(1), to rectify a mistake apparent from the record. Four things fix its shape. The mistake must be apparent — an error of fact or of law that stares from the record and needs no long argument; a point on which two views are reasonably possible is outside the section, which is what T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers decided. The power runs both ways, and section 154(2)(b) expressly allows an amendment on an application made by the assessee, so it is not confined to the authority's own motion. Section 154(3) requires notice and a hearing before any amendment that has the effect of enhancing an assessment or reducing a refund. And section 154(7) sets the outer limit — no amendment once four years have run from the close of the financial year in which the order under correction was passed, a period measured from the order and not from the assessment year. Where the assessee applies, section 154(8) gives the authority six months to pass its order, counted from the close of the month the application reached it.

citation.ref: Sections 154(1), 154(2)(b), 154(3), 154(7) and 154(8), read with T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers (1971) 82 ITR 50 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Section 264 — Revision at the assessee's instance
concepts.statement: Section 264 is the assessee's revision and section 263 is the revenue's, and almost every difference between them follows from that. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may act either on his own motion or on an application by the assessee, may call for the record of any proceeding under the Act, and may pass such order thereon, not being an order prejudicial to the assessee, as he thinks fit — so the worst outcome of a section 264 application is that it is refused. There is no requirement that the order be erroneous or that it be prejudicial to the revenue; those words belong to section 263. The power is wide enough to grant relief on a claim that was never made in the return, the restriction in Goetze (India) being a restriction on the Assessing Officer and not on the revisional authority. Section 264(3) gives the assessee one year from the date on which the order was communicated to him or he otherwise came to know of it, with power to condone delay, and section 264(5) requires a fee of five hundred rupees. Section 264(4) is the bar — no revision while the time for an appeal has not expired and the right of appeal has not been waived, and none where the order has been made the subject of an appeal; once the appeal time has run out unused, the bar lifts. Section 264(6) requires the order within a year of the close of the financial year the application was made in.

citation.ref: Sections 264(1) to 264(6), read with Section 263(1) and Goetze (India) Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Sections 260A and 261 — Appeal to the High Court and to the Supreme Court
concepts.statement: The Appellate Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority, and everything above it is about law only. Section 260A(1) lets an appeal go up to the High Court against any order the Tribunal has passed in an appeal, and only where the High Court is satisfied a substantial question of law arises in it. Section 260A(2)(a) allows one hundred and twenty days from the date the order is received, section 260A(3) requires the High Court itself to formulate the question where it is satisfied one exists, and section 260A(4) confines the hearing to that question, with a proviso letting the court hear the appeal on any other substantial question of law for reasons recorded. Section 260B requires a bench of not less than two judges. A disagreement about how the Tribunal weighed the evidence is not a substantial question of law, and a finding of fact stands unless it is perverse in the sense of resting on no evidence or on irrelevant material. Section 261 then allows an appeal to the Supreme Court from a judgment of the High Court delivered on an appeal under section 260A, and only where the High Court certifies the case to be a fit one — it is not a route that bypasses the High Court. Beside all this sits section 254(2), which lets the Tribunal rectify a mistake apparent from the record and is not a rehearing.

citation.ref: Sections 260A(1) to 260A(4), Section 260B and Section 261, read with Section 254(2)

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 199 and Rule 37BA — Who gets credit for tax deducted, and in which year
concepts.statement: Deducting tax and getting credit for it are two different questions, and section 199 answers the second. Sub-section (1) treats the tax deducted and paid as a payment of tax on behalf of the person from whose income the deduction was made. Sub-section (3) leaves the details to rules, and Rule 37BA does the real work in two sub-rules. Rule 37BA(2) deals with the wrong person — where the whole or a part of the income on which tax has been deducted is assessable in the hands of somebody other than the deductee, credit goes to that other person, provided the deductee files a declaration with the deductor naming him and the deductor reports it in the statement. That is how a clubbed income, a joint holding or an income assessed in a successor's hands is dealt with. Rule 37BA(3) deals with the wrong year — credit is given for the assessment year for which the income is assessable, and where the income is assessable over more than one year, the credit is split over those years in the ratio the income itself is spread in. Credit therefore follows the income, never the deduction, which is why an advance taxed over two years splits its credit over the same two years.

citation.ref: Sections 199(1) and 199(3), read with Rule 37BA(2) and Rule 37BA(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 206AA — Deduction at a higher rate where the PAN is not furnished
concepts.statement: Section 206AA begins with a non obstante clause and lays the duty on the deductor, not on the payee. Where the deductee fails to furnish his permanent account number to the person responsible for deducting, tax shall be deducted at the highest of three figures — the rate specified in the relevant provision of the Act, the rate or rates in force, and twenty per cent. Sub-section (6) treats a permanent account number that is invalid or does not belong to the deductee as one that was never furnished, so a wrong number is no better than none. Sub-section (2) makes a declaration under section 197A invalid unless it carries the number, and sub-section (4) forbids the grant of a certificate under section 197 unless the application carries it, which closes both escape routes at once. The consequence of getting this wrong falls on the payer — a short deduction leaves him an assessee in default under section 201(1), with interest under section 201(1A) and disallowance under section 40(a)(ia). Sub-section (7) is the only relief, taking certain payments to a non-resident or a foreign company out of the section where the conditions in Rule 37BC are met.

citation.ref: Sections 206AA(1), 206AA(2), 206AA(4), 206AA(6) and 206AA(7), read with Rule 37BC and Sections 201(1) and 201(1A)

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Article 5 of a treaty — Permanent establishment and its three routes
concepts.statement: A treaty lets India tax a foreign enterprise's business profits only through a permanent establishment, so Article 5 decides whether Article 7 ever opens. The general definition in Article 5(1) turns on a fixed place of business that the enterprise runs its own business through, in whole or in part, and Article 5(2) gives the familiar illustrative list — a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, a mine or a quarry. Article 5(3) is the construction clause, which makes a building site, construction, assembly or installation project a permanent establishment once it lasts longer than the period the particular treaty names, and that period differs from treaty to treaty. Article 5(4) is the exclusion, taking out a place maintained solely for storage, display or delivery of goods, solely for processing by another enterprise, solely for purchasing goods or collecting information, or solely for any other activity of a preparatory or auxiliary character. Article 5(5) is the agency route, which needs no premises at all — a person acting on behalf of the enterprise who habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to their conclusion, is a permanent establishment. Article 5(6) takes back out an agent of independent status acting in the ordinary course of his own business, such as a broker or a general commission agent.

citation.ref: Article 5(1) to 5(6) of India's double taxation avoidance agreements on the OECD and UN Model pattern, read with Article 7 and Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Rule 10CA — The arm's length range and the use of multiple year data
concepts.statement: Comparables almost never give one number, and Rule 10CA is the machinery that turns a spread of them into an answer. It applies only where the most appropriate method is the comparable uncontrolled price method, the resale price method, the cost plus method or the transactional net margin method, and only where the dataset holds six or more entries. Where both are true, the arm's length range is the set of data points lying from the thirty-fifth percentile to the sixty-fifth percentile of the dataset arranged in ascending order, and Rule 10CA(4) is what builds it. Rule 10CA(5) then gives the test — if the price at which the international transaction has actually been undertaken is within that range, it shall be deemed to be the arm's length price and no adjustment is made. Rule 10CA(6) gives the consequence of failing it, and it is not the nearest edge of the range — where the transaction price is outside the range, the arm's length price is the median of the dataset. Rule 10CA(8) fixes how a percentile is read: multiply the number of data points by the percentile, and where the product is not a whole number take the data point at the next higher whole number, while where it is a whole number take the average of that data point and the one after it. Rule 10CA(2) and 10CA(3) allow the weighted average of up to three years of the comparable's data where the enterprise's own data for the current year is not available at the time the return is furnished. Where the dataset holds fewer than six entries the range has no application at all, and the arithmetic mean under section 92C(2) with the tolerance band in its second proviso is what governs instead.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(2) to Rule 10CA(8) read with Section 92C(1) and Section 92C(2) with its second proviso

concepts.subsection: Section 92CE — The secondary adjustment and the money that stayed abroad
concepts.statement: A primary adjustment fixes the profit figure on paper; the money is still sitting with the associated enterprise abroad. Section 92CE exists to reach that money. Sub-section (1) names five triggers, and only the first is voluntary — an adjustment made suo motu by the assessee in his return, an adjustment made by the Assessing Officer and accepted by the assessee, an adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement under section 92CC, an adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules under section 92CB, and an adjustment arising from a resolution under a mutual agreement procedure under a treaty. Sub-section (2) is the machinery. Where the primary adjustment lifts total income or trims the loss, any excess money left sitting with the associated enterprise that does not come home inside the window Rule 10CB fixes — ninety days, counted from the date the return was due where the assessee made the adjustment himself and from the date of the order in the other cases — is deemed to be an advance the assessee has made to that enterprise, and interest on that deemed advance is computed in the manner prescribed and charged year after year until the money comes home. That interest rate is not one rate but two, and which one applies turns on the currency the international transaction was denominated in: a rupee transaction carries the State Bank of India's one-year marginal cost of funds lending rate as it stood on 1 April of the relevant previous year, plus 3.25 per cent, while a transaction in foreign currency carries the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate as it stood on 30 September of that year, plus 3 per cent. Two escapes sit in the proviso to sub-section (3), and they are joined by "or", so either one alone is enough on its own: the whole secondary adjustment falls away where the primary adjustment for that previous year is not above ₹1 crore, and it falls away equally where the primary adjustment relates to assessment year 2016-17 or an earlier year. Reading them as cumulative — demanding both a small adjustment and an old year — is the mistake to guard against. India's design is a deemed advance bearing imputed interest, not the deemed dividend some other countries use, and it never taxes the primary adjustment a second time. Sub-section (2A) offers the way out — instead of repatriating, the assessee may pay a one-time additional tax on the excess money at 20.9664 per cent, which is tax at 18 per cent lifted by a surcharge of 12 per cent and a cess of 4 per cent, and is paid on the excess money itself rather than on any income figure; the tax is final, so after it no further interest is imputed, no credit for that tax is available to him or to anybody else, and no deduction of it is allowed.

citation.ref: Sections 92CE(1), 92CE(2), 92CE(2A), 92CE(2B) and the proviso to Section 92CE(3), read with Rule 10CB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Sections 92CB and 92CC

concepts.subsection: Section 92CB — Safe harbour, and how it differs from an advance pricing agreement
concepts.statement: Section 92CB(1) makes the whole exercise of fixing an arm's length price answerable to the safe harbour rules, whether that price is being worked out under section 92C or by the officer acting under section 92CA, and its Explanation says what a safe harbour is: the situations where the department will take the price the assessee has himself put forward, and go no further. Two words in that Explanation carry the section — accept, and declared. It is not a margin the officer imposes and it is not a cap on an adjustment he is otherwise making; where the option is validly exercised the declared price is simply taken, and no determination of the arm's length price is made for that transaction at all. The rules are in Rule 10TA to Rule 10TG. The assessee exercises the option in Form 3CEFA for the eligible international transactions and the eligible assessees the rules describe, and the Assessing Officer or Transfer Pricing Officer may hold the option invalid, with an appeal against that to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner whose decision is final. Safe harbour and an advance pricing agreement are not two sizes of the same thing. An agreement under section 92CC is negotiated between the Board and one taxpayer for a stated set of transactions, binds both sides for the years specified and may be rolled back under section 92CD; safe harbour is a set of margins already notified in the Rules, open to anybody who fits the description and negotiated with nobody. A price fixed under the safe harbour rules is still a primary adjustment for the purposes of section 92CE(1)(d).

citation.ref: Section 92CB(1) with its Explanation, read with Rules 10TA to 10TG of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and Sections 92CC, 92CD and 92CE(1)(d)

concepts.subsection: Section 9A — Fund management from India without a business connection
concepts.statement: Before section 9A, a global fund that let its manager sit in India risked two things at once — the manager's activity being read as a business connection under section 9(1)(i), and the fund itself being called resident in India. Section 9A removes both, and removes nothing else. Sub-section (1) says that notwithstanding section 9(1)(i), where an eligible fund manager runs the fund management work for an eligible investment fund, that work by itself hands the fund no business connection in India. Sub-section (2) says the fund does not turn resident here just because the manager doing that work for it happens to sit in India. Neither sub-section is an exemption. Income of the fund that has an independent Indian source is charged as it always was, and section 9A(3) and 9A(4) hedge the relief with conditions on both sides. The fund must be a non-resident, resident of a country with which India has an agreement or a notified country, must not carry on or control a business in India, must be broad based in the way the sub-section describes, and must satisfy the corpus, membership and participation tests. The manager must not be an employee of the fund or a connected person, must be registered as a fund manager or portfolio manager or investment adviser under the relevant regulations, and must be paid at arm's length for the fund management activity. That last condition is the point most often missed — the manager's own remuneration is Indian income and is taxed here in full.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2), 9A(3) and 9A(4), read with Section 9(1)(i) and Section 6(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 115JH — The year a foreign company first becomes resident in India
concepts.statement: A foreign company can become resident in India under section 6(3) because its place of effective management is here, and the moment it does, the whole Act begins to apply to a company that has never kept its records for the Act. It has no written down value computed under section 32, no brought forward loss determined under this Act, no unabsorbed depreciation carried under section 32(2), and no history of collection and recovery here. Section 115JH is the transition provision written for exactly that year. Take a foreign company that counts as resident here in a previous year when no earlier previous year had made it resident: then, whatever else the Act may say to the contrary, the rules on working out total income, on what becomes of unabsorbed depreciation, on setting off losses and carrying them forward, on collection and recovery, and on the anti-avoidance chapter all reach it — but only with whatever exceptions, modifications and adaptations the Central Government has notified. Sub-section (2) requires that notification to be laid before each House of Parliament. Sub-section (3) is the sanction — where in any previous year any of the conditions specified in the notification is not complied with, the benefit of the exceptions, modifications and adaptations is denied, and the Act applies to that company without them as if the notification had never been made. The section eases the mechanics of a transition; it exempts nothing and it charges nothing.

citation.ref: Sections 115JH(1), 115JH(2) and 115JH(3), read with Section 6(3) and Section 32(2)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Sections 44BBA and 44BBB — Aircraft operations and turnkey power projects
concepts.statement: Both sections deem a percentage of a stated aggregate to be the profits of a non-resident, and the work in an exam is always in the aggregate rather than the percentage. Section 44BBA covers a non-resident whose business is running aircraft, and its aggregate has two limbs that are deliberately not symmetrical. Limb one gathers everything handed over to him, or still owed to him, for carrying passengers, livestock, mail or cargo out of a place in India, and it counts whether he or somebody collecting for him takes the money, and whether the money moves inside the country or outside it — where payment happened does not matter, because the journey started here. Limb two gathers only what reaches him in India, actually or by deeming, through him or through an agent, for carrying those same four things from a place abroad — the journey did not start here, so receipt in India is the one connecting factor left. A sum for an inbound carriage that is also collected abroad answers neither limb and stays out of the aggregate altogether. Section 44BB for mineral oil services and section 44B for shipping are built on the same two-limb pattern with their own connecting factors. Section 44BBB is different in shape — its subject is an overseas company doing civil construction, or erecting, testing or commissioning plant or machinery, for a turnkey power project that the Central Government has approved and that an international aid programme pays for, and it takes a percentage of the amount paid or payable to it for that work.

citation.ref: Sections 44BBA(1) and 44BBA(2)(a) and (b), and Section 44BBB(1), read with Sections 44B and 44BB(2)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 44BB — Services and plant for prospecting for or extraction of mineral oils
concepts.statement: Section 44BB(1) picks up the non-resident whose business is to render services, to put facilities at somebody's disposal, or to hire out plant and machinery, all of it for the work of searching out mineral oils or getting them up from the ground, and it deems a percentage of the sub-section (2) aggregate to be his business income. Sub-section (2) has the same two-limb shape as sections 44B and 44BBA and the same asymmetry. Clause (a) gathers everything handed over to him, or still owed to him, whether the money moves inside the country or outside it, and whether he or somebody collecting for him takes it, for services, facilities or hired equipment put to that mineral oil work inside India. Clause (b) gathers only what reaches him in India, actually or by deeming, through him or through an agent, for services, facilities or hired equipment put to that same mineral oil work abroad. Work done outside India paid for outside India therefore falls in neither clause. Sub-section (3) is the escape from the presumption — the assessee may claim lower profits, but only if he keeps and maintains the books and other documents required by section 44AA, gets his accounts audited and furnishes the report under section 44AB, in which case the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment under section 143(3). The proviso to sub-section (1) shuts the section out altogether where the profits are computed under section 42, section 44DA, section 115A or section 293A.

citation.ref: Section 44BB(1) with its proviso, Section 44BB(2)(a) and (b), and Section 44BB(3), read with Sections 44AA, 44AB and 143(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(1)(vi) — Royalty as Explanation 2 defines it
concepts.statement: Royalty is not defined by what it feels like; it is defined by a list. Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) gathers the money paid for six things. One: parting with rights over a patent, an invention, a model, a design, a secret formula, a process, a trade mark or property of that kind, and granting a licence over such property counts as parting with rights. Two: telling somebody how such property works, or how it is to be put to use. Three: the use of such property itself. Four: handing over know-how, which is to say knowledge, experience or skill of a technical, industrial, commercial or scientific sort. Five: letting somebody use equipment of an industrial, commercial or scientific kind, out of which whatever section 44BB already takes is carved. Six: parting with rights over a copyright, or over literary, artistic or scientific work, and film and video tape made for television, and tape made for radio, sit inside this sixth limb. That last clause carries the one exclusion worth memorising — it does not include consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films. Three later Explanations shut escape routes. Explanation 4 says the transfer of all or any rights includes and has always included the transfer of a right for the use of or the right to use computer software, including the granting of a licence, irrespective of the medium. Explanation 5 says it does not matter whether the payer has possession or control of the right, property or information, whether he uses it directly, or where it is located. Explanation 6 says process includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fibre or any similar technology, whether or not it is secret. What none of them can do is change a treaty: section 90(2) lets the assessee take the treaty definition where it is more beneficial, which is the ground on which Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence held that payment for a copyrighted article rather than the copyright is not royalty.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 clauses (i) to (v), Explanation 4, Explanation 5 and Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(vi), read with Section 90(2) and Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence P Ltd v. CIT (2021) 432 ITR 471 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Sections 115AC and 115ACA — Bonds and global depository receipts
concepts.statement: The two sections look alike and are written for opposite people. Section 115AC applies to a non-resident, and covers three kinds of income — interest on bonds of an Indian company issued in accordance with a scheme notified by the Central Government, or on the bonds that the Government has itself sold of a public sector company, dividends on global depository receipts of an Indian company or of a public sector company issued under such a scheme and purchased in foreign currency, and long-term capital gains on the transfer of those bonds or receipts. Section 115ACA applies to a resident, and not to every resident — the assessee must be an individual who is resident in India and who is or was an employee of an Indian company engaged in a specified knowledge based industry or service, or of its subsidiary engaged in such an industry, and the receipts must have been issued under an employees' stock option scheme and purchased in foreign currency. Below that difference the machinery is the same. No deduction under any of sections 28 to 44C or under clause (i) or clause (iii) of section 57 is allowed in computing the income, no deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowed from it, and the first and second provisos to section 48 — the foreign currency conversion rule and indexation — do not apply in computing the long-term capital gain. Section 115AC(4) then relieves a non-resident of filing a return under section 139(1) where his total income consisted only of income of the kinds that section covers and tax has been deducted from it.

citation.ref: Sections 115AC(1) to 115AC(4) and Sections 115ACA(1) to 115ACA(3) with its Explanation, read with the first and second provisos to Section 48

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Sections 196A to 196D — The collection sections written for particular non-residents
concepts.statement: Section 195 is the general provision for a payment to a non-resident, and sections 196A to 196D are four special ones that take particular payments out of it. Section 196A covers what a non-resident who is not a company, or a foreign company, is paid on the units of a Mutual Fund that section 10(23D) specifies, and on the units of the Specified Undertaking of the Unit Trust of India, with deduction at the time of credit or of payment, whichever is earlier, and a proviso allowing the treaty rate where a tax residency certificate is furnished. Section 196B covers income from units referred to in section 115AB and the long-term capital gain on their transfer paid to an offshore fund. Section 196C covers income by way of interest or dividends on bonds or global depository receipts referred to in section 115AC and the long-term capital gain on their transfer, paid to a non-resident. Section 196D covers income in respect of securities referred to in section 115AD(1)(a) paid to a Foreign Institutional Investor, again with a proviso for the treaty rate on a tax residency certificate. The distinction that decides questions is inside section 196D itself. Sub-section (1) requires deduction from the income in respect of the securities, and sub-section (2) says in terms that no deduction shall be made from any income by way of capital gains arising from the transfer of those securities. The investor is not outside the chapter; one stream is deducted from and the other is not, and the gain is charged in the assessment instead.

citation.ref: Sections 196A, 196B, 196C, 196D(1) and 196D(2), read with Sections 115AB, 115AC, 115AD(1)(a) and 195

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: The Multilateral Instrument and the principal purpose test
concepts.statement: The Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting does not sit beside India's treaties; it modifies them. Where both parties have listed a treaty as a covered tax agreement and their positions match, the Convention's terms are read into that treaty and applied as part of it. Two of its articles do most of the work. Article 6 rewrites the preamble, so that the two states are stated to want double taxation gone without at the same time opening doors to income being taxed nowhere at all or taxed too lightly — whether by evasion, by avoidance, or by shopping around for a treaty. Article 7(1) is the principal purpose test, and its words are the exam — notwithstanding any provisions of a covered tax agreement, a benefit under that agreement shall not be granted in respect of an item of income or capital if it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining that benefit was one of the principal purposes of any arrangement or transaction that resulted directly or indirectly in that benefit, unless it is established that granting it in these circumstances would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions of that agreement. One of the principal purposes is a far lower bar than the sole or the dominant purpose, and the burden then shifts to the taxpayer on the object-and-purpose limb. The test is a treaty rule and works without Chapter X-A being invoked at all, which matters because section 90(2A) makes Chapter X-A apply to an assessee even where it is not beneficial to him, and because section 90(4) makes a tax residency certificate a condition of claiming treaty relief rather than proof of entitlement to it.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 6(1) and Article 7(1) of the Convention, read with Sections 90(1), 90(2A) and 90(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 10 — An exclusion from total income is not a deduction from it
concepts.statement: Section 10 opens with the words "in computing the total income of a previous year of any person, any income falling within any of the following clauses shall not be included", and everything that puzzles students about it follows from those words. The income never enters total income at all, so it is not something taken out later. A Chapter VI-A deduction works the other way — under section 80A(1) it is allowed from the gross total income, and under section 80A(2) the aggregate of such deductions can never exceed the gross total income, which is only a sensible rule because the income was in the total in the first place. Three consequences follow from the difference and they are what an examiner tests. Where money is spent to earn income that never enters total income at all, section 14A disallows the spending, because it is being laid out to earn something the Act is not charging. An amount excluded by section 10 is not part of gross total income, so it neither creates room for a Chapter VI-A deduction nor is reduced by one. And a partner's position illustrates all of it: section 10(2A) excludes his share in the total income of a firm separately assessed as such, with the Explanation fixing that share as the same proportion of the firm's total income as his share of profits under the deed bears to those profits, while section 28(v) charges the interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration he receives from the firm as his business income to the extent it was allowed to the firm under section 40(b). One stream is outside his total income and the other is squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Opening words of Section 10 and Section 10(2A) with its Explanation, read with Section 28(v), Section 14A(1) and Sections 80A(1) and 80A(2)

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Specified persons and the dealings that are deemed to benefit them
concepts.statement: Section 13(1)(c) withdraws the exemption where a trust's income or property is used or applied, openly or in a roundabout way, so that somebody named in section 13(3) gains by it, and section 13(2) saves the Assessing Officer from having to prove a benefit by deeming eight dealings to be one. Money lent to such a person without either adequate security or adequate interest or both. Land, building or other property made available for his use without charging adequate rent or other compensation. An amount paid to him by way of salary, allowance or otherwise for services rendered to the trust which is in excess of what may reasonably be paid for those services — the excess is what is caught, so a market-rate salary for real work is not hit at all. Services of the trust made available to him without adequate remuneration. Property purchased from him for more than adequate consideration, or sold to him for less. Income or property diverted to him in excess of one thousand rupees. And funds invested for any period in a concern in which he has a substantial interest. Section 13(3) is the list of who those persons are — the author of the trust or founder of the institution, a person whose total contribution up to the end of the relevant previous year exceeds fifty thousand rupees, a member of a Hindu undivided family which is such an author or contributor, a trustee or manager, a relative of any of them, and a concern in which any of them has a substantial interest, being not less than twenty per cent of the voting power in the case of a company. Section 13(1)(d) sits alongside and withdraws the exemption for funds invested otherwise than in the modes specified in section 11(5).

citation.ref: Sections 13(1)(c), 13(1)(d), 13(2)(a) to (h) and 13(3)(a) to (e), read with Section 11(5) and the Explanation to Section 13

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Section 13A — What a political party is exempt on, and on what conditions
concepts.statement: A political party holding its registration under section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 gets exemption from section 13A on four things and no more — income which is chargeable under the head income from house property, income which is chargeable under the head income from other sources, income by way of capital gains, and income by way of voluntary contributions received from any person. Business income is not on that list, so a party that runs a trade is taxed on it like anybody else. The exemption is conditional, and the conditions are cumulative. The party must keep and maintain such books of account and other documents as would enable the Assessing Officer to properly deduce its income. It must keep a record of each voluntary contribution above the amount specified in the clause, with the name and address of the person who made it, other than a contribution by way of an electoral bond. Its accounts must be audited by an accountant as defined in the Explanation to section 288(2). And it must not receive a donation exceeding two thousand rupees otherwise than by an account payee cheque or draft, through a bank account or through an electoral bond. Two further conditions sit in the provisos — the treasurer or an authorised person must submit the report under section 29C(3) of that Act for the financial year, and the return of income must reach the department under section 139(4B) by the due date that section 139(1) fixes. Missing the return deadline costs the exemption outright.

citation.ref: Section 13A clauses (a) to (d) with its first, second and third provisos, read with Section 139(4B) and Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951

concepts.subsection: Section 44C — Head office expenditure of a non-resident and the adjusted total income
concepts.statement: A non-resident running a branch in India inevitably carries a share of the head office abroad, and section 44C caps what that share may cost the Indian exchequer. Whatever sections 28 to 43A may otherwise say, the branch's business income gets no deduction for head office expenditure beyond the ceiling this section works out. That ceiling is the lower of two figures — a fixed percentage of the adjusted total income, and the amount of head office expenditure attributable to the business or profession in India. The definition of adjusted total income in the Explanation is where the marks are. Begin with the total income the Act's own rules produce, then put four things back in before reading the figure: the section 44C allowance itself, unabsorbed depreciation carried forward under section 32(2), the unabsorbed capital expenditure on scientific research, and the brought forward losses under section 72(1), section 73(3), section 74(1) and 74(3) and section 74A(3). Every one of those is added back, so a branch sitting on a large brought forward loss does not thereby shrink its head office allowance. The Explanation also defines head office expenditure as executive and general administration expenditure incurred outside India, including rent, rates, taxes, repairs or insurance of premises used for the business, salary and allowances of an employee or officer employed in head office management, travelling of any such employee, and such other matters connected with executive and general administration as may be prescribed.

citation.ref: Section 44C with clauses (a) and (b) and the Explanation defining adjusted total income and head office expenditure, read with Sections 32(2), 72(1) and 73(3)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 35AD and Section 73A — Specified businesses and the loss they throw off
concepts.statement: Section 35AD(1) allows a deduction of the whole of any expenditure of a capital nature incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of a specified business carried on by the assessee, in the previous year in which the expenditure is incurred, and the specified businesses are the ones listed in section 35AD(8) with their own commencement dates — a cold chain facility, a warehousing facility for agricultural produce, a pipeline network laid across the country to move natural gas, crude or petroleum oil, a hospital with the prescribed number of beds, a hotel of the prescribed category, developing and building a housing project under a notified scheme, and the others named there. Section 35AD(2) requires the business not to be set up by splitting up or the reconstruction of an existing business and not to be set up by the transfer of previously used plant and machinery beyond the permitted proportion. Section 35AD(4) bars any deduction under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A in relation to that same specified business, for that or any other year, once a deduction under this section has been claimed and allowed. Section 35AD(7A) then ties the asset down for eight years beginning with the year of its acquisition or construction, and section 35AD(7B) makes the deduction already allowed, reduced by the depreciation that would have been allowable under section 32 had no deduction under this section been given, the business income of the year in which the asset is put to any other use. A hundred per cent write-off of capital cost usually produces a loss, and section 73A is the provision for it — a loss of a specified business may be set off only against the profits of another specified business, and section 73A(2) carries whatever is left forward with no limit on the number of assessment years.

citation.ref: Sections 35AD(1), 35AD(2), 35AD(4), 35AD(7A) and 35AD(7B), read with Sections 73A(1) and 73A(2) and Section 80A(1)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43(1) — Actual cost and the Explanations that cut it down
concepts.statement: Section 43(1) defines actual cost as what the asset cost the assessee, less any slice of that cost which somebody else — another person, or an authority — has borne for him, openly or in a roundabout way. Everything else in depreciation flows from that one number, and five riders decide what it is. The proviso, inserted with effect from assessment year 2018-19, keeps money spent on acquiring an asset out of actual cost where more than ten thousand rupees goes to one person on one day and the money does not travel by one of the four safe roads: an account payee cheque, an account payee bank draft, a bank account, or the electronic mode the rules prescribe. Explanation 1 deals with an asset used for scientific research and afterwards brought into the business — actual cost is the actual cost as reduced by the deduction already allowed under section 35. Explanation 3 lets the Assessing Officer, with the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner, substitute the amount he determines as the actual cost where an asset previously used by another person is acquired and he is satisfied the main purpose was the reduction of tax by claiming depreciation on an enhanced cost. Explanation 8 settles a question that used to be litigated — where interest is paid, or falls due, on money borrowed to buy an asset, none of the interest belonging to the stretch after that asset went into use may sit in actual cost, and it never could have sat there, so it is a revenue deduction under section 36(1)(iii) instead. Explanation 10 says that where a portion of the cost has been met directly or indirectly by the Central Government, a State Government, any authority or any other person in the form of a subsidy, grant or reimbursement, so much of the cost as is relatable to it shall not be included in the actual cost.

citation.ref: Section 43(1) with its proviso and Explanations 1, 3, 8 and 10, read with Section 36(1)(iii) and its proviso and Section 32(1)

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Sections 179 and 167C — When the tax follows the directors and the partners
concepts.statement: Limited liability protects a shareholder from the company's debts, and sections 179 and 167C are the two places where the Act sets that aside for its own dues. Section 179(1) bites once a private company's tax on the income of some previous year cannot be got out of the company itself. Everybody who held a directorship in that private company at any point in the year the income arose is then jointly and severally liable to pay it — the test is directorship during the year the income arose, not directorship on the day the demand was raised or the day recovery failed. The escape is in the same sub-section and the burden of it sits on the director: he walks away only by showing that the failure to collect owes nothing to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his side in the running of the company. It is not enough to say he was not involved; he must show the failure to recover was not his doing. The Explanation makes clear that tax due takes in penalty, interest, fees and anything else the Act makes payable. Section 179 reaches a private company only, and there is no counterpart for a public company. Section 167C is the parallel provision for a limited liability partnership in liquidation, putting the same joint and several liability, with the same defence in the same words, on every person who was a partner at any time during the relevant previous year. Section 178 is the different case again, and puts a duty to set aside funds on the liquidator of a company.

citation.ref: Section 179(1) with its Explanation and Section 167C with its Explanation, read with Section 178

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 281 — Certain transfers to be void against the revenue
concepts.statement: Section 281(1) covers the assessee who sees a demand coming and moves his property. While a proceeding under the Act is still running, or once it has ended but before the Rule 2 recovery notice of the Second Schedule is served on him, an assessee may charge one of his assets, or let go of possession of it to somebody else — by selling it, mortgaging it, gifting it, exchanging it, or by any other road a transfer can take. That charge or that transfer counts for nothing against a claim for tax, or for any other sum the finished proceeding, or anything else, leaves him owing. The window therefore opens with the proceeding and does not close when the assessment order is passed; it closes only on the recovery notice. The proviso gives two ways out and only two. The transfer is not void if it is made for adequate consideration and without notice of the pendency of the proceeding or of the tax or other sum payable, which protects a genuine buyer who paid a real price and knew nothing; or if it is made with the previous permission of the Assessing Officer, which is the safe route for a transfer the assessee knows about. Sub-section (2) confines the section to cases where the tax or other sum payable exceeds five thousand rupees and the assets charged or transferred exceed ten thousand rupees in value. The Explanation defines assets narrowly — land, building, machinery, plant, shares, securities and fixed deposits in banks, to the extent to which any of them does not form part of the stock-in-trade of the business of the assessee — so a trader selling his stock in the ordinary way is outside the section altogether.

citation.ref: Section 281(1) with its proviso, Section 281(2) and the Explanation to Section 281, read with Rule 2 of the Second Schedule

concepts.subsection: Section 94A — Transactions with a notified jurisdictional area
concepts.statement: Section 94A is what India does when a country will not exchange information. Sub-section (1) lets the Central Government, having regard to the lack of effective exchange of information with any country or territory outside India, specify it by notification as a notified jurisdictional area, and four consequences then follow for anybody dealing with a person located there. Sub-section (2) is a double deeming — where an assessee enters into a transaction and one of the parties to it is a person located in such an area, all the parties to that transaction shall be deemed to be associated enterprises and the transaction shall be deemed to be an international transaction, so the whole of the transfer pricing machinery in sections 92 to 92F applies whether or not anybody holds a share in anybody. Its second proviso denies the benefit of the tolerance band in the second proviso to section 92C(2). Sub-section (3) is a conditional disallowance rather than a flat one — no deduction is allowed for a payment made to a financial institution located in that area unless the assessee furnishes an authorisation in the prescribed form allowing the tax authorities to seek relevant information from that institution on his behalf, and no deduction is allowed for any other expenditure or allowance, including depreciation, arising from a transaction with a person located there unless the assessee maintains and furnishes the prescribed documents and information. Sub-section (4) deems any sum received from a person located in that area to be the income of the assessee where he offers no satisfactory explanation about the source of that money in the hands of the payer or the beneficial owner. Sub-section (5) sets its own floor for deduction at source — the highest of the rate specified in the relevant provision of the Act, the rates in force, and thirty per cent.

citation.ref: Sections 94A(1) to 94A(6), read with Sections 92 to 92F, the second proviso to Section 92C(2) and Section 206AA

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 2 — what makes a mismatch hybrid, the four recommended amendments, the two-limbed primary rule, and the branch mismatches added in 2017
concepts.statement: Action Plan 2 is about hybrid mismatch arrangements, and the arrangement has to be understood before the remedy makes sense. What such an arrangement works off is a difference between the way two or more tax jurisdictions treat the same entity, or the same instrument, for tax purposes; what it is built to produce is double non-taxation, or a deferral of tax that runs for years. Four uses of these arrangements are listed. One borrowing can be made to yield two deductions. A deduction can be generated in one country with no matching income taken into account anywhere. Participation exemption regimes can be turned to the same end. So can misuse of foreign tax credit. Where a country's own law lets a taxpayer elect how a domestic or a foreign entity is to be taxed, these structures become easier to build. Working out which treasury actually lost the revenue is hard, because every country's law has been complied with; what is not in doubt is that the parties taken together pay less than they otherwise would, and that competition, economic efficiency, transparency and fairness all suffer for it. Four general amendments are recommended. Transparency is refused to an entity where the country in which the non-resident investors are resident regards that entity as opaque. An exemption, or a credit for underlying foreign tax, is refused on a dividend the payer was allowed to deduct. A credit for foreign withholding tax is refused where the same tax has already been credited to somebody else. And controlled foreign company regimes and their like are amended so that a local shareholder is attributed the income of a foreign entity that local law treats as transparent. On the treaty side a new provision is proposed for income earned through a transparent entity, under which only so much of that income as is treated as belonging to a resident of a State gets the benefit of the treaty, with a saving rule preserving a State's power to tax its own residents largely free of treaty restriction. Then come the dedicated domestic anti-hybrid rules, which operate in two stages. At the first stage the primary rule refuses the payer his deduction in either of two situations: where the payment will never enter the recipient's ordinary income, or where the identical amount is at the same time being deducted by another entity. The 2017 report then added branch mismatches. Those arise where the ordinary rules for splitting income and expenditure between a head office and its branch leave part of the taxpayer's net income untaxed in the branch jurisdiction and in the residence jurisdiction both. The dividing line to hold on to is this: a hybrid mismatch grows out of a conflict over the legal treatment of an entity or an instrument, while a branch mismatch grows out of the two arms of one taxpayer accounting differently for a payment the branch makes or receives. Five basic types of branch mismatch arrangement are identified, and between them they give rise to three mismatch outcomes — deduction with no inclusion, double deduction, and indirect deduction with no inclusion. The answer offered is in two parts: improvements to domestic law that would make branch mismatches rarer, and targeted branch mismatch rules that adjust the tax result in either the residence jurisdiction or the branch jurisdiction, so as to neutralise the mismatch while leaving every other tax, commercial and regulatory consequence where it was.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 2, neutralising the effects of hybrid mismatch arrangements — the four recommended general amendments, the treaty provision for transparent entities, the two-limbed primary anti-hybrid rule, and the branch mismatch arrangements and outcomes added by the 2017 report

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 4 — the common approach that ties net interest relief to economic activity, and the three elements it is built from
concepts.statement: Action Plan 4 is the OECD's answer to base erosion carried out with interest and with other financial payments that come to the same thing economically. Three ways of doing it are named: putting third party borrowing into the countries that tax most heavily; lending within the group so that the deductions claimed come to more than what the group actually pays outsiders in interest; and borrowing, from a related party or an outsider, to fund income that is exempt or on which tax is deferred. Money is fluid and one unit of it is as good as another, so the proportions of debt and equity inside a controlled entity are easy to change, which is what makes this among the simplest profit-shifting techniques there is. The result in both inbound and outbound situations can be double non-taxation: the interest reduces the operating company's taxable profit, while in the hands of the recipient it meets a low rate or no rate at all. What the 2015 report settled on is called a common approach, and its idea is to tie the net interest an entity may deduct to how much economic activity that entity actually has, measured by taxable earnings before interest income and expense, depreciation and amortisation. Three elements make it up. A fixed ratio rule works from a benchmark ratio of net interest to that earnings measure. A group ratio rule lets an entity deduct more interest than the benchmark would allow, by reference to the position of its worldwide group. Targeted rules deal with specific risks that the two ratio rules do not reach. India's own response to this Action is section 94B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which caps interest paid to a non-resident associated enterprise; the machinery and the figures of that section are taught elsewhere in this bank and no item here turns on them.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 4, interest deductions and other financial payments — the 2015 common approach linking an entity's net interest deduction to its economic activity by reference to taxable earnings before interest, depreciation and amortisation, built from a fixed ratio rule, a group ratio rule and targeted rules

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 6 in India's own treaties — the Mauritius protocol, the transition cap, the shell and conduit expenditure test, and the Singapore variant
concepts.statement: Treaty shopping is what Action Plan 6 is against, and the minimum standard it sets is a floor of protection every country has committed to. India's own practice on that floor is best seen in two treaties. A protocol amending the treaty with Mauritius was signed at Mauritius on 10 May 2016. For the first time it allowed India to tax gains on the alienation of shares in a company resident in India, provided those shares were acquired on or after 1 April 2017. Gains arising between 1 April 2017 and 31 March 2019 were given a transition benefit: the rate on them could not go above half of the rate India would otherwise apply to such gains. A limitation of benefits clause was written in to keep that half-rate honest. It does two things. A resident of a Contracting State loses the transition benefit where its affairs have been arranged with the primary purpose of getting at the concessional rate. And a company claiming residence in a Contracting State loses it if the company is a shell or a conduit, which the treaty defines as a legal entity that answers the description of a resident while having business operations that are negligible or absent, or carrying on nothing real or continuous by way of business in that State. There is a bright line inside that definition: a resident is deemed to be a shell or conduit company if what it spent on its operations in that State over the twelve months running back from the date the gains arose comes to less than Mauritian rupee 15,00,000, or less than ₹7,00,000 where the State in question is India. The treaty with Singapore was amended along the same lines. Before the amendment, a Singapore resident's gains on shares of an Indian company were taxable in Singapore alone, and that remains the position for shares acquired before 1 April 2017. After it, such gains are taxed the way the Mauritius treaty taxes them and are subject to the same limitation of benefits clause, with a transition benefit of the same shape. For shares acquired after 1 April 2017 and sold before 1 April 2019 the expenditure test has to be satisfied for the twelve months running back from the date of transfer.

citation.source: India-Mauritius Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, protocol of 10 May 2016; India-Singapore Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, as amended
citation.ref: The limitation of benefits clauses introduced into India's treaties with Mauritius and Singapore in implementation of the Action 6 minimum standard — taxation in India of gains on shares acquired on or after 1 April 2017, the cap of half the Indian rate during the transition from 1 April 2017 to 31 March 2019, the primary purpose test, and the shell or conduit expenditure thresholds of Mauritian rupee 15,00,000 and ₹7,00,000 over twelve months

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 13 on the OECD's side — which of the three documents goes straight to a tax administration and which one travels between governments
concepts.statement: Action Plan 13 exists because the data on corporate taxation was too poor for anyone to measure what avoidance was costing, which made transfer pricing assessments hard and audits harder. The report reworks the standards for transfer pricing documentation into a structure of three tiers and recommends that countries adopt it as a standard approach. The master file is the top tier: high-level information about a group's worldwide business and its transfer pricing policies, standardised so that it serves for every member of the group. The local file is the second: transactional detail for one country, covering the transactions with related parties and the amounts involved, together with the financial information for those transactions, a comparability analysis, and the reasoning behind the choice and the application of the most appropriate transfer pricing method. The country-by-country report is the third: an annual return, made for every tax jurisdiction the group does business in, of revenue, profit before income tax, income tax paid and income tax accrued, along with indicators of where the economic activity in the group actually sits. How each document reaches a tax administration is the part that decides a question. The master file and the local file are handed by the group straight to the local tax administrations. The country-by-country report is not; it is filed in the jurisdiction where the ultimate parent entity is tax resident, and it then reaches other jurisdictions through an automatic exchange of information between governments. To make that work the report carries an implementation package, which has two parts. One is model legislation a country can use to require the ultimate parent of a group to file in its own jurisdiction of residence, backup filing included. The other is three model agreements between competent authorities, each resting on a different existing instrument: agreements for the exchange of tax information are the base of one, bilateral tax conventions are the base of the second, and the third rests on the Multilateral Convention on Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters. The package is there to see that reports arrive on time, that what is in them stays confidential, and that it is put to proper use.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 13, re-examining transfer pricing documentation — the three-tier structure of master file, local file and country-by-country report, direct delivery of the first two to local tax administrations against filing of the third in the ultimate parent's jurisdiction of residence with automatic government-to-government exchange, and the implementation package of model legislation and three model competent authority agreements

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Actions 8, 9 and 10 — which of the three hard transfer pricing areas each one owns
concepts.statement: Actions 8, 9 and 10 are the OECD's transfer pricing work and they are reported together, under the heading of aligning transfer pricing outcomes with value creation. The problem they answer is a weakness in the arm's length principle as it had come to be applied. That principle asks what associated enterprises would have agreed had they been independent and dealing in comparable transactions in comparable conditions, and as a practical standard it has served both administrations and taxpayers well and has prevented a good deal of double taxation. But the guidance around it leaned heavily on how a group had allocated functions, assets and risks by contract, and a contract is easy to write, so the guidance proved open to manipulation and the profits could end up somewhere other than where the economic activity that earned them was carried on. Each Action takes one of the hard areas. Action 8 is intangibles, which by their nature move easily and resist valuation, and where misallocating the profit an intangible generates is a major source of base erosion; the work on it includes an agreed way of pricing hard-to-value intangibles from inside the arm's length principle. Action 9 is risk and capital. Its rule on risk is that an allocation of risk written into a contract counts only where the party said to bear it makes the decisions and exercises control over that risk; and its second half is about what return a capital-rich member of the group may earn on funding it provides, where the return does not answer to the level of activity that funding member undertakes. Action 10 is the other high-risk areas, and there are three of them: profit allocations arising out of controlled transactions that are not commercially rational, transfer pricing methods used in a way that pulls profit away from the group's most economically important activities, and payments between group members of a kind that erodes the base without matching value creation, management fees and head office expenses being the examples given.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plans 8 to 10, aligning transfer pricing outcomes with value creation — Action 8 on intangibles and hard-to-value intangibles, Action 9 on contractual risk allocation requiring actual decision-making and control and on returns to a capital-rich funding member, and Action 10 on non-commercially-rational transactions, methods that divert profit from the most economically important activities, and management fees and head office expenses

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 7 — the commissionnaire arrangement, the anti-fragmentation rule, split contracts, and where the changes were put
concepts.statement: A treaty normally lets a country tax a foreign enterprise's business profits only so far as they are attributable to a permanent establishment the enterprise has there, so the definition of permanent establishment decides whether a non-resident pays income tax in that country at all. Action Plan 7 was a review of that definition, aimed at the strategies used to stay outside it. The one it names is the commissionnaire arrangement. A commissionnaire sells products in a country in its own name, but on behalf of a foreign enterprise which owns them; because the seller never owns what it sells, the profit on the sales cannot be taxed in its hands and it is taxable only on what it is paid for its services, usually a commission, while the foreign owner has no permanent establishment to carry the sales either. Groups replaced distributor subsidiaries with arrangements of this kind and the profit left the country where the selling was done, though what was actually being done there had not changed. Tax administrations in many countries regarded this as a serious problem. The changes work in two directions. Where an intermediary's activities in a country are meant to lead to contracts being concluded regularly for a foreign enterprise to perform, that enterprise is treated as having a taxable presence there, unless the intermediary is doing this as an independent business of its own. And the exceptions to the definition are cut back to activities that are genuinely preparatory or auxiliary, with an anti-fragmentation rule that adds together what an enterprise does in a State and what its closely related entities do there, where those operations are cohesive and the split produces a tax mismatch; the same aggregation test also answers the question whether what an enterprise does in a State is preparatory or auxiliary at all. The construction site exception gets its own guard, against contracts split up between closely related enterprises. These changes went into the 2017 OECD Model Tax Convention and into Part IV of the multilateral instrument, which is Articles 12 to 15 of it. The instrument was signed by close to ninety jurisdictions, and about half of the signatories have so far taken up the articles that carry the permanent establishment changes.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 7, preventing the artificial avoidance of permanent establishment status — the commissionnaire arrangement and the treatment of an intermediary concluding contracts, the narrowing of the preparatory or auxiliary exceptions with an anti-fragmentation rule, the guard against splitting up construction contracts between closely related enterprises, and implementation through the 2017 OECD Model Tax Convention and Articles 12 to 15 in Part IV of the multilateral instrument

concepts.subsection: The 2013 diagnosis — why no single rule is to blame, and why a developing country loses more
concepts.statement: Base erosion and profit shifting is the name for the planning multinational enterprises use to get at gaps and mismatches between one country's tax rules and another's and so avoid paying tax. The report that opened the whole project, published in 2013, made a finding about cause that governs everything built afterwards: there is no one tax rule which by itself makes this possible, and what makes it possible is the way several things act on one another. Three of them are named. Domestic rules are written in each country without being coordinated with anybody else's across a border. The standards governing taxation between countries have not kept up with the way global business has changed. And the people who need to see what is happening — the tax administrations, and those who make policy — are short of the relevant information almost everywhere. Alongside those three the report identified the availability of harmful tax practices as a further pressure area. Who loses by this is not evenly spread: corporate income tax carries a larger share of the revenue in a developing country than elsewhere, and that greater reliance on it is why such countries suffer disproportionately. The answer agreed on is a comprehensive package of measures, meant to be brought in domestically and through treaty provisions in a coordinated way, backed by targeted monitoring and by stronger transparency; and the aim set for it is to reach the root causes of these structures comprehensively rather than to treat what shows on the surface. That package was delivered in 2015 as fifteen Action Plans, meant at once to counter avoidance, to make the international tax rules cohere, and to leave the tax environment more transparent than it was. Beyond delivery, the OECD and G20 countries agreed to go on working as equals to watch how the measures are implemented — an assessment of compliance, the minimum standards above all, in the form of reports on what each country has actually done.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2013 report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting — its finding that the cause lies in the interaction of uncoordinated domestic rules, international tax standards that have lagged behind global business, and a widespread shortage of information at tax administrations and policymakers, with harmful tax practices as a further pressure area; the disproportionate effect on developing countries through their greater reliance on corporate income tax; and the design aim of addressing root causes rather than symptoms

concepts.subsection: The two ways an agreement gives relief, and the one India writes into most of its own
concepts.statement: Relief from double taxation reaches a taxpayer down one of two roads, and the roads are told apart by who agreed to them. Bilateral relief is relief two Governments settled between themselves in an agreement, working out together the basis on which it will be given; India has agreements of this kind with close to a hundred countries. Unilateral relief is relief a single country hands its own residents for tax they paid abroad, with no agreement behind it at all, and in India that is what section 91 does. Bilateral relief itself comes in two shapes. Under the exemption shape only one of the two countries charges a particular income and the other stands back from it entirely. Under the credit shape both countries charge the income, each under its own law read with the agreement, and the country where the taxpayer resides then lets him set against its own demand the tax the source country took. The difference matters because the two produce different arithmetic on the same facts, and because the choice is negotiated rather than natural. India follows the credit shape in the greater part of its agreements, and Rule 128 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 is the machinery through which a resident's credit for foreign tax is worked out and given.
