citation.ref: Sections 90, 90A and 91 read with Rule 128 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — bilateral relief by agreement against unilateral relief without one, the exemption shape against the credit shape, and India's practice of using credit in most of its agreements

concepts.subsection: Which slice of the foreign income is doubly taxed, and why the sum is done one country at a time
concepts.statement: Section 91 gives a deduction worked out on the doubly taxed income, so everything turns on what that phrase covers. It covers only so much of the foreign income as survives into the assessee's total income in India. Where a Chapter VI-A deduction has been allowed against that income — section 80QQB on the royalty from a literary or artistic work is the module's own recurring example — the slice taken out by the deduction was never charged in India at all, so it was not taxed twice and carries no relief. The Rajasthan High Court settled that in CIT v. Dr. R.N. Jhanji. Expenses allowed against the same receipt come out for the same reason. A loss suffered in the foreign business also reduces the figure, and it does so even where the other country's own law would not let that loss be set off there, because the set-off is being made under India's section 70 against India's own total income. Then the rate. Two average rates are struck. India's is its income-tax on the total income, taken after any relief the Act itself allows and before any double taxation relief, spread over that total income. The foreign one is the tax actually paid in that country, after the reliefs its own law allows and before its own double taxation relief, spread over the whole income it assessed. Where the foreign income came from more than one country with which India has no agreement, the comparison is made afresh for each of them: the single Indian average rate is set against that country's own average rate, the lower of the two is applied to that country's slice of doubly taxed income, and the separate answers are added. So one country's slice can be relieved at a foreign rate and another country's at the Indian rate in the same computation, and aggregating the foreign income before comparing rates gives the wrong figure.

citation.ref: Section 91 with its Explanation, read with sections 70 and 80QQB and CIT v. Dr. R.N. Jhanji (1990) 185 ITR 586 (Raj.) — doubly taxed income confined to what enters total income, the Chapter VI-A slice excluded, a foreign business loss set off, and the lower-of-two-rates comparison made separately for each foreign country

concepts.subsection: Where the meaning of a treaty word comes from, and what an agreement leaves to the Act
concepts.statement: An agreement under section 90 or 90A does not carry a dictionary of its own for every word it uses, so the Act sets out where a meaning comes from. Three cases. A word the agreement itself defines takes the meaning the agreement gives it, and nothing else. A word the agreement does not define but the Act does takes the Act's meaning, together with any explanation of it the Central Government has issued. And a word the Central Government has assigned a meaning to by a notification in the Official Gazette that is still in force takes that notified meaning, which is treated as having operated from the day the agreement came into force rather than from the day the notification was published — subject always to the context requiring otherwise, and to the meaning not cutting across the Act or the agreement. Behind that sits a wider division of labour the CBDT stated in Circular No. 333 dated 2 April 1982. Where an agreement makes specific provision on a question, that provision governs over the Act's general provision; where the agreement says nothing about the question, the Act governs it. And an agreement is in the main an allotment of taxing rights between the country where the taxpayer resides and the country where the income arises. It rarely tells anybody how to arrive at a figure, so the machinery of computing income and charging tax on it stays with each country's own domestic law.

citation.ref: Section 90(1) and section 90A(1) on the meaning of a term used in an agreement, read with CBDT Circular No. 333 dated 2 April 1982 — a specific agreement provision prevailing over a general provision of the Act, the Act governing where the agreement is silent, and the computation machinery remaining with domestic law

concepts.subsection: When work handed to an Indian unit makes it the foreign enterprise's establishment, and what gets taxed if it does
concepts.statement: The Act and an agreement ask different questions of the same facts. Under the Act, business profits of a non-resident are reached through a business connection in India under section 9(1)(i). Under an agreement they are reached only through a permanent establishment, which Article 5(1) of a typical agreement and section 92F(iiia) both describe as a fixed place of business through which the enterprise carries on its business wholly or in part. A business connection is the wider net of the two, so a non-resident can be caught by the Act and still escape under an agreement. The CBDT applied that to outsourcing in Circular No. 5/2004 dated 28 September 2004, and the rules there are not in the Act at all. Where a foreign enterprise hands work to an Indian entity and there is no business connection between them, the Indian entity is simply assessed on its own income as a separate taxpayer, it is not the foreign enterprise's permanent establishment, and the foreign enterprise picks up no Indian liability from the arrangement. Where a business connection does exist, the Indian entity may be treated as the permanent establishment, and only then does the foreign enterprise become taxable here. What is then taxed is not everything the enterprise earns. It is so much of the profit as can be attributed to the establishment, and the attribution is done by pretending the establishment is a separate enterprise, engaged on work of the same kind under comparable conditions, dealing at complete arm's length with the business it forms part of. Put the other way, the profit given to it is the profit it would have made had it been trading with an unconnected business at prices the open market was charging, which is the arm's length principle wearing another name. Expenses laid out for the purposes of the establishment are deducted in arriving at that profit, executive and general administrative expenses included, and it makes no difference whether they were spent in the country where the establishment stands or somewhere else. Which expenses qualify is then settled by accepted accounting principles and by the Act.

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 5/2004 dated 28 September 2004 read with section 9(1)(i) and section 92F(iiia) — an outsourcing entity as a permanent establishment only where a business connection exists, profits limited to what is attributable to the establishment, the establishment treated as a distinct and separate enterprise at arm's length, and expenses for its purposes deductible wherever they were incurred

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Residence and source as the links that create a tax claim, and the two different things called double taxation
concepts.statement: A country's right to tax a foreign enterprise hangs on a link, and the international vocabulary for such a link is a connecting factor. There are two of them, residence and source, so a company can be taxed on the strength of where it belongs or on the strength of where its income arose. Whether the second link exists usually depends on a distinction that turns on one preposition. A company doing business in a host country — running a branch there, working inside its territory — takes a source link there on top of the residence link it already has at home, and both countries have a claim. A company merely doing business with that country, an exporter shipping goods to buyers there and doing nothing else, is generally taxed at home alone, because it is not carrying on business inside the other country's territory. That is a general position and not an immovable one: an enterprise with a significant economic presence in the other country can pick up a liability there without ever setting foot in it, and India's own law says so. When the links do overlap, two quite different things can happen and the module names them separately. Juridical double taxation is the ordinary case: source rules overlap and two or more countries tax the same person on the same income under their own laws. That is what an agreement is for, and where there is none, section 91 answers it one-sidedly. Economic double taxation is the other case: the same income is taxed in two countries but in the hands of two different persons, so the subject is not the same person twice. The module's example is a country charging a company a tax on the profits it distributes while a second country taxes the shareholder living there on the very dividend those profits became.

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of connecting factors in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, read with section 9(1)(i) on significant economic presence and section 91 — residence and source as the two links, business done in a country against business done with it, and juridical double taxation distinguished from economic double taxation by identity of the person taxed

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: What a treaty is, how much of the field it covers, and why an assigned right holds even if nobody uses it
concepts.statement: A treaty is any instrument binding under international law that two or more parties with international legal personality have concluded between themselves, whatever it happens to be called; the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 describes one in Article 2 as an agreement between States, put in writing, governed by international law, and no less a treaty for being spread over several related documents. Using the word signals that the parties meant to create rights and duties international law will enforce. Tax treaties come in two widths. A limited one reaches only the kinds of income it names, and India's agreement with Pakistan is the module's example, confined to income from international air transport. A comprehensive one reaches nearly every kind of income a model convention deals with, and some go further and take in wealth, gift or surtax as well. What a treaty of either width does is narrower than it looks. It hands out jurisdiction. It never itself imposes a charge — once the jurisdiction has been allotted, each country's own domestic law decides how the income is computed and what tax falls on it. English lawyers called this handing out the Classification and Assignment Rule and German jurists called it the Distributive Rule, and the consequence both names carry is the important part: where the parties have agreed that one of them will stand back from an income, that standing back operates whether or not the other party actually charges anything. So an income can end up taxed nowhere. The argument made for tolerating that is a forward-looking one — the country that holds the right may withdraw its exemption or start levying later, and the rule then works without renegotiation. India's power to make these agreements at all runs from Article 253 of the Constitution and entries 10 and 14 of the Union List, and Parliament has passed it to the Central Government through sections 90 and 90A.

citation.ref: Article 2 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 and sections 90 and 90A of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 253 of the Constitution and entries 10 and 14 of the Union List — limited against comprehensive agreements, the rule that a treaty allots jurisdiction without imposing tax, and the double non-taxation that can follow from an assigned right nobody exercises

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: The parity clause in a protocol, the four conditions the CBDT attaches to it, and why a notification decides the case
concepts.statement: A protocol is a supplement fastened to the end of a treaty to put borderline questions beyond argument, and it binds exactly as the articles above it bind. One thing protocols and exchanges of notes commonly carry is a parity clause, known as the most-favoured-nation clause. Its effect is that a country promises the other party's residents whatever better treatment it may later promise the residents of some third country, so that residents of different countries are not treated unequally. The promise is normally confined to a stated group, such as members of the OECD. India's protocols with several European OECD members hold one — the Netherlands, France, Switzerland, Sweden, Spain and Hungary among them — and although each is worded differently, the common effect is that if India afterwards agrees with another OECD member to a lower rate or a narrower reach for dividends, interest, royalties or fees for technical services, the earlier partner may claim the same. The benefit can also take the shape of a larger allowance for a head office's executive and general administrative expenses. The CBDT set out in Circular No. 3/2022 dated 3 February 2022 that four things must all be true before the better treatment may be claimed. The second agreement must have come after the first one was signed or entered into force, whichever the clause names. The other country must already have been in the OECD on the day India signed with it, so a country that joined afterwards does not count. India must in that second agreement have actually cut its rate or narrowed its reach on the income in question. And India must have issued a separate notification carrying the benefit of the second agreement across into the first. The last of the four is where these cases are usually lost. The Supreme Court held in Assessing Officer v. Nestle SA that a notification under section 90 is not a formality but a necessary step, because without it nothing has altered the law as it stands.

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 3/2022 dated 3 February 2022 read with section 90(1) and Assessing Officer v. Nestle SA (2023) 458 ITR 756 — the parity clause in a protocol, the four conditions including OECD membership tested at the date of signature, and the separate notification held to be a mandatory step

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: When a treaty points at a meaning that has since changed, which vintage of the meaning is taken
concepts.statement: Treaties are long-lived and the things they point at are not. Where an agreement leaves a term undefined and sends the reader to domestic law, or where a reader turns to a Model Commentary for help with a term, the law and the commentary will both have moved on since the agreement was signed. Two answers are possible and both have names. The static answer takes the meaning the term bore on the day the agreement was signed, so the parties are held to what they can be supposed to have had in mind. The ambulatory answer takes the meaning the term bears on the day the agreement is being applied, so the reading keeps pace. Every Model Commentary, including the technical explanation published with the United States Model, prefers the ambulatory answer, and it does so for a practical reason: a later version usually exists because the earlier wording was unclear, so the newer explanation is generally the better guide to what the term was always meant to cover. An agreement drawn on the 1977 OECD Model can therefore be read with the help of a 2017 clarification, provided the clarification only makes plainer what was there. The preference carries one limit, and the limit is where questions on this ground are usually decided. Where a domestic amendment has not clarified the term but changed what it is — altered its substance, so that it now covers something the parties never bargained over — the ambulatory answer is not available and the meaning current when the agreement was signed governs. So the test is not how old the wording is; it is whether the later wording explains the same idea or replaces it with a different one.

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of the static and ambulatory approaches in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties — the Model Commentaries preferring the meaning current at the date of application, and the exception where a domestic amendment alters the substance of the term rather than clarifying it

concepts.subsection: The OECD, UN and US Models — where each came from, and whose taxing right each favours
concepts.statement: A Model Convention is a starting point for negotiation and is not legally binding on anybody; countries have adopted its articles verbatim, with minor changes, or not at all. Three Models matter. The OECD Model's ancestry runs back to 1927 and a draft Model Form the League of Nations' Fiscal Committee drew up for every country to work from. In 1946 the Fiscal Committee sitting under the UN's Social and Economic Council put out a convention at Geneva, and a further one came from the OEEC in 1963. The OECD itself came into being in 1961 as the OEEC's successor, its membership drawn from developed countries, and it took up the draft the OEEC had before it; the final draft in its present form came in 1977 and has been revised several times, most recently in 2017. It is essentially a model treaty between two developed nations and it advocates residence-based taxation. The UN Model began with an Ad hoc Group of Experts from developed and developing countries set up in 1968; the Group finalised the Model in its present form in 1980, and it has been updated in 2001, 2011, 2017 and most recently 2021. It is a compromise between the source principle and the residence principle which gives more weight to source, designed to encourage the flow of investment from developed countries to developing ones and to take account of sharing tax revenue with the country providing the capital. Its articles rest on the source country recognising three things — that income from foreign capital should be taxed on a net basis after expenses allocable to earning it, that the tax should not be so high as to discourage investment, and that revenue should appropriately be shared with the country providing the capital. The US Model is the one the United States uses in its own treaties and was last revised in 2016. Both the OECD and the UN Models are arranged in seven chapters; the OECD Model comprises 32 articles and the UN Model 31. The titles and preambles are almost identical, and the only difference is the order of two words — the UN title says the prevention of tax avoidance and evasion where the OECD says tax evasion and avoidance. Each preamble then disclaims any intention of opening up chances to escape tax altogether, or to pay less of it, by avoidance, by evasion, or by treaty shopping got up so that residents of a third State pick up the relief indirectly.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The introduction and comparative overview in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — the 1927 League of Nations draft through the OECD's 1977 form and 2017 revision, the UN Ad hoc Group of 1968 and the Model finalised in 1980 and last updated in 2021, the US Model of 2016, seven chapters with 32 OECD articles against 31 UN articles, and the residence principle set against the source principle

concepts.subsection: Article 4 — what makes a person a resident, and how the two Models break a tie
concepts.statement: Article 4 decides who may reach a treaty at all, and it does three jobs — it fixes the convention's scope of application, it settles double taxation arising from double residence, and it settles double taxation arising from taxation in both the residence and the source state. Take paragraph 1 of the UN Model first. A person counts as a resident of a Contracting State where that State's own law makes him taxable there on the strength of his domicile, his residence, the place he was incorporated, the place from which he is managed, or a comparable test of the same character; the State itself, its political subdivisions and local authorities, and a recognised pension fund of that State all fall within the term as well. The OECD Model's paragraph 1 is worded on the same lines with two things missing: it makes no reference to place of incorporation and it does not bring in a recognised pension fund. Neither Model treats as a resident a person liable to tax in a State only on income sourced there or capital situated there. Where an individual is a resident of both States under paragraph 1, paragraph 2 breaks the tie in a fixed sequence which is abandoned the moment one test decides. First comes the State where a permanent home stands available to him; where both offer one, the State with which his personal and economic relations are closer, the centre of vital interests; if that cannot be determined, or he has a permanent home in neither, the State of his habitual abode; if he has an habitual abode in both or in neither, the State of which he is a national; and if he is a national of both or of neither, the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. For a person other than an individual paragraph 3 no longer uses a tie-breaker at all. Dual residence for a company arises where one State attaches importance to place of incorporation and the other to place of effective management, and place of effective management was traditionally the tie-breaker, used by India in some of its treaties. In the latest OECD and UN updates that has been replaced by a case-by-case approach, because of the number of tax avoidance cases involving dual resident companies: the competent authorities endeavour to determine the State of residence by mutual agreement, having regard to place of effective management, place of incorporation or constitution and any other relevant factor, on a determination the taxpayer requests through Article 25. Where they do not agree, the person gets no relief or exemption under the Convention except so far as they agree, though it remains a resident of each State for every purpose other than treaty relief.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 4(1), 4(2) and 4(3) of both Models — place of incorporation and a recognised pension fund in the UN definition and absent from the OECD's, the four-step tie-breaker for an individual, and the case-by-case competent-authority approach that has displaced place of effective management for companies

concepts.subsection: Article 5 — the four places the UN Model reaches a permanent establishment and the OECD Model does not
concepts.statement: A permanent establishment is what gives the source State the right to tax business profits under Article 7, so the article matters most to developing countries and it is where the UN Model departs from the OECD Model furthest. The comparable term in Indian domestic law is business connection in section 9(1)(i); business connection is the wider concept, so one may exist without a permanent establishment, though the absence of a business connection indicates the absence of a permanent establishment. The basic rule in Article 5(1) is the same in both Models and is cumulative — there must be an enterprise, it must be carrying on a business, there must be a place of business, that place must be at the disposal of the enterprise in the sense that it has the effective power to use it whether owned or rented, the place must be fixed in that it is established at a distinct place with a certain degree of permanence, and the business must be carried on wholly or partly through it. The definition carries no qualifying words such as unless the context otherwise requires, so it governs in all cases unless something specifically excludes it. Article 5(2) illustrates the term with a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, and a mine, oil or gas well, quarry or other place of extraction of natural resources. Four divergences then follow. Under Article 5(3)(a) of the OECD Model a building site or construction or installation project is a permanent establishment only if it lasts more than twelve months; the UN Model is wider, since it also covers an assembly or installation project and supervisory activities connected with one, and it requires only six months. Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model creates a Service PE where an enterprise furnishes services, consultancy included, using its own staff or hired personnel for spells adding up past 183 days within any twelve months beginning or ending in the fiscal year under review; the OECD Model has no such provision and the presence must be tested under Article 5(1) instead. On agency, both Models reach a dependent agent who makes contracts as a matter of habit, or who is habitually the main mover behind contracts the enterprise then signs off routinely and without altering them in substance; the UN Model goes further and constitutes a permanent establishment where the person does neither of those things but habitually maintains a stock of goods or merchandise in that State from which he regularly delivers goods on behalf of the enterprise. Finally the UN Model carries an additional Article 5(6) under which an insurance enterprise of one State is deemed to have a permanent establishment in the other if it collects premiums in that other State's territory or insures risks situated there through a person, except in regard to re-insurance; with no such article in the OECD Model, an insurer's permanent establishment falls to be decided under Article 5(1) or 5(2).

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 5(1), 5(2), 5(3)(a), 5(3)(b), 5(5) and 5(6) of the two Models, read with Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 — twelve months against six for a construction site, the 183-day Service PE the OECD Model does not have, the delivery-of-stock limb of agency PE, and the UN Model's insurance article

concepts.subsection: Article 7 and Article 21 — the limited force of attraction, and where the UN Model lets the source State back in
concepts.statement: Both Models start from the same place on business profits: they may be taxed only by the residence State, and the source State gets a right to tax them only if a permanent establishment exists in its jurisdiction. What differs is how much the source State may then take. Under the OECD Model, once a permanent establishment is proven the source State may tax only such profits as are attributable to that permanent establishment, and nothing else. The UN Model amplifies that attribution principle with a limited force of attraction rule. The rule means that when a foreign enterprise sets up a permanent establishment in the source State it brings itself within that State's fiscal jurisdiction to such a degree that profits the enterprise derives from that State, whether through the permanent establishment or not, can be taxed there. So under Article 7 of the UN Model the profits taxable in the other State are those attributable to three things and not one — the permanent establishment itself; goods the enterprise sells there directly, where they are of the same or similar kind as what moves through the establishment; and further trading it carries on there, again of the same or similar kind as the establishment's own work. It is called limited because the second and third limbs reach only goods and activities of the same or similar kind, not everything the enterprise does in that State. Article 21, other income, shows the same asymmetry on the ground that is left over after every specific article. Both Models say that income effectively connected with a permanent establishment maintained in a Contracting State by a resident of the other is governed by Article 7; the UN Model adds that income effectively connected with a fixed base is governed by Article 14 instead. But the OECD approach gives the residence State the exclusive right to tax other income, whereas the UN Model contains an additional paragraph, Article 21(3), under which the source State may also tax it.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 7 of the two Models and Article 21(2) and 21(3) — attribution to the permanent establishment alone under the OECD Model against the UN Model's three limbs of permanent establishment, same or similar sales and same or similar business activities, and the extra paragraph letting the source State tax other income

concepts.subsection: Articles 11 and 12 — the one rate the OECD Model actually names, and the royalty the two Models define differently
concepts.statement: On interest the two Models agree on the structure and differ on one number. Paragraph 1 of Article 11 gives the residence State the right to tax interest and paragraph 2 confers a right on the source State as well, interest generally being taxed in the source State at a given rate on a gross basis. That source-State charge is capped once the person beneficially entitled to the interest lives in the other Contracting State: the charge may not run past a stated share of what is paid over before any deduction. Ten per cent is the figure the OECD Model writes in. The UN Model names no figure at all and leaves the ceiling to bilateral negotiation. Both Models define interest the same way, and widely — anything yielded by a debt, mortgage-backed or not, and no matter whether the lender also shares in what the borrower earns, with government paper, bonds and debentures named expressly and any premium or prize riding on them swept in as well. Penalty charges for late payment fall outside the definition in both. On royalties the difference is larger and runs both ways. The OECD Model hands the residence State an exclusive right: a royalty with its source in one State, whose beneficial owner lives in the other, may be taxed by that other State alone. The UN Model departs from that: royalties may be taxed in the residence State, and the source State may tax them too, subject to a ceiling on the gross amount where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other State, and that ceiling is again left to bilateral negotiation. The definitions differ as well. The UN Model's royalty covers whatever is paid for permission to exploit a copyright over literary, artistic or scientific work, and it says in terms that cinematograph films count and so do films or tapes made for broadcast on radio or television; it goes on to patents, trademarks, designs, models, plans and secret formulae or processes, to the hire of industrial, commercial or scientific plant, and to know-how of an industrial, commercial or scientific sort. Two of those are missing from the OECD Model's version: hire of films or tapes made for broadcasting, and equipment rentals such as rentals for industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 11(1) and 11(2) and Article 12 of the two Models — the OECD's 10 per cent ceiling on interest against a UN percentage left to bilateral negotiation, the residence State's exclusive right to royalties under the OECD Model against shared taxation under the UN Model, and the two categories of rental the OECD definition of royalties excludes

concepts.subsection: Articles 12A and 12B — two articles the UN Model has and the OECD Model does not
concepts.statement: Two whole articles exist in the UN Model with no counterpart in the OECD Model, and both give the source State a right the OECD Model withholds. Article 12A covers fees for technical services. India is the pioneer of the concept, which entered the Income-tax Act, 1961 in 1976, and several Indian treaties carry a specific provision for it. Paragraph 1 of Article 12A provides that fees for technical services may be taxed in the residence State but does not make them exclusively taxable there; paragraph 2 establishes the right of the country in which the fees arise to tax them in accordance with its own domestic law, subject to a limit on the maximum rate of tax on the gross amount where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other Contracting State, that maximum being established through bilateral negotiation. Fees for technical services means payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, and it excludes three things — a payment to an employee, a payment for teaching in an educational institution or for teaching by one, and a payment by an individual for services for his personal use. Managerial involves applying knowledge, skill or expertise to the control or administration of a commercial enterprise; technical involves applying specialised knowledge, skill or expertise to a particular art, science, profession or occupation, so fees of regulated professions such as law, accounting, architecture, medicine and engineering qualify; and consultancy involves advice or services of a specialised nature. A financial institution's research, analysis or advice for a specific client is fees for technical services, while its payment and transmission services and its card services are not, because they apply no specialised knowledge on behalf of a particular client. Article 12B covers income from automated digital services and was added to the UN Model in its 2021 update, to preserve domestic-law taxing rights for States from which payments for such services are made. Its paragraphs 1 and 2 follow the same pattern as Article 12A — the residence State may tax but not exclusively, and the source State may tax under its own law subject to a percentage of the gross payments to be established through bilateral negotiation. Paragraph 5 defines automated digital services: the service has to be delivered over the Internet, or over some other electronic network, and the supplier's own people must barely be needed for it — minimal human involvement is the phrase. In practice the question is whether taking on new users takes more staff. An automated business can scale up without them; a digital business that is not automated watches its cost per unit climb roughly in step. Paragraph 6 lists nine examples, including online advertising, supply of user data, online search engines, online intermediation platforms, social media platforms, digital content services, online gaming, cloud computing and standardised online teaching, but the list is only an indication and the paragraph 5 requirement must still be met. Paragraph 7 settles priority: Article 12B does not apply at all if the underlying payments qualify as royalties or as fees for technical services under Article 12 or Article 12A.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12A and Article 12B of the UN Model, neither of which appears in the OECD Model — the definition and three exclusions of fees for technical services, the 2021 introduction of Article 12B, the minimal-human-involvement definition of automated digital services in paragraph 5, and the paragraph 7 rule that royalties and fees for technical services take priority

concepts.subsection: Articles 13 and 14 — the share test the Models share, and the article the OECD deleted
concepts.statement: Article 13 is the most commonly used article and it taxes gains from the transfer of a capital asset, including a transfer of shares. The right may be exclusively the residence State's or shared with the source State. The article says nothing about what a capital gain is or how it is computed, both of which are left to domestic law, and it lays down rules for gains from alienating immovable property, immovable property forming part of a permanent establishment, ships and aircraft and so on. On shares the two Models are identical: the source State gets the right where, at some point in the preceding 365 days, immovable property lying in that State accounted — directly, or through a chain of holdings — for more than 50 per cent of what the shares were worth. Otherwise the residence State has the exclusive right. The UN Model adds one thing the OECD Model does not have — it lets a State tax gains from alienating rights granted under its own law where those rights allow the use of resources naturally present in that State and under its jurisdiction, which covers a fishing quota, a right to fell timber, a right to extract water, a right to explore part of the territory for oil, gas or minerals, a right to install wind or tidal turbines and a right to use the radiofrequency spectrum. It does not cover rights granted contractually between private parties even if the law protects them, so the alienation of an exclusive right to use know-how is outside it. On gains from alienating any property not covered by the other paragraphs, both Models give the residence State the exclusive right. Article 14, independent personal services, survives in the UN Model alone. The OECD struck it out with effect from 29 April 2000, acting on its own 2000 report into the issues that article raised, and the consequence is that a professional's earnings fall to be handled as business profits under Article 7 of the OECD Model. Under the UN Model a resident of one Contracting State who earns from a profession, or from any other work carried on for his own account, is taxed on it in that State and nowhere else — save in two situations that let the other State in. Where a fixed base is kept regularly at his disposal in that other State for the work, whatever part of the income belongs to the base is taxable there. Where instead his days in that other State reach or pass 183 in total across any twelve months that begin or end in the fiscal year in question, the other State may reach whatever part of the income he earned by working on its soil. The term professional services is opened up rather than closed off: scientific, literary, artistic, educational and teaching work carried on independently is named, and so is independent practice by a physician, a lawyer, an engineer, an architect, a dentist or an accountant. The list explains; it does not exhaust. It leaves out industrial and commercial activities, which are business profits; professional services rendered in employment, such as a physician serving as a medical officer in a factory, which are dependent personal services; the income of artistes and sportspersons; and fees for technical services.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 13 of the two Models and Article 14 of the UN Model — the more-than-50-per-cent test over the preceding 365 days for shares deriving value from immovable property, the UN Model's natural-resource rights, and the deletion of Article 14 from the OECD Model on 29 April 2000 with its fixed base and 183-day alternatives

concepts.subsection: Article 25 — the mutual agreement procedure, and the four things arbitration turns on
concepts.statement: A taxpayer who thinks one or both Contracting States have taxed him in a way the treaty does not allow takes the Article 25 route, which puts the two competent authorities under a duty to try to settle the disagreement between themselves. The UN Model offers two alternatives for the whole article, Alternative A and Alternative B, introduced in 2011. Under the OECD Model the taxpayer may make his request to either Contracting State; under Alternative A of the UN Model he must go to the residence State or the country of his nationality. Alternative B bolts arbitration on to that procedure, and what comes out of it binds both States unless a person it directly affects refuses to accept it. Four differences separate the OECD Model's Article 25 from Alternative B of the UN Model and each is examinable on its own. First, the trigger. Article 25B(5) of the UN Model opens arbitration once three years have run from the day the case was presented with the two authorities still not agreed; Article 25(5) of the OECD Model allows two years, counted instead from the day the last piece of information the authorities had asked for reached them both. Second, who asks. The UN Model puts the request in the hands of one State's competent authority, with the taxpayer told once it is made; the OECD Model wants it in writing, and from the taxpayer who set the case going. Third, whether the outcome can be set aside. The UN Model lets the two authorities agree between themselves, inside six months of being told the result, to go a different way; the OECD Model gives them no such licence. Fourth, the article that supplies the relief once the case is settled is not Article 25 at all but Articles 23A and 23B, exemption and credit, and those articles address only juridical double taxation — one and the same person taxed on one and the same income in two States. Economic double taxation, where two different persons are taxed on the same income, sits outside them and the two States must settle it between themselves.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 25 of the OECD Model and Article 25 Alternatives A and B of the UN Model, read with Articles 23A and 23B — three years from presentation of the case against two years from the information being complete, the competent authority against the taxpayer as the party who requests arbitration, the six-month window to depart from the decision, and juridical rather than economic double taxation as what the relief articles address

concepts.subsection: The Inclusive Framework and the Two-Pillar Solution — what BEPS 2.0 actually is
concepts.statement: The fifteen Action Plans delivered in 2015 were the first BEPS package. What followed is called BEPS 2.0 and it is a different thing: not a further set of anti-avoidance measures but a reallocation of taxing rights and a floor under the rate. Two steps got there. First, an institution. Globalisation needed a dialogue wider than the OECD and G20 countries could hold on their own, and what the OECD's Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes had taught them was carried across: in early 2016 those countries settled on a wider framework in which countries and jurisdictions would sit as equals. In June 2016, at the G20's request, the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS was established at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and as at 28 May 2024 it has 147 members. Its members commit to implementing the minimum standards and to taking part in the peer reviews. Second, an agreement. July 2021 brought 134 of those members, between them more than 90 per cent of world GDP, to terms on a two-pillar answer: one pillar for the tax problems digitalisation had created, the other setting a worldwide floor under what the largest multinationals pay on their profits. By 8 October 2021 the count had reached 139 countries and jurisdictions, and that day's text is the October 2021 Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution. It is the outcome of the work under Action 1, which had found in its 2015 report that the whole economy was digitalising and that it would therefore be difficult if not impossible to ring-fence the digital economy; that report gave options rather than recommendations and left countries to act in their own domestic law, which is what unilateral measures such as an equalisation levy were. Each Pillar has two parts. Pillar One is Amount A, the international framework for reallocating taxing rights over the profits of large and highly profitable multinationals, and Amount B, a simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity. Pillar Two is the Global Anti-Base Erosion or GloBE Rules, which put a floor under tax in every jurisdiction a large multinational operates in, and the Subject to Tax Rule, which lets a source jurisdiction tax back where it has ceded taxing rights under a treaty and the payment bears only a low nominal rate in the residence jurisdiction.

citation.ref: The October 2021 Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution agreed by the Inclusive Framework, read with the establishment of that Framework at Kyoto in June 2016 — 89 initial members against 147 as at 28 May 2024, 134 members representing more than 90 per cent of worldwide GDP in July 2021, and 139 countries joining the October 2021 Statement

concepts.subsection: Pillar One Amount A — who is in scope, how much moves, and which market gets it
concepts.statement: Amount A modifies both the nexus rule and the profit allocation rule, and it redistributes what the OECD calls super-profits to the market jurisdictions of a group, treating the multinational as a consolidated entity and allocating by formula rather than by attribution to an establishment. Three separate tests do the work and an examiner can build a question on any of them. Scope first. An in-scope company is a multinational with global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent, profitability being profit before tax divided by revenue; extractives and regulated financial services are out of scope whatever their size. Quantum second. Amount A is 25 per cent of the residual profit, and residual profit is defined as profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue. So the same 10 per cent figure does two jobs — it is the profitability threshold that decides whether the group is in scope at all, and it is the routine return above which profit counts as residual. The residual is then allocated to market jurisdictions with nexus, using revenue-based allocation keys. Nexus third. There is a new special-purpose nexus rule which applies solely to decide whether a jurisdiction qualifies for reallocation under Amount A and which alters nexus for no other tax or non-tax purpose; Amount A is allocated to a market jurisdiction only if that nexus exists, and it exists on a market revenue threshold that depends on the size of the market itself — revenue of at least 1 million for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more, and at least 250,000 for a jurisdiction with annual GDP below 40 billion. The smaller the economy, the lower the bar. To apply that test the group must first source its revenue, and revenue is sourced to the end market jurisdictions where the goods or services are used or consumed, with detailed rules by category of revenue, revenue falling in more than one category sourced by its predominant character, and revenue from supplementary transactions sourced with the revenue it supplements. For online advertising the sourcing principle follows the eyeballs of the viewer rather than the location of the advertiser, identified from an IP address, geolocation or other reliable commercial information. Where the end user genuinely cannot be located — cloud computing, where the group may not know where its customer's employees use the service — the group may use targeted proxies or allocation keys such as aggregated headcount data or macroeconomic proxies. The whole point of Amount A is that it transfers taxing rights over residual profits to jurisdictions where there is business activity regardless of physical presence.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A of the Two-Pillar Solution — global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent for scope, extractives and regulated financial services excluded, 25 per cent of the profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue as the reallocated amount, and market revenue of 1 million or 250,000 depending on whether the jurisdiction's annual GDP reaches 40 billion

concepts.subsection: Pillar One Amount B — a simplified arm's length return for baseline distribution
concepts.statement: Amount B is the half of Pillar One that has nothing to do with reallocating super-profits. Where Amount A updates the international framework for large and very profitable groups, Amount B simplifies existing transfer pricing rules for all taxpayers, and it is aimed at one fact pattern — baseline marketing and distribution activities carried on in a country, which is the most frequent arrangement multinationals meet in the jurisdictions where they operate. Its purpose is to increase tax certainty, cut compliance and administrative cost, and particularly to assist low-capacity jurisdictions that often have no local market comparables to benchmark against. The Inclusive Framework released its report on Amount B on 19 February 2024 and published the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024. The framework runs in two steps. Step 1 is scoping: a tested party's activities are in scope where it is involved in a qualifying transaction and that transaction meets the scoping criteria. Step 2 is pricing, and it applies only if the transaction is in scope and only unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available — a reliable internal CUP displaces the whole simplified approach. Pricing itself has three sub-steps. Step 2-1 applies the pricing matrix to determine a return on sales percentage, the matrix being built out of worldwide financial data for companies doing that same baseline marketing and distribution work, screened against benchmarking criteria and the scoping conditions so that what is left approximates arm's length returns expressed as return on sales; the matrix is read across three pre-defined industry groupings and down bands of operating asset intensity and operating expense intensity. Step 2-2 applies the operating expense cross-check, a corroborative check that tests the matrix return against the tested party's own operating expense level and adjusts its profitability where the return on sales falls outside a pre-defined cap-and-collar range. Step 2-3 applies the data availability mechanism, which adjusts the matrix return upwards where the global dataset holds no or insufficient data for a particular tested party jurisdiction and there is evidence that the jurisdiction could reasonably be considered higher risk. To keep the compliance burden down the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary. The approach as published is elective, and the Inclusive Framework continues to work on something wider than an elective version, tied in with Amount A.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount B of the Two-Pillar Solution, reported on 19 February 2024 with the pending design aspects published on 17 June 2024 — scoping, then pricing by the matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism, a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price displacing the approach, and the matrix updated every five years with the data reviewed annually

concepts.subsection: The GloBE Rules — who they catch, and how the effective tax rate that triggers them is worked out
concepts.statement: December 2021 brought the GloBE Model Rules, the machinery of the minimum tax. Each jurisdiction is meant to write them into its own law, so that the pieces interlock and run in step. Jurisdictions are not required to adopt them; this is a common approach, meaning that a jurisdiction which chooses to adopt them agrees to implement them consistently with the agreed outcomes. They introduce a 15 per cent global minimum tax. On scope, the rules bite on Constituent Entities belonging to a multinational group whose yearly revenue, as the Ultimate Parent Entity's Consolidated Financial Statements report it, reached 750 million euros or more in at least two of the four fiscal years that run immediately before the year being tested, so a single year over the line does not bring a group in and a single year under it does not take a group out. A group counts as multinational once at least one entity, or one permanent establishment, sits outside the jurisdiction the Ultimate Parent Entity belongs to. Certain Excluded Entities are not subject to the rules — government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations, and pension funds or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities, together with holding vehicles used by them — but their revenue still counts towards the consolidated revenue test, and the exclusion does not take the group they control out of scope. The trigger is the effective tax rate and it is computed for each fiscal year on a jurisdictional basis, not entity by entity: the Effective Tax Rate is the total of the Adjusted Covered Taxes of each Constituent Entity located in the jurisdiction divided by the Net GloBE Income of that jurisdiction. Adjusted Covered Taxes are the taxes attributable to a Constituent Entity's income, taken as its current taxes for the year adjusted for certain timing differences, with allocation between entities in certain cases and with later additions or reductions identified and allocated to a jurisdiction and period. Net GloBE Income is the GloBE Income of all Constituent Entities in the jurisdiction less the GloBE Losses of all of them, and it is a positive amount if any — where there is a net GloBE loss the effective tax rate need not be computed at all and in most cases no top-up tax is due. That subtraction is jurisdictional blending, and it is the reason a profitable subsidiary and a loss-making one in the same country are looked at together. Note the asymmetry the examiner is likely to build on: whether the rules apply at all is decided on global revenue, while the effective tax rate that decides whether top-up tax is payable is computed jurisdiction by jurisdiction. If the jurisdictional effective tax rate is below the 15 per cent minimum, the jurisdiction is a low-tax jurisdiction and its entities are low-taxed constituent entities.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules released in December 2021 — annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in the Ultimate Parent Entity's consolidated financial statements in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years, the Excluded Entities whose revenue still counts, and the Effective Tax Rate as Adjusted Covered Taxes over Net GloBE Income computed on a jurisdictional blending basis against a 15 per cent minimum

concepts.subsection: QDMTT, IIR and UTPR — who collects the top-up tax, and how much it is
concepts.statement: Pillar Two answers two separate questions and they must be kept apart: how much top-up tax there is, and which country gets to collect it. On how much, the Jurisdictional Top-up Tax for a fiscal year is the positive amount, if any, of the Top-up Tax Percentage multiplied by the Excess Profit, plus any Additional Current Top-up Tax, less any Domestic Top-up Tax. The Top-up Tax Percentage is the positive percentage point difference between the minimum rate and the effective tax rate. The Excess Profit is the Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion. Notice which base each factor uses: the percentage is worked out on the aggregate profits, the Net GloBE Income, but it is applied to the excess profit after the substance carve-out, and that is deliberate so that groups keep the benefit of incentives on substantive activity. The Substance-based Income Exclusion is the sum of a payroll carve-out and a tangible asset carve-out for each Constituent Entity in the jurisdiction, equal to 5 per cent of the carrying value of tangible assets located there plus 5 per cent of the payroll costs of employees performing activities there; there is a ten-year transition in recognition of the impact on existing incentives and investment, during which the figures start at 8 per cent of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs and phase down to 5 per cent over the ten years. A de-minimis exclusion is available at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity for the low-taxed constituent entities of a jurisdiction where the Average GloBE Revenue of that jurisdiction is less than 10 million euros and its Average GloBE Income or Loss is a loss or is less than 1 million euros; the policy is to avoid a full effective tax rate computation where the top-up tax would not justify the compliance and administrative cost. On who collects, the model rules set a priority order of three rules. First is the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, which lets the low-tax jurisdiction itself collect the jurisdictional top-up tax computed under the GloBE rules by introducing the charge in its own domestic law, preserving its primary right of taxation over its own income. Second, where the low-tax jurisdiction has no such charge, is the Income Inclusion Rule, under which a Constituent Entity that is the Ultimate Parent Entity located in an implementing jurisdiction that held, at any point during the year, an ownership interest in a low-taxed entity below it pays tax equal to its allocable share of that entity's top-up tax. Third, where neither the low-tax jurisdiction imposes the domestic charge nor the parent's jurisdiction has an Income Inclusion Rule, is the Undertaxed Payment Rule, which denies deductions or requires an equivalent adjustment in the other jurisdictions that have implemented the GloBE rules; it is a backstop to the Income Inclusion Rule and it transfers the levy to the group's other constituent entities.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, then the Income Inclusion Rule, then the Undertaxed Payment Rule as backstop; Jurisdictional Top-up Tax as the Top-up Tax Percentage on Excess Profit plus additional current top-up tax less domestic top-up tax; the substance-based income exclusion at 5 per cent of tangible assets and 5 per cent of payroll with a ten-year phase down from 8 and 10 per cent; and the de-minimis exclusion at average revenue below 10 million euros and average income below 1 million euros

concepts.subsection: The Subject to Tax Rule — the treaty half of Pillar Two, and the 9 per cent that drives it
concepts.statement: The Subject to Tax Rule is the second component of Pillar Two and it is not a domestic-law rule at all; it is a treaty-based rule, and it works in priority to the GloBE Rules rather than after them. Its purpose is to let developing countries, as source jurisdictions, tax certain intra-group payments at source where those payments bear only a nominal corporate income tax rate in the hands of the payee. The understanding behind it is that where a source State has ceded taxing rights on outbound intragroup payments under a treaty, it should be able to recover some of them where the income is taxed, if at all, in the residence State at a rate below 9 per cent. It was developed for the priorities of developing countries, and Inclusive Framework members can adopt it by signing the Multilateral Instrument or by amending their treaties bilaterally when a developing member asks. Four limits define it. First, who: it applies only to covered payments made by an entity in a developing country to a group entity in another country, that is to connected persons, and developing country is defined by reference to gross national income per capita calculated on the World Bank Atlas method of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019, a figure to be updated regularly. Connected persons are defined by legal control, direct or indirect ownership of more than 50 per cent of the interests, or by a de facto control relationship. Second, how much: the rule bites only once covered income arising in the source country adds up past a threshold of 250,000 or 1 million a year, depending on whether that country's GDP is above or below 40 billion. Third, what: covered payments are interest and royalties; whatever is paid for rights to distribute a product or a service; premiums on insurance and reinsurance; guarantee or financing fees; hire of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment; and payments for services. Fourth, at what rate: the specified rate is the difference between 9 per cent and the nominal rate the residence State applies, cut down further by whatever source taxation other articles of the treaty have already allocated to the source jurisdiction. The worked example is the shape to hold: a source State entitled under the treaty to withhold 5 per cent on a royalty, and a residence State taxing that royalty at a nominal 1 per cent, keeps its 5 per cent withholding and may impose an additional tax of 3 per cent, being 9 less 5 less 1.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two, which works in priority to the GloBE Rules — a nominal corporate income tax rate below 9 per cent in the residence State, developing country defined as gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method, connected persons at more than 50 per cent of the interests, a covered income threshold of 250,000 or 1 million by reference to a source-country GDP of 40 billion, and a specified rate of 9 per cent less the nominal rate less source taxation already allocated

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: The fifteen Action Plans — the three pillars they are grouped under, and the four that bind
concepts.statement: Base erosion and profit shifting names the planning that turns gaps and mismatches between one country's tax rules and another's into an advantage, so that taxable profit vanishes on paper or moves to somewhere with barely any real activity going on and a low rate to go with it, and little or no corporate tax is paid overall. Following the 2009 financial crisis the G20 mandated the OECD to address tax avoidance; the OECD published its report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting in February 2013, the draft Action Plan in July 2013, and the final package in October 2015 with fifteen Actions. The Actions are structured round three fundamental pillars — introducing coherence in the domestic rules that affect cross-border activities, reinforcing substance requirements in existing international standards so that taxation aligns with where value is created, and improving transparency and tax certainty. Coherence holds Actions 2, 3 and 4; substance holds the preferential-regimes half of Action 5 and Actions 6, 7 and 8 to 10; transparency holds the ruling-exchange half of Action 5 and Actions 11, 12, 13 and 14; and Actions 1 and 15 sit across all three as horizontal. What separates the Actions from one another is not their subject but the level of commitment attached to them, and the OECD uses three words for it. A new minimum standard is a new rule to be implemented by all States, because non-implementation would spill over onto other countries, including on competitiveness; there are four, and they are Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14. Each is subject to peer review so that implementation is timely and accurate and the playing field stays level, and every member of the Inclusive Framework commits both to implementing them and to taking part in the review. A revision of an existing standard means an existing standard has been updated and will be implemented, with the caveat that not all BEPS participants have endorsed the underlying standards on tax treaties or transfer pricing. A best practice is not a standard at all but an optional recommendation, and it is what supports countries acting on mandatory disclosure initiatives or controlled foreign company legislation — which is why Action 3 on CFC rules and Action 12 on disclosure of aggressive tax planning are best practice and not minimum standards. On Action 3 the OECD's final report expressly declines to propose a minimum standard, because the policy behind CFC regimes drew fundamental disagreement — above all over whether one State ought to run its regime so as to shield another State's tax base from earnings stripping.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2015 BEPS package of fifteen Action Plans, structured on coherence, substance and transparency — Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14 as the four minimum standards subject to peer review, against a revision of an existing standard and a best practice, with the controlled foreign company rules of Action 3 and the mandatory disclosure rules of Action 12 left as best practice

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 1 — the three options the OECD offered for the digital economy, and which one India kept
concepts.statement: Action 1 addresses the tax challenges of the digital economy, where business is conducted without regard to national boundaries and the link between an income-producing activity and a specific location dissolves. Before it, the physical location of a digital business's servers was used to fix the jurisdiction that could tax its profits, with the predictable result that servers were placed in tax-efficient jurisdictions while the income and the customers came from elsewhere. The typical taxation issues it names are two: the difficulty of characterising the nature of a payment and establishing a nexus between a taxable transaction or activity and a taxing jurisdiction, and the difficulty of locating the transaction or activity and identifying the taxpayer for income-tax purposes. The report offered three options for the direct tax challenges and recommended none of them, leaving countries to act in their own domestic law. The first reworked the existing permanent establishment rule: a business whose activities had gone wholly digital would have a permanent establishment wherever it kept a significant digital footprint inside another country's economy. The second built a virtual fixed place of business — a permanent establishment arising where a firm runs its website off a server belonging to somebody else in a jurisdiction and trades through that site. The third taxed at source, either as a final withholding charge on what is paid abroad for digital goods and services, or as an equalisation levy on what a non-resident collects for certain digital dealings with a resident, or with another non-resident holding a permanent establishment in the other contracting State. India acted on all three and now stands on two of them. The concept of significant economic presence, which resembles the virtual fixed place of business permanent establishment, was introduced by Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i): a non-resident's significant economic presence in India is itself a business connection, and it means either that the aggregate of payments arising from transactions in goods, services or property with any person in India, including the provision of download of data or software in India, exceeds 2 crore rupees during the previous year, or that a systematic and continuous drive for business, or engagement with users in India, reaches at least 3 lakh users. Either limb bites regardless of where the agreement was made, regardless of whether the non-resident keeps a home or a place of business on Indian soil, and regardless of whether he performs any service here; and where the business connection is established this way, only so much of the income as is attributable to those transactions or activities is deemed to accrue or arise in India. The withholding option is section 194-O: where an e-commerce operator uses its digital or electronic facility or platform to help an e-commerce participant sell goods or supply services, it deducts tax at source at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of those sales or services or both. The equalisation levy option is the one India has now abandoned in both its forms.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) and Section 194-O, read against the three options offered by the OECD under BEPS Action Plan 1 — payments exceeding 2 crore rupees or interaction with at least 3 lakh users as the two limbs of significant economic presence, income deemed to accrue only to the extent attributable to them, and tax deducted at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount by an e-commerce operator

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 15 and the Multilateral Instrument — what makes a treaty a Covered Tax Agreement, and when the Convention bites
concepts.statement: Action 15 is the machinery Action: it exists to put the anti-avoidance solutions proposed in the other Actions into the treaty network. The problem it solves is arithmetic. There are more than 3,000 active bilateral tax treaties, India alone having entered into treaties with more than 90 countries, and amending each one separately is slow and legally cumbersome, while putting the solutions only into domestic law would leave the treaties themselves available to tax evaders. February 2015 saw the mandate for an ad hoc Group to build a multilateral instrument cleared by the OECD's Committee on Fiscal Affairs and backed by the G20's Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors; the Group, of more than 100 countries and jurisdictions including India, began work in May 2015 and adopted the text of the Convention and its Explanatory Statement on 24 November 2016. It was signed at Paris on 7 June 2017 by more than 65 countries. The United States and Brazil have not signed it, so an India-USA or India-Brazil treaty is governed by the treaty alone. The Convention has 7 parts and 39 articles, of which Articles 3 to 17 are the substantive provisions: Part I scope and interpretation in Articles 1 and 2, Part II hybrid mismatches in Articles 3 to 5, Part III treaty abuse in Articles 6 to 11, Part IV avoidance of permanent establishment status in Articles 12 to 15, Part V improving dispute resolution in Articles 16 and 17, Part VI arbitration in Articles 18 to 26, and Part VII final provisions in Articles 27 to 39. The Instrument does not amend the text of a treaty; it applies alongside it and modifies the application of some of its clauses on the later-in-time principle, so the treaty is not superseded. Everything turns on the Covered Tax Agreement. Article 2 defines one as a treaty for relieving double taxation of income which is in force between the parties and which each of them has notified to the Depositary as a listed agreement, so the matching principle governs: both sides must notify each other's treaty. India notified 93 jurisdictions when it ratified. India-Australia is a Covered Tax Agreement because both notified; India-Mauritius is not, because Mauritius did not notify India, its treaty having been amended in 2016 to carry BEPS provisions already. Flexibility comes from compatibility clauses, which resolve conflict between the Instrument and the treaty and come in four kinds — in place of, in the absence of, applies to or modifies, and in place of or in the absence of, the last being the most commonly used and the only one that can apply where only one party notifies — and from reservations, which are the opt-out. A reservation is defined by the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties as a unilateral statement by which a State purports to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain provisions, and a party may reserve for all of its covered treaties or a subset; reservations generally apply symmetrically and, exceptionally, asymmetrically. Reservations against a minimum standard are possible only in limited situations and on conditions, and of the four BEPS minimum standards only Actions 6 and 14 are minimum standards inside the Instrument, Actions 5 and 13 being implemented in domestic law instead. Timing is the last piece and it has two clocks. The Convention takes force for a party once 3 calendar months have run from the day it deposits its instrument of ratification, and then on the first day of the month after. Once it is in force for both Contracting States, its provisions have effect for withholding taxes from the first day of the next calendar year beginning on or after the later of the two entry-into-force dates, and for all other taxes for a taxable period beginning on or after the expiry of 6 calendar months from that later date. India signed on 7 June 2017, deposited its instrument on 25 June 2019, and the Convention entered into force for India on 1 October 2019, with effect from 1 April 2020 at the earliest, notified under section 90(1) by Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019. Where the other State has notified but has not ratified — Italy is the module's example — the Instrument does not apply to that treaty at all.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Articles 2, 34 and 35 of the Convention, read with Section 90(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019 — 7 parts and 39 articles with Articles 3 to 17 substantive, the matching principle on a Covered Tax Agreement notified by both parties, the four compatibility clauses and the reservation mechanism, entry into force on the first day of the month after 3 calendar months from deposit, and effect from the next calendar year for withholding taxes and after 6 calendar months for other taxes

concepts.subsection: Articles 1 and 2 — the persons a Convention reaches, and how much of a payment through a see-through entity it protects
concepts.statement: The first two articles settle who may use a Convention and what it bites on, and both Models say much the same thing with one addition on each side. Under Article 1 a Convention applies to persons who are residents of one of the two States or of both. Where an entity or an arrangement is treated as wholly or partly see-through under the tax law of either State, income running through it is treated as a resident's income — but only so far as that State, for its own taxing purposes, treats the income as belonging to somebody resident there. The measurement matters more than the label. Suppose one State regards a body set up in the other as a company and taxes it on interest paid out of the first State, while the State it was formed in regards it as a partnership and taxes each member on his share: the treaty follows the second State's treatment, so the share of a member resident there is what the interest article protects and the share of a member resident in a third country reached by no treaty is not. Apart from the benefits certain articles confer, a Convention leaves each State free to tax its own residents as its law provides. The UN Model's Article 1 then carries a provision the OECD's does not, applying the Convention to collective investment vehicles. Those are funds held by many investors, holding a spread of securities, and regulated for the protection of investors where they are established; a real estate investment trust is one. They take whatever legal shape suits — a company, a partnership, a trust, or a contract creating joint ownership — and the point of the provision is that an investor putting money in through such a fund at home should carry the same tax burden he would have carried buying his share of the underlying assets directly. Article 2 then fixes the taxes. Both Models apply to taxes on income and on capital levied for a State, or for its political subdivisions or its local authorities, and how the levy is collected makes no difference. What counts is drawn widely: a charge on the whole of income, on the whole of capital, or on any part of either, and the article says specifically that a charge on gains from parting with property, movable or immovable, is inside, as is a charge measured on everything an employer pays out as wages or salaries, and a charge on capital that has appreciated. Each State's existing taxes have to be named in the treaty itself. The Convention carries forward as well to any tax that is the same, or substantially so, brought in after the treaty is signed, whether it is added to the taxes already named or put in their place, and each competent authority has to tell the other when its tax law changes significantly.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Articles 1 and 2 of both Models — persons covered, the see-through entity rule and how far it reaches, the collective investment vehicle provision the UN Model alone carries, and the taxes on income and on capital the Convention applies to, including taxes brought in after signature that are substantially similar

concepts.subsection: The article map — the article only the OECD Model carries, the three the UN Model offers in two texts, and where one article number has two different subjects
concepts.statement: Both Models are laid out in seven chapters — scope, definitions, taxation of income, taxation of capital, methods for the elimination of double taxation, special provisions, and final provisions — and the OECD Model runs to 32 articles against the UN Model's 31. Reading the two article lists side by side shows three things the counts alone do not. First, the divergence at the end. The OECD Model has an article on territorial extension for which the UN Model has no counterpart, so from that point the UN numbering runs one behind: entry into force and termination are articles 31 and 32 in the OECD Model and articles 30 and 31 in the UN Model. Second, three UN articles are set out in two alternative texts, marked A and B, from which the negotiating States take one — international shipping and air transport, pensions and social security payments, and the mutual agreement procedure. The exemption method and the credit method are not a pair of that kind, and reading them as one is a mistake worth naming: they are two separate articles, 23A and 23B, in both Models, and a single treaty may use one of them for some kinds of income and the other for the rest. Third, three articles carry the same number in both Models and a different subject or a different name. The article on income earned in employment is headed income from employment in the OECD Model and dependent personal services in the UN Model. The directors' article is confined to directors' fees in the OECD Model, while the UN Model's names the remuneration of top-level managerial officials alongside them, which is a wider subject and not merely a longer heading. And the performers' article is headed entertainers and sportspersons in the OECD Model against artistes and sportspersons in the UN Model.
