The three articles the UN Model carries which the OECD Model has no counterpart for — fees for technical services, income from automated digital services, and independent personal services — belong to concepts of their own elsewhere in the bank and are named here only so that the map is whole.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The list of articles of both Models set out in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — VII chapters with 32 OECD articles against 31 UN ones, territorial extension in the OECD Model alone, Alternatives A and B on the UN Model's articles 8, 18 and 25, and the differing subjects of articles 15, 16 and 17

concepts.subsection: Article 26 — what the article is for, and the two refusals it allows against the one it does not
concepts.statement: A country cannot finish a tax case on facts that sit in somebody else's country, and Article 26 is how it asks. The article does two things: it fixes what information the two States may pass between them, and it fixes the manner in which one of them puts a request to the other. The two Models say much the same thing here, which is worth noticing because so many of the articles around it do not — this is not one of the places the UN Model adds something for the benefit of a developing country. What the chapter does say about developing countries is why the article matters to them: it cuts across evasion and avoidance carried on across a border, and it cuts across the flight of capital that such evasion and avoidance are often used to arrange. Then the limits, and they are the examinable part because two of them favour the State being asked and one is refused to it. First, no State is to be expected to part with confidential financial material unless it is satisfied that the material will not reach people who have no business seeing it, so confidence in the other side's handling of it is a real condition of the exchange rather than a courtesy. Second, a State may hold material back by showing that it is a communication between a lawyer and his client which its own domestic law protects from being disclosed. Third, and against the State being asked, it may not excuse itself on the ground that the information is of no interest or of no use to it — having no reason of its own to look at something is not a reason to refuse to co-operate over it.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 26 of both Models — what may be exchanged and how a request is made, its importance to developing countries against evasion, avoidance and the capital flight arranged through them, and the confidentiality, legal-advice and want-of-interest limits

concepts.subsection: Sections 245R(9) to (11) and 245W(2) to (4) — the two schemes, what each is for, and the last day a direction under either could issue
concepts.statement: Two schemes sit behind this chapter and they are not the same scheme written twice. The first is for the giving of rulings: the Central Government may make it by notification in the Official Gazette, and three ends are named for it — cutting out the contact between a Board for Advance Rulings and the applicant while a proceeding is running, so far as the technology allows; getting more out of the resources by working at scale and by letting officers specialise in the work they do; and running the jurisdiction dynamically instead of tying a case to one place. The second scheme is for the appeal an Assessing Officer takes to the High Court, and it is provided for separately in section 245W(2) with two ends rather than three — the same use of resources by scale and by specialisation, and a mechanism worked by a team, again with jurisdiction that is not fixed. Both schemes are made for the same three qualities: greater efficiency, greater transparency and greater accountability. Each carries a power to bend the rest of the Act to it. The Central Government may direct, by notification, that a provision of the Income-tax Act, 1961 shall not apply at all, or shall apply subject to whatever modification, exception or adaptation the notification specifies. That power to give a fresh direction stopped on 31 March 2023 and no direction of the kind may issue after that day — though a direction already given on or before it may still be amended by a further notification, so the schemes did not freeze. And nothing here is done out of Parliament's sight: every notification issued under either scheme, and every direction issued under the powers that go with them, must go before both Houses of Parliament once it has issued, and as soon after that as it can be done.

citation.ref: Sections 245R(9), 245R(10) and 245R(11) and sections 245W(2), 245W(3) and 245W(4) — the scheme for giving advance rulings and its three objects, the separate scheme for the Assessing Officer's appeal and its two, the power to direct that a provision shall not apply or shall apply with modifications, the 31 March 2023 stop on fresh directions with amendment still open, and the laying of every notification before each House of Parliament

concepts.subsection: Section 245R — the papers that move between the Board and the Commissioner, and the two hearings, only one of which has to be asked for
concepts.statement: Section 245R governs what happens between an application landing on a Board for Advance Rulings and a ruling coming out of it, and most of it is about who sees what. On receiving an application the Board sends a copy of it to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner concerned, and where it considers it necessary it calls on that officer for the relevant records, which go back to him as soon as they can be returned. Having read the application and the records it called for, the Board does one of two things — it allows the application or it rejects it. It may not reject one without first giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, and where it does reject, the order has to state the reason; a copy of every order goes to the applicant and to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner alike. Where the application is allowed, the Board pronounces its ruling on the question the application states, and in doing so it is not confined to the applicant's own papers: it may act on further material the applicant places before it and on material it obtains for itself. Here is the asymmetry worth holding on to. The hearing before a rejection is owed whether or not it is sought; the hearing before a ruling is pronounced has to be requested, and where the applicant does request one the Board must give it, either to him in person or to a representative he has duly authorised. The ruling then has to be pronounced within six months of the Board receiving the application, and a copy of it, signed by the Members and certified, is sent to the applicant and to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as soon as may be after it is pronounced.

citation.ref: Section 245R — the copy of the application to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the records called for and returned, rejection only after an opportunity of being heard with the reason stated and a copy of every order to both sides, further material placed by the applicant or obtained by the Board, a hearing before pronouncement where the applicant requests one, and the signed and certified ruling sent to both

concepts.subsection: Sections 131(1), 131(1A) and 131(3) — Civil court powers, and how long books may be impounded
concepts.statement: Section 131 hands named income-tax authorities four of the powers a Civil Court holds under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and no fifth. They may order discovery and inspection; they may make somebody turn up, a banking company's officer included, and question him on oath; they may call for books and papers to be produced; and they may issue commissions. Holding those four are the Assessing Officer, the Joint Commissioner, the Joint Commissioner (Appeals), the Commissioner (Appeals), the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and section 144C's Dispute Resolution Panel. They act in a quasi-judicial capacity when they use them. Section 131(1A) lets the investigation wing — the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Joint Director, Assistant Director or Deputy Director, and the authorised officer referred to in section 132(1) before he acts — exercise those same powers where he has reason to suspect that income has been concealed or is likely to be concealed, even though no proceeding is pending against anybody. What section 131 never gives is a power to seize, and that is the distinction the section is asked on. Section 131(3) allows the authority to impound books of account or other documents produced before it and retain them for such period as it thinks fit, and the power is unrestricted for every authority except the Assessing Officer and an Assistant Director or Deputy Director, who must record reasons for impounding and must obtain the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director before retaining them for more than 15 days, holidays excluded.

citation.ref: Sections 131(1), 131(1A), 131(2) and 131(3) — the four Civil Court powers, their exercise by the investigation wing where no proceeding is pending, and the 15-day limit on retention by an Assessing Officer or an Assistant or Deputy Director without prior approval

concepts.subsection: Section 132 — who may authorise a search, what may be seized, and what may only be restrained
concepts.statement: A search is authorised by a Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; an Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may also authorise one, but only if empowered by the Board, and the officer he may then name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. The authorising officer must have reason to believe, on information in his possession, one of three things — that somebody who was served under section 131(1), or given a section 142(1) notice, did not produce the books he was asked for, that a person who has been or might be served will not produce them, or that a person holds money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable articles representing income not disclosed. That reason to believe is not disclosed to any person, any authority or the Appellate Tribunal. What the authorised officer may then do divides into three. He may seize money, bullion, jewellery and other valuable articles found, except that bullion, jewellery or another valuable article which is the stock-in-trade of the business is never seized and only a note or inventory of it is made. Where the thing cannot physically be moved because of its volume, weight, other physical characteristics or dangerous nature, he serves an order under the second proviso to section 132(1) forbidding its removal, and that order is deemed to be a seizure — though even this deeming does not reach stock-in-trade. Where the reason for not seizing is anything else, the order he serves is under section 132(3), it is not a seizure at all, and it lapses after 60 days under section 132(8A); contravening it is punishable under section 275A with imprisonment for up to two years and a fine. Everything found in a person's possession during a search carries the rebuttable presumption in section 132(4A) — that it belongs to him, that the contents of the books are true, and that the handwriting, signature, stamping, execution and attestation are what they appear to be — and section 292C extends that presumption to anything found in a survey under section 133A and to anything delivered to a requisitioning officer under section 132A.

citation.ref: Section 132(1) with its first and second provisos and section 132(1A), read with sections 132(3), 132(4A) and 132(8A), section 275A and section 292C — the authorising ladder, the three limbs of reason to believe, stock-in-trade excluded from seizure, deemed seizure against a 60-day restraint order, and the rebuttable presumption extended to survey and requisition

concepts.subsection: Sections 132(8), 132(9A), 132(9B), 132(9C) and 132(9D) — the clocks that start when a search ends
concepts.statement: Four separate periods run from the end of a search, and the exam tests them against each other. For all of them the last of the authorisations for search is deemed executed on the conclusion of the search as recorded in the last panchnama, or, for a requisition under section 132A, on the actual receipt of the books or assets. Within 60 days of that date the authorised officer must hand seized material to the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction where he has none himself, and from then on that officer exercises the retention powers [section 132(9A)]. Within the same 60 days, or during the search itself, he may provisionally attach any property of the assessee to protect the revenue, for reasons recorded in writing and with the prior approval of the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director [section 132(9B)]; that attachment dies on its own after six months from the date of the order [section 132(9C)]. Within the same 60 days, or during the search, he may also refer the property to a Valuation Officer under section 142A or to an approved valuer, who must report the fair market value within 60 days from the date he receives the reference [section 132(9D)]. Seized books of account and other documents run on a different clock altogether — they are returned within one month from the end of the quarter in which the assessment, reassessment or recomputation order is made, unless reasons for retaining them are recorded in writing and approved by a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director; and even with that approval they cannot be kept for more than 30 days after the assessment proceedings for the years to which they are relevant are completed [section 132(8)]. A person legally entitled to the books who objects to that approval may apply to the Board, which decides after hearing him [section 132(10)].

citation.ref: Sections 132(8), 132(9A), 132(9B), 132(9C), 132(9D) and 132(10) with Explanation 1 to section 132 — 60 days for handover, provisional attachment and a valuation reference, six months for the life of the attachment, 60 days for the valuer's report, and one month from the end of the quarter for the return of seized books with a 30-day outer limit after the proceedings are completed

concepts.subsection: Section 132B — what happens to the money and the assets taken in a search
concepts.statement: Assets seized under section 132 or requisitioned under section 132A may be applied against any existing liability under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the Black Money Act, 2015 and the other named enactments, and against the liability determined on completion of the assessment, reassessment, recomputation or block assessment that follows the search, including the penalty and interest connected with it, once the assessee has defaulted or is treated as having done so. Advance tax is not an existing liability. Where the seized assets are money, or partly money, the Assessing Officer applies the money and the assessee is discharged to that extent; other assets are deemed to be under distraint and may be sold in the manner laid down in the Third Schedule, and whatever is left after the liabilities are met is handed back at once to the person from whose custody it was taken. There is a route out for money the assessee can explain. The month of seizure has to end first; he then gets 30 days to apply to the Assessing Officer and satisfy him where the asset came from and how it was paid for. The asset is then released, after meeting existing liabilities and with the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, within 120 days from the date the last of the authorisations was executed. Where the assets seized turn out to exceed the liabilities, the assessee is entitled to simple interest at one half per cent for every month or part of a month, running from the expiry of those 120 days to the date the assessment, reassessment or recomputation is completed. In Hemant Kumar Sindhi the Allahabad High Court held that an existing liability means one crystallised by adjudication and a liability is determined only on completion of the assessment, so an assessee cannot have seized gold sold and the proceeds set against tax on income he surrendered during the search before any assessment is made.

citation.ref: Section 132B with the proviso to section 132B(1)(i) and section 132B(4), read with Hemant Kumar Sindhi and Another v. CIT (2014) 364 ITR 555 (All) — the 30-day application, the 120-day release, interest at one half per cent a month thereafter, and advance tax excluded from existing liability

concepts.subsection: Section 133A — the power of survey, when it may be exercised and what it stops short of
concepts.statement: A survey is not a small search, and every limit on it is examinable. An income-tax authority may enter a place within the area assigned to him, or occupied by a person over whom he has jurisdiction, or one he is authorised for, at which a business, a profession or an activity for a charitable purpose is carried on, whether or not it is the principal place, and any other place at which the person says his books or valuable articles are kept. He may require the proprietor, trustee, employee or anyone helping in the work to let him inspect the books and documents, to let him check or verify the cash, stock or other valuable articles, and to furnish information. On timing the section draws a line between two kinds of place — a place of business or profession may be entered only during the hours at which it is open for business, and any other place only after sunrise and before sunset. The hour of entry is fixed and the hour of leaving is not, so a survey lawfully begun at ten at night in a shop trading until eleven may carry on past closing. He may place marks of identification on the books, take extracts and copies, make an inventory of the cash, stock or valuable articles checked, and record the statement of any person; he may impound books after recording his reasons, but may not retain them beyond 15 days excluding holidays without the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director. Under section 133A(4) he may not remove any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place at all — there is no seizure in a survey. Where a person refuses or evades, section 133A(6) gives him all the powers under section 131(1) to compel compliance. Section 133A(5) lets him collect information and record statements about a function, ceremony or event after it is over and before assessment proceedings for the relevant year begin. Every survey needs the approval of a Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner. A survey under section 133A(2A) is a narrower thing done for one purpose only, verifying that tax has been deducted or collected under Chapter XVII-B or XVII-BB: it may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset even at a place of business, and in it the authority may neither impound books nor make an inventory of cash, stock or valuable articles.

citation.ref: Sections 133A(1) to 133A(6) with the Explanation to section 133A — business hours against sunrise to sunset, the 15-day limit on impounding excluding holidays, the bar in section 133A(4) on removing cash, stock or valuable articles, and the narrower powers in a section 133A(2A) survey for verifying deduction or collection at source

concepts.subsection: Sections 133, 133B and 133C — calling for information, collecting it, and the faceless scheme
concepts.statement: Section 133 lets the Assessing Officer, the Joint Commissioner, the Joint Commissioner (Appeals) and the Commissioner (Appeals) call for named information — the partners of a firm and their shares, the manager and members of a Hindu undivided family, the beneficiaries of a trustee, guardian or agent, a statement of everyone to whom the assessee paid rent, interest, commission, royalty, brokerage or a non-salary annuity of more than ₹1,000 in a previous year, the payments and receipts of a dealer, broker or agent connected with a stock or commodity exchange, and under section 133(6) any information at all from any person including a banking company that will be useful for or relevant to an enquiry or proceeding. Section 133(6) is also exercisable by the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Joint Director, Deputy Director and Assistant Director. Where no proceeding is pending, no authority below the rank of Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may exercise it without their prior approval — but a Joint Director, Deputy Director or Assistant Director may, and the Supreme Court settled the point in Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank. Section 133B is a smaller power still: an income-tax authority, meaning a Joint Commissioner, Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assessing Officer or an authorised Inspector, may enter a place of business only during business hours and only to collect prescribed information, may on no account remove any books of account or valuable articles, and a failure to furnish what he asks for attracts a penalty of up to ₹1,000 under section 272AA. Section 133C lets a prescribed authority, not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner and authorised by the Board, issue a notice requiring information or documents to verify what it already holds, and process what comes back under the scheme made under section 135A for the faceless collection of information — the e-Verification Scheme, 2021.

citation.ref: Sections 133, 133B, 133C and 135A read with Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. CIT (CIB) (SC), reported at (2014) 360 ITR 243 — the ₹1,000 reporting threshold in section 133(4), prior approval for section 133(6) where no proceeding is pending and the exemption for a Joint, Deputy or Assistant Director, the ₹1,000 penalty under section 272AA, and the e-Verification Scheme, 2021

concepts.subsection: Sections 119 and 119(2)(b) — what the Board may direct, and who condones a delay
concepts.statement: Section 119 lets the Central Board of Direct Taxes issue orders, instructions and directions to income-tax authorities, and section 119(2)(b) lets it authorise an authority to admit an application or claim for an exemption, deduction, refund or any other relief after the period allowed by the Act has expired, to avoid genuine hardship. A claim to carry forward a loss in a return filed late is a claim for other relief within that clause, which is what the Delhi High Court held in Lodhi Property Company Ltd. when a return carrying a loss was one day late. Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 puts the power in the hands of different officers by the size of the claim — a claim up to ₹1 crore for any one assessment year goes to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, a claim above ₹1 crore and up to ₹3 crore to the Chief Commissioner, and a claim above ₹3 crore to the Principal Chief Commissioner. What the Board cannot do is legislate: in CIT v. S.V. Gopala the Supreme Court held that it has no power to amend a legislative provision by issuing a circular. Circulars issued under section 119 bind the officers and persons employed in executing the Act and do not bind the appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts or the taxpayer, though a taxpayer may take the benefit of a circular that favours him.

citation.ref: Section 119 and section 119(2)(b) read with CBDT Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 and with CIT and Anr v. S.V. Gopala and Others (2017) 396 ITR 694 (SC) and Lodhi Property Company Ltd. v. Under Secretary (ITA-II) (2010) 323 ITR 441 — the ₹1 crore and ₹3 crore ladder for condoning delay, and the limits of a circular

concepts.subsection: Sections 269SU and 271DB — the duty to offer an electronic payment facility
concepts.statement: Section 269SU reaches anybody in business whose sales, turnover or gross receipts crossed ₹50 crore in the immediately preceding previous year. He must put in place a way for customers to pay by the electronic modes that stand prescribed, over and above whatever electronic facilities he already offers. Rule 119AA prescribes three and only three modes — a debit card powered by RuPay, the Unified Payments Interface, and the Unified Payments Interface Quick Response Code. The duty is to offer them, not to be paid through them. Failure attracts a penalty under section 271DB of ₹5,000 for every day during which the failure continues, imposed by the Assessing Officer, and no penalty is imposed if the person proves there were good and sufficient reasons for the failure. Two things narrow it. Circular No. 12/2020 dated 20 May 2020 says the section does not apply to a person having only business-to-business transactions, with no transaction with a retail customer or consumer, where at least 95 per cent of all amounts received during the previous year, including receipts for sales, turnover or gross receipts, come by a mode other than cash. And the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 was amended so that no bank or system provider may charge anyone, directly or indirectly, for using these modes, with Circular No. 16/2020 telling banks to refund charges collected on or after 1 January 2020.

citation.ref: Section 269SU with Rule 119AA and section 271DB, read with CBDT Circular No. 12/2020 dated 20 May 2020 — the ₹50 crore turnover trigger, the three prescribed electronic modes, the ₹5,000 a day penalty and the 95 per cent business-to-business relief

concepts.subsection: Section 281B — provisional attachment during a proceeding, and the bank guarantee that lifts it
concepts.statement: Section 281B lets the Assessing Officer lay a provisional attachment, by a written order, on any property the assessee holds, in the manner the Second Schedule provides, where he thinks it necessary to protect the interests of the revenue. It is available during the pendency of an assessment or a reassessment of income that has escaped assessment, and also for the imposition of a penalty under section 271AAD for a false entry in the books where the penalty likely to be imposed exceeds ₹2 crore, and it needs the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director. The attachment is valid for six months from the date of the order. It may be extended for reasons recorded in writing by the same authorities, but the total period of extension cannot exceed two years, or 60 days after the date of the assessment or reassessment, whichever is later. The assessee can buy his property back out of it: where he furnishes a guarantee from a scheduled bank for not less than the fair market value of the attached property, or for an amount sufficient to protect the revenue, the Assessing Officer must revoke the attachment — within 45 days of receiving the guarantee where he has referred the property to a Valuation Officer, who must report within 30 days of the reference, and within 15 days in any other case. The guarantee is then live security. If a notice of demand is served and the sum is not paid in time the Assessing Officer may invoke it wholly or partly; if the assessee fails to renew it or furnish a new one for an equal amount fifteen days before it expires the Assessing Officer must invoke it; what is realised goes first against the existing demand and any balance to the Personal Deposit Account of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; and where the guarantee is no longer needed to protect the revenue it is released forthwith.

citation.ref: Sections 281B(1) to 281B(9) — six months' validity with the extension capped at two years or 60 days after the assessment whichever is later, the ₹2 crore section 271AAD trigger, and the 45-day and 15-day windows for revoking an attachment against a scheduled bank guarantee with the Valuation Officer reporting within 30 days

concepts.subsection: Section 285BA with Rule 114E — the statement of financial transactions and what a default costs
concepts.statement: Section 285BA obliges the persons it names — an assessee, a prescribed person in a Government office, a local authority, a Registrar or Sub-Registrar, a motor vehicle registering authority, the Post Master General, a Collector under the land acquisition law, a recognised stock exchange, an officer of the Reserve Bank, a depository, a prescribed reporting financial institution and any other prescribed person — to furnish a statement of specified financial transactions or reportable accounts they register, record or maintain. Rule 114E sets the values and the reporting person for each. A banking company or co-operative bank reports cash purchases of drafts, pay orders or banker's cheques and of Reserve Bank pre-paid instruments aggregating ₹10 lakh or more in a financial year, and cash deposits or withdrawals aggregating ₹50 lakh or more in one or more current accounts; cash deposits of ₹10 lakh or more in accounts that are neither current accounts nor time deposits, and time deposits of ₹10 lakh or more, are also reported. Credit card bills are reported at ₹1 lakh or more in cash or ₹10 lakh or more by any other mode. Bonds or debentures, shares including share application money, a listed company's buy-back, mutual fund units and the sale of foreign currency are each reported at ₹10 lakh or more in a financial year. A Registrar or Sub-Registrar reports the purchase or sale of immovable property for ₹30 lakh or more, or valued by the stamp valuation authority at ₹30 lakh or more. And a person liable to audit under section 44AB reports the receipt of cash exceeding ₹2 lakh for the sale of any goods or services not already covered. The statement goes in Form No. 61A on or before 31 May immediately following the financial year in which the transaction is recorded. A defective statement may be rectified within 30 days of the intimation of the defect, or such further time as is allowed, and if it is not the Act applies as though inaccurate information had been furnished. Where nothing is filed the prescribed authority may serve a notice allowing not more than 30 days. Where the filer later discovers an inaccuracy he must inform the authority and furnish the correct information within ten days.

citation.ref: Section 285BA with Rule 114E and Form No. 61A — the ₹10 lakh, ₹30 lakh and ₹50 lakh reporting values, the ₹2 lakh cash receipt reported by a person liable to audit under section 44AB, the 31 May due date, and the 30-day and ten-day windows in sections 285BA(4) to 285BA(6)

concepts.subsection: Sections 285BB and 285BAA — the annual information statement, and the new crypto-asset statement
concepts.statement: Section 285BB puts the flow of information the other way round. The prescribed income-tax authority, or a person authorised by it, uploads into the assessee's own registered account an annual information statement containing the prescribed information in its possession. Rule 114-I names the officer — Income-tax (Systems) has its own Principal Director General and its own Director General, and either may authorise somebody else — names the form as Form No. 26AS, and fixes the timing at three months, counted from the close of the month in which the information reached him. Six categories go into it: tax deducted or collected at source, specified financial transactions, payment of taxes, demand and refund, pending proceedings and completed proceedings. The Board may let that same officer add more: what reaches him from any officer, authority or body carrying out a function under any law; what arrives under a section 90 or a section 90A agreement; and what any other person supplies — to whatever extent the Board thinks the revenue's interest served. Section 285BAA is the newest of these obligations and runs on the same machinery as section 285BA: a prescribed reporting entity furnishes a statement of transactions in crypto-assets for the prescribed period, in the prescribed form and to the prescribed authority; a defect may be rectified within 30 days of the intimation or such further period as is allowed, failing which the Act applies as though inaccurate information had been furnished; a person who has filed nothing may be given a notice of not more than 30 days; and a filer who discovers an inaccuracy must correct it within ten days. A crypto-asset here is the digital representation of value that section 2(47A)(d) defines: value whose dealings are validated and kept safe by a distributed ledger secured through cryptography, or by technology of that kind.

citation.ref: Section 285BB with Rule 114-I and Form No. 26AS, and section 285BAA read with section 2(47A)(d) — the six categories of information, the three-month upload window, and the 30-day and ten-day windows on the crypto-asset statement

concepts.subsection: Section 288 — who may appear for an assessee, and who is shut out
concepts.statement: An assessee entitled or required to attend before an income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal may attend by an authorised representative, meaning a person authorised by him in writing to appear on his behalf — except where section 131 requires him to attend personally for examination on oath or affirmation, which nobody may do for him. The people who may be authorised are a relative or a person regularly employed by the assessee, an officer of a scheduled bank with which he keeps a current account or has other regular dealings, a legal practitioner entitled to practise in any Civil Court in India, an accountant, and a person who has passed an accountancy examination recognised by the Board under Rule 50. Accountant means a chartered accountant holding a valid certificate of practice, and it is here that the section does its work, because it excludes exactly the people who are too close to the assessee to audit him. For a company the excluded list is the section 141(3) list of the Companies Act, 2013 — a body corporate other than a limited liability partnership, an officer or employee, a partner or employee of an officer or employee, a person whose relative or partner is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5 lakh or has given a guarantee or security for a third person's debt to it in excess of ₹1 lakh, a person or firm with a prescribed business relationship, a person whose relative is a director or key managerial personnel, a person already auditing more than 20 companies, and a person convicted of an offence involving fraud where ten years have not elapsed; a relative may hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000. For an individual, firm, association of persons or Hindu undivided family it is the assessee himself or a member or partner and their relatives; for a trust or institution it is the author or founder, anyone whose total contribution up to the end of the relevant previous year exceeds ₹50,000, a member of a Hindu undivided family that is one of them, any trustee or manager, and their relatives. A relative of the assessee may hold security or interest in him of a face value not exceeding ₹1 lakh, be indebted to him for not more than ₹1 lakh and guarantee a third person's debt to him up to ₹1 lakh. And there is a rider that decides cases: being ineligible to audit an assessee or to furnish a report or certificate for him does not make an accountant ineligible to appear for him as an authorised representative. Where the matter is the valuation of an asset, section 287A lets the taxpayer attend by a registered valuer instead.

citation.ref: Section 288 with section 288(2) and the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and section 287A — the ₹5 lakh indebtedness and ₹1 lakh guarantee limits, the ₹1,000 and ₹1 lakh security limits for a relative, the ₹50,000 substantial contribution to a trust, and the rider that audit ineligibility does not bar appearance

concepts.subsection: Sections 245N, 245-OB, 245P and 245U — what an advance ruling is, who may ask for one, and who gives it
concepts.statement: An advance ruling settles a question before the issue arises, so that the litigation never happens. Section 245N(a) gives it five limbs, and each has its own applicant. A non-resident may ask about a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake. A resident may ask what a non-resident's tax will come to on a dealing he has already entered into with that non-resident, or plans to. A resident of a class notified by the Central Government may ask about his own tax liability arising out of his own transaction, and the notification of 28 November 2014 makes that a resident whose one or more transactions total ₹100 crore or more. A resident of a notified class may ask about an issue relating to the computation of total income that is already pending before an income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal, and the notified class there is a public sector company. And any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether an arrangement he proposes to undertake is an impermissible avoidance arrangement under Chapter X-A. Section 245RR stops a resident applicant running both remedies at once — where he has applied to the Board for a decision on an issue, no income-tax authority or Tribunal may decide that issue. Three Boards for Advance Rulings have given rulings since 1 September 2021, two with their headquarters in Delhi and one in Mumbai, constituted under section 245-OB; each consists of two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner nominated by the Board, and what it pronounces is appealable to the High Court. Under section 245P a vacancy or a defect in the constitution of a Board does not make its proceedings or its ruling open to question. Under section 245U a Board carries every Civil Court power over discovery and inspection; over making somebody appear — a banking company's officer counts — and questioning him on oath; over issuing commissions; and over calling for books of account to be produced; it is deemed a Civil Court for section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and every proceeding before it is a judicial proceeding, but it is not a Civil Court for Chapter XXVI of that Code.

citation.ref: Sections 245N(a) and 245N(b), 245-OB, 245P, 245RR and 245U with Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 and Notification No. 725(E) dated 3 August 2000 — the five limbs of advance ruling, the ₹100 crore notified resident and the public sector company, three Boards of two members each not below the rank of Chief Commissioner from 1 September 2021, and the Civil Court powers

concepts.subsection: Sections 245Q, 245R, 245T and 245W — the fee, the grounds of rejection, the six months and the appeal
concepts.statement: An application for an advance ruling is made under section 245Q(1) stating the question, in quadruplicate, and section 245Q(2) attaches a fee — ₹10,000, set against whatever higher figure stands prescribed, the larger of the two being payable. Rule 44E sets those prescribed fees by the size of the transaction for an applicant falling in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of section 245N(b) — ₹2 lakh where the transactions in respect of which the ruling is sought do not exceed ₹100 crore, ₹5 lakh where they exceed ₹100 crore but do not exceed ₹300 crore, and ₹10 lakh where they exceed ₹300 crore — while any other applicant pays ₹10,000 in all cases. The applicant may withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application. On receiving it the Board sends a copy to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and may call for the records, and then allows or rejects. It shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before any income-tax authority, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, though a notified resident may ask even then; where it involves the determination of the fair market value of any property; or where it relates to a transaction or issue designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, except for a notified resident applicant and except where the question is whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement. No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard and the order must give the reason. Where the application is allowed the Board pronounces its ruling within six months from the receipt of the application, giving a hearing in person or by an authorised representative if one is asked for. Under section 245T, where the Board finds on a representation by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or otherwise that a ruling was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, it may declare it void ab initio, and the Act then applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after excluding the period from the date of the ruling to the date of that order. Under section 245W(1) the High Court hears an appeal from an applicant aggrieved by a ruling or order of the Board, and from the Assessing Officer too where the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner so directs; either has 60 days from the communication of the ruling or order, and where the High Court is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented him it may grant a further period of 30 days.

citation.ref: Sections 245Q, 245R, 245T and 245W with Rule 44E — the ₹10,000 minimum fee and the ₹2 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹10 lakh slabs against ₹100 crore and ₹300 crore, withdrawal within 30 days, the three grounds on which an application shall not be allowed, the six-month time limit for pronouncing a ruling, a ruling declared void ab initio for fraud with the intervening period excluded, and an appeal to the High Court within 60 days extendable by 30 days

concepts.section: Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
concepts.subsection: Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Black Money Act, 2015 — the charge, the year, and what may be deducted
concepts.statement: Under section 3(1) of the Black Money Act, 2015 the charge falls on every assessee at 30 per cent, and what it falls on is his undisclosed foreign income and asset for the previous year. The proviso moves the year for an asset. However long ago an undisclosed asset abroad was acquired, it is charged at the value it carries in the previous year during which the Assessing Officer first learns of it. An undisclosed asset located outside India is one held by the assessee in his own name or of which he is the beneficial owner, and about the source of investment in which he has no explanation or gives one the Assessing Officer finds unsatisfactory; its value under section 3(2) is the fair market value determined under Rule 3. Total undisclosed foreign income and asset under section 4 is foreign-source income not disclosed in a return filed under section 139(1), 139(4) or 139(5), foreign-source income for which no return was filed at all, and the value of any undisclosed foreign asset — and what this Act charges stays outside total income for the purposes of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Section 5 computes it harshly on one side and fairly on the other. No deduction is allowed for any expenditure or allowance, and no loss may be set off, whether or not the Income-tax Act would have allowed it. But from the value of an undisclosed asset abroad the assessee may reduce any income that has already been assessed to tax under the Income-tax Act for an assessment year before this Act applied, and any income assessable or assessed under this Act, provided he furnishes evidence satisfying the Assessing Officer that the asset was acquired out of it. Where the asset is immovable property the deduction is proportionate. Work out what fraction the assessed or assessable foreign income makes of what the property cost altogether, then apply that fraction to the property's value on the opening day of whichever financial year the Assessing Officer learns of it in.

citation.ref: Sections 3(1) and 3(2) with the proviso, section 4 and section 5(1) and (2) — tax at 30 per cent, an undisclosed foreign asset charged in whichever previous year the Assessing Officer comes to know of it, no expenditure or set-off allowed, and the proportionate deduction for immovable property measured on the value at the first day of that financial year

concepts.section: Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
concepts.subsection: Sections 41 to 56 of the Black Money Act, 2015 — the penalties, the ₹20 lakh let-off and the prison terms
concepts.statement: The penalties under the Black Money Act are deliberately out of scale with the Income-tax Act. Where tax has been computed on undisclosed foreign income and asset, section 41 lets the Assessing Officer direct the assessee to pay, in addition to the tax, a sum equal to three times that tax. Section 42 charges ₹10 lakh on a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who holds a foreign asset as beneficial owner or otherwise, or is the beneficiary of one, or has foreign-source income, and fails to furnish the return required by section 139(1) before the end of the relevant assessment year. Section 43 charges another ₹10 lakh where he files but fails to furnish the information about such an asset in the return or furnishes inaccurate particulars of it. The proviso to both is the practical relief and the thing to remember: neither penalty applies in respect of an asset or assets, other than immovable property, whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20 lakh. Where the balance is in a foreign currency account the rupee value is taken at the State Bank of India telegraphic transfer buying rate on the relevant date. Section 44 charges a penalty equal to the tax arrears on an assessee in default, and paying the tax before the penalty is levied does not save him. Section 45 charges not less than ₹50,000 and up to ₹2 lakh for failing without reasonable cause to answer a question, sign a statement, or attend or produce books in response to a summons under section 8. Under section 46(4) an order imposing a penalty needs the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where it exceeds ₹1 lakh and is levied by an Income-tax Officer, or exceeds ₹5 lakh and is levied by an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant or Deputy Director. On the criminal side, wilful failure to furnish the return under section 49 is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for not less than six months and up to seven years and a fine, but prosecution is not attracted if the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year. Wilful failure to furnish information about a foreign asset under section 50, a false statement in a verification under section 52 and abetment under section 53 carry the same six months to seven years. A wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest under section 51 carries rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years and up to ten years; a wilful attempt to evade payment of it carries three months to three years. Under section 54 the court presumes a culpable mental state and the accused must prove he had none, and under section 55 no prosecution under sections 49 to 53 is begun except with the sanction of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or the Commissioner (Appeals).

citation.ref: Sections 41, 42, 43 with their proviso, 44, 45, 46(4), 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 and 55 — three times the tax, ₹10 lakh each under sections 42 and 43 with no penalty where assets other than immovable property do not exceed ₹20 lakh in aggregate, ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh under section 45, the ₹1 lakh and ₹5 lakh approval limits, and rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years under section 49 with three to ten years under section 51

concepts.subsection: Explanations 5, 6 and 7 to Section 9(1)(i) — when a share of a foreign company counts as an Indian asset
concepts.statement: Capital gain on the transfer of a capital asset situated in India is deemed to accrue here whatever the asset is made of, wherever the transfer deed is registered and wherever the price is paid. Explanation 4 puts that beyond argument by giving the word "through" the sense of by means of, in consequence of, or by reason of. Explanation 5 then goes further and reaches a share or interest in a company or entity that was registered or incorporated abroad, treating that share as having been situated in India all along where it draws its value substantially, directly or indirectly, from assets lying in India. Explanation 6 supplies the measure, and it has two limbs which have to be satisfied together rather than either one on its own — on the specified date the Indian assets must be worth more than ₹10 crore, and they must make up at least half of everything the foreign company or entity owns. Value here means fair market value worked out under Rule 11UB, taken gross without knocking off any liability attached to the asset. The specified date is ordinarily the close of the accounting period that ended before the transfer, but it shifts to the transfer date itself where the book value of the assets on that date runs at least 15 per cent above the book value at the preceding balance sheet date. Explanation 7 then lets the small holder out. Nothing is deemed to accrue to a transferor who, taken with his associated enterprises, held throughout the twelve months before the transfer neither a right of management or control nor more than 5 per cent of the voting power, share capital or interest — measured in the foreign company that directly owns the Indian assets where the holding is direct, and in the entity that would carry control or a stake in that direct owner where the chain is longer. Where the exemption does not apply and the foreign entity also owns assets outside India, only the part of the gain reasonably attributable to the Indian assets is deemed to accrue here, computed under Rule 11UC. Two carve-outs sit in the provisos to Explanation 5 for investments held through Category-I and Category-II foreign portfolio investors, and a CBDT circular keeps a foreign company's own dividend declared abroad outside the clause even where the shares behind it are Indian-heavy.

citation.ref: Explanations 4, 5, 6 and 7 to Section 9(1)(i), read with Rules 11UB and 11UC of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Circular No. 4/2015 dated 26 March 2015

concepts.subsection: Sections 115C, 115D and 115E — what Chapter XII-A charges a non-resident Indian, and at what rate
concepts.statement: Chapter XII-A has run since 1 June 1983 and holds seven sections. It reaches one person only — a non-resident Indian, meaning an individual who is not a resident and who is either a citizen of India or of Indian origin, origin being traced through a birth in undivided India of himself, a parent or a grandparent. It reaches two kinds of income only: investment income from a foreign exchange asset, and long-term capital gain on such an asset. A foreign exchange asset is a specified asset that was bought, acquired or subscribed to with convertible foreign exchange as the Reserve Bank treats that term for the purposes of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, so the money that paid for it matters as much as the asset itself. The list of specified assets is closed and its wording is exact — shares in an Indian company; debentures issued by an Indian company that is not a private company; deposits with an Indian company that is not a private company; any security of the Central Government; and anything else the Central Government notifies. Shares are the only entry with no public-company qualifier attached, so a private company's debenture or deposit falls outside however it was paid for. Section 115D then taxes what is caught on a gross footing: no expenditure or allowance may be set against investment income at all. It also shuts out Chapter VI-A and indexation where the gross total income is nothing but investment income or such a long-term gain or both, and where the gross total income holds other income as well, the Chapter VI-A deductions attach only to that other slice. Section 115E then fixes the charge as a sum of three parts — 20 per cent on the investment income, 12.5 per cent on the long-term gain from the transfer of a specified asset bought in foreign currency, and ordinary rates on whatever else the total income holds — with surcharge where it applies and health and education cess at 4 per cent on top.

citation.ref: Sections 115C(a) to 115C(f), 115D(1), 115D(2) and 115E

concepts.subsection: Section 115F — the long-term gain a non-resident Indian keeps by putting the proceeds back into a specified asset
concepts.statement: Where a non-resident Indian makes a long-term capital gain on a foreign exchange asset and puts the money back into a specified asset within six months of the transfer, section 115F lifts the charge under section 45 off some or all of that gain. The comparison the section makes is the one candidates get wrong: the new asset's cost is set against the net consideration, never against the gain. Net consideration is the full value of the consideration less whatever was spent wholly and exclusively on the transfer itself. Buy a new asset costing at least that net consideration and the whole gain escapes. Buy a cheaper one and the escaping slice is the gain multiplied by the new asset's cost over the net consideration, so a taxpayer who reinvests four fifths of what he received keeps four fifths of his gain out of charge and pays on the rest. The relief is then conditional on holding, and the clock for that runs from the acquisition of the new asset rather than from the transfer of the old one. Sell the new asset, or turn it into money, inside three years of acquiring it, and the gain that escaped charge earlier is deemed to be income under the head Capital Gains relating to a long-term capital asset in the previous year in which the new asset goes — taxed then, in that later year, and not by reopening the year in which the relief was first allowed. Any gain on the new asset itself is charged in that same later year on its own footing, short-term or long-term according to how long the new asset was held.

citation.ref: Section 115F(1) and 115F(2), read with Section 115C(b) and Section 45

concepts.subsection: Sections 115G, 115H and 115-I — the three choices Chapter XII-A leaves open to a non-resident Indian
concepts.statement: Three sections close Chapter XII-A and each of them is a choice or a relief rather than a charge. Section 115G excuses the return. A non-resident Indian need not furnish one under section 139(1) where two things hold together — his total income for the year consists of nothing but investment income, or long-term capital gain of the kind this Chapter deals with, or both of those and nothing else; and tax has been deducted at source from that income. One rupee of any other income, a horse-race winning or a rent, takes the excuse away and the return has to be filed. Section 115H deals with the year the person stops being a non-resident. He may file a declaration in writing along with his return under section 139 for the assessment year in which he first falls to be assessed as a resident, asking that this Chapter go on applying to him. If he does, it does — for that year and every year after it, until the asset is transferred or converted into money. But what the declaration carries forward is narrower than what the Chapter covered while he was non-resident: it reaches the investment income from foreign exchange assets that are debentures, deposits, Central Government securities and other notified assets, and shares of an Indian company are not in that list even though they head the list of specified assets in section 115C. Section 115-I is the door out. A non-resident Indian may choose that the Chapter shall not govern him for a particular assessment year, by furnishing his return for that year with a declaration to that effect in it; his total income for that year is then charged under the ordinary provisions of the Act, which is what a person wants where the general provisions leave him better off — a Chapter VI-A deduction, for instance, which section 115D otherwise denies. The election is made year by year and binds nothing beyond the assessment year it names.

citation.ref: Sections 115G, 115H and 115-I, read with Sections 115C(e), 115D(2) and 139(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 172 — levy and recovery on a single voyage, and the option to be assessed the ordinary way instead
concepts.statement: Section 44B tells you how much of a non-resident shipper's receipts is taxable and stops there; it carries no machinery for assessing or collecting anything. Section 172 is the complete code for the occasional voyage, and it does the whole job. Where a ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident takes on passengers, livestock, mail or goods at a port in India, one fortieth of the amount paid or payable for that carriage — 7.5 per cent — is deemed to be income accruing in India to the owner or the charterer, and demurrage, handling and anything of that nature are drawn into the amount. The master of the ship must prepare and furnish a return of the full amount to the Assessing Officer, ordinarily before the ship leaves that Indian port. A person the master authorises may file it instead, within 30 days of departure, but only where the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the master could not have filed before departure and the master has made satisfactory arrangements for somebody else to file and pay. The Assessing Officer then makes a summary assessment on the deemed income at the rates in force for a foreign company, and the order has to be made within nine months, the clock starting when the financial year in which that return went in comes to a close. The master is liable to pay for it. The Collector of Customs will not grant port clearance to the ship until he is satisfied that the tax has been paid or that satisfactory arrangements exist for paying it, so the levy has teeth a demand notice would not give it. Section 172(7) then offers the owner or charterer a way out of the summary route. He gets the whole of the assessment year that goes with the previous year his ship sailed in, and inside that window he may claim to be assessed on his total income for that previous year under the ordinary provisions instead. A regular assessment follows, whatever was paid under the summary route counts as tax paid in advance, and the difference either way is paid or refunded. The Supreme Court in A.S. Glittre v. CIT described the summary assessment as an ad hoc one that the regular assessment supersedes, and a refund is a real prospect for a non-corporate non-resident, whose own rates sit below the foreign company rate the summary assessment used. Once the regular route is taken, interest under sections 234B and 234C runs against the assessee and interest under section 244A runs in his favour.

citation.ref: Sections 172(2) to 172(8), read with Section 44B; A.S. Glittre v. CIT (1997) 225 ITR 739 (SC) and Circular No. 9/2001 dated 9 July 2001

concepts.subsection: Section 44BBC with Section 10(15B) — the presumptive rate for a cruise operator and the lease rental beside it
concepts.statement: Cruise shipping has been carved out of section 44B and given a scheme of its own. A non-resident running a cruise ship business that meets the prescribed conditions is deemed to earn 20 per cent of two amounts added together — what is paid or becomes payable to him or to anybody on his behalf for carrying passengers, and what he or anybody on his behalf receives or is deemed to receive on that account. Section 44B expressly stands aside for a ship covered by this section, and the two rates differ by a wide margin, 7.5 per cent against 20 per cent. Two things this section does not carry are worth as many marks as the rate. It offers no option to declare a lower figure on audited books, which sections 44BB and 44BBB do offer, so the deemed 20 per cent is the whole computation. And where the deemed figure is declared, no unabsorbed depreciation and no brought-forward loss may be set against it for that year, which is the same restriction section 44BBD carries. Rule 6GB, inserted by CBDT Notification No. 9/2025 of 21 January 2025, sets the conditions: the ship must carry more than 200 passengers or be 75 metres or longer, it must be run for leisure and recreation with proper dining and cabin facilities, it must sail a scheduled voyage or shore excursion touching at least two sea ports in India or the same Indian sea port twice, it must be run mainly to carry passengers and not cargo, and it must follow whatever the Ministry of Tourism or the Ministry of Shipping lays down. Section 10(15B) then completes the design from the other side. Lease rental of a cruise ship, by whatever name it goes, is exempt in the hands of a foreign company receiving it from a specified company — a company other than a domestic company that runs cruise ships in India and has opted into section 44BBC — provided the two are subsidiaries of one and the same holding company, a holding company being one that controls more than half of the total share capital of each, itself or through other subsidiaries. That exemption runs to A.Y. 2030-31 and no further.

citation.ref: Sections 44BBC and 10(15B), read with Section 44B and Rule 6GB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 inserted by Notification No. 9/2025 dated 21 January 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 115BBA with Section 194E — the twenty per cent on a sportsman, an entertainer and a sports association
concepts.statement: Section 115BBA charges 20 per cent on three kinds of receipt and section 194E deducts the same 20 per cent from them at source, so the two sections have to be read as one machine. The first kind is what a sportsman, an athlete included, who is not an Indian citizen and is a non-resident receives or is to receive for taking part in a game or sport in India, for an advertisement, or for contributing articles about a game or sport to a newspaper, magazine or journal in India. Advertising and writing are inside the section even though neither is playing. Winnings from crossword puzzles, races including horse races, card games and other gambling are outside it, because section 115BB charges those at 30 per cent with its own deduction under section 194BB. The second kind is any amount guaranteed to be paid to a non-resident sports association or institution in relation to a game or sport played in India; the Supreme Court in PILCOM held that the words "in relation to" do the work, so guarantee money paid abroad out of a foreign bank account to associations whose teams came and played here was still their Indian income and the payer still had to deduct under section 194E. The third kind is what a non-resident entertainer who is not an Indian citizen receives for performing in India. Against none of the three may any expenditure or allowance be claimed under any provision of the Act, so travel and training costs simply do not enter. Deduction under section 194E happens at credit or payment, whichever comes first, and health and education cess at 4 per cent rides on the 20 per cent because the payee is a non-resident. Where a person's total income for the year is nothing but income of these kinds and tax has been fully deducted from it, he need not file a return under section 139(1). And the section has an edge: the Calcutta High Court in Indcom v. CIT (TDS) held that match referees and umpires are professional or technical people rather than sportsmen, so their fees fall outside section 115BBA and outside section 194E altogether — the fees are still income accruing in India, and tax on them is deducted under section 195 at the rates in force instead.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBA(1) and 115BBA(2) and Section 194E, read with Sections 115BB, 194BB and 195; Indcom v. CIT (TDS) (2011) 335 ITR 485 (Cal) and PILCOM v. CIT (2020) 425 ITR 312 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Section 92A(2) — the deeming limbs, each with its own figure
concepts.statement: Section 92A(1) states the ordinary test. Two enterprises are associated where one takes part in the management, the control or the capital of the other, or where the same person or persons take part in the management, the control or the capital of both; participation counts whether it is direct, indirect, or routed through intermediaries, so a parent that controls a subsidiary is associated with that subsidiary's own subsidiary as well. Section 92A(2) then supplies thirteen situations in which the relationship is simply deemed to exist, and it is the list an examiner reaches for, because most of the limbs are numbers. Voting power of twenty-six per cent or more, held directly or indirectly, by one enterprise in the other or by a common person in each of two enterprises. A loan from one enterprise to the other worth fifty-one per cent or more of the book value of the borrower's total assets. A guarantee by one enterprise covering ten per cent or more of what the other has borrowed. The power to put more than half the board of the other in place, or even to put a single executive director on it — and the same test again where one person wields that power over each of two enterprises. Manufacture by one enterprise that leans entirely on know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences or similar rights belonging to the other or exclusively available to it. Ninety per cent or more of one enterprise's raw materials and consumables coming from the other or from suppliers the other names, on terms the other influences. Goods made by one enterprise going to the other or to buyers the other names, again on terms the other influences. Control of one enterprise by an individual while a relative of his controls the second. Control of one by a Hindu undivided family while a member of that family, or his relative, controls the second. An interest of ten per cent or more in an enterprise that is a firm, an association of persons or a body of individuals. Two things about the list decide questions. Any single limb is enough, so a shareholding well under twenty-six per cent settles nothing on its own; and the relationship has only to hold at some point during the previous year, not throughout it.

citation.ref: Sections 92A(1) and 92A(2), read with the definition of enterprise in Section 92F(iii)

concepts.subsection: Section 92B(2) — a deal with a stranger that counts as a deal with the group
concepts.statement: An enterprise that wants its transfer prices left alone could route the sale through somebody unrelated and let that person pass the goods on to the group. Section 92B(2) closes that road. Where an enterprise transacts with a person who is not its associated enterprise, and either an agreement about that very transaction was already in place between that other person and the associated enterprise, or the terms of it were in substance settled between those two, and either the enterprise or its associated enterprise is a non-resident, then the deal between the enterprise and the outsider is treated as an international transaction between associated enterprises. The sub-section says in terms that this holds whether or not the outsider is himself a non-resident, so his residence is never the question — what matters is the earlier understanding standing behind him and the non-residence of somebody in the pair of associated enterprises. Two further points come from the definitions rather than from the sub-section. A transaction under section 92F(v) takes in an arrangement, an understanding or action in concert, put in writing or not, and enforceable at law or not; so an informal understanding is enough. And section 92B(1) itself reaches beyond buying and selling to the provision of services, to lending and borrowing, to capital financing of any tenure, to business restructuring or reorganisation, and to any other dealing that bears on the profits, the income, the losses or the assets of the enterprises.

citation.ref: Section 92B(1) and Section 92B(2), read with the definition of transaction in Section 92F(v)

concepts.subsection: Dealings inside one legal person — which branch can have an international transaction
concepts.statement: Chapter X bites only where at least one of the two associated enterprises is a non-resident, and that single condition decides every question about branches. Take an Indian company first. A company resident in India is resident for the whole of itself, so its branches abroad are limbs of a resident; what the head office charges a foreign branch, and what one foreign branch charges another, are dealings between residents and fall outside the definition altogether. There is nothing for the machinery to correct either, because the profits of every one of those branches are already inside the Indian tax net. Now turn the picture round. A foreign company's Indian branch is its permanent establishment here and is taxed in India on what it does here, while the head office abroad is taxed abroad. Money can therefore be moved between them across a tax boundary, and it is: what that Indian branch pays its own head office, or pays a fellow branch of the same company in a third country, is an international transaction and has to stand at an arm's length price. The same is true of dealings between an Indian parent and its foreign subsidiary, which are two separate persons to begin with. The lesson worth carrying is that the question is never whether the two sides are separate legal persons — inside one foreign company they are not — but whether the profit can leave the Indian tax net by the price that is charged.

citation.ref: Section 92B read with Section 92(1) and the residence rules in Section 6(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 92CA(3B) — one arm's length price carried across the next two years
concepts.statement: The Finance Act, 2025 added a way to settle a recurring transaction once instead of every year. Where the Transfer Pricing Officer has determined an arm's length price for a transaction for one previous year, that price may be applied to a similar international transaction for the two previous years immediately following, and three things have to happen before it is. The assessee has to exercise an option for those two years; the option has to go in the prescribed form and manner and inside the prescribed period; and the officer has to declare it valid by an order in writing, which he must pass within one month counted from the end of the month in which the option was exercised. Search assessments are outside the scheme. Once the option stands declared valid, no reference for those years is to be made, and a reference already made — before that declaration or after it — is treated as though it had never been made. The officer then examines and determines the price for those two following years in his own order, and on receiving it the Assessing Officer recomputes the total income of both years under section 155(21). The Board may issue guidelines to clear up any difficulty in working the scheme, with the Central Government's prior approval, but its power to do so runs out two years after 1 April 2026. What the scheme does not do is make the option a substitute for the officer's judgement: he still determines the price for both following years, and what the assessee is spared is the reference and the separate proceeding, not the determination.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(3B) and Section 92CA(4A) with the provisos to Section 92CA(1), read with Section 155(21), as inserted by the Finance Act, 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 92CA(3A) — the sixty days the Assessing Officer must be left
concepts.statement: A reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer sits inside the Assessing Officer's own limitation period, and the assessment cannot be completed until his order arrives. Section 92CA(3A) therefore makes the officer finish first, and by a stated margin: his order determining the arm's length price has to be passed at any time before the sixtieth day preceding the day on which the limitation for making the assessment order under section 153, or under section 153B, runs out. That margin is what the Assessing Officer then has to give effect to the order and frame the assessment. Two things can eat into the officer's own time without being his fault — a court staying the assessment proceedings, and a request for information sent to another country under an agreement made under section 90 or section 90A. So the section repairs the damage rather than simply excluding the lost days: where, after taking out the period of the stay or the time spent waiting for the information, what is left to him is under sixty days, the remaining period is stretched to sixty days. The consequence worth holding is that the clock is not merely paused; the officer is guaranteed a floor of sixty days, which can push the assessment's own outer date out with it.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(3A) with its proviso, read with Sections 153 and 153B and Sections 90 and 90A

concepts.subsection: Section 92D and Rule 10D — who keeps transfer pricing records, and for how long
concepts.statement: Section 92D lays two separate duties. Anybody who enters into an international transaction keeps the prescribed information and documents about it. Separately, a constituent entity of an international group keeps prescribed information about the group, and that duty does not wait on the entity having transacted with anybody — it applies whether or not the entity itself undertook any international transaction at all, and what it keeps goes to the authority named under section 286(1). Rule 10D(1) is the list the first duty points at: the ownership structure, a profile of the group, a description of the business and the industry, the nature and terms and value of each transaction, the functions performed and risks assumed and assets employed, the economic analyses, the uncontrolled transactions used as comparables and the comparability study, the methods considered with reasons for the one chosen, the actual workings, the assumptions and negotiations that moved the price, and the adjustments made. It runs to thirteen heads. Rule 10D(2) then lifts that list where the aggregate value of the international transactions does not go past one crore rupees — and lifts only the list. The assessee still has to be able to show that the income arising from those transactions is what section 92 requires, so records and evidence enough to prove the arm's length character are needed at any size. Rule 10D(4) requires the documents to be contemporaneous and to be in existence by the specified date, which is one month before the section 139(1) due date and falls on 31 October of the assessment year; where a transaction runs on across financial years, fresh documents are not needed each year unless something has changed enough to move the price. Rule 10D(5) fixes how long they are kept, and it is eight years counted from the end of the relevant assessment year — a period that outlives the assessment itself. Section 92D(3) is the production duty: on a notice, the information has to be furnished within ten days of receiving it, and that may be extended, on a request, by a further period which cannot go beyond thirty days.

citation.ref: Sections 92D(1), 92D(2) and 92D(3), read with Rules 10D(1), 10D(2), 10D(4) and 10D(5) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Section 286(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 271G — the penalty measured against the transaction, not against the tax
concepts.statement: Where a person who has entered into an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction is asked under section 92D(3) for information or documents and does not produce them inside the ten days allowed, or inside the extension of up to thirty days if one was granted, section 271G makes him liable to a sum of two per cent of the value of that transaction, and it bites separately for each failure. Two features of it are worth holding. The measure is the size of the transaction, not the tax on any income — so a penalty can run even where the pricing turns out to have been right and no adjustment was ever made. And the Transfer Pricing Officer is himself competent to direct it, alongside the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals); his authority does not end with the order determining the price. Around it sit two neighbouring penalties with different triggers. Section 271AA charges two per cent of the value of each such transaction where the prescribed documents were never kept at all, where a reportable transaction went unreported, or where what was kept or furnished was incorrect — and it is charged in addition to, never instead of, the penalty for not furnishing the accountant's report. All three are subject to the general relief for a failure the assessee can show a reasonable cause for.

citation.ref: Section 271G read with Sections 92D(3), 271AA and 273B

concepts.subsection: Section 270A(6)(d) — the transfer pricing addition that is not under-reported income
concepts.statement: An upward adjustment lifts assessed income above returned income, which is the ordinary shape of under-reporting, and under-reported income normally draws a penalty of fifty per cent of the tax on it. Section 270A(6)(d) takes a transfer pricing addition out of that reckoning, but only for a taxpayer who did everything the chapter asked of him first. Three conditions have to be met together: he kept the information and documents section 92D prescribes, he declared the international transaction as Chapter X requires, and he disclosed every material fact about it. Where all three hold, the amount added in line with the arm's length price the Transfer Pricing Officer determined does not enter under-reported income at all, so there is nothing to charge the fifty per cent on. Two limits on the relief decide questions. It is written for an international transaction and stops there, so an addition the officer makes on a specified domestic transaction stays inside under-reported income however carefully the taxpayer documented and declared it. And a taxpayer who never reported the transaction is in a worse position than one who priced it wrongly: failing to report an international transaction, or a transaction deemed to be one, is treated as misreporting under section 270A(9), and misreported income carries two hundred per cent of the tax rather than fifty.
