concepts.statement: An impairment loss on a cash-generating unit is allocated in a fixed order, first against any goodwill allocated to the unit until that goodwill is nil, and only then across the unit's other assets pro rata on their carrying amounts. No individual asset may be written below the highest of its own fair value less costs of disposal where measurable, its value in use where determinable, and zero; whatever the floor blocks is reallocated pro rata to the remaining assets. Goodwill written off this way can never be reversed in a later period, even if the unit recovers.

citation.ref: para 104 and 105, with the reversal bar in para 124

concepts.section: Ind AS on Measurement based on Accounting Policies
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 113 — Principal market and the price used
concepts.statement: Fair value is measured in the principal market, the market with the greatest volume and level of activity that the entity can access, and only where no principal market exists does the most advantageous market answer. Where a principal market exists, its price is used even if a different market would net the entity more. That price is not adjusted for transaction costs, which are specific to a transaction rather than a characteristic of the asset, but it is adjusted for transport costs where location is a characteristic of the asset.

citation.ref: para 16, 18, 25 and 26

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — Presenting a discontinued operation
concepts.statement: A discontinued operation is a component disposed of or classified as held for sale that is a separate major line of business or geographical area, part of a single coordinated plan to dispose of one, or a subsidiary acquired exclusively for resale. Its post-tax result and the post-tax gain or loss on measurement or disposal are collapsed into a single amount in the statement of profit and loss, with the analysis given in the notes. The profit or loss figures for prior periods are re-presented on the same basis; the balance sheets of prior periods are expressly left alone.

citation.ref: para 32, 33, 34 and 40

concepts.section: Ind AS on Liabilities of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 19 — Past service cost
concepts.statement: When a plan amendment or a curtailment moves the present value of the obligation the entity owes its employees, the size of that move is the past service cost. It is recognised as an expense in full at the earlier of the date the amendment or curtailment occurs and the date the entity recognises related restructuring costs or termination benefits. There is no spreading over a vesting period and no distinction between vested and unvested benefits, and past service cost is part of service cost in profit or loss, not a remeasurement in other comprehensive income.

citation.ref: para 102 and 103, with the components in para 120

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Attributing results to non-controlling interests
concepts.statement: Every result of a subsidiary is split between two claimants — the parent's owners on one side and the non-controlling interests on the other. Profit or loss is split that way, so is each separate component of other comprehensive income, and so is the total of the two, even where the split drives the minority into a deficit balance. There is no floor at nil here, unlike the equity method for an associate. Where a subsidiary has cumulative preference shares classified as equity and held outside the group, the group works out its share only after taking off the dividends on those shares, declared or not.

citation.ref: para B94, read with B95

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — The investment entity exception
concepts.statement: An investment entity is one that takes funds from investors to provide them with investment management services, commits to invest solely for capital appreciation or investment income, and measures performance on a fair value basis. It does not consolidate its subsidiaries and does not apply Ind AS 103 on obtaining control; it measures each investment in a subsidiary at fair value through profit or loss. The one carve-out is a subsidiary providing services relating to the investment entity's own investment activities, which is consolidated. A parent that is not itself an investment entity consolidates everything it controls, including what it controls through an investment entity subsidiary.

citation.ref: para 27, 31, 32 and 33

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — Upstream and downstream transactions with an associate
concepts.statement: Gains and losses on sales between an investor and its associate or joint venture are recognised only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests, so the investor's own percentage of the unrealised profit is eliminated and no more. A downstream sale reduces the investor's own profit by its share; an upstream sale reduces its share of the associate's profit. Elimination is never in full, which is where an associate parts company with a consolidated subsidiary. Where the transaction evidences a fall in net realisable value or an impairment, that loss is recognised in full on a downstream sale.

citation.ref: para 28, read with para 29

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 111 — Acquiring an interest in a joint operation that is a business
concepts.statement: Where the activity of a joint operation constitutes a business, an entity acquiring an interest in it applies, to the extent of its share, all the Ind AS 103 business combination principles that do not conflict with Ind AS 111 — identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, acquisition-related costs expensed, goodwill recognised and tested annually. This holds for an additional interest as much as the first. The departure from a step acquisition is that previously held interests are not remeasured where the joint operator retains joint control.

citation.ref: para 21A, with B33A and B33C

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Translating a foreign operation into the presentation currency
concepts.statement: To carry a foreign operation into a different presentation currency, assets and liabilities for every balance sheet presented go at the closing rate at that balance sheet date, income and expenses go at the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions with an average rate accepted as an approximation, and all resulting exchange differences go to other comprehensive income. Those differences come from two sources, retranslating the opening net assets at a new closing rate and translating the result at a rate that is not the closing rate, and they accumulate in a separate component of equity until disposal.

citation.ref: para 39, read with 40 and 41

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Measuring a cash flow hedge
concepts.statement: The cash flow hedge reserve is adjusted to the lower, in absolute amounts, of the cumulative gain or loss on the hedging instrument and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows, both from inception. That effective portion goes to other comprehensive income and everything left over is hedge ineffectiveness in profit or loss. If the hedged forecast transaction later produces a non-financial asset or liability, the accumulated reserve is removed and included directly in that item's initial cost, which is not a reclassification adjustment; in every other case it is reclassified to profit or loss in the periods the hedged cash flows affect profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 6.5.11(a) to (d)

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — The general expected credit loss model
concepts.statement: Outside the simplified approach, a loss allowance is measured at 12-month expected credit losses unless credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, when it moves to lifetime expected credit losses. The test compares the risk of a default occurring at the reporting date with that risk at initial recognition, not the change in the amount of the losses. Two shortcuts sit either side of it — an entity may assume no significant increase where the instrument has low credit risk at the reporting date, and there is a rebuttable presumption of a significant increase once contractual payments are more than 30 days past due.

concepts.section: Ind AS on Liabilities of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Measuring a provision
concepts.statement: Measured at the reporting date, a provision is what the entity best estimates it will have to spend to be rid of the present obligation. Where a large population of items is involved the estimate is the expected value, weighting all possible outcomes by their probabilities; where a single obligation is involved the most likely outcome may be the best estimate. Discounting is required only where the effect of the time value of money is material, at a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments and the risks specific to the liability. A reimbursement is recognised only when it is virtually certain, as a separate asset capped at the provision, and may be netted only in the statement of profit and loss.

citation.ref: para 36, 39, 45, 47 and 53, with the presentation in para 54

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 20 — Repaying a government grant
concepts.statement: A government grant that becomes repayable is a change in accounting estimate, never a prior period error. Repayment of a grant related to income is applied first against any unamortised deferred credit, with the excess straight to profit or loss. Repayment of a grant related to an asset is recognised by increasing the carrying amount of the asset or reducing the deferred income balance, and the cumulative additional depreciation that would have been charged in the absence of the grant goes immediately to profit or loss. The pre-2018 Indian text allowed only the deferred income route and carried no depreciation catch-up.

citation.ref: para 32 as substituted in 2018, with para 33

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 41 — Government grants for biological assets
concepts.statement: Ind AS 41 deliberately departs from Ind AS 20 for a biological asset measured at fair value less costs to sell. An unconditional grant on such an asset goes to profit or loss when, and only when, it becomes receivable — not when it is received and not spread over anything. A conditional grant goes to profit or loss when, and only when, the conditions are met, with time-apportionment allowed only where the terms let part of the grant be retained as time passes. Ind AS 20 returns only where the biological asset is measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment.

citation.ref: para 34, 35 and 36, with the scope split in para 37 and 38

concepts.section: Ind AS 115 Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix C — Service concession arrangements
concepts.statement: Infrastructure inside a public-to-private service concession is never the operator's property, plant and equipment, because the arrangement does not convey the right to control its use. The operator is a service provider, and what it books for construction depends on what the grantor gives back. An unconditional contractual right to receive cash from the grantor produces a financial asset; a right, or licence, to charge users of the public service produces an intangible asset, because those amounts turn on how much the public uses the service. That split also decides borrowing costs — expensed under the financial asset model, capitalised during construction under the intangible asset model.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 11, 16, 17 and 22

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 23 — Capitalisation rate on general borrowings
concepts.statement: Funds borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset yield the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. Funds borrowed generally yield a capitalisation rate applied to the expenditure on the asset, the rate being the weighted average of the borrowing costs on the entity's borrowings outstanding during the period other than those made specifically for a qualifying asset. Whatever the two limbs produce, the amount capitalised in a period can never exceed the borrowing costs actually incurred in that period.

citation.ref: para 12 and 14

concepts.section: Ind AS on Disclosures in the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 33 — Rights issue and the bonus element
concepts.statement: A rights issue priced below fair value is part fresh money and part gift, and only the gift is retrospective. The shares outstanding before the issue are multiplied by the fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share, that theoretical price being the aggregate fair value of the existing shares plus the proceeds of the rights, divided by the shares outstanding after the exercise. The adjusted number is used for all periods before the rights issue, so the comparative earnings per share is restated, while the new shares themselves enter the weighted average from their own date.

citation.ref: para 27(b), with Appendix A, para A2

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 34 — Income tax in an interim period
concepts.statement: The tax charge in an interim period comes from a single rate — the entity's own best estimate, taken across the year as a whole, of its weighted average annual income tax rate — put against profit measured from the start of the year to that date. When the estimate of that annual rate changes, the amount accrued in an earlier interim period of the same financial year is adjusted through the later interim period, so the catch-up lands in the current quarter. Amounts reported in earlier interim periods are not retrospectively adjusted, and no interim period is measured as though it stood alone.

citation.ref: para 30(c), read with para 28 and para 36

concepts.section: Ind AS on Disclosures in the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 108 — Entity-wide disclosures
concepts.statement: Three disclosures bind every entity within Ind AS 108, including one with a single reportable segment, and are given only where the segment note has not already given them. Revenues from external customers by product or service; revenues and non-current assets, leaving out financial instruments, deferred tax assets, assets for post-employment benefits and rights under insurance contracts, split between the country of domicile and all foreign countries in total with any material individual country shown separately; and the fact of any single external customer at 10 per cent or more of revenues, with the amount and the reporting segment but not the customer's name.

citation.ref: para 31, 33 and 34

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 — Modifying and cancelling an equity-settled award
concepts.statement: Whatever is done to an equity-settled award afterwards, the entity recognises as a minimum the services received at the grant date fair value of the instruments granted, unless they fail a vesting condition other than a market condition. On top of that it recognises the effects of modifications that increase the total fair value or are otherwise beneficial to the employee. The incremental fair value is the difference between the modified and the original instrument, both measured at the modification date, spread from that date to vesting. A modification that reduces fair value is ignored, and a cancellation or settlement during the vesting period is an acceleration of vesting.

citation.ref: para 27 and 28, with Appendix B, para B43 and B44

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Changes in liabilities arising from financing activities
concepts.statement: An entity must let a reader move from the opening to the closing balance of every liability whose cash flows sit in financing activities, and the movement is split five ways — what the financing cash flows themselves did to it; what taking over a subsidiary or another business, or letting one go, brought in or carried away with it; what the exchange rates did; what fair value did; and whatever is left after those four. The disclosure covers the non-cash movements as well as the cash ones, which is what makes it more than a repeat of the financing section, and a reconciliation between opening and closing balance sheet amounts is the way the Standard itself suggests fulfilling it.

citation.ref: para 44A, 44B, 44C and 44D

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Supplier finance arrangements
concepts.statement: A supplier finance arrangement is one where a finance provider offers to pay what the entity owes its suppliers and the entity agrees to pay the provider on the same date or later, so the entity gets extended payment terms or its suppliers get early payment. Reverse factoring, payables finance and supply chain finance are the usual names. Two things are expressly not such arrangements — instruments that are solely credit enhancements for the entity, such as letters of credit used as guarantees, and instruments used to settle directly with a supplier, such as credit cards. Where the arrangement exists the entity discloses the terms and conditions, the carrying amounts and the balance sheet line items, how much of that the finance providers have already paid the suppliers, the range of payment due dates against comparable ordinary trade payables, and the non-cash changes. In India this bites for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025.

citation.ref: para 44F, 44G and 44H, with the Indian application date in the effective date section

concepts.section: Ind AS on Measurement based on Accounting Policies
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Choosing a policy where no Ind AS applies
concepts.statement: Where no Ind AS covers a transaction, management develops a policy giving information that is relevant to users and reliable, and it must first work down a two-step order it cannot skip — the requirements in Ind ASs dealing with similar and related issues, then the definitions, recognition criteria and measurement concepts in the Framework. Only after that may it look further, and the Indian text orders even that optional layer: it may first consider the most recent pronouncements of the International Accounting Standards Board, and in the absence of those, the pronouncements of other standard-setting bodies using a similar conceptual framework, other accounting literature and accepted industry practice — none of which may conflict with the mandatory two steps.

citation.ref: para 10, 11 and 12

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 — Depreciating significant parts separately
concepts.statement: A part whose own cost is significant against the total cost of an item of property, plant and equipment is depreciated on its own, the airframe and the engines of an aircraft being the Standard's own example. Parts with the same useful life and the same depreciation method may be grouped. Once any part is depreciated separately the remainder of the item — the parts that are individually not significant — is depreciated separately too, with approximation techniques allowed where expectations for those parts vary. An entity may also choose to depreciate a part separately even where its cost is not significant.

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 Appendix A — Changes in an existing decommissioning liability
concepts.statement: A change in the estimated timing or amount of a decommissioning outflow, or in the discount rate, is not a gain or a loss on the day it happens. Under the cost model the change is added to or deducted from the cost of the related asset in the current period, the deduction is capped at the asset's carrying amount, and any excess of a decrease over that carrying amount goes immediately to profit or loss; an addition is an indication to test the asset for impairment. Under the revaluation model the change moves the revaluation surplus instead. Once the asset has reached the end of its useful life every later change goes straight to profit or loss. The periodic unwinding of the discount is a finance cost in profit or loss, and capitalisation of it under Ind AS 23 is not permitted.

citation.ref: Appendix A, para 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 38 — Recognising expenditure in the development phase
concepts.statement: An intangible asset arising from development is recognised if, and only if, the entity can demonstrate all six of technical feasibility of completing the asset so that it will be available for use or sale, its intention to complete and use or sell it, its ability to use or sell it, how it will generate probable future economic benefits, the availability of adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete it, and its ability to measure reliably the expenditure attributable to it during development. The cost is the sum of expenditure incurred from the date the criteria are first met and no earlier, and expenditure once recognised as an expense may never be reinstated as part of the cost of the asset.

citation.ref: para 57, read with 65, 67 and 71

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 40 — Transfers into and out of investment property
concepts.statement: A transfer to or from investment property is made when, and only when, there is a change in use, evidenced by commencement of owner-occupation, commencement of development with a view to sale, end of owner-occupation, or commencement of an operating lease to another party. A decision to dispose of an investment property without developing it is not a change in use, so the property stays investment property until it is derecognised; redevelopment of an investment property for continued use as investment property is not one either. Because India permits only the cost model for investment property, no transfer between investment property, owner-occupied property and inventories changes the carrying amount of the property or its cost for measurement or disclosure.

citation.ref: para 57, 58 and 59, read with para 56

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 2 — Costs that stay out of the cost of inventories
concepts.statement: Cost of inventories is costs of purchase, costs of conversion and other costs of bringing the inventories to their present location and condition. Costs of purchase take in the purchase price, import duties and other taxes not subsequently recoverable, and transport and handling, less trade discounts and rebates. Four things are named as excluded and expensed as incurred — abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour or other production costs; storage, unless the goods must be held before a further production stage; administrative overheads that add nothing to getting the inventories where and as they are; and selling costs. Where inventories are bought on deferred settlement terms containing a financing element, that element is interest expense over the period of the financing, not part of cost.

concepts.section: Ind AS 115 Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix B — A licence as a right to access or a right to use
concepts.statement: Where a licence of intellectual property is a separate performance obligation, its nature is a right to access only if three criteria are all met — the contract requires, or the customer reasonably expects, activities by the entity that significantly affect the intellectual property; the licence directly exposes the customer to the positive or negative effects of those activities; and those activities do not themselves transfer a good or service. Activities significantly affect the property where they are expected to change its form or functionality, or where the customer's benefit substantially depends on them, which is why a brand usually differs from a completed film or a piece of software with significant stand-alone functionality. A right to access is satisfied over time; a right to use is satisfied at a point in time, and never before the customer can use and benefit from the licence. A sales-based or usage-based royalty is recognised only at the later of the sale or usage occurring and the performance obligation being satisfied.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, B59A, B60, B61, B62 and B63

concepts.section: Ind AS 115 Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix B — Assurance-type and service-type warranties
concepts.statement: A warranty the customer can buy separately is a distinct service and therefore a performance obligation, and part of the transaction price is allocated to it. A warranty the customer cannot buy separately goes to Ind AS 37 as a provision, unless it, or part of it, gives the customer a service beyond the assurance that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications, in which case that part is a performance obligation. Where both kinds are promised and cannot reasonably be accounted for separately, they are accounted for together as a single performance obligation. A law making the entity liable for damage its products cause, and an indemnity against infringement claims, create no performance obligation at all.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B28 to B33, with para 74, 76 and 81

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Classifying a sublease
concepts.statement: An intermediate lessor classifies a sublease by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, not by reference to the underlying asset, so the comparison is with what is left of the head lease term rather than with the economic life of the building or the machine. The one exception runs the other way — where the head lease is a short-term lease the entity has taken the recognition exemption on, the sublease is an operating lease. Where the sublease comes out as a finance lease the intermediate lessor uses the interest rate implicit in the sublease, and if that cannot be readily determined it may use the discount rate used for the head lease, adjusted for initial direct costs on the sublease.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, with para 68 and the Appendix A definition of a sublease

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 Appendix C — Uncertainty over income tax treatments
concepts.statement: An uncertain tax treatment is one where it is uncertain whether the taxation authority will accept it under tax law. The entity first decides whether to look at each uncertainty on its own or grouped with others, on whichever better predicts the resolution. It must then assume the authority will examine every amount it has a right to examine and will have full knowledge of all related information — there is no allowance for the chance of not being caught. If acceptance is probable, the filed treatment is used. If it is not probable, the effect of the uncertainty is reflected using either the most likely amount, where the outcomes are binary or concentrated on one value, or the expected value, being the probability-weighted sum, where they are neither. A later change in facts or new information is a change in accounting estimate.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14

concepts.section: Ind AS on Disclosures in the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 24 — The government-related entity exemption
concepts.statement: A reporting entity is exempt from the paragraph 18 disclosures for transactions and balances with a government that controls, jointly controls or significantly influences it, and with any other entity the same government controls, jointly controls or significantly influences. The exemption is bought, not free: the entity must instead give the name of the government and the nature of the relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction, and a qualitative or quantitative indication of the extent of the transactions that are collectively but not individually significant. Judgement on how much detail turns on the closeness of the relationship, the size of the transaction and whether it was on non-market terms. Nothing in the exemption reaches key management personnel compensation or the disclosure of the parent's name.

citation.ref: para 25, 26 and 27

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Splitting a compound financial instrument
concepts.statement: A bond convertible by the holder into a fixed number of the issuer's own ordinary shares is a single non-derivative instrument holding both a liability and an equity component, and the two are presented separately in the balance sheet. The split is a residual one and only in that direction: the liability component is measured first, as the fair value of a similar liability without the conversion feature, and the equity component is whatever is left of the fair value of the instrument as a whole. Any embedded derivative other than the equity conversion option stays inside the liability component. No gain or loss arises on splitting, and the classification is never revised because conversion has become more or less likely.

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 107 — Liquidity and market risk disclosures
concepts.statement: For each type of risk arising from financial instruments the entity gives the qualitative picture — the exposures and how they arise, its objectives, policies and processes for managing the risk, the methods used to measure it, and any change from last year — and summary quantitative data on the basis of what goes internally to key management personnel. For liquidity risk it gives a maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities and a separate one for derivative financial liabilities showing remaining contractual maturities, at contractual undiscounted cash flows rather than balance sheet carrying amounts, with an issued financial guarantee contract entering at its maximum amount in the earliest period the guarantee could be called. For market risk it gives a sensitivity analysis for each type, showing the effect on profit or loss and on equity of changes that were reasonably possible at the reporting date, unless it uses a value-at-risk analysis instead.

citation.ref: para 33, 34, 39 and 40, with Appendix B, para B11C and B11D

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 27 — Measuring investments in separate financial statements
concepts.statement: In separate financial statements an entity accounts for investments in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates either at cost or in accordance with Ind AS 109, and it must apply the same accounting for each category of investments. There is no third option: the equity method that IAS 27 permits was deliberately left out of Ind AS 27, on the reasoning that the equity method is a manner of consolidation rather than a measurement basis like cost or fair value. An investment carried at cost moves to Ind AS 105 when it is classified as held for sale, while one carried under Ind AS 109 does not change. A dividend from a subsidiary, joint venture or associate is recognised in profit or loss when the right to receive it is established.

citation.ref: para 10, 11A and 12, with the Comparison with IAS 27, item 2

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 29 — Restating in a hyperinflationary economy
concepts.statement: Ind AS 29 sets no absolute rate at which hyperinflation arises; it lists indicators, of which cumulative inflation over three years approaching or exceeding 100 per cent is only one, and leaves the call to judgement. Once made, the Standard applies from the beginning of the reporting period in which the entity identifies the hyperinflation, not from the day the index crossed anything. Financial statements are then stated in the measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period, comparatives included. Balance sheet amounts not already in that unit are restated by a general price index; monetary items are not restated because they are already in it; all items in the statement of profit and loss are restated; and the gain or loss on the net monetary position goes to profit or loss and is separately disclosed.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 106 — Exploration and evaluation assets
concepts.statement: Exploration and evaluation assets are measured at cost on recognition, and after recognition the entity may keep the cost model or apply a revaluation model consistent with whether it has classified the assets as tangible or intangible. Expenditure on the development of mineral resources is outside the definition and cannot be recognised as an exploration and evaluation asset. The moment the technical feasibility and commercial viability of extracting a mineral resource are demonstrable the assets stop being exploration and evaluation assets, and they must be tested for impairment and any loss recognised before they are reclassified. For impairment the entity sets its own policy for allocating the assets to cash-generating units, but no such unit or group of units may be larger than an operating segment.

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Cash flows on acquiring and disposing of a subsidiary
concepts.statement: The aggregate cash flows from obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary are presented as a single separate line and classified as investing, and the amount shown is the cash consideration actually paid or received NET of the cash and cash equivalents that came in or went out with the subsidiary. Consideration settled in the acquirer's own shares is a non-cash transaction and never enters the statement. A change in ownership interest that does NOT cost the parent control is a transaction with owners, so its cash flows are financing, not investing. Alongside all this the entity discloses in aggregate the total consideration, how much of it was cash and cash equivalents, the cash and cash equivalents in the subsidiary, and the other assets and liabilities involved.

citation.ref: para 39 to 42B, with the exclusion of non-cash transactions in para 43

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Treasury shares
concepts.statement: An entity's own equity instruments reacquired by the entity, or by any other member of the consolidated group, are treasury shares and are deducted from equity. No gain and no loss goes to profit or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation, whatever happens to the market price, and the consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity. The shares are not a financial asset of the group, so they are never fair-valued through profit or loss and never impaired. The amount of treasury shares held is disclosed separately, in the balance sheet or in the notes.

citation.ref: para 33 and 34

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Offsetting a financial asset against a financial liability
concepts.statement: A financial asset and a financial liability are offset and the net amount presented when, and only when, both conditions hold together — the entity's right to set the two recognised amounts against each other must be one the law will enforce and must be available now rather than only on some future event, and it must intend either to settle net or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Now is the word that does the work: a right exercisable only on a future event such as the counterparty's default is not a current right, which is why an ordinary master netting arrangement does not on its own permit offsetting. Both conditions must also survive the ordinary course of business, not merely the event of default or insolvency.

citation.ref: para 42, read with the conditions elaborated in paras 43 to 50

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Reversing an impairment loss
concepts.statement: At the end of every reporting period the entity looks for any indication that an impairment loss recognised in an earlier period on an asset other than goodwill no longer exists or has decreased, and reverses it if, and only if, the estimates used to determine recoverable amount have changed since that loss was recognised. The reversal is capped: the increased carrying amount must not exceed the carrying amount, net of depreciation, that would have stood had no impairment loss ever been recognised. The reversal goes to profit or loss unless the asset is carried at a revalued amount, and the depreciation charge is then reset over the remaining life. An impairment loss recognised for goodwill is never reversed.

citation.ref: para 110, 114, 117 and 119, with the goodwill bar in para 124

concepts.section: Ind AS on Liabilities of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — What goes into a restructuring provision
concepts.statement: Once a restructuring provision is due to be recognised, its amount is confined to the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring — those both necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. Retraining or relocating continuing staff, marketing, and investment in new systems and distribution networks are named as excluded, because they relate to the future conduct of the business. Identifiable future operating losses up to the date of the restructuring are excluded too, unless they arise on a contract that is itself onerous.

citation.ref: para 80, 81 and 82, read with the obligating event in para 72

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Offsetting and presenting tax balances
concepts.statement: Current tax assets and current tax liabilities are netted off only where two things sit together: a right of set-off the law will enforce, and a plan either to settle net or to realise the asset and discharge the liability at one time. Deferred tax assets and liabilities carry a harder test: that same enforceable right over the CURRENT tax balances must exist, and both deferred balances must arise on taxes charged by one and the same taxation authority — either on a single taxable entity, or on different taxable entities that intend to settle net in every future period in which material amounts reverse. Two members of one group are two taxable entities, so their deferred tax balances do not offset in the consolidated balance sheet merely because they are consolidated. No deferred tax balance is ever classified as current.

citation.ref: para 71 and 74, with the classification bar in Ind AS 1 para 56

concepts.section: Ind AS on Liabilities of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 19 — The asset ceiling on a plan surplus
concepts.statement: A surplus in a defined benefit plan is not automatically an asset of the employer. Where plan assets exceed the present value of the obligation, the net defined benefit asset is measured at the LOWER of that surplus and the asset ceiling, the asset ceiling being today's value of whatever the employer can genuinely extract from the plan — money handed back to it, or contributions it will not have to pay in later years. Any change in the effect of the asset ceiling, other than the part already inside net interest, is a remeasurement: it goes to other comprehensive income and is never reclassified to profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 64, with the remeasurement components in para 127 and the OCI treatment in para 120 and 122

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — A change in functional currency
concepts.statement: A functional currency, once determined, changes only when the underlying transactions, events and conditions relevant to it change — it is not a policy choice and it is not revisited for convenience. When it does change, the translation procedures for the new functional currency are applied PROSPECTIVELY from the date of the change: every item is translated into the new functional currency at the exchange rate ruling on that date, and the translated amounts of non-monetary items are treated from then on as their historical cost. Nothing is restated, and exchange differences already accumulated in other comprehensive income on translating a foreign operation stay in equity until that operation is disposed of.

citation.ref: para 35 to 37 on a change in functional currency, read with the reclassification on disposal in para 48

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — When the plan of sale changes
concepts.statement: When an asset no longer meets the held-for-sale criteria, classification ceases, and the asset comes back onto the balance sheet at the LOWER of two figures: its carrying amount before it was ever classified as held for sale, adjusted for the depreciation, amortisation or revaluation that would have been recognised had it never been classified; and its recoverable amount at the date of the decision not to sell. The suspended depreciation is caught up, not forgiven. Any adjustment falls in profit or loss from CONTINUING operations in the period the criteria stop being met, in the same caption used for a gain or loss on remeasurement.

citation.ref: para 26, 27 and 28

concepts.section: Ind AS on Disclosures in the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 108 — Aggregating operating segments
concepts.statement: Two or more operating segments may be combined into one only where the aggregation is consistent with the core principle of the Standard, the segments have similar economic characteristics, AND they are alike on each of five counts — what the products and services are, how production is carried on, the type or class of customer served, the route by which the goods or services reach that customer, and, where applicable, the regulatory environment the segments trade under. Similar economic characteristics alone is not enough, and geography is not on the list. Segments that fail the quantitative thresholds may be combined with each other only where they share similar economic characteristics and a majority of those five respects; anything left over goes into an all other segments category.

citation.ref: para 12, read with para 14 and 16

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 112 — Disclosing interests in other entities
concepts.statement: Ind AS 112 is the disclosure standard that sits behind Ind AS 110, 111 and 28, and it asks two distinct things. First, the significant judgements and assumptions made in deciding that the entity has control, joint control or significant influence, and in deciding the type of joint arrangement — so a conclusion of control on less than half the voting rights has to be explained, not merely reached. Second, entity-by-entity information about each subsidiary whose NON-CONTROLLING INTERESTS are material to the reporting entity, including the proportion of ownership interests and voting rights held by those interests, the profit or loss allocated to them, their accumulated balance, and summarised financial information about the subsidiary. The trigger is the materiality of the non-controlling interests, not the size of the subsidiary. Ind AS 112 does not apply to separate financial statements prepared under Ind AS 27.

citation.ref: para 7 and 12, with the separate financial statements carve-out in para 6

concepts.section: Ind AS on Measurement based on Accounting Policies
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 113 — Highest and best use of a non-financial asset
concepts.statement: The fair value of a non-financial asset assumes the use that maximises its value in the hands of MARKET PARTICIPANTS, whether by using the asset themselves or by selling it to another market participant who would. The use must be physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible, and all three are tested. The entity's own current use is presumed to be the highest and best use, but the presumption falls the moment market or other factors show a different use would maximise value, and the entity's intention is irrelevant — an asset bought and deliberately left idle to protect a competitive position is still measured on the use a market participant would make of it. Costs a market participant would have to incur to reach that use, such as clearing a site, come off the price.

citation.ref: para 27, 28, 29 and 30

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — The discount rate and variable lease payments
concepts.statement: A lessee discounts the lease payments at the interest rate implicit in the lease where that rate can be readily determined, and otherwise at its own incremental borrowing rate — the rate this lessee itself would be charged to borrow, over a comparable term and against comparable security, the money needed to obtain an asset of similar value in a similar setting. A cost of capital is not that rate. The payments discounted are fixed payments less lease incentives receivable, variable payments that depend on an INDEX OR A RATE measured using the index or rate at the commencement date, amounts expected to be payable under residual value guarantees, the exercise price of a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, and termination penalties. A payment that varies with sales or usage is none of those, so it stays out of the liability and is charged to profit or loss in the period the triggering event occurs.

citation.ref: para 26 and 27, with the treatment of excluded variable payments in para 38(b)

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — The statement of changes in equity
concepts.statement: The statement of changes in equity is a primary statement, not a note. It shows total comprehensive income for the period split between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests, the effects of retrospective application or retrospective restatement recognised under Ind AS 8 shown for each component of equity, and, for each component, a reconciliation from opening to closing balance separately disclosing the changes from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income, and from transactions with owners in their capacity as owners. Dividends are a distribution to owners: they are presented here or in the notes, with the amount per share, and never as an expense in profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 106, 106A and 107, read with the restatement requirement in Ind AS 8 para 42

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 Appendix B — A cash-settled award modified to equity-settled
concepts.statement: Where the terms of a cash-settled share-based payment are modified so that it becomes equity-settled, three things happen on the modification date and all three happen at once. The equity-settled award is measured by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments granted AT THE MODIFICATION DATE, and the amount taken to equity is the portion of that fair value relating to the goods or services already received up to that date. The liability for the cash-settled award is derecognised on that date. Any difference between the carrying amount of the liability derecognised and the amount recognised in equity goes immediately to profit or loss. Nothing is carried forward and nothing is remeasured afterwards.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B44A, B44B and B44C

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 34 — Segment disclosure in an interim report
concepts.statement: Segment information appears in an interim report only where Ind AS 108 already obliges that same entity to publish a segment note with its ANNUAL financial statements — an entity outside Ind AS 108 does not acquire segment reporting by publishing a half-year report. Where it does apply, what is given is a short list, not the annual note: revenues from external customers and intersegment revenues where they sit in or are provided to the chief operating decision maker's measure, a measure of segment profit or loss, total assets and liabilities of a segment only where those are regularly provided to the chief operating decision maker AND have changed materially since the last annual balance sheet, a description of any change in the basis of segmentation or of measurement, and a reconciliation of the reportable segments' profit or loss to the entity's own.

citation.ref: para 16A(g), read with para 15

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — What Schedule III prescribes and what it does not
concepts.statement: Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 fixes the format and content of a company's financial statements and stops there. It does not prescribe the accounting treatment to be adopted, so the fact that a particular item appears in the format of the balance sheet does not imply that the item may be recognised — recognition is a matter for the notified standards, which Schedule III itself acknowledges and to which it grants overriding status. Three further consequences follow. Schedule III prescribes only the vertical format of the balance sheet and offers no horizontal alternative, though a company may itself add or substitute line items, sub-line items and sub-totals of its own wherever doing so helps a reader understand where the company stands or how it has performed. Its disclosure requirements are in addition to, and not in substitution of, those in the notified standards, and the terms it uses take their meaning from those standards. And the proviso to section 129(1) keeps insurance companies and banking companies outside it altogether, their formats being prescribed by their own regulators.

citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — Schedule III, read with the proviso to section 129(1)

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — Materiality as the filter for disclosure
concepts.statement: Materiality is the filter that decides what goes into the financial statements and what stays out, and the lack of clarity in how to apply it is one of the main drivers of overloaded financial statements. Information is disclosed only if it is material, meaning only if it could influence the decisions users take on the basis of those statements. The filter runs in both directions. Downwards it strips clutter. Upwards it catches what is individually immaterial and material in aggregate — several separately small commitments to buy items of property, plant and equipment together amount to a material capital commitment and are disclosed as one. Size is not the whole of the judgement either: a revenue stream under five per cent of total revenue may still warrant separate segment disclosure where the company has told its stakeholders that it is the strategic direction of the business and the revenue is growing rapidly, even though other streams of similar size are combined into other revenue. Once the line items needing disclosure are settled, the same judgement decides how much detail to give about each and how best to organise it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, materiality

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — Integrating notes, policies and judgements
concepts.statement: The notes cover the largest portion of a set of financial statements and have the greatest effect on how well those statements communicate, so best practice is to group them into categories, place the most critical information prominently, and integrate the main note on a line item with the accounting policy for that item and with the key estimates and judgements behind it. An inventory note carries the cost formula, the lower of cost and net realisable value policy, the estimation uncertainty in net realisable value and the figures together, in one place. The matching discipline runs the other way for policy text: one place holds the policies, rather than a sentence of policy sitting in whichever note happens to need it — a policy of writing off in full assets costing less than five thousand rupees belongs in the accounting policy for fixed assets, not buried in the fixed asset note. Only material accounting policies are disclosed, and non-material policy text that adds no value is removed. Disclosures about estimates focus on the most difficult, subjective and complex of them, with how the estimate was derived, the key assumptions, the review process and a sensitivity analysis.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, integration of notes and disclosure of material accounting policies

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — A staff housing loan below the market rate
concepts.statement: A housing loan advanced to an employee below the market rate is a financial asset and an employee benefit at the same time, and recording it at the amount disbursed gets both of them wrong. Ind AS 109 measures the loan on initial recognition at fair value, which here is the contracted receipts discounted at the market rate for a similar housing loan, so a loan carrying a below-market rate comes on to the balance sheet below the sum lent. The shortfall is not a loss of the year. It is the value the employee receives, and because the employee has to remain in service to keep the concession it is carried as prepaid employee cost and amortised over the loan period on a straight line basis as an employee benefit under Ind AS 19 — irrespective of the employee not being required to give any specific performance against the benefit. Interest is then recognised as finance income at the effective interest rate, which is the market rate used to discount, not at the rate contracted. Deferred tax is recognised on the temporary differences the restatement creates.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — case study on a concessional staff housing loan, read with Ind AS 109 and Ind AS 19

concepts.section: Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — The five fundamental principles
concepts.statement: ICAI's Code of Ethics of 2019, applicable from 1 July 2020 and derived from the IESBA Code of 2018, sets five fundamental principles and a Chartered Accountant shall comply with each of them. Integrity is to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships. Objectivity means bias, a conflicting interest, or pressure applied by anybody else must never be allowed to sway a judgement made in professional or business work. Professional competence and due care is to attain and maintain the knowledge and skill a client or employing organisation needs for competent service, and to act diligently in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards. Confidentiality is to respect information acquired through professional and business relationships. Professional behaviour is to comply with relevant laws and regulations and to avoid any conduct the accountant knows or should know might discredit the profession. Where local regulation differs from the Code the more stringent provision applies unless the law forbids it. Where two principles conflict the accountant might consult others in the firm or employing organisation, those charged with governance, the Institute or legal counsel — but no consultation relieves him of the responsibility to exercise professional judgement and, if necessary, to disassociate from the matter creating the conflict.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the fundamental principles

concepts.section: Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — The conceptual framework and the informed third party test
concepts.statement: The Code does not attempt to list every situation. It gives a conceptual framework the accountant applies in three steps — identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, evaluate the threats identified, and address them by eliminating them or reducing them to an acceptable level. In applying it the accountant shall exercise professional judgement, stay alert to information that is new and to facts that have since shifted, and put the matter to the reasonable and informed third party test. That test asks what another party would probably conclude on the same material — every relevant fact available to the accountant, both what he knows and what it is fair to expect of him, as at the moment his conclusion is reached. Being an accountant is not asked of that third party. What is asked is enough knowledge and enough experience to weigh the conclusion impartially. Professional judgement here means asking whether relevant information might be missing, whether the known facts sit oddly against expectations, whether the accountant's own expertise is sufficient, whether someone else should be consulted, and whether the accountant's own preconception or bias might be affecting the judgement.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the conceptual framework

concepts.section: Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Confidentiality and the circumstances that override it
concepts.statement: Confidentiality binds the accountant to information acquired through professional and employment relationships, and it survives the relationship: on changing employer or taking a new client, prior experience stays the accountant's own to draw upon, while confidential information picked up earlier is neither his to put to work nor his to pass on. It is not absolute. Disclosure may be required by law — producing documents or other evidence in legal proceedings, or disclosing infringements of law that come to light to the appropriate public authorities. It may be permitted by law and authorised by the client or employing organisation. And there may be a professional duty or right to disclose where the law does not prohibit it: meeting what a peer review, or a quality review, of the Institute asks for; answering a professional body or a regulator that has opened an inquiry or an investigation; defending the accountant's own professional interests once proceedings are on foot; and satisfying technical standards, professional standards and the ethics requirements that sit with them. Confidentiality is never a cover for the accountant's own advantage or a third party's, which is why insider trading breaches it, and it is not a reason to hide material facts that require disclosure — reporting fraud, illegal activity or non-compliance with laws and regulations does not constitute a breach at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — confidentiality

concepts.section: Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Information that is or might be misleading
concepts.statement: When preparing or presenting information the accountant shall use a relevant reporting framework, shall not intend to mislead or to influence a contractual or regulatory outcome inappropriately, shall represent the facts accurately and completely in all material respects, describe clearly the true nature of the transactions, classify and record in a timely and proper manner, and omit nothing with the intention of misleading. Discretion is where this bites, and the Code names the misuses: determining a fair value estimate in order to misrepresent profit or loss, selecting between policies permitted by the framework in order to misrepresent profit or loss, timing the sale of an asset near the year end in order to mislead, structuring a financing transaction in order to misrepresent assets and liabilities or the classification of cash flows, and selecting disclosures so as to omit or obscure information about financial or operating risk. Where the accountant knows or has reason to believe that information he is associated with is misleading, the response is a ladder — raise it with the superior, management or those charged with governance and ask for correction and, where it has already gone out, for the users to be told; consult the organisation's own ethics or whistle-blowing policy; then consult the Institute, the internal or external auditor or legal counsel, and determine whether anything must be communicated to third parties or to regulatory and oversight authorities. If after every feasible option is exhausted what sits on the page still misleads, then the accountant refuses to be — or to go on being — associated with it, and resigning may be the right step.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — preparation and presentation of information

concepts.section: Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
concepts.subsection: Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 — The clause a member in service is charged under
concepts.statement: A member in employment who lets a wrong accounting treatment through is not charged under the clauses written for a member in practice, and knowing which Schedule and Part applies is the whole of the answer. Section 22 makes professional or other misconduct include any act or omission in any of the Schedules, and section 21 is the disciplinary route. Professional misconduct sits in Parts I, II and III of the First Schedule and Parts I and II of the Second Schedule; other misconduct sits in the First Schedule's Part IV, together with the Second Schedule's Part III. Part I of the Second Schedule holds ten clauses and applies to a Chartered Accountant in practice — among them failing to disclose a material fact necessary to a financial statement he is concerned with professionally (clause 5), failing to report a known material misstatement (clause 6), not exercising due diligence or being grossly negligent in professional duties (clause 7), and failing to obtain information sufficient for the expression of an opinion (clause 8). Part II of the Second Schedule holds four clauses and applies to members generally, and its clause 1 is contravening any provision of the Act, the regulations, or any guidelines issued by the Council — read with the Council Guidelines, under which an employed member owes due diligence in the work he is put to and is not to be grossly negligent in doing it. That is the route by which a CFO or an accountant in service is held guilty. Part III of the Second Schedule holds one clause: a member, whether in practice or not, is guilty of other misconduct if held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the Schedules, read with sections 21 and 22 and the Council Guidelines

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Robotic process automation in the reporting cycle
concepts.statement: Robotic process automation puts software robots, called bots, on the manual, repetitive and rule-bound parts of financial data processing, analysis and reporting. The bots mimic a person's interactions with the digital systems rather than replacing those systems. On a group consolidation they extract financial data from each subsidiary's own system and consolidate it into the parent's, perform the necessary currency conversions, identify and reconcile intercompany transactions and generate the elimination entries Ind AS 110 requires so that nothing is counted twice, compute the amounts attributable to non-controlling interests and the comprehensive income attributable to the parent, and turn out the consolidated statements themselves — the balance sheet, the profit and loss, the cash flows, and the movement in equity. What that buys is accuracy, timely reporting, cost saving and data integrity, and it frees finance people for work that needs judgement. What it does not buy is judgement itself — a bot applies the rules it was given and nothing more.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — robotic process automation, read with Ind AS 110

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Cloud service models and what they change
concepts.statement: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet, and the shapes it takes differ by how much of the stack the provider runs. Cloud storage keeps files reachable and synchronised from any connected device. Software as a service delivers finished cloud-based applications over the internet, with nothing installed — accounting and financial management, customer relationship management, team collaboration. Infrastructure as a service rents virtualised computing resources, being servers, storage and networking, on a pay-as-you-go basis, so a business scales its IT infrastructure on demand without buying physical hardware. Platform as a service gives developers a cloud-based platform on which to build, deploy and manage applications without the complexity of managing the infrastructure underneath. What the accounting function gains is accessibility from any location, security features such as encryption, firewalls and multi-factor authentication, scalability without new hardware, lower upfront and maintenance cost, real-time collaboration with version control that leaves an audit trail of revisions, and stronger reporting and analytics. What it risks is that an entirely online system is exposed to attackers who could steal data or passwords or compromise the integrity of processed data, and that it depends on connectivity, which is not evenly developed outside the metros.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — cloud computing, its applications, benefits and challenges

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Building internal control over financial reporting into an ERP
concepts.statement: An ERP is built on one defined data structure sitting over a shared database. Whatever a department keys in shows up at once for every other user cleared to see it, so a figure is authenticated in one place instead of reconciled between several versions of itself. Integrating internal control over financial reporting into it turns controls into system behaviour rather than a checklist run afterwards. The illustrative steps include keeping the financial closing process aligned with the reporting requirements and deadlines the regulators set; tracking and validating every change to the closing and reporting process through the system's change management functionality, and confirming from the system logs and audit trail that the change was authorised by a designated individual with the appropriate authority; defining roles through the user access matrix configuration together with a responsibility assignment matrix, which records who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed; assessing the qualifications and training records of the people in financial reporting roles; documenting and approving the choice between alternative accounting treatments and communicating it to the audit committee; running KYC validation controls on account masters and separate ledger coding for related parties so that Schedule III disclosure can be tabulated automatically; and using the audit trail with the accounting period configuration controls, and the posting date against the transaction date, to confirm every posting fell in the correct period and to prevent backdating or unauthorised adjustments.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — illustrative steps for integrating internal control over financial reporting within an ERP

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Cybersecurity threats and the measures against them
concepts.statement: The threats an accounting function faces are named and distinct, and each aims at stealing sensitive financial data, disrupting operations or extracting a ransom. Phishing tricks a user into clicking a malicious link or providing sensitive information. Malware infects computers or networks with software that steals data or disrupts operations. Ransomware encrypts files or locks users out of systems and demands a payment in exchange for restoring access. An insider threat is a malicious act by an employee or other insider who already has access to sensitive data. A denial of service attack overwhelms a system or network with traffic to disrupt it. A supply chain attack compromises third-party software or hardware in order to get in. The proactive measures are equally specific: complex passwords changed regularly, encryption of sensitive data in transmission and in storage, access control limited to authorised personnel and reviewed whenever the management or employee structure changes, network security with firewalls, employee training, regular data backups stored securely, and an incident response plan with procedures for detecting, containing and mitigating an attack. A breach is not only an IT matter — the Information Technology Act, 2000 governs the collection, storage and transmission of financial data, organisations have legal and ethical obligations to disclose incidents with financial implications, and the reporting guidelines of regulators such as SEBI and RBI address disclosure of cybersecurity incidents in financial statements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — cybersecurity in accounting

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Blockchain and financial reporting
concepts.statement: A blockchain is a decentralised ledger shared across a network, in which each transaction is verified by multiple participants and encrypted so that it cannot afterwards be altered, which removes the need for intermediaries and central authorities. For financial reporting that changes several things at once. Transparency, because the record is visible and tamper-proof and can be audited easily. Data integrity, because unauthorised modification is prevented rather than merely detected afterwards. Audit, because the auditor can access the ledger directly to verify transactions instead of reconciling data pulled from different systems. Reconciliation, because a single shared source of truth removes the need to reconcile multiple versions of the same data across systems. Cost, because third-party verification and reconciliation fall away. The audit trail, which is comprehensive and immutable, so an irregularity or discrepancy is easier to identify and investigate. And timeliness, because real-time data availability lets financial reporting be done more frequently and still accurately.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — key impacts of blockchain on financial reporting

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — Convergence with IFRS is not adoption of IFRS
concepts.statement: Adoption means the country applies IFRS in the same manner as issued by the IASB and is one hundred per cent compliant with it. Convergence means the national standard setter works with the IASB to develop the standards over time, having adopted IFRS with some exceptions and working towards a point where no differences are left. India converged. Ind AS carry carve-outs and carve-ins made for the local regulatory landscape, business practice, tax and other provisions, so they are not IFRS as issued. The consequence is a hard one and it comes from the IASB's own rule: full application of its standards and interpretations, including IFRS 1 on first-time adoption, is what allows an entity to assert that its financial statements comply with IFRS; where a local authority has amended those standards first, the entity applying the amended version cannot assert compliance with IFRS. Canada, Bahrain and Cambodia are among the jurisdictions that adopted; India, China and Hong Kong are among those that converged.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — convergence versus adoption of IFRS

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — Net worth for the Ind AS roadmap
concepts.statement: Whether Ind AS applies to a company under the MCA roadmap turns on net worth, and net worth carries the meaning in clause 57 of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013. Working from the audited balance sheet, add up paid-up share capital, the securities premium account and every reserve built out of profits; from that total take away accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off. Left out of the sum altogether are reserves thrown up by revaluing assets, by writing depreciation back, or by an amalgamation. It is computed on the standalone financial statements as at 31 March 2014, or on the first audited financial statements for a period ending after that date for a company not then in existence or crossing a threshold for the first time later. A company that does not meet the criteria on the cut-off date reassesses at each balance sheet date, and a company that meets them once stays in, whatever its net worth does afterwards. Ind AS once required applies to the standalone and the consolidated financial statements alike. Phase I covers listed companies with net worth of five hundred crore or more and unlisted companies of that size, plus their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies, from periods beginning on or after 1 April 2016; Phase II covers listed companies below five hundred crore and unlisted companies of two hundred and fifty crore or more, and their group companies, from 1 April 2017. Companies listed only on an SME exchange are outside the roadmap.

citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — roadmap for applicability, read with section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — How an Ind AS is made and who notifies it
concepts.statement: Accounting standards in India are formulated by the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI, but the ICAI does not put them into force. The sequence is fixed. The ASB prepares a preliminary draft carrying the carve-ins and carve-outs it considers necessary, giving weight to the local regulatory landscape, business practice and tax provisions. The draft goes to the Council members of the ICAI and to specified outside bodies — the MCA, SEBI, the C&AG and the CBDT among them — and the ASB meets their representatives to hear their views. An exposure draft is then finalised and issued for public comment. The comments are considered, the ASB finalises and submits to the Council of the ICAI for approval, and the Council may modify the draft in consultation with the ASB. The final draft goes to the NFRA with the ICAI's recommendation, the NFRA reviews and provides its inputs, and only then does the MCA notify the standard under the Companies Act by publishing it in the Gazette of India, with an announcement of the applicability date. The central government is the body that prescribes a standard. It does so on the ICAI's recommendation, having consulted the NFRA and worked through what the NFRA put forward, and only a notified standard is authoritative under Indian law.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — process of development and finalisation of Indian Accounting Standards

concepts.section: Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — Previous GAAP carrying amount as deemed cost, all or nothing
concepts.statement: A first-time adopter has four ways of measuring property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and right-of-use assets in the opening Ind AS balance sheet, and they do not all behave the same way. Applying the relevant standards retrospectively, using fair value at the date of transition, and using a previous GAAP revaluation that was at its date broadly comparable to fair value or to cost or depreciated cost adjusted for a general or specific price index may each be chosen item by item, one plant retrospectively and another at fair value. The fourth is different: continuing with the previous GAAP carrying amount is available only where there is no change in functional currency, and only if it is applied to all of the asset classes and every item within them. It also extends to investment property, which is the only route to deemed cost there, since Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model and fair value as deemed cost is therefore not available for investment property. Carrying amount means the net book value on the date of transition and not the original cost, so future depreciation runs on that net book value over the remaining useful life, reviewed at least annually as Ind AS 16 requires. Different entities within a group may choose different bases in their own standalone financial statements; for the consolidated financial statements the entire group is treated as one reporting entity and different bases across its entities are not permissible.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — deemed cost for property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and right-of-use assets, paragraphs D5 to D7AA

concepts.section: Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — The mandatory exception for derecognition
concepts.statement: Ind AS 101 has two kinds of relief and they run in opposite directions. An optional exemption is an election the first-time adopter may take. A mandatory exception is a prohibition on going back, and it binds whether the entity wants it or not.
