A rate change announced in a way that is treated as having the substantive effect of enactment counts even though the legislature has not finished with it, and a change enacted after the reporting date does not count at all, however certain it now looks — it is disclosed instead. And because the test is the period of reversal, a single rate rarely does the whole job when a rate change takes effect part way through the reversals — the differences reversing before the change go at the old rate and the rest at the new one. When a rate change moves a balance that is already there, the resulting deferred tax goes to profit or loss, except to the extent it relates to something previously recognised outside profit or loss, in which case it follows that item into other comprehensive income or directly into equity. And no discounting anywhere, however long the reversals run.

citation.ref: the rule fixing which rate a deferred balance takes — the one expected to be in force when the asset is realised or the liability settled — and the enactment or substantive-enactment test applied at the reporting date; where the effect of a rate change is taken, which follows wherever the underlying item was put in the first place; and the bar on discounting

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — carrying the non-controlling interest forward from acquisition to the year end
concepts.statement: The non-controlling interest is measured once at the acquisition date and then rolled forward, and both halves are arithmetic. At acquisition it is either its fair value or its proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets, whichever the group elected for that combination, and whichever figure is used goes into the goodwill computation alongside the consideration. After that the balance moves with the subsidiary — plus the non-controlling share of profit or loss, plus its share of other comprehensive income, less its share of dividends the subsidiary declares, and the balance sits inside equity, presented separately from the equity of the owners of the parent. Two things decide most of the marks. The subsidiary's results are consolidated only from the date control is obtained, so an acquisition part way through a year brings in only the months after it. And a dividend paid by the subsidiary takes money out of the non-controlling interest as surely as a profit puts it in, even though the group's own profit is unaffected because the parent's share of the same dividend is eliminated.

citation.ref: the requirement that consolidation of an investee begins from the date the investor obtains control and ceases when it loses control, together with the measurement of the non-controlling interest at the acquisition date and the attribution of profit or loss and other comprehensive income to the non-controlling interests thereafter

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — rolling the carrying amount of an associate through a year
concepts.statement: The equity method is a single running balance, and every year adds the same four movements to it. Start at cost, which already contains the goodwill on acquisition — the excess of the cost over the investor's share of the net fair value of the associate's identifiable assets and liabilities — and that goodwill is never amortised and is never shown separately. Add the investor's share of the associate's profit, taken to profit or loss. Add its share of the associate's other comprehensive income, taken to other comprehensive income. Deduct distributions received, which reduce the investment rather than producing income, because the profit they came out of has already been picked up. The step candidates lose most often sits inside the share of profit — where the fair value of a depreciable asset at the acquisition date exceeded its carrying amount in the associate's books, the associate's own depreciation is too low for the investor's purposes, and the investor's share of the extra depreciation on the uplift is deducted before the share of profit is recognised. The other trap runs the other way, when the investor's share of net fair value exceeds the cost — that excess is a capital reserve recorded directly in equity, not income and not negative goodwill sitting inside the investment.

citation.ref: the equity method — the investment enters at cost, and from then on its carrying amount tracks what the investor's slice of the investee's net assets does after acquisition: profit or loss goes into profit or loss, other comprehensive income into other comprehensive income, distributions come off the carrying amount, and the profit share is cut by depreciation computed on the fair values fixed at acquisition; goodwill sits inside the carrying amount and is never amortised, while a share of net fair value that tops the cost becomes a capital reserve booked straight to equity

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 111 — what a joint operator actually puts in its own statements
concepts.statement: A joint operator does not carry an investment and does not equity account. Five lines go straight into its own books: everything it holds by itself plus the slice it holds of whatever the arrangement holds together; everything it owes by itself plus the slice it owes of what was taken on together; what it earns selling the output that falls to it; the slice due to it when the arrangement itself makes the sale; and what it spends by itself plus the slice it bears of what was spent together. Each of those is then accounted for under the Ind AS that governs that kind of asset, liability, revenue or expense. Two features of the arithmetic separate a good answer from a plausible one. The share is not automatically the capital ratio — where the contract gives one operator the rights to the whole of a particular asset, or the obligation for the whole of a particular liability, that operator takes all of it and the others take none, and only the assets and liabilities the contract leaves unallocated are split. And an operator's own selling and other costs are its own in full, not shared, because they were never incurred jointly.

citation.ref: paragraph 20, which tells a joint operator to book five lines directly in both its separate and its consolidated statements — what it holds and what it owes, alone and jointly, what it earns on its own slice of the output, what falls to it when the arrangement sells, and what it spends alone and jointly — and then to apply whichever Ind AS governs each line

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Assessing whether a currency is exchangeable
concepts.statement: The May 2025 amendment to Ind AS 21 puts a first step in front of every translation: is the currency exchangeable into the other currency at the measurement date, for the particular purpose the entity needs it for. Exchangeability is a question about a purpose and a date, not a standing property of a currency, so the same currency can pass for settling imports and fail for repaying a loan. What is tested is the ability to obtain the other currency, directly or through a second currency, and not the intention to do so; only markets that give the entity enforceable rights and obligations count; a normal administrative delay does not defeat exchangeability; and a currency fails the test when no more than an insignificant amount can be obtained for that purpose, measured against the whole amount that purpose needs.

citation.ref: the lack of exchangeability amendment notified by MCA vide G.S.R. 291(E) dated 7 May 2025, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025 — the first step of its two-step approach, and the five factors it lists for deciding whether a currency is exchangeable

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Estimating the spot rate when a currency is not exchangeable
concepts.statement: Once the first step answers no, the entity has to build a rate of its own. The only thing the standard asks of that rate is that it be the rate at which an orderly exchange would happen at the measurement date between market participants under the economic conditions then prevailing. Two routes reach it. The entity may take an observable rate and use it unchanged, once it has weighed whether several observable rates exist, what purpose each of them serves, what kind of rate it is and how often it is refreshed; a rate quoted for some other purpose, or the first rate available once the block lifts, are both observable rates. Or it may adjust an observable rate as far as the objective requires, and a quote from a market that gives no enforceable rights may feed that adjustment even though it was ignored at the first step. No order of preference between the two routes is laid down.

citation.ref: para 19A for what an estimated spot rate has to achieve, and para A17 for the route that adjusts an observable rate instead of taking one unchanged

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Disclosure and transition when a currency is not exchangeable
concepts.statement: An entity that has had to estimate a rate says so at length. It names the currency and describes what is blocking it, describes the transactions caught, gives the carrying amount of the assets and liabilities caught, gives the rates used and says of each whether it was observable and untouched or built by another technique, describes that technique with its inputs and assumptions, and gives qualitative information about every kind of risk the block exposes it to together with the carrying amount exposed to each. A further set is owed only where the currency in question is a foreign operation's own functional currency: that operation is named, what kind of investment it is and where it principally trades are stated, summarised financial information about it is given, and any arrangement that could oblige the entity to support it is described. On first applying the amendment nothing is restated — the effect lands in opening retained earnings, or in the translation differences held in their own component of equity.

citation.ref: the disclosures the lack of exchangeability amendment requires when a currency is not exchangeable, the further disclosures owed where the currency belongs to a foreign operation, and its transition, which asks for no comparative information to be restated

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — The Pillar Two temporary exception
concepts.statement: Pillar Two legislation means the OECD's Pillar Two Model Rules and any tax law enacting them, a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax included. Ind AS 12 carves those taxes out of deferred tax altogether: an entity neither recognises nor discloses anything about deferred tax assets and liabilities arising from Pillar Two income taxes. The carve-out is compulsory rather than an option, and it stops deferred tax and no further — current tax on top-up income taxes is accounted for and, more than that, is shown on its own. Three things are said in the notes. That the exception has been taken. The current tax expense or income attributable to Pillar Two income taxes, separately. And, for a jurisdiction where the law is enacted or substantively enacted but has not yet bitten, whatever is known or can reasonably be estimated about the exposure, qualitative and quantitative, which may be given as an indicative range — and where even that cannot be estimated, a statement saying so and an account of how far the assessment has got.

citation.ref: the amendment notified by MCA vide G.S.R. 549(E) dated 13 August 2025 — the exception from recognising and disclosing deferred tax on Pillar Two income taxes, and the four disclosures that come with it

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — clean price, accrued interest and the dirty price
concepts.statement: A bond bought between two coupon dates carries interest the seller has earned and not yet been paid, and the market handles that by quoting two prices. The clean price is the quoted figure and it excludes accrued interest. The dirty price is what actually changes hands — the clean price plus interest accrued from the last coupon date to settlement, computed on the face value at the coupon rate for the days elapsed. Every settlement amount is built on the dirty price, never on the quoted one, and a repurchase agreement makes that visible in two steps. The first leg is the nominal value taken at the dirty price and then reduced by the initial margin the lender of money holds back as a haircut. The second leg is that first-leg amount carried forward at the repo rate for the exact days of the deal. The two mistakes that show up in the answer are settling on the clean price, which underpays the seller by the accrued interest, and adding the margin instead of deducting it, which lends more against the collateral than the collateral is worth.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — the duration of a portfolio of bonds
concepts.statement: A portfolio's duration is the weighted average of the durations of the bonds in it, weighted by the market value each bond represents, not by the number of bonds and not by a simple average across the holdings. Once that figure exists it does the same job it does for a single bond. Divide it by one plus the yield to get the modified duration, which the study material also calls volatility, and multiply that by the change in yield to get the predicted percentage change in the portfolio's value, with the sign reversed because price moves against yield. Applied to the portfolio's rupee value it gives the rupee gain or loss for a stated move in rates, which is what a fund manager is actually asked for. Three errors move the answer far enough to be visible in an option set — averaging the durations without weighting them where nothing on the paper says to, using the Macaulay figure where the modified one belongs, and multiplying by one plus the yield instead of dividing by it. One thing overrides all of the above. Where the question carries its own note naming the method, that note decides the answer, and ICAI does write such notes: the November 2026 revision paper directs a plain unweighted average of the durations of a five-bond government portfolio, and it directs it even though those five holdings were bought at five different prices and so are not of equal value. Read the note under a question before weighting anything. An instruction printed on the paper wins; the value-weighted rule is what governs wherever no such instruction appears.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — approximating the yield to maturity from a price
concepts.statement: Yield to maturity is properly the discount rate at which the present value of a bond's cash flows equals its market price, which means solving for a rate rather than computing one. The approximation the study material uses instead takes the annual coupon, adds the discount or subtracts the premium spread evenly over the remaining years, and divides by the average of the redemption value and the market price. Three things about it decide the marks. The numerator uses the redemption value rather than the face value where the two differ, so a bond redeemable at a premium is amortising towards the redemption figure. The denominator is an average, so dividing by the market price alone or by the face value alone gives a different and wrong answer. And the sign of the second term follows the price — a bond bought below its redemption value gains, so the term is added, and a bond bought above it loses, so the term is deducted, which is why a premium bond's yield to maturity is below its current yield and its current yield is below its coupon rate.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit
concepts.statement: A treasury bill, a commercial paper and a certificate of deposit pay no coupon. They are issued below face value and redeemed at it, and the whole return is that gap. The yield is the gap divided by what the investor actually paid, not by the face value, and then annualised by the days or months in a year over the days or months the instrument runs. Dividing by the face value understates the yield, because the investor never had the face value to invest, and this is exactly why an instrument discounted at a stated rate always yields more than that rate to the buyer. Two conventions matter and they are not the same convention. The study material annualises these money market yields on a 365-day year, or on twelve months where the period is given in months. It uses a 360-day year for accrued interest and for repo interest, which is a different calculation on a different instrument. And a front-ended discount is deducted from the face value to give the issue price before any yield is computed, so a hundred rupees discounted at nine per cent for six months is issued at ninety-five rupees and fifty paise, not at ninety-one.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Analysis — the relative strength index and its bands
concepts.statement: Relative strength is the technical idea that some shares keep outrunning others and that a buyer is better off in the ones that have. The relative strength index turns that idea into a single bounded number for one share. Over a fixed window, conventionally fourteen trading days, the day-on-day price changes are split into gains and losses. Both totals are averaged over the whole window, not over the days on which each actually happened, so a window with four up days and ten down days still divides both totals by fourteen. The relative strength is the average gain divided by the average loss, and the index is a hundred less a hundred divided by one plus that ratio, which pins the answer between nought and a hundred however violent the moves were. Reading it is a matter of four bands and two lines. Above seventy is overbought and below thirty is oversold; between them, fifty is the line that separates positive momentum from weak momentum, so a reading of fifty to seventy is bullish and a reading of thirty to fifty is bearish. That middle line is what most readings turn on, and it is the one a rising index is most often mistaken for. An index climbing out of oversold territory has left the bottom band and has not thereby become bullish — until it is above fifty it is still describing weak momentum, and the direction of travel is not the signal. After the first window the two averages are rolled forward rather than recomputed from scratch, each new day's figure being the previous average carried over the window less one day plus the new day's own gain or loss.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

concepts.subsection: Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — ranking projects by the coefficient of variation
concepts.statement: Standard deviation measures how far a project's cash flows scatter around their own expected value, and it does that job well for one project on its own. It stops working the moment two projects of different sizes have to be ranked, because a large project can scatter by more rupees while scattering by less in proportion to what it is expected to earn. The coefficient of variation fixes exactly that. It is the standard deviation divided by the expected return or expected cash flow, so it states the risk borne for every unit of expected return, and the project with the lower figure offers the better trade between the two. The order of the division is the whole of it: putting the expected return on top gives return per unit of risk, where higher is better, and carrying the lower-is-better rule across to that inverted figure reverses the answer. The denominator is the expected return, not the money put in, so dividing by the initial outlay gives spread per rupee invested, which is a different question nobody asked. And the measure earns its place only where the projects differ in size. Where two projects have the same expected value the coefficient ranks them in exactly the order the standard deviation already did, and adds nothing; where the expected values differ, the standard deviation is the one that cannot be trusted on its own.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

concepts.subsection: Mutual Funds — gilt funds, their net asset value and the duration they carry
concepts.statement: A gilt fund is the debt fund that holds nothing but treasury bills and dated securities issued by the central and state governments. A fund holding corporate debentures or money market paper beside government bonds is a bond fund, so what the portfolio contains, and not merely that it contains bonds, is what names it. Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Because the borrower is the government, the default risk that a debt fund otherwise carries is not what moves this one. Because government paper is long dated, interest rate risk is, and it is not softened at all by the quality of the issuer — a unit holder can lose money in a gilt fund without any borrower missing a rupee, since the units are priced off the market value of the holdings and bond prices fall when yields rise. Net asset value per unit is built from what the fund actually holds: a bond quoted at a rate per hundred rupees of face value is worth that rate applied to the face value held, so a security bought above par costs more than its face value and one bought below par costs less, and the sum of those amounts, over the units outstanding, is the figure per unit. Face value is not that figure and never was. The fund's exposure to rates is then measured by the average duration of its holdings, and it is managed by churning the portfolio against an expected move: lengthen the average duration when rates are expected to fall, so the price gain is larger, and shorten it when they are expected to rise, so the price loss is smaller. A swap of one holding for another leaves the number of holdings unchanged, so the divisor in the average does not move.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

concepts.subsection: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — the replicating portfolio beside the risk-neutral route
concepts.statement: There are two routes to a one-period option price and they are not rivals — they reach the same figure and they ask you to hold different things on the way. The replicating route builds a position in the share and in borrowing whose payoff matches the option's in both future states. The share leg is the payoff spread divided by the price spread, the same ratio the study material calls the composition of the riskless hedge portfolio, and it is a fraction of a share rather than a whole one. Holding that fraction and writing one option leaves a position worth the same amount whichever way the share goes, so that amount is discounted at the risk-free rate to say what must be borrowed today, and the option's price is what the share leg costs less what is borrowed. Nothing in that argument mentions any probability at all. The risk-neutral route instead computes a probability from the risk-free growth factor and the two share prices, takes the expected payoff under it, and discounts that at the risk-free rate; it hands you a price and no position. The two agree because both rest on there being no arbitrage, which is also why a real-world probability offered alongside the question changes neither of them. A stated view that the share will rise with some chance is a view about risk preferences, and the price is independent of those — the replicating route shows it directly, by never using a probability, and the risk-neutral route uses only the probability implied by the prices themselves.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

concepts.subsection: Securitization — the market risks, as against the credit and legal ones
concepts.statement: The study material sorts the risks an investor in a securitisation faces into groups, and market risk is the group that sits outside the transaction altogether. Beside it, credit or counterparty risk is the risk of bankruptcy and of the servicer failing to perform, and legal risk is the absence of settled statutory provision or judicial precedent on these transactions in India, so that a dispute over who owns the pooled assets leaves investor payouts uncertain. Market risk has three parts. Macroeconomic risk reaches the pool through the borrowers: an industry downturn cuts what they earn and so what they can pay, and a fall in the price of whatever secures their loans makes walking away cheaper than paying on, so the financier repossesses an asset now worth less. Prepayment risk bites when rates fall and retail borrowers repay ahead of schedule, which returns the investor's money early and forces him to put it back to work at the lower yield then going. Interest rate risk is a mismatch inside the structure rather than a failure outside it: a pool paying a floating rate against paper promising a fixed one, or the reverse, can leave collections short of the payout even when every borrower pays in full and on time, and an interest rate swap hedges part of that. Which group a fact belongs in is the thing worth getting right. A borrower defaulting because his industry turned down is macroeconomic, not credit; a shortfall arising from the rate and not from the recovery is interest rate risk, and no amount of credit enhancement addresses it, because enhancement absorbs losses from money that never came.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the heads of the balance sheet under the Third Schedule
concepts.statement: The Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 sets out two prescribed forms. A banking company draws its balance sheet on the first of them, Form A, and puts its profit and loss account on Form B, or as near thereto as the circumstances admit. The form is not a presentational nicety: because the heads are fixed, a great deal of the auditor's work on a bank is deciding which head a balance belongs under, and several of the answers are counter-intuitive. Interest accrued but not due on deposits is not included under Deposits; it is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions, which comprises bills payable, inter-office adjustments (net), interest accrued, and others including provisions — and the auditor specifically examines that interest accrued has not been clubbed with the figures of deposits and borrowings. A current account standing in debit is not set off against the credit balances beside it on the liabilities side; the amount is money owed to the bank, so it belongs under Advances. The balance in the inter-office adjustments account is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions if it is in credit, and inter-office transactions are not borrowings and are not presented as such. Borrowings are shown as borrowings in India, split between the Reserve Bank of India, other banks and other institutions and agencies, and borrowings outside India, with the total amount of secured borrowings shown by way of a note to the relevant schedule; a clear distinction is made between rediscount and refinance, because rediscount does not figure under that head. The call money market is treated the same way: what the bank has placed there is never set off against what it has taken. And the figures of advances and investments in the balance sheet exclude the provisions made in respect of them to the satisfaction of the auditors.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the prescribed forms of a banking company's financial statements, the items grouped under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and the heads under which interest accrued, a debit current-account balance, an inter-office balance, rediscount and call money placed are shown

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the items grouped under Other Assets
concepts.statement: Other Assets on a bank's balance sheet is a residual head that carries four things an auditor has to look at separately. Inter-office adjustments, where inter-branch accounts are normally reconciled centrally: the auditor's report says how those accounts stood at the year end — the dates up to which all or any segments have been reconciled, how many entries were still outstanding and for how much, with debits and credits given separately — and he draws that information primarily from branch audit reports. Interest accrued, which is examined to see that interest has been accrued on the entire loans and advances portfolio, with special consideration to overdue bills purchased or discounted, and that the head carries no more interest than the bank can expect to be realised in the ordinary course of business, a limit that rests on AS 9, under which revenue is not recognised while there is significant uncertainty about its collectability. Stationery and stamps, which includes only exceptional items of expenditure such as a bulk purchase of security paper to be written off over a period, valued at cost, normal stationery expenditure being charged to the profit and loss account; security stationery is physically verified at the year end and any shortage inquired into, because it can expose the bank to loss from misuse. And non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims — immovable property or tangible assets that came to the bank in settlement of debts due to it or of its other claims, and that it holds meaning to dispose of them, verified against the terms of settlement, the court's order or the arbitration award, with ownership legally vested in the bank, recorded at the date of acquisition at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value of the asset acquired, and subject to section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which stops a banking company holding immovable property — however it came by that property — beyond seven years from the date it was acquired, unless the bank needs it for its own use.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the audit procedures for the items under Other Assets, including the reporting on the year-end status of inter-branch accounts, the recognition of only such interest accrued as can be realised in the ordinary course of business on the AS 9 principle, the confinement of Stationery and Stamps to exceptional items valued at cost, and the recording of non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value, read with section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 on the seven year holding period for immovable property

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — contingent liabilities and bills for collection
concepts.statement: A great deal of a bank's exposure never reaches its balance sheet, and the Third Schedule requires it to be disclosed all the same. Six heads carry it. Claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts come first, then the liability for partly paid investments, then the liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, then guarantees given on behalf of constituents, split between those within India and those outside India, then acceptances, endorsements and other obligations, and last a catch-all for any other item on which the bank is contingently liable. Separate from all six sits bills for collection, because the bank holds those bills as an agent and they are not its own liability at all. The auditor's concern is that every contingent liability is identified and properly valued, and he obtains a management representation covering, among other things, that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into, after following the due procedure laid down and supported by the underlying documents; that nothing contingent standing at the year end has been left out of what is disclosed; that what is disclosed carries no crystallised liability of the nature of a loss or expense, which require a provision or adjustment in the financial statements instead; that the estimated financial effects are based on best estimates in terms of AS 29, including consideration of any reimbursement; that where guarantees have been issued on behalf of the bank's directors, arrangements are in place, adequate and effective, under which the party's own resources answer the sum guaranteed and nobody comes to the bank for a loan or advance when the guarantee is invoked, keeping the guarantee clear of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; and that where a contingent liability has not been disclosed because the possibility of its outcome is remote, management's justification for that view is given.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the contingent liabilities disclosed under the Third Schedule and the separate disclosure of bills for collection, with the management representations the auditor obtains, including that crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense are not shown as contingent, that estimated financial effects follow AS 29, that guarantees issued on behalf of directors do not violate section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and that a justification is given for liabilities not disclosed as remote

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the principal business test and registration
concepts.statement: Whether a company is a non-banking financial company is a question of fact answered by a quantitative test, not by what the company calls itself. Section 45-I(f) of the Reserve Bank of India Act reaches three kinds of body. A financial institution that is a company is one. So is a company which, though not a bank, makes its principal business the taking of deposits — under a scheme, under an arrangement, or in any other way — or the lending of money in any manner. And so is any other non-banking institution, or class of them, that the Reserve Bank specifies by notification in the Official Gazette, the Central Government having approved it first. To identify the principal business, both the asset pattern and the income pattern are taken as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet of the company. The company is treated as a non-banking financial company where its financial assets constitute more than 50 per cent of its total assets, netted off by intangible assets, and its income from financial assets constitutes more than 50 per cent of its gross income. Both limbs must be satisfied; a company meeting one and not the other does not qualify. A company that does qualify must register. Section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 bars it from starting or continuing the business of a non-banking financial institution on two counts at once: it must hold a certificate of registration granted by the Reserve Bank, and it must have net owned fund of twenty-five lakh rupees, or whatever larger figure the Bank notifies, capped at one hundred crore rupees. The Bank may set different figures for different categories, and it has notified higher ones for particular categories, with a phased timeline for existing companies in those categories. The auditor meets the same test from the other direction under clause 3(xvi)(a) of CARO 2020, which puts to him the question whether a company required to be registered under section 45-IA has in fact been registered.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — section 45-I(f) on what a non-banking financial company is, the two-limb principal business test read off the last audited balance sheet, section 45-IA on registration and net owned fund, and clause 3(xvi)(a) of CARO 2020

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xvii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xvii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 puts two years to the auditor in one question: he reports whether a cash loss arose in the year under audit and again in the year immediately before it, and where one did, the amount of that cash loss goes in as well. Four things follow from those words. The clause asks about a cash loss, which is not the same figure as the loss shown in the statement of profit and loss and not the same figure as an operating loss, so a company can show one without the other in either direction. The clause reaches back a year: the immediately preceding financial year is inside it whether or not the present auditor audited that year. The answer is not a yes or a no — where there are cash losses the amount goes in, and where there are none the clause is still answered, because paragraph 3 says the report shall include a statement on the matters specified rather than a statement only where something is wrong. And the clause reports a fact; it is not an opinion on the company's future and does not by itself modify the audit opinion. Two further provisions of the Order govern how the answer is given. Paragraph 4 has two limbs: an answer to a paragraph 3 question that goes against the company, or that is qualified, carries with it the basis on which it was reached; and an auditor who cannot reach any view on a matter the Order specifies records that inability instead, with his reasons for it. Paragraph 2 then keeps the Order off a report covering consolidated financial statements and leaves clause (xxi) alone to operate there, so a subsidiary's cash losses are reported in the subsidiary's own CARO report and not under this clause in the consolidated one.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 2 on the matters every report under section 143 shall contain and on the Order's application to a report on consolidated financial statements, and with paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 4(b) on stating the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer and on indicating an inability to express an opinion together with the reasons

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Sections 6, 8 and 20 with Regulations 10 and 11 — the certificate of practice, suspension, and the disabilities
concepts.statement: Section 6 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 makes the Council's certificate the gate to practice: a member who holds none may not practise at all, and the bar follows him abroad as well as at home; the annual fee for it is payable on or before the 1st day of April each year, and the certificate may be cancelled by the Council in the prescribed circumstances. A member who is not in practice is precluded from accepting any engagement to render services of the types normally rendered by a chartered accountant, even where the service needs no special qualification. The Council's settled view is that a member has no other capacity, separable from his capacity as a member, in which he can take up such practice: once he is a member he is bound by the Act and the Regulations, so a member suspended from practice, or whose name has been removed for misconduct, cannot during that period appear before the tax authorities or any other body as an income-tax representative and cannot argue that he does so in some other capacity. Regulation 10 makes the certificate liable to cancellation where the holder's name is removed from the Register, where the Council is satisfied after a hearing that it was issued on incorrect, misleading or false information or by mistake, where the member has ceased to practise, or where the annual fee has not been paid by the 30th day of September of the relevant year; a cancelled certificate is surrendered to the Secretary. Regulation 11 lets the Council restore a certificate cancelled for non-payment of the fee, with effect from the date of cancellation, on an application in the approved form with the fee, received by the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year. Behind the certificate stand the disabilities of section 8, which debar a person from having his name entered in or borne on the Register: not having attained the age of 21 years when applying; being of unsound mind and so adjudged by a competent court; being an undischarged insolvent; being a discharged insolvent who has not obtained from the court a certificate that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part; having been convicted by a competent court, inside the country or outside it, either of an offence that carries a prison sentence and involves moral turpitude, or of an offence done in his professional capacity that is more than merely technical, unless he is pardoned or the Central Government lifts the disability by written order; and having been removed from membership on being found on inquiry guilty of professional or other misconduct, a person removed for a specified period being ineligible until that period expires. Failing to disclose that one suffers from any of these disabilities is itself professional misconduct. Section 20 lets the Council remove from the Register the name of a member who is dead, who asks for it, who has not paid a prescribed fee, or who is found to have been subject to a section 8 disability when his name was entered or to have become subject to one since, and requires it to remove the name of a member against whom an order removing him from membership has been passed; a name removed for non-payment of fee may be entered again on application and payment of the arrears.

citation.ref: Sections 6(1), 6(2) and 6(3), section 8 clauses (i) to (vi), and section 20, read with Regulations 10 and 11 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988, and the Council's view on a suspended member appearing before the income-tax authorities as set out in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.1 and its Illustration 1

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: The Council's Know Your Client norms for members in practice
concepts.statement: The financial services industry worldwide is required to obtain information about its clients under Know Your Client norms, and the Council of ICAI, keeping in mind the standards of the profession in India, approved KYC norms of its own to be observed by members in practice. The Council put the norms in mandatory terms and fixed their reach as every assignment that pertains to attestation functions, and the module's own illustration holds a member who gave consultancy, a compilation engagement and advisory services to a company that turned out to be part of a money-laundering group to have been bound to keep the information — his contention that he was not supposed to keep any information about the company is not valid. What must be kept depends on who the client is. For an individual or proprietor: the name, the PAN or Aadhaar number, a business description and a copy of the last audited financial statement, together with the type of engagement. For a corporate entity: the name and address, a business description, the name of the parent company where the client is a subsidiary, and a copy of the last audited financial statement; the type of engagement; and regulatory information — the company's PAN, its Company Identification Number, and the directors' names, addresses and Director Identification Numbers. For a non-corporate entity: the name and address, a copy of the PAN, a business description, the partners' names and addresses with their PAN, Aadhaar or DIN, and a copy of the last audited financial statement, together with the type of engagement. The three lists differ by design: the regulatory block belongs to the corporate client alone, the parent company is asked for only where there is one, and the individual is identified by PAN or Aadhaar where the entity is identified by its registration.

citation.source: Council of ICAI — KYC Norms for members in practice
citation.ref: Know Your Client norms approved by the Council of ICAI, mandatory in nature and applicable to all assignments pertaining to attestation functions, as set out in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.7, with the three client types — individual or proprietor, corporate entity, non-corporate entity — and the general, engagement and regulatory information required for each

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Audit risk in a not-for-profit body
concepts.statement: A not-for-profit body is audited under the same standards as anything else, and what changes is where the risk sits. Taking the three components in turn. Inherent risk rises with the field the body works in: an organisation operating where political and social questions meet can have its activities made risky by that alone, and where accusations and counter-accusations are being traded the auditor is not looking at an ordinary set of records. Receipt of foreign funds makes transactions inherently risky. Crowdfunded donations have to be seen in relation to the constitution of the body itself, which may make them risky — money raised for a purpose the objects do not authorise is a problem before it is ever spent. The credibility and integrity of the persons behind the body matter, because bodies of this kind can be used for money laundering and for misutilising funds given by donors. And where the previous year's accounts were not audited at all, inherent risk rises again through the probable effect of any misstatement in them. Control risk rises where a body whose activities were small has suddenly received substantial donations: formal controls may simply not be in place, and the absence of them can lead to non-compliance with laws whose consequences are severe — non-compliance with the foreign contribution law can lead to the cancellation of the body's certificate. Detection risk rises because the engagement is a first one: there may be a lack of understanding of what the body actually does, and that leads to inappropriate sampling or to a faulty application of the procedures chosen. Where deviations from established controls are found during the audit, the control risk assessment is revised, the revision flows into the assessment of the risks of material misstatement, and it may result in a modification of the nature, timing and extent of the planned substantive procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — audit risk in the audit of a not-for-profit body: the political and social field, foreign funds and crowdfunded donations seen against the constitution of the body as sources of inherent risk, the credibility and integrity of the persons behind it, the prior year's accounts being unaudited, the absence of formal controls after a sudden increase in donations and the consequences of non-compliance with the foreign contribution law as sources of control risk, the first-year engagement as a source of detection risk, and the revision of control risk and of the risks of material misstatement where established controls are found not to be operating

concepts.subsection: Foreign contributions and the audit plan
concepts.statement: Where a society or other not-for-profit body is registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 for the receipt of foreign contributions, the verification of those receipts is ordinarily where the audit goes deepest — the purpose being to rule out round-tripping, money that leaves and returns wearing a different name. The examinable point is not the procedure but what happens to the plan when the procedure changes. The audit plan must describe the nature, timing and extent of the procedures to be performed, and the extent includes deciding the sample sizes to be tested: leaving sample size to be settled later, at the moment each procedure is performed, is not a proper plan. The plan and the related programme are then reconsidered as the audit progresses, on the auditor's review and preliminary evaluation of internal control and on the results of the compliance and substantive procedures. And the auditor documents the audit plan and every significant change made to it during the engagement, together with the reasons for the change. Writing the plan down fixes three things in advance about every procedure — what it is, when it happens and how far it goes — for the risk assessment work first and then for the further audit procedures pitched at the assertion level, each of them answering a risk the auditor has already assessed. It also shows that the work was laid out well enough to be reviewed and approved before anybody performed it. So an auditor who embarks on far more extensive work on foreign contributions than she first envisaged, and documents the procedures performed and the findings but not how the work was planned or why it changed, has left the gap the standard exists to close: the risk of not having conducted the audit according to professional standards in a qualitative manner, with nothing on the file able to show otherwise.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the requirement that the audit plan include the nature, timing and extent of procedures with the extent covering sample sizes, the reconsideration of the plan and programme as the audit progresses, and the requirement to document the audit plan and the significant changes made to it during the engagement together with the reasons, illustrated by the audit of a society registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 whose procedures on the receipt of foreign contributions were extended to rule out round-tripping

concepts.subsection: A first-year not-for-profit engagement and receipts that cannot be vouched at source
concepts.statement: Two evidence problems recur in a first audit of a charitable body and they pull in opposite directions. The first is the opening balances. An initial audit engagement is one where the prior period financial statements were not audited or were audited by a predecessor, and a body whose accounts have never been audited is squarely inside it. The auditor reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor's report where there is one, determines whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determines whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and performs procedures on the opening balances themselves. Two reporting consequences follow. If he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, the opinion is qualified or disclaimed. If he concludes that the opening balances contain a misstatement that materially affects the current period, or that policies are not consistently applied or a change is not properly accounted for, presented and disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse. The second problem is a receipt nobody can trace to its source — cash dropped into a collection box, a donation given at an event without a name, money handed to a volunteer and brought in later. There is no external document behind it, so the completeness of the receipt can only be supported by the controls the body operates over the collection itself, and where those controls are absent the auditor should not expect to close the gap by asking for a certificate: written representations provide necessary audit evidence but do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own, and the fact that management has given reliable representations does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains. Nor does the expense of the work excuse it: where a procedure has no substitute, difficulty, time or cost is not on its own a reason for leaving it undone, and none of the three lets the auditor rest on evidence he can see is less than persuasive. Where sufficient appropriate audit evidence cannot be obtained at all, what is left is a limitation on scope and the opinion is determined accordingly.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510 on initial audit engagements where the prior period was not audited: the four procedures on opening balances and the consequences of being unable to obtain evidence about them or of finding them misstated; read with SA 200 as reproduced in the same chapter, on why expense, delay or inconvenience alone cannot excuse a procedure that has no substitute or make weak evidence adequate, and with SA 580, on a written representation never being enough by itself

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A material misstatement is not always a wrong number, and SA 705 (Revised) gives the Basis for Opinion section three different jobs depending on what is wrong. Where what is wrong is a figure — an amount carried in the statements themselves, or a number given in a note — the auditor sets out in that section what the effect is and how large it is; where he cannot practicably size it, the section says that sizing it is not practicable. Where what is wrong is written disclosure rather than a figure, he explains instead in what respect the wording misstates the position. Where the fault is that a disclosure the framework demands has been left out altogether, three steps follow: the omission is taken up with those charged with governance, the section says what kind of thing is missing, and — where the law does not forbid it, where it can practicably be done, and where he holds evidence enough about what was left out — the auditor sets the absent disclosure out himself. Where the modification instead comes from evidence he could not get, the section carries why he could not get it. Pervasiveness is tested the same way whatever the misstatement looks like, and its third limb exists for exactly these facts — a defect in what is told to readers can be pervasive because of how central it is to their understanding, even though no figure in the primary statements moves.

citation.ref: para 21 on what the Basis for Opinion section must carry where specific amounts are misstated — the effect described and sized, unless sizing it is impracticable — together with the requirements that follow it for a wrongly worded disclosure and for one left out altogether, namely raising the omission with those charged with governance, naming what kind of thing is missing, and supplying the absent disclosure where the law permits, where it can practicably be done and where the evidence is held — read with para 5 on pervasiveness as it bears on disclosures

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: There are two roads to a disclaimer of opinion, and only the first one is about missing evidence. On the first, the evidence an opinion would have to rest on cannot be got, and the auditor judges that misstatements nobody has detected could, if they are there at all, be both material and pervasive in what they do to the statements. On the second, he holds the evidence on every one of the uncertainties in front of him and disclaims anyway: in extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties, he concludes that no opinion can be formed even so, because of how the uncertainties may act on one another and what they may come to together. Nothing is missing from the file. What is missing is the ability to say what the combination comes to. The word extremely is the standard's own, and it marks the road as rare rather than as an alternative to doing the work: a single uncertainty, however large, is dealt with under going concern reporting, under an emphasis of matter paragraph or under a modification for misstatement, and several uncertainties that can each be evaluated and added up are not this case either.

citation.ref: the ground for disclaiming where several uncertainties are open at once — evidence held on each of them separately, yet no opinion formable, because of how they may act on one another and what they may come to in total; a road the standard opens only in extremely rare circumstances — read with para 5 on pervasiveness and para 8 on the adverse opinion

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: Management would usually rather explain a disagreement in a note than have it in the auditor's report, and the note is management's stand on the matter while the qualification is the auditor's. The two are not interchangeable. Full disclosure by management does not by itself discharge the auditor; he exercises his own judgement on whether disclosure alone suffices or whether he must also modify the opinion, and an emphasis of matter paragraph is not a substitute for a modification. An emphasis of matter is open to him only where the matter is appropriately presented and he already holds the evidence he needs about it. Once he concludes that a modification is warranted he may refer to management's note and then go on to give the facts, his own assessment, and the quantification and impact on the various captions of the financial statements so far as he can. The qualification is expressed in a clear and unambiguous manner as "except for" the effects of the matter; phrases such as "subject to" or "with the foregoing explanation" are not sufficiently clear or forceful and are not appropriate in the opinion paragraph. Where notes of a qualificatory nature appear in the accounts, the auditor states all his qualifications independently in his report so that a reader can weigh them, and a bare cross-reference to a note is not, of itself, a qualification at all. Whatever the note may say, the auditor writes the matter up as he himself sees it, never as management has framed it. Where he answers any statutory affirmation in the negative or with a qualification, his report states the reasons, and all qualifications are contained in the auditor's report itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the distinction between notes on accounts and qualifications, the requirement that a qualification be expressed in a clear and unambiguous manner as "except for" rather than "subject to" or "with the foregoing explanation", the independent statement of all qualifications in the report, and the rule that a reference to a note does not automatically become a qualification

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: SA 705 (Revised) has its own communication requirement, and it is narrower and harder than the general one. Once the auditor sees a modification coming, those charged with governance are owed two things before he signs: why he expects to modify, and the sentence he expects to write. Two consequences follow. The trigger is the expectation, not the signature, so the communication happens while the matter can still be discussed and the misstatement still corrected — the auditor is required to discuss and deliberate the audit findings and the type of misstatements with those charged with governance. And the wording itself goes across, not merely the fact that there will be a modification; a board that is told "there will be a qualification" and first sees the sentence in the signed report has not been given what the standard asks for. This sits alongside, and does not replace, the SA 260 (Revised) requirement about matters bearing on how the report is framed and what goes in it, and the separate SA 706 (Revised) requirement to communicate an expected emphasis of matter or other matter paragraph and its wording. Communicating a matter never makes a modification unnecessary, and agreement from those charged with governance is not one of the conditions for modifying.

citation.ref: the requirement that an expected modification be put to those charged with governance in two parts before the report is signed — why the auditor expects to modify, and the sentence he expects to write — read with SA 260 (Revised) para 16 on matters bearing on how the report is framed and what goes in it

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: Knowing the gates is not the same as recognising the facts, and SA 706 (Revised) offers four examples of situations in which such a paragraph may be thought necessary. A dispute or a regulator's action well outside the ordinary run of the entity's affairs, where nobody can yet say how it will end. Something of consequence that happens to the entity after the reporting date and before the report is signed. A new accounting standard taken up a year ahead of the date it becomes compulsory, where the standard allows that and the year's figures move materially because of it. And a disaster on a large scale that has struck the entity's finances and still shows in them. Two things run through all four. Each is a matter the financial statements themselves present or disclose, which is what makes an emphasis of matter rather than an other matter paragraph the right vehicle. And in each the auditor is content with the accounting — the paragraph draws attention to something correctly done, and states that the opinion is not modified in respect of it. The list is illustrative and not a checklist: a matter on it still has to pass both gates, so it must be one that requires no modification under SA 705 (Revised) and, where SA 701 applies, must not have been determined to be a key audit matter. A widespread use of these paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication.

citation.ref: the four illustrative circumstances the standard sets out for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, read with para 8(a) and para 8(b) on the two provisos and para 9 on content and placement

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An other matter paragraph is the report's way of telling the reader something about the audit rather than about the accounts. Where the auditor judges that a reader needs to know something the financial statements do not carry — because it bears on how the audit was done, on what the auditor was answerable for, or on the report itself — he sets it out in an other matter paragraph, and two conditions have to hold. Law or regulation must not forbid the communication. And on an engagement where SA 701 bites, the matter must not already have been picked as a key audit matter for that section of the report. The first condition has no counterpart on the emphasis of matter side and is the one that is forgotten. When he includes the paragraph he puts it in a separate section of the report under the heading "Other Matter" or another appropriate heading. The recurring use in Indian practice is the division of responsibility: where the financial statements of branches or components included in the statements have been audited by other auditors, the paragraph names those branches, gives the total assets and the revenue they account for, records that their statements were audited by those auditors and that their reports have reached the principal auditor, and says that for the amounts and disclosures those branches contribute his opinion rests only on what those reports say; ICAI's illustration of that paragraph also states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter. The test is always the subject matter, not the importance: a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements can never take an other matter paragraph however relevant it is, and a matter outside them can never take an emphasis of matter paragraph, which may point only at information the statements themselves carry.

citation.ref: para 10 on the two provisos for an Other Matter paragraph — no prohibition in law or regulation, and, on an SA 701 engagement, no prior determination of the matter as a key audit matter — with the requirement to include the paragraph within a separate section under the heading "Other Matter" or other appropriate heading, read with para 9 and with the illustration of an Other Matter paragraph on branch financial statements audited by branch auditors in Ch. Reporting

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An emphasis of matter paragraph and a key audit matter answer two different questions, and the difference is where the importance sits. A key audit matter is one the auditor, on his professional judgement, ranks among the most significant things in this period's audit, chosen out of what he communicated to those charged with governance — the importance is to the AUDIT, and it is what required significant auditor attention. An emphasis of matter points at a matter appropriately presented or disclosed which the auditor judges so important that a USER could not properly understand the financial statements without it. The two tests can pull apart in both directions. A matter may be fundamental to users' understanding — a subsequent event is the standard example — and yet not have required significant auditor attention, so it is not a key audit matter and goes in an emphasis of matter paragraph. A matter determined to be a key audit matter may also, in the auditor's judgement, be fundamental to users' understanding; it does not then get both, because an emphasis of matter is barred where SA 701 applies and the matter has been determined to be a key audit matter, and the auditor may instead highlight its relative importance by presenting it more prominently than the other matters in the Key Audit Matters section, for instance as the first matter, or by including additional information in the description of it. Where SA 701 applies, the use of emphasis of matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of the individual key audit matters.

citation.ref: the relationship between Emphasis of Matter paragraphs and key audit matters — that a matter not determined to be a key audit matter because it did not require significant auditor attention may nonetheless be fundamental to users' understanding and be included in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, that where a key audit matter is also fundamental the auditor may present it more prominently in the Key Audit Matters section or add information to its description, and that the use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters where SA 701 applies — read with para 8(b)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6
concepts.statement: Clause (6) makes it professional misconduct for a member in practice to go after clients or professional work — whether he does it face to face, in a letter, through a circular, in an advertisement, at an interview, or by some route the clause does not trouble to list. The words that decide most questions are "indirectly" and "by any other means": work canvassed through a solicitor, a banker, an employee or a partner is the member's own solicitation, and a member may not do through another hand what he may not do with his own. Two provisos sit inside the clause itself. A chartered accountant may apply for, request, invite or secure professional work from another chartered accountant in practice — approaching the profession is not approaching the public. And a member may respond to tenders or enquiries issued from time to time by users of professional services or by organisations, and may secure work as a consequence. The second proviso is then narrowed by the Council's own guideline. Where a tender is floated by a user of professional services, or by an organisation, for work that only a chartered accountant may do — audit and attestation are the guideline's own examples — a member in practice leaves it alone. Two things reopen it: a floor for the fee written into the bidding papers by whoever issued them, or a field thrown open to other professionals alongside chartered accountants. That floor has to match the size, value, volume, manpower requirement and nature of the work it is being set for. Paying a reasonable earnest money deposit or security deposit where the area is not exclusive is not interfered with, though an exorbitant one may be looked into by the Ethical Standards Board case by case, and a member responding to a tender maintains a cost sheet showing the persons involved and the hours to be spent, which the Institute may call for. The restraint exists so that a member keeps his independence of judgement and commands the respect of prospective clients; the satisfaction of existing clients is the advertisement the profession allows.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the bar on soliciting clients or professional work, by whatever route and at whatever remove, with the proviso permitting a chartered accountant to seek work from another chartered accountant in practice and the proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders and enquiries, read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 on responding to tenders in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants and on earnest money deposits and the cost sheet

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6: the Council's website guidelines
concepts.statement: The Council approved the posting of particulars on a website by members and firms in practice under Clause (6), and every stipulation in those guidelines is an answer to the same question: does this reach out to people who did not ask? No format is prescribed and there is no restriction on the colours used. The website must run on a pull model and not a push model, so that a person who wishes to locate the member gets the information only on a specific pull request, and nothing on the site may be circulated by the firm on its own, by email or by any other technique except on such a request. A member may not issue any circular, advertisement or material of any kind soliciting people to visit the site, though the website address may be mentioned on professional stationery and email. The permitted content is a list: name, year of establishment, addresses of the head office and branches with telephone, fax and email, the partners and employees with their qualifications and particulars, job vacancies including articleship, and — displayable only on a specific pull request — the nature of the services rendered, the areas of experience, the number of articled assistants and the nature of the assignments handled. Names of clients and the fees charged may not be given at all, except where a regulator in India or outside requires it, only to the extent of that requirement, only while it is in force, and with a statement in italics below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule or directive requiring it. A passport style photograph is permitted. Articles, professional information, bulletin boards, professional updates and educational videos on topics of professional relevance are permitted. Chat rooms between members and between a firm and its clients are permitted with the confidentiality protocol observed, and a document management facility with distinct log-in and password may be provided. A firm may link to its page on a social networking site but may not solicit people to visit or like it. No advertisement in the nature of a banner or of any other nature is permitted. The address should be as near as possible to the name of the member or the firm, the site should ensure secrecy of client matters, it may link to the sites of ICAI, its Regional Councils and Branches and of Government, regulators and other professional bodies, and the information on it must not be at material variance from ICAI's own records.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's guidelines for posting particulars on the website of a member or firm in practice, included under the Guidelines for Advertisement pursuant to the decision of the Council at its 388th meeting held on 6th and 7th February 2020: the pull and not push model, the bar on circulating the content or soliciting visits, the permitted particulars and those displayable only on a specific pull request, the bar on naming clients or fees except where a regulator requires it with the italicised statement below the disclosure, the passport style photograph, the social networking link without soliciting likes, and the bar on banner advertisements

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6: the forms of soliciting the Council has ruled on
concepts.statement: Under Clause (6) the Council has ruled on particular forms of seeking work, and the pattern across them is that a bare statement of fact sent to people who already know the member is allowed while anything that reaches strangers or praises the member is not. In the press a member may not advertise for work or in a manner that could be read as offering to undertake work, and circulating letters to a small field of possible clients is equally barred; the exceptions are a request to another chartered accountant in practice, an announcement of a change in partnership, a dissolution, a change of address or of telephone number limited to a bare statement of facts with thought given to the area of circulation and the number of insertions, and a classified advertisement in the Institute's own journal or newsletter for sharing work, partnership or salaried employment carrying only the name, address, telephone, fax, email and social networking addresses with the factual position of experience and area of specialisation. Where a Government department, company, court, co-operative society or bank maintains a panel and the member knows of it, he may write asking to be placed on that panel and may quote fees on an enquiry received from it, but roving enquiries to any organisation that may have a panel are improper. A member may not mention his own or his firm's professional attainments in a book, an article or a presentation, though he may use the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm. Greeting cards and invitations carrying the designation and the firm name are permitted only to clients, relatives and friends. Advertising an event organised by a firm is not permitted, but an advertisement for the firm's silver, golden, diamond, platinum or centenary celebrations may be published in a newspaper or newsletter. A member or firm may not sponsor an event unless it is conducted by a Programme Organising Unit of ICAI with the prior approval of the CPE Directorate, and a member sponsoring a corporate social responsibility activity may use his own name with the prefix CA but not the firm name or the CA logo. A firm profile may be shared with a prospective client only in response to that client's specific query. In a public interview or to the press, details must not highlight professional attainments and must be given only in answer to a specific question and only as fact. Advertisements under box numbers are barred, educational videos may be uploaded without naming the firm or giving contact details or the website address, and letters, emails or circulars addressed specifically to persons likely to need a chartered accountant amount to advertisement. A member may not accept original professional work from a client introduced to him by another member and should ask the client to come through that member. And the representation an auditor may make on removal is not a right to the audit: it must set out in a dignified manner how he acted independently and conscientiously and may state his willingness to continue if reappointed, without directly or indirectly canvassing for his continuance.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the forms of soliciting work on which the Council has ruled: press advertisements and their three exceptions, empanelment and the bar on roving enquiries, books, articles and presentations, greeting cards and invitations, celebration and sponsorship advertisements, sharing a firm profile only against a specific query, public interviews, box numbers, educational videos, work emanating from a client introduced by another member, and the scope of the representation an auditor may make under section 140(4) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 194N — Tax deducted on cash withdrawn from a bank account
concepts.statement: A banking company, a co-operative society carrying on the business of banking, and a post office must deduct tax when the cash it pays out of a person's accounts crosses a limit for the year. For an ordinary recipient the limit is ₹1 crore, raised to ₹3 crores where the recipient is a co-operative society, and the rate is 2 per cent of the sum above that limit. A recipient who has filed no return of income for each of the three assessment years whose filing dates have already gone by is treated differently: the limit falls to ₹20 lakhs, and what is paid above ₹20 lakhs draws 2 per cent until the year's withdrawals reach ₹1 crore (₹3 crores for a co-operative society), and 5 per cent after that. Deduction is made when the cash is handed over. Four classes of recipient sit outside the section altogether — the Government, a banking company or a co-operative society carrying on banking or a post office, a business correspondent, and a white label ATM operator — and the Central Government may notify others.

citation.ref: Section 194N with its first and second provisos

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43CB — Profits from a construction contract or a service contract
concepts.statement: Profits from a construction contract, and from a service contract, are computed by the percentage of completion method laid down in the notified computation standard, whatever the books do. A service contract has two exits from that: where the contract runs for ninety days or less the profits are taken when the service is finished, and where the contract asks for an indeterminate number of acts spread over a stated period they are spread evenly over that period. Whichever of the three applies, two adjustments are fixed by the section itself — money the customer holds back until the defect liability period ends is still part of contract revenue, and interest, dividend or capital gains earned on the side may not be knocked off the contract cost.

citation.ref: Section 43CB read with the construction and revenue recognition standards notified under Section 145(2)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43D — Interest on a bad or doubtful debt of a bank or a financial institution
