concepts.statement: Six kinds of lender are let off the mercantile basis for one kind of income: a public financial institution, a scheduled bank, a co-operative bank of any kind except the primary agricultural credit society and the primary co-operative bank for agricultural and rural development, a State financial corporation, a State industrial investment corporation, and a notified class of non-banking financial company. Where the advance falls in the categories of bad and doubtful debt the Income-tax Rules prescribe, drawn up against the Reserve Bank's own guidelines, the interest on it is taxed in whichever year comes first — the year the lender takes it to its profit and loss account, or the year the money actually arrives. Accrual on its own brings nothing to tax. Interest on any other advance of the same lender is taxed the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Section 43D read with the categories of bad and doubtful debt prescribed under the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 36(1)(viia) with the proviso to Section 36(1)(vii) — A bank's provision and the debt it writes off
concepts.statement: A lender that may claim for a provision claims twice over and is then held back once. An Indian scheduled or non-scheduled bank, and a co-operative bank of any kind except the primary agricultural credit society and the primary co-operative bank for agricultural and rural development, may deduct up to 8.5 per cent of total income worked out before this clause and before Chapter VI-A, and on top of that up to 10 per cent of the aggregate average advances of its rural branches. A foreign bank, a public financial institution, a State financial corporation, a State industrial investment corporation and a non-banking financial company get 5 per cent of total income on the same footing and no rural limb at all. The holding back is the proviso to section 36(1)(vii): for a lender inside clause (viia), only so much of a bad debt written off is deductible as stands above the credit already sitting in the provision account. One account serves every advance including a rural one, and section 36(2)(v) will not let the write-off through unless it was debited to that account.

citation.ref: Sections 36(1)(viia) and 36(2)(v), read with the proviso and Explanation 2 to Section 36(1)(vii)

concepts.subsection: Section 292B with Section 292BB — The defect a notice survives and the one it does not
concepts.statement: Section 292B keeps a return, an assessment order, a notice, a summons or any other proceeding alive despite a mistake, a defect or an omission in it, so long as the document still does what the Act sent it to do — a mistyped figure, a slip in arithmetic, a wrong word. It reaches no further than that. A notice issued in the name of a company that had already been swallowed by an amalgamation, where the surviving company had told the Assessing Officer so before the notice went out, is aimed at nobody, and the Supreme Court in Principal CIT v. Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. held that taking part in the proceedings afterwards mends nothing. Section 292BB is a separate rule with a separate reach: once an assessee has appeared or co-operated, it stops him arguing that a notice reached him late, or by the wrong route, or not at all — but in CIT v. Laxman Das Khandelwal the Court held that it cannot conjure up a notice the officer never issued.

citation.ref: Section 292B and Section 292BB, read with Principal CIT v. Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. and CIT v. Laxman Das Khandelwal

concepts.subsection: Rule 138(14) — the trip to be weighed, and the twenty kilometres it lasts
concepts.statement: Rule 138(14) lists movements that need no e-way bill at all, whatever the goods are worth, and the trip to be weighed is one of them. Goods going out from the consignor's own place of business to a weighbridge, and the same goods coming back from the weighbridge to that place of business, sit outside the requirement so long as the leg is twenty kilometres or less and a delivery challan drawn under rule 55 travels with the vehicle. Both halves of the trip are named, not merely the outward one. Stretch a leg past twenty kilometres and nothing in the clause helps any more — the ordinary test comes back, so a consignment worth more than fifty thousand rupees needs a bill and a vehicle stopped without one is open to detention. Two neighbouring figures are easy to reach for and neither is this one. Fifty kilometres excuses filling in the conveyance details in Part B on an intra-State hop between the consignor and his transporter, and the bill itself is still generated. Twenty kilometres appears again in rule 138(10) as a validity step for over dimensional cargo, which is a different question altogether.

citation.ref: Rule 138(14), read with rule 55

concepts.subsection: Rule 41A — moving unused credit when a place of business takes its own registration in the same State
concepts.statement: Section 25 lets one person hold more than one registration inside a single State or Union territory, one for each place of business. When a place of business is broken out that way, rule 41A lets the person who already holds the registration pass his unused balance in the electronic credit ledger, wholly or in part, to any or all of the newly registered places. He furnishes FORM GST ITC-02A on the common portal within thirty days of obtaining the separate registration, the newly registered person accepts it there, and only on that acceptance does the credit reach the transferee's ledger. The share is fixed by the value of assets each of them holds when the registration is taken, and the rule's own explanation puts the trap beyond argument — value of assets means the whole of the business's assets, whether or not any credit was ever taken on them. So a schedule of assets that carried input tax credit is the wrong numerator and the wrong denominator both, and the figure it produces is the one an examiner puts in front of you.

citation.ref: Rule 41A, read with section 25 of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 37 with rule 59 — the sale to a consumer that has to be listed one by one
concepts.statement: GSTR-1 carries every invoice raised on a registered buyer separately, inter-State and intra-State alike, because that buyer will claim credit against it and the two sides have to meet. A sale to somebody who is not registered is different — he claims nothing, so as a rule only a consolidated figure goes in. One class of consumer sale is pulled back out of that rule. Where the supply is inter-State and the invoice value exceeds one lakh rupees, that invoice is reported on its own. Inter-State consumer invoices at or below a lakh go in as a State-wise total for each rate of tax, and intra-State consumer invoices go in as a rate-wise consolidated total however large they are. The reason is the destination principle. Tax on a consumer sale belongs to the State where the goods are consumed, and a large sale across a State line has to be identifiable before the revenue can be sent to the right place. Two details decide every question of this kind and both are easy to skip past — whether a State line was crossed, and whether the value exceeded a lakh rather than merely reached it.

citation.ref: Section 37(1), read with rule 59(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sub-rule (10) of rule 96 is gone — the exporter who bought cheap may now export on payment of tax
concepts.statement: A merchant exporter may buy the goods he is going to ship at a concessional rate of 0.1 per cent, on the conditions the notifications of 23 October 2017 set, and he takes credit of that small tax in the ordinary way. What he once could not do was export on payment of integrated tax and claim that tax back. Sub-rule (10) of rule 96 shut that road to anybody who had received supplies at the concessional rate, leaving him one route only — a letter of undertaking or a bond, an export without payment, and a refund of unused credit. Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8 October 2024 omitted the sub-rule. Both routes are open to him now: export under a letter of undertaking or bond and claim back the unused credit, or export on payment of integrated tax and claim back the tax paid. His supplier is unaffected either way — selling at a tenth of a per cent while buying inputs at ordinary rates leaves credit piling up that cannot be used, and the supplier claims that as a refund on account of the inverted duty structure. Material printed before October 2024 still says the exporter has one road, and that sentence has stopped being true.

citation.ref: Rule 96, sub-rule (10) omitted by Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8 October 2024, read with Notification No. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and Notification No. 41/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) both dated 23 October 2017

concepts.subsection: Board meeting quorum — section 174
concepts.statement: Quorum for a board meeting is the higher of one-third of the total strength of directors (any fraction rounded up) or two directors. A director interested in an item under section 184(2) is left out of the count for that item, and telephonic assent from a director not participating by the prescribed video-conferencing means does not count as presence. Absent quorum, the meeting stands automatically adjourned to the same day the following week, same time and place, unless the articles say otherwise.

citation.ref: Section 174

concepts.subsection: Frequency of board meetings — section 173
concepts.statement: Every company holds at least four board meetings a year, with the gap between two consecutive meetings never exceeding one hundred and twenty days, and the first meeting within thirty days of incorporation. A one person company, small company, dormant company or private start-up needs only one meeting in each half of the calendar year, with a minimum gap of ninety days between the two — a relaxation, not the general rule.

citation.ref: Section 173

concepts.subsection: Board powers needing shareholder approval — section 180
concepts.statement: The board cannot, by its own resolution, part with an undertaking — sell it, lease it or dispose of it in any other way — where what goes is the whole of that undertaking or substantially so, or borrow beyond the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium (ordinary-course temporary bank loans excepted) — both need a special resolution of the shareholders first, obtained before the act, not disclosed to them after it.

citation.ref: Section 180

concepts.subsection: Retirement by rotation — section 152
concepts.statement: Independent directors are never liable to retire by rotation. Of the remaining directors of a public company, at least two-thirds must be liable to rotation, of which one-third (or the number nearest to one-third) retires at every annual general meeting, the director longest in office retiring first and being eligible for reappointment. Articles cannot exempt directors from rotation below this statutory floor.

citation.ref: Section 152(6)

concepts.subsection: Disclosure of directors' interest — section 184
concepts.statement: Every director discloses his concern or interest in any company, body corporate, firm or association of individuals at the first board meeting he attends in a financial year, and again on any change — a duty owed regardless of the size of the interest. Separately, an interested director discloses that interest in a specific contract or arrangement and does not participate in the board's discussion or vote on it; a contract entered in breach is voidable at the company's option.

citation.ref: Section 184

concepts.subsection: Contract of employment with managing or whole-time director — section 190
concepts.statement: A company keeps at its registered office a copy of its managing or whole-time director's contract of service, or a written memorandum of its terms where the contract is not in writing, open for inspection by members without charge during business hours — a members' right the board or the company secretary cannot narrow to itself or to the auditor.

citation.ref: Section 190

concepts.subsection: Consolidated financial statements — section 129(3)
concepts.statement: A company with one or more subsidiaries, including associate companies and joint ventures, prepares a consolidated financial statement in addition to its standalone statements, in the same form and manner, following the applicable accounting standards, and lays it before the annual general meeting alongside the standalone statements. Consolidation covers every subsidiary; it is not a management choice of which ones to fold in.

citation.ref: Section 129(3)

concepts.subsection: Board's report contents — section 134
concepts.statement: The board's report states, among other prescribed particulars, a director's responsibility statement under section 134(5), particulars of loans, guarantees and investments under section 186, particulars of related-party contracts in the prescribed form, the CSR policy and initiatives, and — for listed and other prescribed companies — a statement on the formal annual evaluation of the board, its committees and individual directors. These are matters the report must itself state, not particulars merely available on request.

citation.ref: Section 134(3)

concepts.subsection: Annual return and its certification — section 92
concepts.statement: Every company files its annual return with the Registrar within sixty days of the annual general meeting, or of the date by which the AGM should have been held where none took place, in which case a statement of the reasons for the default goes with it. Section 92(2) leaves the size line to the rules, and Rule 11(2) draws it at a listed company, or a company with paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more, or turnover of ₹50 crore or more: such a return must additionally be certified by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8. The two size tests are alternatives — crossing either is enough — and listing is a third, independent route in.

citation.ref: Sections 92(2) and 92(4), read with Rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 (Form MGT-8)

concepts.subsection: Rights issue procedure — section 62
concepts.statement: A rights issue offer goes to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holding, stays open for not less than fifteen days and not more than thirty days, and carries a right of renunciation in favour of another person unless the articles exclude it. The board cannot allot before the offer period lapses or ahead of renunciation choices being exercised or declined.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Debentures — trustee and redemption reserve, section 71
concepts.statement: Section 71(5) stops a company from issuing a prospectus, or making an offer or invitation to the public or to more than five hundred of its members, for subscription of its debentures unless it has appointed one or more debenture trustees before that issue or offer. What pulls the trustee in is the kind of offer, not the size of the borrowing — the section names no rupee figure at all. Rule 18(1)(c) adds that the trustee comes before the prospectus or letter of offer goes out, and the debenture trust deed is executed within sixty days of allotment, so an independent party holds the security and enforces the debenture-holders' rights; the issuer's own guarantee is not a substitute for that office. Section 71(4) separately requires a debenture redemption reserve out of profits available for dividend, but Rule 18(7) as it now stands excuses listed companies, NBFCs registered under section 45-IA of the RBI Act and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank; other unlisted companies keep a reserve of ten per cent of the outstanding value of the debentures.

citation.ref: Sections 71(4) and 71(5), read with Rules 18(1)(c) and 18(7) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Moratorium under the IBC — section 14
concepts.statement: On admission of a corporate insolvency resolution application, the adjudicating authority declares a moratorium barring institution or continuation of suits against the corporate debtor, transfer or disposal of its assets, enforcement of any security interest, and recovery of property by an owner or lessor in the debtor's possession; supply of essential goods and services to the debtor cannot be terminated during this period. The moratorium does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee for the corporate debtor.

citation.ref: Section 14

concepts.subsection: CIRP time limit — section 12 of the IBC
concepts.statement: A corporate insolvency resolution process must be completed within one hundred and eighty days of the insolvency commencement date. The committee of creditors may resolve, by a vote of sixty-six per cent of voting share under section 12(2), to instruct the resolution professional to seek one extension of up to ninety days — one only, never a second. The proviso to section 12(3) then caps the whole process at three hundred and thirty days from the insolvency commencement date, and that outer figure expressly swallows the time taken in legal proceedings relating to the process. The Supreme Court in Essar Steel read down the word "mandatorily" so a tribunal may go past three hundred and thirty days in an exceptional case where the delay is the tribunal's own, but that is a rescue, not the rule.

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and the proviso to section 12(3), as inserted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2019

concepts.subsection: Committee of creditors — related parties and voting thresholds
concepts.statement: The committee of creditors comprises all financial creditors of the corporate debtor, but the first proviso to section 21(2) strips a financial creditor that is a related party of the corporate debtor of any right of representation, participation or voting in the committee. Losing the vote is not losing the claim — the related party remains a financial creditor whose debt is admitted and paid in its class. The committee's ordinary decisions need fifty-one per cent of voting share under section 21(8); the actions listed in section 28(1) need sixty-six per cent under section 28(3), and so does approval of a resolution plan under section 30(4). "Related party" here is the IBC's own definition in section 5(24), which is wider than section 2(76) of the Companies Act — and the corporate debtor's related-party disclosure under Ind AS 24 continues through the process regardless of who may vote.

citation.ref: Sections 5(24), 21(2) first proviso, 21(8), 28(3) and 30(4)

concepts.subsection: Liquidation waterfall — section 53 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 53(1) distributes liquidation proceeds in a fixed order that overrides anything to the contrary in any other law - (a) insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs in full; (b) workmen's dues for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished its security, ranking equally between themselves; (c) wages and unpaid dues of employees other than workmen for the twelve months preceding that date; (d) financial debts owed to unsecured creditors; (e) government dues for the two years preceding that date and any amount left unpaid to a secured creditor that enforced its own security, ranking equally; (f) any remaining debts and dues; (g) preference shareholders; (h) equity shareholders or partners. Section 327(7) of the Companies Act, 2013 shuts sections 326 and 327 — the Companies Act's own preferential payments — out of a liquidation under the Code, and the Supreme Court upheld that exclusion in Moser Baer Karamchari Union.

citation.ref: Section 53(1), read with section 327(7) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Ineligible resolution applicant — section 29A and the MSME relaxation
concepts.statement: Section 29A lists the persons who may not submit a resolution plan, and section 30(4) obliges the committee of creditors to check eligibility before approving one. Clause (c) catches a person whose account, or an account of a corporate debtor under his management, has been classified as a non-performing asset with at least one year gone from that classification to the insolvency commencement date. Clause (h) catches a person who has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor of the corporate debtor where that guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid. Section 240A switches off clauses (c) and (h) alone where the corporate debtor is a micro, small or medium enterprise, so a promoter of an MSME may bid for his own company — but every other clause of section 29A, including clause (b) on an undischarged insolvent and clause (d) on a conviction, applies to him unchanged.

citation.ref: Sections 29A(b), 29A(c), 29A(h), 30(4) and 240A

concepts.subsection: Pre-packaged insolvency resolution process — Chapter III-A of the IBC
concepts.statement: Chapter III-A, sections 54A to 54P, opens the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process to one class of debtor only — a corporate debtor classified as a micro, small or medium enterprise under section 7(1) of the MSMED Act, 2006. The minimum default is ten lakh rupees, notified under the second proviso to section 4 by S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021, against the one crore rupees that gates an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process. Before filing, the corporate debtor must obtain the approval of unrelated financial creditors representing not less than sixty-six per cent in value of the financial debt owed to them, and must place a base resolution plan on the table. The whole process is built to close within one hundred and twenty days, against the outer three hundred and thirty of a full process, and management stays with the existing board — a debtor-in-possession process supervised by a resolution professional, not an ouster of the board.

citation.ref: Sections 54A and 54C of Chapter III-A, read with the second proviso to section 4 and notification S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021

concepts.subsection: FDI receipt — the Companies Act clock and the FEMA clock
concepts.statement: A single foreign investment starts two clocks with two regulators. Under company law, section 42(6) requires allotment within sixty days of receipt of the application money, refund within fifteen days of that period if allotment does not happen, and interest at twelve per cent beyond that; section 42(8) then requires the return of allotment with the Registrar within fifteen days of the allotment, and section 42(4) blocks the company from using the money until it is filed. Under FEMA, Regulation 4(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019 requires the issue to be reported to the Reserve Bank in Form FC-GPR not later than thirty days from the date of issue of the equity instruments, and Regulation 5 makes a late filing payable through a late submission fee. The two filings run from the same allotment, to different authorities, on different lengths of leash — filing one never satisfies the other.

citation.ref: Regulations 4(1) and 5 of the FEM (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019, read with sections 42(4), 42(6) and 42(8) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Overseas direct investment against overseas portfolio investment
concepts.statement: Rule 2(1)(q) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 makes an investment overseas direct investment where it is an acquisition of unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity, or a subscription to its memorandum, or an acquisition of ten per cent or more of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity, or any investment below ten per cent that carries control. Rule 2(1)(s) leaves everything else in foreign securities as overseas portfolio investment. The Explanation to Rule 2(1)(q) is the sting — once an investment is classified as ODI it stays ODI even if the holding later falls below ten per cent or control is lost, so the reporting and exit discipline follows the original classification, not today's percentage. Paragraph 3(1) of Schedule I caps an Indian entity's total financial commitment in all foreign entities at four hundred per cent of its net worth as per the last audited balance sheet, Rule 19(1) bars ODI into real estate activity, gambling and rupee-linked financial products without approval, and reporting, including the Annual Performance Report, runs through Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022.

citation.ref: Rules 2(1)(q) with its Explanation, 2(1)(s) and 19(1), and paragraph 3(1) of Schedule I, of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, read with Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022

concepts.subsection: Compounding a FEMA contravention — section 15 and the 2024 Rules
concepts.statement: A contravention of FEMA carries a penalty under section 13, and section 15 lets the contravener compound it — admit it, pay a sum, and close the matter — on an application made after the contravention. The Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024, notified on 12 September 2024, superseded the 2000 Rules and moved every figure: the application fee is now ten thousand rupees plus tax, and the Reserve Bank officer who may compound is fixed by the amount involved — an Assistant General Manager below sixty lakh rupees, a Deputy General Manager below two crore fifty lakh rupees, a General Manager below five crore rupees, and a Chief General Manager above five crore rupees. The compounding order is to be passed within one hundred and eighty days of receipt of a complete application, and the amount is payable within fifteen days of the order, failing which the application is void and FEMA applies to the contravention as though nothing had happened. A contravention of clause (a) of section 3 — dealing in foreign exchange with an unauthorised person — is not compounded by the Reserve Bank at all; it goes to the Directorate of Enforcement.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 15, read with the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024 (notified 12 September 2024)

concepts.subsection: Insider trading — continual disclosure and the contra trade bar
concepts.statement: Regulation 7(2)(a) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 makes every promoter, member of the promoter group, designated person and director disclose to the company the securities acquired or disposed of, within two trading days, once the value traded — in one transaction or a series over any calendar quarter — exceeds ten lakh rupees. Regulation 7(2)(b) then makes the company notify the stock exchange within two trading days of receiving that disclosure. Separately, clause 10 of Schedule B to Regulation 9 makes the company's code of conduct forbid a designated person who has traded from executing a contra trade for a period that can never be shorter than six months; a contra trade done in breach has its profits disgorged to SEBI for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund. The compliance officer may relax the restriction for reasons recorded in writing, but a relaxation can never permit what the Regulations themselves prohibit.

citation.ref: Regulations 7(2)(a) and 7(2)(b), and clause 10 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9

concepts.subsection: Substantial acquisition — when an open offer is triggered
concepts.statement: Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 triggers an open offer the moment an acquirer with persons acting in concert crosses twenty-five per cent of the voting rights of a target company for the first time. Regulation 3(2) is the creeping acquisition route and is available only to someone already holding twenty-five per cent or more but below the maximum permissible non-public shareholding: he may add up to five per cent of voting rights in a financial year without an offer, and an open offer is due the moment he acquires more than that. Regulation 4 triggers an offer on the acquisition of control however few shares change hands. The offer must be for at least twenty-six per cent of the target's voting capital under Regulation 7(1). The public announcement is made on the date of agreeing to acquire under Regulation 13(1), the detailed public statement follows within five working days under Regulation 13(4), and Regulation 29(1) separately makes any person crossing five per cent disclose to the company and the exchanges within two working days.

citation.source: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions of a listed entity — LODR Regulation 23
concepts.statement: A listed entity answers to three regimes on the same related party transaction and they do not line up. Section 188 of the Companies Act lets a transaction out of its board and shareholder approvals where the company struck it on an arm's length basis while going about its ordinary business. Regulation 23(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 grants no such exemption — every related party transaction needs the prior approval of the audit committee, and only the independent directors on that committee may give it. Regulation 23(4) sends a material related party transaction to the shareholders, and Regulation 23(7) makes every related party abstain from voting on the resolution whether or not it is a party to that particular transaction. Regulation 23(5) exempts a transaction between a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiary whose accounts are consolidated, and transactions between two such wholly-owned subsidiaries. Materiality under Regulation 23(1) is the lower of a rupee ceiling SEBI prescribes and ten per cent of annual consolidated turnover per the last audited financial statements — SEBI replaced the flat rupee cap with a turnover-scaled ceiling with effect from 19 December 2025, so confirm the figure applicable to your attempt before quoting one. Over and above all of it, Ind AS 24 requires the relationship and the transaction to be disclosed in the financial statements whether or not any approval was needed.

citation.ref: Regulations 23(1), 23(2), 23(4), 23(5) and 23(7), read with section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Ind AS 24

concepts.subsection: Significant beneficial owner — section 90 and the SBO Rules
concepts.statement: Section 90(1) speaks of an individual holding a beneficial interest of not less than twenty-five per cent "or such other percentage as may be prescribed", and Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018 prescribes ten per cent — so ten is the working line and twenty-five is a figure the Rules have overtaken. The test is not the size of a shareholding but its route: a significant beneficial owner holds indirectly, or indirectly together with any direct holding, not less than ten per cent of the shares, or of the voting rights, or of the distributable dividend, or exercises significant influence or control. A purely direct holding, however large, makes a person a registered member and not a significant beneficial owner. He declares in Form BEN-1 within thirty days; the company files Form BEN-2 within thirty days of that declaration and keeps the register in Form BEN-3. Section 90(4A) puts the company under a duty to go and identify its significant beneficial owners, section 90(5) lets it serve notice in Form BEN-4, section 90(6) gives the recipient thirty days to answer, and on no answer or an unsatisfactory one section 90(7) sends the company to the Tribunal within fifteen days for an order restricting the shares, which the Tribunal passes within sixty days under section 90(8).

citation.ref: Sections 90(1), 90(4A), 90(5), 90(6), 90(7) and 90(8), read with Rules 2(1)(h), 3 and 4 of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018

concepts.subsection: Scheme of compromise or arrangement — section 230
concepts.statement: A scheme under section 230 clears three separate gates. The meeting gate is section 230(6): a majority of the persons voting, representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or class of creditors or members or class of members voting in person, by proxy or by postal ballot — a majority in number and three-fourths in value, both, of those who actually vote. The objection gate is the proviso to section 230(4): only a person holding not less than ten per cent of the shareholding, or having outstanding debt of not less than five per cent of the total outstanding debt as per the latest audited financial statement, may object at all. The accounting gate is the proviso to section 230(7): the Tribunal cannot sanction the scheme unless a certificate from the company's auditor has been filed with it stating that the accounting treatment proposed in the scheme conforms to the accounting standards prescribed under section 133. That last one is where company law reaches into the audit file — an accounting treatment engineered inside a scheme does not escape the standards by being carried in a court-sanctioned document.

citation.ref: Sections 230(4) proviso, 230(6) and the proviso to section 230(7)

concepts.subsection: Re-opening and revising filed accounts — sections 130 and 131
concepts.statement: Financial statements once adopted and filed cannot be pulled back by the board on its own. Section 130 allows a re-opening and recasting only on an order of a court or the Tribunal, and only on an application by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or any person concerned — never on the company's own motion — and no order may reach a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year. Accounts so revised are final. Section 131 is the directors' own route: with the Tribunal's approval they may prepare a revised financial statement or a revised Board's report for any of the three preceding financial years, only where the original does not comply with section 129 or section 134, confined to that non-compliance, and not more than once in a financial year. Neither section is engaged by an Ind AS 8 prior period error — restating the comparative figures in the current year's financial statements is ordinary accounting and needs nobody's approval. The Tribunal enters the picture only when the earlier year's own filed statements are to be replaced.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1), 130(3) and 131(1), read with Ind AS 8

concepts.subsection: Preferential transactions — section 43 and the two look-back periods
concepts.statement: Section 43(2) makes a transaction preferential where the corporate debtor transfers property or an interest in it for the benefit of a creditor, surety or guarantor on account of an antecedent debt, and the transfer puts that person in a better position than he would have been in on a distribution under section 53. Section 43(4) then fixes two different windows measured back from the insolvency commencement date — two years for a related party, one year for anybody else — and a transfer outside the applicable window cannot be a preference however unfair it looks. Section 43(3) carves out transfers made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of the corporate debtor or the transferee, and transfers creating a security interest for new value; the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain (Jaypee Infratech) read that "or" as "and", so the transaction must be ordinary for both sides. Section 44 lists the orders the Tribunal may pass, chiefly restoring the property to the corporate debtor. Section 26 is the sting for the timetable: filing an avoidance application does not affect the corporate insolvency resolution process, so the plan is neither held up by the application nor discharged by the plan's approval.

concepts.subsection: Fraudulent and wrongful trading — sections 66 and 67 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 66(1) is fraudulent trading. It applies in a corporate insolvency resolution process or a liquidation, it reaches any persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on the business with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, and it requires that intent to be proved. Section 66(2) is wrongful trading and is a much lower bar: on an application by the resolution professional the Tribunal may direct a director or partner to contribute to the assets where, before the insolvency commencement date, he knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding the commencement of a corporate insolvency resolution process, and he did not exercise due diligence in minimising the potential loss to creditors. No dishonesty is needed. The Explanation measures due diligence against a reasonably diligent person having the knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out the same functions. Section 67 lets the Tribunal make the liability a charge on the person's assets. This is where the audit file becomes evidence: a going-concern paragraph written under SA 570, and the board minutes that answered it, are the record of what the directors knew and when. Contrast section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, whose fraudulent-conduct liability still needs the intent section 66(2) does without.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1), 66(2) with its Explanation, and 67, read with SA 570 and section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Insolvency of a personal guarantor — sections 60(2) and 94 to 100
concepts.statement: A personal guarantor to a corporate debtor is dealt with under Part III of the Code, but he is not sent to the Debt Recovery Tribunal whenever the company is already in front of the National Company Law Tribunal. Section 60(2) requires an application relating to the insolvency resolution or bankruptcy of a personal guarantor to be filed before, or stand transferred to, the same National Company Law Tribunal where a corporate insolvency resolution process or liquidation of the corporate debtor is pending, and section 60(4) arms that Tribunal with all the powers of the Debt Recovery Tribunal for the purpose. The debtor applies under section 94 and a creditor under section 95, in either case through a resolution professional. Section 96 then starts an interim moratorium from the date of the application itself — not from admission — staying pending legal proceedings in respect of any debt and barring fresh ones. Section 97 confirms or appoints the resolution professional, section 99 gives him ten days from his appointment to examine the application and report recommending admission or rejection, and section 100 gives the Tribunal fourteen days from that report to admit or reject. On admission the interim moratorium ends and the section 101 moratorium of one hundred and eighty days begins.

concepts.subsection: Voluntary liquidation of a solvent company — section 59
concepts.statement: Section 59(1) opens voluntary liquidation only to a corporate person that has not committed any default — it is an exit for the solvent, not a route out of debt. Section 59(3) sets the order of steps and each has its own clock. A declaration of solvency is made by a majority of the directors, verified by affidavit, saying the company has no debt or will be able to pay its debts in full from the proceeds of the assets, and that it is not being liquidated to defraud any person; it is accompanied by the audited financial statements and a record of the business operations for the previous two years or since incorporation, whichever is later, and a valuation report of the assets where there are assets. Within four weeks of that declaration the members pass a special resolution to wind up voluntarily and appoint an insolvency professional as liquidator. Where the company owes any debt, creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt must approve that resolution within seven days of it. Section 59(5) makes the liquidation commence on the date of the resolution — or the creditors' approval where one was needed. Section 59(6) then applies sections 35 to 53 to the process, so the section 53 waterfall governs the order of payment even here; the difference is that in a solvent liquidation the water reaches the bottom and the surplus goes to the members.

concepts.subsection: The clean slate for a rescued company — section 32A of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 32A(1) stops the corporate debtor being prosecuted for an offence committed before the commencement of the corporate insolvency resolution process, from the date the Tribunal approves a resolution plan under section 31, but only where the plan results in a change in the management or control of the corporate debtor to a person who was not a promoter, was not in the management or control of the corporate debtor, is not a related party of such a person, and against whom no investigating authority has reported or complained of having abetted or conspired in the offence. Section 32A(2) carries the same protection to the property of the corporate debtor, which then ceases to be liable to attachment, seizure, retention or confiscation for that offence — this is the provision on which attachments made under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act have been ordered released. What the section does not do is clear anybody else. The proviso to section 32A(1) says every person who was a designated partner, officer in default or in any manner in charge of or responsible to the corporate debtor for the conduct of its business shall continue to be liable to prosecution and punishment, and section 32A(3) obliges the corporate debtor and such persons to extend all assistance and co-operation to the investigating authority. The company walks away; the people who ran it do not.

citation.ref: Sections 32A(1) with its proviso, 32A(2) and 32A(3), read with section 31

concepts.subsection: Delisting under an approved resolution plan — Delisting Regulation 3(2)
concepts.statement: A listed company that comes out of insolvency is usually delisted, and the ordinary delisting machinery is impossible there — reverse book building assumes a promoter with money and a market with a discovered price, and an insolvent company has neither. Regulation 3(2)(b) of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 therefore takes the whole of the Regulations off a delisting made pursuant to a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, where the plan either provides for the delisting of the shares or gives the existing public shareholders an exit at a specified price. Two conditions ride on the exemption. The first proviso fixes a floor on fairness rather than on value: the exit price for the public shareholders shall not be less than the price at which a promoter, any entity of the promoter group, or any other shareholder is given an exit under that plan. The second proviso requires the details of the delisting, together with the justification for the exit price, to be disclosed to the recognised stock exchanges within one day of the approval of the resolution plan. The Bombay High Court upheld the validity of the carve-out in December 2024.

citation.ref: Regulation 3(2)(b) and its two provisos, read with section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

concepts.subsection: Preferential issue by a listed company — ICDR pricing and lock-in
concepts.statement: A preferential allotment by a listed company answers to company law and to SEBI at the same time, and SEBI's conditions are the ones company law never imposes. Section 62(1)(c) with section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 supplies the special resolution, the valuation and the private placement machinery. Chapter V of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 then adds a floor price and a lock-in. Regulation 164 fixes the floor for frequently traded shares at the higher of the volume weighted average price of the ninety trading days preceding the relevant date and the volume weighted average price of the ten trading days preceding it — the amendment of 2022 replaced the old twenty-six weeks and two weeks with those trading-day windows. Regulation 167 locks the allotted shares in: eighteen months for an allotment to promoters or the promoter group up to twenty per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital, six months for the part above that twenty per cent, and six months for an allottee who is not a promoter, all reduced from three years and one year by the 2022 amendment. Regulation 160 separately shuts out an allottee who has sold or transferred any equity shares of the issuer in the ninety trading days preceding the relevant date.

citation.source: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
citation.ref: Regulations 160, 164 and 167 of Chapter V, read with sections 42 and 62(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Material events — LODR Regulation 30 and its three clocks
concepts.statement: Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 splits events into two lists in Schedule III Part A. Para A events are disclosed on their own, with no materiality test applied at all. Para B events are disclosed only where the listed entity's own materiality policy or the quantitative test bites. That quantitative test, in Regulation 30(4)(i)(c), is the lower of three numbers, computed on the last audited consolidated financial statements: two per cent of turnover, two per cent of net worth except where net worth is negative, and five per cent of the average of the absolute value of profit or loss after tax for the last three financial years. Taking the lower makes the trigger easier to cross, not harder, which is the opposite of what most readers assume. Regulation 30(6) then supplies three clocks: thirty minutes from the closure of the board meeting in which the decision was taken; twelve hours where the event emanates from within the listed entity; and twenty-four hours where it does not. None of this answers the accounting question. An event after the reporting date is separately tested under Ind AS 10 for whether it gives evidence of a condition that existed at the reporting date, and the auditor tests the same facts under SA 560 — a twenty-four-hour exchange filing and a non-adjusting event disclosure can be, and often are, the correct answer to the same fact together.

citation.ref: Regulations 30(4)(i) and 30(6), read with Schedule III Part A, Ind AS 10 and SA 560

concepts.subsection: NFRA's reach and the boundary with the Institute — section 132
concepts.statement: The National Financial Reporting Authority does not oversee every auditor. Rule 3(1) of the NFRA Rules, 2018 fixes the classes: companies whose securities are listed on any stock exchange in India or outside India; unlisted public companies having paid-up capital of not less than five hundred crore rupees, or annual turnover of not less than one thousand crore rupees, or outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of not less than five hundred crore rupees in aggregate as on the thirty-first of March of the immediately preceding financial year; insurance companies, banking companies and companies engaged in generation or supply of electricity; and any body corporate referred by the Central Government in the public interest. Those three unlisted-public-company tests are alternatives — crossing any one is enough. Section 132(4) gives NFRA the power to investigate professional or other misconduct of a member or firm auditing such a company, and its proviso shuts the door on everyone else: no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct where NFRA has initiated an investigation. Section 132(4)(c) sets the penalty at not less than one lakh rupees extending to five times the fees received for an individual, and not less than five lakh rupees extending to ten times the fees received for a firm, with debarment from audit or valuation work for a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years. Outside those classes, the disciplinary route under sections 21A and 21B of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 continues to be the only one.

citation.ref: Sections 132(2), 132(4) with its proviso and 132(4)(c), read with Rule 3(1) of the NFRA Rules, 2018

concepts.subsection: CSR set-off under Rule 7(3) and what the Income-tax Act does with the spend
concepts.statement: Overspending on corporate social responsibility is not lost. Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 lets a company set the excess off against the requirement of up to the immediately succeeding three financial years, on two conditions — the excess must not include any surplus arising out of the CSR activities themselves, and the Board must pass a resolution to that effect. Section 135(9) removes the need for a CSR Committee altogether where the amount required to be spent does not exceed fifty lakh rupees, the Board doing its work instead. Section 135(6) sends an unspent amount relating to an ongoing project to a separate Unspent CSR Account within thirty days of the end of the financial year, to be spent within three financial years; anything not relating to an ongoing project goes to a Schedule VII fund within six months of the end of the year. Now the tax side, which pulls the other way. Explanation 2 to section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 says expenditure incurred on activities relating to corporate social responsibility referred to in section 135 shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purposes of the business, so it is not deductible under section 37(1) at all. Section 80G still allows a deduction for a qualifying donation made as CSR, except that it expressly denies it for a CSR sum paid to the Swachh Bharat Kosh and to the Clean Ganga Fund. Deductions that stand on their own feet, such as section 35, are unaffected by the label.

citation.ref: Sections 135(6) and 135(9) with Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, read with Explanation 2 to section 37(1) and section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Producer companies — Chapter XXIA of the Companies Act
concepts.statement: Chapter XXIA, sections 378A to 378ZU, was inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2020 with effect from 11 February 2021, carrying Part IXA of the 1956 Act into the present one. Section 378C admits exactly three ways of forming a producer company — ten or more individuals, each of them a producer; or two or more producer institutions; or a combination of ten or more individuals and producer institutions. On registration it becomes a body corporate as if it were a private limited company, but with two departures written into the section itself: the limit on the number of members does not apply to it, and it can never become or be deemed to be a public company. Section 378D(1)(a) gives every member a single vote irrespective of his shareholding or patronage where the membership is all individuals, which is the co-operative principle sitting inside a company. Section 378O requires at least five and not more than fifteen directors. Section 378ZG is where audit meets the chapter: the auditor reports, over and above everything section 143 already requires, on the amount of debts due along with particulars of bad debts, the verification of cash balance and securities, the details of assets and liabilities, all transactions that appear contrary to the provisions of the chapter, loans given to directors, and donations or subscriptions given by the producer company.

citation.ref: Sections 378C, 378D(1), 378O and 378ZG of Chapter XXIA, read with section 143

concepts.subsection: Land-border investment and downstream investment under the NDI Rules
concepts.statement: Two rules of the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 decide more structuring questions than any sectoral cap. The proviso to Rule 6(a), which carries Press Note 3 of 2020 into law, says an entity of a country which shares a land border with India, or an investment whose beneficial owner is situated in or is a citizen of such a country, may invest only with Government approval — and that applies whatever the sector's own entry route, so a hundred per cent automatic sector gives such an investor nothing. Rule 23 governs what happens one level down. Where an Indian company that is owned or controlled by a person resident outside India invests in another Indian company, that investment is a downstream investment and counts as indirect foreign investment in the second company; it must comply with the entry route, the sectoral caps, the pricing guidelines and the other attendant conditions that would have applied had the money come directly from abroad. Rule 23 also requires the funds for a downstream investment to be brought in from abroad and forbids leveraging funds borrowed in the domestic market for it, and the investment is reported to the Reserve Bank in Form DI. An Indian company that is neither owned nor controlled by a non-resident makes no downstream investment at all — its investment is domestic, however much foreign money sits on its share register.

citation.ref: Proviso to Rule 6(a) and Rule 23 of the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, read with Press Note 3 (2020 Series) dated 17 April 2020

concepts.subsection: Branch and liaison offices — FEMA 22(R) and the tax that follows
concepts.statement: The Foreign Exchange Management (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016, notified as FEMA 22(R), set two different entry tests. A branch office needs a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding five financial years in the home country and a net worth of not less than USD 100,000 or its equivalent, certified by the applicant's auditor. A liaison office needs a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding three financial years and a net worth of not less than USD 50,000 or its equivalent. What the two may do differs even more than what they must show. A branch office may carry on the permitted activities and earn income in India. A liaison office may act only as a communication channel between the head office and parties in India — it may not undertake any commercial, trading or industrial activity, it may not earn any income in India, and it must meet its expenses wholly through inward remittances of foreign exchange from the head office. Both file an Annual Activity Certificate from a chartered accountant with the authorised dealer bank and the Director General of Income-tax (International Taxation) on or before 30 September each year. That certificate is where the tax exposure is usually discovered: an office that negotiates prices, concludes contracts or secures orders is doing more than preparatory or auxiliary work, and it creates a business connection under section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and a permanent establishment under the relevant treaty, making the foreign enterprise taxable in India on the profits attributable to it.

citation.ref: Regulation 4 and the Annex to the FEM (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016 (FEMA 22(R)), read with section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Liberalised Remittance Scheme and the tax collected at source on it
concepts.statement: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme lets a resident individual, including a minor, remit up to USD 250,000 or its equivalent in a financial year for whatever current account transaction the rules permit, for a capital account one, or for a mix of the two — one aggregate ceiling for the year across all purposes and all authorised dealers, not a limit per remittance. It runs under Schedule III to the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 read with the Reserve Bank's Master Direction on the Scheme, requires a PAN, and is the route through which a resident individual makes overseas direct or portfolio investment under the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022. It cannot be used at all for margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges, for trading in foreign exchange abroad, for lottery and banned publications, or for remittances to countries identified by the Financial Action Task Force as non-co-operative. The same remittance is a tax event. Section 206C(1G) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 makes the authorised dealer collect tax at source, and the Finance Act, 2025 moved the figures with effect from 1 April 2025: the threshold rose from seven lakh rupees to ten lakh rupees of aggregate remittance in a financial year, the rate is five per cent for education and medical purposes and twenty per cent for everything else on the amount exceeding that threshold, and no tax at all is collected where the remittance for education is made out of a loan obtained from a financial institution referred to in section 80E. Tax collected is not a cost — section 206C(4) credits it against the individual's own tax liability.

citation.ref: Schedule III to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 and the RBI Master Direction on the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, read with section 206C(1G) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 as amended by the Finance Act, 2025

concepts.subsection: Combinations — the deal value threshold and the standstill obligation
concepts.statement: Section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002 tells you when an acquisition, merger or amalgamation is a combination that must be notified to the Competition Commission of India. Clauses (a) to (c) do it on the assets and turnover of the enterprises and their group, on figures the Central Government revises by notification. Clause (d), inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 and brought into force in September 2024, added a wholly different gate: any transaction whose value exceeds two thousand crore rupees is a combination if the enterprise being acquired, merged or amalgamated has substantial business operations in India. That clause was written for the deal that buys a large user base holding almost no assets and earning almost no revenue here, and it means an asset and turnover analysis showing nothing is only half the answer. Section 6(2) requires notice of a combination to the Commission, and section 6(2A) supplies the standstill: no combination shall come into effect until one hundred and fifty days have passed from the day the notice was given, or the Commission has passed an order under section 31, whichever is earlier. Closing before that is gun-jumping, and section 43A lets the Commission impose a penalty which may extend to one per cent of the total turnover or assets or the value of the transaction referred to in clause (d) of section 5, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Sections 5(d), 6(2), 6(2A) and 43A, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

concepts.subsection: Investment advice by a chartered accountant — SEBI registration and Council permission
concepts.statement: Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 forbids any person acting as an investment adviser or holding himself out as one without obtaining a certificate of registration from the Board. Regulation 4 lists who is outside that requirement, and one of the exemptions covers a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India who provides investment advice to his clients incidental to his professional service. The word doing the work is incidental. SEBI's own frequently asked questions give the example that passes — a chartered accountant acting as a tax consultant who, in the course of tax planning, advises a client to invest in an equity linked savings scheme — and state the condition that fails it: where a member provides investment advisory services in securities as an activity or business to clients or investors, not incidental to his main activity, registration is required. A separately marketed, separately charged advisory service is not incidental to anything. Company law and SEBI are not the whole answer either. Clause 11 of the First Schedule (Part I) to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 makes a member in practice guilty of professional misconduct if he engages in any business or occupation other than the profession of accountancy without the general or specific permission of the Council, so a registration granted by SEBI does not by itself make the activity permissible for him.

citation.ref: Regulations 3(1) and 4, read with Clause 11 of the First Schedule (Part I) to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

concepts.subsection: Dormant companies — section 455 and the significant accounting transaction
concepts.statement: Section 455(1) lets a company formed and registered for a future project or to hold an asset or intellectual property, and which has no significant accounting transaction, apply to the Registrar for the status of a dormant company; so may an inactive company. The Explanation defines both words and the second one decides most cases. An inactive company is one which has not been carrying on any business or operation, or has not made any significant accounting transaction during the last two financial years, or has not filed financial statements and annual returns during the last two financial years. A significant accounting transaction is any transaction other than four — payment of fees by the company to the Registrar, payments made by it to fulfil the requirements of the Act or any other law, allotment of shares to fulfil the requirements of the Act, and payments for the maintenance of its office and records. Anything else is significant, and that includes money coming in: interest credited on a deposit, or a gain on the sale of an idle asset, is as fatal to the status as a trading sale would be. Section 455(4) works the other way, letting the Registrar put a company that has not filed financial statements or annual returns for two financial years consecutively on the register of dormant companies after issuing it a notice. Section 455(5) requires a dormant company to have the prescribed minimum number of directors, file the prescribed documents and pay the annual fee to retain the status, which it does by filing the return of dormant company in Form MSC-3, and it returns to active status on an application in Form MSC-4. Section 455(6) is the sanction: the Registrar shall strike off the name of a dormant company which has failed to comply with the requirements of the section. The status does not switch the company off. Section 173(5) deems a dormant company to have complied with section 173 only if at least one meeting of the Board is conducted in each half of a calendar year and the gap between the two meetings is not less than ninety days, and the books of account under section 128 are kept as before.

citation.ref: Sections 455(1) with its Explanation, 455(4), 455(5) and 455(6), read with section 173(5) and Rules 3, 7 and 8 of the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Disqualification and vacation of office — sections 164 and 167
concepts.statement: Section 164(1) disqualifies a person for reasons personal to him — unsoundness of mind, an undischarged insolvency, certain convictions, an order of a court or Tribunal disqualifying him, calls unpaid for six months, a conviction of an offence dealing with related party transactions under section 188 at any time during the preceding five years, and the absence of a Director Identification Number. Section 164(2) disqualifies him for what a company he sat on did. Where a company has not filed financial statements or annual returns for any continuous period of three financial years, or has failed to repay the deposits accepted by it or pay interest on them, or to redeem any debentures on the due date or pay interest due on them, or to pay any declared dividend, and that failure continues for one year or more, then a person who is or has been a director of that company shall not be eligible to be re-appointed as a director of it or appointed in any other company for five years from the date on which the company so failed. The proviso, inserted in 2017, protects the person brought in to clean it up: a person appointed as a director of a company already in default does not incur the disqualification for six months from the date of his appointment. Section 167(1)(a) then vacates his office, and its own proviso is the part most often got wrong — where the disqualification is one under section 164(2), the office becomes vacant in all the companies other than the company which is in default, so the board responsible for the failure is not emptied of the people who must repair it. Section 167(2) punishes a person who functions as a director knowing his office has become vacant. Section 164(3) lets a private company's articles add grounds of its own. The auditor is drawn in by section 143(3)(g), which requires his report to state whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2) — a Companies Act duty, not a CARO 2020 one.

citation.ref: Sections 164(1), 164(2) with its proviso, 164(3), 167(1)(a) with its proviso and 167(2), read with section 143(3)(g)

concepts.subsection: Class action under section 245 and the auditor's exposure
concepts.statement: Section 245 lets the prescribed number of members or depositors, or any class of them, apply to the Tribunal where they are of the opinion that the management or conduct of the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members or depositors. The orders they may seek run from restraining an act that is ultra vires the memorandum or articles, through declaring void a resolution altering the memorandum or articles where it was passed by suppression of material facts or obtained by mis-statement, to the one that makes the section matter to a chartered accountant. Section 245(1)(g) allows a claim of damages or compensation or any other suitable action against the company or its directors for a fraudulent, unlawful or wrongful act, against the auditor including the audit firm of the company for an improper or misleading statement of particulars made in his audit report or for a fraudulent, unlawful or wrongful act or conduct, and against any expert, advisor or consultant for an incorrect or misleading statement made to the company. Section 245(2) refuses to let the firm absorb it: where damages are sought from an audit firm, the liability shall be of the firm as well as of each partner who was involved in making the improper or misleading statement of particulars in the audit report or who acted in a fraudulent, unlawful or wrongful manner. Section 245(7) binds the company, all its members, depositors, and the auditor, audit firm, expert, consultant or advisor to the order; section 245(8) punishes a company that fails to comply with it. Section 245(9) puts one class of company outside the whole section — nothing in it applies to a banking company. That is the line against sections 241 and 244, which give members a remedy for oppression and mismanagement running against the company and its management alone, and give a depositor no standing at all.

citation.ref: Sections 245(1)(g), 245(2), 245(7), 245(8) and 245(9), contrasted with sections 241 and 244

concepts.subsection: Merger under section 232 — the appointed date, the auditor's certificate and Ind AS 103
concepts.statement: Section 232 supplies the machinery for a scheme involving a merger or amalgamation, and two things inside it decide more questions than the rest. The proviso to section 232(3) forbids the Tribunal from sanctioning any compromise or arrangement unless a certificate of the company's auditor has been filed with it to the effect that the accounting treatment, if any, proposed in the scheme is in conformity with the accounting standards prescribed under section 133 — so the accounting answer is a condition of the court's order and is settled before the order, not after it. Section 232(6) makes the scheme itself name its appointed date in plain terms, and the scheme then takes effect on that named date and on no later one. The General Circular No. 09/2019 dated 21 August 2019 issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs clarified three things about that date: it may be a specific calendar date or may be tied to the occurrence of a trigger event; the date so identified shall be deemed to be the acquisition date and the date of transfer of control for the purposes of conforming to the accounting standards, including Ind AS 103; and where the appointed date is significantly antecedent to the date of filing, the justification must be specifically brought out in the scheme. What the circular does not do is disturb Appendix C to Ind AS 103. A business combination of entities under common control is outside acquisition accounting altogether and is accounted for by the pooling of interests method — each combining entity carries its assets, and equally its liabilities, across at the amounts already sitting in its own books; no goodwill is recognised, the identity of the reserves is preserved, the difference between the consideration and the amount of share capital of the transferor is transferred to capital reserve, and the financial information in the financial statements is restated from the beginning of the preceding period presented or from the date the entities came under common control, whichever is later. A deemed acquisition date does not create an acquisition where the standard says there is none.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 232(3) and section 232(6), read with section 133, MCA General Circular No. 09/2019 dated 21 August 2019 and Appendix C to Ind AS 103

concepts.subsection: Cost records and cost audit — section 148
concepts.statement: Section 148(1) lets the Central Government direct by order that particulars relating to the utilisation of material or labour or other items of cost be included in the books of account of a class of companies engaged in the production of goods or the provision of services; section 148(2) lets it direct that the cost records of such a class be audited. The Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 do the work, dividing the covered industries into a regulated sector in Table A and a non-regulated sector in Table B, and setting turnover thresholds for the keeping of records and higher ones, differing between the two tables, for the audit. Rule 4(3) exempts a company whose revenue from exports in foreign exchange exceeds seventy-five per cent of its total revenue, a company operating from a special economic zone, and a company engaged in the generation of electricity for captive consumption. Who may do the audit is decided by section 148(3), and its proviso is the trap: the audit shall be conducted by a cost accountant appointed by the Board, and no person appointed under section 139 as an auditor of the company shall be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records. Section 144 lists the services the statutory auditor may not render and cost audit is not on that list — the bar sits in section 148 instead. Rule 14 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 routes the appointment: in a company required to constitute an audit committee, the Board appoints the cost auditor on the recommendation of the audit committee, which also recommends the remuneration, the Board approves it and the shareholders ratify it subsequently. Rule 6 of the Cost Records and Audit Rules supplies the clocks — appointment within one hundred and eighty days of the commencement of the financial year, intimation to the Central Government in Form CRA-2, the cost auditor's report to the Board in Form CRA-3 within one hundred and eighty days from the closure of the financial year — and section 148(6) with Rule 6 requires the company to furnish the report to the Central Government in Form CRA-4 within thirty days of receiving it, with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification in it. Section 148(5) applies the qualifications, disqualifications, rights, duties and obligations of an auditor under Chapter X to the cost auditor so far as they can be applied.

citation.ref: Sections 148(1), 148(2), 148(3) with its proviso, 148(5) and 148(6), read with Rules 4 and 6 of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 and Rule 14 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Who is a related party — the Companies Act, Ind AS 24 and the LODR do not agree
concepts.statement: Three definitions sit on the same facts and none of them is either of the others, which is why a single transaction can need a disclosure without an approval, or an approval without a disclosure. Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013 lists relationships — a director or key managerial personnel or their relatives, a firm in which a director or manager or his relative is a partner, a private company where any one of those three is a member or sits on its board, a public company on whose board a director or manager of this company sits while he and his relatives between them hold above two per cent of that company's paid-up share capital, a holding, subsidiary or associate company, a fellow subsidiary, an investing company or the venturer of the company, and a person on whose advice, directions or instructions a director or manager is accustomed to act otherwise than in a professional capacity. It has no shareholding limb at all, so a large outside shareholder is not a related party under it. Ind AS 24 works instead on control, joint control and significant influence, judges a relationship by its substance and not merely by its legal form, and reaches three things the Act does not name — the key management personnel of the parent, the close members of the family of any related individual, and a post-employment benefit plan for the benefit of employees of the entity or of an entity related to it. Regulation 2(1)(zb) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 starts from both of those and then adds the limb neither has: anybody who sits inside the listed entity's own promoter group, or is its promoter, whether that is a person or a body corporate, and any person or entity holding equity shares of the listed entity above the prescribed shareholding limb, directly or on a beneficial interest basis, at any time during the immediately preceding financial year. The auditor is on a fourth footing again — SA 550 requires him to test management's identification of related parties against the framework the financial statements are prepared under, which for an Ind AS company is Ind AS 24, while the approvals the same transaction needs come from section 188 and from Regulation 23 of the LODR on their own definitions.

citation.ref: Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013 with section 188, Ind AS 24 and Regulation 2(1)(zb) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, read with SA 550

concepts.subsection: Financial creditor's application — section 7 and the allottees' proviso
concepts.statement: Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 defines financial debt as a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and then lists the limbs it includes; section 5(7) makes a financial creditor any person to whom a financial debt is owed, including a person to whom the debt has been legally assigned or transferred. The Explanation to clause (f) of section 5(8), inserted in 2018, deems any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project to be an amount having the commercial effect of a borrowing, which turns a homebuyer into a financial creditor rather than an operational creditor. The second proviso to section 7(1), inserted by the amendment of 2020 and upheld in Manish Kumar v Union of India, then puts a numerical gate in front of that right: an application by allottees under a real estate project shall be filed jointly by not less than one hundred allottees under the same real estate project, or not less than ten per cent of the total number of allottees under the same project, whichever is less. Section 7(5) requires the Adjudicating Authority to admit the application where a default has occurred, the application is complete and no disciplinary proceeding is pending against the proposed resolution professional; the minimum default for any application is the amount notified under section 4. What section 7 does not have is the machinery section 9 has. There is no demand notice, and a pre-existing dispute is no defence — Innoventive Industries held that once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a default has occurred, the application must be admitted. Section 238A applies the Limitation Act, 1963, so the three-year period under Article 137 runs from the date of default, extendable only by an acknowledgement of liability under section 18 of that Act, which a balance sheet entry can supply.

citation.ref: Sections 5(7), 5(8) with the Explanation to clause (f), the second proviso to section 7(1), section 7(5) and section 238A

concepts.subsection: When liquidation begins — sections 33 and 34 and the end of the going concern basis
concepts.statement: Section 33 has four doors into liquidation and only one of them is the expiry of the clock. Section 33(1) requires the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation where it does not receive a resolution plan under section 30(6) before the expiry of the resolution process period or the maximum period permitted, or where it rejects the plan under section 31 for non-compliance. Section 33(2) opens the second door: where the resolution professional intimates the Adjudicating Authority of a decision of the committee of creditors approved by not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share to liquidate the corporate debtor, the Authority shall pass a liquidation order, and the Explanation says the committee may take that decision at any time after its constitution and before the confirmation of the resolution plan, including at any time before the preparation of the information memorandum. Sections 33(3) and 33(4) open the third, on the application of any person other than the corporate debtor whose interests are prejudicially affected by a contravention of an approved plan. Three consequences follow the order. Section 33(5) bars any suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, subject to section 52, and its proviso lets the liquidator alone institute one, with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority. Section 33(7) deems the order to be a notice of discharge to the officers, employees and workmen of the corporate debtor, except where the business is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator. Section 34(1) makes the resolution professional appointed for the resolution process the liquidator, unless the Adjudicating Authority replaces him. The accounting consequence is separate and is the one candidates miss.
