Ind AS 1 takes the financial statements off the going concern basis where management intends to liquidate the entity or has no realistic alternative but to do so, and SA 570 then requires the auditor to test whether the alternative basis is appropriate and to draw attention to it. The liquidator's power under section 35(1)(e) to carry on the business for the beneficial liquidation of the corporate debtor is a way of selling the assets to advantage; it is not an intention that the entity continue.

citation.ref: Sections 33(1), 33(2) with its Explanation, 33(5), 33(7), 34(1) and 35(1)(e), read with Ind AS 1 and SA 570

concepts.subsection: Undervalued, fraudulent and extortionate transactions — sections 45 to 51
concepts.statement: Below the preference in section 43 sit three more avoidance provisions and they do not share one look-back. Section 45(2) makes a transaction undervalued where the corporate debtor makes a gift to a person, or enters into a transaction with a person involving the transfer of one or more assets for a consideration the value of which is significantly less than the value of the consideration provided by the corporate debtor, and the transaction has not taken place in the ordinary course of business; section 45(1) obliges the liquidator or the resolution professional to apply to the Adjudicating Authority on determining that one was made in the relevant period. Section 46(1) fixes that relevant period at two years preceding the insolvency commencement date where the counterparty is a related party and one year in any other case. Section 47(1) is the safety valve: where an undervalued transaction has not been reported by the liquidator or the resolution professional, a creditor, member, partner or a person interested may apply himself, and section 47(3) lets the Adjudicating Authority order the Board to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the professional who failed to report it. Section 49 is different in kind and this is where the marks are. Where an undervalued transaction was deliberately entered into for keeping assets beyond the reach of any person entitled to make a claim against the corporate debtor, or in order to adversely affect the interests of such a person, the Adjudicating Authority may restore the position and protect the interests of the victims — and section 49 has no relevant period at all, so age is no defence where the intent is shown. Its own limit is that the order shall not prejudice an interest in property acquired in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances. Section 50 covers the extortionate credit transaction, a transaction of credit involving the receipt of financial or operational debt during the two years preceding the insolvency commencement date under which the terms require exorbitant payments, and section 50(2) excludes any debt extended by a person providing financial services in compliance with any law for the time being in force. Section 51 lists the orders — restoring the position, setting aside the whole or part of the debt, modifying the terms, requiring repayment, and requiring any security to be released.

concepts.subsection: Fair value and liquidation value in a resolution process — CIRP Regulations 27 and 35
concepts.statement: Regulation 27 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 requires the resolution professional to appoint two registered valuers to determine the fair value and the liquidation value of the corporate debtor, within seven days of his own appointment and in any event by the forty-seventh day from the insolvency commencement date. Regulation 35(1) says how the two figures are arrived at: each of the two registered valuers submits an estimate of the fair value and of the liquidation value, computed in accordance with internationally accepted valuation standards, after physical verification of the inventory and fixed assets; and where in the resolution professional's opinion the two estimates are significantly different, he may appoint another registered valuer, in which case the average of the two closest estimates shall be considered. Regulation 35(2) requires him, after the receipt of resolution plans, to provide the fair value and the liquidation value to every member of the committee of creditors in electronic form, against a confidentiality undertaking, and the professional and the valuers are bound to maintain that confidentiality. The definitions run the other way from what the names suggest: fair value is the estimated realisable value of the assets if they were exchanged on the insolvency commencement date between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm's length transaction after proper marketing, and liquidation value is the estimated realisable value if the corporate debtor were liquidated on that date. Neither is a reserve price. The Code's only floor is in section 30(2)(b), which requires a resolution plan to provide for payment to operational creditors of not less than the amount that would be paid to them under section 53 in the event of a liquidation, and to financial creditors who did not vote in favour of the plan of not less than the amount payable to them under section 53 in that event. Beyond that floor, the Supreme Court in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited v Satish Kumar Gupta placed the commercial wisdom of the committee on the distribution among classes outside judicial review. The valuers themselves are registered under section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017.

citation.ref: Regulations 27 and 35 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, read with section 30(2)(b) of the Code and section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Board composition of a listed entity — LODR Regulation 17
concepts.statement: Regulation 17 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 is stricter than the Companies Act at every point where the two overlap, and a listed entity has to satisfy both, which in practice means it satisfies the Regulation. Regulation 17(1)(a) requires an optimum combination of executive and non-executive directors with at least one woman director, at least half the board being non-executive, and an independent woman director on the board of the top one thousand listed entities by market capitalisation. Regulation 17(1)(b) sets the independence ratio by who chairs: at least one-third of the board must be independent directors where the chairperson is a non-executive director, and at least half where there is no regular non-executive chairperson or the chairperson is an executive director, or is a promoter or related to a promoter or to a person occupying a management position at board level or one level below it. Regulation 17(1)(c) requires the board of the top two thousand listed entities by market capitalisation to comprise not less than six directors. Regulation 17(1A) forbids a listed entity to appoint or continue the directorship of a non-executive director who has attained the age of seventy-five years unless a special resolution is passed to that effect, with the justification set out in the explanatory statement. Regulation 17(1C) requires shareholders' approval for an appointment to the board at the next general meeting or within three months of the appointment, whichever is earlier. Regulation 17(2) requires at least four board meetings a year with a maximum gap of one hundred and twenty days between two of them. Regulation 25(2A) then makes the appointment, re-appointment or removal of an independent director subject to the approval of shareholders by special resolution. Against that, the Companies Act asks for three directors in a public company under section 149(1), one-third independent directors in a listed public company under section 149(4), four board meetings with a gap of not more than one hundred and twenty days under section 173(1), and an ordinary resolution to appoint a director in general meeting under section 152(2) — with independent directors kept out of retirement by rotation by section 149(13).

concepts.subsection: Material subsidiary of a listed entity — LODR Regulations 24 and 24A
concepts.statement: Regulation 16(1)(c) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 makes a subsidiary material where its income or its net worth exceeds the prescribed proportion of the consolidated income or net worth respectively of the listed entity and its subsidiaries in the immediately preceding accounting year — two alternative limbs, either of which is enough — and requires the listed entity to formulate a policy for determining a material subsidiary. Regulation 24 then follows the money down. Regulation 24(1) requires at least one independent director on the board of the listed entity to be a director on the board of an unlisted material subsidiary. Regulation 24(2) requires the audit committee of the listed entity to review the financial statements of the unlisted subsidiary and in particular the investments made by it; Regulation 24(3) requires the minutes of the subsidiary's board meetings to be placed before the board of the listed entity; and Regulation 24(4) requires the subsidiary's management to bring a statement of all significant transactions and arrangements to that board periodically. The two provisions that change what a group may do without asking its public shareholders are the last two. Regulation 24(5) forbids a listed entity to dispose of shares in its material subsidiary so as to reduce its shareholding, on its own or together with other subsidiaries, to fifty per cent or less, or to cease to exercise control over the subsidiary, without a special resolution in general meeting. Regulation 24(6) requires the same special resolution, in advance, for the selling, disposing of or leasing of assets amounting to more than twenty per cent of the assets of the material subsidiary on an aggregate basis during a financial year. Both are carved out where the transaction is made under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, or under a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, in which case the event is disclosed to the exchanges within one day of the approval. This is ground the Companies Act cannot cover, because section 180(1)(a) puts the special resolution to the members of the company whose undertaking is being sold, and the members of a wholly owned subsidiary are the parent's board, not its public. Regulation 24A extends secretarial audit beyond section 204 in the same way, requiring every listed entity and its material unlisted subsidiaries incorporated in India to undertake a secretarial audit and annex the report of a company secretary in practice to the annual report.

citation.ref: Regulations 16(1)(c), 24(1) to 24(6) and 24A, read with sections 180(1)(a) and 204 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Financial results of a listed entity — LODR Regulation 33
concepts.statement: Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 runs two clocks and imposes one condition on the auditor that has nothing to do with the numbers. Regulation 33(3)(a) requires quarterly and year-to-date financial results to be submitted to the stock exchange within forty-five days of the end of each quarter, other than the last quarter. Regulation 33(3)(d) requires the annual audited financial results for the year to be submitted within sixty days from the end of the financial year, with the audit report and, where the audit report carries a modified opinion, a Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications. Regulation 33(2) requires the results to be approved by the board of directors after review by the audit committee, and the limited review or audit report to be placed before the board. A listed entity with subsidiaries submits consolidated results as well, and for the quarterly consolidated results at least eighty per cent of each of the consolidated revenue, assets and profits must have been subjected to audit or, where unaudited, to limited review. Regulation 33(1)(c) is the condition firms forget: the listed entity shall ensure that the limited review or audit reports submitted to the stock exchanges on a quarterly or annual basis are given only by an auditor who has subjected himself to the peer review process of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and holds a valid certificate issued by its Peer Review Board. The assurance itself differs between the two clocks. A quarterly limited review is performed under SRE 2410, where the practitioner performs inquiry and analytical procedures and expresses a conclusion in the negative form that nothing has come to his attention causing him to believe the statements are not prepared in accordance with the framework; the annual results carry an opinion under SA 700 (Revised), and a modified one is qualified, adverse or a disclaimer under SA 705 (Revised) — all three of which are a modified opinion for the purpose of the Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications.

citation.ref: Regulations 33(1)(c), 33(2), 33(3)(a) and 33(3)(d), read with SRE 2410, SA 700 (Revised) and SA 705 (Revised)

concepts.subsection: Employee stock options — who may be granted them, and what the expense is
concepts.statement: Section 62(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a special resolution before a company offers shares to employees under a scheme of employees' stock option, and Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 then decides who may receive them and on what terms. Rule 12(1) excludes from the meaning of employee an employee who is a promoter or a person belonging to the promoter group, and a director who either himself or through his relative or through any body corporate, directly or indirectly, holds more than ten per cent of the outstanding equity shares of the company; an independent director is outside the definition altogether. Its proviso relaxes both exclusions for a start-up company for a period from incorporation prescribed in the Rule. Rule 12(3) requires a separate resolution of the shareholders for the grant of options to the employees of a subsidiary or holding company, and for the grant to identified employees during any one year of options equal to or exceeding one per cent of the issued capital of the company at the time of grant. Rule 12(6)(a) fixes a minimum period of one year between the grant of options and their vesting, the only relaxation being where the options are granted in lieu of options held under a scheme of a transferor company on a merger or amalgamation, in which case the period already served counts. Rule 12(5) leaves the lock-in on the shares issued on exercise to the company. A listed company answers to the SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 2021 in parallel, which carry the same exclusions and their own shareholder approval requirements. Ind AS 102 then measures the cost, and it measures it once. For an equity-settled share-based payment the entity measures the goods or services received by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments granted, measured at the grant date, and does not remeasure that amount afterwards for movements in the share price — remeasurement at each reporting date belongs to a cash-settled award, whose liability is carried at fair value until settlement. The expense is spread over the vesting period and trued up for the number of awards expected to vest on service and non-market performance conditions; but once an award has vested, no reversal is made merely because the option expires unexercised, since the entity has already received the services the award paid for, and any transfer is within equity.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(b) with Rules 12(1), 12(3), 12(5) and 12(6)(a) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, read with Ind AS 102 and the SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 2021

concepts.subsection: Person resident in India — FEMA against the Income-tax Act, and the property that follows
concepts.statement: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 opens with a day count and then overrides it. A person residing in India for more than one hundred and eighty-two days during the course of the preceding financial year is a person resident in India, but the clause then excludes a person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India for taking up employment outside India, for carrying on a business or vocation outside India, or for any other purpose in such circumstances as would indicate his intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period; and it includes, by the mirror image, a person who has come to or stays in India for any of those purposes. So the status can change on the day a person leaves, whatever the preceding year's count says. Section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 counts days in the previous year itself, adds a sixty-day limb with its own exceptions for a citizen leaving India for employment and for a visiting citizen or person of Indian origin, and asks nothing at all about intention. The same individual is often resident under one statute and not the other in the same twelve months. The property rules ride on the FEMA answer. Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 a Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India may acquire any immovable property in India other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property, and may acquire such property by gift from a person resident in India or from an NRI or OCI who is a relative as defined in section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013; agricultural land, a farm house and plantation property may come to him only by inheritance from a person resident in India. A person resident outside India who is neither an NRI nor an OCI needs the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, save for a lease not exceeding five years, and so does a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong or the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, whatever his residential status. Section 6(5) of the Act protects what was already owned: immovable property in India that he bought while he was still resident here stays his after the change, and he is free to keep it, to pass it on, or to put further money into it, as a person resident outside India.

citation.ref: Sections 2(v) and 6(5) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 with the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, read with section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Realisation of export proceeds — the FEMA clock against the GST clock
concepts.statement: Section 7(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 obliges every exporter of goods to furnish to the Reserve Bank or another prescribed authority a declaration containing true and material particulars including the full export value, and section 7(3) does the same for the exporter of services. Section 8 puts the positive duty on the exporter: a person resident in India to whom any amount of foreign exchange is due or has accrued shall take all reasonable steps to realise and repatriate it to India within the period and in the manner prescribed. Regulation 9(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 supplies the period — the full export value shall be realised and repatriated to India within nine months from the date of export, for all exporters — and goods exported to a warehouse established outside India are given fifteen months from the date of shipment. The Reserve Bank watches this through the Export Data Processing and Monitoring System, on which an entry stays outstanding until the proceeds are matched to it; the write-off facility, including the exporter's own self write-off within a limit and subject to conditions, is for a bill that has genuinely become irrecoverable after the exporter has taken all reasonable steps, and is not an extension of the nine months. Goods and services tax runs its own clock on the same shipment and it is not the same clock. Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 lets a registered person export without payment of integrated tax under a bond or letter of undertaking, on his undertaking to pay the tax with interest if the goods are not exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months, or such further period as the Commissioner may allow, from the date of issue of the export invoice; and, in the case of services, if the payment is not received in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees where permitted by the Reserve Bank, within fifteen days after the expiry of one year, or such further period as the Commissioner may allow, from the date of issue of the invoice. For goods the tax clock measures the shipment and the exchange clock measures the money; for services both measure the money, and the exchange clock is the shorter of the two.

citation.ref: Sections 7 and 8 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 with Regulation 9(1) of the FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, read with Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Anti-competitive agreements — section 3 and the two standards of proof
concepts.statement: Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 forbids any agreement in respect of production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India, and section 3(2) makes such an agreement void. Everything after that is about who has to prove what. Section 3(3) covers agreements between enterprises or persons engaged in identical or similar trade of goods or provision of services, including a cartel, which directly or indirectly determine purchase or sale prices, limit or control production, supply, markets, technical development, investment or provision of services, share the market or source of production by allocation of geographical area or type of goods or number of customers, or directly or indirectly result in bid rigging or collusive bidding — and it says such an agreement shall be presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition. The Commission proves the agreement; the parties have to displace the effect, and no market share is in issue. The first proviso saves an agreement entered into by way of a joint venture where it increases efficiency in production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services. A proviso inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 closes the hub-and-spoke gap by presuming an enterprise or association of enterprises, or a person or association of persons, to be part of a section 3(3) agreement where it participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of that agreement, even though it is not engaged in an identical or similar trade. Section 3(4) is the vertical list — tie-in arrangement, exclusive supply agreement, exclusive distribution agreement, refusal to deal and resale price maintenance — and nothing is presumed there: an agreement among enterprises at different stages of the production chain is caught only where it causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition, established on the factors in section 19(3). Section 3(5) puts two things outside the section entirely — the reasonable conditions a holder may impose to restrain infringement of or to protect his rights under the intellectual property statutes the clause lists, and the right of any person to export goods from India to the extent the agreement relates exclusively to production, supply, distribution or control of goods or services for such export.

citation.ref: Sections 3(1), 3(2), 3(3) with its provisos as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, 3(4) and 3(5), read with section 19(3)

concepts.subsection: Abuse of dominance — section 4 and why dominance itself is lawful
concepts.statement: Section 4(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 says no enterprise or group shall abuse its dominant position. It does not say that no enterprise shall be dominant, and that distinction is the whole of the section. Section 4(2) lists the abuse — directly or indirectly imposing unfair or discriminatory conditions or prices in the purchase or sale of goods or services, including predatory prices; limiting or restricting production of goods or provision of services or the market, or technical or scientific development relating to goods or services to the prejudice of consumers; indulging in practices resulting in denial of market access in any manner; making the conclusion of contracts subject to acceptance by other parties of supplementary obligations which by their nature or according to commercial usage have no connection with the subject of such contracts; and using its dominant position in one relevant market to enter into, or protect, another relevant market. Explanation (a) defines a dominant position as a position of strength enjoyed by an enterprise in the relevant market in India which enables it to operate independently of competitive forces prevailing in the relevant market, or to affect its competitors or consumers or the relevant market in its favour. Explanation (b) defines a predatory price as the sale of goods or provision of services at a price below the cost, as may be determined by regulations, of production of the goods or provision of the services, with a view to reduce competition or eliminate the competitors. No figure in the Act creates dominance. The Commission reaches the finding on the factors in section 19(4) — market share, size and resources of the enterprise, size and importance of competitors, economic power including commercial advantages over competitors, vertical integration, dependence of consumers, entry barriers, countervailing buying power, market structure and size of market, social obligations and social costs, and the relative advantage contributing to economic development — after defining the relevant market under sections 19(5) to 19(7), which fix the relevant product market on interchangeability and the relevant geographic market on conditions of competition distinctly homogeneous and distinguishable from neighbouring areas, so a single state can be the market. On penalty, section 27 permits a penalty on a proportion of the average turnover or income for the three preceding financial years, and the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 defined turnover to mean global turnover derived from all products and services, so a contravention confined to one Indian market is priced off the whole enterprise.

citation.ref: Sections 4(1) and 4(2) with Explanations (a) and (b), read with sections 19(4) to 19(7) and section 27 as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

concepts.subsection: Lesser penalty for a cartel — section 46 and what it does not buy
concepts.statement: Section 46 of the Competition Act, 2002 lets the Commission impose upon a producer, seller, distributor, trader or service provider included in a cartel a lesser penalty than that leviable under the Act, where that person has made a full, true and vital disclosure in respect of the alleged violations. The provisos take it back. No lesser penalty shall be imposed where the report of the Director General has been received before the disclosure was made, so the applicant is racing the investigation rather than the final order. The Commission may impose a lesser penalty subject to such conditions as it thinks fit, and where the applicant does not comply with those conditions, or has given false evidence, or the disclosure is found not to be vital, he is liable to the full penalty and to be dealt with as though he had never applied. The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 added the lesser penalty plus: an applicant who has already made a disclosure about one cartel may make a further full, true and vital disclosure about a second, unrelated cartel, and the Commission may then grant him an additional reduction in the penalty for the first cartel as well as a lesser penalty in the second. The Competition Commission of India (Lesser Penalty) Regulations, 2024 supply the machinery — the marker and the priority status fixed by the order in which applications are received, the requirement of continuing and expeditious co-operation throughout the investigation, the bar on concealing, destroying, manipulating or removing relevant documents, the procedure for withdrawal, and a graded ceiling on the reduction that is highest for the first applicant in the queue and progressively lower for those behind him. Three limits are examined more than the machinery. The section speaks of a cartel, which is a section 3(3) matter, so an enterprise facing a section 4 abuse of dominance case has no leniency route at all. Section 48 makes every person who at the time of the contravention was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business liable for it, so an officer not covered by the company's application does not share its benefit. And a lesser penalty is a reduction in penalty and nothing more — the contravention stands, and a person who has suffered loss may still claim compensation under section 53N.

citation.ref: Section 46 with its provisos and section 48, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, read with the CCI (Lesser Penalty) Regulations, 2024 and section 53N

concepts.subsection: Tax after a resolution plan — sections 79(2)(c), 115JB and 170A
concepts.statement: A resolution plan does to a company's share register exactly what section 79 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was written to punish, and the Act makes room for it in three places. Section 79(1) refuses the carry forward and set off of a loss of a company in which the public are not substantially interested where, on the last day of the previous year, shares carrying not less than fifty-one per cent of the voting power are not beneficially held by the same persons who held them on the last day of the year in which the loss was incurred. Section 79(2)(c) lifts that restriction where the change in shareholding takes place pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. The second place is minimum alternate tax. Clause (iih) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2) ordinarily lets a company reduce from book profit only the lower of the amount of loss brought forward and the unabsorbed depreciation; a proviso to that clause lets a company against which an application for a corporate insolvency resolution process has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority reduce the aggregate of the two instead, which is often the difference between paying minimum alternate tax on the write-back a plan produces and not paying it. The third is section 170A, which lets the successor to a business reorganisation, including one effected by an order of a Tribunal, furnish a modified return of income for any assessment year to which the order applies, within six months from the end of the month in which the order was issued. None of the three makes the plan's accounting gain tax-free by itself. Section 31 of the Code binds the Central Government and every authority to whom a statutory due is owed and so settles the claims for past dues, but the character of an amount written back is decided by the Income-tax Act — the remission or cessation of a trading liability is tested under section 41(1), and the waiver of a loan taken for a capital purpose is tested on ordinary principles, so the write-back is analysed line by line.

citation.ref: Sections 79(1), 79(2)(c), 41(1) and 170A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the proviso to clause (iih) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2), read with sections 7 and 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

concepts.subsection: Statutory registers, their place and their inspection — sections 94 and 95
concepts.statement: Section 88(1) requires every company to keep and maintain a register of members showing separately for each class of equity and preference shares held by each member residing in or outside India, a register of debenture-holders and a register of any other security holders; section 88(2) requires an index of the names in the register of members. Section 88(3) deems the register and index of beneficial owners maintained by a depository under the Depositories Act, 1996 to be the corresponding register and index for the purposes of the Act, so a company whose shares are entirely dematerialised does not keep a second one. Section 94(1) fixes where those registers and the copies of the annual return filed under section 92 are kept — at the registered office — and its proviso allows them to be kept at any other place in India in which more than one-tenth of the total number of members entered in the register of members reside, if a special resolution is passed to that effect at a general meeting. Section 94(2) opens them up: the registers, their indices and the copies of the annual return shall be open for inspection during business hours by any member, debenture-holder, other security holder or beneficial owner without payment of any fee, and by any other person on payment of the prescribed fee. Section 94(3) lets any of those persons take extracts and require a copy on payment of the prescribed fee, and the copy shall be furnished within seven days; its proviso allows the particulars prescribed under the Rules to be excluded from what is shown or copied, which is how a member's address and identifying numbers are kept out of an outsider's hands. Section 94(4) is the sanction and the remedy together — a refusal of inspection or a failure to send the copy within the time attracts a penalty on the company and every officer in default, and the Tribunal may by order compel an immediate inspection or direct that the copy be sent forthwith. Section 95 then makes the registers, their indices and the copies of the annual return prima facie evidence of any matter directed or authorised to be inserted in them by or under the Act. Section 91(1) is the only lawful way to shut the register: a company may close the register of members, debenture-holders or other security holders after giving previous notice of at least seven days, or such lesser period as may be specified by the Securities and Exchange Board of India for a listed company, for a period not exceeding thirty days at any one time and not exceeding forty-five days in the aggregate in each year.

citation.ref: Sections 88(1) to 88(3), 91(1), 94(1) with its proviso, 94(2), 94(3) with its proviso, 94(4) and 95, read with Rule 14 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Periodical financial results — section 129A against LODR Regulation 33
concepts.statement: An unlisted company's accounting duties under the Companies Act are annual. Section 129(1) requires the financial statements to give a true and fair view and to comply with the accounting standards notified under section 133; section 129(2) requires the Board to lay them at every annual general meeting; section 137(1) requires a copy of the financial statements adopted at that meeting, with all the documents annexed to them, to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the meeting. Nothing in that machinery asks for a quarterly number. Section 129A, inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019, is the provision that could ask for one, and it is written as an enabling power rather than as a standing duty. It lets the Central Government require such class or classes of unlisted companies as may be prescribed to prepare the financial results of the company on such periodical basis and in such form as may be prescribed, to obtain the approval of the Board of Directors and to complete an audit or a limited review of those periodical financial results in such manner as may be prescribed, and to file a copy with the Registrar within a period of thirty days of the completion of the relevant period with such fees as may be prescribed. Every limb of it runs on rules, so until the Central Government prescribes the class and the form there is no unlisted company on which the section bites. A listed entity is on an entirely different footing and waits for nobody to prescribe anything: Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 binds it directly and requires quarterly and year-to-date financial results to be submitted to the stock exchange within forty-five days of the end of each quarter other than the last, and the annual audited results within sixty days from the end of the financial year. The three routes therefore answer three different questions — Regulation 33 asks whether the entity is listed, section 129A asks whether the Central Government has prescribed its class, and sections 129 and 137 ask nothing at all beyond the annual cycle every company is already on. The assurance differs with the route as well: a quarterly limited review is an SRE 2410 engagement expressing a conclusion in the negative form, while the audit or limited review section 129A contemplates would be whatever the rules prescribing it require.

citation.ref: Section 129A of the Companies Act, 2013 with sections 129(1), 129(2) and 137(1), read with Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and SRE 2410

concepts.subsection: Sending the accounts to the members — section 136 and the twenty-one days
concepts.statement: Section 136(1) requires a copy of the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statements if any, the auditor's report and every other document required by law to be annexed or attached to them, to be sent to every member of the company, to every trustee for the debenture-holders and to all other persons so entitled, not less than twenty-one days before the date of the general meeting. The first proviso gives a listed company an alternative and not an escape: the requirement is deemed to be complied with if the copies are made available for inspection at the registered office during working hours for a period of twenty-one days before the date of the meeting and a statement containing the salient features of those documents in the prescribed form, or copies of the documents as any member may ask for, is sent not less than twenty-one days before the date of the meeting. Both limbs of that alternative have to be satisfied, and both are measured by the same twenty-one days. Further provisos require a listed company and every other company having a website to place the documents on it, and require a company having a subsidiary to place on its website the separate audited accounts of each subsidiary and to provide a copy to any member who asks for one. A website is therefore an additional duty, never a substitute for sending. Section 136(2) requires the company to allow every member or trustee to inspect the documents at the registered office during business hours. Section 137(1) is the separate duty that follows the meeting rather than preceding it — a copy of the financial statements adopted at the annual general meeting, with all the documents attached, filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the meeting — and section 137(2) covers the case where no annual general meeting is held, requiring the filing within thirty days of the last date on which the meeting should have been held, together with the reasons for not holding it. The three clocks are distinct and none of them substitutes for another: twenty-one days before the meeting for the members under section 136(1), thirty days after it for the Registrar under section 137(1), and the notice of the meeting itself on its own twenty-one clear days under section 101(1).

citation.ref: Sections 136(1) with its provisos and 136(2), read with sections 137(1), 137(2) and 101(1)

concepts.subsection: Branch audit — section 143(8), Rule 12 and SA 600
concepts.statement: Section 143(8) decides who audits a branch and what happens to what he writes. Where a company has a branch office, the accounts of that office shall be audited either by the auditor appointed for the company under the Act, or by any other person qualified for appointment as an auditor of the company under the Act and appointed in that behalf under section 139; and where the branch office is situated in a country outside India, by the company's auditor, or by an accountant, or by any other person duly qualified to act as an auditor of the accounts of the branch office in accordance with the laws of that country. The branch auditor is therefore appointed under section 139 and not by the company's auditor, and a foreign branch may lawfully be audited by someone who could not be appointed the auditor of an Indian company at all. The sub-section then requires the branch auditor to prepare a report on the accounts of the branch office examined by him and to send it to the auditor of the company, who shall deal with it in his report in such manner as he considers necessary. The branch auditor's report goes to the company's auditor, not to the members and not to the Board, and the words "as he considers necessary" leave the company's auditor to form his own opinion on the company's financial statements as a whole. The proviso applies the duties and powers of the company's auditor under sub-sections (1) to (4) of section 143 to the audit of the branch and to the branch auditor, so the branch auditor has the same right of access to the books and vouchers and the same right to require information and explanation. Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 carries the same two points and adds the one that surprises people: the branch auditor submits his report to the company's auditor, and the duty of reporting a fraud extends to the branch auditor to the extent it relates to the concerned branch, so he reports it himself under section 143(12) and Rule 13 rather than passing it up as an audit matter for somebody else to decide. SA 600, Using the Work of Another Auditor, then governs the professional judgement. The principal auditor performs procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the work of the other auditor is adequate for his purposes, considers the significance of the component to the financial statements as a whole, and where he concludes that the other auditor's work cannot be used and he cannot perform sufficient additional procedures, expresses a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion because of a limitation on the scope of the audit.

citation.ref: Section 143(8) with its proviso, read with Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, section 143(12) with Rule 13 and SA 600

concepts.subsection: Powers a Board may use only at a meeting — section 179(3) and section 175
concepts.statement: Section 179(1) gives the Board of Directors of a company the entitlement to exercise all such powers and to do all such acts and things as the company is authorised to exercise and do, subject to the Act, the memorandum and the articles and to any regulation made by the company in general meeting. Section 179(3) then names the powers that may be exercised only by means of resolutions passed at meetings of the Board — to make calls on shareholders in respect of money unpaid on their shares; to authorise a buy-back of securities under section 68; to issue securities, including debentures, whether in or outside India; to borrow monies; to invest the funds of the company; to grant loans or give guarantee or provide security in respect of loans; to approve the financial statement and the Board's report; to diversify the business of the company; to approve an amalgamation, merger or reconstruction; to take over a company or acquire a controlling or substantial stake in another company; and any other matter which may be prescribed. Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 prescribes further powers under that last clause, among them making political contributions, appointing or removing key managerial personnel, and appointing the internal auditor and the secretarial auditor. The proviso to section 179(3) allows delegation of three of those powers and no others — the Board may, by a resolution passed at a meeting, delegate to any committee of directors, the managing director, the manager or any other principal officer of the company the powers to borrow monies, to invest the funds of the company and to grant loans or give guarantee or provide security in respect of loans, on such conditions as it may specify. Section 175(1) is what makes the list bite: no resolution shall be passed by circulation on any matter which is required by the Act or otherwise to be placed before the Board at a meeting, and its proviso lets not less than one-third of the total number of directors require that a resolution being circulated be decided at a meeting instead. Delegation does not enlarge the power delegated. A managing director exercising a delegated power to borrow is still bound by section 180(1)(c), which requires a special resolution of the members before the Board or its delegate borrows money where the money already borrowed together with the money to be borrowed exceeds the aggregate of the company's paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium, leaving aside the short-term money a company's own bankers advance to it while ordinary trading goes on.

citation.ref: Sections 179(1) and 179(3) with its proviso, read with Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, section 175(1) and section 180(1)(c)

concepts.subsection: Non-cash transactions with directors — section 192 against section 188
concepts.statement: Section 192(1) stops an arrangement under which assets change hands for consideration that is not cash, in either direction, between the company on one side and, on the other, its own director, a director of any holding, subsidiary or associate company of it, or someone connected with such a director — the members must have said yes to that arrangement first, by resolution in general meeting. Where the director in question sits on the board of this company's holding company, the holding company's members must pass a resolution in general meeting too. Two things about that sentence decide most questions. The approval is prior, so a ratification after the event does not cure the contravention; and there is no value threshold, no ordinary-course carve-out and no arm's-length carve-out anywhere in the section. Section 192(2) requires the notice for the resolution to include the particulars of the arrangement along with the value of the assets involved, duly calculated by a registered valuer, so the valuation is a condition of the notice and not something produced afterwards. Section 192(3) supplies the consequence: an arrangement entered into by the company or its holding company in contravention of the section is voidable at the instance of the company, unless the restitution of the money or other consideration which is the subject-matter of the arrangement is no longer possible and the company has been indemnified by any other person for the loss or damage caused to it, or unless rights have been acquired bona fide for value and without notice of the contravention by any other person. Section 188 runs alongside and is not the same test. It catches the contracts and arrangements it lists — including the sale, purchase or supply of any goods or materials and the selling or otherwise disposing of, or buying, property of any kind — with a related party as defined in section 2(76), requires the consent of the Board by a resolution at a meeting and, above the prescribed limits, a prior resolution of the members; and its fourth proviso takes out of the section altogether any transaction entered into by the company in its ordinary course of business which is on an arm's length basis. A director is a related party under section 2(76), so the same swap of an asset for shares can be outside section 188 for being at arm's length in the ordinary course and still require the general meeting resolution and the registered valuer's figure under section 192, which knows nothing of either exemption. The valuer himself is registered under section 247 with the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017.

citation.ref: Sections 192(1), 192(2) and 192(3), read with section 188 and its fourth proviso, section 2(76) and section 247

concepts.subsection: Appointment of a managing director — section 196 and Schedule V
concepts.statement: Section 196(1) forbids a company to appoint or employ at the same time a managing director and a manager. Section 196(2) fixes the term: five years is the longest run any single appointment or re-appointment to the office of managing director, whole-time director or manager may have, and a re-appointment cannot be made more than a year ahead of the sitting term running out. Section 196(3) then lists who may not hold the office at all — a person below the age of twenty-one years or who has attained the age of seventy years; an undischarged insolvent or a person who has at any time been adjudged an insolvent; a person who has at any time suspended payment to his creditors or made a composition with them; and a person who has at any time been convicted by a court of an offence and sentenced for a period of more than six months. The proviso to clause (a) is the way past the age, and it is a shareholder route and not a government one: the appointment of a person who has attained the age of seventy years may be made by passing a special resolution, in which case the explanatory statement annexed to the notice for the motion shall indicate the justification for appointing him. Section 196(4) sequences the approvals. The appointment and the terms and conditions and the remuneration payable are approved by the Board of Directors at a meeting, subject to approval by a resolution at the next general meeting of the company, and subject to the approval of the Central Government where the appointment is at variance with the conditions specified in Part I of Schedule V; the notice convening the Board or general meeting shall include the terms and conditions, the remuneration payable and such other matters as are prescribed; and a return in the prescribed form shall be filed with the Registrar within sixty days of the appointment. Section 196(5) protects what was done in the meantime: where the appointment is not approved by the company at a general meeting, any act done by the person before that approval shall not be deemed to be invalid. Two other provisions travel with the appointment. Section 203(1) requires every listed company and every other company of the prescribed class to have a managing director or chief executive officer or manager and in their absence a whole-time director, a company secretary and a chief financial officer as whole-time key managerial personnel, so in those companies the office is not optional. Section 197 with Schedule V then caps what he may be paid, measuring the overall managerial remuneration against the net profits computed under section 198 and sending a company with no profits or inadequate profits to the limits in Part II of Schedule V, which the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 made exceedable by a special resolution of the members rather than by an approval of the Central Government.

citation.ref: Sections 196(1), 196(2), 196(3) with the proviso to clause (a), 196(4) and 196(5), read with Schedule V, section 197 and section 203(1)

concepts.subsection: The Registrar's inspection and inquiry — sections 206 to 209
concepts.statement: Section 206 is a ladder and each rung needs more before it may be climbed. Section 206(1) lets the Registrar, where on scrutiny of a document filed or on information received he is of the opinion that further information or explanation or further documents are necessary, require the company by written notice to furnish them within the time he specifies; section 206(2) obliges the company and every officer to furnish it to the best of their knowledge and power. Section 206(3) is the next rung: where nothing is furnished within the time, or the Registrar on examination considers the information inadequate, or he is satisfied on scrutiny that an unsatisfactory state of affairs exists and the information does not disclose a full and fair statement, he shall by a written notice call on the company to produce such further books, papers and explanations as he requires at the place and time he specifies — and he shall record his reasons in writing before issuing that notice. Section 206(4) is the inquiry proper: where the Registrar is satisfied, on information available with or furnished to him or on a representation made to him by any person, that the business of a company is being carried on for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or not in compliance with the Act, or that the grievances of investors are not being addressed, he may, after informing the company of the allegations and giving it a reasonable opportunity of being heard, call for information and carry out such inquiry as he deems fit; and its proviso lets the Central Government direct the Registrar or an inspector appointed by it to carry out the inquiry. Section 206(5) lets the Central Government direct an inspection of the books and papers by an inspector it appoints, and section 206(6) lets it authorise a statutory authority to carry one out. Section 207(1) obliges every director, officer and employee to produce the books and documents called for and to render all assistance. Section 207(2) lets the Registrar or inspector require the production of further books and keep them in his custody for a period not exceeding one hundred and eighty days, after which they are returned, with liberty to call for them again if necessary. Section 207(3) gives him the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in respect of the discovery and production of books and documents, and of summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath. Section 208 requires him, after the inspection or inquiry, to submit a written report to the Central Government, which may include a recommendation, with reasons, that a further investigation into the affairs of the company is necessary. Section 209 is the only coercive power in the Chapter and it is not his to exercise alone: where the Registrar or inspector has reasonable ground to believe that the books and papers of a company, or those relating to its key managerial personnel, any director, auditor or company secretary in practice, are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he may enter and search the place and seize such books and papers as he considers necessary only after obtaining an order from the Special Court, and only after allowing the company to take copies of or extracts from them; and section 209(2) requires the seized books to be returned as soon as may be and in any case not later than one hundred and eighty days, subject to their being called for again for a further like period by an order in writing.

concepts.subsection: Who can order an investigation — sections 210 and 213, and the boundary with 212
concepts.statement: Three doors lead into an investigation and each is opened by a different hand. Section 210(1) lets the Central Government order an investigation into the affairs of a company where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208, on intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest. Section 210(2) removes the discretion in one case: where an order is passed by a court or the Tribunal in any proceeding before it that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall order an investigation. Section 210(3) then lets the Central Government appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate and to report in such manner as it directs. Section 213 is the members' door, and it opens onto the Tribunal rather than onto the Central Government. The Tribunal may order that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated on an application by not less than one hundred members or by members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in the case of a company having a share capital, or by not less than one-fifth of the persons on the company's register of members in the case of a company having no share capital, supported by evidence showing good reason for seeking the order; or on an application by any other person or otherwise, where it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or that persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members, or that the members have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. The order is made after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, and once it is made the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors — so the Tribunal decides that there will be an investigation and the Central Government decides who conducts it. The second proviso to section 213 adds that where the fraudulent conduct is proved on the investigation, every officer in default and every person concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs is punishable for fraud under section 447. Section 212 is the third door and it is the Central Government's alone: it may assign the investigation to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office on the same grounds as section 210 plus a request from any Department of the Central Government or a State Government, and section 212(2) then clears the field — where a case has been assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government shall proceed with an investigation in that case in respect of any offence under the Act, and one already begun shall not be proceeded with, the relevant documents and records being transferred to that Office.

citation.ref: Sections 210(1), 210(2) and 210(3) and section 213 with its second proviso, read with sections 212(1), 212(2) and 447

concepts.subsection: Winding up by the Tribunal — sections 271 to 273 after the Code took the debts away
concepts.statement: Section 271 as it now stands lists five grounds on which a company may, on a petition under section 272, be wound up by the Tribunal: that the company has by special resolution resolved that it be wound up by the Tribunal; that the company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality; that on an application by the Registrar or any other person authorised by the Central Government the Tribunal is of the opinion that the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent manner, or that the company was formed for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose, or that the persons concerned in its formation or the management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct in connection with it, and that it is proper that the company be wound up; that the company has made a default in filing with the Registrar its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years; and that the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up. What is not on that list is the ground the section used to be remembered for. Inability to pay debts was taken out by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, which sent the unpaid creditor to sections 7 and 9 of the Code instead; section 255 of the Code with its Eleventh Schedule rewrote Chapter XX of the Companies Act accordingly. So a creditor with an unpaid invoice has no winding-up petition on that ground at all, and the Companies Act route survives for the company itself, for the State and for the Registrar. Section 272(1) says who may petition — the company; any contributory or contributories; all or any of those persons together; the Registrar; any person authorised by the Central Government in that behalf; and, on the sovereignty and integrity ground, the Central Government or a State Government. Its provisos keep the Registrar on a leash, requiring the previous sanction of the Central Government before he petitions on the fraudulent-conduct ground and requiring the company to be given a reasonable opportunity of making representations first; and a petition presented by the company itself is admitted only if it is accompanied by a statement of affairs in the prescribed form. Section 273(1) gives the Tribunal its choices — to dismiss the petition with or without costs, to make an interim order, to appoint a provisional liquidator until the winding up order is made, to order the winding up of the company with or without costs, or to make any other order it thinks fit — and its provisos require the order to be made within ninety days from the presentation of the petition and require notice to the company and a reasonable opportunity to make representations before a provisional liquidator is appointed, unless special reasons for dispensing with the notice are recorded in writing. Section 273(2) closes the obvious escape: the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order merely because the assets of the company have been mortgaged for an amount equal to or in excess of those assets, or because the company has no assets at all.

citation.ref: Sections 271, 272(1) with its provisos, 273(1) with its provisos and 273(2), read with sections 7, 9 and 255 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

concepts.subsection: Foreign companies — sections 379 to 384 and the accounts of the Indian business
concepts.statement: Section 2(42) defines a foreign company as any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which has a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and conducts any business activity in India in any other manner. Section 379(1) applies sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393 to all foreign companies, subject to the Central Government's power to exempt a class of them by an order published in the Official Gazette. Section 379(2) is the provision that turns a foreign company into something close to an Indian one: where not less than fifty per cent of the paid-up share capital, whether equity or preference or partly one and partly the other, of a foreign company is held by one or more citizens of India or by one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, whether singly or in the aggregate, the company shall comply with the provisions of that Chapter and with such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed, with regard to the business carried on by it in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India. Section 380(1) is the registration clock: every foreign company shall, within thirty days of the establishment of its place of business in India, deliver to the Registrar for registration a certified copy of the charter, statutes, memorandum and articles or other instrument constituting or defining its constitution, the full address of its registered or principal office, a list of its directors and secretary with the prescribed particulars, the name and address of one or more persons resident in India authorised to accept service of process and notices on its behalf, the full address of its principal place of business in India, particulars of any earlier opening and closing of a place of business in India, a declaration that none of its directors or its authorised representative in India has ever been convicted or debarred from the formation of companies and management in India or abroad, and such other information as may be prescribed; and section 380(3) requires a return of any alteration in those particulars within thirty days of the alteration. Section 381(1) then requires every foreign company to make out, in every calendar year, a balance sheet and profit and loss account in the prescribed form and containing the prescribed particulars, with the prescribed documents annexed, and to deliver a copy to the Registrar; and section 381(2) requires the documents prescribed by the Rules to be attached, which include a statement of related party transactions, a statement of repatriation of profits and a statement of the transfer of funds between the place of business in India and any other related party of the foreign company outside India. Rule 5 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014 requires those accounts to be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India or by a firm or limited liability partnership of practising chartered accountants. Section 384 then imports four more pieces of the Act — section 92 on the annual return; section 128 to the extent of requiring books of account with respect to monies received and spent, sales and purchases made, and assets and liabilities, in the course of or in relation to its business in India, kept at its principal place of business in India; Chapter VI on the registration of charges over property created or acquired by the foreign company; and Chapter XIV on inspection, inquiry and investigation, all of which apply mutatis mutandis. None of this touches, or is touched by, the Reserve Bank's separate permission for a branch, liaison or project office under the Foreign Exchange Management (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any Other Place of Business) Regulations, 2016. The exchange regulator decides whether the office may exist at all; the Registrar keeps the register and takes the accounts.

citation.ref: Sections 2(42), 379(1), 379(2), 380(1), 380(3), 381(1), 381(2) and 384, read with Rules 4 and 5 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: How many layers a group may have — the proviso to section 2(87) against section 129(3)
concepts.statement: The proviso to section 2(87) empowers the making of a restriction rather than imposing one: such class or classes of holding companies as may be prescribed shall not have layers of subsidiaries beyond such numbers as may be prescribed, and Explanation (d) to the same clause defines a layer, in relation to a holding company, as its subsidiary or subsidiaries. Rule 2(1) of the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017 supplies the number: no company, other than one belonging to a class specified in the Rule, shall have more than two layers of subsidiaries. Two provisos qualify it and both are examined. The restriction does not affect a company from acquiring a company incorporated outside India which has subsidiaries beyond two layers as per the laws of that country; and for computing the number of layers, one layer consisting of one or more wholly owned subsidiary or subsidiaries is not taken into account. Rule 2(2) puts four classes outside the restriction altogether — a banking company, a non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank of India and considered as a systemically important non-banking financial company, an insurance company, and a Government company. Rule 2(3) says the restriction is not in derogation of the proviso to section 186(1), which is a separate and narrower rule: a company shall make investment through not more than two layers of investment companies, with its own carve-outs for the acquisition of a company incorporated outside India having investment subsidiaries beyond two layers under the laws of that country, and for a subsidiary having an investment subsidiary in order to meet a requirement of any law or of any rule or regulation framed under any law. Rule 3 deals with a group that was already too deep when the Rules came into force: it files the prescribed return with the Registrar, may not add a layer, and having once reduced the number may not go back above the reduced number or two, whichever is higher. What none of this touches is the accounts. Section 129(3) requires a company having one or more subsidiaries, or one or more associate companies, to prepare a consolidated financial statement of the company and of all the subsidiaries and associates in the same form and manner as its own and to lay it before the annual general meeting along with its own, and the Explanation to that sub-section includes an associate company and a joint venture in the word "subsidiary" for this purpose. Ind AS 110 then consolidates on control, however far down the chain control runs, and the wholly owned layer that Rule 2(1) does not count is consolidated like every other. A structural restriction and a reporting boundary are two different questions, and a group can breach the first while consolidating perfectly under the second.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 2(87) with Explanation (d), Rules 2 and 3 of the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017 and the proviso to section 186(1), read with section 129(3) and Ind AS 110

concepts.subsection: Who may and may not apply — sections 10 and 11 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 10(1) lets a corporate applicant file an application to initiate a corporate insolvency resolution process where the corporate debtor has committed a default. Section 5(5) defines the corporate applicant widely — the corporate debtor itself; a member or partner of the corporate debtor who is authorised to make the application under its constitutional document; an individual who is in charge of managing the operations and resources of the corporate debtor; or a person who has the control and supervision over its financial affairs. Section 10(3) fixes what must accompany the application: the information relating to the corporate debtor's books of account and such other documents for the period specified, the information relating to the resolution professional proposed to be appointed as the interim resolution professional, and the special resolution passed by the shareholders of the corporate debtor or the resolution passed by at least three-fourths of the total number of partners approving the filing of the application. So a company cannot take itself into insolvency on a board resolution alone. Section 10(4) requires the Adjudicating Authority, within fourteen days of receipt, either to admit the application if it is complete and no disciplinary proceeding is pending against the proposed interim resolution professional, or to reject it if it is incomplete or such a proceeding is pending; and its proviso requires notice to the applicant to rectify the defect within seven days before rejection. Section 11 lists the persons not entitled to apply — a corporate debtor undergoing a corporate insolvency resolution process; a financial creditor or an operational creditor of a corporate debtor undergoing a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process; a corporate debtor having completed a corporate insolvency resolution process in the twelve months preceding the application; a corporate debtor in respect of whom a resolution plan has been approved under Chapter III-A in those twelve months; a corporate debtor or a financial creditor who has violated any of the terms of a resolution plan approved twelve months before the application; and a corporate debtor in respect of whom a liquidation order has been made. Two Explanations added in 2020 settle what the section is for. Explanation I says the corporate debtor includes one against whom an application has been admitted and is pending. Explanation II says that nothing in the section shall prevent a corporate debtor referred to in those clauses from initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process against another corporate debtor — so section 11 disqualifies a company from being taken into a fresh process of its own and does not disable it from collecting what it is owed. Section 4 fixes the floor for the whole Part at the minimum amount of default notified under it.

citation.ref: Sections 5(5), 10(1), 10(3), 10(4) with its proviso, and section 11 with Explanations I and II, read with section 4

concepts.subsection: Public announcement and the claims that follow — sections 13 and 15 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 13(1) requires the Adjudicating Authority, after admitting an application under section 7, 9 or 10, to do three things by the same order: declare a moratorium for the purposes referred to in section 14, cause a public announcement of the initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process and call for the submission of claims under section 15, and appoint an interim resolution professional in the manner laid down in section 16. Section 13(2) then requires the public announcement to be made immediately after the appointment of the interim resolution professional, which is why the announcement is his act and not the Authority's. Section 15(1) lists what it must contain — the name and address of the corporate debtor; the name of the authority with which the corporate debtor is incorporated or registered; the last date for submission of claims, as may be specified; details of the interim resolution professional who shall be vested with the management of the corporate debtor and be responsible for receiving claims; the penalties for false or misleading claims; and the date on which the corporate insolvency resolution process shall close, which shall be the one hundred and eightieth day from the date of admission of the application. Regulation 6 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 carries the machinery: the announcement is made in the specified form within three days of the interim resolution professional's appointment, published in one English and one regional language newspaper with wide circulation at the location of the registered office and the principal office of the corporate debtor, on the website of the corporate debtor if it has one, and on the website designated by the Board, and the last date for the submission of claims is fourteen days from the date of that appointment. A creditor who misses that date is not immediately shut out — Regulation 12 lets him submit his claim with proof up to the ninetieth day of the insolvency commencement date, after which the resolution professional updates the list of claims. What does shut him out is the approval of a plan. Section 31(1) makes the approved plan binding on the corporate debtor and its employees, members, creditors, including the Central Government, any State Government or any local authority to whom a statutory due is owed, guarantors and other stakeholders, and the Supreme Court in Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons Private Limited v Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited held that on the approval of a plan all claims not part of it stand extinguished and no person is entitled to start any proceeding in respect of a claim not dealt with in the plan. The claim is therefore lost by the approval of the plan, not by the passing of the announcement's date.

citation.ref: Sections 13(1), 13(2) and 15(1), read with Regulations 6 and 12 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 and section 31(1)

concepts.subsection: The interim resolution professional — sections 16 to 20 and the going concern mandate
concepts.statement: Section 16(2) requires that where the application was made by a financial creditor or by the corporate debtor, the resolution professional proposed in the application be appointed as the interim resolution professional if no disciplinary proceedings are pending against him; section 16(3) covers the operational creditor's application, where the Adjudicating Authority makes a reference to the Board for a recommendation if none is proposed, and appoints the professional proposed if one is. Section 16(5) makes his term run till the date of appointment of the resolution professional under section 22. Section 17(1) is the transfer of the company: from the date of his appointment the management of the affairs of the corporate debtor vests in the interim resolution professional, the powers of the board of directors or the partners stand suspended and are exercised by him, the officers and managers report to him and give him access to documents and records, and the financial institutions maintaining the accounts of the corporate debtor act on his instructions and furnish him all the information they hold. Section 17(2) gives him the authority to act and execute in the name and on behalf of the corporate debtor, to access its electronic records from an information utility and its books and records held with government authorities, statutory auditors and accountants, and makes him responsible for complying with the requirements of any law for the time being in force on behalf of the corporate debtor. Section 18(1) sets his duties — to collect all information relating to the assets, finances and operations of the corporate debtor, to receive and collate all claims submitted pursuant to the public announcement, to constitute a committee of creditors, to monitor the assets and manage the operations until a resolution professional is appointed, to file the information collected with an information utility if necessary, and to take control and custody of any asset over which the corporate debtor has ownership rights. The Explanation to section 18 then removes three things from the word "assets", and one of them decides case questions: assets owned by a third party in possession of the corporate debtor held under trust or under contractual arrangements including bailment, the assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor, and such other assets as may be notified. A subsidiary is consolidated in the corporate debtor's financial statements and is still outside the interim resolution professional's custody. Section 19 obliges the personnel, promoters and anyone associated with the management to extend all assistance and cooperation, and lets him apply to the Adjudicating Authority for directions where they do not.
