concepts.subsection: Rule 42 — Reversal of ITC on inputs and input services
concepts.statement: Where inputs and input services are used partly for taxable or business supplies and partly for exempt supplies or non-business purposes, credit attributable exclusively to the exempt or non-business use is reversed in full at the outset. The remaining common credit — used for both — is reversed monthly by a formula keyed to the ratio of exempt turnover to total turnover, and the reversal is trued up once a year against the actual annual figures.

citation.ref: Rule 42

concepts.subsection: Section 18(6) — ITC on capital goods, disposal before useful life
concepts.statement: Credit on capital goods is available in full at the time of receipt, without the staggering that the earlier VAT regime used. If capital goods on which credit was taken are later supplied outward, the registered person must pay an amount equal to the credit taken reduced by the prescribed percentage points for each quarter of use, or the tax on the transaction value of that supply — whichever of the two is higher. Disposal claws back whatever share of the credit the period of use has not yet earned.

citation.ref: Section 18(6)

concepts.subsection: QRMP scheme — quarterly return, monthly payment
concepts.statement: A registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year is up to ₹5 crore, and who files GSTR-3B, may opt to file that return quarterly while still paying tax in each of the first two months of the quarter in Form GST PMT-06 by the 25th of the following month — either a fixed sum (35 per cent of the tax paid in cash in the preceding quarter, where that return was quarterly) or a self-assessed amount. Crossing ₹5 crore during any quarter of the current year puts the person out of the scheme from the next quarter. Invoices for the first two months can be uploaded through the Invoice Furnishing Facility, up to ₹50 lakh a month, between the 1st and the 13th of the succeeding month, so recipients see credit without waiting for the quarterly return.

citation.ref: Rule 61A (manner of opting) and Rule 59(2) (Invoice Furnishing Facility), read with Notification No. 84/2020-Central Tax dated 10.11.2020 issued under the proviso to section 39(1), and CBIC Circular No. 143/13/2020-GST dated 10.11.2020

concepts.subsection: Section 44 — Annual return
concepts.statement: Every registered person, other than the specified exceptions such as a casual taxable person, a non-resident taxable person, an Input Service Distributor and persons subject to TDS or TCS, must furnish an annual return for the financial year on or before the thirty-first of December following its end. The annual return reconciles the year's periodic returns; it is a summary instrument, not a fresh assessment. Section 44(1) also lets the Commissioner exempt a class of registered persons by notification, and he has: for FY 2024-25 onwards a registered person whose aggregate turnover in the financial year is up to two crore rupees is exempt from filing the annual return for that year. So the duty now turns on two questions — whether the person is one of the excepted kinds, and whether the year's turnover cleared two crore.

citation.ref: Section 44, read with Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025 exempting registered persons with aggregate turnover up to two crore rupees from FY 2024-25 onwards

concepts.subsection: Sections 73, 74 and 74A — Demands, and the FY 2024-25 dividing line
concepts.statement: Which section governs a GST demand now turns first on the period, and only then on honesty. For tax pertaining to periods up to FY 2023-24, section 73 covers shortfalls arising for reasons other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, and section 74 covers the identical shortfalls where one of those is present, with a longer limitation and a heavier penalty. Sub-section (12) of each, inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, stops both at that year. From FY 2024-25 onwards section 74A governs instead, whether or not there was fraud, and its heading says so. It gives one common limitation — notice within forty-two months of the due date for the annual return, order within twelve months of the notice, extendable by six — and pushes the fraud line into the penalty alone: under section 74A(5), ten per cent of the tax or ₹10,000 whichever is higher without fraud, and the whole of the tax with it. No notice issues at all where the amount for the financial year is under ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 74A (inserted by section 138 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, brought into force 01.11.2024 by Notification No. 17/2024-Central Tax dated 27.09.2024), read with sections 73(12) and 74(12)

concepts.subsection: Section 107 — Appeal to the Appellate Authority, pre-deposit
concepts.statement: An appeal to the first Appellate Authority is not entertained unless the appellant has paid the full amount admitted as due, plus ten per cent of the remaining disputed tax. That ten per cent is capped: at twenty crore rupees of CGST, a figure the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 brought down from twenty-five crore. Where the order demands a penalty without demanding any tax, a proviso inserted with effect from 1 October 2025 sets the pre-deposit at ten per cent of that penalty instead. This pre-deposit is what buys a stay on recovery of the balance disputed amount while the appeal is pending — it is a precondition to the appeal being heard at all, not a discretionary figure an officer can vary.

citation.ref: Section 107(6) and its proviso — the maximum reduced from twenty-five to twenty crore rupees by section 141 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, and the penalty-only proviso inserted with effect from 1 October 2025 by section 129 of the Finance (No. 7) Act, 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 60 — Provisional assessment
concepts.statement: A taxable person unable to determine the value of a supply or the applicable rate of tax may request provisional assessment, executing a bond with security for the differential tax. The proper officer must finalise the assessment ordinarily within six months, extendable, and interest on any additional tax found due at finalisation runs from the original due date for payment of that tax, not from the date of the final order.

citation.ref: Section 60

concepts.subsection: Section 36 — Period of retention of accounts
concepts.statement: Every registered person must retain the accounts and records section 35 requires for seventy-two months from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year they relate to. A registered person who is party to an appeal, revision or any other proceeding, or under investigation, must keep the relevant records for a further year after the proceeding's final disposal, or to the seventy-two-month mark, whichever is later.

citation.ref: Section 36

concepts.subsection: Customs — Warehousing, the two clocks under section 61
concepts.statement: Goods deposited in a licensed customs warehouse under a warehousing bond remain there without payment of duty until an ex-bond bill of entry is filed for home consumption or the goods are re-exported. Two separate clocks then run, and confusing them is the usual mistake. For ordinary imported goods — clause (c) of section 61(1) — the warehousing period is one year from the date of the proper officer's order under section 60(1) permitting the deposit, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner by not more than a year at a time. Interest under section 61(2) starts much sooner: once those goods sit beyond ninety days from that same section 60(1) order, interest at the section 47 rate runs on the duty payable at clearance, from the ninety-first day until the duty is paid. On clearance, the rate of duty and tariff value are those on the date the ex-bond bill of entry is presented under section 68, while the value of the goods stays as assessed on the into-bond bill of entry.

citation.ref: Sections 61(1)(c) and 61(2) (ninety days from the order under section 60(1)), read with sections 68 and 15(1)(b)

concepts.subsection: Baggage Rules, 2026 — personal effects and the General Free Allowance
concepts.statement: The Baggage Rules, 2026 replaced the Baggage Rules, 2016 with effect from 2 February 2026, and the old test of which country the passenger flew back from is gone. Rule 3 clears, free of duty and with no value ceiling at all, the used personal effects a traveller needs for daily living, together with travel souvenirs — other than the articles listed in Annexure-I, which is firearms, cartridges over 50, cigarettes over 100 sticks or cigars over 25 or tobacco over 125 grams, alcohol over two litres, gold or silver in any form other than ornaments, and television. Rule 5 then gives a General Free Allowance, for articles outside Annexure-I, of ₹75,000 to a resident, a tourist of Indian origin or a foreigner holding a valid visa that is not a tourist visa — provided he is no infant, and does not arrive by land; ₹25,000 to a tourist of foreign origin on the same terms. A passenger arriving by land gets used personal effects only, whatever his category. Rule 5 also clears one new laptop or notepad free of duty for a passenger of eighteen or above who is not a crew member, and no passenger may pool his allowance with another's.

citation.ref: Rules 3 and 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2026 (Notification No. 14/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, in force 02.02.2026), read with CBIC Master Circular No. 4/2026-Customs dated 01.02.2026

concepts.subsection: Section 27 — Casual taxable person, registration validity
concepts.statement: A casual taxable person must apply for registration at least five days before commencing business and deposit an amount equal to the estimated tax liability for the period of registration, as advance tax. The certificate runs for whichever ends sooner: the period the applicant himself asked for, or ninety days counted from the date his registration takes effect. One extension, of up to ninety further days, is available on top of that.

citation.ref: Section 27

concepts.subsection: Section 12(2) — Place of supply of services, general rule
concepts.statement: Where supplier and recipient are both in India, and the service is not one of the special cases in sub-sections (3) to (14), the place of supply is the location of the recipient if he is registered. If the recipient is unregistered, it is the address on record with the supplier, and only where no address is on record does it fall back to the supplier's own location. Where the service is physically performed has nothing to do with it.

citation.ref: Section 12(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 12(6) and 12(7) — Place of supply for events
concepts.statement: Admission to a cultural, artistic, sporting, scientific, educational or entertainment event, or to an amusement park, is supplied where the event is actually held or the park is located — whoever buys the ticket, registered or not. Organising such an event, services ancillary to organising it, and assigning of sponsorship, follow a different rule — the place of supply is the location of the recipient where he is registered, and only where the recipient is unregistered does it become the place the event is held. Admission looks at the venue; organisation looks at the customer.

citation.ref: Sections 12(6) and 12(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 13(3)(a) — Place of supply where goods are made physically available
concepts.statement: Where either the supplier or the recipient is outside India, and the service needs goods to be made physically available by the recipient to the supplier, the place of supply is where the service is actually performed. Two provisos cut that back. Where the service is rendered from a remote location by electronic means, the place of supply is where the goods are at the time of supply. And where goods come into India on a temporary footing for repair, or for any other treatment or process, and go out again afterwards without having been used here beyond what the work itself required, this clause does not apply at all — the general rule in section 13(2), the location of the recipient, takes over. The second proviso once covered repairs alone and was later widened to any other treatment or process.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a) with its second proviso

concepts.subsection: Sections 12(3) and 13(3) — Time of supply under reverse charge
concepts.statement: Under reverse charge the clock is the recipient's, not the supplier's. For goods, the time of supply is the earliest of the date the goods are received, the date payment is entered in the recipient's books or debited from his bank account, and the day immediately following thirty days from the supplier's invoice. For services the list drops the receipt limb and stretches the outer limit — the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice. Where none of these can be determined it is the date the entry is made in the recipient's books. Thirty days for goods, sixty for services, is the whole distinction.

citation.ref: Sections 12(3) and 13(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(4) — Reverse charge on supplies from unregistered persons
concepts.statement: As first enacted, section 9(4) put every registered person on reverse charge for anything bought from an unregistered supplier. That version was suspended and then replaced with effect from 1 February 2019. What stands now is narrow — tax under reverse charge falls on a notified class of registered persons, on notified supplies, and on nobody else. The live notification covers promoters in real estate, who must pay under reverse charge on the shortfall where less than eighty per cent of the inputs and input services for a project are bought from registered suppliers. An ordinary trader buying from an unregistered supplier owes nothing under this sub-section.

citation.ref: Section 9(4), as substituted with effect from 1 February 2019, with Notification 07/2019-Central Tax (Rate)

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5)(c) and (d) — Blocked credit on construction
concepts.statement: Clause (c) blocks credit on works contract services for construction of immovable property, unless they are an input service for further supplying works contract service. Clause (d) blocks credit on goods or services received for construction of immovable property on the taxpayer's own account, and says so even where the property is used in the course or furtherance of business — business use is no answer to this block. Construction here takes in reconstruction, renovation, addition, alteration and repairs, to the extent the spending is capitalised. Plant and machinery is carved out of both clauses, and that carve-out expressly excludes land, buildings and other civil structures.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) and (d), with the explanation to section 17

concepts.subsection: Section 17(4) — Banking company option, fifty per cent credit
concepts.statement: A banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company supplying services by way of accepting deposits or extending loans may either do the ordinary proportionate reversal under section 17(2), or take a flat fifty per cent of the eligible input tax credit each month on inputs, capital goods and input services. The choice is made for the year and cannot be withdrawn during the rest of that financial year, and the half not taken simply lapses. One proviso matters more than the rule — the fifty per cent restriction does not touch tax paid on supplies received from another registered person holding the same PAN, so credit on inward supplies from the taxpayer's own other registrations comes in full.

citation.ref: Section 17(4) with its provisos

concepts.subsection: Section 19 — Input tax credit on inputs sent for job work
concepts.statement: The principal keeps his input tax credit on inputs sent to a job worker, and section 19(2) says so even where the inputs go straight from the supplier to the job worker's premises without ever reaching the principal. If the inputs are not received back, or supplied out from the job worker's premises, within one year — three years for capital goods — the despatch is deemed a supply on the day the inputs went out. Where the goods were sent directly to the job worker, that one year is counted from the date the job worker received them, not from any earlier date. Moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools sit outside the time limit altogether.

citation.ref: Section 19, with sub-sections 19(2), 19(3) and 19(7)

concepts.subsection: Rule 138(10) — Validity period of an e-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is valid for one day for the first 200 kilometres, and one further day for every 200 kilometres or part thereof after that. Over dimensional cargo, and a multimodal shipment with at least one leg by ship, run on the tighter scale — one day for the first 20 kilometres and one more for every 20 kilometres or part. The period runs from the date and time the transporter first enters vehicle details in Part B, and a part of a stretch counts as a whole one. The 200-kilometre figure replaced an earlier 100-kilometre one, so a validity worked out on the old scale comes out roughly twice as long as the law now allows.

concepts.subsection: Section 54(6) — Provisional refund of ninety per cent
concepts.statement: On a refund claim arising from zero-rated supplies, the proper officer sanctions ninety per cent of the amount claimed on a provisional basis, ahead of the detailed verification that precedes final sanction, and rule 91 gives him seven days from the acknowledgement to do it. Rule 91(2), as amended with effect from 1 October 2025, ties that provisional sanction to the system's own identification and evaluation of risk, and lets the officer decline the provisional route in a given case for reasons recorded in writing and proceed instead to an order under rule 92; that order does not have to be revalidated. The route itself remains confined to a claim arising from zero-rated supplies, which is how ICAI's own November 2026 statutory update reproduces section 54(6).

citation.ref: Section 54(6) with Rule 91(2), as substituted by Notification 13/2025-Central Tax with effect from 1 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Rule 28 — Value of supply between distinct or related persons
concepts.statement: A supply between distinct persons under section 25, or between related persons, is valued at open market value; failing that, at the value of goods or services of like kind and quality; failing both, by rule 30 or rule 31. Two provisos do most of the work in practice. Where the goods are meant for onward supply as such by the recipient, the supplier may opt for ninety per cent of the price the recipient charges his unrelated customer. And where the recipient is eligible for full input tax credit, whatever value is declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value. Separately, rule 28(2) deems the value of a corporate guarantee given to a bank or financial institution on behalf of a related person at one per cent per annum of the amount guaranteed, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Rule 28, with its second proviso and rule 28(2)

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Section 31(2) — Time limit for issuing a tax invoice
concepts.statement: For goods, the tax invoice goes out before or at the time of removal where the supply involves movement, and otherwise on delivery or on making the goods available. For services, rule 47 allows thirty days from the date of supply, stretched to forty-five days for an insurer, a banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company. Rule 47A, in force from 1 November 2024, fixes the other invoice people forget — the self-invoice a recipient paying under reverse charge must raise under section 31(3)(f) where his supplier is unregistered — at thirty days from the date he receives the supply.

citation.ref: Section 31(2) and 31(3)(f), with Rules 47 and 47A of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 10(2) — Transport and insurance in the customs value
concepts.statement: To the price paid or payable are added the cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling associated with delivering the imported goods to the place of importation, and the cost of insurance. Where the cost of transport cannot be ascertained it is taken at twenty per cent of the free on board value; where insurance cannot be ascertained it is taken at 1.125 per cent of the free on board value. Both are fallbacks — an actual, documented figure is used as it stands. The flat one per cent landing charge that the older rules loaded on top of the CIF value was removed with effect from 26 September 2017 and is no longer added to anything.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2), as amended by Notification 91/2017-Customs (N.T.) dated 26 September 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 75 — All Industry Rate and brand rate of drawback
concepts.statement: Section 75 gives back the duty suffered on inputs used in making goods that are then exported. The Central Government fixes All Industry Rates for classes of goods. Where no All Industry Rate has been determined for the exporter's product, he applies for a brand rate under rule 6 of the Drawback Rules. Where an All Industry Rate does exist but recovers less than eighty per cent of the duties actually paid on his materials, he applies under rule 7 for a special brand rate. Both applications run to three months from the relevant date, extendable on payment of the prescribed fee, and rule 9 caps any amount or rate at one third of the market price of the export product.

citation.ref: Section 75, with Rules 3, 6, 7 and 9 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Circular 254/11/2025 — Monetary limits for a section 74A notice and order
concepts.statement: Section 74A says what may be demanded; it does not say who may demand it. Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025 does, extending to section 74A the scheme Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST had set for sections 73 and 74. Taking central tax alone: a Superintendent of Central Tax issues the show cause notice and passes the order up to ₹10 lakh, a Deputy or Assistant Commissioner above that and up to ₹1 crore, and an Additional or Joint Commissioner above ₹1 crore with no ceiling. For integrated tax both steps double, to ₹20 lakh and ₹2 crore. Where one notice covers central tax, integrated tax and cess together, the officer is fixed on the combined amount tested against the doubled steps, never on any single tax read on its own. The same three-tier structure governs a penalty-only notice under section 122, and where the demand grows past an officer's limit during adjudication the case moves up by corrigendum.

citation.ref: Section 74A, read with Tables II and III of Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025, which extends to section 74A the scheme of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018

concepts.subsection: Rules 9A and 14A — Three-day registration and the simplified scheme
concepts.statement: The Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025 — Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, in force from 1 November 2025 — opened two new routes into registration. Rule 9A lets the system grant registration electronically within three working days of the application, on its own data analysis and risk parameters, with an officer stepping in only where a risk parameter is flagged. Rule 14A is an optional simplified scheme a small supplier may choose: he qualifies where his total output tax liability — central tax, State or Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess together — on supplies made to registered persons does not exceed ₹2,50,000 in a month, and where Aadhaar is authenticated for the primary authorised signatory and at least one promoter or partner. That ₹2,50,000 is a monthly output tax figure on business-to-business supplies; it is neither a turnover limit nor the section 22 registration threshold. The scheme is also capped in number, and the cap is drawn round a single State or Union territory: against one PAN only one rule 14A registration may be held there. That cap displaces rule 11, which would otherwise let a person hold separate registrations for several places of business inside the same State. It stops at the State line — a second State or Union territory is a fresh question, decided on its own facts, and a person already on the scheme in one State is not shut out of it in another.

citation.ref: Rules 9A and 14A, inserted by the Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025, Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, with effect from 1 November 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 109(8) and rule 110A — When a single Member hears a GST appeal
concepts.statement: An appeal before the Appellate Tribunal is normally heard by two Members, one Judicial and one Technical. Section 109(8) carves out an exception: where the tax or input tax credit involved, or the fine, fee or penalty determined by the order appealed against, does not exceed ₹50 lakh, and the appeal involves no question of law, it may be heard by a single Member with the President's approval, and subject to such further conditions as may be prescribed on the Council's recommendations. So three things must hold together: the amount is within ₹50 lakh, no question of law arises, and the President has approved. Rule 110A, in force from 22 September 2025, settles how the amount is counted: the ₹50 lakh is read cumulatively across every issue and every tax period the order covers, not issue by issue.

citation.ref: Section 109(8), read with Rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017, inserted by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18(1B) — Time limit for finalising a provisional customs assessment
concepts.statement: A provisional assessment under section 18(1) of the Customs Act once had no outer date; the Finance Act, 2025 gave it one. Section 18(1B) requires the proper officer to finalise within two years from the date of the provisional assessment, and its first proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs extend that by one further year on sufficient cause recorded in writing. The Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025 — Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025 — work the detail, and there are two clocks inside them rather than one. Where the assessment went provisional because the importer or exporter had not produced the papers, the proper officer asks for them within fifteen days, the importer or exporter has two months to hand them over, the proper officer may allow two months more and an officer above him may allow such further time as he thinks fit, but no extension of that kind reaches beyond fourteen months from the date of the provisional assessment; papers that never arrive do not stop the finalisation, which then proceeds on whatever record there is. Where it went provisional instead because the officer wanted to make further enquiry, the enquiring officer has his own fourteen months from that same date to finish the enquiry and pass the papers, with a written report, to the proper officer. Finalisation then follows within three months of the papers arriving or the enquiry ending. All of that still sits under the two years. Certain periods stand outside the two years and the clock restarts when the reason ends — a stay by a court or tribunal, a direction of the Board, a pending request to a foreign authority, a matter before the Settlement Commission. Where a provisional assessment was already pending on 29 March 2025, the two years run from that date, not from the original assessment.

citation.ref: Section 18(1B) with its first proviso, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with regulations 4, 5 and 8 of the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025

concepts.subsection: RoDTEP and section 51B — The electronic duty credit ledger
concepts.statement: Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products gives an exporter back the embedded central, State and local taxes no other scheme refunds — value added tax and excise on the fuel his transport burns, mandi tax, electricity duty, stamp duty on export documents. It is a remission of taxes actually borne, not a bounty, and that is what keeps it inside India's obligations at the World Trade Organization; it replaced the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme for the same reason. The claim is made in the shipping bill at the time of export and the benefit arrives as duty credit in the electronic duty credit ledger that section 51B of the Customs Act, 1962 creates, issued as an e-scrip under the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021. Three limits carry the marks. The credit pays only the duties of customs specified in the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — basic customs duty — and never the integrated tax or compensation cess collected at import. The e-scrip is valid for two years from its creation in the ledger, a period the 2022 amendment raised from one year, and anything unused at the end lapses and is not regenerated. And an e-scrip transfers to another Importer-Exporter Code holder only whole: part transfer is not permitted, and the transfer leaves the two years running as they were. Who may claim it has moved as well. The scheme opened to eligible exports from Domestic Tariff Area units, and Advance Authorisation holders, Export Oriented Units and Special Economic Zone units were shut out of it; they were brought in later, and Notification No. 35/2025 dated 30 September 2025 followed by Notification No. 74/2025-26 dated 31 March 2026 carry the scheme for all four classes up to 30 September 2026. So an Advance Authorisation holder asking whether RoDTEP is open to him is asking a question whose answer changed: it is, and the older position that it is not is the misconception to watch for.

citation.ref: Section 51B, read with regulations 6 and 7 of the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021, as amended by the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger (Amendment) Regulations, 2022, Notification No. 79/2022-Customs (N.T.) dated 15 September 2022

concepts.subsection: Entries 36C to 36E — Individual life and health insurance exempted
concepts.statement: Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 put three entries into the exemption notification, Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), with effect from 22 September 2025. Entry 36C lifts life insurance business out of tax wherever the person covered is a single insured and not a group — a contract over an individual, or over an individual and his family. Entry 36D does the same for health insurance business on the same terms. Entry 36E exempts reinsurance of the services covered by 36C and 36D. What sits outside stays taxable at eighteen per cent: a group term policy, a group credit life policy, a group health policy an employer takes for his staff. The exemption follows the description of the service and the identity of the insured, not the size of the premium — and because it is an exemption rather than zero rating, it breaks the insurer's input tax credit chain on those supplies instead of preserving it.

citation.ref: Serial numbers 36C, 36D and 36E, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Rule 7 — The composition rate, and the turnover it applies to
concepts.statement: Section 10 settles who may compound; rule 7 settles at what rate, and on what. A manufacturer, other than of goods the Government has kept out of the scheme, pays one per cent — half central tax, half State tax — of the turnover in State or turnover in Union territory. A restaurant not serving alcohol pays five per cent of that same turnover in State. Any other supplier eligible under section 10(1) and 10(2), which in practice means a trader, also pays one per cent, but of the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State — and that difference is the whole point of the rule. A trader dealing partly in exempt goods leaves the exempt turnover out of his base; the manufacturer's one per cent runs on the entire turnover in State, exempt supplies included. A supplier of services under the section 10(2A) scheme pays six per cent of turnover in State. In every case the amount comes out of the supplier's own pocket: section 10(4) forbids him to collect it from his customer, and he takes no input tax credit.

citation.ref: Rule 7, read with sections 10(1), 10(2A) and 10(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 148A — Track and trace, and the section 122B penalty
concepts.statement: The Finance Act, 2025 built an enabling frame for marking goods that are easy to evade tax on. Section 148A lets the Government notify goods, and the persons or classes of persons in possession of or dealing with them, and require a unique identification marking to be affixed and the prescribed information about it to be stored and shared electronically. Section 2(116A) defines that marking — a digital stamp, digital mark or similar marking that is unique, secure and non-removable. Section 148A by itself carries no punishment; section 122B, in force from 1 October 2025, supplies it. A person covered by clause (b) of section 148A(1) who acts in contravention pays a penalty of ₹1,00,000 or ten per cent of the tax payable on those goods, whichever is higher, and that amount is in addition to any penalty under Chapter XV or under the penalty chapter itself, not a substitute for it.

citation.ref: Sections 148A and 122B with the definition in section 2(116A), inserted by the Finance Act (No. 7) of 2025, section 122B in force from 1 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18A — Voluntary revision of an entry after clearance
concepts.statement: Before the Finance Act, 2025 an importer who found his own mistake after clearance had no clean way to correct it: section 149 amended a document, and anything touching the assessment waited for the department to issue a notice under section 28. Section 18A now lets the importer, the exporter or an authorised person voluntarily revise an entry already filed — whether it sits in a bill of entry, a shipping bill or a bill of export — after the goods are cleared, and the revised entry is treated as a self-assessment. Where the revision shows duty short paid, he pays it with interest, no penalty attaches and no notice under section 28 issues. Where it shows duty paid in excess, the application is itself treated as a claim for refund under section 27, so no separate refund application is needed. The route is closed in defined cases — where an audit, search, seizure or investigation has already been started and intimated, and where the entry has already been reassessed under section 17, 18 or 84. The Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025 and in force from 1 November 2025, prescribe an electronic application filed at the port where the duty was paid, with a fee of ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 18A, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025, and Circular No. 26/2025-Customs dated 31 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) — Three years and the return is barred
concepts.statement: A late GST return was once late for ever and could still be filed, with late fee and interest. The Finance Act, 2023 shut that door by inserting a sub-section into each of the four return provisions — section 37(4) for the statement of outward supplies, section 39(11) for the return, section 44(2) for the annual return and section 52(15) for the electronic commerce operator's statement — barring the furnishing of any of them after three years from the due date. Those sub-sections came into force on 1 October 2023 under Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023, and the portal began enforcing the bar from 1 October 2025. The three years runs from the due date of that return itself, not from the end of the financial year and not from the annual return's due date. Each of the four sub-sections carries a proviso letting the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify conditions on which a barred return may still be furnished — so the bar is hard, not absolute.

citation.ref: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) with their provisos, inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023 by Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

concepts.subsection: Second proviso to section 16(2) and rule 37 — Paying the supplier within 180 days
concepts.statement: Credit taken on an invoice the recipient has not paid does not stay taken. The second proviso to section 16(2) says that where the recipient fails to pay the supplier the value of the supply together with the tax within 180 days from the date of the invoice, an amount equal to the credit availed is added to his output tax liability, with interest. Rule 37, as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022, works out how much and when: the reversal is proportionate to the amount left unpaid, it goes into the return for the tax period immediately following the 180 days, and interest runs on it under section 50. When the recipient later pays, rule 37(4) lets him take the credit back, and that re-availment is expressly outside the section 16(4) time limit. Supplies on which tax is payable under reverse charge sit outside the proviso altogether, because there is no supplier's tax to hand across.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2), read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted by Notification No. 26/2022-Central Tax dated 26 December 2022 with effect from 1 October 2022

concepts.subsection: Sections 100 and 101 — Appeal against an advance ruling
concepts.statement: An advance ruling under section 98 is not the end of the road. Section 100 gives an appeal to the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling — to the applicant, or to the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer who disagrees with the ruling — within thirty days from the date the ruling is communicated, and the proviso lets the Appellate Authority allow a further thirty days where it is satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. Section 101(2) requires the Appellate Authority to pass its order within ninety days of the appeal being filed. Section 101(3) holds the trap: where the two members of the Appellate Authority differ on any point, it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point. There is no casting vote and no further appeal — the applicant is left exactly where he began. The Advance Ruling Authority below must itself pronounce within ninety days of receiving the application.

citation.ref: Sections 100(2) with its proviso, 101(2) and 101(3), read with section 98(6)

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: Section 25(4A) — Two-year sunset on a conditional customs exemption
concepts.statement: Section 25(1) lets the Central Government exempt goods from customs duty by notification in the public interest — a general exemption, open to anyone importing those goods. Section 25(2) is a different power: it exempts goods of a strategic or secret nature, or goods for a charitable purpose, by special order made in each individual case, and needs no notification. Section 25(4A), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, puts a clock on the first kind wherever it carries conditions. A conditional exemption granted under section 25(1) is given two years to run, and then dies on the 31st day of March that comes next after them — unless the notification itself specifies otherwise, or the Government varies or rescinds it sooner. For conditional exemptions already in force when the provision came in, the two years count from 1 February 2021. Section 25(4B) keeps whole classes outside the sunset, among them exemptions flowing from a multilateral or bilateral trade agreement and from obligations under international agreements, treaties or conventions. An unconditional exemption is not touched by the sunset at all.

citation.ref: Sections 25(4A) and 25(4B), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, read with sections 25(1) and 25(2)

concepts.subsection: Rule 96A — Export under bond or LUT, and the two clocks
concepts.statement: An exporter who chooses to export without payment of integrated tax furnishes a bond or a Letter of Undertaking under rule 96A, undertaking to pay the tax with interest if the export does not in fact happen. Two different clocks then run, and they measure different things. For goods, the tax falls due within fifteen days after three months from the date the export invoice was issued, if the goods have not left India by then — or such further period as the Commissioner allows. For services the test is money, not movement: the tax falls due within fifteen days after one year from the invoice date if payment has not been received in convertible foreign exchange, again subject to extension by the Commissioner. Missing either date costs more than tax and interest — the facility of exporting under bond or Letter of Undertaking is withdrawn until the amount is paid, and restored once it is. Non-receipt of payment does not by itself set off the goods clock; for goods the only question is whether they were exported.

citation.ref: Rule 96A(1)(a) and 96A(1)(b), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15 March 2018

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: IGCR Rules, 2022 — One year for the end use, and a quarterly statement
concepts.statement: An importer claiming a concessional rate of duty that depends on what he does with the goods runs on the IGCR Rules, 2022 — the customs rules covering goods brought in at a reduced duty rate, or for a stated end use. He files a one-time prior intimation estimating quantity and value, obtains an identification number, executes a continuity bond, and accounts for the goods in a prescribed record. Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025, in force from 2 February 2025, loosened two periods. The time within which the imported goods must be put to the intended purpose, and the time within which unutilised or defective goods may be re-exported or cleared on payment of the differential duty, both became one year in place of six months. And the statement in Form IGCR-3 became quarterly — a quarter being three consecutive calendar months ending in March, June, September or December — in place of the monthly statement the rules first demanded. Failing the end use does not undo the import: it makes the differential duty payable, with interest.

citation.ref: Rules 6, 7 and 10 of the IGCR Rules, 2022 — the customs rules on reduced-rate and stated-end-use imports — as amended by Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025 with effect from 2 February 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 20 as substituted — Input Service Distributor becomes compulsory
concepts.statement: Until 31 March 2025 the Input Service Distributor route was a choice: a head office receiving common input services for its branches could distribute the credit through an ISD registration or cross-charge the service to them as a distinct person. From 1 April 2025 the choice is gone. Section 2(61) and section 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, say that an office receiving tax invoices for input services for or on behalf of distinct persons shall distribute the credit through the ISD mechanism, and section 24(viii) makes a separate ISD registration compulsory for that office. Two things widened with the substitution. The definition now expressly takes in invoices for services on which tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3) or section 9(4), so a reverse-charge input service received on a branch's behalf goes through the ISD as well — the office pays that tax under its ordinary registration and then distributes the credit through its ISD registration. And distribution now covers central tax, State or Union territory tax and integrated tax, with rule 39 saying which head goes out as which. The word that changed is one syllable and decides everything: may became shall.

citation.ref: Sections 2(61) and 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025, read with section 24(viii) and rule 39 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 65 and rule 101 — Audit by the tax authorities, and when the clock starts
concepts.statement: The Commissioner or an officer authorised by him may undertake the audit of any registered person for a financial year or part of it. Section 65(3) requires not less than fifteen working days' prior notice in FORM GST ADT-01. Section 65(4) then gives three months from the commencement of the audit to complete it, and lets the Commissioner — nobody lower — extend that by a further period not exceeding six months, for reasons recorded in writing. The whole difficulty sits in the Explanation to section 65(4), which fixes what commencement means: the date on which the records and other documents called for by the tax authorities are made available by the registered person, or the actual institution of audit at the place of business, whichever is later. An officer who walks in before the records arrive has not started the clock. Findings, the reasons for them and the rights and obligations of the registered person are communicated within thirty days in FORM GST ADT-02, and where the audit shows tax unpaid, short paid, wrongly refunded or credit wrongly availed, the officer may proceed under section 74A.

citation.ref: Sections 65(3), 65(4) with its Explanation and 65(6), read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ADT-01 and ADT-02

concepts.subsection: Section 66 and rule 102 — Special audit by a nominated accountant
concepts.statement: A special audit is not an audit the taxpayer arranges. At any stage of scrutiny, inquiry, investigation or other proceedings, an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner may form a view, weighing how intricate the case is against what revenue stands to lose, that value has been understated or that the credit taken sits outside normal limits. On that view, and only with the Commissioner's prior approval, he may direct the registered person in FORM GST ADT-03 to place his records before a chartered accountant, or a cost accountant, whom the Commissioner nominates, for examination and audit. The report is due within ninety days, extendable by a further ninety days on an application by the registered person or the accountant, or for material and sufficient reason. Section 66(3) makes the power available notwithstanding that the accounts have already been audited under any other provision of this Act or under any other law, so a company audit is no shield. Section 66(4) guarantees an opportunity of being heard on any material gathered and proposed to be used. Section 66(5) puts the expenses of the examination and audit, including the accountant's remuneration, on the Commissioner, and makes his determination final.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1) to 66(6), read with rule 102 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ADT-03 and ADT-04

concepts.subsection: Section 67 and rule 140 — Seizure, the six months, and provisional release
concepts.statement: Section 67(1) lets an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner, on reasons to believe recorded by him, authorise in writing in FORM GST INS-01 an inspection of any place of business of a taxable person, of a person engaged in transporting goods, or of the owner or operator of a warehouse or godown. Section 67(2) carries that to search and seizure where goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things useful to the proceedings, are secreted; where seizure is not practicable the proper officer may instead serve a prohibition order in FORM GST INS-03 forbidding removal without his permission. Two consequences matter more than the machinery. Section 67(7) returns the seized goods to the person from whom they were seized if no notice is given within six months of the seizure, a period the proper officer may extend on sufficient cause by a further period not exceeding six months and no more. And section 67(6) keeps a door open throughout — seized goods are released provisionally on execution of a bond and furnishing of security, which rule 140 fixes as a bond for the value of the goods in FORM GST INS-04 together with a bank guarantee equal to the applicable tax, interest and penalty. Goods of a perishable or hazardous nature may be disposed of at once under section 67(8).

citation.ref: Sections 67(1), 67(2), 67(6) and 67(7), read with rules 139 and 140 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST INS-01, INS-03 and INS-04

concepts.subsection: Section 69 — Who may authorise an arrest, and what the five crore line decides
concepts.statement: The power to authorise an arrest under GST sits in one office. Section 69(1) lets the Commissioner, where he has reasons to believe that a person has committed an offence specified in clause (a), (b), (c) or (d) of section 132(1) which is punishable under clause (i) or clause (ii) of that sub-section, or under section 132(2), authorise by order any officer of central tax to arrest that person. No officer below the Commissioner may give that authorisation, and the contrast with section 67 — where a Joint Commissioner authorises an inspection or a search — is the usual place candidates slip. What the amount decides is not whether an arrest may happen but what follows it. Section 132(5) makes the listed offences cognizable and non-bailable only where the amount of tax evaded, or credit wrongly availed or utilised, or refund wrongly taken, exceeds five crore rupees; section 132(4) leaves every other offence non-cognizable and bailable. Where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable, section 69(2) requires the arresting officer to inform the person of the grounds of arrest and produce him before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours. Where it is not, section 69(3) requires the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner to admit him to bail or forward him to the custody of the Magistrate, with the same powers as an officer in charge of a police station.

citation.ref: Sections 69(1), 69(2) and 69(3), read with sections 132(4) and 132(5)

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Sections 125 and 126 — The residual penalty and the minor-breach relief
concepts.statement: Section 125 is the sweeper. Break any provision of the Act or the rules for which no penalty has been separately laid down, and the exposure is a penalty of up to twenty-five thousand rupees — a ceiling, not a fixed amount, and available only where nothing else fits. Section 126 runs the other way. Sub-section (1) bars an officer from penalising a minor breach of a tax regulation or a procedural requirement, and bars him specifically where paperwork carries a slip that can be put right easily, with neither fraudulent intent nor gross negligence behind it. Its Explanation supplies both tests: a breach is minor where the amount of tax involved is less than five thousand rupees, and a documentation omission is easily rectifiable where it is an error apparent on the face of record. Sub-section (2) requires any penalty to be commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach; sub-section (3) forbids a penalty without notice and an opportunity of being heard; sub-section (5) lets voluntary disclosure before discovery be treated as a mitigating factor. And sub-section (6) is the trap that decides most questions: the whole of section 126 stands aside wherever the Act itself has already pinned the penalty down, whether as a stated sum or as a stated percentage.

citation.ref: Sections 125 and 126(1) with its Explanation, 126(2), 126(3), 126(5) and 126(6)

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 138 — Compounding an offence, and the one offence that cannot be compounded
concepts.statement: Section 138(1) lets the Commissioner compound an offence under the Act, on payment of the compounding amount, either before or after the institution of prosecution — but only after the tax, interest and penalty involved in the offence have been paid. The proviso carves out cases, and the sharpest of them is the offence under clause (b) of section 132(1), issuing an invoice or bill without any supply of goods or services, which cannot be compounded at all. Section 138(2) fixes the amount at not less than twenty-five per cent and not more than one hundred per cent of the tax involved, a band that replaced the earlier fifty to one hundred and fifty per cent range with its rupee floors. Section 138(3) gives compounding its point: on payment of the compounding amount no further proceedings shall be initiated under the Act against the accused in respect of the same offence, and any criminal proceeding already instituted stands abated. Compounding settles the criminal side alone; it does not touch proceedings under any other law, and it does not wipe out the tax.

citation.ref: Sections 138(1) with its provisos, 138(2) and 138(3), read with section 132(1)(b) and rule 162 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rules 27, 30 and 31 — The ladder when transaction value fails
concepts.statement: Section 15(1) gives transaction value on two conditions held together: supplier and recipient must be unrelated, and nothing but price may move as consideration. Fail either limb and section 15(4) sends the valuation to Chapter IV of the rules. Rule 27 governs a consideration not wholly in money and works down in order — the open market value of the supply; failing that, the sum of the consideration in money and the money equivalent of the non-monetary part, where that equivalent is known at the time of supply; failing that, the value of a supply of like kind and quality; and failing that, rule 30 or rule 31. Rule 30 values the supply at one hundred and ten per cent of the cost of production or manufacture, the cost of acquisition of the goods, or the cost of provision of the services, whichever limb fits. Rule 31 is the residual — any reasonable method will do, so long as it sits with what section 15 and this Chapter lay down in principle. For goods the order is strict, rule 30 before rule 31. For services it is not: the proviso to rule 31 lets the supplier of a service opt for rule 31 disregarding rule 30 altogether.

citation.ref: Rules 27, 30 and 31 with the proviso to rule 31, read with sections 15(1) and 15(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 34 — The rate of exchange, and why goods and services differ
concepts.statement: A supply priced in a foreign currency has to be turned into rupees before any tax can be computed, and rule 34 gives two different answers depending on what was supplied. Rule 34(1) sends taxable goods to whatever rate the Board has notified under section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, read for the date on which the time of supply of those goods falls. Rule 34(2) sends taxable services somewhere else: to the rate that generally accepted accounting principles yield, again read for the date fixed by the time of supply. Two things follow. The converting date is the date of the time of supply in both cases — never the invoice date as such, never the date the money is received, and never the date the service was performed, except so far as one of those events happens to fix the time of supply under section 12 or section 13. And the customs rate notified by the Board reaches goods only; a service converts at the accounting rate even where a customs rate for the same day exists and differs.

citation.ref: Rules 34(1) and 34(2), read with sections 12 and 13 of the CGST Act, 2017 and section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962

concepts.subsection: Rule 35 — Backing the tax out of a tax-inclusive price
concepts.statement: A retail price marked as including all taxes is not a taxable value, and treating it as one taxes the tax. Rule 35 supplies the arithmetic. Where a supply's stated value already carries the tax — integrated tax, or else central tax with State tax or Union territory tax and cess — the tax amount for a head is the value inclusive of taxes multiplied by the rate of tax in per cent for that head, divided by one hundred plus the sum of all the applicable rates in per cent. On an intra-State supply at eighteen per cent the denominator is one hundred and eighteen, and the numerator is nine for central tax and nine again for State tax, so each head takes nine one-hundred-and-eighteenths of the marked price and the taxable value is what remains. Running the whole eighteen through the same denominator gives the total tax on the sale, which is a useful check but is not the figure for any one head. The rates to use are the live ones — five, eighteen and forty per cent since 22 September 2025; the twelve and twenty-eight per cent slabs were abolished that day and a denominator built on them is wrong before the arithmetic starts.

citation.ref: Rule 35, read with section 15(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 43 — Capital goods credit spread over sixty months
concepts.statement: Rule 42 apportions credit on inputs and input services; rule 43 does the same job for capital goods, and it does it over time. Credit on a capital good used exclusively for non-business purposes or exclusively for exempt supplies is not credited to the electronic credit ledger at all. Credit on one used exclusively for taxable supplies, zero-rated supplies included, is credited in full. What is left is the common capital goods credit, denoted A for each item and aggregated as Tc. Rule 43 fixes the useful life of a capital good at five years, so the common credit attributable to a tax period is Tm equal to Tc divided by sixty. The part of that monthly slice attributable to exempt supplies is Te equal to E divided by F multiplied by Tm. E stands for what that tax period's exempt supplies add up to; F stands for the whole turnover in the State over the same period. Te is added to the output tax liability of the registered person for every tax period of the useful life, along with interest. Where a capital good used at first exclusively for exempt supplies or non-business purposes is later put to common use, A is arrived at by reducing the input tax by five per cent for every quarter or part of a quarter that has passed.

citation.ref: Rule 43(1), clauses (a) to (h), read with sections 17(1) and 17(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 35 and rules 56 to 58 — Records, and what unaccounted goods cost
concepts.statement: Section 35(1) puts on every registered person a duty to hold accounts that are true and correct, kept at whichever principal place of business the registration certificate names, and covering production or manufacture, inward and outward supplies, stock, input tax credit availed, output tax payable and paid, and whatever else is prescribed; where more than one place of business is on the certificate, the accounts relating to each place are kept at that place. Section 35(2) reaches beyond registration — every owner or operator of a warehouse, godown or other place used for storage, and every transporter, must maintain records of the consigner, the consignee and the goods, whether or not he is registered. Rules 56 to 58 supply the detail, including serial numbering of manual records, scoring out with attestation rather than erasure, and a log of every electronic entry edited or deleted. Two points carry the marks. Section 35(5), which had required accounts to be audited by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant above a turnover limit, was omitted with effect from 1 August 2021, and FORM GSTR-9C is now a self-certified reconciliation statement. And section 35(6) says that where the registered person fails to account for goods or services, the proper officer shall determine the tax payable on them as if they had been supplied by that person, and proceed under section 74A.

citation.ref: Sections 35(1), 35(2) and 35(6), with section 35(5) as omitted with effect from 1 August 2021, read with rules 56, 57 and 58 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 89(5) — What Net ITC means in an inverted duty refund
concepts.statement: Section 54(3) allows a refund of accumulated credit in two cases only, and where the case is an inverted duty structure the amount is not the accumulation itself but a figure rule 89(5) computes. The whole weight of that computation sits in one defined term. The Explanation to rule 89(5) confines Net ITC to the credit taken on inputs in the relevant period, leaving out any credit whose refund is being claimed under sub-rule (4A) or (4B). An input, per section 2(59), is a good put to use, or meant for use, in the course or furtherance of business, with capital goods carved out of the definition. Two whole categories therefore never enter Net ITC: the credit on input services, and the credit on capital goods. Both remain perfectly good credit, usable against output tax without limit — they are simply outside the refund. The Supreme Court settled the point in Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (P) Ltd, holding the exclusion of input services from the formula to be within the rule-making power and not discriminatory. The practical consequence is that a manufacturer whose ledger swells on credits for services will find his inverted refund much smaller than his balance, and the gap is not an error.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) with its Explanation, read with section 54(3) and section 2(59) of the CGST Act, 2017, and Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (P) Ltd

concepts.subsection: Export Goods Valuation Rules, 2007 — Valuing an export, and the method that does not exist
concepts.statement: Section 14(1) of the Customs Act values export goods at the transaction value: the amount a buyer pays, or still owes, on a sale for export out of India, reckoned as at the moment exportation occurs and the place it occurs from, provided buyer and seller are unrelated and price alone is the consideration. The proviso that adds cost of transport, loading, unloading, handling and insurance belongs to imported goods; an export is valued at the place of exportation, so ocean freight and insurance beyond that point are never added. Where the declared value is rejected — rule 8 lets the proper officer do that where he has reason to doubt its truth or accuracy, after asking the exporter for an explanation — the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 run in order. Rule 4 looks sideways, to what comparable goods — alike in kind and in quality — fetched on an export to the same destination around the same date, adjusted for differences in nature, quality and quantity. Rule 5 builds a computed value from the cost of production, manufacture or processing, the charges for design or brand, and an amount towards profit. Rule 6 falls back on reasonable means consistent with the principles of the rules and of section 14(1), and says in terms that the local market price of the export goods shall not be the basis. There is no deductive value method for exports; that belongs to the import rules.

citation.ref: Section 14(1) with its proviso, read with rules 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007

concepts.subsection: Sections 53 to 56 — Transit, transhipment, and where the duty falls
concepts.statement: The two words are not interchangeable and the difference is physical. Transit under section 53 is goods that arrive in a conveyance, are mentioned in the arrival manifest as for transit, and continue in the same conveyance to a place outside India or to another customs station; they are allowed to pass without payment of duty. Transhipment under section 54 is goods moved onto a different conveyance, and it needs a document — a bill of transhipment presented to the proper officer, or, where the transhipment is under an international treaty or bilateral agreement, a declaration for transhipment. Section 54(2) allows transhipment to a place outside India without payment of duty; section 54(3) allows transhipment to another customs station in India without payment of duty at the port of arrival, subject to the conditions prescribed for the due arrival of the goods at the destination. Section 55 then decides where the duty falls — goods transited under section 53 or transhipped under section 54(3) to a customs station are treated, on arrival there, as if they had been imported into that station, so assessment and duty happen at the destination and not at the port of entry. Section 52 keeps baggage, goods imported by post and stores outside the chapter altogether.

citation.ref: Sections 52, 53, 54(1), 54(2), 54(3), 55 and 56, read with the Goods Imported (Conditions of Transhipment) Regulations, 1995

concepts.subsection: Section 65 and the MOOWR Regulations, 2019 — Manufacture inside a bonded warehouse
concepts.statement: Section 65(1) of the Customs Act lets the owner of warehoused goods carry on any manufacturing process or other operations in relation to them inside the warehouse, with the permission of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs. The Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019 work it — one application to the jurisdictional Commissioner for a licence under section 58 and permission under section 65 together, a one-time bond under section 59, digital accounts of the goods received and consumed, and a monthly return. The point of the scheme is deferment, not exemption. Nothing is paid when the goods enter. When the resultant goods are exported, the deferred import duty on the warehoused goods used in them is never collected at all. When the resultant goods are cleared into the domestic tariff area, the import duty on the warehoused goods contained in them becomes payable at that moment, and goods and services tax is charged on the domestic supply of the resultant product. Section 65(2)(a) settles waste — remitted where the resultant goods are exported, charged where they go into home consumption. And section 61(1)(a) gives capital goods in such a warehouse a warehousing period running till their clearance and other goods a period running till their consumption or clearance, so the ninety-day interest clock in section 61(2), which belongs to ordinary goods under section 61(1)(c), never starts.

citation.ref: Sections 65(1) and 65(2), read with sections 58, 59, 61(1)(a) and 61(2), and the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse (No. 2) Regulations, 2019, Notification No. 69/2019-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 October 2019

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: Heading 9801 and the Project Imports Regulations, 1986
concepts.statement: Project imports is a classification device, not an exemption. Everything imported for the initial setting up, or for the substantial expansion, of a specified project is classified under a single heading — 9801 of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — and assessed at one uniform rate, whatever heading each turbine, cable, pump or steel section would carry if imported on its own. The specified projects are an industrial plant, an irrigation project, a power project, a mining project, a project for the exploration of oil or other minerals, and any other project the Central Government notifies. Industrial plant is defined narrowly and expressly leaves out a hospital, hotel, photographic studio, film processing laboratory, photocopying studio, laundry, garage and workshop, as well as a single machine or a composite machine dressed up as a plant. The Project Imports Regulations, 1986 attach the conditions. The contract must be registered with the proper officer at the port of import before any goods are cleared, on the recommendation of the sponsoring authority certifying that the goods are required for the project. Spare parts, raw materials and consumable stores are covered only up to ten per cent of the value of the goods registered, and only if the contract shows them. After the last consignment clears, a statement of the goods actually imported is filed and the contract is finalised.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule, read with regulations 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the Project Imports Regulations, 1986

concepts.subsection: Section 9A, Customs Tariff Act — Anti-dumping duty and the lesser duty rule
concepts.statement: Where an article is exported to India at less than its normal value, section 9A(1) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 lets the Central Government impose an anti-dumping duty not exceeding the margin of dumping, that being the difference between the normal value and the export price. That cap is not the levy. Rule 4 of the Anti-dumping Rules, 1995 requires the designated authority to recommend the amount of duty which, if less than the margin of dumping, would be adequate to remove the injury to the domestic industry — the lesser duty rule — so the duty imposed is the lower of the dumping margin and the injury margin. Section 9A(2) allows a provisional duty on a preliminary finding, which shall not remain in force for more than six months, extendable by the Central Government to nine months on a request from exporters accounting for a significant percentage of the trade. Section 9A(5) ends a final duty five years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and lets the Government extend it by a further five years after a sunset review, with the duty continuing pending a review begun before expiry for up to one year. Section 9A(2A) keeps the duty off imports by a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking or a unit in a special economic zone unless the notification specifically applies it, and section 9B forbids both anti-dumping and countervailing duty on the same article to compensate for the same situation.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2), 9A(2A) and 9A(5), read with rule 4(d) of the Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and Collection of Anti-dumping Duty on Dumped Articles and for Determination of Injury) Rules, 1995, and section 9B

concepts.subsection: Section 8B, Customs Tariff Act — Safeguard measures and the developing-country carve-out
concepts.statement: Anti-dumping answers unfair pricing; a safeguard answers a surge. Section 8B, as substituted, is headed as a power to apply safeguard measures rather than merely to levy a safeguard duty, and the measures it allows are a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota, and such other measure as may be prescribed. The trigger is that an article is imported into India in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to the domestic industry. A provisional measure may be applied on a preliminary determination and stays in force for not more than two hundred days. A final measure ceases four years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and even with extensions the total period may not exceed ten years. Two carve-outs decide most questions. A safeguard measure does not apply to an article originating in a developing country so long as that country's share of the imports of that article into India does not exceed three per cent; and where the article comes from more than one developing country each with less than three per cent, the measure reaches none of them so long as their imports together do not exceed nine per cent of the total imports of that article. And the measure does not apply to articles imported by a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking or a unit in a special economic zone unless it is specifically made applicable to them.

citation.ref: Section 8B as substituted — the power to apply safeguard measures, the two hundred day provisional measure, the four-year life with a ten-year outer limit, and the developing country carve-out — read with the Customs Tariff (Identification and Assessment of Safeguard Measures) Rules, 2021

concepts.subsection: Section 16(1)(b) IGST — Supplying an SEZ, and the authorised-operations test
concepts.statement: Section 16(1) of the IGST Act zero-rates two things: an export of goods or services, and a supply of goods or services to a Special Economic Zone developer or unit for authorised operations. Those last three words were added by the Finance Act, 2021 and settled an argument. A zone is deemed to be outside the customs territory of India for the purposes of authorised operations, and no further — a supply into a zone that has nothing to do with the unit's letter of approval is an ordinary inter-State supply on which integrated tax is charged in the normal way. It is not exempt, and it is not zero-rated; the distinction matters because exemption breaks the supplier's credit chain while zero rating preserves it, and an ordinary taxable supply does neither. The endorsement of the specified officer of the zone is what evidences authorised operations when a refund is claimed. Movement the other way is not a supply by the unit at all: section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 treats a clearance from a zone into the domestic tariff area as an import, so the domestic buyer files a bill of entry and pays customs duty together with integrated tax under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and the unit charges nothing on an invoice.

citation.ref: Sections 16(1)(b) and 16(3), read with section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, rule 89(2)(f) of the CGST Rules, 2017, and section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

concepts.subsection: Section 147 and Notification 48/2017 — Deemed exports, and why they are not zero-rated
concepts.statement: Section 147 lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify certain supplies of goods as deemed exports, where the goods supplied do not leave India, payment is received in Indian rupees or in convertible foreign exchange, and the goods are manufactured in India. Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017 notified four categories: goods supplied by a registered person against an Advance Authorisation; capital goods supplied against an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation; goods supplied to an Export Oriented Unit; and gold supplied by a bank or a notified Public Sector Undertaking against an Advance Authorisation. Three limits define the concept. Section 147 speaks only of goods, so a service can never be a deemed export however the recipient is described. A deemed export is not a zero-rated supply under section 16 of the IGST Act, so it cannot be made under a bond or LUT — the tax is charged and paid, and relief comes afterwards. And the third proviso to rule 89(1) lets the refund of that tax be claimed either by the recipient or by the supplier, the conditions in Circular No. 14/14/2017-GST governing which, including that where the supplier claims it the recipient must not have availed the input tax credit and must say so.

citation.ref: Section 147, read with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017, the third proviso to rule 89(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017, and Circular No. 14/14/2017-GST dated 6 November 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 7 — What counts as a supply, and the club that cannot plead mutuality
concepts.statement: Every GST question starts at section 7(1), which sorts a transaction into one of four gates. Clause (a) is the widest: any exchange, sale, barter, disposal, lease, licence, rental or transfer of goods or services, in any combination, counts so long as it is priced and done while carrying on business — the price and the business link are what matter, not the label put on the deal. Clause (aa) arrived later, added by the Finance Act, 2021 and backdated by Parliament to 1 July 2017 so that it would apply from the first day of GST. It reaches dealings a body — anything other than a lone individual — has with its own members or constituents, run either way, paid for in cash, on credit, or in any other valuable form. Its Explanation is the operative sentence: it treats the body and its members as two distinct persons trading with each other, and it says so despite anything to the contrary in any statute or in any court's judgment, decree or order — wording aimed squarely at unwinding the mutuality reasoning the Supreme Court had applied in State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd, so that reasoning no longer holds for GST. Clause (b) picks up an imported service that is paid for, regardless of its business connection, and clause (c) picks up the no-consideration dealings that Schedule I lists. Section 7(1A) is a pure sorting rule and adds no new supply of its own — once something is already a supply because of section 7(1), it tells you whether Schedule II labels it a goods supply or a services one. The earlier version, section 7(1)(d), had let Schedule II manufacture a supply on its own; the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 removed it, again with retrospective effect to 1 July 2017. Section 7(2) takes Schedule III's list and notified government or local-authority activities out of supply altogether, and section 7(3) lets the Government re-badge a goods supply as a services one, or the reverse.

citation.ref: Sections 7(1)(a), 7(1)(aa) with its Explanation, 7(1)(b), 7(1)(c), 7(1A), 7(2) and 7(3), read with Schedules I, II and III, the Finance Act, 2021 and the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018

concepts.subsection: Section 2(31) — Consideration, and the deposit that is not one yet
concepts.statement: Section 2(31) builds consideration out of two limbs, one for money and one for anything else of value. Under the first, a payment already made or still owed — whoever actually hands it over, the recipient or someone else — counts once it is made for, towards, or to bring about the supply, in whatever form it takes. Under the second, where the recipient does something, or holds back from doing something, in return for the supply, that act or restraint is priced at its money value and counts just the same. Two exceptions sit inside this. A grant handed out by the Centre or a State is carved out entirely — section 2(31) does not treat it as consideration, and section 15(2)(e) does not fold it into value either. And a proviso keeps a deposit out of the reckoning for as long as it stays a deposit: it turns into payment for the supply only once the supplier actually sets it against the price, and not before. Money held as security, however long it sits there, stays outside the levy; the tax attaches the moment the supplier appropriates it. Two further things follow from the wording.
