The person who pays need not be the recipient at all — a third party's payment still funds a taxable supply. And nothing here requires cash: an act or a forbearance is valued in money, which is exactly the case rule 27 exists to price.

citation.ref: Section 2(31) with its proviso, read with section 15(2)(e) and section 7(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(17), 2(84) and 2(107) — Business, person, and who is a taxable person
concepts.statement: Three definitions between them decide whether GST reaches a transaction at all. Section 2(84) casts a wide net over who counts as a person — an individual sits alongside a Hindu Undivided Family, a company, a firm, an LLP, an association of persons, a co-operative society, a local authority, a government, a trust, and any other artificial juridical body. Section 2(107) then narrows who is taxable: only someone already registered, or required to be, under section 22 or section 24. Section 2(17) is the one doing the real work, because business is stretched well past ordinary trade. It swallows a wager, a profession, a vocation, an adventure, and every kind of commerce or manufacture, whether or not money is the point; anything tied to one of those, directly or as a side matter; the same regardless of how often or how regularly it happens; a club's or society's provision of facilities to its own members; and letting people onto premises for a fee. None of the three, though, turns everything a registered person does into a taxable event. Section 7(1)(a) still needs the supply to be made in the course or furtherance of business, so when he parts with something he has only ever held as his own, never claimed credit against, and never carried on the business's books, that disposal sits outside supply altogether — his registration decides who must account for tax on what he supplies, not what counts as a supply in the first place.

citation.ref: Sections 2(17), 2(84), 2(105) and 2(107), read with section 7(1)(a) and paragraph 1 of Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Schedule II paragraph 4 — Transfer of business assets, and the going-concern carve-out
concepts.statement: Paragraph 4 of Schedule II handles business assets across three separate situations, each with its own outcome. The owner-directed exit, clause (a), catches a business asset that the person running the business takes out of the business — sold, given away, or simply moved off the books so it no longer counts as business property — and treats that exit as a goods supply whether or not any price changed hands. The private-use case, clause (b), catches an asset the business still holds but lets be used privately, by the owner or by anyone else, for something that has nothing to do with the business; that usage itself is treated as a services supply. The exit-from-the-system case, clause (c), catches a person who stops being a taxable person altogether: whatever business assets he still holds are treated as supplied by him, in the course of that business, at the last moment before he drops out of the system — unless the business passes on whole, as a running concern, to someone else, or unless a personal representative keeps it running and is himself treated as the taxable person. The trap sits in the machinery around this paragraph. After the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 rewrote section 7(1A) and dropped the earlier section 7(1)(d) — both changes reaching back to 1 July 2017 — Schedule II lost the power to invent a supply; it can only sort something that is already a supply under section 7(1). Paragraph 4 keeps working regardless, because each of its clauses is itself a deeming rule, and because paragraph 1 of Schedule I separately deems a supply, with no price needed, whenever a business gives up an asset it had claimed input tax credit against.

citation.ref: Paragraph 4 of Schedule II, read with section 7(1A), paragraph 1 of Schedule I, and the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 omitting section 7(1)(d) with effect from 1 July 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 10(1)(c), (d), (e) and 11 IGST — Place of supply where nothing moves, and where it is installed
concepts.statement: Section 10 of the IGST Act fixes place of supply for goods by working through the physical journey rather than the paperwork. The default, clause (a), covers goods that move — the answer there is simply wherever that movement ends, at the point of handing over to the recipient. Three other clauses cover what clause (a) cannot reach. When nothing moves at all, whether that is because the supplier holds still or the recipient does, clause (c) points to wherever the goods physically sit at the moment of handover. When the goods only become usable after being put together or fixed in place on site, clause (d) points to that site itself. When the goods are handed over aboard something in transit — a vessel, an aircraft, a train, any motor vehicle — clause (e) points to wherever they were loaded on. Section 11 covers the border crossing: an import lands at the importer's own location, and an export lands wherever outside India it ends up. Two mistakes recur. Clause (d) turns on a physical fact — the spot where the thing gets bolted down — never on the address printed on the invoice or the State the recipient is registered in; that recipient-location test belongs to section 12(2), and only for services, never for goods. And once a place of supply is settled, section 7 or section 8 of the IGST Act decides whether the supply is inter-State or intra-State by measuring it against where the supplier sits, so a supplier in one State and a place of supply fixed in another together make it an inter-State supply carrying integrated tax.

citation.ref: Sections 10(1)(c), 10(1)(d) and 10(1)(e), and section 11, read with sections 7(1) and 8(1) of the IGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Vouchers — what is taxed when a voucher changes hands
concepts.statement: A voucher is an instrument that carries an obligation to accept it as consideration for a supply, and the difficulty has always been that three different things happen around it: the voucher is created and sold, it is passed down a chain of distributors, and it is finally redeemed against goods or services. The settled position, taken by the GST Council at its 55th meeting and put into words by Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST, separates them. Where the voucher is a pre-paid instrument recognised by the Reserve Bank of India it is money, and a transaction in money is excluded from the definitions of goods in section 2(52) and of services in section 2(102), so the transaction in the voucher itself is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Where the voucher is not such an instrument it is an actionable claim, and Schedule III keeps actionable claims other than the specified ones outside supply. Distribution of vouchers on a principal-to-principal basis is therefore not a supply either. What is a supply is the service: where a distributor or an agent earns a commission, a fee or a discount for distributing or marketing the vouchers, that is a supply of services by him to the issuer and it is taxable. Unredeemed vouchers — breakage — are not consideration for any supply, because no supply is ever made against them. The redemption is taxed on its own terms, as the supply of whatever the voucher buys. Sections 12(4) and 13(4), which used to fix the time of supply of a voucher, and rule 32(6), which valued one, were taken out as part of the same exercise.

citation.ref: Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST dated 31 December 2024, read with sections 2(52) and 2(102) and paragraph 6 of Schedule III, and with the omission of sections 12(4) and 13(4) and rule 32(6)

concepts.subsection: Section 49(5) and rule 88A — The order in which the credit ledger is spent
concepts.statement: Section 49(5) fixes the order in which the electronic credit ledger is used, and rule 88A, inserted with effect from 29 March 2019, loosens one part of it. Integrated tax credit is applied first towards integrated tax, and the balance may then go towards central tax and State or Union territory tax in any order and in any proportion — that freedom is rule 88A's contribution, and it replaced a rigid sequence that made the balance go to central tax first. Section 49B with rule 88A then adds the gate: the whole of the integrated tax credit must be exhausted before any central tax or State tax credit is used at all. Central tax credit is applied towards central tax and then towards integrated tax; State tax credit towards State tax and then towards integrated tax; and clauses (e) and (f) of section 49(5) forbid the two ever crossing — central tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of State tax, and State tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of central tax. The practical consequence is that the choice rule 88A gives away is worth money. Splitting the leftover integrated tax credit unevenly between the central and State heads can leave a stranded balance on one head and a cash payment on the other, while splitting it so that both heads finish together can leave nothing to pay in cash. Rule 86B separately restricts how much of the output liability a person above a prescribed monthly turnover may discharge from the credit ledger, but it caps the proportion; it does not change the order.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5)(a) to 49(5)(f), 49A and 49B, read with rules 88A and 86B of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 49(3), 49(4) and 49(8) — The three ledgers, and what each one may pay
concepts.statement: Three registers live on the portal, and each does something the other two cannot. Money paid in by challan through FORM GST PMT-06 lands in the electronic cash ledger, governed by section 49(1) and rule 87, and section 49(3) gives that balance a wide reach — it can settle a tax liability, interest, a penalty, a fee, or practically any other sum the Act or its rules call for. Credit self-assessed in a return lands in the electronic credit ledger instead, under section 49(2) and rule 86, and section 49(4) narrows its reach right down: it may only settle output tax, nothing more. Section 2(82) draws that boundary by defining output tax as what a person, or his agent, owes on his own taxable supplies — carving out anything he owes because a reverse charge shifted the liability onto him. That carve-out is what pushes three items permanently into cash: reverse-charge tax itself, plus interest, plus any penalty or fee, none of which the credit ledger may ever touch. The third register, the electronic liability ledger under rule 85, is just a running record of what is owed, nothing more. Section 49(8) then fixes the queue a payment clears: older periods' self-assessed dues first, this period's self-assessed dues next, and only after both of those anything else outstanding, a demand raised under section 73, 74 or 74A included. Section 49(10) lets a registered person move a cash-ledger balance between heads, or between two registrations held by the same PAN, by filing FORM GST PMT-09 — a facility the credit ledger has no equivalent of.

citation.ref: Sections 49(1) to 49(4), 49(8) and 49(10), with section 2(82), read with rules 85, 86 and 87 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST PMT-06 and PMT-09

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5)(b) and (h) — Free samples, gifts, and what an employer must provide by law
concepts.statement: Section 17(5) shuts the door on credit for a fixed list of situations, and two clauses in particular catch spending every business does routinely. Clause (h) reaches goods a business no longer really has — pilfered, ruined, missing from stock and written off, or simply handed out as a gift or a sample rather than sold. Two consequences follow from that. Handing goods out free earns no output tax, since nothing was paid for them — but whatever credit had been claimed on those goods still has to be given up, and it is clause (h) that takes it, not any apportionment worked out under the ordinary rules. A book write-off works the same way even where nothing was stolen and nothing was gifted; the clause asks only what happened to the goods, not why. Clause (b) is the longer list — catering and food, a beauty or wellness treatment, cosmetic or plastic surgery work, hiring or renting a motor vehicle, vessel or aircraft whose own credit is itself blocked, either kind of insurance, a club or gym membership, and a paid holiday or home-town trip given to staff. What rescues some of this spending is the proviso tucked inside clause (b): a business gets its credit back wherever some other statute, not a company policy and not a contract, actually compels it to give that benefit to its staff. A canteen the Factories Act forces a factory to run clears that bar; a canteen the factory simply chooses to run does not. Clause (b) has a second escape besides the proviso — credit survives where the very same category of inward supply is turned around and supplied onward as a taxable output, or folds into a taxable composite or mixed supply.

citation.ref: Sections 17(5)(b) with its provisos and 17(5)(h), read with section 7(1)(a) and paragraph 1 of Schedule I

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Section 31(3) and rule 55 — Which document goes with which event
concepts.statement: Section 31(3) pairs a document with each event in a transaction's life, and reaching for the wrong one is itself a lapse under the Act. A person dealing only in exempt goods or services, or one paying tax under the composition scheme in section 10, drops the tax invoice altogether and raises a bill of supply — rule 49 sets what it must contain, and it never carries a tax amount. Money received up front before the supply happens is acknowledged through a receipt voucher under rule 50. If that advance is later returned because nothing was ever supplied and no invoice ever followed, a refund voucher under rule 51 undoes the receipt voucher. A separate pair of documents covers the reverse charge case, under clause (f): a person who owes tax under section 9(3) or 9(4) on something bought from an unregistered supplier writes himself an invoice — the self-invoice — as soon as he receives the goods or the service, and then, quite separately, raises a payment voucher under rule 52 once he actually pays that supplier. Neither document can stand in for the other in the reverse charge situation: one marks the inward supply arriving, the other marks the money leaving. Rule 55 covers a document that is not an invoice at all — a delivery challan travels with liquid gas whose exact quantity will only be known on delivery, with goods sent out for job work, with goods moved for a reason that is not a supply, and with other notified movements, including a machine shipped in pieces where the tax invoice travels with the first consignment and a challan rides with every later one.

citation.ref: Sections 31(3)(c), 31(3)(d), 31(3)(e), 31(3)(f) and 31(3)(g), read with rules 49, 50, 51, 52 and 55 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(117), 37(4) and 39(10) — A valid return, and the order the returns must go in
concepts.statement: What makes a return valid, under section 2(117), is not merely filing it but clearing the whole of the self-assessed tax that goes with it — a return furnished but left unpaid does not count. That word carries weight downstream, most of all for the buyer's credit: section 16(2)(c) and (d) need the money to have actually reached the Government and the return itself to have been filed before credit is allowed. The monthly filings then run in a strict sequence, each one bolted to the one before. Outward-supply figures for a period go into FORM GSTR-1 under section 37(1), but section 37(4) shuts that door if any earlier period's figures are still outstanding. Rule 59(6) shuts it from the other direction too — GSTR-1 cannot go in unless the preceding period's GSTR-3B already has. And section 39(10) closes the loop entirely: a return under section 39 for a period is refused if either the previous period's return or that same period's own GSTR-1 is missing. Put together, this month's GSTR-1 needs last month's GSTR-3B filed first, and this month's GSTR-3B needs this month's GSTR-1 filed first — nothing can be jumped and quietly filed later. The annual return under section 44 sits above all of this reconciling what the monthly filings already said; it replaces none of them, and filing it never cures a month that was simply never filed.

citation.ref: Sections 2(117), 37(1), 37(4), 39(1), 39(7) and 39(10), read with rule 59(6) of the CGST Rules, 2017 and section 16(2)(c)

concepts.subsection: Sections 61 to 64 — Scrutiny, best judgement, the unregistered person and the summary order
concepts.statement: Four sections sit between the return and the demand, and picking the wrong one is the usual error. Section 61 is scrutiny: the proper officer may scrutinise the return and the particulars furnished to verify their correctness, inform the registered person of the discrepancies noticed in FORM GST ASMT-10 and seek his explanation, and where the explanation in ASMT-11 is found acceptable he informs him in ASMT-12 and takes no further action. Where no explanation is furnished within the prescribed period, or the explanation is not satisfactory, or the person does not take corrective measures after accepting the discrepancy, the officer may launch audit under section 65 or 66, inspection under section 67, or proceedings under section 73, 74 or 74A. Section 62 is best judgement assessment and it reaches only a registered person who fails to furnish a return even after a notice under section 46; the officer assesses to the best of his judgement using the material available, and the order stands withdrawn if the person afterwards furnishes a valid return within the period the section allows, though interest and late fee continue. Section 63 is the one for the person outside the net — a taxable person who fails to obtain registration though liable, or whose registration has been cancelled but who was liable to pay tax, may be assessed to the best of the officer's judgement within five years from the date the annual return for the relevant financial year was due, and only after a show cause notice and an opportunity of being heard. Section 64 is summary assessment, allowed only where the officer has evidence of a liability and sufficient grounds to believe that delay will adversely affect the interest of revenue, and only with the previous permission of the Additional Commissioner or Joint Commissioner; section 64(2) lets the taxable person apply within thirty days for it to be withdrawn.

citation.ref: Sections 61, 62, 63 and 64 with section 64(2), read with rules 98 to 100 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ASMT-10, ASMT-11 and ASMT-12

concepts.subsection: Sections 78, 79 and 80 — The three months, the six modes of recovery, and instalments
concepts.statement: Section 78 starts a clock running: whatever an order under the Act says is owed must be cleared within three months of the order being served, and once that window shuts, recovery can begin. A proviso lets the officer shorten that window on his own, but only where he thinks revenue is at risk and only if he writes down why. Section 79 is a toolbox, not a single road, and the officer may pick any of its modes, together or one after another. He can simply intercept money that is already owed to the defaulter, wherever it sits under his own control or under another officer's. He can seize and auction goods belonging to the defaulter that are within his reach. He can write to anyone else who owes the defaulter money, or who is holding money on the defaulter's behalf, and tell that third party to pay the Government instead — and if that person ignores the notice, he steps into the defaulter's shoes for that sum and answers for it himself. He can attach movable or immovable property and hold it until payment comes, or sell it once thirty days pass unpaid. He can hand the matter to the district Collector to be recovered the way land revenue arrears are. Or he can go to a Magistrate, who then treats the sum exactly as a fine the Magistrate's own court had imposed. Section 80 offers a way out under pressure: on a request, the Commissioner may push the due date back or spread payment across monthly instalments running up to twenty-four, with interest added — except this facility never reaches a sum the taxpayer already declared and assessed himself in a return, and missing even one instalment brings the whole remaining balance due immediately.

citation.ref: Sections 78 with its proviso, 79(1)(a) to 79(1)(f) with section 79(4), and 80, read with rules 143 to 155 and rule 158 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(91), 5 and 6 — Who is a proper officer, and the bar on parallel proceedings
concepts.statement: A function decides who counts as proper officer, not rank by itself. Section 2(91) ties the label to a specific function under the Act, naming as proper officer either the Commissioner or whichever central tax officer the Commissioner's own assignment gives that function to. Two things follow: nobody is "the" proper officer in general, only for a named function, and the assignment order or circular is what confers the authority, not seniority alone. Sections 5 and 6 then say how that authority moves. Section 5(1) hands a central tax officer the powers and duties his own appointment carries, subject to whatever conditions and limitations attach. Section 5(2) lets that officer additionally step into the powers and duties of a subordinate officer of central tax — seniority runs downward, never up. Section 5(3) lets the Commissioner delegate his own powers to a subordinate. Section 5(4) then closes the loop firmly: an Appellate Authority is fenced off from taking on the powers and duties belonging to any other central tax officer at all. Section 6 crosses the two administrations — an officer appointed under the State or Union territory GST law can double as a proper officer here too, on whatever conditions the Government notifies, per section 6(1) with 6(2)(a). The rule that stops both administrations chasing the same case is section 6(2)(b): once a State or Union territory officer has opened proceedings on a matter, this Act's own proper officer may not open a second set on that same matter.

citation.ref: Sections 2(91), 5(1) to 5(4), and 6(1) with 6(2)(a) and 6(2)(b), read with sections 3 and 4

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 130 — Confiscation, the redemption fine, and how it came apart from section 129
concepts.statement: Detention and confiscation run on separate tracks, and one is not a gateway to the other. Section 130(1) sets out confiscation's own list of triggers: supplying or receiving goods against the Act or its rules meaning to dodge tax, leaving goods unaccounted for where tax is owed on them, supplying taxable goods without ever applying for registration, breaching any provision with the same intent to dodge tax, or moving goods in contravention using a conveyance — unless its owner shows the transport happened without his knowledge or his agent's or the person in charge's. That last phrase, meaning to dodge tax, is what marks confiscation off from section 129, which stops goods in transit purely for being moved wrongly and asks nothing about what the person intended. A drafting change to section 130's opening words severed the automatic link the two sections once had, so a case under one no longer carries into the other by itself. Once confiscation is on the table, section 130(2) forces the officer's hand: the owner must be offered a fine as an alternative, capped so it never runs past the goods' market value once the tax due on them is subtracted, and floored so the fine plus any penalty together never come in under hundred per cent of that tax. A confiscated conveyance carries its own version of the same choice — a fine pegged to the tax on whatever it was hauling. Section 130(3) leaves the tax, penalty and other charges on the goods payable regardless of the fine, and section 130(7) gives the owner three months to pay before the officer may dispose of what was seized.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1), 130(2) with its provisos, 130(3), 130(6) and 130(7), read with section 129 and rule 139 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 18(1) and 18(4) — Credit on entering the net, and the amount payable on leaving it
concepts.statement: Section 18 handles the moments when a person's status changes, letting credit in at one end and taking it back at the other. Sub-section (1) is the entry point. Clause (a) covers someone who applies for registration inside thirty days of becoming liable and is granted it: he may claim credit on raw material still on hand and on material already built into semi-finished or finished goods still on hand, valued as of the day before his liability began. Clause (b) gives a person taking voluntary registration under section 25(3) the identical benefit, valued instead as of the day before the grant of registration. Clause (c) covers someone stepping out of the composition levy: he gets the same credit on that stock, plus credit on capital goods (cut down by the prescribed percentage points), valued as of the day before section 9 makes him liable to pay tax in the ordinary way. Clause (d) extends the same treatment to an exempt supply turning taxable. Two limits sit across all four clauses. Section 18(2) is a hard cutoff — nothing claimable through sub-section (1) may be claimed once a full year has run from the date the tax invoice was issued. And rule 40 needs a declaration in FORM GST ITC-01 filed within thirty days, certified by a chartered accountant or cost accountant once the claim crosses the prescribed amount. Sub-section (3) allows unutilised credit to move across on a sale, merger, demerger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the business, provided liabilities are specifically provided for, using FORM GST ITC-02. Sub-section (4) reverses the flow: a person who has already availed credit but now opts into the composition levy, or whose supplies turn wholly exempt, must pay back an amount matching the credit on that stock and on capital goods, and whatever remains afterward in the electronic credit ledger simply lapses.

citation.ref: Sections 18(1)(a) to 18(1)(d), 18(2), 18(3) and 18(4), read with rules 40 and 44 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ITC-01 and ITC-02

concepts.subsection: Sections 29 and 30 — Cancelling a registration, and getting it back
concepts.statement: An end to registration comes about two different ways, and which one applies changes what happens next. Section 29(1) covers the person walking away from it himself, or his legal heirs applying after his death, and it fires on the business closing down, being handed over whole for any reason (death included), merging into another legal entity, splitting apart or being wound up some other way; a change in how the business is constituted; or the person simply falling below what sections 22 and 24 require for registration to stay compulsory. Section 29(2) is the officer's own initiative, and it targets defaults: prescribed provisions contravened, a composition taxpayer's returns unfiled for the prescribed stretch, any other registered person's returns unfiled across a continuous prescribed stretch, a voluntary registrant who has not commenced business within six months of registering, or a registration got through fraud, a wilful lie or a hidden fact. Its proviso insists on a hearing before cancellation goes through. Section 29(3) then draws a firm line: cancelling the registration leaves untouched whatever tax and other dues were owed for the time before cancellation, no matter when that liability actually gets worked out. Section 29(5) is where cancellation bites: the person must debit either ledger — credit or cash — for an amount matching whichever is larger between the output tax on goods still held and the credit already claimed on raw material on hand, on material worked into semi-finished or finished goods still on hand, and on capital goods. Section 30 opens a way back for someone the officer cancelled unilaterally: apply for revocation in the manner and within the period prescribed, with rule 23 first demanding every return due across the gap, tax, interest, penalty and late fee included.

citation.ref: Sections 29(1), 29(2) with its proviso, 29(3), 29(4) and 29(5), and section 30, read with rules 20, 21, 22 and 23 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and rule 44

concepts.subsection: Sections 17, 46 and 47 — Who assesses a bill of entry, and the order for clearance
concepts.statement: The importer assesses his own goods. Section 17(1) says an importer entering goods under section 46, or an exporter entering goods under section 50, shall self-assess the duty leviable on them. Section 17(2) lets the proper officer verify the entries and the self-assessment, and may for that purpose examine or test the goods or require the importer to produce any document or information. Section 17(4) lets him re-assess the duty where, on verification, examination, testing or otherwise, he finds the self-assessment was not done correctly. Section 17(5) then gives the importer a safeguard: if he never confirms in writing that he accepts a re-assessment that runs against his own self-assessment, the officer owes him a speaking order, and the clock on that duty is fifteen days counted from when the re-assessment itself was made, whether the document was a bill of entry or a shipping bill. The self-assessment scheme replaced an older sequence in which the officer assessed the duty in the first instance and the importer merely made the entry. Section 46(1) requires the importer to make entry by presenting electronically a bill of entry for home consumption or for warehousing, and section 46(3) requires it to be presented before the end of the day, including any holiday, preceding the day of arrival of the vessel, aircraft or vehicle carrying the goods, and permits it to be presented in advance within the prescribed period before that expected arrival; charges for late presentation are prescribed. Section 46(4) requires the importer to make and subscribe a declaration as to the truth of the contents and produce the invoice and other supporting documents. Section 47(1) is the last step — where the proper officer is satisfied that the goods are not prohibited and that the import duty, if any, assessed and any charges payable have been paid, he shall make an order permitting clearance of the goods for home consumption. Section 47(2) charges interest where the duty is not paid within the prescribed period from the date on which the bill of entry is returned for payment.

citation.ref: Sections 17(1), 17(2), 17(4) and 17(5), 46(1), 46(3) and 46(4), and 47(1) and 47(2), read with the electronic filing procedure under the Bill of Entry Regulations, 2018

concepts.subsection: Section 28 — Two years, five years, and paying before the notice arrives
concepts.statement: Section 28 is the customs demand provision and it splits on conduct, not on amount. Where duty has not been levied, not been paid, has been short-levied or short-paid, or where it has been erroneously refunded, or where interest has not been paid, part paid or erroneously refunded, for any reason other than collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, section 28(1)(a) gives the proper officer two years from the relevant date to serve a notice requiring the person to show cause. Where any of those three things is the reason, section 28(4) gives him five years from the relevant date. Section 28(2) is the escape before the notice: the person may pay the duty, on the basis of his own ascertainment or of the ascertainment made by the proper officer, together with interest under section 28AA, and inform the proper officer in writing of that payment, and the proper officer shall not serve any notice in respect of the amount so paid, though he may still proceed for any amount short paid. The escape from a section 28(4) case is dearer and is in section 28(5): the person may pay the duty in full or in part as accepted by him, with interest and with a penalty equal to fifteen per cent of the duty, before the notice is served, and inform the officer, and the proceedings in respect of that amount are deemed conclusive. Section 28(6) keeps the same door open for thirty days after a notice under section 28(4) is served. Section 28(9) requires the proper officer to determine the amount within the prescribed period, extendable once by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and where it is not determined within that period the notice is treated as if it had never been issued.

citation.ref: Sections 28(1)(a), 28(2), 28(4), 28(5), 28(6) and 28(9), read with section 28AA and the Explanation defining the relevant date

concepts.subsection: Sections 85 to 90 — Stores, and what a foreign-going vessel may consume free of duty
concepts.statement: Section 2(38) defines stores broadly — anything meant for use aboard a vessel or aircraft, a definition that reaches beyond fuel to spare parts and any other article of equipment, fitted immediately or kept in reserve. Chapter XI builds a separate set of rules around that definition, and every one of them hinges on the vessel or aircraft being foreign-going. Section 85 permits imported goods entered for warehousing — meant to become stores aboard a foreign-going vessel or aircraft — to sit in the warehouse without duty being assessed on them yet. Section 86 lets stores already aboard such a vessel or aircraft stay there and leave India without duty, and lets imported stores move across to another vessel or aircraft on the same terms. Section 87 supplies the core benefit: stores already aboard may be consumed duty-free for as long as the vessel or aircraft counts as foreign-going. Section 88 brings in drawback for imported stores by applying section 74 with adjustments, so the full duty is refunded and the usual reduction for time in use is set aside. Section 89 covers the reverse direction — goods made in India that a foreign-going vessel or aircraft needs as stores may leave the country free of duty, on the same footing as any other export. Section 90 stretches sections 87 and 89, adjusted, to stores handed over to a ship of the Indian Navy. Everything above turns on section 2(21)'s definition of a foreign-going vessel or aircraft — one carrying goods or passengers between a port or airport in India and one outside it, and one out fishing or working beyond India's territorial waters counts too. A coastal vessel running only between two Indian ports falls outside that definition, so its stores are dutiable in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Sections 85, 86, 87, 88, 89 and 90, read with sections 2(38) and 2(21) and with section 74

concepts.subsection: Section 11 — The power to exempt, and the explanation that can be backdated
concepts.statement: GST carries no exemption that Parliament did not choose to delegate, and section 11 is where the delegation sits. Sub-section (1) is the general instrument: acting on the Council's recommendation and only once satisfied that public interest demands it, the Government may issue a notification taking a described category of goods or services — wholly or in part, unconditionally or subject to stated conditions — out of the tax that would otherwise fall on it, from a date the notification itself names. Sub-section (2) is the narrow instrument beside it, built for one transaction at a time rather than a class of them: a special order, naming the unusual circumstance that justifies it, letting a named supply escape the levy. A notification speaks to the world at large and a special order speaks to one case, and each has to justify itself on its own terms. Sub-section (3) is the trap for the unwary. When the Government later wants to pin down what a notification under sub-section (1) or an order under sub-section (2) actually covers, it can add an explanation to that earlier instrument, but only inside a one-year window measured from the original issue — and whatever it adds within that window is treated as though it had been there from day one. Miss the window and the same words would only bind going forward. The Explanation to section 11 carries a separate discipline: once a supply is exempted without any condition attached, the supplier loses the choice to charge tax on it anyway above the rate that already applies. Section 6 of the IGST Act gives the Government the identical three levers for integrated tax.

citation.ref: Sections 11(1), 11(2) and 11(3) with the Explanation to section 11, read with section 6 of the IGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Notification 13/2017 entry 6 — A director's services, and the personal-capacity line
concepts.statement: Section 9(3) is the Government's power, exercised on the Council's recommendation, to name a category of service supply and shift who pays the tax onto the recipient rather than the supplier; entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) uses that power for services supplied by a director of a company or a body corporate to the said company or the body corporate. The recipient company pays under reverse charge, and because that liability is not output tax within section 2(82) the payment must come in cash, not out of the credit ledger. Three payments to the same person can therefore be treated three different ways. Remuneration to a whole-time or executive director that the company books as salary and on which it deducts tax at source under section 192 of the Income-tax Act is not a supply at all — entry 1 of Schedule III keeps an employee's services to his employer, rendered as part of that employment, outside the scope of supply altogether. Sitting fees, commission and similar payments to a non-executive or independent director, on which tax is deducted under section 194J, are not employment income and do fall under entry 6, so the company pays under reverse charge. That split is what Circular No. 140/10/2020-GST settled. And where a director supplies something to the company in his private or personal capacity rather than as a director — renting out immovable property he owns personally being the standing example — Circular No. 201/13/2023-GST says entry 6 does not reach it, so there is no reverse charge on the company and the director accounts for the tax himself if he is otherwise liable. The test is the capacity in which the service is supplied, not the identity of the person supplying it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), read with entry 1 of Schedule III, section 2(82), Circular No. 140/10/2020-GST and Circular No. 201/13/2023-GST

concepts.subsection: Schedule II paragraph 5(b) — Construction sold before completion, and the entire-consideration test
concepts.statement: Selling a flat can sit on either side of GST depending purely on timing, and paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II draws the line. A building put up for sale counts as a service under that paragraph unless one thing is true of the buyer's money: every rupee of it arrived only after the earlier of two events — a completion certificate from the competent authority, where one is called for, or the building's first occupation. Flip that exception around and it becomes the operating rule. Let even a token booking sum land before that earlier event, and the whole transaction — not just the early instalment — is pulled back inside the levy as a service. Note which of the two events is decisive when both are in play: first occupation need not wait on paperwork, and where people have already moved in before any certificate is issued, it is the moving in that fixes the date. Paragraph 5 of Schedule III works alongside this and bends to it — land sold outright sits outside both supply of goods and supply of services altogether, and so, ordinarily, does a building, but that second limb only holds subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II. A finished building sold after that event is therefore untouched by GST, while the identical building sold off a booking taken mid-construction is taxed as a service from the first rupee. The Explanation to paragraph 5 defines the competent authority and reads construction broadly enough to take in an addition, an alteration, a replacement or a remodelling of a structure already standing.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II with its Explanation, read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III and section 7(1A)

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Rule 46 and Notification 14/2020 — The dynamic QR code on a business-to-consumer invoice
concepts.statement: Two separate obligations put a machine-readable code on an invoice and they point in opposite directions. Rule 48(4) is electronic invoicing — a registered person above the notified turnover must prepare an invoice for a supply to a registered person, for an export, or for a supply to a special economic zone unit or developer, by uploading the particulars to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an Invoice Reference Number together with a signed QR code. That code is static. It carries the identity of the invoice so anyone can verify it, and an invoice within rule 48(4) that has not been issued this way is not a valid invoice at all. Business-to-consumer invoices are outside rule 48(4) entirely and are never uploaded to the Portal. Rule 46 carries the other obligation, notified by Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax — an invoice issued by a registered person above the notified turnover to an unregistered person must have a Dynamic Quick Response code. A dynamic code is not an identity token but a payment instruction; it carries the payee details and the amount so that the customer can scan it and pay. The notification treats the requirement as met where the supplier makes the dynamic code available to the recipient through a digital display and the invoice carries a cross-reference of the payment made using that code, and where payment is made by any other mode the invoice must carry a cross-reference of that payment instead. So the same supplier may owe both duties at once, on different invoices, and the code printed by the Portal on a business-to-business invoice does nothing for the counter invoice handed to a walk-in customer.

citation.ref: Rule 46 (the Dynamic Quick Response code requirement) read with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax and rule 48(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1) — Getting money back out of the cash ledger
concepts.statement: Money deposited by challan sits in the electronic cash ledger and is not yet tax. It becomes tax only when it is debited against a liability, and until then it belongs to the person who deposited it. Section 49(6) is what lets that leftover come back out: once every liability — tax, interest, penalty, fee or anything else charged against either the cash or the credit ledger — has been met, whatever remains in either ledger is available for refund under section 54. The proviso to section 54(1) gives the cash side its own shortcut: rather than filing a separate refund application, a taxpayer can pull an unused cash-ledger balance straight through the return filed under section 39, in the prescribed manner. Nothing lapses and nothing is forfeited, however long the balance sits. The credit ledger is not the same animal. Input tax credit is refundable only in the two situations section 54(3) allows — zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and an inverted duty structure where the rate on inputs is higher than the rate on output supplies, subject to the exclusions in the provisos to that sub-section. A registered person making ordinary domestic taxable supplies who has accumulated credit simply carries it forward and uses it; he cannot ask for it back. There is also a middle route for cash that avoids a refund altogether — section 49(10) with FORM GST PMT-09 lets an amount in the cash ledger be transferred from one head or major head to another, and between registrations of the same person holding the same Permanent Account Number. Nothing similar exists for the credit ledger.

citation.ref: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1), read with section 54(3) and section 49(10)

concepts.subsection: Section 56 — Interest when a refund is late, and the date the clock starts
concepts.statement: Section 56 makes the Government pay for its own delay, and it fixes the starting point at an event the applicant controls rather than one the department controls. Take a refund ordered under section 54(5): the clock is sixty days, counted from when the department received the section 54(1) application, and if the money has not moved by then, interest starts running the day after that window closes and keeps running till the refund is actually paid, at a rate the section caps at six per cent and a notification fixes. The date the officer got round to sanctioning is irrelevant, and so is the date of any order. The proviso raises the stakes where the claim comes out of litigation — where a refund arises from an order passed by an adjudicating authority, an Appellate Authority, the Appellate Tribunal or a court which has attained finality, and is not refunded within sixty days from the date of receipt of the application filed consequent to such order, interest runs from the date immediately after the expiry of those sixty days till the date of refund, at a rate the section caps at nine per cent. Note what the proviso does and does not do. It lifts the rate, but it keeps the same trigger — sixty days from the receipt of an application, and specifically the application filed consequent to the order, not the original claim that was rejected years earlier. The Explanation closes the circle by deeming an order of refund made by an appellate authority, the Tribunal or a court against an order of the proper officer to be an order passed under section 54(5), so a refund the department never sanctioned is still a refund ordered under that sub-section for the purposes of the section.

citation.ref: Section 56 with its proviso and Explanation, read with sections 54(1) and 54(5)

concepts.subsection: Sections 107(2) and 107(11) — What the Appellate Authority may do, and the one thing it may not
concepts.statement: The first appeal under GST is not confined to the taxpayer's side of the table. Section 107(1) opens the door to any person aggrieved by a decision or order, who gets three months from its communication to reach the Appellate Authority, with a further month available on sufficient cause shown under section 107(4). Section 107(2) hands the department a route that the section never labels an appeal yet functions as one: the Commissioner, acting on his own motion or at the request of his State counterpart, may pull the record of any proceeding an adjudicating authority has decided, satisfy himself whether it was legally and properly done, and then direct a subordinate officer to place specified points before the Appellate Authority — a step the law treats as an appeal once taken. Section 107(11) is where the examinable content sits. Having made whatever further inquiry the case still needs, the Appellate Authority may confirm the order appealed against, modify it, or annul it altogether — three outcomes only, and sending the file back to the officer who passed it is not a fourth. GST's first appellate stage carries no power of remand, so a gap in the record has to be closed by the Appellate Authority's own further inquiry rather than by returning the matter downward. Two provisos then hem the power in. Raising a fee, a penalty, or a fine standing in for confiscation, ordering the confiscation of goods worth more than before, or cutting down a refund or a credit already allowed — none of that may happen unless the appellant first gets a fair chance to show cause against it. And where the Authority concludes that tax has gone unpaid, been underpaid, been refunded by mistake, or that credit was wrongly claimed or used, it cannot order recovery without first issuing a show cause notice and keeping to the time limits the demand sections lay down. Section 107(12) makes the order state the points decided and the reasons for each; section 107(13) sets a one-year target from filing, where that is achievable.

citation.ref: Sections 107(2), 107(11) with its two provisos, 107(12) and 107(13), read with sections 107(1) and 107(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 108 — Revision, and the four bars on the Revisional Authority
concepts.statement: Revision gives the department its own second look at an order nobody chose to appeal. Subject to section 121, the Revisional Authority — acting on his own motion, on information that comes his way, or on a request from his counterpart holding State or Union territory tax — may call for and go through the record of any proceeding. Where he judges that a subordinate officer's decision or order works against the revenue's interest and is either unlawful, improper, or reached without regard to material facts that existed then or came to light later — including a fact surfaced by an observation of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India — he may put that order on hold and, once the affected person has had a hearing and any further inquiry he thinks necessary has been made, pass whatever order seems just: confirming it, cutting it down, enlarging it, or wiping it out. Note carefully which way the power points — it exists only for orders that hurt the revenue, never for ones that hurt the taxpayer. Sub-section (2) then closes four doors on him. He may not revise an order that has already gone in appeal under section 107, 112, 117 or 118; one where the section 107(2) window is still running, or where more than three years have gone by since it was passed; one already taken up for revision once before; or one that was itself the product of an earlier revision. A proviso softens the first of those bars — on a point the appeal never raised or decided, the Revisional Authority may still act, so long as he does so before one year runs from the date of the appellate order, or before the three years in clause (b) run out, whichever finishes later. A second proviso stops the clock for any stretch during which a court or the Appellate Tribunal has stayed the making of the order. The Explanation reads record to mean everything on file at the time of examination, and reads decision to take in even an intimation issued by an officer junior to the Revisional Authority.

citation.ref: Section 108(1), section 108(2) clauses (a) to (d) with its two provisos, and the Explanation to section 108, read with section 121

concepts.subsection: Section 161 — Rectifying an error apparent on the face of the record
concepts.statement: Section 161 is the small repair kit, and it is deliberately narrow. Whichever authority passed or issued a decision, order, notice, certificate or other document can go back and fix a mistake that is obvious on the face of it — one visible without argument — either of its own accord, or once an officer working the CGST Act or the State or Union territory Act flags it, or once the affected person points it out within three months of the document's issue. Two limits and a safeguard follow. The first proviso says no rectification shall be done after six months from the date of issue of the document — the authority's own outer limit, longer than the affected person's three months to point the error out. The second proviso drops that six-month cap altogether for a purely clerical or arithmetical slip — a wrong addition or a transposed digit traced to an accidental omission can be put right whenever it is found. The third proviso is the safeguard — where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice shall be followed by the authority carrying it out. What section 161 will not do is reopen a matter. An error apparent on the face of record is one visible without argument; a debatable question of law, a fresh appreciation of evidence, or a change of mind is not one, and the route for those is appeal or revision. The section opens without prejudice to section 160, which protects a notice or order from being held invalid merely for a mistake, defect or omission where it is in substance in conformity with the Act.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its three provisos, read with section 160

concepts.subsection: Section 171 — Passing the benefit on, and what an order against a profiteer contains
concepts.statement: Section 171(1) states an obligation in one sentence: whenever the tax rate on a supply of goods or services drops, or an extra input tax credit becomes available to the supplier, the recipient must see prices come down by a matching amount — the reduction has to reach him, and it has to be commensurate with what triggered it. Two triggers, and only two. A fall in the supplier's own costs, a cheaper raw material, a better freight contract, none of these engage the section, and a supplier who has cut his price for one of those reasons has not thereby discharged an obligation created by a rate cut. Commensurate is measured against the benefit, not against last year's price list. Section 171(2) lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, constitute an Authority or empower an existing authority to check whether an availed credit or a cut tax rate genuinely showed up on the price tag as a matching reduction, and a proviso added in 2024 lets the Government notify a date from which that Authority shall not accept any request for examination. The machinery has moved twice — the National Anti-profiteering Authority first, then the Competition Commission of India, and then the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 109, with a notified cut-off after which no fresh request is entertained. Read the current notification for the dates before quoting them. What an order does is fixed by section 171(3) with the rules — it may direct a reduction in prices, and the return of the amount not passed on to the recipient with interest, and where the recipient does not claim it or cannot be identified, deposit of that amount in the Consumer Welfare Fund. Section 171(3A) adds a penalty equivalent to ten per cent of the profiteered amount, with no penalty if that amount is deposited within thirty days of the order. The profiteered amount is the recipient's money being routed back to him; it is not a demand of tax, and it does not travel through sections 73, 74 or 74A.

citation.ref: Section 171(1), 171(2) with its proviso, 171(3) and 171(3A) with the Explanation to section 171, read with rules 127 and 133 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and section 109

concepts.subsection: Sections 151 and 152 — Calling for information, and the bar on using it unheard
concepts.statement: Section 151, as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021, is short and wide. A Commissioner, or an officer he authorises, can order any person to hand over information touching anything the Act deals with, and the order itself fixes the deadline, the format and the manner the information has to be given in. It stands beside section 150, which obliges specified persons — registering authorities, banks, stock exchanges, income-tax authorities and others — to furnish an information return. Between them the department can build a picture of a taxpayer out of material the taxpayer never supplied and may never have seen. Section 152 is the fence around that power and it has two limbs. Sub-section (1) says no information of any individual return or part of it, given for the purposes of section 150 or section 151, shall without the previous consent in writing of the person concerned or his authorised representative be published in a manner enabling the particulars to be identified as referring to a particular person; and the same information cannot be used in any proceedings under the Act unless the person it concerns has first been given a hearing. Publication and use are two separate prohibitions, and the second is the one that bites in an assessment. A proviso lets the Commissioner publish information about a class of taxable persons or a class of transactions where he considers it desirable in the public interest, because nothing there identifies an individual. Sub-section (2) keeps the files shut — no person not engaged in the collection of statistics under the Act, or in compiling or computer processing it for the purposes of the Act, shall be permitted to see or have access to any information or any individual return referred to in section 151.

citation.ref: Sections 151 and 152(1) with its proviso and 152(2), as substituted and amended by the Finance Act, 2021, read with section 150

concepts.subsection: Section 23 — Persons not liable to register, and the overriding words added in 2023
concepts.statement: Section 23(1) names two classes who shall not be liable to registration. The first is a person whose business is nothing but supplying goods or services, or both, that carry no liability to tax or sit wholly exempt from it under the CGST Act or the IGST Act — exclusivity is the condition, not the mere presence of an exempt line among others. The second is an agriculturist, but only for what he supplies by cultivating his own land — anything beyond that falls outside the carve-out. Sub-section (2) lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify further categories exempted from obtaining registration. Two words in sub-section (1) carry the work. Not liable to tax points at a non-taxable supply under section 2(78) — alcoholic liquor for human consumption, and the petroleum products on which GST is not yet levied — while wholly exempt points at section 2(47). And exclusively means exclusively; one taxable supply, however small, takes a person out of the clause and back to sections 22 and 24. The important change is at the front of the sub-section. As originally enacted, section 23 sat awkwardly against section 24, which opens with its own overriding words and makes registration compulsory for named categories irrespective of turnover, among them a person required to pay tax under reverse charge and a person making an inter-State taxable supply. Which provision won was argued for years. The Finance Act, 2023 substituted the opening of section 23(1) so that it now reads notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sub-section (1) of section 22 or section 24, and the substitution was given retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. Section 23 therefore prevails. A person who supplies nothing but exempt or non-taxable goods is outside the register even where a compulsory category in section 24 would otherwise have caught him — and he was outside it from the first day of the levy, not from the date of the amendment.

citation.ref: Section 23(1) as substituted by the Finance Act, 2023 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, and section 23(2), read with sections 22(1), 24, 2(47) and 2(78)

concepts.subsection: Section 121 — The four orders no appeal lies against
concepts.statement: Not every decision of a tax officer can be appealed, and section 121 marks out the exceptions. Overriding every other provision of the Act, it closes the door on an appeal against a decision or order an officer of central tax has made wherever that decision touches one of four things. One, a Commissioner (or another empowered authority) moving a proceeding from one officer's desk to another's. Two, an order about seizing or hanging on to books of account, a register, or other documents. Three, an order that greenlights a prosecution. Four, an order made under section 80, the provision letting the Commissioner stretch out payment time or allow instalments on anything other than tax the person self-assessed. All four share the same character — each is a step in running a case rather than a ruling on how much is owed: which officer hears it, what the department may hold on to, whether a criminal case goes ahead, how long the taxpayer gets to pay. Liability itself stays fully open to appeal throughout. Two things follow from this. The closed door is specifically an appeal, not every remedy, so an arbitrary order on one of these four points can still be taken to the High Court by writ. And because section 108(1) itself opens subject to the provisions of section 121, the same four matters sit beyond the reach of revision too — a department that could not let the taxpayer appeal a thing cannot revise it either.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (a) to (d), read with sections 80, 107(1) and 108(1)

concepts.subsection: Sections 59 and 73 — The warehousing bond, and when it comes back
concepts.statement: Warehousing defers duty, and the security for the deferred duty is a bond. Section 59(1) requires the importer of goods for which a bill of entry for warehousing has been presented under section 46 and assessed under section 17 or section 18 to execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed, binding himself to comply with all the provisions of the Act, the rules and the regulations in respect of those goods, to pay on or before the date specified in a notice of demand all duties and interest payable under section 61(2), and to pay all penalties and fines incurred for any contravention in respect of those goods. Section 59(2) lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner permit a general bond covering goods to be imported within a specified period, and section 59(3) requires security in addition to the bond. The bond continues in force notwithstanding the transfer of the goods to another warehouse, and where the goods are transferred to another person the transferee executes his own bond and security. Section 71 fixes the only lawful exits, and there are just three of them plus a residual class — a warehoused item may go out cleared for home use, go out cleared for export, or move on to a different warehouse, and anything beyond those three needs its own separate authority in the Act. Section 72 deals with the unlawful exit, letting the proper officer demand the full amount of duty chargeable together with all penalties, rent, interest and other charges, and, if the owner does not pay, detain and sell after notice a sufficient portion of his goods in the warehouse. Section 73 closes the loop. Once every last item under a section 59 bond has left the warehouse — sold for home use, shipped abroad, moved on, or accounted for by whatever other lawful route applies — and once every rupee owed on those goods has actually reached the department, the bond has done its work: the officer has to mark it discharged in full and hand it back on demand to whoever executed it or is now entitled to hold it. Nothing about the calendar decides this; only the goods leaving and the money arriving do.

citation.ref: Sections 59(1), 59(2) and 59(3), 71, 72(1) and 72(2), and 73, read with sections 46, 61(2) and 68

concepts.subsection: Section 49 — Storing imported goods in a warehouse without warehousing them
concepts.statement: Section 49 exists for the importer who has entered his goods for home consumption and then cannot take them away. Where the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner is satisfied, on the importer's application, that imported goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, the goods may pending clearance be permitted to be stored in a public warehouse for a period the section fixes, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. What makes the section examinable is a status the closing words deny the goods — the Act refuses to treat them as warehoused goods at all, however long they sit there, so the whole warehousing chapter is switched off for them. Everything follows from that. No bond under section 59 is taken, because there is nothing to bond. No interest under section 61(2) accrues, because interest there attaches to warehoused goods left beyond their free period. No manipulation of the goods under section 64 is available. And, most often tested, the rate of duty and tariff valuation stay where section 15(1)(a) put them — the date of presentation of the bill of entry for home consumption — instead of moving to section 15(1)(b), which fixes the rate for warehoused goods by the date on which the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of them is presented under section 68. The goods are physically in a warehouse and legally are not warehoused goods; a building does not change their status, an order under section 60 permitting deposit does. The importer pays rent and charges for the storage, but nothing about the levy moves while he waits.

citation.ref: Section 49 with its provisos, read with sections 15(1)(a), 15(1)(b), 46, 59, 60, 61(2) and 68

concepts.subsection: Sections 28-I and 28J — When a customs advance ruling cannot be given, and who it binds
concepts.statement: A customs advance ruling is a written decision on a question raised by an applicant in respect of goods before their importation or exportation, given by the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings constituted under section 28EA. An applicant is a person holding a valid Importer-exporter Code Number, a person exporting goods to India, or a person with a justifiable cause to the satisfaction of the Authority. Section 28H(2) fixes what may be asked — classification of goods, the applicability of a notification issued under section 25(1) having a bearing on the rate of duty, the principles to be adopted for determining value, the applicability of notifications in respect of duties under the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff Act or any other law where the duty is chargeable in the same manner as customs duty, the determination of origin of the goods under a trade agreement, and any other matter the Central Government notifies. Section 28-I(2) lets the Authority allow or reject the application by order, and its proviso is a bar rather than a discretion — the Authority shall not allow the application where the question raised in it is already pending in the applicant's case before any officer of customs, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, or where the same question has already been decided by the Appellate Tribunal or any court. The bar looks at the question, not at the consignment, so a future import does not escape it while the identical question is alive in the applicant's own earlier matter. No application is rejected without giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, and the order must give reasons. Section 28J sets the reach of a ruling that is given — it is binding only on the applicant who sought it, in respect of the questions listed in section 28H(2), and on the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs and the customs authorities subordinate to him in respect of that applicant, and it stays binding unless there is a change in the law or the facts on which it was pronounced. Section 28K makes a ruling void from the start where the Authority finds it was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 28-I(2) with sections 28-I(4), 28E, 28EA, 28H(2), 28J(1), 28J(2) and 28K

concepts.subsection: Sections 68 and 71 — A duty-free shop is a warehouse, and duty falls when the goods leave it
concepts.statement: A duty-free shop at an international airport is not foreign territory and is not outside the Customs Act. It is a warehouse licensed under the warehousing chapter, and the goods on its shelves are warehoused goods on which duty has been deferred rather than remitted. That single fact answers most questions asked about it. Section 71 allows warehoused goods to leave a warehouse in only a few ways — cleared for home consumption, cleared for export, removed to another warehouse, or as otherwise provided by the Act — so the sale across the counter is not itself the taxable event; the exit route is. Where an arriving passenger buys at an arrival duty-free shop, the goods take the home-consumption exit, and section 68 governs it. A bill of entry for home consumption in respect of the warehoused goods is presented, the import duty and any charges are paid, and the proper officer makes an order for clearance. Section 15(1)(b) then fixes the rate of duty and tariff valuation by the date that bill of entry is presented, not by the date the shop imported the stock, so a rate change between the two dates counts. Where a departing passenger buys at a departure duty-free shop, the goods leave the country instead of entering it, so no clearance for home consumption occurs and no import duty falls due at all. The shop is the same, the customer is the difference, and the levy follows the exit the goods take rather than the contract of sale.

citation.ref: Sections 68 and 71, read with sections 15(1)(b), 12 and 61

concepts.subsection: Rule 10(1)(c) — Royalties and licence fees, and the condition-of-sale test
concepts.statement: Rule 10(1) of the customs valuation rules lists what gets added on top of the price actually paid or payable once the transaction value is built. Clause (c) is the royalty limb: it brings in a royalty or licence fee tied to the imported goods that the buyer must pay, in whatever form, as the price of being allowed to buy the goods at all, to whatever extent that sum has not already found its way into the invoiced price. Getting this clause right needs both tests satisfied, not just one — the payment has to connect to the imported goods, and separately the buyer has to have no choice but to pay it if the sale is to go through. A royalty the buyer is free to walk away from fails on the second limb no matter how tightly it is pegged to the goods; a sum the supplier will not ship without clears that limb even where its amount is worked out from sales made long after the goods land. Two explanations then pull specific payments back out of the clause. A charge paid purely for the right to make copies of the imported goods within India stays out of the price. And a sum the buyer pays for the right to sell or distribute the goods on also stays out, but only where paying it was never a precondition of the export sale itself. Clause (d) beside it brings in whatever share of a later resale, disposal or use of the goods flows back to the seller, directly or through another route, and clause (e) mops up every other sum the buyer pays as a condition of the sale — to the seller himself, or to a third party in discharge of something the seller owed — to the extent it has not already been counted.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) with its two explanations, read with rules 10(1)(d), 10(1)(e) and 3, and section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

concepts.subsection: Sections 111, 112 and 125 — Confiscation, penalty, and when the fine must be offered
concepts.statement: Section 111 lists the goods brought from a place outside India that are liable to confiscation. Three of its clauses do most of the work in a case study. Clause (d) catches goods that are imported, attempted to be imported, or even just brought into Indian customs waters heading toward import, in breach of a prohibition that sits either in the Customs Act itself or in any other statute currently on the books. Clause (m) catches goods which do not correspond in respect of value or in any other particular with the entry made under the Act, or in the case of baggage with the declaration made under section 77. Clause (o) catches goods conditionally exempted from duty or from a prohibition where the condition is not observed, unless the non-observance was sanctioned by the proper officer. Section 112 attaches a personal penalty to the same conduct — on a person who does or omits to do an act that renders the goods liable to confiscation under section 111, or abets it, and on a person who acquires possession of or is in any way concerned in carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping, concealing, selling or purchasing, or otherwise dealing with, goods he knows or has reason to believe are liable to confiscation. Section 125 is where the two words that decide the answer sit. Whenever confiscation is authorised, the officer adjudging it may, in the case of goods whose importation or exportation is prohibited, and shall, in the case of any other goods, give the owner, or the person from whose possession the goods were seized, an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation. The discretion belongs to the prohibited case; redemption of ordinary goods is not a favour the officer can withhold. A proviso caps the fine at the market price of the goods, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable on them. Section 125(2) adds that where a fine is imposed the owner is in addition liable to any duty and charges payable in respect of the goods, so redemption never replaces the duty.

citation.ref: Sections 111(d), 111(m) and 111(o), section 112, and sections 125(1) with its proviso and 125(2)

concepts.subsection: Sections 30, 31 and 32 — The arrival manifest, entry inwards, and what may be unloaded
concepts.statement: Before a single package comes ashore, three sections have to be satisfied and they apply to different conveyances. Section 29 requires a vessel or aircraft entering India from outside India to call or land only at a customs port or customs airport, except with the Board's permission or for accident, stress of weather or other unavoidable cause. Section 30(1) requires the person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft carrying imported goods or export goods, or any other person the Central Government specifies, to deliver to the proper officer an arrival manifest or import manifest before the arrival of the vessel or aircraft, and in the case of a vehicle an import report after its arrival at the customs station; late delivery without sufficient cause draws a penalty. Section 30(3) requires the person delivering it to subscribe to a declaration as to the truth of its contents, and section 30(4) lets the proper officer permit an incorrect or incomplete manifest to be amended or supplemented where he is satisfied there was no fraudulent intention. Section 31 then adds a step that exists for one kind of conveyance only. A vessel's master is barred from letting any imported cargo come off the ship unless and until the proper officer has first granted that vessel entry inwards, and that grant itself waits on an arrival manifest or import manifest having reached the officer — or on him being satisfied the delay in delivering one had sufficient cause. There is no entry inwards for an aircraft — the section speaks of the master of a vessel throughout. Section 31(3) carves out a passenger's or crew member's baggage, mail bags, animals, and goods that are perishable or hazardous, letting those come off without waiting. Section 32 is the independent check on every conveyance — no imported goods shall be unloaded unless they are mentioned in the arrival manifest, import manifest or import report for that conveyance. Sections 33 and 34 confine unloading to approved places and to the supervision of a customs officer.

citation.ref: Sections 30(1), 30(3) and 30(4), 31(1), 31(2) and 31(3), and 32, read with sections 29, 33 and 34

concepts.subsection: Section 2(6) — Aggregate turnover, and what it counts
concepts.statement: Aggregate turnover is the measuring stick the whole Act reaches for — registration under section 22, eligibility for the composition levy, the e-invoicing obligation, the audit and annual return duties all read off it — and section 2(6) defines it once for all of them. Four heads are added up and the sum is taken PAN-wide, right across the country, rather than registration by registration: supplies that bear tax, supplies that are exempt, goods and services sent out of India, and whatever one PAN moves from one State into another. Struck out of that total before it is read are the purchases on which the buyer himself discharges the levy under the reverse charge mechanism. Each of those four heads catches candidates out in a different way. Exempt supplies count, so a person whose sales are largely exempt can still be pushed over the registration line by them. Exports count, though they carry no tax. Supplies made from a second State under the same PAN count, so the test is never registration-wise. And the figure is aggregate value, not taxable value, so it is read before any deduction. Two things stay out. The value of inward supplies on which the person himself pays tax under reverse charge is excluded — he is the recipient there, and his own purchases are not his turnover. And the taxes themselves are excluded: central tax, State tax, Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess are all stripped out of the figure. The explanations to the section add that the value of activities in Schedule III, and interest on deposits, loans and advances, do not enter the composition scheme's reading of it.

citation.ref: Section 2(6), read with sections 22 and 10

concepts.subsection: Article 246A — What GST replaced, and what it left standing
concepts.statement: GST needed a constitutional amendment before it could exist, because the old scheme split the taxing power — the Union taxed manufacture and services, the States taxed sale of goods, and neither could reach the other's field. The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted Article 246A, which gives Parliament and every State legislature simultaneous power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax, with Parliament alone competent for inter-State supply under Article 269A. Central excise duty, additional duties of excise and customs, service tax, State value added tax, central sales tax, entry tax, octroi, luxury tax, entertainment tax levied by a State, and the several cesses and surcharges on supply were subsumed. What was left standing is the more useful half of the list. Basic customs duty survives untouched on imports and sits beside the integrated tax charged there. Stamp duty on instruments survives, being a duty on the document rather than a tax on supply. State excise and State VAT on alcoholic liquor for human consumption survive, because Article 366(12A) defines goods and services tax as a tax on the supply of goods or services or both except the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption — that supply is outside GST by definition and not merely exempt. Electricity duty and property tax survive. And five petroleum products — crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel — are inside the GST framework but not yet inside the levy, tax on them beginning only from a date the Council recommends.

citation.ref: Article 246A with Articles 269A and 366(12A), inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016

concepts.subsection: Article 279A — The GST Council, and how far its word goes
concepts.statement: Article 279A creates the Goods and Services Tax Council — the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson, the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance, and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation, or any other Minister, nominated by each State Government, who choose one of their number as Vice-Chairperson.
