Its function is to make recommendations to the Union and the States on the taxes to be subsumed, the goods and services to be exempted, model laws and principles of levy, the threshold below which supplies may be exempted, and rates including floor rates with bands. Half the total number of Members is the quorum. A decision is taken by a majority of not less than three fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, the Central Government's vote weighing one third of the votes cast and all the State Governments' votes together weighing two thirds — so neither side can carry a decision alone. The word that matters is recommendations. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations have persuasive value and are not binding on the Union and the States, since Article 246A gives both simultaneous power to legislate and the Council is a forum for that dialogue rather than an authority above it. The practice is that recommendations are followed and notified; the law is that they are not commands.

citation.ref: Article 279A, sub-articles (1) to (9), read with Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022)

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 74 — Health care services, and where the exemption stops
concepts.statement: Entry 74 lifts tax off health care given by a clinical establishment, by an authorised medical practitioner and by para-medics, and off carrying a patient in an ambulance. Everything then turns on how the notification builds the term health care, because that wording is both the width of the exemption and its edge. What counts is diagnosis, treatment or care aimed at an illness, an injury, a deformity, an abnormality or a pregnancy, delivered under a system of medicine that India recognises; taking the patient to a clinical establishment and bringing him back again is folded in as well. Two things are pushed out — a hair transplant, and cosmetic or plastic surgery — but the second walks back in whenever the surgeon is restoring or rebuilding a part of the body, or the working of one, that a congenital defect, a developmental abnormality, an injury or a trauma has damaged. So the same operation performed by the same surgeon in the same hospital falls on either side of the line depending on why it is being done. A clinical establishment is a hospital, nursing home, clinic, sanatorium or any institution offering services requiring diagnosis or treatment, including a place established as an independent entity or part of an establishment for diagnosis or investigation. The exemption attaches to the service, not to the building, which is why a hospital's shop rentals, its canteen sales to visitors and its cosmetic work are all outside it while its ward and its operating theatre are inside.

citation.ref: Entry 74, read with the definitions of health care services and clinical establishment in paragraph 2 of the notification

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 66 — An educational institution, and the services bought in
concepts.statement: Entry 66 has two halves and candidates lose marks by reading only the first. Clause (a) exempts services supplied by an educational institution to its students, faculty and staff, and services by way of conduct of an entrance examination against a fee. The notification builds the term educational institution out of three alternatives: a body teaching at pre-school level and on through to the higher secondary stage or its equivalent; a body delivering a course that forms part of the curriculum laid down for a qualification the law recognises; or a body running an approved vocational education course. So a degree college and a school are both educational institutions for what they supply to their own students. Clause (b) runs the other way — it exempts services supplied to an educational institution by way of transportation of students, faculty and staff, catering including any mid-day meals scheme sponsored by the Government, security or cleaning or house-keeping services performed in such institution, and services relating to admission to or conduct of examination. But clause (b) is cut down: the first three of them are exempt only if the institution receiving them teaches at pre-school level and on through to the higher secondary stage or its equivalent. The inward leg therefore stops at the school gate. A bus operator, a caterer or a housekeeping agency serving a school is exempt; the same three serving a degree college are taxable, and the college takes credit if it has any taxable output to set it against. Examination-related services and online educational journals have their own, differently drawn, treatment.

citation.ref: Entry 66, clauses (a) and (b), read with the definition of educational institution in paragraph 2 of the notification

concepts.subsection: Renting a residential dwelling, and the reverse charge that follows registration
concepts.statement: Renting of a residential dwelling for use as residence has always been exempt, and the exemption used to turn on the building and the use alone. It no longer does. The entry now reads except where the recipient is a registered person, so the moment the tenant is registered under GST the supply leaves the exemption. Nothing about the flat has changed; the status of the tenant has. Having taken the supply out of exemption, the law then moves the liability: the notified entry under section 9(3) makes the registered recipient pay the tax on renting of a residential dwelling under reverse charge, which is how a landlord who is unregistered, and who may have no idea GST is involved, is left with nothing to do. The company or firm renting a flat for a director, a guest house or a staff hostel therefore self-invoices and pays in cash. One carve-out was added because the first version swept too wide — the exemption survives where the registered tenant is a proprietor who takes the flat privately, to live in it himself, and on his own account rather than on the account of his business. The test is the capacity in which the tenant takes the flat, not merely whether his name appears on a GST registration.

citation.ref: Entry 12 as amended, read with entry 5AA of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and the proviso on renting in a personal capacity

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 1 — Charitable activities, and what a trust is still taxed on
concepts.statement: Entry 1 reaches an entity that holds registration under section 12AA or section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and it reaches only what such an entity supplies by way of charitable activities. Both limbs have to be satisfied and students routinely forget the second. Registration under the Income-tax Act qualifies the entity; it does not exempt everything the entity does. Charitable activities is a defined expression and the definition is a closed list — activities relating to public health by way of care or counselling of terminally ill persons or persons with severe physical or mental disability, of persons afflicted with HIV or AIDS, or of persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance, together with work that spreads public awareness of preventive health, of family planning, or of how HIV infection is prevented; advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga; advancement of educational programmes or skill development relating to abandoned, orphaned or homeless children, physically or mentally abused and traumatised persons, prisoners, or persons over the age of sixty-five years residing in a rural area; and preservation of environment including watershed, forests and wildlife. Anything else the trust supplies for a consideration is taxable in the ordinary way — commercial coaching, hall hire, publication sales, sponsorship. Separate entries deal with religious places and with religious ceremonies, and they have their own conditions rather than riding on this one.

citation.ref: Entry 1, read with the definition of charitable activities in paragraph 2 of the notification and section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Section 77 and section 19 of the IGST Act — Tax paid under the wrong head
concepts.statement: Getting the place of supply wrong is the commonest mistake in GST and it is the one the law is gentlest about, because the mistake costs the exchequer nothing — the money was paid, only into the wrong pocket. Under section 77(1), a supplier who treated a supply as intra-State and paid central tax with State or Union territory tax on it gets that money back, in the manner and on the conditions the rules lay down, once the supply is later held to have been inter-State. Section 77(2) adds the second half of the relief: no interest is charged on the integrated tax he must now pay. Section 19 of the IGST Act carries the identical rule the other way for a person who paid integrated tax on what turns out to be an intra-State supply. Three things follow. The correct tax has to be paid — the section forgives interest, not tax. The wrong tax is refunded rather than adjusted, so a refund claim is made and the limitation for it runs from the date the correct-head tax is paid rather than from the original payment. And the relief does not depend on the mistake being innocent in any moral sense; it depends only on the supply having been treated one way and held to be the other.

citation.ref: Sections 77(1) and 77(2), read with section 19 of the IGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 70 — Summons, and why the proceeding is a judicial one
concepts.statement: Section 70(1) lets the proper officer, while any inquiry is on foot, call in anybody whose presence he thinks necessary — to be questioned, or to hand over a document or any other article — and he does it wielding the powers a civil court has. Two words carry the weight. Any person — the power is not confined to the registered person under investigation, and reaches a supplier, a customer, a transporter, a bank official or an employee, none of whom need be suspected of anything. And inquiry — the power exists during an inquiry and does not wait for a show cause notice or an assessment. Section 70(2) then provides that every such inquiry shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of the penal provisions on giving false evidence and on intentionally insulting or interrupting a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding. That deeming is the sanction behind the summons: a statement recorded under section 70 is evidence, and an untrue one is not a compliance lapse to be met with a penalty but an offence under the general criminal law. A summons is therefore a different instrument from the inspection, search and seizure powers of section 67 — it compels a person and a document rather than entering a place, needs no reason to believe an offence has occurred, and produces sworn testimony rather than seized goods.

citation.ref: Sections 70(1) and 70(2)

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 122(1) — The penalty for a specified offence, and the floor beneath it
concepts.statement: Section 122(1) is the list of specified offences and it names twenty-one of them — supplying without an invoice, issuing an invoice without a supply, issuing an invoice using another registered person's identification number, collecting tax and failing to pay it over within three months, taking or utilising input tax credit without receiving the goods or services, obtaining a refund by fraud, falsifying records, failing to register when liable, obstructing an officer, transporting goods without the prescribed documents, and the rest. All twenty-one carry one penalty formula rather than a scale. Work out whichever of these the conduct produced — tax evaded; tax that section 51 required to be deducted and was not, or was deducted short; tax that section 52 required to be collected and was not, or was collected short; credit taken, handed on or distributed against the rules; a refund got by fraud — then set that figure against the fixed sum the sub-section names, and the higher of the two is the penalty. The fixed sum is a floor, not a cap, and not an alternative the officer may pick. Sub-section (1A) reaches the person who retains the benefit of certain of those transactions and at whose instance they are conducted, and sub-section (2) deals separately with tax short paid or not paid otherwise than by fraud, and with the same conduct where fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is present. Section 125 is the residual penalty and it applies only where no penalty is separately provided, so conduct on the section 122 list never reaches it.

citation.ref: Section 122(1), read with sections 122(1A), 122(2) and 125

concepts.subsection: Section 83 — Provisional attachment, and the year it lasts
concepts.statement: Section 83(1) lets the Commissioner, where proceedings under the specified chapters are pending and he is of the opinion that it is necessary so to do for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, by order in writing attach provisionally any property including a bank account belonging to the taxable person or to a person who retains the benefit of certain transactions. Three limits sit inside that sentence. Proceedings must actually be pending — the power is ancillary and cannot be used to open an investigation. The opinion must be formed and recorded, and in Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh the Supreme Court called the power draconian and held that the formation of the opinion must rest on tangible material bearing a live link to the need to protect revenue, not on a mechanical recital. And the attachment must be of property belonging to the person against whom the proceedings run. Section 83(2) then supplies the clock: one year on from the date the order was made, the attachment dies of its own accord. That lapse is automatic and needs no application, no order releasing it and no adjudication in the meantime. Rule 159(5) gives the affected person a separate remedy while it runs — an objection to the Commissioner within seven days that the property was not liable to attachment, with an opportunity of being heard.

citation.ref: Sections 83(1) and 83(2), read with rule 159 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2021)

concepts.section: Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
concepts.subsection: Section 85 — Selling the business, and the tax that follows it
concepts.statement: Chapter XVI attaches GST liability to people other than the person who incurred it, and section 85 is its widest provision. A taxable person who owes tax, interest or penalty and hands his business on — the whole of it or a slice of it, and it makes no difference whether the vehicle is a sale, a gift, a lease, a leave and licence arrangement, a hire or anything else at all — does not thereby put the debt behind him. He and the person taking the business over become liable together and each of them separately, either for the whole or only so far as the transfer goes, for everything owed by him down to the moment of transfer: dues fixed before that moment and left unpaid, and dues worked out long after it. Two consequences follow that buyers regularly miss. A liability quantified two years after the sale, for a period before it, still lands on the buyer — the words are whether determined before or after. And a clause in the sale agreement allocating pre-transfer taxes to the seller is enforceable between the two of them and worth nothing against the department, which may proceed against either. Where the transferee carries the business on, under his own name or under some other, he pays tax on what he supplies from the date of transfer, and if he is registered he must apply within the prescribed time to have his registration amended. Sections 87 to 90 do the same work for other events — amalgamation, dissolution of a firm, liquidation of a company and partners' liability — and section 93 for the estate of a deceased person.

citation.ref: Section 85(1) and 85(2), read with sections 87 to 90

concepts.subsection: Sections 117 and 118 — When the appeal from the Tribunal skips the High Court
concepts.statement: An appeal lies to the High Court from every order passed by the State Bench or Area Benches of the Appellate Tribunal, and one condition guards the door: the Court must be satisfied that a substantial question of law arises. The memorandum states precisely that question, the Court formulates it if satisfied one exists, and the appeal is heard on the question so formulated — the Court does not re-open the facts. It is filed within one hundred and eighty days of the order being communicated, and the Court may admit a late appeal on being satisfied there was sufficient cause. A Bench of not less than two Judges hears it and decides by majority. Then comes the exception that examiners like. The proviso to section 117(1) takes out of the High Court's reach any order of the Appellate Tribunal relating to a matter where two or more States, or a State and the Centre, have a difference of views regarding the place of supply — because such a dispute is not one State's High Court's to settle. Section 118 sends that appeal directly to the Supreme Court, and also gives a direct appeal to the Supreme Court from any order of the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal. So the route upward depends not on the amount or on the taxpayer, but on what the dispute is about.

citation.ref: Section 117(1) with its proviso and sections 117(2) to 117(5), read with section 118

concepts.subsection: Rule 86A — Blocking the credit ledger, and what blocking is not
concepts.statement: Rule 86A works on a belief that input tax credit sitting in the electronic credit ledger was got by fraud or was never eligible in the first place. Holding that belief, the Commissioner — or any officer he authorises, so long as that officer is of at least Assistant Commissioner rank — may stop a debit of the matching amount being made, whether the taxpayer wants to settle a liability with it or to ask for a refund of what is lying unused. The grounds are listed — credit on an invoice issued by a supplier found non-existent or not conducting business from the registered place, credit on an invoice without receipt of the goods or services, credit on tax not paid to the Government, credit taken by a registered person found non-existent, and credit taken without an invoice or debit note. What the rule does is narrow, and the words say so: it disallows a debit. It does not determine a liability, reverse a credit or recover anything — a demand still needs a notice and an order under section 73 or 74A, with the hearing those carry. The reasons must be recorded in writing before the order, and the courts have repeatedly struck down blocking done on a borrowed instruction rather than the officer's own belief. Sub-rule (2) lets the same officer lift the restriction once satisfied the conditions no longer exist, and sub-rule (3) ends it anyway — one year on from the day it was imposed, the block falls away whether or not anybody asks.

concepts.subsection: Rules 3 to 9 — The order the customs valuation methods must be tried in
concepts.statement: Customs valuation is a ladder and the rungs must be taken in order. Rule 3(1) says the value of imported goods shall be the transaction value adjusted under rule 10, subject to rule 12 — the power to raise doubts about the truth or accuracy of the declared value and, after telling the importer the grounds and hearing him, to reject it. Rule 3(4) then provides that if the value cannot be determined under sub-rule (1), it shall be determined by proceeding sequentially through rules 4 to 9. Rule 4 is the value of identical goods sold for export to India at or about the same time, at the same commercial level and in substantially the same quantity. Rule 5 is the same for similar goods — not identical, but with like characteristics and component materials performing the same functions. Rule 7 is deductive value: start from what the consignment, or an identical or a similar import, actually fetches per unit when sold on in India in the largest total quantity, then strip out commissions, transport, insurance and duties. Rule 8 is computed value, built up from the cost of materials and fabrication, profit and general expenses. Rule 9 is the residual method, using reasonable means consistent with the principles of the rules and the data available in India. Rule 6 holds the sequence together and grants the one permitted departure from it: rules 7 and 8 are worked in that order, unless the importer asks for them the other way round and the proper officer agrees, in which case rule 8 is taken first. Nothing else in the ladder may be skipped.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 3(4) with rule 6, read with rules 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 12

concepts.subsection: Section 26A — Import duty back on goods that were not what was ordered
concepts.statement: Section 26A is the customs answer to a bad delivery. Duty already paid on goods cleared for home consumption comes back where those goods turn out to be defective, or fail in some other way to match what the importer and his supplier had agreed the specification would be — but the section fences the relief with conditions and each of them is a possible exam point. The goods must not have been worked on, repaired or put to use once they landed. One use alone is forgiven: the use without which the defect could not have been found, or the specification could not have been tested against them. The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner as the goods that were imported. The importer must not claim drawback on them. And the goods must be exported, or the importer must relinquish his title to them and abandon them to customs, or they must be destroyed, or made commercially worthless, with the proper officer watching it done, within the period the section allows from the date of clearance, extendable on sufficient cause. The refund claim itself is filed within the further period prescribed. The section does not apply at all to perishable goods, to goods now past their shelf life or past the storage-before-use period recommended for them, or to goods against which an offence appears to have been committed under the Act or any other law. Distinguish it from section 74, which is drawback on re-export of duty-paid goods generally, and from section 27, which refunds duty paid in excess of what was due.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1) with its provisos and section 26A(3)

concepts.subsection: Social Welfare Surcharge — What it is charged on
concepts.statement: The Social Welfare Surcharge replaced the education cesses on imported goods and is levied by section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018 to finance education, health and social security. Its character decides every question asked about it: it is a surcharge on duty, not a duty on value. What the prescribed rate is applied to is the total of the duties, taxes and cesses the Central Government levies and collects under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962, together with any sum that some other statute charges on the article as an addition to a duty of customs and in the same way as one — so the assessable value never enters the computation, and where the basic customs duty is nil the surcharge on it is nil too. Three levies are expressly kept out of that base: the integrated tax charged on imports under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, the goods and services tax compensation cess under section 3(9), and the safeguard, countervailing and anti-dumping duties under sections 8B, 9 and 9A of that Act. The surcharge is collected as a duty of customs, and all the machinery provisions of the Customs Act on refunds, exemptions, interest, recovery and penalties apply to it. Because it is not the integrated tax, it is not creditable — like the basic customs duty it rides on, it is a cost.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods, read with sections 3(7) and 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

concepts.subsection: Section 7 of the FTDR Act — The Importer-Exporter Code, and who does not need one
concepts.statement: Section 7 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 says that no person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General of Foreign Trade or an officer authorised by him. It is the licence to trade across the border and the first thing an exporter obtains, before any scheme, scrip or authorisation. The code is now the Permanent Account Number of the person, issued in the format of an IEC by the DGFT on an online application, so one entity holds one code across all its branches, and the details must be updated electronically every year even where nothing has changed — an IEC not updated is liable to be deactivated. Two classes of person are outside the requirement. A Ministry or department of the Central Government or of a State Government, and other categories the policy notifies, may import and export without one. And goods imported or exported for personal use, not connected with trade, manufacture or agriculture, need no code — which is what lets a traveller bring in a personal effect and a person import equipment for a family member without registering as a trader. Import and export by categories such as notified charitable institutions are similarly relieved. The code is a permission to trade and not a benefit: holding it confers no exemption and no duty concession by itself.

citation.ref: Section 7, read with the Importer-Exporter Code provisions of the Foreign Trade Policy and the exempt categories notified under them

concepts.subsection: Local delivery — out of entry 18 and into section 9(5)
concepts.statement: Two notifications of 17 September 2025, both effective 22 September 2025, moved local delivery in one step. Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) added an Explanation to entry 18 of the exemption notification: the exemption for transportation of goods does not apply to local delivery services provided by an electronic commerce operator, or through one. Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) then added local delivery to the services notified under section 9(5), so the operator pays the tax as if it were the supplier — except where the person supplying through the operator is himself liable for registration under section 22(1), in which case that supplier pays in the ordinary way. Read together: the first instrument decides that the service is taxable at all, and the second decides whose liability it is. A delivery rider below the registration threshold delivering through a platform is the case both were written for. The same day's exemption notification also rewrote what a goods transport agency is, putting outside that definition an operator that carries out local delivery and an operator through whom it is carried out, so a consignment note does not turn a platform into a goods transport agency.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025, read with entry 18 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Omnibus under section 9(5) — and the company that falls out of it
concepts.statement: Passenger transport by omnibus was notified under section 9(5) with effect from 22 September 2025, and it carries an exception the other passenger-transport entry does not. Where the person supplying the omnibus service through the electronic commerce operator is a company, the tax is not payable by the operator: the company pays it itself. Every other omnibus supplier through a platform leaves the liability with the operator. The radio-taxi entry beside it is drawn the other way — it covers a motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle or any other motor vehicle and expressly excludes an omnibus, so the two entries divide the vehicles between them rather than overlapping. The test is therefore two questions in order: which vehicle, and then, if it is an omnibus, is the supplier a company.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 16 — Input tax credit conditions
concepts.statement: Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

citation.ref: Section 16(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(3) — Reverse charge
concepts.statement: For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

citation.ref: Section 9(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 22 — Registration
concepts.statement: Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

citation.ref: Section 22

concepts.subsection: Section 10 — Composition levy
concepts.statement: A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation
concepts.statement: Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

citation.ref: Section 16(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where goods move as part of the supply, the place of supply is wherever that movement ends for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Time of supply — advances
concepts.statement: An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

citation.ref: Section 12 and 13, with Notification 66/2017-CT

concepts.subsection: Section 15 — Value of supply
concepts.statement: A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Interest on delayed payment
concepts.statement: Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143 — Job work
concepts.statement: Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

citation.ref: Section 143(3) and 143(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Zero-rated supply
concepts.statement: Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

citation.ref: Section 16

concepts.subsection: Rule 138 — E-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

citation.ref: Rule 138

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Schedule I — Supply without consideration
concepts.statement: Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

citation.ref: Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

citation.ref: Schedule III

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Refunds
concepts.statement: A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

citation.ref: Section 54(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 10(2A) — Composition for service providers
concepts.statement: A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A)

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5) — Blocked credits
concepts.statement: Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs — Duty drawback on re-export
concepts.statement: Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

citation.ref: Section 74

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
concepts.statement: Services directly relating to immovable property — architects, surveyors, engineers, hotel accommodation, letting, construction-linked services — are supplied where the property sits, whatever the locations of supplier and recipient. The property anchors the tax, and if it lies outside India the default recipient-location rule takes over.

citation.ref: Section 12(3)

concepts.subsection: Schedule II — Works contract as a service
concepts.statement: A works contract — a contract for building, construction, fabrication or similar work on immovable property involving transfer of property in goods — is deemed wholly a supply of services by Schedule II. One levy, one classification: the old VAT-plus-service-tax split of a single contract is gone, and works contract input credit has its own restrictions in section 17(5).

citation.ref: Schedule II, para 6(a)

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation — Transaction value
concepts.statement: Customs duty is assessed on transaction value — the price actually paid or payable where goods are sold for export into India — plus prescribed additions, at the time and place of importation. A relationship between buyer and seller displaces that price only where it influenced it; a related-party price the importer shows to be at arm's length stands.

citation.ref: Section 14

concepts.subsection: Section 15(2) — Inclusions in value
concepts.statement: The value of supply includes taxes other than GST itself, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid, incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier, interest or penalty for delayed payment of consideration, and subsidies directly linked to price from anyone other than the Government. Each inclusion widens the base beyond the bare price.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)

concepts.subsection: IGST — Export of services definition
concepts.statement: A service is exported only when all five conditions hold: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and supplier and recipient not merely two establishments of one person. Failing any one, the supply is not an export and zero-rating is lost.

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Section 34 — Credit and debit notes
concepts.statement: A supplier who has charged too much tax — goods returned, deficient supply, price revised down — issues a credit note and reduces output liability, but only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of supply (or the annual return, if earlier), and only if the incidence of tax has not been passed to someone who bears it. A commercial credit note without GST can issue any time, adjusting price but not tax.

citation.ref: Section 34(2)

concepts.subsection: IGST on imported goods
concepts.statement: Import of goods is taxed as inter-State supply, but the IGST is levied and collected as customs duty — under the Customs Tariff Act, on the value determined under the Customs Act at the point of importation, together with basic customs duty. The importer generally takes credit of the IGST so paid; basic customs duty is never creditable.

citation.ref: Section 5(1) proviso

concepts.subsection: Section 25 — Distinct persons
concepts.statement: Registrations of one entity in different States are distinct persons, and supplies between them — stock transfers, services of one office to another — are taxable supplies even without consideration, valued under the rules with full input credit typically flowing. One legal person, several taxable persons: the design keeps each State's revenue whole.

citation.ref: Section 25(4) with Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Customs — Pilferage and remission
concepts.statement: Goods pilfered after unloading but before clearance attract no duty from the importer — unless restored — and the custodian pays instead; goods lost or destroyed before clearance earn remission on the Assistant Commissioner's satisfaction, and goods relinquished before clearance drop the duty too. Pilferage is automatic by the section's operation; remission must be sought and shown.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 23

concepts.subsection: E-commerce — TCS and section 9(5)
concepts.statement: An e-commerce operator collects tax at source on the net value of supplies made through it by others — a collection mechanism, not a levy. For the notified services section 9(5) goes further: the operator is liable to pay the tax as if it were the supplier, and the actual supplier's registration position changes accordingly. TCS and 9(5) never apply to the same supply. Six categories are notified — passenger transport by radio-taxi and similar motor vehicles; passenger transport by omnibus, unless the supplier through the operator is a company, in which case the company pays; accommodation; housekeeping; restaurant service other than at specified premises; and local delivery. Accommodation, housekeeping and local delivery each fall out of section 9(5) where the supplier through the operator is itself liable for registration under section 22(1).

citation.ref: Sections 52 and 9(5), read with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended

concepts.subsection: Exempt, nil-rated, non-taxable and zero-rated
concepts.statement: Four different fates: a nil-rated supply is taxable at zero in the tariff; an exempt supply is freed by notification and includes nil-rated and non-taxable supplies for definition purposes; a non-taxable supply is outside the levy itself, like alcohol for human consumption; zero-rated means exports and SEZ supplies — taxable in principle, taxed at zero, with input credit preserved. Only zero-rating keeps the credit; exemption breaks the credit chain.

citation.ref: Sections 2(47), 2(78) and IGST 16

concepts.subsection: Advance ruling — binding scope
concepts.statement: An advance ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and the jurisdictional officers in respect of that applicant — not other taxpayers, however identical their facts, and not other States' authorities. It holds unless law, facts or circumstances change, and a ruling obtained by fraud or suppression is void from the start. Other taxpayers may read it as persuasive weather, never as shelter.

citation.ref: Section 103

concepts.subsection: Section 51 — Tax deduction at source
concepts.statement: Government departments, local authorities and notified entities deduct tax at source at two per cent from payments to suppliers where a contract's taxable value exceeds two and a half lakh rupees — the deduction tested contract-wise, on value excluding GST. No deduction where the supplier's State and the place of supply differ from the recipient's State. The deductee takes the amount as cash ledger credit, not as input tax.

citation.ref: Section 51

concepts.subsection: Section 54(3) — Refund of unutilised input tax credit
concepts.statement: Accumulated input tax credit is refundable in exactly two cases: zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and the inverted duty structure — input tax rates exceeding output rates. Credit piling up because sales are slow, or because outputs are exempt, earns no refund; the inverted-structure refund runs on the rule's formula and excludes input services from the computation.

citation.ref: Section 54(3)

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: Customs — Date for rate of duty
concepts.statement: The rate of duty and tariff valuation for imports is taken on the date of filing the bill of entry for home consumption — or, for warehoused goods, the date of the ex-bond bill of entry when the goods leave the warehouse for home consumption. A rate change while goods sit in bond therefore lands on the importer; the vessel's arrival date matters only where the bill was filed in advance.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 24 — Compulsory registration
concepts.statement: Certain persons register regardless of turnover: inter-State taxable suppliers of goods, persons liable under reverse charge, casual taxable persons with no fixed place in the State, non-resident taxable persons, e-commerce operators, TDS deductors, and agents supplying for others. The threshold exemption belongs to section 22; section 24's list overrides it — though inter-State suppliers of services enjoy a notified threshold relaxation the goods side never got.

citation.ref: Section 24

concepts.subsection: Foreign trade policy — EPCG
concepts.statement: The Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme imports capital goods at zero customs duty against an export obligation of six times the duty saved, to be discharged over six years from authorisation — with the goods installed and put to use, and the obligation over and above the average of past exports. Default surrenders proportionate duty with interest; the scheme buys machinery cheap with a promise, and the promise is enforced.

citation.ref: EPCG scheme (export obligation 6x duty saved in 6 years)

concepts.subsection: IGST — Bill-to-ship-to supplies
concepts.statement: Where goods are delivered to one person on the instruction of another, the law sees two supplies: supplier to the instructing buyer, and instructing buyer to the actual recipient — with the first leg's place of supply deemed to be the instructing buyer's principal place of business, wherever the goods physically went. Tax type on each leg follows its own deemed geography, and each leg carries its own invoice.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(b)

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: Customs — General rules of interpretation
concepts.statement: Tariff classification walks the General Interpretative Rules in order: headings and their notes first; incomplete articles classify as complete if they have the essential character; mixtures and composites classify by the material giving essential character; and only when goods remain equally classifiable under two headings does the later heading win. The specific description always beats the general one before any tie-breaker is reached.

citation.ref: General Rules for Interpretation 1-4

concepts.subsection: Rule 32(5) — Margin scheme for second-hand goods
concepts.statement: A dealer in second-hand goods, selling them as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, may pay GST only on the margin — selling price less purchase price, with a negative margin ignored — provided no input tax credit was taken on the purchase. Buying from unregistered consumers is the scheme's habitat; take credit on the inward side and the whole selling price becomes taxable.

citation.ref: Rule 32(5)

concepts.subsection: Rule 33 — Pure agent
concepts.statement: Costs a supplier incurs as a pure agent of the recipient stay out of the value of supply when every condition holds: the supplier contracts as the recipient's authorised agent for that payment, the recipient alone uses what was procured, the actual amount is separately indicated on the invoice and recovered without markup, and it is in addition to the supplier's own services. Mark it up, or bundle it, and the exclusion is gone.

citation.ref: Rule 33

concepts.subsection: Section 8 — Composite and mixed supplies
concepts.statement: A composite supply bundles naturally — two or more taxable supplies ordinarily supplied together with one principal supply — and takes the principal supply's rate. A mixed supply is an artificial bundle for a single price whose parts could be sold separately, and it takes the highest rate among them. Natural bundling is tested by trade practice: what buyers expect to come together.

citation.ref: Sections 2(30), 2(74) and 8

concepts.subsection: Actionable claims and specified activities
concepts.statement: Actionable claims are goods by definition, yet Schedule III keeps them outside GST — except the specified ones: lottery, betting, gambling, and since the 2023 amendments, online money gaming, which are taxable, valued on their own rules. An unsecured debt assigned, an insurance claim transferred — outside the levy; a lottery ticket sold — squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Schedule III with section 2(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 50(3) — Interest on wrongly availed credit
concepts.statement: Interest on wrongly availed input tax credit runs only where the credit is also utilised — credit that sat unused in the electronic credit ledger until reversal costs nothing. The same mercy governs delayed payment interest under section 50(1): where the return is late but the tax was paid by balance in the cash ledger, interest applies on the portion paid through cash late, computed on the net cash liability. Both rules arrived as retrospective corrections of harsher readings.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

concepts.subsection: Customs refunds — unjust enrichment
concepts.statement: A customs duty refund is paid to the claimant only on proof that the duty's incidence was not passed on to any other person; otherwise the refund is sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund. The presumption runs against the claimant — passing on is assumed until displaced by evidence such as a chartered accountant's certificate and unchanged prices. Captive consumption and duty paid under protest walk the same test.

citation.ref: Section 27

concepts.subsection: Import of services — reverse charge
concepts.statement: Services imported for business bear IGST in the recipient's hands under reverse charge — the foreign supplier is beyond the levy's practical reach, so the Indian recipient self-assesses, pays in cash, and takes credit where eligible. Import by an individual for personal purposes stays outside as not being in the course of business — except OIDAR services, which are taxed even to consumers with the foreign supplier itself required to register.

citation.ref: Section 5(3) with 2(11)

concepts.subsection: OIDAR services
concepts.statement: Online information and database access or retrieval services — streaming, cloud storage, e-books, online advertising, essentially automated digital delivery with minimal human intervention — are taxed in India even when supplied to unregistered consumers. The foreign supplier (or its appointed person) registers under the simplified scheme and pays; for registered business recipients, ordinary reverse charge applies instead. The 2023 amendments deleted the minimal-human-intervention escape arguments by tightening the definition.

citation.ref: Section 2(17) and 14

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: E-invoicing
concepts.statement: Registered persons with aggregate annual turnover above five crore rupees (in any year from 2017-18) must report B2B invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and QR code — without which the invoice is not a valid invoice at all. B2C supplies, and notified exclusions like banks, insurers, GTAs and passenger transporters, stay outside. The e-invoice auto-populates GSTR-1 and travels with the e-way bill system.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) (₹5 crore threshold from 1 August 2023)

concepts.subsection: FTP — Advance authorisation
concepts.statement: Advance authorisation imports inputs duty-free for physical incorporation in export products, on actual user condition — the inputs and the resulting goods cannot be sold domestically until the export obligation is discharged. The scheme demands minimum value addition (generally fifteen per cent) and export within the specified period, with inputs quantified by standard input-output norms or self-declaration. It frees inputs; EPCG frees capital goods — parallel schemes, different subject matter.

citation.ref: Advance Authorisation scheme

concepts.subsection: Goods transport agencies — the two routes
concepts.statement: A GTA's services are taxed one of two ways: reverse charge at five per cent paid by the specified recipient with the GTA taking no input credit, or forward charge by the GTA's own annual declared option — at five per cent without credit or eighteen per cent with full credit. The credit-preserving rate was twelve per cent until 21 September 2025 and became eighteen per cent on 22 September 2025, when the twelve per cent slab went. Services to unregistered persons largely ride exemptions. The declaration binds for the financial year; recipients must know which regime their transporter elected, since the liability moves with it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with the notified GTA options, the forward-charge rate with credit raised to eighteen per cent by Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — concurrent audit, its appointment and its reporting
concepts.statement: Concurrent audit is the examination of a bank's transactions as they happen or as near to it as possible, and it is treated as part of the bank's early warning system rather than as a second statutory audit. Four things about it are examinable and none of them is about technique. Its head of internal audit settles what it covers — which lines of business, which branches — and that settlement stands only once the Audit Committee of the Board has approved it beforehand. Risk sensitive areas thrown up by the bank's own business model must be brought inside it. Who does it is the bank's choice between its own officials and external auditors; where its own officials are used they must be experienced, well trained and sufficiently senior, and they must be independent of the branch being audited. How long they may do it is fixed at two levels: the Audit Committee of the Board decides the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors, which generally is not more than five years on a continuous basis with the bank, and no concurrent auditor may continue with a branch or business unit for more than three years. And where the findings go is fixed too — major deficiencies go at once to the branch and the controlling office in a special note, a quarterly review of key features goes before the Audit Committee of the Board along with zone-wise reporting and an annual appraisal of the system, minor irregularities are rectified in a timely manner while serious ones go to the controlling or head offices for immediate action, and a fraudulent transaction is reported immediately to the Inspection and Audit Department at head office, to the Chief Vigilance Officer and to the branch managers concerned, unless the branch manager is himself involved. Where an external firm is appointed and serious acts of omission or commission are noticed in its working, the appointment may be cancelled and the fact reported to the Reserve Bank and to the Institute. Terms of appointment and remuneration of external firms are fixed by the Audit Committee of the Board, and the bank reviews the effectiveness of the whole system once a year.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — concurrent audit: the scope left to the head of internal audit with the prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board, the choice between the bank's own officials and external auditors, the maximum tenure of five years with the bank and three years with a branch or business unit, the quarterly review and zone-wise reporting to the Audit Committee, and the immediate reporting of fraudulent transactions to the Inspection and Audit Department, the Chief Vigilance Officer and the branch managers concerned

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 200 — audit risk and its three components
concepts.statement: Audit risk names the danger that the auditor signs off wrongly — an unmodified opinion given on statements that are in fact materially misstated — and it is the product of three separate risks. Inherent risk is the susceptibility of an assertion to a misstatement that could be material, individually or when aggregated with others, assuming there are no related controls; it is addressed both at the financial statement level and at the assertion level. Control risk is the risk that the entity's system of internal control will not prevent, or detect and correct on a timely basis, a misstatement that could be material, and some control risk will always exist because every system of internal control has inherent limitations. Detection risk is the risk that the auditor will not detect a misstatement that exists, and it is the only one of the three the auditor controls; it arises from selecting an inappropriate audit procedure, from misapplying an appropriate one, and from misinterpreting the results of one. The relationships are fixed. Audit risk is inherent risk multiplied by control risk multiplied by detection risk. Inherent risk and control risk together are the risk of material misstatement, which is the risk that the statements are misstated before the audit begins and which exists independently of the audit. Audit risk is therefore the risk of material misstatement multiplied by detection risk, and the acceptable level of detection risk for a given level of audit risk bears an inverse relationship to the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level — the higher the assessed risk, the less detection risk the auditor may accept and the more persuasive the evidence he must obtain. Audit materiality is also inversely related to audit risk.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — audit risk as the product of inherent risk, control risk and detection risk, the risk of material misstatement as inherent risk multiplied by control risk, the inverse relationship between the combined inherent and control risk and detection risk, and the inverse relationship between audit materiality and audit risk

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — assertions and the two levels at which risk is assessed
concepts.statement: Assertions are the representations by management, explicit or otherwise, that are embodied in the financial statements, and the auditor uses them to consider the different types of potential misstatement that may occur. They fall into three categories and the names are not interchangeable. About classes of transactions and events for the period under audit there are five — occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut-off and classification. About account balances at the period end there are four — existence, rights and obligations, completeness, and valuation and allocation. About presentation and disclosure there are four — occurrence and rights and obligations, completeness, classification and understandability, and accuracy and valuation. Separately, risk is assessed at two levels, and the difference decides what the auditor does about it. A risk at the overall financial statement level relates pervasively to the statements as a whole and potentially affects many assertions, so it is answered by an overall response rather than by a procedure on one balance; an incompetent chief accountant is the standard example, because the errors that follow will not be confined to one balance or to one assertion. A risk at the assertion level is identified with a particular class of transactions, account balance or disclosure, and an assessment is made for each individual assertion — the valuation of payables may be a low risk in the same audit in which the valuation of obsolescent inventory is a high one.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the three categories of assertions used by the auditor and the assertions named in each, and the difference between assessing the risks of material misstatement at the overall financial statement level and at the assertion level

concepts.subsection: SA 300 — the audit programme, how it is drawn up and when it is altered
concepts.statement: The audit programme is the document that allocates work to the members of the engagement team. It contains the audit objectives for each area and enough detail to serve both as a set of instructions to the assistants and as a means of controlling the proper execution of the work, and spelling out the objective for each area is what links the procedures to a purpose. Six matters are considered in formulating it: the nature of the business the organisation is engaged in, the overall plan, the system of internal control and the accounting procedures, the size of the organisation and the structure of its management, information about the organisation of the business, and the accounting and management policies followed. The overall plan governs — if drawing the programme makes a divergence from the overall plan necessary, the plan is modified first and only then is the specific matter taken into the programme. On a first appointment the programme is developed in three stages: a broad outline is drawn up to begin with; the detail is then filled in once the accounting and internal procedures have been looked over, with whatever control weaknesses that review turned up deciding what that detail has to be; and when the detailed checking is finished the extent of the special first-time and opening balance procedures is settled. At each subsequent engagement the programme is reviewed and modified on account of the experience gained during previous audits, important changes in the business, and the evaluation of internal control made for the current year. Four circumstances in particular force an alteration during the audit: the volume of turnover has substantially increased beyond what the procedures were designed for, or there have been significant changes in the accounting organisation, procedures or personnel; it is discovered that the internal control procedures were not as effective as assumed when the programme was framed; there has been an extraordinary increase in book debts or in the value of stocks compared with the previous year; and a suspicion has arisen, or information has been received, that assets have been misappropriated.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — formulating an audit programme and the matters to be considered, the three stages in which a programme is developed on a first appointment, the grounds on which it is reviewed and modified at each subsequent engagement, and the circumstances in which it has to be suitably altered during the audit

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 265 — the letter of weakness and what it does not excuse
concepts.statement: The letter of weakness, also called the management letter, is how the auditor communicates deficiencies in internal control in writing. Four things are said about it and they pull in different directions. It lists the areas of weakness in the system and offers suggestions for improvement. It must clearly indicate that it discusses only the weaknesses that came to the auditor's attention as a result of his audit, and that his examination was not designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for management's own purposes. It serves as a reference document management can use to revise the system and to insist on its strict implementation. And should a weak control later let through a large defalcation, or some comparable loss, the letter can cut down what the auditor is answerable for at law — in one reported case an auditor was acquitted of a charge of negligence over an employee's fraud precisely because he had already informed the client about the unsatisfactory state of specific areas and had suggested improvements that the management did not act upon. But the letter is not a substitute for the report. Having put the system's weaknesses to management in writing, the auditor still owes a qualification in the report itself over any shortcoming in the accounts that was left uncorrected to his satisfaction, judged on how material those weaknesses are and what they do.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the letter of weakness: what it lists, the statement it must carry that it discusses only weaknesses noticed during the audit and that the examination was not designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for management, its value as a reference document and in minimising legal liability, and the rule that writing it does not absolve the auditor from qualifying the report where the defects are uncorrected

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — the additional procedures and the cash flow forecast
concepts.statement: Once something has turned up that throws real doubt over whether the entity can carry on as a going concern, the auditor has to gather sufficient appropriate audit evidence on whether a material uncertainty exists, and he gathers it by running extra procedures and by weighing what might mitigate the doubt. The examinable list runs like this. He takes the cash flow, profit and other forecasts and talks them through with management. He does the same with whatever interim accounts the entity has published most recently. He goes to the loan documents to see whether a covenant has already been broken. He reads what shareholders, those charged with governance and the standing committees minuted, hunting for any mention of trouble raising money. He asks the entity's lawyers what litigation and claims are outstanding and whether management's view of how they will end, and of what they will cost, holds up. Where a related party or an outsider has promised to fund the entity or to keep funding it, he checks that the promise is real, lawful and capable of being enforced, and he sizes up whether that party could actually find the money. He runs procedures over events after the reporting date that either soften the doubt or bear on the ability to carry on. He checks that borrowing lines exist, on what terms and in what amount. Where management has not made its assessment at all, he asks for one. And he tests what management intends to do next — whether it would improve matters if it came off, and whether it can be done at all in the circumstances. Where the entity has prepared a cash flow forecast and the analysis of that forecast is a significant factor in considering the future outcome, the auditor does two specific things — he asks how dependable the forecast's input data is, given the way it was produced, and he asks whether the assumptions the forecast rests on are adequately supported. Where management is unwilling to make or to extend its assessment, the auditor considers the implications for his report. And where approval of the financial statements is delayed, he inquires into the reasons and, if he believes the delay relates to the going concern events or conditions, performs the additional procedures and considers the effect on his conclusion.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — the additional audit procedures where events or conditions casting significant doubt on the ability to continue as a going concern have been identified, the two things done where a cash flow forecast has been prepared, the position where management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment, and the inquiry into a delay in the approval of the financial statements

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — acceptance as principal auditor and the other auditor's competence
concepts.statement: Before accepting the work as principal auditor, the auditor considers four matters: the materiality of the portion of the financial information which he himself audits; his own degree of knowledge regarding the business of the components; the risk of material misstatement in the financial information of the components audited by the other auditors; and the performance of the additional procedures the Standard sets out regarding those components, which may result in his having significant participation in that audit. Two further points govern the relationship afterwards. Where a statute gives him the right to go to a component and inspect its books and records, and that component already has an auditor of its own, he may as a rule lean on that auditor's work instead of going, unless something out of the ordinary makes the visit or the inspection essential. And where the auditor he plans to lean on does not belong to the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, he must first weigh that auditor's professional competence against what this particular assignment demands — such a person may not be a qualified auditor at all, which happens where a component sits in a country whose law allows it. The documentation runs the same way: the principal auditor documents the components audited by other auditors, the procedures performed and the conclusions reached, and the results of his discussions and of his review of the written summary of the other auditor's procedures. Reasons for limiting those procedures, though, need not be documented at all where he already holds sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the other auditor's practice runs on acceptable quality control policies and procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — acceptance as principal auditor and the four matters considered, the right to visit and examine the books of a component and the entitlement to rely on the component's auditor absent special circumstances, the consideration of the professional competence of an other auditor who is not a member of the Institute, and the documentation requirement with its exception where quality control compliance has been established

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — deciding whether an auditor's expert is needed at all
concepts.statement: SA 620's first question is not how to use an expert but whether to use one at all. Knowing little about some field outside accounting and auditing does not by itself force the auditor to bring in an auditor's expert: he may still pick up enough of that field to carry the audit himself. That grounding can come from having audited other entities where the same expertise mattered, from courses or other professional development in the subject, or from talking to auditors who have done engagements like it. Such a discussion is a different thing from consultation with an auditor's expert about a specific set of circumstances on the engagement, where the expert is given all the relevant facts so that he can give informed advice on the particular matter. Where he does conclude that one is needed, four things weigh on the decision: whether management itself leaned on a management's expert when the statements were drawn up; how significant the matter is and how complex it gets; what risks of material misstatement it carries; and what procedures those risks will call for, set beside whatever other sources of audit evidence are open to him. An expert's help may be wanted at any of five points: understanding the entity and its internal control; picking out the risks of material misstatement and sizing them up; settling on overall responses at the financial statement level and then carrying them out; building and running further audit procedures at the assertion level; and judging whether the evidence gathered is sufficient and appropriate. How much the auditor does over the expert's work, when, and how far, turns on what kind of matter it is, what risk of material misstatement it carries, how much the audit as a whole rests on that expert's contribution, how well he knows that expert's earlier work from having used it, and whether the expert falls inside the firm's own quality control policies and procedures. Four things in particular call for procedures that differ or go further than they otherwise would: the work relates to a significant matter involving subjective and complex judgments; the auditor has not previously used that expert and has no prior knowledge of his competence, capabilities and objectivity; the expert is performing procedures integral to the audit rather than being consulted for advice on an individual matter; and the expert is an external expert and is therefore not subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — determining the need for an auditor's expert, the ways in which an auditor who is not an expert may obtain a sufficient understanding of the field without one, the considerations when deciding whether to use an expert, the matters governing the nature, timing and extent of the auditor's procedures, and the four factors suggesting more extensive procedures

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — a report whose wording is prescribed, and a report under two sets of standards
concepts.statement: Two situations take the auditor's report out of the layout SA 700 (Revised) itself sets out, and in both the question is the same: may the report still say the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing? Take the first. An entity's own law or regulation may fix the report's layout, or its wording, word for word. Such a report keeps its reference to the Standards on Auditing only where thirteen elements are all present in it as a floor. Counting them off: a title; an addressee, settled by what the engagement's circumstances require; an Opinion section, which both expresses the opinion and names the reporting framework the statements were drawn up under; a line saying which audited statements are meant; an independence statement, which also records that the auditor's remaining ethical duties were discharged and which points to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI; a section meeting SA 570's reporting requirements, and not cutting across them, where that standard bites; a Basis for Qualified or Adverse Opinion section, where there is one; a section carrying whatever SA 701 calls for, or whatever extra detail the law demands about the audit, so long as it sits consistently with the standard; management's responsibilities, described, and beside them the naming of whoever oversees how financial reporting gets done; a pointer to the Standards on Auditing and to the law or regulation, with the auditor's own responsibilities described; the signature; where it was signed; and when. What is not on the list is as examinable as what is: the Other Information section, the location of the description of the auditor's responsibilities and the other reporting responsibilities section are all absent from it. The second situation is an audit run under the Standards on Auditing and, at the same time, under the International Standards on Auditing or another jurisdiction's auditing standards. Both may be named only where the two bodies of requirement do not collide — no collision that would push the auditor to a different opinion, and none that would cost the report an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph the Standards on Auditing demand in the circumstances — and only where those same thirteen elements are, again, all present. A report naming both identifies them clearly, the other standards' jurisdiction of origin included.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): an auditor's report prescribed by law or regulation may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it carries the thirteen listed minimum elements, and a report on an audit conducted in accordance with both the Standards on Auditing and the International Standards on Auditing or the standards of another jurisdiction may refer to both only where no conflict would lead the auditor to a different opinion or to omitting a required Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — supplementary information presented with the financial statements
concepts.statement: Information not required by the applicable financial reporting framework is often printed alongside the audited financial statements, and SA 700 (Revised) makes the auditor decide whether his opinion covers it. He evaluates whether, in his professional judgement, the supplementary information is nevertheless an integral part of the financial statements because of its nature or because of how it is presented. Where it is an integral part, it shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, and no label saying otherwise changes that. Where it is not an integral part, he evaluates whether it is presented in a way that sufficiently and clearly differentiates it from the audited financial statements; if it is not, he asks management to change how the unaudited supplementary information is presented, and if management refuses he identifies the unaudited supplementary information and explains in his report that it has not been audited. The module's two examples are the ones to hold. First, a note sitting inside the financial statements that explains, or reconciles, how far those statements line up with a second reporting framework: that note may be supplementary information which cannot be told apart from them clearly, and on the same reasoning the opinion reaches any note or schedule the statements themselves cross-reference. Second, an extra profit and loss account breaking out particular heads of expenditure, set out as its own schedule and bound in as an appendix: that one may be supplementary information which can be told apart clearly.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): supplementary information not required by the applicable financial reporting framework that is an integral part of the financial statements by its nature or by how it is presented shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, and where it is not an integral part but is not sufficiently and clearly differentiated the auditor asks management to change the presentation and, on refusal, identifies it and explains in his report that it has not been audited

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — comparative financial statements, and an opinion that has changed
concepts.statement: SA 710 offers two approaches and the reporting consequences are opposite. Where corresponding figures are used, only the current period is spoken to by the opinion on the statements.
