Where comparative financial statements are used, every period put on show is one the opinion speaks to, and that is what makes the prior period live again. Two rules follow from it. When reporting on the current period's audit, if the auditor's opinion on the prior period financial statements differs from the opinion he previously expressed on them, he shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph in his report — the changed opinion goes in the opinion, the reasons for the change go in the paragraph. And if he concludes that a material misstatement is present in previously audited figures on which a predecessor auditor reported, he shall report it to the appropriate level of management and request that the predecessor auditor be informed; if the prior period statements are then amended and the predecessor auditor agrees to issue a new report on them, the auditor shall report only on the current period. The treatment common to both approaches is unchanged: where the prior period was audited by a predecessor auditor and the auditor is permitted to refer to that report, he states the fact, the type of opinion the predecessor expressed and the date of that report; where the prior period was not audited at all, he says so, and saying so does not relieve him of obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the opening balances contain no misstatement materially affecting the current period.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 710: with comparative financial statements the auditor's opinion refers to each period presented; where the opinion on the prior period differs from the opinion previously expressed the substantive reasons are disclosed in an Other Matter paragraph; and where a material misstatement is found in previously audited figures the auditor reports it to management and requests that the predecessor auditor be informed, reporting only on the current period if the prior statements are amended and the predecessor issues a new report

concepts.subsection: SA 720 (Revised) — the contents of the Other Information section
concepts.statement: Whether the Other Information section appears at all is one question; what goes inside it is another, and SA 720 (Revised) fixes five things. One: the section says management owns the other information. Two: it identifies what other information the auditor had in hand before his report was dated and — where the audited entity is a listed one — what he expects will reach him once it has been dated. Three: it says the opinion stops short of the other information, so no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion of any kind is being given on it, or will be. Four: it sets out what the standard makes the auditor do with the other information — read it, weigh it, report on it. Five: where other information did reach him ahead of the report's date, the section either records that nothing arises or, if he has settled that a material misstatement in the other information stands uncorrected, spells that misstatement out. A qualified or adverse opinion under SA 705 (Revised) pulls on the third of these: the auditor weighs what the matter behind the modification means for that statement. And where the reference to other information must follow a layout, or a wording, that law or regulation lays down, three things are the floor for a report that still names the Standards on Auditing — what other information reached the auditor before his report was dated, what his duties over it were, and, said outright, what came of the work he did on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 720 (Revised): the five contents of the Other Information section, and the three elements a report must carry at a minimum where law or regulation prescribes the layout or wording of the reference to other information

concepts.subsection: SA 800 — planning a special purpose audit, and describing the framework in the report
concepts.statement: Between accepting a special purpose engagement and writing the alert, SA 800 makes three adjustments that are routinely missed. On materiality: SA 320 ordinarily pitches what counts as material at the financial information a whole group of users has in common, and a special purpose audit pitches it instead at what the intended users need. Management may also have settled with those intended users on a figure beneath which misstatements thrown up over the course of the audit are left uncorrected and unadjusted; that arrangement leaves the auditor's own duty untouched, and he still fixes materiality under SA 320 so that he can plan and perform the audit. On communication: SA 260 (Revised) has the auditor work out which people inside the entity's governance structure are the right ones to talk to, and where a complete set of general purpose financial statements is prepared as well, whoever oversees the special purpose set need not be the same body charged with governance that oversees the general purpose one. On the report: it sets out why the statements were drawn up and, where that is needed, who they were drawn up for, or else sends the reader to a note carrying the same thing; and where management could have picked between frameworks, the passage on management's responsibility also carries its responsibility for settling that the framework picked is acceptable in the circumstances. Where the auditor also considers it appropriate to indicate that his report is intended solely for the specific users, the paragraph alerting readers may be expanded to include those other matters and the heading modified accordingly.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 800: materiality judgements based on the financial information needs of the intended users and an agreed correction threshold that does not relieve the auditor of determining materiality under SA 320; the persons responsible for oversight of the special purpose financial statements who may not be those charged with governance for the general purpose statements; the report describing the purpose and the intended users and management's responsibility for determining the framework is acceptable; and the alerting paragraph expanded, with the heading modified, to restrict distribution or use

concepts.subsection: SA 805 — accepting and planning an audit of a single financial statement or a specific element
concepts.statement: SA 805 asks a question before it asks anything else: is an audit of this in accordance with the Standards on Auditing practicable at all? Under SA 200 every SA bearing on the audit binds the auditor, and it binds him whether or not the complete set of the entity's financial statements is his engagement too — so where the complete set is not his, he settles first whether auditing the one statement, or the one element, to the SAs can be done at all. It may not be, and the standard says why. An auditor who takes the complete set as well knows the entity, its surroundings and its internal control in a way this auditor commonly does not. He holds no evidence bearing on how good the accounting records, or any other accounting information, are in general — the sort an audit of the whole set throws off — so he may want more evidence to back up whatever the accounting records gave him. And on a specific element, some SAs call for work out of all proportion to the element in front of him. Where practicability looks doubtful, the conversation to have with management is whether some other kind of engagement would sit better. Acceptability of the financial reporting framework is decided on the same narrow ground: does applying it end in a presentation whose disclosures are enough for the intended users to make sense of what the statement, or the element, is telling them, and of what material transactions and events did to it? In planning and performing the audit he adapts all relevant SAs. Where he audits the element alongside the complete set he may use audit evidence obtained in that audit, but the SAs still have him plan and perform the element's audit so as to reach sufficient appropriate audit evidence to rest its opinion on. Because the statements and many of the elements, including their notes, are interrelated, he may not be able to consider the element in isolation and may need to perform procedures on the interrelated items. And the materiality determined for the element may be lower than that for the complete set, which affects the nature, timing and extent of the procedures and the evaluation of uncorrected misstatements.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 805: determining whether an audit in accordance with the SAs is practicable where the auditor is not also engaged on the complete set, the acceptability of the framework turning on adequate disclosures to the intended users, the use of evidence from the audit of the complete set without displacing the requirement to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the element, the interrelated items, and materiality for the element which may be lower than for the complete set

concepts.subsection: SA 810 — the report on summary financial statements, its date, and auditor association
concepts.statement: The report on summary financial statements is short and almost every line of it is prescribed. Its introductory paragraph names the summary financial statements being reported on, each statement by its own title; names the audited financial statements; and points to the auditor's report on those, giving its date and, where nothing in it was modified and it carried neither an Emphasis of Matter nor an Other Matter paragraph, saying that the opinion expressed was unmodified. Two further statements belong there. Should the summary's report bear the later date of the two, it says that events arising after the audited statements' report was dated show up in neither set of figures. And it says the summary leaves out disclosures the reporting framework behind the audited statements calls for, so nobody should treat a reading of the summary as standing in for a reading of the audited statements. The addressee gets its own rule. Where the summary is addressed to somebody other than whoever the report on the audited statements was addressed to, the auditor weighs whether that different addressee is appropriate, looking at what the engagement's terms say, at what sort of entity this is, and at what the summary is for. The report is dated no earlier than the later of two dates — the date the auditor got hold of enough appropriate evidence to rest his opinion on, which takes in evidence that the summary was prepared and that responsibility for it has been asserted by whoever holds the recognised authority, and the date the audited statements' own report carries. Association is the last requirement and it works in two directions. Where the entity plans to state in a document containing the summary financial statements that the auditor has reported on them but does not plan to include his report, he requests management to include it, and if management does not, he settles on and takes whatever further steps will keep management from tying him inappropriately to the summary financial statements in that document. Where he was engaged to report on the financial statements but not on the summary, and the entity plans to refer to him and to the fact that the summary is derived from statements he audited, he must be satisfied that the reference is made in the context of his report on the audited financial statements and that the statement does not give the impression that he has reported on the summary; if not, he requests management to change the statement or not to refer to him, and if management does neither he advises management that he disagrees with the reference and carries out other appropriate actions to prevent an inappropriate reference.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 810: the elements of the auditor's report on summary financial statements including the statement required where that report is dated later than the report on the audited financial statements, the report dated no earlier than the later of the date evidence was obtained on the summary and the date of the report on the audited financial statements, and the auditor association requirements where the entity refers to the auditor without including his report

concepts.subsection: SRS 4400 — agreeing the terms of an agreed-upon procedures engagement
concepts.statement: An agreed-upon procedures engagement is defined by what was agreed, so SRS 4400 spends its opening on the agreement. The auditor is to see that the entity's representatives — and, ordinarily, whichever other specified parties are to be sent the report of factual findings — all hold the same clear understanding of what procedures were agreed and on what conditions the engagement runs. Five matters are to be agreed. What sort of engagement this is, which carries with it the point that no audit and no review is being performed here, so nothing by way of assurance follows. Why it is being done. Which financial information the agreed-upon procedures are to be run against. What those specific procedures are, when they happen and how far they go. And what limits the report of factual findings will carry on its distribution — a limit that cannot stand against legal requirements, and where it would, the engagement is one the auditor turns down. Both sides gain from an engagement letter setting the appointment's key terms on paper: it confirms his acceptance of the appointment and heads off misunderstanding about the objectives and scope of the engagement, the extent of his responsibilities and the form of reports to be issued, and it lists the procedures the parties agreed he would perform and says that only those specified parties who agreed to the procedures will be sent the report of factual findings. The procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis; recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks; observation; inspection; and obtaining confirmations. The report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority. Whoever performs a related service need not be the same person who audits the entity's financial statements.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the five matters to be agreed including limitations on distribution, with the auditor not accepting the engagement where such a limitation would conflict with legal requirements; the matters included in the engagement letter; the procedures that may be applied; and the report of factual findings addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority

concepts.subsection: SRS 4410 — what a compilation engagement is, and the terms it cannot begin without
concepts.statement: Where a practitioner is brought in to help management put historical financial information together and present it, picking up no assurance on that information along the way, and then to report on what he did, SRS 4410 is the standard that governs him. The engagement itself is this: a practitioner brings accounting and financial reporting expertise to bear so that management can prepare and present an entity's financial information under whichever reporting framework applies, and he issues a report at the end. It is not an assurance engagement. Nothing in it obliges him to test whether what management handed over for the compilation is accurate or complete, and nothing obliges him to gather evidence towards an audit opinion or towards a review conclusion. Management retains responsibility for the financial information and for the basis on which it is prepared and presented, including the judgement required for its preparation, the selection and application of appropriate accounting policies and, where needed, the development of reasonable accounting estimates. Because it is a non-assurance engagement the independence requirements do not apply, though independence may still be the subject of a requirement, or of a disclosure rule, that a law or a regulation lays down; the relevant ethical requirements do apply, and threats to compliance with them are identified and appropriately addressed. SQC 1 applies to the firm in respect of its compilation engagements, because it applies to all Engagement Standards. Acceptance is conditional. Terms have to be settled first with management — and with the engaging party too, where that is somebody else — covering: what use the financial information is intended for, how far it will travel, and what limits either of those carries; which reporting framework applies; what the engagement is for and how far it reaches; what the practitioner is on the hook for, relevant ethical requirements included; the responsibilities of management for the financial information and its preparation and presentation under an acceptable framework, for such internal control as management determines is necessary, for the accuracy and completeness of the records, documents, explanations and other information provided, and for the judgements needed in preparing and presenting the information; and what shape and substance the practitioner's report will take. Those settled terms go on paper — an engagement letter, or another written form that suits it — before any of the work begins.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: a compilation engagement carries no assurance, so nothing in it obliges the practitioner to test management's material for accuracy or for completeness; management retains responsibility for the information and its basis; independence requirements do not apply unless a law or a regulation specifies them; and the engagement is not accepted until the listed terms are agreed and put into an engagement letter, or another written agreement, ahead of the work

concepts.subsection: SRS 4410 — proposing amendments, withdrawing, and the practitioner's report
concepts.statement: A compilation engagement gives the practitioner no opinion to modify, so everything he can do about a defect he does before the report is issued. He gets to know the entity's business and how it runs, its accounting system and accounting records included, and he gets to know the reporting framework in play and how the entity's own industry applies it. He then compiles, working from whatever records, documents and explanations management handed him, and from any other material and any significant judgements it supplied. Significant judgements he assisted with are talked through with management, or with those charged with governance. And before finishing he reads the compiled financial information against everything he has understood. Where what management has provided is incomplete, inaccurate or otherwise unsatisfactory, he brings that to management's attention and requests the additional or corrected information; where the engagement cannot be finished at all because management never supplied it, he withdraws from the engagement and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons. Where he becomes aware that the compiled financial information does not adequately refer to or describe the applicable financial reporting framework, that amendments are required for it not to be materially misstated, or that it is otherwise misleading, he puts the amendments that are needed to management; should management refuse them, or refuse to allow them, he withdraws and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons; and if withdrawal is not possible he determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances. Management, or those charged with governance, must then acknowledge to him that the final version of the compiled financial information is theirs to answer for. The report is in writing and is not a vehicle to express an opinion or conclusion in any form. It carries the title; the addressee as required by the terms of the engagement; a line saying that what the practitioner compiled, he compiled out of material management supplied; a description of management's responsibilities; the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework and, where a special purpose framework is used, a description of it or a reference to its description; the identification of the financial information including the title of each element and the date or period; a description of the practitioner's responsibilities, including that the engagement was performed in accordance with the standard and that he has complied with relevant ethical requirements; a description of what a compilation engagement entails; explanations that, no assurance being carried here, he was under no duty to test management's material for accuracy or completeness, and that no audit opinion and no review conclusion is therefore given on whether the financial information follows the framework that applies; where a special purpose framework is used, an explanatory paragraph describing the purpose for which the information is prepared and, if necessary, the intended users, or referring to a note that discloses it, and flagging for readers that a special purpose framework is what the information was drawn up under, which may make it unsuitable elsewhere; the date of the report; the practitioner's signature; and the place of signature. The documentation holds the significant matters arising and how they were addressed; a reconciliation showing how the compiled financial information ties back to the records, documents and explanations underlying it and to the rest of what management supplied; and a copy of the final version of the compiled information for which responsibility was acknowledged, together with the practitioner's report.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: proposing amendments where the compiled information does not adequately describe the framework, requires amendment not to be materially misstated or is otherwise misleading, withdrawing and informing management and those charged with governance where amendments are declined or where management fails to provide what was requested, the elements of the practitioner's report including the two explanations and the special purpose framework paragraph, and the three documentation requirements

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — the factors against acceptance, and the preconditions
concepts.statement: SRE 2400 (Revised) applies where the practitioner performing the review is not the auditor of the entity's financial statements, and it keeps two separate gates in front of the engagement. The first is a list of circumstances in which, unless required by law or regulation, he shall not accept the engagement at all. He shall not accept it if he is not satisfied that there is a rational purpose for the engagement — and it may be unlikely that there is one where there is a significant limitation on the scope of work, where he suspects association of his name with the financial statements in an inappropriate manner, or where the engagement is intended to meet compliance requirements of a law or regulation that requires the financial statements to be audited. He shall not accept it if he is not satisfied that a review engagement would be appropriate in the circumstances; where it would not be, he may recommend another type of engagement, an audit where that is more appropriate, or, where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement altogether, a compilation or other accounting services engagement. He shall not accept it if there is reason to think the relevant ethical requirements, independence among them, will go unmet; if his preliminary understanding indicates that the information needed to perform the review is likely to be unavailable or unreliable; if management's integrity is doubtful enough that the review is likely to suffer for it in the doing; or if a limit is written into the proposed engagement's terms by management, or by those charged with governance, that narrows his work so far that he expects to end in a disclaimer of conclusion. The second gate is the preconditions. Before accepting, he shall determine whether the financial reporting framework applied is acceptable, which on special purpose financial statements means grasping why they are being drawn up and for whom; and he shall obtain management's agreement that it acknowledges and understands its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with that framework, for such internal control as is necessary to enable their preparation free from material misstatement, and to provide him with access to all relevant information, with additional information he may request, and with unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. If he is not satisfied as to a precondition he discusses the matter with management or those charged with governance, and if changes cannot be made the engagement is turned down — unless a law or a regulation compels him to take it. Taken on that footing, it falls outside the standard, so his report carries no reference at all to the review having been conducted in accordance with it. If he discovers after acceptance that a precondition is not satisfied, he discusses it and determines whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and how to communicate the matter in his report.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the factors affecting acceptance, including the absence of a rational purpose where law or regulation requires the financial statements to be audited, and the preconditions, with the consequence that an engagement accepted without them because law or regulation requires it carries no reference to the review having been conducted in accordance with the standard

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — materiality in a review, and the written representations
concepts.statement: Two things in a review are not scaled down to match the assurance. Materiality is the first. A materiality figure is fixed for the statements taken as a whole, and it governs both how the procedures are designed and how their results are weighed. What the practitioner counts as material, taking those statements as a whole, does not shift with the level of assurance behind the conclusion he will express. He shall revise it if he becomes aware of any information during the review that would have caused him to determine a different amount initially. Written representations are the second. He asks for a signed statement from management confirming that every responsibility the agreed terms put on it has in fact been carried out, and that confirmation shall include that management has discharged what it owes on drawing the statements up under the framework that applies, fair presentation included where that is relevant, and has provided him with all relevant information and access as agreed, and that every transaction has found its way into the records and shows in the statements. He shall also request written representations that management has disclosed to him who the entity's related parties are, together with every related party relationship, and every transaction with one, that it knows of; significant facts relating to any frauds or suspected frauds known to it that may have affected the entity; any non-compliance with a law or a regulation, actual or possible, that it knows of and whose effects reach the statements; all information relevant to the use of the going concern assumption; that all subsequent events requiring adjustment or disclosure have been adjusted or disclosed; material commitments, contractual obligations or contingencies affecting the statements, their disclosures included; and any material transaction in the period that was non-monetary or that carried no consideration. Sometimes a law or a regulation obliges management to say publicly and in writing what it is responsible for, and where such a statement already carries some or all of the representations wanted, those matters need not be gone over again. If management does not provide one or more of the requested representations, he discusses the matter with management and those charged with governance, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the conclusion. And he shall disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements, or withdraw where withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation, if management's integrity is doubtful enough that its written representations cannot be relied on, or if management does not provide the required representations about its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements and the recording of all transactions.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): materiality determined for the financial statements as a whole, the practitioner's judgement about what is material being the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained, with revision where later information would have changed it; and the written representations, with a disclaimer of conclusion or withdrawal where management does not provide those about its responsibilities or where its integrity is in sufficient doubt

concepts.subsection: SRE 2410 — a limitation on scope, and a material uncertainty about going concern
concepts.statement: A limitation on scope ordinarily prevents the auditor from completing an interim review, and SRE 2410 answers it differently depending on where the limitation came from. Where it is imposed by management, the auditor does not accept the engagement at all if his preliminary knowledge indicates that he would be unable to complete the review because of it. Where management imposes it after acceptance, he requests its removal; if management refuses, he is unable to complete the review and express a conclusion, and why the review cannot be finished goes in writing both to the right level of management and to those charged with governance — and if a matter has come to his attention causing him to believe that a material adjustment is needed to the interim financial information, he communicates that too. He then considers his legal and regulatory responsibilities, including whether he is required to issue a report; where he is, the conclusion is disclaimed and the report itself carries why the review could not be finished, again communicating any material adjustment he believes necessary. Where the limitation arises from circumstances other than management, he is ordinarily unable to complete the review and express a conclusion; but in some rare circumstances the limitation may be penned in to one or two particular matters which, material though they are, he does not judge pervasive to the interim financial information, and then he modifies the report by indicating that, except for the matter described in an explanatory paragraph, the review was conducted in accordance with the standard, and qualifies the conclusion. Going concern is answered on the state of the disclosure rather than on the state of the entity. A material uncertainty may come to his notice which could throw significant doubt over whether the entity can carry on as a going concern; where the interim financial information discloses it adequately, he modifies the report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph. Where he had already added such a paragraph to a prior audit or review report and the material uncertainty still exists with adequate disclosure made, he modifies the current report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty. Where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, he should express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, and the report should point expressly at the existence of a material uncertainty of that kind.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: a limitation on scope imposed by management, with a disclaimer of conclusion and the reason given where a report is required, against a limitation arising otherwise and clearly confined to specific matters that are not pervasive, which is met by an explanatory paragraph and a qualified conclusion; and going concern, where adequate disclosure of a material uncertainty is met by an emphasis of matter paragraph and inadequate disclosure by a qualified or adverse conclusion

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3402 — what the standard covers, and what a type 1 and a type 2 report each comprise
concepts.statement: SAE 3402 bites only where the service organisation either answers for the suitable design of controls or is otherwise in a position to assert it. Two kinds of engagement fall outside it. One reports on nothing but whether a service organisation's controls ran as the description said. The other reports on nothing but controls that lie away from any service bearing on the user entities' internal control over their financial reporting — controls over a user entity's production or its quality control, for example. Within that scope, each report is built of three components and the difference between the two is a date against a period. A type 1 report comprises the service organisation's description of its system; a written assertion by the service organisation that, in all material respects and based on suitable criteria, the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented at the specified date and the controls related to the control objectives stated in the description were suitably designed as at the specified date; and a service auditor's assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters. A type 2 report comprises the description; a written assertion with three limbs rather than two — that across the whole of the specified period the description fairly presents how the system was designed and put in place, that across that same period the controls tied to the stated control objectives were suitably designed, and that across it those controls also operated effectively; and a service auditor's assurance report that conveys reasonable assurance about those matters and sets out the tests of controls he ran and what they showed. The service auditor's opinion is expressed in the positive form, and a type 1 report says besides that operating effectiveness was not something the service auditor put any procedure to, so no opinion on it is given.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the standard applies only where the service organisation is responsible for or able to assert the suitable design of controls and does not deal with engagements to report only on whether controls operated as described or only on controls unrelated to user entities' financial reporting; and the three components of a type 1 and of a type 2 report, the type 2 assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb on operating effectiveness and the report including a description of the tests of controls and their results

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — who the Order applies to, and the five exempt classes
concepts.statement: Paragraph 1 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 casts the net over companies generally, foreign ones included — clause (42) of section 2 supplies that meaning — and then lifts exactly five classes out again. Banking companies come first, taking their sense from section 5(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Insurers under the Insurance Act, 1938 are second. Third are companies holding a licence issued under section 8. Fourth, two creatures of section 2 — the One Person Company of clause (62), and the small company of clause (85). Fifth, and the only class with arithmetic in it, a private limited company which is neither subsidiary nor holding company of any public company and which clears three money tests together: paid up capital plus reserves and surplus of one crore rupees or less on the balance sheet date; borrowings never touching one crore rupees at any moment of the year, taken from banks and financial institutions; and total revenue, as Schedule III to the Companies Act discloses it and counting revenue from discontinuing operations, staying at ten crore rupees or under for that year. Four features of that fifth class decide most questions on it. The three tests hold together, so one failure alone drags the company back under the Order. Public-company parentage, or being such a company's subsidiary, defeats the exemption however small the figures look. Borrowing is judged across the whole year rather than on one date, so a facility drawn and cleared before closing still counts. And revenue means total revenue with discontinuing operations inside it, not turnover. Paragraph 2 then settles what the Order does. Where it applies, the report the auditor gives under section 143 has to carry paragraph 3's matters and paragraph 4's as well — the Order rides on that report instead of standing as a report of its own. Consolidated financial statements sit outside it, saving clause (xxi) of paragraph 3 alone.

citation.ref: paragraph 1 on the companies to which the Order applies and the classes it exempts, including the private limited company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and passes the paid up capital and reserves and surplus, borrowings and total revenue tests, read with paragraph 2 on the matters every report under section 143 shall in addition contain and on the Order's application to a report on consolidated financial statements

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(vi)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(vi) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 packs two questions into a single sentence. Has the Central Government, acting under section 148(1) of the Companies Act, specified that this company keep cost records? And if it has, were those accounts and records in fact made and kept that way? The two are asked in order, because the second only arises if the first is answered yes. Three confusions follow from reading it as one question. The clause is not about a cost audit. Section 148 carries both the power to specify that cost records be kept and the power to direct that they be audited, and clause 3(vi) reaches only the first; whether a cost auditor was appointed and whether the cost audit was carried out are not what this clause states on. The clause is not skipped where the Central Government has specified nothing, because paragraph 3 requires the auditor's report to include a statement on the matters specified rather than a statement only where something is wrong — the answer is simply that maintenance of cost records has not been specified for the company, and the second limb does not arise. And where either limb is answered unfavourably, paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for that answer, which a bare "no" does not do.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi) — its two limbs on cost records, the Central Government's specification of them under section 148(1) and whether the company then kept them — read with paragraph 3 on stating the matters specified and paragraph 4(a) on an unfavourable answer

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(viii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(viii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 puts two limbs to the auditor. Did any transaction the books of account never carried get surrendered, or disclosed as income, in the year's assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961? And where one did, has the company since brought that previously unrecorded income properly into its ledgers inside the same year? The second limb is where companies fail: money surrendered to the tax authorities is very often left out of the accounts, on the view that the tax has been paid and the matter is closed. The clause says otherwise — the books must show that previously unrecorded income, brought in properly and within the year — and an unfavourable answer carries paragraph 4(a) with it, so the report states the basis for it. Two things the clause does not do are as examinable as what it does. It does not decide whether the unrecorded transactions were a fraud; that is answered under section 143(12) with Rule 13 and, inside the Order itself, under clause 3(xi), and it is possible for clause 3(viii) to be answered in the affirmative with no fraud reported at all. And it does not reach a surrender made after the year end, because it asks about what has been surrendered or disclosed during the year.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii) — its two limbs, a surrender or disclosure of income in the year's assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961 covering transactions the books never carried, and the proper bringing in of that previously unrecorded income within the same year — read with paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 3(xi)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 applies to a Nidhi company and carries three separate questions, each of which is answered on its own. Sub-clause (a) turns on the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio, which the Order pegs at 1:20 for meeting the liability — so deposits above twenty times net owned funds breach it, and because this is a ratio and not an absolute amount, a growing Nidhi can fail it without any single deposit being irregular. Sub-clause (b) turns on term deposits: ten per cent of them, unencumbered, are to be held against the liability, the Nidhi Rules, 2014 being where that percentage sits; the word deciding it is unencumbered, since a term deposit pledged against a borrowing is not available to meet the liability. Sub-clause (c) asks after default — in paying interest on deposits, or in repaying them — over any period at all, with the details where there has been one, and "for any period" means a default that has since been made good is still reported. All three are answered whatever the answers are, because paragraph 3 requires a statement on the matters specified, and an unfavourable answer to any of them carries paragraph 4(a), so the report states the basis for it.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(a), (b) and (c) — the 1:20 Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio, the ten per cent of term deposits to be held unencumbered under the Nidhi Rules, 2014, and default over any period in paying interest on deposits or in repaying them — read with paragraph 4(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3)(j) and Rule 11 — the other matters the report must carry
concepts.statement: Clause (j) of section 143(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the auditor's report to state such other matters as may be prescribed, and Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 is what prescribes them. Six matters sit there and they are a list to be known as a list. One: has the company shown, in its financial statement, what pending litigation does to its financial position, where there is any such effect at all. Two: where material foreseeable losses arise on long term contracts, derivative contracts among them, has provision been made as law or the accounting standards demand. Three: were amounts due to be handed over to the Investor Education and Protection Fund handed over late. Four, the funding chain, three sub-limbs and the one most often stated wrongly: has management represented that the company advanced, loaned or invested nothing in other persons or entities, foreign entities included — the Intermediaries — on an understanding that the Intermediary would then lend or invest onward, whether directly or by some further step, in persons or entities the company identified or had identified for it, the Ultimate Beneficiaries, or would stand guarantee or security or the like for them; has management represented that nothing was received by the company from persons or entities, foreign ones included — the Funding Parties — on an understanding that the company would itself lend or invest onward in Ultimate Beneficiaries the Funding Party identified or had identified for it, or would stand guarantee or security or the like for them; and, on audit procedures the auditor judged reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, did anything reach the auditor's notice giving cause to believe either representation materially mis-stated. Five: was the year's dividend, whether declared or whether paid, compliant with section 123 of the Companies Act, 2013. Six, the audit trail: did the company keep its books of account on accounting software carrying an audit trail feature; did that feature run the whole year across every transaction the software recorded; was it left untampered with; and has the company preserved the trail for as long as the statutory record retention rules require. Separately from Rule 11, section 197(16) requires the auditor to make a statement in his report under section 143 on directors' remuneration — whether what the company paid them accords with that section, whether any director was paid beyond the ceiling it lays down, and such other details as may be prescribed; ICAI's advisory of 9 September 2019 places that statement, for auditors of public companies, under the section headed "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements".

citation.ref: Rule 11, prescribing the other matters to be included in the auditor's report under clause (j) of sub-section (3) of section 143 — pending litigations, provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts, delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, the representations on Intermediaries and Funding Parties with the auditor's own statement on them, compliance of dividend with section 123, and the accounting software's audit trail — read with section 197(16) on directors' remuneration

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the five international frameworks and what each counts
concepts.statement: Five internal control frameworks are followed internationally and the module names each with the counts that identify it. The Internal Control - Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of the Sponsoring Organisations of the Treadway Commission, the COSO Framework, was introduced in 1992; it articulates seventeen principles across five components — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — every one of which must be present and functioning for a system of internal control to be effective, and it lists three categories of objectives: operations objectives, reporting objectives and compliance objectives. The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants' Guidance on Assessing Control — the Criteria of Control, or CoCo framework — was developed to lift how an organisation performs and how it decides, by way of better control, better risk management and better corporate governance, and includes twenty criteria for effective control in four areas: purpose or direction, commitment or identity and values, capability or competence, and monitoring and learning or evolution. Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology, COBIT, was created by ISACA for IT governance and management and has thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives, sorted into four domains: planning and organisation; next, acquisition and implementation; then delivery and support; and finally monitoring and evaluation. Internal Control: Guidance for Directors on the Combined Code — the Turnbull Report — came from ICAEW, the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales. It puts on the board a duty to keep internal control sound, so that what shareholders have put in and what the company owns are both safeguarded. It asks the directors to test how well the group's internal control is working — financial, operational and compliance controls, with risk management among them — no less often than once a year, and to tell shareholders they have done it. And a company running without an internal audit function is to revisit, now and then, whether one is needed. Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, an American statute, puts a duty on every company whose shares are publicly traded in that country: it has to put internal controls over financial reporting in place, along with the procedures that go with them, and then write those down, test them and keep them current. That section was followed by the constitution of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, and under the SEC rules and the PCAOB standard management performs a formal assessment of its controls over financial reporting and includes an assessment of internal control over financial reporting in its annual report, while two opinions come from the external auditors inside one integrated audit — a standalone opinion on how effective internal control over financial reporting is, alongside the traditional opinion on the financial statements. The COSO framework itself acknowledges that internal control has limitations and provides reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the international internal control frameworks: COSO's seventeen principles across five components and its three categories of objectives, CoCo's twenty criteria in four areas, COBIT's thirty-four high-level processes and two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains, the Turnbull Report's key principles, and Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 with the two opinions of a single integrated audit

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the questionnaire, the check list and the flow chart
concepts.statement: Three techniques are used to evaluate a system of internal control, and the examinable part is what separates them rather than what each looks like. An internal control questionnaire gathers, functional area by functional area, an organised body of questions, put there to weigh how effective control is and to bring its weaknesses out; it is meant to be filled in by the company executives in charge of the various areas, questions are framed so that generally a "No" answer reflects a weakness, and answers are given as Yes, No or Not applicable. A check list puts instructions and questions on internal control in front of the auditor himself, who must work through them or answer them; its character is a prompt, reminding him of what still wants checking. The three distinctions the module draws between them are the answer to most questions on this: the questionnaire incorporates a large number of detailed questions while a check list stays with the principal control objective of whichever area is under review; in a questionnaire the questions are usually answered by company executives while in a check list they are answered by the auditor or his staff; and a "No" in a questionnaire indicates a weakness but not the significance of that weakness, whereas a check list demands a statement in terms wherever a weakness on its face could turn out material to the accounts taken as a whole. A flow chart is a graphic presentation of internal controls drawn to show the controls in each section or sub-section; it provides the most concise and comprehensive way of reviewing internal controls and gives a bird's eye view of the system. Two periods go with the techniques. For the first year of an engagement, issue of a questionnaire is necessary; for subsequent years the auditor may instead ask the client to confirm whether the control system has changed, but it is good practice in a continuing engagement to issue a questionnaire irrespective of any change every third year, which alerts the client to unnoticed changes and makes it more control-conscious. And where the auditor is already aware of the features and efficacy of the controls through a continuing relationship, he may review only the changes in the intervening period, but even then a review covering the whole ground falls due once in roughly every three years. The review is ordinarily undertaken as a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme, though where the size of operations is rather small it can be undertaken in conjunction with other audit procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the techniques of evaluation of internal control: the internal control questionnaire and its basic assumptions, the check list, the flow chart, the three distinctions between a questionnaire and a check list, the issue of a questionnaire in the first year and every third year, and the comprehensive review of the system at an interval of about three years

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the internal check system
concepts.statement: An internal check system is the way the book-keeping as a whole is organised and the staff's duties laid out, so that one hand alone cannot put a transaction through and record it in every one of its aspects. It is part of the overall control system and operates as a built-in device so far as the organisation and job-allocation aspects of control are concerned: the routine itself carries a continuous check over each day's transactions, whereby the work of each person is either proved independently or made complementary to the work of another. Six aims sit behind it. Errors and frauds should surface easily. The chance that any one of the staff commits such an error or fraud should be cut down as far as it can be. The staff inside the organisation should end up working more efficiently for it. Where something did go wrong, the system should point to the area answerable for it, or to the very stage at which the fraud or error happened. The business should keep its integrity, because nothing settles into the accounts without a second hand scrutinising and checking it. And cash should be neither misappropriated nor embezzled, and the accounts not falsified. Whether such a system runs efficiently rests on four considerations: clarity of responsibility, so that the responsibility of the different persons engaged in the various operations is properly identified, for which a well-integrated organisational chart helps; division of work, segregated so that the free flow of work is not interrupted and the work of one person is complementary to that of another, with rotation of employees through the various components of the job; standardisation of the entire accounting process by suitable policies commensurate with the nature of the business; and appraisal, a periodic review of the chain of operations and workflow, for which an audit flow chart can be drawn up. The general conditions of the system are a list in their own right: no one person is to hold in his own hands the whole of any important part of the business, and another person's review must fall on whatever each employee does; duties are rotated among the staff, so that nobody stays on one and the same function for long stretches; leave is encouraged for each member of the staff, at least once in every year; whoever holds assets in physical custody is kept clear of the books of account; there should be an accounting control for each class of assets together with periodical inspection to establish their physical condition; mechanical devices should be used wherever practicable to prevent loss or misappropriation of cash; budgetary control should be exercised and wide deviations reconciled; when inventory is taken at the year's close, trading is halted wherever that can be managed, and the counting spread across staff drawn from several sections of the organisation; financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously among different officers with the manner of their exercise reviewed periodically; and procedures should be laid down for the periodical verification and testing of the accounting records.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the internal check system: its meaning, its six objectives, the four considerations its effectiveness depends on, and the general conditions including rotation of duties, compulsory leave, the separation of custody of assets from access to the books, and the suspension of trading during inventory taking

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Public sector audit — compliance audit, and where it sits beside the other two
concepts.statement: Compliance audit asks, independently, whether some subject matter squares with the criteria that apply to it. The work is done by holding activities, financial transactions and information up against the regulatory and other rules the audited entity is governed by, and asking whether they conform in every material respect. Two things concern it at once. Regularity — does the subject matter hold to the formal criteria which flow out of the laws, regulations and agreements binding the entity. And propriety — are the general principles of sound financial management kept, and do public officials conduct themselves ethically. Regularity is emphasised in compliance auditing, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector context, where the public holds expectations about how money is managed and how officials behave — so a transaction that satisfies every rule can still be a compliance audit finding. A compliance audit sits inside a combined audit which may reach other aspects too, and it is generally conducted in one of three ways: in relation with the audit of financial statements, or separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing. Where a performance audit is the setting, compliance counts as one aspect of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and a failure to comply may be what caused the state of the activities under examination, or what explains it, or what followed from it. Its process runs from general principles and an annual compliance audit plan, through planning the individual audits, performing them and gathering evidence, evaluating evidence and forming conclusions, to reporting — with documentation, communication and quality control running alongside all of it.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance audit: its concern with regularity and with propriety, the three ways in which it is generally conducted, and its relation to performance auditing where compliance is one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Public sector audit — the C&AG's report on undertakings, and the Audit Board
concepts.statement: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on the audit of public sector undertakings are presented to Parliament in several parts, and there are four of them. First, an introduction reviewing in general terms how Government companies, deemed Government companies and corporations have worked out. Second, what came of the comprehensive appraisals the Audit Board made of the undertakings it selected. Third, a resume — of the reports company auditors filed against directions the C&AG issued to them, and of his own comments on the accounts of the Government companies. Fourth, whatever significant audit results arose in those undertakings the Audit Board never took up for appraisal. For certain specified states a separate audit report on commercial matters goes from the C&AG to the legislature, while for other States and Union Territories with a legislature there is a commercial chapter in the main audit report; a state audit report carries both the results of the audit appraisal of the performance of selected companies and corporations and important individual instances of financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure and system deficiencies noticed by the statutory auditors. The Audit Board is something only the Indian Audit and Accounts Department's audit has: it is constituted so that the working of public sector enterprises across diverse sectors can be appraised comprehensively, associates with itself experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisal, and discusses its findings and conclusions with the managements of the enterprises and with their controlling ministries and departments before finalisation, so that their view points are ascertained first. Two things about its standing are examinable and easy to get wrong: an Audit Board is no separate legal entity of its own, and it answers to the Comptroller and Auditor General for supervision and control. Behind all of it sits section 143(5) of the Companies Act, 2013: where a Government company is being audited, the manner of that audit may be directed by the C&AG, and the auditor's report must then carry those directions, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts and financial statements of the company.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the parts of the C&AG's audit report on public sector undertakings, the constitution and standing of the Audit Boards, which are no separate legal entity of their own and answer to the C&AG for supervision, and the directions under section 143(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 with the action taken on them and their impact reported by the auditor

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: BRSR — who files it, from when, and the three sections of the questionnaire
concepts.statement: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report arrived at the end of a decade of widening requirements, and the dates and the ranks are the examinable part. In 2012 SEBI required the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation to file a Business Responsibility Report. In 2015 the BRR became part of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations and the top 500 listed companies by market capitalisation were required to file it. In 2017 SEBI advised the top 500 listed companies which were required to prepare a BRR to adopt Integrated Reporting on a voluntary basis from the financial year 2017-18. In 2019 the fifth amendment to the Listing Regulations, taking effect on 26 December that year, pushed the rank down to 1,000: every listed entity inside that band by market capitalisation had to carry a business responsibility report within its annual report. Then in 2021 SEBI brought in fresh ESG-parameter reporting under a new name, the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, asking for disclosure of how a company has performed against nine principles laid down in the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23; in the financial year 2021-22 disclosure was voluntary only. Three sections make up the reporting questionnaire, each with its own content. Section A, General Disclosures, contains the details of the listed company, its products, services and operations, employee related details, and its holding, subsidiary and associate companies. Section B, Management Process and disclosures, contains the questions related to policy and management processes, governance, leadership and oversight. Section C, Principle-wise performance disclosures, is where companies report key performance indicators in alignment with the nine principles, classified into essential indicators which are mandatory and leadership indicators which are voluntary. The point of the whole design is comparability: the BRSR is intended to have quantitative and standardised disclosures on ESG parameters so that companies, sectors and periods can be compared, and it is expected to become the single means of disclosing sustainability related information in India.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the evolution of ESG reporting in India from the top 100 listed companies in 2012 to the top 500 and then the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, the introduction of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report in 2021, its mandatory application from the financial year 2022-23 after a voluntary year, and the three sections of the reporting questionnaire

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — a digital audit against auditing digitally
concepts.statement: Two phrases in this chapter sound alike and mean opposite things, and telling them apart is the first thing the chapter asks for. A digital audit puts assurance over how effectively an organisation's implemented IT systems work — the IT systems are the subject matter, and the work exists because organisations must review their technology-related controls to identify gaps and risks, to improve continuously and to ensure regulatory compliance. Auditing digitally turns advances in technology to the conduct of an audit that is effective and efficient — the technology is the tool, and the subject matter is whatever the audit was about anyway; using a sampling tool to select a sample from a population based on materiality, or a bot to analyse compliance with statutory payments, is auditing digitally. The features of a digital audit are that it encourages the auditee to embrace technological advancement and gives it confidence to stay updated, improves the quality of the opinion and so leads to a more reliable audit report, saves time, cost and human effort which can be spent on more productive tasks, allows processes to be standardised and controls to be implemented to mitigate risk, helps the organisation gain a comprehensive overview of end-to-end processes, and helps the auditee make informed decisions. Its advantages are enhanced effectiveness and efficiency, better audit quality, lower costs, better analytics and improved risk assessment. And its considerations are cautionary rather than promotional: know what business benefits the organisation wants from automation; think people first and do not underestimate how difficult change is; target the right processes, which is the key to successful automation; ensure the process works and is standardised before automating it, because bots do not easily adapt to process change; treat automation as part of a broader digitalisation strategy rather than a stand-alone solution; and do not forget governance and data security in the risk framework.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — a digital audit, which puts assurance over how effectively an organisation's IT systems work, set against auditing digitally, which turns technological advance to the conduct of an audit that is effective and efficient, with the features and advantages of a digital audit and the considerations and challenges that go with automation

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — the five IT dependencies and the three areas of general IT controls
concepts.statement: An IT dependency arises wherever the entity leans on IT to initiate a transaction, to authorise it, to record it, to process it or to report it — and equally for other financial data on its way into the financial statements. Identifying them is what tells the auditor where the entity actually relies on IT, what risks arise from that reliance, which general IT controls are related, and therefore what an effective and efficient audit approach looks like. There are five types. Automated controls, designed into the IT environment to enforce business rules — a purchase order approved by workflow, a format check, an existence check that a duplicate customer number cannot exist, a reasonableness check on a maximum payment amount. Reports, being information generated by IT systems, often used in the entity's execution of a manual control such as a business performance review, or used by the auditor himself when selecting items for testing or performing substantive procedures — a vendor master report, a customer ageing report. Calculations, being accounting procedures performed by an IT system instead of a person, such as the system applying the straight-line formula to compute depreciation or computing an invoice by multiplying price by quantity shipped. Security, segregation of duties among it: the IT environment is what makes it possible to fence information off and to split apart roles and responsibilities which would otherwise let one employee both commit an error or a fraud and hide it. And interfaces, being programmed logic that transfers data from one IT system to another, such as an interface transferring data from a payroll sub-ledger to the general ledger. Management responds to the risks arising from those dependencies by implementing information technology general controls, and the module groups them into three areas, each with its own control objective. Access security, whose objective is to ensure that access to programs and data is authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives — access requests reviewed and authorised, a terminated user's access removed on a timely basis, access rights periodically monitored for appropriateness, transactions of administrative and sensitive generic IDs monitored, security policies maintained, and access to the operating system and database restricted. Program change, whose objective is to ensure that modified systems continue to meet financial reporting objectives — a change management policy, development, testing and production environments segregated, changes tracked and recorded, changes tested and approved before migration into production, emergency changes approved, and segregation of duties maintained between developer and implementor. And data centre and network operations, whose objective is to ensure that production systems are appropriately backed up to meet financial reporting objectives — backup and recovery policies, data backed up and recoverable, restoration testing performed, service level agreements monitored, and batch job schedules monitored for failures with access restricted. The consequence is the part that decides audit work: the auditor scopes general IT controls into testing where IT dependencies are identified, and if the controls around the IT environment are not implemented or are not operating effectively, the general IT controls cannot be relied upon, which means the IT dependencies cannot be relied upon either.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the five types of IT dependency, being automated controls, reports, calculations, security and interfaces, and the three areas of general IT controls with their control objectives, being access security, program change, and data centre and network operations, read with the consequence that ineffective general IT controls leave the IT dependencies unrelied upon

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — remote audit
concepts.statement: A remote or virtual audit is one in which the auditor uses online or electronic means to conduct the audit, either partially or completely, leaning on technology to gather audit evidence, or to run a documentation review in which the auditee takes part. The auditor must develop tailored strategies so that the remote audit meets the requirements and delivers results equivalent to a traditional onsite audit, and the module groups what he considers under three heads. Feasibility and planning — agreeing the audit timelines, the meeting platform to be used for audit sessions, the data exchange mechanisms and any access authorisation requests, and determining that the technology is available and that auditors and auditees have the competencies for it; the execution phase involves video or tele conferencing with auditees, and the documentation for audit evidence is transferred through a document sharing platform. Confidentiality, security and data protection — access to the document sharing platform is sufficiently restricted and secured by encrypting the data sent across the network, information once reviewed and documented is removed from the platform and stored according to the applicable archiving standards and data protection requirements, legislation and regulations may require additional agreements from both sides, the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees and any screenshot of a document or record used as evidence should be previously authorised by the audited organisation, and access to the auditee's IT system should be through a virtual private network, which creates a safe and encrypted online connection. And risk assessment — the risks to achieving the audit objectives are identified, assessed and managed, and the assessment of whether a remote audit would be sufficient to achieve the audit objectives is made and written down audit by audit, drawing in every member of the audit team along with the audited organisation's representative. Its advantages are no travel time or cost, comfort and flexibility for the team, evidence gathering spread over several weeks instead of concentrated into a short period that takes personnel away from their daily activities, first-hand evidence directly from the IT system where direct access is given, and a wider selection of auditors from a global network of experts. Its disadvantages are interrupted meetings from network issues, limited or no ability to see the facility, the culture of the organisation or the body language of the auditees, time zone problems, security and confidentiality violations, remote access to sensitive IT systems not being allowed, cultural challenges and a lack of knowledge of local laws, the impossibility of physical verification of assets and stock taking, and — the one with a consequence attached — an increased opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information, which may call for additional planning and some additional or different audit procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — remote or virtual audit: the three considerations of feasibility and planning, confidentiality, security and data protection, and risk assessment, including the restriction and encryption of the document sharing platform, the prior authorisation of screenshots used as evidence and the use of a virtual private network, together with the advantages and the disadvantages including the increased opportunity to present doctored documents

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — who appoints the auditor, and what is settled before the audit starts
concepts.statement: A bank's auditor is appointed by a different body according to what the bank is, and neither appointment may be made until the Reserve Bank has approved it. Shareholders appoint the auditor of a banking company, and they do it at the annual general meeting; a nationalised bank's own Board of Directors appoints that bank's auditor, acting for the bank. The Reserve Bank's approval comes first in both cases. Most nationalised and public sector banks appoint four or more firms of chartered accountants to act jointly as statutory central auditors, while a statutory branch audit is carried out by a single firm. The appointment letter of a statutory central auditor carries the period of appointment, the particulars of the other central auditors and of the previous auditors, the procedural requirements for accepting, a statement of the division of work among the joint auditors in a nationalised bank, and the scope including any special reports or certificates; a branch auditor's letter is on similar lines except for the particulars of other auditors and the division of work. Before the audit starts, three things are settled. The Reserve Bank has advised banks to obtain from the auditor a declaration of indebtedness, a written confirmation that the auditor, the firm, its partners and their family members have not been declared wilful defaulters by any bank or financial institution, and this is in addition to the declaration about the absence of the disqualifications in section 141 of the Companies Act. An audit firm should not undertake a statutory audit assignment while it is associated with internal assignments in the bank during the same year. And under SA 210 the terms of the engagement are agreed with the bank and documented before significant portions of fieldwork begin.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — audit of accounts and appointment of auditor: four or more firms as statutory central auditors, a single firm for a branch, the contents of the appointment letter, the annual general meeting for a banking company and the Board for a nationalised bank with the Reserve Bank's approval in either case; Stage I initial considerations: the declaration of indebtedness, internal assignments in the same year, and the terms of the engagement under SA 210

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — verifying the statutory liquidity ratio and compiling the demand and time liabilities
concepts.statement: The Reserve Bank requires the statutory central auditors of a bank to verify compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements on 12 odd dates in different months of the fiscal year, not being Fridays. Two addressees receive the report that results: the Reserve Bank, and the bank's own top management. The two things verified are the correctness of the compilation of the demand and time liabilities position and the maintenance of liquid assets under section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act. The branch auditors send weekly trial balances as on Fridays, consolidated at head office into the position for every reporting Friday; the central auditor asks the branch auditors to verify the trial balances on the dates he selects and to examine the cash balance at the branch on those dates, and he examines the consolidation on a test basis and the valuation of securities against the Reserve Bank's guidelines. In compiling the liabilities he checks that the excluded items have been excluded — paid-up capital, reserves, any credit balance in the profit and loss account, loans from the Reserve Bank, refinance from EXIM Bank, NHB, SIDBI and NABARD, part recoveries of debts considered bad and doubtful, and margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities — and that the included items have been included: the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts, and borrowings from abroad, which are liabilities to others and are taken at gross, so that an adverse balance in the Nostro mirror account is a liability to others, unlike liabilities towards the banking system in India, which may be netted against assets towards that system.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — compliance with CRR and SLR requirements: 12 odd dates in different months not being Fridays, the report to top management and the Reserve Bank, the weekly Friday trial balances and their consolidation, the items excluded from and included in the demand and time liabilities, and borrowings from abroad taken at gross as liabilities to others

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — drawing power, temporary deficiencies, unreviewed limits and quick mortality
