concepts.statement: Four rules decide whether a working capital account is merely irregular or has become non-performing. Drawing power is calculated net of the stipulated margin, on the stock and the eligible book debts, and in a consortium the calculation and allocation made by the lead bank bind the member banks; for a construction company the work in progress must be valued consistently and the mobilisation advance received is reduced in arriving at it, and a stock audit including book debts is carried out for every account whose funded exposure exceeds the stipulated limit. A bank does not classify an account as non-performing merely because of deficiencies that are temporary in nature — the non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, the balance temporarily exceeding the limit, or the non-renewal of limits on the due date. But the stock statements relied on for drawing power must not be older than 3 months, and the outstanding based on drawing power calculated from a stock statement older than 3 months is irregular. And an account whose regular or ad hoc limit is not reviewed within 180 days from the due date or the date of the ad hoc sanction is treated as non-performing, the auditor also checking that ad hoc or short reviews are not done repetitively. Among the accounts the auditor selects for examination are quick or early mortality cases: an advance that slips to non-performing within 12 months of its sanction.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — drawing power calculated net of margin, the lead bank's calculation binding in a consortium, mobilisation advances in construction and the stock audit; accounts with temporary deficiencies not classified as non-performing; stock statements not older than 3 months; limits not reviewed within 180 days treated as non-performing; quick or early mortality within 12 months of sanction

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — Basel III, the two tiers of capital and the 9 per cent ratio
concepts.statement: Basel III is the global standard on the capital adequacy of banks, stress testing and market liquidity risk, and three purposes sit behind it. A banking sector that can take the shock of financial or economic stress, whatever set it off, is the first; better risk management and governance is the second; more transparency and disclosure from banks is the third. In India the Reserve Bank has prescribed since 1992 a uniform methodology for scheduled commercial banks other than regional rural banks. Capital is split for supervisory purposes into two tiers by quality. Share capital and disclosed reserves make up most of Tier I, which counts as the highest quality a bank holds, since losses can be met out of it in full. Tier II consists of certain reserves and certain types of subordinated debt and has a lower loss absorption capacity. The capital to risk-weighted assets ratio is eligible total capital funds divided by risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items, multiplied by 100, and the Reserve Bank requires a minimum of 9 per cent on an ongoing basis. Each exposure is weighted before it enters the denominator — a secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh at 50 per cent subject to conditions, above ₹75 lakh at 75 per cent, commercial real estate at 100 per cent, so a housing loan of ₹60 lakh contributes ₹30 lakh — and a non-performing asset purchased from another bank carries a 100 per cent weight. The authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, including its disclosures and the other ratios in the notes, is one of the certificates the statutory central auditors give beside the main report.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — Basel III framework: its three aims, the uniform methodology of 1992, Tier I and Tier II capital, the CRAR formula with risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items in the denominator, the minimum of 9 per cent, the housing loan risk-weight example, the 100 per cent weight on purchased non-performing assets, and the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio among the certificates

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — deposits, inoperative accounts, non-resident accounts and window-dressing
concepts.statement: Deposits are of two kinds, repayable on demand — current and savings accounts — and repayable after a fixed term, including recurring deposits. Savings accounts are opened for individuals, Hindu undivided families and some approved institutions, never for a business or professional concern, whose transactions run through current accounts; no interest is generally paid on a current account, and a debit balance in a current account is not netted on the liabilities side but shown under advances. A savings or current account with no transactions for over two years is inoperative or dormant, a high-risk area for fraud, and it may be revived only with proper authority. On term deposits the auditor checks that receipts are issued serially, that the correct rate has been offered on bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above for scheduled commercial banks, that the foreclosure penalty has been deducted on premature closure, and that a 360-day year, not a 365-day one, was the basis on which interest was paid. Foreign currency non-resident deposits are opened by non-resident Indians as fixed deposits only and are converted at the rate notified by head office, the difference going to the profit and loss account. Non-resident Indians and persons of Indian origin may hold an NRE account, whose balance is repatriable; any non-resident at all may hold an NRO account, from which repatriation is barred but for current income, on conditions; both are in rupees and may be savings, current, recurring or fixed. Deposits must not be inflated for presentation: overdrafts granted near the balance sheet date and placed back as deposits, with further advances on their security, inflate both deposits and advances, and where that window-dressing is indicated the auditor considers a suitable qualification in the main audit report.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — deposits: current and savings accounts, no savings account for a business concern, debit balances shown under advances, inoperative accounts after two years revived only with proper authority, bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above, the foreclosure penalty, interest on the basis of 360 days, FCNR accounts as fixed deposits, NRE and NRO accounts and repatriability, and window-dressing calling for a qualification in the main report

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the nationalised bank's report to the Central Government and the certificates beside it
concepts.statement: Five matters go into the report a nationalised bank's auditor makes to the Central Government. Is the balance sheet full and fair, does it carry every particular it needs, and has it been drawn up to exhibit a true and fair view of how the bank stands — that is the first. Does the profit and loss account show a true balance of profit or loss over the period — that is the second. Where explanation or information was called for, was it supplied, and was what came back satisfactory — the third. Did the bank's transactions that he came across stay inside the bank's own powers — the fourth. Were the returns from its offices and branches adequate for him to audit on — the fifth. Anything else he thinks the Central Government ought to be told of goes in beside these. Beside the report, the terms of appointment require a long form audit report and a set of reports and certificates: on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting, on compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements, on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines, on any serious irregularity needing immediate attention in line with section 143(12), a certificate on the custody and utilisation of unused Bank Receipt forms, the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, the status of compliance with the Ghosh Committee's recommendations on frauds and malpractices and the Jilani Committee's on internal control and inspection, instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas, asset liability management, the corporate governance certificate for a listed bank, and certification of claims of interest subsidies and subventions.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — auditor's report of a nationalised bank to the Central Government: the balance sheet and profit and loss account, explanations called for, transactions within the powers of the bank, adequacy of branch returns, other matters; and the reports and certificates required by the terms of appointment beside the long form audit report

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the 15 per cent capital ratio, and when an asset is sub-standard or lost
concepts.statement: Every applicable non-banking financial company must keep its capital ratio — Tier I and Tier II taken together — at 15 per cent or more, measured against its aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet plus the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items; each asset is multiplied by its risk weight and the aggregate is what the ratio is measured against, so a ratio computed on the balance sheet alone overstates the position. Alongside the ratio sits the classification of assets. A sub-standard asset includes an asset whose terms as to interest or principal have been renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured after the commencement of operations, and it stays sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance under the new terms. A loss asset is one identified as such by the company, by its internal or external auditor or by the Reserve Bank on inspection, to the extent not written off, and also an asset adversely affected by a potential threat of non-recoverability due to erosion in the value of the security, the non-availability of security, or any fraudulent act or omission on the part of the borrower. The auditor checks compliance with the prudential norms as a whole — income recognition, accounting for investments, classification, provisioning, capital adequacy, the prohibition on loans against the company's own shares, and the norms for concentration of credit and investments — and that the Board of a company granting demand or call loans has framed and implemented a policy for them.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — prudential norms: the minimum capital ratio of 15 per cent of aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items; sub-standard assets including renegotiated or restructured assets until one year of satisfactory performance; the definition of a loss asset; the prohibition on loans against own shares; the demand and call loan policy

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — a downgraded credit rating, matured deposits and what counts as a fraud
concepts.statement: A deposit-taking non-banking financial company's ceiling on public deposits is tied to a credit rating from an approved agency, and the auditor checks that the rating is in force and that the company has informed the Reserve Bank of any revision. Where the rating is downgraded below the minimum investment grade, an investment and credit company or a factor regularises the excess deposits in a fixed way: with immediate effect it stops accepting fresh public deposits and renewing existing ones, all existing deposits run off to maturity, and within 15 working days it must report where it stands to whichever Regional Office of the Reserve Bank holds its registration; and no matured public deposit is renewed without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor. The auditor's report on such a company says whether it is accepting public deposits without a minimum investment grade rating, whether deposits in excess of the permissible quantum have been regularised in the manner provided, and whether the capital adequacy ratio in the return to the Reserve Bank is correctly determined. On frauds, the company's classification runs from misappropriation and criminal breach of trust through fraudulent encashment, unauthorised credit facilities for reward, negligence and cash shortages, cheating and forgery, irregularities in foreign exchange transactions, and any other fraud. Negligence and cash shortages, and foreign exchange irregularities, are reported as fraud where an intention to cheat is suspected or proved; where it is not, a cash shortage is still treated and reported as fraud if it exceeds ₹10,000, or exceeds ₹5,000 and was detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported on its occurrence by the person handling the cash.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions: the credit rating ceiling, the procedure on downgrade below investment grade with the report within 15 working days, no renewal of a matured deposit without express and voluntary consent, the audit report items for a deposit-taking company; Monitoring of Frauds Directions: the classes of fraud and the ₹10,000 and ₹5,000 cash-shortage lines

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 2(2), Regulation 191 and sections 24 and 25 — who is in practice, and who is punished for pretending
concepts.statement: Section 2(2) treats a member as being in practice when he takes remuneration, received or still to come, for any of four kinds of work — alone, or in partnership with chartered accountants in practice or with members of the other prescribed professions. Practising accountancy is the first. The second is offering or doing work that audits or verifies financial transactions, books, accounts or records, or that prepares, verifies or certifies financial accounting and related statements; so is putting himself before the public as an accountant. Third comes professional service or assistance where the subject is accounting procedure, or how financial facts are recorded, presented or certified. Fourth is any other service the Council thinks a chartered accountant in practice may render — under which the Council permits the entire range of management consultancy and other services. A person is in practice not only when he serves clients but when he offers to: setting up an establishment offering accounting services is practice though no client has been served, and a member rendering service with the armed forces is deemed in practice. The Explanation narrows one case. Where a member draws a salary from a chartered accountant in practice, or from such a firm, one purpose alone counts as practice for him — the training of articled assistants. Regulation 191 adds more. Acting in his professional capacity, and neither personally nor as somebody's employee, a member is in practice when he is a receiver, a liquidator, a trustee, an executor, an administrator or an arbitrator, or an adviser or representative on costing, financial or taxation matters; when the Central Government, a State Government, a court or another legal authority appoints him; or when he is a secretary, unless he holds that post on a salary-cum-full-time basis. The Ethical Standards Board reads a court mediator as within arbitrator. Two sections punish pretence. Section 24 catches two people. The first is an outsider who gives himself out as a member, or writes the designation chartered accountant after his name. The second is a member who holds no certificate of practice and yet lets it be understood that he practises. Either is punishable on first conviction with a fine up to ₹1,000 and on a subsequent conviction with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ₹5,000 or both. Under section 25 no company, wherever incorporated, may practise as chartered accountants, company here including a limited liability partnership with a company as a partner, and every director, manager, secretary or other officer knowingly a party to a contravention is punishable with a fine up to ₹1,000 on first conviction and ₹5,000 on any subsequent one.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — members deemed to be in practice under section 2(2) and its Explanation, offering to render services as practice, service with the armed forces, Regulation 191, section 24 on falsely claiming membership or practice with its fine and imprisonment, section 25 on companies not to engage in accountancy with its fines

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I Clause 11 — the Director Simplicitor, the general and specific permissions, and the twenty per cent test
concepts.statement: Clause 11 forbids a member in practice to engage in any business or occupation other than the profession unless the Council permits, and the Council's permission comes in two resolutions. Under the general resolution a member may, without asking, take employment under a chartered accountant in practice, private tutorship, authorship of books and articles, a life insurance agency licence for renewal commission only, attending classes and sitting examinations, public elective office as a Member of Parliament or of a legislature, honorary office of a charitable, educational or other non-commercial organisation, acting as notary public, justice of the peace or special executive magistrate, part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute, valuation of papers and acting as paper-setter, head-examiner or moderator, editorship of professional journals, acting as surveyor and loss assessor under the Insurance Act, acting as recovery consultant in the banking sector, and owning agricultural land and carrying on agriculture. Under the specific resolution he needs the Council's specific and prior approval for full-time or part-time employment in a business concern where neither he nor his relatives hold a substantial interest, employment in a non-business concern, the office of managing or whole-time director where he and his relatives hold no substantial interest, interest in a family business in whose management he takes no active part, interest in an educational institution, lectureship for courses other than the Institute's, tutorship under an educational institution other than the Institute's coaching organisation, editorship of journals other than professional journals, and any other occupation the Executive Committee allows; and a member who takes teaching work may undertake attest functions only if the teaching hours together do not exceed 25 hours a week. A relative is the husband, wife, brother, sister or any lineal ascendant or descendant, and a substantial interest is not less than twenty per cent of the voting power of a company, or of the profits of any other concern, held by the member, his relatives or concerns in which they hold such an interest. A Director Simplicitor is an ordinary director who is not a managing or whole-time director, is required only at board meetings and is paid nothing but for attending them; a member in practice is permitted generally to be one in any company, including a board-managed company, without specific permission unless he or any partner is interested in the company as an auditor, and he may be a promoter or subscriber to the memorandum and become its Director Simplicitor, but the Council prohibits him from auditing a company of which he is a director whether or not he holds a substantial interest, and the Board reads signing the company's Registrar forms as a direct conflict of role. A managing or whole-time director's office needs the Council's specific prior approval, is barred where the member, his partners or relatives hold a substantial interest, and once granted shuts him out of attest functions; a person entrusted with the whole or substantially the whole of the management is deemed a managing or whole-time director whatever his title. Interest in a family business may be taken as a proprietor, a partner or the Karta or member of a Hindu undivided family, with evidence that it devolved by inheritance, succession or partition, that the member is not actively engaged in it and that he did not create it; a Karta stays within the limit if he invests only the family's funds and takes no active part in management. And a member in practice may transact in equity and currency derivatives in his personal capacity without the Council's permission, but not in his professional capacity for clients.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule: the general and specific resolutions, relative and substantial interest at twenty per cent, the Director Simplicitor and the auditor exception, promoter-directors, managing and whole-time directors and the attest bar, interest in a family business and the Karta, the 25 teaching hours, and equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I Clause 2 — a deceased member's share, the sale of goodwill and the firm name kept in abeyance
concepts.statement: Clause 2 forbids sharing the fees or profits of professional business with anyone but a member, and the Council has drawn the line for the dead. In a partnership firm of two or more partners, when one dies his legal representative, say his widow, may continue to receive a share of the firm only if the partnership agreement contains such a provision; the same applies where all the partners die at the same time. In a proprietorship there is no sharing of fees between the legal representative and the purchaser of the goodwill, but the goodwill of a proprietary firm may be sold or transferred to another eligible member after the proprietor's death, and payments may be made in instalments if the sale agreement so provides. Where the proprietor died on or after 30 August 1998 the sale must be completed in all respects within a year of the death; the legal heir must obtain the Council's permission within a year of the death; and the firm's name is kept in abeyance, not removed, only up to one year from the death. Where there is a dispute as to the legal heir and the Institute receives information of it within a year of the death, the name is kept in abeyance till one year from the settlement of the dispute. A widow selling her husband's practice for a price that includes the right to use the firm name is in effect selling the goodwill, which is permissible, and the buyer may continue to practise in that name as a proprietor.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule: share of profit of a deceased partner only under the partnership agreement, no fee sharing in a proprietorship, sale of the goodwill of a proprietary firm after death completed within a year, the legal heir's permission from the Council within a year, the firm name in abeyance for one year from death or from settlement of a dispute, and the illustration of the widow's sale

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Council General Guidelines 2008 Chapters V, X and XI — books of account, indebtedness, and the incoming auditor's duty
concepts.statement: Three chapters of the Council General Guidelines bind a member in practice, and a breach of any of them is misconduct under Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule. Chapter V requires a member in practice, or the firm of which he is a partner, to maintain proper books of account of the professional practice including a cash book and a ledger, whether or not section 44AA of the Income-tax Act applies. Chapter X forbids a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm, or a relative of the member or partner to accept appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it, or while he has given a guarantee or provided security for the indebtedness of a third person to it, for the limits fixed in the statute and in other cases for an amount exceeding ₹1,00,000; an auditor who under the terms of engagement recovers his fees progressively as parts of the work are done is not indebted at any stage. The Ethical Standards Board applies the same limit to a member who holds the credit card of a bank he audits, provided the outstanding does not exceed ₹1,00,000 beyond the prescribed credit period, and it does not permit a member to accept the audit of a bank from which he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit. Chapter XI requires a member to follow a direction of the Council or its committee, given to him as the incoming auditor, not to accept appointment in a case of unjustified removal of the earlier auditor. The Board's procedure feeds that direction: where an auditor resigns or does not offer himself for reappointment, he sends a written communication of his professional reasons to the Board of Directors with a copy to the Institute, and the incoming auditor must obtain a copy from the Board of Directors and consider it before accepting; where an auditor willing to continue is not reappointed, he files with the Institute a copy of the statement he sent to management for circulation to the shareholders, and the incoming auditor must obtain a copy from the company and consider it; the Board may call for further information from either auditor or the company and report to the Council; and the same procedure applies to removal by the government or another statutory authority.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Council General Guidelines 2008: Chapter V maintenance of books of account with a cash book and a ledger; Chapter X appointment when indebted beyond ₹1,00,000 and the progressive-fee opinion; Chapter XI directions on unjustified removal; the Ethical Standards Board's guidelines on resignation and non-reappointment and the incoming auditor's duty; the Board's decisions on a bank's credit card and a loan against a fixed deposit

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: The Council's recommended self-regulatory measures — branch audits, joint audits, the staff ratio, disclosure and the scale of fees
concepts.statement: Self-regulatory measures adopted by the Council aim at two things: the profession growing in good health, and work flowing round it equitably. They are recommendatory, and the Council expects every member to implement them. Where a firm of statutory auditors runs to ten members or more, that firm should leave a company's branch audits to local firms of fewer than ten members — without cutting into the statutory auditors' right of access to branch accounts under the Companies Act. Two situations relax the restriction: branch accounting records kept at the head office, and significant operations of the company carried out at the branch. In large companies the practice of associating a firm of fewer than five members as joint auditor should be encouraged, and where the client wants such a firm the senior firm should not object. On staffing, a firm doing audit work needs one member at least for each five non-qualified people it employs, leaving out of that count articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and anyone not directly engaged in professional work. As a good and healthy practice, auditors should disclose the payments they receive for other services through a different firm of which the auditor is a partner or proprietor. And the Institute has issued a recommended minimum scale of fees for professional assignments, graded for Class A, B and C cities.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recommended self-regulatory measures: branch audits by local firms of fewer than ten members with two exceptions, joint audits with firms of fewer than five members, one member for every five non-qualified staff, disclosure of interest in other firms, and the recommended minimum scale of fees

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Recent decisions of the Ethical Standards Board — what a member in practice may and may not take on
concepts.statement: The Ethical Standards Board publishes decisions on the borderline cases members bring it, and the module lists them. Permitted: an internal auditor of a company may acquire its shares; a firm may register on the Udyog Aadhar portal; a member may provide services through a kiosk if they are the professional activities of a practising chartered accountant; two or more members may run a training session jointly for their clients on GST, sharing the fees between them; a member holding a certificate of practice may be a member of the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank, and a non-executive or independent director of a co-operative bank if not involved in its day-to-day activity and neither he nor a partner is its auditor; a member may be the authorised representative of a foreign company if he is not its auditor; a member in service may take e-return registration if it does not conflict with his employment, but cannot certify the return; a member may be an equity research adviser but cannot publish a retail report; a member may be a registration authority for digital signatures; a member may act as a court mediator, mediator being within arbitrator under Regulation 191; a member may charge a percentage of the utilisation certified for an educational institute's grant; professional advice on intellectual property rights is routine professional work; and there is no conflict in a member of a trust being its auditor unless the statute governing it prohibits it. Not permitted: a statutory auditor of a bank may not simultaneously be the agency for specialised monitoring of a customer of the same bank, and takes either one at a time; a member may not be internal auditor and procurement officer of the same organisation; a member may not accept the statutory audit of a society where his spouse or a dependent holds an honorary position on a managing committee of an institute it governs; a member may not use messaging applications to make people aware of his practice and its services; a member may not act as a trademark or patent attorney; a Director Simplicitor may not sign the company's Registrar forms; a member who is a non-executive director of a company, or his firm, may not accept the statutory audit of that company's joint venture; a member may not be a financial adviser receiving fees or commission from mutual funds, insurance companies or non-banking financial companies; and a member may not exercise a lien over a client's documents for non-payment of fees.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recent decisions of the Ethical Standards Board, items 10 to 35: the agency for specialised monitoring, internal auditor and procurement officer, the society audit, messaging applications, the Board of Management of urban co-operative banks, trademark and patent attorneys, the internal auditor's shares, Udyog Aadhar, kiosks, joint GST training, co-operative bank directors, Registrar forms, authorised representatives of foreign companies, e-return registration, joint venture audits, equity research, registration authorities, credit cards, mediators, loans against fixed deposits, financial advisers and the lien over client records

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — acceptance and continuance of client relationships, and the policy on withdrawing
concepts.statement: Three moments trigger the enquiry — a client the firm has never had, a decision on whether an existing relationship should run on, and a fresh engagement for somebody already on the books. At each the firm gathers what it judges it needs, and if it goes ahead in spite of what it found, it records how that was settled. Integrity is read from who the principal owners, key management, related parties and those charged with governance are and what reputation they carry in business; from how the client operates and trades; from that group's appetite for stretching accounting standards and its attitude to internal control; from pressure to hold the audit fee down as far as it will go; from signs that the work is to be fenced in; from signs of money laundering or of other criminal conduct; and from why this firm is being asked and why the last one is not being asked again. Capability is a separate question: do the firm's people know this industry, this subject matter and the reporting and regulatory rules that go with it, or can they learn them in time; are there enough of them; can an expert be brought in; is somebody available to carry out an engagement quality control review where one is called for; and can the reporting deadline be met. Any conflict of interest as between firm and client is settled before the work is taken on. Should something surface afterwards that would have stopped the firm taking the work at all, its continuance policies send it back to its professional and legal duties — whether the appointing person has to be told, whether a regulator has to be told in some instances, and whether to step out of the engagement, out of the client relationship, or out of both. Stepping out has policies of its own: talk the possible action over at the right level of management and with those charged with governance; if going is the right answer, tell them so and say why; ask whether a professional, regulatory or legal duty pins the firm in place, or obliges it to report its departure and the reasons for it to a regulator; and write down the significant issues, the consultations, the conclusions and what they rest on.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements: the matters on the integrity of a client, the matters on capabilities, competence, time and resources, documenting how issues were resolved, information that would have caused the firm to decline, and the policies on withdrawal from an engagement or from the client relationship

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — the annual independence confirmation, the familiarity threat and rotation of the engagement partner
concepts.statement: The ethical requirements element asks the firm's policies to do four things: tell its people what independence demands of them; spot and weigh up the situations and relationships that put independence at risk; deal with those risks, either by killing them off or by cutting them down to a level that can be lived with; and, where nothing else will serve, leave the engagement. The flow of information runs both ways — an engagement partner tells the firm what its client work involves, staff report a threatening situation or relationship as soon as they meet it, and any independence breach goes to the firm at once so that it can act. Once a year, at a minimum, every member of staff who has to be independent under the Code signs a written confirmation that the firm's independence policies have been complied with. Familiarity gets particular weight in SQC 1: leave the same senior people on an assurance engagement year after year and performance quality can suffer, so the firm writes down when a safeguard becomes necessary, weighing how much public interest the engagement carries and how long those seniors have already served. Two safeguards are named — move the senior people off, or put an engagement quality control review over the work. Listed-entity audits are where this bites hardest, and there the engagement partner comes off after a set span, as a rule no longer than seven years. One exception survives: a sole practitioner auditing a listed entity, whose quality is instead assured by a peer review that is compulsory.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 ethical requirements: communicating independence requirements, identifying and evaluating threats, prompt notification of breaches, the annual written confirmation of compliance from all personnel required to be independent, the familiarity threat and its criteria, rotation or an engagement quality control review as safeguards, and rotation of the engagement partner on listed entities after normally not more than seven years except for a sole practitioner subject to mandatory peer review

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — monitoring, the sixth element, and the six things it must take into account
concepts.statement: Four claims are made about the firm's own quality control rules — that they bear on the work, that they go far enough, that they actually function, and that people follow them — and monitoring is what keeps those claims honest. It runs continuously as a weighing-up of the whole system, and it periodically picks finished engagements out of the pile and inspects them. Six matters go into it. Was the system built properly in the first place, and was it genuinely put into operation? Have shifts in professional standards, and in law and regulation, been carried through into the firm's own rules? Has the job of monitoring been handed to a partner, or to somebody else, holding enough of the right experience and authority inside the firm? Are complaints and allegations being handled — that the firm, or one of its employees, fell short of professional standards or of what a regulator requires, whoever raises it, insider or outsider? Where a member of staff has departed from the quality rules, is remedial action following? And where the rules themselves are found wanting in how they were designed or how they run, or where the system is simply not being complied with, is something being done about it?

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 monitoring: ongoing consideration and evaluation with periodic inspection of a selection of completed engagements, and the six factors — design and implementation, new developments, responsibility to a partner or person of sufficient experience and authority, complaints and allegations, remedial action, and action on deficiencies

concepts.subsection: Mechanisms for review of quality control — the Peer Review Board, the Quality Review Board and NFRA, and who reviews whom
concepts.statement: Three bodies review the quality of members' work. The Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council of the Institute to ensure that in assurance assignments members comply with technical, professional and ethical standards including regulatory requirements, and that proper systems including documentation are in place demonstrating the quality of assurance services. Peer review examines the systems and procedures a practice unit has put in place for the quality of its assurance services; once a unit is reviewed its assurance engagement records for the period are examined, and a peer review certificate is issued where the reviewer's report is unqualified, while on a qualified report the unit is told the certificate cannot be issued, with the reasons and the due date for a follow-on review decided by the Board. The Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government, with members nominated by the Central Government and the Council, and has three functions: to make recommendations to the Council on the quality of services provided by members, to review the quality of services including audit services, and to guide members to improve quality and adherence to statutory and regulatory requirements; statutory auditors of companies are identified for review on a risk-based approach, and the reviews are carried out by technical reviewers empanelled by the Board on an engagement basis from across the country. The National Financial Reporting Authority is constituted under section 132(1) of the Companies Act. Compliance with the accounting standards, and with the auditing standards, is its to watch over and to enforce; the service quality of the professions that deliver that compliance is its to oversee, with improvements to be suggested; and it may undertake investigation under section 132(4) of the auditors of the classes of companies in Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018 — listed companies, insurance companies, banking companies and the others the rule names. Audit quality at a listed company is therefore NFRA's ground. What the Quality Review Board may look at is the rest: entities Rule 3 leaves out, together with whatever NFRA sends across to it.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — mechanisms for review of quality control: the Peer Review Board constituted by the Council, the peer review certificate and the follow-on review after a qualified report; the Quality Review Board set up by the Central Government with its three functions, risk-based selection and empanelled technical reviewers; NFRA under section 132 with its duties, investigation under section 132(4) and the Rule 3 companies; and the Quality Review Board's review confined to entities outside Rule 3 or referred by NFRA

concepts.subsection: Porter's five forces — putting a fact under the force it belongs to
concepts.statement: The five forces model asks one question about an industry: how much of the money the industry earns is competed away, and by whom. Five sources of pressure are named. Rivalry counts how hard the firms already inside are fighting each other. Entry asks how easily a new firm can set up and take a share. Substitution asks whether some other product, belonging to another industry altogether, does the same job for the customer. Supplier leverage asks whether the people selling inputs can dictate terms. Buyer leverage asks the same of the people paying for the output. The examinable skill is almost never reciting the list; it is taking a sentence out of a situation and putting it under the right heading, because the same fact answers a different question depending on where it lands. A shortage of berths at the one port a company ships through is leverage held by whoever controls those berths, not a sign that rivals are multiplying. A customer who can move to a competitor without paying anything to switch is leverage held by buyers, not rivalry. A household that stops buying the product because it now does the job at home is substitution, and the firm supplying that household alternative is not a new entrant to this industry — it never joined it. Two habits cause most of the wrong placements: reading any new competitive threat as entry, and reading any squeeze on price as rivalry. Both collapse five distinct questions into one, and the answer to each is a different move.

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model, as worked in the digest's case solutions and its objective answers on classifying an industry fact under a force

concepts.subsection: Porter's five forces — what the reading is for, and what it cannot tell you
concepts.statement: Having placed the facts, a candidate still has to say what follows, and the digest's marks go to the answer that ends somewhere. Two conclusions are wanted. First, whether the industry as a whole is one where profit survives: where several forces press hard at once, the margin leaks out of the industry no matter which firm holds the share. Second, what this particular firm should do about the force that presses hardest on it, which always means changing its own position against that force rather than hoping the force weakens — owning the input it kept having to bid for, giving buyers a reason to stay that is not price, making itself expensive to imitate so that a new arrival needs more than money. The second limb is what separates a description from an analysis. The model also has a boundary that ICAI has rewarded a student for stating. It describes the structure of an industry at one moment. It says nothing about what this firm owns that others do not, so it cannot on its own explain why one firm inside a hostile industry earns more than its neighbours — a look at the firm's own activities and resources answers that. And it sits still while the world around the industry moves, so a scan of the wider environment belongs beside it. A board that treats a five forces reading as the whole case for a five-year commitment has taken a good starting point and stopped there.

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model — the digest's objective answer on why the analysis is not used in isolation, and its worked descriptive solutions on industry attractiveness

concepts.subsection: The value chain — sorting an activity into the right primary link
concepts.statement: A value chain breaks a business into the separate pieces of work that turn a bought input into something a customer pays for. Five of those pieces are called primary, because the product physically passes through them. Goods arrive, are checked and are held until needed. They are then worked on, so that what leaves is not what came in. What has been made is gathered, held and moved out to whoever ordered it. Somewhere alongside, the firm finds buyers and closes sales. And after the sale it answers for what it sold — repairs, complaints, training, replacement. The sorting rule is about the goods and not about the department: ask where the item stood at that moment and what was being done to it. Storage is the trap, because a warehouse handles both ends of the chain, and stock waiting to be worked on sits at the front of the business while stock waiting to be despatched sits at the back. A quality check is the second trap, because it happens at every link, and the answer depends on what is being checked — material arriving, work in progress, or finished goods on their way out. In a service business the same five links exist without a physical good: what is received and held is a booking, a specimen or a file, the work done on it is the operation, and the handover to the customer is the outbound step. Sorting matters because cost, and the chance to be better than a rival, sit in particular links, and a firm that has not separated them is improving an average.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — the five primary activities, as classified in the digest's objective answers matching listed activities to links in the chain

concepts.subsection: The value chain — support activities, linkages, and where the margin sits
concepts.statement: Beside the five links the product passes through sit four kinds of work that serve all of them. Buying — the function that sources materials, equipment and services — is support work wherever in the firm it happens, and it is not the same thing as the arrival and handling of goods, which is a primary link. Building and improving the methods, tooling and systems the business runs on is support work. Recruiting, paying and training the people is support work. And the general machinery of the company — the board, planning, finance, the legal function, quality governance — is support work too. Whatever is left of the price after every one of these has been paid for is the margin, which is why the chain is drawn as a whole rather than as a list of departments. The idea that earns marks is the linkage: money spent in one activity that removes a larger amount of cost, or creates a larger amount of value, in a different one. Tighter specifications when material is bought, and more testing when it arrives, cost money in two links and can take far more out of rework, scrapped batches, warranty claims and lost customers further down. The consequence for a case is a rule about who is judged on what: a firm that manages each activity to its own budget will cut exactly the spend that was holding a later link together, and will report the saving as an improvement. Outsourcing and integration decisions are read off the same picture — a link where the firm has no advantage and no linkage worth keeping is a link somebody else can run.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — support activities and margin, as evaluated in the digest's worked descriptive solutions on a company's chain

concepts.subsection: Competitive advantage — the kind that survives a season and the kind that does not
concepts.statement: A firm has an advantage when a customer picks it over the alternatives at a price that still covers what it cost to serve that customer. Whether the advantage lasts is a separate question from whether it exists, and it is the question a case usually turns on. Ask three things of it. Do buyers actually care about the thing, or is it a distinction only the firm can see. Can a competitor with money and a year copy it, or buy something that does the same job for the buyer. And is the firm arranged so as to use it — the skill exists, but does anything in the way the business is run turn that skill into a sale. Most claimed advantages fail the second question. A price cut is matched in a week; a new machine is ordered by everyone from the same maker; a feature is on a rival's product by the next season. What holds longer is what a rival cannot simply purchase: exclusive access to a scarce input, a position built up over years in the places the customers are, a body of accumulated know-how spread across many people rather than sitting with one, a name that already means something specific to buyers, a cost base that comes from the way the whole chain is arranged rather than from one machine. The practical use in an examination is brutal and simple. When a company lists what makes it special, take each entry and ask what would stop the nearest rival having the same thing within twelve months. Whatever survives that question is the advantage; the rest is a promotion.

citation.ref: Competitive advantage and its sustainability, as assessed in the digest's worked solutions on what strengthened and what failed to protect a company's market position

concepts.subsection: Core competence — the questions that decide whether a capability qualifies
concepts.statement: A core competence is a bundle of skills and know-how, usually spread across several parts of a company, that lets it do something its rivals struggle to do. Three questions decide whether a capability is one. Does it reach something the customer actually values, so that the buyer would notice its absence. Would a competitor find it hard to copy, which normally means it was accumulated rather than bought. And does it open a breadth of markets — could the same underlying skill carry the firm into products it does not sell today. Being cheaper is not on that list, and ICAI has set an objective question whose whole point is that it is not. Cost is a result, and it is the result a particular strategy aims at; a company that has chosen to win by being different from its rivals rather than by being the cheapest of them may have a genuine core competence that raises its costs. Reading a cost advantage as proof of a competence therefore does two things wrong at once: it tests an outcome instead of a capability, and it imports the yardstick of a strategy the firm may not be following. Two further slips are common in a case. A single asset — one plant, one licence, one machine — is rarely a competence, because a competence is knowledge held by people and processes. And a competence attached to exactly one product is usually a product strength; the breadth question exists precisely to separate the two.

citation.ref: Core competency analysis — the digest's objective answer on which parameter is not a test of a core competency

concepts.subsection: Cost leadership and differentiation — choosing one, and the price of choosing neither
concepts.statement: Across a broad market there are two ways to earn more than the next firm. One is to be the producer with the lowest cost, and then to price where rivals cannot follow and still make money. The other is to be different in some way buyers will pay extra for, and to keep the extra above what the difference costs to provide. A narrower version of each aims the same choice at one segment rather than at the whole market. What makes this examinable rather than decorative is that the two demand opposite things from the operating model. Winning on cost wants sameness — few variants, long runs, thin overhead, tight specifications, distribution stripped to what is necessary. Winning on difference wants the reverse — variety, attentive service, spending on the brand, people who can respond, a willingness to carry cost where the buyer notices the result. A company that reaches for both at once usually ends with the cost base of the second and the prices of the first, and is then beaten from each side: undercut by whoever is genuinely cheapest, and passed over by whoever is genuinely better. The exam version of this shows up as a firm proudly listing standardisation programmes and premium launches in the same plan. The right answer is not that both are bad ideas; it is that each of them belongs to a different position, and the firm has to say which one it is holding and let the other go, or run them at arm's length as separate businesses with separate cost structures.

citation.ref: Generic competitive strategies — cost leadership and product differentiation, as applied in the digest's case solutions on how a company chose to win its market

concepts.subsection: Diversification — related, unrelated, and what each one has to prove
concepts.statement: Diversification is entering a business the firm is not in. It is called related when the new business genuinely shares something with the old one — the same plant, the same route to the shop, the same technical know-how, a brand the new customer already trusts — and unrelated when the only things shared are cash and the attention of the people at the top. The label is not a description; it decides what the board has to demonstrate. For a related move, naming the shared thing is not enough: the case has to say which activity is shared, and roughly what that sharing is worth, because a claimed overlap that nobody can point to in the chain of activities is a story rather than a saving. For an unrelated move the argument has to be different in kind, since there is no overlap to measure. It rests on the firm being a better owner of that business than whoever holds it now, or on earnings that rise when the existing business falls. Both claims are hard, and investors usually mark the second one down, because a shareholder can spread risk across industries far more cheaply than a company can. So an unrelated move carries the heavier burden of proof, and the commonest error in a case is to shrink that burden by inventing a relationship — two businesses called related because both sell to households, or because both are consumer facing, or because the same board would run them. None of those is a shared activity.

citation.ref: Related and unrelated diversification, and stakeholder reaction to it, as discussed in the digest's preface and applied in its case solutions on strategic adaptation

concepts.subsection: Backward, forward and horizontal integration — naming the move and testing whether it helps
concepts.statement: Three moves are constantly confused in Paper 6 answers because all three are acquisitions. Going backward means taking over the stage that supplies the firm — the plantation, the mine, the crushing unit, the component maker. Going forward means taking over the stage that stands between the firm and the person who finally buys — the distributor, the branch network, the shop. Going sideways means buying somebody doing the same thing at the same stage, which is another word for buying a competitor. The names matter because the moves answer different problems and attract different scrutiny: only the sideways move removes a rival from the market, which is why it is the one that raises a competition-law question before it raises a strategic one. Naming the move is the first mark, and the second mark is the harder one: does the move touch the pressure the firm is actually under. Buying the supplier is an answer to dependence on that supplier — an input that is scarce, or inconsistent, or priced by somebody with leverage — and it converts a purchase price into fixed assets and a plant the firm now has to keep busy. It does nothing about a customer who can walk away without paying to switch, and nothing about a rival cutting prices. A board that reaches for integration whenever the margin is thin has read the symptom rather than the force, and the cost of that mistake is a heavier balance sheet standing next to the original problem.

citation.ref: Backward, forward and horizontal integration, as identified in the digest's objective answers and applied in its case solutions on control over the supply chain

concepts.subsection: Strategic alliance or joint venture — how much shared control the work needs
concepts.statement: Two firms that want to work together choose between a contract and a company. Under a contract — an alliance — each side keeps its own assets and its own employees, each still decides its own matters, the obligations are whatever the agreement says, and either party can leave when the term ends without unwinding anything. By forming a company together — a joint venture — they create a third legal person that both own, which holds the assets, employs the people, and is governed by a board on which both are represented, so decisions about it are taken jointly and leaving means selling a shareholding. Choosing between them is not a matter of formality or of cost; it is a question of how much shared control the work actually needs. Where the partners are building or running one thing together, where the money at risk is large and long-dated, where a regulator wants a licensed entity in the country with identified owners, or where each side has to rely on decisions the other makes day to day, the separate company is what supplies the governance. Where the cooperation is narrower — selling each other's products, sharing a channel, licensing a technology, a joint bid — the contract does the job and costs far less to end. Two misreadings recur. The first treats the joint venture as the looser arrangement of the two, on the reasoning that a new company is free to run itself; in fact it is the tighter one, because neither owner can move it alone. The second picks the structure for access to the other side's intellectual property, which is a licensing term either structure can carry.

citation.ref: Strategic alliance compared with a joint venture — the digest's objective answer on why shared ownership and control decided the structure

concepts.subsection: The balanced scorecard — four perspectives, and a measure taken from the strategy
concepts.statement: A balanced scorecard sets out what a company is trying to achieve under four headings, and puts a measure against each aim. The money heading covers returns, costs and the use of assets. The customer heading covers who is being kept, who is being won, and what they think of what they get. The process heading covers the internal work that has to run well for those customers to be satisfied. The people heading covers the skills, information and culture the firm has to build for the processes to keep improving. The reason the last three exist is that they move first: a company sees its training, its cycle times and its customer complaints turn before it sees the effect in its accounts, which is why an answer that fills all four rows with money measures has missed the instrument. The mark that gets dropped most often, though, is the second one. A measure has to be taken from the strategy the firm is running, not from a general list of things worth measuring. A business winning on low cost measures the things that drive cost out of each unit of capacity it operates and each unit it sells; a business winning on being different measures the things the premium is being paid for. Swap the two sets over and every row is still full, every heading is still covered, and the scorecard now tracks a plan the company has not adopted. Balance means the four viewpoints are represented, and it has never meant that every initiative in the company deserves a row.

citation.ref: The balanced scorecard — the digest's worked descriptive solution constructing goals and performance measures under each perspective for a low-cost operator

concepts.subsection: The McKinsey 7S framework — putting an observed fact under the right element
concepts.statement: The 7S framework cuts an organisation into seven parts whose names all begin with the same letter and asks whether they fit one another. Three are called hard, because each one is written down somewhere and can be read off a document. Strategy is the plan by which the firm means to stay ahead of its rivals. Structure is who reports to whom and where a decision is allowed to be taken. Systems are the routines and procedures by which the daily work actually gets done. The other four are called soft, because nobody writes them down and they live in the people. Skills are what the workforce is able to do. Staff is how many people there are and of what kinds. Style is how those in charge behave and what the place feels like to work in. Shared values are what the organisation believes it is for. The objective questions almost always hand over one observed fact and ask which heading it belongs under, and the sorting rule is to ask what kind of thing the fact IS rather than which department reported it. A written procedure for inspecting a returned item before a refund is issued is a routine, so it is a system, whichever team follows it. A decision to buy a competitor is a plan for staying ahead, so it is strategy, whoever signed the cheque. Two pairs cause most wrong placements. A shortage of hands is staff when the count is short and skills when the count is right and the capability is not. And a decision nobody is taking is structure when the right to take it was never granted, but style when the right exists on paper and the manner of the person in charge is what stops anyone using it.

citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — the digest's objective answers classifying one observed fact under a single element, and its worked descriptive solution taking an operation element by element

concepts.subsection: The McKinsey 7S framework — what follows when two elements do not fit each other
concepts.statement: Naming the seven parts earns almost nothing. The whole point of the model is that they have to fit one another, and that a change made to one of them fails when the other six are left where they were. Shared values sit in the middle of the diagram because every other part is judged against what the organisation says it is for. Three claims about the framework come up again and again in examinations and all three are wrong. The first is that the hard three outrank the soft four. They do not — being written down makes them easier to spot and quicker to alter, and easy to alter is not the same as worth altering. The second is that strategy is the element the rest hang off. It is not the centre; it is one of seven, and a plan is exactly the thing that fails silently when nothing around it moves. The third is that the soft four can be dealt with afterwards. Because they live in the people and shift only as the people do, they take the longest, which is a reason to start on them first rather than last. The framework earns its marks in two uses. It diagnoses why something already decided is not landing, by naming the specific part that was left standing when the plan changed. And it tests an organisation before or during a change, by asking of each of the seven whether it will survive what is about to happen. A useful answer therefore names the pair that is out of step, says which of the two is going to be moved, and says how long the firm should expect to wait for it.

citation.source: ICAI Paper 6 Revision Test Paper, November 2026
citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — the suggested descriptive answer diagnosing an operational collapse element by element, read with the case study digest's objective answer testing three contentions about the relative weight of hard and soft elements

concepts.subsection: The Kano model — sorting what a customer wants, and what each sort is worth spending on
concepts.statement: The Kano model sorts the things a customer might want by asking two questions about each of them — what happens to satisfaction when it is there, and what happens when it is not. A basic requirement is one the customer assumes without ever saying so. Meeting it earns nothing and failing it causes real anger, and it is exactly what gets left out when a customer is asked what matters, because nobody lists what they take for granted. A performance requirement moves satisfaction in step with how much of it there is, so more is better and less is worse; this is the group customers talk about and compare between suppliers. A delighter is something the customer never thought to ask for, so it lifts satisfaction when it appears and costs nothing when it is missing, because nobody misses what they did not expect. Two further sorts are examined. An indifferent feature moves satisfaction neither way, so money spent on it buys nothing at all. A reverse feature makes matters worse by existing — take it away and nobody thanks you, leave it and people complain — so the answer to one is removal rather than improvement, which is usually the cheapest fix on the list. The sort is never a permanent property of the feature. It is a statement about one customer at one moment, so a delighter stops being one the day customers begin to expect it. And the whole ranking collapses when a basic requirement fails, because a customer who did not get the thing he came for stops caring how good the rest of it was.

citation.ref: The Kano model of customer satisfaction — the digest's objective answers on basic, performance, delight and reverse attributes, read with the November 2026 revision test paper's assertion-and-reason question on an attribute ceasing to matter during a failure

concepts.subsection: Push and pull inventory systems — what each needs, and which products suit which
concepts.statement: There are two ways of deciding when to make something. Under a push system the plant produces ahead of demand, on a forecast, and holds what it has made until orders arrive. Under a pull system nothing is made until a customer has ordered, so the order is what starts production. Each buys one thing and gives up its opposite. Producing ahead lets the plant run long uninterrupted batches, which lowers what each unit costs to make and to deliver, and it keeps goods on hand so a customer asking today is served today. What it costs is everything that can happen to stock sitting in a store: goods that pass their date, goods that go out of fashion, money tied up in what nobody has yet asked for, and a forecast that turns out wrong. Producing to order removes most of that and pays for it twice over, because the plant loses the economies of the long run and a customer whose order arrives faster than the line can make it either waits or goes elsewhere. Two things are commonly claimed for a pull system and neither is true. It does not do away with planning, since capacity, materials, people and the production schedule all still have to be planned, and planned more tightly, because there is no finished stock to absorb a mistake; what falls away is only the weight resting on a forecast of what will sell. And it does not guarantee availability, which is the other system's promise and not its own. Which products suit which is settled product by product, on five questions. Is demand steady and foreseeable, or does it arrive in bursts nobody can time. How long will the goods keep. Can the line make the quantity a single order asks for without a costly changeover, or does the process only work in a fixed batch. How long from order to delivery, set against how long the customer will wait. And what does being out of stock cost — an inconvenience, or something the company cannot accept. A short-lived, high-margin, occasionally ordered product made on a line whose quantity can be varied is the strongest case for pull. A long-lived, steadily selling product with high turnover belongs on push. A product that can only be made in a fixed batch cannot be pulled however short its life, and a product that has to be there the moment it is wanted cannot be pulled however unpredictable its demand.

citation.source: ICAI Revision Test Paper, Paper 6, November 2026
citation.ref: Push and pull inventory management, as worked in the revision test paper's case study on a manufacturer choosing a system for each of its product categories

concepts.subsection: Centralised decision-making, divisional measures, and keeping the two aims pointed the same way
concepts.statement: Goal congruence is the state in which what a person or a division below is working towards points in the same direction as what the organisation as a whole is trying to achieve. It fails in two opposite ways, and a case usually turns on which of the two is in front of you. The first failure comes from taking every decision at the top. Deciding centrally buys uniformity, and it buys tight control over spending, and both of those are real. What it costs is that the people who can see the ground never influence the decision, so the aims set at the centre and the conditions faced below drift apart; the feedback that would have corrected the drift is filed and not answered, staff who watch their information ignored stop supplying it, the organisation loses the ability to bend when circumstances move, and eventually the people leave. A structure is judged on all of that together, not on the one number it was designed to hold. The second failure is the price of the cure. Pushing decisions down to divisions restores the feedback and gives a manager something to be accountable for, and it creates a fresh problem: a manager judged on a divisional number will take the decision that improves that number even where the company is worse off for it. Return on investment is the standing example. A division already earning well above the company's cost of capital will refuse a project that earns above that cost but below its own current return, because accepting it drags the divisional percentage down. Residual income removes the pull by measuring what the division controls after charging it for the capital it uses at the company's own cost of capital, so every project earning above that cost improves the measure. The same question arises whenever divisions trade with each other, where a price only works if it sits between what the supplying division gives up by not selling outside and what the buying division would pay to buy outside. The habit worth carrying into the exam is short: when a manager behaves oddly on a divisional number, look at the measure before you look at the manager.

citation.source: ICAI Paper 6 Case Study Digest and Revision Test Paper, Paper 6, November 2026
citation.ref: Goal congruence — the revision test paper's objective answer on the behavioural effect of centralised top-down decision-making, and the digest's worked case on divisional return on investment against residual income

concepts.subsection: Reviewing a product line for withdrawal — what leaves with it and what does not
concepts.statement: A reported loss on a product line is a reason to look, not a decision, and three separate things have to be sorted out before anything is withdrawn. The first is which costs actually stop. A line's own materials, the wages of people who work only on it, promotion bought only for it and any licence or insurance taken out only for it all disappear with it. A share of factory rent, a share of head office cost, and depreciation on plant already bought and paid for do not; they were put on the line by an apportionment and they will simply be put on whatever remains. So the honest arithmetic is never the reported result. It is what the line earns after its own variable costs, less only the costs that leave with it, and a line reported as loss-making after apportionment can still be paying for fixed costs the company will carry either way. The second thing is what else leaves with it. A line can be genuinely loss-making even on that stricter test and still be the reason a set of customers walks in and buys something profitable, in which case the profit walking out is not only the line's own. The third is what refuses to leave: a lease with years to run, staff who cannot be redeployed, a supply agreement that requires the range to be carried, a customer contract, a regulatory duty to keep the product available. Beyond the money sit commitments the arithmetic never sees at all — obligations under a dealership or a licence, undertakings given to customers, and the part the line plays in what the business intends to be in five years, which is why identifying a line as a candidate for review and deciding to withdraw it are two different findings. Two errors account for most wrong answers. One takes the apportioned result as the effect of the decision. The other counts what the line earns as lost and forgets the costs that stop alongside it.

citation.source: ICAI Paper 6 Case Study Digest and Revision Test Paper, Paper 6, November 2026
citation.ref: Product portfolio review and the continue-or-withdraw decision — the digest's worked relevant-cost statement in which fixed, apportioned and sunk charges are excluded, and the revision test paper's answer distinguishing a candidate for review from a decision to discontinue

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

citation.ref: para 5

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: The audit is planned and performed with professional skepticism — a questioning mind alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement, and a critical assessment of evidence. It neither assumes management dishonest nor assumes it honest; records are accepted as genuine absent reason to believe otherwise, and doubted the moment there is one.

citation.ref: para 15

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

citation.ref: para 6

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

citation.ref: para 7

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: On recurring audits the auditor assesses whether circumstances require the engagement terms to be revised and whether the entity needs reminding of the existing terms. A fresh letter every year is not demanded; a changed situation — new management, changed ownership, a changed framework, misunderstood scope — is what calls for one.

citation.ref: para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.

citation.ref: para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

citation.ref: para 14 and A21

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: Audit documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the procedures performed, the results and evidence obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions. The file must speak for itself; the auditor's memory is not part of the record.

citation.ref: para 8

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

citation.ref: para 31

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

citation.ref: para 26 and 47

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Auditor resignation under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who resigns files a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar within thirty days of resignation, stating the reasons and any relevant facts. For specified companies the statement also goes to the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Failure invites a penalty on the auditor personally.

citation.ref: Section 140(2) and (3)

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

citation.ref: para 6

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

citation.ref: para 15 and 16

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

citation.ref: para 9

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.
