citation.ref: para 13 and 14

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

citation.ref: para 12(l), 26(a)(i) and 32

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

citation.ref: para 9 and 11

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

citation.ref: para 21

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: However low the assessed risk falls, every material class of transactions, every material account balance and every material disclosure still gets substantive procedures designed and performed for it. Excellent controls reduce substantive work; they never reduce it to zero for anything material.

citation.ref: para 18

concepts.section: General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities
concepts.subsection: SA 402 — the standard titled Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

citation.ref: para 8 and 17

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.

citation.ref: para 11 and 12

concepts.subsection: SA 500 — Audit Evidence
concepts.statement: Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

citation.ref: para 5(b), 5(e)

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: Material inventory obliges the auditor to be present at the physical count himself, and only impracticability excuses that attendance.

citation.ref: para 4

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations
concepts.statement: Where inventory held by a third party is material, the auditor obtains evidence of its existence and condition by requesting confirmation from the custodian, or by inspection, or both — and considers whether more is needed where the custodian's integrity or independence is in doubt.

citation.ref: para 8

concepts.subsection: SA 505 — External Confirmations
concepts.statement: Negative confirmations may stand alone as the substantive procedure only where four things hold together — assessed risk is low, the population is large and alike throughout, hardly any exceptions are looked for, and nothing the auditor knows of suggests recipients will brush the request aside.

citation.ref: para 15

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: On a first-year engagement two things have to be established, with enough appropriate evidence behind each. One: that no figure carried in as an opening balance is wrong by an amount that would matter to the statements of this year. Two: that the accounting policies sitting behind those balances were applied the same way as before, or that a change was accounted for and disclosed properly.

citation.ref: para 6

concepts.subsection: SA 520 — Analytical Procedures
concepts.statement: Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

citation.ref: para 6

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

citation.ref: para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 540 — Auditing Accounting Estimates
concepts.statement: The auditor reviews the outcome, or subsequent re-estimation, of the prior period's accounting estimates — not to second-guess last year's audit, but to learn how management estimates: where its judgments proved biased, where uncertainty was understated, and where this year's risk therefore sits. Estimates resolved far from their booked amounts are risk assessment gold, not automatic prior-period errors.

citation.ref: para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and asks what the stated business rationale really points at — a genuine commercial purpose, or one of two other things: fraudulent financial reporting, or a misappropriation of assets being kept out of sight.

citation.ref: para 18 and 23

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

citation.ref: para 12(b)

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: Between the financial statements' date and the auditor's report date, the auditor actively performs procedures to catch events needing adjustment or disclosure. After the report's date the duty to search ends — but a fact coming to the auditor's knowledge before the statements are issued, which would have changed the report, must be pursued: discuss, determine amendment, and act on the outcome.

citation.ref: para 6 and 10

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — Going Concern
concepts.statement: Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

citation.ref: para 22

concepts.subsection: SA 580 — Written Representations
concepts.statement: A signed representation counts as audit evidence. Standing alone, though, it never rises to sufficient appropriate audit evidence for whatever it asserts, and obtaining one leaves the nature and the extent of the auditor's other procedures exactly where they already stood.

citation.ref: para 4

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, indicating the extent of the financial information audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor, except where circumstances should have aroused suspicion about its reliability.

citation.ref: para 24 and 25

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) permits internal auditors to provide direct assistance under the external auditor's direction, supervision and review — but never for procedures that involve significant judgments, relate to higher assessed risks where more than limited judgment is required, or cover work the internal audit function has itself reported on. Written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors come first.

citation.ref: para 28, 30 and 33

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

citation.ref: para 14 and 15

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report presents the Opinion as its first section, and the Basis for Opinion comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.

citation.ref: para 23 and 28

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: A listed entity whose auditor reports on a complete set of general purpose financial statements must be given a key audit matters section. So must any audit where law demands one, and any where the auditor takes it on without being obliged to.

citation.ref: para 5

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

citation.ref: para 5, 7(a)

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: Where the matter already sits inside the financial statements, the auditor writes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph. Where it sits nowhere in them, and a reader still needs it to follow how the audit ran, what the auditor was answerable for, or the report itself, an Other Matter paragraph carries it.

citation.ref: para 8 and 10

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

citation.ref: para 10 and 15

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

citation.ref: para 14, 18 and 22

concepts.subsection: SA 800 — Special Considerations, Special Purpose Frameworks
concepts.statement: Financial statements prepared for specific users under a special purpose framework — a tax basis, a regulator's format, a contract's accounting clauses — are audited with the SAs applied to that framework, and the report carries an Emphasis of Matter alerting readers that the statements follow a special purpose framework and may be unsuitable for any other purpose; the auditor may also restrict distribution. The opinion itself is not modified by the framework being special.

citation.ref: special purpose framework reporting — Emphasis of Matter alert

concepts.subsection: Section 15 of the SEZ Act — Who receives a proposal to set up a Unit, who decides it, and who hears the appeal
concepts.statement: Setting up a Unit in a zone runs through three different bodies and each has one job. A person who intends to set up a Unit for carrying on the authorised operations submits his proposal to the DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER concerned, who on receipt submits it to the Approval Committee. The Development Commissioner is the door, not the decision. The APPROVAL COMMITTEE may approve the proposal without modification, approve it with such terms and conditions as it thinks fit, or reject it — and where it modifies or rejects, it must give the person a reasonable opportunity of being heard and record its reasons. A person aggrieved by that order may appeal to the BOARD of Approval within the prescribed time, and an appeal filed late may still be admitted if he satisfies the Board that he had sufficient cause. An existing Unit is deemed to have been set up in accordance with the Act and needs no approval under it at all. The appeal to the High Court in section 24 belongs to a different chapter entirely: it lies from a decision of the court designated under section 23, within sixty days, and has nothing to do with a refused proposal.

citation.ref: Section 15, sub-sections (1) to (7) with the proviso to sub-section (1), read with section 24 for the appeal that does NOT apply

concepts.subsection: Rule 53 of the SEZ Rules — Positive net foreign exchange, and what actually goes on the other side of it
concepts.statement: A Unit shall achieve positive net foreign exchange, calculated cumulatively for a period of five years from the commencement of production, on a stated formula: A minus B greater than nought. A is the free-on-board value of exports, and it expressly includes exports to Nepal and Bhutan made against freely convertible currency, together with certain deemed-export style supplies such as goods supplied against an advance authorisation or a Duty Free Import Authorisation and capital goods supplied to an EPCG licence holder. B is where most of the marks are, because it is wider than it looks. It takes in the cost, insurance and freight value of all imported inputs used for authorised operations and of all imported capital goods — INCLUDING goods bought on a high seas basis even though paid for in Indian rupees — and all payments made in foreign exchange by way of export commission, royalty, fees, DIVIDENDS, interest on external commercial borrowings or any other charges. It also takes in goods obtained from another Unit, an EOU or a technology park, and goods imported duty free, leased, received free of cost or on loan for the period they stay with the Unit. Because the test is cumulative, a bad year is answered by the rest of the block rather than by a default; and where the Unit cannot achieve it because of adverse market conditions or any ground of genuine hardship, the Board of Approval may extend the five year block by a further period of up to one year, case by case.

citation.ref: Rule 53, the formula and the definitions of A and B, with the proviso allowing the Board of Approval a further period of up to one year

concepts.subsection: Sections 51, 49 and 53 of the SEZ Act — How far the Act overrides other law, and how far the zone is really outside India
concepts.statement: Two provisions are constantly run together and they do different things. SECTION 51 is a plain overriding clause: this Act wins over whatever is inconsistent with it, whether that inconsistency sits in another law currently in force or in an instrument that draws its effect from some law other than this one. There is no list in it and no notification behind it — it bites on every inconsistent law by its own force. SECTION 49 is the separate power that people mistake it for: the Central Government may, BY NOTIFICATION, direct that any provision of this Act other than sections 54 to 56, or of any other Central Act or rule made under it, shall not apply to a zone or shall apply only with the exceptions and modifications specified. One works automatically and the other needs a notification naming what it touches. SECTION 53 is a third thing again, and its own words fence it: a zone shall be deemed to be a territory outside the customs territory of India FOR THE PURPOSES OF UNDERTAKING THE AUTHORISED OPERATIONS, so the fiction reaches the authorised operations and stops. Sub-section (2) separately deems a zone to be a port, airport, inland container depot, land station or land customs station under section 7 of the Customs Act, 1962 with effect from a date the Central Government notifies, which is about the zone being a place where customs business is done and not about widening the fiction in sub-section (1).

citation.ref: Sections 51, 49(1) and 53(1) and (2)

concepts.subsection: Section 10AA — deduction for a unit in a Special Economic Zone
concepts.statement: Section 10AA allows an entrepreneur holding a letter of approval under the SEZ Act, 2005 a deduction from total income for the profits derived from the export of articles, things or services by a unit that began to manufacture, produce or provide services in a Special Economic Zone in the previous year relevant to A.Y. 2006-07 or later but not later than A.Y. 2020-21 (a unit whose letter of approval was issued by 31 March 2020 could begin by 31 March 2021 and is treated as having begun in A.Y. 2020-21). The deduction runs in three bands: 100% of the export profits for five consecutive assessment years beginning with the year the unit begins, 50% for the next five, and for a further five years so much of the profit, not exceeding 50%, as is debited to the profit and loss account and credited to a Special Economic Zone Re-investment Reserve Account to be used for new plant or machinery first put to use within three years following the year the reserve was created; an amount misused, or unused at the end of those three years, is deemed profit of the year of misuse or of the year following the period. Export profits are the unit's profits multiplied by export turnover over total turnover. Export turnover is the consideration for exports received in, or brought into, India in convertible foreign exchange within six months from the end of the previous year, or such further period as the competent authority allows, and excludes freight, telecommunication charges and insurance attributable to delivery outside India and expenses incurred in foreign exchange in rendering services outside India; by Circular 4/2018, following the Supreme Court, whatever is excluded from export turnover on that account is excluded from total turnover too. The deduction is allowed from the total income computed before giving effect to the section and cannot exceed it. It is lost if the return is not furnished by the due date under section 139(1), and the report of a chartered accountant certifying the claim must be furnished one month before that date. An individual, HUF, AOP or BOI gets it only after shifting out of the default regime under section 115BAC(1A), and a company or co-operative society only when it pays tax under the normal provisions rather than sections 115BAA, 115BAB, 115BAD or 115BAE.

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1) to (3) and (7) with Explanation 1 (export turnover), the Explanation below section 10AA(1) (deduction not to exceed total income), and CBDT Circular No. 4/2018 dated 14 August 2018 on exclusions from both export and total turnover

items.stem: What is the company's WACC for discounting project cash flows?

options.text: 12.0 per cent, using the book-value weights of 625:375 with the after-tax cost of debt
options.misconception: weights the sources of capital by book value instead of the market value the firm actually raises money at
options.why: The book split is 500:300, or weights of 0.625 and 0.375. Applying those to 15% and 7% gives 9.375% + 2.625% = 12.0% — the after-tax cost of debt is right here, but market value, not book value, is what WACC must weight.

options.text: 14.0 per cent, using market-value weights but the pre-tax cost of debt of 10 per cent
options.misconception: omits the tax shield on interest, using debt's quoted rate instead of its after-tax cost
options.why: Interest is tax-deductible, so debt's true cost to the firm is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%, not 10%. Using the pre-tax figure gives 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 10% = 14.0%, overstating the discount rate.

options.text: 13.4 per cent, using market-value weights of 80:20 and an after-tax cost of debt of 7 per cent
options.why: Weights come from market value: 800/1000 = 0.8 for equity, 200/1000 = 0.2 for debt. Debt's after-tax cost is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%. WACC = 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 7% = 12% + 1.4% = 13.4%.

options.text: 8.6 per cent, using the market-value weights but assigning equity's weight to debt and debt's weight to equity
options.misconception: swaps the equity and debt weights before applying them to their respective costs
options.why: Swapping the weights gives 0.2 × 15% + 0.8 × 7% = 3% + 5.6% = 8.6%, understating WACC by crediting the cheaper source with the larger share it does not actually have.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company's equity has a market value of ₹800 crore and a cost of equity of 15 per cent. Its debt has a market value of ₹200 crore and a pre-tax cost of 10 per cent. The tax rate is 30 per cent. The same company's books show equity at ₹500 crore and debt at ₹300 crore.

items.stem: Under real options reasoning, what should the firm do and why?

options.text: Reject — total value is −5 − 9 = −₹14 crore, since the option adds another cost on top of the shortfall
options.misconception: subtracts the option value instead of adding it, treating flexibility as a further cost rather than a source of value
options.why: An option the firm holds, not one it owes, only ever adds to value — it is the right, not the obligation, to expand. It is added to static NPV, giving +4 crore, not subtracted.
keywords: added to static NPV, giving +4 crore, not subtracted

options.text: Reject — the static NPV is −5 crore and real options do not change accept-or-reject decisions
options.misconception: treats real options as inapplicable and evaluates the project on static NPV alone
options.why: The whole point of real options is that flexibility has value discounting misses. A project rejected on static NPV alone can still be strategically positive once its embedded options are priced in, as here.
keywords: rejected on static NPV alone can still be strategically positive

options.text: Accept — total strategic value is −5 + 9 = ₹4 crore, since the expansion option is worth more than the pilot's shortfall
options.why: Real options add the option's value to the static NPV rather than ignoring it: −5 + 9 = +4 crore. Discounting alone prices the pilot as if the expansion choice did not exist, which is exactly what real options corrects.
keywords: add the option's value to the static NPV
as if the expansion choice did not exist

options.text: Accept, with total value of ₹9 crore, since only the option matters once one exists
options.misconception: credits the option value alone and drops the underlying project's own negative static NPV
options.why: The option sits on top of the base project, not instead of it. Both figures belong in the total: −5 crore from the pilot itself, +9 crore from the option to expand, netting to +4 crore.
keywords: sits on top of the base project, not instead of it
Both figures belong in the total

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A pilot plant has a static NPV of −₹5 crore on its own cash flows. It also carries the option to expand into a full plant in three years if the pilot succeeds; that option, valued separately, is worth ₹9 crore.

items.stem: Which technique is this, and what does it give that changing one variable at a time cannot?

options.text: Scenario analysis — because it uses a set of named cases such as best, base and worst
options.misconception: mistakes the description of scenario analysis's few discrete bundles for a method that draws thousands of random combinations
options.why: Scenario analysis bundles a handful of internally consistent cases by name. Ten thousand random draws from each variable's own distribution is a different exercise entirely — simulation, not a short list of scenarios.
keywords: bundles a handful of internally consistent cases by name
not a short list of scenarios

options.text: Sensitivity analysis — because several variables are varied at the same time
options.misconception: defines sensitivity analysis by the number of variables moved, when its defining trait is moving exactly one at a time
options.why: Sensitivity analysis isolates one variable, holding the rest fixed, precisely so each variable's own break-even point is visible. Moving several together, randomly, is what simulation does.

options.text: Simulation — a full probability distribution of NPV, including the chance of a negative outcome, not just a handful of break-even points
options.why: Drawing many random combinations from probability distributions and building the full outcome spread is Monte Carlo simulation. Sensitivity analysis only ever answers "what if this one variable moves," never the chance of any particular result.
keywords: building the full outcome spread is Monte Carlo simulation
never the chance of any particular result

options.text: The certainty equivalent approach — because it converts risky flows into a single risk-adjusted figure
options.misconception: confuses simulation's output, a distribution of outcomes, with the certainty equivalent method's output, a single deflated cash flow
options.why: Certainty equivalents shrink each risky flow to one certain-equivalent number and discount it at the risk-free rate. That produces one adjusted NPV, not the spread of ten thousand outcomes described here.
keywords: discount it at the risk-free rate
not the spread of ten thousand outcomes

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: An analyst reruns a project's NPV model ten thousand times, each run drawing sales volume, selling price and unit cost independently from their own probability distributions, and plots the resulting spread of ten thousand NPV outcomes.

items.stem: What is the one-step binomial value of the call?

options.text: ₹12.00, the expected payoff at the correct risk-neutral probability, left undiscounted
options.misconception: computes the correct expected payoff but forgets to discount it back to the present at the risk-free rate
options.why: 0.6 × 20 = ₹12 is the expected payoff one period from now, not its value today. The option's price is that payoff discounted at 1.08, giving ₹11.11, not ₹12.00.
keywords: expected payoff one period from now, not its value today

options.text: ₹9.26, taking the up and down moves as equally likely instead of computing the risk-neutral probability
options.misconception: substitutes a naive 50-50 probability for the no-arbitrage risk-neutral probability the model requires
options.why: At p = 0.5 the expected payoff would be 0.5 × 20 = ₹10, discounting to 10/1.08 ≈ ₹9.26. But 0.5 is not the probability that removes arbitrage here — 0.6 is, from the risk-free rate and the up and down factors.
keywords: 0.5 is not the probability that removes arbitrage
from the risk-free rate and the up and down factors

options.text: ₹11.11: risk-neutral probability 0.6, expected payoff ₹12, discounted at 1.08
options.why: p = (1.08 − 0.9) / (1.2 − 0.9) = 0.18/0.3 = 0.6, using u = 1.2 and d = 0.9. Payoffs are ₹20 up and ₹0 down, so expected payoff = 0.6 × 20 = ₹12, discounted at 1.08 gives 12/1.08 ≈ ₹11.11.

options.text: ₹7.41, swapping u and d in the risk-neutral probability formula
options.misconception: swaps the up and down factors inside the probability formula, inverting which state is which
options.why: Swapping gives p = (1.08 − 1.2)/(0.9 − 1.2) = 0.4, not 0.6. Expected payoff falls to 0.4 × 20 = ₹8, discounting to 8/1.08 ≈ ₹7.41 — a probability drawn from the wrong pairing of factor to state.
keywords: wrong pairing of factor to state

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trading at ₹100 will move in one period to either ₹120 or ₹90. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.08. A call option on the share has a strike of ₹100.

items.stem: What happens to the two premiums?

options.text: The call rises and the put falls by the same amount, to keep put-call parity satisfied
options.misconception: misapplies put-call parity, which fixes call-minus-put, to mean the two must move in opposite directions
options.why: Parity fixes C − P at a value independent of volatility, which both premiums rising together, by the same amount, still satisfies exactly. Parity requires them to move together, not apart.
keywords: requires them to move together, not apart

options.text: Only the call premium rises, since higher volatility only helps a bet on the price going up
options.misconception: assumes volatility only benefits upside bets, when a put profits just as much from a large favourable (downward) move
options.why: A put gains from a big fall the same way a call gains from a big rise; both are bets on movement, not direction. Volatility raises the value of optionality on both sides at once.
keywords: raises the value of optionality on both sides

options.text: Both premiums fall, since higher volatility is priced as a risk cost the way it would depress a bond's price
options.misconception: treats volatility like a bond's default or duration risk, which lowers value, instead of like optionality, which volatility raises
options.why: Unlike a bond holder, an option holder's downside is fixed at the premium already paid while the upside is open-ended, so more volatility can only help, never hurt, the option's value.
keywords: downside is fixed at the premium already paid

options.text: Both the call and the put premium rise
options.why: Higher volatility raises the chance of a large favourable move for either option, while the loss on each stays capped at its premium — so both gain value together, and by the same amount, since put-call parity's right-hand side does not depend on volatility.
keywords: the loss on each stays capped at its premium

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A dealer revises only her volatility estimate for an underlying share upward, holding spot, strike, time to expiry and the risk-free rate unchanged, and reprices both a call and a put on that share with Black-Scholes.

items.stem: What price does the convexity-adjusted estimate give, and how does it compare with the duration-only estimate?

options.text: ₹880 — the duration-only fall of 12 per cent, with convexity ignored entirely
options.misconception: uses the linear duration estimate alone and skips the convexity correction altogether
options.why: −6 × 0.02 = −12% gives ₹880, but that straight-line estimate overstates the loss for a positive-convexity bond — the true fall is smaller once the 1.6% convexity add-back is included.
keywords: overstates the loss for a positive-convexity bond
once the 1.6% convexity add-back is included

options.text: ₹896 — a 10.4 per cent fall, softer than the 12 per cent duration-only fall because convexity adds back 1.6 per cent
options.why: Duration-only: −6 × 0.02 = −12%. Convexity term: 0.5 × 80 × 0.02² = 0.5 × 80 × 0.0004 = 1.6%. Combined: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, so price = 1,000 × 0.896 = ₹896 — less severe than the straight-line estimate, as positive convexity always is on a yield rise.
keywords: less severe than the straight-line estimate
positive convexity always is on a yield rise

options.text: ₹912 — omitting the one-half factor in the convexity term
options.misconception: drops the standard one-half multiplier on the convexity term, overstating the correction
options.why: The convexity adjustment is 0.5 × C × (Δy)², not C × (Δy)²  — the one-half comes from the second-derivative term in the Taylor expansion the estimate is built on. Skipping it gives 3.2% instead of 1.6%, and an overstated ₹912.
keywords: the one-half comes from the second-derivative term

options.text: ₹864 — subtracting the convexity term from the duration estimate instead of adding it
options.misconception: subtracts the convexity term from the duration-only estimate, doubling the mis-estimate of the loss instead of correcting it
options.why: The convexity term is always added, not subtracted: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, not −12% − 1.6% = −13.6%. Positive convexity works in the bondholder's favour on both a rise and a fall in yield, so it can only soften a loss, never worsen it.
keywords: can only soften a loss, never worsen it

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 6 years and a convexity of 80. Its yield rises by 200 basis points.

items.stem: What is the bond's current yield, and how does it sit against the coupon rate and the yield to maturity?

options.text: 8.33 per cent, dividing the coupon by the average of price and face value
options.misconception: applies the approximate-YTM shortcut, which averages price and face value in its denominator, to a plain current-yield question
options.why: Current yield only ever divides by the market price: 80/920 ≈ 8.70%. Averaging price and face value, 80/960 ≈ 8.33%, belongs to an approximation of YTM, a different figure answering a different question.
keywords: only ever divides by the market price
belongs to an approximation of YTM

options.text: 8.70 per cent — above the 8.00 per cent coupon, with YTM higher again, since a discount bond also gains from the pull to par
options.why: Current yield = 80/920 ≈ 8.70%, above the 8.00% coupon because the price sits below face value. YTM adds the capital gain to par at redemption on top of that, so the order is coupon rate < current yield < YTM for any discount bond.
keywords: above the 8.00% coupon because the price sits below face value
coupon rate < current yield < YTM for any discount bond

options.text: 8.70 per cent, but with YTM the lowest of the three since the discounted price marks the bond as cheap
options.misconception: reverses the ordering, reading a discount price as depressing the yield instead of raising it further still through the pull to par
options.why: A price below par is exactly what makes YTM the highest of the three, not the lowest — the buyer collects both the coupon stream and the gain to par at maturity. The current yield figure of 8.70% is right; the ordering claimed after it is not.
keywords: makes YTM the highest of the three, not the lowest
the ordering claimed after it is not

options.text: 8.00 per cent, dividing the coupon by the face value rather than the market price
options.misconception: computes current yield on face value instead of the bond's actual market price
options.why: Current yield is defined against what the bond actually costs today, ₹920, not its ₹1,000 face value. 80/1,000 = 8.00% is just the coupon rate restated, not the yield an investor buying at ₹920 earns.
keywords: defined against what the bond actually costs today

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: An 8 per cent coupon bond with face value ₹1,000 is trading at ₹920.

items.stem: Ignoring time value of money, what is the bank's net cash flow across the premiums paid and the default payout?

options.text: Net gain of ₹6 crore, the payout alone, with the premiums paid left out of the reckoning
options.misconception: reports the default payout as the net benefit and forgets to deduct the premiums paid over the life of the position
options.why: The premiums are a real cost the buyer paid every year the contract ran, ₹0.30 crore in total here, and belong in the net figure alongside the ₹6 crore payout: 6 − 0.30 = ₹5.70 crore.
keywords: premiums are a real cost the buyer paid

options.text: Net gain of ₹9.70 crore, with the payout set at the full ₹10 crore face value
options.misconception: pays out the full face value instead of the loss given default, ignoring the stated 40 per cent recovery rate
options.why: The seller's obligation is the loss given default, ₹10 crore × (1 − 0.4) = ₹6 crore, not the whole face value. Paying the full ₹10 crore ignores the recovery the bond still returns.
keywords: obligation is the loss given default
ignores the recovery the bond still returns

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.70 crore — a ₹6 crore payout on the 60 per cent loss given default, less ₹0.30 crore of premiums actually paid
options.why: Protection ends at the default, so only the premiums actually paid count: ₹10 crore × 1.5% × 2 years = ₹0.30 crore. Payout: (1 − 0.4) × ₹10 crore = ₹6 crore, since the seller covers only the loss given default, not the whole face value. Net: 6 − 0.30 = ₹5.70 crore.
keywords: only the premiums actually paid count
the seller covers only the loss given default, not the whole face value

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.25 crore, continuing to count premiums for the full five-year tenor even though default ended the contract in year 3
options.misconception: keeps paying CDS premiums out to the original five-year tenor instead of stopping at the default that ends the contract
options.why: Protection ends when the reference entity defaults; only the premiums actually paid up to that point, two years' worth or ₹0.30 crore here, count. Charging the full five years, ₹0.75 crore, against a contract that ended in year 3 overstates the cost and understates the net gain: it gives 6 − 0.75 = ₹5.25 crore instead of ₹5.70 crore.
keywords: Protection ends when the reference entity defaults
overstates the cost and understates the net gain

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A bank holds a ₹10 crore bond and buys five-year CDS protection on it at a spread of 150 basis points a year, paid annually. The reference entity defaults at the start of year 3, after two full annual premiums have been paid, and the recovery rate is 40 per cent.

items.stem: What is the theoretical ex-rights price, and what is the value of the right attached to one existing share?

options.text: TERP ₹130; value of the right ₹5 per existing share, taking a simple average of the cum-rights and issue prices
options.misconception: averages the cum-rights and subscription prices equally instead of weighting them by the number of shares outstanding at each price
options.why: A simple average, (150 + 110)/2 = ₹130, ignores that four times as many shares trade at ₹150 as are issued at ₹110. The weighted figure, ₹142, reflects that four-to-one mix; a plain average does not.
keywords: ignores that four times as many shares trade at ₹150

options.text: TERP unchanged at ₹150; value of the right ₹40, the gap between the cum-rights price and the subscription price
options.misconception: ignores the dilution the new shares cause, comparing the subscription price to the undiluted cum-rights price instead of the ex-rights price
options.why: Once the new shares are issued, the price settles at the blended ex-rights figure, ₹142, not the pre-issue ₹150. The right's value is 142 − 110 = ₹32, spread over four shares — ₹150 − 110 = ₹40 skips the dilution the rights issue itself causes.
keywords: skips the dilution the rights issue itself causes

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹8 per existing share
options.why: TERP = (4cr × 150 + 1cr × 110) / 5cr = (600 + 110)/5 = ₹142. The right to buy one new share is worth 142 − 110 = ₹32; spread over the four old shares needed to earn it, that is ₹8 per existing share.
keywords: spread over the four old shares needed to earn it

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹6.40 per existing share, dividing by the post-issue share count of five instead of four
options.misconception: divides the right's value by the total post-issue share count instead of the subscription ratio of old shares needed for one new share
options.why: The right's ₹32 value belongs to the four old shares that earn one new share under a 1-for-4 issue, so 32/4 = ₹8. Dividing by five, the post-issue total, answers a different question and understates the figure.
keywords: belongs to the four old shares
Dividing by five, the post-issue total, answers a different question

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company with 4 crore shares outstanding, trading cum-rights at ₹150, offers a 1-for-4 rights issue — one new share for every four held — at a subscription price of ₹110.

items.stem: What does Walter's model give as the share price at this payout, and what does it say the firm should do?

options.text: About ₹73.33, inverting the ratio to Ke/r instead of r/Ke
options.misconception: inverts the r/Ke multiplier in Walter's formula, understating what retained earnings contribute for a growth firm
options.why: Using Ke/r = 0.12/0.15 = 0.8 gives [4 + 0.8 × 6]/0.12 = 8.8/0.12 ≈ ₹73.33. The formula's multiplier is r/Ke = 1.25, which rewards a firm earning above its cost of equity — the inverted ratio does the opposite.
keywords: the inverted ratio does the opposite

options.text: About ₹95.83; since r (15%) exceeds Ke (12%), the firm should retain more and cut its payout further to raise the price above this
options.why: P = [4 + (0.15/0.12)(10 − 4)]/0.12 = [4 + 1.25 × 6]/0.12 = 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83. Because the firm earns more on retained cash than shareholders' own opportunity cost, Walter's rule says push retention toward 100%, not hold it at 40%.
keywords: earns more on retained cash than shareholders' own opportunity cost

options.text: About ₹95.83, but since r exceeds Ke the firm should raise its payout toward 100 per cent to maximise price
options.misconception: reverses Walter's decision rule, recommending higher payout for a growth firm when full retention is what maximises price
options.why: The price figure is right, but the direction is backwards. When r > Ke the firm compounds shareholders' money better than the market does, so the rule calls for retaining more, not distributing more.

options.text: ₹11.50, stopping at the formula's numerator and forgetting the final division by Ke
options.misconception: computes the numerator of Walter's formula correctly but omits the final division by the cost of equity
options.why: 4 + 1.25 × 6 = 11.5 is only the bracketed numerator; Walter's price is that figure divided by Ke, 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83, not the undiscounted 11.5 itself.
keywords: Walter's price is that figure divided by Ke

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company has EPS of ₹10, pays a dividend of ₹4 per share, earns an internal return of 15 per cent on retained earnings, and has a cost of equity of 12 per cent.

items.stem: What money multiple (MOIC) does the sponsor earn on exit, and what drove it?

options.text: 2.5x — exit equity of 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore against ₹100 crore of sponsor equity, driven purely by debt paydown
options.why: Exit equity value is enterprise value less the debt still outstanding: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore. Against the ₹100 crore the sponsor put in, that is a 2.5x return, and since EBITDA and the multiple never moved, debt paydown alone explains it.
keywords: enterprise value less the debt still outstanding

options.text: 1.5x — treating the ₹150 crore of debt paid down as if it were itself the exit equity value
options.misconception: equates the amount of debt paid down with the exit equity value, instead of computing exit enterprise value less remaining debt
options.why: Debt paid down (400 − 250 = 150) measures how much less is owed, not what the equity is worth. Equity value is what is left after debt: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore, not the ₹150 crore paydown itself.
keywords: measures how much less is owed, not what the equity is worth
Equity value is what is left after debt

options.text: 5.0x — treating the full ₹500 crore exit enterprise value as belonging to the sponsor, with no debt netted off
options.misconception: forgets that debt still outstanding at exit belongs to the lenders, not the sponsor, and credits the whole enterprise value to equity
options.why: ₹250 crore of debt is still owed at exit and comes off the top before anything belongs to the sponsor. 500/100 = 5.0x skips that deduction entirely.
keywords: comes off the top before anything belongs to the sponsor

options.text: 1.0x — measuring the return on the unchanged ₹500 crore enterprise value rather than on the sponsor's equity slice
options.misconception: measures the return on the whole, unchanged enterprise value instead of the sponsor's leveraged equity slice, which is where the paydown accrues
options.why: The enterprise value did stay flat, but the sponsor never owned the whole enterprise — only the ₹100 crore equity slice beneath ₹400 crore of debt. That slice grew to ₹250 crore precisely because the debt above it shrank.
keywords: because the debt above it shrank

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A sponsor buys a company for ₹500 crore, funded with ₹400 crore of debt and ₹100 crore of sponsor equity. Over five years the debt is paid down to ₹250 crore from the company's own cash flow; EBITDA and the exit multiple are unchanged, so the exit enterprise value is again ₹500 crore.

items.stem: What is the portfolio's standard deviation?

options.text: 24.0 per cent, the simple weighted average of the two standard deviations
options.misconception: takes the weighted average of the two standard deviations, which is only correct at perfect positive correlation, ignoring the actual 0.2 correlation's diversification benefit
options.why: 0.6 × 20% + 0.4 × 30% = 24% is what the formula gives only when correlation is +1. At 0.2 the assets do not move together nearly that closely, and the true portfolio risk, 18.6%, sits well below the weighted average.
keywords: sits well below the weighted average

options.text: About 35.3 per cent, plugging the 0.2 correlation directly into the covariance term without multiplying by the two standard deviations
options.misconception: uses the correlation coefficient as if it were the covariance itself, skipping the multiplication by each asset's standard deviation
options.why: The cross term is 2 × wA × wB × ρ × σA × σB, not 2 × wA × wB × ρ alone. Leaving out the two standard deviations inflates the cross term to 0.096 and the standard deviation to ≈35.3%, far above the correctly weighted 18.6%.
keywords: Leaving out the two standard deviations inflates the cross term

options.text: About 18.6 per cent, using the full variance formula with the covariance term at correlation 0.2
About 17.0 per cent, dropping the covariance term as if the assets were uncorrelated
options.misconception: sets the cross term to zero as though correlation were 0, when the stated correlation of 0.2 still contributes a small positive covariance term
options.why: At zero correlation, variance would be just 0.0144 + 0.0144 = 0.0288, giving ≈17.0%. But 0.2 correlation is not zero — it adds a further 0.00576 to variance, lifting the true figure to 18.6%.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: A portfolio holds 60 per cent in Asset A, with a standard deviation of 20 per cent, and 40 per cent in Asset B, with a standard deviation of 30 per cent. The correlation between the two assets is 0.2.

items.stem: Which machine should the plant buy, and on what comparison?

options.text: Machine A, because its capital outlay of ₹9 lakh is lower than Machine B's ₹12 lakh
options.misconception: decides on the purchase price alone, ignoring both the running costs and the number of years each machine serves
options.why: The ₹3 lakh saved on purchase is repaid several times over by ₹30,000 a year of extra running cost and by having to buy again after three years instead of five. Both belong in the comparison, and once they are in, B wins.
keywords: having to buy again after three years instead of five

options.text: Machine B, at about ₹3.31 lakh a year against Machine A's ₹4.24 lakh, dividing each total present value of cost by the number of years
options.misconception: divides the present value by the plain count of years instead of by the annuity factor, dropping the time value that the annuity factor carries
options.why: 12,73,050 / 3 = ₹4,24,350 and 16,54,920 / 5 = ₹3,30,984 both understate the annual charge, because a rupee due in year 5 is not the same rupee as one due in year 1. Dividing by the annuity factor — 2.487 and 3.791 — is what converts a present value back into a level annual amount, giving ₹5.12 lakh and ₹4.37 lakh.
keywords: converts a present value back into a level annual amount

options.text: Machine B, at an equivalent annual cost of about ₹4.37 lakh against Machine A's ₹5.12 lakh
options.why: Machine A's total PV of cost is 9,00,000 + 1,50,000 × 2.487 = ₹12,73,050, and dividing by its own annuity factor gives 12,73,050 / 2.487 ≈ ₹5,11,881 a year. Machine B's is 12,00,000 + 1,20,000 × 3.791 = ₹16,54,920, and 16,54,920 / 3.791 ≈ ₹4,36,539 a year. Because the machine will be replaced indefinitely, the annual charge is the only fair comparison, and B's is about ₹75,000 lower.
keywords: dividing by its own annuity factor
the annual charge is the only fair comparison

options.text: Machine A, because its total present value of cost is ₹12.73 lakh against Machine B's ₹16.55 lakh
options.misconception: compares total present values of assets with unequal lives, which credits the shorter-lived machine for simply carrying fewer years of cost
options.why: Machine A's total is smaller only because it covers three years while B's covers five. Put on the same footing — cost per year of service — A is the dearer of the two at ₹5.12 lakh against ₹4.37 lakh. Totals over different spans are not comparable at all.
keywords: smaller only because it covers three years
Totals over different spans are not comparable

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A plant needs one packing machine and will need one indefinitely. Machine A costs ₹9,00,000, lasts 3 years and runs at ₹1,50,000 a year. Machine B costs ₹12,00,000, lasts 5 years and runs at ₹1,20,000 a year. Neither has any salvage value. The cost of capital is 10 per cent; the annuity factors are 2.487 for 3 years and 3.791 for 5 years.

items.stem: What is the project's adjusted present value, and what does the firm do?

options.text: ₹6 crore, so accept — the ₹12 crore tax shield less ₹1 crore of issue costs outweighs the ₹5 crore base-case shortfall
options.why: The annual tax shield is 40 × 10% × 30% = ₹1.2 crore, and in perpetuity at the 10 per cent cost of debt that is 1.2 / 0.10 = ₹12 crore, which is the same as debt times the tax rate, 40 × 0.30. APV = −5 + 12 − 1 = +₹6 crore, so the financing side effects turn a reject into an accept.
keywords: the same as debt times the tax rate
financing side effects turn a reject into an accept

options.text: ₹7 crore, so accept — base-case NPV of −₹5 crore plus the ₹12 crore tax shield
options.misconception: counts the tax shield but omits the issue costs, taking only the financing side effect that helps
options.why: Issue costs are a financing side effect exactly as the tax shield is, and APV requires every one of them, favourable or not. −5 + 12 − 1 = ₹6 crore, not ₹7 crore.
keywords: Issue costs are a financing side effect
APV requires every one of them, favourable or not

options.text: −₹5 crore, so reject — the base-case NPV is the project's value and financing is a separate matter
options.misconception: stops at the all-equity base case and treats financing side effects as irrelevant to the accept-or-reject decision, which is the one thing APV exists to prevent
options.why: Separating the two halves is not the same as discarding one of them. APV values the project ungeared precisely so the financing benefit can be added explicitly rather than buried in a discount rate — and here that benefit, +₹11 crore net, is what decides the case.
keywords: not the same as discarding one of them
the financing benefit can be added explicitly

options.text: ₹34 crore, so accept — the debt supports ₹40 crore of interest payments in present value terms, less ₹1 crore of issue costs
options.misconception: treats the whole interest payment as the financing benefit instead of only the tax saved on it, valuing a cost as though it were a gain
options.why: Interest of ₹4 crore a year discounted in perpetuity at 10 per cent gives ₹40 crore, and −5 + 40 − 1 = ₹34 crore. But interest is money paid out, not received; the only benefit is the tax it saves, ₹1.2 crore a year, worth ₹12 crore in perpetuity.
keywords: interest is money paid out, not received
the only benefit is the tax it saves

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project needs ₹100 crore. Valued as if it were entirely equity funded, discounted at the ungeared cost of equity, its NPV is −₹5 crore. The firm will fund ₹40 crore of it with perpetual debt at 10 per cent, incurring ₹1 crore of issue costs on that debt. The tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What value per share does the comparable multiple imply?

options.text: ₹50 — enterprise value of ₹400 crore plus net debt of ₹100 crore, over 10 crore shares
options.misconception: reverses the bridge, adding net debt to enterprise value when the direction from EV to equity is to subtract it
options.why: Adding net debt is the bridge run backwards — that is how you get from equity value to enterprise value, not the other way. Starting at EV, the debt comes off: 400 − 100 = ₹300 crore, or ₹30 a share.
keywords: Adding net debt is the bridge run backwards
from equity value to enterprise value, not the other way

options.text: ₹28 — enterprise value of ₹400 crore less debt of ₹120 crore, over 10 crore shares
options.misconception: deducts gross debt without crediting the cash the buyer also acquires, so the company is charged for its borrowings but given no credit for the money sitting against them
options.why: The bridge runs on net debt, not gross. ₹20 crore of cash comes to the buyer along with the ₹120 crore of borrowings, so only ₹100 crore is deducted and the answer is ₹30, not ₹28.
keywords: The bridge runs on net debt, not gross

options.text: ₹30 — enterprise value of ₹400 crore, less net debt of ₹100 crore, over 10 crore shares
options.why: EV = 8 × 50 = ₹400 crore. Net debt = 120 − 20 = ₹100 crore, since the buyer takes on the debt but also acquires the cash. Equity value = 400 − 100 = ₹300 crore, and over 10 crore shares that is ₹30 a share.
keywords: the buyer takes on the debt but also acquires the cash
over 10 crore shares that is ₹30 a share

options.text: ₹40 — the ₹400 crore enterprise value divided by 10 crore shares
options.misconception: treats enterprise value as though it belonged to shareholders, skipping the bridge that removes what belongs to lenders
options.why: An EV/EBITDA multiple prices the whole enterprise — the claims of lenders as well as shareholders. The ₹100 crore of net debt has to come off before anything is divided among shares, giving ₹30, not ₹40.
keywords: come off before anything is divided among shares

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A listed peer of similar size and growth trades at an EV/EBITDA multiple of 8. The company being valued has EBITDA of ₹50 crore, debt of ₹120 crore, cash of ₹20 crore, and 10 crore shares outstanding.

items.stem: What spot rate does relative purchasing power parity expect in one year?

options.text: ₹86.25 per dollar — the rupee depreciating by the ratio of the two inflation rates
options.why: Expected spot = 83 × (1.06 / 1.02) = 83 × 1.0392 ≈ ₹86.25. India's prices rise faster, so the rupee must buy fewer dollars for the same basket to cost the same in either country — the higher-inflation currency is the one PPP expects to weaken.
keywords: the higher-inflation currency is the one PPP expects to weaken

options.text: ₹84.66 per dollar — applying the US 2 per cent inflation to the spot rate
options.misconception: uses the foreign country's inflation rate where the home country's belongs, moving the rate by the wrong one of the two figures
options.why: 83 × 1.02 = ₹84.66 takes the smaller of the two inflation rates on its own. The rate moves on the ratio of both — 1.06 over 1.02 — which is a 3.92 per cent depreciation, not 2 per cent.
keywords: takes the smaller of the two inflation rates on its own
moves on the ratio of both

options.text: ₹79.87 per dollar — the rupee appreciating over the year
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, putting foreign inflation in the numerator, which makes the higher-inflation currency strengthen — the opposite of what purchasing power parity says
options.why: 83 × (1.02 / 1.06) = ₹79.87 is the formula upside down. A currency whose prices rise 6 per cent against another's 2 per cent loses purchasing power, so it depreciates; it cannot strengthen on faster inflation.

options.text: ₹87.98 per dollar — applying India's 6 per cent inflation to the spot rate
options.misconception: adjusts for domestic inflation alone and forgets that US prices are also rising, so the whole gap is charged to the rupee instead of only the differential
options.why: 83 × 1.06 = ₹87.98 assumes American prices stand still. They rise 2 per cent too, so only the 4 per cent gap between the two should move the rate, giving ₹86.25.
keywords: only the 4 per cent gap between the two should move the rate

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: The spot rate is ₹83.00 per US dollar. Expected inflation over the coming year is 6 per cent in India and 2 per cent in the United States.

items.stem: What crosses a border once the group settles by multilateral netting?

options.text: ₹10 lakh — one payment, from C to B
options.why: Netting each company group-wide: A receives 40 + 50 = 90 and pays 60 + 30 = 90, so A is square at zero. B receives 60 + 15 = 75 and pays 40 + 25 = 65, a net receipt of ₹10 lakh. C receives 30 + 25 = 55 and pays 50 + 15 = 65, a net payment of ₹10 lakh. One transfer of ₹10 lakh from C to B settles the whole month, against ₹220 lakh gross.
keywords: One transfer of ₹10 lakh from C to B settles the whole month

options.text: ₹20 lakh — B's net receipt of ₹10 lakh plus C's net payment of ₹10 lakh
options.misconception: adds up every company's net position, counting each transfer twice — once in the payer's figure and once in the receiver's
options.why: B's ₹10 lakh receipt and C's ₹10 lakh payment are the two ends of the same single transfer, not two transfers. The money that actually crosses a border is ₹10 lakh, half the sum of the net positions.
keywords: the two ends of the same single transfer, not two transfers
half the sum of the net positions

options.text: ₹50 lakh — ₹20 lakh from A to B, ₹20 lakh from C to A and ₹10 lakh from B to C
options.misconception: stops at the pairwise stage, which is the correct first step but not the whole procedure; the group-wide pass still has to follow, and it strikes out flows that two companies on their own could never cancel
options.why: Pair by pair, A owes B 20, C owes A 20 and B owes C 10 — ₹50 lakh in three transfers. But A's ₹20 lakh receipt and ₹20 lakh payment cancel exactly, and once they are struck out only ₹10 lakh from C to B remains.
keywords: receipt and ₹20 lakh payment cancel exactly

options.text: ₹220 lakh — netting changes how the balances are recorded, not the amounts that move
options.misconception: treats netting as a bookkeeping presentation rather than a settlement mechanism, when the whole saving is that the offset flows are never converted or transferred at all
options.why: Netting is settled through a central desk, so the offsetting amounts are never converted and never sent. That is precisely where the saving on conversion spread, transfer charges and float comes from: ₹10 lakh moves instead of ₹220 lakh.
keywords: conversion spread, transfer charges and float

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A group has three subsidiaries in three countries. Over the month A owes B ₹60 lakh and B owes A ₹40 lakh; A owes C ₹30 lakh and C owes A ₹50 lakh; B owes C ₹25 lakh and C owes B ₹15 lakh. Settled gross, ₹220 lakh would cross borders.

items.stem: What position in the share does she take, and why that size?

options.text: Sell 600 shares — 0.6 × 1,000, matching the short option position with a short share position
options.misconception: matches the direction of the option position instead of offsetting it, so both legs lose together on a rise rather than cancelling
options.why: A written call already loses on a rise; shorting shares loses again on the same rise. The hedge has to move the other way, which means buying shares, not selling them.
keywords: shorting shares loses again on the same rise

options.text: Buy 600 shares — 0.6 × 1,000, so the shares gain roughly what the written calls lose on a small move
options.why: A written call loses value when the share rises, and it loses ₹0.60 per rupee per share covered. On a ₹1 rise the calls cost her about 0.6 × 1,000 = ₹600, and 600 shares held long gain exactly ₹600. Delta is the hedge ratio, so the hedge is delta times the shares the options cover.
keywords: A written call loses value when the share rises
the hedge is delta times the shares the options cover

options.misconception: uses one minus delta as the hedge ratio, a figure that belongs to no hedge at all
options.why: Delta itself, 0.6, is the hedge ratio. On a ₹1 rise, 400 shares gain ₹400 against about ₹600 lost on the calls, leaving ₹200 of the exposure unhedged.
keywords: Delta itself, 0.6, is the hedge ratio

options.text: Buy 1,000 shares — one share for every share the options cover
options.misconception: hedges one for one, ignoring that the option's value moves by only 60 paise for each rupee the share moves
options.why: On a ₹1 rise, 1,000 shares gain ₹1,000 while the written calls lose only about ₹600 — a ₹400 gain, not a neutral position. Over-hedging leaves exposure just as under-hedging does; it merely points the other way.
keywords: a ₹400 gain, not a neutral position
Over-hedging leaves exposure just as under-hedging does

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A market maker has written 10 call option contracts on a share, each contract covering 100 shares, so 1,000 shares in all. The calls have a delta of 0.6. She wants the position delta neutral against a small move in the share.

items.stem: Which swaption position does that description call for?

options.text: Enter a forward-start swap now, fixing the rate for the five-year period beginning in six months
options.misconception: locks the rate with a binding commitment, which removes the benefit of a fall — the one thing the treasurer said he wanted to keep
options.why: A forward swap is an obligation, not an option, so it does fix his cost but at the price of the upside. He asked to keep the gain if rates fall, and only a bought option keeps it — which is what the premium buys.
keywords: A forward swap is an obligation, not an option
only a bought option keeps it

options.text: Write a payer swaption — collecting the premium on the right for someone else to pay fixed
options.misconception: confuses receiving the premium with buying protection, when the writer holds the obligation and the buyer holds the right
options.why: Writing hands the choice to the counterparty and leaves the treasurer with an obligation he cannot decline. The premium comes in, but so does the exposure: he would be receiving fixed and paying floating just as his own borrowing cost rises.
keywords: Writing hands the choice to the counterparty

options.text: Buy a receiver swaption — the right to enter the swap as the fixed-rate receiver
options.misconception: takes the side that gains when rates fall, which is the opposite of a borrower's exposure
options.why: A receiver swaption pays off when rates fall, which is the very outcome the treasurer is happy to live with unhedged. His risk is rates rising, and only the right to pay fixed covers that.
keywords: A receiver swaption pays off when rates fall
only the right to pay fixed covers that

options.text: Buy a payer swaption — the right, not the obligation, to enter the five-year swap as the fixed-rate payer
options.why: Paying fixed and receiving floating is what converts a floating loan into a fixed one, so the right to pay fixed is the protection he wants. Buying it, rather than writing it, gives him the right and leaves the choice with him: exercise if rates rose, walk away and borrow floating if they fell. The premium is what that choice costs.
keywords: converts a floating loan into a fixed one
Buying it, rather than writing it, gives him the right

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer has agreed to draw a five-year floating-rate loan six months from now. He wants protection if rates have risen by then, but wants to be free to borrow at the floating rate if they have fallen instead — and he is prepared to pay a premium for that freedom.

items.stem: What does the CPPI rule require the fund to do now?

options.text: Sell ₹12 lakh of equities, cutting the equity holding from ₹48 lakh to ₹36 lakh
options.why: Equities fall to 60 × 0.8 = ₹48 lakh, so the portfolio is 48 + 40 = ₹88 lakh. The cushion is now 88 − 70 = ₹18 lakh and the target equity holding is 2 × 18 = ₹36 lakh. Holding ₹48 lakh, the fund sells ₹12 lakh. CPPI sells into a fall, which is exactly how the floor survives a deeper one.

options.text: Buy ₹4.8 lakh of equities, restoring the original 60:40 split of the ₹88 lakh portfolio
options.misconception: applies constant-mix rebalancing, which restores a fixed percentage split and therefore buys into a fall, where CPPI's cushion rule sells into it
options.why: 0.6 × 88 = ₹52.8 lakh against ₹48 lakh held would mean buying ₹4.8 lakh. That is constant mix, a different discipline with no floor in it. CPPI's target comes from the cushion, and it says sell ₹12 lakh.
keywords: That is constant mix, a different discipline with no floor in it
CPPI's target comes from the cushion

options.text: Nothing — the equity holding is already down to ₹48 lakh from ₹60 lakh, below where it started
options.misconception: treats the opening rupee allocation as the target and holds through the move, which is buy-and-hold rather than any rebalancing rule
options.why: CPPI recomputes the target after every move; the opening ₹60 lakh has no standing once the portfolio is worth ₹88 lakh. The new target is 2 × (88 − 70) = ₹36 lakh, so ₹12 lakh must go.
keywords: recomputes the target after every move
the opening ₹60 lakh has no standing

options.text: Sell ₹30 lakh of equities, cutting the equity holding to ₹18 lakh
options.misconception: sets the equity holding equal to the cushion itself and drops the multiplier from the formula
options.why: ₹18 lakh is the cushion, not the equity target. The rule is multiplier times cushion, 2 × 18 = ₹36 lakh, so the sale is ₹12 lakh. Selling ₹30 lakh would de-risk far below what the floor requires and give up the recovery.
keywords: is the cushion, not the equity target
The rule is multiplier times cushion

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: A fund runs constant proportion portfolio insurance with a floor of ₹70 lakh and a multiplier of 2. It starts at ₹100 lakh, so ₹60 lakh sits in equities and ₹40 lakh in treasury bills. Equities then fall 20 per cent; ignore interest on the bills over the period.

items.stem: Which securities enter the optimal portfolio under Sharpe's single index model?

options.text: All four — every security has an expected return above the risk-free rate
options.misconception: uses a positive excess return as the admission test, ignoring the cut-off rate entirely
options.why: Beating the risk-free rate is not the standard. Q's ratio of 4.0 is positive but sits below the 4.5 per cent cut-off, which means adding Q would pull the portfolio's own reward-to-risk below where P, R and S leave it.
keywords: Beating the risk-free rate is not the standard
pull the portfolio's own reward-to-risk below

options.text: P alone — the security with the highest excess return to beta
options.misconception: treats the ranking as a contest the top name wins, when the cut-off rate is a threshold that admits every security standing above it
options.why: Ranking is only the first step; the cut-off then decides how far down the list to go. Three of the four clear 4.5 per cent, and leaving R and S out abandons the diversification the model is built to capture.
keywords: Ranking is only the first step
the cut-off then decides how far down the list to go

options.text: P, R and S — every security whose excess return to beta clears 4.5 per cent
options.why: The ratios are P (18 − 6)/1.5 = 8.0, Q (14 − 6)/2.0 = 4.0, R (12 − 6)/1.0 = 6.0 and S (10 − 6)/0.8 = 5.0. P, R and S are all above the 4.5 per cent cut-off and go in; Q at 4.0 is below it and stays out, despite having the second-highest expected return of the four.
keywords: all above the 4.5 per cent cut-off and go in
Q at 4.0 is below it and stays out

options.text: P and Q — the two securities with the highest expected returns
options.misconception: ranks on raw expected return instead of on excess return per unit of beta, so a security is credited for a high return without being charged for the risk that produced it
options.why: Q's 14 per cent comes on a beta of 2.0, so it earns only 4.0 per cent of excess return per unit of beta — the worst of the four. R at 12 per cent and S at 10 per cent both buy their returns more cheaply, at 6.0 and 5.0, and both belong ahead of Q.
keywords: excess return per unit of beta

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: The risk-free rate is 6 per cent. Four securities are under consideration — P, expected return 18 per cent and beta 1.5; Q, expected return 14 per cent and beta 2.0; R, expected return 12 per cent and beta 1.0; S, expected return 10 per cent and beta 0.8. The cut-off rate for this set has been computed as 4.5 per cent.

items.stem: Which form of restructuring is this?

options.text: An equity carve-out, since a new company has been floated around the division
options.misconception: confuses a pro rata distribution to existing shareholders with a sale of a minority stake to new outside investors
options.why: A carve-out sells part of the subsidiary's equity to outside investors and raises cash for the parent while the parent keeps control. Neither happens here: no new investor comes in and not a rupee is raised.
keywords: sells part of the subsidiary's equity to outside investors

options.text: A reverse merger, since a new listed entity has come into existence
options.misconception: mistakes a route to a stock market listing for a way of separating a division
options.why: A reverse merger is a private company merging into an existing listed shell to get listed without an offer. Nothing merges here — one company becomes two, and the direction is the opposite.
keywords: merging into an existing listed shell
one company becomes two, and the direction is the opposite

options.text: A sell-off, since the division has been separated from the parent
options.misconception: assumes any separation of a division must be a sale, when a sell-off requires a third-party buyer paying consideration
options.why: A sell-off transfers the division to an outside buyer and brings cash into the parent. Here there is no buyer at all and no consideration — the division goes to the people who already owned it.
keywords: transfers the division to an outside buyer

options.text: A demerger — the same shareholders now hold two separately priced companies instead of one
options.why: The defining marks are all present: shares go to the parent's own shareholders pro rata, there is no buyer and no consideration, and no cash moves. Ownership of the underlying businesses is unchanged in substance; what changes is that the market can now price the chemicals business on its own terms rather than inside a conglomerate discount.
keywords: shares go to the parent's own shareholders pro rata

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A conglomerate separates its chemicals division into a newly incorporated company. Every existing shareholder of the parent receives shares in the new company in proportion to the holding they already have. No outside investor subscribes, the parent receives no consideration, and no cash enters or leaves the group.

items.stem: At what premium or discount is the depository receipt trading?

options.text: A premium of 315 per cent, the ₹3,320 receipt against the ₹800 share price
options.misconception: compares the receipt with a single share and ignores the ratio, so the receipt looks four times dearer than it is
options.why: One receipt is a claim on four shares, not one. The comparison has to be receipt against 4 × ₹800 = ₹3,200, which gives 3.75 per cent. Against a single share the figure is 3,320/800 − 1 = 315 per cent, and it measures nothing.
keywords: One receipt is a claim on four shares, not one
The comparison has to be receipt against 4 × ₹800

options.text: A premium of 3.61 per cent, the ₹120 gap against the ₹3,320 receipt price
options.misconception: divides the premium by the receipt's own price instead of by the value of the underlying shares the premium is measured against
options.why: 120 / 3,320 = 3.61 per cent answers a different question — what share of the receipt's price the gap is. The premium is measured against what the receipt is a claim on, ₹3,200, giving 3.75 per cent.
keywords: measured against what the receipt is a claim on

options.text: A premium of ₹120 per receipt, or 3.75 per cent over the underlying shares
options.why: Four underlying shares are worth 4 × 800 = ₹3,200. The receipt converts to 40 × 83 = ₹3,320. The gap is ₹120, and measured against the ₹3,200 the receipt is a claim on, that is 120 / 3,200 = 3.75 per cent — the receipt is the dearer side.
keywords: the receipt is the dearer side

options.text: A discount of 3.75 per cent, since ₹3,200 is less than ₹3,320
options.misconception: computes the gap correctly but reads its direction backwards, calling the more expensive side the discounted one
options.why: The receipt costs ₹3,320 for what is worth ₹3,200 in Mumbai, so the receipt is dear, not cheap — a premium. Whoever pays more is paying the premium, and here that is the buyer of the receipt.
keywords: the receipt is dear, not cheap
Whoever pays more is paying the premium

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company's share trades at ₹800 on the domestic exchange. Its depository receipt trades abroad at $40.00, and one receipt represents four underlying shares. The spot rate is ₹83 per dollar.

items.stem: What is EPS after the buyback?

options.text: ₹11.11 — profit of ₹1,000 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.misconception: counts the benefit of the buyback, the reduced share count, but not its cost, the after-tax income the cash was earning
options.why: The cash did not leave without taking its earnings with it. ₹84 lakh of after-tax income goes when the ₹1,500 lakh goes, so the numerator is ₹916 lakh, not ₹1,000 lakh, and EPS is ₹10.18 rather than ₹11.11.
keywords: did not leave without taking its earnings with it
the numerator is ₹916 lakh, not ₹1,000 lakh

options.text: ₹9.78 — profit of ₹880 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.misconception: deducts the forgone interest gross of tax, forgetting that the company was only ever keeping 70 paise in the rupee of it
options.why: The gross ₹120 lakh was taxed at 30 per cent, so only ₹84 lakh ever reached profit after tax. Charging the full ₹120 lakh double-counts the tax and understates EPS: the right numerator is ₹916 lakh, giving ₹10.18.
keywords: only ₹84 lakh ever reached profit after tax
double-counts the tax and understates EPS

options.text: ₹9.16 — profit of ₹916 lakh over 100 lakh shares
options.misconception: charges the cost of the buyback but leaves the share count untouched, which is the one thing a buyback certainly changes
options.why: Ten lakh shares have been cancelled, so 90 lakh remain. Dividing the correctly reduced profit by the old count shows only the cost and none of the benefit, turning a small rise into a fall.
keywords: by the old count shows only the cost and none of the benefit
turning a small rise into a fall

options.text: ₹10.18 — profit of ₹916 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.why: The ₹1,500 lakh of cash was earning 1,500 × 8% = ₹120 lakh before tax, or 120 × 0.7 = ₹84 lakh after tax, and that income is now gone. Profit falls to 1,000 − 84 = ₹916 lakh and the share count falls to 90 lakh, giving 916 / 90 = ₹10.18. The smaller share count outweighs the lost income, so EPS rises slightly.
keywords: The smaller share count outweighs the lost income

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company earns profit after tax of ₹1,000 lakh on 100 lakh shares, so EPS is ₹10. It buys back 10 lakh shares at ₹150 each, paying ₹1,500 lakh out of surplus cash that had been earning 8 per cent a year before tax. The tax rate is 30 per cent, and nothing else changes.

items.stem: What is the conversion premium, and what is the debenture's floor value?

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹80, with a floor of ₹880
options.misconception: measures the premium against the straight bond value rather than the conversion value, so it reports the downside cushion instead of what conversion costs
options.why: 960 − 880 = ₹80 is the premium over the straight bond value, and it answers a different question — how far the price can fall before the bond floor catches it. The conversion premium is measured against what the shares fetch on conversion, ₹840, and it is ₹120.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹160, with a floor of ₹880
options.misconception: takes the ₹1,000 face value as the debenture's price, when the premium is measured from the market price actually paid
options.why: 1,000 − 840 = ₹160 uses face value where the market price belongs. The buyer gives up ₹960 today, not ₹1,000, so the conversion premium is ₹120. Face value matters at redemption; it is not what anyone pays now.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹120, with a floor of ₹840
options.misconception: takes the conversion value as the floor, when the floor is whichever of the conversion value and the straight bond value is higher — and here the bond value is
options.why: The premium is right and the floor is not. Conversion value of ₹840 acts as a floor only while it exceeds the straight bond value. Here the bond alone is worth ₹880, and that claim survives whatever the share does, so ₹880 is the floor.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹120, or 14.29 per cent, with a floor of ₹880
options.why: The conversion value is 20 × ₹42 = ₹840, so the conversion premium is 960 − 840 = ₹120, which is 120 / 840 = 14.29 per cent over conversion value. The floor is the higher of the two lower bounds: the straight bond value of ₹880 stands above the conversion value of ₹840, so a holder who never converts still has an ₹880 claim and the debenture will not sensibly trade below it.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A convertible debenture of ₹1,000 face value converts into 20 equity shares. The share trades at ₹42. A non-convertible debenture of the same issuer, coupon and maturity would be worth ₹880. The convertible itself trades at ₹960.
