The net asset figure of ₹80 crore is what the business is worth broken up; a going concern earning ₹12 crore a year is worth what those earnings support, ₹120 crore. Taking the lower of the two by habit would hand the buyer the goodwill for nothing.

options.text: Net assets ₹80 crore and capitalised earnings ₹120 crore, the ₹40 crore gap being goodwill
options.why: The net asset method gives 120 − 40 = ₹80 crore, what the assets would realise less what is owed. The earnings method gives 12 / 0.10 = ₹120 crore, the maintainable profit capitalised at the rate for the risk. The ₹40 crore between them is goodwill — what the business earns over and above what its assets on their own would justify, and the reason a going concern is worth more than a breaking-up one.

options.text: Net assets ₹80 crore and capitalised earnings ₹1.20 crore
options.misconception: multiplies the maintainable profit by the capitalisation rate instead of dividing by it, which values a permanent income stream at a tenth of one year of it
options.why: 12 × 0.10 = ₹1.20 crore multiplies the maintainable profit by the rate. Capitalising means asking what sum, earning 10 per cent, would produce ₹12 crore a year — which is 12 / 0.10 = ₹120 crore. The answer must be far larger than one year's profit, never a fraction of it, and a figure below the annual earnings is the signal that the division has been inverted.

options.text: Both ₹120 crore, since the assets and the earnings agree
options.misconception: reads the gross asset figure as the value of the business, forgetting that the lenders are paid before the shareholders see anything
options.why: The ₹120 crore of assets is not the shareholders' to keep — ₹40 crore of it answers to the creditors, so the net asset method gives ₹80 crore. That it coincides with the capitalised earnings figure of ₹120 crore is a coincidence of these numbers, and treating them as agreeing hides the ₹40 crore of goodwill sitting between the two.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company's assets would realise ₹120 crore and it owes ₹40 crore. It earns a maintainable profit after tax of ₹12 crore a year, and the capitalisation rate for a business of this kind is 10 per cent. It is being sold as a going concern.

items.stem: What separates internal credit enhancement from external?

options.text: Credit enhancement lifts the rating of every tranche in the deal equally
options.misconception: reads enhancement as adding safety to the whole structure, when subordination lifts the senior paper precisely by pushing loss onto the junior paper below it
options.why: Subordination moves risk about rather than adding safety. The senior tranche is rated higher because the junior tranches stand in front of it, and those junior tranches are rated lower for the same reason. What lifts one class is what depresses another, so an equal lift across the deal is not what happens.

options.text: An external guarantee makes the senior paper risk-free, since the guarantor rather than the pool stands behind it
options.misconception: forgets that an external enhancement substitutes the guarantor's credit standing for part of the pool's and can never be better than the guarantor
options.why: A guarantee is only as good as the guarantor. External enhancement swaps part of the pool's risk for the credit standing of the party giving the guarantee or the letter of credit, so the paper is capped by that party's own rating and falls with it. That dependence is the standing objection to external enhancement and the reason internal devices are preferred.

options.text: Internal enhancement uses the deal's own material — a pool larger than the paper issued, junior tranches, excess spread and a cash collateral account; external enhancement is a third party's promise, such as a guarantee or a letter of credit
options.why: Internal credit enhancement is built out of the transaction itself. Overcollateralisation transfers a pool worth more than the paper issued, junior tranches take loss first, excess spread is the surplus of pool interest over what the paper pays, and a cash collateral account is money set aside inside the structure. External enhancement brings in a third party by guarantee or letter of credit, and the paper then depends on that party staying solvent.

options.text: Overcollateralisation means the vehicle holds cash equal to the securities it has issued
options.misconception: confuses overcollateralisation with a cash reserve, when it means the receivables transferred are worth more than the paper issued against them
options.why: Overcollateralisation is about the pool, not about cash. Receivables worth more than the securities issued are transferred to the vehicle, so ordinary losses are absorbed by the surplus before any investor is touched. Cash set aside is a separate device, the cash collateral account, and holding cash equal to the paper would defeat the purpose of raising it.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An originator wants the senior paper from a securitisation rated above its own corporate rating, and is offered several ways of achieving it.

items.stem: What has the plan produced?

options.text: 1,000 units at an average cost of ₹24.75
options.misconception: buys the same number of units each month rather than investing the same sum, which lands the investor exactly on the simple average of the prices
options.why: Buying 250 units a month gives 1,000 units for 250 × (30 + 25 + 20 + 24) = ₹24,750, an average cost of ₹24.75. That is the simple average of the prices, and it is what a fixed number of units produces. A fixed sum buys more units when the price is low, which is what drags the average cost down to ₹24.24.

options.text: 990 units, and the plan cannot lose, because buying more units when prices fall guarantees a gain
options.misconception: mistakes a lower average cost for a guaranteed profit, when averaging only beats the simple average of the prices and does nothing to make the price recover
options.why: What averaging guarantees is that the average cost, ₹24.24, comes out below the simple average of the prices paid, ₹24.75. It guarantees nothing about where the price ends up. Here it ends at ₹24, below the average cost, and the plan is ₹240 down despite the averaging having worked exactly as advertised.

options.text: 990 units at an average cost of about ₹24.24, and a holding worth ₹23,760 — a loss of ₹240
options.why: The instalments buy 6,000 / 30 = 200 units, then 240, then 300, then 250 — 990 units in all for ₹24,000, an average cost of 24,000 / 990 = ₹24.24. That is below the simple average of the four net asset values, (30 + 25 + 20 + 24) / 4 = ₹24.75, because more units were bought when the price was low. At ₹24 the holding is worth 990 × 24 = ₹23,760, so the plan is ₹240 down.

options.text: 990 units, and the investor is ahead, since the closing value of ₹24 is above the ₹20 paid at the low point
options.misconception: judges the plan against its best instalment rather than against the average cost of all four
options.why: The ₹20 instalment was one of four. What the investor paid on the whole holding is the average cost of ₹24.24, and the closing net asset value of ₹24 is below it, so he is ₹240 down. Measuring against the cheapest purchase would make almost every plan look successful.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor puts ₹6,000 into a scheme on the first of each month for four months. The net asset values on those four dates are ₹30, ₹25, ₹20 and ₹24, and the value on the last of them is also the value at which the holding stands today.

items.stem: How does the loss fall under each form of consideration?

options.text: Under the cash deal Q Ltd's shareholders lose ₹11.25 crore of the price they were promised
options.misconception: attaches the share exchange's loss to the cash alternative, when a cash price is fixed on signing and the seller has no further exposure to the outcome
options.why: ₹11.25 crore is what Q Ltd's shareholders lose under the share exchange, where they still own a slice of the combined company. Under the cash deal they were paid ₹180 crore and walked away, so whatever happens afterwards is nothing to do with them and the entire ₹30 crore falls on P Ltd's shareholders.

options.text: The two are identical, since both hand Q Ltd's shareholders ₹180 crore
options.misconception: reads the share offer as a fixed amount, when it is a fixed proportion whose value moves with whatever the combined company turns out to be worth
options.why: The two are identical only if the combined company really is worth ₹800 crore. Cash fixes an amount; a share exchange fixes a proportion, and 22.5 per cent of ₹750 crore is ₹168.75 crore rather than ₹180 crore. The moment the outcome differs from the forecast the two forms of consideration part company.

options.text: Under the share exchange P Ltd's shareholders bear the whole ₹50 crore shortfall, since shares once issued cannot be taken back
options.misconception: reverses the effect of issuing shares, which is precisely what makes the incoming shareholders share the disappointment rather than escape it
options.why: Issuing shares is what spreads the loss. Q Ltd's shareholders now own 22.5 per cent of the combined company, so 22.5 per cent of every rupee of disappointment is theirs — ₹11.25 crore of it. P Ltd's shareholders carry ₹18.75 crore. It is the cash deal, where nothing is shared, that leaves the acquirer holding the whole ₹30 crore.

options.text: Under cash P Ltd's shareholders lose the whole ₹30 crore; under the share exchange they lose ₹18.75 crore and Q Ltd's shareholders lose ₹11.25 crore
options.why: With cash, Q Ltd's shareholders take ₹180 crore and go, leaving P Ltd's shareholders with 750 − 180 = ₹570 crore against ₹600 crore standalone, a loss of ₹30 crore. Under the share exchange, Q Ltd's shareholders hold 22.5 per cent of ₹750 crore, that is ₹168.75 crore, so they lose ₹11.25 crore of the ₹180 crore forecast, and P Ltd's shareholders keep ₹581.25 crore and lose ₹18.75 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: P Ltd is worth ₹600 crore on its own and Q Ltd ₹150 crore on its own. P Ltd forecasts a combined value of ₹800 crore. It offers Q Ltd's shareholders either ₹180 crore in cash, or shares giving them 22.5 per cent of the combined company — which on the forecast is also worth ₹180 crore. In the event no synergy at all arrives and the combined company is worth only ₹750 crore.

items.stem: How does the study material classify the two approaches?

options.text: The first is technical analysis and the second is fundamental analysis
options.misconception: swaps the two labels
options.why: The labels run the other way round. Reading growth, inflation, an industry's demand and a company's margins is fundamental analysis; reading a chart of price and traded volume is technical analysis.

options.text: Both are technical analysis, since both work from published data
options.misconception: separates the two by where the number was published rather than by what the number is about
options.why: Fundamental analysis uses published financial and economic data; technical analysis uses market data alone — price, volume and open interest. What separates them is the subject matter, not whether somebody printed the figures.

options.text: Only the first is analysis; the second is guesswork with no stated method
options.misconception: dismisses technical analysis instead of describing it
options.why: Technical analysis has three stated principles — the market discounts everything, price moves in trends, and history tends to repeat itself — and the study material sets it out as one of the two approaches to security analysis. Whether it works is a separate argument from what it is.

options.text: The first is fundamental analysis and the second is technical analysis
options.why: Fundamental analysis works from the economy to the industry to the company to reach an intrinsic value, and recommends buying where the market price sits below it. Technical analysis reads price and volume alone, on the assumptions that price discounts everything, that prices move in trends and that history tends to repeat itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: Two analysts study the same share. The first works through the country's growth rate and inflation, then the industry's demand supply gap, then the company's margins and net worth. The second looks only at a chart of the share's daily price and traded volume over two years.

items.stem: Which type of risk does this illustrate?

options.text: Compliance risk
options.misconception: reaches for the regulatory label wherever a company suffers a loss
options.why: Compliance risk is the risk of failing the rules and regulations a business must live under, and it bites hardest when a company enters a new state or a new line of business under laws it does not know. No rule was broken here.

options.text: Financial risk
options.misconception: calls the money consequence the risk itself
options.why: Financial risk is unexpected change in financial conditions — prices, exchange rates, interest rates, credit standing. The collapse in sales is what the strategic failure cost, not a movement in a financial variable.

options.text: Strategic risk
options.why: Strategic risk is a strategy becoming less effective so the company struggles to reach its goals — technological change, a new competitor, a shift in customer demand. Shelving its own digital camera is the study material's own worked example of exactly this.

options.text: Operational risk
options.misconception: files a failure of direction under a failure of daily running
options.why: Operational risk is people and process going wrong in the day-to-day running — the clerk who pays ₹1,00,000 where ₹10,000 was due. Nothing in the running failed here; the running was fine and the direction was not.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A camera maker builds a working digital camera in its own laboratory and shelves it, because selling it would eat into the film business that pays for everything. Ten years on, rivals sell digital cameras, film sales collapse and the company never recovers.

items.stem: Which structure fits?

options.text: An interval scheme
options.misconception: reads a periodic window as continuous access
options.why: An interval scheme opens for purchase and redemption only during pre-specified intervals — monthly, quarterly, annually. Between those windows the investor is locked in, and "at any time" is precisely what he said he needed.

options.text: An open-ended scheme
options.why: An open-ended scheme lets the investor enter and exit at any time. Its capital is unlimited and its redemption period indefinite, and the fund itself buys the units back at a price based on NAV — which is both conditions he asked for.
keywords: enter and exit at any time

options.text: Any of the three, since every mutual fund buys its own units back on demand
options.misconception: assumes redemption on demand is a feature of all mutual funds
options.why: Only the open-ended structure buys its own units back on demand. That single difference is what the functional classification of mutual funds is drawn on, and it is why the question has an answer at all.

options.text: A close-ended scheme
options.misconception: treats a listing on an exchange as the same thing as redemption by the fund
options.why: A close-ended scheme has a fixed life and a fixed corpus. Before maturity the only way out is to sell to another buyer on the stock exchange at whatever the market offers, which can sit well below NAV. The fund is not the counterparty.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor says he may need his money at any time and wants a scheme that will buy his units back itself, at a price tied to the value of what the fund holds.

items.stem: Which source of startup finance is built for exactly this position?

options.text: Crowdfunding
options.misconception: picks the best-known modern source instead of the one that matches the shortage
options.why: Crowdfunding gathers small amounts of capital from a large number of individuals through social media and crowdfunding websites to finance a new business initiative. It funds an idea over weeks of campaigning; it does not put material into a supplier's hands against one confirmed order.

options.text: Purchase order financing
options.why: Purchase order financing exists for the startup that has found a large new order and lacks the cash to produce and deliver against it. The financier advances the funds directly to the supplier so the goods can be made, and is repaid out of the transaction the order completes.

options.text: Microloans
options.misconception: takes a small-ticket source to a need sized by the order
options.why: Microloans are small loans given at lower interest rates by an individual, or by several individuals each contributing a portion. The small size is the whole point of them, and an order large enough for the bank to refuse is not what they are for.

options.text: Factoring of accounts receivable
options.misconception: funds money already earned when what is needed is money for production not yet done
options.why: Factoring advances most of an amount already outstanding on a credit sale and pays the balance when the customer settles. Here nothing has been delivered, so there is no receivable to sell — the cash is needed before the invoice can exist.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A two-year-old manufacturer has just won its largest ever order from a retail chain. It has no cash to buy the raw material and produce the goods, and the bank has refused a working capital limit for want of a track record. Nothing has been delivered and no invoice has been raised.

items.stem: What do the two findings together say about this market's efficiency?

options.text: Semi-strong efficient, but not weak form efficient
options.misconception: treats the three forms as independent tests rather than nested ones
options.why: The levels nest. Semi-strong includes everything the weak form covers, because past prices are themselves public information, so no market can pass the higher test and fail the lower one. This combination cannot exist.

options.text: Nothing, since efficiency is about whether prices are fair and not about whether anyone can profit
options.misconception: separates efficiency from the returns it is actually defined by
options.why: Efficiency is tested exactly by whether abnormal returns can be earned from a stated set of information after adjusting for risk. That is what the serial correlation, run and filter rule tests measure at the weak level, and what the announcement studies measure at the semi-strong level.

options.text: Strong form efficient
options.misconception: jumps to the top level on evidence about the bottom one
options.why: Strong form efficiency means price reflects all information, private as well as public, so even corporate insiders would earn nothing extra. The finding here is that even public information still pays, which is two levels short of that.

options.text: Weak form efficient, but not semi-strong efficient
options.why: Weak form efficiency means price already reflects everything in the record of past prices and volumes, so chart study pays nothing — which is the first finding. The semi-strong level adds all other publicly available information, and an earnings announcement is public, so a trader still profiting from it says that level has not been reached.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A researcher finds two things in the same market. A trader who studies past price charts and volumes earns nothing above the market after adjusting for risk. A trader who acts on an earnings announcement in the minutes after it is published still earns an abnormal return.

items.stem: What did the analysis leave out?

options.text: The economy and industry stages, which come before company analysis
options.why: Fundamental analysis is three concentric circles worked from the outside in — economy analysis, then industry analysis, then company analysis. A company's fortunes are tied to its industry and the industry's to the economy, so a contracting economy and a demand supply gap in the industry sink a good company along with a bad one.

options.text: Nothing — a low price earnings ratio against peers is a complete case on its own
options.misconception: treats one ratio as the whole of company analysis
options.why: The study material warns that the price earnings ratio should in theory be alike for two similar companies and in practice never is, and that EPS cannot be the sole basis of an investment decision. A low multiple is a question to be answered, not the answer.

options.text: The quality of management, which is the only company factor that matters
options.misconception: elevates one company-level factor above the framework it belongs to
options.why: Quality of management is one company-level factor among many — net worth, growth record, competitive advantage, corporate governance, marketability of the shares — and it is the one thing the analyst did look at. Naming it as the answer leaves the economy and the industry out for a second time.

options.text: Technical analysis, since a price chart would have shown the fall coming
options.misconception: replaces the missing layers of one method with a different method altogether
options.why: A chart might well have shown a downtrend, but the gap sits inside fundamental analysis itself — two of its three layers were never worked. Technical analysis is the alternative approach, not the missing stage of this one.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: An analyst decides a company is well run and cheap on its price earnings ratio against its peers, and buys. The economy is contracting and the industry is running with heavy surplus capacity. The share falls anyway.

items.stem: What does the advanced role of the CFO now cover?

options.text: Nothing beyond that list, which already describes the whole role
options.misconception: keeps the CFO inside the role the material calls traditional
options.why: Governance, compliance, controls and business ethics are named as the traditional role and are still carried. The point of the chapter is what has been added on top of them, driven by globalisation, the growth of information and communications, and the pandemic.

options.text: A new objective, since wealth maximisation for shareholders is no longer the goal
options.misconception: reads a widened job as a changed objective
options.why: Wealth maximisation is still the objective. What the chapter says has changed is the range of responsibilities used to reach it, and it adds that the value creation is now expected to be sustainable over a longer period. The goal held still; the work did not.

options.text: Day-to-day marketing and product design, since finance pays for them
options.misconception: stretches the expanded role into functions the material never gives it
options.why: The expansion named is into risk, the supply chain, mergers and sustainability financing — places where money is the deciding constraint. Funding a function is not running it, and the chapter puts marketing at the functional level of strategy rather than on the CFO's desk.

options.text: The risk management framework, the financial viability of the supply chain, mergers and restructuring, and ESG financing
options.why: The four areas the role has grown into are the overall risk management framework of the organisation, the financial viability of the supply chain, mergers and corporate restructuring, and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) financing — the shift from traditional financing to sustainability financing. Together they make the CFO a leader in value creation.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: A board is rewriting its CFO's job description after the pandemic. It already lists governance, compliance, controls, business ethics and financial reporting, and asks what the study material says has been added to that in recent years.

items.stem: What does a technical analyst expect near ₹125, and what would a clean move above it mean?

options.text: A move above ₹125 confirms the range, so the share should return towards ₹100
options.misconception: treats a breakout as evidence that the old band still holds
options.why: A breach is the evidence against the range, not for it. Once the price passes the resistance level convincingly, the analyst stops expecting the old band and starts looking for newer levels to form.

options.text: Selling pressure at ₹125, which is the resistance level; a clean breach signals a departure from the range and an attempt at new levels
options.why: The peak a price falls away from becomes the resistance level, because every holder who failed to sell at the high is keen to liquidate there. The trough it rebounds from becomes the support level. A breach of either indicates a distinct departure from the status quo and an attempt to set newer levels.

options.text: Nothing in particular, since support and resistance are one line described twice
options.misconception: collapses two levels doing opposite jobs into a single idea
options.why: They are two different prices doing opposite work. ₹100 is the support level below, where buying appears; ₹125 is the resistance level above, where selling appears. The price is expected to travel between them.

options.text: Buying pressure at ₹125, since a rising price draws buyers in
options.misconception: reads momentum into a level the pattern says is made of supply
options.why: Momentum is not what the level is built from. ₹125 is where the holders who wish they had sold last time will sell, and that supply is exactly what has turned the price back before.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A share fell from a peak of ₹125, traded down to ₹100 and rebounded, and for two months has moved between those two prices. It is now at ₹123 and rising.

items.stem: Which obstacle is this, and what does the study material say about it?

options.text: Lack of standardisation, of which the duty is a symptom
options.misconception: relabels a tax cost as a documentation problem
options.why: Lack of standardisation is that every originator follows its own format for documentation and administration, so no two deals read alike and each has to be understood from scratch. It slows the market; it is not what a stamp office charges for.

options.text: Stamp duty, and a pass through certificate escapes it because it evidences a receivable rather than a debt
options.why: Stamp duty on a mortgage debt under the Transfer of Property Act is named first among the problems holding securitisation back in India. The material adds that a pass through certificate does not evidence any debt but only a receivable, so it is exempt, and that some states have reduced the duty on securitised instruments.

options.text: Ineffective foreclosure laws, which are the reason the duty is charged
options.misconception: joins two separate obstacles into a cause and an effect
options.why: Foreclosure laws are a separate item on the same list. Weak ones make it hard for a lender to take the property when a borrower defaults, which makes mortgage backed securities less attractive to investors. They have nothing to do with why a transfer attracts duty.

options.text: Taxation, and the SPV will certainly be taxed as an entity on the pool's whole income
options.misconception: turns an unsettled tax question into a settled rule
options.why: Taxation is on the list precisely because it is unsettled. There is no specific provision for securitised instruments, and expert opinion divides between taxing the SPV in a representative capacity and taxing the investors on their share. Certainty is what nobody has here.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: A finance company in India wants to securitise a pool of housing loans. Its counsel warns that transferring the mortgage debt to the special purpose vehicle will attract a duty running into double digits as a percentage in some states, and asks whether the instrument chosen changes that.

items.stem: At which level of strategy does each decision sit?

options.text: All three are corporate, because the group board approved all three
options.misconception: reads the level of strategy off who signed rather than off what was decided
options.why: The level is a property of the question, not of the approver. Senior management decides strategy, middle management tactics and line management operations, but a board approving a departmental system does not turn that system into a decision about which businesses to be in.

options.text: Corporate, functional and business unit, in that order
options.misconception: swaps the last two levels
options.why: Pricing against a rival to hold share is competitive advantage for one unit's products, which is business unit level. A treasury system is a departmental process, which is functional level. Reversing them puts a departmental process above a competitive decision.

options.text: Corporate, business unit and functional, in that order
options.why: Corporate level strategy selects the businesses a company competes in and coordinates that portfolio, so cement against chemicals is corporate. Business unit level strategy is about sustaining competitive advantage for one unit's products, which is the paints pricing question. Functional level strategy sits in the operating divisions and departments, and a treasury system is exactly that.

options.text: Business unit, business unit and functional, since a group of divisions has no corporate level
options.misconception: denies the corporate level to a group that is organised into divisions
options.why: The corporate level is exactly what a group of several divisions has, and its whole job is which businesses to be in and how the portfolio fits together. Selling one division to enter a different industry is that decision and no other.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: One group board meeting settles three things. Whether to sell the cement division and enter speciality chemicals. How the paints unit should price against its nearest rival to hold share. Whether the treasury department should move to a new cash-pooling system.

items.stem: How does the Dow Theory classify the three, and what can it tell the investor?

options.text: The four-week fall ended the bull market, because the direction reversed
options.misconception: reads a secondary movement as a change in the primary one
options.why: A secondary movement is opposite in direction to the primary by definition — that is what makes it a correction rather than a reversal. Under the theory the trend turns when successive highs and successive lows are both lower, not when one four-week fall happens.

options.text: Primary movement, secondary movement and daily fluctuations — and it gives direction only, never how far
options.why: The primary movement is the main trend, running from a year to thirty-six months or longer, and it is what bull or bear names. The secondary movement is shorter and runs opposite to it. The daily fluctuations are the narrow day-to-day moves. The theory's stated purpose is to say where the market is and where it is going, although not how far or high.

options.text: It will give the level the index should reach before the primary movement ends
options.misconception: expects a magnitude from a theory that offers only direction
options.why: The theory determines where the market is and where it is going, and the material says plainly that it does not say how far or high. Direction without magnitude is the limit of what it claims, and reading a target out of it is reading something that is not there.

options.text: The daily moves carry the signal, since they are the most recent evidence
options.misconception: prefers the freshest data to the trend the theory is actually built on
options.why: The daily fluctuations are explicitly no part of the Dow Theory's interpretation of the market. They are watched only because they add up to the longer movement; on their own they say nothing about where the market is going.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A market index has risen for eighteen months. Inside that stretch there was a four-week fall of 12 per cent, and there have been moves of about a per cent either way almost every day throughout.

items.stem: What pattern is this, and what does a fall below ₹150 imply?

options.text: A head and shoulders top; a fall below the neckline is a sell signal, with a drop of about ₹70 expected
options.why: The left shoulder at ₹180, the head at ₹220 and the right shoulder at ₹182 form a head and shoulders top, the single most important pattern for a reversal of trend. The neckline joins the points where head and shoulders meet, here ₹150, and the drop expected equals the distance from the top of the head to it — ₹220 less ₹150.

options.text: A triangle or coil, so the direction cannot be predicted
options.misconception: reaches for the pattern of uncertainty instead of reading the one on the chart
options.why: A triangle or coil is the formation the material describes as a pattern of uncertainty, where it is difficult to predict which way the price will break out. Three peaks around a higher middle one is not that shape; it is the reversal pattern with the clearest published reading of the lot.

options.text: A double top, complete at ₹182, so the level at ₹150 does not matter
options.misconception: names a two-peak pattern where there are three, and drops the level the signal depends on
options.why: A double top has two peaks of about the same height; this has three, with the middle one clearly highest, which is the head. And the price movement after the second shoulder is precisely what is crucial — the signal is the break of the level at ₹150, not the shoulder.

options.text: An inverse head and shoulders, so the fall below ₹150 confirms a coming rise
options.misconception: applies the inverted pattern's reading to the upright one
options.why: An inverse head and shoulders has its head as the lowest point between two higher troughs, and there it is a rise above the neck line that signals a purchase. Here the head is the highest point of the three, so this is the top formation and its signal runs downward.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A share chart shows a rise to ₹180, a fall to ₹150, a rise to ₹220, a fall back to ₹150, and a rise to ₹182 followed by a decline. The line joining the two troughs sits at ₹150.

items.stem: How does the study material classify these four?

options.text: Only the last is financial risk; the other three are operational risks
options.misconception: narrows financial risk down to a shortage of cash
options.why: Operational risk is people and process inside the company — a payment made for the wrong amount. A government blocking remittances, a customer defaulting and a rate resetting are all changes in financial conditions arriving from outside, which is what the chapter means by financial risk.

options.text: They are four separate risk types, so none of them is financial risk
options.misconception: treats the sub-categories as rivals to the heading above them
options.why: Financial risk is the heading and these are its categories, not alternatives to it. The chapter's other headings — strategic risk, compliance risk and operational risk — sit beside financial risk, and not one of these four belongs under them.

options.text: The conversion restriction is currency risk rather than political risk
options.misconception: files a government action under the exposure that action happens to touch
options.why: Currency risk is exchange rate movement changing cash flows. A restriction on converting the local currency is an adverse action by the host government, which the chapter lists under political risk beside confiscation, rationing of remittance and price control of products.

options.text: Political, counter party, interest rate and liquidity risk — all four are categories of financial risk
options.why: Financial risk is unexpected change in financial conditions, and the chapter divides it into counter party risk for a customer not honouring its obligation, political risk for adverse action by a host government including restriction on conversion of local currency, interest rate risk for a rate change moving assets and liabilities, and liquidity risk for an inability to meet liabilities as they fall due.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian company with a plant abroad lists four worries. The host government may restrict conversion of its local currency. A large customer may not pay. Its floating-rate borrowing may reprice upward. It may not hold cash on the day a repayment falls due.

items.stem: Which stage of the venture capital investment process is this, and what comes next?

options.text: Post investment activity, since the fund is already deeply involved
options.misconception: mistakes heavy engagement before an investment for engagement after it
options.why: Post investment activity begins once the money is in, and it is where the fund nominates its nominee to the board of the company. Nothing has been invested here; the fund is still deciding whether to.

options.text: Screening, followed by deal origination
options.misconception: puts sourcing after the first look rather than before it
options.why: Deal origination is where the proposal comes from — the fund working directly or through intermediaries — and it is the first stage, not a later one. Screening is the quick sort that follows it, and it is already behind this fund.

options.text: Deal structuring, since terms are always agreed before the facts are checked
options.misconception: reverses verification and negotiation
options.why: Deal structuring comes after the case has passed due diligence. Agreeing terms on unverified claims is what the ordering exists to prevent, which is why structuring is the fourth stage and not the third.

options.text: Due diligence, followed by deal structuring
options.why: The process runs deal origination, screening, due diligence, deal structuring, post investment activity and exit plan. Verifying the claims before deciding is due diligence, and once the case passes it the terms are negotiated — deal structuring — before any money moves.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A venture fund met a founder through an intermediary, read the summary and liked it, and is now verifying the revenue figures, the technology and the background of the team before it decides anything.

items.stem: What has the fund done, and what does the separation achieve?

options.text: Charged an exit load, so that the cost of leaving keeps investors in
options.misconception: substitutes a charge on redemption for a separation of assets
options.why: An exit load is a percentage deducted from the NAV when an investor redeems, and it goes into the scheme's own pool of funds rather than to the asset management company. It prices an exit; it does not quarantine an asset.

options.text: Something not permitted, since a scheme must carry every holding it owns inside one NAV
options.misconception: treats one NAV per scheme as a rule with no exception
options.why: Side pocketing is described as an established practice, quite common internationally and much discussed in India after the IL&FS default left several schemes writing off their exposure. It is the recognised answer to a stressed holding, not a breach of anything.

options.text: Protected the investor who is leaving rather than the one who stays
options.misconception: gets the beneficiary of the separation backwards
options.why: The separation is built for the investor who wants to hold the units of the main fund for the long term, and it exists so that good assets are not sold cheaply to meet redemptions. The one leaving takes the value of the liquid assets and waits on the side pocket.

options.text: Side pocketing — the stressed holding is locked away and the main scheme's NAV then reflects the liquid assets
options.why: Side pocketing separates the risky or doubtful assets from the other investments and cash holdings. Money linked to the stressed asset stays locked until the fund recovers it, so the manager avoids distress selling of illiquid securities, and the NAV of the main scheme then reflects the actual value of the liquid assets.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A debt scheme holds a bond of a company that has just been downgraded. The bond cannot be sold except at a distress price, and redemption requests are coming in. The fund separates that one holding from the rest of the portfolio.

items.stem: What signal does the study material read from this?

options.text: No signal, since a moving average only smooths the data and never produces a decision
options.misconception: treats the average as description when it is used as a rule
options.why: Moving averages are plotted with prices precisely to make buy and sell decisions, and the material sets out three buy signals and three sell signals from the crossings. Smoothing is how the tool works, not the whole of what it is for.

options.text: A sell signal, since a 200-day average that has been falling shows a long-term downtrend
options.misconception: reads the average's recent direction in place of the crossing rule
options.why: A 200-day average is used to identify a long term trend, and its recent fall is exactly why the flattening matters. The sell signal is the price line falling through the moving average line while that line flattens out — the opposite crossing to this one.

options.text: A buy signal
options.why: The buy signals listed are the price line rising through the moving average line when the graph of that line is flattening out; the price line falling below an average that is rising; and a price line above the average that falls but turns back up before reaching it. The first of the three is exactly the picture described.

options.text: A buy signal only if the average were exponential, since an arithmetic one weights stale prices too heavily
options.misconception: makes the signal depend on which kind of average was chosen
options.why: An exponential moving average assigns decreasing weights with the highest on the latest price, while an arithmetic moving average weights every period alike, so the two turn at different speeds. The signal is read off the crossing either way; the choice changes how soon it appears, not whether it counts.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A chartist plots a 200-day arithmetic moving average against the daily closing price. The average has been falling for weeks and has now begun to flatten out. The price line, which was below it, rises through it.

items.stem: What is the ten-trading-day 99 per cent value at risk?

options.text: About ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: scales the volatility across ten days but never applies the confidence multiple
options.why: ₹4 lakh × 10 leaves the Z score out altogether. The standard deviation is the typical daily move; a 99 per cent figure needs 2.33 of them, and stating a confidence level is the whole reason the multiple exists.

options.text: About ₹9.32 lakh
options.misconception: answers the one-day question when ten days were asked
options.why: ₹9.32 lakh is the one-day 99 per cent figure and the right starting point. VaR is defined over a stated time horizon, and changing the horizon changes the number — which is why a VaR quoted without its horizon says nothing at all.

options.text: About ₹29.47 lakh
options.why: Two per cent of ₹2 crore is ₹4 lakh of daily volatility, and 4 × 2.33 gives a one-day VaR of ₹9.32 lakh. A longer horizon of independent daily moves scales by the square root of the number of days, so 9.32 × 3.1623 comes to about ₹29.47 lakh.

options.text: About ₹93.20 lakh
options.misconception: multiplies the one-day figure by ten instead of by the square root of ten
options.why: 9.32 × 10 assumes ten days of loss all pulling the same way. Independent daily moves partly cancel each other, which is why the horizon enters as its square root and ten days costs about three times one day rather than ten times.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A trader holds ₹2 crore of one share whose market price has a daily standard deviation of 2 per cent. Prices are taken as normally distributed, and the Z score for 99 per cent confidence is 2.33.

items.stem: What happens to the two instruments?

options.text: The principal only strip gains, because principal is the safer half of the cash flow
options.misconception: reasons from credit safety when the question turns on timing
options.why: Credit is not what moved. The principal is still expected in full; it is expected later, and money later is worth less, so the PO price falls when yields rise and rises when they fall and borrowers repay early.

options.text: The interest only strip gains and the principal only strip falls
options.why: Stripped securities divide the pool's cash flows into an Interest Only security and a Principal Only security. When yields in the market rise, borrowers prefer to postpone repayment on their cheaper existing loans, so the PO price tends to fall as its principal is pushed further out, while the IO gains because interest keeps being calculated on borrowings that stay outstanding.

options.text: Neither moves, since the two together must still be worth the whole pool
options.misconception: reads a constraint on the sum as a constraint on each half
options.why: The two together are worth the pool, and the pool's own value changes with rates as well. The identity constrains the pair; it says nothing about how the value is divided between them, and the division is precisely what a rate move alters.

options.text: Both fall, since every fixed income instrument falls when yields rise
options.misconception: applies the plain bond rule to a strip whose cash flows themselves move with rates
options.why: A plain bond has a fixed schedule, so only the discount rate changes. A strip's schedule is not fixed — prepayment behaviour moves with rates — and that is exactly why the two halves of one pool can move in opposite directions.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: The cash flows of a housing loan pool are divided into two instruments — one paying only the interest collected, the other only the principal collected. Market yields then rise sharply.

items.stem: Which test is this, and what is it testing?

options.text: A test of the semi-strong form, since a price series is public information
options.misconception: reads any use of public data as a test of the semi-strong form
options.why: The weak form is about the record of past prices and volumes specifically, and that record is all this test uses. The semi-strong form is tested with announcements — earnings, stock splits, mergers — by asking how quickly prices adjust once the news is out.

options.text: The filter rule test, since it hunts for a pattern that could be traded
options.misconception: names the trading-rule test for a procedure that places no trades
options.why: The filter rule test buys after a rise of at least N per cent and sells after a fall of at least N per cent from a subsequent high, then asks whether that beat a buy and hold strategy once commission is counted. It places trades; the procedure described places none.

options.text: The run test, one of three ways the weak form of efficient market theory is checked
options.why: A run is an unbroken stretch of changes carrying the same sign, and a new run begins when the sign changes. Comparing the number of runs against a purely random series of the same size is the run test, and it is used alongside the serial correlation test and the filter rule test to check the weak form. By and large the results support the random walk model.

options.text: The serial correlation test, which is the same procedure counted differently
options.misconception: merges two distinct tests because both work on the same price changes
options.why: The serial correlation test correlates the price change in one period with the change in another period, and it uses the sizes of those changes. The run test throws the sizes away and keeps only the signs. Same hypothesis, different arithmetic, which is why the material lists them separately.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A researcher marks each day's price change as a plus or a minus, counts the unbroken stretches of one sign, and compares that count against what a purely random series of the same size would produce. No trades are placed and the sizes of the changes are never used.

items.stem: What does the sustainable growth model say about this plan?

options.text: The target is reachable as long as the company simply borrows the difference
options.misconception: treats borrowing as free of the very constraint the board itself imposed
options.why: Borrowing more while equity grows only by retention pushes the debt to equity ratio up, and the board has fixed that ratio. Extra debt is available only in proportion to the retained earnings that can carry it, which is the arithmetic the model is made of.

options.text: Growing faster than the sustainable rate is nothing to worry about, since growth is what shareholders want
options.misconception: treats growth as costless whatever it is funded by
options.why: Growing above the sustainable rate means funding the gap with more debt or new equity or both. Doing it while the board forbids both is what creates the risky position the model exists to expose — too much debt and too little equity.

options.text: The three rules together fix the growth rate, so one of them has to give or the target has to come down
options.why: The sustainable growth model assumes a target capital structure held without issuing new equity, a target dividend payment ratio held, and sales growing as fast as conditions allow. Hold the first two and the only source of new equity is retained earnings, so sales and assets cannot grow faster than retained earnings plus the debt those earnings support.

options.text: The model does not apply, since the sustainable growth rate measures borrowing capacity and not sales
options.misconception: narrows the model down to a test a lender runs
options.why: The sustainable growth rate is defined as the maximum rate of growth in sales achievable given the firm's profitability, asset utilisation, desired dividend payout and leverage. It is often reached for when a borrower asks for more, but what it measures is sales.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: A board sets a sales growth target well above the rate the firm can fund out of retained profits. It also rules that the dividend payment ratio will not change, that the debt to equity ratio will not change, and that no new equity will be issued.

items.stem: Which risk is the portfolio still carrying?

options.text: Liquidity risk, since twelve industries cannot all be sold at once
options.misconception: substitutes a trading concern for the pricing question asked
options.why: Liquidity affects the cost of exiting, not why the valuation tracked the index. The co-movement with the market is systematic risk by definition.
keywords: the cost of exiting, not why the valuation tracked the index
co-movement with the market is systematic risk by definition

options.text: Unsystematic risk, because thirty stocks are too few
options.misconception: believes firm-specific risk lingers until the portfolio holds the whole market
options.why: The gain from diversification flattens quickly — most firm-specific risk is gone well before thirty stocks. The 9 per cent fall tracking a 10 per cent market fall is market behaviour, not stock-picking noise.

options.text: None — a fall proves the portfolio was badly constructed
options.misconception: reads any loss as evidence of avoidable risk
options.why: A diversified portfolio is supposed to move with the market; that is what remains after the removable risk is removed. A loss in a falling market is the priced risk showing up.
keywords: supposed to move with the market

options.text: Systematic risk, which diversification cannot remove
options.why: Thirty stocks across twelve industries has diversified away nearly all firm-specific risk. What moves the portfolio now is the market itself — interest rates, the cycle, policy — and that risk is common to every security, so holding more of them does not dilute it.
keywords: diversified away nearly all firm-specific risk
common to every security, so holding more of them does not dilute it

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: An investor holds a portfolio of 30 stocks spread across twelve industries and asks why its value still fell 9 per cent in a month when the market index fell 10 per cent.

items.stem: What are the put's intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic value nil, time value ₹11
options.misconception: applies the call test to a put and reads spot below strike as out of the money
options.why: For a call this spot would mean no intrinsic value, and that is the reflex being tested. A put gains when the share falls, so spot below strike is in the money.
keywords: For a call this spot would mean no intrinsic value
spot below strike is in the money

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹11, time value nil
options.misconception: equates the whole premium with intrinsic value
options.why: The premium is the price of the option, not its exercise value. Intrinsic value comes from strike against spot alone, and here that is ₹8.
keywords: the price of the option, not its exercise value
Intrinsic value comes from strike against spot alone

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹8, time value ₹3
options.why: The put lets its holder sell at ₹100 what the market prices at ₹92, so exercising now is worth ₹8 — the intrinsic value. The premium's remaining ₹3 is time value, paid for the chance the share falls further before expiry.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹3, time value ₹8
options.misconception: swaps the two components
options.why: The split runs the other way. Exercise value first — strike ₹100 less spot ₹92 — and only the remainder of the premium is time value.
keywords: The split runs the other way
only the remainder of the premium is time value

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A put option on a share has a strike price of ₹100. The share trades at ₹92 and the put's premium is ₹11.

items.stem: Where must the one-year forward rate sit, relative to spot?

options.text: Above ₹84 — the dollar at a forward premium, the rupee at a discount
options.why: A depositor could otherwise convert to rupees, earn 7 per cent against 3, and convert back with nothing lost. The forward rate removes that free profit by making future dollars dearer — roughly by the 4 per cent differential, near ₹87.2.
keywords: removes that free profit by making future dollars dearer
roughly by the 4 per cent differential

options.text: Below ₹84 — the rupee at a forward premium because its interest rate is higher
options.misconception: gives the forward premium to the high-rate currency
options.why: This is parity read backwards. The higher rate is compensation for the currency expected to weaken; if the rupee also strengthened forward, holding rupees would win twice and arbitrage would close the gap at once.
keywords: compensation for the currency expected to weaken

options.text: It depends only on expected inflation in the two countries
options.misconception: answers with purchasing power parity when the question fixes interest rates
options.why: Inflation drives the long-run story through PPP, but the covered forward rate is pinned by interest rate parity — the rates given are the whole calculation.
keywords: the covered forward rate is pinned by interest rate parity
the rates given are the whole calculation

options.text: Exactly ₹84, because forward rates track spot when markets are efficient
options.misconception: treats efficiency as making the interest differential irrelevant
options.why: Efficiency is what forces the gap open, not shut. A forward equal to spot with a 4 per cent rate differential is a money machine, and efficient markets price it away.
keywords: forces the gap open, not shut
a money machine, and efficient markets price it away

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year interest rates are 7 per cent in India and 3 per cent in the United States. The spot rate is ₹84 per dollar. Markets are free of arbitrage.

items.stem: A fund expects interest rates to fall and wants the largest price gain. Which bond should it hold?

options.text: A floating-rate bond resetting every six months
options.misconception: reaches for the bond that adjusts to rates rather than the one that gains from them
options.why: A floater's coupon resets to the market, so its price barely moves — near-zero duration. It is the instrument for avoiding the bet, not winning it.

options.text: A ten-year bond with a 12 per cent coupon
options.misconception: picks the highest coupon as the biggest gainer
options.why: Large coupons return money early, which shortens duration and dampens the price move. Same maturity, less sensitivity than the zero.
keywords: shortens duration and dampens the price move

options.text: A ten-year zero-coupon bond
options.why: Price sensitivity follows duration, and a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its full maturity because every rupee arrives at the end. Ten years of duration is the most leverage to a rate fall among these choices.
keywords: every rupee arrives at the end

options.text: A two-year zero-coupon bond
options.misconception: remembers zeros are sensitive but forgets maturity drives it
options.why: Being a zero helps only as far as the maturity allows. Two years of duration moves far less than ten when rates shift.
keywords: Being a zero helps only as far as the maturity allows
Two years of duration moves far less than ten

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.stem: How many futures contracts should the fund sell?

options.misconception: applies beta twice
options.why: ₹12.6 crore already carries the beta adjustment. Multiplying by 1.4 again hedges an exposure the fund does not have, and the excess contracts are a speculative short.
keywords: hedges an exposure the fund does not have

options.misconception: hedges the portfolio's value while ignoring its beta
options.why: ₹9 crore ÷ ₹10.5 lakh gives about 86, which hedges a beta-one portfolio. This portfolio swings 40 per cent harder than the market, and 86 contracts leave that excess exposed.

options.text: 120 contracts bought, not sold
options.misconception: gets the size right and the direction backwards
options.why: Long futures gain when the market rises — added to a long portfolio, that doubles the bet. A hedge against a fall needs the futures to pay when the market drops, which means selling.
keywords: added to a long portfolio, that doubles the bet
needs the futures to pay when the market drops

options.why: The exposure to hedge is value times beta — ₹9 crore × 1.4 = ₹12.6 crore, because the portfolio moves 1.4 times the market. Divided by ₹10.5 lakh per contract, that is 120 contracts sold.
keywords: The exposure to hedge is value times beta

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A fund holds a ₹9 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 1.4 against the index. Index futures trade at 21,000 with a lot size of 50, making one contract worth ₹10.5 lakh. The fund wants a full hedge against a market fall.

items.stem: Which hedge fits that requirement?

options.text: Sell a put option on the dollar
options.misconception: confuses writing options with buying protection
options.why: Selling a put collects a premium and takes on obligation — if the dollar falls, the importer is put dollars at the strike. It provides no protection at all against a rise.
keywords: Selling a put collects a premium and takes on obligation
no protection at all against a rise

options.text: Do nothing, since a payable in dollars gains when the dollar weakens
options.misconception: keeps the exposure because one side of it is pleasant
options.why: The open position gains on a fall and loses on a rise; the loss side is the risk to be managed. Doing nothing is a bet, not a hedge.
keywords: the loss side is the risk to be managed
Doing nothing is a bet, not a hedge

options.text: Buy a call option on the dollar
options.why: A dollar call caps the buying rate at the strike if the dollar rises, and lapses if the dollar falls, letting the importer buy cheaper in the market. That asymmetry is exactly what was asked for, and the premium is its price.
keywords: caps the buying rate at the strike

options.text: Buy dollars forward
options.misconception: reaches for the standard hedge and gives away the benefit that was wanted
options.why: A forward locks the rate in both directions. It removes the risk of a rise but equally removes the gain from a fall, which the finance head specifically wanted to keep.
keywords: locks the rate in both directions
removes the gain from a fall

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An importer must pay $500,000 in three months. The rupee has been volatile, and the finance head wants protection if the dollar rises but would like the benefit if it falls.

items.stem: Which project should be accepted, and why?

options.text: A — the smaller outlay carries less risk for the same decision
options.misconception: substitutes an outlay-size intuition for a discounting answer
options.why: Risk is already priced into the 12 per cent discount rate. Introducing outlay size as a separate criterion double-counts caution.
keywords: already priced into the 12 per cent discount rate

options.text: B — with mutually exclusive projects, the higher NPV measures the wealth added
options.why: Only one can be taken, and B adds ₹52 lakh of value against A's ₹28 lakh at the firm's actual cost of capital. IRR's higher rate on A is a rate on a much smaller base, and its reinvestment assumption at 24 per cent is not available to the firm.
keywords: at the firm's actual cost of capital
reinvestment assumption at 24 per cent is not available to the firm

options.text: A — its IRR of 24 per cent beats B's 17 per cent
options.misconception: ranks mutually exclusive projects by rate of return
options.why: A high rate on ₹1 crore can add less wealth than a modest rate on ₹4 crore. Ranking by IRR answers which project is more efficient per rupee, not which makes the firm richer.
keywords: add less wealth than a modest rate
not which makes the firm richer

options.text: Both, since each has a positive NPV and an IRR above the cost of capital
options.misconception: forgets that mutual exclusivity means choosing
options.why: Independent projects with positive NPV are all accepted. These are mutually exclusive — taking one forecloses the other, which is the whole reason the ranking conflict matters.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: Two mutually exclusive projects at a 12 per cent cost of capital. Project A needs ₹1 crore and has NPV ₹28 lakh with IRR 24 per cent. Project B needs ₹4 crore and has NPV ₹52 lakh with IRR 17 per cent.

items.stem: What is the NAV per unit?

options.misconception: drops the accrued income and the liabilities together
options.why: ₹840 over 40 crore units alone is a portfolio-only shortcut. NAV is the whole balance sheet in one number — everything owned less everything owed.
NAV works on market value, not cost — ₹840 plus ₹12 minus ₹22 gives net assets of ₹830 crore, and over 40 crore units that is ₹20.75. The unrealised gain over cost is already inside it.
keywords: NAV works on market value, not cost
unrealised gain over cost is already inside it

options.misconception: values the portfolio at cost instead of market
options.why: ₹700 plus ₹12 minus ₹22 over 40 crore units gives ₹17.25, a number that hides ₹140 crore of gains from every unitholder transacting today. Cost is history; NAV is a price.
keywords: Cost is history; NAV is a price

options.misconception: forgets the liabilities and expenses
options.why: ₹840 plus ₹12 over 40 crore units ignores ₹22 crore that unitholders owe. Gross assets per unit overstate what a redeeming investor actually gets.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A fund holds investments with market value ₹840 crore and cost ₹700 crore, accrued income of ₹12 crore, and liabilities plus accrued expenses of ₹22 crore, with 40 crore units outstanding.

items.stem: What is the value of the share under the dividend growth model?

options.why: The model discounts the coming dividend — ₹6 grown one year at 8 per cent is ₹6.48 — divided by the 6 per cent spread between the 14 per cent required return and the growth rate. ₹6.48 over 0.06 is ₹108.
keywords: The model discounts the coming dividend
spread between the 14 per cent required return and the growth rate

options.misconception: uses the dividend just paid instead of the next one
options.why: ₹6 over 0.06 forgets that the valuation stands at the start of a growth year. The formula runs on the expected dividend, and the ₹8 difference is exactly the missed growth step.
keywords: stands at the start of a growth year

options.misconception: divides by the required return alone, ignoring growth
options.why: ₹6.48 over 0.14 values a dividend frozen forever. Perpetual growth is the model's whole engine, and it lives in the denominator's subtraction.

options.misconception: swaps the growth and required-return roles
options.why: ₹6.48 over 0.08 discounts at the growth rate — a rate at which the investor requires nothing and the model means nothing. The spread, not either rate alone, prices the share.
keywords: The spread, not either rate alone, prices the share

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company has just paid a dividend of ₹6 per share. Dividends are expected to grow at 8 per cent for the foreseeable future, and equity investors require a 14 per cent return.

items.stem: What does the FRA deliver?

options.text: The counterparty compensates the company for the 1.5 per cent difference, settled at the start of the borrowing period at its discounted value
options.why: The buyer of an FRA is protected against rates rising past the agreed 8 per cent. The settlement pays the rate difference on the notional for three months, discounted because it arrives at the period's start while borrowing costs bite at its end.
keywords: protected against rates rising past the agreed 8 per cent
discounted because it arrives at the period's start

options.text: The company pays the counterparty, since it locked 8 per cent and rates moved to 9.5
options.misconception: reverses who wins when rates rise
options.why: Paying away when rates rise would make the hedge a double loss. The buyer fixed a borrowing cost; the market moving above it is precisely the event the buyer is paid for.
keywords: would make the hedge a double loss
the market moving above it is precisely the event the buyer is paid for

options.text: Nothing — the FRA lapsed because it was not exercised within six months
options.misconception: treats a binding forward as an option needing exercise
options.why: An FRA is a firm contract, not an option. Settlement happens automatically on the fixing date, whichever way rates went.
keywords: a firm contract, not an option
Settlement happens automatically on the fixing date

options.text: The company borrows the ₹50 crore from the FRA counterparty at 8 per cent
options.misconception: expects the FRA to deliver the loan itself
options.why: An FRA is a contract on a rate, not a source of funds. The company borrows wherever it chooses at 9.5 per cent, and the settlement brings the effective cost back to 8.
keywords: a contract on a rate, not a source of funds
the settlement brings the effective cost back to 8

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A company will need to borrow ₹50 crore for three months, starting six months from now. Its treasurer buys a 6x9 FRA at 8 per cent. Six months later the three-month reference rate sets at 9.5 per cent.

items.stem: Is there an arbitrage, and on which side?

options.text: No — the call costing more than the put is the natural order of things
options.misconception: eyeballs the two premiums instead of testing the parity equation
options.why: Which option costs more is not the question; the equation is. The gap between ₹7 and ₹18.50 is the mispricing, whatever the premiums' order.
keywords: Which option costs more is not the question
the mispricing, whatever the premiums' order

options.text: Yes — sell both options and pocket ₹83 of premium
options.misconception: mistakes premium income for arbitrage
options.why: A short straddle collects ₹83 and stands naked to every large move in the share. Arbitrage means a locked, riskless difference; this is a bet wearing its costume.
keywords: stands naked to every large move

options.text: Yes — the call is cheap relative to parity; buy the call, sell the put, short the share, invest the strike's present value
options.why: Parity wants call minus put equal to share minus present value of strike: ₹18.50. The market offers ₹45 minus ₹38, only ₹7. The left side is underpriced, so buy it — long call, short put — against a short share and lending, locking ₹11.50 without risk.
keywords: call minus put equal to share minus present value of strike

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the share's expected volatility
options.misconception: drags valuation inputs into a no-arbitrage identity
options.why: Volatility prices each option; parity binds their difference regardless. The identity holds for any volatility, which is what makes its breach a free lunch.
keywords: The identity holds for any volatility

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹500. A one-year European call at strike ₹520 costs ₹45, and the matching put costs ₹38. The one-year risk-free rate makes the present value of the strike ₹481.50.

items.stem: What explains the disagreement, and which measure fits an investor holding only this fund?

options.text: X carries diversifiable risk that Treynor ignores; a sole-fund investor should trust Sharpe
options.why: Treynor prices only systematic risk, so X's extra, diversifiable volatility vanishes from its denominator and the funds tie. An investor whose whole wealth rides on one fund bears total risk, and Sharpe is the measure that charges for all of it.
keywords: Sharpe is the measure that charges for all of it

options.text: The measures conflict, so the data must contain an arithmetic error
options.misconception: expects consistent rankings from measures built on different denominators
options.why: The disagreement is the information. Identical Treynor with worse Sharpe is the signature of an underdiversified portfolio, not of a miscalculation.
keywords: the signature of an underdiversified portfolio

options.text: Treynor, because beta is the more scientific risk measure
options.misconception: picks the measure by prestige instead of by what the investor bears
options.why: Beta is the right charge for a fund inside a diversified portfolio. Held alone, the fund's diversifiable risk is not diversified away by anyone, and a measure that ignores it flatters X.
keywords: the right charge for a fund inside a diversified portfolio
a measure that ignores it flatters X

options.text: Sharpe always, since total risk always exceeds systematic risk
options.misconception: right choice here, universalised for the wrong reason
options.why: For a fund that is one sleeve of a larger portfolio, Treynor is the better lens — the holder's other sleeves absorb the unsystematic part. The choice follows the investor's position, not a fixed hierarchy.
keywords: follows the investor's position, not a fixed hierarchy

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Fund X and Fund Y both earned 14 per cent against a risk-free rate of 6 per cent. X has standard deviation 20 per cent and beta 1.6; Y has standard deviation 10 per cent and beta 1.0. On Sharpe, Y wins (0.8 against 0.4); on Treynor, X and Y tie at 8. An investor asks which measure to trust.

items.stem: What does CAPM say about this stock?

options.text: Required return is 15 per cent; the stock offers 16, so it is underpriced — buy
options.why: CAPM charges 6 + 1.5 × (12 − 6) = 15 per cent for this stock's systematic risk. An expected 16 per cent sits one point above the security market line — positive alpha. The market price is too low for the return on offer, which is the definition of a buy.
keywords: sits one point above the security market line
The market price is too low for the return on offer

options.text: Required return is 15 per cent; expecting more means the stock is overpriced — sell
options.misconception: inverts the alpha rule
options.why: Overpricing shows up as expected return below the line — paying too much shrinks the return. Extra return above the charge for risk is the reward being too big, not the price.
keywords: Overpricing shows up as expected return below the line
the reward being too big, not the price

options.text: CAPM cannot judge the stock without its standard deviation
options.misconception: imports total risk into a model that prices only systematic risk
options.why: CAPM's whole claim is that diversifiable risk earns nothing, so beta is the only risk input the line needs. Standard deviation belongs to Sharpe's world, not the SML's.
keywords: beta is the only risk input the line needs

options.text: Required return is 18 per cent, so the stock falls short — sell
options.misconception: multiplies beta into the whole market return instead of the premium
options.why: Beta scales the market risk premium of 6, not the market return of 12. The risk-free 6 per cent is earned without any beta at all.
keywords: scales the market risk premium of 6, not the market return of 12
earned without any beta at all

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Risk-free rate 6 per cent, expected market return 12 per cent. A stock with beta 1.5 is expected by analysts to return 16 per cent. An investor concludes the stock should be sold, since 16 per cent is a higher return and higher return means higher risk.

items.stem: What does an arbitrageur do?

options.text: Sell the stock (or short it), invest the proceeds, and buy the cheap futures
options.why: The futures trade ₹7 below fair value, so the reverse cash-and-carry runs: shorting the stock raises ₹500 that earns interest to about ₹515, while the futures lock repurchase at ₹508. The ₹7 is collected whichever way the stock itself moves.
keywords: below fair value, so the reverse cash-and-carry runs
collected whichever way the stock itself moves

options.text: Buy the futures and wait for the stock to rise above ₹508
options.misconception: replaces arbitrage with a directional bet
options.why: Needing the stock to rise means carrying market risk. The arbitrage earns the gap with both legs locked, indifferent to direction — that indifference is what makes it arbitrage.
keywords: Needing the stock to rise means carrying market risk

options.text: Buy the stock with borrowed money and sell the futures against it
options.misconception: runs the cash-and-carry in the wrong direction
options.why: That trade profits when futures are rich. Here it locks in buying at ₹500 plus ₹15 of interest to deliver at ₹508 — a guaranteed loss of the same ₹7.
keywords: a guaranteed loss of the same ₹7

options.text: Nothing — ₹508 for a ₹500 stock already includes a fair carrying charge
options.misconception: eyeballs the premium instead of computing it
options.why: The question is never whether futures exceed spot but whether the gap equals the carry. Three months of 12 per cent on ₹500 is about ₹15; a ₹8 premium is ₹7 short.
keywords: whether the gap equals the carry

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A stock trades at ₹500 and pays no dividend. Money costs 12 per cent a year. The three-month futures contract on the stock trades at ₹508, while the cost-of-carry fair value works out to about ₹515.

items.stem: What does the EPS rise actually prove?

options.text: Only that T's earnings were bought at a lower multiple than A's — the market may still mark the deal down
options.why: Shares worth ₹400 crore at A's price bought ₹25 crore of earnings — a multiple of 16 against A's own 20, so the arithmetic guarantees accretion. Whether value was created depends on what T's earnings deserve; if their quality merits only a low multiple, the higher EPS can price at a lower P/E and shareholders gain nothing.
keywords: the higher EPS can price at a lower P/E

options.text: That A overpaid, since issuing 2 crore shares diluted control
options.misconception: confuses ownership dilution with earnings dilution
options.why: Existing holders do own a smaller fraction of a bigger company — that is every share-funded deal. Overpayment is measured against T's value, and a 16-times price for earnings A's own market rates at 20 is not overpayment on its face.
keywords: a smaller fraction of a bigger company
Overpayment is measured against T's value

options.text: That the merger created value for A's shareholders
options.misconception: reads bootstrap arithmetic as wealth creation
options.why: EPS accretion follows mechanically from buying low-multiple earnings with high-multiple paper. Value creation needs synergies or underpricing — neither is shown by the ₹0.42.
keywords: buying low-multiple earnings with high-multiple paper
Value creation needs synergies or underpricing

options.text: Nothing — EPS should fall whenever new shares are issued
options.misconception: sees only the denominator of the fraction
options.why: The new shares arrive carrying T's ₹25 crore of earnings. Whether EPS rises or falls is the race between the two, settled by the relative multiples.
keywords: The new shares arrive carrying T's ₹25 crore of earnings

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: Acquirer A earns ₹100 crore on 10 crore shares (EPS ₹10) and trades at a P/E of 20. Target T earns ₹25 crore and A buys it by issuing 2 crore new shares. The CFO announces the merger is a success because combined EPS rises to about ₹10.42.

items.stem: How does the money market hedge run, and roughly what does it lock in?

options.text: The hedge fails because rupee interest is higher than dollar interest
options.misconception: reads the rate differential as a barrier instead of the price
options.why: The differential is exactly what sets the locked rate above spot. Higher home interest is why the exporter's manufactured forward is favourable, not why the hedge breaks.
keywords: sets the locked rate above spot

options.text: Borrow about $0.98 million now, convert at ₹84, invest in rupees — locking roughly ₹85.6 per dollar
