items.scenario: A group consolidates nine components. One of them, an overseas trading entity carrying 4 per cent of consolidated total assets and 3 per cent of consolidated revenue, has never been audited; the parent's management supplies a certificate confirming its figures. The team proposes to issue an unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph naming the component and saying its financial statements are unaudited.

items.stem: Is the partner right?

options.text: No — SSAE 3000 is ICAI's umbrella standard for assurance engagements on sustainability information, it covers both reasonable and limited assurance, and it has been mandatory for assurance reports covering periods ending on or after 31 March 2024
options.why: SSAE 3000, Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information, applies to all assurance engagements on sustainability information and to both levels of assurance. This engagement covers a period ending 31 March 2026, well inside the mandatory window.

options.text: No — SSAE 3000 applies, but only to reasonable assurance engagements, so a limited assurance engagement on sustainability information falls outside any standard
options.misconception: assumes the standard reaches only the higher level of assurance
options.why: The standard states its application to engagements providing reasonable or limited assurance on sustainability information. Both levels are inside it.

options.text: Yes — the Standards on Auditing govern historical financial information, and no ICAI pronouncement reaches non-financial sustainability data
options.misconception: assumes the field is unregulated because the subject matter is not financial
options.why: It is true that the SAs are for historical financial information, which is why a separate standard exists. ICAI's Sustainability Reporting Standards Board issued SSAE 3000 to occupy exactly this ground.

options.text: No — the governing standard is SAE 3410, which is the umbrella standard for sustainability assurance in India
options.misconception: promotes the greenhouse-gas-specific standard into the umbrella standard
options.why: SAE 3410 deals with assurance engagements on greenhouse gas statements — one slice of sustainability information. SSAE 3000 is the umbrella above it.

citation.ref: Scope of the Standard and effective date of application

items.scenario: A firm is asked to give limited assurance on the sustainability information in a listed company's annual report for the year ended 31 March 2026. The engagement partner tells the team that ICAI has no standard covering sustainability assurance, so they should borrow the reporting format of SA 700 and describe the work in their own words.

items.stem: What is the position on the two omissions?

options.text: Neither omission matters, because Section C is required only of entities that voluntarily seek assurance on BRSR Core
options.misconception: confuses the obligation to report with the separate obligation to have the report assured
options.why: Reporting under BRSR and obtaining assurance on it are two separate obligations. The principle-wise performance disclosures in Section C are part of the report itself, whatever assurance is or is not sought.

options.text: Leaving the leadership indicators blank is permitted because they are optional disclosures; the two essential indicators are mandatory disclosures and their omission is a reporting gap the provider must raise
options.why: Section C classifies its key performance indicators into essential indicators, which are mandatory, and leadership indicators, which are optional. Not collecting the data is a reason the gap exists, not a reason it is permitted.

options.text: Both omissions are acceptable, because everything in Section C runs on a comply-or-explain basis and the company has explained
options.misconception: treats the whole of the principle-wise performance section as voluntary with an explanation
options.why: The essential indicators are mandatory disclosures, not comply-or-explain items. An explanation for why the data is absent does not convert a required disclosure into an optional one.

options.text: Both omissions are breaches, because every indicator in Section C becomes mandatory once BRSR applies to the entity
options.misconception: collapses the essential and leadership split and makes optional data compulsory
options.why: That would erase the distinction the format itself draws. Leadership indicators are where an entity may go further than the floor; a blank there is not a breach.

citation.ref: Regulation 34(2)(f) read with the prescribed BRSR format, Section C

items.scenario: A listed company among the top 1,000 by market capitalisation files its BRSR. Section C is partly blank: the whole of the leadership indicators is left empty across all nine principles, and two essential indicators under Principle 6 are also left empty, the company explaining that it does not collect that data. The assurance provider is asked whether the report is complete.

items.stem: What should the auditor do?

options.text: Add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the sustainability section of the annual report
options.misconception: points an Emphasis of Matter at narrative outside the financial statements
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter points at something the statements themselves already carry, appropriately presented or disclosed there. It cannot be aimed at a section of the annual report sitting outside them, and it would not cure an unadjusted carrying amount in any case.

options.text: Include a Key Audit Matter describing the sustainability disclosure so that readers of the report are alerted to it
options.misconception: uses a Key Audit Matter to report on other information rather than on a matter of most significance in the audit of the financial statements
options.why: Key audit matters come out of what was communicated to those charged with governance, and only the matters carrying most significance for that year's audit of the statements themselves qualify. Impairment of the plant could well be one; the narrative disclosure itself is not.

options.text: Treat the retirement commitment as evidence bearing on the plant's useful life and on impairment inside the financial statements, and challenge the carrying amount, the depreciation and the absence of any climate-related disclosure before considering anything in the auditor's report
options.why: A management commitment to retire an asset nine years earlier than its booked useful life is audit evidence about an estimate that already sits in the financial statements. The auditor first determines whether the entity has appropriately disclosed the relevant climate-related information under the applicable financial reporting framework; only then does the question of what the report says arise.

options.text: Nothing, because sustainability narrative is other information on which the auditor expresses no opinion
options.misconception: reads "no opinion on other information" as "climate information is never audit evidence about a balance"
options.why: Expressing no opinion on the other information is not the same as ignoring what it tells you. Here the narrative contradicts an estimate inside the statements, and a material inconsistency is itself something the auditor must respond to.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — role of the auditor, consideration of climate-related risks

items.scenario: You audit a listed thermal power company. The sustainability section of its annual report commits to retiring its oldest plant by 2032 under tightening emission norms, and names the plant. In the financial statements that plant is carried at full carrying amount and depreciated over a remaining useful life running to 2041, with no impairment note and no mention of the retirement plan. The team's plan is to say nothing, because the sustainability section is outside the financial statements and carries no opinion.

items.stem: What breaches Regulation 18?

options.text: Only the independence count — four meetings in the year satisfies Regulation 18 whatever the gaps between them
options.misconception: reads the four-meeting requirement as replacing the 120-day cap rather than sitting alongside it
options.why: The two requirements are cumulative. Four meetings bunched into one half of the year would leave the committee blind for months, which is why the 120-day cap sits beside the count.

options.text: The independence count and the meeting gap — two-thirds of six is four independent directors, not three, and 130 days exceeds the outer limit of 120 days between two meetings
options.why: Regulation 18(1) requires two-thirds of the members to be independent directors, so a six-member committee needs four. Regulation 18(2) requires at least four meetings a year and not more than 120 days between two of them; both limbs must hold, and the second one fails here.

options.text: Only the meeting gap — Regulation 18 asks for a majority of independent directors, and three out of six satisfies that
options.misconception: imports Section 177's "majority of independent directors" test into Regulation 18, which sets a two-thirds bar
options.why: Section 177 of the Companies Act sets a majority test for the companies it covers; the LODR bar for a listed entity is higher at two-thirds. Three of six is not even a majority.

options.text: Nothing — the chairperson is independent, the company secretary is the secretary, and the quorum of two members including two independent directors was met
options.misconception: checks the conditions that were satisfied and stops, treating Regulation 18 as a menu rather than a set of cumulative requirements
options.why: Those three features are indeed compliant — quorum here is the greater of two members and one-third of six, which is two, with at least two independent directors present. That does not rescue the composition or the meeting gap.

citation.ref: Regulation 18(1) and Regulation 18(2)

items.scenario: A listed company's audit committee has six directors, three of them independent. It met four times during the year, and the longest gap between two consecutive meetings was 130 days. At one of those meetings only two members were present, both independent directors. The chairperson of the committee is an independent director, and the company secretary acts as secretary to the committee.

items.stem: Is the auditor's reasoning sound?

options.text: Yes — the certificate travels with the audit opinion, so a clean opinion on the financial statements supports a clean certificate
options.misconception: treats the corporate governance certificate as an extension of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The certification is neither an audit nor an expression of opinion on the financial statements. The two conclusions are reached on different subject matter and can point in opposite directions on the same company.
keywords: neither an audit nor an expression of opinion

options.text: No — the certificate is on the factual implementation of the conditions in the LODR Regulations, and an audit committee that met three times under a chairman who is not independent is exactly the kind of fact requiring an adverse or qualified statement in the certificate, whatever the financial statements show
options.why: The auditor's responsibility here is verification and certification that the stipulated conditions were factually implemented. Both facts — fewer than four meetings, and a chairman of the audit committee who is not an independent director — are named situations calling for an adverse or qualified statement.

options.text: Yes — the certificate speaks to the company's viability and to how effectively management has run its affairs, and both are plainly sound here
options.misconception: reads the certificate as an assurance about future viability and management effectiveness, which it expressly is not
options.why: The certificate is expressly neither an assurance as to the future viability of the company nor as to the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted its affairs. Profitability answers a question the certificate never asks.

options.text: No — but the right response is to qualify the audit opinion on the financial statements, since a breach of the LODR Regulations is non-compliance with a law under SA 250
options.misconception: moves a defect belonging in a separate certificate into the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: SA 250 would bite only if the non-compliance had a material effect on the financial statements, which a short-staffed audit committee does not. The defect is reported where it belongs — in the certificate.
keywords: material effect on the financial statements

citation.ref: Regulation 34(3) read with Schedule V — compliance certificate on conditions of corporate governance

items.scenario: A listed company's audit committee met three times during the year, and its chairman is a non-independent director. The statutory auditor, who is also issuing the certificate on compliance with the conditions of corporate governance, argues that the certificate can go out clean: the financial statements are free from material misstatement, the company is comfortably profitable, and there is no going concern doubt whatsoever.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The statutory auditor must withdraw his report and reissue it incorporating the CAG's comments
options.misconception: confuses supplementing an audit report with reissuing it
options.why: Section 143(6)(b) lets the CAG comment upon or supplement the audit report. The auditor's own report stands as signed; the supplement travels alongside it.

options.text: The comments are valid, but they feed the CAG's own reporting to Parliament and there is no obligation to put them before the members
options.misconception: treats supplementary audit as an internal government process invisible to shareholders
options.why: The proviso to Section 143(6) does the opposite: it routes the comments to the same people who get the audited financial statements and onto the AGM agenda beside the audit report.

options.text: The comments are within time, being 51 days after the CAG received the audit report, and Section 143(6) requires them to be sent to everyone entitled to copies of the audited financial statements and placed before the annual general meeting in the same manner as the audit report
options.why: The sixty days run from the date the CAG receives the audit report under Section 143(5), so 10 August is comfortably inside the window. The proviso then makes the comments public: they go to every person entitled to copies under Section 136(1) and are laid before the AGM at the same time and in the same manner as the audit report itself.

options.text: The finance head is right that the window has closed, because the CAG's sixty days run from the balance sheet date
options.misconception: measures the sixty days from the balance sheet date instead of from the date the CAG receives the audit report
options.why: Section 143(6) fixes the start of the clock at the date of receipt of the audit report under sub-section (5). From 20 June, the CAG had until roughly 19 August.
keywords: date of receipt of the audit report

citation.ref: Section 143(6) and the proviso to Section 143(6)

items.scenario: The statutory auditor of a government company signs an unmodified report on 20 June and sends a copy to the Comptroller and Auditor-General the same day. On 10 August the CAG issues comments supplementing that report, pointing out an understated provision. The annual general meeting is fixed for 25 September. The company's finance head says the comments came too late to matter and will simply be filed with the CAG's own records.

items.stem: On the earliest permissible date, when may this engagement documentation be destroyed?

options.text: 31 March 2033 — seven years from the balance sheet date of the financial statements audited
options.misconception: counts the retention period from the financial year-end instead of from a report date
options.why: Nothing in SQC 1 measures retention from the year-end. It runs from a report date, which is always later than the year-end and can be much later on a delayed audit.

options.text: 12 May 2033 — seven years from this firm's own audit report, since the group auditor's report belongs to another firm
options.misconception: drops the "or, if later, the date of the group auditor's report" limb because the group report was signed by someone else
options.why: The limb exists precisely for the component auditor whose papers may be needed to support a group opinion signed after his own. Whose firm signed the group report is not the test.

options.text: 30 June 2033 — seven years counted from the later of the two report dates, which here is the group auditor's report
options.why: SQC 1 fixes the retention period as a floor of seven years, and it runs from the later of two dates: when the auditor signed his own report, or the date of the group auditor's report. Here the group auditor's report of 30 June 2026 is the later of the two, so that is where the count begins.
keywords: date of the group auditor's report

options.text: 11 July 2026 — sixty days after the auditor's report, when the final audit file must be assembled
options.misconception: confuses SA 230's sixty-day file assembly period with SQC 1's retention period
options.why: Assembly and retention are different obligations. The sixty days is the outer limit for putting the file together; retention is how long the assembled file is then kept.

citation.ref: para 83 — retention period for engagement documentation

items.scenario: Your firm audits a subsidiary and signs its audit report on 12 May 2026. The group auditor, a different firm, signs its report on the group's consolidated financial statements on 30 June 2026. Your firm's quality manual says engagement documentation is destroyed seven years after the financial year audited, which the office manager reads as 31 March 2033 for this file.

items.stem: What provision is required, and by how much is the branch short?

options.text: ₹40 lakh is required, being 40 per cent of the outstanding balance for an asset doubtful for one to three years, so the branch is correct
options.misconception: applies the graded doubtful percentage to the whole outstanding and leaves the unsecured portion entirely unprovided
options.why: The graded rate attaches only to the secured portion. Applying it to the total quietly gives the unsecured ₹40 lakh a 40 per cent provision when the norm demands 100 per cent on it.

options.text: ₹64 lakh is required — 40 per cent on the ₹60 lakh secured portion, which is ₹24 lakh, plus 100 per cent on the ₹40 lakh unsecured portion — so the branch is short by ₹24 lakh
options.why: On a doubtful asset the portion not covered by the realisable value of the security carries 100 per cent, and only the secured portion is graded by how long the asset has been doubtful — 40 per cent in the one to three year band. ₹24 lakh plus ₹40 lakh is ₹64 lakh.

options.text: ₹100 lakh is required, because an asset that has remained doubtful for more than one year is provided in full
options.misconception: applies the "more than three years" rate at the one-year mark
options.why: Full provision on the secured portion arrives only beyond three years in the doubtful category. At two years the secured portion sits in the 40 per cent band.

options.text: ₹49 lakh is required — 15 per cent on the ₹60 lakh secured portion, which is ₹9 lakh, plus 100 per cent on the ₹40 lakh unsecured portion
options.misconception: carries the 15 per cent substandard rate across into an asset that has moved to doubtful
options.why: Fifteen per cent is the general provision on a substandard asset, on its total outstanding. Once the asset is doubtful the secured portion is graded at 25, 40 or 100 per cent by age.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on IRACP — paras 5.3.1 and 5.3.2

items.scenario: As branch auditor you examine an advance of ₹100 lakh that has been classified as doubtful for two years. The realisable value of the security, assessed on a realistic basis, is ₹60 lakh. The branch has provided ₹40 lakh, computed as 40 per cent of the outstanding balance.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Both investigations may continue, because Section 212(2) bars only agencies of the Central Government and leaves a State Government's agency untouched
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering central agencies alone when the sub-section names Central and State agencies in the same breath
options.why: The words are "no other investigating agency of Central Government or any State Government". The state wing is squarely inside the bar.

options.text: The state agency must stop, and the statutory auditor must also suspend the audit and hand his working papers to the SFIO
options.misconception: extends a bar on parallel investigation to the statutory audit, which is a separate engagement and not an investigating agency
options.why: The bar is on other investigating agencies. The auditor is not one; his duty to report fraud and to respond to a request for information is a separate matter from being ordered off the engagement.

options.text: The state agency must stop and transfer its relevant documents and records to the SFIO; the statutory audit is not an investigation under the Act and continues
options.why: Section 212(2) bars any other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government from proceeding once a case is assigned to the SFIO, and requires an investigation already initiated to stop and its documents and records to be handed over. A statutory audit is an engagement under Section 143, not an investigation under the Act.

options.text: The state agency may finish what it has already begun; the bar operates only on investigations not yet started when the case is assigned
options.misconception: treats the bar as prospective only, letting a head start survive the assignment
options.why: The sub-section deals with that case expressly — where an investigation has already been initiated it shall not be proceeded further with, and the documents go to the SFIO.

citation.ref: Section 212(1) and Section 212(2)

items.scenario: Acting on a Registrar's report under Section 208, the Central Government assigns an investigation into a listed company's affairs to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office. A state economic offences wing had already opened its own investigation into the same alleged offences under the Companies Act and proposes to carry on in parallel. The company's statutory auditor, midway through the year's audit, asks whether he too must stop.

items.stem: What does the file still need?

options.text: A record of how the alternative audit procedures performed achieve the aim of the requirement departed from, and the reasons for the departure
options.why: SA 200 lets the auditor depart from a relevant requirement in exceptional circumstances, on condition that alternative audit procedures achieve the aim of that requirement. SA 230 then requires both halves of that judgement to be written down — how the alternatives achieve the aim, and why the departure happened. The results of the alternative procedures are only one of the three things needed.

options.text: Nothing more — the alternative procedures and their results are documented, and the reason for departing is a matter of professional judgement that need not be reduced to writing
options.misconception: treats the auditor's judgement as evidence the file does not have to carry, when the file must speak to an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit
options.why: The whole point of SA 230 is that the reasoning has to survive the auditor's memory. A file showing what was done and not why the standard route was abandoned leaves the departure invisible to any reviewer.

options.text: Nothing can save it — a requirement of an SA is absolute, so the auditor must qualify the opinion for the inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
options.misconception: treats every SA requirement as absolute and converts a permitted departure into a scope limitation
options.why: SA 200 expressly contemplates a departure in exceptional circumstances, and the aim of external confirmation — evidence about existence from outside the entity — was met by subsequent receipts and sanction orders. The evidence was obtained, so there is nothing to qualify.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph in the auditor's report disclosing that a requirement of an SA was departed from
options.misconception: moves a documentation requirement into the auditor's report
options.why: The departure is documented, not published. Nothing in SA 230 or SA 705 puts a permitted departure into the report, and the alternative procedures here obtained the evidence, so there is no inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to report on.

citation.ref: para 12, read with SA 200 para 23

items.scenario: Trade receivables of a company include ₹22 crore owed by four state government departments. Those departments are under a court-ordered payments freeze and their accounts officers are barred from confirming balances to anyone. The engagement partner judges the circumstances exceptional, does not send confirmation requests, and instead vouches the subsequent receipts, the sanction orders and the tender files for all four balances. The senior's working paper records the alternative procedures performed and their results, and nothing else — the partner's reasoning stayed in the room.

items.stem: What does SA 620 require of you?

options.text: Accept the valuation but name the valuer in the Basis for Opinion section so that readers know the volume assumption came from a specialist
options.misconception: names the expert in the report, which reads as dividing a responsibility the auditor cannot divide
options.why: SA 620 keeps the expert out of the auditor's report unless law or regulation requires the reference, and even then the report must say the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility. Naming him does not make an unreasonable assumption reasonable.

options.text: Accept the valuation — the auditor may not go behind an expert's assumptions in a field outside his own expertise, which is the reason the expert was engaged
options.misconception: reads the auditor's lack of specialist expertise as a bar on evaluating the expert's assumptions and source data
options.why: The auditor is not asked to form his own view of a cement plant's value. He is asked whether the assumptions are relevant and reasonable in the circumstances and whether the source data is accurate, and a figure contradicting the client's own budget can be challenged without any valuation expertise at all.

options.text: Treat the contradiction as an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence and qualify the opinion at once
options.misconception: jumps to a modification before performing the further work SA 620 requires first
options.why: A modification is what happens if the further work still leaves the auditor without sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The standard's sequence is to fix the evidence first — more work by the expert, or additional audit procedures by the auditor.

options.text: Evaluate the relevance and reasonableness of the significant assumptions and methods and the relevance, completeness and accuracy of the source data, and — the work being inadequate — either agree further work with the expert or perform additional audit procedures yourself
options.why: Competence, capabilities and objectivity are a separate, earlier test. Adequacy is tested on the work itself, and a volume assumption contradicting the entity's own board-approved budget and its entire operating history fails both the reasonableness of the assumption and the accuracy of the source data. SA 620 then gives exactly two routes forward, and neither is acceptance.

citation.ref: para 12 and para 13

items.scenario: You engage a registered valuer as an auditor's expert to value a cement plant carried at ₹310 crore, for an impairment test. The valuer is qualified, experienced and has no relationship with the client. His report supports the carrying amount on a value-in-use basis, using a production volume of 4.1 million tonnes a year supplied to him by the client's planning head. The board-approved budget you already hold in the file projects 2.6 million tonnes, and the plant has never exceeded 2.9 million tonnes. The manager proposes to accept the valuation, noting that volumes are outside the auditor's field of expertise.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 510 require this year?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the customer's liquidation
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where a modification is required, and where nothing has been appropriately disclosed to emphasise
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter points readers at something the financial statements already carry, properly presented or properly disclosed. Here the matter is neither disclosed nor provided for — that is a misstatement, and a misstatement is answered in the opinion.

options.text: An adverse opinion, because the unprovided amount is more than four times overall materiality
options.misconception: treats any large multiple of materiality as pervasive, skipping the separate test of whether the effect is confined to specific elements of the financial statements
options.why: Pervasiveness is not a multiple of materiality. The effect here is confined to one receivable and its related provision, is not a substantial proportion of the financial statements, and is not a disclosure fundamental to users' understanding — so it stays material but not pervasive.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph stating that the predecessor auditor's report on the corresponding figures was qualified and why
options.misconception: uses the Other Matter paragraph about a predecessor's report to carry a misstatement that is still sitting in this year's figures
options.why: That paragraph exists to tell readers who audited the comparatives and what he said. It says nothing about the current year, and the ₹9 crore is unprovided in the current balance sheet, not only in the comparatives.

options.text: A qualified opinion — the matter remains relevant and material to the current period's financial statements, so your own opinion is modified, and the misstatement is material but not pervasive
options.why: Where the predecessor's opinion was modified and the matter remains relevant and material to the current period, SA 510 requires the current opinion to be modified too. At ₹9 crore against materiality of ₹2 crore the misstatement is plainly material; being confined to one receivable in a ₹180 crore balance sheet, it is material but not pervasive, which points to a qualified opinion rather than an adverse one.

citation.ref: para 11 and para 13

items.scenario: You are appointed in place of the previous auditor of a trading company. The predecessor's report on the previous year carried a qualified opinion because ₹9 crore due from a single customer, already three years overdue and in liquidation, was carried without any provision. That receivable is still carried in full at the current year-end and is still unprovided. Overall materiality for the current year is ₹2 crore, and receivables are one line of a balance sheet totalling ₹180 crore. The manager proposes an unmodified opinion this year with an Other Matter paragraph recording that the predecessor's report was qualified.

items.stem: What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Two things — an Other Matter paragraph must state that the corresponding figures are unaudited, and that statement does not remove the requirement to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the opening balances contain no misstatement materially affecting the current period
options.why: SA 710 requires the unaudited status of the corresponding figures to be stated in an Other Matter paragraph, and says in the same breath that stating it does not relieve the auditor of the opening-balance work under SA 510. Accepting the firm's brought-forward figures without procedures fails the second half.

options.text: Only the opinion — the corresponding figures being unaudited is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, so the opinion is qualified in respect of them
options.misconception: converts an unaudited comparative into a scope limitation on an opinion that does not cover the comparative
options.why: The opinion does not extend to the corresponding figures, so there is nothing there to qualify. A modification arises only if the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the opening balances themselves, which is a separate question and one the team has not even attempted.

options.text: Only the reporting — an Emphasis of Matter paragraph should state that the corresponding figures are unaudited, and the opening balances need no separate work because they are the firm's audited closing figures carried forward
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where the standard names an Other Matter paragraph, and assumes the firm's books were audited when they were not
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter points at something disclosed in the financial statements; a matter about the scope of the audit itself belongs in an Other Matter paragraph. And the firm's figures were never audited, so there is nothing to carry forward on trust.

options.text: Nothing — the opinion covers only the current period when comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, so the prior period is outside the auditor's report altogether
options.misconception: reads the rule that the opinion does not refer to corresponding figures as removing every reporting obligation about them
options.why: Not referring to the corresponding figures in the opinion is one thing. SA 710 separately requires an Other Matter paragraph in the very situations where readers would otherwise be misled about who, if anyone, audited them.

citation.ref: para 14

items.scenario: A partnership firm converted into a private limited company during the year. The company's first statutory financial statements present the firm's prior period figures as corresponding figures. Those figures were never audited by anyone. The team plans to say nothing at all about them, reasoning that the opinion refers only to the current period in any event, and to accept the opening balances as brought forward from the firm's books.

items.stem: What has gone wrong with this procedure?

options.text: Analytical procedures may never be the sole substantive procedure for a material balance, so tests of details on interest expense were mandatory
options.misconception: invents a bar on substantive analytical procedures that SA 520 does not contain
options.why: SA 520 makes substantive analytical procedures a choice about how to respond to an assessed risk, and they can stand alone where they are suitable for the assertion. Suitability, not a prohibition, is the test the team failed.

options.text: The expectation should have been developed by management from its own loan records and then tested by the auditor for reasonableness
options.misconception: hands the auditor's own expectation to management, which is the one party whose figure the procedure is meant to challenge
options.why: An expectation developed by the entity is not independent of the recorded amount it is compared with. SA 520 has the auditor develop the expectation, using data whose reliability he has evaluated.

options.text: Nothing — a substantive analytical procedure is permitted for a material balance and the difference is barely 2 per cent of the recorded amount
options.misconception: judges a substantive analytical procedure by the size of the variance instead of by the precision of the expectation and the reliability of the data
options.why: A small variance from an imprecise expectation built on unreliable data proves nothing. The expectation has to be precise enough to identify a misstatement that could make the financial statements materially misstated before its closeness means anything.

options.text: The reliability of the data from which the expectation was developed was never evaluated, and no amount of acceptable difference was determined in advance, so the ₹40 lakh gap was judged only after it appeared
options.why: SA 520 requires the auditor to evaluate the reliability of the data used to build the expectation, taking account of its source and the controls over its preparation, and to determine the amount of difference acceptable without further investigation. An unreconciled schedule kept by the person whose work is being tested fails the first, and a threshold set after seeing the answer is not a threshold.

citation.ref: para 5

items.scenario: Interest expense of ₹18 crore is tested only by a substantive analytical procedure. The senior multiplies the average of the opening and closing borrowing balances by the weighted average rate taken from the loan agreements, arrives at ₹18.4 crore, compares it with the recorded ₹18 crore and concludes the balance is reasonable. The borrowing balances came from a loan schedule kept by the treasury clerk, which the team has not reconciled to the general ledger or to lender statements. No figure for an acceptable difference was set before the comparison was made. Performance materiality is ₹1.1 crore.

items.stem: How should the ₹6 lakh be treated?

options.text: Leave it out of the projection to the population, because the cause is isolated and the whole affected sub-population has been examined — but still add the ₹6 lakh itself, in full, to the projected misstatement of the rest when evaluating the results
options.why: Establishing an anomaly needs a high degree of certainty that the misstatement is not representative of the population, obtained by additional audit procedures — which examining all 210 affected invoices supplies. That earns exclusion from the projection only. The misstatement is real money and is still uncorrected, so its own effect is added to the projected misstatement of the rest.

options.text: Extend the sample until the projected misstatement falls comfortably below performance materiality, then conclude
options.misconception: uses sample size to dilute a misstatement already found instead of to respond to an assessed risk
options.why: A larger sample answers a question about sampling risk, not about a misstatement already identified. Sampling more to make a number look better is designing the procedure around the answer wanted.

options.text: Drop it entirely from the evaluation — once a misstatement is established as an anomaly it is not representative of the population, so it carries no weight
options.misconception: reads exclusion from the projection as exclusion from the evaluation, so a real uncorrected misstatement disappears
options.why: Only the projection is affected. The ₹6 lakh was actually charged to actual customers and is still in the financial statements uncorrected, so it goes into the accumulation of misstatements and into the evaluation alongside the projected figure.

options.text: Project it to the whole population like any other misstatement — a misstatement found in a sample is always evidence about the population it came from
options.misconception: denies that the anomaly exists as a category, when SA 530 defines it and allows it in extremely rare circumstances
options.why: That is the default and the right instinct, but SA 530 defines an anomaly as a misstatement demonstrably not representative of the population and permits exclusion from the projection once a high degree of certainty is obtained. Here it has been.

citation.ref: para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: Sales are tested by sampling 80 invoices from a population of 12,000 invoices totalling ₹90 crore. One misstatement of ₹6 lakh is found. Investigating the cause, you establish that it arose from a pricing table that failed during a two-day billing system migration, that only invoices raised on those two days could be affected, and that you have examined every one of the 210 invoices raised on those two days and found no other error. The other 79 sample items are clean. The senior wants to call the ₹6 lakh an anomaly and leave it out of the evaluation altogether. Performance materiality is ₹80 lakh.

items.stem: What must the new auditor's report contain, over and above the opinion?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph or Other Matter paragraph referring to the note that more extensively discusses the reason for the amendment of the previously issued financial statements, and to your earlier report
options.why: SA 560 requires the new or amended report to carry that signpost, so a reader holding two differently dated reports on the same year can see why the second exists. You also review the steps management takes to ensure everyone who received the earlier financial statements and report is informed.

options.text: Nothing at all is required, because after the financial statements have been issued the auditor has no obligation to perform any audit procedures on them
options.misconception: reads the end of the duty to search as the end of the duty once a fact has actually arrived
options.why: That sentence removes the obligation to go looking. The next sentence of the same requirement sets out what happens when a fact reaches the auditor anyway, and that is exactly what has happened here.

options.text: Nothing beyond the fresh date — the new report replaces the old one, which is superseded and no longer speaks
options.misconception: reissues without the required reference to the amendment and the earlier report, leaving two reports on the same year and nothing to reconcile them
options.why: The earlier financial statements and report went out to members and were laid before the annual general meeting. They are in the world, and the standard requires the new report to point at the note explaining why it exists.

options.text: A key audit matter describing the unrecorded guarantee and the amendment it forced
options.misconception: uses a key audit matter to explain why an earlier report was replaced, rather than to communicate a matter of most significance in the audit of the financial statements
options.why: Key audit matters are selected from matters communicated to those charged with governance that were of most significance in the audit of the current period's financial statements. The reason a previously issued report was amended is not one of them, and SA 560 names the paragraph it wants.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 16

items.scenario: The financial statements and your report were issued to members on 12 August and the annual general meeting was held on 28 September. On 5 October you learn that the company gave a ₹40 crore corporate guarantee on 20 March for a promoter group entity, and that it was neither recorded nor disclosed. Had you known of it at the date of your report you would have modified your opinion. Management accepts the position and agrees to amend the financial statements and have you report on them afresh.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 580 lead to?

options.text: A qualified opinion, the matter being material but not pervasive
options.misconception: grades a refused responsibilities representation as a narrow limitation, when the standard names a disclaimer without any pervasiveness test
options.why: SA 580 does not send this through the usual material-versus-pervasive sorting. A refusal to confirm that all relevant information and access were provided touches every part of the audit, and the standard prescribes a disclaimer directly.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion — management has not provided a written representation about its own responsibilities, and SA 580 answers that with a disclaimer
options.why: The struck-out paragraph is one of the two representations about management's own responsibilities. Where those are not provided, or where the auditor concludes there is sufficient doubt about the integrity of management such that they are not reliable, SA 580 requires a disclaimer of opinion. The auditor also discusses the matter with management and re-evaluates management's integrity before getting there.

options.text: An unmodified opinion — no misstatement has been identified, and a written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence about anything in any case
options.misconception: treats a refused representation about management's own responsibilities as harmless because the figures look clean
options.why: It is true that a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own. But its absence here is not about a balance; it is management declining to say it gave you everything, which puts the completeness of all your evidence in doubt.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph recording that management declined to give the representation
options.misconception: uses a paragraph in the report to record a refusal the standard answers by withholding the opinion
options.why: Recording a problem is not the same as responding to it. A paragraph noting the deletion would leave an unmodified opinion standing on evidence management will not confirm is complete.

citation.ref: para 19 and para 20

items.scenario: Management returns the written representation letter signed, but with one paragraph struck out — the one confirming that it has provided you with all relevant information and access as agreed in the terms of the audit engagement. The finance director explains that he cannot vouch for what forty branches did or did not send you. Every other representation you asked for has been given, your procedures have identified no misstatement, and the figures look clean.

items.stem: What does SA 550 require beyond correcting the disclosure?

options.text: Correcting the note is enough, because once the transaction is disclosed the financial statements are free from material misstatement in this respect
options.misconception: treats a related party discovered by the auditor as a disclosure defect alone, ignoring the control failure and the fraud indicator behind it
options.why: The corrected note says nothing about how many other related parties the same broken control missed, and nothing about whether the omission was an accident. Both are questions the standard makes the auditor ask.

options.text: Obtain a fresh written representation from management that the related party list is now complete, and rely on it for the remaining risk
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation for the procedures the standard requires, from the management whose list was just proved wrong
options.why: The list you were given was already wrong once. A second list, certified by the same people, is not audit evidence about the completeness of related parties, and a written representation is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own.

options.text: Report the matter to the Central Government under section 143(12) at once, an undisclosed related party payment of this size being a fraud against the company
options.misconception: escalates to statutory fraud reporting before the auditor has reason to believe an offence of fraud has been committed
options.why: Section 143(12) is triggered by reason to believe an offence of fraud has been or is being committed. An omission from a related party list, without more, is not yet that — the substantive procedures SA 550 requires are what tell you whether it becomes that.

options.text: Communicate promptly to the engagement team, ask management to identify all transactions with that party, inquire why the controls failed to identify or disclose it, perform substantive procedures on the newly identified transactions, reconsider the risk that other related parties are undisclosed, and where the non-disclosure appears intentional evaluate the implications for the audit as a fraud risk
options.why: A related party the auditor found for himself is evidence of two things at once — a disclosure gap and a control that did not work. SA 550 sets out each of those steps, and the last one connects a non-disclosure that appears intentional to a risk of material misstatement due to fraud.

citation.ref: para 22

items.scenario: Reviewing bank statements you notice ₹12 crore paid during the year to a consultancy firm. Its partnership deed, obtained from the public record, shows the managing director's son as a partner. The firm appears nowhere on management's related party list and nowhere in the related party note. The finance controller says the accounts department simply missed it. The audit senior proposes to have the disclosure added to the note and to move on.

items.stem: What does SA 250 require of you?

options.text: Note the matter in the file and move on, because environmental law is not a law with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, so the auditor's duty stops at the specified procedures
options.misconception: uses the other-laws category to switch off the auditor's response after non-compliance has actually been identified
options.why: The two categories decide how hard the auditor looks. Once non-compliance is identified or suspected, the response requirements apply whichever category the law sits in — and a ₹30 crore demand is fundamental to the operating aspects of this business in any event.

options.text: Express an adverse opinion, because the ₹30 crore demand is unprovided and is more than seven times overall materiality
options.misconception: modifies for a misstatement when the problem is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
options.why: You do not know the demand is ₹30 crore or that it is payable — the correspondence was withheld. The auditor cannot assert a misstatement he was prevented from measuring; the modification arises from the preclusion itself.

options.text: Communicate the matter to the next higher level of authority, the audit committee, and — being precluded by management from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether non-compliance that may be material has occurred — express a qualified opinion or disclaim an opinion, because the scope of the audit was limited
options.why: Where the auditor suspects management is involved in the non-compliance, SA 250 sends the communication up to the next higher level of authority, the audit committee here. And where management precludes the auditor from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence, the answer is a scope-limitation modification, qualified or disclaimed according to how pervasive the possible effects are.

options.text: Add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the cancelled environmental clearance and the pollution control board's demand
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter to carry a limitation on the scope of the audit
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter can only point at something the statements themselves carry, properly presented or properly disclosed, and it never signals a limitation. Here nothing is disclosed and the evidence was blocked — that is a modification, not an emphasis.

citation.ref: communication to a higher level of authority and the effect of a preclusion by management on the opinion

items.scenario: A chemical manufacturer's environmental clearance was cancelled in November and the state pollution control board has raised a demand you believe runs into ₹30 crore. The finance director, who is also an executive director on the board, instructs the plant head in writing not to give you the board's correspondence or the show-cause notices, and the audit committee has not been told anything. Your alternative procedures produce nothing you can rely on. Overall materiality is ₹4 crore.

items.stem: What is the auditor's responsibility on each?

options.text: Neither — compliance with law is management's responsibility and the auditor's opinion is on the financial statements
options.misconception: reads management's responsibility for compliance as removing the auditor's own
options.why: Preventing non-compliance is indeed management's responsibility, and the standard says so. It does not follow that the auditor has none: a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures is a matter for the opinion itself.

options.text: Sufficient appropriate audit evidence on both, every law that could cost money being audited alike
options.misconception: collapses the two categories into one, which would make the auditor an examiner of all law
options.why: An auditor cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with every law a company is subject to, and the standard does not ask it. Only the first category — a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures — carries the sufficient appropriate audit evidence obligation.

options.text: Sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the tax matter, and specified procedures — inquiry and inspection of correspondence with the authority — on the licence
options.why: The standard splits laws and regulations in two. One group bears a direct effect on what the statements must record and show by way of material amounts and disclosures — tax law does exactly that to the tax provision — and there the auditor must obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the entity has complied. The other group touches the figures only at a remove, yet complying with it is fundamental to how the business runs or to staying clear of penalties that would matter; there the auditor runs specified procedures able to bring a breach to light — asking management and, where it fits, those charged with governance, plus inspection of correspondence with whoever licenses or regulates the activity.

options.text: Only the licence matter, being the one that threatens the ability to continue in business
options.misconception: keeps the graver-sounding matter and drops the one the opinion actually rests on
options.why: The threat to the business makes the licence matter important, but it is the tax matter that has a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, and that one carries the heavier procedure of the two.

citation.ref: Consideration of Laws and Regulations in an Audit of Financial Statements — the two categories of laws and regulations and the auditor's differing responsibility for each

items.scenario: While auditing a manufacturer the auditor comes across two matters. The company has computed its tax provision on a reading of the tax law that understates the charge. Separately, the plant has been operating outside the terms of its environmental licence, which carries a penalty large enough to matter and could cost the company the licence.

items.stem: What does SA 501 require you to do?

options.text: Issue an unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph noting that a legal matter exists whose outcome could not be quantified
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter to carry a scope limitation, and emphasises a matter that is not disclosed in the financial statements at all
options.why: There is no disclosure in the financial statements to emphasise, and an Emphasis of Matter never signals that the auditor was blocked. The inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence goes into the opinion.

options.text: Accept the written representation, since management is the party that knows what claims exist and confidentiality is a legitimate reason to withhold correspondence
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation for direct communication with the entity's external legal counsel
options.why: A representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any matter it deals with, least of all one that management has an interest in keeping quiet. The standard names the external legal counsel precisely because the answer must come from outside management.

options.text: Modify the opinion — management's refusal, combined with alternative audit procedures that did not yield sufficient appropriate audit evidence, is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
options.why: SA 501 states the outcome plainly. Where management refuses permission to communicate with the external legal counsel and the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by alternative procedures, the auditor modifies the opinion. Both limbs are made out here.

options.text: Write to the external legal counsel directly without management's permission, since the auditor's statutory right of access overrides the client's wish for confidentiality
options.misconception: bypasses the requirement that the letter of inquiry is prepared by management and sent by the auditor, and ignores the privilege binding the lawyer
options.why: The letter of inquiry is prepared by management and sent by the auditor for a reason — the lawyer's duty runs to his client, and without management's authority he cannot answer. A letter sent around management would go unanswered and would not cure anything.

citation.ref: para 10 and para 11

items.scenario: Reviewing legal expense accounts you find ₹1.4 crore paid during the year to a law firm that does not appear on the client's schedule of pending litigation. Management says the matter is confidential, refuses permission for you to write to or meet the company's external legal counsel, and offers instead a written representation that no material claim is outstanding. Your alternative procedures — board minutes, subsequent payments, inquiries of the company secretary — produce nothing about the matter. Overall materiality is ₹1 crore.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require of you?

options.text: Take it up with the chief financial officer, since SA 240 requires communication to the appropriate level of management and he is the officer responsible for the payments
options.misconception: communicates to the very person suspected, ignoring the rule that communication goes at least one level above those apparently involved
options.why: Telling the suspect first is how evidence disappears. The standard fixes the level expressly, and where the suspicion touches management it adds a separate channel to those charged with governance.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement immediately, since exceptional circumstances have arisen that bring your ability to continue into question
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as the first step rather than as a matter to be considered after determining the applicable professional and legal responsibilities
options.why: The standard has the auditor determine the professional and legal responsibilities applicable, then consider whether withdrawal is appropriate and possible under law, and if he withdraws, discuss the reasons with management and those charged with governance. Walking out first skips all of it.

options.text: Say nothing outside the audit file, because disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement without the client's consent is itself professional misconduct
options.misconception: reads professional confidentiality as absolute when the clause itself excepts a disclosure required by any law in force
options.why: The confidentiality clause excepts disclosure required by any law for the time being in force, and both SA 240 and section 143(12) sit inside that exception. Confidentiality protects the client's information, not the client's officers.

options.text: Communicate the matter to those charged with governance on a timely basis, the suspected fraud involving management, and to a level of management above the chief financial officer — then consider whether the circumstances bring your ability to continue the engagement into question, taking legal advice on any duty to report outside the entity
options.why: Communication to management goes at least one level above the persons who appear to be involved, so the chief financial officer is the wrong addressee. Where the suspected fraud involves management, SA 240 requires timely communication to those charged with governance as well, whatever management would prefer.

citation.ref: para 40 and para 41

items.scenario: You establish that the chief financial officer personally authorised ₹3 crore of payments to a vendor with no premises, no employees and no earlier trading history, and that the supporting purchase orders were raised after the payments. The chairman of the audit committee is the chief financial officer's brother-in-law. The managing director asks you to take the matter up with the chief financial officer alone, saying the board should not be troubled until the facts are settled.

items.stem: What do you do once the forty-five days have expired?

options.text: Forward your report to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, together with a note containing the details of the report earlier sent to the audit committee and not replied to
options.why: Rule 13 provides for exactly this case. Where the auditor gets no reply or observations within the stipulated forty-five days, he forwards his report to the Central Government with a note giving the details of the report earlier sent for which no reply was received. The report goes to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs in a sealed cover, in Form ADT-4.

options.text: Wait until the audit committee replies, because the report to the Central Government must carry the committee's observations and your comments on them
options.misconception: makes the reply a precondition to reporting, when the rule expressly provides for its absence
options.why: The reply travels with the report only if one arrives. Making it a precondition would let any company kill the report by staying silent, which is the reason the rule spells out the alternative.

options.text: Record the fraud in the Board's report with its nature, approximate amount and the parties involved, that being the route the rules prescribe
options.misconception: applies the below-one-crore route to a fraud above the threshold
options.why: Disclosure in the Board's report is what happens to frauds below one crore rupees, which go to the audit committee or the Board and no further. At ₹2.4 crore the report is owed to the Central Government.

options.text: Nothing further — the duty was discharged when you reported to the audit committee within two days, and its silence is its response
options.misconception: treats the intimation to the audit committee as the report to the Central Government rather than as the first step towards it
options.why: Above one crore rupees the report is owed to the Central Government. The audit committee stage exists to attach the company's side to it, not to absorb it — which is why the rule says what to do when nothing comes back.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) read with Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: On 3 June you come to have reason to believe that the procurement head of an unlisted public company has defrauded it of ₹2.4 crore through a chain of inflated purchase invoices. On 4 June you report the matter to the audit committee, seeking its reply or observations within forty-five days. The forty-five days pass and no reply of any kind arrives. The company secretary tells you the file is closed because the committee chose not to respond.

items.stem: Which forum hears the case, and is counsel right about the worst outcome?

options.text: The Board of Discipline hears it, and counsel is right — removal for a period not exceeding three months is the outer limit
options.misconception: sends a Second Schedule charge to the forum that hears only First Schedule cases
options.why: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties sits in the Second Schedule, which takes the case out of the Board of Discipline entirely. The three-month cap belongs to the Board and travels no further.

options.text: The two charges are heard separately — the First Schedule charge by the Board of Discipline and the Second Schedule charge by the Disciplinary Committee
options.misconception: splits one case across two forums, when a case touching both Schedules goes whole to the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: The Act sends a case falling under both Schedules to the Disciplinary Committee as one case. Splitting it would put the same facts before two bodies and could produce two inconsistent findings on one audit.

options.text: The Disciplinary Committee hears it, because the case falls under both the Schedules, and counsel is wrong — that Committee may remove the member's name from the Register of Members permanently or for such period as it thinks fit
options.why: Routing follows the Schedule. A case under the First Schedule alone goes to the Board of Discipline; a case under the Second Schedule, or under both Schedules, goes to the Disciplinary Committee. Permanent removal is available only to the Disciplinary Committee, so the three-month ceiling counsel is relying on is the wrong forum's.

options.text: Neither — the Director (Discipline), having formed a prima facie opinion of guilt, may impose the punishment himself
options.misconception: treats the Director (Discipline)'s prima facie opinion as a finding of guilt and gives him a punishing power he does not have
options.why: A prima facie opinion decides only which forum the case goes to. Guilt is found, and punishment imposed, by the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee after the member has been given an opportunity of being heard.

citation.ref: Section 21A(3) and Section 21B(3), read with the routing under Section 21(3)

items.scenario: A complaint against a member in practice carries two charges. The first is that he accepted appointment as statutory auditor of a company without first communicating in writing with the retiring auditor — a clause of Part I of the First Schedule. The second is that he was grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties on the same audit — a clause of Part I of the Second Schedule. The Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion that the member is guilty on both. The member's counsel argues that the worst outcome available is removal for three months.

items.stem: What does SA 260 require?

options.text: Reporting to the group financial controller was enough, since he is the officer who can fix the delays
options.misconception: treats a report to the very management that created the obstruction as a communication to those charged with governance
options.why: SA 260 directs the communication at those charged with governance. Management is a different body with a different role, and here it is the party whose conduct is the subject of the communication.

options.text: Nothing, because the evidence was ultimately obtained and the opinion is unmodified
options.misconception: makes the communication conditional on how the audit turned out rather than on the matter having arisen
options.why: A clean opinion says the financial statements are not materially misstated. It says nothing about a finance function that made the audit take seven extra weeks, which is exactly the kind of thing the body overseeing the financial reporting process is there to hear about.

options.text: Mention the difficulties orally at the closing meeting, since SA 260 leaves the form of every communication to the auditor's judgement
options.misconception: treats the form as unconstrained, when significant findings go in writing wherever oral communication would not be adequate
options.why: SA 260 does allow oral communication, but only where it would be adequate. Significant findings from the audit go down in writing whenever the auditor, weighing it on his own professional judgement, decides that saying them aloud would leave the communication short — and a difficulty management itself created is precisely where a written record earns its place.

options.text: Communicate the difficulties to the audit committee as part of the significant findings from the audit, alongside your views on the significant qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices, the significant matters discussed with management and the written representations you are requesting
options.why: SA 260 names significant difficulties encountered during the audit as one of the significant findings that must reach those charged with governance, and the requirement is not written as an exception report — the difficulty itself is what governance oversees, whatever opinion came out at the end. The same list carries the auditor's view on significant qualitative aspects — how the entity's own accounting choices strike him — together with the written representations he still means to ask management for.
keywords: significant difficulties encountered during the audit

citation.ref: para 16

items.scenario: Your team spent seven weeks waiting for a subsidiary's ledgers, was refused access to the treasury system until March, and was told the group financial controller had no time for the cut-off walkthrough. Every one of those obstacles was eventually overcome, and the opinion will be unmodified. The manager reported each delay to the group financial controller as it happened and proposes to say nothing about any of it to the audit committee, on the ground that the evidence was obtained in the end.

items.stem: What is missing from the letter?

options.text: Nothing — the description and the potential effects are the whole of the requirement, and what a recipient does with the letter is not the auditor's affair
options.misconception: reads the content requirement as ending at the description, treating the context statements as courtesy rather than requirement
options.why: The context statements sit in the requirement itself, not in the application guidance. SA 265 sets them out as the second limb of what the written communication shall include.

options.text: A restriction on use, stating that the letter is for the addressee alone and may not be relied upon by any other party
options.misconception: substitutes a restriction-on-use paragraph for the context the standard actually prescribes
options.why: A restriction on use is sensible practice and SA 265 does not require it. What the standard requires is the three statements about the purpose of the audit, the limited reason internal control was considered, and the limits of what is being reported.

options.text: An opinion on whether the four deficiencies, taken together, amount to a material weakness
options.misconception: imports internal financial controls reporting into a SA 265 letter, which carries no opinion at all
options.why: Reporting on internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a separate requirement under section 143(3)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, and it produces an opinion inside the auditor's report. A SA 265 communication to those charged with governance expresses no opinion on internal control.

options.text: The context statements SA 265 prescribes — that the purpose of the audit was to express an opinion on the financial statements, that internal control was considered only in order to design audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances, and that the deficiencies reported are limited to those identified during the audit
options.why: SA 265 requires the written communication to say what each deficiency is and spell out their potential effects, plus carry sufficient information to enable the reader — governance and management both — to understand the context behind the letter. Those statements exist precisely to stop a list of four deficiencies being read as an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control, which is how the chairman has just used it.
keywords: opinion on the effectiveness of internal control

citation.ref: para 11

items.scenario: You write to the audit committee describing four significant deficiencies in internal control and the amount each could expose. The letter contains nothing else — no explanation of why you looked at internal control, and no statement of what your list does and does not cover. The chairman forwards it to the company's lenders as "our auditor's assessment of the company's internal controls".

items.stem: What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Only the period is a problem, and a bridging letter from the service organisation covering January to March closes it
options.misconception: treats an assertion by the service organisation as audit evidence about the operation of its own controls
options.why: A bridging letter is the service organisation saying that nothing changed. It is not evidence obtained by the auditor or by a service auditor, and it leaves the three controls at the client untouched in any case.

options.text: Refer to the service auditor's report in the Basis for Opinion section, so readers know part of the evidence came from another auditor
options.misconception: refers to the service auditor in a report carrying an unmodified opinion, and treats disclosure as a substitute for the missing work
options.why: SA 402 bars the user auditor from referring to the work of a service auditor in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires it, and such a reference would not diminish the user auditor's own responsibility in any event. Naming the provider does not test a control the client was supposed to run.

options.text: Nothing — an unmodified type 2 report is evidence that the controls operated effectively throughout the period it covers, which is what reliance requires
options.misconception: reads the type 2 report as covering the whole control system, when the complementary user entity controls it names were never within its scope
options.why: It is evidence about the provider's controls and only those. The description names three controls the provider assumed the client would run, and nobody has yet looked at whether the client ran them.

options.text: Two things — the three controls the provider named sit at the client, so they must be understood and their operating effectiveness tested there; and the report stops at 31 December, so the time elapsed since the service auditor's tests and the three uncovered months must both be dealt with
options.why: The service auditor tested nothing at the user entity, so an unmodified type 2 report says nothing about whether the client authorised new joiners, reviewed the exception report or reconciled the charge. SA 402 makes the user auditor go back to the complementary user entity controls the service organisation named, decide which are relevant here, and — for those — find out whether the client designed and implemented them, then test their operating effectiveness directly. Separately, he has to weigh whether the stretch that was tested still holds up against the time elapsed since those tests were performed.

citation.ref: para 8(a), with the type 2 report requirements on complementary user entity controls and on the time elapsed since the tests of controls

items.scenario: Your client outsources payroll. The provider gives you a type 2 report for 1 April to 31 December with an unmodified service auditor's opinion. Its description of the system lists three complementary user entity controls: the client must authorise every new joiner in the provider's portal, must review the monthly exception report, and must reconcile the payroll charge to the general ledger. The year end is 31 March. The manager proposes to rely on the type 2 report for the whole year and do no controls work at the client at all.

items.stem: Which reliance survives SA 330?

options.text: Both — neither control has changed and neither has reached its third audit
options.misconception: applies the three-year rotation to controls over a significant risk, which are carved out of it
options.why: The rotation rule is general; the carve-out for a significant risk is written into the same standard. Revenue recognition carries a presumed fraud risk under SA 240, and controls over a significant risk are tested in every period the auditor relies on them.

options.text: The bank reconciliation control only — it may be relied on without retesting this year, the change test having been satisfied; the revenue cut-off control must be tested this year because it addresses a significant risk
options.why: SA 330 lets unchanged controls be tested at least once in every third audit, so a control last tested two years ago can still be relied on once the auditor has obtained audit evidence about whether significant changes have occurred. That concession stops at a significant risk: where the auditor plans to rely on controls over a risk determined to be a significant risk, those controls are tested in the current period.
keywords: at least once in every third audit

options.text: Both, provided management confirms in writing that neither control has changed since it was last tested
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation for the evidence SA 330 requires to establish continuing relevance
options.why: Continuing relevance is established by audit evidence obtained through inquiry combined with observation or inspection, not by management's word. A written representation is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it deals with.
keywords: inquiry combined with observation or inspection

options.text: Neither — evidence about a control's operating effectiveness speaks only for the period in which it was obtained, so every control must be tested afresh each year
options.misconception: denies the rotation SA 330 permits and turns every audit into a full test of every control relied on
options.why: SA 330 expressly allows audit evidence obtained in previous audits to be used once the auditor has established its continuing relevance. Testing everything every year is not what the standard asks for and is not what the file has to show.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 15

items.scenario: Two controls are in question. The first is a three-way bank reconciliation over cash. The second is a management review control over revenue cut-off; you have assessed revenue recognition as a significant risk under the SA 240 presumption. Both were tested two years ago and found effective, and inquiry combined with observation shows that neither has changed since. The senior plans to rely on both this year without testing either, since neither has reached its third audit.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require?

options.text: Cover the remaining period with procedures that give a reasonable basis for extending the interim conclusion to the year end, and — the December error being one you did not expect — reassess the risk and reconsider the remaining-period work before performing it
options.why: SA 330 gives two routes across the remaining period: substantive procedures combined with tests of controls for the intervening period, or further substantive procedures only where the auditor determines that is sufficient. Either has to provide a reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions from the interim date to the period end.
