First, the team has established that the purchase manager, working with a dye supplier, raised invoices for 1.8 crore rupees of dyes that were never delivered and had them paid in full during the year, and that a storekeeper separately removed yarn worth 30 lakh rupees, which the company found and recovered in January 2026. The finance head accepts both, says the company will recover the 1.8 crore rupees from the supplier, and asks that the matter be placed before the audit committee at its scheduled meeting in five weeks; on the yarn, he says that anything under a crore is not the auditor's business to report anywhere. The audit manager's view is that a fraud above a crore goes straight to the Central Government and the committee can be told afterwards. Second, the ledger shows an advance of 4 crore rupees, interest-free, to a partnership firm of the managing director's brother against a mortgage of land whose title deed the company has never held; 60 lakh rupees of club subscriptions and the expenses of a family wedding charged to business promotion; and shares of a listed company bought during the year for 2.1 crore rupees and sold in March 2026 to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees. The finance head says these are matters the auditor merely looks into under sub-section (1) of section 143 and never reports on, so the report stays as it is whatever she finds; the manager says the report must answer each of the six matters one by one, the way it answers the clauses of the Order. Third, the company has refused the team's request for the minutes of the remuneration committee and the change log of the vendor master, calling both confidential; the Panipat branch auditor's report has not been sent to the firm; and one director was disqualified under sub-section (2) of section 164 in June 2025 through another company's default, which the finance head says is that company's auditor's concern. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the three ledger entries alone, what does Meera do?

options.text: The manager is right. The six matters in sub-section (1) are answered one by one in a separate paragraph of the report, favourable or not, in the way the clauses of the Order are answered, so the report will carry six statements.
options.misconception: The six inquiry matters are a checklist reported clause by clause, like the Order.
options.why: Nothing about these six reaches the report unless the auditor has something particular to say, and where she is satisfied the report reads exactly as it would have; only an adverse answer is reported, and there is no clause-by-clause paragraph.

options.text: The finance head is right. Sub-section (1) is a duty of inquiry and nothing more: Meera looks into the advance, the expenses and the share sale, records her inquiry in the working papers, and the report stays as it is whatever she finds.
options.misconception: Section 143(1) is a duty to inquire with no reporting consequence at all.
options.why: The auditor is not required to report on the sub-section (1) matters unless he has special comments to make, and an adverse answer is a special comment reported to the members; the working papers are where a satisfied inquiry rests, not an adverse one.

options.text: The three entries are frauds by the managing director against the company, so they leave sub-section (1) and are reported to the Central Government under sub-section (12) within the prescribed time, and the audit report itself says nothing about them.
options.misconception: An adverse answer under section 143(1) is automatically a fraud to be reported under section 143(12).
options.why: Sub-section (1) asks whether an advance is properly secured or on prejudicial terms, whether personal expenses sit in revenue and whether securities were sold below cost, none of which is a finding of fraud; an adverse answer on these is reported to the members, and the route under sub-section (12) needs reason to believe an offence of fraud by an officer or employee, which the inquiry has not established.

options.text: Meera inquires into each of the three and reports only where the answer is adverse, which here is all three. Her duty under sub-section (1) is to inquire into six named matters, and three of them meet these facts: a secured loan or advance that is not truly covered by its security, or lent on terms that work against the company or its members; private spending put through the revenue account; and securities that left the company for less than it paid for them. She is not required to report on any of them where the inquiry satisfies her, and the report then stays exactly as it is. But an interest-free advance against land the company holds no title to, a wedding charged to business promotion and shares sold to a group company for 70 lakh rupees less than they cost are each an answer in adverse, so she reports each to the members. The finance head is right that inquiry is not reporting and wrong that the report never changes; the manager is wrong that the six are answered clause by clause.
options.why: Sub-section (1) hands the auditor a duty to ask, not a duty to announce, and the chapter sets out six things she must ask about: whether money lent against security is genuinely covered by it and whether the terms of the lending run against the company or its members; whether transactions existing only as book entries hurt the company; whether a company that is neither an investment nor a banking one let shares, debentures and other securities go for less than it paid; whether loans have been dressed up as deposits; whether somebody's private spending has been put through the revenue account; and whether cash actually came in for shares said to have been issued for cash. What follows from all that is settled by the Research Committee opinion the chapter carries. She need say nothing about these six where the asking leaves her satisfied, and then the wording of her report is unchanged; but she must put each question and think about what the answer gives her before deciding that nothing needs saying. Where an answer comes back in adverse, she makes a report to the members on it. An interest-free advance to the managing director's brother's firm, mortgaged on land whose title deed the company has never held, is neither truly covered nor on terms that leave the company unharmed; club subscriptions and a family wedding sitting in business promotion are private spending in the revenue account; shares that cost 2.1 crore rupees and went to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees left for less than the company paid. Each is something particular to say. In short, Meera must inquire into the six matters, is not required to report on them where satisfied, and reports to the members on each answer she finds in adverse, which here is all three.

citation.ref: section 143(1): a duty to inquire into six named matters — among them whether a secured loan or advance really is secured and whether its terms work against the company or its members, whether securities went out for less than they cost, and whether personal spending has been put through the revenue account — with nothing said in the report about them unless the auditor has something particular to say, and a report to the members on any answer found in adverse

The audit manager's view is that a fraud above a crore goes straight to the Central Government and the committee can be told afterwards. Second, the ledger shows an advance of 4 crore rupees, interest-free, to a partnership firm of the managing director's brother against a mortgage of land whose title deed the company has never held; 60 lakh rupees of club subscriptions and the expenses of a family wedding charged to business promotion; and shares of a listed company bought during the year for 2.1 crore rupees and sold in March 2026 to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the refused documents, the branch report and the disqualified director alone, what does Meera's report state?

options.text: The report says nothing about the two documents. Board and committee papers are the company's to withhold as confidential, and a refused paper affects the report only if Meera concludes the resulting limitation is material, in which case it appears as a scope paragraph and not otherwise.
options.misconception: Management may withhold papers as confidential and the report stays silent unless the auditor decides the gap is material.
options.why: Clause (a) of sub-section (3) has the report state whether all the information and explanations necessary for the audit were obtained and, if not, the details thereof and the effect on the financial statements; the company's view of confidentiality does not change what the clause requires the report to say.

options.text: The report answers each of the three under sub-section (3), and a refusal is reported, not absorbed. It says whether Meera asked for and got every piece of information and explanations her audit needed and, where she did not, what was withheld and what the gap does to the financial statements — so the minutes and the vendor master change log are named, with their effect. It says whether the Panipat branch report, made under sub-section (8) by another firm, reached her and what she did with it in building her own. And it says whether any director of Beas is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2), which is answered for Beas's own director whichever company's default caused it. Confidentiality is an answer to none of the three.
options.why: Sub-section (3) lists what the report shall state, and three of its clauses land on these facts. Clause (a) is about what the auditor was given: did she ask for all the information and explanations her audit needed, on her own honest judgement of what it needed, and did she get them — and where she did not, the report has to name what was missing and say what the gap does to the financial statements. A company that keeps back its remuneration committee minutes and the change log of its vendor master has not given the auditor what she judged necessary, and the clause wants that written down with its effect rather than quietly worked around by narrowing the audit. Clause (c) is about a branch somebody else audited under sub-section (8): did that firm's report come to her, and what did she do with it in building her own? A branch report that never arrived is answered in those same terms. Clause (g) asks whether a director of the company is disqualified from being appointed as a director, on the grounds section 164(2) sets out; it asks about this company's own board, and a disqualification triggered by another company's default disqualifies the director all the same. In short, the report states whether the information and explanations needed were obtained and, where they were not, what is missing and to what effect; whether the branch report under sub-section (8) reached her and how she dealt with it; and whether a director of Beas is disqualified from being appointed as a director on the grounds section 164(2) sets out.
keywords: disqualified from being appointed as a director

options.text: The Panipat branch is another auditor's work. Its report belongs to that firm and to the branch, so Meera's report on the company does not mention whether it was received, and she audits the branch figures herself if it does not arrive.
options.misconception: A branch audited by another auditor is outside the company auditor's report.
options.why: Clause (c) has the company auditor's own report say whether a branch report made under sub-section (8) by another firm reached her and what she did with it, so an absent branch report is stated rather than silently worked around.

options.text: The disqualification is answered by the auditor of the defaulting company, whose report carries the director. Meera's report on Beas states nothing on the director, because Beas itself has not defaulted.
options.misconception: Director disqualification is reported only by the auditor of the company where the default occurred.
options.why: Clause (g) asks whether any director of this company is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2); it is this company's own board that is being asked about, whatever company's default produced the disqualification.

citation.ref: section 143(3): the report says whether every piece of information and explanations the audit needed was asked for and given and, where it was not, what is missing and what that does to the financial statements; whether a branch report made under sub-section (8) by somebody else reached the auditor and how it was used; and whether any director stands disqualified under section 164(2)

Second, the ledger shows an advance of 4 crore rupees, interest-free, to a partnership firm of the managing director's brother against a mortgage of land whose title deed the company has never held; 60 lakh rupees of club subscriptions and the expenses of a family wedding charged to business promotion; and shares of a listed company bought during the year for 2.1 crore rupees and sold in March 2026 to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees. Third, the company has refused the team's request for the minutes of the remuneration committee and the change log of the vendor master, calling both confidential; the Panipat branch auditor's report has not been sent to the firm; and one director was disqualified under sub-section (2) of section 164 in June 2025 through another company's default, which the finance head says is that company's auditor's concern. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the receivable and the tunnel fire alone, can either matter go in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph?

options.text: The receivable can, because the note is complete and the paragraph will say the opinion is not modified; the fire cannot, because it is a key audit matter.
options.misconception: Applies the key audit matter gate and forgets the modification gate.
options.why: The second half is right and the first is the mistake the module names: management's disclosure through the notes does not remove the auditor's duty to modify where evidence is lacking, and an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for a modification of opinion. The paragraph's statement that the opinion is not modified would be untrue.

options.text: Neither. The paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and the receivable is a matter on which the file says a qualification is required; a complete note does not change that, because an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for a modification. The tunnel fire fails the other gate: where SA 701 applies, a matter already determined to be a key audit matter is not placed in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph as well.
options.why: Two conditions sit on this paragraph, and the two matters fail one each. The first is that the matter must not be one that leaves the auditor required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised). The second, where SA 701 is in play, is that the matter must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter for the report. The receivable runs into the first, and it is the very trap the module warns of: management presses for an unmodified opinion on the ground that the notes tell the whole story, but the auditor still has to judge whether disclosure by itself will do or the report has to be modified, and the paragraph is not a substitute for a modification. The module adds that this paragraph is used only where sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the matter is already in hand, and the firm holds none on whether the 38 crore rupees will be recovered. So the opinion is qualified for the evidence the firm could not get, the note is pointed to inside the basis for that qualification, and the matter stays out of a paragraph that announces an unmodified opinion. The fire runs into the second gate: the team has already settled on it as a key audit matter, and the module's table on how the two relate says such a matter is described in the key audit matters section rather than lit up a second time here. In short, a matter that forces a modification is shut out because this paragraph is not a substitute for one, and a matter already settled on as a key audit matter is shut out by the other gate.

options.text: The fire can, because a key audit matter of that importance may be highlighted twice; the receivable cannot, because it requires a qualification.
options.misconception: Applies the modification gate and forgets the key audit matter gate.
options.why: The second gate is that, where SA 701 is in play, the matter must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter, and the module's table on the two says emphasis paragraphs used freely weaken what they are meant to carry; a key audit matter is described in the key audit matters section and is not emphasised on top of that.

options.text: Both. The purpose of the paragraph is to draw attention to matters fully disclosed in the notes, which both are, and a qualification would be disproportionate where management has hidden nothing.
options.misconception: Treats a complete note as curing a limitation on evidence.
options.why: Full disclosure is the entry condition for the paragraph, not the whole test; the module requires that the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter and that it is not a key audit matter. A qualification for an inability to obtain evidence turns on the evidence, not on candour, and the module says the paragraph is not a substitute for a modification.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) puts two gates on an Emphasis of Matter paragraph: the matter must not be one that leaves the auditor required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised), and, where SA 701 is in play, it must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter for the report; the paragraph is no stand-in for a modification

items.scenario: Iyer & Lakhani audit Betwa Hydro Power Limited, a listed company at Jabalpur with revenue of 1,150 crore rupees from three run-of-river stations. Radhika Iyer is the engagement partner and the draft report for the year ended 31 March 2026 is on her desk with three requests from the chief financial officer. First, a receivable of 38 crore rupees from a state distribution company has been under dispute for two years; the note describes the dispute in full, but the firm has been unable to obtain evidence about its recoverability and Radhika's file concludes that a qualification is required; the chief financial officer asks for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph instead, "since the note is complete and your opinion need not change", and asks that the same paragraph also cover the fire in the headrace tunnel at the Bargi station, which the team has already determined to be a key audit matter for its impairment assessment. Second, the accounts of the three stations are audited by three branch auditors, whose reports have been furnished to the firm, and the stations account for total assets of 610 crore rupees and revenue of 290 crore rupees; the manager proposes to say nothing of this in the report "because the Companies Act lets us rely on branch auditors anyway", while the chief financial officer suggests that if it must be mentioned it belongs under Emphasis of Matter "as it is important". Third, the manager's draft places under a single heading "Emphasis of Matter" both the company's early application, where permitted, of an amendment to an accounting standard that has a material effect and is disclosed in a note, and the fact that the comparative figures for the previous year were audited by another firm which issued an unmodified opinion.

items.stem: On the branch auditors alone, what does the report say about the three stations, and where?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph, because the stations are more than half the company's assets and a matter of that importance must be emphasised, with a statement that the opinion is not modified.
options.misconception: Chooses the paragraph by how important the matter is rather than by what it is about.
options.why: Importance is not the test between the two paragraphs; subject matter is. The module's Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and the fact that other auditors audited the stations is not presented in them. A matter relevant to understanding the audit takes an Other Matter paragraph.

options.text: Nothing. The branch auditors' reports are the principal auditor's evidence and the Act permits reliance on them; a paragraph would suggest the firm's opinion is weaker than it is.
options.misconception: Reads statutory permission to rely as a reason not to disclose the reliance.
options.why: The module's own illustration of the Other Matter paragraph is the branch paragraph, and its text says the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter; the paragraph informs the reader who audited what, which is a matter relevant to understanding the audit, and the reliance the Act permits is what it records.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph, in a separate section under that heading, and not an Emphasis of Matter paragraph: that the firm did not audit the financial statements of three stations reflecting total assets of 610 crore rupees and revenue of 290 crore rupees, that they were audited by branch auditors whose reports have been furnished to the firm, and that the opinion so far as it relates to those amounts and disclosures is based solely on those reports. The paragraph is available because it is not prohibited by law or regulation and the matter is not a key audit matter; the Companies Act's leave to rely on the branch auditors is why the opinion is unmodified, not a reason to be silent about it.
options.why: The module gives the rule and then this very paragraph as its worked illustration. The rule: where the auditor judges that a reader needs to be told something the accounts do not carry — something bearing on the audit itself, on what the auditor answered for, or on the report — an Other Matter paragraph is where it goes, so long as no law or regulation forbids it and, where SA 701 is in play, the matter has not already been settled on as a key audit matter; and it goes in a separate section, headed "Other Matter" or whatever other heading fits. The illustration is a company whose branches were audited by branch auditors, and the paragraph there gives the branches' assets and revenue, says their statements were audited by those auditors and that their reports have reached the principal firm, says the opinion so far as it touches those amounts and disclosures is based solely on those reports, and adds that the opinion is not modified. What that reports is the audit and who performed it — which is exactly why it can never be emphasised instead: an emphasis may take in only what the accounts themselves carry, and how the audit work was split between firms is not in them, however large the stations are. The manager has it backwards: the statute's leave to rely on other auditors is what makes the reliance sound, and the paragraph is how the reader learns the reliance happened. Where such a paragraph is expected, its wording goes to those charged with governance beforehand. In short, the branch paragraph is an Other Matter paragraph in a separate section, open because it is not prohibited by law or regulation, and it tells the reader that the opinion on those amounts is based solely on the branch auditors' reports.
keywords: not prohibited by law or regulation

options.text: A qualified opinion, because the firm did not itself audit assets of 610 crore rupees and cannot take responsibility for figures it has not examined.
options.misconception: Treats reliance on another auditor's report as a limitation on scope.
options.why: The branch auditors' reports have been furnished and the module's illustration treats reliance on them as consistent with an unmodified opinion, recorded in an Other Matter paragraph that states the opinion is based solely on those reports; there is no inability to obtain evidence and no misstatement, so nothing under SA 705 (Revised) is engaged.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) on the Other Matter paragraph: it carries something the accounts do not, which the auditor judges a reader needs in order to grasp the audit, the auditor's duties or the report; it is open where no law or regulation forbids it and where the matter has not already been settled on as a key audit matter, and it sits in its own section under that heading; the module's illustration is the branch paragraph

items.stem: On the manager's single heading alone, is the draft right to put both matters under Emphasis of Matter?

options.text: Yes. Both matters are important to a reader of the report and neither modifies the opinion, which is all an Emphasis of Matter paragraph requires; two headings for two short matters would clutter the report.
options.misconception: Uses importance as the test instead of subject matter.
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph may take in only what the statements themselves carry, and the identity of last year's auditor is not among that; it is a fact bearing on a reader's understanding of the audit and takes an Other Matter paragraph in its own section. Importance to the reader is not the dividing line.

options.text: No; the two matters take two paragraphs. The early application of the amendment is presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and the module lists it among the occasions for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — which may refer only to information the statements themselves carry, with a pointer to the note and a line saying the opinion is not modified. That another firm audited the comparatives is nowhere in the accounts; it bears on a reader's understanding of the audit and of this firm's report, so it goes in a separate Other Matter paragraph.
options.why: What separates the two paragraphs is the subject, not the size. One of them is for something the accounts themselves already say — a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements which a reader must grasp to make sense of them — and where the auditor uses it, the paragraph may refer only to information the statements carry, must point to the note that describes the matter, and must say the opinion is not modified. Adopting an amendment early, where that is permitted, when it bites materially and is disclosed in a note, is on the module's own list of occasions for such a paragraph, and this company's note is that case. The other paragraph is for something the accounts do not say at all: a fact bearing on a reader's understanding of the audit, of what the auditor answered for, or of the report itself, and it sits in its own section headed "Other Matter" or under whatever other heading fits. Who audited last year's figures appears nowhere in the accounts. It is a fact about the audit, and about what this firm's report does and does not reach, so it cannot be filed under a heading whose paragraph may refer only to information inside the statements. One heading over both is not a small drafting slip: it files a statement about the audit inside a paragraph defined as being about the accounts. In short, the amendment is presented or disclosed in the financial statements and takes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which may refer only to information in them, while the previous auditor bears on a reader's understanding of the audit and takes an Other Matter paragraph.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements

options.text: No; both belong under Other Matter, because neither concerns a figure in the accounts and each is about the circumstances of this year's reporting.
options.misconception: Sends a disclosed accounting matter to the paragraph reserved for matters about the audit.
options.why: The early application of the amendment is disclosed in a note and has a material effect on the financial statements, which is a matter presented or disclosed in them and one the module lists among the circumstances for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph; only the previous auditor is a matter outside the financial statements and relevant to users' understanding of the audit.

options.text: No; the comparatives audited by another firm should not be mentioned at all, because that firm's opinion was unmodified and mentioning it implies doubt, while the amendment is correctly under Emphasis of Matter.
options.misconception: Confuses an Other Matter paragraph with an expression of doubt.
options.why: The amendment is rightly emphasised, but the module's Other Matter paragraph exists for a matter not presented in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit or the auditor's report, and which firm audited the comparatives is that; telling the reader is the purpose, and it implies no doubt where the paragraph reports an unmodified opinion.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) on the two paragraphs beside the opinion: one is for a matter the accounts already present or disclose which is fundamental to reading them, and it may take in only what the statements themselves carry; the other is for a matter the statements do not carry, bearing on a reader's grasp of the audit, of the auditor's duties or of the report; and early application of a new standard with a material effect is on the module's own list of occasions for the first

items.stem: On property, plant and equipment alone, what does the report state?

options.text: The land is not reported, because the company occupies it and pays its tax and is its owner in substance; only the revaluation is stated, since a change of twelve per cent crosses the line, and the dies are left to next year's write-off.
options.misconception: Beneficial ownership and possession satisfy the title-deed clause.
options.why: Clause (i)(c) asks in whose name the title deed is held and, where not the company's, asks for the details in the format including the reason and whether in dispute; ownership in substance is not the question, and the discrepancy is reported under (i)(b) as noticed and not dealt with.

options.text: Since there is no dispute and the promoter holds the land for the company, Lakshmi takes a written confirmation from him and reports the deed as held for the company; the dies go to a qualification of the opinion rather than to the Order.
options.misconception: A promoter's confirmation converts his name into the company's for the title-deed clause.
options.why: Clause (i)(c) asks whether the deed is held in the name of the company, not for whom it is held, and a confirmation does not change the name on the deed; the discrepancy is stated under (i)(b) whatever the opinion paragraph does about it.

options.text: The revaluation needs no statement because the note to the accounts already discloses it and the clause asks only whether a revaluation took place; the missing dies are not a discrepancy until they are written off, so only the land is reported.
options.misconception: A note in the accounts discharges the revaluation clause, and a discrepancy exists only once written off.
options.why: Clause (i)(d) wants to know who did the valuing, which has to be a Registered Valuer, and wants the change quantified once it reaches a tenth of the class; the auditor states that whatever the note says. And a discrepancy is what the count turned up, the write-off being the dealing-with the clause asks after.

options.text: Three statements, none of them the finance head's. Under clause (i)(c) the report states that the title deed of the factory land is not held in the name of the company and gives the details in the prescribed format: the description, the gross carrying value of 14 crore rupees, whose name it stands in, that he is a promoter and director, the period since 2009, the reason, and that it is not in dispute; the property tax changes nothing. Under clause (i)(d) it states that the company revalued its plant and machinery during the year, that the revaluation is not based on the valuation by a Registered Valuer, and specifies the amount of change, because twelve per cent is 10% or more of the net carrying value of that class. Under clause (i)(b) it states that material discrepancies were noticed on physical verification and that they have not been properly dealt with in the books of account.
options.why: Each sub-clause puts a question of fact, and the report answers it as a fact. Take the deeds first. What is wanted is the name the deeds of the immovable properties in the accounts stand in, and where that name is not the company's a table has to be filled: what the property is, its gross carrying value, the name it is held in, whether that person is a promoter, a director, or a relative or employee of one, how long it has been that way, why, and whether anybody disputes it. Land standing in a promoter-director's name since 2009 answers no, with every column filled, and who pays the property tax is not one of the columns. Next, the write-up. Where a class has been revalued in the year, the Order wants to know who did the valuing — and the answer has to be a Registered Valuer — and it wants the change quantified once that change reaches a tenth of the class's net carrying value taken together. The company's own chief engineer is not a Registered Valuer, twelve per cent clears the tenth for plant and machinery, and a note in the accounts is the company's disclosure rather than the auditor's statement. Last, the count. Management's verification is asked about, and where it throws up a material difference the books are asked what became of it. Dies and moulds of 1.2 crore rupees that nobody could find and that still sit in the books are a difference nobody dealt with, and an intention to write them off next year is the answer no, not the absence of a discrepancy. In short, the report states that the deed is not held in the name of the company with the format's details, that the revaluation is not based on a Registered Valuer with the amount of change, and that material discrepancies were noticed and not properly dealt with in the books of account.
keywords: held in the name of the company
properly dealt with in the books of account

citation.ref: the three fixed-asset questions this item turns on — paragraph 3(i)(b), on how often management counts the assets and what the books then do about a material difference it turns up; 3(i)(c), on whose name the deeds of land and buildings stand in, with a set table to be filled where that name is not the company's; and 3(i)(d), on who is allowed to put a fresh value on a class and how large a change must be before the auditor has to quantify it

items.scenario: Krishnan & Pillai are the statutory auditors of Bhavani Pumps Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore with a revenue of 310 crore rupees, and Lakshmi Krishnan is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Her report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order is in draft and the finance head has answered three of its clauses in writing. First, on property, plant and equipment: the title deed of the factory land, with a gross carrying value of 14 crore rupees, has stood since 2009 in the name of the promoter-director, who says he holds it for the company, and there is no dispute; the plant and machinery was revalued in March 2026 by the company's own chief engineer, raising the net carrying value of that class by twelve per cent, and a note to the accounts says so; and the management's verification of assets in January 2026 could not find dies and moulds of 1.2 crore rupees, which remain in the books because the finance head intends to write them off next year. His answer is that property tax paid by the company makes the land the company's, that a note in the accounts is enough for the revaluation, and that a shortfall to be written off next year is not a discrepancy. Second, on loans: the company lent 18 crore rupees to its subsidiary, on which interest of 1.1 crore rupees was more than 120 days overdue at the year end; 7 crore rupees to a partnership owned by the managing director's brother, repayable on demand with no terms of repayment; and 5 crore rupees to a dealer, which fell due in September 2025 and was extended by a year on the same day. His answer is that the board approved each loan under section 186, so the clause has nothing to report. Third, on corporate social responsibility: of the obligation for the year ended 31 March 2025, 50 lakh rupees not tied to any project was never transferred to any fund, and 30 lakh rupees of it was spent on new projects during the year under audit; of the current year's obligation, 80 lakh rupees unspent on an ongoing school building was transferred to the special account the company opened for it. His answer is that the report should say the company has complied with section 135, because spending is better than transferring and the school money went where it should. Lakshmi has to settle what each clause says.

items.stem: On the three loans alone, what does the report state?

options.text: Only the loan to the partnership is reported, because it is the one to a related party; the subsidiary's loan and the dealer's loan are ordinary commercial loans with repayment schedules and need no mention.
options.misconception: Clause (iii) is a related-party clause.
options.why: The related-party amount is one column of sub-clause (f), not the scope of the clause; interest overdue for more than ninety days is reported under (d) and a loan renewed or extended after falling due under (e), whoever the borrower is.

options.text: The overdue interest is reported only if it is still overdue on the date of the report, and because the dealer's loan was extended on the very day it fell due nothing ever fell overdue on it, so nothing is stated under the renewal sub-clause.
options.misconception: An extension granted on the due date is not a renewal, and overdue amounts are judged at the report date.
options.why: Sub-clause (d) asks the total amount overdue for more than ninety days at the balance sheet date, and sub-clause (e) asks whether a loan that has fallen due during the year has been renewed or extended, which an extension on the due date is; the overdue question and the renewal question are different sub-clauses.

options.text: Section 186 is the question of clause (iv); clause (iii) asks its own, and each of the three loans answers one. The report gives the aggregate amount granted during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, with the 18 crore rupees to the subsidiary shown apart from the loans to parties other than subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates; states whether the terms of each are prejudicial to the company's interest; states that on the subsidiary's loan interest of 1.1 crore rupees is overdue for more than ninety days, and says what has been done to get it in; states that the dealer's loan of 5 crore rupees, which fell due during the year, was renewed or extended, with the aggregate and its percentage of the loans granted during the year; and states that 7 crore rupees to the partnership is repayable on demand without terms of repayment, with the aggregate, its percentage of the total loans, and the amount of it granted to related parties.
options.why: Board approval under section 186 answers clause (iv), which asks whether sections 185 and 186 have been complied with, and it answers nothing in clause (iii), which is a set of factual questions about the loans themselves. Sub-clause (a) asks the aggregate during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties, so the subsidiary's loan is the first line of the answer and not outside it. Sub-clause (b) asks whether the terms of all loans are not prejudicial to the company's interest, which is stated for each. Sub-clause (d) wants the sum that has sat unpaid past ninety days, principal and interest alike, together with what has been done to get it in; interest of 1.1 crore rupees still unpaid after 120 days at the year end is overdue for more than ninety days, and it is stated along with the steps taken. Sub-clause (e) wants to know whether a loan was given a fresh lease of life once it fell due in the year, and if it was, how much was so renewed or extended and what share that is of the year's lending; a loan that fell due in September 2025 and was extended by a year on that day is exactly that, and the extension being prompt does not take it out. Sub-clause (f) asks whether any loans repayable on demand or without specifying terms or period of repayment have been granted, and if so the aggregate, its percentage of the total loans, and the amount granted to promoters and related parties; a loan to the managing director's brother's partnership repayable on demand with no terms fills every column. In short, the report states the amounts by class of borrower, the terms, the interest overdue for more than ninety days with the recovery steps, the dealer's loan renewed or extended with its percentage, and the partnership's loan repayable on demand with the related-party amount.
keywords: overdue for more than ninety days

options.text: The finance head is right: each loan was approved by the board under section 186, so the clause is answered favourably, and the subsidiary's loan is in any case outside it as a loan within the group.
options.misconception: Board approval under section 186 disposes of clause (iii), and group loans are outside it.
options.why: Section 186 is clause (iv)'s question; clause (iii)(a) asks the aggregate and balance outstanding to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates by name, so a group loan is the first thing reported, and the overdue interest, the extension and the demand loan are each a separate sub-clause.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(iii), the lending clause, and its six questions: how much the company put out in the year and how much is still owed, group borrowers kept apart from the rest; whether the terms hurt the company; whether repayment was scheduled and whether it is being kept to; what sum has sat unpaid past ninety days, with the steps taken to get it in; loans given a fresh lease of life after they fell due, with how much and what share of the year's lending they are; and loans lent with no stated term, with how much, what share, and how much of it went to promoters and related parties

items.stem: On the corporate social responsibility money alone, what does the report state?

options.text: Because the ongoing project's money reached the special account, the clause is answered favourably as a whole; the 50 lakh rupees belongs to the previous year's obligation and was a matter for the previous year's report.
options.misconception: Clause (xx) is one answer, and last year's unspent amount belongs to last year's report.
options.why: The two limbs are answered separately, and the six months for the previous year's unspent amount expired on 30 September 2025, within the year under audit, so the failure to transfer to a Fund specified in Schedule VII is a fact of this year's report whatever last year's said.

options.text: Spending the money on corporate social responsibility is a better outcome than parking it in a fund, so the 30 lakh rupees spent satisfies the clause for that part and only the 20 lakh rupees still lying with the company is reported as not transferred.
options.misconception: Later spending on projects substitutes for the transfer to a Schedule VII fund.
options.why: Limb (a) asks whether the unspent amount was transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year; spending after that date is not a transfer, and the unspent amount the limb asks about is the whole 50 lakh rupees.

options.text: Corporate social responsibility is the board's matter under section 135 and is reported in the board's report; the auditor's report under the Order carries it only where the company has no corporate social responsibility committee at all.
options.misconception: Corporate social responsibility is for the board's report, not the auditor's.
options.why: Paragraph 3 of the Order has the auditor's report include a statement on every listed matter for a company to which the Order applies, and clause (xx) asks about the transfer to a Fund specified in Schedule VII and to the special account without any condition about a committee.

options.text: Two statements, one unfavourable and one favourable, and neither of them is that the company has complied with section 135. Under clause (xx)(a) the report states that, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the company has not transferred the unspent amount of 50 lakh rupees to a Fund specified in Schedule VII inside the six months that followed the close of the year it belonged to, and that spending 30 lakh rupees of it on new projects afterwards is not that transfer. Under clause (xx)(b) the report states that the amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project, 80 lakh rupees, has been transferred to the special account in compliance with section 135(6); a favourable answer is still a statement, not a silence.
options.why: Clause (xx) has two limbs with two destinations, and the report answers each in its own words. Limb (a) is about money left over on nothing that counts as a running project: it has to reach a Fund specified in Schedule VII, and it has to get there inside the six months following the close of the year, which is what the second proviso to section 135(5) requires. The 50 lakh rupees for the year ended 31 March 2025 was tied to no project; the six months ran out on 30 September 2025, a date inside the year under audit; and nothing was transferred. So the answer is no, with the amount, and the later spending of 30 lakh rupees on new projects is a use of the money rather than the transfer this limb asks after. Limb (b) is about money left over on a running project, which has its own destination — the special account section 135(6) provides for. The 80 lakh rupees for the school building was, so the answer is yes, and the Order asks for the statement on every matter in paragraph 3, favourable or not, with reasons required only where the answer is unfavourable. A single line that the company has complied with section 135 is neither limb and is wrong on the first. In short, the report states that the unspent amount for other than ongoing projects was not transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months, and that the ongoing project's unspent amount was transferred to the special account.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx) and its two limbs, each with its own destination and its own clock: limb (a), where money left unspent on nothing that counts as a running project has to reach one of the funds Schedule VII lists, and the six months after the year closes in which it has to get there under the second proviso to section 135(5); and limb (b), where money left unspent on a running project has to reach the special account section 135(6) provides for

items.scenario: Krishnan & Pillai are the statutory auditors of Bhavani Pumps Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore with a revenue of 310 crore rupees, and Lakshmi Krishnan is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Her report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order is in draft and the finance head has answered three of its clauses in writing. First, on property, plant and equipment: the title deed of the factory land, with a gross carrying value of 14 crore rupees, has stood since 2009 in the name of the promoter-director, who says he holds it for the company, and there is no dispute; the plant and machinery was revalued in March 2026 by the company's own chief engineer, raising the net carrying value of that class by twelve per cent, and a note to the accounts says so; and the management's verification of assets in January 2026 could not find dies and moulds of 1.2 crore rupees, which remain in the books because the finance head intends to write them off next year. His answer is that property tax paid by the company makes the land the company's, that a note in the accounts is enough for the revaluation, and that a shortfall to be written off next year is not a discrepancy. Second, on loans: the company lent 18 crore rupees to its subsidiary, on which interest of 1.1 crore rupees was more than 120 days overdue at the year end; 7 crore rupees to a partnership owned by the managing director's brother, repayable on demand with no terms of repayment; and 5 crore rupees to a dealer, which fell due in September 2025 and was extended by a year on the same day. His answer is that the board approved each loan under section 186, so the clause has nothing to report. Third, on corporate social responsibility: of the obligation for the year ended 31 March 2025, 50 lakh rupees not tied to any project was never transferred to any fund, and 30 lakh rupees of it was spent on new projects during the year under audit; of the current year's obligation, 80 lakh rupees unspent on an ongoing school building was transferred to the special account the company opened for it. His answer is that the report should say the company has complied with section 135, because spending is better than transferring and the school money went where it should. Lakshmi has to settle what each clause says.

items.stem: On the chief financial officer's list alone, which matters are key audit matters and why?

options.text: Whichever matters the chief financial officer selects, since key audit matters are chosen from matters communicated with management and management is best placed to say which were significant to the company.
options.misconception: Hands the selection of key audit matters to management.
options.why: The module's starting pool is the matters communicated with those charged with governance, and the judgment of which required significant auditor attention and which were of most significance is the auditor's professional judgment. Significance to the company is not the test; significance in the audit is.

options.text: The contract revenue and the plant impairment, and not the other three. The starting pool is the matters communicated with those charged with governance; out of it the auditor keeps whatever demanded significant auditor attention — an area assessed as riskier, a significant risk, an estimate carrying wide uncertainty, the audit effect of a large one-off event — and from those picks the ones of most significance. Routine work that went through without difficulty never enters, however many items the company would like listed.
options.why: The module gives the term a meaning and then a funnel for reaching it. The meaning: out of one period's audit, the handful of matters the auditor's own judgment ranks as weightiest. The funnel: begin with the matters communicated with those charged with governance, keep the ones that genuinely demanded significant auditor attention — areas the auditor assessed as riskier, or flagged as significant risks under SA 315; areas where management had to exercise wide judgment, estimates above all, where the uncertainty in the number runs high; and whatever the period's large one-off events or transactions did to the audit — and out of what survives, take the ones of most significance. Revenue on long-term contracts and the impairment of a plant are the module's own worked examples, and the senior's paper puts both down as significant risks that consumed the team's judgment. A register reconciliation, a tax reconciliation and bank confirmations that passed without trouble demanded no such attention. Five is not a target: the count falls out of the judgment and is never fed into it. In short, the two matters that were communicated with those charged with governance, demanded significant auditor attention and stood out as of most significance are the key audit matters.
keywords: communicated with those charged with governance

options.text: None of them should be described. Naming the contract revenue and the impairment would amount to separate opinions on those two balances, which SA 701 forbids.
options.misconception: Reads the "no separate opinion" sentence as a bar on communicating key audit matters.
options.why: The introductory language the module prescribes says that the matters were addressed in the context of the audit as a whole and that the auditor does not provide a separate opinion on them; that sentence is how a key audit matter is described without becoming a separate opinion, not a reason to describe none.

options.text: All five. A key audit matter is any area the audit covered in depth, and listing more of them increases the transparency the standard is designed to give the reader.
options.misconception: Treats a key audit matter as anything audited carefully rather than what required significant attention.
options.why: Transparency is the purpose the module states, but the selection rule is the module's funnel: matters communicated with those charged with governance that required significant auditor attention, and among those the ones of most significance. Routine procedures that went through without difficulty fail the first test, and a longer list dilutes rather than increases the communicative value.

citation.ref: SA 701 on what makes a matter a key audit matter. It sets a definition — the weightiest matters of the period's audit, ranked so by the auditor's own judgment — and a narrowing to reach them: begin with what was raised with those charged with governance; keep whatever genuinely demanded the auditor's attention, which means areas assessed as riskier or flagged as significant risks, areas where management's judgment ran wide and estimates carried broad uncertainty, and what the period's large one-off events did to the audit; then select the weightiest of what survives

items.scenario: Menon & Saxena are the statutory auditors of Bhima Wind Components Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore that fabricates towers for wind turbines, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Revenue is 720 crore rupees. The company's lenders asked for a report that names the matters the auditors spent most of their effort on, and the engagement letter records the firm's decision to communicate key audit matters. Three matters are open before signing. First, the chief financial officer has sent the partner a list of five matters he wants shown as key audit matters, "because five shows how thorough the audit was": revenue on long-term tower contracts, impairment of the Tuticorin plant, the reconciliation of the fixed asset register, GST reconciliations, and the year-end bank confirmations. The senior's working paper records that the contract revenue and the impairment were significant risks that took most of the team's judgment and time, and that the other three were routine and went through without difficulty. Second, the company breached the debt-to-equity covenant on a 150 crore rupee term loan at the year end, the lender has not yet waived it, and note 38 discloses the breach and the resulting material uncertainty about going concern completely and accurately; the partner has drafted a key audit matter headed "Liquidity and covenant compliance" and intends to use it in place of a going concern section "so the report does not carry a heading the lenders dislike". Third, the managing director has written that the company is not listed, that SA 701 therefore cannot apply to it, and that the whole Key Audit Matters section must be dropped from the report.

items.stem: On the covenant breach alone, may the partner report it as a key audit matter instead of under going concern?

options.text: Neither. Because note 38 already discloses the uncertainty completely and accurately, nothing further is required in the auditor's report; the auditor reports on the financial statements, not on what the notes already say.
options.misconception: Assumes an adequate note discharges the auditor's own going concern reporting.
options.why: Adequate disclosure by management is the condition for an unmodified opinion, not a reason to say nothing: the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section exists to draw attention to that very note. The module also says a key audit matter is no substitute for the disclosures the framework requires, and the reverse is equally true.

options.text: No. Communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for reporting under SA 570 when a material uncertainty exists. The breach and its consequence go under a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, drawing attention to note 38, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to that section rather than a description of the matter under a heading of the partner's choosing.
options.why: The module lists the things this section is not a substitute for, and the third entry settles the question. Where a material uncertainty has arisen — events or conditions throwing real doubt on whether the entity can carry on — the reporting SA 570 (Revised) calls for still has to happen, in its own place, exactly as a modified opinion under SA 705 still has to be given and management's own disclosures still have to be made. An unwaived covenant breach on a 150 crore rupee loan, which the company itself discloses as a material uncertainty, is that case, and what it calls for is a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section. The module's illustration then shows the two sitting side by side: the key audit matters section records that, apart from what the going concern section already describes, nothing else was determined — a reference, not a second description. What the lenders think of a heading is nothing the standard weighs, and a report that buried the going concern section under a liquidity label would tell them less than the standard means them to be told. In short, a key audit matter is not a substitute for the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, and the key audit matters section carries a reference to it.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

options.text: Yes. The matter took significant auditor attention and involved significant judgment, so it meets the definition of a key audit matter, and the heading is the auditor's to choose.
options.misconception: Lets the definition of a key audit matter override the separate reporting SA 570 requires.
options.why: A matter can meet the definition and still go undescribed in the Key Audit Matters section. SA 570 (Revised) reporting is not something this section may stand in for, and the module's illustration has it point at the going concern section instead of describing the matter again. Meeting the definition is why the pointer is there at all; it is no licence to relabel.

options.text: Yes, provided the key audit matter description also explains that a material uncertainty exists; a description that says the same thing as a going concern section is equivalent to it.
options.misconception: Treats matching content under a different heading as compliance with SA 570.
options.why: The module rules out the substitution in terms, whatever the words used, because the reader is entitled to find a material uncertainty under the heading the standards give it. The going concern section is required, and the key audit matters section refers to it.

citation.ref: SA 701 on what the key audit matters section does not stand in for. It cannot take the place of the going-concern reporting SA 570 (Revised) calls for once a material uncertainty has arisen, nor of a modified opinion under SA 705, nor of the disclosures the framework puts on management. The illustration prints the pairing: the section sends the reader to the going-concern heading and records that nothing else was determined

items.stem: On the managing director's objection alone, does SA 701 apply to this report?

options.text: Yes. Listed entities are where the standard is compulsory, but they are not the whole of its reach: it governs equally where the auditor otherwise decides to put key audit matters in the report, and where law or regulation says he must. This firm decided, and wrote the decision into the engagement letter, so the section stays and the standard runs over it whole. The single bar the module names is a report in which the auditor disclaims an opinion, which this is not.
options.why: Three ways into the standard, the module says, on an audit covering a full set of general purpose financial statements. A listed entity is one. An auditor who otherwise decides to report key audit matters is the second. A legal or regulatory requirement to report them is the third. Being unlisted closes the first road only, and the managing director stops reading at the first. The second road is the one this firm took, prompted by the lenders and recorded in the engagement letter, and once that decision is taken the standard governs how the matters are determined and how they are described, no differently than at a listed company. The module then names its single prohibition, which sits in SA 705 (Revised): where the auditor disclaims an opinion, no key audit matters go in the report at all, unless the law requires that they do. An opinion is being expressed here, so nothing is barred. In short, SA 701 reaches past listed entities to the auditor who otherwise decides, and the section falls away only where the auditor disclaims an opinion.

options.text: No. SA 701 is confined to listed entities, and an auditor who includes a Key Audit Matters section in an unlisted company's report is reporting outside the standard's scope, so the section must be dropped.
options.misconception: Reads the listed-entity requirement as the whole scope of the standard.
options.why: The module's second circumstance is exactly an auditor who otherwise decides to communicate key audit matters, in an entity where the standard does not require it. That decision brings the audit within SA 701, and the section is prepared under it.

options.text: It applies, but because the company is unlisted the section may be limited to a statement that key audit matters were considered, without naming or describing any.
options.misconception: Invents a reduced form of the section for a voluntary adopter.
options.why: Once SA 701 applies, its requirements for determining and describing key audit matters apply without a lighter form for unlisted entities; where matters are determined they are described, and a statement that there are none is used only when the auditor has determined that there are none.

options.text: It applies only if the lenders' request is written into a loan covenant, because a requirement imposed by a third party is the "law or regulation" limb of the standard's scope.
options.misconception: Mistakes a contractual request for the law-or-regulation limb of the standard.
options.why: A lender's request is not law or regulation; what it did here was prompt the auditor's own decision, and the module's second circumstance, where the auditor otherwise decides, is met by that decision recorded in the engagement letter, covenant or no covenant.

citation.ref: SA 701 on when it applies at all, and the one report it is kept out of. Three doorways, on an audit covering a full set of general purpose financial statements: the entity is listed; or the auditor chooses to report key audit matters when nothing obliged him to; or law or regulation requires him to. The bar sits in SA 705 (Revised) — where the auditor disclaims an opinion, key audit matters are not reported at all unless the law demands it
