items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on the deposits at the Rourkela branch. The balance sheet placement and the investment book are noise for this one. On the deposits alone, what does Sujata conclude?

options.text: Every one of the six is wrong. A savings account is not opened for a business or professional concern, so the rice mill's turnover belongs in a current account. An overdrawn current account is never set off against deposits; the two crore rupees must be included under the head advances instead. An account with no transactions for over two years is inoperative, so the forty-one are misclassified and the revival on an unwritten instruction was not made with proper authority. The four crore rupee deposit is a bulk deposit, two crore rupees and above, and needed the bulk rate verified. Interest accrued but not due goes under other liabilities and provisions, not inside the term deposits figure. And the March round trip inflates both deposits and advances, which is window dressing; for that Sujata should consider a suitable qualification in the main audit report. In short, the netted overdrafts must be included under the head advances, the dormant accounts are those with no transactions for over two years, and the March reversal calls for a suitable qualification in the main audit report.
options.why: The chapter settles each of the six separately. A trading or professional business does not bank in a savings account; its turnover runs through a current account. Where such an account is overdrawn the bank does not shrink its deposits by that amount — the overdraft is an asset and is included under the head advances, so both the deposits figure and the advances figure here are wrong by two crore rupees. An account is treated as inoperative or dormant when there are no transactions for over two years, and an inoperative account is revived only with proper authority — a telephone instruction nobody recorded is not that, and the chapter marks inoperative accounts as a high-risk area of fraud. Bulk deposits are two crore rupees and above for scheduled commercial banks presently, so the correct rate had to be verified rather than the retail card rate applied. Interest accrued but not due on deposits is shown under other liabilities and provisions and not clubbed with the deposits. And the module's own example of window dressing is this exact round trip — overdrafts near the balance sheet date, the overdrawn money placed as deposits, further advances against those deposits, reversed after the close of the year — for which the auditor should consider making a suitable qualification in the main audit report besides other applicable reporting.
keywords: no transactions for over two years
suitable qualification in the main audit report

options.text: The March overdraft-to-deposit round trip is a presentation matter only, and since the transactions were reversed on 4 April it is enough to disclose it as a subsequent event without touching the audit report.
options.misconception: Treating a transaction reversed shortly after the year end as self-correcting, when what is being tested is the figure that stood on the balance sheet date and the intention that put it there.
options.why: The reversal is the evidence of window dressing, not the cure for it. The balance sheet at 31 March carries inflated deposits and inflated advances, and where the figures point to window dressing the chapter asks the auditor to weigh a suitable qualification in the main audit report, on top of whatever else he has to report.

options.text: The netting of the three overdrawn current accounts is correct, because the same customer's debit and credit balances at one branch are two sides of one relationship and the net figure is the true liability of the bank.
options.misconception: Carrying the offsetting rule for a customer's several accounts over from an ordinary company's books, where a net receivable is normal, into a balance sheet whose form is fixed by the Third Schedule.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite in terms. An overdrawn balance is not allowed to shrink the deposits shown on the liabilities side; it crosses over and is included under the head advances. Netting understates deposits and understates advances at the same time, which is why the rule is written as a prohibition rather than a preference.

options.text: The forty-one accounts are not yet inoperative, because an account becomes dormant only after three years without a transaction, and the revival in January restarted that clock in any event.
options.misconception: Borrowing the three-year period from unclaimed deposits and the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund and applying it to the inoperative-account test, which is a different and shorter clock.
options.why: The period in the chapter is over two years, not three, so all forty-one were already inoperative at the year end. And a revival does not cure the earlier misclassification — it is itself the risk the rule is aimed at, which is why an inoperative account may be revived only with proper authority and why a large fall in the balance of such an account calls for the withdrawal authorisation to be examined.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — audit of deposits: savings accounts and business concerns, debit balances in current accounts, inoperative accounts, bulk deposits, interest accrued but not due, and deposits inflated for balance sheet presentation.

items.scenario: Mahapatra & Sahu are a firm of chartered accountants at Bhubaneswar, and Sujata Mahapatra is the partner in charge of the audit of a nationalised bank, where her firm is one of four appointed jointly as statutory central auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the week the branch returns are being consolidated. First, the deposits at the Rourkela branch. A savings account has been opened in the name of a rice-milling partnership firm and the whole of that firm's business turnover has passed through it. Three current accounts at the branch were overdrawn at the year end by two crore rupees between them, and the branch has shown its deposits figure on the liabilities side net of that overdrawn amount. Forty-one savings and current accounts in which nothing at all has moved since February 2024 are still being counted as operative, and one of them was revived in January and emptied a week later on a telephone instruction nobody wrote down. A term deposit of four crore rupees placed in November was given the rate the bank publishes for its retail depositors. Interest accrued but not due on term deposits, seven crore rupees, has been added into the term deposits figure itself. And in the last week of March the branch sanctioned overdrafts to four borrowers, the overdrawn money came back the same day as fresh term deposits, further advances were drawn against the security of those deposits, and the whole arrangement was reversed on 4 April. Second, where three balances sit in the balance sheet. The inter-office adjustments account is in credit by twelve crore rupees at the year end and the bank has set that credit off against advances. Advances are shown at their gross figure, with provisions of three hundred and forty crore rupees disclosed separately on the liabilities side. And a contractor's claim, on which the High Court passed a decree against the bank in February that the bank has decided not to appeal, is still listed among claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts. Third, the investment book. In December the bank moved securities of a face value of nine hundred crore rupees from available for sale to held to maturity; the shift was cleared by the investment committee and by the asset liability committee, and the finance head says that is the competent authority because the Board delegated investment decisions to those committees years ago. On one security the interest has been in arrears since 12 November 2025 and the bank has gone on taking the coupon to income, because the issuer is a state undertaking and the finance head expects the money. Sujata has to settle all three before the consolidated statements go up.

items.stem: QUESTION 2 OF 3 — turns on where the three balances sit in the balance sheet. The branch's deposits and the investment book are noise for this one. On the placement alone, what does Sujata require?

options.text: Only the decree must move. The inter-office set-off and the gross presentation of advances are both acceptable, because the Third Schedule fixes the heads of the balance sheet and not the arithmetic that produces the figure under each head.
options.misconception: Reading a prescribed form as a list of captions to be filled in however the entity likes, when for a bank the form carries the measurement and the offsetting rules with it.
options.why: The chapter fixes the arithmetic as well as the heads. A credit on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit at the year end, has a home of its own under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and what is shown for advances and for investments already excludes provisions against them. Both of the two treatments the bank has adopted are therefore wrong on their own, before the decree is reached.

options.text: The provisions of three hundred and forty crore rupees are correctly shown as a separate liability, because showing advances net of provisions would hide the size of the bank's bad loan book from the reader of the balance sheet.
options.misconception: Letting a sound instinct about transparency override a prescribed presentation, when the same information is required to reach the reader by a route the form already provides.
options.why: The concern is real and the Third Schedule answers it elsewhere, through the disclosures and the notes, not by grossing up the face of the balance sheet. The rule in the chapter is flat: a bank presents both advances and investments net, with the provisions held against them — tested and accepted by its auditors — already taken off the figure that reaches the reader.

options.text: All three must move. A balance standing on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, has its own home under Other Liabilities and Provisions and cannot be set off against advances. What a bank shows for its advances and its investments already excludes provisions held against them, tested to the auditors' satisfaction, so the three hundred and forty crore rupees comes off the advances figure instead of standing as a separate liability. And a decree the bank has decided not to appeal is no longer contingent: the disclosed contingent liabilities must not include crystallised liabilities of the nature of a loss or expense, which require a provision to be made instead. In short, an inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, belongs under Other Liabilities and Provisions, the advances figure excludes provisions made to the auditors' satisfaction, and crystallised liabilities come out of the contingent list and into a provision.
options.why: Each of the three is a placement rule and none of them is a matter of judgement. The Third Schedule requires bills payable, inter-office adjustments (net), interest accrued and others including provisions to be disclosed under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and the chapter places the balance on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, squarely under that same head; netting it off against advances understates both sides of the balance sheet at once. On the asset side the chapter is equally flat: what a bank shows for advances and for investments already excludes provisions against them, tested to the auditors' satisfaction, so those figures are presented net and the provision never surfaces as a liability of its own. And among the representations the auditor obtains on contingent liabilities is that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require the creation of a provision or adjustment — an unappealed decree is exactly such a liability, and leaving it in the contingent list keeps a real charge off the face of the accounts.
keywords: inter-office adjustments account, if in credit

options.text: The contractor's decree stays where it is until the appeal period expires and the bank actually pays, since until money leaves the bank the amount remains a claim against the bank not acknowledged as a debt.
options.misconception: Tying recognition to the cash going out rather than to the point at which the obligation stopped being contingent, which is the whole distinction between a provision and a contingent liability.
options.why: The bank has decided not to appeal, so the liability has crystallised and the label no longer fits — the bank does acknowledge the debt. The representation the auditor obtains is that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require a provision. Payment is when the provision is used, not when it arises.

citation.ref: Third Schedule, Form A — Other Liabilities and Provisions, the inter-office adjustments balance in credit, advances and investments stated net of provisions, and contingent liabilities.

items.scenario: Mahapatra & Sahu are a firm of chartered accountants at Bhubaneswar, and Sujata Mahapatra is the partner in charge of the audit of a nationalised bank, where her firm is one of four appointed jointly as statutory central auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the week the branch returns are being consolidated. First, the deposits at the Rourkela branch. A savings account has been opened in the name of a rice-milling partnership firm and the whole of that firm's business turnover has passed through it. Three current accounts at the branch were overdrawn at the year end by two crore rupees between them, and the branch has shown its deposits figure on the liabilities side net of that overdrawn amount. Forty-one savings and current accounts in which nothing at all has moved since February 2024 are still being counted as operative, and one of them was revived in January and emptied a week later on a telephone instruction nobody wrote down. A term deposit of four crore rupees placed in November was given the rate the bank publishes for its retail depositors. Interest accrued but not due on term deposits, seven crore rupees, has been added into the term deposits figure itself. And in the last week of March the branch sanctioned overdrafts to four borrowers, the overdrawn money came back the same day as fresh term deposits, further advances were drawn against the security of those deposits, and the whole arrangement was reversed on 4 April. Second, where three balances sit in the balance sheet. The inter-office adjustments account is in credit by twelve crore rupees at the year end and the bank has set that credit off against advances. Advances are shown at their gross figure, with provisions of three hundred and forty crore rupees disclosed separately on the liabilities side. And a contractor's claim, on which the High Court passed a decree against the bank in February that the bank has decided not to appeal, is still listed among claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts. Third, the investment book. In December the bank moved securities of a face value of nine hundred crore rupees from available for sale to held to maturity; the shift was cleared by the investment committee and by the asset liability committee, and the finance head says that is the competent authority because the Board delegated investment decisions to those committees years ago. On one security the interest has been in arrears since 12 November 2025 and the bank has gone on taking the coupon to income, because the issuer is a state undertaking and the finance head expects the money. Sujata has to settle all three before the consolidated statements go up.

items.stem: QUESTION 3 OF 3 — turns on the investment book. The branch's deposits and the balance sheet placement are noise for this one. On the investments alone, what does Sujata conclude?

options.text: Both are wrong. Moving a security out of available for sale and into held to maturity is a step the bank's own board has to sanction: it is duly approved by the Board of Directors and by nobody below them, however wide the standing delegation the investment committee or the asset liability committee holds. Those committees are competent to fix a category on the day the security is bought, which is a different decision altogether. And a coupon in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days makes it a non-performing investment, so from the second week of February the bank should have stopped reckoning income and made provision for the depreciation in its value; the identity of the issuer and the finance head's expectation of payment change nothing. In short, the shift out of available for sale needed approval duly approved by the Board of Directors, and interest in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days makes it one of the bank's non-performing investments.
options.why: The chapter separates the two decisions on purpose. Which category a security enters on the day it is bought turns on what the bank meant to do with it, and the proof of that intention is a decision by a competent authority — the board, but a committee will do. Shifting one out of a category later is the tighter rule, and there the auditor looks for a move duly approved by the Board of Directors itself; a delegation handed to two committees years ago is not that approval. On the arrears the test is mechanical rather than a matter of judgement. An investment goes bad for this purpose once either the interest or the principal has stood in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days. From that point the security sits among the bank's non-performing investments, the income stops being taken to the profit and loss account, and a provision is made for the fall in its value. Ninety days from 12 November 2025 runs out in the second week of February, so the coupon taken to income after that date should not have been.
keywords: duly approved by the Board of Directors
in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days

options.text: The security is not yet a non-performing investment, because the issuer is a state undertaking and payments backed by a state government are not treated as being in arrears while recovery is expected.
options.misconception: Importing the comfort of a government-linked borrower into a rule that was deliberately written to be counted rather than judged.
options.why: There is no such carve-out in the chapter. The test is the age of the arrears alone: an investment is non-performing once either sum has sat in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days. Who the issuer is and what management expects have no place in it, which is the point of writing the test as a number of days.

options.text: The shift is properly approved. The chapter names the Board, the asset liability committee and the investment committee as competent authorities for the categories of the investment portfolio, and both committees cleared this one.
options.misconception: Reading one list of competent authorities as though it governed every decision about the investment book, when the chapter attaches it to the acquisition decision and puts a higher bar on the shift.
options.why: Those three bodies are named for classification at the time of acquisition, where the question is what the bank intended when it bought the security. Shifting an existing holding out of available for sale into held to maturity carries its own requirement, and the chapter states it separately: the auditor examines whether the shift is duly approved by the Board of Directors of the bank.

options.text: The bank may go on taking the coupon to income so long as it makes provision for the depreciation in the value of the investment, because the provision already reflects the loss and stopping the income as well would count the same thing twice.
options.misconception: Treating a provision as a substitute for stopping accrual, which leaves an uncollected coupon sitting in the profit and loss account of the year it was never earned in.
options.why: The chapter requires both, not a choice between them: in the case of a non-performing investment banks have not to reckon income on the securities and are required to make provisions for depreciation in the value of the investment. Income recognition and valuation are separate consequences of the same classification, and the second does not buy off the first.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — examination of classification and shifting between HTM, HFT and AFS, the approval required for a shift out of available for sale, and non-performing investments.

items.stem: On the planning memo alone, what must Zeenat do before the strategy is set?

options.text: Nothing further. Acceptance is a one-time decision that was taken and documented before the appointment, and planning under SA 300 begins with the overall audit strategy; the tax partner's work is a firm-level matter for the firm's quality control, not the engagement.
options.misconception: Treats acceptance as a tender-stage event rather than a beginning-of-engagement activity.
options.why: All three of them belong at the opening of this year's engagement, in front of any strategy anybody writes: the acceptance and continuance checks, the ethical evaluation with independence inside it, and the terms agreed with the client. The engagement partner has to be satisfied with what they conclude. And a partner's new personal work for the promoter is exactly a threat this engagement's own independence evaluation has to weigh, not something that can be handed off to the firm at large.

options.text: Evaluate independence and issue the firm's own engagement letter, but the acceptance procedures need not be repeated because the company was accepted at the tender and nothing in the standard requires them twice.
options.misconception: Keeps two of the three preliminary activities and drops the first.
options.why: First in the order comes the acceptance and continuance work SA 220 calls for, and part of what it asks about is anything significant that has surfaced since the last look. A review done months earlier at tender stage cannot answer a question the standard deliberately puts at the opening of this year's engagement.

options.text: All three preliminary activities have to be done again at the beginning of the current audit engagement, whatever was settled at the tender: the acceptance and continuance checks SA 220 asks for, which reach the owners' and the management's integrity, whether this team has the skill and the hours, whether the ethical rules can be kept, and anything significant that has come up since; a fresh evaluation of independence, which the tax partner's new work for the promoter now makes urgent; and the terms of the engagement, agreed with this company and put in a letter of this firm's own under SA 210, not another firm's letter with the name changed.
options.why: Three activities sit in front of the strategy, and the standard fixes when they happen — at the beginning of the current audit engagement, meaning every year, not once when the relationship opened. The first is the set of acceptance and continuance checks that SA 220 and the quality-control standard require, and they run to the integrity of the owners, of key management and of those charged with governance; to whether this team has the skill, the expertise, the hours and the resources for the job; to whether firm and team alike can keep to the ethical rules; and to anything significant that has surfaced, this year or last. The second is a fresh look at whether the firm is independent. The third is settling the terms of the engagement with the company under SA 210. All three are treated as very important, and it is the engagement partner who has to be satisfied both that they were carried out and that what they concluded was right. Now apply the timing to the memo. A tender in February is not where this engagement begins, and what has happened since is precisely the sort of thing these activities exist to catch: a partner of the firm has taken on personal tax work for the promoter, which is a question for the independence evaluation and for nothing else. And the terms are this firm's own to agree and to record; a predecessor's letter with a new name typed on it records an agreement nobody here ever made. In short, all three activities belong at the beginning of the current audit engagement, independence is evaluated again in the light of the tax partner's work, and the terms of the engagement go into a letter of this firm's own.
keywords: beginning of the current audit engagement

options.text: Use the previous auditors' engagement letter as it stands, since the terms of a statutory audit are fixed by law and do not change with the auditor, and record the acceptance and independence work after the strategy so that fieldwork is not delayed.
options.misconception: Borrows another firm's terms and reorders the preliminary activities behind the strategy.
options.why: Terms have to be settled between this firm and this company. A statutory audit takes its duties from the Act, but the engagement is still an agreement, and a predecessor's letter records somebody else's. All three activities also come in front of the strategy, not behind it.

citation.ref: the work that comes in front of the strategy in every year and not merely the first — the acceptance and continuance checks SA 220 calls for, a fresh look at whether the firm is independent, and settling with the client what this engagement is, under SA 210

items.scenario: Rao & Farooqui were appointed statutory auditors of Chambal Auto Castings Limited, an unlisted public company at Bhilwara with revenue of 640 crore rupees, for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditors completed their term. Zeenat Farooqui is the engagement partner and three matters are open at the planning stage. First, the manager's planning memo opens with the overall audit strategy and records that "acceptance was completed at the tender stage in February 2026, so no further preliminary work is needed"; since then the firm's tax partner has begun advising the promoter on his personal tax affairs, and no engagement letter has been issued because the manager intends to reuse the previous auditors' letter with the firm's name changed. Second, the senior proposes to accept the opening balances as they stand, "because last year was audited by a firm of standing and the closing figures are in the signed accounts", and the chief financial officer has said that opening balances are last year's problem and this year's audit should start from 1 April. Third, the previous auditors' report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carried a qualified opinion because they could not attend the physical count of inventory of 22 crore rupees at the Bhilwara foundry, which is the opening inventory for this year and has flowed into this year's cost of sales; the chief financial officer wants the new report to say in an Other Matter paragraph that the previous year was audited by another firm whose report was qualified, and nothing more.

items.stem: On the senior's proposal alone, what does SA 510 require of the new auditors for the opening balances?

options.text: Evidence, not acceptance. Zeenat's team reads last year's signed accounts along with the predecessor auditor's report; checks that the closing figures were brought forward into this year unchanged; satisfies itself that the policies behind them are the right ones and were applied the same way; and performs audit procedures on opening balances to see whether anything in them throws this year out materially. The previous firm's standing is something to read about, not evidence in itself, and for an auditor the year does not begin on 1 April.
options.why: An initial engagement, in this standard's sense, is one where last year was either not audited at all or audited by somebody else — which is Rao & Farooqui's position exactly. What the team needs from the opening figures is evidence, of two things: that nothing hiding in them throws this year's statements out materially, and that the policies behind them are the right ones and were carried through unchanged from one year into the next. Five steps follow from that. Read last year's signed accounts, and what the predecessor auditor's report said about them. Set last year's closing figures against this year's opening ones, so that what was signed is what was brought forward. Satisfy yourself about the policies. Then perform audit procedures on opening balances — real work, chosen for the balance in front of you. And where something wrong in those figures has thrown this year's statements out, take it to management or to those charged with governance. Not one item on that list is discharged by the previous firm's reputation, however good it is; the module's own worked example turns on a new auditor left with a doubt about opening inventory, which is the senior's question in different words. As for the chief financial officer's line, the opening figures are this year's problem for a plain reason — they sit inside this year's statements, at the top of every account. In short, the team reads the predecessor auditor's report, checks what was brought forward, and performs audit procedures on opening balances of its own.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the opening balances are correct, which discharges the responsibility because the previous year's accounts were approved by the members.
options.misconception: Substitutes a representation and a shareholder vote for audit procedures.
options.why: Nothing on the list is a representation, and a vote at a general meeting is not audit evidence about a figure. The work itself is what discharges this — procedures on the opening balances, the match across the year end, and the policies behind them.

options.text: Accept them. Opening balances audited by a predecessor are outside the current engagement, and the new auditor's responsibility begins with the transactions of the current year; the predecessor's report is the evidence.
options.misconception: Treats the predecessor's audit as the current auditor's evidence.
options.why: SA 510 was written for exactly this engagement, and what it asks for is work on the opening figures rather than acceptance of them. The outgoing firm's report is read, and last year's closing figures are checked against this year's opening ones — but evidence that nothing is wrong inside those figures is this auditor's to obtain, nobody else's.

options.text: Re-audit the previous year in full, because an initial engagement makes the new auditor responsible for the prior period's statements as well as the current one.
options.misconception: Overshoots from procedures on opening balances to a second audit of last year.
options.why: What is wanted is evidence that nothing inside the opening figures throws this year out materially — reached by reading last year's accounts and report, matching the figures across the year end, testing the policies, and doing work on the balances themselves. That is not an opinion on last year, and nobody is asking for a second audit of it.

citation.ref: what a firm taking over from another owes to figures it did not audit — reading what the outgoing auditor said, checking that last year's closing figures arrived intact, testing the policies sitting behind them, doing real work on the figures themselves, and speaking up when what is wrong in them has distorted this year's accounts

items.scenario: Rao & Farooqui were appointed statutory auditors of Chambal Auto Castings Limited, an unlisted public company at Bhilwara with revenue of 640 crore rupees, for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditors completed their term. Third, the previous auditors' report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carried a qualified opinion because they could not attend the physical count of inventory of 22 crore rupees at the Bhilwara foundry, which is the opening inventory for this year and has flowed into this year's cost of sales; the chief financial officer wants the new report to say in an Other Matter paragraph that the previous year was audited by another firm whose report was qualified, and nothing more.

items.stem: On the predecessor's qualification alone, does an Other Matter paragraph settle the new auditors' report?

options.text: Yes. The qualification belongs to the previous auditors and the previous year; an Other Matter paragraph referring to it is the module's own device for a predecessor's report, and this year's opinion is on this year's figures.
options.misconception: Lets a reference to the predecessor's qualification stand in for the current auditor's own.
options.why: What the outgoing firm qualified over has to be weighed for its effect on this year, and where it still bites here the report of this year gets modified. Opening inventory sitting in this year's cost of sales is what makes last year's matter this year's, and a paragraph describing another firm's report is no substitute for a modification of this firm's own.

options.text: Yes, provided the Other Matter paragraph also states that the new auditors place no reliance on the opening inventory; a disclaimer of reliance is the same as a modification.
options.misconception: Confuses words of non-reliance with a modified opinion.
options.why: Saying in a paragraph that you place no reliance on a figure does not modify an opinion. Where the matter behind the outgoing firm's qualification still bites this year, this year's report is the thing that has to change — and opening figures nobody can verify take that to a qualified opinion or a disclaimer under SA 705, not to a paragraph.

options.text: No; the new auditors must give an adverse opinion, because a qualification on inventory that remains unresolved has become pervasive by carrying into a second year.
options.misconception: Reaches for an adverse opinion on a limitation rather than a known misstatement.
options.why: Which situation applies turns on the kind of problem, never on how many years it has run. Being unable to reach evidence about the opening figures leads to a qualified opinion or a disclaimer; the road that can end in adverse is for something actually found wrong in those figures and then left undisclosed. Nobody here has found anything wrong yet.

options.text: No. Where the outgoing firm modified its report, this firm has to work out what the underlying matter does to this year's accounts, and where it is relevant and material to them it must modify the current period audit report. Opening inventory nobody counted, now sitting inside this year's cost of sales, is that case — unless Zeenat's team can reach evidence about it now. If it cannot, what follows is a qualified opinion or a disclaimer over figures it could not verify, and a paragraph reciting what another firm once said discharges nothing.
options.why: Three situations get separate treatment on reporting, and this is the third of them. Where the outgoing firm modified its report, the incoming firm has to work out what the underlying matter does to this year's accounts, and modify this year's report if that matter is both relevant and material to them. Apply it here. Inventory of 22 crore rupees that nobody independent ever counted is the opening figure of this year's cost of sales, so what went wrong last year is sitting in this year's profit — relevant on one count and material on the other. There is one road out of a modification, and it is not a paragraph: Zeenat's team obtains evidence about that opening inventory itself, through procedures on the opening balances — reconciliations, later movements, production records, whatever will actually reach it. Fail at that and the first of the three situations takes over: opening figures nobody can get evidence about produce a qualified opinion or a disclaimer, depending on how much of the accounts they carry. The second situation, the one running as far as adverse, is for something wrong actually found in the figures and left undisclosed, and nothing here has found anything yet. Then look at what the chief financial officer's paragraph would do. It would tell a reader that another firm qualified last year, while this year's opinion sits clean over a figure this firm has not verified either — the requirement turned exactly backwards. In short, a matter that is relevant and material to this year obliges the auditor to modify the current period audit report, and opening figures that cannot be verified bring a qualified opinion or a disclaimer.
keywords: modify the current period audit report

citation.ref: how the report is modified when figures a firm inherited cannot be stood behind — treated separately where no evidence about them can be got at all, where something wrong is found in them and left undisclosed, and where the outgoing auditor had already modified and the same matter still bites this year

items.stem: On the warranty provision alone, can the audit senior close the area on the chief financial officer's signed statement?

options.text: Yes, provided the statement is included in the formal representation letter signed by both the managing director and the chief financial officer rather than as a separate note.
options.misconception: Treats the form of the representation as the source of its evidential weight.
options.why: Who signs it, and where on the page it sits, change nothing about what such a statement is worth. It never settles a matter by itself, and that holds just as firmly for a line inside the full letter as for a note handed over separately.

options.text: No, because a written representation is not audit evidence at all; SA 580 requires the letter only as a formality of the engagement, and nothing in the audit file may rest on it.
options.misconception: Swings from "enough by itself" to "worth nothing".
options.why: A signed statement is evidence the auditor is required to obtain, and one of SA 580's own objectives is to lean on such statements in support of other evidence about the accounts or about particular assertions. So they count as evidence. What they never are is enough by themselves. Right conclusion here, wrong reason.

options.text: Yes, because a warranty provision is an accounting estimate and estimates are management's responsibility; the auditor's only evidence about them is management's own assertion that the assumptions are reasonable.
options.misconception: Confuses whose responsibility the estimate is with whose evidence supports it.
options.why: That management makes the estimate is the reason the auditor tests it, not a reason to take management's word for it. A reliable signed statement leaves the kind and the amount of other work on that assertion exactly where it stood. The claims history, the assumptions and the money actually paid out in the year are all evidence the auditor gathers herself.

options.text: No. A signed statement is evidence the auditor is required to obtain, and it is still not sufficient on its own to settle any matter it speaks to; holding a reliable one does not reduce the work owed on the same assertion. The provision has to be tested against the claims history, the assumptions underneath it and the 9 crore rupees actually paid out in the year — the statement stands beside that work and never in place of it.
options.why: Two propositions govern this, and they point the same way. The first: a statement signed by management is evidence the auditor is required to get, and getting it settles nothing by itself about any matter the statement happens to speak to. The second: the reliability of that statement, however high, leaves untouched both the kind and the amount of other evidence owed on the same responsibilities and the same assertions. So the letter never buys a reduction in work — it sits beside the work. Now take the warranty provision. A line saying the assumptions behind an estimate are reasonable is one of the standard lines in such a letter, and it is asked for in addition to the auditor's own testing of that estimate, never as a swap for it. And look at the figures the senior wants to close on: 6 crore rupees carried against 9 crore rupees of claims paid in the very same year. That is exactly the kind of number whose basis has to be examined first-hand. In short, the chief financial officer's statement is not sufficient on its own, and holding it does not reduce the testing the estimate still needs.

citation.ref: how far a signed statement from management carries — evidence the auditor needs, yet never enough by itself to settle a matter it speaks to, and no reason at all to do less work on the assertion it touches

items.scenario: Chenab Auto Components Private Limited makes wiring harnesses at Chakan for three vehicle makers. Its revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was 310 crore rupees and its profit before tax 21 crore rupees. Fernandes & Sethi are the statutory auditors, and the partner intends to sign the report on 28 August 2026. Three things stand between her and the signature. First, the provision for warranty claims is 6 crore rupees, against 9 crore rupees of claims paid in the year; the chief financial officer has signed a statement that the provision is adequate and the assumptions behind it reasonable, and the audit senior proposes to close the area on that statement alone, "since a signed representation from the CFO is audit evidence". Second, the firm asked for a written representation that all related party relationships and transactions known to management have been disclosed to the auditors; the managing director, whose brother owns the company's largest wire supplier, has struck that line out of the draft letter, saying "you have been told everything that matters, and I will not sign a line that reads like an accusation". Third, the audit found that for eight months of the year one accounts executive raised purchase orders, approved supplier invoices and released the payments, with nobody reviewing what she released, across 140 crore rupees of purchases; the chief financial officer says a second person was hired in July 2026 to split the work and asks that "nothing be put in writing about a problem that no longer exists".

items.stem: On the struck-out line alone, what does SA 580 require of the partner now?

options.text: Qualify the opinion "except for" the related-party disclosures in the note, since the refusal concerns one disclosure and its effect is confined to that note.
options.misconception: Reads a refusal about completeness of information as a misstatement of one disclosure.
options.why: What was refused is not a disclosure; it is a statement that nothing on the related-party side has been kept back from the firm — a claim about the completeness of what the auditor has been given. Since the partner cannot name what she was never told about, the possible effect has no edge to it, and qualifying one note misdescribes where the audit actually stands.

options.text: Nothing further. The managing director has given the information orally, and SA 580 accepts oral representations from the person responsible for the financial statements.
options.misconception: Treats an oral statement as satisfying a requirement for a written one.
options.why: SA 580 deals in statements set down in writing, and where one asked for does not arrive the road is a conversation, a fresh judgement on integrity, and action under SA 705. An oral assurance from the very person whose family connection is the question is not what was asked for — and a refusal to put it on paper is itself evidence about integrity.

options.text: Discuss the refusal with the managing director, re-evaluate the integrity of management and what that does to every other representation and piece of evidence, and take appropriate action on the report under SA 705. The line refused is about the completeness of the information given to the auditor, which goes to the whole audit rather than one balance, so a persisting refusal leads to a disclaimer of opinion, not an "except for" qualification of the related-party note.
options.why: Three things follow from a line being struck out, and signing anyway is not among them. Talk to management about why. Then ask again how far this management can be believed at all — not only on the line refused, but on every other statement it has signed and on the reliability of what the audit has already gathered. Then act, and one of the actions is what the report itself says, under SA 705. Weigh who refused, and what. A managing director whose own brother owns the largest wire supplier will not confirm that the related parties have all been disclosed. As reasons to re-open the integrity of management go, this file will not produce a stronger one, and doubt of that kind does not stay in its corner — it reaches back across everything management has told the firm. Now measure the reach. The line struck out is one of the statements SA 580 itself requires about management's own responsibilities, and what it speaks to is the completeness of the information handed to the auditor. The partner cannot say what else was never mentioned, so the possible effect is not fenced inside the related-party note; it has no boundary. In short, the partner discusses the refusal, re-opens the integrity of management, and where the refusal holds, a line about the completeness of the information brings a disclaimer of opinion rather than a qualification of one note.

options.text: Drop the line and sign, provided the partner performs additional procedures on the supplier owned by the brother; extra evidence on the known relationship makes the representation unnecessary.
options.misconception: Assumes evidence on the known relationship can stand in for a representation about unknown ones.
options.why: Work on the one relationship the firm happens to know about cannot answer the question the line was asking, which is whether there are others. Statements about management's own responsibilities, the completeness of what has been handed over among them, are required whatever else the file holds — and where one is refused the road is a fresh judgement on integrity and action under SA 705, not a substitute.

citation.ref: what a refusal to sign a line the auditor asked for sets in motion — a conversation about why, a fresh judgement on how far management can be believed at all and what that does to everything else already collected, and the consequence for the report under SA 705, which reaches the whole opinion where the line refused was about the completeness of what the auditor has been told

items.scenario: Chenab Auto Components Private Limited makes wiring harnesses at Chakan for three vehicle makers. Its revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was 310 crore rupees and its profit before tax 21 crore rupees. Fernandes & Sethi are the statutory auditors, and the partner intends to sign the report on 28 August 2026. Three things stand between her and the signature. First, the provision for warranty claims is 6 crore rupees, against 9 crore rupees of claims paid in the year; the chief financial officer has signed a statement that the provision is adequate and the assumptions behind it reasonable, and the audit senior proposes to close the area on that statement alone, "since a signed representation from the CFO is audit evidence". Second, the firm asked for a written representation that all related party relationships and transactions known to management have been disclosed to the auditors; the managing director, whose brother owns the company's largest wire supplier, has struck that line out of the draft letter, saying "you have been told everything that matters, and I will not sign a line that reads like an accusation". Third, the audit found that for eight months of the year one accounts executive raised purchase orders, approved supplier invoices and released the payments, with nobody reviewing what she released, across 140 crore rupees of purchases; the chief financial officer says a second person was hired in July 2026 to split the work and asks that "nothing be put in writing about a problem that no longer exists".

items.stem: On the payments clerk alone, what does SA 265 require, and what must the communication contain?

options.text: One employee raising orders, approving invoices and releasing 140 crore rupees of payments with nobody reviewing any of it is a deficiency serious enough to report, and this audit found it. It goes in writing to those charged with governance, promptly, and in writing to management as well — put right since or not. The letter sets out the fault and its potential effects, and frames itself: the audit existed to produce an opinion on the accounts, controls were looked at only to shape the procedures and not to give an opinion on its effectiveness, and only what this audit found and judged worth reporting appears in it.
options.why: Start with the judgement. The auditor decides whether the faults thrown up by the audit work are, one at a time or taken together, serious enough to count. Once one is, it goes in writing — to those charged with governance without undue delay, and to management at a level senior enough to do something about it. What sets the duty off is finding the fault during this audit. A second person hired in July is the answer to that letter, not a reason to keep it back, and the eight months in which one employee ordered, approved and paid are the months the accounts now being reported on were built in. Then the content. The letter has to say what the fault is and what it could lead to — its potential effects — and it has to give the reader enough to place it: the audit was there to produce an opinion on the accounts; controls were examined only so that the procedures could be shaped sensibly, and not to give an opinion on its effectiveness; and what is listed is confined to what this audit turned up and thought important enough to set down. In short, a deficiency of that seriousness found during the audit goes in writing to those charged with governance and to management, carrying the fault and its potential effects, and framed so nobody can read it as a verdict on the control system — it is there to describe and explain, not to give an opinion on its effectiveness.
keywords: not to give an opinion on its effectiveness

options.text: Report it orally to the chief financial officer, who is the appropriate level of management, and record the conversation in the audit file; a written letter is only for deficiencies management disputes.
options.misconception: Invents a written-only-if-disputed rule and stops at management.
options.why: Writing is the form for both recipients. Those charged with governance get it on paper, and so does management, unless dealing with management directly would be inappropriate in the circumstances. Whether management agrees with the finding has no bearing on the form at all.

options.text: Nothing in writing is required. The deficiency has been remedied before the report date, and SA 265 is concerned only with deficiencies that still exist when the auditor reports.
options.misconception: Reads a remedy after the year end as cancelling the duty to report the year's deficiency.
options.why: Finding the fault during the audit is what sets the duty off, and nothing else does. One serious enough to count goes to those charged with governance in writing, without undue delay. Nowhere is a fault excused because management says it has since been put right — and nobody has tested the July arrangement in any case.

options.text: Communicate it in writing to the audit committee, and include in the letter an opinion that the company's internal control over purchases was ineffective for the year, so that the board understands the seriousness.
options.misconception: Turns the letter of weakness into an opinion on internal control, which it disclaims.
options.why: The letter does the reverse of that. One of the things SA 265 makes it explain is that controls were looked at only so the procedures could be shaped, and never so that anybody could pronounce on how well those controls work. It sets out the fault and what it could lead to; it carries no verdict on the control system.

citation.ref: what happens when an audit turns up a control broken badly enough to matter — who has to be told, in what form, how quickly, and what the letter itself must carry: the fault, what it could lead to, and the framing that stops a reader taking the letter for a verdict on the control system

items.stem: On the manager's weekend alone, was he right that no auditor's expert is needed?

options.text: No. Going without is allowed only where the auditor already carries a sufficient understanding of the field — built by auditing companies of this kind, by study or a formal course, or by talking to auditors who have handled work of the same sort. A weekend with a textbook and a call to a friend is none of the three, and the moment that friend is asked about this reserve he becomes an auditor's expert himself. Every consideration then points one way: a management's expert produced the figure, the matter is large and intricate, the risk after a one-fifth cut is high, and for ore still in the ground there are no alternative sources of audit evidence to fall back on.
options.why: Two questions sit inside the manager's note and SA 620 answers both. The first is whether a team may take on an unfamiliar field alone. It may, where the auditor holds a sufficient understanding of that field already, and the standard names how such an understanding is come by: auditing entities whose accounts need that expertise, study or a formal course in the subject, or conversation with auditors who have done work of the same kind. All three build the auditor's own capacity, in general and in advance. Ringing a geologist to ask whether this company's reserve stands up is a different act altogether — it is advice on the particular facts of this engagement, given by somebody who has been handed those facts, and it turns the geologist into an auditor's expert whose competence, objectivity and work the firm must then evaluate. The second question is whether to engage one at all, and four considerations settle it. Did management itself use an expert? How large and how tangled is the matter? What risk of misstatement does it carry? And what work is in prospect — is there any other road to evidence? Take them here in turn. The staff engineer is a management's expert, which is a reason for Priya to want one of her own rather than a reason to go without. The reserve drives amortisation on 310 crore rupees of assets and has just moved by a fifth. And no ledger, no confirmation and no supplier's invoice can say how much manganese lies underground; estimating what a deposit holds is exactly the kind of field the standard has in view. In short, a weekend is not a sufficient understanding of the field, the engineer being a management's expert argues for the auditor's own rather than against it, and for ore in the ground there are no alternative sources of audit evidence at all.

options.text: Yes, provided the manager's reading is documented and the geologist he calls is given the drilling data, because SA 620 lets an auditor obtain the understanding through discussion with individuals possessing expertise in the field.
options.misconception: Dresses a consultation on the engagement's facts as professional development.
options.why: This is the very line the standard draws. Talking to people in a field to raise the auditor's own capacity is one thing; asking somebody who has been given this engagement's facts to advise on this engagement's problem is another. A geologist handed the company's drilling data and asked whether the reserve holds sits on the second side of that line, so competence, an agreement and an evaluation of his work all become due.

options.text: No; the auditor must engage an expert whenever management has, because SA 620 requires the auditor's expert to match management's expert field for field.
options.misconception: Turns a judgement on the considerations into a mechanical rule.
options.why: Management's use of an expert is one weight among several — how big and how tangled the matter is, what risk it carries, whether evidence can be reached another way. No rule pairs an expert with an expert, and a team that genuinely knows the field may proceed alone. The answer reached here is right, but off a rule that was never written.

options.text: Yes. The reserve was prepared by a qualified mining engineer, and where management has used an expert the auditor's task under SA 500 is to evaluate that expert's competence and work, not to hire a second expert to do it again.
options.misconception: Treats management's expert as a substitute for the auditor's own.
options.why: Management having used an expert is one of the things weighed when deciding whether the auditor needs an expert too — it does not settle the question the other way. Judging a mining engineer's reserve model is itself geology, which nobody on this team knows; SA 500 has the firm assess that engineer's competence, and no such assessment hands the team the science it lacks.

citation.ref: the routes by which an auditor picks up enough of an unfamiliar field to audit it without engaging anyone, and the point at which asking somebody about this engagement's own facts crosses out of that; and what the decision to engage an expert is weighed on — the expert management itself used, how large and how tangled the matter is, the risk it carries, and whether any other route to evidence exists at all

items.scenario: Venkatesh & Bose audit Damodar Ferro Alloys Limited, an unlisted public company at Rourkela with revenue of 860 crore rupees, which mines its own manganese ore under a lease. Mine development assets of 310 crore rupees are amortised on the units-of-production method over the ore reserve, and the reserve estimate, prepared for the company by a mining engineer on its staff, was cut by a fifth this year after new drilling. Priya Venkatesh is the engagement partner and three things happen in the course of the audit. First, the audit manager records that the team will assess the reserve estimate itself, "after reading up on reserve estimation over a weekend and a phone call to a geologist I know", and that no auditor's expert is needed because the company's engineer is qualified and the figure is his. Second, when Priya overrules him and engages Dr Anjali Sethi, an independent geologist who has never worked with the firm, the manager briefs her by telephone: "look at the reserve and tell us if it holds", hands her the company's drilling logs and the engineer's model, and puts nothing in writing, saying a written engagement would "slow things down and she is a professional". Third, when Dr Sethi's report supports the reduced reserve, the chief financial officer asks that the auditor's report name her and her firm "so the lenders can see an independent expert stood behind the number", and the manager suggests adding the words "in reliance on the report of Dr Sethi" to the opinion paragraph to limit the firm's own exposure.

items.stem: On the telephone briefing alone, what should have passed between the firm and Dr Sethi before she began?

options.text: A written representation from Dr Sethi that she has no interest in or relationship with the company, which settles her objectivity, after which the work can proceed on the oral briefing.
options.misconception: Substitutes the objectivity check for the agreement on the work.
options.why: A statement about interests and relationships belongs to a separate exercise, the one testing whether the expert is objective, and asking for it may well be right. It is not the agreement on what the work is, who does what, how she reports and what she keeps quiet, and it stands in for none of that.

options.text: Nothing more than the briefing given. An auditor's external expert is engaged for her expertise and the standard leaves the terms of the work to the expert's own professional standards; a written scope would amount to directing her judgement.
options.misconception: Confuses agreeing the scope of the work with directing the expert's conclusions.
options.why: The standard obliges the auditor to settle four things with the expert, on paper where that is appropriate: what the work is for, who does what, how she reports, and what she keeps confidential. Fixing what is to be done is what lets the firm judge afterwards whether it was done adequately, and it leaves her judgement inside that task entirely her own.

options.text: An agreement, and in writing here, on four matters: the nature, scope and objectives of her work, so that "tell us if it holds" becomes a defined task the firm can later evaluate; the respective roles and responsibilities of the firm and of her; the nature, timing and extent of communication between them, including the form of the report she will give; and the need for her to observe confidentiality requirements, because the drilling logs are the company's confidential information and an external expert is not bound by the firm's professional duty merely by being engaged. Writing is appropriate because she is external, new to the firm, working on a complex matter and holding sensitive data.
options.why: An agreement belongs between the decision to engage an expert and the day she starts, and SA 620 says what it settles: four things, in writing wherever writing is appropriate. What she is being asked to do and how far it reaches — the nature, scope and objectives of her work. Who is answerable for which part, as between the firm and her. How the two of them will be in touch, how often, and in what form her conclusions come back; where the work bears on a significant risk the standard has in mind a formal report at the end with oral ones as she goes. And the confidentiality requirements she is to observe, because the secrecy the ethical code lays on the auditor has to be made to bind the expert too, along with whatever more the law, a regulator or the company itself imposes. A telephone call settles none of the four. "Tell us if it holds" is not a scope; the roles were never stated; no form of report was fixed; and an outside geologist now holds this company's drilling logs under no undertaking whatever. The missing scope costs twice over. The reason a firm is asked to understand the expert's field at all is so that it can frame the task at the start and judge the work against that frame at the end — an undefined task cannot be measured against anything later, so the evaluation the standard requires has nothing to bite on. As for the manager's justification, that she is a professional: that is the difficulty, not the answer. Dr Sethi's professional standards are hers, and the agreement is the thing that ties her work to what this audit needs from it. In short, the firm settles with her in writing the nature, scope and objectives of the work, who does what, how and when she reports, and the confidentiality requirements she must observe.

options.text: A written agreement on the fee and the timetable, since those are the only terms that differ from one expert to another; the scope is self-evident from the matter and confidentiality follows from her professional status.
options.misconception: Assumes confidentiality away, which the module names as the matter to be agreed.
options.why: The four matters are the task and its purpose, the roles, how she reports, and secrecy. The standard says plainly that the duty of confidence binding the auditor has to be made to bind the expert as well, and an outside geologist's own professional standing does not accomplish that by itself. Fee and timetable are contract terms, not the four.

citation.ref: what has to be settled with an expert before the work starts, and when that settlement belongs on paper — what the work is for and how far it reaches, who is answerable for which part, how the two will talk and in what form the expert reports back, and the duty of secrecy binding the auditor that must be made to bind the expert as well

Mine development assets of 310 crore rupees are amortised on the units-of-production method over the ore reserve, and the reserve estimate, prepared for the company by a mining engineer on its staff, was cut by a fifth this year after new drilling. Priya Venkatesh is the engagement partner and three things happen in the course of the audit. First, the audit manager records that the team will assess the reserve estimate itself, "after reading up on reserve estimation over a weekend and a phone call to a geologist I know", and that no auditor's expert is needed because the company's engineer is qualified and the figure is his. Second, when Priya overrules him and engages Dr Anjali Sethi, an independent geologist who has never worked with the firm, the manager briefs her by telephone: "look at the reserve and tell us if it holds", hands her the company's drilling logs and the engineer's model, and puts nothing in writing, saying a written engagement would "slow things down and she is a professional". Third, when Dr Sethi's report supports the reduced reserve, the chief financial officer asks that the auditor's report name her and her firm "so the lenders can see an independent expert stood behind the number", and the manager suggests adding the words "in reliance on the report of Dr Sethi" to the opinion paragraph to limit the firm's own exposure.

items.stem: On the request to name the geologist alone, can the report refer to Dr Sethi?

options.text: No, because an expert's report is not audit evidence at all and can never be mentioned in any auditor's report; the firm must obtain its own evidence on the reserve by other means.
options.misconception: Denies the expert's work its status as evidence in order to reach the right answer.
options.why: Once her work is judged adequate, what Dr Sethi found in her own science may be taken as evidence, and the standard does contemplate a naming where a law demands one, or in a modified report where it matters. The firm leaves her out here because nothing obliges it to put her in — not because her report counts for nothing.

options.text: No, to both. The firm alone answers for the opinion — that is its sole responsibility, and leaning on Dr Sethi's work does not reduce it by a rupee, so "in reliance on" would be untrue as well as improper. And where the opinion is unmodified the report stays silent about an expert altogether, unless required by law or regulation, which nothing here does. On the rare occasion a law does demand the name, the report must add that the mention does not reduce what the auditor is answerable for — the exact opposite of what the manager is reaching for.
options.why: Two rules, and they come in that order: who answers for the opinion, and only then what the report may say. The firm answers for it alone. Nothing about drawing on an expert's work shrinks that — sole responsibility survives Dr Sethi's engagement whole. What the standard does permit is narrower than a shared signature: having worked through its requirements and satisfied itself that her work will serve the audit's purposes, the firm may treat what she found within her own science as evidence. Evidence sitting on the file, that is, and not a second name on the opinion. On the report itself the standard is flat. An unmodified opinion carries no mention of an auditor's expert unless required by law or regulation, and nothing reaches a private manganese miner that way; the requirement turns up here and there for transparency in public-sector reporting, which this is not. Where it does bite, the report has to add that naming the expert does not reduce what the auditor is answerable for. Now read the two requests against that. The chief financial officer wants lenders to see a second name standing behind the number — and a reader who takes that name as a second guarantor is exactly the misreading the rule was written to stop. The manager's wording is worse than a mention, because it is drafted to cut down a responsibility that cannot be cut down. In short, the firm carries sole responsibility which Dr Sethi's work does not reduce, and an unmodified report names no expert unless required by law or regulation, in which case it must say the naming changes nothing.
keywords: unless required by law or regulation

options.text: Yes to both, provided the report also states that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility, which is the form SA 620 prescribes for a reference to an expert.
options.misconception: Reads the mandatory rider as permission to refer.
options.why: That sentence is what a report must carry when a law forces the expert's name into it. It is not a formula that unlocks a naming nobody required, and the words "in reliance on" sitting in the opinion paragraph contradict it in the very same breath.

options.text: Yes to the chief financial officer's request, because naming an independent expert increases the transparency of the report and the lenders are its users; no to the manager's phrase, because it limits responsibility.
options.misconception: Treats the public-sector transparency exception as a general licence.
options.why: Where the opinion is unmodified an expert goes unmentioned unless a law or a regulator says otherwise. Transparency is the reason such laws exist in public-sector reporting; it is not a ground on which a firm may volunteer a name of its own accord. The second half of this answer is right and the first is the very case the rule forbids.

citation.ref: who answers for the opinion once an expert's work has been used, and the narrow case in which an unmodified report may name that expert at all — only where a law or a regulator makes it do so, and then only with a line saying the naming shifts nothing
