items.stem: On the bank's letter and the internal auditor's request alone, what does Meera do?

options.text: Nothing goes to the bank on the finance head's telephone call. What an engagement teaches the firm stays inside the firm unless a law compels it out or the client releases it, and in a company that release — the consent of the client — is the Board of Directors' to give by resolution, or a Managing Director's where the Board has handed him powers wide enough to carry it. A finance head on the telephone is neither, so Meera asks the company for that consent before any note on the supplier leaves the firm. The working papers sit outside that question altogether: they are hers, nobody, bank, client or internal auditor, can demand sight of them, and extracts to the client are hers to offer or withhold.
options.why: The clause has two doors and the finance head's call opens neither. Telling anyone outside the client what an engagement taught the firm is misconduct unless the client has agreed to it or a law demands it, and a lender's letter is a request rather than a demand of law. Agreement has to come from someone competent to give it: section 179 of the Companies Act puts that power in the Board of Directors, so the consent of the client here means a resolution of that Board, or a Managing Director acting under a delegation broad enough to carry it. A finance head speaking on the telephone holds no such power, and a note sent to the bank on his say-so would be a disclosure nobody authorised. The working papers are governed separately and more simply: the Code owes no sight of them to the client, and none to another auditor of the same enterprise either, a description it reads as covering the internal auditor, leaving extracts to the client as a courtesy the member may choose. So the bank's copies are not owed, the internal auditor's access is not owed, and a valid consent would have changed nothing on that half of the answer. In short, information leaves only on the consent of the client given by the Board of Directors or a managing director it has empowered, and no one, bank, client or internal auditor, has a right to her working papers.

options.text: Once the Board of Directors consents, Meera must send both the note and the working papers, because a valid consent removes every restriction and refusing the papers would then be a breach of her duty to the client.
options.misconception: A valid consent obliges the auditor to hand over the working papers as well.
options.why: A client's agreement opens the door for information and creates no right at all over the auditor's working papers, which she need not hand across and may share in extract if she chooses.

options.text: The bank is a lender with 40 crore rupees at stake, so its request is a disclosure required by law in substance; the note and the working papers go to the bank, and the internal auditor, being part of the client, has access to the working papers as of right.
options.misconception: A lender's request for information about its borrower is disclosure required by law.
options.why: A lender's interest in its borrower is not a legal demand, and the clause opens on two doors only: the client's agreement, or a law. On the papers themselves the Code owes nothing to another auditor of the same enterprise, and it reads that description as taking in the internal auditor.

options.text: The finance head's telephone consent is enough, since he is the officer who deals with the auditor day to day; the working papers, however, are the property of the company and go to whoever the company names, including the bank and the internal auditor.
options.misconception: The officer who deals with the auditor can consent for the company, and working papers belong to the client.
options.why: Consent must come from a person competent to give it, which for a company is the Board of Directors by resolution or a managing director with delegated powers wide enough; and the working papers are the auditor's, to which the Code gives the client and other auditors no right of access.

citation.ref: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule — the confidentiality clause. It covers when a member in practice may pass on what an engagement taught him, who inside a company is competent to release him from that duty, and, as a separate question, whether anyone can demand sight of his working papers

items.scenario: Bhargava & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Panchkula with two partners, Meera Bhargava and Rohit Iyer, and Meera is the engagement partner on the statutory audit of Ghaggar Foods Limited, an unlisted public company with a revenue of 180 crore rupees. Three matters sit on her desk in the first week of September 2026. First, the inspection team of the bank that has lent 40 crore rupees to Ghaggar Foods has written directly to the firm asking for a note on the company's purchases from a supplier owned by a director's brother and for copies of the firm's working papers on the stock count; the company's finance head has said on the telephone that the bank may have whatever it asks for, and in the same week the company's internal auditor has asked for access to the firm's working papers on debtors for his own review. Second, three engagements have been offered to the firm: the audit of a charitable trust that runs two schools, of which Rohit is a trustee; the audit of a management college where Meera teaches two evenings a week as a part-time lecturer; and a certificate of stock and debtors for a bank on behalf of a trading partnership in which Rohit is a partner, on which Rohit says the clause is about opinions and not certificates and that Meera, not he, will sign. Third, a shareholder of Ghaggar Foods has filed a complaint with the Institute on two counts: that in the previous year the firm certified the company's export turnover for a government incentive from a printout of the sales management information system without examining the books of account, and that in the current year the firm signed its audit report forty days after the date the company needed it to meet a statutory filing, because the firm's staff were engaged elsewhere; Rohit's answer is that the certified figure later proved right, that the company lost nothing, and that nobody has alleged dishonesty, so there is nothing to answer. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the three engagements offered to the firm alone, what does Meera decide?

options.text: None of the three is taken as offered. Where the member, the firm, or a partner in his firm holds a substantial interest in an enterprise, that enterprise is one this firm cannot report on; and the Council has ruled a trust's audit away from a firm one of whose partners sits as a trustee of it, and a college's audit away from a member who is a part-time lecturer there. The certificate is caught on the same footing: reports, certificates and attest work of every kind sit inside this clause beside the audit opinion, the bar attaches to the firm rather than to whoever holds the pen, and a member who is himself a partner in a trading concern may not certify what it reports, so moving the signature from Rohit to Meera cures nothing.
options.why: The clause is written for the firm, not for the signature. It shuts a member out of reporting on any enterprise in which he, the firm, or a partner in his firm carries a substantial interest, and the Code reads its reach wide: anything given out after an examination of accounts, and any attest work an enactment asks for, stands on the same footing as an audit opinion, with the Council adding that certificates and audits done for banks are no exception. Take the three in turn. The trust: the Council's decision keeps a firm away from a trust's audit where a partner of that firm is a trustee of it, or for that matter an employee of it, and Rohit is a trustee. The college: the same decision keeps a member away from a college's audit while he holds a part-time lecturer's post there, and Meera teaches two evenings a week. The trading partnership: an interest held as a partner in a concern that is not a company is treated by the Council as touching the member's independence of mind, so his firm may neither audit nor certify what that concern reports; and because the bar runs to every partner in his firm, moving the engagement from Rohit's signature to Meera's moves it nowhere. In short, a trust with a partner of the firm on its board of trustees, a college where the member is a part-time lecturer, and a partnership in which a partner in his firm holds an interest are all outside what this firm may certify or audit.

options.text: Only Rohit's two engagements are affected, because it is Rohit who is a trustee and a partner; Meera's lecturing is teaching, not a financial interest, so the college audit may be accepted in her own name.
options.misconception: A teaching post is not an interest that bars the college's audit.
options.why: The Council's ruling on colleges turns on the post, not on money: a member holding a part-time lecturing job there is not to take that college's audit, in his own name or under the firm's. That is exactly where Meera stands.

options.text: The trust and the college audits may be accepted provided the relationship is disclosed in the report, since disclosure is what independence rules ask for; only the certificate for the partnership is barred outright.
options.misconception: Disclosing the relationship in the report cures a substantial-interest bar.
options.why: What the clause forbids is the giving of the opinion at all, and the Council's rulings say the engagement is not to be taken, under the member's own name or under the firm's. Neither is answered by a paragraph of disclosure.

options.text: The certificate for the bank is outside the clause because a certificate of stock and debtors is not an opinion on financial statements, and it is safe if Rohit does not sign it; the trust and the college are the two to refuse.
options.misconception: Clause (4) is about audit opinions, not certificates.
options.why: Certificates and attest work of every kind fall inside this clause beside the audit opinion, the Council presses the point for work done for banks in particular, and the bar follows a partner in his firm whoever ends up signing.

citation.ref: Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule — the substantial-interest bar. It covers which enterprises a member, his firm or a fellow partner is shut out of reporting on, why certificates and attest work stand beside the audit opinion inside it, and the Council's decisions on a college lectureship and on a trusteeship

items.scenario: Bhargava & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Panchkula with two partners, Meera Bhargava and Rohit Iyer, and Meera is the engagement partner on the statutory audit of Ghaggar Foods Limited, an unlisted public company with a revenue of 180 crore rupees. Three matters sit on her desk in the first week of September 2026. First, the inspection team of the bank that has lent 40 crore rupees to Ghaggar Foods has written directly to the firm asking for a note on the company's purchases from a supplier owned by a director's brother and for copies of the firm's working papers on the stock count; the company's finance head has said on the telephone that the bank may have whatever it asks for, and in the same week the company's internal auditor has asked for access to the firm's working papers on debtors for his own review. Second, three engagements have been offered to the firm: the audit of a charitable trust that runs two schools, of which Rohit is a trustee; the audit of a management college where Meera teaches two evenings a week as a part-time lecturer; and a certificate of stock and debtors for a bank on behalf of a trading partnership in which Rohit is a partner, on which Rohit says the clause is about opinions and not certificates and that Meera, not he, will sign. Third, a shareholder of Ghaggar Foods has filed a complaint with the Institute on two counts: that in the previous year the firm certified the company's export turnover for a government incentive from a printout of the sales management information system without examining the books of account, and that in the current year the firm signed its audit report forty days after the date the company needed it to meet a statutory filing, because the firm's staff were engaged elsewhere; Rohit's answer is that the certified figure later proved right, that the company lost nothing, and that nobody has alleged dishonesty, so there is nothing to answer. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the complaint's two counts alone, what does Meera tell Rohit the firm faces?

options.text: The late report is misconduct because a statutory date was missed, but the certificate is not, because an auditor is a watchdog and not a bloodhound and may rely on the company's own system report unless something excites suspicion.
options.misconception: Watchdog not bloodhound means the auditor may certify from management's reports.
options.why: The watchdog line frees an auditor from starting every job in suspicion; it does not let him certify a figure while the books of account stay shut, which a decided case treats as a failure of due diligence and as gross negligence.

options.text: The certificate is misconduct, but the late report is a matter between the firm and its client under the engagement letter and not professional misconduct, since the Institute does not police delivery dates.
options.misconception: Missing an audit deadline is a contractual matter, not professional misconduct.
options.why: There is a decided case squarely on this: a member whose audit was unfinished and whose report did not reach the client in time for a statutory obligation to be met was held guilty under Clause (7). The date missed was the client's statutory one, not a date in an engagement letter, and the clause reaches it.

options.text: Neither count can stand, because gross negligence needs either dishonesty or a loss to somebody, and here the figure was right and the company lost nothing; at most the Institute writes to the firm asking for more care in future.
options.misconception: Gross negligence needs dishonesty or a loss.
options.why: The clause bites the moment one has to ask whether the member worked honestly and reasonably, and the decided cases under it found misconduct where no dishonesty and no loss had been alleged. A word asking for more care answers a minor slip, which a certificate signed with the books unopened is not.

options.text: Both counts are answerable under the clause, and Rohit's three points answer neither. The clause is failing to exercise due diligence or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, and it needs no dishonesty and no loss; certifying a turnover figure from a management information system printout without examining the books of account is the very case of failing to exercise due diligence, whatever the figure later proved, and not completing the audit and submitting the report in due time to let the company meet a statutory requirement is misconduct under the same clause. What the clause does not reach is a minor error or lapse, which is brought to the member's attention rather than taken to the Disciplinary Committee.
options.why: One question runs through the clause: did the member do his work honestly and reasonably? The Code says the clause bites the moment that question has to be answered. Carelessness under it stretches the whole distance from the frontiers of fraud down to slight negligence, so an absence of dishonesty proves nothing, and no loss to anybody is an ingredient of it. Count one: the reported case is a member who certified circulation figures off a management information report while the books of account stayed shut, and he was held to have failed in due diligence and to be grossly negligent, because a figure lifted from statistical records and never traced back to the financial ones has not been verified at all. An export turnover certified off a sales system printout is that same act, and the figure turning out right afterwards supplies no examination that nobody performed. Count two: the Code's other case is a member whose audit work was unfinished and whose report reached the company too late for a statutory obligation to be met, held guilty under this clause; a report signed forty days past the date the company needed, because staff were busy elsewhere, is that case again. Outside the clause sits the minor error or lapse, which the Council answers with a word to the member asking for more care, and neither count is of that size. In short, a certificate given without examining the books of account and a report not delivered in due time are each a failure of due diligence, and neither dishonesty nor loss is an element of the clause.
keywords: without examining the books of account

citation.ref: Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule — the due-diligence clause. It covers the standard of care a member owes in professional work, the decided cases the Code places inside it (a certificate signed off a management report with the books unopened; an audit report that arrived too late for the client's statutory filing), and the minor lapse it leaves outside

items.stem: On the opening stock alone, can the senior take the 48 crore rupees on the predecessor's unmodified report?

options.text: Yes. An unmodified report from a qualified predecessor is sufficient appropriate evidence about the opening balances, and the new auditor's responsibility begins with the transactions of the year of appointment.
options.misconception: Treats the predecessor's report as evidence about the opening balances rather than as a document the new auditor reads on the way to obtaining evidence.
options.why: What SA 510 asks the new auditor to obtain is evidence about whether anything carried in at the start of the year is wrong enough to distort this year's statements, and reading another auditor's opinion does not supply that. The predecessor auditor's report is one step on the way; work on the opening balances themselves comes after it.

options.text: No, and because the predecessor's working papers are unavailable the opening inventory is unauditable, so the opinion must be qualified for a scope limitation on opening stock without further work.
options.misconception: Jumps to a modified opinion before performing the procedures that could produce the evidence.
options.why: The working papers are one possible source of evidence, not the only one. The module's additional procedures for opening inventory, reconciling the current count to the opening quantities and testing the valuation of the opening inventory, do not depend on the predecessor. A qualified or disclaimed opinion is the result where the auditor is unable to obtain the evidence after trying, not the starting point.

options.text: Yes, provided the year-end count agrees with the books; a clean closing count proves the stock system works and so proves the opening figure the same system produced.
options.misconception: Assumes a closing count carries evidence backwards to the opening balance.
options.why: This is the very reasoning the standard turns down: work done on the closing stock gives little audit evidence about what was on hand when the year began. A count at 31 March 2026 establishes what stood there that day, not what stood there twelve months earlier.

options.text: No. Reading the predecessor auditor's report and last year's statements is the first step, not the evidence. The firm has to get evidence of its own that nothing carried in as opening inventory is wrong enough to matter to this year's figures, and a count taken at this year end gives little audit evidence about what stood in the freezers on 1 April 2025; so it does further work aimed at that date, tracing the current count back through the year's movements to the opening quantities and testing how the opening inventory was valued.
options.why: A first-year engagement puts three things on the auditor before anything else. Last year's statements and the predecessor auditor's report go in front of her. She settles whether last year's closing figures came across intact and on accounting policies that hold. Then she works on the opening balances themselves. What she is after is evidence that nothing carried in at 1 April is wrong enough to distort what this year's statements say, and part of the judgement is whether the year's ordinary work reaches back that far or whether something aimed squarely at the opening figure is needed instead. Inventory is where it does not reach: work on the closing stock gives little audit evidence about what was on hand when the year began, so the standard asks for more — attend a count now and reconcile it backwards through the year's movements to the opening quantities, and test the valuation put on the opening inventory. A clean report from the man before is read; it does not stand in for that work, and his silence over his working papers changes nothing about what has to be obtained. In short, the predecessor auditor's report is read rather than relied on, this year's count gives little audit evidence about the opening inventory, and the firm does its own procedures on it.

citation.ref: SA 510 on a first-year engagement — what the previous statements and the predecessor auditor's report are read for, and why they are only the start; and the standard's warning that stock work done at this year end carries almost nothing backwards about what was in store twelve months before, so procedures aimed at the opening figure itself become necessary

items.scenario: Godavari Frozen Foods Private Limited freezes and stores vegetables at a cold-storage plant near Nashik and sells to retail chains. Kulkarni & Menon were appointed its statutory auditors in September 2025 for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditor, a sole practitioner, retired from practice; his report on the year ended 31 March 2025 was unmodified. Revenue for the year was 380 crore rupees and profit before tax 19 crore rupees. The partner has three notes from the senior on her desk. First, opening stock at 1 April 2025 was 48 crore rupees of frozen produce, the firm attended no count at that date, the retired auditor has not answered two letters asking for his working papers, and the senior proposes to accept the opening figure "on the strength of a clean report from a qualified predecessor". Second, trade receivables at the year end are 65 crore rupees, of which 40 crore rupees is owed by five retail chains; the managing director has refused to let the firm send confirmation requests to those five, saying "the chains resent audit letters and it costs us shelf space", and has offered instead statements of account which his sales team will collect from the chains and hand to the firm. Third, the company revalued the cold-storage plant at 31 March 2026 from 70 crore rupees to 120 crore rupees on a valuer's report; the firm engaged its own chartered engineer, who has twenty years in refrigeration plant, and he has returned a two-page opinion agreeing with 120 crore rupees, resting on a remaining useful life of twenty-five years and on a replacement cost taken from a 2019 supplier quotation which the company gave him. The senior has filed the opinion as the evidence for the revaluation, "since an engineer with twenty years' experience has signed it".

items.stem: On the refused confirmations alone, what does SA 505 require of the firm?

options.text: Inquire into the reasons for the refusal and seek evidence that they are valid and reasonable; evaluate what the refusal does to the assessed risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and to the other procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures on the 40 crore rupees, such as subsequent receipts and shipping documents. Statements collected by the sales team are received indirectly and are not confirmations. If the refusal is found unreasonable, the firm communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the opinion.
options.why: SA 505 sets out three things to do when a client will not let the request go. Ask why, and look for evidence that the reason given is a real and reasonable one. Weigh what the refusal itself says about the risks already assessed, fraud included, and about the nature, timing and extent of everything else planned. Then do other work in the confirmation's place: alternative audit procedures chosen to bring in evidence that is both relevant and reliable, such as cash received afterwards matched to the invoices, and the despatch records behind them. Should the reason turn out not to hold, the matter goes to those charged with governance and the firm considers what it means for the audit and for the opinion. Control of the confirmation exercise, from picking the party written to through to taking in the reply, is the auditor's throughout, and a reply reaching her by an indirect route is one the standard flags as less reliable for that reason alone; a statement carried in by the client's own sales staff is exactly that case. In short, the firm asks the reasons for the refusal, performs alternative audit procedures, and takes an unreasonable refusal to those charged with governance.

options.text: Accept the managing director's offer. A statement of account signed by the customer is external evidence whoever carries it, and for a private company the confirmation process is a matter for management's convenience.
options.misconception: Treats a document that originated outside the company as an external confirmation regardless of who handled it on the way.
options.why: The confirmation process is controlled by the auditor, including sending the request and receiving the reply directly, and the module names a response received indirectly as a reason to doubt its reliability. A statement handed over by the client's sales team gives the auditor no assurance that it came from the chain unaltered, and nothing in SA 505 turns on whether the company is private.

options.text: Treat the refusal as a scope limitation imposed by management and disclaim the opinion, since 40 crore rupees is over half of receivables and confirmations were necessary.
options.misconception: Moves straight from a refusal to a disclaimer without the inquiry and the alternative procedures SA 505 requires first.
options.why: The module's steps come before any conclusion on the opinion: inquire into the reasons, evaluate the risk implications, and perform alternative audit procedures. Only if the refusal is unreasonable does the auditor communicate with those charged with governance and consider the implications for the opinion, and even then the form of any modification depends on whether alternative procedures produced the evidence.

options.text: Send the confirmation requests regardless, since the auditor controls the confirmation process and management cannot forbid it; a refusal is noted in the letter of weakness.
options.misconception: Reads the auditor's control of the process as a power to override the client rather than a responsibility for how requests are handled.
options.why: SA 505 recognises that management may refuse and prescribes what the auditor does then, which is inquiry, evaluation, alternative procedures and, for an unreasonable refusal, communication with those charged with governance. Writing to a customer over the client's objection is not among the steps, and the letter of weakness is about control deficiencies, not this.

citation.ref: SA 505 on a management refusal to let a confirmation request go out — asking why and looking for evidence that the reason holds; weighing what the refusal does to the risks already assessed, fraud among them, and to the rest of the planned work; doing other procedures in place of the confirmation; and carrying an unreasonable refusal to those charged with governance, with the opinion in view

items.stem: On the valuer's report alone, is the engineer's signed opinion the evidence for the 120 crore rupees?

options.text: Yes, but the auditor's report must refer to the engineer by name and state that the revaluation was verified by him, so that responsibility for the figure is shared.
options.misconception: Believes referring to an expert in the report divides responsibility for the opinion.
options.why: SA 620 says the auditor's responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by using an expert, and the report does not refer to the expert unless law or regulation requires it, in which case it states that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility. There is no sharing of responsibility, and naming the engineer does not replace evaluating his work.

options.text: No, because an auditor may not use an expert on a matter that management has already had valued; the firm must obtain a third valuation from an independent valuer chosen jointly with the company.
options.misconception: Invents a bar on using an auditor's expert alongside a management's expert.
options.why: Nothing in SA 620 bars an auditor's expert where management used an expert of its own; the two are different things and the standard exists for exactly this use. What the module requires is the evaluation of the auditor's expert's work, its assumptions and methods and source data, not a further valuation.

options.text: Yes. Once the firm has satisfied itself about the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity, his conclusion in his own field is audit evidence, and second-guessing an engineer on refrigeration plant would be the auditor acting outside her competence.
options.misconception: Stops at the expert's qualifications and treats the evaluation of his work as beyond the auditor.
options.why: Competence, capabilities and objectivity are assessed before the expert is used; the module then requires the auditor to evaluate the adequacy of the work itself, including the assumptions and methods and the source data. Asking whether a 2019 quotation is complete and accurate for a 2026 value, or whether the findings are consistent with other evidence, is not engineering, and the auditor's sole responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by the expert's signature.

options.text: Not yet. The engineer's competence is the entry ticket, not the evaluation. The firm must evaluate whether his work is adequate for its purposes: whether his findings are relevant and reasonable and consistent with other evidence, whether the twenty-five-year life and the replacement-cost approach are relevant and reasonable as assumptions and methods, and whether a 2019 quotation supplied by the company is relevant, complete and accurate source data for a 2026 value. The firm keeps sole responsibility for the opinion; using an expert does not reduce it.
options.why: The opinion belongs to the firm and to nobody else, and bringing in a specialist shaves nothing off that: sole responsibility stays exactly where it was. His findings turn into audit evidence only once the firm, having worked through SA 620, is satisfied that the work is good enough for what the firm needs it for. That judgement has three parts. Do his conclusions bear on the question, are they reasonable, and do they sit comfortably beside the other evidence on file? Where the work rests on assumptions and methods of any weight, are those apt in these circumstances and sound in themselves? And where it draws on source data that matters to the result, is that data on point, complete and accurate? A twenty-five-year remaining life and a replacement-cost route to value are assumptions and methods of exactly that weight; a quotation seven years old, handed over by the company itself, is source data on which a 50 crore rupees uplift is being made to rest. In short, the assumptions and methods and the source data are the firm's to evaluate, and the firm keeps sole responsibility for the opinion.

citation.ref: SA 620 on using an auditor's expert — the opinion stays the auditor's alone and engaging a specialist lightens nothing; and what has to be judged about that specialist's work before it can be leaned on: whether his conclusions bear on the question and sit beside the rest of the evidence, whether the assumptions and methods behind them are apt, and whether the data he worked from is fit for the purpose

items.stem: On the four uncertainties alone, what does Aparna settle?

options.text: Aparna disclaims an opinion on the financial statements as a whole because of the way the four uncertainties interact, and gives the clean opinion on the statement of cash flows in the same report, since none of the four touches it and the reader is better served by knowing which part of the statements is sound.
options.misconception: Reading the bar on a piecemeal opinion as a matter of usefulness to the reader, rather than a contradiction the standard forbids outright.
options.why: The opinion is right and the addition undoes it. A report that disclaims, or gives an adverse opinion, on the statements as a whole may not also carry a clean opinion beside it — same framework, one statement, or particular elements, accounts or items — because the two things contradict each other inside one document. A reader told that no opinion can be formed on the statements, and then told that one of those statements is fine, will take the second sentence and read the first as a formality. The four uncertainties also reach the cash flow statement through the recallable borrowing, whatever the finance head says.

options.text: Aparna gives a qualified opinion with all four matters set out in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section. She has sufficient appropriate audit evidence about every one of them and no single matter is pervasive, so the statements are true and fair except for the four, and the clean opinion on the statement of cash flows is left out as unnecessary.
options.misconception: Treating pervasiveness as a test applied to each matter one at a time, so four non-pervasive matters can only add up to a qualification.
options.why: Adding up four matters that are each not pervasive does not settle whether the statements as a whole can be reported on, and that is the judgement the standard asks for. A qualified opinion is a statement that everything outside the named matters is true and fair. She cannot make that statement here, because the four matters are not separate exceptions to an otherwise settled picture — the licence decides the plant, the plant decides the borrowing, and the possible cumulative effect runs through every figure. The standard provides for precisely this: where the auditor has evidence about each individual uncertainty and still cannot form an opinion because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties, the opinion is disclaimed.

options.text: Aparna gives an unmodified opinion with four emphasis of matter paragraphs, one for each uncertainty, since all four are disclosed in the notes and she has evidence about each. Drawing the reader's attention to them is what the reporting standards provide for when a matter is properly disclosed and the auditor has no disagreement with the accounting.
options.misconception: Using emphasis of matter as a way of reporting doubt, when it decorates an opinion the auditor is still able to express.
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph leaves the opinion unmodified, and the opinion is the thing in doubt. It is used where the auditor can say the statements are true and fair and wants the reader to notice something that is already disclosed. Here she cannot say that, because the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect make it impossible to form the opinion at all. Four paragraphs of attention attached to a clean opinion would tell the reader the statements can be relied on subject to being read carefully, which is a stronger assurance than she is in a position to give.

options.text: Aparna disclaims an opinion, and refuses the clean opinion on the one statement. Holding enough evidence on each uncertainty separately does not settle the question. What she cannot form a view on is the potential interaction of the uncertainties — the licence decides the plant, the plant decides the borrowing, the borrowing is already recallable, and the arbitration and the tax demand sit on top of all of it — and the possible cumulative effect that interaction has across every figure. That is the case the standard reserves for extremely rare circumstances and answers with a disclaimer, not with a qualified opinion carrying four limbs and not with four emphasis of matter paragraphs. And once the opinion on the whole is disclaimed, the report cannot carry a clean opinion beside it under the same framework on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items, so the statement of cash flows does not get one.
options.why: The finance head's two proposals both assume the difficulty is a list of separate problems, and it is not. A qualified opinion says the statements are true and fair except for named matters, which requires the auditor to know what the rest of the statements look like once those matters are set aside; here she does not, because each uncertainty changes what the others are worth. That is why the standard has a second route to a disclaimer beside the ordinary one. The ordinary route is an inability to obtain evidence whose possible effects are material and pervasive. The second route is written for exactly this case, and the standard calls it extremely rare: the auditor holds enough evidence on every uncertainty taken by itself, and an opinion is still beyond her because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties — what each of them does to the others — and the possible cumulative effect of the four together. Emphasis of matter paragraphs fail for a further reason: they draw attention to something disclosed while leaving the opinion unmodified, and an unmodified opinion is the one thing she cannot give. The last part follows from the first. A disclaimer on the statements as a whole and a clean opinion on the cash flow statement in the same report would contradict each other, which is why the standard bars a clean opinion, under the same framework, on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items alongside it. In short, she disclaims because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties and of the possible cumulative effect of the four together, and she does not add a clean opinion on specific elements, accounts or items to the same report.

citation.ref: the second route the standard gives to a disclaimer — evidence held on every uncertainty taken singly, an opinion still beyond reach because of how the uncertainties would work on one another and what they might come to together, and the standard calling that extremely rare — together with its bar on a report that disclaims, or gives an adverse opinion, on the statements as a whole also carrying a clean opinion beside it under the same framework, whether on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items

items.scenario: Sinha & Varma are a firm of chartered accountants at Lucknow, and Aparna Sinha is the engagement partner on the audit of Gomti Polymers Limited, a listed company, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters are open in the week the report is to be signed. First, four uncertainties. An arbitration on a terminated supply contract, where the award is reserved and the claim against the company is 210 crore rupees; a tax demand of 96 crore rupees under appeal; a covenant on a borrowing of 340 crore rupees that the company breached in December 2025 and that lets the lender recall the whole amount on notice; and the renewal of the manufacturing licence for the company's only plant, pending with the state authority since October 2025. Aparna has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about each of the four on its own, and no one of them taken alone is pervasive; what she cannot see is how the four would work out together, since each turns on the others and their possible cumulative effect runs through every figure in the statements. The finance head proposes a qualified opinion carrying four separate limbs, or failing that an emphasis of matter paragraph for each, and adds that since the statement of cash flows is untouched by any of the four she should give a clean opinion on that one statement inside the same report. Second, the annual report. The board's report, which she received before the date of her own report, puts segment revenue for the speciality division at 480 crore rupees where the audited statements show 380 crore rupees, and repeats the higher figure twice more in the management discussion. She asked for the correction; management refused; she wrote to the audit committee, which also declined, saying the board's report is a management document that nobody audits. The finance head's position is that her opinion does not cover the other information at all, so the most she may do is say that she read it. Third, the shape of the report itself. The finance head has sent back a redrafted report in which a two-page background to the arbitration comes first, then the basis on which the audit was conducted, then the two responsibilities sections, with the opinion paragraph at the very end, where he says a reader will finally have the context to understand it; he has kept the heading Opinion over that paragraph, and has left standing the sentence saying that the financial statements have been audited. Aparna has to settle all three before she signs.

items.stem: On the figure in the board's report alone, what does Aparna settle?

options.text: Aparna modifies her opinion on the financial statements for the misstatement in the board's report. A figure a hundred crore rupees away from the audited revenue, repeated three times, is material, and once management and those charged with governance have both refused to correct it the only instrument left to the auditor is a qualification.
options.misconception: Reaching for the opinion because it is the strongest instrument, when the misstatement is outside what the opinion covers.
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements, and the financial statements are not wrong — the audited segment revenue is 380 crore rupees and stays 380 crore rupees. The misstatement is in the other information, which the opinion does not cover, and the standard gives it its own place in the report for that reason: a statement in the Other Information section that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Qualifying the opinion would tell readers something untrue about the statements, and it would also hide the real point, which is that the board's report and the audited figures do not agree.

options.text: Aparna has already done the two things that come first — she asked management to correct it and, on the refusal, took it to those charged with governance and asked them to correct it. What follows now is not silence. She weighs the implications for the auditor's report and tells those charged with governance how she plans to address the misstatement in it, and because the board's report reached her before the date of her own report, the Other Information section must carry a statement that describes the uncorrected material misstatement instead of a statement that she has nothing to report. Resigning the engagement is the other action open to her where the law allows it. The finance head is right that her opinion does not cover the other information, and the section says so in terms; that is a different thing from having nothing to say about it.
options.why: The finance head has taken a true sentence and drawn the wrong conclusion from it. The auditor's opinion does not cover the other information, and the Other Information section says exactly that — that management is responsible for it and that no opinion or assurance conclusion is expressed on it. But the same section also reports the outcome of the auditor's reading of it, and that outcome is not optional. Where the other information was obtained before the date of the report, the section ends either with a statement that the auditor has nothing to report or, where a material misstatement has been left uncorrected, with one that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Saying only that she read it would be the first of those two endings, which would be untrue. The steps before that point have all been taken: the request to management, then the same request put to those charged with governance. What the standard requires once they too refuse is that she weigh the implications for the auditor's report and tell them how she plans to address the matter in it, and it names resigning the engagement, where the law permits it, as the other course. In short, the matter goes to those charged with governance, she weighs the implications for the auditor's report, and the Other Information section describes the uncorrected material misstatement rather than reporting nothing.

options.text: Aparna accepts that nothing further is open to her. She read the other information and found the inconsistency, she asked for a correction and she escalated it, which is the whole of the duty; her opinion does not cover the board's report, so the Other Information section states that management is responsible for it and that no opinion is expressed on it, and stops there.
options.misconception: Reading the escalation as the whole of the duty, so the report says nothing about what the escalation failed to fix.
options.why: Three of the steps are right and the report is where it goes wrong. The section that says the opinion does not cover the other information is the same section that must report what came of reading it. Where the other information was obtained before the date of the report, that section ends either with a statement that the auditor has nothing to report or with one that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Stopping after the responsibility sentence leaves the reader with the first of those by implication, and the reader is the person the whole exercise is for — a segment revenue figure a hundred crore rupees above the audited one, repeated three times, is what the section exists to surface.

options.text: Aparna signs the report with a statement in the Other Information section that describes the uncorrected material misstatement, and treats the matter as closed with that. Since the audit committee has already been told and has declined, there is nothing to be gained by writing to them again about what the report will say.
options.misconception: Treating the earlier request for a correction as the same communication as telling governance how the report will address the matter.
options.why: The statement in the report is right and the step left out is the one that gives those charged with governance a last chance to act. The standard asks her to weigh what the misstatement means for her report and then to tell governance how the report is going to deal with it — a different communication from the earlier request to correct the figure. A board that has refused a correction in the abstract often behaves differently when it is told, before the report is signed, what the report is going to say. Skipping it also leaves the auditor without a record that the outcome was put to them.

citation.ref: what the standard asks once a material misstatement of the other information is found — the request to management, then the same request to those charged with governance on a refusal; and where the other information came in before the report is dated and is still wrong, the auditor weighs the implications for the auditor's report, tells governance how the report is going to deal with it, and may resign where the law allows it — together with the two ways the Other Information section can end for information obtained before that date: nothing to report, or a statement describing the material misstatement left uncorrected

items.scenario: Sinha & Varma are a firm of chartered accountants at Lucknow, and Aparna Sinha is the engagement partner on the audit of Gomti Polymers Limited, a listed company, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters are open in the week the report is to be signed. First, four uncertainties. An arbitration on a terminated supply contract, where the award is reserved and the claim against the company is 210 crore rupees; a tax demand of 96 crore rupees under appeal; a covenant on a borrowing of 340 crore rupees that the company breached in December 2025 and that lets the lender recall the whole amount on notice; and the renewal of the manufacturing licence for the company's only plant, pending with the state authority since October 2025. Aparna has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about each of the four on its own, and no one of them taken alone is pervasive; what she cannot see is how the four would work out together, since each turns on the others and their possible cumulative effect runs through every figure in the statements. The finance head proposes a qualified opinion carrying four separate limbs, or failing that an emphasis of matter paragraph for each, and adds that since the statement of cash flows is untouched by any of the four she should give a clean opinion on that one statement inside the same report. Second, the annual report. The board's report, which she received before the date of her own report, puts segment revenue for the speciality division at 480 crore rupees where the audited statements show 380 crore rupees, and repeats the higher figure twice more in the management discussion. She asked for the correction; management refused; she wrote to the audit committee, which also declined, saying the board's report is a management document that nobody audits. The finance head's position is that her opinion does not cover the other information at all, so the most she may do is say that she read it. Third, the shape of the report itself. The finance head has sent back a redrafted report in which a two-page background to the arbitration comes first, then the basis on which the audit was conducted, then the two responsibilities sections, with the opinion paragraph at the very end, where he says a reader will finally have the context to understand it; he has kept the heading Opinion over that paragraph, and has left standing the sentence saying that the financial statements have been audited. Aparna has to settle all three before she signs.

items.stem: On the redrafted layout alone, what does Aparna settle?

options.text: Aparna sends the layout back. The opinion is the first section of the auditor's report, before any background and before the responsibilities sections, and the basis on which the audit was conducted belongs in a section headed Basis for Opinion directly following the Opinion section, not in front of it. Two of his other edits go as well: because she is disclaiming, the heading over that first section reads Disclaimer of Opinion and not Opinion, and the sentence saying the financial statements have been audited is amended to say that she was engaged to audit them. A two-page background to the arbitration written by the company has no place in her report at all; what she has to say about the arbitration goes in the section that gives the basis for her conclusion.
options.why: The order of the sections is a requirement, not a house style, and the reason is the reader. A report that arrives at its conclusion on the last page can be read for two pages by somebody who does not yet know whether there is an opinion at all, and the company's own account of the arbitration would be the first thing that reader met. The standard puts the auditor's opinion in the first section of the auditor's report under the heading Opinion, and puts the Basis for Opinion section directly following the Opinion section — the conclusion first, then why. The heading changes with the opinion: Qualified Opinion, Adverse Opinion or Disclaimer of Opinion as appropriate, so keeping Opinion over a disclaimer would tell the reader at a glance the opposite of what the section says. The last edit is the subtlest and the one most easily left standing: a report that disclaims an opinion does not say the financial statements have been audited, because the auditor could not complete what an audit ends in; the wording is amended to say the auditor was engaged to audit them. In short, the opinion is the first section of the auditor's report, the Basis for Opinion section comes directly following the Opinion section, and the disclaimer carries its own heading with the amended statement that she was engaged to audit the statements.
keywords: first section of the auditor's report

options.text: Aparna restores the opinion to the front under the heading Disclaimer of Opinion and amends the sentence to say she was engaged to audit the statements, and keeps the two-page background to the arbitration as the section directly following the opinion, since a reader facing a disclaimer needs the fullest account of what could not be resolved.
options.misconception: Filling the place directly after the opinion with the fullest explanation available, rather than the section the standard puts there.
options.why: The heading and the amended sentence are right, and the section kept in second place belongs to somebody else. The section directly following the Opinion section is the Basis for Opinion section, which is the auditor's own: it says the audit was run under the Standards on Auditing, points to the section describing her responsibilities, states her independence under ICAI's Code of Ethics, and says whether the evidence she obtained is sufficient and appropriate — and where the opinion is disclaimed it gives the reasons. Putting the company's account of the arbitration there hands the most read part of the report to the party being reported on, and displaces the section the standard requires.

options.text: Aparna keeps his order but fixes the headings. Where the opinion sits is a presentation choice and a reader who has the background and the basis first will understand the conclusion better; what matters is that the section is headed Disclaimer of Opinion and that the sentence is amended to say she was engaged to audit the financial statements.
options.misconception: Treating the order of the report's sections as a matter of presentation, when it is specified.
options.why: The two headings are right and the order is not a choice. The standard puts the opinion in the report's first section and the Basis for Opinion section immediately after it. The sequence carries the meaning: the reader is told the conclusion, then the grounds for it, and nothing of the company's own drafting stands in front of either. A two-page background supplied by the finance head, placed first, also blurs whose words the report is, which is the one thing an independent auditor's report cannot afford.

options.text: Aparna restores the opinion to the front, with the Basis for Opinion section directly following it and the background dropped, and leaves his two other edits alone. The heading Opinion covers every kind of opinion including a disclaimer, and the sentence that the financial statements have been audited is a statement of fact — she did audit them, and what she cannot do is form an opinion on the result.
options.misconception: Reading Opinion as a heading that covers every outcome, and the audited wording as a description of work done rather than of a completed audit.
options.why: The order is right and both of the edits left standing say something the report must not say. Where the opinion is modified the heading of the first section is Qualified Opinion, Adverse Opinion or Disclaimer of Opinion as appropriate, so a heading reading Opinion over a disclaimer is wrong on the page a reader looks at first. And a disclaimer amends the statement that the financial statements have been audited to say the auditor was engaged to audit them. That is not word play: an audit ends in an opinion, and a report that says the statements were audited while expressing no opinion invites the reader to think the audit was completed and the auditor is merely being cautious.

citation.ref: the shape the standard gives the report — the opinion carried in the first section of the auditor's report under a heading naming it, which reads Qualified Opinion, Adverse Opinion or Disclaimer of Opinion where the opinion is modified; the Basis for Opinion section sitting directly following the Opinion section, saying the audit followed the Standards on Auditing, pointing to the section on the auditor's responsibilities, setting out her independence under the relevant ethical requirements and ICAI's Code of Ethics, and saying whether the evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate; and the amendment a disclaimer makes to the sentence about the statements having been audited, which then says the auditor was engaged to audit them

items.stem: On the unpaid fee alone, may Desai & Kulkarni accept the appointment?

options.text: Yes. A fee dispute is not a professional reason for refusing an audit, and the retiring auditor has said in writing that it has no objection, which is all Clause 8 asks for.
options.misconception: Treats every unpaid fee as a fee dispute; a fee agreed in the signed accounts is undisputed, and that is the case the clause bars.
options.why: A fee dispute is indeed not a professional reason, but nothing here is disputed: the fee is provided for in accounts signed by both sides. That is exactly what the module defines as an undisputed audit fee, and its non-payment is a professional reason that makes accepting professional misconduct, whatever the retiring auditor says about the change.

options.text: Yes. The letter went by registered post acknowledgement due and the card came back signed, so the communication required by Clause 8 has been made and the firm is free to accept.
options.misconception: Reads Clause 8 as a rule about proving delivery, when the delivery is only the means of finding out whether a professional reason exists.
options.why: Registered post acknowledgement due is one of the ways the Council accepts as positive evidence of delivery, so the communication has been made. But the purpose of the letter is to learn whether there is a professional reason for not accepting, and the reply disclosed one: undisputed audit fees unpaid by a company that is not a sick unit.

options.text: No. The fee is provided for in accounts signed by both sides and the travel was spent on the audit, so this is an undisputed audit fee for a statutory audit, and Harihar is not a sick unit; the firm must not accept until it is paid, and accepting would be professional misconduct.
options.why: Under Clause (8) a fee dispute is not by itself a professional reason for refusing, but non-payment of an undisputed audit fee for a statutory audit, other than by a sick unit, is one of the three professional reasons, and an auditor who accepts in that case is guilty of professional misconduct. The provision in accounts signed by both auditee and auditor plus the auditor's expenses is the undisputed audit fee, and a sick unit is one registered for at least five years whose accumulated losses equal or exceed its net worth; a company profitable for seven years is not one. So the firm must not accept until the 3.4 lakh rupees is paid.

options.text: No, and the firm cannot accept this audit at all until a court settles what Bhandari & Co. is owed, however long that takes.
options.misconception: Confuses an undisputed fee with a disputed one, and misses that payment, not litigation, removes the bar.
options.why: Nothing needs a court. The fee is undisputed, so the way is cleared by the company paying it; the module even provides for the case where the previous auditor is not available to receive payment, by having the client buy a demand draft for the amount which the incoming auditor verifies before accepting.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause (8) — non-payment of undisputed audit fees for a statutory audit, other than by a sick unit, is a professional reason for not accepting; undisputed audit fee is the provision in accounts signed by both plus the auditor's expenses; demand draft where the previous auditor is not available

items.scenario: Harihar Agro Industries Limited is an unlisted public company that mills rice at Raichur; it was registered seven years ago and has reported a profit in every year since. Its auditors, Bhandari & Co., resigned in July 2026, and the company has asked Desai & Kulkarni, a firm of chartered accountants, to take up the statutory audit. The engagement partner has three matters on his desk before the firm accepts. First, the firm's letter to Bhandari & Co. went by registered post acknowledgement due and the signed card has come back; Bhandari's reply says the firm has no objection to the change, but adds that its audit fee of 3 lakh rupees for the year ended 31 March 2026, provided for in accounts signed by both the company and the firm, and 40,000 rupees of travel it spent on that audit, remain unpaid. The managing director says "the fee is between them and us, and no reason to keep you out". Second, the board passed a resolution in July appointing Desai & Kulkarni and no general meeting has been held since; the managing director hands the partner a certificate he has signed saying that sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been duly complied with, and says the minute book and the meeting notices are "not for outsiders to leaf through". Third, on the first day the company transfers 9 lakh rupees to the firm's office account: 1.5 lakh rupees as an advance against the audit fee, 50,000 rupees for the filing fees and stamp paper on the annual return to be filed that week, and 7 lakh rupees to meet a customs duty demand that falls due the following March. The partner leaves the whole 9 lakh rupees in the office account.

items.stem: On the certificate alone, has the firm done what Clause 9 requires before accepting?

options.text: Yes. Clause 9 requires the auditor to ascertain compliance from the company, and a certificate signed by the managing director is the company telling him so in writing.
options.misconception: Reads "ascertain from the company" as asking the company; the module reads it as finding out for certain from the company's records.
options.why: The guidance meets this head on. A certificate handed across by management, however categorically it is worded, is not the thing the clause asks an incoming auditor to lean on; he has to open the relevant records and find out for certain himself. And the company's refusal to show the minute book and the notices is no neutral inconvenience — on its own it is a reason to decline the work.

options.text: Clause 9 does not arise. The board resolution filled a casual vacancy, and the clause is only about cases where an auditor is removed by special notice at a general meeting.
options.misconception: Limits Clause 9 to removals under section 140, when the module lists resignation as its own case with its own record to check.
options.why: Clause (9) covers every appointment as auditor of a company, and the guidance lists the records to verify for each kind: a first auditor, a casual vacancy, a resignation, a removal, and a joint auditor not reappointed. For a vacancy that arose by resignation the incoming auditor sees whether a proper resolution filling it has been passed at the general meeting, which has not happened here.

options.text: No. To ascertain is to find out for certain, so a certificate from the managing director is not sufficient; the firm must verify the records itself, and for a vacancy caused by resignation must see a proper resolution filling it passed at the general meeting. If the company will not let the records be seen, the firm should not accept.
options.why: "Ascertain" is the word the whole clause turns on, and the Council reads it strictly: to find out for certain, not to be told. An assurance signed by the managing director that the appointment provisions were followed settles nothing, because the man giving it is the man whose compliance is the question. The incoming auditor goes instead to the company's own papers and satisfies himself there. A seat vacated by resignation has its own item on that list: he looks for a resolution properly passed at the general meeting to fill it. And the guidance closes the door on the very situation facing this partner — a company that will not let him verify the records is a company whose audit he should decline. Nothing has been checked here, no general meeting has met, and the minute book is being withheld.

options.text: Yes, through Clause 8. The retiring auditor replied that it has no objection to the change, and an outgoing auditor who was not properly displaced would have objected.
options.misconception: Lets the Clause 8 communication stand in for the Clause 9 verification, which is a different question answered from a different source.
options.why: Clause 8 and Clause 9 are separate duties. The letter to the retiring auditor is how the firm learns of professional reasons for not accepting; whether the company followed sections 139 and 140 is found out for certain from the company's own records, and the retiring auditor's silence about the procedure proves nothing about it.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause (9) — "ascertain" means to find out for certain; a certificate from management is not sufficient, the incoming auditor verifies the company's records, and where the vacancy arose by resignation sees that a proper resolution filling it has been passed at the general meeting; if the company will not allow verification, do not accept

items.stem: On the 9 lakh rupees alone, which part of it had to go into a separate banking account?

options.text: None of it. Clause 10 is breached only when a member uses client money for his own purposes, and the partner has spent none of it.
options.misconception: Reads the clause as a rule against misuse only, when keeping the money apart is itself the duty.
options.why: The clause has two limbs, and failing to keep client moneys in a separate banking account is a breach on its own, before any question of misuse; the module's illustration finds misconduct where a firm merely left a client's money sitting in its own savings account. The 7 lakh rupees for a demand eight months away had to be separated immediately.

options.text: The 7 lakh rupees and the 50,000 rupees. Both are money for expenses rather than fees, and only the advance against the fee is exempt.
options.misconception: Misses the reasonably-short-time exception for expense money.
options.why: Expense money is not one single category. The Council divided it by how soon the money will go out again: a sum meant for statutory charges and stamp paper on a return being filed that same week will be gone almost immediately, and it may be left in the office account. The 50,000 rupees is precisely that sum. What has to be banked apart on arrival is money for an outgoing the firm will not make for a long while yet — here the customs demand due next March, and only the 7 lakh rupees answers that description.

options.text: All 9 lakh rupees. Every rupee a client hands to a practising member, other than a fee already earned, must go into a separate banking account the day it arrives.
options.misconception: Ignores both exceptions the Council has written into the clause.
options.why: The clause leaves fees and remuneration out on its own terms, and the Council has added that a sum paid ahead for services still to come does not engage it either. It has also said that money meant for an outgoing the firm will make almost at once may be left where it is. Between those two, the 1.5 lakh rupees advance and the 50,000 rupees for that week's filing were lawfully sitting in the office account.

options.text: Only the 7 lakh rupees for the duty demand. An advance against the fee is outside Clause 10, and money for expenses to be spent within a reasonably short time need not be separated; money for an expense eight months away goes into a separate bank account immediately.
options.why: Three different lines run through this one transfer, and the Council has drawn each of them. Money handed over ahead of work still to be done is not client money of the sort the clause governs, so the 1.5 lakh rupees against the fee never engaged it at all. Money given for an outgoing the firm will make almost at once — the filing charges and stamp paper for a return leaving that same week — may sit in the office account, since the Council saw no purpose in a separate bank account for a sum that will have gone within days. The third line is where the rule bites. Where the outgoing is not one the firm will make within a reasonably short time, the money is set aside the moment it arrives, and a customs demand falling due the following March is eight months off by any reckoning. So the advance and the 50,000 may stay where they are; the 7 lakh rupees had to be moved on the day it came in.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause (10) — client moneys other than fees go into a separate banking account; an advance against services does not fall under the clause; money for expenses to be spent within a reasonably short time need not be separated; money for expenses not to be spent within a reasonably short time goes into a separate account immediately

items.stem: On the revenue presumption alone, what does Kavya decide?

options.text: The presumption is rebutted for the distributor sales, which are simple, and kept for the institutional contracts, and the sales director's assurance about standard terms is taken as the documented reason for the first half.
options.misconception: Management's assurance can serve as the documented reason for rebutting the presumption.
options.why: Evaluating the streams separately is what the standard asks, but the reason documented for a rebuttal has to be the auditor's conclusion about the revenue, and an assurance from the director whose bonus turns on the total is a fraud risk factor rather than a reason to drop the presumption on any stream.

options.text: The presumption cannot be rebutted in any audit, so the manager's proposal is rejected on that ground alone and every stream of revenue is treated as a significant risk without further evaluation.
options.misconception: The revenue presumption is irrebuttable, like the presumption on management override.
options.why: SA 240 allows the presumption to be rebutted, and it asks the auditor to pin the risk to particular streams, particular transactions and particular assertions rather than treat all revenue alike; the answer here comes from the facts, not from an absolute rule.

options.text: The presumption stands and is worked through, not rebutted. Kavya begins where the standard makes her begin, with the presumption that there are risks of fraud in revenue recognition, and asks which of Hemavati's three streams, and which assertions inside them, carry that risk: institutional contracts with year-end rebates and rights of return, renegotiated in February 2026, sitting beside franchise fees, are nothing like the one simple kind of revenue that lets the assumption go, and a bonus payable only above 450 crore rupees hangs an incentive on the very figure being audited. It may be rebutted on reasons about the revenue itself, and the auditor must then document the reasons; a clean prior year and the sales director's word are neither. The manager's proposal fails on the facts and on the missing paper.
options.why: SA 240 does not let revenue sit inside the auditor's general risk assessment. Fraud risk in revenue is assumed before any evidence is gathered, and the work left to the auditor is to say where it lands — which stream, which transaction, which assertion. The assumption is not immovable; it may be rebutted, and the illustration the standard itself offers is an entity earning one simple kind of revenue, rent from a single property, while a tangled revenue structure or weak control over the recognition of revenue points the other way entirely. Hemavati has three streams, one of them carrying rebates and return rights renegotiated in the last quarter, so the real question is not whether bottles are exotic but which assertions in which stream are exposed; and a bonus turning on a revenue target is precisely the sort of pressure the standard names as a fraud risk factor. A clean prior year, and an assurance from the man whose bonus rides on the figure, are not conclusions about the revenue at all. Where an auditor does decide the assumption has no place on his engagement, he must document the reasons, which makes a rebuttal with nothing written down no rebuttal the standard would recognise. In short, the presumption that there are risks of fraud in revenue recognition survives here: it goes only on written reasons about the revenue, and Hemavati's streams are evaluated one by one and kept.
keywords: risks of fraud in revenue recognition

options.text: The manager's proposal is accepted. The presumption is a starting point and not a rule, the company's revenue is the sale of goods, last year's audit found nothing, and an experienced auditor's judgment that the risk is low needs no separate note.
options.misconception: The revenue presumption is rebutted by the auditor's general comfort with the client.
options.why: The presumption may be rebutted where the revenue is a single type of simple transaction, which three streams with rebates, return rights and a target-linked bonus are not; and where the auditor concludes the presumption is not applicable he shall document the reasons, so a judgment without a note does not rebut it.

citation.ref: fraud risk in revenue is assumed from the start, and the work is to say where it lands — which stream, which transaction, which assertion; the assumption can be displaced, and one simple kind of revenue is the illustration the standard itself offers, but an engagement where the auditor decides it has no place must carry his written reasons for saying so

items.scenario: Rao & Hegde are the statutory auditors of Hemavati Beverages Limited, an unlisted public company at Hassan with a revenue of 430 crore rupees from three streams: sales of bottled drinks to distributors, institutional supply contracts with hotels and canteens that carry year-end volume rebates and rights of return, and franchise fees from bottlers in two neighbouring states. Kavya Rao is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026, and the audit manager has brought her three matters in the planning memorandum. First, the manager proposes to rebut the presumption of fraud in revenue recognition, on the ground that the company sells bottles and nothing exotic, that last year's audit found nothing, and that the sales director has assured him the contracts are standard; the manager does not intend to write the reasons down. Kavya notes from the same memorandum that the sales director's bonus for the year is payable only if revenue crosses 450 crore rupees, and that the institutional contracts were renegotiated in February 2026. Second, the manager proposes to drop the testing of journal entries and other year-end adjustments, because the company's new enterprise software passed the firm's tests of general information-technology controls, the finance head has been in post for fourteen years, and the risk of management override is therefore low; he also proposes no work on the sale in March 2026 of a bottling line to a newly formed company owned by a friend of a director, with a lease of the same line back to Hemavati, because the board approved the sale and the gain of 9 crore rupees is disclosed. The finance head has asked that the matter be reported to him alone and kept from the audit committee until his own inquiry is complete in six weeks, and the manager has asked Kavya whether the firm should now withdraw from the audit.
