items.stem: On the override work alone, what does Kavya decide?

options.text: The journal-entry testing stays, but the sale needs no work because the board approved it and the gain is disclosed; a transaction that is authorised and shown in the notes cannot be a means of fraudulent reporting.
options.misconception: Board approval and disclosure take an unusual transaction outside the override procedures.
options.why: For a significant transaction outside the normal course of business the auditor evaluates whether its business rationale suggests fraudulent financial reporting or concealment; authorisation and disclosure are what override looks like from the outside and are not the rationale the procedure asks about.

options.text: The manager is right on the journal entries: SA 240 asks the auditor to assess the risk of override and respond to it, and where general controls have been tested and passed and the finance head is trusted, the assessed risk is low enough that the entries need no separate testing; the sale is looked at only as a related-party question.
options.misconception: Management override is an ordinary assessed risk that strong controls can lower below the need for procedures.
options.why: Those tests of journal entries and year-end adjustments are owed whatever the auditor makes of the override risk, because every entity carries it and the standard ranks it as significant; and the sale, sitting well outside the ordinary run of the business, is examined for whether a business reason for it holds.

options.text: Neither proposal survives. The testing of journal entries and other adjustments is performed irrespective of the auditor's assessment of the risk of override, so a passed test of general controls and a long-serving finance head do not lower it into something that can be dropped: the risk is present in all entities because management can override controls that otherwise appear to operate effectively, and it is a significant risk. The sale of the bottling line to a company formed for the purpose and owned by a director's friend, with the line leased straight back, is a significant transaction outside the normal course of business, and Kavya evaluates whether its business rationale suggests it was entered into for fraudulent financial reporting; board approval and a disclosed gain describe the transaction and do not explain it.
options.why: SA 240 treats management override unlike every other fraud risk. Whoever runs a company can rewrite what its books say and dress the statements to match, stepping over controls that look, from outside, as though they are working; every entity carries that exposure, and because it surfaces in ways nobody can predict the standard ranks it as significant. Hence three procedures that do not wait on the auditor's own rating of the risk: the entries put through the ledger and the adjustments made when the statements are drawn up are tested for whether they belong there, estimates are re-read for a management lean in one direction, and any significant transaction lying outside the ordinary course of the business, or simply looking odd, is examined to see whether a business reason for it exists and whether that reason, or its absence, points at dressed-up reporting or a covered-up theft. Strong general controls and a trusted finance head are the very things a manager overrides, so they argue for the procedures rather than against them. A production line sold to a company formed to buy it, owned by a director's friend, then leased straight back, is what the third procedure was written for, and a board minute plus a note disclosing a gain of 9 crore rupees answers neither question it asks. In short, the journal entries are tested irrespective of the auditor's assessment of the risk, and the business rationale of the sale and lease-back is evaluated.

options.text: Because the software passed the firm's tests, Kavya relies on the system's own change log as the test of journal entries, and treats the sale as a matter for the accounting of leases rather than for fraud, since the gain is computed correctly.
options.misconception: A control log substitutes for the auditor's own test of journal entries, and correct accounting settles rationale.
options.why: The procedure is a test by the auditor of the appropriateness of journal entries and other adjustments, which a system log does not perform, and the question on the sale is its business rationale, which correct accounting for the gain does not answer.

citation.ref: whoever runs a company can set its controls aside from above, so override counts as a risk every entity carries and one the standard ranks as significant; three procedures follow whatever the auditor's own rating says — the entries put through the ledger and the adjustments made when the statements are drawn up are tested for whether they belong, estimates are re-read for a management lean, and any significant transaction lying outside the ordinary course is examined for whether a business reason for it holds up

Third, during the audit the team has found that the head of institutional sales, who reports to the sales director, recorded 2.6 crore rupees of supplies to three canteens that never received them, reversing them in April 2026, and one of the three canteens has written that the sales director himself asked it to confirm the balance. items.stem: On the canteen supplies alone, what does Kavya do?

options.text: Kavya communicates now, to the audit committee as well as to management, and does not withdraw on these facts. A fraud has been identified, so it goes without delay to the appropriate level of management; and because the canteen's letter gives reason to suspect that the sales director is in it, the matter goes just as promptly to those charged with governance, and she settles with them the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures that finishing the year now calls for. The finance head's request to keep it from the audit committee for six weeks is refused, because promptness is the standard's own demand. Withdrawal is not the next step: it arises only where a fraud throws up circumstances exceptional enough to put the firm's capacity to carry on in doubt, and 2.6 crore rupees the team itself found, and can now audit around, calls for more procedures rather than for leaving.
options.why: SA 240 fixes who hears about a fraud and how fast. Once the auditor has found one, or holds information pointing at one, the right level of management hears it without delay, that being where the duty to prevent and detect fraud sits in the first place; the fictitious supplies are a fraud already found, so management is told now. The body charged with governance is a second addressee, reached whenever the suspicion runs to management, to staff carrying real weight in the control system, or to anyone else whose fraud leaves the statements materially wrong — and the only entity spared that second call is one whose governing body and management are the same people, which Hemavati is not. A canteen writing that the sales director asked it to confirm the balance is information that a fraud reaching management may exist, so the audit committee hears it now as well; and where management is the suspect the auditor also works out with the governance side the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures the discovery now demands, which here means the April reversal and the two remaining canteens. Six weeks of silence at the finance head's request would surrender the promptness the standard insists on and would confine a suspected management fraud to management. Withdrawal answers a different question on a different trigger: the fraud has to raise circumstances so exceptional that the firm's capacity to keep auditing is itself in doubt, and only then does the auditor settle his professional and legal position, weigh withdrawal where the law permits it, and, if he goes, explain his reasons to management and to the governance side and decide whether anyone else must be told. Nothing here yet puts that capacity in doubt. In short, Kavya reports the fraud promptly to the appropriate level of management and, management being suspected, to those charged with governance, agrees with them the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures still needed, and stays on the engagement.
keywords: nature, timing and extent of audit procedures

options.text: Kavya withdraws from the engagement, because a fraud that reaches a director means the firm can no longer rely on any representation from management, and SA 240 requires the auditor to step away once management is implicated.
options.misconception: Suspected fraud involving management requires the auditor to withdraw.
options.why: Leaving is reached only where the fraud throws up circumstances exceptional enough to put the firm's capacity to carry on in doubt, and even then it is weighed, where the law permits, after the auditor's own responsibilities are settled; what suspecting management actually requires is telling those charged with governance and agreeing with them the further work the audit now needs.

options.text: Because the entries were reversed in April 2026 and the year-end figures are now right, there is nothing to communicate; Kavya records the matter in the working papers and raises it, if at all, in the management letter after the report is signed.
options.misconception: A fraud that has been reversed and does not misstate the year-end figures needs no communication.
options.why: The duty to communicate is triggered by identifying a fraud or information that one may exist, whatever its effect on the final figures, and it is owed on a timely basis to the appropriate level of management and, where management is suspected, to those charged with governance; a reversal after the year end is part of what those charged with governance are told, not a reason to say nothing.

options.text: The finance head's request is accepted: management is the appropriate level for a fraud by an employee, the audit committee is told once the company's own inquiry has established the facts, and an unproven suspicion about a director is not something the auditor puts before the board.
options.misconception: Those charged with governance are told only once a fraud involving management is proved.
options.why: Where the auditor suspects fraud involving management he shall communicate to those charged with governance on a timely basis and discuss with them the procedures needed to complete the audit; the standard is triggered by suspicion and information, not by a concluded inquiry, and a six-week delay is not timely.

citation.ref: a fraud found, or information pointing at one, goes promptly to the right level of management; where the suspicion runs to management itself, to staff carrying real weight in the control system, or to anyone else whose fraud leaves the statements materially wrong, the body charged with governance is told promptly as well, unless every one of its members already runs the entity, and a suspicion about management is talked through with them so far as it changes the audit work still needed; leaving the engagement is a separate question, reached only when the fraud raises circumstances so exceptional that carrying on is itself in doubt, and then the auditor settles his professional and legal position, weighs withdrawal where the law permits it, and on going explains why to management and to the governance side and decides whether anyone else must be told

items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on whether the report is owed at all and how its parts are made up. The indicators and the mapping to the nine principles are noise for this one. On the reach of the report and its parts alone, what does Vasudha conclude?

options.text: None of the three positions holds. What triggers the report is where a company ranks by size at the time, and Indravati now sits inside the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, so it is caught this year; nothing gives a newcomer a settling-in period, and the one free pass the market was handed belonged to an earlier year altogether. Reporting has been mandatory from financial year 2022-23 for whoever the size test catches. Nor are the parts of the return interchangeable. One part describes the company; a second asks how the company is run, which is where the board's oversight and the policies behind it are answered; the third carries the principle-wise performance disclosures. Collapsing the second into the first wipes out a prescribed part, and the subsidiaries, associates and headcount describe the company, so they belong in the opening part and not among the principle-wise performance disclosures.
options.why: Start with who has to file. The obligation was written as a test of size and it is applied afresh every year: a company inside the largest thousand by market value files, a company outside it does not, and there is nothing in between that lets a first-timer take a year to settle in. Indravati is inside the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation for the year under review, so it files. The free year the secretary has in mind was a one-off, handed to the whole market when the new format arrived, and it had run out well before this year opened — the reporting has been mandatory from financial year 2022-23. Now the build of the return. Its three parts are told apart by what goes inside them, not by the order they are printed in. The opening part is the description of the business: what it sells, where it works, how many people it employs, and which companies sit above and below it in the group. The middle part is about stewardship — the policies, who owns them, and how the board keeps watch. The last part is the principle-wise performance disclosures, measured against the nine principles. Each of the committee's rearrangements carries material over one of those lines, and a reader setting Indravati beside a competitor would find neither piece where the form promises it. In short, Indravati is inside the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, the reporting has been mandatory from financial year 2022-23, and a description of the group has no business sitting among the principle-wise performance disclosures.
keywords: top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation

options.text: Only the subsidiaries and the headcount need moving back. Folding the policy and oversight questions into the opening part does no harm, because how a company manages itself is a general fact about the company in any event.
options.misconception: Treating the word general as a bin that will take any disclosure not tied to a numbered principle, when the opening part has a settled content of its own.
options.why: It is not. The return keeps what the business is apart from how the business is run, because the two answer different questions and different readers go hunting for them. The subsidiaries and the headcount do have to go back, but so do the policy and oversight answers, and that is the larger of the two corrections.

options.text: The two-part draft will do. The parts are a recommended running order, and a company that answers every question put to it does not become non-compliant by gathering the policy and oversight answers under a heading of its own choosing.
options.misconception: Reading a prescribed return as though it were a narrative report, where the headings are the author's to choose, rather than a form whose parts are fixed so that two companies can be compared.
options.why: Order is not what defines them; content is. A separate part exists for stewardship so that any reader can find a company's policies and its board's watch in the same named place in every report filed. The reason the return is fixed at all is so that one company's answers can be set beside another's, and that collapses at the first company allowed to rename the parts.

options.text: Indravati has a free year. The format was voluntary in the year it first appeared, and the same concession begins afresh for each company in the year it first enters the list.
options.misconception: Turning a one-off transitional year into a rolling entitlement, so that every company newly crossing a threshold collects a grace period of its own.
options.why: The concession was a single transitional year given to the market as a whole when the format changed. It was never written as a personal allowance travelling with each new entrant. From the following year onwards the filing is compulsory for whoever the size test catches in that year, and a company that has only just crossed the line is caught in the year it crosses it.

citation.source: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
citation.ref: Regulation 34(2)(f), as amended in 2019 to carry business responsibility reporting into the annual reports of the thousand largest listed entities by market capitalisation, and the SEBI notification of 5 May 2021 that replaced that report with the BRSR and settled its parts.

items.scenario: Kanitkar & Bhagat are a firm of chartered accountants at Raipur, and Vasudha Kanitkar is the partner asked to review the first business responsibility and sustainability report of Indravati Alloys Limited, a listed maker of ferro-alloys, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the fortnight before the annual report is signed. First, whether the report is owed at all and how it is built. Indravati stands within the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation and entered that list only this year, having sat outside it until now; the company secretary's note argues that a first year inside the list is a voluntary year, in the way the whole market once had a voluntary year, and that the report may therefore be filed as a courtesy. The draft itself has two sections rather than three: the questions on the company's policies, its governance and the oversight its board exercises have been folded into the opening section of general details, which the ESG committee says reads better, and the list of subsidiary and associate companies together with the headcount of permanent and contract workers has been moved out of that opening section and placed inside the principle-wise part under the employees principle. Second, which disclosures the company was obliged to make. The draft leaves out the energy consumed, the emissions released, the water drawn and the waste handled at two of the four furnaces, and it leaves out the number of workers put through safety training during the year, the ESG committee having decided that plant-level environmental figures and training counts are optional detail. In their place the draft carries a forty-page life cycle assessment of one alloy grade and a long note on the biodiversity around the mine lease, both of which the committee told the board were compulsory and both of which took a full quarter to assemble. The chief financial officer has concluded from the exercise that the company should stop producing material of that kind next year. Third, how activities have been mapped to the principles. Indravati belongs to three industry chambers and has sent the state government written comments on a draft rule about slag disposal, and the draft reports both under the principle on inclusive growth and equitable development. The company has redesigned its packaging so that a buyer can tell a dust-prone grade from a safe one and now prints handling, reuse and disposal instructions in three languages, and the draft reports that under the environment principle. A footnote to the section says the nine principles divide four to the environmental component, three to the social and two to the governance. Vasudha has to settle all three before she signs anything.

items.stem: QUESTION 2 OF 3 — turns on which of the draft's disclosures were compulsory and which were optional. The reach of the report and the mapping to the nine principles are noise for this one. On the indicators alone, what does Vasudha conclude?

options.text: Nothing has gone wrong. Both halves are disclosures the company chose to make, and a company that publishes a full assessment of a product and a study of the wildlife around its lease has plainly gone beyond the minimum, whatever it left out of the furnace numbers.
options.misconception: Judging a report by its bulk instead of by whether the compulsory items are inside it — the same error as writing at length on an optional question and leaving the compulsory one blank.
options.why: Doing more is not the same as doing what was asked. One half of the section is compulsory and the other is not, and a report missing the compulsory half is short however long the rest of it runs. A reader of a fixed form is owed the compulsory figures by every company that files, and nothing else in the report stands in for them.

options.text: The furnace numbers may be left out. Plant-level environmental data becomes compulsory only where the plant matters to the company as a whole, and half the furnaces is not the whole company.
options.misconception: Carrying the financial statement notion of materiality into a fixed disclosure form, which exists precisely so that the preparer does not choose what counts.
options.why: No filter of that kind exists in the split. The compulsory side is compulsory as a class, and plant environmental data is named inside it. A fixed form exists so that a reader need not rely on the preparer's view of what was worth reporting, and a plant-by-plant materiality test would hand exactly that judgement back to the preparer.

options.text: The quarter went the wrong way round. Furnace-level energy, emissions, water and waste figures, and the headcount put through safety training, are of the sort required on a mandatory basis, so dropping two furnaces and the training number is a hole in the compulsory half of the section rather than a saving on optional detail — and a figure covering half a plant can be set beside no other company's. Life cycle assessments and extra biodiversity work sit on the optional side, so the committee spent a quarter on what it was free to postpone while the compulsory numbers went missing. The chief financial officer then errs in the opposite direction, because a listed company is asked to endeavour to report the leadership indicators, not to drop them.
options.why: Every principle's performance measures are split in two, and which side a figure falls on decides whether it may be left out at all. The compulsory side is required on a mandatory basis, and the module's own worked examples of it are precisely what the committee waved away as detail: how many workers were trained in the year, and the plant numbers for energy, emissions, water and waste. Reporting half the furnaces also defeats the point of having a fixed form, which is to produce figures that line up against other companies, other sectors and earlier years; half a plant lines up against nothing. On the optional side the module puts life cycle assessments and further biodiversity work, so the heaviest lifting in the draft was the lifting that could have waited. Optional is not the same as unwanted, though. A listed company is asked to endeavour to report the leadership indicators as well, so the cure for a misspent quarter is to get the compulsory half in first rather than to give up the other half. In short, the furnace and training numbers were required on a mandatory basis, life cycle assessments were not, and Indravati should still endeavour to report the leadership indicators next year.
keywords: endeavour to report the leadership indicators

options.text: The chief financial officer is right to stop. What is optional is optional, dropping it costs the company nothing, and the hours are better spent on the compulsory half.
options.misconception: Reading voluntary as discouraged rather than as encouraged but not compelled, which is the ordinary sense of the word in a reporting framework.
options.why: Half right, and wrong in the half that matters. The hours should indeed go to the compulsory side first. But the module does not treat the optional side as spare — it asks companies to attempt it too — and a company that publicly abandons it after a single year tells its investors something it may not have meant to say.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — how the BRSR divides its principle-wise measures into a compulsory class and an optional one, what the module places on each side, what it says about attempting the optional side, and why the form is standardised.

items.stem: QUESTION 3 OF 3 — turns on how the draft has mapped three matters to the nine principles. The reach of the report and the indicators are noise for this one. On the nine principles alone, what does Vasudha conclude?

options.text: All three are wrong. Sitting on industry bodies and writing to the state government about a draft rule is advocacy, and advocacy has a principle of its own — influence on public and regulatory policy — which points a company down exactly this road, naming trade groups and industry chambers as the vehicles to use. Telling a buyer how to handle a grade, reuse it and get rid of it safely is something owed to the customer, so it belongs with the consumer principle and not with the environmental one. And the footnote has the arithmetic backwards: Environment takes two of the nine, Social three and Governance four.
options.why: Each of the three has a home the module names. The advocacy principle begins from the plain fact that a company works inside rules somebody else writes, and its core elements send a company that wants a say towards collective bodies — trade groups and industry chambers — as the proper road. Indravati's memberships and its letter to the state government are that activity and nothing else, so they sit under influence on public and regulatory policy. Inclusive growth is a different subject: what a company's activities do to the social, cultural and economic life of the people near it, land taken, families moved, communities on the margin, where the CSR money goes. The packaging is different again. Warning a buyer which grade throws dust, and telling him how to reuse it and dispose of it, is the consumer principle at work, since that principle asks a company to teach its customers safe handling and safe disposal. The environmental principle looks inward instead, at what the company itself consumes and spoils, and the fact that the environment gains here too does not move the disclosure across. The footnote's count is simply reversed. In short, the chamber work falls under influence on public and regulatory policy, the principle that names trade groups and industry chambers as the road to take, and Environment takes two of the nine, Social three and Governance four.
keywords: influence on public and regulatory policy
Environment takes two of the nine

options.text: The footnote is right and only the two mappings need correcting. The environmental component holds the largest share of the nine, because the environment is where sustainability reporting started.
options.misconception: Assuming that because ESG is talked about as an environmental subject, the environmental component must hold the most principles, when the framework puts its weight on governance.
options.why: The count runs the other way about. Environment takes two of the nine, Social three and Governance four, so governance holds the largest share — which is itself a signal about what the framework thinks drives the other two.

options.text: The packaging belongs under the environmental principle. Instructions that lead to reuse and safe disposal cut waste, and cutting waste is environmental.
options.misconception: Sorting a disclosure by the outcome it produces rather than by the relationship it governs, which ends with every good thing a company does filed under the environment.
options.why: The environmental principle does reach reuse and recycling, but as things a company does about its own consumption and its own mess. What Indravati has done is teach a customer how to use a product and get rid of it safely, which the module writes into the consumer principle. The test is which relationship the disclosure is about, not which good outcome happens to fall out of it.

options.text: The memberships and the letter are correctly placed. Industry bodies exist to raise a whole industry, and raising a whole industry is inclusive growth and equitable development.
options.misconception: Reading the word inclusive as covering anything that benefits more than one party, when the principle is aimed at the communities a business affects.
options.why: Inclusive growth in the module is about people rather than industries — what a company's own operations do to the communities around it, whom it displaces, whom it leaves out, and how it picks where its CSR money goes. Talking to government through a trade body has a principle of its own, and the collective bodies are named inside that one.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the nine principles of the NGRBC, how many of them fall to each ESG component, the principle on advocacy through collective bodies, and the principle on what a buyer is told about using and disposing of a product.

items.scenario: Kanitkar & Bhagat are a firm of chartered accountants at Raipur, and Vasudha Kanitkar is the partner asked to review the first business responsibility and sustainability report of Indravati Alloys Limited, a listed maker of ferro-alloys, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the fortnight before the annual report is signed. First, whether the report is owed at all and how it is built. Indravati stands within the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation and entered that list only this year, having sat outside it until now; the company secretary's note argues that a first year inside the list is a voluntary year, in the way the whole market once had a voluntary year, and that the report may therefore be filed as a courtesy. The draft itself has two sections rather than three: the questions on the company's policies, its governance and the oversight its board exercises have been folded into the opening section of general details, which the ESG committee says reads better, and the list of subsidiary and associate companies together with the headcount of permanent and contract workers has been moved out of that opening section and placed inside the principle-wise part under the employees principle. Second, which disclosures the company was obliged to make. The draft leaves out the energy consumed, the emissions released, the water drawn and the waste handled at two of the four furnaces, and it leaves out the number of workers put through safety training during the year, the ESG committee having decided that plant-level environmental figures and training counts are optional detail. In their place the draft carries a forty-page life cycle assessment of one alloy grade and a long note on the biodiversity around the mine lease, both of which the committee told the board were compulsory and both of which took a full quarter to assemble. The chief financial officer has concluded from the exercise that the company should stop producing material of that kind next year. Third, how activities have been mapped to the principles. Indravati belongs to three industry chambers and has sent the state government written comments on a draft rule about slag disposal, and the draft reports both under the principle on inclusive growth and equitable development. The company has redesigned its packaging so that a buyer can tell a dust-prone grade from a safe one and now prints handling, reuse and disposal instructions in three languages, and the draft reports that under the environment principle. A footnote to the section says the nine principles divide four to the environmental component, three to the social and two to the governance. Vasudha has to settle all three before she signs anything.

items.stem: On the drawing power sheet alone, what is the drawing power Sunita works with?

options.text: The lead bank's 31 crore rupees, and the account is 7 crore rupees over it. In a consortium the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on member banks, so the branch's own sheet does not govern; and the sheet is wrong on its own terms in any case, because drawing power is calculated net of stipulated margin on stock from which sundry creditors for goods and stock covered by the bank's letters of credit are excluded, and on book debts net of the bills discounted with the bank, none of which the branch deducted.
options.why: The module gives four rules for the sheet and the branch broke all four. The starting document is the sanction letter, which carries the bank's own credit policy, and the figure is only struck once the margin stipulated there has been taken off — so gross stock and gross debtors give a limit the borrower never had. Next, stock the borrower still owes its suppliers for, and stock the bank has itself financed through a letter of credit, cannot be counted as cover: a declared stock figure may not stand as security for a liability the borrower carries as sundry creditors for goods, nor for what the bank has already paid for once. That strips 14 crore rupees and 6 crore rupees out of the 52 crore rupees before any margin is applied. Where the facility is against book debts, the net value of debtors is arrived at as eligible trade debtors per the sanction less bills discounted with banks, so the 6 crore rupees already discounted comes off the 18 crore rupees. And because the account is in a consortium, the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on member banks: the branch does not get to compute a friendlier figure, and its 45 crore rupees gives way to the 31 crore rupees allocated to it. Against that the outstanding of 38 crore rupees is over the drawing power by 7 crore rupees, which is the fact the rest of the advances work starts from. In short, drawing power is net of stipulated margin, sundry creditors for goods and stock under the bank's letters of credit do not count, book debts are net of bills discounted, and the lead bank's allocation binds the branch.

options.text: The branch's 45 crore rupees. The sanction fixes the margins and the branch has applied them to the borrower's own declared figures; what the borrower owes its suppliers is a matter for the balance sheet, not for the security cover.
options.misconception: Treats unpaid-for stock as security for the bank that financed it.
options.why: Stock a borrower has not yet paid its suppliers for, and stock the bank financed under its own letter of credit, cannot stand as cover for that same bank; a book-debts figure is taken after the bills already discounted come off; and where several banks lend together the leader's computation and allocation binds each member, so the branch's own figure does not govern even on the occasions when it happens to be right.

options.text: Sunita's own recomputation from the corrected figures, whatever it comes to. A member bank is not bound by the lead bank's arithmetic and the branch auditor reports the drawing power the sanction supports on the evidence she has examined.
options.misconception: Makes the branch auditor a second lead bank.
options.why: The module states that in the case of consortium accounts the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on member banks; the auditor tests the branch's adherence to that allocation rather than substituting a figure of her own.

options.text: The sanctioned limit of 40 crore rupees, because drawing power is a monitoring figure and an account is irregular only when the outstanding exceeds the limit itself.
options.misconception: Collapses drawing power into the sanctioned limit.
options.why: The module requires all accounts to be kept within both the drawing power and the sanctioned limit, and lists accounts that exceed the drawing power among those to be examined; the limit is a ceiling and the drawing power is the security-backed figure beneath it, and the lower governs.

citation.ref: what fixes a borrower's drawing power — the document it is read out of, the deduction that comes off before it is struck, the stock that cannot be pledged twice because it is still owed for or already financed by the bank's own credit, what is taken out of a book-debts figure, and whose computation governs where several banks lend together

items.scenario: Rathi & Deshmukh are the statutory branch auditors of the Hosur industrial branch of Dakshin Vaibhav Bank Limited, a branch with advances of 1,240 crore rupees, and Sunita Rathi is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three things come out of the branch's returns. First, the largest borrower, Kabini Alloys Private Limited, has a cash credit limit of 40 crore rupees in a consortium led by another bank, with a margin of 25 per cent on stock and 40 per cent on book debts; the branch's drawing power sheet takes the gross stock of 52 crore rupees and gross book debts of 18 crore rupees and arrives at 45 crore rupees, without deducting sundry creditors for goods of 14 crore rupees, stock of 6 crore rupees procured under the bank's own letters of credit, or 6 crore rupees of the debts already discounted with the bank, while the lead bank's allocation to this branch works out at 31 crore rupees against an outstanding of 38 crore rupees. Second, the branch's list of outstanding guarantees of 96 crore rupees includes 11 crore rupees of guarantees that expired during the year and were never marked off in the register, a guarantee of 5 crore rupees for Kabini Alloys that the state electricity board invoked in March and the branch paid in April but still shows as contingent, and its bills for collection of 23 crore rupees include 9 crore rupees of bills that another branch of the same bank sent it for collection. Third, an instalment on Kabini Alloys' term loan at the branch has been overdue for 110 days at the year end, and a letter of credit that devolved in February sits in a separate "LC devolvement" account of 3 crore rupees; the branch has classified the term loan as non-performing and kept the cash credit and the devolvement account standard, "because those two are being serviced".

items.stem: On the guarantee list and the bills alone, what does Sunita change?

options.text: All 96 crore rupees of guarantees should be provided for in full, because once one guarantee has been invoked the bank's exposure on the rest is no longer remote, and the bills stay as they are.
options.misconception: Lets one invocation reprice every guarantee on the list.
options.why: The module's AS 29 consideration attaches to a guarantee on which a claim has arisen, not to the whole head; the remaining guarantees are disclosed as contingent after expired ones are excluded, and bills from other branches of the bank still come out of bills for collection.

options.text: Only the expired guarantees. An invoked guarantee stays contingent until the bank's liability is finally settled with the customer, and bills for collection are shown at the branch that physically holds the bills, whichever branch they came from.
options.misconception: Keeps a paid claim contingent and counts a bill at every branch that touches it.
options.why: The module says that where a claim has arisen the auditor considers whether a provision is required under AS 29, and the payment in April shows the claim was good; and it says bills drawn on other branches of the bank are not included in bills for collection so that they are not taken twice in the amalgamated balance sheet.

options.text: Nothing on the guarantees, because a branch auditor reports the register as it stands and the central statutory auditors reconcile the head; only the 9 crore rupees of bills needs reversing at the branch.
options.misconception: Hands the branch auditor's own procedures to the central auditors.
options.why: The module places the examination of the guarantee register, the exclusion of expired guarantees and the AS 29 consideration on the auditor verifying the branch's contingent liabilities; a branch auditor who reports the register as it stands passes a known error up to be consolidated.

options.text: Three things. The 11 crore rupees of expired guarantees come out of the head, because the auditor examines that expired guarantees are not included and the register is to be marked off. The invoked guarantee of 5 crore rupees is no longer only contingent: a claim has arisen, so she considers whether a provision is required under AS 29, and the April payment settles that it is. And the 9 crore rupees of bills sent by another branch of the same bank come out of bills for collection, because bills drawn on other branches of the bank are not included there and would be counted twice in the amalgamated balance sheet.
options.why: Each of the three entries meets a different step in the branch's off-balance-sheet work. The guarantee register is where the first one is settled: she looks for evidence that this branch really does mark a guarantee off once its life has run out, ties the register back to the list still live so that nothing outstanding has gone missing, and keeps expired guarantees out of the head altogether — which is what takes the 11 crore rupees off it. The invoked guarantee changes character rather than amount. Once a claim has been made against the bank, AS 29 governs, and the question she has to put to herself is whether a provision is required; the electricity board invoked in March, the branch paid in April, and that payment tells her the obligation already existed at the year end. So the 5 crore rupees is provided for, not disclosed as a contingency. The bills are a double-counting rule. A branch may not carry, inside its own bills for collection, paper drawn on other branches of the bank; and where one branch has sent bills to a second for collection, the amalgamated balance sheet must not finish by showing them at both, the receiving branch reversing those entries at the year end for closing purposes. The 9 crore rupees therefore drops out here, because the sending branch is already carrying it. In short, expired guarantees are not included, a claim that has arisen makes her consider whether a provision is required under AS 29, and bills from other branches of the bank are not included in bills for collection.

citation.ref: the work on guarantees given for constituents — keeping ones that have run out off the head, proving the register against the outstanding list, and what a claim already made turns a guarantee into under AS 29; and the two traps that would show one bill for collection at two branches of the same bank

Three things come out of the branch's returns. Second, the branch's list of outstanding guarantees of 96 crore rupees includes 11 crore rupees of guarantees that expired during the year and were never marked off in the register, a guarantee of 5 crore rupees for Kabini Alloys that the state electricity board invoked in March and the branch paid in April but still shows as contingent, and its bills for collection of 23 crore rupees include 9 crore rupees of bills that another branch of the same bank sent it for collection. Third, an instalment on Kabini Alloys' term loan at the branch has been overdue for 110 days at the year end, and a letter of credit that devolved in February sits in a separate "LC devolvement" account of 3 crore rupees; the branch has classified the term loan as non-performing and kept the cash credit and the devolvement account standard, "because those two are being serviced".

items.stem: On the classification alone, is the branch right to keep the cash credit and the devolvement account standard?

options.text: Yes, provided the branch reviews the classification again at the next quarter, because the term loan itself has only just crossed the ninety-day line and the borrower-wise rule applies once an account has stayed non-performing for a full quarter.
options.misconception: Invents a grace quarter before the borrower-wise rule bites.
options.why: The module's rule that classification is borrower wise carries no waiting period; it applies as soon as one facility is non-performing, and the classification is made as per the position on the balance sheet date, with all the facilities to the borrower treated as NPA from then.

options.text: No. Asset classification is borrower wise and not facility wise, so once the term loan is non-performing all the facilities granted to Kabini Alloys are treated as NPA, the cash credit included, however well that account is being serviced. And the devolved letter of credit kept in a separate account is not a standard asset of its own: the outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms, so it takes the borrower's classification and its provisioning too.
options.why: The module answers both halves of the branch's argument in one passage. The auditor is to ensure that asset classification is borrower wise and not facility wise; once one account goes bad, all the facilities standing in that borrower's name at the bank turn non-performing with it, not merely the one that fell irregular. The term loan has an instalment overdue for 110 days at the year end, which makes it non-performing, and the borrower's other facilities follow it; a cash credit that is within limit and being operated does not stand apart, because the rule looks at the borrower's ability to service the bank as a whole and a borrower who cannot pay a term loan instalment is not a standard borrower in another ledger. The module continues that if debits arising out of devolvement of letters of credit or invoked guarantees are kept in a separate account, the outstanding balance should be treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the purpose of application of the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. The 3 crore rupees the bank paid on the borrower's behalf in February is money owed by the borrower, parked under a different name; it is added to the borrower's account and classified, recognised and provided with it. The branch's reason, that the two accounts are being serviced, is the facility-wise view the rule exists to exclude. In short, classification is borrower wise, all the facilities to the borrower become NPA with the term loan, and the devolved letter of credit is part of the borrower's principal account.

options.text: Yes for both. Each facility has its own repayment terms and its own record of recovery, and a cash credit that is within limit and in operation is by definition not out of order; the devolvement account is a fresh advance with no overdue of its own.
options.misconception: Classifies each account on its own conduct.
options.why: The module requires classification to be borrower wise and not facility wise, so all the facilities granted to the borrower are treated as NPA and not only the one that became irregular; and a devolved letter of credit kept in a separate account is treated as part of the borrower's principal account, not as a fresh advance.

options.text: No for the cash credit, yes for the devolvement account. The borrower-wise rule carries the cash credit down with the term loan, but a devolved letter of credit is a contingent liability that crystallised and is disclosed rather than classified.
options.misconception: Leaves a paid-out letter of credit on the off-balance-sheet side.
options.why: The module says that debits arising out of devolvement of letters of credit kept in a separate account are treated as part of the borrower's principal account for asset classification, income recognition and provisioning; once the bank has paid, the amount is an advance to the borrower and no longer a contingent liability.

citation.ref: asset classification is borrower wise and not facility wise, so all the facilities granted by a bank to a borrower are treated as NPA and not only the particular facility that has become irregular; where debits arising out of devolvement of a letter of credit or an invoked guarantee are kept in a separate account, the outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning

Second, the branch's list of outstanding guarantees of 96 crore rupees includes 11 crore rupees of guarantees that expired during the year and were never marked off in the register, a guarantee of 5 crore rupees for Kabini Alloys that the state electricity board invoked in March and the branch paid in April but still shows as contingent, and its bills for collection of 23 crore rupees include 9 crore rupees of bills that another branch of the same bank sent it for collection. Third, an instalment on Kabini Alloys' term loan at the branch has been overdue for 110 days at the year end, and a letter of credit that devolved in February sits in a separate "LC devolvement" account of 3 crore rupees; the branch has classified the term loan as non-performing and kept the cash credit and the devolvement account standard, "because those two are being serviced".

items.stem: On the Bhavani Rice Mills account alone, is the branch right to show it as regular, and what does the auditor do?

options.text: Yes. Drawing power is the bank's own computation on its own sanction terms, and the branch auditor checks only that the arithmetic from the statement on file is right
options.misconception: confines the auditor to checking the branch's arithmetic, when the module asks him to test the basis of the drawing power including the age of the statement
options.why: Recomputing the drawing power from the latest stock and book-debt statement is part of the auditor's own work on advances — net of the stipulated margin, net of creditors for goods, net of bills discounted against book debts — and the age of the statement is the first thing that computation tests. An auditor who checks the arithmetic of a four-month-old statement has verified the branch's sum and not the borrower's security, and the module's three-month rule is written for exactly that gap.

options.text: Yes. The outstanding has stayed within the drawing power all year and every stock statement on file supports it, so the account is regular
options.misconception: treats a drawing power computed once as valid until replaced, when the module ties its validity to the age of the stock statement it rests on
options.why: The drawing power on file was computed from a statement dated 30 November 2025, and the module is direct that statements relied upon for drawing power should not be older than three months, with an outstanding based on an older one considered irregular. A limit that rests on stock nobody has declared for four months is not a limit the borrower has today; the stock may have been sold, pledged or eaten by creditors for goods since. Staying under a stale figure proves nothing about the security now.

options.text: No. A drawing power worked out from a stock statement older than three months does not make the outstanding regular, so the account is irregular; the auditor calls for the latest stock statement, recomputes the drawing power, and does not classify the account as NPA merely for this deficiency while it is temporary
options.why: The module holds two rules side by side. A bank should not classify an advance as NPA merely because of a deficiency that is temporary in nature, and it names drawing power not being available on the latest stock statement as one of those deficiencies. But the stock statements a bank relies on for drawing power should not be older than three months, and an outstanding based on a drawing power calculated from a statement older than three months is considered irregular. Bhavani's statement is four months old at the year end, so the 2.55 crore rupees is irregular whatever the branch's returns say — being inside a stale figure is not being inside a drawing power. What the auditor does is what the deficiency asks for: obtain the latest statement, recompute the drawing power net of margin and creditors for goods, and judge the account on that. Irregular is the finding; NPA is not, unless the recomputed figure or the conduct of the account takes it there.

options.text: No. A stock statement more than three months old means the security cannot be verified at all, so the account is classified NPA from the day the statement went stale
options.misconception: turns every irregularity into an NPA, when the module keeps a temporary deficiency and non-performance apart
options.why: The module says the opposite in terms: a bank should not classify an account as NPA merely due to deficiencies which are temporary in nature, and it lists non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement as one. A stale statement makes the outstanding irregular and sends the auditor to get a fresh one; it does not on its own crystallise a date of NPA. The account becomes non-performing on the conduct of the account, not on the age of a piece of paper.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — accounts with temporary deficiencies; stock statements relied on for drawing power not to be older than three months, and an outstanding based on an older one treated as irregular

items.scenario: Kaveri Bank is a nationalised bank, and Rao & Bhat are the statutory branch auditors of its Hosur industrial branch for the year ended 31 March 2026. Advances at the branch are 96 crore rupees and three matters stand out from the review. First, Bhavani Rice Mills holds a cash credit limit of 3 crore rupees against stock and book debts. The latest stock statement on the branch file is dated 30 November 2025, the drawing power of 2.7 crore rupees was worked out from it, and the outstanding of 2.55 crore rupees has stayed within that figure all year, so the branch's returns show the account as regular. Second, Deccan Forgings has a term loan of 5 crore rupees whose instalment due on 15 December 2025 is still unpaid, and a cash credit of 2 crore rupees that has run within its limit with regular credits all year; a letter of credit opened for Deccan devolved in February 2026 and the 40 lakh rupees the branch paid under it sits in a separate account. The branch has classified the term loan alone as non-performing. Third, a loan of 4 crore rupees to a housing scheme carrying a guarantee of the Central Government has been overdue since August 2025; the branch has not invoked the guarantee, has kept the account standard, and has credited 32 lakh rupees of interest on it to income for the year.

items.stem: The branch has classified Deccan Forgings' term loan alone as non-performing. How do Deccan's facilities stand at 31 March 2026?

options.text: All of Deccan's facilities are non-performing from 31 March 2026, the date on which the auditor found the overdue instalment
options.misconception: dates the NPA from the audit rather than from the day the ninety days ran out, which moves the provision and the income reversal
options.why: The facilities are all non-performing, but the date is wrong, and the date decides the provision and the reversal of income. The account became non-performing when the instalment had stayed overdue for more than ninety days, which is in March 2026 counted from 15 December 2025, not on the day of the auditor's visit or the balance sheet date. The module asks the auditor to verify that the bank's system crystallises the date of NPA accurately and to compare the date of NPA with the previous year's; an NPA dated by discovery rather than by default is exactly what that check is for.

options.text: The term loan is non-performing and the cash credit stays standard, since it has run within its limit with regular credits and each facility is judged on its own conduct
options.misconception: classifies facility by facility on each account's own conduct, when the module requires the borrower's facilities to move together
options.why: This is the branch's classification and it is the one the module names as wrong. Asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise; all the facilities granted to a borrower are treated as NPA when one of them becomes irregular. The cash credit's regular credits are a fact about that account's operations, and the norm is deliberately blind to them: a borrower in default on one facility is a borrower whose every exposure carries the doubt.

options.text: Both facilities are non-performing, and the 40 lakh rupees stays as a separate standard account because a devolved letter of credit is a crystallised contingent liability, not an advance
options.misconception: keeps a devolved letter of credit outside the borrower's classification because it sits in a separate account, when the module folds it into the principal account
options.why: Half right, and the half that is wrong is the half the separate account was designed to hide. The module says in terms that debits arising out of the devolvement of a letter of credit or invoked guarantees kept in a separate account are treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the purpose of the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. The money the branch paid under Deccan's letter of credit is money Deccan owes the bank; it takes the classification of Deccan, which is non-performing.

options.text: All of Deccan's facilities are non-performing — the term loan, the cash credit and the 40 lakh rupees of the devolved letter of credit — because classification is borrower-wise and the separate account is part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms
options.why: A term loan whose instalment has stayed unpaid for more than ninety days is non-performing, and the 15 December instalment is more than a hundred days overdue at the year end. The module then asks the auditor to ensure that asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise: all the facilities granted by a bank to a borrower have to be treated as NPA, not only the particular facility that has become irregular. The cash credit's good conduct does not rescue it — it belongs to a borrower who cannot service his term loan. And the module adds the point the branch's bookkeeping hides: where debits arising from the devolvement of a letter of credit or an invoked guarantee are kept in a separate account, the outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. So the 40 lakh rupees is an NPA balance of Deccan's, not a standalone entry.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — asset classification to be borrower-wise and not facility-wise; debits from a devolved letter of credit kept in a separate account treated as part of the borrower's principal account

Second, Deccan Forgings has a term loan of 5 crore rupees whose instalment due on 15 December 2025 is still unpaid, and a cash credit of 2 crore rupees that has run within its limit with regular credits all year; a letter of credit opened for Deccan devolved in February 2026 and the 40 lakh rupees the branch paid under it sits in a separate account. Third, a loan of 4 crore rupees to a housing scheme carrying a guarantee of the Central Government has been overdue since August 2025; the branch has not invoked the guarantee, has kept the account standard, and has credited 32 lakh rupees of interest on it to income for the year.

items.stem: The housing scheme loan is guaranteed by the Central Government, has been overdue since August 2025, and the guarantee has not been invoked. What is the auditor's position on its classification, on the 32 lakh rupees of interest, and on his report?

options.text: The account is non-performing, with the interest reversed and provision made, because it has been overdue for more than ninety days and the guarantee has not been invoked
options.misconception: applies the ninety-day rule to a Central Government guaranteed advance, when the module reserves NPA status for repudiation of the guarantee
options.why: Ninety days of arrears is the general rule, and an advance carrying the Centre's guarantee is lifted out of it: what turns such a facility bad is a refusal by the guarantor after being called on, not the passing of time. Leaving the guarantee uncalled gives the auditor something to ask about and something to write into the LFAR; it is not the event that makes the account non-performing. Had the guarantor been a State Government this answer would have been right, since that lifting-out was never extended to the States — but the promise here is the Centre's.

options.text: The account becomes non-performing on the day the bank invokes the guarantee, so the auditor insists that the branch invoke it now and classify the account from that date
options.misconception: makes invocation the event that creates the NPA, when the module makes it repudiation, and puts the auditor in the bank's seat on whether to invoke
options.why: Calling the guarantee is not the trigger; refusing it is. A guarantee that gets called and is then honoured leaves behind an account that has been paid off, not a bad one, so invocation on its own decides nothing. Nor is it the auditor's decision whether the bank calls a guarantee at all — that seat belongs to the bank. Where money has been outstanding a long while and nobody has called, his work is to get the branch's reasoning, put it in the LFAR, and meanwhile take back out of income the interest that was credited but never collected.

options.text: The account stays standard and the interest stays in income, because a sovereign guarantee secures both the principal and the interest and removes the doubt about recovery
options.misconception: stretches the classification exemption for Central Government guarantees to income recognition, when the module confines it to asset classification
options.why: Half of this is right and the half that is wrong is the money. The shelter a sovereign guarantee gives was written for classification alone; the norms governing when interest may be called income were deliberately left outside it, and on an advance of this kind interest counts as earned only once it has actually been collected. A guarantee is a promise to pay if the borrower does not; it is not a receipt, and booking income against a promise is what the norm forbids. So the account stays standard and the 32 lakh rupees comes back out.

options.text: The account stays standard for classification and provisioning, because a Central Government guaranteed advance becomes NPA only when the Central Government repudiates the guarantee on invocation; but the 32 lakh rupees of unrealised interest is reversed, since the exemption does not extend to income recognition; and the branch's reason for not invoking the guarantee is obtained and reported in the LFAR
options.why: Three separate questions hide inside this one advance, and the branch has answered only one of them correctly. Classification comes first. Where the Centre stands behind a facility, the prudential norms refuse to let mere lateness turn the account bad; what does that is the Centre saying no — the moment it repudiates a guarantee somebody has actually called in. Nobody has called this one, so repudiation cannot yet have arisen, and the branch is right to leave the account standard and to carry no provision against it. Income sits under a different roof, because the norms on income recognition were never given that same shelter: interest on an advance of this kind belongs in the profit and loss account only so far as the money has come in, so the 32 lakh rupees booked and never received has to come back out. The third answer is the report. A guarantee left uncalled while the money has sat outstanding since August is a thing the auditor asks the branch to explain, and the explanation is written up and reported in the LFAR, the long form audit report. Standard, reversed, reported — three answers to what read as one question.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — Central Government guaranteed advances treated as NPA only on repudiation of the guarantee when invoked; the exception not available for income recognition; the reason for not invoking a long-overdue guarantee reported in the LFAR

items.scenario: Kaveri Bank is a nationalised bank, and Rao & Bhat are the statutory branch auditors of its Hosur industrial branch for the year ended 31 March 2026. Advances at the branch are 96 crore rupees and three matters stand out from the review. First, Bhavani Rice Mills holds a cash credit limit of 3 crore rupees against stock and book debts. The latest stock statement on the branch file is dated 30 November 2025, the drawing power of 2.7 crore rupees was worked out from it, and the outstanding of 2.55 crore rupees has stayed within that figure all year, so the branch's returns show the account as regular. Second, Deccan Forgings has a term loan of 5 crore rupees whose instalment due on 15 December 2025 is still unpaid, and a cash credit of 2 crore rupees that has run within its limit with regular credits all year; a letter of credit opened for Deccan devolved in February 2026 and the 40 lakh rupees the branch paid under it sits in a separate account. The branch has classified the term loan alone as non-performing. Third, a loan of 4 crore rupees to a housing scheme carrying a guarantee of the Central Government has been overdue since August 2025; the branch has not invoked the guarantee, has kept the account standard, and has credited 32 lakh rupees of interest on it to income for the year.

items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on the terms in the appointment letter. The warehouse report and last year's open issues are noise for this one. On those terms alone, what does Ananya tell the company before she signs?

options.text: Refuse the automation role but accept the receivables assignment, since the redesign was delivered fourteen months ago and a completed past engagement no longer affects the firm's objectivity.
options.misconception: Believes a self-review threat expires with the passage of time rather than with a change of the activity being reviewed.
options.why: Time does not dissolve a self-review. The receivables process on this year's plan is the very process the firm built, so any finding about it is a finding about the firm's own work, and the temptation not to make it is exactly what the rule against reviewing an activity you were previously responsible for is there to remove. The gap of fourteen months changes nothing about who designed the controls being tested.

options.text: Accept both extra responsibilities, because the module expressly allows the internal auditor to give advisory inputs on matters such as automation of activities and process re-engineering.
options.misconception: Reads permission to advise as permission to own the operational responsibility and later audit it.
options.why: Being asked for a view is not the same as being handed the job. The module does allow the internal auditor to offer advice on how a process is run, and automation is one of the places it says so. Advice ends where ownership begins. Take charge of the automation and he becomes answerable for an operational area; test a process his own firm designed and he is marking his own work, which is the whole reason the module keeps him away from anything he was previously responsible for.

options.text: The terms have to change. The internal audit function must sit outside the functions it audits and report directly to the audit committee, because independence has to hold not only in mind but also in appearance; the audit committee or the board settles the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology after talking to the internal auditor, and one executive cannot settle it alone; and since nobody may sit in judgement on work he was himself previously responsible for, the firm can take neither the automation role nor this year's receivables assignment.
options.why: Putting the head of internal audit under the chief financial officer places him beneath the very officer whose function he examines. Freedom from pressure is the first thing the module asks of him, and it sets the test twice over: the independence has to be real and it has to be visible, not only in mind but also in appearance. A line that merely looks compromised has already failed. Where the company is listed, the reporting is expected to run past the executives and land with those charged with governance, so the committee rather than a finance officer is who the head of internal audit answers to, and the function is meant to sit clear of anything it examines. Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 then hands the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology to the audit committee, or to the board, after they have talked it over with the internal auditor — one executive deciding it alone is not what the rule describes. Automating purchase to pay is an operational job, and deciding how an area works before auditing that area is the conflict the module warns of; the receivables assignment is the same fault in a cleaner form, because the firm would be marking work it was previously responsible for. In short, independence must hold not only in mind but also in appearance, the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology are the committee's to settle, and nobody audits what he was previously responsible for.
keywords: not only in mind but also in appearance

options.text: Accept the reporting line as drafted, and ask instead that the audit committee ratify the year's scope after the work is finished, which restores the committee's authority without disturbing the company's management structure.
options.misconception: Treats a later sign-off by the audit committee as curing a reporting line that runs into the finance function.
options.why: Ratification after the event is not the same thing as formulation before it. Under rule 13(2) the year's scope, its periodicity and the method are settled at the start, by the committee or the board and in consultation with the internal auditor; a committee told afterwards what was covered cannot decide what should have been covered. And the reporting line is the larger problem, because it is what the outside world sees.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — integrity, objectivity and independence of the internal auditor, the position and reporting of the chief internal auditor within the organisation structure, rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 on who formulates the scope, and the conflict in reviewing an activity the auditor was previously responsible for.

items.scenario: Basu & Kanungo are a firm of chartered accountants at Ranchi, and Ananya Basu is the partner who leads its internal audit practice. The firm has been offered the internal audit of a listed steel fabrication company for the year ending 31 March 2027, as an outside service provider, and three parts of the arrangement reach her in the week the engagement is being set up. First, the terms in the appointment letter. It says the head of internal audit will report to the chief financial officer, that the chief financial officer alone will settle the scope, the periodicity and the methodology for the year, and that the audit committee will be told what was covered once the work is finished. Beneath that, two further responsibilities are offered to the firm: taking charge of automating the company's purchase to pay process, and owning the redesign of the receivables process, which this same firm was paid fourteen months ago to redesign and which stands on this year's internal audit plan. The chief financial officer says those two pieces are worth more in fees than the audit itself. Second, the reporting. The plan for the year holds eleven assignments, the first of them the Jamshedpur warehouse. Ananya's team will finish the warehouse work in November, and the company wants the findings held back until the whole year is done so that one report goes up in April. Warehouse management has asked not to be copied on anything, on the ground that the plant head will pass on whatever matters. The chief financial officer has also asked her to confirm in writing that the standard her firm follows on reporting results governs the comprehensive report on the entity as a whole, because the audit committee has begun asking for one every quarter and nobody in the company wants to write it. Third, what became of last year's findings. The previous internal auditor's files list thirty-four issues raised in the year just ended. Nineteen of them carry a management action plan with a named owner and a date; twenty-two are still open. The chief financial officer's position is that the internal auditor raised them and the internal auditor should therefore close them, and he has asked Ananya's team to do the remediation work on nine of the nineteen for a separate fee. On six others the management accepted the recommendation, began the work and then stopped, and nobody has asked why. There is no agreed process for tracking any of this, and the audit committee has never been told that anything is open. Ananya has to settle all three before the engagement letter is signed.

items.stem: QUESTION 2 OF 3 — turns on the reporting arrangement. The appointment letter's terms and last year's open issues are noise for this one. On the reporting arrangement alone, what does Ananya settle with the company?

options.text: Issue the warehouse report in November but send it only upwards, to executive management and the audit committee, since the warehouse is the audited unit and should not receive the findings against it.
options.misconception: Thinks the auditee is a party to be reported about rather than the party the report is addressed to.
options.why: This inverts the addressee. The Internal Audit Report is issued to the auditee — the unit whose area was examined — with copies going to local and executive management as agreed during the planning phase. Withholding a report from the people whose processes it describes leaves nobody positioned to correct anything.

options.text: There are two reports and neither absorbs the other. One is written at the end of a particular audit assignment, goes to the unit that was audited, and is copied to local and executive management on terms fixed while the work was being planned — so the warehouse findings go out in November and warehouse management is copied; the report covering the whole plan period is a separate document, normally quarterly, sent up by the engagement partner to the audit committee; and she cannot sign the confirmation asked for, because the Standard reaches only the first type of reports.
options.why: Results are normally reported in two stages, and the company is trying to fold them into one. The narrow report comes first: it takes one area, one function or one part of the business, is written at the end of a particular audit assignment, says how the work was done and what was found, goes to the unit that was audited, and is copied to local and executive management on terms fixed while the assignment was being planned. That is why warehouse management cannot opt out of a copy, and why sitting on November's findings until April drains the report of any use. The wider report comes second: it covers everything internal audit did across the plan period, is written by the chief internal auditor — or by the engagement partner where the work is outsourced, as here — comes round quarterly as a rule, and goes up to the body that answers for internal audit, which will usually be the audit committee. The Standard says in its own scope that it reaches only the first type of reports and leaves the entity-wide one alone, so the confirmation the chief financial officer wants would be a false statement. In short, the assignment report is written at the end of a particular audit assignment and copied to local and executive management, the entity-wide report is a separate quarterly one for the audit committee, and the Standard governs only the first type of reports.
keywords: at the end of a particular audit assignment
only the first type of reports

options.text: Give the written confirmation, because a Standard on reporting results necessarily governs every report an internal auditor signs, including the quarterly one for the entity.
options.misconception: Assumes a Standard named for an activity covers every instance of that activity, without reading its stated scope.
options.why: The Standard fixes its own boundary and says so: it deals with the internal auditor's responsibility to issue the assignment report, not the periodic reporting for the whole entity under the annual or quarterly plan. Signing a confirmation that it governs the quarterly report would misstate the Standard, and it would also hand the firm a duty the company is trying to avoid writing itself.

options.text: Agree to the single report in April, since the audit committee is the body that internal audit results are owed to and one complete report serves it better than eleven partial ones.
options.misconception: Treats the audit committee as the only real recipient and the assignment report as an optional interim step.
options.why: The assignment report is not a draft of the periodic report; it is a report in its own right, owed to the auditee at the end of the assignment so that the people who run the area can act on the findings while acting still helps. Waiting until April means the warehouse carries a known weakness for five months. The committee's quarterly report is a separate obligation and does not discharge this one.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: The two stages in which internal audit results are reported — the report that closes one assignment and who receives a copy of it, the periodic report for the whole plan period and who it goes up to — and which of the two the Standard itself governs.

items.scenario: Basu & Kanungo are a firm of chartered accountants at Ranchi, and Ananya Basu is the partner who leads its internal audit practice.
