Priya has to settle each of the three before the report is signed.

items.stem: On the Angul receivable alone, whose responsibility is the Angul work, and must Deshpande & Rao re-perform it?

options.text: The Angul receivables work, including the procedures that missed the insolvency, is the responsibility of Bhattacharya & Sen alone, because it was allocated to them. Deshpande & Rao are entitled to assume that the other joint auditors carried out their part in accordance with the Standards, and it is not necessary for them to review or test that work; re-performing it is not required. The provision now needed is a matter brought to all three firms' notice, and its treatment in the statements and the report is a shared responsibility.
options.why: Responsibility here follows the allocation. A firm handed a unit answers for that unit alone — for getting and weighing the information and explanations it needs there, and for running its procedures properly. Angul and trade receivables went to Bhattacharya & Sen, so a confirmation that stopped short of the customer's insolvency is their execution and their lapse. The module then says what the other firms may take for granted: each of them is entitled to assume that the rest did their share to the Standards on Auditing, and no firm has to go back over another's papers or run tests of its own to find out whether it was done that way. So "so that we are covered" asks for work nobody is obliged to do; it is not necessary, and doing it would move the responsibility nowhere. What all three firms do share, once the receivable is known to every one of them, is the joint and several responsibility for a matter brought to their notice and agreed on, for how the statements present and disclose it, and for the report itself. In short, the work allocated to Bhattacharya & Sen stays theirs, the other firms are entitled to assume it was done to the Standards, and it is not necessary for Deshpande & Rao to do it again.

options.text: All three firms are jointly and severally responsible for the Angul receivable, because joint auditors sign one report and the law does not divide liability by plant; Deshpande & Rao should re-perform the work before signing.
options.misconception: Reads a common report as common responsibility for every allocated area.
options.why: The module's joint and several responsibility is a listed set: work not divided, common planning decisions, matters brought to notice and agreed, statutory compliance, presentation and disclosure, and the report. Work allocated to one joint auditor is that auditor's responsibility only, and the others are entitled to assume it was properly done without reviewing or testing it.

options.text: Nobody is responsible for it as auditors, because the balance was confirmed by the customer and a confirmation is the evidence the Standards ask for on a receivable; the insolvency is a valuation question for management.
options.misconception: Treats a confirmation as the end of the receivables work.
options.why: Proper execution of the audit procedures for an allocated area is the allocated joint auditor's responsibility, and a confirmation that establishes existence does not answer recoverability. The lapse is Bhattacharya & Sen's, not nobody's.

options.text: Bhattacharya & Sen are responsible, but since the fault has come to light Deshpande & Rao must now review the whole Angul file and test the receivables, because the entitlement to assume proper work falls away once one lapse is found.
options.misconception: Invents a trigger that converts one firm's allocated work into everybody's.
options.why: The module states the entitlement and the absence of any duty to review or test without a condition of that kind. What a discovered matter does create is a joint responsibility for its treatment once it is brought to the notice of all the joint auditors and agreed; it does not transfer the allocated work.

citation.ref: SA 299 (Revised) on divided work: a firm answers for the area allocated to it and for running its procedures there properly; the other firms may take it that it did its part to the Standards on Auditing, and none of them has to go back over that firm's work or test it to find out whether it was done that way

items.scenario: Mahanadi Steel Limited, a listed steel maker with plants at Rourkela, Angul and Kalinganagar and revenue of 4,800 crore rupees, is audited for the year ended 31 March 2026 by three joint auditors. The signed work allocation gives Rourkela and treasury to Deshpande & Rao, Angul and trade receivables to Bhattacharya & Sen, and Kalinganagar and inventory to Kulkarni Associates; compliance with the statutes, presentation and disclosure, and the audit report were left undivided. Meera Deshpande is the engagement partner at Deshpande & Rao, and three matters are open a week before the signing date the company has fixed. First, a 30 crore rupee receivable from an Angul customer that entered insolvency in February 2026 carries no provision, and Bhattacharya & Sen's file shows the balance was confirmed but the insolvency was not picked up; the chief financial officer found it after the draft reports circulated, and Meera's senior asks whether Deshpande & Rao must now re-perform the Angul receivables work "so that we are covered". Second, during the treasury work Deshpande & Rao found that a 90 crore rupee loan to a company owned by the promoter's family, booked at Kalinganagar, has been reclassified as an advance to a supplier; Meera told Kulkarni's partner about it on the telephone and treats that as done, and she wants the opinion qualified for the classification, while the other two firms consider an Emphasis of Matter paragraph enough and say that two firms against one settles the common report. Third, Deshpande & Rao's engagement quality control reviewer has not completed his review, Meera has not yet read the file on the loan classification herself, and her manager proposes that she sign on the agreed date on the strength of the manager's review, with the partner's review and the quality control review "to follow within the week".

items.stem: On the Kalinganagar loan alone, has Meera done what SA 299 asks of her, and does two against one settle the report?

options.text: Not yet, and no. A matter one firm meets that falls in another's area goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes, so a telephone call to one of them is not the communication the standard asks for. On the opinion, Meera is not bound by the views of the majority: if the disagreement survives the firms talking their conclusions over, she gives her own opinion in a separate audit report, and each report points at the other under an Other Matter paragraph.
options.why: Two rules answer the two halves. Take coordination first. When a firm, doing its own work, runs into something belonging to another firm's area — something that deserves their attention, or has to be disclosed, or needs talking over or judging by them — that something goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes. A loan to a promoter's company booked at Kalinganagar and relabelled as a supplier advance sits squarely in Kulkarni's area and in the disclosure all three firms answer for. What happened instead was one partner, on the telephone: one firm rather than every firm, spoken rather than written, and Bhattacharya & Sen have heard nothing at all. Now reporting. One report signed by all of them is the ordinary outcome, and the standard provides for the other one beside it: where the firms cannot agree on the opinion, or on anything else the report has to cover, each puts its own view in its own report, the two reports point at each other in an Other Matter paragraph as per SA 706, and Meera is not bound by the views of the majority. Before any of that the firms talk their conclusions over and pass them between themselves, so the disagreement is tested rather than assumed — but if she still lands on a qualification, counting firms settles nothing. In short, the matter goes to every other firm in writing, Meera is not bound by the views of the majority, and a firm that still disagrees signs a separate audit report.
keywords: not bound by the views of the majority

options.text: Yes, and yes. Telling the joint auditor whose area it is discharges the duty of coordination, and joint auditors resolve a difference on the opinion by majority so that the entity receives a single report, which is the purpose of a joint audit.
options.misconception: Imports voting into a standard that provides for separate reports instead.
options.why: The duty runs to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes — not to the one firm concerned, by telephone. And the standard holds no majority rule: a firm that disagrees is not bound by the views of the majority and puts its differing opinion in a separate audit report, with the two reports pointing at each other.

options.text: Meera has no duty to communicate at all, because the loan sits in Kulkarni's area and each joint auditor is responsible only for the work allocated to them; whether to qualify is therefore Kulkarni's call alone.
options.misconception: Stretches the division of work into a division of the opinion.
options.why: Allocated responsibility limits who performs the work, not who must be told. The module requires a joint auditor who comes across a matter relevant to another's area to communicate it to all the other joint auditors in writing, and the opinion is a matter on which every joint auditor forms and, if necessary, separately expresses their own view.

options.text: Not yet on communication, but on the report Meera must fall in with the other two: the standard requires a common audit report, and a joint auditor who cannot agree with it should withdraw rather than issue a second report.
options.misconception: Reads "common report" as absolute and misses the separate-report provision beside it.
options.why: The common report is the ordinary case, and the exception sits in the very same sentence: firms that cannot agree on the opinion each express their own in a separate audit report. Withdrawal is nowhere in it.

citation.ref: SA 299 (Revised) on coordination and on reporting: a matter one firm meets that falls in another's area goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes; the firms issue one report, but a firm that cannot agree on the opinion, or on anything else the report must cover, gives its own report instead, is not held to what the others think, and the reports point at each other in an Other Matter paragraph as per SA 706

items.stem: On the signing date alone, may Meera sign on the manager's review with her own review and the quality control review to follow?

options.text: No, but only because of the quality control review; the partner may rely on the manager's review of the loan file, since the standard allows review to be performed by a more experienced member of the team.
options.misconception: Takes the team's layered review as a substitute for the partner's own.
options.why: Work of less experienced members being reviewed by more experienced ones is the team's layering; it does not remove the module's requirement that review of audit documentation before issue of the report is the engagement partner's responsibility, and that sufficient appropriate audit evidence supports the conclusions before the report is issued.

options.text: Yes, provided the three joint auditors sign together, because in a joint audit the quality control review by any one of the firms covers the common report.
options.misconception: Lets a joint audit pool one firm's quality control across the others.
options.why: SA 220 attaches to each firm's own engagement and its own partner: it is Deshpande & Rao's reviewer whose review must be complete before Meera dates the report, and the partner's own review of documentation is not transferred to another firm by a joint appointment.

options.text: Yes. The partner's responsibility for quality is discharged through the team, the manager's review is the firm's review, and the quality control review is a firm-level monitoring step that may be completed after the report is dated.
options.misconception: Confuses the engagement quality control review with the firm's monitoring after the fact.
options.why: Direction, supervision, performance and the reading of the documentation before the report goes out are the partner's own, and the standard says in terms that at a listed entity no date goes on the report until the engagement quality control review has finished. That is a condition on dating, not monitoring after the fact.

options.text: No. Direction, supervision and the performance of the engagement are the partner's, and so is reading the audit documentation before the report goes out; a manager's review does not stand in for her own on a judgment as significant as the loan classification. Before she dates the report she has to be satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence sits behind the conclusions drawn, and at a listed company she may put no date on it until the engagement quality control review has finished. The company's chosen date yields to both.
options.why: Engagement performance sits on the partner herself. She directs the engagement, oversees it and performs it to the professional standards and the law that govern it; the report being right for the circumstances is hers to answer for; and reading the audit documentation before the report goes out is hers too, as is being satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind what the report concludes. A partner who has not read the file on a 90 crore rupee related-party classification cannot say that of her own report, and handing the reading to the manager hands over the work without handing over the answerability. Then the rule that attaches at a listed company: the partner establishes that a quality control reviewer is in place, talks the significant matters through with him, and puts no date on the report until the engagement quality control review has finished. A review "to follow within the week" means a report dated ahead of its own review, which is the one thing that rule shuts out. In short, direction, supervision and review belong to the partner, the report is dated only once sufficient appropriate audit evidence supports it, and never before the engagement quality control review is done.

citation.ref: SA 220 (Revised) on the engagement partner's own job: directing, supervising and performing the engagement, and reading the audit documentation before the report goes out, satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind what was concluded; and, at a listed entity, no date on the report before the engagement quality control review has finished

items.stem: On the bank's report on the financial statements alone, what does Radhika do?

options.text: Radhika does not sign on the strength of the finance head's papers, and she may engage the chartered accountant at Anand. Under clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule the firm's name goes on a report about financial statements only where the statements and the related records were gone over by hands the clause names — hers, a partner or an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice. Company accounts staff and a consultancy of commerce graduates are outside that list, however closely she reads their schedules, so the firm does the examining itself. Anand is the one piece she may pass on, to a chartered accountant in practice there, and the report then stands on that work and her own.
options.why: Four sets of hands are named and nobody else: Radhika herself, a partner or an employee in his firm, and another chartered accountant in practice. The chapter explains the point of the restraint — a member is not to put his name under a report on a statement he has not had gone over by one of those, the object being that the job he was trusted with was actually done by him, or by people working under his eye, before the report leaves his desk. The company's own accounts staff are the very people whose figures are under examination, and a consultancy of commerce graduates is nobody the clause knows; going through their working papers is not doing the work, and a firm short of staff this month is a firm short of a report this month. Now the part the finance head reached by accident. Because the clause admits another chartered accountant in practice, two or more members may take an assignment jointly, or one member may draw on the help of another — which is exactly what makes the Anand suggestion sound. So the Anand records go to the member there, the rest is done by the firm, and the report in the firm's name then rests on work the clause will accept. In short, the report can rest only on an examination of the statements and the related records done by Radhika herself, by a partner or an employee in his firm, or else by another chartered accountant in practice, and the finance head's examiners are none of the three.
keywords: a partner or an employee in his firm

options.text: Radhika signs, but the report states in a paragraph that the examination of the records was carried out by the company's staff and an outside consultancy and that the firm relied on their work, so that the bank is not misled about who did what.
options.misconception: A report may rest on any examiner provided the report discloses who it was.
options.why: The clause has no disclosure exception; a report of an examination made by anybody outside the four permitted hands is misconduct whether or not the report says so, and telling the bank who examined does not turn the consultancy into an employee of the firm.

options.text: Radhika signs after reading the papers. The clause is about the quality of the examination, the finance head's staff and the consultancy have produced complete working papers, and a partner who has read and questioned them has supervised the work in the sense the clause requires.
options.misconception: Reading another examiner's working papers carefully is the same as making the examination.
options.why: The clause turns on who made the examination, not on how good the papers look: it must be made by the member, a partner or an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice, and reading somebody else's schedules is not making it.

options.text: Radhika cannot engage the Anand member either. The clause requires the examination to be made within her own firm, so every record, including the Anand unit's, must be examined by her, her partner or the firm's employees before the report is signed.
options.misconception: Every part of the examination must be made inside the member's own firm.
options.why: The clause expressly accepts an examination made by another chartered accountant in practice, and the chapter explains that this exception is what allows joint assignments and assistance from another member in practice.

citation.ref: clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule — misconduct where a report on an examination of financial statements goes out under a member's own name or the firm's while the statements, and the related records sitting behind them, were examined by somebody the clause does not name. It names only the member himself, a partner or an employee in his firm, and another chartered accountant in practice

items.scenario: Desai & Trivedi are a firm of chartered accountants at Vadodara, and Radhika Desai is the partner in charge of Mahi Agro Processors Private Limited, a client that is seeking a term loan of 40 crore rupees from a bank for a second plant at Anand. Three matters have come to her from the company's finance head, a retired bank manager with a management degree who is not a member of the Institute. First, the bank wants a report from the firm on the company's financial statements for the three years to 31 March 2026, with the stock and receivables examined. The finance head has had the records examined by his own accounts staff and by a consultancy of commerce graduates that he engaged for the purpose, has sent the firm their working papers and schedules, and asks Radhika to certify the report in the firm's name after reading them, since the firm has no staff to spare this month; for the Anand unit's records, which sit at Anand, he suggests that the firm engage a chartered accountant in practice there to examine them. Second, the bank wants a five-year projection of profits. The company's own team has prepared it, Radhika has reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, and the loan proposal that the company has printed carries on its cover the words "Projections certified by Desai & Trivedi, Chartered Accountants"; the finance head says the word is deserved because the review was careful, and that the bank is used to seeing it. Third, the finance head proposes to join the firm as a partner from October 2026, bringing with him the loan-syndication work of a dozen companies he knows, and Radhika's friend, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Gujarat, has asked at the same time to join the firm as a partner to handle its tax litigation. Radhika's own partner, Nikhil Trivedi, says a partner who brings work is worth more than a rule, and that in any case the advocate belongs to a recognised profession and so does the banker. Radhika has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the five-year projection alone, what does Radhika do?

options.text: The word "certified" comes off the cover before the proposal goes, and the firm's report on the projection says plainly what the projection is. What clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule strikes at is the firm's name being attached to an estimate of earnings that rests on transactions still to happen, attached in a way that could leave the bank thinking the firm vouches for the accuracy of the figures. The Council's own opinion leaves the work open: a chartered accountant may help build such a forecast or go over one, provided the report is open about the sources of information used, the footing the figures stand on and the major assumptions behind them, and provided she does not stand behind the outcome. Careful work does not change what a reader takes from the word "certified"; what counts is what the document invites the bank to believe.
options.why: Nothing in the clause keeps a member away from a forecast. The chapter carries the Council's opinion, settled when the guidance on accountants' reports about profit and financial forecasts was finished: taking part in building one is open to a member, and so is going over one somebody else built, on two conditions — the report says openly where the sources of information came from, what footing the figures rest on and what the major assumptions were, and the member stops short of standing behind how it all turns out. Projections put together on hypothetical assumptions about future events and management action are treated the same way. What the clause punishes, then, is not the association but the dressing: a use of the name that could leave a reader believing the member vouches for the accuracy of the figures. A loan proposal whose cover calls the projections certified by the firm says precisely that to a bank — whatever the assumptions were, and however closely Radhika went through them — because the question is what the document invites the reader to believe, not how good the work behind it was. The chapter's own illustration is a member who issued projection statements for individuals, a bank lent against them, and clause (3) was among the findings against him. So the firm's report on the projection sets out the sources of information, the footing and the major assumptions, says in terms that it does not stand behind the outcome, and the cover is corrected. In short, the firm may go over the forecast and say so, naming the sources of information, the footing and the major assumptions, but may not let its name sit where a reader would think it vouches for the accuracy — which is where "certified" puts it.

options.text: The word stays. Radhika reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, so the firm can stand behind the projection, and a certificate that rests on careful work is not the mischief the clause was written for.
options.misconception: Careful work on a forecast entitles the member to certify it.
options.why: The clause turns on the manner in which the name is used and whether it may lead to the belief that the member vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, not on how careful the review was; the Council's opinion permits review only so long as the member does not vouch for the accuracy.

options.text: The word stays because the reader is a bank. A lender's credit department knows that a projection is an estimate, so no belief that the firm vouches for its accuracy can arise, and the clause is aimed at documents put before the public.
options.misconception: A sophisticated reader cures a forecast the firm has called certified.
options.why: The clause asks whether the manner of use may lead to the belief that the member vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and the chapter's own case of projection statements issued to a bank ended in a finding of misconduct; the reader's expertise is not the test.

options.text: The firm withdraws from the projection altogether. A chartered accountant's name may not be connected with an estimate of future earnings in any form, so Radhika's review is withdrawn and the company sends the projection to the bank without any reference to the firm.
options.misconception: A chartered accountant may not be associated with a forecast or projection at all.
options.why: The Council's opinion is that a member can participate in the preparation of forecasts and can review them, provided the report indicates the sources of information, the basis and the major assumptions and does not vouch for the accuracy; the clause bars a manner of use, not the association.

citation.ref: clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule — misconduct where a member lets his own name, or the firm's, be attached to an estimate of earnings resting on transactions still to happen, and attached in a way that could leave a reader thinking he vouches for the accuracy of it. Against that, the Council's opinion: a member may help build such a forecast or go over one, so long as his report is open about the sources of information he worked from, the footing the figures stand on and the major assumptions behind them, and so long as he does not stand behind the outcome

The finance head has had the records examined by his own accounts staff and by a consultancy of commerce graduates that he engaged for the purpose, has sent the firm their working papers and schedules, and asks Radhika to certify the report in the firm's name after reading them, since the firm has no staff to spare this month; for the Anand unit's records, which sit at Anand, he suggests that the firm engage a chartered accountant in practice there to examine them. Second, the bank wants a five-year projection of profits. The company's own team has prepared it, Radhika has reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, and the loan proposal that the company has printed carries on its cover the words "Projections certified by Desai & Trivedi, Chartered Accountants"; the finance head says the word is deserved because the review was careful, and that the bank is used to seeing it. Third, the finance head proposes to join the firm as a partner from October 2026, bringing with him the loan-syndication work of a dozen companies he knows, and Radhika's friend, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Gujarat, has asked at the same time to join the firm as a partner to handle its tax litigation. Radhika's own partner, Nikhil Trivedi, says a partner who brings work is worth more than a rule, and that in any case the advocate belongs to a recognised profession and so does the banker. Radhika has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the two proposed partners alone, what does Radhika decide?

options.text: Both may join. Banking and law are recognised professions, the clause was written to keep unqualified people out of a chartered accountant's practice, and a retired branch manager with a management degree and an enrolled advocate are each qualified in their own field.
options.misconception: Any recognised profession qualifies its member for partnership with a chartered accountant.
options.why: The clause admits only a Chartered Accountant in practice or a member of a professional body prescribed by the Council, and Regulation 53B lists company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, engineers, architects and actuaries; a management degree and a banking career are on no list, and even the advocate waits for the Council's guidelines on multi-disciplinary partnerships.

options.text: The banker cannot be a partner, and the advocate not yet. Clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule shuts a member in practice, here or abroad, out of partnership with anybody who is neither a Chartered Accountant in practice nor a member of some other professional body whose qualifications the Council has prescribed. A retired bank manager holding a management degree belongs to no prescribed body, and the work he would bring is not an argument the clause listens to. An advocate on the Bar Council is on the Regulation 53B list, beside company secretaries, cost accountants, engineers, architects and actuaries; but the Council's caution is that Multi-Disciplinary partnerships have to wait until the other regulators open the same door from their side and guidelines come out, so the advocate waits on that.
options.why: The list is closed. Partnership is open to a Chartered Accountant in practice, and to somebody belonging to another professional body whose qualifications the Council has prescribed — which takes in a person living abroad who would be entitled to registration here but for that, and a person whose qualifications the Central Government or the Council recognises for the purpose. After those, nobody, in India or outside it. The bodies themselves sit in Regulation 53B: the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India, the Bar Council of India, the Institution of Engineers or a recognised engineering degree, the Indian Institute of Architects, and the Institute of Actuaries of India. A retired banker with a management degree belongs to none of them, and Nikhil's point about the work is not a point the clause hears — a dozen companies' business is exactly what such a partnership would be splitting. The advocate does belong to a prescribed body, and that is where the chapter adds its warning: even for somebody on the list, the door is not open yet. A Multi-Disciplinary partnership waits on two things happening — the regulators of the other calling permitting their own members to join up with chartered accountants, and the Council putting out guidelines. In short, only a Chartered Accountant in practice or a member of a body named in Regulation 53B may come in at all, the banker is neither, and even the advocate waits until Multi-Disciplinary partnerships are cleared from both sides.

options.text: Neither may ever join. A chartered accountant in practice may be in partnership only with other chartered accountants in practice, so the advocate is refused on the same footing as the banker and the firm stays as it is.
options.misconception: Clause (4) allows partnership with chartered accountants in practice and nobody else.
options.why: The clause itself extends to members of other professional bodies having such qualifications as may be prescribed, and Regulation 53B prescribes advocates among others; the advocate is refused for now because of the Council's note on multi-disciplinary partnerships, not because the clause bars him.

options.text: The banker may join and the advocate may not. A partner who brings syndication work and will never sign an audit report is outside the mischief of the clause, while a lawyer in the partnership would put the firm in litigation, which a chartered accountant's firm may not carry on.
options.misconception: A non-member partner who does not sign reports is outside clause (4).
options.why: The clause turns on who the partner is, not on what he signs: a person who is neither a Chartered Accountant in practice nor a member of a prescribed body is barred whatever his role; and an advocate is on the Regulation 53B list, held back only by the Council's note on multi-disciplinary partnerships.

citation.ref: clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule — who a member in practice may take into partnership, here or abroad: a Chartered Accountant in practice, or somebody belonging to another professional body whose qualifications the Council has prescribed, and nobody else. Regulation 53B is where those bodies are named — company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, engineers, architects, actuaries — and the chapter's caution is that Multi-Disciplinary partnerships have to wait until the other regulators open the same door from their side and the Council issues its guidelines

items.scenario: Desai & Trivedi are a firm of chartered accountants at Vadodara, and Radhika Desai is the partner in charge of Mahi Agro Processors Private Limited, a client that is seeking a term loan of 40 crore rupees from a bank for a second plant at Anand. Three matters have come to her from the company's finance head, a retired bank manager with a management degree who is not a member of the Institute. First, the bank wants a report from the firm on the company's financial statements for the three years to 31 March 2026, with the stock and receivables examined. The finance head has had the records examined by his own accounts staff and by a consultancy of commerce graduates that he engaged for the purpose, has sent the firm their working papers and schedules, and asks Radhika to certify the report in the firm's name after reading them, since the firm has no staff to spare this month; for the Anand unit's records, which sit at Anand, he suggests that the firm engage a chartered accountant in practice there to examine them. Second, the bank wants a five-year projection of profits. The company's own team has prepared it, Radhika has reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, and the loan proposal that the company has printed carries on its cover the words "Projections certified by Desai & Trivedi, Chartered Accountants"; the finance head says the word is deserved because the review was careful, and that the bank is used to seeing it. Third, the finance head proposes to join the firm as a partner from October 2026, bringing with him the loan-syndication work of a dozen companies he knows, and Radhika's friend, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Gujarat, has asked at the same time to join the firm as a partner to handle its tax litigation. Radhika's own partner, Nikhil Trivedi, says a partner who brings work is worth more than a rule, and that in any case the advocate belongs to a recognised profession and so does the banker. Radhika has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the two fee arrangements alone, how does Meenakshi answer Vikram?

options.text: Both are in order. Suresh Rao is being paid for bringing business, which is consultancy, and an office allowance is an expense of the firm rather than a share of its fees; the company secretary did half of the work and is paid for that half.
options.misconception: Treating the label on a payment as settling its character, when the Council looks at the substance of the transaction and has already held an office allowance to a non-member to be a share of profits.
options.why: Anything paid out of what the practice earns, directly or through somebody else, is caught by the clause, and the Council has already treated a non-member's office allowance as a division of profits in substance; what a firm writes in its ledger does not settle what the money is. The company secretary is in order for a different reason entirely — his body is prescribed under Regulation 53A.

options.text: The 10 per cent to Suresh Rao is professional misconduct under Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule whatever the ledger calls it, and the share with the company secretary is in order. Only a short list of people may lawfully take a slice of what a practice earns, whether the slice goes out as a share, a commission or brokerage: members of the Institute, present partners, retired ones, the heir standing in a dead partner's place, and members of the bodies or holders of the qualifications the Council has prescribed. A garment exporter appears on none of those lists, and what a payment really is decides the question, not the heading it is booked under — the substance of the transaction, not its name. The company secretary belongs to the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, a body named under Regulation 53A, so a fee may be shared with him.
options.why: The clause polices money going out of a practice, and it names the only hands that may receive any of it: a member of the Institute; a partner, serving or retired; the heir standing in a dead partner's place; and a member of another professional body, or the holder of a qualification, that the Council has prescribed. Suresh Rao holds no qualification at all and is simply a tax client, so his 10 per cent is a share, a commission or brokerage landing outside every one of those categories, and that it bought an introduction is precisely the mischief the clause was written against. The ledger heading rescues nothing. A decided case had a member handing a non-member half of his audit fees for years, booked as an office allowance; the Council looked past the label and found he had in truth divided his profits, because a transaction takes its character from what it does and not from the name written over it. The company secretary sits on the other side of the same line. Regulation 53A of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988 is where the Council has set down the bodies whose members may take a share — company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, architects, actuaries — so paying him for the half of the work he actually did is squarely allowed. In short, the exporter's 10 per cent is a share, commission or brokerage measured by the substance of the transaction and is misconduct, while the company secretary's share is permitted by Regulation 53A.

options.text: Both are professional misconduct. Clause (2) permits a share of fees only to a member of the Institute or a partner, so a company secretary is as much outside the clause as a garment exporter, and the firm must recover both payments.
options.misconception: Reading the clause as ending at members and partners, and missing the prescribed professional bodies and qualifications added by the Council under Regulation 53A.
options.why: The clause itself extends to a member of any other professional body or a person with such other qualification as may be prescribed, and the Council has prescribed under Regulation 53A the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, the cost accountants' institute, the Bar Council, the architects' institute and the actuaries' institute, and a list of qualified persons besides; the share with the company secretary is expressly allowed.

options.text: The 10 per cent is in order because it is a one-time payment for a single introduction rather than a continuing arrangement, and the company secretary must be paid a fixed fee rather than a percentage, because a percentage is what the clause forbids.
options.misconception: Inventing a distinction between a one-off commission and a continuing one, and a rule about percentages, neither of which is in the clause; the clause turns on who receives the share, not on how often or in what form.
options.why: The clause is broken by paying or allowing, or agreeing to pay or allow, any share, commission or brokerage to a person outside its list, and it draws no line between a single payment and a continuing one; and it forbids nothing about the form of a payment to a person inside its list, so a company secretary may be paid a share of the fee for the work he did.

citation.ref: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule — the fee-sharing bar. It covers who outside the practice may lawfully be handed a slice of what it earns, the bodies and qualifications the Council has prescribed under Regulation 53A, and its rule that a payment is judged by what it really is rather than by the heading it is booked under

items.scenario: Iyer & Bhonsle, a firm of two partners at Hyderabad, leaves the firm's own compliance to Meenakshi Iyer, and three things reach her desk in April 2026. First, the firm's largest new audit client of the year came through Suresh Rao, a garment exporter who is himself a tax client of the firm and holds no professional qualification of any kind; Vikram Bhonsle, the other partner, has agreed to pay him 10 per cent of the first year's audit fee from that client, entered in the firm's ledger as an office allowance, and in the same month has agreed to share the fee from a secretarial compliance assignment with a company secretary in whole-time practice who did half of that work. Second, Meenakshi has accepted a seat on the board of Golconda Foods Limited, a listed company the firm has never audited, as an ordinary director holding no executive office, and Vikram became a working partner in his brother's granite export business on 1 April 2026 and filed his application for the Council's permission on 20 April. Third, while Meenakshi was abroad from 6 to 18 April, the firm's audit manager, a chartered accountant of nine years' standing who holds a power of attorney from both partners, signed and issued the audit report of a private company client and a net worth certificate for its bank, and in the same fortnight signed the audit queries on two other audits and the letters forwarding draft observations to their managements. Vikram's view is that a power of attorney and nine years of experience settle the third matter, that the ledger description settles the first, and that a permission applied for is as good as one granted.

items.stem: On the directorship and the granite business alone, where does each partner stand?

options.text: Both need the Council's specific permission before they begin. A directorship is an occupation other than the profession like any other, and Vikram's application of 20 April protects him from that date onward, so only Meenakshi is presently in breach.
options.misconception: Reading the clause without its proviso, and treating an application as if it were the approval, when the module's illustration holds a member guilty for the days between taking up the office and applying.
options.why: A plain board seat falls outside the clause altogether by its proviso, so long as no executive office comes with it and the firm has no audit relationship with the company; Meenakshi needs no permission. An application protects nobody, either: what the clause asks for is the Council's specific and prior approval, and Vikram had none of it from 1 April onwards.

options.text: Neither needs anything. An interest in a family business is within the Council's general permission because it came through the family, and a seat on a board is not an occupation at all, so neither partner has engaged in anything the clause reaches.
options.misconception: Stretching the Council's concession for an inherited and passive family interest to cover a member who is actively working in a relative's business.
options.why: The Council's indulgence for a family business is for an interest that devolved on the member by inheritance, succession or partition, in a business he did not create and is not actively engaged in carrying on; Vikram joined his brother's business as a working partner, which is active engagement in a business concern and needs the specific and prior approval of the Council. Meenakshi is safe, but by the proviso, not because a board seat is nothing.

options.text: Meenakshi may hold the seat only after obtaining the Council's specific permission, because Golconda Foods is a listed company, while Vikram is safe because he applied within thirty days of joining the business, which is the time the Council allows.
options.misconception: Adding a listing test and a grace period that the clause does not contain; the only tests are executive office, audit interest, and approval before the engagement begins.
options.why: The proviso to Clause (11) draws its line at managing director or whole time director and at the firm being interested in the company as an auditor, and says nothing about listing; and there is no thirty-day window anywhere in the clause or the Council's resolutions, the approval has to be specific and prior, and the module holds a member guilty for the nine days between taking office and applying.

options.text: Meenakshi needs no permission, and Vikram is guilty of professional misconduct for the days before he applied. A seat on a board is left alone by the clause's proviso so long as the member holds no executive office there, being neither managing director nor whole time director, and so long as neither he nor any partner of his stands towards that company as an auditor; the firm has never audited Golconda Foods. Working as a partner in a business sits nowhere in what the Council has allowed everybody in advance: it calls for the specific and prior approval of the Council. So from 1 April to 20 April Vikram carried on another business unpermitted, and an application filed afterwards does not reach back over those days.
options.why: The clause shuts a practising member out of trades and occupations beyond the profession itself unless the Council has said yes, and then its own proviso lifts one thing back out: a seat on a board, provided the member is neither managing director nor whole time director of that company and neither he nor any partner of his stands towards it as an auditor. Meenakshi's is a plain seat, no executive office, at a company the firm has never audited, so the proviso covers her and she needs nobody's leave; the company being listed adds nothing, because the proviso never asks about listing. Vikram holds no permission of any kind. What the Council has allowed everybody in advance is a fixed list — working under a practising chartered accountant, private tuition, writing books, honorary office in a charity, editing a professional journal, owning farmland and farming it, and others of that character. A working partnership in a granite export business is on none of them; joining a business concern as employee or partner falls under the Council's other resolution, which asks for the specific and prior approval of the Council case by case. The module's illustration is a member who stepped into an executive chairmanship on the first of a month and wrote to the Council on the tenth: he was held guilty for the nine days he had run without leave, and Vikram's 1 April to 20 April is that same gap. In short, a plain director who holds no executive office needs no permission unless his firm stands towards the company as an auditor, while a partnership in a business needs the Council's specific and prior approval before it starts.

citation.ref: Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule — the other-occupation bar. It covers when a member in practice may hold work outside the profession at all, the proviso that leaves a plain seat on a board alone, and the Council's division between what it has permitted everybody in advance and what a member must have approved before he starts

First, the firm's largest new audit client of the year came through Suresh Rao, a garment exporter who is himself a tax client of the firm and holds no professional qualification of any kind; Vikram Bhonsle, the other partner, has agreed to pay him 10 per cent of the first year's audit fee from that client, entered in the firm's ledger as an office allowance, and in the same month has agreed to share the fee from a secretarial compliance assignment with a company secretary in whole-time practice who did half of that work. Second, Meenakshi has accepted a seat on the board of Golconda Foods Limited, a listed company the firm has never audited, as an ordinary director holding no executive office, and Vikram became a working partner in his brother's granite export business on 1 April 2026 and filed his application for the Council's permission on 20 April. Third, while Meenakshi was abroad from 6 to 18 April, the firm's audit manager, a chartered accountant of nine years' standing who holds a power of attorney from both partners, signed and issued the audit report of a private company client and a net worth certificate for its bank, and in the same fortnight signed the audit queries on two other audits and the letters forwarding draft observations to their managements. items.stem: On what the audit manager signed alone, what does Meenakshi conclude?

options.text: The audit report is misconduct but the net worth certificate is not, because the clause names a balance sheet, a profit and loss account, a report and financial statements, and a certificate to a bank is none of those four.
options.misconception: Reading the word report narrowly as the audit report alone, when the module reads it as any expression of a professional opinion, and holds a certificate signed by a member who is not a partner to be within the clause.
options.why: A report for the purposes of the clause is any document arising out of a professional assignment whose subject matter is the expression of a professional opinion, whether financial or non-financial, and a certificate of net worth is exactly that; the module's illustration of an assistant chartered accountant signing a stock certificate for a bank on the absent member's instruction ends in misconduct under Clause (12).

options.text: Nothing is misconduct. The manager is a chartered accountant, so section 26 of the Act is satisfied, and a power of attorney from both partners makes his signature the firm's own for every document on the list.
options.misconception: Stopping at section 26's requirement that the signatory be a member, and missing the clause's second limb that the signatory must be a partner; authority does not travel by power of attorney.
options.why: Section 26 is the floor and not the whole rule: Clause (12) adds a second limb keeping out a member not being his partner, so the firm's reporting work is closed to an employee however qualified, and the module's illustration of a power of attorney given to an employee chartered accountant ends in a finding of misconduct under Clause (12) and under the Second Schedule for section 26 besides.

options.text: The audit report and the net worth certificate are professional misconduct under Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule, and the rest is not. The firm's reporting work — a balance sheet, a profit and loss account, a report, financial statements — goes out over a partner's signature or over nobody's: someone outside the Institute cannot put his name to it, and neither can a member of the Institute who is not a partner of that firm. The manager is a member but not a partner, and the power of attorney changes nothing, since the clause catches a member not being his partner whatever authority has been handed to him, with section 26 of the Act compounding it. Audit queries and letters forwarding draft observations carry no professional opinion at all; they are routine documents, and the Council has said their signing may be delegated.
options.why: Clause (12) has two limbs and it is the second that catches this manager. One limb keeps out anybody who is not a member of the Institute in practice; the other keeps out a member not being his partner, so a chartered accountant on the firm's payroll, however senior, however many years in the profession, cannot put his name to a balance sheet, to a profit and loss account, to a report or to financial statements for the firm. Report is read broadly here: any document coming out of a professional assignment whose point is the expression of a professional opinion, financial or otherwise. That puts the bank's net worth certificate inside the clause exactly where the audit report sits, and the module illustrates it with a member abroad who told his assistant, himself a chartered accountant, to sign and issue a stock certificate to a bank; he was guilty. Nor does a power of attorney help. The module's second illustration has a practising member arming an employee chartered accountant with one and letting him sign the firm's reports and statements; that was misconduct under Clause (12) and, because section 26 lets nobody but a member sign for a practising accountant or his firm in a professional capacity, under Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule as well. What the clause leaves alone is audit paperwork that carries no opinion. The Council has said in terms that signing may be handed on where a document calls for neither a professional opinion nor an authentication, and the list it gives opens with queries raised while an audit is running and takes in letters that forward draft observations, so the manager's second fortnight of signing is in order. A warning comes with it: once signing has been delegated, a firm cannot defend itself in an enquiry by saying no chartered accountant signed the document. In short, a member not being his partner cannot sign a report or a certificate for the firm and a power of attorney does not alter that, while audit queries and forwarding letters are routine documents whose signing may be delegated.

options.text: Everything the manager signed is misconduct, the audit queries and the forwarding letters included, because nothing may leave a firm of chartered accountants in its professional capacity over a signature other than a partner's.
options.misconception: Reading Clause (12) as covering every document of the firm, when the Council has listed the routine documents whose signing may be delegated and audit queries are the first of them.
options.why: Where a document calls for neither a professional opinion nor an authentication, the Council has said its signing may be passed on without Clause (12) biting, and the list it gives names queries raised while an audit is running and letters carrying draft observations out to a management. The clause is about what leaves the firm bearing an opinion, not about its correspondence.

citation.ref: Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule — the signing bar. It covers whose signature may go on the firm's reporting work and whose may not, read beside section 26 of the Act; how widely the word report is read for this purpose; and the Council's list of routine paperwork whose signing may be handed to somebody else

First, the firm's largest new audit client of the year came through Suresh Rao, a garment exporter who is himself a tax client of the firm and holds no professional qualification of any kind; Vikram Bhonsle, the other partner, has agreed to pay him 10 per cent of the first year's audit fee from that client, entered in the firm's ledger as an office allowance, and in the same month has agreed to share the fee from a secretarial compliance assignment with a company secretary in whole-time practice who did half of that work. Third, while Meenakshi was abroad from 6 to 18 April, the firm's audit manager, a chartered accountant of nine years' standing who holds a power of attorney from both partners, signed and issued the audit report of a private company client and a net worth certificate for its bank, and in the same fortnight signed the audit queries on two other audits and the letters forwarding draft observations to their managements. Vikram's view is that a power of attorney and nine years of experience settle the third matter, that the ledger description settles the first, and that a permission applied for is as good as one granted.

items.stem: On the quarterly statements alone, what does the auditor report under CARO 2020, and where?

options.text: Under clause (ii)(b), because the limits sanctioned on the security of current assets exceed five crore rupees in aggregate: state that the quarterly statements filed with the banks are not in agreement with the books of account, and give the details — the June and September statements and the differences of 1.3 crore rupees and 70 lakh rupees in inventory
options.why: Clause (ii)(b) has two limbs and Meghdoot trips both. The first is a size test with a date range attached: did the company, at any moment in the year, hold sanctioned facilities resting on the security of its current assets that came, in aggregate across every bank and financial institution, to more than five crore rupees? Six crore rupees at Sahyadri and three crore at Konkan, both against hypothecated stock and receivables, make nine, so the clause switches on. The second limb then puts a plain question of fact — are the quarterly returns handed to those lenders in agreement with the books of account — and where the answer is no, it wants the particulars. Inventory shown at 6.4 crore rupees against 5.1 crore rupees in the books is a gap of 1.3 crore rupees; 5.9 against 5.2 is another 70 lakh rupees. That the figures were called provisional and that neither bank ever objected is an explanation the company may owe its lenders. It is not one the clause accepts from the auditor, whose task here is to say the returns do not match, and by how much.

options.text: Nothing under CARO, since neither bank's limit on its own exceeds five crore rupees and the clause is applied lender by lender
options.misconception: applies the five crore rupee test to each bank separately, when the clause says in aggregate
options.why: The threshold is counted across lenders, not within one. Aggregate is the operative word: every bank and financial institution is added together before the five crore rupee line is drawn. Six crore at Sahyadri plus three crore at Konkan is nine, and the clause applies. Testing each lender on its own would let any company step outside the clause by splitting its working capital between two banks — the opposite of what a provision about returns filed with lenders is there to do.

options.text: Qualify the opinion on the financial statements, since statements filed with lenders that overstate inventory are a misstatement the auditor cannot pass over
options.misconception: turns a CARO clause finding into a modified opinion on the financial statements, when the books themselves are not shown to be wrong
options.why: The financial statements are not what was overstated; the statements filed with the banks were. The books show 5.1 crore rupees and 5.2 crore rupees, and if the audit finds those figures right, the accounts are not misstated by a return that said something else. CARO is a report on matters specified in the order, given as an annexure, and clause (ii)(b) is where this goes — as a statement that the returns do not agree with the books and the details of how they differ. Whether the gap also says something about the reliability of the company's controls is a separate question for the audit; it is not a qualification of the opinion.

options.text: Nothing under clause (ii)(b), because the statements were marked provisional and the banks accepted them without query, so there is no disagreement to report
options.misconception: treats the bank's acceptance of a statement as settling whether it agrees with the books, when the clause asks only whether it agrees
options.why: The clause asks one factual question — are the statements filed with the banks in agreement with the books of account — and it does not ask whether the bank minded. A statement that shows 6.4 crore rupees of inventory when the books show 5.1 crore rupees is not in agreement with the books, whatever word is written across the top of it. The auditor reports the fact and the details; how the company explains the gap to its lenders is the company's business.

citation.ref: paragraph 3, clause (ii)(b) — the size test that switches the clause on where facilities backed by current assets pass five crore rupees across all lenders, and what the annexure must say when the periodic returns given to those lenders do not match the books

items.scenario: Meghdoot Agro Industries Limited is an unlisted public company that mills and packs pulses, and Desai & Kulkarni are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. CARO 2020 applies to it. Three matters are on the partner's list. First, the company holds cash credit limits of 6 crore rupees from Sahyadri Bank and 3 crore rupees from Konkan Bank, both secured by hypothecation of stock and receivables; the quarterly stock and receivable statements filed with the two banks for June and September 2025 show inventory of 6.4 crore rupees and 5.9 crore rupees, against 5.1 crore rupees and 5.2 crore rupees in the books on those dates, and the finance manager says the statements were "provisional figures, and neither bank has ever raised a query". Second, GST of 42 lakh rupees for June 2025 was still unpaid on 31 March 2026 because of a cash crunch, and an income-tax demand of 1.6 crore rupees dated August 2025 is also unpaid; the company has written twice to the Assessing Officer objecting to it but has filed no appeal. Third, a term loan instalment of 75 lakh rupees due to Sahyadri Bank on 31 December 2025 was paid on 20 February 2026, and during the year 3 crore rupees drawn on the cash credit was used to buy a new packaging line, which the board minutes describe as "temporary, pending a term loan".

items.stem: On the GST and the income-tax demand alone, how are they reported under clause (vii) of CARO 2020?

options.text: Both under clause (vii)(a): the company has not been regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues, and the arrears outstanding at 31 March 2026 for more than six months from the date they became payable are stated — the 42 lakh rupees of GST and the 1.6 crore rupees of income tax — with nothing under clause (vii)(b), because letters to the Assessing Officer are a mere representation and not a dispute
options.why: Clause (vii)(a) opens on punctuality — is the company handing over the statutory dues nobody contests when they fall due, Goods and Services Tax and income-tax among them — and where it is not, the annexure has to carry a figure. That figure is what was still owed at the close of the year, counting only dues that had by then been sitting unpaid for more than six months. June 2025 GST unpaid on 31 March 2026 clears that line, and so does a demand raised in August 2025. The demand looks at first as though it belongs in (vii)(b), the home of dues withheld because a fight is on — until the bracket inside that clause is read. Writing to the department that raised a demand is a mere representation, and the clause refuses to dignify it as a dispute. Two letters to the Assessing Officer with no appeal behind them is precisely that, so the 1.6 crore rupees is undisputed for this purpose and sits beside the 42 lakh rupees under (vii)(a). A cash crunch explains why the money never went; it does not move the amount to a different clause.

options.text: The GST under clause (vii)(a) as an arrear of more than six months, and the income-tax demand under clause (vii)(b) as a disputed due, naming the Assessing Officer as the forum where the dispute is pending
options.misconception: treats objections written to the department as a dispute with a forum, when the clause says a mere representation is not a dispute
options.why: This is the reading the company would prefer, and the clause shuts it inside its own bracket: a mere representation made to the department concerned is not to be counted as a dispute. What (vii)(b) is built for is a due held back because a matter is live before some forum — an appellate authority, a tribunal, a court — which is why it wants the amount and the forum named together. Letters to the officer who issued the demand give you a correspondent, not a forum. The demand is therefore undisputed for the clause, and joins the arrears of more than six months under (vii)(a).

options.text: Only a statement under clause (vii)(a) that the company has not been regular, without amounts, since the arrears will be stated in the notes to the accounts and the clause only asks about regularity
options.misconception: reads clause (vii)(a) as a yes-or-no on regularity, when it requires the arrears over six months to be quantified in the report
options.why: Regularity is the clause's opening question, not its only one. Where a company has not been regular, the clause goes on to demand a number: how much was still owed when the year closed, limited to dues that had been payable for over six months by that date. The figure is the report. Whatever the notes to the accounts carry, the CARO annexure states the arrears itself — 42 lakh rupees of GST and 1.6 crore rupees of income tax standing at 31 March 2026.

options.text: Nothing, if both amounts are paid before the auditor signs the report, since clause (vii) looks at the position on the date of the report
options.misconception: measures the arrears at the date of the report, when the clause measures them on the last day of the financial year
options.why: The clause pins its own measuring date, and it is the close of the financial year, not the day of signature: what stood in arrears then, counting dues payable for over six months by then. Money paid in April or May 2026 cannot alter what was unpaid on 31 March 2026, and the clause's opening question — was the company punctual with these dues — is answered by the whole year's conduct rather than by the state of play on signing day. A payment made afterwards can be recorded as a fact; it does not lift the arrears out of the annexure.

citation.ref: paragraph 3, clause (vii)(a) — whether statutory dues that nobody contests are paid over on time, and the figure the annexure must carry when they are not; clause (vii)(b) — dues held back over a live dispute, the particulars wanted, and the bracket that keeps a letter to the department from counting as one

items.scenario: Meghdoot Agro Industries Limited is an unlisted public company that mills and packs pulses, and Desai & Kulkarni are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. CARO 2020 applies to it. Three matters are on the partner's list. First, the company holds cash credit limits of 6 crore rupees from Sahyadri Bank and 3 crore rupees from Konkan Bank, both secured by hypothecation of stock and receivables; the quarterly stock and receivable statements filed with the two banks for June and September 2025 show inventory of 6.4 crore rupees and 5.9 crore rupees, against 5.1 crore rupees and 5.2 crore rupees in the books on those dates, and the finance manager says the statements were "provisional figures, and neither bank has ever raised a query". Second, GST of 42 lakh rupees for June 2025 was still unpaid on 31 March 2026 because of a cash crunch, and an income-tax demand of 1.6 crore rupees dated August 2025 is also unpaid; the company has written twice to the Assessing Officer objecting to it but has filed no appeal. Third, a term loan instalment of 75 lakh rupees due to Sahyadri Bank on 31 December 2025 was paid on 20 February 2026, and during the year 3 crore rupees drawn on the cash credit was used to buy a new packaging line, which the board minutes describe as "temporary, pending a term loan".

items.stem: On the late instalment and the packaging line alone, what goes into the report under clause (ix) of CARO 2020?

options.text: Under clause (ix)(a), the default to Sahyadri Bank — term loan, 75 lakh rupees of principal not paid on the due date, 51 days of delay — even though it was made good before the year end; and under clause (ix)(d), that funds raised on a short-term basis have been used for long-term purposes, stating the nature and the amount: 3 crore rupees of cash credit spent on a packaging line
options.why: Clause (ix)(a) asks whether the company has defaulted in repayment of loans or borrowings or in the payment of interest to any lender, and its format is built for exactly this case: the nature of the borrowing, the lender, the amount not paid on the due date, whether principal or interest, and the number of days of delay "or unpaid". A column for days of delay only makes sense for a default that was later paid; an instalment due on 31 December and paid on 20 February is 51 days of delay on 75 lakh rupees of term loan principal, and the report says so, lender by lender. Clause (ix)(d) asks the separate question whether funds raised on a short-term basis have been utilised for long-term purposes, and if yes, the nature and the amount to be indicated. A cash credit is short-term money and a packaging line is a long-term asset; the board's word "temporary" and the term loan it hopes for describe an intention, and the clause reports what was done: 3 crore rupees.

options.text: The late instalment under clause (ix)(a), and the packaging line under clause (ix)(c) as a term loan not applied for the purpose for which it was obtained
options.misconception: treats a cash credit spent on a fixed asset as a diverted term loan under (ix)(c), when it is short-term funds used for long-term purposes under (ix)(d)
options.why: Clause (ix)(c) is about term loans: whether term loans were applied for the purpose for which they were obtained, and if not, the amount diverted and the purpose it was used for. The 3 crore rupees was not a term loan; it was drawn on the cash credit, a working capital facility raised on a short-term basis, and spent on a long-term asset. That is the question clause (ix)(d) asks — funds raised on short-term basis utilised for long-term purposes — and it is answered with the nature and the amount. Putting it under (ix)(c) names the wrong facility and the wrong test.

options.text: Nothing under clause (ix)(a), because the instalment was paid before 31 March 2026 and there was no default outstanding at the year end; the packaging line under clause (ix)(d)
options.misconception: reports only defaults still unpaid at the balance sheet date, when the clause and its format cover defaults during the year with their days of delay
options.why: The clause asks whether the company has defaulted, not whether a default is outstanding at the year end, and the format it prescribes carries a column for the number of days of delay — a column that would be empty in every report if only unpaid defaults were reported. A 75 lakh rupee instalment paid 51 days after its due date was a default in repayment during the year, and it is reported as such with the days of delay. The packaging line is rightly placed under (ix)(d), which is why this option is half the answer.

options.text: Under clause (ix)(a), a default of 3 crore rupees to Sahyadri Bank, because using the cash credit for a machine breaches the sanction terms, with the late instalment noted as cured
options.misconception: reads a breach of the sanction's purpose as a repayment default under (ix)(a), and softens the real default into a note
options.why: Spending a cash credit on a machine may breach the sanction, but a breach of terms is not a default in repayment: nothing fell due on the 3 crore rupees and went unpaid. Clause (ix)(a) reports amounts not paid on their due date, and the only one of those is the 75 lakh rupee instalment, 51 days late, which is reported in full and not merely "noted as cured". The 3 crore rupees has its own home in clause (ix)(d), as short-term funds used for long-term purposes, with the nature and amount stated.

items.stem: On the vendor master alone, what does SA 265 require of the auditors?

options.text: Leave it out, since a deficiency is significant only where the audit has found a misstatement that flowed from it, and the sample was clean
options.misconception: makes a found misstatement the test of significance, when SA 265 tests likelihood and potential magnitude
options.why: This is the finance head's argument, and SA 265 rejects it in terms: significance depends not only on whether a misstatement has actually occurred but also on the likelihood that one could occur and the potential magnitude of it, and significant deficiencies may exist even though no misstatement was identified during the audit. A control whose absence lets one person create a supplier and pay it is judged by what it could let through, not by whether it did this year.

options.text: Treat it as a significant deficiency, because significance turns on the likelihood and potential magnitude of a misstatement and not only on whether one has occurred, and communicate it in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and to management
options.why: A deficiency in internal control exists where a control needed to prevent, or detect and correct, misstatements on a timely basis is missing, and no review of changes to the vendor master by the person who also pays the vendors is a missing control over a route by which money leaves the company. SA 265 says the significance of a deficiency depends not only on whether a misstatement has actually occurred but on the likelihood that one could and its potential magnitude, so significant deficiencies may exist even though the auditor found no misstatement, and the susceptibility to loss of an asset is a factor. Sixty clean payments out of nine thousand say the year happened to be clean; they do not make the control exist. Once it is significant, the standard is precise: in writing, to those charged with governance, on a timely basis, and also to management at an appropriate level.

options.text: Mention it orally to the finance head, because deficiencies go to management and only matters affecting the opinion go to the board
options.misconception: routes every deficiency to management alone, when a significant one goes in writing to those charged with governance
options.why: SA 265 sends significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance, and separately to management; the board is not spared them because the opinion is unaffected. Other, lesser deficiencies of sufficient importance go to management, and that is the only tier where the board drops out. An oral word to the finance head meets neither requirement for a significant deficiency, and the standard's reason for writing is that a letter the board has read is what a later loss will be measured against.

options.text: Qualify the audit report, since a control over supplier payments is missing and the auditor cannot rely on the payables balance
options.misconception: turns a control deficiency into a modification, when the evidence on the balance was obtained by other means
options.why: The auditors tested payments directly and found them correct, so they have their evidence on the balance by substantive work; a weak control changes how much of that work is needed, not whether an opinion can be formed. SA 265 exists precisely for deficiencies that do not reach the opinion: they are communicated in writing to those charged with governance and management rather than reported to the shareholders. A qualification needs a material misstatement or an inability to obtain evidence, and there is neither here.
