items.scenario: Nandini Dairy Products Limited is an unlisted public company that collects milk from forty village centres and sells packaged curd and ghee, and Pillai & Associates are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The company's only directors are the two brothers who founded it, and between them they run purchasing, finance and sales; there is no audit committee and no independent director. The audit manager is drafting the closing letter to the board and has three notes on his desk. First, the accounts clerk who processes supplier payments can also add and change entries in the vendor master file, and nobody reviews those changes; the auditors tested a sample of 60 payments of the year's 9,000 and found every one of them correct, and the finance head says "nothing went wrong, so there is nothing to write". Second, the manager's draft letter sets out at length the written representations the firm is requesting and the four accounting questions the audit team argued over with the finance head during the year, "because SA 260 lists them". Third, the fixed asset register reached the auditors five weeks after it was asked for, the payables to milk centres could be verified only by sending two staff to read paper registers at eleven centres, and the audit finished three weeks past the agreed date; the manager has left all this out of the letter as "our problem, not the board's".

items.stem: On the manager's second note alone, is he right that SA 260 requires those two matters in the letter to this board?

options.text: No: since the directors are the management, SA 260 does not apply at all and no governance letter is needed for a company without an audit committee
options.misconception: treats an owner-managed board as outside SA 260, when the standard names that case and keeps most of the list
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) applies whatever shape the board takes. Its definition of a governing body turns on the job — overseeing where the company is headed and answering for how it is run — not on whether the people doing that job also hold executive posts, and the standard expressly contemplates boards where some or all of them do. When they do, two entries drop out of the findings; the letter itself does not. The brothers are still told what the auditor is responsible for, how the audit was planned and timed, what the auditor makes of their accounting practices, the significant difficulties met along the way, and anything bearing on the report.

options.text: No: the arguments with the finance head and the written representations being sought are the two entries SA 260 drops where every member of the governing body is also involved in managing the business, which is Nandini's position exactly; the views on accounting practices, significant difficulties and matters affecting the report still go
options.why: Two entries on the SA 260 (Revised) roster of significant findings come with a proviso the rest lack. Where a board oversees people other than itself, the auditor tells it what was argued out with those people during the year and what written representations are being asked for; where the board IS those people, both entries drop away. Nandini's governing body is the two founding brothers, and purchasing, finance and sales are run between them, so every member of it is also involved in managing the business — and telling the brothers what the brothers disputed with their own finance head, or what they will shortly be handed to sign, tells them nothing they did not already know. Nothing else on the roster moves. This board is still owed the auditor's view of how good its accounting practices are, the significant difficulties the audit ran into, anything that will shape the report, and whatever else bears on its oversight.

options.text: Yes: every item on the SA 260 list of significant findings is communicated to those charged with governance whoever they are, and the manager should keep both in
options.misconception: reads the SA 260 list as unconditional, when two of its items apply only where governance and management are different people
options.why: The roster is not flat. Two of its entries — what was argued out with management, and the representations the auditor is asking for in writing — carry a proviso the rest do not: they are owed only where the people who govern and the people who run the business are different sets. Nandini's board is its two founding brothers, who between them run purchasing, finance and sales, so the proviso bites and those two entries are not required. Reading every entry as unconditional is exactly the mistake the manager has made.

options.text: Yes for the written representations, no for the accounting disagreements, because representations are a formal document the board must approve
options.misconception: splits the two conditional items, when SA 260 attaches the same condition to both
options.why: One proviso governs both entries, and SA 260 (Revised) sets them side by side under it: the arguments had with management and the representations sought in writing are owed only where the governing body is made up of people other than those running the business. Nothing separates them. The representations here will be signed by these same brothers under SA 580, wearing their management hats; handing them as a governance matter a document they will sign as managers adds nothing, and that is the whole reason the proviso exists.

citation.ref: which of the audit's significant findings reach the governing body, and the two entries on that roster — the arguments had with management, and the representations being sought in writing — that fall away where the same people both govern and run the business

items.scenario: Nandini Dairy Products Limited is an unlisted public company that collects milk from forty village centres and sells packaged curd and ghee, and Pillai & Associates are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The company's only directors are the two brothers who founded it, and between them they run purchasing, finance and sales; there is no audit committee and no independent director. The audit manager is drafting the closing letter to the board and has three notes on his desk. First, the accounts clerk who processes supplier payments can also add and change entries in the vendor master file, and nobody reviews those changes; the auditors tested a sample of 60 payments of the year's 9,000 and found every one of them correct, and the finance head says "nothing went wrong, so there is nothing to write". Second, the manager's draft letter sets out at length the written representations the firm is requesting and the four accounting questions the audit team argued over with the finance head during the year, "because SA 260 lists them". Third, the fixed asset register reached the auditors five weeks after it was asked for, the payables to milk centres could be verified only by sending two staff to read paper registers at eleven centres, and the audit finished three weeks past the agreed date; the manager has left all this out of the letter as "our problem, not the board's".

items.stem: On the manager's third note alone, what does SA 260 say about leaving these matters out?

options.text: The manager is right: the cost and timing of the audit are matters between the firm and the management under the engagement letter, not findings from the audit
options.misconception: files the audit's difficulties under fees and timing, when SA 260 lists them as a finding to communicate
options.why: Fees and dates are the engagement letter's business. Quite separately, SA 260 (Revised) makes the trouble met during the audit a significant finding owed to the governing body, and the shapes it names are exactly these — management taking too long, papers that were not there, effort nobody expected to spend. Telling the board is not a complaint about time. It is that trouble of this kind can harden into a limit on scope, and the people who oversee the reporting ought to hear it from the auditor rather than read it in a modified opinion.

options.text: They are significant difficulties encountered during the audit and must be communicated: SA 260 names significant delays by management and extensive unexpected effort to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence among them, and such difficulties can amount to a scope limitation
options.why: The trouble an audit runs into is its own entry on the SA 260 (Revised) roster of significant findings, and no proviso hangs off it. What the standard treats as significant difficulties runs to a handful of familiar shapes: delays by management, the people or the papers the auditor expected not being there, a window too short to finish in, unexpected effort on a scale nobody budgeted for, and limits management itself imposes. A fixed asset register that took five weeks to appear is the first shape; two staff sent to read paper registers at eleven village centres is the fourth. The standard then adds the reason a board hears about any of it — difficulties like these can, in the right circumstances, harden into a limit on scope and pull the opinion with them. That makes them the board's problem well before they become the report's.

options.text: They are communicated in writing to management under SA 265 as a deficiency in internal control, not to the board under SA 260
options.misconception: confuses the audit's difficulties with a control deficiency, when SA 260 and SA 265 cover different things
options.why: SA 265 is about deficiencies in internal control — a control that fails to prevent or detect misstatements, or a needed control that is missing. A late register and paper records at village centres may say something about record-keeping, but what the audit manager is sitting on is the audit's own experience of delay and extra effort, and SA 260 (Revised) names that experience as a significant difficulty to be communicated to those charged with governance. The two standards answer different questions and one does not stand in for the other.

options.text: They go in only if the auditor ends up modifying the opinion because of them; an audit that finished with a clean opinion had no significant difficulty
options.misconception: makes a modified opinion the trigger for reporting difficulties, when SA 260 lists them as a finding on their own
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) keeps these two apart on its roster. Whatever will shape how the report reads is one entry; the trouble the audit ran into is a different entry, and the second does not wait on the first. The standard puts it as a possibility — difficulties like these may, in some circumstances, become a limit on scope — and it wants them reported as difficulties whether or not they ever get that far. A clean opinion at the end says the evidence was got in spite of the delays; it does not say the delays were small.

citation.ref: the entry on the significant-findings roster covering the trouble the audit itself ran into — what the standard counts as such trouble, and when trouble of that kind starts to look like a limit on the audit's scope

items.stem: On the Kenyan subsidiary alone, what does the guidance require of the partner?

options.text: Consolidate the management accounts as they are and add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph stating that the Kenyan component is unaudited; the reader is then informed and the opinion stays unmodified.
options.misconception: Uses a paragraph that describes a matter as a cure for evidence that was never obtained.
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph draws attention to something properly presented in the financial statements; it does not supply the audit evidence the module says is missing for the unaudited amounts. The module's route for an unaudited component is an evaluation of a possible modification under SA 705, not a paragraph.

options.text: The component's figures should be audited or subjected to audit procedures, by the firm itself if nobody else will, and the absence of a local audit requirement does not change that. If the figures still remain unaudited, the partner treats them as consolidated amounts for which sufficient appropriate audit evidence has not been obtained, evaluates both qualitative and quantitative factors on their possible effect, and considers a modification of the opinion under SA 705. A paragraph describing them as unaudited is not a substitute for that evaluation.
options.why: The module sets the rule in two steps. The starting expectation is that everything folded into a group's accounts has been audited, or has at least had audit procedures run over it, in a group spread across locations — and the work may be done either by the firm signing the group report or by the component's own auditor. So the first answer to a component nobody audits is that the group auditor performs the procedures himself. Should a component still be unaudited when the group report is drawn, the firm signing that report has to bring it into the question of whether the opinion is modified, and the module gives the reason: nothing has furnished the auditor sufficient appropriate audit evidence over those amounts and balances. What the gap could mean is then weighed both in kind and in size, with SA 705 in hand. A director's certificate is not audit evidence, and a paragraph that says so describes a hole rather than filling it. In short, the figures are subjected to audit procedures, and what remains unaudited is weighed on qualitative and quantitative factors for a modification under SA 705.

options.text: Leave the Kenyan subsidiary out of the consolidation until it is audited and disclose the exclusion; a set of consolidated statements should carry only audited components.
options.misconception: Fixes the auditor's evidence problem by editing the group.
options.why: The consolidation is management's, and the group's composition is not changed to suit the auditor's evidence. The module's answer to an unaudited component is procedures on it and, failing that, an evaluation of a possible modification of the report, not the removal of a subsidiary from the group.

options.text: Because Kenyan law does not require an audit, the component is outside the guidance; consolidate the figures on the CFO's certificate and report nothing.
options.misconception: Lets the component's local audit exemption stand in for the group auditor's evidence.
options.why: The module's rule is that all components in a consolidation should be audited or subjected to audit procedures, and it addresses components that "continue to remain unaudited" without any exception for a jurisdiction that does not require an audit. Local law decides whether the subsidiary needs its own audit; it does not decide what evidence the group's auditor needs.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: every component folded into a group's accounts is expected to have been audited, or at least to have had audit procedures run over it, whether by the firm signing the group report or by the component's own auditor; a component still unaudited when that report is drawn goes into the group auditor's thinking on whether to modify, since nothing has furnished him sufficient appropriate audit evidence over those amounts, and he weighs what the gap could mean in kind and in size with SA 705 in hand

items.scenario: Rathi & Iyer are the auditors of Narmada Agro Holdings Limited, a listed company in Indore that consolidates six subsidiaries, and the partner is finalising the report on the consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Consolidated revenue is 1,600 crore rupees and consolidated total assets are 2,100 crore rupees. Three matters are open. First, Narmada East Africa Limited, a seed distributor in Kenya, carries 9 per cent of consolidated total assets and 6 per cent of consolidated revenue; the law of its country does not require an audit for a company of its size, and its accounts have arrived certified by its own directors and nobody else. The group CFO says the firm should "consolidate the management accounts, and add a paragraph to the report saying the Kenyan numbers are unaudited, the way a note would". Second, two Indian subsidiaries are audited by other firms and together carry 28 per cent of consolidated total assets and 31 per cent of consolidated revenue; their reports are unmodified and have been furnished to the partner. The CFO wants the Other Matter paragraph to state those percentages "after eliminating the intra-group sales, because that is what the group really reports", and the senior on the job has written that the paragraph "reads like a qualification we do not mean". Third, during the year the parent raised its holding in Narmada Fertilisers Private Limited from 60 per cent to 75 per cent, and that subsidiary sold fertiliser stock to the parent at a margin of 20 per cent, of which 14 crore rupees remained in the parent's closing inventory at the year end. The CFO's consolidation file treats both under one heading, "acquisition adjustments, done once and carried forward", and the elimination of unrealised profit in inventory is the figure computed at the previous year end, brought forward without change.

items.stem: On the two subsidiaries audited by other firms alone, how are they shown in the report, and are the CFO and the senior right?

options.text: Because the two reports are unmodified, no reference to the other auditors is needed at all; the paragraph exists only to carry a component auditor's qualification up to group level.
options.misconception: Confuses the Other Matter reference with the treatment of a component auditor's modified opinion.
options.why: The paragraph is about magnitude and divided responsibility, not about modifications: the module has it disclose the portion of the statements audited by others whenever the auditor considers such a reference necessary, and it is precisely not a qualification. A component auditor's modification is dealt with separately, through the group auditor's own evaluation of materiality to the group.

options.text: The senior is right: naming another auditor's work in the report limits the parent's auditor's responsibility for those components, and a limit on responsibility is a qualification, so the paragraph should be dropped and the opinion left clean.
options.misconception: Reads a statement of divided responsibility as a modification of the opinion.
options.why: The module says that reference is no qualification of the opinion; it marks divided responsibility as between the two sets of auditors. It discloses who did which audit, and dropping it would hide from the reader that 28 per cent of the assets were audited by somebody else.

options.text: The report discloses the magnitude of what the other auditors audited, as rupee amounts or percentages of total assets, revenues and cash flows, and those figures are presented before giving effect to the consolidation adjustments, so the CFO's post-elimination percentages are wrong. The senior is wrong too: nothing in that paragraph is a qualification of the opinion. It marks divided responsibility — part of the underlying audit work was done by the parent's auditors and part by the subsidiaries'.
options.why: One passage of the module disposes of both objections. Where the firm signing the group report judges a reference to the other auditors' work to be called for, the report has to make plain how large that slice was, and the way to make it plain is a rupee total, or a share of the assets, the revenue and the cash flows brought in by components the parent's auditor did not audit. Then comes the sentence the CFO has not read: those component figures go in before giving effect to any permanent or current period consolidation adjustment. So the 31 per cent of revenue is stated as the subsidiaries' own revenue, intra-group sales and all, because the paragraph exists to say how much of the underlying audit work belonged to somebody else, and eliminations are the parent's arithmetic rather than the component auditor's. The senior's worry is answered in the same place: saying that other auditors did part of the group's audit is no qualification of the opinion at all, but a statement of divided responsibility as between the parent's auditors and those of its subsidiaries. In short, magnitudes are presented before giving effect to the consolidation adjustments, and the paragraph marks divided responsibility rather than a qualification of the opinion.

options.text: The CFO is right: the paragraph describes the consolidated financial statements, so the percentages must be of the consolidated figures after eliminations, otherwise they overstate the other auditors' share of what the group reports.
options.misconception: Measures the other auditors' share against the group's arithmetic instead of their own audited figures.
options.why: The module is explicit that the component figures go in before giving effect to any permanent or current period consolidation adjustment. The figure measures the other auditors' work, which was done on the components' own statements before any elimination.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: an auditor who thinks a reference to the other auditors' work is called for must make the report show plainly how large that slice was — rupee totals, or shares of the assets, the revenue and the cash flows brought in by components the parent's auditor did not audit, taken before any permanent or current period consolidation adjustment is applied; and that reference reads as responsibility divided between the parent's auditors and those of its subsidiaries, never as a qualification of the opinion

items.stem: On the Narmada Fertilisers adjustments alone, is the CFO's single heading right, and what does the partner verify?

options.text: No. The rise from 60 to 75 per cent is a change in shareholding, which is a permanent consolidation adjustment: goodwill or capital reserve and the equity attributable to non-controlling interests are redetermined, with attention to the date of investment and the pre-acquisition reserves. The unrealised profit in the parent's inventory is a current period adjustment made afresh for this year on the 14 crore rupees actually held, with the deferred tax on the elimination, and the previous year's figure cannot be carried forward.
options.why: The module keeps the two kinds of adjustment apart by when they fall due. A permanent consolidation adjustment is made the first time an entity is consolidated, and again whenever the parent's holding in that entity moves: goodwill or capital reserve is worked out, and so is the equity belonging to the minority, or non-controlling, interest. The auditor checks those computations, looks hard at the pre-acquisition reserves and at the dates on which the investments were made, and checks what a later purchase of shares in a component does to them. Going from 60 to 75 per cent is such a later purchase. A current period adjustment, by contrast, belongs to the year being consolidated, and the module puts unrealised intra-group profit on assets moved between components, together with the deferred tax booked on that elimination, among them. Profit sitting in this year's closing inventory is this year's figure: 20 per cent margin on the 14 crore rupees held at 31 March 2026, not on whatever was held a year earlier, so a brought-forward elimination is wrong in amount as well as in kind. In short, the shareholding change is a permanent consolidation adjustment, the unrealised profit is a current period adjustment, and the two are verified on their own terms.

options.text: Yes. Both items arise from the parent's relationship with the same subsidiary, and once an adjustment for a subsidiary has been computed on acquisition it is carried forward until the subsidiary is disposed of.
options.misconception: Treats every adjustment involving a subsidiary as a one-time acquisition entry.
options.why: Only the permanent adjustments are carried between periods, and even those are recomputed when the shareholding changes. The module places the elimination of unrealised intra-group profit among the current period adjustments, made in the period being consolidated, so a figure brought forward from last year is not an adjustment for this year at all.

options.text: The unrealised profit needs no elimination, because the sale was at arm's length and the subsidiary is 75 per cent owned rather than wholly owned; only wholly owned subsidiaries' intra-group profits are eliminated.
options.misconception: Limits intra-group elimination to wholly owned subsidiaries.
options.why: The module lists unrealised intra-group profits on assets transferred between components as a current period consolidation adjustment without any condition on the percentage held or on the pricing of the transfer. A 75 per cent subsidiary is consolidated in full, and the profit its sale left in the parent's inventory has not been earned by the group.

options.text: Both are current period adjustments, because both happened during the year; goodwill is simply remeasured every year like any other balance.
options.misconception: Sorts adjustments by when the event happened instead of by what kind of adjustment it is.
options.why: The module defines permanent adjustments by the occasion that triggers them: the first consolidation or a change in shareholding, when goodwill or capital reserve and the non-controlling interest are determined. An increase from 60 to 75 per cent is that occasion, and the adjustment it produces is permanent, not a yearly remeasurement.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: permanent consolidation adjustments are made only on the first occasion, or on subsequent occasions when there is a change in the shareholding of a consolidated entity, and consist of determining goodwill or capital reserve and the equity attributable to non-controlling interests, with particular attention to pre-acquisition reserves and the dates of investment; current period consolidation adjustments are made in the accounting period being consolidated and relate mainly to eliminating intra-group transactions and balances, including unrealised intra-group profits on assets transferred between components and the deferred tax on that elimination

items.scenario: Rathi & Iyer are the auditors of Narmada Agro Holdings Limited, a listed company in Indore that consolidates six subsidiaries, and the partner is finalising the report on the consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Consolidated revenue is 1,600 crore rupees and consolidated total assets are 2,100 crore rupees. Three matters are open. First, Narmada East Africa Limited, a seed distributor in Kenya, carries 9 per cent of consolidated total assets and 6 per cent of consolidated revenue; the law of its country does not require an audit for a company of its size, and its accounts have arrived certified by its own directors and nobody else. The group CFO says the firm should "consolidate the management accounts, and add a paragraph to the report saying the Kenyan numbers are unaudited, the way a note would". Second, two Indian subsidiaries are audited by other firms and together carry 28 per cent of consolidated total assets and 31 per cent of consolidated revenue; their reports are unmodified and have been furnished to the partner. The CFO wants the Other Matter paragraph to state those percentages "after eliminating the intra-group sales, because that is what the group really reports", and the senior on the job has written that the paragraph "reads like a qualification we do not mean". Third, during the year the parent raised its holding in Narmada Fertilisers Private Limited from 60 per cent to 75 per cent, and that subsidiary sold fertiliser stock to the parent at a margin of 20 per cent, of which 14 crore rupees remained in the parent's closing inventory at the year end. The CFO's consolidation file treats both under one heading, "acquisition adjustments, done once and carried forward", and the elimination of unrealised profit in inventory is the figure computed at the previous year end, brought forward without change.

items.stem: On the resignation alone, how should clause (xviii) be answered?

options.text: By stating that there was a resignation and what Deepa made of what the outgoing auditors had raised. The second limb is about the issues, objections or concerns themselves, so she first has to find out what they were: a letter offering only "professional pre-occupation" names the one reason ICAI's announcement puts out of bounds at an unlisted company, so the departing firm is asked in writing for its real ones, and the useful-life disagreement she was told of on the telephone is a concern raised, to be followed through in the audit of the spinning frames and reported as considered. "No issues raised" is neither the question the clause puts nor the truth on the file.
options.why: The clause has two limbs and the draft answers the first while misstating the second. The first limb is the bare fact that an auditor went during the year. The second reports what the incoming partner made of the issues, objections or concerns the departing firm had raised — which only means anything if she found out what they were. The letter on the file does not tell her. ICAI's announcement, carried in the module, shuts off "professional pre-occupation" as a reason an unlisted company's auditor may give, and asks instead for the reasons set out plainly in the letter to the company; so a letter resting on that phrase alone is one the departing firm should not have written and one Menon & Thakur cannot take as the whole account. What the telephone call supplied is the concern the letter left out — a disagreement over the useful life of the spinning frames — and a concern is no less raised for having been spoken rather than typed. Considering it means what it sounds like: the useful life goes into this year's audit of property, plant and equipment, its effect on the opening balances and on the depreciation charge is worked out, and the clause then records that the concern was weighed. Nothing here makes Deepa adopt the outgoing auditors' view of the useful life; she must weigh it and say she did. In short, the answer records that an auditor went, says what became of the issues, objections or concerns the outgoing auditors had raised, and treats a letter pleading professional pre-occupation as the reason to go and ask for them.

options.text: By stating the resignation and adopting the outgoing auditors' position on the useful life of the spinning frames, since the clause exists to stop a company shopping for a more agreeable auditor and the incoming firm must therefore hold the outgoing firm's line.
options.misconception: Turns "taken into consideration" into "bound by".
options.why: The clause asks whether the auditor has taken into consideration what the outgoing auditors raised, not whether she has adopted it; the useful life is audited on its own evidence this year, and the answer reports that the concern was considered and what came of it.

options.text: The clause is not engaged, because it applies only where the auditors resigned in protest or over a dispute with the company, and a resignation for pre-occupation is a routine casual vacancy reported under section 139 rather than under CARO.
options.misconception: Narrows "any resignation" to a contested one.
options.why: Clause 3(xviii) reaches every resignation by a statutory auditor in the year and sorts them into no kinds at all; and the reason actually given is the one ICAI's announcement says shall not be given, so it is no ground for calling this departure routine.

options.text: As drafted. The clause asks only whether a resignation occurred and whether the outgoing auditors raised issues in writing; the letter raises none, and a remark on the telephone before appointment is not something the clause can be answered on.
options.misconception: Reads "raised" as "raised in a letter".
options.why: The clause speaks of issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors and does not confine them to writing, and the module's own announcement makes the letter's sole reason one an auditor of an unlisted company shall not give; a concern the incoming partner was told of is one she has to take into consideration and report on.

citation.ref: clause 3(xviii) on a statutory auditor's resignation in the year and on what the incoming auditor made of anything the departing firm had raised, read with ICAI's announcement, which puts "professional pre-occupation" out of bounds as the stated reason at an unlisted company and asks for the real ones, plainly, in the letter

items.scenario: Menon & Thakur were appointed in September 2025 to fill a casual vacancy at Penna Spinning Mills Limited, an unlisted public company at Guntur with revenue of 420 crore rupees, after the previous auditors resigned in August. Deepa Menon is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026, and three things sit in the draft of the CARO annexure. First, the outgoing firm's resignation letter to the company gives "professional pre-occupation" as its only reason; when Deepa telephoned its partner before accepting, she was told of a disagreement with the company over the useful life assigned to the spinning frames that "was never put in writing", and the manager's draft under clause (xviii) reads that there was a resignation and that the outgoing auditors raised no issues. Second, the company's own working, checked by the team, shows cash losses of 12 crore rupees this year and 9 crore rupees in the year before, and the manager proposes to answer clause (xvii) with a bare "yes" for the current year only, without amounts, since the earlier year was audited by the previous firm and "a figure invites questions". Third, the current ratio is 0.7, three-tenths of the receivables are older than 180 days, a term loan instalment of 60 crore rupees falls due in November 2026, and the board's plan is a rights issue supported by a promoter's letter of comfort; the manager proposes to answer clause (xix) that no material uncertainty exists, on the strength of the promoter's letter alone, and to leave the going-concern assessment out of the audit report "because CARO now covers it".

items.stem: On the loss figures alone, how is clause (xvii) answered?

options.text: As the manager drafts it, but with the basis added. A "yes" is a complete answer where the amounts are visible in the financial statements, and paragraph 4 requires only that the basis for an unfavourable answer be stated, which the loss figures in the accounts supply.
options.misconception: Lets the accounts answer a clause that asks for a figure.
options.why: The clause itself says "if so, state the amount of cash losses", so the amount is part of the answer and not something the reader is sent to the accounts to find; paragraph 4's requirement to state the basis is in addition to the amount, not instead of it.

options.text: The current year only, with its amount. The immediately preceding year was audited and reported on by the previous firm, whose CARO annexure already dealt with it, and an auditor cannot report under CARO on a year he did not audit.
options.misconception: Ties the clause's reach to the auditor's own tenure.
options.why: The clause names the immediately preceding financial year in the same breath as the current one and does not condition it on who audited that year; the present auditor answers for both on the evidence available, and states the amount for each.

options.text: Neither year, because the clause reports a fact that the financial statements already show and CARO exists to report matters the accounts do not; the losses are addressed instead under the going-concern paragraph of the main report.
options.misconception: Treats CARO as a report only on what is otherwise hidden.
options.why: Paragraph 3 requires a statement on each specified matter, and clause 3(xvii) asks for the cash losses of both years with their amounts whether or not the accounts show them; the going-concern reporting is a separate matter and does not replace a CARO clause.

options.text: Both years, both amounts. Two years are inside the clause — the one under audit and the immediately preceding financial year — and where cash losses were run in them it asks the auditor to state the amount for each; who held the appointment in the earlier year narrows nothing, so the answer carries 12 crore rupees this year and 9 crore rupees the year before. A "yes" with no figures leaves out what was asked for, and paragraph 4 makes an unfavourable or qualified answer carry its basis as well.
options.why: Each of the manager's three shortcuts is disposed of by the clause's own reach. Two years are named in it, the one under audit and the immediately preceding financial year, so the reach back belongs to the clause and does not turn on who held the appointment then; the earlier year is answered on the evidence now to hand, which here is the company's working that the team has checked. Next it asks the auditor to state the amount for each of those years, so a bare "yes" answers half of it — the figures are the substance of the report, and a worry that a number invites questions argues for the number rather than against it. Paragraph 4 of the Order adds one thing more: an answer to any paragraph 3 matter that is unfavourable or qualified comes with the basis on which it was given, so the losses reported bring the working behind them. What is reported here is a fact about two years that has run; by itself it says nothing about what happens next, which is the business of the going-concern work and of a different clause, and that is no licence to soften this one. In short, both years are covered, the auditor must state the amount for each, and an unfavourable or qualified answer comes with its basis.

citation.ref: clause 3(xvii) on cash losses across two years — the one under audit and the immediately preceding financial year — with the amount to be given for each; and paragraph 4 of the Order, which adds a basis to any paragraph 3 answer that is unfavourable or qualified

First, the outgoing firm's resignation letter to the company gives "professional pre-occupation" as its only reason; when Deepa telephoned its partner before accepting, she was told of a disagreement with the company over the useful life assigned to the spinning frames that "was never put in writing", and the manager's draft under clause (xviii) reads that there was a resignation and that the outgoing auditors raised no issues. items.stem: On the ratios and the loan alone, how is clause (xix) answered?

options.text: The clause cannot be answered until the rights issue closes, because the opinion is given as on the date of the audit report and the auditor should hold the report until the money is in.
options.misconception: Turns a reporting date into a reason to delay reporting.
options.why: The clause asks for the auditor's opinion as on the date of the audit report on the basis it lists, which includes the auditor's knowledge of management plans; a plan that has not yet produced money is weighed as a plan, and where a material uncertainty remains the answer says so rather than waiting for it to clear.

options.text: As drafted. The clause turns on the auditor's knowledge of the board's plans, and a rights issue backed by the promoter in writing is the plan; the ratios describe the past and the clause is about the year ahead.
options.misconception: Reads one item on the clause's list as the whole list.
options.why: The clause lists the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of assets and payment of liabilities, and other accompanying information alongside the auditor's knowledge of management plans, so the ratios are part of the basis and not history to be set aside; and the going-concern work under SA 570 is not displaced by the clause.

options.text: On everything the clause lists, not on the letter alone. The opinion — that nothing material stands in the way, judged as at the date of the audit report — is built on the financial ratios, on when assets will turn into money and liabilities have to be met, on what travels alongside the accounts, and on what the auditor knows of the board's and management's plans; the promoter's letter is one of those inputs, set against a current ratio of 0.7, slow receivables and an instalment of 60 crore rupees falling due inside the one year from the balance sheet date. And the clause is added to the going-concern work under SA 570; it does not stand in its place.
options.why: The clause names its own evidence and its own window, and the manager's draft respects neither. Its evidence is a list: the financial ratios; how old the receivables and payables are and when each is expected to turn into money or have to be met; whatever information travels alongside the accounts; and what the auditor knows of the board's and management's plans. Its window is the twelve months after the balance sheet date, and the liabilities in question are the ones the company already carried on that date. The plan sits last on the list rather than alone on it, and it is weighed with the rest: a rights issue backed by a letter of comfort goes against a current ratio below one, receivables three-tenths of which are past 180 days, and a 60 crore rupees instalment due in November 2026 — inside the one year from the balance sheet date. Because the opinion speaks as at the date of the audit report, what has become of the rights issue by that day counts, and a letter of comfort that has not turned into money by then is weighed for what it is. The draft's second move fails too: the module's going-concern illustration has the auditor report the going concern basis and the material uncertainty under SA 570 and SA 705, and then report under clause (xix) as well. The CARO clause is an extra reporting duty and the going-concern assessment stays where it was, in the main report. In short, the whole of the clause's list is weighed together, the question is whether liabilities come due inside the one year from the balance sheet date, and the answer is given as at the date of the audit report beside the going-concern reporting rather than instead of it.
keywords: one year from the balance sheet date

options.text: By leaving clause (xix) blank and dealing with the matter under SA 570 instead, since a material uncertainty about going concern belongs in the main report and reporting it twice would contradict the opinion.
options.misconception: Treats the CARO clause and SA 570 as alternatives.
options.why: The module's going-concern illustration reports the material uncertainty in the main report under SA 570 and SA 705 and then states that the auditor is also required to report under clause (xix); the two are answered together, on the clause's own basis and window, and a blank clause is no answer at all.

citation.ref: clause 3(xix), which wants an opinion — built on the financial ratios, on when assets will turn into money and liabilities have to be met, on what travels alongside the accounts, and on what the auditor knows of the board's and management's plans — as to whether anything material stands in the way of the company meeting the liabilities it already had, over the one year from the balance sheet date, judged as at the date of the audit report; and the module's going-concern illustration, which reports under SA 570 and SA 705 and then under clause (xix) as well

items.stem: On the fraud clause alone, what does Anjali write?

options.text: Only the ADT-4 limb needs a positive answer. Because the fraud went to the Central Government under section 143(12), it is reported there and not repeated under clause (xi), and the complaints limb is answered only where the company has a formal whistle-blower policy, which an unlisted company need not have.
options.misconception: Treating the three limbs as alternatives and reading a vigil-mechanism requirement into a clause that asks only whether complaints received were considered.
options.why: The first limb reaches every fraud by or on the company that came to notice or was reported over the year, with its nature and its amount, and the second asks separately whether a section 143(12) report was filed; one does not replace the other. The third limb asks what the auditor did with whistle-blower complaints the company took in during the year, and it says nothing about a policy; a complaint received is a complaint received.

options.text: Three answers, each on its own. A fraud on the company was noticed during the year, and the nature and the amount involved is indicated: fictitious vendor invoices passed by a purchase clerk in collusion with the vendor, 1.4 crore rupees. A report under section 143(12) was filed with the Central Government in Form ADT-4, and the clause says so. And a whistle-blower complaint was received by the company during the year, so Anjali considers it herself before she answers the third limb; the clause asks whether the auditor has considered whistle-blower complaints received by the company, not whether the company found them substantiated, and a complaint closed without inquiry has not been considered by anyone.
options.why: Clause (xi) is three questions and the finance head's draft answers none of them. The first reaches every fraud, one the company committed and one worked on it, that came to notice or was reported over the year, and where there is one its nature and the amount involved go into the report; an employee's swindle of his own employer, found in August, is such a fraud, and what the clause wants is what it was and how much, not a formula leaning on what management chose to report. The second limb is about the report under sub-section (12) of section 143, made to the Central Government in Form ADT-4. This fraud was of one crore rupees or above and the hand was an employee's, so it went to the audit committee inside two days, the reply came back, and the form went in — precisely what the limb is about, and the answer is yes. The third limb turns on whistle-blower complaints the company took in during the year, and on whether the auditor turned her mind to them. One arrived. What the human resources head made of it is beside the point, because the limb is about the auditor's own work on complaints the company received, and "not applicable" belongs to a company that received none. Anjali reads the email, asks what became of it, and runs her own procedures over the dealer commissions; only then can the clause say the complaint was considered. In short, the nature and the amount involved of the fraud are stated, the report in Form ADT-4 is stated, and the whistle-blower complaints the company took in are considered by the auditor herself.

options.text: The finance head's wording is acceptable. The fraud was found by the company and reported by management, so "no fraud noticed except as reported by management" is accurate, and an email that the company itself closed as a grievance is not a whistle-blower complaint within the clause.
options.misconception: Letting management's own description of the fraud and its own closing of the complaint stand in for the auditor's answer, when both limbs are about what the auditor states and did.
options.why: The clause reaches any fraud worked on the company that came to notice or was reported over the year and wants its nature and the amount involved put down, so a formula giving neither does not answer it; and the third limb asks what the auditor did with complaints the company received, which turns on receipt, not on how the company labelled what it received.

options.text: The fraud is reported under the clause, but the Form ADT-4 limb is answered no, because a report to the audit committee under section 143(12) is what the rules require for a fraud by a clerk and the filing with the Central Government was a step too far; the email is mentioned as a matter considered.
options.misconception: Reversing the one crore rupees line in rule 13, so that the larger fraud is thought to stop at the audit committee when it is the smaller one that does.
options.why: Rule 13 sends a fraud of one crore rupees or above by officers or employees to the board or audit committee within two days and then, with their reply, to the Central Government in Form ADT-4; only a fraud below one crore rupees stops at the audit committee, and 1.4 crore rupees is above it, so the filing was required and the limb is answered yes.

citation.ref: clause (xi) of paragraph 3 puts three questions: has a fraud by the company, or one worked on it, come to notice or been reported over the year, its nature and the amount involved being stated if so; has a report gone to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 under section 143(12); and has the auditor turned her mind to whistle-blower complaints the company took in during the year

items.scenario: Sharma & Venkat are the statutory auditors of Periyar Pumps Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore with two plants, a revenue of 310 crore rupees and an audit committee, and Anjali Sharma is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three things sit in the CARO file. First, in August 2025 the company's own checks found that a purchase clerk had passed fictitious invoices from a vendor he was in league with, 1.4 crore rupees over two years; the company went to the police, Anjali reported it to the audit committee within two days, received its reply, and filed her report with the Central Government in Form ADT-4. In January 2026 an anonymous email to the company alleged that a sales manager takes kickbacks from dealers; the human resources head closed it as a personal grievance without any inquiry, and the finance head wants the fraud clause answered as "no fraud noticed except as reported by management" with the complaints limb marked not applicable "because nothing was substantiated". Second, the company bought castings worth 38 crore rupees during the year from Periyar Foundries Private Limited, a company owned by the managing director's brother, on the same price list and credit terms as its two unrelated foundries; the finance head says the purchases are in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, so section 188 does not apply, the audit committee was not told, and the draft accounts carry no related party note on them. Third, the company's internal audit for the year was done by a retired accounts clerk engaged part time, whose three short reports cover petty cash and stationery at the head office and never reached either plant or the purchase function; the finance head says the clause is answered yes because an internal auditor has been appointed, and Anjali's audit senior has not read the three reports "since they cover nothing material".

items.stem: On the castings alone, what does the related party clause require of Anjali?

options.text: Anjali answers the clause with the words "where applicable" and stops, because the clause itself allows the auditor to leave out a transaction whose status under the sections is arguable; the audit committee is a governance matter for the board's report, not for the auditor's.
options.misconception: Reading where applicable as a discretion to omit, when it only decides which of the two sections applies to a transaction that is in the clause either way.
options.why: The words where applicable qualify which of sections 177 and 188 applies to a given transaction, and they do not let the auditor drop a related party transaction from the clause; the audit committee's approval under section 177 is one of the two sections the clause names, and a missing approval is reported with its basis under paragraph 4.

options.text: The clause is not exhausted by section 188. Its subject is all transactions with the related parties, and it asks two things of them: do they comply with sections 177 and 188 where applicable, and are the details in the financial statements as the applicable accounting standards demand. Ordinary course and arm's length may carry the castings outside the approval regime of section 188, but the purchases remain a transaction with a related party: section 177 applies because the company has an audit committee that was never told, and the accounting standard wants the relationship and the dealing disclosed whether or not section 188 reaches them. Anjali reports the failure under section 177 and the missing disclosure, with the basis stated, unless the note is added and the committee's approval obtained.
options.why: The clause names three things and each can fail on its own. It reports on all transactions with the related parties, a population wider than the transactions section 188 regulates, so a transaction is not out of the clause because it is out of section 188. The words where applicable work in both directions: the section 188 limb may fall away for a purchase in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis, and the finance head is entitled to that argument if the price list and terms bear it out, but the section 177 limb does not fall away with it, because the company has an audit committee and related party transactions go to it, and this one never did. The disclosure limb stands apart from both sections: the applicable accounting standards require the details of the transaction with the managing director's brother's company to be disclosed in the financial statements, and "section 188 does not apply" is no reason for a silent note, because the standard does not ask whether section 188 applied. So the clause is answered unfavourably on section 177 and on disclosure, with the basis for that answer stated as paragraph 4 requires, unless the company puts the note in and takes the transaction to the committee before the report is signed. In short, the clause covers all transactions with the related parties, sections 177 and 188 apply where applicable and the audit committee limb applies here, and the details are disclosed as required by the applicable accounting standards regardless of section 188.
keywords: all transactions with the related parties

options.text: Every purchase from the foundry is a breach of section 188, because a transaction with a director's relative can never be at arm's length, and the clause is answered unfavourably on that ground alone; the note in the accounts is a separate matter for the audit of the financial statements and not for CARO.
options.misconception: Treating relationship as proof of non arm's length dealing and pushing the disclosure limb out of the clause, when the clause names it.
options.why: Section 188's approval regime does not reach transactions in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis, and the same price list and credit terms as two unrelated foundries is evidence of exactly that, so the section 188 limb is not the failure here; and disclosure under the applicable accounting standards is a limb of the clause itself, not a matter outside it.

options.text: The finance head is right and the clause is answered favourably. Clause (xiii) tracks section 188, and a purchase in the ordinary course of business at arm's length is outside that section, so there is nothing to approve and nothing to report; the accounting standard follows the Act.
options.misconception: Reading clause (xiii) as a report on section 188 alone, when the clause has three limbs and the disclosure limb and the audit committee limb survive the ordinary course and arm's length argument.
options.why: The clause reports on all transactions with the related parties and asks about sections 177 and 188 where applicable and about disclosure under the applicable accounting standards; the standard's disclosure requirement does not depend on section 188, and the section 177 limb applies to a company with an audit committee whether or not section 188 does.

citation.ref: clause (xiii) of paragraph 3 asks whether every dealing the company had with a related party stands within sections 177 and 188 of the Act so far as those sections reach it, and whether the details sit in the financial statements as the applicable accounting standards demand; paragraph 4 has the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer stated

items.scenario: Sharma & Venkat are the statutory auditors of Periyar Pumps Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore with two plants, a revenue of 310 crore rupees and an audit committee, and Anjali Sharma is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three things sit in the CARO file. First, in August 2025 the company's own checks found that a purchase clerk had passed fictitious invoices from a vendor he was in league with, 1.4 crore rupees over two years; the company went to the police, Anjali reported it to the audit committee within two days, received its reply, and filed her report with the Central Government in Form ADT-4. In January 2026 an anonymous email to the company alleged that a sales manager takes kickbacks from dealers; the human resources head closed it as a personal grievance without any inquiry, and the finance head wants the fraud clause answered as "no fraud noticed except as reported by management" with the complaints limb marked not applicable "because nothing was substantiated". Second, the company bought castings worth 38 crore rupees during the year from Periyar Foundries Private Limited, a company owned by the managing director's brother, on the same price list and credit terms as its two unrelated foundries; the finance head says the purchases are in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, so section 188 does not apply, the audit committee was not told, and the draft accounts carry no related party note on them. Third, the company's internal audit for the year was done by a retired accounts clerk engaged part time, whose three short reports cover petty cash and stationery at the head office and never reached either plant or the purchase function; the finance head says the clause is answered yes because an internal auditor has been appointed, and Anjali's audit senior has not read the three reports "since they cover nothing material".

items.stem: On the internal audit arrangement alone, how is clause (xiv) answered?

options.text: The first limb is answered yes because the company is under section 138 and has complied with it, and the second is answered no because reports of this quality are not the kind the statutory auditor is required to consider, which is reported as a deficiency of the company.
options.misconception: Answering the fit limb with a section 138 compliance answer, and turning the auditor's own consideration limb into a comment on the company.
options.why: Limb (a) is a question about fit, not about section 138: a company can be inside that section and have appointed someone and still fail the limb because the coverage does not match the size and nature of its business. Limb (b) is about what the statutory auditor did with the reports for the period, whatever their quality, and a no there is a statement about the auditor, not a deficiency of the company.

options.text: Two limbs, and neither is answered by the appointment. The first is a question of fit: is the internal audit arrangement commensurate with the size and nature of what this company does? A part-time retired clerk checking petty cash and stationery at the head office of a 310 crore rupee manufacturer with two plants, never once looking at purchases, is not, so the limb is answered unfavourably with the basis stated. The second limb is a statement about Anjali's own work: three reports of the Internal Auditors exist for the year, and the limb is true only if they were considered by the statutory auditor. The senior reads all three before the report is signed, and considering them is not the same as relying on them.
options.why: The clause puts two different questions and the finance head has answered a third that it does not ask. Limb (a) is not whether an internal auditor has been appointed; it asks whether the internal audit function the company actually runs is commensurate with the size and nature of what the company actually does. That is a test of fit between the function and the company, and a company can have an appointee and fail it: here the function is one part-time person, the coverage is petty cash and stationery at one office, and the two plants and the purchase function, where the year's fraud came from, were never looked at, so the arrangement is not commensurate with a two-plant manufacturer of this size and the answer is unfavourable, with the basis for that answer stated as paragraph 4 requires. Limb (b) is about the statutory auditor's own conduct rather than the reports' worth: three thin reports are still the reports of the Internal Auditors for the year, and the clause cannot truthfully say they were considered by the statutory auditor if nobody on the engagement opened them. Reading them is the whole of what that limb asks; whether any of their work can be leaned on is a separate question for SA 610, and a report considered is not a report relied on. In short, the arrangement is judged by whether it is commensurate with the size and nature of what the business does rather than by an appointment, and the reports of the Internal Auditors for the year have to be considered by the statutory auditor before the limb can be answered yes.
keywords: commensurate with the size and nature

options.text: Both limbs are answered yes. The company has appointed an internal auditor, which is what the clause looks for, and reports that cover nothing material need not be read to be considered; the senior's judgement that they are immaterial is itself the consideration.
options.misconception: Reading an appointment as a system, and a decision not to read as a form of considering.
options.why: Limb (a) asks whether the system is commensurate with the size and nature of the business, not whether an appointment exists, and a part-time check of petty cash at a two-plant manufacturer is not; limb (b) asks whether the reports were considered by the statutory auditor, and a report nobody has read has not been considered by anyone.

options.text: The clause is not applicable and is answered so, because an unlisted company that engages a part-time person has no internal audit system in the sense the clause means, and where there is no system there are no reports to consider.
options.misconception: Turning an inadequate system into an inapplicable clause, which hides the very finding the clause exists to report.
options.why: The clause does apply to this company, and what it asks is whether the internal audit arrangement is commensurate with the size and nature of what the company does; an arrangement that falls short answers the limb unfavourably with the basis stated, it does not answer that the clause does not apply. And three reports for the year exist, so the second limb has something to be considered by the statutory auditor.

items.stem: On the turnover alone, was the company required to have an internal auditor for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes. A private company is covered when its turnover in the preceding financial year is two hundred crore rupees or more, and the 236 crore rupees of the year ended 31 March 2025 is the preceding year for this audit; the borrowings limit is a separate, alternative test. The company had six months from the applicability commencing to comply.
options.why: Two roads bring a private company inside rule 13, and either one on its own is enough. The first is money through the door: sales reaching two hundred crore rupees in the year before. The second is money owed: bank or financial-institution debt standing above a hundred crore rupees at any moment in that same year. For an audit of the year to 31 March 2026 the year before is the one that closed on 31 March 2025, so the figure that matters is 236 crore rupees, and it clears the first road whatever the loan book looked like. The company was therefore inside the requirement, and the rules then allow a company already trading six months from the day the requirement attaches to put an internal auditor in place — a window that had run out long before this year end. In short, the preceding financial year is the one ended 31 March 2025, its 236 crore rupees carries the company past the two hundred crore mark on the sales limb alone, and the six months allowed to comply had already expired.

options.text: No. The managing director is right that a private company is covered only through its bank borrowings, and the turnover test in rule 13 applies to unlisted public companies.
options.misconception: Carries the private company's exemption from two of the four public-company tests over to all of them.
options.why: A private company has two tests of its own and either one catches it: sales past the two hundred crore mark, or bank debt past a hundred crore. What such a company is spared is the pair of tests built on paid-up capital and on deposits, and those reach only unlisted public companies.

options.text: Not yet. Turnover is measured over the year being audited, so the 251 crore rupees of the year ended 31 March 2026 brings the company in only from the year that follows.
options.misconception: Reads the test as applying to the current year's figures.
options.why: Every one of these tests looks backwards, at the year before the one being audited, never at the year under audit itself. Here that is the year closed on 31 March 2025, whose sales were 236 crore rupees; the requirement had already bitten, and the six months allowed for complying started running from that point.

options.text: No, because the tests are cumulative: a private company must exceed both the turnover figure and the borrowings figure, and this one fails the borrowings limb.
options.misconception: Reads the rule's "or" as "and".
options.why: The two limbs are alternatives, joined by "or" rather than "and", and a company whose borrowings sit nowhere near the limit is caught on sales alone. Clearing one figure in the year before is enough by itself.

citation.ref: section 138 read with rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — the two figures that pull a private company inside the internal-audit requirement, sales made or bank debt carried in the year before, either one being enough by itself; and how long a company already trading is given to put an internal auditor in place once it is caught

items.scenario: Prithvi Packaging Private Limited makes corrugated boxes at two plants near Nashik. Its paid-up share capital is 8 crore rupees, its borrowings from banks never exceeded 60 crore rupees in any year, and it has never accepted deposits. Its turnover was 172 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2024, 236 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2025, and 251 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2026, and it has never had an internal auditor. Verma & Goel are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026, and the engagement partner has three matters in front of him. First, when the audit senior raised internal audit, the managing director said that "internal audit is for public companies, and for private ones only when bank loans cross a hundred crore, and ours are nowhere near". Second, to close the point, the board in February 2026 named the company's own finance manager, a chartered accountant who left practice six years ago and has been an employee since, as internal auditor; the audit senior objects that an internal auditor must be a chartered accountant in practice and cannot be an employee of the company. Third, the firm is short of staff for the year-end count, and the partner plans to have the finance manager's two-person internal audit team do three things for the statutory audit: attend and test-count the box stock at both plants, assess the risk of material misstatement in revenue for the audit plan, and evaluate the provision for slow-moving stock, which is the largest estimate in the accounts.

items.stem: On the finance manager alone, is the audit senior's objection to the appointment right?

options.text: Partly. An employee may be internal auditor, but only a chartered accountant may hold the post, so a cost accountant or any other professional would have been ineligible.
options.misconception: Narrows the eligible professions to chartered accountants only.
options.why: Cost accountants are named beside chartered accountants, and beyond the pair the Act leaves a further door for whatever other professional the Board settles on. The employee half of this answer is right; the qualification half is not.

options.text: Yes on both counts. The internal auditor must hold a certificate of practice, and an employee cannot audit the company that pays him.
options.misconception: Imports the statutory auditor's independence rules into an appointment the Act deliberately leaves open to employees.
options.why: The Act says the opposite on both counts. A certificate of practice is not the test — the qualification serves whether its holder practises or not — and employment is permitted in terms. An in-house internal audit department is the ordinary arrangement the section has in view, not an exception to it.

options.text: Yes, because a person who has left practice for more than five years has lost the eligibility that section 138 attaches to being a chartered accountant.
options.misconception: Invents a currency-of-practice condition the section does not contain.
options.why: Nothing in the section counts the years since somebody left practice. The qualification serves whether its holder practises or not, so a chartered accountant six years on a payroll stands exactly where a partner in a firm stands.

options.text: No. The post is open to a chartered accountant, to a cost accountant, in practice or not, and to such other professional as the Board settles on; the appointee may or may not be an employee, the Act saying so in terms. A chartered accountant on the company's payroll is eligible on both of the senior's counts.
options.why: Both halves of the objection fall, and they fall for different reasons. On qualification, the Act names a chartered accountant and a cost accountant side by side, in practice or not, and then leaves a further door open to such other professional as the Board settles on — so a certificate of practice was never the test, and six years away from practice costs the finance manager nothing. On employment the Act is explicit rather than silent: the person appointed may or may not be an employee, which is precisely how in-house internal audit departments come to exist across the country. Now, whether a man who runs the finance function can be genuinely detached about his own department is a real question — but it is a different question from eligibility, and it is asked in a different place. It belongs to Verma & Goel, who weigh it under SA 610 before leaning on any of his work; it is no bar on the board's appointment. In short, the board could appoint him: the Act covers a chartered accountant or a cost accountant in practice or not, and such other professional as it decides, and the appointee may or may not be an employee.
keywords: may or may not be an employee

items.stem: On the partner's plan alone, which of the three tasks may the internal auditors be given as direct assistance?

options.text: The test-counting and the risk assessment, but not the provision; risk assessment is planning rather than evidence, so the judgement rule does not reach it.
options.misconception: Excludes planning judgements from the significant-judgement rule.
options.why: Sizing the risk of misstatement heads the list of judgements the signer must make personally, and it does so precisely because the whole plan is built on top of it. Planning is not a lesser kind of work. It can no more be handed to the internal auditors than the provision can.

options.text: None of them. Internal auditors employed by the company can never provide direct assistance to the statutory auditor, whatever the task.
options.misconception: Reads the limits on direct assistance as a ban on it.
options.why: Direct assistance is permitted, and the standard says how far it may go: on how much judgement the task demands, on how risky the area is, and on what threatens the internal auditors' detachment and how able they are. A test-count run under the firm's direction and reviewed by it falls inside that.

options.text: All three, provided the partner reviews the internal auditors' working papers and the firm's own staff re-perform a sample of each task.
options.misconception: Treats supervision as a substitute for the external auditor making the significant judgements himself.
options.why: Reviewing papers afterwards and re-doing a sample do not reopen a door SA 610 has shut. Where a task turns on a judgement the opinion rests on — sizing the risk, or settling an estimate — the bar is absolute, because those judgements belong to the person who signs.

options.text: Only the test-counting, and only after the partner has evaluated threats to the internal auditors' objectivity and their competence and obtained the written agreements. Assessing the risk of material misstatement and evaluating the slow-moving stock provision are significant judgements that stay with the external auditor, who has sole responsibility for the opinion.
options.why: Direct assistance stops at the point where a task calls for a significant judgement, and two of the partner's three tasks sit on the far side of that line. Sizing the risk of misstatement in revenue is one of them; forming a view on the slow-moving stock provision is the other. Both are judgements the opinion itself stands on, and the reason neither can be passed across is that Verma & Goel carry sole responsibility for that opinion — a responsibility discharged by making the judgement, not by watching somebody else make it. Counting boxes is work of a different order. It is looking and arithmetic, and the internal audit team may be given it, but not before the partner has done two things. First he weighs what threatens the internal auditors' objectivity and how serious each threat is, alongside how competent they are — which here means facing squarely that the team answers to the finance manager whose own figures are being counted. Second he obtains the written agreements: from the company, that it will not interfere with the work; and from the internal auditors, that they will keep to themselves what they learn on it. All of that goes on the file, with the name of whoever reviewed what they did. In short, only the test-count may be assigned, and only once the threats to their objectivity have been weighed; the risk assessment and the estimate involve significant judgements and stay with the auditor carrying sole responsibility for the opinion.
