items.scenario: Ambekar & Nabar are a firm of chartered accountants at Nagpur, and Rukmini Ambekar is the partner in charge of the audit of a state government owned company that mines lignite and burns it at two power stations of its own, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the same fortnight. First, four findings from the field inspection, to every one of which the company answers that the money was sanctioned by the officer empowered to sanction it, under rules in force on the day. A residential training hostel was built at the older mine at a cost of forty crore rupees and has stood locked since it was handed over three years ago, because the training centre it was meant to serve was never shifted there. A consultancy contract for a coal handling study went to a firm in which the sanctioning director's brother is a partner, and the sanction file records no comparison against any other quotation. A welfare grant voted for all contract workers at both mines was released in full to the men of one contractor. And the whole senior cadre has been taking a fortnight each summer at a hill station guest house the company pays for, an arrangement appearing nowhere in the remuneration the board approved. Second, where three papers go and who answers them. The C&AG's report on this company has been laid before the State Legislature; a second report in the same volume deals with the state mining department's own disbursements and asks whether they were authorised, whether they went to the purpose the House voted them for, and whether transfers between heads followed the rules; and a third body has written asking the company what economies and improvements in organisation could be effected, and says it proposes to suggest alternative policies. The finance director's reading is that all three papers belong to one committee, that no committee may question the state's lignite policy at all because the Legislature approved it, and that once a committee has presented its recommendations the company's part in the matter is finished. Third, three engagements are running at once out of the Accountant General's office. One team is auditing the company's financial statements. A second is examining whether the expansion of the second power station was economical, efficient and effective. A third is testing whether royalty was paid on the lignite despatched in accordance with the mining rules. The company intends to hand each team a statement it drew up itself before the work begins, and the finance director says this makes all three attestation engagements, and that the benchmark each team measures against is therefore whatever that statement has used. Rukmini has to settle all three matters before the audit report is signed.

items.stem: QUESTION 3 OF 3 — turns on the three engagements running out of the Accountant General's office. The four field findings and where the three papers go are noise for this one. On the engagements alone, what does Rukmini conclude?

options.text: All three are direct reporting engagements, because the C&AG's own office is running every one of them, and a Supreme Audit Institution always reaches its own view rather than attesting anybody else's.
options.misconception: Reading the auditor's independence or standing as deciding the type of engagement, when the classification turns on which party produced the subject matter information.
options.why: Who the auditor is does not decide it either. An audit of financial statements sits on the attestation side whoever conducts it, because the statements remain a presentation the entity has made and the auditor's work is to gather evidence about that presentation. The C&AG's office doing the work changes nothing about where the subject matter information came from.

options.text: The finance director has the yardstick right at least: audit criteria come from the procedure manuals and the statements of the entity under audit, so each team measures against whatever that statement has used.
options.misconception: Taking one item off a list of sources as the whole list, which lets the auditee choose the standard it is measured against and empties the audit of its criteria.
options.why: The entity's manuals are the first source the chapter lists and nothing like the only one. It draws criteria also from the policies, standards and directives that apply, from what the same body or a comparable one is held to on similar work, from independent expert opinion, from settled scientific knowledge, and from the technical literature of the subject. An entity that fixed its own benchmark would be marking its own paper.

options.text: One of the three is an attestation engagement, the other two are not, and the yardstick is not the company's to set. The split turns on which side does the measuring. Where the entity weighs its own position against the criteria and hands over the result, the auditor is testing somebody else's work and gathering evidence about it; that is an attestation engagement, and what was handed over is the subject matter information. Where the auditor does the weighing himself, it is a direct reporting engagement. An audit of accounts is always the first kind, because financial statements are by their nature the entity's own presentation. Performance work and compliance work are normally the second, so the expansion review and the royalty testing stay direct reporting however many statements the company volunteers first. In short, the accounts audit is the attestation engagement because the company presents the subject matter information, while the expansion team and the royalty team each measure for themselves and each runs a direct reporting engagement.
options.why: Chapter 15 divides the two types by who performs the evaluation, not by who produces a document. In the first, the entity measures its own position against the criteria and puts the outcome forward as the subject matter information; the auditor then collects enough suitable evidence to reach a conclusion about that presentation, and that is an attestation engagement. In the second the auditor evaluates the subject matter himself and reports what he found, which is a direct reporting engagement. From that division the chapter draws a flat consequence: an audit of accounts always falls on the first side, since a set of accounts is financial information the entity has put forward, while performance and compliance work generally falls on the second. A statement volunteered to the expansion team or the royalty team is a piece of evidence for that team to test, not something it may attest. And the criteria are the yardstick, drawn from the rules and standards that bind the entity, from what comparable bodies are held to, and from expert and technical knowledge — the company's own manual is one source among several, never the whole of it.

options.text: All three are attestation engagements, because in every one the company hands the team a statement it drew up before the work starts, and an engagement is an attestation engagement whenever the auditor is given a management assertion to test.
options.misconception: Making the existence of a management document the test, when the test is which party performs the evaluation against the criteria.
options.why: Handing over a document does not decide it. What decides it is which party measured the position against the criteria. A team asked to judge whether the expansion was economical, efficient and effective is doing that measuring itself, whatever paper it was given on the first day.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — elements of PSU audits: the two types of engagement and which party does the measuring, where financial, performance and compliance audit fall between them, and the sources audit criteria are drawn from.

items.stem: On cost records alone, what does the standalone report state?

options.text: The clause has no application, as the finance head says: it is the cost audit clause, and no cost audit has been ordered for the company, so the report states that clause (vi) is not applicable.
options.misconception: Clause (vi) is about a cost audit and falls away where none is ordered.
options.why: Clause (vi) turns on two facts — that the Central Government has prescribed cost records for these products under section 148(1), and that the company kept them. An order for a cost audit is neither of those facts and the clause does not mention one, so its absence changes nothing.

options.text: Two answers, the second of them unfavourable with its reason. The report says yes to the first question, because the Central Government has prescribed cost records for these alloy products under section 148(1); it then splits the second, since the records exist at Jamshedpur and do not exist at Rourkela, so across the company they were not kept, and paragraph 4(a) makes the report give the reason — the plant bought in August 2025 has kept none since. A cost audit is a different thing altogether and the clause never mentions one, and records promised for next year are not records kept in this one.
options.why: Clause (vi) puts two questions in a single sentence, and the second only arises if the first is answered yes. The first is whether the Central Government has told this industry to keep cost records at all, under section 148(1). Here it has, so that answer is yes. The second is whether the company actually kept them, and it is settled against what exists on the ground rather than against what was meant to happen: Jamshedpur has the records, Rourkela has had none since the company bought it in August 2025, so for the company the answer is no. Paragraph 4(a) then stops the report from leaving a bare no on the page — the reason has to go with it. The finance head is answering a question nobody asked. An order for a cost audit is not what switches this clause on; prescription of the records under section 148(1) is, and a year in which no audit was ordered leaves the clause standing and still unanswered. A promise about next year sits outside the year being reported on. In short, the report says cost records are prescribed for this company under section 148(1), that they were kept only at Jamshedpur, and gives the Rourkela gap as the reason.

options.text: The report answers the clause favourably, because cost records are maintained at the plant the specification was written for and the Rourkela plant was bought in the year, so its records belong to the first full year of ownership.
options.misconception: A plant acquired during the year is outside the cost records clause until the next year.
options.why: The second question is about the whole company for the year, not about the one plant the prescription was written around; a plant owned since August 2025 with no cost records makes the answer unfavourable, and paragraph 4(a) requires the reason in the report.

options.text: Ritu examines the Jamshedpur cost records herself and, finding them complete, reports that the records are made and maintained; the Rourkela plant is mentioned in the letter to those charged with governance rather than in the report, because a missing record is a control weakness and not a reportable answer.
options.misconception: A partial failure on a clause goes to the governance letter and the report stays favourable.
options.why: Paragraph 3 requires the report to include a statement on each matter, and paragraph 4(a) requires the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer to be stated in the report itself; a plant with no cost records is an unfavourable answer to the second limb, not a matter for a letter.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi), the cost records clause — records prescribed for an industry under section 148(1), and whether the company in fact kept them; paragraph 4(a), which makes the report give its reason whenever an answer is not a clean yes

items.scenario: Sinha & Das are the statutory auditors of Subarnarekha Alloys Limited, an unlisted public company at Jamshedpur with a revenue of 520 crore rupees, and Ritu Sinha is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. The company prepares consolidated financial statements that include three subsidiaries: Subarnarekha Castings Private Limited, audited by another firm whose report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order carries a qualification under clause (vii)(a) for provident fund dues in arrears for more than six months; Subarnarekha Ferro Limited, whose auditor's report under the Order carries an adverse remark under clause (ix)(a) for defaults in repaying a term loan; and Subarnarekha Logistics Limited, whose report under the Order is clean. Ritu's own report on the standalone statements is in draft and the finance head has answered three points. First, the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records for the company's alloy products under sub-section (1) of section 148, and the company keeps such records at its Jamshedpur plant; the Rourkela plant, bought in August 2025, keeps none, and the finance head's answer is that no cost audit has been ordered for the company, so the clause has nothing to say, and that records for Rourkela will be set up next year in any case. Second, during a survey by the income-tax department in November 2025 the company admitted cash sales of 3.4 crore rupees that had never been entered in its books and surrendered the amount as income in the assessment for the year; the tax was paid in January 2026; the amount appears in the tax computation and nowhere in the books of account, because, the finance head says, the tax is paid and the matter is closed. In May 2026, after the year end, the company surrendered a further 90 lakh rupees for an earlier year in a reassessment, and the finance head would like the report to say in one line that there were no unrecorded transactions. Third, on the consolidated statements, the finance head says the Order does not apply to a report on consolidated financial statements, so the consolidated report carries nothing under it; the Castings qualification and the Ferro remark are in those companies' own reports and are their auditors' business, and Logistics is clean anyway. Ritu has to settle what each report states.

items.stem: On the surrendered income alone, what does the standalone report state?

options.text: Both surrenders are reported under the clause this year, the 3.4 crore rupees as unrecorded and the 90 lakh rupees as a subsequent event, since the earlier year's unrecorded income is as much a fact of the company's books as this year's.
options.misconception: A surrender after the year end is reported under clause (viii) for the year it relates to.
options.why: The clause is fixed to the year in which the surrender was made, so a surrender in May 2026 is answered in the next report; the older year the income belongs to does not pull it back into this one.

options.text: Yes to the first question and no to the second, with the reason, and the May surrender is not this year's. The report says that cash sales of 3.4 crore rupees, which the ledgers never carried, were given up as income in the year's tax assessment, and that this unrecorded income has still not been written into the books of account; under paragraph 4(a) it gives the reason, that the amount sits in the tax computation and nowhere else. The 90 lakh rupees given up in May 2026 was not given up inside this year, so it belongs to the next report rather than to this answer.
options.why: Clause (viii) asks two things. The first is a question about the assessment: did the company own up to income it had kept out of its ledgers when the tax department assessed it inside the year? The cash sales were never entered and were given up in November 2025, so the answer is yes and the amount is named. The second only arises on that yes, and it is a question about the ledgers: has that income since been written in? Paying the tax and carrying the figure in a tax computation puts nothing in the ledgers, so the answer is no, and paragraph 4(a) makes the report give the reason. The finance head's single line fails on both counts — there were such transactions, and they are still missing from the books. The 90 lakh rupees is a separate matter because the clause is fixed to when the surrender was made and not to the year the income came from, so a May 2026 surrender is the next report's answer. In short, the report says unrecorded income was given up in the year's tax assessment, that it has still not reached the books of account, and why.

options.text: The report states that no unrecorded transactions were found by the auditor, because the clause is about what the audit uncovers, and the cash sales came to light through a survey by the tax department and not through audit procedures.
options.misconception: Clause (viii) reports only unrecorded transactions the auditor found.
options.why: What sets the clause going is the surrender or disclosure made in the assessment itself, whatever brought the transactions to light; nothing in the clause asks who found them.

options.text: The finance head's line stands. The surrender was made to the tax department and the tax has been paid, so the transactions are now recorded where they matter; the clause is satisfied by the surrender itself and the report states that the company has disclosed the income in its assessment.
options.misconception: Surrendering income in the tax assessment discharges clause (viii) without entering it in the books.
options.why: The surrender settles the first question only. The second asks a different thing — whether the company has since written that income into its own ledgers — and money showing up in a tax computation alone has not been written anywhere. The report answers no and gives the reason.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii), the clause on income a company owns up to in a tax assessment after leaving it out of its ledgers, and on what it did about the ledgers afterwards; paragraph 4(a), which requires the reason behind an unfavourable answer

items.stem: On the consolidated statements alone, what does the consolidated report state?

options.text: One clause and nothing else. The finance head has the general rule right — a report on consolidated financial statements is outside the Order — but paragraph 2 carves clause (xxi) out of that rule, and the consolidated report answers it. It says that component auditors have modified their own CARO reports, and it names where: Subarnarekha Castings Private Limited at clause (vii)(a) and Subarnarekha Ferro Limited at clause (ix)(a), giving the paragraph numbers in each of those reports. Subarnarekha Logistics Limited is clean and so adds nothing here, and the group is given no other clause of the Order.
options.why: Paragraph 2 sets a rule and one exception in a single breath: a report on consolidated financial statements is outside the Order, except for clause (xxi). The finance head read as far as the comma and stopped. Clause (xxi) puts a narrow question to the group auditor — did the auditors of the companies consolidated here modify their own CARO reports, and if they did, which companies were they and at which paragraphs? The clause is a signpost rather than fresh audit work: it points whoever reads the group accounts back to the spots where a component's own report already carries a qualification or an adverse remark, so that what was said about a subsidiary does not vanish into the consolidation. Castings and Ferro are both consolidated here and both have modified reports, so both are named with their paragraph numbers; Logistics has nothing to name. The other twenty clauses are not run over the group a second time, because paragraph 2 keeps them out. In short, the consolidated report answers clause (xxi) by naming the two consolidated companies whose CARO reports carry a qualification or an adverse remark, with the paragraph numbers, and answers nothing else under the Order.

options.text: The finance head is right and the consolidated report carries nothing under the Order; the Castings qualification and the Ferro remark are answered in those companies' own reports by their own auditors, and repeating them would report on companies Ritu does not audit.
options.misconception: The Order has nothing at all to say in a report on consolidated financial statements.
options.why: Clause (xxi) is the one thing paragraph 2 lifts out of the exclusion, and it asks for exactly this — the modifications sitting in the component auditors' own CARO reports, with the companies named and the paragraph numbers given.

options.text: Clause (xxi) is answered by modifying the opinion on the consolidated financial statements, because a qualification in a subsidiary's CARO report is a qualification of the group, so the Castings and Ferro matters go into the basis for qualified opinion paragraph rather than into a separate statement.
options.misconception: A component's CARO qualification modifies the consolidated opinion.
options.why: Clause (xxi) wants the companies named and the paragraph numbers given; it is a statement made under the Order, not a change to the opinion, and whether the consolidated opinion is modified is judged separately on the consolidated statements.

options.text: Ritu prepares a full report under the Order on the consolidated figures, answering each clause for the group as a whole, since the consolidated statements are the accounts of the company to which the Order applies and the components' issues are best captured clause by clause.
options.misconception: The consolidated report carries a clause-by-clause CARO statement on the group figures.
options.why: Paragraph 2 keeps every clause but (xxi) out of a report on consolidated financial statements; each of the others is answered in a company's own standalone report by its own auditor and is not run again over the group figures.

citation.ref: paragraph 2, which keeps the Order out of a report on consolidated financial statements save for one clause; and clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, which has the group auditor point at the modifications already carried in the component auditors' own CARO reports, naming the companies and the paragraph numbers

items.stem: On the audit report alone, what does Simran advise Harpreet?

options.text: Simran tells her that the report is open on three clauses, each on its own limb. The 6 crore rupee loan is clause (5): a material fact known to him, on Harpreet's own review note, that the statements had to carry and never did. The stock at 21 crore rupees against a count of 18 is clause (6): a material misstatement sitting in the statements, known to her, with a working paper marked for management to explain, no explanation on file, and nothing said in the report. The investments are clause (8): an opinion signed without the sufficient information an opinion needs, and where the reservation runs that large the chapter's worked example says an auditor may not shelter behind a "subject to" and has to disclaim in terms nobody can misread. That the statements are the directors' answers none of the three, because each clause asks what the member, professionally concerned with those statements, failed to do.
options.why: The three clauses sort a report's failures by kind, and this file supplies one of each. Clause (5) is about something missing: a material fact known to him that never reached the statements although they could not properly be made without it, he being professionally concerned with them. A term loan of 6 crore rupees kept out of the books entirely is that fact, and the review note in Harpreet's own hand supplies the knowledge the clause asks for. Clause (6) is about something present and wrong: a material misstatement she knew was there, in statements she was professionally concerned with, and left unreported. Stock carried at 21 crore rupees against a count of 18 crore rupees is that misstatement, and the chapter says of both clauses alike that materiality has to be established, measured against the balance sheet and against the profit and loss account. Clause (8) is about the ground under the opinion: either the evidence an opinion needs was never obtained, or the reservations weigh so heavily that they cancel the opinion out. The chapter works that through on investments an auditor could not verify, and says he may not write that the balance sheet is true and fair once somebody has checked them; he has to disclaim, in terms that leave no room. A "subject to" laid over four-tenths of the assets is the very phrasing that example forbids. Whose statements they are never enters any of the three clauses; they speak of the member professionally concerned with them, and of what she knew and did not say. In short, a material fact known to him and left out is clause (5), a material misstatement known and unreported is clause (6), an opinion given without sufficient information is clause (8), and the words "subject to" rescue nothing.

options.text: Simran tells her that only the stock can be charged. Clause (6) catches a wrong figure that appears in the statements; a loan that appears nowhere in them is the company's omission and not a misstatement, and the investments were reported on with a qualification, so neither of those is a reporting failure of hers.
options.misconception: Only a wrong figure present in the statements is a reporting failure; a material fact the statements leave out altogether is the company's business.
options.why: A fact the member knew of, needed by the statements and absent from them, is exactly what clause (5) was written for — which is why the Schedule carries a clause for the missing fact alongside the clause for the wrong figure. The investments fail on clause (8) instead, for want of the evidence an opinion needs.

options.text: Simran tells her that the report is not open to any charge. The financial statements are the directors' statements under the Companies Act, the auditor reports on what management prepared, and a member cannot be guilty of misconduct for a fact the company chose not to record or a figure the company chose to carry.
options.misconception: Because the financial statements belong to the directors, the auditor's report cannot be misconduct for what they leave out or misstate.
options.why: Each of the three clauses asks about the member, not about the company: what she knew, and what she then failed to disclose, to report, or to obtain before signing. Whose statements they are is a defence under none of them, and the chapter's own illustration of a loan left out of the books puts the guilt on the auditor who passed over it in the report.

options.text: Simran tells her that the loan and the stock are exposed but the investments are safe. By writing that the statements are true and fair subject to verification of the investments she disclosed the limitation to every reader, which is all that clause (8) asks of an auditor who could not obtain the evidence.
options.misconception: A "subject to" qualification discharges the auditor whatever the size of what could not be verified.
options.why: Reservations heavy enough to cancel an opinion out are themselves the breach of clause (8), and the chapter's example of unverifiable investments tells the auditor to put down a disclaimer nobody can misread instead of a "subject to". Four-tenths of the assets unchecked is that example.

citation.ref: Clauses (5), (6) and (8) of Part I of the Second Schedule — the three reporting clauses. items.stem: On the draft statement and the advance-tax money alone, what does Simran do?

options.text: Simran leaves the sentence in. A written statement in reply to a complaint is the member's defence, it is for the Director (Discipline) to test it against the file, and a member is entitled to put her best case in her own words without that case becoming a fresh charge.
options.misconception: A member's reply to a complaint is a privileged defence and cannot itself be misconduct however false it is.
options.why: Clause (3) of Part II names the Director (Discipline) among the bodies to which a statement carrying particulars known to be false is misconduct, and the chapter's case of a wrong statement duly verified before the Disciplinary Committee shows that the member's own defence is exactly where the clause bites.

options.text: Simran tells her that neither point belongs before the Institute. A false statement and a misuse of money are dishonesty, which is a matter for a court, and the Schedules to the Act deal only with how a member does professional work, so the complaint should be met by saying that these allegations are outside the Act.
options.misconception: Dishonesty is for the courts and the Schedules cover only the technical quality of professional work.
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule is written for members generally and its clauses (3) and (4) are precisely false particulars to the Institute's bodies and defalcation of money received in a professional capacity; the chapter treats both as professional misconduct before the Disciplinary Committee.

options.text: Simran strikes the sentence about the loan out of the statement and tells Harpreet that the money is not a wrong-account matter. A statement submitted to the Director (Discipline) that includes particulars knowing them to be false is clause (3) of Part II of the Second Schedule on its own, whatever becomes of the audit charge, and a verified statement that the loan was never brought to her notice, against a review note in her own hand, is that clause; the chapter's decided case is a member found guilty for a wrong statement duly verified before the Disciplinary Committee. The 15 lakh rupees the company handed the firm for its advance tax was money received in a professional capacity, and paying it into her own account and spending it on her house is a member who defalcates or embezzles money received in his professional capacity under clause (4) of Part II, not the failure to keep it in a separate banking account under clause (10) of Part I; making it good two months later does not move it back.
options.why: Clause (3) of Part II reads on the reply itself. A member who puts particulars she knows to be untrue into anything she files with the Institute's machinery is guilty under it, and the clause names that machinery at length — the Council and its committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board, the Appellate Authority. The draft here is a statement bound for the Director (Discipline); the particular is that the loan never came to her notice; and the review note in her own hand is what makes it a particular she knows to be false. The chapter's cases run the same way — a member held guilty over a wrong statement he had duly verified, another over a statement sworn while he knew it to be untrue. A defence that puts a false fact in front of the Director (Discipline) adds a charge to the complaint instead of answering it, and that charge is complete on the day the statement is filed. The money engages the other Part II clause. Clause (4) is the member who defalcates or embezzles money that reached her in a professional capacity, and the chapter calls such a defalcation fraud. The 15 lakh rupees was the company's advance tax, handed to the firm to be passed on. What Harpreet offers instead is clause (10) of Part I, a custody failure: client money not held in its own bank account, or not applied to its purpose in reasonable time. But a member who moves that money into her personal account and spends it on her house has gone past custody and into taking. Paying the tax and the interest two months afterwards is restitution, and neither clause carries a repayment limb. In short, a statement to the Director (Discipline) with particulars knowing them to be false is clause (3) of Part II, and a member who defalcates or embezzles client money received in her professional capacity is clause (4), whether or not she later makes it good.

options.text: Simran tells her the money is clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule and nothing worse. The clause requires a client's moneys to be kept in a separate banking account and used for their purpose within a reasonable time; the account was wrong and the time was two months, and since the company lost nothing the matter ends there.
options.misconception: Repayment turns a defalcation of client money back into a failure to keep it in the right account.
options.why: Clause (10) is a custody failure; paying client money into her own account and spending it on her house is a member who defalcates or embezzles money received in her professional capacity under clause (4) of Part II, which the chapter says amounts to fraud, and making it good later is not a limb of either clause.

citation.ref: Clauses (3) and (4) of Part II of the Second Schedule. The first covers particulars a member knows to be untrue and files with the Institute's own machinery — the Council and its committees, the Director (Discipline), either disciplinary forum, the Quality Review Board, the Appellate Authority. The second covers a member who takes for himself money that reached him professionally

items.stem: On the forum alone, what does Simran now tell Harpreet?

options.text: Simran holds to her view. The Director (Discipline) screens every complaint, and one that is careless rather than dishonest is one he can close or dispose of with a warning himself; only where he finds dishonesty does a case go to either forum.
options.misconception: The Director (Discipline) can dispose of a minor complaint with a penalty of his own.
options.why: The Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion and places the matter before the Board or the Committee according to the Schedule; the powers to reprimand, remove and fine belong to those two bodies and he has none of them.

options.text: Simran tells Harpreet that the Board of Discipline will hear it, because most of the allegations are of carelessness and the forum follows the weight of the complaint, and that the worst outcome is therefore removal of her name for three months and a fine of one lakh rupees.
options.misconception: The forum and the ceiling on punishment are set by how serious the complaint feels, not by the Schedule the clauses sit in.
options.why: The forum follows the Schedule in which the alleged misconduct is mentioned, not the proportion of careless to dishonest limbs, and a matter in the Second Schedule or in both goes before the Disciplinary Committee, whose powers include removal permanently or for any duration and a fine up to five lakh rupees.

options.text: Simran withdraws what she told Harpreet. The Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion on the complaint and decides nothing else; he punishes nobody. Where that opinion is that the matter falls in the Second Schedule or in both Schedules, he places it before the Disciplinary Committee, and a complaint that mixes First Schedule and Second Schedule matters goes there whole, not to the Board of Discipline. The Committee, on finding a member guilty, may reprimand her, remove her name from the Register permanently or for any duration it thinks fit, or fine her up to five lakh rupees, so permanent removal is on the table and the mixed bag is the reason it is, not the reason it is not. The three-month ceiling and the one lakh rupees belong to the Board of Discipline, which hears only matters falling in the First Schedule alone.
options.why: The procedure in the chapter runs from a complaint or information to the Disciplinary Directorate, which forms a prima facie opinion; the Director (Discipline) is the person who routes the matter and he has no power to reprimand, remove or fine, so the expectation that he will deal with a careless case himself has nothing to rest on. The routing follows the Schedule, not the seriousness anyone feels: where the opinion is that the member is guilty of misconduct mentioned in the First Schedule, the matter is placed before the Board of Discipline; where it is that the member is guilty of misconduct mentioned in the Second Schedule or in both the Schedules, it is placed before the Disciplinary Committee. The words "or in both" answer Simran's mixed bag: a complaint with any Second Schedule limb goes to the Committee entire. The powers differ with the forum. The Board of Discipline may reprimand, remove the member's name up to a period of three months, or fine up to one lakh rupees. The Disciplinary Committee may reprimand, remove the name permanently or for any duration it thinks fit, or fine up to five lakh rupees. So the three-month ceiling Simran quoted is the Board's, and the Committee that will hear this complaint has permanent removal in its hands; a member or the Director (Discipline) aggrieved by either order may appeal to the Appellate Authority within ninety days, which is the next step after an order, not a reason to expect a lighter forum. In short, the Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion and punishes nobody, a matter in the Second Schedule or in both goes before the Disciplinary Committee, and the Committee may remove a name permanently.

options.text: Simran tells Harpreet the complaint will be split. The Director (Discipline) sends the First Schedule limbs to the Board of Discipline and the Second Schedule limbs to the Disciplinary Committee, each body deals with its own limbs, and the punishments are then added together.
options.misconception: A complaint under both Schedules is divided between the two forums limb by limb.
options.why: The chapter's rule is that misconduct mentioned in the Second Schedule or in both the Schedules is placed before the Disciplinary Committee, so a mixed complaint goes there whole and the Board of Discipline hears only matters falling in the First Schedule alone.

citation.ref: sections 21, 21A and 21B read with the Rules of 2007: the Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion; a matter in the First Schedule is placed before the Board of Discipline, which may reprimand, remove the name up to three months or fine up to one lakh rupees; a matter in the Second Schedule or in both Schedules is placed before the Disciplinary Committee, which may reprimand, remove the name permanently or for any duration it thinks fit or fine up to five lakh rupees

items.stem: On the Kandla warehouse alone, what does SA 705 (Revised) require of Iyer & Menon now?

options.text: Withdraw from the audit, since management has refused the auditors access and the standard treats a refused limitation as grounds for withdrawal
options.misconception: reaches for withdrawal on any refused access, when withdrawal is the response to a possible effect that is both material and pervasive
options.why: Walking away is held back for the case where the damage could be both material and spreading, so that qualifying would understate how serious the position is — and even then only where leaving is practicable and the law allows it, with a disclaimer where it is not. An inability confined to one warehouse's stock is material and nothing more, and the answer to that is a qualified opinion rather than the auditor's resignation.

options.text: Accept a note from management explaining the lessor dispute and add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph pointing to it, leaving the opinion unmodified
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter to cover a scope limitation, when it is barred wherever a modification is required
options.why: Such a paragraph is open only where the matter forces no modification of the opinion, and it is never a way round one. The gap here belongs to the auditor and not to the reader: no evidence at all was obtained on 14 crore rupees of stock, and no note written by management can supply what an auditor was stopped from getting. A paragraph of that kind points at something properly set out in the accounts and fully evidenced — the opposite of this position.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion, because a limitation that management itself imposed is by its nature pervasive whatever the balance concerned
options.misconception: treats management's refusal as making the effect pervasive, when pervasiveness is judged by the effect on the financial statements
options.why: Pervasive describes what an effect does to the accounts, never who caused the gap in the evidence. An effect earns the word when it does not stay inside particular elements or items, or when it does stay inside them but they make up a substantial slice of the statements, or when a disclosure it touches is fundamental to a reader's understanding. Stock in one warehouse, with every other balance well supported, stays inside — and missing inventory evidence is the module's own example of an effect that stays local. Management being the source of the limitation changes which steps come first; it leaves untouched the test that decides between qualifying and disclaiming.

options.text: Ask management to remove the limitation; if it refuses, communicate the matter to those charged with governance and look for alternative procedures; and, since the possible effects of undetected misstatement in one warehouse's stock could be material but not pervasive, express a qualified opinion
options.why: What the chief financial officer's letter did was shut off evidence after the engagement had already been taken on — a limitation with management's own hand behind it. The order of response is fixed. Ask management to remove the limitation. If it will not, take the matter to those charged with governance, and go looking for some other route to the same evidence. Only when no route exists does the report come into it, and then the question is what an undetected misstatement could do to the accounts. Here it could do a great deal to one line and nothing whatever to any other. Stock in a single warehouse is unverified while receivables, property, loans and payables are all properly supported — the very shape the module uses as its example of an inability that stays local. An effect that is material but stays inside one element is answered by a qualified opinion. Fourteen crore rupees is large enough to matter; large is not the same as everywhere. In short, the partner asks for the limitation to be lifted, tells those charged with governance if it is not, and where nothing else will reach the stock, signs a qualified opinion.

citation.ref: what follows when management itself shuts off the evidence after the engagement has been taken on and no other route will reach it; and what makes an effect on the accounts a spreading one rather than a confined one

items.scenario: Suvarna Textiles Limited is listed on the National Stock Exchange and spins and weaves cotton, and Iyer & Menon are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026, their first year on the company. Three matters are on the partner's list. First, inventory of 14 crore rupees out of a total of 38 crore rupees lies in a leased warehouse at Kandla; in February 2026 the CFO wrote that the auditors were not to visit Kandla "while the dispute with the lessor is live" and declined to arrange a count by anyone else, and because that warehouse's stock records are a spreadsheet updated once a month, no roll-forward from an earlier count was possible. Every other balance in the accounts is well supported. Second, a customs demand of 22 crore rupees disputed before the Tribunal is disclosed as a contingent liability in note 34 with counsel's opinion; the auditors obtained the evidence they needed and agree with the disclosure; the matter was a significant risk from planning, took much of the team's time, was discussed with the audit committee, and is on the partner's list of key audit matters, and the partner now proposes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph on it as well "so that nobody misses it". Third, the previous year's financial statements were audited by Rao & Rao, whose report dated 28 May 2025 was qualified over an unprovided gratuity liability that has since been provided; the corresponding figures appear in this year's statements and the CFO says the new auditors "need not mention last year at all".

items.stem: On the customs demand alone, what does the partner's proposal get wrong, and where does the matter go in the report?

options.text: Give it an Emphasis of Matter instead of a key audit matter, because a matter fundamental to users' understanding belongs in an Emphasis of Matter and key audit matters are for areas where evidence was hard to get
options.misconception: sorts matters into Emphasis of Matter or key audit matter by how important they are, when the test for a key audit matter is significance in the audit
options.why: What makes something a key audit matter is that the auditor judged it of most significance in this audit — drawn from what was discussed with those charged with governance, weighing higher assessed risk, the judgements that were hardest, and the events of the year. The customs demand answers to that on its facts. Being fundamental to a reader's understanding does not lift it out of SA 701 either: one matter can be both, and the auditor then says so where the key audit matter is described. Dropping it altogether would breach SA 701 on a listed company as well.

options.text: Give it both — a key audit matter and an Emphasis of Matter — since nothing stops an important matter from being flagged twice
options.misconception: treats the two paragraphs as stackable, when SA 706 bars an Emphasis of Matter on a matter already determined to be a key audit matter
options.why: Something does stop it. On a report SA 701 governs, the second of the two conditions is that the matter must not already have been picked out as a key audit matter — and this one has been. The reason behind the bar is plain: such a paragraph is no substitute for the description of a key audit matter, and a report strewn with them dilutes what the auditor is trying to say. Wanting the reader to notice is met inside the key audit matter itself, where the auditor may draw further attention to its relative importance.

options.text: With SA 701 in play, an Emphasis of Matter is reserved for something that has not been determined a key audit matter, and this one has been; so the demand is described in the Key Audit Matters section, where the partner is free to draw attention to how much it mattered, and no Emphasis of Matter is added
options.why: Suvarna is listed, so SA 701 is in play, and the customs demand — a significant risk carried from planning, a large share of the team's hours, taken to the audit committee — already sits on the partner's list of key audit matters. Now the test for an Emphasis of Matter. Two conditions have to hold at once: nothing about the matter would force the opinion to be modified, and, on a report SA 701 governs, the paragraph is reserved for something that has not been determined a key audit matter. The first condition is satisfied here. The second plainly is not. And what the partner actually wants — that a reader should not miss the demand — is answered inside the Key Audit Matters section itself: a matter of most significance in the audit can also be fundamental to a reader's understanding, and where it is, the auditor may draw attention to how much weight it carried in the very passage that describes it. A second paragraph adds nothing. It is no stand-in for the description of a key audit matter, and a report strewn with such paragraphs communicates less rather than more. In short, the demand has already been picked out as a key audit matter, which bars the Emphasis of Matter, and the partner may draw attention to its importance where it is described.

options.text: Express a qualified opinion, since 22 crore rupees is far too large a matter to be left to a note and a paragraph
options.misconception: modifies the opinion because the amount is large, when the auditor has evidence and agrees with the disclosure
options.why: A modification follows from a material misstatement or from an inability to obtain evidence, and here there is neither: the auditors obtained the evidence they needed and agree with the disclosure of the demand as a contingent liability with counsel's opinion. The size of a disclosed and properly supported matter does not turn agreement into disagreement. A qualified opinion would say the accounts are wrong about the demand, which is not what the auditors found.

citation.ref: the two conditions that must both hold before an Emphasis of Matter may be used at all — no modification of the opinion called for by the matter, and, on a report the key-audit-matters standard governs, no prior selection of it as one; and how the two paragraphs stand to each other

items.stem: On the previous year's audit alone, what does SA 710 require of Iyer & Menon's report, given that they decide to refer to it?

options.text: Say nothing about last year, because the corresponding figures are not covered by the current opinion and the qualification has been resolved
options.misconception: reads "the opinion does not cover the corresponding figures" as "the report says nothing about them", when SA 710 prescribes what is stated about a predecessor's report
options.why: Both halves of that are true on their own — the opinion speaks to this year, and a gratuity matter now provided for calls for no modification. Neither makes the earlier report disappear. The stem has Iyer & Menon deciding to mention it, and once they do, three facts are fixed: who audited last year, what opinion that firm gave, and when. A chief financial officer's preference for silence is nowhere in the standard.

options.text: Put the predecessor's qualified opinion in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, since it is a matter fundamental to users' understanding of the figures
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter for a fact about the prior audit, when the paragraph may refer only to what is in the financial statements
options.why: A paragraph of that kind may point only at something set out inside the accounts, and another firm's report is not inside the accounts. Something a reader needs in order to understand the audit or the report itself, yet found nowhere in the statements, is exactly what an Other Matter paragraph is for under SA 706 (Revised) — which is why the facts about last year's auditor go there.

options.text: Add an Other Matter paragraph carrying three facts: that last year's accounts were audited by another firm, the type of opinion that predecessor auditor gave — a qualified one — and the date of that report, 28 May 2025; the gratuity matter, provided for since, leaves this year's opinion unmodified
options.why: With corresponding figures, the opinion signed this year speaks to this year. Where a different firm audited the year before, and this firm is neither barred from mentioning that earlier report nor minded to stay silent about it, SA 710 fixes exactly three facts to put on the page: that a predecessor auditor did last year's audit, the type of opinion that firm gave, and the date of that report. Notice what kind of facts those are. Every one of them is about an audit and about an auditor's report — not about anything presented or disclosed inside the accounts themselves — and that is precisely the work an Other Matter paragraph does. As for the qualification: the gratuity liability has since been provided for, so nothing in this year's figures calls for a modification at all. The reader hears about last year's qualification through the paragraph, never through this year's opinion. In short, the paragraph names the predecessor auditor, the type of opinion that firm gave and the date of that report, and this year's opinion is left unmodified.

options.text: Repeat the predecessor's qualification in a Basis for Qualified Opinion section, since the corresponding figures still carry the year in which the gratuity was left unprovided
options.misconception: carries a predecessor's qualification forward as the current auditor's, when the matter is resolved and the current opinion covers the current period
options.why: Qualifying this year's report is a statement that this year's accounts are materially wrong, and they are not — the gratuity liability has been provided for. With corresponding figures the opinion speaks to this year, and the short list of occasions on which it reaches back to last year's numbers does not include a prior-year matter that has since been put right. Last year's opinion is reported as a fact about last year's audit — what kind it was and when it was signed — inside an Other Matter paragraph, not taken over as this auditor's own modification.

citation.ref: corresponding figures where last year's accounts were audited by a different firm — and, for an auditor who is allowed to mention that earlier report and chooses to, the three facts the report then has to carry

items.stem: On the forecast and the refused representation alone, what does the partner require of the senior before the going concern conclusion can be reached?

options.text: Confirmation of the plot sale and the promoter's undertaking from the buyer and the promoter in writing, after which the forecast may be accepted as reliable without further analysis.
options.misconception: Treats one confirmation as a substitute for evaluating the whole forecast and the plans behind it.
options.why: Confirming the existence, terms and enforceability of arrangements for financial support is one of the module's procedures, and it is not the whole of them. The forecast's data and assumptions are still evaluated, the plans still judged feasible in the circumstances, later facts still considered, and the written representation still requested.

options.text: Work of the auditor's own. The cash flow forecast is analysed and discussed with management, the reliability of its data and the support for its assumptions evaluated, the plot sale and the promoter's undertaking tested for whether they are feasible in the circumstances, and any facts arising since the assessment considered. A written representation on the plans and their feasibility is requested; if management stays unwilling to give it, that refusal is weighed for its implications for the auditor's report rather than accepted.
options.why: A forecast agreed to the assessment it was built from is not audit work; it is the same document read twice. Once warning signs are on the file the auditor owes a set of steps of his own. The forecast gets gone through with management. The figures underneath it are asked whether they can be relied on, and every assumption is asked what stands behind it. The plans are weighed for whether they can practicably be carried through in the position this company is actually in. Whatever has come to light since the assessment was made gets picked up. And a written representation is asked for — of management, and of the board where that is called for — covering those plans and whether they will work. A plot sale agreed only in principle and a promoter's word are precisely the assumptions whose support has to be seen before anyone leans on them. A management unwilling to make or extend its assessment is not merely noted either: the standard sends the auditor to work out what that silence costs the report, and a refusal to sign for the plans is treated in the same spirit rather than filed. In short, the cash flow forecast is tested, the written representation is requested, and a refusal carries implications for the auditor's report.

options.text: Nothing further. The forecast is management's document and the going concern assessment is management's responsibility; the auditor's job is to check that an assessment was made, and a representation about future plans cannot be demanded because plans are not facts.
options.misconception: Confuses management's responsibility for the assessment with the auditor's responsibility to obtain evidence about it, and treats a representation about plans as outside SA 580.
options.why: Management makes the assessment; the auditor still has to gather evidence about it, and that means work on the forecast, on its figures, on its assumptions and on the plans, not a tick confirming an assessment exists. A representation covering those plans and whether they will work is one of the things the auditor is told to ask for, so it is squarely something that can be demanded.

options.text: A qualified opinion at once, because a refused representation is a scope limitation and the senior's file note cannot be improved after the fact.
options.misconception: Jumps from a refusal to a modified opinion without performing the procedures the module lists first.
options.why: The order is wrong. The procedures come first: the forecast is analysed, the plans evaluated for feasibility and the representation requested, and only if management stays unwilling does the auditor consider the implications for the report. Nothing has yet been asked for and refused in a way that fixes the form of the opinion, and the senior's file can be reopened.

citation.ref: the extra work owed once warning signs are on the file — going through the forecast with management, asking whether its underlying figures can be relied on and whether anything supports its assumptions, judging the plans behind it for practicability, picking up what has come to light since the assessment was made, and asking for a signed representation about those plans — and what an unwilling management costs the report

items.scenario: Tapti Spinning Mills Private Limited runs a cotton spinning mill near Surat. Its revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was 420 crore rupees, its loss after tax 38 crore rupees following a loss of 22 crore rupees the year before, and at the year end its current liabilities exceeded its current assets by 55 crore rupees. In June 2026 the principal lender recalled its 90 crore rupees term loan and demanded repayment within twelve months. Bhatt & Deshmukh are the statutory auditors, and the partner intends to sign the report on 20 August 2026. Three things are on her desk. First, the chief financial officer's cash flow forecast shows the company through the next year on the strength of two plans, the sale of a spare plot for 70 crore rupees to a buyer who has agreed terms in principle and a promoter's undertaking to bring in 40 crore rupees; the audit senior has filed the forecast with the note "management's forecast, agreed to management's assessment" and no work of his own, and the chief financial officer has declined to sign any representation about the plans, "since plans are hopes and I sign only facts". Second, the draft note 41 sets out the losses, the lender's demand and the negative working capital, describes both plans, and ends with a sentence saying plainly that there is a material uncertainty which may cast significant doubt over whether the company can carry on as a going concern, and that it may not be able to turn its assets into cash or settle what it owes in the ordinary way of trade; the partner has concluded that the plans are feasible and the going concern basis appropriate, and the senior proposes an "except for" qualification, or at least an emphasis of matter, "since there is a going concern problem". Third, the managing director wants that last sentence of note 41 struck, keeping the events and the plans, "because the plans are in the note and the sentence reads like an obituary".

items.stem: On note 41 as drafted alone, and taking the partner's conclusions as sound, what form does the auditor's report take?

options.text: A qualified opinion, "except for" the going concern uncertainty, because a company that may be unable to pay its debts cannot receive a clean report whatever its notes say.
options.misconception: Believes doubt about survival is itself a reason to modify the opinion, regardless of the disclosure.
options.why: A qualified opinion answers a misstatement or a lack of evidence, and a material uncertainty that is adequately disclosed is neither. The module's road for this case is an unmodified opinion with the separate section; the qualified or adverse road is reserved for the case where adequate disclosure is not made, and note 41 makes it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern". That section points the reader at note 41, says the matters set out there raise a material uncertainty over whether the mill can carry on trading, and records that the opinion is not modified on account of it. Note 41 is adequate — it carries the events, the plans and the plain admission of the uncertainty — so there is nothing to qualify and no emphasis of matter to write.
options.why: Three conditions hold together here: the basis of preparation is still the right one, the doubt is real, and the accounts have said so properly. Where all three hold, the opinion is left alone and the matter is given a section to itself. The heading of that section is fixed — "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" — and inside it the auditor points at the note carrying the disclosure, sets out what the events come to, and records that the opinion has not been changed on account of the matter. Whether a note has said so properly is settled in three parts as well: the events or conditions themselves, what management proposes to do about them, and a plain sentence admitting the uncertainty and the risk that the company will not be able to turn its assets into cash and settle what it owes as a trading business does. Note 41 as drafted carries all three. And a doubt disclosed properly is not a misstatement, so "except for" has nothing to bite on; the separate section is this report's own way of carrying the matter, which is why an emphasis of matter is not reached for either. In short, the disclosure is adequate, the section is headed Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern, and the opinion is not modified.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

options.text: An adverse opinion, because two years of losses, negative working capital and a recalled loan mean the going concern basis cannot be appropriate whatever management plans.
options.misconception: Confuses events that cast significant doubt with a conclusion that the basis itself is wrong.
options.why: The adverse opinion belongs to the case where management's use of the going concern basis is inappropriate in the auditor's judgement. Here the partner has concluded the plans are feasible and the basis appropriate, and the question takes that as sound; a material uncertainty that is adequately disclosed leads to the separate section, not to an adverse opinion.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph that refers to note 41, since the matter is fundamental to users and is properly disclosed.
options.misconception: Uses the general emphasis of matter paragraph where SA 570 prescribes a specifically headed section.
options.why: The reasoning is right about the opinion and wrong about the paragraph. The module gives the going concern uncertainty its own separately headed section, "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern", with its own required statements, and that section is used in place of an emphasis of matter for this matter.

citation.ref: the road the report takes when the basis of preparation still holds, the doubt is real and the accounts disclose it properly: the opinion itself is left alone, and a section carrying the set heading "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" points the reader at the note, says what the doubt is, and says in terms that the opinion has not been changed on account of it

items.stem: On the managing director's edit alone, if the last sentence of note 41 is struck and the board approves the accounts without it, what happens to the auditor's report?

options.text: The separate going concern section falls away and the opinion is modified. Strike the plain admission that the doubt exists and that the company may not manage to turn its assets into cash and settle what it owes as a trading business does, and the uncertainty is not adequately disclosed; the partner then gives a qualified or adverse opinion as far as the omission warrants, and says in the basis for opinion paragraph that the doubt is real and the accounts do not properly disclose it.
options.why: A note that does its job has two halves. One is the events themselves and what management means to do about them. The other is a plain sentence admitting that the doubt is real and that the company may not manage to turn its assets into cash and settle what it owes as a trading business does. Striking the last sentence of note 41 takes the second half away, and events with plans beside them do not on their own amount to an adequate disclosure. What follows is settled. The basis of preparation still holds and the doubt is still real, but the accounts have stopped saying so, and for that case the opinion is qualified or adverse according to how far the omission reaches, with the matter set out in the basis for opinion paragraph. The separately headed section belongs to the other case, the one where the note does say what it should, so it cannot be pressed into repairing a note that does not. In short, the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse, and the basis for opinion paragraph says why.

options.text: An adverse opinion in every case, because omitting a going concern statement means the going concern basis has become inappropriate.
options.misconception: Confuses inadequate disclosure of a material uncertainty with inappropriate use of the going concern basis.
options.why: The basis has not changed; the partner's conclusion that it is appropriate stands. What has changed is the adequacy of the disclosure, and for that the module's road is a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate, the choice depending on how pervasive the omission is. The adverse opinion in every case belongs to the different road where the basis itself is inappropriate.

options.text: Nothing changes. The events and the plans are still in note 41, the reader can draw the conclusion for herself, and the auditor's own separate going concern section says the uncertainty exists, which cures whatever the note leaves out.
options.misconception: Treats the auditor's report as a place to supply a disclosure the financial statements should have made.
options.why: The module's definition of adequate disclosure requires the clear statement itself, in the financial statements, not a reader's inference from events and plans. The separate section is written only where adequate disclosure is made and draws attention to the note; it does not stand in for words the note lacks, and the road for inadequate disclosure is a modified opinion.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph that supplies the missing sentence, since an emphasis of matter is the auditor's tool for drawing attention to what the accounts say too quietly.
options.misconception: Uses an emphasis of matter to fill a gap in disclosure, which is the one thing it can never do.
options.why: An emphasis of matter refers only to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and here the disclosure is not adequate, so the paragraph cannot be used at all. The module's road is a qualified or adverse opinion with the matter in the basis for opinion paragraph.

citation.ref: what a note must contain before the disclosure counts as an adequate one, including the plain admission that the doubt exists and that the company may not manage to turn its assets into cash and settle what it owes as a trading business does; and the road the report takes when the basis of preparation holds but that admission is missing — an opinion modified as far as the omission warrants, with the reason given in the basis for opinion paragraph
