items.stem: On the partner's idea alone, can describing the Kesar receivable as a key audit matter take the place of a qualification?

options.text: No. SA 701 applies to this listed company, and it says in terms that communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when SA 705 requires one. A matter that requires a qualification is dealt with in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section; the Key Audit Matters section cannot be used to keep the report clean.
options.why: SA 701 governs this audit — a listed company's full financial statements — and its scope paragraph, printed in the module, rules out four uses of the section at once. It is not a substitute for the disclosures the framework puts on management, not a substitute for the modified opinion SA 705 calls for once the circumstances demand one, not a substitute for the going concern reporting SA 570 requires, and never an opinion on one matter standing alone. What the section does is tell the reader how the audit went in the areas that mattered most, inside an opinion already formed on the statements taken as a whole; it has no power over what that opinion says. Where the facts demand a qualification, the reasons go in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the opinion is qualified. Wanting a clean report for the exchange is not a consideration the standard knows about.

options.text: Yes. For a listed company the Key Audit Matters section is the place where matters of most significance are reported, and a matter fully described there with the procedures performed need not also modify the opinion.
options.misconception: Treats the key audit matters section as an alternative form of modification.
options.why: Being of most significance in the audit is what makes a matter a key audit matter; it is not what decides the opinion. SA 701's scope paragraph excludes exactly this use: describing a matter as a key audit matter is not a substitute for a modified opinion when SA 705 requires one. The two operate together, not in place of each other.

options.text: No, because a matter that gives rise to a modified opinion can never be mentioned anywhere else in the report, so the Key Audit Matters section must stay silent about the receivable.
options.misconception: Reaches the right answer through an invented rule of silence.
options.why: The bar is on substitution, not on mention. What SA 701 forbids is using the key audit matters section instead of the modified opinion the circumstances require; the matter is described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the opinion is qualified. The conclusion that the partner's plan fails is right, but the reason given, a rule of total silence, is not in the standard.

options.text: Yes, provided the description in the Key Audit Matters section quantifies the possible loss and states that the auditor disagrees with management, which gives users the same information as a qualification.
options.misconception: Assumes the content of a paragraph can do the work of the opinion.
options.why: A key audit matter description is not a separate opinion on an individual matter, and SA 701 says so; the auditor does not express disagreement with management inside it. Giving users "the same information" is not the test. If the statements are materially misstated the opinion itself must say so, in the form SA 705 prescribes.

citation.ref: SA 701 on reach and on limits. It governs listed-entity audits, and it shuts out four uses of the key audit matters section: it cannot replace the disclosures the framework puts on management, nor the modified opinion SA 705 calls for, nor the going concern reporting under SA 570, and it is never an opinion on any single matter

Iyer & Rao are the statutory auditors, and the engagement partner is settling the report with three matters in front of her. Second, a receivable of 12 crore rupees from Kesar Trading, the company's largest distributor, has been outstanding since September 2025; a resolution professional was appointed over Kesar in January 2026, the debt is unsecured, and the company has made no provision; note 38 sets out these facts and management's view that the amount is recoverable in full, and the chief financial officer says that "the note discloses it fully, so an Emphasis of Matter pointing at the note is the most you need". Third, to keep the report clean for the exchange, the partner is minded to describe the Kesar receivable as a key audit matter, setting out the procedures performed and the judgement involved, in place of any qualification.

items.stem: On the liabilities compilation alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali corrects all four entries in the liabilities statement — the branch adjustment credit balance goes in, the borrowings from abroad go in at gross level, the accrued interest goes in and the NABARD refinance stays out — and accepts the twelve Fridays as satisfying the liquidity ratio verification, since Friday is the reporting day the whole system is built on.
options.misconception: Treating the Friday reporting cycle as the audit test dates, when the requirement is written to fall away from it.
options.why: The liabilities are right and the dates are not, and the reason given is the reason the requirement exists. Friday is the reporting day for the weekly trial balances from the branches and for the liabilities position consolidated at head office. The auditor's verification of compliance with the liquidity ratio is set on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, so that the dates tested are not the dates the bank already prepares for. Accepting a Friday compilation as the verification means the bank has been checked only on the days it was ready to be checked, and the report to the top management and the Reserve Bank would say compliance was verified when it was not.

options.text: Anjali tells him one of the four entries is right and the liquidity ratio work has not started. Leaving out the refinance from NABARD is correct; refinance from NABARD, SIDBI, the National Housing Bank and EXIM Bank is excluded. The net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is not an internal item that cancels itself — it is included in liabilities. Borrowings from abroad are reported at gross level as liabilities to others; only liabilities towards the banking system in India may be set off against assets with that system, and a bank abroad is not that system. The 26 crore rupees of interest that had accrued by the reporting date goes in whether or not the books had caught up with it. And the twelve Fridays are the wrong dates: compliance is verified on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, the Friday statements being the basis on which the liabilities position is struck, not the basis of the verification. Her report goes to the top management and to the Reserve Bank, and says how many branches were unaudited and that she relied on their returns.
options.why: Three of the general manager's four readings turn on the same mistake, which is treating a liability as something the bank owes to an outsider on the balance sheet date. The Reserve Bank's list works the other way round. The exclusions are named one by one, and refinance from NABARD is on that list, which is why leaving it out is right. What is not on the list stays in. The net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is money the bank holds unsquared between its own offices, and it is included; calling it internal does not make it disappear. Borrowings from abroad are the clearest case: the netting permitted for liabilities towards the banking system in India is permitted because both sides of it are inside the same system, so a borrowing from a bank abroad is reported at gross level as a liability to others and nothing is set off against it. Interest that has accrued by the reporting date is a liability from that date, and the bank's habit of writing it into the books at the quarter end is a bookkeeping rhythm, not a rule about when it is owed. The liquidity ratio dates are a separate error of the same family: the weekly Friday trial balances are how the liabilities position is determined, while the auditor's compliance verification is deliberately set on dates the bank cannot anticipate. In short, the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is included in liabilities, borrowings from abroad are reported at gross level, and the verification is done on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays.
keywords: net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts

options.text: Anjali corrects the branch adjustment accounts and the accrued interest, both of which go into liabilities, and accepts the rest. The refinance from NABARD is rightly excluded, the borrowings from abroad are dealings between banks and may be set off against the balances held with banks abroad, and a compilation on twelve Fridays through the year meets the verification requirement.
options.misconception: Reading the netting allowed within the banking system in India as a netting allowed between any two banks, and treating the Friday reporting rhythm as the verification dates.
options.why: Two of the three are right and the two that are wrong are the ones the general manager most wants agreement on. Netting is allowed only for liabilities towards the banking system in India against assets with that same system; borrowings from abroad by banks in India are outside it and are shown as liabilities to others at their full amount, so setting the balances abroad against them understates the liabilities on which both ratios are worked. And the twelve Fridays are the dates on which the liabilities position is struck, not the dates on which compliance is verified — the Reserve Bank asks for odd dates in different months that are not Fridays precisely so that the bank cannot arrange itself for them.

options.text: Anjali corrects only the borrowings from abroad, which are shown at their full amount as liabilities to others. The branch adjustment accounts are internal and net to nothing outside the bank, interest not yet written into the books is not yet a liability, the NABARD refinance is rightly out, and the twelve Fridays are the required verification dates.
options.misconception: Treating internal accounts and unposted accruals as outside liabilities, so only the item owed to an identifiable outsider on a posted date is counted.
options.why: The one correction made is correct, and three of the four things left alone are wrong. A net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is included in liabilities; it is an unsquared amount the bank holds, and the fact that both sides of the entry are its own offices is not a reason to leave it out. Interest accrued by the reporting date is included even though the bank records it periodically, because the accrual and the posting are two different dates and the liability follows the first. And the compliance verification is done on odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, which is a different set of dates from the Friday trial balances the liabilities position is built on.

items.scenario: Kelkar & Deshmukh are a firm of chartered accountants at Nagpur, and Anjali Kelkar is the partner in charge of the statutory central audit of Wainganga Bank Limited, a scheduled commercial bank, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters have come to her from the general manager (accounts) in the week the report is to be signed. First, the compilation of demand and time liabilities. The bank's statement leaves out a refinance of 300 crore rupees taken from NABARD; it also leaves out a net credit balance of 42 crore rupees in the branch adjustment accounts, which the general manager calls an internal account that cancels against itself; it shows borrowings from abroad of 180 crore rupees netted against the bank's own balances with banks abroad, on the footing that both are dealings with the banking system; and it omits 26 crore rupees of interest that had accrued on deposits by the reporting date but was written into the books only at the following quarter end. For the statutory liquidity ratio, he has handed her a compilation prepared as on twelve Fridays spread through the year and says the verification is complete. Second, the head other assets. Interest accrued of 55 crore rupees includes 9 crore rupees on bills purchased and discounted that are long overdue, where the branch's own note records that recovery is uncertain, and the general manager's position is that interest accrues by contract whether or not anybody collects it. A suspense account carries 7 crore rupees, of which 4.2 crore rupees are entries more than three years old for which no reason for the delay is on record, and he says a suspense balance is temporary by definition and so needs no provision. And a building taken over in 2019 from a defaulting borrower in satisfaction of a debt of 12 crore rupees stands in the books at 12 crore rupees, though its net realisable value on the date it was taken over was 9.5 crore rupees; he says the bank will sell it at a profit one day. Third, the reports beyond the audit report itself. The general manager suggests that the long form audit report for the bank is a management document, so it should go before the board only if the board asks for it and nothing about it need reach the Reserve Bank; and he asks whether authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on the conduct of treasury operations belong to this engagement at all, or are a separate assignment the bank would have to commission. Anjali has to settle each of the three before the report is signed.

items.stem: On the other assets alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali takes the interest out and examines the suspense entries, and leaves the building at 12 crore rupees. The asset was taken over in full and final settlement of a debt of that amount, so 12 crore rupees is what the bank gave up for it, and the realisable value matters only when it is sold.
options.misconception: Measuring an asset taken in satisfaction of a claim at the amount of the claim, and deferring the shortfall to the sale.
options.why: A non-banking asset acquired in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, measured when it is taken over, so the figure is 9.5 crore rupees. The claim given up is not the cost, because the bank did not choose this asset as an investment — it took what was available for a debt that was not being paid, and the rule exists so that the shortfall is recognised then rather than carried as an asset until a sale finally proves it. Since 2019 the difference has sat in other assets as a profit the bank still expects.

options.text: Anjali requires the suspense account to be examined entry by entry and the building to be brought down to 9.5 crore rupees, but leaves the interest accrued alone. Interest on bills purchased and discounted accrues under the contract and the bills have not been written off, so the whole 55 crore rupees stands until the advances themselves are treated as bad.
options.misconception: Treating a contractual accrual as income until the underlying advance is written off, instead of testing what can be realised.
options.why: The interest is the item the head exists to test. Other assets carries interest accrued only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, which does not wait for the advance to be written off; it is the accounting rule that revenue is not recognised where there is significant uncertainty about collectability, and the branch's own note that recovery is uncertain is precisely that. Leaving the 9 crore rupees in overstates both the asset and the year's income, and it does so in the head where such an amount is least likely to be asked about again.

options.text: Anjali requires all three to change. Interest accrued is carried only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, so the 9 crore rupees on long overdue bills, where the branch's own note records the doubt, comes out; a contractual right to interest is not revenue where collection is significantly uncertain. On the suspense account she asks for the details of the old outstanding entries with the reasons for the delay, and where a balance calls for a provision or a write-off she examines whether it has been made — 4.2 crore rupees standing over three years unexplained is the reason the head is looked at at all. And the building came in at the wrong figure: an asset acquired in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, which is 9.5 crore rupees and not 12. She also reads the terms of the settlement, checks that ownership is legally vested in the bank, and looks at section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, since the asset is held to be disposed of and has been there since 2019.
options.why: Each of the three answers is the same idea in a different place: other assets is the head where an amount that will never be collected can sit for years looking like an asset, so each item in it is tested against what the bank will actually get. Interest accrued is included only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, which is the accounting rule that revenue is not recognised where there is significant uncertainty about collectability; the branch's own note is that uncertainty in writing, so the 9 crore rupees is not carried whatever the contract says. The suspense account is examined by obtaining the details of the old outstanding entries and the reasons for the delay, because the age is the evidence — an entry nobody has been able to explain in three years is not a temporary parking of a receipt, and where the balance requires a provision or a write-off the auditor sees whether one has been made rather than accepting that the head is temporary by nature. The building is measured by a rule written for this exact hope: an asset taken in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, so the shortfall is taken when the asset comes in and is not carried as a future profit. In short, interest goes in only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, the old outstanding entries in suspense are obtained with their reasons and provided for where needed, and the building enters at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired.
keywords: realised in the ordinary course of business
net book value of the advance or the net realisable value

options.text: Anjali takes the 9 crore rupees of interest out and brings the building down to 9.5 crore rupees, and accepts the suspense account as it stands. A suspense balance is a holding place for entries awaiting classification, so its age is a housekeeping matter for the bank rather than something the audit provides against.
options.misconception: Reading the suspense account as a housekeeping matter because of what it is called, rather than examining the old entries for a provision.
options.why: Two right and the third is where the loss usually hides. The suspense account is examined by obtaining the details of the old outstanding entries and the reasons for the delay, and where a balance requires a provision or a write-off the auditor examines whether it has been made. An entry more than three years old with no reason on record is not awaiting classification; it is an amount nobody can account for, and treating the head as temporary by definition is what lets it stay. Age is the evidence here, not the excuse.

items.stem: On the reports after the audit report alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali agrees that the certificates, authentication of the capital adequacy ratio among them, are part of this engagement, and accepts that the long form audit report is addressed to the management. Once she has given it to the management the bank decides what to do with it, and whether it goes further is the board's affair.
options.misconception: Treating the report as delivered when it reaches management, so the stages after that are read as the bank's own business.
options.why: The first half is right and the second stops one step too early. The long form audit report is submitted to the management, and it does not stop there: it is placed before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed, and a copy of it with the relative agenda note and the Board's views goes to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. Those stages are not the bank's discretion, and they are the reason the report is worth writing — a report that reaches only the people it comments on is a report with no reader who can act on it.

options.text: Anjali says the long form audit report goes to the management, before the Audit Committee of the Board and to the Reserve Bank within 60 days with the agenda note and the Board's views. On the second question she agrees with the general manager: authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on treasury operations are certificates outside the statutory audit, which the bank engages an auditor for separately.
options.misconception: Reading a bank audit as a company audit plus optional extras, so the regulatory certificates look like separate assignments.
options.why: The route of the report is right and the second half misreads what a bank audit includes. The statutory central auditor of a bank gives a list of reports and certificates as part of the same engagement, and authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on whether treasury operations were conducted in accordance with the Reserve Bank's instructions are both on it, beside the liquidity ratio report, the income recognition and asset classification report and the Ghosh and Jilani committee reports. Treating them as separate work would leave the regulator without figures it depends on the statutory auditor to certify, and would make the engagement look like a company audit with an opinion and nothing else.

options.text: Anjali says both parts of his suggestion are wrong. The long form audit report is not a paper that waits to be asked for: it goes from her to the management, it is placed before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed on each matter in it, and a copy of it with the relative agenda note and the Board's views is submitted to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. And the certificates are not a separate assignment for the bank to commission — authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on whether treasury operations were conducted in accordance with the Reserve Bank's instructions are among the reports the statutory central auditor gives as part of this engagement, along with the report on compliance with the liquidity ratio, the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, and the reports on the Ghosh and Jilani committee recommendations.
options.why: The general manager has read both things as favours the bank may decline. Neither is. The long form audit report has a route written for it, and every stage of that route is somebody else's check on the bank: management first, then the Audit Committee of the Board, which must record what is being done about each matter, and then the Reserve Bank, which receives the report together with the agenda note and the Board's own views within 60 days. Making it depend on the board asking would break the route at the point where it stops being internal. The second half is a mistake about what a bank audit is. A company audit ends at an opinion on the financial statements; a bank audit carries a list of reports and certificates alongside it, because the regulator relies on the auditor for figures it cannot verify itself — the capital adequacy ratio is authenticated by her, treasury operations are reported against the Reserve Bank's instructions, and the liquidity ratio, income recognition and asset classification and the Ghosh and Jilani committee reports sit in the same list. In short, the long form audit report goes to management, then before the Audit Committee of the Board, and to the Reserve Bank within 60 days with the agenda note and the Board's views, and authentication of the capital adequacy ratio is part of this engagement rather than a separate one.

options.text: Anjali says the long form audit report goes to the management, then before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed, and that a copy reaches the Reserve Bank; the bank sends it with its other returns whenever those are due, there being no separate time limit. The certificates, including authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, are part of this engagement.
options.misconception: Remembering the route the report takes but not that it carries a time limit of its own.
options.why: Everything here is right except the timing, and the timing is the part that decides whether the report is of any use. A copy of the long form audit report together with the relative agenda note and the Board's views is submitted to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. Letting it travel with whatever return happens to be due next means the regulator reads the auditor's observations on a year that is already well past, and it also removes the pressure that makes the Board record its views at all.

items.stem: On the board note about the four contractors alone, what should the board be told?

options.text: It is horizontal integration, because Alaknanda and the contractors serve the same developers, and the purchase would bring two firms with one customer under one roof.
options.misconception: reads two firms serving the same customer as two firms standing at the same stage
options.why: Sideways means buying somebody doing the same work at the same stage, which is another way of saying buying a competitor. The contractors do not build turbines and Alaknanda does not erect them; they are consecutive stages of one chain that happen to end at the same developer. Sharing a customer is not sharing a stage, and no rival leaves the market if this purchase goes through.

options.text: It is backward integration, because the contractors are the source of every order Alaknanda receives and the note is really about securing supply.
options.misconception: names the direction from where the orders come rather than from where the acquired business sits between the company and the person who finally buys
options.why: Backward means taking on the stage that supplies the company with what it works on — the foundry, the forging shop, the plate mill. The contractors supply nothing of the kind. They take a finished machine and put it in the ground for a developer. An order is not an input, and a business standing between the maker and the buyer is on the customer side of the chain however much work it sends back up the line.

options.text: It is forward integration, and the direction fits the pressure the facts describe — what Alaknanda depends on is the contractor standing between it and the developer, and there is nothing on the supply side for a purchase to fix.
options.why: Direction is read off the stage the acquired business occupies. The contractors sit between Alaknanda and the person who finally buys the machine: they carry it to the site, they hold the developer's signature and they keep the service work for the life of the plant. Taking them on is a move towards the buyer, and that is forward integration. Naming the move is the first mark; the second and harder one is whether the move touches the pressure the company is actually under, and here it does. The facts put nothing on the supply side — many small foundries, prices that have not moved in three years, no shortage of castings or forgings. Everything that has changed sits in the channel, where two of the four largest contractors now fit a rival's machine beside Alaknanda's and can move a developer from one supplier to another for nothing. Buying that stage removes the dependence the facts actually describe rather than one somebody has imagined. In short, this is forward integration, and it answers the dependence the facts describe.
keywords: the stage the acquired business occupies
it answers the dependence the facts describe

options.text: It is not integration at all but diversification, since erection and commissioning is a service business and Alaknanda is a manufacturer, so the board should judge it as an entry into a new industry.
options.misconception: treats a different kind of work on the same chain as an unrelated business, when every integration buys a stage that does something the company does not do
options.why: A foundry melts metal, a contractor puts machines in the ground, and neither builds turbines. If a different activity were enough to make a move diversification, no integration could exist at all. What marks this one is that the activity sits on the chain carrying Alaknanda's own machine to Alaknanda's own buyer, and what is being bought is the service revenue on those very machines.

items.scenario:
Alaknanda Hydel Systems Limited is an unlisted public company at Dehradun that builds turbines, gates and penstocks for small hydro plants in the hills. Its revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was 486 crore rupees, it has an audit committee constituted under section 177, and CA Ira Nauriyal is the engagement partner on its statutory audit. Five matters sit in front of the board and its auditor in June 2026, and two of them are carried in the annexures.
The first is the route to market. Alaknanda never sells to a power developer directly. Forty independent erection and commissioning contractors carry its machines to the site, install them and hold the service contract afterwards; the developer signs with the contractor, and the contractor decides whose turbine goes in. Castings and forgings come from many small foundries at prices that have not moved in three years, and the works has never been short of either. What has changed is at the other end. Two of the four largest contractors have begun fitting an imported turbine beside Alaknanda's, they keep the service revenue that follows every machine for its whole life, and they have moved developers from one supplier to another without paying anything to do it. A board note proposes buying those four contractors outright and asks for approval on the strength of the service revenue the group would then keep.
The second is measurement. The board has built a scorecard on four perspectives and has set, under the customer heading, the goal of getting a stopped machine generating again faster than anybody else in the industry, because a developer loses a day of sales for every day a turbine stands still. Four measures have been put up for that row: the hours of training given to service engineers during the year, the number of regional service depots opened, the average time from a developer's breakdown call to the machine generating again, and the rupees spent on spares held near the sites.
The third is the overseas arm. Alaknanda holds eight per cent of the paid-up equity capital of Himal Turbine Works Limited, a company whose shares are listed on the Nepal exchange, and a shareholders' agreement gives Alaknanda the right to appoint three of Himal's five directors. The finance head has classified the holding as overseas portfolio investment, on the reasoning that eight is below ten and that a board seat is a management matter rather than an investment one.
The fourth is a customer in trouble. Mandakini Power Limited, a developer that owes Alaknanda 34 crore rupees, was admitted into a corporate insolvency resolution process on 6 January 2026 and a moratorium has been in force since. Annexure 1 is what the Dehradun paper carried about it this month.
ANNEXURE 1 — BUSINESS NEWS
State authority moves to take back Mandakini's water concession. Dehradun, 2 June 2026. The state water resources authority has served a notice on Mandakini Power Limited proposing to cancel the thirty-year concession under which it draws water for its 24 MW plant, on the ground that a company in insolvency cannot be relied on to run a river. Mandakini's resolution professional has replied that every charge falling due for the use of the concession since the process began has been paid on the day it fell due, that nothing is outstanding, and that the plant has generated without a break throughout. The notice itself alleges no arrears. A rival developer is understood to have written to the authority the same week asking for the concession if it falls free.
ANNEXURE 2 — INTERNAL EMAIL
From: Vivek Bahuguna, finance head. Sent: 5 June 2026, 09:40. To: CA Ira Nauriyal, Nauriyal and Rawat. Subject: two matters for the audit file.
Ira, internal audit has closed two investigations and I set out below what was found and what I think follows from it.
The first is the stores in-charge at the Dehradun works. He sold scrap gates to a firm he owns himself on four occasions during the year, for 42 lakh rupees, 55 lakh rupees, 38 lakh rupees and 61 lakh rupees. One man, one method, four times, one crore ninety-six lakh rupees in all. Because the total is well past a crore I take it this has to go to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, routed through the audit committee for its reply.
The second is our freight contractor. He billed us against forged weighbridge slips and took 2.4 crore rupees more than he was owed, over fourteen months. items.stem: On the customer-perspective goal alone, which of the four proposed measures should carry it?

options.text: The number of regional service depots opened, because a depot near the site is what makes a fast repair possible and a count of them is easy to verify.
options.misconception: counts a resource put in place instead of the outcome it was meant to produce, and treats ease of verification as what makes a measure right
options.why: A depot is a means to the goal, not the goal. Five of them opened and eleven days still taken to restore a machine is a perfectly possible year, and this measure would call it a success. Being easy to count is not the test either; a measure is chosen because the goal cannot be reached without it moving, and a depot can sit there unused.

options.text: The average time from a developer's breakdown call to an engineer reaching the site, since that is the part of the delay Alaknanda controls, and holding people to a number they cannot control is unfair.
options.misconception: narrows the measure to the part the company finds comfortable, which stops short of the goal the board actually set
options.why: Reaching the site is a step on the way, not the thing the developer is waiting for. A machine reached in four hours and repaired in nine days has not been restored quickly, and a measure that stops where the company's comfort stops will report success through a year of long stoppages. Where part of the delay sits outside Alaknanda's hands — a part on a truck, a road closed by rain — that is an argument for taking it in hand, which is what the goal says.

options.text: The average time from a developer's breakdown call to the machine generating again, which is the only one of the four that says whether the goal was reached.
options.why: A measure earns its row by answering the goal it is put against. The goal is a stopped machine generating again faster than anybody else, so the measure has to be the length of the stoppage as the developer experiences it — from the call to the first unit sent out again. options.text: The hours of training given to service engineers during the year, because a faster repair comes from a better trained engineer and training is where the improvement has to start.

items.stem: On the water concession alone, may the state authority cancel it?

options.text: No. While the moratorium runs, a grant of this kind cannot be taken back for the reason that the company is insolvent, and the single condition attached to that shelter is met — every charge for using the concession since the process began has been paid.
options.why: Section 14 does more than freeze suits and recovery. It also holds in place the permissions a company needs in order to keep trading — a licence, a permit, a registration, a quota, a concession, a clearance — whether the grant came from a government, a local authority or a sectoral regulator; none of them may be suspended or terminated while the moratorium runs on the ground of insolvency. The shelter is not unconditional. It holds only where the company keeps paying whatever falls due for the use of the grant during the moratorium period itself, which is why the resolution professional's reply talks about payments and why the notice's silence about arrears matters more. Mandakini has paid every charge on the day it fell due, nothing is outstanding, and the only ground the notice offers is the one the section closes off. A rival's letter asking for the concession is not a ground at all. In short, a concession cannot be taken back on the ground of insolvency while the moratorium runs, so long as the dues for using it during the moratorium period are paid.
keywords: a licence, a permit, a registration, a quota, a concession, a clearance
keeps paying whatever falls due for the use of the grant
taken back on the ground of insolvency

options.text: Yes. The moratorium binds courts, tribunals and creditors chasing the company for money. A regulator acting under its own statute is none of those, and an insolvency law cannot take away a power another statute gives the authority.
options.misconception: reads the moratorium as reaching only legal proceedings and creditors, when it also holds a debtor's regulatory permissions in place
options.why: Only the first limb of section 14 is about suits and proceedings. The explanation under that sub-section says in terms that a grant made by a government, a local authority or a sectoral regulator is not to be suspended or terminated during the moratorium for the reason that the company is insolvent, and it says so notwithstanding any other law. The authority's power is real; the ground it has chosen is the one the Code shuts while the process runs.

options.text: No, and for a wider reason — once a moratorium is declared, nothing touching the company's permissions or contracts may change at all until the process ends, so the authority could not even alter the concession's terms.
options.misconception: widens a shelter that carries one stated condition into a general freeze on everything touching the company
options.why: What the section gives is narrower and sharper: a grant is not to be suspended or terminated on the ground of insolvency, and that holds only while the dues for using the grant during the moratorium keep being paid. Read as a general freeze it stops being arguable — a student holding that reading cannot say why the resolution professional's reply is about payments at all, and would answer this notice correctly for a reason the section does not contain.

options.text: Yes. The concession belongs to the authority and was only lent to Mandakini, so it is not property of the corporate debtor, and a moratorium that protects the debtor's assets has nothing to say about it.
options.misconception: treats a grant as outside the moratorium because the debtor does not own it, when the shelter was written for exactly the things a debtor holds without owning
options.why: A business in resolution is worth more running than stopped, and what keeps it running is usually held rather than owned — permission to operate, a registration, a right to draw water from a river. That is why those are named separately from the debtor's assets in the first place. Ownership is not the test here and never was.

items.stem: On the Himal Turbine Works holding alone, is the finance head's classification right?

options.text: No, and the classification would be the same at any percentage, because control is what separates the two: any investor holding a board seat holds overseas direct investment, whether the foreign entity is listed or not.
options.misconception: makes control the dividing line everywhere, when it decides only a sub-ten-per-cent holding in a listed entity, and treats one seat on a board as control
options.why: Control settles one limb of one case. Any unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity is direct investment on grounds that mention no percentage at all; ten per cent or more of a listed one is direct investment with or without control; and control is asked about only below ten per cent in a listed entity. One seat out of five is also not control — three out of five is, because that is a majority of the board.

options.text: Yes. For a listed foreign entity the ten per cent line is the whole test and eight is below it. The right to name directors comes from a private agreement and is a management right, which has nothing to do with how an investment is classified.
options.misconception: takes the percentage as the only test for a listed entity, when a second limb brings a smaller holding in the moment it carries control
options.why: Were the percentage the whole test, the Rules would not have written a second limb for listed entities at all. That limb exists for exactly this case: a small stake that comes with the power to run the company, because what makes an investment direct is the ability to direct. A shareholders' agreement is where such a power usually lives, so it is the first place the classification looks rather than a private matter standing outside it.

options.text: No. In a listed foreign entity a holding under ten per cent is still overseas direct investment where it carries control, and a right to name three of five directors is control; only a holding under ten per cent with no control is portfolio investment.
options.why: The definition of overseas direct investment runs in four limbs, and two of them reach a listed foreign entity. The first of those is arithmetic: ten per cent or more of the paid-up equity capital is direct investment whether or not the investor has any say in how the entity is run. The second is the limb that decides this holding — an investment below ten per cent is also overseas direct investment if it carries control. Control is the power to appoint a majority of the board, or to settle the management or policy decisions of the entity, and it may come through a shareholding, through management rights or, as here, through a shareholders' agreement. Three of Himal's five directors is squarely that, whatever the percentage sitting beside it. Overseas portfolio investment is what is left over once the four limbs have taken what they take, which for a listed entity means a stake below ten per cent with no control attached. In short, a holding below ten per cent of a listed foreign entity is overseas direct investment where it carries control, and the power to appoint a majority of the board is control.
keywords: an investment below ten per cent is also overseas direct investment if it carries control
the power to appoint a majority of the board
a stake below ten per cent with no control attached

options.text: No, but the reason is the size of the commitment. An investment abroad is overseas direct investment once the company's total financial commitment passes the ceiling set against its net worth, and Alaknanda's is past it.
options.misconception: confuses the ceiling on how much may go abroad with the test that says what kind of investment a particular holding is
options.why: The ceiling and the classification answer different questions. An Indian company's total financial commitment in foreign entities is capped at four hundred per cent of its net worth as per its last audited balance sheet, which is a limit on the amount and a breach of it is a breach. Whether one holding is direct or portfolio investment turns on the nature of that holding, and it would read the same way if Alaknanda had spent a tenth as much.

citation.ref: Rules 2(1)(q) and 2(1)(s) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, read with the definition of control in the same Rules — a holding below ten per cent of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity is overseas direct investment where it carries control

items.stem: On the two matters in the finance head's email alone, what does the auditor do?

options.text: The finance head is right about the scrap sales. Four takings by one man using one method are one continuing fraud, so they are added together, and one crore ninety-six lakh rupees goes to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 through the audit committee.
options.misconception: adds separate frauds by the same person together to cross the threshold, when the rule measures each one on its own
options.why: The rule fixes the threshold on what a fraud involves by itself. Four sales on four occasions are four frauds however alike they look, and adding them is the auditor applying a test the rule does not contain. The consequence is not academic either: the higher road puts a statement on the Ministry's desk and the company on a list, on a reading nothing supports.

options.text: Nothing is reported yet. A police complaint is filed and the company's own investigation is closed but untested, so the auditor waits until a court or the police establishes that a fraud was committed before anything leaves the firm.
options.misconception: waits for proof, when the duty is set off by the auditor's own reason to believe and its clock starts on the day she knows
options.why: The sub-section speaks of an auditor who, doing her work as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud is being or has been committed. Reason to believe is a long way short of a finding by a court, and it has to be, because the clock in the rule is measured in days from the auditor's knowledge. Waiting for the police would make every report years late, and the two days would have run out long before the first hearing.

options.text: The freight overbilling is the one that goes up. At 2.4 crore rupees it is past the threshold, so it goes to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, and the scrap sales, being small, are noted in the management letter and left there.
options.misconception: reads the amount as the whole test, forgetting that the sub-section reaches only a fraud committed on the company by its own officers or employees
options.why: The amount is the second question and there is a first one in front of it. The sub-section is about an offence of fraud on the company by its officers or employees, and an outside contractor with nobody inside helping him is not that at any figure. The scrap sales are the ones that do belong to the sub-section, and being under a crore does not send them to a management letter; it sends them to the audit committee and into the Board's report.

options.text: Each fraud is measured on its own, so the four scrap sales are not added up and none of them reaches a crore: all four go to the audit committee within two days of Ira knowing, and the company sets out their details in the Board's report. The freight overbilling is outside the sub-section altogether, because it reaches a fraud on the company by its own officers or employees; it is answered in the CARO report instead, and no Form ADT-4 is filed for it.
options.why: The rule asks whether a fraud involves, or is expected to involve, individually one crore rupees or more, and the word doing the work is individually. Four sales of scrap on four occasions for 42, 55, 38 and 61 lakh rupees are four frauds, each measured against the threshold by itself, however plainly one man used one method four times. None reaches a crore, so the lower road is the one that opens: the audit committee within two days of the auditor coming to know, told what the fraud was, roughly how much went and who was in it, and the company then setting those details out in the Board's report. Nothing goes to the Central Government and no statement in Form ADT-4 is filed. The freight matter fails a different test, and fails it before the money is even reached: the sub-section is about an offence of fraud on the company by its own officers or employees, and the company's own investigation found nobody inside it. An outsider who defrauds the company is still reported, under clause (xi) of the Order, which asks about a fraud by the company and a fraud on the company noticed or reported in the year. In short, the threshold is measured against each fraud individually rather than against the total, so the four scrap sales go to the audit committee and into the Board's report, and the freight fraud sits outside the sub-section because no officer or employee was in it.
keywords: individually one crore rupees or more
measured against each fraud individually rather than against the total
because no officer or employee was in it

items.stem: On the industry reading and the market share alone, what should the board conclude about the fall in margin?

options.text: That the reading explains nothing about a margin. Margin is made or lost inside a company, so the fall is a costing failure at Bhagirathi and the answer is a cost programme.
options.misconception: Treats profitability as entirely internal and industry structure as background colour.
options.why: Costs are one half of a margin and the price the industry allows is the other, and this reading is about the second half. Four chains charging for shelf space and an own-label pack beside every brand set a ceiling on price that no amount of internal cost work lifts. A cost programme may well be worth running; it is not an answer to the question of why the whole industry is earning less than it did.

options.text: That the five headings are a register of risks. The conclusion is to score each of them every quarter and report the movement to the board.
options.misconception: Turns an analysis that is supposed to end in a conclusion about profit into a monitoring exercise with no conclusion at all.
options.why: Monitoring is what you do with a thing you have already understood. The reading is used to reach a conclusion about whether profit survives in this industry, and a quarterly score sheet postpones that conclusion instead of arriving at it. A board that has been given a table and a review date has been told nothing it can act on.

options.text: That with the largest share Bhagirathi can lead prices upwards and the smaller brands will follow, so the reading supports a price rise rather than a change of plan.
options.misconception: Reads market share as pricing power, in an industry where buyers are concentrated and a substitute sits on the same shelf.
options.why: Leading a price upwards needs somebody on the other side who has nowhere else to go. Here four chains carry three-quarters of the volume, each of them sells its own label, and several hundred regional brands are waiting for a gap. Share in an industry shaped like that buys volume, not pricing power, and a brand that moves first on price loses the shelf rather than gaining the margin.

options.text: That the profit in this industry is being competed away, so holding the largest share of it does not exempt Bhagirathi. Four headings pressing at once — easy entry, concentrated buyers who charge for shelf space, their own labels standing in for the brands, and crops reaching processors through a few traders — describe an industry in which whatever margin is made gets handed to somebody else. The first thing the reading is for is the answer to whether profit survives here at all, and the answer is that not much of it does. Share is a claim on the profit an industry has left; it does not create any.
options.why: An industry reading is a statement about how much money is available to compete for, and that is the first of the two conclusions it is meant to reach. Where several forces press at once the margin leaks out of the industry as a whole: entry costs so little that no price stays high for long, four chains between them decide who reaches a shelf and take a fee for it, an own-label pack sitting alongside caps what a brand can charge, and a concentrated set of traders holds the price of the crop. None of those pressures asks how large the firm bearing them is. So the largest share of a thin industry is a large share of very little, and reading the fall as evidence that costs at Bhagirathi in particular are being run badly mistakes an industry result for a company one. a large share of very little
mistakes an industry result for a company one

items.scenario:
Bhagirathi Foods Limited is listed on both exchanges and sells packaged spice mixes and ready-to-cook meals across India. Its financial year ended on 31 March 2026 and the audit report has not yet been signed. Four matters sit with the audit committee, and the finance head has written to its chairperson about every one of them.

Bhagirathi holds the largest share of the packaged spice market at twenty-two per cent, and its operating margin has fallen for the third year running. The planning team's reading of the industry runs like this. Several hundred regional brands compete; a grinding and packing line costs little to put up; four retail chains carry three-quarters of the volume and charge a fee before a new pack reaches a shelf; each of those chains now sells its own label beside the brands; and the chilli and turmeric crops reach processors through a small number of large traders. The team graded four of the five headings as pressing hard, put the grading in a table, and stopped there.

The chief executive tells the board that Bhagirathi has taken the cost leadership position, because after discounts its 200 gram pack sits at a lower shelf price than any other national brand. The costing team's own figures say something else. Making, packing and delivering that pack costs Bhagirathi about three rupees more than it costs the nearest competitor, and the shelf price is being held down by a rebate a large packaging supplier agreed to for two years, of which one year is left.

During the year the company placed three orders for printed cartons on Anvi Packaging LLP, a firm in which the managing director's brother is a partner: eighteen crore rupees in June 2025, fourteen crore rupees in November 2025, and a fourth order of twenty crore rupees is now proposed. Two other suppliers had quoted about nine per cent less for the same board, printing and delivery, and the purchase file records that the difference was accepted to keep the supply steady. Turnover in the audited accounts of the preceding financial year was four hundred and eighty crore rupees. The managing director says he will sit through the Board's discussion of the fourth order but will not vote on it.

Sarayu Cold Storage Private Limited is a subsidiary of Bhagirathi and is audited by a different firm. Its turnover for the year was forty-one crore rupees. It borrowed thirty crore rupees from a bank in August 2025 to build a warehouse at Nashik and had brought the outstanding down to eighteen crore rupees by 31 March 2026. Sarayu has filed its financial statements and its annual returns with the Registrar on time in every year of its existence. Its auditor is settling what his report must say about internal financial controls.

On 18 April 2026 a fire destroyed Bhagirathi's cold store at Vapi and the stock lying in it, which stood in the books at 31 March 2026 at nine crore rupees. The company reported the fire to both exchanges under Regulation 30 of the listing regulations, inside the time that regulation allows.

ANNEXURE 1, a trade weekly of 6 April 2026, under the heading Spice brands cut again. The tenth round of price cuts this year landed last week, and two of the four national chains have widened their own-label spice ranges since January. A brand manager who asked not to be named said that putting a new pack on a shelf now costs more than advertising it used to. Nobody in this business earns what it earned three years ago, a distributor in Indore told us. The volumes are there. The money is not.

ANNEXURE 2, an internal email of 22 April 2026 from the finance head to the chairperson of the audit committee. Four things before Friday. One, the fall in margin is ours to fix, because we hold the biggest share in the country and nobody can tell me the market is the problem. Two, we are the cost leader, since our pack is the cheapest on the shelf and that is what the phrase means. Three, the fourth carton order is a contract of its own and each of the three earlier ones is well under a tenth of our turnover, so a Board resolution covers it. Four, Sarayu's borrowing on the closing day was eighteen crore rupees, so its auditor need say nothing about controls; and the fire has gone to the exchanges inside the time Regulation 30 allows, so the closed year's accounts need nothing further and our audit work stopped on 31 March in any case.

items.stem: On the shelf price and the costing figures alone, is the chief executive right that Bhagirathi holds the cost leadership position?

options.text: Yes. The cheapest pack on the shelf is exactly what cost leadership means, since the buyer meets the position at the price and nowhere else.
options.misconception: Confuses selling at the lowest price with producing at the lowest cost.
options.why: The buyer meets the price, and the position is what lets the firm survive at it. Two firms can print the same number on the same shelf and only one of them makes money doing so. The question the position answers is which of them can hold that number through a price war, and on these figures Bhagirathi cannot.

options.text: No. The position is being the producer whose costs are lowest, and Bhagirathi's are three rupees a pack above its nearest rival's. What it holds is the lowest price, bought with somebody else's rebate for one more year. A cost leader prices where its rivals cannot follow and still earns; Bhagirathi is pricing where its rivals could follow comfortably and is earning less than they do while it does so.
options.why: The two things being confused here are a price and a position. Winning on cost means the operating model itself produces the lowest cost — the range kept short, the runs kept long, the overhead kept thin, distribution stripped to what is needed — and the low price is then something the firm can afford and its rivals cannot match without losing money. Bhagirathi has the second half and not the first. Its cost per pack is above the nearest competitor's, so every rupee it takes off the shelf price hurts it more than the same cut hurts them, which is the exact reverse of what the position is for. And the gap between the two is being filled by a supplier's rebate held at that supplier's option with a year left to run, so what looks like an advantage is a term of somebody else's contract. A low price paid for out of somebody else's pocket is not a cost position, and the year the rebate ends is the year the board finds that out.
keywords: the operating model itself produces the lowest cost
a term of somebody else's contract

options.text: Yes, so long as the rebate is renewed next year. A cost advantage obtained from a supplier agreement is a cost advantage like any other, and the position stands while it lasts.
options.misconception: Mistakes a bought discount held at another party's option for a cost structure of the firm's own.
options.why: A discount somebody else grants can be withdrawn by somebody else, and a rival can be offered the same terms tomorrow. A position is what a firm has built into how it makes and moves its goods, which is why it survives a renegotiation. Reading a two-year rebate as a position leaves the board planning on a year of grace it does not control.

options.text: No, and it follows that Bhagirathi must move to differentiation and raise its price, since a firm which is not the cheapest has to be the most different.
options.misconception: Reads the two positions as an exhaustive pair a firm can simply switch between, rather than as two positions each of which has to be built.
options.why: Failing to hold one position does not confer the other. Winning on difference has to be built and paid for — something the buyer can see, would miss, and will pay extra for — and nothing in these facts says Bhagirathi has it. Raising the price first and finding the difference afterwards is how a firm ends up with the costs of one position and the prices of the other.

citation.ref: Generic competitive strategies — volume 1, the airline whose stated position is cost leadership and whose revenue per seat kilometre sits below its cost per seat kilometre, and volume 2, where making a raw material in-house is read as cost leadership and not as differentiation

items.stem: On the carton orders alone, what does the company need before it places the fourth one?

options.text: The members' prior approval by ordinary resolution, on top of the Board's resolution. Nine per cent above two other quotations is not arm's length, so the exemption for ordinary-course dealings closes and the section applies. The limit for a purchase of goods is ten per cent of turnover, taken from last year's audited accounts, which is forty-eight crore rupees, and it is applied to the year's orders of that kind added together: eighteen and fourteen already placed, twenty now proposed, fifty-two crore rupees in all. The managing director's offer is also short of what the rule asks — an interested director does not sit through the discussion, not merely the vote.
options.why: Three questions, taken in order. Is the section engaged? Its exemption needs the deal to be both in the ordinary course and at arm's length, and paying nine per cent more than two other suppliers quoted for the same board, printing and delivery fails the second limb whatever the purchase file says about steady supply. What does the section then ask for? At least a resolution of the Board. Do the members have to be asked as well? For a purchase of goods the prescribed limit is ten per cent or more of turnover, and two things about how it is measured decide this case. Turnover is taken from the audited accounts of the preceding financial year, so the base is four hundred and eighty crore rupees and the limit is forty-eight crore. And the limit is applied to the transactions of that kind entered into during the financial year taken together with the earlier ones, not to each contract on its own, so the figure to compare is fifty-two crore rupees. The limit is crossed, so the members must approve by ordinary resolution before the order is placed. One more thing goes with it: where a director is interested in the contract, the rule keeps him out of the meeting while it is discussed, so offering to abstain from the vote and stay in the room does not meet it.
keywords: both in the ordinary course and at arm's length
the audited accounts of the preceding financial year
taken together with the earlier ones

options.text: Only a resolution of the Board, because the ten per cent test for a purchase of this size is measured against the company's net worth, which the orders come nowhere near.
options.misconception: Uses the base prescribed for property transactions on a purchase of goods.
options.why: The base differs with the kind of transaction, and for a sale, purchase or supply of goods or materials it is turnover. Net worth is the base the rule uses for buying or disposing of property. Reading across from one row of that rule to another moves the limit far out of reach and lets a purchase through that the section requires the members to approve.

options.text: The members' prior approval by special resolution, a related party purchase above the prescribed limit being a matter reserved for a three-fourths majority.
options.misconception: Carries forward the special resolution the section required before it was amended.
options.why: The first proviso asks for prior approval by a resolution, and the rule describes that resolution as an ordinary one. A special resolution was what the section called for before it was amended, which is why the requirement is remembered that way; putting the higher majority back today asks the company for something the law has stopped requiring.

options.text: Only a resolution of the Board. Each order is a contract of its own, and no single one of them comes near a tenth of the company's turnover.
options.misconception: Reads a limit that aggregates the year's transactions as one applied to each contract on its own.
options.why: The prescribed limit is not applied contract by contract. It is applied to the transaction or transactions of that kind entered into during the financial year, individually or taken together with the previous ones, which is what stops a purchase being split into instalments that each sit under the line. Added together the four orders are fifty-two crore rupees against a limit of forty-eight crore.

citation.ref: Section 188(1) with its fourth proviso and its first proviso, read with sub-rules (2) and (3) of rule 15 of the 2014 rules made under the Act on Board meetings — a purchase of goods from a related party that is not at arm's length needs the Board's resolution, and the members' prior approval by ordinary resolution once its value, taken together with the year's earlier transactions of that kind, reaches ten per cent or more of turnover computed from the preceding year's audited financial statement

items.stem: On Sarayu alone, must its auditor's report carry a statement on internal financial controls?

options.text: Yes. The exemption a private company can claim from that clause is not available to Sarayu. The route the finance head has in mind needs two things at once — turnover under fifty crore rupees and borrowings under twenty-five crore rupees — and the borrowing side is measured at any point of time during the financial year, not on the closing day. Sarayu's borrowing stood at thirty crore rupees from August 2025, so it fails that limb however low the outstanding had come by 31 March 2026, and its clean filing record is a condition of the exemption rather than a way of qualifying for it.
options.why: The notification lets a private company out of the controls clause by one of two routes, and Sarayu is on neither. The second route is the one the figures invite, and it has two limbs joined by an and: turnover below fifty crore rupees as per the latest audited financial statement, and aggregate borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate below twenty-five crore rupees at any point of time during the financial year. Sarayu clears the first at forty-one crore rupees and fails the second, because the thirty crore rupees it drew in August 2025 to build the Nashik warehouse is inside the year the test asks about. A wording that says at any point of time during the financial year is deliberately not a closing-day figure — otherwise a company could borrow heavily all year, repay in March and be exempt on the strength of one day. The filing record matters in the other direction: a private company that has defaulted with the Registrar loses the exemption even after meeting the criteria, so filing on time keeps a door open rather than opening it. Sarayu's auditor therefore reports on the adequacy of its internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and on whether they operated effectively.
keywords: two limbs joined by an and
at any point of time during the financial year
keeps a door open rather than opening it

options.text: No. Turnover is forty-one crore rupees, under the fifty crore rupee limit, and the turnover and borrowing tests are alternatives — meeting either one is enough.
options.misconception: Reads two cumulative conditions as a choice between two tests.
options.why: The two are joined and have to be satisfied together. A company can be small by turnover and heavily borrowed, and that is precisely the company whose controls somebody outside it has an interest in, which is why the notification asks for both. Treating them as alternatives would exempt every borrower whose sales happen to be modest.

options.text: No. Sarayu is a private company that has never missed a filing with the Registrar, and the exemption is written for private companies that are up to date with their filings.
options.misconception: Mistakes the condition attached to an exemption for the test of who gets it.
options.why: Being up to date is a condition attached to the exemption, not the exemption itself. A company still has to fall inside one of the two routes — a one person company or a small company, or the turnover and borrowing route — and the filing record then decides whether it may keep what it has qualified for. Sarayu qualifies under neither route.

options.text: No. Borrowings on the reporting date were eighteen crore rupees, well inside the limit, and the balance sheet figure is what a limit expressed in rupees is tested against.
options.misconception: Reads a test written for any point during the year as a test of the year-end balance.
options.why: The test names the period it looks at, and the period is the whole financial year. A peak of thirty crore rupees in August is inside it, so the limb fails even though the closing figure is comfortable. Reading it as a year-end balance would let a company arrange its repayments around the reporting date and claim an exemption on the strength of one day's position.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i), read with the notification exempting a private company from that clause where it is a one person company or a small company, or where its turnover is under fifty crore rupees as per the latest audited financial statement and its aggregate borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate are under twenty-five crore rupees at any point of time during the financial year, the exemption being open only to a private company that has not defaulted in its filings with the Registrar

items.stem: On the fire alone, does telling the exchanges settle what the closed year's accounts and the audit still have to do?

options.text: Yes. The event has been put before the market under the listing regulation, and a company that has told the exchanges has told everybody; the closed year's accounts are about the closed year and carry nothing about it.
options.misconception: Treats a disclosure made under securities law as discharging the disclosure the financial statements have to carry.
options.why: A filing and a set of financial statements are read by different people for different purposes, and neither discharges the other. The accounts are what a lender, a supplier or a shareholder reads months later, and a loss of this size affecting the company they are reading about belongs in them.

options.text: No. The filing answers the listing regulation and nothing else. The auditor's work does not stop on the closing day: he has to perform procedures reaching up to the date of his report to find events between the two dates that need the figures changed or a disclosure made. Here the fire happened after 31 March 2026, so the stock is not written down in those accounts, but the fire and an estimate of what it cost are disclosed in them.
options.why: Three separate questions are being answered by one act in the finance head's email, and only one of them has actually been answered. Telling the exchanges is a duty owed under the listing regulations to the market; it says nothing about what the financial statements for the year just closed must contain, and no regulator treats a filing as a substitute for a note in the accounts. The audit question comes next. The standard on subsequent events puts the auditor's procedures over the stretch between the date of the financial statements and the date of his report, so a fire on 18 April is squarely inside the period he is responsible for and reaches him as work rather than as news. The accounting question is the third, and it turns on when the condition arose. An event giving evidence of something that already existed at the reporting date is put into the figures; an event whose cause arose afterwards is not, and is disclosed instead where it matters enough to affect what a reader decides. The store was standing and the stock was there on 31 March, so nine crore rupees of inventory is not written off in that year — and a fire of that size is disclosed, with its nature and an estimate of its financial effect, in the very accounts the finance head says need nothing further.
keywords: a duty owed under the listing regulations
the date of the financial statements and the date of his report
it turns on when the condition arose

options.text: No, and the nine crore rupees of stock must therefore be written off at 31 March 2026, because by the time the accounts are approved the company knows the stock is gone.
options.misconception: Treats knowledge gained before approval as evidence of a condition that existed at the reporting date.
options.why: What is asked is not whether the loss is known by the time of approval but whether the thing that caused it existed at the reporting date. The store and the stock were both intact on 31 March and the fire came three weeks later, so the condition arose after the period ended. Writing the stock off in the closed year would report a loss in a year in which it had not happened.

options.text: No, but the matter belongs to management. The auditor's procedures ended on the closing day, and an event after it concerns him only if it surfaces after his report has been signed.
options.misconception: Reads the auditor's responsibility for subsequent events as beginning only after the report is signed.
options.why: The standard on subsequent events gives the auditor an active duty over the period from the date of the financial statements to the date of his report — enquiring, reading what the board has minuted since the year end, and asking whether anything needs the figures changed or a disclosure made. What happens after the report is signed is a further and separate part of the same standard, not the whole of it.

citation.ref: The auditor's procedures over events arising after the accounts are drawn up and before he signs, read with Ind AS 10 on events after the reporting period and Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015

items.scenario:
Bhagirathi Foods Limited is listed on both exchanges and sells packaged spice mixes and ready-to-cook meals across India. Its financial year ended on 31 March 2026 and the audit report has not yet been signed. Four matters sit with the audit committee, and the finance head has written to its chairperson about every one of them.

Bhagirathi holds the largest share of the packaged spice market at twenty-two per cent, and its operating margin has fallen for the third year running. The planning team's reading of the industry runs like this. Several hundred regional brands compete; a grinding and packing line costs little to put up; four retail chains carry three-quarters of the volume and charge a fee before a new pack reaches a shelf; each of those chains now sells its own label beside the brands; and the chilli and turmeric crops reach processors through a small number of large traders. The team graded four of the five headings as pressing hard, put the grading in a table, and stopped there.

The chief executive tells the board that Bhagirathi has taken the cost leadership position, because after discounts its 200 gram pack sits at a lower shelf price than any other national brand. The costing team's own figures say something else. Making, packing and delivering that pack costs Bhagirathi about three rupees more than it costs the nearest competitor, and the shelf price is being held down by a rebate a large packaging supplier agreed to for two years, of which one year is left.

During the year the company placed three orders for printed cartons on Anvi Packaging LLP, a firm in which the managing director's brother is a partner: eighteen crore rupees in June 2025, fourteen crore rupees in November 2025, and a fourth order of twenty crore rupees is now proposed. Two other suppliers had quoted about nine per cent less for the same board, printing and delivery, and the purchase file records that the difference was accepted to keep the supply steady. Turnover in the audited accounts of the preceding financial year was four hundred and eighty crore rupees. The managing director says he will sit through the Board's discussion of the fourth order but will not vote on it.

Sarayu Cold Storage Private Limited is a subsidiary of Bhagirathi and is audited by a different firm. Its turnover for the year was forty-one crore rupees. It borrowed thirty crore rupees from a bank in August 2025 to build a warehouse at Nashik and had brought the outstanding down to eighteen crore rupees by 31 March 2026. Sarayu has filed its financial statements and its annual returns with the Registrar on time in every year of its existence. Its auditor is settling what his report must say about internal financial controls.

On 18 April 2026 a fire destroyed Bhagirathi's cold store at Vapi and the stock lying in it, which stood in the books at 31 March 2026 at nine crore rupees. The company reported the fire to both exchanges under Regulation 30 of the listing regulations, inside the time that regulation allows.

ANNEXURE 1, a trade weekly of 6 April 2026, under the heading Spice brands cut again. The tenth round of price cuts this year landed last week, and two of the four national chains have widened their own-label spice ranges since January. A brand manager who asked not to be named said that putting a new pack on a shelf now costs more than advertising it used to. Nobody in this business earns what it earned three years ago, a distributor in Indore told us. The volumes are there. The money is not.

ANNEXURE 2, an internal email of 22 April 2026 from the finance head to the chairperson of the audit committee. Four things before Friday. One, the fall in margin is ours to fix, because we hold the biggest share in the country and nobody can tell me the market is the problem. Two, we are the cost leader, since our pack is the cheapest on the shelf and that is what the phrase means. Three, the fourth carton order is a contract of its own and each of the three earlier ones is well under a tenth of our turnover, so a Board resolution covers it. Four, Sarayu's borrowing on the closing day was eighteen crore rupees, so its auditor need say nothing about controls; and the fire has gone to the exchanges inside the time Regulation 30 allows, so the closed year's accounts need nothing further and our audit work stopped on 31 March in any case.

items.stem: Which facts block the appointment?

options.text: All three — any financial connection with an audit client disqualifies
options.misconception: replaces the statutory thresholds with a zero-tolerance rule
options.why: Parliament drew money lines precisely so trivial connections would not bar appointment. Reading them as zero makes the limits in the rule meaningless.
keywords: trivial connections would not bar appointment
makes the limits in the rule meaningless
