They are provided for, and a liability raised, only so far as the investor has taken on legal or constructive obligations of the associate's, or has already paid money out for it — which is why the ₹90 lakh sat unrecognised. When the associate turns profitable again the investor resumes recognising profit only once the later earnings have caught up with the share of losses not recognised. The ₹40 lakh of 2026 is absorbed in full and ₹50 lakh of the shortfall remains; of the ₹70 lakh of 2027, ₹50 lakh clears the rest and ₹20 lakh is recognised.

options.text: ₹40 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹70 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2027, the unrecognised losses having lapsed when they were not recognised
options.misconception: treats losses that were never put on the balance sheet as though they had been written off for good
options.why: They were not written off; they were held back. The equity method is a running measure of the investor's share of the associate's net assets, and letting the profits through while the matching losses are forgotten would carry the investment back above what the share is actually worth. The standard keeps a memorandum record precisely so the two meet.

options.text: ₹22.50 lakh and ₹52.50 lakh — the investor's 25 per cent share of the ₹90 lakh shortfall is made good first and the rest is recognised
options.misconception: applies the ownership percentage a second time to a figure that is already the investor's share
options.why: The ₹90 lakh is already the investor's own share of the losses, not the associate's total, and so are the ₹40 lakh and the ₹70 lakh. Taking a quarter of a share gives a sixteenth of the associate, which is not what the investor owns.

citation.ref: para 38 and 39

items.scenario: An investor holds 25 per cent of an associate. By 31 March 2025 its share of the associate's losses had reduced the carrying amount of every part of its interest to nil, and a further ₹90 lakh of its share of losses went unrecognised. The investor has guaranteed nothing, has incurred no legal or constructive obligation on the associate's behalf and has made no payments for it. The associate returns to profit: the investor's share is ₹40 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹70 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2027.

items.stem: How much of each loss does X Ltd recognise?

options.text: 60 per cent of each — ₹12 lakh and ₹15 lakh — since gains and losses alike are recognised only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests
options.misconception: applies the unrelated-investors restriction to losses that evidence a real fall in value
options.why: The restriction exists to stop an investor booking profit on a sale to itself. A loss that evidences a reduction in net realisable value or an impairment is not that; the asset is genuinely worth less, and the standard sets it apart for exactly this reason. Restricting it would leave part of a real fall in value unrecorded by anyone.

options.text: The whole ₹20 lakh and the whole ₹25 lakh, both losses being recognised in full
options.misconception: reads the full-recognition rule as covering the upstream leg too
options.why: Full recognition is written for downstream transactions, where the investor is the seller of the asset that has fallen in value. For an upstream transaction the investor recognises its share in those losses, because the asset was the associate's and the associate has already taken the loss in full through its own profit. Taking all of it would count the other 60 per cent that belongs to the associate's other owners.

options.text: Nothing on either, because both transactions were at market value and no unrealised profit therefore arises
options.misconception: looks only for unrealised profit and misses that the standard also governs losses
options.why: The absence of an unrealised gain is not the end of the question. Ind AS 28 deals separately with transactions that provide evidence of a reduction in net realisable value or of an impairment, and both of these do. Selling inventory carried at ₹100 lakh for ₹80 lakh is a real ₹20 lakh loss for X Ltd however fair the price was.

options.text: The whole ₹20 lakh on the sale to Y Ltd, and 40 per cent of the ₹25 lakh on the purchase from Y Ltd — ₹10 lakh, reaching X Ltd through its ₹80 lakh share of Y Ltd's profit
options.why: The rule that restricts gains to unrelated investors' interests does not run in the same way for losses that tell you an asset is worth less. Where the investor is the seller, a price that shows the goods have fallen below what they will fetch — a drop in net realisable value — or that shows the asset is impaired puts the whole loss on the investor's own books, recognised in full and not cut down to a fraction. The ₹20 lakh therefore comes off X Ltd's profit entire. Where the associate is the seller, the same kind of evidence about the asset being bought leads the other way: the investor takes only its share in those losses, and the ₹25 lakh already sits inside Y Ltd's ₹200 lakh, so 40 per cent of it reaches X Ltd through the equity method.

citation.ref: para 29, read with para 28

items.scenario: X Ltd holds 40 per cent of Y Ltd, an associate it equity accounts. During the year ended 31 March 2026 X Ltd sold inventory to Y Ltd for ₹80 lakh; its carrying amount in X Ltd's books was ₹100 lakh and ₹80 lakh was its market value, so the sale is evidence of a fall in the net realisable value of that inventory. In the same year X Ltd bought a machine from Y Ltd for ₹60 lakh; the machine's carrying amount in Y Ltd's books was ₹85 lakh and the sale is evidence of an impairment loss on it. Y Ltd's profit for the year, after that ₹25 lakh loss, was ₹200 lakh.

items.stem: How much of what each employee shareholder receives is consideration for the acquired business?

options.text: ₹1 crore for each of the three, because all three sold the same one-third stake and the consideration must be the same for the same thing sold
options.misconception: equalises the price across shareholders, when the difference is what tells you part of the payment is not for shares
options.why: The difference in what each receives is evidence rather than a problem to be smoothed away. The non-employee gets ₹1 crore for a third of the company; the employees get ₹60 lakh for a third of the company plus a great deal more for staying. Forcing them to be equal would put two years of somebody's salary into goodwill.

options.text: The whole ₹60 lakh and the additional payment, at its acquisition-date fair value, because a payment measured on the acquired business's own earnings is by its nature consideration for that business
options.misconception: takes the earnings formula as decisive and ignores the employment condition attached to it
options.why: Both remuneration and contingent consideration can be measured on earnings, so the formula settles nothing. What separates them is who has to do what to earn the money, and this payment requires the shareholder to keep working. The standard names that condition first among its indicators.

options.text: Only the ₹60 lakh is consideration, and the additional payment is disclosed as a contingent liability until the two years are served
options.misconception: gets the classification right and then defers the expense that follows from it
options.why: Calling it remuneration decides where it goes, not whether it goes anywhere. Compensation for post-combination services is recognised as an expense over the period the services are rendered under the Ind AS that governs employee benefits. A contingent liability is a possible obligation from a past event, and these services have not been rendered yet.

options.text: Only the ₹60 lakh — the additional payment is remuneration for post-combination services, because it is automatically forfeited if the employment terminates
options.why: Ind AS 103 gives the forfeiture condition as the indicator that settles this. Where an earn-out dies with the job — where the payments are automatically forfeited the moment the employee walks out — what is being bought is the work of the next two years, so the payment is remuneration for post-combination services. An earn-out that survives a departure points the other way, and may be additional consideration for the business. Here the whole of the additional payment goes if the employee leaves, so it is compensation for the two years he serves and is accounted for under the other Ind AS, not as part of the consideration transferred. Only the ₹60 lakh is exchanged for the business.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B55(a), read with the consideration transferred in para 37

items.scenario: ABC Ltd acquires all the shares of XYZ Ltd from its three shareholders, who held equal stakes. Two of them were senior employees of XYZ Ltd and will stay on after the acquisition; the third was not an employee. Each of the two employee shareholders receives ₹60 lakh on completion plus an additional payment of between ₹1.5 crore and ₹2 crore based on a multiple of earnings over the next two years, and that additional payment is forfeited in full if he leaves XYZ Ltd's employment at any time in those two years. The non-employee shareholder receives ₹1 crore and nothing more. The salaries the two employees draw are reasonable remuneration for their services.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 7 require instead?

options.text: Two separately presented investing amounts — a ₹260 lakh outflow and a ₹220 lakh inflow — because a disposal's cash effects are not deducted from those of obtaining control, with aggregate disclosure of the total consideration, the portion consisting of cash and cash equivalents, the cash and cash equivalents in each business, and the other assets and liabilities by major category
options.why: Money paid out to take control of a business, and money taken in on giving control up, are each totalled on their own side and shown as a separate line inside investing activities. The standard says in terms that a disposal's cash effects are not deducted from those of obtaining control. Each side is then reported net of the cash and cash equivalents that came or went with the business, which gives ₹300 lakh less ₹40 lakh and ₹250 lakh less ₹30 lakh. Alongside, the entity discloses in aggregate for both the total consideration paid or received, how much of that was cash and cash equivalents, how much cash and cash equivalents sat inside the businesses whose control changed hands, and what the other assets and liabilities came to, summarised by each major category.
keywords: not deducted from those of obtaining control

options.text: The ₹260 lakh in investing activities and the ₹220 lakh in financing activities, a disposal of shares in a subsidiary being a transaction with owners
options.misconception: applies the financing classification for an ownership change to a transaction that loses control
options.why: Financing is where cash flows go when the parent's ownership interest changes without losing control, because those are equity transactions with the group's own co-owners. Losing control is not one — the group has parted with a business — so it is an investing flow, presented separately.

options.text: A single net investing figure of ₹40 lakh, since both are changes in the composition of the group and the standard requires them to be aggregated
options.misconception: reads the word aggregate as permission to net an acquisition against a disposal
options.why: Aggregate means each side is added up across the transactions of its own kind, not that the two sides are set against each other. The separate presentation exists so that the reader can see how much cash went into buying businesses and how much came back from selling them, which a single net figure destroys — a busy year of both would look like a quiet one.

options.text: A ₹300 lakh outflow and a ₹250 lakh inflow, the cash held by the subsidiaries being part of the group's own cash and not a deduction
options.misconception: presents the gross consideration and forgets that cash came with the business
options.why: The cash inside A Ltd became the group's cash on the same day the ₹300 lakh left it, so the group parted with ₹260 lakh net to acquire the business. Reporting the gross figure would show an outflow larger than the group actually suffered and would double-count the ₹40 lakh, which also appears in the closing cash balance.

citation.ref: para 39, 40 and 42, read with para 42A and 42B

items.scenario: During the year ended 31 March 2026 P Ltd obtained control of A Ltd, paying ₹300 lakh in cash; A Ltd held ₹40 lakh of cash and cash equivalents on that date. In the same year P Ltd lost control of B Ltd, receiving ₹250 lakh in cash; B Ltd held ₹30 lakh of cash and cash equivalents on the date control passed. The finance manager proposes to show a single net investing outflow of ₹40 lakh and to add no further note, on the ground that both transactions are acquisitions and disposals of subsidiaries and the reader can see the net effect.

items.stem: What must the company disclose for credit risk beyond the expected credit loss note?

options.text: The maximum exposure to credit risk, measured after deducting the collateral held over the dealers' stock, since collateral is what the exposure actually reduces to
options.misconception: nets the collateral into the exposure figure the standard asks to be given before it
options.why: The exposure is disclosed without taking account of any collateral held or other credit enhancements, and the collateral is then described separately along with its financial effect. Netting the two would hide both the size of the risk and the quality of what stands behind it, and would make companies with worthless collateral look like companies with good collateral.

options.text: Nothing further — the expected credit loss allowance is the credit risk disclosure, and an instrument measured at fair value through profit or loss already carries its credit risk in its carrying amount
options.misconception: treats the impairment note as the whole of credit risk disclosure and the fair value as a substitute for exposure information
options.why: Fair value tells the reader what the instrument is worth, not how much the entity stands to lose if every counterparty defaults, and a guarantee given may have a small or nil carrying amount while exposing the company to its full face value. The standard therefore asks separately for the amount that best represents the maximum exposure for instruments outside the impairment requirements.

options.text: For the instruments the Ind AS 109 impairment rules do not touch, the figure that comes closest to its maximum exposure to credit risk before any security is counted, together with a description of what is held as security, of any other credit enhancements standing behind the exposure, and of the financial effect of both — the first of those being unnecessary where the carrying amount already comes closest to the exposure
options.why: Ind AS 107 splits credit risk disclosure in two. Where the impairment requirements of Ind AS 109 are applied, the expected credit loss information carries the weight. For all financial instruments to which those requirements are not applied — the dealer loans at fair value through profit or loss and the guarantees — the entity gives, class by class, the figure that comes closest to its maximum exposure to credit risk on the reporting date, arrived at while ignoring anything pledged to it and any other support standing behind the exposure. It then describes what collateral held as security comes to, what other credit enhancements exist, and what difference they make — quantifying, for instance, how far they cut the risk. The first of those is not required for an instrument whose carrying amount already comes closest to that exposure.

options.text: A maturity analysis of the guarantees showing their remaining contractual maturities, which is the credit risk disclosure for a guarantee given
options.misconception: gives the liquidity risk disclosure in answer to a credit risk question
options.why: The maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities, into which an issued financial guarantee enters, is the liquidity risk disclosure — it tells the reader when cash might have to leave. Credit risk asks a different question, which is how much the company loses if the people who owe it money do not pay.

citation.ref: para 35K and 36, read with the collateral disclosures in para 15

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company holds ₹500 crore of trade receivables, on which it applies the impairment requirements of Ind AS 109 and discloses the expected credit loss allowance. It also holds ₹150 crore of dealer loans measured at fair value through profit or loss, to which the impairment requirements do not apply and which are secured by a charge over the dealers' stock, and it has given ₹200 crore of financial guarantees on behalf of a joint venture. The chief financial officer says the expected credit loss note on the receivables discharges the company's credit risk disclosure for everything.

items.stem: What must the company disclose?

options.text: Only the 11 per cent customer, with its name and the amount each segment earned from it; the products-and-services disclosure is indeed unnecessary because the entity reports three segments
options.misconception: treats any segment disclosure as satisfying the entity-wide requirement, and over-discloses on the customer
options.why: The entity-wide disclosures are given where the reportable segment information does not already provide them, and geographic segments do not provide a product split. On the customer, what has to be said is that the ten per cent line has been crossed, how much revenue each such buyer brought in, and which segment or segments booked it — not the customer's name, and not a segment-by-segment split of what that one buyer paid.

options.text: Only the products-and-services split; the three related companies are separate legal persons contracting separately, so none of them reaches 10 per cent
options.misconception: counts legal persons where the standard counts a group under common control
options.why: A group of entities known to the reporting entity to be under common control is considered a single customer, because the concentration of risk the disclosure exists to reveal sits with whoever controls the buying, not with the entity that signs. Judgement is required for a government and the entities it controls, where the extent of economic integration matters, but an ordinary commercial group is caught.

options.text: External revenue broken down product by product and service by service, or across each group of similar products and services, because segments organised by geography do not already give it — the only let-out being figures that cannot be assembled without excessive cost, which must itself be stated; and reliance on both customers, because buyers the company knows to sit under common control count as one between them
options.why: The entity-wide disclosures exist for the case where the segments do not happen to answer the question. Reportable segments built on geography say nothing about how much revenue comes from cement as against paints, so external revenue has to be split product by product and service by service, or across each group of similar products and services where a finer split would be artificial. The one escape is cost: where the figures are not there to be had and the cost to develop it would be excessive, the entity discloses that fact instead. On customers, a single external buyer accounting for a tenth or more of total revenue has to be reported, and buyers the reporting entity knows to sit under common control count as one between them — so 6 plus 6 plus 6 is 18 per cent and the line is crossed.
keywords: group of similar products and services
cost to develop it would be excessive

options.text: Both customers, but the products-and-services disclosure only if the company chooses to re-organise its segments around products
options.misconception: makes an entity-wide disclosure depend on how the entity is managed, which is the one thing it is designed not to depend on
options.why: Entity-wide disclosures are required of every entity within the standard's scope, including one with a single reportable segment, precisely so that the information does not disappear because of how management happens to organise itself. Reorganising the segments is not on offer as an alternative to disclosing.

citation.ref: para 32, 33 and 34

items.scenario: A company's three reportable segments are North, South and West, organised on geography because that is how the chief operating decision maker runs it. Within each segment it sells cement, paints and logistics services, which are essentially different from one another. Revenue from one customer is 11 per cent of total revenue. Revenue also comes from three separate companies at 6 per cent each, and the company knows all three to be under the common control of one group. The finance head says the products-and-services disclosure is unnecessary because the company already reports segments, and that no single one of the three related companies crosses the threshold.

items.stem: What diluted per-share amounts does the company report?

options.text: ₹2.50 for continuing operations, a loss of ₹3.00 for the discontinued operation and an overall diluted loss per share of ₹0.50 — the options are included even though the overall loss per share falls from ₹0.60 to ₹0.50
options.why: An entity that reports a discontinued operation uses income from continuing operations, adjusted for preference dividends and similar adjustments, as the control number in deciding whether potential ordinary shares are dilutive. The same number of potential ordinary shares that dilutes the continuing-operations figure then governs every other diluted per-share amount the entity reports, even where its effect there runs the wrong way against the matching basic amount. Continuing operations fall from ₹3.00 to ₹2.50 on 12,00,000 shares, so the options are dilutive and go in everywhere: ₹36,00,000 over 12,00,000 is a ₹3.00 loss, and ₹6,00,000 over 12,00,000 is a ₹0.50 loss.
keywords: same number of potential ordinary shares

options.text: The options are excluded altogether, because including them reduces the overall loss per share from ₹0.60 to ₹0.50 and is therefore antidilutive
options.misconception: tests dilution against the overall result, when the control number is the result from continuing operations
options.why: Testing against the bottom line lets a one-off discontinued loss decide how the recurring business is presented, and would flip the answer from year to year on facts that have nothing to do with the options. That is why the standard fixes the control number as what the continuing business earned for the parent's own ordinary shareholders, and here that number is diluted.

options.text: No diluted amounts are reported at all, because the company has made an overall loss and diluted earnings per share is not presented in a loss year
options.misconception: believes a loss suspends diluted reporting, when it changes only which potential shares are dilutive
options.why: A loss does not switch the diluted presentation off. It usually means potential ordinary shares are antidilutive against the control number and are excluded, which is a different matter from not presenting the figure. Here the control number is a profit and is diluted, so the options are included and the diluted amounts are reported.

options.text: ₹2.50 for continuing operations, with the discontinued operation and the overall figure left on 10,00,000 shares at a loss of ₹3.60 and ₹0.60
options.misconception: uses two different share counts in one set of diluted figures
options.why: The whole point of the control number is that one denominator governs the set. The same number of potential ordinary shares that dilutes continuing operations carries over to every other diluted per-share amount reported, so that the three figures still add up and the reader can trace one to another. Mixing counts would leave a set of numbers that does not reconcile.

citation.ref: para 41 and 42, applied to an entity reporting a discontinued operation

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a company reports income from continuing operations of ₹30,00,000 and a loss from discontinued operations of ₹36,00,000, giving a net loss of ₹6,00,000. The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding is 10,00,000, and its outstanding stock options would add 2,00,000 incremental shares. Basic figures are therefore ₹3.00 for continuing operations, a loss of ₹3.60 for the discontinued operation and an overall loss per share of ₹0.60.

items.stem: How is each scheme accounted for?

options.text: P Ltd's as cash-settled; Q Ltd's as equity-settled, with the whole ₹90 lakh debited to equity because a settlement of an equity-settled award never touches profit or loss
options.misconception: puts the entire payment through equity and misses the cap at the fair value of the instruments
options.why: A repurchase of equity is a transaction with owners only up to what the equity is worth. The payment is deducted from equity to the extent of the fair value of the equity instruments repurchased, measured at the repurchase date, and any excess over that is recognised as an expense. Putting the whole ₹90 lakh through equity would let the company pay ₹15 lakh more than the award was worth without that ever reaching the year's result.

options.text: Both as cash-settled, since in the event both were settled in cash and the accounting must follow what actually happened
options.misconception: decides the classification with hindsight, when it is made from the obligation the entity has at the time
options.why: The classification is made on whether a present obligation to settle in cash exists, judged as the services are received, not on what the entity later chose to do. Q Ltd could have issued shares and had said nothing to suggest it would not, so it had no such obligation; its later decision to pay is a repurchase of the equity it had already granted.

options.text: P Ltd's as cash-settled, because past practice and a stated policy give it a present obligation to settle in cash; Q Ltd's as equity-settled, with the cash settlement treated as the repurchase of an equity interest — ₹75 lakh debited to equity and the ₹15 lakh excess recognised in profit or loss
options.why: Where the entity has the choice of settlement, the whole award is treated as cash-settled or as equity-settled depending on whether the entity has a present obligation to settle in cash. That obligation is taken to exist where there is no commercial substance to issuing equity — a restriction on issuing new share capital, for instance — or where there is a past practice or stated policy of settling in cash, which is P Ltd exactly. Q Ltd has neither, so equity-settled accounting was right; and where equity-settled accounting has been applied but the settlement is made in cash, it is accounted for as the repurchase of an equity interest, debiting the amount previously credited to equity and putting through profit or loss whatever the cash paid came to over and above the worth of the shares the entity would otherwise have issued.
keywords: present obligation to settle in cash

options.text: Both as equity-settled, because the entity's freedom to choose means no liability has been incurred in either case
options.misconception: reads a contractual right to choose as conclusive, when practice and policy can create the obligation anyway
options.why: A right to settle in shares is worth nothing if the entity has told everybody it will pay cash and has done so six times running. The standard looks for a present obligation however it arises, and a past practice or a stated policy of cash settlement creates one just as a restriction on issuing capital would.

citation.ref: para 41, 42 and 43, read with the repurchase rule in para 29

items.scenario: Two companies each grant share options under which the entity, not the employee, chooses whether to settle in cash or by issuing shares. P Ltd has settled every one of its six previous schemes of this kind in cash and has told employees it will do so again. Q Ltd has always settled in shares, is under no restriction on issuing new capital and has stated no policy, so it accounted for its scheme as equity-settled and credited ₹75 lakh to equity over the vesting period. On settlement Q Ltd nonetheless paid ₹90 lakh in cash; on that date the shares it would otherwise have issued were worth ₹75 lakh.

items.stem: What does the company recognise on the cancellation?

options.text: ₹16,46,667 charged at once as an acceleration of vesting, plus ₹90,000 of expense — ₹16,20,000 of the payment being a deduction from equity at the ₹90 fair value on the repurchase date and only the ₹5 an option excess reaching profit or loss
options.why: A grant cancelled or settled during the vesting period, otherwise than by forfeiture when the vesting conditions are not satisfied, is accounted for as an acceleration of vesting, so the amount that would otherwise have been recognised over the remainder of the vesting period is recognised immediately. On 9 directors the total grant date charge is 9 times 2,000 times ₹130, or ₹23,40,000, of which ₹6,93,333 has been taken, leaving ₹16,46,667. Whatever is paid over on the cancellation counts as buying back an equity interest, which makes it a deduction from equity — but only as far as the worth of the instruments granted on the repurchase date reaches, and anything paid beyond that figure is an expense. Nine times 2,000 at ₹90 is ₹16,20,000 taken off equity, and the remaining ₹90,000 goes through profit or loss.

options.text: ₹16,46,667 as an acceleration of vesting, with the whole ₹17,10,000 payment recognised as an expense of the year
options.misconception: expenses the entire settlement payment instead of treating it first as a repurchase of equity
options.why: The payment buys back an equity interest the employees already hold, and a transaction with holders in that capacity is a deduction from equity. Only what is paid over and above the fair value of those instruments at the repurchase date is an expense — ₹5 an option here, not ₹95.

options.text: A credit reversing the ₹6,93,333 already charged, since the options will now never vest and no shares will ever be issued
options.misconception: treats a cancellation like a failed service condition, which is the one case the rule expressly excludes
options.why: Reversal is what happens when a vesting condition fails, because the entity never received the services it was paying for. Here the directors gave the service and the company chose to end the scheme, so it must recognise immediately what it would otherwise have spread. Letting a cancellation claw the charge back would let any board erase its option cost by cancelling in the last year.

options.text: ₹16,46,667 as an acceleration of vesting, with the whole ₹17,10,000 payment deducted from equity
options.misconception: puts the entire payment through equity and ignores the cap at the fair value on the repurchase date
options.why: The deduction from equity is capped at what the instruments were worth on the day they were bought back, which is ₹90 an option. Paying ₹95 for something worth ₹90 is a cost of ending the scheme early, and the ₹90,000 that represents is an expense of the period rather than a distribution to owners.

citation.ref: para 28(a) and 28(b)

items.scenario: On 1 April 2024 a company granted 2,000 share options to each of its 10 directors, vesting on 31 March 2027 subject to three years' service. The grant date fair value was ₹130 an option and at the end of the first year 8 directors were expected to remain, so ₹6,93,333 was charged for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the year ended 31 March 2026 the board cancelled the scheme outright. Nine directors were then in employment; the fair value of an option at the date of cancellation was ₹90 and the company agreed to pay each of the nine ₹95 an option, a total of ₹17,10,000. The cancellation is not a forfeiture — the service condition had not failed.

items.stem: Which positions are presented net in the balance sheet?

options.text: The first only — gross settlement through a clearing house qualifies, but a right of set-off can never run against a party other than the counterparty
options.misconception: treats the different-counterparties rule as absolute, when a three-party agreement is the recognised exception
options.why: The general case is indeed that amounts owed to and by different parties are not offset. The standard sets out the exception in terms: now and then a debtor is entitled to set what a third party owes him against what he himself owes his creditor, so long as the three of them have an agreement that establishes that right of set-off plainly. That agreement exists here and is enforceable in every state the criteria name.

options.text: The third only — settlement through a clearing house is settlement in full on both sides, so nothing is being settled net
options.misconception: reads the criterion as requiring literal net settlement, when an equivalent outcome suffices
options.why: The criterion is met where the outcome is in effect equivalent to net settlement, and a single settlement cycle with margining that leaves credit and liquidity risk insignificant is exactly the arrangement contemplated. Insisting on a single net payment would make the presentation turn on a plumbing detail rather than on the exposure the entity actually carries.

options.text: The first and the third — the clearing house cycle is in effect equivalent to net settlement, and a three-party agreement can create the legal right of set-off; the synthetic instrument's two legs are presented gross
options.why: The intention limb is satisfied not only by settling net but where the entity can settle in a way whose outcome is in effect equivalent to net settlement. That is a narrow test. The gross mechanism has to strip credit and liquidity risk down to something insignificant, and it has to put receivables and payables through a single settlement process or cycle — which the clearing house does. A right of set-off can also, rarely, reach past the counterparty: a debtor may be entitled to set what a third party owes him against what he himself owes his creditor, so long as the three of them have signed something that establishes that right plainly. That is the third position. Offsetting is inappropriate where several instruments emulate a single one — a synthetic instrument — because each leg is a separate right or obligation, transferable and settleable on its own and exposed to its own risks.

options.text: All three — each pair has the same economic effect as a single net position, and substance governs presentation
options.misconception: reasons from economic substance past the two criteria the standard sets
options.why: Substance is what the two criteria are for, and the synthetic instrument fails them. Each of the borrowing and the swap is a contractual right or obligation with its own terms, each may be transferred or settled separately, and each is exposed to risks the other is not. Netting them would hide a ₹200 lakh borrowing behind a ₹12 lakh derivative.

citation.ref: para 42 and 48, with para 45 and 49(a)

items.scenario: A company holds three positions at 31 March 2026. The first is a ₹80 lakh receivable and a ₹80 lakh payable with the same counterparty, settled gross through a clearing house that processes receivables and payables in a single settlement cycle on the same day, with margining that leaves credit and liquidity risk insignificant; a legally enforceable right of set-off exists. The second is a ₹200 lakh floating rate borrowing combined with an interest rate swap under which the company receives floating and pays fixed, together synthesising a fixed rate borrowing; the swap is an asset of ₹12 lakh and no right of set-off exists between the two. The third is a ₹50 lakh receivable from X and a ₹50 lakh payable to Y, with a written agreement between the company, X and Y establishing the company's right to set the two off, enforceable in the normal course of business and on default and insolvency, and the company intends to settle net.

items.stem: What are the cash-generating units here, and what does the transfer pricing do to the measurement?

options.text: X and Y together are one cash-generating unit, because sixty per cent of X's output goes to Y and X's cash inflows therefore depend on demand for Y's products
options.misconception: treats the internal share of the output as decisive, when the existence of an active market is what settles independence
options.why: That reasoning is right where there is no active market for the intermediate product, because then X's inflows really do depend on demand for Y's. Here X can sell the same product to outsiders, so the inflows it would generate are largely independent of Y whatever proportion currently goes internally. The market, not the current routing of the goods, is the test.

options.text: X and Y are separate units, and the value in use of each is measured on the internal transfer prices actually charged, since those are the prices at which the transactions really occur
options.misconception: measures value in use on prices the entity sets for itself
options.why: Internal transfer prices here do not reflect market prices — they are set to pass all margins to X and are above the market. Measuring on them would overstate X's recoverable amount and understate Y's by the same amount, so that an impairment in one unit could be hidden by the pricing policy. The budgets are adjusted to what the goods would fetch at arm's length.

options.text: Neither is a cash-generating unit, because the two plants are managed together and the smallest group generating independent inflows is the entity as a whole
options.misconception: goes to the entity level, which is the answer for the case where no active market exists
options.why: Being managed together matters when the recoverable amount of one plant cannot be assessed independently of the other, which is the no-active-market case. Here it can. Testing at the entity level would let a profitable business absorb an impairment in a plant that is failing on its own terms, which is the outcome the cash-generating unit exists to prevent.

options.text: X and Y are each a separate cash-generating unit, because an active market exists for X's output even though part of that output is used internally; and in determining value in use for both, the budgets are adjusted to management's best estimate of future prices achievable in arm's length transactions for the output used internally
options.why: What settles a unit is whether the output can be sold, not where it happens to go. Once an active market stands ready for what a plant makes, that plant is a cash-generating unit in its own right, and it stays one even where the whole of what it makes is used internally, because the entity could sell that output on the market and so bring in cash inflows largely independent of the rest of the entity. X could sell to outsiders what it sends to Y, so X is a unit; Y sells eighty per cent of its own production outside, so Y is another. Transfer pricing then interferes with the measurement: X charges Y more than the market pays, so the budgets and forecasts of both units are restated to management's best estimate of what the goods moved inside the entity would fetch in arm's length transactions.

citation.ref: para 70, read with para 6 and the value in use requirements in para 30

items.scenario: Plant X makes an intermediate product. Sixty per cent of X's output goes to plant Y of the same entity at a transfer price that passes all margins to X, and the other forty per cent is sold to outside customers. Y uses the intermediate product as a significant raw material and sells eighty per cent of its own final production outside the entity. An active market exists for X's intermediate product, and the internal transfer prices X charges Y are higher than the prices in that market.

items.stem: On what valuation premise is each measured?

options.text: Both in combination with other assets, and with other assets and liabilities — the machine as installed or otherwise configured for use alongside the rest of the line, and the customer relationships valued together with the right to future updates
options.why: Once highest and best use is settled, a second question remains: whether the maximum value to market participants comes from the asset used in combination with other assets, or with other assets and liabilities, or instead on a standalone basis. That is the valuation premise, and it is decided by what market participants would do rather than by whether the asset could in principle be sold on its own. The machine gives its maximum value installed and configured for use with the other assets of the line, and that deployment is the one market participants ordinarily use, so it is measured on that premise. The customer relationships would have little or no value without the free updates that come with them, so market participants would value the two together and the same premise applies.

options.text: The machine in combination with other assets, but the customer relationships on a standalone basis, since the update right is a separately identifiable intangible with a fair value of its own
options.misconception: reads separate identifiability as requiring a separate valuation premise
options.why: Being separately identifiable and being separately valuable are different things. The premise asks where the maximum value lies, and the relationships would have little or no value without the updates. Splitting them would produce two figures neither of which any buyer would pay, and would lose value that plainly exists in the pair.

options.text: The machine on a standalone basis, because it was bought from an outside vendor and could be resold to one, and the customer relationships in combination
options.misconception: lets the asset's history and its resaleability choose the premise
options.why: Where the asset came from and whether a market exists for it alone do not decide the premise; what market participants would do with it does. The customisation, light though it was, and the way such machines are ordinarily deployed both point to use in combination, and there is no evidence pointing the other way.

options.text: Both on a standalone basis, because fair value is an exit price and an exit means each asset leaving on its own, at whatever a buyer would pay for that asset alone
options.misconception: reads the exit-price definition as forcing a standalone premise on every asset
options.why: An exit price is what market participants would pay, and market participants here would be buying a machine installed in a line and relationships that come with their update right. The valuation premise follows where the value actually lies, not the mechanics of a hypothetical removal. A standalone premise would price the machine at little more than scrap and freight.

citation.ref: para 31 and 32, read with the highest and best use requirements in para 27 to 30

items.scenario: A Ltd obtains control of B Ltd and must fair value two of the assets acquired. It has already established that each asset's highest and best use is the use it is being put to now, so no alternative use is in question for either. The first asset is a machine B Ltd bought from an outside vendor and lightly customised for its production line; a market participant would get the most value from it installed and configured alongside the other assets and liabilities of that line, and that is how such machines are ordinarily deployed in this industry. The second is a customer relationship intangible sold together with a contractual right for those customers to receive all future technology updates free — a right that is a separate intangible in its own terms, and without which the relationships would have little or no value.

items.stem: What happens to the ₹10,000 in other comprehensive income on each block?

options.text: On both it is reclassified from equity to profit or loss, since a cumulative amount in other comprehensive income on a debt instrument is always recycled when the measurement basis changes
options.misconception: recycles on both moves, when only the move to fair value through profit or loss recycles
options.why: Recycling happens where the asset goes on being carried at fair value and the loss has therefore been suffered in the reported carrying amount. Where it goes to amortised cost the carrying amount is put back to what amortised cost would have been, so the loss has been undone rather than realised, and passing it through profit or loss would report a loss the balance sheet has just reversed.

options.text: On the first it is removed from equity and adjusted against the fair value, so the bonds are carried at ₹1,00,000 as if they had always been measured at amortised cost, with nothing reaching profit or loss; on the second it leaves equity for profit or loss, as a reclassification adjustment
options.why: On a move from fair value through other comprehensive income to amortised cost, the asset is measured at fair value on the reclassification date, but the cumulative gain or loss previously recognised in other comprehensive income is removed from equity and adjusted against that fair value. The asset is therefore measured as if it had always been measured at amortised cost, which brings the first block back to ₹1,00,000; the adjustment affects other comprehensive income and does not affect profit or loss, so it is not a reclassification adjustment. On a move to fair value through profit or loss the asset simply continues to be measured at fair value, and whatever gain or loss has piled up in other comprehensive income comes out of equity on the reclassification date and lands in profit or loss, which makes it a reclassification adjustment. In neither case is the effective interest rate adjusted.
keywords: as if it had always been measured at amortised cost

options.text: On both it stays in equity untouched, because reclassification is applied prospectively and amounts already recognised are never restated
options.misconception: reads the no-restatement rule as leaving the accumulated other comprehensive income where it is
options.why: Prospective application and no restatement govern the periods before the reclassification date — previously recognised interest, gains and losses are not rewritten. What happens to the balance standing in equity on the reclassification date is a separate instruction, and the standard gives a different one for each destination.

options.text: On the first the bonds are carried at ₹90,000 with the ₹10,000 left in equity, and on the second at ₹90,000 with the ₹10,000 also left in equity, since fair value on the reclassification date is the new carrying amount in both cases
options.misconception: stops at the fair value measurement and never deals with the balance sitting in other comprehensive income
options.why: Fair value on the reclassification date is where the measurement starts, not where it ends. Leaving the ₹10,000 in equity on the amortised cost block would carry an asset at ₹90,000 against a loss that has been cancelled, and on the other block would leave a realised loss permanently parked in equity on an instrument that no longer has an other comprehensive income route at all.

citation.ref: para 5.6.5 and 5.6.7

items.scenario: A company holds two identical blocks of bonds, each with an amortised cost of ₹1,00,000 and each currently measured at fair value through other comprehensive income, with a cumulative loss of ₹10,000 sitting in other comprehensive income on each. Fair value on the reclassification date is ₹90,000 for each block. A change in the business model requires the first block to be reclassified to amortised cost and the second to fair value through profit or loss.

items.stem: What deferred tax does the acquirer recognise on the goodwill at each of the two dates?

options.text: A deferred tax liability on the ₹35 crore at acquisition, which increases goodwill by the same amount, and a matching credit when the goodwill is written down
options.misconception: recognises the goodwill liability and grosses goodwill up, which is the circularity the prohibition exists to stop
options.why: Grossing goodwill up creates a larger temporary difference, which demands a larger liability, which grosses goodwill up again. The figure never settles, and every rupee of the increase would be an asset the acquirer did not buy. That is why the standard closes the door at initial recognition rather than working the circle towards a limit.

options.text: None at acquisition, but a deferred tax credit on the ₹9 crore fall, because the exception governs only the initial recognition and a subsequent movement is an ordinary change in a temporary difference
options.misconception: reads the exception as expiring after the acquisition date, letting the movement in through the back door
options.why: The standard closes that route in terms. A change in the temporary difference that arises because the carrying amount of goodwill has been reduced is itself regarded as arising from the initial recognition of that goodwill, and so is not recognised. Otherwise an impairment would create through profit or loss exactly the liability the acquisition date was forbidden to create.

options.text: None at either date — no deferred tax liability is recognised on the initial recognition of goodwill, and a later change in the temporary difference that arises from that same initial recognition is treated as arising from it too, so it is not recognised either
options.why: Goodwill with a nil tax base carries a taxable temporary difference equal to its whole carrying amount. Recognising the deferred tax liability on it would increase goodwill, because goodwill is measured as a residual, which would increase the temporary difference, which would increase the liability again — a circular computation the standard shuts down by prohibiting recognition on the initial recognition of goodwill outright. The prohibition then carries forward: a reduction in the carrying amount of goodwill that changes the temporary difference is also regarded as arising from that initial recognition, so no deferred tax is recognised on the movement from ₹35 crore to ₹26 crore either.

options.text: A deferred tax liability on the goodwill at both dates, since a difference between carrying amount and tax base always produces deferred tax where the entity is taxable at all
options.misconception: reads the general rule as having no exception for goodwill
options.why: The general rule recognises a deferred tax liability for every taxable temporary difference except in the cases the standard names, and the initial recognition of goodwill is the first of them. Applying the rule here would make goodwill a self-inflating number that no computation could close.

citation.ref: para 15(a), read with para 21 and 21A

items.scenario: An acquirer pays ₹100 crore for a subsidiary whose identifiable net assets have an acquisition date fair value of ₹65 crore, so goodwill of ₹35 crore is recognised. The tax authority allows no deduction for that goodwill at any time, including when the subsidiary later disposes of the underlying business, so the goodwill's tax base is nil. Two years later the acquirer writes the goodwill down by ₹9 crore for impairment, which the tax authority does not allow either, so the taxable temporary difference on the goodwill falls to ₹26 crore.

items.stem: What does the company do about the ₹80 lakh at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Recognise a liability when the obligation arises, to the extent the contributions payable will not be available as a refund or as a reduction in future contributions after they are paid into the plan; that liability adds to the deficit already carried, so that no gain or loss is expected
options.why: The company's general point is ordinarily right — a requirement to contribute does not affect the measurement, because once paid the contributions become plan assets and the additional net liability is nil. The Appendix to Ind AS 19 identifies the case where that breaks down. Where a minimum funding requirement obliges an entity to put money in against a shortfall for service already received, the question to ask is what becomes of that money once it is in the plan: will it be available as a refund, or as a reduction in future contributions? To the extent the answer is neither, a liability is recognised when the obligation arises, and it adds to the deficit already carried, so that no gain or loss is expected when the money actually goes in.
keywords: no gain or loss is expected

options.text: Nothing at 31 March 2026, because the asset ceiling applies only where the plan is in surplus and this plan is in deficit
options.misconception: reads the whole Appendix as being about the ceiling, when it also asks when a funding requirement creates a liability
options.why: The ceiling limits a surplus, and there is no surplus here. The Appendix addresses three issues, and the third is when a minimum funding requirement might give rise to a liability — which does not depend on the plan being in surplus at all. A deficit plan whose contributions are irrecoverable is exactly the case it was written for.

options.text: Nothing — the company is right, because a contribution becomes a plan asset on payment and so leaves the net defined benefit liability unchanged
options.misconception: applies the general position to the one case the Appendix carves out of it
options.why: The reasoning holds only while the money remains the company's in some form once it is in the plan, whether as a refund it can draw or as contributions it will not have to make later. Here the rules allow no refund and the actuary has found no reduction in future contributions, so the ₹80 lakh leaves the company and never comes back in any shape. That is a cost the company is already committed to, and it belongs on the balance sheet now.

options.text: Disclose the ₹80 lakh as a contractual commitment, since it is a future contribution and Ind AS 19 requires disclosure of expected contributions for the next annual period
options.misconception: answers a recognition question with the disclosure that sits beside it
options.why: Expected contributions for the next annual reporting period are indeed disclosed, and that disclosure exists alongside the recognition rule rather than instead of it. Where the contributions payable to meet an existing shortfall will not be available afterwards, the Appendix requires a liability to be recognised, and a note cannot stand in for an amount the standard says goes on the face of the statements.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para 23 and 24, read with the asset ceiling in para 64

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company's defined benefit plan is in deficit on the Ind AS 19 measurement. A statutory minimum funding requirement obliges the company to pay ₹80 lakh of contributions during the year to 31 March 2027 to make good a shortfall for past service measured on the minimum funding basis. The plan rules permit no refund to the company in any circumstances, and the actuary determines that once these ₹80 lakh are in the plan they will not reduce the contributions the company must make for future service either. The company's view is that a contribution can never affect the measurement of a defined benefit liability, because the money becomes a plan asset the moment it is paid.

items.stem: How is the ₹100 crore attributed between the owners of the parent and the non-controlling interests?

options.text: ₹90 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹10 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.misconception: carries the potential-voting-rights test from the question of power across to the question of attribution, where the standard excludes it
options.why: Potential voting rights are weighed in deciding whether an investor has power over an investee, and that is where their work ends. Attribution is on present ownership interests alone. Counting the options twice would give the parent 90 per cent of a profit on which it has no present claim, and would leave the minority carrying a share of the results of shares they still own.

options.text: ₹65 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹35 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.why: Splitting a year's profit, and every movement in equity, between parent and non-controlling interests rides on present ownership interests only. Whatever a holder might one day convert or take up — potential voting rights, written options, derivatives of that kind — sits outside the split. So the 25 per cent of options move nothing here, however certain their exercise looks, and the instruments themselves are accounted for under Ind AS 109. One narrow exception cuts the other way. Where a bargain already hands the holder what an owner gets, giving him access to the returns on those shares from today, the split is worked as though the shares were already his. P Ltd's contract over the further 5 per cent is that bargain, so 65 per cent goes to the parent.

options.text: ₹65 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹35 crore to the non-controlling interests, with the 25 per cent of options presented within non-controlling interests in the consolidated balance sheet
options.misconception: treats an instrument conferring no present ownership as a component of the equity attributable to non-controlling interests
options.why: The split of the profit is right and the balance sheet is not. Non-controlling interest is the equity in a subsidiary not attributable to the parent, and an option that entitles its holder to nothing until exercise is not equity of the subsidiary held by anybody. Ind AS 109 governs the options, which is what the attribution rule expressly leaves them to.

options.text: ₹60 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹40 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.misconception: applies the general rule to both instruments and misses the in-substance ownership exception that reaches the second one
options.why: Ignoring the options is right; ignoring the 5 per cent contract is not. The narrow exception asks one thing — has the arrangement already put the rewards of ownership into this holder's hands? A contract paying over the dividends from today has. Where it bites, the instrument is not measured under Ind AS 109 at all.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B89 and B90

items.scenario: P Ltd holds 60 per cent of the ordinary shares of S Ltd and consolidates it. P Ltd also holds currently exercisable options over a further 25 per cent of S Ltd's ordinary shares, deeply in the money, which carry no right to any dividend or to any share of net assets until they are exercised; the options were counted in concluding that P Ltd has power over S Ltd. Separately, P Ltd has a contract over another 5 per cent of S Ltd's shares which, from today, entitles it to the dividends and other returns on those shares. S Ltd's profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹100 crore and it has no other comprehensive income.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 112 require of the note?

options.text: The significant judgements and assumptions behind the conclusion on the type of joint arrangement, and information presented separately for each class of interest with an explanation of how interests have been aggregated
options.why: An entity discloses the significant judgements and assumptions it has made in determining the nature of its interest in another entity or arrangement and the type of joint arrangement in which it has an interest. An arrangement carried on through a separate vehicle is a joint venture unless the legal form, the contractual terms or other facts give the parties rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities, so concluding that this one is a joint operation is exactly the kind of judgement a reader cannot reconstruct from the figures. The Standard also requires information to be presented separately for interests in subsidiaries, joint ventures, joint operations, associates and unconsolidated structured entities, and requires the entity to disclose how it has aggregated its interests in similar entities.

options.text: The judgement disclosure is needed only where the conclusion is that the arrangement is a joint venture, that being the outcome that keeps assets off the balance sheet
options.misconception: makes the disclosure turn on which answer was reached rather than on a judgement having been made at all
options.why: The requirement attaches to the judgement, not to its outcome. A joint operation puts the company's share of the assets and liabilities on its own balance sheet and a joint venture puts one equity-accounted line there, so a reader needs the reasoning whichever way the classification went.

options.text: Nothing at all for the structured entity, since the company does not control it and it is therefore outside the group the note describes
options.misconception: reads Ind AS 112 as reaching only what is consolidated
options.why: Unconsolidated structured entities are one of the classes the Standard names, and they are the class it was most concerned to bring into view — an interest that carries risk without appearing in the consolidated figures is precisely what a reader cannot otherwise see. The scope covers interests in subsidiaries, joint arrangements, associates and unconsolidated structured entities alike.

options.text: One combined table is enough, provided every interest the company holds appears somewhere in it
options.misconception: aggregates across the five classes the Standard requires to be presented separately
options.why: Aggregation is allowed within a class of similar entities and is not allowed across the classes. Information is presented separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures, joint operations, associates and unconsolidated structured entities, because the risks a reader is being told about differ completely between them, and the entity must say how it aggregated whatever it did aggregate.

citation.ref: para 7, read with the requirement to present information separately by class of interest and to disclose how interests have been aggregated

items.scenario: A company has three sets of interests. It and one other party jointly control an arrangement carried on through a company incorporated for the purpose, and after weighing the legal form, the contractual terms and the other facts it has concluded that the arrangement is a joint operation rather than a joint venture. It holds interests in two associates. And it holds an interest in a structured entity that it does not consolidate. The draft note sets out one combined table headed "interests in other entities", and says nothing about how the joint arrangement came to be classified, on the ground that Ind AS 111 already gives the test.

items.stem: What stands between the fund and the definition of an investment entity?

options.text: The perpetual debt alone — an exit strategy is needed for debt that has the potential to be held indefinitely but not for the five-year bonds, and having one investor and two investments does not by itself disqualify the fund
options.why: A fund of this kind must write down how it gets out. Nearly every share it owns, and nearly every non-financial holding, needs an exit strategy saying how the value built up in it will be turned into cash. Debt joins that list only where the paper could run on with no end in sight, which is why perpetual debt needs a plan of its own. A bond that matures in five years cannot run on, so its own redemption date is the way out and no plan is called for. Several holdings, several investors, and investors who are outsiders rather than group companies are typical characteristics of such a fund. Falling short on one of those typical characteristics does not by itself put the fund outside the definition; it means the call has to be made on judgement and shown.

options.text: Nothing — the equity exit strategies are documented and debt repays itself, so the fund already meets the definition
options.misconception: treats every debt instrument as self-liquidating, when perpetual debt has no maturity to rely on
options.why: A fixed-maturity bond does repay itself and needs no plan. Perpetual debt does not, which is why the requirement names it. Without an exit strategy for it the fund is holding an investment it has no documented intention of ever realising, which is the opposite of what an investment entity does.

options.text: Nothing, because an exit strategy is required only for equity investments and both debt holdings are outside the requirement
options.misconception: stops at the equity limb of a requirement that reaches debt with no maturity as well
options.why: The requirement runs to substantially all equity and non-financial asset investments and then, expressly, to debt instruments that have the potential to be held indefinitely. Reading it as equity-only would let a fund hold perpetual paper forever and still call itself an investment entity.

options.text: The single investor and the two investments — those are conditions of the definition and the fund fails them outright
options.misconception: turns the typical characteristics into conditions of the definition
options.why: The definition has three elements — obtaining funds from investors to provide them with investment management services, committing to invest solely for capital appreciation or investment income, and measuring and evaluating performance on a fair value basis. The typical characteristics sit beside those elements, and their absence indicates that additional judgement is required rather than settling the matter.

citation.ref: para 27 and 28, read with the application guidance in Appendix B on exit strategies and on the typical characteristics of an investment entity

items.scenario: A fund obtains money from investors, provides them with investment management services, commits in its offering document to invest solely for capital appreciation and investment income, and measures and evaluates every holding on a fair value basis. It has documented how it plans to realise each of its equity investments within five to eight years. It also holds perpetual debt issued by one investee, for which it has no exit plan, and five-year bonds issued by another, for which it also has no exit plan. The fund has one investor and two investments, both substantial.

items.stem: What must the finished statement show?

options.text: The ₹20 lakh in profit or loss, being the excess of what the parent paid over the carrying amount of the interest it acquired
options.misconception: routes a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners through performance
options.why: Buying out a minority that the parent already controlled is a dealing between the owners of a business, not a purchase of one. It has its own named line inside transactions with owners, and nothing about it reaches the year's result.

options.text: One combined adjustments line is enough, both amounts arising under Ind AS 8 and both landing in equity
options.misconception: merges two adjustments the standard requires to be shown separately from each other
options.why: A change in accounting policy and a correction of an error say different things about the company. One is a decision about how to report; the other is an admission that an earlier report was wrong. The requirement to show them separately, component by component and period by period, exists so that a reader can tell which happened.

options.text: The ₹60 lakh and the ₹15 lakh shown separately by component of equity as adjustments to the opening balances, for each prior period and at the beginning of the period, and the ₹20 lakh inside transactions with owners as a change in ownership interest that does not result in a loss of control
options.why: Each column of equity carries two adjustment figures, not one: what changes in accounting policies did to that column, and beside it what corrections of errors did to it. Both are shown for every earlier period presented and again at the start of this one. Neither is a movement of the year to 31 March 2026. Restating backwards resets the opening balance of retained earnings, or of whatever other column an Ind AS points to, and the revaluation surplus is the column the ₹15 lakh resets. Working down the same column, the standard then wants the owners' own dealings pulled out and labelled — what they subscribed, what was handed back to them, and any move in how much of a subsidiary the group holds while the parent still keeps hold of it, a move that stops short of a loss of control.

options.text: Both adjustments among this year's movements, with the ₹20 lakh correctly placed inside transactions with owners
options.misconception: gets the ownership change right and leaves retrospective adjustments in the wrong period
options.why: The half that is right does not save the half that is not. A retrospective adjustment restates the opening balance of the earliest period presented; showing ₹75 lakh as movements of the year to 31 March 2026 would make this year look ₹75 lakh worse and leave the earlier periods still reported on the old basis.

citation.ref: para 110, read with para 106(b) and 106(d)

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a company does three things. It changes an accounting policy retrospectively, which reduces the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented by ₹60 lakh. It corrects a prior period error, which reduces the opening revaluation surplus by ₹15 lakh. And it buys a further 10 per cent of a subsidiary from the minority, ₹20 lakh of the price being taken directly to equity attributable to the owners of the parent. The draft statement of changes in equity shows a single line called "adjustments" of ₹75 lakh among this year's movements and puts the ₹20 lakh inside profit for the year.

items.stem: Over which periods must the segment information be presented?

options.text: For the nine months and its comparative alone, since interim information is reported on a year-to-date basis
options.misconception: reads the year-to-date basis as replacing the interim period rather than accompanying it
options.why: Year-to-date describes the basis of the cumulative column, not the whole requirement. The current interim period is presented as well, and without it the movement inside the latest three months is invisible.

options.text: For the three months and the nine months, with a comparative for the year ended 31 March 2025 rather than for the corresponding periods
options.misconception: compares an interim period against a full prior year instead of against the comparable interim period
options.why: The comparative for a statement of profit and loss is the comparable interim period of the immediately preceding financial year. Only the balance sheet takes the end of the immediately preceding financial year as its comparative, and it does so because a balance sheet is a position at a date rather than a performance over a stretch of time.

options.text: For the three months and its comparative alone, as drafted, a quarterly report being about the quarter
options.misconception: drops the cumulative year-to-date columns that sit alongside the interim period
options.why: A quarter on its own can be flattered or spoiled by timing. The cumulative figures exist so that a reader can see the year as it has actually run, which is why the standard asks for both and not for a choice between them.

options.text: For the three months ended 31 December 2025 and cumulatively for the nine months to that date, each with a comparative for the corresponding periods of the previous financial year
options.why: Interim reporting runs on a financial year-to-date basis, and that is what sets the columns. One statement of profit and loss covers the current interim period, here the three months to 31 December 2025. A second runs from 1 April and carries the figures year to date. Each of the two is then set against the matching stretch of the year before — the comparable interim periods for the quarter and for the nine months alike. Segment information inside an interim report takes exactly those periods, so the note runs to four columns and not to two.

citation.ref: para 20, read with the interim segment disclosure in para 16A(g)

items.scenario: A listed company with a 31 March year end publishes quarterly interim reports and discloses segment information in its annual financial statements under Ind AS 108. It is preparing the report for the quarter ended 31 December 2025, its third quarter. The draft gives segment revenue and a measure of segment result for the three months ended 31 December 2025, with a comparative for the three months ended 31 December 2024, and nothing further.

items.stem: Which of the four enter the disclosure?

options.text: The lease liabilities, the swap and the overdraft, an overdraft being borrowed money like any other
options.misconception: treats an overdraft that forms part of cash management as a financing liability
options.why: Where a bank overdraft is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of an entity's cash management, it is included as a component of cash and cash equivalents. The balance swings between positive and negative as part of one cash position, and no cash flow from financing activities arises on it at all.

options.text: The lease liabilities alone, since the disclosure is about liabilities and a derivative asset cannot enter it
options.misconception: reads the heading and misses the express extension to financial assets that hedge those liabilities
options.why: The heading is a description, not the boundary. The requirement is extended in terms to changes in financial assets where the cash flows from them run through financing activities, and the example the standard itself gives is an asset that hedges a financing liability. Leaving the swap out would show the borrowing moving with exchange rates and hide the instrument that offsets it.

options.text: All four, since every one of them will be settled in cash sooner or later
options.misconception: makes eventual cash settlement the test, when the test is how that cash flow is classified
options.why: Everything on a balance sheet is settled in cash eventually. What decides membership is the classification of the cash flow — financing, operating or investing — and trade payables for raw materials are operating however certainly they will be paid.

options.text: The lease liabilities and the swap; the overdraft and the trade payables stay out
options.why: One test decides it: where does the money show up in the cash flow statement? A balance joins the liabilities arising from financing activities once its payments have been presented, or are going to be presented, under the financing heading. Lease liabilities pass that test. Trade payables fail it, their payments being operating. The reconciliation is then stretched across to the other side of the balance sheet, because assets that hedge such borrowings are drawn in on that identical test — which is what puts the cross-currency swap inside it, whichever side it happens to sit on. The overdraft is another matter again. It counts as one component of cash and cash equivalents, so its swings live inside the balance the statement sets out to explain, and there is no financing flow left to reconcile.

citation.ref: para 44A and 44C, read with the definition of cash equivalents in para 8

items.scenario: A company is drawing up the disclosure on liabilities arising from financing activities and argues over four balances. Its lease liabilities, on which the cash payments are presented as financing cash flows. A bank overdraft repayable on demand which forms an integral part of the company's cash management and is included in cash and cash equivalents. Trade payables for raw materials. And a cross-currency swap taken out to hedge a dollar borrowing, whose settlements are presented within financing cash flows.

items.stem: Is the consultant right?

options.text: No, but Company B measures in the most advantageous market instead, the exchange being closed to it
options.misconception: reaches for the fallback when the entity does have a principal market of its own
options.why: The most advantageous market answers only in the absence of a principal market. Company B has one — the regional market is the market with the greatest volume and level of activity that B can access — so the fallback is never reached and no comparison of net proceeds across markets is made.

options.text: Yes for a commodity traded on an exchange, though Company B would use its own market for an asset that had no exchange at all
options.misconception: makes access relevant only where no larger market exists, when it qualifies the identification of the principal market in every case
options.why: Whether a market is an exchange or not changes nothing. The question in every case is which market with the greatest volume and level of activity the entity can access, and an exchange the entity cannot deal on fails that question exactly as a closed private market would.

options.text: Yes — fair value is a market-based measurement, so the deepest market for the commodity fixes one price for every holder
options.misconception: reads a market-based measurement as one that ignores which markets the holder can actually reach
options.why: Market-based means the measurement uses the assumptions market participants would use rather than the entity's own intentions. It does not mean the entity is priced in a market it cannot trade in. Access at the measurement date is written into the identification of the principal market for that reason.

options.text: No — the exchange is Company A's principal market and the regional market is Company B's, so the two properly report different fair values for the same commodity
options.why: Measurement happens in the principal market, and that market is picked from the ones this entity can access on the measurement date — of those, the busiest, the one where most of the asset changes hands. Depth on its own settles nothing: a market shut to the holder can never be his principal market, however large it is. Two companies can therefore have different principal markets while sitting inside one group, and the question is put afresh for each asset held. Two holders of one commodity landing on two fair values is what the standard expects, then, and not an inconsistency somebody has to iron out.

citation.ref: para 16 and 19

items.scenario: Two unrelated companies each hold the same commodity at 31 March 2026. Company A is a member of the national exchange, which has by far the greatest volume and level of activity for the commodity, and deals there routinely. Company B is not a member, cannot become one before the reporting date, and can deal only in a regional market with much lower volumes, where it has always transacted.
