A consultant tells Company B that fair value is a property of the asset, so B must measure at the exchange price too.

items.stem: Does either contract contain a significant financing component?

options.text: The retention contract only, a customer who withholds money being in substance lent it back
options.misconception: reads a performance-protection retention as consideration deferred for the sake of finance
options.why: The money is withheld because the work may prove defective, and the amount withheld is proportional to that risk rather than to the passage of time. That is the difference arising for reasons other than the provision of finance, which the standard names as taking the contract outside the financing rules.

options.text: Both of them, since the one-year practical expedient is unavailable and more than a year passes in each case
options.misconception: treats the length of the gap as the whole test, when the overriding provision is reached first
options.why: The practical expedient removes the adjustment where the gap is a year or less. Failing the expedient does not create a financing component; it only means the entity must go and ask whether one exists, and the overriding provision answers that neither of these has one.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: Ind AS 115 puts an overriding provision above the general rule, and two situations answer to it. In the first, cash arrives up front but the buyer picks the moment of delivery inside a stated band, so the timing sits at the discretion of the customer; the standard illustrates it with a prepaid mobile card. In the second, the gap between the promised price and the cash selling price opened for reasons other than the provision of finance and moves in step with whatever opened it, the illustration being a payment term that shields one side against the other walking away from its obligations. A defect retention is that second situation. So neither contract holds a significant financing component and neither is discounted for the time value of money.
keywords: reasons other than the provision of finance

options.text: The prepaid card only, since the customer parts with cash before receiving anything at all
options.misconception: makes advance payment by itself decisive, which is the very case the discretion limb removes
options.why: Advance payment is what makes the question worth asking, not what answers it. Where the customer decides when the service is taken, the entity is not being financed by the delay — the customer is choosing it — and the standard removes such a contract by name.

citation.ref: para 62(a) and 62(c), read with para 60 and the practical expedient in para 63

items.scenario: Two contracts are under review. In the first, a construction company is paid by milestones that coincide with its performance, and the customer retains 10 per cent of each milestone payment until one year after completion as protection against defects. In the second, a telecom company sells prepaid cards; the customer pays now and decides when, within a stated band of time, to use the minutes. In both contracts more than a year passes between some of the cash and the related performance, so the one-year practical expedient is unavailable.

items.stem: How does the operator recognise its consideration for the construction services?

options.text: Wholly an intangible asset, since the operator must run the metro for twenty-five years before it earns anything at all
options.misconception: reads the obligation to operate as making every entitlement contingent
options.why: Having to perform is not the same as having to hope. The annuity is payable whatever the ridership, so once the operator performs, the amount is not contingent on anything the public does. Only the fare entitlement carries demand risk.

options.text: Wholly a financial asset, the authority having guaranteed part of the return under a single arrangement with a single grantor
options.misconception: lets a partial guarantee carry the whole consideration into a financial asset
options.why: A financial asset arises only so far as the operator has an unconditional right to receive cash. Nothing is guaranteed on the fare side, so the operator carries the ridership risk on ₹500 crore of its consideration, and that risk is precisely what the split exists to show.

options.text: Split it, recognising a financial asset for the guaranteed portion and an intangible asset for the fare-based portion, each component measured initially at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable
options.why: One contract can hand the builder two different kinds of reward, and Appendix C will not let them be merged. Where part of what is earned for building is a promise of money and part is only a licence to charge the people who ride the line, the operator has to account separately for each strand, putting both on the books at the fair value of the consideration it has earned or is owed. The annuity falls due whatever the ridership, so the right to it is unconditional and it is a financial asset. The fare stream is no more than a right to charge the travelling public, worth whatever that public decides to travel, so it is an intangible asset.

options.text: Split, but with the intangible asset taken as the residual once the financial asset has been recognised at the present value of the guaranteed annuity
options.misconception: applies a residual method the Appendix does not use
options.why: Each of the two components enters the books in its own right, at the fair value of what the operator is entitled to receive for that component; neither half is a leftover taken after the other has been measured. A residual would make the intangible asset absorb every error in measuring the other component, and would make the two halves of one contract measured on two different bases.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 18, read with para 16 and 17

items.scenario: An operator builds a metro line for a state authority under a twenty-five-year concession, spending ₹1,200 crore. Under the contract the authority pays a guaranteed annuity whatever the ridership, and the operator additionally collects fares from passengers, with no guarantee of any kind on the fare side and no shortfall made good. On the model both parties used to price the bid, ₹700 crore of the consideration for the construction services is attributable to the guaranteed annuity and ₹500 crore to the fare entitlement.

items.stem: May the company take the low-value recognition exemption on both head leases?

options.text: On neither — an intermediate lessor may take no recognition exemption at all
options.misconception: overstates a bar that reaches the low-value election and leaves the short-term one standing
options.why: The short-term exemption survives a sublease. Where the head lease is a short-term lease that the entity has accounted for under that exemption, the sublease is simply classified as an operating lease. It is the low-value election alone that a sublease closes off.

options.text: On the first only — a lessee that subleases an asset, or expects to sublease it, cannot account for that head lease as a lease of a low-value asset
options.why: Once a head lease has been sublet, or the lessee merely expects to sublease what it has taken, that head lease is shut out of the low-value asset election, and what the furniture is worth never enters the argument. The company is an intermediate lessor on the second item, so a right-of-use asset and a lease liability go on its balance sheet for it. The consequence runs past presentation: a sublease is classified against the right-of-use asset the head lease throws off, and a head lease sheltering inside the exemption throws off nothing for the sublease to be measured against.

options.text: On both, provided the sublease itself turns out to be an operating lease
options.misconception: makes the bar depend on how the sublease is classified, when it bites before the classification is reached
options.why: Classification comes later and depends on the right-of-use asset the head lease creates. The bar operates first, on the fact of subleasing or expecting to sublease, and it is what brings that right-of-use asset into existence in the first place.

options.text: On both — the low-value election is available asset by asset, and an item does not stop being of low value because somebody else uses it
options.misconception: applies the low-value election to a head lease the standard removes from it
options.why: The election is indeed made asset by asset, and that is not the point. The standard takes a subleased head lease out of the election altogether, before the value of the underlying item is ever considered, because the lessee has stopped being a user and become a lessor.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B7, read with para 5 and 6 and the sublease classification in para B58

items.scenario: A company takes two head leases on the same day, each of a single item of office furniture that is of low value when new, each for three years, and neither carrying a purchase option. It intends to use the first item itself. At the same time it subleases the second item to a tenant for the whole three years.

items.stem: How does the company account for the ₹90 crore?

options.text: Add the ₹90 crore to the cost and take the ₹50 crore to other comprehensive income against the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: applies the revaluation-model route to an asset carried at cost, and to an impairment rather than to the liability change
options.why: Two things go wrong at once. The revaluation route in the Appendix applies only where the related asset is measured using the revaluation model, and this one is not; and even there it governs the liability change itself, not an impairment loss arising afterwards. There is also no revaluation surplus on this asset for the amount to sit in.

options.text: Add the ₹90 crore to the cost of the refinery and depreciate ₹210 crore over eight years, an increase in a provision not being an impairment indicator
options.misconception: takes the addition to cost as the end of the matter, when the Appendix names it as the trigger to look further
options.why: The Appendix does not leave this to the general list of impairment indicators; it makes the addition to cost itself the thing the entity must consider. The reason is plain enough — a bigger obligation to clean up does not make the plant more valuable, so a carrying amount that has just been raised by one is exactly where recoverability is in doubt.

options.text: Add it to the cost of the refinery, then test the asset for impairment because the addition is an indication that the new ₹210 crore carrying amount may not be fully recoverable, recognise a ₹50 crore impairment loss and depreciate the remaining ₹160 crore over eight years
options.why: An asset kept at cost absorbs the movement in its decommissioning or restoration provision into its own carrying amount: this year's remeasurement is added to that amount, or taken off it, with the liability restated to the same figure. Where the movement pushes the carrying amount up, the Appendix does not stop there. It treats the increase itself as a warning sign that an asset now sitting at a bigger number may no longer be fully recoverable, and it sends the entity into Ind AS 36 to work out the recoverable amount and book whatever impairment loss the comparison throws up. ₹210 crore measured against ₹160 crore leaves a shortfall of ₹50 crore, and the ₹160 crore that survives is written off across the eight years still to run.

options.text: Recognise the ₹90 crore as an expense of the year, since it arises from a regulation and a rate change rather than from anything the refinery gained
options.misconception: expenses a change the Appendix capitalises under the cost model
options.why: Under the cost model the change is added to, or deducted from, the cost of the asset. Only a decrease that exceeds the asset's carrying amount reaches profit or loss, and separately the periodic unwinding of the discount is a finance cost. Expensing the increase would leave the asset and the provision measured on different bases from the same estimate.

citation.ref: Appendix A, para 5(a) and 5(c), read with Ind AS 36

items.scenario: A refinery carried under the cost model has a carrying amount of ₹120 crore at 31 March 2026 and a remaining useful life of eight years. A new regulation and a fall in the market discount rate raise the present value of the decommissioning obligation by ₹90 crore at that date. The refinery's recoverable amount at 31 March 2026, measured under Ind AS 36, is ₹160 crore. There is no revaluation surplus in existence for this asset.

items.stem: What deferred tax asset does the parent recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: None
options.why: Two hurdles stand in front of any asset here and both have to be cleared. Take a stake in a subsidiary, a branch, an associate or a joint venture: its deductible temporary differences give an asset only where the unwinding is probable inside the foreseeable future, and only where taxable profit will be available to soak up the deduction when it lands. The signed sale agreement clears the first hurdle. The run of losses and a forecast showing nothing to tax knock out the second, so the certainty of the reversal buys nothing and no asset is put up.

options.text: ₹14 crore, because a deductible temporary difference is always recognised in full, the restrictions in Ind AS 12 on investments applying only to taxable temporary differences
options.misconception: reads the investment rules as reaching deferred tax liabilities alone
options.why: Both sides are addressed. Taxable temporary differences on such investments give a liability unless a two-part exception is met, and deductible temporary differences give an asset only where a two-part condition is met. The second rule exists because an investor may have no way of turning a book loss on an investment into a tax deduction it can use.

options.text: ₹14 crore, the binding agreement making reversal in the foreseeable future certain
options.misconception: takes the reversal condition as the whole test, when the recognition rule joins two conditions with "and"
options.why: Reversal only creates the deduction; it does not create anything to deduct it from. A company with no taxable profit gets no benefit from a deductible amount, and a deferred tax asset is an asset precisely because a benefit is expected. Both conditions are required together.

options.text: None, because a deductible temporary difference on an investment in a subsidiary can never be recognised
options.misconception: turns a test with two conditions into a prohibition
options.why: It is recognised whenever both conditions are met, and they often are — a committed sale producing a deduction against expected taxable profit is exactly the case the rule was written to allow. What defeats it here is the absence of taxable profit, not the fact that the investment is in a subsidiary.

citation.ref: para 44

items.scenario: A parent's investment in a foreign subsidiary carries an amount of ₹180 crore in the consolidated financial statements against a tax base of ₹250 crore, a deductible temporary difference of ₹70 crore. The parent has signed a binding agreement to sell the subsidiary in the year ending 31 March 2027, so the difference will certainly reverse. The parent has, however, a long record of tax losses in the jurisdiction where the relief would arise and its forecasts show no taxable profit there in any year covered by them. The rate the parent is told applies to such a deduction is 20 per cent.

items.stem: How are the three amounts treated?

options.text: The ₹80 lakh deducted from equity and the other two charged to profit or loss, a buy-back being a use of cash rather than an equity transaction
options.misconception: leaves a reacquisition of the entity's own shares outside the meaning of an equity transaction
options.why: Reacquiring the entity's own equity instruments is an equity transaction as surely as issuing them is — the consideration paid is deducted from equity and no gain or loss on the instruments reaches profit or loss. The costs of doing it follow the transaction they belong to.

options.text: The whole ₹117 lakh to profit or loss, costs of raising or returning capital being period costs like any other
options.misconception: treats the cost of a transaction with owners as an operating expense of the business
options.why: These costs buy nothing that is used in trading. They are the cost of a movement in the company's own capital, so they are set against that movement rather than against the year's results, which is what deducting them from equity does.

options.text: The whole ₹117 lakh deducted from equity, the abandoned issue included, since an equity transaction was intended in every case
options.misconception: deducts from equity a cost that produced no equity transaction at all
options.why: The deduction attaches to an equity transaction that happens. Where the issue is abandoned there is no movement in equity for the cost to attach to, and the standard says in terms that money spent on a share issue which is called off goes to profit or loss as an expense of the period.

options.text: The ₹80 lakh and the ₹12 lakh are deducted from equity, with any related income tax dealt with under Ind AS 12, and the ₹25 lakh on the abandoned issue is an expense; the amount taken out of equity is disclosed separately
options.why: What it costs to move a company's own capital is set against that capital and not against the year's trading. Such costs come off as a deduction from equity so far as they are incremental costs directly attributable to the deal and would never have been borne had it not gone ahead. Putting shares out and buying them back are both dealings in the entity's own equity, so the ₹12 lakh on the buy-back travels the road the ₹80 lakh on the rights issue travels. An issue that is abandoned produces no such dealing, so its ₹25 lakh becomes an expense of the year. Ind AS 12 takes care of any income tax on these costs, and the total lifted out of equity during the year has to be disclosed separately in the notes.

citation.ref: para 37 and 39, read with para 35A

items.scenario: A company incurs three lots of costs during the year ended 31 March 2026. It pays ₹80 lakh of merchant banker and legal fees on a rights issue that completes. It pays ₹25 lakh on a second issue that it abandons after market conditions turn, so no shares are ever issued. And it pays ₹12 lakh of stamp duty and brokerage on buying its own shares back through the exchange. The finance head proposes to charge the whole ₹117 lakh to profit or loss as professional and regulatory expenses.

items.stem: What does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹40 lakh in other comprehensive income, and then an immediate reclassification of ₹15 lakh out of the reserve into profit or loss, leaving ₹25 lakh in the reserve
options.why: Two cumulative figures are put side by side and the smaller of them, taken without regard to sign, is what the cash flow hedge reserve is set at: ₹40 lakh of loss sitting on the forward contract, against ₹42 lakh of movement in the present value of the sales being hedged. ₹40 lakh is the smaller, so ₹40 lakh goes through other comprehensive income and no ineffectiveness falls out. A second rule then bites. Once a company has worked out that some slice of an accumulated hedging loss will simply not be recovered, in this period or any later one, that slice leaves the reserve there and then and lands in profit or loss as a reclassification adjustment. ₹15 lakh has been judged unrecoverable, so ₹15 lakh moves now and ₹25 lakh stays behind. Holding all ₹40 lakh back until the sales happen would postpone a loss the company has already accepted.

options.text: ₹15 lakh left in the reserve and ₹25 lakh reclassified to profit or loss, the unrecoverable part being the effective portion
options.misconception: reverses which part of the accumulated loss is reclassified
options.why: The amount reclassified is the amount that is not expected to be recovered, which is the ₹15 lakh. What stays in the reserve is the part that still relates to cash flows the forecast sales will produce, and it will move to profit or loss when they do.

options.text: ₹40 lakh in other comprehensive income and nothing in profit or loss until the forecast sales occur, as the finance head proposes
options.misconception: applies the ordinary timing rule to a loss the standard requires to be taken now
options.why: Ordinarily the reserve empties into profit or loss as and when the forecast sales it was taken out against reach profit or loss themselves, and that timing is the rule the finance head has in mind. Written into it, in mandatory terms, is an exception for the part of a loss that will not be recovered, and the company has already concluded that ₹15 lakh will not be.

options.text: ₹42 lakh in other comprehensive income, being the cumulative change in the hedged item, with ₹2 lakh of ineffectiveness in profit or loss
options.misconception: takes the higher of the two cumulative amounts, when the reserve is set at the lower in absolute amounts
options.why: The test is a lower-of test taken in absolute amounts, and ₹40 lakh is the smaller. An under-hedge leaves part of the hedged item's movement unhedged rather than creating ineffectiveness to book, so there is nothing for the ₹2 lakh to be.

citation.ref: para 6.5.11(a), (b) and (d)(iii)

items.scenario: A company designated a forward contract as the hedging instrument in a cash flow hedge of highly probable forecast dollar sales expected in the year ending 31 March 2027. Every qualifying criterion is met. At 31 March 2026 the cumulative loss on the hedging instrument since inception is ₹40 lakh and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows since inception is ₹42 lakh. The forecast sales remain highly probable, but the company has assessed that ₹15 lakh of the accumulated loss will not be recovered in any future period. The finance head proposes to leave the whole ₹40 lakh in the cash flow hedge reserve until the sales occur.

items.stem: Are the terms substantially different, and how do the two fees enter the answer?

options.text: Yes — only the ₹3 crore paid to the lender enters the test, giving ₹353 crore against ₹395 crore and a difference of about 10.6 per cent, so the old loan is extinguished, and both fees are then recognised as part of the gain or loss on the extinguishment
options.why: The 10 per cent test counts a narrow set of fees, netting what came in against what went out. Only money moving between the borrower and the lender is admitted, and money either of them settles on the other's account is admitted with it. A law firm stands outside that pair, so its ₹5 crore never enters the arithmetic — ₹350 crore plus the ₹3 crore amendment fee gives ₹353 crore, set beside ₹395 crore, a gap of about 10.6 per cent. Past ten, the terms count as substantially different and the old loan is treated as extinguished. Once that verdict is reached the net widens: every cost and fee of the renegotiation, the law firm's included, is swept into the gain or loss on the extinguishment.

options.text: Yes, but only the ₹3 crore paid to the lender enters the gain or loss, the ₹5 crore of legal advice being a period expense
options.misconception: carries the test's restriction forward into the measurement of the gain or loss, where it does not apply
options.why: The restriction to fees between the borrower and the lender belongs to the test alone, where it exists so that a borrower cannot manufacture a 10 per cent difference by hiring advisers. Once the old liability is treated as extinguished, everything spent on the renegotiation is folded into the gain or loss recognised on it, and that takes in the law firm's ₹5 crore as well.

options.text: No, because a renegotiation with the same lender on the same principal can never be substantially different, nothing having been exchanged
options.misconception: reads the rule as reaching only an exchange of instruments, when a substantial modification of terms is treated the same way
options.why: Two routes reach the same place. Swapping one debt instrument for another on substantially different terms, between a borrower and a lender already in a relationship, kills the old liability — and so does a substantial reworking of the terms of a liability that stays where it is, whether or not the debtor is in financial difficulty. Who sits on the other side settles nothing; the test does.

options.text: No — both fees belong in the test, giving ₹358 crore against ₹395 crore and a difference of about 9.4 per cent, so the loan survives and both fees adjust its carrying amount
options.misconception: puts a third party's fee into a test the standard confines to fees between the borrower and the lender
options.why: The costs counted for the test are not the costs counted once the answer is known. For the test the standard names only fees paid or received between the borrower and the lender; it is afterwards, and only where the modification does not result in derecognition, that any costs or fees incurred adjust the carrying amount and are amortised over the remaining term of the modified liability.

citation.ref: para 3.3.2 and 3.3.3, with the 10 per cent test and the fees included in it in Appendix B, para B3.3.6

items.scenario: A company renegotiates a term loan with the same lender on 1 October 2025. Its carrying amount is ₹400 crore. The company pays the lender an amendment fee of ₹3 crore and pays an independent law firm ₹5 crore for advice on the amendment. Discounted at the original effective interest rate, the remaining cash flows of the old loan have a present value of ₹395 crore, and the cash flows under the new terms, before any fee, have a present value of ₹350 crore.

items.stem: What is open to each company?

options.text: The first may take it if it translates the previous GAAP carrying amounts into the new functional currency at the transition-date rate
options.misconception: tries to cure a closed gate with a translation, when the condition is that the functional currency has not changed at all
options.why: The condition is absolute — the election is available where there is no change in functional currency on the date of transition. Translating old amounts into a new functional currency is exactly the exercise the condition exists to prevent, because those amounts were never measured on that basis.

options.text: The first may not take the election at all; the second may, and may take it for its investment property too
options.why: D7AA lets a first-time adopter leave every item of property, plant and equipment at the amount its old GAAP already carried and treat that amount as deemed cost — but it opens that door on one condition, that there is no change in the entity's functional currency on the date of transition to Ind AS. The first company's currency changes on exactly that date, so the door is shut and it must either apply the standard retrospectively or take fair value at transition as deemed cost. The second company's currency holds, so the door is open, and the same choice extends to its investment property.

options.text: The first may take it, and the second may not extend it to investment property, the election being written for property, plant and equipment alone
options.misconception: inverts both limbs of the answer
options.why: The functional currency condition is what stops the first company, and the option is expressly available for investment property as well, so the second company is the one with the wider choice rather than the narrower.

options.text: Both may take it, a change in functional currency being a translation matter that does not touch the deemed cost election
options.misconception: misses the condition the election opens with
options.why: The condition is the first thing the election says. It exists because previous GAAP amounts were measured in the old functional currency, and carrying them forward once the currency of measurement has changed would give a starting cost expressed in a currency the entity no longer reports in.

citation.ref: para D7AA

items.scenario: Two companies adopt Ind AS from 1 April 2026, with 1 April 2025 as the date of transition. The first company's functional currency changes on the date of transition from the rupee to the dollar, and it wants to continue with the previous GAAP carrying amounts of all its property, plant and equipment as deemed cost. The second company's functional currency does not change, and it wants the same treatment for all its property, plant and equipment and for its investment property as well.

items.stem: What do the 2021 amendments to Division II require?

options.text: The benami and virtual currency disclosures only, the surrendered income being covered by the current tax note
options.misconception: lets the tax note absorb a disclosure Schedule III asks for by name
options.why: The tax note explains the charge for the year. This disclosure exists because income was surrendered and never entered the books at all, which is a fact about the reliability of the records rather than about the tax computation, and Schedule III asks for it separately for that reason.

options.text: Only the ratio note — the other three are income-tax and regulatory matters that sit outside the financial statements
options.misconception: reads the 2021 amendments as a ratio note and nothing else
options.why: The amendments were written precisely to bring matters of this kind onto the face of the notes, where an auditor sees them and a reader can find them. A prescribed disclosure does not stop being one because the underlying subject is also dealt with by another regulator.

options.text: All three, but in the Board's report rather than in the notes to the financial statements
options.misconception: moves a prescribed note into the directors' report
options.why: Schedule III prescribes the format and content of the financial statements, and what it requires goes in them. The Board's report carries its own list under the Companies Act, and reporting something there does not discharge a Schedule III requirement.

options.text: All three carry their own disclosure alongside the ratio note — details of the benami proceedings, the income surrendered and not recorded in the books, and the dealings in the virtual currency
options.why: The 2021 amendments added a block of additional information to Division II of which the ratio note is one item among several. Others require details of any proceedings initiated or pending against the company for holding any benami property, disclosure of any income surrendered or disclosed in a tax assessment that has not been recorded in the books of account, and details of any crypto currency or virtual currency traded or invested in during the year. Each is a prescribed note, and a company cannot select among them.
keywords: not been recorded in the books

citation.ref: Schedule III Division II — additional regulatory information inserted by the 2021 amendments

items.scenario: A company preparing its financial statements under Division II of Schedule III has three matters on the table. Proceedings have been initiated against it under the law prohibiting benami transactions. It surrendered income during a search assessment which has not been recorded in its books of account. And it bought and sold units of a virtual digital currency during the year. The chief financial officer says the ratio note is the only thing the 2021 amendments added, so none of the three needs anything in the notes.

items.stem: Under which provision, if any, can he be held guilty?

options.text: Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule — a member in anybody's employment who lets out confidential matter that reached him through the job, with only two ways out — a law in force made him speak, or his employer agreed to it
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule carries four clauses and it reaches every member of the Institute, certificate of practice or none. Clause 2 is the one written for a member who is somebody's employee: it catches him when confidential matter that reached him through the job is passed to an outsider, and it lets him out in two situations only — a law in force at the time compels him to speak, or the disclosure was permitted by the employer. Neither is available. No statute called for the pricing file and nobody at the company agreed to it. A marking on the document decides nothing; what the clause asks is whether the information was confidential and whether the job is how he came by it.
keywords: Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: Clause 1 of Part I of the Second Schedule, for disclosing information acquired in the course of his professional engagement without his client's consent
options.misconception: charges a member in employment under a clause written for a member in practice
options.why: Part I of the Second Schedule is headed professional misconduct in relation to Chartered Accountants in practice, and its clause 1 speaks of information acquired in the course of a professional engagement and of the consent of a client. This member has an employer, not a client, and holds no certificate of practice.

options.text: No clause reaches him, since he certified nothing and expressed no opinion
options.misconception: assumes professional misconduct requires an audit, a report or a certificate
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule reaches members of the Institute generally, and none of its four clauses asks whether the member reported on anything. Clause 2 is written for the member who is somebody's employee, which is exactly what he is.

options.text: Clause 4 of Part II of the Second Schedule, for defalcating money received in his professional capacity
options.misconception: reaches for the wrong clause of the right Part
options.why: Clause 4 covers a member who defalcates or embezzles money received in his professional capacity. No money moved here; what left the company was information, and clause 2 of the same Part addresses that by name.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, clause 2

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant employed as a group financial controller, holding no certificate of practice, gives a friend at a rival company a copy of his employer's customer pricing file. He says two things in his defence. He certified nothing and expressed no opinion, so no clause of the Schedules reaches him. And the file carried no confidentiality marking, so his employer's permission was not needed.

items.stem: How many of the four offend the principle of confidentiality?

options.text: All four, but only the partner and the manager can be answerable, an articled assistant not being a member of the Institute
options.misconception: locates the duty in the assistant alone when the accountant who controls him carries it
options.why: Whether the assistant is a member is not the question the principle asks. It puts the burden on the accountant above him, who must do what is reasonable to see that the people working under his direction respect the same duty — so a firm that never told the assistant a word about confidentiality has failed that requirement in its own right.

options.text: Two — a prospective client is owed nothing until the engagement is accepted, and a family conversation is private
options.misconception: makes the duty start with the engagement letter and stop at the front door
options.why: Both limbs are written out expressly. Information disclosed by a prospective client is covered, which is why a firm that declines an engagement may not trade on what it learned while considering it; and the accountant must be alert to inadvertent disclosure in a social environment and particularly to an immediate or close family member.

options.text: Three — the file passed inside the firm is not a breach, the duty running to outsiders
options.misconception: reads confidentiality as a wall around the firm rather than around the information
options.why: The principle names confidentiality within the firm or employing organisation as its own requirement. A client hands information to the accountant for a purpose, and a colleague with no part in that purpose is as much a stranger to it as anybody outside the door.

options.text: All four
options.why: Section 114 breaks the duty into sub-paragraphs, and each of the four episodes lands on one of them. A remark to a brother over dinner is the very slip the Code has in mind when it warns about inadvertent disclosure — words let go socially, and above all in front of somebody close in business or in the family. Handing a file to a colleague with no part in the work offends the separate requirement to keep a client's information confidential within the firm or the employing organisation. Discussing a prospective client's projections after the work has been declined is caught as well, because the duty attaches from the moment the figures arrive and does not wait for an engagement letter. And the untaught articled assistant is the firm's own failure: personnel under the accountant's control, along with anybody brought in to advise or help, have to be held to the same silence. Nothing rescues any of the four — no law compelled the words, no client authorised them, and no professional duty or right called for them.

citation.ref: Section 114 — Confidentiality, sub-paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (g)

items.scenario: Four things happen in one firm in a month. A partner describes a client's forthcoming results at a family dinner to his brother, who has no connection with the client. A manager forwards a client's file to a colleague in another service line who has no need of it. A prospective client's projections are discussed with an outsider after the firm decides not to accept the engagement. And an articled assistant, who has been told nothing about confidentiality, mentions a client's name at a college reunion.

items.stem: Which of them may use the relief?

options.text: The first and the third, and the second for its transactions with the department alone
options.misconception: splits the relief transaction by transaction, when it attaches to the status of the reporting entity
options.why: The relief is available to a reporting entity that is itself government-related, and it then covers that entity's dealings with the government and with other entities under the same government. An entity that is not government-related has nothing to be relieved of, since a customer relationship generated no disclosure in the first place.

options.text: The first and the third only
options.why: Ask who stands behind the reporting company. Where a government controls it, shares control of it, or merely carries significant influence over it, the company answers to the description of a government-related entity and the relief is open to it. The first is significantly influenced by a state, the third is owned outright by a municipal corporation, so both are in. The second is not: a department buying the whole output year after year on tender is a customer, and however dependent the seller becomes on that trade, dependence by itself makes nobody a related party. With no related party relationship in the first place there is nothing for the relief to relieve.

options.text: All three, any entity whose fortunes depend on a government being government-related
options.misconception: reads economic dependence as the test, when the definition names control, joint control and significant influence
options.why: Dependence is a commercial fact rather than a relationship the standard recognises. Ind AS 24 says the opposite in terms: an arm of a government that neither controls the reporting entity, nor shares control of it, nor holds significant influence over it stays outside the related party circle, however much ordinary business the two of them do together.

options.text: The third only, the relief being written for entities a government controls
options.misconception: drops joint control and significant influence out of a definition that names all three
options.why: The definition lists control, joint control and significant influence together, and the relief follows the definition. A government holding significant influence over a listed company can still produce the very problem the relief was written for — dealings with a long list of other entities under the same government.

citation.ref: para 9 definition of a government-related entity, and para 11(d) and (e), read with para 25

items.scenario: Three companies want to use the relief Ind AS 24 offers to government-related entities. The first is a listed company in which a state government holds 26 per cent and has the right to appoint two of its nine directors; the government is treated as having significant influence over it. The second sells the whole of its output to a central government department under an annual tender and has no government shareholding of any kind. The third is wholly owned by a municipal corporation.

items.stem: Do the Ind AS 103 business combination principles apply on the formation of this joint operation?

options.text: Yes, and the same answer would follow even if A Ltd, B Ltd and C Ltd were companies under the common control of one group
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out that sends a common control transaction to Appendix C of Ind AS 103 instead
options.why: The first half is right and the second half is not. Where the transaction is a common control transaction as defined in Ind AS 103, the entity does not apply these requirements at all — it applies the accounting specified in Appendix C of Ind AS 103 instead. These three companies are unrelated, so the carve-out is not reached, but the answer would change if they were not.

options.text: No — the requirements apply only where every party to the joint operation contributes a business, and here two of the three contribute assets
options.misconception: turns "one of the parties" into "all of the parties" and reads the exclusion backwards
options.why: The exclusion runs the other way round. It bites only where not one contributor brings a business — where everything put in is assets, or bundles of assets, and none of it amounts to a business. Demanding a business from every party would leave the exclusion with nothing to exclude, since a single business going in is already what makes the setting-up an acquisition of a business.

options.text: No — the Ind AS 103 principles reach a joint operation only when an entity buys an interest in one that already exists, and a formation is by definition not an acquisition
options.misconception: reads the provision as covering purchases alone and misses the sentence that extends it to a formation
options.why: The extension to a formation is written into the Standard in terms, and it is not an afterthought — it is the reason a party cannot escape business combination accounting by arranging for the business to be dropped into a new vehicle instead of sold into an old one. What is true is that a formation has no previously held interest to worry about, so the question of remeasuring one does not arise here at all.

options.text: Yes — Ind AS 103's principles bite here because A Ltd handed over a going terminal business as its stake when the arrangement was set up, and only one contributor needs to have done that
options.why: Two questions decide this and the second is the one in dispute. Ind AS 103's accounting reaches an interest in a joint operation whose own activity is a business; it reaches the formation of a joint operation as well, but only where somebody hands over an existing business — a business in the Ind AS 103 sense — as their stake when the arrangement is set up. One contributor doing so is enough. A Ltd's terminal, with its berths, cranes, staff and contracts, is exactly that. Read the negative limb and the same point falls out: nothing carries across where every contributor puts in bare assets, or groups of assets, that fall short of a business. Land from B Ltd and cash from C Ltd are bare assets; A Ltd's terminal is not, so one of the parties has opened the gate for all three.

citation.ref: para 21A read with Appendix B paras B33A and B33D, and the common control carve-out to Appendix C of Ind AS 103

items.scenario: Three unrelated companies form a joint operation on 1 April 2026 to run a port terminal, each taking a one-third interest and the three sharing joint control. On formation, A Ltd transfers into the arrangement an existing terminal it has been operating for years, with its berths, cranes, staff, customer contracts and operating processes, which everybody agrees is a business as defined in Ind AS 103. B Ltd contributes a plot of adjoining land and nothing else. C Ltd contributes cash. The activity of the joint operation itself constitutes a business. The finance teams disagree about whether the Ind AS 103 principles come into play at all on a formation, as opposed to on a later purchase of an additional interest.

items.stem: Which of the three balances is, in substance, part of the net investment in S Ltd?

options.text: All three, since every one of them is a monetary balance with a foreign operation that has in practice stayed outstanding
options.misconception: treats a balance that happens to persist as a balance nobody plans to settle
options.why: Persisting is not the test, and the Standard excludes trade receivables and trade payables by name so that a rolling trading balance cannot be dressed up as permanent funding. Each year's invoices here ARE expected to be paid in the ordinary course; what stays constant is the level of trading, not the debt.

options.text: Only the third — the trade receivable is excluded whatever its age, the twelve-year loan does not qualify merely for being long, and the loan routed through T Ltd qualifies whatever currency it is denominated in
options.why: A balance owed either way between the group and a foreign operation counts towards the net investment on one condition. Nobody intends to settle it, and no settlement looks likely within any period one can see ahead. Long-dated loans and receivables can meet that condition; two categories never do, and the Standard names them in its own words, trade receivables or trade payables. Age is not the test, so the six-year-old trading balance stays outside however long it has sat there. Nor does a distant due date carry a loan in by itself. A twelve-year maturity is still a date, and only a documented intention to renew, pushing repayment out beyond sight, would take it out of the ordinary. That has to rest on auditable evidence, minuted at board level for instance, and P Ltd's board minuted nothing either way. T Ltd's advance is the one that qualifies. Seen from the group, the money funds a stake in an operation abroad, and it does so irrespective of the currency the lending happens to be written in.

options.text: The second and the third, a twelve-year maturity being long enough that repayment is not in the foreseeable future
options.misconception: reads duration as a substitute for the absence of a planned settlement
options.why: A fixed maturity is itself a plan. Where the board has said nothing about rolling the loan over, the due date on the paper is the settlement date, and a date on the paper is a settlement both planned and foreseeable, however distant it is. Ten to fifteen years is the very span the study material picks to make that point. Renewal must be shown, never assumed.

options.text: Only a loan made by the parent itself can be part of the parent's net investment, so none of the three qualifies
options.misconception: requires the lender to be the reporting entity, when the consolidated statements look at the group's position
options.why: The funding here was arranged by P Ltd and provided by T Ltd on its direction, and in the consolidated financial statements the exchange difference on it goes to other comprehensive income. Seen from the group, what T Ltd advanced is money put behind an operation abroad. Which group company wrote the cheque does not change what the money is.

citation.ref: para 15 and 15A, with the study material's worked examples on a rolling trading balance and on funding routed through a fellow subsidiary

items.scenario: An Indian parent P Ltd is preparing consolidated financial statements and has three balances with its foreign subsidiary S Ltd. The first is a trade receivable for inventory P Ltd sells to S Ltd; the balance has stood on the books at every year end for six years running, though each year's invoices are expected to be paid in the ordinary course. The second is a loan from P Ltd to S Ltd with a fixed maturity twelve years away, on which the board has minuted no intention one way or the other about renewal. The third is a loan to S Ltd made, on P Ltd's direction, by T Ltd, another subsidiary of P Ltd, which nobody expects to be repaid and which is denominated in T Ltd's own functional currency, a third currency.

items.stem: How should the restated figures be translated into rupees?

options.text: Every amount — assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses — converted at one single rate, being the closing rate on the most recent balance sheet date, with the comparative column left at the figures the prior year already reported as its own current-year amounts
options.why: A subsidiary reporting in a hyperinflationary currency gets one rate, not two. Assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses, and the prior year's column with them, so that the list runs to everything including comparatives, all go over at a single rate — closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet. An average rate would be wrong here rather than merely rough, because Ind AS 29 has already pulled every figure on to one measuring unit and a second rate on income and expenses would pull them apart again. One carve-out follows. Translate into a currency that is not itself inflating away, a non-hyperinflationary economy, which the rupee is, and the comparative figures stay as the prior year reported them. Neither subsequent changes in the price level nor a movement in rates since then reopens last year's column.
keywords: closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet
subsequent changes in the price level

options.text: All amounts including the comparatives at the closing rate at 31 March 2026, so that both columns are stated in the same rupees
options.misconception: applies the general rule and misses the carve-out for a non-hyperinflationary presentation currency
options.why: This is the rule as it stands for translation into the currency of another hyperinflationary economy, and the words "except that" immediately following it are what this answer drops. Where the presentation currency is not itself hyperinflationary, last year's column holds whatever that year's own statements showed as their current-year figures. Restating them again would move a figure the reader has already seen reported, for a price-level change that has nothing to do with the rupee.

options.text: Assets and liabilities at the closing rate, income and expenses at the average rate for the year, with the comparatives re-translated at this year's closing rate
options.misconception: applies the ordinary translation method to a hyperinflationary operation and then restates the comparatives it should have left alone
options.why: Both halves fail. The ordinary method, closing rate for assets and liabilities and transaction or average rates for income and expenses, is displaced once the functional currency is a hyperinflationary one, and every single amount then moves at the balance sheet date's closing rate instead. The second half fails too, since comparatives going into a currency that is not hyperinflationary are never re-translated for a later movement in exchange rates.

options.text: Translate the subsidiary's unrestated local currency figures at the closing rate, since translation at a single current rate already deals with the inflation
options.misconception: treats a closing-rate translation as a substitute for the Ind AS 29 restatement
options.why: Restatement comes first and translation second. An entity whose functional currency is hyperinflationary must put its accounts through Ind AS 29 before it translates anything, and the single exception to that order is the comparative column heading into a currency that is not hyperinflationary. One exchange rate cannot do the restatement's work, because it says nothing about which balances were monetary and gives no gain or loss on the net monetary position.

citation.ref: paras 42 and 43, on carrying a hyperinflationary operation's restated figures into a different presentation currency, read with Ind AS 29

items.scenario: An Indian parent reports in rupees, which is not the currency of a hyperinflationary economy. Its subsidiary's functional currency is that of a hyperinflationary economy, and the subsidiary's own financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 have already been restated under Ind AS 29 into the measuring unit current at that date. The group accountant now has to bring the subsidiary into the consolidated statements, which show the year ended 31 March 2026 and the comparative year ended 31 March 2025. She proposes to translate assets and liabilities at the closing rate, income and expenses at average rates for the year, and to re-translate last year's comparative column at this year's closing rate so that the two columns are on one footing.

items.stem: Is the company right that there is no transfer to test?

options.text: No — an entity that retains the rights but assumes an obligation to pay the cash flows to eventual recipients has made a transfer if all four conditions are met, and only then does the risks-and-rewards test begin
options.why: Two roads lead to a transfer and this is the second of them. Where the entity keeps the contractual right to collect but takes on a matching obligation to hand what it collects to one or more eventual recipients, that pass-through arrangement counts as a transfer, provided four things are all true of it. First, money is owed onward only once money has come in, so nothing is payable to the investors until the company has taken equivalent amounts off the borrowers. Second, the pool itself is locked, the contract stopping the company from selling it or pledging it anywhere except as security to the eventual recipients. Third, whatever is collected must be handed over without material delay. Fourth, in the gap before it is handed over the cash may sit only in cash or near-cash, for the short settlement period alone, and the interest it earns follows the principal. All four hold on these facts. The risks-and-rewards question comes after this gate, never instead of it.

options.text: No, and since the four conditions are met the whole pool is derecognised, the conditions being the test for derecognition
options.misconception: stops at the pass-through gate and never runs the risks-and-rewards test behind it
options.why: Meeting the four conditions establishes that there is a transfer; it does not decide the outcome. The proportion sold is derecognised only if the entity has then also transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership of that proportion. And even where it has, the 10 per cent the company kept for itself is not part of the transfer and stays on its balance sheet.

options.text: Yes — derecognition is available only where the contractual rights to the cash flows are legally assigned to the buyer or expire
options.misconception: reads the first derecognition test as the only one and misses the pass-through route
options.why: There are two ways in. The rights to receive the cash flows may be transferred, which is what a sale of a debenture or an assignment of a receivable does. Or the rights may be retained while an obligation to pay them over to eventual recipients is assumed, which is the shape most Indian securitisations take, and the Standard treats that as a transfer once the four conditions are satisfied.

options.text: Yes, because a short-term advance the company might make to smooth a month's collections would break the first condition in any event
options.misconception: treats a recoverable short-term advance as an obligation to pay irrespective of collection
options.why: That condition survives an advance the company can get back. Lend into a thin month, keep the right to recover every rupee of it together with interest at a market rate, and the first condition is untouched. What breaks it is recourse of another kind, a guarantee or an option letting the transferee push the receivables back, and this company has given none of that.

citation.ref: para 3.2.4(b) and 3.2.5, the four pass-through conditions, read before the risks-and-rewards evaluation in para 3.2.6

items.scenario: A non-banking finance company keeps the contractual right to collect instalments on a pool of vehicle loans, but has settled a trust and agreed to pass 90 per cent of everything it collects to the investors in that trust. The agreement says the company owes the investors nothing unless and until it collects the equivalent amount from the borrowers, and it gives no guarantee about how the pool performs. The company is barred by the contract from selling or pledging the loans other than as security to the investors. It must remit what it collects without material delay, and it may not reinvest the collections except in cash equivalents during the short settlement period, with any interest earned on that passed on to the investors. The company argues that because it still holds the contractual right to receive the loan cash flows, no transfer has occurred and nothing can be derecognised.

items.stem: Which of the four designations does Ind AS 109 permit?

options.text: All four, since inception documentation is in place and every one of the four instruments has a genuine economic relationship with what it is meant to hedge
options.misconception: treats documentation and an economic relationship as the whole of the qualifying criteria
options.why: Documentation at inception and an economic relationship are two of the criteria, not all of them. The one this answer skips comes first. Everything inside the relationship has to be eligible to begin with, both the instrument side and the item side. Eligibility is exactly where a written option, an internal contract and a part-period designation each fail, before the other criteria are ever reached.

options.text: The first and the third, a written option being a derivative measured at fair value through profit or loss like any other
options.misconception: treats the written option as eligible because it meets the measurement description
options.why: The measurement description is followed immediately by the exception. A written option is carved out because the writer's upside is capped at the premium while the downside is not, so it cannot offset a hedged item's risk in the way hedge accounting assumes. A purchased option is a different instrument and is eligible.

options.text: The second and the third, an intragroup contract being a real contract that fixes a real price for the division that entered it
options.misconception: forgets that hedge accounting is applied to the reporting entity being reported on
options.why: Only contracts with a party external to the reporting entity — external to the group or the individual entity being reported on — can be designated as hedging instruments. The internal forward may well be designated in the manufacturing division's own individual financial statements, but in the consolidated statements it nets to nothing, and there is no exposure left for it to hedge.

options.text: Only the third — a written option cannot be a hedging instrument, an internal contract cannot be one in the consolidated statements, and an instrument may not be designated for part of the period it is outstanding
options.why: Take the four proposals in turn. A derivative carried at fair value through profit or loss is eligible as a hedging instrument, with one class carved out, the written option. Combine a written option with a purchased one and the carve-out still bites where the combination is, on the day of designation, a net written position. Next, hedge accounting looks outward. The counterparty has to be external to the reporting entity, meaning outside the group whose statements these are, so a forward struck between treasury and manufacturing nets to nothing on consolidation and cannot be designated. Third, an eligible instrument has to be designated in its entirety, and only three departures from that are allowed — splitting an option's intrinsic value from its time value and taking the intrinsic change alone, splitting a forward's spot element from its forward element and taking the spot alone, and taking a stated proportion of the whole instrument, 50 per cent of the nominal amount for instance. Slicing off a portion of the time period an instrument is alive for is not on that list, which is why the two-years-of-five swap designation fails.

citation.ref: para 6.4.1(a) with the qualifying instruments and designation rules in paras 6.2.1 to 6.2.6

items.scenario: A company's treasury proposes four designations for the coming year. It wants to designate a written call option on its own commodity purchases as the hedging instrument for those purchases. It wants to designate an internal forward contract between its treasury division and its manufacturing division as the hedging instrument in the consolidated financial statements. It wants to designate only the change in the intrinsic value of a purchased option and to leave the time value out. And it wants to designate a five-year interest rate swap as a hedging instrument for the first two years of its life only. All the documentation is in place at inception in every case.

items.stem: What goes into the opening Ind AS balance sheet at 1 April 20X5?

options.text: The receivables stay off, but every derivative is brought on at fair value and the deferred loss shown as an asset is eliminated
options.why: The exception is written for items that are NOT derivatives, and the word non-derivative is load-bearing. An adopter that took financial assets or liabilities of that kind off its books under its old GAAP, for a transaction that happened before the transition date, leaves them off; the factored receivables therefore stay off. Not a word of that reaches a derivative. The opening balance sheet does something else with those. At the transition date an entity measures all derivatives at fair value, and it sweeps away the deferred losses and gains that the old GAAP had allowed to sit on the balance sheet as though they were assets or liabilities in their own right. So the swaps come on at fair value and the deferred loss asset goes.
keywords: measures all derivatives at fair value

options.text: Both come on — the receivables at their carrying amount and the swaps at fair value — because the opening balance sheet must show everything Ind AS 109 would have shown
options.misconception: applies full retrospection where a mandatory exception forbids it for one of the two
options.why: Retrospective application is the general principle and the mandatory exceptions are where it is switched off. Derecognition is one of them, so the receivables stay off even though Ind AS 109's criteria might not have been met on the 20X3 factoring. The swaps are a different matter, and they come on.

options.text: Both stay off, since the derecognition exception applies prospectively to every financial asset and liability derecognised before the date of transition
options.misconception: drops the word "non-derivative" out of the exception and stretches it over derivatives
options.why: The exception is expressly limited to non-derivative financial assets and non-derivative financial liabilities, and the limitation is doing real work. A derivative that previous GAAP left off the balance sheet was never derecognised in a transaction; it was simply never recognised, and the opening Ind AS balance sheet recognises all assets and liabilities that Ind AS requires.

options.text: The receivables stay off and the swaps come on at fair value, but the deferred loss is carried forward and written off over the swaps' remaining life as previous GAAP intended
options.misconception: recognises the derivative but leaves the previous GAAP deferral standing beside it
options.why: The requirement has two limbs and this answer takes only the first. Bringing every derivative on at fair value is one half; wiping out the deferral the old GAAP had parked on the balance sheet, as though a loss still to be written off were an asset, is the other. Keep the deferred loss and the same loss is counted twice, once inside the swaps' fair value and once again as an asset waiting to be amortised.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — mandatory exceptions, derecognition of financial assets and financial liabilities, read with the hedge accounting exception on derivatives at the date of transition

items.scenario: A company's date of transition to Ind AS is 1 April 20X5. Two things sat off its previous GAAP balance sheet. The first is a portfolio of receivables factored to a bank in 20X3 and derecognised then under previous GAAP. The second is a set of currency swaps entered into in 20X4 and carried nowhere on the balance sheet under previous GAAP, with the losses on them deferred and shown as an asset, to be written off over the swaps' remaining life. The controller says that whatever the mandatory exception does for the receivables it must do for the swaps too, since both were kept off the balance sheet before transition.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 106 allow after initial recognition?

options.text: Only the cost model is available, exploration and evaluation assets being measured at cost
options.misconception: reads the initial measurement rule as though it governed subsequent measurement too
options.why: Cost is the measurement on recognition and it is not the end of the matter. After recognition the entity may keep the cost model or move to a revaluation model, which is a real choice and one of the few places the Standard leaves an accounting policy open.

options.text: Both models are available, and the classification may be revisited each year according to what the asset was mainly used for in that year
options.misconception: treats a classification fixed by the nature of the asset as a use-based label reviewed annually
options.why: The classification follows the nature of the assets acquired and is applied consistently, which is what stops an entity moving assets between bases to suit the year's result. Using a tangible asset to develop an intangible asset does not change the tangible asset into an intangible one, however much of its life goes into that work.

options.text: It may keep the cost model or apply a revaluation model, and the revaluation model it applies must be the one consistent with its classification of those assets as tangible or intangible — but the classification itself follows the nature of the assets acquired and is applied consistently, so the rigs cannot become intangible
options.why: After recognition an entity applies either the cost model or a revaluation model to exploration and evaluation assets, and if the revaluation model is applied it must be consistent with the classification of the assets. That classification is a separate decision made first — the entity classifies exploration and evaluation assets as tangible or intangible according to the nature of the assets acquired and applies the classification consistently. Rigs and vehicles are tangible by nature and stay tangible; using a tangible asset in work that produces an intangible one does not turn it into an intangible asset. So revaluing the rigs on the Ind AS 16 model while holding the licences and studies at cost is open to the company; reclassifying the rigs is not.

options.text: Both models are available, and the company may pick whichever revaluation model it prefers for each asset regardless of how the asset is classified
options.misconception: unhooks the choice of revaluation model from the tangible or intangible classification
options.why: The revaluation model applied has to be consistent with the classification of the assets, so a tangible exploration and evaluation asset is revalued on the Ind AS 16 model and an intangible one on the Ind AS 38 model, with the conditions each of those carries. Picking freely between the two would let an entity take the Ind AS 16 model for an intangible asset that has no active market and could not be revalued at all.

citation.ref: para 12 on measurement after recognition and para 15 on classifying exploration and evaluation assets as tangible or intangible

items.scenario: A mining company has recognised two kinds of exploration and evaluation asset. Drilling rigs and vehicles bought for a survey campaign are physical items it expects to use across several blocks. Licences to explore particular blocks, and the geological survey studies bought in for them, have no physical substance. The company has been carrying every exploration and evaluation asset at cost, and now wants to revalue upwards the rigs and vehicles, whose market prices have risen, while continuing to carry the licences and studies at cost. It also proposes to reclassify the rigs as intangible assets in years when they are used mainly to develop the survey studies.

items.stem: Is anything further required?

options.text: No — an asset carried at ₹86 lakh after a repayment cannot be impaired, since ₹86 lakh is what it would have stood at had the grant never been given
options.misconception: confuses restoring the pre-grant carrying amount with establishing that the amount is recoverable
options.why: What the asset would have cost is not what the asset is now worth. The repayment mechanics are designed to put the carrying amount back where it would have been without the grant, and that is a computation about history. Whether ₹86 lakh can still be recovered from using or selling the plant is a question about the future, and here the answer is no.

options.text: No — the repayment has been accounted for as a change in accounting estimate and an estimate change is applied prospectively, so nothing else follows from it
options.misconception: treats the change in estimate label as closing off every other requirement
options.why: Accounting for the repayment as a change in accounting estimate settles how the repayment itself is recorded and says nothing about whether the resulting asset is recoverable. The Standard adds the impairment consideration precisely because the two questions are separate, and Ind AS 36 applies to the plant whether or not a grant was ever repaid.

options.text: Yes — the ₹34 lakh shortfall is added to the repayment charge and presented as part of the government grant repaid in profit or loss
options.misconception: merges an impairment loss into the grant repayment rather than recognising it under Ind AS 36
options.why: The two are different charges arising under different standards and are not run together. Ind AS 20 governs the repayment and the immediate cumulative additional depreciation; Ind AS 36 governs the write-down to recoverable amount, with its own measurement, its own disclosure and its own possibility of reversal in a later period if the recoverable amount recovers.

options.text: Yes — the possible impairment of the new carrying amount must be considered, and on these facts the plant is written down from ₹86 lakh to ₹52 lakh
options.why: Ind AS 20 says in terms that in circumstances giving rise to repayment of a grant related to an asset it may be necessary to give consideration to the possible impairment of the new carrying amount of the asset. The reason is plain once the mechanics are done — the repayment puts ₹40 lakh back on to an asset without asking whether the asset is worth it, and the very event that triggered the repayment is often a sign that it is not. Here the recoverable amount of ₹52 lakh is below the new carrying amount of ₹86 lakh, so an impairment loss of ₹34 lakh is recognised under Ind AS 36 on top of the repayment accounting.

citation.ref: para 32 with para 33, the possible impairment of the new carrying amount of the asset

items.scenario: A company received a government grant of ₹40 lakh towards a plant and presented it by deducting it from the plant's carrying amount. Four years later the company breaches a condition and the whole grant becomes repayable. It has correctly accounted for the repayment by increasing the plant's carrying amount by the ₹40 lakh and charging the cumulative additional depreciation to profit or loss immediately, which leaves the plant at ₹86 lakh. Since the grant was given the market for the plant's output has collapsed and the plant's recoverable amount is now ₹52 lakh. The finance manager says the repayment has been dealt with and nothing further arises.

items.stem: What must the notes disclose about government grants relating to agricultural activity?

options.text: The nature and extent of the grants recognised, the unfulfilled conditions and other contingencies attaching to grants, and the significant decreases expected in the level of government grants
options.why: Ind AS 41 asks for three things here and the preparer's proposal covers less than one of them. The first goes past the figure to what was granted and how far it reached, the nature and extent of what has been recognised. The second reaches the grant nothing has been recognised on. Conditions not yet met, and any other contingency hanging off a grant, must be described, so the five-year farming undertaking belongs in the notes with two of its years still to run; those are the unfulfilled conditions. The third looks forward rather than back. Where the level of grants is expected to fall away sharply, that expectation is itself a required disclosure, so the state's announcement about scaling the scheme back goes into this year's notes, significant decreases in prospect being news the reader is entitled to.

options.text: The amount recognised, plus a reconciliation of the opening and closing balance of grants receivable and deferred
options.misconception: imports a movement reconciliation the Standard does not ask for and drops the two it does
options.why: The reconciliation Ind AS 41 does ask for tracks biological assets and not grants, namely how the standing crop's carrying amount moved from its opening figure to its closing one. Putting a grants-balance table in place of the three named grant disclosures would still leave the conditions not yet met, and the fall in grants ahead, unsaid.

options.text: Only the amount recognised in profit or loss, the other two matters being events of later years
options.misconception: limits the note to amounts already recognised and misses the two disclosures aimed at what has not been recognised
options.why: Two of the three required disclosures are about things that have NOT gone through profit or loss — the conditions still unfulfilled on a grant held back, and the decreases expected in the level of grants to come. A reader who is told only what was recognised cannot see that a recognised income stream is about to fall away.

options.text: The amount recognised and the unfulfilled conditions, but not the expected decrease, which is a forecast and belongs in the management discussion
options.misconception: treats a forward-looking disclosure the Standard requires as narrative outside the financial statements
options.why: Significant decreases expected in the level of government grants is one of the three disclosures Ind AS 41 requires for grants relating to agricultural activity. A requirement in the Standard is not satisfied by putting the information somewhere adjacent to the financial statements, however sensible it may also be to discuss it there.

citation.ref: para 57, disclosure for government grants relating to agricultural activity

items.scenario: A plantation company is drafting the notes to its financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. During the year it recognised a government grant on its standing crop, a biological asset measured at fair value less costs to sell. It holds a second grant on the same crop which requires it to keep farming the same land for five years, of which two have passed, so nothing has been recognised on it yet. And the state has announced that the scheme under which both grants were made will be scaled back sharply from the next financial year. The preparer proposes to disclose the amount recognised in profit or loss and nothing else, on the ground that the other two matters are not amounts in this year's statements.

items.stem: Which of the three must apply Ind AS for the year ended 31 March 2027?

options.text: Only P, a voluntary adopter being free to revert and an SME-listed company being outside
options.misconception: treats a voluntary adoption as reversible because it was never compelled
options.why: The clause covers a company that starts following Ind AS "either voluntarily or mandatorily", and it is drafted that way deliberately — an entity that has already restated its comparatives and told the market it reports on Ind AS cannot hand that back without making its own history incomparable. Q is in for good.

options.text: All three, R's net worth of ₹700 crore putting it above the Phase I threshold
options.misconception: applies the net worth test to a company the roadmap never reaches
options.why: The thresholds only matter to a company the roadmap applies to. A company listed solely on an SME exchange is excluded by the Rules themselves, and the exclusion is drawn by where the shares are listed rather than by how large the company is. R may adopt voluntarily, and would then be caught by the same one-way rule as Q.

options.text: P and Q, but not R
options.why: Entry into Ind AS is a one-way door, and the Rules say so in a single clause. A company that has begun reporting on Ind AS, whether it did so voluntarily or mandatorily under the criteria, keeps doing so in every set of subsequent financial statements it prepares, and keeps doing so even after those criteria stop describing it. P is that case. Its net worth has fallen, which changes nothing, because once the threshold has been crossed a later fall below it releases nobody. Q is the same clause read on its other limb, so a voluntary adopter cannot go back either. R never enters at all. The roadmap is switched off for a company whose shares sit, or are being put, on an SME exchange alone, and ₹700 crore of net worth does not switch it back on.

options.text: Only Q and R, P having fallen out of the criteria and being free to revert to the earlier standards
options.misconception: reads the roadmap criteria as a test applied afresh every year in both directions
options.why: A company that does NOT meet the criteria on the cut-off date reassesses at each balance sheet date, so the criteria are tested again on the way in. There is no way out.
