If the net worth threshold criteria are once met, the company complies with Ind AS irrespective of the fact that at a later date its net worth falls below the criteria specified.

citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — clause 9 of the notification on continuing with Ind AS, and the exclusion of companies listed only on an SME exchange

items.scenario: Three companies ask the same question in 2026. Company P crossed the net worth threshold on the cut-off date, has prepared Ind AS financial statements since 2016, and its net worth has now fallen well below the threshold after several loss-making years. Company Q is unlisted, has never met any threshold, and adopted Ind AS voluntarily in 2022 because its overseas lenders wanted it; it would now like to go back to the earlier standards to save cost. Company R's shares are listed only on an SME exchange and its net worth is ₹700 crore.

items.stem: What are the steps before an exposure draft of an Ind AS is issued for public comment?

options.text: The ASB prepares a preliminary draft already carrying the carve-ins and carve-outs it thinks necessary, circulates it to the Council members of the ICAI and to specified outside bodies such as the MCA, SEBI, the C&AG and the CBDT, and meets their representatives to hear their views — and only then is the exposure draft finalised and issued
options.why: The consultation with the regulators comes before the public one, not after. The ASB considers a preliminary draft prepared with the requisite carve-in and carve-out and revises it as needed, giving weight to the local regulatory landscape, business practices, tax and other relevant provisions. That draft is circulated to the Council members of the ICAI and to specified outside bodies such as the MCA, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and the Central Board of Direct Taxes. The ASB then meets the representatives of those specified outside bodies to ascertain their views. The exposure draft is finalised and issued for public comment after that.

options.text: The NFRA reviews the preliminary draft and provides its inputs before the exposure draft is issued for public comment
options.misconception: moves the NFRA's review to the front of the process, where the ICAI's own consultation sits
options.why: The NFRA comes in at the far end. The final draft Ind AS is submitted to the NFRA with the ICAI's recommendations for notification, and the NFRA reviews and provides its inputs before the MCA notifies. Nothing goes to the NFRA before the exposure draft has been issued and its comments considered.

options.text: The ASB issues the exposure draft first so that the regulators comment on it alongside the public, and the carve-outs are settled from the comments received
options.misconception: puts the regulator consultation inside the public comment process instead of ahead of it
options.why: The regulators are consulted on a preliminary draft that already carries the proposed carve-ins and carve-outs, and the ASB meets their representatives specifically to ascertain their views before anything goes out publicly. Treating them as ordinary commentators would leave the departures from the IFRS to be settled in public, which is not how the sequence runs.

options.text: The ASB converges the IFRS without change and any Indian departure is inserted by the MCA at the notification stage
options.misconception: moves the carve-ins and carve-outs from the drafting stage to the notification stage
options.why: The carve-ins and carve-outs are made at the start, by the ASB, when it prepares the preliminary draft, giving consideration to the local regulatory landscape, business practices, tax and other relevant provisions. The MCA's act at the end is notification in the Gazette, not redrafting.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — process of development and finalisation of Indian Accounting Standards, the steps up to issuance of the exposure draft

items.scenario: The IASB has issued a new IFRS and the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI has begun work on the corresponding Ind AS. A trainee asks what happens between the IASB issuing the IFRS and the exposure draft appearing for public comment, and whether the differences from the IFRS are argued out with the regulators after the public sees the draft or before.

items.stem: How does Schedule III deal with the three points?

options.text: The terms used in Schedule III have their own statutory meaning, which prevails over the meaning in the notified standards where the two differ
options.misconception: gives the Schedule's vocabulary a life independent of the standards
options.why: Where the Schedule uses a word, the notified Standards supply its meaning, and nothing in the Schedule sets up a rival definition. That is what keeps a line on the face of the balance sheet and the note behind it talking about one and the same thing, and it fits the overriding status the Schedule gives those Standards.

options.text: Its disclosure requirements sit on top of those in the notified standards rather than replacing them, its vocabulary borrows the standards' meanings, and every disclosure it calls for now belongs in the notes
options.why: Schedule III answers all three itself. On the first, what its Part I and its Part II or Part III require is stated to run alongside what the notified Standards ask for, in addition to and not in substitution, so an Ind AS 107 disclosure does not vanish merely because the Schedule says nothing about it. On the second, the terms used in Schedule III take their meaning from those same Standards, which leaves the preparer no room to widen "borrowings" on his own authority. On the third, the amended Schedule puts every disclosure it requires in one place. They are given as a part of the notes, and that settles where the bracketed additions belong.
keywords: in addition to and not in substitution
as a part of the notes

options.text: Disclosures may be made either on the face of the financial statements or in the notes, at the company's choice, so long as they are made somewhere
options.misconception: treats the location of a disclosure as a free choice after the amendments
options.why: Under the amended Schedule every disclosure it calls for goes into the notes. What is still a matter of choice is a different thing altogether. A line item, a sub-line item or a sub-total may be added on the FACE, or shown there instead, where doing so helps a reader see where the company stands or how it performed, or where the industry calls for it.

options.text: Schedule III is the complete list of what must be disclosed, so a requirement it does not carry need not be met
options.misconception: reads a presentation schedule as an exhaustive disclosure list
options.why: Schedule III grants overriding status to the Standards and says its own disclosure requirements are in addition to and not in substitution of theirs. Treating it as the complete list would put a company in breach of the standards while it believed itself compliant with the Act.

citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — Schedule III, the disclosure requirements being in addition to and not in substitution of the notified standards

items.scenario: A company's draft financial statements are being reviewed. The preparer has left out three disclosures that Ind AS 107 requires about financial instruments, saying Schedule III does not ask for them and Schedule III is what governs the format. He has used the word "borrowings" in the balance sheet with a meaning of his own, wider than the one the notified standards give it. And he has put several disclosures on the face of the balance sheet as bracketed additions rather than in the notes, saying it makes no difference where they appear.

items.stem: What further work does the materiality judgement have to do?

options.text: Only the first point stands — an accounting policy affecting small balances is by definition immaterial and is removed
options.misconception: settles policy materiality on the size of the affected balances alone
options.why: Size is one factor and not the whole of it. In judging whether an accounting policy is material, the balances and transactions the policy bears on count, and so do other things, among them what kind of business the company actually runs. A policy about measuring deferred tax on indefinite-life brands can be the very thing a reader needs to make sense of the numbers, whatever this year's balances happen to be.

options.text: None — materiality is a filter on which items appear, and once an item is in, the standards decide everything that is said about it
options.misconception: treats materiality as a one-off gate at the line item level
options.why: The assessment runs at both levels. After the line items are settled, the same judgement decides what to say about them, how much detail to provide and how best to organise it — and that second stage is where a set of financial statements either communicates or becomes the overloaded document the lack of clarity about materiality is blamed for producing.

options.text: Only the second point stands — a policy is judged on its own materiality, but there is no judgement left about how much to say once a line item is in
options.misconception: accepts the policy judgement while denying the same judgement at the line item level
options.why: The two are one idea used twice. Deciding what a material line item's disclosure should say, the depth of it and the arrangement that makes it readable, is named as the step that follows the choice of line items, and it is not optional.

options.text: It decides what to disclose about each material line item, how much detail to give and how best to organise it — and whether a policy is material turns on more than the size of the balances it affects, the nature of the company's operations counting as well
options.why: Choosing the line items is the first judgement, not the last. Once an item is in, the same judgement decides what gets said about it, how much detail belongs there, and how best to organise it so a reader can find and follow it. Copying the fullest disclosure available, in whatever sequence the standard happens to print its requirements, is a judgement skipped rather than a judgement made safely. Policies are tested the same way. Whether a policy is material is not settled by the size of what it touches. The balances and transactions it affects are one factor among several, and the nature of the company's operations is another. That is why a policy on how deferred tax is measured on brands and licences management treats as indefinite-lived can matter while the balances stay small.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, materiality and the disclosure of material accounting policies

items.scenario: A company has decided that its inventories, its revenue and its deferred tax are all material line items and must be disclosed. The preparer treats that as the end of the materiality question and copies the fullest disclosure he can find for each of the three, in the order the standards happen to list the requirements. Separately, the company has an accounting policy on deferred tax for certain brands and licences acquired in past business combinations, which management considers to have an indefinite life; the balances affected by that policy are small, and the preparer proposes to leave the policy out on that ground alone.

items.stem: What does good practice in presenting the notes and the annual report require?

options.text: Rewrite the governance and strategy sections to repeat the wording of the notes, since only the audited text may describe the restructuring
options.misconception: turns the requirement for a consistent message into a requirement for identical text
options.why: What is asked for is that the annual report be considered as a whole and deliver a consistent and coherent message throughout. Different sections speak to different questions and properly use different words; the fault is a message that changes between them, not the existence of more than one account.

options.text: Group the notes into categories, place the most critical information more prominently, or do both — and consider the annual report as a whole so that one consistent and coherent message runs through it
options.why: The notes take up more of a set of financial statements than anything else, and how well those statements communicate turns largely on them. Hence the advice to group notes into categories, or to bring what matters most forward so that it sits more prominently, or to do both together. An order that simply records the sequence in which the drafting happened buries the one note a reader is looking for. The second half of the answer reaches past the financial statements. An annual report also carries governance, strategy, business developments and business responsibility reporting, each often written by a different team, and it is read as one document, so it has to be built as one, with a consistent and coherent message running the length of it.

options.text: The order of the notes is a matter of drafting convenience so long as the cross-references are complete
options.misconception: treats navigation aids as a substitute for the arrangement of the document
options.why: A cross-reference helps a reader who already knows what to look for. Grouping the notes into categories and placing the most critical information more prominently is what helps the reader who does not, and it is named as a practice in its own right rather than as an alternative to referencing.

options.text: Move the restructuring note to the front and leave the rest of the report alone, the financial statements being the only part within the preparer's control
options.misconception: fixes the prominence point and abandons the whole-report point
options.why: Prominence is half the answer and the annual report read as one document is the other half. The financial statements are just one part of the company's communication with its stakeholders, and a restructuring described three different ways across one report is a failure of communication however well the note itself is placed.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, integration of notes and the integrated approach to the annual report

items.scenario: A company's notes run to ninety pages presented in the order the disclosures were drafted, with the note explaining a major restructuring sitting at number 47 between two routine schedules. The reporting team argues that the sequence does not matter because everything is there and cross-referenced. Elsewhere in the same annual report, the governance section, the business responsibility report and the strategy commentary each describe the restructuring in different terms, having been written by different teams.

items.stem: How do these balances appear in the balance sheet at 31 March 20X2, and is anything else required?

options.text: The loan split ₹8,38,068 and ₹2,61,994 as in the first answer, but the whole ₹1,16,318 of prepaid employee cost shown as a current asset because it is charged to profit or loss every year
options.misconception: calls the entire prepayment current because some of it is released annually
options.why: Being released annually is what makes one year of it current, not all of it. The balance is amortised over the loan period on a straight line basis at ₹29,080 a year, so ₹29,080 is the current portion and the ₹87,238 that will be released in the four years after that is another non-current asset.

options.text: Loan to employee ₹8,38,068 as a non-current financial asset and ₹2,61,994 as a current financial asset, prepaid employee cost ₹87,238 as another non-current asset and ₹29,080 as another current asset, and deferred tax on the temporary differences arising on those balances
options.why: Each of the two assets is split, and they are split on different logic. The current portion of the loan is what the amortised cost balance will fall by in the coming year — the ₹3,72,000 instalment less the ₹1,10,006 of finance income that will accrue on it, being ₹2,61,994 — which leaves ₹8,38,068 non-current. The prepaid employee cost is amortised on a straight line basis at ₹29,080 a year, so ₹29,080 of it is a current asset and the remaining ₹87,238 is non-current. The loan is a financial asset and the prepaid employee cost is not, so they sit on different lines and are never netted. And deferred tax on the temporary differences arising on the above account balances should be recognised, because restating a loan from ₹15,00,000 to its fair value and creating a prepayment out of the difference moves the carrying amounts away from the tax bases.

options.text: The loan at the contractual amount still outstanding of ₹12,00,000, the prepaid employee cost having been created only to arrive at the first year's income
options.misconception: treats the fair value measurement as a computation for the income statement rather than the basis of the asset
options.why: The loan is measured at amortised cost using the 10% effective interest rate, which is ₹11,00,062 at this date, and the prepaid employee cost is an asset in its own right representing the benefit the employee has still to earn by staying in service. Putting the contractual ₹12,00,000 back on the balance sheet would undo the initial measurement altogether.

options.text: Loan to employee ₹11,00,062 and prepaid employee cost ₹1,16,318, both wholly non-current because the loan runs for four more years, with no deferred tax
options.misconception: leaves both balances undivided and never asks what falls due within twelve months
options.why: An instalment loan produces a current asset every year it runs, and the amount is the reduction in the amortised cost the coming year will bring, not the whole cash instalment. The prepaid employee cost is amortised evenly, so a year of it is current on the same reasoning. Deferred tax on the temporary differences arising on these balances is required as well.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — case study on a concessional staff housing loan, the balance sheet extract at the first year end and the deferred tax on the resulting temporary differences

items.scenario: On 1 April 20X1 Star Limited advanced a housing loan of ₹15,00,000 to an employee at 6% a year, repayable in five equal annual instalments of principal with interest at each year end. The market rate for a similar housing loan is 10%. The loan was correctly recognised at its fair value of ₹13,54,602 with ₹1,45,398 taken as prepaid employee cost. During the year ended 31 March 20X2 finance income of ₹1,35,460 was recognised, ₹3,90,000 was received, and ₹29,080 of the prepaid employee cost was amortised, so the loan stands at ₹11,00,062 and the prepaid employee cost at ₹1,16,318. Next year's instalment is ₹3,72,000 and next year's finance income at 10% will be ₹1,10,006.

items.stem: What does integrating internal control over financial reporting into the ERP require for these findings?

options.text: Identify related parties from the audited financial statements of the counterparties at the year end, which is more reliable than a coding scheme inside the company's own ledger
options.misconception: pushes a continuous identification control out to an annual external procedure
options.why: Separate ledger coding for related parties exists so that the transactions can be auto-tabulated for Schedule III presentation as they arise, which is a control that runs all year. Reading counterparties' accounts after the year end finds relationships late, misses transactions with parties whose accounts say nothing, and leaves the company's own ledger unable to produce the disclosure.

options.text: Decisions on alternative accounting treatments documented and approved within the ERP with the rationale and the communication to the audit committee, standardised voucher types with the journal voucher listing reviewed to identify non-routine transactions, and KYC validation controls on account masters with separate ledger coding for related parties
options.why: Three of the illustrative steps answer the three findings directly. Decisions on alternative accounting treatments for significant events or transactions are validated as documented and approved by management, and the ERP is reviewed for documentation of accounting treatment decisions including the approvals and the communication to the audit committee — the rationale, analysis and conclusions being recorded rather than recalled. Non-routine transactions are identified by reviewing the journal vouchers listing, supported by standardising voucher types, which are predefined templates for different kinds of journal entry that keep the recording consistent. And proper KYC validation controls are put in place for creating account masters, with separate ledger coding for related parties so that those transactions can be auto-tabulated for presentation as required by Schedule III.

options.text: A year-end memorandum recording the treatment chosen, the related parties identified and the new account masters opened is enough, since it captures the same facts
options.misconception: substitutes an annual narrative for controls configured inside the system
options.why: A memorandum written after the year has closed cannot show that the treatment was approved before it was applied, cannot identify a related party the spreadsheet missed, and cannot stop an account master being opened without a check. Automating and standardising the procedures is what reduces manual effort and minimises the risk of errors; a memorandum describes the year, it does not control it.

options.text: Restrict the choice of accounting treatment to the statutory auditor, so that management never selects between alternatives
options.misconception: hands a management responsibility to the auditor instead of documenting how management discharged it
options.why: Choosing between two defensible treatments is management's job, and the control is that the choice be written down and signed off by management for any significant event or transaction, with that record, and the fact that it went to the audit committee, visible inside the system. Management chooses and records; the auditor and the committee then have something to look at.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — illustrative steps 9, 10, 12 and 13 for integrating internal control over financial reporting within an ERP

items.scenario: A listed company runs everything through an ERP. Its audit committee finds that a large sale and leaseback was accounted for on one of two defensible treatments with no record of who chose it or why, and that the committee itself heard about the choice only when the draft accounts arrived. The same review finds that account masters are opened without any identity checks, that related party transactions are picked out by hand from a spreadsheet at the year end, and that non-routine journal entries are indistinguishable in the system from routine ones. The finance head proposes a year-end memorandum recording all such matters.

items.stem: How far is the managing partner wrong?

options.text: Wrong only on the law — the Act does regulate the storage of financial data, but with no theft and no ransom there is nothing here that could affect any set of financial statements
options.misconception: measures the effect of a breach by what was taken rather than by what could be altered
options.why: Reading data is the mild end of the range. The severe end is modifying the financial statements without the knowledge of the management, and an intruder with write access to the working papers for four months sat at that end. What was taken is one question; what could have been changed is a different and larger one.

options.text: On all three counts — a breach can reach as far as modifying the financial statements without management's knowledge, the Information Technology Act, 2000 governs the collection, storage and transmission of financial data, and non-compliance with data protection law brings financial penalties and reputational damage
options.why: The managing partner is wrong on each of the three. Take the reach of a breach first. What an intruder can do to an accounting firm runs from simply reading the firm's or a client's financial data at the mild end, all the way to modifying the financial statements while nobody in management knows it happened, and write access to the working papers for four months puts this intrusion at that end. Second, the storage is regulated. India's Information Technology Act, 2000, as it stood after the 2008 amendment, is the framework governing how financial data is collected, held and passed on, and it does not switch off because nothing was stolen. Third, the price of getting that wrong is not confined to cash. Breaching data protection law brings financial penalties and reputational damage, and neither of those waits for a rupee to go missing.

options.text: Right on all three, since the consequences of a breach crystallise only when a financial loss can be quantified
options.misconception: waits for a quantified loss before treating a breach as having any consequence
options.why: A breach hits financial reporting along three lines, money lost, standing damaged and the law's own consequences, and only the first of the three is a number. A four-month intrusion with write access to client working papers has consequences from the moment it is found, whatever the eventual arithmetic says.

options.text: Wrong only about financial reporting — the reporting risk is real, but no Indian statute governs how an accounting firm stores client financial data
options.misconception: treats data protection as a matter of contract and good practice rather than of law
options.why: The statute is there, and it has been there since 2008. India's law on information technology, as amended that year, reaches how financial data is gathered, kept and passed on, which is exactly what an accounting firm does with a client's records. Falling short of data protection law carries its own consequences, money penalties and a name that is harder to trade on afterwards, so the firm's exposure sits outside anything it agreed with its clients.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — cybersecurity in accounting, the impact of a breach and the legal and regulatory framework

items.scenario: An accounting firm discovers that an intruder held access to its systems for four months. No ransom was demanded and no money left any account, but the intruder could read client financial data and had write access to the working papers from which several clients' financial statements were built. The managing partner says that since the attacker took nothing, the matter is an IT problem, that no law governs how the firm stores client financial data, and that nothing about it can touch financial reporting.

items.stem: What does the Code say about his position?

options.text: Nothing, because a threat exists only where the accountant has a direct shareholding, and a bonus is remuneration rather than a financial interest
options.misconception: reads financial interest as meaning shares alone, when the Code names compensation and incentive arrangements among the interests that create the threat
options.why: The examples run wider than a shareholding. The Code catches pay and incentive arrangements whose value moves with the very reporting and decisions the accountant makes, and it lists eligibility for a profit-related bonus whose value might be directly affected by the accountant's own decisions as one on its own. A direct or indirect holding is one example among several, not the boundary of the idea.

options.text: The threat is unavoidable, so he must resign from the company before the classification is settled
options.misconception: jumps to the most drastic response when the framework asks first for an evaluation and allows a threat to be reduced rather than eliminated
options.why: Threats are addressed by eliminating them or by reducing them to an acceptable level, and which of the two is right follows from the evaluation. Withdrawing from this particular decision, obtaining appropriate oversight, or having the classification settled by somebody with no stake in the bonus are all responses short of resigning, and the Code expects the evaluation before the response.

options.text: He is right that the pay arrangement is separate, provided he discloses the bonus formula in the related party note
options.misconception: treats disclosure of the arrangement as discharging the duty to address the threat the arrangement creates
options.why: Disclosing a bonus formula tells a reader the arrangement exists; it does nothing about the threat the arrangement creates for the very decision in front of him. The framework asks him to identify the threat, evaluate it and then address it by eliminating it or reducing it to an acceptable level, and none of those three steps is satisfied by a note.

options.text: The compensation arrangement and the deferred bonus shares each create a self-interest threat that he must identify, evaluate and address, and he may not use his position to influence the classification for personal gain
options.why: The Code's list of self-interest threat sources reaches financial interests of this kind — holdings and rights whose worth turns on the very reporting and decision the accountant is making. A profit-related bonus whose value might be directly affected by his decisions, and deferred bonus share rights whose value might move the same way, are both named as examples of it. And separately, the Code forbids using his position to manipulate information, or using confidential information, for his own or another's financial gain — so the arrangement is not a private matter standing outside the decision.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the self-interest threat created by pay tied to the outcome of the accountant's own reporting and decisions, and the separate bar on manipulating or misusing information for gain

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant employed as financial controller is paid a bonus computed as a percentage of cash generated from operations. His own holding of deferred bonus shares in the company vests next year. He is deciding how to classify a large receipt in the statement of cash flows, and one of the two available classifications would lift cash generated from operations above the bonus threshold. He tells the audit committee that his pay arrangement is a matter between him and the company and has nothing to do with the classification.

items.stem: What does the study material say about those two effects?

options.text: Neither changes, because outside confirmations are required by the auditor and a blockchain entry still has to be audited
options.misconception: assumes the audit procedure is fixed, when the material's point is that the auditor works differently against a shared ledger
options.why: Auditing does not disappear, but what it costs and how it is done both move. The auditor can access the ledger directly to verify transactions rather than reconciling data pulled from several systems, and it is the intermediary standing between the two parties whose fee falls away.

options.text: Cost rises, since every participant must now store and verify the whole ledger, which is the price paid for removing the middleman
options.misconception: reads distributed verification as a new cost centre, when the material counts it as the saving
options.why: The material treats the distributed verification as what makes the saving possible, not as a charge against it. Its stated impact is a reduction in cost, achieved by eliminating intermediaries and central authorities, and the participants doing the verifying are the same parties who were previously paying somebody else to do it.

options.text: Cost falls, but the reporting frequency cannot change, because a set of financial statements can only be drawn up once the period has closed and the entries have been reviewed
options.misconception: treats the periodic close as a property of accounting rather than of the systems that feed it
options.why: The material puts real-time financial reporting among the impacts precisely because the constraint is the system and not the concept. Where the data is available continuously and each transaction is verified as it is recorded, the reporting can be more frequent and still accurate, and that is the change the technology is credited with.

options.text: Cost falls because third-party verification and reconciliation drop away with the intermediaries, and reporting can be done more often because the data is available in real time and agreed by consensus as it arrives
options.why: Two of the named impacts answer his two questions directly. On cost, by eliminating intermediaries and central authorities the technology reduces the cost of third-party verification and reconciliation. On timing, real-time data availability together with the consensus mechanism lets financial reporting be done more frequently and still accurately, rather than only at a periodic close. Both follow from the same feature — a single record the parties verify between themselves.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — key impacts of blockchain on financial reporting: cost reduction and real-time financial reporting

items.scenario: A group closes its books once a quarter and pays outside agents to confirm balances with three trading partners before each close. Its finance director asks what a blockchain would do about those two things in particular — the cost of the outside confirmations, and the fact that the numbers are only trustworthy on four days a year.

items.stem: What does the cost model require each year?

options.text: Depreciate the building, but the annual valuation may be stopped, since fair value has no role once the cost model is applied
options.misconception: reads the removal of the fair value MODEL as removing the fair value DISCLOSURE
options.why: What India removed is the option to carry the property at fair value. The requirement to disclose fair value survives and applies to every entity, which is why a valuation is still commissioned. Stopping it would leave the notes short of the one figure that tells a reader what the property is actually worth.

options.text: Depreciate the whole ₹100 crore over forty years at ₹2.5 crore a year, since the land and the building are one investment property
options.misconception: depreciates land along with the building because the two were acquired and are held as a single property
options.why: Being one property for classification does not make it one asset for depreciation. Land normally has an unlimited useful life and is not depreciated, and the building is depreciated over its own forty years. Charging ₹2.5 crore writes off ₹1 crore a year of an asset that is not wasting.

options.text: Depreciate the building at ₹1.5 crore a year under Ind AS 16's requirements, leave the land undepreciated, test for impairment under Ind AS 36 where there is an indication, and still obtain the fair value, because Ind AS 40 requires it to be disclosed
options.why: Where the cost model applies, the property is measured in accordance with Ind AS 16's requirements for that model, which brings depreciation and impairment with it. Sixty crore over forty years is ₹1.5 crore a year on the building, while land with an unlimited useful life is not depreciated. Impairment is tested under Ind AS 36 in the ordinary way. And the valuation is still needed, because the fair value of investment property must be disclosed whichever measurement model is used — in India that disclosure is the only place it appears.

options.text: No depreciation at all, because investment property is held for rentals and capital appreciation rather than for consumption in the business
options.misconception: carries the fair value model's consequence across to the cost model, where the absence of depreciation was the whole point of the model
options.why: Not depreciating is a feature of the fair value model, which India did not adopt. Under the cost model the building is measured in accordance with Ind AS 16's requirements, and systematic depreciation over the useful life is one of them. Why the property is held decides its classification, not whether it wastes.

citation.ref: measurement after recognition under the cost model, with the fair value disclosure requirement and Ind AS 16's depreciation requirements

items.scenario: A company holds one investment property: land bought for ₹40 crore and an office block on it built for ₹60 crore with a forty-year useful life and no residual value, both let out to tenants. Its new accountant, coming from an IFRS group that used the fair value model, asks what has to be done year by year now that the property is carried at cost, and whether the annual valuation the group used to commission is still needed for anything.

items.stem: How are the two movements classified and measured?

options.text: Both transfer, but each is brought in at fair value on the date of the change in use, ₹45 crore and ₹24 crore, with the uplift recognised in profit or loss
options.misconception: applies the fair value model transfer rules, which the Indian text does not carry
options.why: Para 59 says a transfer between investment property, owner-occupied property and inventories does not change the carrying amount of the property transferred, nor its cost for measurement or disclosure purposes. The paragraphs that revalue a property on transfer are marked as not adopted in Ind AS 40, so ₹17 crore and ₹5 crore of uplift are recognised nowhere.

options.text: Neither transfers, because a change in use moves a property out of investment property and never into it
options.misconception: reads para 57 as a one-way list, when two of its four triggers are transfers into investment property
options.why: Para 57's list runs both ways. Two of the four triggers move a property out — commencement of owner-occupation, and commencement of development with a view to sale — and two move a property in: owner-occupation ending, and a lease to an outside party beginning. Leaving both properties where they were would carry a let building under Ind AS 16 and a let block of flats under Ind AS 2.

options.text: The old head office transfers on 1 September 2025, but the flats stay as inventories, because property built for sale remains stock in trade until it is sold
options.misconception: makes the original intention decisive for the flats, when para 57(d) makes the inception of the operating lease the change in use
options.why: What the flats were built for decided their classification until the use changed. Para 57(d) is what fires here: letting the flats out to a tenant is the moment an operating lease to someone outside the entity begins, and that is the change in use that moves them from inventories to investment property from 1 January 2026, whatever they were built for.

options.text: The old head office transfers from owner-occupied property to investment property on 1 September 2025 and the flats transfer from inventories to investment property on 1 January 2026, each at its existing carrying amount of ₹28 crore and ₹19 crore, with no gain recognised on either
options.why: Para 57 ties a transfer to a change in use, not to intention alone, and it names two moves in this direction. Sub-paragraph (c) treats the end of owner-occupation as the trigger: once a property stops being owner-occupied, it becomes investment property, which is the old head office on 1 September 2025. Sub-paragraph (d) treats the inception of an operating lease as the trigger where the tenant is a party other than the entity itself: letting the flats out from 1 January 2026 moves them from inventories to investment property the same way. Because India permits only the cost model, para 59 carries each across at its existing carrying amount, so ₹28 crore and ₹19 crore stand and neither uplift is recognised.

citation.ref: para 57(c) and 57(d), read with para 59

items.scenario: A property company reports two movements in the year ended 31 March 2026. It vacated its old head office on 1 September 2025, moved the staff into a new building and let the old one to a tenant on a long lease; it had been carried as owner-occupied property under Ind AS 16 at ₹28 crore, and its fair value on 1 September 2025 was ₹45 crore. Separately, it holds a block of unsold flats built for sale and carried as inventories at ₹19 crore; unable to sell them, it let the whole block to a company on an operating lease beginning 1 January 2026, when their fair value was ₹24 crore.

items.stem: How is materiality judged for the interim report?

options.text: Against the interim period's data, but the amount may still be omitted because the estimates behind an interim measurement are less reliable than annual ones
options.misconception: turns the Standard's acknowledgement that interim measurement leans more on estimates into a licence to leave items out
options.why: The Standard does flag that estimates carry more weight in an interim figure than in an annual one, precisely because less of the year has run and less is yet known for certain. That flag explains why an interim number leans harder on judgement — it is not permission to leave the number out. Judgement is always required in assessing materiality; the item is still recognised and disclosed.

options.text: Against whichever base gives the more prudent answer, since the Standard leaves the choice to the entity's judgement
options.misconception: reads the presence of judgement as the absence of a rule
options.why: Judgement operates inside a stated base, and the base is fixed: what the interim period's own figures show, not a base the entity may pick for itself. A free choice of base would let the same item be material in one company's half year and not in another's on identical facts, which is exactly what a stated base prevents.

options.text: Against the interim period's own financial data, so the ₹9 crore is measured against the six months' ₹40 crore and is recognised and disclosed in the interim report
options.why: Materiality here turns on one base only: what the six months' own figures show, not the year's. Judged against that measure — item by item, whether to recognise it, how to measure it, how to classify it or whether to disclose it — the ₹9 crore is weighed against the interim period financial data taken by itself, without reference to how the full year might look. Nine crore against ₹40 crore is more than a fifth of the half year's profit, so the item goes in, and unusual items are flagged on that footing so a reader is not left with misleading inferences that a silent set of accounts would invite.

options.text: Against the forecast annual result, so the finance head is right and the ₹9 crore waits for the annual financial statements
options.misconception: measures an interim item against the year it sits in, which is the comparison the Standard rules out
options.why: The Standard is explicit about the base: what a half year's own numbers show, judged on their own, not what the year end might look like. Measuring against the year would let almost anything be left out of a half year and would defeat the point of publishing one, since a reader of the interim report has only the interim figures in front of him.

citation.ref: para 23, 24 and 25

items.scenario: A company publishes half-yearly interim reports. In the six months to 30 September 2025 it settles a dispute for ₹9 crore. Profit before that settlement for those six months is ₹40 crore, and budgeted profit for the full year is ₹300 crore. The finance head proposes to leave the settlement out of the interim report altogether, on the ground that ₹9 crore is three per cent of the year's expected profit and so immaterial, and that it will be disclosed in the annual financial statements where it belongs.

items.stem: What liability stands at 31 March 2026 and what is charged for the year then ended?

options.text: A liability of ₹16,20,000 and a charge for the year of ₹9,07,500
options.why: The rights are earned across the four-year vesting period, so at each reporting date the liability is the fair value of the rights expected to vest multiplied by the fraction of the period served. At 31 March 2026, 36 employees × 500 rights × ₹180 is ₹32,40,000, and two of the four years have run, so the liability is half of that, ₹16,20,000. A year earlier it was 38 × 500 × ₹150 × one quarter, which is ₹7,12,500. The charge for the year is the movement, ₹16,20,000 less ₹7,12,500, being ₹9,07,500.

options.text: A liability of ₹18,00,000 and a charge for the year of ₹10,87,500
options.misconception: counts all 40 employees rather than the 36 expected to satisfy the service condition
options.why: 40 × 500 × ₹180 × one half is ₹18,00,000. The number that goes into the measurement is the number expected to become entitled, which the company has estimated at 36, and that estimate is revised at each reporting date as employees leave or stay. Counting all 40 measures an obligation to people the company does not expect to owe.

options.text: A liability of ₹32,40,000 and a charge for the year of ₹25,27,500
options.misconception: measures the liability at the full fair value of the rights expected to vest without spreading it over the period the employees must still serve
options.why: 36 × 500 × ₹180 is the whole of what the rights are worth if all four years are served. The employees have served two, so only half of that has been earned. Recognising the full amount charges the company for services it has not yet received, and would leave nothing to charge in the two years still to come.

options.text: A liability of ₹14,40,000 and a charge for the year of ₹7,80,000
options.misconception: freezes the measurement at the grant date fair value of ₹160, which is the equity-settled treatment
options.why: 36 × 500 × ₹160 × one half is ₹14,40,000 and uses the ₹160 fixed at grant. A cash-settled award does not freeze like that — its liability is revalued afresh every time the entity reports, right through to the day it is finally settled, so ₹180 is the figure that goes in at 31 March 2026. It is the equity-settled award whose grant date measurement is never revisited for the share price.

citation.ref: para 30, 32 and 33

items.scenario: On 1 April 2024 a company granted 500 cash-settled share appreciation rights to each of 40 employees, exercisable only if the employee stays four years, so the vesting date is 31 March 2028. The fair value of one right was ₹160 at grant. At 31 March 2025 the fair value was ₹150 and 38 employees were expected to stay; at 31 March 2026 the fair value is ₹180 and 36 employees are expected to stay. Nothing has been exercised.

items.stem: May the earlier calculation be used for this year's annual test?

options.text: No — an annual test means a fresh detailed calculation every year, which is what makes it annual
options.misconception: reads the annual requirement as a requirement to redo the arithmetic, when the Standard allows a rolled-forward calculation on conditions
options.why: The unit must be tested annually, but the Standard says in terms that the most recent detailed calculation from a preceding period may be used in the current period's test where the three criteria are met. Requiring the model to be rebuilt every year on a unit that nothing has happened to would spend audit effort where there is no question to answer.

options.text: Yes, if all three conditions are met — the unit's assets and liabilities are essentially unchanged since the calculation was made, that calculation cleared the carrying amount by a substantial margin, and a look at what has happened since makes a current shortfall remote
options.why: The most recent detailed calculation made in a preceding period of a unit's recoverable amount may be carried forward and used in the current period's test, but only where all three criteria are satisfied together. They ask whether the unit is still essentially the same collection of assets and liabilities as when the figure was worked out, whether that figure cleared the carrying amount by a substantial margin, and whether, on an analysis of events and changed circumstances since, the likelihood of a current determination being less than the carrying amount is remote. All three hold here, so the earlier figure may be used.

options.text: Yes, provided only that the earlier calculation exceeded the carrying amount by a substantial margin, headroom being the point of the relief
options.misconception: keeps one of the three criteria and drops the other two
options.why: Headroom is one criterion of three and it looks backwards. The other two ask whether the unit is still the same unit, and whether anything since has made a shortfall likely — and a unit can have had large headroom last year and have lost a major customer this year. All three must be met before the earlier figure may stand.

options.text: Yes, and no conditions attach, since goodwill impairment is tested at the same time each year and the timing is all the Standard prescribes
options.misconception: takes the permission without the three criteria that are the price of it
options.why: The permission is conditional and the conditions are cumulative. A unit whose assets and liabilities have changed significantly, or whose earlier headroom was thin, or where events since make a shortfall more than remote, must be measured afresh. Timing is a separate requirement and does not displace them.

citation.ref: para 99, read with para 96

items.scenario: A company allocated goodwill to a cash-generating unit and computed that unit's recoverable amount in detail last year, arriving at a figure far above its carrying amount. This year it wants to use that same calculation rather than build a new one. The unit's assets and liabilities are unchanged, nothing in the market or the business has moved against it, and management considers a fall below carrying amount remote.

items.stem: What impairment does the company recognise on the contract cost asset, and in what order?

options.text: No impairment, because the ₹60 lakh still to be received comfortably exceeds the ₹42 lakh carrying amount
options.misconception: compares the asset with the gross consideration and never deducts the costs still to be incurred to earn it
options.why: The test is not against the consideration but against the consideration less any directly related contract costs yet to be recognised. Twenty-five lakh of those costs are still to come, so the amount available to support the asset is ₹35 lakh, and ₹7 lakh of the ₹42 lakh is not recoverable.

options.text: The Ind AS 16 impairment on the plant is recognised first, and then ₹7 lakh on the contract cost asset, being its ₹42 lakh carrying amount less the ₹60 lakh of expected consideration reduced by the ₹25 lakh of costs still to be recognised
options.why: An impairment loss bites once the carrying amount of the asset outruns what is left to come in against it — the remaining amount of consideration still due under the contract for the goods or services concerned, cut down by whatever directly related costs the entity has not yet recognised. Sixty lakh less ₹25 lakh is ₹35 lakh, against a carrying amount of ₹42 lakh, so ₹7 lakh is written off. Before that test is applied, the entity recognises impairment losses on assets related to the contract that are accounted for under another Standard, Ind AS 16 among them, so the plant is dealt with first.

options.text: ₹7 lakh, and if the contract later recovers the write-down may never be added back, as with goodwill
options.misconception: imports the goodwill rule that no impairment may be reversed
options.why: A previously recognised impairment loss on a contract cost asset is reversed when the impairment conditions no longer exist or have improved, subject to the increased carrying amount not exceeding what it would have been, net of amortisation, had no impairment been recognised. The permanent bar belongs to goodwill and not here.

options.text: ₹7 lakh on the contract cost asset, recognised before the plant's own impairment, since Ind AS 115 governs the contract
options.misconception: reverses the order, when the Standard requires assets under other Standards to be impaired first
options.why: The amount is right and the sequence is not. The entity recognises impairment losses on contract-related assets accounted for under another Standard — Ind AS 2, Ind AS 16 and Ind AS 38 are the examples given — before applying this test. Doing it the other way would measure the contract cost asset against consideration that a still-unimpaired plant is also being asked to support.

citation.ref: para 101, 103 and 104, with the amortisation requirement in para 99

items.scenario: A company capitalised costs of obtaining and fulfilling a service contract, and the resulting contract cost asset stands at ₹42 lakh. Reviewing it at the year end, the company expects to receive ₹60 lakh of remaining consideration in connection with the related services, and expects to incur a further ₹25 lakh of directly related contract costs that have not yet been recognised. Plant used on the same contract, carried under Ind AS 16, is itself impaired.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 8 say about the two omissions?

options.text: The second is permitted if the company discloses in its notes that the classification requirement has not been applied and explains why
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a departure the Standard describes as inappropriate
options.why: Disclosure does not convert an inappropriate departure into an acceptable one. The Standard's objection is to making or leaving uncorrected an immaterial departure in order to achieve a particular presentation, and a note explaining that the presentation was the reason states the objection rather than answering it.

options.text: Both are permitted, since neither has a material effect and materiality is the only test the Standard applies
options.misconception: stops at the first sentence and drops the sentence that follows it
options.why: Materiality excuses the first omission and not the second, because the second sentence attaches a further condition to departures of any size. A departure made deliberately to achieve a particular presentation is not saved by being small — the smallness is what makes it usable for that purpose in the first place.

options.text: The first is permitted, because a policy need not be applied where the effect of applying it is immaterial; the second is not, because it is inappropriate to make or leave uncorrected immaterial departures made to achieve a particular presentation
options.why: The Standard says both things in the same breath. Ind AS set out accounting policies meant to produce relevant and reliable information, and it grants a size-based relief: a policy need not be followed where the effect of applying them is immaterial. But that relief has a limit the Standard states just as plainly — it is inappropriate to make, or to leave sitting uncorrected, a departure chosen because of what it does to the picture the accounts present: shaping a particular presentation of the entity's position, performance or cash flows rather than following an honest reading of the rule. Saving the cost of a trivial working is the first case; keeping a subtotal above a lenders' threshold is the second, and repeating it for four years is leaving it uncorrected.
keywords: effect of applying them is immaterial

options.text: Neither is permitted, because a requirement of an Ind AS is a requirement whatever its effect
options.misconception: treats every requirement as absolute and ignores the immateriality relief the Standard gives in terms
options.why: The relief is written into the Standard in plain terms: a policy carries no obligation where following it would change nothing material — the effect of applying them is immaterial and so the requirement falls away. Insisting on every requirement regardless of effect would make the accounts more expensive without making them more useful, which is the opposite of what materiality exists to prevent.

citation.ref: para 7 and 8

items.scenario: A company identifies two Ind AS requirements it has not followed. The first is a measurement requirement whose effect on every figure in the financial statements would be trivial, and the company has ignored it to save the cost of the working. The second is a classification requirement, also trivial in amount, which the company has deliberately not applied in each of the last four years because leaving it out keeps a subtotal on the face of the balance sheet above a level its lenders watch.

items.stem: How is the error corrected?

options.text: Charge the whole cumulative effect against profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026, since the earlier years cannot be restated
options.misconception: falls back on a current-year catch-up whenever full restatement is impracticable
options.why: Impracticability limits how far back the restatement reaches; it does not turn the correction into a charge of the current year. The years that can be restated are restated, and the balance is carried into the opening position of the earliest period for which restatement is practicable rather than through this year's result.

options.text: Leave the comparatives alone and disclose the error and its effect in the notes, since a partial restatement is worse than none
options.misconception: abandons the restatement that is practicable because a full one is not
options.why: The relief is limited to the periods for which restatement cannot be made. The year ended 31 March 2025 and the opening position at 1 April 2024 can be determined in full, so they are restated, and disclosure accompanies that rather than replacing it.

options.text: Restate every year from 1 April 2021 using the best assumptions management can make now about what it would have intended then
options.misconception: treats an impracticable restatement as merely a difficult one, and supplies the missing judgement with hindsight
options.why: Supplying what management would have intended is precisely what the Standard names as making a restatement impracticable. Estimates built now from information that was not available then are hindsight, and a restatement built on hindsight reports a past that never existed.

options.text: Restate the comparative for the year ended 31 March 2025 and the opening balances at 1 April 2024, and say so — the earlier years being ones for which retrospective restatement is impracticable
options.why: Retrospective restatement is required only so far as it is practicable. The Standard's own test for when it is not: the entity has made every reasonable effort and still cannot apply the requirement, which is what impracticable means here. Two situations it treats as meeting that test are reconstructing what management's intent would have been at a date now impossible to know, and building an estimate from facts that only came to light later, which cannot honestly be separated from that later knowledge. Both apply to 2021-22 through 2023-24, so the restatement runs from the earliest date at which it is practicable, being 1 April 2024, and the fact and the reason are disclosed.

citation.ref: para 5, the definition of impracticable, read with para 43, 44 and 45

items.scenario: In the year ended 31 March 2026 a company discovers that a class of contracts has been measured wrongly since 1 April 2021. It presents one comparative year. Reconstructing the figures for 2021-22 to 2023-24 would need assumptions about what management would have intended at each of those dates, and estimates that cannot be separated from what is known only now, but the company can determine the effect on the year ended 31 March 2025 and on the opening position at 1 April 2024 in full.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: Yes — the assumptions and the discount rate are set once, at the start of the annual reporting period, and a plan amendment does not disturb them
options.misconception: applies the opening-assumptions rule without the exception that a remeasurement triggers
options.why: The opening rule holds until something forces a remeasurement. A plan amendment does force one, and the Standard then requires the remainder of the period to run on the remeasured figures — otherwise the entity would keep charging service cost for benefits the plan no longer offers, and interest at a rate the obligation is no longer measured on.

options.text: No — the past service cost is recognised on 30 September, but net interest for the whole year is left on the opening figures, only the current service cost moving to the updated assumptions
options.misconception: applies the remeasurement to one of the two components and not to the other
options.why: Both move. The Standard deals with current service cost and net interest in turn and gives each the same treatment: once a plan amendment, curtailment or settlement forces a remeasurement, everything from that point to the year end runs on the updated numbers — net interest using the remeasured liability and the discount rate used to remeasure it.

options.text: No — for the six months after 30 September the current service cost and the net interest are both determined using the assumptions and the discount rate used on the remeasurement, which are the 8 per cent rate and the updated assumptions
options.why: Current service cost and net interest are ordinarily determined using the actuarial assumptions and the discount rate set at the start of the annual reporting period. But where the entity remeasures the net defined benefit liability on a plan amendment, curtailment or settlement, it determines current service cost for the remainder of the annual reporting period using the assumptions used to remeasure it, and determines net interest for that remainder using the remeasured liability and the discount rate used to remeasure it. The 7 per cent rate governs the first six months and the 8 per cent rate the second.
keywords: remainder of the annual reporting period

options.text: No — the whole year's current service cost and net interest must be recomputed on the 8 per cent rate and the updated assumptions, including the six months before the amendment
options.misconception: pushes the new assumptions backwards over the whole year instead of applying them from the amendment forward
options.why: The Standard says the remainder of the annual reporting period after the plan amendment, not the whole of it. The first six months were correctly measured on the assumptions current at the time, and recomputing them would fold what is really a remeasurement of the obligation into the service cost and net interest of a period it does not belong to.

citation.ref: para 99(b), read with the current service cost and net interest requirements that follow it

items.scenario: A company's year ends 31 March 2026. At 1 April 2025 the net defined benefit liability was ₹90 crore and the discount rate set at that date was 7 per cent. On 30 September 2025 it amends the plan, and the actuary remeasures the obligation on that date using a discount rate of 8 per cent and updated demographic assumptions, giving a net defined benefit liability of ₹120 crore immediately after the amendment. The finance team proposes to recognise the past service cost on 30 September and then run the year's current service cost and net interest on the assumptions and the rate fixed at 1 April 2025 throughout, because those were the opening assumptions.

items.stem: How do the seller-lessee and the buyer-lessor account for the transaction?

options.text: A sale has occurred, so the seller-lessee derecognises the warehouse, recognises a right-of-use asset at the retained proportion of the ₹6 crore, and takes to profit or loss only the gain relating to the rights transferred
options.misconception: applies the qualifying-sale route without first testing control, which the repurchase option defeats
options.why: That is the right treatment where the transfer is a sale, and this transfer is not one. A substantive right to repurchase means the buyer-lessor never obtained control, and the proportionate right-of-use measurement and partial gain only arise once the control test has been passed. The existence of a leaseback alone would not have defeated the sale; the repurchase option does.

options.text: No sale has occurred, so the seller-lessee keeps the warehouse and treats the ₹10 crore as deferred income released over the eight years of the leaseback
options.misconception: turns the financing into deferred income, when the amount received is a financial liability the payments repay
options.why: The ₹10 crore is money the company must work off through the lease payments, not income waiting to be earned. Ind AS 116 requires a financial liability under Ind AS 109 for any amount received from the buyer-lessor, decreased by the payments made less the portion treated as interest expense. Releasing it as income would report a profit the company never made and leave the obligation off the balance sheet.

options.text: No sale has occurred — the seller-lessee keeps the warehouse at ₹6 crore, recognises a financial liability of ₹10 crore and no gain, and reduces that liability by the payments made less the portion treated as interest; the buyer-lessor does not recognise the warehouse and recognises a financial asset of ₹10 crore
options.why: Whether there has been a sale is decided by Ind AS 115's control test, and a substantive repurchase option fails that test here: since the seller-lessee can compel the asset back, the buyer-lessor never gained the ability to direct it, so nothing counts as sold. The consequence is a financing on both sides: the seller-lessee continues to recognise the underlying asset, recognises a financial liability under Ind AS 109 for the amount received, and decreases it by the payments made less the portion treated as interest expense; the buyer-lessor does not recognise the underlying asset and instead recognises a financial asset for the amount paid.

options.text: A sale has occurred and the whole ₹4 crore gain is recognised, since the proceeds are cash and the price is fixed
options.misconception: reads cash proceeds at a fixed price as proof that control passed
options.why: How the price is settled says nothing about control. A financier who must hand the asset back if the option is exercised has not obtained the ability to direct its use or to obtain substantially all its benefits, and no gain of any size is recognised on a transfer that is not a sale.

citation.ref: para 99, 100 and 103, with the substantive repurchase option point in para 99

items.scenario: A company sells a warehouse carried at ₹6 crore to a financier for ₹10 crore in cash and leases it back for eight years. Under the same agreement the company holds an option, exercisable at the end of year five at a fixed price, to buy the warehouse back, and the option is substantive.

items.stem: Which source of startup finance is this?

options.text: Purchase order financing
options.misconception: reaches for the source that funds a large order, when purchase order financing brings in a third party who pays the supplier, and here the supplier itself is doing the funding
options.why: Purchase order financing answers the startup that has won a large new order and lacks the cash to produce and deliver it, and the financing company advances the funds directly to the supplier. There is no such third party here — the manufacturer is both the seller and the source of the money, which is what makes it vendor financing instead.

options.text: Vendor financing
options.why: Vendor financing covers two related moves a supplier makes for its own customer, both seen here. First, the supplier itself lends money so the customer can buy its products in the first place. Second, the manufacturer persuades the distributor to defer payment until the stock has actually sold through, stretching a thirty-day term out to sixty or ninety. Both limbs are present here, and both come from the supplier rather than from a financier standing outside the trade.

options.text: Peer-to-peer lending
options.misconception: names a source in which a group of unconnected people lend to each other, when the money here comes from the counterparty to the trade
options.why: Peer-to-peer lending brings a pool of otherwise unconnected individuals onto one platform, where they lend money to each other directly, often small or ethnic business groups with a shared faith or interest supporting one another's ventures. Nobody outside the sale is lending anything here.

options.text: Factoring of accounts receivable
options.misconception: funds a receivable the distributor would owe rather than one it is owed, reversing who is waiting to be paid
options.why: In factoring, a seller who has sold goods on credit gets most of the outstanding amount upfront from a factoring company and the balance when the customer pays. The distributor here has sold nothing yet; it is the buyer, and what it needs is time to pay rather than early payment of something owed to it.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A young distributor wants to stock a larger consignment of a manufacturer's goods but cannot pay for them for several months. The manufacturer, wanting the volume, agrees to extend the distributor's payment terms from thirty days to ninety and, for part of the order, to lend the distributor the money to buy those same goods.

items.stem: What are the four called?

options.text: Bear hug, greenmail, white knight and crown jewels
options.misconception: names four manoeuvres that exist but describe different things, and puts an acquirer's strategy among the target's defences
options.why: A bear hug is the acquirer threatening an open offer so that the target's board settles for a change of control, and it belongs to the acquirer's side. Greenmail is the target paying the raider a price above market for his block so he goes away. A white knight is a friendly acquirer the target invites in. Crown jewels is the divestiture of the target's own prized business. None of the four is a counter bid, a manager's compensation, a passive shareholder or a bond issue.

options.text: Street sweep, strategic alliance, brand power and divestiture
options.misconception: lists three of the acquirer's takeover strategies alongside one defence, when all four manoeuvres described are the target's
options.why: Street sweep, strategic alliance and brand power are techniques the acquiring company uses — accumulating shares before an open offer, offering partnership instead of a buyout, and allying with powerful brands to displace the target's. Only divestiture is a defence, and it is the target spinning off a business rather than any of the four described.

options.text: Pac-man defence, golden parachutes, white knight and poison pill
options.misconception: mistakes the passive buyer for a rival bidder and the bond issue for the convertible debenture defence
options.why: A white knight actually acquires the target to save it from the hostile bidder; the company here buys shares and stays out of the contest, which is a white squire. And a poison pill in the study material's example is a large issue of convertible debentures to existing shareholders, making the bidder's task harder by increasing the shares carrying voting control; a bond that lets the holder cash in at a higher price and drains the target of cash is a poison put.

options.text: Pac-man defence, golden parachutes, white squire and poison put
options.why: The Pac-man defence aims at the target making a counter bid for the acquirer company, forcing the acquirer to defend itself. Golden parachutes are hefty compensations offered to managers if they are ousted due to takeover, which reduces the acquirer's interest. A white squire places a block of the target's shares with a friendly, passive company uninterested in taking it over itself, so the target's management retains control. A poison put gives bondholders the right to redeem at rising prices once a bid succeeds, and it is the resulting cash drainage that makes the target unattractive.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A target's board considers four further manoeuvres against a hostile bidder: making a counter bid for the bidder itself; promising its own managers heavy compensation if they are ousted; selling a block of shares to a company that has no interest in taking it over; and issuing bonds that encourage the holder to cash in at higher prices.

items.stem: What actually separates the two?

options.text: They are identical in structure — local shares go to a domestic custodian and a depository issues receipts against them — and the difference is where and in what they trade, an American depository receipt being issued in the United States under the Securities and Exchange Commission's rules and denominated in dollars, while a global depository receipt is not tied to a single currency or a single market, and can change hands both inside and outside the United States
options.why: A depository receipt is a negotiable certificate that stands for shares priced in a currency other than the issuer's own, representing the company's local currency equity shares. Receipts issued in the United States are American depository receipts, subject to the stringent provisions stipulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and denominated in dollars. A global depository receipt is, in the material's words, identical in structure to an American one, but it is free of the single-currency, single-market limits an American receipt carries: pricing can run in more than one currency at once, and dealing happens both inside and outside the United States. Indian issues take the global form because they are marketed globally rather than in one country.

options.text: A global depository receipt lists the company's own shares on a foreign exchange, while an American depository receipt leaves the shares at home
options.misconception: confuses a receipt issued against shares held by a custodian with a direct listing of the shares themselves
options.why: Neither instrument lists the company's shares abroad. In both, the local currency shares are delivered to the depository's local custodian bank and the depository bank issues receipts against them; it is the receipts that trade overseas, on a foreign stock exchange, over the counter, or among a restricted group such as qualified institutional buyers.

options.text: An American depository receipt represents equity and a global depository receipt represents debt
options.misconception: splits the two by the instrument underlying them, when both ordinarily represent equity shares
options.why: Both represent the company's publicly traded local currency equity shares. In theory a depository receipt can also represent a debt instrument, but in practice it rarely does, and nothing in the distinction between the American and the global form turns on it.

options.text: A global depository receipt is always denominated in euro and an American one always in dollars, which is why the two names exist
options.misconception: fixes the global form to a single currency when its defining feature is that it is not fixed to one
options.why: Most global depository receipts are denominated in United States dollars, with a few in euro and pound sterling. The point of the global form is that it is not tied to one currency or one market, and reading it as a euro instrument reverses the very feature that separates it from the American one.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company is advised that it may raise foreign currency equity either through an American depository receipt programme or through a global depository receipt issue. Its treasurer believes the two are entirely different instruments, and that a global depository receipt is the one used when the company wants to list its own shares on a foreign exchange.

items.stem: What does each cover cost, and below what closing spot would the option have been the cheaper choice?

options.text: Forward ₹1,74,40,000 against option ₹1,74,00,000, so the option is cheaper by ₹40,000
options.misconception: compares the strike with the forward rate and leaves the premium out of the option's cost
options.why: A strike of ₹87.00 does sit below a forward of ₹87.20, but the strike is not what the cover costs. The premium of ₹1,80,000 is paid whether the option is exercised or not, so the option's total is ₹1,75,80,000 and the forward is ₹1,40,000 cheaper at this closing spot.

options.text: Forward ₹1,74,40,000, and the option can never be the cheaper cover, because its premium is paid on top of whatever rate is eventually used
options.misconception: forgets that the option lapses when the dollar falls, letting the importer buy at a spot well below the forward rate
options.why: The premium is a certain cost and the rate under the option is not. Where the dollar falls, the call is abandoned and the importer buys at the cheaper spot, so the option's total can fall below the forward's fixed ₹1,74,40,000 — and it does so at any closing spot below ₹86.30.

options.text: Forward ₹1,74,40,000 against option ₹1,75,80,000, so the forward wins here, and the option would only have been cheaper had the spot ended below ₹86.30
options.why: The forward fixes the rate, so 2,00,000 × 87.20 is ₹1,74,40,000. The call is exercised at a spot of ₹89.00 because the strike is lower, giving 2,00,000 × 87.00 = ₹1,74,00,000, and the premium of 2,00,000 × 0.90 = ₹1,80,000 sits on top, making ₹1,75,80,000. The option is cheaper only where the dollar falls far enough for the premium to be recovered: its total matches ₹1,74,40,000 when the rupees paid for the currency itself fall to ₹1,72,60,000, which is a spot of ₹86.30.

options.text: Forward ₹1,74,40,000 against option ₹1,75,80,000, and the option would have been cheaper below a spot of ₹86.10
options.misconception: works the break-even by deducting the premium from the strike instead of comparing the option's whole cost with the forward's
options.why: 87.00 − 0.90 = ₹86.10 answers a different question. The comparison is between the option's total outlay and the forward's ₹1,74,40,000, and since the premium of ₹1,80,000 is spent in either case, the currency itself must cost no more than ₹1,72,60,000 — a spot of ₹86.30.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
