items.scenario: An importer must pay $2,00,000 in three months. Spot is ₹86.00. The three-month forward is ₹87.20. A three-month call on the dollar struck at ₹87.00 costs a premium of ₹0.90 a dollar, payable now; ignore interest on the premium. Take the spot three months hence as ₹89.00.

items.stem: What do the two versions give?

options.text: Both give ₹180, because the capitalisation rate is the reciprocal of the price-earnings ratio — 12 × 15 on one route, and 12 divided by 6.67 per cent on the other
options.why: Under the price-earnings multiplier the price per share is earnings per share multiplied by the price-earnings ratio, so 12 × 15 = ₹180. Under capitalisation of earning, the value is the expected maintainable profit divided by the required earning yield, and the study material gives that yield as the reciprocal of the price-earnings ratio, which is 1 ÷ 15 = 6.67 per cent. Twelve divided by 0.0667 is ₹180. They are the same arithmetic written two ways, which is why they cannot disagree when the same ratio is used.

options.text: The multiplier gives ₹0.80 and capitalisation gives ₹180
options.misconception: divides earnings by the multiple instead of multiplying, which produces the yield rather than the price
options.why: Twelve divided by 15 is 0.80, and that is the earning yield expressed in rupees per rupee of price, not a share price. The price per share is earnings per share multiplied by the price-earnings ratio, and a value below one year's earnings is the signal that the multiplication has been inverted.

options.text: Both give ₹180, but the figure must then be reduced, because a multiplier drawn from quoted companies is never usable for a target
options.misconception: applies the unquoted-company adjustment to a target that is itself listed
options.why: The downward adjustment for additional risk belongs to the step of valuing an unlisted company off a quoted comparable's ratio. This target is listed, so the comparable ratio is being applied to a share that already trades, and there is no non-listing risk to discount for.

options.text: The multiplier gives ₹180 and capitalisation gives ₹80, at a capitalisation rate of 15 per cent
options.misconception: reads the price-earnings ratio of 15 as a capitalisation rate of 15 per cent, when the rate is its reciprocal
options.why: Fifteen is a multiple, not a percentage. Twelve divided by 0.15 gives ₹80 and prices the share as though investors demanded a 15 per cent earning yield, when a multiple of 15 means they accept 6.67 per cent. The rate to use is the reciprocal of the price-earnings ratio.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A listed target has future maintainable earnings per share of ₹12. Comparable quoted companies trade on a price-earnings ratio of 15. The buyer's analyst wants to value the share both by the price-earnings multiplier and by capitalising the earnings, and expects the two to disagree.

items.stem: Which levels does the chart set, and what shape is it?

options.text: Resistance about ₹166 and support about ₹136, taking the most recent turning points as the current levels
options.misconception: takes the latest swing rather than the peak the price fell away from and the trough it rebounded from
options.why: The levels are set by the peak the price went down from and the trough it rebounded after reaching, which are ₹168 and ₹132. The later turns at ₹166 and ₹136 come close to those levels and are what confirms them; treating each new swing as a fresh level would move the band every week and leave nothing to be breached.

options.text: No levels can be read, because a breach would be needed before either could be identified
options.misconception: makes a breach the thing that creates the levels, when a breach is what ends them
options.why: The levels are drawn from the peak and the trough already on the chart, and the price is then expected to move between them. A breach of either indicates a distinct departure from the status quo and an attempt to set newer levels, so it destroys the band rather than defining it.

options.text: Support about ₹168 and resistance about ₹132
options.misconception: swaps the two, putting the level buyers appear at above the level sellers appear at
options.why: The names follow the direction. Resistance sits above the price, at the peak it fell from, because everyone who failed to sell at the high is keen to liquidate there; support sits below, at the trough it rebounded from, because everyone who failed to buy at the low would like to purchase. A support level above a resistance level would leave the price with nowhere to move.

options.text: Resistance about ₹168 and support about ₹132, and it is a range rather than a wedge, since the tops and the bottoms are each holding roughly level
options.why: When the price goes down from a peak, that peak becomes the resistance level; when it rebounds after reaching a trough, the lowest value reached becomes the support level. The fall runs from ₹168 and the rebound turns at ₹132, so those are the two levels, and the later touches at ₹166, ₹164, ₹166 and at ₹133 and ₹136 confirm them. A wedge would need the tops and bottoms to change in opposite directions or at different rates; here both are roughly flat, so the price is simply expected to move between the two levels.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A share's closing prices over two months, in rupees and in order, are 168, 160, 145, 132, 140, 152, 166, 158, 141, 133, 147, 164, 155, 136 and 166. Nothing is known about the company; only the chart is being read.

items.stem: Which variable moves the net present value most, and by how much?

options.text: The initial capital cost — it rises to ₹410 crore, and net present value falls to ₹124.60 crore, a fall of 7.43 per cent
options.misconception: assumes the variable carrying the biggest rupee figure must be the most critical, when a 2.5 per cent move on it is a smaller move than 2.5 per cent on a margin
options.why: The arithmetic is right — ₹534.60 crore less ₹410 crore is ₹124.60 crore, 7.43 per cent below base. But a 2.5 per cent change in a cost that appears once is a ₹10 crore change, whereas 2.5 per cent off the selling price takes ₹2.50 off a ₹50 contribution, five per cent of the margin, in each of the three years. The largest number is not the most sensitive variable.

options.text: The fixed cost per year — it rises to ₹51.25 crore, and net present value falls to ₹131.26 crore, a fall of 2.48 per cent
options.misconception: picks the variable with the smallest effect, reading a cost that is fixed as the one a project is most exposed to
options.why: A 2.5 per cent rise in fixed costs is ₹1.25 crore a year against a contribution of ₹250 crore, so the annual inflow falls only to ₹198.75 crore and the net present value to ₹131.26 crore. That 2.48 per cent is the smallest of the five moves, which is precisely what the exercise is meant to reveal — this project's risk sits in its price, not in its overheads.

options.text: The selling price — net present value falls from ₹134.60 crore to ₹101.19 crore, a fall of 24.82 per cent
options.why: At base, contribution is ₹50 a unit on 5 crore units, that is ₹250 crore, less ₹50 crore of fixed costs, so the annual inflow is ₹200 crore. Two hundred times 2.673 is ₹534.60 crore, less the ₹400 crore outlay, giving a net present value of ₹134.60 crore. Cut the selling price by 2.5 per cent to ₹97.50 and contribution falls to ₹47.50 a unit, so the annual inflow is 237.50 − 50 = ₹187.50 crore, whose present value is ₹501.19 crore and whose net present value is ₹101.19 crore — 24.82 per cent below base, the largest of the five moves.

options.text: The variable cost per unit — it rises to ₹51.25, and net present value falls to ₹117.89 crore, a fall of 12.41 per cent
options.misconception: stops at the variable that also squeezes contribution, without noticing that the selling price squeezes it twice as hard
options.why: The figures are correct — contribution falls to ₹48.75, the annual inflow to ₹193.75 crore, the present value to ₹517.89 crore and the net present value to ₹117.89 crore. But 2.5 per cent of a ₹50 variable cost is ₹1.25 while 2.5 per cent of a ₹100 selling price is ₹2.50, so the selling price takes twice as much out of the same contribution and moves the net present value 24.82 per cent instead of 12.41 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project needs ₹400 crore now and runs three years. It sells 5 crore units a year at ₹100 each, variable cost is ₹50 a unit, and fixed costs are ₹50 crore a year. The discount rate is 6 per cent and the three-year annuity factor at that rate is 2.673. Each of the five variables is now moved 2.5 per cent in the adverse direction, one at a time, with the others held at base.

items.stem: What are the two net asset values after the segregation, and what does an investor redeeming the next day receive?

options.text: Main scheme ₹90 a unit and side pocket ₹8 a unit; a redeeming investor is paid ₹90 a unit now and keeps his side pocket units until the bond is recovered
options.why: Net asset value is the net value of all assets less liabilities, computed per unit. Before segregation it is (1,000 − 20) ÷ 10 = ₹98. Moving the ₹80 crore bond out leaves the main scheme with 1,000 − 80 − 20 = ₹900 crore over 10 crore units, that is ₹90 a unit, and the side pocket carries ₹80 crore over 10 crore units, that is ₹8. The redeeming investor takes the value of the liquid assets, ₹90, and his side pocket units stay with him until the fund recovers what it can on the bond.

options.text: Main scheme ₹90 a unit, and side pocket units go only to investors who stay, a redeeming investor being paid the full ₹98
options.misconception: rewards the investor who leaves with value the segregation was designed to hold back
options.why: Side pocketing exists for the investor who wishes to hold on to the units of the main fund for the long term, so that good assets are not sold cheaply to meet redemptions. Paying a leaver ₹98 would take ₹8 a unit of the stressed bond's value out in cash and leave those who stay carrying the whole of the risk.

options.text: Main scheme ₹98 a unit and side pocket nil; segregation does not change what a unit is worth
options.misconception: treats the side pocket as a book entry, when the whole point is that the stressed asset leaves the main scheme's net asset value
options.why: Segregation separates the risky or doubtful assets from the other investments and cash holdings, so the main scheme's net asset value then reflects the actual value of the liquid assets — ₹90, not ₹98. Leaving it at ₹98 would let a redeeming investor take value out against a bond that cannot be sold except at a distress price.

options.text: Main scheme ₹92 a unit and side pocket ₹8 a unit
options.misconception: deducts the segregated bond from assets but never deducts the scheme's liabilities
options.why: (1,000 − 80) ÷ 10 = ₹92 forgets the ₹20 crore the scheme owes. Net asset value is total assets less total liabilities attributable to them, on a per unit basis, so the main scheme is (1,000 − 80 − 20) ÷ 10 = ₹90.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A debt scheme holds assets of ₹1,000 crore, of which one downgraded bond is carried at ₹80 crore, against liabilities of ₹20 crore. It has 10 crore units outstanding. The trustees segregate the downgraded bond into a side pocket, and every unit holder receives one side pocket unit for each unit of the main scheme he holds.

items.stem: What is the warrant's theoretical value, and what would it be if the share fell to ₹380?

options.text: ₹180 now, so the warrant is quoted ₹30 above it; and nil at ₹380, not a negative figure
options.why: The theoretical value of a warrant is the market price of the share less the exercise price, multiplied by the number of equity shares one warrant converts into. That is (460 − 400) × 3 = ₹180, and the ₹210 quote stands ₹30 above it because the market is also paying for the time the warrant has left to run. At a share price of ₹380 the difference turns negative, but the holder simply does not subscribe, so the theoretical value is nil.

options.text: ₹1,380 now, being three shares at their market price of ₹460
options.misconception: values the shares the warrant would buy rather than the advantage of buying them at the exercise price
options.why: 460 × 3 = ₹1,380 is what the three shares are worth, and the holder would still have to pay ₹1,200 to get them. What the warrant is worth is the difference, (460 − 400) × 3 = ₹180, so the exercise price has to come out.

options.text: ₹60 now, and negative ₹20 at ₹380
options.misconception: works the difference per share and never multiplies by the three shares one warrant carries
options.why: 460 − 400 = ₹60 is the gain on one share. One warrant carries three, so the theoretical value is ₹180. The number of equity shares convertible with one warrant is part of the formula, and leaving it out understates the value by two thirds.

options.text: ₹180 now, and negative ₹60 at ₹380, since the holder is committed to subscribe at ₹400
options.misconception: treats the warrant as an obligation to subscribe, when it is a right the holder simply declines to use
options.why: A warrant gives its holder an option, never an obligation — he may subscribe for the equity shares on offer within the period fixed for it, at the price fixed for it, or simply let the right lapse. At ₹380 he buys in the market instead, so the worst the warrant can be worth is nil. A negative theoretical value would mean the instrument cost its holder money to hold, which a right never does.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company's share trades at ₹460. Each of its listed warrants entitles the holder to subscribe three equity shares at ₹400 a share. The warrant itself is quoted at ₹210.

items.stem: What is free cash flow to equity, and is the director right?

options.text: ₹430 crore, the firm figure less interest net of tax
options.misconception: makes the interest adjustment and stops, treating new borrowing as irrelevant to equity cash flow
options.why: 500 − 70 = ₹430 crore is the right first step and only the first step. Money raised from lenders during the year is cash the shareholders did not have to provide, so net new borrowing of ₹100 crore is added, giving ₹530 crore. Ignoring it makes a company that gears up look poorer than one that does not.

options.text: ₹580 crore, the firm figure less interest net of tax plus the ₹150 crore drawn
options.misconception: counts the gross drawdown as the borrowing adjustment and forgets the ₹50 crore repaid in the same year
options.why: The adjustment is net new borrowing, which is the ₹150 crore drawn less the ₹50 crore repaid, that is ₹100 crore. Counting the drawdown alone credits the shareholders with money that went straight back out to a different lender, and overstates the figure by ₹50 crore.

options.text: ₹530 crore — larger than the firm figure, because the ₹100 crore of net new borrowing exceeded the ₹70 crore of after-tax interest
options.why: Free cash flow to the firm is measured before the claims of lenders, so getting to the equity figure means taking out what the lenders were actually paid and adding back what they newly advanced. Interest net of tax is 100 × 0.70 = ₹70 crore and net new borrowing is 150 − 50 = ₹100 crore, so 500 − 70 + 100 = ₹530 crore. The two are not the same figure and the equity one is larger here, which is why the firm figure is discounted at the weighted average cost of capital and the equity figure at the cost of equity.

options.text: ₹400 crore, the firm figure less the ₹100 crore of interest paid
options.misconception: deducts interest gross of tax and ignores the borrowing raised during the year
options.why: Interest is deductible, so the company only ever bore ₹70 crore of the ₹100 crore. And the ₹100 crore raised net from lenders reached the business in the same year. Both adjustments are part of the bridge, and leaving them out understates the equity figure by ₹130 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: For the year just ended a company's free cash flow to the firm is ₹500 crore. It paid interest of ₹100 crore, the tax rate is 30 per cent, and during the year it drew a new term loan of ₹150 crore and repaid ₹50 crore of an old one. Take free cash flow to equity as the free cash flow to the firm less interest net of tax plus net new borrowing. A director says the two figures must be the same because the same business generated them, and that in any case the equity figure can never be the larger of the two.

items.stem: What does an internal rate of return analysis, done properly, say?

options.text: Take L — the extra ₹200 lakh it needs brings in an extra ₹255 lakh, an incremental return of 27.5 per cent, which is above the 10 per cent cost of capital, so the larger project is worth the extra money
options.why: Where two projects are mutually exclusive, the question is not which has the higher rate but whether the extra outlay the bigger one demands earns enough. The difference between them is an outlay of 300 − 100 = ₹200 lakh returning 390 − 135 = ₹255 lakh, so the incremental return is 255 ÷ 200 − 1 = 27.5 per cent. Against a cost of capital of 10 per cent that increment is worth committing, so L is chosen — the same answer the net present values give, ₹54.55 lakh against ₹22.73 lakh, which is what a properly run rate analysis must reach.

options.text: Take S — the increment's 27.5 per cent is below S's own 35 per cent, so committing the extra ₹200 lakh lowers the return on the money
options.misconception: compares the incremental return with the smaller project's rate instead of with the cost of capital
options.why: The test for the increment is the cost of capital, because that is what the extra ₹200 lakh costs to raise and what it would otherwise earn. Twenty-seven and a half per cent against 10 per cent means the increment adds value. Insisting that every rupee earn as much as the best rupee would rule out most of the profitable investment a company ever makes.

options.text: The increment earns 30 less 35, that is minus 5 per cent, so the extra ₹200 lakh destroys value and S wins
options.misconception: subtracts one project's rate from the other's, when a rate on an increment has to be computed from the incremental cash flows themselves
options.why: Rates cannot be subtracted, because each is computed on a different outlay. The incremental return is worked from the incremental cash flows — ₹200 lakh out and ₹255 lakh back — which gives a positive 27.5 per cent, not a negative 5 per cent. Its present value is ₹31.82 lakh, exactly the gap between the two projects' net present values.

options.text: Take S — 35 per cent beats 30 per cent, and the board asked for the choice to be made on rates
options.misconception: ranks mutually exclusive projects by their own rates of return, which measures return per rupee rather than what the extra rupees earn
options.why: A rate says how hard each rupee works, not how many rupees are working. S leaves ₹200 lakh of the available money uncommitted, and that ₹200 lakh would have earned 27.5 per cent in L. Choosing S on the strength of 35 per cent trades a 27.5 per cent return on ₹200 lakh for nothing at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: Two mutually exclusive projects each run one year, at a cost of capital of 10 per cent. Project S costs ₹100 lakh now and returns ₹135 lakh in a year, an internal rate of return of 35 per cent. Project L costs ₹300 lakh now and returns ₹390 lakh in a year, an internal rate of return of 30 per cent. The board wants the choice settled on rates of return rather than on rupees.

items.stem: When does the maker recognise revenue on the spare parts?

options.text: Never on a bill-and-hold basis, since revenue on goods always waits for delivery
options.misconception: reads the standard as forbidding revenue before delivery, when it sets out the terms on which such revenue is recognised
options.why: The standard devotes a section of Appendix B to these arrangements precisely because they can support revenue. The discipline is in the four criteria, which stop a seller from invoicing goods it has not finished and calling the difference revenue.

options.text: On the date the four criteria for a bill-and-hold arrangement are met, even though the parts never leave the maker's warehouse
options.why: A customer can obtain control of a product that stays in the seller's physical possession, because it can direct the use of and obtain substantially all the remaining benefits from it while choosing not to take delivery. For a bill-and-hold arrangement, four criteria must be met on top of the ordinary indicators — the reason for the arrangement must be substantive, the product must be identified separately as belonging to the customer, the product must currently be ready for physical transfer, and the seller must be barred from putting those goods to its own use or sending them to any other buyer. All four hold here. The storage that follows is a separate custodial service.
keywords: identified separately as belonging to the customer

options.text: On despatch to the customer's own store, because control follows physical possession
options.misconception: treats physical possession as the whole test of control, when it is one indicator among several
options.why: Physical possession is an indicator of the transfer of control, not the definition of it. If it were the definition, no consignment would ever be excluded and no bill-and-hold arrangement would ever be recognised. The question is who can direct the use of the parts and take their benefits, and on these facts that is the customer.

options.text: On the invoice date, the customer having been billed and having taken the risk of loss
options.misconception: takes billing and risk of loss as sufficient, skipping the three criteria that ask whether the goods exist, are set aside and are beyond the seller's use
options.why: Invoicing and risk of loss are the easiest facts for a seller to arrange and the least probative. A maker could bill for parts still on the line and shift the risk by a clause. The other three criteria are what make the arrangement substantive.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B79 to B82, read with the indicators of transfer of control in para 38

items.scenario: A machine tool maker finishes a batch of spare parts a customer ordered. The customer asks the maker to keep them because its own store is full. The parts are labelled with the customer's name and kept on a rack set aside for that customer, they are ready to be shipped the moment the customer calls for them, and the maker cannot use them or divert them to anyone else. The customer has been invoiced and has accepted the risk of loss while the parts sit in the warehouse.

items.stem: What revenue does the contractor recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹25,00,000, being ₹20,00,000 of costs incurred over ₹40,00,000 of total expected costs, applied to the whole transaction price
options.misconception: leaves the uninstalled lifts inside the measure of progress, so a purchase order manufactures half a project's revenue
options.why: Half of ₹50,00,000 is the ₹25,00,000 here, and it says the contractor is halfway through a refurbishment on which it has laid one-fifth of the service work. Buying a lift is not progress towards refurbishing a building. That mismatch between cost and progress is exactly what the adjustment to the input method exists to correct.

options.text: Nil on the lifts until they are installed, so ₹7,00,000 for the year
options.misconception: withholds revenue on goods the customer already controls, on the ground that the contractor has not yet used them
options.why: Control of the lifts passed on delivery to the site. The adjustment does not defer their revenue; it strips out their margin, recognising revenue equal to cost so that buying them neither creates nor destroys profit.

options.text: ₹22,00,000 — ₹15,00,000 for the lifts at cost with no margin, plus 20 per cent of the remaining ₹35,00,000 of the transaction price
options.why: Where a cost incurred is not proportionate to the entity's progress, the input method is adjusted and revenue is recognised only to the extent of that cost incurred. The four conditions for that adjustment all hold — the lifts are not a distinct performance obligation, the customer takes control of them well before receiving the service, their cost is significant against total expected costs, and the contractor merely procures them. So the lifts are excluded from the measure of progress, which becomes ₹5,00,000 over ₹25,00,000, or 20 per cent. Twenty per cent of the ₹35,00,000 attributable to the service is ₹7,00,000, and the lifts add ₹15,00,000 of revenue equal to their cost.
keywords: only to the extent of that cost incurred

options.text: ₹6,25,000, being ₹5,00,000 over ₹40,00,000 applied to the whole transaction price
options.misconception: strips the lifts out of the numerator of the progress fraction but leaves their cost in the denominator, and gives them no revenue at all
options.why: This excludes the lifts twice over. Once their cost is taken out of the measure of progress, the ₹15,00,000 of expected lift cost comes out of the denominator too, leaving ₹5,00,000 over ₹25,00,000. And the lifts still carry revenue equal to their cost, because the customer controls them.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B19, read with para 39 to 41

items.scenario: A contractor refurbishes a building under a single performance obligation satisfied over time. The transaction price is ₹50,00,000. Expected costs are ₹15,00,000 for lifts bought in from a third party and ₹25,00,000 for construction services, ₹40,00,000 in all. The lifts reach the site half a year ahead of the date they go in, the customer obtains control of them on delivery, the contractor modifies nothing about them, and they are not a distinct performance obligation. By 31 March 2026 the lifts have been delivered and ₹5,00,000 of the other costs have been incurred. The contractor measures progress by a cost-to-cost input method.

items.stem: What revenue should the retailer report on each jacket sold?

options.text: Either ₹3,000 or ₹1,200, provided the basis is disclosed and applied consistently
options.misconception: turns a facts-driven determination into a presentation policy
options.why: Nothing offers an option here. The capacity in which an entity acts is a conclusion drawn from the facts, and two retailers with identical facts must report identically — which is the whole point of having indicators rather than a preference.

options.text: ₹3,000, because gross presentation is required whenever the entity issues the invoice to the customer in its own name
options.misconception: promotes invoicing into the test, which would make every agent a principal
options.why: The number is right and the reason would produce the wrong answer everywhere else. Agents routinely invoice and collect in their own name; the travel portal that only arranges a hotel room does exactly that. Invoicing is not among the indicators the standard lists.

options.text: ₹1,200, its margin, because the manufacturer made the jackets and the retailer only sells them
options.misconception: reads who produced the goods as deciding the capacity, when the test is who controls them immediately before transfer
options.why: Almost nothing a retailer sells was made by the retailer, and if manufacture decided the question no shop would report gross revenue. The standard asks about control of the specified good before it reaches the customer, and here the shop bought, stored, priced and risked it.

options.text: ₹3,000 — it is the principal, so it reports the gross amount of consideration
options.why: The indicators all point one way. The retailer is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise, it carries the inventory risk on unsold jackets and on returns, and it has discretion in establishing the price. Together those show that it obtains control of the jackets before they are transferred to the customer, which makes it the principal, and a principal recognises revenue in the gross amount of consideration to which it expects to be entitled.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B34A, B35 and B37, with the gross presentation in para B35B

items.scenario: A specialty retailer buys 5,000 winter jackets outright from a manufacturer at ₹1,800 each, takes them into its own warehouse, and sets its own shelf price of ₹3,000. It cannot return unsold stock, it handles every return and defect claim itself, and it bears the loss on whatever is left at the end of the season. It reports only its ₹1,200 margin per jacket as revenue, arguing that all it really does is put the maker's coat on a shopper's back.

items.stem: Which method of estimating variable consideration fits each contract?

options.text: The expected value for both, as the controller proposes, because it uses more of the available information
options.misconception: treats the more elaborate method as always the better predictor, when the standard picks the method that fits the shape of the outcomes
options.why: A probability-weighted figure on an all-or-nothing bonus produces an amount the contract can never pay — a number between nil and ₹5 crore that no outcome delivers. More arithmetic is not a better prediction when the arithmetic describes an impossible result.

options.text: The most likely amount for the commissioning bonus and the expected value for the volume rebate
options.why: An entity estimates variable consideration using either the expected value or the most likely amount, whichever it expects to better predict the consideration to which it will be entitled. The expected value, being the sum of probability-weighted amounts across a range of possible outcomes, suits an entity with a large number of contracts with similar characteristics, which the 4,000 rebate contracts are. The most likely amount, being the single most likely outcome, suits a contract with only two possible outcomes, which the all-or-nothing bonus is. The selection is not a free choice.

options.text: The most likely amount for both, since each contract in the end settles at one figure
options.misconception: reads the eventual single settlement as the test, when the choice turns on how many outcomes the contract can produce
options.why: Every contract settles at one figure eventually; that says nothing about how to estimate it today. Across 4,000 rebate contracts the single most likely tier ignores the whole distribution the company has years of data on.

options.text: Either method for either contract, provided the choice is applied consistently and disclosed
options.misconception: turns the selection into an accounting policy election
options.why: Consistency is required within a contract once a method is chosen, and that is a constraint, not a permission. The method itself is selected on the facts of each contract, and different types of variable consideration inside one contract may even take different methods.

citation.ref: para 53, read with para 54 and 55

items.scenario: A company has two contracts on hand. Under the first it will receive a single ₹5 crore bonus if a plant is commissioned by a fixed date and nothing at all if it is not, and there are no other outcomes. Under the second it supplies goods to 4,000 retailers under a volume rebate that settles at nil, 2 per cent, 5 per cent or 8 per cent depending on each retailer's purchases for the year, and the company has several years of data on how that population behaves. The financial controller wants the probability-weighted figure used for both, calling it the more scientific method.

items.stem: How are these items classified at 31 March 2026?

options.text: The inventories are current, but the trade payable is non-current because it falls due in fifteen months
options.misconception: keeps the operating-cycle limb for assets and drops it for liabilities
options.why: The liability test carries the same limb. A payable settled within the entity's normal operating cycle is current even if it is due more than twelve months after the reporting period, and showing the barley as working capital while its own supplier is long-term misstates the working capital position.

options.text: Everything but the overdraft is non-current, since a 26-month operating cycle is not clearly identifiable and the cycle defaults to twelve months
options.misconception: overrides a stated operating cycle with the twelve-month default, which applies only where the cycle cannot be identified
options.why: The default is a fallback for entities whose cycle cannot be pinned down. Here the cycle is stated as clearly identifiable at 26 months, so it governs, and a distiller's ageing period is the textbook case of a cycle longer than a year.

options.text: Only the bottled whisky and the overdraft are current; the barley and the spirit sit more than twelve months from cash and are non-current
options.misconception: applies the twelve-month test to items the operating-cycle limb has already made current
options.why: The two limbs are alternatives, not a sequence. An item that fails the twelve-month test can still be current on the operating-cycle test, which is why raw materials in a long process are shown as working capital rather than as long-term assets.

options.text: All three inventories and the fifteen-month trade payable are current, and the overdraft is current as well
options.why: An asset is current when the entity expects to realise it in its normal operating cycle, even where realisation is not expected within twelve months after the reporting period, so the barley, the spirit in barrels and the bottled whisky are all current. The same operating-cycle limb makes a trade payable current when it is settled in that cycle, whatever its due date, so the fifteen-month payable is current too. The overdraft is current on a different ground — no right to defer settlement for at least twelve months exists at the reporting date.
keywords: twelve months after the reporting period

citation.ref: para 66 and 68 for assets, para 69 and 70 for liabilities

items.scenario: A distiller ages whisky for 24 months before it can be sold, and its normal operating cycle is clearly identifiable at 26 months. At 31 March 2026 it holds barley and yeast, part-distilled spirit in barrels, and bottled whisky ready for sale, none of which will turn into cash within twelve months. It owes trade payables for the barley on supplier terms of fifteen months, set to match the ageing cycle, and it has a bank overdraft the bank may call at any time.

items.stem: What basic earnings per share is reported for the year ended 31 March 2026, and what happens to the comparative?

options.text: ₹10 for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹9 for the comparative, both on 1,00,00,000 shares
options.why: Where the number of ordinary shares increases as a result of a capitalisation or bonus issue, basic and diluted earnings per share are adjusted retrospectively for all periods presented. Where the change falls in the gap between the reporting date and the day those statements are approved for issue, the per-share calculations for the current and every prior period presented are based on the new number of shares. Ten crore over 1,00,00,000 shares is ₹10, and the ₹18 comparative halves to ₹9.

options.text: ₹20 for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹9 for the comparative
options.misconception: inverts the adjustment, restating the prior year alone
options.why: This restates the one year that is not being reported on and leaves alone the one that is. The adjustment applies to the current period and to every prior period presented, on the same new share count.

options.text: ₹10 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the ₹18 comparative left as published because it was reported before the bonus was even announced
options.misconception: restates the current year and leaves the comparative on a different share base
options.why: Two figures on two different share counts cannot be compared, which is the whole purpose of the restatement. Leaving the comparative at ₹18 would show earnings per share almost halving in a year when profit did not move.

options.text: ₹20 for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹18 for the comparative, the bonus issue belonging to the following year
options.misconception: treats a bonus issue after the reporting date as an event of the next year, when the rule reaches back across every period presented
options.why: Ten crore over 50,00,000 shares is the ₹20 here. It would make next year's figure fall by half for no reason a reader could see. The bonus adds shares without adding resources, so the same profit is simply divided among more shares in every year shown.

citation.ref: para 64, read with para 26 to 28 and the disclosure carve-out in para 71(d)

items.scenario: A company had 50,00,000 equity shares in issue throughout the year ended 31 March 2026 and profit attributable to equity holders of ₹10 crore for that year. Its published basic earnings per share for the previous year was ₹18. On 5 May 2026 it made a one-for-one bonus issue. The financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 were approved for issue on 20 May 2026.

items.stem: What combination does Ind AS 108 permit?

options.text: None of them may be combined, because combination requires the segments to be similar in each of the five respects
options.misconception: applies the test for aggregating reportable segments, which demands all five, to below-threshold segments, where a majority is enough
options.why: The two tests sit at deliberately different heights. Aggregating segments that would otherwise have been reported separately hides something the reader would have seen, so it demands similarity in each of the five respects. Segments below every threshold were never going to appear on their own, so the bar for combining them is a majority of the same respects.

options.text: P and Q may be combined, and R must then be reported as a segment of its own, since it can be combined with nothing
options.misconception: turns an inability to combine into a requirement to report separately
options.why: Failing to qualify for combination does not promote a segment across thresholds it has already failed. A below-threshold segment that cannot be combined is reported in an all other segments category, whose sources of revenue are described.

options.text: All three may be combined, all three having similar economic characteristics and none of them being separately reportable in any event
options.misconception: reads similar economic characteristics as the whole of the lower test as well
options.why: Similar economic characteristics is the first condition of both tests and the whole of neither. R is alike to P in one respect out of five, so combining them would report as one business two things that share almost nothing a reader would recognise.

options.text: P and Q may be combined into one reportable segment; R may be combined with neither and goes into an all other segments category
options.why: Operating segments that do not meet the quantitative thresholds may be combined to produce a reportable segment only where a majority of the aggregation criteria are satisfied by both and the two have similar economic characteristics. P and Q share three of the five respects, which is a majority, so the combination is open to them. R shares one, which is not, so it stands apart and its information goes into an all other segments category alongside the other business activities that are not separately reportable.

citation.ref: para 14, read with the aggregation criteria in para 12 and the all other segments category in para 16

items.scenario: A group has three operating segments that all fall below every quantitative threshold. Segments P and Q have similar economic characteristics and are alike in the nature of their products, the nature of their production processes and the class of customer they serve, but they distribute through different channels and work under different regulatory environments. Segment R has similar economic characteristics to P but is alike to it in only one of the five respects. Management asks whether any of them may be combined.

items.stem: At what amount are the inventories carried at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹52,50,000, absorbing the whole ₹15,00,000 of fixed overhead into the 3,75,000 units at ₹4 a unit
options.misconception: absorbs fixed overhead on actual production, which carries the cost of idle capacity into the value of the stock
options.why: Dividing an unchanged ₹15,00,000 by a reduced 3,75,000 units gives ₹4 a unit and quietly capitalises the power failure. The rate is set by what the plant is built to make, not by what a bad year happened to produce, so that the loss falls in the year it arose.

options.text: ₹48,75,000, with ₹3,75,000 of unallocated fixed overhead recognised as an expense
options.why: Fixed production overheads are allocated to the costs of conversion on the basis of the normal capacity of the production facilities, being the production expected on average over a number of periods under normal circumstances. Fifteen lakh over five lakh units is ₹3 a unit, so the 3,75,000 units actually made absorb ₹11,25,000. A year that falls short of normal output leaves unallocated overheads behind, and those are expensed in the very year they arise rather than parked in stock, so the remaining ₹3,75,000 goes to profit or loss. Variable production overheads are allocated on the basis of the actual use of the production facilities, so the whole ₹7,50,000 stays in cost, giving ₹30,00,000 plus ₹7,50,000 plus ₹11,25,000.
keywords: actual use of the production facilities

options.text: ₹46,87,500, allocating both the fixed and the variable overheads on the basis of normal capacity
options.misconception: applies the normal-capacity basis to variable overheads, which are allocated on actual use
options.why: Variable overheads move with volume by definition, so there is no idle capacity inside them to strip out. Spreading ₹7,50,000 over five lakh units and charging only 3,75,000 of them would leave ₹1,87,500 of real, incurred, volume-driven cost outside inventory for no reason.

options.text: ₹41,25,000, the whole of the fixed overhead being expensed because production was abnormally low
options.misconception: takes an abnormally low year as putting every fixed overhead outside cost, when only the unallocated part goes
options.why: The units that were made still consumed their proper share of the plant. Only the share attributable to capacity that stood idle is unallocated, which is ₹3,75,000 of the ₹15,00,000, and the other ₹11,25,000 is a genuine cost of conversion.

citation.ref: para 13, read with the definition of the costs of conversion in para 12 and the exclusions in para 16

items.scenario: A plant has a normal capacity of 5,00,000 units a year and incurs fixed production overheads of ₹15,00,000, which do not move with output. A prolonged power failure held actual production for the year ended 31 March 2026 to 3,75,000 units. Direct materials and direct labour for those units came to ₹30,00,000, and variable production overheads, which vary directly with volume, were ₹7,50,000. Every unit is still unsold at the year end and net realisable value is well above cost.

items.stem: How much of the ₹155 lakh enters the carrying amount of the factory?

options.text: ₹30 lakh, the December testing cost alone
options.why: A factory stops absorbing further cost into its carrying amount once it stands where management meant it to stand and works as management meant it to work — the point at which it becomes capable of operating in the manner intended by management, here 1 January 2026. Testing whether the asset functions properly came before that date and is directly attributable, so it capitalises. Everything after it is named in the standard as excluded — costs incurred while an item capable of operating has yet to be brought into use, initial operating losses while demand builds up, and the costs of relocating or reorganising part of an entity's operations.
keywords: capable of operating in the manner intended by management

options.text: ₹95 lakh, everything except the initial operating losses
options.misconception: capitalises the idle-period salaries and the relocation, which the standard names as exclusions alongside the operating losses
options.why: All three are on the same list. Relocating or reorganising part of an entity's operations is expenditure on the business, not on the building, and idle-period costs buy nothing the asset did not already have on 1 January.

options.text: ₹155 lakh, everything spent getting the factory into production
options.misconception: capitalises every cost up to the first sale, which would put a start-up's trading losses into its buildings
options.why: On this logic a loss-making launch would raise the carrying amount of the plant that caused it. Capitalisation stops at readiness, and losses while demand builds up are the clearest case of a cost the asset did not need.

options.text: ₹70 lakh, the testing plus the idle-period salaries, since production had not yet begun
options.misconception: takes the start of production as the cut-off, when the cut-off is the date the asset became capable of operating as intended
options.why: The two dates are two months apart here and the standard uses the earlier one. Once the factory could have run, the delay was the company's own choice about staffing, and a company cannot lengthen an asset's cost by taking its time.

citation.ref: para 20, read with para 16 and 17

items.scenario: A new factory is complete and capable of operating in the manner management intended on 1 January 2026, but the company does not start production until 1 March while it recruits operators. It incurred ₹30 lakh in December 2025 testing whether the plant functioned properly. Between January and March 2026 it incurs ₹40 lakh of salaries for plant staff while the factory stood ready but unused, ₹60 lakh of losses in February and March because demand for the output has yet to build up, and ₹25 lakh moving a department out of an old site and into the new factory.

items.stem: When does capitalisation of borrowing costs begin, and what happens on 31 January 2026?

options.text: It begins on 18 July 2025, when physical construction started, and ceases for the first building on 31 January 2026
options.misconception: leaves technical and administrative work out of the activities necessary to prepare the asset
options.why: Those activities include technical and administrative work before physical construction begins, such as obtaining permits. What they exclude is merely holding an asset while nothing is being done to change its condition, which is why interest on land held with no development on it does not capitalise.

options.text: It begins on 19 June 2025 and runs on every building until the last one is finished, the park being a single project
options.misconception: keeps capitalising on a part already fit for use because other parts are unfinished
options.why: The commencement date is right and the ending is not. Where each part can be used independently, cessation is judged part by part, so the first building's borrowing costs stop on 31 January 2026 while the rest carry on.

options.text: It begins on 19 June 2025, and on 31 January 2026 it ceases for the first building alone while continuing on the other three
options.why: Capitalisation begins on the commencement date, which is the date on which the entity first satisfies all three conditions — it incurs expenditures for the asset, it incurs borrowing costs, and preparatory work on the asset itself has begun. Interest began on 15 May and the preparatory activities on 2 June, but the first expenditure came only on 19 June, so the latest of the three dates governs. Where a project finishes building by building, and one finished building is capable of being used even though work carries on elsewhere on the site, capitalisation stops for that building once the work needed to ready it is substantially done.

options.text: It begins on 15 May 2025, when interest first accrued, and ceases for the whole park only when the last building is ready
options.misconception: starts on the first of the three dates instead of the last, and treats a park of separately usable buildings as one indivisible asset
options.why: Interest running is one condition of three, and interest incurred before any money has gone into the asset has bought the asset nothing. At the other end, a building tenants have already moved into is finished whatever the neighbours look like.

citation.ref: para 17, read with para 18 and 19, and the completion in parts in para 24

items.scenario: A company is building a business park of four buildings, each of which can be used on its own while work continues on the others. The project is funded entirely by borrowing. Loan interest on the project began to accrue on 15 May 2025. Technical site planning and the work of obtaining permits began on 2 June 2025. The first expenditure on the project was incurred on 19 June 2025. Physical construction started on 18 July 2025. The first building was substantially ready for its intended use on 31 January 2026, with the other three still unfinished.

items.stem: What reversal is recognised at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹34 lakh in all — ₹4 lakh on the patent, ₹15 lakh on the plant and ₹15 lakh on the building — leaving the unit at ₹142 lakh, with nothing credited to goodwill
options.why: A reversal for a cash-generating unit is spread across the unit's assets pro rata with what each of them is carried at, except for goodwill, which takes none of it. No asset may then be increased above the lower of its recoverable amount and the carrying amount, net of depreciation, it would have shown had the earlier impairment never been recognised at all. Those ceilings are ₹4 lakh, ₹15 lakh and ₹15 lakh, and an amount one ceiling blocks is reallocated pro rata to the others until they fill too. That exhausts ₹34 lakh of the ₹42 lakh headroom, and the ₹8 lakh no asset can absorb is not credited anywhere, because an impairment loss recognised for goodwill is never reversed.

options.text: No reversal at all, because the unit's original loss fell first on goodwill and a goodwill impairment cannot be reversed
options.misconception: extends the bar on reversing goodwill to every other asset in the same unit
options.why: The bar is on goodwill and nothing else. The patent, the plant and the building each carry a loss that the standard requires to be reversed once the estimates behind recoverable amount have changed, and ₹34 lakh of it can be.

options.text: ₹42 lakh allocated pro rata on carrying amounts, being ₹7 lakh on the patent and ₹17.5 lakh on each of the plant and the building
options.misconception: applies the pro rata step without the ceiling that sits on each individual asset
options.why: Pro rata on ₹18, ₹45 and ₹45 lakh does give those figures, and every one of them breaches its own ceiling — the patent would reach ₹25 lakh against a ₹22 lakh limit and the plant and building ₹62.5 lakh against ₹60 lakh. A reversal may not carry an asset above where it would have stood had it never been impaired.

options.text: ₹42 lakh, taking the unit to its ₹150 lakh recoverable amount, with the ₹8 lakh the individual ceilings block credited back to goodwill
options.misconception: reverses an impairment loss recognised for goodwill, which the standard prohibits outright
options.why: Goodwill is the one asset whose impairment loss is never reversed, because any later increase in its recoverable amount is likely to be internally generated goodwill, which cannot be recognised. The ₹8 lakh simply is not recognised, and the unit stops at ₹142 lakh.

citation.ref: para 122 and 123, with the bar on reversing goodwill in para 124

items.scenario: A cash-generating unit was impaired two years ago, and the loss was large enough to write its goodwill down to nil. At 31 March 2026 it carries a patent at ₹18 lakh, plant at ₹45 lakh and a building at ₹45 lakh, ₹108 lakh in all. Recoverable amount has risen to ₹150 lakh and the indicators for a reversal are clearly met. Had no impairment loss ever been recognised, the carrying amounts net of depreciation at this date would have been ₹22 lakh for the patent, ₹60 lakh for the plant and ₹60 lakh for the building.

items.stem: How is the ₹9 crore treated?

options.text: Recognised in profit or loss as incurred, while the acquired brand itself stays on the balance sheet at ₹60 crore
options.why: Where a brand, a masthead, a publishing title or a customer list is already on the books, subsequent expenditure aimed at it is recognised in profit or loss as incurred, whether the item was externally acquired or internally generated, because such expenditure cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. The acquisition gave the brand a cost, measured in a transaction with a third party. The campaign gives it none, and the acquired asset is unaffected either way.
keywords: recognised in profit or loss as incurred
developing the business as a whole

options.text: Recognised in profit or loss, and the ₹60 crore brand written off as well, since brands cannot sit on a balance sheet
options.misconception: extends the bar on internally generated brands to a brand acquired in a business combination
options.why: The bar is on internally generated brands. A brand acquired as part of a business combination is recognised separately from goodwill where it is identifiable, and its acquisition-date fair value is its cost. Only the spending that follows is expensed.

options.text: Capitalised into the brand's carrying amount, the brand being a recognised asset already
options.misconception: applies the ordinary subsequent-expenditure test to a class of item the standard singles out by name
options.why: Ordinary subsequent expenditure on an intangible can be capitalised where it meets the recognition criteria. Brands and their cousins are carved out of that, precisely because nobody can tell where spending on the brand ends and spending on the business begins.

options.text: Capitalised to the extent an independent valuer certifies that the brand's value has risen by at least ₹9 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a valuation for a recognition rule
options.why: A valuer can price the brand, and the answer changes nothing. Recognition is settled before measurement is reached, and here the standard settles it against capitalisation whatever the value has done.

citation.ref: para 20, read with para 63

items.scenario: A company acquires a business and, as part of it, recognises an acquired brand at its ₹60 crore acquisition-date fair value. Over the following year it spends ₹9 crore on advertising, sponsorship and a repositioning campaign aimed squarely at that same brand. The marketing director says the ₹9 crore should be added to the brand's carrying amount, because it plainly makes the brand stronger and the brand is already an asset on the balance sheet.

items.stem: What is wrong with the accounting, and how does the plant stand at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — an asset still physically capable of use is depreciated whatever its classification, and the classification stands
options.misconception: keeps depreciating an asset whose carrying amount is now to be recovered by sale rather than by use
options.why: Depreciation allocates cost over the period an asset's benefits are consumed in use. Once recovery is through a sale transaction, there is no consumption to allocate, which is why the standard stops the charge at the classification date.

options.text: The plant is written up to ₹24 lakh, fair value less costs to sell now exceeding its carrying amount
options.misconception: reads the measurement rule as a two-way test rather than as a ceiling
options.why: The rule takes the lower of the two figures, so it can only ever write an asset down. Fair value above carrying amount changes nothing, and a gain is recognised only to the extent of impairment losses previously recognised on that asset.

options.text: The ₹5 lakh of depreciation should never have been charged; the plant remains classified as held for sale and is carried at ₹20 lakh
options.why: A non-current asset is not depreciated while it is classified as held for sale, because it is being recovered through sale rather than through use, so the ₹5 lakh comes back. The one-year period is extended where the delay is caused by events or circumstances beyond the entity's control and there is sufficient evidence that the entity remains committed to its plan to sell, and contamination found by a buyer's inspection is precisely that. Measurement stays at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, so ₹20 lakh stands.

options.text: The depreciation is rightly reversed, but classification must cease because the sale did not complete within one year
options.misconception: applies the one-year period as absolute, ignoring the extension for delays outside the entity's control
options.why: The one-year expectation is tested at classification, and the standard then provides for exactly this — a delay caused by circumstances beyond the entity's control, with the entity still committed to its plan. Declassifying here would reverse the presentation and restart depreciation on an asset that is genuinely for sale.

citation.ref: para 25 for depreciation, with the extension to the one-year period in Appendix B, para B1

items.scenario: A plant was classified as held for sale on 1 April 2025, when the criteria were plainly met. It then had a carrying amount of ₹20 lakh, fair value less costs to sell of ₹24 lakh, and four years of useful life left. The company went on charging depreciation of ₹5 lakh through the year. In February 2026 a committed buyer withdrew after its inspection found contamination nobody had known about; the company began remediation at once, is still actively marketing the plant and expects to sell within the following year. Fair value less costs to sell at 31 March 2026 is still ₹24 lakh.

items.stem: At what amounts are the two measured, and in which levels do the measurements sit?

options.text: The shares at ₹22.50 but still as a Level 1 measurement, the input remaining an exchange price for the identical share
options.misconception: keeps the Level 1 label on a measurement whose quoted price has been adjusted
options.why: The amount is right and the label is not. Level 1 is defined by quoted prices, unadjusted, in active markets for identical assets, and the word unadjusted does the work. The moment judgement is applied to the quote, the measurement drops out of that level.

options.text: The shares at ₹22.50 as a Level 2 measurement, and the unlisted security as a Level 3 measurement
options.why: A quoted price in an active market is used without adjustment whenever it is available, but a quoted price may fail to represent fair value where a significant event occurs on the measurement date after the close of trading. The non-approval was a condition of the asset existing at the measurement date and the ₹22.50 opening price shows how market participants priced it, so the closing price is adjusted, and once adjusted the measurement is no longer a Level 1 measurement. If the adjustment to a price seen in the market has to be built out of an unobservable input, and it moves the result significantly, the measurement is categorised within Level 3.

options.text: The shares at ₹36 as a Level 1 measurement, an exchange closing price being used unadjusted, and the unlisted security as a Level 2 measurement
options.misconception: applies the unadjusted-quoted-price rule to a price that no longer reflects a condition existing at the measurement date, and ignores what a significant unobservable adjustment does to the level
options.why: The unadjusted rule holds while the quote is faithful. Here the market had not yet been told what the regulator had decided, so the closing price values a drug that had already failed. And an observable starting point does not keep a measurement in Level 2 once an unobservable adjustment is what drives it.

options.text: The shares at ₹36, with the fall disclosed as a non-adjusting event after the reporting period, and the unlisted security as a Level 3 measurement
options.misconception: treats the regulator's decision as an event after the reporting period, when it was a condition of the asset existing at the measurement date
options.why: The decision was taken and communicated on 31 March. What arrived afterwards was the market's reaction to it, and a reaction is evidence of a condition that already existed rather than a new event.

citation.ref: para 77 and 79, read with the level determination in para 73 and 75

items.scenario: A company holds listed shares in a biotechnology firm and measures them at fair value at 31 March 2026. The shares closed at ₹36 that day. After trading closed on 31 March the drug regulator told the firm that its lead drug had not been approved, the firm put out a press release that evening, and the shares opened at ₹22.50 on the next trading day. The company also holds an unlisted security priced from the quoted price of a similar traded instrument, reduced by a significant adjustment for a restriction on sale that no market data supports.

items.stem: How does the lessor classify this lease?

options.text: A single finance lease over the whole property, the thirty-year term covering the major part of the building's economic life
options.misconception: treats land and buildings as one unit when the land element is far from immaterial
options.why: A lessor may treat them as a single unit only where the amount for the land element is immaterial to the lease, in which case the building's economic life stands for the whole. Land worth ₹80 crore against a building worth ₹120 crore is not immaterial by any reading.

options.text: A single finance lease, because payments over one title cannot be split between the two elements
options.misconception: reaches for the fallback that applies where allocation is unreliable, when the scenario says the split can be made reliably
options.why: The fallback is real — where the lease payments cannot be allocated reliably the whole contract is classified as a finance lease, and only plain evidence that each of the two elements is an operating lease keeps it out of that class. It is reached only when allocation fails, and here the relative fair values are given.

options.text: The two elements are assessed separately — the building element is a finance lease and the land element an operating lease
options.why: For a lease that includes both land and buildings, the lessor assesses the classification of each element separately, given that land normally has an indefinite economic life. The lease payments are allocated between them in proportion to the relative fair values of the leasehold interests at the inception date, which is 60 to 40 here. Thirty years over a thirty-year building whose fair value is substantially recovered transfers substantially all the risks and rewards, so that element is a finance lease. Thirty years over land that will still be there afterwards transfers nothing like all of them, so that element is an operating lease.

options.text: A single operating lease over the whole property, land of indefinite life never transferring substantially all the risks and rewards
options.misconception: lets the land element decide the classification of the building element as well
options.why: The conclusion about land is right and it does not travel. Assessing the elements separately exists so that a building whose value is substantially recovered is recognised as sold on credit, whatever the ground it stands on.

citation.ref: para 55 and 56, read with the classification criteria in para 63

items.scenario: A lessor grants a thirty-year lease of a plot with a factory building standing on it. The building's remaining economic life is thirty years; the land's is indefinite. At the inception date the leasehold interests are worth ₹120 crore for the building and ₹80 crore for the land, and the annual rent can be reliably allocated in that proportion. The present value of the payments allocated to the building amounts to substantially all of the building's fair value.

items.stem: What deferred tax is recognised on the land?

options.text: None, because land is a non-depreciable asset and non-depreciable assets give rise to no temporary differences
options.misconception: denies that a difference exists at all, when one plainly does and it is the exception rather than its absence that blocks recognition
options.why: A temporary difference is the gap between carrying amount and tax base, and ₹50 crore against nil is a gap whether the asset depreciates or not. Getting the right answer from the wrong premise fails the moment the same land is revalued or sold under a regime that does allow a deduction.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore, being 25 per cent of the ₹50 crore difference
options.misconception: applies the general rule to a difference the initial recognition exception carves out
options.why: The general rule is real and it has three exceptions written into the same paragraph. This transaction falls squarely inside the second of them, so the arithmetic is right and the recognition step never opens.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore, with the matching debit added to the cost of the land
options.misconception: grosses up the asset, which is the outcome the exception was written to prevent
options.why: Carrying the land at ₹62.5 crore would report a plot at more than anyone paid for it, and then depreciate or impair that inflated figure. The standard names this and refuses it.

options.text: None, even though a ₹50 crore taxable temporary difference plainly exists
options.why: A deferred tax liability is recognised for all taxable temporary differences save in one case: the difference came out of the initial recognition of an asset or of a liability, the deal itself was not a business combination, and on the day it was struck it moved neither accounting profit nor taxable profit. Both conditions hold on this purchase, so the exception bites and nothing is recognised. The alternative would be to gross up the cost of the land itself, which the standard says would make the financial statements less transparent.
keywords: neither accounting profit nor taxable profit

citation.ref: para 15(b) and para 22, read with the deferred tax asset mirror in para 24

items.scenario: A company buys a plot of land for ₹50 crore in a transaction that is not a business combination. Under the tax law the land carries no depreciation allowance and no deduction of any kind, on purchase or on eventual sale, so its tax base is nil. The purchase affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit at the time it happens. The tax rate is 25 per cent. The finance team proposes a deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore on the ₹50 crore taxable temporary difference.

items.stem: What goes to profit or loss and what goes to other comprehensive income?

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and a ₹17 crore gain in other comprehensive income
options.why: Net interest is found by applying the discount rate to the net defined benefit liability, so 7 per cent of the ₹120 crore deficit is ₹8.4 crore, and that with the ₹30 crore of current service cost gives ₹38.4 crore in profit or loss. The return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest is a remeasurement, and the amount included in net interest is 7 per cent of the ₹500 crore of plan assets, being ₹35 crore. The actual return of ₹52 crore, already stated after the costs of managing plan assets, exceeds that by ₹17 crore, and the excess is recognised in other comprehensive income.

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and a ₹19 crore gain in other comprehensive income, adding back the ₹2 crore spent on managing the plan assets
options.misconception: treats the costs of managing plan assets as a separate expense, when the return on plan assets is defined net of them
options.why: The return on plan assets is interest, dividends and other income together with realised and unrealised gains, less the costs of managing plan assets and any tax payable by the plan itself. The ₹52 crore is already that net figure, so adding the ₹2 crore back counts it twice.

options.text: ₹30 crore charged to profit or loss, with the whole ₹52 crore earned on the plan assets credited there as investment income
options.misconception: puts the entire actual return through profit or loss, when only the part measured at the discount rate belongs there
options.why: Splitting the return at the discount rate is the whole design. The part the entity could have expected from the passage of time sits in profit or loss inside net interest; the part that depends on how markets happened to move is a remeasurement and stays out of the operating result.

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and nothing in other comprehensive income, there having been no actuarial gain or loss this year
options.misconception: reads remeasurements as meaning actuarial gains and losses alone
options.why: Remeasurements are three things and not one — actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets outside net interest, and any change in the effect of the asset ceiling outside net interest. The obligation was quiet this year and the assets were not.

citation.ref: para 123 and 127, with the definition of the return on plan assets in para 8 and the profit or loss and OCI split in para 120

items.scenario: At 1 April 2025 a company's gratuity plan holds plan assets with a fair value of ₹500 crore against a defined benefit obligation of ₹620 crore, and the discount rate at that date is 7 per cent. Through the year the plan assets earn ₹52 crore after ₹2 crore of costs of managing them. Current service cost is ₹30 crore. There were no contributions, no benefits paid, no plan amendment and no change in any actuarial assumption, and the timing of cash flows within the year may be ignored.

items.stem: What is provided for at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing — neither the ₹4 crore fitting cost nor any fine, because no present obligation exists at the reporting date for either
options.why: A provision answers only to a duty the company already carries — past events existing independently of whatever it may decide to do next. The company can avoid the fitting cost entirely by its own future actions — by changing its method of operation, or by closing or selling the factory — so there is no present obligation for it. The fine has a different obligating event, which is operating the factory without filters once the law bites, and that has not happened yet.

options.text: ₹4 crore, since the law is already enacted and the company cannot lawfully run the factory without filters
options.misconception: reads an enacted law as the obligating event, when the entity can still avoid the expenditure by changing what it does
options.why: Enactment fixes what will be required of anyone who chooses to operate; it does not oblige this company to operate. A law that can be sidestepped by the entity's own future decisions creates no liability today, however certain the company is that it will comply.

options.text: Nothing for the fitting, but a provision for the fines expected from 1 June 2026 onwards
options.misconception: provides for a penalty whose obligating event, operating without filters, has not yet occurred
options.why: A fine for unlawful operation is a genuine obligation once the unlawful operation happens, which is why penalties and clean-up costs for damage already caused are provided. Here nothing has been operated unlawfully at the reporting date.

options.text: Nothing recognised, but the ₹4 crore is disclosed as a contingent liability
options.misconception: calls a future cost the entity can avoid a contingent liability, when there is no possible obligation arising from a past event at all
options.why: A contingent liability is a possible obligation arising from past events whose existence depends on uncertain future events. There is no past event here. Future expenditure the entity controls is not disclosed as a contingency; it is simply next year's cost.

citation.ref: para 19, read with the recognition conditions in para 14 and the definition in para 10

items.scenario: A law taking effect on 1 June 2026 requires factories of a certain type to be fitted with smoke filters. At 31 March 2026 a company's factory has no filters and none has been ordered. Fitting them will cost ₹4 crore. A factory that operates after 1 June 2026 without filters attracts a fine. The company intends to keep the factory running and has not decided when it will fit them.

items.stem: How does Ind AS 32 classify the three instruments?

options.text: All three are equity, since none of the triggering events is within the issuer's control
options.misconception: inverts the rule — an event outside the issuer's control is what makes the instrument a liability, not what saves it
options.why: Control by the issuer is what would allow it to avoid payment. Where the issuer cannot avoid the settlement because the trigger is beyond its control, the obligation is real and the instrument is a liability.

options.text: The first is a financial liability; the second and third are equity
options.why: A contingent settlement provision that could require the issuer to deliver cash should some doubtful event come to pass, an event beyond the control of both parties to the contract, makes the instrument a financial liability, and a revenue test is exactly such an event. Two exceptions rescue the others. An obligation that can arise only on liquidation of the issuer does not create a liability, and neither does a part of the provision that is not genuine, meaning one with no commercial substance.

options.text: The first is equity because the revenue test may never be met, and the second and third are liabilities
options.misconception: classifies on how likely the trigger is rather than on whether a contingent obligation exists
options.why: Probability plays no part. The question is whether the issuer has an obligation it cannot avoid should the event occur, and a revenue test the company cannot control is such an obligation whether it fires or not.

options.text: All three are financial liabilities, each of them being redeemable in cash on some event
options.misconception: applies the contingent settlement rule without the two exceptions written into it
options.why: The rule and its exceptions sit in one paragraph. Without them, every perpetual instrument would become a liability the moment somebody wrote a liquidation clause into it, and an absurd trigger would carry the same weight as a real one.

citation.ref: para 25, read with the exception for obligations arising on liquidation in para 16(b) and the definition in para 11

items.scenario: A company issues three instruments. The first must be redeemed in cash if the company's revenue falls below ₹500 crore in any of the next five years, an outcome neither the company nor the holders control. The second must be redeemed in cash only if the company goes into liquidation. The third carries a redemption clause triggered if a named director's grandchild is born on 29 February, a possibility both parties accept has no commercial substance whatever.

items.stem: Where is the simplified approach compulsory and where is it a choice?

options.text: Compulsory only for the 45-day receivables; for the other two, lifetime expected credit losses are an accounting policy the company may adopt but need not
options.why: The simplified approach is mandatory for trade receivables and contract assets that result from transactions within the scope of Ind AS 115 and contain no significant financing component. Where a trade receivable does contain a significant financing component, and for lease receivables, the entity may choose as its accounting policy to measure the loss allowance at lifetime expected credit losses; if it does not, the general three-stage model governs those balances. The policy is elected separately for trade receivables and for lease receivables.

options.text: Compulsory for all three, since the simplified approach exists precisely so that receivables need no staging assessment
options.misconception: reads the simplified approach as covering every receivable, when its mandatory limb is confined to those without a significant financing component
options.why: The convenience is real and its scope is not unlimited. Once a receivable carries a financing component it starts to behave like a loan, which is why the standard offers the simplification there instead of imposing it.

options.text: Compulsory for the first two and unavailable for the lease receivables, leasing being outside the scope of Ind AS 115
options.misconception: reads the scope of Ind AS 115 as the boundary of the election, when the standard extends it separately to lease receivables under Ind AS 116
options.why: Lease receivables are named in their own limb of the same paragraph, with their own election. And the second set is not compulsory, because its financing component is exactly what moves it into the optional limb.

options.text: Compulsory for none of them — the simplified approach is an election available across all three
options.misconception: turns a mandatory rule into an election
options.why: For plain trade receivables there is no choice at all. The word used is that an entity shall always measure the loss allowance at lifetime losses for them, which is why a provision matrix is the ordinary practice rather than an option.

citation.ref: para 5.5.15, read with the general model in para 5.5.3 and 5.5.5

items.scenario: A company holds three sets of balances at 31 March 2026. The first are trade receivables from ordinary 45-day sales with no financing element in them. The second are trade receivables on a three-year deferred-payment arrangement that does contain a significant financing component. The third are finance lease receivables from equipment the company lets out. The credit controller says the simplified approach must be applied to all three, since all three are receivables.

items.stem: What happens to each reserve balance?

options.text: All three are reclassified in full to profit or loss, each being a disposal of part of the group's interest
options.misconception: treats every reduction in a holding as a disposal of the whole foreign operation
options.why: Full reclassification belongs to a full disposal, or to a partial one that costs the group control. A 10 per cent sale that leaves control intact is a transaction with the group's own co-owners and never touches profit or loss.

options.text: All three balances stay in equity until the last share of each operation has been sold
options.misconception: waits for a complete exit before anything is recycled
