items.scenario: The representation letter on your file deals with three matters, each of them a point the team raised during the audit: contingent liabilities, related party transactions and events after the reporting date. It says nothing about management's responsibility for the financial statements and nothing about whether everything relevant was given to you. It is dated the same day as your report and states that it covers the year ended 31 March 2026, although your report also covers the comparative figures for the previous year.

items.stem: What does SA 600 require of the principal auditor beyond the statement in the report?

options.text: Advise the other auditor of the use to be made of his work and report and make sufficient arrangements for coordination — the areas requiring special consideration, the procedures for identifying inter-component transactions and the timetable — and then consider the significant findings of the other auditor, which may be done by discussing the audit procedures applied or by reviewing a written summary of his procedures and findings
options.why: SA 600 puts work at both ends. Before the other auditor starts, the principal auditor advises him of the use to be made of his work and report and coordinates the areas needing special consideration, the identification of inter-component transactions and the timetable. After it, the principal auditor considers the significant findings of the other auditor, and may either talk through the procedures that were applied or read a written summary — a completed questionnaire or checklist — of what was done and what came out of it.
keywords: use to be made of his work

options.text: Re-audit the three branches himself, since he cannot state a division of responsibility for work whose quality he has not established
options.misconception: replaces a review of another auditor's work with a second audit the standard does not require
options.why: Ordinarily the principal auditor may lean on what the other auditor did, and only special circumstances — ones making a visit to the component or an examination of its books essential — displace that. Re-auditing every branch would make the division of work pointless.

options.text: Obtain the other auditors' complete working paper files in every case and re-perform a selection of their tests before signing
options.misconception: turns an exceptional step into the routine requirement
options.why: Visiting the component and examining its records is available where special circumstances call for it. As a standing practice it ignores the ordinary route the standard sets out — discussion of procedures, or a written summary of them and of the findings.

options.text: Nothing — a signed report from a member of the same profession is itself the evidence, and the statement of division in the report is what tells the reader where responsibility sits
options.misconception: treats receipt of another auditor's report as the whole of the principal auditor's work
options.why: The statement of division tells the reader how much of the audit was somebody else's. It does not tell the principal auditor anything, and he is the one who has to conclude on the financial statements as a whole.

citation.ref: the principal auditor's procedures — advising the other auditor of the use to be made of his work, coordination, and consideration of the other auditor's significant findings — read with the statement of division of responsibility

items.scenario: You are the principal auditor of a company with three branches audited by other firms. You never told those firms what use you would make of their work, what areas needed special attention, how inter-branch transactions were to be identified, or when you needed their reports. Each firm sent you a signed audit report on its branch in due course. You have filed all three, read none of the reasoning behind them, asked no questions, and drafted your report stating the division of responsibility and the magnitude of the divided portion.

items.stem: What is missing from the Basis for Opinion section?

options.text: A cross-reference to the part of the report that sets out what the auditor is responsible for under the Standards on Auditing, and a statement that he is independent of the entity under the ethical requirements bearing on this audit and has met his other ethical duties, naming the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section carries four things and the draft has two. It states that the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing, refers to the section of the report describing the auditor's responsibilities under those standards, includes a statement that the auditor is independent of the entity and has fulfilled his other ethical responsibilities — referring to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI — and states whether the auditor believes the evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate.

options.text: A description of the audit procedures performed on each material account balance, so that the reader can judge whether the evidence really was sufficient
options.misconception: turns the basis section into an account of the audit programme, which no standard requires
options.why: The report says whether the auditor believes the evidence is sufficient and appropriate; it does not set out the evidence. Where a matter of most significance needs describing, that is done in the Key Audit Matters section and only where SA 701 applies.

options.text: Nothing — the two sentences present are the whole of what the standard asks for under that heading
options.misconception: keeps the two elements everyone remembers and drops the cross-reference and the independence statement
options.why: The independence statement is the part a reader cannot get anywhere else in the report, and it is required in every report rather than only where independence has been in question. The section is short, and it is not two sentences short.

options.text: The key audit matters, which belong inside the Basis for Opinion section because they are the matters the opinion actually rests on
options.misconception: puts key audit matters inside the basis section, when SA 701 gives them a section of their own
options.why: Key audit matters have their own section, later in the report, and the standard states in terms that the auditor does not provide a separate opinion on them. Folding them into the basis would read as though the opinion turned on those matters alone.

citation.ref: the Basis for Opinion section, directly following the Opinion section

items.scenario: A draft auditor's report on a company's financial statements carries an Opinion section and then a Basis for Opinion section of two sentences. One says the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing. The other says the firm believes the evidence it gathered is sufficient and appropriate for the opinion it has given. Nothing else appears under that heading.

items.stem: What does SA 701 require?

options.text: Keep the section and state under the Key Audit Matters heading that the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate in the report
options.why: The section stays. Where the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate, the report carries a Key Audit Matters heading and says so in terms. The point is that a reader of a listed company's report knows the section is required, so its absence would read as an omission and its presence with that sentence is a positive statement the auditor is standing behind.
keywords: no key audit matters to communicate

options.text: Leave the section out — a heading with nothing under it conveys less than silence, and the requirement is to communicate matters, not to announce their absence
options.misconception: reads the requirement as conditional on there being something to say
options.why: Silence and a statement look identical to a reader and mean opposite things. One of them says the auditor considered the question and reached an answer; the other could equally mean the section was forgotten.

options.text: Move the statement into the Basis for Opinion section, which is where the report explains what the opinion rests on
options.misconception: relocates a required section into another, when each carries its own heading
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section has its own four elements and this is not among them. A reader looking for the Key Audit Matters heading in a listed company's report would not find it.

options.text: Determine a key audit matter from the largest balance in the financial statements so that the section is not empty
options.misconception: fills the section by size, when the determination runs on matters that required significant auditor attention
options.why: A balance being large is not a reason it required significant auditor attention. Manufacturing a matter tells the reader that something was of most significance in the audit when nothing was, which misdescribes the audit.

citation.ref: the presentation where the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate

items.scenario: A listed company has had an uneventful year. There are no higher assessed risks of material misstatement, no significant management judgements, no unusual transactions and no going concern question. Working through the matters communicated with those charged with governance, you conclude honestly that none of them was of most significance in the audit. The partner proposes to leave the Key Audit Matters heading out of the report altogether, on the ground that an empty heading looks like an oversight.

items.stem: Which of the two may be left out of the Key Audit Matters section?

options.text: Both, since describing either would damage the company and the auditor is not required to harm the entity he audits
options.misconception: reads commercial harm as a general licence to omit, when the second exception is extremely rare and closed once the entity has itself disclosed
options.why: Damage to the entity is the beginning of the enquiry, not the end. The exception asks whether the adverse consequences would outweigh the public interest benefits, and a company that has already told the stock exchange has answered that itself.

options.text: Neither — a matter determined to be a key audit matter is described in the report without exception, which is what makes the section reliable
options.misconception: denies the two exceptions the standard states in the same requirement
options.why: The exceptions are written into the requirement. The first exists because an auditor cannot be asked to break a statute in order to comply with a standard, and the second exists for the extremely rare case where publication would do more harm than good.

options.text: Only the regulatory investigation, because law precludes public disclosure about the matter; the customer dispute must be described, because the extremely rare adverse-consequences exception does not apply where the entity has itself publicly disclosed information about the matter
options.why: SA 701 describes every key audit matter in the report unless one of two things is true. Either law or regulation precludes public disclosure about the matter, which the governing statute here does; or, in extremely rare circumstances, the auditor determines that the adverse consequences of communicating would reasonably be expected to outweigh the public interest benefits — and that second exception is expressly unavailable where the entity has publicly disclosed information about the matter, which this stock exchange filing did.

options.text: Only the customer dispute — commercial damage is the plainer case for omission, while a regulator's investigation is a matter of public interest that must be described
options.misconception: inverts the two exceptions, omitting the one the standard closes and describing the one law forbids
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. The statute settles the investigation without any weighing at all, and the company's own filing removes the dispute from the only exception that could have covered it.

citation.ref: para 14

items.scenario: Two matters in a listed company's audit have been determined to be key audit matters. The first is a confidential regulatory investigation into the company, which the governing statute forbids anybody from disclosing publicly until it concludes. The second is a dispute with the company's largest customer; management argues that any public mention would wreck the renegotiation now under way, though the company itself has already filed a disclosure with the stock exchange naming the customer and the amount at stake.

items.stem: What does SA 706 require of the paragraph?

options.text: Only a heading — the wording inside is the auditor's own, and pointing at the note is a courtesy to the reader rather than a requirement
options.misconception: treats the reference to the disclosure as optional, when the standard requires the paragraph to point at where the matter is fully described
options.why: The reference is what keeps the paragraph tied to the financial statements. Without it the auditor is telling the reader about something the reader cannot go and read, which is the opposite of drawing attention to a disclosure.

options.text: The placement is right — the Basis for Opinion section is where a matter of this importance belongs, so that the reader meets it immediately after the opinion
options.misconception: puts the paragraph inside another required section, when the standard asks for a separate section of its own
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section has its own contents and a fire is none of them. Burying an emphasis inside it also removes the heading a reader scans for.

options.text: The paragraph is right in substance, and the auditor's own doubt about recoverability is exactly what an Emphasis of Matter paragraph exists to convey
options.misconception: uses the paragraph to introduce the auditor's own view, when it refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: The paragraph points at the entity's disclosure and adds nothing to it. A doubt about recoverability that the financial statements do not carry is either a matter for the opinion or a matter to be disclosed by the entity, and in neither case does it belong in an emphasis.

options.text: A separate section with a heading that includes the term "Emphasis of Matter"; a clear reference to the matter being emphasised and to where the relevant disclosures that fully describe it can be found in the financial statements, referring only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements; and a signal to the reader that what has been emphasised leaves the audit opinion unmodified
options.why: SA 706 states three things. The paragraph goes in a separate section of the report under a heading that includes the term Emphasis of Matter. It carries a clear reference to the matter and to where the relevant disclosures fully describing it can be found, and it refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements. And the reader has to be told the opinion is not modified on account of the matter emphasised, without which he cannot tell the paragraph from a qualification.

citation.ref: the requirements when the auditor includes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — separate section with an appropriate heading, clear reference to the matter and to the relevant disclosures, and an indication that the opinion is not modified

items.scenario: A fire destroyed a company's Nashik plant after the year end. It is fully and correctly disclosed in note 34, no modification of the opinion is required as a result of it, and SA 701 does not apply to this audit. You have decided an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is proper. The draft puts a single sentence inside the Basis for Opinion section, reading, "Attention is drawn to the fire at the Nashik plant, which in our view casts doubt on the recoverability of the related insurance claim." There is no reference to note 34 and nothing about the opinion.

items.stem: What does section 141 require?

options.text: The firm vacates the office of auditor now — a person is disqualified where a relative of his holds a directorship in the company or works there as a director or as key managerial personnel, one disqualified partner disqualifies the firm, and a disqualification incurred after appointment obliges the auditor to vacate, the vacancy so caused being deemed a casual vacancy
options.why: Two provisions run together. A person is not eligible to be appointed auditor if a relative of his sits on the company's board, or is employed by it as a director or as key managerial personnel; and where a firm is appointed, the disqualification of any partner disqualifies the firm. Section 141 then deals with the disqualification arising later: where a person appointed as auditor incurs any of the disqualifications after his appointment, he shall vacate his office and such vacation shall be deemed to be a casual vacancy in the office of the auditor.

options.text: The engagement partner steps aside and the second partner signs, the disqualification attaching to the individual rather than to the firm
options.misconception: builds a wall inside the firm, when the statute disqualifies the firm on any partner's disqualification
options.why: Where a firm is appointed as auditor, the disqualification of a partner is the firm's disqualification. Moving the signature changes who holds the pen and not who is appointed.

options.text: Nothing happens this year — the eligibility tests are applied on the date of appointment, and a fact arising afterwards is dealt with by not seeking reappointment
options.misconception: reads section 141 as a test applied once, when the section deals expressly with a disqualification incurred after appointment
options.why: The section has a sub-section written for exactly this sequence. If eligibility were tested only at appointment, an auditor could become as interested as he liked the day after and still sign the report.

options.text: The firm may continue for the remainder of the year if the audit committee records that it is satisfied with the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a governance body approve past a statutory disqualification
options.why: The audit committee recommends and oversees; it cannot make an ineligible person eligible. The statute names the disqualifications and no committee is given a power to waive them.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(f) read with Section 141(3) proviso on firms and Section 141(4)

items.scenario: A firm is appointed auditor of a company in August and is clean on every test on that date. In January the engagement partner's brother is appointed chief financial officer of the same company and is designated as its key managerial personnel. The firm proposes to complete the year's audit and simply not offer itself for reappointment, on the footing that the disqualification tests in section 141 are applied as at the date of appointment. A second partner offers to sign the report instead, having no relative anywhere near the company.

items.stem: What must the report state?

options.text: Both, but they belong in the report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order rather than in the auditor's report under section 143
options.misconception: moves two statutory statements from the section that requires them into an Order that does not
options.why: The Order adds matters to the auditor's report; it does not take any away. These two are section 143(3) clauses and are answered in the auditor's report itself.

options.text: Both of the omitted matters — whether the branches he never went to sent him returns adequate for the purposes of his audit, and whether the report on each branch audited by somebody other than the company's auditor reached him, together with what he did with that report when drawing his own
options.why: Section 143(3) asks its own list of questions and two of them are about branches. The books-of-account clause runs on into a second question about the branches not visited by him: did proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit reach the auditor from them? A separate clause then asks whether the report on any branch audited under section 143(8) by somebody other than the company's auditor was sent to him, and the manner in which he has dealt with it when drawing his own report.
keywords: proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit
the manner in which he has dealt with it

options.text: Only the branch returns statement; what passed between the company's auditor and a branch auditor is a professional matter between the two of them
options.misconception: keeps the clause about returns and drops the clause about the branch auditor's report, which the section states separately
options.why: The section asks in terms whether the branch auditor's report reached him and how he dealt with it, which is precisely the reader's interest — the principal auditor's opinion covers the whole company including branches he never saw.

options.text: Neither — those statements are required only where the auditor has something adverse to say about a branch, and here he has not
options.misconception: reads the section 143(3) matters as exception reporting, when each is answered expressly in every report
options.why: They are statements, not exceptions. A reader checks the answers as given, and a blank where an answer should be tells him nothing about whether the question was even asked.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(b) and Section 143(3)(c), read with Section 143(8)

items.scenario: A company has eleven branch offices. You visited two of them. Four branches were audited under section 143(8) by other chartered accountants, whose reports reached you before you signed. Your draft report answers the books-of-account question — proper books have been kept, so far as your examination of them shows — and stops there. You have left out any mention of the branches you did not visit and any mention of the branch auditors' reports, on the footing that the branch auditors answer for their own work and any reader may read their reports for himself.

items.stem: Which of the three breach section 144?

options.text: The first and the second — for a firm the section reaches services rendered through any entity in which the firm or any partner has significant influence or control and through any entity whose name, trade mark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners, and the prohibition covers services to the holding company as well as to the company
options.why: The Explanation to section 144 defines rendering services directly or indirectly, and for a firm it reaches services rendered by itself, by any of its partners, by its parent, subsidiary or associate entity, by any entity in which the firm or any partner of the firm has significant influence or control, and by any entity whose name or trade mark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners. Design and implementation of a financial information system and actuarial services are both on the prohibited list, and the list applies to the company, its holding company and its subsidiary company alike.

options.text: Only the second — a separately registered foreign entity is a separate person, however similar its name, and control is the only connection the section recognises
options.misconception: reads the brand limb out of the Explanation, leaving a network that shares a name outside the section
options.why: The Explanation names the shared name, trade mark or brand as a connection in its own right, precisely because a network can be built without any shareholding at all. Ignoring that limb leaves the easiest arrangement untouched.

options.text: None — the prohibition binds the appointed auditor, and neither the brand-sharing entity nor the controlled associate is the appointed auditor of this company
options.misconception: confines the section to the appointed auditor, when the Explanation exists to reach services rendered indirectly
options.why: If the section stopped at the appointed auditor it would be answered by incorporating a second entity. The Explanation was written to say who else counts, and both of these entities are inside it.

options.text: All three — any service rendered to an audit client by anyone connected with the auditor is prohibited once the audit is held
options.misconception: reads the prohibition as covering every service, when the section bars a named list and routes the rest through approval
options.why: The section bars nine categories and leaves the door open to any other service that the Board of Directors, or the audit committee, has approved. Representation before a tax authority is not on the list and it had the approval the section contemplates.

citation.ref: the Explanation to Section 144 on services rendered directly or indirectly in the case of a firm, read with the prohibited list and its extension to the holding company and the subsidiary company

items.scenario: A firm is the statutory auditor of a company. During the year three things happen. An entity registered in another country, which is not a partner of the Indian firm but trades under the same brand name that the firm and its partners use, designs and implements the company's new financial information system. An entity in which the audit firm holds control provides actuarial services to the company's holding company. And a partner of the firm, in his personal capacity, appears for the company before the goods and services tax appellate authority, an engagement the audit committee approved in advance.

items.stem: Who appoints the first auditor now, and how long does the appointee hold office?

options.text: The members, at an extraordinary general meeting, the Board's own window having passed — and the appointee holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, not for a term of five years
options.why: Section 139(7) sets a cascade for a government company and each step opens only when the one before it fails. The Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints first; on his failure the Board appoints within its own window; on the Board's failure the company informs the members, who appoint the first auditor at an extraordinary general meeting. Whoever makes the appointment, the first auditor holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, which is what makes him the first auditor rather than an auditor with a term.

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General, whose power over a government company's audit cannot lapse whatever period the section names
options.misconception: treats the constitutional auditor's role as making the statutory period ornamental
options.why: The Comptroller and Auditor-General's powers over a government company are wide and this particular one is time-bound. The section says what happens if he does not appoint within the period, which it would not need to say if the power never lapsed.

options.text: The Board, whose power revives once the Comptroller and Auditor-General has failed and is not limited by any period
options.misconception: keeps a lapsed power alive by reading the Board's window as open-ended
options.why: The Board's power is the second step of a cascade and it carries its own period. Reading that period away would delete the members' step entirely, and the section would then have no way of ever producing an auditor if the Board did nothing.

options.text: The members, and the appointee holds office for five years, subject to ratification by the members at each annual general meeting
options.misconception: gives the first auditor the five-year term of a subsequent auditor and revives a ratification requirement that has been omitted from the Act
options.why: The first auditor's office ends at the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, which is where the ordinary appointment machinery takes over. The requirement of annual ratification was omitted from the Act and is no part of the answer either way.

citation.ref: Section 139(7), read with Section 139(6)

items.scenario: A government company within the meaning of section 2(45) is registered on 1 April. The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India does not appoint a first auditor within the sixty days the section allows him from the date of registration. The Board then lets its own thirty-day window pass without appointing anybody either. It is now 15 July and the company still has no auditor. The company secretary advises the Board that on the Comptroller and Auditor-General's failure the power simply reverts to the Board with no time limit on it, and that whoever is appointed will hold office for five years like any other auditor.

items.stem: What does clause 3(i) require the auditor to report?

options.text: That the company keeps no proper record of its Property, Plant and Equipment — nothing setting out full particulars, quantitative details and situation — and none of its intangible assets; that nobody has verified those assets physically at any reasonable interval; and that benami proceedings are pending against the company, with an answer on whether their details have been disclosed in the accounts
options.why: Clause 3(i) is a set of separate questions and three of them are answered badly here. One asks whether the records of Property, Plant and Equipment are proper ones — full particulars, quantitative details and situation, and the same again for intangible assets. Another asks whether management has physically verified those assets at intervals that are reasonable. A third asks whether proceedings for holding benami property have been begun against the company or are pending against it, and, where they have, whether the details of them were disclosed in the accounts.

options.text: Nothing — the title deeds are all in the company's name and there was no revaluation during the year, so the clause is answered clean
options.misconception: answers the two sub-clauses the auditor remembers and leaves the records, the verification and the benami sub-clauses unread
options.why: Title deeds and revaluation are two sub-clauses of five. A clean answer on those says nothing about whether the company can tell anybody what assets it owns or where they are.

options.text: The record-keeping and verification failures, but not the benami proceedings, which are a legal matter for the company's own disclosure and not for the auditor to raise
options.misconception: hands a named CARO reporting duty to the company's disclosure and off the auditor's report
options.why: The sub-clause asks the auditor two things about the proceedings — that they exist, and whether the company has appropriately disclosed the details. The second question only makes sense because the first is his to report.

options.text: Only the physical verification point, the maintenance of registers being a matter of internal record-keeping and the benami notice being sub judice
options.misconception: reduces three reportable findings to one, on grounds the clause does not recognise
options.why: The clause asks about the records in terms, and it asks about proceedings that have been initiated or are pending — which is what a pending proceeding is. Neither is excused by being internal or by being before an authority.

citation.ref: Clause 3(i)(a), Clause 3(i)(b) and Clause 3(i)(e)

items.scenario: A company's fixed asset register shows only the total cost of each class of plant. It carries no quantitative details and no situation, and the company's intangible assets appear in no register at all. Property, plant and equipment have not been physically verified by anybody for four years. The Initiating Officer under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 has issued a notice to the company in respect of a warehouse and those proceedings are pending; the notes to the accounts say nothing about them. Every title deed is in the company's own name and there was no revaluation during the year.

items.stem: What does clause 3(ii) require?

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(a) on whether physical verification was conducted at reasonable intervals by the management and whether, in the auditor's opinion, the coverage and procedure of such verification is appropriate — the part coverage and the walk-through both speak to that — and report that discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate for a class of inventory were noticed and how they were dealt with in the books of account; clause 3(ii)(b) does not arise, no working capital limits having been sanctioned
options.why: Clause 3(ii)(a) asks three things. Has management verified the inventory physically, and at intervals that are reasonable? Is the coverage and procedure of that verification, in the auditor's own opinion, appropriate? And were discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate found in any class of inventory — where they were, the second half of the sub-clause asks whether such discrepancies ended up properly dealt with in the books of account. Clause 3(ii)(b) bites only on a company holding working capital limits above five crore rupees sanctioned against current assets, and this one holds none.
keywords: properly dealt with in the books of account

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(b) as well, since the sub-clause applies to every company that finances inventory, whether or not limits were sanctioned
options.misconception: applies the quarterly-returns sub-clause to a company with no sanctioned working capital limits against current assets
options.why: That sub-clause has its own trigger — working capital limits in excess of five crore rupees sanctioned at any point in the year on the basis of security of current assets. With no limits there are no quarterly returns to compare with anything.

options.text: Nothing at all — the discrepancy was written off before the year end, so the books are right and the accounts carry no misstatement
options.misconception: reads a disclosure clause as though it asked whether the accounts are wrong
options.why: Correcting the books is the second half of the sub-clause, not an escape from it. The clause asks whether the discrepancy was noticed and how it was dealt with, and a write-off is the answer to the second question rather than a reason to skip the first.

options.text: Report the discrepancy only — how much of the inventory management chose to count and by what method are management's own arrangements, on which the auditor expresses no view
options.misconception: drops the auditor's own opinion on coverage and procedure, which the sub-clause asks for by name
options.why: The sub-clause says in terms, in the opinion of the auditor. Coverage of sixty-two per cent and an estimate in place of a count for work in progress is exactly the fact pattern that question exists to surface.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ii)(a), read with Clause 3(ii)(b)

items.scenario: A company counts its inventory once a year, on 31 March. This year management's team counted only the two largest of its five warehouses, which hold sixty-two per cent of the value, and used a walk-through estimate rather than a count for work in progress. In one of the warehouses counted, the shortfall in a class of raw material was fourteen per cent of that class in the aggregate; the shortfall was written off in the books before the year end. The company has never been sanctioned working capital limits by any bank or financial institution.

items.stem: What does clause 3(ix) require?

options.text: Only the pledge, since it is the single arrangement on which any default has actually occurred
options.misconception: uses default as the trigger for sub-clauses whose triggers are the transaction itself
options.why: The short-term-for-long-term sub-clause and the subsidiary-obligation sub-clause are triggered by the utilisation and by the taking of the funds. Default appears only inside the pledge sub-clause, as an extra question once a pledge is reported.

options.text: Three separate reports — that money raised on a short term basis was put to a long term use, with the nature and amount; that funds were taken to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, with the nature of the transaction and the amount; and that a loan was raised on the pledge of securities held in a joint venture, with details and with the default in repayment of that loan
options.why: Clause 3(ix) is six questions and the company has answered the first three cleanly and the last three badly. A cash credit facility repayable on demand and spent on a warehouse is money borrowed on a short term basis and then put to a long term use, which the auditor reports with its nature and amount. The borrowing that paid the subsidiary's instalment is funds taken to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures. And where a loan comes against the pledge of securities the company holds in a subsidiary, a joint venture or an associate, the sub-clause wants the details and asks on top of that whether repayment of such a loan has been defaulted on.

options.text: Nothing — there was no default on any borrowing of the company's own, it is not a wilful defaulter, and every term loan went where it was meant to go
options.misconception: answers the first three sub-clauses of the clause and treats them as the whole of it
options.why: Those are three sub-clauses and there are six. The three the company fails are about where the money came from and what it was pledged against, which no amount of punctual repayment touches.

options.text: All three, and the auditor must in addition report the company as a wilful defaulter, two missed instalments being a default deliberately made
options.misconception: has the auditor make a declaration the clause asks him only to report if a lender has made it
options.why: The sub-clause asks only this: has some bank, financial institution or other lender declared the company a wilful defaulter? The declaration is theirs to make and the auditor's to report; he does not reach the conclusion himself from missed instalments.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ix)(d), Clause 3(ix)(e) and Clause 3(ix)(f)

items.scenario: During the year a company draws ₹12 crore on its cash credit facility, repayable on demand, and builds a new warehouse with it. It borrows ₹8 crore from a non-banking finance company expressly to pay an instalment falling due on its subsidiary's loan. And it raises a ₹20 crore loan by pledging the shares it holds in its joint venture, and has since missed two instalments on that loan. On its own term loans the company has never defaulted, every rupee was spent on the purpose for which it was raised, and it is not a declared wilful defaulter.

items.stem: Where does Clause 7 of Part I of the First Schedule bite?

options.text: On all three, a letterhead being a professional document and everything printed on it a statement about the member
options.misconception: treats every fact on a letterhead as an advertisement, when the objection is to attainments and to the practice date rather than to the firms' names
options.why: The clause reads what is being said. Firm names identify where the member practises; a date of establishment is a claim of standing, which is why one is permitted and the other is not.

options.text: On none — the member did not write the offer document and a letterhead is not published to the world at large
options.misconception: excuses the member from a publication he is named in, when the Council places on him the duty to see that it does not advertise his attainments
options.why: The Council's position is that the member concerned has to take the necessary steps. It is his name and his attainments in the document, and a member who lets them appear has not taken them.

options.text: On the offer document and on the practice date — a description of the member's expertise and specialisation in a company's offer document is misconduct and he must take steps to see that it does not appear, and a letterhead may not carry the date of setting up of practice; naming all three firms on his personal letterhead is permitted
options.why: The Council has said that a prospectus or an announcement put out by a company on whose board a practising chartered accountant sits is misconduct if it describes his expertise, his specialisation and his knowledge of a field; the member has to take the steps needed to keep his professional attainments out of it. Separately, the date of setting up of practice, and the date the firm itself was established, may not be printed on a letterhead. Nothing bars a member holding a certificate of practice from printing on his personal letterhead the names of every firm in which he is a partner.
keywords: date of setting up of practice

options.text: On the offer document alone — a letterhead advertises nothing once it carries no description of services
options.misconception: reads the clause as reaching only descriptions of services, when it separately restrains claims a member may not print
options.why: The practice date describes no service and still says something about the member's attainments. That is why the position on letterheads is stated separately from the position on write-ups describing services.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 7, read with the Council's decisions on a prospectus of a company in which a member is a director and on what a letterhead may carry

items.scenario: CA Bhatt holds a certificate of practice and is a partner in three firms. He is also a director of a listed company, and that company's offer document names him as a director and sets out his areas of specialisation and his standing in the profession. His own personal letterhead names all three firms in which he is a partner. Beneath the names, the letterhead adds the line "In practice since 1998".

items.stem: Where does Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule bite?

options.text: On CA P — failing to complete the work and submit the report in time, so that the company could not meet its statutory requirement, is a failure to exercise due diligence; CA Q's slip is one of the minor errors and lapses which do not amount to gross negligence and do not constitute professional misconduct
options.why: A member falls inside the clause when his professional duties are carried out without due diligence, or with gross negligence. Delivering late, so that the client cannot comply with a statute, is a want of care of that kind even where the work itself was sound. At the far end sit minor errors and lapses: carelessness of that order is not by itself the gross negligence the clause is about, and the Council draws such matters to a member's attention instead of referring him.

options.text: On both — the clause reaches negligence of every degree, and each member fell short of the care his client was entitled to
options.misconception: flattens a clause that distinguishes minor lapses from gross negligence into a single standard
options.why: Negligence is a word with a very wide field. At one edge it runs up against fraud; at the other it shades into collateral minor negligence. Professional misconduct sits at the serious end of it, and a ₹4,000 slip the member found and fixed himself is at the other end.

options.text: On CA Q alone — an arithmetical error is a failure of care, while a missed deadline is a matter of the engagement letter rather than of professional conduct
options.misconception: sends a want of due diligence into the contract and treats a self-corrected slip as the misconduct
options.why: It is the wrong way round. A slip the member caught himself is evidence that his review worked, and delay that costs the client its statutory compliance is the classic instance of the clause.

options.text: On neither — no set of accounts was misstated in either case, so nobody was misled and there is nothing for the clause to punish
options.misconception: measures the clause by whether the financial statements ended up wrong, when it asks whether the member brought reasonable skill, care and caution to his duties
options.why: The test is the skill, care and caution a reasonably competent, careful and cautious auditor would use. A report that arrives too late to be used has failed the client whatever the accounts said.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 7

items.scenario: Two members are complained against. CA P accepted a company audit, did not complete his work and did not submit his audit report in time, so the company could not comply with the statutory requirement that depended on it; nothing he did do is criticised as wrong. CA Q, auditing a manufacturer, made an arithmetical slip in one schedule which overstated a note by ₹4,000; he found it himself and corrected it before the report was signed, and no other part of his file is criticised.

items.stem: Where does Clause 9 leave him?

options.text: Not guilty — Clause 9 applies where an auditor is appointed in place of a retiring auditor at an annual general meeting, and a vacancy arising mid-year is outside it
options.misconception: narrows the clause to one route of appointment, when the duty to ascertain runs on any appointment as auditor of a company
options.why: The clause speaks of accepting an appointment as auditor of a company, with no route excluded. The Council's own guidance sets out the checks for a first auditor, for an appointment after a resignation or removal, and for a joint auditor not reappointed.

options.text: Not guilty — a casual vacancy caused by a resignation is filled by the Board alone, so there were no general meeting records for him to inspect in the first place
options.misconception: stops at the Board's power to fill a casual vacancy, when an appointment to fill a vacancy caused by resignation must also be approved by the company at a general meeting
options.why: The Board fills the vacancy, and where the vacancy arose from a resignation the appointment must also be approved by the company in general meeting. Those are precisely the records the incoming auditor should have seen and was refused.

options.text: Guilty — to ascertain means to find out for certain, so a certificate from the management is not sufficient; the incoming auditor verifies the company's relevant records himself, and where the company will not allow that verification he should not accept the audit assignment
options.why: The Council has spelt out what the clause asks of an incoming auditor. To ascertain is to find out for certain, and a management certificate that the provisions have been complied with will not be sufficient for that purpose; the relevant records of the company have to be verified by the auditor himself. Where the company will not let him look at them, the incoming auditor should not accept the audit assignment. Iyer did the opposite of both.
keywords: should not accept the audit assignment

options.text: Not guilty — a written certificate from the company is exactly the ascertainment from the company that the clause calls for, and he obtained it before accepting
options.misconception: reads ascertaining from the company as receiving the company's own assurance, when the Council requires verification of the records
options.why: The clause exists because the company is the party whose compliance is in question. Taking its word for it would make the duty circular, which is why the Council put the word ascertain under a microscope.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 9, read with the Council's guidelines on the records an incoming auditor is to verify and with Section 139(8) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: CA Iyer is offered the audit of a company whose previous auditor resigned in the middle of the year. He asks the company whether the appointment provisions have been complied with, and the managing director hands him a signed certificate saying that all the requirements of sections 139 and 140 have been duly complied with. Iyer then asks to see the board minutes and the notice and resolution of the general meeting. The company refuses, saying the certificate should be enough for anybody. Iyer accepts the appointment.

items.stem: What do section 138 and Rule 13 say?

options.text: Covered, and the general manager may be appointed, and as internal auditor he settles the scope, functioning and periodicity of the internal audit himself
options.misconception: leaves the scope with the internal auditor, when the Audit Committee or the Board formulates it in consultation with him
options.why: Consultation is not delegation. An internal auditor who sets his own scope decides which parts of the company will never be looked at, which is the one decision the rule takes away from him.

options.text: Not covered — the tests for an unlisted public company are paid-up share capital and turnover, and this company is under both
options.misconception: reads the unlisted public company criteria as two, when borrowings and deposits stand beside capital and turnover
options.why: There are four criteria and any one of them brings the company in. Deposits sit there because a company holding public money has depositors with an interest in its controls whatever its size on the other measures.

options.text: Covered, but the appointment is invalid — an internal auditor must be a chartered accountant in practice and must not be an employee of the company he audits internally
options.misconception: imports the independence conditions of a statutory audit into an office the rule expressly opens to employees and to members not in practice
options.why: The rule says the opposite twice over. It names a cost accountant as eligible, it adds the words whether engaged in practice or not, and it leaves the office open to somebody who may or may not be an employee of the company.

options.text: The company is covered, because deposits standing at twenty-five crore rupees or above at any time in the year before are on their own enough to bring an unlisted public company in; the appointment is valid, because a cost accountant is eligible whether or not he practises, and the office is open to somebody on the company's own payroll; but the Audit Committee or the Board formulates the scope and periodicity, in consultation with him
options.why: An unlisted public company is tested on four criteria joined by "or", and one of them is outstanding deposits standing at twenty-five crore rupees or above at any point in the year before, so thirty-one crore brings the company in whatever capital and turnover do. Rule 13 opens the office to a chartered accountant, to a cost accountant — whether engaged in practice or not — and to any other professional the Board settles on, adding that the person appointed may or may not be an employee of the company. The scope, the functioning, the periodicity and the methodology of the internal audit are then fixed by the Audit Committee, or by the Board, after consulting the internal auditor.
keywords: whether engaged in practice or not
may or may not be an employee

citation.ref: Section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — the unlisted public company criteria including outstanding deposits, who may be appointed as internal auditor, and the formulation of the scope by the Audit Committee or the Board

items.scenario: An unlisted public company has paid-up share capital of twelve crore rupees, turnover of ninety crore rupees, no borrowings at all from banks or public financial institutions, and outstanding deposits of thirty-one crore rupees at one point during the preceding financial year. It proposes to appoint its own general manager (finance) as internal auditor. He is a cost accountant, he is an employee of the company, and he is not in practice. The managing director says internal audit does not apply because capital and turnover are both under the limits, and that in any event an employee cannot be an internal auditor. He adds that if it does apply, the general manager will settle the scope and periodicity himself.

items.stem: Where do these three sit under SA 220 (Revised)?

options.text: Only the shareholding is his — the competence of the team is a staffing decision for whoever allocates people, and continuance was settled when the engagement was accepted
options.misconception: drops the assignment of engagement teams from the engagement partner's list and treats continuance as a one-off decision
options.why: The assignment of engagement teams is one of the heads the standard names, and continuance is a conclusion revisited rather than a door that shuts at acceptance. A partner who cannot say who on his team can audit a derivative book has not discharged either.

options.text: The engagement partner's responsibility is the review of the audit documentation before the report is issued, so all three are premature
options.misconception: confines the engagement partner to engagement performance, which is one head among several
options.why: Review is the last of the partner's responsibilities, not the whole of them. By the time the file reaches him, an independence breach and an under-skilled team have already shaped every working paper he is reading.

options.text: All three are the engagement partner's own responsibility — he spots the independence threat that no safeguard can bring down to an acceptable level and takes it to the relevant persons within the firm, so that whatever creates the threat is removed or the firm walks away where the law lets it walk away; he satisfies himself that the conclusions reached on acceptance and continuance of the client relationship are appropriate; and he makes sure the team, taken together with any auditor's expert brought in from outside it, has between them the competence and the capabilities this engagement needs
options.why: The standard describes the engagement partner's responsibilities under named heads, and only one of them is engagement performance. On ethics, the partner identifies a threat to independence and reports it to the relevant persons within the firm, so the activity or interest can be eliminated or the firm can withdraw where legally permitted. On acceptance and continuance, the conclusions reached about the client relationship are his to be satisfied about, not the risk partner's alone. And on the assignment of the engagement team, he ensures the team together with any auditor's expert outside it collectively have the appropriate competence and capabilities for the work.

options.text: All three belong to the firm's system of quality control, and the engagement partner is entitled to rely on that system, so nothing here is for him to do
options.misconception: treats the firm's system of quality control as discharging the engagement partner's own engagement-level responsibilities
options.why: An engagement team may rely on the firm's system, but that reliance ends the moment information in front of the team says otherwise — and a shareholding, a missing competence and an unresolved integrity doubt are exactly such information. The system sets the policy; the partner applies it to this engagement.

citation.ref: the engagement partner's responsibilities for relevant ethical requirements, for acceptance and continuance of the client relationship, and for the assignment of engagement teams

items.scenario: Three things surface in the third week of an audit. A senior on the engagement team has bought shares in the client, and the engagement partner cannot see any safeguard that would reduce the threat. The client has opened a derivative book during the year and nobody on the team, and no expert engaged by the firm, has ever audited one. And the doubts about the promoter's integrity that were raised when the firm decided to continue the relationship were never taken any further. The manager's view is that all three belong to the firm's risk partner, and that the engagement partner's own responsibility begins with the review of the file at the end.

items.stem: What does SQC 1 require on each of the three?

options.text: Nothing turns on any of the three because the firm audits no listed entity, SQC 1's requirements on independence and leadership applying to firms with listed clients
options.misconception: reads a listed-entity scope into SQC 1, which applies to the firm in respect of all its assurance and related services engagements
options.why: SQC 1 applies to the firm across all its audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements. Only the engagement quality control review carries a listed-entity trigger, and that is one part of one element.

options.text: Only the independence confirmation is a requirement — how a firm balances deadlines against quality is a matter of its own commercial judgement, and who the engagement partner is concerns the firm and not the client
options.misconception: treats the leadership and human resources elements as aspiration rather than requirement
options.why: All six elements are requirements in the same sense. The leadership element exists precisely because a firm's own commercial judgement is the pressure it has to be insulated from, and the client is told who the engagement partner is so that the person answerable is known outside the firm as well as inside it.

options.text: A three-yearly confirmation from partners is enough, staff being covered by the partners' supervision, and the rest is a matter for the engagement quality control reviewer
options.misconception: shortens the annual confirmation and narrows it to partners, and pushes the firm-level elements onto the engagement quality control review
options.why: The confirmation is annual and it reaches all personnel required to be independent. The engagement quality control review sits inside engagement performance and looks at one engagement's judgements; it was never the place where a firm's independence policy or its leadership policy is discharged.

options.text: The firm's policies must be such that commercial considerations do not override the quality of the work performed; written confirmation of compliance with the firm's policies and procedures on independence must be obtained at least annually from all firm personnel required to be independent; and the identity and role of the engagement partner are communicated to the client's management and to those charged with governance
options.why: Each of the three is a stated requirement of a different element. Under the leadership element, quality has to outrank commercial considerations in the way the firm hands out its management roles — a deadline that beats a quality step is the failure the element was written against. Ethical requirements carry the rule that the firm obtains written confirmation of compliance with its independence policies at least annually, and from all personnel required to be independent, not from partners alone. And human resources carries the requirement that the identity and role of the engagement partner are communicated to the client's key management and to those charged with governance.
keywords: identity and role of the engagement partner

citation.ref: the leadership responsibilities, ethical requirements and human resources elements — commercial considerations not overriding quality, the annual written confirmation of independence from all personnel, and communication of the engagement partner's identity and role to the client

items.scenario: A firm's quality control manual says three things. Where a quality step would cost a reporting deadline the deadline wins, because the managing partner's business plan sets the targets. Written independence confirmations are taken from the partners once every three years and are never taken from staff at all. And the identity of the engagement partner is recorded in the firm's internal allocation sheet but is never told to the client.

items.stem: What follows a qualified peer review report?

options.text: The Quality Review Board issues the certificate, the Peer Review Board's role ending with the appointment of the reviewer
options.misconception: swaps the two bodies, which have different constitutions and different functions
options.why: The Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council of the Institute and runs the peer review process end to end. The Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government to review the quality of services, recommend to the Council and guide members — it issues no peer review certificate.

options.text: The certificate is issued in every case once the review is complete, the qualification being recorded on the file for the next review to pick up
options.misconception: treats the certificate as an attendance record rather than the outcome of an unqualified report
options.why: A certificate that issued whatever the reviewer found would say nothing. It is the unqualified report that the certificate reports, which is why a qualified one produces a follow-on review instead.

options.text: A peer review certificate is issued only where the reviewer's report is unqualified — on a qualified report the practice unit is informed that the certificate cannot be issued, told the reasons, and given the due date for a follow-on review as decided by the Peer Review Board, which is constituted by the Council of the Institute; the Quality Review Board is a separate body set up by the Central Government
options.why: The outcome turns on the report. Where the peer reviewer issues an unqualified report a peer review certificate is issued. Where the report is qualified the practice unit is informed that the certificate cannot be issued along with the reasons, and is told the due date for conducting a follow-on review as the Board may decide. The body doing this is the Peer Review Board, constituted by the Council of the Institute; the Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government and works on a risk-based approach through technical reviewers, which is a different mechanism altogether.

options.text: A qualified report means the practice unit's attestation reports for the review period must be withdrawn and reissued
options.misconception: turns a review of the unit's systems into a re-audit of its clients
options.why: The review examines the systems and procedures the practice unit has put in place, not the accounts of any auditee. Nothing in the process reaches back into a report already issued to a client.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — the Peer Review Board, the peer review certificate on an unqualified report, and the follow-on review where the report is qualified

items.scenario: A practice unit has been through a peer review and the reviewer's report is qualified. The managing partner's position is that the review is now over, that the certificate follows as a matter of course because the unit submitted to the process, and that in any event it is the Quality Review Board and not the Peer Review Board that issues it.

items.stem: What do SA 240's risk assessment procedures require beyond the questionnaire?

options.text: The margin movement is a matter for SA 520 alone, to be investigated as an analytical difference and not as a fraud consideration
options.misconception: treats an unexplained analytical result as belonging to one standard only, when SA 240 requires it to be evaluated for fraud risk as well
options.why: The same fluctuation is read twice for two purposes. SA 520 asks whether the difference is explained; SA 240 asks what an unexpected relationship says about the risk of material misstatement due to fraud, and a nine-point margin jump in one division answers both.

options.text: Nothing more on the inquiries — management's own assessment of the risk of fraud is the matter SA 240 puts the question to, and the chief financial officer speaks for management
options.misconception: collapses four risk assessment activities into one inquiry of one officer
options.why: Management's assessment is one topic among several and management is one source among several. Asking only the officer with the most to lose from an answer is the shape of inquiry the standard was written to widen.

options.text: Inquiries of management and of others within the entity; an understanding of the oversight those charged with governance keep over the way management goes about spotting fraud risks, answering them, and running the internal control it has built to hold them down; and an evaluation of what unexpected relationships thrown up by analytical work say about the risk of material misstatement from fraud
options.why: The standard names four risk assessment activities and the questionnaire is a fragment of one. Inquiries run to management and to others within the entity — legal counsel, internal audit, and the people who initiate, process or record the unusual transactions are exactly who is meant. Separately the auditor obtains an understanding of how those charged with governance exercise oversight of management's fraud processes and of the internal control established to mitigate the risks. And unexpected relationships identified in performing analytical procedures are evaluated for what they say about the risk of fraud, which is why the margin jump could not simply be handed back to management.
keywords: those charged with governance exercise oversight

options.text: Those charged with governance need not be approached at the risk assessment stage — they are communicated with later, and only if a fraud is actually identified or suspected
options.misconception: confuses the risk assessment understanding of governance oversight with the later communication of an identified fraud
options.why: Two different requirements sit at two different points. The understanding of how governance exercises oversight is obtained while risks are being assessed; the communication of an identified or suspected fraud comes afterwards and does not replace it.

citation.ref: the risk assessment procedures — inquiries of management and others within the entity, the understanding of how those charged with governance exercise oversight of management's fraud processes, and the evaluation of unexpected relationships identified in performing analytical procedures

items.scenario: The whole of a team's fraud risk assessment is a questionnaire signed by the chief financial officer. The audit committee was asked nothing. The in-house legal counsel, the head of internal audit and the operating staff who process the unusual year-end rebate credits were never approached. And an analytical procedure threw up a nine-point jump in one division's gross margin that was left where it lay, the senior noting that margins are a management matter.

items.stem: What more does SA 260 require for a listed entity?

options.text: The independence communication is required only where the auditor has identified a threat he could not reduce to an acceptable level
options.misconception: makes an unconditional listed-entity requirement conditional on a problem having been found
options.why: The communication happens whether or not a threat was found; its purpose is to let those charged with governance form their own view rather than to report the auditor's. A clean position still has to be shown.

options.text: Oral communication is sufficient throughout provided the audit committee raises no objection, documentation being needed only for written communications
options.misconception: reverses the documentation rule, which exists precisely for the matters communicated orally
options.why: Where a communication is written the auditor retains a copy; where it is oral he records the matter, the date and the persons in the audit documentation. The oral route is the one that needs the note, because nothing else survives it.

options.text: Confirmation that the relevant ethical requirements on independence have been complied with by the engagement team, by others in the firm where that applies, by the firm itself and by network firms where any exist; every relationship, and every other matter, between the firm, the network firms and the entity that a reasonable person might think bears on independence, including the total fees billed for audit and for non-audit services, split into categories that let those charged with governance weigh the effect on independence; and the safeguards applied — and where any matter is communicated orally the auditor includes it in the audit documentation with when and to whom it was communicated
options.why: For a listed entity the independence communication is a set of four things, not a sentence. It states the compliance of the engagement team, the firm and the network firms with the relevant ethical requirements on independence; it names every relationship, and every other matter, a reasonable person might think bears on independence; it gives the total fees the firm and the network firms billed for audit and for non-audit work, split into categories so that those charged with governance can weigh the effect; and it sets out the safeguards applied. Separately, a matter communicated orally goes into the audit documentation together with when and to whom it was communicated, which is why a conversation nobody recorded fails even where its content was right.

options.text: Nothing further — a statement of independence is the requirement, and the fees of network firms are their own commercial affair rather than a matter for this audit committee
options.misconception: treats network firms as outside the independence communication, when the requirement names them expressly
options.why: Network firms are inside the communication for the same reason they are inside the independence rules — what a sister firm bills the client bears on whether the auditor is independent in appearance, and the committee cannot assess that without the figure.

citation.ref: the communication of auditor independence to those charged with governance of a listed entity, and the documentation of matters communicated orally

items.scenario: The auditor of a listed company communicated the planned scope and timing of the audit, and his findings, to the audit committee's chairman over lunch. His file records neither the date of that conversation nor who was present. On independence he handed across one line — that the firm is independent — and nothing about the group's three network firms, which billed the company substantial consulting fees during the year.

items.stem: What does SA 320 require?

options.text: Revise materiality — the trigger includes a change in the auditor's understanding of the entity as a result of performing further audit procedures, not only a change in the entity's results — and select an appropriate benchmark, total cost or net cost being the example given for a public utility programme, profit before tax from continuing operations being the benchmark for a profit-oriented entity and gross profit or total revenues where profit before tax is volatile
options.why: Materiality is revised on new information, on a change in circumstances during the audit, and on a change in the auditor's understanding of the entity as a result of performing further audit procedures. The third trigger is the one at work here: nothing about the undertaking changed, the auditor's grasp of it did. On the benchmark, the factors include the nature of the entity and the items on which the attention of its users tends to be focused, and the worked examples run profit before tax from continuing operations for a profit-oriented entity, gross profit or total revenues where that figure is volatile, total cost or net cost for a public utility programme, and assets where the entity has custody of assets.

options.text: Raise materiality to whatever figure makes the firm's computed sample sizes workable, since the audit cannot be performed at fifty-five thousand rupees
options.misconception: sets materiality from the convenience of the audit rather than from what could influence the decisions of users
options.why: Materiality is a judgement about the users of these financial statements, and sample sizes follow from it rather than the other way round. A figure reverse-engineered from a workload has stopped measuring anything.

options.text: Apply five per cent of total assets, that being the benchmark prescribed for any entity not run for profit
options.misconception: turns the illustrative benchmarks into a prescribed rule and ignores what the users of this entity actually look at
options.why: The standard gives factors and examples, not a table to look a figure up in. Assets are the example where the entity has custody of assets; a water supply scheme funded by a grant is judged on what it costs to run.

options.text: Keep the fifty-five thousand rupee figure — materiality is determined at planning, and a benchmark once chosen is held so that the audit is not designed around its own answer
options.misconception: treats the planning figure and the benchmark as fixed, when the standard names a change in the auditor's understanding as a trigger for revision
options.why: Holding a figure that was built on a misunderstanding is not discipline. The standard asks the auditor to revise on information that would have led him to a different amount initially, and a benchmark that was wrong from the start is exactly that.

citation.ref: the revision of materiality as the audit progresses, read with the factors affecting the identification of an appropriate benchmark and the examples of benchmarks

items.scenario: A manager sets materiality for a municipal water supply undertaking at five per cent of profit before tax. The undertaking is not run for profit; its surplus for the year is eleven lakh rupees, so materiality comes out at fifty-five thousand rupees and every sample size the firm's software computes is unworkable. Half way through the audit he understands for the first time that the undertaking's income is a fixed municipal grant and that what its users and its funders look at is what the scheme costs to run. He proposes to leave materiality where it is, on the ground that it was set at planning and that the benchmark, once chosen, is not revisited.

items.stem: What must the user auditor be satisfied about before using a type 1 or type 2 report?

options.text: The service auditor's professional competence and his independence of the service organisation, and the adequacy of the standards under which the type 1 or type 2 report was issued — and, where the report is a type 2, whether the tests of controls ran over a long enough stretch and how much has changed since they were done, which here leaves six months of the year untested
options.why: Before a service auditor's report becomes evidence in someone else's audit, the user auditor satisfies himself about the service auditor's professional competence and independence from the service organisation, and about the adequacy of the standards under which the report was issued — an unnamed framework answers neither. Where the report is type 2, he also asks whether the time period covered by the tests of controls stretches far enough, and how long ago those tests were run. A report stopping on 30 September says nothing about the six months that follow it.
keywords: time period covered by the tests of controls

options.text: That the service organisation has agreed in writing that the user auditor may rely on the report, reliance being a matter of the service organisation's consent
options.misconception: substitutes a permission from the service organisation for the auditor's own evaluation of the report
options.why: Consent is not evidence. Nothing the service organisation agrees to changes whether its auditor was competent, independent, working to adequate standards, or testing the right months.

options.text: Nothing beyond the type of the report — a type 2 report reports on operating effectiveness over a period, and that is what makes it usable
options.misconception: treats the type of the report as the whole test, ignoring who wrote it, under what standards, and over which period
options.why: The type tells you what the report set out to do. Whether it did it turns on the competence and independence of the person who wrote it, the standards he worked to, and whether the period he tested is the period you are auditing.

options.text: That the gap between 30 September and the year end is covered by a written representation from the client's management about the service organisation's controls
options.misconception: uses a representation from the user entity to fill an evidence gap about controls operating elsewhere
options.why: A user entity's management cannot represent about the operation of controls it does not run and cannot see. The gap is closed by tests of controls at the service organisation, by a report covering the period, or by substantive work — not by a sentence in a letter.

citation.ref: the user auditor's evaluation of a type 1 or type 2 report — the service auditor's professional competence and independence, the adequacy of the standards under which the report was issued, and the time period covered by the tests of controls

items.scenario: A service organisation hands your client a type 2 report covering 1 April to 30 September. Your client's year ends on 31 March. The report is signed by a firm you have never heard of and does not say under what standards it was prepared. Your manager plans to rely on it for the whole year because it is a type 2 report and type 2 reports cover operating effectiveness.

items.stem: What does SA 500 require when the evidence an auditor leans on was built out of work done by an expert of management's own?

options.text: Engage an auditor's expert of the firm's own to re-perform the actuarial valuation, an auditor being unable to evaluate work in a field outside his competence
options.misconception: makes a second expert the only route, when the standard asks for an understanding sufficient to evaluate the work
options.why: A second expert is sometimes the right response and it is never the required first step. What the standard asks for is an understanding of the field sufficient to evaluate the work, which is a lower bar than doing the work again.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the actuary is independent, which settles the objectivity question
options.misconception: substitutes management's assertion about the expert for the auditor's own evaluation of him
options.why: Management's view of its own expert is the very thing under examination. A representation may be obtained, but the evaluation of competence, capabilities and objectivity remains the auditor's work.

options.text: Only the appropriateness of the work matters — the expert's relationships and fee sources are the entity's affair, since it is the entity and not the auditor who engaged him
options.misconception: drops objectivity from the three matters the standard names, on the ground that the expert was engaged by the entity
options.why: That the entity engaged him is the reason objectivity is in the list, not the reason it is out of it. A valuation prepared to please the person who pays for it is unreliable however the arithmetic checks.
