options.text: Evaluate the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert — objectivity is one of the three, and a close family relationship with the finance director together with a dependence on the group's fees goes directly to it — and obtain an understanding of the work of that expert sufficient to evaluate its appropriateness as audit evidence for the relevant assertion
options.why: The standard puts three things in front of the auditor and objectivity is the third of them: he evaluates the competence, capabilities and objectivity of the management's expert. Family relationships with the entity's officers and financial dependence on the entity are the circumstances that erode objectivity, and no amount of technical skill answers them. The second requirement is that the auditor obtains an understanding of the work of that expert — not that he re-performs it, and not that he defers to it, but that he understands it well enough to evaluate whether it is appropriate as audit evidence.

citation.ref: what an auditor owes when an expert engaged by the entity has produced something he means to rely on — judging that expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and grasping his work well enough to weigh it as evidence

items.scenario: The actuary who valued a company's gratuity and leave encashment liabilities is the finance director's brother-in-law, and roughly four-fifths of his professional income comes from the group. The audit senior says objectivity is beside the point because SA 500 is about the work rather than the person, and that no understanding of the actuary's work is possible in any event since actuarial science is outside the auditor's own field.

items.stem: What does SA 501 have the auditor do here?

options.text: Once something the auditor learns casts doubt on the custodian's integrity and objectivity, go past the confirmation or replace it — stand at the third party's stock count where that can be arranged, or send another auditor to stand there; get a report, from another auditor or from a service auditor, on whether the custodian's own controls are strong enough to see the stock counted right and kept safe; and inspect the papers covering stock lying with third parties
options.why: Confirmation from the custodian is the first route the standard offers, and it is the route that stops working when the custodian is the problem. Where what he learns casts doubt on the custodian's integrity and objectivity, the auditor performs other procedures instead of or in addition to the confirmation, and the standard names them: attending the count himself or arranging for another auditor to attend, taking a report from another auditor, or from a service auditor, on how well the third party's own controls see stock counted and safeguarded, and inspecting documentation covering the goods held.
keywords: arranging for another auditor to attend

options.text: Nothing further — the confirmation came directly from the custodian rather than through the client, which is the requirement the standard sets
options.misconception: treats directness as the whole test of a confirmation, ignoring the reliability of the party confirming
options.why: A confirmation is only as good as the party writing it. Directness removes one risk, that the client edited the reply, and leaves untouched the risk that the custodian's own word is worth nothing.

options.text: Qualify the opinion at once for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, no procedure being available where a custodian is under investigation
options.misconception: goes to the report before performing the alternative procedures the standard names
options.why: The standard supplies three further procedures before any question of the opinion arises. A modification that skipped them would be reporting the auditor's convenience rather than a limitation.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the client's management confirming the quantities and condition of the inventory lying with the custodian
options.misconception: replaces evidence about inventory held elsewhere with an assertion from management that has no better access to it
options.why: Management is no closer to the goods than the auditor is, and its representation adds no knowledge. The requirement is evidence about existence and condition, which is obtained by going to where the goods are or by testing the controls of whoever holds them.

citation.ref: inventory under the custody and control of a third party — confirmation, and the other audit procedures where information raises doubt about the third party's integrity and objectivity

items.scenario: A material part of your client's inventory sits with a third-party custodian. During the year the tax authorities raided that custodian over a fake-invoicing scheme and its proprietor is in custody. A confirmation nevertheless comes back directly from the custodian's office confirming the quantities and condition of everything held. Your manager treats the confirmation as obtained directly and closes the point.

items.stem: What does SA 520 require when a result differs from the expected value by a significant amount?

options.text: Reduce the extent of the tests of details on revenue and receivables, the analytical result being favourable in both cases
options.misconception: reads an unexplained favourable movement as assurance rather than as a risk indicator
options.why: A movement in the direction management would have wanted is not a comfort. Both of these are the classic signatures of revenue recorded early and receivables netted off, which is why the standard sends the auditor towards the difference rather than away from it.

options.text: Treat the two movements as a scope limitation, management having failed to substantiate them, and modify the opinion
options.misconception: jumps from an unexplained difference to the report without performing the other audit procedures the standard requires
options.why: A difference the auditor has not yet investigated is not a limitation on his scope. It becomes one only after the further procedures have been performed and have failed.

options.text: Record management's explanation, which is what inquiry of management means, and move on where the explanation is plausible on its face
options.misconception: stops at the inquiry and drops the evidence relevant to the response, which is the other half of the same requirement
options.why: Plausibility is the quality a fabricated explanation is designed to have. The standard asks for evidence relevant to the response for that reason, and a product-mix claim is testable against the sales ledger in an afternoon.

options.text: Investigate the difference: put the question to management, then go and obtain audit evidence that is appropriate to whatever answer comes back, and perform such other audit procedures as the circumstances call for — the need for those arising where management cannot explain, or where the explanation together with the evidence obtained relevant to it is not adequate
options.why: The requirement has two halves and the senior has done the first. Where analytical procedures identify fluctuations or relationships inconsistent with other relevant information, or differing from expected values by a significant amount, the auditor inquires of management and obtains appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses. An explanation on its own is a statement, not evidence. Beyond that he performs other audit procedures as necessary, which is what happens where management cannot explain the movement or where the explanation and the evidence together still do not answer it.
keywords: appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses

citation.ref: what an auditor does with an analytical result that misses his expectation by a wide margin — asking management, backing whatever comes back with evidence of its own, and going further still where that pair is not enough

items.scenario: The analytical procedures performed near the end of an audit throw up two results well outside expectation: gross margin nine percentage points above last year, and debtor days forty days shorter. The finance head explains both in one sentence — a better product mix. The senior records the sentence in the file and closes the point, the explanation having been obtained from the person best placed to give it.

items.stem: What does SA 550 require of you now?

options.text: Obtain audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved, and evaluate whether the terms of the transaction are consistent with management's explanations to you, and whether the transaction has been accounted for, and disclosed, the way the applicable financial reporting framework demands
options.why: Inspecting the contract and testing the business rationale is one part of the response to a significant related party transaction outside the normal course of business, and three parts remain. The auditor obtains audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved — a sale of an asset of this kind with no board minute and no members' resolution fails that at once. He evaluates whether the terms are consistent with management's explanations, which a price thirty per cent below the term sheet is not. And he evaluates whether it has been properly accounted for and disclosed, which a gain routed to reserves without a note is not.

options.text: Nothing further on the audit side — report the absence of board approval to those charged with governance and leave the accounting to management
options.misconception: turns a set of audit requirements into a communication, and hands the accounting question back to the party being audited
options.why: Communication with those charged with governance sits alongside the work; it does not replace it. And whether the gain is correctly presented is an audit conclusion, not a preference management is entitled to.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the sale was on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, which answers the price point and the approval point together
options.misconception: substitutes an arm's length representation for the separate requirements on authorisation, on consistency with explanations and on accounting
options.why: An arm's length assertion is itself an assertion to be audited, and it says nothing about whether the board approved the sale or whether the gain was accounted for correctly. Three separate requirements cannot be answered by one sentence about price.

options.text: Treat the price difference as a matter for the valuation of the brand alone, the term sheet being a negotiating document with no evidential value
options.misconception: dismisses the inconsistency between the terms and management's own explanation, which the standard requires to be evaluated
options.why: The term sheet matters here not as a valuation but as what management told you. A transaction whose terms contradict the explanation given for it is the specific thing the standard asks the auditor to evaluate.

citation.ref: identified significant related party transactions outside the entity's normal course of business — evidence of appropriate authorisation and approval, consistency of the terms with management's explanations, and proper accounting and disclosure

items.scenario: A manufacturer sells its oldest brand to an entity owned by the promoter's family. You have identified the sale as a significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business, inspected the assignment deed, and satisfied yourself that the stated rationale — exiting a line the company no longer makes — is genuine. Three things are still open. The board minutes for the year do not mention the sale and no members' resolution was passed. The price in the deed is thirty per cent below the figure in the term sheet management showed you. And the gain has been credited straight to reserves with no note.

items.stem: What must SA 560 have the auditor do in the stretch running from the balance sheet date to the day he signs his report?

options.text: Interim financial statements prepared for a bank are outside the audit and need not be read, being unaudited and prepared for a single user
options.misconception: excludes the latest subsequent interim financial statements, which the standard names among the required procedures
options.why: The standard asks for the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements without any qualification about who they were prepared for. They are read as a source of subsequent events, not as a statement anyone is opining on.

options.text: Only the written representation is required in this window; active procedures begin only where something comes to the auditor's notice
options.misconception: reverses the two windows, applying the reactive duty of the post-report window to the period before the report
options.why: The reactive duty belongs after the report is signed. Before that date the auditor performs procedures designed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that subsequent events have been identified, and a representation is the last step of that work rather than a substitute for it.

options.text: Obtain an understanding of any procedures management has established to ensure that subsequent events are identified; inquire of management and, where appropriate, of those charged with governance whether any subsequent events have occurred which might affect the financial statements; read the minutes of meetings of the entity's owners, management and those charged with governance held after the date of the financial statements; and read the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements — with written representations that all subsequent events have been adjusted or disclosed
options.why: In this window the auditor is actively looking, and the standard lists what looking means. He obtains an understanding of any procedures management has established for identifying subsequent events. He inquires of management and, where appropriate, of those charged with governance. He reads the minutes of meetings of owners, management and those charged with governance held after the date of the financial statements — which is why stopping at 31 March misses the whole point. He reads the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements. And he requests written representations that all subsequent events have been adjusted or disclosed.

options.text: Reading the board minutes up to the date of the financial statements is the requirement, minutes after that date relating to the following year
options.misconception: reads minutes only up to the balance sheet date, when the requirement is for meetings held after it
options.why: A meeting held in May is precisely where an insolvency, a fire or a settlement occurring in April will be recorded. Reading only up to 31 March closes the file on the window the standard opens.

citation.ref: what the auditor must do in the gap running from the balance sheet date to the day he signs, read with the written representation on subsequent events

items.scenario: A company's year ended on 31 March and the report is to be signed on 20 June. The subsequent events section of the file holds two things: a note that the board minutes were read up to 31 March, and the signed representation letter. Nobody asked management or the audit committee anything; the minutes of the April and May board meetings were never called for; and the interim accounts the company prepared for its bankers in April and May were not read.

items.stem: What does SA 700 (Revised) require in that section, and what does it permit?

options.text: The sentence is sufficient — the section states what the auditor did, and the limitations of an audit are a matter of professional knowledge rather than of the report
options.misconception: treats the description of reasonable assurance and materiality as background rather than as required content of the section
options.why: The section is written for a reader who has no professional knowledge. Telling him that reasonable assurance is not a guarantee, and what makes a misstatement material, is the work the section does.

options.text: Two statements are compulsory. The section has to say that reasonable assurance, high a level of assurance though it is, is still not a guarantee: an audit run under the SAs will not always turn up a material misstatement that is sitting there. And it has to say that a misstatement may come from fraud or from error, and counts as material where it could, on its own or added to others, reasonably be expected to sway what users decide on the strength of these accounts. The longer description may then sit in an appendix to the report or, where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly permit, give way to a pointer to an appropriate authority's website, so long as the description there covers the same ground and contradicts none of it
options.why: The single sentence in the draft records the conclusion and leaves out the two things the section exists to say. First, that reasonable assurance, though a high level of assurance, is still not a guarantee: an audit carried out under the SAs can miss a material misstatement that is sitting there. Second, that a misstatement springs from fraud or from error, and is material where it could, by itself or piled on others, reasonably be expected to sway the economic choices users make on the strength of these accounts. On placement the standard is kinder than the partner was told: the detailed description may be lifted into an appendix to the report, and where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly permit, a pointer to an appropriate authority's website may stand in its place.

options.text: The section may be shortened to a cross-reference to the Standards on Auditing themselves, since the responsibilities are set out there in full
options.misconception: replaces the required statements with a citation of the standards, which is not one of the permitted routes
options.why: A reference to the standards is not a reference to a website of an appropriate authority carrying the description, and it leaves the reader with nothing. The permitted shortcuts are the appendix and, where expressly permitted, the named website.

options.text: The whole description must appear in the body of the report, an appendix or a website reference being a dilution of the auditor's own statement of his responsibilities
options.misconception: denies the placement options the standard expressly allows
options.why: The standard permits the material to be located in an appendix, and permits a website reference where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly allow it and the description there is not inconsistent. Neither route changes what the auditor is responsible for.

citation.ref: the two statements that must appear in the section headlined Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements, and the permission to move the description into an appendix or, where expressly permitted, onto an appropriate authority's website

items.scenario: In a draft auditor's report the part headlined Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements runs to one sentence: "We audited the financial statements in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and obtained reasonable assurance that they are free from material misstatement." The partner wants to move the fuller description out of the body of the report, and has been told that an appendix is not permitted and that pointing the reader at a regulator's website is never allowed.

items.stem: Which of the matters in the proviso do these four engage?

options.text: None — the proviso creates a duty to inquire and the auditor reports nothing under it, all his reporting obligations being in section 143(3)
options.misconception: reads the absence of routine reporting as an absence of any reporting, when an adverse finding is stated
options.why: Nothing is said where the inquiry is satisfied, which is not the same as nothing being said at all. Where the inquiry produces an adverse answer the auditor reports it to the members, and four adverse answers are what these facts produce.

options.text: Only the sale of securities below cost, the other three being matters for CARO 2020 rather than for section 143(1)
options.misconception: moves three of the proviso's own matters into CARO, which is a separate reporting order
options.why: CARO adds reporting; it does not remove the proviso's matters from section 143(1). Loans shown as deposits and shares allotted for cash without cash are named in the proviso itself and are answered there.

options.text: All four, and each must also be positively confirmed in the auditor's report every year along with the other two matters in the proviso
options.misconception: turns the proviso into an annual positive-assurance report, when only adverse findings are stated
options.why: The duty is to inquire and to apply the mind; the report speaks only where an answer is adverse. An auditor who prints six clean answers every year has told the reader nothing about which years the answer was tested.

options.text: All four — whether a loan or advance given against security has in fact been secured properly, and whether the terms it was given on damage the company or the people who own it; whether the company, being neither an investment company nor a banking company, has parted with shares, debentures or other securities for less than it paid for them; whether what are really loans and advances sit in the balance sheet dressed as deposits; and whether cash truly came in where the books record shares as allotted for cash
options.why: The proviso names six matters and the manager has remembered two of them. A loan on a second charge over land already fully charged, at two per cent for twelve years, goes to whether it was properly secured and whether the terms are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members. Securities costing seven crore sold for three crore goes to the matter about assets consisting of shares, debentures and other securities sold below their purchase price, which applies because this company is neither an investment company nor a banking company. Loans described as security deposits go to whether loans and advances have been shown as deposits. And shares recorded as allotted for cash where no cash arrived goes to the last matter in the proviso.

citation.ref: Section 143(1), proviso clauses (a), (c), (d) and (f)

items.scenario: Four things come out of an unlisted manufacturing company's books. Eighteen crore rupees lent against a second charge on land already fully charged to a bank, carrying two per cent interest and repayable after twelve years. Quoted securities that cost seven crore rupees sold to a promoter entity for three crore; the company is neither an investment company nor a banking company. Five crore rupees of loans to a supplier shown in the balance sheet under the heading "security deposits". And nine crore rupees of shares recorded in the books as allotted for cash, against which the bank statements show nothing received. The manager says the proviso to section 143(1) is about book entries and personal expenses, neither of which arises.

items.stem: Is the reporting requirement met?

options.text: Yes — the reporting requirement is that the software has the feature and that the feature operated throughout the year, both of which hold
options.misconception: stops at the operation limb and drops both the tampering limb and the preservation limb
options.why: Operation is one of three limbs. A trail that anybody could edit and that is thrown away after a year fails the other two, whatever the switch said all year.

options.text: No — a third limb asks whether the company kept the audit trail for as long as the law on record retention lays down, which a twelve-month backup cycle does not satisfy; and whether the feature was tampered with is tested through the controls over the trail itself, which fail here on shared user IDs, on unrestricted access with no access logs, and on unauthorised changes to the audit trail's configuration
options.why: The reporting requirement asks three things and the manager has answered one. The third asks whether the company has preserved the audit trail for the whole span the law on record retention fixes, and a company that overwrites its logs after twelve months has not preserved them. Tampering is not established by nobody having alleged it either: the controls the auditor examines are that the feature cannot be disabled or deactivated, that access to the audit trail is restricted with access logs maintained, that user IDs are assigned to each individual and not shared, that changes to the audit trail's configuration are authorised and logged, and that periodic backups are taken and archived for the statutory period.

options.text: The access controls, the shared logins and the retention of backups are matters for the internal financial controls reporting and have no bearing on this requirement
options.misconception: separates the audit trail reporting from the controls that make the trail reliable, when those controls are how the tampering limb is tested
options.why: The two reports overlap and neither swallows the other. A trail anybody can edit is how the auditor answers whether the feature was tampered with, so those controls are read for this requirement whether or not they are read again elsewhere.

options.text: No, and the consequence is a qualification of the opinion on the financial statements, since books maintained without a preserved audit trail are not proper books of account
options.misconception: converts a separate reporting requirement into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: This is a reporting requirement answered in its own place, and answering it adversely is not the same as concluding the financial statements are misstated. The books can be complete and accurate while the trail over them is not preserved.

citation.ref: Rule 11 — the auditor's reporting on the use of accounting software with an audit trail feature, its operation throughout the year without being tampered with, and its preservation as per the statutory requirements for record retention

items.scenario: A company's accounting software had the audit trail feature switched on for the whole year. Four other things are true. The database administrators share one login between them. Anyone in the finance team can open and edit the table the log is written to, and no record is kept of who opened it. The log's configuration was changed twice during the year without anyone's approval. And the logs for the two earlier years are gone, the company keeping backups for twelve months. The manager proposes a clean report: the feature was on all year and nobody has alleged tampering.

items.stem: What else does clause 3(xi) require?

options.text: Nothing — sub-clause (b) is answered only where a report was actually filed, and sub-clause (c) is answered only where the company refers a whistle-blower complaint to the auditor
options.misconception: treats both sub-clauses as conditional, when each is answered every year and the second requires the auditor to obtain the complaints
options.why: Both are standing questions. A nil answer on Form ADT-4 is still an answer, and the second sub-clause places the initiative on the auditor rather than on whoever happens to forward him a complaint.

options.text: The thirty lakh fraud must in any event be reported in Form ADT-4, and sub-clause (b) then answered in the affirmative
options.misconception: ignores the threshold in rule 13 that decides whether the report goes to the Central Government or to the audit committee
options.why: Rule 13 splits the route by amount: at or above the prescribed figure the report goes to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, and below it to the audit committee or the Board. The CARO answer follows what the rule actually required, not what would be tidier.

options.text: The other two sub-clauses — whether the auditors put in any section 143(12) report to the Central Government on Form ADT-4, the form rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 lays down, a question answered even when nothing at all was filed; and whether the auditor took account of any whistle-blower complaints the company received in the year, which means getting hold of them first and then reading them
options.why: The clause has three sub-clauses. Sub-clause (b) has the auditor say whether he himself put a section 143(12) report to the Central Government on Form ADT-4, the form rule 13 prescribes — a question about his own conduct, and one answered even when the answer is that nothing was filed. Sub-clause (c) asks whether he has considered any whistle-blower complaints the company received in the year, which an auditor who never called for them cannot answer; three complaints alleging invoice inflation in one division are exactly what the sub-clause was written to reach.

options.text: The whistle-blower complaints are covered by clause 3(xiv) on the internal audit system, the vigil mechanism being part of that system
options.misconception: moves the whistle-blower question to a different clause, when clause 3(xi)(c) names it
options.why: Clause 3(xiv) asks about the internal audit system and whether its reports were considered. Whistle-blower complaints are named in clause 3(xi)(c) and are answered there, alongside the frauds and the Form ADT-4 question they sit with.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)(b) and clause 3(xi)(c), read with rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: During the year the auditor found one fraud, of thirty lakh rupees, and reported it to the audit committee because the amount fell below the threshold for reporting to the Central Government. No report in Form ADT-4 was therefore filed. Separately, the company's vigil mechanism received nine complaints, three of them alleging invoice inflation in the same division; the audit senior never asked for them, on the view that the vigil mechanism belongs to the audit committee. He drafts clause 3(xi) covering the thirty lakh fraud and nothing else.

items.stem: What does section 143(3)(i) require the report to state?

options.text: Two things — first, whether adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements exist at all, and second, how effectively those controls actually worked — so a control that was not performed for four months is reported however the financial statements came out, the internal financial controls opinion being a separate opinion from the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The clause puts two questions. One asks whether adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements exist at all; the other asks about the operating effectiveness of the controls that do. Design and operation are two questions, and a control that exists on paper and was not performed for a third of the year fails the second whatever the closing figures show. The auditor's substantive work is what kept the financial statements right; it is not evidence that the company's own control operated. The internal financial controls opinion is a separate opinion and is reached on its own evidence.
keywords: adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements

options.text: A modified opinion on the financial statements, since an internal financial controls failure of this size cannot leave the opinion on the financial statements unqualified
options.misconception: ties the opinion on the financial statements to the internal financial controls opinion, when the two are formed separately
options.why: The two opinions travel separately. An adverse conclusion on internal financial controls does not by itself modify the opinion on financial statements that the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence about by other means.

options.text: That adequate internal financial controls are in place — operating effectiveness being demonstrated by the absence of any uncorrected misstatement in the financial statements
options.misconception: reads a clean set of financial statements as evidence that the company's controls operated
options.why: A clean set of financial statements can be the product of the audit rather than of the entity's controls, which is exactly what happened here. Operating effectiveness is tested on the control, not inferred from the outcome.

options.text: Nothing on this control — the failure is a deficiency to be communicated to those charged with governance, and the clause reports only on the design of the system as a whole
options.misconception: narrows the clause to design and pushes an operating failure into a communication
options.why: Communicating the deficiency is required and it is not a substitute. The clause names operating effectiveness in terms, so a control that did not operate is answered in the report and not only in a letter.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i) — the two matters the report must state: that adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements exist, and how effectively they operate

items.scenario: An unlisted public company with a turnover of nine hundred crore rupees is audited. The control over revenue cut-off — a review of despatch documents against invoices at each month end — was simply not performed for four months of the year. Your own substantive work found the errors it would have caught, management corrected all of them, and the financial statements carry no uncorrected misstatement. The manager proposes to report that adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements were there all year and worked as they should, because the numbers ended up right.

items.stem: How should the three accounts stand?

options.text: All three are non-performing, since each departs in some way from the terms of sanction
options.misconception: collapses the distinction between a temporary deficiency and a weakness in the credit itself
options.why: If every departure from sanction made an account non-performing, the norms would not have named temporary deficiencies separately. The purpose of the distinction is that a stock statement arriving late and a borrower who has vanished are not the same event.

options.text: The first two require the account to be treated as non-performing unless the branch obtains a fresh stock statement and a renewal sanction before the accounts are signed
options.misconception: makes classification turn on post-year-end paperwork rather than on whether the deficiency is temporary
options.why: Whether the deficiency is temporary is judged on the position at the balance sheet date, not on how quickly the branch can produce documents afterwards. Curing the paperwork later changes nothing about the classification on the date it is made.

options.text: The other way round — the first two are temporary deficiencies, and an account is not classified as non-performing merely because drawing power based on the latest stock statement is unavailable, because the balance outstanding exceeded the limit temporarily, or because limits were not renewed on the due date; the third indicates inherent weakness and is deemed non-performing whatever the position on the limit
options.why: The norms separate a deficiency in paperwork from a weakness in the credit. An account is not to be classified as non-performing merely because of temporary deficiencies such as the non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, a balance outstanding exceeding the limit temporarily, or limits not renewed on the due date — the first two accounts are that and nothing more. Where an account indicates inherent weakness, it is deemed non-performing, and a shut factory with an untraceable borrower is the plainest case of it even though no instalment has fallen due.

options.text: The branch manager is right on all three — a missing stock statement and an expired limit are irregularities in the account, while an account within its limit with nothing overdue cannot be non-performing
options.misconception: treats every documentary irregularity as an NPA trigger and treats "nothing overdue" as conclusive against one
options.why: The record of recovery is the ordinary test and inherent weakness is the exception written beside it. Paperwork that is late does not make a good account bad, and a limit that has not yet been breached does not make a dead one good.

citation.ref: Ch. Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies — accounts with temporary deficiencies, and accounts indicating inherent weakness

items.scenario: Three cash credit accounts at a branch on 31 March. In the first, the borrower has not submitted his latest stock statement, so drawing power on the latest statement could not be worked out; the outstanding is inside the sanctioned limit and every interest debit has been served. In the second, the limit expired on 15 February and the renewal proposal is with the sanctioning authority; the account operates regularly and is within the old limit. In the third, the borrower's factory has been shut for seven months and he is untraceable, though nothing is overdue and the outstanding is inside the limit. The branch manager classifies the first two as non-performing and the third as standard.

items.stem: How does Clause 1 of Part I of the Second Schedule answer the three?

options.text: All three may be answered in full once the member records in his file that disclosure is in the client's own commercial interest
options.misconception: invents an exception for the member's own view of the client's interest, which the clause does not contain
options.why: The clause admits two exceptions and neither is the member's judgement about what would suit the client. A note in a file is not consent and it is not a law.

options.text: His working papers are his own: neither the client, nor another auditor of the same enterprise, nor the auditor of a parent or of a subsidiary, can demand access to them, though he may at his discretion make portions of or extracts from them available; sharing working papers and sharing information are different things, and information may be given to the client or to a regulatory body after obtaining the client's consent; and for a company that consent comes from the Board of Directors by resolution, unless the Board's powers have been delegated to the managing director comprehensively enough to include it
options.why: Three different rules answer the three requests. Nobody can demand sight of a member's audit working papers — not the client, not another auditor of the same enterprise, not the auditor of a related enterprise such as a parent or a subsidiary — and a principal auditor has no right of access to a branch auditor's papers either; the member may hand over portions or extracts if he chooses. Information is a separate question from working papers, and information may be given to the client or to a regulatory body once the client's consent has been obtained. And in the case of a company the consent must come from the Board of Directors by resolution, unless the Board's powers have been delegated to the managing director widely enough to cover it.

options.text: The holding company's auditor is entitled to the working papers, a group audit being one audit, and the managing director's instruction binds the member because he is the company's chief executive
options.misconception: creates a right of access for another auditor and treats an officer's instruction as the company's consent
options.why: The other auditor may rely on the member's work without ever seeing his papers, which is the arrangement the profession works on. And consent belongs to the company, expressed the way the company expresses decisions, not to whichever officer asks.

options.text: Nothing may go to the regulator either, because a request that is not backed by legal compulsion cannot be answered whatever the client says
options.misconception: forgets that consent is the other door out of the duty, alongside legal compulsion
options.why: The clause bars disclosure without the client's consent or otherwise than as required by law. Consent is a door in its own right, so a client that wants the regulator informed can open it.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 1 — access to audit working papers, the difference between sharing working papers and sharing information, and who may give the client's consent

items.scenario: Three requests land on a practising member in one week. The auditor of his client's holding company asks for his audit working papers on the subsidiary, so that the group opinion can be supported. The client's managing director, whose board has passed no resolution delegating the point to him, asks him to send those working papers to the company's banker. And a regulator writes asking for information about the client's export incentive claims; the client is entirely willing for the information to go.

items.stem: Which of the three does Clause 4 of Part I of the Second Schedule bar?

options.text: Only the second — a certificate for a tax assessment is an attest function, while a net worth certificate for a bank is a private commercial document outside the clause
options.misconception: reads "financial statements" narrowly and excludes certificates given after an examination of the accounts
options.why: A net worth certificate given after an examination of the accounts is precisely a report or certificate of the kind the clause names. Who asked for it does not change what it is.

options.text: None, because twenty-six per cent of voting power is below the threshold at which a member is deemed to have a substantial interest
options.misconception: misplaces the threshold, which is reached at shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power
options.why: Appendix 9 puts the line at shares carrying twenty per cent or more of the voting power, held at any point across the years in question, and beneficially owned either by the member himself or by the persons the definition groups with him. Twenty-six is above that, not below it.

options.text: All three, because the clause reaches every document a member with a substantial interest signs, whatever it is for and whoever sees it
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out for statements prepared by a member in employment purely for his employer
options.why: The carve-out exists because such a pack is not an opinion offered to anyone outside. It is also prepared for a different company altogether, in which the member's shareholding is not in issue at all.

options.text: The first two — in this clause the words "financial statements" stretch to a report or a certificate of the kind handed over once the accounts have been gone through, and to any attest function a statute demands or an income-tax assessment calls for — while the third stays outside, being a pack a salaried member draws up for his own employer's information as part of his ordinary work, which never travels to anyone outside
options.why: The clause is not confined to a document headed "financial statements". Its reach takes in reports and certificates of the sort a member hands over once he has been through the accounts, and any attest function a statute demands or that income-tax assessments call for — so both the net worth certificate and the tax certificate fall inside it. What falls outside is the third: a pack a salaried member draws up for his own employer's eyes, as part of his ordinary work, which never travels to any outside authority. Twenty-six per cent of the voting power is beyond the twenty per cent at which substantial interest is reached under Appendix 9 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 4 — the meaning of "financial statements" for the clause, read with the definition of substantial interest in Appendix 9 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A member holds shares carrying twenty-six per cent of the voting power in a private company. Three documents are put in front of him. A net worth certificate on that company for its banker, given after an examination of its accounts. A certificate accompanying that company's income-tax return, an attest function for the purposes of the assessment. And a monthly management accounts pack that he prepares as a salaried employee of an entirely different company, purely for that employer's own information and never sent outside it.

items.stem: Which of the four need the Council's permission, and what else follows?

options.text: Editorship of professional journals, and owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity, are within the general permission and need no specific permission; part-time or full-time lectureship for courses other than the Institute's, and tutorship under an educational institution other than the Institute's coaching organisation, need the specific and prior approval of the Council — and the permission is subject to the direct teaching hours taken together not exceeding 25 hours a week if he is to undertake attest functions
options.why: The Council has passed two resolutions and the answer turns on which list an activity falls in. The general permission covers, among other things, private tutorship, authorship of books and articles, editorship of professional journals, acting as a notary public, holding public elective office, acting as surveyor and loss assessor under the Insurance Act, 1938, recovery consultancy in the banking sector, and owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity. The specific and prior approval of the Council is needed for employment in business or non-business concerns, for the office of managing director or whole-time director, for interest in family business concerns, for editorship of journals other than professional journals, and for lectureship and tutorship outside the Institute's own coaching organisation. On top of that sits the condition that direct teaching hours taken together must not exceed 25 hours a week for the member to be able to undertake attest functions.

options.text: None needs permission, because none of the four is a business — teaching, farming and editing are professional or personal pursuits rather than trade
options.misconception: reads Clause 11 as reaching only business, when it reaches any business or occupation other than the profession
options.why: The clause covers any business or occupation other than the profession of accountancy. A lectureship is an occupation, which is why the Council had to name it in the list requiring specific approval.

options.text: Only the lectureship needs permission, and the hours he teaches are a private matter that affects nothing
options.misconception: drops the tutorship outside the Institute's coaching organisation and drops the hours condition attached to the permission
options.why: Tutorship under an educational institution other than the Institute's coaching organisation is on the specific list beside the lectureship, and the permission is granted subject to the 25-hour condition. Thirty hours a week puts his attest work in question.

options.text: All four need specific permission, the proviso to Clause 11 saving only a directorship simpliciter and nothing else
options.misconception: ignores the Council's general resolution, which permits a listed set of occupations without any application
options.why: The proviso about a directorship is one thing and the Council's general permission is another. Editing a professional journal and farming one's own land are on the general list and need no application at all.

citation.ref: Regulation 190A with the Council's general and specific resolutions in Appendix 9, read with First Schedule Part I, Clause 11 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: A practising member takes on four things in one year and asks nobody about any of them. He edits a professional journal. He owns agricultural land and farms it. He accepts a full-time lectureship at a private college. And he takes a part-time tutorship at a private coaching institute that has nothing to do with the Institute's own coaching organisation. Between the last two he teaches thirty direct hours a week, and he continues to sign audit reports.

items.stem: Which of the four breach Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule?

options.text: The company secretary, the advocate and the commerce graduate — fees may be shared only with a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner or a deceased partner's legal representative
options.misconception: stops at the four categories in the clause and omits the members of other professional bodies and prescribed persons the Council has added
options.why: The clause itself names a member of any other professional body and such other persons having such qualifications as may be prescribed. Regulation 53A is where those are prescribed, and it is why a company secretary and an advocate are inside the line.

options.text: Only the referral fee to the other chartered accountant, a payment for the introduction of work being the very thing the clause was written against
options.misconception: confuses the outflow of fees to a non-member with a referral fee between two members, which is permitted
options.why: Clause 2 polices where the fee went, and a fellow member in practice is the one recipient nobody has ever doubted. The introduction that offends is the one by a person outside the permitted lists.

options.text: Only the payment to the commerce graduate — the Council has prescribed under Regulation 53A the professional bodies and the persons qualified in India with whom fees may be shared, and they include a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant, an Actuary and holders of a Bachelor in Engineering, Technology, Architecture or Law and a Master in Business Administration, alongside the Bar Council of India and the other named bodies; a Bachelor of Commerce appears on neither list, and a referral fee between two members in practice is not prohibited at all
options.why: The clause bars payment of any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to anyone outside a named set, and the Council has prescribed that set under Regulation 53A. The professional bodies are the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India, the Bar Council of India, the Indian Institute of Architects and the Institute of Actuaries of India. The persons qualified in India are a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant, an Actuary, and a Bachelor in Engineering, in Technology, in Architecture or in Law, and a Master in Business Administration. A commerce graduate is on neither list, and it is not prohibited for a member in practice to charge a referral fee from another member in practice.

options.text: All four, since a share of professional fees may never leave the firm's own partners
options.misconception: reads the clause as an absolute bar, when it names permitted recipients and the Council has prescribed more
options.why: Sharing with another member of the Institute or with a firm of chartered accountants is in order on the face of the clause, and the referral fee between two members in practice is expressly not prohibited.

citation.ref: Regulation 53A(1) and Regulation 53A(3), read with First Schedule Part I, Clause 2 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: A firm makes four payments out of its professional fees during the year. A share to a practising company secretary who worked with it on a secretarial due diligence. A share to an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of India who worked on the same file. A share to a commerce graduate who introduced the assignment and did none of the work. And a referral fee to another chartered accountant in practice for passing on an assignment.

items.stem: Which of the four are professional misconduct under Clause 10 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: The third and the fourth — an advance received against services to be rendered stays outside the clause, and money given for an expense the member will meet within a reasonably short time may sit in the office account; but money for an expense he will not meet within a reasonably short time goes into a separate bank account straight away, and so does anything reaching him in the capacity of trustee, executor or liquidator
options.why: The Council has drawn four lines through this clause. An advance received against services to be rendered is the member's own money on account and does not fall under it. Where a client hands over cash for an outlay the member will make almost at once — stamp paper, prescribed statutory fees — the office account will do. Where the outlay is months away, and so sits well outside any reasonably short time, the sum belongs in a separate bank account at once, which the eight lakh rupees sitting from April to December plainly does. And moneys received in the capacity of trustee, executor or liquidator must be put in a separate bank account immediately, whatever the amount and whatever the intention.
keywords: advance received against services to be rendered

options.text: Only the fourth, moneys received as liquidator being trust moneys, while everything received from a client in the course of practice is the member's to hold in his office account
options.misconception: treats every client receipt other than a fiduciary one as the member's own money
options.why: The duty attaches to moneys of the client, and eight lakh rupees held for eight months to meet a duty demand is client money in every sense. Only the fee advance and the short-term float are outside the duty.

options.text: None, provided the office account never falls below the total held and every payment is eventually made on time
options.misconception: treats a sufficient balance and an eventual payment as a substitute for a separate banking account
options.why: The offence is the mixing, not the shortfall. Keeping enough in a common account does not separate the client's money from the firm's, which is the whole of what the clause asks for.

options.text: All four — client moneys of every description must be kept in a separate banking account, the clause admitting no distinction
options.misconception: ignores the exclusions the clause and the Council both draw, for fees and for money meant to be spent shortly
options.why: The clause itself excepts fees or remuneration and money meant to be expended, and the Council has said in terms that a fee advance and a short-term expense float are outside it. A rule with no exceptions would make a stamp-paper float misconduct.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 10, read with the Council's suggestions on fee advances, short-term expense moneys and moneys received as trustee, executor or liquidator

items.scenario: Four receipts reach a practising member's office in one month, and all four are put into the firm's office account. Two lakh rupees as an advance against next year's audit fee. Fifteen thousand rupees to buy stamp paper and pay filing fees that week. Eight lakh rupees handed over in April to meet a duty demand that falls due in December. And forty lakh rupees received by him in his capacity as liquidator of a company.

items.stem: Where does he stand under Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Clause 9 reaches both — what the clause punishes is staying silent about a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit that the circumstances called for, and the circulation certification carries a special procedure the member accepted in writing and undertook to report any lapse of; and doing a statutory duty the wrong way is not excused merely by giving a qualification, or a reservation, in the report, so the sentence about the unverified cash does not save him
options.why: Clause 9 is about the audit's own method rather than about the figures. It catches a member who says nothing about a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit that the circumstances called for, and what is generally accepted takes its content from the Institute's own pronouncements — engagement and quality control standards, statements, guidance notes and the rest. Certifying circulation for the Audit Bureau of Circulations carries its own special procedure, which members accept in writing and undertake to report any lapse of, so a silent departure from it is squarely within the clause. And a bare disclosure cures nothing, because a statutory duty carried out the wrong way is not excused merely by giving a qualification, or a reservation, in the report itself; where he does qualify, he would be well advised to say why he could not follow the accepted procedure.
keywords: not excused merely by giving a qualification

options.text: Neither is misconduct — the cash position was disclosed in the report, which is all the Schedule asks, and a circulation certificate is not an audit of financial statements
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing the omitted procedure, and treats a special-purpose certification as outside the accepted-procedure clause
options.why: Disclosure is not performance. And a certification with its own prescribed procedure is exactly where the clause bites, because the accepted procedure in those circumstances is the one the member agreed in writing to follow.

options.text: Both, but under Clause 7 for gross negligence, Clause 9 applying only where the auditor departs from a Standard on Auditing that expressly binds him
options.misconception: narrows generally accepted procedure of audit to the Standards on Auditing alone
options.why: What constitutes generally accepted audit procedure depends on the facts, and guidance comes from the whole body of the Institute's pronouncements and from the special rules governing particular certifications. Clause 7 may run alongside; it does not displace Clause 9.

options.text: Only the cash, and under Clause 8 rather than Clause 9, the failure being a failure to obtain sufficient information necessary for expression of an opinion
options.misconception: reads the cash failure only as an evidence failure and misses the departure from accepted procedure that Clause 9 addresses
options.why: Clause 8 is about the evidence behind the opinion and it is engaged here too, but it says nothing about the circulation certificate. Clause 9 is the clause that reaches a departure from the method itself, in both engagements.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 9 — material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit, and the rule that a failure to perform a statutory duty is not excused by a qualification in the report

items.scenario: An auditor did not verify cash balances of one crore forty lakh rupees held at three depots, in circumstances where verification was necessary, feasible and material. He performed no alternative procedure and wrote one sentence in his report: "We have not verified the cash balances at the depots." In the same year he certified a magazine's circulation for the Audit Bureau of Circulations, departing from the special procedure he had accepted in writing, and said nothing about the departure. His position is that having disclosed the first in his report he is safe, and that the second is a private arrangement with a trade body.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require of the response?

options.text: The substantive procedures must include tests of details, the approach to this significant risk consisting only of substantive procedures
options.why: SA 330 adds a condition where the auditor's approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures: those procedures shall include tests of details. A substantive analytical procedure on its own does not satisfy it, however carefully the expectation is built, so the plan has to add work on the cut-off itself — the despatch and acceptance documents on either side of the year end.

options.text: Tests of controls over cut-off must be performed, a significant risk always obliging the auditor to test the controls that address it
options.misconception: turns the duty to understand the controls relevant to a significant risk into a duty to test their operating effectiveness
options.why: The auditor obtains an understanding of the entity's controls relevant to a significant risk, but he tests their operating effectiveness only where he intends to rely on them in setting the nature, timing and extent of substantive procedures. Here he does not.

options.text: Nothing more — a substantive analytical procedure is a substantive procedure, so a response made of them is responsive to the risk
options.misconception: reads the requirement as "some substantive work of any kind" and misses the extra condition attaching to a substantive-only approach
options.why: The requirement to perform substantive procedures specifically responsive to a significant risk is one sentence and the condition on a substantive-only approach is the next one. Both have to be met, and the second one names tests of details.

options.text: The assessment must be revised downwards, a substantive-only approach being open only for a risk that is not significant
options.misconception: invents a bar on responding to a significant risk with substantive procedures alone
options.why: A substantive-only approach is perfectly available for a significant risk. What the standard controls is the content of those substantive procedures, not whether the approach may be taken at all.

citation.ref: Substantive procedures related to a significant risk, read with the requirement to test controls only where reliance is intended

items.scenario: Revenue cut-off at a project engineering company is a significant risk. You do not intend to rely on any control over cut-off, so the whole response is substantive. The senior's plan holds one procedure: a month-by-month comparison of gross margin against the prior year, with an acceptable difference set in advance. He says analytical procedures are substantive procedures, so a response made only of them is specifically responsive to the risk and the standard asks for nothing more.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require?

options.text: Express an unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph recording that the receivables were not circularised
options.misconception: treats an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence as something a paragraph can disclose away
options.why: An Other Matter paragraph is never a substitute for a modification. The auditor has no evidence over the largest balance in the financial statements, and no paragraph converts that into a basis for an opinion.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion on the financial statements, withdrawal before issuing the report being neither practicable nor possible
options.why: Once the auditor has concluded that undetected misstatements could be material and pervasive in their possible effects, SA 705 (Revised) opens a branch with two steps. Step one: withdraw from the audit, provided the law or regulation he works under makes leaving both practicable and possible. Step two is reached only when leaving before the report goes out is neither of those: disclaim an opinion. The regulator's directive shuts step one here, so step two is the one that operates.

options.text: Withdraw at once, the standard preferring withdrawal to a disclaimer wherever the effects are pervasive
options.misconception: reads the preference for withdrawal as an instruction and drops the condition attached to it
options.why: Withdrawal is offered only where it is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation. On these facts it is neither, and an auditor who leaves anyway breaches the directive rather than complying with the standard.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, setting out the receivables you were unable to verify in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.misconception: applies the material-but-not-pervasive branch to effects the auditor has already concluded are pervasive
options.why: A qualification is the answer where the possible effects could be material but not pervasive. Seventy-two per cent of total assets is the paradigm of pervasive, and the standard says in terms that a qualification would then be inadequate to communicate the gravity of the situation.

citation.ref: What follows when management blocks the evidence after the engagement has been accepted and the auditor can get no sufficient appropriate audit evidence any other way

items.scenario: Six weeks before the report on a listed company is due, management refuses to let you circularise trade receivables of ₹640 crore, being 72 per cent of total assets, and refuses the ageing behind them. You request that the limitation be removed; management refuses. You communicate the refusal to the audit committee and attempt alternative procedures, which produce nothing you can rely on. You conclude that misstatements you have not been able to detect could affect the financial statements in ways that are both material and pervasive. Your counsel confirms that the directive the Securities and Exchange Board of India has issued about auditors stepping down does not let you leave without issuing the report for the period.

items.stem: What does SA 700 (Revised) require beyond the checklist?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the netting and to the single expense line
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to flag a presentation failure the auditor is required to evaluate and, if it is material, to modify for
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter draws attention to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed. These are matters the auditor has concluded are not appropriately presented, which is a different road entirely.

options.text: Nothing beyond the checklist — compliance with the framework's requirements is what forming an opinion means
options.misconception: collapses a fair presentation framework into a compliance framework
options.why: Under a compliance framework the question stops at whether the requirements were met. Under a fair presentation framework the standard adds the further evaluation in terms, which is the whole reason the two kinds of framework are distinguished.

options.text: Only a check that the framework being applied is named or described somewhere in the statements
options.misconception: takes one element of the evaluation and treats it as the whole of it
options.why: Whether the statements adequately refer to or describe the framework is one item on the list. It sits alongside the accounting policies, the estimates, the disclosures, the terminology and the fair presentation evaluation, and none of them stands in for the others.

options.text: An evaluation of whether the financial statements achieve fair presentation — the overall presentation, structure and content, and whether they represent the underlying transactions and events in a manner that achieves it
options.why: The opinion SA 700 (Revised) calls for turns on one question: were these statements drawn up, in every material respect, under the framework that applies to them? Where that framework is a fair presentation one, a second evaluation is bolted on — do the statements achieve fair presentation? Two things feed it. One is the overall presentation, structure and content of what has been produced. The other is whether the statements and their notes, read together, portray the underlying transactions and events so that fair presentation results. Ticking off the framework's named disclosures answers neither.

citation.ref: Forming an opinion on the financial statements — the additional evaluation under a fair presentation framework

items.scenario: A company reports under a fair presentation framework. Every disclosure the framework names is present, every accounting policy is one the framework permits, and there are no uncorrected misstatements. The balance sheet nonetheless sets ₹180 crore receivable from one customer group against ₹176 crore payable to the same group and shows the ₹4 crore difference as a single line, and "other expenses" of ₹640 crore carries no breakdown anywhere in the notes. The manager says the framework's disclosure checklist is complete, so the opinion is unmodified.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require of you on withdrawing?

options.text: Send the resignation and stop there — the standard permits withdrawal and says nothing about how it is done
options.misconception: treats the permission to withdraw as the whole of the requirement and skips the two steps attached to it
options.why: The standard attaches both a determination and a discussion to a withdrawal in these circumstances. Silent departure is exactly the outcome those two steps exist to prevent, because it leaves the fraud with nobody outside the boardroom knowing why the auditor left.

options.text: Continue the engagement and qualify the opinion, the standard never permitting withdrawal where the members made the appointment
options.misconception: invents a bar on withdrawal drawn from who appointed the auditor
options.why: SA 240 contemplates withdrawal in exactly these circumstances and says so. Who made the appointment bears on whom the auditor may have to report the withdrawal to, not on whether he may withdraw.

options.text: File the report on the fraud under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and treat that as discharging everything the standard asks on withdrawal
options.misconception: lets a statutory fraud report stand in for the standard's own requirements about leaving the engagement
options.why: A report under section 143(12) may well be required on these facts, and it runs alongside SA 240 rather than instead of it. It is not a discussion with those charged with governance about the withdrawal, and it does not answer whether the person who made the appointment must be told.

options.text: Work out what his professional and legal responsibilities are here, including whether anyone has to be told he has left — the people who appointed him, and in some cases a regulator — and then discuss the withdrawal, and why it happened, with management at the appropriate level and with those charged with governance
options.why: SA 240 does not leave withdrawal as a private act. Two steps attach to it. The first is a determination: what are this auditor's professional and legal responsibilities on these facts, and do they oblige him to tell whoever appointed him — or, in some situations, a regulator — that he has gone? Regulatory authorities are named in the standard for exactly that reason. The second is a discussion, with management at the appropriate level and with those charged with governance, covering both the departure itself and the reasons for the withdrawal. A one-line letter discharges neither, and the managing director is not the person who decides which of them applies.

citation.ref: The auditor unable to continue the engagement — determining responsibilities and communicating the withdrawal

items.scenario: You have established that the promoter-directors routed ₹18 crore through three vendors with no premises and no employees. You communicated the matter to those charged with governance in writing. The audit committee will not act and the board has resolved that the payments were commercial. You conclude that exceptional circumstances have arisen that bring into question your ability to continue the engagement, and you decide to withdraw. The managing director asks you to send in a one-line resignation and say nothing to anyone, since the members appointed you and the members can be told at the next general meeting.

items.stem: What has the senior still not considered under SA 520?

options.text: That an analytical procedure may never be the sole substantive procedure for a material balance, so tests of details are required on both
options.misconception: turns a judgement about suitability into an absolute bar the standard does not contain
options.why: A substantive analytical procedure may be the only substantive procedure for a balance where it is suitable and the expectation is precise enough. The depreciation charge is a fair example; the objection here is to the professional fees, not to the technique.

options.text: Nothing — reliability of the data and an acceptable difference are the two requirements, and both were met
options.misconception: takes the two limbs the senior did satisfy as the whole of the requirement
options.why: Four things are required before a substantive analytical procedure is relied on: suitability for the assertion, reliability of the data, precision of the expectation, and the amount of acceptable difference. Two of the four have been done.

options.text: That the expectation must be built by management from its own records and then tested by the auditor for reasonableness
options.misconception: hands the auditor's own expectation to the entity, which would make the test circular
options.why: The expectation is the auditor's. An expectation supplied by the entity being audited tells the auditor only that the entity's records agree with themselves.

options.text: The suitability of the particular procedure for the assertion — analytical procedures being generally more applicable to large volumes of transactions that tend to be predictable over time — and whether the expectation is sufficiently precise to identify a misstatement that may be material
options.why: Before any of this is relied on, SA 520 asks whether the particular procedure suits the assertion it is aimed at — a judgement about suitability that takes in the assessed risks and any tests of details covering the same ground. Analytical work fits best where transactions come in large volumes and are predictable over time, which the depreciation charge is and the professional fees plainly are not. A second and separate question follows: is the expectation sufficiently precise that a misstatement big enough to matter, on its own or added to others, would show up as a difference? A comparison with last year's number on an unpredictable balance gives no such precision.

citation.ref: Substantive analytical procedures — suitability for the assertion and precision of the expectation

items.scenario: Two balances are to be tested by substantive analytical procedures alone. The first is depreciation on a fleet of delivery vans: opening cost, additions and disposals are verified elsewhere, the rate is fixed by policy, and an expected charge can be built to within ₹40,000. The second is consultancy and professional fees of ₹9 crore — eighty-one invoices from thirty-one unrelated suppliers, none of them recurring, with no operating driver in the business that predicts the total. Performance materiality is ₹1.1 crore. The senior plans a comparison with last year's figure for both, and has evaluated the reliability of the data and fixed an acceptable difference in each case.

items.stem: What does SA 530 make the sample size turn on?

options.text: Nothing that has to be reasoned, once a non-statistical approach is chosen and the firm's manual gives a number
options.misconception: reads "non-statistical" as "unreasoned", when it means only that the size is not computed by a statistical formula
options.why: A non-statistical approach uses judgement in place of a formula, and the judgement is over the same three inputs. A number taken from a manual with none of them considered is not a sample size the standard recognises.

options.text: A fixed proportion of the population, so that a larger population always draws a larger sample
options.misconception: makes sample size a percentage of the population, which SA 530 does not do
options.why: For a large population the size of the population itself has almost no effect on the sample size needed. What drives it is how much risk the auditor will accept and how far the tolerable rate sits from the expected rate.

options.text: The level of sampling risk the auditor is willing to accept, the tolerable rate of deviation and the rate of deviation he expects to find — the size being one sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level, whether the approach is statistical or non-statistical
options.why: SA 530 requires the auditor to determine a sample size sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level. What moves that size is the level of sampling risk the auditor is willing to accept, the tolerable rate of deviation for a test of controls or the tolerable misstatement for a test of details, and the rate of deviation or the misstatement he expects to find. Sampling risk is the risk that the conclusion drawn from a sample differs from the conclusion the same procedure would reach on the whole population. The reasoning is owed whether the approach is statistical or non-statistical: the approach changes how the size is arrived at, not whether it must be arrived at.

options.text: Non-sampling risk, which the auditor reduces by taking more items
options.misconception: swaps the two risks, and attaches to sample size the one no sample size can touch
options.why: Non-sampling risk is the risk of an erroneous conclusion for any reason not related to sampling — a badly designed procedure, a misread document. Enlarging the sample does nothing about it; only better procedures and supervision do.

citation.ref: Sample size and the factors influencing it, read with the definitions of sampling risk and non-sampling risk

items.scenario: Two seniors argue about the sample size for a test of the purchase authorisation control. One says the sample must be at least a tenth of the population, because a larger population needs a proportionately larger sample. The other says the firm's standard number is enough and that, because he is using a non-statistical approach, the size needs no reasoning behind it at all. Neither has written down the rate of deviation he would tolerate, nor the rate he expects to find, nor how much risk of a wrong conclusion he is prepared to run.

items.stem: What does SA 620 require before the expert's work is used?

options.text: Objectivity is evaluated only for a management's expert, the auditor's own expert being answerable to the auditor
options.misconception: reverses the two, when the requirement to evaluate competence, capabilities and objectivity is written for the auditor's expert
options.why: SA 620 governs the auditor's expert, and the evaluation of competence, capabilities and objectivity is its requirement. A management's expert is dealt with under SA 500, where the auditor evaluates that expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity as well.

options.text: An evaluation of whether the expert has the necessary competence, capabilities and objectivity — inquiring of the entity about interests and relationships including financial interests, business and personal relationships and other services the expert provides it, and obtaining a written representation from the expert about them
