options.why: Competence, capabilities and objectivity are evaluated before the expert's work is relied on, and they are a separate and earlier question from whether the work itself turns out to be adequate. Where the expert is an external expert the auditor inquires of the entity about interests and relationships that may create a threat to objectivity — financial interests, business and personal relationships, and the provision of other services by the expert to the entity — and it is appropriate to obtain a written representation from the expert about any such interest or relationship, and to discuss with him whether any safeguards are adequate. An eleven-year retainer, a fee, and a brother in the entity's management are precisely what that evaluation exists to surface.

options.text: Nothing before the work arrives — objectivity is judged from the report, and a report that stands up is a report from an objective expert
options.misconception: pushes an entry test to the end of the work, where the answer can no longer change what was relied on
options.why: The evaluation comes before reliance because it decides whether the work may be relied on at all. Work that happens to look sound is not evidence that the person who produced it was free of a threat to his objectivity.

options.text: The expert may not be engaged at all, a retainer with the entity and a relative inside it being an absolute bar
options.misconception: converts a threat the auditor must evaluate into a prohibition the standard does not impose
options.why: SA 620 does not bar an expert with a relationship to the entity. It requires the relationships to be identified, the threats evaluated, and safeguards considered — and an expert engaged by the entity is common enough that the standard sets out how to handle it.

citation.ref: Competence, capabilities and objectivity of the auditor's expert, and the inquiry into interests and relationships

items.scenario: You propose to engage an actuary as an auditor's expert on a company's gratuity and pension liability. He is an external expert, not part of your firm. His own firm has been the company's retained actuarial adviser for eleven years and draws a fee from the company for that retainer, and his brother is the company's head of human resources. Your manager says none of this matters, because the objectivity question is about the audit firm rather than the expert, and in any case the work will be evaluated for adequacy when it arrives.

items.stem: What does SA 620 say about naming the expert there?

options.text: Name the expert and state that responsibility for the valuation of the investment rests with him
options.misconception: uses the reference to divide a responsibility the standard says is undivided
options.why: The auditor has sole responsibility for the opinion expressed, and that responsibility is not reduced by his use of the work of an auditor's expert. A sentence apportioning it to the expert states the opposite of the standard.

options.text: The reference may be made, being relevant to an understanding of the modification — and the report must then indicate that the reference does not reduce your responsibility for the opinion
options.why: SA 620 keeps the auditor's expert out of a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires the reference. Where the auditor refers to the work of an auditor's expert because that reference is relevant to an understanding of a modification to the opinion, the standard permits the reference and attaches a condition to it: the report shall indicate that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility for that opinion. The same condition applies where law or regulation requires the reference to be made.

options.text: The reference is permitted here and needs no further wording, the disclaimer itself making clear that nothing has been concluded
options.misconception: makes the reference and drops the sentence the standard requires to accompany it
options.why: The added sentence is a requirement, not a courtesy. Without it a reader may take the mention of a specialist as a division of responsibility, which is the exact misreading the sentence exists to close off.

options.text: The expert may never be named in an auditor's report in any circumstances
options.misconception: takes the default silence for an absolute rule and loses the two exceptions written next to it
options.why: Silence is the default, not the rule. Law or regulation may require the reference, and the auditor may make it where it is relevant to understanding a modification.

citation.ref: Reference to the auditor's expert in the auditor's report

items.scenario: You disclaim an opinion on a company's financial statements because you could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the fair value of an unlisted investment. To make the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section understandable you want to describe the work of the auditor's expert you engaged on that valuation and why it did not resolve the matter.

items.stem: What has he left out of the engagement quality control review?

options.text: Reading a selection of the working papers behind the team's significant judgments and the conclusions drawn from them, talking the significant matters over with the engagement partner, and — this being a listed client — looking at how the team satisfied itself that the firm was independent on this engagement
options.why: An engagement quality control review is, in SQC 1's own framing, an objective look at the significant judgments the team arrived at and at where those judgments landed in the auditor's report — and the standard then lists the four things such a review is made of. Significant matters are discussed with the engagement partner. The financial statements and the draft report are read. A selection of the working papers sitting behind those judgments is read too. And the conclusions drawn for the report are evaluated. A listed client adds three more: how the team satisfied itself about the firm's independence here, whether difficult or contentious matters and differences of opinion drew the consultation they should have, and whether the papers chosen do show the work done on the significant judgments.

options.text: Only the independence point, the review of working papers belonging to the engagement partner rather than to the reviewer
options.misconception: hands the documentation review back to the engagement partner, whose own judgments are the thing being reviewed
options.why: The engagement partner reviews the file as part of directing the engagement. The reviewer looks at selected documentation precisely because his subject is the significant judgments the partner and the team made, and he cannot evaluate those from the finished statements alone.

options.text: He should have re-performed the significant audit procedures himself, a review being worth nothing unless the work is done again
options.misconception: turns an objective evaluation of judgments into a second audit
options.why: SQC 1 asks for an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions, not a re-performance. The reviewer reads selected documentation to test the reasoning; he does not redo the testing.

options.text: Nothing — the review is of the judgments and the report, and both were read before the report was dated
options.misconception: treats the output of the audit as the whole subject of the review and drops the documentation behind it
options.why: Reading the statements and the proposed report is one of four named steps. Without the selected documentation behind the significant judgments, the reviewer has nothing against which to test whether those judgments were sound.

citation.ref: The nature, timing and extent of an engagement quality control review, and the additional considerations for the audit of a listed entity

items.scenario: The engagement quality control reviewer on a listed company's audit reads the draft financial statements and the proposed auditor's report, is satisfied with both, and signs off before the report is dated. He opens no working paper, saying the engagement partner has already reviewed the file and a second reading of the same papers adds nothing. He also does not look at the engagement team's conclusion on the firm's independence, saying independence is settled centrally by the firm and is not an engagement matter.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xxi) actually reach?

options.text: The clause requires the opinion on the consolidated financial statements to be modified for the two component qualifications
options.misconception: reads a signpost as a modification, and a component's qualification as automatically material to the group
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) points the reader at where a component's own report already carries a qualification. Whether that matter is material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole is a separate evaluation under SA 705 (Revised), and it may well not be.

options.text: Only the components that are themselves covered by the Order — so the three Indian subsidiaries, of which two carry remarks to be reported; the small company, the banking subsidiary, the foreign subsidiary and the limited liability partnership contribute nothing to the clause and are not reported as clean either
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) puts a single question: did any of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements draw a qualification or an adverse remark from its own auditor? Where one did, the auditor gives the details of that company along with the paragraph numbers of the report carrying them. A component with no CARO report of its own supplies nothing to answer with. The Order leaves out a banking company, a small company and a section 8 company, and it never reaches an entity that is not a company under the Act at all — so a foreign body corporate and a limited liability partnership sit outside it too, and calling them free of adverse remarks asserts something nobody examined.
keywords: companies included in the consolidated financial statements

options.text: Every component included in the consolidation, each answered clause by clause, since the reader of the consolidated statements is entitled to the same information as the reader of a standalone one
options.misconception: reads the one clause that survives consolidation as a licence to run the whole Order over the group
options.why: Only clause 3(xxi) operates on a report on consolidated financial statements. The other clauses attach to the auditor's report on the standalone financial statements of the companies the Order covers.

options.text: All seven components, with the four outside the Order reported as carrying no adverse remarks so that the clause is complete
options.misconception: fills a gap in the clause with a positive statement about entities that have no CARO report at all
options.why: A clean answer is an assertion. For a component the Order never touched there is no CARO report and no examination behind such an assertion, so the honest position is that the clause does not reach it.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xxi), read with the paragraph of the Order listing the companies to which it does not apply

items.scenario: The consolidated financial statements you are reporting on include three Indian subsidiaries covered by CARO 2020, one Indian subsidiary that is a small company, a banking subsidiary, a subsidiary incorporated outside India, and a limited liability partnership joint venture. Two of the three CARO-covered subsidiaries have qualifications in their CARO reports. Your manager proposes to state under clause 3(xxi) that the small company, the banking subsidiary, the foreign subsidiary and the limited liability partnership carry "no adverse remarks".

items.stem: What else does clause 3(iii) require to be reported?

options.text: The split between related and other borrowers is asked only of a company whose principal business is to give loans, so a manufacturer reports one aggregate
options.misconception: reverses the carve-out, which takes lending companies out of that sub-clause instead of confining it to them
options.why: The words in brackets exempt a company whose principal business is to give loans from sub-clause (a), and from the renewal disclosure in sub-clause (e). A manufacturer is squarely inside both.

options.text: The aggregate during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date shown separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties; whether the schedule of repayment of principal and interest is stipulated and whether the receipts are regular; and the total amount overdue for more than ninety days with whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery
options.why: Sub-clause (a) asks for the aggregate amount during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, split between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and other parties on the other, so one figure of ₹55 crore does not answer it. Sub-clause (c) asks separately whether a schedule of repayment of principal and interest has been stipulated and whether the receipts are regular — a schedule that exists and is not being met fails the second half. And where anything is unpaid, sub-clause (d) wants the amount more than ninety days overdue, and whether reasonable steps went into getting the principal and the interest back, which on these facts is nothing at all.
keywords: balance outstanding at the balance sheet date

options.text: The overdue limb does not arise, a schedule having been stipulated and only one borrower being late
options.misconception: reads the overdue disclosure as a consequence of having no schedule, when it is triggered by the amount being unpaid
options.why: Sub-clause (d) is triggered by an amount being overdue, whatever the paperwork says. One hundred and forty days is beyond ninety, so the amount and the steps taken both have to be stated.

options.text: Nothing more — the terms are not prejudicial, and that is the judgement the clause exists to draw out
options.misconception: answers one sub-clause and reports the whole of clause 3(iii) as satisfied
options.why: Whether the terms are prejudicial is sub-clause (b). It sits beside the amounts, the schedule, the overdue position, the renewals and the on-demand loans, and each of those is answered on its own.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)(a), clause 3(iii)(c) and clause 3(iii)(d)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company, whose principal business is not to give loans, granted ₹40 crore of loans to two subsidiaries and ₹15 crore to unrelated parties during the year. Every loan carries a written schedule for repayment of principal and interest. ₹6 crore of the subsidiary loans fell due and has been unpaid for one hundred and forty days, and the company has done nothing about it. The audit senior drafts clause 3(iii) as a single aggregate of ₹55 crore with a sentence that the terms are not prejudicial to the company's interest.

items.stem: Is the senior right?

options.text: No, and the whole consolidation must be rebuilt from the original acquisition date as though the 85 per cent had been held throughout
options.misconception: turns a fresh determination on the new tranche into a restatement of every earlier year
options.why: What is redone is the determination of goodwill or capital reserve and of the amount attributable to the non-controlling interests, on the new tranche and from its own date. Prior periods are not rewritten to pretend the holding was always 85 per cent.

options.text: No — permanent consolidation adjustments are made on the first occasion and again on any subsequent occasion on which there is a change in the shareholding of a consolidated entity, so the further 15 per cent reopens the determination of goodwill or capital reserve and of the amount attributable to the non-controlling interests
options.why: Two occasions call for permanent consolidation adjustments, not one: the first time a component is consolidated, and any later date on which a change in the shareholding of that component takes place. Buying a further 15 per cent is such a date. Two adjustments are then remade — goodwill or capital reserve, and the slice of equity belonging to the minority or non-controlling interests. The auditor pays particular attention to the pre-acquisition reserves of the component, which the dates of investment fix, and checks that they have been split properly between the parent and the non-controlling interests.

options.text: Yes — permanent adjustments take their name from being made once, on the first occasion of consolidation, and never revisited
options.misconception: keeps half the definition and drops the second trigger written into it
options.why: The definition has two occasions in it, not one: the first consolidation, and any later change in the shareholding. "Permanent" describes an adjustment that is not remade every year, not one that is never remade.

options.text: Yes, because the change happened part-way through the year rather than on the first day of it, so it falls into next year's consolidation
options.misconception: makes the trigger a date in the calendar rather than the change in shareholding itself
options.why: The trigger is the change in shareholding, and the date of investment is what fixes the pre-acquisition reserves to be allocated. A mid-year purchase is dealt with in the year it happens.

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — permanent consolidation adjustments and current period consolidation adjustments

items.scenario: A parent has held 70 per cent of a subsidiary for five years. On 1 October this year it bought a further 15 per cent, taking its holding to 85 per cent. The consolidation senior proposes to carry goodwill and the non-controlling interests' share of net assets forward at the figures computed on the original acquisition, on the ground that permanent consolidation adjustments are made only on the first occasion of consolidation, and to treat the intra-group eliminations as the only work of this year.

items.stem: What is the position under section 129?

options.text: Nothing need be attached about the subsidiaries, the consolidated statements already carrying their figures; and the consolidated statements are audited but are not laid before the members
options.misconception: assumes consolidation absorbs the component disclosure, and stops the audit short of adoption
options.why: Consolidation merges the numbers and hides the individual entities, which is why the separate statement of salient features exists. And section 129(4) carries the whole preparation, adoption and audit regime across, laying included.

options.text: The consolidated financial statements are prepared for information only, so no audit of them is required and Form AOC-1 replaces them
options.misconception: treats consolidated statements as a voluntary annexure rather than as statements the Act requires and the auditor reports on
options.why: Section 129(3) requires the consolidated financial statements themselves, and section 129(4) brings the audit requirement with them. Form AOC-1 sits beside them and replaces nothing.

options.text: The full financial statements of every subsidiary must be attached to the company's own financial statements
options.misconception: reads a statement of salient features as a requirement to annex the components entire
options.why: What is attached is a separate statement of the salient features in the prescribed form, not each subsidiary's complete financial statements.

options.text: Form AOC-1 must be attached, carrying the salient features of each subsidiary's financial statement; and whatever the Act says about preparing, adopting and auditing a holding company's financial statements applies, mutatis mutandis, to the consolidated ones
options.why: The proviso to section 129(3) makes the company annex Form AOC-1 to its own financial statement, and what goes into that form is a statement of each subsidiary's salient features — with subsidiary reading, for this purpose, as taking in an associate company and a joint venture too. Section 129(4) then carries across, mutatis mutandis, everything the Act says about how a holding company's financial statements are prepared, adopted and audited, and it carries it to the consolidated set — so those are audited, adopted and put before the members just as the standalone ones are.

citation.ref: Proviso to Section 129(3) with Rule 5 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, and Section 129(4)

items.scenario: A listed company with four subsidiaries and one associate is preparing consolidated financial statements for the first time. The company secretary asks two things: whether anything about the individual subsidiaries has to be attached to the financial statements, and whether the consolidated financial statements themselves have to be audited, adopted and laid before the members in the way the company's own financial statements are.

items.stem: What breaches Regulation 18?

options.text: Only the marketing director's membership — the expertise requirement and the chairperson's attendance are recommendations of good practice rather than requirements
options.misconception: sorts one requirement into the binding column and two identically worded ones into the advisory column
options.why: All three sit in the same sub-regulation and are worded the same way. Nothing marks the expertise requirement or the attendance requirement as advisory.

options.text: Nothing — three independent directors out of four satisfies the two-thirds test, and the rest of Regulation 18 is best practice
options.misconception: stops at the arithmetic of composition and treats every qualitative requirement as optional
options.why: The arithmetic is the part that passes. What fails is the set of qualifications and duties attaching to the members and to the chairperson, which the Regulation states as requirements.

options.text: Only the chairperson's absence — financial literacy is left to the board's judgement and the Regulation prescribes no expertise requirement
options.misconception: drops the two qualifications Regulation 18(1) states in terms and keeps only the attendance rule
options.why: Both qualifications are written into the Regulation, and financial literacy is even defined in it, so neither is a matter of the board's judgement.

options.text: Three things — every member must be financially literate, at least one member must have accounting or related financial management expertise, and the chairperson must be present at the annual general meeting to answer shareholder queries
options.why: Regulation 18(1) requires that all members of the audit committee shall be financially literate, meaning able to read and understand a balance sheet, a statement of profit and loss and a statement of cash flows, and that at least one member shall have accounting or related financial management expertise. It separately requires that the chairperson of the committee shall be an independent director and shall be present at the annual general meeting to answer shareholder queries. The counting is fine here: four directors with three independent clears the two-thirds test, and five meetings inside ninety-day gaps clears Regulation 18(2).
keywords: accounting or related financial management expertise

citation.ref: Regulation 18(1) — financial literacy of every member, accounting or related financial management expertise of at least one, and the chairperson's presence at the annual general meeting

items.scenario: A listed entity's audit committee has four directors, three of them independent, and met five times during the year with no gap longer than ninety days. Its chairperson is an independent director but did not attend the annual general meeting, the company having routed every shareholder question through the managing director. One member, the marketing director, says openly that he cannot read a statement of cash flows, and no member has any accounting or related financial management background.

items.stem: What do sections 177(5) and 177(6) allow the committee?

options.text: The chairman is right on both — the committee's investigative jurisdiction begins with a reference from the Board, and access to records and to outside advisers runs through the Board
options.misconception: reads the Board's reference as the only gateway, when the section gives two and neither depends on the Board
options.why: The section reads "in relation to the items specified in sub-section (4) or referred to it by the Board". Capital work in progress goes to the financial statement and to internal financial controls, both of which are in the terms of reference, so the committee is already inside its own jurisdiction.

options.text: To investigate any matter in relation to the items specified in the terms of reference or referred to it by the Board, with power to obtain professional advice from external sources and full access to information contained in the records of the company; and to call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems and the scope of audit including their observations, and to review the financial statement before its submission to the Board
options.why: Section 177(6) gives the audit committee authority to investigate into any matter in relation to the items specified in sub-section (4) or referred to it by the Board, and for that purpose the power to obtain professional advice from external sources and full access to information contained in the records of the company. A reference from the Board is one way in, not the only way, and neither the outside advice nor the records need the Board's leave. Section 177(5) lets the committee call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems, the scope of audit including the observations of the auditors, and review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board, and discuss any related issues with the internal and statutory auditors and with the management.

options.text: The committee may call for the auditors' comments but may not review the financial statement before it goes to the Board, review being the Board's own function
options.misconception: takes review of the financial statement out of a sub-section that names it
options.why: Section 177(5) names review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board as one of the things the committee may take up with the auditors. The Board's own review comes after, not instead.

options.text: The committee may investigate and may take outside advice, but access to the records is a matter for management, the committee being a committee of the Board rather than an authority over the company
options.misconception: grants the power and withholds the access the same sub-section grants alongside it
options.why: Full access to information contained in the records of the company is written into the same sub-section as the power to investigate and the power to take external advice. An investigation without the records would be the power without its subject.

citation.ref: Sections 177(5) and 177(6)

items.scenario: An audit committee suspects that ₹22 crore of capital work in progress at a plant is fictitious. The chairman of the Board tells the committee that it may look only into what the Board refers to it, that it cannot engage an outside forensic firm without the Board's sanction, and that the company's records are the Board's to release. The committee separately wants the statutory auditor's comments on the internal control systems and on the scope of the audit, and wants to review the financial statement before it goes to the Board.

items.stem: How do the four sit across the control types?

options.text: The first three are general IT controls — access security, program change, and data centre and network operations in that order — and the fourth is an application control inside the sales system
options.why: General IT controls govern the environment and are grouped by objective. Access security is about access to programs and data being authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives, and removing a terminated user's access on a timely basis sits there. Program change is about modified systems continuing to meet those objectives, and covers segregating development from production and having changes tested and approved before migration. Data centre and network operations is about production systems being backed up and monitored, and batch job schedules being monitored for failures. A validation that refuses an invoice with no customer code lives inside one system and tests one transaction, which is what an application control is.

options.text: All four are general IT controls, because every one of them is a failure of the company's information technology
options.misconception: sorts by where the failure happened rather than by what the control does
options.why: The split is not between technology and business. General controls hold the environment steady; application controls test individual transactions inside one system, which is exactly what the customer-code validation does.

options.text: The first is an application control and the fourth a general IT control, access being granted inside the application and a validation rule being part of the platform
options.misconception: reverses the two clearest cases by looking at where a setting is typed rather than at what it governs
options.why: Access provisioning is a general control however it is administered, because it governs who may reach the programs and the data. A field validation inside the sales system governs one transaction, so it is an application control.

options.text: All four are application controls, since each one is a rule the company's software was supposed to enforce
options.misconception: reads anything a computer does as an application control
options.why: User access administration, change management and batch scheduling are not features of one application. They are the environment every application on the platform runs inside.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — what each area of general IT controls is there to achieve, and the application controls that sit beside them

items.scenario: Four weaknesses come out of one company's information technology environment. A terminated employee's login was still active four months after he left. A change to the pricing master was migrated into production without testing and without approval. The overnight batch job failed twice in March and nobody was told. And the sales system accepts and posts an invoice that carries no customer code.

items.stem: How many of the Board's four instructions match how an investigation actually runs?

options.text: The materiality instruction and the timetable, an investigation still being bound by the same thresholds and the same reporting cycle as the audit it grows out of
options.misconception: carries the audit's sampling and reporting rhythm into a probe that is defined by not having them
options.why: Materiality and a fixed reporting cycle belong to an audit, which uses test checking and sampling to form an opinion. An investigation requires a detailed study and examination of the facts and figures in the selected area, on whatever period the question needs.

options.text: All four — an investigation by a chartered accountant follows the same materiality, evidence and reporting discipline as an audit, only aimed at a narrower question
options.misconception: treats an investigation as an audit with a smaller scope, when the evidence standard and the reporting audience both change
options.why: Narrowness of subject is only one of the differences. The evidence sought is conclusive rather than persuasive, nothing is taken on a stated fact, the period is open, and the report goes to whoever commissioned it.

options.text: The reporting instruction only, because an investigation ordered by the Board of a company must ultimately be reported to the members who own it
options.misconception: routes the report to the owners because the entity is a company, when the subject is who commissioned the work
options.why: An audit's outcome is reported to the owners of the business entity. An investigation's outcome goes to the person or persons on whose behalf it was carried out, and even a third party may appoint an investigator.

options.text: None of the four — an investigation seeks conclusive evidence rather than persuasive, does not accept a stated fact until it is substantiated, is not limited by a rigid time frame and may cover several years, and reports to the person or persons on whose behalf it is carried out
options.why: The differences from an audit are what the examiner asks for. An investigation seeks substantive and in some cases conclusive evidence, where an audit is mainly concerned with evidence that is prima facie or persuasive. An investigator treats nothing as fact on the strength of having been told it; he gets there only once the point is substantiated, whereas an auditor may rely on what he is told where nothing looks suspicious. The work is not limited by a rigid time frame and may cover several years, because the outcome is not certain at the start. And the outcome is reported to the person or persons on whose behalf the investigation is carried out — here the Board that ordered it, not the shareholders in general meeting.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — audit versus investigation

items.scenario: The Board asks you to establish whether the head of procurement took kickbacks over the last four years. It hands you four instructions with the engagement letter: work only to the current year's audit materiality; accept the procurement head's written explanations where nothing on the file contradicts them; present your findings to the shareholders at the annual general meeting; and finish inside the statutory audit's timetable.

items.stem: What is the position under sections 22A and 22G?

options.text: Both may appeal, an appellate body existing to hear anyone dissatisfied with the decision below
options.misconception: assumes a general right of appeal for a complainant, which section 22G does not create
options.why: The section names who may appeal, and a complainant is not on the list. A general right of appeal for anybody dissatisfied would have to be written in, and it is not.

options.text: The Director (Discipline) may appeal where the Council so authorises him and the complainant company may not, the appeal lying to a member aggrieved by an order and to the Director (Discipline) alone — and the Authority is a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government
options.why: Section 22A has the Central Government constitute an Appellate Authority consisting of a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government from among persons of ability, integrity and standing having special knowledge of law, economics, business, commerce or accountancy. Section 22G opens the appeal to a member of the Institute aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or of the Disciplinary Committee, and by a proviso to the Director (Discipline) where the Council so authorises him. A complainant is neither of those, so the company has no appeal to the Authority.

options.text: The complainant may appeal and the Director (Discipline) may not, an officer of the Institute having no standing to challenge the Institute's own Committee
options.misconception: inverts both halves of the section
options.why: It is the other way round. The member and the Director (Discipline) have the appeal; the complainant does not.

options.text: Neither may appeal, the Authority hearing only a member on whom a penalty has been imposed, so an officer of the Institute has no standing
options.misconception: keeps the member's right and loses the proviso that gives the Director (Discipline) his
options.why: The proviso to section 22G is exactly the answer to that: the Director (Discipline) may also appeal against a decision of the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee, if so authorised by the Council.

citation.ref: Section 22A on the constitution of the Appellate Authority, and Section 22G with its proviso on who may prefer an appeal

items.scenario: The Board of Discipline finds a member not guilty and closes a complaint. The complainant, a company, wants to take the closure to the Appellate Authority. In an unrelated matter the Council considers an order of the Disciplinary Committee far too lenient and wants the Director (Discipline) to challenge it. A member sitting in on both asks who actually sits on the Authority.

items.stem: Which of the four is professional misconduct under Clause 10?

options.text: All four, Clause 10 admitting no exception once a fee moves with an outcome
options.misconception: reads the clause without the words that carry the exception into Regulation 192
options.why: The clause itself says "except as permitted under any regulation made under this Act". Three of the four sit inside those permitted cases, which is the whole point of reading the clause and the regulation together.

options.text: The second and the fourth — a percentage of working capital is a percentage of profits under another name
options.misconception: treats a permitted base for a co-operative society audit as if it were the prohibited profit base
options.why: Regulation 192 names the paid-up capital, the working capital, the gross or net income and the profits, all four, as permitted bases for the auditor of a co-operative society. Working capital is on the list in terms.

options.text: Only the fourth
options.why: Clause 10 bars fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the professional employment, except as permitted under any regulation made under the Act, and the exception is Regulation 192. That regulation permits a valuer for the purposes of direct taxes and duties to charge on a percentage of the value of the property valued, and permits the auditor of a co-operative society to charge on a percentage of the paid-up capital, the working capital, the gross or net income or the profits. The Council has separately permitted a percentage or contingent basis for debt recovery services, alongside certain management consultancy services, fund raising services and cost optimisation services. A certification fee that rises with the credit limit a bank chooses to sanction is outside every one of those cases, and it is contingent on the result of the very work certified.
keywords: percentage of the value of the property valued

options.text: None, Regulation 192 permitting a percentage fee wherever the client has agreed to one in writing
options.misconception: turns a closed list of permitted engagements into a consent rule
options.why: Regulation 192 permits particular engagements on a percentage basis, and consent is not one of the conditions. A client's agreement cannot bring an engagement inside a list it is not on.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A member in practice takes four engagements in one year, each on a percentage basis agreed in writing. As a valuer of a factory building for the purposes of direct taxes, at a stated percentage of the value he determines. As auditor of a co-operative society, at a stated percentage of its working capital. Providing a debt recovery service to a manufacturer, at a stated percentage of the debt actually recovered. And certifying a company's turnover for its bankers, at a stated percentage of the credit limit the bank goes on to sanction.

items.stem: What happens next?

options.text: Neither is right — the Director (Discipline) places all the information and the complaint before the Board of Discipline whatever Schedule was invoked, and the Board either agrees with him and closes the matter or disagrees, in which case it may advise him to investigate further, proceed with the matter itself where it is allied to the First Schedule, or refer it to the Disciplinary Committee where it is allied to the Second Schedule or to both
options.why: Which Schedule the clause sits in decides the forum only where the prima facie opinion is that the member is guilty. Where the Director (Discipline) is of the opinion that the member is not guilty, he submits all the information and complaints to the Board of Discipline whatever the clause complained of, and it is the Board that decides what happens. If it agrees, the matter is closed. If it disagrees, it may advise the Director (Discipline) to further investigate the matter, may proceed with the matter itself if it is allied to the First Schedule, or may refer the matter to the Disciplinary Committee if it is allied to the Second Schedule or to both the Schedules.

options.text: The complainant is right — a Second Schedule allegation goes to the Disciplinary Committee whatever the Director (Discipline) thinks of it
options.misconception: applies the guilty routing to a not-guilty opinion, so that the Schedule decides the forum in every case
options.why: The routing by Schedule operates on a prima facie opinion of guilt. On a not-guilty opinion there is one destination whatever the Schedule, and that is the Board of Discipline.

options.text: The complaint goes to the Appellate Authority, which is where a complainant dissatisfied with the closure of his complaint takes it
options.misconception: reaches for the appeal route before the first-instance body has even seen the matter
options.why: The Appellate Authority hears appeals against orders of the Board of Discipline and the Disciplinary Committee, from a member on whom a penalty was imposed or from the Director (Discipline) where the Council authorises him. Nothing has yet reached it, and a complainant has no appeal to it in any case.

options.text: The member is right — a prima facie opinion that he is not guilty closes the file, the Director (Discipline) being the officer the Act charges with forming it
options.misconception: gives the Director's opinion a finality the Act deliberately withholds
options.why: The Director (Discipline) forms the opinion; he does not dispose of the complaint. A not-guilty opinion goes to the Board of Discipline for it to accept or reject, which is what stops one officer from closing complaints alone.

citation.ref: Section 21, read with the 2007 Rules on the Institute's procedure for investigating professional and other misconduct — the route taken where the prima facie opinion is not guilty

items.scenario: A complaint against a member alleges gross negligence in the conduct of his professional duties, which is a clause of Part I of the Second Schedule. The Director (Discipline) examines it and forms a prima facie opinion that the member is not guilty. The complainant insists the matter must still go to the Disciplinary Committee, because the clause complained of sits in the Second Schedule. The member insists the Director's opinion ends the matter there and then.

items.stem: Are the two a network, and what follows for P?

options.text: No — a network requires common ownership, control or management, and two firms with no common partner cannot have it
options.misconception: reads one alternative test as the essential one, so that separate ownership settles the question
options.why: Common ownership, control or management is again one entry among six. Separate partners, separate profits and separate deeds do not undo a network built on any of the others.

options.text: Yes, but the consequence stops at disclosure — P discloses the relationship to those charged with governance and continues
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for the independence requirement that membership of a network actually attracts
options.why: Membership of a network makes the independence requirements applying to an audit client of the firm apply to the network firm too. A material financial interest in the audit client is not a matter that disclosure cures.

options.text: Yes — a larger structure aimed at co-operation that shares common quality control policies and procedures, or that shares a common business strategy, is a network on either of those tests standing alone, so Q's shareholding is treated as though P held it and P is not independent of the audit client
options.why: A network is a larger structure aimed at co-operation between firms which also does any one of a list of things: shares profits or costs, has common ownership, control or management, shares common quality control policies and procedures, shares a common business strategy, uses a common brand name, or shares a significant part of professional resources. Each of those tests stands on its own, so a quality control manual applied across both firms with cross review, or a signed common business strategy, makes a network with no brand, no shared people and no shared money anywhere in the arrangement. The consequence is the reason the definition exists: the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of the firm apply to a network firm too, so a financial interest that is material to Q is treated as though P held it.

options.text: No — a network needs a common brand name or a significant part of the professional resources shared, and neither is present
options.misconception: takes two of the alternative tests as the only two, when the list is disjunctive
options.why: The brand and the shared resources are two entries on a list of six, and any one entry is enough. Two other entries are met here in terms.

citation.ref: The definition of a network and of a network firm, and the application to a network firm of the independence requirements for an audit client of the firm

items.scenario: Two firms practise in different cities under different names. They share no brand, no letterhead, no office, no staff, no specialists and no profits or costs; they have no common partner and no common ownership, control or management. What they do share is one written quality control manual adopted by both, under which each reviews a sample of the other's engagements, and a signed three-year business plan setting common target sectors and a common pricing policy. Firm P audits a listed company. Firm Q holds a shareholding in that same company which is material to Q.

items.stem: What does the Code require?

options.text: Both may be assigned, the Code's provisions running only the other way — on a partner or employee leaving the firm for the client
options.misconception: keeps only the outward movement and misses that the Code answers both directions separately
options.why: The Code deals with both directions. Going out, a former partner joining the client raises a familiarity or intimidation threat unless no significant connection remains with the firm. Coming in is the case here, and it has its own rule.

options.text: The first may not be assigned to the audit team at all, his employment having occurred during the period covered by the audit report; the second may be, the threats from his earlier service being evaluated and addressed, for example by having an appropriate reviewer review the work he performs
options.why: Take someone who has been a director or officer at the audit client, or an employee whose position let him exert significant influence over how the client's accounting records or financial statements were prepared. If he joins the firm, he may not be put on that client's audit team where the service or employment fell inside the period covered by the audit report. That is a bar rather than a threat to be weighed, and no reviewer cures it, because the individual would be auditing records he himself prepared. Where the service was before the period covered by the report, the firm evaluates the self-interest, self-review and familiarity threats and addresses those that are not at an acceptable level, and having an appropriate reviewer review the individual's work is one of the actions available.
keywords: period covered by the audit report

options.text: Both may be assigned, the reviewing partner being the safeguard the Code asks for in either case
options.misconception: treats an outright bar as a threat that a safeguard can bring to an acceptable level
options.why: For service during the period covered by the report the Code does not offer safeguards; it says the individual shall not be assigned to the team. Safeguards belong to the other case, where the service predates that period.

options.text: Neither may be assigned, anybody who has ever worked for the client being barred from its audit team
options.misconception: extends the bar to any past employment, losing both the timing test and the significant-influence test
options.why: The bar is drawn by two conditions: the individual's role at the client, and whether the service fell within the period covered by the audit report. A treasury employee of three years ago meets neither.

citation.ref: Employment with an audit client — an individual who has served with the client joining the firm

items.scenario: Two recruits join an audit firm in April. One was until March the financial controller of a listed audit client of the firm and personally prepared the accounting records for the year now under audit. The other left the same client's treasury department three years ago and was never in a position to exert significant influence over the preparation of its accounting records or its financial statements. The engagement partner proposes to put both on that client's audit team, with a second partner reviewing whatever they do.

items.stem: What provision do the three actually require?

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹45 lakh on C
options.misconception: treats pending recovery proceedings as a reason to hold a loss asset at a part provision
options.why: A loss asset is one where loss has been identified but the amount has not been written off. So long as it stays on the books the whole outstanding is provided; the recovery proceedings do not scale the provision down.

options.text: ₹12 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.misconception: nets the ECGC cover off the outstanding before applying the substandard rate, which the norm forbids in terms
options.why: The 15 per cent on a substandard asset is computed on the total outstanding without any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover or for securities available. Deducting the cover first is the single commonest error on this norm.

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹7.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.misconception: applies the same 15 per cent to a secured and an unsecured substandard exposure
options.why: An unsecured exposure identified as substandard carries an additional 10 per cent over the general provision, taking it to 25 per cent. On ₹50 lakh that is ₹12.5 lakh, not ₹7.5 lakh.

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.why: A substandard asset carries a general provision of 15 per cent of the total outstanding, and the norm says in terms that it is made without making any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover and securities available — so A needs 15 per cent of the whole ₹200 lakh, which is ₹30 lakh, and the branch is short by ₹18 lakh. An exposure identified as substandard that is unsecured carries an additional 10 per cent, 25 per cent in all, so B needs ₹12.5 lakh. A loss asset should be written off, and where it is permitted to remain on the books 100 per cent of the outstanding is provided, so C needs the whole ₹90 lakh.
keywords: 15 per cent of the total outstanding

citation.ref: Prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning — the provisioning norms for substandard assets and for loss assets

items.scenario: A branch has three advances at the year end. Advance A of ₹200 lakh is classified substandard and is fully secured; it also carries ECGC guarantee cover of ₹120 lakh, and the branch has provided ₹12 lakh, being 15 per cent of the ₹80 lakh left after deducting that cover. Advance B of ₹50 lakh is classified substandard and is wholly unsecured; the branch has provided ₹7.5 lakh. Advance C of ₹90 lakh has been identified as a loss asset and remains on the books while recovery proceedings run; the branch has provided ₹45 lakh.

items.stem: What else must the additional report cover?

options.text: Whether the company is engaged in the business of a non-banking financial institution and, on its asset pattern and income pattern, is entitled to continue to hold the certificate; whether the Board has passed the resolution the directions require for a company not accepting public deposits and whether any have in fact been accepted; whether the prudential norms on income recognition, accounting standards, asset classification and provisioning have been complied with; and, where it applies, whether the capital adequacy ratio has been correctly determined and reported
options.why: The directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies set out the matters the additional report to the Board must carry, and whether the company holds the certificate of registration that section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 requires is only the first of them. Continued entitlement to hold that certificate turns on the asset pattern and the income pattern as at the year end. For a company that does not accept public deposits, the board resolution to that effect and whether any deposits were in fact accepted are separate matters. Compliance with the prudential norms on income recognition, accounting standards, asset classification and provisioning is another, and where the requirement applies to the company, the correct determination and reporting of the capital adequacy ratio is another again.

options.text: Nothing else — the certificate of registration is the whole subject of the additional report, everything else being covered by the report under section 143
options.misconception: shrinks a report with a named list of matters down to its first item
options.why: The directions list the matters, and registration is one of several. The report under section 143 is on the financial statements and answers a different question for different readers.

options.text: The capital adequacy ratio and the prudential norms only, the registration and deposit matters applying to deposit-taking companies alone
options.misconception: assumes the deposit-related matters drop out for a company that takes no deposits, when they are precisely the matters it must report on
options.why: For a company not accepting public deposits the directions ask exactly that: whether the Board has passed the required resolution and whether the company has nonetheless accepted any. The duty exists because the company says it takes none.

options.text: A summary of the observations in the report under section 143, the additional report being the regulator's copy of the statutory one
options.misconception: treats the additional report as a duplicate rather than as a separate report on separate matters
options.why: The additional report is a distinct report to the Board on matters the directions specify. It is not a précis of the opinion on the financial statements, and most of what it covers appears nowhere in that opinion.

citation.source: Reserve Bank of India directions to auditors of non-banking financial companies
citation.ref: The matters to be included in the auditor's additional report to the Board of Directors, read with section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

items.scenario: You are drafting the additional report to the Board of Directors of a non-banking financial company that does not accept public deposits. Your assistant has covered one matter only — whether the company holds a certificate of registration — and says everything else belongs in the report on the financial statements under section 143, because the Board already sees that.

items.stem: Which of the three positions does the Act support?

options.text: Only the refusal of inspection — the qualifications go before the general meeting and no further, and the auditor has a standing right to attend whether or not notice reaches him
options.misconception: swaps the two limbs, denying the inspection section 145 gives and inventing a right to attend that does not depend on the notice the company must send
options.why: Section 145 makes the qualifications open to inspection by any member as well as read before the meeting, and section 146 requires the notices to be forwarded to the auditor.

options.text: Only the exemption — the company may exempt the auditor from attending, but the notice of the meeting must still be forwarded to him, and the qualifications in his report are open to inspection by any member
options.why: Section 146 requires that all notices of, and other communications relating to, any general meeting be forwarded to the auditor, and that he shall attend the meeting either himself or through his authorised representative unless otherwise exempted by the company. So the exemption is the company's to give and the notice is not its to withhold. Section 145 then works on a separate track. Whatever the auditor has qualified, observed or commented upon — where it bites adversely on the company's dealings or on how the company runs — is read out to the members in general meeting, and it is left open to inspection by any member.
keywords: unless otherwise exempted by the company
open to inspection by any member

options.text: All three — attendance is the auditor's own choice, so no notice is needed, and inspection of an audit report is a matter between the company and the Registrar
options.misconception: treats attendance as the auditor's discretion, when section 146 makes it a duty that only the company can waive, and treats the member's inspection right as if it did not exist
options.why: The notice is forwarded to the auditor as a matter of right under section 146, and section 145 gives every member inspection of the qualifications. Neither depends on what the auditor would prefer to do.

options.text: None — the notice must be sent, the company has no power to excuse the auditor from attending, and the member is entitled to inspect
options.misconception: reads the attendance duty in section 146 as absolute and misses the words "unless otherwise exempted by the company" sitting inside it
options.why: Two of the three limbs here are right, which is what makes the option tempting, but the section does allow the company to exempt the auditor from attending.

citation.ref: Section 146 read with section 145

items.scenario: A company is preparing for its annual general meeting. It does not send the notice of the meeting to its auditor, saying he has no business at a meeting of shareholders. Its board separately passes a resolution exempting the auditor from attending this year's meeting and writes to tell him so. After the meeting a member asks the company to let him inspect the two qualifications carried in the auditor's report, and is refused on the ground that inspection of an audit report is a matter for the Registrar.

items.stem: How does the financial due diligence treat them?

options.text: All three are deducted in arriving at normalised earnings, because each will reduce the profits the buyer earns after completion
options.misconception: runs a one-off structural exposure through an earnings multiple, which prices a single event as though it recurred every year
options.why: Normalisation strips out what will not recur and puts in the costs the business will bear year after year; a one-time acceleration or a lost lease is neither.

options.text: None — a contingency that has not crystallised is outside a due diligence, which reports on the figures the accounts actually carry
options.misconception: confuses due diligence with an audit of the past, when the assignment is to price what the buyer is acquiring going forward
options.why: The report states findings of fact about the target's whole position for the party who engaged it, and a term that fires on completion is part of that position.

options.text: All three are reported as liabilities the transaction itself will trigger — they sit outside the historical accounts and outside the earnings adjustment, and they drive the price, the warranties and the indemnities, and the consents to be obtained before completion
options.why: A due diligence works out what the buyer is actually buying rather than verifying last year's profit, so a lease, a borrowing or a customer contract carrying a change-of-control clause that the transaction itself will trigger is exactly the kind of hidden liabilities the assignment exists to find. None of them is an adjustment to normalised earnings, because none describes the sustainable trading of the business; they change what the buyer must pay, promise or obtain, which is why they feed the price, the warranties and the indemnities.

options.text: Only the loan, which is added to net debt because it becomes repayable; the lease and the customer contract are ordinary commercial risks the buyer simply accepts and no report is needed on them
options.misconception: reports one of the three and drops the two that can destroy the value being bought, when all three are triggered by the same event
options.why: Net debt collects what is debt-like at completion on the existing terms. Whether the acceleration is shown there or as a hidden liability, the lease and the customer contract still have to be reported, because each can remove what the buyer is paying for.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — hidden liabilities identified in a financial due diligence, including guarantees, onerous contracts and change-of-control clauses that the transaction itself triggers

items.scenario: On a share purchase of a manufacturer, the diligence turns up three things the audited accounts show nothing about. The factory lease lets the landlord terminate on a change in the target's controlling shareholder. A term loan becomes immediately repayable on a change of control. And the target's largest customer contract lets the customer walk away if the target is acquired by a competitor, which the buyer is. The seller says none of them is a liability today, so none belongs in the report.

items.stem: What is the defect in what the team did?

options.text: Nothing of substance — the copies carry the same content as the originals, and the content is what the findings rest on
options.misconception: treats forensic evidence as information, when what makes it evidence is that its handling can be proved from the moment it was taken
options.why: A perfect copy whose handling cannot be traced proves nothing about where it came from, which is the first question it will be asked.

options.text: The team should have obtained the suspect's written consent before examining the laptop, without which nothing found on it may be used
options.misconception: invents a consent precondition; the failing here is the record of handling, not permission to look at a machine the entity itself owns
options.why: The investigator's problem is not that he looked. It is that he cannot show what he did with what he found.

options.text: The chain of custody is broken and nothing records who held the evidence when — a gap of that kind lets the evidence be challenged or makes it inadmissible, and deleting the originals destroys the source the copies would have to be proved against
options.why: A forensic engagement produces evidence meant to stand where it will be read, so the team must be able to trace who held each item, unbroken, from the moment it was seized to the day it is presented in court. Break that chain of custody, or leave a finding inconclusive, and the other side gets to attack it — a judge may rule the whole thing inadmissible. Copying to a personal device with no record of handling, and deleting the originals from the machine they came from, leaves findings that may well be true sitting on evidence nobody can rely on.

options.text: Only that the laptop was returned too soon; the copying and the deletion were sound precautions against tampering by the suspect
options.misconception: calls destruction of the source a precaution, when removing the original is the one step that cannot be undone and is the suspect's strongest argument
options.why: Preserving the original and imaging it is how tampering is guarded against; deleting it removes the only thing the copy could ever be checked against.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — collecting evidence that can be used in court and keeping a clear chain of custody, gaps in which may leave the evidence challengeable or inadmissible

items.scenario: Investigating a suspected procurement fraud, the team takes the suspect's laptop, copies the folders it wants onto a team member's personal pen drive, deletes those folders from the laptop so the suspect cannot alter them, and returns the laptop the same evening. No record is kept of who held the laptop, the pen drive or the files at any point. The findings that come out of the copies are clear, and the team writes them up.

items.stem: What has to happen before the working paper's claim to a complete population can stand?

options.text: The 4 per cent difference should be projected across the flagged exceptions so that its effect on the financial statements can be measured
options.misconception: projects from a sample when the problem is that the population was never obtained; projection answers a sampling question, not a completeness one
options.why: There is nothing to project from here. The missing records were never tested, so no conclusion about them can be extrapolated from the ones that were.

options.text: The extraction has to be reconciled to a control total in the accounting records and the parameters it was run with have to be checked — here the date range is a month short and the extracted total does not agree to the trial balance, so the analytic covered part of the population and the coverage claim is unsupported
options.why: Data extracted from the entity's systems is information produced by the entity, so the auditor obtains audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness before relying on anything run over it — reconciling the extraction to the general ledger or to another control total, and checking the parameters the extraction was run with. A date range ending in February leaves March out, and a total below the trial balance says records are missing. Until both are resolved, one hundred per cent describes the extract and not the population.
keywords: parameters the extraction was run with

options.text: A written representation from management that the download given to the team was complete and accurate
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for evidence about information the entity itself produced, which is the one thing a representation cannot supply
options.why: A representation is not audit evidence about the accuracy of the very data the entity handed over, and the reconciliation that would settle it is available in the file.

options.text: Nothing — the analytic ran over every record the system returned, and what the system returns is the population
options.misconception: treats the extract as the population, when the extract is only what somebody asked the system for on the parameters he happened to type
options.why: The system returned what it was asked for. Whether that was the population is the question the reconciliation answers.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance, read with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

items.scenario: The team asks the client's IT department for a download of all sales invoices for the year and runs an analytic over it looking for credit notes issued to the same customer within seven days of the invoice. The working paper records that the population tested was complete. Two things sit in the file that nobody has looked at: the extraction request names a date range running from 1 April to 28 February, and the total of the invoices extracted is 4 per cent below the revenue figure in the trial balance.

items.stem: Has the team put the disclosures in the right sections?

options.text: No — all three are in the wrong place. Section A carries the general description of the entity, Section B carries the policy and management process disclosures, and Section C carries the performance against the nine principles
options.why: The report has three sections and each has its own content. Section A is general disclosures about the entity, its products, operations, employees and group companies. Section B is management process and policy disclosures covering governance, leadership and oversight. Section C is principle-wise performance disclosures, taken one principle at a time across the nine that the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct lay down, and Section C alone is the one that splits into essential and leadership indicators.

options.text: Only the policy disclosures are misplaced; product and employee details belong in Section C alongside the performance figures
options.misconception: pulls the entity's general description into the performance section, which reports against the nine principles rather than describing the company
options.why: Products, operations and employee numbers are the general disclosures Section A asks for. Section C reports what the entity did against each principle.

options.text: Yes — the prescribed format leaves the ordering to the entity so long as every required disclosure appears somewhere in the report
options.misconception: treats a prescribed format as a checklist with no structure, when the three sections are what make one company's report comparable with another's
options.why: Each section is defined by what belongs in it, and a reader looking for the entity's governance policies goes to Section B because that is where the format puts them.

options.text: No, but only because Section B has been left empty — Sections A and C may be completed in either order
options.misconception: invents an ordering freedom the format does not give, and misses that Section A's own content has been moved out of it
options.why: Section B is not empty here; the policy disclosures that belong in it have been put in Section A, and Section A's own content has gone to Section C.

citation.ref: Regulation 34(2)(f) read with the prescribed BRSR format, Sections A, B and C

items.scenario: A listed company is drafting its first Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. Its team puts the details of the company's products, its plant locations and its employee numbers into Section C; its policy on responsible business conduct and how the board oversees that policy into Section A; and its principle-wise performance figures into Section B.

items.stem: Under which principles do the two disclosures belong?

options.text: The first under Principle 5, respect for and promotion of human rights, privacy being a right; the second under Principle 2, safe and sustainable goods and services
options.misconception: sends a consumer disclosure to the human rights principle and a life-cycle environmental disclosure to the design principle, leaving Principles 6 and 9 with nothing to report
options.why: Principle 5 is human rights read against the Constitution, national law and the International Bill of Human Rights, and Principle 2 is about design, production methods and reduce, reuse and recycle. Neither is where these two disclosures sit.

options.text: The first under Principle 1, ethics, transparency and accountability, data handling being a governance matter; the second under Principle 8, inclusive growth and equitable development
options.misconception: treats every disclosure about conduct as Principle 1 and every environmental harm to communities as Principle 8, which is how candidates collapse nine principles into two
options.why: Principle 1 carries the anti-bribery and disclosure machinery, and Principle 8 carries inclusive growth including land acquisition and displacement. Neither reaches these facts.

options.text: The first under Principle 9, providing value to consumers responsibly; the second under Principle 6, protection and restoration of the environment
options.why: Principle 9 is providing value to consumers responsibly — reducing negative impacts, not restricting freedom of choice, disclosing adverse impacts accurately, and respecting the customer's right to privacy when handling customer data. Principle 6 is protection and restoration of the environment across the whole life cycle of the product, with measurement of pollution, waste, energy and land use and a contribution to climate resilience in line with India's commitments including the Paris Agreement.

options.text: Both under Principle 6, since electronic waste and customer data are both things the product leaves behind
options.misconception: reads Principle 6 as covering everything a product leaves behind, when personal data is not an environmental impact and has its own principle
options.why: Principle 6 is measured in pollution, waste, energy and land use. Data privacy is disclosed under the consumer principle.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Principle 6 on protection and restoration of the environment across the life cycle of the product and Principle 9 on providing value to consumers responsibly

items.scenario: A consumer electronics company is mapping two disclosures to the principles for Section C of its report. The first sets out how it handles the personal data its customers give it and how it avoids restricting a customer's freedom to choose between its own accessories and other makers'. The second sets out the environmental impact of the product across the whole of its life, from the materials drawn in to the electronic waste left at the end, together with the company's contribution to India's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

items.stem: How does section 27 treat the two new offices?

options.text: Raipur complies and the second Nagpur office fails, because an exemption cannot be claimed where no member has been named at all
options.misconception: treats the exemption as something claimed by naming somebody, when it removes the requirement of a second member altogether
options.why: Where the exemption applies, both offices may be under the same charge and no second member is needed. Raipur is the office that fails, because the man named is neither a partner nor an employee nor actually in charge.

options.text: Both comply — the Nagpur office is in the same city and Raipur has a member of the Institute named as in charge, which is all the section asks for
options.misconception: reads "a member of the Institute" on its own and drops the requirement that he be a partner or in whole-time employment, and that he actually be in charge
options.why: The words are met on their face and the substance is not: a monthly visitor with his own separate practice is not in separate charge of the office.

options.text: Both fail — the Council's exemptions relieve only a second office in the same premises, and every office anywhere else needs its own member
options.misconception: shortens the exemptions to the same-premises case and drops the same-city limb and the prescribed-distance limb sitting beside it
options.why: The exemptions cover the same premises, the same city, and a distance from the municipal limits that the Council's guidelines prescribe.

options.text: The second Nagpur office is covered by the Council's exemption for an office in the same city, so it needs no second member; Raipur fails, because the member in charge of a firm's office must ordinarily be a partner or in the firm's whole-time employment and must actually be in charge
options.why: Section 27 requires each office of a member or a firm in India to be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and the Council's general exemptions relieve that where the second office is in the same premises or in the same city as the first. Naming an outside practitioner does not satisfy the section: the member in separate charge must ordinarily be either a partner of the firm or a member in whole-time employment with it, and he is expected to be actually in charge, attending the office rather than merely named on a letter.

citation.ref: Section 27, read with the Council's general exemptions from separate charge of a second office and the requirement that the member in separate charge of a firm's office be a partner or in whole-time employment with the firm

items.scenario: A firm has its head office in Nagpur. It opens a second office across the same city, and a third in Raipur. For Raipur it names CA Deshpande, a member of the Institute who is neither a partner of the firm nor in its employment; he runs his own practice elsewhere, has agreed to let his name be given as the member in charge, and visits once a month. For the second Nagpur office it names nobody at all.

items.stem: Which of the three disclosures is within Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Only the first — the board's written authorisation is the employer's permission; her own view that the study is harmless is not an exception, and the customer's consent cannot release her because the confidence is not the customer's to waive
options.why: Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule bites on the member who holds a job rather than a practice. What she learns only because of that job — information acquired in the course of his employment, in the clause's own words — she must keep shut, and letting it out is professional misconduct. Two doors lead out and there is no third. The first is compulsion: a disclosure required by any law then in force. The second is consent from above: a disclosure permitted by the employer. The board's written authorisation is the second of them. A member's own judgement that a disclosure is harmless is not a door, and a customer's consent is not the employer's permission.
keywords: acquired in the course of his employment

options.text: None — an employee may never disclose information acquired in the course of his employment, the clause admitting no exception at all
options.misconception: drops both exceptions the clause writes out, one of which is the employer's own permission
options.why: The clause names two exceptions on its face, and the board's written authorisation is squarely inside one of them.

options.text: The first and the third — consent from the person the information is about releases the member in either case
options.misconception: borrows the consent rule from the confidentiality clause that binds a member in practice, where it is the client's consent that counts, and applies it to information the employer holds
