options.why: The practice clause sits in Part I and turns on the client's consent. This one sits in Part II and turns on the employer's permission, and the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: The first and the second — a disclosure that harms nobody and serves the whole industry is outside the mischief the clause is aimed at
options.misconception: reads a harm test into a clause that has none; the clause turns on permission and on legal compulsion, not on consequences
options.why: Whether the benchmarking study hurts anyone is not the question the clause asks. It asks whether a law required the disclosure or the employer permitted it.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 2

items.scenario: CA Nandini is the financial controller of a manufacturing company. Three disclosures come up in one month. Her board authorises her in writing to give the company's product costing data to a prospective joint-venture partner. A trade body asks her for the same data for an industry benchmarking study; she judges the study harmless and useful to the whole industry, and sends it. And a customer whose pricing data the company holds writes to her consenting to her sharing that data with the customer's own bank; the company knows nothing of this.

items.stem: Is Bhatt exposed under Clause 3 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: No — he wrote a correct report, and the brochure is the company's document; a member answers only for words he wrote himself
options.misconception: reads the clause as being about authorship, when what it prohibits is permitting the use of the name
options.why: The clause is aimed at the name, not the draft. A member who watches his name being used that way and does nothing has allowed it.

options.text: Yes — knowing of the brochure and letting it run is permitting his name to be used in a manner that may lead the reader to believe he vouches for the forecast, and his own report does not travel with the brochure
options.why: Clause 3 reaches the member who lends his name, or his firm's, to a projection of what a business will earn if things it has not yet done come off. He permits his name to be used alongside an estimate of earnings turning on future transactions, in a way that invites the reader to think he vouches for the accuracy of that forecast. Permitting is not confined to drafting the words: a member who is shown the document, understands what it says about him and allows it to keep circulating has permitted it. The test is the impression the document as it stands invites, and a report the reader never sees cannot correct that impression.

options.text: Yes, but only from the moment the projections turn out to be wrong, until which no reader has been misled
options.misconception: dates the misconduct from the outcome, when the breach is complete the moment the name is lent in that manner
options.why: Whether the forecast comes true is not the test. The clause looks at what the document invited the reader to believe when he read it.

options.text: No — the brochure says only "reviewed", which is a weaker word than certified and carries no warranty of the numbers
options.misconception: hunts for a forbidden word, when the clause tests the impression the document creates as a whole
options.why: A professional name printed beside a profit chart with nothing else on the page is the impression the clause is about, whatever single word was chosen.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 3

items.scenario: CA Bhatt gives a company a carefully worded report on its five-year projections, saying that the assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the projection and that actual results are likely to differ. The company then prints a fundraising brochure carrying only the line "Projections reviewed by CA S. Bhatt" beside a chart of the projected profits, with every caveat left out. Bhatt is sent a copy, sees what has been done with his name, decides that his own report is on file and says nothing. The brochure circulates for four months.

items.stem: Does Part II of the First Schedule reach the arrangement?

options.text: Yes, but the misconduct is cured once the company is told about it and raises no objection
options.misconception: treats the employer as the person wronged and free to waive it, when what the clause protects is the standing of the profession
options.why: No consent by the employer appears anywhere in the clause, and the misconduct is complete on the payment.

options.text: No — Part II catches only what he receives from his employer's lawyers, brokers and agents; what he does with his own salary is his own affair
options.misconception: keeps the accepting limb of Part II and drops the paying limb sitting immediately beside it
options.why: The Part holds both limbs. Paying away a share of his emoluments is the first of them.

options.text: Yes — a member in employment who pays any person a share of the emoluments of his employment commits professional misconduct, and it makes no difference that the money is his own or that his employer has lost nothing
options.why: Part II of the First Schedule binds a member in service, and its first limb is the paying limb: he is guilty of professional misconduct if he pays any person a share of the emoluments of his employment. The clause does not ask whether the employer was out of pocket or whether the recipient did any work. The profession's fee-sharing discipline follows the member into service and runs in both directions — paying out of his emoluments, and accepting a share of the fees of a lawyer, chartered accountant, broker or agent engaged by his employer.

options.text: No — the schedules bind a member in practice, and a member in employment answers to his contract of service rather than to the Institute
options.misconception: the practice-only reading that Part II exists to defeat; it binds a member in service in terms
options.why: Part II is headed for members in service precisely because the discipline does not stop at the door of a practice.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part II

items.scenario: CA Mehra is employed as a company's group financial controller. A former colleague introduced him to the company, and under a private arrangement Mehra pays him 5 per cent of his own monthly salary as thanks. The colleague is not a member of the Institute, does no work for the company and has no dealings with it. The company knows nothing about the arrangement. Mehra says his salary is his own money to do with as he likes.

items.stem: Which of the three does the framework reach?

options.text: All three — a member who becomes aware of any breach of law at a client, or by any of its directors, is inside the framework
options.misconception: drops both exclusions, which would push every trivial filing default and every director's private affair through an escalation built for matters that damage the entity or the public
options.why: The framework names its own boundaries so that the escalation it requires is reserved for the matters that need it.

options.text: Only the third — the framework reaches non-compliance and suspected non-compliance in the conduct of the client's business, and it puts outside itself matters that are clearly inconsequential and personal misconduct unrelated to the business
options.why: The framework is engaged by non-compliance or suspected non-compliance with laws and regulations at the client, and it excludes two things by its own terms: a matter that is clearly inconsequential, which a late filing settled by a nominal fee is, and personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client, which the managing director's own rental income is. Two sets of production records kept for three years to under-declare output is neither of those, and it is material to the financial statements besides.
keywords: personal misconduct unrelated to the business

options.text: The first and the third — a managing director's own tax evasion goes to his integrity, which bears directly on the audit
options.misconception: integrity may well matter to the auditor's risk assessment, but the framework itself excludes personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client
options.why: What the auditor does with a doubt about integrity is a separate question from whether this framework is engaged, and on that question the exclusion is express.

options.text: The second and the third, a late statutory filing being the plainest case of non-compliance there is
options.misconception: reads "non-compliance" without the filter of consequence, when a breach that is clearly inconsequential does not start the response at all
options.why: The filing was late and was paid for. Nothing about it calls for the member to escalate, press for rectification or weigh a disclosure in the public interest.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations — the scope of the framework, and its exclusion of matters that are clearly inconsequential and of personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client

items.scenario: Auditing a mid-sized company, a member comes across three things. The managing director has been under-reporting the rent from a private property of his own that has nothing to do with the company. The company filed one statutory return eleven days late and paid the nominal fee for it. And the company has for three years kept two sets of production records so as to under-declare its output to an excise authority, which if unwound would materially change the financial statements. The engagement partner asks which of the three engages the NOCLAR framework.

items.stem: Is that advice right?

options.text: No — the clause bars a member in practice from entering into partnership, in or outside India, with anyone other than a chartered accountant in practice or a member of a body the Council has notified, so where the firm sits does not save it
options.why: Clause 4 of Part I of the First Schedule reaches a partnership entered into in or outside India, and those words are in the clause itself rather than read into it. The permitted co-partners are a chartered accountant in practice and a person belonging to a professional body the Council has notified, subject to the Council's conditions. A foreign qualification outside that list is not one of them, and neither the location of the firm nor the absence of Indian clients is a condition the clause carries.
keywords: professional body the Council has notified

options.text: Yes, provided he intimates the Institute of the foreign partnership and the firm takes no Indian assignments
options.misconception: invents an intimation cure; the clause admits permitted categories of partner, not permitted disclosures about a partner who is not one of them
options.why: Telling the Institute about an arrangement the clause forbids does not make the arrangement permitted.

options.text: Yes — the Chartered Accountants Act governs conduct in India, and a partnership formed and operating abroad is outside its reach
options.misconception: the territorial argument the clause answers on its own face by naming a partnership entered into in or outside India
options.why: The Act follows the member rather than the firm's address, and the clause says so in as many words.

options.text: No — and the same bar would catch a plain fee-sharing referral arrangement with the same Singapore accountant, Clause 4 reaching every commercial link with a non-member
options.misconception: stretches Clause 4 beyond partnership; a fee-sharing arrangement is dealt with by the clauses on paying out and on accepting a share of profits, not by the partnership clause
options.why: Clause 4 is about entering into partnership. A referral or fee-sharing arrangement is governed by different clauses of the same Part.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 4

items.scenario: CA Sharma, in practice in Chennai, is invited to become a partner in a professional firm in Singapore. The proposed co-partner is a Singapore-qualified accountant who is not a member of the Institute and does not belong to any professional body the Council has notified. Sharma's Indian practice will continue unchanged, and the Singapore firm will take no Indian work. He is advised that the First Schedule stops at the Indian border.

items.stem: Does Clause 1 of Part I of the First Schedule permit the arrangement?

options.text: No — the person allowed to practise in the member's name must be a chartered accountant in practice and be in partnership with him or employed by him, and Fernandes, running an independent practice, meets the first requirement and not the second
options.why: Clause 1 makes it professional misconduct for a member in practice to let anybody hold himself out under that member's name. Two things must both be true of the other man before it is allowed. He has to be a chartered accountant in practice himself; and he has to stand, towards the member, in partnership with or employed by him. Both conditions have to hold at once. Fernandes holds a certificate of practice, so the first is satisfied; he is neither a partner nor an employee, so the second fails, and two independent practices cannot lend each other a name however well qualified each of them is.
keywords: in partnership with or employed by him

options.text: No — and it would fail just as surely if Fernandes were Kulkarni's salaried employee, because a member may practise only in his own name
options.misconception: reads the clause as an absolute bar, when it expressly permits a chartered accountant in practice who is a partner or an employee to practise in the member's name
options.why: The clause opens the door for exactly that case. What it shuts out is the person who is not in practice, or not a partner or employee.

options.text: Yes — the mischief the clause is aimed at is an unqualified person working in a member's name, and Fernandes is fully qualified
options.misconception: keeps the qualification condition and drops the partnership-or-employment condition standing beside it
options.why: The clause protects the public's ability to know whose judgement stands behind the work, and that needs a relationship the Institute can trace, not only a qualification.

options.text: Yes, provided Kulkarni reviews and signs everything issued from the Hubli office
options.misconception: offers supervision in place of the relationship the clause requires, when the clause names partnership or employment and nothing else answers it
options.why: Supervision is not one of the two things the clause asks for, and a member cannot supply by arrangement what the clause requires by status.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 1

items.scenario: CA Kulkarni practises in Belgaum and has built a name there. CA Fernandes, also a chartered accountant holding a certificate of practice, runs his own firm in Hubli. They agree that Fernandes may hold out and work in Kulkarni's firm name at Hubli while keeping his own clients, his own fees and his own separate firm. No partnership deed is signed and neither employs the other. Kulkarni is content, since Fernandes is a fully qualified practising member.

items.stem: What does Clause 3 of Part I of the First Schedule say about the two offers?

options.text: Clause 3 is the receiving side — it bars a member from taking in any slice of what an outsider to the Institute earns from professional work — so the tax-return preparer's offer is misconduct, while the company secretaries' arrangement falls inside the Council's carve-out
options.why: Clause 3 points at what comes in. A member in practice who accepts or agrees to accept a slice of what somebody outside the Institute earns from professional work is caught by it; what a member pays out of his own professional fees is the subject of the clause before it. An unqualified tax-return preparer is not a member, so a fixed share of that practice's profits is squarely inside it. The Council has made a carve-out for prescribed arrangements with the professional bodies it has notified, and a firm of company secretaries in practice is within that carve-out.

options.text: Neither offer concerns him — Clause 3 is about a member paying a share of his own fees to an outsider, so nothing he receives is caught by it
options.misconception: runs Clause 3 in the wrong direction; paying out is the neighbouring clause, and Clause 3 is about what the member takes in
options.why: The two clauses sit next to each other and face opposite ways. Reading only one of them is how the first offer gets missed.

options.text: Both are permitted, since Iqbal does none of the referred work himself and so shares in nothing he has earned
options.misconception: makes the member's own effort the test, when the clause bars accepting a share of another person's professional profits precisely because he did not earn it
options.why: Doing none of the work is the reason the clause bites, not a reason it does not.

options.text: Both are misconduct — Clause 3 admits no exception, so a share of profits from any firm outside the Institute is barred
options.misconception: drops the Council's carve-out for the professional bodies it has notified, which sits in the clause as a proviso
options.why: The clause carries a limited exception for prescribed reciprocal arrangements with certain other recognised professional bodies, and that is the second offer.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 3

items.scenario: CA Iqbal, in practice, is offered two arrangements. An unqualified tax-return preparer with a large local following offers him a fixed one-third of the profits of the preparer's own practice in return for Iqbal being available to him for advice. Separately, a firm of company secretaries in practice offers him a share of the profits of work referred between the two firms, under an arrangement of the kind the Council has permitted with the professional bodies it has notified. Iqbal believes Clause 3 is about what he pays out, so he thinks neither offer concerns him.

items.stem: What does SIA 370 say about the two decisions?

options.text: The fraud may wait for the report, but the effective controls must go in, since the report has to be balanced
options.misconception: gets the balance rule right and the urgent one wrong, which is the more expensive half of the pair
options.why: Five weeks is five weeks in which the stock keeps moving. That is why the Standard takes the fraud out of the reporting timetable altogether.

options.text: The fraud must be reported at once to the audit committee rather than to management, and the effective controls may be left out
options.misconception: sends the immediate report to the wrong recipient and keeps the one-sided draft
options.why: SIA 370 has the matter brought to management's attention immediately. The audit committee receives the Chief Internal Auditor's periodic comprehensive report at the close of a plan period.

options.text: Both are wrong — a suspected fraud goes to management at once rather than waiting for the report, and the report's conclusions rest on everything found, with controls that worked acknowledged rather than passed over
options.why: Where the internal auditor comes across any actual or suspected fraud or other misappropriation of assets, he brings it to management's attention immediately and does not wait for the report at all. And the report's conclusions are based on all the findings rather than on a few deviations, which is why controls found to be operating effectively are acknowledged: a report that lists only failures misdescribes the entity it is describing.

options.text: Both are right — the report is the internal auditor's channel to management, and a report that dwells on working controls wastes the reader's time
options.misconception: treats the assignment report as the only channel, when a suspected misappropriation is the one finding that cannot wait for it
options.why: The report is the ordinary channel and the fraud is the exception to it, and the balance rule exists because a one-sided report is a misleading one.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: the immediate reporting of an actual or suspected fraud to management, and conclusions based on all the findings with controls operating effectively acknowledged

items.scenario: Halfway through an internal audit of a warehouse, the internal auditor finds what looks like a systematic misappropriation of stock by a storekeeper. He notes it for the report he will issue at the end of the assignment, five weeks away. In drafting that report he also decides to list only the failures, leaving out the three controls he tested and found operating effectively, on the view that a report exists for problems.

items.stem: What must the Central Government do in each case?

options.text: In the first it must order an investigation, the section leaving it no discretion where a court or the Tribunal so orders; in the second it may order one, the special resolution being a ground on which it forms its own opinion
options.why: Section 210 puts the Central Government on two different footings. On the receipt of a report of the Registrar or of an inspector under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest, it may order an investigation where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so. But where a court or the Tribunal, in any proceeding before it, orders that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall order an investigation. In every case it is the Central Government that appoints one or more persons as inspectors.
keywords: appoints one or more persons as inspectors

options.text: It must refer both to the Tribunal under section 213, the Tribunal being the only forum that may order an investigation into a company's affairs
options.misconception: section 213 is the Tribunal's route on an application by members or another person; section 210 is the Central Government's own and does not pass through the Tribunal
options.why: The two sections differ in who moves. Section 210 needs no application and no Tribunal order, except in the one case where a court or the Tribunal has already given one.

options.text: It must order an investigation in both, a special resolution of the members binding the Government as firmly as a court's order does
options.misconception: raises the special resolution from a ground to a command, when the section leaves the Government its own opinion on that ground
options.why: The resolution opens the door; whether to walk through it is still the Central Government's judgement.

options.text: It may decline in both, the section saying only that the Central Government may order an investigation
options.misconception: reads the discretionary limb across the whole section and misses the court-or-Tribunal limb, which says shall
options.why: The section carries both words, and which one applies depends on where the case came from.

citation.ref: Section 210 — the grounds on which the Central Government may order an investigation, and its duty to order one where a court or the Tribunal directs

items.scenario: In a proceeding before it, a court records that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated and orders accordingly. In a different company and on separate facts, the members pass a special resolution that the company's affairs ought to be investigated, and the resolution is intimated to the Central Government, which takes the view that nothing in it merits appointing an inspector.

items.stem: Which of the three must stop?

options.text: Only the State economic offences wing — the bar reaches another investigating agency proceeding in respect of an offence under the Companies Act, so it does not touch an investigation under a different statute or a review the company itself commissioned
options.why: Section 212(2) provides that once a case has been assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government shall proceed with an investigation in that case in respect of an offence under this Act, and an investigation already initiated is not proceeded with further, its relevant documents and records being transferred to the SFIO. The bar is bounded by those words, so a money-laundering investigation under another statute continues, and a forensic review commissioned by the company is not an investigating agency at all.

options.text: None — the section asks agencies to coordinate rather than to stop, and each keeps the documents it gathered
options.misconception: softens a prohibition into a request, and ignores the requirement that the relevant documents and records be handed over to the SFIO
options.why: The section stops the other agency and moves its papers, which is the opposite of running in parallel.

options.text: The State wing and the Directorate of Enforcement — once the SFIO has the case every other agency stands down, so that one investigation runs
options.misconception: reads the bar as a general takeover of the company, when it is confined by its own words to an offence under the Companies Act
options.why: A separate statute creates separate offences, and the section says nothing about them.

options.text: All three, the company's own forensic review included, since parallel work would compromise the evidence the SFIO is gathering
options.misconception: extends a bar written for investigating agencies of the Central or a State Government to a private engagement the section does not touch
options.why: A firm engaged by the audit committee is not an investigating agency of any Government, so the section does not reach it.

citation.ref: Section 212(2) — the bar on any other investigating agency proceeding in respect of an offence under the Act once a case is assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office

items.scenario: The Central Government assigns a case to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office. Three other bodies are already looking at the same company. A State economic offences wing is investigating the same facts as offences under the Companies Act. The Directorate of Enforcement is investigating them as offences under a separate money-laundering statute. And the company's own audit committee has engaged a firm of chartered accountants to run a forensic review of the same transactions.

items.stem: Where do the three sit under the scale-based framework?

options.text: A housing finance company sits outside the scale-based framework altogether, being regulated as a housing lender rather than as an NBFC
options.misconception: leaves housing finance companies outside a framework they were expressly brought inside
options.why: A housing finance company is placed in the middle or the upper layer like any other covered NBFC, and the layer decides the prudential requirements the audit must test against.

options.text: All three follow asset size alone — the small deposit taker in the base layer, and the other two in the upper layer if they are large enough
options.misconception: reduces a framework built on size, activity and perceived riskiness to a single size test, which is exactly what the activity-based placements override
options.why: Some placements are fixed by what the NBFC does rather than by how large it is, and the deposit taker and the housing financier are both of that kind.

options.text: Each company decides its own layer and reports it, the Reserve Bank publishing only the top layer
options.misconception: gives the entity a choice it does not have; the upper layer is a list the Reserve Bank identifies and the top layer is one it populates
options.why: Placement is not a self-assessment. The auditor confirms it against the framework and the Reserve Bank's own identification.

options.text: A deposit-taking NBFC is in the middle layer whatever its size; a housing finance company is in the middle or the upper layer and never in the base layer; and a Government-owned NBFC is placed in the base or the middle layer, and not in the upper layer until the Reserve Bank says otherwise
options.why: Under scale-based regulation the layer is fixed by the framework and by the Reserve Bank, not by the entity or by its auditor. All deposit-taking NBFCs sit in the middle layer irrespective of asset size. A housing finance company is included in the middle layer or the upper layer as the case may be, and not in the base layer. Government-owned NBFCs are placed in the base layer or the middle layer and will not be placed in the upper layer till further notice. The upper layer itself comprises those NBFCs the Reserve Bank specifically identifies as warranting enhanced regulatory requirement.

citation.ref: Ch. Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies — the four layers of scale-based regulation and the placement of deposit-taking, housing finance and Government-owned NBFCs

items.scenario: Three NBFCs come up in a firm's planning meeting. One is a deposit-taking NBFC with a small balance sheet. One is a housing finance company. One is a large Government-owned NBFC that the audit senior expects to find in the upper layer because of its size. The senior proposes to put the first in the base layer because it is small, and to take the other two companies' own view of where they belong.

items.stem: What may the Authority order, and where does an appeal lie?

options.text: A monetary penalty, and debarment of the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for at least six months and at most ten years; an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal
options.why: Where misconduct is proved, section 132 lets the Authority impose a monetary penalty and debar the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for a minimum period of six months and up to a maximum of ten years. An appeal against such an order lies to the Appellate Tribunal, and not to the Appellate Authority constituted under the Chartered Accountants Act.

options.text: It may impose a monetary penalty but it cannot debar, debarment being reserved to the Disciplinary Committee of the Institute
options.misconception: keeps half the power and gives the rest away, when debarment is named in section 132 itself
options.why: Debarment from audit, internal audit and valuation under section 247 is written into the Authority's own powers.

options.text: It may debar permanently, and its order is final, the section providing no appeal
options.misconception: removes both the floor and the ceiling the section sets, and the appeal it provides
options.why: The section fixes a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years, and an appeal lies against the order.

options.text: It may only recommend action to the Institute, which passes the order, with an appeal to the Appellate Authority under the Chartered Accountants Act
options.misconception: makes the Authority an advisory body, when section 132 gives it the power to penalise and to debar in its own right
options.why: The Authority investigates and orders. The Institute's own forums are the ones the proviso to section 132(4) stops from running alongside it.

citation.ref: Section 132 — monetary penalty and debarment for a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years, with an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal

items.scenario: The National Financial Reporting Authority finds professional misconduct proved against an audit firm and its engagement partner in the audit of a large listed company. The firm asks what the Authority can actually order against it, and where it can go if it disagrees with the order.

items.stem: What are the three parties, and where has the trainee gone wrong?

options.text: The auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and the department is the responsible party, not the intended user; the criteria are the benchmarks the subject matter is measured against, and the subject matter information is the outcome of that measurement
options.why: Every public sector audit has three parties. The auditor, a role filled by the Supreme Audit Institution of India. The responsible party, whose responsibilities are determined by constitutional or legislative arrangement, generally the auditable entity and those charged with its governance. And the intended users, the individuals or organisations for whom the auditor prepares the report. The department whose procurement is examined is the auditable entity, and so the responsible party. The subject matter is what is measured or evaluated, the criteria are the benchmarks used to evaluate it, and the subject matter information is the outcome of measuring the subject matter against those criteria.

options.text: The auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and the trainee is right, an entity being the intended user of a report addressed to it
options.misconception: gets the three roles and then collapses two of them into one
options.why: The party responsible for the subject matter and the users for whom the report is prepared are distinct roles, which is what gives the engagement its structure.

options.text: The auditor, the entity and the legislature — and the trainee is right, since the department reads the report and acts on it
options.misconception: names the reader of the day instead of the role, when the entity being examined is the responsible party whatever it does with the report afterwards
options.why: The three roles are auditor, responsible party and intended users, and the legislature is one intended user among others rather than a party in its own name.

options.text: There are only two parties in a compliance audit, the auditor and the entity; the three-party structure belongs to attestation engagements alone
options.misconception: confines the three-party structure to one type of engagement, when it is common to every public sector audit
options.why: What separates attestation from direct reporting is who measures the subject matter against the criteria, not how many parties there are.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the three parties to a public sector audit, and the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information

items.scenario: A team is planning a compliance audit of a State department's procurement. The planning file has to name the three parties to the engagement and identify the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information. A trainee writes that the intended user is the department being audited, since the report will be addressed to it.

items.stem: Which statement corrects him?

options.text: Only the second half is wrong; his purview is confined to bodies in which Government holds equity, financing alone giving no right of audit
options.misconception: makes equity the only gateway, when substantial financing from Union or State revenues is itself a ground of audit purview
options.why: Both halves of what the trainee was told are wrong, and the financing ground is the one this option keeps out.

options.text: Nothing needs correcting — an audit purview fixed by the Constitution cannot extend to a body the Government neither owns nor controls
options.misconception: leaves out the financing ground, when a body substantially financed from Union or State revenues is within the purview even where it is neither owned nor controlled
options.why: Money voted by a legislature is followed by that legislature's auditor, whoever owns the body that spends it.

options.text: Only the first half is wrong; the appraisals are indeed his officers' alone, the Audit Boards being advisory committees of Parliament
options.misconception: moves the Audit Boards to Parliament, when they are constituted within the Indian Audit and Accounts Department
options.why: The Boards have no separate legal entity and work under the Comptroller and Auditor General's supervision and control.

options.text: His purview also reaches autonomous bodies owned or controlled by the Union or the States and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues; and comprehensive appraisals are made through Audit Boards, which associate experts and discuss their findings with the enterprise and its controlling ministry before finalising them
options.why: The bodies within the Comptroller and Auditor General's audit purview run wider than departments and government companies: they include non-commercial autonomous bodies and authorities owned or controlled by the Union or the States, and authorities and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues. For comprehensive appraisals of public enterprises he constitutes Audit Boards, which bring in experts from whatever disciplines the appraisal calls for. Such a Board then sits down with the enterprise's own management, and with the ministry above it, to talk its draft through before finalisation. The Boards have no separate legal entity and work under his supervision and control.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the bodies within the audit purview of the Comptroller and Auditor General, and the Audit Boards constituted for comprehensive appraisals

items.scenario: A trainee is told two things about the Comptroller and Auditor General. First, that his audit stops at Government departments and the companies in which Government holds a majority. Second, that his comprehensive appraisals of public enterprises are carried out by his own officers alone, and that the findings go into his report without the enterprise ever seeing them first.

items.stem: Is the board's objection sound?

options.text: No — comprehensive audit examines management's decisions and their results, so any decision the auditor thinks was wrong is fair reporting
options.misconception: reads "examines management decisions" as a licence to prefer a different decision, when what is examined is performance against criteria drawn from the enterprise's own objectives
options.why: The audit does go into management's decisions, but it measures them against the enterprise's stated purpose rather than against the auditor's commercial view.

options.text: Yes, and it follows that a comprehensive audit may report nothing beyond the financial statements, on which it expresses its opinion
options.misconception: answers a question about criteria by shrinking the audit into a financial one
options.why: A comprehensive audit expresses no opinion on the financial statements and certifies nothing. It reports findings, the reasons behind them and recommendations, to Parliament through the Comptroller and Auditor-General's report.

options.text: No — the objection would hold in a propriety audit, which tests one transaction, but a comprehensive audit has no criteria at all and reports whatever it finds
options.misconception: an audit with no criteria is not an audit; the absence of a fixed rulebook is not the absence of criteria
options.why: The criteria exist and are drawn from the enterprise itself. What is not fixed in advance is which areas the appraisal takes up.

options.text: Yes, on both findings as framed — the criteria in a comprehensive audit are drawn from a study of the enterprise, its stated objectives, its published policy, its board's decisions and its reports to Government, and that is what keeps the exercise from collapsing into an opinion about management
options.why: The areas a comprehensive audit examines are not fixed by any rule; they are selected after a study of the enterprise, its stated objectives, its published policy, the decisions of its board and the reports it makes to Government, and the criteria against which performance is judged are drawn from those sources rather than from the auditor's own preference. A finding that the enterprise should have entered a market nobody set as an objective, or priced against a policy it never adopted, is a preference and not a measured shortfall.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — comprehensive audit of a public enterprise, the selection of the areas examined and the criteria drawn from the enterprise's stated objectives, published policy and board decisions

items.scenario: In a comprehensive audit of a public sector shipyard, the team reports that the yard should have entered the offshore-vessel market five years ago, and that its pricing is too conservative. The yard's board answers that the audit is substituting the auditor's commercial preferences for the board's own judgement, and that nothing in the yard's stated objectives, in its published policy or in any decision of the board called for either thing.

items.stem: Is the department right about economy?

options.text: Yes — economy is the price paid, and the quality and the delay are questions for efficiency and effectiveness
options.misconception: strips quality and timeliness out of economy, when the definition puts both inside it
options.why: Economy is not the lowest price. It is the least cost consistent with the quantity and quality the activity needs, obtained in due time.

options.text: No — economy is minimising the cost of the resources used having regard to appropriate quantity and quality and the best price, so resources acquired late and below the required grade fail it even at the lowest price; the relaying is then a further loss of efficiency
options.why: Economy asks what an activity's inputs cost it. The test is the smallest outlay that still delivers the right amount, of the right standard, at the best price — and judging it means asking as well whether those inputs turned up in due time and in appropriate quantity. Cement delivered late and below the specified grade fails on time and on quality, so the lowest price does not answer the question. Efficiency is the input-output ratio, and relaying a section consumes inputs that produce no additional output.

options.text: Yes, and the relaying belongs to propriety audit rather than performance audit, being a question of prudence on one transaction
options.misconception: sends a performance question to the propriety rail, when the relaying is measured as inputs consumed without output
options.why: Propriety asks whether a particular item of expenditure was wisely incurred. What is measured here is the conversion of money into a completed bridge.

options.text: No — the failing is effectiveness alone, since the bridge was eventually built and the intended outcome was reached
options.misconception: reaches for the third E when the first two are where the loss actually shows
options.why: Effectiveness asks whether the intended outcome was achieved, and on these facts it was. What was lost was economy on the purchase and efficiency on the rework.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — performance audit and the definitions of economy, efficiency and effectiveness

items.scenario: A State department buys the cheapest cement on offer for a bridge. It arrives four months late and is of a grade below what the design required, so one section has to be taken up and relaid at further cost. The department tells the performance audit team that economy is not in question, since it paid the lowest price available in the market.

items.stem: What is wrong in each case?

options.text: The first is on the wrong standard, SRE 2410 applying where the review is performed by the entity's own auditor; and in the second the understanding has to be updated and extended to internal control over the interim process, which can differ from the annual one
options.why: SRE 2410 is written for the man who already audits the company and is then asked to look at a quarter. It bites where the review is done by the independent auditor of the entity, and a practitioner who is not that auditor reviews under SRE 2400 instead. Nor does the annual audit stand in for the planning work. Planning a review, the auditor updates what he knows of the business, of its surroundings and of the controls running inside it — and he goes one step further, because he must grasp how the controls bearing on a quarter's interim financial information actually work. Those need not be the controls that carried the year-end figures.

options.text: The second is wrong, but the first is right — SRE 2410 is available to any practitioner engaged to review interim figures
options.misconception: drops the applicability the standard's own title carries
options.why: SRE 2410 is confined to a review performed by the independent auditor of the entity. SRE 2400 is the standard for a practitioner who is not the auditor.

options.text: The first is wrong, but the second is right — an interim review is the lighter engagement and the annual audit's understanding carries it
options.misconception: the lighter procedures rest on the understanding being current, which is exactly why the standard requires it to be updated and extended to the interim process
options.why: Inquiry and analytical procedures are enough only because the auditor already knows the entity, and that knowledge has to be brought up to date before it can carry anything.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — any firm may perform a limited review, and an auditor fresh from the annual audit already knows the controls
options.misconception: ignores both the standard's own applicability and the fact that the controls over an interim close are not always the controls over a year end
options.why: The standard is titled for a review performed by the independent auditor of the entity, and it requires the understanding to be updated rather than assumed.

citation.source: SRE 2410 — reviewing interim figures, where the reviewer is the entity's own auditor
citation.ref: applicability where the review is performed by the entity's own auditor, and the requirement to bring the understanding of the business and of its controls up to date, reaching the controls that bear on a quarter's reporting

items.scenario: Two engagement letters cross a partner's desk. In the first, a listed company has appointed a firm that is not its statutory auditor to review its quarterly results, and the letter cites SRE 2410. In the second, the firm's own review of a different listed client's quarter records that no further understanding of internal control is needed, because the annual audit just completed covered it.

items.stem: What is the memorandum of changes, and what is done where the auditor proposes no change?

options.text: A section of the long form audit report, so a nil position needs no separate statement
options.misconception: files the memorandum inside the long form audit report, which is a different document answering a different reader
options.why: The long form audit report is a separate questionnaire prescribed by the Reserve Bank and answered alongside the branch audit report. The memorandum of changes is annexed to the branch audit report itself, and where there is nothing to propose the memorandum says so.

options.text: A statement annexed to and forming part of the branch audit report, setting out every change the auditor considers necessary in the returns the branch has submitted, each change described, quantified and grouped by its effect — and where he proposes none he states the memorandum as nil rather than omitting it
options.why: A branch auditor cannot alter the branch's books, so this is how he records what he thinks is wrong: it is annexed to and forming part of the branch audit report and sets out every change he considers necessary in the returns the branch has submitted, each one described, quantified and grouped by its effect on the profit and loss account, on the classification of advances, on provisioning and on the balance sheet heads. Where he proposes no change he states the memorandum as nil, because a missing memorandum reads at the head office as one not yet received rather than as one with nothing in it.
keywords: annexed to and forming part of the branch audit report

options.text: An internal working paper for the central statutory auditors, prepared only where the branch has refused a change the auditor considers material
options.misconception: treats the memorandum as an internal paper confined to material disputes, when it forms part of the report and carries every change proposed
options.why: It forms part of the branch audit report and is not a working paper, and it is not confined to material refusals. Every change the auditor considers necessary in the branch's returns goes in, whether or not the branch has accepted it, and where there are none the memorandum is stated as nil.

options.text: The branch auditor's opinion on the branch's returns, so where he proposes no change the branch audit report is itself the memorandum
options.misconception: merges the memorandum into the audit report, when it is a separate statement annexed to the report and answering a different question
options.why: The two documents do different jobs. The report carries the opinion; the memorandum carries the changes the auditor considers necessary in the returns, quantified so that the head office can apply them, and it is annexed to the report rather than being it.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the memorandum of changes annexed to and forming part of the branch audit report, and the statement of a nil memorandum

items.scenario: A first-year assistant on a branch audit asks what the memorandum of changes actually is. This year the branch auditor has proposed no change at all, and the assistant suggests simply leaving the memorandum out of the file, since a document listing nothing has nothing to say.

items.stem: What else does the audit approach to advances direct you to select for examination?

options.text: Problem accounts that have not yet slipped into the non-performing category, taken from the branch's SMA-1 and SMA-2 lists; accounts adversely commented upon by the concurrent auditors, by the bank's internal inspection or by the Reserve Bank's inspection team; restructured accounts; and quick or early mortality accounts, being advances that turned non-performing within twelve months of sanction
options.why: Large advances are examined in full and the rest on a sample basis, but the sample is directed rather than random. The approach names accounts showing stress while still standard, which the SMA-1 and SMA-2 lists identify; accounts adversely commented upon by the concurrent auditors, by internal inspection or by the Reserve Bank's inspection team; restructured accounts, because a restructured portfolio requires additional provisioning; and quick or early mortality accounts, an advance slipping to non-performing within twelve months of its sanction being a signal about the appraisal rather than about the borrower alone.
keywords: adversely commented upon by the concurrent auditors

options.text: Nothing else — value is the only defensible criterion, and an account below the cut-off is immaterial by definition
options.misconception: reads a sampling cut-off by value as a statement that smaller accounts carry no risk
options.why: Value shows where the money is; it does not show where the risk is. A ₹2 crore account restructured twice and commented on by the concurrent auditor says more about the branch's credit process than a much larger account running normally, and the branch's own records already name both.

options.text: Accounts already classified as non-performing, those being the ones where the provision is at stake
options.misconception: looks where the branch has already conceded the problem rather than where it has not
options.why: Accounts the branch has already classified are the easier half of the work, because the disagreement is over. The examination is aimed at the accounts the branch still calls standard, which is why the stress lists, the inspection comments and the early mortality cases are named.

options.text: A fresh sample drawn without reference to the branch's own lists, a list produced by the branch being information produced by the entity
options.misconception: turns the duty to test information produced by the entity into a reason not to use it at all
options.why: Those lists are information produced by the entity, so their accuracy and completeness are established rather than assumed — which is a reason to test them, not a reason to look away from them. Refusing to read them throws away the branch's own record of where its trouble is.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the audit approach to advances, including examination of the SMA-1 and SMA-2 lists, of accounts adversely commented upon by concurrent auditors and inspection teams, of restructured accounts and of quick or early mortality accounts

items.scenario: You are planning the advances work at a large branch carrying 4,200 borrowal accounts. The manager proposes to examine every advance above ₹5 crore in full and then to pick the rest at random, on the footing that once the large ones are covered size is the only sensible criterion left.

items.stem: What is wrong with that description?

options.text: Only the quarterly filing — a treasury under concurrent audit needs no separate review of the investment portfolio, the ground being covered already
options.misconception: reads coverage of the same subject as coverage of the same question
options.why: Concurrent audit verifies transactions shortly after they take place. The half-yearly review examines the portfolio as a whole, the amendments made to the investment policy, and adherence to that policy and to the Reserve Bank's guidelines, which no amount of transaction testing answers.

options.text: Nothing — a monthly concurrent audit reaching the Chairman and Managing Director is stronger than any half-yearly review, and a regulator is entitled to copies of it
options.misconception: treats transaction-level concurrent audit as covering a portfolio-level review, and invents a filing that is not required
options.why: The monthly report is right and it does not displace the review, which asks a different question: it looks at the portfolio and at the investment policy rather than at individual transactions, and it certifies adherence to that policy and to the regulator's guidelines. Copies of the internal audit report are not required to reach the Reserve Bank at all.

options.text: Two things — the bank should undertake half-yearly reviews of its investment portfolio as at 30 September and 31 March, covering the operational aspects, any amendments to the investment policy and adherence to the laid-down policy, procedures and Reserve Bank guidelines; and copies of the internal audit report need not be forwarded to the Reserve Bank, though major irregularities and the position of compliance may be carried into that half-yearly review
options.why: The monthly part he has right: the concurrent audit of treasury transactions is separately conducted by the internal auditors and the results are placed before the Chairman and Managing Director once every month. The rest is wrong. Banks should undertake half-yearly reviews of their investment portfolio as at 30 September and 31 March, covering not only the operational aspects but also the amendments made to the investment policy, and certifying adherence to the laid-down internal investment policy and procedures and to the Reserve Bank's guidelines. And copies of the internal audit report need not be forwarded to the Reserve Bank; major irregularities observed and the position of compliance may instead be incorporated in that review.
keywords: half-yearly reviews of their investment portfolio
adherence to the laid-down internal investment policy and procedures
need not be forwarded to the Reserve Bank

options.text: Only the review is missing — the monthly report should go to the audit committee of the board rather than to the Chairman and Managing Director, and copies to the Reserve Bank are required
options.misconception: redirects a report the guidance places with the Chairman and Managing Director, and keeps a filing that is not required
options.why: The results of the concurrent audit of treasury transactions are placed before the Chairman and Managing Director once every month, and copies of the internal audit report need not be forwarded to the Reserve Bank. Two of the three things this option leaves standing are the two that are wrong.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — treasury and investments: the half-yearly reviews of the investment portfolio as at 30 September and 31 March, and the concurrent audit of treasury transactions conducted by the internal auditors with monthly reporting to the Chairman and Managing Director

items.scenario: A bank's treasury is covered by a concurrent audit conducted by the bank's internal auditors. The general manager tells you the concurrent auditor's reports go to the Chairman and Managing Director every month, that copies are forwarded to the Reserve Bank every quarter, and that because concurrent audit already covers treasury the bank sees no need for any periodic review of the investment portfolio itself.

items.stem: Is that drafting right?

options.text: No, and the auditor must also report whether the board's approval of the ₹9 crore purchase was commercially justified
options.misconception: turns a compliance-and-disclosure clause into an opinion on the wisdom of the transaction
options.why: The clause reports compliance with the two sections and disclosure under the accounting standards. Whether the price was right belongs to any assertion the company makes that the transaction was on arm's length terms, and to the auditor's evidence about that assertion; it is not what clause 3(xiii) asks.

options.text: No, but only the ₹9 crore purchase is reportable, the second transaction being in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis
options.misconception: extends the section 188 carve-out for ordinary-course arm's length transactions to the disclosure limb, which has no such carve-out
options.why: Those words take a transaction outside the approval regime of section 188. They do nothing to the disclosure limb, which asks whether the details have been disclosed as the applicable accounting standards require, and that limb applies to a related party transaction however it was priced.

options.text: No — the words "where applicable" switch off the section 177 limb alone, so the clause is still answered on compliance with section 188 and on disclosure as the applicable accounting standards require
options.why: Clause 3(xiii) asks whether all transactions with related parties are in compliance with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 where applicable, and whether the details have been disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards. Where a company has no audit committee the section 177 limb simply does not arise, and the other two are untouched: the ₹9 crore purchase is reported as not in compliance with section 188, and the ₹40 lakh sale is still answered under the disclosure limb.
keywords: sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 where applicable
disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards

options.text: Yes — a clause that names section 177 cannot be answered by a company that has no audit committee
options.misconception: reads "where applicable" as switching off the whole clause rather than the one limb that does not arise
options.why: The clause names two sections and a disclosure requirement, and "where applicable" exists so that each is answered on its own footing. Reading the absence of an audit committee as switching the clause off would take every company without one outside a clause that plainly reaches them.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiii), read with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A private company outside the classes required to constitute an audit committee has two related party transactions in the year. A ₹9 crore purchase of goods from a firm in which a director is a partner, not in the ordinary course of business, approved by the board but not by the shareholders where section 188 required their approval. And a ₹40 lakh sale of services to a director's relative, in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis, disclosed in the notes. The manager drafts clause 3(xiii) as not applicable, the company having no audit committee.

items.stem: What do the Listing Regulations require?

options.text: It is printed inside the auditor's report on the financial statements, so that one document carries both conclusions
options.misconception: folds a separate certificate into the report carrying the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The two are reached on different subject matter and can point in opposite directions on the same company. Putting the certificate inside the audit report would attach a conclusion about governance conditions to a report that expresses none.

options.text: Only the statutory auditor may give it, a company secretary having no standing to certify compliance for a listed entity
options.misconception: narrows to the statutory auditor a certificate the Regulations expressly allow a practising company secretary to give
options.why: Schedule V names both, and many listed entities take the certificate from a practising company secretary rather than from their auditors. Nothing in the Regulations reserves it to the firm that audits the accounts.

options.text: It goes to the stock exchange alone, the directors' report being confined to the matters section 134(3) lists
options.misconception: keeps the certificate away from the shareholders, and treats the directors' report as a closed list
options.why: The certificate is annexed to the directors' report, which is how the shareholders reach it. And section 134(3) is not a closed list — other laws and regulations add to what that report must carry, which is exactly how this certificate gets there.

options.text: The certificate may be obtained from either the auditors or a practising company secretary, and it is annexed to the directors' report
options.why: Regulation 34(3) read with Schedule V has the listed entity obtain a certificate from either the auditors or a practising company secretary regarding compliance of the conditions of corporate governance, and that certificate is annexed to the directors' report. It stands on its own because it reports the factual implementation of the stipulated conditions, which is a different subject matter from the financial statements.
keywords: either the auditors or a practising company secretary

citation.ref: Regulation 34(3) read with Schedule V — the certificate from the auditors or a practising company secretary annexed to the directors' report

items.scenario: A listed company's board is settling who will give the certificate on compliance with the conditions of corporate governance and where it will appear. The company secretary says only the statutory auditor may give it. The managing director says it should be printed inside the auditor's report on the financial statements so that shareholders read one document instead of two.

items.stem: What does section 139 allow?

options.text: He may be re-appointed provided he joins a firm and a different partner of that firm signs the report, the bar attaching to the signature
options.misconception: reads a limit on tenure as a limit on the signature
options.why: The bar attaches to the individual appointed as auditor of that company. Who may sign is governed elsewhere, and an arrangement that keeps the same individual in the appointment while moving the pen answers nothing section 139(2) asks.

options.text: He may not be re-appointed, and the members' resolution is not open to them either, rotation being fixed by statute and not a matter for the members
options.misconception: reads the statutory rotation as occupying the field, missing the separate power section 139(3) gives the members
options.why: Statutory rotation of the auditor is not a matter for the members, and section 139(3) gives them a separate and additional power alongside it — to resolve on rotation of the auditing partner and his team, or on the audit being conducted by more than one auditor.

options.text: He may be re-appointed for a second term, the ceiling of ten years being the same for an individual and for a firm
options.misconception: equalises the individual's cap with the firm's, when section 139(2) sets them at one term and at two terms
options.why: The section states the two ceilings in separate clauses and they are not the same figure. An individual is capped at one term of five consecutive years; only an audit firm may serve two such terms.

options.text: He may not be re-appointed — an individual is capped at one term of five consecutive years and is then barred from re-appointment in the same company for five years — while the members' resolution is open to them under section 139(3)
options.why: Section 139(2) sets two different ceilings on purpose: an individual as auditor for no more than one term of five consecutive years, and an audit firm for no more than two terms of five consecutive years. Its proviso then makes an individual who has completed his term ineligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of that term, so a second term is not available to him. Section 139(3) is a separate power and it permits exactly what the members want: they may resolve that the auditing partner and his team shall be rotated at such intervals as they resolve, or that the audit shall be conducted by more than one auditor.
keywords: one term of five consecutive years

citation.ref: Section 139(2) capping an individual at one term of five consecutive years, with its proviso on ineligibility for re-appointment for five years, read with Section 139(3)

items.scenario: CA Bhatia, a sole practitioner, has been the auditor of a listed company for one term of five consecutive years, ending at the 2026 annual general meeting. The company proposes to appoint him again for a second term of five years, arguing that the cap belongs to firms and that an individual should be allowed the same total tenure. Separately, a group of members wants a resolution that the audit partner and his team be rotated every three years and that the audit be conducted by two auditors.

items.stem: What has the finance head misread?

options.text: Only the appointment — the order does direct a cost audit, but the Central Government appoints the cost auditor for every company it covers
options.misconception: keeps the misreading of the order and adds an appointment power the Central Government does not exercise
options.why: The order under section 148(1) directs cost records, not an audit of them. And where an audit is directed under section 148(2), the Central Government's part is the direction; the appointment is made by the Board of Directors of the company.

options.text: Nothing — an order to include cost particulars in the books is a cost audit order, and the statutory audit firm arranges the appointment as part of its engagement
options.misconception: collapses the records direction into the audit direction, and hands the appointment to a firm the Act keeps out of it
options.why: The two orders are separate and only one of them brings an audit into existence. And even where a cost audit is directed, the appointment is the Board's, and the auditor appointed under section 139 is barred from conducting the cost audit at all — so arranging it is no part of the statutory audit engagement.

options.text: Section 148(1) directs cost particulars into the books of account, which is a records requirement; a cost audit arises only on the separate direction under section 148(2), and where one exists the cost auditor is appointed by the Board of Directors
options.why: Section 148 carries two different orders. Under section 148(1) the Central Government may direct that particulars relating to the utilisation of material or labour or to other items of cost be included in the books of account kept by such class of companies as may be prescribed — an obligation to maintain cost records and nothing more. Under section 148(2), where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, it may direct that the cost records of such class of prescribed companies, having a net worth or turnover of the prescribed amount, be audited. Only the second creates a cost audit, and the cost auditor is then appointed by the Board of Directors.
keywords: included in the books of account
cost records of such class of prescribed companies
appointed by the Board of Directors

options.text: Only the identity of the appointing body — the order does direct a cost audit, and the audit committee appoints the cost auditor and fixes his remuneration
options.misconception: leaves the two directions merged, and turns the audit committee's recommendation into an appointment
options.why: The direction under section 148(1) is about what goes into the books of account. And the appointment is the Board's; in a company that has an audit committee the committee's part is to recommend the cost auditor and his remuneration, not to appoint him.

citation.ref: Section 148(1) on the inclusion of cost particulars in the books of account and Section 148(2) on the direction that cost records be audited, with the appointment of the cost auditor by the Board of Directors

items.scenario: A manufacturing company receives an order of the Central Government under section 148 directing that particulars relating to the utilisation of material and labour be included in its books of account. The finance head reads that as an order for a cost audit, and asks the statutory audit firm to find a cost accountant, appoint him and settle his remuneration.

items.stem: Has the firm done everything section 140(2) requires?

options.text: No — for a company covered by section 139(5) the resigning auditor must file the same statement with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India as well
options.why: Section 140(2) requires the auditor who has resigned to file, within thirty days of the resignation, a statement in the prescribed form indicating the reasons and other facts relevant to the resignation — with the company and with the Registrar, and in the case of companies referred to in section 139(5) with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India as well. A government company owned by the Central Government is such a company, so the third filing is the one that is missing.
keywords: reasons and other facts relevant to the resignation

options.text: Yes — the company and the Registrar are the only addressees the section names
options.misconception: reads the general addressees as the whole list and misses the limb written for a company covered by section 139(5)
options.why: They are the addressees for an ordinary company. The section carries a further limb for companies referred to in section 139(5), and a government company is exactly what engages it.

options.text: Yes, and in any event the thirty days run from the next annual general meeting rather than from the resignation
options.misconception: ties the filing period to the meeting calendar rather than to the date of the resignation
options.why: Two things are wrong. The third filing is missing, and the clock runs from the date of the resignation — which is what makes a mid-year exit reportable at all, and mid-year exits are the ones whose reasons matter most.

options.text: No, but the omission is the company's to cure, the company being the one that ordinarily corresponds with the Comptroller and Auditor-General
options.misconception: moves the auditor's own statutory filing onto the company
options.why: The filing is the resigning auditor's personal duty and the penalty for failing to make it falls on him. Who ordinarily corresponds with the Comptroller and Auditor-General has nothing to do with whose filing this is.

citation.ref: Section 140(2), including the filing with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India for companies referred to in Section 139(5)

items.scenario: An audit firm resigns mid-year from the audit of a government company owned by the Central Government. Within thirty days it files the prescribed statement of reasons and relevant facts with the company and with the Registrar, and treats the matter as closed.

items.stem: What else must the firm be satisfied about before performing the service?

options.text: That the service is approved by those charged with governance, an approval settling the matter whatever management's own capability
options.misconception: treats governance approval as a safeguard for a risk the Code addresses through the client's own capability to decide
options.why: Communicating with those charged with governance is often appropriate and it does not substitute for the client having someone able to make and own the decision. Approval by a body is not the same thing as competence to evaluate what the firm produced.

options.text: Nothing further — once management takes the decision the firm has not assumed a management responsibility, and that is the whole of the test
options.misconception: stops at the formal fact that management decided, when the Code also asks whether management was in a position to decide
options.why: Management taking the decision is necessary and it is not sufficient. A board signing a recommendation it has nobody able to evaluate has decided in form only, which is why the Code asks for a designated individual of suitable skill, knowledge and experience and for oversight of the work.

options.text: That the firm's fee for the service is not contingent on which financing structure the board chooses, that being the safeguard the Code calls for here
options.misconception: reaches for the contingent fee rule, which answers a different threat from the one these facts create
options.why: A contingent fee creates a self-interest threat of its own and the Code deals with it separately. It says nothing about whether the firm is taking a decision that belongs to management, which is the question these facts raise.

options.text: That client management designates an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience to be responsible for the client's decisions and to oversee the service, provides oversight of the activities and evaluates the adequacy of the results, and accepts responsibility for the actions to be taken
options.why: Providing advice and recommendations to assist management is not assuming a management responsibility, and the Code does not leave the matter at management having taken the decision. To avoid the risk of assuming a management responsibility the firm must be satisfied that client management designates an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience to be responsible for the client's decisions and to oversee the service, preferably from senior management; that it provides oversight of the activities and evaluates the adequacy of the results; and that it accepts responsibility for the actions to be taken arising from those results.
keywords: designates an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience
provides oversight of the activities and evaluates the adequacy of the results
accepts responsibility for the actions to be taken

citation.ref: the prohibition on a firm assuming a management responsibility for an audit client, with the requirement that client management designate an individual possessing suitable skill, knowledge and experience to be responsible for the client's decisions and to oversee the services

items.scenario: A firm agrees to build a detailed working capital model for its audit client and to recommend which of three financing structures the board should adopt. The board will take the decision itself. The engagement partner says that because management decides, nothing further is needed and the firm has plainly not assumed a management responsibility.

items.stem: How does the Code of Ethics answer him?

options.text: He is right — the rule on gifts and hospitality governs what is accepted from an audit client, and this company is not yet a client and nothing was accepted
options.misconception: answers with the acceptance rule for audit clients and misses the separate prohibition on offering an inducement
options.why: There are two rules and he has answered only one. The trivial-and-inconsequential test governs what a firm or an audit team member may accept from an audit client. The prohibition on an inducement made with the intent to improperly influence behaviour applies to offering as much as to accepting, and it is not confined to existing clients.

options.text: He is wrong, but the rule reaches him personally alone, so the firm and the rest of the engagement team are unaffected by what he arranged
options.misconception: confines to one individual a prohibition that reaches the firm and anyone offering on the accountant's behalf
options.why: The prohibition runs against the professional accountant and against allowing another to offer for him, and the Code applies it to the firm as well as to individuals. A firm that wins an appointment this way has not stayed clear of the rule because only one partner did the arranging.

options.text: An inducement is not confined to gifts and hospitality — employment or other commercial opportunities and preferential treatment are within it — and the Code bars an accountant from offering one, or encouraging others to offer one, with the intent to improperly influence behaviour, an immediate or close family member included
options.why: The Code treats an inducement as an object, situation or action used as a means to influence another individual's behaviour, and its examples run well past gifts: entertainment, political or charitable donations, appeals to friendship or loyalty, employment or other commercial opportunities, and preferential treatment, rights or privileges. An internship offered to a decision-maker's daughter while the decision is open is squarely inside that. And the routing does not save him, because the accountant shall not offer, or encourage others to offer, an inducement made with the intent to improperly influence behaviour, and shall not allow an immediate or close family member to offer one for him.

options.text: He is wrong, but the answer is to apply the conceptual framework and weigh the value, the timing and the cumulative effect of the internship
options.misconception: applies the evaluate-and-address route to an inducement the Code prohibits outright
options.why: The framework governs where there is no intent to improperly influence behaviour. Where there is such intent the Code prohibits the inducement outright and stops asking what it was worth, and an opportunity handed to the decision-maker's daughter while the decision is open is not a case for weighing factors.

citation.ref: the inducements provisions — the meaning of an inducement, and the prohibition on offering an inducement, or encouraging or allowing another to offer one, with the intent to improperly influence behaviour
