items.scenario: A firm wants the audit of a large company. While the appointment is being decided, the engagement partner arranges for his wife, who has nothing to do with the firm, to offer the finance director's daughter a paid internship at the wife's own business. The partner points out that he offered nothing himself, that no gift changed hands, and that an internship is not a gift or a piece of hospitality at all.

items.stem: What should he put to the company before accepting?

options.text: That he must refuse the operational areas outright, an internal auditor being barred from any operational involvement whatever
options.misconception: hardens a limited and time-bound allowance into a total prohibition
options.why: The bar is not absolute. He may accept a limited operational role and for a short duration; what he may not do is take operational decisions in areas that will later be subject to internal audit, and the caveat has to be given before he accepts rather than argued afterwards.

options.text: That the department belongs outside the departments it audits, with its reporting line running straight to those charged with governance — in a listed company that means the audit committee; and that he can accept only a limited operational role, for a short spell, and cannot take operational decisions in areas that will later come before him as auditor
options.why: Independence inside an entity comes from position and from reporting line. Internal audit sits positioned outside the functions which are subject to internal audit — finance and accounts among them — and its head may be required, in a listed company, to report directly to those charged with governance, which there means the audit committee, rather than to the chief executive officer or the chief financial officer. System automation and process re-engineering are operational duties, so he may accept a limited operational role and only for a short spell, and may not decide operational matters that will later be subject to internal audit.
keywords: positioned outside the functions which are subject to internal audit
report directly to those charged with governance

options.text: Nothing — internal audit is an internal function, so the Chief Financial Officer is the natural reporting line, and an operational role gives him knowledge no outsider would have
options.misconception: treats internal audit's position inside the entity as removing the safeguards its independence depends on
options.why: Being inside the entity is the reason the reporting line matters, not a reason to set it aside. A function reporting to the officer whose department it audits has nothing to fall back on when its scope is trimmed or its findings are softened.

options.text: That the reporting line is for the board to settle, and that any conflict of interest can be set out in his annual report to the audit committee
options.misconception: defers a conflict of interest to a periodic report instead of raising it at once, and leaves the reporting line to the body being audited
options.why: An actual or apparent conflict of interest is brought to the attention of the appropriate level of management immediately, so that corrective action can be taken while it still can be. And the reporting line is what makes any report to the audit committee worth reading in the first place.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — the function positioned outside the functions subject to internal audit and reporting directly to the audit committee, and the limits on an internal auditor accepting operational responsibilities

items.scenario: A retired officer is offered the post of Chief Internal Auditor of a listed company. The offer letter has him reporting to the Chief Financial Officer. It also gives him responsibility for "system automation" and "process re-engineering" across the finance function, which the company says will make him more useful than an auditor who only inspects.

items.stem: Who appoints the auditor for that financial year, by when, and for how long does he hold office?

options.text: The Board appoints him within thirty days of the commencement of the financial year, the Comptroller and Auditor-General's role being confined to the supplementary audit
options.misconception: gives the Board an appointment power section 139(5) places with the Comptroller and Auditor-General
options.why: Thirty days from registration is the Board's window for a first auditor under section 139(6), and that section does not reach a government company. The Comptroller and Auditor-General both appoints the auditor under section 139(5) and may conduct a supplementary audit under section 143(6); the second power does not replace the first.

options.text: The members appoint him at the annual general meeting on the Board's recommendation, for a term of five consecutive years
options.misconception: applies the ordinary section 139(1) appointment to a company section 139(5) expressly governs
options.why: That is the machinery of section 139(1), written for companies section 139(5) does not reach. For a government company the appointment belongs to the Comptroller and Auditor-General and the tenure runs to the conclusion of the annual general meeting rather than for five years.

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India appoints him within one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, and the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting
options.why: Section 139(5) takes a government company out of the ordinary appointment machinery for every year and not only the first. In respect of a financial year the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India appoints an auditor duly qualified to be appointed as an auditor of companies under the Act, within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, and the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting. Neither the Board nor the members have a part in it.
keywords: one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year
till the conclusion of the annual general meeting

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints him within sixty days, and he holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting
options.misconception: carries the first-auditor timetable of section 139(7) into the annual appointment section 139(5) governs
options.why: Sixty days and the first annual general meeting belong to section 139(7), which deals with the first auditor of such a company and runs from the date of its registration. This company is many years past that, so section 139(5) governs.

citation.ref: Section 139(5) — appointment by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India within one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, the auditor holding office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting

items.scenario: A government company has been in existence for many years and its first auditor's term ended long ago. For the financial year beginning 1 April the board asks its audit committee to recommend a firm, and proposes to place the appointment before the members at the annual general meeting in September.

items.stem: How is the Comptroller and Auditor General's relationship with the financial committees described?

options.text: He is a witness before the Committees and nothing more, so checking a draft report would compromise his independence
options.misconception: reduces a standing advisory role to that of a witness, and reads assistance to the legislature as a threat to independence
options.why: The described role goes well past giving evidence and it is the settled practice rather than a departure from it. Helping a committee of the legislature verify the figures in its own draft is assistance to the body the auditor reports to in the first place.

options.text: He has no continuing relationship with them, the reports standing referred to the Committees automatically and being taken up without him
options.misconception: reads the automatic reference of the reports as ending the auditor's part in the process
options.why: The reports do stand referred automatically, and that is where his involvement begins rather than ends. He scrutinises the ministries' notes and assists on the facts and figures, the ministries then inform the Committees of the action taken, and Action Taken Reports are presented to the legislature in turn.

options.text: He is recognised as the friend, philosopher and guide of the Committees — what he has reported is ordinarily where their work starts, though a Committee is not precluded from examining issues not brought out in his reports, and he goes through the notes the ministries put in and helps check the correctness of facts and figures in a draft report
options.why: The Comptroller and Auditor General is central to how the financial committees of Parliament and of the State Legislatures do their work, and has come to be recognised as their friend, philosopher and guide. What he has reported is ordinarily the starting point for what they take up, though a Committee is not precluded from examining issues not brought out in his reports. He goes through the notes the ministries put before the Committees, and helps them test the correctness of what is submitted and of the facts and figures in their draft reports.
keywords: not precluded from examining issues not brought out in his reports
facts and figures in their draft reports

options.text: He acts as the secretariat of the Committees, which is why they are confined to the matters his reports raise
options.misconception: turns a role that supplies the Committees' agenda into a limit on what they may examine
options.why: The Committees are expressly not precluded from examining issues not brought out in his reports, and he is not their secretariat. What he has reported is where their work usually starts, which is a starting point and not a boundary.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Comptroller and Auditor General's role as the friend, philosopher and guide of the financial committees

items.scenario: A financial committee of Parliament is examining a ministry. Its secretariat asks the Comptroller and Auditor General's office to look over the notes the ministry has submitted and to check the facts and figures in the committee's own draft report. A member objects that this makes the auditor a party to the committee's report, and adds that the committee may in any case take up only matters the auditor's reports have raised.

items.stem: Which general principles have long been recognised as the standards of financial propriety?

options.text: That every item of expenditure carries a sanction, that the sanction is from a competent authority, and that the expenditure falls within the grant voted
options.misconception: recites the regularity tests, which propriety audit was developed to go beyond
options.why: Those are the tests of regularity audit — legality, authority and the appropriation. Propriety audit exists because expenditure can pass all three and still be wasteful, so its standards are a separate list rather than a longer version of that one.

options.text: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness, measured against the targets the entity set itself for the year
options.misconception: answers with the performance audit criteria, which measure results rather than the propriety of the transaction
options.why: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness are the subject of performance audit, which asks whether the money achieved what it was meant to achieve. Propriety asks about the wisdom and faithfulness of the transaction itself, and it is answered against the standards of financial propriety rather than against anybody's targets.

options.text: There are none written down, propriety being a moral term that each auditor applies as he sees fit
options.misconception: treats the acknowledged subjectivity of propriety as meaning that no standards exist
options.why: Propriety does carry an element of subjectivity, and that is precisely why the general principles were laid down in the Audit Code and why the Comptroller and Auditor General has developed norms of propriety for the expenditure of public funds. The subjectivity is what the standards answer, not a licence to do without them.

options.text: That spending stays, on the face of it, inside what the occasion calls for, every official watching it as closely as a prudent man watches money of his own; that whoever sanctions an order takes nothing from it for himself, directly or by a roundabout route; that public money is not steered to one person or to one set of people; and that beyond the remuneration or reward already agreed, no side door is left ajar through which management, staff or anyone else gains something indirectly
options.why: Those four are the general principles laid down in the Audit Code and long recognised as the standards of financial propriety. The first is a prudence test, measuring the care taken against the care a person of ordinary prudence would exercise over his own money. The second stops a sanctioning authority ordering a benefit for itself. The third keeps public funds from a particular person or group of persons. The fourth shuts the side door: beyond the agreed remuneration or reward, nothing further may be left open through which management, staff or others gain indirectly.
keywords: a person of ordinary prudence would exercise over his own money
particular person or group of persons

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the general principles laid down in the Audit Code and recognised as the standards of financial propriety

items.scenario: A trainee joining a government audit team has been told only that propriety audit looks at the wisdom, faithfulness and economy of a transaction. He asks what he is actually testing against, since none of those three words appears in any rule book he has been given.

items.stem: Does SA 210 bar you from accepting this engagement?

options.text: Yes, unless the company first agrees in the engagement letter that the opinion may be qualified
options.misconception: treats the client's advance agreement to a qualification as the thing that makes acceptance permissible
options.why: A term agreed in advance cannot settle an opinion the auditor forms only after doing the work. The acceptance question turns on what he expects the limitation to produce, and the client's willingness to live with a qualification is no part of it.

options.text: Yes — any limitation imposed by management before acceptance bars the engagement, whatever its size
options.misconception: attaches the bar to management-imposed limitations generally, rather than to those expected to end in a disclaimer
options.why: Who imposed the limitation is not the whole of the test. What the standard asks is whether the auditor believes the limitation will result in his disclaiming an opinion, and a restriction reaching part of one balance is a long way from that.

options.text: No, and the limitation may then be left out of the report, having been known and accepted before the engagement began
options.misconception: reads a permitted acceptance as a licence to leave the consequence out of the report
options.why: Accepting decides only that the engagement may be undertaken. If the alternative procedures do not produce sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the quantities, the inability goes into the opinion under SA 705 (Revised), and a limitation is no less a limitation for having been known in advance.

options.text: No — the bar operates where the auditor believes the limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, and a limitation expected to produce at worst a qualification does not engage it
options.why: SA 210 says that where management imposes a limitation on the scope of the auditor's work in the terms of a proposed audit engagement such that the auditor believes the limitation will result in the auditor disclaiming an opinion on the financial statements, he shall not accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement, unless required by law or regulation to do so. The test is the consequence he expects, not the mere existence of a restriction. Here one warehouse is closed, alternative procedures are available, and the worst expected outcome is a qualification.
keywords: will result in the auditor disclaiming an opinion
unless required by law or regulation

citation.ref: para 7

items.scenario: Before appointing you, a company tells you that you may not attend the physical inventory count at one of its eleven warehouses, the landlord of that site having closed it to visitors. That warehouse holds 6 per cent of inventory, and inventory is 20 per cent of total assets. Alternative procedures on the location are open to you, and you expect at worst that they will leave you qualifying the opinion on quantities there. Every other area is unrestricted.

items.stem: Why does SA 250 treat the two differently?

options.text: It does not — the risk is the same and the standard merely lists extra procedures for laws and regulations
options.misconception: denies a difference the standard states expressly and then explains
options.why: The standard says in terms that the risk of not detecting a material misstatement arising from non-compliance is higher than the risk of not detecting one arising from error, and it sets out why. The procedures follow from those reasons rather than standing on their own.

options.text: Because non-compliance is always intentional, and an intentional misstatement is harder to find than an unintentional one
options.misconception: hardens a possibility of concealment into a claim that all non-compliance is deliberate
options.why: Non-compliance may be intentional and it may not — a company can breach a licence condition through carelessness. What the standard says is that non-compliance may involve conduct designed to conceal it, which is one of three reasons rather than a rule about every case.

options.text: Because a great many laws bear on how the entity operates rather than on its figures, so the financial statements are untouched and the reporting systems never record them; because those who breach a law often set out to hide the breach; and because it takes a court, in the end, to say whether an act was non-compliance at all
options.why: SA 250 says an audit's built-in limits bite harder here, and gives three reasons. Many laws bear principally on the operating aspects of the entity; they leave the financial statements alone, and the systems that feed financial reporting never pick them up. Second, there may be conduct designed to conceal it — forged papers, staff acting together, transactions deliberately left unrecorded, controls overridden by management, or untruths told to the auditor on purpose. Third, whether a given act amounts to non-compliance at all is in the end a question of legal determination by a court.

options.text: Because the auditor is responsible for preventing non-compliance, which sets a higher standard of work than error does
options.misconception: inverts the standard's allocation of responsibility, which puts compliance on management and limits the auditor expressly
options.why: SA 250 says the opposite in the same breath: stopping a breach is no part of the auditor's responsibility, and nobody can expect him to pick up every breach of every law and regulation there is. The higher risk of non-detection is part of the reason for those limits, not a reason to widen his duty.

citation.ref: the higher risk of non-detection where a material misstatement springs from non-compliance rather than from error, and the three reasons the Standard gives for it

items.scenario: A partner reviewing a planning file writes that the programme should treat the risk of an undetected material misstatement arising from non-compliance with laws and regulations exactly as it treats the risk of one arising from error, since both end in a wrong figure in the same set of accounts.

items.stem: What else does SA 265 require in writing?

options.text: Nothing — a significant deficiency is addressed to those charged with governance alone, and deficiencies below that level may be raised orally
options.misconception: reads the communication to those charged with governance as the whole requirement, and treats lesser deficiencies as needing no written record
options.why: The standard names management as a second addressee for the significant ones, and it puts the other deficiencies of sufficient importance in writing to management as well. A mention at a closing meeting satisfies neither.

options.text: The two significant deficiencies also go in writing to management at an appropriate level of responsibility, unless it would be inappropriate to communicate directly to management — and the other four go to management in writing as well
options.why: SA 265 sends a significant deficiency in two directions. It is communicated in writing to those charged with governance, and it is communicated in writing to management at an appropriate level of responsibility as well, unless it would be inappropriate to communicate directly to management. Separately, any other deficiency the audit turned up which nobody else has already put to management, and which carries sufficient importance to merit management's attention, is communicated to management in writing too.
keywords: management at an appropriate level of responsibility
inappropriate to communicate directly to management
sufficient importance to merit management's attention

options.text: All six go in writing to those charged with governance, management needing no copy once governance has been told
options.misconception: raises every deficiency to the governance level and drops the separate written communication the standard directs at management
options.why: Only significant deficiencies go to those charged with governance. Other deficiencies of sufficient importance go to management, and telling governance does not discharge the separate communication the standard directs at management.

options.text: Only the other four go to management, the significant ones being reserved for those charged with governance so that management cannot bury them
options.misconception: withholds significant deficiencies from management, when the standard sends them to both bodies
options.why: Nothing in the standard reserves a significant deficiency from management. It goes to management at an appropriate level of responsibility as well, and the single exception is where it would be inappropriate to communicate directly to management.

citation.ref: para 9 and para 10

items.scenario: You have identified two significant deficiencies in internal control and four other deficiencies you think the finance director ought to know about. You write to the audit committee about the two significant ones. The manager says nothing further is owed to anybody: significant deficiencies are the audit committee's business, and the other four can be mentioned in passing at the closing meeting.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) say about that proposal?

options.text: It is not needed, and P may also assume that anything Q found and did not mention was immaterial
options.misconception: converts an entitlement to assume the others communicated into an inference about matters they never raised
options.why: The entitlement is that the others have brought relevant matters to his notice, and the standard's coordination requirement is what supports it — a joint auditor who comes across a matter relevant to another's responsibilities communicates it to all the others in writing before the audit is completed. Silence is not evidence that there was nothing to say.

options.text: It is not needed — each joint auditor is entitled to assume that the others have carried out their work in accordance with the Standards and have brought to his notice any departure from the framework or any significant observation relevant to his responsibilities, and where a division's financial statements are audited by one joint auditor the others may proceed on the basis that those statements comply with the legal and regulatory requirements
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) makes each joint auditor entitled to assume that the other joint auditors have carried out their work in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and that the work has actually been performed, so it is thus not necessary for a joint auditor to review the work another of them has done. He is entitled to assume too that they have brought to his notice any departure from the applicable financial reporting framework and any significant observations relevant to his responsibilities. And where the financial statements of a division or branch are audited by one of the joint auditors, the others are entitled to proceed on the basis that those statements comply with all the legal and regulatory requirements.
keywords: not necessary for a joint auditor to review the work
significant observations relevant to his responsibilities

options.text: It is needed for the division's financial statements alone, a branch audited by one auditor being work of another auditor within the meaning of SA 600
options.misconception: treats a fellow joint auditor as a component auditor and imports SA 600's procedures into a joint audit
options.why: A joint auditor is not another auditor under SA 600; he is an auditor of the same financial statements, appointed alongside. Where a division's financial statements are audited by one of the joint auditors, the others are entitled to proceed on the basis that they comply with the legal and regulatory requirements.

options.text: It is needed — a joint auditor signs a common report on the whole of the financial statements, so he must satisfy himself about every part of the work behind it
options.misconception: reads the common report as making each joint auditor responsible for performing the whole audit
options.why: A common report is issued on one set of financial statements, and the standard divides responsibility for performing the work precisely so that each joint auditor answers for his own part of it. If everyone had to re-perform everyone else's work the division would achieve nothing at all.

citation.ref: the entitlement of each joint auditor to assume that the other joint auditors have carried out their work in accordance with the Standards on Auditing, read with para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: Three firms are joint auditors of a company. P takes payables, Q takes inventory and R takes receivables, and the financial statements of one division are audited by Q alone. Before signing the common report, P proposes to re-perform a sample of Q's inventory testing and to re-audit the division's financial statements, saying he cannot sign an opinion covering work he has not seen. Nothing has been brought to his notice suggesting anything is wrong with Q's work.

items.stem: What does SA 450 require before any of that?

options.text: To communicate on a timely basis all misstatements accumulated during the audit with the appropriate level of management, unless prohibited by law or regulation, and to request management to correct them
options.why: SA 450 puts management first and puts it early: the auditor shall communicate on a timely basis all misstatements accumulated during the audit with the appropriate level of management, unless prohibited by law or regulation, and shall request management to correct those misstatements. Timeliness is the point of it — it gives management the chance to examine each item while the accounts can still be changed, and where management does correct them the auditor then determines whether misstatements remain.
keywords: all misstatements accumulated during the audit

options.text: To obtain a written representation that management believes the effects of the misstatements are immaterial, and to treat that as the request to correct
options.misconception: substitutes the closing written representation for the timely communication and request the standard requires
options.why: That representation is obtained at the end, deals with the misstatements that remain uncorrected, and carries a summary of them. It records what management believes; it is not a request that anything be corrected, and it is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own.

options.text: To determine which of the eleven are clearly trivial and to communicate only the remainder
options.misconception: applies the clearly trivial threshold a second time, to the communication rather than to the accumulation
options.why: The clearly trivial threshold works at the point of accumulation — misstatements other than clearly trivial ones are what get accumulated in the first place. What has been accumulated is then communicated in full rather than filtered again.

options.text: Nothing — the schedule of misstatements is put to those charged with governance at the end, and management sees it only if governance asks for corrections
options.misconception: skips the communication to management and starts at the communication to those charged with governance
options.why: The communication to those charged with governance is a separate and later requirement and it deals with the misstatements that remain uncorrected. Before it, all accumulated misstatements go to the appropriate level of management on a timely basis with a request that they be corrected.

citation.ref: para 8, read with para 9

items.scenario: You have accumulated eleven misstatements during the audit. The manager plans to hold all of them until the closing meeting, present the schedule to the audit committee there, and put it to the finance director only if the audit committee asks for corrections. Two of the eleven, if corrected, would change the position on a bank covenant ratio.

items.stem: What procedures does SA 501 require in order to identify litigation and claims involving the entity?

options.text: Inquiry of management and, where applicable, of others within the entity including in-house legal counsel; review of the minutes of meetings of those charged with governance and of the correspondence between the entity and its external legal counsel; and review of the legal expense accounts
options.why: SA 501 does not let the auditor wait to be told. He designs and carries out work aimed at finding the lawsuits and claims the entity is caught up in, wherever one of them could carry a risk of material misstatement, and the Standard names three such procedures. He puts questions to management, and, where the client keeps one, to its in-house legal counsel. He then reads two records: the minutes of meetings of those charged with governance, plus whatever letters have passed between the company and the outside solicitors acting for it. Third comes reviewing the legal expense accounts, which is the one that finds a matter nobody put on any schedule.
keywords: minutes of meetings of those charged with governance

options.text: A schedule of pending cases from the company, agreed to the contingent liability note, which is sufficient where nothing on it looks unusual
options.misconception: relies on a list produced by the entity to establish the completeness of that same list
options.why: A schedule is information produced by the entity and it can only show what the entity chose to put on it. The standard's procedures exist to find what the schedule leaves off, which is exactly why one of them is a review of the legal expense accounts.

options.text: Written representations from management that all litigation and claims have been disclosed, which put the responsibility where it belongs
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for procedures the standard requires the auditor to perform himself
options.why: A written representation is audit evidence and it is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any matter it deals with. Responsibility for disclosing claims does sit with management, and that is precisely why the standard has the auditor go looking for them.

options.text: A letter of inquiry to the entity's external legal counsel in every audit, whatever the risk assessment says
options.misconception: starts with the letter of inquiry, which the standard makes conditional, and skips the identification procedures that decide whether it is needed
options.why: The letter of inquiry comes later and on a condition — where the auditor assesses a risk of material misstatement regarding identified litigation or claims, or where his procedures indicate that other material litigation or claims may exist. Identification comes first and is done from the entity's own records and people.

citation.ref: para 9

items.scenario: You are planning the work on litigation and claims at a manufacturing client. The senior proposes to obtain a schedule of pending cases from the company secretary, agree it to the contingent liability note, and do nothing further unless something on the schedule looks odd.

items.stem: Is your work on the opening balances complete?

options.text: Yes, because a change in accounting policy is dealt with by the reporting framework rather than by SA 510
options.misconception: hands the consistency question to the reporting framework and leaves the auditor with nothing to test
options.why: The framework says when a change is permitted and how it is presented; SA 510 makes the auditor test that in relation to the opening balances in an initial audit engagement. The two work together rather than as alternatives.

options.text: No — the change is a misstatement of the opening balances, which must be restated on the previous basis
options.misconception: converts a requirement to test a change into a rule that no change may be made
options.why: Consistency is not a bar on change. Where a change is appropriately accounted for and adequately presented and disclosed in accordance with the framework there is nothing to correct, and the auditor's work is to establish whether it was.

options.text: No — SA 510 sets a second objective, that the accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied in the current period's financial statements, or that changes to them are appropriately accounted for and adequately presented and disclosed
options.why: SA 510 gives the auditor two objectives about opening balances. One asks whether the opening balances contain misstatements big enough to distort what this year's accounts report. The other is whether appropriate accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied in the current period's financial statements, or whether changes to them are appropriately accounted for and adequately presented and disclosed in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. A move from weighted average to first-in first-out is such a change, and it has to be tested rather than accepted as an improvement.
keywords: consistently applied in the current period's financial statements

options.text: Yes — once the opening figure is shown to be free from misstatement the requirement is discharged
options.misconception: treats the freedom of the opening balance from misstatement as the whole of SA 510
options.why: That is one of the two objectives. The second is about the accounting policies those opening balances reflect, and an untested policy change can misstate this year's figures even where last year's closing number was right.

citation.ref: para 6

items.scenario: This is your first year as auditor of a trading company. The previous year's auditor valued inventory on a weighted average basis; this year the company has moved to first-in first-out and calls the change an improvement. You have satisfied yourself that the opening inventory figure itself contains no misstatement.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 510 point to?

options.text: A qualified or adverse opinion, opening inventory at 22 per cent of total assets being material to the current period's financial statements
options.misconception: applies the misstatement pair of opinions to a case that is an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: Qualified or adverse is the answer where the opening balances contain a misstatement that is not properly dealt with. Nothing here says the figure is wrong; what is absent is the evidence, and absent evidence produces a qualification or a disclaimer.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph recording that the prior period was not audited
options.misconception: uses an Other Matter paragraph to carry an inability to obtain audit evidence
options.why: A paragraph recording that fact tells the reader who audited the comparatives and nothing more. It supplies no evidence about a balance that flows into this year's cost of sales, and a paragraph never carries a modification.

options.text: An unmodified opinion, provided the notes disclose that the comparative figures are unaudited
options.misconception: treats a disclosure by the entity as curing the auditor's own inability to obtain evidence
options.why: A disclosure by the entity is not audit evidence, and the difficulty is not with the comparatives as such. The opening balances feed this year's figures, so the auditor's inability to obtain evidence about them is answered in his opinion rather than in the company's notes.

options.text: A qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, as appropriate, this being an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances
options.why: SA 510 separates the two ways an opening balance damages the current opinion, and this is the first of them. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, he expresses a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, as appropriate, under SA 705 (Revised). The qualified-or-adverse pair belongs to the other case, where an opening balance contains a misstatement that materially affects the current period and the effect is not properly accounted for or adequately presented or disclosed.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances
qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion

citation.ref: para 10, read against para 11

items.scenario: You are appointed for the first time to audit a company whose previous year was audited by nobody, the company having been below the threshold then. Opening inventory is 22 per cent of total assets. The records of the previous count are missing, the goods are perishable and the population has turned over several times, so no roll-back from the current count is possible. Nothing suggests the figure is wrong; you simply cannot obtain evidence about it.

items.stem: What follows in each case?

options.text: Neither — in each case the answer is to have the sentence about arm's length terms taken out of the notes
options.misconception: answers a problem with a disclosure by removing the disclosure, dropping a requirement of the framework in the process
options.why: Deleting the sentence would remove a disclosure the applicable financial reporting framework requires where the assertion is made, and would leave the reader knowing less than before. The auditor obtains evidence about the assertion and then reports what his work found.

options.text: Both are inabilities to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, neither company having supported the assertion it made
options.misconception: files a contradicted assertion as missing evidence, when the evidence exists and disproves it
options.why: The first file is not empty. It holds evidence, and that evidence points the other way. Evidence contradicting an assertion is a finding about the disclosure rather than an absence of evidence about it, and treating it as unaudited would leave a disclosure the auditor has disproved standing in the notes.

options.text: In the first the assertion is misstated and is dealt with as any other misstatement; in the second there is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about a disclosure the framework requires, with the consequences SA 705 (Revised) attaches
options.why: SA 550 requires the auditor to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about an assertion that a related party transaction was conducted on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, and that work can end in two different places. Where the audit evidence contradicts the assertion, the disclosure is wrong and it is a misstatement, accumulated and evaluated like any other. Where there is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about an assertion the framework requires to be disclosed, SA 705 (Revised) decides what the opinion says.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction

options.text: Both are misstatements, because an assertion the auditor cannot support is an assertion that should never have been made
options.misconception: converts an inability to obtain evidence into a misstatement, which asserts more than the auditor knows
options.why: Unsupported and disproved are not the same thing. Where nothing can be obtained about an assertion the framework requires to be disclosed, what the auditor has is an inability to obtain evidence, and SA 705 (Revised) is where that is answered.

citation.ref: para 24, read with SA 705 (Revised)

items.scenario: Two companies in the same group each pay a ₹40 crore management fee to the parent, and the notes of each state that the fee was on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, which the applicable financial reporting framework requires to be disclosed where the assertion is made. In the first company your work produces market data showing that unrelated providers charge a third of that fee for the same services. In the second you can find no comparable at all, and management's process for supporting the assertion produces nothing you can test.

items.stem: What must the practitioner do before agreeing to accept the engagement?

options.text: Begin the work and raise each of these matters in the report, acceptance turning on the engagement letter alone and every one of them being describable as a limitation
options.misconception: converts a set of pre-acceptance determinations into matters to be disclosed in the report
options.why: The standard makes them acceptance matters, which means they decide whether there is an engagement at all. A practitioner who cannot obtain a sufficient understanding of the acquiree cannot perform the procedures, and describing that in a report he was never in a position to write answers nothing.

options.text: Accept, provided the modified opinion on the sources is quoted in full in his own report, which puts the reader in the same position as the practitioner
options.misconception: answers a question about what the law permits by doing the very thing whose permissibility is in doubt
options.why: The question put by the standard is one of permission: does the applicable statute or rulebook let him lean on sources carrying a modified audit opinion at all, and let him point his own readers at that modification? Whether he may quote it is the question, and quoting it assumes the answer.

options.text: Accept on the footing that a prospectus is a statutory document, so the responsible party's acknowledgement of its responsibilities is implied by law and need not be obtained
options.misconception: treats the statutory character of the document as substituting for an acknowledgement the standard requires the practitioner to obtain
options.why: The standard requires the practitioner to obtain the responsible party's agreement acknowledging and understanding its responsibility for describing the applicable criteria to the intended users where these are not publicly available, for compiling the information on the basis of those criteria, and for giving him access to all relevant information, to any additional information he requests, and to the people from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. Nothing about a prospectus supplies that agreement.

options.text: Work through the acceptance matters — his capabilities and competence; that the applicable criteria are suitable and it is unlikely the information will be misleading for the purpose intended; that he will likely be able to express the prescribed opinion; whether law or regulation permits use of, or reference to, the modified opinion on the sources; whether he can obtain a sufficient understanding of the never-audited acquiree; and obtain the responsible party's acknowledgement of its responsibilities
options.why: SAE 3420 puts a defined list before acceptance rather than after it. The practitioner determines that he has the capabilities and competence to perform the engagement; on a preliminary knowledge of the circumstances and discussion with the responsible party, that the applicable criteria are suitable and that the compiled information is unlikely to be misleading for the purpose for which it is intended; and, where the wording is prescribed by law or regulation, that he will likely be able to express the opinion so prescribed on the basis of the procedures this standard specifies. Where the sources carry a modified audit opinion he considers whether the relevant law or regulation permits their use or a reference to them in his report; where an acquiree's historical financial information has never been audited or reviewed he asks whether enough can be learned about that acquiree — how it keeps its accounts and how it reports them. And he obtains the responsible party's agreement acknowledging its responsibilities, which cannot wait for a draft.
keywords: capabilities and competence to perform the engagement
misleading for the purpose for which it is intended

citation.ref: the matters the practitioner settles before he agrees to take the engagement on, including the responsible party's acknowledgement of its responsibilities

items.scenario: A practitioner is asked to report on whether pro forma financial information in a prospectus has been compiled on the basis of the applicable criteria. The transaction is the acquisition of a family-owned target whose historical financial information has never been audited or reviewed. The issuer's own unadjusted financial information is extracted from statements carrying a modified audit opinion. The regulator prescribes the exact wording of the practitioner's opinion. The responsible party says it will discuss its own responsibilities "once the report is drafted".

items.stem: What does SA 540 (Revised) require of you?

options.text: Accept the ₹185 crore, since it falls inside a range the company's own expert produced and any figure inside an expert's range is by definition reasonable
options.misconception: treats a number sitting inside somebody's range as proof that management addressed the estimation uncertainty, when the choice of where to sit inside it is the whole question
options.why: A range is the measure of the estimation uncertainty, not an answer to it. Management chose a point near one end and recorded no reasoning for that choice, which is exactly the gap the standard fills by having the auditor build his own range.

options.text: Compute your own single best figure, substitute it for management's, and treat the whole difference as a misstatement to be corrected
options.misconception: replaces management's estimate with the auditor's own point figure, when the standard has him develop a range to test reasonableness rather than to supplant the estimate
options.why: The auditor evaluates the reasonableness of management's estimate; he does not make the estimate. Where his range and management's figure do not overlap there is a misstatement to discuss, but a single auditor's figure imposed on the accounts turns the reviewer into the preparer.

options.text: Qualify the opinion at once for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, an outcome spread of that width not being auditable
options.misconception: converts high estimation uncertainty into a scope limitation before performing the procedures the standard prescribes for exactly that situation
options.why: High estimation uncertainty is the condition SA 540 was written for, not a reason to stop. The standard supplies the response — the auditor's own range, tests of the data and assumptions, and evidence from events up to the report date — and a modification is considered only after those have been performed and have failed.

options.text: Develop a range with which to evaluate the reasonableness of the estimate, management not having adequately addressed the effects of the estimation uncertainty on an estimate giving rise to a significant risk; and, among your responses, test what happened between the year end and the signing of your report for what it says about the provision
options.why: Where management has not adequately addressed the effects of estimation uncertainty on an accounting estimate that gives rise to a significant risk, the auditor shall develop a range with which to evaluate the reasonableness of the estimate. The responses to the assessed risk also include testing the data used, evaluating whether the method of measurement is appropriate and the assumptions reasonable, and asking what the provision looked like by the time the report was signed — events occurring up to the date of the auditor's report can settle it, an actual tender or settlement after the year end being worth more than a debate about the model.
keywords: events occurring up to the date of the auditor's report

citation.ref: the responses to the assessed risks of material misstatement for an accounting estimate, and the auditor's range where management has not adequately addressed the effects of estimation uncertainty on an estimate giving rise to a significant risk

items.scenario: A company carries a decommissioning provision for an offshore platform. Its own consultant gave a range of plausible outcomes running from ₹180 crore to ₹520 crore, and management has booked ₹185 crore, near the bottom of that range. The file records no assessment by management of the effect of the estimation uncertainty on the amount chosen, and you have assessed the provision as an estimate giving rise to a significant risk.

items.stem: What does SA 560 require of you now?

options.text: Issue a new auditor's report with an Other Matter paragraph describing the fact, a fresh report being the only lever the auditor has once the statements are out
options.misconception: reports afresh on financial statements management has not amended, when the amendment is the condition on which a new report is issued at all
options.why: The new or amended report with its Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph belongs to the case where management does amend. Reporting again on unamended statements would put a second report on the same wrong numbers and leave the members no better off.

options.text: Resign as auditor and say nothing further, the duty of confidentiality barring any step that reaches the members directly
options.misconception: uses confidentiality to bar the step the standard names, and treats resignation as a substitute for it
options.why: The standard directs the auditor to seek to prevent future reliance on his own report, which is his document and his name. Resigning leaves the report standing and the members relying on it, which is the outcome the requirement exists to prevent.

options.text: Nothing further — after the financial statements have been issued the auditor has no obligation to perform any audit procedures on them, and management's refusal ends the matter
options.misconception: reads the end of the duty to search as the end of the duty once a fact has arrived and management has refused to act on it
options.why: The sentence removing the obligation removes the duty to go looking. It says nothing about what happens once a fact has reached the auditor, and the requirement that follows it is written for precisely the refusal described here.

options.text: Notify management and those charged with governance that you will seek to prevent future reliance on the auditor's report, and if they still do not act, take appropriate action to seek to prevent that reliance
options.why: Where management does not take the steps needed to ensure that everyone in receipt of the previously issued financial statements is informed, and does not amend them when the auditor requires it, the auditor shall notify management and those charged with governance that he will seek to prevent future reliance on the auditor's report. If they still do not act, he takes appropriate action to seek to prevent that reliance. The discussion, the determination whether amendment is needed and the inquiry into management's intentions have already happened here; this is the step after them.
keywords: notify management and those charged with governance

citation.ref: the auditor's action where management neither amends the previously issued financial statements nor informs those who received them

items.scenario: The financial statements and your report went to members on 12 August and were laid before the annual general meeting. On 5 October a fact reaches you that, had you known it at the date of your report, would have caused you to modify your opinion. You discuss it with management and with those charged with governance and ask how they intend to address it. They decline to amend the financial statements and decline to inform anyone who already holds them.

items.stem: What does SA 610 (Revised) still require before that work is used?

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the head of internal audit that the counts were properly performed, and place it on file instead of the evaluation
options.misconception: substitutes a representation from the party whose work is being judged for the external auditor's own evaluation of that work
options.why: A representation from the function is not evidence about the quality of the function's work, and a written representation is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own. The standard asks the external auditor to read the reports, evaluate the work and perform his own procedures on it.

options.text: Re-perform every procedure the function carried out at all nine depots, since responsibility for the opinion is the external auditor's alone
options.misconception: turns a sample of reperformance into a duplicate audit, which would make using the work pointless and is not what the standard asks for
options.why: Sole responsibility for the opinion is real and it does not mean doing the work twice. The requirement is to perform sufficient audit procedures on the body of work as a whole, reperformance included, so that the external auditor can judge the work — not to repeat all of it, which would leave nothing for the function's work to contribute.

options.text: Nothing more — the three conditions have been met, so the function's work may be taken as it stands
options.misconception: treats the gate on the function as a gate on every file the function produces, when the two are separate evaluations
options.why: The first evaluation is about the function; the second is about the work. A competent and objective function applying a disciplined approach can still produce a file that was under-supervised or that reaches a conclusion its own evidence does not support, and the standard asks the external auditor to look.

options.text: Read the function's reports on the work being used and evaluate whether that work was properly planned, performed, supervised, reviewed and documented, whether sufficient appropriate audit evidence was obtained and whether the conclusions reached are appropriate; perform audit procedures on the body of that work as a whole, including reperformance; and communicate to those charged with governance how the use of the function's work has been planned
options.why: Passing the three conditions decides that the function's work may be used at all. Before any particular body of work is used the external auditor reads the relevant reports and evaluates whether the work was properly planned, performed, supervised, reviewed and documented, whether sufficient appropriate audit evidence was obtained to support the conclusions, and whether those conclusions are appropriate; and he performs audit procedures on that body of work as a whole, including reperformance of some of it. He also communicates the planned use to those charged with governance, so the people who oversee the audit know what rests on the function.
keywords: properly planned, performed, supervised, reviewed and documented

citation.ref: the evaluation of the internal audit function's work before it is used, the audit procedures on the body of work as a whole including reperformance, and the communication to those charged with governance of the planned use of that work

items.scenario: You have evaluated the internal audit function on all three counts the Standard names — where it is placed in the reporting line and the rules it works to, its level of competence, and whether it applies a systematic and disciplined approach — and all three are satisfactory. The team now plans to take the function's inventory count files for nine depots straight into the audit file, having read the one-page dashboard the function circulates to the audit committee, and to tell nobody outside the team that it has done so.

items.stem: What does SA 710 require in your report on the current period?

options.text: Withdraw last year's auditor's report and issue a fresh report on last year's financial statements
options.misconception: reopens a completed engagement instead of dealing with the corresponding figures in the report the auditor is about to sign
options.why: SA 710 deals with the misstatement where it now sits, in the corresponding figures of the current period's financial statements. Reissuing a prior year report is the machinery of SA 560 for facts known after that report was issued, and it is not what this requirement directs.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph describing the prior year error, the opinion itself being left unmodified
options.misconception: answers a misstatement with a paragraph that carries no opinion, when the standard answers this one inside the opinion
options.why: An Other Matter paragraph communicates a matter relevant to users' understanding of the audit or the report. It does not cure figures that are wrong. Where the misstatement has not been dealt with under the framework, the standard calls for a modified opinion.

options.text: Verify whether the misstatement has been dealt with as required by the applicable financial reporting framework and, since it has not, express a qualified or an adverse opinion on the current period's financial statements, in respect of the corresponding figures
options.why: The rule that the opinion does not refer to the corresponding figures carries exceptions, and this is one of them. Where the auditor obtains evidence that a material misstatement exists in prior period financial statements on which an unmodified opinion was previously issued, he verifies whether the misstatement has been dealt with as required under the applicable financial reporting framework and, if it has not, expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion on the current period's financial statements, modified in respect of the corresponding figures included in them.

options.text: Nothing in the opinion — where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures the opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to them
options.misconception: reads the general rule as absolute, when SA 710 sets out the exceptions in which the current opinion does reach the corresponding figures
options.why: That rule is the starting point and it has named exceptions. One is a prior modification still unresolved; the other is this one, a material misstatement discovered in a prior period that carried an unmodified opinion. The corresponding figures sit inside this year's financial statements, so a misstatement left in them is a misstatement in the statements you are reporting on.

citation.ref: the exceptions to the rule that the auditor's opinion does not refer to the corresponding figures, where a material misstatement exists in prior period financial statements on which an unmodified opinion was issued

items.scenario: You audited this company last year and issued an unmodified opinion. During this year's audit you obtain evidence that last year's closing inventory was overstated by ₹31 crore, an amount material to last year. The comparatives are presented as corresponding figures. Management has left the corresponding figures exactly as they were reported and has made no restatement or disclosure of the error anywhere in this year's financial statements.

items.stem: What must the Other Matter paragraph in your report state?

options.text: That the corresponding figures are unaudited
options.misconception: uses the paragraph written for figures nobody audited on figures a predecessor auditor did audit and did report on
options.why: That statement belongs to the different case where the prior period financial statements were not audited at all. Saying it here would be untrue, and it would also drop the predecessor's opinion out of sight.

options.text: That the corresponding figures were audited by the predecessor auditor, the type of opinion the predecessor expressed and, if that opinion was modified, the reasons for the modification, and the date of that report
options.why: SA 710 names three things for the Other Matter paragraph in exactly this situation — that the corresponding figures were audited by the predecessor auditor, the type of opinion he expressed together with the reasons for any modification, and the date of that report. A reader then knows who stood behind last year's figures, what he concluded and as at when.

options.text: Only that a change of auditor took place during the year and the name of the outgoing firm
options.misconception: names the person and omits the two facts a reader actually needs, being what the predecessor concluded and the date on which he concluded it
options.why: The identity of the predecessor is one of three elements. Without the type of opinion and the date of the report a reader cannot tell whether the corresponding figures were reported on cleanly, or as at what point in time.

options.text: Nothing — where the prior period was audited by another firm the incoming auditor says nothing about it, the opinion covering the current period only
options.misconception: reads the rule that the opinion does not refer to the corresponding figures as removing every reporting obligation about them
options.why: Not referring to the corresponding figures in the opinion is one thing; the Other Matter paragraph is another, and SA 710 requires it in the situations where a reader would otherwise not know who audited the comparatives or what he found.

citation.ref: the Other Matter paragraph where the prior period financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor

items.scenario: This is your first year as auditor of a company. The prior period's financial statements were audited by the outgoing auditor, whose report was unmodified and was dated 12 July 2025. The comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, and nothing in law or regulation prohibits you from referring to the predecessor's report.

items.stem: Is the manager right?

options.text: No, and the section should state that the auditor has audited the other information and found it consistent with the financial statements
options.misconception: converts a section whose whole purpose is to say that no opinion is given into one that gives a clean opinion
options.why: The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it. The section says so in terms, and a sentence claiming an audit of it would contradict the statement immediately above.

options.text: No — for an unlisted entity the section is included where the auditor has obtained some or all of the other information at the date of his report, and where nothing is wrong it carries a statement that the auditor has nothing to report
options.why: The Other Information section is triggered by the other information having been obtained, not by a finding. For an unlisted entity it is included where the auditor has obtained some or all of the other information at the date of his report. It identifies what was obtained, says that management is responsible for it, states that the auditor's opinion does not cover it and that no opinion or conclusion is expressed on it, describes his responsibilities for reading and considering it, and then either says he has nothing to report or describes the uncorrected material misstatement.

options.text: He is wrong about unlisted entities but right about listed ones, where the section covers only other information actually obtained before the date of the report
options.misconception: drops the half of the listed-entity trigger that reaches other information the auditor expects to obtain after the date of his report
options.why: For a listed entity the section is included where the auditor has obtained, or expects to obtain, other information, and it identifies both the other information obtained before the date of the report and that expected after it. Leaving out what is expected would hide the part of the annual report that is usually typeset last.

options.text: Yes — the section is there to describe an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information, so with nothing to describe it is omitted
options.misconception: makes the section conditional on a finding, when it is conditional on other information having been obtained or, for a listed entity, expected
options.why: The section tells the reader what the auditor did with the other information and, just as importantly, what he did not do with it. A reader who sees no such section cannot tell whether the auditor read the directors' report or never saw it.

citation.ref: the Other Information section of the auditor's report — when it is included for a listed and for an unlisted entity, and what it contains

items.scenario: You are signing the report of an unlisted company. Before the date of your report you obtained the directors' report and the management discussion and analysis, read both, and found no material inconsistency and nothing else materially misstated. The manager proposes to leave the Other Information section out of the report altogether, saying that the section exists to describe a problem and there is no problem, and that in any event it is a listed company requirement.

items.stem: What does SA 800 require of the auditor here?

options.text: Qualify the opinion for the ambiguity, since a reader cannot tell which reading produced the revenue figure
options.misconception: modifies the opinion before performing the step the standard requires first, which is to obtain the understanding of the interpretation management adopted
options.why: The understanding comes first. It may show that management's reading is the one the contract bears, or that the interpretation adopted needs disclosing. A modification is what happens after that work, not instead of it.

options.text: Nothing — the contract is the framework, and interpreting a contract is a question of law for the parties rather than a matter for the auditor
options.misconception: treats the framework's own ambiguity as somebody else's problem, when the framework is the measure against which the opinion is given
options.why: The opinion says whether the statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the framework. Where the framework itself can be read two ways and the readings differ materially, the auditor cannot form that opinion without understanding which reading management took and why.

options.text: Refuse the engagement, a framework capable of two reasonable readings not being an acceptable financial reporting framework
options.misconception: rejects a contractual framework outright, when the standard provides for one and asks instead about its attributes and about management's interpretations of it
options.why: Financial reporting provisions of a contract are one of the standard's own examples of a special purpose framework. Ambiguity in a clause is dealt with by understanding and, where needed, by disclosure of the interpretation adopted — not by declining the work.

options.text: Obtain an understanding of the significant interpretations of the contract that management made in preparing the financial statements — an interpretation being significant where the adoption of another reasonable interpretation would have produced a material difference in the information presented — a contractual framework being acceptable only where it exhibits the attributes normally exhibited by an acceptable financial reporting framework
options.why: Where financial statements are prepared under the provisions of a contract, SA 800 has the auditor obtain an understanding of any significant interpretations of the contract that management made. An interpretation is significant where the adoption of another reasonable interpretation would have produced a material difference in the information presented in the financial statements, which is exactly what the second reading does here. At acceptance the question is whether the framework the contract sets up exhibits the attributes normally exhibited by an acceptable financial reporting framework — a framework laid down by an authorised body or prescribed by law is presumed acceptable, but a contract is not.

citation.ref: acceptability of the financial reporting framework, and the significant interpretations of a contract where the financial statements are prepared under the financial reporting provisions of that contract

items.scenario: A concession agreement requires the operator to deliver audited financial statements prepared under the accounting clauses of that agreement. One clause defines the revenue the operator may recognise in language that bears two readings. Management has adopted one of them; on the other, equally reasonable, reading, revenue for the year would be ₹64 crore lower on a stated top line of ₹300 crore.

items.stem: What does SA 805 require?

options.text: Nothing — both opinions are unmodified, so no reader is worse off for the two sitting side by side
options.misconception: treats presentation as cosmetic, when the risk being guarded against is a reader taking a report on one element as a report on the whole
options.why: The hazard is not the content of either opinion but the confusion between them. A reader who takes a clean opinion on a receivables schedule for a clean opinion on the financial statements has been misled by the layout alone.

options.text: Combine the two engagements into one auditor's report carrying one opinion covering the financial statements and the schedule together
options.misconception: merges two engagements the standard deliberately keeps apart, each with its own scope, its own materiality and its own opinion
options.why: The two are separate engagements. Materiality determined for a specific element may be lower than for the complete set, and the procedures differ accordingly, so one combined opinion would describe neither engagement accurately.

options.text: Ask management to rectify the presentation, because the audited specific element is being published together with the complete set and the presentation does not sufficiently differentiate it from them, and do not issue the report on the specific element until you are satisfied with the differentiation; a separate opinion is expressed for each engagement
options.why: Where an audited single financial statement or specific element is published together with the entity's complete set of financial statements and the presentation does not sufficiently differentiate the one from the other, the auditor asks management to rectify the situation, and his report carrying the opinion on that specific element is withheld until the differentiation satisfies him. Where the same auditor does both, he expresses a separate opinion for each engagement.

options.text: Add an Other Matter paragraph to the report on the complete set cross-referring to the report on the schedule
options.misconception: answers a presentation problem with a paragraph, leaving the presentation that caused it unchanged
options.why: A cross-reference does not separate two documents a reader sees as one. The standard's answer is to have the presentation itself put right before the report on the element is released.

citation.ref: publication of an audited single financial statement or specific element together with the complete set of financial statements, and the separate opinion for each engagement

items.scenario: You audited a company's complete set of financial statements and issued an unmodified opinion. You were separately engaged to audit its schedule of trade receivables, and that work is also complete and clean. The company now proposes to print your report on the schedule immediately after the financial statements in the same annual report, under the same running heads and with continuous page numbering, so that the schedule reads as one further statement in the set.

items.stem: What does SA 810 require your report on the summary financial statements to say?

options.text: That the audited statements were reported on with a disclaimer of opinion, describing the basis on which that disclaimer was given, and that the disclaimer makes any opinion on the summary set inappropriate
options.why: A modification on the source set governs what may be said about anything derived from it. Because your earlier report carried a disclaimer of opinion, this one names that fact, describes the basis the earlier report gave for it, and then says that it is in consequence inappropriate to express an opinion on the summary financial statements at all. A summary cannot be sounder than what it summarises, however faithfully it reproduces it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion that the summary set is consistent, in all material respects, with the statements you audited, judged against the criteria the company applied
options.misconception: applies the ordinary consistency test to a source on which no opinion was expressed, so a faithful summary of unaudited numbers would carry a clean opinion
options.why: Consistency with the audited financial statements is the ordinary form of the opinion, and it presupposes an opinion on those statements. Where the auditor disclaimed one, a statement that the summary is consistent with them would tell a reader far more than the audit supports.

options.text: The disclaimer itself should be repeated as the opinion on the summary financial statements
options.misconception: expresses a disclaimer on the summary, when the standard has the auditor say that expressing any opinion on it is inappropriate
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion on the summary would suggest the auditor was unable to obtain evidence about the summary. The problem lies with the source, and the standard's wording says exactly that.

options.text: The engagement must be refused outright, no report of any kind being possible where the source carried a disclaimer
options.misconception: treats a report the standard actually prescribes as an engagement that cannot be accepted at all
options.why: The standard does not close the engagement; it fixes what the report says. The report is issued, it states the disclaimer and its basis, and it says that expressing an opinion on the summary is inappropriate — which is a good deal more informative to a reader than silence.

citation.ref: what the report on summary financial statements must say where the source set was reported on adversely or with a disclaimer

items.scenario: You audited a company's financial statements and disclaimed an opinion on them, having been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about a large intangible asset. The company now asks you to report on a summary set derived from those same financial statements. It points out that you were the auditor of the source statements, that the criteria applied are disclosed, and that the summary agrees line for line with what you audited.

items.stem: Is there any route other than the additional date?

options.text: Yes — the auditor may instead provide a new or amended auditor's report that includes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph or an Other Matter paragraph stating that his procedures on subsequent events are restricted solely to the amendment of the financial statements as described in the relevant note
options.why: Where law, regulation or the financial reporting framework does not prohibit management from restricting the amendment to the effects of the subsequent event, and those responsible for approving the statements are not prohibited from restricting their approval to that amendment, the auditor is permitted to restrict his subsequent-event procedures to the amendment. He may then either amend the report to include an additional date restricted to that amendment, or provide a new or amended report containing an Emphasis of Matter paragraph or an Other Matter paragraph saying that his procedures on subsequent events are restricted solely to that amendment. Both routes rest on the same permission.
keywords: Emphasis of Matter paragraph or an Other Matter paragraph

options.text: No — the additional date is the only mechanism the standard provides for restricting the procedures to the amendment
options.misconception: keeps one of the two routes the standard offers and treats the other as unavailable
options.why: The standard offers a choice of two forms for the same restriction, and the paragraph route exists precisely for an auditor who does not want a second date on the report. What cannot be done is to restrict the procedures without saying so in one form or the other.

options.text: Yes — leave the report dated 20 May and say nothing, the amendment being management's own act
options.misconception: leaves a report dated before an amendment it does not mention, so the report on file does not match the statements it accompanies
options.why: The amended financial statements need a report that addresses them. A report predating the amendment and silent about it would be a report on a different set of statements from the one the members receive.

options.text: Yes — simply re-date the whole report to 4 June, which avoids two dates and needs no additional wording
options.misconception: takes a later date without the work a later date carries, which is subsequent-event procedures up to that date
options.why: Re-dating the report to 4 June extends the auditor's responsibility for subsequent events to 4 June and requires procedures up to that day.
