The restricted routes exist so that he may avoid that, and choosing the new date without the work would claim a responsibility he has not discharged.

citation.ref: the two routes where management restricts the amendment to the effects of a subsequent event — the additional date, and the Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph

items.scenario: Your report on the 31 March financial statements is dated 20 May. On 4 June, before the statements are issued, a major debtor is declared insolvent. Management amends the financial statements for that event alone and describes it in a note. Neither law nor the financial reporting framework prohibits management from restricting the amendment to that event, and those approving the statements are not prohibited from restricting their approval to the amendment. The engagement partner does not want two dates printed under his signature.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require?

options.text: Express an adverse conclusion, a refusal of access on that scale meaning the financial statements do not give a true and fair view
options.misconception: uses the misstatement half of the modification grid to answer a problem sitting on the evidence half
options.why: An adverse conclusion says the financial statements are wrong. Nothing here says that; what has happened is that the practitioner has not been allowed to find out. Inability to obtain evidence leads to a qualified conclusion or a disclaimer, not to an adverse one.

options.text: Where the practitioner is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence he expresses a qualified conclusion if the possible effects could be material but not pervasive, and disclaims a conclusion if they could be both material and pervasive; and where management imposed the limitation after acceptance such that he believes he may need to disclaim, and the engagement is not required by law or regulation, he withdraws where practicable and possible
options.why: Modification in a review follows two tracks. Where the financial statements are materially misstated the conclusion is qualified or adverse. Where the practitioner is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence he expresses a qualified conclusion if the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be material but not pervasive, and disclaims a conclusion if they could be both material and pervasive. A limitation imposed by management after acceptance adds a further step — where he believes he may need to disclaim a conclusion because of it, and the engagement is not required by law or regulation, he withdraws from the engagement where withdrawal is practicable and possible.

options.text: Issue the unmodified conclusion — a review gives only limited assurance, so restricted access is already contemplated by the level of assurance
options.misconception: treats limited assurance as a licence to conclude on whatever evidence happens to be available
options.why: Limited assurance describes the level of the conclusion, not the amount of evidence needed to reach it. The practitioner must still obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for the conclusion he gives, and where he cannot, the conclusion is modified or withdrawn from.

options.text: Convert the engagement into an audit, so that access to the branch records can be insisted on as a matter of right
options.misconception: answers a scope limitation by changing the level of assurance, which is a change in the terms of the engagement and not a response to the limitation
options.why: Changing a review into an audit changes what was agreed with the client and needs its own justification and a new agreement. It would also give management, which has just restricted access, the choice of whether the change happens at all.

citation.ref: the modified conclusions where the practitioner is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, and the withdrawal where management imposes a limitation after acceptance

items.scenario: You accepted an engagement to review a company's half-yearly financial statements. It is not required by any law or regulation; the company asked for it to satisfy a lender. After acceptance, management refuses you access to the records of four branches that between them carry a large part of revenue, and offers no alternative. You conclude that the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive.

items.stem: May those two sentences be deleted?

options.text: Yes to the first and no to the second — a report can hardly speculate about findings from procedures nobody performed
options.misconception: reads a statement about the limits of the procedures as speculation about what an audit would have found
options.why: The sentence makes no claim about what other work would have shown. It says that the procedures were the agreed ones and that others were not performed, which is why the reader draws his own conclusions rather than relying on an opinion.

options.text: Yes — both say in a longer way that no assurance is expressed, and the report states that once already
options.misconception: treats two statements about the limits of the work as a repetition of the statement about the level of assurance
options.why: Saying that no assurance is expressed tells the reader what the conclusion is worth. These two tell him what was and was not looked at, which is a different thing and the thing a reader of a seven-procedure report most needs.

options.text: No, but they belong in the engagement letter rather than in the report, where the parties agreed the scope in the first place
options.misconception: moves statements the report is required to carry into a document only the engaging parties hold
options.why: The engagement letter also records the procedures and the restriction on distribution, and it does not travel with the report. The statements are required in the report itself, where whoever reads the findings will see them.

options.text: No — both are elements the report of factual findings is required to contain
options.why: SRS 4400 lists what the report of factual findings contains, and both sentences are on the list. The first tells the reader what a narrow engagement cannot show: had additional procedures been carried out, or a full audit, other matters might have come to light and would then have been reported to him. The second fences the work in — the report speaks only to the elements listed in it and does not extend to the company's financial statements as a whole. Between them they stop a reader treating a set of seven procedures as an examination of the company.
keywords: other matters might have come to light

citation.ref: the elements of the report of factual findings — the statement that additional procedures, an audit or a review might have brought other matters to light, and the statement that the report relates only to the elements specified

items.scenario: You have drafted the report of factual findings on seven procedures agreed with a bank and its borrower. It lists each procedure and what it showed. The engagement partner wants two sentences struck out as boilerplate — one saying that further work, or a full audit or a review, might have brought other matters to light that would then have been reported; the other saying that the report speaks only to the elements listed in it and reaches nothing about the company's financial statements as a whole.

items.stem: What is the position under SAE 3400?

options.text: The Standard is not engaged at all where the forward-looking information is put in general or narrative terms, a management discussion and analysis page being exactly that; where it is engaged, the work need not fall to the statutory auditor of the financial statements, and the assurance it conveys is moderate
options.why: An outlook page written in words sits outside SAE 3400 altogether: the Standard passes over forward-looking information put in general or narrative terms, and the study material's own example of that is management discussion and analysis in an annual report. Where it does bite, the work is not reserved to the statutory auditor of the financial statements, and the assurance is moderate — a negative assurance statement on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, with an opinion on preparation and presentation.

options.text: The Standard applies to any forward-looking statement in an annual report, and only the statutory auditor of the financial statements may perform the engagement
options.misconception: stretches the Standard over any words about the future and reserves the work to the statutory auditor, neither of which it does
options.why: Two separate errors. The scope is prospective financial information, not narrative outlook, and the Standard says so; and the examination is not reserved to the statutory auditor, who may or may not be the person engaged.

options.text: The Standard applies and would give reasonable assurance on the narrative, that being the highest level available for an assurance engagement
options.misconception: keeps a subject matter the Standard excludes and raises the level of assurance above the one it provides
options.why: The level of assurance under this Standard is moderate, not reasonable, because the evidence about future events is itself future-oriented and speculative. And a narrative outlook is outside its scope in any case.

options.text: No standard reaches any forward-looking information, so the firm may design and word the engagement as it wishes
options.misconception: reads one scope exclusion as an absence of any standard governing prospective financial information
options.why: The exclusion is narrow — information in general or narrative terms. Prospective financial information itself is squarely within SAE 3400, which sets the acceptance considerations, the examination procedures and the form of the report.

citation.ref: the scope of the Standard, which does not extend to prospective financial information expressed in general or narrative terms, and the moderate level of assurance provided

items.scenario: A company asks your firm to examine, under SAE 3400, the outlook section of its annual report — a page of management discussion and analysis in words, with no figures and no schedules. The company adds that the work must be done by its statutory auditor and that it wants the highest level of assurance available.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require on presentation and disclosure?

options.text: Neither is required so long as the arithmetic on the stated assumptions is correct and the assumptions themselves are listed
options.misconception: reduces presentation and disclosure to arithmetic, when the Standard sets out a list of disclosures the auditor assesses in addition
options.why: Correct arithmetic on the assumptions is what the opinion on proper preparation covers. The separate assessment is whether the presentation is informative and not misleading, and a forecast with no preparation date and an unannounced change of policy is neither.

options.text: The date is required, but the policy is not — a forecast is free to adopt whatever accounting policy management thinks best represents the future
options.misconception: lets the forecast float free of the historical financial statements it will inevitably be compared against
options.why: A reader compares a forecast with the last set of historical figures. Where the policy has moved between them, the reason for the change and its effect on the prospective financial information must be disclosed, or the comparison misleads without either document being wrong on its own.

options.text: The notes must give the date as of which the forecast was drawn up, with management confirming the assumptions are appropriate as of that date even where the inputs behind them were accumulated over a period of time spanning months; and a change of accounting policy away from the one shown in the latest historical statements must be disclosed too, with the reason for the change and what it does to the forecast
options.why: Both sit on the Standard's own checklist for presentation and disclosure. The notes must give the date as of which the forecast was drawn up, and management must confirm the assumptions are appropriate as of that date even where the inputs behind them were accumulated over a period of time spanning months — otherwise a reader cannot tell how stale those inputs are. A change of accounting policy away from the one shown in the latest historical statements is disclosed too, with the reason for the change and what it does to the forecast, because a forecast is read against the history it grew out of.
keywords: accumulated over a period of time

options.text: Both are matters for the date of the auditor's report on the forecast rather than for the notes to the prospective financial information
options.misconception: moves an entity disclosure into the auditor's report, where a reader of the notes alone would never find it
options.why: The date of the auditor's report says when his work finished. The date as of which the information was prepared, and the change in accounting policy, are disclosures in the notes to the prospective financial information, made by the entity that prepared it.

citation.ref: the assessment of presentation and disclosure — the date as of which the prospective financial information was prepared and management's confirmation of the assumptions as of that date, and the disclosure of a change in accounting policy from the most recent historical financial statements

items.scenario: A forecast you are examining carries its assumptions and its accounting policies in the notes. Two things are missing. The notes nowhere say as of what date the forecast was prepared, although the underlying information was accumulated over four months. And the company has moved to a different revenue recognition policy from the one disclosed in its most recent historical financial statements, with no mention of the change or of what it does to the forecast.

items.stem: What is the position under SAE 3402?

options.text: Without the service organisation's written assertion — that the description fairly presents the system, that the controls were suitably designed and, in a type 2 report, that they operated effectively throughout the specified period — the service auditor does not accept or continue the engagement unless law or regulation requires otherwise; and he must be independent of the service organisation but is not required to be independent of the user entities
options.why: The written assertion is what the report is built on. It says that, in all material respects and on suitable criteria, the description fairly presents the service organisation's system, that the controls were suitably designed, and, in a type 2 report, that they operated effectively throughout the specified period. Where the service organisation will not provide it, the service auditor does not accept or continue the engagement unless law or regulation requires otherwise. On independence, he must be independent of the service organisation, which is the party being reported on; he is not required to be independent of the user entities.

options.text: The assertion is needed only for a type 1 report, where there is no testing of operating effectiveness to stand behind the description
options.misconception: makes the assertion a substitute for testing, when it is required for both types and covers more ground in a type 2 report
options.why: Both types of report rest on a written assertion. In a type 2 report the assertion covers more, not less: that the description is fairly presented, that the controls were suitably designed, and that they operated effectively right through the period specified.

options.text: The assertion may be replaced by a management representation letter taken at the end of the engagement
options.misconception: substitutes the closing representations for the assertion the whole report is addressed to, when the Standard requires both and they do different work
options.why: Written representations are requested as well, and they reaffirm the assertion rather than replace it. The assertion is the responsible party's public statement, which the service auditor's opinion then reports on; a letter to the auditor at the end is not that.

options.text: The assertion is optional where management cooperates fully in every other way, and independence is required of every user entity as well as of the service organisation
options.misconception: drops the one document the opinion attaches to and extends independence to fifty parties the service auditor does not report on
options.why: Cooperation is not the same as a signed statement of responsibility. And independence attaches to the party being reported on. A service auditor with fifty user entities to be independent of could not accept the engagement at all, which is not what the Standard contemplates.

citation.ref: the service organisation's written assertion and the consequence where it is not provided, and the service auditor's independence of the service organisation

items.scenario: A payroll processing organisation engages you to issue a type 2 report. Its management will prepare a description of the system and will answer whatever you ask, but declines to sign any written assertion, saying the description speaks for itself and a signature adds nothing. It also asks whether you have to be independent of the fifty user entities whose auditors will read the report.

items.stem: What does SAE 3420 actually require?

options.text: Audit the source financial statements afresh, since the practitioner cannot express any opinion resting on work another firm performed
options.misconception: turns an engagement on the compilation into a re-audit of the historical figures, which the Standard expressly says the practitioner has not performed
options.why: The opinion is on whether the pro forma financial information has been compiled on the basis of the applicable criteria. Re-auditing the source would answer a question nobody asked, and the report itself states that the practitioner has not audited or reviewed the historical financial information used.

options.text: Read nothing outside the pro forma tables and their notes, the subject matter of the engagement being the compilation alone
options.misconception: keeps the narrow subject matter and drops the requirement to read the document the information sits inside
options.why: The subject matter is narrow and the reading requirement is real. The practitioner reads the other information in the prospectus to identify material inconsistencies with the pro forma financial information, because a prospectus that contradicts its own illustration misleads whichever half the reader believes.

options.text: Obtain evidence that the source the unadjusted figures were taken out of was an appropriate one, and that the responsible party took them out of it properly — not audit it again, the practitioner being neither responsible for reissuing any report on the historical financial information used nor having audited or reviewed it — and read the other information in the prospectus to identify material inconsistencies with the pro forma financial information
options.why: The engagement is on the compilation, and the steps run from identifying the source, through extracting the unadjusted financial information from it and making the pro forma adjustments, to presenting the information with its disclosures. The practitioner obtains evidence about the appropriateness of the source and about whether the responsible party appropriately extracted the unadjusted financial information from it. His report says that he is not responsible for reissuing any report on the historical financial information used and that he has not audited or reviewed that information. He also reads the other information in the prospectus to identify any material inconsistency with the pro forma financial information.

options.text: Decline the engagement wherever there is no audit or review report on the source, no evidence about the unadjusted information being obtainable in that case
options.misconception: treats an unaudited source as a bar, when the Standard has the practitioner perform procedures to satisfy himself that the source is appropriate
options.why: Where there is no audit or review report on the source, the practitioner performs procedures to be satisfied that the source is appropriate. Whether he can obtain a sufficient understanding of the entity is a question at acceptance, not an automatic refusal.

citation.ref: the procedures on the source of the unadjusted financial information and its extraction, the statement that the practitioner is not responsible for reissuing any report on the historical financial information used, and the reading of the other information in the prospectus

items.scenario: The unadjusted financial information in a prospectus was extracted from financial statements audited by another firm. Your manager proposes two things: to audit those financial statements again himself, because an opinion cannot rest on another firm's work; and to ignore the rest of the prospectus, because the practitioner's subject matter is the pro forma tables and nothing else.

items.stem: What must the principal auditor still do?

options.text: Nothing further — a component reporting on group policies produces figures already on the group's framework, so there is nothing left to check
options.misconception: takes the absence of conversion adjustments as the absence of any question about the policies the components were told to apply
options.why: The conversion adjustments have gone; the question they answered has not. It has moved upstream to the manual, and if the manual departs from the framework the parent must report under, every component departs with it and no adjustment anywhere reveals it.

options.text: Rely on the local auditors' reports on the manual-based statements without more, the manual being the parent's own document and therefore consistent with the parent's framework by construction
options.misconception: treats a document the parent wrote as proof that it complies with the framework the parent reports under
options.why: The local auditors report on compliance with the manual, not on whether the manual itself is right. Somebody has to test the manual against the accounting principles applicable to the parent, and the guidance puts that on the principal auditor.

options.text: Perform the procedures necessary to determine that the group accounting policies set out in the group accounting manual comply with the generally accepted accounting principles applicable to the parent
options.why: A component may prepare its financial statements on the parent's accounting policies as set out in the group accounting manual instead of being converted afterwards, and the local auditor may then audit and report on statements prepared on those group accounting policies. When that route is used, the principal auditor performs the procedures necessary to determine the compliance of the group accounting policies with the generally accepted accounting principles applicable to the parent — the manual being the parent's own document and not evidence of its own correctness.

options.text: Require the conversion route in any event, the group accounting manual approach not being open where a component's local generally accepted accounting principles differ from the parent's
options.misconception: closes an alternative the guidance expressly provides, and treats a difference in local principles as ruling it out
options.why: The manual route is offered precisely for components whose local principles differ. It works by having them report on group accounting policies from the start, rather than by correcting local figures afterwards.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: component financial statements prepared on the parent's accounting policies as set out in the group accounting manual, and the principal auditor's procedures on the compliance of those policies with the parent's generally accepted accounting principles

items.scenario: Rather than convert each foreign subsidiary's audited financial statements after the event, a listed parent issues a group accounting manual and requires every component to prepare its financial statements on the accounting policies it sets out. The local auditors audit those statements and report on them. The parent's auditor plans to take the component figures into the consolidation with no further work, since no conversion adjustments now arise.

items.stem: Which requirements of the internal audit engagement has the team failed?

options.text: Only the sampling, SIA 5 being the sole Standard on Internal Audit that governs fieldwork
options.misconception: picks one Standard out of a step that names five, leaving the source of the data, the analytics, the evidence, the documentation and the review unanswered
options.why: Sampling is one of them. Analytical procedures, audit evidence, documentation and the review of work before an interim report is issued each have their own Standard, and the failure here runs across all of them.

options.text: Information must so far as possible be obtained directly from the source with checks on its correctness and integrity; analytical procedures are performed under SIA 6, samples selected under SIA 5, evidence collected and stored under SIA 320, work papers documented under SIA 330, and an interim report issued only after proper review of the work performed under SIA 350
options.why: Step three of the engagement has the internal auditor obtain the required information and perform checks to ensure its correctness and integrity, obtaining it directly from the source so far as possible — the process owner's own spreadsheet is not that. Step four then names the Standards: analytical procedures to identify key trends and outliers under SIA 6, sampling where needed under SIA 5, evidence collected and stored under SIA 320, work papers documented under SIA 330, and interim reports issued only after proper review of the work performed under SIA 350.

options.text: None — the conduct of fieldwork is a matter for the internal auditor's professional judgement, the Standards on Internal Audit reaching only planning and reporting
options.misconception: confines the Standards on Internal Audit to the two ends of the engagement, when they name the procedures in the middle of it as well
options.why: Professional judgement decides how much testing is enough; it does not decide whether evidence is collected, whether work papers exist or whether an interim report is reviewed before it goes out. Each of those has a Standard on Internal Audit of its own.

options.text: Only the interim report, which should never have been issued at all — an internal auditor reports once, at the end of the assignment
options.misconception: bars interim reporting outright, when the requirement is that an interim report is issued only after proper review of the work performed
options.why: Interim reports are contemplated and are useful where a finding cannot wait. What the requirement adds is the review before issue, so that a report going to management rests on work somebody senior has looked at.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — gathering the required information directly from the source with checks on its correctness and integrity, and performing the audit checks under SIA 6, SIA 5, SIA 320, SIA 330 and SIA 350

items.scenario: The scope of an internal audit of the purchase-to-pay cycle has been approved by the audit committee and the Board and fieldwork has begun. The team takes its vendor master data from a spreadsheet the process owner maintains rather than from the enterprise resource planning system, runs no analytical work over the year's transactions, picks a handful of invoices by eye, and emails an interim report to the chief financial officer the same evening without anyone reviewing it.

items.stem: What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Nothing — reading the working papers and signing them off is the review the Standard asks for, and the written agreements cover the rest
options.misconception: treats reading a conclusion as reviewing the work behind it, which is the distinction the Standard draws for staff who are not independent of the entity
options.why: A working paper records what its preparer says he did. Because the preparers here are the entity's own employees, the Standard asks the external auditor to go behind some of those papers to the underlying audit evidence itself rather than to accept the record of the work.

options.text: The internal auditors' work must be re-performed in full by the external auditor, precisely because they are not independent of the entity
options.misconception: converts checking back to the underlying evidence for some of the work into a duplicate of all of it, which would leave direct assistance no purpose
options.why: What the review must reach is the evidence sitting behind a portion of what was done, and direction, supervision and review must go far enough for the external auditor to satisfy himself that the conclusions rest on sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Redoing everything is neither required nor what an assistance arrangement is for.

options.text: Reviewing what internal auditors do on direct assistance is not finished until the external auditor has gone behind their papers to the evidence itself on a portion of that work; the nature, timing and extent of direction, supervision and review must be set with their lack of independence from the entity in mind; and the planned use of direct assistance, its nature and its extent, is communicated to those charged with governance
options.why: Two things are missing. The nature, timing and extent of direction, supervision and review must be settled with one fact in front of you: these two draw the entity's pay and are therefore not independent of the entity. The review is not finished until the external auditor has gone behind their conclusions, checking back to the underlying audit evidence on a portion of what they did — reading a signed-off working paper is not enough. And the planned use of direct assistance, its nature and its extent, is communicated to those charged with governance, so the people who oversee the audit know how much of it was done by the entity's own staff.
keywords: checking back to the underlying audit evidence

options.text: The communication to those charged with governance is required only where the internal auditors are used on a significant risk, and no significant risk is involved here
options.misconception: attaches a condition to the communication that the Standard does not impose, so that the arrangement most likely to go unmentioned is the routine one
options.why: The external auditor communicates the nature and extent of the planned use of direct assistance to those charged with governance, and the requirement is not limited to significant risks. Areas involving significant judgments and higher assessed risks are dealt with separately, by being closed to direct assistance altogether.

citation.ref: the direction, supervision and review of internal auditors providing direct assistance, the reach of that review into the evidence behind part of their work, and the communication to those charged with governance of the planned use of direct assistance

items.scenario: Two internal auditors are providing direct assistance on work that is not prohibited — vouching a sample of expense claims and tracing goods received notes to purchase orders. The written agreements are in place. The manager plans to read the working papers the two produce and sign them off, and to say nothing about the arrangement to the audit committee, on the view that how the firm staffs its own audit is an internal matter.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Only the inventory point is a departure, attendance at physical inventory counting being an absolute requirement of SA 501 that admits of no condition
options.misconception: reads a conditional requirement as an absolute one by dropping the condition that opens it
options.why: The attendance requirement is conditional on inventory being material to the financial statements. A company with no inventory at all does not meet that condition, so the requirement is not relevant rather than departed from.

options.text: Both are departures, and the file must record how the alternative audit procedures performed achieve the aim of each requirement and the reasons for departing from it
options.misconception: treats a requirement whose condition never arose as a requirement the auditor abandoned, which would put a departure note in every file for every SA the entity does not engage
options.why: That documentation belongs to a genuine departure — a relevant requirement the auditor judged it necessary to depart from in exceptional circumstances. A condition that never arose is not a departure, and recording one would say in the file that a rule was broken when none applied.

options.text: Neither is a departure, because a departure from a requirement of an SA never needs documenting in any event
options.misconception: reaches the right conclusion through a rule that does not exist, and would leave a real departure invisible in the file
options.why: A genuine departure is documented, and documented twice over — how the alternative audit procedures performed achieve the aim of the requirement, and the reasons for the departure. The answer here is that no departure occurred, not that departures go unrecorded.

options.text: Neither is a departure — a requirement binds the auditor only while it is relevant, and it is not relevant either where the SA as a whole has no application to the entity or where the condition the requirement hangs on never arose; both of those hold here, so the file records no departure
options.why: The auditor complies with a requirement in all cases where it is relevant, and a requirement is not relevant in two situations — where the entire SA is not relevant, and where the requirement is conditional and the condition does not exist. Inventory attendance is conditional on inventory being material to the financial statements, and SA 610 is not relevant to an entity with no internal audit function. Nothing has been departed from, so nothing about a departure goes in the file.
keywords: conditional and the condition does not exist

citation.ref: compliance with the requirements of an SA, and the two situations in which a requirement is not relevant, read with the documentation of a departure at SA 230 para 12

items.scenario: You are completing the audit of a small trading company that carries no inventory of any kind and has no internal audit function. An article on documentation has left a junior worried. He asks whether the file must record a departure from SA 501's requirement to attend physical inventory counting, and from SA 610, together with the alternative procedures that achieved the aim of each.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is the body that resulted from the merger of the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council
options.why: The Value Reporting Foundation is a non-profit organisation that was the result of the merger between the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council. It belongs to the consolidation phase of sustainability reporting, in which a crowded field of frameworks began combining rather than multiplying.

options.text: It is the framework created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board for consistent climate-related disclosures
options.misconception: gives the Financial Stability Board's creation the wrong name
options.why: What the Financial Stability Board created in 2015 is the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, written for businesses whose dealings are mainly financial ones — banks and insurers above all.

options.text: It is the body the IFRS Foundation Trustees announced on 3 November 2021 to deliver a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards
options.misconception: gives the Value Reporting Foundation the announcement and the mandate that belong to the International Sustainability Standards Board
options.why: That announcement created the International Sustainability Standards Board, whose purpose is a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards for investors and other capital market participants. It is a different body from the merged foundation, and it came later.

options.text: It is the result of the merger of the Global Reporting Initiative and the Carbon Disclosure Project
options.misconception: merges the two bodies whose names come up most often rather than the two that actually merged
options.why: The Global Reporting Initiative is an independent international organisation based in Amsterdam and remains one; the Carbon Disclosure Project collects environmental performance data and reports to investors, buyers and other stakeholders. Neither was part of this merger.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Value Reporting Foundation as the result of the merger between the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council

items.scenario: Reading about the consolidation among sustainability bodies, a colleague comes across the Value Reporting Foundation and asks you what it is and where it came from.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: It is the better of the two approaches, since numbers in a sustainability section invite challenge that narrative does not
options.misconception: prefers the form that cannot be checked, when the material says the mixed approach adds the most to the quality of the disclosure
options.why: Being hard to challenge is not a virtue in a disclosure. Metrics and key performance indicators are what let a reader see progress against goals, and a mixed approach that combines them with the narrative adds the maximum value.

options.text: It is qualitative ESG reporting, which describes strategy and policy; quantitative reporting carries metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area to measure progress against goals; and a mixed approach using both tends to add the maximum value to the quality of the disclosures
options.why: ESG reporting can be both quantitative and qualitative in nature. A qualitative report describes the company's strategy or policy around the relevant topics, which is what this board has produced. A quantitative approach carries metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area, so progress against goals can be measured and achievements reported. A mixed approach that uses both tends to add the maximum value to the quality of the disclosures, so the answer is to add the numbers rather than to replace the words.

options.text: It is quantitative reporting, a stated policy being a measurable commitment in itself
options.misconception: calls a policy a measure, when the quantitative form is defined by the metrics and indicators attached to it
options.why: A policy states an intention. Quantitative reporting is the metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area, which is precisely what this section does not have.

options.text: It is not ESG reporting at all, ESG reporting being by definition the disclosure of metrics and key performance indicators
options.misconception: recognises only the quantitative half of ESG reporting and dismisses the qualitative half the same material describes
options.why: Reporting on strategy and policy in words is one of the two recognised forms. It is incomplete on its own, which is a different criticism from saying it is not ESG reporting.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — qualitative and quantitative ESG reporting and the value of a mixed approach

items.scenario: A company's ESG section describes its climate policy, its supplier code and its diversity policy in words. It carries no numbers, no targets and no measures of progress. The board asks whether what it has produced counts as ESG reporting, and whether it should be doing something else instead.

items.stem: Which list is it?

options.text: Energy and transportation; agriculture, food and forestry products; materials and buildings; and banks and insurance
options.why: Climate-related risk is taken in as part of understanding the entity, and the material says it weighs more in some industries than in others: energy and transportation; agriculture, food and forestry products; materials and buildings; and banks and insurance. The list is a starting point for where to look, not a boundary on the requirement.

options.text: Listed entities in any sector, and no unlisted entity in any sector
options.misconception: turns a question about the nature of a business into a question about whether its shares are traded
options.why: Listing determines what an entity must disclose. It does not determine whether a warming climate affects its assets, its liabilities or its estimates, which is what makes the risk relevant to the audit.

options.text: None — climate-related risks sit outside the auditor's understanding of the entity in every sector
options.misconception: excludes from the understanding of the entity a risk the material puts expressly inside it
options.why: The consideration of climate-related risks is part of developing the understanding of the entity and its environment. The sector list says where it bites hardest, not whether it applies at all.

options.text: Energy and mining alone, climate-related risk being a question about carbon emissions and nothing else
options.misconception: reduces climate-related risk to the emitting industries and misses the financing, transport, construction and food sectors the material names
options.why: Emissions are one route by which climate reaches the financial statements. Financing exposure, transport assets, building materials and agricultural output are others, and the sectors named cover all of them.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the sectors in which climate-related risks could be more relevant to the audit

items.scenario: A firm is deciding where in its client portfolio to build climate-related risk into the understanding of the entity first. A partner asks which sectors the study material actually names as ones where climate-related risks could be more relevant to an audit.

items.stem: Which Social Audit Standards govern the three?

options.text: SAS 200, SAS 1300 and SAS 1100 respectively
options.why: The series runs by the field the social enterprise works in. SAS 200 is the health standard: health care and mental healthcare, sanitation, and getting safe drinking water to people who lack it. SAS 1300 covers the promotion of financial inclusion. SAS 1100 is the cities standard: slum redevelopment, housing people can afford, and the other work that makes a city sustainable and able to withstand shocks.

options.text: None of them — the Social Audit Standards govern the audit of a social enterprise's financial statements rather than an assessment of its impact
options.misconception: reads the series as a financial audit series, when each Standard guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement
options.why: Each Standard guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise working in a particular field, and sets out the audit steps and procedures for conducting the social impact assessment. The financial statements of the enterprise are a separate matter.

options.text: SAS 500, SAS 800 and SAS 1000 respectively
options.misconception: sends a water and sanitation programme to the environmental standard, financial inclusion to the incubator standard and housing to the livelihoods standard
options.why: SAS 500 is environmental sustainability and climate change including forest and wildlife conservation; SAS 800 is supporting incubators of social enterprises; SAS 1000 is promoting livelihoods for the rural and urban poor. None of the three matches the engagements described.

options.text: SAS 100 governs all three, the later numbers merely elaborating the general standard it lays down
options.misconception: treats the first number in the series as a general standard the rest expand on, when each Standard is tied to its own field
options.why: SAS 100 is itself a field standard — eradicating hunger, poverty, malnutrition and inequality. There is no general standard sitting above the series; the number follows the work the social enterprise does.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Social Audit Standards SAS 100 to SAS 1600 and the fields to which each of them applies

items.scenario: Your firm takes on three impact assessment engagements in the same month. The first is for a social enterprise running rural sanitation and safe drinking water programmes. The second is for one working on the promotion of financial inclusion. The third is for one carrying out slum area development and affordable housing.

items.stem: How do the Council's guidelines answer him, and under which clause would a breach be charged?

options.text: The wife's debt is outside the guideline, which reaches only the member's own indebtedness; but the fee taken in full before the report was signed is indebtedness and bars him
options.misconception: drops the relative from a bar that names her and turns a permitted progressive recovery of fees into a debt
options.why: Both halves are the wrong way round. The guideline names a relative of the member or of a partner in terms, so the wife's ₹4,00,000 is squarely within it, and fees recovered as and when a part of the work is done are not a debt owed to the client at all.

options.text: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines bars a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm, or a relative of such member or partner from accepting appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it beyond the limit fixed in the statute or, in other cases, ₹1,00,000 — a partnership firm is a concern and the wife is a relative, so the appointment is barred — while fees recovered on a progressive basis are not indebtedness; and a breach is misconduct under Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule
options.why: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 is written far wider than section 141. It reaches a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm itself, and a relative of such member or partner; it applies to a concern of any kind and not only to a company; and the ceiling is the limit fixed in the statute where a statute fixes one and ₹1,00,000 in other cases. On the fee, the Research Committee has already answered this: where a member draws his money on a progressive basis, taking each instalment as that slice of the work is finished rather than holding out until the engagement closes, no debt to the client arises at any point along the way. Because the source of the bar is a Council guideline, the charge for breaching it is Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule, which makes contravention of any guidelines issued by the Council professional misconduct.
keywords: a relative of such member or partner
Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: Nothing bars him — section 141(3)(d) is the only rule on an auditor's indebtedness, it applies to companies, and a partnership firm engagement falls outside it altogether
options.misconception: treats the Companies Act as the only source of the indebtedness bar, missing the Council guideline that applies to a concern of any kind
options.why: Section 141(3)(d) is one rule and the Council General Guidelines are another, and the second is the wider of the two. It bars accepting appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it, and a partnership firm is a concern. A member who is outside the Companies Act is not therefore outside the guidelines.

options.text: Both facts bar him, because any money moving between an auditor and his client before the report is signed is indebtedness
options.misconception: reads every pre-report receipt as indebtedness, when a fee earned as the work is done is payment and not a loan
options.why: A fee is money the client owes the auditor, not money the auditor owes the client, and the Research Committee has said that progressive recovery does not make the member indebted at any stage. What bars this appointment is the ₹4,00,000 the wife owes the firm.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 1, read with Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 on appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it

items.scenario: CA Bhatia is asked to become the auditor of Sahaj Traders, a partnership firm. At the date he is asked, his wife owes the firm ₹4,00,000 on an interest-free advance she took to buy a car. He says that section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs an auditor's indebtedness, that it applies to companies and not to a partnership firm, and that in any case the debt is his wife's and not his. On a separate engagement he has been recovering his fee on a progressive basis as parts of the work were completed, and had received the whole fee before he signed, which he now worries about.

items.stem: What does the Council's guidance on the relative size of fees require of the firm?

options.text: The trading company requires disclosure, the proportion being far past any trigger; the exemption for a small practice goes to the size of the fee and cannot answer a question about the proportion
options.misconception: reads the exemption out of the guidance by treating it as answering a different question from the one the trigger asks
options.why: An exemption exists precisely to take a case outside a trigger that would otherwise be met. The guidance exempts a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount from the provision altogether, and a proportion computed inside an exempt practice is not reported.

options.text: No disclosure in either case — the exemption for a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount answers the first, and the exemption for the audit of a nationalised bank, and generally where the appointment of the auditor is made by the Government, answers the second; and where the guidance does bite, the trigger is a higher proportion for an entity that is not a public interest entity than for one that is, in each case for two consecutive years
options.why: The guidance has a differentiated trigger and then two exemptions, and this firm is inside both exemptions. The trigger differs by the kind of client: disclosure is called for once an audit client's gross annual professional fees run past a stated proportion of the firm's own total fees and stay past it for two consecutive years, and that proportion is set higher for a client that is not a public interest entity than for one that is. The first exemption is for a practice whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount, which this firm's do not. The second is for the audit of government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions and regulators, and generally where appointments of auditors are made by the Government.

options.text: Only the bank audit requires disclosure, a regulated entity's auditor being held to the stricter public interest entity proportion whatever the exemptions say
options.misconception: applies the stricter trigger to an appointment the guidance expressly exempts, so the exemption is never reached
options.why: The order of the questions is the point. A case that falls inside an exemption never reaches the trigger at all, and the audit of a nationalised bank whose auditors are appointed by the Government is one of the cases the guidance exempts by name.

options.text: Both require disclosure — the exemptions cover government companies alone, and a nationalised bank is a banking company rather than a government company
options.misconception: reads the exemption list too narrowly, missing that it names nationalised banks and, more widely, appointments made by the Government
options.why: The list is longer than government companies. It names public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions and regulators, and it extends to any case where the appointment of the auditor is made by the Government — which is how this bank's auditors were appointed.

citation.ref: the Council's guidance on Fees–Relative Size — the differentiated disclosure requirement for public interest entities and other entities where the gross annual professional fees from an audit client exceed the stated proportion of the firm's total fees for two consecutive years, and the exemptions for a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount and for government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions, regulators and appointments made by the Government

items.scenario: A four-partner firm has two clients that worry a new partner. The first is an unlisted trading company, not a public interest entity, which has for two consecutive years produced well over half of the firm's gross annual professional fees. The second is a nationalised bank whose auditors are appointed by the Government, and the fees from it also run far above the proportion at which the Council's guidance on the relative size of fees would otherwise call for disclosure. The firm's total fees for the year are below the amount at which the guidance's exemption for a small practice stops applying.

items.stem: What does the Code have the firm evaluate, and how does it then address what it finds?

options.text: Whether the client is content with the two individuals, and whether any error has been found in the nine years, an unblemished record showing that objectivity has survived
options.misconception: measures a familiarity threat by the client's satisfaction and by hindsight, rather than by the factors the Code names
options.why: A familiarity threat is measured before the damage, not after it. The client's contentment is not one of the factors, and an absence of errors found is at least as consistent with a threat having taken effect as with its absence.

options.text: There is nothing to weigh — the Code's fixed rotation and cooling-off requirement applies to every audit client, and both individuals are already past it
options.misconception: extends the prescribed rotation and cooling-off, which the Code writes for a public interest entity, to every audit client
options.why: The Code does two different things in the same section. For a public interest entity it prescribes a term and a cooling-off period. For every other audit client it requires the firm to evaluate the familiarity and self-interest threats and to address them, which is why the factors exist at all.

options.text: The nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, his role on the engagement team, the extent to which the client's management has changed, and the nature or complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues — and it then addresses what it finds by rotating the individual off the team, changing his role, putting the finished work in front of an appropriate reviewer drawn from outside the engagement team, or arranging an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement
options.why: Where the Code leaves long association to evaluation rather than prescribing a term, it names what the evaluation weighs: the nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, the individual's role on the engagement team, the extent to which the client's management has changed, and the nature or complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues. Nine years on a company whose management has not changed and whose accounting is simple reads differently from nine years on one that has been through both. The actions that follow are also named — rotating the individual off, changing his role, an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team, or an independent quality review.

options.text: Only the length of service — the Code's factors are all ways of measuring time on the engagement, so the nine years and the seven years answer the question by themselves
options.misconception: reduces a four-factor evaluation to the one factor that can be counted, so the client's own circumstances never enter it
options.why: Length is one factor of four. The individual's role, how far the client's management has changed, and how complex the client's accounting and reporting issues are all bear on whether the relationship has made him too sympathetic or too accepting, and two of those have nothing to do with the calendar.

citation.ref: the long association provisions — the evaluation of the familiarity and self-interest threats created by long association, the factors that evaluation weighs, and the actions by which the firm addresses the threat where the client is not a public interest entity

items.scenario: Kesari Mills is an unlisted family company and is not a public interest entity. The senior manager has been on its audit for nine years and the engagement partner for seven. The firm accepts that a familiarity threat exists and that no fixed rotation requirement applies to a client of this kind. The audit manager asks what the firm is actually supposed to weigh before deciding what to do.

items.stem: Under which head does each fall?

options.text: Iyer falls under Second Schedule Part III and Rao under First Schedule Part IV — she went to prison and he did not
options.misconception: measures by the sentence served, so the heavier charge follows the person the court treated more harshly rather than the graver offence
options.why: This reads the two Schedules off the sentences, which is exactly the swap they are drafted to prevent. Both Schedules describe an offence punishable with imprisonment for a stated term, and neither asks what punishment the court chose within its powers.

options.text: Rao falls under Second Schedule Part III and Iyer under First Schedule Part IV — the line is drawn by the term of imprisonment the offence carries, not by the sentence the court actually awarded
options.why: Second Schedule Part III catches a member held guilty by any civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, and Rao's offence carries up to seven years however lightly he was dealt with. First Schedule Part IV catches an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, and Iyer's does, however long she was actually inside. The term of imprisonment the offence carries is what the Schedules measure; the sentence awarded is what the court decided about the person, and it moves nothing.
keywords: term of imprisonment the offence carries

options.text: Rao falls under Second Schedule Part III and Iyer under neither — a fine or a short sentence is too small a matter to engage other misconduct at all
options.misconception: adds a threshold of seriousness the Schedules do not contain, when First Schedule Part IV exists precisely for the lighter offence
options.why: There is no floor. First Schedule Part IV is written for the offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, so a conviction of that kind is other misconduct and goes before the Board of Discipline rather than falling out of the code altogether.

options.text: Both fall under Second Schedule Part III — an offence carrying seven years in one case and an actual term of imprisonment served in the other
options.misconception: puts an offence punishable with up to six months into the Second Schedule because the sentence happened to be custodial
options.why: Rao belongs there and Iyer does not. Her offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, which is First Schedule Part IV, and serving four months of that term does not enlarge the offence.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part IV, and Second Schedule, Part III — the dividing line being the term of imprisonment the offence is punishable with

items.scenario: Two members come before the Institute. Mr Rao is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years; the magistrate takes a lenient view of his circumstances and imposes a fine of ₹5,000, with no imprisonment at all. Mrs Iyer is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of up to six months, and is sentenced to four months, which she serves.

items.stem: Which of the four is a safeguard as the Code of Ethics uses that word?

options.text: None — a self-review threat can never be reduced by a safeguard, so the only answer is to decline or end the professional activity
options.misconception: turns the Code's last resort into a rule about a whole category of threat, when declining follows from the facts rather than from the label
options.why: Declining or ending the activity is one of three ways of addressing a threat, and it is reached where the circumstances creating the threat cannot be eliminated and no safeguard is capable of being applied. That is a conclusion on facts. A self-review threat is not in a class of its own, and the Code offers a reviewer who was not on the team as an action that might address it.

options.text: All four — anything that makes an improper conclusion less likely is a safeguard, and the four together are stronger than any one of them
options.misconception: treats every favourable feature of the environment as a safeguard, so nothing is ever left to be done about the threat
options.why: Counting the environment as a safeguard is how a threat gets talked down without anything changing. A certification and a regulator existed before the threat arose and will exist after it; the Code asks what the accountant did about this threat.

options.text: The first three — a safeguard is something already in place before the engagement begins, and a review carried out after the work is done comes too late to be one
options.misconception: puts a timing condition on the word that the Code does not, and rules out the very example the Code gives
options.why: The Code names having an appropriate reviewer review the work performed as an action that might address a self-review threat, and a review is by its nature after the work. What matters is whether the action effectively reduces the threat, not when in the engagement it falls.

options.text: Only the last — a safeguard is an action, individually or in combination, that the accountant takes and that effectively reduces a threat to an acceptable level, and an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team reviewing the work is one of the Code's own examples; the other three are conditions, policies and procedures that might affect the evaluation of whether a threat is at an acceptable level, and are not themselves safeguards
options.why: The Code defines the word narrowly on purpose. Safeguards are actions — one on its own, or several working together — by which the accountant himself brings a threat down to what the Code will treat as an acceptable level, and every example it gives is something a person does: putting extra hours and better-qualified people on to the tasks that need them; asking an appropriate reviewer from outside the team to go back over the finished work, or to advise while it is still being done; splitting non-assurance work off to different partners and teams that report up a separate line; bringing a second firm in to carry out, or to carry out again, some piece of the engagement; and walling one team off from another where confidential matters are in play. A certification, a regulator and a training requirement are conditions, policies and procedures in the environment: they might affect the evaluation of whether a threat is at an acceptable level, and none of them is an action taken against this threat.

citation.ref: the conceptual framework — addressing threats by eliminating the circumstances, applying safeguards, or declining or ending the professional activity, with the definition of safeguards as actions the accountant takes and the examples of such actions

items.scenario: A team has identified a self-review threat and is listing what it will rely on to bring it to an acceptable level. The list has four entries: the firm's ISO certification; the fact that the client is a regulated entity that files with a regulator; the profession's continuing education requirements; and a look over the finished work by an appropriate reviewer who sat outside the engagement team.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No — Clause 3 of Part II of the Second Schedule names the Quality Review Board among the bodies to which the information, statement, return or form may be submitted, alongside the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee and the Appellate Authority
options.why: Clause 3 does not stop at the Institute. Its reach is fixed by a list of recipients, and that list is a long one: the Institute itself, the Council and any Committee of it, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board, and the Appellate Authority. Put a particular into an information, a statement, a return or a form headed for any one of them, knowing them to be false, and the clause bites. That this Board was set up by the Central Government rather than by the Council changes nothing, because the clause lists it by name.

options.text: No, but only if the false statement affected the Board's conclusion on the quality of the engagement
options.misconception: adds a consequence the clause does not require, when the wrong is complete on including particulars known to be false
options.why: The clause is complete when the member includes particulars knowing them to be false. Whether anyone was misled goes to what the Disciplinary Committee makes of it, not to whether the clause is engaged.

options.text: Yes — Clause 3 reaches the Institute and its own organs, and a false statement to the Quality Review Board is a matter for that Board's own procedures and for nobody else
options.misconception: reads the clause as protecting the Institute's own machinery only, when it lists the bodies it protects and the Board is one of them
options.why: The clause is a list, and reading the list settles it. The Quality Review Board appears in it expressly, so a knowing falsehood in a submission to the Board is professional misconduct whatever the Board itself decides to do about the review.

options.text: No, but the charge is Clause 2 of Part III of the First Schedule, for not complying with the requirements asked for by the Quality Review Board
options.misconception: picks the clause about silence when the member spoke, and spoke falsely, which is what moves the case into the Second Schedule
options.why: Clause 2 of Part III is aimed at the member who goes silent — who never hands over the information the body called for, or who leaves undone what it required of him. This member complied and lied while doing it, and knowledge of the falsity is exactly what carries the case across into the Second Schedule.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 3 — the bodies to which a statement, return or form carrying particulars known to be false may be submitted

items.scenario: A member's firm is selected for a review by the Quality Review Board. In the information he submits to the Board he states that a second partner reviewed the engagement file before the report was signed, knowing that nobody did. When this is put to him he says that Clause 3 speaks of information submitted to the Institute, and that the Quality Review Board is a separate body set up by the Central Government, so the clause cannot reach him.

items.stem: Which clause reaches these two, and before which forum?

options.text: Clause 3 of Part III of the First Schedule reaches both — it catches a member who gives information knowing it to be false while inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, and equally while advertising through a write-up — and being a First Schedule matter, the Board of Discipline hears it
options.why: Clause 3 of Part III polices three routes at once: inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, responding to tenders or enquiries, and advertising through a write-up or anything provided for in items (6) and (7) of Part I. The letter to the larger firm is the first route and the circulated write-up is the third, and both carried information the member knew to be false. Because Part III sits in the First Schedule, the Board of Discipline hears the case.
keywords: inviting professional work from another chartered accountant

options.text: Only the write-up, under Clause 7 of Part I, because it advertises the firm's attainments; a letter between two members is a private commercial approach and outside the Schedules
options.misconception: files a knowing falsehood under the advertising clause and treats an approach to another member as beyond the disciplinary code
options.why: Clause 7 of Part I is about advertising attainments and about designations, and it would be engaged by a write-up whether or not anything in it was false. What is wrong here is the knowledge, and the clause that turns on knowledge across all three routes — the letter included — is Clause 3 of Part III.

options.text: Only the letter — Clause 3 names inviting work from another chartered accountant, while a write-up is governed by the Council's write-up guidelines, and a departure from a guideline is not misconduct
options.misconception: takes the write-up route out of a clause that names it, and treats a Council guideline as advisory
options.why: The clause names advertising through a write-up in the same breath as inviting work from another chartered accountant. And a guideline is not advisory in any event: Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule makes contravention of any guidelines issued by the Council professional misconduct in itself.

options.text: Neither — Clause 3 catches false information only in a response to a tender or an enquiry from a user of professional services, and neither a letter to another chartered accountant nor a write-up is that
options.misconception: shrinks a clause with three named routes down to one of them, so the two routes the profession opened up go unpoliced
options.why: Tenders and enquiries are one of the three routes the clause names. Inviting professional work from another chartered accountant is another, and advertising through a write-up is the third, and the clause treats a knowing falsehood on any of them alike.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part III, Clause 3 — false information given when work is invited from another chartered accountant, when a tender or an enquiry is answered, or in a write-up put out to advertise

items.scenario: CA Sengupta writes to a larger firm offering to take sub-contracted certification work, stating that his firm holds an ISO certification and has branch offices in two cities, knowing that it has neither. Separately he circulates a write-up describing his services, in which he states that his firm has completed more than two hundred bank audits, knowing the true number is under thirty.

items.stem: Which of the two breaches Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Neither — in both cases the examination was made by a chartered accountant, which is the whole of what the clause requires
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring a chartered accountant, when it requires one of four specified relationships to the member
options.why: A chartered accountant in the client's whole-time employment is neither in practice nor an employee in his firm, and the clause names relationships rather than qualifications. Reading it as a qualification test would let the client audit itself and have the member sign.

options.text: Only the first — an outsider is an outsider, and the fourth permitted person means a chartered accountant to whom the whole engagement has been sub-contracted with the client's consent
options.misconception: adds a consent condition the clause does not contain, and reads the fourth permitted person almost out of existence
options.why: The clause says another chartered accountant in practice and stops there. It asks nothing about the client's consent and nothing about whether the whole engagement or only the examination was passed on.

options.text: Only the second — Clause 2 lets the examination be made by any one of four people: the member himself, a partner of his, somebody employed inside his own firm, or a different chartered accountant who is in practice; CA Pillai is the fourth of those; the client's own accounts department is none of the four, and the qualification of the person heading it does not put him inside the list
options.why: Clause 2 names four pairs of hands and CA Pillai is one of them: another chartered accountant in practice, engaged for the work, is expressly permitted, and it makes no difference that he is outside the firm. The client's accounts head fails on both halves of the test — he is not an employee in his firm, being employed by the client, and he is not in practice at all. Being a chartered accountant is not the qualification the clause asks about; whose chartered accountant he is, is.

options.text: Both — the examination has to be made inside the firm, by the member himself, by a partner or by an employee of the firm, and anybody else is an outsider
options.misconception: drops the fourth permitted person from a list of four, so a lawful arrangement is condemned along with an unlawful one
options.why: The list has four entries and the fourth is another chartered accountant in practice. The clause was drafted that way so that a firm may bring in a practising member for work it cannot do itself, which is what happened in the first engagement.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 2 — the four persons by whom the examination of the financial statements and the related records may be made

items.scenario: Two certification engagements are reviewed. In the first, the firm engaged CA Pillai, a chartered accountant in practice on his own account who is neither a partner of the firm nor employed by it, to carry out the examination of the financial statements and the related records; the engagement partner then signed the certificate. In the second, the examination was carried out entirely by the client's own accounts department, whose head is a chartered accountant in the client's whole-time employment, and the engagement partner signed after reading their file.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: Yes, because responding to an empanelment is expressly permitted, and what a partner pays outside the engagement is a matter between him and the officer
options.misconception: reads the permission to respond to a tender or an enquiry as covering the means by which the response was made to succeed
options.why: The permission is to answer an invitation, not to buy the outcome. Nothing in it touches how the member conducted himself while the decision was being made, which is precisely what the second limb of Clause 5 reaches.

options.text: Yes — Clause 5's first limb names a person who is not an employee or a partner, so where the member acts himself there is nobody to bring the clause into play
options.misconception: reads a two-limbed clause as though it had only its first limb, so a member who does the improper thing himself escapes
options.why: Reading only the first limb would mean a member could do personally what he may not pay an agent to do. The second limb exists for that case: it is about the means and not about the hands.

options.text: No, but the charge is Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule, for paying a share of professional fees to a person who is not a member of the Institute
options.misconception: reaches for the fee-sharing clause when the money was not a share of any fee but a payment made to procure the work
options.why: Clause 2 polices the outflow of professional fees — a share, commission or brokerage out of the fees earned. A lump sum paid to an officer to obtain an empanelment is not a share of the fees on the work, and the clause that fits what was done is Clause 5's second limb.

options.text: No — Clause 5 has a second limb, securing any professional business by means which are not open to a chartered accountant, and that limb asks how the work was obtained rather than who obtained it; a private payment to the officer who controls the empanelment is such a means
options.why: Clause 5 has two limbs and either one is enough. The first asks who brought the work in — a person who is not an employee of the member and not his partner. The second limb asks by what means it was secured, and it catches means which are not open to a chartered accountant whoever employed them, the member himself included. A payment made privately to the officer who decides the empanelment is the paradigm case, and the firm's own hands on it make it worse rather than safer.
keywords: means which are not open to a chartered accountant

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 — the second limb, securing professional business by means which are not open to a chartered accountant

items.scenario: A firm wants a place on a state undertaking's audit panel. No outsider is involved at any stage: the managing partner meets the undertaking's finance director himself and pays him ₹2,00,000 privately to have the firm's name put on the panel. The firm is empanelled and takes the work. The partner's position is that Clause 5 is aimed at touts and agents, and that since nobody outside the firm brought the work in, the clause cannot be engaged.

items.stem: Who may lawfully sign?

options.text: CA Shah and CA Dutt — firms in one network share quality control and standards, so a network firm's partner signs as a partner for this purpose
options.misconception: treats network membership as partnership, when the network's consequence is for independence and not for who may sign
options.why: A network exists for other purposes: where a firm is a network firm the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of one apply to the other. It does not make the partners of one firm the partners of another, and Clause 12 asks about partnership in this firm.

options.text: None of the three — nobody who did not himself perform the examination may sign the report, and none of them did
options.misconception: merges the clause about who may sign with the clause about who may make the examination, and misreads the second one as well
options.why: Two different clauses answer two different questions. Clause 12 fixes who may sign, and Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule fixes who may make the examination — permitting the member, a partner, an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice. A partner may therefore sign on work done by the firm's employees.
