items.scenario: Your client's billing runs on a cloud provider. The type 2 report covers the full year and carries an unmodified service auditor's opinion. Its description of the system names one complementary user entity control: the user entity must review and approve the monthly rate table before it is loaded, and the report says this control is necessary to achieve the control objective on the accuracy of billed amounts. You establish that the client's finance head signs the loading form each month without opening the rate table, and has done so all year.

items.stem: What does SA 580 require of you?

options.text: Disclaim the opinion, because SA 580 answers any refused written representation with a disclaimer
options.misconception: applies the rule for the two responsibilities representations to every representation in the letter
options.why: The disclaimer is not the standard's answer to refusal in general. It is prescribed where management does not provide the representations about its own responsibilities, or where the auditor concludes that doubt about management's integrity makes those unreliable. Everything else runs through the graded response, which may still end at a disclaimer but only after the evaluation.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management; re-evaluate the integrity of management and the effect that has on the reliability of representations, oral and written, and of audit evidence in general; and take appropriate actions, including determining the possible effect on the opinion — the automatic disclaimer is prescribed for the two representations about management's own responsibilities, and this is not one of them
options.why: Where a requested written representation is not provided, SA 580 sets a sequence rather than an outcome. The auditor discusses the matter with management, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect that has on the reliability of representations and of audit evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the opinion. The disclaimer the standard prescribes without that grading is for the two representations about management's responsibilities, both of which were given here; what was refused is a specific representation, and a refusal on it still contaminates the rest, which is why the re-evaluation reaches audit evidence in general rather than only this paragraph.

options.text: Nothing follows — a written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence about any matter it deals with, so an absent one leaves the evidence exactly where it was
options.misconception: reasons from what a representation is worth as evidence to what its refusal is worth as information
options.why: It is true that a representation is never sufficient on its own. But a refusal is not the same event as an absence: management has been asked to confirm something and has declined, and SA 580 treats that as information about management, reaching the reliability of the representations it did give and of audit evidence in general.
keywords: refusal is not the same event as an absence

options.text: Accept an oral confirmation from the group legal head in place of the struck-out paragraph and complete the file note
options.misconception: substitutes an oral statement from a third officer for a written representation management has deliberately declined to give
options.why: The standard requires the representation in writing from management, and the significant fact here is the deliberate deletion, not the absence of words on the subject. Taking a spoken assurance from someone else records agreement that management has just refused to give.

citation.ref: para 19 — the actions where requested written representations are not provided — read with para 20, which prescribes a disclaimer for the representations about management's responsibilities

items.scenario: Management signs the representation letter, including both representations about its own responsibilities — that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements, and that it has provided you with all relevant information and access agreed in the terms of the engagement. It strikes out one other paragraph: the one confirming that it has disclosed to you all known instances of non-compliance with laws and regulations. The finance director says the group legal head would not put his name to that sentence and offers no further explanation.

items.stem: Is that split defensible under SA 620?

options.text: Yes — the four matters must be agreed with both experts, but the standard requires the agreement to be in writing when appropriate, and access to confidential information, an expert not previously used, the extent and significance of the work and its complexity are the factors that make writing appropriate; all of them point at the engineer and none at the actuary
options.why: The agreement itself is not optional for either. The same four matters are agreed with every auditor's expert: the nature, scope and objectives of the work, the respective roles and responsibilities, the nature, timing and extent of communication including the form of any report, and the need to observe confidentiality requirements. What varies is the form. The standard asks for it in writing when appropriate, and the factors it names are whether the expert will see confidential entity information, whether this is an expert whose work the auditor has not previously used, how much of the audit turns on the work and how much rides on it, and how complex the matter is.

options.text: No — every agreement with an auditor's expert must be in writing, without exception
options.misconception: hardens a standard that says "when appropriate" into an unqualified rule
options.why: The standard's words are that the auditor shall agree, in writing when appropriate, on the four matters. Reading the qualification out of it turns a judgement the standard asks the auditor to make into a formality, and gives no way to tell the engineer's engagement apart from the actuary's.

options.text: Yes, but for a different reason — writing is required for an external expert and never for an internal one, and that line settles it by itself
options.misconception: promotes one of several factors into the whole test, so a first-time internal expert on a highly complex matter would need nothing in writing
options.why: Whether the expert is internal or external is one factor among several, and the others can carry the answer on their own. An internal expert given confidential information for a large and complex matter he has never worked on before is a case where writing would be appropriate, and a rule drawn on the internal-external line alone would miss it.

options.text: No — an internal expert is a member of the firm and needs no agreement at all, the four matters being covered by the firm's own quality management system
options.misconception: uses membership of the firm to remove the agreement rather than to inform the judgement about its form
options.why: Membership of the firm bears on whether writing is appropriate, not on whether there is anything to agree. Somebody still has to fix what the actuary is valuing, on what basis, by when and in what form, and a system of quality management does not answer any of those for a particular engagement.

citation.ref: para 11 — the four matters agreed with the auditor's expert, in writing when appropriate — read with the factors bearing on whether writing is appropriate

items.scenario: Two experts are used on one audit. The first is an actuary who is a partner in your own firm's actuarial team, has worked on this client for six years, and is doing a routine review of a small gratuity valuation. The second is an external petroleum engineer the firm has never used before, engaged on a large and technically complex reserves estimate, and given the client's confidential reserve data to do it. The manager proposes a written agreement with the engineer and a short file note recording the arrangement with the actuary.

items.stem: Which of these fall within SA 720?

options.text: Only the bound volume — other information has to be published together with the financial statements it accompanies, so a separately issued booklet is outside the standard
options.misconception: makes physical packaging the test, when the definition turns on purpose and allows a combination of documents
options.why: A combination of documents that serve the same purpose is an annual report, and the separate booklet is one of them. Deciding scope by what is between the same covers would let an entity move its most optimistic commentary out of the volume and out of the audit's reach at once.

options.text: All four — everything the company published about the year's results reaches owners and carries the same figures, so all of it is other information
options.misconception: treats subject matter and audience as the test, when the standard excludes two categories by name
options.why: Overlapping figures do not make a document part of the annual report. SA 720 excludes preliminary announcements of financial information and securities offering documents, including prospectuses, and reporting on the second of those has its own regime rather than none.

options.text: The bound volume and the management discussion and analysis booklet — one year's reporting to owners can be spread over more than one publication, and a combination of documents put out for that purpose is the annual report — while the standard does not apply to preliminary announcements of financial information or to securities offering documents, including prospectuses
options.why: The definition does the work. What makes something an annual report is who issues it and why: management, or those charged with governance, putting it out year by year because law, regulation or custom asks them to, so that owners learn how the entity traded and where it stands. One publication or several — a combination of documents can be the annual report between them. A booklet issued the same day and described as part of the year's reporting is inside that; binding is not the test. And SA 720 says in terms that it does not apply to preliminary announcements of financial information, or to securities offering documents including prospectuses.

options.text: The bound volume and the prospectus — a prospectus reproduces the audited financial statements and goes to investors, which is what other information is for
options.misconception: brings in by reasoning the one document the standard excludes by name
options.why: Reproducing the financial statements is not the test either, and here the standard leaves no room to reason: it does not apply to securities offering documents, including prospectuses. What a practitioner does about the other information in a prospectus is a separate engagement under its own standard.

citation.ref: the definition of an annual report as a document or combination of documents, and the exclusion of preliminary announcements of financial information and securities offering documents including prospectuses from the scope of the SA

items.scenario: A listed company issues four documents around its results. A bound volume carrying the directors' report, the corporate governance report and the audited financial statements. A separate management discussion and analysis booklet, posted to shareholders on the same day and described in the bound volume as forming part of the year's reporting. An unaudited preliminary announcement of the year's results, released to the exchanges three weeks before your report is signed. And a prospectus for a bond issue two months later, which reproduces the audited financial statements. The finance head tells you only the bound volume is the annual report.

items.stem: What does SAE 3402 require?

options.text: Modify the opinion for the description and disclaim separately on the access control, so the report carries a modification and a disclaimer side by side
options.misconception: splits one opinion into two conclusions on the same subject matter, when the standard answers multiple faults with one modified opinion carrying all the reasons
options.why: There is one opinion on the description, the design and, in a type 2 report, the operating effectiveness. Where more than one thing is wrong, the answer is a single modified opinion whose report contains a clear description of all the reasons for the modification, not two conclusions that a reader has to reconcile.
keywords: all the reasons for the modification

options.text: Both are grounds for modification — the description does not fairly present the system, and you are unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence — and the report shall contain a clear description of all the reasons for the modification, not the one that is easiest to state
options.why: The service auditor modifies the opinion where the description does not fairly present the system as designed and implemented, where the controls were not suitably designed, where in a type 2 report the controls tested did not operate effectively, or where he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence. Two of the four are engaged here. And the standard settles the drafting as well as the grounds: the report shall contain a clear description of all the reasons for the modification, so a user auditor reading it knows everything that is wrong and not only the part that was convenient to write.
keywords: does not fairly present the system
unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
all the reasons for the modification

options.text: Neither is a ground — in a type 2 report the opinion is modified only where the controls tested did not operate effectively, and both problems are about something else
options.misconception: keeps one of the four grounds and discards the other three
options.why: Operating effectiveness is one ground of four. Fair presentation of the description, suitability of the design and an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence each stand alongside it, and an inability to obtain evidence is precisely what four months of purged logs leaves.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence

options.text: Modify for the purged logs alone — a description that management has undertaken to correct next year is a matter for a letter to the service organisation
options.misconception: treats a promise about next year's document as curing this year's, and drops a named ground for modification out of the report
options.why: The report describes the system for the period reported on, and for that period the description asserts a control nobody performs. A user auditor relying on the description would be relying on a reconciliation that does not exist, which is why "does not fairly present the system" is a ground in its own right.
keywords: does not fairly present the system

citation.ref: the grounds on which the service auditor's opinion is modified — a description that does not fairly present the system, controls not suitably designed, controls tested that did not operate effectively in a type 2 report, and an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence — with the requirement that the report contain a description of all the reasons for the modification

items.scenario: You are the service auditor completing a type 2 report. Two problems stand. The service organisation's description of its system says a daily reconciliation between the ledger and the settlement file is performed, and it is not performed at all. Separately, you could not test one access control because the system logs for four months were purged under a retention setting nobody had reviewed. You propose to modify the opinion naming only the purged logs, on the ground that the description point is minor and management has undertaken to correct the wording next year.

items.stem: What is missing from the report under SAE 3400?

options.text: Three elements — that responsibility for the forecast, and for the assumptions underneath it, rests with management; where it applies, a note of what the forecast was drawn up for and of who alone may be handed it; and a description of the work, namely that the evidence behind the assumptions, the amounts and the disclosures was examined on a sample of items
options.why: The three gaps map onto three named elements of the report. Saying in the report that management is responsible for the prospective financial information, assumptions and all, answers who prepared it, and matters most on a document about the future, where a reader may otherwise take the numbers for the auditor's. Naming the purpose, and any restricted distribution that goes with it, answers what a forecast built for one lender's covenant is doing in anyone else's hands. And saying that the work involved examining, on a test basis, the evidence behind the assumptions, the amounts and the rest of the disclosures tells the reader what was actually done.
keywords: management is responsible for the prospective financial information

options.text: A statement that the auditor is responsible for the assumptions, since it is the assumptions he gave negative assurance on
options.misconception: reads assurance given on assumptions as responsibility taken for them
options.why: Giving negative assurance on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis is a statement about somebody else's assumptions. The prospective financial information, and the assumptions it is built on, belong to management, and a report saying otherwise would put the auditor behind a forecast of events that may never occur.

options.text: Nothing — those three belong in the engagement letter, and the report is complete once it carries the negative assurance, the opinion and the caveat
options.misconception: moves three named elements of the report into the engagement letter, leaving the report silent on responsibility, purpose and work performed
options.why: The engagement letter records the arrangement between two parties; the report speaks to whoever reads it. Responsibility for the information, the purpose it was prepared for and the nature of the examination are elements of the report itself, and a reader who never sees the engagement letter would otherwise learn none of them.

options.text: Only the reference to restricted distribution — responsibility and the nature of the procedures are implied by the reference to the applicable standard
options.misconception: lets a citation of the standard stand in for the statements the standard says the report shall contain
options.why: Naming a standard tells a reader which rules were followed, not what the auditor did or who made the forecast. The standard sets out the elements a report shall contain precisely so that a reader does not have to go and look them up, and the statements on responsibility and on the test-basis examination are two of them.

citation.ref: the elements a report on an examination of prospective financial information must contain — among them who is responsible for that information and for the assumptions under it, a reference where it applies to what the information was prepared for and to any limit on who may receive it, and a statement of what the examination consisted of, the evidence behind the assumptions, the amounts and the disclosures having been tested on a sample of items

items.scenario: You have examined a three-year forecast prepared solely for one lender under a covenant in its loan agreement, and you are satisfied with the assumptions and the preparation. The draft report carries a title, an addressee, an identification of the forecast, a reference to the applicable standard, the negative assurance sentence on the assumptions, the opinion on preparation and presentation, a caveat about achievability, the date, the place of signature and the signature. It says nothing about who prepared the forecast, nothing about the fact that it was prepared only for the lender, and nothing about what your examination consisted of.

items.stem: Which file breaches the standard's effective date of application?

options.text: Neither file — both periods end before the standard became mandatory, which is for periods ending on or after 31 March 2026
options.misconception: moves the mandatory date two years later than the standard sets it
options.why: The mandatory stage begins with assurance reports covering periods ending on or after 31 March 2024. The year ended 31 March 2025 is inside it, and a report drafted without reference to the standard for that period is a breach.

options.text: File B only — SSAE 3000 applied on a voluntary basis to assurance reports covering periods ending on 31 March 2023 and on a mandatory basis to assurance reports covering periods ending on or after 31 March 2024
options.why: The effective date is written in two stages. On a voluntary basis it applied to assurance reports covering periods ending on 31 March 2023, so File A departed from a standard nobody was yet obliged to follow. On a mandatory basis it applied to assurance reports covering periods ending on or after 31 March 2024, which catches a report on the year ended 31 March 2025 squarely.

options.text: Both files — the standard bound every assurance engagement on sustainability information from the day ICAI issued it
options.misconception: treats the date of issue as the date of application, ignoring a two-stage effective date the standard states in terms
options.why: A standard's effective date is a separate question from when it was issued, and this one was deliberately phased. The voluntary stage for periods ending on 31 March 2023 exists so that firms could adopt it early without a breach hanging over anyone who did not.

options.text: Neither file — SSAE 3000 binds only assurance engagements for the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation, and this company is outside that class
options.misconception: imports a reporting threshold that applies to entities into a standard that applies to the engagement
options.why: The top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation is the class on which a reporting obligation was placed; it is not a limit on an assurance standard. SSAE 3000 applies to assurance engagements on sustainability information, and what decides its application is the period the report covers.

citation.ref: Effective date of application — voluntary where a report covers a period that ends on 31 March 2023, and mandatory once the period covered ends on or after 31 March 2024

items.scenario: A firm's quality review picks up two files. File A is a limited assurance report on a listed company's sustainability information for the year ended 31 March 2023; it makes no reference to SSAE 3000 and follows a format of the team's own. File B is a limited assurance report on the same company's sustainability information for the year ended 31 March 2025, also drafted without reference to SSAE 3000. Neither company is among the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation.

items.stem: What does SA 250 require you to do about telling an authority outside the company?

options.text: Say nothing to anyone outside the company in any circumstances, confidentiality being absolute once an engagement letter records it
options.misconception: reads confidentiality as absolute, when SA 250 contemplates that law or regulation may require the auditor to report
options.why: Confidentiality is a strong duty and it is not an absolute one. SA 250 expressly contemplates reporting where law or regulation requires it, and in India several statutes do exactly that in their own fields.

options.text: Report the matter to the municipal authority and to the police at once — a suspected bribe is a matter of public interest and public interest overrides confidentiality
options.misconception: treats public interest as a self-executing override of the professional duty of confidentiality, when SA 250 asks first whether reporting is required by law or regulation
options.why: Public interest is the reason the law sometimes compels reporting; it is not itself the authority to report. The standard sends the auditor to the law of the jurisdiction, and a disclosure made without that footing is a breach of confidence rather than a duty discharged.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement and treat the withdrawal as your answer to the question of external reporting
options.misconception: substitutes withdrawal for the determination the standard requires, when withdrawal answers a different question and does not settle whether anyone outside must be told
options.why: Withdrawal is a separate consideration in SA 250, and it does not dispose of the reporting question. An auditor who resigns still has to decide whether the law obliges him to tell somebody, and resigning may well leave that duty exactly where it was.

options.text: Determine whether you have a responsibility to report the suspected non-compliance to a party outside the entity, bearing in mind that your professional duty of confidentiality ordinarily prevents it unless reporting is required by law or regulation — and consider obtaining legal advice
options.why: SA 250 makes this a determination rather than a reflex. The auditor shall determine whether he has a responsibility to report — whether the non-compliance he has identified or suspects should reach somebody outside the entity. His professional duty of confidentiality ordinarily precludes such reporting unless it is required by law or regulation, and because the answer turns on the law of the place the standard treats legal advice as an appropriate step.

citation.ref: para 28 and para 29, read with para 24 on withdrawal

items.scenario: Auditing a construction company, you identify payments routed through a consultant that you suspect are bribes paid to obtain municipal clearances. You discuss the matter with management and then with those charged with governance. Both accept that the payments happened, decline to investigate further, and decline to inform anybody outside the company. Your engagement letter contains an ordinary confidentiality clause and no statute names you as a reporter of this kind of conduct.

items.stem: How does SA 299 (Revised) allocate responsibility for the two problems?

options.text: The missing disclosure is the responsibility of all three jointly and severally; the inventory overstatement is L's alone
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) splits responsibility in two. Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to him, so the badly performed stock count belongs to L. Presentation and disclosure sit outside that division — whether the financial statements meet what the applicable financial reporting framework demands is one of the matters for which the joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible, along with undivided work carried out by all of them and with ensuring that the audit report complies with the requirements.
keywords: audit report complies with the requirements

options.text: Both are the responsibility of all three jointly and severally, joint auditors sharing one appointment and one report
options.misconception: collapses the division of work into joint responsibility, when SA 299 makes each joint auditor responsible for the work divided to him
options.why: A common appointment and a common report do not make the work common. The standard divides the work precisely so that responsibility for performing it can be located, and a stock count divided to one firm is that firm's to answer for.

options.text: Both are L's, the inventory being his area and the missing disclosure relating to inventory quantities he was closest to
options.misconception: uses the subject matter of a disclosure to move a joint and several responsibility onto the joint auditor whose area it touches
options.why: Disclosure is not allocated by topic. It sits on the joint and several list because the financial statements are presented as a whole, and no joint auditor may point at another when the statements do not comply with the framework.

options.text: Neither can be allocated, because responsibility among joint auditors is settled by the engagement letter rather than by the standard
options.misconception: treats a professional responsibility fixed by the standard as something the parties can contract about
options.why: An engagement letter records the division of work; it cannot rewrite who answers for what. SA 299 (Revised) sets the allocation itself and names the matters that stay joint and several however the work is split.

citation.ref: para 13 on division of work and para 14 on joint and several responsibility

items.scenario: Three firms are joint auditors of a company. The work is divided: L takes inventory and fixed assets, M takes payables and payroll, N takes receivables. The notes to the financial statements, the presentation of the statements and the audit report itself were settled by all three together. After the report is signed two problems surface. A disclosure the applicable framework requires is missing from the notes. Separately, a stock count L attended was performed badly and inventory is overstated.

items.stem: What does SA 300 say about that file?

options.text: It is incomplete — the documentation must show the strategy, the plan, and any significant changes made to either during the engagement together with the reasons for those changes
options.why: SA 300 requires the audit documentation to hold three things: the strategy, the plan, and a record of whatever significant changes were made to either one as the engagement went on, together with the reasons for such changes. Holding only the final version records the destination and loses the journey, and the acquisition is exactly the kind of event those reasons are meant to capture.

options.text: It is complete, because a mid-audit acquisition is a change in the entity rather than a change in the audit strategy
options.misconception: separates the entity from the audit of it, when a new location and a new accounting package change the scope, timing and direction of the audit
options.why: A new location and a second accounting package change what the audit has to cover and how it is resourced. That is a change to the overall audit strategy in the ordinary sense of the words, whatever caused it.

options.text: It is incomplete, but only because the superseded documents were deleted — keeping them would have satisfied the requirement without any note
options.misconception: treats retaining the old version as equivalent to recording the change and the reason for it
options.why: Two documents side by side show that something changed and leave the reader to guess why. The standard asks for the reasons, which is the part that cannot be reconstructed from the papers later.

options.text: It is complete — SA 300 asks for a strategy and a plan, and the file holds a correct one of each
options.misconception: reads the documentation requirement as two documents, when it has a third element covering changes and the reasons for them
options.why: The requirement lists three things and the file holds two. A reviewer reading it cannot tell that the scope of the audit moved mid-engagement, which is the single most important planning fact of this year.

citation.ref: para 12 on documentation, read with para 10 on changes to planning decisions during the audit

items.scenario: Halfway through an audit the client acquires a business, which brings in a new location and a second accounting package. The engagement partner reworks the overall audit strategy and the team rewrites the audit plan. The old versions of both are deleted from the working papers because, the senior says, a file holding two plans confuses the reviewer. The new documents are complete and correct and carry no note about what changed or why.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require?

options.text: Reliance is permissible without testing, because the control addresses no significant risk and this is only its second audit since it was last tested
options.misconception: applies the three-audit rotation to a control that has changed, when the rotation is conditional on the absence of changes
options.why: The absence of a significant risk removes one restriction and leaves the other standing. The rotation was never a fixed licence to skip two years; it operates only once the auditor has satisfied himself that the control is still the control he tested.

options.text: Reliance is barred outright, because audit evidence about a control's operating effectiveness can never be carried forward from a previous audit
options.misconception: denies a carry-forward that SA 330 permits, and answers a rule about changed controls with a rule about no controls
options.why: Evidence from previous audits may be used once its continuing relevance is established. The answer here is that the control must be tested this year because it changed, not that carrying evidence forward is never allowed.

options.text: The control must be tested in the current audit, the three-audit rotation being available only for a control that has not changed
options.why: Before using audit evidence from a previous audit the auditor establishes its continuing relevance by obtaining audit evidence about whether significant changes in those controls have occurred since. Where there have been changes that affect that continuing relevance, SA 330 requires the auditor to test the controls in the current audit. The rotation of at least once in every third audit applies to controls that have not changed, and a new system with reset limits and a reduced approval requirement is a change.
keywords: test the controls in the current audit

options.text: Reliance is permissible, provided the auditor tests the general information technology controls over the new system instead of the purchase order control itself
options.misconception: substitutes testing of the system's general controls for testing of the application control the auditor actually plans to rely on
options.why: General controls over the environment support an application control; they are not that control. Evidence that the new system is well administered says nothing about whether the reset approval limits work as the auditor assumes.

citation.ref: para 15(a) on changed controls, read with para 14 and para 15(b)

items.scenario: A purchase order approval control was tested two years ago and found effective. Since then the company has replaced its accounting package: approval is now applied inside the new system, the approval limits have been reset, and a category of purchase that used to need two approvals now needs one. Purchases are not a significant risk. The senior plans to rely on the control without testing it, on the footing that a control need be retested only in every third audit.

items.stem: What does SA 505 require next?

options.text: Communicate the refusal to those charged with governance in every case, a refusal to permit a confirmation being reportable whether or not it was reasonable
options.misconception: makes the escalation automatic, when SA 505 attaches it to an unreasonable refusal or to alternative procedures that do not deliver
options.why: The standard states its own trigger. Reporting every refusal regardless of the reason turns a graded response into a formality and tells those charged with governance nothing they can act on.

options.text: Modify the opinion for a scope limitation, since a confirmation you planned was not obtained
options.misconception: treats a planned procedure not performed as an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, when the alternative procedures supplied that evidence
options.why: A limitation exists where the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The evidence was obtained by another route, and the audit plan is a means to evidence rather than the evidence itself.

options.text: Nothing further — the inquiry, the evaluation and the alternative procedures are complete, and the escalation step does not arise
options.why: SA 505 answers a refusal with three steps: inquire into management's reasons and seek audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness, evaluate the implications of the refusal for the assessment of the risks of material misstatement, and perform alternative audit procedures. Escalation follows only where the auditor concludes that the refusal is unreasonable or the alternative procedures fail to deliver relevant and reliable evidence. Here counsel's letter makes the reason reasonable and the subsequent receipts deliver, so neither trigger is met.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the balance is correct, and rely on that in place of the confirmation
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for audit evidence, when a written representation is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it deals with
options.why: A written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it deals with. The alternative procedures here are real evidence from outside management's assertion, which is why they answer the problem and a representation would not.

citation.ref: para 8 and para 9

items.scenario: You select nine customers for positive confirmation. Management asks you not to write to one of them, a customer with whom the company is in confidential arbitration, and shows you the arbitration file and a letter from its counsel advising that no direct contact be made pending the award. You read both and find the reason genuine. You then vouch the balance to the signed contract, the despatch documents and the amounts actually received after the year end, and that evidence fully supports the balance.

items.stem: Is the fraud work complete?

options.text: No — the review of estimates for bias is required whatever the assessed risk of management override, and the file must show it was performed with that purpose in mind
options.why: SA 240 requires certain procedures irrespective of the auditor's assessment — they stand whatever he has concluded about the risks of management override of controls, and reviewing accounting estimates for bias is one of them. That work asks whether the judgements and assumptions of management indicate a possible bias on the part of management, which is a different question from the one the risk assessment review asks, even where the same underlying comparison of estimate against outcome serves both.
keywords: possible bias on the part of management

options.text: No, and the remedy is to modify the opinion, an incomplete fraud file being a scope limitation
options.misconception: jumps to the report when the procedure can simply be performed before the audit is completed
options.why: A procedure not yet done is a procedure to do. A limitation arises where the auditor cannot obtain evidence, and nothing here suggests the estimates and the prior year file are unavailable to him.

options.text: Yes — the retrospective review was performed, and one review of the same estimates cannot sensibly be done twice
options.misconception: treats the two reviews as the same procedure because they look at the same estimates, when they are performed for different purposes and only one of them is on the file
options.why: Nobody has to do the comparison twice. What is missing is the second question being asked of it and answered on the file, and a reviewer reading this file cannot tell that the bias question was ever put.

options.text: Yes — a low assessed risk of management override justifies leaving the review of estimates out
options.misconception: makes a required procedure conditional on the risk assessment, when SA 240 requires it whatever the assessment says
options.why: The whole point of the required procedures in SA 240 is that they do not bend to the auditor's own assessment. Management override is by definition the risk the auditor is least able to see coming, so the standard removes the auditor's discretion about it.

citation.ref: para 32(b) on reviewing accounting estimates for bias irrespective of the assessed risk of management override, read with SA 540 (Revised) para 14

items.scenario: Your file shows a thorough retrospective review of last year's warranty provision and expected credit loss, performed at the risk assessment stage and used to shape this year's procedures on those two estimates. The section of the file dealing with the risk of management override of controls contains journal entry testing and a review of significant unusual transactions, and records that a review of estimates for bias was not needed because the risk of management override was assessed as low.

items.stem: What does SA 720 require, the other information having reached you after the date of your report?

options.text: Notify those charged with governance of your concerns about the other information and take any further appropriate action, including obtaining legal advice — or, if the law or regulation you operate under allows it, withdraw from the engagement altogether
options.why: Where other information obtained after the date of the auditor's report is materially misstated and management refuses to correct it, SA 720 sets out the actions open to the auditor: notifying those charged with governance of his concerns and taking any further appropriate action, including obtaining legal advice, or — where applicable law or regulation leaves that door open — withdrawing from the engagement entirely. There is no Other Information section left to write, because the report has already been issued.

options.text: Recall the auditor's report and reissue it with the material misstatement of the other information described in the Other Information section
options.misconception: treats an issued report as amendable for other information that arrived later, when SA 720 sends the auditor to those charged with governance and to legal advice instead
options.why: Describing the misstatement in the report is the route for other information obtained before the date of the report, because the section can be written before signing. After issue the standard changes the remedy rather than reopening the report.

options.text: Perform the procedures in SA 560 for facts that become known after the financial statements have been issued, and ask the entity to revise the financial statements
options.misconception: applies the subsequent-events machinery for a fact about the financial statements to a misstatement sitting in the other information
options.why: SA 560 works where the financial statements themselves would have been changed had the fact been known. These financial statements are right, and it is the Chairman's statement beside them that is wrong.

options.text: Nothing, the auditor's responsibility for other information ending on the date of the auditor's report
options.misconception: reads the auditor's responsibility as closing on the date of the report, when SA 720 deals expressly with other information obtained after that date
options.why: The standard has a separate limb for exactly this timing, so the responsibility plainly does not end at signing. What changes after the date of the report is which action is open to the auditor, not whether any is.

citation.ref: para 18(b) on other information obtained after the date of the auditor's report, read with para 18(a)

items.scenario: You signed your report on 12 June. The annual report is published on 30 June and you read the Chairman's statement in it for the first time. It claims a market share figure that contradicts a note in the audited financial statements, and the contradiction is material. You are satisfied the financial statements themselves are right. You ask management to correct the statement. Management refuses.

items.stem: What is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Neither — engagement documentation belongs to the firm, so the firm may deal with its own property as it chooses once the audit is over
options.misconception: reads ownership of the documentation as freedom to dispose of it, when the same standard that vests ownership in the firm also fixes how long it must be kept
options.why: Ownership settles who may show the papers to a third party; it does not settle how long they live. SQC 1 states both, and the second obligation is not cancelled by the first.

options.text: Only the destruction — storage arrangements are a matter of office practice, the retention rule being about time rather than about custody
options.misconception: reads retention as a period only, when SQC 1 attaches conditions to how the documentation is held during that period
options.why: A period with no custody conditions would be met by papers nobody can find or trust. The standard names confidentiality, safe custody, integrity, accessibility and retrievability precisely so that the file is still a file at the end of the years.

options.text: Only the storage — keeping the report and the financial statements preserves the audit conclusion, which is what the retention period exists to protect
options.misconception: treats the conclusion as the thing retained, when the documentation retained is the evidence and reasoning that supported it
options.why: The report is already public and needs no protection. What retention protects is the record of what was done and why, which is the only thing that can answer a question about the audit years later.

options.text: Both halves — nothing may be deleted or discarded before the end of the retention period, and the firm must keep the documentation in safe custody with its confidentiality, integrity, accessibility and retrievability maintained throughout
options.why: Once the final audit file is assembled, a clock starts running and nothing may leave the file before it ends: the auditor may not delete or discard audit documentation of any nature until the retention period is over, so weeding out the working papers at year three is not open to him. SQC 1 separately requires the firm to have policies protecting how the file is held throughout that period — its confidentiality, its safe custody, its integrity, and its accessibility and retrievability — which an unlocked corridor cupboard does not provide.

citation.ref: the retention period and the requirement for policies on confidentiality, safe custody, integrity, accessibility and retrievability of engagement documentation, read with SA 230 para 16

items.scenario: A firm is moving to a smaller office. Three years into the retention period for a batch of completed audits, a partner proposes to keep only the signed audit report and the financial statements for each of those engagements and to destroy the rest of the working papers, on the basis that the conclusion is what anyone would ever want to see. He also proposes to store what remains in an unlocked corridor cupboard, the sensitive years having passed.

items.stem: How does the Companies Act answer the two points?

options.text: No duty you are subject to is regarded as contravened by reporting in good faith; and the fraud reporting provisions apply mutatis mutandis to the cost accountant conducting the cost audit and to the company secretary in practice conducting the secretarial audit
options.why: The Act protects the reporter: whatever duty an auditor of a company answers to, that duty is treated as unbroken by his reporting the matter, provided he reported it in good faith. A report that turns out to be mistaken is still a report made in good faith. The Act also extends the same provisions mutatis mutandis to the cost accountant conducting cost audit under section 148 and to the company secretary in practice conducting secretarial audit under section 204, so the cost auditor's silence was his own default.

options.text: You are protected, but only against the company — the shareholders and the person named in the report may still proceed against you
options.misconception: narrows a protection expressed in terms of any duty the auditor is subject to down to the company alone
options.why: The words are general and do not pick out the company as the only party against whom the protection runs. Reading it that way would leave the auditor exposed to whoever is unhappy, which is the situation the provision exists to prevent.

options.text: The confidentiality clause in the engagement letter governs, a contract between the parties being enforceable on its own terms
options.misconception: lets a contractual clause displace a statutory protection written for exactly this situation
options.why: The protection is written into the Act and speaks of any duty to which the auditor may be subject, which takes in a duty owed under a contract. A company cannot buy its way out of the reporting scheme by drafting.

options.text: The protection covers you only where a fraud is finally established, and the cost accountant is right that the duty is the statutory auditor's alone
options.misconception: makes the protection depend on the outcome, when the statute attaches it to good faith, and confines to the statutory auditor a duty the Act extends to two other professionals
options.why: A protection available only when the suspicion proves correct would protect nobody, because the auditor has to report before he knows. The Act tests the auditor's state of mind, and it names the cost auditor and the secretarial auditor in the same section.

citation.ref: Section 143(13) and Section 143(14), read with Section 143(12)

items.scenario: You report a suspected fraud in the manner the section and the rules require. A later internal investigation shows there was no fraud — the trail you saw came from a badly designed inter-branch account. The company writes threatening action for breach of the confidentiality clause in your engagement letter. Separately, the cost accountant conducting the company's cost audit tells you he saw the same trail and said nothing, because fraud reporting is the statutory auditor's duty and not his.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the two points?

options.text: Neither point is right — the CAG's role in a government company is confined to appointing the auditor, everything after that being the auditor's own
options.misconception: reduces a scheme of appointment, direction, supplementary audit and test audit down to appointment alone
options.why: Appointment is the first of several powers, not the whole of them. The same section goes on to give directions, a supplementary audit within a fixed period and a test audit, which is why a government company audit is not an ordinary company audit with a different appointer.

options.text: The directions belong in the report, but a test audit may be ordered only where the CAG has first conducted a supplementary audit and found the report deficient
options.misconception: makes one power conditional on the other, when the Act imposes no such sequence
options.why: Nothing ties the test audit to a prior supplementary audit or to a finding of deficiency. The sub-section conferring it turns on the CAG considering it necessary, and no more.

options.text: The audit report itself must include the directions, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts and financial statements; and a test audit may be ordered, being a separate power from supplementary audit
options.why: Where the CAG appoints the auditor of a government company and directs the manner in which the accounts are to be audited, the auditor submits a copy of his audit report to the CAG, and that report is to include the directions issued, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts and financial statements of the company. A separate provision lets the CAG, if he considers it necessary, by an order cause a test audit to be conducted, and it sits beside the supplementary audit rather than inside it.

options.text: A separate letter to the CAG is the right route for the directions, and the test audit objection is good — supplementary audit is the CAG's only power over a signed report
options.misconception: keeps the directions out of the report the Act requires them to be in, and reduces the CAG's powers to the one the company has heard of
options.why: The Act puts the directions and their impact inside the audit report, which is what makes them visible to the members rather than only to the CAG. The test audit is a distinct power conferred by its own sub-section.

citation.ref: Section 143(5) on directions and the auditor's report, read with Section 143(6) and Section 143(7) on test audit

items.scenario: The Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints the statutory auditor of a government company and issues directions on the manner in which the accounts are to be audited. The auditor answers each direction in a separate letter addressed to the CAG's office and keeps his statutory audit report silent about them, saying the directions are correspondence between him and the CAG. The CAG later orders a test audit of the accounts. The company objects that the Act allows the CAG only a supplementary audit.

items.stem: What does clause 3(vii)(a) require?

options.text: Report that the company was not regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues, and state no arrears, the arrears figure being taken as it stands on the last day of the financial year
options.why: The clause asks two things and the team is answering only the second. It first asks whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues, which on these facts it was not. It then asks, if not, for the extent of the arrears — measured, as the clause fixes it, on the last day of the financial year, and counting only those unpaid for more than six months from the date they became payable — and there are none, because everything was cleared in March.
keywords: last day of the financial year

options.text: Report the whole of the provident fund paid during the year as an arrear, the company having been irregular throughout
options.misconception: turns a finding of irregularity into a money figure, when the arrears figure counts only dues still outstanding at the year end and then only those older than six months
options.why: Irregularity and arrears are answered separately. Dues actually paid are not arrears, and converting a year's contributions into an outstanding amount would put a number in the report that nothing in the accounts supports.

options.text: Report nothing at all, no amount being outstanding at the balance sheet date
options.misconception: answers only the arrears half of the clause and drops the question about regularity in depositing
options.why: Clearing the dues before the year end fixes the arrears and does not undo nine months of irregular payment. A reader of the report is entitled to know that the company was running behind, which is precisely what the first half of the clause tells him.

options.text: Report the seven-month arrear as it stood in January, that being the point at which the six-month line was crossed
options.misconception: reports the arrears at their worst point during the year, when the clause fixes the measuring date as the last day of the financial year
options.why: The clause fixes one measuring date, the last day of the financial year concerned. An arrear that existed in January and was paid in March is history by then, and reporting it as an outstanding amount would misstate the balance sheet position.

citation.ref: Clause 3(vii)(a), read with Clause 3(vii)(b)

items.scenario: A company fell behind on provident fund contributions from June onwards. By January the oldest unpaid contribution was seven months old. In March, before the year end, the company cleared every rupee of provident fund dues. At the balance sheet date nothing at all is outstanding, and nothing is disputed. The audit team plans to report nothing under the statutory dues clause, since there is no arrear on the last day of the year.

items.stem: What does section 141(3)(g) make of that?

options.text: The appointments in both firms are counted collectively against the one specified number attaching to Mr T, so he is over the limit and cannot take another
options.why: The section deals expressly with a partner who is also a partner of any other firm or firms of auditors, and says the number of companies which may be taken into account collectively by all the firms shall not exceed the specified number in relation to each of the partners. The ceiling belongs to the person, so two registers that each look clean do not create two allowances.
keywords: any other firm or firms of auditors

options.text: Only the appointments in the firm where Mr T is the engagement partner count; appointments signed by his fellow partners do not touch his number
options.misconception: counts the audits a partner personally signs, when the count runs on appointments held in his name in a firm of which he is a partner
options.why: The count is of appointments held, not of reports signed. Reading it the other way would let a firm move a name onto the report to free up somebody's headroom, which is the manoeuvre the section is written against.

options.text: Nothing — being a partner in two firms is itself a disqualification, so the counting question never arises
options.misconception: invents a bar on multiple partnerships, when the section assumes it is possible and only regulates how the appointments are counted
options.why: Nothing in the section forbids a member from being a partner in more than one firm. The provision is drafted on the footing that he may be, and deals with the consequence for the count.

options.text: Each firm has its own ceiling, so both managing partners are right and Mr T may take further appointments in either
options.misconception: gives the ceiling to the firm, when the section fixes it in relation to each partner and adds his appointments across firms
options.why: A ceiling that multiplied with the number of firms a person joined would be no ceiling at all. The provision anticipates exactly this arrangement and closes it by counting collectively.

citation.ref: The Explanations to Section 141(3)(g) on a partner of more than one firm and on the specified number for a firm

items.scenario: Mr T is a partner in two audit firms at once, firm X and firm Y, and is in full-time practice. Company audits are held in his name in both firms. Firm X's managing partner checks only firm X's register and finds Mr T well inside the limit there. Firm Y's managing partner checks only firm Y's register and reaches the same conclusion. Neither register shows the other firm's appointments. Together the two sets exceed the specified number.

items.stem: What is the consequence in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Nothing happens, the bonds not having been sold, redeemed or transferred and Mrs Rao remaining their owner throughout
options.misconception: reads the lock-in as broken only by a sale, when the section reaches conversion into money and expressly deems a loan against the bonds to be one
options.why: Ownership is not the test. The Explanation was written because a loan against the security puts the money in the assessee's hands while leaving the paper in her name, which is economically the same as cashing the bonds in.

options.text: The amount is charged in previous year 2025-26, but as a short-term capital gain, the bonds having been held for only about three years
options.misconception: applies the holding period of the bonds when the section deems the charge to relate to the long-term capital asset originally transferred
options.why: The charge is not on a gain from the bonds. It restores the gain on the original asset, which was long-term, and the section says so by deeming the amount to be income chargeable under capital gains relating to a long-term capital asset.

options.text: The exemption allowed for the year of the original sale is withdrawn by rectifying that year's assessment
options.misconception: reopens the year in which the exemption was allowed, when the section charges the year of the transfer or conversion
options.why: Nothing about the earlier assessment was wrong when it was made — the investment was genuine and within time. The section charges the previous year in which the specified asset is transferred or converted, which is 2025-26.

options.text: The exempted gain is deemed to be long-term capital gains of previous year 2025-26, taking a loan on the security of the bonds being a deemed conversion of them into money
options.why: The section withdraws the exemption where the specified asset is transferred or converted into money within five years from the date of its acquisition, and its Explanation says that an assessee who takes any loan or advance on the security of such specified asset is deemed to have converted it into money on the date the loan is taken. September 2022 to November 2025 is inside the five years, so the gain earlier exempted is charged as long-term capital gains of the year the loan is taken.
keywords: loan or advance on the security

citation.ref: Section 54EC(2) with its Explanation, read with Section 54EC(1)

items.scenario: Mrs Rao sold a plot of land in June 2022 and invested the whole of the resulting long-term capital gain in specified bonds in September 2022, within the time the section allows. The exemption was allowed in full. She still holds the bonds. In November 2025 she pledges them with her bank as security for a personal loan, and the bank sanctions the loan against that security. The bonds themselves are not sold, redeemed or transferred to anybody.

items.stem: What is the full value of the consideration for computing capital gains?

options.text: ₹80 lakh, the price actually agreed and actually received
options.misconception: ignores the deeming altogether once an agreement date exists
options.why: An agreement fixes the price between the parties. Section 50C substitutes the stamp value for the price wherever the tolerance is crossed, and the agreement only decides which stamp value is looked at.

options.text: ₹1.05 crore, the stamp value on the date of registration
options.why: The first proviso does let the stamp value on the date of the agreement be taken where the agreement date and the registration date differ, but the second proviso allows that only where part of the consideration was received by way of an account payee cheque or bank draft, by electronic clearing system, or by another prescribed electronic mode, on or before the date of the agreement. Cash fails that condition, so the registration date governs, and ₹1.05 crore exceeds one hundred and ten per cent of ₹80 lakh, which is ₹88 lakh, so the stamp value replaces the price in full.
keywords: on or before the date of the agreement

options.text: ₹1.05 crore, and the seller cannot ask for the plot to be referred to a Valuation Officer, having agreed the price himself in 2023
options.misconception: denies a reference the Act allows whenever the assessee claims the stamp value exceeds fair market value and has not disputed it before the stamp authority
options.why: The figure is right and the second half is wrong. Where the assessee claims that the stamp value exceeds the fair market value and has not disputed that value in any appeal or revision before the stamp authority, the Assessing Officer may refer the valuation to a Valuation Officer. Having signed an agreement two years earlier takes nothing away from that.

options.text: ₹84 lakh, the stamp value on the date of the agreement, an advance having been paid on that day
options.misconception: applies the first proviso without the payment-mode condition the second proviso attaches to it
options.why: The provisos work as a pair. The relief for a delayed registration is available only to a seller who took part of the price through the banking system on or before the agreement date, and cash is exactly what the condition excludes.

citation.ref: The first and second provisos to Section 50C(1), read with Section 50C(2)

items.scenario: An agreement to sell a plot was signed in May 2023 fixing the consideration at ₹80 lakh. On that day the buyer handed over ₹6 lakh in cash as advance, and nothing was paid by cheque, draft or through a bank. The conveyance was registered in previous year 2025-26 and the balance was then paid by bank transfer. The stamp valuation authority's value was ₹84 lakh on the date of the agreement and ₹1.05 crore on the date of registration.

items.stem: How is the ₹5,00,000 dealt with?

options.text: As income from other sources of previous year 2025-26, an advance received on the transfer of a capital asset being chargeable in the year of receipt
options.misconception: charges an advance that was neither forfeited nor followed by a failed negotiation, when both are conditions of the charge
options.why: There is no charge on advances as such. The provision is aimed at money the seller keeps when the deal collapses, and it names both the forfeiture and the failure of the negotiations as conditions.

options.text: As income from other sources in previous year 2025-26 and again as part of the consideration in the capital gains computation
options.misconception: charges the same receipt under two heads, which the scheme of section 51 and its proviso exists to prevent
options.why: The Act is careful never to tax a forfeited advance under other sources and to deduct it from cost as well. The same instinct rules out charging an advance that became part of the price under two heads at once.

options.text: As part of the ₹90,00,000 full value of consideration in the capital gains computation, and nowhere else
options.why: The charge on an advance in the income from other sources chapter bites only where the seller keeps the money and the talks do not result in transfer of that capital asset. Both conditions fail here, because the money was never forfeited and the sale went through. So the advance is simply part of the price, and it enters the computation as part of the full value of consideration received on the transfer.

options.text: As a deduction from the cost of acquisition of the house under section 51
options.misconception: applies section 51, which deals with an advance retained on a failed negotiation, to an advance that became part of the sale price
options.why: Section 51 reduces the cost by money the owner kept for nothing. Here the ₹5,00,000 bought the buyer part of a house, so treating it as a cost reduction would tax the same amount twice — once as consideration and once as a smaller cost.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(ix), read with Section 51 and its proviso and Section 48

items.scenario: Mr Sen owns a house he bought in 2009. In April 2025 a buyer pays him ₹5,00,000 as an advance under an agreement to sell. The sale goes through in December 2025 and the buyer pays the balance, so the total consideration Mr Sen receives is ₹90,00,000 including that advance. Nothing was forfeited and no negotiation failed.

items.stem: What does section 194-IA require?

options.text: Deduction on ₹8,00,000, the excess of the stamp duty value over the consideration
options.misconception: applies the rate to the difference between the two figures rather than to the higher of them
options.why: The section does not tax a gap. It names one base, the higher of the two, and the rate runs on the whole of it.

options.text: No deduction at all, the consideration being below fifty lakh rupees
options.misconception: reads the exclusion as turning on the consideration alone, when it requires the consideration and the stamp duty value both to be below the figure
options.why: The word "both" is doing the work in that sub-section. It was written that way so that a price recorded below the threshold could not take a property out of the section while the stamp value sat well above it.

options.text: Deduction on ₹48,00,000, tax at source being a deduction out of a payment and no payment being made of the stamp duty value
options.misconception: assumes the base must be money that actually moves, when the section names the higher of the consideration and the stamp duty value
options.why: Tax at source is deducted out of the payment, and the section still measures it on the higher figure. That is deliberate: the same anti-understatement idea runs through the capital gains provisions for immovable property.

options.text: Deduction on ₹56,00,000, the stamp duty value being the higher of the two figures — the exclusion needs the consideration and the stamp duty value to be below fifty lakh
options.why: The section fixes the deduction by reference to such sum or the stamp duty value of the property, whichever is higher, so ₹56,00,000 is the base. The exclusion in the section is worded so that it applies only where the consideration and the stamp duty value are both less than fifty lakh rupees, and here one of them is not.
keywords: both less than fifty lakh rupees

citation.ref: Section 194-IA(1) and Section 194-IA(2), read with the Explanation to Section 194-IA

items.scenario: An individual buys a flat from a resident seller. The agreed price is ₹48,00,000. The stamp duty value of the flat is ₹56,00,000. The buyer says no deduction is due because the price is under the fifty lakh figure the section mentions, and in any event that if anything is deductible it can only be on the money he actually pays.

items.stem: Is twenty per cent right?

options.text: No — and no deduction at all is due, a tax residency certificate exempting the payment from deduction of tax at source
options.misconception: turns evidence of residence into an exemption from deduction, when it only removes the higher-rate rule and leaves the ordinary rate to apply
options.why: A tax residency certificate proves where the payee lives and lets the treaty be applied. It does not remove the charge or the duty to deduct; the treaty rate on royalty is still a rate.

options.text: Yes — the absence of a permanent account number is fatal in every case, the section admitting no exception
options.misconception: reads section 206AA as absolute, when it carries its own sub-section carving out prescribed payments to non-residents and foreign companies
options.why: The exception is inside the section itself. It exists because a foreign payee with no Indian income other than the payment has no reason to hold a permanent account number, and the details prescribed give the department the same traceability.

options.text: No — the section does not apply to this payment, the prescribed details having been furnished, so tax is deducted at the rate under the Act or the treaty, whichever is more beneficial
options.why: Section 206AA has a sub-section taking certain payments to a non-resident or a foreign company out of it subject to prescribed conditions, and Rule 37BC prescribes them for royalty among other payments: the name, e-mail address, contact number and address in the country of residence, a tax residency certificate where that country issues one, and the Tax Identification Number in that country. All of them have been given, so the higher-rate rule is displaced.

options.text: Yes — the relief for a payee with no permanent account number is confined to interest on long-term bonds, and royalty is outside it
options.misconception: stops at the first clause of the exempting sub-section and misses the limb covering any other payment subject to prescribed conditions
options.why: Interest on long-term bonds is named in the sub-section, and the clause after it covers any other payment subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Rule 37BC is that prescription and it names royalty in terms.

citation.ref: Section 206AA(7) read with Rule 37BC of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Section 90(2)

items.scenario: Orion Ltd pays royalty to a company incorporated and resident in the United Kingdom that has no permanent account number in India. Before the payment the UK company gives Orion its name, its e-mail address, its contact number, its address in the United Kingdom, a tax residency certificate issued by the UK authorities and its UK taxpayer identification number. Orion's accountant proposes to deduct at twenty per cent because no permanent account number was quoted.

items.stem: How is the credit for the tax deducted allocated?

options.text: Half to Mrs Iyer, provided Mr Iyer files a declaration with the tenant and the tenant reports the deduction in her name in its statement
options.why: Rule 37BA(2) meets the case where income carrying the deducted tax — all of it, or only a slice — proves assessable in the hands of a person other than the deductee. The credit then goes to that other person and not to the deductee. It is conditional: the deductee files a declaration with the deductor giving the other person's name, address and permanent account number and the reasons, and the deductor reports the deduction in that person's name.
keywords: assessable in the hands of a person other than the deductee

options.text: The whole to Mr Iyer, credit belonging to the person named as deductee in the tenant's statement and in the certificate
options.misconception: ties credit to the name on the certificate, when the rule follows the person in whose hands the income is assessable
options.why: The certificate records who the money was paid to. The rule was written because that is often not the person taxed on it, and co-owned property is the plainest example of the mismatch.

options.text: Half to Mrs Iyer automatically, the moment she offers her share of the rent in her return
options.misconception: drops the declaration and the deductor's reporting, which the rule makes conditions of the transfer of credit
options.why: The rule gives the credit and then says how. Without the declaration and the corresponding reporting there is nothing in the department's records linking her return to the tenant's deduction, and the credit cannot be matched.

options.text: Neither may claim it as credit; Mrs Iyer must instead apply for a refund of her share of the tax under section 239
options.misconception: sends a credit the rules allocate down a refund route, when the refund follows from the credit rather than replacing it
options.why: A refund arises where the credit allowed exceeds the tax payable. It is the consequence of getting the credit, not an alternative to it, so the allocation question has to be answered first either way.

citation.ref: Rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, read with Section 199(1) and Section 199(3)

items.scenario: A house is owned equally by Mr and Mrs Iyer. The tenant pays the whole rent into Mr Iyer's bank account and deducts tax at source on it, showing Mr Iyer as the deductee in its statement. Half the rent is assessable in Mrs Iyer's hands as a co-owner, and she offers it in her return. Mr Iyer offers his half in his. Both then claim the whole of the tax deducted, each saying the other cannot have it.

items.stem: In whose hands, if anyone's, is the ₹7,00,000 chargeable?

options.text: Basalt Ltd's, in previous year 2025-26, as the successor in business
options.why: Section 41(1) has a second limb for exactly this pattern. Where the successor in business obtains, in cash or in any other manner, a benefit in respect of a trading liability by way of remission or cessation of it, the value of that benefit is deemed to be profits and gains of business of the successor and is charged as his income of that previous year. An amalgamated company taking over the amalgamating company's business is a successor in business for this purpose.
keywords: deemed to be profits and gains of business

options.text: Nobody's — the deduction was allowed to Aster Ltd, and Aster Ltd has ceased to exist
options.misconception: reads section 41(1) as reaching only the person allowed the deduction, when the sub-section names the successor in business separately
options.why: That is what the first limb alone would produce, and it is why the second limb was written. Otherwise every allowed deduction could be made unrecoverable by a reorganisation, which is a result the drafting closes off.

options.text: Basalt Ltd's, but under income from other sources, Basalt never having claimed the deduction
options.misconception: shifts the head of income when the sub-section deems the amount to be profits and gains of business or profession
options.why: The sub-section fixes the head itself, and it says profits and gains of business or profession. Whether the successor claimed the original deduction is not a question the provision asks.

options.text: Aster Ltd's, by reopening the assessment of the year in which the amalgamation took effect
options.misconception: reopens an earlier year, when the charge falls in the previous year in which the benefit is obtained
options.why: Nothing about the amalgamation year was wrong. The charge attaches to the year in which the remission occurs and the benefit is obtained, which is previous year 2025-26.

citation.ref: Section 41(1)(b) read with Explanation 2 to Section 41(1) defining successor in business

items.scenario: Aster Ltd amalgamated into Basalt Ltd in 2023 and the whole of Aster's business was taken over as a going concern. In 2018 Aster had bought goods on credit and had been allowed a deduction for the purchase in its own assessment. In previous year 2025-26 that supplier writes off the unpaid balance of ₹7,00,000 and tells Basalt the debt is closed. Aster no longer exists.

items.stem: What survives the conditions in section 40(b)?

options.text: Only the two active partners' remuneration from 1 October 2025 onwards; R's is disallowed in full and the retrospective half-year is disallowed as well
options.why: The ceiling is the last gate, not the first. Remuneration to a partner who is not a working partner is disallowed outright, and R takes no part in the conduct of the business. Remuneration to the working partners is authorised by the deed, but the payment for 1 April to 30 September relates to a period prior to the date of that deed and no earlier deed authorised it, so that part is disallowed too.

options.text: All of it, every amount being inside the statutory ceiling and the deed being binding on the partners according to its own terms
options.misconception: treats the ceiling as the whole test, when three qualifying conditions have to be met before the ceiling is ever reached
options.why: Being within the ceiling is necessary and not sufficient. The section first asks who was paid, whether the deed authorised it, and what period it relates to, and only then applies the limit on book profit.

options.text: Everything except the retrospective half-year — R's remuneration is authorised by the deed, and authorisation is what the section asks for
options.misconception: reads deed authorisation as curing the requirement that the recipient be a working partner, when they are separate conditions
options.why: The conditions stack rather than substitute. A deed may authorise a payment to a sleeping partner and the payment is still disallowed, because the first condition asks what the partner does and not what the deed says.

options.text: Everything except R's remuneration — the deed's own words make the authorisation effective from 1 April 2025
options.misconception: lets partners backdate an authorisation, when the Act measures the period against the date of the deed rather than against the date the deed nominates
