items.scenario: Konark Cements Ltd is a company. Its turnover for previous year 2025-26 is above the limit at which section 44AB requires a person carrying on business to get his accounts audited. Its accounts for that year have been audited by its statutory auditor under the Companies Act, 2013, and that audit was completed well before the specified date. The finance head takes the view that the statutory audit is the end of the matter and that nothing further is owed under section 44AB.

items.stem: Which of the two amounts does section 43B(h) push out of previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Neither — both were paid on 30 June 2026, before the due date for furnishing the return, which preserves the deduction for previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: applies the first proviso to section 43B, which rescues the other clauses but was not extended to clause (h)
options.why: The first proviso to section 43B saves a deduction where the money actually goes out by the date the return is due. Clause (h) was deliberately left out of that rescue, so a payment in June does nothing for the year that ended in March.

options.text: Only the ₹18,00,000, the larger sum being the one the clause was aimed at
options.misconception: sizes the disallowance by the amount owed rather than by the class the supplier is registered in
options.why: Clause (h) has no monetary floor and no ceiling. What decides it is whether the supplier is a micro or small enterprise and whether the sum is outstanding beyond the section 15 time limit at the year end.

options.text: Only the ₹9,00,000 owed to Anand Tools
options.why: Clause (h) of section 43B bites where a micro or small enterprise is still owed money after the time limit specified in section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006 has gone by. A medium enterprise is not named in the clause, so the ₹18,00,000 owed to Suraj Components stays outside it and is deducted on accrual. The ₹9,00,000 owed to Anand Tools is past the agreed forty-day term and still unpaid at the year end, so it waits for previous year 2026-27, the year of actual payment.

options.text: Both amounts, the payment discipline of the MSMED Act running to every enterprise registered under it
options.misconception: extends clause (h) to a medium enterprise, which the clause does not name, when the MSMED Act's own registration covers all three sizes
options.why: Registration under the MSMED Act, 2006 is one thing and the class of supplier clause (h) names is another. The clause names a micro or small enterprise and stops there, which is why the size of the supplier has to be read off the registration before anything else.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h) with the first proviso to Section 43B, read with Section 15, Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006

items.scenario: Vindhya Ltd bought goods on 5 December 2025 from two suppliers, under written agreements fixing payment within forty days of delivery in each case. It owes ₹18,00,000 to Suraj Components, which is registered under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 as a medium enterprise, and ₹9,00,000 to Anand Tools, registered under the same Act as a small enterprise. Both amounts are unpaid at 31 March 2026 and both are paid on 30 June 2026. The company's return for assessment year 2026-27 is due on 31 October 2026.

items.stem: How much of the ₹50,00,000 is deductible under section 37(1)?

options.text: ₹18,00,000 — the amounts covered by section 80G and section 35CCD, allowed through section 37(1)
options.misconception: routes the two other reliefs through the residuary section, when each is a claim under its own section with its own computation
options.why: A deduction under section 80G is made from gross total income and a deduction under section 35CCD is a business deduction under its own section. Neither becomes a section 37(1) claim, and the arithmetic of ₹12,00,000 plus ₹6,00,000 belongs to those sections.

options.text: ₹32,00,000 — everything except the two sums that find relief elsewhere
options.misconception: nets the other reliefs out of section 37(1), when Explanation 2 disallows the whole corporate social responsibility spend under that section and the others stand on their own
options.why: Explanation 2 is not a rule about double deduction. It removes the whole class of spending from section 37(1), so there is no residue to allow under that section after the other claims are taken out.

options.text: ₹50,00,000 — the spending is compulsory under the Companies Act, so it is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business
options.misconception: argues from the compulsion, when Explanation 2 deems the expenditure not to be for the business whatever made the company incur it
options.why: Compulsion under another statute is what created the class of expenditure, and Parliament answered it directly. The Explanation deems the spending not to be for the purposes of the business, which settles the wholly and exclusively test before it is reached.

options.text: Nothing under section 37(1), although ₹12,00,000 may still be claimed under section 80G and ₹6,00,000 under section 35CCD
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 37(1) picks up whatever an assessee spends on the activities relating to corporate social responsibility that section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 imposes, and says such outgo shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred in running a business at all. That shuts section 37(1) on the whole ₹50,00,000. The other two claims survive because section 80G and section 35CCD are separate provisions with their own conditions, and the Explanation speaks only to the residuary section.
keywords: activities relating to corporate social responsibility
shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred

citation.ref: Explanation 2 to Section 37(1), read with Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, Section 80G and Section 35CCD

items.scenario: Bharat Alloys Ltd spends ₹50,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 discharging its corporate social responsibility obligation under section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. Of that, ₹12,00,000 was a contribution to a fund for which a deduction under section 80G is available to the company, and ₹6,00,000 was spent on a skill development project of the kind section 35CCD covers, whose conditions the company satisfies. The whole ₹50,00,000 is debited to the profit and loss account and claimed under section 37(1).

items.stem: How do the reach of the standards and the conflict work out?

options.text: They bind Mr Bose and Coral Ltd but not Ms Anita, and where a standard conflicts with the Act the Act prevails
options.why: The standards notified under section 145(2) apply to a person following the mercantile system of accounting, and reach only two heads of income — profits and gains of business or profession, plus whatever falls under other sources. They do not apply to an individual or Hindu undivided family who is not required to get his accounts audited under section 44AB. Ms Anita has neither head and keeps cash accounts, so nothing in them reaches her. On the second question the standards themselves say that where there is a conflict the provisions of the Act shall prevail to that extent.
keywords: profits and gains of business or profession
the provisions of the Act shall prevail

options.text: They bind Coral Ltd alone, a company being the only assessee section 145(2) reaches
options.misconception: confines the standards to companies, when they turn on the method of accounting and the head of income rather than on the form of the assessee
options.why: Section 145(1) reaches income taxed under the business-or-profession head and income taxed under other sources, computed in accordance with the cash or mercantile system regularly employed by the assessee. Mr Bose is squarely within it.

options.text: They bind Mr Bose and Coral Ltd, and on a conflict the standard prevails, that being the point of notifying them
options.misconception: gets the reach right and inverts the conflict rule, reading the standards as an override rather than a computation aid
options.why: The standards exist to detach the tax computation from accounting choices, not to displace the charge. The conflict rule runs the other way and the Act governs.

options.text: They bind all three as notified standards of general application, and on a conflict the later notification prevails over the Act
options.misconception: gives a notification precedence over the statute it was issued under, when the standards say the opposite in their own terms
options.why: A standard notified under section 145(2) draws its whole force from the section. It cannot displace the Act, and it says so, which is why the conflict question has only one answer.

citation.ref: Sections 145(1) and 145(2), read with the preamble and scope of the notified Income Computation and Disclosure Standards I to X

items.scenario: Three assessees ask whether the income computation and disclosure standards apply to them for previous year 2025-26. Ms Anita has only salary income and income from house property and keeps her personal accounts on the cash basis. Mr Bose carries on a business, follows the mercantile system and is required to get his accounts audited under section 44AB. Coral Ltd follows the mercantile system and has business income and interest income. Separately, Coral Ltd finds one requirement in a standard that cannot stand with an express provision of the Act.

items.stem: How does section 2(47) treat what she did?

options.text: Nothing in section 2(47) reaches it — a flat moves for tax purposes only on a registered conveyance, and none was executed
options.misconception: reads section 2(47) as needing a conveyance, when the definition is inclusive and clause (vi) was written for exactly the route taken here
options.why: Section 2(47) opens with the word includes and then names relinquishment, extinguishment of rights, compulsory acquisition, part performance and the arrangement in clause (vi) alongside a sale. A conveyance is one route into the definition, not the gate to it.

options.text: Clause (v) reaches it — the buyer was let into possession of the flat in part performance of a contract
options.misconception: reaches for the part-performance clause, which needs the immovable property itself to sit under a contract answering section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
options.why: Clause (v) is about immovable property whose possession the buyer is allowed to take or keep under a contract answering section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. What was contracted for and sold here was the shares, and clause (vi) is the limb that catches an arrangement of that shape.

options.text: Nothing in section 2(47) reaches it, and the ₹95,00,000 is a capital receipt not chargeable to tax
options.misconception: reads the absence of a conveyance as the absence of any transfer, when the sale of the shares is itself a transfer under clause (i)
options.why: A sale of shares is the sale of a capital asset and is a transfer under clause (i) of section 2(47) whatever else is true of the flat. Clause (vi) is what closes the further argument that the immovable property did not move.

options.text: Clause (vi) reaches it — a transaction which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of immovable property, including by acquiring shares in a co-operative society
options.why: Clause (vi) of section 2(47) covers any transaction, whether by way of becoming a member of or acquiring shares in a co-operative society, company or other association of persons, or by way of any agreement or arrangement or in any other manner whatsoever, which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of any immovable property. Handing over the shares handed over the flat, and the clause was written so that the society's ownership of the building answers nothing.
keywords: acquiring shares in a co-operative society

citation.ref: Section 2(47)(vi), read with Section 2(47)(i), Section 2(47)(v) and Section 45(1)

items.scenario: Mrs Rao holds shares in a co-operative housing society which carry with them the right to occupy flat 12B in the society's building. In January 2026 she sells those shares to a buyer for ₹95,00,000 and the buyer moves into the flat. The flat itself is never conveyed to anyone; the society's records simply show a new shareholder in her place, and the building stays in the society's name throughout. She says no immovable property was transferred by her at all.

items.stem: What arises in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: A short-term capital gain of ₹2,00,000, a depreciated item having no cost left to set against it
options.misconception: treats the whole consideration as gain, when section 50(1) sets it against the opening written down value of the block before anything is left over
options.why: The block, not the individual item, is the unit of computation. Section 50(1) subtracts the opening written down value of the whole block, which is ₹9,00,000, so there is nothing for the ₹2,00,000 to exceed.

options.text: No capital gain and no capital loss — the ₹2,00,000 comes off the block and depreciation runs on the reduced written down value of ₹7,00,000
options.why: Section 50 operates in two cases and no others. Section 50(1) creates a short-term capital gain only where the consideration exceeds the aggregate of the transfer expenditure, the opening written down value and the actual cost of any asset acquired during the year, and section 50(2) creates a gain or loss only where the block ceases to exist. Neither happens here: ₹2,00,000 is well below ₹9,00,000 and assets remain in the block. The money received is simply deducted from the written down value under section 43(6)(c), leaving ₹7,00,000 to depreciate.
keywords: deducted from the written down value

options.text: A short-term capital loss of ₹7,00,000, being the written down value less the consideration
options.misconception: strikes a loss on a block that survives, when section 50(2) reaches only the case where the block ceases to exist at the end of the year
options.why: A loss under section 50(2) needs every asset in the block to have gone. While assets remain, the shortfall is not a loss at all; it stays inside the block as written down value and is recovered through depreciation over the following years.

options.text: No capital gain, and no depreciation either for the year, an asset having gone out of the block during it
options.misconception: reads a sale out of a block as stopping depreciation, when depreciation continues on whatever written down value the block still carries
options.why: Depreciation under section 32 is computed on the written down value of the block as it stands after the year's additions and deductions. A sale reduces that value; it does not switch the allowance off.

citation.ref: Sections 50(1) and 50(2), read with Section 43(6)(c) and Section 32(1)

items.scenario: Nilgiri Associates, a firm, has one block of furniture and fittings. The written down value of the block on 1 April 2025 is ₹9,00,000. Nothing is bought for the block during previous year 2025-26. One item out of the block is sold in October 2025 for ₹2,00,000, with no expenditure on the transfer. Several items remain in the block on 31 March 2026. The partner preparing the computation wants to strike a short-term capital loss on the sale.

items.stem: What is charged in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Business profit of ₹20,00,000 on the plot sold, being ₹26,00,000 less the indexed cost of ₹6,00,000, and no capital gain
options.misconception: collapses the two charges into one, when section 45(2) splits the surplus at the fair market value on the date of conversion
options.why: The rise up to the date of conversion accrued to him as the owner of a capital asset and stays under capital gains with its indexation and its long-term character. Only the rise after conversion was earned as a trader.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 and business profit of ₹6,00,000, on the one plot alone
options.why: Section 45(2) charges the capital gain in the previous year in which the stock-in-trade is sold or otherwise transferred, so only the plot actually sold is charged and the other three wait for the years in which they go. On that plot the fair market value on the date of conversion, ₹20,00,000, is the deemed full value of consideration, and against the indexed cost of ₹6,00,000 it gives ₹14,00,000. The excess of the ₹26,00,000 sale price over that same ₹20,00,000 is business profit of ₹6,00,000.
keywords: in which the stock-in-trade is sold
fair market value on the date of conversion

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 in previous year 2023-24 and business profit of ₹6,00,000 in previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: charges the capital gain in the year of conversion, when section 45(2) postpones it to the year the stock is sold
options.why: Conversion is a transfer under section 2(47)(iv), which is why a capital gain arises at all, but section 45(2) exists to move the charge to the year of sale. Nothing is taxable in 2023-24.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹56,00,000 on all four plots and business profit of ₹6,00,000 on the one sold
options.misconception: charges the gain on the whole of the converted stock in the year any part of it is sold, when section 45(2) is applied plot by plot as each is sold
options.why: The charge is tied to the sale of the stock-in-trade, and three plots have not been sold. Their gain is computed on the same conversion-date value when their turn comes, in the year each of them goes.

citation.ref: Section 45(2) read with Section 2(47)(iv) and Section 48

items.scenario: Mr Sinha bought four identical plots in 2010. On 1 July 2023 he converted all four into stock-in-trade of his property business, when the fair market value of each plot was ₹20,00,000. The indexed cost of acquisition of each plot, taken up to the year of conversion, is ₹6,00,000. In previous year 2025-26 he sold one of the four plots for ₹26,00,000. The other three are still held as stock on 31 March 2026.

items.stem: In which previous year is the ₹9,00,000 charged under the head capital gains?

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, but under income from other sources rather than capital gains, her entitlement not being final
options.misconception: moves an interim payment of compensation to another head, when section 56(2)(viii) sends only the interest on compensation there
options.why: Section 56(2)(viii) puts interest received on compensation or on enhanced compensation under income from other sources. The compensation itself, interim or final, is deemed by section 45(5) to be income under capital gains.

options.text: In the previous year in which the final order of the High Court is made, so neither previous year 2025-26 nor previous year 2026-27
options.why: The proviso to section 45(5) deals with compensation an assessee has collected under an interim order of a court, a Tribunal or some other authority. Such a receipt is treated as chargeable under the head capital gains only in the year the final order of that court, Tribunal or authority arrives. Receipt is the test for enhanced compensation under clause (b), and this proviso is the one exception to it, because money paid under an interim order can still be taken back.
keywords: chargeable under the head capital gains

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, section 45(5)(b) charging enhanced compensation in the year it is received
options.misconception: applies the receipt rule in clause (b) without its proviso, which is written for a payment made under an interim order
options.why: Clause (b) does charge enhanced compensation in the year of receipt, and that is the right rule for money paid under a final decree. The proviso carves out the interim payment precisely because the entitlement to it is not yet settled.

options.text: Previous year 2025-26, the year in which the interim order was made
options.misconception: takes the date of the interim order as the charging event, when the proviso points at the final order and not at the interim one
options.why: The proviso names the previous year in which the final order is made. The interim order is what triggers the proviso; it is not the date the proviso fixes.

citation.ref: Proviso to Section 45(5), read with Section 45(5)(b) and Section 56(2)(viii)

items.scenario: Ms Fernandes's land was compulsorily acquired and she went to court for more compensation. On 12 March 2026, with the appeal still pending, the High Court made an interim order directing the acquiring authority to pay her ₹9,00,000 against her claim for enhancement. The ₹9,00,000 reached her on 20 May 2026. The final order in the appeal had still not been made by 31 March 2027, and the authority may yet recover the money if the appeal fails.

items.stem: Is the transaction a slump sale under section 2(42C)?

options.text: Yes, but only because the consideration is wholly in shares; had any part of it been cash the definition would have failed
options.misconception: makes the form of the consideration the test, when the clause asks only that it be a lump sum with no values assigned to individual assets and liabilities
options.why: Cash, shares or a mixture of the two are all capable of being a lump sum consideration. What the clause forbids is the assignment of values to the individual assets and liabilities, which is what would turn the deal into an itemised sale.

options.text: No — a slump sale needs a sale, and shares issued in exchange for an undertaking are not a sale
options.misconception: reads the clause as it stood before the 2021 amendment, which replaced the requirement of a sale with a transfer by any means
options.why: Before 2021 the clause spoke of the transfer of an undertaking as a result of the sale, and a slump exchange was argued to be outside it. The amendment was made to end that argument and it did.

options.text: No — the land was valued at ₹8 crore, so values were assigned to individual assets and the definition fails
options.misconception: counts a stamp duty valuation as an assignment of values, which Explanation 2 to the clause says it is not
options.why: A stamp duty valuation is forced on the parties by another law and says nothing about how they priced the undertaking between themselves. Explanation 2 was written so that complying with the stamp law does not cost the transaction its character.

options.text: Yes on both points — the clause now covers a transfer by any means, and a valuation made only for stamp duty is not an assignment of values
options.why: Section 2(42C) treats a slump sale as one or more undertakings passing across by any means for a single price, without values being assigned to what each separate asset and each separate liability is worth. The words by any means were put into the clause in 2021 to bring an exchange, and every other mode of transfer, inside it. Explanation 2 to the clause then says that fixing what an asset or a liability is worth is not an assignment of values to the separate items, where the reason for fixing it is the sole purpose of payment of stamp duty, a registration charge or a like levy.
keywords: sole purpose of payment of stamp duty

citation.ref: Section 2(42C) with Explanation 2, as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, read with Section 50B

items.scenario: Kaveri Ltd transfers its packaging undertaking to Nila Ltd as a going concern. Nila Ltd pays no cash; it issues its own equity shares to Kaveri Ltd for the undertaking. The agreement fixes no value for any individual asset or liability of the undertaking, but the land inside it was separately valued at ₹8 crore for the sole purpose of working out the stamp duty on the conveyance. Kaveri Ltd says this cannot be a slump sale: there was no sale, only an exchange, and in any case a value was assigned to the land.

items.stem: What is the annual value of the four unsold flats for those two years?

options.text: Nil for both years — the relief runs for two further financial years after the one in which the completion certificate was obtained
options.why: Section 23(5) reaches a building, or the land attached to one, that a business keeps as unsold stock. Where such a flat is held as stock-in-trade and nobody occupies it on rent for the whole previous year or for any slice of it, its annual value is taken as nil, and that relief lasts two further financial years after the one in which the local authority issued the certificate of completion. Here it came on 10 September 2024, inside financial year 2024-25, so the relief runs to 31 March 2027 and covers both previous years.

options.text: Nil in both years and in every later year as well, a building held as stock-in-trade being a trading asset outside the head altogether
options.misconception: reads section 23(5) as putting stock-in-trade outside house property, when it is a time-limited relief written inside the head
options.why: The sub-section sits in section 23, which computes annual value under the head income from house property, and it fixes the annual value at nil only for the stated period. Once that period ends, section 23(1) applies to the unsold flats again.

options.text: The expected rent in both years — the company is the owner and section 23(1)(a) taxes the sum for which the property might reasonably be let
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 23(1)(a) without section 23(5), which was inserted for a builder's unsold stock
options.why: Section 23(1)(a) is the default and would tax an empty flat on what it might fetch. Section 23(5) suspends that default for a limited period so that a builder is not taxed on rent he never had while the stock is still fresh.

options.text: Nil for previous year 2025-26 and the expected rent for previous year 2026-27, the two years running from the date of the certificate
options.misconception: measures the two years from the date of the certificate, when the sub-section runs them from the end of the financial year in which it was obtained
options.why: Running from the date would end the relief on 10 September 2026 and split previous year 2026-27 in half. The sub-section avoids that by measuring from the end of the financial year, so the relief ends on a 31 March.

citation.ref: Section 23(5), read with Section 22 and Section 23(1)(a)

items.scenario: Meru Developers Ltd builds flats for sale and holds them as stock-in-trade of its business. The certificate of completion of construction for one building was obtained from the local authority on 10 September 2024. Four flats in that building were unsold and were not let at any time during previous year 2025-26 or previous year 2026-27. The Assessing Officer proposes to tax a notional annual value on the four flats in both years.

items.stem: How much of the ₹6,00,000 is clubbed with Mr Deshmukh for previous year 2025-26, and under which head?

options.text: Nothing — once the money is put into her own business the income is her business income and section 64(1)(iv) has nothing to work on
options.misconception: reads the change of form as ending the clubbing, when Explanation 3 was written for exactly that change
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) speaks of income arising directly or indirectly from the transferred asset, and Explanation 3 spells out what that means when the asset has been folded into a business. Changing the form of the money does not release it.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, as business income
options.why: Explanation 3 to section 64(1) says that where an asset transferred to the spouse is invested in a business, the income to be clubbed is that part of the business income which bears the same proportion to it as the value of the asset invested bears to the total investment in the business as on the first day of the previous year. ₹5,00,000 against ₹20,00,000 is one fourth, and one fourth of ₹6,00,000 is ₹1,50,000. Clubbed income keeps the head it bore in the transferee's hands, so it comes to him as business income.
keywords: first day of the previous year

options.text: ₹6,00,000, as business income — the gift was without consideration, so the whole income of the business it funded clubs with him
options.misconception: clubs the whole business income, when Explanation 3 clubs only the proportion the transferred asset bears to the total investment
options.why: Fifteen lakh rupees of the capital in the business was never his. Explanation 3 exists to apportion the income so that only what the transferred money earned comes back to the transferor.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, but as income from other sources in his hands
options.misconception: changes the head on clubbing, when section 64 brings the income into the transferor's total income under the head it already bore
options.why: The proportion is right. Section 64 moves income between persons, not between heads, so business income of the wife comes to him as business income and is set off and computed accordingly.

citation.ref: Explanation 3 to Section 64(1), read with Section 64(1)(iv)

items.scenario: On 1 May 2024 Mr Deshmukh gifted his wife ₹5,00,000 for nothing in return. On 1 August 2024 she put the whole ₹5,00,000 into her own proprietary trading business as capital. Her total investment in that business on 1 April 2025 was ₹20,00,000, of which the gifted money is part. The business earned a profit of ₹6,00,000 in previous year 2025-26. They are married throughout and are not living apart under any agreement.

items.stem: For which of the two does partial integration operate?

options.text: For neither — agricultural income is exempt under section 10(1) and can never touch the rate on anything else
options.misconception: reads the exemption as putting agricultural income out of sight for every purpose, when the rate schedule brings it back for the rate alone
options.why: Section 10(1) keeps agricultural income out of total income, and the aggregation in the rate schedule never taxes it. It only decides which slabs the rest of the income sits in, which is why the exemption survives the exercise intact.

options.text: For Mr Prakash alone
options.why: Partial integration is a rate device carried in the Finance Act's rate schedule, and it is written for an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons or body of individuals and an artificial juridical person. A firm is charged at a flat rate on the whole of its income, so there are no lower slabs for the farm income to push its business income out of and the device has nothing to work on. Mr Prakash is taxed on a slab scale, so it works on him.

options.text: For both — the gates are net agricultural income above ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income above the basic exemption limit, and each assessee clears them
options.misconception: applies the two gates without first asking whether the assessee belongs to a class the scheme is written for
options.why: Those two gates are real and they come second. The first question is whether the assessee is one of the persons the rate schedule applies the scheme to, and a firm is not.

options.text: For Ganga Traders alone — its partners are individuals, so the farm income integrates at the firm's level on their behalf
options.misconception: looks through the firm to its partners, when a firm is a separate person assessed on its own income at its own rate
options.why: A firm is its own assessee under the Act and its income is not the partners' income. What the partners receive from it is dealt with by section 10(2A) and section 28(v), not by the firm's rate computation.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) read with the rate schedule in the Finance Act, 2025 providing for aggregation of agricultural income

items.scenario: Two assessees for previous year 2025-26. Ganga Traders is a partnership firm with business income of ₹30,00,000 and net agricultural income of ₹9,00,000. Mr Prakash is a resident individual with business income of ₹30,00,000 and net agricultural income of ₹9,00,000. Both ask whether the agricultural income affects the rate at which their non-agricultural income is taxed.

items.stem: What can he do?

options.text: He may switch between the two regimes every year, the choice being made afresh with each year's return
options.misconception: applies the year-by-year choice, which belongs to a person with no business income, to a person who has it
options.why: A person with no income from business or profession does choose afresh each year along with the return, and nothing binds him. Sub-section (6) writes a much tighter rule for the person who has business income, and Mr Varun is inside it.

options.text: He may withdraw and opt out again as often as he likes, provided each Form 10-IEA goes in by the due date under section 139(1)
options.misconception: treats the due-date condition as the only condition, missing the limit of one withdrawal
options.why: The due date governs when the form may be filed. What limits how often the switch may be made is the separate sentence in the sub-section allowing the option to be withdrawn only once.

options.text: He may withdraw the option once and return to the default regime for assessment year 2026-27, but he can never opt out again while he has business income
options.why: Section 115BAC(6) lets a person having income from business or profession exercise the option to be taxed outside the default regime on or before the due date under section 139(1), and provides that the option once exercised may be withdrawn only once. After that withdrawal the person shall never be eligible to exercise the option again, unless he ceases to have any income from business or profession.

options.text: He cannot return to the default regime at all — an option once exercised binds him for every later year
options.misconception: reads the option as irrevocable, when the sub-section expressly allows one withdrawal
options.why: The sub-section allows a single withdrawal, and it is the second exit that is shut, not the first. Reading it as irrevocable would leave a person permanently in a regime he chose once on one year's numbers.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(6), read with Section 115BAC(1A) and Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Mr Varun runs a proprietary business. For assessment year 2025-26 he opted out of section 115BAC by filing Form 10-IEA before the due date under section 139(1) and was taxed under the old regime. Having recomputed, he now wants to go back into the default regime for assessment year 2026-27, and then to opt out again from assessment year 2027-28. He will continue to have business income throughout.

items.stem: What is the book profit for section 115JB?

options.text: ₹50,00,000, the loss and depreciation figures being taken from the income-tax computation
options.misconception: takes the figures from the tax computation, when the clause says as per books of account
options.why: Book profit is struck from the accounts, and the whole of section 115JB is a computation on the books rather than on the return. Carrying the tax figures in would defeat the point of a separate book-profit base.

options.text: ₹50,00,000 — the brought forward loss shown in the books comes off in full
options.misconception: deducts the loss on its own, when the clause allows only the lower of the loss and the unabsorbed depreciation
options.why: The clause pairs the two figures deliberately, so that a company cannot take the benefit of a book loss that is made up entirely of items other than depreciation. The pairing is what the word less is doing there.

options.text: ₹80,00,000 this year, and the ₹30,00,000 is lost for book profit purposes for good
options.misconception: treats this year's failure of clause (iii) as extinguishing the book loss, when the clause is applied afresh to the books of each year
options.why: Clause (iii) reads the books as they stand in the year of computation. A year in which unabsorbed depreciation is nil yields no deduction, and it does not destroy the brought forward loss for a later year in which both figures are positive.

options.text: ₹80,00,000 — nothing comes off
options.why: Clause (iii) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB reduces the book profit by the amount of loss brought forward or unabsorbed depreciation, whichever is less, as per the books of account, and it says in terms that if either of them is nil the deduction shall be nil. Unabsorbed depreciation is nil here, so the lower of the two is nil and the whole ₹30,00,000 of brought forward loss stays where it is.
keywords: as per the books of account

citation.ref: Clause (iii) of Explanation 1 to Section 115JB(2)

items.scenario: Zeta Ltd's statement of profit and loss for previous year 2025-26 shows a profit of ₹80,00,000 before any adjustment under section 115JB. Its books of account show a brought forward loss of ₹30,00,000 and unabsorbed depreciation of nil. No other adjustment under Explanation 1 is called for, and the company has not opted for section 115BAA. The chief financial officer reduces the book profit by the ₹30,00,000.

items.stem: What is the adjusted total income for section 115JC?

options.text: ₹17,50,000 — the ₹4,00,000 of total income plus the ₹13,50,000 of depreciation that would otherwise have been allowed
options.misconception: adds back the notional depreciation instead of the section 35AD deduction net of it, which inverts the arithmetic the sub-section directs
options.why: The notional depreciation is the amount taken out of the add-back, not the amount put into it. What goes in is the section 35AD deduction, reduced by that figure.

Section 115JC(2) adds back the deduction claimed under section 35AD, but it adds it back as reduced by the depreciation allowable under section 32 that the asset would have carried had section 35AD never been touched. The net add-back is ₹90,00,000 less ₹13,50,000, that is ₹76,50,000, and on top of the total income of ₹4,00,000 it gives ₹80,50,000.

options.text: ₹94,00,000 — the whole ₹90,00,000 goes back on top of the ₹4,00,000
options.misconception: adds the section 35AD deduction back gross, when the sub-section nets the notional depreciation off it first
options.why: Adding the deduction back gross would tax the firm on capital cost it would have written off under section 32 in any event. The netting exists so that the add-back reaches only the accelerated part of the write-off.

options.text: ₹4,00,000 — adjusted total income is the total income, the add-backs being confined to Chapter VI-A heading "C" and section 10AA
options.misconception: leaves section 35AD out of the add-back list, when section 115JC(2) names it alongside the other two
options.why: Section 115JC(2) names three things: deductions under Chapter VI-A heading "C", the deduction under section 10AA, and the deduction under section 35AD as reduced by notional depreciation. Leaving the third out would let the largest incentive of the three escape the minimum tax.

citation.ref: Section 115JC(2), read with Section 35AD and Section 32

items.scenario: Sagar Warehousing LLP's total income for previous year 2025-26, computed under the normal provisions, is ₹4,00,000. In arriving at it the firm claimed a deduction of ₹90,00,000 under section 35AD on a warehousing facility. Depreciation that would have been allowable under section 32 on that asset, had no deduction under section 35AD been claimed, is ₹13,50,000. The firm claimed no deduction under Chapter VI-A heading "C" and none under section 10AA.

items.stem: Is section 68 the right provision for this addition?

options.text: No — and no addition can be made at all, every one of sections 68 to 69D requiring books of account to be maintained
options.misconception: reads the books requirement into section 69A, which applies precisely where the money is not recorded in any books
options.why: Sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C were enacted for assets and expenditure found outside the books, or where no books exist. The absence of books is the trigger for them rather than a defence against them.

options.text: No — with no books kept, the addition belongs under section 69A as unexplained money
options.why: Section 68 opens only where a credit entry sits within the books of an assessee maintained for any previous year. A bank passbook or statement is the bank's record of its dealings with its customer and not books maintained by the assessee, so the opening condition of the section is not met. Section 69A is written for this case: where the assessee is found to be the owner of any money which is not recorded in the books of account, and offers no explanation, the money is deemed to be his income.
keywords: books of an assessee maintained for any previous year
not recorded in the books of account

options.text: Yes, because he is a salaried employee and section 68 is the only deeming provision open against a person with no business
options.misconception: ties the deeming provisions to the head of income the assessee otherwise has, when they turn on what is found and where it is recorded
options.why: None of the deeming sections asks what the assessee does for a living. They ask whether a sum, an asset or an expenditure has been explained, and section 69A reaches a salaried person as readily as a trader.

options.text: Yes — a credit entry in a bank account is a sum credited in the assessee's books for section 68
options.misconception: treats a bank statement as the assessee's own books, when it is the bank's record of its dealings with him
options.why: The books section 68 speaks of are books the assessee maintains. A bank writes its own records for its own purposes and gives the customer a copy, which is why the section cannot be anchored on them.

citation.ref: Section 68 read with Section 69A

items.scenario: Mr Sethi is a salaried employee with no business and no profession. He keeps no books of account of any kind. During previous year 2025-26 a total of ₹18,00,000 in cash is deposited into his savings bank account, and when asked he offers no explanation of where the money came from. The Assessing Officer proposes to add the ₹18,00,000 as a cash credit under section 68, pointing to the credit entries in the bank statement.

items.stem: Is the ₹40,00,000 a deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)?

options.text: Yes in part — a deemed dividend arises on so much of the loan as exceeds what an unrelated borrower could have obtained
options.misconception: invents an arm's length comparison inside clause (e), when the exclusion either applies to the payment or does not
options.why: Section 2(22)(e) deems the payment itself to be dividend to the extent of accumulated profits; it never apportions by reference to what someone else might have borrowed. Clause (ii) then removes the whole payment from the definition.

options.text: No — the exclusion for a company whose business is lending takes it out
options.why: The exclusions sit inside section 2(22) itself. Clause (ii) of the definition says dividend does not include any advance or loan made to a shareholder by a company in the ordinary course of its business, where the lending of money is a substantial part of the business of the company. A finance company lending on its standard terms is the case that exclusion was written for, and the size of the accumulated profits is then beside the point.
keywords: lending of money is a substantial part

options.text: Yes — she holds well over ten per cent and the loan is comfortably within accumulated profits
options.misconception: applies the trigger in clause (e) without reading the exclusions that sit in the same definition
options.why: Substantial shareholding and sufficient accumulated profits are what bring clause (e) into play, and both are present. The definition then removes certain payments from dividend altogether, and this loan is one of them.

options.text: No, but only because the loan carries market interest; an interest-free loan on the same facts would be a deemed dividend
options.misconception: makes the rate of interest the test, when the exclusion turns on the company's business and on the loan being in the ordinary course of it
options.why: Clause (ii) says nothing about interest. What it asks is whether lending money is a substantial part of the company's business and whether this loan was made in the ordinary course of that business.

citation.ref: Clause (ii) of Section 2(22), read with Section 2(22)(e)

items.scenario: Sarita holds 30 per cent of the equity shares of Ratna Finance Ltd, a non-banking finance company whose registered and actual business is the lending of money and which does substantially nothing else. In previous year 2025-26 the company lends her ₹40,00,000 on its standard terms, on the same security and at the same rate of interest it charges unrelated borrowers, and the loan is recorded like any other in its loan book. The company's accumulated profits are ₹6 crore.

items.stem: What is the route open to the trust for the ₹15,00,000 it has not received?

options.text: Accumulate it under section 11(2), that being the only route for income a trust has not spent
options.misconception: reaches for accumulation, which is for income received but not spent, when the Explanation deals with income not received at all
options.why: Section 11(2) is the shelter for money the trust holds and chooses not to spend yet, and it carries its own conditions and its five-year clock. Money the trust has not been paid is a different problem, and the Explanation is the answer written for it.

options.text: Exercise the option, but the money may then be spent at any time within five years of the year to which it relates
options.misconception: borrows the five-year window from section 11(2), when the Explanation gives the year of receipt and the one immediately following
options.why: Five years is the accumulation period under section 11(2), which is a different route with different conditions. The Explanation's window is much shorter, because the only reason the money was not spent was that it had not arrived.

options.text: Exercise the option under the Explanation to section 11(1), in Form 9A before the due date for furnishing the return, and spend the money in the year of receipt or the year after
options.why: The Explanation to section 11(1) covers income which has not been received during the previous year. Where that is so, the trust may exercise an option in the prescribed form, Form 9A, on or before the due date for furnishing the return under section 139(1), and the income is then deemed to have been applied to charitable purposes in the year to which it relates. It must then be applied in the previous year in which it is received or in the previous year immediately following, failing which it is treated as income of that later year.
keywords: not been received during the previous year

options.text: Nothing is needed — income not received is not income of the trust, so only the ₹65,00,000 received enters the eighty-five per cent test
options.misconception: reads the trust as taxed on receipts, when the income of the previous year is what the eighty-five per cent test is applied to
options.why: The grant fell due during the year and is income of that year. That is precisely why the Explanation exists — without it, a trust would fail the application test on money it never had a chance to spend.

citation.ref: Explanation to Section 11(1) and the option in Form 9A, read with Section 139(1) and Section 11(2)

items.scenario: A charitable trust registered under section 12AB has income of ₹80,00,000 for previous year 2025-26. Of that, ₹15,00,000 is a grant which fell due to it during the year but which the grantor did not actually pay until August 2026. The trust applied ₹50,00,000 to its objects during previous year 2025-26. It does not want to accumulate anything under section 11(2), and it intends to spend the ₹15,00,000 in the year it receives it.

items.stem: Under which provision must Orion Ltd withhold on each of the two purchases?

options.text: Section 194Q on the resident's ₹4 crore, and section 195 on the non-resident's ₹3 crore
options.why: Section 194Q makes a specified buyer responsible for deducting tax on any sum paid or credited to a resident for purchase of goods, so it reaches the ₹4 crore and stops there. A payment to a non-resident is governed by section 195, which requires deduction on any sum chargeable under the provisions of this Act, and the parties accept that this sum is. The size of the purchase does not move a non-resident seller into section 194Q.
keywords: paid or credited to a resident for purchase of goods
chargeable under the provisions of this Act

options.text: Section 194Q on both, the buyer test and the per-seller test being crossed for each of them
options.misconception: applies section 194Q to a non-resident seller, when the section speaks only of a sum paid to a resident
options.why: Both tests are indeed crossed, and they are the tests that decide whether the buyer is within the section at all. Who the seller is comes first, and the section names a resident.

options.text: Section 195 on both, that being the general withholding provision for a purchase of goods
options.misconception: treats section 195 as a general provision, when it is written for a payment to a non-resident
options.why: Section 195 opens by naming any person responsible for paying to a non-resident. It has no application to the resident supplier, whose purchases are dealt with by section 194Q.

options.text: Section 194Q on the resident's ₹4 crore and nothing on the non-resident, a purchase of goods from abroad being outside withholding
options.misconception: reads the absence of section 194Q as the absence of any obligation, when section 195 stands behind it for a non-resident payee
options.why: The obligation moves rather than disappears. Section 195 applies to any sum chargeable under the Act paid to a non-resident, and a purchase of goods is not carved out of it.

citation.ref: Section 194Q(1), read with Section 195(1)

items.scenario: Orion Ltd's turnover for the preceding financial year was above the limit that makes a buyer a specified buyer under section 194Q, and its purchases from each of the two sellers below are above the per-seller limit in that section. In previous year 2025-26 it buys goods worth ₹4 crore from a resident supplier and goods worth ₹3 crore from a supplier which is a non-resident. It is common ground that the sum paid to the non-resident is chargeable to tax in India.

items.stem: Must Mr Naik deduct tax under section 194R on the motorcycle?

options.text: No — section 194R reaches a benefit given in money, and a motorcycle is not money
options.misconception: confines the section to cash, when it names a benefit or perquisite whether convertible into money or not
options.why: The right answer for the wrong reason. Section 194R was enacted precisely for benefits in kind, and its first proviso deals with how tax is to be ensured where the benefit is wholly in kind.

options.text: Yes — the turnover exclusion for a small individual is written into section 194Q and not into section 194R
options.misconception: attributes the turnover exclusion to the wrong section, when section 194R carries its own in a proviso
options.why: Section 194Q has a turnover test that decides who is a specified buyer. Section 194R separately excludes a small individual or Hindu undivided family by its own proviso, and that is the provision Mr Naik relies on.

options.text: Yes — the ₹90,000 is well past the value at which section 194R starts to bite, and nothing else matters
options.misconception: applies the threshold on the value of the benefit and stops, without asking whether the section casts any duty on this provider at all
options.why: The value threshold decides whether a benefit given by a person within the section is large enough to be caught. It says nothing about whether the giver is a person the section reaches, which is the prior question here.

options.text: No — the exclusion for a small individual takes him out of the section
options.why: The obligation in section 194R falls on the person responsible for providing a benefit or perquisite arising from business or the exercise of a profession. Its second proviso excludes an individual, or a Hindu undivided family, if its total sales, gross receipts or turnover in the preceding financial year stayed inside the stated limits, and Mr Naik's ₹70,00,000 is below the ₹1 crore business limit. The benefit is still income of the agent; what is absent is Mr Naik's duty to deduct on it.
keywords: total sales, gross receipts or turnover

citation.ref: Section 194R(1) with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: Mr Naik carries on a proprietary retail business and carries on no profession. His total sales for financial year 2024-25 were ₹70,00,000. In previous year 2025-26 he gives the agent of one of his suppliers a motorcycle worth ₹90,000 as a reward for meeting a target, and the benefit arises out of Mr Naik's business. The limits written into section 194R for an individual are ₹1 crore of total sales, gross receipts or turnover from business, and ₹50 lakh from a profession, in the preceding financial year.

items.stem: Is the company right on either of the two points?

options.text: On the first point only — a completed statutory audit bars a direction, though the nomination is indeed the Commissioner's
options.misconception: reads an earlier audit as a bar on the direction, when the sub-section opens by saying that it is not
options.why: The words about an audit under any other law are there because the ordinary case is a company whose accounts are already audited. A special audit is an additional audit into the complexity of accounts that have been audited, not a substitute for a missing one.

options.text: On the second point only — the direction may be made, but the assessee names the accountant since it bears the cost
options.misconception: ties the nomination to who pays for the audit, when the nomination is the Commissioner's and the expenses are met by the Central Government
options.why: Since 1 June 2007 the expenses of a special audit, including the auditor's remuneration, are fixed by the Principal Chief Commissioner, the Chief Commissioner, the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner and met by the Central Government under section 142(2D). The premise of the answer is wrong as well as the conclusion.

options.text: On both points — the section is a last resort for accounts never audited, and the assessee chooses the accountant so the audit is not one-sided
options.misconception: reads section 142(2A) as filling a gap where no audit exists, when it is directed at accounts whose complexity or volume the officer cannot penetrate
options.why: The grounds in the sub-section are the nature and complexity of the accounts, their volume, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions and the specialised nature of the business. Every one of those assumes accounts that exist and have been kept.

options.text: On neither point
options.why: Section 142(2A) applies notwithstanding that the assessee's accounts have already been audited under any other law in force at the time, or audited otherwise, so an audit already done is no answer to a direction. The same sub-section hands the choice of auditor to the revenue — the accountant must be one nominated by the Principal Chief Commissioner, or by the Chief Commissioner, the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner, which puts that choice outside the assessee's hands altogether.
keywords: nominated by the Principal Chief Commissioner

citation.ref: Section 142(2A) with its proviso, read with Section 142(2D)

items.scenario: Trident Ltd's accounts for previous year 2025-26 have been audited by its statutory auditor under the Companies Act, 2013, and a tax audit report under section 44AB has been filed. During the scrutiny the Assessing Officer, having regard to the volume of the accounts and the multiplicity of transactions in them, wants to direct a special audit under section 142(2A). The company answers that its accounts have already been audited twice, so the section cannot be used, and that if an audit is nevertheless ordered it will appoint its own firm of accountants to carry it out.

items.stem: Can the Commissioner (Appeals) admit the appeal as it stands?

options.text: Yes — section 249(4) applies only where no return of income has been furnished at all
options.misconception: takes clause (b), which covers the case of no return, for the whole of section 249(4)
options.why: Clause (b) covers a person who has furnished no return and asks him for an amount equal to the advance tax which was payable by him. Clause (a) is the limb that governs a person who has filed a return, and it is the one that bites here.

options.text: Yes — the appeal is in time and in form, and the tax in dispute is the very thing the appeal is about
options.misconception: reads the payment condition as attaching to the disputed demand, when it attaches to the tax on the income the assessee returned
options.why: The condition was written so that a taxpayer cannot appeal while withholding tax on income he has himself admitted. Tax on the additions is what the appeal is for, and none of it has to be paid to get in.

options.text: Not until he pays the balance ₹3,00,000 of the tax due on his returned income
options.why: Section 249(4)(a) says no appeal shall be admitted unless, at the time of filing the appeal, the assessee has paid the tax due on the income returned by him. What has to be paid is the tax on the income he himself declared, ₹4,00,000, not the tax on the additions he is disputing. Until the remaining ₹3,00,000 goes in the appeal cannot be admitted, and the form and the fee do not cure it.
keywords: tax due on the income returned

options.text: Not until he pays the whole demand raised by the assessment, additions included
options.misconception: raises the condition to the whole demand, when the sub-section asks only for the tax on the income returned
options.why: Requiring the whole demand would make the right of first appeal turn on the assessee's ability to fund the addition he is challenging. The sub-section stops at the admitted income, and a stay of the balance is a separate matter.

citation.ref: Section 249(4)(a), read with Section 249(4)(b) and Section 246A

items.scenario: Mr Bakshi filed his return for assessment year 2026-27 declaring an income on which the tax due was ₹4,00,000. He has paid ₹1,00,000 of that and no more. The assessment added further income and raised a demand well above the ₹4,00,000. He files an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against the additions, within time, in the prescribed form and with the fee paid, and he disputes nothing about his own returned income.

items.stem: What is the amount of the under-reported income?

options.why: Where the under-reporting has the effect of reducing a loss or converting a loss into income, section 270A(3) measures the under-reported income as the difference between the loss claimed and the income or loss assessed or reassessed. A returned loss of ₹40,00,000 against an assessed income of ₹15,00,000 gives ₹55,00,000, and it is the change of sign that makes the two figures add rather than subtract.

options.text: ₹40,00,000, being the loss claimed and disallowed
options.misconception: stops at the loss that was knocked out and leaves out the positive income the assessment produced
options.why: Removing the loss is only half of what the assessment did. It also produced ₹15,00,000 of income, and the sub-section adds both parts by taking the difference between the loss claimed and the income assessed.

options.text: ₹15,00,000, being the income actually assessed
options.misconception: measures the under-reporting by the assessed income alone, leaving out the loss that was wrongly claimed and would have sheltered later years
options.why: A loss claimed and lost is a real benefit taken away, because it would otherwise have been carried forward against future profits. The measure has to pick that up as well as the income assessed.

options.text: Nil — a company that returned a loss has under-reported nothing, there being no tax on the returned income to compare anything with
options.misconception: reads under-reporting as needing tax on the returned income, when section 270A expressly covers a loss reduced or converted into income
options.why: Section 270A was drafted with the loss case in mind, because the old regime argued about it endlessly. The tax on the under-reported income is then computed as the section directs and the penalty follows on that.

citation.ref: Section 270A(3), read with Section 270A(1) and Section 270A(7)

items.scenario: Mistral Ltd furnished its return for assessment year 2026-27 declaring a loss of ₹40,00,000. In the assessment under section 143(3) the Assessing Officer disallowed several items and assessed a positive total income of ₹15,00,000. The case is one of under-reporting of income and is not a case of misreporting, and no carve-out in section 270A(6) is claimed.

items.stem: Is that argument good?

options.text: No — section 90(2) is available only to a resident, so a foreign company cannot invoke it at all
options.misconception: confines section 90(2) to residents, when it speaks of the assessee to whom the agreement applies
options.why: Section 90(2) applies in relation to the assessee to whom the agreement applies, and a non-resident of a treaty country is the ordinary case. The argument fails on the Explanation, not on the company's residence.

options.text: Yes — section 90(2) is a general rule that the taxpayer takes whichever treatment is better, and the domestic rate is better
options.misconception: reads section 90(2) as a free choice of the lowest figure available anywhere, when the Explanation shuts this comparison out expressly
options.why: Section 90(2) compares what the Act gives with what the agreement gives on the same question. It does not let a taxpayer compare himself with a different class of assessee under the same Act, which is what this argument does.

options.text: Yes, but only if the company gives up the agreement for every other stream of its income as well, the choice being all or nothing
options.misconception: makes the section 90(2) choice a blanket election, when it is exercised provision by provision
options.why: A taxpayer may take the treaty for one stream of income and the Act for another, because the comparison is made wherever the two overlap. The all-or-nothing rule described here is not in the section.

options.text: No — the Act declares in terms that the higher rate on a foreign company is not less favourable treatment
options.why: Section 90(2) does let an assessee take whichever of the Act or the agreement is more beneficial to him, provision by provision. Explanation 1 to section 90 then removes this particular argument. Taxing a foreign company at a rate that sits above the rate at which a domestic company is chargeable is declared by that Explanation not to be a less favourable charge, and not a less favourable levy either, on the foreign company. The residency certificate opens the treaty; it does not create a rate the treaty never gave.
keywords: rate at which a domestic company is chargeable

citation.ref: Section 90(2) with Explanation 1 to Section 90, read with Section 90(4)

items.scenario: A foreign company resident in a country with which India has a comprehensive agreement under section 90 carries on business in India through a permanent establishment. Its Indian business profits are charged under the Act at the rate applicable to a foreign company, which is higher than the rate at which a domestic company is charged. The company holds a valid tax residency certificate. It says that being charged more than a domestic company is less favourable treatment, and that section 90(2) therefore entitles it to the domestic company rate.

items.stem: How much of the ₹6,00,000 can be allowed?

options.text: ₹6,00,000, the gross total income of ₹14,00,000 being more than enough to absorb it
options.misconception: reads the gross total income as one undifferentiated figure, which is the reading section 112A(6) exists to prevent
options.why: Nothing in Chapter VI-A allows a deduction to be set against income charged at the special rate section 112A fixes. Treating the gross total income as a single pool is exactly what that sub-section forbids.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, because section 80A(2) imposes the only ceiling and the claim is far below the gross total income
options.misconception: treats the section 80A(2) ceiling as the only limit and misses the separate direction in section 112A(6)
options.why: Section 80A(2) is a ceiling on the total amount deducted, not a rule about which income the deduction may be taken from. Both provisions operate, and the narrower one decides this case.

options.text: ₹4,00,000 — the Chapter VI-A deduction is given from the gross total income as reduced by the long-term capital gains charged under section 112A
options.why: Section 112A(6) directs that where the gross total income includes long-term capital gains charged under that section, the deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowed from the gross total income as reduced by such capital gains. Section 80A(2) adds that the aggregate of the deductions cannot exceed the gross total income. The ₹10,00,000 of capital gains is therefore set aside and only ₹4,00,000 of business income is left to absorb the claim.
keywords: as reduced by such capital gains

options.text: Nil, a person whose income includes gains charged at a special rate being outside Chapter VI-A altogether
options.misconception: turns a restriction on the income available for set-off into a bar on the person
options.why: Chapter VI-A is not shut to a person merely because part of his income bears a special rate. His ₹4,00,000 of business income is ordinary income and the deduction runs against it.

citation.ref: Section 112A(6) and Section 80A(2), read with Chapter VI-A and Section 111A(2)

items.scenario: Mr Anand's gross total income for assessment year 2026-27 is ₹14,00,000. It is made up of ₹4,00,000 of business income and ₹10,00,000 of long-term capital gains on listed equity shares charged under section 112A. He has made investments and payments that would, on their own terms, earn him ₹6,00,000 of deductions under Chapter VI-A. He files his return in time and claims the whole ₹6,00,000.

items.stem: What does section 80JJAA allow on account of these 40 workmen?

options.text: The full deduction for previous year 2025-26, the workmen being on the payroll on the last day of that year
options.misconception: reads additional employee as anyone on the payroll at the year end, ignoring the days-employed test
options.why: The Explanation fixes a minimum period of employment inside the previous year. Standing on the payroll on 31 March proves nothing about how long the person was employed during it.

options.text: Nothing, in this year or in any other, the workmen having failed the test in the year they joined
options.misconception: applies the exclusion and stops there, missing the proviso that carries the employee into the next year
options.why: The exclusion would have that effect but for the proviso written immediately after it, which exists precisely so that a late-year recruit is not lost for good. He is picked up in the following year instead.

options.text: Nothing for previous year 2025-26, but the deduction on their emoluments runs from previous year 2026-27, in which they are deemed to have been employed
options.why: The Explanation to section 80JJAA(2) takes out of the expression additional employee anyone employed for fewer than 240 days in the previous year, so 121 days fails the year of joining. The proviso written immediately below it provides that where such an employee is employed for 240 days or more in the immediately succeeding year, he is deemed to have been employed in that succeeding year and the section applies accordingly.

options.text: The deduction for previous year 2025-26, scaled down in the proportion 121 days bears to the year
options.misconception: turns a pass-or-fail day count into a pro-rata apportionment
options.why: The section allows a fixed percentage of additional employee cost and knows nothing of proportioning that cost for part of a year. The day count decides whether a person is an additional employee at all, and there is nothing in between.

citation.ref: The Explanation to Section 80JJAA(2) defining additional employee, with the proviso to that Explanation, read with Section 80JJAA(1)

items.scenario: Talwar Castings Ltd, whose accounts are audited, takes on 40 new workmen on 1 December 2025, so each of them is employed for 121 days in previous year 2025-26. It does not manufacture apparel, footwear or leather products. Every workman is paid below the monthly emoluments ceiling the section sets, is paid by bank transfer and participates in a recognised provident fund, and there is a net increase in the total number of employees. All 40 stay on and work through the whole of previous year 2026-27. Form 10DA is furnished in time for both years.

items.stem: What deduction under section 80M survives?

options.text: The full ₹40,00,000, the distribution having been made before the return was actually furnished on 28 October 2026
options.misconception: substitutes the date the return was filed for the date the proviso names
options.why: The proviso does not look at when the return goes in. It fixes a date computed backwards from the due date under section 139(1), and a company gains nothing by filing early or late.

options.text: The full ₹40,00,000, section 80M carrying no time condition on the onward distribution
options.misconception: reads the main limb of section 80M alone and misses the proviso attached to it
options.why: The main limb does read as a plain matching of dividend received against dividend distributed. The proviso beneath it is what turns that matching into a dated condition.

options.text: ₹40,00,000, but in assessment year 2027-28, the distribution falling in that year
options.misconception: moves the deduction to the year of distribution, which section 80M does not do
options.why: Section 80M gives the deduction in the year in which the dividend is received, measured against the dividend distributed by the dated deadline for that same year. There is no rule carrying an unclaimed deduction into another year.

options.text: None of it — the onward dividend had to be distributed by 30 September 2026
options.why: The proviso to section 80M fixes the last date for the onward distribution as one month prior to the date for furnishing the return under sub-section (1) of section 139. With the due date 31 October 2026 that date is 30 September 2026, and a distribution on 15 October 2026 is too late.

citation.ref: The proviso to Section 80M(1), read with Section 80M(1) and Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Kestrel Holdings Ltd, a domestic company, receives a dividend of ₹40,00,000 from another domestic company in October 2025. Its due date for furnishing the return of income for assessment year 2026-27 is 31 October 2026. It declares and distributes a dividend of ₹40,00,000 to its own shareholders on 15 October 2026, and claims the full deduction under section 80M in its return, which it files on 28 October 2026.

items.stem: Has the company gone to the right forum?

options.text: Yes, because an order under section 263 merely directs a fresh assessment and is therefore an assessment order for the purposes of appeal
options.misconception: reclassifies the revision order as the assessment it directs
options.why: The revision order and the fresh assessment made in obedience to it are two different orders with two different routes. The fresh assessment, when made, is appealable to the Commissioner (Appeals) in the ordinary way; the revision order is not.

options.text: Yes — every order under the Act is first appealable to the Commissioner (Appeals), and only his order then goes to the Tribunal
options.misconception: treats the appeal chain as a single ladder every order must climb from the bottom rung
options.why: The Act sends some orders to the Commissioner (Appeals) and others straight to the Tribunal. An order made by the Principal Commissioner himself is one that skips the first rung, since otherwise an officer of lower rank would be hearing an appeal against his superior.

options.text: No — an order under section 263 is not appealable at all and can be challenged only by a writ petition in the High Court
options.misconception: invents a bar on appeal where section 253(1) expressly provides one
options.why: Section 253(1) names the section 263 order among the orders that may be appealed to the Tribunal. The statutory remedy exists, and it is the one to be used.

options.text: No — an order under section 263 is appealable directly to the Appellate Tribunal, and the Commissioner (Appeals) has no jurisdiction over it
options.why: Section 253(1) lists the orders an assessee may take straight to the Appellate Tribunal, and an order passed by a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under section 263 is one of them. The Commissioner (Appeals) hears appeals against the orders listed in section 246A, and a revision order is not among those.

citation.ref: Section 253(1), read with Section 246A and Section 263(1)

items.scenario: The Principal Commissioner passes an order under section 263 holding an assessment erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue, and directing the Assessing Officer to make a fresh assessment. The company wants to challenge that order at once and files an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals).

items.stem: Is Mr Rege's transfer of his Nilgiri shares taken out of the charge by section 47(vii)?

options.text: No — the clause covers the shareholder only where the consideration is the allotment of shares in the amalgamated company, and part of what he received was cash
options.why: Clause (vii) of section 47 takes a shareholder's transfer under an amalgamation scheme out of the charge only where what he gets back for it is an allotment of shares in the amalgamated company, that company being Indian. Cash paid alongside the shares is not an allotment of shares, so the clause does not cover this transfer.

options.text: Yes, because the amalgamating and the amalgamated company are both Indian companies
options.misconception: reads the condition about the amalgamated company being an Indian company as the whole of the clause
options.why: That condition is satisfied here and it is a real one. It sits beside the share-consideration condition, which is not satisfied, and both have to be met.

options.text: No, because section 47(vii) covers the amalgamating company's transfer of its own assets and never a shareholder's shares
options.misconception: confuses clause (vi), which covers the company's transfer of its property, with clause (vii), which covers the shareholder
options.why: Clause (vi) deals with the transfer by the amalgamating company of its capital assets to the amalgamated company. Clause (vii) is the separate clause written for the shareholder, so a shareholder is squarely within the section's contemplation.

options.text: Yes — section 47(vii) covers any transfer by a shareholder in a sanctioned scheme of amalgamation, whatever form the consideration takes
options.misconception: drops the condition that the consideration be shares in the amalgamated company
options.why: The clause is written around the form of the consideration. A sanctioned scheme is the setting in which the clause operates, not the test it applies.

citation.ref: Section 47(vii), read with Section 47(vi) and Section 45(1)

items.scenario: Under a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the Tribunal, Nilgiri Ltd amalgamates into Sahyadri Ltd. Both are Indian companies. Mr Rege held shares in Nilgiri Ltd which had cost him ₹5,00,000. Under the scheme he receives shares of Sahyadri Ltd worth ₹6,00,000 and, in addition, ₹2,00,000 in cash.

items.stem: How does section 54B affect the computation on this second sale?

options.text: The ₹20,00,000 exempted earlier is charged as capital gains of previous year 2025-26, and the new land keeps its ₹22,00,000 cost
options.misconception: imports the section 54F(3) mechanism, which charges the earlier gain in the later year, into section 54B, which instead cuts the cost
options.why: Section 54F(3) does charge the earlier exempted gain as income of the year the condition is broken. Section 54B chose the other mechanism, and the two must not be swapped.

options.text: Nothing changes — the ₹20,00,000 was exempt once and for all and the new land carries its full ₹22,00,000 cost
options.misconception: treats the exemption as unconditional and misses the three-year condition attached to it
options.why: The exemption is conditioned on the new land being held for three years. Selling inside that period is the very case the clause is written for.

options.text: The cost of the new land drops to ₹2,00,000, so ₹28,00,000 is chargeable on this sale
options.why: Clause (ii) of section 54B(1) applies where the new agricultural land costs at least as much as the capital gain. The gain is not charged, and for computing any capital gain on a transfer of the new asset within a period of three years of its purchase, its cost is reduced by the amount of the capital gain. ₹22,00,000 less ₹20,00,000 leaves ₹2,00,000 against the ₹30,00,000 received.
keywords: within a period of three years

options.text: The ₹20,00,000 exempted earlier is charged as capital gains of previous year 2023-24, that assessment being rectified, and the new land keeps its ₹22,00,000 cost
options.misconception: reopens the year in which the exemption was allowed, which section 54B does not do
options.why: Section 54B works forward, through the cost of the new asset in the year that asset is sold. Nothing in it disturbs the completed assessment of the year in which the exemption was given.

citation.ref: Clause (ii) of Section 54B(1), read with clause (i) of Section 54B(1) and Section 48

items.scenario: Mr Chauhan sold agricultural land in previous year 2023-24 and made a capital gain of ₹20,00,000. Within the year he bought other agricultural land for ₹22,00,000, and the whole gain was exempted under section 54B. In previous year 2025-26, twenty months after buying it, he sells that new land for ₹30,00,000.

items.stem: Is the exemption available?

options.text: Yes, the reinvestment having been made well inside the three years section 54D allows
options.misconception: satisfies the reinvestment condition and treats it as the only condition
options.why: The reinvestment window governs what the company must do after the transfer. The use condition governs what must have happened before it, and both have to be met.

options.text: No — the land and the shed had to be in use for the business of the industrial undertaking in the two years immediately preceding the transfer, and fourteen months is short of that
options.why: Section 54D(1) opens with a capital asset being land or building forming part of an industrial undertaking which, in the two years immediately preceding the date of the transfer, was being used by the assessee for the purposes of the business of that undertaking. Fourteen months of use does not meet that condition, and prompt reinvestment cannot cure it.
