options.text: No, because section 54D is available only to an individual or a Hindu undivided family
options.misconception: imports the assessee-class restriction of sections 54 and 54B into section 54D
options.why: Section 54D names no class of assessee, so a company is within it. What defeats this claim is the period of use, not the company's status.

options.text: Yes — the company used the assets for its business right up to the acquisition, and section 54D asks for nothing more
options.misconception: reads the use condition as use at the moment of transfer rather than throughout the two preceding years
options.why: The section fixes a period, not a moment. Use on the date of acquisition is necessary but it does not answer the two-year requirement written into the sub-section.

citation.ref: Section 54D(1), read with Section 54D(2)

items.scenario: Torrent Alloys Ltd bought land and a shed fourteen months before they were compulsorily acquired in previous year 2025-26, and used them for the business of its industrial undertaking from the day it bought them right up to the acquisition. Within a year of the acquisition it buys other land and puts up a new shed to re-establish the same undertaking, and claims exemption under section 54D.

items.stem: Under which provision does the officer make the reference in each case?

options.text: Section 55A for both, every reference to a Valuation Officer being made under it
options.misconception: treats section 55A as the only route to a Valuation Officer
options.why: Section 55A is confined to ascertaining fair market value for the capital gains provisions. An estimate of what was actually spent on a construction is a different exercise, and the Act gives it its own section.

options.text: Section 55A for Mr Dua's file and section 142A for Ms Roy's
options.why: Section 55A lets the Assessing Officer refer the valuation of a capital asset to a Valuation Officer with a view to ascertaining its fair market value for the purposes of the capital gains provisions. Section 142A is the separate power to require an estimate of the value of any investment, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article, or of any expenditure, where an addition as unexplained investment or expenditure is in contemplation.

options.text: Section 142A for both, the officer in each case doubting a figure the assessee has put forward
options.misconception: reads section 142A as a general power to test any value the officer doubts
options.why: Section 142A is tied to an estimate of an investment or an expenditure that the officer proposes to bring in as unexplained. It does not reach the fair market value of a capital asset on a sale.

options.text: Neither — a Valuation Officer can be brought in only by the Principal Commissioner
options.misconception: moves the power of reference to an authority neither section names
options.why: Both sections put the reference in the hands of the Assessing Officer himself. Neither requires the approval of any higher authority before the reference is made.

citation.ref: Section 55A(a) and Section 55A(b), read with Section 142A(1) and Sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C

items.scenario: Two files sit on the Assessing Officer's desk. In the first, Mr Dua has sold a house and has adopted a fair market value as on 1 April 2001 taken from a registered valuer's report to work out his cost of acquisition; the officer thinks that value is inflated. In the second, Ms Roy has built a house during the year and the officer thinks the amount actually spent on the construction is far more than her books show, and wants an estimate so that the difference can be brought in as unexplained investment.

items.stem: What does section 184 require of the firm?

options.text: Nothing further — once a deed is on record the firm is assessed as a firm for every later year, changes included
options.misconception: reads section 184(3) alone and misses the exception section 184(4) makes for a year of change
options.why: Section 184(3) carries the position forward only while the constitution and the shares stay as the deed on record says. The sub-section that follows it is written for the year they change.

options.text: Nothing, because the retirement dissolved the old firm and a new firm is simply filing its first return
options.misconception: treats a change in constitution as the end of the assessable entity
options.why: A retirement with the business continuing is a change in constitution, not a dissolution, and section 184(4) is written for exactly that case. The same firm carries on and the revised deed must be filed.

options.text: A certified copy of the revised deed had to go with the return for the year of the change, and without it the firm loses its deduction for interest and remuneration for that year
options.why: Section 184(3) does carry a firm's assessment as a firm into every subsequent year without a fresh deed. Section 184(4) then requires that where there is a change in the constitution of the firm or in the shares of the partners during a previous year, a certified copy of the revised instrument must go in with the return of income filed for the assessment year to which the change relates.
keywords: certified copy of the revised instrument

options.text: A fresh certified copy with the return every year, whether or not anything has changed
options.misconception: turns a filing triggered by a change into an annual formality
options.why: Section 184(3) exists precisely so that a firm need not file its deed again year after year. Only a change brings the requirement back.

citation.ref: Section 184(4), read with Section 184(3), Section 184(1) and Section 185

items.scenario: Wadia and Sons was assessed as a firm for assessment year 2024-25, a certified copy of its partnership deed having been filed with that year's return. On 1 July 2025 one partner retires and the remaining partners execute a fresh deed changing the profit-sharing ratio, the business carrying on without a break. The firm files its return for assessment year 2026-27 with no deed attached, taking the view that the deed already on record serves for all later years.

items.stem: Which of the four payments is NOT a payment to a person covered by section 40A(2)(b)?

options.text: The fee paid to Mr Marwah's wife's brother
options.why: Section 40A(2)(b) reaches a director, a relative of a director and a person in whose business a director has a substantial interest. Relative is defined by section 2(41), and the list is short: a husband or wife, a brother or sister, and any lineal ascendant or descendant of the individual. A brother-in-law is in none of those categories, so the fourth payee falls outside the clause.

options.text: The consultancy fee paid to Mr Marwah himself
options.misconception: overlooks that the first person section 40A(2)(b) names for a company is its own director
options.why: Where the assessee is a company, the clause names any director of the company. A payment to the managing director is the plainest case it covers.

options.text: The fee paid to Mr Marwah's sister
options.misconception: reads relative narrowly as spouse and children only, when section 2(41) includes a brother or sister
options.why: Section 2(41) includes a brother or sister of the individual. A director's sister is a relative of a director and so is inside section 40A(2)(b).

options.text: The purchase from Sundar Traders
options.misconception: misses the limb that reaches a concern in whose business a director has a substantial interest
options.why: The Explanation to section 40A(2)(b) treats a person as having a substantial interest in a business where, in a case other than a company, he is entitled to not less than twenty per cent of the profits. A 30 per cent share of the profits of the firm crosses that.

citation.ref: Section 40A(2)(b) with its Explanation, read with Section 2(41) and Section 40A(2)(a)

items.scenario: Marwah Ceramics Ltd makes four payments in previous year 2025-26, each of them generous. The first is a consultancy fee to Mr Marwah, its managing director. The second is a fee to Mr Marwah's sister. The third is a purchase from Sundar Traders, a firm in which Mr Marwah beneficially holds a 30 per cent share of the profits. The fourth is a fee to Mr Marwah's wife's brother, who is in no other way connected with the company.

items.stem: Can the disallowance stand?

options.text: No — the Act says in terms that the deduction is not to be denied merely because the approval was withdrawn after the payment was made
options.why: The Explanation that follows clause (iii) of section 35(1) provides that the deduction shall not be denied merely on the ground that, subsequent to the payment made by the assessee, the approval granted to the association, university, college or other institution has been withdrawn. The company's position is tested as at the date of payment.

options.text: Yes — a deduction under section 35(1)(ii) is available only while the payee holds a valid approval, and the withdrawal takes it away for every year
options.misconception: makes the payee's continuing approval a condition of the payer's deduction, which the Explanation expressly rejects
options.why: The Explanation exists because a payer cannot police what an approved institution does years later. Approval on the date of payment is what the clause asks for.

options.text: Yes, because the research was in a field unconnected with the company's own business
options.misconception: imports the related-to-the-business condition of section 35(1)(i) into the payment clauses that follow it
options.why: Section 35(1)(i) allows revenue expenditure on scientific research related to the assessee's own business. A sum paid to an approved association under clause (ii) carries no such requirement, which is the point of allowing the payment at all.

options.text: No, but only because the reopening is out of time, the deduction itself being bad
options.misconception: concedes the substantive point and rests the answer on a limitation argument the scenario does not raise
options.why: The deduction is good on its own terms because of the Explanation. Deciding the case on a time limit would leave the company exposed the moment the department got its dates right.

citation.ref: The Explanation to Section 35(1) following clause (iii), read with Section 35(1)(ii) and Section 35(1)(i)

items.scenario: Ambar Polymers Ltd pays ₹20,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 to a research association approved under section 35(1)(ii), to be used for scientific research in a field unconnected with the company's own business. Two years later the approval granted to that association is withdrawn. The Assessing Officer reopens previous year 2025-26 and disallows the whole ₹20,00,000 on the ground that the payee is no longer an approved association.

items.stem: How long may Aravalli Metals Ltd carry the ₹5,00,00,000 forward?

options.text: It cannot be carried forward at all, a loss being personal to the company that suffered it
options.misconception: states the general rule and ignores section 72A, which is the exception to it
options.why: A loss is ordinarily personal to the assessee who incurred it, and that is why section 72A exists. Where its conditions are met the loss moves across.

options.text: Only the unexpired part of Girnar's own period, so up to assessment year 2027-28 and no further
options.why: Girnar merges into Aravalli on 1 October 2025, so the cap that applies to a re-organisation from 1 April 2025 onwards governs. The eight years run from assessment year 2019-20, the year the loss was first determined for Girnar, and that takes the loss no further than assessment year 2027-28. Aravalli inherits what is left of that run and nothing beyond it, which is two assessment years.

options.text: A fresh period runs, the loss being treated as Aravalli's own loss of previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: reads the deeming of the loss into the year of amalgamation as also restarting the eight-year count, which an amalgamation from 1 April 2025 onwards no longer gets
options.why: Section 72A(1) does hand the accumulated loss and the unabsorbed depreciation across, and in the successor's hands they are deemed to be the loss and the depreciation allowance of the amalgamated company, sitting in the previous year in which the amalgamation was effected. That settles whose loss it is, and it is where this answer comes from. It does not settle how many years are left. For an amalgamation on or after 1 April 2025 the outer limit is measured from the year the loss was first worked out in the original predecessor's hands, so Girnar's own clock carries across and no new one is started.
keywords: previous year in which the amalgamation was effected

options.text: Indefinitely, section 72A placing no limit on the number of years
options.misconception: gives a business loss the indefinite carry-forward that belongs to unabsorbed depreciation
options.why: Unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2) carries forward without a time limit. A business loss does not: eight assessment years is its outer limit, and for an amalgamation from 1 April 2025 onwards those years are measured from where the predecessor's own count began rather than handed out again.

citation.ref: Section 72A(4), read with Sections 72A(1), 72A(2), 72A(3) and 72(3) and Rule 9C of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Girnar Steels Ltd owns an industrial undertaking and has an accumulated business loss of ₹5,00,00,000 determined for assessment year 2019-20. On 1 October 2025 it amalgamates into Aravalli Metals Ltd. Every condition in section 72A and in Rule 9C is satisfied. Aravalli's finance team wants to know for how long it may carry the ₹5,00,00,000 forward, since in Girnar's own hands the loss would have run out after assessment year 2027-28.

items.stem: Does the scheme meet the definition of a demerger in section 2(19AA)?

options.text: No — all the property and all the liabilities of the undertaking had to become the property and liabilities of the resulting company
options.why: Clauses (i) and (ii) of section 2(19AA) require that all the property of the undertaking being transferred, and all the liabilities relatable to it, immediately before the demerger become the property and the liabilities of the resulting company. Holding back two warehouses and the loan raised on them breaks both clauses, whatever else the scheme gets right.

options.text: Yes, provided the warehouses and the loan are transferred to Summit Ltd within a reasonable time after the appointed date
options.misconception: invents a grace period for completing the transfer that the definition does not allow
options.why: The clauses speak of the position immediately before the demerger. A later transfer is a separate transaction and cannot repair a scheme that did not answer the definition when it took effect.

options.text: No, because a demerger requires the demerged company to cease to exist once the undertaking has gone
options.misconception: confuses a demerger with an amalgamation, where the transferor company does cease to exist
options.why: A demerged company survives a demerger and carries on whatever it has kept. What defeats this scheme is the property and the liability left behind, not Ridge's continued existence.

options.text: Yes — the shareholder condition and the book-value condition are the substance of section 2(19AA) and both are met
options.misconception: keeps the two conditions most often examined and drops the completeness conditions that open the definition
options.why: Those two conditions are real and they are satisfied. They are two clauses of a definition with several, and a definition fails on any one of its limbs.

citation.ref: Clauses (i) and (ii) of Section 2(19AA), read with clauses (iii), (iv) and (vi) of Section 2(19AA) and Section 47(vib)

items.scenario: Ridge Ltd demerges its logistics undertaking to Summit Ltd under a court-approved scheme. All the property and liabilities are recorded at the values appearing in Ridge's books immediately before the demerger, and shareholders holding far more than three-fourths in value of Ridge's shares become shareholders of Summit on a proportionate basis. The scheme leaves with Ridge two warehouses that the logistics undertaking used, and the bank loan taken to buy them, on the view that Summit does not need either.

items.stem: Which of the four is a specified violation for which the registration may be cancelled under section 12AB(4)?

options.text: The first and the fourth
options.misconception: adds the late audit report to the list of specified violations, when the Act meets that default in a different way
options.why: Furnishing the audit report late has its own consequence under section 12A(1)(b), which is that the exemption under sections 11 and 12 is not available for that year. It is not among the violations that cost the trust its registration.

options.text: The first alone — applying income for an object other than the objects it is registered for
options.why: The Explanation to section 12AB(4) defines a specified violation, and its first limb is a trust that has put income to some object outside the objects for which it is established. An accumulation made under section 11(2) with the statement filed, and a corpus donation held in a mode section 11(5) allows, are things the Act permits.
keywords: objects for which it is established

options.text: All four, section 12AB(4) reaching any departure from the ordinary working of sections 11 and 12
options.misconception: turns a defined list of violations into a general power to cancel
options.why: The Explanation names the violations. A power to cancel on any departure at all would make that list pointless, and would put the registration at the mercy of every procedural slip.

options.text: The second — accumulating income instead of applying it in the year of receipt
options.misconception: treats an accumulation the Act expressly permits as a violation
options.why: Section 11(2) allows a trust to accumulate income for a stated purpose on filing the prescribed statement in time. Using a facility the Act gives cannot be a specified violation.

citation.ref: The Explanation to Section 12AB(4), read with Section 12AB(4), Section 12AB(5), Section 11(2) and Section 12A(1)(b)

items.scenario: A trust registered under section 12AB does four things in previous year 2025-26. It spends ₹8,00,000 on the relief of poverty, which is not among the objects for which it was registered. It accumulates ₹20,00,000 under section 11(2) for a stated purpose and files the prescribed statement in time. It receives a corpus donation of ₹15,00,000 and holds it in a mode section 11(5) permits. It files its audit report a fortnight after its return.

items.stem: What does section 13(4) allow?

options.text: Exemption is denied on the whole ₹80,30,000, the investment breaching section 13(1)(d)
options.misconception: applies the forfeiture to the trust's whole income and ignores the confining rule in section 13(4)
options.why: Section 13(1)(d) does deny exemption where funds are invested otherwise than in the modes section 11(5) allows. Section 13(4) is the provision that limits the damage where the holding is small, and it applies on these facts.

options.text: Nothing is denied, a holding of 3 per cent being too small for section 13 to reach
options.misconception: reads the five per cent rule as an escape from section 13 rather than as a limit on what is forfeited
options.why: The small holding does not make the investment a proper one. It confines the loss to the income arising from that investment, which is the ₹30,000, and does not wipe the loss out.

options.text: Exemption is denied on the whole ₹80,30,000 unless the shares are sold before the end of the previous year
options.misconception: invents a cure by disposal that section 13(4) does not offer
options.why: Section 13(4) turns on the size of the holding, not on when it is disposed of. Selling the shares would end the problem for later years but would change nothing for the year in question.

options.text: Exemption is denied only on the ₹30,000 arising from that investment; the ₹80,00,000 keeps its exemption
options.why: Section 13(4) provides that where the trust's funds put into a concern in which a specified person has a substantial interest stay within five per cent of that concern's capital, the exemption is not denied in relation to any income other than the income arising from that investment. A 3 per cent holding is inside that limit.

citation.ref: Section 13(4), read with Sections 13(1)(d), 13(2)(h), 13(3) and 11(5)

items.scenario: A registered charitable trust holds shares in Meridian Trading Private Ltd, a concern in which the trust's founder has a substantial interest. The investment cost ₹4,00,000 and represents 3 per cent of the nominal capital of that company. The shares are held throughout previous year 2025-26 and yield ₹30,000 of dividend. The trust's other income for the year is ₹80,00,000, all of it properly applied to its objects. The Assessing Officer proposes to deny exemption on the whole ₹80,30,000.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: Yes — a donation is anonymous unless the donor's permanent account number is on record
options.misconception: adds a permanent account number requirement that the definition does not contain
options.why: The definition asks for the name and the address of the donor and such other particulars as may be prescribed. It does not name the permanent account number, and the trust cannot be judged against a condition the section has not laid down.

options.text: No — a donation is anonymous only where the trust has kept no record of the donor's identity showing his name and address, and the register does exactly that
options.why: The definition in section 115BBC(3) turns on the record the trust keeps, not on whether the donor can afterwards be traced. A register showing the name and address of each donor, together with such other particulars as may be prescribed, takes the donation out of the definition, and an undelivered letter does not put it back in.
keywords: such other particulars as may be prescribed

options.text: Yes, because three of the four letters came back, which shows the register is not genuine
options.misconception: converts a failure of later verification into a failure of the record itself
options.why: Whether the record was kept, and what an enquiry two years later turns up, are two different questions. If the officer says the register was fabricated he must say so and prove it; an undelivered letter is not that finding.

options.text: No, but only because the trust runs a school, which is outside section 115BBC altogether
options.misconception: confuses the exclusion written for a wholly religious trust with a general exclusion for educational institutions
options.why: Section 115BBC excludes a trust created wholly for religious purposes, and in a limited way a wholly religious and charitable one. A school run by a charitable trust is squarely inside the section, and this trust escapes on the record it kept.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(3), read with Section 115BBC(1) and Section 115BBC(2)

items.scenario: A charitable trust running a school collects ₹18,00,000 in donations at a fundraising evening. For every donation it entered the donor's name and address in its register, as its standing practice requires. It did not collect anyone's permanent account number, and when the Assessing Officer later wrote to four of the donors, three letters came back undelivered. He treats the whole ₹18,00,000 as anonymous donations.

items.stem: What does section 13A give the party for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: The full exemption — a late return is met by penalty and interest, not by the loss of an exemption
options.misconception: treats a condition written into section 13A itself as an unrelated procedural default
options.why: A late return does draw its own consequences elsewhere in the Act. It also happens to be one of the conditions section 13A attaches to its own exemption, and that is what decides this.

options.text: The exemption on everything except the voluntary contributions, the return condition attaching to those alone
options.misconception: splits the exemption stream by stream, when the condition governs the section as a whole
options.why: The record-keeping conditions are indeed written around contributions. The return condition is not; it is a condition of the section applying at all, so no stream survives it.

options.text: The full exemption, a return under section 139(4B) having no due date of its own
options.misconception: reads section 139(4B) as free-standing, when the due date it works to is the one section 139(1) fixes
options.why: Section 139(4B) requires the chief executive officer of the party to furnish a return where the income, computed without giving effect to section 13A, exceeds the maximum amount not chargeable to tax. The date it must be furnished by is the one section 139(1) fixes.

options.text: Nothing at all — the late return costs it the whole exemption
options.why: The provisos to section 13A are gateways to the exemption as a whole, the section providing that nothing contained in it shall apply unless the conditions are satisfied. One of them is that the political party files its return of income for the previous year as section 139(4B) requires, and files it on or before the due date that section 139 fixes. Filing on 20 December 2026 misses 31 October 2026.
keywords: on or before the due date
nothing contained in it shall apply

citation.ref: The provisos to Section 13A, read with Section 13A clauses (a) to (d) and Section 139(4B)

items.scenario: A registered political party keeps proper books of account, has them audited, records the name and address of every contributor above the amount the section specifies, and takes no cash donation above the limit the section allows. Its due date under section 139(1) for assessment year 2026-27 is 31 October 2026. It furnishes its return under section 139(4B) on 20 December 2026.

items.stem: What is the officer to do with the application?

options.text: Grant the certificate, the permanent account number being a matter for the deductor's quarterly statement and not a condition of the certificate
options.misconception: treats the permanent account number as a reporting detail rather than the express condition section 206AA(4) makes it
options.why: The number is needed in the statement of deduction as well, and that is a separate requirement. Section 206AA(4) puts it on the application itself as a condition of the certificate.

options.text: Refuse the certificate, section 197 being open only to a person other than a company or a firm
options.misconception: imports the restriction on the self-declaration under section 197A into section 197 itself
options.why: Section 197 is open to any person receiving income on which tax is deductible under the sections it lists, a company included. It is section 197A that confines its declarations to persons other than a company or a firm.

options.text: Grant the certificate at the higher rate section 206AA prescribes for a deductee without one
options.misconception: mixes the rate section 206AA sets for a deductee with the bar the same section places on the certificate
options.why: A certificate under section 197 exists to bring a rate down. One issued at the section 206AA rate would give the applicant nothing, and the section does not contemplate it.

options.text: Refuse the certificate, a missing permanent account number being fatal to the application
options.why: Section 206AA(4) provides that no certificate under section 197 shall be granted unless the application made under that section contains the permanent account number of the applicant. The officer has no discretion to look past its absence, however sound the estimate is.
keywords: no certificate under section 197 shall be granted

citation.ref: Section 206AA(4), read with Section 197(1), Section 197A(1) and Rule 28 (Form 13)

items.scenario: A contractor working on thin margins applies to the Assessing Officer in Form 13 for a certificate under section 197 authorising his customers to deduct tax at a lower rate. The application sets out his estimated income for the year and his existing tax liabilities in full, and the officer is satisfied that the estimate is honest. The permanent account number field on the application is blank, the contractor having applied for one that has not yet been allotted.

items.stem: At what rate and for what period does interest run under section 201(1A)?

options.text: At one per cent for every month or part of a month, from 7 June 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.misconception: uses the failure-to-deduct rate and starts the period at the due date for payment
options.why: One per cent is the rate section 201(1A)(i) sets for a failure to deduct, and that clause runs from the date the tax was deductible to the date it is deducted. Once the tax has been deducted, clause (ii) governs and both the rate and the starting point change.

options.text: At one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month, from 7 June 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.misconception: takes the right rate but starts the period at the due date for payment instead of at the date of deduction
options.why: The clause names the date of deduction as the starting point. The company held the Government's money from 12 May 2025, and the interest is computed for the whole of that time.

options.text: No interest, the tax having been paid before the end of the financial year
options.misconception: treats payment within the year as compliance, which section 201(1A) does not
options.why: Section 201(1A) has no end-of-year grace. Interest runs for every month or part of a month of the delay, however and whenever the delay ends.

options.text: At one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month, from 12 May 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.why: Section 201(1A)(ii) governs tax that has been deducted but not paid. Interest on that tax runs at one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month, from the date on which it was deducted right up to the day it is actually paid. The date on which payment fell due does not start the clock.
keywords: from the date on which it was deducted

citation.ref: Section 201(1A)(ii), read with Section 201(1A)(i) and Section 201(1)

items.scenario: Halcyon Media Ltd deducted ₹2,00,000 of tax under section 194J from a payment it made on 12 May 2025. The tax was due to be paid to the credit of the Central Government by 7 June 2025. The company in fact paid it on 20 January 2026.

items.stem: Was the Transfer Pricing Officer entitled to take up the loan?

options.text: Yes — a transaction that comes to his notice during the proceedings before him is treated as though it had been referred to him
options.why: Section 92CA(2A) provides that where any other international transaction comes to the notice of the Transfer Pricing Officer during the course of the proceedings before him, the provisions of the Chapter apply as if that transaction were one referred to him under sub-section (1). No fresh reference from the Assessing Officer is needed.

options.text: No — his jurisdiction is confined to the transactions the Assessing Officer actually referred, so the loan needed a fresh reference
options.misconception: reads section 92CA(1) as the whole of the Transfer Pricing Officer's jurisdiction, missing sub-section (2A)
options.why: That was the position before sub-section (2A) was inserted, and it is the reason the sub-section exists. A transaction the Assessing Officer never spotted is exactly the case it was written for.

options.text: No, because the loan was reported in the section 92E report and a reported transaction cannot be taken up without the assessee's consent
options.misconception: invents a consent requirement and inverts the effect of reporting
options.why: Reporting a transaction does not immunise it. A transaction not reported under section 92E is dealt with by a separate sub-section, and a reported one sits squarely inside sub-section (2A).

options.text: Yes, but only if the Principal Commissioner approves the widening of the reference
options.misconception: carries the approval condition attached to the Assessing Officer's reference over to the Transfer Pricing Officer's own power
options.why: The previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner is a condition of the reference the Assessing Officer makes under section 92CA(1). Sub-section (2A) operates on its own once the transaction comes to the Transfer Pricing Officer's notice.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(2A), read with Section 92CA(1), Section 92CA(2B) and Section 92CA(3)

items.scenario: With the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner, the Assessing Officer refers one international transaction — a royalty paid to the German parent — to the Transfer Pricing Officer. While examining the royalty, the Transfer Pricing Officer notices a second international transaction, an interest-free loan to a fellow subsidiary. That loan was reported in the company's section 92E report but was never referred to him. He determines its arm's length price as well, and the company objects that he had no jurisdiction over it.

items.stem: Who is right, and whom does the agreement bind?

options.text: The officer, because an advance pricing agreement binds the taxpayer alone and never the revenue
options.misconception: makes the agreement one-sided, which section 92CC(5) does not
options.why: The sub-section binds the person and the authorities together. An agreement binding one side only would be worth nothing to the taxpayer who applied for it.

options.text: The company — the agreement binds the Board alone, an Assessing Officer being no party to it
options.misconception: reads the agreement as a private contract between the Board and the company, binding nobody else
options.why: Section 92CC(5) reaches the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the authorities subordinate to him, so the Assessing Officer is bound while the agreement stands. It is the change in law that releases him, not any want of privity.

options.text: The company — an advance pricing agreement binds both sides for its full term, whatever happens afterwards
options.misconception: treats the agreement as immune to a change in the very law it was written under
options.why: The certainty an agreement buys is certainty about the application of the law as it stood when the agreement was made. Section 92CC(6) says so in terms.

options.text: The officer — the agreement ceases to bind on a change in law, and while it stands it binds the company and the tax authorities alike on that transaction
options.why: Section 92CC(5) binds the person in whose case the agreement is entered into, only in respect of the transaction it covers, and binds the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the authorities subordinate to him in respect of that person and that transaction. Section 92CC(6) then provides that the agreement shall not be binding if there is a change in law or facts having a bearing on it.

citation.ref: Sections 92CC(5) and 92CC(6), read with Section 92CC(1) and Section 92CD(1)

items.scenario: An advance pricing agreement is entered into with Vasant Systems Ltd covering the arm's length price of a management fee paid to its parent, for five consecutive previous years. In the third of those years Parliament amends the very provision on which the agreed method rests. The Assessing Officer for that year says the agreement no longer binds him. The company says an agreement is an agreement and both sides are held to it for its full term.

items.stem: Does section 9A still keep the manager's activity from creating a business connection in India?

options.text: Yes, provided he gives up the salaried post before the end of the previous year
options.misconception: invents a cure by later resignation that the section does not provide
options.why: The conditions describe the arrangement under which the activity was actually carried on during the year. Nothing in section 9A lets a condition be satisfied afterwards for the months during which it was broken.

options.text: No, and the consequence is that the fund becomes resident in India for the year
options.misconception: overstates the consequence, confusing the loss of the section 9A protection with a finding on residence
options.why: Losing section 9A means the two deemings in sections 9A(1) and 9A(2) are not available, so the manager's activity may create a business connection and the place of control may be examined. Residence still has to be decided under section 6(3) on its own facts.

options.text: No — the manager must not be an employee of the fund, and his salaried post breaks that condition
options.why: Section 9A(1) gives its protection only where the fund management activity is carried out through an eligible fund manager, and section 9A(4)(a) opens that definition by requiring that the manager is not an employee of the fund he manages, nor a connected person of it. A man on the fund's payroll fails it, and the conditions that are met cannot supply the one that is not.

options.text: Yes — the employment is beside the point, section 9A caring only that the manager is registered and paid at arm's length
options.misconception: keeps the conditions most often quoted and drops the independence condition that opens the definition
options.why: Registration and arm's length remuneration are two of the conditions in section 9A(4). The first of them is independence from the fund, and a definition fails on any one of its limbs.

citation.ref: Section 9A(4)(a), read with Sections 9A(1), 9A(2) and 9A(3) and Section 6(3)

items.scenario: Meridian Offshore Fund appoints Mr Sridhar, based in Mumbai, as its fund manager. He is registered with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, acts in the ordinary course of his business, is paid at arm's length for the activity, and neither he nor his connected persons are entitled to more than the share of the fund's profits that section 9A(4) permits. He is also on the fund's own payroll as its whole-time head of research and draws a salary from it. Every condition in section 9A(3) is satisfied.

items.stem: What does the Act say on the officer's proposal and on Mr Bhalla's question?

options.text: The complaint may be filed only at the instance of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and the offence may be compounded either before or after proceedings are instituted
options.why: Section 279(1) bars a prosecution for a section 276CC offence save at the instance of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, so the Assessing Officer cannot launch the prosecution on his own. Section 279(2) allows the offence to be compounded by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, and says it may be done either before or after the institution of proceedings.

options.text: Neither sanction nor compounding arises, an offence under section 276CC being a matter for the criminal court alone
options.misconception: treats the offence as one the Act sets in motion by itself
options.why: The Act creates the offence and also says who may set it in motion and who may compound it. The criminal court tries the complaint; it does not initiate one.

options.text: The complaint needs the Principal Commissioner's sanction, but compounding is possible only before the complaint is filed
options.misconception: states the sanction requirement correctly and then halves the compounding power
options.why: The sanction half of this is right. Section 279(2) then allows compounding either before or after the institution of proceedings, so the filing of the complaint is not a cut-off.

options.text: The Assessing Officer may file the complaint himself, and once it is filed the offence can no longer be compounded
options.misconception: skips the sanction requirement and denies a compounding power the Act expressly gives after institution
options.why: The sanction of a senior authority stands between an officer's satisfaction and a criminal court. And compounding survives the filing of the complaint, the sub-section saying so in terms.

citation.ref: Sections 279(1) and 279(2), read with Section 276CC and Section 278E

items.scenario: The Assessing Officer is satisfied that Mr Bhalla wilfully failed to furnish his return for assessment year 2023-24 and that the case falls outside the proviso to section 276CC. He proposes to file a complaint in the criminal court himself, without troubling anyone above him. Mr Bhalla, hearing of it, wants to know whether the matter can still be settled without a trial.

items.stem: For what period does interest under section 244A run on this refund?

options.text: From 18 September 2025 to 14 July 2026
options.why: Section 244A(1)(b) covers a refund of any amount other than those the earlier clauses name, and gives interest at one-half per cent for every month or part of a month from the date of payment of the tax or penalty to the date on which the refund is granted. The tax was paid on 18 September 2025 and refunded on 14 July 2026.
keywords: date on which the refund is granted

options.text: From 2 May 2026 to 14 July 2026
options.misconception: treats the appellate order as the event that creates the refund and so starts the interest
options.why: The appellate order establishes that the money should never have been collected. Section 244A therefore compensates from the date it was collected, not from the date the mistake was found.

options.text: From 1 April 2026 to 14 July 2026
options.misconception: applies the starting point clause (a) sets for advance tax and tax deducted at source to a payment made against a notice of demand
options.why: The first of April is the starting point in clause (a), which deals with refunds out of advance tax and tax collected or deducted at source. Tax paid against a notice of demand is refunded with interest from the day it was paid.

options.text: No interest is payable, the refund arising from an appellate order rather than from the assessment
options.misconception: reads section 244A as confined to refunds thrown up by the assessment itself
options.why: Section 244A applies to any amount becoming due to an assessee under the Act, and a refund following an appellate order is squarely within it.

citation.ref: Section 244A(1)(b), read with Section 244A(1)(a) and Section 244A(2)

items.scenario: A demand of ₹5,00,000 was raised on Ms Fernandes by a notice under section 156 following her assessment, and she paid the whole of it on 18 September 2025. None of it was advance tax, tax deducted at source or self-assessment tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition by an order dated 2 May 2026, and the refund of ₹5,00,000 was granted to her on 14 July 2026.

items.stem: What is his due date for furnishing his return for assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: 31 July 2026, since his own accounts need no audit and the ordinary date applies to him
options.misconception: reads the audit-case date as attaching to the assessee's own accounts, when Explanation 2 extends it to a partner of an audited firm
options.why: 31 July is the residual date for any other assessee, and it would be right if the Explanation stopped at the person whose own accounts are audited. It does not. A partner is taken out by name, because his share of the firm's profit is not known until the firm's audited accounts are ready.

options.text: 31 October 2026, a partner of a firm whose accounts must be audited taking the audit-case date even though his own accounts are not audited
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 139(1) gives 31 October of the assessment year not only to an assessee whose own accounts must be audited but also, by name, to a partner of a firm that is itself under audit. The date follows the firm's audit rather than anything of the partner's, so Mr Sethi files by 31 October 2026.

options.text: 30 September 2026, the firm's audit report being due by then and the partner's return following it
options.misconception: takes the date for the audit report as the date for the return, when the two are fixed separately
options.why: The tax audit report has a date of its own, set a month ahead of the return. The return date is fixed by Explanation 2 to section 139(1), and for an audit case, and for a partner of an audited firm, that date is 31 October.

options.text: 30 November 2026, the firm being under audit and the extended date for audited entities passing to the partner
options.misconception: uses the 30 November date, which section 139(1) reserves for an assessee required to furnish a report under section 92E
options.why: 30 November belongs to an assessee who is required to furnish a report under section 92E for an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction. Mr Sethi has neither, and an audit under section 44AB does not move any date to 30 November.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 to Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Mr Sethi is a partner in Vasudha Associates, a firm whose accounts are required to be audited under section 44AB for previous year 2025-26. His own income is his share from the firm, his remuneration from it and some bank interest. Nothing of his own is required to be audited, and he has no international transaction and no specified domestic transaction.

items.stem: Does section 195 require anything else of Trident Ltd?

options.text: Yes, it must first apply to the Assessing Officer under section 195(2) for a determination, even on a sum that is not chargeable
options.misconception: makes the section 195(2) application compulsory, when it is a remedy for a payer who thinks only part of a sum is chargeable
options.why: Section 195(2) is an option for a payer who considers that only a proportion of a payment bears tax and wants that proportion fixed before he pays. It is not a gate every remittance has to pass through, and it has nothing to do on a sum that bears no tax at all.

options.text: No, once the sum is not chargeable to tax the whole of section 195 falls away
options.misconception: reads every part of section 195 as switched off by non-chargeability, when sub-section (6) is drafted the other way round
options.why: Sub-section (1) is switched off, because it deducts only from a sum chargeable to tax. Sub-section (6) was written with the opposite words and applies whether or not the sum is chargeable, which is how the department sees remittances it would otherwise never hear of.

options.text: Yes, the German supplier must first obtain a certificate under section 197 authorising nil deduction
options.misconception: uses section 197, which is the payee's route for a lower or nil deduction on income that is chargeable
options.why: Section 197 lets a payee whose income is chargeable ask for a certificate authorising deduction at a lower rate or at no rate. Where nothing is chargeable in the first place there is no deduction for such a certificate to reduce.

options.text: Yes, section 195(6) requires the payer to furnish the prescribed information on the payment whether or not the sum is chargeable to tax
options.why: Section 195(6) stands apart from the duty to deduct. It obliges the person responsible for paying any sum to a non-resident to furnish the information relating to that payment in the prescribed form and manner, and it says in terms "whether or not chargeable" under the Act. A finding that nothing is chargeable therefore settles the deduction and leaves the reporting duty exactly where it was.

citation.ref: Section 195(6), read with Sections 195(1) and 195(2)

items.scenario: Trident Ltd remits ₹15,00,000 to a supplier in Germany for goods manufactured and delivered wholly outside India. Its consultant confirms that the sum is not chargeable to tax in India, so nothing is deducted under section 195(1). The company concludes that section 195 has nothing further to say to it and makes the remittance through its bank, filing nothing.

items.stem: What does the failure to furnish the report attract?

options.text: No penalty, the report being a formality where the pricing has been accepted
options.misconception: makes the reporting duty conditional on its outcome, when section 271BA penalises the failure itself
options.why: Section 92E requires the report because an international transaction exists, and section 271BA then penalises the failure to furnish it. Neither section asks whether an adjustment followed, which is what makes the report a filing obligation rather than an admission.

options.text: A penalty of ₹1,00,000 under section 271BA, whether or not any adjustment was made
options.why: Section 271BA provides that where a person fails to furnish a report from an accountant as required by section 92E, the Assessing Officer may direct him to pay a penalty of one hundred thousand rupees. The penalty attaches to the failure itself and is a fixed sum, so what the benchmarking produced makes no difference to it.

options.text: A penalty measured at two per cent of the value of the international transactions
options.misconception: uses the proportionate measure that other transfer pricing defaults carry, when section 271BA fixes a flat sum
options.why: A penalty scaled to the value of the transaction belongs to other defaults in this chapter. Section 271BA names one figure and it does not grow with the size of the transactions, so a small exporter and a large one face the same sum for the same failure.

options.text: A penalty under section 271AA, which is the transfer pricing penalty section
options.misconception: reaches for the documentation penalty when the default is in the accountant's report, which has its own section
options.why: Section 271AA is aimed at a failure in the information and documents kept under section 92D and at a transaction reported wrongly or not at all. The accountant's report under section 92E is a separate obligation and section 271BA is its separate penalty.

citation.ref: Section 271BA, read with Section 92E

items.scenario: Sarvesh Exports Ltd entered into international transactions with its associated enterprises during previous year 2025-26 and neither obtained nor furnished the accountant's report under section 92E. The Transfer Pricing Officer examined the pricing and made no adjustment. The company says that since nothing was lost to the revenue, no penalty can follow.

items.stem: Must Mr Bhagat deduct tax at source under section 194A?

options.text: Yes, because the exclusion of an individual covers interest on a personal borrowing, and this loan was taken for his business
options.misconception: makes the exclusion turn on the purpose of the borrowing, when the sub-section turns on the payer's status and the proviso on his turnover
options.why: The words of the sub-section look at who is paying, not at what the borrowed money was for. What can bring a proprietor inside the section is his turnover in the preceding year crossing the limits in the proviso, and that is an entirely different test.

options.text: No, because section 194A does not reach an individual payer unless the proviso brings him in, and it does not on these figures
options.why: Section 194A(1) fastens the duty on any person "not being an individual or a Hindu undivided family". The proviso pulls such a person back in only where his sales, gross receipts or turnover in the preceding financial year crossed the limits it states, and Mr Bhagat's ₹40,00,000 is below them. No duty arises, whatever the size of the interest.
keywords: not being an individual or a Hindu undivided family

options.text: Yes, because ₹1,40,000 is far above the general threshold in section 194A, so tax must be deducted
options.misconception: applies the threshold before asking whether the payer is a person section 194A(1) reaches at all
options.why: A threshold answers how much, and it is reached only after the section has found a payer it applies to. Section 194A(1) begins by taking an individual and a Hindu undivided family out, so on these facts the threshold is never argued.

options.text: No, because interest paid to a friend rather than to a bank or a finance company is outside section 194A
options.misconception: invents an exclusion for a private lender, when the section reaches interest paid to any resident
options.why: Section 194A covers interest other than interest on securities paid to a resident, and the lender's identity is not the test of whether the section applies. Who the payee is decides only which threshold would be used, and the case is settled before that by who the payer is.

citation.ref: Section 194A(1) with its proviso

items.scenario: Mr Bhagat runs a small retail shop as a sole proprietor. His turnover in previous year 2024-25 was ₹40,00,000, which is below the monetary limits stated in the proviso to section 194A(1), and his accounts were not required to be audited. During previous year 2025-26 he pays ₹1,40,000 of interest on a business loan taken from Mr Chawla, a resident friend who has furnished his permanent account number.

items.stem: Is the accountant right?

options.text: Yes, because a payment to a sub-lessor is a licence fee rather than rent, and section 194-I reaches only rent
options.misconception: renames the payment instead of reading the definition, which covers any agreement or arrangement for the use of the property
options.why: The Explanation opens with "any payment, by whatever name called" and then names lease, sub-lease, tenancy and any other agreement or arrangement. Calling the payment a licence fee changes none of the things the section actually turns on.

options.text: No, but at two per cent, a sub-lease being the hire of a facility rather than the letting of a building
options.misconception: moves a building into the rate section 194-I reserves for machinery, plant or equipment
options.why: The rate follows the thing let, not the kind of interest the payee holds in it. A warehouse is a building, and the two per cent rate belongs to plant, machinery and equipment, so nothing about a sub-lease changes which limb of the section applies.

options.text: No, because the Explanation to section 194-I defines rent as a payment under a lease, sub-lease, tenancy or any other agreement for the use of the property, whether or not the payee owns it
options.why: The definition names a sub-lease alongside a lease and a tenancy, and it ends by saying that none of the listed assets need be owned by the payee. Ownership is therefore not a condition of the section at all, and what Vega Ltd pays Mr Deshpande is rent for a building on which it must deduct.
keywords: none of the listed assets need be owned by the payee

options.text: Yes, but only because Mr Deshpande holds no title; the deduction would be due had the owner let the warehouse directly
options.misconception: keeps ownership as the test after conceding the point, when the Explanation removes it in terms
options.why: Title has nothing to do with it. The section asks whether a payment is made for the use of land, a building, machinery, plant, equipment, furniture or fittings, and then adds expressly that it does not matter whether the payee owns them.

citation.ref: Section 194-I with the Explanation defining rent

items.scenario: Vega Ltd takes a warehouse on rent from Mr Deshpande for ₹1,20,000 a month through previous year 2025-26, well above the section 194-I threshold. Mr Deshpande does not own the warehouse. He holds it on a long lease from its owner and has sub-let it to Vega Ltd. Vega's accountant says nothing is deductible, because section 194-I reaches rent paid to an owner.

items.stem: Must Vindhya Ltd deduct tax under section 194J?

options.text: No, because a sitting fee is paid for attending a meeting rather than for a service rendered, so it is outside section 194J
options.misconception: reads clause (ba) as needing a service, when it covers remuneration or fees by whatever name called
options.why: Clause (ba) uses the words "any remuneration or fees or commission by whatever name called", which are drafted wide enough to catch a sitting fee without asking what was done for it. The only thing it excludes is a sum on which section 192 already operates.

options.text: No, because ₹18,000 is below the limit in the first proviso, which governs every payment the section covers
options.misconception: applies the proviso's monetary limit to clause (ba), which the proviso does not name
options.why: The proviso lists by letter the clauses it applies to, and clause (ba) was deliberately left out of that list when it was inserted. A director's fee is therefore deductible from the first rupee, which is the whole point of the omission.

options.text: Yes, because clause (ba) covers a director's remuneration or fees other than salary and the first proviso's limit is not written for that clause
options.why: Section 194J(1)(ba) reaches any remuneration, fees or commission, by whatever name called, paid to a director of a company, other than a sum on which tax is deductible under section 192. The first proviso then sets a monetary limit for the sums in clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d), and clause (ba) is not one of them, so the ₹18,000 bears tax however small it is.
keywords: other than a sum on which tax is deductible under section 192

options.text: No, because a director is an officer of the company and the deduction, if any, belongs to section 192
options.misconception: sends a non-employee director's fee to section 192, which reaches only a payment taxable as salary
options.why: Section 192 deducts from income chargeable under the head salaries, which needs a relationship of employer and employee. Clause (ba) exists for the director who is not an employee, and it excludes by name any sum on which section 192 already bites.

citation.ref: Section 194J(1)(ba) with the first proviso to Section 194J(1)

items.scenario: Vindhya Ltd pays Mr Salim, a non-executive director who is not its employee, sitting fees of ₹18,000 for attending board meetings during previous year 2025-26. That is the only sum it pays him in the year, and it is below the monetary limit in the first proviso to section 194J(1). He draws no salary from the company, so nothing is deductible under section 192. The accountant leaves the payment alone.

items.stem: On which of the two must tax be deducted under section 194H?

options.text: On Mr Rane's ₹90,000 only, the Explanation to section 194H excluding a transaction relating to securities from the meaning it gives those words
options.why: The Explanation catches a payment for services rendered other than professional services, a payment for services in the course of buying or selling of goods, and a payment tied to a dealing in any asset, valuable article or thing — with the words "not being securities" cutting securities back out. Brokerage on listed shares is a dealing in securities and falls outside the meaning of commission or brokerage; procuring orders for steel sits inside it.
keywords: services in the course of buying or selling of goods

options.text: On both, each being commission or brokerage paid to a resident above the threshold
options.misconception: applies the section without reading its own Explanation, which carves securities out
options.why: The payee and the threshold are satisfied for each payment, which is what makes this read well. What decides the case is the Explanation, and it closes with the words "not being securities" for exactly this situation.

options.text: On Ms Sohal's ₹1,20,000 only, brokerage being the very word the section uses
options.misconception: takes the label instead of the definition, when the section's own Explanation excludes a securities transaction
options.why: The section is headed commission or brokerage and then defines those words for itself. A payment that answers the ordinary meaning of brokerage can still sit outside the statutory definition, and brokerage on securities is the case the Explanation names.

options.text: On neither, because section 194H reaches only a payment made by a principal to his own selling agent
options.misconception: narrows the section to one kind of agency, when it covers any payment for the services the Explanation describes
options.why: The Explanation covers a payment received by a person acting on behalf of another for services rendered, or for services in the course of buying or selling goods. Mr Rane procuring orders is squarely inside that, whatever the two of them call their arrangement.

citation.ref: Explanation (i) to Section 194H

items.scenario: Anantam Trading Ltd pays two amounts to residents during previous year 2025-26. It pays ₹90,000 to Mr Rane for procuring orders for its steel division. It pays ₹1,20,000 to Ms Sohal, a stockbroker, as brokerage on its own purchases and sales of listed shares on a recognised stock exchange. Both have furnished their permanent account numbers and each amount is well above the section 194H threshold.

items.stem: What may be recovered from Mr Kapoor under section 179?

options.text: The ₹9,00,000 of tax and the ₹2,00,000 of interest, but not the penalty, a penalty being personal to the defaulter
options.misconception: splits the Explanation's own list, which names penalty alongside interest
options.why: The Explanation makes no such division. Penalty stands first in the list of things the expression tax due includes, so a penalty imposed on the company is recoverable from the director on exactly the same footing as the tax.

options.text: Only the ₹9,00,000 of tax, interest and penalty remaining liabilities of the company alone
options.misconception: reads "tax due" in its narrow sense, when the Explanation to section 179 widens it
options.why: That would be right if the section stopped at the words tax due. The Explanation was added to stop precisely this argument, and it names penalty, interest and fees among the things the expression takes in.

options.text: The whole ₹12,50,000, the Explanation to section 179 making the expression "tax due" include penalty, interest, fees and any other sum payable under the Act
options.why: Section 179(1) makes a director liable for the tax due from the company, and the Explanation to section 179 says that expression includes penalty, interest, fees or any other sum payable under the Act. The ₹2,00,000 of interest and the ₹1,50,000 of penalty therefore travel with the ₹9,00,000 of tax, and ₹12,50,000 may be recovered from him.

options.text: Nothing, because a sum of this size must first be pursued under the Second Schedule against the company itself
options.misconception: invents a procedural condition, when section 179 fixes the liability once recovery from the company has failed
options.why: The condition in section 179(1) is that the tax cannot be recovered from the company, and that is exactly what has happened here. Once it has, and once the director's defence fails, he is jointly and severally liable and the recovery machinery then runs against him.

citation.ref: Explanation to Section 179, read with Section 179(1)

items.scenario: Recovery against Sarita Fabrics Pvt Ltd, a private company, has failed and the company has no assets. What remains outstanding for previous year 2022-23 is tax of ₹9,00,000, interest of ₹2,00,000 and a penalty of ₹1,50,000. Mr Kapoor was a director throughout that previous year and cannot show that the non-recovery is free of any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part.

items.stem: Must he furnish a return of income under section 139(1)?

options.text: Yes, because deduction at source is a collection mechanism and never removes the duty to file
options.misconception: treats deduction at source as never dispensing with a return, when section 115AC(4) does exactly that in this narrow case
options.why: That is the general position and it is why the exception had to be written. Section 115AC(4) is a specific relief for a non-resident whose whole Indian income is this dividend or interest and has already borne tax at the full rate.

options.text: No, because a non-resident is outside section 139(1) altogether
options.misconception: reads a non-resident out of the return provision, when section 139(1) applies to him and section 115AC(4) is a narrow exception to it
options.why: Section 139(1) reaches every person whose total income exceeds the maximum amount not chargeable to tax, resident or not. What saves Mr Halim is one specific sub-section written for one narrow case, and not any general immunity from filing.

options.text: No, and the relief would hold just the same had he sold some of the receipts during the year at a gain
options.misconception: extends section 115AC(4) to capital gains, when the sub-section names only the income in clause (a)
options.why: The relief is tied to the income referred to in clause (a) of section 115AC(1), which is the interest or the dividend. A capital gain on transfer of the receipts falls under clause (b), and once such a gain is in his total income the exemption from filing is gone.

options.text: No, because section 115AC(4) excuses a non-resident whose income consisted only of such dividend or interest and from which tax has been deducted
options.why: Section 115AC(4) says it shall not be necessary for a non-resident to furnish a return under section 139(1) where his total income consisted only of the income referred to in clause (a) of section 115AC(1) and the tax deductible under Chapter XVII-B has been deducted from it. Mr Halim satisfies both conditions, so no return is due from him.

citation.ref: Section 115AC(4), read with Section 115AC(1)(a)

items.scenario: Mr Halim is a non-resident. His only Indian income for previous year 2025-26 is ₹6,00,000 of dividend on global depository receipts of an Indian company, purchased by him in foreign currency under a scheme notified by the Central Government. Tax has been deducted at source on the whole of it under Chapter XVII-B. He sold none of the receipts during the year.

items.stem: Which section deems the profits of Kessel Power GmbH?

options.text: Section 44BBA, which covers any non-resident earning from a project carried out in India
options.misconception: reads section 44BBA as a general presumptive section, when it is confined to the business of operation of aircraft
options.why: Section 44BBA opens with a non-resident engaged in the business of operation of aircraft and goes no wider. Nothing in it reaches construction or the erection of plant, which is exactly why section 44BBB was enacted beside it.

options.text: Section 44BB, the erection and commissioning of plant being services connected with an extraction project
options.misconception: borrows section 44BB, which is tied to the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils
options.why: Section 44BB is written for services and plant supplied in connection with the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils. A power project is not that, however similar the engineering work may look on the ground.

options.text: Section 44BBB, which is written for a foreign company engaged in civil construction, erection, testing or commissioning in connection with an approved turnkey power project
options.why: Section 44BBB names its own assessee and its own work — a foreign company whose business is civil construction, or erecting plant or machinery, or testing and commissioning what it has erected, for a turnkey power project the Central Government has approved. Kessel Power GmbH answers that description exactly, while section 44BBA is confined to the business of operation of aircraft, which is Skylark's business and not its.

options.text: Section 44BBB, but only if Kessel Power GmbH is a non-resident of any kind rather than specifically a foreign company
options.misconception: loosens the status the section requires, when section 44BBB names a foreign company and not merely a non-resident
options.why: The status matters here and is narrower than in the neighbouring sections. Section 44BBB applies "in the case of an assessee, being a foreign company", where sections 44B, 44BB and 44BBA each address a non-resident. Kessel Power GmbH is a foreign company, so it fits.

citation.ref: Section 44BBB(1), read with Section 44BBA(1)

items.scenario: Two non-residents earn from Indian work in previous year 2025-26. Skylark Air Inc operates aircraft and carries passengers out of Indian airports. Kessel Power GmbH, a foreign company, erects and commissions generating plant for a turnkey power project the Central Government has approved, and is paid ₹50,00,000 for that work.

items.stem: Is the interest deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.text: Yes, but only to the extent the Government's project abroad remitted money back to India
options.misconception: invents an apportionment, when clause (a) deems the whole of the interest to accrue in India
options.why: Clause (a) contains no proportion and no tracing of any kind. Once the Government is the payer the whole of the interest is deemed to accrue in India, and what the borrowed money went on to earn abroad is beside the point.

options.text: No, because interest on money borrowed and used for a business carried on outside India is taken out of section 9(1)(v)
options.misconception: applies the clause (b) exception, which is written for a resident payer, to a payment by the Government under clause (a)
options.why: The exception is real and it belongs where it is written. It removes from clause (b) the interest on money borrowed and used for a business carried on outside India, and clause (a) has no counterpart to it at all.

options.text: Yes, because section 9(1)(v)(a) sources interest payable by the Government and attaches no condition about how the borrowing was used
options.why: Section 9(1)(v) has three limbs and only two of them carry a use test. Section 9(1)(v)(a) covers interest payable by the Government and stops there. The exception for money borrowed and used for a business carried on outside India sits inside clause (b), which is about interest payable by a resident, so it never touches a payment made by the Government.

options.text: No, because Meridian Bank has no business connection or place of business in India
options.misconception: asks for a presence in India, when section 9(1)(v) sources interest by reference to the payer and, in two limbs, the use of the money
options.why: Section 9(1)(v) works on who is paying and, in two of its three limbs, on what the money was used for. A presence in India is what section 9(1)(i) turns on for a business connection, and that is a different clause answering a different question.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(v)(a), read with Section 9(1)(v)(b)

items.scenario: The Government of India borrows from Meridian Bank, a non-resident, and pays it ₹40,00,000 of interest during previous year 2025-26. The whole of the borrowing was used for a project the Government runs outside India. Meridian Bank has no office, agent or business connection in India, and argues that the interest cannot be Indian income because the money was used abroad.

items.stem: Is section 10(2A) available to Mr Iqbal?

options.text: Yes, the association having borne tax on the whole ₹24,00,000, so the same reasoning exempts his share
options.misconception: carries the reason behind section 10(2A) across to a body the clause does not name
options.why: The reason is much the same and the clause is not written that way. Section 10(2A) names a firm, and where Parliament wanted a comparable result for an association of persons it wrote section 86, which reaches it by a different route.

options.text: No, but his share is kept out of his total income all the same, the association having already been charged on it
options.misconception: reaches the right conclusion on section 10(2A) and then borrows its mechanism for section 86
options.why: Section 86 is drafted as a relief from tax and says that income-tax shall not be payable in respect of the share. Where the association has been charged at ordinary rates the share still forms part of the member's total income, and relieving a tax is not the same act as removing an income.

options.text: Yes, and section 86 is simply the machinery through which section 10(2A) is given effect for an association
options.misconception: treats section 86 as machinery for section 10(2A), when the two sit in different places and do different work
options.why: Section 10(2A) keeps a partner's share outside total income altogether. Section 86 leaves a member's share inside total income and relieves the tax on it, which is why that share can still affect the rate borne by the rest of his income.

options.text: No, section 10(2A) being confined to a partner of a firm assessed as such, and a member's share in an association of persons being governed by sections 67A and 86
options.why: Section 10(2A) speaks of a person being a partner of a firm which is separately assessed as such, and an association of persons is not a firm, so the clause cannot stretch to Mr Iqbal. His share is computed under section 67A. Section 86 then provides that income-tax shall not be payable by a member in respect of that share, but it works by relieving the tax rather than by keeping the share out of total income, which is what section 10(2A) does for a partner.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A), read with Sections 67A and 86

items.scenario: Mr Iqbal is a member of Konark Associates, an association of persons, with a one-fourth share. For previous year 2025-26 the association's total income is ₹24,00,000 and it has been charged to tax at the rates applicable to an association of persons, not at the maximum marginal rate. Mr Iqbal's accountant keeps his ₹6,00,000 share out of his total income, relying on section 10(2A).

items.stem: What goes into the aggregate on which section 44B operates?

options.text: ₹8,40,00,000, demurrage being a charge on the cargo but handling charges being a separate service that stays outside
options.misconception: splits the Explanation's own list, which names handling charges beside demurrage
options.why: The Explanation names demurrage charge and handling charge in one breath and then adds any other amount of a similar nature. Neither can be taken out on the footing that it pays for a service rather than for carriage.

options.text: ₹8,00,00,000, with the demurrage and handling charges computed separately as ordinary business income under section 28
options.misconception: takes the two charges out of the presumptive aggregate and computes them again elsewhere, which the Explanation prevents
options.why: Section 44B opens with a non-obstante clause displacing sections 28 to 43A for this business, so no separate computation runs beside it. The Explanation puts the two charges inside the presumptive aggregate, which is the only computation there is.

options.text: ₹8,60,00,000, the Explanation to section 44B(2) putting demurrage and handling charges into the amount along with any other amount of a similar nature
options.why: The Explanation widens what section 44B(2) takes in. An amount paid or payable as a demurrage charge or handling charge is drawn in, and so is any other amount of similar nature. The ₹40,00,000 and the ₹20,00,000 therefore join the ₹8,00,00,000, and the aggregate is ₹8,60,00,000 before the presumptive percentage is applied to it.
keywords: any other amount of similar nature

options.text: ₹8,00,00,000, only freight for the carriage of goods answering the description in section 44B(2)
options.misconception: reads section 44B(2) without its Explanation, which names demurrage and handling charges
options.why: The sub-section on its own does read as freight for carriage, which is why the Explanation had to be added. A shipping line's bill routinely carries these charges beside the freight, and leaving them out would let the aggregate be shrunk by relabelling.

citation.ref: The Explanation to Section 44B(2)

items.scenario: Meridian Lines Inc, a non-resident, operates cargo ships. For previous year 2025-26 it receives ₹8,00,00,000 in India as freight for goods shipped at Kandla port. On the same shipments it also receives in India ₹40,00,000 of demurrage charges and ₹20,00,000 of handling charges. Its accountant puts only the freight into the section 44B aggregate, saying demurrage is a charge for delay and handling is a service charge, and neither is freight.

items.stem: Can it be assessed on the ₹40,00,000 instead?

options.text: Yes, because section 44BB(3) lets an assessee who keeps those books and furnishes that audit report claim lower profits, and the Assessing Officer then assesses him under section 143(3)
options.why: Section 44BB(3) provides that notwithstanding sub-section (1) an assessee may claim lower profits and gains than the presumptive figure, if he keeps and maintains the books and documents required under section 44AA(2) and gets his accounts audited and furnishes the report required under section 44AB. The Assessing Officer thereupon makes an assessment of the total income or loss under section 143(3). Corvid Energy has met both conditions.

options.text: No, because a claim under section 44BB(3) is open only where the whole of the work was done outside India
options.misconception: invents a geographical condition, when sub-section (3) turns on books and audit and not on where the work was done
options.why: Where the work was done decides which receipts enter the aggregate under sub-section (2). Sub-section (3) is about proving the real profit earned on that aggregate, and it is available wherever the work was done.

options.text: Yes, and it may do so simply by declaring the lower figure in its return, the books and the audit report being matters of good practice
options.misconception: drops the conditions the sub-section attaches, which are what buy the right to claim less
options.why: The claim is open only to an assessee who keeps the section 44AA(2) books and furnishes the section 44AB report. Those conditions are the price of leaving the presumptive figure, not advice about record-keeping, and without them the deemed profits stand.

options.text: No, because the presumptive figure is conclusive, which is what makes section 44BB a presumptive section
options.misconception: reads section 44BB as an irrebuttable deeming, when sub-section (3) provides the way out
options.why: Some presumptive charges are indeed conclusive and this one is not. Sub-section (3) opens with a non-obstante clause aimed at sub-section (1) and lets the assessee show a lower figure on stated conditions.

citation.ref: Section 44BB(3), read with Sections 44AA(2), 44AB and 143(3)

items.scenario: Corvid Energy Ltd, a non-resident company, provides services in connection with the extraction of mineral oils in India. Its receipts for previous year 2025-26 produce a presumptive figure of ₹1,50,00,000 under section 44BB(1). Its accounts for the Indian operations show an actual profit of ₹40,00,000. It keeps and maintains the books of account and other documents required under section 44AA(2), has had them audited, and furnishes the report required under section 44AB.

items.stem: Does section 9(1)(vii) deem this fee to accrue or arise in India?

options.text: Yes, the payer being a resident and the Explanation to section 9(2) making the deeming apply whether or not the services were rendered in India
