citation.ref: Serial number 36C, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025, read with serial number 36D

items.scenario: In July 2026 a life insurer issues two policies. One is an endowment policy taken by a salaried man on his own life, with his wife as nominee. The other is a group term policy taken out by a factory over its four hundred workers, the factory paying the whole premium.

items.stem: How does paragraph 4 of Schedule II classify the two?

options.text: Both are supplies of goods, the same asset being involved in each case
options.misconception: classifies by what the asset is rather than by whether it left the business for good
options.why: The asset is a red herring in both clauses. What separates them is whether the goods have stopped being assets of the business, which the guillotine has and the camera has not.

options.text: Both are supplies of services, neither having been sold for money
options.misconception: treats the absence of a sale as making the transaction a service, when clause (a) applies whether or not for a consideration
options.why: Clause (a) says in terms that it applies whether or not for a consideration. A free disposal is inside it, and it produces a supply of goods.

options.text: The guillotine is a supply of goods and the camera is a supply of services
options.why: Clause (a) covers goods forming part of the assets of a business that are transferred or disposed of so as no longer to form part of those assets, and calls that a supply of goods, whether or not for a consideration — the guillotine has gone for good. Clause (b) covers goods held for the business that are put to any private use or made available for a purpose other than a purpose of the business, and calls the usage a supply of services — the camera came back, so what was supplied was its use and not the thing.
keywords: no longer to form part of those assets

options.text: Neither is a supply, because no consideration passed in either case
options.misconception: requires a consideration where paragraph 4 is written as a set of deeming provisions that do not need one
options.why: Paragraph 4 exists to catch exactly these two cases. Both clauses are deeming provisions that work without any money changing hands, and the credit taken on the goods is why they were written.

citation.ref: Clauses (a) and (b) of paragraph 4 of Schedule II, read with section 7(1A)

items.scenario: A printing firm does two things with equipment on which it had taken input tax credit. It gives an old guillotine away to a school, for nothing. And it lets its proprietor take the office camera home for his son's wedding for a fortnight, after which the camera comes back to the shop floor.

items.stem: What does section 49 actually allow?

options.text: Storage in any warehouse with space, public or private, the section caring only that the goods are secure
options.misconception: treats the two kinds of warehouse as interchangeable, when the section names only one of them
options.why: A private warehouse is licensed for the goods of the person who holds the licence. The section sends goods that cannot be cleared to a public warehouse, and that word is doing work rather than describing.

options.text: Storage in a public warehouse, but only with the permission of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner
options.misconception: puts the first permission at the rank that the section reserves for extending the period
options.why: The senior officer appears later in the section, on the extension of the period, not at the start. The permission to store is given at the level of the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner.

options.text: Storage in a public warehouse, on his application, if the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner is satisfied the goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time
options.why: Section 49 has three conditions written into its opening lines and he has missed two of them. The permission is that of the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner, not any officer to hand; it follows an application by the importer and a satisfaction that the goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time; and the place named is a public warehouse.

options.text: Nothing — an importer who cannot pay must warehouse the goods under section 60 instead
options.misconception: sends him to the warehousing chapter, which is what section 49 exists to spare him
options.why: Warehousing under section 60 needs a bill of entry for warehousing and a bond, and it moves the rate of duty. Section 49 is the door for an importer who has already entered his goods for home consumption and simply needs time.

citation.ref: Section 49

items.scenario: An importer has entered a consignment for home consumption and cannot pay the duty for another few weeks. He asks the customs house to let the goods sit in his own private bonded warehouse down the road, which has space, and says the Superintendent on the docks can sign it off.

items.stem: To which of these do the transit and transhipment provisions in Chapter VIII apply?

options.text: To the cargo and to the stores, stores also continuing in the same conveyance
options.misconception: reasons from the fact that the stores stay aboard, which is true and is not what decides it
options.why: Stores do continue in the same conveyance and are still excluded by name. They are governed by their own sections on consumption aboard and on supply without payment of duty, not by the transit provisions.

options.text: To everything aboard, the chapter following the conveyance rather than the goods
options.misconception: reads the chapter as attaching to the ship, when its first section removes three classes of goods from it
options.why: The chapter is about goods and not about vessels. Its opening section names three classes it does not apply to, and all three of them are aboard this ship.

options.text: To the cargo and the postal parcels, both being goods brought into an Indian port for onward movement
options.misconception: keeps goods imported by post inside a chapter that names them in its exclusion
options.why: Goods imported by post are one of the three named exclusions and have a separate chapter of their own. Being onward-bound does not put them back into Chapter VIII.

options.text: Only the cargo containers
options.why: Section 52 opens the chapter by taking three things out of it — baggage, goods imported by post, and stores. Each of those has its own chapter elsewhere in the Act, so the suitcases, the parcels and the ship's fuel and provisions are all outside sections 53 to 56, and the manifested cargo is the only consignment those sections reach.

citation.ref: Section 52, read with sections 53, 54 and 55

items.scenario: A vessel calls at Kochi on its way to Male. Aboard it are cargo containers manifested for Male, the ship's own fuel and provisions declared as stores, a passenger's suitcases, and a sack of parcels for delivery to addresses in India through the post.

items.stem: Can he, and what does the summons let him do?

options.text: No, because a summons may only require attendance to give evidence and never the production of documents
options.misconception: halves the power, which names giving evidence and producing a document as alternatives
options.why: The sub-section names both. A summons may require a person to attend and speak to what he knows, or to bring in a document or any other thing, or to do the two together — the officer asks for whichever the inquiry needs.

options.text: Yes, and the summons also lets him go to the office and take the ledgers if the accountant does not bring them
options.misconception: reads a summons as authorising the entry and seizure that only an authorisation under section 67 can permit
options.why: A summons produces a person and a paper across a table. Going to the premises and taking the books is a search and a seizure, and it needs the written authorisation and the recorded reason to believe that section 67 requires.

options.text: No — without material suggesting an offence he has no power to call for anything at all
options.misconception: imports section 67's threshold into section 70, when the summons power is exercisable in any inquiry
options.why: The threshold he is thinking of belongs to search and seizure. The summons power exists during an inquiry and does not wait for a suspicion of an offence, which is what makes it the ordinary opening move of an investigation.

options.text: Yes — a summons needs no reason to believe and no authorisation, but it compels a person and a document and does not let him enter or seize anything
options.why: Section 70 and section 67 are different instruments. A summons compels a named person to attend and to produce a document in an inquiry, and it needs neither a reason to believe nor a written authorisation. What it does not carry is any power to enter premises, to search them or to seize what is found there — that is section 67, and it is fenced with the conditions this officer has not met.

citation.ref: Section 70(1), read with section 67(1) and section 67(2)

items.scenario: An officer wants a taxpayer's purchase ledgers and the delivery challans behind them. He has no material suggesting an offence, and no written authorisation from a Joint Commissioner. He proposes to issue a summons to the accountant requiring him to bring the records.

items.stem: Is the adviser right on either point?

options.text: No on both — the penalty is ten per cent of the profiteered amount, and none is leviable if that amount is deposited within thirty days of the order
options.why: Section 171(3A) fixes the penalty at ten per cent of the profiteered amount, so the base is the money he kept and not his turnover. Its proviso then says no penalty shall be leviable if the profiteered amount is deposited within thirty days of the date of passing of the order, which leaves the manufacturer a month in which the penalty can still be avoided altogether.

options.text: Right on the second — the penalty is measured on turnover, the profiteering being spread across sales
options.misconception: puts the penalty on turnover when the sub-section measures it on the amount not passed on
options.why: Turnover is nowhere in the sub-section. It fixes the penalty as a percentage of the profiteered amount, which is the sum the order says should have come off the price and did not.

options.text: No on both, and in any case the amount is recovered as a demand of tax with interest under the demand provisions
options.misconception: routes the recovery through the demand sections, when the amount was never tax
options.why: The money is the recipient's, not the Government's. It is returned to him with interest, or sent to the Consumer Welfare Fund where he cannot be identified, and it does not travel through the demand provisions at all.

options.text: Right on the first — the penalty follows the order automatically and nothing he does afterwards touches it
options.misconception: misses the proviso, which makes the penalty avoidable by paying within a fixed window
options.why: The sub-section has a proviso and the proviso is the useful half. Depositing the profiteered amount inside the window written into it means no penalty is leviable at all.

citation.ref: Section 171(3A) with its proviso, read with sections 171(1) and 171(3)

items.scenario: An order finds that a manufacturer kept ₹40 lakh of a rate reduction to himself and directs him to return it. His adviser tells him two things: that a penalty will follow whatever he does now, and that the penalty is charged on his turnover for the period.

items.stem: When is the time of supply for that ₹700?

options.text: There is no time of supply, an amount not covered by an invoice not being consideration for any supply
options.misconception: treats an unbilled overpayment as outside the levy, when the proviso exists precisely because it is inside it
options.why: Money received against a taxable supply is consideration whether or not an invoice covers it yet. The proviso would have nothing to do if the excess were outside the levy; it is there to say when the tax on it falls due.

options.text: The date of issue of the invoice for the excess, and the supplier has no say in it
options.misconception: reads a relief the supplier may take as a rule he must follow
options.why: The words "at the option of the said supplier" are in the proviso. It is a concession he may use, not a mandatory shift of the time of supply, and a supplier who finds it simpler to tax the excess on receipt may do that.

options.text: At the architect's option, the date on which he issues the invoice relating to the excess
options.why: The proviso to section 13(2) picks up a small overpayment: the supplier has been paid more than his tax invoice asked for, and the surplus is one thousand rupees or less. For that surplus the time of supply moves, at the option of the supplier, to the date of issue of invoice for the surplus itself. The relief is optional, so he may take the excess into tax on receipt if he prefers, and the proviso simply spares him from having to.

options.text: The date of receipt, without exception, every rupee received against a service being taxable when it comes in
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 13(2) and never reaches the proviso sitting under it
options.why: Receipt is the general rule and the proviso is written as an exception to it for small overpayments. Ignoring the proviso makes an architect account for tax on seven hundred rupees of rounding in the month it arrives.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 13(2), read with the corresponding proviso to section 12(2)

items.scenario: An architect invoices a client ₹47,300 for a design. The client rounds the transfer up and pays ₹48,000 in the same month, ₹700 more than the invoice. The extra ₹700 is not returned and will be set against the next job.

items.stem: Is the fee outside GST, and is the consultant's reason right?

options.text: Outside, but by section 7(2)(b) and the notification under it, not by Schedule III
options.why: Section 7(2) has two clauses and they work differently. Clause (a) sends you to Schedule III, which is a fixed list in the Act. Clause (b) is a standing power to notify instead: work done by a local authority, or by either government, while acting in its public capacity sits outside supply once it is named in a notification the Council has recommended — "as may be notified" is the whole of it. A municipality is a local authority and this activity has been notified, so it is clause (b) that keeps the fee out.

options.text: Outside, because a local authority is not a person and cannot make a supply at all
options.misconception: denies a local authority the status the definition of person expressly gives it
options.why: A local authority is named in the definition of person, and a government is too. Both can and do make taxable supplies; what takes this one out is the notification, not the identity of the supplier.

options.text: Outside, and Schedule III is the right reason, since Schedule III is where everything outside supply is listed
options.misconception: treats Schedule III as the only door out of supply, when section 7(2)(b) is a second and separate one
options.why: Schedule III is a closed list written into the Act and it does not mention this activity. The second clause of section 7(2) is a standing power to notify, and it is by a notification under that power that the activity is outside.

options.text: Inside GST, because a fee is a consideration and the municipality supplied something for it
options.misconception: applies section 7(1)(a) without reading section 7(2), which overrides it
options.why: Section 7(2) opens with words that make it prevail over sub-section (1). An activity it covers is not a supply however neatly it fits the definition in clause (a).

citation.ref: Section 7(2)(b), read with section 7(2)(a), section 2(84) and Notification No. 14/2017-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: A municipality carries out an activity in relation to a function entrusted to it under the Constitution, and charges the residents a fee for it. That activity has been notified by the Government on the Council's recommendation. The municipality's consultant says the fee is outside GST, and puts it down to Schedule III.

items.stem: Is the consultant right, and what still has to happen?

options.text: Wrong, because an exporter who pays integrated tax on exports has no refund at all and must set it against domestic output tax
options.misconception: denies the second of the two routes section 16 gives an exporter
options.why: Section 16 offers two routes and this is the second of them — pay the integrated tax and claim it back. An exporter with no domestic output tax would otherwise have nothing to set it against.

options.text: Right, and nothing else is needed, the shipping bill being complete in itself the moment it is filed
options.misconception: takes the deeming and stops before the conditions that decide when the deemed application is filed
options.why: The deeming and its timing are in the same rule. Until the manifest or report is filed and the return is furnished, there is no application on foot and nothing for the system to process.

options.text: Right — the shipping bill is deemed to be the refund application, but it is treated as filed only once the export manifest or report is filed and a valid return is furnished
options.why: Rule 96(1) deems the shipping bill filed by an exporter of goods to be an application for refund of the integrated tax paid on the goods exported, so no separate application is made. The same rule then holds that deemed application back until two things happen — the person in charge of the conveyance files an export manifest or an export report covering the shipping bill, and the exporter furnishes a valid return.

options.text: Wrong — a refund of integrated tax paid on exports is claimed like any other refund, on an application to the proper officer
options.misconception: puts the payment route through the ordinary refund application, which is what rule 96 replaces for goods
options.why: The ordinary application belongs to the letter of undertaking route, where unutilised credit is refunded. Where the tax was paid on the export invoice, the shipping bill itself is the application and the refund is worked out from the customs system.

citation.ref: Rule 96(1), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter chooses the second route and pays integrated tax on his export invoices rather than going under a letter of undertaking. He asks his consultant when to file the refund application on the common portal, and is told the shipping bill has already done that job.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No, but the only consequence is a general penalty, the invoices themselves remaining valid
options.misconception: separates the requirement from rule 48(5), which is what gives the requirement its bite
options.why: Rule 48(5) says a document required to be issued in the manner rule 48(4) prescribes, and issued otherwise, shall not be treated as an invoice. That is a heavier consequence than a penalty and it reaches the refund and the recipient as well.

options.text: Yes — an overseas buyer has no registration and no input tax credit, so nothing turns on the number
options.misconception: reasons from the recipient's credit, when the requirement follows the class of supply and not what the buyer can claim
options.why: The buyer's credit is why the rule matters for a domestic sale; it is not why the rule applies. The sub-rule names exports on its own account, and the exporter's own refund runs on documents that have to be valid.

options.text: No — the rule covers supplies to a registered person and exports alike, and a supply to a special economic zone unit is inside it too
options.why: Rule 48(4) names supplies to a registered person and supplies for export in the same breath, so an export invoice needs an Invoice Reference Number exactly as a domestic business invoice does. A supply to a unit in a special economic zone is treated the same way. The consequence in rule 48(5) follows the requirement, so the invoices he has not reported are not valid invoices.

options.text: Yes for exports, no for the special economic zone unit, which is a registered person in India
options.misconception: gets the second half right for the wrong reason and keeps exports out, when the sub-rule names them expressly
options.why: Both are in, and exports are in by name rather than by any argument about registration. It is the class of supply the sub-rule lists that decides, and it lists exports.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4), read with rule 48(5)

items.scenario: An exporter well above the turnover line issues three kinds of invoice: to Indian registered customers, to buyers abroad against shipping bills, and to a unit inside a special economic zone. He has been reporting only the first kind to the Invoice Registration Portal, on the view that the requirement is for supplies to registered persons in India.

items.stem: What does section 126 require of the officer?

options.text: To make the penalty commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach, and to consider the voluntary disclosure as a mitigating factor
options.why: Section 126(2) requires the penalty imposed to be commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach, so a maximum imposed without regard to the facts is not a penalty the sub-section allows. Section 126(5) then says that where a person voluntarily discloses the circumstances of a breach to the officer prior to its discovery, the officer may consider that as a mitigating factor when quantifying the penalty.

options.text: Nothing — the officer fixes the penalty within the statutory range and the taxpayer's conduct afterwards is irrelevant
options.misconception: reads the range as the whole of the discretion, when the section directs how the discretion is to be exercised inside it
options.why: The range is where the section starts, not where it ends. Two sub-sections tell the officer how to choose within it, one on proportionality and one on disclosure before discovery.

options.text: To cancel the penalty altogether, a voluntary disclosure before discovery being a complete defence
options.misconception: turns a mitigating factor into an immunity, which the sub-section does not give
options.why: The words are that the officer may consider the disclosure as a mitigating factor. That lightens the penalty and does not remove it, and the section keeps the power to impose one.

options.text: To impose no penalty, because a breach the taxpayer found himself is by definition a minor breach
options.misconception: pulls in the minor-breach bar, which turns on the amount of tax and on the error being apparent on the face of record
options.why: Minor is defined in the Explanation by the amount of tax involved, and easily rectifiable by the error being apparent on the face of record. Who found the breach does not enter either test.

citation.ref: Sections 126(2) and 126(5), read with section 126(1) and its Explanation

items.scenario: A registered person finds a contravention in his own records and tells the officer about it before any audit or scrutiny has reached it. The contravention carries no fixed penalty and no fixed percentage, so the penalty has to be worked out. The officer proposes to impose the maximum, saying the facts of the disclosure are none of his concern.

items.stem: Will that application succeed?

options.text: No, because a person with a place of business in two States cannot use rule 14A at all
options.misconception: stretches a cap on how many registrations one State may hold into a ban on the scheme itself once a person has premises in two States
options.why: Premises in two States take nobody out of the scheme. He keeps what he has in Madhya Pradesh and may take the simplified route in Maharashtra as well; what he could not do is hold it twice inside one State, and that is not what he is asking for.

options.text: Yes, provided the two States' monthly output tax figures are added and the total stays within the ceiling
options.misconception: invents an adding-up test across States, when each application is measured on the output tax arising in the State applied for
options.why: There is nothing to add. The ceiling is applied to the applicant in the State he is applying in, on the output tax arising there, and the Maharashtra figure is well inside it. The application succeeds without any all-India total being struck.

options.text: Yes — registration is State-wise, so each State is looked at separately and both may be under rule 14A
options.why: Registration is taken State by State, and the cap in this scheme sits inside a State or Union territory rather than across them. What it displaces is rule 11, which would otherwise allow separate registrations for several places of business within one State; it says nothing about a person who registers in a second State. Maharashtra is therefore looked at on its own, and on these facts the monthly ceiling and the Aadhaar condition are both met there.

options.text: No — a person registered under rule 14A in one State cannot take a second rule 14A registration on the same permanent account number in another State
options.misconception: reads a cap drawn round one State or Union territory as a bar running across the whole country, so a scheme used once is thought to be spent everywhere
options.why: Rule 14A caps the scheme at one registration inside a State or Union territory against a single permanent account number, and that cap is worded for one State rather than for the country. Madhya Pradesh has used its one; Maharashtra is untouched by it, and an application there stands on its own monthly output tax figure and its own Aadhaar authentication.

citation.ref: Rule 14A, inserted by Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025 with effect from 1 November 2025

items.scenario: A supplier already registered under rule 14A in Madhya Pradesh opens a second place of business in Maharashtra on the same permanent account number. His monthly output tax on supplies to registered persons in Maharashtra will be small, and Aadhaar is authenticated for the signatory and for one partner. He applies for the Maharashtra registration under rule 14A as well.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: No — where no certificate is required from the authority, the Explanation lets a registered architect, a chartered engineer or a licensed surveyor be the competent authority
options.why: The carve-out in paragraph 5(b) is drafted as a completion certificate issued "where required" by the competent authority, and the Explanation then defines competent authority as the Government or any authority authorised to issue such a certificate under any law and, where no such certificate is required from that authority, an architect registered with the Council of Architecture, a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers, or a licensed surveyor of the local body. The engineer's certificate therefore starts the clock, and the entire consideration came afterwards.

options.text: Yes, unless the flats had also been first occupied, first occupation being the only event available where no certificate is issued
options.misconception: makes first occupation the sole fallback and leaves the Explanation's list of substitute authorities out of account
options.why: First occupation is the other event and it works on its own. It is not the only route open where the local body issues nothing, because the Explanation supplies a competent authority for exactly that situation.

options.text: No, and for the further reason that a small block is not construction within paragraph 5(b) at all
options.misconception: reads construction narrowly, when the Explanation stretches it to additions, alterations, replacements and remodelling
options.why: Size does not come into it, and the definition runs the other way. Construction is defined to include additions, alterations, replacements or remodelling of any existing civil structure, so the expression is wider than a new building rather than narrower.

options.text: Yes — without a certificate from the local body the carve-out cannot be satisfied at all
options.misconception: reads the certificate as having to come from the authority in every case, past the words where required
options.why: The words "where required" are what save this builder. A place where no certificate is required is exactly the case the Explanation was written for, and it names three professionals who may issue one instead.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II with the Explanation to paragraph 5

items.scenario: A builder finishes a small block in a village where the local body issues no completion certificate for buildings of that size. He obtains a certificate of completion from a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers and sells every flat afterwards, taking not a rupee before that certificate. A buyer's adviser says paragraph 5(b) still catches the sales because no competent authority issued anything.

items.stem: Is the sale a deemed export?

options.text: No — section 147 reaches only goods manufactured in India, and these were imported and resold as they were
options.why: Section 147 lets the Government notify supplies as deemed exports where the goods supplied do not leave India, where payment is received in Indian rupees or in convertible foreign exchange, and where such goods are manufactured in India. The first two are satisfied here and the third is not, so the notification cannot reach this sale however the recipient is described.

options.text: No, because a deemed export requires the goods to leave India and these do not
options.misconception: inverts the condition, which requires precisely that the goods do not leave India
options.why: Goods that leave India are an export and are zero-rated. The whole idea of a deemed export is that the goods stay here, which is why the section says so in terms.

options.text: Yes, provided he pays the tax and does not go under a letter of undertaking, the origin of the goods being irrelevant
options.misconception: gets the tax mechanics right and drops the manufacture condition, which is the one that decides this case
options.why: Paying the tax rather than using a letter of undertaking is right for a deemed export and is beside the point here. The supply never becomes a deemed export in the first place because the pumps were not made in India.

options.text: Yes — the recipient is an Export Oriented Unit, which is one of the notified categories, and that is what the notification turns on
options.misconception: reads the notified category as the whole test and skips the conditions section 147 sets before any notification can bite
options.why: The notification works inside the section that authorises it. Section 147 states three conditions and the goods must satisfy all of them before a notified category has anything to attach to.

citation.ref: Section 147, read with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017

items.scenario: A registered trader imports finished pumps, pays the customs duties on them and clears them for home consumption. He then sells the same pumps, untouched, to an Export Oriented Unit under the prescribed procedure. He proposes to treat the sale as a deemed export and to have the refund claimed by the unit.

items.stem: Is that second demand good?

options.text: Yes — the shipping line is outside India, so the Indian recipient must self-assess on reverse charge as with any imported service
options.misconception: applies the ordinary import-of-services rule to a service already inside the value of the imported goods
options.why: The ordinary rule works where the service stands on its own. Here the freight is inside the assessable value of the goods and has already borne integrated tax at the customs station, which is why the Court refused a second charge.

options.text: No — the Supreme Court struck the levy down, the import being a composite supply on which integrated tax has already been paid
options.why: In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals the Supreme Court held that an import on cost, insurance and freight terms is a composite supply of goods and of transport, that integrated tax on it is already collected at the customs station on a value that takes the freight in, and that a second levy on the transport limb alone would tax the same transaction twice. The notifications creating the reverse charge on ocean freight were held to be ultra vires.

options.text: No, but only where the contract is on free on board terms and the importer himself pays the freight
options.misconception: reverses the two kinds of contract, when it is the cost, insurance and freight case in which the freight is already inside the customs value
options.why: Where the importer pays the freight himself he contracts directly with the carrier and the position is different. The case decided was the cost, insurance and freight contract, which is the one in front of this company.

options.text: Yes, and the importer is not even the recipient — the levy is on the foreign seller, so it is he who must register in India
options.misconception: fixes on who contracted with the shipping line, which was one of the difficulties with the levy rather than a cure for it
options.why: The importer's not being a party to the transport contract was among the reasons the levy failed. Naming a foreign seller as the person liable does not revive a charge the Court has set aside.

citation.ref: Section 5(3) with section 5(1), read with section 8 of the CGST Act, 2017, section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.

items.scenario: An Indian company buys machinery abroad on cost, insurance and freight terms, so the foreign seller arranges and pays the shipping line. Integrated tax has been paid at the customs station on the value assessed under the Customs Act, which included the freight. The department now demands integrated tax again from the importer, under reverse charge, on the transport service the foreign shipping line supplied to the foreign seller.

items.stem: What is payable?

options.text: Tax on one per cent a year of the amount guaranteed, that being the value the rules fix for a guarantee
options.misconception: applies the deemed value written for a corporate guarantee to a guarantee given personally by a director
options.why: That deemed value is for a guarantee given by one company for a related company. A director's personal guarantee is dealt with separately, and the circular puts its value at zero where he takes nothing for it.

options.text: Nothing, because a guarantee given without payment is not a supply at all
options.misconception: stops at the absence of consideration, when Schedule I makes a supply between related persons a supply without one
options.why: Schedule I is the answer to that. A supply between related persons made without consideration is a supply, so the guarantee is inside the levy and it is the value, not the existence of a supply, that produces the nil answer.

options.text: Tax on a value the company must estimate, since the parties are related and cannot use the invoice value
options.misconception: reaches for an estimate where the circular has already fixed the value at zero for this case
options.why: There is nothing to estimate. Where no consideration has passed and none may pass, the open market value of the guarantee is taken as zero and no tax is payable on it.

options.text: Nothing — the guarantee is a supply, but with no consideration paid to the director its open market value is treated as zero
options.why: A director and his company are related persons, so a guarantee given without consideration is still a supply under Schedule I and reverse charge would apply to it. The Board's circular then settles the value: where the director has taken no consideration in any form for the guarantee, and the regulator's rules bar him from taking any, the open market value of the supply is treated as zero, and tax on zero is nothing.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule I, read with section 15(4), rule 28 of the CGST Rules, 2017, entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and Circular No. 204/16/2023-GST

items.scenario: A bank sanctions a working capital limit to a private company against the personal guarantee of its managing director. The regulator's rules forbid the company paying him anything for the guarantee, and it pays him nothing. The company's auditor says integrated tax must be paid on a notional value of the guarantee under reverse charge.

items.stem: Is it?

options.text: No — interest on deposits, loans or advances is left out of the turnover that decides eligibility, so he is at ₹46 lakh
options.why: An Explanation to section 10 carves a hole in the eligibility test. When aggregate turnover is measured to see whether a person may pay tax under this section, one exempt supply is left out of the count: lending, in the shape of deposits, loans or advances, where what the lender takes is interest or discount. Those receipts do not enter the figure at all. Taking the ₹6 lakh out leaves him inside the fifty lakh gate.

options.text: Yes — aggregate turnover takes in every supply, exempt supplies included, and ₹52 lakh is over the line
options.misconception: applies the general definition of aggregate turnover without the exclusion the section writes into it for this test
options.why: The general definition does take exempt supplies in, which is why an express exclusion was needed and written. For this eligibility test the interest limb is carved out of it.

options.text: Yes, because a person with income from two different activities cannot use the scheme for service providers at all
options.misconception: invents a single-activity condition that the section does not contain
options.why: Nothing in the section confines the scheme to one line of work. What it does is fix a turnover gate and then tell you which receipts are counted in measuring it.

options.text: No, because interest is not a supply at all and never enters turnover in any computation
options.misconception: treats interest as outside supply, when lending is a supply of services whose consideration happens to be exempt
options.why: Extending deposits, loans or advances is a supply of services and the interest is its consideration; the entry that exempts it says as much. It enters turnover in the ordinary way and is taken out only for this test by the Explanation.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A), read with the Explanations to section 10 and section 2(6)

items.scenario: A management consultant's receipts for the preceding financial year were ₹46 lakh of professional fees and, separately, ₹6 lakh of interest on money he had lent out. His accountant adds the two, gets ₹52 lakh, and tells him the special composition scheme for service providers is closed to him.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The department must apply to a court for permission to sell, the owner not having consented
options.misconception: sends a statutory power of disposal to a court that the section does not involve
options.why: The section gives the power to the proper officer and sets its own condition, which is the lapse of three months without payment. No court is in the sequence at any point.

options.text: Title passed to the Government on confiscation, and the proper officer may now dispose of the goods, the fine having gone unpaid for three months
options.why: Section 130(5) vests the title of confiscated goods in the Government from the confiscation, and section 130(6) has the proper officer take and hold possession, with every police officer bound to assist him on requisition. Section 130(7) then provides that where the fine in lieu of confiscation is not paid within three months from the date of the order, or such further time as the officer may allow, the proper officer may dispose of the goods and deposit the sale proceeds with the Government.

options.text: The option of a fine keeps the goods alive indefinitely, since the section sets no time within which it must be taken
options.misconception: reads the option as open-ended, when the same section closes it after three months
options.why: The option is bounded. Three months from the confiscation order, or such further time as the officer allows, and after that the goods may be sold whether or not the owner still wants to pay.

options.text: The goods remain the owner's until a sale takes place, confiscation only barring him from taking them away
options.misconception: treats confiscation as a detention, when the section transfers the title on the order itself
options.why: Confiscation is not detention. The sub-section says the title of such goods shall thereupon vest in the Government, so ownership moves at the order and the sale afterwards is the Government selling its own goods.

citation.ref: Sections 130(5), 130(6) and 130(7), read with section 130(2)

items.scenario: Goods are confiscated by an order that offers the owner the option of a fine in lieu of confiscation. Four months pass. The owner has paid nothing, has asked for no further time, and the goods are still in the department's godown. He says the goods remain his until somebody auctions them and that only a court can order a sale.

items.stem: Where does he stand on interest?

options.text: He is entitled to interest on the withheld refund from the date immediately after the expiry of sixty days from the refund application until the refund is paid
options.why: Section 54(11) is what allows the Commissioner to withhold the refund while the appeal runs, after giving the taxable person an opportunity of being heard. Section 54(12) then says that where a refund is withheld under that sub-section, the taxable person shall be entitled to interest at the notified rate if he becomes entitled to the refund as a result of the appeal, and the period runs from the day after sixty days from the application to the date of the refund.

options.text: No interest, because the delay was caused by an order lawfully passed and not by any failure of the department
options.misconception: reads interest as compensation for a departmental default, when the section attaches it to the withholding itself
options.why: Lawful withholding is exactly the case the sub-section covers. It exists to pay for the use of money the department kept while it was entitled to keep it, and it is not a penalty for anybody's fault.

options.text: No interest, since the withheld refund is not a refund delayed beyond sixty days but a refund not yet due
options.misconception: treats the withholding order as postponing the due date, when the section keeps the clock running behind it
options.why: The withholding stops the payment and not the clock. The taxpayer's entitlement is worked out as though the refund had been due, which is why the interest is calculated from the same sixty-day point.

options.text: Interest, but only from the date on which the appeal was decided in his favour
options.misconception: starts the interest at the successful order, when the section runs it from the sixty days after the application
options.why: The order decides that he was entitled all along. The interest is measured from the point at which a refund becomes overdue, not from the day the argument about it ended.

citation.ref: Sections 54(11) and 54(12), read with section 56

items.scenario: A refund was sanctioned in the taxpayer's favour. The department has appealed, and the Commissioner, of the opinion that paying it out now would be hard to recover if the appeal succeeds, has heard the taxpayer and passed an order withholding the refund. The taxpayer eventually wins the appeal. He assumes he has lost the money's use for nothing.

items.stem: On what amount does the section 50 interest run for each?

options.text: On ₹6 lakh for the first and on the whole ₹20 lakh for the second
options.why: The proviso to section 50(1) confines interest to the portion paid by debiting the electronic cash ledger, and then excepts a return furnished after the commencement of any proceedings under section 73 or section 74. The first taxpayer is inside the proviso and pays on the cash portion. The second is inside the exception, so the proviso does not reach him and the main limb charges interest on the whole liability.

options.text: On the whole ₹20 lakh for both, the proviso applying only where the return is filed on time
options.misconception: reads the proviso as a reward for punctuality, when it was written for the late filer
options.why: A return filed on time carries no interest at all. The proviso exists for the late filer and confines his interest to the cash portion, so long as he files before proceedings begin.

options.text: On ₹6 lakh for the first and on ₹14 lakh for the second, the credit portion being what the exception withdraws
options.misconception: reads the exception as reversing the proviso rather than as switching it off
options.why: Losing the proviso puts the taxpayer back on the main limb, which charges interest on the tax that remains unpaid. That is the whole liability of ₹20 lakh and not the credit half of it.

options.text: On ₹6 lakh for both, the proviso protecting the credit portion whenever the return is eventually filed
options.misconception: takes the proviso without the exception written into the middle of it
options.why: The exception is inside the proviso itself and it is the part most notes leave out. Filing only after the department has started proceedings takes the relief away entirely.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 50(1) with its exception, read with section 50(1)

items.scenario: Two taxpayers file a late return for a period in FY 2023-24, each with a liability of ₹20 lakh met ₹14 lakh from credit and ₹6 lakh in cash. The first files it of his own accord. The second files it only after the department has begun proceedings against him under section 73 for that very period.

items.stem: Can the order stand?

options.text: Yes for a year, after which it lapses in any case, so the quality of the reasoning never has to be examined
options.misconception: uses the automatic lapse as an answer to a challenge that can be brought while the attachment runs
options.why: The lapse ends the attachment; it does not validate the months before it. A person whose account is frozen for a year has a live grievance and the Court has said what he may attack.

options.text: No — the opinion has to rest on tangible material with a live link to the need to protect revenue, and a bare recital is not that
options.why: In Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh the Supreme Court called the power draconian and held that the formation of the opinion must be based on tangible material bearing a live link to the necessity of protecting the revenue. Reciting the statutory words is not forming an opinion, so an order with nothing behind it fails even though the proceedings are pending and the year has not run.

options.text: Yes — the section asks only that the Commissioner be of the opinion, and he has said he is
options.misconception: treats the opinion as subjective and unreviewable, when the Court has held it must rest on material
options.why: The opinion is the Commissioner's to form and it is not beyond review. What the Court required was material behind it, precisely because the section otherwise reads as though saying the words were enough.

options.text: No, because an attachment can never be made before a demand has been determined
options.misconception: requires a determined demand, when the section works on pending proceedings and would be useless if it waited
options.why: The power is ancillary to pending proceedings and exists to hold the position while they run. Waiting for a determined demand would defeat the reason the section is there.

citation.ref: Section 83(1), read with Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh and rule 159 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An order attaching a taxpayer's bank account recites, in one sentence, that the Commissioner is of the opinion that the attachment is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. There is nothing else on the file — no working of any liability, no note of any attempt to move money and no reference to any material. Proceedings are properly pending and the order is three weeks old.

items.stem: What has he left out?

options.text: A separate application to the jurisdictional Commissioner for permission for this particular consignment
options.misconception: describes the case-by-case permission the older scheme used, which the 2022 rules replaced with a one-time intimation on the portal
options.why: There is no consignment-by-consignment permission to obtain. The rules run on a single prior intimation and an identification number on the common portal, which is what made the scheme workable.

options.text: The one-time prior intimation, the identification number it generates and the continuity bond — all of which have to be in place before the goods are imported
options.why: The rules are front-loaded. An importer who wants the concessional rate gives a one-time prior intimation estimating the quantity and value of the goods, obtains an identification number on the common portal, and executes a continuity bond, and only then may he claim the rate on a bill of entry. Writing afterwards is not the procedure; the intimation is a condition of the exemption and not a report on it.

options.text: Only a bond, the intimation being needed just once a year and after the first import
options.misconception: keeps the bond and drops the intimation and the number, which are the two things the bond is registered against
options.why: The bond does not stand alone. It is executed alongside the intimation and the identification number, and the number is what the imports and the records are afterwards tracked under.

options.text: Nothing before the import — the rules work on what he does with the goods afterwards, through the periodic statement and the end-use period
options.misconception: sees only the back end of the rules, when the entitlement to the rate is created by steps taken before the goods arrive
options.why: The statement and the end-use period are real and they come later. What lets him claim the concessional rate on the bill of entry at all is the intimation, the number and the bond, and none of the three can be done retrospectively.

citation.ref: IGCR Rules, 2022 — the customs rules governing goods brought in at a reduced duty rate, or for a stated end use — rules 4 and 5

items.scenario: A manufacturer has found an exemption notification giving a concessional rate on a raw material if it is used in his own factory. His consignment is already on the water and he plans, on the day it lands, to file the bill of entry at the concessional rate and to write to the customs house afterwards explaining what the goods are for.

items.stem: Will the State authority entertain it?

options.text: No, because rectification is not available at all against an order once it has been issued
options.misconception: denies the rectification remedy altogether, when the Act provides for it and only fixes where it lies
options.why: Rectification of an error apparent on the face of the record is expressly available. What section 6(3) decides is where the application goes, and it goes to the officer who passed the order.

options.text: No — section 6(3) says proceedings for rectification, appeal and revision of an order passed by an officer under this Act shall not lie before an officer appointed under the State Act
options.why: Cross-empowerment is about who may initiate proceedings, not about who may sit over another administration's order. Section 6(3) closes that door in terms: proceedings for rectification, appeal and revision of an order passed by an officer appointed under this Act shall not lie before an officer appointed under the State or Union territory Act. The order goes back up the side it came down.

options.text: Yes, provided the central officer who passed the order gives his consent, since the bar is for his protection
options.misconception: treats a statutory bar on jurisdiction as a matter the officer whose order it is can waive
options.why: Jurisdiction is not waivable by the officer whose order is under attack. The sub-section says such proceedings shall not lie, and consent cannot create a forum the Act has closed.

options.text: Yes — section 6(1) makes State officers proper officers for this Act, so a State officer may do anything a central officer may
options.misconception: reads the cross-empowerment in section 6(1) as covering the appellate and rectification chain, which the very next sub-sections carve out
options.why: Section 6(1) authorises State officers as proper officers for this Act, and section 6(3) then removes one class of work from that authority. The two sub-sections are read together and the later one governs this case.

citation.ref: Section 6(3), read with sections 6(1), 6(2)(b) and 161

items.scenario: A central tax officer passes an order against a taxpayer. The order contains an arithmetical slip on its face. The taxpayer's consultant, knowing that the two administrations are cross-empowered and that either can act for the other, files the rectification application with the State tax authority because its office is nearer.

items.stem: May the appeal be heard that way?

options.text: Yes, if both parties consent to a single Member hearing it
options.misconception: puts the decision with the parties, when the section puts it with the President
options.why: Nothing in section 109(8) turns on what the parties want. The approval it names is the President's, and the other two conditions are facts about the order appealed against rather than matters anybody can agree to.

options.text: No — the President's approval is a condition in its own right, and the amount and the absence of a question of law do not supply it
options.why: Section 109(8) lets a single Member hear an appeal only where three things hold together: the tax or input tax credit involved, or the fine, fee or penalty determined, does not exceed ₹50 lakh; the appeal involves no question of law; and the President has approved, subject to such further conditions as may be prescribed on the Council's recommendations. Two out of three is not the exception. Everything else is heard by one Judicial Member and one Technical Member sitting together.
keywords: one Judicial Member and one Technical Member

options.text: Yes — ₹40 lakh is inside the ceiling, which is what the exception turns on
options.misconception: treats the money limit as the whole test when it is one of three conditions
options.why: The ceiling is necessary and not sufficient. An appeal can sit well inside ₹50 lakh and still have to go to two Members, because the approval was never given or because a question of law is involved.

options.text: No — an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal is always heard by two Members, one Judicial and one Technical
options.misconception: reads the ordinary constitution of a Bench as admitting no exception, when section 109(8) writes one
options.why: Two Members is the rule and it is not the whole rule. Section 109(8) provides expressly for a single Member in the narrow case, which is why the conditions matter: they are what keeps the exception narrow.

citation.ref: Section 109(8), read with Rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An order of the Appellate Authority confirms tax of ₹40 lakh against a company for one tax period. Nobody suggests the appeal raises a question of law. The Registrar lists it before a single Member of the State Bench, and the President's approval has not been sought.

items.stem: May he?

options.text: No — the daily penalty follows a notice requiring the return, and it runs from the expiry of the period that notice allows
options.why: The machinery has two steps and the notice is the first of them. Where an information return has not been furnished in time, the authority serves a notice requiring it within a period the notice specifies, and only a failure to comply with that notice attracts the penalty of one hundred rupees for each day the failure continues, subject to a ceiling of five thousand rupees. Counting from the original due date skips the step the penalty section is built on.

options.text: Yes — the obligation to file is in the Act, so the penalty runs from the day the return was due
options.misconception: attaches the penalty to the statutory due date, when the penalty section attaches it to the period allowed by a notice
options.why: The obligation and the penalty have different starting points. Missing the due date is what brings the notice; missing the notice's period is what brings the penalty.

options.text: No, and no penalty is possible at all, since a bank filing an information return is not a taxable person under this Act
options.misconception: assumes the penalty provisions reach only registered taxpayers, when this one is written for the persons obliged to file the return
options.why: The section is written for a person required to furnish an information return, and the list of such persons is deliberately wide — banks, registering authorities, stock exchanges, income-tax authorities and others, none of whom need be taxable persons.

options.text: Yes, and without any ceiling, the penalty running for as long as the default continues
options.misconception: drops the cap, when the section carries an express maximum in its proviso
options.why: The daily amount is capped. The proviso fixes an outer limit on the penalty however long the failure runs, which is what keeps a small compliance default from becoming ruinous.

citation.ref: Section 123 with its proviso, read with section 150

items.scenario: A bank that is required to file an information return has not filed one for the year. No notice has been served on it. The officer proposes to impose the daily penalty straight away and to count the days from the original due date.

items.stem: What is the position under section 88?

options.text: Nothing can be recovered from any director, because the company is in liquidation and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code overrides section 88
options.misconception: applies the IBC saving of section 93 to section 88, which has no such saving
options.why: The words "save as otherwise provided in the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016" sit in section 93, not in section 88. Section 88 is the provision written for liquidation.

options.text: The liquidator's intimation was late — it was due within 30 days; the Commissioner must notify the provision within 3 months of receiving it; and Mr Desai is jointly and severally liable for the ₹40 lakh unless he proves the non-recovery is not attributable to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part
options.why: Section 88(1) requires the liquidator to give intimation within 30 days of appointment, and 25 July is past that; section 88(2) requires the Commissioner to notify, within 3 months of receiving the intimation, the amount sufficient to provide for tax, interest or penalty. Section 88(3) reaches anyone who was a director at any point within the period for which the tax was due and makes him jointly and severally liable when the dues cannot be recovered from a private company — resignation before the order does not matter, the period does — unless he satisfies the Commissioner that the non-recovery is not traceable to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part. Leaving the finances to someone else is the thing he has to answer for, not the answer.
keywords: gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty

options.text: Mr Desai is liable only for his proportionate share of the ₹40 lakh, divided among all the directors of that year
options.misconception: reads joint and several liability as a pro-rata split
options.why: Joint and several means the department may recover the whole from any one of them, who is left to seek contribution from the others. The section does not apportion.

options.text: Mr Desai is not liable, because he had ceased to be a director before the winding-up order and section 88 reaches only the directors in office at liquidation
options.misconception: reads the section as fixing directors by the date of the order, when it fixes them by the period for which the tax was due
options.why: Section 88(3) names every person who was a director at any point within the period for which the tax was due. He was a director for the whole of that year, so the section reaches him whatever happened afterwards.

citation.ref: Section 88(1), (2) and (3)

items.scenario: Kaveri Fabrics Pvt Ltd is ordered to be wound up on 10 June. The liquidator informs the Commissioner of his appointment on 25 July. Tax of ₹40 lakh for the year before the winding-up cannot be recovered from the company. Mr Desai was a director throughout that year but resigned before the winding-up order; he says he attended every board meeting and left the finances to the managing director.

items.stem: What can be recovered from Ms Rao under section 89?

options.text: Both the ₹12 lakh and the ₹50,000 — the dues relate to a year in which the company was private and she was a director
options.misconception: applies section 89(1) without its conversion carve-out
options.why: The dues do relate to the private period, and that is exactly the case section 89(2) addresses: conversion before recovery lifts sub-section (1) from the former directors, leaving only a personal penalty.

options.text: The ₹12 lakh only — a personal penalty is a penalty on the company for which the director cannot be pursued
options.misconception: inverts section 89(2), which spares the company's dues and keeps the personal penalty
options.why: A personal penalty is imposed on the director for her own act, and section 89(2) says in terms that its relief does not extend to it. It is the company's tax that conversion lifts from her.

options.text: Nothing — a director's liability under section 89 arises only in liquidation, and the company is a going concern
options.misconception: confines section 89 to a company in liquidation, which is section 88's field
options.why: Section 89 applies to a private company that is not being wound up; section 88(3) is the liquidation counterpart. She escapes the ₹12 lakh under section 89(2), not because the company is solvent.

options.text: Only the ₹50,000 personal penalty — section 89(2) frees the former private company's directors from its unrecovered dues once it converts into a public company, but not from a personal penalty imposed on the director
options.why: Section 89(1) would make a director of a private company jointly and severally liable for its unrecovered tax, interest or penalty, but section 89(2) provides that once such a company has been converted into a public company, with its private-period dues still unrecovered at the conversion, sub-section (1) does not apply to any person who was a director of the private company in relation to those dues. The same sub-section keeps one thing on her: nothing in it applies to any personal penalty imposed on such director, so the ₹50,000 stands.

citation.ref: Section 89(1) and (2)

items.scenario: Tapti Tools Pvt Ltd owed ₹12 lakh of tax for 2024-25 that the department could not recover. On 1 April 2026 the company converted into a public company. In July 2026 the department seeks the ₹12 lakh, and a personal penalty of ₹50,000 imposed on Ms Rao for a false statement, from Ms Rao, who was a director throughout 2024-25.

items.stem: For which dues is Mr Bhat liable, and what does the deed do?

options.text: For the dues up to 10 January only — a partner's liability ends with retirement, and the deed confirms it
options.misconception: stops the liability at the retirement date and gives the deed effect against the department
options.why: That is the position only where the retirement is intimated within 1 month. Without the notice, the proviso to section 90 keeps his liability running until the Commissioner receives it, and the deed is a contract to the contrary that section 90 overrides.

options.text: For his proportionate share of the dues up to 10 January, according to his profit-sharing ratio
options.misconception: apportions a joint and several liability by profit share
options.why: Joint and several liability lets the department recover the whole from any partner; the profit-sharing ratio governs contribution between partners and nothing else.

options.text: For nothing — the firm alone is the taxable person, and partners are reached only under section 93 when the firm is dissolved
options.misconception: treats the firm as a shield while it exists
options.why: Section 90 makes the firm and each of its partners jointly and severally liable while the firm carries on; section 93(3) is the further rule for a dissolved firm. Both reach the partners.

options.text: For the dues up to the date the Commissioner receives intimation of his retirement — because none was given within 1 month, his liability runs past 10 January into February and March — and the deed binds only the partners, not the department, because section 90 applies notwithstanding any contract to the contrary
options.why: Section 90 makes the firm and each partner jointly and severally liable for the firm's tax, interest and penalty notwithstanding any contract to the contrary. A retiring partner is liable for the dues up to his retirement whether determined or not, and the retirement must be intimated to the Commissioner by notice in writing; the proviso says that if no intimation is given within 1 month from the date of retirement, his liability continues until the date the Commissioner receives it. No notice was sent, so he stays liable for the February and March supplies. The deed settles who bears the cost between the partners; it cannot shrink the department's recourse.
keywords: until the date the Commissioner receives
notwithstanding any contract to the contrary

citation.ref: Section 90 with its proviso

items.scenario: Mr Bhat retired from Sahyadri Traders, a registered firm, on 10 January. Neither he nor the firm wrote to the Commissioner. On 5 April the firm's tax for the quarter ended 31 March, including supplies made in February and March, is found unpaid. The partnership deed provides that Mr Bhat bears no liability for the firm's taxes after retirement.

items.stem: Who is liable for the ₹8 lakh?

options.text: The LLP alone — section 90 speaks of a firm, and an LLP is a body corporate with limited liability
options.misconception: treats the LLP's corporate form as taking it outside the Chapter
options.why: Whatever the LLP Act says about limited liability, the Explanation to Chapter XVI deems an LLP a firm for these provisions, and section 90 makes its partners jointly and severally liable.

options.text: A, B and C only — D was not a partner when the supplies were made, and a person cannot be liable for a period before he joined
options.misconception: reads section 90 alone and misses section 94(2), which was written for the incoming partner
options.why: Section 94(2) reaches the partners as the firm exists after the reconstitution for a period before it. The incoming partner is liable with the rest; his remedy is contribution from the others, not exemption from the department.

options.text: A, B, C and D, jointly and severally — an LLP is a firm for this Chapter, and under section 94(2) the partners as the firm stood before and after the reconstitution are all liable for a period before it
options.why: The Explanation to Chapter XVI says a limited liability partnership formed and registered under the LLP Act, 2008 shall also be considered as a firm, so sections 90 and 94 apply. Section 94(2) provides that where a change has occurred in the constitution of a firm, the partners of the firm as it existed before and as it exists after the reconstitution are, without prejudice to section 90, jointly and severally liable to pay the tax, interest or penalty due for any period before its reconstitution. D's joining after the period is the very case the sub-section addresses.
keywords: before and as it exists after

options.text: A and B only — C retired and D joined after the period, so only the continuing partners are liable
options.misconception: drops both the outgoing and the incoming partner, when section 94(2) keeps both sets
options.why: C was a partner during July and August and remains liable under section 90 for dues up to his retirement, and section 94(2) adds the partners as they stand after the change. Neither end of the reconstitution is released.

citation.ref: Section 94(2); the Explanation to Chapter XVI treating an LLP as a firm

items.scenario: Narmada Associates LLP had three partners, A, B and C, until 30 September, when C left and D joined. In the following year a demand of ₹8 lakh is raised for supplies made in July and August. D argues that section 90 does not apply to an LLP, and that in any case he joined after the period.

items.stem: Is Krishna Ltd right?

options.text: No — the ₹3 crore is taxable because goods were supplied, but the ₹40 lakh of services is not, as section 87 speaks only of goods
options.misconception: narrows section 87 to goods
options.why: Section 87(1) covers goods or services or both supplied or received to or from each other. Both streams are included in the respective turnovers.

options.text: No — under section 87 the supplies between the effective date and the date of the order are included in the turnover of the respective companies and taxed, the two are treated as distinct companies up to 15 November, and the registrations are cancelled with effect from the date of the order
options.why: Section 87(1) applies where companies are amalgamated by an order taking effect from a date earlier than the order and any two of them supplied or received goods or services to or from each other in the period from the effective date to the date of the order: each such dealing counts in the turnover of both companies — as a supply for one and a receipt for the other — and each is liable to pay tax accordingly. Section 87(2) keeps the two as distinct companies right up to 15 November, the date of the order, and cancels their registration certificates from that date, not from 1 April.

options.text: Yes — a supply to oneself is no supply, and the order speaks from 1 April
options.misconception: gives the retrospective effect of the order the tax consequence section 87 was enacted to deny
options.why: Company law may treat the two as one from 1 April, but section 87 keeps them distinct for GST until the order and taxes what passed between them in the meantime.

options.text: Yes as to tax, but Godavari's registration is cancelled from 1 April and it must file nil returns for the period
options.misconception: dates the cancellation from the effective date instead of the order
options.why: The registration certificates are cancelled with effect from the date of the order, 15 November. Godavari remains a registered, distinct company until then and reports its supplies to Krishna in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Section 87(1) and (2)

items.scenario: By an order of the Tribunal dated 15 November, Godavari Ltd is amalgamated into Krishna Ltd with effect from 1 April of the same year. Between 1 April and 15 November Godavari supplied goods worth ₹3 crore to Krishna and received services worth ₹40 lakh from it. Krishna Ltd contends that, the amalgamation being effective from 1 April, those were transactions with itself and no GST is payable, and that Godavari's registration lapsed on 1 April.

items.stem: What is she liable for in each case under section 93(1)?

options.text: Nothing in either case — tax dues abate on death and the department's remedy is against the estate in probate only
options.misconception: treats death as extinguishing GST dues
options.why: Section 93(1) exists to say the opposite: dues determined before or after the death are payable by the legal representative, from the estate or in full depending on whether the business goes on.

options.text: In both cases she pays nothing beyond ₹6 lakh, since a liability cannot exceed what the deceased left
options.misconception: extends the estate ceiling to a continued business
options.why: The estate ceiling belongs to the discontinued case. A person who continues the business is liable for the dues under section 93(1) and as transferee under section 85, without reference to the estate.

options.text: In both cases she pays the full ₹9 lakh, because a legal representative steps into the shoes of the deceased
options.misconception: ignores the estate ceiling that section 93(1) gives when the business is discontinued
options.why: When the business is discontinued the liability is expressly limited to the estate's capacity to meet it. Only continuing the business takes the ceiling away.

options.text: If the business is discontinued, she pays out of the estate to the extent it can meet the charge — ₹6 lakh; if she continues the business, she is liable for the ₹9 lakh due from him, as legal representative and as transferee on the death of a sole proprietor
options.why: Section 93(1) draws the line at whether the business continues. Where it is discontinued, whether before or after the death, the dues — tax, interest or penalty, settled before the death and left unpaid, or settled afterwards — fall on the legal representative and come out of the deceased's estate, and only to the extent to which the estate is capable of meeting them: here ₹6 lakh. Where the business is continued after the death by the legal representative or any other person, that person is liable to pay the dues, and Circular 96/15/2019 adds that on a sole proprietor's death the transferee is liable for the transferor's dues under section 85.
keywords: to the extent to which the estate is capable

citation.ref: Section 93(1); Circular No. 96/15/2019-GST

items.scenario: Mr Pillai, a registered sole proprietor, died on 3 May leaving tax of ₹9 lakh unpaid and an estate worth ₹6 lakh. His daughter is his legal representative. Case one: she closes the business. Case two: she continues it in her own name.

items.stem: Which parts of the advice are right?

options.text: Neither the need to register first nor the place-of-supply question — an applicant is any person registered or desirous of obtaining registration, and place of supply is not among the seven questions in section 97(2), because the Authority is a State body whose ruling cannot run across States; classification is a proper question
options.why: Section 95(c) defines an applicant as any person registered or desirous of obtaining registration, so Mr Ranjan may apply before registering. Section 97(2) lists seven questions — classification, applicability of a notification, time and value of supply, admissibility of input tax credit, liability to pay tax, whether registration is required, and whether a thing amounts to a supply — and place of supply is not one of them; the module explains that the Authority and Appellate Authority are constituted under the State Act and their rulings run only within that State, which is why a place-of-supply question cannot be raised. Classification of the goods is the first question on the list.

options.text: Only the place-of-supply point — he need not register first, and place of supply may be asked because export is a matter of central law under the IGST Act
options.misconception: reasons that the IGST Act makes place of supply askable, when the Authority's State constitution is the bar
options.why: Section 20 of the IGST Act applies the advance ruling provisions, but the Authority remains a State body and section 97(2) does not list place of supply. The question cannot be raised whatever Act the supply falls under.

options.text: Both — only a registered person can apply, and every question about a proposed supply can be put to the Authority
options.misconception: narrows the applicant and widens the questions, both against the text
options.why: The definition of applicant reaches a person desirous of registration, and section 97(2) is a closed list of seven questions that does not include place of supply.

options.text: Only the registration point — he must register first, but once registered he may ask about classification and not about place of supply
options.misconception: keeps the registration precondition that section 95(c) removes
options.why: The place-of-supply half is right and the registration half is wrong: a person desirous of obtaining registration is an applicant, and may seek a ruling on a proposed supply.

citation.ref: Sections 95(c) and 97(2); section 96 — the module's Test Your Knowledge case of Ranjan

items.scenario: Mr Ranjan intends to start selling certain goods from Delhi. He is not yet registered. His adviser says he must register first before applying for an advance ruling, and that he can seek a ruling on the classification of the goods and on the place of supply for sales to buyers in the United States.

items.stem: What happens to Meghna's application, what does it cost, and can the officer appeal the other ruling?

options.text: The application is admitted and the officer may appeal the other applicant's ruling on paying ₹10,000 under each Act
options.misconception: gives the officer a fee-bearing appeal against a stranger's ruling
options.why: An officer's appeal is free of fee, and it lies only in respect of the applicant whose ruling it is. Meghna's own application fails on pendency regardless.

options.text: The application is admitted, because the pending show cause notice concerns an earlier period and a ruling would settle the future
options.misconception: reads the pendency bar as period-specific, when it turns on the question
options.why: Section 98(2) speaks of the question raised being pending in any proceedings in the applicant's case. The same classification question is under adjudication, so the application is not admitted; the ruling route is not a second forum for a live dispute.

options.text: The application is rejected without a hearing, since the pendency is a matter of record, and the fee is refunded
options.misconception: skips the hearing and the speaking order the proviso requires
options.why: The proviso to section 98(2) forbids rejecting an application until the applicant has been heard, and requires the rejecting order to speak its reasons. Nothing in the section provides for a refund of the ₹5,000 fees.

options.text: The application is not admitted because the question is already pending in proceedings in the applicant's own case, and rejection must be by a speaking order after a hearing; the application fee would have been ₹5,000 under CGST and ₹5,000 under SGST; an officer's appeal carries no fee but lies only against a ruling given in respect of an applicant within his jurisdiction
