items.scenario: A company's employee stock option scheme is running normally. Three questions reach the company secretary in one week. An employee has died in service holding four thousand vested and six thousand unvested options, and his widow asks for all ten thousand. A second employee has resigned holding three thousand vested and five thousand unvested options and wants to keep both lots. A third wants to transfer two thousand of his vested options to his brother, who is willing to pay him for them.

items.stem: What does section 92(3) require of this company?

options.text: Neither, because a return filed with the Registrar is already a public document and the company owes no separate disclosure
options.misconception: treats a filing with the Registrar as discharging a duty owed to the members
options.why: The filing and the placing are separate duties in separate sub-sections. Section 92(3) is aimed at the member or the lender who wants to read the return without paying for a copy from the Registrar's portal.

options.text: The annual return on the website, and nothing in the Board's report
options.misconception: reads the first half of the sub-section and stops
options.why: The sub-section has two limbs and the second is the one that reaches the reader: the web link is to be disclosed in the Board's report, so a member reading the report knows the return exists and where it sits.

options.text: The extract in Form MGT-9 annexed to the Board's report, exactly as before
options.misconception: carries forward a requirement the amended sub-section removed
options.why: The extract was the old form of the same idea — giving members the substance of the return without making them go and find it. The sub-section now does that with a link to the full return instead of a summary of it.

options.text: A copy of the annual return placed on the company's website, if it has one, with the web link disclosed in the Board's report — and the extract in Form MGT-9 is no longer required at all
options.why: Section 92(3) as it now stands says every company shall place a copy of the annual return on the website of the company, if any, and that the web link of such annual return shall be disclosed in the Board's report. The extract the Board's report used to carry went when that sub-section was substituted, so annexing Form MGT-9 answers a requirement that has ceased to exist while leaving the one that has replaced it unmet.

citation.ref: Section 92(3), as substituted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017

items.scenario: A company secretary is assembling the Board's report for 2025-26. He proposes to annex the extract of the annual return in Form MGT-9, as the firm has done every year since 2015, and says the company's website need carry nothing, because the annual return is filed with the Registrar and anybody who wants it can pay for a copy there.

items.stem: Which of the four are operational creditors?

options.text: The employees and the supplier — a tax department is a creditor of a different kind altogether and stands outside the Code's two classes
options.misconception: leaves government dues outside a definition that names them
options.why: There is no third class. Section 5(21) puts a debt in respect of dues arising under any law and payable to the Central Government, a State Government or a local authority squarely inside operational debt, which is why tax departments appear regularly as applicants under section 9.

options.text: Only the supplier, since operational debt means what a company owes its trade suppliers
options.misconception: shrinks operational debt to trade payables
options.why: Goods are one limb of three. The sub-section names services, says "including employment" in terms, and adds dues payable to a Government or a local authority under any law.

options.text: All four, because anybody a company owes money to is an operational creditor unless he holds security
options.misconception: makes security the line between financial and operational debt
options.why: The line is what the money was for, not what secures it. An unsecured term loan is still financial debt, because it was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and a secured supplier is still an operational creditor.

options.text: The employees, the State Government and the supplier — each of them holds operational debt; the bank holds financial debt and its route is section 7
options.why: Section 5(21) defines an operational debt as a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services including employment, or a debt in respect of the payment of dues arising under any law for the time being in force and payable to the Central Government, any State Government or any local authority. Unpaid salary is the employment limb, the tax is the statutory dues limb and the supplier's bill is the goods limb, so each of the three is an operational creditor under section 5(20) and applies under section 9. The bank's term loan was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, which puts it in section 5(8) and sends it to section 7 instead.

citation.ref: Sections 5(20) and 5(21), read with sections 5(8), 7 and 9

items.scenario: A company has stopped paying everybody. It owes unpaid salary to its own employees, goods and services tax to a State Government, a term loan to a bank, and the price of raw material to a supplier. Each of the four amounts is above the minimum notified under section 4, none of them is disputed, and all four want to move the Adjudicating Authority.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two decisions?

options.text: The point about the rights issue is right, but the shares may be held, since destruction is a SEBI requirement that binds listed companies alone
options.misconception: moves a Companies Act condition into the SEBI regulations
options.why: Section 68(7) sits in the Act and applies to every company that buys back its own shares, listed or unlisted. The SEBI regulations add to it for a listed company; they are not the source of it.

options.text: The shares had to be extinguished and physically destroyed within seven days of the last date of completion of the buy-back, so they cannot be held for resale; and no further issue of the same kind of shares may be made within six months, which catches the rights issue
options.why: Section 68(7) requires a company that has bought back its own shares to extinguish and physically destroy them within seven days of the last date of completion of the buy-back, which is why treasury shares are not an outcome the section allows. Section 68(8) then bars a further issue of the same kind of shares or other specified securities within a period of six months of the completion, and it names the further issue under section 62(1)(a) among the issues it stops. Its exceptions are a bonus issue and the discharge of subsisting obligations such as the conversion of warrants, a stock option scheme, sweat equity, or the conversion of preference shares or debentures into equity shares.

options.text: The point about the shares is right, but the rights issue is free because section 68(8) stops only a fresh public issue
options.misconception: reads "further issue of the same kind" as a public issue
options.why: The sub-section speaks of a further issue of the same kind of shares or other specified securities and mentions the allotment of new shares under section 62(1)(a) in terms. A rights issue of equity after a buy-back of equity is exactly what it stops.

options.text: Nothing — once the buy-back has been lawfully completed the section has no more to say
options.misconception: treats completion as the end of the section's conditions
options.why: Two of the conditions are written to bite after completion. One destroys the shares so that capital is actually reduced, and the other stops the company putting the same capital back within six months, which would make the whole exercise a device for supporting the price.

citation.ref: Sections 68(7) and 68(8), read with section 62(1)(a)

items.scenario: A company completes a buy-back of forty lakh equity shares on 12 June 2026, every condition of section 68 having been satisfied on the way in. The board then decides to keep the bought-back shares in the company's own name so that they can be sold when the price recovers, and three months later resolves on a rights issue of equity shares to fund a new plant. The company secretary sees no difficulty: the buy-back is over and its conditions were met.

items.stem: Is the chief financial officer right on either proposal?

options.text: On neither — section 129(4) applies the provisions on preparation, adoption and audit to the consolidated financial statements mutatis mutandis, and section 129(5) puts the disclosure of a deviation, its reasons and its financial effects on the company itself
options.why: Section 129(4) says the provisions of the Act applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to the consolidated financial statements, so they are audited, laid before the annual general meeting and adopted exactly as the standalone statements are. Section 129(5) then says that where the financial statements do not comply with the accounting standards, the company shall disclose the deviation, the reasons for it and the financial effects, if any, arising out of it — a duty of the company, discharged in its own statements.

options.text: On both — consolidated statements are prepared for information and the auditor is the proper person to flag a departure
options.misconception: treats the consolidated statements as a supplementary schedule rather than as financial statements
options.why: Section 129(4) exists to stop exactly that reading. Once a company has to prepare consolidated statements they carry the whole apparatus of the Act — audit, laying, adoption, filing — and the company's own disclosure duty under section 129(5) runs on them as well.

options.text: Right on the audit only — the consolidated statements need no separate opinion, but the company must disclose the deviation itself
options.misconception: keeps half of section 129(4)
options.why: The sub-section carries preparation, adoption and audit across together; it does not split them. A consolidated statement that nobody has audited is one nobody has tested, and it is the statement on which the group's true picture depends.

options.text: Right on the deviation only — the auditor's report is where non-compliance with an accounting standard is reported
options.misconception: moves the company's own disclosure duty onto its auditor
options.why: The auditor reports under section 143(3)(e) whether, in his opinion, the financial statements comply with the accounting standards. That is his obligation and it does not relieve the company of the separate disclosure section 129(5) requires it to make.

citation.ref: Sections 129(4) and 129(5), read with section 143(3)(e)

items.scenario: A holding company prepares consolidated financial statements for the year. Its chief financial officer proposes that they be sent to members for information but not put to the annual general meeting for adoption and not audited, since the standalone statements already carry an audit opinion. He also proposes that a departure from one accounting standard in a group measurement be left for the auditor to describe in his report, rather than mentioned by the company anywhere in its own statements.

items.stem: What has the board missed?

options.text: The committee is needed, but the managing director may chair it, since he is the person answerable to shareholders
options.misconception: puts an executive at the head of a committee the section reserves for a non-executive
options.why: Section 178(5) says the chairperson shall be a non-executive director. The committee exists to look at the company's dealings with its own security holders from outside the executive line, which is why the section names the class of director rather than the office.

options.text: Nothing — grievances about transfers and dividends are administrative and belong with the company secretary
options.misconception: treats a statutory committee as an optional layer over an existing process
options.why: The section makes it a committee of the Board once the count of security holders is crossed, and puts a non-executive director at its head, so that the people whose grievances are being answered are not answered by the management they are complaining about.

options.text: The committee is needed only where the company has securities listed on a stock exchange
options.misconception: reads a Companies Act committee as a listing requirement
options.why: The trigger in section 178(5) is a count of shareholders, debenture holders, deposit holders and other security holders, and it says nothing about listing. An unlisted company past that count owes the committee.

options.text: A Stakeholders Relationship Committee chaired by a non-executive director, to consider and resolve the grievances of the security holders; and that the chairperson of each committee constituted under section 178, or a member he authorises, must attend the general meetings
options.why: Section 178(5) requires the Board of a company which consists of more than one thousand shareholders, debenture holders, deposit holders and any other security holders at any time during a financial year to constitute a Stakeholders Relationship Committee, whose chairperson shall be a non-executive director. Section 178(6) gives that committee the work of considering and resolving the grievances of the security holders. Section 178(7) requires the chairperson of each of the committees constituted under the section, or in his absence a member of the committee authorised by him, to attend the general meetings.

items.scenario: A company has about fourteen hundred shareholders and three hundred debenture holders. Its board has an audit committee and a nomination and remuneration committee, and says nothing further is needed. Complaints about share transfers and unpaid dividends go to the company secretary, who answers to the managing director. At the last annual general meeting the chairperson of the audit committee did not attend and sent nobody, and the chairman of the meeting told a member that a committee chairperson has no business at a general meeting.

items.stem: Is counsel right?

options.text: No, but no offer is needed here because the rights come out of an agreement rather than out of shares
options.misconception: reads control as something only shares can carry
options.why: Regulation 2(1)(e) names shareholders agreements and voting agreements inside the definition itself, precisely so that control acquired on paper is treated the same as control acquired by buying votes.

options.text: No, but the trigger is Regulation 3(1), because acquiring control is deemed to be an acquisition of twenty-five per cent of the voting rights
options.misconception: invents a deemed shareholding to force control into a percentage trigger
options.why: Nothing is deemed. Regulation 3(1) is about crossing twenty-five per cent of the voting rights, and Regulation 4 stands beside it for the acquirer who takes control without crossing anything.

options.text: No — Regulation 4 requires an open offer for the acquisition of control irrespective of the acquisition or holding of any shares or voting rights
options.why: Regulation 4 of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 says that irrespective of acquisition or holding of shares or voting rights in a target company, no acquirer shall acquire, directly or indirectly, control over such target company unless he makes a public announcement of an open offer. Regulation 2(1)(e) defines control to include the right to appoint a majority of the directors or to control the management or policy decisions, exercisable by shareholding, management rights, shareholders agreements, voting agreements or in any other manner. The right to appoint a majority of the board is control on the face of that definition, and the percentage is beside the point.

options.text: Yes — the Regulations are a set of shareholding thresholds and he has crossed none of them
options.misconception: reads the code as being about percentages alone
options.why: The percentage triggers are one route to an open offer and the acquisition of control is a separate one, written in its own regulation and opening with the words "irrespective of acquisition or holding of shares or voting rights".

citation.source: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
citation.ref: Regulation 4, read with Regulation 2(1)(e) and Regulation 3(1)

items.scenario: An investor holds nine per cent of the voting rights of a listed company and does not propose to buy a single further share. Under a shareholders' agreement signed on 1 September 2026 he obtains the right to appoint a majority of the board of directors and a veto over the annual business plan. His counsel advises that no open offer arises, because the takeover code works on shareholding percentages and nine per cent is nowhere near any of them.

items.stem: What is wrong with what he has told the Adjudicating Authority?

options.text: The one hundred and twenty days is right, but within it the plan may be filed whenever the resolution professional is ready
options.misconception: reads a single deadline where the section sets two
options.why: Section 54D sets an outer limit for the process and an earlier one for the submission of the approved plan, so that the Adjudicating Authority has time to consider it inside the outer limit rather than on its last day.

options.text: The timetable could have been extended by the committee of creditors on a sixty-six per cent vote, so nothing is lost
options.misconception: borrows the extension in section 12(2) for a chapter that has none
options.why: Section 12(2) lets the committee resolve to extend a corporate insolvency resolution process beyond one hundred and eighty days. Chapter III-A has no equivalent — its answer to a process that has run out of time is termination under section 54D(3), not extension.

options.text: Both clocks have already run out — the process had to be completed within one hundred and twenty days of the commencement date, and the approved plan had to be submitted to the Adjudicating Authority within ninety days of it
options.why: Section 54D(1) requires the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process to be completed within a period of one hundred and twenty days from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date, so a process that commenced on 1 April 2026 was over at the end of July. Section 54D(2) separately requires the resolution professional to submit the resolution plan as approved by the committee of creditors to the Adjudicating Authority within ninety days from that date. Section 54D(3) is what happens when he cannot: he files an application for termination of the process the day after that period expires.

options.text: Nothing — the one hundred and eighty days runs for every process the Code creates
options.misconception: carries the section 12 timetable into Chapter III-A
options.why: The one hundred and eighty days belongs to section 12 and to the corporate insolvency resolution process. Chapter III-A was written to be faster because the debtor stays in possession and the plan is largely settled before the process begins, and section 54D carries its own two clocks.

citation.ref: Sections 54D(1), 54D(2) and 54D(3), read with section 12

items.scenario: A pre-packaged insolvency resolution process for an eligible micro enterprise commences on 1 April 2026. On 20 August 2026 the resolution professional tells the Adjudicating Authority that the committee of creditors approved a resolution plan on 15 August and that he will file it in the next few weeks. He adds that there is no hurry, because the pre-packaged process has the same one hundred and eighty day outer limit as an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process, with the same extension available on a vote of the committee.

items.stem: How do the two stand under section 4?

options.text: The matched discount is protected by the Explanation to section 4(2)(a), which takes out a discriminatory condition or price adopted to meet the competition; cutting output and shelving the upgrade is abuse under section 4(2)(b)
options.why: Section 4(2)(a) makes it an abuse to impose an unfair or discriminatory condition or price in the purchase or sale of goods or services, and its Explanation says that this shall not include such discriminatory condition or price which may be adopted to meet the competition. A discount confined to the one customer a rival has quoted for, and still above cost, is that case exactly. Section 4(2)(b) is a separate limb and it is where the second act lands: limiting or restricting production of goods or provision of services, or technical or scientific development relating to goods or services, to the prejudice of consumers.

options.text: Neither is an abuse — a producer decides its own output and its own research priorities, and matching a rival's price is ordinary trade
options.misconception: treats output and research as commercial freedoms a dominant enterprise keeps intact
options.why: They are freedoms for everybody else. Section 4(2)(b) names limiting or restricting production and technical or scientific development to the prejudice of consumers as an abuse precisely because a dominant enterprise's restraint is felt by the whole market rather than absorbed by it.

options.text: Both are abuses, because a dominant enterprise may never charge two customers different prices
options.misconception: reads section 4(2)(a) without the Explanation attached to it
options.why: The Explanation is part of the same provision and it says the discriminatory price does not include one adopted to meet the competition. Without it a dominant firm could never respond to a rival's quote at all, which would protect the rival rather than the customer.

options.text: The discount is an abuse and the output cut is not, since discrimination between customers is the clearest case the section contains
options.misconception: keeps the general words of section 4(2)(a) and ignores both its Explanation and section 4(2)(b)
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both halves. The Explanation takes the matched discount out, and section 4(2)(b) puts the output cut in.

citation.ref: Sections 4(2)(a) with its Explanation and 4(2)(b), read with section 4(1)

items.scenario: An enterprise that is dominant in the supply of industrial gas does two things in the same quarter. In one city a new rival quotes a lower price to a large hospital, and the enterprise offers that hospital — and nobody else — a matching discount, which still leaves its price above its own cost of production. Separately it cuts back output of the small cylinder size hospitals prefer, so that buyers move to its larger and costlier size, and shelves a purification upgrade its engineers had ready for release.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: Section 273(1) gives the Tribunal five courses, an interim order and a provisional liquidator among them; an order under that sub-section must be made within ninety days of the presentation of the petition; and before appointing a provisional liquidator the Tribunal must give the company notice and a reasonable opportunity to make representations, unless it records special reasons in writing for dispensing with the notice
options.why: Section 273(1) lets the Tribunal dismiss the petition with or without costs, make any interim order it thinks fit, appoint a provisional liquidator of the company till the making of a winding up order, make an order for winding up with or without costs, or make any other order it thinks fit — five courses and not two. Its first proviso requires the order to be made within ninety days from the date of presentation of the petition. Its second proviso is the safeguard the Registrar is asking the Tribunal to skip: notice to the company and a reasonable opportunity to make its representations before a provisional liquidator is appointed, unless for special reasons recorded in writing the Tribunal dispenses with it.

options.text: A provisional liquidator may be appointed at once and without notice as a matter of course, since urgency is the whole reason the power exists
options.misconception: reads an exception as if it were the rule
options.why: The exception exists and it is conditional. The Tribunal may dispense with the notice only for special reasons recorded in writing, and a dispensation given as a matter of course would swallow the safeguard the second proviso was written to create.

options.text: The company is right — the Tribunal either winds the company up or dismisses the petition, and it has no timetable
options.misconception: reads the jurisdiction as all or nothing and reads the provisos out of the sub-section
options.why: Interim orders and the appointment of a provisional liquidator are clauses (b) and (c) of the same sub-section, and the first proviso puts a ninety-day limit on the decision. A petition that can neither be disposed of nor policed in the meantime would be the worst of both.

options.text: The ninety days is directory only, and in any case no interim order may be made, because an interim order in a winding up would prejudge the petition
options.misconception: treats an interim order as a partial final order
options.why: An interim order preserves the position while the petition is decided, which is the opposite of deciding it. The Act contemplates it in clause (b) of section 273(1) and puts the outer limit on the decision in the proviso that follows.

citation.ref: Section 273(1) with both its provisos, read with section 272(1)

items.scenario: The Registrar presents a petition for the winding up of a company on 5 January 2026, with the previous sanction of the Central Government. At the first hearing he asks the Tribunal to appoint a provisional liquidator at once and without notice, because the directors are said to be moving assets out. The company replies that the Tribunal's only choice on a winding up petition is to order a winding up or to dismiss the petition, that it may take as long as it likes to decide, and that a provisional liquidator cannot be appointed before the order.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Section 192 catches it — the section covers a director, or a person connected with him, acquiring assets from the company for consideration other than cash just as it covers the company acquiring from him, so prior approval by a resolution in general meeting was needed, with the value of the assets calculated by a registered valuer set out in the notice
options.why: Section 192(1) has two halves. Clause (a) covers a director — of this company, or of another in the same group, holding, subsidiary or associate, or a person connected with him — who acquires, or is to acquire, assets from the company where what passes back the other way is consideration other than cash; clause (b) covers the company acquiring such assets from him. A flat going to the whole-time director's son against shares is clause (a), and a son is a relative within section 2(77) and plainly a person connected with him. Section 192(2) then requires the notice for the resolution to include the particulars of the arrangement along with the value of the assets involved, duly calculated by a registered valuer.

options.text: The section does not apply, because the son is not a director of the company or of any company in its group
options.misconception: drops the connected person from a sub-section that names him
options.why: Section 192(1) names a director, whether of this company or of another in the same group — holding, subsidiary or associate — and then adds, "or a person connected with him". Without those words the section could be avoided by routing every arrangement through a relative, which is exactly what has happened here.

options.text: The section applies, but a Board resolution with the audit committee's note is enough where the counterparty is not the director himself
options.misconception: substitutes a board approval for the general meeting the section requires
options.why: Section 192(1) requires prior approval by a resolution of the company in general meeting, and it makes no distinction between the director and a person connected with him. The Board cannot approve for the members what the section reserves to them.

options.text: The section does not apply, because it catches only assets the company acquires from a director
options.misconception: reads one half of section 192(1) and stops
options.why: The sub-section is written in both directions on purpose. A company handing a valuable asset to a director's family against paper is the mischief just as much as a company buying an asset from him at a price nobody outside has tested.

citation.ref: Sections 192(1)(a) and 192(2), read with section 2(77) and section 247

items.scenario: A company owns a flat it no longer uses. It transfers the flat to the son of its whole-time director and, instead of taking money, accepts from the son shares he holds in an unlisted company. The Board approves the transfer at a meeting and the audit committee notes that the son holds no office in the company and that the flat is not worth very much. Nothing is put to any general meeting and no valuation is obtained from outside the company.

items.stem: What has been left out?

options.text: Nothing after the sanction — filing the certified copy of the order with the Registrar within thirty days completes everything the company owes
options.misconception: treats registration of the order as the end of the scheme's compliance
options.why: Section 232(5) does require the certified copy to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of receipt of the order, and section 232(7) then runs for as long as the scheme takes to implement, with a certified annual statement to the Registrar each year until it is completed.

options.text: Nothing — the scheme itself and a valuation report are what a member needs in order to vote
options.misconception: treats the notice requirements as a matter for the companies to judge
options.why: Section 232(2) writes the list out and does not leave it to be judged. The directors' own report is the item that matters most to a small holder, because it is where the effect on his class, as against the promoters' class, has to be spelled out.

options.text: The notice had to carry a confirmation that a copy of the draft scheme had been filed with the Registrar, a directors' report explaining the effect of the compromise on each class of shareholders, key managerial personnel, promoters and non-promoter shareholders, and a supplementary accounting statement because the transferor's last annual accounts are more than six months old; and a certified statement has to be filed with the Registrar every year until the scheme is completed
options.why: Section 232(2) lists what must be circulated for the meetings the Tribunal orders — the draft of the proposed terms of the scheme adopted by the directors, a confirmation that a copy of it has been filed with the Registrar, a report adopted by the directors explaining the effect of the compromise on each class of shareholders, key managerial personnel, promoters and non-promoter shareholders and laying out in particular the share exchange ratio and any special valuation difficulties, the expert's report on valuation if there is one, and a supplementary accounting statement where the last annual accounts of any of the merging companies relate to a financial year ending more than six months before the first meeting. Section 232(7) then requires every company in relation to which the order is made to file a statement with the Registrar every year until the scheme is completed, certified by a chartered accountant, a cost accountant or a company secretary in practice, saying whether the scheme is being complied with.

options.text: Only the directors' report — the accounts are recent enough, since the six months runs from the Tribunal's order and not from the meeting
options.misconception: measures the six months from the wrong event
options.why: The sub-section measures it from the first meeting of the company summoned for the purpose of approving the scheme. Members vote on the scheme at that meeting, so the accounts have to be fresh when they vote rather than when the Tribunal later signs.

items.scenario: Two unrelated companies file a scheme of amalgamation and the Tribunal orders meetings of members and creditors. The companies circulate the notice with the draft scheme and a registered valuer's report on the share exchange ratio, and nothing else. The last annual accounts of the transferor relate to a financial year that ended eleven months before the first meeting. After the Tribunal sanctions the scheme, the transferee files the certified copy of the order with the Registrar and treats the matter as closed, although the scheme will take about three years to implement fully.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way the two assets are being held?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — CSR is measured by what is spent, and both years' money has gone on the projects
options.misconception: reads CSR as a test of money spent and not of what the money leaves behind
options.why: Money spent is the obligation's measure and not its whole content. The Rule on capital assets exists because an asset held in the company's own name can be sold, mortgaged or simply repurposed, and the spend would then have bought the company an asset rather than the community a school.

options.text: The school block is acceptable because the company will maintain it, and only the ambulances are wrongly held
options.misconception: reads an undertaking to maintain as a substitute for the ownership the Rule prescribes
options.why: Maintenance is not on the Rule's list. It names four holders and the company is not among them, however carefully it promises to look after what it built.

options.text: A capital asset created or acquired out of CSR spend may be held only by a section 8 company or a registered public trust or registered society having charitable objects and a CSR registration number, by the beneficiaries of the project in the form of self-help groups, collectives or entities, or by a public authority — and not by the company itself
options.why: Rule 7(4) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 permits the CSR amount to be spent for the creation or acquisition of a capital asset and then says who may hold it: a company established under section 8 of the Act, or a registered public trust or registered society having charitable objects and a CSR registration number, or the beneficiaries of the CSR project in the form of self-help groups, collectives or entities, or a public authority. A school block sitting in the company's own fixed assets and ambulances registered in the company's own name fail that in both years, and handing the ambulances to a district hospital to operate does not cure it, because the Rule is about who holds the asset.

options.text: Both are wrong, because a capital asset can never be created out of CSR spend at all
options.misconception: reads a rule about who holds an asset as a bar on creating one
options.why: Rule 7(4) opens by permitting the CSR amount to be spent for the creation or acquisition of a capital asset. What it controls is the name the asset is held in, not whether the project may build anything.

citation.ref: Rule 7(4) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, read with section 135(5)

items.scenario: A company discharges its corporate social responsibility obligation by building a school block on land it owns, and records the building in its own fixed assets, saying that it will maintain it and that a school on the company's own land is easier to look after. Its CSR committee proposes to spend next year's obligation on a fleet of ambulances, registered in the company's name, which a district hospital will operate.

items.stem: Which of them is a related party under Ind AS 24?

options.text: Only the joint venture itself. The supplier, the bank and the company with the common director are not related parties on these facts, and two venturers are not related parties to each other merely because they share joint control
options.why: Ind AS 24 sets out what is not a related party, and three of these four sit in that list: two entities simply because they have a director or other member of key management personnel in common; two venturers simply because they share joint control over a joint venture; providers of finance, trade unions, public utilities and government departments simply by virtue of their normal dealings with the entity; and a customer, supplier, franchisor, distributor or general agent with whom the entity transacts a significant volume of business, simply by virtue of the resulting economic dependence. The joint venture is on the other side of the line — a joint venture in which the entity is a venturer is a related party of that entity.

options.text: The bank and the joint venture, since a lender with a covenant over dividends has significant influence
options.misconception: reads a contractual covenant as significant influence
options.why: Significant influence is the power to participate in the financial and operating policy decisions of an investee, and it is not control or joint control of those decisions. The standard names providers of finance among those who are not related parties simply by virtue of their normal dealings with the entity, and a dividend covenant is a normal dealing between a lender and a borrower.

options.text: All four, because Ind AS 24 is wider than section 2(76) and reaches every close commercial relationship
options.misconception: reads the standard's width as unlimited
options.why: It is wider in the places where it says it is wider. It also states four categories that are not related parties, and three of these four sit inside them, so width in one direction is not width in every direction.

options.text: The supplier and the joint venture, because dependence on that scale is control in substance
options.misconception: reads commercial dependence as a related party relationship
options.why: The standard answers that argument in terms. A customer or supplier with whom an entity transacts a significant volume of business is not a related party simply by virtue of the resulting economic dependence, however uncomfortable the dependence is.

citation.ref: Ind AS 24, Related Party Disclosures — the paragraph listing persons who are not related parties, read with section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company preparing its financial statements under Ind AS has to decide on four relationships. A supplier from whom it buys eighty per cent of its raw material, and who earns most of his own revenue from it. A bank which has lent it a large term loan and has taken a covenant restricting dividends. Another company with which it shares one non-executive director and nothing else. And a joint venture over which it and one other venturer have joint control — the venture itself, and that other venturer.

items.stem: What is wrong with the omnibus approval?

options.text: It cannot run for three years — an omnibus approval is valid for a period not exceeding one year and needs a fresh approval afterwards; it must specify the maximum amount of the transactions and the indicative base price or current contracted price with the formula for any variation; and the committee must review the transactions made under it at least once a quarter
options.why: Regulation 23(3) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 lets the audit committee grant an omnibus approval, and then attaches the conditions. The committee must lay down criteria and satisfy itself that the approval is in the interest of the listed entity. The approval must specify the name of the related party, the nature, period and maximum amount of the transactions to be entered into, and the indicative base price or current contracted price along with the formula for any variation. The committee must review, at least on a quarterly basis, the details of the transactions entered into under each omnibus approval. And the approval is valid for a period not exceeding one year, requiring a fresh approval on expiry.

options.text: Only the review is wrong; a three-year approval is permitted where the underlying contract itself runs for three years
options.misconception: ties the life of the approval to the life of the contract
options.why: Regulation 23(3) fixes the life of the approval at not exceeding one year whatever the term of the contract beneath it, so a three-year arrangement comes back to the audit committee each year for a fresh look at prices and volumes.

options.text: Only the period is wrong; the details can be filled in later, since the point of an omnibus approval is that the transactions are not yet known
options.misconception: reads the provision made for unforeseen transactions as the general rule
options.why: The Regulation deals with the unforeseen case separately, and caps such approvals at the amount per transaction it names. For everything else the specified details — the party, the nature, the period, the maximum amount and the indicative price — are conditions of the approval rather than paperwork to follow it.

options.text: Nothing — an omnibus approval exists precisely so that a committee need not return to the same dealing again
options.misconception: reads the convenience of an omnibus approval as removing the review that comes with it
options.why: What it saves is a fresh approval for each transaction, and what it does not save is oversight. The quarterly review and the one-year life are the price of the convenience, written into the same sub-regulation that grants it.

citation.ref: Regulation 23(3), read with Regulation 23(2)

items.scenario: In April 2026 the audit committee of a listed entity grants an omnibus approval covering purchases from a promoter group company for the next three years. The minute records the name of the related party and the nature of the transaction, but no maximum amount and no indicative price, on the footing that the volumes will vary with demand. It adds that the committee will look at the transactions when the three years are up.

items.stem: What is wrong with what he has done?

options.text: The values should not go to the committee at all, since confidentiality is what the Regulation is protecting
options.misconception: reads confidentiality as secrecy from the committee itself
options.why: The committee is who the values are for; it is the body that has to weigh a plan against them. Regulation 35(2) governs when they go and on what condition, not whether they go.

options.text: Both values go to the members of the committee only after the receipt of resolution plans, and only on an undertaking from each member that he will keep them confidential and will not use them to cause an undue gain or undue loss to himself or anyone else
options.why: Regulation 35(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 says that after the receipt of resolution plans the resolution professional shall provide the fair value and the liquidation value to every member of the committee in electronic form, on receiving an undertaking that the member shall maintain confidentiality of the values and shall not use them to cause an undue gain or undue loss to itself or any other person. Sending them out before the plans are in, and without the undertaking, hands a member who may itself bid the one number every other bidder is trying to beat.
keywords: after the receipt of resolution plans

options.text: The timing is right, and the undertaking is a formality that can be collected afterwards
options.misconception: reads a condition precedent as a piece of record-keeping
options.why: The Regulation makes the disclosure conditional on receiving the undertaking, so it comes first. An undertaking signed after the value has been read protects nothing that had not already been given away.

options.text: Nothing — the committee has to judge the plans against the values, so the earlier it has them the better
options.misconception: treats the committee's entitlement to the values as an entitlement to have them at any time
options.why: The committee does need both values, and the Regulation gives them to it. What it controls is the moment: after the plans have been received, when the numbers can no longer shape what is bid.

citation.ref: Regulation 35(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, read with Regulation 27 and section 29(2) of the Code

items.scenario: A resolution professional circulates the fair value and the liquidation value to every member of the committee of creditors along with the invitation for expressions of interest, before a single resolution plan has come in, and takes no undertaking from anybody. One committee member is a financial creditor which is itself considering submitting a resolution plan through a group company. When a dissenting member objects, the professional answers that the committee is entitled to everything he knows and that the objection is a delaying tactic.

items.stem: How should the application be dealt with?

options.text: The conditions cannot bite here, because the Public Prosecutor did not appear and the first of them is therefore impossible to satisfy
options.misconception: reads an opportunity to oppose as an actual appearance
options.why: The sub-section requires that the Public Prosecutor be given an opportunity to oppose the application, which the court secures by notice. His absence on one date neither converts his silence into consent nor makes the condition impossible; the second condition only comes into play if he does oppose.

options.text: The twin conditions apply, but they replace the ordinary bail law, so nothing in the Code of Criminal Procedure need be considered
options.misconception: reads section 212(6) as a complete code for bail
options.why: Section 212(7) says the limitation is in addition to the limitations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. An accused therefore has to get past both sets, not the harsher set alone.

options.text: It cannot be granted unless the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose it and, where he opposes, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail — conditions that are in addition to those in the Code of Criminal Procedure
options.why: Section 212(6) makes an offence covered under section 447 cognizable and provides that no person accused of it shall be released on bail or on his own bond unless the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application and, where he opposes it, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. Section 212(7) says that limitation on granting of bail is in addition to the limitations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The proviso relaxes the twin conditions for a person under the age of sixteen, a woman, a sick or infirm person, or a case below the amount it names, and this accused is none of those.

options.text: Bail should follow as a matter of course, since the offence involves no violence and arises under a company law statute
options.misconception: reads the nature of the statute as deciding the bail regime
options.why: Parliament decided otherwise when it made the section 447 offence cognizable and attached the twin conditions to it. The mischief the conditions guard against is the destruction of records and the pressure on witnesses, which does not need violence to be effective.

citation.ref: Sections 212(6) with its proviso and 212(7), read with section 447

items.scenario: Officers of the Serious Fraud Investigation Office arrest a promoter — a healthy adult man — for an offence punishable under section 447 involving a large sum, well above the amount named in the proviso to section 212(6). He applies for bail before the Special Court. The Public Prosecutor is engaged elsewhere that day and does not appear. Counsel for the promoter says bail should follow as a matter of course because no violence is alleged and the offence is under a company law statute, and that the ordinary bail principles of the Code of Criminal Procedure are the only ones that apply.

items.stem: May he?

options.text: He may, but only with the prior approval of the Central Government — section 219 lets an inspector extend the investigation to a subsidiary or holding company or a subsidiary of the holding company, to a body corporate accustomed to act on the instructions of the company or its directors, and to a person who is or has at any relevant time been the company's managing director, manager or employee
options.why: Section 219 says that if an inspector appointed under section 210, 212 or 213 considers it necessary for the purposes of the investigation to investigate also the affairs of any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been the company's subsidiary or holding company or a subsidiary of its holding company, or a body corporate whose Board comprises nominees of the company or is accustomed to act in accordance with the directions or instructions of the company or any of its directors, or any person who is or has at any relevant time been the company's managing director or manager or employee, he shall, subject to the prior approval of the Central Government, investigate into and report on their affairs. The reach is there; the safeguard is the approval, and it comes before the extension rather than after it.

options.text: He may reach the two bodies corporate, but not the former managing director, since a person is not a body corporate and the section is about the affairs of companies
options.misconception: stops at the corporate limbs of a section that names an individual too
options.why: The last limb of section 219 names any person who is or has at any relevant time been the company's managing director or manager or employee. The words "has been" are what reach a man who left two years ago.

options.text: He may, as of right, because an order of investigation carries the inspector wherever the money went
options.misconception: reads an inspector's mandate as extending itself
options.why: His appointment names a company and his powers run against that company. Section 219 is what lets him go further, and it makes him ask first — the bodies corporate he wants to look at are not the ones the Central Government decided to investigate.

options.text: He may not, because a separate order under section 210 is needed for each body corporate
options.misconception: turns an approval into a fresh order of investigation
options.why: Section 219 exists so that one investigation can follow the money without a new order for each entity. What it requires is the prior approval of the Central Government, given inside the investigation that is already running.

citation.ref: Section 219, read with sections 210(1), 212 and 213

items.scenario: The Central Government orders an investigation into a company's affairs under section 210 and appoints an inspector, whose order of appointment names that company alone. Working through the books, the inspector concludes that money left through a fellow subsidiary of the company's holding company and through a firm whose board is accustomed to act on the instructions of the company's directors, and that the company's former managing director, who left two years ago, holds part of the answer. He proposes to extend the investigation to both bodies corporate and to the former managing director on his own authority.

items.stem: Is the consultant right?

options.text: No — the general permission for a project office rests on the contract plus one of four funding conditions, none of which is satisfied here, so the German company has to approach the Reserve Bank of India for approval
options.why: A person resident outside India may establish a project office in India under the general permission only where it has secured from an Indian company a contract to execute a project in India and one of four things is also true: the project is funded directly by inward remittance from abroad, or it is funded by a bilateral or multilateral international financing agency, or it has been cleared by an appropriate authority, or the Indian company awarding the contract has been granted a term loan by a public financial institution or a bank in India for the project. Where none of them is met, the foreign entity has to approach the Reserve Bank of India for approval. A signed contract is half the test.

options.text: Yes, provided the project office remits nothing out of India until the contract is finished
options.misconception: swaps an entry condition for a condition on remittance
options.why: The four conditions are about how the project is funded and are tested at entry. Remittance of the surplus is a separate matter altogether, allowed on completion once the authorised dealer is satisfied that the project is over and the tax position settled.

options.text: No, and a project office is out of reach altogether — the German company would have to open a branch office instead
options.misconception: turns a case that needs approval into a case that is barred
options.why: The Regulations do not close the route; they send it to the Reserve Bank of India for a decision on the facts. A branch office carries its own entry conditions and its own list of permitted activities, and it is not a substitute the applicant is forced into.

options.text: Yes — the contract is the condition, and how the Indian company chooses to fund the work is its own affair
options.misconception: reads the contract as the whole of the general permission
options.why: The funding conditions are there because they tell the Reserve Bank where the foreign exchange for the project is coming from. A project paid for entirely out of Indian rupees raises a different question from one funded by an inward remittance, which is why the second half of the test exists.

citation.ref: FEM (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016 — the conditions for a project office

items.scenario: A German engineering company has won a contract from an Indian private company to build a plant in India. The Indian company is funding the project entirely out of its own accruals: there is no inward remittance from abroad, no bilateral or multilateral international financing agency behind it, no clearance from any appropriate authority, and no term loan from a public financial institution or a bank in India. The German company wants to set up a project office to run the contract, and its consultant says no approval is needed at all, a signed contract being the only condition a project office has to meet.

items.stem: Is the firm within Clause 6?

options.text: No — the clause bars a member from soliciting clients or professional work directly or indirectly, so work canvassed through somebody else's hands is caught exactly as a letter from the firm would be
options.why: Clause 6 sits in Part I of the First Schedule — the misconduct list the 1949 Act lays on a member who holds a certificate of practice. It makes it misconduct for a chartered accountant in practice to solicit clients or professional work either directly or indirectly, by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means. The word indirectly and the closing words by any other means are what defeat the argument: a brochure pushed at a prospective client through a solicitor or a banker is still the firm's own circular, and a member may not do through another hand what he may not do with his own.

options.text: No breach, because the clause reaches only an approach the member makes himself to a prospective client
options.misconception: reads the word "directly" and stops before the word that follows it
options.why: The clause names both routes in the same breath. Confining it to what the member does with his own hand would leave every firm free to hire a channel, which is the arrangement the word "indirectly" was written to catch.

options.text: No breach, because the solicitors and the bankers decided for themselves which company to give a brochure to, so the choice of recipient was never the firm's
options.misconception: treats the intermediary's discretion as breaking the chain back to the member
options.why: The firm printed the material, chose the channel and asked for it to be passed on to companies looking for an auditor. Who handed over which copy is a detail of execution; the soliciting was done when the arrangement was made.

options.text: No breach, because nothing was paid to the solicitors or the bankers, and solicitation requires the member to have bought the introduction
options.misconception: adds a payment element the clause does not contain
options.why: Payment raises questions under other clauses of the same Schedule. Clause 6 asks only whether professional work was solicited, and is silent about consideration — an unpaid channel solicits just as effectively as a paid one.

citation.ref: Clause 6, Part I, First Schedule

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants writes to nobody. It prints a brochure describing its audit practice, leaves a stack of them with a friendly firm of solicitors and with two branch managers of its bankers, and asks them to hand one to any company they hear is looking for a new auditor. Nothing is paid to the solicitors or to the bankers. A partner says Clause 6 cannot be engaged, because the firm has approached no company at all.

items.stem: Has a default occurred within section 3(12)?

options.text: No, because the debt is the loan and the loan is not yet due; an instalment is only the manner in which the debt is being paid
options.misconception: reads the definition of debt without the words "part or instalment" in the definition of default
options.why: The Code answers this in the definition itself. Section 3(12) does not ask whether the debt has matured — it asks whether the whole, or any part, or any instalment has become due and payable and has not been paid.

options.text: Yes — default is the non-payment of a debt when the whole or any part or instalment of it has become due and payable and is not paid, so the unpaid instalment is itself a default even though the rest of the loan has not fallen due
options.why: Section 3(12) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 defines default as non-payment of a debt when the whole or any part or instalment of the amount of debt has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor. Section 3(11) defines debt as a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person, and includes a financial debt and an operational debt. Put together, the instalment that fell due on 30 April 2026 and was not paid is a default on its own, and nothing waits for the maturity of the loan in 2029.

options.text: No, because default requires the debtor to have refused to pay, and this borrower has not refused
options.misconception: adds an element of refusal that the definition does not contain
options.why: There is no mental element in section 3(12). The sub-section asks two things only: has the amount become due and payable, and has it been paid. A borrower who cannot pay is in default as surely as one who will not.

options.text: Yes, and the whole of the loan is in default, non-payment of one instalment putting the entire debt in default under the Code
options.misconception: reads a definition as an acceleration clause
options.why: Section 3(12) decides that a default has occurred; it does not accelerate anything. Whether the rest of the loan becomes immediately payable is a question for the acceleration clause in the loan agreement, not for the definition.

citation.ref: Sections 3(11) and 3(12), read with section 4

items.scenario: A company borrowed on a term loan repayable in quarterly instalments, the last of which falls due in 2029. The instalment due on 30 April 2026 — an amount well above the minimum notified under section 4 — has still not been paid on 30 August 2026. Every other instalment has been paid on time. The borrower's counsel says there is no default within the Code, because a debt means the whole liability and the loan does not mature until 2029.

items.stem: Who verifies the company's return of income?

options.text: The insolvency professional appointed by the Adjudicating Authority, a proviso to section 140(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 saying so in terms once an insolvency application has been admitted
options.why: Section 140(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ordinarily has the return of a company verified by the managing director, and by any director where there is no managing director or he is unable to verify. A proviso to that clause carries the position through an insolvency: where an application for corporate insolvency resolution process has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the return shall be verified by the insolvency professional appointed by that Adjudicating Authority. It sits with section 17(1) of the Code, which suspends the powers of the board and vests the management of the company's affairs in the professional.

options.text: Any director, under the ordinary rule in section 140(c), the proviso beginning to operate only when a resolution plan is approved
options.misconception: starts the proviso at the approval of the plan instead of at the admission of the application
options.why: The proviso runs from the admission of the application by the Adjudicating Authority, which is also the moment section 17(1) suspends the board. Waiting for the plan would leave the company with no one able to verify a return for the whole of the process.

options.text: The suspended managing director, who remains the managing director on the company's records until somebody removes him
options.misconception: keeps the office doing work after section 17(1) has taken its powers away
options.why: He holds the title and not the power. Section 17(1) vests the management of the affairs of the company in the insolvency professional, and the Income-tax Act follows that with its own proviso naming the professional as the person who verifies.

options.text: Nobody, until a resolution plan is approved; the return is filed late and the delay is explained by the process
options.misconception: treats an insolvency as suspending the company's tax obligations
options.why: The process changes who acts for the company, not what the company owes. The proviso exists precisely so that the return can be verified and filed on time while the board sits suspended.

citation.ref: The proviso to section 140(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 17(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

items.scenario: An application for a corporate insolvency resolution process against a company was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority in March 2026, and the resolution professional is running the business. The company's return of income for the year is now due. The suspended managing director offers to verify it as he has every year; the chief financial officer says nobody can verify it until a resolution plan is approved and the return will simply have to be late.

items.stem: What does section 25 say about the two?

options.text: Taking immediate custody and control of all the assets, including the business records, is his own duty and not a request he makes item by item; and he may appoint accountants, legal and other professionals in the manner specified by the Board, an appointment that is not on the section 28(1) list at all
options.why: Section 25(1) puts the resolution professional under a duty to preserve and protect the assets of the corporate debtor, including the continued business operations. Section 25(2)(a) then requires him to take immediate custody and control of all the assets of the corporate debtor, including the business records — the initiative is his and the management has no say in the pace. Section 25(2)(d) lets him appoint accountants, legal and other professionals in the manner specified by the Board. Section 28(1) is a closed list of the actions he may not take without the committee's prior approval, and appointing his own professionals is not on that list.

options.text: The suspended management may insist on an itemised written request, because section 17 transfers the powers of the board and not the possession of the company's property
options.misconception: separates possession from the control the Code hands over
options.why: Section 25(2)(a) is written in terms of custody and control of all the assets, and section 19(1) requires the personnel of the corporate debtor, its promoters and any other person associated with its management to extend all assistance and cooperation to the professional. Nothing in either lets the outgoing management set the terms of the handover.

options.text: He may take custody at once, but the appointment of the accountants and the lawyer has to be ratified by the committee at its next meeting
options.misconception: invents a ratification step the Code does not contain
options.why: Ratification is not a mechanism section 28 uses at all — an action on its list taken without prior approval is void under section 28(4), not curable later. And an appointment under section 25(2)(d) never needed the committee in the first place.

options.text: Both need the committee's approval, section 28(1) covering everything the professional does that costs the corporate debtor money
options.misconception: treats section 28(1) as a general spending control rather than a closed list of named actions
options.why: Section 28(1) names its actions one by one and the professional's own professional advisers are not among them. A section that had been meant as a spending control would not have needed thirteen clauses.

citation.ref: Sections 25(1), 25(2)(a) and 25(2)(d), read with sections 19(1) and 28(1)

items.scenario: A resolution professional takes charge. He asks the suspended management for the keys, the seals and the books; they say they will hand over whatever he asks for in writing, item by item, as and when he identifies it. He also wants to engage a firm of accountants to help him verify the claims and a lawyer to defend a pending suit. The chief financial officer tells him that every one of those appointments needs the committee's approval under section 28.

items.stem: Was the allotment made in time?

options.text: Yes, because the fifteen-day period applies only where an application for an approval or permission of a regulatory authority is pending
options.misconception: reads the proviso as if it were the rule
options.why: The fifteen days are the rule for every allotment pursuant to a special resolution. The proviso only moves the starting point where an application for an approval or permission is pending, counting the fifteen days from the date of that approval instead.

options.text: No, but the lapse is cured by a Board resolution ratifying the delay and recording the reasons for it
options.misconception: lets the Board cure a lapse the Regulation puts back to the members
options.why: The Regulation names the cure itself and it is a fresh special resolution of the members, with the relevant date taken again. A Board cannot ratify its way past a requirement written in terms of a members' resolution.

options.text: No — the allotment had to be completed within fifteen days of the date of passing the special resolution, so it was due by 20 June 2026, and where it is not completed in that period a fresh special resolution must be passed and the relevant date taken afresh
options.why: Regulation 170 of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 requires an allotment pursuant to a special resolution to be completed within a period of fifteen days from the date of passing of that resolution, and provides that where it is not, a fresh special resolution shall be passed and the relevant date for pricing shall be reckoned afresh. That is the discipline behind the floor price: a resolution passed on one set of market prices cannot be held in a drawer and used months later.

options.text: Yes, because the fifteen days run from the receipt of the subscription money rather than from the date of the resolution
options.misconception: starts the clock at the money instead of at the members' approval
options.why: Regulation 170 counts from the date of passing of the special resolution. Receipt of money starts a different clock in a different statute — section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 — and it does not move this one.

citation.source: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
citation.ref: Regulation 170 with its proviso

items.scenario: A listed company passes the special resolution approving a preferential allotment on 5 June 2026. No approval of any regulatory authority is needed for it. The allotment is completed on 10 July 2026. The company secretary records that the timing raises nothing, since the ICDR Regulations fix no period within which an approved preferential allotment must be made.

items.stem: What does section 204 require on the two points?

options.text: The report is annexed and must in addition be filed separately with the Registrar in a form of its own within thirty days
options.misconception: invents a separate filing for a document that travels with another
options.why: There is no separate filing. The secretarial audit report is annexed to the Board's report, and the Board's report goes to the Registrar with the financial statements — which is why the annexure is the whole of the requirement.

options.text: Producing the report to any member who asks is enough, the Act requiring it to be given to the Board rather than published to the members
options.misconception: stops at the delivery of the report and misses where the section makes it travel
options.why: Section 204(1) does not stop at the Board. It requires the report to be annexed to the Board's report, which goes to every member and is filed with the Registrar, so the report reaches the people whose compliance it describes.

options.text: The report has to be annexed to the Board's report, and the company, its officers and its auditors are under a statutory duty to give the company secretary in practice all assistance and facilities necessary for conducting the secretarial audit
options.why: Section 204(1) requires the prescribed companies to annex a secretarial audit report given by a company secretary in practice to the Board's report made under section 134(3). It is annexed because that is how the members and the Registrar come to see it, and a report kept in the minute book for anyone who asks is not compliance. Section 204(2) puts the other side of it on the company: it shall be the duty of the company, its officers and its auditors to give all assistance and facilities to the company secretary in practice for the purpose of conducting the secretarial audit. Section 204(4) then makes the company, every officer in default and the company secretary in practice punishable for a contravention.

options.text: The report is annexed, but the practitioner's access to records is whatever his engagement with the Board gives him, since it is the Board that appointed him
options.misconception: makes a statutory right of access a term of the engagement letter
options.why: Section 204(2) is addressed to the company and its officers, not to the Board's terms of appointment. The duty to give assistance and facilities exists independently of what any engagement letter says and a department head cannot decline it.

citation.ref: Sections 204(1), 204(2) and 204(4), read with section 134(3)

items.scenario: A company covered by section 204 receives its secretarial audit report a week before the Board's report is signed. The company secretary proposes to keep the report in the minute book and produce it to any member who asks for it, rather than putting it with the Board's report. Separately, the head of one department has refused the practising company secretary access to a statutory register, saying the practitioner's mandate comes from the Board and the department answers to the managing director.

items.stem: Is that classification right?

options.text: Yes, because ten per cent is the line between the two classifications and this holding is well below it
options.misconception: applies the listed-entity percentage test to an unlisted foreign entity
options.why: The ten per cent test is written into the limb that speaks of a listed foreign entity. The Rules deliberately treat an unlisted foreign entity differently, because a stake in a company whose shares nobody can buy or sell on an exchange is not a portfolio holding however small it is.

options.text: No, and the answer would change if the holding fell below one per cent, a stake that small being portfolio by its nature
options.misconception: invents a de minimis floor the Rules do not contain
options.why: There is no floor. The first limb of Rule 2(1)(q) reaches any unlisted equity capital, and a single share of an unlisted foreign entity is overseas direct investment on the same reasoning as two per cent.

options.text: No — the acquisition of any unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity is overseas direct investment whatever the percentage and whether or not there is control; the percentage and control tests belong to a listed foreign entity
options.why: Rule 2(1)(q) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 defines overseas direct investment as the acquisition of any unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity, or subscription as part of the memorandum of association of a foreign entity, or investment in ten per cent or more of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity, or investment with control where the investment is less than ten per cent of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity. The first limb has no percentage in it at all. Two per cent of an unlisted foreign entity is on that limb, so it is overseas direct investment and carries the reporting, exit and end-use discipline that goes with it.

options.text: Yes, because overseas portfolio investment is investment without control and this company has none
options.misconception: makes control the dividing line for every foreign entity
options.why: Control divides the two only inside a listed foreign entity, where an investment below ten per cent is overseas direct investment if it carries control and portfolio investment if it does not. In an unlisted foreign entity the question never arises, the first limb of Rule 2(1)(q) having already answered it.

citation.ref: Rules 2(1)(q) and 2(1)(s) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022

items.scenario: An Indian manufacturing company subscribes to two per cent of the equity capital of a company incorporated in Dubai whose shares are not listed on any exchange anywhere. It takes no board seat and has no control of any kind. Its finance head classifies the holding as overseas portfolio investment, on the reasoning that two per cent is far below ten and there is no control.

items.stem: What does the Act provide?

options.text: The shares may be transferred to anybody the Board approves, the restriction being about the Board's approval rather than about who the transferee is
options.misconception: keeps the approval requirement and drops the condition on the transferee
options.why: The section imposes both. The previous approval of the Board is one condition and the transferee being an active member is another, with the price fixed at par so that the transfer cannot be used to extract a premium out of the company's reserves.

options.text: The shares are not transferable at large — a member may transfer them only to an active member, at par value, and only with the previous approval of the Board; every member nominates, within three months of becoming a member, the person in whom his shares vest on his death; and where the Board is satisfied that a member has ceased to be a primary producer it may direct the surrender of his shares
options.why: Section 378ZB makes the shares of a member of a producer company non-transferable save as the section itself allows. A member may, after obtaining the previous approval of the Board, transfer the whole or part of his shares along with any special rights to an active member, at par value — so the son, who is not a member and not a producer, cannot take them at any price. The section requires every member, within three months of becoming a member, to nominate in the manner specified in the articles the person to whom his shares shall vest in the event of his death, and that nominee becomes entitled on the death. And where the Board is satisfied that a member has ceased to be a primary producer or has failed to retain his qualifications, it may direct the surrender of his shares.

options.text: The shares are freely transferable like the shares of any other company, subject only to whatever the articles say
options.misconception: treats a producer company's share as an ordinary share in a private company
options.why: A producer company's membership is tied to production, not to capital, which is why its shares are non-transferable except within the membership. Free transferability would let the company be bought by people who produce nothing.

options.text: On a member's death his shares lapse to the company, a producer company having no room for a holder who is not himself a producer
options.misconception: overlooks the nomination the section requires every member to make
options.why: Nothing lapses. The section requires the nomination within three months of becoming a member precisely so that there is somebody in whom the shares vest, and the nominee becomes entitled to all the rights in the shares on the death.

citation.ref: Section 378ZB

items.scenario: Three questions reach the board of a producer company on the same day. A member wants to sell his shares to his son, who farms nothing and is not a member. A member has died and his family asks what becomes of his shares. And a third member sold his land two years ago and has not produced anything since.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The March lease stands — no regulation made by the company in general meeting invalidates a prior act of the Board which would have been valid had that regulation not been made — and counsel has the Board's authority the wrong way round, the Board being entitled to exercise all the powers the company itself may exercise, subject to the Act, the memorandum, the articles and any such regulation
