And the opportunity of being heard is granted on a request from the assessee, not automatically, and when it is granted it is through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible. A personal appearance was never on offer.

options.text: The committee may not reject the application for silence alone; it must decide the application on its merits and record why the assessee's case fails
options.misconception: reads silence as leaving the committee with a duty to decide the merits, when the rule makes silence itself a ground for rejection
options.why: The rule is explicit that where no response is furnished by the assessee the committee may reject the application. It is not obliged to construct a case for a person who did not answer its notice.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — a show-cause notice before rejection, an opportunity of being heard on the assessee's request through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible, extension of time on an application made in that behalf, and rejection where no response is furnished

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee doubts that an application should be admitted. It sends the assessee a show-cause notice setting a date and time for a response. The assessee neither responds nor asks for anything. His counsel later says the committee could not lawfully reject the application without first hearing him in person.

items.stem: By when must the committee have passed its order, and by when must the Assessing Officer act on it?

options.text: The committee by 14 November 2026 and the Assessing Officer by 9 January 2027, each period running from the date of the event
options.misconception: runs both periods from the date of admission and the date of receipt, when each runs from the end of the month in which the event falls
options.why: Neither period is measured from a date. The committee's six months and the Assessing Officer's one month both start at the end of the month in which the triggering event happened, which pushes each deadline out to a month end.

options.text: The committee by 31 May 2027, being six months from the end of the assessment year, and the Assessing Officer by 31 January 2027
options.misconception: attaches the committee's period to the end of the assessment year rather than to the month of admission
options.why: The committee's period is tied to its own admission of the application and to nothing about the assessment year. Six months from the end of May 2026 is 30 November 2026.

options.text: The committee by 30 November 2026, being six months from the end of the month of admission, and the Assessing Officer by 31 January 2027, being one month from the end of the month in which he received the order
options.why: Both clocks run from the end of a month rather than from a date. The committee has six months from the end of the month during which it admitted the application for dispute resolution, so from 31 May 2026, which is 30 November 2026. Section 245MA(2A) then gives the Assessing Officer one month from the end of the month in which the committee's order is received, so from 31 December 2026, which is 31 January 2027.
keywords: six months from the end of the month
one month from the end of the month

options.text: The committee by 30 November 2026, and the Assessing Officer by 8 January 2027, being thirty days from receipt
options.misconception: gets the committee's clock right and then swaps the Assessing Officer's month for a thirty-day period counted from receipt
options.why: Section 245MA(2A) gives one month measured from the close of the month during which the order reached him, not thirty days counted from receipt. On these facts that is 31 January 2027.

citation.ref: Section 245MA(2A) read with Rule 44DAB — the committee's order within six months of the close of the month of admission, and the Assessing Officer's conforming or modified order within one month of the close of the month in which the committee's order reaches him

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee admitted an application on 14 May 2026. It passed its order of resolution and served a copy on the Assessing Officer, who received it on 9 December 2026.

items.stem: What can he do about the variations now?

options.text: He may make a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel, the draft order under section 144C(1) having remained a draft order throughout
options.misconception: leaves the Panel route open after the committee has acted, when the two are alternatives for an eligible assessee
options.why: Once the committee has dealt with a specified order that was a draft order under section 144C(1), the assessee is not eligible to file a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel against the modified order. The Assessing Officer passes an order of assessment in conformity with the committee's order, and that is the end of it.

options.text: Nothing — no appeal or revision lies against the modified order, and having gone to the committee he can neither make a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel nor appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against it
options.why: The rule closes both doors. No appeal and no revision lie against the modified order. And where the specified order was that of an eligible assessee referred to in section 144C(1), he is not eligible to file a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel or an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against the modified order. An eligible assessee chooses between the Panel and the Committee at the start and does not get both.

options.text: He may seek revision under section 264, which is not an appeal and so is untouched by the bar
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering appeals only, when the rule shuts out revision in the same breath
options.why: The words are that no appeal or revision would lie against the modified order. Section 264 is a revision and is shut out with the rest.

options.text: He may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), because an order making no modification to the variations is prejudicial to his interest and the bar applies only to an order in his favour
options.misconception: assumes an order that changes nothing is prejudicial, when all three decisions open to the committee are treated as not prejudicial to the assessee
options.why: All three outcomes are treated as orders not prejudicial to the interest of the assessee — a modification not prejudicial to him, a refusal to modify coupled with waiver and immunity, and a plain disposal with no modification. The bar on appeal does not turn on which of the three he got.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB read with section 245MA(2A) — the three decisions open to the committee, each of them counted as an order not prejudicial to the assessee's interest, no appeal or revision against the modified order, and no reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel or appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) by an eligible assessee under section 144C(1)

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee has heard an eligible assessee whose specified order was a draft order under section 144C(1). It decides to make no modification at all to the variations, but to waive the penalty and grant immunity from prosecution. The Assessing Officer passes his order in conformity and serves it with a notice of demand. The assessee wants to take the variations further.

items.stem: What may the committee grant?

options.text: Neither, since a prosecution launched before the application makes the whole of Rule 44DAC unavailable to him
options.misconception: extends a bar written only for immunity so that it also swallows the waiver of penalty
options.why: The bar is written about immunity alone. Waiver of the penalty imposable and immunity from prosecution are separate reliefs and the committee may grant either or both; only the second is closed by a prosecution already begun.

options.text: Both, provided the prosecution is withdrawn by the income-tax authority before the committee passes its order
options.misconception: invents a cure by withdrawal, when the rule fixes the position by reference to the date the application was received
options.why: The rule fixes the point in time at the date of receipt of the application. What happens to the prosecution afterwards does not reopen an immunity the rule has already closed.

options.text: Both, the prosecution being irrelevant once the committee has resolved the dispute and the demand has been paid
options.misconception: treats resolution and payment as curing everything, and misses the one express bar in the rule
options.why: Resolution and payment are what open the reliefs, not what override the exception. Where the prosecution was initiated before the committee received the application, immunity cannot be granted at all.

options.text: Waiver of the penalty, but not immunity, because prosecution proceedings had been initiated before the date on which it received his application
options.why: The two reliefs are granted on the same conditions — payment of the tax due on the returned income in full where such tax is available, co-operation with the committee, and confirmation that the demand has been paid — and he satisfies all three. But there is one separate bar and it goes only to immunity: no immunity is granted where a prosecution for an offence was already on foot before the date of receipt of the application by the committee. The penalty waiver is unaffected.
keywords: tax due on the returned income
before the date of receipt of the application

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC read with section 245MA(2) — waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution on confirmation of payment of the demand where the tax on the returned income has been paid in full and the assessee has co-operated, and no immunity where prosecution proceedings were initiated before the date of receipt of the application

items.scenario: An application has been resolved and the assessee has paid the demand and confirmed the payment to the Dispute Resolution Committee. He had also paid in full the tax due on the income he had returned, and he answered every notice the committee sent. He asks for waiver of the penalty and immunity from prosecution. The department points out that a prosecution for an offence under the Act was launched against him two months before he applied to the committee.

items.stem: What is the effect on the immunity and the waiver?

options.text: The immunity stands withdrawn, and the provisions of the Act then apply as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted at all
options.why: The rule makes the grant conditional and says exactly what a breach does. An immunity granted to a person stands withdrawn if he fails to comply with any of the conditions subject to which it was granted, and once it goes, the Income-tax Act, 1961 works on him as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted. It is not a prospective withdrawal; the relief is treated as never having existed.
keywords: as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted

options.text: Nothing happens to the immunity, which once granted is final; the breach of the condition can only be visited with a fresh penalty
options.misconception: treats the grant as unconditional, when the rule lets the committee attach conditions and provides for withdrawal on breach
options.why: The committee grants the relief subject to such conditions as it thinks fit, for reasons recorded in writing, and a failure to comply with any of them withdraws the immunity.

options.text: The immunity is withdrawn only for the future, so a prosecution may be launched for anything done after the breach but the earlier period stays protected
options.misconception: makes the withdrawal prospective, when the rule undoes the grant from the beginning
options.why: The words are that the Act applies as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted. There is no protected earlier period left behind.

options.text: The waiver of penalty survives and only the immunity from prosecution falls, the rule speaking of immunity alone
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal as touching only one of the two reliefs, when the rule restores the position as if neither had been granted
options.why: The withdrawal provision ends by saying that the provisions of the Act apply as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted, which names both.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC — waiver or immunity granted subject to conditions for reasons recorded in writing, withdrawn on failure to comply with any of them, with the Act applying as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee granted an assessee immunity from prosecution and waived the penalty, recording its reasons in writing and imposing a condition on him. Eighteen months later he has failed to comply with that condition.

items.stem: What must it do, and what happens next?

options.text: It may terminate the proceedings for reasons recorded in writing and after giving him an opportunity of being heard, and it then intimates the income-tax authority so that the action the Act provides for may be taken
options.why: Concealment of a particular material to the proceedings or the giving of false evidence is one of the four grounds on which the committee may decide to terminate at any stage. Two safeguards run with the power — reasons to be recorded in writing and an opportunity of being heard — and where the proceedings are terminated the committee has to intimate the income-tax authority so that whatever the Act provides for may be done.
keywords: reasons to be recorded in writing

options.text: It may terminate at once and without a hearing, an assessee who has given false evidence having forfeited the right to be heard
options.misconception: drops the opportunity of being heard, which the rule requires before termination on any of the four grounds
options.why: The rule attaches the safeguard to the power itself, without exception for the seriousness of the ground. The committee terminates only once it has recorded its reasons in writing and given the assessee a chance to be heard.

options.text: It must reject the application, since false evidence goes to admission and a rejected application never reaches the merits
options.misconception: confuses rejection at the admission stage with termination, which is what the rule provides for a proceeding already admitted
options.why: Rejection belongs to the screening stage and is decided on the application itself. Once the application has been admitted the committee's power is to terminate the proceedings, and false evidence is one of the four listed grounds for doing so.

options.text: It must pass an order of resolution making no modification, which is the only order it is permitted to pass once an application has been admitted
options.misconception: treats the three decisions on the merits as the committee's only exits, when termination is a separate route out
options.why: The three decisions are what the committee does when it disposes of an admitted application on the merits. Termination is a distinct power exercisable at any stage of the proceedings on one of four grounds, and it ends the proceeding rather than deciding it.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — termination of dispute resolution proceedings where the assessee has concealed a material particular or given false evidence, for reasons recorded in writing and after an opportunity of being heard, with intimation to the income-tax authority

items.scenario: A dispute resolution proceeding is well past the admission stage. The committee finds that the assessee has given false evidence on a point material to the proceedings. It wishes to end the proceeding.

items.stem: In which of the four may the committee terminate the proceedings?

options.text: The first and the fourth only, non-payment of the demand being a matter for recovery rather than for the committee
options.misconception: leaves out the fourth ground, which the rule states in terms
options.why: Failure to pay the demand as required in the notice of demand is itself listed as a ground for termination, and it has to be, because waiver and immunity under Rule 44DAC depend on confirmation that the demand has been paid.

options.text: The first, the third and the fourth — a disagreement with what the committee proposes is not one of the four grounds
options.why: The grounds are a closed list of four: failure to co-operate during the proceedings, failure to respond to or submit information in response to a notice, satisfaction that the assessee has concealed a material particular or given false evidence, and failure to pay the demand as required in the notice of demand. Ignoring notices, not paying the demand and ceasing to attend are the first, fourth and again the first of those. Saying in writing that he disagrees is participation, not a ground.

options.text: All four, since the committee may terminate at any stage if it considers it necessary
options.misconception: reads the opening words as a free-standing discretion, when they are followed by an exhaustive list of grounds
options.why: The power is exercisable at any stage of the proceedings, but only if one of the four listed things has happened. An assessee who argues his case has done none of them.

options.text: The third only, the other three being matters the committee must decide against the assessee on the merits rather than grounds for termination
options.misconception: treats non-cooperation as something to be weighed in the decision instead of a listed ground for ending the proceeding
options.why: Failure to co-operate and failure to respond to a notice are each a listed ground. The rule does not require the committee to construct a decision on the merits out of an assessee's silence.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — the four grounds for terminating a dispute resolution proceeding, being failure to co-operate, failure to respond to or submit information in answer to a notice, concealment of a material particular or false evidence, and failure to pay the demand

items.scenario: Four things happen in four different admitted proceedings. In the first the assessee ignores two notices calling for information. In the second the assessee tells the committee in writing that he disagrees with the modification it proposes and asks it to think again. In the third the assessee does not pay the demand raised by the notice of demand. In the fourth the assessee stops attending altogether and answers nothing.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: No application under section 245C can be made on or after 1 February 2021, the Commission having ceased to operate from that date, and the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 were sent to seven Interim Boards for Settlement constituted by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021
options.why: The Settlement Commission ceased to operate with effect from 1 February 2021 and no application under section 245C for settlement of a case can be made on or after that date. To dispose of the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 the Central Government constituted seven Interim Boards for Settlement by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021.

options.text: Pending applications were transferred to the Dispute Resolution Committees, which took over the Commission's work
options.misconception: treats the Committee as the Commission's successor, when it is a separate forward-looking route with its own narrow limits
options.why: The Dispute Resolution Committee is not the Settlement Commission's successor. It hears a dispute arising from a variation in a specified order within the ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh limits, and the old settlement applications went to the Interim Boards instead.

options.text: The Commission ceased to operate from 1 April 2021, and pending applications lapsed with it
options.misconception: borrows the date on which the Dispute Resolution Committee scheme began and assumes the pending applications died
options.why: 1 April 2021 is when the new scheme of dispute resolution took effect. The Commission ceased on 1 February 2021, and the applications pending on the day before did not lapse — seven Interim Boards were set up precisely so that they could be disposed of.

options.text: Applications may still be made under section 245C, but they are heard by the Interim Boards rather than by the Commission
options.misconception: turns the Interim Boards into a continuing forum, when they exist only to clear a closed set of applications already pending
options.why: The Interim Boards were constituted to dispose of the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 and nothing else. The door to new applications under section 245C shut on 1 February 2021.

citation.ref: Section 245C read with Chapter XIX-AA — the Income-tax Settlement Commission ceasing to operate from 1 February 2021, seven Interim Boards for Settlement constituted by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021 for applications pending as on 31 January 2021, and the Dispute Resolution Committee scheme with effect from 1 April 2021

items.scenario: A client has heard that the Income-tax Settlement Commission still takes applications and wants to make one for a case that has been running for years. He also wants to know what happened to the applications that were pending when the Commission stopped.

items.stem: What is the answer, and why?

options.text: It does not, because a company is not a person the Board may specify for dispute resolution under Chapter XIX-AA at all
options.misconception: rules the company out on its status when what actually rules it out is the size of the variation and of the returned income
options.why: The Chapter operates in the case of such persons or class of persons as the Board may specify, and it does not exclude companies as a class. What defeats this company is the arithmetic — ₹40,00,000 of variations and ₹9 crore of returned income.

options.text: It does, the Dispute Resolution Committee having inherited the Settlement Commission's jurisdiction over any case a taxpayer wishes to settle
options.misconception: reads the Committee as a replacement of the Settlement Commission rather than a differently designed and much narrower route
options.why: Nothing was inherited. The Commission's pending work went to the Interim Boards, and the Committee was created separately, with effect from 1 April 2021, for small and medium taxpayers on a specified order.

options.text: It does, provided the company withdraws any appeal, since the monetary limits apply only to non-corporate assessees
options.misconception: invents a corporate exemption from the two monetary tests, which are written without reference to the kind of assessee
options.why: The ₹10 lakh limit on variations and the ₹50 lakh limit on returned income are conditions on the order and the return, not on the status of the assessee. Withdrawing an appeal is a step after admission and cannot cure a failure of the limits.

options.text: It does not, because the new scheme was formulated to give early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers and reaches only a specified order within the ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh limits, neither of which this company meets
options.why: The purpose is written into the reason the Chapter exists — to prevent tax disputes in future and settle issues at the initial stage, providing early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers. The limits follow from that purpose: the aggregate of variations must not exceed ₹10 lakh and the returned income must not exceed ₹50 lakh. Variations of ₹40,00,000 on a returned income of ₹9 crore fail both.

citation.ref: Chapter XIX-AA with section 245MA and the Explanation defining a specified order — the scheme formulated with effect from 1 April 2021 to give early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers, confined to variations not exceeding ₹10 lakh on a returned income not exceeding ₹50 lakh

items.scenario: A large company with variations of ₹40,00,000 in its assessment order, and a returned income of ₹9 crore, asks whether Chapter XIX-AA gives it the sort of one-stop settlement the Settlement Commission once offered.

items.stem: How are the four classified?

options.text: Tax planning, tax management, tax avoidance and tax evasion, in that order
options.misconception: treats a wrong classification of an asset as lawful planning gone too far, when it is a false particular
options.why: The generator is not at the factory. Describing it as plant fitted there so as to claim a higher rate of depreciation is furnishing of false particulars in an attempt to evade tax, which is the module's own classification of this fact pattern, and not avoidance.

options.text: Tax planning, tax management, tax evasion and tax evasion, in that order
options.why: Depositing in a term deposit to claim a deduction the statute offers is tax planning — full advantage of a relief the Act permits, without violating anything. Keeping a register so that deductions are deposited on time reduces no liability at all and is tax management, which is compliance. Recording a generator at the chairman's farmhouse as factory plant is a misstatement of fact that unjustifiably raises the depreciation from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, and furnishing false particulars to reduce tax is evasion. A credit note recording a commission that moves ₹80,000 to a person who will pay nothing on it is a fictitious transaction, and reducing liability by recording one is evasion too.

options.text: Tax planning, tax planning, tax avoidance and tax avoidance, in that order
options.misconception: folds compliance into planning and then treats two misstatements of fact as avoidance, which is lawful in form
options.why: Tax management is a separate label from tax planning: the register saves no tax and exists to meet an obligation. And avoidance means methods which technically satisfy the requirements of law while circumventing it. Neither the generator entry nor the credit note satisfies the requirements of law even technically; both misstate what happened.

options.text: Tax management, tax management, tax evasion and tax planning, in that order
options.misconception: calls an ordinary deduction claim compliance, and calls a fictitious commission planning because the recipient's rebate is itself lawful
options.why: A section 80C deduction claimed on a real deposit is the textbook example of planning, not management. And the fact that the daughter's own rebate under the default regime is lawful does not make the company's credit note lawful; the transaction it records did not happen.

citation.ref: Section 270A read with the Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee (Wanchoo Committee) distinction between tax evasion and tax avoidance — planning as full advantage of permitted reliefs, tax management as compliance, and false particulars and fictitious transactions as evasion

items.scenario: Four things happened at Kadam Textiles Ltd during previous year 2025-26. Its promoter put ₹1,50,000 into a five-year bank term deposit to claim a deduction under section 80C. The accounts department kept a monthly register of every payment liable to deduction of tax at source so that nothing was deposited late. A generator installed at the chairman's farmhouse was recorded in the fixed asset register as plant in the factory, so that depreciation ran at 15 per cent instead of the 10 per cent that furniture and fittings attract. And a credit note for commission of ₹80,000 was raised in favour of the chairman's daughter, whose total income under the default regime stays within ₹12,00,000 and who therefore pays nothing on it, while the company's income fell by the same amount.

items.stem: How does the module treat these two failures?

options.text: Both are evasion but the penalty is 50 per cent, which is the rate for a case where income has not been correctly returned
options.misconception: applies the under-reporting rate to conduct the Act classifies as misreporting
options.why: Fifty per cent is the rate for under-reporting. Conduct in the list of common forms of evasion is misreporting, and misreporting carries 200 per cent.

options.text: Only the unrecorded receipt is evasion; a failure to report a specified domestic transaction is a reporting default and carries its own separate penalty instead
options.misconception: separates the transfer pricing reporting default from evasion, when the module puts it in the same list as suppression of a receipt
options.why: A separate penalty for a reporting default does not take the failure out of the list. The module names the failure to report a specified domestic transaction under Chapter X as one of the common forms of tax evasion alongside the suppression of a receipt.

options.text: Both are named among the common forms of tax evasion, and both amount to misreporting of income carrying penalty at 200 per cent
options.why: The list of common forms of tax evasion has six entries and these are two of them. One is a receipt that bears on total income and never reaches the books at all. The other is a failure to report an international transaction, a deemed international transaction, or a specified domestic transaction that Chapter X covers. The module says of the whole list that these constitute misreporting of income attracting penalty at 200 per cent under section 270A.

options.text: Both are tax avoidance rather than evasion, since neither involves a false document
options.misconception: requires a forged document before conduct can be evasion, when suppression and non-reporting are themselves listed forms of it
options.why: Evasion is described as a manoeuvre involving deceit, misrepresentation of facts, falsification of accounting calculations or downright fraud, and the list of its common forms begins with misrepresentation or suppression of facts. No document need be forged.

citation.ref: Section 270A read with the module's list of common forms of tax evasion — failure to record a receipt bearing on total income and failure to report an international, deemed international or specified domestic transaction under Chapter X, both constituting misreporting of income at 200 per cent

items.scenario: Two failures come to light in a scrutiny. The company failed to record in its books a receipt that bore on its total income. Separately, it failed to report a specified domestic transaction under Chapter X, which its finance head says is a transfer pricing compliance matter and nothing to do with evasion of tax.

items.stem: Which proposition actually emerges from the module's account of the case law?

options.text: Neither — where a transaction is genuine its form governs and not its substance, and it is only where the transaction is colourable or a mere device that the question becomes one between appearance and truth, at which point the authorities may pierce the corporate veil
options.why: The principles are stated as a pair. A transaction put through in one form the law knows is taxed by that form, and had it gone through in another form equally open to the parties it might not have been, so what governs is the form actually chosen. That rule applies only to genuine transactions; where the transaction is not genuine but colourable or a mere device, the contest is no longer form against substance but appearance and truth, and the authorities may then pierce the corporate veil and look past the legal facade.

options.text: The officer is right — Duke of Westminster survives untouched in India, so no arrangement may ever be looked through
options.misconception: ignores the departure Mc Dowell made from the earlier Indian decisions following Westminster
options.why: The Supreme Court in Mc Dowell expressly disassociated itself from the earlier observations echoing the Westminster principle, listed the evil consequences of avoidance, and held that it is for the court to expose sophisticated legal devices for what they are.

options.text: The partner is right — Mc Dowell established that substance prevails over form in every case, so a genuine transaction may be recharacterised whenever it results in less tax
options.misconception: reads Mc Dowell as abolishing the form rule rather than confining it to genuine transactions
options.why: Mc Dowell held tax planning to be legitimate only while it keeps inside the boundaries the law sets, and that a colourable device can be no part of tax planning. The Gujarat High Court in Minal Rameshchandra read it as directed at artificial and transparent devices and sham practices, and held that where an arrangement cannot be dismissed as an artificial device the subject is taxed by the strict letter of the law.

options.text: The proposition that survives is Kharwar's — that the legal effect of a transaction may be displaced by probing into its substance
options.misconception: keeps the one sentence of Kharwar that Mc Dowell expressly disapproved and drops the one that survives
options.why: Kharwar said the opposite of that. Where a transaction has a legal effect, an enquiry into the substance underneath it cannot displace that effect, though the authority is bound to determine the true legal relation and may unravel a device. It is that sentence which has since been expressly disapproved in Mc Dowell.

citation.ref: Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 154 ITR 148 (SC) read with CIT v. Motor and General Stores (P) Ltd. (1967) 66 ITR 692 (SC), CIT v. B.M. Kharwar (1969) 72 ITR 603 (SC) and CIT v. Smt. Minal Rameshchandra (1987) 61 CTR 80 (Guj) — form governs a genuine transaction, and appearance against truth governs a colourable one

items.scenario: A partner in a firm argues before an Assessing Officer that after Mc Dowell the substance of a transaction always prevails over its form, so the officer may look through any arrangement he dislikes. The officer argues that Mc Dowell changed nothing, and that Duke of Westminster still governs India without qualification.

items.stem: How did the Supreme Court deal with an arrangement of this shape?

options.text: It held that a validly incorporated subsidiary is a separate legal person, so the transfer had to be respected in the absence of direct evidence of motive
options.misconception: treats separate legal personality as conclusive, which is the argument the Court declined to accept
options.why: The Court accepted that nobody had produced direct evidence of the subsidiary having been set up as a device, and decided against the holding company anyway, on the footing that the true state of affairs was there to be found behind the structure.

options.text: It declined to interfere, holding that a dispute about a payment under welfare legislation is not a tax matter and the tax reasoning had no place in it
options.misconception: assumes the reasoning is confined to tax, when the Court applied it to a welfare statute in terms
options.why: The case was about a payment of bonus rather than about tax, and that is the point of citing it. The Court applied the same reasoning it had laid down in Mc Dowell, and said the duty arises where ingenuity is expended to avoid liability to taxation and to welfare legislation alike.

options.text: It held that the arrangement was tax avoidance and applied the General Anti-Avoidance Rules to disregard the subsidiary
options.misconception: reads a 1986 decision as an application of Chapter X-A, which came into force from assessment year 2018-19
options.why: The decision is from 1986 and the General Anti-Avoidance Rules took effect from assessment year 2018-19. What the case supplies is the judicial reasoning that Chapter X-A later codified, not an application of it.

options.text: It held on the facts that the transfer was a device to reduce the gross profits, and that where ingenuity is spent on escaping a liability the court must get behind the smoke screen to find what is truly going on
options.why: This is Associated Rubber Industries. The subsidiary had no asset except the transferred investments and no income except the dividend on them, and the Court held that the purpose of the transfer was to reduce the gross profits of the holding company and so the payment due under the Payment of Bonus Act. The absence of direct evidence did not save it: the Court said that in every case where ingenuity is spent on escaping a liability — to tax or to welfare legislation alike — its duty is to get behind the smoke screen and find what is really there.

citation.ref: Associated Rubber Industries (1986) 157 ITR 77 (SC) read with Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 154 ITR 148 (SC) — a subsidiary holding nothing but transferred investments treated as a device, and the duty of the court to get behind the smoke screen

items.scenario: A holding company forms a wholly owned subsidiary that has no assets of its own except a block of investments transferred to it by the holding company, and no income of its own except the dividend on those investments. The effect is to reduce the holding company's gross profits and with them a liability it owes under welfare legislation. There is no direct evidence that the subsidiary was formed for that purpose.

items.stem: Which of these is a tax benefit for the purpose of section 96?

options.text: All except the treaty-driven refund, tax benefit being defined by reference to amounts payable under the Act alone
options.misconception: drops the two limbs that are written specifically about a tax treaty
options.why: Two of the six limbs are written about a treaty — a reduction, avoidance or deferral that would be payable as a result of a tax treaty, and an increase in a refund as a result of a tax treaty. Chapter X-A was drafted to reach treaty benefits, so leaving them out would empty it.

options.text: Only those arising in the relevant previous year; the deferral and the unused loss arise in a later year and so are outside the definition
options.misconception: confines the definition to the year under examination, when it says the relevant previous year or any other previous year
options.why: The closing words of the definition are in the relevant previous year or any other previous year, which is what lets a deferral into a later year and an unused loss count.

options.text: Only the reduction in total income, the other three producing no reduction in the tax eventually payable
options.misconception: reads a tax benefit as a permanent saving of tax, when the definition covers deferral and an increase in a loss as well
options.why: The definition does not ask whether tax is permanently saved. It names deferral in the same breath as reduction and avoidance, and names an increase in a loss separately, precisely because those two produce no immediate saving.

options.text: All four, section 102(10) covering a deferral, an increase in a loss, an increase in a refund as a result of a tax treaty and a reduction in total income
options.why: The definition has six limbs and these fall within four of them. A reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or other amount payable under the Act; an increase in a refund; the same two again where they arise as a result of a tax treaty; a reduction in total income; and an increase in a loss — in the relevant previous year or in any other previous year. So a pure deferral qualifies with no permanent saving at all, and an unused loss qualifies before it has been used.

citation.ref: Section 102(10) read with section 96 — the six limbs of a tax benefit including deferral, an increase in a refund, treaty-driven reduction or refund, a reduction in total income and an increase in a loss, in the relevant previous year or any other previous year

items.scenario: Four results are put to an Assessing Officer who is considering whether the purpose test in Chapter X-A is met. An arrangement defers tax by three years without reducing the total tax ever paid. An arrangement increases a business loss that has not yet been set off against anything. An arrangement increases a refund because of a tax treaty. An arrangement reduces total income without reducing the rate.

items.stem: Is that argument good?

options.text: Yes — an impermissible avoidance arrangement is an arrangement, so the whole reorganisation must be struck down or none of it
options.misconception: treats the arrangement as indivisible, which is the reading section 95 and Rule 10UA exist to defeat
options.why: Nothing has to be struck down as a whole. A single step may be declared impermissible and the consequences confined to it, leaving the other six steps and their tax treatment alone.

options.text: No, but only if the fourth step is itself a separate agreement; a step within a single agreement is not an arrangement
options.misconception: makes the definition turn on how many documents there are, when it covers a step whether or not the understanding is even enforceable
options.why: An arrangement takes in any step in a transaction, operation, scheme, agreement or understanding, or one part of such a thing, or the whole of it, and it does not matter whether the thing is enforceable. Whether the step sits inside one document or several decides nothing.

options.text: No — section 95 lets Chapter X-A be brought to bear on any step in, or a part of, an arrangement just as on the arrangement itself, and Rule 10UA then confines the tax consequences to that part
options.why: The Chapter was drafted against exactly this argument. Section 95 lets the Chapter's provisions reach any step in, or one part of, an arrangement in the same way they reach the whole of it, and section 102(1) defines an arrangement to include any step in a transaction. Rule 10UA completes it: once a part of an arrangement is held to be an impermissible avoidance arrangement, the tax consequences are worked out by reference to such part only.

options.text: Yes, unless the sixth other steps are also shown to lack commercial substance, since the purpose test applies to the arrangement as a whole
options.misconception: requires the purpose test to be satisfied for the whole arrangement when the section allows it to be applied to a step
options.why: The section applies the Chapter to a step exactly as it applies to an arrangement, and that includes the purpose test. The question is whether the main purpose of that step is a tax benefit, not whether the reorganisation as a whole was commercially motivated.

citation.ref: Sections 95, 102(1) and 102(9) read with Rule 10UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — Chapter X-A applied to any step in or part of an arrangement, with the tax consequences determined with reference to that part only

items.scenario: A commercial reorganisation runs through seven steps. Six of them have obvious business reasons. The fourth step routes a payment through an entity that does nothing else and exists only to change where the receipt is taxed. The assessee argues that Chapter X-A is written about arrangements, that this reorganisation is plainly a genuine commercial arrangement taken as a whole, and that the Chapter therefore cannot touch any part of it.

items.stem: Can the arrangement be deemed to lack commercial substance?

options.text: Yes — it involves round trip financing, which is judged without any regard to whether the funds can be traced, to the time or sequence in which they moved, or to the means by which they moved
options.why: Section 97 deems an arrangement that involves round trip financing to lack commercial substance, and defines round trip financing as any arrangement in which funds are transferred among the parties through a series of transactions with no substantial commercial purpose other than obtaining the tax benefit. It then removes the obvious defence: the limb applies without having any regard to whether the money can be traced back to sums any party moved out or took in, to the time or sequence of those movements, or to the means, manner or mode by which they were made. The subsidiary does nothing else, so the interest may be taxed in Meghna Ltd's hands by disregarding it.

options.text: No — round tripping requires the funds to come back to the person who put them out, and here they cannot be traced to Meghna Ltd at all
options.misconception: reads a tracing requirement into round trip financing, which the section removes in terms
options.why: The definition says the test applies without any regard at all to whether the money involved can be traced back to sums that some party to the arrangement moved out or took in. Untraceability is the ordinary state of affairs in these structures and is why the words were written.

options.text: Only if the tax benefit exceeds ₹3 crore in the year and the subsidiary is a connected person of Tarun Ltd
options.misconception: adds a connected-person requirement that the section does not impose for round trip financing
options.why: The ₹3 crore floor in Rule 10U is real, but nothing in the round trip financing limb requires any party to be a connected person. That requirement does not even attach to an accommodating party, who may be connected or not.

options.text: No — the loan is at a commercial rate of 11 per cent to an unrelated borrower, so the arrangement is at arm's length and no tainted element is present
options.misconception: answers the first tainted element, non-arm's-length dealings, and leaves the third one untouched
options.why: Arm's length pricing answers a different limb. The third tainted element is that the arrangement lacks commercial substance or is deemed to, and an arrangement involving round trip financing is deemed to lack it however commercial the interest rate is.

citation.ref: Section 97(1)(b)(i) with section 97(2) — round trip financing deemed to make an arrangement lack commercial substance, judged without regard to tracing, to the time or sequence of transfers or to the means, manner or mode of transfer

items.scenario: Meghna Ltd, an Indian company, incorporates a subsidiary in a low tax jurisdiction with equity of ₹5 crore. The subsidiary lends ₹5 crore to Tarun Ltd, an unrelated Indian company, at 11 per cent a year, and Tarun Ltd claims the interest as a deduction. The subsidiary has no other activity of any kind. The department cannot trace the money Tarun Ltd pays back to Meghna Ltd.

items.stem: What weight do those three facts carry?

options.text: The payment of taxes under the arrangement is conclusive, since an arrangement on which tax has been paid has by definition produced no tax benefit
options.misconception: reads payment of some tax as proof that no benefit arose, when a benefit is measured against the alternative course
options.why: Tax having been paid under an arrangement is expressly one of the relevant but insufficient factors. A tax benefit is the difference between the liability under the arrangement and the liability under the alternative course available, and paying some tax says nothing about that difference.

options.text: Each is a relevant factor and none is sufficient — section 97(4) names the period of existence, the payment of taxes and the provision of an exit route as relevant but not sufficient
options.why: Section 97(4) names three facts as relevant but not sufficient when the question is whether an arrangement wants commercial substance. First, the period or time over which the arrangement and the operations inside it have lasted. Second, payment of taxes made under it, whether that payment was direct or indirect. Third, the presence of an exit route, which includes a route by which an activity, a business or the operations can be transferred out. All three point the assessee's way and none of them decides the question.

options.text: An arrangement that has existed for more than five years is outside the General Anti-Avoidance Rules, so the first fact is decisive
options.misconception: turns a relevant factor into the five-year safe period that the Board was asked for and refused to give
options.why: The Board was asked to provide a definite timeline of five to ten years of existence during which the rules would not apply, and answered that how long an arrangement has been in existence counts as a relevant factor under section 97(4) and never as a sufficient one.

options.text: None of the three has any bearing, section 97 listing only the deeming limbs and nothing else
options.misconception: overlooks section 97(4), which exists precisely to say what these three facts are worth
options.why: Section 97(4) is part of the section and names all three. They are relevant, and an assessee is entitled to rely on them; what he cannot do is treat any of them as settling the matter.

citation.ref: Section 97(4) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the period of existence, the payment of taxes and an exit route as relevant but not sufficient factors, and the refusal to fix a five to ten year period outside the rules

items.scenario: An assessee resists a finding that his arrangement lacks commercial substance on three grounds. It has been in place for eight years. Tax has been paid under it every year. And it contains an exit route allowing the business to be transferred out.

items.stem: Is that the limit of the consequences?

options.text: No — section 98 illustrates consequences including treating equity as debt, reallocating a receipt or an expenditure among the parties, treating the situs of an asset as being elsewhere, and disregarding a corporate structure altogether
options.why: Whatever consequence fits the circumstances may be settled on, and section 98 gives illustrations that go far beyond a denial. Steps may be disregarded, combined or re-characterised; the arrangement may be treated as if it had never been entered into; an accommodating party may be disregarded or merged with another; connected persons may be deemed one person; accruals, receipts, expenditure, deductions, relief and rebates may be reallocated among the parties; the place of residence of a party or the situs of an asset or transaction may be treated as elsewhere; and any corporate structure may be looked through. It adds expressly that equity may be treated as debt or the reverse.

options.text: Yes as regards recharacterisation, but a receipt may be reallocated between parties only where they are connected persons
options.misconception: attaches a connected-person condition to the reallocation power that the section does not carry
options.why: Reallocation is available among the parties to the arrangement. Treating connected persons as one and the same person is a separate illustration in the same list, not a precondition for the reallocation one.

options.text: Yes — the only consequence the Chapter provides is denial of the tax benefit under the Act or under a tax treaty
options.misconception: stops at the opening words of section 98 and ignores the illustrations that follow them
options.why: Denial of the benefit is where the section starts, not where it ends. It goes on to leave the manner of the consequence to whatever the circumstances make appropriate, and then lists seven kinds of manner.

options.text: No, but a re-characterisation may only reduce a deduction; income of a capital nature can never be treated as revenue
options.misconception: denies one of the three re-characterisations the section states in terms
options.why: The section lets an accrual or a receipt that is capital in nature be treated as revenue, and revenue as capital, alongside treating equity as debt and re-characterising any expenditure, deduction, relief or rebate.

citation.ref: Section 98 with section 98(2) — consequences including disregarding, combining or re-characterising a step, treating the arrangement as never entered into, reallocation among the parties, relocation of residence or situs, looking through a corporate structure, and treating equity as debt or a capital receipt as revenue

items.scenario: An arrangement has been declared an impermissible avoidance arrangement. The assessee accepts that the tax benefit claimed under it must be denied, but says that is the limit of what may be done: the department cannot rewrite the transaction, move anybody's residence or reallocate receipts between the parties.

items.stem: What is the Board's position on that request?

options.text: A corresponding adjustment will not be made in the hands of the other participant, because Chapter X-A is an anti-avoidance provision with deterrent consequences and matching adjustments across taxpayers would blunt the deterrence
options.why: The Board was asked to clarify that where a consequence is applied in the hands of one participant there would be a corresponding adjustment for another, and it declined. Its answer is that adequate procedural safeguards ensure the rules are invoked in a uniform, fair and rational manner, but that once a consequence lands on one participant, a corresponding adjustment for the other will not be made, because tax adjustments carried across different taxpayers could militate against deterrence.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment must be made, since taxing the same receipt twice would be double taxation of one amount
options.misconception: assumes symmetry follows from fairness, which is exactly the request the Board refused
options.why: The clarification is explicit that no corresponding adjustment will be made. The consequence is deliberately asymmetric, and that asymmetry is described as part of the deterrent.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment is made automatically wherever both participants are resident in India, the asymmetry being intended only for cross-border cases
options.misconception: confines the Board's answer to cross-border arrangements, when it is written about participants generally
options.why: The answer is not limited by residence. It speaks of a consequence applied in the hands of one participant and of corresponding adjustments across different taxpayers, without distinguishing domestic arrangements from cross-border ones.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment is available only on an application to the Approving Panel, which may direct it while issuing its directions
options.misconception: invents a route to symmetry through the Approving Panel, which issues directions about the declaration rather than adjustments in another taxpayer's hands
options.why: The Approving Panel issues directions on whether the arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement and for which previous years. Nothing gives it a power to make an adjustment in another participant's assessment, and the Board's answer is that no such adjustment is made at all.

citation.ref: Sections 98 and 99 read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — no corresponding adjustment in the hands of another participant where a consequence is applied to one, corresponding adjustments being treated as militating against deterrence

items.scenario: An arrangement between two Indian companies has been declared impermissible, and a receipt has been reallocated so that it is taxed in the hands of the first company. The second company, which had already offered the same receipt to tax, asks for a corresponding adjustment reducing its own income by the same amount.

items.stem: Which of these is protected by the grandfathering in Rule 10U(1)(d)?

options.text: The original shares, the split shares and the bonus shares, but neither the aircraft lease nor the loan
options.why: The grandfathering covers income arising from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017. The Board has clarified that shares brought into existence by way of split or consolidation of a grandfathered holding, and bonus shares issued in respect of shares acquired before that date in the hands of the same investor, are eligible. It has equally clarified that on accounting principles an investment is an asset held for income by way of dividends, interest or rentals and for capital appreciation, and that lease contracts and loan arrangements are by themselves not investments, so grandfathering is not available for them.

options.text: All four, since each was entered into before 1 April 2017 and the rule protects everything of that vintage
options.misconception: reads the grandfathering as covering anything dated before 1 April 2017, when it is confined to income from the transfer of investments
options.why: The words of the rule are income from transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017. A lease and a loan are not investments, so their date does not help them, and an arrangement of any other kind is expressly still within the Chapter for a benefit obtained on or after that date.

options.text: None, the grandfathering having lapsed because the Chapter applies to any arrangement irrespective of the date on which it was entered into
options.misconception: reads the sentence that keeps old arrangements inside the Chapter as cancelling the investment grandfathering, when it is expressly subject to it
options.why: That sentence begins by excepting the grandfathered investments. It says the provisions apply to any arrangement other than the one specified in that clause, irrespective of the date on which it was entered into, for a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017.

options.text: The original shares alone, the split and the bonus shares having come into existence after 1 April 2017
options.misconception: dates the investment by when the new share certificates appeared rather than by when the underlying investment was made
options.why: The clarification deals with exactly that. Shares brought into existence by split or consolidation, and bonus shares issued on shares acquired before 1 April 2017 in the hands of the same investor, are grandfathered, because the investment behind them was made before the date.

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(d) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — grandfathering of income from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017, extended to splits, consolidations, bonus issues and compulsorily convertible instruments, and denied to lease contracts and loan arrangements

items.scenario: An investor holds four things acquired before 1 April 2017 and disposes of them in previous year 2025-26. Shares of an Indian company bought in January 2016. Shares that came out of a split of that same holding in 2019. Bonus shares issued in 2021 on the January 2016 holding, still in his own hands. And his rights under an aircraft lease and under a loan he advanced, both entered into in 2016.

items.stem: How do the two objections stand?

options.text: Both succeed, the two objections reinforcing each other because a pre-2017 arrangement is tested only against the benefit of the assessee actually assessed
options.misconception: combines both misreadings, and adds a rule about who is assessed that appears nowhere in the exclusion
options.why: Neither objection stands on its own and putting them together does not help. The Chapter reaches an old arrangement for a new benefit, and the floor is an aggregate across the parties for the relevant assessment year.

options.text: The date objection succeeds — an arrangement entered into before 1 April 2017 is outside the Chapter altogether
options.misconception: extends the grandfathering of investments to arrangements, which the rule expressly separates
options.why: Only income from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017 is protected by date. For everything else the rule says the opposite in terms, applying the Chapter irrespective of when the arrangement was entered into so long as the benefit is obtained on or after that date.

options.text: The threshold objection succeeds — the ₹3 crore limit is applied taxpayer by taxpayer, and none of the three crossed it
options.misconception: divides an aggregate limit among the parties, which the rule and the Board both refuse
options.why: The exclusion is written about the tax benefit arising in aggregate to all the parties to the arrangement, and the Board has answered a request to read it per taxpayer by saying the limit cannot be read in respect of a single taxpayer only.

options.text: Both fail — the Chapter applies to an arrangement irrespective of the date it was entered into for a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017, and the ₹3 crore floor is tested on the aggregate benefit to all the parties in the relevant assessment year
options.why: The date objection is answered by the rule itself, which applies the provisions to any arrangement other than a grandfathered investment irrespective of the date on which it was entered into, in respect of a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017. The threshold objection is answered by the words of the exclusion: it applies where the total tax benefit for that assessment year, in aggregate to all the parties, stays at ₹3 crore or below. The Board has confirmed that the limit cannot be read in respect of a single taxpayer only. Here the aggregate is ₹4 crore.
keywords: in aggregate to all the parties

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(a) and the proviso to Rule 10U(1) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the ₹3 crore floor measured on the aggregate tax benefit to all parties in the relevant assessment year, and the Chapter applying irrespective of the date the arrangement was entered into for a benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017

items.scenario: An arrangement was entered into in 2014. It produces a tax benefit for the first time in previous year 2025-26, and the benefit that year comes to ₹4 crore spread over three parties to the arrangement, no single one of whom gets more than ₹2 crore. The assessee says the arrangement predates the Chapter and that in any case no party crossed ₹3 crore.

items.stem: Which of the five are virtual digital assets?

options.text: The crypto token, the non-fungible token and the gift voucher, a voucher being a digital representation of value exchanged for consideration
options.misconception: keeps the voucher inside the first limb and misses that it has been notified out of the definition
options.why: A gift card or a voucher is a record that will buy goods, a service or a price cut, and it is one of the three things expressly excluded from the definition by notification.

options.text: All five, the definition covering anything of value that can be transferred, stored or traded electronically
options.misconception: applies the width of the first limb without the exclusions the Central Government has notified under the same section
options.why: The definition is wide, and the section then lets the Central Government exclude digital assets by notification. Three classes have been excluded — vouchers and gift cards, reward and loyalty points, and subscriptions — precisely because the first limb would otherwise have swallowed them.

options.text: The crypto token only, a non-fungible token being outside the definition unless it is issued by a regulated exchange
options.misconception: adds a regulated-issuer condition to the non-fungible token limb, which turns instead on notification and on what the token carries
options.why: A non-fungible token is a limb of the definition in its own right, and the Central Government has notified it as the class of token that answers the description of a virtual digital asset. Who issued it is not the test.

options.text: The crypto token and the non-fungible token only
options.why: A crypto-asset that relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions is a virtual digital asset in its own limb of section 2(47A), and a notified non-fungible token is another. The other three were taken out by notification: gift cards and vouchers usable to obtain goods or services or a discount on them; mileage points, reward points and loyalty cards handed over with no money paid for them under a scheme of awards, rewards, benefits, loyalty, incentives, rebates or promotions, redeemable for nothing but goods, services or a price cut; and a subscription to a website, platform or application.

citation.ref: Section 2(47A) read with CBDT Notification No. 74/2022 dated 30 June 2022 — the crypto-asset and non-fungible token limbs of the definition, and the exclusion of gift cards and vouchers, mileage, reward and loyalty points, and subscriptions to a website, platform or application

items.scenario: A client lists five things he holds and asks which of them the Act treats as a virtual digital asset. A crypto token recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger. A gift voucher from a department store, usable only against goods there. Airline mileage points earned under a loyalty programme and redeemable only for flights. A twelve-month subscription to a streaming platform. And a non-fungible token that carries no claim to anything physical.

items.stem: How does the notification on non-fungible tokens treat the two?

options.text: The first is a non-fungible token and so a virtual digital asset; the second is not, because its transfer results in the transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset and that transfer of ownership is legally enforceable
options.why: The Central Government notified the non-fungible token as the class of token that qualifies as a virtual digital asset, with one carve-out: a non-fungible token is left out where its transfer carries ownership of an underlying tangible asset with it, and that transfer of ownership is legally enforceable. The artwork token carries no such title and stays inside; the warehouse token carries an enforceable title and falls out, so its transfer is dealt with under the ordinary provisions instead.

options.text: Both are non-fungible tokens and so virtual digital assets, the carve-out applying only to tokens representing immovable property registered under the Registration Act
options.misconception: narrows the carve-out to registered immovable property, when it is written about any underlying tangible asset
options.why: The carve-out speaks of an underlying tangible asset and of a legally enforceable transfer of ownership in it. It is not confined to any particular class of property or to any register.

options.text: The second is a virtual digital asset and the first is not, since only a token backed by something real has inherent value
options.misconception: inverts the carve-out by assuming backing by a real asset is what brings a token in
options.why: Backing by a real asset is what takes the token out, not what brings it in, provided the transfer of ownership in that asset is legally enforceable. A token with nothing behind it stays inside the definition.

options.text: Neither is a virtual digital asset, a non-fungible token being covered only if the Central Government notifies each token individually
options.misconception: reads the notification as requiring token-by-token specification rather than a class notification with a carve-out
options.why: The notification specifies a class — a token which qualifies to be a virtual digital asset — and then carves out the enforceable-title case. No individual token has to be named.

citation.ref: Section 2(47A)(b) read with CBDT Notification No. 75/2022 dated 30 June 2022 — a token qualifying as a virtual digital asset specified as a non-fungible token, excluding one whose transfer results in a legally enforceable transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset

items.scenario: Two tokens are sold in the same week. The first is a token representing a piece of digital artwork; nothing physical passes and no title to any physical thing is created. The second is a token whose transfer transfers ownership of a warehouse, and the transfer of that ownership is legally enforceable against the seller.

items.stem: What is the tax on the income from the virtual digital asset?

options.text: ₹1,91,880 — being 31.2 per cent of ₹6,15,000, after allowing the ₹35,000 of exchange and brokerage charges as a cost of transfer
options.misconception: allows the cost of transfer, when the section allows the cost of acquisition and nothing else
options.why: The words are that no deduction is allowed in respect of any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition. Brokerage and exchange charges are expenditure on the transfer and are outside that single exception, which is what makes this head harsher than capital gains.

options.text: ₹2,02,800 — being 30 per cent of ₹6,50,000 plus cess, the ₹35,000 of charges not being deductible and the business loss not being available against this income
options.why: Section 115BBH shuts out every deduction the Act might otherwise give for expenditure or for an allowance, except the cost of acquisition, so the income is ₹8,10,000 less ₹1,60,000, which is ₹6,50,000, and the ₹35,000 of charges is simply lost. No set off of any loss is allowed against that income, so the business loss cannot touch it and is carried forward instead. Tax at 30 per cent on ₹6,50,000 is ₹1,95,000, and cess at 4 per cent brings it to ₹2,02,800.
keywords: No set off of any loss

options.text: ₹1,95,000 — 30 per cent of ₹6,50,000, no cess being chargeable on a special rate under section 115BBH
options.misconception: exempts a special-rate income from health and education cess, which applies to income-tax however computed
options.why: The computation of the income is right and the cess is not optional. The module's own worked illustrations under this section apply the rate as 31.2 per cent, being 30 per cent with cess at 4 per cent on it.

options.text: ₹1,40,400 — being 31.2 per cent of ₹4,50,000, after setting off the business loss of ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: sets a business loss against income taxed under section 115BBH, which the section forbids
options.why: The section says no set off of any loss shall be allowed against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset. The business loss of ₹2,00,000 has to be carried forward for set off against business income of a later year instead.

citation.ref: Section 115BBH — income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset taxed at 30 per cent, with no deduction for any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition and no set off of any loss against that income

items.scenario: Mr Pathak, aged 34, transferred a virtual digital asset during previous year 2025-26 for ₹8,10,000. It had cost him ₹1,60,000 and he paid ₹35,000 of exchange and brokerage charges on the sale. He also has a business loss of ₹2,00,000 for the year, which he wants set off. Take health and education cess at 4 per cent and ignore surcharge and any other income.

items.stem: What is taxable, and what happens to the loss?

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, and the ₹40,000 loss may be set off against her other income of the year because only set off against virtual digital asset income is barred
options.misconception: reads the bar as one-directional, when the section blocks the loss against income computed under any provision of the Act
options.why: There are two separate prohibitions. One stops other losses coming into this income. The other stops this loss going out — no head of income anywhere in the Act may take it.

options.text: ₹50,000 is taxable, losses and gains on virtual digital assets being netted against each other before the rate is applied
options.misconception: assumes an intra-head netting, when the section forbids the set off of any loss against this income including a loss on another such asset
options.why: There is no netting. The section allows no set off of any loss against this income and does not make an exception for a loss on another virtual digital asset, which is why each transfer is computed on its own.

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, but the ₹40,000 loss may be carried forward for eight assessment years for set off against gains on virtual digital assets
options.misconception: gets the current year right and then borrows the capital loss carry-forward rule, which this section expressly denies
options.why: The section says the loss shall not be allowed to be carried forward to succeeding assessment years. There is no eight-year window and no future gain it can be used against.

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, and the ₹40,000 loss is neither set off against the gain nor carried forward to any later year
options.why: The bar is written twice over and it catches this. No set off of any loss is allowed against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and a loss from the transfer of a virtual digital asset is not allowed to be set off against anything the Act computes as income, nor allowed to be carried forward to a succeeding assessment year. So the gain of ₹90,000 is taxed in full at 30 per cent and the ₹40,000 dies in the year it arose.
keywords: No set off of any loss
not allowed to be set off

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(2) — no set off of any loss against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and a loss from such a transfer neither set off against income computed under any provision of the Act nor carried forward to a succeeding assessment year

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26 Ms Devika made a gain of ₹90,000 on the transfer of one virtual digital asset and a loss of ₹40,000 on the transfer of another. She proposes to offer ₹50,000 to tax, and to carry the loss forward if the department disagrees.

items.stem: Who has to deduct tax under section 194S, and how much?

options.text: Mr Harsh need not deduct, his consideration of ₹48,000 being within the ₹50,000 threshold for a specified person; Corniche Ltd must deduct ₹120, being 1 per cent of ₹12,000, the threshold for any other person being ₹10,000
options.why: The section has two thresholds. For a specified person — an individual or Hindu undivided family with no business or professional income under that head at all, or whose turnover did not exceed ₹1 crore in business or ₹50 lakh in a profession in the preceding financial year — the aggregate consideration must exceed ₹50,000 in the financial year before any deduction is due, and Mr Harsh is inside it. For anybody else the figure is ₹10,000, which Corniche Ltd has crossed, so it deducts at 1 per cent.

options.text: Both must deduct at 1 per cent, the single threshold under section 194S being ₹10,000 for everybody
options.misconception: applies one threshold to both, missing the higher figure the section gives a specified person
options.why: The section sets out a table with two rows. A specified person has a threshold of ₹50,000 and every other person a threshold of ₹10,000, and Mr Harsh is inside the higher one.

options.text: Neither must deduct, both being below the ₹50,000 threshold that applies to a transfer of a virtual digital asset
options.misconception: applies the specified person's threshold to a company, which gets the lower one
options.why: The ₹50,000 figure is available only to a specified person, which is an individual or a Hindu undivided family answering the turnover or no-business-income test. A company is in the other row, where the threshold is ₹10,000.

options.text: Mr Harsh must deduct ₹480 but cannot, having no tax deduction account number; Corniche Ltd must deduct ₹120
options.misconception: puts Mr Harsh over a threshold he is under, and treats the absence of a deduction account number as an obstacle when the section disapplies that requirement for him
options.why: Mr Harsh is below his ₹50,000 threshold, so nothing is due from him at all. And if he had been over it, the want of a deduction account number would not have stopped him: section 203A does not apply to a specified person under this section.

citation.ref: Section 194S with the table of thresholds and the disapplication of section 203A — deduction at 1 per cent, ₹50,000 for a specified person being an individual or Hindu undivided family with turnover within ₹1 crore in business or ₹50 lakh in a profession or with no business income, and ₹10,000 for any other person

items.scenario: Two buyers pay for virtual digital assets during financial year 2025-26. Mr Harsh is salaried, has no income under the head profits and gains of business or profession, and pays ₹48,000 in the year for an asset bought from a resident. Corniche Ltd, a company, pays ₹12,000 in the year for an asset bought from a resident.

items.stem: What is the answer to the three questions?

options.text: Deduction is on ₹5,00,000 excluding the goods and services tax but including the ₹6,000 of platform charges, which are part of what the buyer paid
options.misconception: excludes the tax but keeps the deductor's own service charge, when the clarification excludes both
options.why: The clarification is that the withholding is on the net consideration after excluding the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor for rendering the service. Both come out.

options.text: Deduction is on the consideration net of the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor, section 194Q does not apply once tax has been deducted under section 194S, and the payment gateway need not deduct where the person required to deduct has done so
options.why: The Board's guidelines answer all three. The tax required to be withheld under section 194S is on the net consideration after excluding the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor for rendering the service. Once tax is deducted under section 194S, tax is not required to be deducted under section 194Q, and the Board declined to decide whether a virtual digital asset is goods at all. And a payment gateway is not required to deduct on a transaction where the person required to make the deduction has already done so, and may take an undertaking to that effect.

options.text: Deduction is on the gross ₹5,96,000, section 194Q applies in addition because a virtual digital asset is goods, and the payment gateway must also deduct
options.misconception: takes the gross figure and then stacks three deductions on one payment, which is the outcome the guidelines were issued to prevent
options.why: Every limb is answered the other way. The deduction is on the net consideration, section 194Q is displaced once section 194S has been applied, and the payment gateway is relieved where the payer has deducted.

options.text: Deduction is on the net consideration, but where tax is deductible under section 194-O as well the deduction is made under section 194-O and not under section 194S
options.misconception: reverses the priority between the two sections, which the Act settles in favour of section 194S
options.why: The section says that where both section 194-O and section 194S bite on the same payment, it is section 194S that governs the deduction and section 194-O that gives way.

citation.ref: Section 194S with CBDT Circular No. 13/2022 dated 22 June 2022 and Circular No. 14/2022 dated 28 June 2022 — deduction on the consideration net of goods and services tax and the deductor's charges, section 194S in preference to section 194-O, section 194Q displaced once section 194S has been applied, and no deduction by a payment gateway where the payer has deducted

items.scenario: A company buys a virtual digital asset from a resident dealer for ₹5,00,000 plus goods and services tax of ₹90,000, and the platform charges the buyer ₹6,000 for the service of executing the trade. The payment is routed through a payment gateway. The company's tax head asks whether tax is to be deducted on ₹5,96,000, whether section 194Q applies because the asset might be goods, and whether the payment gateway must deduct as well.
