items.stem: Which form does each report go in, and what opinion does the tax auditor give in each?

options.text: Form 3CA for both, Form 3CB being used only where the accounting year differs from the financial year
options.misconception: turns the one situation the module singles out for Form 3CB into the only situation it covers
options.why: A company whose accounting year differs from the financial year does have to prepare and audit accounts for the financial year and report in Form 3CB, but that is a particular case, not the rule. Form 3CB is used wherever no other law requires an audit.

options.text: Form 3CB for the company and Form 3CA for the firm, the more demanding form being reserved for the corporate assessee
options.misconception: reverses the two forms by assuming the choice turns on the status of the assessee rather than on whether another law already requires an audit
options.why: The choice turns on one fact only — whether the accounts are already required to be audited under another law. It is a company that usually is, which puts it in Form 3CA, the form where the tax auditor gives the fewer opinions because somebody else has already given the other one.

options.text: Form 3CD for both, Forms 3CA and 3CB being alternative annexures to it
options.misconception: inverts the relationship, when Form 3CD is the statement of particulars annexed to whichever report is used
options.why: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars required under section 44AB and is annexed to the audit report, which is in Form 3CA or Form 3CB. The report is not annexed to the particulars.

options.text: Form 3CA for the company, where the tax auditor gives no true and fair opinion and only says whether the Form 3CD particulars are true and correct; Form 3CB for the firm, where he gives the true and fair opinion on the balance sheet and the profit and loss account as well
options.why: Form 3CA is used where the accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law, such as the Companies Act, 2013 or the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. There the tax auditor is not required to give his opinion on whether the accounts give a true and fair view; he annexes the audited accounts and the statutory auditor's report and opines only on the particulars in Form 3CD. Form 3CB is for a person no other law obliges to have his accounts audited, and there he opines that the balance sheet shows the state of affairs as at the last date of the accounting year and the profit and loss account the profit or loss for that year, as well as on the Form 3CD particulars.

citation.ref: Rule 6G with Circular No. 561 dated 22 May 1990 — Form 3CA where the accounts are audited under another law and the tax auditor gives no true and fair opinion, Form 3CB where they are not and he does, and Form 3CD annexed to whichever report is used

items.scenario: Two clients need a tax audit report for previous year 2025-26. One is a private company whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act, 2013. The other is a partnership firm whose accounts no other law requires to be audited.

items.stem: What does Rule 6G(3) permit here?

options.text: A revised report may be issued by the same auditor at any time up to the completion of the assessment, the assessment year limit applying only to the original report
options.misconception: stretches the deadline for a revision to the completion of the assessment
options.why: The rule fixes the outer date for the revised report itself: it must go in by the close of the assessment year the report relates to.

options.text: No revision is possible once the report has been uploaded; the payment can only be dealt with in the return
options.misconception: treats a signed report as final, when the rule provides expressly for this one situation
options.why: This is the situation Rule 6G(3) was written for. A payment made after the report which changes a section 40 or section 43B disallowance is the ground of revision the rule names.

options.text: A revised report may be issued by any chartered accountant, and there is no time limit because the rule places no limit on the number of revisions
options.misconception: reads the absence of a limit on the number of revisions as the absence of a time limit and of a rule about who may revise
options.why: There is no restriction on how many times a report may be revised, and there are restrictions on who and when. The same tax auditor does the revision, and the revised report goes in before the end of the relevant assessment year.

options.text: A revised report may be issued, because a payment has been made after the report which necessitates recalculation of the disallowance under section 43B, but it has to be issued by the same tax auditor and furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year
options.why: Rule 6G(3) allows a revision where there is a payment by the person after the report was furnished which necessitates recalculation of the disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, and requires the revised report to be furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year. Revision of a tax audit report has to be done by the same tax auditor who did the original audit and not by another. The revised report must carry a reference to the earlier report, be signed on the current date, and be issued under a fresh unique document identification number.
keywords: before the end of the relevant assessment year

citation.ref: Rule 6G(3) — a revised tax audit report where a payment after the report necessitates recalculation of a disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year, by the same tax auditor, with a reference to the earlier report and a fresh unique document identification number

items.scenario: A tax audit report for previous year 2025-26 was signed and uploaded in September 2026. In November 2026, before filing the return, the assessee paid a sum covered by section 43B whose payment changes the disallowance the report had computed. He asks a second chartered accountant to issue a revised report, saying the original auditor is unavailable.

items.stem: What penalty may the Assessing Officer direct under section 271B?

options.text: Nothing, because section 273B keeps a penalty under section 271B out wherever the assessee is otherwise compliant
options.misconception: reads section 273B as a general exemption rather than a defence that has to be made out on reasonable cause
options.why: Section 273B says no penalty shall be imposed if the person proves that there was reasonable cause for the failure. It is a defence to be established, and on these facts there is no explanation at all.

options.text: ₹8,50,000, being the fixed sum of ₹1,50,000 in addition to one half of one per cent of turnover
options.misconception: adds the two figures, when the section offers them as alternatives and takes the lesser
options.why: The two figures are alternatives, not cumulative. The Assessing Officer directs payment of a sum equal to the percentage or to ₹1,50,000, whichever is less.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, being lower than one half of one per cent of the ₹14 crore turnover
options.why: The penalty is one half of one per cent of the total sales, turnover or gross receipts in business, or ₹1,50,000, WHICHEVER IS LESS. Half a per cent of ₹14 crore is ₹7,00,000, which is the larger of the two, so the penalty is the flat ₹1,50,000. The percentage only ever bites where turnover is below ₹3 crore.
keywords: one half of one per cent

options.text: ₹7,00,000, being one half of one per cent of the turnover of ₹14 crore
options.misconception: takes the percentage as the penalty, when the section directs the lower of the percentage and the fixed sum
options.why: The section ends with the words whichever is less. Where the percentage works out above ₹1,50,000 it is the fixed sum that applies, so a large business never pays more than ₹1,50,000 under this section.

citation.ref: Section 271B read with section 273B — penalty of one half of one per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts or ₹1,50,000, whichever is less, and no penalty where reasonable cause for the failure is proved

items.scenario: Sarvesh Traders had turnover of ₹14 crore for financial year 2025-26 and did not get its accounts audited under section 44AB at all. It has no explanation to offer. Ignore any other default.

items.stem: What follows for the company and for the chartered accountant?

options.text: The company is not in default at all, since each business is tested separately and neither crossed the ₹10 crore limit on its own
options.misconception: tests the threshold business by business, when the aggregate sales, turnover and gross receipts of all businesses are taken
options.why: The aggregate sales, turnover or gross receipts of all businesses carried on by the assessee are taken in deciding whether the prescribed limit has been exceeded. On ₹18 crore it plainly has been.

options.text: The company is in default and the penalty is computed on the whole ₹18 crore, the report furnished for part of the turnover being of no effect
options.misconception: ignores that a report was in fact furnished for the larger business when fixing the base of the penalty
options.why: The example in the module is exactly this. The Assessing Officer wanted to charge on ₹18 crore and the answer is that, the report having been furnished for ₹15 crore, the penalty is invoked only on the ₹3 crore left uncovered.

options.text: The company is in default because the turnovers of all its businesses are aggregated to ₹18 crore, but the section 271B penalty is computed on the ₹3 crore for which no report was furnished; the chartered accountant is liable to ₹10,000 under section 271J for that certificate
options.why: Where a person runs more than one business the results of every one of them are clubbed, so the threshold is tested on ₹18 crore and section 44AB was attracted for the whole. The module's own example then limits the penalty base: a report having already gone in for the ₹15 crore business, the penalty is invoked only on the turnover of ₹3 crore and not on ₹18 crore. Section 271J is a separate charge on the accountant, of ₹10,000 for each report or certificate in which incorrect information is furnished.

options.text: The company is in default, but section 271J has no application to the chartered accountant because it is confined to a registered valuer
options.misconception: confines section 271J to one of the several persons it names
options.why: Section 271J reaches an accountant, a merchant banker and a registered valuer alike, and charges ₹10,000 for each report or certificate in which incorrect information is furnished under the Act or the Rules.

citation.ref: Section 271B read with section 44AB and section 271J — the turnover of all businesses aggregated for the threshold, the penalty computed only on the turnover for which no report was furnished, and ₹10,000 for each report or certificate carrying incorrect information

items.scenario: Nandini Ltd runs two businesses, one with turnover of ₹15 crore and the other with turnover of ₹3 crore, all receipts and payments being through banking channels. It prepared financial statements only for the first, got them audited and furnished the report in time, believing the second business too small to matter. Its chartered accountant separately furnished a certificate under the Act carrying information he had not verified and which turned out to be incorrect.

items.stem: Which form does each need?

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29B for the company, Form 3CEA for the slump sale and Form 15CB for the remittance
options.why: Section 12A(1)(b) requires a trust or institution to have its accounts audited and to furnish Form 10B or Form 10BB before the specified date to claim exemption under section 11 or section 12. A company to which section 115JB applies furnishes Form 29B certifying the correctness of the computation of book profit. A slump sale under section 50B needs Form 3CEA certifying the net worth of the undertaking or division. And a remittance to a non-resident chargeable under the Act needs a certificate in Form 15CB where the remittance, or the aggregate of such remittances, exceeds ₹5 lakh during the financial year, which ₹7,00,000 does.

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29C for the company, Form 10CCB for the slump sale and Form 15CB for the remittance
options.misconception: swaps the minimum alternate tax form for the alternate minimum tax one and uses the profit-linked deduction form for a slump sale
options.why: Form 29C is for a person to whom alternate minimum tax under section 115JC applies, not a company under section 115JB, which uses Form 29B. Form 10CCB is the audit report for a deduction under sections 80-IA to 80-IE, prescribed by Rule 18BBB, and has nothing to do with a slump sale.

options.text: Form 3CD for all four, being the statement of particulars required under the Act
options.misconception: treats one form as covering every report, when each provision prescribes its own
options.why: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars annexed to a tax audit report under section 44AB. Each of the other provisions prescribes a form of its own.

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29B for the company, Form 3CEA for the slump sale, and no form for the remittance, which is below the ₹10 lakh limit for a Form 15CB
options.misconception: raises the Form 15CB limit to ₹10 lakh, when it is ₹5 lakh in the financial year
options.why: The certificate is required where the remittance, or the aggregate of such remittances, is more than ₹5 lakh in the financial year and the sums remitted are chargeable to tax under the Act. A remittance of ₹7,00,000 is over that.

citation.ref: Sections 12A(1)(b), 115JB, 115JC, 50B and 80-IA(7) with Rules 18BBB and 37BB — Form 10B or 10BB for a trust, Form 29B for minimum alternate tax, Form 29C for alternate minimum tax, Form 3CEA for the net worth on a slump sale, Form 10CCB for a deduction under sections 80-IA to 80-IE, and Form 15CB where a remittance or the aggregate of remittances exceeds ₹5 lakh in the financial year

items.scenario: A practice is preparing four filings. A trust claiming exemption under section 11. A company to which minimum alternate tax under section 115JB applies. An assessee who has sold an undertaking by way of a slump sale under section 50B. And a client remitting ₹7,00,000 to a non-resident, the remittance being chargeable under the Act.

items.stem: How does each fare under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 — Part I of its Second Schedule?

options.text: Both are guilty, an incorrect report being professional misconduct whatever the accountant does afterwards
options.misconception: makes the misconduct strict, when what the clauses ask about is diligence and the sufficiency of the information obtained
options.why: The clauses are about conduct, not outcome. The second accountant's report was wrong and he was held not guilty, because on discovering the error he withdrew it and informed the assessee immediately, which is what due diligence required of him at that point.

options.text: The first is guilty under clauses (7) and (8), and the second is not guilty, having withdrawn his report as soon as he knew and told the assessee at once
options.why: Clause (7) covers a failure to exercise due diligence or gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties and clause (8) a failure to obtain sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion. Given the nature of the business the onus was on the first to extend his verification to cash payments, mere reliance on a management certificate is not acceptable, and certifying that there were no such instances against ₹30 crore of them attracts both clauses. The second acted the moment he knew — he withdrew the report in Form 10CCB, informed the assessee, who filed a revised return withdrawing the claim — and was held not guilty under clause (7).

options.text: The first is guilty under clause (7) only, clause (8) being confined to a statutory audit under the Companies Act, 2013
options.misconception: confines clause (8) to company audits, when it applies to the expression of any opinion by a chartered accountant in practice
options.why: Clause (8) applies to a chartered accountant in practice who fails to obtain sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion, and it was applied alongside clause (7) in the tax audit case.

options.text: Neither is guilty, since the first carried out test checks and held a certificate from the management, which is the evidence an auditor is entitled to rely on
options.misconception: treats test checks and a management certificate as sufficient regardless of what the business is and what the sums involved are
options.why: The contention that test checks did not reveal the violations was held not tenable. Considering the nature of the business the onus was on the chartered accountant to verify the position, such payments can be identified independently of bank transactions, and mere reliance on a certificate issued by the management is not acceptable.

citation.ref: Clauses (7) and (8) in Part I of the Second Schedule, Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, read with section 40A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 18BBB with Form 10CCB — want of due diligence and failure to obtain sufficient information, and withdrawal of a report on discovery of the error with immediate communication to the assessee

items.scenario: Two chartered accountants are before the Disciplinary Committee. The first certified in Form 3CD that there were no payments in breach of section 40A(3) by a jewellery business, when such payments in fact ran to ₹30 crore; his defence is that his test checks did not reveal them and that he relied on a certificate from the management. The second issued Form 10CCB for a deduction under section 80-IA, later discovered that the ten year period had already expired, withdrew his report at once and told the assessee, who filed a revised return giving up the claim.

items.stem: Which of the four are agricultural income?

options.text: The seedlings and the sub-tenant's rent only
options.why: Explanation 3 to section 2(1A) makes a nursery's receipts from saplings or seedlings agricultural income even where nobody performed any basic operation on the land at all, so the ₹75,000 qualifies. Rent from agricultural land in India is agricultural income and ownership is not one of the conditions, so rent received by an original tenant from a sub-tenant qualifies too. The house rent fails on Explanation 2, which takes out income derived from a building used for any purpose other than agriculture, including letting for residential purposes. And poultry farming is one of the activities the module says the term agriculture cannot be stretched to.

options.text: The sub-tenant's rent only, income from a nursery being business income unless the basic operations were carried out on the land
options.misconception: applies the pre-Explanation case law and misses the deeming provision that settles it
options.why: That was the position under Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy, and Explanation 3 was inserted to settle it the other way. Income from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery is deemed agricultural whether or not the basic operations were carried out on land.

options.text: The house rent, the seedlings and the sub-tenant's rent
options.misconception: treats rent from a building standing on agricultural land as agricultural income whatever the building is used for
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 2(1A) says that income derived from any building from its use for any purpose other than agriculture, including letting for residential purposes or for a business or profession, is not agricultural income. Houses occupied by industrial workers as homes are that use exactly.

options.text: The seedlings only, rent being agricultural income only in the hands of the owner of the land
options.misconception: reads ownership of the land into the first limb, which asks only that the rent be derived from land in India used for agriculture
options.why: Three conditions have to hold — rent or revenue derived from land, land situated in India, and land used for agricultural purposes — and ownership is not among them. Rent received by an original tenant from a sub-tenant is agricultural income.

citation.ref: Section 2(1A) with Explanations 2 and 3 read with section 10(1) — rent from land in India used for agriculture without any requirement of ownership, a building used for a non-agricultural purpose taken out by Explanation 2, nursery saplings and seedlings deemed agricultural by Explanation 3, and poultry farming outside the term agriculture

items.scenario: Four receipts for assessment year 2026-27. Rent of ₹60,000 from tenants living in houses built on land used for agriculture, the tenants being workers at a nearby factory who occupy them as homes. ₹75,000 from the sale of seedlings raised in a nursery without carrying out all the basic operations on land. ₹2,40,000 of rent received by an original tenant of agricultural land in India from his sub-tenant. And ₹4,00,000 from a poultry farm run on the same holding.

items.stem: How are the three treated?

options.text: Only the potted plants are agricultural income, Explanation 3 covering anything grown in a container
options.misconception: stretches the nursery deeming provision to plants that were never part of a nursery operation
options.why: Explanation 3 is about saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery. It does not turn every plant raised in a pot into agricultural produce; the module keeps the pot-grown case on the other side of the line.

options.text: The store house income is agricultural, the Sri Lankan orchard income is fully taxable, and the potted plants grown directly in pots do not give agricultural income
options.why: Income from a farm building is agricultural where the building is on or in the immediate vicinity of the land and the cultivator requires it as a dwelling house or store house by reason of his connection with the land, and both conditions hold. The land has to be situated in India, so income from agricultural land in a foreign country is taxable in full. And on Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy the basic operations must be performed on the land before income can be agricultural, so income derived from the sale of plants grown directly in pots is not agricultural income.

options.text: All three are agricultural income, the source in each case being the growing of a crop
options.misconception: ignores the requirement that the land be in India and the basic operations rule for plants never grown on land
options.why: Two of the three fail. Land in a foreign country takes the income entirely outside the exemption, and plants raised directly in pots never involve the basic operations on land that Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy requires.

options.text: The store house income and the Sri Lankan orchard income are agricultural, and only the potted plants are taxable, since exemption follows the nature of the activity and not the place
options.misconception: drops the requirement that the land be situated in India from the definition
options.why: The definition names the place expressly. Rent or revenue must be derived from land situated in India and used for agricultural purposes, and if the agricultural land is situated in a foreign country the entire income is taxable.

citation.ref: Section 2(1A) read with CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy (1957) 32 ITR 466 (SC) — the farm building conditions of immediate vicinity and connection with the land, the requirement that the land be situated in India, and the basic operations test for plants grown directly in pots

items.scenario: A grower keeps a store house on the edge of the field where his crop is cleaned and bagged, and he needs it as a store house because of his connection with the land. In the same year he also earns ₹9,00,000 from an orchard he owns in Sri Lanka, and he sells potted ornamental plants grown directly in pots on a terrace, with no operations of any kind carried out on land.

items.stem: What are his business income and his agricultural income?

options.text: Business income ₹6,40,000 and agricultural income ₹9,60,000, applying the 40 and 60 per cent split
options.misconception: uses the tea and roasted-coffee percentages for rubber
options.why: Forty per cent business and 60 per cent agricultural is Rule 8 for tea, and Rule 7B for coffee that is also roasted and ground. Rubber under Rule 7A is 35 and 65.

options.text: Business income ₹5,60,000 and agricultural income ₹10,40,000, being 35 per cent and 65 per cent of the ₹16,00,000 of profit on sale
options.why: Rule 7A applies to income derived from the sale of centrifuged latex manufactured from field latex obtained from rubber plants grown by the seller in India, and it splits the PROFIT, not the sale proceeds. The profit is ₹52,00,000 less ₹22,00,000 of growing cost less ₹14,00,000 of manufacturing cost, which is ₹16,00,000. Thirty-five per cent of that, ₹5,60,000, is business income and the balance 65 per cent, ₹10,40,000, is agricultural income and exempt.

options.text: Business income ₹18,20,000 and agricultural income ₹33,80,000, being 35 per cent and 65 per cent of the ₹52,00,000 of sale proceeds
options.misconception: applies the percentages to the sale proceeds rather than to the profit on sale
options.why: The rule speaks of profits on sale. Applying the split to turnover would tax him on business income of ₹18,20,000 when the whole enterprise made ₹16,00,000.

options.text: Business income ₹10,40,000 and agricultural income ₹5,60,000, being 65 per cent and 35 per cent of the profit
options.misconception: reverses the two percentages, giving the taxable share the larger figure
options.why: Under Rule 7A it is 35 per cent that is taxable as business income and 65 per cent that is agricultural and exempt. The exempt share is the larger one, which is the point of the rule.

citation.ref: Rule 7A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — 35 per cent of the profit on sale of centrifuged latex manufactured from field latex obtained from rubber plants grown by the seller in India taxable as business income, and the balance 65 per cent agricultural income

items.scenario: Mr Nilekani grows rubber plants in India and manufactures centrifuged latex from the field latex obtained from them. The latex is sold for ₹52,00,000. Growing the rubber plants cost him ₹22,00,000 and manufacturing the latex cost him ₹14,00,000.

items.stem: What is the business income of each?

options.text: ₹8,00,000, ₹5,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, roasting and grinding being a further agricultural process that increases the exempt share
options.misconception: swaps the two coffee percentages by assuming more processing makes more of the profit agricultural
options.why: More manufacturing makes more of the profit business income, not less. Coffee grown and cured is 25 per cent business; coffee also roasted and ground is 40 per cent business, because the extra processing is a manufacturing activity.

options.text: ₹7,00,000, ₹7,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, coffee being 35 per cent business income however it is processed
options.misconception: uses the rubber percentage for coffee and collapses the two coffee cases into one
options.why: Thirty-five per cent is Rule 7A for rubber. Coffee has two figures of its own — 25 per cent where it is grown and cured, and 40 per cent where it is also roasted and ground.

options.text: ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, being 25 per cent, 40 per cent and 40 per cent of the profit
options.why: Rule 7B gives 25 per cent as business income for coffee grown and cured by the seller in India, leaving 75 per cent agricultural, and 40 per cent for coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground by the seller in India with or without chicory or other flavouring ingredients, leaving 60 per cent agricultural. Rule 8 gives 40 per cent for tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India, leaving 60 per cent agricultural. Applied to ₹20,00,000 those are ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹8,00,000.

options.text: ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹12,00,000 respectively, tea being 60 per cent business income
options.misconception: inverts the tea split, which gives 40 per cent to business and 60 per cent to agriculture
options.why: Rule 8 taxes 40 per cent of the profit on sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India as business income and leaves the balance 60 per cent as agricultural income.

citation.ref: Rules 7B and 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — 25 per cent of the profit taxable as business income on coffee grown and cured by the seller in India, 40 per cent on coffee also roasted and ground with or without chicory, and 40 per cent on tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India

items.scenario: Three growers in India each made a profit of ₹20,00,000 on sale in previous year 2025-26. The first grew and cured coffee. The second grew, cured, roasted and ground coffee, mixing chicory into it. The third grew tea leaves and manufactured tea from them.

items.stem: Is stopping the analysis at section 9B correct?

options.text: Yes — once section 9B taxes the land, section 45(4) does not apply again to the same reconstitution
options.misconception: treats the two sections as alternatives rather than cumulative charges
options.why: The sections tax different components of the same event: 9B taxes the asset transfer, 45(4) taxes the excess over the capital account. Both can apply to a single reconstitution without double-taxing the same rupee.
keywords: 45(4) taxes the excess over the capital account
Both can apply to a single reconstitution

options.text: No — but the liability falls on partner A personally, not on the firm
options.misconception: shifts the charge to the retiring partner
options.why: Both section 9B and section 45(4) tax the entity — the firm, AOP or BOI — not the partner receiving the assets. The partner's own capital gains, if any, arise separately on disposal of what was received.
keywords: Both section 9B and section 45(4) tax the entity
not the partner receiving the assets

options.text: No — section 45(4) must also be tested, taxing any excess of money plus the fair market value of assets received by A over A's capital account balance, as the firm's capital gains
options.why: The two sections operate in sequence on the same event: 9B taxes the deemed transfer of the capital asset at fair market value; 45(4) separately catches any excess consideration — in cash or assets — over the partner's capital account, taxable as capital gains for the firm. Skipping 45(4) misses this second charge.
keywords: operate in sequence on the same event

options.text: No — but section 45(4) only applies when the firm dissolves entirely, not on a partner's retirement
options.misconception: narrows reconstitution to dissolution only
options.why: Reconstitution covers a change in the constitution of the firm — including a partner's retirement, admission, or change in profit-sharing ratio — not only a full dissolution.
keywords: Reconstitution covers a change in the constitution of the firm

citation.ref: Sections 9B and 45(4)

items.scenario: A partnership firm has three partners. On reconstitution, partner A retires and receives a plot of land — a capital asset that had never appeared on the firm's books — plus a cash payment. The firm's accountant reports the land's fair market value as the firm's income under section 9B and stops there, treating the cash payment as a settlement outside the Act.

items.stem: Is the "no capital gains ever" claim correct?

options.text: No — section 47 only shields transfers between individuals and their HUF, not between companies
options.misconception: confuses the HUF-partition clause of section 47 with the subsidiary-holding company clause
options.why: Section 47 lists several independent transactions; the HUF partition clause and the wholly-owned subsidiary clause are separate limbs, and this transfer squarely fits its own limb.
keywords: the HUF partition clause and the wholly-owned subsidiary clause

options.text: Yes — section 47 permanently exempts all intra-group transfers between an Indian company and its subsidiary, in either direction, without conditions
options.misconception: drops the wholly-owned and continuing-holding conditions
options.why: The exemption needs the parent to hold the entire share capital of the subsidiary, and needs that holding to continue — it is not a blanket exemption for any group transfer.
keywords: needs the parent to hold the entire share capital
not a blanket exemption for any group transfer

options.text: No — the transfer is exempt only if the subsidiary is a foreign company
options.misconception: inverts the actual condition, which requires an Indian holding company
options.why: The clause requires the holding company to be an Indian company; a foreign parent does not qualify under this limb of section 47.
keywords: requires the holding company to be an Indian company
a foreign parent does not qualify

options.text: No — section 47 only defers the gain; if the parent later transfers the asset otherwise than within a similar wholly-owned structure, or ceases to hold the entire share capital, the exemption can be withdrawn under section 47A
options.why: Section 47 keeps the transfer outside section 45's charge at the time it happens, but section 47A claws the exemption back if the parent-subsidiary shareholding condition breaks or the asset leaves the group within the specified period — the tax is deferred, not cancelled.
keywords: the tax is deferred, not cancelled

citation.ref: Section 47

items.scenario: A wholly-owned subsidiary transfers a capital asset to its holding company, a 100 per cent Indian parent, for no separate consideration, as part of an internal restructuring. The subsidiary's tax team argues no capital gains tax applies to this transfer at all, ever.

items.stem: Can he claim the exemption despite the gain being short-term?

options.text: No — section 54B, like section 54, applies only to long-term capital gains
options.misconception: imports the long-term-only condition from section 54 into section 54B
options.why: Several capital gains exemptions apply only to long-term gains, but 54B is a deliberate exception — its use condition, not a holding-period condition, does the gatekeeping.
keywords: its use condition, not a holding-period condition

options.text: No — the new land must be purchased before the sale, not after
options.misconception: reverses the reinvestment window
options.why: The window runs from the date of transfer — reinvestment within two years afterward qualifies; the section does not require a purchase in advance of the sale.
keywords: The window runs from the date of transfer
does not require a purchase in advance of the sale

options.text: Yes, but only up to fifty lakh rupees of reinvestment
options.misconception: imports the section 54EC monetary cap into section 54B
options.why: Section 54B carries no such ceiling; the entire capital gain can be exempted if the new agricultural land's cost covers it. The fifty lakh cap belongs to the bonds under section 54EC.
keywords: fifty lakh cap belongs to the bonds under section 54EC

options.text: Yes — section 54B exempts both short-term and long-term gains on qualifying agricultural land; the two-year test attaches to agricultural use before the transfer, not to how long the land itself was held
options.why: Section 54B is unusual among the capital gains exemptions in reaching short-term gains too. What it insists on is that the land was used for agriculture by the assessee or a parent in the two years before transfer — a condition met here regardless of how briefly he owned the land.
keywords: used for agriculture by the assessee or a parent

citation.ref: Section 54B

items.scenario: An individual sells agricultural land that he personally cultivated for the three years before the sale, earning a short-term capital gain because he had held the land itself for only fourteen months. He buys another agricultural plot within a year of the sale and claims exemption under section 54B.

items.stem: Can the company, not being an individual or HUF, claim exemption under section 54D?

options.text: No — only individuals and HUFs can claim capital gains exemptions on compulsory acquisition
options.misconception: generalises the individual/HUF restriction from other sections to all compulsory-acquisition relief
options.why: That restriction belongs to specific sections such as 54 and 54B. Section 54D was drafted for industrial undertakings precisely because companies, not just individuals, run them.
keywords: That restriction belongs to specific sections such as 54 and 54B

options.text: Yes — section 54D is open to any assessee, including a company, unlike sections 54 and 54B which are restricted to individuals or HUFs
options.why: Section 54D's own words name no restriction on the class of assessee. It answers a different problem — compulsory loss of an industrial undertaking's premises — and is available to whichever assessee, individual or company, runs that undertaking.
keywords: name no restriction on the class of assessee
available to whichever assessee, individual or company

options.text: No — the three-year reinvestment window has already expired since the company built the shed after two years, which falls outside the window
options.misconception: misreads a reinvestment made within the window as falling outside it
options.why: Building the replacement within two years of receiving compensation is comfortably inside the three-year window the section allows; the exemption is not lost.
keywords: within two years of receiving compensation
inside the three-year window the section allows

options.text: Yes, but only if the new asset is also compulsorily acquired land
options.misconception: invents a mirror-image acquisition condition for the replacement asset
options.why: The section requires the new land or building to be for shifting or re-establishing the undertaking; it does not require the replacement itself to come from a compulsory acquisition.
keywords: for shifting or re-establishing the undertaking
does not require the replacement itself to come from a compulsory acquisition

citation.ref: Section 54D

items.scenario: A private limited company runs a factory on land that the state government compulsorily acquires for a highway. The company had used this land for its factory for the preceding four years. Compensation is received in March, and the company builds a replacement factory shed within two years of receiving it.

items.stem: Can the company still claim the section 80-IA deduction?

options.text: No — section 80AC requires the specific deductions it names to be claimed in a return filed by the section 139(1) due date; a belated return under 139(4), however timely otherwise, does not qualify
options.why: Section 80AC's condition is not merely that a return exists before assessment — it names the 139(1) due date specifically. A belated return filed under 139(4) fails this condition even though it is otherwise a valid return.
keywords: belated return filed under 139(4) fails this condition

options.text: Yes — any return filed before the assessment is completed satisfies Chapter VI-A's requirements
options.misconception: substitutes a general before-assessment test for section 80AC's specific due-date test
options.why: That general idea describes ordinary computation, not the stricter gate section 80AC places in front of the named profit-linked deductions.
keywords: not the stricter gate section 80AC places in front

options.text: No — because Chapter VI-A deductions are never available to companies
options.misconception: invents a blanket bar on companies claiming Chapter VI-A deductions
options.why: Nothing in Chapter VI-A excludes companies as a class; several deductions, including profit-linked ones under sections 80-IA and similar, are squarely aimed at companies running eligible undertakings.
keywords: Nothing in Chapter VI-A excludes companies as a class

options.text: Yes, because Chapter VI-A deductions can never exceed gross total income and are otherwise unconditional
options.misconception: confuses the ceiling on the amount of deduction with the separate timing condition on claiming it
options.why: The gross-total-income ceiling limits how much can be deducted; it says nothing about when the return must be filed, which is a distinct condition under section 80AC.
keywords: gross-total-income ceiling limits how much can be deducted
says nothing about when the return must be filed

citation.ref: Section 80AC read with Chapter VI-A (Sections 80C to 80U)

items.scenario: A company eligible for a deduction under section 80-IA misses the due date under section 139(1) but files its return two months later, within the period allowed for a belated return under section 139(4), still before the assessment is completed.

items.stem: Is the disallowance under section 40A(2) sustainable?

options.text: No — but only because the brother is not a "relative" as the section defines it
options.misconception: misreads the definition of relative, which does include a sibling of a person with substantial interest
options.why: The disallowance fails for want of evidence of excess, not because the relationship falls outside the definition — a sibling is squarely within it.
keywords: fails for want of evidence of excess
a sibling is squarely within it

options.text: No — the section disallows only the excess over fair market value or legitimate business need, and the relationship alone, without a finding that the amount is unreasonable, cannot support disallowing the whole payment
options.why: Section 40A(2) is not a bar on related-party dealing; it is a check on overpayment. The Assessing Officer must show the amount paid is excessive against a comparable benchmark — here, the company's own dealings with unrelated consultants at the same rate undercut any such finding.
keywords: not a bar on related-party dealing; it is a check on overpayment
show the amount paid is excessive against a comparable benchmark

options.text: Yes, since section 40A(2) applies automatically whenever a company deals with a director's family member
options.misconception: skips the substantial-interest condition the section actually requires
options.why: The section targets persons having a substantial interest in the business, and their relatives — a director's family member qualifies only if that condition is independently met, and even then, only the excess is disallowed.
keywords: persons having a substantial interest in the business, and their relatives

options.text: Yes — payments to a relative of a person with substantial interest are disallowed in full, regardless of reasonableness
options.misconception: treats section 40A(2) as an absolute bar rather than a reasonableness test
options.why: The section only ever disallows the excess portion; a payment shown to be at arm's length, as here, survives it entirely.
keywords: only ever disallows the excess portion
at arm's length, as here, survives it entirely

citation.ref: Section 40A(2)

items.scenario: A company pays consultancy fees to a firm in which the company's managing director's brother is a partner. The fee matches what the company pays unrelated consultants for comparable work. The Assessing Officer disallows the entire fee, citing only the related-party relationship as the reason.

items.stem: Does the voucher-splitting protect the deduction?

options.text: No — but because cash payments to suppliers are disallowed in full regardless of amount
options.misconception: drops the threshold entirely, as if any cash payment triggers disallowance
options.why: The section only bites once the daily aggregate to one person crosses the prescribed limit; cash payments below it are deductible in the ordinary way.
keywords: daily aggregate to one person crosses the prescribed limit
cash payments below it are deductible

options.text: No — section 40A(3) tests the aggregate of payments to one person in a day, not each voucher separately; splitting one day's payment across vouchers does not take it outside the section
options.why: The section looks at total cash paid to a single person on a single day. Two ₹9,000 payments to the same supplier on the same day add up to ₹18,000, which is what gets tested — the paperwork split changes nothing.
keywords: total cash paid to a single person on a single day

options.text: Yes — the section applies voucher by voucher, so each payment under the limit escapes disallowance
options.misconception: reads the limit as applying per voucher rather than per day per payee
options.why: That reading would defeat the section's purpose by inviting exactly this kind of splitting, which is why the aggregation is by payee and by day, not by voucher.
keywords: aggregation is by payee and by day, not by voucher

options.text: Yes, provided the trader can prove the supplier's identity and the genuineness of the purchase
options.misconception: imports a genuineness defence the section does not recognise
options.why: Genuineness and the payee's identity are irrelevant to section 40A(3) — the disallowance turns solely on the mode and aggregate amount of payment, not on whether the transaction was real.
keywords: payee's identity are irrelevant to section 40A(3)
turns solely on the mode and aggregate amount of payment

citation.ref: Section 40A(3) and (3A)

items.scenario: A trader pays a supplier ₹18,000 in cash in a single day for goods purchased, splitting it as two separate cash payments of ₹9,000 each recorded in two different vouchers to keep each voucher under the disallowance limit. He claims the full deduction, arguing no single voucher crossed the threshold.

items.stem: On which of these can additional depreciation be claimed, and at what rate for the year?

options.text: Only the new plant and machinery qualifies, and even that draws half the normal additional depreciation rate because it was used for less than 180 days
options.why: Additional depreciation is for new plant and machinery used in manufacturing or power generation — the trucks fail as road transport vehicles and the used machinery fails as second-hand. What survives, the new plant, is still caught by the general half-rate rule for assets used under 180 days in the year of acquisition.
keywords: trucks fail as road transport vehicles and the used machinery fails as second-hand
half-rate rule for assets used under 180 days

options.text: None of the three qualifies, because additional depreciation is available only in the year following installation, not the year of acquisition itself
options.misconception: invents a one-year lag before additional depreciation can be claimed
options.why: Additional depreciation is claimed in the very year the new plant and machinery is acquired and put to use, subject only to the half-rate rule for short usage — no such lag exists.
keywords: claimed in the very year the new plant and machinery is acquired

options.text: Only the new plant and machinery qualifies, at the full rate, because the 180-day rule applies only to normal depreciation and not to additional depreciation
options.misconception: exempts additional depreciation from the 180-day restriction that in fact applies to it as well
options.why: The half-rate-for-short-use rule under section 32 governs additional depreciation exactly as it governs normal depreciation; nothing in the section carves additional depreciation out of it.
keywords: governs additional depreciation exactly as it governs normal depreciation
nothing in the section carves additional depreciation out of it

options.text: All three qualify at the full additional depreciation rate, since all were bought new to the company's use
options.misconception: ignores both the asset-class exclusions and the 180-day rule
options.why: Road transport vehicles and second-hand plant are excluded by name from additional depreciation, and even the one qualifying asset is capped at half-rate for the year because of the short usage period.
keywords: excluded by name from additional depreciation
capped at half-rate for the year

citation.ref: Section 32(1) and (1)(iia)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company buys new plant and machinery in December and puts it to use the same month, well within 180 days of the year's end. In the same month it also buys a fleet of new delivery trucks and a batch of used machinery from another factory. It claims additional depreciation on all three purchases.

items.stem: What is the consequence of discontinuing the business and selling the assets?

options.text: The set-off loss already claimed becomes taxable as Y's income in the year the conditions are violated — section 72A reverses the relief rather than merely disallowing future set-off
options.why: Section 72A conditions the relief on the amalgamated company continuing the business and holding the fixed assets for the specified period. Breaking that condition does not just stop future benefit — it claws back what was already set off, taxing it in the year of breach.
keywords: continuing the business and holding the fixed assets for the specified period
claws back what was already set off

options.text: The consequence falls on Company X's erstwhile shareholders, who must individually offer the loss to tax
options.misconception: shifts the reversal to the wrong taxpayer
options.why: The taxable consequence lands on the amalgamated company, Y, which claimed and benefited from the set-off — not on X's former shareholders, who have no assessment role here.
keywords: lands on the amalgamated company, Y

options.text: Y simply loses the right to carry forward any remaining unabsorbed loss from that year onward, with no effect on what was already set off in earlier years
options.misconception: understates the consequence as prospective only
options.why: The section's consequence for breach is a clawback of what was already allowed, taxing it as income in the year of failure — not merely a stop to future set-off.
keywords: clawback of what was already allowed
not merely a stop to future set-off

options.text: Nothing changes — once the loss has passed to Y and been set off, the relief is final regardless of what Y does afterward with the business or assets
options.misconception: treats the section 72A relief as unconditional once granted
options.why: The relief is conditional throughout the specified holding period, not just at the moment of amalgamation; the continuity conditions must hold afterward too.
keywords: conditional throughout the specified holding period
continuity conditions must hold afterward too

citation.ref: Section 72A

items.scenario: Company X, running a hotel business, amalgamates into Company Y. Y takes over the carried-forward business loss of X and sets it off in full against its own profits. Three years later, Y sells off most of the fixed assets it acquired from X and discontinues the hotel business, without meeting the specified holding conditions.

items.stem: Is the company's reasoning to skip the section 92E report correct?

options.text: Yes — the report is only needed where the pricing understates the Indian company's profit
options.misconception: reads section 92E as reporting only unfavourable outcomes
options.why: The section requires the report for the transaction as such, regardless of whether the arm's length analysis favours or disfavours the Indian taxpayer.
keywords: requires the report for the transaction as such
regardless of whether the arm's length analysis favours

options.text: No — section 92E requires the report whenever an international transaction exists, whatever the pricing outcome; the report is a filing obligation triggered by the transaction, not a confession of profit shifting
options.why: The duty to obtain and furnish the accountant's report attaches to the existence of an international transaction with an associated enterprise. Being at arm's length is the correct outcome the report itself is meant to demonstrate — it does not excuse filing it.
keywords: existence of an international transaction with an associated enterprise
it does not excuse filing it

options.text: No, but the obligation only arises if the transaction value exceeds a specified aggregate threshold in the year
options.misconception: imports a domestic-transaction-style threshold into the international transaction reporting duty
options.why: Unlike the specified domestic transaction limb, which does carry an aggregate threshold, the international transaction reporting duty under section 92E is not conditioned on crossing a value threshold.
keywords: specified domestic transaction limb, which does carry an aggregate threshold
not conditioned on crossing a value threshold

options.text: Yes — reports under section 92E are needed only for specified domestic transactions, not international ones with a foreign subsidiary
options.misconception: inverts which category needs the report by dropping international transactions
options.why: Section 92E squarely covers international transactions with associated enterprises — a sale to a wholly-owned foreign subsidiary is the paradigm case, not an exception.
keywords: sale to a wholly-owned foreign subsidiary is the paradigm case

citation.ref: Section 92E

items.scenario: An Indian company sells goods to its wholly-owned foreign subsidiary at a price it can demonstrate is exactly at arm's length, supported by a benchmarking study. It decides no accountant's report under section 92E is needed, because the pricing is already correct and there is no profit shifting to report.

items.stem: Is deducting tax on the entire sum the correct approach?

options.text: No — but only because fees for technical services are exempt from section 195 entirely
options.misconception: invents a blanket exemption for fees for technical services
options.why: Fees for technical services paid to a non-resident are a classic case that section 195 does reach; the error here is deducting on the non-chargeable goods component, not on the services fee.
keywords: Fees for technical services paid to a non-resident
the error here is deducting on the non-chargeable goods component

options.text: No — section 195 reaches only the portion of the sum that is chargeable to tax in India; the company should have applied under section 195(2) to have the Assessing Officer determine the taxable proportion, rather than withholding on the whole payment
options.why: The trigger for section 195 is chargeability, not mere payment to a non-resident. Where a composite sum mixes chargeable and non-chargeable components, the payer's remedy is to seek the Assessing Officer's determination of the taxable slice under section 195(2), not to deduct on everything by default.
keywords: trigger for section 195 is chargeability, not mere payment
determination of the taxable slice under section 195(2)

options.text: Yes, and the vendor's only recourse is to claim a refund after filing a return in India
options.misconception: skips the section 195(2) and 197 routes available before the deduction happens
options.why: Both the payer and the payee have upfront mechanisms — the payer under section 195(2), the payee under section 197 — to fix the deduction at the right level before money changes hands, rather than over-deducting and sorting it out only through a later refund.
keywords: the payer under section 195(2), the payee under section 197

options.text: Yes — any sum paid to a non-resident is chargeable to tax in India and must suffer TDS under section 195 in full
options.misconception: equates "paid to a non-resident" with "chargeable to tax," which section 195 does not
options.why: Chargeability depends on where income accrues or is deemed to accrue; goods supplied from outside India need not be chargeable at all, so treating every rupee paid to a non-resident as taxable overstates the section's reach.
keywords: Chargeability depends on where income accrues or is deemed to accrue
goods supplied from outside India need not be chargeable

citation.ref: Section 195 (with Sections 195(2) and 197)

items.scenario: An Indian company pays a lump sum to a non-resident vendor for a mix of goods supplied from outside India (not chargeable to tax in India) and technical services rendered (chargeable as fees for technical services). The company deducts tax under section 195 on the entire lump sum, reasoning that any payment to a non-resident must suffer TDS in full.

items.stem: Can the department appeal the Tribunal's factual finding to the High Court in the ordinary course?

options.text: Yes, provided the department first files a cross-objection before the Tribunal itself
options.misconception: confuses the cross-objection procedure, which operates within a pending Tribunal appeal, with the separate right of appeal to the High Court
options.why: A cross-objection lets a respondent raise its own grievance inside an appeal already filed by the other side at the Tribunal stage; it has no bearing on whether a subsequent High Court appeal is confined to legal questions.
keywords: cross-objection lets a respondent raise its own grievance
no bearing on whether a subsequent High Court appeal

options.text: Yes — either party can appeal any part of the Tribunal's order to the High Court as of right, on facts or law
options.misconception: treats the High Court appeal as a general second appeal on facts
options.why: Section 260A confines the High Court's jurisdiction to substantial questions of law; an ordinary factual disagreement, without more, does not qualify.
keywords: confines the High Court's jurisdiction to substantial questions of law
factual disagreement, without more, does not qualify

options.text: No — because only the assessee, never the department, may appeal a Tribunal order to the High Court
options.misconception: invents a one-sided right of appeal
options.why: Section 260A is available to either the assessee or the department; the bar here is the nature of the question raised (fact versus law), not which party is appealing.
keywords: available to either the assessee or the department
the nature of the question raised (fact versus law)

options.text: No — appeal to the High Court under section 260A lies only on a substantial question of law; the Tribunal's finding of fact, being the end of the fact-finding chain, is not reopened there merely because the department disagrees with it
options.why: The statutory scheme makes the Tribunal the last authority on facts. A section 260A appeal exists to test whether the Tribunal went wrong in law — including, in limited cases, whether a finding was perverse for want of any evidence — not to re-litigate which view of the facts was correct.
keywords: makes the Tribunal the last authority on facts
not to re-litigate which view of the facts was correct

citation.ref: Sections 253 and 260A

items.scenario: An assessee loses before the Commissioner (Appeals) partly on a factual finding — whether a particular receipt was capital or revenue — and partly on a point of law. He appeals to the Tribunal, which reverses the factual finding in his favour but upholds the legal point against him. The department wants to appeal the Tribunal's factual reversal to the High Court, treating it like any other appeal.

items.stem: Is the specified domestic transaction machinery attracted for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Yes — the aggregate of ₹22 crore exceeds the ₹20 crore threshold, so both the inter-unit transfers and the payments to directors and their relatives must be benchmarked at arm's length price
options.misconception: still counts section 40A(2)(b) payments as specified domestic transactions after their omission from section 92BA
options.why: This is the pre-2017 position. Adding the ₹8 crore is exactly what produces the false ₹22 crore aggregate and the false conclusion. Related-party payments left the transfer pricing net when clause (i) was omitted; they never re-enter the section 92BA aggregate.
keywords: left the transfer pricing net when clause (i) was omitted

options.text: No — payments covered by section 40A(2)(b) ceased to be specified domestic transactions when clause (i) of section 92BA was omitted with effect from 1 April 2017, so only the ₹14 crore of inter-unit power transfers counts, and that is below the ₹20 crore aggregate threshold
options.why: Only transactions still listed in section 92BA go into the aggregate. The ₹8 crore paid to persons covered by section 40A(2)(b) is not one of them any more, so the aggregate is ₹14 crore, not ₹22 crore. Fourteen crore does not exceed twenty crore, so no specified domestic transaction arises and no report or arm's length benchmarking is required. The ₹8 crore is still open to a reasonableness challenge, but under section 40A(2) alone.
keywords: Only transactions still listed in section 92BA go into the aggregate
Fourteen crore does not exceed twenty crore

options.text: Yes — the threshold is ₹5 crore, which the ₹14 crore of inter-unit transfers crosses on its own
options.misconception: uses the pre-A.Y. 2016-17 ₹5 crore threshold instead of the current ₹20 crore
options.why: The threshold was raised from five crore rupees to twenty crore rupees with effect from assessment year 2016-17. On the correct figure, ₹14 crore falls short and nothing is attracted.
keywords: raised from five crore rupees to twenty crore rupees

options.text: Yes — once an assessee claims a deduction under section 80-IA, its inter-unit transfers are specified domestic transactions regardless of any monetary threshold
options.misconception: drops the ₹20 crore aggregate threshold in section 92BA altogether
options.why: The section 80-IA claim decides which transactions are of the right kind; the ₹20 crore aggregate decides whether the machinery switches on at all. Both must be satisfied, and here the second is not.
keywords: ₹20 crore aggregate decides whether the machinery switches on
Both must be satisfied, and here the second is not

citation.ref: Section 92BA (clause (i) omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2017) read with Section 80-IA(8) and (10)

items.scenario: Alpha Ltd claims a deduction under section 80-IA for its captive power unit. During previous year 2025-26 the power unit transferred electricity to Alpha's other manufacturing units at an internal price, the transfers aggregating ₹14 crore. In the same year Alpha paid ₹8 crore as consultancy and rent to its directors and their relatives, all persons covered by section 40A(2)(b). Alpha's accountant adds the two, arrives at ₹22 crore, and concludes that the transfer pricing machinery for specified domestic transactions is attracted.

items.stem: How much of the ₹10 crore can carry the section 10AA deduction?

options.text: The whole ₹10 crore — an arm's length adjustment cannot be made at all on a unit whose income is already exempt, because there is no revenue effect to protect
options.misconception: assumes transfer pricing does not apply to a tax-holiday unit
options.why: A tax-holiday unit is the case transfer pricing most needs to reach, because profits shifted into it escape tax. That is why the machinery applies and why the proviso then denies the deduction on what the adjustment adds.
keywords: the proviso then denies the deduction on what the adjustment adds

options.text: Only ₹8 crore — the proviso to section 92C(4) denies any deduction under section 10AA or Chapter VI-A on income enhanced by an arm's length price adjustment, so the ₹2 crore adjustment is taxed in full
options.why: The proviso exists precisely for a tax-holiday unit. If the deduction rode on the enhanced figure, understating the transfer price would cost nothing and the adjustment would be toothless. The returned ₹8 crore keeps its deduction; the ₹2 crore added by the Transfer Pricing Officer is taxable income with no shelter over it.
keywords: The returned ₹8 crore keeps its deduction
₹2 crore added by the Transfer Pricing Officer is taxable income with no shelter

options.text: The whole ₹10 crore — the adjustment raises the unit's profits, and section 10AA exempts the profits of the unit as computed after every adjustment
options.misconception: treats income enhanced by a transfer pricing adjustment as eligible profits of the unit
options.why: Section 10AA computes the deduction on the unit's profits, but the proviso to section 92C(4) sits above that and strips the enhancement out of the eligible base. Beta gets its deduction on ₹8 crore and no more.
keywords: strips the enhancement out of the eligible base
deduction on ₹8 crore and no more

options.text: Nothing — once a transfer pricing adjustment is made, the section 10AA claim is forfeited for the year in its entirety and all ₹10 crore is taxed
options.misconception: overstates the proviso as forfeiting the whole claim rather than only the enhancement
options.why: The proviso reaches only the amount of the enhancement. The deduction on the ₹8 crore originally returned is untouched; nothing in section 92C(4) cancels a claim that was properly made.
keywords: reaches only the amount of the enhancement
nothing in section 92C(4) cancels a claim that was properly made

citation.ref: Section 92CA read with the proviso to Section 92C(4)

items.scenario: Beta Ltd runs a unit in a special economic zone and returned profits of ₹8 crore from that unit for previous year 2025-26, on which it claimed a hundred per cent deduction under section 10AA. On a reference under section 92CA, the Transfer Pricing Officer determines the arm's length price of Beta's exports to its associated enterprise and makes an upward adjustment of ₹2 crore. Beta now shows unit profits of ₹10 crore and claims the section 10AA deduction on the whole ₹10 crore.

items.stem: What rollback is available to Gamma, and can it choose the years?

options.text: Rollback is available for five preceding previous years — 2020-21 to 2024-25 — matching the five-year span the agreement itself covers going forward
options.misconception: confuses the four-year rollback span with the five-year forward validity of the agreement
options.why: The two numbers are different by design: the agreement may cover up to five consecutive previous years going forward, while the rollback reaches back at most four. Previous year 2020-21 is outside the rollback window.
keywords: the rollback reaches back at most four
Previous year 2020-21 is outside the rollback window

options.text: Rollback is available for up to four previous years preceding the first year of the agreement — previous years 2021-22 to 2024-25 — and Gamma must apply for all four years in which the transaction was undertaken, not a chosen two
options.why: The agreement's first year is 2025-26, so the four preceding years are 2024-25, 2023-24, 2022-23 and 2021-22. Rule 10MA requires the rollback application to cover every rollback year in which the transaction was undertaken; cherry-picking the favourable years is expressly shut out, which is the point of the rule.
keywords: the four preceding years are 2024-25, 2023-24, 2022-23 and 2021-22
cover every rollback year in which the transaction was undertaken

options.text: No rollback is available; an advance pricing agreement binds only prospectively, from the first previous year it covers
options.misconception: describes the position before the rollback provisions were introduced
options.why: Rollback was added to section 92CC precisely so that an agreed price could settle the past as well as the future, sparing both sides litigation over identical transactions in earlier years.
keywords: settle the past as well as the future

options.text: Rollback is available for four preceding previous years, and Gamma may confine its application to the two years in which the agreed price is favourable to it
options.misconception: reads the rollback as optional year by year rather than all-or-nothing
options.why: The four-year span is right, but the choice is not. The applicant either applies for all the rollback years in which the transaction was undertaken or does not apply at all.
keywords: The four-year span is right, but the choice is not
or does not apply at all

citation.ref: Sections 92CC and 92CD read with Rules 10MA and 10RA

items.scenario: Gamma Ltd enters into an advance pricing agreement with the Board in December 2025. The agreement covers the arm's length price of a single recurring international transaction for previous years 2025-26 through 2029-30. Gamma has undertaken that same transaction in every year since 2019-20 and wants the agreed position applied backwards as well, but only for the two years in which the agreed price would reduce its assessed income.

items.stem: Is the accountant right that the alternate minimum tax provisions do not apply?

options.text: Yes — adjusted total income of ₹17,00,000 is below the ₹20,00,000 threshold, so the alternate minimum tax provisions are not attracted
options.misconception: applies the section 115JC(4) twenty lakh floor to a person it does not cover
options.why: The floor is person-specific, not a general exemption. Reading it as available to every non-corporate assessee is the single most common slip on this section, and it is what this scenario is built around.
keywords: The floor is person-specific, not a general exemption

options.text: No — the ₹20 lakh floor in section 115JC(4) is available only to an individual, HUF, association of persons, body of individuals or artificial juridical person; a limited liability partnership has no floor, so alternate minimum tax applies to its adjusted total income of ₹17,00,000
options.why: The add-back is right: ₹11,00,000 of total income plus the ₹6,00,000 deduction under section 80-IA, which sits in Chapter VI-A heading "C", gives adjusted total income of ₹17,00,000. The error is applying the twenty lakh floor. Section 115JC(4) names the persons it protects, and a limited liability partnership is not among them.
keywords: a limited liability partnership is not among them

options.text: Yes — alternate minimum tax bites only where a deduction under section 10AA or section 35AD has been claimed, and this firm claimed neither
options.misconception: leaves Chapter VI-A heading "C" deductions out of the trigger for alternate minimum tax
options.why: Section 115JC is triggered by a deduction under Chapter VI-A heading "C" as well as by section 10AA or section 35AD. Section 80-IA sits under that heading, so the claim brings the firm squarely inside.

options.text: No — alternate minimum tax applies, and adjusted total income is ₹11,00,000, being the total income as returned
options.misconception: omits the add-back of the Chapter VI-A deduction when computing adjusted total income
options.why: Adjusted total income is total income with the specified deductions added back. Leaving the ₹6,00,000 out defeats the whole purpose of the computation, which is to measure income before the incentive deduction.
keywords: total income with the specified deductions added back
measure income before the incentive deduction

citation.ref: Sections 115JC(1), 115JC(2) and 115JC(4)

items.scenario: A limited liability partnership returns a total income of ₹11,00,000 for previous year 2025-26 after claiming a deduction of ₹6,00,000 under section 80-IA. Its accountant computes adjusted total income at ₹17,00,000, notes that this is below twenty lakh rupees, and concludes that the alternate minimum tax provisions do not apply.

items.stem: Does the scheme qualify as a demerger under section 2(19AA)?

options.text: Yes — 80 per cent exceeds the three-fourths shareholder requirement, and that is the condition on which the definition turns
options.misconception: treats the shareholder test as the only substantive condition in section 2(19AA)
options.why: Section 2(19AA) sets out several conditions and every one of them must hold. Clearing the shareholder test does nothing for a scheme that fails the book-value test.
keywords: every one of them must hold
a scheme that fails the book-value test

options.text: No — the definition requires shareholders holding not less than 90 per cent in value to become shareholders of the resulting company, and 80 per cent falls short
options.misconception: raises the three-fourths shareholder threshold to 90 per cent
options.why: The threshold is three-fourths, that is 75 per cent in value, which 80 per cent satisfies. The scheme fails on the revaluation, not on the shareholding.
keywords: The threshold is three-fourths, that is 75 per cent in value
fails on the revaluation, not on the shareholding

options.text: No — property and liabilities must be transferred at the values appearing in the books immediately before the demerger, disregarding any revaluation; recording the assets at ₹40 crore instead of ₹25 crore breaks the definition even though the shareholder condition is met
options.why: Eighty per cent comfortably clears the three-fourths shareholder test, so that condition is not where the scheme fails. The book-value condition is, and it is absolute: the ₹15 crore of revaluation must be ignored, and once the assets go in at ₹40 crore the transaction is not a demerger. The exemptions under section 47 and the loss carry-forward under section 72A(4) all fall with it.
keywords: the ₹15 crore of revaluation must be ignored
once the assets go in at ₹40 crore the transaction is not a demerger

options.text: Yes — a revaluation is permitted so long as it is supported by a registered valuer's report and the same values are recorded by both companies
options.misconception: invents a valuer's-report exception to the book-value condition
options.why: No such exception exists. The condition is that the values disregard any increase on revaluation, and consistency between the two companies' books does not cure a departure from book value.
keywords: the values disregard any increase on revaluation
does not cure a departure from book value

citation.ref: Section 2(19AA) read with Sections 47(vib), 47(vid) and 72A(4)

items.scenario: Delta Ltd transfers its logistics undertaking to Epsilon Ltd under a court-approved scheme. The undertaking's assets stood at ₹25 crore in Delta's books immediately before the transfer; Delta has them valued at ₹40 crore and Epsilon records them at ₹40 crore. Shareholders holding 80 per cent in value of Delta's shares become shareholders of Epsilon, and Epsilon issues its shares to them on a proportionate basis.

items.stem: For how long will the renewed registration be granted?

options.text: Indefinitely — once a trust has been registered and has not violated any condition, the registration continues until it is cancelled
options.misconception: carries the old section 12AA position, where registration was perpetual, into section 12AB
options.why: Perpetual registration ended with section 12AA. Every section 12AB registration is for a fixed term and lapses if the trust does not apply for renewal at least six months before it expires.
keywords: lapses if the trust does not apply for renewal

options.text: Three years — that is the period for which registration under section 12AB runs before it must be applied for again
options.misconception: confuses provisional registration, which runs three years, with a renewed regular registration
options.why: Three years is the life of a provisional registration under section 12AB(1)(c). A trust already holding regular registration and renewing it is on a different footing.
keywords: Three years is the life of a provisional registration under section 12AB(1)(c)

options.text: Five years — registration granted under section 12AB is always renewed for a five-year period, whatever the size of the trust
options.misconception: applies the pre-1 April 2025 position, under which every renewal ran for five years
options.why: Five years is now the period for a trust that crosses the ₹5 crore mark in either of the two preceding years. This trust does not, so it takes the ten-year period the proviso gives.
keywords: Five years is now the period for a trust that crosses the ₹5 crore mark
it takes the ten-year period the proviso gives

options.text: Ten years — the trust's income computed without sections 11 and 12 did not exceed ₹5 crore in either of the two immediately preceding previous years, so the proviso to section 12AB(1), which took effect from 1 April 2025, applies
options.why: Both figures, ₹3.2 crore and ₹4.1 crore, are below five crore rupees, and the proviso needs the threshold met in each of the two years, not on average. This is a recent change: before 1 April 2025 every renewal was for five years, and a trust of this size now gets ten. The application must still go in at least six months before expiry.
keywords: the threshold met in each of the two years, not on average
at least six months before expiry

citation.ref: Section 12AB(1) with its proviso (inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2025), read with Section 12A(1)(ac)

items.scenario: A charitable trust registered under section 12AB holds a registration that expires with assessment year 2026-27. Its total income, computed without giving effect to sections 11 and 12, was ₹3.2 crore in the first of the two previous years immediately preceding the year of application and ₹4.1 crore in the second. The trust applies for renewal in good time.

items.stem: What is charged under section 115TD, and on what amount?

options.text: Accreted income of ₹7,50,00,000 — the fair market value of total assets less liabilities on the specified date — bears additional income-tax at the maximum marginal rate, payable even though the trust had no income that year
options.why: The computation is ₹9,00,00,000 less ₹1,50,00,000, giving ₹7,50,00,000. Section 115TD is an exit charge on accreted net worth, not a tax on income, so the absence of income in the year is beside the point. The rate is the maximum marginal rate, and the charge is in addition to any income-tax otherwise payable.
keywords: an exit charge on accreted net worth, not a tax on income
The rate is the maximum marginal rate

options.text: ₹7,50,00,000 is charged, but at the rates applicable to an association of persons rather than at the maximum marginal rate
options.misconception: applies the ordinary slab rates for an association of persons instead of the maximum marginal rate section 115TD prescribes
options.why: The amount is right and the rate is wrong. Section 115TD names the maximum marginal rate, which is why slab-rate reasoning has no place in this computation.
keywords: The amount is right and the rate is wrong

options.text: ₹9,00,00,000 bears additional income-tax at the maximum marginal rate, the fair market value of the assets being the accreted income
options.misconception: omits the deduction of liabilities from the fair market value of total assets
options.why: Accreted income is a net figure. Ignoring the ₹1,50,00,000 of liabilities overstates the charge by taxing money the trust owes to others.
keywords: Accreted income is a net figure
Ignoring the ₹1,50,00,000 of liabilities overstates the charge

options.text: Nothing is charged — section 115TD taxes income, and the trust had no income in the previous year in which the registration was cancelled
options.misconception: reads section 115TD as a charge on income rather than on accreted net worth
