options.why: The whole design of the section is to recover the benefit built up over the years when a trust leaves the charitable régime. Tying it to the income of the exit year would let a dormant trust walk away with everything it accumulated.
keywords: recover the benefit built up over the years
Tying it to the income of the exit year

citation.ref: Sections 115TD(1), 115TD(2) and 115TD(3)

items.scenario: A trust registered under section 12AB has its registration cancelled and does not apply for fresh registration within the time allowed. On the specified date the fair market value of its total assets is ₹9,00,00,000 and its liabilities are ₹1,50,00,000. The trust earned no income at all in that previous year, having suspended all activity.

items.stem: Who has the obligation, under which provision, and for how much?

options.text: Neither applies — section 194Q requires the buyer's turnover in the preceding year to exceed ₹50 crore, and Mehta's ₹12 crore falls well short
options.misconception: raises the section 194Q buyer turnover test from ₹10 crore to ₹50 crore, confusing it with the ₹50 lakh transaction threshold
options.why: The buyer's turnover test is ₹10 crore, which Mehta's ₹12 crore crosses. The ₹50 lakh figure in the section is the threshold on the value of purchases from a single seller, not a turnover test at all.
keywords: The buyer's turnover test is ₹10 crore
the threshold on the value of purchases from a single seller, not a turnover test

options.text: Both provisions apply to the transaction, and under the tie-break rule section 194Q prevails, so Mehta deducts and Sunder is relieved of collecting
options.misconception: applies the pre-2025 priority rule between two live provisions when only one of them still exists
options.why: There is no overlap left to resolve. The tie-break mattered when a single transaction could attract both; with section 206C(1H) omitted, section 194Q applies on its own terms and nothing has to give way to it.
keywords: There is no overlap left to resolve
section 194Q applies on its own terms

options.text: Sunder must collect ₹4,000 as tax at source under section 206C(1H), being 0.1 per cent of the ₹40,00,000 by which receipts exceed ₹50,00,000
options.misconception: applies section 206C(1H), which was omitted with effect from 1 April 2025 and does not operate in previous year 2025-26
options.why: The arithmetic is the arithmetic of a provision that no longer exists. The figure of ₹4,000 happens to be right, but it is payable by the buyer as deduction under section 194Q, not by the seller as collection under section 206C(1H).
keywords: payable by the buyer as deduction under section 194Q, not by the seller

options.text: Sunder collects nothing — section 206C(1H) stands omitted from 1 April 2025; the obligation is Mehta's, to deduct ₹4,000 under section 194Q, being 0.1 per cent of ₹40,00,000, the purchase value above the ₹50,00,000 threshold
options.why: For previous year 2025-26 there is no tax collection at source on a sale of goods at all. Mehta's own turnover of ₹12 crore is above the ₹10 crore that section 194Q requires of the buyer, so the buyer deducts: ₹90,00,000 less ₹50,00,000 is ₹40,00,000, and 0.1 per cent of that is ₹4,000. The seller's ₹18 crore turnover is now irrelevant to this transaction.
keywords: there is no tax collection at source on a sale of goods at all

citation.ref: Section 206C(1H) (omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2025) read with Section 194Q

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26, Mehta Industries buys goods worth ₹90,00,000 from Sunder Traders, a resident seller. Sunder's turnover in the preceding financial year was ₹18 crore; Mehta's was ₹12 crore. Sunder's accountant prepares to collect tax at source on the transaction, reasoning that the seller's turnover is well above ₹10 crore and the receipts are well above ₹50,00,000.

items.stem: What is Ridge Ltd's position on the tax and on interest?

options.text: Ridge remains an assessee in default for the whole tax not deducted, because the proviso protects a payer only where the payee is a non-resident
options.misconception: inverts the proviso, which applies where the payee is a resident
options.why: The first proviso is expressly for a resident payee, who is the person able to file a return under section 139 and pay the tax on the receipt. A payment to a non-resident is governed by section 195 and does not attract this relief in the same terms.
keywords: does not attract this relief in the same terms

options.text: Ridge is not in default, and interest runs from 10 June 2025 until the date Ridge itself pays the interest demand raised by the Assessing Officer
options.misconception: takes the wrong end date for the section 201(1A) interest period
options.why: The period closes on the date the payee furnished his return of income, here 30 September 2026, not on the date the payer settles the demand. Once the payee has declared and paid, the exchequer is no longer out of pocket.
keywords: closes on the date the payee furnished his return of income
not on the date the payer settles the demand

options.text: Ridge is neither in default nor liable to interest, since the revenue has been paid in full by the payee and has suffered no loss
options.misconception: reads the first proviso to section 201(1) as waiving interest along with the tax
options.why: The proviso relieves the payer of the tax alone. Interest under section 201(1A) is compensation for the period the money sat with the payer instead of the exchequer, and the payee's later payment does not erase that period.
keywords: relieves the payer of the tax alone
the payee's later payment does not erase that period

options.text: Ridge is not deemed an assessee in default, because the first proviso to section 201(1) is satisfied, but interest under section 201(1A) still runs at one per cent per month from 10 June 2025 to 30 September 2026
options.why: The proviso needs a resident payee who filed a return under section 139, took the sum into account, paid the tax, and a certificate from an accountant — all present here, so the tax cannot be recovered from Ridge. The relief stops there. Interest under section 201(1A) runs from the date the tax was deductible, 10 June 2025, to the date the payee furnished his return, 30 September 2026.
keywords: the tax cannot be recovered from Ridge
Interest under section 201(1A) runs from the date the tax was deductible

citation.ref: Section 201(1) with its first proviso, and Section 201(1A)

items.scenario: Ridge Ltd pays ₹20,00,000 as commission to a resident agent on 10 June 2025 and deducts no tax under section 194H. The agent includes the commission in his return of income for assessment year 2026-27, files that return on 30 September 2026 and pays the tax due on it. Ridge Ltd obtains and furnishes the accountant's certificate in the prescribed form.

items.stem: Is the notice issued on 20 August 2026 within time?

options.text: No — a section 148 notice can never be issued more than three years from the end of the relevant assessment year, the longer period being confined to search and requisition cases
options.misconception: confines the extended limb to search cases, when it turns on the quantum of escaped income
options.why: The extended period depends on the Assessing Officer holding material showing escaped income of ₹50,00,000 or more. It is not restricted to searches, and a survey or third-party information can equally support it.
keywords: It is not restricted to searches
a survey or third-party information can equally support it

options.text: No — the limit is three years and three months from the end of the relevant assessment year, which expired on 30 June 2026, so the notice is out of time
options.misconception: ignores the extended limb available where escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more
options.why: Three years and three months is the ordinary limit. Where the Assessing Officer has material showing escaped income of at least ₹50,00,000, section 149 gives him five years and three months, and ₹80,00,000 clears that bar.
keywords: Three years and three months is the ordinary limit
gives him five years and three months

options.text: Yes — the escaped income of ₹80,00,000 is above ₹50,00,000, so the outer limit is five years and three months from the end of assessment year 2022-23, that is 30 June 2028
options.why: Assessment year 2022-23 ends on 31 March 2023. Three years and three months from that date is 30 June 2026 and five years and three months is 30 June 2028. The notice on 20 August 2026 is past the first date but well inside the second, and the extended limb is available because the documents show escaped income of ₹50,00,000 or more.
keywords: Three years and three months from that date is 30 June 2026

options.text: Yes — where escaped income exceeds ₹50,00,000 a notice may be issued up to ten years from the end of the relevant assessment year, so the notice is comfortably in time
options.misconception: uses the ten-year outer limit that applied before section 149 was substituted with effect from 1 September 2024
options.why: The conclusion is right for the wrong reason, which in an examination is a wrong answer. The ten-year limit is gone; the correct outer limit is five years and three months, and it is that date the notice must be tested against.
keywords: the correct outer limit is five years and three months

citation.ref: Section 149(1) as substituted with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Section 148A

items.scenario: For assessment year 2022-23 the Assessing Officer holds documents showing that income of ₹80,00,000 chargeable to tax has escaped assessment. He completes the section 148A procedure and issues a notice under section 148 on 20 August 2026. The assessee objects that the notice is time-barred.

items.stem: What follows from the objections being filed on 20 June 2026?

options.text: The objections are out of time, and the company's only remedy is a writ petition, since no appeal lies against a final order passed on an unobjected draft
options.misconception: assumes a final order passed under section 144C(3) is not appealable
options.why: The lateness is right; the consequence is not. The final assessment order remains an appealable order before the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A. What the company loses is the Dispute Resolution Panel route, not its right of appeal.
keywords: remains an appealable order before the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A
loses is the Dispute Resolution Panel route, not its right of appeal

options.text: The objections are in time — section 144C allows sixty days from receipt of the draft order for an eligible assessee to object
options.misconception: uses sixty days in place of the thirty days section 144C(2) actually allows
options.why: The period is thirty days, and it is short by design so that the Dispute Resolution Panel can issue its directions within nine months from the end of the month the draft order was forwarded.
keywords: issue its directions within nine months

options.text: The objections are in time — the thirty days runs from the Transfer Pricing Officer's order under section 92CA(3), not from the draft assessment order
options.misconception: takes the wrong starting point for the thirty-day period
options.why: The clock starts on receipt of the draft order by the eligible assessee. The Transfer Pricing Officer's order feeds into the draft order but does not start the objection period.
keywords: The clock starts on receipt of the draft order
does not start the objection period

options.text: The objections are out of time — they were due within thirty days of receipt, that is by 4 June 2026 — so the Assessing Officer may complete the assessment on the basis of the draft order
options.why: Section 144C(2) gives thirty days from receipt of the draft order. Counting from 5 May 2026, the thirtieth day is 4 June 2026, and objections lodged on 20 June are sixteen days late. Where no objections are validly filed in time, section 144C(3) lets the Assessing Officer pass the final order on the draft as it stands.
keywords: gives thirty days from receipt of the draft order
objections lodged on 20 June are sixteen days late

items.scenario: A foreign company receives a draft assessment order under section 144C on 5 May 2026, carrying a transfer pricing variation prejudicial to it. The company files its objections with the Dispute Resolution Panel and the Assessing Officer on 20 June 2026, forty-six days after receiving the draft order.

items.stem: What equalisation levy is payable on these two payments?

options.text: ₹4,80,000 — six per cent of the ₹80,00,000 paid for online advertisement; the e-commerce payment attracts nothing
options.misconception: applies the six per cent advertisement levy, which ceased from 1 April 2025
options.why: The arithmetic of the withdrawn levy is correct and the levy is not. The advertisement levy applied to consideration up to 31 March 2025 and not to a payment made in previous year 2025-26.
keywords: The arithmetic of the withdrawn levy is correct and the levy is not
applied to consideration up to 31 March 2025

options.text: ₹4,00,000 — two per cent of the ₹2,00,00,000 paid to the e-commerce operator; the advertisement payment attracts nothing
options.misconception: applies the two per cent e-commerce levy, which ceased from 1 August 2024
options.why: The e-commerce levy was the first of the two to go, on consideration received or receivable on or after 1 August 2024. It cannot reach a payment made in previous year 2025-26.
keywords: It cannot reach a payment made in previous year 2025-26

options.text: ₹8,80,000 in all — six per cent on the advertisement payment and two per cent on the e-commerce payment, both levies being in force
options.misconception: treats both equalisation levies as still operating, when each was withdrawn on its own date
options.why: This is the position as it stood up to 31 July 2024 and no later. Both levies were withdrawn on separate dates, and neither survives into previous year 2025-26.
keywords: the position as it stood up to 31 July 2024 and no later

options.text: None on either — the two per cent levy on e-commerce supply or services ceased from 1 August 2024 and the six per cent levy on online advertisement from 1 April 2025, so chargeability for previous year 2025-26 is tested under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the applicable treaty instead
options.why: Both levies had gone before previous year 2025-26 began. The section 10(50) exemption that kept levy-bearing receipts outside the Income-tax Act goes with them, so the right question is now whether the non-residents have a business connection or significant economic presence under section 9, what section 195 requires on payment, and what the double taxation avoidance agreement permits.
keywords: Both levies had gone before previous year 2025-26 began
business connection or significant economic presence under section 9

citation.ref: Chapter VIII, Sections 165 and 165A of the Finance Act, 2016 (levies withdrawn w.e.f. 1-8-2024 and 1-4-2025), read with Section 10(50) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26, Orbit Ltd, an Indian company, pays ₹80,00,000 to a non-resident for online advertisement space targeted at customers in India, and ₹2,00,00,000 to a non-resident e-commerce operator for goods supplied to Indian customers through its platform. Neither non-resident has a permanent establishment in India. Orbit's consultant prepares to discharge equalisation levy on both payments.

items.stem: Is the company right that no income is deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.text: No — and the amount is taxable in full at the rate in force, because section 9 is a deeming provision of the Act and a treaty cannot cut down what the Act deems to accrue
options.misconception: treats a domestic deeming provision as overriding the treaty, when section 90(2) lets the assessee take whichever is more beneficial
options.why: Section 90(2) gives the non-resident the benefit of the treaty where it is more favourable than the Act. Establishing chargeability under section 9 is the first step, not the last.
keywords: the benefit of the treaty where it is more favourable
the first step, not the last

options.text: Yes — services rendered wholly outside India by a person with no presence here cannot give rise to income deemed to accrue in India
options.misconception: relies on the rendered-in-India argument the Explanation to section 9(2) was inserted to override
options.why: That was a live argument before the Explanation. It is not one now: the Explanation says in terms that the deeming applies whether or not the services were rendered in India.
keywords: whether or not the services were rendered in India

options.text: Yes — fees for technical services are taxable in India only where the non-resident has a permanent establishment here, and this consultant plainly has none
options.misconception: applies the permanent establishment test for business profits to fees for technical services
options.why: A permanent establishment governs the taxation of business profits. Fees for technical services are dealt with by their own article, which typically taxes them on a gross basis in the source country without needing any permanent establishment.
keywords: A permanent establishment governs the taxation of business profits

options.text: No — the Explanation to section 9(2) deems fees for technical services to accrue in India whether or not the non-resident has a residence, place of business or business connection here and whether or not the services were rendered in India, though the Singapore treaty's fees-for-technical-services article, including any make-available condition, still has to be tested under section 90(2)
options.why: The source rule in section 9(1)(vii) turns on where the services are utilised and who bears the cost, not on where the consultant sat. The Explanation was inserted to close exactly the argument the company is making. Chargeability under the Act is therefore established, and the next step is the treaty, which may narrow or remove the charge if the services do not make available technical knowledge to the Indian company.
keywords: turns on where the services are utilised and who bears the cost
if the services do not make available technical knowledge

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(vii) with the Explanation to Section 9(2), read with Section 90(2)

items.scenario: An Indian manufacturing company pays ₹50,00,000 to a technical consultant resident in Singapore for advice on a production process used at its Indian plant. The consultant does all the work from Singapore, never sets foot in India, and has no office, agent or business connection here. The Indian company takes the view that nothing is deemed to accrue in India, so no tax need be withheld.

items.stem: What are its presumptive profits chargeable under section 44B?

options.text: ₹37,50,000 — seven and a half per cent of ₹5,00,00,000, the two Chennai shipments counting but not the Dubai to Rotterdam carriage
options.misconception: applies only the first limb of section 44B(2) and overlooks the second, which catches freight received in India for carriage between two foreign ports
options.why: The first limb is applied correctly here, which is what makes the slip convincing. The ₹60,00,000 still belongs in the aggregate, because it was received in India for carriage from a port outside India.
keywords: The ₹60,00,000 still belongs in the aggregate
received in India for carriage from a port outside India

options.text: ₹42,00,000 — seven and a half per cent of ₹5,60,00,000, all three receipts entering the specified aggregate
options.why: Both Chennai shipments count whether the freight was collected in India or abroad, because the first limb covers amounts paid or payable, in India or outside, for goods shipped at a port in India. The Dubai to Rotterdam carriage counts under the second limb because the freight was received in India. The aggregate is ₹4,00,00,000 plus ₹1,00,00,000 plus ₹60,00,000, that is ₹5,60,00,000, and 7.5 per cent of that is ₹42,00,000.
keywords: counts under the second limb because the freight was received in India

options.text: ₹56,00,000 — ten per cent of ₹5,60,00,000, that being the presumptive rate for a non-resident's shipping business
options.misconception: uses section 44BB's ten per cent rate for mineral oil services instead of section 44B's seven and a half per cent
options.why: The aggregate is right and the rate is wrong. Section 44B deems seven and a half per cent; ten per cent belongs to section 44BB, and five per cent to section 44BBA for the operation of aircraft.
keywords: Section 44B deems seven and a half per cent
ten per cent belongs to section 44BB

options.text: ₹30,00,000 — seven and a half per cent of ₹4,00,00,000, only the freight received in India for goods shipped from an Indian port qualifying
options.misconception: requires both an Indian port and receipt in India, when each limb of section 44B(2) needs only one of the two
options.why: This drops ₹1,60,00,000 from the base. The first limb does not care where the freight was received, and the second does not care where the goods were shipped, so requiring both conditions together shrinks the aggregate wrongly.
keywords: requiring both conditions together shrinks the aggregate wrongly

citation.ref: Section 44B(1) and (2), read with Sections 44BB and 44BBA

items.scenario: A non-resident shipping company operating cargo vessels has the following receipts for previous year 2025-26 — ₹4,00,00,000 received in India as freight for goods shipped at Chennai port; ₹1,00,00,000 received in Athens as freight for other goods also shipped at Chennai port; and ₹60,00,000 received in India as freight for a consignment carried from Dubai to Rotterdam. It operates no cruise ships.

items.stem: What tax is deductible under section 194A in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: ₹5,600 in all — only Mr Bakshi's interest crosses its threshold, and tax is deducted at 10 per cent on the whole ₹56,000
options.why: From 1 April 2025 the section 194A threshold where the payer is a bank, a co-operative society engaged in banking or a post office is ₹1,00,000 for a resident senior citizen and ₹50,000 for anyone else, and ₹10,000 in any other case. Mr Ahuja's ₹95,000 is under ₹1,00,000, and Mr Chandra's ₹9,500 is under ₹10,000, so nothing is deducted from either. Mr Bakshi's ₹56,000 is over ₹50,000, and the deduction is on the whole sum at ten per cent, which is ₹5,600.

options.text: ₹15,100 in all — ₹9,500 from Mr Ahuja and ₹5,600 from Mr Bakshi, the non-banking company's payment being too small
options.misconception: applies the ₹50,000 general bank threshold to a senior citizen instead of the ₹1,00,000 figure reserved for him
options.why: The threshold for a resident senior citizen is higher, not the same. Reading ₹50,000 across the board takes ₹9,500 from Mr Ahuja that the section does not authorise; his ₹95,000 is below ₹1,00,000 and bears nothing.

options.text: ₹16,050 in all — ₹9,500 from Mr Ahuja, ₹5,600 from Mr Bakshi and ₹950 from Mr Chandra, every payment crossing its limit
options.misconception: uses the pre-1 April 2025 thresholds of ₹50,000 for a senior citizen, ₹40,000 for others and ₹5,000 in any other case
options.why: On the old figures all three would indeed be deducted from and the total would be ₹16,050. The thresholds were raised on 1 April 2025 to ₹1,00,000, ₹50,000 and ₹10,000, and on the current numbers Mr Ahuja and Mr Chandra both fall below.

options.text: ₹600 — 10 per cent of ₹6,000, being the amount by which Mr Bakshi's interest exceeds the ₹50,000 threshold
options.misconception: deducts on the excess over the threshold rather than on the whole sum once the threshold is crossed
options.why: The threshold decides whether section 194A applies at all, not how much of the payment it reaches. Once ₹50,000 is crossed the deduction is on the entire ₹56,000. Collecting on the excess is the pattern of section 206C(1G), not of the deduction provisions.

citation.ref: Section 194A(1) and Section 194A(3)(i) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26, Sunrise Co-operative Bank Ltd, a co-operative society engaged in the business of banking, credits interest on time deposits of ₹95,000 to Mr Ahuja, a resident aged 68, and ₹56,000 to Mr Bakshi, a resident aged 45. Separately, Vardhan Finance Ltd, a non-banking finance company, credits ₹9,500 as interest on a loan taken from Mr Chandra, a resident aged 40. All three have furnished their PAN.

items.stem: What tax is deductible under section 194-I in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: ₹4,000 — 2 per cent of ₹2,00,000, being the amount by which the plant and machinery hire exceeds ₹6,00,000
options.misconception: treats the threshold as an exempt slab and deducts only on the excess above it
options.why: Section 194-I gives a threshold, not an exemption. Once the rent crosses it the deduction is on the entire ₹8,00,000, so the figure is ₹16,000 and not ₹4,000.

options.text: ₹80,000 — 10 per cent of ₹8,00,000 on the plant and machinery hire, the office building rent being below the threshold
options.misconception: applies the section 194-I(b) rate of ten per cent to plant and machinery, which falls under section 194-I(a) at two per cent
options.why: The threshold is handled correctly here, which is what makes the slip convincing. Rent for the use of plant, machinery or equipment carries two per cent; the ten per cent rate is for land, a building, furniture or fittings.

options.text: ₹70,000 — 10 per cent of ₹5,40,000 on the office building and 2 per cent of ₹8,00,000 on the plant and machinery
options.misconception: applies the pre-1 April 2025 threshold of ₹2,40,000 for the financial year, which the office rent would have crossed
options.why: The rate on a building is right at ten per cent, and the arithmetic of ₹54,000 plus ₹16,000 is right for the old threshold. What has changed is the threshold itself, and ₹5,40,000 no longer reaches it.

options.text: ₹16,000 — nothing on the office building rent, and 2 per cent of ₹8,00,000 on the plant and machinery hire
options.why: The threshold from 1 April 2025 is ₹50,000 for a month or part of a month, which on an even rent is ₹6,00,000 for a year. Mr Dhar's rent is ₹45,000 a month and ₹5,40,000 for the year, under the limit on either reading, so nothing is deducted. Falcon's ₹80,000 a month is over it, and rent for plant and machinery carries the two per cent rate, giving ₹16,000 on the whole ₹8,00,000.
keywords: ₹50,000 for a month or part of a month

citation.ref: Section 194-I(a) and (b) with its second proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

items.scenario: Kestrel Ltd pays rent during previous year 2025-26 as follows. It pays Mr Dhar ₹45,000 a month for all twelve months for the use of an office building, ₹5,40,000 for the year. It pays Falcon Equipment Ltd ₹80,000 a month for ten months for the hire of plant and machinery, ₹8,00,000 for the year. Both payees are residents and have furnished their PAN.

items.stem: What tax is deductible under section 194J in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: ₹21,040 — nothing on the advocate's fees, ₹1,040 on the technical fees at 2 per cent, and ₹20,000 on the royalty at 10 per cent
options.why: The ₹50,000 threshold from 1 April 2025 applies separately to each category in section 194J, so the advocate's ₹48,000 of professional fees stands on its own and falls below it. Fees for technical services other than professional services carry two per cent, giving ₹1,040 on ₹52,000. Royalty not connected with cinematographic films carries ten per cent, giving ₹20,000 on ₹2,00,000, and the total is ₹21,040.

options.text: ₹25,840 — the three payments aggregate ₹3,00,000, which crosses ₹50,000, so the advocate's fees are also deducted from, at 10 per cent
options.misconception: applies the ₹50,000 threshold to the aggregate of all payments under section 194J rather than to each category separately
options.why: The proviso sets the limit for each of the four categories the section covers — professional fees, technical fees, royalty, and a sum for not carrying out an activity. Aggregating them pulls in ₹4,800 from the advocate that is not deductible.

options.text: ₹30,000 — 10 per cent on each of the three payments, all of them crossing the threshold
options.misconception: uses the pre-1 April 2025 threshold of ₹30,000 and applies ten per cent to fees for technical services as well
options.why: Two errors compound here. The threshold is ₹50,000 now, not ₹30,000, so the advocate's fee is out; and fees for technical services carry two per cent, not ten, so ₹5,200 is wrong for the engineer.

options.text: ₹5,040 — 2 per cent on the technical fees and 2 per cent on the royalty, the advocate's fees being below the threshold
options.misconception: extends the two per cent rate to royalty generally, when it is confined to royalty for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films
options.why: The threshold is handled correctly and only the rate is wrong. Royalty under section 194J carries ten per cent unless it is consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films, which this royalty to an author is not.

citation.ref: Section 194J(1) with its first proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

items.scenario: Meridian LLP makes three payments to residents during previous year 2025-26 — ₹48,000 as fees for professional services to an advocate, ₹52,000 as fees for technical services to an engineer who is not rendering professional services, and ₹2,00,000 as royalty to an author, the royalty having nothing to do with cinematographic films. All payees have furnished their PAN.

items.stem: What must Harbour Ltd deduct under section 194H, and on what amount?

options.text: ₹500 — the aggregate of ₹25,000 crosses the ₹20,000 threshold, so tax is deducted in January at 2 per cent on the whole ₹25,000 including the April payment
options.why: The section 194H threshold is on the aggregate credited or paid during the financial year, so nothing was due in April but the January credit takes the total to ₹25,000 and past ₹20,000. The deduction is then on the whole aggregate, at the two per cent rate that has applied since 1 October 2024, which is ₹500.
keywords: aggregate credited or paid during the financial year

options.text: ₹100 — 2 per cent of ₹5,000, being the amount by which the aggregate exceeds ₹20,000
options.misconception: deducts on the excess over the threshold instead of on the whole aggregate once the threshold is crossed
options.why: The rate is right and the base is wrong. Crossing ₹20,000 makes the entire ₹25,000 deductible, including the ₹19,000 credited in April from which nothing was taken at the time.

options.text: Nothing — neither payment on its own reaches ₹20,000, so no liability to deduct arises in either month
options.misconception: reads the ₹20,000 threshold as a per-payment test rather than an aggregate for the financial year
options.why: Section 194H tests the amount credited or paid, or the aggregate of the amounts credited or paid, during the financial year. Splitting a payment into instalments below the limit is exactly what the aggregate wording defeats.

options.text: ₹1,250 — 5 per cent of the aggregate ₹25,000
options.misconception: uses the five per cent rate that section 194H carried before 1 October 2024
options.why: The base is right and the rate is stale. The rate on commission or brokerage fell from five per cent to two per cent for sums credited or paid on or after 1 October 2024, and both these payments fall after that date.

citation.ref: Section 194H with its first proviso, rate amended with effect from 1 October 2024 and threshold with effect from 1 April 2025

items.scenario: Harbour Ltd credits commission of ₹19,000 to Mr Iyer, a resident selling agent, on 20 April 2025, and a further ₹6,000 to the same agent on 12 January 2026. No other commission is paid to him in the year. Harbour's accountant deducted nothing in April because the payment was below the limit, and now asks what to do in January.

items.stem: What tax must the authorised dealer collect from each of them under section 206C(1G)?

options.text: ₹1,80,000 from Mr Rao and ₹3,500 from Ms Iyer
options.misconception: uses the pre-1 April 2025 threshold of ₹7,00,000 and the old 0.5 per cent rate on a loan-funded education remittance
options.why: Both figures are the previous year's law. On the ₹7,00,000 threshold Mr Rao's base would be ₹9,00,000 and twenty per cent of it ₹1,80,000, and a loan-funded education remittance bore half a per cent on ₹7,00,000, which is ₹3,500. The threshold is now ₹10,00,000 and the education-loan rate is nil.

options.text: ₹3,20,000 from Mr Rao and nothing from Ms Iyer
options.misconception: collects twenty per cent on the whole remittance instead of on the amount in excess of the threshold
options.why: Ms Iyer's position is right. Mr Rao's is not: section 206C(1G) says in excess of, so the base is ₹6,00,000 and not ₹16,00,000. This section differs from the deduction provisions in Chapter XVII-B, which reach the whole payment once their threshold is crossed.

options.text: ₹1,20,000 from Mr Rao and nothing from Ms Iyer
options.why: Section 206C(1G) collects on the amount in excess of ₹10,00,000, so Mr Rao's base is ₹16,00,000 less ₹10,00,000, that is ₹6,00,000, and the rate for a purpose other than education or medical treatment is twenty per cent, giving ₹1,20,000. Ms Iyer's remittance is for education out of a loan from a financial institution under section 80E(3)(b), and from 1 April 2025 no tax is collected on such a remittance at all, whatever its size.

options.text: ₹1,20,000 from Mr Rao and ₹20,000 from Ms Iyer
options.misconception: applies the five per cent education and medical rate to a remittance funded by a qualifying education loan, ignoring the nil rate
options.why: Mr Rao's figure is right. Five per cent of the ₹4,00,000 by which Ms Iyer's remittance exceeds ₹10,00,000 would be ₹20,000, and that is the rate for an education remittance funded from her own money. Where the money comes from a section 80E(3)(b) loan, nothing is collected.

citation.ref: Section 206C(1G) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025, read with Section 80E(3)(b)

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26 an authorised dealer handles two remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme. Mr Rao remits ₹16,00,000 to buy shares of a foreign company; this is his only remittance in the year. Ms Iyer remits ₹14,00,000 for her daughter's university fees abroad, the whole of it drawn from an education loan sanctioned by a bank that is a financial institution as defined in section 80E(3)(b); this is her only remittance in the year.

items.stem: What documentation does the Indian company owe under Rule 10DA and section 286?

options.text: Nothing under either provision, because the Indian company had no international transactions in intangible property during the year
options.misconception: reads the ₹50 crore and ₹10 crore limbs of Rule 10DA as cumulative when they are alternatives
options.why: The second condition in Rule 10DA is satisfied by either aggregate international transactions above ₹50 crore or intangible property transactions above ₹10 crore. The ₹60 crore of ordinary transactions satisfies it on its own.

options.text: Nothing under either provision, because the parent entity is resident in Germany and the documentation duties fall on the parent
options.misconception: treats the master file as an obligation of the parent alone, when Rule 10DA falls on the Indian constituent entity itself
options.why: Rule 10DA places the duty on the constituent entity in India, not on the group's parent. What does depend on where the parent sits is the Country-by-Country report, and that question does not arise here because the group is below the ₹6,400 crore threshold.

options.text: Both the master file in Form 3CEAA and the Country-by-Country report in Form 3CEAD, the ₹500 crore consolidated revenue test governing both
options.misconception: applies the Rule 10DA master file revenue threshold to the Country-by-Country report, whose threshold is ₹6,400 crore
options.why: The two obligations have separate triggers by design. The Country-by-Country threshold is ₹6,400 crore, aligned with the OECD's 750 million euro figure, and it is not reduced because a master file happens to be due.

options.text: The master file in Form 3CEAA, because both Rule 10DA thresholds are crossed; no Country-by-Country report arises, because ₹2,000 crore is far below the ₹6,400 crore the section 286 obligation needs
options.why: Rule 10DA needs consolidated group revenue above ₹500 crore, which ₹2,000 crore clears, and in addition either international transactions above ₹50 crore, which ₹60 crore clears, or intangible property transactions above ₹10 crore. Both limbs are satisfied so Form 3CEAA is due. The Country-by-Country report threshold is a different and far higher one, and a group of this size owes nothing under section 286.

citation.ref: Rule 10DA and Rule 10DB read with Section 286 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and Notification No. 31/2021

items.scenario: Nordic Instruments India Pvt Ltd is a constituent entity of an international group whose parent is resident in Germany. For the accounting year preceding previous year 2025-26 the group's consolidated revenue was ₹2,000 crore. The Indian company's international transactions with associated enterprises during the year aggregate ₹60 crore, none of them in intangible property.

items.stem: What foreign tax credit is she entitled to under Rule 128?

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — the whole of the foreign tax paid, with the excess ₹90,000 refunded to her
options.misconception: ignores the Rule 128 cap limiting credit to the Indian tax on the doubly taxed income
options.why: Credit relieves double taxation; it does not turn a foreign government's higher tax into an Indian refund. The cap is the Indian tax on that income, here ₹2,10,000, and nothing above it is available.

options.text: ₹2,10,000, and she may set the credit against her interest under section 234B as well as against her tax
options.misconception: extends the credit to interest, when Rule 128 allows it only against tax, surcharge and cess
options.why: The amount of the credit is right and its reach is not. Rule 128 gives credit against the tax, surcharge and cess payable under the Act, and expressly not against any interest, fee or penalty.

options.text: ₹2,10,000 — the lower of the foreign tax paid and the Indian tax on that income; the excess ₹90,000 is neither refunded nor carried forward, and Form 67 was in time
options.why: Rule 128 caps the credit at the tax arrived at by applying the Indian rate to the doubly taxed income, so the credit is the lower of ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,10,000. The remaining ₹90,000 of Country X tax simply falls away. Form 67 filed on 15 February 2027 is within the relevant assessment year, which ends on 31 March 2027, so the timing condition is met.

options.text: Nothing — Form 67 was not furnished by the due date for filing the return under section 139(1), and the credit is lost
options.misconception: applies the pre-2022 Rule 128, under which Form 67 had to be furnished by the section 139(1) due date
options.why: Rule 128 was amended by Notification No. 100/2022 so that Form 67 may be furnished at any time on or before the end of the relevant assessment year. Her filing on 15 February 2027 is comfortably inside that.

citation.ref: Rule 128(1), 128(2) and 128(9) as amended by Notification No. 100/2022, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Ms Kaul, resident in India, earns ₹10,00,000 from a source in Country X during previous year 2025-26 and pays ₹3,00,000 of tax there. The Indian tax attributable to that same ₹10,00,000, computed by applying her Indian rate of tax to it, is ₹2,10,000. She files her return under section 139(1) on 30 July 2026 and furnishes the statement in Form 67 on 15 February 2027. She also owes interest under section 234B for the year.

items.stem: What is the tax on the royalty in each case?

options.text: Case 1 — ₹20,00,000 at 20 per cent on the gross amount; Case 2 — ₹24,00,000 at 40 per cent on the net amount
options.misconception: uses the forty per cent foreign company rate that ceased to apply from assessment year 2025-26
options.why: Case 1 is right and Case 2 uses a rate that no longer exists. The rate for a foreign company was reduced from forty per cent to thirty-five per cent by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so the figure is ₹21,00,000.

options.text: Case 1 — ₹20,00,000, being 20 per cent of the gross ₹1,00,00,000 under section 115A; Case 2 — ₹21,00,000, being 35 per cent of the net ₹60,00,000 under section 44DA
options.why: With no permanent establishment, section 115A charges the gross receipt at twenty per cent with no deduction for expenditure, giving ₹20,00,000. Where the royalty is effectively connected with a permanent establishment, section 115A steps aside and section 44DA taxes ₹1,00,00,000 less ₹40,00,000, that is ₹60,00,000, at the ordinary foreign company rate of thirty-five per cent, giving ₹21,00,000.

options.text: ₹20,00,000 in both cases — section 115A charges royalty at 20 per cent on the gross amount whether or not there is a permanent establishment
options.misconception: overlooks section 44DA, which takes effectively connected royalty out of section 115A altogether
options.why: The whole point of section 44DA is that effective connection with a permanent establishment moves the income to the business head, taxed net at the ordinary rate, with books required under section 44AA and an audit report in Form 3CE. Section 115A(1) itself excludes such income.

options.text: Case 1 — ₹10,00,000 at 10 per cent on the gross amount; Case 2 — ₹21,00,000 at 35 per cent on the net amount
options.misconception: uses the ten per cent section 115A rate that applied before assessment year 2024-25
options.why: Case 2 is right. The section 115A rate on royalty and fees for technical services was doubled from ten per cent to twenty per cent with effect from assessment year 2024-25, so Case 1 is ₹20,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 115A(1)(b) and Section 44DA(1) with its provisos, read with Section 90(2) and Rule 6GA (Form 3CE)

items.scenario: Lyra GmbH, a foreign company, receives royalty of ₹1,00,00,000 from an Indian company during previous year 2025-26 under an agreement made after 31 March 1976. In Case 1 it has no permanent establishment in India. In Case 2 the agreement is effectively connected with its permanent establishment in India, and it has incurred ₹40,00,000 of expenditure wholly and exclusively for that permanent establishment. Ignore surcharge, cess and any treaty relief.

items.stem: Which state does Article 4(2) treat him as a resident of, and by which test?

options.text: India, on the habitual abode test — he spent more nights in India than in Country Y during the year
options.misconception: jumps to the habitual abode test while the centre of vital interests test is still capable of deciding
options.why: Habitual abode is the third test and is reached only where a centre of vital interests cannot be determined. Here it plainly can, and where the sequence decides earlier the later tests are simply not applied.

options.text: Whichever state he is a national of, nationality being the test the Article applies where a person has a home in both states
options.misconception: promotes nationality, which is the fourth test, above the centre of vital interests and habitual abode
options.why: Nationality comes fourth, after permanent home, centre of vital interests and habitual abode, and it is reached only where he has an habitual abode in both states or in neither. If he is a national of both or of neither, the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement.

options.text: India — section 6(1) makes him a resident of India, and a treaty cannot displace a residential status conferred by the Act
options.misconception: denies the treaty any effect on residence, when section 90(2) lets the assessee take whichever of the Act and the treaty is more beneficial
options.why: Section 90(2) is what makes Article 4(2) operate at all. He remains a resident under section 6 for the Act's own purposes, but for the treaty's purposes he is treated as a resident of one state only, and that decides which state may tax what.

options.text: Country Y, on the centre of vital interests test — a permanent home is available in both, so the tie is broken by his closer personal and economic relations, which are in Country Y
options.why: Article 4(2) is worked in order and stops at the first test that decides. The permanent home test does not decide because a home is available in both states, so the next test applies: the centre of vital interests, being the state with which his personal and economic relations are closer. His family and his only business are in Country Y, so the tie breaks there and the habitual abode test is never reached.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital
citation.ref: Article 4(2), as adopted in India's double taxation avoidance agreements, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Mr Sethi is a resident of India for previous year 2025-26 under section 6(1), having stayed 190 days in India, and is at the same time a resident of Country Y under Country Y's own law. India and Country Y have a treaty carrying the standard Article 4(2) tie-breaker. He owns and keeps available a permanent home in both countries. His wife, children and his only business are in Country Y, though he spent more nights in India than in Country Y during the year.

items.stem: How is the ₹2,00,00,000 of undisclosed income of the block period charged to tax?

options.text: At the slab rates applicable to Mr Batra as an individual, the undisclosed income being added to his other income of the years concerned
options.misconception: assesses undisclosed income year by year at ordinary rates instead of as one block at the section 113 rate
options.why: Block assessment exists precisely so that undisclosed income found in a search is not folded back into each year's ordinary computation. It is assessed as one figure for the block period and charged at the flat rate section 113 sets.

options.text: 60 per cent on the undisclosed income of the part-period from 1 April 2025 to the date of the search only, the six preceding years being reopened by separate notices under section 148 and taxed at ordinary rates
options.misconception: splits the block period, when section 158BC assesses the whole of it in a single block assessment
options.why: The part-period from the first day of April of the year of search is part of the block period, not a separate assessment. Everything inside the block period is determined together under section 158BC, which is what makes a separate reassessment for those years unnecessary.

options.text: ₹1,20,00,000 — a flat 60 per cent under section 113, applied to the undisclosed income of the whole block period as one, whatever Mr Batra's status
options.why: Section 113 puts one rate on whatever the block assessment throws up: the block period's undisclosed income in total, as settled by section 158BC, bears tax at sixty per cent, and sixty per cent of ₹2,00,00,000 is ₹1,20,00,000. The rate is flat and does not vary with the assessee's status, and it is increased by the surcharge levied by the Central Act applicable in the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the search was initiated.

options.text: ₹1,50,00,000 — 60 per cent tax of ₹1,20,00,000 plus a mandatory surcharge of 25 per cent on that tax
options.misconception: imports the twenty-five per cent surcharge that section 115BBE carries for unexplained credits into the section 113 charge
options.why: The sixty per cent is right; the surcharge is borrowed from the wrong section. Section 113 adds the surcharge levied by the Central Act for the relevant year, not the fixed twenty-five per cent that rides on section 115BBE.

citation.ref: Sections 158B(b), 158BA and 158BC read with Section 113, as inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024

items.scenario: A search under section 132 is initiated at Mr Batra's premises on 10 December 2025. The block assessment under section 158BC determines the total undisclosed income of the block period at ₹2,00,00,000. Mr Batra's other income for the years in the block period was returned and assessed in the ordinary way and is not in dispute. Ignore surcharge and cess.

items.stem: By when must the section 143(2) notice be served, and by when must the section 143(3) order be passed?

options.text: Notice by 30 September 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.misconception: uses the six-month period for a section 143(2) notice that the Finance Act, 2021 cut to three months
options.why: The order date is right. With effect from 1 April 2021 the notice period came down from six months to three, counted from the close of the financial year in which he filed the return, so the last date is 30 June 2027.

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2027 and order by 31 December 2027
options.misconception: uses the nine-month completion period that applied to assessment years before 2022-23
options.why: The notice date is right. For assessment year 2022-23 and every year after it the section 153(1) period is twelve months from the end of the assessment year, not nine, so the order date is 31 March 2028.

options.text: Notice by 30 January 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.misconception: counts the three months from the date the return was filed instead of from the end of the financial year in which it was filed
options.why: Three months from 30 October 2026 would indeed be 30 January 2027, and that is the wrong starting point. Section 143(2) starts counting at the close of the financial year during which the return went in, and that is 31 March 2027.

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.why: The return was furnished in financial year 2026-27, which ends on 31 March 2027, and section 143(2) allows three months from that end, giving 30 June 2027. Assessment year 2026-27 also ends on 31 March 2027, and section 153(1) allows twelve months from the end of the assessment year — the year that income first became liable to be assessed — giving 31 March 2028.
keywords: twelve months from the end of the assessment year

citation.ref: Section 143(2) proviso as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, and Section 153(1)

items.scenario: Cobalt Ltd furnishes its return of income for assessment year 2026-27 on 30 October 2026, within the due date under section 139(1). The Assessing Officer wishes to take the case up for scrutiny. No reference is made to the Transfer Pricing Officer and no other extension applies.

items.stem: Can Mr Nair take the order to a Dispute Resolution Committee under section 245MA?

options.text: Yes — the variations of ₹9,00,000 are within ₹10,00,000 and the returned income of ₹46,00,000 is within ₹50,00,000, so it is a specified order; the committee may also reduce or waive the penalty and grant immunity from prosecution
options.why: A specified order is one where the aggregate of the variations does not exceed ₹10,00,000 and the returned income does not exceed ₹50,00,000, and both tests are satisfied here. What makes this route worth taking is the relief no appellate authority can give: the committee may grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, and its order is due six months after the close of the month in which it admits the application.

options.text: No — his returned income of ₹46,00,000 exceeds the ₹10,00,000 limit the section sets for eligibility
options.misconception: applies the ₹10 lakh variation limit to the returned income and drops the separate ₹50 lakh income limit
options.why: The section has two different figures for two different things. Ten lakh rupees is the cap on the aggregate variations; fifty lakh rupees is the cap on the returned income. Reading one into the other rules out cases the section was written for.

options.text: Yes on the figures, but the committee has no power to touch the penalty, which he must contest separately before the Commissioner (Appeals)
options.misconception: denies the committee the penalty and prosecution powers section 245MA expressly gives it
options.why: The power to grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, exercised in accordance with Rule 44DAC, is the distinguishing feature of the Dispute Resolution Committee. Without it the route would offer nothing an appeal does not.

options.text: No — an assessment order can only be challenged by an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A
options.misconception: treats the appellate route as exclusive, when section 245MA offers an alternative for a specified order
options.why: Section 245MA was inserted to give a small taxpayer an option other than appeal. It is confined to a specified order and excludes search, survey and treaty-information cases, but within those limits it stands beside section 246A.

citation.ref: Section 245MA with the Explanation defining a specified order, read with Rule 44DAC and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022

items.scenario: Mr Nair returned an income of ₹46,00,000 for assessment year 2026-27. The assessment order proposes variations aggregating ₹9,00,000 and initiates penalty. The order is an ordinary scrutiny assessment — it is not founded on a search or survey, and no information under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A is involved. He would rather not appeal.

items.stem: What is taxable in the company's hands on this issue of shares?

options.text: ₹40,00,000 is taxable, but in the hands of the subscribers under section 56(2)(x) rather than in the company's hands
options.misconception: confuses the two provisions — section 56(2)(x) taxes a recipient who pays below fair market value, not one who pays above it
options.why: Section 56(2)(x) charges a person who receives property for less than its fair market value. These subscribers paid ₹500 for shares worth ₹300, which is more than fair market value, so nothing arises to them either.

options.text: Only the premium attributable to the non-resident subscribers is taxable, resident subscribers having always been outside the charge
options.misconception: reverses the position — the charge originally covered resident subscribers and was extended to non-residents in 2023, and the whole clause is now gone
options.why: Section 56(2)(viib) applied to resident subscribers from the start and was extended to non-residents with effect from assessment year 2024-25. Both limbs went together when the clause was omitted, so the distinction decides nothing now.

options.text: Nothing — section 56(2)(viib) was omitted with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so the ₹40,00,000 of premium above fair market value is not chargeable at all
options.why: The excess is ₹200 a share over the ₹300 fair market value on 20,000 shares, which is ₹40,00,000, and before the omission that whole amount would have been income from other sources. Section 56(2)(viib) was omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so nothing arises in previous year 2025-26. Section 68 would still be open had the subscribers not been established, but on these facts it is not.

options.text: ₹40,00,000 is taxable as income from other sources, being the consideration received in excess of the fair market value of the shares
options.misconception: applies section 56(2)(viib), which stands omitted from assessment year 2025-26
options.why: The arithmetic is the arithmetic of a provision that no longer exists. Two hundred rupees a share on 20,000 shares is ₹40,00,000, and that figure had a charge on it up to assessment year 2024-25 and none after.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025 (A.Y. 2025-26), read with Sections 68 and 56(2)(x)

items.scenario: Ardent Systems Pvt Ltd, an unlisted company in which the public are not substantially interested, issues 20,000 equity shares during previous year 2025-26 at ₹500 each to a mix of resident and non-resident investors. The fair market value determined under Rule 11UA is ₹300 a share. The company can establish the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of every subscriber.

items.stem: How is the ₹12,00,000 charged under section 115BBI?

options.text: At the maximum marginal rate rather than at 30 per cent, because income applied for the benefit of a specified person forfeits exemption
options.misconception: applies the maximum marginal rate that section 164(2) once carried, when section 115BBI now prescribes a rate of its own
options.why: Section 115BBI names thirty per cent for specified income and that rate displaces the older maximum marginal rate reasoning. Surcharge and cess ride on top of the thirty per cent but they do not turn it into the maximum marginal rate.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — 30 per cent of ₹10,00,000, the ₹2,00,000 of expenditure incurred in earning the income being deductible first
options.misconception: allows a deduction for expenditure against specified income, which section 115BBI(2) expressly forbids
options.why: The rate is right and the base is not. Sub-section (2) is the operative bar: no expenditure, no allowance and no set-off of loss may reduce specified income, so the ₹2,00,000 stays in.

options.text: ₹3,60,000 — 30 per cent of the whole ₹12,00,000, with no deduction for the ₹2,00,000 of expenditure and no set-off of the brought forward deficit
options.why: Income spent to benefit a person section 13(3) describes is specified income, and section 115BBI(2) allows no deduction for any expenditure, allowance or set-off of loss against it. The charge is therefore on the gross ₹12,00,000 at thirty per cent, which is ₹3,60,000. The trust's remaining income continues to be governed by sections 11 to 13 in the ordinary way.

options.text: The whole of the trust's income for the year loses exemption and is charged at 30 per cent, not merely the ₹12,00,000
options.misconception: treats a section 13 violation as forfeiting the trust's exemption entirely, when section 115BBI isolates only the specified income
options.why: Section 115BBI takes out the specified income and taxes it separately. Income applied for the charitable objects keeps its exemption under sections 11 and 12, which is what makes the section a targeted charge rather than a cancellation of registration.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBI(1) and 115BBI(2) with the Explanation, read with Sections 11(5) and 13(3)

items.scenario: A trust registered under section 12AB applies ₹12,00,000 of its income during previous year 2025-26 to benefit a person of the kind section 13(3) describes. It incurred ₹2,00,000 of expenditure in earning the income so applied, and it has a brought forward deficit it wishes to set off. Its remaining income is applied wholly for its charitable objects. Ignore surcharge and cess.

items.stem: What is its gross total income for previous year 2025-26, and what is carried forward?

options.text: Gross total income nil, with ₹1,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation carried forward indefinitely
options.why: Current year depreciation goes first, leaving business income of ₹7,00,000. The brought forward business loss of ₹5,00,000 goes next, leaving ₹2,00,000. The unabsorbed depreciation of ₹6,00,000 then absorbs that ₹2,00,000 and, being deemed part of the current year's allowance, a further ₹3,00,000 against house property income, leaving ₹1,00,000 to be carried forward indefinitely.

options.text: Gross total income ₹3,00,000, with ₹4,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation carried forward
options.misconception: confines unabsorbed depreciation to business income, when section 32(2) lets it be set off against income under any head except salaries
options.why: The order of set-off is handled correctly here, which is what makes the slip convincing. Unabsorbed depreciation is deemed part of the current year's allowance and can meet income under any head other than salaries, so it takes the ₹3,00,000 of house property income and only ₹1,00,000 remains.

options.text: Gross total income ₹5,00,000, the unabsorbed depreciation of previous year 2016-17 having lapsed after eight years
options.misconception: applies the eight-year carry-forward limit for a business loss to unabsorbed depreciation, which is carried forward without any time limit
options.why: Section 32(2) sets no time limit. The eight-year limit belongs to section 72 and governs the business loss of previous year 2019-20, which is still within time in assessment year 2026-27.

options.text: Gross total income ₹3,00,000, with ₹4,00,000 of business loss carried forward
options.misconception: sets off unabsorbed depreciation before the brought forward business loss, stranding the loss it should have absorbed first
options.why: Taking the ₹6,00,000 of depreciation against the ₹7,00,000 leaves only ₹1,00,000 for the business loss, so ₹4,00,000 of it is stranded and the house property income stays taxable because a business loss cannot reach it. The settled order puts the business loss ahead precisely to avoid that.

citation.ref: Section 32(2) read with Sections 72(2), 72(3) and 80

items.scenario: For previous year 2025-26 Meridian Ltd has business profits of ₹15,00,000 before depreciation, current year depreciation of ₹8,00,000, and income from house property of ₹3,00,000. It carries forward a business loss of ₹5,00,000 from previous year 2019-20 and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹6,00,000 from previous year 2016-17. All returns were filed within the time allowed by section 139(1).

items.stem: What is the disallowance under section 14A read with Rule 8D?

options.text: ₹10,50,000 — ₹1,50,000 of direct expenditure plus 1 per cent of ₹9,00,00,000; the absence of exempt income during the year is no answer
options.why: Rule 8D adds the expenditure directly relating to the exempt income to one per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the investment balances, so ₹1,50,000 plus ₹9,00,000 gives ₹10,50,000. That is below the ₹18,00,000 of total expenditure claimed, so the rule's own ceiling does not bite. The Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022 makes the section apply whether or not exempt income accrued during the year.

options.text: ₹9,00,000 — 1 per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the investment balances
options.misconception: applies only the one per cent limb of Rule 8D and drops the direct expenditure limb
options.why: Rule 8D has two limbs and both are added. Leaving out the ₹1,50,000 that relates directly to the exempt investments understates the disallowance by exactly that amount.

options.text: ₹1,50,000 — only the expenditure directly relating to the investments, the 1 per cent limb applying only in a year when exempt income is actually earned
options.misconception: makes the one per cent limb of Rule 8D conditional on exempt income having been earned, a condition neither the rule nor section 14A contains
options.why: Neither limb of Rule 8D is switched off by the absence of exempt income. Once the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee's own working, the rule is applied in full and both limbs are added.

options.text: Nothing — no exempt income was earned in the year, so there is no income in relation to which expenditure could have been incurred
options.misconception: relies on the pre-2022 case law that no disallowance arises in a year without exempt income, which the Explanation to section 14A now overrides
options.why: That argument won for years and was closed by statute. The Finance Act, 2022 added a non-obstante clause and an Explanation saying the disallowance is made whether or not such exempt income has accrued or arisen or been received during the previous year.

citation.ref: Section 14A(1) with its Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022, read with Rule 8D(2) and 8D(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Halcyon Ltd claims total expenditure of ₹18,00,000 in computing its business income for previous year 2025-26. Of that, ₹1,50,000 relates directly to investments whose income stays outside total income. Averaging each month's opening and closing balance for those investments, and then averaging those monthly figures across the year, gives ₹9,00,00,000. The company received no dividend and no other exempt income during the year. The Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the company's claim that nothing should be disallowed.

items.stem: Which of the three gains is long-term?

options.text: Only the listed shares are long-term; gold needs 36 months and the unlisted shares 24 months
options.misconception: keeps the thirty-six month category that was withdrawn on 23 July 2024
options.why: Gold did sit in a thirty-six month class until 23 July 2024, and on that reading 30 months would fall short. That class no longer exists — every asset outside the listed-security group is now long-term after twenty-four months, so the jewellery qualifies.

options.text: All three are long-term, shares of any company being long-term after 12 months
options.misconception: extends the twelve-month period for a listed security to shares of an unlisted company
options.why: The twelve-month period is given to a security listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, to a unit of an equity oriented fund, to a unit of the Unit Trust of India and to a zero coupon bond. Shares of an unlisted private company are none of those and take the twenty-four month period.

options.text: The listed shares and the gold jewellery are long-term; the unlisted shares are short-term
options.why: After the rationalisation of 23 July 2024 section 2(42A) leaves two periods only. A security listed on a recognised stock exchange is long-term after twelve months, so 14 months qualifies. Every other capital asset is long-term after twenty-four months, so the gold at 30 months qualifies and the unlisted shares at 20 months do not.

options.text: Only the gold jewellery is long-term; the 12-month period went when indexation went, leaving a single 24-month test for every asset
options.misconception: reads the rationalisation as collapsing everything into one period, when two survive
options.why: The amendment reduced three periods to two, not to one. The listed shares held 14 months are long-term on the twelve-month test, and the unlisted shares held 20 months remain short-term.

citation.ref: Section 2(42A) as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024

items.scenario: Mr Anand makes three sales during previous year 2025-26, all of them after 23 July 2024. He sells equity shares of a company listed on a recognised stock exchange in India that he had held for 14 months, gold jewellery he had held for 30 months, and equity shares of an unlisted private company he had held for 20 months. None of the three is a market linked debenture or a specified mutual fund.

items.stem: Is the gain long-term or short-term?

options.text: Short-term, the thirty-six month period still applying to a transfer made before 23 July 2024
options.why: The rationalisation of section 2(42A) reaches a transfer made on or after 23 July 2024. This transfer is three weeks earlier, so the position before it governs, and gold sat in the thirty-six month class. Thirty months falls short of it.

options.text: Long-term, twenty-four months being the period for every asset outside the listed-security group
options.misconception: states the rule correctly and applies it to a transfer it does not reach
options.why: Twenty-four months is right for a transfer made on or after 23 July 2024. This transfer was made before it, and an amendment cannot reach backwards over a sale already made.

options.text: Long-term — the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 governs the whole of previous year 2024-25, so the twenty-four month period applies to every transfer in it
options.misconception: applies the amendment across the entire previous year instead of from the date the amendment itself names
options.why: An amendment to a holding period is not applied by previous year but by the date named in it, and this one names 23 July 2024 for the transfer. A sale on 1 July 2024 and a sale on 1 December 2024 fall on opposite sides of the same previous year.

options.text: Neither — jewellery is a personal effect, so it is not a capital asset and no capital gain arises
options.misconception: forgets that jewellery is written out of the personal effects exclusion by name
options.why: Personal effects are indeed excluded from the meaning of a capital asset, but jewellery is named as an exception to that exclusion and stays a capital asset. So a gain does arise, and the only question is which period it is measured against.

citation.ref: Section 2(42A) as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024, read with the exclusion of personal effects in section 2(14) and the exception for jewellery within it

items.scenario: Ms Deepa sells gold jewellery on 1 July 2024. She had held it for 30 months. She holds nothing else that is sold in that year.

items.stem: What is the tax on the long-term capital gain?

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — the lower of 12.5 per cent on the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000 and 20 per cent on the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000
options.why: The proviso to section 112(1) lets a resident individual transferring land or a building acquired before 23 July 2024 take the lower of the two packages. Without indexation the gain is ₹40,00,000 less ₹10,00,000, that is ₹30,00,000, and 12.5 per cent of it is ₹3,75,000. With indexation the gain is ₹40,00,000 less ₹25,00,000, that is ₹15,00,000, and 20 per cent of it is ₹3,00,000. The lower figure stands.

options.text: ₹1,87,500 — 12.5 per cent of the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000
options.misconception: mixes the two limbs, taking the new rate on the indexed base when the proviso offers rate and base only as a pair
options.why: Both halves of this figure exist in the section and neither belongs with the other. The choice is between 12.5 per cent without indexation and 20 per cent with it; nobody is given indexation at the lower rate.

options.text: ₹6,00,000 — 20 per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: keeps the pre-amendment twenty per cent rate while dropping the indexation that went with it
options.why: This is the worst of both regimes and is nowhere in the section. Twenty per cent is available only on the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000, and on the unindexed gain the rate is 12.5 per cent.

options.text: ₹3,75,000 — 12.5 per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000, indexation having been withdrawn for every transfer made on or after 23 July 2024
options.misconception: overlooks the proviso preserving the comparison for a resident individual or HUF on land or a building acquired before 23 July 2024
options.why: The general rule is stated correctly and one exception has been missed. Indexation is gone as a general matter, but the proviso keeps the twenty per cent computation alive purely as a ceiling for this narrow class of taxpayer and asset.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) with its proviso, as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024

items.scenario: Mr Bhatia, a resident individual, sells on 1 December 2025 a plot of land he bought in June 2010 for ₹10,00,000. The sale consideration is ₹40,00,000, and the stamp duty value is lower than that. The indexed cost of acquisition, if indexation were applied, would be ₹25,00,000. Ignore surcharge and cess, and assume he claims no exemption under section 54EC or section 54F.

items.stem: What is the tax on the long-term capital gain?

options.text: ₹5,00,000 — twelve and a half per cent of the unindexed gain, with no comparison available
options.why: The proviso to section 112(1) is open to a resident individual and a Hindu undivided family and to nobody else. A firm gets the general rule alone: the gain is ₹60,00,000 less ₹20,00,000, that is ₹40,00,000, and twelve and a half per cent of it is ₹5,00,000. The date of purchase and the fact that the asset is land, which would matter for an individual, decide nothing here.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — twenty per cent of the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000, indexation surviving for a firm
options.misconception: treats the withdrawal of indexation as something the proviso took away rather than the general rule
options.why: Indexation was withdrawn for every transfer made on or after 23 July 2024, whoever makes it. The proviso does not preserve indexation for anyone; it gives a resident individual or Hindu undivided family a ceiling computed as though indexation had survived.

options.text: ₹8,00,000 — twenty per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹40,00,000
options.misconception: keeps the pre-amendment rate while dropping the indexation that went with it
options.why: Twenty per cent never applies to an unindexed gain. It survives only inside the proviso, and only on the indexed figure, and only for a resident individual or Hindu undivided family.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — the lower of the two computations, as for any resident selling land bought before 23 July 2024
options.misconception: reads the proviso as turning on the asset and the date alone, when it also names who may use it
options.why: The asset and the date are two of the three conditions and this firm meets both. The third is the taxpayer, and the proviso names a resident individual and a Hindu undivided family. A firm, a company, an association of persons, a body of individuals and a non-resident are all outside it.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) with its proviso, as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024 — the proviso being available to a resident individual or Hindu undivided family only

items.scenario: A partnership firm resident in India sells on 1 December 2025 a plot of land it bought in June 2010 for ₹20,00,000. The sale consideration is ₹60,00,000 and the stamp duty value is lower. The indexed cost of acquisition, if indexation were applied, would be ₹45,00,000. Ignore surcharge and cess, and assume no exemption is claimed.

items.stem: What is charged, under which head, and in which previous year?

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹21,00,000 in previous year 2023-24 and business profit of ₹12,00,000 in previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: charges the capital gain in the year of conversion instead of the year the stock is sold
options.why: Both amounts are computed correctly and one is put in the wrong year. Conversion is a transfer, but section 45(2) postpones the charge to the previous year in which the stock-in-trade is actually sold, which is the whole purpose of the sub-section.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹21,00,000 and business profit of ₹12,00,000, both in previous year 2025-26
options.why: Section 45(2) charges the capital gain in the year the stock is sold, so both figures fall in previous year 2025-26. The fair market value on the date of conversion is the deemed full value of consideration, giving ₹30,00,000 less the indexed cost of ₹9,00,000, that is ₹21,00,000. The surplus of the sale price over that same fair market value, ₹42,00,000 less ₹30,00,000, is business profit of ₹12,00,000.
keywords: fair market value on the date of conversion

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹33,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 and no business profit
options.misconception: takes the actual sale price as the full value of consideration for the capital gain, when section 45(2) deems the fair market value on the date of conversion to be it
options.why: Using ₹42,00,000 against the indexed cost of ₹9,00,000 gives ₹33,00,000 and taxes the whole rise as capital gain. The split exists because everything above the conversion-date value was earned as a trader, not as an investor.

options.text: Business profit of ₹37,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 and nothing under capital gains
options.misconception: treats the entire surplus over the original cost as business income, denying the split section 45(2) creates
options.why: Taking ₹42,00,000 less the original ₹5,00,000 produces ₹37,00,000 and loses both the indexation and the concessional long-term rate. The gain up to the date of conversion accrued to her as owner of a capital asset and stays under capital gains.

citation.ref: Section 45(2) read with Section 2(47)(iv) and Section 48

items.scenario: Ms Chitra acquired a plot in 2012 for ₹5,00,000. On 10 May 2023 she converted it into stock-in-trade of her real estate business, when its fair market value was ₹30,00,000. She sold the plot from that stock on 20 June 2025 for ₹42,00,000. The indexed cost of acquisition, taken up to the year of conversion, is ₹9,00,000.

items.stem: What is taxable in previous year 2025-26, and what happens to the earlier forfeiture?

options.text: ₹4,00,000 is income from other sources in previous year 2025-26, both forfeitures being taxed in the year the second one occurred
options.misconception: applies section 56(2)(ix) to an advance received before 1 April 2014, which the section does not reach
options.why: The charge attaches to the sum received on or after 1 April 2014. The ₹1,00,000 of 2010-11 was never within it, and pulling it into this year taxes an amount that is already destined to reduce the cost of the house.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 is taxable as capital gain in previous year 2025-26, forfeiture being the extinguishment of the buyer's right in the house
options.misconception: forces the receipt into capital gains when there is no transfer by the owner and the statute places it under other sources
options.why: Mr Deshpande still owns the house and has transferred nothing, so no capital gain can arise to him. Parliament settled the head by naming the receipt in section 56(2)(ix), which sits in the income from other sources chapter.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 is income from other sources in previous year 2025-26; the ₹1,00,000 forfeited in 2010-11 is not taxed now and will reduce the cost of acquisition when the house is sold
options.why: Section 56(2)(ix) taxes a forfeited advance received on or after 1 April 2014 as income from other sources in the year of forfeiture, so the ₹3,00,000 is charged in previous year 2025-26 and the proviso to section 51 keeps it out of the cost computation. The ₹1,00,000 was received before that date, so section 51 alone governs it and it is deducted from the cost of acquisition whenever the house is eventually transferred.

options.text: Nothing is taxable in previous year 2025-26; both amounts reduce the cost of acquisition when the house is sold
options.misconception: applies the pre-2014 section 51 treatment to a current forfeiture, ignoring the proviso that now excludes it
options.why: That was the law for the ₹1,00,000 and it is no longer the law for the ₹3,00,000. Once section 56(2)(ix) taxes a forfeited sum, the proviso to section 51 stops it being deducted from cost as well, so it is not taxed twice and not relieved twice.
