citation.ref: Taxation in India of gains on shares in an Indian company acquired on or after 1 April 2017, the cap of half the Indian rate on gains arising between 1 April 2017 and 31 March 2019, and the limitation of benefits clause denying that cap where affairs are arranged with the primary purpose of obtaining the concessional rate or where the claimant is a shell or conduit company

items.scenario: A company resident in Mauritius bought shares in an Indian company in June 2017 and sold them in January 2019 at a gain. It has a substantial operating business in Mauritius and did not acquire the shares with any Indian tax advantage in mind.

items.stem: How does the shell and conduit test apply to the two of them?

options.text: The Mauritius company keeps the benefit because it is under the limit, and the Singapore company is outside the test because Singapore has no such clause
options.misconception: reads the threshold as a floor a company must stay under, and assumes the Singapore treaty was left unamended
options.why: Both halves are wrong. Spending under the threshold is what triggers the deeming, so being under the limit is the losing position and not the safe one. And the Singapore treaty was amended along the same lines as the Mauritius treaty, with a limitation of benefits clause and a transition benefit of the same shape.

options.text: Neither is affected, because the expenditure thresholds bind only a company that has no employees at all
options.misconception: treats the threshold as an illustration of what a shell looks like rather than as a rule that deems
options.why: The treaty does not leave it to impression. It defines a shell or conduit company by reference to negligible or absent business operations, and then deems a resident to be one where its expenditure on operations in that State falls under the stated figure. Once spending is below the line the deeming applies, whatever the payroll shows.

options.text: Both are tested against ₹7,00,000, because the shares sold are shares of an Indian company
options.misconception: attaches the rupee figure to where the shares are, when it belongs to the State in which the expenditure was incurred
options.why: The figure follows the State whose operations are being measured. Expenditure in Mauritius is measured against Mauritian rupee 15,00,000; the figure of ₹7,00,000 is the one used where the State in question is India. Where the shares are issued has nothing to do with which threshold applies.

options.text: The Mauritius company is deemed a shell or conduit and loses the benefit; the Singapore company must meet the same expenditure test for the twelve months before the transfer
options.why: Spending in Mauritius below Mauritian rupee 15,00,000 over the relevant twelve months puts the first company inside the deeming provision, and a company deemed a shell or conduit gets no transition benefit. The second company's shares were bought after 1 April 2017 and sold before 1 April 2019, and for that combination the Singapore treaty applies the expenditure test to the twelve months running back from the date of transfer rather than from the date the gain arose.
keywords: twelve months running back from the date of transfer

citation.source: India-Mauritius Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, protocol of 10 May 2016; India-Singapore Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, as amended
citation.ref: The shell or conduit deeming provision and its expenditure thresholds of Mauritian rupee 15,00,000 and ₹7,00,000 over the twelve months preceding the date the gains arise, and the Singapore variant applying the expenditure test over the twelve months preceding the date of transfer for shares acquired after 1 April 2017 and sold before 1 April 2019

items.scenario: Two claims to the transition benefit come up together. A Mauritius company spent Mauritian rupee 12,00,000 on its operations in Mauritius over the twelve months running back from the date its gain arose. A Singapore company bought shares in an Indian company in August 2017 and sold them in December 2018.

items.stem: Which description matches the report?

options.text: All three are delivered by the group directly to each local tax administration that wants them
options.misconception: extends direct delivery to the country-by-country report, missing the government-to-government mechanism entirely
options.why: The country-by-country report is aggregate data on the whole group across every jurisdiction it operates in, and it is filed once, in the jurisdiction of tax residence of the ultimate parent entity. The rest of the world gets it through an automatic exchange arrangement, not by direct filing.

options.text: All three are filed in the jurisdiction of the ultimate parent and then exchanged between governments
options.misconception: extends the country-by-country filing mechanism to the whole three-tier structure
options.why: Only one of the three travels between governments. Pushing all three through an exchange mechanism would delay information that a local administration is meant to have in its hands, which is why the master file and the local file are delivered to it directly.

options.text: The country-by-country report can be exchanged only under a bilateral tax convention, so two countries with no such convention cannot exchange it
options.misconception: assumes a single legal base for the exchange, when the implementation package supplies three
options.why: Three model agreements between competent authorities sit in the implementation package, each built on a different base. Agreements made for the exchange of tax information are one such base. Bilateral tax conventions are another. The third is the Multilateral Convention on Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters, and two countries joined to it can exchange without any bilateral treaty between them.

options.text: The master file and the local file go from the group straight to the local tax administrations; the country-by-country report is filed where the ultimate parent is resident and reaches other jurisdictions by automatic exchange between governments
options.why: That is the division the structure rests on. Both the master file and the local file are delivered by the group directly to local tax administrations. The third document is not handed over that way at all: it is filed in the jurisdiction where the ultimate parent entity is tax resident, and the other jurisdictions receive it through automatic exchange between governments, which is why the implementation package needed model legislation and model agreements between competent authorities to make the exchange work.
keywords: delivered by the group directly to local tax administrations
where the ultimate parent entity is tax resident

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 13 — direct delivery of the master file and the local file to local tax administrations, filing of the country-by-country report in the ultimate parent's jurisdiction of tax residence with dissemination by automatic government-to-government exchange, and the implementation package of model legislation with three model competent authority agreements

items.scenario: A group is working out how each of the three documents required by the Action 13 structure is meant to reach the tax administrations that will read it.

items.stem: Which of the three carries what he is after, and what would he find in the other two?

options.text: The country-by-country report, but it carries only revenue and profit; tax paid and tax accrued are not part of it
options.misconception: remembers the report as a profit table and drops the two tax figures that make it useful
options.why: Both tax figures are in it, and setting them beside one another is much of the point: what a group paid in a jurisdiction and what it accrued there can differ, and the difference is itself something worth a question. Beside those two the report carries the revenue, the profit before income tax and indicators of where the economic activity in the group sits.

options.text: The country-by-country report; the master file describes the group's business and its transfer pricing policies at a high level, and the local file holds one country's transactional detail
options.why: The third tier is an annual return covering every tax jurisdiction the group does business in, and those four figures with the activity indicators are what it is made of. Neither of the other two would answer him. The master file carries high-level information about the group's worldwide business and its transfer pricing policies, standardised so that it serves every member of the group. The local file holds one country's transactional detail with its comparability analysis, the amounts involved in the related party transactions, and the reasoning behind the method chosen.
keywords: an annual return covering every tax jurisdiction the group does business in
high-level information about the group's worldwide business and its transfer pricing policies
one country's transactional detail with its comparability analysis

options.text: The master file, because it is the tier that looks at the group as a whole and so carries the figures for each jurisdiction
options.misconception: assumes the tier that takes the widest view must be the one holding the numbers for every country
options.why: The master file is wide but it is descriptive. It says what the group's business is and what its transfer pricing policies are; it is not a table of figures broken out jurisdiction by jurisdiction. Those figures sit in the third document, and it is there that tax paid and tax accrued are set out side by side.

options.text: The local file, because the financial information for the transactions is exactly what the local file is required to carry
options.misconception: stretches the local file's financial information to cover the group's position in every country
options.why: The financial information in a local file is about the transactions of that one country and the parties to them, and it sits beside a comparability analysis and the reasoning for the transfer pricing method selected. Nothing in it reaches across jurisdictions, which is why a separate document had to be designed for that purpose.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 13 — what each tier of the documentation structure contains: the master file's high-level account of the group's worldwide business and transfer pricing policies, the local file's transactional detail, amounts, comparability analysis and choice of method for one country, and the country-by-country report's annual figures for revenue, profit before income tax, income tax paid and income tax accrued with indicators of economic activity

items.scenario: An officer wants, for every country a group does business in, the revenue, the profit before income tax, and the income tax both paid and accrued, together with something that shows where the group's economic activity actually sits. The group has prepared all three documents the Action 13 structure calls for.

items.stem: Which Action Plan is aimed directly at this?

options.text: Action 9
options.why: Action 9 covers risk and capital, and both halves of it are in this fact pattern. Its rule on risk is that an allocation of risk written into a contract is respected only where the party said to bear it makes the decisions and exercises control over that risk. Its second half is about the return a capital-rich member of the group may earn on the funding it provides, where that return does not answer to the level of activity the funding member actually undertakes.
keywords: makes the decisions and exercises control over that risk
does not answer to the level of activity

options.text: Action 8
options.misconception: reaches for the intangibles Action because both are about profit ending up in a low-tax country
options.why: Action 8 is about controlled transactions involving intangibles, which move easily and are hard to value, and about pricing hard-to-value intangibles inside the arm's length principle. There is no intangible in this arrangement; the asset provided is cash.

options.text: Action 13
options.misconception: confuses the Action that prices a transaction with the Action that documents it
options.why: Action 13 is about transfer pricing documentation, so it would decide what this group must write down and to whom, not what return the funding member is entitled to. The pricing question belongs to the value creation Actions.

options.text: Action 10
options.misconception: treats every remaining transfer pricing problem as falling into the residual Action
options.why: Action 10 takes the other high-risk areas, and its three are transactions that are not commercially rational, methods used so as to pull profit away from the group's most economically important activities, and payments such as management fees and head office expenses that erode the base without matching value creation. Funding and risk have their own Action.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 9 within Actions 8 to 10 — contractual allocations of risk respected only where supported by actual decision-making and control, and the return to funding provided by a capital-rich group member where that return does not correspond to the activity undertaken

items.scenario: A group member in a low-tax country holds the cash and funds the rest of the group. Its contracts with the operating companies place the commercial risk of the funded projects on it, and it is paid a large return for bearing that risk. It has two employees, takes no decisions about the projects and controls nothing.

items.stem: What weakness were the three Actions written to answer?

options.text: The principle had itself become a leading cause of double taxation, and the three Actions exist to relieve that
options.misconception: inverts the record, since the principle is credited with preventing double taxation rather than causing it
options.why: The arm's length principle is treated as a practical and balanced standard which has kept a good deal of double taxation from arising, and that is one of the reasons it was kept in place. The complaint against it is different: the guidance on applying it could be manipulated, so the reported outcome stopped matching the economic activity.

options.text: The rules bind only associated enterprises, so groups escaped by routing their dealings through unrelated intermediaries
options.misconception: puts the weakness in the boundary of the rules rather than in the way they were being applied
options.why: Actions 8 to 10 say nothing about who the rules reach. They take three hard areas inside those rules — intangibles, risk and capital, and other high-risk transactions such as management fees and head office expenses — and not one of them turns on an unrelated intermediary being brought in.

options.text: The guidance around the principle leaned on how the group had allocated functions, assets and risks by contract, so profit could end up away from the activity that earned it
options.why: The principle asks what associated enterprises would have agreed had they been independent and dealing in comparable transactions in comparable conditions, and as a working standard it has served administrations and taxpayers alike. The weakness sat in the guidance around it, which leaned on how the group had allocated functions, assets and risks by contract; a contract is quickly written, so that guidance proved open to manipulation and profit could end up away from the activity that earned it. The three Actions close the gap without discarding the standard, and even hard-to-value intangibles are priced from inside the arm's length principle rather than outside it.
keywords: how the group had allocated functions, assets and risks by contract
profit could end up away from the activity that earned it
priced from inside the arm's length principle

options.text: The principle had been found unworkable, so these Actions replace it with a formula that splits a group's profit between countries by sales, assets and payroll
options.misconception: reads the phrase about aligning outcomes with value creation as the abandonment of the arm's length principle for a formulary split
options.why: Nothing was replaced. The existing standards were clarified and strengthened, and the agreed way of pricing hard-to-value intangibles was reached within the principle rather than as an alternative to it. What changed is that a contractual allocation of risk no longer settles the answer on its own; it counts only where the party said to bear the risk takes the decisions and controls it.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plans 8 to 10, aligning transfer pricing outcomes with value creation — the arm's length principle as a practical standard that has prevented double taxation, the vulnerability of the existing guidance through its emphasis on contractual allocations of functions, assets and risks, and the clarification and strengthening of the standards with hard-to-value intangibles priced within the principle

items.scenario: Transfer pricing between associated enterprises was already governed by the arm's length principle long before the BEPS project began, and a student cannot see what was left for Actions 8, 9 and 10 to do.

items.stem: Why did this keep the manufacturer outside the country's tax net, and what does Action 7 do about it?

options.text: It escaped tax because selling on behalf of another is preparatory or auxiliary, and Action 7 removes that exception altogether
options.misconception: puts the sales activity inside the preparatory or auxiliary exception, and reads the anti-fragmentation work as abolishing the exception
options.why: Selling a principal's goods to customers is the business itself, not something preparatory to it. The work on the exceptions runs alongside the commissionnaire changes rather than explaining them, and it narrows rather than abolishes: the exceptions are confined to activities genuinely preparatory or auxiliary, an anti-fragmentation rule adds together what an enterprise and its closely related entities do in a State where those operations are cohesive, and the construction exception is guarded against contracts split between closely related enterprises. All of it went into the 2017 OECD Model Tax Convention and into Part IV of the multilateral instrument, Articles 12 to 15.

options.text: It escaped tax because the goods were transferred at arm's length prices, and Action 7 tightens the pricing rules for such sales
options.misconception: treats an avoided taxable presence as a pricing problem
options.why: Pricing does not arise until there is something in the country to price profits into. The whole difficulty was that there was no taxable presence at all, which is a question about the definition of permanent establishment rather than about the arm's length principle.

options.text: The local seller never owned the goods, so it could be taxed only on its commission and the manufacturer had no permanent establishment to carry the sales; Action 7 treats the manufacturer as having a taxable presence where the intermediary's activities are meant to lead to contracts being concluded regularly for it, unless the intermediary acts as an independent business
options.why: Both halves are the point of the Action. Because the person concluding the sales does not own what it sells, no profit on the sales can be taxed in its hands, so it is taxed only on its commission, which is what it earns for the service it renders. The foreign owner meanwhile has no permanent establishment for the sales to be attributed to, so the profit leaves the country where the selling happens without the selling itself changing. The revised definition treats the enterprise as having a taxable presence where the intermediary's activities are meant to lead to contracts being concluded regularly for it, with an exception only for an intermediary carrying this on as an independent business of its own.
keywords: no permanent establishment for the sales to be attributed to
carrying this on as an independent business of its own

options.text: The arrangement always created a permanent establishment; what Action 7 changed was only how much profit is attributed to it
options.misconception: assumes the old definition already caught the arrangement, so the review looks like a profit attribution exercise
options.why: It did not create one, and that is why the definition had to be reviewed. Groups adopted these arrangements precisely because the former definition let the foreign enterprise sell in a country without a permanent establishment there.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 7 — commissionnaire arrangements and the revised treatment of an intermediary whose activities lead to the regular conclusion of contracts, the narrowing of the preparatory or auxiliary exceptions with an anti-fragmentation rule and a guard against split construction contracts, and implementation through the 2017 OECD Model Tax Convention and Articles 12 to 15 of the multilateral instrument

items.scenario: A foreign manufacturer used to sell through a distributor subsidiary in a country. It replaced that subsidiary with an arrangement under which a local company sells the goods in its own name, on the manufacturer's behalf, while the manufacturer keeps ownership of the goods until each sale. The local company keeps a commission. Nothing about what is done in that country has changed.

items.stem: How does Action 7 answer a structure of this shape?

options.text: What the enterprise does in the State and what its closely related entities do there are added together, where the operations are cohesive and the split produces a tax mismatch
options.why: This is the arrangement the anti-fragmentation rule was written for. The exceptions to the definition are confined to activities genuinely preparatory or auxiliary, and to stop a group getting round that by cutting one business into pieces, what the enterprise does in the State and what its closely related entities do there are added together, where the operations are cohesive and the split produces a tax mismatch. The same aggregation also settles whether an activity is preparatory or auxiliary in the first place, so no arm of the structure gets judged on its own.
keywords: added together, where the operations are cohesive and the split produces a tax mismatch
settles whether an activity is preparatory or auxiliary in the first place
confined to activities genuinely preparatory or auxiliary

options.text: Nothing in Action 7 reaches this, because the aggregation applies only within one enterprise and these are three separate companies
options.misconception: reads the words about closely related entities out of the rule, so separate incorporation looks like a defence
options.why: The rule is written for exactly that case. It aggregates what an enterprise does in a State with what its closely related entities do there, and if separate incorporation were a defence then fragmentation would succeed every time, since setting up another company is the cheapest step in the whole structure.

options.text: The guard against splitting a contract between closely related enterprises applies, so the three activities are read as one contract
options.misconception: reaches for the construction site guard, which answers a different way of dividing something up
options.why: That guard is real and it answers another device altogether: a building project cut into shorter contracts shared among closely related enterprises, so that no single one of them runs long enough for the site to become a permanent establishment. It is about a period of time on one site, not about several different activities carried on at once.

options.text: The enterprise has a taxable presence because the office concludes contracts on its behalf, so the exceptions never come into it
options.misconception: reaches for the better known intermediary limb where the facts do not support it
options.why: That limb bites where an intermediary's activities are meant to lead to contracts being concluded regularly for the foreign enterprise. Here the office takes orders and nothing in the facts says it settles the terms of any sale, so the answer has to run through the exceptions to the definition instead, which is the work the aggregation test does.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: Action Plan 7 — the narrowing of the exceptions to the permanent establishment definition to genuinely preparatory or auxiliary activities, the anti-fragmentation rule aggregating the activities of an enterprise with those of its closely related entities in the same State where the operations are cohesive and the division creates a tax mismatch, and the separate guard against construction contracts split between closely related enterprises

items.scenario: A foreign enterprise keeps a warehouse in a country from which goods are delivered to customers. One company closely related to it runs an office in the same country that takes customer orders, and a second closely related company does the after-sales work there. Each of the three says its own activity is preparatory or auxiliary and so creates no permanent establishment. Put together the three make one selling operation, and the split lowers what the group pays in that country.

items.stem: What did it conclude?

options.text: That no single tax rule brings it about on its own, and that it becomes possible through the way several things act on one another
options.why: The finding is about interaction, not about any one defective provision, and everything built afterwards follows from it. Three things were named as combining. Domestic rules are written in each country without being coordinated across borders with anybody else's. The standards governing taxation between countries have not kept up with the way global business has changed. And tax administrations, along with those who make policy, are short of the relevant information almost everywhere. The availability of harmful tax practices was identified as a further pressure area.

options.text: That transfer pricing rules are the single point of failure, so the package had to be built around the arm's length principle
options.misconception: elevates one workstream into the whole diagnosis because it produced the most Action Plans
options.why: Transfer pricing takes three of the fifteen Actions, but the report did not put the cause in it. Naming one rule as the point of failure is exactly the conclusion the report declined to reach.

options.text: That the cause is illegality, since these structures work only where a taxpayer breaks the law of one of the countries involved
options.misconception: reads avoidance as evasion, so the answer looks like enforcement rather than rule design
options.why: These arrangements are built out of compliance with each country's law, which is why it is hard even to say which treasury lost the revenue. That is what makes the answer a matter of designing and coordinating rules rather than of catching people breaking them.

options.text: That the cause is the gap between statutory rates, so the answer had to be a common minimum rate agreed between countries
options.misconception: reads back the later Pillar Two minimum into the 2013 diagnosis
options.why: A global minimum rate arrived years afterwards, with the two-pillar work. The 2013 report was pointing at uncoordinated rules, lagging standards and missing information, and the package it led to in 2015 was fifteen Action Plans rather than a rate.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2013 report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting — the conclusion that the cause lies in interaction rather than in any single rule, the three combining factors of uncoordinated domestic rules, lagging international tax standards and absent information at tax administrations and policymakers, and harmful tax practices as a further pressure area

items.scenario: A student is asked what the 2013 report concluded about the cause of base erosion and profit shifting, before any Action Plan had been written.

items.stem: What reason is given for that?

options.text: They are outside the Inclusive Framework, so the measures agreed were not designed with them in mind
options.misconception: assumes developing countries were left out of the framework, when it was created so that they could take part as equals
options.why: The Inclusive Framework was set up so that countries and jurisdictions outside the OECD and the G20 could take part on an equal footing, developing economies particularly, and it reviews and monitors implementation with them in it. Their exposure comes from the shape of their revenue, not from exclusion.

options.text: They have fewer tax treaties, so they cannot obtain information from other countries
options.misconception: substitutes a plausible administrative weakness for the reason actually given
options.why: A shortage of information is named, but as one of the three things that combine to make these strategies possible everywhere, and it is described as sitting at tax administrations and policymakers generally. It is not the reason given for the uneven burden between rich and poor countries.

options.text: They rely more heavily on corporate income tax for their revenue
options.why: Corporate income tax carries a larger share of the revenue in a developing country than it does elsewhere, so the same loss of taxable corporate profit takes a bigger bite out of what the state has to spend. The reason is about the composition of the revenue base and not about weak administration or a shortage of treaties.
keywords: larger share of the revenue in a developing country

options.text: Their statutory corporate tax rates are higher, so the incentive to shift profit out of them is greater
options.misconception: reasons from where profit would be shifted from rather than from what the loss costs the state
options.why: The reason given is what corporate tax contributes to the budget, not what the headline rate is. A country can have a modest rate and still depend on that tax for much of what it collects, and it is the dependence that decides how much the erosion hurts.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2013 report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting — the disproportionate effect on developing countries arising from their greater reliance on corporate income tax

items.scenario: The material states that developing countries suffer from base erosion and profit shifting disproportionately.

items.stem: What are these two drafts called, and which shape does India put in most of its agreements?

options.text: The first is the exemption method and the second is the credit method, and India uses the exemption method in the greater part of its agreements
options.misconception: has both names right and then attaches the wrong one to India's own practice
options.why: The two names are right here and the practice is not. Exemption does appear in India's agreements, but credit is the shape the majority of them use, and a candidate who knows the definitions and stops there gets the second half of this question wrong.

options.text: The first is the credit method and the second is the exemption method, and India uses the exemption method in the greater part of its agreements
options.misconception: swaps the two names, so that leaving an income alone reads as giving credit for it
options.why: The names are the wrong way round. Credit is what the second draft describes, because a credit only makes sense where both countries have charged the income and one of them is setting the other's tax off. A country that charges nothing has nothing to set anything against.

options.text: Both drafts describe unilateral relief, since in each of them the relief comes out of the residence country's pocket
options.misconception: decides bilateral against unilateral by asking which country bears the cost, when the question is whether two Governments agreed it
options.why: What makes relief bilateral is that two Governments settled it between themselves in an agreement and worked out the basis on which it would be given. Which of the two ends up giving up revenue is a different question. Unilateral relief is relief a country gives its own residents with no agreement behind it at all, and in India that is section 91.

options.text: The first is the exemption method and the second is the credit method, and India uses the credit method in the greater part of its agreements
options.why: Bilateral relief is given in one of two shapes. Under the exemption shape a particular income is charged in only one of the two countries. Under the credit shape it is charged in both, each country applying its own law read with the agreement, and the country where the recipient resides then allows him credit for what the source country took. The greater part of India's agreements are built on credit rather than on exemption, which is also why Rule 128 exists to work the credit out.
keywords: charged in only one of the two countries
allows him credit for what the source country took

citation.ref: Sections 90 and 90A read with Rule 128 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — bilateral relief in its exemption and credit shapes, and India's use of the credit shape in most of its agreements

items.scenario: Two draft articles are on the table in a treaty negotiation. Under the first draft, a particular class of income would be charged in one of the two countries only, and the other country would leave it alone altogether. Under the second draft, both countries would charge the income under their own laws as modified by the agreement, and the country in which the recipient resides would then let him set the source country's tax against its own demand.

items.stem: Has she read the agreement correctly?

options.text: Yes — since the agreement lets both countries charge the fee, she may offer it in whichever of the two taxes it more lightly
options.misconception: turns an allotment of taxing rights into a choice of where the taxpayer would rather pay
options.why: An agreement is not a menu. Where it lets both countries charge an income, both of them may charge it, and the relief arrives as a set-off in the country where she lives. What she may choose is a different thing — whether the agreement or the Act governs her, where one of them treats her better — and that choice does not move the fee off the Indian return.

options.text: No — on that footing the fee still enters her Indian total income, and the agreement works by letting her set the Country R tax against India's demand rather than by taking the fee out of the return
options.why: The article she is describing is built on the credit shape. There, the fee is charged in both countries, each country charging under its own law as the agreement modifies it, and India, being where she lives, then gives her credit for what Country R collected. Dropping a receipt out of total income belongs to the other shape, under which one of the two countries stands back from the income entirely. India writes the credit shape into the greater number of its agreements, so this is the reading she will meet most often.
keywords: the fee is charged in both countries
gives her credit for what Country R collected
stands back from the income entirely

options.text: No, but the set-off she wants is open to her only where India has no agreement with the other country, section 91 being the provision that gives credit
options.misconception: ties credit to the absence of an agreement, leaving bilateral relief with only one shape
options.why: Section 91 does give credit where no agreement covers the country, and it is not the only place credit is found. Two Governments commonly settle the credit shape in the agreement itself, and relief given that way is bilateral. Section 91 is what a resident falls back on when there is no agreement at all.

options.text: Yes — a receipt that has already suffered tax in the source country is left out of total income in India, which is what relief from double taxation means
options.misconception: reads every kind of relief as an exemption, so any foreign tax paid becomes a reason to drop the income here
options.why: Relief comes in two shapes and only one of them removes the income. Under the exemption shape a particular income is charged in one of the two countries alone. Under the credit shape both of them charge it and the country of residence allows a set-off, which is the shape this article uses. Reading the first into an agreement written on the second takes an amount off the return that the agreement never meant to remove.

citation.ref: Sections 90 and 90A on bilateral relief read with section 91 — the credit shape charging an income in both countries with a set-off in the country of residence, against the exemption shape under which one country alone charges it

items.scenario: Malini is resident in India. She earns a fee from a client in Country R, and Country R has already taxed that fee under its own law. India's agreement with Country R deals with this class of income on the footing that both countries may charge it and that the country where the recipient lives will then set off what the other one took. Filing her return in India, Malini leaves the Country R fee out of her total income altogether, saying it has already borne tax once and that stopping a second charge is what the agreement is for.

items.stem: What is the doubly taxed royalty income, and at what rate is the section 91 deduction worked out on it?

options.text: ₹2,50,000, at 16 per cent
options.misconception: applies the Indian rate because Indian tax is what the deduction reduces
options.why: The amount is right and the rate is not. Section 91 takes the lower of the Indian average rate and that country's average rate, and applies the Indian rate only where the two are equal. Relieving at 16 per cent here would hand back more Indian tax than the other country ever collected.

options.text: ₹5,50,000, at 10 per cent
options.misconception: takes the expenses out but leaves the Chapter VI-A deduction in the doubly taxed figure
options.why: This gets the expenses right and stops one step early. A deduction under Chapter VI-A removes its amount from the charge in India just as surely as an expense does, so the ₹3,00,000 was taxed in the other country and not here. It was not taxed twice, and relief is only for what was.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, at 10 per cent
options.misconception: uses the gross receipt because that is the figure the other country taxed
options.why: What the other country charged is only one half of the test. The section relieves income charged in both places, so the Indian side has to be measured too, and on the Indian side this royalty entered total income at ₹2,50,000 after expenses and after section 80QQB.

options.text: ₹2,50,000, at 10 per cent
options.why: Only the part of the royalty that actually reaches his total income in India has been charged in both countries. The ₹50,000 of expenses never entered it and neither did the ₹3,00,000 the Chapter VI-A deduction took out, so ₹6,00,000 less ₹50,000 less ₹3,00,000 leaves ₹2,50,000. That is the point the Rajasthan High Court settled in Dr. R.N. Jhanji. The rate is the lower of the two averages, and 10 per cent is below 16 per cent.
keywords: Only the part of the royalty that actually reaches his total income
the Chapter VI-A deduction took out

citation.ref: Section 91 read with section 80QQB and CIT v. Dr. R.N. Jhanji (1990) 185 ITR 586 (Raj.) — doubly taxed income confined to the part entering total income, and the lower of the Indian average rate and the foreign average rate

items.scenario: Mr Bhatia is resident in India for previous year 2025-26. He wrote a novel and earned royalty of ₹6,00,000 gross from a publisher in a country with which India has no agreement, spending ₹50,000 to earn it, and the other country charged him tax on that royalty. In computing his total income he is allowed ₹3,00,000 as a deduction under section 80QQB. His average rate of tax in India works out to 16 per cent and his average rate of tax in that country to 10 per cent. Every condition in section 91 is satisfied.

items.stem: How much relief does section 91 give her in total?

options.text: ₹84,000 — 12 per cent of the whole ₹7,00,000
options.misconception: finds the lowest rate anywhere in the problem and applies it to everything
options.why: The lower-of-two test is run once for each country, and Country P's rate has nothing to do with the income that arose in Country Q. Carrying one country's rate across understates the relief on the Q slice by ₹36,000.

options.text: ₹1,26,000 — 18 per cent of the whole ₹7,00,000
options.misconception: applies the single Indian average rate to the aggregate foreign income without comparing it with anything
options.why: The Indian average rate is one number for the year, but it is a candidate in each comparison rather than the answer to any of them. Applied to Country P's slice it loses to the lower 12 per cent, so ₹24,000 of this figure is relief the section does not give.

options.text: ₹1,20,000 — 12 per cent of ₹4,00,000 plus 24 per cent of ₹3,00,000
options.misconception: uses each country's own rate throughout, treating the foreign rate as the measure of the relief
options.why: Country Q's 24 per cent is the higher of the two rates in that comparison, so it is exactly the one the section does not use. Relief is capped by what India charged on the income; a country that taxes more heavily than India cannot make India refund the difference.

options.text: ₹1,02,000 — 12 per cent of ₹4,00,000 plus 18 per cent of ₹3,00,000
options.why: The comparison is made country by country, not once over the whole foreign income. Against Country P the Indian 18 per cent is set beside Country P's 12 per cent, and 12 per cent is the lower, giving ₹48,000. Against Country Q the same Indian 18 per cent is set beside Country Q's 24 per cent, and this time the Indian rate is the lower, giving ₹54,000. The two answers are then added, and one slice ends up relieved at a foreign rate while the other is relieved at India's.
keywords: this time the Indian rate is the lower

citation.ref: Section 91 with its Explanation — the Indian average rate compared separately with each foreign country's average rate, the lower applied to that country's doubly taxed income, and the results added

items.scenario: Ms Prabhu is resident in India for previous year 2025-26 and has income from two countries, with neither of which India has an agreement. Her doubly taxed income from Country P is ₹4,00,000 and her average rate of tax in Country P is 12 per cent. Her doubly taxed income from Country Q is ₹3,00,000 and her average rate of tax in Country Q is 24 per cent. Her average rate of tax in India is 18 per cent. Every condition in section 91 is satisfied for both countries.

items.stem: How is the term to be read?

options.text: Neither the Act nor a notification can supply the meaning, so the article cannot be applied until the two Governments amend the agreement
options.misconception: reads a gap in the agreement as a gap in the law, when the Act says where the meaning comes from
options.why: An agreement is not expected to define every word it uses, and the Act sets out the order in which a meaning is found — the agreement's own definition, then the Act's, then a notified meaning. An undefined term is an ordinary event, not a breakdown.

options.text: The term takes its ordinary dictionary meaning, an agreement being an international instrument that domestic definitions cannot reach
options.misconception: keeps the agreement and the Act in separate compartments, which is the opposite of what section 90 does
options.why: The agreement operates in India through section 90, and the same section says where an undefined term gets its meaning. A separate question — which is not this one — is whether the meaning taken is the one current when the agreement was signed or the one current when it is applied.

options.text: The notified meaning applies, and it is treated as having operated from the day the agreement came into force rather than from the day it was published
options.why: Where a term used in an agreement is not defined in the agreement or in the Act but the Central Government has assigned it a meaning by a notification still in force, that meaning is what the term carries, and the Act deems it to have taken effect from the day the agreement came into force. Where the Act itself defines a term the agreement leaves alone, the Act's meaning applies together with any explanation the Central Government has given it. Either way the reading is settled by law rather than left open, and the assessee's date argument is the thing the deeming provision was written to close.
keywords: the Central Government has assigned it a meaning
the day the agreement came into force

options.text: The notified meaning applies, but only to years beginning after the notification was published, earlier years being read on the Act's definition
options.misconception: treats the notification like an ordinary amendment that speaks from its own date
options.why: This is the argument the section answers in terms. A notification of this kind is not an amendment of the agreement; it declares what a word in the agreement has meant, and the Act therefore backdates its effect to the day the agreement came into force.

citation.ref: Section 90(1) and section 90A(1) on the meaning of a term used in an agreement — the agreement's own definition, the Act's definition with any Central Government explanation, and a notified meaning deemed effective from the date the agreement came into force

items.scenario: An article of India's agreement with a foreign country uses a term that the agreement nowhere defines. The Income-tax Act, 1961 does define it, and the Central Government has since issued a notification in the Official Gazette assigning that term a meaning for the purposes of agreements of this kind. The notification is still in force. The assessee argues that the notified meaning can bite only from the date the notification was published, so that earlier years must be read some other way.

items.stem: Must the notified meaning be applied to this article?

options.text: No — and because there is no third place to look for a meaning, the article cannot be applied at all until the agreement is amended
options.misconception: reads the failure of one route to a meaning as leaving the article unusable
options.why: Setting a notified meaning aside does not leave the reader with nothing. The article is then read in its own context in the ordinary way, which is exactly what the words about the context calling for something else contemplate. A term nobody has defined is a common event in an agreement and it does not disable the article that uses it.

options.text: No — the notified meaning is taken subject to the context calling for something else, and it cannot be used to produce a reading at odds with the Act or with the agreement
options.why: A notified meaning is the answer where a term is left undefined by both the agreement and the Act, and the same provision attaches two limits to it in the same breath: the meaning yields where the context requires another reading, and it may not be given an effect that cuts across the Act or the agreement. Those limits belong to the rule; they are not an exception argued around it. From what date such a meaning operates once it does apply is a separate question and not this one.
keywords: the meaning yields where the context requires another reading
cuts across the Act or the agreement
undefined by both the agreement and the Act

options.text: Yes — a notification of the Central Government has statutory force, so once one is in force the term can bear no other meaning
options.misconception: takes the notified meaning as absolute and drops the two conditions the same provision fastens to it
options.why: The notified meaning is the ordinary answer and it is not an unconditional one. The provision supplying it says in the same sentence that it gives way where the context calls for something else, and that it holds only so far as it does not run against the Act or the agreement. A notification that cannot be squared with the article it is being read into is not doing the work the provision gave it.

options.text: Yes, but only where the two Governments have accepted the notified meaning between themselves in some later exchange
options.misconception: demands the treaty partner's consent for a step India's own Act provides for
options.why: A notification of this kind is a domestic instrument, and nothing in the Act makes it wait on the other country. What confines it is the context of the article and its fit with the Act and the agreement, and those are judged by the authority applying it rather than negotiated across a table.

citation.ref: Section 90(1) and section 90A(1) on a term left undefined by the agreement and by the Act — a notified meaning applying unless the context calls for something else, and only so far as it does not run against the Act or the agreement

items.scenario: A term in India's agreement with a foreign country is left undefined by the agreement and by the Income-tax Act, 1961 alike. The Central Government has notified a meaning for that term and the notification is in force. Carrying the notified meaning into the article in dispute would produce a reading that sits against what the agreement provides elsewhere, and the article's own context points the other way. The Assessing Officer says a notification of the Central Government is binding and there is nothing further to argue.

items.stem: What is the Indian tax position of the two companies?

options.text: Anvaya Services Ltd is the permanent establishment, but only the margin it earns on this contract is taxed in Meridian Corp's hands
options.misconception: skips to the attribution question without first asking whether an establishment exists at all
options.why: Attributing profit is the step that follows a finding that an establishment exists. Here there is no business connection, so there is nothing to attribute anything to, and the margin is simply Anvaya's own taxable income.

options.text: Meridian Corp is taxable in India on the profit from this work, because the work itself is being done inside India
options.misconception: locates the taxable event in where the work happens rather than in whether the foreign enterprise has an establishment here
options.why: Under an agreement a non-resident's business profits are reached only through a permanent establishment. Work being physically performed in India by somebody else's employees does not by itself give the foreign enterprise a fixed place of business through which it carries on its own business.

options.text: Anvaya Services Ltd is Meridian Corp's permanent establishment, as an Indian entity doing a foreign enterprise's work always is
options.misconception: makes every outsourcing arrangement an establishment, which removes the business-connection question the circular turns on
options.why: The circular sets the two cases side by side precisely because they part company. With no business connection the Indian entity stands alone; with one, it may be treated as the establishment. An independent contractor serving many customers on its own terms is the clearest example of the first case.

options.text: Anvaya Services Ltd is assessed on its own income as a separate taxpayer, it is not Meridian Corp's permanent establishment, and Meridian Corp picks up no Indian liability from the arrangement
options.why: Where a foreign enterprise outsources work to an Indian entity and no business connection runs between them, the Indian entity is taxed on what it earns as a taxpayer in its own right and is not the foreign enterprise's permanent establishment. The foreign enterprise becomes liable here only if the Indian unit does amount to its permanent establishment, and on these facts it does not.
keywords: taxed on what it earns as a taxpayer in its own right
is not the foreign enterprise's permanent establishment
only if the Indian unit does amount to its permanent establishment

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 5/2004 dated 28 September 2004 read with section 9(1)(i) — an outsourcing entity assessed separately where no business connection exists, and the foreign enterprise liable only where the Indian unit is its permanent establishment

items.scenario: Meridian Corp, resident in a country with which India has a comprehensive agreement, hands its claims-processing work to Anvaya Services Ltd, an unrelated Indian company that does the same kind of work for a dozen other customers and prices each contract on its own terms. On the facts there is no business connection between Meridian Corp and Anvaya Services Ltd. Meridian Corp has nothing else in India.

items.stem: What is taxed in India, and how is the figure arrived at?

options.text: The profit attributable to the establishment, but with no deduction for the head office's executive and general administrative expenses, since those were spent outside India
options.misconception: makes deductibility turn on the country the money was spent in
options.why: The rule is the opposite. Expenses incurred for the purposes of the establishment are deducted whether they were incurred in the country where it stands or elsewhere, executive and general administrative expenses among them. Which expenses qualify is then a question for accepted accounting principles and the Act.

options.text: Only so much of the enterprise's profit as is attributable to the establishment, worked out as though it were a distinct enterprise dealing at arm's length with its own head office, with expenses laid out for its purposes deducted whether they were spent in India or abroad
options.why: The charge reaches the profit attributable to the establishment and no more. The attribution is made by treating the establishment as a distinct enterprise, engaged on work of the same kind under comparable conditions, dealing wholly independently with the business it forms part of, so the services passing between them are priced as though an unconnected business were on the other side — the arm's length principle. Expenses incurred for the establishment's purposes are allowed, executive and general administrative expenses included, and where they were spent makes no difference.
keywords: the profit attributable to the establishment and no more
where they were spent makes no difference

options.text: Whatever the unit and the head office have recorded between themselves, a figure agreed inside one enterprise being the only price there is
options.misconception: accepts an internal recharge as the price, which is exactly what the arm's length fiction exists to displace
options.why: There is no bargain between two parties inside one enterprise, so the recorded figure proves nothing about value. The profit given to the establishment is the profit it would have made had it been dealing with an entirely separate business at the prices ruling in the ordinary market.

options.text: The whole of the enterprise's worldwide profit, a permanent establishment in India making it taxable here on everything it earns
options.misconception: reads a permanent establishment as making the foreign enterprise resident in India
options.why: A permanent establishment gives the source country a claim on the profits that belong to that establishment. It does not turn a non-resident into a resident, and worldwide income is a residence-based charge.

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 5/2004 dated 28 September 2004 — profits limited to what is attributable to the permanent establishment, the establishment treated as a distinct and separate enterprise dealing independently, and expenses for its purposes deductible wherever incurred

items.scenario: On different facts, a foreign enterprise is found to have a business connection with the Indian back-office unit that handles its work, and the unit is treated as its permanent establishment in India. The enterprise's head office abroad ran the recruitment, technology and senior management functions that the unit depends on, and it spent that money outside India. The enterprise says that since the unit is not a separate company, no price need be put on what passes between the two.

items.stem: What is being described here?

options.text: Neither, because a tax on distributed profits falls on the company's own act of distributing and is not a tax on the dividend at all
options.misconception: treats the two charges as landing on different things, when the point of the example is that they land on one economic sum
options.why: The two charges reach the same profits, once as the company's and once as the shareholder's. That is precisely why the case is given a name of its own rather than being dismissed as two unrelated taxes.

options.text: Juridical double taxation — the same income has been taxed twice, and that is what the term means
options.misconception: defines juridical double taxation by the income alone, dropping the requirement that the same person be taxed twice
options.why: Juridical double taxation is what happens when source rules overlap and two countries charge the same person on the same income under their own laws. Here two different taxpayers are charged, which is the distinction the two names exist to mark.

options.text: Economic double taxation — the same income is reached in two countries but in the hands of two different persons, so there is no identity of subject
options.why: Two countries have taxed one economic sum, but the taxpayers are not the same person: one charge falls on the company and the other on its shareholder. That absence of subject identity is what separates this from the ordinary case, and the module's own illustration is this one — a distribution tax on the company in one country and a tax on the shareholder in the other.
keywords: the taxpayers are not the same person

options.text: Economic double taxation, and Ms Rao may claim unilateral relief under section 91 for the tax Country X charged Helio Ltd
options.misconception: reads unilateral relief as covering any income taxed twice, when it answers the case of one person taxed twice on his own income
options.why: The classification is right and the remedy is not. Section 91 relieves a resident for tax he himself paid abroad on income assessed in his own hands. Ms Rao did not pay Country X's tax; Helio Ltd did, on its own profits.

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of juridical and economic double taxation in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, read with section 91 — the two kinds distinguished by whether the same person is taxed twice

items.scenario: Country X charges Helio Ltd, a company resident there, a tax on the profits it distributes to its shareholders. Ms Rao, who lives in Country Y and holds shares in Helio Ltd, is charged tax by Country Y on the dividend she receives out of those same profits.

items.stem: How do the connecting factors fall for the two companies?

options.text: Karnik Exports Ltd is doing business with Country Z, and nothing it might later do short of opening a place of business there could ever make it taxable in Country Z
options.misconception: hardens a general position into an absolute one, and misses that a significant economic presence can create a liability without any physical place
options.why: The first half is right and the word "ever" is wrong. An enterprise with a significant economic presence in another country can be taxed there without a place of business in it — India's own law reaches a non-resident that way — so the general position holds until such a presence arises.

options.text: Both are doing business in Country Z, since in each case goods end up in that country's market
options.misconception: locates the business wherever the goods arrive, which erases the distinction the two connecting factors rest on
options.why: Where the goods finish is not the test. The question is whether the enterprise is itself carrying on business inside the other country's territory, and an exporter selling from India is not.

options.text: Karnik Exports Ltd has a source link in Country Z because its customers are there, so both companies are taxable in Country Z
options.misconception: builds a source link out of the customer's location alone
options.why: A customer abroad is what makes an export an export. If the buyer's address created a source link, every exporter everywhere would be taxable in every market it sells to, and the with-against-in distinction would have no work to do.

options.text: Karnik Exports Ltd is doing business with Country Z and is generally taxed at home on its residence link alone, while Sarode Ltd is doing business in Country Z and takes a source link there in addition to its residence link at home
options.why: The distinction turns on one preposition. Selling to buyers abroad without carrying on any business inside their country leaves an enterprise with its residence link and nothing else, so it is generally taxed at home alone. Running a branch inside the other country is carrying on business there, which adds a source link, and both countries then have a claim.
keywords: leaves an enterprise with its residence link and nothing else
Running a branch inside the other country

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of connecting factors in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, read with section 9(1)(i) on significant economic presence — residence and source as the two links, and business done with a country distinguished from business done in it

items.scenario: Karnik Exports Ltd, resident in India, ships machine parts to buyers in Country Z. It has no office, no staff and no plant there; the goods are sold from India and shipped out. Its competitor, Sarode Ltd, also resident in India, has instead set up a branch in Country Z which buys, stores and sells locally.

items.stem: Is the officer right?

options.text: Yes — a treaty allots the right and each country's own law then imposes the tax, so if Country M's law imposes none, the charge falls back to India
options.misconception: reads "domestic law supplies the charge" as letting the country that gave up the right pick it up again
options.why: Domestic law supplies the charge for the country that holds the right, and it has nothing to give back to the country that gave the right away. The allotment is the first step and it is not conditional on what the second step produces.

options.text: No, but only because the agreement is a comprehensive one; under a limited agreement India could charge the income anyway
options.misconception: turns the limited-against-comprehensive distinction into a rule about how firmly an allotted right binds
options.why: Whether an agreement is limited or comprehensive settles which incomes it covers at all, not how strongly it binds on the ones it does cover. India's agreement with Pakistan is limited to income from international air transport; within that field its allocations bind exactly as any other agreement's do.

options.text: Yes — a treaty exists to relieve double taxation, so where no double taxation has in fact arisen the article has nothing to operate on
options.misconception: reads the purpose of an agreement as a condition attached to each of its articles
options.why: Relieving double taxation is why the countries negotiated, not a test each article must separately pass before it applies. An allocation article says which country may charge, and it says so once and for all rather than year by year according to what the other country did.

options.text: No — once the right has been allotted, the article works whether or not the other country actually charges anything, and an income taxed nowhere is a known consequence of allotting rights rather than a reason to take one back
options.why: A treaty hands out jurisdiction; it does not itself levy. Where one country has agreed to stand back from an income, that standing back holds independently of whether the other country charges it, which is what the Distributive Rule means. The result can be an income taxed nowhere, and the reason for tolerating it is forward-looking — the country holding the right may withdraw its exemption later, and the article then bites without anything being renegotiated.
keywords: holds independently of whether the other country charges it

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of the Classification and Assignment or Distributive Rule in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties — an agreement allotting jurisdiction while domestic law imposes the tax, and the double non-taxation that can follow

items.scenario: A comprehensive agreement between India and Country M gives Country M the sole right to charge a particular class of income. Country M's own law happens to exempt that class of income altogether, so the recipient pays nothing anywhere. An Assessing Officer says the article cannot have been meant to produce that result, and that India may therefore charge the income after all.

items.stem: Can the demand stand on the article alone?

options.text: Yes — the agreement is notified under section 90 and operates as law here, so an article giving India the right is by itself enough to charge
options.misconception: reads an instrument that carries the force of law as though every article in it were a charging provision
options.why: Carrying the force of law and imposing a charge are two different things. The article names which of the two countries may tax; it does not say who is liable, on what amount, or at what rate, and a charge has to answer all three. Those answers come from the Act.

options.text: Yes, but only up to the rate the article names, that rate being the charge the agreement itself lays down
options.misconception: mistakes a ceiling written into an allocation article for a rate at which the agreement levies
options.why: A rate in an article of this kind is a ceiling on what the country holding the right may take. It is not a demand of its own, and it has something to cap only where that country's own law has charged something first, which here it has not.

options.text: No, because under section 90(2) the assessee may take whichever of the agreement and the Act treats him better, and he elects the Act
options.misconception: reaches for the more-beneficial rule where the real answer is that no charge ever arose
options.why: That rule chooses between two charges. Here only one of the two instruments could ever have charged the receipt and it does not reach it, so there is nothing to choose between and nothing to elect. The conclusion is the same as the right answer and the reason is not, and the reason is what the next question of this shape will turn on.

options.text: No — the article settles which country may tax the receipt, and a charge must still be found in the Act, so where the Act reaches nothing there is nothing to collect
options.why: An agreement shares out taxing jurisdiction between the two countries and levies nothing itself. Once the jurisdiction has been allotted, each country's own law decides what is taxed and at what rate, so a right handed to India is permission to use the Act and not a replacement for it. If the Act is amended later to reach the receipt, the article is already in place and nothing has to be renegotiated.
keywords: shares out taxing jurisdiction between the two countries
each country's own law decides what is taxed

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of a tax treaty sharing out taxing jurisdiction in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, read with section 90 — jurisdiction allotted by the agreement and the charge supplied by each country's own law

items.scenario: An article of India's comprehensive agreement with Country T says that a particular receipt of a resident of Country T may be taxed in India. On the facts before the Assessing Officer nothing in the Income-tax Act, 1961 reaches that receipt at all — it neither accrues nor arises here and no deeming provision brings it in. The officer raises a demand anyway, saying the agreement operates as law in India and the article plainly hands India the right.

items.stem: Does the parity clause carry the 10 per cent rate across to Country A?

options.text: Yes — the later agreement's lower rate simply displaces the earlier one, later agreements governing earlier ones on the same subject
options.misconception: invents a rule that a later treaty overrides an earlier one, when each agreement binds only its own two parties
options.why: Two agreements with different countries do not compete. India's agreement with Country B binds India and Country B, and the only route by which anything in it can reach a resident of Country A is the parity clause in Country A's own protocol, on the conditions that clause and the circular impose.

options.text: No — a parity clause never reaches dividends, being confined to royalties and fees for technical services
options.misconception: narrows the clause to the wrong list of incomes
options.why: The reach of the clause is a matter of how it is worded, and the incomes commonly named include dividends alongside interest, royalties and fees for technical services. This claim fails on the OECD timing, not on the kind of income.

options.text: No — Country B was not in the OECD on the day India signed with it, and that condition is tested at the date of signature, not at the date of the claim
options.why: One of the conditions the CBDT set out is that the second agreement must be with a country that was already an OECD member when India signed with it. India signed with Country B on 20 June 2020 and Country B joined in 2022, so the condition fails on those dates however satisfactory the rest of the picture looks. Timing is where these claims are usually decided.
keywords: already an OECD member when India signed with it
the condition fails on those dates

options.text: Yes — Country B is an OECD member today, and membership at the time the benefit is claimed is what the condition asks about
options.misconception: tests OECD membership on the date of the claim instead of the date India signed the second agreement
options.why: Reading the condition that way would let a country's later decision to join reopen agreements India signed years before, which is the opposite of the certainty the condition is there to give. The date fixed is the date of signature.

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 3/2022 dated 3 February 2022 — the conditions for a parity clause, including that the later agreement be with a country that was an OECD member at the time India signed it

items.scenario: India's agreement with Country A entered into force on 1 January 2019 and charges dividends at 15 per cent. Its protocol carries a parity clause of the usual kind. Country A has been an OECD member since 2012. India then signed an agreement with Country B on 20 June 2020 which limits dividend tax to 10 per cent. Country B joined the OECD in 2022. A resident of Country A claims the 10 per cent rate on a dividend from its Indian subsidiary.

items.stem: Can the lower rate be applied?

options.text: No — a protocol sits outside the treaty and can never carry a benefit into it
options.misconception: reaches the right answer by denying a protocol any force at all
options.why: The conclusion is right for the wrong reason, which would mislead on the next set of facts. A protocol is part of the treaty and binds accordingly; the claim fails here because the notification the clause depends on has not been issued.

options.text: Yes — a protocol has the same binding force as the treaty's own articles, so the parity clause operates without anything further being done
options.misconception: takes a true proposition about a protocol's status and treats it as answering a different question about what the clause needs to operate
options.why: A protocol is an integral part of its treaty and does bind as the articles bind. What it binds India to is the parity clause on that clause's own terms, and the CBDT and the Supreme Court have both said those terms are not complete without the notification.

options.text: No — a separate notification under section 90(1) importing the benefit is one of the conditions, and the Supreme Court has held it to be a necessary step rather than a formality
options.why: Three conditions being met is not enough; the fourth asks whether India has issued a separate notification carrying the benefit of the later agreement into the earlier one. In Nestle SA the Supreme Court held that a notification is required wherever the effect would be to change the law as it stands, so until one is issued the earlier rate continues to apply.
keywords: a separate notification carrying the benefit
required wherever the effect would be to change the law

options.text: Yes — the notification is procedural, so its absence affects only the date from which the lower rate runs
options.misconception: downgrades the notification to a formality that changes timing rather than entitlement
options.why: That is precisely the reading the Supreme Court rejected. Where giving effect to a protocol would alter the law as it stands, the notification is what does the altering, so without one there is no lower rate to date from.

citation.ref: CBDT Circular No. 3/2022 dated 3 February 2022 read with section 90(1) and Assessing Officer v. Nestle SA (2023) 458 ITR 756 — the separate notification held to be a necessary condition for a parity clause to operate

items.scenario: On a different set of facts every timing condition is met: the second agreement came after the first, the other country was in the OECD when India signed with it, and India did limit its source taxing right on the income in question. India has issued no notification importing that benefit into the earlier agreement. The assessee argues that a protocol binds as strongly as the articles it is attached to, so the lower rate must apply of its own force.

items.stem: Which vintage of meaning applies to each?

options.text: Neither approach is open, because an agreement built on the 1977 Model can be read only with the Commentary of that year
options.misconception: ties a treaty to the Commentary contemporaneous with its Model, which is the question the two approaches exist to answer
options.why: The vintage of the Model does not lock the reading to the Commentary of the same year. A clarificatory 2017 explanation may be used for an agreement drawn on the 1977 Model, and it is the character of the later text — explanation or replacement — that decides.

options.text: The current meaning governs both, the ambulatory approach being the settled rule with no exception to it
options.misconception: takes the ambulatory preference as absolute and drops the limit that goes with it
options.why: The preference comes with one caution written into it. Where an amendment changes the sum and substance of a term, the ambulatory reading would import into the agreement something the parties never bargained over, and that is where it gives way.

options.text: The 1985 meaning governs both, an agreement being read as at the day the two countries agreed it
options.misconception: applies the static approach to everything, which the Model Commentaries do not do
options.why: The static reading is one of the two answers and it is not the preferred one. Refusing every later clarification would leave an agreement being read on wording its own authors later admitted was unclear.

options.text: The 2017 Commentary may be used, the Model Commentaries favouring the meaning current when the agreement is applied; but where the amendment has altered the substance of the term rather than clarified it, the meaning it bore when the agreement was signed governs
options.why: The ambulatory approach takes the meaning current at the date of application and is the one the Model Commentaries prefer, including the technical explanation issued with the United States Model, because a later version usually exists to clear up an earlier want of clarity. That preference stops where a domestic amendment has changed what the term is rather than explained it, and there the static reading applies, so the meaning it bore when the agreement was signed governs.
keywords: takes the meaning current at the date of application
to clear up an earlier want of clarity
the meaning it bore when the agreement was signed

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of the static and ambulatory approaches in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties — the Model Commentaries preferring the meaning current at the date of application, and the exception where a domestic amendment alters the substance of the term

items.scenario: An agreement India signed in 1985 was drawn on the OECD Model as it stood in 1977 and leaves a term undefined. Two later developments are pressed on the Tribunal. A Commentary published in 2017 explains that same term more fully, saying nothing new but setting out plainly what the earlier wording had left ambiguous. Separately, an amendment to the domestic law has since altered what the term covers, so that it now takes in a class of receipt the parties never discussed.

items.stem: Which vintage of the meaning applies?

options.text: The 1993 meaning governs, an agreement being read on the law the two countries had in front of them when they signed it
options.misconception: makes the static reading the general rule, when it is kept for the case where a later change alters what the term covers
options.why: Reading every agreement as at its signature would leave an old one being applied on wording its own authors afterwards admitted was unclear. The static reading has its place, and its place is where an amendment has changed the term rather than explained it.

options.text: Thirty years is too long — a later text can help only where it followed reasonably soon after the agreement was signed
options.misconception: uses the age of the agreement as the test, which is the one thing the two approaches do not turn on
options.why: There is no period after which a clarification stops being usable. An agreement drawn on an old Model may be read with the help of a much later explanation, so long as the later text explains what was already there. Length of time is the assessee's argument and it is not the one that decides.

options.text: The amended wording may be used only if Country W has made a matching amendment or has otherwise accepted the new reading
options.misconception: turns a rule about how a term is read into an alteration of the agreement needing the other country's consent
options.why: Nothing is being added to the agreement here. The article itself sends the reader to domestic law for this term, so reading that law as it now stands is using the article rather than altering it, and the other country's concurrence is not what the question turns on.
