options.text: The amended wording may be used, a later text that explains the same idea being the one the Model Commentaries prefer, and the length of the gap deciding nothing
options.why: Where later wording only makes plainer what the term already covered, the reading that takes the meaning current when the agreement is applied is the preferred one, and every Model Commentary says so. What settles it is the character of the change and not its date: a clarification may be used however long after signature it arrived, and a change that alters the substance of the term is refused however soon it arrived. Here nothing new has been brought inside the term, so the objection is about the calendar rather than about the term.
keywords: the meaning current when the agreement is applied
the character of the change and not its date
nothing new has been brought inside the term

citation.ref: ICAI's treatment of the static and ambulatory approaches in Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties — the current domestic wording usable where a later amendment clarifies the term, and the static reading kept for an amendment that changes what the term covers

items.scenario: India signed an agreement with Country W in 1993, and one of its articles leaves a term undefined and sends the reader to domestic law for the meaning. That domestic law has since been amended. The amendment brings no class of receipt inside the term that was not inside it before; it puts into plain words what the earlier wording had left arguable. The assessee says an agreement of 1993 can only be read on the law as it stood in 1993, and that thirty years is far too long a gap for a later amendment to be read into it.

items.stem: Which line of the comparison is correct?

options.text: The OECD Model was last revised in 2017 and comprises 32 articles; the UN Model was last updated in 2021 and comprises 31 articles; both are arranged in seven chapters
options.why: The OECD Model reached its present form in 1977 and has been revised several times, the latest being 2017. The UN Model was finalised in 1980 and updated in 2001, 2011 and 2017, with the latest update in 2021. Both are arranged in seven chapters, and the OECD Model comprises 32 articles against the UN Model's 31 — a count worth holding, because the UN Model adds Articles 12A and 12B and keeps Article 14, and still ends up one article shorter.

options.text: Both Models were last updated in 2017 and both carry 31 articles
options.misconception: stops at 2017 for the UN Model, which is the update before its latest, and gives both Models the same count
options.why: 2017 is the UN Model's second-to-last update, not its last; the 2021 update is what introduced Article 12B on automated digital services. And the two counts differ.

options.text: The OECD Model was last revised in 2017 and comprises 31 articles; the UN Model was last updated in 2021 and comprises 32 articles
options.misconception: has the years right and the article counts the wrong way round
options.why: The years are right and the counts are swapped. The OECD Model is the longer of the two at 32 articles and the UN Model carries 31.

options.text: The OECD Model was last revised in 2021 and comprises 32 articles; the UN Model was last updated in 2017 and comprises 31 articles
options.misconception: attaches 2021 to the OECD Model, when 2021 is the UN Model's latest update and 2017 is the OECD's
options.why: 2017 belongs to the OECD Model and 2021 to the UN Model. 2017 is a year in which both were updated, which is exactly why it is easy to stop there: the UN Model was updated in 2001, 2011 and 2017 before its latest update in 2021.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The comparative overview in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — the OECD Model in its 1977 form as revised in 2017 with seven chapters and 32 articles, and the UN Model finalised in 1980 and updated in 2001, 2011, 2017 and 2021 with seven chapters and 31 articles

items.scenario: An articled assistant is drawing up a one-page comparison of the two Model Conventions for a client note. Two columns of it are the year each Model was last updated and how many articles each carries, and he has to get both right before the note goes out.

items.stem: Which Model is Q arguing from, and how does the other Model lean?

options.text: The OECD Model, which gives more weight to the source principle; the UN Model advocates residence-based taxation
options.misconception: reverses the two Models, giving the source leaning to the OECD Model
options.why: It is the other way round. The OECD's membership is developed countries, which are capital-exporting, and a residence-based Model serves them; the UN Model was written for the developed-to-developing pairing and leans to source.

options.text: The US Model, which was last revised in 2016 and is the Model developing countries negotiate from
options.misconception: treats the US Model as a developing-country Model, when it is the one the United States uses in its own treaties
options.why: The US Model is used by the United States when entering into treaties with various countries, and it was last revised in 2016. It is not a developing-country instrument and Country Q would not be arguing from it.

options.text: The UN Model, which gives the source State the exclusive right to tax and leaves the residence State nothing
options.misconception: reads "more weight to the source principle" as exclusive source taxation
options.why: The UN Model is a compromise, not a reversal. It seeks to be balanced, and it embodies the idea that the residence country should extend relief from double taxation through a foreign tax credit or an exemption, exactly as the OECD Model does. Giving more weight to source is not the same as giving source everything.

options.text: The UN Model, which is a compromise between the source principle and the residence principle giving more weight to source; the OECD Model advocates residence-based taxation and is essentially a model treaty between two developed nations
options.why: Those three propositions are the UN Model's own stated corollaries to taxation at source, and they are why the UN Model exists — it was drafted by an Ad hoc Group of experts from developed and developing countries to encourage the flow of investment from the former to the latter and to take account of sharing tax revenue with the country providing the capital. It is a compromise between the source principle and the residence principle, weighted towards source. The OECD Model is the counterpart: a model treaty between two developed nations, which advocates residence-based taxation and lays emphasis on the right of the state of residence to tax the income.
keywords: compromise between the source principle and the residence principle

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The introduction to ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — the UN Model as a compromise weighted to the source principle, resting on net-basis taxation, a rate that does not discourage investment and appropriate revenue sharing, against the OECD Model's residence-based approach between developed nations

items.scenario: Two delegations are negotiating a first treaty. Country P is a capital-exporting developed economy whose residents will make the investment. Country Q is a developing economy in which the investment will be made. Q's team presses for provisions that let it tax at source, arguing that income from foreign capital should be taxed on a net basis after the expenses allocable to earning it, that the tax should not be so high as to discourage the investment, and that revenue should be shared appropriately with the country providing the capital.

items.stem: Which statement is right?

options.text: The UN Model Convention was finalised in its present form in 1968 by an Ad hoc Group of Experts from developed and developing countries
options.misconception: takes the year the expert group was set up for the year its Model was finalised
options.why: 1968 is when the Group was set up. It finalised the UN Model in its present form in 1980, twelve years later, and the Model has been updated four times since.

options.text: The OECD was established in 1963 to succeed the OEEC, and the first draft of a Model Form applicable to all countries was prepared in 1968
options.misconception: moves the OECD's founding to the year of the OEEC publication and the first draft to the year the UN set up its expert group
options.why: The OECD was established in 1961, with developed countries as its members, to succeed the OEEC; 1963 is the year the OEEC itself published a model convention. 1968 is the year the United Nations set up its Ad hoc Group of Experts, not the year of any OECD draft.

options.text: The first draft of a Model Form applicable to all countries was prepared in 1927 by the Fiscal Committee of the League of Nations; the OECD was established in 1961 to succeed the OEEC, which had published a model convention in 1963; and the OECD Model reached its present form in 1977
options.why: That is the chain the module sets out. A Fiscal Committee of the League of Nations put together the first draft of a Model Form for every country to work from, in 1927; Geneva saw a convention published in 1946, that one the work of the Fiscal Committee sitting under the UN's Social and Economic Council, and the OEEC issued its own in 1963; the OECD, established in 1961 and drawing its members from the developed world, took over from the OEEC and approved the draft that body had before it; and the final draft in the present form was settled in 1977, revised several times since.

options.text: The first draft of a Model Form applicable to all countries was prepared in 1927 by the Fiscal Committee of the United Nations Social and Economic Council
options.misconception: attributes the 1927 draft to the United Nations, which did not exist then
options.why: The 1927 draft was the League of Nations' work — its Fiscal Committee prepared it. The Fiscal Committee of the UN Social and Economic Council is the body that published a model convention at Geneva in 1946, nineteen years later.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017
citation.ref: The historical introduction in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — the 1927 League of Nations draft, the 1946 Geneva publication, the OEEC in 1963, the OECD established in 1961, and the final draft in its present form in 1977

items.scenario: A paper on the history of tax treaties makes four statements about where the present Model Conventions came from. Only one of them is accurate.

items.stem: How does the definition of a resident in Article 4(1) differ between the two Models?

options.text: The OECD Model names place of incorporation and the UN Model does not; the recognised pension fund appears in both
options.misconception: reverses which Model carries the wider definition
options.why: Place of incorporation is in the UN Model and absent from the OECD Model, and the recognised pension fund is in the UN Model alone. The UN Model is the wider of the two on both counts, which fits its purpose of letting more persons reach the treaty.

options.text: Neither Model names place of incorporation; residence under both rests on place of effective management alone
options.misconception: imports the old corporate tie-breaker into the paragraph 1 definition of residence
options.why: Place of effective management is not the paragraph 1 definition at all; it was the traditional tie-breaker in paragraph 3, used where a person is already a resident of both States. Paragraph 1 lists several criteria and place of management is only one of them.

options.text: The UN Model names place of incorporation among the criteria and expressly brings in a recognised pension fund of that State; the OECD Model's paragraph 1 contains neither reference
options.why: Under paragraph 1 of the UN Model a person is a resident of a Contracting State if that State's law taxes him there because of his domicile, his residence, his place of incorporation, the place he is managed from, or a comparable test of the same character; the term also takes in the State, its political subdivisions and local authorities, and a recognised pension fund of that State. The OECD Model's paragraph 1 runs on similar lines but does not contain a reference to place of incorporation and does not include a recognised pension fund. Both Models agree on the exclusion at the end: a person liable to tax in a State only on income from sources there or capital situated there is not a resident.

options.text: It does not differ — both Models list place of incorporation among the criteria and both expressly include a recognised pension fund
options.misconception: assumes the two definitions have converged, when this is one of the places they have not
options.why: They differ in exactly these two respects, and this is one of the few places in Article 4 where they do. The OECD Model's paragraph 1 is worded on similar lines to the UN Model's but contains neither reference.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 4(1) of the two Models — place of incorporation and a recognised pension fund among the UN Model's criteria and absent from the OECD Model's, with both excluding a person liable to tax only on income sourced in that State

items.scenario: A fund recognised as a pension fund under the law of State B, and a company incorporated in State B whose place of management is in a third country, both want to claim benefits under State B's treaty with State A. Their adviser tells them that whether either is a resident of State B for treaty purposes may depend on which Model the treaty was drafted from.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: Yes, but only where the treaty follows the UN Model; a treaty on the OECD pattern leaves the company resident in both States
options.misconception: invents a divergence between the two Models on a paragraph where both were changed the same way
options.why: The change to a case-by-case approach was made by both the OECD and the UN in their latest updates. This is not a place where the two Models part company.

options.text: No — a company that is a resident of both States is simply denied the treaty, and there is no mechanism to resolve it
options.misconception: treats the absence of an automatic rule as the absence of any route at all
options.why: There is a mechanism, and it is the competent authorities. Denial is only what happens if they fail to agree, and even then it is denial of relief or exemption under the Convention rather than of the Convention wholesale.

options.text: No — the latest updates replaced the automatic rule with a case-by-case determination by the competent authorities by mutual agreement, having regard to place of effective management, place of incorporation and any other relevant factors, and the taxpayer has to request it through Article 25
options.why: Paragraph 3 now leaves it to the competent authorities, who are to try by mutual agreement to settle which State the person counts as a resident of. What they weigh is the place of effective management, where the entity was incorporated or otherwise brought into being, and any other relevant factors. The determination is requested by the concerned taxpayer through Article 25, the mutual agreement procedure, so doing nothing is the one thing that does not work. In the absence of such agreement the person is not entitled to any relief or exemption from tax under the Convention except to the extent and in the manner the competent authorities agree — though it stays a resident of each State for purposes other than treaty relief.

options.text: Yes — place of effective management is the tie-breaker for a company in both Models and the result follows without any application by the taxpayer
options.misconception: states the rule as it traditionally stood, before the latest OECD and UN updates replaced it
options.why: Place of effective management was traditionally the tie-breaker and India has used it in some of its treaties, which is why this answer feels right. In the latest update by the OECD and the UN it has been replaced, because of the number of tax avoidance cases involving dual resident companies.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 4(3) of the two Models — the case-by-case competent-authority determination that has displaced place of effective management as the corporate tie-breaker, requested through Article 25, with no relief or exemption where the authorities do not agree

items.scenario: A company is a resident of State A because it is incorporated there and a resident of State B because its place of effective management is there. The treaty between them follows the latest OECD and UN updates. The company's adviser tells the board that the tie is broken automatically in favour of the place of effective management, so the company is a resident of State B and need do nothing.

items.stem: Does a permanent establishment arise in State S under each?

options.text: Under the UN Model yes, because it covers an assembly or installation project and supervisory activities connected with it and requires only six months; under the OECD Model no, because Article 5(3)(a) requires the site or project to last more than twelve months
options.why: Article 5(3)(a) of the OECD Model makes a building site or construction or installation project a permanent establishment only if it lasts more than twelve months, so eight months falls short. The UN Model is wider in two ways at once: it covers an assembly or installation project and supervisory activities in connection with it, and it requires the activity to continue only for six months. Eight months clears that.

options.text: Under both, yes — eight months exceeds the six-month period, which is common to both Models
options.misconception: applies the UN Model's six-month period to the OECD Model as well
options.why: Six months is the UN Model's figure alone. The OECD Model's period is more than twelve months, and it is the single most-tested difference between the two on this article.

options.text: Under both, no — the twelve-month test in Article 5(3)(a) is common to both Models
options.misconception: applies the OECD Model's twelve-month period to the UN Model as well
options.why: The twelve-month figure is the OECD Model's. The UN Model's Article 5(3)(a) needs only six months, and it also brings in assembly, installation and supervisory activity that the OECD wording does not name.

options.text: Under the OECD Model yes and under the UN Model no, the OECD Model being the wider of the two on construction projects
options.misconception: has the right two periods but attaches each to the wrong Model
options.why: On this article the UN Model is the wider, which is what the whole design is for — the permanent establishment concept is what gives the source State the right to tax, so a Model written for developing countries lowers the bar rather than raising it.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 5(3)(a) of the two Models — more than twelve months for a building site or construction or installation project under the OECD Model, against six months under the UN Model, which also covers assembly or installation projects and connected supervisory activities

items.scenario: An enterprise of State R carries out an installation project in State S which lasts eight months, and its own personnel carry out supervisory activities in connection with that project throughout. It has no other presence in State S. Two treaties are put in front of the assessing officer: one that reproduces the OECD Model's Article 5 word for word, and one that reproduces the UN Model's.

items.stem: Under which Model does State S get a permanent establishment, and by what route?

options.text: Under neither, because without a place of business at the enterprise's disposal Article 5(1) cannot be satisfied and no other route exists
options.misconception: is right about Article 5(1) and forgets that the UN Model supplies a second route that needs no premises
options.why: The first half is sound — Article 5(1) is cumulative and a place of business at the enterprise's disposal is one of its conditions, so it fails here. But the UN Model does not stop at Article 5(1); its Article 5(3)(b) creates a Service PE that needs no premises.

options.text: Under the UN Model, through Article 5(3)(b): services furnished through employees that run for more than 183 days in aggregate inside a twelve-month window opening or closing in the fiscal year concerned give a Service PE; under the OECD Model presence has to be tested under Article 5(1), which fails on these facts
options.why: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model reaches services an enterprise furnishes, consultancy among them, using employees or other personnel taken on for the job — but only where work of that kind carries on inside a Contracting State for more than 183 days in aggregate within a twelve-month window that opens or closes in the fiscal year concerned. Two hundred days clears it. The OECD Model has no such article, so presence must be ascertained through the general principles under Article 5(1) — and Article 5(1) is cumulative, needing a place of business at the enterprise's disposal, which these facts do not give.

options.text: Under the UN Model, but only once the services have continued for twelve months, the same period its construction clause uses
options.misconception: carries the construction period across to the service test, when the two clauses of Article 5(3) use different periods
options.why: Article 5(3) has two limbs with two different periods. Limb (a), construction, uses six months in the UN Model. Limb (b), services, uses more than 183 days in any twelve-month period — which is a length of activity, not a length of the project, and it is measured across a window rather than continuously.

options.text: Under both, because furnishing services for more than 183 days in any twelve-month period is a permanent establishment in each Model
options.misconception: attributes the UN Model's Service PE article to the OECD Model as well
options.why: The 183-day service test lives in Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model, and there is no corresponding provision in the OECD Model at all. Its absence is the point: where the OECD Model applies, the presence has to be ascertained through the general principles of Article 5(1).

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model, which has no counterpart in the OECD Model — services furnished through employees for more than 183 days in aggregate within a twelve-month window opening or closing in the fiscal year concerned, against the cumulative conditions of Article 5(1)

items.scenario: An enterprise of State R furnishes consultancy services in State S through its own employees for periods aggregating 200 days in a twelve-month period ending in the fiscal year concerned. It rents no premises in State S, and no place there is at its disposal in the sense of a place it has the effective power to use.

items.stem: Under which Model does each of these amount to a permanent establishment?

options.text: Both amount to a permanent establishment under the UN Model, and neither has an article of its own in the OECD Model, where each falls to be tested under Article 5(1) or 5(2)
options.why: The UN Model finds a permanent establishment even where the person neither makes contracts as a matter of habit nor is the main mover behind them, provided he keeps up in that State a stock of the enterprise's goods or merchandise out of which he regularly delivers goods for it. And the UN Model has an additional Article 5(6) under which an insurance enterprise of a Contracting State, except in regard to re-insurance, is deemed to have a permanent establishment in the other State if it collects premiums in that territory or insures risks situated there through a person. The OECD Model has neither provision, so an insurer's permanent establishment there has to be determined in accordance with Article 5(1) or 5(2).

options.text: Both amount to a permanent establishment under both Models
options.misconception: assumes the two Models treat agency and insurance alike, when both of these limbs are UN Model additions
options.why: Both Models reach a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts or habitually plays the principal role leading to their conclusion. Neither of these two facts is that, and both of the provisions that catch them are in the UN Model only.

options.text: The insurer under the UN Model, including its re-insurance business, and the delivery agent under neither
options.misconception: reads the insurance article without its carve-out and drops the UN Model's extra agency limb
options.why: Article 5(6) of the UN Model applies except in regard to re-insurance, so re-insurance is expressly outside it — which does not matter on these facts, since none of the business is re-insurance. And the delivery agent is caught, by the UN Model's own extension of agency.

options.text: The delivery agent under both Models, the insurer under neither
options.misconception: treats the delivery-of-stock limb as common to both Models
options.why: The delivery-of-stock limb is a UN Model addition, exactly like the insurance article. Both Models were amended together to reach an agent who plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts; only the UN Model went the further step to a person who merely holds stock and delivers from it.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The agency provision of Article 5 and Article 5(6) of the UN Model, neither having a counterpart in the OECD Model — habitual maintenance of a stock of goods with regular delivery, and an insurance enterprise collecting premiums or insuring risks through a person except in regard to re-insurance

items.scenario: Two separate facts arise in State S. A person there neither habitually concludes contracts for an enterprise of State R nor plays the principal role leading to their conclusion, but he does habitually maintain a stock of that enterprise's goods from which he regularly makes deliveries on its behalf. Separately, an insurance enterprise of State R collects premiums in State S through a person there; none of the business is re-insurance.

items.stem: What may State S tax under a treaty on the UN Model, and how would the OECD Model differ?

options.text: Under both Models State S may tax only the profits attributable to the permanent establishment
options.misconception: denies the UN Model its force of attraction rule, which is the whole of the difference on this article
options.why: That is the OECD Model's position and only the OECD Model's. The UN Model amplifies the attribution principle with a limited force of attraction rule, and that rule is what adds the second and third limbs.

options.text: Under the UN Model State S may tax everything the enterprise derives from State S, including the insurance business, because once a permanent establishment exists the enterprise is within State S's fiscal jurisdiction
options.misconception: reads a limited force of attraction as a full one, taxing every profit sourced in the State
options.why: The rule is limited and the word does the work. Article 7 of the UN Model reaches sales of goods of the same or similar kind as those sold through the permanent establishment, and other business activities of the same or similar kind as those effected through it. Insurance is neither.

options.text: Under the OECD Model the direct sales are taxable because they are of the same or similar kind; under the UN Model they are not
options.misconception: attaches the force of attraction rule to the OECD Model instead of the UN Model
options.why: The same or similar kind test belongs to the UN Model. Under the OECD Model, once a permanent establishment is shown to exist, State S reaches the profits attributable to that establishment and no others — nothing turns on whether other sales are similar.

options.text: Under the UN Model State S may tax the profits attributable to the permanent establishment and the profits from the direct sales of the same or similar goods, but not the insurance business; under the OECD Model it may tax only the profits attributable to the permanent establishment
options.why: Under Article 7 of the UN Model the profits taxable in the other State are those attributable to three things: the permanent establishment itself; goods the enterprise sells there directly, where they are of the same or similar kind as what moves through the establishment; and further business it carries on there, again of the same or similar kind. The direct sales of machine tools are the second limb. The insurance business is neither of the same or similar kind nor effected through the permanent establishment, so the limited force of attraction does not reach it. Under the OECD Model none of that applies and attribution to the establishment is the whole rule.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 7 of the UN Model against Article 7 of the OECD Model — the limited force of attraction rule and its three limbs of the permanent establishment, sales of goods of the same or similar kind, and other business activities of the same or similar kind

items.scenario: An enterprise resident in State R has a permanent establishment in State S which sells machine tools. In the same year the enterprise also sells machine tools of the same kind directly from its head office to customers in State S, without routing them through the permanent establishment at all. Separately again, it sells insurance products in State S through an unrelated broker.

items.stem: Which State may tax that income?

options.text: Under both Models only the source State
options.misconception: reverses the residual rule, which in both Models starts from the residence State
options.why: Neither Model gives the source State an exclusive right over other income. The OECD Model gives the residence State an exclusive right and the UN Model gives both a right.

options.text: Under both Models only the residence State
options.misconception: applies the OECD Model's exclusivity to the UN Model as well
options.why: Exclusivity is the OECD position. The UN Model's extra paragraph is precisely a departure from it.

options.text: Under the OECD Model only the residence State; under the UN Model the source State may tax it as well, because the UN Model carries an additional paragraph, Article 21(3), which the OECD Model does not
options.why: Article 21 deals with items of income not specifically taxable under any other article. The OECD approach is that the exclusive right to tax lies with the residence State. An additional paragraph in the UN Model, Article 21(3), goes the other way: the source State may also tax other income. That single extra paragraph is the difference, and it fits the pattern of the whole UN Model — wherever the OECD Model gives the residence State exclusivity, the UN Model tends to let the source State back in.

options.text: Under the UN Model taxation is governed by Article 7 in every case, whether or not the income is connected with a permanent establishment
options.misconception: extends Article 21(2) beyond the effectively connected income it is written for
options.why: Article 21(2) of both Models routes to Article 7 only income effectively connected with a permanent establishment maintained in a Contracting State, and the UN Model adds a route to Article 14 for income effectively connected with a fixed base. These facts say the income is connected with neither, so paragraph 2 never engages.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 21(2) and Article 21(3) of the two Models — the residence State's exclusive right to other income under the OECD Model, the UN Model's additional paragraph letting the source State tax, and the routing of effectively connected income to Article 7 or, in the UN Model, Article 14

items.scenario: A resident of State R receives an item of income arising in State S which no specific article of the treaty deals with, and which is not effectively connected with any permanent establishment or fixed base in State S.

items.stem: What is the answer under each Model?

options.text: Both Models specify 10 per cent of the gross amount of the interest
options.misconception: treats a figure the OECD Model states as a figure common to both
options.why: Only the OECD Model names a figure. The UN Model leaves the percentage to be established through bilateral negotiations, which is consistent with a Model written for pairs of countries with very different bargaining positions.

options.text: The OECD Model leaves the percentage to bilateral negotiation and the UN Model specifies 10 per cent
options.misconception: attaches the stated figure to the wrong Model
options.why: It is the OECD Model that names 10 per cent. Leaving the rate open is the UN Model's approach, on interest and on royalties and on fees for technical services alike.

options.text: Neither Model specifies a figure, because interest is taxable only in the residence State under both
options.misconception: carries the OECD Model's exclusive-residence rule for royalties across to interest
options.why: Exclusive residence taxation is the OECD Model's rule for royalties under Article 12, not for interest. On interest both Models give the source State a right, and it is the ceiling on that right which differs.

options.text: The OECD Model specifies 10 per cent; the UN Model specifies no figure at all and leaves the percentage to be established through bilateral negotiations
options.why: Paragraph 1 of Article 11 gives the residence State the right to tax interest and paragraph 2 confers a right on the source State too, interest generally being taxed at source at a given rate on a gross basis. Once the beneficial owner lives in the other State, that source charge is capped at a stated share of the interest before deductions. The OECD Model sets that share at 10 per cent. The UN Model names none and leaves the ceiling to bilateral negotiations. This is the only rate the OECD Model actually names in the articles compared here, which is why it is worth remembering as a number rather than as a principle.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 11(1) and 11(2) of the two Models — the source State's right to tax interest on a gross basis, capped at 10 per cent by the OECD Model and at a percentage left to bilateral negotiations by the UN Model

items.scenario: Two countries are drafting a treaty and have agreed to follow one Model's Article 11 word for word. The source State's negotiator asks what ceiling the Model itself puts on the tax it may charge on the gross amount of interest where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other Contracting State.

items.stem: Which Model lets State S tax these payments as royalties, and does its definition reach both?

options.text: Both Models let the source State tax, and both definitions cover both payments
options.misconception: assumes the two Models agree on royalties, where in fact they differ on the taxing right and on the definition
options.why: They differ twice over on this article. On the right, the OECD Model gives the residence State an exclusive right; on the definition, the OECD Model leaves out both of these categories.

options.text: The OECD Model lets State S tax at up to 10 per cent of the gross royalties
options.misconception: carries the OECD Model's interest ceiling across to royalties, where the OECD Model gives the source State no right at all
options.why: 10 per cent is the OECD Model's ceiling under Article 11 on interest. Under Article 12 the OECD Model does not cap the source State's right, because it does not give the source State a right to cap.

options.text: Only the UN Model lets the source State tax royalties, the OECD Model reserving them exclusively to the residence State where the beneficial owner is a resident there; and the UN definition reaches both payments, both of which the OECD definition of royalties leaves out
options.why: The OECD Model gives royalties to one side only. A royalty with its source in one State, whose beneficial owner lives in the other, is taxable only in the residence State. The UN Model departs from that: royalties may be taxed in the residence State, and the source State may also tax them, subject to a specified percentage of the gross amount to be established through bilateral negotiations where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other State. On the definition, the UN Model's royalties includes payments for the use of films or tapes used for radio or television broadcasting and for the use of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment; the OECD definition expressly does not include rentals for films or tapes used for radio or television broadcasting, or equipment rentals.
keywords: taxable only in the residence State

options.text: The UN Model lets State S tax, but its definition of royalties, like the OECD's, excludes equipment rentals
options.misconception: gets the taxing right right and then attributes the OECD Model's two exclusions to the UN definition
options.why: The exclusions run the other way. Hire of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment sits expressly inside the UN definition, and it is the OECD definition that leaves equipment rentals and broadcasting tape rentals out.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12 of the two Models — the residence State's exclusive right under the OECD Model against shared taxation subject to a negotiated ceiling under the UN Model, and the two categories of rental the OECD definition of royalties excludes

items.scenario: A resident of State R receives two payments from a payer in State S. The first is for the right to use tapes for television broadcasting. The second is rent for scientific equipment leased to the payer. The treaty between R and S reproduces one Model's Article 12 exactly, and the recipient is the beneficial owner in both cases.

items.stem: Which of these four payments is fees for technical services?

options.text: All four, since each is a payment for services rendered from State R
options.misconception: applies the definition without the three exclusions written into it
options.why: The definition is not simply payments for services. It is payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, and it carries three express exclusions which take out three of these four payments.

options.text: The accountants' fee and the university fee
options.misconception: keeps the teaching payment inside the definition when it is one of the three named exclusions
options.why: Teaching is expressly excluded, in both directions — a payment for teaching in an educational institution and a payment for teaching by an educational institution are both outside the definition.

options.text: Only the accountants' fee
options.why: Fees for technical services means payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, and three things are carved out of it: a payment to an employee; anything paid for teaching, whether the teaching happens inside an educational institution or is teaching by an educational institution; and a payment an individual makes for services put to personal use. Those three exclusions take out the salary, the university fee and the managing director's decorator. What is left is the accountants' fee, and it is squarely inside: accounting is one of the regulated professions the commentary names, and advice on a specific restructuring is consultancy of a specialised nature given to a particular client.

options.text: None, since a regulated profession such as accountancy is outside the definition of technical services
options.misconception: reads the regulated professions as excluded, when the module gives them as the clearest examples of what is included
options.why: The opposite is true. Technical points to specialised knowledge, skill or expertise being brought to bear in some particular art, science, profession or occupation, and a fee charged by a regulated profession — law, accountancy, architecture, medicine, engineering — is fees for technical services.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12A of the UN Model — fees for technical services as payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, excluding a payment to an employee, a payment for teaching in or by an educational institution, and a payment by an individual for services for personal use

items.scenario: In one year a company resident in State S makes four payments to residents of State R under a treaty that carries Article 12A. It pays a salary to one of its own employees who is a resident of State R; a fee to a firm of chartered accountants in State R for advice on a specific restructuring; a fee to a university in State R for teaching a course to its staff; and its managing director personally pays a decorator in State R for redecorating his own house.

items.stem: Which article of the treaty applies to each stream?

options.text: Neither, because Article 12B was added to the UN Model in 2017 and applies only to treaties concluded from that year
options.misconception: dates Article 12B to the 2017 update rather than the 2021 one
options.why: Article 12B reached the United Nations Model Tax Convention with the 2021 update, not the 2017 one, and its purpose was to keep a taxing right under domestic law for the State out of which payment for an automated digital service goes. The scenario says the treaty follows the 2021 update, so the article is there.

options.text: Both fall under Article 12B, since digital content services are one of the nine categories listed in paragraph 6
options.misconception: reads the paragraph 6 list as self-standing and ignores the paragraph 7 priority rule
options.why: Paragraph 6 is expressly not self-standing: the list only signals that an activity might be an automated digital service, and it does not settle that a listed activity is one — the paragraph 5 requirements must also be met. And paragraph 7 puts royalties and fees for technical services ahead of Article 12B in any event.

options.text: Both fall under Article 12, since Article 12B appears in the OECD Model only
options.misconception: puts Article 12B in the wrong Model, when it is one of two articles the UN Model has and the OECD Model does not
options.why: The OECD Model carries no counterpart to Article 12B, just as it carries none to Article 12A. Both are UN Model additions, and both exist to preserve a source State's taxing rights.

options.text: The streaming subscription falls under Article 12B if it meets the paragraph 5 test of minimal human involvement; the patented process is a royalty under Article 12, and paragraph 7 of Article 12B disapplies that article where the payments qualify as royalties or as fees for technical services
options.why: Automated digital services is defined in paragraph 5 as any service provided on the Internet or another electronic network requiring minimal human involvement from the service provider, and the indicator is the ability to scale up to new users with minimal human involvement — which is exactly what the facts describe of the catalogue. Paragraph 6 lists digital content services as an example, but the list is only an indication and paragraph 5 must still be met. The patent is a royalty under Article 12, and paragraph 7 settles the overlap in terms: Article 12B does not apply if the payments underlying the income qualify as royalty or as fees for technical services under Article 12 or Article 12A.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12B of the UN Model, added in its 2021 update — automated digital services defined in paragraph 5 by minimal human involvement, the paragraph 6 list as an indication only, and paragraph 7 disapplying the article where the payments qualify as royalties or fees for technical services

items.scenario: A resident of State R receives two streams of payment from customers in State S under a treaty that follows the UN Model as updated in 2021. The first is subscription income from a music-streaming catalogue delivered over the internet, which the business can supply to one user or to a million on the same automated processes. The second is consideration for the right to use a patented manufacturing process.

items.stem: Which State may tax the gain, and does the answer differ between the Models?

options.text: State S, and the answer is the same under both Models, which are identical on shares — the source State gets the right where immovable property there accounted, directly or through a chain, for more than 50 per cent of the share value at some point in the preceding 365 days
options.why: In respect of shares both Models are identical. The source State gets a right to tax once immovable property lying there accounted — directly, or through a chain of holdings — for more than 50 per cent of what the shares were worth at some point in the preceding 365 days; otherwise the residence State has the exclusive right to tax. Sixty-two per cent, held throughout the 365 days, clears it. Note what the article does not do: it does not say what a capital gain is or how it is computed, both of which are left to the applicable domestic law.

options.text: State S, but only if more than 50 per cent of the value was so derived throughout the preceding 12 months
options.misconception: substitutes a twelve-month period for the 365 days the article actually uses
options.why: The article says 365 days, and the answer here happens to be the same, but the habit is the problem: twelve months is the period in the OECD Model's construction PE clause, and carrying periods from one article to another is how these questions are lost.

options.text: State S, but under the UN Model only; the OECD Model reserves gains on shares to the residence State
options.misconception: assumes a divergence on shares where the two Models are word for word the same
options.why: In respect of shares both Models are identical, and it is one of the few substantial places in this chapter where they are. Assuming a UN-versus-OECD split on every article is the trap; here there is none.

options.text: Only State R, because Article 13 gives the residence State the exclusive right to tax gains on shares
options.misconception: applies the article's residual rule to a case the article expressly deals with
options.why: Exclusive residence taxation is what Article 13 gives for gains from the alienation of any property other than the property covered in its other paragraphs. Shares deriving their value from immovable property are covered by one of those other paragraphs, so the residual rule never reaches them.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 13 of the two Models, identical in respect of shares — the source State's right where immovable property there accounted, directly or through a chain, for more than 50 per cent of the share value at any point in the preceding 365 days, with computation left to domestic law

items.scenario: A resident of State R sells shares of a company resident in State S. At every point during the 365 days preceding the sale, 62 per cent of the value of those shares was derived from immovable property situated in State S. The adviser is not sure which Model the treaty follows and wonders whether it matters.

items.stem: How is her income dealt with under each Model?

options.text: Under the UN Model, Article 14 lets State S tax so much of the income as is derived from her activities performed there, because her stay reaches 183 days in the aggregate in a twelve-month period; under the OECD Model, Article 14 was deleted on 29 April 2000 and the income is dealt with as business profits under Article 7, so State S taxes only if she has a permanent establishment there
options.why: Article 14(1) of the UN Model makes income from professional services taxable only in the residence State except in two cases. One is a fixed base regularly available in the other State, where only the income attributable to the fixed base may be taxed there. The other is a stay in that other State reaching or passing 183 days in total across any twelve months that begin or end in the fiscal year in question, where the State may tax only what she earned by working on its soil. One hundred and ninety days meets the second. The effect of the deletion of Article 14 from the OECD Model is that income from professional services is now dealt with as business profits under Article 7, which needs a permanent establishment.

options.text: Under neither Model, since income of an independent professional is always taxable only in the State of residence
options.misconception: takes the opening words of Article 14(1) and stops before the exceptions
options.why: Article 14(1) does begin by making the income taxable only in the residence State, but it continues with the words "except in the following circumstances", and both circumstances let the other State tax. And under the OECD Model the income falls to Article 7, which also lets the source State tax where a permanent establishment exists.

options.text: Under both Models Article 14 applies and State S may tax the income derived from activities performed there
options.misconception: keeps Article 14 in the OECD Model, which deleted it
options.why: Article 14 is present only in the UN Model. The OECD struck it out with effect from 29 April 2000, acting on its own 2000 report into the issues that article raised.

options.text: Under the UN Model State S may tax only if she has a fixed base regularly available to her; the days test is not an alternative but a further condition
options.misconception: turns two alternative gateways into one gateway with two conditions
options.why: The article sets out the two circumstances as alternatives, joined by "or". A fixed base lets the other State tax the income attributable to that base; a stay of 183 days or more lets it tax the income derived from activities performed there. Either alone is enough.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 14 of the UN Model, deleted from the OECD Model on 29 April 2000 — income from professional services taxable only in the residence State except where a fixed base is regularly available or the stay amounts to or exceeds 183 days in the aggregate in any twelve-month period, with the OECD Model treating such income as business profits under Article 7

items.scenario: An architect resident in State R performs professional services in State S for 190 days in a twelve-month period ending in the fiscal year concerned. No fixed base is regularly available to her in State S and she has no permanent establishment there.

items.stem: When may arbitration be initiated under each, and who has to ask for it?

options.text: Under the UN Model after two years and under the OECD Model after three years
options.misconception: has both periods and attaches each to the wrong Model
options.why: Three years belongs to Article 25B(5) of the UN Model and two years to Article 25(5) of the OECD Model.

options.text: Under both, after three years, and in both cases only the competent authorities may request arbitration
options.misconception: applies the UN Model's period and applicant to the OECD Model as well
options.why: Under the OECD Model the written request has to come from the taxpayer — the person who initiated the case — and the period is two years. Only the UN Model puts the request in the hands of a competent authority.

options.text: Under both, after two years from the presentation of the case, on the taxpayer's written request
options.misconception: merges the two provisions into one, taking the OECD period and applicant and the UN starting point
options.why: Every element of that is half right, which is what makes it dangerous. The two-year period and the taxpayer's written request are the OECD Model. The presentation of the case as the starting point is the UN Model. The OECD clock runs from the information being complete, not from presentation.

options.text: Under the UN Model's Article 25B(5), after three years from the presentation of the case, on a request by the competent authority of one of the Contracting States, the taxpayer being notified; under the OECD Model's Article 25(5), after two years from the date all the information required by the competent authorities was provided to both of them, on a written request by the person who initiated the case
options.why: Two things differ and they are easy to run together. On the clock, the UN Model uses three years from the presentation of that case, while the OECD Model allows two years counted from the day the last piece of information the authorities had asked for to deal with the case reached them both — a different length and a different starting point. On the applicant, the UN Model has the competent authority of one of the Contracting States request arbitration, with the taxpayer notified once the request is made, while the OECD Model has the person who initiated the case request it in writing.
keywords: the person who initiated the case

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 25(5) of the OECD Model and Article 25B(5) of the UN Model — two years from the date all required information was provided to both competent authorities against three years from the presentation of the case, and a written request by the person who initiated the case against a request by the competent authority of one of the Contracting States

items.scenario: A taxpayer has presented a case to the competent authorities and they have not reached agreement. Two treaties are being compared: one reproduces the OECD Model's Article 25, and one reproduces Alternative B of the UN Model's Article 25.

items.stem: May the authorities depart from the decision, and do Articles 23A and 23B relieve the second complaint?

options.text: They may depart at any time by agreement; and the complaint is juridical double taxation, because the same income is taxed twice
options.misconception: defines juridical double taxation by the income being taxed twice rather than by the same person being taxed twice
options.why: Juridical double taxation happens when one and the same person is taxed on one and the same income, or capital, in more than one State. The test is the person, not the income. Two different persons taxed on the same income is economic double taxation.

options.text: They may depart from it if they agree to do so within six months after it has been communicated to them, which the OECD Model does not allow; and Articles 23A and 23B do not reach the second complaint, because it is economic double taxation, which the two States must solve in bilateral negotiation
options.why: Article 25B(5) of the UN Model lets the two competent authorities set the arbitration outcome aside, provided they agree to do that inside six months of being told what it was; the OECD Model has no equivalent provision. On the second point, the double taxation Articles 23A and 23B address is juridical — one and the same person taxed on one and the same income, or capital, in more than one State. A company taxed on its profits and a shareholder taxed on the dividend are two different persons, so this is economic double taxation, which those articles do not encompass; if two States wish to solve it they must do so in bilateral negotiations.

options.text: They may not depart from an arbitration decision at all; and Articles 23A and 23B relieve both kinds of double taxation
options.misconception: reads the arbitration decision as final in every case and treats the relief articles as covering economic double taxation too
options.why: Alternative B of the UN Model expressly lets the competent authorities depart from the decision, within a window. And the relief articles are limited to juridical double taxation; economic double taxation is not encompassed by them.

options.text: They may depart from it if they agree within three years; and the articles relieve economic double taxation
options.misconception: borrows the three-year arbitration trigger as the departure window and extends the relief articles beyond juridical double taxation
options.why: Three years is the period after which arbitration may be initiated, not the window for departing from its result. The departure window is six months. And the articles address juridical double taxation only.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 25B(5) of the UN Model and Articles 23A and 23B of the two Models — a six-month window for the competent authorities to depart from an arbitration decision, with no such provision in the OECD Model, and relief confined to juridical double taxation with economic double taxation left to bilateral negotiation

items.scenario: An arbitration decision under a treaty on Alternative B of the UN Model's Article 25 has been communicated to both competent authorities, and both would like to depart from it. In a separate matter the same taxpayer complains that profits of a company are taxed in the source State in the company's hands and the dividend out of them is taxed again in the residence State in the shareholder's hands.

items.stem: Which line is right?

options.text: It was established in 2015 alongside the final BEPS package and has 139 members
options.misconception: dates the Framework to the year the fifteen Action Plans were delivered and takes the count of countries that joined the October 2021 Statement for its membership
options.why: 2015 is the year the fifteen Action Plans were delivered, a year before the Framework was set up, and 139 is the number of countries and jurisdictions that joined the 8 October 2021 Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution, not the membership of the Framework.

options.text: It was established in 2013 when the OECD published its report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, with 65 members
options.misconception: dates it to the first BEPS report and takes the number of countries at the first MLI signing ceremony for its membership
options.why: February 2013 is when the report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting was published, three years before the Framework existed, and more than 65 countries is the number that signed the Multilateral Instrument at Paris on 7 June 2017.

options.text: It was established in July 2021, when 134 of its members agreed the two-pillar solution
options.misconception: takes the agreement the Framework reached for the moment the Framework itself was created
options.why: July 2021 was when 134 members of the Inclusive Framework, between them more than 90 per cent of worldwide GDP, reached the historic agreement on a two-pillar solution. That the Framework already had 134 members that month is itself the answer to whether it was founded then.

options.text: It was established in June 2016 at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and as at 28 May 2024 it had 147 members
options.why: The idea came out of the strong interest developing countries had shown in the BEPS Project. What the OECD's Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes had taught them carried across, and in early 2016 the OECD and G20 countries settled on a wider framework in which countries would sit as equals. In June 2016, at the request of the G20, the Inclusive Framework was established at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions. As at 28 May 2024 it includes 147 members, who on an equal footing monitor the implementation of the BEPS measures and contribute to their development.

citation.ref: The establishment of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS at Kyoto in June 2016 with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and 147 members as at 28 May 2024

items.scenario: A briefing note has to state, in one line each, when and where the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS was established, how many members it began with and how many it has on the latest count in the study material.

items.stem: Which description is right?

options.text: Pillar One has two parts — Amount A, the framework for reallocating taxing rights over the residual profits of large and highly profitable groups, and Amount B, a simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity; Pillar Two also has two — the GloBE Rules, a minimum tax framework in each jurisdiction, and the Subject to Tax Rule, which lets a source jurisdiction tax back a payment that bears a low nominal rate in the residence jurisdiction
options.why: Both Pillars are built in two complementary halves and it is worth holding them as four things rather than two. Amount A is the reallocation of taxing rights over the residual profit of the largest and most profitable groups; Amount B is the simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity. The Global Anti-Base Erosion Rules put a floor under tax in every jurisdiction a large group operates in, and the Subject to Tax Rule lets a source State tax back where a treaty made it give up the right and the payment meets only a low nominal rate where the recipient is resident.

options.text: Pillar One is Amount A alone; Amount B belongs to the transfer pricing guidelines and forms no part of the Two-Pillar Solution
options.misconception: treats Amount B as ordinary transfer pricing work outside the agreement
options.why: Amount B is described by the Inclusive Framework as a critical component of Pillar One, and the final package on Pillar One is the text of a Multilateral Convention for Amount A together with a framework for Amount B. It simplifies transfer pricing, but it is part of the Pillar.

options.text: Amount A and Amount B are both parts of Pillar Two, and the GloBE Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule are both parts of Pillar One
options.misconception: keeps the four parts and attaches each pair to the wrong Pillar
options.why: Amount A and Amount B belong to Pillar One; the GloBE Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule belong to Pillar Two.

options.text: Pillar One is the global minimum tax on the profits of large groups and Pillar Two is the reallocation of taxing rights to market jurisdictions
options.misconception: swaps the two Pillars
options.why: Pillar One is the reallocation and Pillar Two is the minimum tax. Pillar One is designed to deliver a fairer distribution of taxing rights over the largest and most profitable groups; Pillar Two exists so that groups pay a minimum level of tax wherever they operate.

citation.ref: The Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution of 8 October 2021 — Pillar One as Amount A and Amount B, and Pillar Two as the Global Anti-Base Erosion Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule

items.scenario: A note for a client describes the Two-Pillar Solution agreed on 8 October 2021 and has to set out what each Pillar is made of before it goes any further.

items.stem: Which of the four groups is in scope of Amount A?

options.text: Group I and Group IV
options.misconception: applies the turnover and profitability tests correctly and forgets that extractives are carved out whatever their size
options.why: Group IV passes both quantitative tests and is still out, because extractives and regulated financial services are excluded from the scope of Amount A.

options.text: Group I and Group III
options.misconception: treats high profitability as enough without the turnover threshold
options.why: Group III is very profitable at 25 per cent and is far short of the turnover threshold at 15 billion euros. Amount A is aimed at the largest and most profitable groups, which means both, not either.

options.text: Group I only
options.why: In-scope companies are multinationals with global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent, profitability being profit before tax divided by revenue, and extractives and regulated financial services are out of the scope. Group I clears both numbers at 26 billion and 14 per cent and is in a sector that is not carved out. Group II fails on profitability, Group III fails on turnover, and Group IV, which passes both numbers, is an extractives group and is excluded for that reason alone.

options.text: Group I, Group II and Group IV
options.misconception: treats turnover alone as the scope test, dropping the profitability limb
options.why: Group II is over the turnover line at 26 billion euros and under the profitability line at 7 per cent. Both tests have to be passed, and Group IV is excluded by its sector in any event.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A — global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent measured as profit before tax over revenue, with extractives and regulated financial services out of scope

items.scenario: Four multinational groups are tested against the scope of Amount A. Group I has global turnover of 26 billion euros and profit before tax of 14 per cent of revenue, and sells consumer goods. Group II has global turnover of 26 billion euros and profit before tax of 7 per cent of revenue. Group III has global turnover of 15 billion euros and profit before tax of 25 per cent of revenue. Group IV has global turnover of 40 billion euros and profit before tax of 20 per cent of revenue, and its business is oil and gas extraction.

items.stem: How much profit is reallocated to market jurisdictions as Amount A?

options.text: 750 million euros
options.why: Amount A is 25 per cent of the residual profit, and residual profit is defined as profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue. Ten per cent of revenue is 3,000 million euros, so the residual profit is 6,000 less 3,000, that is 3,000 million euros, and Amount A is 25 per cent of that, 750 million euros. The 10 per cent is doing a second job here that is worth naming: it is the same figure as the profitability threshold that decides whether the group is in scope at all, and it is also the routine return the group keeps before anything is reallocated.

options.text: 600 million euros
options.misconception: reads the 10 per cent as the share of profit reallocated rather than as the routine return that defines the residual
options.why: Ten per cent of the profit before tax is 600 million euros, but 10 per cent is not a share of anything that moves. It is a percentage of revenue, and it marks the line above which profit becomes residual.

options.text: 3,000 million euros
options.misconception: reallocates the whole residual profit and drops the 25 per cent share
options.why: 3,000 million euros is the residual profit itself. Only a quarter of it is reallocated; the rest stays where the ordinary rules put it.

options.text: 1,500 million euros
options.misconception: applies the 25 per cent to the whole profit before tax rather than to the residual profit
options.why: Twenty-five per cent of 6,000 million euros is 1,500 million, but the base is wrong. Amount A reaches only the residual — the profit above a routine return of 10 per cent of revenue — and never the whole profit.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A — 25 per cent of the residual profit, residual profit being the profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue, allocated to market jurisdictions with nexus using revenue-based allocation keys

items.scenario: A group is in scope of Amount A. For the year its revenue is 30,000 million euros and its profit before tax is 6,000 million euros.

items.stem: Which of the two countries has nexus for Amount A?

options.text: Both, since each exceeds 250,000
options.misconception: applies the lower threshold to every jurisdiction regardless of its GDP
options.why: 250,000 applies only where annual GDP is below 40 billion. Country Y's GDP is 60 billion, so its threshold is 1 million.

options.text: Neither, since neither reaches 1 million
options.misconception: applies the higher threshold to every jurisdiction regardless of its GDP
options.why: 1 million applies only where annual GDP is 40 billion or more. Country X's GDP is 25 billion, so its threshold is 250,000 and it clears it comfortably.

options.text: Country Y only, because it is the larger economy
options.misconception: reads the GDP figure as the thing being tested, when it only selects which revenue threshold applies
options.why: The GDP figure does not decide nexus; it decides which revenue bar the market revenue is measured against. Being the larger economy raises Country Y's bar rather than clearing it.

options.text: Country X only
options.why: The market revenue threshold is 1 million or more for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more, and 250,000 or more for a jurisdiction with annual GDP below 40 billion. Country X, with GDP of 25 billion, is measured against 250,000 and its 600,000 clears it. Country Y, with GDP of 60 billion, is measured against 1 million and its 800,000 falls short. The smaller economy has the lower bar, which is the design: nexus is meant to reach markets that would otherwise be too small to register.

citation.ref: The special-purpose nexus rule for Pillar One Amount A — market revenue of at least 1 million for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more and at least 250,000 for one with annual GDP below 40 billion, applying solely for Amount A and altering nexus for no other purpose

items.scenario: An in-scope group has applied the revenue sourcing rules and finds market revenue of 600,000 in Country X, whose annual GDP is 25 billion, and market revenue of 800,000 in Country Y, whose annual GDP is 60 billion.

items.stem: How is the transaction priced?

options.text: By the matrix, and then adjusted towards the internal comparable uncontrolled price under the data availability mechanism
options.misconception: uses the data availability mechanism as a general adjustment when it exists for a different problem
options.why: The data availability mechanism adjusts the return upwards when the global dataset holds nothing, or too little, for the particular tested party jurisdiction and there is evidence that the jurisdiction could reasonably be considered higher risk. It is not a route for reconciling the matrix to a comparable the taxpayer already has.

options.text: By the Amount B pricing matrix, which overrides any comparable once the transaction is in scope
options.misconception: treats the Amount B approach as mandatory for every in-scope transaction
options.why: Step 2 turns the Amount B framework on for an in-scope transaction only where no reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price can be found for it. The exception is written into the step itself.

options.text: Neither — a transaction for which an internal comparable uncontrolled price exists can never be in scope at step 1
options.misconception: moves the comparable-price test from step 2 back into the step 1 scoping test
options.why: Step 1 asks only whether the tested party is involved in a qualifying transaction meeting the scoping criteria. The comparable uncontrolled price is a step 2 question, and the two steps do different work.

options.text: By the internal comparable uncontrolled price, which displaces the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism
options.why: The pricing step applies only unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available, so where one is, the whole of the three-sub-step framework falls away — the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check that tests the matrix result against the tested party's operating expense level, and the data availability mechanism. That ordering makes sense of what Amount B is for: it approximates an arm's length return where local comparables are absent, which is why it is aimed at low-capacity jurisdictions in the first place. Where a reliable comparable exists there is nothing to approximate.
keywords: unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount B — step 1 scoping and step 2 pricing, the pricing framework applying unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available, with the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism as its three sub-steps

items.scenario: A distributor in a low-capacity jurisdiction carries on baseline marketing and distribution for its group and is in scope of Amount B at step 1, being party to a qualifying transaction that meets the scoping criteria. The group also has a reliable internal comparable uncontrolled price for the same transaction.

items.stem: Which statement is right?

options.text: Both are refreshed annually, so the matrix percentages change every year
options.misconception: collapses the same two cadences into the shorter of the two
options.why: The annual review is of the financial data and other datapoints. The analysis behind the matrix itself is on a five-year cycle, unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update — which is what keeps the approach usable as a simplification.

options.text: Amount B was published in December 2021 with the GloBE Model Rules, and every figure in it is refreshed annually
options.misconception: dates Amount B to the release of the Pillar Two rules, which are a different Pillar and two years earlier
options.why: December 2021 is when the GloBE Model Rules for the minimum tax were released, and those are Pillar Two. The Amount B report came on 19 February 2024 and the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024.

options.text: Both the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the underlying financial data are updated every five years, with no annual review
options.misconception: collapses two different cadences into the longer of the two
options.why: There are two cadences on purpose. The analysis supporting the pricing matrix and the operating expense cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years; the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary.

options.text: The Inclusive Framework reported on Amount B on 19 February 2024 and published the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024; the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually
options.why: Those are the two dates and the two cadences. The report of 19 February 2024 set out to make the arm's length principle simpler and smoother to apply where a distributor does baseline marketing and selling inside one country, with the needs of low-capacity jurisdictions particularly in view, and the pending design aspects followed on 17 June 2024. The analysis behind the matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is on a five-year cycle, updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary. The split cadence exists to simplify compliance: a matrix that moved every year would be no simpler than a benchmarking study.

citation.ref: The Inclusive Framework's report on Pillar One Amount B of 19 February 2024 and its pending design aspects of 17 June 2024 — the pricing matrix and operating expense cap-and-collar analysis updated every five years unless market conditions warrant an interim update, with the financial data reviewed annually

items.scenario: A firm is briefing a client on how settled the Amount B figures are — when the Inclusive Framework published them, and how often they will change.

items.stem: Is the group within the scope of the GloBE Rules for the tested fiscal year?

options.text: No — the test looks at the fiscal year immediately preceding the tested year, in which revenue was 640 million euros
options.misconception: reads the test as a one-year test, so a single year below the line takes the group out
options.why: The immediately preceding year is only one of the four the test looks at. It is precisely because a single year can fall below the line that the test is written as two of four.

options.text: No — the threshold must be met in each of the four preceding fiscal years
options.misconception: reads the two-of-four test as a test that must be satisfied in all four years
options.why: The rule says at least two of the four, not all four. A four-year requirement would take almost every group out of scope in the year after a bad year.

options.text: Yes, but because the average of the four years exceeds 750 million euros
options.misconception: satisfies the test by averaging the four years rather than by counting how many of them clear the threshold
options.why: The average here is 755 million euros, so the answer comes out the same, and that is what makes the method dangerous: it will give the wrong answer whenever one very large year carries three small ones. The rule counts years over the threshold; it does not average them.

options.text: Yes — the test asks for annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in at least two of the four fiscal years that run before the tested one, and two of these four reach it
