options.why: The GloBE Rules catch Constituent Entities of a multinational group whose annual revenue, as reported in the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Ultimate Parent Entity, stood at 750 million euros or more in at least two of the four fiscal years that run before the year under test. Here the 900 and the 780 reach it, which is two of the four, so the group is in scope. The design of the test is what matters: a single year over the line does not bring a group in, and a single year under it does not take a group out.
keywords: at least two of the four

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — annual revenue of 750 million euros or more, as the Ultimate Parent Entity's consolidated financial statements report it, in at least two of the four fiscal years that run before the tested one

items.scenario: A group's annual revenue, as its Ultimate Parent Entity's consolidated financial statements report it, ran like this over the four fiscal years before the tested one: 900 million euros in the earliest, then 700 million euros, then 780 million euros, and 640 million euros in the year just before the tested one.

items.stem: What does the Excluded Entity status of the pension fund do to the group?

options.text: The whole group is out of scope, because the Ultimate Parent Entity is an Excluded Entity
options.misconception: reads the exclusion of the parent as an exclusion of everything beneath it
options.why: The rules say in terms that this exclusion does not affect the multinational group owned by such entities: that group stays inside the GloBE Rules so long as it clears the consolidated revenue threshold when taken as a whole.

options.text: A pension fund is not an Excluded Entity at all; only government entities and international organisations are
options.misconception: truncates the list of Excluded Entities to its first two members
options.why: The list runs wider than that: government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations, and pension funds or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities, plus holding vehicles used by them.

options.text: The pension fund is not subject to the rules and its revenue is left out of the consolidated revenue test as well
options.misconception: extends the exclusion from liability to the measurement of the threshold
options.why: The rules separate the two questions. An Excluded Entity is not subject to the charge; its revenue nevertheless counts when the consolidated revenue test is applied.

options.text: The pension fund and the holding vehicle it uses are not themselves subject to the rules, but the fund's revenue still counts for the consolidated revenue test and the group it controls stays in scope
options.why: The list of Excluded Entities runs like this: government entities; international organisations; non-profit organisations; pension funds; investment funds that sit at the head of a group as its Ultimate Parent Entity; and the holding vehicles any of them use. Two things follow and they pull in opposite directions, which is why this is examinable. The excluded entity is not subject to the rules. But its revenue still counts when the consolidated revenue test is applied, and the exclusion does not touch the group it owns, which remains in scope if that group as a whole meets the threshold. The exclusion protects sovereign, non-profit and charitable entities and the policy of not adding a layer of tax between the investment and the investor; it is not a way out for the operating group.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Excluded Entities being government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations and pension or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities together with their holding vehicles, whose revenue is still counted for the consolidated revenue test and whose exclusion leaves the group they control in scope

items.scenario: A pension fund is the Ultimate Parent Entity of a group. Beneath it sit a holding vehicle used by the fund and a chain of operating companies in several countries. Taken as a whole the group is well above the revenue threshold.

items.stem: What is the effective tax rate for Country B, and what would it be if B Co had instead made a GloBE loss of 5,000,000 euros?

options.text: 20 per cent on the facts, being the tax measured against C Co's income alone, and 20 per cent again on the loss facts
options.misconception: computes the effective tax rate entity by entity rather than on a jurisdictional blend
options.why: The effective tax rate is calculated on a jurisdictional basis, not per entity. The denominator is the Net GloBE Income of the jurisdiction, which is 15,000,000 euros on the first set of facts.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and unchanged if B Co made the loss, since a loss-making entity is left out of the computation
options.misconception: leaves a loss-making entity out of the jurisdictional figure instead of netting its loss against the other entity's income
options.why: Under jurisdictional blending the profits, the losses and the taxes of every constituent entity sitting in one jurisdiction are pooled before the effective tax rate is worked out. Net GloBE Income is the GloBE income of all constituent entities less the GloBE losses of all of them, so a loss reduces the denominator rather than dropping out of it.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and 40 per cent if B Co made the loss
options.why: The Effective Tax Rate is the total of the Adjusted Covered Taxes of each constituent entity located in the jurisdiction divided by the Net GloBE Income of that jurisdiction. Net GloBE Income here is 5,000,000 plus 10,000,000, that is 15,000,000 euros, so the rate is 2,000,000 over 15,000,000 or 13.3333 per cent, below the 15 per cent minimum. If B Co had made a loss of 5,000,000 instead, jurisdictional blending would net that loss against C Co's 10,000,000, leaving Net GloBE Income of 5,000,000 euros, and the rate would be 2,000,000 over 5,000,000, that is 40 per cent. Note which way it moves: a loss in the jurisdiction raises the effective tax rate, because the taxes are being spread over less income.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and nil if B Co made the loss, because a net GloBE loss means no effective tax rate need be computed
options.misconception: applies the net-loss rule to a jurisdiction that is still in net profit after the blend
options.why: It is true that where there is a net GloBE loss the effective tax rate need not be calculated and in most cases no top-up tax is due. But the blend here is 10,000,000 less 5,000,000, which is a net income of 5,000,000 euros, not a loss. The rule bites only when the jurisdiction as a whole is in loss.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Effective Tax Rate as the Adjusted Covered Taxes of the jurisdiction over its Net GloBE Income, Net GloBE Income being the GloBE income of all constituent entities less the GloBE losses of all of them on a jurisdictional blending basis, against a 15 per cent minimum rate

items.scenario: In Country B an in-scope group has two constituent entities. B Co has GloBE income of 5,000,000 euros and C Co has GloBE income of 10,000,000 euros. The adjusted covered taxes of the two taken together are 2,000,000 euros.

items.stem: Who bears the top-up tax attributable to the Country C subsidiary?

options.text: The subsidiaries in Countries A and B, under the Undertaxed Payment Rule, because the priority runs domestic minimum top-up tax first, then the Income Inclusion Rule at the parent, and the Undertaxed Payment Rule only where neither of the first two applies
options.why: The model rules prescribe a priority ranking. Where Country C imposes a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax the jurisdictional top-up tax is imposed on the Country C subsidiary itself. Where it does not, the Ultimate Parent Entity in Country X pays an amount equal to its allocable share of that subsidiary's top-up tax under the Income Inclusion Rule, provided Country X has implemented it. Where neither happens, and Countries A and B have implemented the Undertaxed Payment Rule, those two subsidiaries bear the top-up tax in their own jurisdictions by a denial of deductions or an equivalent adjustment. The rule transfers the levy to the group's other constituent entities located where the GloBE rules are in force.

options.text: Nobody — with no domestic minimum top-up tax in Country C and no Income Inclusion Rule in Country X, the top-up tax falls away
options.misconception: stops at the first two rules and forgets that the third exists as a backstop
options.why: The Undertaxed Payment Rule is triggered precisely where the Ultimate Parent Entity's jurisdiction does not implement the Income Inclusion Rule or does not adopt the GloBE rules. It is the backstop, and its whole purpose is that the top-up tax does not fall away.

options.text: The Country C subsidiary, because the low-tax jurisdiction always has the first right to collect
options.misconception: applies the domestic minimum top-up tax to a jurisdiction that has not enacted one
options.why: A Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax gives the low-tax jurisdiction the right to collect the jurisdictional top-up tax by introducing the charge in its own domestic tax laws. Country C has not introduced it, so there is no charge for it to collect under.

options.text: The parent in Country X, under the Income Inclusion Rule, whether or not Country X has adopted the GloBE rules
options.misconception: applies the Income Inclusion Rule in a jurisdiction that has not implemented the GloBE rules
options.why: The Income Inclusion Rule reaches a constituent entity that is the Ultimate Parent Entity located in a GloBE implementing jurisdiction. Country X has not adopted the rules, so there is nothing there to charge the parent with, and that is exactly the gap the third rule exists to close.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the priority ranking of the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, then the Income Inclusion Rule imposing tax on the parent equal to its allocable share, then the Undertaxed Payment Rule as backstop where the parent's jurisdiction has not implemented the Income Inclusion Rule or adopted the rules

items.scenario: The Ultimate Parent Entity of a group is in Country X and it has three wholly owned subsidiaries, in Countries A, B and C. Country C is a low-taxed jurisdiction. Country C has not introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax. Country X has not adopted the GloBE rules at all. Countries A and B have both implemented the Undertaxed Payment Rule.

items.stem: How is the jurisdictional top-up tax arrived at?

options.text: The percentage is applied to the Net GloBE Income of 15,000,000 euros, the substance-based exclusion being a deduction from the tax rather than from the profit
options.misconception: applies the top-up tax percentage to the wrong base, treating the carve-out as a credit against tax
options.why: The carve-out reduces the profit, not the tax. Excess Profit is defined as Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion, and it is the Excess Profit that the percentage is applied to.

options.text: The full 15 per cent minimum rate is applied to the excess profit, the effective tax rate being relevant only to deciding whether the jurisdiction is low-taxed
options.misconception: charges the whole minimum rate a second time, ignoring the tax the jurisdiction has already collected
options.why: The effective tax rate does two jobs, not one. It decides whether the jurisdiction is low-taxed, and it is then subtracted from the minimum rate to give the percentage charged. Charging the full 15 per cent would tax the same profit twice over.

options.text: The percentage is the effective tax rate itself, 13.333 per cent, applied to the excess profit
options.misconception: charges the effective tax rate rather than the shortfall between it and the minimum
options.why: The Top-up Tax Percentage is the minimum rate less the effective tax rate. It is a shortfall, which is why it is described as a positive percentage point difference.

options.text: The Top-up Tax Percentage is the minimum rate less the effective tax rate, 15 less 13.333, that is 1.6667 per cent, and it is applied not to the Net GloBE Income but to the Excess Profit, which is 15,000,000 less 1,500,000, that is 13,500,000 euros
options.why: The Jurisdictional Top-up Tax is the Top-up Tax Percentage multiplied by the Excess Profit, plus any Additional Current Top-up Tax, less any Domestic Top-up Tax. The Top-up Tax Percentage is the positive percentage point difference between the minimum rate and the effective tax rate. The Excess Profit is the Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion. The two bases are deliberately different: the percentage is worked out on the aggregate profits, the Net GloBE Income, but it is applied to the excess income after the substance carve-out, so that groups keep the benefit of incentives on substantive activity.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Jurisdictional Top-up Tax as the Top-up Tax Percentage on the Excess Profit plus additional current top-up tax less domestic top-up tax, the percentage being the minimum rate less the effective tax rate and the Excess Profit being Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion

items.scenario: For Country B a group has Net GloBE Income of 15,000,000 euros and an effective tax rate of 13.333 per cent. The substance-based income exclusion for the jurisdiction is 1,500,000 euros. There is no additional current top-up tax and no domestic top-up tax.

items.stem: Which answer is right?

options.text: The de-minimis exclusion applies automatically wherever average revenue is below 10 million euros, whatever the income, and no election is needed
options.misconception: drops the second limb of the de-minimis test and the election that switches it on
options.why: Both limbs have to be satisfied — average revenue below 10 million euros and average income or loss that is a loss or is below 1 million euros — and the exclusion is provided at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity rather than applying of its own force.

options.text: The exclusion is 5 per cent of payroll costs only, tangible assets carrying no carve-out; and the de-minimis exclusion applies where average revenue is below 1 million euros
options.misconception: drops the tangible-asset half of the carve-out and swaps the two de-minimis figures
options.why: The exclusion has two halves — a payroll carve-out and a tangible asset carve-out — and the de-minimis figures are 10 million euros of average revenue and 1 million euros of average income, not the other way round.

options.text: The exclusion is 5 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets in the jurisdiction plus 5 per cent of the payroll costs of employees performing activities there, with a ten-year transition starting at 8 per cent of tangible assets and 10 per cent of payroll and phasing down to 5 per cent; and the de-minimis exclusion, at the filing entity's election, applies where the jurisdiction's Average GloBE Revenue is less than 10 million euros and its Average GloBE Income or Loss is a loss or is less than 1 million euros
options.why: For a jurisdiction the substance-based income exclusion adds two things together for each constituent entity there — a payroll carve-out, and a carve-out for tangible assets. Each is 5 per cent: 5 per cent of what the tangible assets sitting in that jurisdiction are carried at, and 5 per cent of the payroll costs for employees who perform activities there. There is a ten-year transition period in recognition of the impact on existing incentives and investment, during which the figures are 8 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs, both phasing down to 5 per cent over the ten years. The de-minimis exclusion has two limbs and both must be met, and it operates at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity — average revenue below 10 million euros and average income or loss that is a loss or below 1 million euros. Its purpose is to avoid a full effective tax rate computation where the top-up tax would not justify the compliance cost.

options.text: The transition starts at 10 per cent of tangible assets and 8 per cent of payroll
options.misconception: has both transitional percentages and attaches each to the wrong carve-out
options.why: It is 8 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs. The payroll figure is the higher of the two.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the substance-based income exclusion at 5 per cent of the carrying value of tangible assets and 5 per cent of payroll costs with a ten-year transition from 8 per cent and 10 per cent, and the de-minimis exclusion at the Filing Constituent Entity's election where average GloBE revenue is below 10 million euros and average GloBE income or loss is a loss or below 1 million euros

items.scenario: A client asks two questions about the GloBE rules. What is the substance-based income exclusion worth, now and during the transitional period? And when may a jurisdiction be left out of the computation altogether?

items.stem: What may Country A do under the Subject to Tax Rule?

options.text: It keeps its 5 per cent withholding and may impose an additional tax of 3 per cent of the covered income
options.why: The specified rate is 9 per cent minus the nominal rate charged where the recipient is resident, and minus again whatever source taxation the treaty's other articles have already allocated to the source jurisdiction. Here that is 9 less 5 less 1, which is 3 per cent. The payor jurisdiction retains its 5 per cent withholding right and imposes the additional 3 per cent on top, so the total tax on the payment reaches the 9 per cent the rule is aimed at.

options.text: It may charge nothing, because the Subject to Tax Rule applies only where the residence State taxes the payment at nil
options.misconception: reads "subject to tax" as requiring the income to bear no tax at all in the residence State
options.why: The rule bites wherever the tax rate nominally charged on the recipient's corporate income sits below 9 per cent. A nominal 1 per cent is below 9, so the rule engages; it is not a rule about untaxed income.

options.text: It may charge an additional 8 per cent, being 9 per cent less the 1 per cent nominal rate in Country B
options.misconception: takes only one of the two reductions, forgetting the source taxation the treaty has already allocated
options.why: The specified rate is the difference between 9 per cent and the nominal rate the resident State applies, cut down further by whatever source taxation other articles of the treaty have already allocated to the source jurisdiction. Country A already has 5 per cent, and that 5 per cent comes off too.

options.text: It may charge 9 per cent in place of the 5 per cent withholding the treaty gives it
options.misconception: treats the 9 per cent as a fresh rate that replaces the treaty rate rather than as a ceiling the source State tops up to
options.why: The 9 per cent is not a rate the source State charges. It is the level below which the residence State's nominal taxation triggers the rule, and the specified rate is the gap between it and what has already been taxed.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two — the specified rate being 9 per cent less the nominal rate applied in the resident State and further reduced by source taxation already allocated to the source jurisdiction under other articles of the treaty

items.scenario: Company A is resident in Country A, a developing country, and pays a royalty to Company B, its group company resident in Country B, for a licence to use a trademark. The treaty between the two countries lets Country A withhold tax at 5 per cent on royalty payments. Country B taxes the royalty at a nominal rate of 1 per cent.

items.stem: Does the Subject to Tax Rule apply to this payment?

options.text: Yes — every condition of the rule is satisfied
options.misconception: works through the payment, the threshold and the connection and misses the developing-country test the rule opens with
options.why: Three of the four conditions are satisfied, which is what makes this tempting. The one that is not is the first: the rule applies to covered payments by an entity in a developing country, and developing country is defined by a gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019.

options.text: No, because the covered income of 400,000 falls below the 1 million threshold
options.misconception: applies the higher covered-income threshold to a country whose GDP is below 40 billion
options.why: The threshold is 250,000 or 1 million a year depending on whether the source country's GDP is above or below 40 billion. This country's GDP is 30 billion, so its threshold is 250,000, and 400,000 exceeds it.

options.text: No, because a management service fee is not a covered payment
options.misconception: reads the list of covered payments as confined to passive income
options.why: Covered payments run wider than passive income: interest and royalties, of course, but also whatever is paid for rights to distribute a product or a service, premiums on insurance and reinsurance, guarantee or financing fees, hire of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, and payments for services. Service fees are expressly in.

options.text: No — the payer's country is not a developing country for this rule, which defines one as having gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method
options.why: The Subject to Tax Rule exists to prevent base erosion in developing countries, and it defines them by income per head: gross national income per capita worked out on the World Bank Atlas method must be 12,535 US dollars or less for 2019, a figure to be regularly updated. At 14,000 dollars the payer's country is outside that. Everything else here is satisfied — the parties are connected persons, since connection is direct or indirect ownership of more than 50 per cent of the interests or a de facto control relationship and the holding is 60 per cent; a payment for services is a covered payment; 400,000 exceeds the 250,000 threshold that applies where the source country's GDP is below 40 billion; and a nominal 4 per cent is below 9 per cent. The first condition still fails, and it fails on its own.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two — applicable to covered payments by an entity in a developing country, defined as one with gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method, made to connected persons at more than 50 per cent of the interests, where covered income in the source country exceeds 250,000 or 1 million by reference to a GDP of 40 billion

items.scenario: A payment is made by an entity in a country whose gross national income per capita on the World Bank Atlas method was 14,000 US dollars in 2019, to a group company that holds 60 per cent of its interests. The payment is a management service fee. The total covered income arising in that source country is 400,000 a year, and the source country's annual GDP is 30 billion. The recipient's country taxes the fee at a nominal 4 per cent.

items.stem: Which of these four are BEPS minimum standards?

options.text: Actions 5 and 13 only
options.why: There are four minimum standards in the whole BEPS package and they are Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14. Two of them appear in this list, so two of these four are binding. Action 3 on controlled foreign company rules and Action 12 on mandatory disclosure are best practices, which the OECD defines as an optional recommendation for States to follow rather than a standard; guidance drawn from best practices is what supports countries proposing to act on mandatory disclosure initiatives or CFC legislation.

options.text: Actions 3 and 12, being the ones a country has to legislate for in its own domestic law
options.misconception: reverses which two bind, on the footing that the domestic-law Actions must be the compulsory ones
options.why: Both minimum standards and best practices can call for domestic legislation, so that is not the dividing line. What makes an Action a minimum standard is that non-implementation would produce negative spill-overs on other countries, including on competitiveness, and Actions 3 and 12 are expressly not minimum standards.

options.text: Actions 5, 6, 13 and 15
options.misconception: puts the multilateral instrument among the minimum standards in place of Action 14 on dispute resolution
options.why: Action 15 is the machinery for putting treaty measures into existing treaties, not a standard of its own. The fourth minimum standard is Action 14, making dispute resolution more effective.

options.text: All four
options.misconception: treats every Action Plan as carrying the same level of commitment
options.why: The Actions carry three different levels of commitment, and that is a distinction the OECD draws in terms: a new minimum standard, a revision of an existing standard, and a best practice. Only four Actions are minimum standards.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2015 BEPS package — Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14 as the four minimum standards subject to peer review, against a revision of an existing standard and a best practice, with the controlled foreign company rules of Action 3 and the mandatory disclosure rules of Action 12 as best practice only

items.scenario: A country is deciding what it is obliged to legislate for and what it may leave alone. Four Action Plans are on the table: Action 3 on controlled foreign company rules, Action 5 on countering harmful tax practices, Action 12 on disclosure of aggressive tax planning arrangements, and Action 13 on transfer pricing documentation.

items.stem: What reason does the study material give for that?

options.text: Because controlled foreign company rules are treaty measures, and a minimum standard can only be a domestic-law measure
options.misconception: classifies CFC rules as treaty measures when they are domestic legislation taxing a resident shareholder
options.why: Controlled foreign company rules are domestic legislation. They tax income in the parent country even where it has not been repatriated, which is a purely domestic charge on a resident shareholder.

options.text: Because CFC rules were superseded by the Income Inclusion Rule under Pillar Two
options.misconception: reads a later development back into a report that predates it by six years
options.why: Action 3 was delivered in 2015 and the GloBE Model Rules came in December 2021. The two coexist; nothing in Action 3 was written by reference to a rule that did not yet exist.

options.text: Because too few countries had CFC rules at the time for a peer review process to be workable
options.misconception: invents a practical obstacle where the study material gives a disagreement of principle
options.why: The obstacle recorded is disagreement about what a CFC regime is for, not the number of countries that had one. CFC rules had been in use for decades before the BEPS Project.

options.text: Because the policy behind CFC regimes drew fundamental disagreement — above all over whether one State ought to run its regime so as to shield another State's tax base from earnings stripping
options.why: The Final Report does not propose a minimum standard for CFC regimes. The OECD regards them as important in tackling base erosion and profit shifting and made a series of best practice recommendations on the building blocks of an effective regime. What stopped it going further than best practice was fundamental disagreement about policy: members could not agree whether one State ought to run a CFC regime so as to shield another State's tax base from earnings stripping. It is a disagreement about purpose, not about technique.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: BEPS Action Plan 3 on strengthening controlled foreign company rules — the Final Report declining to propose a minimum standard because of fundamental disagreement over the policy of CFC regimes, and offering best practice recommendations on the building blocks instead

items.scenario: A student notices that the OECD calls controlled foreign company rules important in tackling base erosion and profit shifting, and yet Action 3 produced only best practice recommendations on the building blocks of an effective regime.

items.stem: Which statement is right?

options.text: Peer review covers all fifteen Actions, so that implementation of the whole package can be monitored
options.misconception: extends peer review from the four minimum standards to the entire package
options.why: Peer review attaches to the minimum standards, because those are the ones every member has committed to implement. Monitoring of the wider package takes the form of assessment reports on what countries have done, which is a different thing from a peer review with a standard to measure against.

options.text: The Actions are grouped on coherence, substance and transparency, with Actions 1 and 15 horizontal across all three; and each of the four minimum standards is subject to peer review, which every member of the Inclusive Framework commits to take part in
options.why: The Action Plans are structured round three fundamental pillars — coherence, substance and transparency — with Action 1 on the digital economy and Action 15 on the multilateral instrument sitting horizontally across them. Action 5 appears twice, its preferential-tax-regimes component under substance and its exchange-of-rulings component under transparency. And each of the four minimum standards goes through peer review, so that implementation is timely and accurate and a level playing field is safeguarded, with all members of the Inclusive Framework committing both to implementing the minimum standards and to participating in the peer review.

options.text: The Actions are grouped by whether each is a treaty measure or a domestic-law measure
options.misconception: substitutes a plausible classification for the one the OECD actually used
options.why: The grouping is by objective, not by instrument. The three fundamental pillars are introducing coherence in domestic rules affecting cross-border activities, reinforcing substance requirements so that taxation aligns with value creation, and improving transparency and tax certainty.

options.text: Action 1 belongs to the coherence pillar and Action 15 to the transparency pillar
options.misconception: forces the two horizontal Actions into pillars when the classification places them across all three
options.why: Action 1 on the digital economy and Action 15 on the multilateral instrument are classified as horizontal. Both cut across the whole package rather than serving one objective, which is why Action 15 is called the machinery Action.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The classification of the fifteen BEPS Action Plans on coherence, substance and transparency with Actions 1 and 15 horizontal, and the peer review to which each of the four minimum standards is subject

items.scenario: A note groups the fifteen Action Plans and describes how compliance with them is checked. Only one of the four statements in it is accurate.

items.stem: Does the company have a significant economic presence in India?

options.text: Yes, and the whole of the company's global income is then deemed to accrue or arise in India
options.misconception: gets the trigger right and ignores the attribution limit written into the same provision
options.why: The provision ends with a limit. Once significant economic presence is what creates the business connection, only the income attributable to the transactions or activities the two limbs describe is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

options.text: No — with no office, employee or agent in India there can be no business connection at all
options.misconception: requires a physical presence, which is the very thing the provision was written to do without
options.why: The provision says the opposite in terms. The transactions or activities make up a significant economic presence regardless of where the agreement was made, regardless of whether the non-resident keeps a home or a place of business on Indian soil, and regardless of whether he performs any service here.

options.text: Yes — the two limbs are alternatives, and although the payments of ₹1.6 crore fall short of the ₹2 crore limb, systematic and continuous soliciting of business or interaction with at least 3 lakh users is the second limb and 4.2 lakh users satisfies it
options.why: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) gives significant economic presence two limbs. The first covers dealings in goods, services or property that a non-resident has with anybody in India — the supply or download of data or software included — where the payments add up during the previous year to more than ₹2 crore. The second is a systematic and continuous drive for business, or engagement with users in India, where the users number at least 3 lakh. Either is enough, and the second is met here. Both apply regardless of where the agreement was made and regardless of whether the non-resident keeps a place of business here — and only the income attributable to those activities is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

options.text: No — the aggregate of payments has to exceed ₹2 crore before there can be a significant economic presence, and ₹1.6 crore falls short
options.misconception: reads the two limbs of the definition as cumulative when they are alternatives
options.why: The definition sets out two separate kinds of transaction, each with its own condition, and satisfying either is enough. The payments limb is not a gateway the user limb has to pass through.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) — significant economic presence as either payments exceeding ₹2 crore in the previous year from transactions in goods, services or property including downloads of data or software, or systematic and continuous soliciting or interaction with at least 3 lakh users, applying whether or not the agreement is entered into in India, with only the attributable income deemed to accrue or arise in India

items.scenario: A non-resident company has no office, employee or agent in India. During previous year 2025-26 it receives ₹1.6 crore from customers in India for downloads of its software, and its platform is used by 4.2 lakh users in India with whom it interacts systematically and continuously. The agreements with the Indian customers are all signed outside India.

items.stem: Which mapping is right?

options.text: All three options were adopted as a single measure, the equalisation levy, which remains in force
options.misconception: collapses three separate Indian provisions into one and misses that the levy has been withdrawn
options.why: Three separate provisions answer the three options, and the equalisation levy is no longer one of them: the 2 per cent levy on e-commerce supply or services was withdrawn by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 and the 6 per cent levy on specified services by the Finance Act, 2025.

options.text: Significant economic presence answers the withholding tax option and section 194-O answers the virtual fixed place of business option
options.misconception: has both provisions and attaches each to the wrong OECD option
options.why: Significant economic presence is a nexus rule — it makes a non-resident's presence a business connection — which is what the virtual fixed place option was about. Section 194-O is a deduction of tax at source, which is the withholding option.

options.text: Significant economic presence under Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) answers the virtual fixed place of business option; section 194-O, at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services facilitated by an e-commerce operator, answers the withholding tax option; and the equalisation levy answered the third, and is the one India has withdrawn
options.why: The OECD offered three options and recommended none, leaving countries to act in their own domestic law. India acted on all three. The concept of significant economic presence, which the study material itself describes as similar to the virtual fixed place permanent establishment recommended in the 2015 Action 1 report, was introduced by Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i). Section 194-O answers the option of a final withholding tax on payments for digital goods or services: where an e-commerce operator uses its digital or electronic facility or platform to help an e-commerce participant sell goods or supply services, it deducts tax at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount. The third option was the equalisation levy, and it is the one India has abandoned in both its forms.

options.text: Section 194-O answers the withholding tax option, at 1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services facilitated
options.misconception: states the section 194-O rate as 1 per cent
options.why: The rate in section 194-O is 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services or both. The mapping is otherwise right, which is what makes the wrong figure worth catching.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) and Section 194-O, read against the three options offered under BEPS Action Plan 1 — a modified permanent establishment rule, a virtual fixed place of business, and a final withholding tax or an equalisation levy, with tax deducted at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount by an e-commerce operator

items.scenario: A firm is mapping the options the OECD offered for the direct tax challenges of the digital economy under Action Plan 1 against the provisions India actually enacted.

items.stem: Does the Multilateral Instrument apply to either treaty?

options.text: To the Country M treaty only, notification by India being the operative act
options.misconception: makes the Instrument apply on the strength of one party's own notification
options.why: It is the only one of the two where notification is not matched, so it is the clearer failure of the two. Each country has to notify its treaty with the other while depositing its instrument with the OECD.

options.text: To both, since India has notified each of them
options.misconception: treats one side's notification as enough to make a treaty a covered tax agreement
options.why: Article 2 requires each party to have notified the agreement to the Depositary as a listed agreement. That is the matching principle, and it needs both.

options.text: To the Country N treaty only, because matched notification is what matters and ratification is a formality
options.misconception: reduces ratification to a formality, when it is what starts the entry-into-force clock
options.why: Ratification is the act that makes the Convention enter into force for a country, and until it has entered into force for both Contracting States its provisions cannot have effect for their treaty. Matched notification decides what the Instrument could modify; ratification decides whether it modifies anything yet.

options.text: To neither — the matching principle needs both parties to notify before a treaty is a Covered Tax Agreement, which fails for Country M; and for Country N the Instrument has not entered into force, since entry into force follows the deposit of an instrument of ratification
options.why: Two different conditions fail in the two cases. Article 2 defines a Covered Tax Agreement as a treaty for relieving double taxation which is in force between the parties and which each of them has notified to the Depositary as a listed agreement — the matching principle — so India-Country M is not a Covered Tax Agreement at all, the same position as India-Mauritius, where India notified and Mauritius did not. For Country N the notification is matched but the Instrument applies only to countries which have signed it and have ratified, accepted or approved it under domestic law and deposited that instrument with the OECD depositary. That is the India-Italy position in the study material: Italy notified its treaty with India as a Covered Tax Agreement and has not ratified, so the Instrument does not apply to that treaty.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 2 and Article 34 of the Convention — a Covered Tax Agreement being one notified to the Depositary by each party as a listed agreement, and the Convention applying only to countries that have signed and have ratified, accepted or approved it and deposited that instrument with the OECD depositary

items.scenario: Two situations are put to an adviser. India and Country M have both signed and ratified the Multilateral Instrument; India has notified its treaty with Country M as a covered tax agreement, but Country M has not notified its treaty with India. Separately, India and Country N have each notified their treaty with the other, but Country N has not ratified the Instrument under its own law.

items.stem: When did the Convention enter into force for India, and from when could its provisions first take effect here?

options.text: 1 October 2019, being the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months beginning on 25 June 2019, with the earliest effect in India on 1 April 2020, six calendar months later
options.why: On deposit of the instrument of ratification three calendar months begin to run, and the Convention comes into force on the first day of the month after they expire. Three calendar months from 25 June 2019 expires in September, so the first day of the following month is 1 October 2019. For taxes other than withholding taxes the provisions have effect for a taxable period beginning on or after the expiration of six calendar months from the later of the entry-into-force dates, which for India is 1 April 2020 — the earliest date on which the Convention could take effect here. The Central Government notified the Convention under section 90(1) by Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019.

options.text: 1 July 2019 and 1 January 2020, the withholding tax rule applying to every kind of tax
options.misconception: shortens the entry-into-force period and applies the withholding-tax effective date rule to all taxes
options.why: Two errors compound. The period before entry into force is three calendar months, not a few days. And the calendar-year rule — the first day of the next calendar year beginning on or after the later entry-into-force date — is the rule for withholding taxes only; for other taxes the period is six calendar months and it runs to the start of a taxable period.

options.text: 25 September 2019 and 25 March 2020, both counted forward from the date of deposit itself
options.misconception: counts three and six months forward from the day of deposit instead of to the first day of the month that follows
options.why: Entry into force is not three months from the date of deposit. It is the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months beginning on that date, which is what moves it from late September to 1 October.

options.text: 1 October 2019 for both, entry into force and entry into effect being one event
options.misconception: collapses the two clocks into one, when the Convention runs them separately
options.why: They are two separate clocks and the second starts only when the first has finished for both Contracting States. Entry into force is when a country becomes a party; entry into effect is when the modified provisions actually begin to govern a taxable period.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention, read with Section 90(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019 — entry into force on the first day of the month after three calendar months from deposit have expired, effect for withholding taxes from the first day of the next calendar year and for other taxes after six calendar months, with India depositing on 25 June 2019, entering into force on 1 October 2019 and taking effect from 1 April 2020

items.scenario: India signed the Multilateral Instrument at Paris on 7 June 2017 and deposited its instrument of ratification with the OECD depositary on 25 June 2019.

items.stem: Which summary is right?

options.text: It replaces each covered tax agreement, the text of the treaty ceasing to have effect once the Instrument enters into force
options.misconception: reads the Instrument as superseding the treaty rather than applying alongside it
options.why: The Instrument modifies tax treaties not by amending their text but by being applied together with the relevant treaty. It does not make the existing agreement otiose; it operates alongside it and modifies the application of some clauses on the later-in-time principle.

options.text: It has 7 parts and 39 articles, of which Articles 3 to 17 are the substantive provisions; a party may reserve out of provisions that do not reflect a BEPS minimum standard and may withdraw the reservation later; and of the four BEPS minimum standards only Actions 6 and 14 are minimum standards inside the Instrument, Actions 5 and 13 being implemented in domestic law
options.why: The Instrument runs to 7 parts and 39 articles: scope and interpretation in Articles 1 and 2, hybrid mismatches in 3 to 5, treaty abuse in 6 to 11, avoidance of permanent establishment status in 12 to 15, improving dispute resolution in 16 and 17, arbitration in 18 to 26, and final provisions in 27 to 39, with Articles 3 to 17 recognised as the substantive provisions. A reservation is a unilateral statement by which a State excludes or modifies the legal effect of certain provisions, and a jurisdiction may opt out only where a provision does not carry a BEPS minimum standard — and may later withdraw the reservation and opt in. Of the four minimum standards under the BEPS package, Actions 6 and 14 are the ones specifically provided as minimum standards under the Instrument.

options.text: It has 7 parts and 39 articles, and no reservation of any kind is permitted, the whole Instrument being a minimum standard
options.misconception: gets the structure right and treats every provision as compulsory, when the reservation mechanism is the reason countries signed
options.why: The structure is right and the rest is not. The Instrument provides flexibility in three ways — a choice among alternative provisions, a choice whether to apply optional provisions such as mandatory binding arbitration, and the right to reserve out. Without that flexibility the tax policies of the signatories would never have converged enough for them to sign.

options.text: All four BEPS minimum standards are minimum standards inside the Instrument as well
options.misconception: assumes the four BEPS minimum standards carry over unchanged into the Instrument
options.why: Only two do. Action 6 on treaty abuse and Action 14 on dispute resolution are specifically provided as minimum standard provisions under the Instrument; the solutions for Action 5 and Action 13 are incorporated under domestic laws instead, which is why they cannot be minimum standards in a treaty instrument.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: The structure of the Convention in 7 parts and 39 articles with Articles 3 to 17 as the substantive provisions, the reservation mechanism limited to provisions that do not reflect a BEPS minimum standard, and Actions 6 and 14 as the minimum standards inside the Instrument with Actions 5 and 13 implemented in domestic law

items.scenario: A firm is summarising the Multilateral Instrument for a training note — how it is built, how much a country may opt out of, and how the BEPS minimum standards sit inside it.

items.stem: How much of that interest does the treaty treat as the income of a resident of Country N?

options.text: The whole of it — Country M, where the payment arises, treats Larkspur as a company set up in Country N, and it is the paying State's view of the recipient that decides
options.misconception: lets the source State's characterisation of the entity decide, when the rule looks to how the other State taxes the income
options.why: The rule is written the other way about. It asks how the State under whose law the entity is see-through treats the income for its own taxing purposes, not how the State the payment comes from classifies the entity. Country M's view that Larkspur is a company does not turn the two Country Z shares into a resident's income.

options.text: One third, but only once the competent authorities of Country M and Country N have settled the point between them, a mismatch of this kind being decided case by case
options.misconception: borrows the case-by-case competent-authority route used for a dual resident company and applies it to the see-through entity rule
options.why: The case-by-case approach through the competent authorities belongs to the residence article, where a person other than an individual is resident in both States. The see-through entity rule needs no such determination: it applies of itself, by measuring how much of the income the other State taxes as a resident's.

options.text: None of it — the two States classify Larkspur differently, and where the classification does not match the Convention cannot reach the payment at all
options.misconception: reads a mismatch of classification as putting the income outside the treaty, when the article exists precisely to resolve one
options.why: A mismatch is the situation the provision was written for, not a reason it fails. It gives an answer in exactly this case, and the answer is that the part of the income the other State taxes in a resident's hands is inside the treaty.

options.text: One third — the share of the single member whom Country N taxes as a resident of Country N
options.why: Where an entity is treated as wholly or partly see-through under the tax law of either State, the income running through it counts as a resident's income only so far as that State, for its own taxing purposes, treats the income as belonging to somebody resident there. Country N looks past Larkspur and taxes three members. Only one of them is resident in Country N, so only his share is protected by the interest article; the two shares belonging to members in Country Z are not, because Country Z has no treaty with either State and Country N is not taxing those shares as the income of its own residents. One third is therefore the answer.
keywords: only so far as that State

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021 and OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017
citation.ref: Article 1 of both Models — income derived through an entity treated as wholly or partly fiscally transparent counts as a resident's income only to the extent that State treats it as the income of a resident

items.scenario: Country M and Country N have a treaty that follows the Model Convention word for word. Larkspur Holdings is set up in Country N and has three members sharing everything equally: one lives in Country N, and the other two live in Country Z, which has no treaty with either M or N. Country M's law treats Larkspur as a company and taxes it on interest a borrower in M pays it. Country N's law treats Larkspur as see-through and taxes each of the three members on his own third.

items.stem: Which of the four does the Convention apply to?

options.text: The provincial wage levy, the tax on the gain from the warehouse and the new surcharge — but not the tax on the value added at each stage of a sale
options.why: The article applies to taxes on income and on capital levied for a State or for its political subdivisions or local authorities, so a province's levy is not outside merely because a province charges it, and a charge measured on everything an employer pays out as wages is named as one of the taxes covered. A charge on the gain from parting with immovable property is named as well. The Convention carries forward to any tax that is the same, or substantially the same, brought in after signature, whether added to the taxes named or put in their place, which is the new surcharge. A tax on the value added at each stage of a sale is neither a tax on income nor a tax on capital, so nothing brings it in.

options.text: Only the tax on the gain from the warehouse and the new surcharge — a levy charged by a province rather than by the national government of State P sits outside a treaty the national government signed
options.misconception: reads the article as reaching only taxes levied by the central government, when it names political subdivisions and local authorities as well
options.why: The article says in terms that it covers taxes levied for a State or for its political subdivisions or its local authorities, and adds that it makes no difference how the levy is collected. A provincial charge measured on wages paid is inside.

options.text: All four — once a treaty is in force it governs every tax the State levies on a resident of the other State, whatever the nature of the tax
options.misconception: forgets that the Convention is confined to taxes on income and on capital, so an indirect tax on a sale is never inside it
options.why: The article draws a boundary and the tax on the value added at each stage of a sale falls outside it. What is covered is a charge on the whole of income, on the whole of capital, or on any part of either, and a turnover-based indirect tax is none of those.

options.text: Only the tax on the gain from the warehouse — a levy on wages paid is a cost of employing people rather than a tax on income, and a tax brought in after signature reaches the treaty only if the two States sign a fresh protocol for it
options.misconception: denies the wage-based levy and requires a new protocol for a later tax, when the article covers both expressly
options.why: Both limbs are written into the article. A tax on the total amounts an enterprise pays out as wages or salaries is listed among the taxes covered, and the Convention applies of its own force to a tax that is identical or substantially similar imposed after the date of signature.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 2 of both Models — taxes on income and on capital levied for a State or its political subdivisions or local authorities, the taxes expressly included, and identical or substantially similar taxes imposed after the date of signature

items.scenario: State P and State Q sign a treaty on the Model Convention, and the treaty names State P's corporate income tax among its existing taxes. Four of State P's levies are then argued over. A province of State P charges an employer a levy worked out on the whole of the wages it pays its staff. State P taxes the gain a seller makes on parting with a warehouse. State P also charges a tax on the value added at each stage of a sale of goods. And two years after the treaty was signed, State P brings in a fresh surcharge on company profits which is substantially the same as the corporate income tax the treaty names.

items.stem: Which reading of those three rows is right?

options.text: The OECD Model heads its employment article income from employment where the UN Model heads it dependent personal services; the UN Model's directors' article names the remuneration of top-level managerial officials as well as directors' fees, which the OECD's does not; and the OECD's performers' article speaks of entertainers where the UN's speaks of artistes
options.why: Those are the three rows where the two article lists diverge without either Model gaining or losing an article. The employment article is called income from employment in one list and dependent personal services in the other. The directors' article is confined to directors' fees in the OECD Model, while the UN Model gives the same article a wider subject by naming the remuneration of top-level managerial officials alongside them. And the performers' article is headed entertainers and sportspersons in the OECD Model against artistes and sportspersons in the UN Model.

options.text: It is the other way round on the first row — the UN Model calls it income from employment and the OECD Model calls it dependent personal services
options.misconception: reverses which Model uses which label, and so misreads the whole column
options.why: Dependent personal services is the UN Model's label and pairs with independent personal services, the article the UN Model keeps and the OECD Model deleted. Income from employment is the OECD Model's.

options.text: Both Models now head that article entertainers and sportspersons — artistes was the older OECD wording and the UN Model adopted the change when the OECD made it
options.misconception: assumes the UN Model followed the OECD's renaming, when the UN Model's own article list still reads artistes and sportspersons
options.why: The two lists do not agree here. The UN Model's article is artistes and sportspersons and the OECD Model's is entertainers and sportspersons, which is one of the three places the same article number carries different words.

options.text: The headings differ but nothing else does — the UN Model's longer heading on the directors' article is a description of the same ground, so both Models reach directors' fees and nothing more
options.misconception: treats the extra words in the UN heading as decoration, when they give that article a subject the OECD's article does not have
options.why: A heading in an article list is what the article is about. The UN Model's article is about directors' fees and about the remuneration of top-level managerial officials; the OECD Model's is about directors' fees. That is a difference in subject, not in wording.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The article lists of both Models in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — articles 15, 16 and 17, where the same number carries a different name or a wider subject

items.scenario: A firm is drawing up a treaty on the UN Model for a client and putting the OECD Model in the next column so the client can see what he is choosing. Three rows in Chapter III carry the same article number in both columns and different words: the article on income earned in employment, the article on what a company pays its directors, and the article on performers.

items.stem: What is the right answer to both questions?

options.text: The permanent establishment article and the royalties article are where the UN Model offers two versions, those being the places it parts company with the OECD Model most sharply
options.misconception: confuses a divergence between the two Models with the UN Model offering two texts of its own to choose between
options.why: Those are indeed the articles where the two Models differ most, and neither of them is offered in alternative versions. Divergence from the OECD Model and a choice inside the UN Model are two different things.

options.text: Only the mutual agreement procedure is offered in two versions; shipping and pensions carry a single text in each Model
options.misconception: knows Alternative B from the arbitration discussion and assumes that is the only place the UN Model offers a choice
options.why: The mutual agreement procedure is the best known of the three because Alternative B is where arbitration comes from, but the article list marks two more the same way: international shipping and air transport, and pensions and social security payments.

options.text: Those three, and the exemption and credit methods are a fourth pair — one article set out in two versions, of which the negotiating States adopt whichever suits them
options.misconception: reads 23A and 23B as two versions of one article, and so misses that a treaty may use both at once
options.why: They are two numbered articles in both Models, not two versions of one, and a treaty may adopt the exemption route for certain kinds of income and the credit route for others. The two are not mutually exclusive.

options.text: Two texts are offered for international shipping and air transport, for pensions and social security payments, and for the mutual agreement procedure; the exemption and credit methods are not such a pair, being two separate articles that a single treaty may use side by side for different kinds of income
options.why: Three entries in the UN Model's article list are marked as carrying Alternatives A and B — international shipping and air transport, pensions and social security payments, and the mutual agreement procedure, whose Alternative B is the one that brings in arbitration. The exemption method and the credit method are different: they stand as articles 23A and 23B in both Models, and a treaty is free to write in one of them for some classes of income and the other for the rest, so choosing one is not choosing against the other.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021 and OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017
citation.ref: The UN Model's article list in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — Alternatives A and B on international shipping and air transport, on pensions and social security payments, and on the mutual agreement procedure, against articles 23A and 23B which stand separately in both Models

items.scenario: A negotiator is told that the UN Model does not always put up a single text — that for some articles it sets out two versions, marked A and B, and the two States take one of them. He asks which articles those are, and whether the exemption method and the credit method are a pair of that kind.

items.stem: Which description of the article is right?

options.text: The two Models word it much alike, so it is not a UN Model addition at all; it settles both what may be passed between the two States and the form an asking has to take; and what makes it matter to a developing country is that evasion and avoidance across a border carry capital out of the country with them
options.why: Two of his assumptions have to go. This is one of the articles on which the two Models are similar, not one the UN Model added, so nothing turns on which Model a treaty follows here. And the article is not merely permissive: it settles both what may be passed between the two States and the form an asking has to take. The reason the chapter singles out developing countries is the second-order loss — the article curtails cross-border evasion and avoidance, and it curtails the flight of capital that is often accomplished through them.
keywords: both what may be passed between the two States and the form an asking has to take

options.text: Both Models carry it, and its value to a developing country is confined to collecting the tax on the transactions it asks about; capital leaving the country is an exchange control matter and has nothing to do with this article
options.misconception: severs the link the chapter draws between cross-border evasion and the capital flight arranged through it
options.why: The chapter draws exactly that link. The article is said to matter to many developing countries not only for curtailing evasion and avoidance across a border but for curtailing the capital flight that is often accomplished through them.

options.text: Both Models carry it, and it does no more than list the information that may be exchanged; how a State asks for that information is left to whatever procedure its own domestic law provides
options.misconception: splits the article in half, when it provides for the manner of making a request as well as for what may be exchanged
options.why: The article provides for both halves. It settles what may be passed across, and it settles the form in which one State is to put its asking to the other. That is the whole point of writing it into the treaty rather than leaving each side to its own procedure.

options.text: He is right that it is a UN Model addition — the OECD Model, being a treaty between developed countries, has no counterpart to it, which is why it is discussed as a developing country's article
options.misconception: assumes an article the chapter ties to developing countries must be one the UN Model added, when the OECD and UN versions of this one are similar
options.why: The articles the UN Model carries alone are fees for technical services, income from automated digital services and independent personal services. The exchange of information article stands in both Models and the two are worded much alike; what is said about developing countries is why it matters to them, not who wrote it.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 26 of both Models — the information which may be exchanged and the manner of requesting it, the similarity of the two Models on this article, and its importance to developing countries against evasion, avoidance and capital flight

items.scenario: A student is going through the articles where the UN Model and the OECD Model part company and has reached the exchange of information article. He assumes it must be another of the places where the UN Model went further for the sake of developing countries, and he is not sure what the article covers beyond saying that information may be passed on.

items.stem: Which of State Y's three grounds does the exchange of information article recognise?

options.text: The lawyer's advice may be held back, and the worry about the material reaching the wrong hands is a real one the article takes account of; but having no use for the material itself is no ground at all
options.why: The article recognises two of the three. A State may hold material back by showing that it is a communication between a lawyer and his client which its own law protects from disclosure. And no State is expected to hand over confidential financial material unless it is satisfied that the material will not reach people with no business seeing it, so State Y's concern about onward disclosure is one the article takes account of. The third ground fails: a State's own want of interest or use in information cannot be the basis on which it declines to co-operate.
keywords: a communication between a lawyer and his client
not reach people with no business seeing it

options.text: The second and third only — a lawyer's papers about a client's tax affairs enjoy no protection, tax information being by its nature not privileged
options.misconception: denies the legal-advice limb the article allows, and accepts the want-of-interest ground it refuses
options.why: The article has it the other way about on both. The legal-advice ground is one it names as available, and the want-of-interest ground is the one it names as unavailable.

options.text: None of them — the obligation is unqualified, so once a request is properly made the State asked must supply whatever it holds
options.misconception: reads the exchange obligation as absolute, missing the protection given to a lawyer's communication with his client
options.why: The obligation has limits. Material protected from disclosure under domestic law as a communication between a lawyer and his client may be withheld, and confidentiality in the hands of the requesting State is a real condition of the exchange.

options.text: All three — a State is asked to gather information for its treaty partner as a courtesy, so any honest reason for declining is enough
options.misconception: treats a State's own lack of interest in the information as a good reason to refuse, which the article rules out expressly
options.why: The article is an obligation and not a courtesy, and the one ground it names as insufficient is precisely this: lack of interest or use in the information cannot form the basis for refusing to co-operate.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 26 of both Models — confidence that information will not be disclosed to unauthorised persons, the domestic-law protection for a lawyer's communication with his client, and that want of interest or use is no ground for refusing to co-operate

items.scenario: Under a treaty on the Model Convention, State X asks State Y for information about a taxpayer's bank dealings. State Y wants to hold three things back. Some of the papers are advice a lawyer gave the taxpayer, which State Y's own law protects from being disclosed. State Y adds that the taxpayer raises no question at all under State Y's tax, so the material is of no use to State Y itself. And State Y says it is not satisfied that State X will keep the material away from people who have no business seeing it.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No — the appeal scheme is the wider of the two, since it alone may cut out the contact between the authority and the party, an appeal being decided on the papers
options.misconception: reverses which scheme carries the interface object
options.why: Removing the interface is named in the scheme for giving advance rulings, not in the scheme for the Assessing Officer's appeal. The appeal scheme's second object is a team-based mechanism with dynamic jurisdiction.

options.text: No — both are made for greater efficiency, transparency and accountability, and both put resources to work through scale and specialisation with a jurisdiction that moves; but removing the contact between the Board and the applicant so far as technology allows is named only for the rulings scheme, and a team-based mechanism is named only for the appeal scheme
options.why: The two schemes overlap and are not the same. Both are made for greater efficiency, transparency and accountability. Both reach for the better use of resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation, and both carry a jurisdiction that is dynamic rather than fixed. The rulings scheme alone speaks of doing away with the interface between the Board and the applicant during a proceeding, so far as it is technologically feasible, which makes sense because that is the scheme where an applicant appears. The appeal scheme alone speaks of a team-based mechanism.
keywords: economies of scale and functional specialisation

options.text: Yes — the same objects are written into both, the faceless wording being a standard form repeated wherever the Act provides for a scheme
options.misconception: treats the objects as boilerplate, when each scheme names its own and the lists are not the same length
options.why: The lists differ. The rulings scheme names three objects and the appeal scheme two, and only one of them mentions removing the interface with the applicant while only the other mentions a team.

options.text: No — there is no scheme for the appeal at all, an appeal to the High Court being governed by that court's own procedure once it is filed
options.misconception: assumes the Act stops providing once a matter reaches the High Court, when a scheme for the Assessing Officer's appeal is expressly provided for
options.why: The Act provides for one. The Central Government is empowered to make a scheme for the purpose of the appeal to the High Court by the Assessing Officer, with its own stated objects, quite apart from anything the High Court does with the appeal afterwards.

citation.ref: Section 245R(9) and section 245W(2) — the scheme for giving advance rulings with its three objects including elimination of the interface, and the separate scheme for the Assessing Officer's appeal with its team-based mechanism

items.scenario: An article student is reading the two places the Income-tax Act, 1961 lets the Central Government make a scheme in this chapter — one for the giving of advance rulings by a Board, and one for the appeal the Assessing Officer takes to the High Court. He tells his principal the two are worded identically and that reading one is enough.

items.stem: What may the Central Government do, and what happens to the notification afterwards?

options.text: Only the fresh direction — a direction once issued has spent itself and cannot be reopened, though the power to issue new directions continues
options.misconception: reverses both limbs, denying the amendment the section preserves and allowing the fresh direction it stops
options.why: It is the other way round on both. Fresh directions stopped on 31 March 2023 and a direction issued on or before that day may still be amended by notification.

options.text: Only the amendment — no such direction may be issued after 31 March 2023, but one issued on or before that day may still be amended by notification; and a notification of either kind is laid before each House of Parliament once it has issued
options.why: The power to direct that a provision of the Act shall not apply, or shall apply with the modifications, exceptions and adaptations specified, was given an end date. No direction may be issued after 31 March 2023. What survives that date is the power to amend: a direction already issued on or before it may be amended by notification afterwards, so a scheme already set up does not freeze. And Parliament sees them all: a notification issued under any of these powers is laid before each House of Parliament, which must be done as soon as it can be once the notification has issued.
keywords: laid before each House of Parliament

options.text: Both — the date governs only the notification setting up the scheme itself, and directions made under the scheme may issue at any time while the scheme runs
options.misconception: attaches the cut-off to the scheme notification rather than to the power to direct that provisions of the Act shall not apply
options.why: The date is written against the power to direct, not against the scheme. It is fresh directions that stopped on 31 March 2023, and the scheme carries on with the directions already made under it.

options.text: Both, and neither notification goes anywhere afterwards — laying before Parliament is required of rules made under the rule-making power and not of a notification of this kind
options.misconception: drops the laying requirement written into this chapter itself, treating it as belonging only to the general rule-making power
options.why: This chapter carries its own laying requirement. A notification issued under the scheme powers, or under the directions that go with them, goes before both Houses of Parliament once it has issued, and as soon after that as it can be done.

citation.ref: Sections 245R(10) and 245R(11) with sections 245W(3) and 245W(4) — the power to direct that a provision shall not apply or shall apply with modifications, no such direction after 31 March 2023 with amendment of an earlier one still open, and every notification laid before each House of Parliament

items.scenario: In 2026 the Central Government wants to do two things about the scheme for giving advance rulings. It wants to issue a fresh direction that a particular provision of the Income-tax Act, 1961 shall not apply to proceedings under the scheme. And it wants to amend a direction of that same kind which it issued in February 2023. The Board's counsel is also asked whether either notification has to go anywhere once it is issued.

items.stem: Whose complaint is good?

options.text: Both complaints are good — a hearing is due at every stage of the proceeding, asked for or not
options.misconception: makes the hearing before a ruling automatic, when the section makes it turn on the applicant asking
options.why: Only the hearing before a rejection is automatic. The hearing before a ruling is pronounced is given where the applicant requests one, and the request is what triggers it.

options.text: Ms Cherian's only — the Board may reject an application on the papers, the applicant's remedy being his appeal, but it may never rule without hearing him
options.misconception: reverses the two hearings, making the rejection summary and the ruling always oral
options.why: The section says the opposite in both places. No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard, and a hearing before the ruling is given on the applicant's request.

options.text: Mr Bakshi's, on both counts — an application may not be rejected without the applicant being offered an opportunity of being heard, and the rejecting order has to state the reason. Ms Cherian's is not, because a hearing before a ruling is given where the applicant asks for one and she did not ask
options.why: The two hearings in this section are not the same. Before rejecting an application the Board must give the applicant an opportunity of being heard, whether or not he has asked for one, and where it does reject, the order has to state the reason it has refused him. Before pronouncing a ruling on an application it has allowed, the Board has to hear the applicant where a request for a hearing has been received, in person or through a duly authorised representative. Mr Bakshi's rejection fails both requirements. Ms Cherian made no request, so nothing obliged the Board to hear her.
keywords: where a request for a hearing has been received

options.text: Neither — the Board settles its own procedure, so it may reject or rule without hearing anybody, and the reason for a rejection is a matter internal to the Board
options.misconception: treats the Board's procedure as unregulated, when the section requires both the hearing before rejection and the reason in the order
options.why: Two things are required of a rejection and both were missing here: the applicant must be given an opportunity of being heard first, and the order must state why the application was rejected. A copy of that order also goes to the applicant and to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner.

citation.ref: Section 245R — no rejection without an opportunity of being heard, the reason to be given in the order, and a hearing before pronouncement where the applicant requests one, in person or through a duly authorised representative

items.scenario: Two applicants complain about a Board for Advance Rulings. Mr Bakshi's application was rejected; he was never told the Board was minded to reject it, and the order says only that his application is not allowed. Ms Cherian's application was allowed, and the Board then pronounced its ruling without hearing anybody at all; she had never asked for a hearing but says the ruling is bad because none was given.

items.stem: Which of the three complaints is right?
