options.text: The third only — a ruling answers the applicant's own question and is served on him alone, the department learning of it only if he later relies on it
options.misconception: forgets that a copy of the ruling goes to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as well
options.why: A copy of the ruling, duly signed and certified, is sent to the applicant and to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner alike, as soon as may be after it is pronounced.

options.text: None of them
options.why: Each of the three describes something the section provides for. On receiving an application the Board sends a copy to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner concerned and, where it considers it necessary, calls on that officer to furnish the relevant records, which are returned to him as soon as they can be. In ruling on an application it has allowed, the Board is not confined to the applicant's papers: it may examine further material placed before it by the applicant and material it has obtained itself. And a copy of the ruling, signed by the Members and certified, is sent to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as well as to the applicant.
keywords: signed by the Members and certified

options.text: The first only — a Board decides between the applicant and the Revenue, so calling for one side's file and reading it puts the Board on that side
options.misconception: treats the Board as an adversarial forum, when the section itself has the application copied to the Commissioner and his records called for
options.why: The section builds that step in. A copy of the application goes to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and where the Board considers it necessary it calls on him for the relevant records, which are then returned to him.

options.text: The second only — once an application is admitted the question is fixed, and the Board rules on the record as it stood when it admitted the case
options.misconception: denies the Board its own power to obtain material after admitting an application
options.why: The Board pronounces its ruling after examining such further material as the applicant places before it or as it obtains itself. Admission fixes the question, not the evidence.

citation.ref: Section 245R — the copy of the application sent to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the records called for and returned, further material placed by the applicant or obtained by the Board, and the signed and certified ruling sent to both

items.scenario: An applicant before a Board for Advance Rulings makes three complaints about how his case was handled. That the Board should never have called for the Commissioner's file, the Commissioner being on the other side. That having admitted his application the Board could only rule on the papers he himself had filed. And that the ruling, once signed, ought to have gone to him alone.

items.stem: Is the Assessing Officer right about section 131(3)?

options.text: Yes — recording reasons is good practice but the section imposes no condition, and the 15-day period runs only after the assessee asks for the books back
options.misconception: turns a statutory condition into practice and makes the clock start on the assessee's request rather than on the impounding
options.why: The recording of reasons is a condition the section states in terms for these three officers, not a matter of practice, and the period is measured from the retention itself. Nothing in section 131(3) makes it depend on the assessee asking.

options.text: No — the outer limit is 30 days from the date the books were produced, and no approval can extend it
options.misconception: puts the limit at 30 days and treats it as absolute, when the figure is 15 days excluding holidays and an approval lifts it
options.why: Thirty days is the outer limit in a different provision — section 132(8), which says seized books cannot be kept more than 30 days after the assessment proceedings are completed even with approval. Under section 131(3) the number is 15 days, holidays are excluded, and the approval of a senior authority carries it further.

options.text: Yes — the restriction bites only where the books were seized in a search, and books produced voluntarily in a proceeding may be retained indefinitely
options.misconception: reads the impounding power as available only after a search, when section 131(3) is about books produced before an authority in an ordinary proceeding
options.why: Section 131(3) is written for exactly this situation — books produced before an authority in any proceeding under the Act. A search is not needed to trigger it and is not what the time limit turns on.

options.text: No — the words he is relying on are unrestricted only for the other authorities; an Assessing Officer, an Assistant Director or a Deputy Director must record his reasons for impounding and must obtain prior approval to retain the books for more than 15 days, holidays excluded
options.why: Section 131(3) does say the authority may impound and retain books for such period as it thinks fit, and for a Commissioner or a Chief Commissioner that is the whole of the rule. The section then subjects three officers to two conditions. The Assessing Officer, the Assistant Director and the Deputy Director must record their reasons for impounding, and if they wish to keep the books for a period exceeding 15 days, excluding holidays, they must first obtain the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director. Both are missing here.

citation.ref: Section 131(3) — the power to impound and retain books produced in a proceeding, unrestricted except for the Assessing Officer, Assistant Director and Deputy Director, who must record reasons and obtain prior approval to retain for more than 15 days excluding holidays

items.scenario: In the course of a scrutiny proceeding the Assessing Officer requires a firm to produce its ledgers, and when they are produced he keeps them. He writes nothing on the file about why. He still has them forty days later, having taken nobody's approval, and tells the partner that section 131(3) lets him retain books for such period as he thinks fit.

items.stem: Is the order good, and what could the Director General have done instead?

options.text: The order is bad — section 131(1A) carries only the four Civil Court powers in section 131(1), which stop at discovery and inspection, attendance and examination on oath, production of books and issuing commissions, and none of them is a power to seize; to reach the ₹50,00,000 he must authorise a search under section 132(1)
options.why: Section 131(1A) does two things and only two. It names the investigation wing, and it lets those officers exercise the powers conferred by section 131(1) even where no proceeding is pending against the person. Those powers are the four a Civil Court has under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — discovery and inspection; making somebody attend, an officer of a banking company among them, and putting him on oath; calling for books of account and documents to be produced; and issuing commissions. Seizure is not among them and never has been. A Director General is, however, one of the authorities who may authorise a search under section 132(1) on the strength of information in his possession that a person holds money representing undisclosed income, and it is that route, not section 131(1A), that reaches the cash.
keywords: even where no proceeding is pending

options.text: The order is good as to the cash but bad as to procedure — he should first have issued a summons under section 131(1) and seized the ₹50,00,000 only on a failure to comply
options.misconception: treats a failure to comply with a summons as converting a section 131 power into a power of seizure
options.why: A failure to produce books after a summons under section 131(1) is one of the three limbs of reason to believe that lets a search be authorised under section 132(1). It does not turn section 131 itself into a seizure power, and it is the authorisation under section 132(1) that does the work either way.

options.text: The order is bad, and there is nothing else the Director General can do himself — a search may be authorised only by a Principal Chief Commissioner or a Principal Commissioner, so he must refer the information onward
options.misconception: leaves a Director General off the list of authorities who may authorise a search under section 132(1)
options.why: The first half is right and the second is not. Section 132(1) names the Principal Director General, the Director General, the Principal Director and the Director alongside the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner and Commissioner, so the Director General can authorise the search himself.

options.text: The order is good — section 131(1A) exists precisely so that the investigation wing can act where no proceeding is pending, and a power to enquire into ₹50,00,000 of concealed cash without a power to hold it would be worthless
options.misconception: reads the removal of the pending-proceeding requirement as an enlargement of the powers themselves
options.why: What section 131(1A) removes is the requirement that a proceeding be pending. The list of powers it lets those officers exercise is unchanged, and it is the section 131(1) list. A power can be usefully exercised without a proceeding and still not include seizure.

citation.ref: Sections 131(1) and 131(1A) read with section 132(1) — the four Civil Court powers available to the investigation wing even where no proceeding is pending, none of which is a power of seizure, and the authorities competent to authorise a search

items.scenario: A Director General of Income-tax receives information that a person holds ₹50,00,000 of unaccounted cash. No proceeding of any kind is pending against that person. The Director General passes an order invoking section 131(1A) and directing that the ₹50,00,000 be seized.

items.stem: How does the challenge stand?

options.text: It fails on its own terms but the search has a different defect — a Joint Commissioner may authorise a search if the Board has empowered him, and where he is the authorising officer the officer he may name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer, so a Joint Director cannot be the authorised officer on his warrant
options.why: Section 132(1) has two rungs. A Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may authorise a search, and each of them may name a Joint Director, Joint Commissioner, Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. An Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may also authorise a search, but only if empowered by the Board, and the officer he may then name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. So the flat proposition that a Joint Commissioner cannot authorise a search is wrong, and the pairing on this warrant is wrong.
keywords: only if empowered by the Board

options.text: It fails entirely — any authority above the rank of Income-tax Officer may authorise a search where he holds information, and the rank of the officer who conducts it is an internal matter
options.misconception: treats the authorising ladder as a general seniority test and the identity of the authorised officer as administrative
options.why: Both halves of section 132(1) are statutory. The authorising officers are named, the officers each of them may authorise are named, and the pairing is part of the condition on which the search is lawful rather than an internal allocation of work.

options.text: It succeeds — section 132(1) lists eight authorising officers and a Joint Commissioner is not among them in any circumstances
options.misconception: reads the list of authorising officers as closed, ignoring the second rung available to an Additional or Joint officer empowered by the Board
options.why: The section carries a second rung expressly. An Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may authorise a search if he is empowered by the Board to do so, and what changes is the seniority of the officer he may send in.

options.text: It succeeds because the Joint Commissioner did not disclose the information in his possession to Ganesh before signing, which the section requires him to do
options.misconception: requires disclosure of the reason to believe, which section 132(1) expressly forbids
options.why: The section says the opposite. What the income-tax authority writes down as its reason to believe is withheld from every person, every authority and the Appellate Tribunal, and the same bar covers the reason to suspect recorded under section 132(1A).

citation.ref: Section 132(1) — the authorities competent to authorise a search, the narrower class of officers an Additional or Joint officer empowered by the Board may authorise, and the bar on disclosing the recorded reason to believe

items.scenario: A search is carried out at Ganesh's premises. The warrant of authorisation was signed by the Joint Commissioner having jurisdiction over him, on information in the Joint Commissioner's possession, and the search was conducted by a Joint Director. Ganesh challenges the search on the ground that section 132(1) does not empower a Joint Commissioner to authorise one at all.

items.stem: What is the position on the three?

options.text: Only the ornaments are properly dealt with, and the two orders are void because an authorised officer may either seize a thing or leave it, with nothing in between
options.misconception: denies the existence of the restraint machinery, which section 132 provides in two distinct forms
options.why: The section provides exactly the middle course this option denies, and provides it twice — the deemed seizure in the second proviso to section 132(1) for things that cannot be moved, and the restraint order in section 132(3) for everything else, with a 60-day life under section 132(8A). It is the seizure of the ornaments that is wrong.

options.text: The ornaments should not have been seized at all because they are stock-in-trade and only a note or inventory of them is made; the order on the machinery is a deemed seizure under the second proviso to section 132(1); and the order on the cartons is a restraint order under section 132(3), which is not a seizure and lapses after 60 days
options.why: Three different rules, one for each. Bullion, jewellery or another valuable article which is the stock-in-trade of the business and is found as a result of a search shall not be seized, and the authorised officer makes a note or inventory of it instead. Where it is not possible or practicable to take physical possession and remove the thing because of its volume, weight, other physical characteristics or its dangerous nature, the order forbidding its removal is deemed to be a seizure under the second proviso to section 132(1) — though the deeming never reaches stock-in-trade. And where the reason for not seizing is anything other than those physical ones, the order served under section 132(3) is expressly not deemed to be a seizure, and under section 132(8A) it cannot stay in force for a period exceeding 60 days counted from the day the order was made.

options.text: All three are lawful seizures, since anything found as a result of a search may be seized and an order forbidding removal is the ordinary substitute where physical removal is awkward
options.misconception: treats every restraint order as a seizure and ignores the stock-in-trade exclusion altogether
options.why: Two of the three fail. Stock-in-trade in the nature of bullion, jewellery or another valuable article is outside the seizure power entirely, and an order served under section 132(3) for reasons other than volume, weight or physical characteristics is stated not to amount to a seizure.

options.text: The ornaments and the machinery are properly dealt with, but the order on the cartons is also a deemed seizure and it too runs without any time limit
options.misconception: extends the deeming in the second proviso to an ordinary restraint order and drops the 60-day limit in section 132(8A)
options.why: The deeming in the second proviso is tied to the physical impossibility of removal. An order served because the officer wants to enquire further is a section 132(3) order, is not a seizure, and cannot remain in force for more than 60 days from its date.

citation.ref: Section 132(1) with its second proviso, read with sections 132(3) and 132(8A) — stock-in-trade inventoried and not seized, an order deemed to be seizure where the thing cannot physically be removed, and a restraint order which is not a seizure and lapses after 60 days

items.scenario: A search at a jeweller's shop and godown turns up three things. Gold ornaments of ₹80,00,000 forming part of the shop's trading stock. A consignment of industrial machinery too heavy to move to a safe place. And forty cartons of loose stones which the authorised officer thinks may or may not be stock, and which he wants left alone while he makes further enquiries. He seizes the ornaments, and serves an order on the proprietor about the machinery and another about the cartons.

items.stem: What does the presumption in section 132(4A) actually give, and how far does it reach?

options.text: It presumes only that the contents of books and documents are true, so the papers relating to the Mumbai company are evidence against that company, but nothing is presumed about who owns an asset
options.misconception: keeps only the second of the three limbs and drops the presumption of belonging, which is the first
options.why: The first limb is exactly the presumption about ownership — that the books, documents, money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article found in a person's possession or control belong to that person. And the presumption runs against the person searched, not against a stranger whose papers happen to be lying there.

options.text: It reaches search material alone, so nothing found in a survey under section 133A or handed over on a requisition under section 132A carries any presumption at all
options.misconception: stops at section 132(4A) and misses the extension section 292C makes to survey and requisition material
options.why: Section 292C states the extension in its own words. Where books, documents, money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable articles are found in a person's possession or control in the course of a search under section 132 or a survey under section 133A, the presumption may be drawn, and section 132A(2) carries it to material delivered to a requisitioning officer.

options.text: It is a conclusive presumption confined to the block assessment that follows the search, so the jewellery is the director's whatever he proves and nothing found can be used in an ordinary assessment
options.misconception: makes the presumption conclusive and confines it to the search assessment, when it is rebuttable and section 292C carries it into any proceeding
options.why: Both halves are wrong. The module says the presumption is rebuttable and that the assessee may prove the facts are otherwise, and section 292C exists precisely so that it can be drawn in any proceeding under the Act, including a regular assessment.

options.text: It presumes that what is found belongs to the person in whose possession or control it was found, that the contents of the books and documents are true, and that the handwriting, signature, stamping, execution and attestation are what they appear to be — it is rebuttable, so the director may prove the jewellery is his daughter's, and section 292C carries the same presumption into any proceeding under the Act, including material found in a survey under section 133A or delivered on a requisition under section 132A
options.why: Section 132(4A) presumes three things about books, documents and assets found in a person's possession or control during a search, and the module says in terms that it is a rebuttable presumption which the assessee may displace on facts and with evidence. That is why the director's claim about his daughter is not hopeless, only something he must prove. Section 292C was inserted to say that the same presumption may be made in any proceeding under the Act and is available in a regular assessment, and it extends it to anything found in the course of a survey under section 133A as well as to books, documents or assets delivered to a requisitioning officer under section 132A.

citation.ref: Sections 132(4A) and 292C read with section 132A(2) — the three-limbed rebuttable presumption about material found in a search, its availability in any proceeding under the Act, and its extension to a survey under section 133A and to a requisition

items.scenario: Three things are found in a search of a company's premises and a director's bedroom. Papers in an accountant's drawer relating to an unconnected Mumbai company. Jewellery worth ₹5,00,000 in the bedroom, which the director says belongs to his married daughter. And loose sheets recording income and expenditure of the company that were never entered in the books, which the director admits are genuine. In a later regular assessment of the company, and in a survey under section 133A at its branch, the Assessing Officer wants to rely on the same kind of presumption.

items.stem: What is wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the attachment and the reference may be made at any time while the assessment arising out of the search is pending, and both lapse only when that assessment is completed
options.misconception: ties the attachment and the valuation reference to the pendency of the assessment rather than to the 60 days after the last authorisation
options.why: Neither power is tied to the assessment. Sections 132(9B) and 132(9D) both start running the day the last search authorisation was executed and both close 60 days after it, and the attachment then dies of its own accord after six months.

options.text: Only the reference to the Valuation Officer is out of time; the attachment is good because section 132(9B) allows 90 days from the conclusion of the search and it lasts until the assessment is made
options.misconception: gives the attachment 90 days instead of 60 and lets it run to the assessment rather than for six months
options.why: Both windows are the same 60 days, and the life of the attachment is fixed independently of the assessment. Section 132(9C) says every provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of six months from the date of the order.

options.text: Both the attachment and the reference are out of time, because each had to be made during the search or within 60 days from 9 August 2025, which expired on 8 October 2025; and even a valid attachment would have ceased to have effect six months after its date, while the valuer had to report within 60 days of receiving the reference
options.why: The last of the authorisations for search is deemed executed on the conclusion of the search as recorded in the last panchnama, so the clock in this case starts on 9 August 2025. Section 132(9B) allows a provisional attachment while the search or seizure is under way, and also within a period of 60 days measured from that date, and section 132(9D) allows a reference to a Valuation Officer or an approved valuer in exactly the same window. Twenty October is outside both. Two further limits would have applied anyway: under section 132(9C) every provisional attachment ceases to have effect after the expiry of six months from the date of the order under section 132(9B), and under section 132(9D) the valuer must submit his report within 60 days from the date he receives the reference.

options.text: Only the attachment is out of time; a reference for valuation may be made at any point because a fair market value is needed before the assessment can be framed
options.misconception: reads the valuation reference as an assessment step, when section 132(9D) confines it to the same 60-day window as the attachment
options.why: Section 132(9D) puts the reference in the same window as the attachment and the handover — during the search or seizure or within 60 days from the date the last authorisation was executed — and adds its own limit that the valuer report within 60 days of receiving it.

citation.ref: Sections 132(9B), 132(9C) and 132(9D) with Explanation 1 to section 132 — the 60-day window for a provisional attachment and a valuation reference measured from the conclusion of the search recorded in the last panchnama, the six-month life of the attachment, and the valuer's 60 days to report

items.scenario: A search concludes on 9 August 2025, and the last panchnama is drawn that day. On 20 October 2025 the authorised officer provisionally attaches a plot of land belonging to the assessee to protect the revenue, recording his reasons and taking the approval required. On the same day he refers the plot to a Valuation Officer. The attachment order is still in force on 1 June 2026, and the valuer's report has not come in.

items.stem: What do the two limbs of section 132 require?

options.text: The books had to go back by 30 April 2026, being one month from the end of the quarter in which the assessment order was made, and could have been kept beyond that only on recorded reasons and approval and in no event for more than 30 days after the proceedings were completed; and the material had to reach the jurisdictional Assessing Officer within 60 days of 3 December 2025
options.why: Section 132(8) fixes the return of seized books at one month from the end of the quarter — the quarter holding the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation — so an order of 12 February 2026 puts the quarter's end at 31 March 2026 and the return at 30 April 2026. Retention beyond that needs reasons recorded in writing and the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director, and even with that approval the books may not be held on for a period exceeding 30 days once the assessment proceedings for the relevant years are over. Section 132(9A) is separate and earlier: where the authorised officer has no jurisdiction over the person, the books, documents and assets are handed to the Assessing Officer who has, within 60 days from the date the last of the authorisations for search was executed, and from then the retention powers are his.
keywords: one month from the end of the quarter

options.text: The books had to go back within one month of the assessment order itself, so by 12 March 2026, and the handover to the jurisdictional Assessing Officer is due within 30 days of the last authorisation
options.misconception: measures the return from the date of the order instead of from the end of its quarter, and shortens the handover window to 30 days
options.why: Section 132(8) measures from the end of the quarter in which the order is made, not from the order, which is why an order in February gives until 30 April. And the handover window in section 132(9A) is 60 days from the execution of the last authorisation.

options.text: Nothing has gone wrong on the books, because an approval to retain is needed only where the assessee applies to the Board under section 132(10), and the handover is a matter of internal administration with no time limit
options.misconception: inverts section 132(10), which is the assessee's remedy against an approval already given, and drops the 60-day handover limit
options.why: Section 132(10) is what a person legally entitled to the books may do when he objects to an approval that has been given — he applies to the Board, which decides after hearing him. It is not the source of the approval requirement, and section 132(9A) states the 60-day handover as a duty.

options.text: The books may be retained until every appeal arising out of the assessment is finally disposed of, and the handover is required only if the assessee objects to the authorised officer's jurisdiction
options.misconception: makes retention run to the end of the appeals and treats the handover as something the assessee must ask for
options.why: Retention is measured against the assessment, not the appeals, and it is capped at 30 days after the assessment proceedings are completed even where approval has been obtained. The handover under section 132(9A) is the authorised officer's own duty and does not wait on an objection.

citation.ref: Sections 132(8), 132(9A) and 132(10) — seized books returned within one month from the end of the quarter in which the assessment order is made, retention beyond that only on recorded reasons and approval and never more than 30 days after the proceedings are completed, and the handover to the jurisdictional Assessing Officer within 60 days of the last authorisation

items.scenario: Books of account seized in a search are still with the department. The assessment order under section 143(3) for the relevant year was passed on 12 February 2026 and the assessment proceedings for every year to which the books relate were completed on the same day. No reason for retaining the books has been recorded and no approval has been taken. Separately, the authorised officer who ran the search has no jurisdiction over the person searched and has not passed the material to the Assessing Officer who does; the last authorisation was executed on 3 December 2025.

items.stem: Is either of the two reasons good?

options.text: Only the advance tax point is good — the application was in time, but a seized asset may be retained against every liability the assessee has or will have, including advance tax
options.misconception: reverses the two answers, allowing the retention against advance tax that the note to section 132B(1) rules out
options.why: It is the timing point the department gets wrong and the advance tax point as well. The note to section 132B(1) states that existing liability does not include advance tax payable in accordance with Part C of Chapter XVII of the Act.

options.text: Both are good — the application had to be made within 30 days of the seizure itself, so by 12 October 2025, and any tax the assessee will owe for the year is an existing liability
options.misconception: measures the 30 days from the date of seizure instead of from the end of the month of seizure, and treats a future advance tax instalment as an existing liability
options.why: The proviso starts its clock only when the month of seizure has closed, which is what makes 27 October in time. And existing liability is defined against the note to section 132B(1), which excludes advance tax payable under Part C of Chapter XVII.

options.text: Only the time point is good — the window is 30 days from the seizure, but the department is right that advance tax cannot be met out of seized cash
options.misconception: keeps the wrong starting point for the 30 days while getting the advance tax point right
options.why: The advance tax half is right and the timing half is not. The proviso allows 30 days once the month of seizure has closed, and the seizure here was in September, so the application on 27 October was well within it.

options.text: Neither — the application was in time, because the 30 days run from the end of the seizure month, taking the window to 30 October 2025; and existing liability against which a seized asset may be held does not include advance tax
options.why: The proviso to section 132B(1)(i) gives the person concerned 30 days from the end of the month of seizure to apply for the asset's release and to satisfy the Assessing Officer where it came from and how it was paid for. The asset was seized in September 2025, so the window closed on 30 October 2025 and an application on 27 October is inside it. On the second reason, the note to section 132B(1) says plainly that existing liability does not include advance tax payable in accordance with Part C of Chapter XVII, so a future advance tax instalment is not something the seized cash can be held against.
keywords: 30 days from the end of the month

citation.ref: The proviso to section 132B(1)(i) with section 132B(4) and the note to section 132B(1) — the application for release within 30 days from the end of the month of seizure, and advance tax excluded from existing liability

items.scenario: Cash of ₹25,00,000 was seized on 12 September 2025 in a search, and that day the last of the authorisations for search was executed. The assessee applied to the Assessing Officer on 27 October 2025 for the release of the cash, setting out its nature and source. The Assessing Officer turned the application down as time-barred and added that in any event the cash would be kept against the advance tax that will fall due for the year.

items.stem: What interest is he entitled to?

options.text: ₹24,000 — simple interest at one half per cent for every month or part of a month on ₹8,00,000, for the six months from 1 February 2026 to 31 July 2026
options.why: Section 132B(4) gives the assessee simple interest at one half per cent for every month or part of a month where the amount of the assets seized exceeds the liabilities eventually determined. The period it names opens immediately after the expiry of 120 days, counted from the day the last search authorisation was executed, and closes on the date the assessment, reassessment or recomputation is completed. That is 1 February 2026 to 31 July 2026, which is six months, and one half per cent of ₹8,00,000 for six months is ₹24,000.

options.text: ₹48,000 — interest at one per cent a month, the rate the Act uses for a default in payment of tax, applied for the six months to completion of the assessment
options.misconception: imports the one per cent rate used for interest payable by an assessee, when section 132B(4) fixes one half per cent
options.why: One per cent a month is the rate an assessee pays under sections 234A, 234B and 234C. Interest payable to him on a surplus of seized assets is fixed by section 132B(4) at one half per cent for every month or part of a month.

options.text: Nothing — interest is payable only where the department has been shown to have retained the assets without justification, and here it retained them under a lawful seizure
options.misconception: treats the interest as a remedy for wrongful retention, when section 132B(4) gives it on any surplus as a matter of course
options.why: Nothing in section 132B(4) asks whether the retention was justified. It gives interest wherever the assets seized eventually exceed the liabilities, for the period after the 120 days, and a lawful seizure is the situation it is written for.

options.text: ₹40,000 — interest for the ten months from the date the search was completed on 3 October 2025 to 31 July 2026
options.misconception: starts the interest at the search instead of at the expiry of the 120 days the department is given to release the asset
options.why: The 120 days are the department's own time to release an explained asset, and no interest runs during them. Section 132B(4) starts the period immediately after they expire, which here is 1 February 2026.

citation.ref: Section 132B(4) — simple interest at one half per cent for every month or part of a month on the excess of the seized assets over the liabilities, running from the expiry of 120 days from the date the last authorisation for search was executed to the completion of the assessment

items.scenario: In a search the last of the authorisations was executed on 3 October 2025, and 120 days from that date expired on 31 January 2026. The assessment was completed on 31 July 2026. After every liability had been met, ₹8,00,000 of the seized assets was left over and was returned to the assessee. He asks what interest the Act gives him on that surplus. Part of a month is treated as a full month.

items.stem: What may the survey party lawfully do?

options.text: Both entries are good — the storeroom is drawn into the survey because the trader has said his books are kept there, and once a survey is lawfully begun it may be carried to any place connected with it at any hour
options.misconception: reads the extension of a survey to a place where books are said to be kept as also extending the hours at which that place may be entered
options.why: The extension and the timing are two different rules. Section 133A(1) does bring in any other place at which the person says his books or valuable articles are kept, and section 133A(2) then says that any other place may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset.

options.text: The entry at the shop is bad because the survey continued past the hour at which the shop closes, and the storeroom entry is good because the trader himself disclosed it
options.misconception: reads the closing hour as an hour by which the survey must end, when the section fixes only the time of entry
options.why: The section prescribes when the authority may enter and says nothing about when he must leave, which is why a survey lawfully begun at 10 at night may continue after the shop closes. And a disclosure that books are kept somewhere brings that place inside the survey without changing the hours at which it may be entered.

options.text: The entry at the shop at 10 at night is good because the place was open for business and the survey may continue past 11; the storeroom may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset, so entering it at one in the morning is not open to them
options.why: Section 133A(2) draws the line by the kind of place. A place of business or profession may be entered only during the hours at which it is open for the conduct of that business or profession, and the module's own example is a place open from 11 in the morning to 11 at night which an income-tax authority may enter at 10 at night, with the survey continuing beyond 11. Any other place may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset. What the section fixes is the hour of entry and not the hour of leaving, which is why the shop survey may run on and why the storeroom cannot be entered in the small hours at all.

options.text: Both entries are bad — an income-tax authority may enter any place only after sunrise and before sunset, and 10 at night is outside that whatever the shop's hours
options.misconception: applies the sunrise-to-sunset rule to a place of business, where the test is the hours for which it is open
options.why: The sunrise-to-sunset rule is the rule for any other place. For a place at which a business, profession or charitable activity is carried on, the test is whether it is open for the conduct of that business, and a shop trading until 11 at night is open at 10.

citation.ref: Sections 133A(1) and 133A(2) — a place of business or profession entered only during the hours at which it is open for business, and any other place only after sunrise and before sunset, with no limit on the hour at which the survey ends

items.scenario: A trader's shop is open for business from 11 in the morning until 11 at night. He also keeps a private storeroom in a residential building which is not a place of business, and he has told the department that some of his ledgers are kept there. The survey party reaches the shop at 10 at night, is still working at half past midnight, and then wants to go on to the storeroom, arriving there at one in the morning.

items.stem: How much of that was open to him?

options.text: None of it as done — he may not remove any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place at all, he may impound the ledgers only after recording his reasons, and he may not retain them for more than 15 days excluding holidays without approval
options.why: A survey is not a seizure. Section 133A(4) tells the income-tax authority he cannot remove a thing from the premises he has entered, and may not have it carried out by somebody else either — no cash, no stock, no other valuable article. So both the cash and the cartons had to stay; what he does with them is make an inventory of what he has checked or verified. Section 133A(3)(b) lets him impound and retain books of account or other documents inspected by him only after recording reasons for doing so, and he cannot retain them for a period exceeding 15 days, excluding holidays, without the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director.

options.text: All of it — a survey carries the same powers as a search once the authority is lawfully inside, and the 15-day limit applies only to a survey under section 133A(2A)
options.misconception: collapses survey into search and confines the impounding limit to the narrower verification survey
options.why: The difference between the two is the whole point of the section. A search may seize and a survey may not, and the 15-day limit in section 133A(3) applies to an ordinary survey. In a survey under section 133A(2A) the authority may not impound books at all.

options.text: The cash could be taken because it is unexplained, but not the stock, and the ledgers could be impounded for up to 15 days including holidays without recording anything
options.misconception: allows unexplained cash to be removed in a survey and counts holidays inside the 15 days while dropping the recording of reasons
options.why: Section 133A(4) makes no exception for cash that looks unexplained; nothing may be removed in a survey, whatever it turns out to be. And the 15 days are counted excluding holidays, with reasons recorded before the books are impounded at all.

options.text: The ledgers could be impounded and kept indefinitely because they are documents rather than assets, but the cash and stock had to stay
options.misconception: treats the bar on removal as the only limit and leaves the impounding of books unlimited
options.why: The bar on removing cash and stock is one limit and the impounding rule is another. Books may be impounded only on recorded reasons and may not be retained beyond 15 days, excluding holidays, without approval from the named authorities.

citation.ref: Sections 133A(3) and 133A(4) — impounding books only after recording reasons and never beyond 15 days excluding holidays without approval, and the bar on removing any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place surveyed

items.scenario: During a survey at a wholesaler's premises the authority finds ₹6,00,000 of cash that the cash book does not explain, stock worth ₹40,00,000, and three ledgers he wants to take away. He puts the cash and two cartons of stock into the departmental vehicle, impounds the ledgers without writing anything on the file about why, and keeps them for 25 working days without taking any approval.

items.stem: Which parts of that are open to him in a survey under section 133A(2A)?

options.text: The inspection and the inventory, but not the impounding — a record of what was found is always permitted, and only the taking away of books is barred
options.misconception: reads the restriction as a bar on taking things away rather than on the two named acts
options.why: Making an inventory is one of the two acts the sub-section names as not available in a verification survey, alongside impounding. It is a narrower power than an ordinary survey in both directions.

options.text: Only the inspection — a survey under section 133A(2A) may be entered at a place of business only after sunrise and before sunset, so the 7 in the evening visit is doubtful whatever the office hours, and in such a survey he may neither impound books nor make an inventory of cash, stock or other valuable articles
options.why: Section 133A(2A) is a narrower power for one purpose, verifying that tax has been deducted or collected under Chapter XVII-B or Chapter XVII-BB. Two things are cut down. On timing, the authority may go in only after sunrise and before sunset, whether the place is an office or somewhere else a business or profession is carried on, so the business-hours rule that governs an ordinary survey does not save an evening visit after sunset. On powers, the section says that while acting under sub-section (2A) the authority shall not impound and retain the books or papers he has inspected, nor draw up an inventory of the cash, stock or other valuable article he has checked or verified. What he may do is inspect the books and require information.

options.text: The inspection and the impounding, but not the inventory — books may always be impounded on recorded reasons, and it is only the counting of cash and stock that a verification survey leaves out
options.misconception: keeps the impounding power in a section 133A(2A) survey, which the section withholds along with the inventory
options.why: The section withholds both in the same breath. Acting under sub-section (2A) the authority shall not impound and retain books of account or documents inspected by him, and shall not make an inventory of cash, stock or other valuable articles checked or verified.

options.text: All of it — section 133A(2A) is a survey like any other, so the business-hours rule applies to a place of business and the ordinary powers to impound and to inventory come with it
options.misconception: treats the verification survey as carrying the same timing and the same powers as an ordinary survey
options.why: It carries neither. The timing for a section 133A(2A) survey is after sunrise and before sunset even at a place of business, and the section expressly withholds the powers to impound books and to make an inventory of cash or stock.

citation.ref: Section 133A(2A) with the closing words of section 133A(3) — entry after sunrise and before sunset for a survey to verify deduction or collection at source, and no impounding of books and no inventory of cash, stock or valuable articles in such a survey

items.scenario: An income-tax authority enters a company's registered office at 4 in the afternoon to verify whether tax has been deducted at source on the expenditure heads in its books. He inspects the ledgers, impounds two of them, makes an inventory of the cash in hand, and records that he will return the next day at 7 in the evening because the office works until 9.

items.stem: How do the two sets of notices stand?

options.text: Both sets are bad — section 133(6) can be exercised only where a proceeding is pending, and the deposits will have to be reached some other way
options.misconception: denies the power altogether where no proceeding is pending, which is the very point Kathiroor settled the other way
options.why: That was the argument the Supreme Court rejected. The power is available for an enquiry in a case where no proceeding is pending, and what the Act adds in that situation is a requirement of prior approval for most authorities.

options.text: Both sets are good — prior approval is needed only where the information is sought from a banking company about a person outside the officer's own jurisdiction
options.misconception: invents a jurisdictional trigger for the approval, when the trigger is that no proceeding is pending
options.why: The trigger is the absence of a pending proceeding, not the identity of the person asked or where he is assessed. On that footing the Assessing Officer's notices needed approval and did not have it.

options.text: The Assessing Officer's notices are good and the Deputy Director's are not — section 133 names the Assessing Officer in its own text and the investigation wing has to borrow the power through an approval
options.misconception: reverses the exception, giving the approval requirement to the officers the module exempts from it
options.why: It is the other way round. The Joint Director, Deputy Director and Assistant Director are the officers who may act without prior approval where no proceeding is pending, and the approval requirement catches the rest below the rank of Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner.

options.text: The Deputy Director's notices are good and the Assessing Officer's are not — where no proceeding is pending the power under section 133(6) may not be exercised by an authority below the rank of Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner without their prior approval, but a Joint Director, Deputy Director or Assistant Director may exercise it without that approval
options.why: Section 133(6) lets an authority call for any information useful for or relevant to an enquiry or proceeding, and the Supreme Court in Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank held that the power extends to an enquiry where no proceeding is pending against the person. The module sets the condition and its exception side by side. Where the enquiry is one in which no proceeding is pending, an authority ranked under a Principal Director, a Director, a Principal Commissioner or a Commissioner must get their prior approval first; only the Joint Director, the Deputy Director and the Assistant Director may act without that approval. An Assessing Officer is not in that carved-out group.

citation.ref: Section 133(6) read with Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. CIT (CIB) (SC), reported at (2014) 360 ITR 243 — prior approval of the Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner where no proceeding is pending, and the exemption for a Joint Director, Deputy Director or Assistant Director

items.scenario: No proceeding is pending against a co-operative bank's depositors. A Deputy Director of Income-tax issues notices under section 133(6) to the bank calling for details of large deposits, taking nobody's approval first. In the same office an Assessing Officer issues identical notices to a second bank, also with no proceeding pending and also without approval. The banks say both sets are bad.

items.stem: What does the Act allow and what does it cost the proprietor?

options.text: The entry was lawful but the files could not be taken, because under section 133B the authority shall on no account remove any books of account or other valuable articles from the place; the refusal attracts a penalty of up to ₹1,000 under section 272AA; and the brokerage statement is called for under section 133 in respect of payments of more than ₹1,000 to any one person in a previous year
options.why: Section 133B is a power to collect information and nothing more. An income-tax authority, which for this section means a Joint Commissioner, Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assessing Officer or an Inspector authorised by the Assessing Officer, may enter a place of business only during the hours at which it is open for business, may require the proprietor or an employee to furnish the prescribed information, and shall on no account remove or cause to be removed any books of account or other valuable articles or things. A failure to furnish the prescribed information attracts a penalty of up to ₹1,000 under section 272AA, imposed after an opportunity of being heard. And section 133 lets the Assessing Officer call from any assessee for a statement of the persons to whom he paid rent, interest, commission, royalty or brokerage, or a non-salary annuity, of more than ₹1,000, with the particulars of the payments.

options.text: Everything done was lawful — section 133B carries the same powers as a survey once the authority is inside during business hours, so the files may be impounded, and the penalty for refusing is ₹10,000 under section 272A
options.misconception: reads section 133B as a survey and reaches for the wrong penalty section
options.why: Section 133B is the smallest of these powers. It cannot impound anything and cannot remove anything, and the penalty attached to a failure to furnish the prescribed information is the one in section 272AA, which is up to ₹1,000.

options.text: The entry and the removal were both lawful, and the brokerage statement can be called for only in respect of payments of more than ₹10,000 to a single person
options.misconception: allows removal under section 133B and raises the section 133 reporting threshold tenfold
options.why: Nothing may be removed under section 133B on any account. And the threshold in section 133 for the statement of rent, interest, commission, royalty, brokerage or a non-salary annuity is more than ₹1,000 — or a bigger figure, should one ever be prescribed.

options.text: The entry was bad because an Inspector is never an income-tax authority for section 133B, and there is no penalty for refusing information to an officer who should not be there
options.misconception: leaves an authorised Inspector out of the definition of income-tax authority in section 133B
options.why: An Inspector of Income-tax counts too, so long as the Assessing Officer has authorised him, and the power he then holds runs over the area that officer has jurisdiction over. The entry was therefore good and the refusal is penalised.

citation.ref: Sections 133 and 133B with section 272AA — the ₹1,000 threshold for the statement of rent, interest, commission, royalty and brokerage, entry under section 133B only during business hours with no removal of books or valuable articles, and a penalty of up to ₹1,000 for failing to furnish the prescribed information

items.scenario: An Inspector of Income-tax authorised by the Assessing Officer enters a shop at 3 in the afternoon, while it is open, to collect prescribed information under section 133B. He takes two files of purchase invoices back to the office. The proprietor refuses to fill in the prescribed form at all. Separately, the same Assessing Officer wants a statement from a manufacturer of everybody to whom it paid brokerage during the year.

items.stem: Who may condone the delay, and may the loss be carried forward at all?

options.text: The Assessing Officer may, since he is the authority who will give effect to the carry forward and the delay of one hour is trivial
options.misconception: gives the condonation power to the Assessing Officer, when section 119(2)(b) places it with the authority the Board authorises and the circular names three
options.why: The power belongs to the Board and, through it, to the authority it authorises. The circular names the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, the Chief Commissioner and the Principal Chief Commissioner by the size of the claim, and the Assessing Officer is not among them however small the delay.

options.text: The Chief Commissioner may, because the claim of ₹3,10,00,000 falls in the band above ₹1,00,00,000 and the Principal Chief Commissioner is reached only above ₹5,00,00,000
options.misconception: puts the top band at ₹5 crore, when the circular's second band closes at ₹3 crore and everything above it goes to the Principal Chief Commissioner
options.why: The circular has three bands and the middle one runs from above ₹1,00,00,000 to ₹3,00,00,000. There is no ₹5,00,00,000 line, so a claim of ₹3,10,00,000 is already with the Principal Chief Commissioner.

options.text: Nobody may — section 119(2)(b) reaches an exemption, a deduction or a refund, and the carry forward of a loss is none of those, so a return filed even an hour late loses the loss under section 80
options.misconception: reads the list in section 119(2)(b) as closed, missing the words for any other relief that Lodhi Property applied to a loss return
options.why: The clause ends with the words any other relief under the Act, and that is exactly where a claim to carry forward a loss was placed in Lodhi Property Company Ltd., where the Court held that refusing to condone a one-day delay would cause genuine hardship.

options.text: The Principal Chief Commissioner may — a claim to carry forward a loss is a claim for other relief within section 119(2)(b), and CBDT Circular No. 11/2024 puts a claim above ₹3,00,00,000 for any one assessment year with the Principal Chief Commissioner
options.why: Section 119(2)(b) lets the Board authorise an income-tax authority to admit an application or claim for an exemption, deduction, refund or any other relief after the period allowed by the Act has expired, to avoid genuine hardship, and the Delhi High Court in Lodhi Property Company Ltd. held that a claim to carry forward a loss in a late return falls in the category of any other relief and condoned a delay of one day. Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 then allocates the power by the size of the claim — up to ₹1,00,00,000 for any one assessment year to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, above ₹1,00,00,000 and up to ₹3,00,00,000 to the Chief Commissioner, and above ₹3,00,00,000 to the Principal Chief Commissioner. A claim of ₹3,10,00,000 is in the top band.

citation.ref: Section 119(2)(b) read with CBDT Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 and Lodhi Property Company Ltd. v. Under Secretary (ITA-II) of the Department of Revenue, (2010) 323 ITR 441 — a carry forward claim as other relief, and the ₹1 crore and ₹3 crore ladder allocating the power to condone

items.scenario: A company files its return for assessment year 2025-26 electronically. The portal fails through the evening of 31 October 2025 and the upload finally succeeds at 1 in the morning on 1 November 2025, one hour late. The return claims to carry forward a business loss of ₹3,10,00,000, and the company records the network failure in an email to the department the same day and applies for the delay to be condoned.

items.stem: How far does a circular under section 119 carry?

options.text: The first circular stands until it is withdrawn, because the Board's reading of a section is authoritative on the officers who must apply it and a court will not go behind it
options.misconception: treats the Board's reading of a provision as beyond challenge, when a circular that amends a provision has no force at all
options.why: What S.V. Gopala decided is that the Board cannot amend a legislative provision through a circular. A circular that shifts a date the section itself fixes is not an authoritative reading, and a court is not shut out from saying so.

options.text: Neither circular can be relied on by the assessee, because a document that does not bind the courts cannot found a claim, so the concession in the second is unenforceable
options.misconception: turns the absence of binding force on the taxpayer into a bar on the taxpayer relying on a beneficial circular
options.why: The freedom runs one way. Because a circular does not bind him, an assessee is not forced to accept an adverse one, and he may still take the benefit of a beneficial circular against the department, which is bound by it.

options.text: Both circulars stand and bind everybody, because section 119 makes the Board's orders, instructions and directions binding on all authorities and on assessees alike
options.misconception: extends the binding force of a circular to the appellate authorities, the courts and the taxpayer
options.why: A circular binds the officers and persons employed in executing the Act, and stops there. The appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts and the taxpayer are outside it, which is what lets an assessee argue against an adverse circular and rely on a favourable one.

options.text: The first circular cannot stand, because the Board has no power to amend a legislative provision by issuing a circular; circulars bind the officers and persons employed in executing the Act and do not bind the appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts or the taxpayer, and a taxpayer may take the benefit of one that favours him
options.why: The Supreme Court in CIT v. S.V. Gopala held that the Board does not have the power to amend legislative provisions in exercise of its powers under section 119 by issuing a circular, so a circular that moves a date the section fixes is worth nothing. On who is bound, the module puts both halves side by side in one paragraph: a circular under section 119 ties the hands of the tax officers, and of everyone else employed in carrying the Act out, while it is not binding on the appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts or the taxpayer — and a taxpayer may still take the benefit of beneficial circulars.
keywords: not binding on the appellate authorities

citation.ref: Section 119 read with CIT and Anr v. S.V. Gopala and Others (2017) 396 ITR 694 (SC) — no power to amend a legislative provision by circular, circulars binding on the department and not on the appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts or the taxpayer, who may take the benefit of a beneficial circular

items.scenario: A circular issued by the Board under section 119 reads a time limit in a section as running from a different date from the one the section names, and a second circular gives an assessee a concession the section does not. An Assessing Officer applies the first against an assessee. In an appeal the assessee relies on the second, and the department says a circular binds nobody but the department.

items.stem: Is the firm in default, and if so from when?

options.text: Yes, from 1 April 2025 — the test is turnover exceeding ₹50,00,00,000 in the immediately preceding previous year, so the ₹1,20,00,00,000 of 2024-25 brings it in, and only the three modes prescribed by Rule 119AA count towards the duty
options.why: Section 269SU reaches anybody in business whose sales, turnover or gross receipts crossed ₹50,00,00,000 in the immediately preceding previous year, so for the previous year 2025-26 the figure that decides it is the ₹1,20,00,00,000 of 2024-25 and not the ₹42,00,00,000 of the year itself. What the section then demands is a way of taking payment by the electronic modes that stand prescribed, alongside whatever else is offered, and Rule 119AA prescribes three and only three — a debit card powered by RuPay, the Unified Payments Interface and the Unified Payments Interface Quick Response Code. Cheques, funds transfers and credit cards are outside that list, so the firm offered nothing that counted until 1 July 2025.

options.text: Yes, but only from 1 April 2026, because the obligation begins in the previous year following the one in which the ₹50,00,00,000 threshold is crossed
options.misconception: pushes the start of the duty a year further out, when the preceding year's turnover is what makes the duty live in the current year
options.why: The preceding year's turnover is the test for the current year, not a warning for the year after. Turnover of ₹1,20,00,00,000 in 2024-25 makes the facility due throughout 2025-26.

options.text: No — turnover of ₹42,00,00,000 in 2025-26 is below the ₹50,00,00,000 line, so the section did not apply to it during that year at all
options.misconception: measures the ₹50 crore turnover in the year of the alleged default instead of in the immediately preceding previous year
options.why: The section fixes the year of measurement itself. It looks at total sales, turnover or gross receipts during the immediately preceding previous year, which for 2025-26 means 2024-25, and that figure was ₹1,20,00,00,000.

options.text: No — the firm already accepts payment electronically by funds transfer and by credit card, which satisfies a section written to move business away from cash
options.misconception: reads the duty as a duty to accept some electronic payment, when Rule 119AA prescribes three named modes and only those discharge it
options.why: The section asks for a facility through the prescribed electronic modes in addition to any other electronic facility already offered, which is a direct statement that existing electronic facilities do not answer it. Rule 119AA names the three that do.

citation.ref: Section 269SU with Rule 119AA — the duty on a person carrying on business whose turnover exceeded ₹50 crore in the immediately preceding previous year to provide a facility through a RuPay debit card, the Unified Payments Interface and the Unified Payments Interface Quick Response Code

items.scenario: Trellis Traders had turnover of ₹1,20,00,00,000 in the previous year 2024-25 and ₹42,00,00,000 in 2025-26. It has always accepted payment by cheque, by national electronic funds transfer and by credit card, and its accountant says that is more than enough. It put up no debit card facility powered by RuPay, no Unified Payments Interface facility and no Unified Payments Interface Quick Response Code until 1 July 2025, having offered none at all from 1 April 2025.

items.stem: What penalty does section 271DB carry on those facts?

options.text: ₹5,000 — the section fixes one penalty for the failure, however long it lasted
options.misconception: reads section 271DB as a single penalty instead of a daily one
options.why: The section fixes ₹5,000 for each day the failure runs on, which makes it a daily penalty. Three months of failure therefore costs ninety-one times the daily figure.

options.text: Nil — no penalty can be levied under section 271DB unless the department first shows that a customer was actually turned away for want of the facility
options.misconception: adds a requirement of demonstrated loss, when the default is the absence of the facility itself
options.why: The default the section penalises is the failure to provide the facility, and nothing in it asks whether anybody tried to use one. The only escape is proof of good and sufficient reasons for the failure.

options.text: ₹4,55,000 — ₹5,000 for every one of the 91 days from 1 April 2025 to 30 June 2025, imposed by the Assessing Officer
options.why: Section 271DB fixes the penalty at ₹5,000 for every day during which the failure to provide the facility prescribed under section 269SU continues, and it is imposed by the Assessing Officer. The failure ran from 1 April 2025 to 30 June 2025, which is 30 plus 31 plus 30 or 91 days, and 91 multiplied by ₹5,000 is ₹4,55,000. The section lets the penalty go only if the person proves there were good and sufficient reasons for the failure, and the cost of terminals is not offered as one.
keywords: every day during which the failure

options.text: ₹1,50,000 — ₹5,000 for each of the three months during which the facility was missing
options.misconception: converts a daily penalty into a monthly one
options.why: Section 271DB counts days, not months. Ninety-one days at ₹5,000 is ₹4,55,000, and the monthly reading understates it by more than ₹3,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 271DB read with section 269SU — a penalty of ₹5,000 for every day during which the failure to provide the prescribed electronic payment facility continues, imposed by the Assessing Officer, with no penalty where good and sufficient reasons are proved

items.scenario: A firm covered by section 269SU offered no prescribed electronic mode at all from 1 April 2025, and put one in place with effect from 1 July 2025, so the failure ran through 30 June 2025. It has no explanation for the three months beyond the cost of the terminals. April has 30 days, May 31 and June 30.

items.stem: How long does the attachment last, and does the penalty matter support a second one?

options.text: It is valid for six months from 1 July 2025 and may be extended for reasons recorded in writing, with the total period of extension not exceeding two years or 60 days after the date of the assessment or reassessment, whichever is later; and no attachment lies for the penalty matter, because that route needs the penalty likely to be imposed under section 271AAD to exceed ₹2,00,00,000
options.why: Section 281B(2) makes a provisional attachment valid for six months from the date of the order. The same senior authorities who approved it may extend it by whatever further period they think fit, having written down their reasons, but the total period of extension shall not exceed two years or sixty days after the date of the assessment or reassessment, whichever is later. The power is available during the pendency of an assessment or of a reassessment of escaped income, and separately for the imposition of a penalty under section 271AAD, but that second route is confined to a case where the amount or aggregate of penalty likely to be imposed under that section exceeds ₹2,00,00,000, which ₹80,00,000 does not.
keywords: six months from the date of the order

options.text: It lasts until the reassessment is completed and for 60 days afterwards in every case, and the penalty matter supports an attachment once the show-cause notice under section 271AAD has been issued
options.misconception: turns the sixty days after the assessment into the whole rule rather than one half of a later-of test on the extension
options.why: The sixty days after the assessment is one arm of the cap on the extension, taken against two years, whichever is later. The order itself lives six months, and the section 271AAD limb turns on the amount of the likely penalty rather than on a notice having issued.

options.text: It is valid for two years from 1 July 2025 without any extension being needed, and the penalty matter supports an attachment because section 271AAD is expressly named in section 281B
options.misconception: reads the two-year cap on the extension as the original life of the attachment and drops the monetary condition attached to the section 271AAD route
options.why: Two years is the outer limit of the extension, not the life of the order, which is six months. And section 271AAD is named subject to a figure — the penalty likely to be imposed must exceed ₹2,00,00,000.

options.text: It is valid for six months and cannot be extended at all, and the penalty matter supports an attachment because any penalty proceeding is a proceeding for the purposes of section 281B
options.misconception: denies the extension the section provides and reads the penalty limb as covering every penalty
options.why: The section provides for extension in terms, by the same authorities, on reasons recorded in writing. And the penalty limb is written for section 271AAD alone and only above ₹2,00,00,000.

citation.ref: Sections 281B(1) and 281B(2) — provisional attachment during an assessment or reassessment or for a section 271AAD penalty likely to exceed ₹2 crore, valid for six months from the date of the order, extendable so that the total extension does not exceed two years or 60 days after the assessment, whichever is later

items.scenario: Reassessment proceedings are pending against an assessee for income said to have escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer provisionally attaches a warehouse belonging to him by an order in writing dated 1 July 2025, having taken the approval of the Principal Commissioner. In a separate matter the same officer wants to attach property to secure a penalty under section 271AAD for a false entry in the books, where the penalty likely to be imposed is ₹80,00,000.

items.stem: What do the guarantee provisions of section 281B require?

options.text: The attachment must be revoked within 15 days of the guarantee in every case, the Valuation Officer has 60 days to report, and a guarantee about to expire simply lapses with the attachment revived
options.misconception: uses one revocation period for both cases, stretches the valuer's time and lets an expiring guarantee revive the attachment
options.why: The section gives two revocation periods, 45 days where a valuation reference is made and 15 days otherwise, and the valuer's own time is 30 days. An expiring guarantee does not revive the attachment; it obliges the Assessing Officer to invoke the guarantee.

options.text: Nothing is required until the assessment is complete, because a guarantee cannot be substituted for an attachment while the proceeding that justified the attachment is still running
options.misconception: denies the substitution that sections 281B(3) to 281B(9) exist to provide
options.why: The substitution is the point of those sub-sections, and it was recommended by the Income Tax Simplification Committee for exactly the situation where the proceeding is still running. A guarantee protects the revenue as well as an attachment and frees the property.

options.text: The attachment must be revoked by an order in writing within 45 days of receiving the guarantee where a reference has been made to the Valuation Officer, who must report within 30 days of receiving the reference, and within 15 days in any other case; and where the assessee fails to renew the guarantee or furnish a new one for an equal amount fifteen days before it expires, the Assessing Officer shall invoke it
options.why: Section 281B(3) obliges the Assessing Officer to revoke the attachment where a guarantee from a scheduled bank is furnished for an amount not less than the fair market value of the attached property or sufficient to protect the revenue. Section 281B(4) lets him refer the property to a Valuation Officer, who must estimate the fair market value and report within 30 days from the date he receives the reference. Section 281B(5) fixes the time for the revoking order — within 45 days from the receipt of the guarantee where such a reference is made, and within 15 days in any other case. Section 281B(7) then protects the revenue: if the assessee fails to renew the guarantee, or to furnish a new one from a scheduled bank for an equal amount, fifteen days before it expires, the Assessing Officer shall invoke it.

options.text: The Assessing Officer may revoke the attachment if he chooses, since a guarantee is only an alternative security, and he may invoke it at any time whether or not a demand has been served
options.misconception: makes revocation discretionary and lets the guarantee be invoked without the demand the section requires
options.why: Revocation is compulsory on a sufficient guarantee — the section says the Assessing Officer shall revoke the attachment by an order in writing. And invoking it for non-payment requires a notice of demand served and unpaid within the time specified in it.

citation.ref: Sections 281B(3) to 281B(9) — revocation of a provisional attachment against a scheduled bank guarantee within 45 days where a reference is made to the Valuation Officer who reports in 30 days and within 15 days otherwise, and invocation where the guarantee is not renewed fifteen days before expiry

items.scenario: A property under provisional attachment is worth more to the assessee working than idle, so he hands over a guarantee from a scheduled bank for no less than what the property would fetch at fair market value. The Assessing Officer has referred the property to a Valuation Officer. Three months later the guarantee is about to expire and the assessee has said nothing about renewing it.

items.stem: How many of the four have to be reported in a statement of financial transactions?

options.text: Two — the cash deposits and the jeweller's receipt; the flat is outside because it changed hands for less than ₹30,00,000 and a stamp value is not a consideration
options.misconception: applies only the price limb of the immovable property entry and drops the stamp valuation limb that stands beside it
options.why: The entry is written with two limbs joined by the word or — an amount of ₹30,00,000 or more, or valued by the stamp valuation authority referred to in section 50C at ₹30,00,000 or more. A stamp value of ₹31,00,000 answers the second even where the price does not answer the first.

options.text: All four — the ₹10,00,000 cash figure applies to every kind of bank account, current accounts included, so ₹38,00,000 of withdrawals is reportable as well
options.misconception: applies one cash threshold to all bank accounts, when Rule 114E sets ₹50 lakh for current accounts and ₹10 lakh for the rest
options.why: The rule separates them deliberately. Cash deposits or withdrawals aggregating ₹50,00,000 or more in current accounts is one entry, and cash deposits of ₹10,00,000 or more in accounts other than a current account and a time deposit is another.

options.text: One — only the cash deposits, because a sale of immovable property is reported by the buyer under section 194-IA and a cash sale by a jeweller is dealt with by section 269ST rather than by any reporting obligation
options.misconception: reads other provisions dealing with the same transactions as displacing the reporting entries in Rule 114E
options.why: Section 194-IA and section 269ST attach their own consequences to the same events and do not remove the reporting entries. Rule 114E names the Registrar or Sub-Registrar as the reporting person for immovable property, and a person liable to audit under section 44AB for cash receipts exceeding ₹2,00,000.

options.text: Three — the ₹22,00,000 of cash deposits, the flat because the stamp value is ₹31,00,000, and the jeweller's cash receipt; the ₹38,00,000 withdrawn from a current account is below the ₹50,00,000 figure Rule 114E sets for current accounts
options.why: Rule 114E fixes a different value for each kind of transaction. Cash deposits aggregating ₹10,00,000 or more in a financial year in one or more accounts of a person other than a current account or a time deposit are reportable by the bank, so ₹22,00,000 into a savings account is caught. Cash deposits or withdrawals in current accounts are reportable only at ₹50,00,000 or more, so ₹38,00,000 is not. The Registrar or Sub-Registrar reports the purchase or sale of immovable property for ₹30,00,000 or more or valued by the stamp valuation authority under section 50C at ₹30,00,000 or more, and the stamp value of ₹31,00,000 satisfies the second limb even though the price does not satisfy the first. And a person liable to audit under section 44AB reports the receipt of cash exceeding ₹2,00,000 for the sale of goods or services of any nature not already listed.

citation.ref: Rule 114E with section 285BA(1) — cash deposits of ₹10 lakh or more in accounts other than a current account or a time deposit, cash deposits or withdrawals of ₹50 lakh or more in current accounts, immovable property at ₹30 lakh or more by price or by stamp value, and cash exceeding ₹2 lakh received for a sale by a person liable to audit under section 44AB

items.scenario: Four things happen during the financial year. A person deposits ₹22,00,000 of cash into his savings bank account over eleven visits. The same person withdraws ₹38,00,000 of cash from his current account with the same bank. A flat is sold for ₹28,00,000 and the stamp valuation authority values it at ₹31,00,000. And a jeweller who is liable to audit under section 44AB receives ₹2,10,000 in cash from one customer for a single sale of ornaments.

items.stem: What do sections 285BA and 271FAA require of it?

options.text: The statement was in time and the defect may be rectified within 30 days, but the penalty for inaccurate information is a flat ₹50,000 whatever the number of accounts affected
options.misconception: stops at the ₹50,000 in section 271FAA and misses the per-account addition for a reporting financial institution
