options.why: Section 271FAA carries two limbs for a prescribed reporting financial institution. The ₹50,000 is the first, and a further ₹5,000 for every reportable account is directed in addition where the inaccuracy is due to false or inaccurate information furnished by the account holder.

options.text: The statement was in time, being due on or before 31 May 2026; the defect had to be rectified within 30 days of the intimation or such further time as was allowed, failing which the Act applies as if inaccurate information had been furnished; and the inaccuracy discovered must be reported and the correct information furnished within ten days, not next year
options.why: Rule 114E requires the statement of financial transactions in Form No. 61A on or before 31 May immediately following the financial year in which the transaction is recorded, so 20 May 2026 is inside the date for 2025-26. Section 285BA(4) gives 30 days from the intimation of a defect to rectify it, with a further period at the authority's discretion on an application, and says that if the defect is not rectified in that time the provisions of the Act apply as if the person had furnished inaccurate information. Section 285BA(6) gives ten days from discovering an inaccuracy to inform the authority and furnish the correct information. Inaccurate information carries a penalty under section 271FAA of ₹50,000, and for a prescribed reporting financial institution a further ₹5,000 for every reportable account where the inaccuracy is due to false or inaccurate information from the account holder.

options.text: The statement was late, being due on 31 March 2026; the defect may be cured at any time before the assessment of the reporting person; and an inaccuracy may indeed be corrected in the following year's statement
options.misconception: puts the due date at the end of the financial year and treats both correction windows as open-ended
options.why: The due date is 31 May immediately following the financial year, and both windows are fixed — 30 days from the intimation of a defect and ten days from the discovery of an inaccuracy.

options.text: The statement was in time, but an unrectified defect has no consequence of its own until the authority issues a notice under section 285BA(5) requiring a fresh statement
options.misconception: treats a defect and a complete failure to file as the same thing, when the section attaches its own consequence to each
options.why: Section 285BA(5) is for a person who has not furnished a statement at all, and gives him a notice allowing not more than 30 days. A defective statement has its own consequence in section 285BA(4) — after the 30 days, the Act applies as though inaccurate information had been furnished.

citation.ref: Sections 285BA(4), 285BA(5) and 285BA(6) with Rule 114E and section 271FAA — the 31 May due date, 30 days to rectify a defect, ten days to report an inaccuracy, and a penalty of ₹50,000 with a further ₹5,000 for every reportable account against a reporting financial institution

items.scenario: A reporting financial institution files its statement for the financial year 2025-26 on 20 May 2026. On 4 June 2026 the prescribed income-tax authority intimates that the statement is defective. The institution does nothing about the defect for two months. On 1 August 2026 it separately discovers that one account was reported with the wrong balance, and its compliance officer proposes to correct it when the next year's statement is filed.

items.stem: What penalty does section 271FA come to?

options.text: ₹81,000 — ₹1,000 a day for all 81 days, the higher rate applying because the bank was in default throughout and a notice was in fact issued
options.misconception: applies the higher rate to the whole period, when it starts only after the date the notice allowed
options.why: The rates run one after the other. The ₹500 rate covers the default from the due date up to the date allowed by the notice, and only from the day after that does ₹1,000 a day begin.

options.text: ₹40,500 — ₹500 a day for all 81 days of default, from 1 June 2026 to 20 August 2026
options.misconception: applies the ₹500 rate to the whole period and ignores the higher rate that runs after the time allowed by the notice
options.why: The higher rate exists precisely because a notice has been served and ignored. Once the time allowed by the notice under section 285BA(5) has passed, the rate is ₹1,000 a day until the statement is furnished.

options.text: ₹50,500 — ₹500 a day for the 61 days from 1 June 2026 to 31 July 2026, which is ₹30,500, plus ₹1,000 a day for the 20 days from 1 August 2026 to 20 August 2026, which is ₹20,000
options.why: Section 271FA carries two rates for two periods. Failure to furnish the statement by the due date under section 285BA(1) costs ₹500 for every day the default continues, and the due date was 31 May 2026, so that rate runs from 1 June 2026 to the last day allowed by the notice, 31 July 2026, which is 30 plus 31 or 61 days and ₹30,500. From the day after that date until the statement is actually furnished the rate is ₹1,000 a day, so 1 August 2026 to 20 August 2026 is 20 days and ₹20,000. Together ₹50,500.

options.text: ₹20,000 — the penalty runs only from the failure to comply with the notice, since the department cannot charge for a period during which it had not asked for the statement
options.misconception: starts the penalty at the notice, when the default begins on the day after the due date whether or not a notice has issued
options.why: The default under section 285BA(1) begins the day after 31 May, and section 271FA charges ₹500 for every day of it. The notice raises the rate for the period after it expires; it does not create the default.

citation.ref: Section 271FA read with sections 285BA(1) and 285BA(5) — ₹500 for every day of continuing default from the due date to the date allowed by the notice, and ₹1,000 for every day thereafter until the statement is furnished

items.scenario: A private bank does not file its statement of financial transactions for the financial year 2025-26 at all. The prescribed income-tax authority issues a notice on 1 July 2026 requiring the statement by 31 July 2026. The bank finally furnishes it on 20 August 2026. June has 30 days, July 31 and the twenty days of August are counted to the date of filing.

items.stem: What does section 285BB with Rule 114-I say?

options.text: The Assessing Officer uploads it within 30 days of the end of the financial year, and it carries only tax deducted or collected at source and the taxes the assessee has paid
options.misconception: gives the duty to the Assessing Officer on an annual clock and keeps only the two oldest categories
options.why: The duty is on Income-tax (Systems) — its Principal Director General or its Director General, or somebody either of them authorises — the clock runs three months from the close of the month the information came in, and the table runs to six categories including demand and refund and pending and completed proceedings.

options.text: It is uploaded on the assessee's request in the prescribed form, and until he asks the department is under no obligation to compile one
options.misconception: turns a standing obligation on the department into something the assessee must apply for
options.why: Section 285BB puts the obligation on the prescribed authority to upload the statement into the registered account, and Rule 114-I times it from the receipt of the information. Nobody has to ask.

options.text: The Principal Director General or Director General of Income-tax (Systems), or a person authorised by him, uploads it in Form No. 26AS into the assessee's registered account, and has three months to do it counted from the close of the month the information came in, and it may carry tax deducted or collected at source, specified financial transactions, payment of taxes, demand and refund, pending proceedings and completed proceedings
options.why: Section 285BB requires the prescribed income-tax authority or a person authorised by it to upload an annual information statement into the assessee's registered account, meaning the electronic filing account he has registered on the designated portal. Rule 114-I names the officer — Income-tax (Systems) has both a Principal Director General and a Director General, and either may authorise somebody else — names the form as Form No. 26AS, and fixes the timing at three months from the end of the month, counted from when the information reached him. The six categories in the table are information relating to tax deducted or collected at source, to specified financial transactions, to payment of taxes, to demand and refund, to pending proceedings and to completed proceedings.
keywords: three months from the end of the month

options.text: It is uploaded three months after the close of the month the information came in, but nothing may go into it beyond what the Act itself collects, so anything arriving under a section 90 agreement cannot appear there
options.misconception: shuts out treaty and third-party information, which section 285BB(2) expressly lets the Board authorise
options.why: The timing is right and the limit is not. The Board may let that same officer upload more: what reaches him from any officer, authority or body carrying out a function under any law; what arrives under a section 90 or a section 90A agreement; and what any other person supplies — to whatever extent the Board deems fit in the revenue's interest.

citation.ref: Section 285BB with Rule 114-I and Form No. 26AS — the Principal Director General or Director General of Income-tax (Systems) uploading the annual information statement into the assessee's registered account inside three months of the close of the month the information came in, and the six categories of information it carries

items.scenario: An assessee finds that his annual information statement shows a demand raised for an earlier year and a proceeding that is still running, and asks his adviser three things — where the statement comes from, what may go into it, and how quickly information reaches it once the department gets it.

items.stem: What does section 285BAA require of it?

options.text: The defect had to be cured within ten days and the inaccuracy reported within 30, the two periods being the other way round
options.misconception: swaps the two windows, giving the defect the shorter period and the inaccuracy the longer one
options.why: The longer period goes to the defect the department has pointed out, because the entity has to find and fix it, and the shorter one to an inaccuracy the entity has itself discovered. Thirty days for the defect, ten days for the inaccuracy.

options.text: Nothing yet — section 285BAA obliges a reporting entity to furnish a statement but attaches no consequence to a defect until the department serves a notice requiring a fresh one
options.misconception: reads the defect provision as inert, when it converts an unrectified defect into inaccurate information by its own force
options.why: The notice provision in sub-section (3) is for an entity that has furnished no statement at all. Where a statement has been filed and is defective, sub-section (2) itself turns an unrectified defect into inaccurate information after the 30 days.

options.text: Nothing, because a crypto-asset is not property under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and a statement about transactions in one has no statutory footing
options.misconception: denies the statutory basis of the obligation, when section 285BAA creates it and section 2(47A)(d) defines the asset
options.why: The obligation is in section 285BAA and the asset is defined in section 2(47A)(d) as a digital representation of value relying on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions.

options.text: The defect had to be rectified within 30 days of the intimation or such further period as was allowed, failing which the Act applies as if it had furnished inaccurate information; and the values it has now found wrong must be corrected with the authority within ten days of the discovery
options.why: Section 285BAA runs on the same machinery as the statement of financial transactions. Sub-section (2) gives 30 days from the intimation of a defect, or such further period as may be allowed, and says that if the defect is not rectified within that period the provisions of the Act apply as if the person had furnished inaccurate information in the statement. Sub-section (4) gives ten days from coming to know of or discovering an inaccuracy to inform the prescribed income-tax authority and furnish the correct information. A crypto-asset for this purpose is the digital representation of value defined in section 2(47A)(d), which relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions.

citation.ref: Sections 285BAA(1) to 285BAA(4) read with section 2(47A)(d) — the crypto-asset statement, 30 days to rectify a defect after which the Act applies as if inaccurate information had been furnished, a notice of not more than 30 days where nothing is filed, and ten days to correct a discovered inaccuracy

items.scenario: A platform through which people buy and sell digital tokens is a prescribed reporting entity for the purposes of the crypto-asset statement. It files its statement, is told on 10 September that the statement is defective, and lets three months pass. A month after that its own audit finds that two users' transactions were reported at the wrong values.

items.stem: Which of them may be authorised as the company's representative under section 288?

options.text: CA Sundar and CA Prakash — the loan is his brother's rather than his own, and the disqualification reaches only the accountant himself
options.misconception: confines the indebtedness test to the accountant, when the list reads a person who, or his relative or partner, is indebted
options.why: The words are a person who, or his relative or partner, is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5,00,000. A brother is a relative and ₹7,00,000 is over the line.

options.text: CA Sundar and CA Tanvi — a fraud conviction is spent after five years and a shareholding of ₹800 is trivial, while the loan and the number of audits both disqualify
options.misconception: puts the fraud disqualification at five years, when the list requires ten to have elapsed
options.why: The period is ten years from the date of conviction, and six have gone. Everything else in the option is right, which is what makes the wrong figure decide the answer.

options.text: None of them — a chartered accountant may never appear for a company before an appellate authority, that being work reserved for a legal practitioner
options.misconception: reads appearance before an income-tax authority as advocacy reserved to lawyers, when section 288 names an accountant among those who may appear
options.why: Section 288 names both. A legal practitioner entitled to practise in any Civil Court in India may appear, and so may an accountant, and it is only the section 141(3) disqualifications that thin the field.

options.text: CA Sundar alone — a relative may hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000, while indebtedness of a relative above ₹5,00,000, holding appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies, and a fraud conviction where ten years have not elapsed each disqualify
options.why: The definition of accountant in section 288 excludes, for a company assessee, a person who is not eligible for appointment as its auditor under section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. That list disqualifies a person whose relative or partner is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5,00,000, so CA Prakash's brother's ₹7,00,000 loan is fatal; a person who at the date of appointment already holds appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies, which catches CA Rehana at 22; and a person convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud where a period of ten years has not elapsed, which catches CA Tanvi at six years. The footnote to the same list permits a relative to hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000, and CA Sundar's wife holds ₹800.

citation.ref: Section 288 with the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 — a relative or partner indebted in excess of ₹5 lakh, appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies and a fraud conviction within ten years disqualifying, while a relative may hold security of face value not exceeding ₹1,000

items.scenario: A company looks for someone to appear for it before the Commissioner (Appeals). Four names come up. CA Prakash, whose brother has taken a loan of ₹7,00,000 from the company. CA Rehana, who is already the statutory auditor of 22 companies. CA Sundar, whose wife holds shares in the company of a face value of ₹800. And CA Tanvi, who was convicted of an offence involving fraud six years ago.

items.stem: What are the three answers?

options.text: He may not appear for the trust; nobody may attend a section 131 examination for the client; and a valuation question must be argued by an accountant because a registered valuer is a witness rather than a representative
options.misconception: gets the section 131 point right and both others wrong, treating a registered valuer as incapable of appearing
options.why: Section 287A says in terms that a taxpayer entitled or required to attend on a matter relating to the valuation of an asset may attend by a registered valuer. And the rider in section 288 lets the partner appear for the trust despite being unable to audit it.

options.text: He may not appear for the trust, because a contribution of ₹75,000 exceeds the ₹50,000 substantial contribution limit and the disqualification runs to representation as well as to audit
options.misconception: carries the audit disqualification into representation, which the rider in section 288 exists to prevent
options.why: The rider was written for this. Being unable to audit an assessee or to sign a report or certificate for him does not stop an accountant appearing for him in a proceeding as authorised representative.

options.text: He may appear for the trust; the firm may also attend the section 131 examination provided it holds a written authority; and a registered valuer may appear only with the Assessing Officer's leave
options.misconception: allows a representative to stand in for a personal examination on oath and adds a permission requirement to section 287A
options.why: Section 288(1) opens by carving out the personal examination: where section 131 calls somebody to appear himself and be examined on oath or on affirmation, no written authority can cure it. And section 287A gives the taxpayer the right to attend by a registered valuer without anybody's leave.

options.text: He may appear for the trust, because ineligibility to audit or to furnish a report or certificate does not make an accountant ineligible to attend as authorised representative; nobody may attend in place of a person required under section 131 to attend personally for examination on oath; and on a question of valuation the taxpayer may attend by a registered valuer under section 287A
options.why: Section 288 carries a rider. Being barred from auditing an assessee, or from giving him a report or a certificate, shall not make an accountant ineligible to appear for that same assessee as his authorised representative in a proceeding of the kind section 288(1) names. So the ₹75,000 contribution, which is above the ₹50,000 that makes a person a substantial contributor and bars him from auditing the trust, does not bar him from appearing for it. Section 288(1) itself carves out one case: where section 131 obliges somebody to attend personally for examination on oath or on affirmation, nobody may do it for him. And section 287A lets a taxpayer who is required to attend on a matter relating to the valuation of an asset attend by a registered valuer, subject to the same section 131 exception.
keywords: shall not make an accountant ineligible
attend personally for examination on oath

citation.ref: Section 288(1) and the rider to the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 287A — appearance by an authorised representative except where section 131 requires personal attendance on oath, the ₹50,000 substantial contribution that bars an audit of a trust but not an appearance for it, and appearance by a registered valuer on a valuation matter

items.scenario: Three questions come to a firm on the same morning. Its partner is not eligible to audit a charitable trust because he gave it ₹75,000 last year, and the trust asks whether he can nonetheless appear for it in an assessment. A client summoned under section 131 to be examined on oath asks whether the firm can go in his place. And another client, whose only dispute is the value of a factory building, asks who may appear on that.

items.stem: How many of the four may apply?

options.text: All four — the ₹100,00,00,000 notification sets the fee band rather than the class of applicant, and any resident may ask about his own liability
options.misconception: confuses the ₹100 crore notification defining the class of resident applicant with the transaction slabs that fix the fee
options.why: Two different figures do two different jobs. The notification of 28 November 2014 makes a resident an applicant only where his transactions total ₹100,00,00,000 or more, and Rule 44E separately uses ₹100,00,00,000 and ₹300,00,00,000 to fix the fee for an applicant who is already qualified.

options.text: Three — Alpha Inc, Bharat Ltd and Mr Dev; Chandra Ltd cannot, because a resident may seek a ruling on his own tax liability only if he falls in a class notified by the Central Government, and the notified class is a resident whose transactions total ₹100,00,00,000 or more
options.why: Section 245N(a) gives an advance ruling five limbs and section 245N(b) gives each of them its applicant. A non-resident may ask about a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake, which covers Alpha Inc. A resident may ask what a non-resident's tax will come to on a dealing he has already entered into with that non-resident, or plans to, which covers Bharat Ltd. Any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether an arrangement proposed to be undertaken is an impermissible avoidance arrangement referred to in Chapter X-A, which covers Mr Dev. A resident asking about his own tax liability must fall within a class notified by the Central Government, and Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 draws that class round a resident whose transactions, taken together, are worth ₹100,00,00,000 or more, so ₹40,00,00,000 leaves Chandra Ltd out.

options.text: Two — only Alpha Inc and Bharat Ltd, because the whole chapter is written for the tax liability of a non-resident and a resident's own affairs are outside it in every case
options.misconception: reads advance rulings as available only where a non-resident's liability is in question
options.why: Two of the five limbs are about a resident's own position. A notified resident may ask about his own tax liability, and any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement.

options.text: Three — Alpha Inc, Bharat Ltd and Chandra Ltd; Mr Dev cannot, because a question of impermissible avoidance is for the Approving Panel under Chapter X-A and never for a Board for Advance Rulings
options.misconception: sends the avoidance question to the Approving Panel, when section 245N(a) expressly makes it a limb of advance ruling
options.why: Section 245N(a) names it as a limb in its own words — a determination or decision whether an arrangement proposed to be undertaken by any person, resident or non-resident, is an impermissible avoidance arrangement referred to in Chapter X-A. It is the one limb open to everybody, and it is Chandra Ltd that fails on the ₹100,00,00,000 test.

citation.ref: Sections 245N(a) and 245N(b) with Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 — the five limbs of advance ruling and their applicants, including the notified resident whose transactions total ₹100 crore or more and the impermissible avoidance question open to any person

items.scenario: Four people want a ruling from a Board for Advance Rulings. Alpha Inc, a non-resident, on the tax effect of a transaction it proposes to undertake in India. Bharat Ltd, a resident, on the tax liability of a non-resident arising out of a supply contract Bharat Ltd proposes to enter into with that non-resident. Chandra Ltd, a resident and not a public sector company, on its own tax liability arising out of transactions totalling ₹40,00,00,000. And Mr Dev, a resident individual, on whether an arrangement he proposes to undertake is an impermissible avoidance arrangement.

items.stem: Which of those is right?

options.text: All except the last — the two remedies may be pursued together, because an advance ruling only clarifies a question and an appeal decides a dispute
options.misconception: allows a resident applicant to run an appeal and an application at once, which section 245RR forbids
options.why: Section 245RR exists to stop exactly that. Where a resident applicant has made an application in respect of an issue for the decision of a Board, no income-tax authority or Tribunal may take any decision on that issue.

options.text: All except the third — a Board may call for the Commissioner's records but has no power over a third party such as a bank, which can only be reached by the Assessing Officer
options.misconception: confines the Board's powers to the departmental record, when section 245U gives it the powers of a Civil Court over any person
options.why: Section 245U names the banking company specifically. The Board may make anybody attend — a banking company's officer among them — put him on oath, and compel the production of books of account and other documents.

options.text: All of them — three Boards for Advance Rulings have given rulings since 1 September 2021, each of two members who are officers not below the rank of Chief Commissioner; a vacancy or defect in the constitution does not make a proceeding or ruling open to question; a Board has the powers of a Civil Court including compelling the production of books and examining on oath; and section 245RR stops any income-tax authority or the Tribunal deciding an issue on which a resident applicant has applied
options.why: Section 245-OB lets the Central Government constitute Boards for Advance Rulings, and three have been constituted for giving rulings on or after 1 September 2021, two with their headquarters in Delhi and one in Mumbai; every such Board consists of two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner nominated by the Board. Section 245P says a proceeding before, or a ruling by, a Board is not questioned or invalid merely because of a vacancy or a defect in its constitution. Section 245U gives it every Civil Court power over discovery and inspection; over making somebody appear, a banking company's officer included, and questioning him on oath; over issuing commissions; and over calling for books of account to be produced. And section 245RR provides that where a resident applicant has applied on an issue, no income-tax authority or Tribunal shall take any decision on it, so the two remedies cannot be run together.
keywords: not below the rank of Chief Commissioner

options.text: Only the last — a Board consists of three members of whom one is a retired judge, and a defect in its constitution invalidates whatever it has done
options.misconception: describes the Dispute Resolution Committee's three-member composition and denies the protection section 245P gives
options.why: Three members, two of them retired officers, is Rule 44DAA and the Dispute Resolution Committee. A Board for Advance Rulings has two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner, and section 245P protects its proceedings against a vacancy or defect.

citation.ref: Sections 245-OB, 245P, 245RR and 245U with Notification No. 96/2021 dated 1 September 2021 — three Boards of two members each not below the rank of Chief Commissioner, a vacancy not invalidating a proceeding, the Civil Court powers, and the bar on an authority or the Tribunal deciding an issue a resident applicant has taken to a Board

items.scenario: A resident applicant is told three things by his adviser and doubts all of them. That the body which will hear him is not a tribunal of judges but a bench of two serving revenue officers. That a vacancy on that bench would not upset its ruling. And that the same bench can compel a bank to produce records and can examine a person on oath. He also asks whether, having applied, he can keep his appeal on the same issue alive before the Tribunal.

items.stem: What fee accompanies each application?

options.text: ₹5,00,000 for both, since the fee follows the value of the transactions and the public sector company's amounts are the larger
options.misconception: applies the transaction slabs to every applicant, when Rule 44E confines them to sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iia) and puts everyone else at ₹10,000
options.why: The slabs are written only for an applicant referred to in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of clause (b) of section 245N. Any other applicant, however large the sums in issue, pays ₹10,000 in all cases.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 for the non-resident and ₹10,000 for the public sector company, the top slab applying to anything above ₹1,00,00,00,000
options.misconception: collapses the middle slab, treating everything above ₹100 crore as attracting the ₹10 lakh fee
options.why: There are three slabs, not two. The ₹10,00,000 fee applies only where the transactions exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹2,50,00,00,000 sits in the middle slab at ₹5,00,000.

options.text: ₹10,000 for both, because section 245Q(2) fixes the fee at ₹10,000 and Rule 44E only prescribes the form of the application
options.misconception: reads section 245Q(2) as fixing a flat fee, when it in fact sets ₹10,000 against any figure that stands prescribed and takes the larger
options.why: The section itself contemplates a higher prescribed fee. It sets ₹10,000 against whatever figure stands prescribed and takes the larger of the two, and Rule 44E prescribes the slabs that are higher for the applicants it names.

options.text: ₹5,00,000 for the non-resident, its transactions exceeding ₹1,00,00,00,000 but not ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹10,000 for the public sector company, which pays that in all cases
options.why: Section 245Q(2) wants the application in quadruplicate with a fee attached — ₹10,000, set against any figure that stands prescribed, whichever is higher — and Rule 44E prescribes the higher fees only for an applicant falling in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of clause (b) of section 245N. For that applicant the fee is ₹2,00,000 where the transactions do not exceed ₹1,00,00,00,000, ₹5,00,000 where they exceed ₹1,00,00,00,000 but do not exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹10,00,000 where they exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000. Any other applicant, which includes the notified public sector company, pays ₹10,000 in all cases.

citation.ref: Section 245Q(2) with Rule 44E — the fee of ₹10,000 or the prescribed fee whichever is higher, and the slabs of ₹2 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹10 lakh against ₹100 crore and ₹300 crore for an applicant under sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of section 245N(b), with ₹10,000 for any other applicant

items.scenario: Two applications are being prepared on the same day. One is by a non-resident falling in sub-clause (i) of section 245N(b), on transactions in respect of which the ruling is sought totalling ₹2,50,00,00,000. The other is by a public sector company notified for the purpose, on an issue pending before the Appellate Tribunal, where the amounts involved are far larger.

items.stem: Which of them may the Board allow, and how long has it to rule?

options.text: The second, the third and the fourth — a valuation question may be answered because section 245U gives the Board the powers of a Civil Court, and only a genuinely pending question is excluded
options.misconception: reads the Board's procedural powers as enlarging the questions it may answer, when the fair market value ground is a separate bar
options.why: Powers of procedure and jurisdiction over a question are different things. The determination of the fair market value of any property is named as a question the Board shall not allow, whatever powers it holds to gather evidence.

options.text: The third and the fourth — the pending question and the fair market value question are grounds on which the Board shall not allow an application, while the avoidance ground has its own exception for a question whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement; and where an application is allowed the ruling must be pronounced within six months from the receipt of the application
options.why: Section 245R lists three questions the Board shall not allow. One already pending before any income-tax authority, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, though a notified resident may ask even then and this applicant is not one. One involving the determination of the fair market value of any property. And one relating to a transaction or issue designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, except in the case of a notified resident applicant or where a resident or non-resident asks whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement, which is exactly the third application. No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard and the order must give the reason. Where an application is allowed, the Board pronounces its ruling within six months from the receipt of the application by the Board.

options.text: Only the fourth — an avoidance transaction is barred without exception, and the Board has twelve months from admission to pronounce
options.misconception: drops the exception written into the avoidance ground and doubles the time limit while measuring it from admission
options.why: The avoidance ground carries its own exception for the question whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement, which is one of the five limbs of advance ruling. And the time limit is six months from the receipt of the application, not twelve from its admission.

options.text: All four — the three grounds are matters the Board takes into account in framing its ruling rather than reasons for refusing to hear a case at all
options.misconception: turns mandatory grounds of rejection into considerations, when the section says the Board shall not allow such an application
options.why: The words are that the Board shall not allow an application where the question raised is one of the three. They govern admission, not the content of a ruling.

citation.ref: Section 245R — the three grounds on which the Board shall not allow an application, the exceptions for a notified resident and for the impermissible avoidance question, the opportunity of being heard before rejection, and the six-month limit for pronouncing a ruling

items.scenario: Four applications reach a Board for Advance Rulings. The first raises a question already pending before the Appellate Tribunal in the applicant's own case, and the applicant is not a notified resident. The second asks the Board to fix the fair market value of a plant in Kerala. The third relates to a transaction the Board considers to be designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, and the applicant is a non-resident asking whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement. The fourth raises an ordinary question of law on a proposed transaction.

items.stem: What is the position in the three cases?

options.text: The withdrawal is too late because it must be sought within 30 days of the Board sending the application to the Commissioner; the 60 days for an appeal cannot be extended; and a void ruling simply falls away with no adjustment of time limits
options.misconception: measures the withdrawal window from a later event, denies the extension the proviso gives, and drops the exclusion of the intervening period
options.why: All three figures are in the sections. Thirty days runs from the date of the application, the High Court may add 30 days on sufficient cause, and the period between the ruling and the order declaring it void is excluded so that the department is not shut out by limitation.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him only with the Board's leave; the further period the High Court may grant is 60 days rather than 30; and where a ruling is void the exclusion runs from the date of the application rather than the date of the ruling
options.misconception: adds a leave requirement to the withdrawal, doubles the extension and starts the exclusion at the application
options.why: Withdrawal within 30 days is the applicant's own right and needs nobody's leave. The further period is 30 days, and the excluded period begins with the date of the advance ruling and ends with the date of the order declaring it void.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him; the appeal against a ruling lies to the Appellate Tribunal rather than the High Court, so the 60 days does not apply; and a void ruling stands until set aside by a court
options.misconception: sends the appeal to the Tribunal, when section 245W takes a ruling of a Board straight to the High Court
options.why: A ruling pronounced or an order passed by a Board for Advance Rulings is appealable before the High Court under section 245W. And the Board itself declares a ruling void ab initio under section 245T, without anybody having to go to court.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him because it was sought within 30 days from the date of the application; the High Court may grant a further period of 30 days beyond the 60 days where it is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented the appeal; and where a ruling is declared void the Act applies as if it had never been made, excluding the period from the date of the ruling to the date of that order
options.why: Section 245Q(3) lets an applicant withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application, and 3 April to 1 May is inside that. Section 245W(1) gives an applicant aggrieved by a ruling or order 60 days from its communication to appeal to the High Court, and the proviso lets the High Court grant a further period of 30 days where it is satisfied on an application that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from presenting it in time. Section 245T lets the Board declare a ruling void ab initio where it finds, on a representation by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or otherwise, that it was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, and the Act then applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after excluding the period beginning with the date of the advance ruling and ending with the date of the order under that section.
keywords: within 30 days from the date of the application
as if the ruling had never been made

citation.ref: Sections 245Q(3), 245T and 245W(1) with its proviso — withdrawal within 30 days from the date of the application, a ruling declared void ab initio for fraud or misrepresentation with the intervening period excluded, and an appeal to the High Court within 60 days extendable by a further 30 days on sufficient cause

items.scenario: A non-resident applied to a Board for Advance Rulings on 3 April 2025 and changed his mind on 1 May 2025, when he asked to withdraw. A different applicant received a ruling and wants to take it to the High Court, but the sixty days ran out while his counsel was ill. And in a third case the Board has found that the ruling it gave was obtained by misrepresentation of facts and has declared it void ab initio.

items.stem: What is chargeable under the Black Money Act, and when?

options.text: ₹90,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26 at 30 per cent, giving ₹27,00,000 of tax, with no deduction for the ₹4,00,000 of fees and no set-off of the loss
options.why: The proviso to section 3(1) settles the year. An undisclosed asset sitting outside India is taxed on the value it holds in whichever previous year the asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, so the year of acquisition is beside the point and 2025-26 is the year of charge. Section 3(1) fixes the rate at 30 per cent of the undisclosed foreign income and asset, and 30 per cent of ₹90,00,000 is ₹27,00,000. Section 5(1) is written to stop exactly the two claims Mr Anand makes — no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance and no set-off of any loss is allowed in computing the total undisclosed foreign income and asset, whether or not the Income-tax Act, 1961 would have allowed it.
keywords: comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer

options.text: Nothing — the asset was acquired in the previous year 2011-12, so any charge belongs to that year and no assessment for it can now be made
options.misconception: charges an undisclosed foreign asset in the year of acquisition, when the proviso moves it to the year it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer
options.why: The proviso to section 3(1) is what makes this Act work on old assets at all. The value is charged in the previous year during which the Assessing Officer comes to know of the asset, however long ago it was acquired.

options.text: ₹90,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26, but taxed at the slab rates applicable to Mr Anand under the Income-tax Act, 1961 because the Black Money Act contains no rate of its own
options.misconception: reads the Black Money Act as borrowing the Income-tax Act's rates, when section 3(1) carries its own flat rate
options.why: Section 3(1) carries a rate of its own — every assessee pays 30 per cent, and what he pays it on is his undisclosed foreign income and asset for the previous year. And section 4 keeps that income out of total income under the Income-tax Act altogether.

options.text: ₹86,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26 at 30 per cent, giving ₹25,80,000, the custody and management fees being an allowable expense against the value of the holding
options.misconception: allows expenditure against the value of an undisclosed foreign asset, which section 5(1) refuses whether or not the Income-tax Act would have allowed it
options.why: Section 5(1) refuses a deduction for any expenditure and for any allowance when the total undisclosed foreign income and asset is being computed, and adds that this holds irrespective of whether it is allowable under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

citation.ref: Section 3(1) with its proviso, section 4(c) and section 5(1) — tax at 30 per cent, an undisclosed foreign asset charged in whichever previous year the Assessing Officer comes to know of it, and no deduction for expenditure or allowance and no set-off of loss

items.scenario: Mr Anand has been resident and ordinarily resident throughout. He acquired shares in a foreign company in the previous year 2011-12 out of sources he cannot explain, and the Assessing Officer comes to know of them during the previous year 2025-26, when their fair market value determined under Rule 3 is ₹90,00,000. Mr Anand says the charge, if any, arose in 2011-12 and is long dead; that in any event he should be allowed the ₹4,00,000 of custody and management fees he has paid on the holding over the years; and that he has a foreign capital loss to set against it.

items.stem: What amount is chargeable to tax under the Black Money Act?

options.text: ₹60,00,000 — the cost of ₹80,00,000 less the ₹20,00,000 already assessed, the charge being on what the asset cost rather than on what it is now worth
options.misconception: charges the historical cost of an undisclosed foreign asset instead of its value in the year it comes to notice
options.why: The charge is on value, not on cost. The proviso to section 3(1) charges an undisclosed foreign asset at the value it holds in the previous year during which the Assessing Officer learns of it, and the cost enters only as the denominator of the proportion in section 5(2).

options.text: ₹2,00,00,000 — no deduction is available, because section 5(1) refuses every deduction in computing the total undisclosed foreign income and asset
options.misconception: reads the bar on expenditure and set-off in section 5(1) as removing the deduction section 5(2) gives for income already taxed
options.why: The two sub-sections do different jobs. Section 5(1) refuses expenditure, allowances and losses; section 5(2) allows a reduction for income already assessed or assessable to tax, on evidence that the asset was acquired out of it.

options.text: ₹1,80,00,000 — the ₹20,00,000 that has already suffered tax is deducted from the ₹2,00,00,000, since a person cannot be taxed twice on the same money
options.misconception: deducts the assessed amount at its historical figure instead of scaling it to the asset's present value
options.why: Section 5(2) does not deduct the historical figure. For immovable property it scales the assessed income up in the same proportion that it bore to the total cost, which is what gives ₹50,00,000 rather than ₹20,00,000 on these numbers.

options.text: ₹1,50,00,000 — the deduction for immovable property is proportionate, so it is ₹2,00,00,000 multiplied by ₹20,00,000 over ₹80,00,000, which is ₹50,00,000, and that comes off the ₹2,00,00,000
options.why: Section 5(2) fixes the size of the deduction where the income already assessed relates to immovable property. Two ratios are set equal. Take the property's value on the day the financial year opens — the year the Assessing Officer learns of it — and ask what fraction of that value the deduction is; it is the same proportion as the assessable or assessed foreign income makes when set against the total cost of the asset. Here the value on 1 April 2025 is ₹2,00,00,000, the assessed income is ₹20,00,000 and the total cost is ₹80,00,000, so the deduction is ₹2,00,00,000 multiplied by 20 over 80, which is ₹50,00,000, and the amount chargeable is ₹1,50,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 5(2) with the proviso to section 3(1) — the deduction for income already assessed where the asset is immovable property, set in the same proportion against the property's value on the opening day of whichever financial year the Assessing Officer learns of it in, as the assessed income makes when set against the total cost of the asset

items.scenario: A house property outside India was acquired by Mrs Bhatia in the previous year 2013-14 for a total cost of ₹80,00,000. Of that investment, ₹20,00,000 had already been assessed to tax in her total income for that year and earlier years under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and she can furnish evidence of it to the Assessing Officer's satisfaction. The asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer during the previous year 2025-26, and its value on 1 April 2025 is ₹2,00,00,000.

items.stem: What penalty does section 43 come to?

options.text: ₹20,00,000 — ₹10,00,000 for each of the two failures, the accounts being one and the flat another
options.misconception: multiplies the penalty by the number of assets, when section 43 fixes one sum for the failure
options.why: Section 43 directs the assessee to pay, by way of penalty, a sum of ₹10,00,000. It is a single figure for the failure and not a rate per asset.

options.text: Nil — the aggregate value of everything he failed to report is what the ₹20,00,000 proviso measures, and on that footing the accounts are below it while the flat is a single asset he has always owned openly
options.misconception: aggregates only the assets that suit the relief and reads immovable property as capable of falling inside it
options.why: Immovable property is put outside the relief by the words of the proviso, which speaks of an asset or assets other than immovable property. No aggregation brings a flat inside it.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 — the proviso relieves an asset or assets other than immovable property whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20,00,000, so the two accounts at ₹18,00,000 would have been covered on their own, but the flat is immovable property and is outside the relief altogether
options.why: Section 43 charges a penalty of ₹10,00,000 on a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who leaves out of his return the information about an asset abroad — one he holds as its beneficial owner, one he holds in some other way, or one he merely benefits from — or about income from a source outside India. The proviso to sections 42 and 43 lifts the penalty where the assets, taken together and other than immovable property, come to a figure that does not exceed ₹20,00,000. The two bank accounts total ₹18,00,000 and would have been inside it; the flat is immovable property, which the proviso puts outside the relief, so the penalty stands at ₹10,00,000.

options.text: Three times the tax computed on the value of the flat, section 41 being the penalty that applies wherever an undisclosed foreign asset is found
options.misconception: reaches for the section 41 penalty on computed tax where the default is a reporting failure under section 43
options.why: Section 41 bites once tax has been worked out on undisclosed foreign income and asset, and it is three times that tax. Section 43 is the separate penalty for failing to furnish information about a foreign asset in the return, and it is ₹10,00,000.

citation.ref: Sections 41 and 43 with the proviso to sections 42 and 43 — a penalty of ₹10 lakh for failing to furnish information about a foreign asset, not applying to assets other than immovable property whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20 lakh, against the section 41 penalty of three times the tax computed

items.scenario: Mr Chetan has been resident and ordinarily resident throughout. He filed his return under section 139(1) on time but gave no information in it about two foreign bank accounts holding ₹18,00,000 between them, or about a flat abroad worth ₹60,00,000 of which he is the beneficial owner. His adviser says the ₹20,00,000 relief in the Black Money Act covers him because the accounts are under it.

items.stem: What follows on the two matters?

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi, because section 49 is not attracted where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year; and the ₹4,00,000 penalty needs no approval of the Joint Commissioner, since approval is required where an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner levies a penalty exceeding ₹5,00,000, while a wilful attempt to evade tax under section 51 carries rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years extending to ten years and a fine
options.why: Section 49 punishes a wilful failure to furnish the return required under section 139(1) in due time by a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who holds a foreign asset or has foreign income, with rigorous imprisonment of not less than six months extending to seven years and a fine, and then carves out the escape Mrs Devi has taken: file that return before the expiry of the assessment year and no prosecution follows. On the penalty, section 46(4) requires the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where the penalty exceeds ₹1,00,000 and the authority levying it is an Income-tax Officer, or exceeds ₹5,00,000 and the authority is an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant or Deputy Director, so ₹4,00,000 levied by an Assistant Commissioner is below the line. Section 51 punishes a wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest with rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years extending to ten years and a fine.
keywords: before the expiry of the assessment year
three years extending to ten years

options.text: Mrs Devi can still be prosecuted because the return was late whatever she did afterwards; the ₹4,00,000 penalty needs approval because the limit for every authority is ₹1,00,000; and section 51 carries six months to seven years like the other offences
options.misconception: denies the escape section 49 gives, applies the ₹1 lakh approval limit to every rank, and levels the sentence for evasion down to the reporting offences
options.why: All three figures are in the sections. Section 49 excludes prosecution where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year, section 46(4) has two limits by rank, and section 51 is the heaviest of the offences at three to ten years.

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi; the penalty needs approval because any penalty over ₹1,00,000 does; and a wilful attempt to evade payment of tax carries the same three to ten years as an attempt to evade tax
options.misconception: uses the ₹1 lakh limit for an Assistant Commissioner and gives evasion of payment the same sentence as evasion of tax
options.why: The ₹1,00,000 limit belongs to a penalty levied by an Income-tax Officer, and for an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner the figure is ₹5,00,000. And section 51 splits the two — three to ten years for a wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest, and three months to three years for a wilful attempt to evade payment of it.

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi and no approval is needed for the penalty, but a prosecution under section 51 may be launched by the Assessing Officer without anybody's sanction once the penalty order is made
options.misconception: drops the sanction section 55 requires before a prosecution under sections 49 to 53 is begun
options.why: Section 55 says a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence under sections 49 to 53 except with the sanction of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or the Commissioner (Appeals). The first two halves of the option are right and this one is not.

citation.ref: Sections 46(4), 49, 51 and 55 — prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where a penalty exceeds ₹1 lakh levied by an Income-tax Officer or ₹5 lakh levied by an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner, no prosecution under section 49 where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year, rigorous imprisonment of three to ten years under section 51, and the sanction required by section 55

items.scenario: Mrs Devi, resident and ordinarily resident, holds a foreign account and did not file her return by the due date under section 139(1). She files it before the end of the relevant assessment year and discloses everything. In a separate matter Mr Eshwar is charged with a wilful attempt to evade tax under the Act, and a penalty of ₹4,00,000 is proposed against him by an Assistant Commissioner.

items.stem: What are the answers under section 245MA and the rules made under it?

options.text: A committee of three members, being two retired officers of the Indian Revenue Service who have held the post of Commissioner of Income-tax or an equivalent or higher post for five years or more and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, deciding by majority; a fee of ₹1,000; one month from the receipt of the specified order; and proof of withdrawal of the appeal within 30 days of the communication that the application is admitted
options.why: Rule 44DAA requires the Central Government to constitute a Dispute Resolution Committee for every region of a Principal Chief Commissioner, consisting of three members — two retired officers who came out of the Indian Revenue Service (Income-tax), each having sat as a Commissioner of Income-tax, or in a post equal to that or above it, for five years or more, and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as specified by the Board — appointed for a period of three years and deciding by majority. Rule 44DAB requires the application in the prescribed form accompanied by a fee of ₹1,000. The time to file is one month from the receipt of the specified order where no appeal is pending, and where an appeal is already pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) it is such time from the constitution of the committee as the Board specifies. And within 30 days of receiving the communication that the application is admitted the assessee must submit proof of withdrawal of the appeal filed under section 246A or of the application before the Dispute Resolution Panel, or say that no such proceeding is pending, failing which the committee may reject the application.

options.text: A committee of three serving officers of the rank of Commissioner or above; no fee, the route being meant for a small taxpayer; one month from the receipt of the specified order; and the appeal may be kept alive because the committee's order is not a decision on the merits
options.misconception: makes the committee wholly serving and fee-free and lets the assessee run the appeal alongside the application
options.why: Two of the three members are retired officers, which is what gives the committee its independence, the application carries a fee of ₹1,000 under Rule 44DAB, and the appeal must be withdrawn with proof furnished within 30 days of the admission.

options.text: A single Commissioner sitting as the committee; a fee of ₹10,000; six months from the receipt of the specified order; and the appeal lapses automatically on admission
options.misconception: turns the committee into one officer, borrows the advance ruling fee, stretches the filing period and assumes the appeal lapses without the assessee doing anything
options.why: Every figure is wrong. Three members under Rule 44DAA, ₹1,000 under Rule 44DAB, one month from the receipt of the specified order, and a positive duty on the assessee to furnish proof of withdrawal within 30 days of the admission.

options.text: A committee of three members with two of them retired; a fee of ₹1,000; but the application may be filed at any time before the appeal period under section 246A expires, and no withdrawal is needed because the two proceedings run in parallel
options.misconception: replaces the one-month filing period with the appeal period and lets both proceedings run at once
options.why: The composition and the fee are right and the last two are not. The time is one month from the receipt of the specified order, and the committee may reject the application where the assessee does not produce proof of withdrawal of a section 246A appeal or a Dispute Resolution Panel application within 30 days of the communication admitting it.

citation.ref: Rules 44DAA and 44DAB read with section 245MA(1) — a three-member committee of two retired Indian Revenue Service officers who have held the post of Commissioner or higher for five years or more and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner, deciding by majority, a fee of ₹1,000, an application within one month of the specified order, and proof of withdrawal of a section 246A appeal within 30 days of admission

items.scenario: An assessee has received a specified order and wants to take it to a Dispute Resolution Committee rather than appeal. He asks four things. Who will actually hear him. What the application costs. How long he has to file it, no appeal having been filed anywhere. And what he must do if the committee admits the application while an appeal of his under section 246A is pending on the same order.

items.stem: Are the Zenith shares treated as an asset situated in India, so that Mr Karan's gain is deemed to accrue here?

options.text: No — the shares are of a Singapore company, the sale happened in Dubai and the money was paid there, so nothing about the transaction touches Indian jurisdiction
options.misconception: treats a transfer made abroad between two non-residents as beyond section 9(1)(i), which is the very gap Explanation 5 was written to close
options.why: This reasoning would defeat the clause entirely. Capital gain on a capital asset situated in India is deemed to accrue here whatever the asset is made of, wherever the deed is registered and wherever the price changes hands, and Explanation 5 exists precisely so that a foreign company's share can itself be that Indian asset. The answer here turns on the ₹10 crore, not on the geography.

options.text: No — the Indian assets have to be worth more than ₹10 crore as well as make up at least half of everything the company owns, and ₹9.4 crore does not reach the first of those
options.why: Both limbs of Explanation 6 have to be satisfied before Explanation 5 can treat a foreign company's share as an Indian asset. The measure is fair market value on the specified date, worked out under Rule 11UB and taken gross without knocking off any liability, and here that is ₹9.4 crore against a ₹10 crore floor. The 67 per cent proportion is therefore irrelevant, and no part of Mr Karan's gain is deemed to accrue in India.
keywords: fair market value on the specified date

options.text: Yes — the ₹11.2 crore at which Zenith's books carry the Indian assets is above ₹10 crore, and a company's own accounts are the natural measure of what it owns
options.misconception: measures the ₹10 crore limb against the carrying amount in the accounts, when the provision measures fair market value
options.why: A book figure is the wrong quantity. What Explanation 6 weighs is fair market value on the specified date, computed the way Rule 11UB prescribes. Book value has one job in this provision and one only — it decides which date is the specified date, because the date of transfer displaces the close of the preceding accounting period where book value on the transfer date runs at least 15 per cent above the last balance sheet figure. Here it did not, so the earlier date stands and the fair market value on it is ₹9.4 crore.

options.text: Yes — the Indian assets are about 67 per cent of everything Zenith owns, which is well past the halfway mark the provision sets
options.misconception: reads Explanation 6's two limbs as alternatives, so that clearing either one is enough
options.why: The proportion is right and it is only half the test. Explanation 6 joins its two limbs with an "and", so a share is treated as Indian only when the Indian assets both exceed ₹10 crore in value and account for at least half of the whole. Zenith's Indian assets clear the second limb comfortably and fall ₹60 lakh short of the first, so the deeming does not reach them.

citation.ref: Explanations 5 and 6 to Section 9(1)(i), read with Rule 11UB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Zenith Holdings Pte Ltd is incorporated in Singapore and has never been registered in India. Its only Indian holding is the entire share capital of an Indian subsidiary, and it owns other assets abroad. Mr Karan, a non-resident, sells his shares in Zenith Holdings to a buyer in Dubai on 4 September 2025; the price is paid in Dubai and the transfer is recorded there. On the specified date the fair market value of Zenith's Indian assets, determined under Rule 11UB and taken without reducing any liability, is ₹9.4 crore, and the fair market value of everything Zenith owns is ₹14 crore. Zenith's own books carry those Indian assets at ₹11.2 crore, and its book values had not moved by anything approaching 15 per cent since its last balance sheet date.

items.stem: How much of Ms Rhea's gain is deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.text: Nothing — she and her associated enterprise together held 4.7 per cent and no right of management or control at any point in the twelve months before the sale, which is what Explanation 7 asks
options.why: Explanation 7 asks two questions of the transferor taken together with his associated enterprises, and it asks them of the whole twelve months before the transfer rather than of the transfer date. Did they hold a right of management or control in the foreign company that directly owns the Indian assets? No. Did they hold voting power, share capital or interest above 5 per cent of that company's total? Their combined 4.7 per cent does not, at any time in the period. Both answers being no, no income is deemed to accrue or arise to her from this transfer.
keywords: taken together with his associated enterprises
whole twelve months before the transfer

options.text: The whole gain, because the 4.1 per cent and the 0.6 per cent belong to two different persons and each is tested on its own against the 5 per cent line
options.misconception: refuses to aggregate an associated enterprise's holding, when Explanation 7 measures the transferor and his associated enterprises together
options.why: The aggregation runs the other way and it works against the taxpayer, not for him. The provision measures what the transferor holds either individually or along with his associated enterprises, so the two stakes are added — which is why the figure to test here is 4.7 per cent and not 4.1. Adding them still leaves her under the line, so she is exempt; had the associated enterprise held 1.2 per cent instead, the aggregate would have crossed 5 per cent and she would not be.

options.text: The whole gain, because she still held 4.1 per cent on the day of the sale and the exemption is only for a transferor who holds nothing at all in the foreign company
options.misconception: reads the exemption as needing a nil holding, when the provision sets a 5 per cent ceiling
options.why: Explanation 7 does not require an empty holding. It sets a ceiling — more than 5 per cent of the total voting power, share capital or interest — and a stake below that line keeps the exemption alive so long as no right of control comes with it. A rule demanding nil would exempt nobody who had anything to sell.

options.text: The whole gain, because once a share is treated as situated in India the size of the shareholder's stake makes no difference to the charge
options.misconception: applies Explanation 5 without Explanation 7, which carves the small holder out of the very charge Explanation 5 creates
options.why: Explanation 7 sits in the same clause and takes the small holder out of it. A transferor who, with his associated enterprises, held neither control nor more than 5 per cent throughout those twelve months has nothing deemed to accrue to him at all. And even where the exemption misses, the charge would not reach the whole gain: only so much of it as is reasonably attributable to the Indian assets is deemed to accrue here, computed under Rule 11UC.

citation.ref: Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i), read with Explanation 5 and Rule 11UC of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Meridian Capital Ltd is registered in Mauritius and owns, directly, shares in an Indian operating company. Those Indian shares are worth ₹260 crore and are 82 per cent of everything Meridian owns, so a share in Meridian is treated as situated in India. Ms Rhea, a non-resident, sold her holding in Meridian outside India in January 2026 for a large gain. Through the whole of the twelve months before that sale she held 4.1 per cent of Meridian's share capital, an enterprise associated with her held a further 0.6 per cent, and neither of them had any right of management or control over Meridian, or any right that could have given them one.

items.stem: Income from which of these is investment income taxable at 20 per cent under section 115E?

options.text: The Aravali shares, the Sarvottam debentures and the Kaveri Mills deposit
options.misconception: allows a private company's debenture, when the list admits a debenture only where the issuing Indian company is not a private company
options.why: Two of the four entries in section 115C(f) exclude a private company by name — debentures issued by an Indian company that is not a private company, and deposits with an Indian company that is not a private company. Sarvottam Traders is private, so its debentures are outside whatever currency bought them. The Kaveri Mills deposit is in because that company is public.

options.text: All four, since each is either a share, a debenture, a deposit or a Government security, which is the whole of the section 115C list
options.misconception: recites the list of specified assets without either qualifier — the public-company requirement on two entries, and the convertible foreign exchange the asset must be bought with
options.why: The list is closed and it carries qualifiers inside it. Two of its entries reach only a company that is not a private company, and every entry has to be paid for with convertible foreign exchange before it becomes a foreign exchange asset. Both qualifiers bite here, and each of them knocks out a different one of Mr Devan's four investments.

options.text: The Aravali shares and the Kaveri Mills deposit only
options.why: Shares in an Indian company are a specified asset with no public-company qualifier attached, and a deposit qualifies where the company is not a private one, so the Aravali shares and the Kaveri Mills deposit are both in — each was bought with convertible foreign exchange, which is what turns a specified asset into a foreign exchange asset. The Sarvottam debentures fail because the issuer is a private company. The Central Government securities fail on the other qualifier: they are a specified asset, but they were paid for out of rupees already in India rather than with convertible foreign exchange.
keywords: the issuer is a private company

options.text: The Aravali shares, the Kaveri Mills deposit and the Central Government securities
options.misconception: treats a Central Government security as inside Chapter XII-A however it was paid for, missing that the asset must be acquired in convertible foreign exchange
options.why: A security of the Central Government is on the list of specified assets, which is the trap — the entry is there and the reader stops. What section 115C(b) adds is that the asset must have been acquired, purchased or subscribed to with convertible foreign exchange before it becomes a foreign exchange asset. Rupees in a non-resident ordinary account are not that, so this holding sits outside the Chapter and its interest is taxed under the general provisions.

citation.ref: Sections 115C(a), 115C(b), 115C(e) and 115C(f), read with Section 115E

items.scenario: Mr Devan is a citizen of India who has lived in Oman for eleven years and is a non-resident for previous year 2025-26. He holds four investments and each has thrown off income this year. He bought shares in Aravali Ltd, a listed Indian company, with dollars remitted from Oman. He bought debentures issued by Sarvottam Traders Pvt Ltd, an Indian private company, also with remitted dollars. He placed a fixed deposit with Kaveri Mills Ltd, an Indian public company, again with remitted dollars. And he bought Central Government securities using rupees already lying in his ordinary non-resident rupee account in India.

items.stem: How is her income charged?

options.text: The ₹6,00,000 at 20 per cent with no deduction for the ₹25,000, the ₹4,00,000 at 12.5 per cent, the rent at ordinary rates, and the Chapter VI-A deduction allowed only against the ₹5,00,000 of rent
options.why: Section 115E splits the charge three ways — 20 per cent on investment income from a foreign exchange asset, 12.5 per cent on a long-term gain from such an asset, and ordinary rates on everything else — with surcharge if it applies and cess at 4 per cent on top. Section 115D(1) refuses any expenditure or allowance against the investment income, so the ₹25,000 collection charge is simply lost. Section 115D(2) then confines the Chapter VI-A deduction to the part of her gross total income that is neither investment income nor such a long-term gain, which here is the rent alone.
keywords: 20 per cent on investment income from a foreign exchange asset
refuses any expenditure or allowance against the investment income
neither investment income nor such a long-term gain

options.text: The ₹6,00,000 and the ₹4,00,000 both at 20 per cent, the rent at ordinary rates, and the Chapter VI-A deduction allowed only against the rent
options.misconception: carries the 20 per cent across to the long-term capital gain, which section 115E charges at its own rate
options.why: Section 115E gives the two limbs two different rates on purpose. Investment income bears 20 per cent; a long-term capital gain on the transfer of a specified asset bought in foreign currency bears 12.5 per cent. Treating them alike overtaxes the gain by 7.5 percentage points.

options.text: The ₹6,00,000 at 20 per cent after deducting the ₹25,000 collection charge, the ₹4,00,000 at 12.5 per cent, and the Chapter VI-A deduction allowed against her whole gross total income
options.misconception: computes investment income on a net footing and spreads the Chapter VI-A deduction over the whole of the gross total income
options.why: Both halves of this go wrong in the same direction. Section 115D(1) lets nothing at all be set against a non-resident Indian's investment income — no expenditure, no allowance, and no provision anywhere in the Act that might have let one in — which is what a gross basis means in practice. And section 115D(2) restricts the Chapter VI-A deduction to the slice of gross total income that carries neither kind of Chapter XII-A income, so it cannot be set against the dividend or the gain.

options.text: Everything at ordinary slab rates, because Chapter XII-A only fixes rates where the taxpayer has no income outside it
options.misconception: treats Chapter XII-A as switching off the moment other income appears, when the Chapter charges its own two limbs and leaves the rest to the general provisions
options.why: Other income does not displace the Chapter; section 115E provides for it in terms, by charging the balance of the total income at the rates that would otherwise apply. What having other income does change is section 115D(2): the Chapter VI-A deduction, denied altogether where the gross total income is nothing but Chapter XII-A income, becomes available against that other slice.

citation.ref: Sections 115D(1), 115D(2) and 115E

items.scenario: Ms Anjali is a non-resident Indian for previous year 2025-26 and has not opted out of Chapter XII-A. Her gross total income is made up of dividend of ₹6,00,000 on shares of an Indian company she had bought with convertible foreign exchange; a long-term capital gain of ₹4,00,000 on the sale of some of those same shares; and rent of ₹5,00,000 from a house property in Pune. She spent ₹25,000 on collection charges relating to the dividend and has paid ₹1,50,000 into an eligible savings scheme for which she wants a deduction under Chapter VI-A.

items.stem: How much of the ₹9,00,000 long-term capital gain escapes charge under section 115F?

options.text: ₹6,00,000, being ₹9,00,000 multiplied by the ₹10,00,000 cost of the new asset over the ₹15,00,000 net consideration
options.why: Net consideration is the ₹15,50,000 received less the ₹50,000 spent wholly and exclusively on the transfer, so ₹15,00,000, and the gain is ₹15,50,000 less ₹50,000 less the ₹6,00,000 cost, so ₹9,00,000. The new asset cost less than the net consideration, so the exempt slice is the gain multiplied by the cost of the new asset over the net consideration — ₹9,00,000 times ₹10,00,000 over ₹15,00,000, which is ₹6,00,000. The remaining ₹3,00,000 is charged. The 20 January purchase is inside six months of the 10 August sale, so the relief is open to him at all.
keywords: Net consideration is the ₹15,50,000 received less the ₹50,000
cost of the new asset over the net consideration

options.text: The whole ₹9,00,000, since the ₹10,00,000 he reinvested is more than the capital gain itself
options.misconception: measures the new investment against the capital gain, the way section 54EC does, when section 115F measures it against the net consideration
options.why: This is the comparison section 115F does not make. Sections that measure a new investment against the gain do exist and this is not one of them: here the cost of the new asset is set against the net consideration, so full exemption needs ₹15,00,000 to go back in, not ₹9,00,000. Beating the gain is not enough.

options.text: ₹3,00,000, the gain being reduced in the proportion that the ₹5,00,000 he did not reinvest bears to the ₹15,00,000 net consideration
options.misconception: applies the section 115F fraction upside down, exempting the reinvested proportion's mirror image instead of the reinvested proportion itself
options.why: The fraction is the right one turned over. Section 115F exempts the gain multiplied by the cost of the new asset over the net consideration — the part that went back in, not the part that stayed out. Reinvesting two thirds of the net consideration exempts two thirds of the gain, ₹6,00,000, and leaves ₹3,00,000 in charge. This option has the two figures the wrong way round.

options.text: Nothing, because he put the money into shares of an Indian company and shares are not a specified asset for this purpose
options.misconception: forgets that shares in an Indian company head the list of specified assets in section 115C
options.why: Shares in an Indian company are the first entry on the list of specified assets, and they are the one entry with no public-company qualifier on it. What the new asset does have to be is a specified asset bought inside six months of the transfer, and his purchase is both.

citation.ref: Section 115F(1), read with Section 115C(b) and Section 115C(f)

items.scenario: Mr Farid, a non-resident Indian, sells listed shares of an Indian company on 10 August 2025 for ₹15,50,000. He had bought them in convertible foreign exchange several years earlier and they cost him ₹6,00,000; brokerage and other expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively on this sale came to ₹50,000. The gain is long-term. On 20 January 2026 he puts ₹10,00,000 into shares of another Indian company. The rupee figures given are those arrived at after any adjustment the first proviso to section 48 requires, so no further currency working is needed.

items.stem: What follows from the sale of the new asset?

options.text: Nothing is disturbed, because the three-year period runs from the transfer of the original asset and more than three years had passed by 5 October 2028
options.misconception: starts the three-year clock at the transfer of the original asset, when section 115F(2) starts it at the acquisition of the new one
options.why: The clock is fixed to the wrong event. Section 115F(2) runs its three years from the date the new asset was acquired, which is 20 January 2026, so the period closes on 19 January 2029. Selling on 5 October 2028 is inside it. Counting from the original transfer would shorten the holding the section actually asks for, and here it flips the answer.

options.text: The ₹6,00,000 becomes chargeable as long-term capital gain in the previous year in which the new asset is transferred, and the ₹1,20,000 gain on the new asset is charged in that same year on its own footing
options.why: The new asset went inside three years of its acquisition, so section 115F(2) brings the relief back. What comes back is deemed to be income under the head Capital Gains relating to a long-term capital asset, and it is charged in the previous year in which the new asset is transferred or converted into money — previous year 2028-29 here, not the year the relief was first allowed. The ₹1,20,000 earned on the new asset itself is a separate gain of that same year, short-term because the asset was held for 32 months.
