keywords: inside three years of its acquisition
Capital Gains relating to a long-term capital asset
not the year the relief was first allowed

options.text: The assessment for A.Y. 2026-27 is reopened and the ₹6,00,000 is brought to charge in that year, since that is the year the gain actually arose
options.misconception: withdraws the relief by reopening the year it was allowed, when the section charges the amount in the later year instead
options.why: No earlier year is touched. Section 115F(2) is written as a fresh charge rather than as a withdrawal: whatever was kept out of charge back then turns into income of the later previous year, the one in which the new asset goes. That design is deliberate, because it needs no reassessment machinery and no reopening of a completed year to work.

options.text: The ₹6,00,000 comes back as short-term capital gain, since the new asset was held for less than three years
options.misconception: takes the character of the revived amount from how long the new asset was held, when the section fixes it as relating to a long-term capital asset
options.why: How long the new asset was held decides two things — whether the relief is withdrawn at all, and the character of the gain on the new asset itself, which is short-term here. It does not decide the character of the revived amount. Section 115F(2) says that amount is income under Capital Gains relating to a long-term capital asset, which is what the original gain was.

citation.ref: Section 115F(2)

items.scenario: In her return for A.Y. 2026-27 Ms Gauri, a non-resident Indian, kept ₹6,00,000 of long-term capital gain out of charge under section 115F. The original foreign exchange asset was transferred on 10 August 2025 and the new specified asset was acquired on 20 January 2026. She sells that new asset on 5 October 2028 — 32 months after acquiring it, and rather more than three years after the original transfer — making a further gain of ₹1,20,000 on it.

items.stem: What does that declaration achieve?

options.text: Chapter XII-A goes on applying to the investment income from the debentures, and to that income alone, for A.Y. 2027-28 and every later year until those debentures are transferred or converted into money
options.why: Section 115H carries forward less than the Chapter covered while he was a non-resident, and the list in it is the whole answer: the investment income it protects is that from foreign exchange assets being debentures, deposits, Central Government securities and other notified assets. Shares are absent from that list even though they head the list of specified assets in section 115C, so the dividend on his shares falls under the general provisions from A.Y. 2027-28. The protection then runs on year after year until the asset is transferred or converted into money.
keywords: debentures, deposits, Central Government securities and other notified assets
Shares are absent from that list
until the asset is transferred or converted into money

options.text: Chapter XII-A goes on applying to the investment income from both holdings and to any long-term capital gain he makes on either of them
options.misconception: extends section 115H to long-term capital gains, when the declaration reaches investment income only
options.why: Section 115H speaks of investment income derived from the listed foreign exchange assets and nothing else. A long-term capital gain is the Chapter's other limb, charged separately by section 115E, and the declaration does not carry it forward. Once he is a resident, a gain on either holding is computed and charged under the general provisions.

options.text: Nothing, because the declaration had to be filed in the last year in which he was a non-resident, not in the first year in which he is assessed as a resident
options.misconception: puts the declaration in the wrong year, when the section asks for it with the return for the year he first becomes assessable as a resident
options.why: The timing in the section is the other way about. The declaration goes in writing along with the return under section 139 for the assessment year in which he becomes assessable as a resident — A.Y. 2027-28 for Mr Hemant. Filing it in a year in which he was still a non-resident would ask for the continuance of something that was already applying to him.

options.text: Chapter XII-A goes on applying to the income from both holdings, since both are foreign exchange assets and the section preserves the treatment of foreign exchange assets
options.misconception: assumes section 115H carries forward every specified asset, when its own list leaves shares out
options.why: The two lists are not the same and that is the point of the question. Section 115C(f) admits shares in an Indian company first of all; section 115H names debentures, deposits, Central Government securities and other notified assets and stops. An asset that was inside the Chapter while he was non-resident can therefore drop out of it the year he becomes resident.

citation.ref: Section 115H, read with Sections 115C(f) and 139

items.scenario: Mr Hemant returned to India for good in June 2026 and is assessable as a resident for the first time in A.Y. 2027-28. He continues to hold two foreign exchange assets bought years ago with convertible foreign exchange — shares in a listed Indian company, and debentures of another listed Indian company. Both throw off income every year. Along with his return for A.Y. 2027-28 he files a declaration in writing asking that Chapter XII-A go on applying to him.

items.stem: What must he do to get it?

options.text: File the declaration under section 115-I, understanding that it takes him out of Chapter XII-A for that year and for every year afterwards as well
options.misconception: treats the section 115-I election as permanent, when it is made for one assessment year at a time
options.why: The election is annual. Section 115-I lets a non-resident Indian elect that the Chapter shall not govern him for any particular assessment year, by a declaration in the return for that year, and it binds nothing beyond the year it names. He may sit inside the Chapter next year and outside it the year after, as the arithmetic of each year decides.

options.text: Nothing can be done for A.Y. 2026-27, because section 115G removes his obligation to file a return and a person who need not file cannot claim a deduction
options.misconception: reads section 115G's excuse from filing as a bar on filing, when it only lifts the obligation
options.why: Section 115G lifts an obligation; it does not take away a right. It says a non-resident Indian need not furnish a return under section 139(1) where his income is only of these kinds and tax has been deducted from it. Nothing in it stops him filing one, and section 115-I positively requires a return as the vehicle for opting out.

options.text: Claim the Chapter VI-A deduction in a return filed under section 139 while remaining within Chapter XII-A, since a deduction and a special rate are separate questions
options.misconception: assumes Chapter VI-A survives inside Chapter XII-A, when section 115D(2) denies it where the gross total income holds nothing but these two kinds of income
options.why: Section 115D(2) shuts the deduction out. Where a non-resident Indian's gross total income consists only of investment income or such a long-term capital gain or both, no deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowed at all, and Mr Imran's income is exactly that. The deduction becomes reachable only if he leaves the Chapter.

options.text: File a return for A.Y. 2026-27 under section 139 and say in it that he wants Chapter XII-A kept off that year, after which his total income for that year is charged under the general provisions and the deduction is available
options.why: Section 115-I is the door out and the return itself is what opens it. He files for the assessment year and says in it that he wants Chapter XII-A kept off that year; his total income is then computed and charged under the general provisions of the Act, which is what lets the Chapter VI-A deduction in. Section 115G would otherwise have excused him from filing at all, since his income is only of the two kinds the Chapter deals with and tax has been deducted from it; choosing to opt out means choosing to file.
keywords: says in it that he wants Chapter XII-A kept off that year
charged under the general provisions of the Act
excused him from filing at all

citation.ref: Sections 115G, 115-I and 115D(2), read with Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Mr Imran is a non-resident Indian. For previous year 2025-26 his entire income is investment income of ₹8,00,000 from foreign exchange debentures of a listed Indian company and a long-term capital gain of ₹2,00,000 on foreign exchange shares he sold. Tax has been fully deducted at source from both. He has paid ₹1,50,000 into an eligible savings scheme and works out that a Chapter VI-A deduction for it would leave him better off than the Chapter XII-A rates do, so he wants the deduction and the refund that would follow.

items.stem: What does section 172 require, and on what amount?

options.text: No return arises under section 172 at all; the Indian charterer deducts tax under section 195 from the freight and that is the end of it
options.misconception: replaces the section 172 code with ordinary withholding, when the section is a complete code carrying its own return, assessment, collection and clearance
options.why: Section 172 is the complete code for the occasional voyage — it charges the income, takes a return, provides a summary assessment, fixes who pays and holds the ship at the port until the money is arranged. That is exactly what section 44B does not carry and what distinguishes the two provisions from one another.

options.text: The ship may not be given port clearance until the master personally files the return, the 30-day extension being available only where the ship has no cargo to declare
options.misconception: makes the master the only possible filer, when the section lets an authorised person file within 30 days on the Assessing Officer's satisfaction
options.why: The master is the person the obligation sits on and he is not the only person who may discharge it. The section provides in terms for a return by a person authorised by the master within 30 days of departure, on the two conditions that are met here, and it exists because a ship on a tide cannot wait for paperwork.

options.text: 7.5 per cent of ₹80,00,000 is deemed to accrue, the demurrage being compensation for delay rather than an amount paid for carriage
options.misconception: leaves demurrage out of the base, which section 172(8) expressly draws in
options.why: Demurrage does read as compensation rather than freight, which is why the sub-section had to say so. Section 172(8) sweeps demurrage into the chargeable sum, and handling with it, along with any other charge of that kind whatever the invoice calls it. Leaving it out would let the base be shrunk by relabelling a line in the bill.

options.text: The agent may file the return within 30 days of the ship's departure; 7.5 per cent of ₹84,00,000 is deemed to accrue in India, and port clearance is withheld until the tax is paid or satisfactorily arranged for
options.why: The return is ordinarily the master's job before the ship sails, but a person the master authorises may file it within 30 days of departure where the Assessing Officer is satisfied the master could not have filed in time and satisfactory arrangements for filing and paying have been made — both of which hold here. The demurrage joins the freight, because section 172(8) draws in demurrage, handling charges and anything of a similar nature, so the base is ₹84,00,000 and 7.5 per cent of it is deemed to accrue. And the Collector of Customs will not grant port clearance until satisfied that the tax has been paid or arranged.
keywords: demurrage, handling charges and anything of a similar nature

items.scenario: The Estrella Bay, a ship owned by a non-resident company that has no other Indian business, loads a single cargo at Kandla port. ₹80,00,000 is payable for the carriage, of which ₹4,00,000 is demurrage. The ship is due to sail on a tide that leaves the master no time to prepare the return before departure, and the master has arranged for the company's Indian shipping agent to file it and pay the tax; the Assessing Officer accepts that the master could not have filed before the ship left.

items.stem: What may he do about the difference?

options.text: Claim a refund by filing a rectification application, since paying at the foreign company rate when he is an individual is a mistake apparent from the record
options.misconception: reaches for rectification, when the higher rate was correct for the summary assessment and section 172(7) provides the route to a regular one
options.why: Nothing was mistaken. Section 172(4) requires the tax on the deemed income to be calculated at the rate in force for a foreign company, whoever the owner is, so the summary assessment was right on its own terms. The relief is not correction of an error but an election for a different kind of assessment, which is what section 172(7) provides.

options.text: Claim the regular assessment at any time within four years, the section fixing no earlier outer limit for an election of this kind
options.misconception: invents a four-year window, when the option shuts once the assessment year for the year of departure has run out
options.why: The window is short and the sub-section writes it in. What it gives him is the whole of the assessment year that goes with the previous year his ship sailed in, and no more. December 2025 sits in previous year 2025-26, whose assessment year ends on 31 March 2027, so an election made after that date reaches nothing.

options.text: Claim, while the assessment year for previous year 2025-26 is still running, to be assessed on his total income for that previous year under the ordinary provisions; what he paid is then treated as tax paid in advance and the difference is refunded
options.why: Section 172(7) lets the owner or charterer make that claim while the assessment year for the previous year of departure is still running — a sailing on 12 December 2025 falls in previous year 2025-26, so the door stays open through A.Y. 2026-27 and shuts on 31 March 2027. A regular assessment then follows, the money already paid under the summary route is treated as tax paid in advance for that assessment year, and the difference is either paid by him or refunded to him. A refund is the likely direction here precisely because an individual's rates sit below the foreign company rate the summary assessment used.
keywords: while the assessment year for the previous year of departure is still running
treated as tax paid in advance
either paid by him or refunded to him

options.text: Nothing; the summary assessment is final once the tax is paid and the ship has been cleared to sail
options.misconception: treats the summary assessment as conclusive, when section 172(7) lets the owner or charterer ask for a regular assessment instead
options.why: It is not final and the Supreme Court said so in A.S. Glittre v. CIT, describing the summary assessment as an ad hoc one that a regular assessment supersedes if the owner opts for it. Section 172(7) gives him that option in terms, and the whole point of it is the case he is in — a non-corporate non-resident taxed provisionally at the higher foreign company rate.

citation.ref: Sections 172(4) and 172(7), read with Section 44B; A.S. Glittre v. CIT (1997) 225 ITR 739 (SC)

items.scenario: Mr Nakamura is a non-resident individual who owns a small cargo vessel. It called at Chennai once during previous year 2025-26, departing on 12 December 2025, and tax was assessed and paid under the summary procedure at the rate in force for a foreign company. Across the whole of previous year 2025-26 his Indian shipping receipts are modest and, computed under section 44B and taxed at the rates that apply to him as an individual, the liability would be appreciably less than what he has already paid.

items.stem: What is its business income under section 44BBC?

options.text: ₹6 crore, its audited profit, since it keeps books under section 44AA(2) and has had them audited under section 44AB
options.misconception: borrows the lower-profits option that sections 44BB and 44BBB give and section 44BBC does not
options.why: Keeping and auditing books buys nothing under this section. The option to claim a lower figure than the presumptive one, with an assessment under section 143(3) to follow, belongs to sections 44BB and 44BBB. Section 44BBC is written without it, and it also refuses any set-off of unabsorbed depreciation or brought-forward loss for a year in which the deemed 20 per cent is declared.

options.text: ₹4.05 crore, being 7.5 per cent of ₹54 crore
options.misconception: applies section 44B's shipping rate to a cruise ship, which section 44B now expressly stands aside for
options.why: Section 44B once covered every ship and now covers every ship other than a cruise ship referred to in section 44BBC. The two rates are far apart — 7.5 per cent against 20 per cent — so reading a cruise operator into the older section understates its income by more than half.

options.text: ₹10 crore, being 20 per cent of the ₹50 crore paid or payable to it, the ₹4 crore collected by the agent lying outside the aggregate
options.misconception: counts only the first limb of the aggregate, dropping what is received in India on the assessee's behalf
options.why: The section adds two amounts, not one. The first is what is paid or payable to the assessee or to anyone on his behalf for carrying passengers; the second is what is received or deemed to be received by him or on his behalf on the same account. The agent's ₹4 crore answers the second limb squarely, so the aggregate is ₹54 crore.

options.text: ₹10.8 crore, being 20 per cent of ₹54 crore, and it may not offer its audited ₹6 crore instead
options.why: Both limbs count — ₹50 crore paid or payable to it and ₹4 crore received in India on its behalf — so the aggregate is ₹54 crore and one fifth of that is the deemed income. What makes the audited figure irrelevant is that section 44BBC carries no option to declare lower profits on audited books. Sections 44BB and 44BBB do carry one; this section does not, so the presumptive figure is the whole computation whichever way the accounts fall.
keywords: no option to declare lower profits on audited books
the presumptive figure is the whole computation

citation.ref: Section 44BBC, read with Sections 44B, 44BB(3) and 44BBB

items.scenario: Azure Voyages Ltd is a non-resident that runs one cruise ship on a scheduled Indian itinerary and satisfies every condition Rule 6GB lays down. For previous year 2025-26, ₹50 crore is paid or payable to it for carrying passengers, and a further ₹4 crore is received in India on its behalf by its Indian booking agent, again for carrying passengers. Its books, which are audited, show an actual operating profit on the Indian itinerary of ₹6 crore.

items.stem: How is that ₹9 crore treated in Coral Charter's hands?

options.text: Taxable, because the exemption reaches only a lease between a holding company and its own subsidiary, and these two companies are merely each other's fellow subsidiaries
options.misconception: requires a direct holding-and-subsidiary relation between lessor and lessee, when the section asks that both be subsidiaries of the same holding company
options.why: The relation the section asks for is the one these two have. It requires the foreign company and the specified company to be subsidiaries of the same holding company, which is what Coral Charter and Azure Voyages are under Pelagic Group. A parent leasing to its own subsidiary would be a different arrangement, and it is not the one the provision describes.

options.text: Exempt under section 10(15B), and the exemption carries on indefinitely because the section fixes no end to it
options.misconception: drops the sunset, when the exemption reaches only an assessment year up to A.Y. 2030-31
options.why: The relief has an end written into it. It reaches income received or accruing for an assessment year up to A.Y. 2030-31, which makes it a temporary encouragement to bring cruise tonnage to Indian ports rather than a permanent feature of the Act.

options.text: Exempt under section 10(15B), the two companies being subsidiaries of one holding company and the lessee being a specified company that has opted into section 44BBC — an exemption that runs up to A.Y. 2030-31
options.why: Section 10(15B) exempts income of a foreign company from lease rentals of cruise ships, by whatever name they go, received from a specified company that operates such ships in India. A specified company is one other than a domestic company that runs cruise ships in India and has opted into section 44BBC, which Azure Voyages has. The condition that both be subsidiaries of the same holding company is met through Pelagic Group, and the relief is time-limited: it is available up to A.Y. 2030-31 and not beyond.
keywords: lease rentals of cruise ships, by whatever name they go

options.text: Taxable as royalty, since a payment for the use of equipment made by an Indian operation to a foreign company is royalty and bears tax at the section 115A rate
options.misconception: routes cruise lease rental through the royalty machinery, when section 10(15B) takes this income out of total income altogether
options.why: An exemption under section 10 comes first: income that does not form part of total income is not reached by a charging or rate provision at all. Section 10(15B) was inserted alongside section 44BBC precisely so that the leasing half of a cruise operation would not be taxed while the operating half sits on a presumptive rate.

citation.ref: Section 10(15B), read with Section 44BBC

items.scenario: Coral Charter Ltd and Azure Voyages Ltd are both foreign companies and both are subsidiaries of Pelagic Group Ltd, which controls more than half of the share capital of each. Coral Charter owns a cruise ship and leases it to Azure Voyages, which operates it in India and has opted to pay tax under section 44BBC. Azure Voyages pays Coral Charter ₹9 crore of lease rental for previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: How should the committee deduct on the two sets of payments?

options.text: 20 per cent under section 194E on the ₹40,00,000 of prize money only, the advertisement fee and the column being ordinary professional income under section 195; and section 195 on Mr Petersen's fee
options.misconception: confines section 115BBA to money earned by playing, when the section names advertisement and written contributions in its own clauses
options.why: Section 115BBA lists three sources for a sportsman, not one. Beside participation in a game or sport in India it names advertisement, and contribution of articles relating to a game or sport in India to newspapers, magazines or journals. All three are inside, which is why an endorsement fee earned by a visiting player bears the same 20 per cent as his match fee.

options.text: 20 per cent under section 194E on all ₹49,00,000 paid to Mr Okonkwo, and 20 per cent under section 194E on Mr Petersen's fee as well, since he too is a non-resident engaged for the same matches
options.misconception: puts a match referee inside section 115BBA because he is at the ground, which the Indcom decision refused
options.why: Being engaged for the matches is not the test. Section 194E deducts only from income referred to in section 115BBA, and that section reaches a sportsman including an athlete, a sports association or institution, and an entertainer. Indcom v. CIT held that umpires and match referees render professional or technical services and are none of those three, so the deduction falls to section 195 instead.

options.text: 20 per cent under section 194E on all ₹49,00,000 paid to Mr Okonkwo; and on Mr Petersen's fee, tax under section 195 at the rates in force, because a match referee is not a sportsman
options.why: All three of Mr Okonkwo's receipts are named in section 115BBA — participation in a game in India, an advertisement, and a contribution of articles about a game to a newspaper — so section 194E deducts 20 per cent from each, with cess on top because he is a non-resident. Mr Petersen is the edge the Calcutta High Court settled in Indcom: a match referee is a professional or technical person rather than a sportsman, so section 115BBA and with it section 194E do not reach him. His fee is still income accruing in India, and tax on it is deducted under section 195 at the rates in force.
keywords: participation in a game in India, an advertisement, and a contribution of articles
a professional or technical person rather than a sportsman
deducted under section 195 at the rates in force

options.text: 20 per cent under section 194E on all ₹49,00,000 paid to Mr Okonkwo, and nothing on Mr Petersen's fee, since income outside section 115BBA is outside the Indian net altogether
options.misconception: reads the Indcom decision as making a referee's fee untaxable, when it only moves it out of section 115BBA and into the general provisions
options.why: The decision moved the fee, it did not exempt it. The Calcutta High Court accepted that payments to non-resident match referees are income which has accrued and arisen in India; what it held was that such income is not taxable under section 115BBA. Ordinary rates and section 195 apply to it instead.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBA(1)(a) and 194E, read with Section 195; Indcom v. CIT (TDS) (2011) 335 ITR 485 (Cal)

items.scenario: A tournament in India is run by an Indian organising committee. It pays Mr Okonkwo, a non-resident footballer who is not an Indian citizen, ₹40,00,000 of prize money for playing, ₹8,00,000 for appearing in a sponsor's television advertisement and ₹1,00,000 for a column he wrote about the tournament in an Indian newspaper. It also pays ₹6,00,000 to Mr Petersen, a non-resident who is not an Indian citizen, for officiating at the same matches as a match referee. The committee asks how much to deduct from each.

items.stem: How is the ₹90,00,000 taxed, and must the committee deduct anything from it?

options.text: The ₹90,00,000 is taxable but at the rates in force under section 195, since section 115BBA reaches individual sportsmen and entertainers and not an association
options.misconception: leaves a sports association out of section 115BBA, which names one in a clause of its own
options.why: The section has three limbs and an association is the middle one. Clause (b) of section 115BBA(1) reaches a guarantee given to a sports association or institution that is non-resident, where what the guarantee relates to is a game or sport played here; it sits beside the limb for a sportsman who is neither resident nor an Indian citizen and the limb for an entertainer in the same position. So the 20 per cent charge and the section 194E deduction both apply.

options.text: The whole ₹90,00,000 is charged at 20 per cent with no deduction for the tour costs, and the committee must deduct 20 per cent under section 194E even though it paid abroad
options.why: Section 115BBA(1)(b) charges any amount guaranteed to be paid to a non-resident sports association in relation to a game or sport played in India, and section 115BBA(2) refuses any expenditure or allowance against it, so the ₹30,00,000 is lost and the full sum bears 20 per cent plus cess. Where the money was routed makes no difference: PILCOM decided that guarantee money paid abroad for matches played here is Indian income and that section 194E bites on the payer. Since tax has been deducted and this is the Board's only Indian income, it need not furnish a return under section 139(1).
keywords: guaranteed to be paid to a non-resident sports association
refuses any expenditure or allowance against it
guarantee money paid abroad for matches played here

options.text: ₹60,00,000 is charged at 20 per cent, the tour costs being deductible against the guarantee money, and the committee deducts under section 194E on that net figure
options.misconception: allows the tour costs against the receipt, when section 115BBA(2) refuses any expenditure or allowance under any provision of the Act
options.why: Nothing may be set against it. Section 115BBA(2) shuts out every expenditure and every allowance in computing this income, whichever provision of the Act might otherwise have carried one, so the ₹30,00,000 of travel and accommodation simply does not enter the computation. The whole ₹90,00,000 is charged and the whole ₹90,00,000 bears the deduction.

options.text: Nothing is taxable in India and nothing is deductible, because the payer paid from an overseas account into an overseas account and no money entered India
options.misconception: locates the income by where the money moved, when the source is the playing of the matches in India
options.why: This is the argument the Supreme Court rejected in PILCOM. Guarantee money was paid from a London account to the boards of countries whose teams came and played here, and the Court held that the source of the income was the playing of the matches in India and that the payer was liable to deduct under section 194E. The phrase in section 115BBA(1)(b) that does the work is "in relation to" a game or sport played in India.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBA(1)(b), 115BBA(2) and 115BBA(3) and Section 194E; PILCOM v. CIT (2020) 425 ITR 312 (SC)

items.scenario: An Indian organising committee guarantees ₹90,00,000 to the Rovers Cricket Board, a non-resident sports association, for bringing its team to India to play a series of matches here. The committee holds an account abroad and pays the whole sum into the Board's own overseas account, so no part of the money passes through India. The Board spends ₹30,00,000 on travel and accommodation for the tour. The Board has no other Indian income.

items.stem: Are the two associated enterprises for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: No — Kestrel's holding is 18 per cent, which is short of the twenty-six per cent the section asks for, and the guarantee is not a shareholding
options.misconception: reads the voting-power limb as the whole of section 92A(2), when the guarantee is a limb of its own
options.why: The voting-power limb is one of thirteen and each of them stands alone. Kestrel does fail that one, which is exactly why the question is worth asking, and the guarantee limb is satisfied independently of it.

options.text: No — the guarantee was given to a bank outside the group, and a guarantee can only make two enterprises associated where it is given to one of them
options.misconception: looks at whom the guarantee was given to rather than whose borrowings it covers
options.why: The limb is about the borrower whose debt is being guaranteed, not about the identity of the lender. A guarantee is worth giving precisely because the lender is an outsider, and the section is written to catch that.

options.text: No — a guarantee brings the two inside the section only where it covers fifty-one per cent or more of the borrowings
options.misconception: carries the fifty-one per cent figure from the loan limb across to the guarantee limb
options.why: Fifty-one per cent belongs to a different limb — a loan advanced by one enterprise to the other worth fifty-one per cent or more of the book value of the borrower's total assets. The guarantee limb sets its threshold much lower, and measures it against borrowings rather than against assets.

options.text: Yes — the guarantee covers 15 per cent of Larkspur's borrowings, and that limb asks only for ten per cent or more
options.why: One enterprise guaranteeing ten per cent or more of the total borrowings of the other is a deeming limb in its own right, and ₹6 crore against ₹40 crore is 15 per cent. Any single limb is enough, so the failure of the voting-power test does not matter.

citation.ref: Section 92A(2), the limb on guaranteeing borrowings, read with the voting-power and loan limbs of the same sub-section

items.scenario: Kestrel Polymers Ltd, an Indian company, holds 18 per cent of the voting power in Larkspur BV, a Netherlands company. Larkspur holds nothing in Kestrel and the two have no directors in common. Larkspur has borrowed the equivalent of ₹40 crore from a European bank that is unconnected with either company, and Kestrel has given that bank a guarantee covering ₹6 crore of the borrowing. During previous year 2025-26 Kestrel sold moulds to Larkspur.

items.stem: Are Sundara and Halcyon associated enterprises?

options.text: No — an appointment cannot make two enterprises associated where the appointer holds no capital in either of them
options.misconception: treats participation in capital under section 92A(1) as a condition every deeming limb must also meet
options.why: Section 92A(1)'s reference to management, control or capital is one route in, and section 92A(2) is a separate one that does not need it. Several of its limbs work with no shareholding anywhere — the raw-material limb and the intangibles limb do the same.

options.text: Yes, but only for the part of the year that ran from the day the second executive director took office
options.misconception: prorates a relationship the section makes annual, treating the deeming as switching on mid-year
options.why: Section 92A(2) asks whether the relationship existed at any time during the previous year. Once it did, the two are associated enterprises for that year, and the transactions of the year are examined on that footing rather than sliced by date.

options.text: Yes — one person appointing more than half of one board and at least one executive director of the other satisfies the limb
options.why: The limb is met where more than half the directors of one enterprise, or one or more of its executive directors, and the same for the other enterprise, are appointed by the same person or persons. Nine of fifteen is more than half on the Sundara side, and an executive director is enough on the Halcyon side.
keywords: one or more of its executive directors

options.text: No — the same person must appoint more than half the board of each of the two companies, and two of eleven is nowhere near half
options.misconception: demands the majority test on both sides, when the limb accepts an executive director on either
options.why: The limb offers two ways of satisfying it on each side, and an executive director is the second way. It is written that way because control follows an executive director in a way it does not follow an ordinary one.

citation.ref: Section 92A(2), the limb on the appointment of directors of two enterprises by the same person, read with Section 92A(1)

items.scenario: Mr Prakash Nadar appoints nine of the fifteen directors on the board of Sundara Ceramics Ltd. He also appoints two of the eleven directors on the board of Halcyon Trading Pte Ltd, Singapore, and both of the two are executive directors. He owns no shares in either company, neither company owns shares in the other, and the two traded with each other throughout previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: How is the sale from Vaayu to Mr Bhatia treated?

options.text: As an international transaction only if Vaayu's contract with Mr Bhatia came first and his contract with Meridian followed it
options.misconception: inverts the order the sub-section requires, when the agreement standing behind the outsider is the earlier one
options.why: The sub-section works on an agreement that was already there — between the outsider and the associated enterprise — when the enterprise dealt with him, which is why the dates here run 30 July and then 12 August. Reversing them would leave the enterprise selling into the open market with nothing behind it.

options.text: As a specified domestic transaction, both parties to it being residents, once such transactions in the year cross twenty crore rupees in the aggregate
options.misconception: routes a transaction the Act deems international into the domestic machinery because both immediate parties are residents
options.why: Section 92BA reaches a listed class of dealings between related domestic parties, chiefly those of an undertaking claiming a profit-linked deduction. A sale caught by section 92B(2) is deemed international, and the two sets of provisions are not alternatives to be chosen between.

options.text: As an international transaction between associated enterprises, because an agreement on that yarn was already in place between Mr Bhatia and Vaayu's associated enterprise
options.why: Meridian is an associated enterprise of Vaayu on the voting-power limb and is a non-resident. An agreement on that yarn was already in place between Mr Bhatia and Meridian when Vaayu sold to him, so the sale to Mr Bhatia is treated as an international transaction between associated enterprises and has to stand at an arm's length price.
keywords: already in place between Mr Bhatia and Meridian
treated as an international transaction between associated enterprises

options.text: As a domestic sale outside Chapter X, because Mr Bhatia is a resident and is not an associated enterprise of Vaayu
options.misconception: tests the residence of the unrelated party, which the sub-section says makes no difference
options.why: Section 92B(2) settles this in terms — the deeming works whether or not the other person is a non-resident. Mr Bhatia's residence is the one fact the sub-section tells you to put aside.

citation.ref: Section 92B(2) read with the voting-power limb of Section 92A(2)

items.scenario: Vaayu Textiles Ltd, an Indian company, agreed on 12 August 2025 to sell 200 tonnes of specialty yarn to Mr Suresh Bhatia, a trader resident in India who is unconnected with the Vaayu group. On 30 July 2025 Mr Bhatia had already agreed to sell that same yarn onward to Meridian Fabrics Ltd, a Mauritius company holding 31 per cent of the voting power in Vaayu. Vaayu says the sale it made was a domestic one between two Indian residents.

items.stem: Is the reorganisation an international transaction?

options.text: Yes, but only from the year in which the arrangement first shows in Ravinder's profits or in the value of its assets
options.misconception: defers the transaction to the year an effect surfaces, when the definition refuses to wait for one
options.why: Waiting for an effect is the one thing this head rules out. It reaches the arrangement when it is entered into, and deferring it would leave the two enterprises choosing the year in which their reorganisation gets examined.

options.text: Yes — a reorganisation agreed with an associated enterprise is inside the definition even where it moves nothing in the accounts, then or later
options.why: The scope of an international transaction takes in a business reorganisation or restructuring agreed with an associated enterprise, and it does so even where it moves nothing in the accounts, then or later. Ravinder's flat figures therefore settle nothing, and the arrangement has to stand at an arm's length price.
keywords: a business reorganisation or restructuring agreed with an associated enterprise
even where it moves nothing in the accounts, then or later

options.text: No — only the sale, purchase or lease of property, the provision of services and the lending or borrowing of money are covered, and a reorganisation is none of them
options.misconception: reads the list of dealings as closed, missing both the reorganisation head and the catch-all beneath it
options.why: The list runs further than those four. Capital financing of any tenure sits in it, a reorganisation has a head of its own, and beneath them all is any other dealing bearing on the profits, the income, the losses or the assets of the enterprises.

options.text: No — nothing was paid for the contracts and the year's accounts show no effect on Ravinder's profits, so there is nothing for the machinery to price
options.misconception: makes an effect on profits a condition of the definition, when the reorganisation head is written to apply where there is none
options.why: A price of nothing is still a price, and the head covering reorganisations was written so that an arrangement showing no immediate effect cannot be argued out of the chapter. What the year's accounts show is not the test.

citation.ref: Section 92B(1) and the head of the scope of an international transaction covering a reorganisation agreed with an associated enterprise

items.scenario: Ravinder Auto Components Ltd is an Indian company whose Austrian parent, Steinweg AG, holds 62 per cent of its voting power. In March 2026 the two reorganised the group's sales arm: Ravinder gave up the distribution rights it had held for South Asia and handed its customer contracts to a newly formed Austrian entity, taking nothing for them. Ravinder's accounts for previous year 2025-26 show no gain, no loss and no movement in its assets from the arrangement, and its tax head says the reorganisation is therefore outside Chapter X.

items.stem: Which of the two has to be priced at arm's length under Chapter X?

options.text: Neither, because a branch is not a person separate from its own company and nobody can transact with himself
options.misconception: makes separate legal personality the condition, when the Act treats a non-resident's Indian permanent establishment as an enterprise for this purpose
options.why: The definition of an enterprise takes in a person together with a permanent establishment of his, which is what allows a branch to be one side of an international transaction. It has to, or a foreign company could set its own internal charges freely.

options.text: Only the payment by Corvus GmbH's Indian branch to its head office in Munich
options.why: The Indian branch is the permanent establishment of a non-resident and is taxed here on what it does here, while the head office is taxed in Germany, so the price charged decides how much profit stays in the Indian tax net. Trident's Dubai branch is part of an Indian resident, which puts its dealings with the head office between two residents.

options.text: Both of them, since each is a payment between two units of one enterprise across a border
options.misconception: reads any cross-border internal charge as an international transaction, missing that a resident's foreign branch is itself resident
options.why: A resident Indian company is resident for the whole of itself, branches included, so no profit can leave the Indian net by what its head office charges a foreign branch. There is nothing for the machinery to correct.

options.text: Only the charge from Trident's Mumbai head office to its Dubai branch
options.misconception: treats the crossing of a national border as the test, when the test is whether either side is a non-resident
options.why: The border is crossed in both cases and that settles nothing. Trident is resident in India and so are all its branches wherever they sit, so this charge runs between two residents and Chapter X does not reach it.

citation.ref: Section 92B read with Section 92F(iii) and Section 92(1)

items.scenario: Two charges are on the table for previous year 2025-26. First, Trident Alloys Ltd, a company resident in India, bills its own branch in Dubai ₹90 lakh for management and engineering support supplied from Mumbai. Second, the Indian branch of Corvus GmbH, a company resident in Germany, pays its head office in Munich ₹1.2 crore for the use of a design library. Neither company is connected with the other.

items.stem: Does Chapter X reach the purchase?

options.text: Only if this purchase and Aravali's other dealings with Zenobia together cross twenty crore rupees for the year
options.misconception: borrows the aggregate threshold that governs specified domestic transactions and applies it to an international one
options.why: Twenty crore rupees is the line for specified domestic transactions between related residents. An international transaction carries no such floor, so a single purchase of ₹3 crore is inside the chapter on its own.

options.text: Yes — the branch is the Indian company itself, and it has bought from a separate company resident abroad in which it holds 80 per cent of the voting power
options.why: A foreign branch of an Indian company is the Indian company, which is why the reasoning gets its first half right and its answer wrong. Zenobia is a non-resident associated enterprise on the voting-power limb, so the two sides are a resident and a non-resident and the purchase has to stand at an arm's length price.
keywords: a non-resident associated enterprise on the voting-power limb
the two sides are a resident and a non-resident

options.text: No — the Dubai branch counts as resident, so what it buys is bought between two residents
options.misconception: carries the rule that a resident's foreign branch is resident across to a counterparty that is a separate company abroad
options.why: Treating the branch as resident settles who the buyer is and says nothing about the seller. Zenobia is a company of its own, resident abroad, and one non-resident on either side is all the chapter asks for.

options.text: No — the goods never came to India and the branch pays tax in the United Arab Emirates on what it does there
options.misconception: makes the movement of the goods and the local tax on the branch the test, when the test is who the two parties are
options.why: Where the goods travelled does not enter the definition, and a foreign country taxing the branch does not put the profit out of India's reach — Aravali is taxed here on its global income, its Dubai branch included.

citation.ref: Section 92B read with the voting-power limb of Section 92A(2) and the residence rules in Section 6(3)

items.scenario: Aravali Steelworks Ltd is resident in India and runs a branch in Dubai. During previous year 2025-26 that branch bought ₹3 crore of finished bar stock from Zenobia Metals FZE, a company resident in the United Arab Emirates in which Aravali holds 80 per cent of the voting power. Aravali's tax head keeps the purchase out of the transfer pricing report, reasoning that a foreign branch of an Indian company counts as resident and that the branch is the buyer.

items.stem: What does the block scheme require before the determination can carry forward?

options.text: The option is open to any assessee, including one whose assessment for the year arises out of a search, so long as the transactions are similar
options.misconception: ignores the exclusion the sub-section makes for search assessments
options.why: Proceedings for the assessment of search cases are kept outside the scheme by the sub-section itself. A block determination assumes a settled, repeating transaction, which is the opposite of what a search proceeding is examining.

options.text: The option covers the two previous years immediately following, and the officer must declare it valid in writing within one month from the end of the month the option was exercised in
options.why: The scheme carries the price to a similar transaction for the two previous years immediately following, on an option exercised in the prescribed form, manner and period, and on the officer declaring it valid in writing within one month from the end of the month in which it was exercised. Search assessments are outside the scheme.
keywords: one month from the end of the month

options.text: Nothing beyond the option, because once it is exercised the earlier year's price simply applies and the officer determines nothing further
options.misconception: reads the block as freezing the earlier figure, when the officer still determines the price for both later years
options.why: What the assessee is spared is the reference and the separate proceeding. The officer still examines and determines the price for both following years in his order, and the Assessing Officer then recomputes the total income of those years under section 155(21).

options.text: The option covers the three following previous years, and it takes effect automatically unless the officer rejects it inside three months
options.misconception: stretches the block to three years and turns a positive declaration of validity into a deemed acceptance
options.why: The block is two following years, not three, and the officer's declaration is something he has to make rather than something that happens by his silence. A scheme built on inaction would leave nobody able to say whether an option had taken effect.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(3B) and Section 92CA(4A) read with Section 155(21), as inserted by the Finance Act, 2025

items.scenario: Ashram Forgings Ltd buys castings from its German parent every year on much the same terms. For previous year 2025-26 the Transfer Pricing Officer determined an arm's length price for that purchase in an order under section 92CA(3). The company wants that determination to cover the same purchase for the years ahead as well, and exercises an option in the prescribed form on 14 September 2026 for both of the following two years. It is not a search case.

items.stem: What follows for previous year 2026-27?

options.text: The option lapses for 2026-27, a year on which a reference is already pending being ineligible for the block
options.misconception: makes a pending reference a bar to the option, when the valid option is what disposes of the reference
options.why: The order of operations runs the other way. The declaration is what empties the reference of effect, and nothing makes a year ineligible because a reference happened to go out on it.

options.text: The earlier reference stands, the bar working only on references that go out after the declaration
options.misconception: reads the bar as forward-looking, when it is written to reach a reference already made
options.why: It is written to reach both — a reference sent before the declaration and one sent after it are treated the same way. Leaving the earlier one alive would run two proceedings on one purchase for one year.

options.text: The reference counts for nothing, and the Assessing Officer must reopen the assessment for 2026-27 to give the price effect
options.misconception: reaches for reassessment machinery when the Act names a recomputation route built for these years
options.why: The first half is right and the road is wrong. On receiving the officer's order the Assessing Officer recomputes the income for the two years under section 155(21), and reopening is a separate power with conditions of its own that the scheme does not use.

options.text: The earlier reference counts for nothing, the officer determines the price for both option years in his own order, and the Assessing Officer then recomputes the total income
options.why: Once a valid option stands, no reference is to be made for those years, and a reference made before the declaration or after it counts for nothing. The officer examines and determines the price for both option years in his own order, and on receiving it the Assessing Officer recomputes the total income for those years under section 155(21).
keywords: a reference made before the declaration or after it counts for nothing

citation.ref: The provisos to Section 92CA(1) and Section 92CA(4A), read with Section 92CA(3B) and Section 155(21)

items.scenario: Sundargarh Bearings Ltd exercised an option under the block scheme for previous years 2026-27 and 2027-28, resting on an arm's length price the Transfer Pricing Officer had determined for 2025-26 on the same recurring purchase from its parent. The officer declared the option valid by an order in writing on 20 October 2027. A fortnight before that order, the Assessing Officer had already made a reference on the same purchase for 2026-27, and he now asks what becomes of it.

items.stem: How long does the Transfer Pricing Officer have to pass his order?

options.text: Until the assessment's own limitation date, the sixty-day margin falling away once the delay was outside the officer's control
options.misconception: treats the sixty-day margin as the officer's own cushion, when it is the time reserved for the Assessing Officer to give effect to his order
options.why: The sixty days ahead of the limitation date exist so that the Assessing Officer can act on the order and frame the assessment. Letting the officer run into that margin would leave the assessment itself unfinishable, which is the mischief the sub-section addresses.

options.text: 60 days, because the period left to him after the exclusion is under sixty days and the section stretches it to sixty
options.why: Where a reference for exchange of information has been made under an agreement under section 90 or section 90A, or the proceedings are stayed by a court, and the time left to the officer after taking that period out is less than sixty days, the remaining period is stretched to sixty days. Twenty-two becomes sixty.
keywords: remaining period is stretched to sixty days

options.text: 22 days, the waiting period being excluded and nothing more being given
options.misconception: applies the exclusion and stops there, missing that the section restores a floor rather than merely pausing the clock
options.why: Excluding the waiting period is only the first step. Where what is left after that exclusion is under sixty days, the section stretches the remaining period to sixty days, so the officer is not left with a fragment.

options.text: 30 days, that being the extension the section allows once information has been sought from another country
options.misconception: invents a thirty-day extension, which belongs to the production of documents under section 92D(3) and not to the officer's own order
options.why: Thirty days is the outer limit of the extension for furnishing information asked for under section 92D(3), and it has nothing to do with the officer's own timetable. His floor is sixty days.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(3A) with its proviso, read with Section 153 and Section 90

items.scenario: A reference under section 92CA is pending before the Transfer Pricing Officer. Partway through, the competent authority sends a request for information to the treaty partner under an agreement made under section 90, and the answer takes several months to come back. When it arrives, the officer works out that after leaving the waiting period out of account he has 22 days left before the day sixty days ahead of the assessment's own limitation date.

items.stem: How long does he in fact have to pass his order?

options.text: Up to the assessment's own limitation date, the sixty-day margin ahead of it holding only where nothing has interrupted the proceedings
options.misconception: treats the margin reserved for the Assessing Officer as forfeited by the stay
options.why: That margin belongs to the assessment and not to the officer. It is left ahead of the limitation date so the Assessing Officer can act on the order and frame the assessment, and an interruption does not release the officer into it.

options.text: 60 days — a stay having intervened, the section gives him the sixty days it names in place of whatever was left
options.misconception: reads the floor as a fixed allowance that replaces the remaining period instead of propping it up
options.why: If sixty days replaced the remainder, an officer with most of a year still in hand would lose it the moment a stay was granted. A remainder above sixty days is simply left as it stands.

options.text: 155 days — the 95 left to him plus the sixty days the stay earns him
options.misconception: reads the sixty days as an extension granted for the delay rather than as the least he may be left with
options.why: Nothing in the sub-section adds a period to what the officer already holds. It names a least amount and raises a short remainder to it, so sixty days is a floor and never a bonus.

options.text: 95 days — the proviso lifts a short remainder up to sixty and adds nothing to one that is already longer
options.why: The proviso works only where what is left after taking out the stayed period is under sixty days, and it then lifts that short remainder up to sixty. Ninety-five days is already longer, so nothing is added and he has 95 days.
keywords: lifts that short remainder up to sixty
nothing is added and he has 95 days

citation.ref: The proviso to Section 92CA(3A), read with Section 153 and the stay of proceedings by a court

items.scenario: In another reference, a High Court stayed the assessment proceedings for five months. When the stay is vacated the Transfer Pricing Officer works out that, once the stayed months are taken out of account, 95 days are left to him before the day sixty days ahead of the assessment's own limitation date. He tells his colleague the stay has earned him a further sixty days on top of those 95.

items.stem: Is that conclusion right?

options.text: Yes — under one crore rupees in the aggregate, Rule 10D lifts the documentation requirement entirely
options.misconception: reads relief from the prescribed list as relief from the duty to substantiate the price
options.why: What the sub-rule lifts is the obligation to keep the listed information and documents. The assessee still has to be able to show that the income arising from those transactions accords with section 92, so records and evidence enough to prove that are still needed.

options.text: No — the prescribed list need not be kept, but the company must still be able to show that the income from those transactions accords with section 92, and its duty as a constituent entity is separate
options.why: Rule 10D(2) relieves an assessee whose international transactions do not exceed one crore rupees from keeping the listed information and documents, and no further. It must still be able to show that the income from those transactions accords with section 92. Section 92D(1) separately requires a constituent entity of an international group to keep prescribed information about the group whether or not it undertook any international transaction.
keywords: do not exceed one crore rupees
show that the income from those transactions accords with section 92
whether or not it undertook any international transaction

options.text: Yes for this year, the duty of a constituent entity arising only in a year in which it has actually entered into an international transaction
options.misconception: makes the group-level duty conditional on the entity having transacted, which is exactly the condition the section removes
options.why: The section says the opposite in terms: a constituent entity keeps and furnishes the prescribed group information whether or not it has undertaken any international transaction of its own. The duty is about the group, not about the entity's dealings.

options.text: No — the one crore threshold applies to each transaction separately, and the company crosses it because the transactions are aggregated only for the accountant's report
options.misconception: makes the threshold transaction-by-transaction, when the sub-rule measures the aggregate value
options.why: The sub-rule measures the aggregate value of the international transactions, so ₹85 lakh across all of them is under the line. The finance head has the threshold right; what he has wrong is what crossing or not crossing it does.

citation.ref: Rule 10D(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 read with Section 92D(1)

items.scenario: Ferrolite Components Pvt Ltd is a constituent entity of an international group. During previous year 2025-26 its own international transactions with associated enterprises came to ₹85 lakh in the aggregate. Its finance head reads Rule 10D(2), sees that the aggregate is under one crore rupees, and concludes that the company owes nothing at all by way of transfer pricing documentation for the year.

items.stem: What are the two answers?

options.text: Kept until the assessment for the year is complete and no appeal is pending, the rule setting no fixed period
options.misconception: replaces a fixed statutory period with a test tied to the progress of the proceedings
options.why: The rule fixes a period and it deliberately outlives the assessment, because a reassessment or an appellate order can send the officer back to the same file years later. Tying retention to the state of the proceedings would leave nobody able to say when the file could go.

options.text: Kept for six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, and in existence by the due date for the return
options.misconception: borrows the six-year period used elsewhere in the Act and puts the documents' deadline on the return's own due date
options.why: Transfer pricing documents run to eight years from the end of the relevant assessment year, longer than several other retention periods in the Act. And they had to exist by the specified date, which sits one month ahead of the return's due date rather than on it.

options.text: Kept for eight years from the end of the relevant assessment year, and in existence by 31 October 2026, one month before the due date for the return
options.why: Rule 10D(5) requires the information and documents to be kept for eight years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Rule 10D(4) requires them to be contemporaneous and to exist by the specified date, which is one month before the due date for the return under section 139(1) and falls on 31 October of the assessment year.
keywords: eight years from the end of the relevant assessment year
one month before the due date

options.text: Kept for eight years from the end of the previous year, and in existence by the date the Transfer Pricing Officer first calls for them
options.misconception: counts the eight years from the wrong year end and makes the papers' deadline the officer's notice, which is what contemporaneous documentation exists to prevent
options.why: The eight years run from the end of the assessment year, not of the previous year, which is a full twelve months' difference. And documents assembled after a notice arrives are not contemporaneous, which is the very thing the rule requires them to be.

citation.ref: Rule 10D(4) and Rule 10D(5) read with Section 92D(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the specified date one month before the Section 139(1) due date

items.scenario: Meghdoot Instruments Ltd keeps the full Rule 10D file for its international transactions of previous year 2025-26. Its records manager wants to know two things before setting a destruction date: how long the file has to be kept, and by when the papers in it had to be in existence. The company's return for the year is due on 30 November 2026.

items.stem: What penalty does the failure attract, and who may direct it?

options.text: Two per cent of the value of the international transaction, but only the Assessing Officer may direct it, the Transfer Pricing Officer's role ending with his order on the price
options.misconception: treats the Transfer Pricing Officer's authority as spent once he has determined the arm's length price
options.why: The measure is right and the authority is not. The section lists three officers who may direct the penalty and the Transfer Pricing Officer is one of them, which matters because it is usually his notice that went unanswered.

options.text: Nothing — the ten days can be stretched by a further thirty, and the papers went in on the thirty-fifth day
options.misconception: treats the further period as running on its own, when it is granted only on a request the assessee actually makes
options.why: The further period of up to thirty days is granted on an application, and this company made none, so the time open to it never went past ten days. A period that ran of its own accord would leave the ten-day limit saying nothing at all.

options.text: A fixed sum of ₹1,00,000, that being the figure every transfer pricing reporting default carries
options.misconception: carries the flat figure attached to the accountant's report across to a section that measures the penalty against the transaction
options.why: A flat one lakh rupees is the penalty for not furnishing the accountant's report, and that is a different default with a different section behind it. This one is measured against the size of the transaction, so it grows with what was at stake.

options.text: Two per cent of the value of the international transaction for the failure, and the Transfer Pricing Officer may direct it himself
options.why: Section 271G measures the penalty at two per cent of the value of the international transaction for each such failure, and it names the Assessing Officer, the Transfer Pricing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) as the authorities who may direct it. So the Transfer Pricing Officer may direct it himself.
keywords: two per cent of the value of the international transaction
the Transfer Pricing Officer may direct it himself

citation.ref: Section 271G read with Section 92D(3)

items.scenario: Fox Instruments Ltd was asked, by a notice under section 92D(3) issued at the Transfer Pricing Officer's instance, for information and documents relating to one international transaction worth ₹12 crore. It never applied for more time and put the papers in on the thirty-fifth day after the notice reached it.

items.stem: What penalties can follow?

options.text: ₹1,00,000 only, the documentation penalty needing a notice calling for the papers before it can be charged
options.misconception: collapses the penalty for keeping nothing into the separate penalty for not producing papers on a notice
options.why: A notice is what the other penalty waits for — the one for failing to produce information inside the ten days allowed. Keeping nothing at all is a failure on its own and does not wait for anybody to ask.

options.text: Nothing, the prices having been at arm's length and no addition having been made
options.misconception: measures a documentation penalty against the tax outcome, when it is measured against the transactions themselves
options.why: Both of these answer a failure to keep records and a failure to file a report, and neither asks whether the price was right. A company that priced everything correctly and kept nothing is exposed to both.

options.text: Two per cent of the value of each transaction only, the flat sum falling away once a documentation penalty is charged
options.misconception: reads the two as alternatives, when one is charged in addition to the other
options.why: They are not alternatives to choose between. The two failures are different — no records kept, and no report filed — and paying for one of them does not repair the other.

options.text: Two per cent of the value of each of the three transactions for keeping no documents, and ₹1,00,000 for the missing accountant's report, the first standing over and above the second
options.why: Keeping none of the prescribed information and documents draws two per cent of the value of each of the three transactions, so all three are charged. The flat ₹1,00,000 for not furnishing the accountant's report answers a separate failure, and the documentation penalty is charged over and above it rather than in its place.
keywords: two per cent of the value of each of the three transactions
charged over and above it rather than in its place

citation.ref: Section 271AA read with Sections 92D(1), 92D(2), 271BA and 273B

items.scenario: Karvir Speciality Chemicals Pvt Ltd had three international transactions with its Swiss parent during previous year 2025-26, worth ₹4 crore, ₹6 crore and ₹10 crore. It kept none of the information and documents the rules list for them, and it neither obtained nor furnished the accountant's report on them. When the transactions are examined the prices turn out to have been at arm's length and no adjustment is made anywhere.

items.stem: How does section 270A treat the two additions?

options.text: Both stay inside under-reported income and both draw two hundred per cent, a transfer pricing addition always being misreporting
options.misconception: treats every transfer pricing addition as misreporting, when misreporting is failing to report the transaction at all
options.why: Two hundred per cent is the misreporting rate, and what makes a transfer pricing case misreporting is failing to report the international transaction or a transaction deemed to be one. Both companies reported theirs; what was in dispute was the price.

options.text: Neither is under-reported income, the three steps both companies took taking any transfer pricing addition out of the charge
options.misconception: extends a carve-out written for an international transaction to a specified domestic one
options.why: The clause is drawn for an international transaction and goes no further. That gap is real and it is worth knowing about, because the same care that protects one company protects the other from nothing.

options.text: Both stay inside under-reported income, the relief being available only where the adjustment is accepted and the tax paid without appeal
options.misconception: confuses the carve-out from under-reporting with the separate immunity that has to be applied for after paying the tax
options.why: Paying the tax and giving up the appeal is the price of a different relief, applied for after the assessment. This one is not applied for at all — it works on how the income is computed, so the amount never becomes under-reported income to begin with.

options.text: Sarvatra's addition is not under-reported income; Nilaya's stays inside it and draws fifty per cent of the tax on it
options.why: Where the assessee kept the documents section 92D prescribes, declared the transaction and disclosed all material facts, an addition made in line with the price the Transfer Pricing Officer determined is left out of under-reported income. That relief is written for an international transaction only, so Nilaya's specified domestic transaction stays inside under-reported income and draws fifty per cent of the tax on it.
keywords: written for an international transaction only
fifty per cent of the tax on it

citation.ref: Section 270A(6)(d) read with Sections 270A(7), 270A(9) and 92D

items.scenario: Two adjustments were made for assessment year 2026-27, each in line with an arm's length price the Transfer Pricing Officer determined. The first is on Sarvatra Ltd, on an international transaction with its Dutch parent. The second is on Nilaya Ltd, on a specified domestic transaction between its tax-holiday unit and another of its own units. Both companies kept the information and documents section 92D prescribes, both declared the transaction, and both disclosed every material fact about it.

items.stem: How does section 270A treat the addition on the licence?

options.text: As misreporting, at two hundred per cent of the tax, because the transaction was never reported at all
options.why: Not reporting an international transaction, or one deemed to be an international transaction, is listed as misreporting, and misreported income is charged at two hundred per cent of the tax on it. The documents do not rescue the company: the relief for a transfer pricing addition also asks that the transaction was declared, and this one was not.
keywords: two hundred per cent of the tax on it
also asks that the transaction was declared

options.text: It is under-reported income at fifty per cent of the tax, that being the rate a transfer pricing addition carries
options.misconception: reaches for the ordinary under-reporting rate when the failure to report has moved the case into the higher one
options.why: Fifty per cent is the rate where income has merely been under-reported. Not reporting the transaction is put in the higher class by the section itself, so the ordinary rate is not where this one lands.

options.text: It is left out of under-reported income, the company having kept everything the documentation section asks for
options.misconception: treats the documentation limb as the whole of the relief, when declaring the transaction is a condition standing beside it
options.why: The relief rests on three things holding together — the documents kept, the transaction declared, and every material fact about it disclosed. A company that documented a transaction it told nobody about fails the second of them.

options.text: No penalty arises, an addition made in line with the officer's own arm's length price never being under-reported income
options.misconception: attaches the relief to where the addition came from rather than to what the taxpayer did before it
options.why: The relief is earned by the taxpayer's own conduct — kept, declared, disclosed — and not by the source of the addition. Read the other way round it would put every transfer pricing addition out of reach of penalty, whatever the taxpayer had done.

citation.ref: Section 270A(9) and Section 270A(8), read with Section 270A(6)(d) and Section 92E

items.scenario: Nirvaan Polymers Ltd had two dealings with its Korean parent in previous year 2025-26. The first, a purchase of compounds, it put in its accountant's report and in its return. The second, a licence of process technology, it never reported anywhere, though it had kept the full documentation file for that one as well and turned it over when asked. The Transfer Pricing Officer makes an addition on the licence in line with the arm's length price he determines.

items.stem: Is the officer entitled to proceed that way?

options.text: No — the courts have held that the test has no statutory backing and that the spend is not an international transaction with any machinery for pricing it
options.why: In the Sony Ericsson case the Delhi High Court held that the test has no statutory backing and that splitting spend into routine and non-routine by measuring it against non-comparables is not authorised. In the Bausch and Lomb case the same court held that the advertising spend is not an international transaction and that no machinery is provided for computing an adjustment on it. Between them the officer has neither a charge nor a method.

options.text: Yes, provided he first shows that the Indian company's spend exceeds what comparable distributors spend by a wide margin
options.misconception: treats the comparison itself as the flaw, when the objection is that the comparison has no statutory foundation whatever the margin
options.why: The size of the gap is not what the objection turns on. The courts refused the method itself, so a bigger gap measured the same way is no better founded than a smaller one.

options.text: No, but only because the parent rather than the subsidiary should have been assessed on the benefit it received
options.misconception: accepts that a chargeable transaction exists and quarrels only about whose hands it is taxed in
options.why: The rulings do not move the charge to somebody else; they say there is no transaction of this kind to charge and no way of computing an adjustment on it. Shifting it to the parent would meet the same two objections.

options.text: Yes — brand building for the parent is plainly a benefit conferred on an associated enterprise, and an arm's length reward for it follows
options.misconception: reasons from the commercial benefit to a chargeable transaction, skipping the questions of whether there is a transaction and whether the Act supplies a way to price it
options.why: A benefit passing to somebody is not by itself a transaction the Act can price. The Delhi High Court has held that the advertising spend is not an international transaction at all, and that no machinery is provided for computing an adjustment on it.

citation.ref: Sections 92B and 92C, on the authority of two Delhi High Court rulings, Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P) Ltd v. CIT, decided 2015, at 374 ITR 118, and Bausch and Lomb Eyecare (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT, decided 2016, at 381 ITR 227

items.scenario: Solstice India Pvt Ltd distributes the products of its foreign parent, which owns the brand. It spent heavily during previous year 2025-26 on advertising, marketing and sales promotion in India. The Transfer Pricing Officer takes what comparable distributors spend as a line, treats everything Solstice spent above that line as a service rendered to the parent in building the parent's brand, and proposes an adjustment bringing in a mark-up on the excess.

items.stem: Does dropping the bright line rescue the adjustment?

options.text: Yes — the spend plainly benefits the parent, and the definition catches any dealing that bears on the profits of the two enterprises
options.misconception: reasons from the width of the definition to a transaction, when the court held that none arises on these facts
options.why: The catch-all still needs a dealing between the two enterprises to fasten on to. The court held there is none in the advertising spend, so the width of the words does not reach it, and a benefit passing to somebody is not by itself something the Act can price.

options.text: Yes, provided he first shows that the parent's worldwide ratio is a reliable measure of what an unrelated distributor would have spent
options.misconception: argues about the quality of the comparison when the objection is that there is nothing here to compare
options.why: Reliability is the wrong question to be answering. A better measure of a share is still a measure of something the court held is outside the definition, and care cannot supply machinery the Act does not contain.

options.text: No — the second of the two rulings goes to whether such a transaction exists and whether the Act supplies any way of computing an adjustment, which no change of method answers
options.why: Refusing the line is only half of what the Delhi High Court decided. The other half holds that the spend is not an international transaction and that the Act gives no machinery for computing an adjustment on it, and a fresh way of estimating the share answers neither point.
keywords: the spend is not an international transaction
no machinery for computing an adjustment on it

options.text: Yes — what the court struck down was the line itself, so a method that draws no line is open to him
options.misconception: reads the two rulings as one objection to a technique, missing the ruling that removes the charge and the means of computing it
options.why: One of them is about the technique and the other says there is nothing to charge and nothing to compute with. The second objection stands whatever replaces the line, which is why the two rulings are cited together.

citation.ref: Sections 92B and 92C, on the authority of the Delhi High Court in Bausch and Lomb Eyecare (India) (P.) Ltd., decided 2016, read with its earlier ruling in Sony Ericsson, decided 2015

items.scenario: Calico Home Products India Pvt Ltd distributes its foreign parent's goods and pays for the advertising and sales promotion in India, while the parent owns the brand. The Transfer Pricing Officer accepts that he may not draw a line from what comparable distributors spend. He proposes instead to work out the share of Calico's spend that went to building the parent's brand from the parent's own worldwide ratio of brand spend to sales, and to charge a mark-up on that share.

items.stem: How is the income from the portfolio taxed?

options.text: It escapes the section, because Mr Rathore has no legal right to the income itself and holds nothing but shares in Calder
