options.why: Clauses 5 to 8 of Part I of the Second Schedule are indeed written for a Chartered Accountant in practice, but Part II of the Second Schedule reaches every member of the Institute, whether he practises or not. Its clause 1 catches a member who breaks the Act itself, a regulation framed under it, or any guidelines issued by the Council — and the Council has laid down, for a member in employment, a standing requirement of due diligence and a bar on being grossly negligent in how he carries out his work. Presenting receipts from the sale of property, plant and equipment and of investments as cash from operations, when Ind AS 7 classifies them within investing activities, is exactly that failure.
keywords: Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: No provision reaches him, since the Schedules bind only members in practice
options.misconception: assumes the Act governs practice alone
options.why: Part II and Part III of the First Schedule, and Parts II and III of the Second Schedule, all reach members in service or members generally. The Council may also inquire into conduct that never arose out of professional work: integrity of the highest order is expected of a Chartered Accountant in his private dealings just as much as in his professional ones.

options.text: Part III of the Second Schedule, being other misconduct by a member whether in practice or not
options.misconception: reaches for the other-misconduct clause instead of the professional one
options.why: Part III of the Second Schedule holds a single clause, and it is triggered only where the member is held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months. Misclassifying a cash flow is professional misconduct, and no court conviction is in question.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — Second Schedule, read with the Council Guidelines and Ind AS 7

items.scenario: The directors of a company are entitled to an incentive computed on cash generated from operations. The company has lost cash from operations, so the CFO, who is a Chartered Accountant in employment and holds no certificate of practice, presents the proceeds of selling under-utilised equipment and investments inside cash from operations, which turns the figure positive. A colleague says he cannot be proceeded against, because clauses 5 to 8 of Part I of the Second Schedule are written for a Chartered Accountant in practice.

items.stem: What can the bots do, and what stays with people?

options.text: Only the data entry — the consolidation adjustments and the statements themselves must stay manual
options.misconception: understates what the technology already covers
options.why: The bots pull the consolidated data together and put through the consolidation adjustments that are needed, work out what belongs to the non-controlling interests and what share of equity and of comprehensive income the parent is left with, and then produce the four statements. Restricting them to data entry leaves most of the three weeks where it was.

options.text: Everything including the accounting judgements, since the bots can be programmed with the standards
options.misconception: reads automation of rules as automation of judgement
options.why: A bot performs the calculations and applies the rules it has been given, which is why it is good at eliminations and currency conversion. Deciding whether an entity is controlled, or whether an estimate is reasonable, is not a rule waiting to be encoded.

options.text: The bots can extract and consolidate the subsidiary data, convert currencies, identify and eliminate intercompany transactions and produce the statements; the judgement calls stay with people
options.why: Robotic process automation uses software robots to automate manual and repetitive tasks by mimicking human interactions with digital systems. On a consolidation the bots extract the financial data from the subsidiary systems and consolidate it into the parent's, perform the necessary currency conversions, identify the intercompany transactions and generate the elimination entries Ind AS 110 requires so that nothing is counted twice, compute the amounts attributable to non-controlling interests, and turn out all four consolidated statements — the balance sheet, the cash flow statement, the statement of changes in equity and the statement of profit and loss. The gain is accuracy, timely reporting, cost saving and data integrity. What a bot does not do is decide anything: it applies the rules it was given.

options.text: Nothing at all, since robotic process automation needs every subsidiary on one system first
options.misconception: confuses automation with system consolidation
options.why: The bots mimic a person's interactions with the existing systems, which is why they work across subsidiaries each maintaining their own financial data. Putting everyone on one system is an ERP question, not a condition of using bots.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — robotic process automation, read with Ind AS 110

items.scenario: A group with eleven subsidiaries, each on its own accounting system, spends three weeks of every quarter pulling trial balances into spreadsheets, converting currencies by hand, chasing intercompany balances and typing elimination entries. The CFO asks what robotic process automation could take over, and whether it would replace the group reporting manager.

items.stem: What are the two arrangements the CFO wants, and what does the IT head's proposal give up?

options.text: The accounting application is software as a service, and the developers need nothing beyond cloud storage
options.misconception: substitutes file storage for a development platform
options.why: Cloud storage lets users save and synchronise files across devices. It gives developers no runtime, no deployment and no managed infrastructure, which is the whole of what platform as a service provides.

options.text: Software as a service for the accounting application and platform as a service for the developers; buying servers is on-premise, and forgoes the pay-as-you-go scaling infrastructure as a service would give
options.why: Software as a service provides cloud-based applications that users access and use over the internet, which is what a subscription accounting and financial management application is. Platform as a service is the second one: the provider hands developers a cloud-based place to build an application, put it live and keep it running, and takes the server and network plumbing off their hands entirely. Installing the application on servers in the company's own building is not cloud computing at all. Infrastructure as a service is what offers virtualised computing resources — servers, storage and networking — on a pay-as-you-go basis, allowing a business to scale its IT infrastructure based on demand without the need for physical hardware.

options.text: Both are infrastructure as a service, since in each case the provider owns the hardware
options.misconception: collapses the three service models into the one that rents hardware
options.why: The models differ by how much of the stack the provider runs. A finished application delivered over the internet is software as a service; a place to build and deploy applications is platform as a service; renting virtualised servers, storage and networking is infrastructure as a service.

options.text: The IT head is right — a private rack in the company's own building is cloud computing, since the finance team reaches it over the network
options.misconception: mistakes network access for the cloud service models
options.why: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet, letting accountants reach their data and software from any device with an internet connection. A traditional client-server architecture in a physical location the entity controls is the arrangement cloud computing is contrasted with.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — common applications of cloud computing

items.scenario: A mid-sized company is moving its finance function. The CFO wants a subscription accounting and financial management application that the team simply logs into, and a place for the in-house developers to build and run a customer portal without anyone managing servers. The IT head proposes instead to buy a rack of servers, install the accounting application on them in the company's own building, and call the result cloud.

items.stem: What does integrating internal control over financial reporting into the ERP actually require here?

options.text: Restrict every finance user to read-only access, since no one then posts anything wrong
options.misconception: replaces segregation of duties with a blanket lockout
options.why: The ERP enables segregation of duties, not the removal of duties. Roles and responsibilities in the closing and reporting process must be clearly defined, documented and communicated, and the people in those roles must have the qualifications, training and accounting knowledge to perform them.

options.text: Move the close out of the ERP into a controlled spreadsheet model, since the ERP has already failed
options.misconception: reads a configuration gap as a reason to abandon the system
options.why: The weaknesses are all things the ERP is designed to control and was not configured to — change management, the access matrix, the period configuration. Moving the close into spreadsheets gives up the audit trail, the segregation of duties and the single source of authentication that made the ERP worth having.

options.text: The monthly spreadsheet review is adequate, since a human reviewer catches anything a system rule would
options.misconception: substitutes a detective review for preventive system controls
options.why: A review after the close cannot stop a posting going into a closed period or record who approved a process change that left no log. Automating and standardising the procedures is what reduces manual effort and minimises the risk of errors; the review is what runs on top of it.

options.text: Use the ERP's own change management with the system logs and audit trail, a responsibility assignment matrix alongside the user access matrix, and the accounting period configuration controls that block backdating
options.why: Integrating internal control over financial reporting into an ERP puts the control inside the system. Changes to the financial closing and reporting process are tracked and validated through the ERP's change management functionality, and it is the system logs and audit trail that confirm the change was authorised by a designated individual with the appropriate authority. Roles are defined by reviewing the user access matrix configurations together with a responsibility assignment matrix, which records who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task. Postings in the wrong period are caught by the accounting period configuration controls and by comparing the posting date with the transaction date, which is also what prevents backdating and unauthorised adjustments. A spreadsheet review outside the system finds these afterwards, if at all.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — illustrative steps for integrating internal control over financial reporting within an ERP

items.scenario: An internal control review at a listed company finds three weaknesses. Changes were made to the financial closing and reporting process with no record of who authorised them. Several journal entries were posted into a period that had already been closed. And nobody can say which finance role is accountable for which step of the close. All the company's transactions run through an ERP. The finance head proposes a monthly spreadsheet review by a manager as the remedy for all three.

items.stem: How should the two incidents be characterised, and is the IT head right on either point?

options.text: A supply chain attack in both cases, because the first email impersonated a client
options.misconception: confuses impersonating a counterparty with compromising one
options.why: A supply chain attack compromises third-party software or hardware in order to gain access to a system or network. An email that merely looks as though it came from a client is phishing; no third-party product was subverted.

options.text: An insider threat followed by a denial of service attack, since a manager's own credentials were used and the firm was locked out
options.misconception: names the threats by their symptoms rather than their mechanism
options.why: An insider threat is a malicious action by an employee or other insider who has access; the manager here was deceived, not malicious. A denial of service attack overwhelms a system or network with traffic; encrypting files and demanding payment is ransomware.

options.text: A phishing attack followed by a ransomware attack; a firewall is one measure among several, and disclosure obligations do not turn on whether cash was lost
options.why: Tricking a user into clicking a malicious link or providing sensitive information is a phishing attack. Scrambling a firm's files, or shutting its people out of their own systems, and then naming a price for handing access back, is a ransomware attack. Network security with firewalls is one proactive measure, but it sits alongside password management, encryption, access control limited to authorised personnel and reviewed as the management or employee structure changes, employee training, regular data backups stored securely, and an incident response plan setting out how an attack is detected, contained and mitigated — and it is training and access control, not a firewall, that address a manager typing his password into a fake page. A breach with money in it is not left to the IT department either: an organisation is under a duty, in law and in ethics, to tell people about it, and the reporting guidelines of regulators such as SEBI and RBI reach the disclosure of such incidents, so the absence of a cash loss does not close the matter.

options.text: Two malware attacks; the IT head is right that a firewall would have stopped both
options.misconception: folds every incident into malware and treats perimeter security as complete
options.why: Malware is infecting computers or networks with malicious software that steals data or disrupts operations, and it is a different named threat from phishing and from ransomware. No firewall stops a person voluntarily entering credentials on a page he was directed to.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — common cybersecurity threats and proactive measures

items.scenario: An accounting firm is attacked twice in a fortnight. First a manager receives an email that looks like a client's and enters his credentials on the page it links to. A week later the firm's files are encrypted and a payment is demanded to unlock them. The IT head says a stronger firewall would have prevented both, and that since no money was actually paid and no client complained, nothing further need be considered.

items.stem: What would blockchain change that the group does not already have?

options.text: Past entries could be corrected in place across all systems at once, keeping the group's history consistent
options.misconception: treats an immutable ledger as an editable shared one
options.why: Every entry goes on to the ledger in the open and, once it is there, cannot be quietly altered; the cryptography is there precisely to stop unauthorised modification. Consistency comes from there being one record, not from being able to rewrite the old ones everywhere at once.

options.text: The records would be centralised on the parent's server, so the subsidiaries stop keeping their own
options.misconception: describes a central database rather than a distributed ledger
options.why: Blockchain spreads the record across a network: many participants hold it, and each of them verifies what goes on to it, which is what makes an intermediary unnecessary. Moving everything on to one company's server is the traditional centralised system it is contrasted with.

options.text: The director is right — the gain is speed of data entry and nothing more
options.misconception: reads blockchain as another input automation tool
options.why: Blockchain changes where the record lives and who can alter it, not how fast a document is read. The reconciliation effort the group is describing is precisely what a single shared ledger removes.

options.text: One shared, tamper-proof record instead of five to be reconciled, with an immutable audit trail the auditor can verify directly
options.why: A blockchain is a decentralised ledger in which each transaction is verified and encrypted so that unauthorised modification is prevented. Because one decentralised ledger stands in place of five sets of books, nothing is left to reconcile: a single shared source of truth, rather than several versions of the same balance to be agreed against each other. It maintains a comprehensive and immutable audit trail of every transaction, so an auditor can access the ledger directly to verify transactions instead of reconciling data pulled from several systems, and an irregularity or discrepancy is easier to identify and investigate. Faster data entry is what automation and optical character recognition give; it is not what this changes.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — key impacts of blockchain on financial reporting

items.scenario: A group spends most of its year-end close reconciling intercompany balances between the separate systems of five subsidiaries, and again between its own records and its bank's. A consultant proposes blockchain. A director objects that the only gain would be faster data entry, which the group already has through scanning software.

items.stem: Can the assertion be made?

options.text: Yes — convergence and adoption mean the same thing in substance
options.misconception: uses the two words interchangeably, as the study material warns against
options.why: Adoption is implementing IFRS as the IASB issued them. Convergence is moving towards them from a different direction, with exceptions that are worked on over time. The two are commonly used interchangeably and there is a significant difference between them.

options.text: No, because India has adopted IFRS in full and the sentence therefore understates the position
options.misconception: gets the right answer from the wrong classification
options.why: India converged with IFRS; Canada, Bahrain and Cambodia are among the jurisdictions that adopted. Treating India as an adopter would make the assertion available, which is the opposite of the position.

options.text: No — convergence with carve-outs is not adoption, and an entity applying standards amended by a local authority cannot make that assertion at all
options.why: Adoption means applying IFRS in the same manner as issued by the IASB and being one hundred per cent compliant with the guidelines issued by the IASB. India is converged, not an adopter: the national standard setter has adopted IFRS with some exceptions and works with the IASB towards removing them, and Ind AS contain carve outs and carve ins that make them contextually relevant in India. The IASB's own position is that nothing short of applying its standards and their related interpretations in full lets an entity say its financial statements comply with IFRS; where a local authority has amended those standards first, the entity cannot assert compliance with the IFRS it says it follows. How few the differences are does not enter into it.

options.text: Yes, provided the company discloses the carve-outs it has applied and their effect
options.misconception: treats disclosure of departures as curing an assertion of compliance
options.why: The assertion is all or nothing. Full application of the standards and interpretations is what allows it, which is why countries aligning their national standards with IFRS have to require IFRS 1 before an entity reporting under them can assert compliance.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — convergence versus adoption of IFRS

items.scenario: A listed Indian company's annual report states that its Ind AS financial statements "comply with IFRS as issued by the IASB". The CFO defends the sentence on two grounds — that India has converged with IFRS, so compliance amounts to the same thing, and that in any case the remaining differences are only a handful of carve-outs.

items.stem: What is the net worth for the Ind AS roadmap, and which phase does Company A fall into?

options.text: ₹505 crore, so Phase I, and Ind AS applies for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2016
options.why: Net worth under section 2(57) is the paid-up share capital plus all reserves created out of the profits and the securities premium account, less accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off. That is 160 plus 200 plus 150 plus 75, less the 80 of miscellaneous expenditure not written off, which is ₹505 crore. The revaluation reserve of 40 is not included, because the definition expressly excludes reserves created out of revaluation of assets. At ₹505 crore the company is above the five hundred crore threshold and is also listed, so it falls in Phase I and applies Ind AS for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2016, with comparatives for the period ending 31 March 2016.

options.text: ₹585 crore, so Phase I, and Ind AS applies from 1 April 2016
options.misconception: never deducts the miscellaneous expenditure not written off
options.why: The definition requires deducting the aggregate value of accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off. The ₹80 crore sitting on the asset side is exactly that, and leaving it in overstates net worth by its whole amount. The phase happens to be the same here, but the figure is wrong and would give the wrong answer the moment the balance sits nearer the threshold.

options.text: ₹545 crore, so Phase I, and Ind AS applies from 1 April 2016
options.misconception: includes the revaluation reserve in reserves
options.why: Three kinds of reserve are shut out of the net worth figure: one thrown up by revaluing assets, one arising from a write-back of depreciation, and one arising on an amalgamation. The ₹40 crore revaluation reserve never enters the computation, so 505 plus 40 is not a net worth figure under section 2(57).

options.text: ₹465 crore, so Phase II, and Ind AS applies from 1 April 2017
options.misconception: reads the exclusion of the revaluation reserve as a deduction from net worth
options.why: Excluding a reserve means not adding it in, not subtracting it. The revaluation reserve was never part of the 505, so taking a further 40 away double-counts the exclusion and pushes the company below the threshold it actually meets.

citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — roadmap for applicability, read with section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Company A's equity shares have been listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange since 2010. Its audited standalone balance sheet as at 31 March 2014 shows, in ₹ crore — equity share capital 160, securities premium 200, general reserve 150, revaluation reserve 40, profit and loss account 75, and other liabilities 160, against fixed assets 455, investments 200, current assets 50 and miscellaneous expenditure not written off 80.

items.stem: Is the standard in force?

options.text: No, because the NFRA notifies accounting standards under the Companies Act
options.misconception: gives the NFRA the notifying power that belongs to the MCA
options.why: The NFRA reviews the final draft and provides its inputs to the ICAI, and the central government examines its recommendations. It is the MCA that notifies the standard by publishing it in the Gazette of India.

options.text: No — the ICAI recommends, the NFRA reviews, and only the MCA's notification in the Gazette puts a standard into force
options.why: Accounting standards in India are formulated by the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI, but it is the central government that prescribes them, acting on the ICAI's recommendation and only after consulting the NFRA and working through what the NFRA has put to it. After the Council of the ICAI approves, the final draft goes to the NFRA with the ICAI's recommendation; the NFRA reviews and provides its inputs; and the MCA then notifies the standard under the Companies Act by publishing it in the Gazette of India, announcing the applicability date. Only a notified standard is authoritative under Indian law.

options.text: Yes — the ICAI formulates accounting standards, so its Council's approval brings the standard into force
options.misconception: treats formulation as enactment
options.why: Formulating and prescribing are different acts done by different bodies. The ICAI's Council approval is one step in the middle of the sequence, with the NFRA's review and the MCA's notification still ahead of it.

options.text: Yes, once the exposure draft's public comment period has closed, since the substance is then settled
options.misconception: mistakes the end of consultation for the end of the process
options.why: The comments received on the exposure draft are considered and the standard is then finalised by the ASB for submission to the Council of the ICAI. Closing the comment window is the beginning of the approval chain, not the end of it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — process of development and finalisation of Indian Accounting Standards

items.scenario: An exposure draft of a new Ind AS has been finalised by the Accounting Standards Board and approved by the Council of the ICAI. A company's technical team argues that it should be applied to the current year's financial statements, since the ICAI is the body that formulates accounting standards in India and it has now approved this one.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 101 permit?

options.text: Both companies must use the same basis even in their own standalone financial statements, because they are one group
options.misconception: extends the consolidation constraint back into the separate statements
options.why: Nothing prevents different entities within a group from choosing different bases for deemed cost in their standalone financial statements. The single-reporting-entity constraint bites only when the consolidated statements are prepared.

options.text: X Ltd may mix freely, since every deemed cost election in Ind AS 101 works item by item
options.misconception: applies the item-by-item rule to the one election that does not allow it
options.why: Retrospective application, fair value at transition and an eligible previous GAAP revaluation may each be chosen item by item. The previous GAAP carrying amount is the exception and can be taken only if applied to all asset classes and items.

options.text: X Ltd may not mix — the previous GAAP carrying amount election is all or nothing across asset classes; the two companies may differ in their standalone statements but not in the consolidated ones
options.why: Where there is no change in functional currency a first-time adopter may elect to continue with the carrying value of its property, plant and equipment as measured under previous GAAP and use that as deemed cost, but if it chooses that option the option of applying it selectively to some items and using fair value for others is not available — it must be applied to all of the asset classes and every item within them. Nothing prevents different entities within a group from choosing different bases for arriving at deemed cost in their respective standalone financial statements. In the consolidated financial statements, though, the whole group counts as one reporting entity — so at the transition date its members may not each carry property, plant and equipment at a deemed cost arrived at on a basis of their own.

options.text: Both may keep their own choices in the consolidated statements, since each subsidiary's figures come from its own audited accounts
options.misconception: lets the source of the figures decide the group's accounting policy
options.why: Consolidation treats the whole group as a single reporting entity. Two companies inside it may not therefore settle on different bases for the deemed cost of the same class of assets at the transition date, whatever each one's own statements say.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — deemed cost for property, plant and equipment, paragraphs D5 to D7AA

items.scenario: X Ltd is the holding company of Y Ltd and both adopt Ind AS from 1 April 20X1, with no change in functional currency. X Ltd wants to continue with the previous GAAP carrying amount for its buildings and to use fair value as deemed cost for its plant. Y Ltd wants fair value as deemed cost for all of its property, plant and equipment. X Ltd asks whether it may mix the two, and whether the group's consolidated financial statements can carry both companies' choices.

items.stem: Is the auditor right?

options.text: No — derecognition is a mandatory exception applied prospectively from the date of transition, so the portfolio stays off, unless the entity elects the retrospective option from a date of its choosing
options.why: Derecognition is a mandatory exception, and it runs forwards only: the tests in Ind AS 109 bite on transactions from the date of transition onward, and a first-time adopter applies them prospectively from there. Non-derivative financial assets and liabilities that previous GAAP had already taken off the books, because of something that happened earlier than that date, stay off — they return only if a later transaction or event qualifies them on its own merits. The study material runs this very fact pattern, a loan portfolio securitised to a trust before transition, and leaves it derecognised even though the Ind AS 109 criteria may not have been met. One alternative exists: the entity may instead apply those same requirements retrospectively, starting from a date of the entity's choosing, and then only where the information Ind AS 109 needs for those past transactions was already in hand when they were first accounted for.

options.text: No, and no election exists either — a first-time adopter can never look at pre-transition derecognitions
options.misconception: hardens the exception into an absolute bar
options.why: The entity may apply the derecognition requirements retrospectively from a date of its own choosing. What it may not do is reconstruct the information afterwards: the information needed must have been obtained at the time of initially accounting for those transactions.

options.text: Yes, provided the entity reconstructs the information about the 20X2 transaction from the trust's records now
options.misconception: allows the retrospective option to be exercised on information gathered later
options.why: The retrospective option is conditioned on the information having been obtained at the time of initially accounting for the transactions. Assembling it now from the trust's records is exactly what the condition rules out.

options.text: Yes — the opening Ind AS balance sheet must show everything as Ind AS 109 would have shown it, so the portfolio comes back
options.misconception: applies full retrospection where a mandatory exception forbids it
options.why: Retrospective application is the general principle, and the mandatory exceptions are where it is switched off. Derecognition is one of them, and an exception is not an election the entity or its auditor can decline.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — mandatory exceptions, derecognition of financial assets and financial liabilities

items.scenario: An NBFC moves on to Ind AS with 1 April 20X5 as its transition date. Back in 20X2 it had securitised a loan portfolio to a trust and taken the loans off its books under previous GAAP. On reviewing the arrangement now, the auditor concludes that the NBFC retained substantially all the risks and rewards, so the Ind AS 109 derecognition criteria would not have been met, and says the portfolio must be restored in the opening Ind AS balance sheet.

items.stem: What does the exemption allow, and what follows on a later disposal?

options.text: The exemption may be taken subsidiary by subsidiary, so the CFO's proposal works
options.misconception: treats an all-or-nothing exemption as an item-by-item election
options.why: If the exemption is used, the cumulative translation differences are set to zero for all foreign operations. Keeping a rebuilt balance for one and zero for the others is the mixture the exemption does not permit.

options.text: It is taken for all foreign operations or for none, so all three are reset to zero at transition, and a later disposal excludes the differences that arose before that date
options.why: The exemption relieves a first-time adopter of recognising some translation differences in other comprehensive income from the beginning and of reclassifying pre-transition cumulative translation differences for a foreign operation to profit or loss as part of the gain or loss on its disposal. If the first-time adopter uses it, the cumulative translation differences are set to zero for all foreign operations, not for a chosen few, so the subsidiary with complete records is reset alongside the other two. The consequence runs to the far end: the gain or loss on a subsequent disposal of a foreign operation shall exclude those differences that arose before the date of transition and include only the differences arising after it.
keywords: set to zero for all foreign operations

options.text: All three are reset, and on a later disposal the whole cumulative amount since acquisition is recycled to profit or loss
options.misconception: resets the balance but leaves the disposal rule untouched
options.why: Resetting to zero would mean nothing if the pre-transition differences came back on disposal. The gain or loss on a subsequent disposal shall exclude the differences that arose before the date of transition, which is the point of the exemption.

options.text: All three are reset, and the amount removed is taken to profit or loss in the year of transition
options.misconception: routes the transition adjustment through profit or loss instead of equity
options.why: A first-time adopter's transition adjustments are recognised directly in retained earnings, or another category of equity where appropriate, in the opening Ind AS balance sheet. Running them through the profit or loss of the transition year would put pre-Ind AS history into a reported result.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — optional exemptions, cumulative translation differences

items.scenario: A first-time adopter has three foreign subsidiaries. Translation records are complete for one, acquired two years ago, and unavailable for the other two, acquired in the 1990s. The CFO proposes to take the Ind AS 101 exemption for the two with missing records and to rebuild the cumulative translation difference for the third, and asks what happens if a foreign subsidiary is sold three years after transition.

items.stem: How should the company decide whether to recognise the customer list?

options.text: By applying the Conceptual Framework, because the Standards are built on it and it states the higher principle
options.misconception: treats the Conceptual Framework as superior law because the Standards were written from it, when it is expressly not a Standard and overrides nothing
options.why: Being the source of the concepts a Standard was drafted from is not the same as ranking above it. The Framework says of itself that it is not a Standard, that it does not override any Standard or any requirement in a Standard, and that it does not form part of the set of standards pronounced by the standard-setter. It is written first for the standard-setter, not as a body of rules a preparer may reach past an Ind AS to use.
keywords: not the same as ranking above it

options.text: By choosing either treatment, because the Framework and Ind AS 38 are both permitted sources
options.misconception: reads the Framework's role where an Ind AS allows a choice of accounting policy as a general freedom to choose between the Framework and a Standard
options.why: The choice limb means something narrower. Where an Ind AS itself offers a choice of accounting policy, the Framework helps the entity pick between the options that Standard gives it. It never creates a choice between following an Ind AS and following the Framework instead, and Ind AS 38's probability criterion offers no option at all.
keywords: where an Ind AS itself offers a choice
never creates a choice between following an Ind AS

options.text: By capitalising the list and disclosing the difference from the Framework as a departure in an appendix
options.misconception: takes the mechanism by which the standard-setter explains a deliberate departure and hands it to a preparer as a way of settling a conflict
options.why: A departure from an aspect of the Framework is something the standard-setter decides when it writes a Standard, and it explains that departure in the Appendix to that Ind AS. It is not a disclosure a company makes about its own accounts, and there is nothing for a preparer to explain here — the narrower gate in Ind AS 38 is a considered part of the Standard, not an inconsistency to be reported.
keywords: not a disclosure a company makes

options.text: By applying the recognition criteria in Ind AS 38, because the Conceptual Framework does not override an Ind AS
options.why: Ind AS 38 applies squarely to a purchased intangible asset, and it asks for the future economic benefits attributable to the asset to be probable before anything is recognised. The Conceptual Framework is not a Standard and does not override any Standard or any requirement in one, so meeting its definition is no answer to a requirement the applicable Ind AS makes. The Framework reaches a preparer only where no Ind AS applies, or where an Ind AS allows a choice of policy, and neither is the case here.
keywords: only where no Ind AS applies

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: the statement that the Conceptual Framework is not a Standard and does not override any Standard or any requirement in a Standard, read with the probability recognition criterion in Ind AS 38

items.scenario: Kalyani Speciality Chemicals Ltd has bought a customer list from a competitor leaving the market. The list is a right the company controls, and it would produce economic benefits in at least one circumstance, but the sales director's own assessment is that only a small minority of those customers will ever place an order, so the inflow is possible rather than probable. The financial controller proposes to capitalise the list, arguing that the Conceptual Framework's definition of an asset is met and that the Framework is the foundation on which every Ind AS is built.

items.stem: In which of these four does the Conceptual Framework govern the answer?

options.text: In the second and the third only
options.why: Those are the two situations in which the Framework reaches a preparer — developing a consistent accounting policy where no Ind AS applies to the transaction, and choosing between the options where an Ind AS allows a choice of accounting policy. In the first, the applicable Ind AS governs. In the fourth, the applicable Ind AS still governs, because the Framework overrides nothing.
keywords: where no Ind AS applies to the transaction
where an Ind AS allows a choice

options.text: In all four, because every Ind AS is built on the Framework's concepts
options.misconception: converts the Framework's role as the source of the concepts behind the Standards into authority over their application
options.why: The Framework's purpose in relation to a Standard already written is to help all parties understand and interpret it, not to decide what it requires. Where a Standard applies and states a requirement, that requirement is the answer, and the Framework does not sit above it.

options.text: In the second, the third and the fourth, since a Standard that departs from the Framework is defective
options.misconception: reads a deliberate departure by the standard-setter as a defect a preparer may correct by applying the Framework instead
options.why: A departure is deliberate, not defective. The standard-setter may specify requirements that depart from aspects of the Framework in order to meet the objective of financial reporting, and where it does so it explains the departure in the Appendix to that Ind AS. The requirement still binds, and the fourth situation is governed by the Standard.
keywords: A departure is deliberate, not defective

options.text: In the second only
options.misconception: remembers the gap-filling role and forgets that the Framework also assists where a Standard allows a choice of accounting policy
options.why: Gap filling is only half of it. The Framework is stated to assist preparers both where no Ind AS applies to a particular transaction or event and where an Ind AS allows a choice of accounting policy, so the third situation is inside its reach as well.
keywords: Gap filling is only half of it
allows a choice of accounting policy

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: the three stated purposes of the Conceptual Framework and the two situations in which it assists preparers, together with the statement that a departure specified by the standard-setter is explained in the Appendix to the relevant Ind AS

items.scenario: The technical team at Sundar Infrastructure Ltd is reviewing four questions for the year ended 31 March 2026. In the first, an Ind AS deals with the transaction squarely and gives one answer. In the second, a new kind of arrangement has arisen that no Ind AS addresses at all. In the third, an Ind AS offers an explicit choice of accounting policy and the team must pick one. In the fourth, a requirement in an Ind AS produces a result the team believes the Framework's concepts would not have produced.

items.stem: What is the right answer to the shareholder?

options.text: The difference is goodwill and should be recognised as an asset
options.misconception: treats the excess of market capitalisation over net assets as internally generated goodwill that may be brought on to the balance sheet
options.why: Nothing here has been acquired in a transaction. The excess of what the market will pay over the carrying amount of net assets is not an item the entity may recognise, and the Framework's answer is the opposite one — the statements were never meant to carry the entity's value in the first place.
keywords: Nothing here has been acquired in a transaction
never meant to carry the entity's value

options.text: The statements have failed, and the remedy is to measure every asset and liability at fair value
options.misconception: believes a full fair value system would make total equity equal the entity's value, when Ind AS is a mixed measurement system and equity is a residual
options.why: Ind AS is not a fair value system. It uses fair value in specific places and measures much else at depreciated historical cost, and even a complete fair value system would not close this gap, because total equity is measured as a residual of recognised assets less recognised liabilities and would still miss what the entity has never recognised.

options.text: The statements are not designed to show the entity's value, only to help users estimate it
options.why: One of the three stated limitations of general purpose financial reports is that they are not designed to show the value of a reporting entity. What they do is provide information that helps existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors estimate that value for themselves. The gap is expected rather than a failure — internally generated intangibles that cannot be recognised are one obvious reason for it.
keywords: not designed to show the value of a reporting entity

options.text: The criticism is misdirected because a shareholder is not a primary user of general purpose financial reports
options.misconception: confuses the limitation about the value of the entity with the question of who the primary users are, and excludes exactly the group the objective names first
options.why: Existing and potential investors are named first among the primary users, and helping them decide whether to buy, sell or hold equity instruments is the first of the three decisions the objective serves. The shareholder is the intended reader. It is the expectation about value that is wrong, not the standing of the person holding it.
keywords: named first among the primary users

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the stated limitation that a general purpose report is not a value gauge for the entity, only an input the reader uses to estimate that value themselves, read together with the objective of the reporting and who its primary users are

items.scenario: At the annual general meeting of Harith Consumer Products Ltd, a shareholder complains that the balance sheet total equity of ₹640 crore bears no relation to the ₹2,100 crore at which the market values the company, and says the financial statements have failed. The finance director is preparing a note for the board on whether the criticism is well founded.

items.stem: Is the finance team right about what general purpose financial reporting sets out to do?

options.text: Yes — the objective is confined to the prospects for future net cash inflows
options.misconception: remembers only the forward-looking half of the objective and drops stewardship, which sits beside it rather than under it
options.why: The forward-looking assessment is one of two, not the whole. Stewardship is stated alongside it wherever the objective is set out, including in the description of what accrual accounting and past cash flow information are useful for.
keywords: one of two, not the whole

options.text: No — assessing management's stewardship of the entity's economic resources is part of the objective itself
options.why: The objective names two assessments and this is one of them. Users need this reporting for two purposes together — judging what cash the entity may bring in later, and separately, being able to assess management's stewardship of the entity's economic resources. Accrual information and information about past cash flows are both stated to help with stewardship, which is why the accounts are the right place to look and not a substitute for it.
keywords: both stated to help with stewardship

options.text: Yes — stewardship is assessed from information about past cash flows only, which sits outside the objective
options.misconception: attaches stewardship to the cash flow statement alone, when accrual information is expressly said to help assess it too
options.why: Both routes are named. Financial performance reflected by accrual accounting is said to help users assess management's stewardship, and so is information about the entity's cash flows during the period. Neither is outside the objective.
keywords: accrual accounting is said to help users assess management's stewardship

options.text: No — but only because this lender is a primary user, and stewardship would be outside the objective for anybody else
options.misconception: makes the content of the objective vary with who is asking, when the objective is fixed and it is the identity of the primary users that is fixed with it
options.why: The objective does not change reader by reader. It is stated once, for existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors as a class, and stewardship is inside it for all of them. A party outside that class is simply not the primary audience, which is a different point altogether.
keywords: does not change reader by reader
stewardship is inside it for all of them

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the twin purpose behind general purpose financial reporting — judging likely future cash inflows and judging how well management has looked after the entity's resources — and how both accrual performance and past cash flow information feed the stewardship half of it

items.scenario: An institutional lender to Bhavani Logistics Ltd wants to judge how well the management has looked after the assets entrusted to it over the last three years, separately from what the company is likely to earn next year. The finance team's view is that the financial statements answer only the second question and that the first belongs outside the accounts, in the directors' report or in the auditor's work.

items.stem: What does the Conceptual Framework say about that decision?

options.text: Both items must be disclosed, because materiality is a matter for the users and the entity cannot decide it
options.misconception: reads the entity-specific character of materiality as removing the entity's judgement, when it is the entity that must exercise that judgement about its own users
options.why: The test is framed by reference to the decisions primary users make, but it is the entity preparing the report that has to apply it. Disclosing everything would defeat the purpose, since obscuring material information among immaterial detail is itself named as a way of failing the test.
keywords: it is the entity preparing the report that has to apply it

options.text: Both items are correctly omitted, because a five per cent threshold is the accepted quantitative test
options.misconception: treats a percentage borrowed from a group manual as the definition of materiality, when no uniform quantitative threshold can be specified at all
options.why: There is no accepted percentage. The standard-setter is expressly unable to specify a uniform quantitative threshold for materiality or to predetermine what could be material in a particular situation, precisely because the judgement depends on the entity and on what its own users would be influenced by.
keywords: unable to specify a uniform quantitative threshold

options.text: The related party payment may well be material despite its size, because materiality turns on nature as well as magnitude
options.why: Materiality is the entity-specific aspect of relevance, and it is assessed on the nature or the magnitude of the item, or both, in the context of that entity's own report. A small figure whose nature is that money went to a person connected with the managing director can reasonably be expected to influence a primary user's decision, so the percentage does not dispose of it.
keywords: the nature or the magnitude of the item, or both
the percentage does not dispose of it

options.text: Neither is material, because materiality only bites on the primary financial statements and not on the notes
options.misconception: confines materiality to the face of the statements, when the test is about omitting, misstating or obscuring information in the report as a whole
options.why: The test speaks of omitting, misstating or obscuring information in the financial report, without confining itself to the face of the statements. A note is where most of the influencing information sits, and a related party payment is a plain example of it.
keywords: without confining itself to the face of the statements
where most of the influencing information sits

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers why materiality is judged for this entity alone, weighing what kind of item it is alongside its size, and why no fixed percentage can stand in for that judgement

items.scenario: Ganesan Textiles Ltd applies a group instruction that treats anything below five per cent of profit before tax as immaterial. Profit before tax for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹90 crore, so the threshold is ₹4.5 crore. Two items fall below it. The first is a routine write-off of ₹3.8 crore of slow-moving cloth. The second is ₹0.6 crore paid during the year to a firm in which the managing director's brother is a partner, on terms the company has not compared with anything. The controller proposes to omit both from the notes.

items.stem: Is the chief financial officer's reasoning sound?

options.text: No — because relevance is judged only on materiality, and a revenue analysis is always material
options.misconception: collapses relevance into materiality and then asserts a blanket answer, when materiality is one entity-specific aspect of relevance rather than the whole of it
options.why: Relevance is the capacity to make a difference to decisions, delivered through predictive value or confirmatory value or both, and materiality is the entity-specific aspect of it. Nothing is material as a category — the judgement is made for the particular entity and its own users.
keywords: delivered through predictive value or confirmatory value
Nothing is material as a category

options.text: No — information need not be a prediction to have predictive value, and this analysis will usually have confirmatory value as well
options.why: Financial information has predictive value if users can employ it as an input to their own processes for predicting future outcomes, and it need not itself be a prediction or a forecast. A revenue analysis is exactly such an input. The same analysis can also be set against what users predicted a year ago, which gives it confirmatory value, and the two are interrelated rather than alternatives.
keywords: need not itself be a prediction or a forecast

options.text: Yes — predictive value belongs to forward-looking information and confirmatory value to historical information
options.misconception: splits the two aspects of relevance by the direction the information faces, when the same historical information routinely carries both
options.why: The split does not exist. Predictive value and confirmatory value are described as interrelated, and information that has one often has the other. Historical revenue is the standard example of a figure serving both purposes at once.

options.text: Yes — but the analysis should be kept anyway, because comparability requires the same notes each year
options.misconception: promotes an enhancing characteristic into a reason to retain information, when comparability cannot make information useful if it is not relevant to begin with
options.why: Comparability could not save the disclosure if it were genuinely irrelevant, because the enhancing characteristics cannot make information useful where it is irrelevant or fails to represent faithfully. The disclosure survives because it is relevant, not because it appeared last year.
keywords: cannot make information useful where it is irrelevant

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers what predictive value means — it is not confined to forecasts, and it interlocks with confirmatory value rather than sitting apart from it

items.scenario: Meenakshi Foods Ltd is deciding whether to keep disaggregating its revenue by product line in the notes. The chief financial officer argues the analysis should go, on the ground that it is a record of what has already happened and therefore has no predictive value, and that only forward-looking information such as an order book or a forecast can be predictive.

items.stem: How does the Framework's requirement of faithful representation apply here?

options.text: Charging no depreciation would be the neutral treatment, since it embeds no judgement
options.misconception: equates neutrality with refusing to make a judgement, when omitting a charge the entity knows is due is itself a slanted depiction
options.why: Neutrality means the depiction is not slanted, weighted, emphasised or de-emphasised. Carrying an asset at cost while it is being consumed is a slanted depiction, not an absence of one, and it would fail completeness as well, since the user would not have the information needed to understand the position.
keywords: not slanted, weighted, emphasised or de-emphasised

options.text: The estimate is acceptable only because relevance has been traded against faithful representation
options.misconception: reaches for the trade-off between the two fundamental characteristics where no trade-off arises, because this estimate satisfies both
options.why: A trade-off arises where the level of measurement uncertainty is so high that it is questionable whether an estimate represents the phenomenon faithfully at all. A useful life estimated on ordinary engineering and operating evidence is not in that territory; it is both relevant and faithfully represented, with nothing given up.
keywords: so high that it is questionable

options.text: The chair is right — an amount that cannot be verified against an outcome is not free from error
options.misconception: reads free from error as accuracy proved by the eventual outcome, when the requirement runs to the description and the process rather than the result
options.why: The outcome turning out differently does not make the estimate erroneous. Free from error addresses errors or omissions in the description of the item and errors in the process used to produce the figure, not the distance between an estimate and what later happens.
keywords: does not make the estimate erroneous
errors in the process used to produce the figure

options.text: An estimate can be a faithful representation if it is described as an estimate, its process and limits are explained, and no error was made in choosing and applying that process
options.why: Free from error does not mean perfectly accurate — an unobservable figure like this one is not the kind of thing that can be called accurate or inaccurate in that sense. What settles the matter here is that the amount is clearly and accurately described as an estimate, its limits are spelled out honestly, and nothing about picking or running the estimating method was done carelessly. Reasonable estimates are treated as an essential part of preparing financial statements, not a defect to be apologised for.
keywords: Free from error does not mean perfectly accurate
clearly and accurately described as an estimate
an essential part of preparing financial statements

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the three marks of a faithful depiction and why an honestly labelled, clearly explained estimate can still meet the free-from-error test

items.scenario: Vaishnavi Renewables Ltd must estimate the useful life of a wind farm and the residual value of its turbines at the end of that life. The audit committee chair objects that no such estimate can be shown to be right or wrong for twenty-five years, so any depreciation charge built on it cannot be free from error, and proposes that the company disclose the cost and charge no depreciation until the position is certain.

items.stem: What is wrong with the draft, and where does the word the trainee used actually belong?

options.text: The characteristics are right, but freedom from error should have been listed as the third fundamental one
options.misconception: raises a limb of faithful representation to the status of a characteristic in its own right
options.why: Free from error is one of the three things a perfectly faithful depiction is, along with complete and neutral. It is a component of faithful representation, not a characteristic sitting beside it.
keywords: one of the three things a perfectly faithful depiction is

options.text: The characteristics are right but prudence is enhancing rather than fundamental
options.misconception: promotes prudence into the list of qualitative characteristics at the wrong tier, when it is in neither list and supports neutrality instead
options.why: Prudence is not among the four enhancing characteristics either — those are comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability. Prudence is the exercise of caution when making judgements under uncertainty, and its stated role is to support neutrality.
keywords: not among the four enhancing characteristics

options.text: The draft is correct, since reliability and faithful representation are two names for the same characteristic
options.misconception: treats the two words as interchangeable, missing that one is a wider test with the other as one of its five limbs
options.why: They are not the same size. Under Ind AS 8 faithful representation is one of five limbs of reliability, sitting beside substance over form, neutrality, prudence and completeness. In the Framework, completeness, neutrality and freedom from error are the three limbs of faithful representation itself, and prudence supports neutrality rather than standing beside it.
keywords: one of five limbs of reliability

options.text: The Framework's two fundamental characteristics are relevance and faithful representation; reliability is Ind AS 8's word, where faithful representation is only one limb of it
options.why: The Framework's fundamental qualitative characteristics are relevance and faithful representation, and it uses no characteristic called reliability at all. Ind AS 8 does use it, in the paragraph telling management how to develop a policy where no Ind AS applies, and there information is reliable if it represents faithfully, reflects economic substance rather than legal form, is neutral, is prudent and is complete in all material respects.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the Framework's two fundamental characteristics and the three limbs of faithful representation, set against Ind AS 8's separate reliability language

items.scenario: A trainee at Nachiket Auto Components Ltd has drafted an accounting policy note that opens by saying the financial statements have been prepared to satisfy the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of the Conceptual Framework, which the draft names as relevance and reliability, and lists prudence as a third. The reviewer has to correct it.

items.stem: Which of the two proposals does the Conceptual Framework permit?

options.text: Both, because prudence means erring on the side of caution in the entity's reported position
options.misconception: reads prudence as conservatism, so that a deliberately worse-looking position is always the safer answer
options.why: Caution in making a judgement is not the same as a deliberate bias in the answer. A depiction weighted to be received unfavourably is as far from neutral as one weighted the other way, and neutrality is what prudence is there to support.
keywords: not the same as a deliberate bias
as far from neutral as one weighted the other way

options.text: Both, provided the amounts and the reasoning are disclosed in the notes
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a cure for a figure that is not neutral, when a note cannot make a slanted measurement into a faithful representation
options.why: Neutrality is about the selection and presentation of the information itself. Explaining that a figure has been slanted does not unslant it, and the depiction still fails to represent faithfully what it purports to represent.
keywords: selection and presentation of the information itself

options.text: Neither, because prudence does not allow liabilities or expenses to be overstated nor assets or income to be understated
options.why: What prudence means, at bottom, is caution when making judgements under conditions of uncertainty, and the Framework states the rule facing in both directions at once. One direction bars overstating assets and income while understating liabilities and expenses; the other bars the mirror-image fault — it does not allow for the understatement of assets or income, run the other way round to inflate liabilities and expenses. The provision proposal breaches the first direction and the land proposal breaches it too.
keywords: caution when making judgements under conditions of uncertainty
does not allow for the understatement of assets or income

options.text: Only the warranty proposal, because caution about liabilities is permitted while caution about assets is not
options.misconception: applies prudence asymmetrically, keeping the half of the rule about not understating liabilities and dropping the half about not overstating them
options.why: There is no asymmetry in the statement of the rule. Overstating a liability is refused in the same sentence that refuses understating an asset, and the ₹6 crore added to the warranty provision is exactly the overstatement that sentence names.
keywords: no asymmetry in the statement of the rule
exactly the overstatement that sentence names

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers neutrality as freedom from bias, prudence as the caution that backs it, and the two-directional bar prudence sets against over- and understatement alike

items.scenario: Two proposals reach the year-end meeting at Devika Engineering Ltd. The best estimate of the warranty obligation is ₹12 crore, and the finance director proposes to provide ₹18 crore because the year has gone well and a cushion would be prudent. The commercial director separately proposes to carry a plot of surplus land at ₹9 crore rather than the ₹15 crore the revaluation supports, on the same reasoning. Both describe their proposals as an exercise of prudence.

items.stem: Does this presentation satisfy the Conceptual Framework?

options.text: No — a neutral depiction is not emphasised or de-emphasised, and neutrality covers presentation as well as selection
options.why: A neutral figure carries no bias in the selection or presentation of what it shows, so nothing here may be slanted, weighted, emphasised, de-emphasised or otherwise manipulated — nudging a reader toward taking it well or badly is exactly the fault the rule targets. Two correctly measured figures arranged so one is buried and the other is spotlighted still fall foul of it, and neutrality is one of the three limbs of faithful representation.
keywords: bias in the selection or presentation

options.text: Yes, because every figure is correctly measured and every required disclosure is made
options.misconception: reads faithful representation as a test of the numbers alone, when neutrality expressly reaches how the information is presented
options.why: Measurement is not the whole of it. The requirement names the presentation of financial information in the same breath as its selection, so a set of correct figures arranged to make one of them harder to notice still fails.
keywords: names the presentation of financial information
arranged to make one of them harder to notice

options.text: No — but the fault is a failure of comparability rather than of neutrality
options.misconception: reaches for comparability because the presentation differs from other entities, when the defect is bias in this entity's own report
options.why: Comparability is about using the same methods for the same items across periods and entities. Nothing here turns on that. The defect is that the depiction has been weighted to be received favourably, which is the definition of a failure of neutrality.
keywords: same methods for the same items

options.text: Yes, because emphasising the improvement makes the report more understandable
options.misconception: uses an enhancing characteristic to justify a breach of a fundamental one, when the enhancing characteristics cannot make information useful if it does not represent faithfully
options.why: Understandability is an enhancing characteristic and it cannot rescue information that is not a faithful representation. The enhancing characteristics are stated to work only on information that is already relevant and already faithfully represented.
keywords: cannot rescue information that is not a faithful representation
already relevant and already faithfully represented

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers neutrality as reaching both how information is selected and how it is presented

items.scenario: Ratnesh Hospitality Ltd is reporting a strong year and its investor relations team asks for the loss on closing two hotels to be shown as a single line low in the statement of profit and loss, with the accompanying note kept short, while the operating margin improvement is given its own note, a chart and a paragraph in the accounting policy section. Every figure involved is correctly measured and every required disclosure is made somewhere.

items.stem: What does the Conceptual Framework say about leaving the arrangement out?

options.text: The omission is right if the cost of explaining the arrangement exceeds the benefit to users
options.misconception: stretches the cost constraint, which the standard-setter applies when writing a Standard, into a preparer's ground for dropping a required disclosure
options.why: The cost constraint is described as something the standard-setter weighs in formulating a proposed Ind AS, considering costs and benefits for financial reporting generally rather than for an individual entity. It is not a switch a company turns to remove information from its own accounts.
keywords: the standard-setter weighs in formulating a proposed Ind AS
not a switch a company turns

options.text: The omission is right, because understandability is one of the qualitative characteristics and the board has applied it
options.misconception: treats understandability as a licence to omit, when it is achieved by classifying, characterising and presenting clearly rather than by leaving things out
options.why: Understandability is delivered by classifying, characterising and presenting information clearly and concisely. It is also an enhancing characteristic, which cannot make a report useful where what remains is not a complete and faithful representation.
keywords: classifying, characterising and presenting information clearly

options.text: Leaving it out would make the report incomplete and possibly misleading, and the reports are written for users who review and analyse diligently
options.why: Complexity in the underlying arrangement will not go away just because it is left unwritten. Dropping it for an easier read leaves the reports incomplete and therefore possibly misleading — a gap dressed up as tidiness is still a gap. The intended reader is somebody with a working grasp of business who is prepared to review and analyse the information diligently, and even that reader may reasonably bring in an adviser for something this hard.
keywords: review and analyse the information diligently

options.text: The arrangement may be omitted from the statements provided its existence is mentioned in the directors' report
options.misconception: moves the information outside the financial statements and treats that as satisfying the requirement, when completeness is a limb of faithful representation inside them
options.why: A complete depiction includes all the information necessary for a user to understand what is being depicted, including the necessary descriptions and explanations. Moving the subject elsewhere in the annual report does not make the financial statements complete.
keywords: all the information necessary for a user to understand
does not make the financial statements complete

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers understandability, why cutting complex content for readability still fails the report, and the cost constraint as the standard-setter applies it

items.scenario: Yamuna Power Ltd has entered into a structured arrangement over its future generation that is genuinely hard to describe. The board proposes to leave it out of the financial statements altogether, on the ground that the shareholder register is largely retail and that an explanation nobody can follow is worse than silence.

items.stem: How should the audit committee's objection be answered?

options.text: The objection fails because comparability is only about comparing this entity with other entities, not with its own earlier periods
options.misconception: halves comparability, dropping the period-to-period dimension that this change actually affects
options.why: Comparability runs both ways. Setting this entity's numbers beside another entity's is only half of it; being able to line them up against the same entity for another period or date is the other half, and it is exactly that second half the changed presentation basis has disturbed.
keywords: the same entity for another period

options.text: One enhancing characteristic may be reduced to maximise another, and a temporary loss of comparability can be worth better relevance or faithful representation in the longer term
options.why: Applying the enhancing characteristics is an iterative process that follows no prescribed order, and sometimes one has to be diminished to maximise another. A temporary reduction in comparability from applying a new Ind AS prospectively is given as an example of a trade worth making, and appropriate disclosures may partially compensate for the non-comparability.

options.text: The objection fails because comparability means uniformity, which prospective application preserves
options.misconception: equates comparability with uniformity, which the Framework distinguishes expressly
options.why: Comparability is neither consistency nor uniformity. Consistency is using the same methods for the same items and is the means of achieving comparability, while uniformity would require like and unlike things to look alike, which is the opposite of what is wanted.
keywords: is the means of achieving comparability

options.text: The objection is sound, because comparability is fundamental and cannot be traded against anything
options.misconception: promotes comparability to the tier of relevance and faithful representation, when it is one of four enhancing characteristics
options.why: The fundamental characteristics are relevance and faithful representation. Comparability is enhancing, along with verifiability, timeliness and understandability, and enhancing characteristics are to be maximised as far as possible rather than treated as absolute.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers why the four enhancing characteristics get traded against one another rather than applied in a set sequence, illustrated by a new Ind AS applied prospectively, and how comparability differs from consistency and from uniformity

items.scenario: Anantha Cements Ltd applies a new Ind AS prospectively from 1 April 2025, so the year to 31 March 2026 is presented on a basis the comparative year is not. The audit committee objects that comparability is a qualitative characteristic and that the company has knowingly given it up, and asks whether the change can be right.

items.stem: Is the company secretary right about what a reporting entity can be?

options.text: No — and the boundary may be drawn wherever the buyer asks, since the primary users decide it
options.misconception: reads users' information needs as the whole test and drops the three faithful representation requirements that constrain the boundary
options.why: Users' information needs drive the boundary, but they do not settle it alone. The set of economic activities inside must not be arbitrary or incomplete, including it must produce neutral information, and how the boundary was determined must be described. A line drawn to flatter the division would fail all three.
keywords: they do not settle it alone

options.text: Yes — only a legal entity, or a parent with its subsidiaries, can be a reporting entity
options.misconception: ties the reporting entity to legal form, which is exactly the tie the Framework cuts
options.why: The Framework says in terms that a reporting entity is not necessarily a legal entity, and it contemplates a portion of an entity as well as combinations of entities that are not linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship. Legal form is one way a boundary gets drawn, not the only one.
keywords: Legal form is one way a boundary gets drawn

options.text: No — a reporting entity can be a portion of an entity and need not be a legal entity, provided the boundary is drawn properly
options.why: A reporting entity is one that is required, or chooses, to prepare financial statements, and it can be a single entity, a portion of an entity, or more than one entity. It is not necessarily a legal entity. Where the boundary is not set by legal form it is driven by the information needs of the primary users, and faithful representation requires that the set of activities inside is not arbitrary or incomplete, that including it produces neutral information, and that the statements describe how the boundary was determined and what the reporting entity consists of.

options.text: No — but the resulting statements would be combined financial statements
options.misconception: applies the label for two or more entities not linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship to a single carved-out portion of one entity
options.why: Combined financial statements are what a reporting entity comprising two or more entities not all linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship produces. A portion of one entity is not that; it is simply a reporting entity whose boundary is drawn other than by legal form.
keywords: two or more entities not all linked
A portion of one entity is not that

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: the definition of a reporting entity as an entity required or choosing to prepare financial statements, which can be a single entity, a portion of an entity or more than one entity and is not necessarily a legal entity, together with the three requirements that faithful representation places on determining the boundary of a reporting entity that is not a legal entity

items.scenario: Kaveri Industries Ltd is negotiating the sale of its packaging division, which is not a separate company and has never had its own registration. The buyer and its bankers want three years of financial statements for the division alone. The company secretary says this cannot be done under Ind AS because a reporting entity has to be a legal entity, and offers a management information pack instead.

items.stem: What is wrong with the chairman's proposal, taking the Framework's position on it?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, provided the consolidated position for each subsidiary is given in the notes to the parent's statements
