options.misconception: inverts what consolidated statements are for, since they are expressly not designed to give information about any particular subsidiary
options.why: A subsidiary's own assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses, taken on their own, are simply not what consolidation is for — consolidated statements are not designed to provide separate information about any one subsidiary picked out from the group; a subsidiary's own statements are designed to do that. Notes about individual subsidiaries are not what is missing.
keywords: not designed to provide separate information
A subsidiary's own statements are designed to do that

options.text: Where consolidated statements are required, unconsolidated statements cannot serve as a substitute for them
options.why: What a parent's own investors, lenders and other creditors need to know is rarely covered by the parent's unconsolidated numbers alone — that information is typically not sufficient to meet what those users need, so where consolidation is required, the unconsolidated set cannot be put in their place. A parent may prepare them in addition, never instead.
keywords: cannot be put in their place

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the subsidiaries' own statements together give the reader the same information
options.misconception: assumes a set of separate statements adds up to a consolidation, which is the assumption consolidated statements exist to defeat
options.why: Consolidated statements present the parent and its subsidiaries as a single reporting entity, which is what a creditor of the parent needs, since the parent's own cash inflows include distributions from subsidiaries that depend on their inflows. Four separate sets do not answer that question.
keywords: Four separate sets do not answer that question

options.text: The proposal is acceptable if the parent's statements are described as combined financial statements
options.misconception: reaches for the combined label as though renaming a set of statements changed what it reports
options.why: Combined financial statements describe a reporting entity comprising two or more entities not all linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship. This group is linked by exactly that relationship, and calling the parent's own statements something else would not add the subsidiaries to them.
keywords: not all linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship
would not add the subsidiaries to them

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers what consolidation is for and is not for — never a way to isolate one subsidiary's own figures, never replaceable by unconsolidated numbers where it is required — read against the separate label for combined statements of unrelated entities

items.scenario: Prithvi Holdings Ltd has four subsidiaries, each of which files complete financial statements of its own. The chairman proposes that the group stop preparing consolidated financial statements and issue only the parent's own unconsolidated statements, on the ground that a reader who wants the subsidiaries' position can read their statements, and that the parent's own creditors care only about the parent's distributable reserves anyway.

items.stem: Applying the Conceptual Framework's definition, is the receivable still an asset?

options.text: Yes — the right exists and has the potential to produce benefits, and the low probability bears on recognition and measurement instead
options.why: Certainty is not the bar for potential to exist, and neither, in fact, is likelihood — for the right to produce benefits it does not need to be certain, or even likely. Even where the probability of benefits is low, that low chance is a question for recognition and measurement, not for whether the right exists at all. What the test actually asks is narrower: does the right already exist, and is there at least one circumstance in which it would produce benefits for this entity beyond those available to everyone else. A low probability of benefits does not stop a right meeting the definition of an economic resource; instead it feeds into whether the asset is recognised and how it is measured, which may leave the carrying amount at nil.
keywords: does not need to be certain, or even likely
even where the probability of benefits is low
whether the asset is recognised and how it is measured

options.text: No — because control has been lost to the resolution professional
options.misconception: confuses the insolvency of the counterparty with the loss of the entity's own right, when what is doubtful is recovery rather than control
options.why: Directing the use of a resource and obtaining what flows from it is what control is; the company still holds the claim and would still receive whatever is distributed on it. What is uncertain is the amount, not who holds the right.
keywords: uncertain is the amount, not who holds the right

options.text: No — an asset requires future economic benefits to be expected to flow to the entity
options.misconception: applies the older wording still carried in Ind AS 38, under which benefits must be expected, to the Framework's definition, which asks only for potential
options.why: Expected inflow is the older formulation, and Ind AS 38 still uses it when it defines an asset as a resource from which future economic benefits are expected to flow. The Framework sets the bar lower: a right just needs the potential, in at least one scenario, to give this entity benefits nobody else gets — the Framework prescribes no probability criterion at all.
keywords: Expected inflow is the older formulation

options.text: Yes — and it must therefore continue to be carried at ₹4 crore until the outcome is known
options.misconception: takes meeting the definition as settling the measurement too, when definition, recognition and measurement are three separate questions
options.why: Meeting the definition decides only that an asset exists. Whether it is recognised turns on the recognition criteria, and what it is carried at turns on the measurement requirements in the applicable Ind AS, which here would reduce the amount to what is expected to be collected.
keywords: decides only that an asset exists

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers how low the bar for potential is set in defining an economic resource, and why a low probability of benefit steers recognition and measurement rather than knocking out the definition itself, read against Ind AS 38's older expected-inflow wording

items.scenario: Shantanu Trading Ltd is owed ₹4 crore by a customer that has gone into insolvency proceedings. The resolution professional's own estimate is that unsecured operational creditors will recover very little, and the company's assessment is that any recovery is unlikely. The junior accountant argues that because an inflow is not expected, the receivable is no longer an asset at all and the whole question is closed.

items.stem: How does the Framework's treatment of expenditure apply to the two items?

options.text: Neither is an asset, because one produces no benefits and the other cost nothing
options.misconception: keeps the correct answer on the study for the wrong reason and applies a cost condition to the water right that the definition does not contain
options.why: Cost is not part of the definition of an asset. The definition asks for a present economic resource controlled as a result of past events, and a twenty-year transferable right to draw water is exactly that, whether it was bought, granted or donated.
keywords: Cost is not part of the definition
whether it was bought, granted or donated

options.text: Both are assets, because expenditure creates one and a granted right is one
options.misconception: treats expenditure as sufficient for an asset, which is the half of the rule the Framework denies
options.why: Money spent is evidence of seeking benefits, nothing more. A study for a product that will not be launched leaves the company with no right that has the potential to produce economic benefits, so there is no economic resource to control.
keywords: evidence of seeking benefits, nothing more
no right that has the potential

options.text: The market study is not an asset despite the spending, and the water right is an asset despite there being none
options.why: Spending money and acquiring an asset tend to happen together, but one is not the price of admission for the other — a close association between incurring expenditure and acquiring assets is not the same as the two always coinciding. Money spent shows the entity was chasing future benefits; on its own it is not conclusive proof that it obtained an asset. Running the logic the other way, having spent nothing is no bar either: the absence of related expenditure does not preclude an item counting as one, and rights granted by a government free of charge are the example given of assets that arrive with no cost.
keywords: not conclusive proof that it obtained an asset
absence of related expenditure does not preclude an item
granted by a government free of charge

options.text: Both should be recognised at nil, since neither has a measurable cost
options.misconception: reaches for a nil carrying amount as a way of avoiding the definition question, when a granted right may be measured at a deemed cost and the study is not an asset at any amount
options.why: Where an item is acquired in an event that is not a transaction on market terms, historical cost may not give a faithful representation and a current value may be used as a deemed cost on initial recognition. That is the route for the water right. The study is not an asset at nil or at any other figure.
keywords: used as a deemed cost on initial recognition
not an asset at nil or at any other figure

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers why spending money neither guarantees an asset nor is required for one, illustrated by a government right granted free of charge

items.scenario: Two items are on the desk at Aparna Speciality Foods Ltd. The company spent ₹2.6 crore during the year on a market study for a product it has now decided not to launch, and the finance team wants to carry that as an asset because the money was actually spent. Separately, the state government has granted the company, free of charge, a transferable right to draw water from a canal for twenty years, and the same team wants to record nothing because nothing was paid.

items.stem: Does Tarun control the stock, and what follows for its balance sheet?

options.text: Both parties control the goods, so both recognise them, each to the extent of its interest
options.misconception: allows control to be shared, when the Framework states that if one party controls a resource no other party does
options.why: Control does not divide that way. The definition is built so only one answer can be right — if one party controls an economic resource, no other party controls it, since holding control includes the ability to prevent others from directing the use or obtaining the benefits.
keywords: if one party controls an economic resource, no other party controls it
prevent others from directing the use

options.text: Yes — because Tarun is exposed to variation in the amount it earns from handling the goods
options.misconception: takes exposure to variability as the test of control, when it is named as one indicator among several and here relates to the fee rather than to the goods
options.why: Exposure to significant variations in the economic benefits produced by a resource may indicate control, but it is only one factor in an overall assessment. Tarun's fee varies with volume; it is not exposed to variation in the benefits the goods themselves produce, which is the exposure the indicator is about.
keywords: only one factor in an overall assessment
not exposed to variation in the benefits the goods themselves produce

options.text: Yes — physical possession gives the present ability to direct the use of the goods
options.misconception: reads custody as control, when control is the present ability to direct the use of the resource and obtain the benefits, which possession alone does not confer
options.why: Two things make up control: the present ability to direct the use of a resource, and the ability to obtain the benefits it produces. Tarun can do neither — it cannot deploy the goods, cannot price them and takes none of the benefit of their value. Holding something is not directing its use.
keywords: present ability to direct the use
Holding something is not directing its use

options.text: No — a resource in an agent's custody that the principal controls is not the agent's asset, and the duty to deliver it is not the agent's liability
options.why: Where a principal engages an agent to act on its behalf, an economic resource in the agent's custody that the principal controls is not an asset of the agent. And where the agent is obliged to transfer that resource to a third party, the obligation is not the agent's liability either, because what would be transferred is the principal's economic resource and not the agent's. Neither line goes on Tarun's balance sheet.
keywords: not an asset of the agent
the obligation is not the agent's liability

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the two limbs that make up control, why control cannot be shared between two parties at once, and how a principal-agent arrangement keeps a resource and its related duty off the agent's own balance sheet

items.scenario: Tarun Distribution Ltd holds stock in its warehouse belonging to Ravindra Appliances Ltd. Under their agreement Tarun may release the goods only against a delivery instruction from Ravindra, cannot set the price, cannot use the goods in its own business, earns a fixed handling fee per unit, and is not exposed to any change in the goods' value. Tarun's accountant proposes to recognise the stock as inventory and a matching liability to deliver it.

items.stem: Which of the three is an economic resource of Sharada Technologies Ltd?

options.text: The confidential method and the bought-back shares
options.misconception: treats an entity's own repurchased instruments as economic resources, when an entity cannot have a right to obtain benefits from itself
options.why: Nothing here can be owed to itself: an entity, under the Framework's rule, cannot have a right to obtain economic benefits from itself. Debt or equity instruments it has issued and then repurchased and holds — treasury shares — are not economic resources of that entity, and the same is true within a group of instruments issued by one member and held by another.
keywords: cannot have a right to obtain economic benefits from itself
are not economic resources of that entity

options.text: Only the confidential method, because control can rest on the ability to keep know-how secret rather than on a registered right
options.why: The textbook case is a legal right — control usually arises from an ability to enforce legal rights — but the Framework does not stop there: it can just as well rest on the entity having some other way of shutting everybody else out of directing the resource and taking its benefits. Access to know-how kept out of the public domain, together with the present ability to keep it secret, is precisely that other route, even without a registered patent behind it.
keywords: usually arises from an ability to enforce legal rights

options.text: None of them, because none is supported by an enforceable legal right
options.misconception: makes legal enforceability the test of control, when the Framework treats it as the usual source rather than the requirement
options.why: Legal enforceability is how control usually arises, not what control is. The test is the present ability to direct the use of the resource and obtain the benefits, together with the ability to prevent others from doing so, and secrecy can deliver that as effectively as a patent.
keywords: how control usually arises, not what control is

options.text: The confidential method and the open standard
options.misconception: recognises a right available to everybody at no significant cost, which is expressly not an asset of the entity holding it
options.why: Rights available to all parties without significant cost are typically not assets of the entities that hold them, and know-how in the public domain is the example given. A right is an asset only where it has the potential to produce benefits for this entity beyond those available to all other parties.
keywords: available to all parties without significant cost
beyond those available to all other parties

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the two routes to control — enforceable legal rights, or some other practical way of shutting everyone else out — illustrated by secret know-how, plus why a right open to everyone at no cost is not an asset and why an entity cannot hold a right against itself

items.scenario: Three items are being argued over at Sharada Technologies Ltd. It has bought back 4,00,000 of its own equity shares and holds them, and the treasurer wants to show them as an investment. It has a proprietary manufacturing method that is not patented but is kept confidential inside a small team, and the legal head says it cannot be an asset because there is no registered right. And it uses a published open standard freely available to every competitor, which the technology head wants recognised because it is central to the product.

items.stem: Which of the two is an obligation at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Both, because the board has resolved on the payment and a board resolution binds the company
options.misconception: treats an internal decision as creating an obligation, when an obligation is always owed to another party and an intention is not enough
options.why: A duty or responsibility owed to another party is what an obligation is, and nothing has been owed to anybody here — the families have not been told and nothing has been held out to them. Wanting to pay is not the same as being unable to walk away from paying: an intention to make a transfer does not establish that the entity has no practical ability to avoid it.
keywords: an intention to make a transfer does not establish

options.text: Neither, because a returns policy is not legally enforceable and an intention is not an obligation
options.misconception: limits obligations to legally enforceable duties, dropping constructive obligations altogether
options.why: Many obligations are established by contract or legislation and are legally enforceable, but obligations can also arise from customary practices, published policies or specific statements. Legal enforceability is one route to an obligation, not the definition of one.
keywords: can also arise from customary practices
one route to an obligation, not the definition of one

options.text: The ex gratia payment only, because it is highly likely to be made while a return may never be requested
options.misconception: makes probability the test of an obligation, when likelihood does not create one and a low probability of transfer does not destroy one
options.why: Likelihood is not the test in either direction. Something the entity is very likely to hand over is not, for that reason alone, something it has no way of escaping; and a low chance of transferring an economic resource does not stop an obligation being a liability.
keywords: Likelihood is not the test in either direction
a low chance of transferring an economic resource does not stop an obligation being a liability

options.text: The returns policy only, because the company has no practical ability to act inconsistently with a published policy it has always honoured
options.why: A constructive obligation is what arises from an entity's customary practices, published policies or specific statements once acting against them is no longer practically open to it. Eleven years of a published policy honoured without exception is that. The ex gratia payment fails a different test: a mere plan inside the boardroom is not enough, since neither an intention to make a transfer nor a high likelihood carries the weight needed to say the company cannot avoid it.
keywords: customary practices, published policies or specific statements
neither an intention to make a transfer nor a high likelihood carries the weight

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers what turns a practice or a policy into a constructive obligation, and why an unspoken boardroom intention — however likely to be carried out — falls short of that test

items.scenario: Two matters sit before the board of Nandini Retail Ltd at 31 March 2026. First, the company has published a returns policy on every till receipt and on its website for eleven years, refunding goods within sixty days without asking for a reason, and it has never refused a request. Second, the board discussed in March making an ex gratia payment to the families of two employees killed in an accident, resolved that it intended to do so, and has told nobody outside the boardroom.

items.stem: How does the going concern basis bear on the finance head's argument?

options.text: The argument succeeds, so the levy is a contingent liability disclosed rather than an obligation
options.misconception: accepts the avoidance argument and then reaches for a disclosure category, when the going concern conclusion has already closed off the avoidance route
options.why: The avoidance argument does not survive. Once the entity concludes it is a going concern, it has concluded it cannot avoid what only shutting down would avoid, so the question is not whether an obligation can exist but when the past event brings it into existence.
keywords: when the past event brings it into existence

options.text: The going concern basis is about disclosure of uncertainties and has no bearing on whether an obligation exists
options.misconception: knows the going concern rule only from the presentation standard and misses the use the Framework makes of it inside the definition of a liability
options.why: Going concern does two jobs. One is the basis on which the statements are prepared and the disclosure of material uncertainties about it. The other is this one — the Framework uses the conclusion itself as evidence about what the entity can and cannot practically avoid.
keywords: as evidence about what the entity can and cannot practically avoid

options.text: A conclusion that the going concern basis is appropriate is itself a conclusion that the entity cannot avoid a transfer escapable only by ceasing to trade
options.why: A duty that only bites if the entity takes some action of its own choosing is still an obligation once the entity has no realistic way to refrain from that action — that is what conditional on an action the entity may itself choose to take means here. And the going concern basis is not neutral on the point: preparing the accounts on that basis is itself a finding that the only escape from the levy is shutting the terminals down, whether that is phrased as by liquidating the entity or by ceasing to trade. Both cannot be said, and the finance head is trying to say both.
keywords: conditional on an action the entity may itself choose to take
by liquidating the entity or by ceasing to trade

options.text: The argument succeeds for later years and fails for the current year, because only the current year's levy is certain
options.misconception: uses certainty to sort the years, when the Framework's sorting is done by the past event test and not by how sure the outcome is
options.why: Certainty is not the sorter. A present obligation arises from a past event only where the entity has already obtained economic benefits or taken an action and as a consequence will or may have to transfer a resource. Operating in the year is the action; that is why the current year is caught, and it has nothing to do with how certain anything is.
keywords: already obtained economic benefits or taken an action

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers how a self-triggered duty still counts as an obligation once avoiding the trigger is not practically open, and how the going concern conclusion itself settles that question, alongside the past-event test that fixes when a present obligation actually arises

items.scenario: A new state law charges every operator of a chemical storage terminal an environmental levy for each year in which it operates a terminal in the state. Ashwini Terminals Ltd operates two terminals there and its financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 are prepared on a going concern basis. The finance head argues that the company has a practical ability to avoid the levy for later years, since it could simply stop operating the terminals, and that no obligation for those years therefore exists at any time.

items.stem: How should the two agreements be treated under the Conceptual Framework?

options.text: As a single unit of account measured at the fair value of the copper at 31 March 2026
options.misconception: gets the unit of account right and then measures something that does not exist, since the combined arrangement creates no rights or obligations to measure
options.why: Choosing the unit of account comes first and it decides what there is to measure. Here the answer is nothing, because the two sets of rights and obligations nullify each other. There is no exposure to the copper price to put a value on.
keywords: decides what there is to measure

options.text: As a single unit of account, whose combined effect is that no rights and no obligations have been created
options.why: Reporting the substance of a group or series of contracts designed to achieve an overall commercial effect can require treating what they produce as a single unit of account rather than several. The Framework's own illustration is this exact pairing — two contracts struck with the same counterparty on the same day, where each side's promise is the exact mirror of the other's, so netted together the pair create no rights or obligations for either party to carry.
keywords: designed to achieve an overall commercial effect

options.text: As two separate contracts, each recognised and measured on its own terms
options.misconception: takes the legal form of two documents as fixing two units of account, when the unit of account is chosen to represent the substance faithfully
options.why: A unit of account is selected to provide useful information, which requires that what is reported about the item faithfully represents the substance of the transaction it arose from. Two agreements negotiated together that cancel each other have a substance the gross presentation would not show.

options.text: As two separate contracts, offset against each other in the balance sheet
options.misconception: confuses offsetting with selecting a single unit of account, which the Framework separates in terms
options.why: Offsetting is recognising and measuring an asset and a liability as separate units of account and then grouping them into one net amount, and it is generally not appropriate because it classifies dissimilar items together. Folding a whole bundle of rights and obligations into one single unit of account before recognition even starts is a different operation, and it is the right one here.
keywords: grouping them into one net amount

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers when a group of contracts gets treated as one unit of account rather than several, using mutually cancelling contracts with one counterparty as the illustration, and how that differs from offsetting two separately recognised items

items.scenario: On 14 February 2026 Chandrika Metals Ltd signed two agreements with the same counterparty on the same day. The first commits it to buy 5,000 tonnes of copper in September at a fixed price. The second commits the same counterparty to buy the same 5,000 tonnes back from Chandrika in September at the same fixed price on the same date. Neither agreement can be assigned separately and the parties negotiated them together as one arrangement. The reporting date is 31 March 2026.

items.stem: Is the manager right that one unit of account must serve both purposes?

options.text: No — but only because the individual contracts are immaterial
options.misconception: reaches for materiality where the answer is the unit of account, so the reasoning would collapse the moment a contract grew large
options.why: The permission does not depend on size. The test is whether the information about the item and about the income and expenses it produces is relevant and faithfully represents the substance, and a portfolio measurement can be the answer for large contracts as readily as for small ones.
keywords: relevant and faithfully represents the substance

options.text: Yes — the unit of account is chosen once and governs recognition, measurement and presentation alike
options.misconception: treats the unit of account as a single decision taken once, when the Framework contemplates different units at different stages
options.why: Even presentation is not tied to it. When it comes to putting the numbers in front of a reader, an item may well need to be split or grouped again — assets, liabilities, income and expenses can each be aggregated or separated into components for that purpose — so the choice is made for a purpose rather than fixed for all purposes.
keywords: made for a purpose rather than fixed for all purposes

options.text: No — recognition and measurement can each be given their own unit of account when the circumstances call for it
options.why: Choosing a unit of account means asking how the recognition criteria and the measurement concepts will apply to it, and that question can get two different answers depending on which stage is under consideration — recognition may point one way, while a different unit of account for measurement can serve the numbers better. Contracts recognised individually but measured as part of a portfolio is the example the Framework itself gives.
keywords: recognition may point one way, while a different unit of account for measurement
measured as part of a portfolio

options.text: Yes — unless the contracts are interdependent, in which case they form one inseparable unit
options.misconception: applies the rule about interdependent rights and obligations arising from the same source to unrelated contracts with different customers
options.why: Interdependence is about rights and obligations arising from the same source, such as the two sides of one contract, which cannot be separated and so form a single asset or liability. Thousands of contracts with different customers are not interdependent; they are simply measured together because that produces the more useful information.
keywords: measured together because that produces the more useful information

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers why recognition and measurement can each get their own unit of account, illustrated by contracts booked one by one but valued together as a portfolio, and the underlying requirement that whatever unit is picked must faithfully represent the transaction's substance

items.scenario: Latika Insurance Broking Ltd writes several thousand small annual service contracts a year, each individually trivial. It brings each contract on to its records as it is signed, so that the contract count and the customer records agree, but it estimates the obligations arising under them across the whole portfolio, because no single contract can be estimated sensibly on its own. A new manager says this is inconsistent and that the recognition and measurement units must match.

items.stem: What does the Conceptual Framework say exists at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A right to receive 12,000 tonnes and a separate obligation to pay ₹50.4 crore, both recognised gross
options.misconception: splits the two sides of the executory contract into an asset and a liability, when they are one inseparable unit of account
options.why: The right and the obligation come from the same source and are interdependent, so they are a single inseparable asset or liability and form a single unit of account. Presenting them gross would report two things where the substance is one.
keywords: report two things where the substance is one

options.text: Nothing, because neither party has performed and no past event has occurred
options.misconception: confuses an equally unperformed contract with no contract, when the Framework treats the executory contract itself as a single asset or liability
options.why: Equally unperformed is precisely what an executory contract is, and the Framework gives it an element rather than nothing. Signing the contract is the past event; what neither party has done is perform under it.
keywords: Equally unperformed is precisely what an executory contract is
Signing the contract is the past event

options.text: A single liability, because the combined right and obligation are inseparable and the terms of the exchange are currently unfavourable
options.why: What an executory contract establishes is a combined right and obligation to exchange economic resources, and neither half of that pairing can be pulled apart from the other, so together, interdependent and cannot be separated, they form one single asset or one single liability. Which of the two turns on price: a liability if they are currently unfavourable, an asset if the opposite holds. At ₹42,000 against ₹31,000 the terms favour the seller, so Nirmala has a liability — whether it goes into the financial statements is the separate question of recognition and measurement, including any onerous test.
keywords: a liability if they are currently unfavourable
the separate question of recognition and measurement

options.text: A liability, which must in every case be recognised immediately at the ₹13.2 crore difference
options.misconception: takes meeting the definition of a liability as compelling recognition and a particular measure, when the Framework separates the definition from both
options.why: Whether such a liability is included in the financial statements depends on the recognition criteria and on the measurement basis selected for it, including any test for whether the contract is onerous. The definition is met; what follows from it is decided by the applicable Ind AS, not by the definition.
keywords: decided by the applicable Ind AS

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers what an executory contract is, why its combined right and obligation cannot be split into two line items, how the direction of price movement decides asset versus liability, and why meeting that definition still leaves recognition and measurement as separate questions

items.scenario: In November 2025 Nirmala Ceramics Ltd contracted to buy 12,000 tonnes of a glaze material in August 2026 at ₹42,000 a tonne. Neither side has done anything under the contract at 31 March 2026 and neither can walk away from it. By that date the price of the same material for August delivery has fallen to ₹31,000 a tonne. The financial controller says that because no goods have been delivered and no money has been paid, there is nothing at all at the reporting date.

items.stem: Is there a present obligation to pay the salary at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes — because a contractual liability to pay cash can exist before the payment falls due
options.misconception: correctly recalls that enforceability may be deferred, then applies it to a contract where nothing has yet been performed on either side
options.why: It is true that a present obligation can exist even though a transfer cannot be enforced until a future date — a liability to pay cash next year exists now. But that presupposes a present obligation, and here there is none, because the company has not yet received anything for which it must pay.
keywords: cannot be enforced until a future date

options.text: Yes — the company has no practical ability to avoid the payments, which is the definition of an obligation
options.misconception: satisfies the no-practical-ability limb and stops there, forgetting that the past event criterion has to be met as well
options.why: All three criteria must hold, not one. There must be an obligation, it must be to transfer an economic resource, and it must be a present obligation as a result of past events. The third is missing until the services are received.
keywords: All three criteria must hold, not one
missing until the services are received

options.text: No — the contract is executory until the services are received, so no present obligation to pay has arisen
options.why: Past events are what a present obligation depends on, and the test asks something specific of them: has the entity already obtained economic benefits or taken an action, such that, as a consequence, it will or may have to transfer a resource it would not otherwise have had to transfer. Nothing in that description fits Pallavi yet — the engineer has not worked a day. Until services are received the contract stays executory: what Pallavi holds is a combined right to future services and obligation to pay for them, bundled together as one inseparable item rather than standing as a liability for the salary on its own.
keywords: already obtained economic benefits or taken an action
a combined right to future services and obligation to pay for them

options.text: No — but only for the second year, since the first year's services are highly likely to be received
options.misconception: splits the contract by likelihood, when likelihood plays no part in whether a past event has occurred
options.why: Nothing has been received for either year. The past event test asks what the entity has already obtained or already done, and expecting to receive services next year is neither. Likelihood does not create a past event.
keywords: what the entity has already obtained or already done
Likelihood does not create a past event

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the past-event test for a present obligation, illustrated by a salary contract that creates no obligation to pay until the employee's services are actually received

items.scenario: Pallavi Analytics Ltd signs a two-year employment contract with a senior engineer on 1 March 2026 at ₹36 lakh a year. The engineer joins on 1 April 2026 and has done no work for the company by 31 March 2026. The chief financial officer proposes to recognise a liability of ₹72 lakh at 31 March 2026 for the salaries the company is committed to pay, on the ground that the contract is signed and the company cannot get out of it.

items.stem: Can the ₹9 crore be carried in the balance sheet?

options.text: Yes — because the future economic benefits from the campaign are probable
options.misconception: imports a probability test as though satisfying it were a permission to recognise, when the definition has to be met first and the Framework sets no probability threshold anyway
options.why: Probability answers a question that does not arise until an asset exists. There is no right here with the potential to produce economic benefits that the company controls, and the Framework itself prescribes no probability criterion — that is Ind AS 38's gate, and it is a further hurdle rather than a doorway.
keywords: a question that does not arise until an asset exists
a further hurdle rather than a doorway

options.text: No — matching is not an objective of the Framework, and nothing may sit in the balance sheet unless it meets the definition of an asset, a liability or equity
options.why: Income and its related expenses sometimes land in the same period, and people call that matching costs with income — but it is a by-product of how the entries fall, not a goal the Framework chases, and matching costs with income is not an objective of the Conceptual Framework. What actually gates the balance sheet is the definition: nothing sits there unless it meets the definition of an asset, a liability or equity, and spending on a campaign leaves the company with no right it controls.
keywords: not an objective of the Conceptual Framework
unless it meets the definition of an asset, a liability or equity

options.text: No — but the ₹9 crore may be recognised in equity as a capital maintenance adjustment
options.misconception: borrows a term from the capital maintenance discussion to park a cost outside profit or loss, when capital maintenance adjustments arise from restating assets and liabilities and not from spending
options.why: Capital maintenance adjustments arise where the revaluation or restatement of assets and liabilities produces increases or decreases in equity that a particular concept of capital maintenance keeps out of profit. Nothing has been revalued or restated here; a cost has been incurred and there is no asset to hold it.
keywords: revaluation or restatement of assets and liabilities

options.text: Yes — as a prepayment, since the benefit relates to a later period
options.misconception: reaches for the prepayment label to hold a cost whose benefit is in the future, when a prepayment is a right to receive goods or services still to be delivered
options.why: A prepayment is an asset because the entity holds a right to goods or services it has paid for and not yet received. Here the services have been received and consumed — the advertisements ran. What remains is a hope about revenue, which is not a right.
keywords: right to goods or services it has paid for and not yet received
a hope about revenue, which is not a right

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers why matching costs to income is not something the Framework sets out to achieve, and why the definition of an asset, a liability or equity is the actual gate for the balance sheet

items.scenario: Ishaan Beverages Ltd spent ₹9 crore during the year ended 31 March 2026 on a launch campaign for a drink that goes on sale in June 2026. The marketing head asks for the ₹9 crore to be carried forward in the balance sheet as deferred launch expenditure and released against the revenue the drink earns, on the ground that the cost was incurred to earn that revenue and that matching costs with income is a principle of financial reporting.

items.stem: Does meeting the definition of a liability compel recognition here?

options.text: No — because the probability of an outflow decides it, and the lawyers cannot say the outflow is probable
options.misconception: applies a probability threshold the Framework does not contain, and misreads advice that an obligation probably exists as advice about the outflow
options.why: The Framework sets no probability threshold for recognition. A low probability of an outflow is one factor that may make recognition irrelevant, and it does not decide the matter on its own. Here it is the measurement, not the probability, that defeats faithful representation.
keywords: sets no probability threshold for recognition
does not decide the matter on its own

options.text: Yes — recognition follows automatically once an item meets the definition of an element
options.misconception: reads the definitions as the whole of the recognition test, when meeting one is necessary and not sufficient
options.why: Only items meeting a definition are recognised, but not all items that meet a definition are recognised. The Framework adds the two criteria of relevance and faithful representation precisely because recognising some items that meet a definition would not give useful information.
keywords: not all items that meet a definition are recognised

options.text: No — where measurement uncertainty is so high that no available measure would be useful, the item is not recognised, and the uncertainty is explained instead
options.why: Recognition requires both relevant information and a faithful representation. In limited circumstances all the relevant measures available may be subject to measurement uncertainty so high that none would provide useful information even accompanied by an explanation, and in those circumstances the asset or liability is not recognised. An exceptionally wide range of outcomes whose probabilities cannot be estimated, and a measure exceptionally sensitive to small changes in them, are two of the named circumstances. Whether or not the item is recognised, explanatory information about the uncertainty may need to be provided.
keywords: both relevant information and a faithful representation

options.text: No — because a high level of measurement uncertainty always prevents recognition
options.misconception: turns a limited circumstance into a rule, when even a high level of measurement uncertainty does not necessarily prevent an estimate from being useful
options.why: The use of reasonable estimates is an essential part of preparing financial information and even a high level of measurement uncertainty does not necessarily stop an estimate providing useful information. It is only in limited circumstances, where no available measure would be useful, that recognition falls away.
keywords: does not necessarily stop an estimate providing useful information

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: the two recognition criteria of relevant information and faithful representation, the circumstances in which the level of measurement uncertainty may be so high that a measure does not provide a sufficiently faithful representation, including an exceptionally wide range of outcomes whose probabilities are exceptionally difficult to estimate and a measure exceptionally sensitive to small changes in those probabilities, the statement that in limited circumstances the asset or liability would not be recognised, and the requirement that explanatory information about the uncertainties may need to be provided whether or not the item is recognised

items.scenario: Bhairavi Pharmaceuticals Ltd is defending a claim brought by a regulator in another country. Its lawyers advise that an obligation probably exists but that the possible outcomes run from nothing to an amount larger than the company's net worth, that the probability of each outcome cannot sensibly be estimated, and that the answer is exceptionally sensitive to small changes in those probabilities. The audit committee is told that because the definition of a liability is met, a number has to go on the balance sheet whatever its quality.

items.stem: What does the Conceptual Framework's derecognition principle say about removing the receivables?

options.text: They stay on, because Meghna keeps exposure to swings in the benefits the receivables produce, which points to continuing control
options.why: Losing control is what triggers derecognition, and control has not gone here even though title has moved. Meghna retains exposure to significant positive or negative variations in what the receivables go on to yield, and that lingering exposure is the sign the Framework treats as evidence the entity might continue to control the asset. A shortfall guarantee on the downside and a return of the excess on the upside leaves both variations with Meghna.
keywords: retains exposure to significant positive or negative variations
might continue to control the asset

options.text: They come off, and Meghna recognises a provision for the shortfall guarantee
options.misconception: derecognises the asset and replaces the retained exposure with a provision, which reports a transfer that in substance has not happened
options.why: Recognising a provision would present the arrangement as a completed transfer plus a separate risk taken on, which is not what has occurred. In substance Meghna still holds the receivables and the ₹52 crore it received is consideration it must account for as a financial liability.
keywords: a completed transfer plus a separate risk taken on
account for as a financial liability

options.text: The ₹52 crore of receivables covered by the guarantee comes off and the remaining ₹8 crore stays
options.misconception: splits the asset by the size of the guarantee, when the transferred and retained components are identified by what has actually gone and not by a money amount
options.why: The distinction the Framework draws is between the component that has expired, been consumed, collected, fulfilled or transferred and the component retained. Nothing here has been collected or genuinely transferred, so there is no transferred component to split off, and the guarantee amount is not a dividing line.
keywords: between the component that has expired
no transferred component to split off

options.text: They come off, because the legal transfer of title means control has passed
options.misconception: settles derecognition on legal form, when faithful representation requires the substance of the rights and obligations to be reported
options.why: Financial statements report the substance of contractual rights and obligations, and where substance and legal form differ, reporting only the form does not faithfully represent the transaction. The title has moved; the exposure to what the receivables actually produce has not.
keywords: report the substance of contractual rights and obligations
the exposure to what the receivables actually produce has not

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers when an apparent transfer of an asset still fails to earn derecognition because control has not actually left — evidenced here by continued exposure to the ups and downs in what the asset produces

items.scenario: On 20 March 2026 Meghna Wires Ltd assigned trade receivables of ₹60 crore to a finance company and received ₹52 crore at once. Under the agreement Meghna must make good any shortfall between ₹52 crore and what the finance company actually collects, and anything collected above ₹52 crore is returned to Meghna after the finance company retains an interest charge. The directors want to remove the receivables from the balance sheet because legal title has passed.

items.stem: What happens to the retained component on this derecognition?

options.text: It continues to be recognised as a unit of account separate from the transferred component, with no income or expense arising on it
options.why: Two things happen on a partial disposal: the piece that has gone is derecognised and its income and expenses recognised, and the piece that stays keeps being recognised as its own unit — it becomes a unit of account separate from the transferred component. Nothing hits profit or loss for that surviving piece purely because a sale happened elsewhere in the same asset, unless the derecognition results in a change in the measurement requirements that apply to it, and here it does not.
keywords: unless the derecognition results in a change in the measurement requirements
becomes a unit of account separate from the transferred component

options.text: The whole right is derecognised and the retained five regions are recognised afresh at fair value
options.misconception: treats a partial derecognition as a disposal and reacquisition, which the retained component rule exists to prevent
options.why: The retained component is continued in recognition, not removed and brought back. That is the point of describing it as a component that carries on, presented separately in the balance sheet, rather than as a new asset.
keywords: continued in recognition, not removed and brought back
presented separately in the balance sheet

options.text: It is remeasured to fair value, with the gain in profit or loss, as happens whenever part of an asset is disposed of
options.misconception: generalises the loss-of-control-of-a-subsidiary rule into a rule for every partial disposal, when that case works only because the measurement requirements themselves change
options.why: The parent that loses control of a subsidiary and keeps a minority holding does remeasure what it retains to fair value, and the Framework gives it as the example of the exception — it works because the measurement principles applicable to the retained holding change. Where they do not change, nothing happens on the retained component.
keywords: gives it as the example of the exception
Where they do not change, nothing happens

options.text: A gain is recognised across the whole eight-region right, since one transaction has established its value
options.misconception: lets a price observed on part of an asset flow through to the part still held, ignoring that the two are now separate units of account
options.why: Once the transferred component goes, the retained component is a separate unit of account and its measurement follows its own requirements. A price obtained for something else is not a reason to remeasure it.
keywords: not a reason to remeasure it

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers how a partial derecognition is handled — the piece disposed of drops out with its income and expense recognised, the piece kept on continues as its own unit of account, and no gain or loss is booked on that surviving piece purely because of the disposal unless the measurement basis for it has itself changed, with the retained piece shown as a separate line

items.scenario: Sarayu Media Ltd held a broadcasting right for eight regions. On 1 January 2026 it sold the right for three of those regions outright, keeping the right for the other five with no continuing involvement in the three. The measurement requirements that apply to the retained five-region right are unchanged by the sale. The financial controller proposes to remeasure the retained right to its current market value and take the increase to profit or loss, arguing that the sale of the three regions has proved what the whole right is worth.

items.stem: Which measurement basis is the company applying?

options.text: Value in use
options.why: Value in use is the present value of the cash flows, or other economic benefits, that an entity expects to derive from the use of an asset and from its ultimate disposal. It reflects entity-specific assumptions rather than those of market participants, cannot be observed directly and is determined using cash-flow-based measurement techniques, and while it ignores the transaction costs incurred on initial recognition it does take in the present value of the costs to be incurred on disposal. Every feature of the description matches.
keywords: from the use of an asset and from its ultimate disposal
present value of the costs to be incurred on disposal

options.text: Current cost
options.misconception: confuses an entry value with an exit value, since current cost asks what would be paid to obtain the asset today rather than what using it will yield
options.why: Current cost is an entry value, like historical cost. For an asset it is the consideration that would be paid to acquire an equivalent asset at the measurement date plus the transaction costs that would be incurred. It looks at what the entity would give, not at what the asset will produce.
keywords: an entry value, like historical cost

options.text: Fulfilment value
options.misconception: applies the liability-side name to an asset, when fulfilment value and value in use are the entity-specific measures for the two different elements
options.why: Fulfilment value is the present value of whatever cash or other economic resources the entity will, on its own reckoning, be obliged to transfer as it fulfils a liability. It is the mirror of value in use on the liability side, and a furnace is not a liability.
keywords: obliged to transfer as it fulfils a liability
the mirror of value in use

options.text: Fair value
options.misconception: reads any present value calculation as a fair value, missing that fair value takes market participants' assumptions and does not deduct the costs of disposal
options.why: What fair value asks is what an orderly sale of the asset would fetch between market participants, so it takes their assumptions rather than the entity's own, and it is measured without deducting the transaction costs that would be incurred on disposal. Both features are the opposite of what this company has done.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers the five measurement bases and what tells them apart — whose assumptions each one uses, entry versus exit, and how each one treats transaction costs

items.scenario: Vidya Steel Ltd measures a purpose-built furnace at the present value of the cash flows it expects to derive from operating the furnace and from selling it for scrap at the end of its working life, less the present value of the costs it expects to incur in that final disposal. The estimates use the company's own assumptions about how it will run the plant, which differ from what an average buyer in the market would assume, and no price for a furnace of this design can be observed anywhere.

items.stem: How should the board answer the shareholder?

options.text: Fair value must be used wherever it can be measured, and historical cost only where it cannot
options.misconception: ranks fair value above the other bases as a default, when the choice turns on the information each produces for the particular asset and business
options.why: There is no such ranking. Where an entity holds assets solely for use or solely to collect contractual cash flows, information reflecting changes in their fair value may not provide predictive value or confirmatory value at all, so a measurable fair value is not automatically the more relevant one.
keywords: may not provide predictive value or confirmatory value

options.text: A mixed measurement approach is deliberate, and for resources used in combination historical cost or current cost is likely to give the more relevant information
options.why: Several economic resources working together to produce and market goods only generate cash indirectly, and for that kind of activity an entry-price basis — historical cost or current cost — tends to be the more informative choice, because it lets margins be derived. A basis built on exit prices earns its keep elsewhere: where an asset produces cash flows directly and can be sold independently without significant penalty. Ind AS is deliberately a mixed system rather than a fair value system, and a mixture of bases chosen for the information each gives is not the same thing as an inconsistency.
keywords: produces cash flows directly and can be sold independently
not the same thing as an inconsistency

options.text: The shareholder is right, because consistency requires the same measurement basis to be used throughout the financial statements
options.misconception: reads consistency as one basis for everything, when it means using the same methods for the same items rather than for all items
options.why: Consistency is using the same methods for the same items, from period to period and across entities, and it is the means of achieving comparability. Applying one basis to unlike items would be uniformity, which the Framework distinguishes and does not ask for.
keywords: the same methods for the same items
which the Framework distinguishes and does not ask for

options.text: Using different bases for different assets is a weakness the standard-setter tolerates, and the company should reduce the number of bases to as few as possible
options.misconception: treats the mixed system as a defect being managed, when it is the considered answer, and turns a remark about understandability into an instruction
options.why: Understandability does depend partly on how many bases are used, and using more of them can make the totals less informative. But the Framework's answer is that it can be appropriate to use more bases where that is necessary to provide useful information, which makes the number a consequence of the choice rather than a target.
keywords: can make the totals less informative
a consequence of the choice rather than a target

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers what steers the choice of measurement basis toward entry prices or exit prices depending on how the business earns cash from the asset, and why a deliberately mixed system is not the same thing as inconsistency

items.scenario: A shareholder of Bhagirathi Papers Ltd writes to the board saying that the company appears to use a mixed measurement approach, that mixed must mean inconsistent, and that everything from the paper machines to the inventory should be carried at fair value so the accounts hold together. The company's machines and its pulp stock produce cash only when used together to make and sell paper, and it has no intention of selling either.

items.stem: What is the retained profit for the year under financial capital maintenance measured in units of constant purchasing power?

options.text: A loss of ₹80,000
options.why: Closing capital is ₹8,80,000, being sales of ₹12,80,000 less drawings of ₹4,00,000, and it is all cash. The capital to be maintained is the opening capital expressed in closing prices, which is ₹8,00,000 multiplied by 120 and divided by 100, or ₹9,60,000. Retained profit is ₹8,80,000 less ₹9,60,000, a loss of ₹80,000, and the negative figure says the business no longer has the purchasing power it started with.
keywords: opening capital expressed in closing prices

options.text: A loss of ₹1,60,000
options.misconception: reports the capital maintenance adjustment itself as the loss, rather than the shortfall of closing capital against the restated opening capital
options.why: ₹9,60,000 less ₹8,00,000 is ₹1,60,000, the amount by which opening capital had to be restated. That figure is the capital maintenance adjustment and it goes to equity. The loss is what is left when the restated capital is set against the ₹8,80,000 actually held.
keywords: the amount by which opening capital had to be restated

options.text: A profit of ₹80,000
options.misconception: answers under financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units, comparing closing capital with the unrestated opening figure
options.why: ₹8,80,000 less the unrestated ₹8,00,000 is ₹80,000, and that is the right answer to the nominal question. Constant purchasing power asks a different one — whether the closing capital buys what the opening capital bought — and the opening figure has to be restated to closing prices before the comparison is made.
keywords: the right answer to the nominal question

options.text: A profit of ₹4,80,000
options.misconception: reports the trading margin as retained profit, ignoring both the drawings and the restatement of opening capital
options.why: ₹12,80,000 less the ₹8,00,000 cost of the units is the margin on trading. Retained profit under any capital maintenance concept compares capital at the end with capital at the beginning after excluding distributions to owners, so the ₹4,00,000 withdrawn comes out and the opening figure is restated.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers financial capital maintenance under both nominal monetary units and constant purchasing power, and how the general price rise gets split off into equity as a capital maintenance adjustment rather than counted as profit

items.scenario: Kaushalya Traders began the year on 1 April 2025 with capital of ₹8,00,000, represented by 4,000 units of a single product bought at ₹200 each. During the year it sold all 4,000 units at ₹320 each and bought no more, and the proprietor withdrew ₹4,00,000. At 31 March 2026 the business holds only cash. The general price index stood at 100 at the beginning of the year and 120 at the end.

items.stem: Under physical capital maintenance, how is the ₹10,00,000 increase treated?

options.text: ₹6,00,000 is profit and ₹4,00,000 is a capital maintenance adjustment
options.misconception: gives the constant purchasing power answer, splitting the rise at the general price index, where the physical concept treats the whole of it as an adjustment
options.why: The split is real arithmetic under the wrong concept. Eight per cent of ₹50,00,000 is ₹4,00,000, the general price effect, and under financial capital maintenance in units of constant purchasing power the remaining ₹6,00,000 would be profit. The physical concept makes no such split, because every price change is a change in the measure of productive capacity.
keywords: real arithmetic under the wrong concept

options.text: Nothing arises under any concept of capital until the metal is sold
options.misconception: answers the recognition question in place of the capital maintenance one, when the concept of capital fixes what profit is whether or not an entry is made
options.why: Recognition and the concept of capital are different questions. It is true that a holding gain may not be recognised until disposal, but that is a statement about when an entry is made under one concept, not about how the concept defines profit. Under the physical concept the ₹10,00,000 is a capital maintenance adjustment now and it will never be profit.
keywords: Recognition and the concept of capital are different questions

options.text: The whole ₹10,00,000 is a capital maintenance adjustment in equity, and the retained profit for the year is nil
options.why: Under the physical concept, capital is the entity's physical productive capacity, and all price changes affecting the entity's assets and liabilities are viewed as changes in the measurement of that capacity, so the whole rise is capital maintenance adjustments that are part of equity rather than earnings passing through the statement of profit and loss. The company can still buy the same 10,000 tonnes, so its productive capacity is unchanged and there is no profit.
keywords: all price changes affecting the entity's assets and liabilities
capital maintenance adjustments that are part of equity

options.text: The whole ₹10,00,000 is profit, because the net assets are worth that much more than at the start
options.misconception: gives the nominal financial capital maintenance answer to a question asked under the physical concept
options.why: Under financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units, holding gains are indeed conceptually profits, though they may not be recognised as such until the assets are disposed of in an exchange transaction. That is a different concept of capital, and the question is asked under the physical one.
keywords: holding gains are indeed conceptually profits

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: covers physical capital maintenance, where every price change on the entity's assets and liabilities is read as a change in productive capacity and booked to equity rather than profit, contrasted with the nominal and constant-purchasing-power answers to the same facts

items.scenario: Nandan Alloys Ltd began the year holding 10,000 tonnes of a metal costing ₹500 a tonne, being net assets of ₹50,00,000, and that stock is the whole of its business. During the year it sold nothing, bought nothing, paid no dividend and issued no shares. At the year end the current cost of the metal is ₹600 a tonne, so the same 10,000 tonnes would now cost ₹60,00,000 to buy. The general price index rose from 100 to 108 over the year. The company applies the physical concept of capital.

items.stem: How much revenue does the manufacturer recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Revenue for the 60 per cent the agent has sold to end customers
options.why: Control of consigned goods does not pass on despatch — the agent can return them and holds them for the manufacturer. Control passes when the agent sells to a customer, so only those units have satisfied a performance obligation under Ind AS 115.
keywords: Control of consigned goods does not pass on despatch
Control passes when the agent sells to a customer

options.text: Revenue spread evenly over the consignment period
options.misconception: converts a point-in-time obligation into an over-time one without meeting any criterion
options.why: Over-time recognition needs one of the Ind AS 115 criteria — the customer consuming the benefit as the entity performs, or the entity creating an asset the customer controls. A consignment of finished goods meets none of them.
keywords: the customer consuming the benefit as the entity performs
A consignment of finished goods meets none of them

options.text: Revenue for the full despatch, since the goods have left the premises
options.misconception: treats despatch as sale, the recognition trigger Ind AS 115 replaced
options.why: Despatch moves the goods, not control. The agent has no obligation to pay for unsold units and can return them, so the manufacturer still controls them.
keywords: Despatch moves the goods, not control
no obligation to pay for unsold units

options.text: No revenue until the agent remits the money
options.misconception: uses receipt of cash as the recognition trigger
options.why: Collection is a separate matter from recognition. Once control of a unit has passed to an end customer, the obligation is satisfied whether or not the agent has remitted.
keywords: Collection is a separate matter from recognition
satisfied whether or not the agent has remitted

citation.ref: para 31

items.scenario: A manufacturer despatches goods to a consignment agent on 28 March 2026. The agent holds the goods, can return any unsold units, and sells to end customers on the manufacturer's behalf. By 31 March the agent has sold 60 per cent of the units to customers.

items.stem: Which inventory cost formula does Ind AS 2 not permit?

options.text: Specific identification
options.misconception: forgets the formula required for non-interchangeable items
options.why: Specific identification is not merely permitted — it is required where items are not ordinarily interchangeable, such as goods segregated for a specific project.
keywords: not merely permitted — it is required
where items are not ordinarily interchangeable

options.text: LIFO
options.why: Ind AS 2 allows specific identification for non-interchangeable items, and FIFO or weighted average for the rest. LIFO is expressly not an option — in a rising price environment it books the newest, dearest cost first and leaves inventory at stale values.
keywords: LIFO is expressly not an option

options.text: Weighted average
options.misconception: assumes averaging is imprecise and therefore barred
options.why: Weighted average is the other permitted formula — each purchase re-averages the cost pool, smoothing price swings instead of tracking layers. Averaging is a choice, not a defect.
keywords: Averaging is a choice, not a defect

options.text: FIFO
options.misconception: confuses the permitted default with the prohibited formula
options.why: FIFO is one of the two permitted formulas for interchangeable items — it assumes the oldest stock sells first, which is how most warehouses actually move goods.
keywords: one of the two permitted formulas for interchangeable items
assumes the oldest stock sells first

citation.ref: para 23 to 25

items.stem: Does the company control the investee under Ind AS 110?

options.text: No, but the investee is a joint venture
options.misconception: mislabels one-sided board control as joint control
options.why: Joint control requires unanimous consent of the sharing parties over relevant activities. A right to appoint four of seven directors is unilateral, not shared.
keywords: requires unanimous consent of the sharing parties

options.text: No, the 45 per cent holding gives significant influence and equity accounting
options.misconception: stops at the shareholding percentage and applies the associate test
options.why: Significant influence is the fallback when control is absent. Here the board rights give actual power, so the investee is a subsidiary and is consolidated.
keywords: the fallback when control is absent

options.text: No, because control requires holding more than half the voting power
options.misconception: equates control with majority shareholding
options.why: Majority voting power is one route to power, not the definition of it. Ind AS 110 was written precisely to catch control held through other means.
keywords: one route to power, not the definition of it
catch control held through other means

options.text: Yes — it has power through the board rights, variable returns, and the link between them
options.why: All three elements of control are present. Power does not have to come from a majority of shares; a contractual right to appoint the majority of the board directs the relevant activities just as effectively.
keywords: All three elements of control are present
Power does not have to come from a majority of shares

citation.ref: para 7

items.scenario: A company holds 45 per cent of the voting shares of an investee. A shareholders' agreement gives it the contractual right to appoint four of the seven directors, and its returns vary with the investee's performance.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 109 require instead?

options.text: An allowance once a receivable is more than 90 days overdue
options.misconception: imports the banking overdue norms into financial reporting
options.why: Ninety days is a prudential banking classification, not an Ind AS measurement rule. There is a rebuttable presumption of default at 90 days past due, but the allowance exists long before that.
keywords: a prudential banking classification, not an Ind AS measurement rule
the allowance exists long before that

options.text: A 12-month expected credit loss allowance unless credit risk has increased significantly
options.misconception: applies the general staging model where the simplified approach governs
options.why: The two-stage general model applies to loans and debt investments. Trade receivables take the simplified approach, which is lifetime losses without a staging test.
keywords: Trade receivables take the simplified approach
lifetime losses without a staging test

options.text: A lifetime expected credit loss allowance on trade receivables from initial recognition
options.why: Ind AS 109 replaced the incurred-loss model with expected credit losses, recognised before any default. For trade receivables the simplified approach removes the staging debate entirely — the allowance is always lifetime expected losses.
keywords: replaced the incurred-loss model with expected credit losses, recognised before any default
the allowance is always lifetime expected losses

options.text: The company's policy is compliant, since losses should not be anticipated
options.misconception: defends the incurred-loss model the standard replaced
options.why: Waiting for the loss event is exactly what Ind AS 109 abolished. Expected losses are an estimate of the future, made from the first day the receivable exists.
keywords: Waiting for the loss event is exactly what Ind AS 109 abolished
made from the first day the receivable exists

citation.ref: para 5.5.15

items.scenario: A company recognises a loss allowance on trade receivables only when a customer has actually defaulted, on the ground that anything earlier would be providing for losses that have not happened.

items.stem: Where does the ₹8 crore gain go under Ind AS 103?

options.text: Other comprehensive income, accumulated in capital reserve
options.why: This is the Indian carve-out. IFRS 3 takes a bargain purchase gain to profit or loss; Ind AS 103 routes it through other comprehensive income into capital reserve, keeping a purchase discount out of earnings.
keywords: routes it through other comprehensive income into capital reserve
keeping a purchase discount out of earnings

options.text: Reduced from the values of the assets acquired
options.misconception: treats the gain as a measurement error to be spread over assets
options.why: Reassessment happens first, and this scenario says it already has. Once the measurements stand, the difference is a recognised gain, not an allocation.
keywords: a recognised gain, not an allocation

options.text: Deferred and amortised to profit or loss over five years
options.misconception: invents an amortisation treatment the standard does not contain
options.why: Nothing in Ind AS 103 spreads a bargain purchase gain over time. It is recognised at once, in other comprehensive income.
keywords: Nothing in Ind AS 103 spreads a bargain purchase gain over time
recognised at once, in other comprehensive income

options.text: Profit or loss immediately
options.misconception: applies the IFRS 3 treatment where the Indian carve-out differs
options.why: Correct under IFRS 3, and the classic trap in an Ind AS paper. The carve-out exists precisely because recognising acquisition-day gains in earnings was thought unsuitable.
keywords: Correct under IFRS 3, and the classic trap in an Ind AS paper
recognising acquisition-day gains in earnings was thought unsuitable

citation.ref: para 34 and 36

items.scenario: A company acquires a business for ₹70 crore when the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is ₹78 crore. After reassessing the identification and measurement, the ₹8 crore difference remains.

items.stem: How is revenue recognised on the two contracts?

options.text: Both at a point in time, on completion of each project
options.misconception: defaults everything to completion without testing the over-time criteria
options.why: The factory meets two routes into over-time recognition. Deferring it all to completion would misstate every year the construction spans.
keywords: meets two routes into over-time recognition
Deferring it all to completion would misstate every year

options.text: Both over time, because construction contracts are always percentage-of-completion
options.misconception: carries the old AS 7 reflex into a standard that tests criteria, not contract type
options.why: There is no contract-type rule any more. Each contract is tested against the para 35 criteria, and the flats fail them — alternative use exists and payment rights do not.
keywords: alternative use exists and payment rights do not

options.text: The flats over time, since forty units means performance is continuous
options.misconception: reads continuous physical work as continuous transfer of control
options.why: Continuous effort is not the test — continuous transfer of control is. Buyers of the flats control nothing until handover, however steadily the builder works.
keywords: Continuous effort is not the test — continuous transfer of control is

options.text: The factory over time; the flats at a point in time on handover
options.why: The factory sits on the customer's land — the customer controls the asset as it is built — and there is an enforceable right to payment for work to date, so the over-time criteria are met. The flats have an alternative use to the builder and carry no right to payment before handover, so control passes only then.
