options.why: A taxable temporary difference reversing in the right period is a future taxable amount by construction — that is what makes it taxable — so it is the first thing to look at, not something outside the test.
keywords: a future taxable amount by construction

options.text: ₹13.75 crore
options.why: Where an entity has a history of recent losses, a deferred tax asset on unused tax losses is recognised only to the extent of sufficient taxable temporary differences, or convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit will be available. Here both exist — ₹35 crore of taxable temporary differences and ₹20 crore of evidenced profit, ₹55 crore in all, at 25 per cent.

options.text: ₹22.5 crore
options.misconception: recognises the asset on the whole of the carried-forward loss because the law allows the loss to be carried forward
options.why: That the law permits a carry forward says nothing about whether there will be profits to set it against. ₹35 crore of the ₹90 crore has nothing at all behind it, and the standard says in terms that to the extent it is not probable that taxable profit will be available, the asset is not recognised.

citation.ref: the recognition criteria for a deferred tax asset arising from the carry forward of unused tax losses, and the guidance that where an entity has a history of recent losses it recognises such an asset only to the extent of sufficient taxable temporary differences or convincing other evidence of sufficient future taxable profit

items.scenario: A company has made losses in each of the last three years and carries unused tax losses of ₹90 crore. It has taxable temporary differences of ₹35 crore relating to the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity, and they will reverse in periods in which the losses can still be set against them. Beyond that, its directors have convincing evidence of a further ₹20 crore of taxable profit from a contract already signed. Nothing else is in prospect. The tax rate is 25 per cent.

items.stem: How do these balances appear in the consolidated balance sheet?

options.text: A single net deferred tax asset of ₹3 crore
options.misconception: offsets across two taxable entities because they are inside one group and one consolidated balance sheet
options.why: Consolidation does not merge the tax positions. The second condition asks about the entities' intention to settle net, and without that intention the parent's asset and the subsidiary's liability are separate assets and liabilities of the group.
keywords: the entities' intention to settle net

options.text: A current asset of ₹7 crore and a current liability of ₹4 crore
options.misconception: gets the offsetting right and then presents deferred tax among current items
options.why: The netting is right and the classification is not. A deferred tax balance is presented as non-current whatever the timing of the reversals, so it never sits among current assets or current liabilities.

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹23 crore and a deferred tax liability of ₹20 crore
options.misconception: refuses to offset anywhere, treating the two conditions as never satisfied
options.why: Both conditions are satisfied inside each company — the same taxation authority, the same taxable entity, and a legally enforceable right to set off current tax. Showing ₹23 crore and ₹20 crore reports gross figures the standard requires to be netted.
keywords: Both conditions are satisfied inside each company

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹7 crore and a deferred tax liability of ₹4 crore, shown separately
options.why: Offsetting is permitted where there is a legally enforceable right to set off current tax and the balances relate to the same taxation authority on the same taxable entity — which is true inside each company and gives a net ₹7 crore asset in the parent and a net ₹4 crore liability in the subsidiary. Across two taxable entities it is permitted only where they intend to settle current tax on a net basis or realise and settle simultaneously, and here they do not, so the two net figures stand side by side.
keywords: intend to settle current tax on a net basis

citation.ref: the two conditions for offsetting deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities — a legally enforceable right to set off current tax, and balances levied by the same taxation authority on the same taxable entity or on different taxable entities that intend to settle net — read with the presentation of deferred tax balances as non-current

items.scenario: A group has two taxable entities, both taxed by the same taxation authority. The parent has a deferred tax asset of ₹18 crore and a deferred tax liability of ₹11 crore, both its own, and it has a legally enforceable right to set off its current tax assets against its current tax liabilities. The subsidiary has a deferred tax asset of ₹5 crore and a deferred tax liability of ₹9 crore, and it too has that right for its own current tax. Neither company intends to settle the other's current tax on a net basis, and no such settlement is possible.

items.stem: How are the two deferred tax benefits recognised?

options.text: ₹15 crore credited to profit or loss with goodwill untouched by it, and ₹5 crore reducing goodwill to ₹85 crore
options.why: The change in the acquirer's own deferred tax asset is recognised in the period of the business combination but is not part of the accounting for the combination, so it does not enter the measurement of goodwill. The acquiree's benefit is different — an acquired deferred tax benefit recognised within the measurement period from new information about facts existing at the acquisition date is applied to reduce the carrying amount of the goodwill on that acquisition.
keywords: not part of the accounting for the combination
applied to reduce the carrying amount of the goodwill

options.text: ₹15 crore reducing goodwill to ₹75 crore, and ₹5 crore credited to profit or loss
options.misconception: swaps the two, sending the acquirer's own benefit into goodwill and the acquiree's into income
options.why: Both figures are right and both are in the wrong place. The one that changes goodwill is the acquiree's, found within the measurement period; the one that goes to profit or loss is the acquirer's own.
keywords: Both figures are right and both are in the wrong place

options.text: Both go to profit or loss, ₹20 crore in all, and goodwill stays at ₹90 crore
options.misconception: sends every deferred tax benefit to profit or loss, ignoring what the measurement period is for
options.why: The measurement period exists so that new information about facts that already existed at the acquisition date corrects the acquisition accounting rather than the current year's result. The ₹5 crore falls squarely inside it.

options.text: Both reduce goodwill, taking it to ₹70 crore
options.misconception: treats every deferred tax benefit the acquisition brings to light as part of the purchase price allocation
options.why: The acquirer's own losses were never something it bought. They belonged to A Ltd before the deal and the deal only changed the odds of using them, so the ₹15 crore is A Ltd's own income and goodwill is not measured on it.

citation.ref: the requirement that a change in the acquirer's own deferred tax asset resulting from a business combination is recognised in the period of the combination but is not included in the accounting for it, and the requirement that acquired deferred tax benefits recognised within the measurement period from new information about facts existing at the acquisition date are applied to reduce the carrying amount of the related goodwill

items.scenario: A Ltd acquired B Ltd on 1 October 2025 and recognised provisional goodwill of ₹90 crore. Two things then happen. A Ltd has unused tax losses of its own on which it had recognised nothing, having had no prospect of profits to use them against; the acquisition makes ₹60 crore of those losses recoverable against B Ltd's future taxable profits. Separately, within the measurement period, new information about facts that existed at 1 October 2025 shows that ₹20 crore of B Ltd's own unused losses, left out of the provisional accounting, do meet the recognition criteria after all. The tax rate is 25 per cent.

items.stem: What goodwill arose on the acquisition, and what is the non-controlling interest at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Goodwill ₹36 crore and non-controlling interest ₹98 crore
options.why: The non-controlling interest at acquisition is 20 per cent of ₹380 crore, which is ₹76 crore, and goodwill is ₹340 crore plus ₹76 crore less ₹380 crore. Rolling the balance forward adds 20 per cent of the two years' profits of ₹135 crore, which is ₹27 crore, and deducts 20 per cent of the ₹25 crore dividend, which is ₹5 crore.
keywords: deducts 20 per cent of the ₹25 crore dividend

options.text: Goodwill ₹45 crore and non-controlling interest ₹107 crore
options.misconception: measures the non-controlling interest at the fair value implied by the price paid for the controlling stake, when the group elected the proportionate share
options.why: Grossing ₹340 crore up from 80 per cent gives ₹425 crore for the whole company and ₹85 crore for the outside 20 per cent, which is the fair value route and also usually wrong on its own terms because the price of control carries a premium. The election here was the proportionate share, so ₹76 crore is the opening figure.
keywords: The election here was the proportionate share

options.text: Goodwill ₹36 crore and non-controlling interest ₹103 crore
options.misconception: rolls the non-controlling interest forward on profits alone and leaves the dividend out
options.why: A dividend takes cash out of the subsidiary and out of every shareholder's stake in it, including the outside shareholders'. Their ₹5 crore share of it comes off the balance, so ₹103 crore overstates them by exactly that.

options.text: Goodwill ₹36 crore and non-controlling interest ₹76 crore
options.misconception: treats the non-controlling interest as an acquisition-date measurement that is never touched again
options.why: The measurement choice is made once, at the acquisition date; the balance is not. Profit or loss and other comprehensive income are attributed to the non-controlling interests every year after that, so ₹76 crore is where the balance starts and not where it stays.
keywords: The measurement choice is made once, at the acquisition date; the balance is not

citation.ref: the attribution of profit or loss and other comprehensive income to the non-controlling interests, read with Ind AS 103 paragraph 19 on measuring the non-controlling interest at the acquisition date

items.scenario: P Ltd acquired 80 per cent of S Ltd on 1 April 2024 for ₹340 crore in cash. S Ltd's identifiable net assets had a fair value of ₹380 crore on that date. P Ltd's policy, applied to this combination, is to measure the non-controlling interest at its proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets. S Ltd made a profit after tax of ₹60 crore in the year to 31 March 2025 and ₹75 crore in the year to 31 March 2026, had no other comprehensive income, and declared and paid a dividend of ₹25 crore during the year to 31 March 2026.

items.stem: What part of T Ltd's profit is attributable to the owners of the parent, and what is the non-controlling interest at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹43.2 crore and ₹148.8 crore
options.why: Consolidation begins from the date control is obtained, so only the nine months from 1 July are consolidated — ₹72 crore of the ₹96 crore. Sixty per cent of that, ₹43.2 crore, goes to the owners of the parent and forty per cent, ₹28.8 crore, is added to the ₹120 crore non-controlling interest.
keywords: Consolidation begins from the date control is obtained

options.text: ₹57.6 crore and ₹158.4 crore
options.misconception: consolidates the subsidiary's whole year including the three months before control was obtained
options.why: The three months to 30 June belong to T Ltd's former owners. Bringing them in reports as group profit ₹24 crore the group did not control when it was earned.
keywords: belong to T Ltd's former owners

options.text: ₹28.8 crore and ₹163.2 crore
options.misconception: swaps the two shares, giving the parent forty per cent and the non-controlling interests sixty
options.why: H Ltd owns 60 per cent, so 60 per cent of the ₹72 crore is the parent's. The two figures are the right arithmetic on the wrong percentages.
keywords: the right arithmetic on the wrong percentages

options.text: ₹43.2 crore and ₹158.4 crore
options.misconception: applies the acquisition date to the parent's share and the whole year to the non-controlling interests
options.why: One profit figure cannot be split on two different bases. The ₹72 crore of post-acquisition profit is what is attributed, and it is attributed 60 to 40.
keywords: One profit figure cannot be split on two different bases

citation.ref: the requirement that an investee is consolidated from the day control over it passes to the investor, read with the split of profit or loss between the parent's owners on one side and the non-controlling interests on the other

items.scenario: H Ltd acquired 60 per cent of T Ltd on 1 July 2025 and obtained control on that date. The non-controlling interest at acquisition was measured at ₹120 crore. T Ltd's profit after tax for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹96 crore, earned evenly through the year. T Ltd had no other comprehensive income and paid no dividend. H Ltd draws up its consolidated financial statements to 31 March 2026.

items.stem: What share of profit does A Ltd recognise, and what is the carrying amount of the investment at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Share of profit ₹25.5 lakh and carrying amount ₹202.5 lakh
options.why: The share of profit starts at 30 per cent of ₹90 lakh, or ₹27 lakh, and is reduced by the investor's share of the extra depreciation on the fair value uplift — ₹120 lakh over 24 years is ₹5 lakh a year, of which 30 per cent is ₹1.5 lakh. The carrying amount is ₹180 lakh of cost plus ₹25.5 lakh of profit plus ₹9 lakh of other comprehensive income less the ₹12 lakh dividend received.
keywords: the extra depreciation on the fair value uplift

options.text: Share of profit ₹27 lakh and carrying amount ₹204 lakh
options.misconception: takes the associate's profit as reported without adjusting for depreciation on the fair value uplift
options.why: B Ltd depreciates the building on its own carrying amount, which is ₹120 lakh below the fair value A Ltd effectively paid for its share of. Without the ₹1.5 lakh adjustment the equity method reports a share of a profit that is measured on the wrong base.

options.text: Share of profit ₹25.5 lakh and carrying amount ₹214.5 lakh
options.misconception: takes the dividend to income and leaves the investment untouched by it
options.why: A dividend from an associate is a return of part of the profit already picked up through the share of profit. Recognising it as income as well would count the same money twice, so it comes off the carrying amount instead.

options.text: Share of profit ₹25.5 lakh and carrying amount ₹193.5 lakh
options.misconception: leaves the share of the associate's other comprehensive income out of the running balance
options.why: The equity method follows the whole post-acquisition change in the investor's share of the associate's net assets, and other comprehensive income is part of that change. The ₹9 lakh goes into the carrying amount and into the investor's own other comprehensive income.

citation.ref: the equity method — cost adjusted for the post-acquisition change in the investor's share of net assets, the share of profit adjusted for depreciation of depreciable assets on their fair values at the acquisition date, the share of other comprehensive income, and distributions received reducing the carrying amount

items.scenario: A Ltd acquired 30 per cent of B Ltd on 1 April 2025 for ₹180 lakh and obtained significant influence. At that date B Ltd's identifiable net assets had a carrying amount of ₹400 lakh and a fair value of ₹520 lakh, the whole ₹120 lakh excess relating to a building with 24 years of remaining useful life which B Ltd depreciates on the straight line basis. For the year ended 31 March 2026 B Ltd made a profit of ₹90 lakh and other comprehensive income of ₹30 lakh, and declared and paid a dividend of ₹40 lakh.

items.stem: What does C Ltd recognise on acquisition, and what is the carrying amount of the investment at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A capital reserve of ₹20 lakh recorded directly in equity, and a carrying amount of ₹308 lakh
options.misconception: credits the capital reserve without carrying the investment at the share of net fair value that produced it
options.why: The credit to equity has to have a debit, and the debit is the investment. Leaving the investment at ₹260 lakh and still crediting ₹20 lakh to equity does not balance.

options.text: A gain of ₹20 lakh in profit or loss, and a carrying amount of ₹328 lakh
options.misconception: takes the excess of the share of net fair value over cost through profit or loss
options.why: The carrying amount is right. The excess is treated as a capital reserve and recorded directly in equity, so nothing about acquiring the associate touches the year's profit.

options.text: A capital reserve of ₹20 lakh recorded directly in equity, and a carrying amount of ₹328 lakh
options.why: C Ltd's share of the net fair value is 40 per cent of ₹700 lakh, or ₹280 lakh, which exceeds the ₹260 lakh cost by ₹20 lakh. That excess is a capital reserve recorded directly in equity, and the investment comes on at ₹280 lakh. The land is not depreciated so there is no adjustment to the share of profit, which is 40 per cent of ₹120 lakh, and ₹280 lakh plus ₹48 lakh is ₹328 lakh.
keywords: capital reserve recorded directly in equity

options.text: Goodwill of ₹20 lakh inside the investment, and a carrying amount of ₹308 lakh
options.misconception: compares cost with the share of net fair value the wrong way round and reads an excess of share over cost as goodwill
options.why: Goodwill arises only where the cost exceeds the share of net fair value. Here the share is the larger of the two, so there is no goodwill to sit inside the investment and ₹308 lakh is the cost carried forward with the excess never recognised at all.
keywords: only where the cost exceeds the share of net fair value

citation.ref: what happens on acquiring an associate where the two sides of the comparison do not match: if the investor's slice of the net fair value carried by the investee's identifiable assets and its liabilities runs above what was paid, the surplus is a capital reserve booked straight to equity; if the price runs above that slice, the difference is goodwill sitting inside the investment's carrying amount

items.scenario: C Ltd acquired 40 per cent of D Ltd on 1 April 2025 for ₹260 lakh and obtained significant influence. D Ltd's identifiable net assets had a fair value of ₹700 lakh at that date, the whole excess over their carrying amount being on a plot of land that is not depreciated. D Ltd made a profit of ₹120 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2026, had no other comprehensive income and paid no dividend.

items.stem: What does X Ltd recognise in its own financial statements?

options.text: Assets of ₹340 lakh and liabilities of ₹210 lakh
options.why: A joint operator recognises its assets including its share of any held jointly and its liabilities including its share of any incurred jointly. The contract gives X Ltd the whole warehouse of ₹240 lakh and the whole term loan of ₹180 lakh, and splits the rest — ₹80 lakh of equipment and ₹20 lakh of cash, and ₹30 lakh of trade payables.
keywords: its share of any held jointly

options.text: Assets of ₹340 lakh and liabilities of ₹120 lakh
options.misconception: reads the specific allocation as applying to the asset but not to the liability that came with it
options.why: The same sentence of the contract gives X Ltd the warehouse and the term loan. Taking the asset in full and the debt at half reports a stake in the operation that no document supports.
keywords: Taking the asset in full and the debt at half

options.text: A single investment of ₹100 lakh, accounted for by the equity method
options.misconception: accounts for a joint operation the way a joint venture is accounted for, as one line rather than as assets and liabilities
options.why: Half of Z's ₹200 lakh equity is ₹100 lakh, which is what the equity method would give. The equity method is for a joint venture, where the parties have rights to the net assets. A joint operator has rights to the assets themselves and obligations for the liabilities, and puts them on its own face.
keywords: puts them on its own face

options.text: Assets of ₹220 lakh and liabilities of ₹120 lakh
options.misconception: applies the capital ratio to every line, ignoring the contractual terms that allocate particular assets and liabilities in full
options.why: Half of everything gives ₹220 lakh and ₹120 lakh, and it is the answer the arrangement would produce if the contract said nothing more than fifty-fifty. The contract does say more, and what a joint operator recognises follows the rights and obligations the contract actually gives it.
keywords: follows the rights and obligations the contract actually gives it

citation.ref: the requirement that a joint operator recognises its assets including its share of any held jointly and its liabilities including its share of any incurred jointly, in accordance with the Ind AS applicable to the particular assets and liabilities

items.scenario: X Ltd and Y Ltd each hold half the capital of a separate vehicle Z, and the arrangement has been concluded to be a joint operation. The contract gives X Ltd the rights to the whole of a warehouse owned by Z and the obligation for the whole of a term loan owed by Z. Rights to all other assets and obligations for all other liabilities are shared in proportion to capital, half each. Z's balance sheet shows a warehouse of ₹240 lakh, equipment of ₹160 lakh and cash of ₹40 lakh, against a term loan of ₹180 lakh, trade payables of ₹60 lakh and equity of ₹200 lakh.

items.stem: What revenue and what expenses does P Ltd recognise for the year?

options.text: Revenue ₹9,600 lakh and expenses ₹6,900 lakh
options.why: A joint operator recognises its revenue from the sale of its share of the output, which is the whole ₹9,600 lakh P Ltd received, and its expenses including its share of those incurred jointly, which is 60 per cent of ₹11,000 lakh. Its own selling costs of ₹300 lakh were never incurred jointly and come in at full value.
keywords: its revenue from the sale of its share of the output

options.text: No revenue and no expenses, but a share of the profit of the joint operation of ₹2,700 lakh
options.misconception: reports a joint operation as one net line, which is what the equity method does for a joint venture
options.why: The profit figure is right and the presentation is not. A joint operator's revenue and expenses go on its own face, line by line; only a joint venture is carried as a single equity-accounted balance.
keywords: go on its own face, line by line

options.text: Revenue ₹5,760 lakh and expenses ₹6,900 lakh
options.misconception: applies the sharing ratio a second time to revenue P Ltd has already earned on its own account
options.why: The 60 per cent has already been applied once, in the 12,000 tonnes P Ltd took. The ₹9,600 lakh is what P Ltd itself sold, so applying the ratio again reports three-fifths of its own sales.

options.text: Revenue ₹9,600 lakh and expenses ₹11,300 lakh
options.misconception: takes its own share of the output and revenue but the whole of the operation's jointly incurred costs
options.why: The costs are shared in the same ratio as the output. Taking 60 per cent of the production and 100 per cent of the cost of producing it turns a profitable year into a loss of ₹1,700 lakh that nobody made.
keywords: shared in the same ratio as the output

citation.ref: the requirement that a joint operator books three things on its own face — what it earns by selling the slice of output that falls to it, the slice that falls to it of what the arrangement itself earns by selling output, and its expenses, those it bears jointly with the other operator included

items.scenario: P Ltd and Q Ltd are the operators of an unincorporated joint operation in the ratio 60 to 40. In the year ended 31 March 2026 the operation produced 20,000 tonnes of output, and each operator took its contractual share and sold it on its own account. P Ltd sold its 12,000 tonnes for ₹9,600 lakh. The operation's jointly incurred operating costs for the year came to ₹11,000 lakh, shared in the same ratio. P Ltd also incurred ₹300 lakh of its own selling and distribution costs on the output it took.

items.stem: What share of E Ltd's profit does D Ltd recognise for the year?

options.text: ₹77 lakh
options.misconception: eliminates the investor's share of the whole intra-group profit instead of the part still held
options.why: Thirty-five per cent of the whole ₹20 lakh is ₹7 lakh, and it treats goods already sold to outsiders as though they were still in stock. Three-quarters of the profit has been realised in a sale to a third party and stays recognised.
keywords: has been realised in a sale to a third party

options.text: ₹84 lakh
options.misconception: eliminates nothing, on the view that an associate is not consolidated so there is no intra-group profit to remove
options.why: The elimination for an associate is not a consolidation adjustment, it is a limit on how much of its own profit the investor may recognise. The rule applies to upstream and downstream transactions alike whether or not the investee is consolidated.
keywords: a limit on how much of its own profit the investor may recognise

options.text: ₹79 lakh
options.misconception: eliminates the whole unrealised profit rather than only the investor's share of it
options.why: ₹5 lakh is the profit still in stock, but 65 per cent of it belongs to E Ltd's other shareholders, who are unrelated investors. Only D Ltd's own 35 per cent, ₹1.75 lakh, is taken out.

options.text: ₹82.25 lakh
options.why: Thirty-five per cent of ₹240 lakh is ₹84 lakh. Against it, the gain on an upstream transaction is recognised only to the extent of the unrelated investors' interests, so the part still unrealised has to come out — a quarter of the ₹20 lakh profit is ₹5 lakh still in D Ltd's inventory, and D Ltd's own 35 per cent of that is ₹1.75 lakh.
keywords: only to the extent of the unrelated investors' interests

citation.ref: the requirement that gains and losses resulting from upstream and downstream transactions between an entity and its associate or joint venture are recognised in the entity's financial statements only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests in the associate or joint venture

items.scenario: D Ltd holds 35 per cent of E Ltd, an associate. During the year ended 31 March 2026 E Ltd sold goods to D Ltd for ₹80 lakh, on which E Ltd made a profit of ₹20 lakh. At 31 March 2026 D Ltd still held a quarter of those goods, the rest having been sold to outside customers. E Ltd's profit for the year was ₹240 lakh. There are no fair value adjustments to consider.

items.stem: How does A Ltd account for the sale in its consolidated financial statements?

options.text: The non-controlling interest goes up by ₹165 crore and ₹45 crore is credited directly to equity
options.misconception: adjusts the non-controlling interest for its share of the net assets only, leaving the goodwill out
options.why: The policy stated is a proportionate share of the net assets and the associated goodwill, so the base is ₹1,300 crore and not ₹1,100 crore. Leaving the goodwill out understates what moves to the non-controlling interest by ₹30 crore and inflates the credit to equity by the same amount.

options.text: The non-controlling interest goes up by ₹195 crore, ₹15 crore is credited directly to equity, and nothing goes through profit or loss
options.why: A change in a parent's ownership interest that does not result in a loss of control is an equity transaction. Paragraph B96 makes A Ltd restate both interests to the new relative holdings, which on this policy shifts 15 per cent of ₹1,300 crore. Whatever gap is left between that restatement and the ₹210 crore actually banked is recognised directly in equity, and A Ltd's own shareholders take it.
keywords: does not result in a loss of control is an equity transaction

options.text: The non-controlling interest goes up by ₹195 crore and a gain of ₹15 crore is recognised in profit or loss
options.misconception: treats a partial disposal that keeps control as a sale producing a gain, the way a disposal that loses control would
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the destination is not. Selling to your own minority while keeping control is a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners, so the difference goes into equity and never through the statement of profit and loss.
keywords: owners in their capacity as owners

options.text: Goodwill is reduced by ₹30 crore, being the 15 per cent sold, and a gain of ₹15 crore is recognised in profit or loss
options.misconception: derecognises a slice of goodwill on a disposal that changes no asset of the subsidiary
options.why: Because control is retained, the subsidiary's assets including its goodwill are untouched by the transaction and no gain or loss is recognised on it. What changes is how the group's equity is split between the owners of the parent and the non-controlling interests.
keywords: the subsidiary's assets including its goodwill are untouched

citation.ref: paragraph 23, that changes in a parent's ownership interest that do not result in a loss of control are equity transactions, and paragraph B96, that the carrying amounts of the controlling and non-controlling interests are adjusted for the change in their relative interests and any difference between that adjustment and the fair value of the consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity and attributed to the owners of the parent

items.scenario: A Ltd owns 90 per cent of B Ltd. On 31 March 2026 it sells a 15 per cent interest in B Ltd to outside investors for ₹210 crore in cash, keeping 75 per cent and retaining control. At that date the carrying amount of B Ltd's identifiable net assets in the consolidated financial statements is ₹1,100 crore, and the goodwill recognised when B Ltd was acquired is ₹200 crore. A Ltd measures subsequent changes in the non-controlling interest at the non-controlling interest's proportionate share of the net assets and the associated goodwill.

items.stem: Is he right about the dividend payable?

options.text: No — FC 15,000 against FC 5,00,000 is 3 per cent, an insignificant amount for that purpose, so FC is not exchangeable for the dividend
options.why: The amendment asks the question one purpose at a time. For capital goods the subsidiary can obtain everything it needs, so FC is exchangeable there. For the dividend it can obtain FC 15,000 against a requirement of FC 5,00,000, and an amount that small measured against what the purpose actually needs is no more than an insignificant amount. The same currency therefore passes for one balance and fails for the other on the same date.
keywords: no more than an insignificant amount

options.text: No, and because FC fails for the dividend the machinery payables must be translated at an estimated rate as well
options.misconception: carries one purpose's failure across to every other purpose
options.why: The failure travels no further than the purpose it was found in. Capital goods have no ceiling here, so that balance is translated under the ordinary requirements of Ind AS 21 and only the dividend needs a rate to be estimated.

options.text: Yes — a currency is either exchangeable or it is not, and this one plainly is, so both balances take the official rate
options.misconception: treats exchangeability as a standing property of the currency rather than of a purpose
options.why: Making it a property of the currency is exactly the reading the amendment closes off. Two permissions with two ceilings are two answers, and the machinery route says nothing about whether the dividend can be remitted.

options.text: Yes, because the subsidiary has not yet applied to remit the FC 5,00,000 and nothing has been refused
options.misconception: waits for an actual refusal instead of measuring the amount obtainable
options.why: The test is what the entity is able to obtain, not what it has been told it cannot have. A ceiling published in advance answers the question at the measurement date; waiting for a rejection letter would put the assessment off for ever.

citation.ref: the requirement to assess exchangeability at the measurement date for a specified purpose, and the factor that treats a currency as not exchangeable where no more than an insignificant amount can be obtained for that purpose

items.scenario: A subsidiary reporting in currency LC has declared a dividend of FC 5,00,000 to its overseas parent and owes FC 90,000 to machinery suppliers. The local authority lets the subsidiary buy FC 15,000 a year for dividend remittances and lets it buy FC freely for capital goods; the two permissions cannot be swapped, and the machinery bills have been paid all year without difficulty. The finance head says that a company buying FC every month is plainly operating in an exchangeable currency, so both balances take the published official rate at 31 March 2026.

items.stem: Is LC exchangeable into PC at that date?

options.text: Yes — the two-leg route is available without limit and clears in four working days, and the board's decision not to use it is beside the point
options.why: What is tested is the ability to obtain the other currency, directly or indirectly, and not the intention or decision to do so. Going through a third currency counts as obtaining it. Four working days is the settlement cycle, which is a normal administrative delay and does not stop a currency being exchangeable.
keywords: and not the intention or decision to do so

options.text: No — nobody quotes LC against PC, and a route through a third currency is not an exchange between these two
options.misconception: requires a direct quotation between the two currencies
options.why: A currency is exchangeable if the other one can be obtained either directly or indirectly, and two legs through FC is the indirect case written down.

options.text: No, because the board has decided against that route and an entity cannot be held to a road it has refused
options.misconception: reads a decision not to convert as an inability to convert
options.why: The amendment separates these two on purpose. An entity that could obtain PC and chooses not to is in an exchangeable currency; only an entity that could not is not.

options.text: No, because a spot rate is a rate for immediate delivery and four working days is not immediate
options.misconception: reads the spot-rate definition as barring any settlement delay
options.why: Legal requirements, holidays and settlement cycles all put a gap between the deal and the currency arriving, and the amendment says in terms that a normal administrative delay does not preclude exchangeability. What counts as normal depends on the facts.

citation.ref: the factors of time frame, of ability rather than intention to obtain the other currency, and of the markets or exchange mechanisms that may be considered

items.scenario: An entity whose functional currency is LC needs currency PC at 31 March 2026. No bank will sell PC against LC directly. LC can be sold for currency FC and FC for PC with no ceiling on either leg, and the whole amount clears in four working days, which is the local settlement cycle. A street market quotes LC against PC directly at a rate 12 per cent away from the official one, but deals struck there give the entity no enforceable rights. The board has decided against the two-leg route because it costs more in fees.

items.stem: At what rate is the borrowing translated, and on what footing?

options.text: LC 1.05, the rate the authority itself has fixed, giving LC 4,20,000
options.misconception: treats an official rate as authoritative without asking how current it is
options.why: How often a rate is refreshed is one of the things the entity has to weigh, and a figure untouched since 2023 cannot describe conditions at this reporting date. Its official standing does not repair that.

options.text: LC 1.40 without adjustment, that market being the only place FC changes hands for this purpose
options.misconception: promotes an unenforceable market's quote straight to the answer
options.why: A quote from such a market may feed an estimate, but only through the route that adjusts it as far as the objective requires. Lifting it unchanged skips the very question the entity is meant to answer, and it does so after the entity has already found a rate that meets the objective.

options.text: LC 1.15 on the FC 50,000 the entity can actually obtain and LC 1.40 on the rest, giving LC 5,27,500
options.misconception: splits one balance across two rates in proportion to what can be obtained
options.why: The entity estimates one spot rate at the measurement date and translates the whole balance at it. Nothing in the amendment blends rates by the fraction of a liability the entity happens to be able to fund.

options.text: LC 1.15, taken as an observable exchange rate without adjustment, giving LC 4,60,000
options.why: A rate quoted for a purpose other than the one being assessed is an observable exchange rate, and it may be used unchanged once the entity has satisfied itself that it meets the estimation objective. The entity has done exactly that, so the borrowing comes in at FC 4,00,000 times 1.15.
keywords: a purpose other than the one being assessed

citation.ref: para 19A for the objective an estimated spot rate must meet, read with the guidance allowing an observable exchange rate to be used without adjustment and the factors for deciding whether such a rate reflects prevailing economic conditions

items.scenario: An entity has concluded that FC is not exchangeable into LC at 31 March 2026 for repaying a borrowing of FC 4,00,000. Three prices are observable. LC 1.15 per FC is the rate at which it may buy FC to pay for imported spares, refreshed daily. LC 1.40 per FC is quoted in a market whose deals give no enforceable rights. LC 1.05 per FC was fixed by the authority in 2023 and has not moved since. The entity concludes that LC 1.15 reflects the economic conditions prevailing at the reporting date.

items.stem: Is the colleague right?

options.text: No — the LC 1.62 quote is barred from the first step but may be adjusted as necessary to build the estimate at the second
options.why: The two steps ask different questions and apply different filters. Whether enforceable rights arise decides which markets count when the entity is asking if it can obtain the currency at all. Once the answer is no, the entity is asking what an orderly exchange would price at, and a rate from such a market may be adjusted as necessary to reach that.
keywords: the two steps ask different questions

options.text: No, but the entity must wait for exchangeability to be restored and take the first rate then available
options.misconception: turns one example of an observable rate into the only permitted answer
options.why: That first later rate is one example of an observable rate and not the required one, and an entity choosing it also has to weigh how long the gap to restoration was and what inflation did in between. A rate is needed at the measurement date, not whenever the block happens to lift.

options.text: Yes — a market excluded when exchangeability was assessed stays excluded when the rate is estimated
options.misconception: carries the enforceable-rights filter from the assessment into the estimation
options.why: Carrying it across would leave an entity in this position with no observable price of any kind, which is the situation the second step exists to solve rather than to repeat.

options.text: No, and the LC 1.62 must be used exactly as it stands, an observable rate ranking above any technique
options.misconception: invents an order of preference the amendment does not lay down
options.why: No hierarchy of observable exchange rates is prescribed. An observable rate goes in unchanged only when it meets the objective on its own, and here treasury has a reason to think it does not.

citation.ref: para A17 for estimating a spot rate by adjusting an observable rate, including a rate from a market that creates no enforceable rights, read with the absence of any prescribed hierarchy among observable rates

items.scenario: An entity has determined that FC is not exchangeable into LC at 31 December 2025 for settling a liability of FC 3,00,000. The only prices anyone can see come from a market where deals create no enforceable rights, running at LC 1.62 per FC, and treasury thinks the figure needs trimming for the risk attaching to that market. A colleague objects that the same market was set aside when the entity decided FC was not exchangeable, so it must be set aside now too.

items.stem: What else does the amendment require in the notes?

options.text: The same three items, plus a sensitivity analysis showing what a 10 per cent movement in the LC 1.28 estimate would do to profit
options.misconception: substitutes a quantified sensitivity for the qualitative risk information asked for
options.why: What is asked for here is qualitative information about each type of risk the entity is exposed to, with the nature and carrying amount exposed to each. A single percentage swing answers a different question and leaves that one unanswered.

options.text: The same three items, plus the name of the supplier, summarised financial information about it, and any obligation to support it
options.misconception: applies the foreign-operation disclosures to an ordinary trade counterparty
options.why: That further set is owed only where the currency that cannot be exchanged is a foreign operation's own functional currency, or the presentation currency against it. A payable to an unrelated supplier does not bring it into play.

options.text: Nothing further — naming the currency, the restriction and the rate is the whole of it
options.misconception: reads the shortest disclosure in the list as the entire list
options.why: Those three are the opening of the list, not the end. Without the amount caught and the technique behind the rate a reader cannot tell whether the estimate matters or how it was reached.

options.text: The transactions affected, the carrying amount affected, whether the rate was observable or built by a technique, that technique with its inputs and assumptions, and each type of risk with the amount exposed to it
options.why: A reader has to be able to see what the block has caught and how much judgement went into the number. So the note describes the affected transactions, gives the carrying amount of the assets and liabilities affected, says of the rate whether it was observable and left alone or estimated by another technique, describes that technique with the inputs and assumptions behind it, and sets out each type of risk the block creates alongside the carrying amount exposed to it.
keywords: the carrying amount of the assets and liabilities affected

citation.ref: the disclosures required when a currency is not exchangeable into another currency, and the additional disclosures owed only where a foreign operation's functional currency is the one affected

items.scenario: An entity has translated a payable of FC 12,00,000 at an estimated spot rate of LC 1.28. Its draft note names the currency, describes the restriction that blocks it, and gives the rate. The audit committee asks whether the note is complete.

items.stem: How is the change brought in?

options.text: The comparative year is left alone and the LC 46 lakh goes to opening retained earnings, or to the accumulated translation differences where it belongs to the foreign operation
options.why: The amendment relieves an entity of restating comparative information when it first applies the lack of exchangeability requirements. The catch-up is taken instead to the opening balance of retained earnings, or, where it relates to a foreign operation, to the cumulative translation differences sitting in their own component of equity.
keywords: the opening balance of retained earnings

options.text: The comparative year is restated in full, this being a change in accounting policy under Ind AS 8
options.misconception: applies the general retrospective route to an amendment that displaces it
options.why: A transition provision written into the amendment governs how that amendment comes in, and this one says comparative information is not required to be restated. Restating anyway would hand the reader two years measured on rules the second of them was never subject to.

options.text: The comparative year is left alone and the LC 46 lakh is taken to profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026
options.misconception: routes a transition catch-up through the current year's income
options.why: A figure belonging to periods before the amendment was applied is not this year's performance. Putting it through profit or loss would move a number that has nothing to do with the year's trading.

options.text: Nothing yet — the amendment applies to annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026, so the year ended 31 March 2026 is untouched
options.misconception: pushes the effective date on by one year
options.why: The lack of exchangeability requirements bite for annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025, so the year ended 31 March 2026 is the first one they govern and the transition falls due now.

citation.ref: the transition to the lack of exchangeability amendment, which requires no comparative information to be restated and takes the effect to opening retained earnings or to the cumulative amount of translation differences held in a separate component of equity

items.scenario: An entity applies the lack of exchangeability amendment for the first time in the year ended 31 March 2026, the amendment being effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025. Working the comparative year on the new basis would move its closing figures by LC 46 lakh. Part of that sits on ordinary foreign currency payables and part on a foreign subsidiary whose translation differences are held in their own component of equity.

items.stem: How are the two balances dealt with?

options.text: The net ₹5.4 crore liability is recognised, the offsetting conditions being satisfied
options.misconception: treats Pillar Two deferred balances as ordinary deferred tax to be offset and recognised
options.why: Offsetting is a question about balances that get recognised in the first place. These do not, so there is nothing to net and nothing to carry.

options.text: Neither is recognised, but both the ₹4.2 crore and the ₹9.6 crore are disclosed in the notes as unrecognised deferred tax
options.misconception: keeps the disclosure after dropping the recognition
options.why: The exception covers both halves in the same breath. Naming the two figures in the notes would put back exactly the information the carve-out exists to keep out.

options.text: Neither is recognised and neither is disclosed; the group states that it has applied the exception
options.why: Ind AS 12 carves Pillar Two income taxes out of deferred tax entirely. The entity neither recognises nor discloses information about deferred tax assets and liabilities related to those taxes, so nothing about the ₹4.2 crore or the ₹9.6 crore reaches the balance sheet or the notes. What does reach the notes is the statement that the exception has been applied.
keywords: the statement that the exception has been applied

options.text: Both are recognised unless the group elects the exception as an accounting policy choice
options.misconception: reads a mandatory carve-out as an option to be elected
options.why: There is no election here. The exception applies to every entity within its scope, and the only thing the entity chooses is the words it uses to say it has applied it.

citation.ref: the exception under which an entity neither recognises nor discloses information about deferred tax assets and liabilities related to Pillar Two income taxes, and the requirement to disclose that the exception has been applied

items.scenario: An Indian parent within the scope of the Pillar Two rules is closing its accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its tax team has worked out a deferred tax asset of ₹4.2 crore and a deferred tax liability of ₹9.6 crore arising from top-up income taxes in two jurisdictions where the group operates and the rules are in force, and proposes recognising the net ₹5.4 crore liability.

items.stem: What do the notes have to carry?

options.text: That the exception has been applied, the ₹1.8 crore shown separately, and for the second jurisdiction a statement that the exposure cannot yet be reasonably estimated with an account of how far the assessment has got
options.why: Current tax on top-up income taxes is not caught by the carve-out and is shown separately, so the ₹1.8 crore stands on its own line. For a jurisdiction where the law is enacted or substantively enacted but not yet in effect, the group gives whatever is known or reasonably estimable about its exposure; where that cannot be estimated it says so and describes the progress it has made in assessing the exposure.
keywords: enacted or substantively enacted but not yet in effect
describes the progress it has made

options.text: That the exception has been applied, the ₹1.8 crore shown separately, and a single point estimate of the second jurisdiction's exposure, a range not being information
options.misconception: refuses the indicative range the amendment expressly allows
options.why: The information need not meet every specific requirement of the Pillar Two legislation and may be given as an indicative range. Forcing a point estimate out of an assessment that is not finished would give the reader a figure with nothing behind it.

options.text: That the exception has been applied, with the ₹1.8 crore left inside the current tax charge, since only deferred tax attracts a separate disclosure
options.misconception: extends the deferred tax carve-out to the current tax figure
options.why: The carve-out reaches deferred tax and stops. Current tax expense or income relating to Pillar Two income taxes is required to be disclosed separately, which is the opposite of leaving it folded into the total.

options.text: That the exception has been applied and the ₹1.8 crore shown separately; the second jurisdiction needs nothing until its rules take effect
options.misconception: reads a law that is not yet in effect as nothing worth telling anyone about
options.why: The period before the rules bite is precisely when a reader most needs warning. The amendment asks for the exposure to be described in exactly those periods, and silence is not one of the permitted answers.

citation.ref: the requirement to disclose separately the current tax expense or income related to Pillar Two income taxes, and to give known or reasonably estimable qualitative and quantitative information about the exposure in periods where Pillar Two legislation is enacted or substantively enacted but not yet in effect

items.scenario: A group is closing the year ended 31 March 2026. In one jurisdiction the Pillar Two rules are in force and ₹1.8 crore of top-up tax sits inside the current tax charge. In a second, the legislation is substantively enacted but takes effect only from the following year, so nothing is payable there yet, and the group cannot presently put a reliable figure on what its exposure there will be.

items.stem: What does the buyer actually pay for each ₹100 of face value?

options.misconception: adds a whole year's coupon instead of the interest accrued to the settlement date
options.why: A full ₹9 would be right only on the day before a coupon falls due. Here 219 of the 360 days have run, so ₹5.475 has accrued and the remainder belongs to whoever holds the bond next.
keywords: only on the day before a coupon falls due

options.misconception: settles on the quoted price, treating the clean price as the amount that changes hands
options.why: The quoted price is deliberately stripped of accrued interest so that a bond's quotation does not sawtooth upward between coupon dates and drop on each payment. The seller has still earned 219 days of interest and is paid for it on top.

Accrued interest is the face value at the coupon rate for the days elapsed, which is ₹100 at 9 per cent for 219 days of a 360-day year, or ₹5.475. The dirty price is the clean price plus that accrued interest, and the dirty price is what settles.
keywords: the dirty price is what settles

options.misconception: deducts the accrued interest from the clean price instead of adding it
options.why: The buyer will collect the whole next coupon, including the part the seller earned, so the buyer pays for it now. Deducting it would have the buyer paid twice for the same interest.
keywords: The buyer will collect the whole next coupon

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A 9 per cent Government of India security with a face value of ₹100 is quoted at a clean price of ₹96.40. At the settlement date 219 days of interest have accrued since the last coupon. The market convention for accrued interest on this security is a 360-day year.

items.stem: What are the dirty price and the amount repayable at maturity?

options.misconception: adds the initial margin to the first leg instead of deducting it
options.why: Adding 2 per cent lends more than the collateral is worth, which is the opposite of what a haircut is for. The margin always comes off the first leg.
keywords: lends more than the collateral is worth

options.misconception: leaves the initial margin out, lending the full market value of the collateral
options.why: The dirty price is right. The margin is the haircut that protects the lender of money if the collateral falls in value before the second leg, so the first leg is ₹4,04,54,400 and not ₹4,12,80,000.

Accrued interest is ₹100 at 8 per cent for 180 days of 360, which is ₹4, so the dirty price is ₹103.20. The first leg is ₹4 crore at that price, ₹4,12,80,000, less the 2 per cent initial margin, giving ₹4,04,54,400. The second leg carries that at 6 per cent for 15 days of 360, which adds ₹1,01,136.
keywords: less the 2 per cent initial margin

options.misconception: uses the quoted clean price as the collateral value and never adds accrued interest
options.why: The collateral is worth its dirty price, because whoever holds the bond collects the accrued interest with it. Starting from ₹99.20 understates the collateral by ₹4 per ₹100 and lends about ₹15.7 lakh less than the deal is worth.
keywords: The collateral is worth its dirty price

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: Bank A enters into a 15-day repurchase agreement with Bank B in 8 per cent Government of India bonds with a nominal value of ₹4 crore, at a repo rate of 6 per cent. The clean price of the bonds is ₹99.20 and 180 days of interest have accrued. The initial margin is 2 per cent. A 360-day year is used throughout.

items.stem: What is the portfolio's Macaulay duration, and what price change does it predict if yields rise by 100 basis points?

options.text: 3.094 years and a fall of about 3.09 per cent
options.misconception: applies the Macaulay duration directly to the yield change instead of the modified duration
options.why: The duration figure is right. Macaulay duration is a time in years, not a price sensitivity — it becomes one only after dividing by one plus the yield, and skipping that step overstates the fall by about a fifth of a percentage point here and by more when yields are higher.
keywords: a time in years, not a price sensitivity

options.text: 3.094 years and a fall of about 3.34 per cent
options.misconception: multiplies the Macaulay duration by one plus the yield instead of dividing by it
options.why: Modified duration is always smaller than Macaulay duration, because dividing by 1.08 can only reduce it. Any answer larger than the duration itself has the operation inverted.

options.text: 2.705 years and a fall of about 2.50 per cent
options.misconception: computes the duration of the coupon bond and never brings the zero coupon holding into the average
options.why: Bond Q is 30 per cent of the portfolio and it has the longer duration of the two, so leaving it out understates both figures. The whole point of a portfolio duration is that every holding contributes in proportion to its market value.
keywords: it has the longer duration of the two

options.text: 3.094 years and a fall of about 2.86 per cent
options.why: Bond P prices at ₹1,103.04 and its Macaulay duration is the present value of each cash flow times its year, divided by that price, which comes to 2.705 years. A zero coupon bond's duration is its maturity, so Bond Q is 4.000 years. The portfolio duration is the value weighted average, 0.7 times 2.705 plus 0.3 times 4.000. Modified duration is that divided by 1.08, which is 2.864, and a 1 per cent rise in yields is predicted to take about 2.86 per cent off the value.
keywords: A zero coupon bond's duration is its maturity

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: Bond P has a face value of ₹1,000, pays a 12 per cent annual coupon and has three years to maturity. Bond Q is a zero coupon bond of the same face value with four years to maturity. The yield to maturity prevailing on both is 8 per cent. Present value factors at 8 per cent are 0.9259 for year one, 0.8573 for year two, 0.7938 for year three and 0.7350 for year four. A fund holds the two so that Bond P is 70 per cent of the portfolio's market value and Bond Q is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What are the portfolio's modified duration and the value change it predicts?

options.text: 4.50, and a fall of about ₹3.375 crore
options.misconception: averages the two durations without weighting them by the money invested in each
options.why: A simple average treats the ₹35 crore holding as though it were as big as the ₹65 crore one. Nearly two-thirds of the money sits in the shorter bond, so the portfolio's true sensitivity is well below the midpoint of the two.
keywords: as though it were as big as

options.text: 3.93, and a fall of about ₹3.93 crore
options.misconception: applies a full one per cent move when the question asks about 75 basis points
options.why: Modified duration is the percentage price change per one per cent change in yield, so it has to be scaled by the actual move. Seventy-five basis points is three-quarters of a per cent.

options.text: 3.93, and a rise of about ₹2.95 crore
options.misconception: gets the size right and the direction wrong, moving price with yield rather than against it
options.why: Bond prices move inversely with yields. Rising yields discount the same fixed cash flows harder, so the portfolio loses.

options.text: 3.93, and a fall of about ₹2.95 crore
options.why: The modified durations are averaged by market value, so 0.35 times 6.4 plus 0.65 times 2.6 gives 3.93. A rise of 0.75 per cent multiplied by 3.93 is 2.9475 per cent, and on ₹100 crore that is a fall of about ₹2.95 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A debt fund holds ₹35 crore of a bond whose modified duration is 6.4 and ₹65 crore of a bond whose modified duration is 2.6. Its manager expects yields across the curve to rise by 75 basis points and wants to know what that would do to the ₹100 crore portfolio.

items.stem: What is the approximate yield to maturity?

options.text: About 10.23 per cent
options.misconception: computes the current yield and stops, leaving out the pull to par over five years
options.why: ₹9 over ₹88 is the current yield, which counts only the coupon. A bond bought at ₹88 and redeemed at ₹100 also earns ₹12 of capital gain, and the yield to maturity is what includes it.

options.text: About 11.40 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the face value instead of by the average of face value and market price
options.why: The investor put in ₹88, not ₹100, so the return has to be measured against something closer to what was invested. The approximation uses the average of the two, ₹94.
keywords: measured against something closer to what was invested

options.text: About 12.13 per cent
options.why: The coupon is ₹9 and the ₹12 discount is spread over five years, adding ₹2.4 a year, so the numerator is ₹11.4. The denominator is the average of the redemption value and the price, which is ₹94, and ₹11.4 over ₹94 is 12.13 per cent.
keywords: the average of the redemption value and the price

options.text: About 9.00 per cent
options.misconception: reports the coupon rate, which is a return on face value and not on the price paid
options.why: The coupon rate is fixed at issue and says nothing about what today's buyer earns. It equals the yield to maturity only for a bond trading exactly at par.
keywords: only for a bond trading exactly at par

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond with a face value of ₹100, redeemable at par, carries a 9 per cent annual coupon and has exactly five years to maturity. It is trading at ₹88.

items.stem: What is the approximate yield to maturity?

options.text: About 9.20 per cent
options.why: The gain to redemption is ₹1,050 less ₹960, which is ₹90 over four years, or ₹22.5 a year on top of the ₹70 coupon. The denominator is the average of the redemption value and the price, ₹1,005, and ₹92.5 over ₹1,005 is 9.20 per cent.
keywords: the average of the redemption value and the price

options.text: About 8.16 per cent
options.misconception: amortises the gain to the face value instead of to the redemption value the bond will actually pay
options.why: The bond redeems at ₹1,050 and not at ₹1,000, so the investor gains ₹90 and not ₹40. Where a bond is redeemable at a premium the redemption value replaces the face value on both sides of the calculation.
keywords: the redemption value replaces the face value

options.text: About 9.64 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the market price rather than by the average of price and redemption value
options.why: The numerator is right at ₹92.5. Dividing by ₹960 instead of ₹1,005 assumes the investment stays at the purchase price for the whole four years, when it is drifting up towards ₹1,050.
keywords: assumes the investment stays at the purchase price

options.text: About 7.29 per cent
options.misconception: reports the current yield and leaves the redemption premium out altogether
options.why: ₹70 over ₹960 counts the coupon and nothing else. The bond is bought at ₹960 and redeemed at ₹1,050, and that ₹90 is a real part of the return.
keywords: counts the coupon and nothing else

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries a 7 per cent annual coupon, has four years left to run and is redeemable at a premium at ₹1,050. It is currently trading at ₹960.

items.stem: What yield does the investor earn?

options.text: About 3.00 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the face value and does not annualise either
options.why: Both steps are missed at once. The base should be the ₹4.85 crore paid, and the 91-day figure should then be annualised by 365 over 91.
keywords: Both steps are missed at once

options.text: About 3.09 per cent
options.misconception: reports the return for the 91-day period without annualising it
options.why: 3.09 per cent is right for 91 days. A yield is quoted per annum, so it has to be scaled by 365 over 91, and money earning 3.09 per cent a quarter is earning far more than 3.09 per cent a year.
keywords: A yield is quoted per annum

options.text: About 12.41 per cent
options.why: The return is ₹15 lakh on the ₹4.85 crore actually invested, which is 3.0928 per cent for 91 days. Annualising by 365 over 91 multiplies it by 4.011, giving 12.41 per cent.

options.text: About 12.03 per cent
options.misconception: divides the discount by the face value rather than by the amount the investor paid
options.why: The investor never had ₹5 crore in the instrument, only ₹4.85 crore, so the return has to be measured against ₹4.85 crore. Dividing by face value understates every discounted instrument's yield, which is why the yield always exceeds the discount rate.
keywords: the yield always exceeds the discount rate

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company issues commercial paper with a face value of ₹5 crore and a tenor of 91 days, and receives ₹4.85 crore for it. The paper is redeemed at face value on maturity. Use a 365-day year.

items.stem: What is the yield on the bill?

options.text: About 7.60 per cent
options.misconception: annualises on a 360-day year, which is the convention for accrued interest and repo interest and not for a treasury bill
options.why: The study material's treasury bill formula uses the actual days to maturity over 365. The 360-day year belongs to the repo working, on a different instrument, and mixing them costs about eleven basis points here.
keywords: uses the actual days to maturity over 365

options.text: About 7.71 per cent
options.why: The discount of ₹3.70 on a purchase price of ₹96.30 is 3.8422 per cent over 182 days. Annualised by 365 over 182, that is 7.71 per cent.

options.text: About 3.84 per cent
options.misconception: gives the return over the 182 days without annualising it
options.why: The 182-day return is right. A treasury bill yield is quoted per annum, so the period return is multiplied by 365 over 182.

options.text: About 7.42 per cent
options.misconception: divides the discount by the face value instead of by the price paid
options.why: ₹3.70 over ₹100 is the discount rate the bill was struck at, not the yield the buyer earns. The buyer parted with ₹96.30, and the return is measured on that.
keywords: not the yield the buyer earns

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: An investor buys a 182-day treasury bill with a face value of ₹100 at a price of ₹96.30 and holds it to maturity. The study material's treasury bill formula annualises on a 365-day year.

items.stem: What are the issue price and the effective yield?

options.text: ₹95.50 and about 9.42 per cent
options.why: The discount is ₹100 at 9 per cent for six of twelve months, which is ₹4.50, so the certificate is issued at ₹95.50. The effective yield is ₹4.50 over ₹95.50 for six months, annualised by twelve over six, which is 9.42 per cent.

options.text: ₹95.50 and about 4.71 per cent
options.misconception: gives the six-month return without annualising it
options.why: 4.71 per cent is what the investor earns in six months. An effective yield is stated per annum, so it is doubled to 9.42 per cent.
keywords: An effective yield is stated per annum

options.text: ₹91.00 and about 9.89 per cent
options.misconception: deducts a full year's discount from a certificate that runs for six months
options.why: The rate is 9 per cent a year and the instrument runs for half a year, so the discount is ₹4.50. Taking ₹9 off prices a six-month deposit as though the bank had held the money twice as long.
keywords: as though the bank had held the money twice as long

options.text: ₹95.50 and about 9.00 per cent
options.misconception: reports the discount rate as the yield, which is only true if the discount were charged on the amount actually lent
options.why: The issue price is right. The 9 per cent was applied to the ₹100 face value while only ₹95.50 was ever invested, so the return on what was invested is higher, and that gap is what a front-ended discount always produces.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bank issues a certificate of deposit with a face value of ₹100 for a period of six months at a discount rate of 9 per cent a year. The discount is front-ended, so it is deducted from the face value at issue and the face value is paid at maturity.

items.stem: What is the bond's current yield now, and what price would a current yield of 8.25 per cent imply?

options.text: 7.50 per cent now, and a price of about ₹133.33
options.misconception: moves the price the wrong way, treating a rise in yield as a rise in price
options.why: ₹133.33 is what a current yield of 6.75 per cent would imply, so this moves the yield down by 75 basis points instead of up. Yield and price move in opposite directions.
keywords: Yield and price move in opposite directions

options.text: 7.50 per cent now, and no change in price
options.misconception: treats the current yield as a fixed property of the bond rather than as an arithmetic consequence of its price
options.why: The coupon is what is fixed. Current yield is simply that coupon divided by whatever price the market is asking, so the yield cannot move unless the price does.
keywords: The coupon is what is fixed

options.text: 9.00 per cent now, and a price of about ₹109.09
options.misconception: reads the current yield off the coupon rate, dividing by face value rather than by market price
options.why: The implied price is right, which is what makes the first figure so easy to slip past. ₹9 over ₹100 is the coupon rate. Current yield always divides by what the bond costs today, ₹120.
keywords: divides by what the bond costs today

options.text: 7.50 per cent now, and a price of about ₹109.09
options.why: Current yield is the coupon over the market price, so ₹9 over ₹120 is 7.50 per cent. Holding the ₹9 coupon fixed and solving ₹9 divided by the price equal to 8.25 per cent gives ₹109.09, and a higher yield means a lower price.
keywords: the coupon over the market price
a higher yield means a lower price

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond with a face value of ₹100 carries a 9 per cent annual coupon and is trading at ₹120. A fund manager wants to know what the bond would be worth if the current yield on bonds of this kind moved to 8.25 per cent, the coupon being fixed.

items.stem: What is the bond worth today?

options.misconception: doubles the number of periods and halves the rate but goes on paying the full annual coupon in each of them
options.why: Six payments of ₹100 is twice the interest the bond actually pays. When the periods are doubled the coupon has to be halved with them, to ₹50.
keywords: twice the interest the bond actually pays

options.text: About ₹951.99
options.misconception: treats the interest as though it arrived once a year and discounts three annual coupons at 12 per cent
options.why: Half-yearly interest is worth more than the same annual total, because the first ₹50 arrives six months sooner and can be reinvested. Pricing it as an annual coupon gives a figure close enough to look right and built on the wrong timing.
keywords: the first ₹50 arrives six months sooner

options.misconception: assumes a bond redeemable at par must be worth par
options.why: A bond sells at par only when the required return equals the coupon rate. Here investors want 12 per cent from a bond paying 10 per cent, so it has to sell at a discount.
keywords: only when the required return equals the coupon rate

options.text: About ₹950.87
options.why: Everything moves to a half-yearly period. The coupon is ₹50, the rate per period is 6 per cent and there are six periods, so the price is ₹50 times the sum of the six factors at 6 per cent, which is 4.9174, plus ₹1,000 times 0.7050.
keywords: Everything moves to a half-yearly period
the rate per period is 6 per cent and there are six periods

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries a 10 per cent coupon paid half-yearly and has exactly three years to maturity, redeemable at par. Investors require 12 per cent a year on bonds of this kind. Present value factors at 6 per cent for periods one to six are 0.9434, 0.8900, 0.8396, 0.7921, 0.7473 and 0.7050. Present value factors at 12 per cent for years one to three are 0.8929, 0.7972 and 0.7118.

items.stem: What are the convexity measure and the convexity adjustment?

options.text: A measure of 14 and an adjustment of plus 0.14 per cent, added in both directions
options.why: The two repriced values less twice the initial price is ₹2.80, and dividing that by twice the initial price times the square of the 0.01 yield change, which is 0.2, gives 14. The adjustment is 14 times 0.0001 times 100. It is added whichever way yields move, which is what positive convexity means — the fall is smaller than duration predicts and the rise is larger.

options.text: A measure of 14 and an adjustment of plus 0.14 per cent on a fall and minus 0.14 per cent on a rise
options.misconception: signs the convexity adjustment like a duration term, so that it moves against the yield
options.why: The measure is right. Convexity is the curvature the straight line of duration misses, and a curve that bends away from the line on both sides gives the holder the better of the two outcomes each time. So the adjustment is added to the duration estimate in both directions.
keywords: the curvature the straight line of duration misses

options.text: A measure of 2.80 and an adjustment of plus 0.028 per cent
options.misconception: stops at the numerator and never divides by twice the price times the square of the yield change
options.why: ₹2.80 is the raw difference in rupees. It has to be scaled by the size of the bond and by the size of the yield move before it can be a measure, which is what the denominator of 0.2 does.

options.text: A measure of 28 and an adjustment of plus 0.28 per cent
options.misconception: omits the factor of two in the denominator, doubling the measure and the adjustment
options.why: The denominator is twice the initial price times the square of the yield change, not the price times that square. Dropping the two doubles everything, and the adjustment then overshoots the actual repriced values.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond is priced at ₹1,000 and its modified duration is 4.9. Repricing it shows that a 100 basis point rise in yields would take it to ₹952.60 and a 100 basis point fall would take it to ₹1,050.20. An analyst wants the convexity measure and the convexity adjustment for a move of that size, using the study material's formula in which the measure is built from the price if the yield rises, the price if it falls and the initial price, and the adjustment is the measure times the square of the change in yield times one hundred.

items.stem: What is the fourteen-day relative strength index, and how is it read?

options.text: 42.86, and the share is showing bearish momentum
options.misconception: counts how many days rose instead of how much they rose, treating the index as the proportion of up days in the window
options.why: Six rising days out of fourteen is 42.86 per cent, and the index is not a count. It weighs the size of the moves, which is why fourteen days holding one large rise and thirteen small falls can read as strength while a simple tally of days would call it weakness.
keywords: the index is not a count
It weighs the size of the moves

options.text: 66.67, and the share is showing bullish momentum
options.misconception: averages each total over the days on which it happened rather than over the whole window, so the two averages are computed on different divisors
options.why: Dividing ₹4.20 by the 6 rising days and ₹2.80 by the 8 falling days gives ₹0.70 and ₹0.35, a ratio of 2 and an index of 66.67. Both totals take the same divisor, which is the length of the window. Note that this slip lands in the same band as the right answer, so the reading does not catch it and only the arithmetic does.
keywords: Both totals take the same divisor

options.text: 40.00, and the share is showing bearish momentum
options.misconception: divides the average loss by the average gain, putting the relative strength ratio upside down and reversing the reading
options.why: Turning the ratio over gives 0.20 over 0.30, and an index of 40.00 instead of 60.00. The gain goes on top. Getting this backwards does not merely shift the figure, it moves it across the fifty line and turns a bullish reading into a bearish one.
keywords: moves it across the fifty line

options.text: 60.00, and the share is showing bullish momentum
options.why: Both totals are averaged over the whole fourteen-day window, so the average gain is 4.20 divided by 14, or ₹0.30, and the average loss is 2.80 divided by 14, or ₹0.20. The relative strength is 0.30 over 0.20, which is 1.5, and the index is 100 less 100 divided by 2.5, which is 60.00. A reading between fifty and seventy is positive momentum.
keywords: averaged over the whole fourteen-day window
between fifty and seventy is positive momentum

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: Over the last fourteen trading days the closing price of a share rose on 6 days, the rises adding up to ₹4.20, and fell on 8 days, the falls adding up to ₹2.80.

items.stem: What does the index actually say here?

options.text: Oversold still, so the share is cheap and the buy stands on that ground
options.misconception: keeps the oversold label after the index has climbed back above 30, reading the recent low rather than today's figure
options.why: Oversold is the band below 30 and the index is at 36.10, so the label no longer fits. It fitted five sessions ago at 26.40. Reading a stale band is how a signal gets used after the condition that produced it has gone.

options.text: Weak momentum still, since 36.10 is above the 30 line but below the 50 line
options.why: The share has climbed out of oversold territory, which is what the 30 line marks, and that is all it has done. The line that separates positive momentum from weak momentum is 50, and at 36.10 the index is in the band from 30 to 50, which reads as bearish. A recovery inside the weak band is not confirmation of anything.
keywords: the index is in the band from 30 to 50

options.text: Nothing either way, since the index only signals at 70 and at 30 and is silent between them
options.misconception: treats the index as a two-state overbought-or-oversold flag and ignores the 50 line that divides the middle ground
options.why: The middle ground is divided. From 50 to 70 is positive momentum and from 30 to 50 is weak momentum, so a reading of 36.10 says something quite definite. Most readings in practice fall between 30 and 70, which is exactly why that division carries the work.

options.text: Positive momentum, since the index has risen in five consecutive sessions
options.misconception: reads the direction the index is travelling instead of the level it has reached, so any run of rises is treated as a signal
options.why: The bands are levels, not slopes. An index can rise for a fortnight and still be under 50 the whole way, and until it is above 50 it is describing weak momentum however steadily it climbs. Five sessions of travel from 26.40 has taken it to 36.10, which is short of the line.
keywords: The bands are levels, not slopes

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis
