items.scenario: The fourteen-day relative strength index of a share stood at 26.40 five sessions ago and has risen in every session since, reaching 36.10 today. A dealer tells the client that the five-session recovery confirms a bull trend and that he should buy.

items.stem: What are the two coefficients of variation, and which project is preferred on them?

options.text: 0.30 and 0.25, and Project Q is preferred
options.why: The coefficient is the standard deviation over the expected cash flow, so 12 over 40 gives 0.30 for P and 15 over 60 gives 0.25 for Q. Q bears 25 paise of variability for every rupee of expected cash flow against P's 30 paise, and the lower figure is the better trade.
keywords: the standard deviation over the expected cash flow
the lower figure is the better trade

options.text: 0.24 and 0.20, and Project Q is preferred
options.misconception: divides the standard deviation by the money put in rather than by the expected return, measuring spread per rupee invested
options.why: 12 over 50 and 15 over 75 give 0.24 and 0.20, which is variability per rupee of outlay. The denominator is what the project is expected to return, because the measure is about the risk borne for each unit of expected return, and outlay and expected return are not the same figure.
keywords: The denominator is what the project is expected to return

options.text: 3.33 and 4.00, and Project P is preferred
options.misconception: puts the expected cash flow on top, so the figure now measures return per unit of risk, and then applies the lower-is-better rule to a figure that means the opposite
options.why: 40 over 12 and 60 over 15 give 3.33 and 4.00, which say how much expected cash flow each rupee of variability buys — and on that figure higher is better, so it picks Q as well. The division runs the other way, and reversing it without reversing the rule turns the answer inside out.
keywords: reversing it without reversing the rule

options.text: 0.30 and 0.25, and Project P is preferred
options.misconception: computes the coefficients correctly and then ranks on the raw standard deviations instead, choosing the smaller absolute spread
options.why: P's spread of ₹12 lakh is smaller than Q's ₹15 lakh in rupees, and that comparison is the one the coefficient exists to replace. P is the smaller project, so a smaller spread is what it should have; measured against what each is expected to earn, P is the riskier of the two.
keywords: the one the coefficient exists to replace

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company must choose one of two projects. Project P costs ₹50 lakh, has an expected annual cash flow of ₹40 lakh and a standard deviation of ₹12 lakh. Project Q costs ₹75 lakh, has an expected annual cash flow of ₹60 lakh and a standard deviation of ₹15 lakh.

items.stem: Which project is accepted, and on what ground?

options.text: Project R, because its expected net present value of ₹250 lakh is the larger
options.misconception: ranks on expected return alone, so risk never enters the decision and the right answer is reached for a reason that would fail on the next pair
options.why: The verdict happens to agree here and the ground does not. Had S carried a spread of ₹8 lakh, its coefficient would have been 0.10 against R's 0.16 and the smaller project would have been the better trade — a test that ignores risk cannot tell those two cases apart.
keywords: The verdict happens to agree here and the ground does not

options.text: Project S, whose standard deviation of ₹24 lakh is below Project R's ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: compares raw standard deviations across projects of very unequal size, which is exactly the comparison the coefficient exists to correct
options.why: A standard deviation ranks honestly only where the expected values are alike, and here one project is expected to return more than three times the other. ₹40 lakh of spread on ₹250 lakh expected is a tighter proposition than ₹24 lakh on ₹80 lakh, which is what the two coefficients of 0.16 and 0.30 say.
keywords: ranks honestly only where the expected values are alike

options.text: Project R, whose coefficient of 0.16 is below Project S's 0.30
options.why: 40 over 250 is 0.16 and 24 over 80 is 0.30. R does scatter by more rupees, and it is also more than three times the size, so the rupees are not comparable. Risk borne for each unit of expected return is the comparison that survives a difference in size, and R bears roughly half of what S bears.
keywords: Risk borne for each unit of expected return

options.text: Neither, on these figures — the coefficient may only be compared between projects of the same size
options.misconception: has the rule the wrong way round, restricting the coefficient to the case in which it adds nothing
options.why: It is the other way about. Where two projects are of the same size the coefficient ranks them in the order the standard deviation already did and adds nothing; where the sizes differ, as here, it is the measure that still works and the standard deviation is the one that misleads.
keywords: It is the other way about

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: Two mutually exclusive proposals reach the board. Project R has an expected net present value of ₹250 lakh with a standard deviation of ₹40 lakh. Project S has an expected net present value of ₹80 lakh with a standard deviation of ₹24 lakh. The finance director notes that the two measures of risk point in opposite directions and asks which one governs.

items.stem: What type of fund is this, and what is its net asset value per unit?

options.text: A gilt fund, and ₹10.00 per unit
options.misconception: values the holdings at face value rather than at what the fund paid, so a security bought above par and one bought below par are counted alike
options.why: Five holdings of ₹4 crore face value is ₹20 crore, and over 2 crore units that is ₹10.00. But a bond quoted at ₹110 cost the fund ₹4.40 crore and one quoted at ₹95 cost ₹3.80 crore, and the premiums here outweigh the discounts by ₹80 lakh. Face value is not what anything is worth.
keywords: the premiums here outweigh the discounts
Face value is not what anything is worth

options.text: A gilt fund, and ₹4.16 per unit
options.misconception: divides the portfolio's value by the number of securities held instead of by the units outstanding
options.why: ₹20.80 crore over the five holdings gives ₹4.16, which is the average size of a holding and not a price for anything. Net asset value per unit divides by the units outstanding, which is 2 crore here, because it answers what one unit holder would receive per unit on redemption.
keywords: the average size of a holding

options.text: A bond fund, and ₹10.40 per unit
options.misconception: names the fund from the fact that it holds bonds, when the category turns on whose bonds they are
options.why: The figure is right and the label is not. A bond fund may hold corporate debentures, convertible debentures and money market paper beside government stock; a scheme holding nothing but treasury bills and dated government securities is the narrower category, and it is called a gilt fund.
keywords: The figure is right and the label is not
nothing but treasury bills and dated government securities

options.text: A gilt fund, and ₹10.40 per unit
options.why: Only central and state government paper is held, which is what names a gilt fund. Each holding is worth its quoted rate applied to ₹4 crore of face value, giving ₹4.08, ₹4.32, ₹3.80, ₹4.40 and ₹4.20 crore, or ₹20.80 crore altogether, and that over 2 crore units is ₹10.40.
keywords: Only central and state government paper is held
its quoted rate applied to ₹4 crore of face value

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A scheme's whole portfolio is five dated Government of India securities, ₹4 crore of face value in each. They were bought at ₹102, ₹108, ₹95, ₹110 and ₹105 per ₹100 of face value. The scheme has 2 crore units outstanding and no other assets and no liabilities.

items.stem: What should the manager do, and what does the portfolio's average duration become?

options.text: Sell the 5.50-year security and buy more of the 14.00-year one, giving 9.70 years
options.misconception: lengthens the average duration in the face of an expected rise, which is the move for an expected fall
options.why: This is the right action for the wrong direction. Lengthening to 9.70 years makes the fund gain more if rates fall and lose more when they rise, and rates are expected to rise. A longer maturity on government paper is not a safer position; it is a more rate-sensitive one.
keywords: the right action for the wrong direction

options.text: Sell the 14.00-year security and buy more of the 5.50-year one, giving 6.30 years
options.why: Rates rising means prices falling, and the longer the duration the harder the fall, so the move is to shorten. Taking 14.00 out of the total of 40.00 and putting 5.50 in leaves 31.50 over five securities, which is 6.30 years against the 8.00 the fund started with.
keywords: the longer the duration the harder the fall

options.text: Sell the 14.00-year security and buy more of the 5.50-year one, giving 7.88 years
options.misconception: divides by four after the sale, forgetting that the proceeds bought another security so the portfolio still holds five
options.why: 31.50 over four gives 7.88, and there are still five securities. The sale and the purchase happen together, so nothing left the portfolio uninvested; the divisor moves only when the number of holdings does.
keywords: the divisor moves only when the number of holdings does

options.text: Do nothing, leaving the average at 8.00 years, since government paper cannot default
options.misconception: reads the absence of default risk as the absence of price risk, when the units are priced off the market value of the holdings every day
options.why: The government paying every rupee it promised is exactly what is assumed here, and the fund can still lose. Units are valued off the market price of the holdings, and government bond prices fall when yields rise, so the 75 basis point move reaches the unit holder whether or not anybody defaults.
keywords: government bond prices fall when yields rise

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A gilt fund holds five government securities whose durations are 3.00, 5.50, 8.00, 9.50 and 14.00 years, and it takes the plain average of those five as the portfolio's duration. Interest rates are expected to rise by 75 basis points. The manager will sell one holding and put the whole proceeds into more of another holding already in the portfolio, leaving five securities as before.

items.stem: What is the call worth under the replicating portfolio route?

options.misconception: deducts the amount the borrowing will repay at the end of the period instead of the amount that has to be borrowed today, so the interest is never accounted for
options.why: The down-move value of ₹109.29 is a figure one period away, and ₹128.57 is a figure today. Subtracting one from the other mixes two dates. Bringing ₹109.29 back at 1.04 gives ₹105.08, and the ₹4.20 of interest between the two is the whole of the ₹4.20 gap between ₹19.29 and ₹23.49.
keywords: Subtracting one from the other mixes two dates

options.why: The call pays ₹45 on the up move and nothing on the down move, so the share leg is 45 over the price spread of 105, which is 0.4286 of a share. That fraction is worth ₹109.29 on the down move, and discounting at 1.04 says ₹105.08 must be borrowed today. The fraction of a share costs ₹128.57 now, and the difference of ₹23.49 is the option. The risk-neutral route reaches the same figure to the paisa.
keywords: the share leg is 45 over the price spread of 105
reaches the same figure to the paisa

options.misconception: quotes the cost of the share leg as the option's price, leaving the borrowing that finances most of it out of the sum
options.why: 0.4286 of a share does cost ₹128.57 today, and that is one leg of two. The portfolio that replicates the call is that holding financed in part by borrowing ₹105.08, and the option is worth what the two legs net to, not what one of them costs.
keywords: that is one leg of two
worth what the two legs net to

options.misconception: holds one whole share against the option instead of the payoff spread divided by the price spread
options.why: One share and borrowing the discounted ₹255 gives 300 less 245.19, or ₹54.81, and that portfolio does not match the call: on the up move it is worth ₹105 while the call pays ₹45. The share leg is a fraction, and it is the fraction that makes the two payoffs equal in both states.
keywords: it is worth ₹105 while the call pays ₹45
The share leg is a fraction

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share stands at ₹300 today and in one period will be worth either ₹360 or ₹255. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.04. A European call on the share has an exercise price of ₹315.

items.stem: What does the 45 per cent do to the call's value?

options.text: It replaces the 54.29 per cent figure, bringing the call to ₹19.47
options.misconception: treats the probability inside the model as an estimate of what will happen, so a better estimate is thought to give a better price
options.why: 0.45 times ₹45 over 1.04 gives ₹19.47, and at that price the call could be bought and the replicating portfolio sold for a certain ₹4.02 with no risk taken. The figure the model uses is the one that removes exactly that opportunity; it is not the market's opinion and was never meant to be.
keywords: a certain ₹4.02 with no risk taken

options.text: It leaves the call unpriceable, since the two routes will now disagree
options.misconception: thinks an extra piece of information can break a no-arbitrage price, when the price rests on the two share prices and the risk-free rate alone
options.why: Extra information about risk preferences cannot unsettle a figure that never rested on them. The two routes are two proofs of the same ₹23.49, and a stated view about the up move sits outside both of them, useful for deciding whether to buy the option and useless for pricing it.
keywords: useful for deciding whether to buy the option

options.text: Nothing, because neither route uses a view about the up move
options.why: The replicating route never mentions a probability at all — it matches the call's payoff in both states with a fraction of a share and some borrowing, and prices the option at what that costs. The risk-neutral route does use a probability, but it is 54.29 per cent, computed from 1.04 and the two share prices, and it is not a forecast of anything.
keywords: never mentions a probability at all
computed from 1.04 and the two share prices

options.text: Nothing to the replicating route, which uses no probability, but the risk-neutral route needs it
options.misconception: reads the risk-neutral route as needing any probability it can be given, when the probability it needs is implied by the prices themselves
options.why: Half of this is right and it is the half that matters least. The risk-neutral route computes its own probability of 54.29 per cent before it discounts anything, and feeding it a forecast instead breaks the agreement between the two routes — which is the very thing that shows the price is the only one no arbitrage allows.
keywords: computes its own probability of 54.29 per cent
the only one no arbitrage allows

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: On the same one-period share, priced at ₹300 and moving to ₹360 or ₹255 with a risk-free growth factor of 1.04 and a call struck at ₹315, both routes have given ₹23.49. The analyst who prepared the note adds that in her own judgement there is a 45 per cent chance of the up move, and asks whether the valuation should be redone with that figure.

items.stem: Under which of the study material's risk headings does this sit?

options.text: Credit or counterparty risk, since borrowers are failing to pay
options.misconception: files every non-payment under credit risk, when that heading in the material is about the servicer failing rather than about the pool's borrowers being squeezed by their own industry
options.why: Credit or counterparty risk here is the risk of bankruptcy and of the servicer not performing — the party that collects from the borrowers and passes the money on. A downturn reaching the pool through the borrowers' own trade is external to the transaction, which is the definition of the market risk group.

options.text: Legal risk, since whether the financier can repossess turns on the law
options.misconception: reads legal risk as any risk that involves a legal right, when the material means the absence of settled law on securitisation itself
options.why: Legal risk on this list is that there is no conclusive judicial precedent and no explicit statutory provision on these transactions, so a dispute about who owns the pooled assets leaves investor payouts uncertain. Taking back a vehicle under an ordinary loan agreement is not that question.
keywords: Taking back a vehicle under an ordinary loan agreement

options.text: Prepayment risk, since these loans are ending before their term
options.misconception: counts a default that closes a loan early as a prepayment, when prepayment means the borrower paying the balance off in full ahead of time
options.why: A prepayment is money arriving early, and it hurts by forcing the investor to put it back to work at a lower yield, which is why it goes with falling rates. Here the money is not arriving at all. Both sit inside market risk; they are different parts of it and they hurt in opposite ways.
keywords: A prepayment is money arriving early
the money is not arriving at all

options.text: Market risk, of the macroeconomic kind
options.why: Market risks are the ones outside the transaction, and a downturn in the industry the borrowers work in is the example the material itself uses. The fall in vehicle prices makes it worse in a second way: when the security is worth less than the balance owed, walking away costs a borrower less than paying on, so the price fall converts hardship into deliberate default.
keywords: walking away costs a borrower less than paying on

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: A special purpose vehicle has issued paper against a pool of commercial vehicle loans. Industrial output falls, freight volumes with it, and operators earn less. Second-hand vehicle prices drop sharply at the same time, and a number of borrowers stop paying and let the financier take the vehicle back rather than keep up their instalments.

items.stem: What is this, and what does the study material offer against it?

options.text: Interest rate risk from the mismatch, and an interest rate swap hedges part of it
options.why: The shortfall is in the rate and not in the recovery, which is why perfect collection does not cure it: the pool now earns less than the fixed promise made to investors. That mismatch between a floating pool and fixed payouts is named on its own inside market risk, and the material offers an interest rate swap as a partial hedge.
keywords: The shortfall is in the rate and not in the recovery
an interest rate swap as a partial hedge

options.text: Macroeconomic risk, since a falling benchmark rate is an economy-wide event
options.misconception: puts anything economy-wide under the macroeconomic heading, when that sub-heading works through what the borrowers can afford rather than through the deal's own pricing
options.why: Macroeconomic risk on this list reaches the pool through the borrowers — an industry downturn, or a fall in the price of what secures their loans. Here the borrowers are unaffected and paying. The damage is done by the structure's own two rates moving apart, which the material lists separately in the same group.
keywords: reaches the pool through the borrowers
the structure's own two rates moving apart

options.text: Prepayment risk, since falling rates send borrowers off to refinance
options.misconception: applies the falling-rate story for a fixed-rate retail pool to a floating-rate one, where the loans reprice on their own and nobody has any reason to leave
options.why: A borrower refinances to escape a rate that has stopped being competitive. These loans reset downward by themselves, so there is nothing to escape and nobody has left. The pool's principal is intact and its income has fallen, which is the opposite shape of problem.
keywords: These loans reset downward by themselves

options.text: Credit risk, and more credit enhancement is what answers it
options.misconception: reaches for enhancement because money is short, when enhancement absorbs losses from money that never came and every borrower here has paid
options.why: Overcollateralisation, junior tranches, excess spread and a guarantee all stand between the investor and a loss on the pool. None of them turns a floating stream into a fixed one. Nothing has gone bad, so there is no loss for enhancement to absorb.
keywords: None of them turns a floating stream into a fixed one
no loss for enhancement to absorb

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: The loans in a securitised pool carry a floating rate that resets with a benchmark. The paper the special purpose vehicle issued against them promises investors a fixed rate. The benchmark falls. Every borrower pays in full and on time, and the pool's collections still come to less than the amount owed to investors that quarter.

items.stem: How many of the four are correctly presented, and what is the position?

options.text: None of them. Interest accrued but not due belongs under Other Liabilities and Provisions and is not clubbed with deposits; debit balances in current accounts are included under Advances rather than netted on the liabilities side; a net credit inter-office adjustments balance goes under Other Liabilities and Provisions because inter-office transactions are not borrowings; and call loans made cannot be netted off against call loans received
options.why: Each of the four is a rule of presentation the auditor examines specifically. Interest accrued is one of the four items disclosed under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and the auditor examines that it has not been clubbed with the figures of deposits and borrowings. A current account in debit is not squared off against the credit balances on the liabilities side; the amount is instead included under the head advances. The balance in inter-office adjustments, if in credit, is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and inter-office transactions are not borrowings. And call money the bank has placed cannot be netted off against call loans received.
keywords: not been clubbed with the figures of deposits and borrowings
cannot be netted off against call loans received

options.text: Three of them. Only the netting of call loans is wrong, because a bank's lending and borrowing in the call money market are separate transactions; the other three are permissible groupings
options.misconception: allows three presentations because each groups related balances, when the Third Schedule fixes the head and forbids the grouping in each case
options.why: Grouping is exactly what the form of the balance sheet is there to prevent. Interest accrued has its own place under Other Liabilities and Provisions, a debit balance in a current account is an advance, and an inter-office balance is not a borrowing. All four are wrong, not one.

options.text: All four are correct, provided the notes to the accounts disclose each grouping, since the Third Schedule allows a bank to prepare its balance sheet in the form set out or as near thereto as the circumstances admit
options.misconception: reads the "as near thereto" latitude as permission to move balances between heads if disclosed
options.why: That latitude is about circumstances that make the prescribed form impracticable, not about moving a balance into a head the form gives to something else. A note does not cure a misclassification, and the auditor is directed to examine for these four specifically.

options.text: Two of them. The interest accrued and the current account netting are right, because both relate to deposits and the head is Deposits; the inter-office and call loan presentations are wrong
options.misconception: places balances by what they relate to rather than by what the Third Schedule calls them
options.why: Relatedness is not the test. Interest accrued but not due on deposits is examined precisely to see that it is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions and not under Deposits, and a debit balance in a current account is an amount owed to the bank, which makes it an advance.
keywords: an amount owed to the bank

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the disclosure of interest accrued under Other Liabilities and Provisions and the examination that it is not clubbed with deposits and borrowings, the inclusion of debit balances in current accounts under advances, the treatment of a credit inter-office adjustments balance and the rule that inter-office transactions are not borrowings, and the rule against netting call loans made against call loans received

items.scenario: You are a statutory central auditor of a bank. Reviewing the draft balance sheet you find four presentations. Interest accrued but not due on term deposits, ₹412 crore, has been added to the figure of term deposits under Deposits. Current accounts with debit balances totalling ₹78 crore have been netted against the credit balances in current accounts, so that Deposits is shown ₹78 crore lower. The inter-office adjustments account has a net credit balance of ₹34 crore and has been shown under Borrowings, on the reasoning that head office has effectively lent the amount to the branches. And call loans of ₹500 crore made to other banks have been netted against call loans of ₹300 crore received from other banks, with ₹200 crore shown as money at call and short notice.

items.stem: What does the form of a bank's balance sheet require?

options.text: A single figure for each of India and outside India is sufficient; the split between classes of lender and the secured total are disclosures for the notes to accounts under the Companies Act rather than requirements of the Third Schedule
options.misconception: moves two requirements of the prescribed form into general company law disclosure, where they are optional in this form
options.why: Both are requirements of the head itself. The breakdown between the Reserve Bank of India, other banks and other institutions and agencies is part of how borrowings in India are shown, and the secured total is shown by way of a note to the relevant schedule.
keywords: part of how borrowings in India are shown
by way of a note to the relevant schedule

options.text: The split is required, but rediscount and refinance are properly added together, since both are ways of raising funds against the bank's own asset portfolio
options.misconception: treats economic similarity as a reason to combine two items the auditor is directed to keep apart
options.why: The auditor is directed to look for a clear distinction between rediscount and refinance when the amount under this head is disclosed, because rediscount does not figure under it. Combining them puts an amount under borrowings that does not belong there.

options.text: Nothing further, provided the branch has been authorised by head office to retain the borrowings and the terms accord with that authorisation
options.misconception: answers a question about presentation with an audit procedure about authorisation, which is a different requirement
options.why: Examining the head office authorisation and the terms is one of the audit procedures on borrowings, and a second asks that what the branch accounts show is properly classified based on security or otherwise. Neither supplies the breakdown the form requires.

options.text: Borrowings in India are split between the Reserve Bank of India, other banks, and other institutions and agencies; the total amount of secured borrowings, in India and outside India, is shown by way of a note to the relevant schedule; and rediscount is distinguished from refinance because rediscount does not figure under this head at all
options.why: The head has a prescribed breakdown — borrowings in India from the Reserve Bank of India, from other banks and from other institutions and agencies, and borrowings outside India — and the total amount of secured borrowings, which for this purpose includes borrowings and refinance in India as well as outside India, is shown by way of a note to the relevant schedule. The auditor examines whether a clear distinction has been made between rediscount and refinance, since rediscount does not figure under this head.
keywords: from other banks and from other institutions and agencies
by way of a note to the relevant schedule
rediscount does not figure under this head

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the presentation of borrowings in India between the Reserve Bank of India, other banks and other institutions and agencies and of borrowings outside India, the note showing the total amount of secured borrowings, and the distinction between rediscount and refinance

items.scenario: A bank's draft schedule of borrowings shows a single figure for borrowings in India and a single figure for borrowings outside India. Within the India figure, refinance taken from a refinancing institution and bills rediscounted with another bank have been added together. Nothing anywhere states how much of the total is secured. The finance team's view is that the split between lenders is management information and that security is a matter for the notes on charges rather than for this schedule.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The provisions are netted, and no separate movement of reserves need be shown, since the closing balance of each reserve tells the reader everything he needs
options.misconception: drops the movement disclosure, which the form requires item by item
options.why: For statutory reserves, capital reserves, share premium and revenue and other reserves including the investment fluctuation reserve, the form asks for three figures apiece — the opening balance, the additions during the year and the deductions during the year — set out separately in respect of each item.
keywords: the opening balance, the additions during the year and the deductions during the year
separately in respect of each item

options.text: The figures of advances and investments in a bank's balance sheet are shown excluding the provisions made in respect of them to the satisfaction of the auditors; and Statutory Reserves is one of the items disclosed under Reserves and Surplus, where opening balance, additions and deductions are shown separately
options.why: The netting is the point. What a bank shows for advances, and what it shows for investments, already excludes provisions in respect thereof made to the satisfaction of auditors, which is why no separate provision line appears. And Reserves and Surplus discloses statutory reserves, capital reserves, share premium, revenue and other reserves including the investment fluctuation reserve, and the balance in the profit and loss account, with the opening balance, the additions during the year and the deductions during the year shown separately for each of those marked.
keywords: made to the satisfaction of auditors
opening balance, the additions during the year and the deductions during the year

options.text: The provisions must be missing from the draft, because a provision is a liability and belongs under Other Liabilities and Provisions in every case
options.misconception: applies the general position for provisions to advances and investments, where the form nets them against the asset
options.why: Other Liabilities and Provisions carries other provisions, and the auditor examines those in the same manner as for any other entity. Provisions against advances and investments are different: the asset figures themselves are shown excluding them.

options.text: The provisions are netted, and the statutory reserve is not a balance sheet item at all but a regulatory computation reported separately to the Reserve Bank
options.misconception: gets the netting right and then removes a head that the Third Schedule actually requires in the balance sheet
options.why: Statutory Reserves is one of the items required to be disclosed under Reserves and Surplus. The auditor verifies the opening balances against the previous year's audited balance sheet and examines whether the requirements of the governing legislation about transferring the prescribed percentage of profits to the reserve fund have been complied with.
keywords: required to be disclosed under Reserves and Surplus

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the netting of provisions against advances and against investments on the face of a bank's balance sheet, and the items disclosed under Reserves and Surplus with the movement on each shown for the year

items.scenario: A newly qualified assistant is reading a bank's balance sheet beside a manufacturing company's and cannot see where the provisions have gone. Advances are shown at ₹1,42,300 crore and investments at ₹58,900 crore, and there is no line anywhere showing the provisions held against either. He also cannot find the reserve the bank is required by its governing legislation to build out of profit each year, though Reserves and Surplus is there.

items.stem: What does the audit of interest accrued require?

options.text: Interest is accrued only on the standard portion of the loan book, so the entire accrual on any account that is not standard comes out, whether or not it is realisable
options.misconception: swings past the rule to a blanket exclusion, when the auditor is directed to check that interest has been accrued on the entire portfolio
options.why: The auditor examines whether interest has been accrued on the entire loans and advances portfolio of the bank. The head is then confined to what can be realised in the ordinary course of business, which is a judgement on each amount rather than a class exclusion.
keywords: the entire loans and advances portfolio

options.text: The head shows no more interest than can be realised in the ordinary course of business, because AS 9 does not let revenue be recognised where there is significant uncertainty about its collectability — and overdue bills purchased or discounted call for special consideration
options.why: Contractual accrual is not the test for what goes under this head. The auditor keeps the figure down to what can be realised in the ordinary course of business, and the reason sits in AS 9: revenue stays unrecognised while there is significant uncertainty about its collectability. He also gives special consideration to overdue bills purchased or discounted, which is exactly the ₹94 crore here.
keywords: realised in the ordinary course of business

options.text: The accrual stands in full, and recoverability is dealt with entirely through provisioning against the advance, so that income and provision are kept as separate questions
options.misconception: keeps a recognition question inside a measurement one, when the rule bars the recognition of interest that cannot be realised in the ordinary course
options.why: Provisioning answers what the advance is worth. What may be shown as interest accrued is a separate rule, and it admits only interest realisable in the ordinary course of business. Accruing income the bank will not receive and then providing against it is not what the head permits.
keywords: realisable in the ordinary course of business

options.text: Interest accrued has no place under Other Assets at all; interest accrued is one of the items disclosed under Other Liabilities and Provisions
options.misconception: remembers interest accrued on the liabilities side and concludes there is no asset-side item of the same name
options.why: Both exist. Interest accrued on the bank's deposits and borrowings is one of the items under Other Liabilities and Provisions; interest accrued on the bank's own loans and advances is one of the items under Other Assets. The name is the same and the balance is on opposite sides.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the audit procedures for interest accrued under Other Assets: accrual across the whole loan book, the special consideration overdue bills purchased or discounted call for, and the AS 9 limit on how much interest the head may carry

items.scenario: A bank's Other Assets schedule shows interest accrued of ₹1,860 crore. Testing it, you find that the accrual has been computed on the whole loan book, which is right, but that it includes ₹94 crore accrued on a group of bills purchased and discounted that are long overdue and where the drawees have stopped responding, and a further ₹120 crore accrued on accounts the bank's own credit team has flagged as unlikely to pay. The finance head's position is that interest has contractually accrued on every one of these accounts, that the bank has not waived it, and that the right place to deal with recoverability is the provision against the advance rather than the accrual itself.

items.stem: What should the auditor examine?

options.text: That the asset is carried at the higher of the two amounts, so that the bank does not understate an asset it has taken over in full settlement of a larger debt
options.misconception: reverses the measurement rule, taking the higher of the two figures instead of the lower
options.why: The rule takes the lower. As at the date of acquisition the asset is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value of the asset acquired, which keeps the bank from booking a gain on a defaulted loan.
keywords: booking a gain on a defaulted loan

options.text: That the asset was recorded at the date of acquisition at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value of the asset — so ₹22 crore, not ₹27 crore — and compliance with section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which bars a banking company from holding immovable property, however it was acquired, for longer than seven years measured from the date of acquisition, unless the property is required for its own use
options.why: Two things are wrong. At the date of acquisition the asset had to go into the books at the lower of the net book value of the advance or, if that was the smaller figure, the net realisable value of the asset acquired — ₹22 crore here, not ₹27 crore. And section 9 stops a banking company holding immovable property, whether it came in on a settlement of claims or in any other way, for a run exceeding seven years from the date of acquisition. The bar takes in every immovable property except such as is required for its own use — so the two floors kept as the regional office stand differently from the vacant part, and nine years have passed.
keywords: lower of the net book value of the advance
net realisable value of the asset acquired
except such as is required for its own use
exceeding seven years from the date of acquisition

options.text: That a provision has been made under AS 29, since a property the bank has failed to sell for nine years is a contingent liability
options.misconception: turns an asset the bank has not disposed of into a contingent liability, which is a liability the bank may owe
options.why: The building is an asset held with the intention of being disposed of, not an obligation. AS 29 comes into the picture where a dispute or other claim about the property arises subsequently and the auditor examines whether a provision for liability or the disclosure of a contingent liability is appropriate.
keywords: held with the intention of being disposed of
a dispute or other claim about the property arises subsequently

options.text: Only the legal title. Once ownership is legally vested in the bank and the settlement, court order or arbitration award supports it, the asset may be held indefinitely, since it is now the bank's own property
options.misconception: stops at the ownership check and misses the statutory limit on how long a banking company may hold immovable property
options.why: Checking that ownership is legally vested in the bank and verifying the terms of settlement, the court's order or the arbitration award are two of the procedures, but they are not the whole of it. Section 9 puts a seven year limit on holding immovable property however acquired, except such as is required for the bank's own use.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims, their recording at the date of acquisition at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value of the asset acquired, the verification of ownership and of the terms of settlement, court order or arbitration award, and compliance with section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949

items.scenario: A bank took possession of a commercial building nine years ago under a settlement with a defaulting borrower, and shows it under Other Assets as a non-banking asset acquired in satisfaction of claims. The advance had a net book value of ₹22 crore at the date of acquisition and the building's net realisable value was assessed then at ₹27 crore; the asset is carried at ₹27 crore. Two floors of the building have been used as the bank's regional office since the year after acquisition and the rest has been vacant. The bank has made no attempt to sell it.

items.stem: What is required of the auditor on the two items?

options.text: Stationery and Stamps includes only exceptional items of expenditure such as a bulk purchase of security paper to be written off over a period, valued at cost, with normal stationery charged to the profit and loss account; and on inter-office adjustments the auditor reports the year-end status, the dates up to which segments have been reconciled, and the number and amount of outstanding entries, separately for debits and credits
options.why: The head is not a store of unconsumed supplies. It includes only exceptional items of expenditure on stationery — a bulk buy of security paper that the bank will have written off over a period, say — valued at cost, and normal expenditure on stationery is charged to the profit and loss account. On inter-office adjustments the auditor's report has to say where the inter-branch accounts stood at the year end: the dates up to which all or any segments have been reconciled, and how many entries were left outstanding and for how much, giving that information separately for debit and credit entries, drawn primarily from branch audit reports.
keywords: the dates up to which all or any segments have been reconciled
separately for debit and credit entries

options.text: Both treatments are acceptable. Unconsumed stationery is an asset of the bank on any view, and the reconciliation position is an internal control matter for the long form audit report rather than something to be reported on the year-end figure
options.misconception: allows a head to swell with ordinary supplies, and moves a required report on the year-end status into a different document
options.why: Normal expenditure on stationery is charged to the profit and loss account rather than carried, and the item may not even appear at branch level since head office supplies much of it. And the auditor is required to report on the year-end status of inter-branch accounts with the dates and the outstanding entries, which is not discharged by a comment elsewhere.
keywords: charged to the profit and loss account

options.text: Neither item needs work at branch level, since stationery is supplied centrally and inter-branch reconciliation is done at the central level
options.misconception: reasons from where the accounting happens to a conclusion that nothing is checked, when both items carry specific branch-level procedures
options.why: Both are still audited. Security stationery on hand is physically verified at the year end and any shortage inquired into because it can expose the bank to loss from misuse, and the branch auditor comments specifically on the adequacy of the relevant internal controls in the long form audit report; the inter-office information itself comes primarily from branch audit reports.
keywords: physically verified at the year end
comes primarily from branch audit reports

options.text: Stationery and Stamps should be written off in full, since no stationery of any kind may be carried as an asset by a bank
options.misconception: overshoots the rule, deleting the exceptional items the head exists to carry
options.why: The head exists for exceptional items — a bulk buy of security paper, say, which the bank will have written off over a period of years — and these are valued at cost. What comes out is the normal expenditure, not everything.
keywords: What comes out is the normal expenditure

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the audit procedures for Stationery and Stamps and for Inter-Office Adjustments under Other Assets, including the confinement of the head to exceptional items valued at cost, the physical verification of security stationery at the year end, and the reporting of the year-end status of inter-branch accounts with the dates reconciled and the outstanding debit and credit entries

items.scenario: Two items in a bank's Other Assets schedule are being discussed at the closing meeting. The first is Stationery and Stamps of ₹41 crore, which the finance team has built by carrying forward the whole of the year's unconsumed stationery at every branch, including ordinary printed forms supplied by head office. The second is Inter-Office Adjustments, where the central reconciliation is complete only to a date four months before the year end and a large number of entries remain outstanding on both sides. The finance head says the outstanding entries will clear in the normal course and that a bare figure in the schedule is all a reader needs.

items.stem: What is wrong?

options.text: Only the partly paid investments. Derivative contracts belong with guarantees given on behalf of constituents, and bills for collection belong with acceptances and endorsements
options.misconception: keeps the items but merges them into neighbouring heads, which defeats the point of a prescribed breakdown
options.why: Outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts have their own head, and bills for collection are not a contingent liability at all — they are shown separately because the bank holds the bills as an agent rather than owing anything on them.
keywords: holds the bills as an agent

options.text: Nothing, provided management represents that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for and all year-end contingent liabilities disclosed
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for the disclosure it is meant to support
options.why: The representation is one of the auditor's procedures and covers, among other things, that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into and that all year-end contingent liabilities have been disclosed. It does not decide which heads the disclosure carries; the Third Schedule does.
keywords: It does not decide which heads

options.text: All three. The liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts and the liability for partly paid investments are each separate heads of contingent liabilities under the Third Schedule, and bills for collection are shown separately rather than within any contingent liability head
options.why: The heads are prescribed and there are six of them. Two cover what somebody may come and claim off the bank: claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts, and the liability for partly paid investments. Then the liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts; then guarantees given on behalf of constituents within and outside India; then acceptances, endorsements and other obligations; and last a residual head for anything else on which the bank is contingently liable. Bills for collection sit apart from all six, because the bank holds those bills as an agent.
keywords: liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts

options.text: Only the bills for collection, since derivative positions carried at fair value and unpaid calls on investments are both recognised in the balance sheet and disclosing them again would double count
options.misconception: assumes recognition in the balance sheet displaces the contingent liability disclosure, when both are prescribed heads of that disclosure
options.why: The Third Schedule names both as heads of contingent liabilities in their own right. The disclosure is of the exposure, not a second recognition of an amount already booked, which is why the auditor's concern is that all contingent liabilities are identified and properly valued.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the heads of contingent liabilities disclosed under the Third Schedule, including liability for partly paid investments and liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, and the separate disclosure of bills for collection

items.scenario: A bank's draft disclosure of contingent liabilities lists claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts, guarantees given on behalf of constituents, and acceptances, endorsements and other obligations. Three things have been left out. Outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, on the view that these are trading positions carried at fair value in the books and so are already in the balance sheet. Liability for partly paid investments, on the view that the unpaid amount is a commitment rather than a liability. And bills held for collection on behalf of customers, which have been added into acceptances, endorsements and other obligations to keep the disclosure short.

items.stem: What does the auditor seek in the management representation on contingent liabilities?

options.text: That all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into, after following the due procedure laid down and supported by the underlying documents — which is the whole of the representation on contingent liabilities
options.misconception: names three real limbs of the representation and treats them as its entirety
options.why: Those three are in the representation and they are not all of it. The representation runs on to the disclosure of all year-end contingent liabilities, to crystallised liabilities, to AS 29 estimates, to guarantees on behalf of directors and section 20, and to the justification for treating an outcome as remote.
keywords: Those three are in the representation and they are not all of it
the justification for treating an outcome as remote

options.text: That the estimated financial effects have been computed under AS 29, which answers all three, since a decreed claim, a director-related guarantee and a remote claim are all matters of estimation
options.misconception: folds three separate representations into the one about measurement, when only one of them is about estimating an amount
options.why: The AS 29 representation is that the estimated amounts of the financial effect of the contingent liabilities are based on best estimates, including consideration of the possibility of any reimbursement. It says nothing about whether a crystallised liability has been wrongly left in the disclosure, about section 20, or about a remote classification.

options.text: A representation is not sought on contingent liabilities at all, because a written representation is not audit evidence and the auditor must verify each item against the underlying documents
options.misconception: rejects a representation the chapter expressly directs the auditor to obtain, on a proposition about representations generally
options.why: The auditor is directed to obtain a representation from management on these matters, alongside his other procedures on the identification and valuation of contingent liabilities. The representation supplements the work on the underlying documents rather than replacing it.

options.text: That the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require a provision or adjustment instead; that where guarantees have been issued on behalf of the bank's directors, arrangements exist for the commitment to be met out of the party's own resources so that section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is not breached; and that management's justification is given for liabilities not disclosed because their outcome is remote
options.why: The representation covers each of the three. It states that the disclosure holds no crystallised liabilities of the loss-or-expense kind — those call for a provision or an adjustment in the financial statements instead. It states that where a guarantee stands in the name of a concern the bank's directors are interested in, the arrangements already made are adequate and effective, the sum guaranteed is to be met out of the party's own resources, nobody will come to the bank for a loan or advance if the guarantee is invoked, and that section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is nowhere breached. And it states that contingent liabilities not disclosed because the possibility of their outcome is remote include management's justification for that decision.
keywords: met out of the party's own resources
section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the management representation obtained on contingent liabilities, including that crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense are not shown as contingent, that estimated financial effects are best estimates in terms of AS 29 including any reimbursement, that guarantees issued on behalf of the bank's directors raise no violation of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and that management's justification is given where an outcome is treated as remote

items.scenario: You are auditing a bank's contingent liabilities. Three matters come up. A claim against the bank in a consumer dispute was decreed against it in February and the bank has decided not to appeal; the amount remains inside claims not acknowledged as debts. A guarantee has been issued on behalf of a company in which two of the bank's directors are interested, and nothing on the file shows what would happen if it were invoked. And a group of claims has been left out of the disclosure entirely on the ground that the possibility of any outflow is remote, with no note of why management takes that view.

items.stem: How is the question decided?

options.text: By the test on assets and income taken from the last audited balance sheet — more than 50 per cent of total assets, after intangible assets are netted off, held as financial assets, and more than 50 per cent of gross income earned on them — and the company meets both, so it is a non-banking financial company and required to register
options.why: Both the asset pattern and the income pattern are considered, as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet, to decide the company's principal business. Two limbs then have to hold. On the asset side, once intangible assets are netted off, what the company holds in financial assets must be more than 50 per cent of the total assets. On the income side, what those assets earn must be more than 50 per cent of the gross income. Here the assets are ₹300 crore against ₹480 crore and the income is ₹38 crore against ₹60 crore, so both limbs are met, and a company which fulfils both criteria would require to be registered.
keywords: as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet
more than 50 per cent of the total assets
more than 50 per cent of the gross income

options.text: By the objects in the memorandum of association, which state what the company's principal business is; a company whose objects are trading is not a non-banking financial company however its balance sheet looks
options.misconception: answers a question of fact from the constitutional documents, when the test is quantitative and taken from the accounts
options.why: The principal business is identified from the asset pattern and the income pattern as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet. What the memorandum says the company was set up to do does not enter the test.
keywords: asset pattern and the income pattern

options.text: By whether the lending is to outside parties. Lending confined to group companies is treasury management within a group and is excluded from financial assets for the purpose of the test
options.misconception: invents an exclusion for intra-group lending that the test does not contain
options.why: The test looks at financial assets and at income from financial assets. It does not ask who the borrower is, and nothing in it carves out lending to group companies.
keywords: does not ask who the borrower is

options.text: By the asset test alone. Financial assets above half of total assets makes the company a non-banking financial company, and the income figures are a cross-check rather than a condition
options.misconception: keeps one limb of a two limb test and demotes the other to corroboration
options.why: Both criteria must be fulfilled. Financial assets have to exceed 50 per cent of total assets after intangible assets are netted off, AND the income those assets throw off has to exceed 50 per cent of gross income; a company which fulfils both these criteria qualifies, and one that clears a single limb does not.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the identification of a non-banking financial company from both the asset pattern and the income pattern as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet, and the two 50 per cent limbs that test is made of

items.scenario: You have been appointed auditor of a company that describes itself in its memorandum as a trading company and has never held a certificate of registration from the Reserve Bank. Its last audited balance sheet shows total assets of ₹500 crore, of which intangible assets are ₹20 crore and financial assets — loans given to group companies and to unrelated borrowers, and investments in securities — are ₹300 crore. Its gross income for that year was ₹60 crore, of which ₹38 crore was interest and dividend income from those financial assets. The directors say the company cannot be a non-banking financial company because lending is not what the company was set up to do and because most of the lending is to group companies.

items.stem: What does the auditor have to do about it in his report?

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvi)(a) but only after the company has applied for registration, since until then it is not established that registration was required
options.misconception: makes the auditor's answer wait on the company's application, when the requirement to register is decided by the test and not by the application
options.why: Whether registration is required is answered by the principal business test on the last audited balance sheet, and the company meets both limbs. The auditor answers the clause on the position as it is, and an application not yet made is part of what makes the answer unfavourable.
keywords: answered by the principal business test
part of what makes the answer unfavourable

options.text: Nothing in the report. Registration is regulatory and the auditor's remedy is to report the matter to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank under the directions issued to auditors of non-banking financial companies
options.misconception: routes the matter to a reporting duty that belongs to the auditor of a registered non-banking financial company, and drops the CARO clause that applies here
options.why: The additional report to the Board and the exception report to the Regional Office are duties under the directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies. This company is not registered and this auditor's duty on these facts is the CARO clause, which asks exactly this question of every company the Order covers.

options.text: Modify the opinion on the financial statements, because carrying on the business of a non-banking financial institution without a certificate of registration is a contravention of law
options.misconception: converts a non-compliance into a modification without asking whether the financial statements are misstated
options.why: A modification requires a material misstatement of the financial statements or an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Non-compliance is reported where the law requires it to be reported, and here that is the CARO clause; whether the opinion is modified turns on the effect of the non-compliance on the financial statements.
keywords: turns on the effect of the non-compliance

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvi)(a) of the Order — it asks whether section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 required this company to register and, where it did, whether the company went and obtained the registration — and state the basis for the unfavourable answer
options.why: The Order puts the question directly to the auditor. Clause 3(xvi)(a) covers every company the Order applies to, and it asks two things in turn. Was this company required to be registered under section 45-IA? That section sits in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. And where the answer to the first question is yes, the clause asks whether the registration has been obtained. On these facts it was required and it has not been, which is an unfavourable answer, and paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for it.
keywords: required to be registered under section 45-IA
whether the registration has been obtained

citation.ref: clause 3(xvi)(a), which asks the auditor whether section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 required the company to register and, where it did, whether the company obtained the registration, read with paragraph 4(a) on stating the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer

items.scenario: The company in the previous engagement meets both limbs of the principal business test and has never registered. It is covered by the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020. The audit manager proposes to raise the matter with the directors, note it in the working papers, and leave the auditor's report alone on the ground that registration is a matter between the company and the Reserve Bank.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(xvii) say?

options.text: That a cash loss arose both in the year under audit and in the year immediately before it, with the amount given for each — ₹2.10 crore and ₹1.45 crore
options.why: The clause asks two things at once. Its first limb reaches across two years — a cash loss arising in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year is what it looks for — and its second limb then tells the auditor to state the amount of the cash losses. Both years sit inside the one question, so both amounts belong in the answer, and a bare "Yes" leaves out the half of the clause that calls for a figure.
keywords: in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year
state the amount of the cash losses

options.text: That the company has incurred cash losses of ₹2.10 crore in the financial year; the preceding year is outside the scope of the current year's report
options.misconception: confines the clause to the year under audit, when its words carry it back one year
options.why: The clause says in terms that it covers the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year. The report is for the current year but the question it answers spans two, and dropping the earlier year answers only half of it.
keywords: the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year

options.text: That the company has incurred operating losses of ₹1.60 crore and ₹0.70 crore in the two years
options.misconception: reports the operating loss, which is a different figure from the one the clause names
options.why: The clause names cash losses. The operating loss is another figure in the same schedule and answering with it means the reader of the CARO annexure is given a number the Order did not ask for.
keywords: a number the Order did not ask for

options.text: That the company has incurred a loss of ₹5.40 crore in the financial year, being the loss before tax shown by the statement of profit and loss
options.misconception: answers with the loss in the profit and loss account, treating a cash loss as though it were the reported loss
options.why: The loss before tax and the cash loss are different figures, which is why the schedule carries both. The clause asks for the cash loss, and it asks about the preceding year too, which this answer leaves out altogether.
keywords: asks about the preceding year too

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii)

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a company to which the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 applies, for the year ended 31 March. The company has had two poor years. Its schedules, which you have verified, give the following for the year under audit and for the year before it. Turnover was ₹63 crore and ₹71 crore. The debit balance in the profit and loss account stood at ₹9.30 crore at the year end. The loss before tax was ₹5.40 crore and ₹3.90 crore. The operating loss was ₹1.60 crore and ₹0.70 crore. The cash loss was ₹2.10 crore and ₹1.45 crore. Your audit manager has drafted the CARO annexure and has answered clause 3(xvii) with the single word "Yes".

items.stem: What should the answer say?

options.text: That the company has not incurred cash losses in the financial year or in the immediately preceding financial year
options.why: The clause asks about cash losses, not about the loss in the statement of profit and loss, and those are different figures. Where the verified position is that no cash loss arose in either year, that is the answer, and the figures from the statement of profit and loss do not belong in it. The clause is still answered rather than left blank.
keywords: still answered rather than left blank

options.text: Nothing. Where the answer is in the negative the clause is not applicable and the annexure omits it
options.misconception: treats the clause as exception reporting, when paragraph 3 requires a statement on each specified matter
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the auditor's report shall include a statement on the matters specified. Every clause that applies to the company is answered, and an omitted clause tells the reader nothing about whether the question was even asked.
keywords: shall include a statement on the matters specified
an omitted clause tells the reader nothing

options.text: That the company has incurred losses of ₹8.40 crore and ₹7.10 crore, since the clause is intended to alert the reader to a loss-making company
options.misconception: replaces the figure the clause names with the one the answerer thinks the clause was for
options.why: What the clause is for is not the test; its words are. It asks whether cash losses were incurred and, if so, for the amount of the cash losses. A reader who wants the loss before tax has the statement of profit and loss.
keywords: the amount of the cash losses

options.text: That the company has not incurred cash losses, together with a statement of the basis on which that answer is given, as paragraph 4 of the Order requires
options.misconception: attaches the basis requirement to a favourable answer, when paragraph 4 attaches it to an unfavourable or qualified one
options.why: Paragraph 4(a) requires the basis to be stated where the answer to a paragraph 3 question is unfavourable or qualified. A plain negative answer to this clause is neither, so no basis is called for.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 3 and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies carries a very large depreciation charge on a plant commissioned three years ago. Its statement of profit and loss shows a loss before tax of ₹8.40 crore this year and ₹7.10 crore last year. The workings you have verified show that the company incurred no cash loss in either year. The audit senior's draft answers clause 3(xvii) by saying that the company has incurred losses of ₹8.40 crore and ₹7.10 crore in the two years, on the view that a loss is a loss and the clause cannot have meant to let a loss-making company answer in the negative.

items.stem: What does the Order require?

options.text: Answer for both years using the preceding auditor's report, and state that the preceding year's answer is based solely on that report
options.misconception: substitutes another auditor's report for evidence on a matter this auditor must state, without the Order providing for such reliance
options.why: The previous year's audit report carries an opinion on the previous year's financial statements; it does not answer this clause for the auditor now signing. Where he cannot form his own view he says so and gives the reasons, which is what the Order provides for.

options.text: Answer for the current year only. A clause cannot require an auditor to report on a year he did not audit, and the previous auditor's report covers that year
options.misconception: reads a limit into the clause from who signed the earlier report, when the clause's words look at the company's position in both years
options.why: The clause asks about the company, not about the auditor's own engagements. The immediately preceding financial year is inside the question whoever audited it, and the Order supplies a route for an auditor who cannot answer rather than an exemption from answering.
keywords: a route for an auditor who cannot answer

options.text: The clause covers both years, so the preceding year must be addressed; and where the auditor is unable to express an opinion on a specified matter his report shall indicate that fact together with the reasons why he cannot
options.why: The clause asks about the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year, and nothing in it turns on who audited the earlier one. Where the auditor cannot answer, the Order lays a road for that as well: he must indicate such fact together with the reasons — the annexure carries both the inability itself and what caused it. Silence is the one answer the Order does not allow.
keywords: indicate such fact together with the reasons

options.text: Answer for both years and, since the position for the earlier year is unknown, modify the audit opinion on the current year's financial statements for a limitation on scope
options.misconception: escalates an unanswerable CARO clause into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The CARO annexure and the opinion are different reports answering different questions. An inability to answer a clause of the Order is dealt with inside the Order, by indicating the fact with reasons; it does not by itself say anything is missing from the evidence supporting the current year's financial statements.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 4(b)

items.scenario: You have been appointed statutory auditor of a company for the year ended 31 March. It is your first year on the engagement. The company has incurred a cash loss this year and the amount is not in dispute. The preceding year was audited by another firm, which has since ceased practice; you have the previous year's signed financial statements but the schedule reconciling the previous year's cash position was never prepared and the underlying records for part of that year were destroyed in a flood before you were appointed. You have performed what alternative procedures you can and cannot satisfy yourself one way or the other about whether a cash loss arose in the preceding year. Your partner's instinct is to answer the clause for the current year only and say nothing about the earlier one.

items.stem: What does paragraph 4 of the Order add?

options.text: Nothing. Clause 3(xvii) asks for the amount and the amount has been given, and paragraph 4 applies only where the auditor qualifies his opinion on the financial statements
options.misconception: reads paragraph 4 as attaching to a qualified audit opinion, when it attaches to an unfavourable or qualified answer inside the annexure
options.why: Paragraph 4 is about the answers to the paragraph 3 questions, not about the opinion on the financial statements. An unfavourable answer inside the annexure triggers it whether or not the opinion itself is modified.
keywords: about the answers to the paragraph 3 questions
whether or not the opinion itself is modified

options.text: Paragraph 4 requires the basis only where the auditor is unable to express an opinion, so it reaches the statutory dues clause but not the cash losses clause
options.misconception: collapses the two limbs of paragraph 4 into one, dropping the limb about unfavourable and qualified answers
options.why: Paragraph 4 has two limbs. Sub-paragraph (a) requires the basis where the answer is unfavourable or qualified. Sub-paragraph (b) is the separate case where the auditor is unable to express any opinion, and then his report indicates that fact together with the reasons.

options.text: Paragraph 4 requires the auditor to modify his opinion on the financial statements wherever an answer under paragraph 3 is unfavourable
options.misconception: turns a requirement to explain an answer into a requirement to change the opinion
options.why: It requires the basis for the answer to be stated, and nothing more. Whether the opinion is modified is decided under SA 705 (Revised) on the audit evidence about the financial statements, and many unfavourable CARO answers sit beside an unmodified opinion.
keywords: requires the basis for the answer to be stated

options.text: Where the answer to any of the paragraph 3 questions is unfavourable or qualified, the report shall also state the basis for that answer — so both clauses need the basis stated, and the rule is general rather than particular to one clause
options.why: Paragraph 4(a) is written across the whole of paragraph 3. Whenever a reply given to any of the questions referred to in paragraph 3 comes out unfavourable or qualified, the annexure shall also state the basis on which that reply rests. A pair of amounts with no basis, and an unpaid statutory due with no explanation, both fall short of it.
keywords: any of the questions referred to in paragraph 3

citation.ref: paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 4(b), read with paragraph 3(xvii) and paragraph 3(vii)

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies incurred cash losses in both the year under audit and the year before it, and the amounts are established and agreed. The audit manager's draft annexure answers clause 3(xvii) with the two amounts and nothing else. The engagement partner asks whether anything more is needed, and separately whether the same treatment applies to clause 3(vii) on statutory dues, where the draft records an unpaid amount without saying anything about why it is unpaid.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Repeat the clause 3(xvii) answer in the consolidated annexure, because the consolidated statements include the subsidiary and its losses are part of the group's result
options.misconception: applies the whole Order to the consolidated report, when paragraph 2 applies only one clause of it there
options.why: Consolidation brings the subsidiary's figures into the group statements; it does not bring the Order's clauses into the group report. Paragraph 2 keeps every clause but one out of a consolidated annexure — except clause (xxi), there is nothing under the Order to answer there.
keywords: does not bring the Order's clauses

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvii) in the consolidated annexure and add the emphasis of matter paragraph, since both draw attention to a matter properly disclosed in the consolidated financial statements
options.misconception: adds a paragraph on top of a clause that does not apply, and treats a component's CARO answer as a matter disclosed in the group statements
options.why: The clause does not apply to that report at all, so there is nothing to answer. And an emphasis of matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; a statement made in another company's CARO annexure is not one, and clause (xxi) is the route the Order provides.
keywords: does not apply to that report
presented or disclosed in the financial statements

options.text: Paragraph 2 leaves only clause (xxi) alive on a report covering consolidated financial statements, so there is no clause 3(xvii) answer to give there; what that report carries under the Order is the clause (xxi) statement about qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO annexures of the companies taken into the group accounts
options.why: Paragraph 2 draws a line around the group report: of everything in the Order, one clause alone is left standing there. Since the carve-out is worded as except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, clause 3(xvii) has no place in the consolidated annexure. A group reader reaches a component's CARO position by that single road — clause (xxi) asks whether the CARO annexures of the companies taken into the group accounts carried any qualifications or adverse remarks, and for the details where they did.
keywords: no place in the consolidated annexure

options.text: Give no answer under the Order at all in the consolidated report, since the holding company itself has incurred no cash losses
options.misconception: reaches the right silence on clause 3(xvii) for the wrong reason, and drops the one clause that does apply
options.why: The reason there is no clause 3(xvii) answer is that the Order does not apply to a report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi), not that the holding company's own position is clean. Clause (xxi) still has to be answered in that annexure.
keywords: does not apply to a report on consolidated financial statements

citation.ref: paragraph 2, which leaves clause (xxi) of paragraph 3 as the only part of the Order still operating on a report that covers consolidated financial statements, read with paragraph 3(xvii) and paragraph 3(xxi)

items.scenario: A holding company to which the Order applies has one Indian subsidiary, also covered by the Order. The subsidiary has incurred cash losses in both the year under audit and the preceding year; the holding company itself has not. You are the auditor of the holding company and are signing both the standalone and the consolidated financial statements. The subsidiary's own auditor has reported the cash losses under clause 3(xvii) in the subsidiary's CARO annexure. The audit manager wants to repeat that statement in the CARO annexure to your report on the consolidated financial statements, so that a reader of the group accounts is not left unaware of it, and separately proposes an emphasis of matter paragraph in the consolidated report drawing attention to the subsidiary's losses.

items.stem: Is CA Ranade right?
