options.misconception: lets cost decide the extent of the work, which is the reasoning the standard rules out in terms
options.why: Expense, delay and inconvenience are not by themselves grounds on which an auditor may drop a procedure that has no substitute, nor grounds for calling weak evidence good enough. Cost may inform how a procedure is designed; it cannot be the reason for settling for weaker evidence.

options.text: Perform the full reconciliation regardless, since a material class of receipts must always be verified to source and no alternative procedure is ever adequate
options.misconception: hardens the rule into a bar on alternative procedures, when what it bars is dropping a procedure because it is expensive where no alternative exists
options.why: What the standard bars is dropping a procedure that has nothing to take its place, on the ground of what it costs. Where an alternative procedure does give sufficient appropriate audit evidence it is available, and the auditor chooses between procedures on what they prove rather than on a rule that only one route can ever do.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 200 as reproduced there, on why expense, delay or inconvenience alone cannot justify dropping a procedure that has no substitute or accepting evidence the auditor knows to be weak, with the position that where a procedure is impracticable alternative audit procedures may provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence and that where they cannot, the scope limitation goes to the opinion

items.scenario: The same trust has one further class of receipts: money collected in a rural fundraising drive by two hundred volunteers, each of whom issued handwritten slips. The slips exist but are held at four district offices, unsorted, and the drive's total is material to the income statement. The auditor proposes to visit the district offices, sort the slips and reconcile them to the amounts banked. The managing trustee objects that the exercise would take three weeks, that the trust would have to pay for the auditor's travel and time, that the cost would exceed a tenth of what the drive raised, and that in a charity every rupee spent on audit is a rupee not spent on beneficiaries. He asks the auditor to accept the district offices' summary statements instead, which are less persuasive but far cheaper, and points out that the trust's own committee has accepted them.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section drawing attention to the closure and the liquidator's appointment, since the facts are fully known to the reader once the auditor points to them
options.misconception: reaches for the treatment reserved for an adequately disclosed uncertainty, where here nothing is disclosed and the basis of preparation is itself wrong
options.why: A separate section drawing attention to a matter presupposes that the financial statements say something for the auditor to draw attention to, and that the basis of accounting is appropriate. Neither holds. There is no note at all, and the question is not whether an uncertainty exists but whether the entity may still be presented as a going concern.

options.text: An adverse opinion — the statements have been prepared on a basis that is no longer appropriate, and that affects everything in them rather than any one balance
options.why: An adverse opinion is the outcome the standard keeps for one situation: management has drawn the accounts up on the going concern footing, and the auditor judges that footing inappropriate. It is not a question of degree here: the plant has closed, the workforce has gone, the members have resolved on a voluntary winding up and a liquidator is in control of the assets, so the entity is not going to continue in operational existence. That the company has not yet been struck off answers a legal question and not an accounting one. Because the wrong footing runs through every asset and every deferral rather than sitting in a few balances, the effects are pervasive and a qualification would not convey the position.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because until the liquidator has realised the assets nobody can say what they are worth and the auditor cannot form a view
options.misconception: turns a misstatement the auditor has identified into an inability to obtain evidence, which is the other of the two circumstances entirely
options.why: The two circumstances requiring a modification are a material misstatement and an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and this is the first. The auditor is not short of evidence; he knows the plant has closed, the workforce has gone and a liquidator is in control. Uncertainty about the eventual realisation is a normal feature of a break-up basis, not a reason to disclaim.

options.text: A qualified opinion, the misstatement being confined to the carrying amounts of the plant, the inventory and the deferred expenditure
options.misconception: treats a wrong basis of preparation as a set of individual valuation errors, when it is a matter affecting the statements as a whole
options.why: A qualified opinion is for a misstatement that is material but not pervasive. Pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items, and a basis of accounting that should not have been used at all is the clearest case of that — it decides how every asset and every liability in the statements has been measured and presented.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — what the report has to say once the auditor decides the going concern footing was the wrong one to use, read with the SA 705 (Revised) material on the two circumstances that force a modification and on when an effect counts as pervasive rather than confined

items.scenario: A company's only manufacturing plant stopped work in November and has not restarted. In December its workforce was paid off. In February the members passed a resolution to wind the company up voluntarily, and in March a liquidator was appointed and took control of the assets. The financial statements for the year ended 31 March have been drawn up exactly as in previous years: plant and machinery at cost less depreciation, inventory at cost, deferred expenditure carried forward and amortised over four more years, and no note anywhere about the resolution, the liquidator or the closure. The managing director tells the auditor that the winding up is not complete, that the company legally exists until it is struck off, and that it would be wrong to write anything down before the liquidator has actually sold it.

items.stem: How should the auditor's report deal with this?

options.text: A qualified opinion, because an uncertainty of this size means the auditor cannot say the statements give a true and fair view without reservation
options.misconception: treats the existence of an uncertainty as a reservation, when the opinion is modified only if the uncertainty is not adequately disclosed
options.why: A qualified opinion arises from a material misstatement or from missing evidence, and there is neither. The company has disclosed the claim, the range of outcomes and the doubt itself; the auditor has concluded the basis is appropriate. Where adequate disclosure of the material uncertainty is made, the opinion is unmodified.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with the matter reported in the Key Audit Matters section, since it is plainly among the matters of most significance in the audit
options.misconception: substitutes the key audit matters section for a reporting requirement that stands on its own and applies whether or not that section exists
options.why: Whether the matter is also a key audit matter is a separate question and does not answer this one. The separate section on a material uncertainty related to going concern is required in its own right, and the key audit matters section is confined in scope to particular audits and is not a substitute for it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with the matter set out in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, that being the paragraph the report uses to point at something already disclosed
options.misconception: uses the general paragraph for drawing attention to a disclosed matter, where a specific and separately headed section is prescribed for this one
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that is fundamental to users' understanding, and it is not the vehicle here. Reporting on a material uncertainty about going concern has its own separate section with its own heading and its own two required statements, and the specific requirement displaces the general one.

options.text: An unmodified opinion, with a separate section under its own heading drawing attention to the note and stating that a material uncertainty exists and that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter
options.why: Three findings line up: the going concern footing is appropriate, a material uncertainty exists, and the notes set it out properly. On that combination the opinion stays unmodified and the report carries a section of its own, headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern". That section does two jobs. It draws attention to the note where the company has written the matter up, and it says in terms that a material uncertainty hangs over whether the company can carry on trading, and that the opinion given is not modified in respect of the matter. Proper disclosure is what keeps the opinion clean; the separate section is what makes the reader see it.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern
not modified in respect of the matter

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the outcome where the going concern footing holds, a material uncertainty is present and the notes carry it properly: a clean opinion plus the separately headed section on that uncertainty, and the two things that section has to tell the reader

items.scenario: A company faces a claim under labour legislation covering nine years of alleged underpayment across three plants. The matter is before a tribunal and the company's counsel cannot predict the outcome. If the claim succeeds in full, the amount would exceed the company's net worth and the company would not be able to pay it out of its own resources. The company is otherwise trading profitably and its bankers have renewed all its facilities for a further year. Note 10 to the accounts sets out the claim, its history, the range of possible outcomes and the company's reasons for resisting it; Note 11 records that, on these conditions, a material uncertainty hangs over whether the company can carry on trading at all. The auditor is satisfied that the going concern basis is appropriate, that a material uncertainty exists and that the disclosure is adequate.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because until the refinancing is settled nobody can know whether the company will continue and the auditor cannot form a view
options.misconception: converts an uncertainty about the future into an inability to obtain evidence about the present
options.why: A disclaimer belongs to an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The auditor here is not short of evidence; he knows the facilities expire, that four lenders have been approached and that the notes are incomplete. What he has found is a misstatement, and a misstatement is answered by a qualification or an adverse opinion.

options.text: A qualified opinion, its basis section saying that a material uncertainty hangs over whether the company can carry on trading and that the notes do not put that in front of the reader
options.why: Take the going concern footing as sound and a material uncertainty as real, but the notes fall short of setting that uncertainty out. The reader is then being misled by an incomplete note, so the opinion is modified — qualified, or adverse where the shortfall runs right through the accounts — and the Basis for Qualified Opinion section has to carry two statements: that a material uncertainty hangs over whether the company can carry on trading, and that the accounts do not adequately disclose it. Here the shortfall is one incomplete note, an effect that is material but not pervasive, so a qualification is the modification that fits.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since financial statements that do not tell the reader the company may be unable to continue are misleading as a whole
options.misconception: escalates to the outcome reserved for a pervasive misstatement, on facts the auditor has assessed as confined
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the misstatement is both material and pervasive. Pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items, or which represent a substantial proportion of the statements, or which are fundamental to users' understanding in relation to disclosures. The auditor has assessed this as confined to one incomplete disclosure, so the qualification is the proportionate answer.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section on the material uncertainty, the notes having disclosed the expiry and the amounts involved
options.misconception: treats partial disclosure as adequate disclosure, when what is missing is the consequence the reader needs
options.why: The unmodified route is available only where adequate disclosure of the material uncertainty is made. These notes give the magnitude, the expiration and the total but do not discuss the impact or the availability of refinancing, so the fact of the uncertainty is not fully disclosed and the statements are materially misstated by the omission.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the outcome where the going concern footing holds and a material uncertainty is real but the notes fall short of setting it out: a modification under SA 705 (Revised), with the basis section naming both the doubt and the shortfall, and the worked illustration of a company whose borrowing is maturing and whose notes stop at the amounts and the dates

items.scenario: A company financed its fixed capital with long-term borrowing and its working capital with short-term lines. Both mature within four months of the year end. The company has approached four lenders and has not been able to renegotiate the existing arrangements or obtain replacement financing, and it has told the auditor that if nothing is arranged it may not be able to turn its assets into cash and pay off what it owes as it trades on. The notes to the financial statements set out the magnitude of the financing arrangements, the dates on which they expire and the total sum involved. They say nothing about what would follow if the money is not replaced and nothing about whether refinancing is available. The auditor accepts that the going concern basis is still appropriate, and considers that the effect of what is missing from the notes, while material, is confined to this one disclosure.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Accept the nine-month assessment supported by the sanction letter, since the limits are in place and the auditor may not require management to do work it considers unnecessary
options.misconception: lets the refusal settle the matter, when the standard treats an unwillingness to make or extend the assessment as something the auditor has to respond to
options.why: A sanction letter for existing limits answers whether facilities exist today, not whether the company can meet its obligations over the period the assessment must cover. Management's unwillingness to extend the assessment when requested is expressly a situation the auditor is required to respond to rather than one he may accept.

options.text: Prepare his own cash flow forecast from the company's records, since the assessment is ultimately about facts the auditor can establish for himself
options.misconception: moves the assessment from management to the auditor, when the responsibility to make it is management's and the auditor's job is to evaluate it
options.why: Making the assessment falls to management. What falls to the auditor is gathering enough of the right evidence about that assessment and then reaching his own conclusion on whether the footing management used holds up. An auditor who builds the forecast himself has audited his own work, and he still has no assessment from those responsible for making one.

options.text: Consider the implications for his report, management being unwilling to extend its assessment when requested to do so
options.why: Three outcomes sit in the implications table and this is the third. Asked to produce or lengthen its judgment of how long the company can keep trading, the board has refused; a board unwilling to make or extend its assessment is the trigger, and what the auditor must do next is consider the implications for his report. The refusal does not by itself decide that the footing is inappropriate or that a material uncertainty exists — it leaves the auditor without evidence he asked for, and what follows depends on whether he can conclude without it. He would also carry out the further procedures still open to him, weigh management's plans for future action and ask for written representations on whether those plans are workable.
keywords: unwilling to make or extend its assessment

options.text: Express an adverse opinion, a refusal to look twelve months ahead being an admission that the going concern basis cannot be supported
options.misconception: reads a refusal as a conclusion about the basis of accounting, when the standard reserves the adverse opinion for a case where the auditor judges the basis inappropriate
options.why: An adverse opinion on this ground follows only once the auditor has judged the going concern footing itself to be the wrong one for accounts drawn up on it. Nothing here establishes that yet. The refusal is a limitation on what the auditor has been given, and the standard directs him to consider its implications rather than to treat it as a finding about the footing.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 570 (Revised) on what the auditor does once events casting doubt have surfaced: asking the board for its assessment, weighing its plans of future action, working through the cash flow forecast, taking written representations on those plans, and the outcome prescribed when the board will not produce or lengthen that assessment

items.scenario: An auditor identifies several conditions during the audit of a company whose year ended on 31 March: the current ratio and the debt service coverage ratio have both deteriorated sharply, creditors are being paid late, salaries were delayed twice during the year, and the bankers have declined a request for additional facilities. He asks the directors to set down their own judgment of how long the company can keep trading. The board's assessment covers the nine months to 31 December only, on the ground that the company's business is seasonal and the December position is the one that matters. The directors decline to extend the assessment to twelve months from the balance sheet date and decline to prepare a cash flow forecast, saying that the auditor already has the bank's sanction letter for the existing limits and that a forecast would be guesswork.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion that names the processor and explains that the auditor was unable to examine its controls, so that the reader knows the limit of what was done
options.misconception: treats naming a limitation in the report as a substitute for modifying the opinion, and refers to the service organisation in an unmodified report
options.why: An explanation is not an opinion. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence he modifies; describing the gap while giving a clean opinion tells the reader the statements are free from material misstatement when the auditor does not know that. And in a report whose opinion is unmodified, a service auditor's work is not to be mentioned at all unless some law or regulation calls for the mention.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since a material part of the accounting has been carried out where the auditor cannot see it and the statements cannot be said to give a true and fair view
options.misconception: answers missing evidence with the outcome reserved for a misstatement the auditor has established
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive. Here he has obtained no evidence at all about the payroll processing and has established no misstatement, so the modification arises from an inability to obtain evidence and is expressed as a qualification or a disclaimer.

options.text: A modified opinion — the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services provided, and because the possible effects are confined to payroll and the balances flowing from it, a qualification rather than a disclaimer
options.why: Outsourcing a material process settles the reporting question through one rule: an auditor who cannot get at evidence about the outsourced work has to modify the opinion. That is the position here, where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the payroll processing — no assurance report on the processor's controls, no access to test them, no records at the company that would let the processing be tested there, and a user control that reconciles a total to a payment without reaching the master data or the computation. Which modification follows turns on pervasiveness, and the possible effects of undetected misstatements are confined to payroll cost and the balances that flow from it, so they are material but not pervasive and the opinion is qualified using the wording for possible effects.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because a whole accounting function has been placed beyond the auditor's reach and the audit as a whole is therefore incomplete
options.misconception: assumes a disclaimer whenever an entire function cannot be tested, without asking whether the possible effects run across the financial statements
options.why: A disclaimer is for possible effects that are both material and pervasive, so that a qualification would be inadequate to communicate the gravity of the situation. Payroll is one function and everything else in this audit is complete and satisfactory, so the possible effects are confined to specific elements rather than fundamental to the statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402 on what the user auditor reports when evidence about the outsourced services cannot be got at, taken with the qualified and disclaimer tests and the meaning of a pervasive effect in Ch. Reporting

items.scenario: A company outsourced its entire payroll to an outside processor two years ago. The processor holds the employee master data, calculates gross pay, statutory deductions and net pay, makes the payments and returns a monthly summary that the company posts as a single journal entry. Payroll is material to the company's results. The auditor asks the processor for an assurance report on its controls and is told none is prepared. He asks to visit and test the processing and is refused. He asks the company for the underlying calculations and is told the company holds only the monthly summaries, having no copy of the master data or of the individual computations. The company's own controls over payroll consist of a finance officer checking that the total in the summary matches the total paid out of the bank, which tests neither the master data nor the calculation. Everything else in the audit is complete and satisfactory.

items.stem: What should go into the report?

options.text: Everything the partner wants, since the custodian's assurance report is audit evidence and a reader is entitled to know the sources the opinion rests on
options.misconception: treats transparency about sources as an entitlement, when the rule exists to stop the reader inferring a shared responsibility
options.why: The report communicates the auditor's opinion and the basis for it, not an inventory of the evidence. The reason a reference is barred in an unmodified report is that it suggests the opinion is partly somebody else's, which is why the only permitted reference carries a statement that it does not diminish the user auditor's responsibility.

options.text: The reference may be included provided the report also states that it does not diminish the auditor's responsibility for the opinion, that statement being what makes any such reference proper
options.misconception: applies the safeguard that accompanies a legally required reference to a reference the auditor has chosen to make
options.why: That statement is required where a reference is required by law or regulation, and it does not create a general permission. Where no law requires the reference, the reference itself is not to be made at all, and adding a disclaimer to it does not cure it.

options.text: The reference should be included in the Other Matter section rather than the Basis for Opinion section, since it explains the conduct of the audit rather than the opinion
options.misconception: solves the question by choosing a paragraph, when the objection is to the reference existing in an unmodified report at all
options.why: Where the reference is not permitted, no section of the report is the right place for it. The rule is about whether the work of a service auditor may be mentioned in a report containing an unmodified opinion, not about where a mention would sit.

options.text: None of it — where the opinion is unmodified, the report is not to mention a service auditor's work at all unless some law or regulation demands it, and the audit committee learns what was done through the communication with those charged with governance instead
options.why: Read the rule backwards from the opinion. So long as the opinion is clean, this auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor at all, and the only door out is a reference some statute forces on him: unless required by law or regulation, the custodian and the firm behind its assurance report stay out of the report altogether. Where a statute does force one in, the report has to add that the mention does not diminish the user auditor's own responsibility for the opinion — which is the point of the whole rule, since the opinion belongs to the user auditor alone and a reference invites the reader to think it is shared. Nothing prevents the partner from telling the audit committee what work was done; that is what the communication with those charged with governance is for.
keywords: shall not refer to the work of a service auditor
unless required by law or regulation

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402 on keeping a service auditor out of a report whose opinion is clean, the narrow statutory exception to that, and the sentence a forced mention has to carry about whose responsibility the opinion remains

items.scenario: A company's investment accounting is performed by a custodian. The auditor obtains the custodian's assurance report covering the whole of the financial year, evaluates the professional competence and independence of the firm that issued it, satisfies himself that the controls tested and their results are relevant to the assertions in the company's financial statements, tests the complementary controls at the company, and concludes that he has sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The opinion will be unmodified. The engagement partner, who has spent a fortnight on this part of the audit, wants the report to name the custodian, name the firm that issued the assurance report and describe the work relied on, so that the audit committee can see what was done and so that responsibility is fairly shared. No law or regulation requires any such reference.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Determine which of the four are relevant to the assertions being tested, test those at the company, and treat the assurance report as supporting only the periods and controls where the complementary controls actually operated — obtaining evidence another way for the rest and modifying the opinion if he cannot
options.why: Call it what the description calls it: a complementary user entity control is one the provider builds its own controls around, expecting the customer to run it, and names in the description because the control objectives cannot be reached without it. An auditor leaning on the report has to settle which of those are relevant to the user entity, find out whether they were put in place, and test how well they ran. Where they did not run, the provider's controls cannot be assumed effective over that stretch either, so the auditor needs evidence about pricing and credit exposure from somewhere else — and if the evidence he needs about the outsourced services cannot be got, he modifies.

options.text: Ask the provider to reissue its assurance report without the assumption about the company's controls, so that the report the auditor holds stands on its own
options.misconception: tries to remove the condition rather than address it, when the assumption reflects how the service is actually designed
options.why: The assumption is not a drafting choice. The provider's controls are designed on the footing that certain things happen at the user entity, and a report that pretended otherwise would describe a system that does not exist. What the auditor has to do is test those controls where they matter and respond to the ones that failed.

options.text: Treat the assurance report as worthless and audit the year's invoicing entirely substantively, since two of the four assumed controls have failed
options.misconception: discards the whole report because part of what it assumes has failed, when the failures are confined to particular controls and particular periods
options.why: Two of the four complementary controls did operate, and the exception report clearance operated for part of the year. The response is proportionate to what failed and when, not an abandonment of everything the report supports.

options.text: Rely on the assurance report as it stands, since the provider's controls were tested by the service auditor and found effective and the company's own lapses are a separate matter for the management letter
options.misconception: reads the service auditor's opinion as free-standing, when the description itself makes the provider's controls conditional on what the user entity does
options.why: The description says the provider's controls over pricing and credit limits are designed on the assumption that the four controls operate at the company. An auditor leaning on such a report has to work out which of the controls the provider expects its customer to run bear on his own audit, understand those, and test whether they worked. An assumption that has failed cannot be treated as a matter for the management letter.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402 on the controls a provider expects its customers to run and names in the description of the system, on what the user auditor must settle, understand and test about them before leaning on a type 1 or type 2 report, and on modifying the opinion when the evidence needed about the outsourced services cannot be got

items.scenario: A company's sales invoicing runs on a platform operated by an outside provider. The auditor obtains the provider's assurance report covering the full year. The description of the system states that the provider's controls over pricing and credit limits are designed on the assumption that four things are done at the company: master price lists are approved by the sales director before upload, credit limits are reviewed monthly by the finance controller, exception reports produced by the platform are cleared within seven days, and user access is recertified each quarter. The auditor finds that the price list approval operates, that the access recertification operates, that the monthly credit limit review has never been performed, and that exception reports were cleared until June and then abandoned when the controller left. The audit plan had assumed reliance on the assurance report for the whole year.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because the amount of the eventual liability cannot be known until the appellate authority has ruled
options.misconception: converts an uncertain amount into an inability to obtain evidence, when the auditor holds the demand, the records and counsel's opinion
options.why: A disclaimer follows an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The auditor has the notice, the quantified demand, the company's own monitoring records and counsel's assessment; he is not short of evidence. What he has found is that a material matter is neither provided for nor disclosed, which is a misstatement.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since a company that broke an environmental law for eleven months and then concealed the consequence has presented accounts that are misleading throughout
options.misconception: escalates on the seriousness of the underlying conduct rather than on the pervasiveness of the effect on the financial statements
options.why: The choice between a qualification and an adverse opinion turns on the auditor's judgment about the pervasiveness of the effects on the financial statements, not on how badly the entity behaved. One omitted provision and its disclosure, material against the results and small against the balance sheet total, is confined.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a paragraph drawing attention to the appeal, the outcome of exceptional regulatory action being the classic case for such a paragraph
options.misconception: uses the paragraph for drawing attention to a disclosed matter where nothing has been disclosed and the statements are misstated
options.why: A paragraph drawing attention to a matter is available only where the matter is appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements. These statements neither provide for the penalty nor mention it, so there is nothing to draw attention to and the reason for the modification is a misstatement rather than a matter needing emphasis.

options.text: A qualified opinion — the breach of law bites materially on the accounts, the accounts do not show it, and what is left out is confined rather than pervasive
options.why: The reporting rule for a breach of law turns on two findings taken together: the breach tells materially on the accounts, and the accounts do not show it. Reach both and the opinion goes out qualified or adverse — a breach with a material effect that has not been adequately reflected is exactly the trigger. Which of the two follows from pervasiveness: the omitted liability and its disclosure sit in particular elements of the accounts and are not a substantial slice of them, so the effect is material but not pervasive and the opinion is qualified. That an appeal is pending goes to how the liability is measured, not to whether the reader should be told about it at all.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250 on what the report says about a breach of law that bites materially on the accounts and is not shown in them, taken with the pervasiveness test in Ch. Reporting that picks between the two modifications

items.scenario: A manufacturer discharged effluent above the permitted limit for eleven months of the year. The State pollution control board issued a show-cause notice in January and a demand for a quantified penalty in March; the amount is material to the results though small against the balance sheet total. The company has filed an appeal and has paid nothing. The auditor has the notice, the demand, the company's own internal monitoring records confirming the breaches and an opinion from the company's counsel putting the chance of success on appeal at less than even. The financial statements neither provide for the penalty nor disclose it; the finance director says that providing for it would prejudice the appeal and that the matter is contingent until the appellate authority rules. The auditor has communicated with those charged with governance and they support the finance director.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion, since the auditor is not responsible for detecting non-compliance with every law and cannot be expected to establish whether an offence has occurred
options.misconception: uses the limit on the auditor's responsibility to excuse a limitation deliberately imposed on him
options.why: True enough that stopping a breach of law is not the auditor's job, and nobody expects him to catch every breach of every statute. That is about how far his duty to look extends, not about what he does when he has looked, has found something material and has been stopped from going further.

options.text: An adverse opinion, the refusal by both management and the audit committee being itself evidence that the payments were improper
options.misconception: treats a refusal as proof of the underlying wrong, and answers missing evidence with the outcome reserved for an established misstatement
options.why: A refusal is not evidence of what the documents would have shown. An adverse opinion requires the auditor to have obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence and concluded that misstatements are material and pervasive, and he has obtained no evidence at all on this point.

options.text: A qualified opinion together with a report of the suspected offence to the enforcement authority, the auditor being obliged to report outside the entity once those charged with governance are themselves involved
options.misconception: states the external reporting duty as automatic, when the standard requires the auditor to determine whether such a responsibility exists
options.why: Where the auditor has identified or suspects non-compliance he shall determine whether he has a responsibility to report it to parties outside the entity — a determination, not a duty that arises by itself. The reporting outcome on the financial statements is the qualification or disclaimer, and whether anything goes outside is a separate question answered against the law that applies.

options.text: A qualified opinion, or a disclaimer, resting on a scope limitation — management and then the audit committee have both shut the auditor out of the evidence that would show whether a material breach of law happened
options.why: Look first at who closed the door. Where the auditor is stopped from getting the evidence that would show whether a material breach of law has happened or probably happened, and the block comes from inside the company — he is precluded by management or those charged with governance — the auditor gives a qualified opinion or disclaims one altogether, resting either way on a limitation on the scope of the audit. Which of the two turns on whether the possible effects of what he could not detect would be material but confined, or material and running right through. Note who refused here: the managing director first, then the audit committee, and that is what puts the case in this limb rather than in the one for a limitation the circumstances imposed.
keywords: precluded by management or those charged with governance
limitation on the scope of the audit

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250 on the reporting outcome where the people inside the company shut the auditor out of evidence about a possible material breach of law, and on the separate step of working out whether anything has to be reported to somebody outside the entity

items.scenario: During the audit of a trading company the auditor notices payments to three overseas intermediaries described only as "facilitation" and totalling a material sum, made in the two months before a large export order was awarded. He asks for the agreements with the intermediaries, the correspondence with the customer's procurement department and the legal advice the company obtained before making the payments. The managing director refuses all three, saying the papers are privileged. The auditor raises it with the audit committee, which meets and resolves that the documents will not be produced to the auditor and that he is not to contact the company's external lawyers. Nothing else in the audit is affected and the auditor cannot tell from anything he does hold whether an offence has been committed.

items.stem: How does the auditor deal with this in the report?

options.text: Request management to remove the limitation and, if it refuses, communicate with those charged with governance and consider withdrawing from the engagement
options.misconception: applies the route built for a limitation management has imposed, where the limitation came from a fire and management has been cooperative
options.why: The request to remove the limitation, the communication with those charged with governance and the possibility of withdrawal belong to a limitation imposed by management after the auditor accepted the engagement. Nobody imposed this one. Asking management to remove a limitation it did not create and cannot lift is a step with nothing behind it.

options.text: Evaluate the effect on the opinion, the limitation having been imposed by circumstances rather than by management or those charged with governance
options.why: Nobody shut the auditor out here; a fire did. Where the reason he cannot tell whether a breach of law happened is that the papers are gone — limitations imposed by the circumstances, not by any person inside the company — what he does is evaluate the effect on his opinion. The distinction earns its keep because the other limb, a block put up by management or by the board, carries consequences of its own, and management here has been cooperative and has itself gone after duplicates. What is left is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on a material matter, and the effect on the opinion is then settled on materiality and pervasiveness in the ordinary way.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: Report the matter to the regulator of that country and delay the report until an answer is received
options.misconception: makes an external enquiry a precondition to reporting, and converts an unanswered request into a duty to report a non-compliance nobody has established
options.why: Nothing has been established to report. Management has already written to the local regulator and had no answer, and an audit report cannot be held open indefinitely against a reply that may never come. The auditor evaluates the effect of the missing evidence on his opinion and reports.

options.text: Give an unmodified opinion, since the loss of records was outside everybody's control and an auditor cannot modify an opinion because of an accident
options.misconception: treats the innocence of the cause as answering the question, when the report speaks to what the auditor could establish and not to whose fault the gap was
options.why: Why the evidence is missing does not change that it is missing. The reader is told whether the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and a fire that nobody could help leaves the same hole in the evidence as a refusal would.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250 on the auditor who cannot tell whether a breach of law happened because events, and not people, took the records away, and on weighing what that does to his opinion under SA 705

items.scenario: A company operates a branch in another country. Six weeks before the auditor's visit a fire in the branch office destroyed the correspondence files, the local statutory registers and the supporting documents for the branch's foreign exchange transactions for the whole year. The accounting records themselves survived on a server, but they show only the amounts and dates and not the underlying approvals or filings. The auditor cannot determine whether the branch complied with the exchange control law of that country, and non-compliance would be material. Nobody at the company prevented the auditor from doing anything; management has been cooperative throughout, has written to the local regulator asking for duplicate filings and has received no answer. There is no other source for the documents.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Ask the company to date the financial statements later so that the insolvency falls inside the period covered and can be accounted for as a current-year event
options.misconception: proposes to move the reporting date to fit the event, when the reporting date is fixed and the question is only how an event after it is treated
options.why: The date of the financial statements is the end of the period they cover and is not a matter of choice. What the standard governs is how events after that date are treated, and this one is treated by adjusting the amounts because it evidences a condition that already existed.

options.text: Treat the event as one requiring adjustment of the receivable, and where the company will not adjust, modify the opinion — the financial statements being materially misstated by an unadjusted balance
options.why: Between the reporting date and the day he signs, the auditor has one objective: to gather enough of the right evidence that whatever happened in that window has been carried into the accounts, either by adjusting a figure or by adding a note. This customer's collapse points back to conditions existing at the reporting date, so what it calls for is adjustment of the receivable and not a note about it. Management's refusal leaves a material misstatement standing, and with the report still unsigned the auditor modifies the opinion; whether that is a qualification or an adverse opinion depends on whether the effect is confined. He would also take a written representation that everything in that window needing a figure changed or a note added has had one.
keywords: conditions existing at the reporting date

options.text: Accept the note, since the event occurred after the reporting date and disclosure is what the financial statements owe the reader in that case
options.misconception: classifies the event by the date it happened rather than by what it proves about the position at the reporting date
options.why: The test is not when the event occurred but what it evidences. This one shows what was already true at the reporting date — defaults to other suppliers before the year end, cheques dishonoured in February, a financial position recited as pre-dating the year end — so the amounts have to be adjusted, and a disclosure does not discharge that.

options.text: Sign an unmodified report and write to those charged with governance recording the disagreement, so that the matter is on record without disrupting the accounts
options.misconception: substitutes a communication with governance for the modification the misstatement requires
options.why: Communicating with those charged with governance is required and is not an alternative to reporting. A material misstatement the entity refuses to correct is reflected in the opinion; a letter that nobody outside the company reads does not tell the reader of the financial statements anything.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560 on the auditor's objective across the window running from the reporting date to the signing of his report, on the written representation covering that window, and SA 705 on the modification an uncorrected material misstatement forces

items.scenario: A company's year ended on 31 March and the audit is nearly complete; the report has not been signed. A customer owing a material sum, shown in full as good in the trade receivables, filed for insolvency on 12 May. The auditor's enquiries establish that the customer had defaulted to three other suppliers before 31 March, that its cheques to this company had bounced twice in February, and that the insolvency petition recites a financial position that existed well before the year end. The auditor asks the company to write the balance down. The finance director refuses, saying that the resolution process may still produce a recovery, that the insolvency happened after the year end and so is a matter for next year's accounts, and that in any case the company has disclosed the filing in a note headed "events after the reporting period".

items.stem: What does the auditor do?

options.text: Take no further step, the events giving rise to the suit having occurred after the reporting date and the auditor's responsibility having ended when the report was signed
options.misconception: reads the date of the report as the end of the auditor's responsibility, when the standard exists precisely for facts that become known afterwards
options.why: The auditor's objective extends to responding appropriately to facts that become known to him after the date of his report which, had they been known at that date, may have caused him to amend the report. That the underlying events post-date the reporting date affects whether the statements are adjusted or the matter disclosed; it does not end the auditor's obligation to respond.

options.text: Resign the engagement and inform the members directly of the judgment, since the board has made clear it will circulate statements the auditor knows to be incomplete
options.misconception: replaces the prescribed sequence with a step of the auditor's own, before the statements have even been issued
options.why: The standard sets out what to do and in what order, and it stops at notifying those charged with governance and then, if the statements are issued anyway, taking appropriate action to prevent reliance on the report. Resigning and approaching the members directly is neither of those and would leave the report standing unqualified in the members' hands.

options.text: Withdraw the report of 15 July and issue a fresh one carrying a modified opinion, since a signed report can always be replaced before the statements are issued
options.misconception: reaches for a modification, which is the route where the report has not yet reached management, and treats withdrawal as freely available
options.why: Modifying the opinion is what the standard directs where the auditor's report has not yet been provided to management. This report has been provided, which puts the case in the other limb: the auditor notifies those charged with governance not to issue the statements before the amendments are made, and acts to prevent reliance if they are issued anyway.

options.text: Tell those charged with governance that the accounts must not go out to anybody outside the company until they have been amended, and if they go out anyway, act to stop anyone relying on the report
options.why: A fact reaching the auditor after his report is dated but before the accounts go out puts him back to work: he takes it up with management or with those charged with governance, decides whether the accounts need amending, and asks how management means to deal with it. If management will not amend, everything then turns on where the report has got to. Had it not yet reached management, the answer would be to modify the opinion. Here it has already been provided, and on that side of the line the auditor warns management and the board not to issue the financial statements to third parties until the amendments are in — and if the accounts go out regardless, he takes the steps open to him to prevent reliance on his report.
keywords: not to issue the financial statements to third parties

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560 on a fact that reaches the auditor after his report is dated but before the accounts are issued: the discussion, the decision on whether the accounts need amending, the enquiry into what management will do, and the two different answers turning on whether the report has yet reached management

items.scenario: An auditor signed her report on 15 July and delivered it to the company that afternoon. The financial statements have not yet been sent to the members, filed, or given to anybody outside the company. On 18 July the company lost a suit brought by a creditor in a fast-track court and must pay a large sum; the events giving rise to the suit all occurred after the reporting date, but the amount is material and the outcome is now certain. The auditor asks the directors to amend the financial statements to reflect the judgment. On 22 July the board replies that it will not amend them, that the report is already signed, and that it intends to circulate the statements to the members with the notice of the annual general meeting the following week.

items.stem: What report should the auditor issue, and dated when?

options.text: A fresh report dated 20 July, that being the date the directors decided to amend and therefore the date on which the auditor's original reservations were met
options.misconception: dates the report from the decision to amend rather than from the approval of the amended statements
options.why: A decision to amend is not an amendment. The report cannot be dated earlier than the date on which the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base his opinion, including evidence that the amended financial statements have been prepared and that those with authority have approved them — and approval came on 25 July.

options.text: Either an amended report carrying an additional date restricted to the amendment, or a new or amended report including a statement in an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph — and the new report cannot be dated earlier than the date the amended financial statements were approved
options.why: Where management amends the financial statements, the auditor carries out the procedures necessary in the circumstances on the amendment and then has two routes: to amend the auditor's report to include an additional date restricted to that amendment, so that the reader can see the original audit was completed earlier and only the amendment was audited to the later date; or to provide a new or amended report including a statement in an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph explaining the reason for the amendment and referring to the earlier report. Whichever is chosen, the report may not be dated earlier than the date of approval the board gave the amended accounts, which here is 25 July.
keywords: Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter
not be dated earlier than the date of approval

options.text: Keep the original report and its date of 15 July, and issue a separate letter to the members explaining the two amendments
options.misconception: leaves a report standing on financial statements that no longer exist in the form audited, and reports the change outside the report
options.why: The financial statements have changed, so a report bearing the earlier date describes a document nobody will now be reading. And a separate letter is not the auditor's report; the reader of the amended statements has to be able to see, from the report attached to them, what was audited and to what date.

options.text: A fresh report dated 25 July with a modified opinion, since the original report was signed on statements that were materially misstated in two respects
options.misconception: carries the original modification into a report on statements from which the misstatements have been removed
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements the report accompanies, and both matters have now been reflected in them. Nothing is left to modify for. What the reader is told about the history comes through the additional date or through the Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, not through an opinion that no longer fits the accounts.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560 where management does amend after a late fact: the extended procedures, the choice between an additional date restricted to the amendment and a fresh report carrying an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, and the earliest date such a report may bear

items.scenario: The same company reconsiders. On 20 July the directors agree to amend the financial statements for the judgment, and while they are at it they also amend them for an earlier matter — a fire that destroyed stock on 27 June, which the auditor had asked them to reflect before the original report was signed and which they had refused. The amended financial statements are approved by the board on 25 July. The auditor extends her audit procedures over both amendments and to the date of the new approval, and is satisfied. She now has to decide what report to issue and what date it should bear. A partner suggests keeping the original date of 15 July, since that is when the audit of the financial statements as a whole was completed.

items.stem: How should the auditor proceed?

options.text: Disclaim an opinion at once, since attendance at the count is the only procedure that gives evidence of the existence of inventory and it can never be replaced
options.misconception: treats attendance as irreplaceable, when the standard provides for alternative procedures where attendance is impracticable
options.why: The standard contemplates alternative procedures precisely for the case where attendance is impracticable, and gives an example of one. Only where those cannot give sufficient appropriate audit evidence does the modification follow, and even then the choice between a qualification and a disclaimer depends on whether the possible effects are pervasive.

options.text: Accept the storekeeper's sheets, supported by a management representation, since attendance was impossible and the cost of anything further is out of proportion to the balance
options.misconception: lets cost decide the extent of the work and treats a representation as filling the gap left by the missing procedure
options.why: How hard, how long or how dear a procedure is decides nothing by itself, and it is no licence to skip a step nothing can replace or to rest on evidence that falls short of persuasive. A written representation is evidence the auditor needs, but it never amounts on its own to sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

options.text: Perform whatever alternative procedures can give sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the existence and condition of the inventory, disregarding the cost objection — and if no alternative can, modify the opinion as a result of the scope limitation
options.why: When nobody could be at the count, alternative audit procedures are what the auditor turns to — tracing goods that were on hand before the year end through to the papers for their later sale is the example the standard itself offers — and their purpose is the same evidence about existence and condition that attendance would have given. Cost has no vote in that decision: difficulty, time or cost is never on its own a reason to drop a procedure nothing can replace, or to settle for evidence weaker than persuasive. Sometimes nothing else will produce the evidence needed, and then the auditor must modify the opinion because his work was limited in scope.

options.text: Attend a count now and roll the quantities back to 31 March, which is always available and removes the need for any modification
options.misconception: assumes a roll-back is always possible, when the entire closing stock has been consumed and the records will not support the reconciliation
options.why: A count at a later date with a roll-back is a real alternative in many audits and it is not one here: the whole of the closing stock was drawn off and consumed in April and May, and the production records do not reconcile inputs to specific tank withdrawals. A procedure that cannot be performed on these facts is not an answer to them.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501 on being present at a stock count and on what the auditor does instead when being present is impracticable, with SA 705 forcing a modification for the scope limitation where nothing else yields the evidence, read with the SA 200 passage reproduced there on cost and difficulty settling nothing by themselves

items.scenario: A firm is appointed in June to audit a chemicals company for the year ended 31 March, so no member of the firm attended the year-end count. The inventory is bulk liquid held in six sealed tanks, material to the financial statements. The company's own count was made by dipping the tanks and applying a density conversion; the working sheets survive but were prepared and signed by one storekeeper alone. The whole of the closing stock was drawn off and consumed in production during April and May, so no item can be identified and traced to a later sale, and the production records do not reconcile inputs to specific tank withdrawals. The auditor proposes to engage an independent engineer to reconstruct the tank movements from the plant's flow meters. The finance director objects that this would cost more than the audit fee, that the exercise would take a month, and that the storekeeper's sheets have been accepted by the company's own management for years.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Insist on personal attendance and refuse to complete the audit until the operator permits a visit, attendance being the only procedure that establishes existence
options.misconception: treats attendance by the auditor himself as the only route, when the standard names several others including attendance arranged through another auditor
options.why: The standard names alternatives: going to the count himself or getting another auditor to go, obtaining a report on the holder's controls, inspecting the paperwork, and confirming with anyone to whom the stock has been pledged. Refusing to move until one particular procedure becomes available leaves the audit stalled where the standard offers routes forward.

options.text: Write the inventory down to nil and issue an unmodified opinion on the restated figures, since stock whose existence cannot be verified should not be carried
options.misconception: has the auditor decide the accounting, and treats unverifiable as equivalent to non-existent
options.why: The auditor does not write down the entity's assets; management prepares the financial statements and the auditor reports on them. And the inability to verify a balance is not evidence that the goods are absent — it is an absence of evidence, which is answered by further procedures and, if those fail, by a modification for a scope limitation.

options.text: Treat the one-line confirmation as sufficient, a reply from an independent third party being external evidence and therefore more reliable than anything generated inside the company
options.misconception: relies on the source of the evidence without weighing what it actually says or what is known about the party who sent it
options.why: External origin raises the reliability of evidence; it does not make a reply evidence of something it does not state. This one gives no quantities, no descriptions and no condition, and the auditor now has information raising doubts about the integrity and objectivity of the party who sent it.

options.text: Perform other procedures — inspecting documentation of subsequent sales, arranging for another auditor to attend or to report on the adequacy of the warehouse's controls over goods held for others — and where sufficient appropriate audit evidence about existence and condition still cannot be obtained, modify the opinion
options.why: Stock lying in somebody else's godown, if it matters to the accounts, still has to be proved: the auditor either asks the holder to confirm what it has, or inspects, or does something else that answers existence and condition. What changes the picture is what he has since learned, because it goes to the integrity and objectivity of the third party — a defaulting operator, a suspended licence, other depositors complaining of shortages. On that footing the standard points him at further steps: going to the operator's count himself or having another auditor go, obtaining a report from that operator's own auditor or from a service auditor on how well its controls count and safeguard goods belonging to others, inspecting the paperwork for stock lodged outside, and confirming with anyone to whom the stock has been pledged. If none of that yields the evidence a material balance needs, a scope limitation is what remains and the opinion is modified.
keywords: integrity and objectivity of the third party

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501 on material stock lying with somebody else: proving existence and condition by confirmation, by inspection or by other procedures, and the further steps to weigh once something casts doubt on the holder's integrity and objectivity, read with SA 705 on a modification where the evidence cannot be got

items.scenario: A trading company holds a material part of its stock at an independent warehouse in another state. The auditor sends a confirmation request to the warehouse operator and receives a one-line reply stating that goods are held to the account of the company, without quantities, descriptions or condition. He then learns three things: the warehouse operator has defaulted on its own borrowings and its accounts show a going concern note; two other depositors have complained publicly about shortages at the same premises; and the operator's licence was suspended for a month during the year. The auditor asks to attend a count at the warehouse and is told visits are not permitted under the operator's insurance policy. He asks for a report from the operator's own auditor on the adequacy of its controls over goods held for others, and is told none exists.

items.stem: What does the auditor do?

options.text: Qualify the opinion, the refusal being a limitation on scope that is material but confined to the two matters the paragraphs deal with
options.misconception: treats the refused representations as one more confined limitation, when what is withheld undermines the reliability of everything else management has said
options.why: These two representations are not about a balance; they are about whether the financial statements were prepared as management undertook and whether the auditor was given everything. Doubt about those is not confined, which is why the standard answers this case with a disclaimer rather than leaving it to the ordinary material-but-not-pervasive test.

options.text: Accept the letter as signed, the missing paragraphs being duplicated in the engagement letter and the substantive representations all having been given
options.misconception: treats the engagement letter as carrying the representation, when the two documents do different work at different times
options.why: The engagement letter records what management agrees to do at the start; the written representation is management's confirmation, at the end and covering the period reported on, that it has done it. They are not interchangeable, which is why the representations about management's own responsibilities are asked for separately and why their absence has a consequence of its own.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management, re-evaluate the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and audit evidence generally, and — these being the representations about management's own responsibilities — disclaim an opinion
options.why: Where management does not provide one or more of the requested representations, the auditor discusses the matter with management, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect that may have on the reliability of representations and of audit evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the opinion. Two situations are answered by a disclaimer rather than a qualification, and this is one of them: where management does not provide the representations that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access agreed in the terms of the engagement. The history of documents produced only on a third request is exactly what the re-evaluation of integrity is for.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement immediately, since an auditor who cannot obtain the basic representations has no basis on which to continue
options.misconception: makes withdrawal the automatic answer, skipping the discussion and re-evaluation the standard requires and the reporting outcome it prescribes
options.why: Withdrawal is one of the actions that may follow and it is not where the standard starts. The auditor first discusses the matter, re-evaluates management's integrity and the effect on the reliability of the evidence he holds, and then takes appropriate action — which on these facts means disclaiming an opinion.

citation.ref: para 19 and para 20, read with para 14 — the steps that follow a representation management will not give (the discussion, the fresh look at management's integrity and at how far anything it says can still be relied on, and the actions that include weighing the effect on the opinion), and the two representations whose absence carries a disclaimer of its own

items.scenario: An audit is complete but for the representation letter. Management signs the representations about related parties, litigation, subsequent events and the valuation of inventory without demur. It strikes out two paragraphs: the one where management confirms it has done its own part in drawing the accounts up under the framework that applies, and the one where it confirms it has given the auditor every piece of information and every access the engagement terms promised. The managing director's explanation is that the engagement letter already records both, that repeating them is a lawyer's device, and that the board will not sign the same undertaking twice. During the audit the auditor has twice found documents that were requested early and produced only after being asked a third time.

items.stem: What is wrong with the manager's note, and what follows?

options.text: The period is the problem — the auditor should obtain a report covering only the part of the year during which the technology provider was engaged, and rely on the existing report for the rest
options.misconception: reads the gap as a gap in time, when it is a gap in scope that runs through the whole period
options.why: The exclusion is not about dates. The technology provider's controls are outside the description and outside the opinion for the entire period the report covers, so no part of the year is covered in respect of them and slicing the period changes nothing.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the excluded controls are technology controls rather than accounting controls, and the assurance report covers the accounting the company relies on
options.misconception: divides controls by their label rather than by whether they bear on the assertions, when access provisioning and data restoration go directly to completeness and accuracy
options.why: What matters is whether a control bears on the assertions in the company's financial statements, not whether it is called a technology control. User access provisioning decides who can change a fund balance and data restoration decides whether the balances survive a failure intact; both go to completeness and accuracy.

options.text: The report is invalid, since an assurance report that excludes controls the user relies on cannot properly be issued
options.misconception: treats a permitted method of dealing with a subservice organisation as a defect in the report
options.why: The carve-out method is one of the two methods the standard provides for, and a report using it is properly issued so long as the description says what is excluded — which this one does. The problem is not the report; it is what the user auditor concluded from it.

options.text: The description uses the carve-out method, so the excluded provider's controls are outside both the description and the service auditor's opinion — the auditor must obtain evidence about those controls separately, and modify the opinion if he cannot
options.why: Where a service organisation uses a subservice organisation, the description of the system may deal with it by the inclusive method, which brings the subservice organisation's relevant control objectives and controls into the description and into the scope of the engagement, or by the carve-out method, which excludes them from both while describing the nature of the services provided. Under a carve-out the service auditor has expressed no opinion on those controls at all, so an assurance report covering the full year says nothing about them, however long the period. The auditor therefore has to obtain evidence about the excluded controls himself, and where the evidence he needs about outsourced services bearing on his audit simply cannot be got, he modifies the opinion.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402 on the two ways a description of the system can deal with a subservice organisation, the carve-out one leaving that organisation's control objectives and controls outside both the description and the service auditor's engagement while still saying what it does, read with SA 402 on the user auditor modifying his opinion when the evidence he needs about outsourced services cannot be got

items.scenario: A company's fund accounting is performed by an administrator, and the auditor obtains the administrator's assurance report for the full year. Reading the description of the system, he finds that the administrator does not itself host the application: the hosting, the database backups and the logical access administration are performed by a separate technology provider, and the description states that the controls at that provider are excluded from the description and from the scope of the service auditor's opinion. The controls excluded include user access provisioning and the restoration of data after a failure, both of which bear directly on the completeness and accuracy of the company's fund balances, which are material. The engagement manager's note reads that the assurance report covers the full year and can therefore be relied on for the whole of the fund accounting.

items.stem: Which opinion does SA 705 (Revised) require, and why?

options.text: An adverse opinion, because the group's most significant asset cannot be supported and the financial statements therefore do not give a true and fair view
options.misconception: applies the misstatement row of the matrix to a matter that is an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive. Here no misstatement has been established at all, and the auditor cannot say the statements do not give a true and fair view when he cannot say what the amount ought to be.
keywords: having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: A qualified opinion, using the phrase "except for the possible effects of the matter", since the difficulty is confined to one investment
options.misconception: reads pervasiveness off the number of line items affected rather than off the proportion of the financial statements those items represent
options.why: The first limb of pervasiveness asks whether the effects are confined to specific elements. The second limb answers the case where they are — if so confined, do they represent or could they represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements. More than nine-tenths of net assets is that proportion, so being confined to one investment does not save the qualification.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an other matter paragraph explaining that the joint venture's records were not made available
options.misconception: uses a paragraph that adds information to the report as a way of not answering the opinion question at all
options.why: A paragraph that describes the difficulty leaves the opinion saying the financial statements give a true and fair view, which is precisely what the auditor is unable to say. The inability to obtain evidence drives the opinion itself; no additional paragraph can carry it.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because the auditor cannot here obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and misstatements nobody has detected could — if they are there at all — be both material and pervasive in what they do to the group's accounts
options.why: The type of modification is decided by two things together — the nature of the matter, and the auditor's judgement about pervasiveness. The nature here is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, not a known misstatement, so the question is about the possible effects of undetected misstatements, if any. A holding that is more than nine-tenths of the group's net assets means those possible effects could be both material and pervasive, and on that row of the matrix the answer is a disclaimer of opinion, not a qualification. Finding no misstatement is not a finding that there is none.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

citation.ref: para 5 on pervasiveness, read with the requirement to disclaim wherever the evidence an opinion would have to rest on cannot be got and the auditor judges that misstatements nobody has detected could, if they exist, be both material and pervasive in what they do to the statements

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a power generating company for the year ended 31 March. The company's own operations are small. Its one substantial holding is a joint venture that runs a transmission line, carried in the consolidated balance sheet at an amount representing more than nine-tenths of the group's net assets. Three weeks before you sign, the joint venture's board declines to give you access to its management or to its auditors, and your request for that firm's audit documentation is refused. The joint venture's own audited financial statements are not made available to you either. You perform every alternative procedure you can think of — public filings, the shareholders' agreement, the group's own records of distributions received — and none of them lets you conclude on the group's share of the joint venture's assets, liabilities, income and expenses. Nothing you have seen suggests the carrying amount is wrong. You simply cannot tell. The rest of the group's balances are properly supported and you have no other unresolved matter. Your engagement partner says that since you have found no misstatement, the honest answer is a qualified opinion saying so.
