citation.ref: para 8(b) and para 10 on the key audit matter proviso attaching to both paragraphs, read with the guidance that the use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters and that a key audit matter which is also fundamental to users' understanding may be presented more prominently or carry additional information in its description

items.scenario: An engagement partner on a listed company has determined four key audit matters and described each of them in the Key Audit Matters section. He considers one of the four — the recoverability of a large loan to a joint venture — to be not only the most demanding part of the audit but also fundamental to a reader's understanding of the financial statements. Rather than describe it at length, he proposes to keep all four descriptions short and equal and to add an emphasis of matter paragraph after the section, drawing attention to the loan.

items.stem: Which of the four go in an emphasis of matter paragraph and which in an other matter paragraph?

options.text: None of them. An unmodified opinion with no key audit matters section carries no additional paragraphs at all
options.misconception: ties the two paragraphs to a modified opinion or to SA 701, when both exist precisely for reports that are otherwise clean
options.why: Both paragraphs are for reports where the opinion is not modified. An emphasis of matter is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and it states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter emphasised.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion
the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

options.text: The early adoption and the fire may take an emphasis of matter paragraph; the position on the predecessor's working papers may take an other matter paragraph; the cured covenant breach takes neither
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements, which the early adoption in note 22 and the fire in note 35 both are. An other matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, of the auditor's own responsibilities, or of the report itself, which is what the predecessor's papers are. The cured covenant breach is neither disclosed in the statements nor about the audit, and no disclosure is required, so nothing in the report attaches to it.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements
relevant to users' understanding of the audit
nothing in the report attaches to it

options.text: The early adoption takes an emphasis of matter paragraph and the other three take an other matter paragraph, since the fire, the predecessor and the covenant are all matters of fact rather than of accounting policy
options.misconception: sorts the matters by whether they concern policy, which is not the distinction the standard draws
options.why: The standard does not divide matters into policy and fact. It divides them by whether they are presented or disclosed in the financial statements. The fire is disclosed in note 35 and so cannot take an other matter paragraph.
keywords: does not divide matters into policy and fact

options.text: All four may take an emphasis of matter paragraph, since the auditor considers each of them worth a reader's attention
options.misconception: makes the auditor's interest the test, when the test is whether the matter is presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph may refer only to information presented or disclosed by the accounts it accompanies. Two of these four are not in the statements at all, so no such paragraph can reach them however much attention they deserve.
keywords: refer only to information presented or disclosed
not in the statements at all

citation.ref: para 8 and para 10 on the two paragraphs and the matters each may carry, read with para 9, which confines an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to information the statements themselves carry and requires it to state that the opinion is not modified

items.scenario: You are signing the report of a manufacturing company for the year ended 31 March. Your opinion is unmodified and SA 701 does not apply. Four things remain to be placed. The company's note 22 discloses that it has adopted a new revenue accounting policy a year early, as the standard permits, and quantifies the effect. Your own audit of the opening balances was constrained because the prior year was audited by a firm that has since been wound up and whose working papers you could not obtain; you performed alternative procedures and are satisfied, and nothing about this appears in the financial statements. Note 35 describes a fire at a leased godown in February and the loss recognised. And a covenant on the company's term loan was breached during the year and cured before the year end, which the company has not disclosed anywhere because nothing was outstanding at the year end and you agree no disclosure is required.

items.stem: What does SA 706 (Revised) say about the practice?

options.text: It is right. Since the paragraph states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter, adding one can never mislead a reader and the only cost is length
options.misconception: assumes the disclaimer inside the paragraph removes every consequence of using it, which is the assumption the standard's warning contradicts
options.why: The sentence that the opinion is not modified protects the opinion, not the communication. Nine paragraphs that each say a matter is fundamental to users' understanding tell the reader that none of them is, which is what the standard means by diminishing effectiveness.
keywords: protects the opinion, not the communication

options.text: It is wrong, and the fix is to put the same matters in other matter paragraphs instead, which carry no such warning
options.misconception: moves matters between the two paragraphs to avoid a warning, when the choice is fixed by whether the matter is in the financial statements
options.why: The paragraphs are not interchangeable. What an other matter paragraph carries is a matter other than those presented or disclosed by the accounts, so a matter that is disclosed there cannot be moved into one.
keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

options.text: It is not a safe addition. A widespread use of emphasis of matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters, and each paragraph is available only where both gates are passed — no modification required as a result of the matter, and, where SA 701 applies, the matter not determined to be a key audit matter
options.why: The standard warns against the practice in terms: a widespread use of emphasis of matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters. And the paragraph is not freely available. The auditor includes one provided he would not be required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised) because of the matter, and provided this particular matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter on an SA 701 engagement.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion
has not been determined to be a key audit matter

options.text: It is wrong, because an emphasis of matter paragraph may be included only where another Standard on Auditing expressly requires one
options.misconception: turns a warning against overuse into a rule that there is no discretion at all, which would delete the auditor's own judgement from the standard
options.why: The auditor's judgement is the trigger. He puts the paragraph in when he thinks readers need pointing at something so weighty that, without it, they would misread the accounts — subject to the two provisos. Other standards do require such paragraphs in particular cases, but they are not the only route.
keywords: The auditor's judgement is the trigger

citation.ref: para 8(a) and para 8(b) on the two provisos, read with para 9 and with the caution that a widespread use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters

items.scenario: A firm's reporting manual tells staff that an emphasis of matter paragraph is a safe addition to any report because it changes nothing, and encourages its use whenever an audit team has been worried about something. On one report last year the team added nine of them. The engagement quality reviewer on this year's audit asks whether that is right.

items.stem: What should the firm do about the three?

options.text: Answer the statutory audit tender but quote a fee the firm can justify against the size and manpower of the assignment, and leave the other two alone as work outside a chartered accountant's field
options.misconception: treats the bidder's own quoted fee as the prescribed minimum fee, and reads the reserved areas as the limit of what a member may pursue
options.why: Both halves are the wrong way round. The exception asks who set the floor: a minimum fee for this purpose is prescribed in the tender document itself and must commensurate with the size, value, volume, manpower requirement and nature of the work, so a figure the bidder chose is the very thing the guideline exists to control. And the restriction bites inside the reserved areas, which means it leaves the non-exclusive areas open — the module's own illustration of a permitted response is a firm bidding to computerise land revenue records.

options.text: Answer the grievance portal tender and the company's enquiry, and leave the statutory audit tender alone — the Council's guideline bars a response in an area exclusively reserved for chartered accountants unless the tender document itself prescribes a minimum fee or the area is open to other professionals
options.why: The proviso opens the door and Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 shut part of it again. Where the work being bought is work exclusively reserved for chartered accountants — audit and attestation are the two the guideline itself names — a firm in practice leaves that tender alone. Two things reopen it and only two: a minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document by whoever floated it, or the field is open to other professionals bidding beside chartered accountants. Statutory audit is reserved work and this document fixes no floor at all, so neither way out is available. The grievance portal is neither audit nor attestation and other trades may bid for it, so the guideline never engages. The company's letter is an enquiry and not a tender, and answering an enquiry sits inside the proviso.
keywords: minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document

options.text: Answer all three, since the proviso permits a member to respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure work as a consequence
options.misconception: reads the proviso on its own and stops before the Council guideline that narrows it for the reserved areas
options.why: The proviso is where the analysis starts and not where it ends. The Council issued a guideline under the same clause that bars a response in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, and audit is the example the guideline itself gives. A member who quotes only the proviso is answering the position as it stood before 2016.

options.text: Answer none of them, because bidding for work advertises the firm's services and the clause that governs an advertisement is Clause (7)
options.misconception: files a solicitation question under the advertising clause, which polices attainments and designations rather than the pursuit of work
options.why: Clause (7) is about advertising professional attainments or services and about using a designation other than chartered accountant on professional documents, cards and sign boards. Nothing here concerns what the firm called itself or what it claimed about its record. The pursuit of work is squarely the soliciting limb, and it is Clause (6) that decides it — including the two provisos that let two of these three be answered.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6), second proviso, read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 — tenders in the areas kept for chartered accountants alone, audit and attestation among them, and the two circumstances that lift the bar: a fee floor set in the bidding papers, or a field other professionals may bid in as well

items.scenario: A four-partner firm is deciding what to do about three invitations that reached it in the same week. A State Government undertaking has floated a tender inviting firms of chartered accountants to bid for its statutory audit; the tender document sets out the scope, the branches to be visited and the timetable, and says nothing whatever about what the assignment will pay, each bidder being asked to quote its own fee. A municipal corporation has floated a second tender, for the design and running of a citizens' grievance portal, open to software houses, management consultancies and firms of chartered accountants alike. And a manufacturing company the firm has never acted for has written asking what the firm would charge to carry out an internal audit of its two plants. The managing partner's view is that all three may be answered, because the clause carries a proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure professional work as a consequence.

items.stem: How should the firm proceed?

options.text: Proceed as planned on all three — the area is not exclusive to chartered accountants so the firm may respond, a reasonable earnest money deposit is not interfered with, and the costing paper is the cost sheet the Council asks a responding member to maintain so that the Institute may call for it
options.why: Computerisation of land revenue records is not audit or attestation and is open to other professionals, so the guideline's restriction never engages and the second proviso to Clause (6) does the work on its own. On the deposit, the Council's view is that interference with the prevailing practice of requiring an earnest money or security deposit is not required, though on a complaint or instance of an exorbitant deposit the Ethical Standards Board may look into the matter case by case. And a member who answers a tender is asked to keep a cost sheet of what the job will cost him, counting the people he will put on it and the hours they will spend, and to keep it precisely because the Institute may want to read it — the senior partner's second worry is the rule stood on its head.

options.text: Proceed with the bid and the cost sheet but withdraw the ₹50,000, a member being barred from putting his own money at risk to obtain professional work
options.misconception: invents a bar on deposits, when the Council expressly declined to interfere with the practice and reserved only the exorbitant case to the Ethical Standards Board
options.why: There is no such bar. The Council considered exactly this and said that interference with the practices prevailing for the requirement of an earnest money or security deposit is not required. What it kept for itself is the outlier: on a complaint or instance of an exorbitant deposit the Ethical Standards Board may look at it case by case. A deposit the tender demands of every bidder alike is not that.

options.text: Proceed with the bid and the deposit but destroy the costing paper, since a document recording what the firm will charge and why is client information the Institute has no business seeing
options.misconception: treats a costing paper about the firm's own effort as client information, when the guideline requires it precisely so that the Institute may call for it
options.why: The cost sheet records the firm's own inputs — persons involved and hours to be spent — and nothing about a client, who at that stage does not exist. The Council wants the paper kept for the very reason that the Institute may want to read it, which is the opposite of a document that has to be destroyed.

options.text: Withdraw from the tender altogether, a chartered accountant in practice being confined to work that only a chartered accountant may do
options.misconception: reads the reserved areas as the limit of what a member may pursue, when the restriction runs the other way and bites only inside them
options.why: The guideline restricts a response inside the exclusively reserved areas, which means it leaves the non-exclusive areas open. The module's own illustration is this exact assignment: computerisation of land revenue records does not fall within the exclusive areas, so the firm may respond and may pay the deposit.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 — the restriction confined to areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, the Council's view that interference with the practice of requiring an earnest money or security deposit is not required with exorbitant deposits left to the Ethical Standards Board, and the cost sheet to be maintained by a member responding to a tender

items.scenario: A State Government invites tenders for the computerisation of its land revenue records. Engineering firms, software houses and firms of chartered accountants are all eligible to bid. A firm of chartered accountants decides to bid and takes three steps before the closing date. It pays ₹50,000 as the earnest money deposit the tender document requires of every bidder. It prepares a working paper setting out the number of people it will put on the job, their grades and the hours it expects them to spend, and files that paper with the tender working papers. And it asks a partner to keep a note of the reasons for the fee it has quoted. A senior partner is uneasy on two counts: he thinks a member may not put the firm's own money at risk to obtain work, and he thinks the costing paper is an internal document that ought not to exist in a form anybody outside the firm could ask for.

items.stem: Which of these may stand and which must not be sent?

options.text: Everything may stand, because the firm is already on the panel and a member on a panel is entitled to be given the work the panel exists to allot, and because the cloth merchants are being offered a service rather than being asked for work
options.misconception: reads empanelment as an entitlement to work, and treats an unsolicited offer of services as something other than solicitation
options.why: Being on a panel means the member may be considered; it confers no claim on any assignment, which is why the Institute allows the letter asking the reason and stops the letter asking for the work. And an unsolicited offer is the clause's own language — soliciting clients or professional work directly or indirectly by circular or personal communication.

options.text: All four letters already sent are misconduct and only the draft is safe, since the clause catches a personal communication seeking work whoever it is addressed to, while a general offer of services to a market is an advertisement governed by Clause (7)
options.misconception: applies the clause without its first proviso and then routes the plainest solicitation to the advertising clause
options.why: Both halves fail. The clause carries the proviso inside itself and it is not narrow: applying for, requesting, inviting or securing professional work from another chartered accountant in practice is permitted. And a letter to persons likely to need a chartered accountant is dealt with under Clause (6) itself, where the Council says it amounts to advertisement.

options.text: The two letters to the firm and the letter asking the reason for no allotment may stand; the letter requesting that work be allowed crossed the line, and the draft to the thirty proprietors must not be sent
options.why: The first proviso sits inside the clause and it is not narrow: a member may ask, apply, invite or secure work from another chartered accountant in practice, so the profession may be approached even though the public may not. On the panel, the Institute lets a member write again and again to ascertain the reasons for not getting the work; what it stops is the letter that turns into a request for allowing the work, and that letter is misconduct under Clause (6). And a circular, an email or a letter aimed at named people because their trade makes them likely to want an accountant is advertisement — which is exactly what a mailing to thirty cloth merchants is.
keywords: from another chartered accountant in practice
ascertain the reasons for not getting the work

options.text: Only the two letters to the firm are misconduct, since seeking work from another firm undercuts the relationships that firm already has
options.misconception: inverts the proviso, treating the one approach the clause expressly protects as the one it forbids
options.why: The proviso protects exactly those letters. Nothing in Clause (6) turns on competition between firms, and the module's own illustration is a member who wrote to two firms asking for work and was held to have committed no misconduct at all.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6), first proviso permitting a chartered accountant to apply for, request, invite or secure professional work from another chartered accountant in practice, read with the Council's position on letters to a body maintaining a panel — writing to ascertain the reasons for not getting the work is permissible while a letter amounting to a request for allowing the work is misconduct — and with the head on soliciting professional work by making roving enquiries, under which letters, emails or circulars addressed specifically to persons likely to require the services of a chartered accountant amount to advertisement

items.scenario: A member who set up in practice eight months ago has written four letters and is drafting a fifth. The first two went to an established firm of chartered accountants, asking whether it had any work it could pass on to him. The third went to the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies, stating that his firm is already on the panel and asking why no audit work has been allotted to it. The fourth went to the same officer a month later, repeating the question and requesting that work now be allowed to the firm. The fifth, still in draft, is addressed to thirty proprietors in the wholesale cloth market near his office, offering to take up their tax work. A friend has told him that all of this is safe because the clause carries a proviso about asking other chartered accountants for work.

items.stem: What is the position of the firm on these four steps?

options.text: All four steps are proper, since a request to be considered for work is not a request for work
options.misconception: collapses the Council's distinction between writing to a panel one knows of and writing to organisations at large
options.why: The Council drew the line inside that very idea. Asking a body known to keep a panel is permitted; broadcasting the same request to organisations chosen because they might have one is a roving enquiry and is not proper. The difference is whether the member is answering a known process or fishing.

options.text: The letter to the bank is proper and so is the fee quoted in reply to a body that asked, but the eleven identical letters and the reminder are roving enquiries and improper
options.why: The Council's position comes in three parts and all three are here. A member who already knows that the organisation keeps a panel of its own may write to it and ask that his name go on that panel. What the Council calls improper is the opposite habit — roving enquiries, posted to bodies picked because one of them might run a panel, which is what eleven blind letters and a reminder chasing one of them are. On fees, a member may quote fees on enquiries being received from a body that runs a panel, so the reply to the company that asked for a figure is unobjectionable. The engagement partner's note misses where the wrong sits: it is in whom the firm wrote to, not in what it asked for.
keywords: already knows that the organisation keeps a panel of its own
quote fees on enquiries being received

options.text: None is proper, because approaching a prospective client in writing is a circular within the meaning of the clause however few copies are sent
options.misconception: treats every letter as a circular, when the clause is read alongside the Council's own permission to write to a body known to maintain a panel
options.why: The clause names a circular among the means of soliciting, and the Council has then said which letters are and are not caught. A single letter to an organisation known to maintain a panel is expressly permitted, so it cannot be a prohibited circular.

options.text: Only the letter to the bank is proper; quoting a fee turns a request to be empanelled into a solicitation of the assignment itself
options.misconception: forbids a quotation given in answer to an enquiry, which the Council expressly allows
options.why: The Council permits a member to quote fees on enquiries being received from bodies which maintain such panels. The firm did not put the number in front of anybody; it answered a question it was asked, and answering is not soliciting.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — application for empanelment for allotment of audit and other professional work: a member may write where the existence of the panel is within his knowledge, roving enquiries by applying to any such organisation are improper, and it is permissible to quote fees on enquiries being received from bodies maintaining such panels

items.scenario: A firm learns from a colleague that a nationalised bank maintains a panel of auditors, and writes to that bank asking that its name be placed on the panel. In the same week it posts an identical letter to eleven Government companies, having no idea whether any of them keeps a panel at all, chosen because they are the largest employers in the district. A month later one of the eleven writes back saying it does maintain a panel, that the firm's name has been added, and asking what the firm would charge for an internal audit; the firm replies with its fee. A second of the eleven does not reply, and the firm sends it a reminder repeating the request. The engagement partner records in the file that no misconduct can arise because the firm has only ever asked to be considered and has never asked for an assignment.

items.stem: How should the episode be classified?

options.text: Two clauses, not one — the invitation to approach the firm and the distribution of cards are soliciting under Clause (6), while calling himself a management expert falls under section 7 read with Clause (7); the explanation of the tax change is what a member is permitted to do from a platform
options.why: The limbs answer different questions. Clause (6) asks whether the member went after work: telling an audience his firm provides services at reasonable rates and inviting them to approach it is solicitation by personal communication, and distributing cards to the audience is misconduct in terms of Clause (6) on its own. Section 7 read with Clause (7) asks what he called himself: management expert is not a degree that any Indian university set up under law, or recognised by the Central Government, confers, and it is not a title showing membership of a body the Central Government or the Council recognises. And the answer on the tax change is inside the permission — a member may lecture, give his name and describe himself as a chartered accountant, and may give special qualifications directly relevant to the subject matter, provided what he says is an objective professional view of the topic rather than promotion of himself or his firm.

options.text: One clause — Clause (6) alone, because everything he did was aimed at getting work and the designation was only the means
options.misconception: folds the designation limb into the soliciting limb, when ICAI's own answer holds the member guilty under both
options.why: The designation is a wrong in itself whether or not it wins any work. Section 7 and Clause (7) restrain a member from using any designation or expression other than chartered accountant in documents and settings through which his professional attainments come to the notice of the public, and that is breached at the moment the words are spoken.

options.text: No misconduct at all, a member being free to speak at a Government conference, to answer questions on the law and to give his contact details to people who ask for them
options.misconception: reads the permission to appear and be identified as a chartered accountant as a permission to promote the firm from the platform
options.why: The permission is real and it is bounded. A member may appear on television, broadcast or lecture, give his name, describe himself as a chartered accountant and give special qualifications directly relevant to the subject matter. What he may say must be an objective professional view of the topic and not promotional of himself or his firm, and no reference should be made by a member in practice to the name, address or services of his firm.

options.text: One clause — Clause (7) alone, since a speech is a form of advertising professional attainments and the cards were handed out only because the delegates asked
options.misconception: treats a request from the audience as consent that cures the solicitation, when the clause looks at what was pushed and not at who asked first
options.why: The Council's answer names the distribution of cards to the audience as misconduct in terms of Clause (6) without any qualification about who asked. And the invitation to approach the firm for services at reasonable rates was not asked for by anybody in the hall.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — solicitation by personal communication and the distribution of business cards to an audience, read with section 7 of the Act and First Schedule Part I, Clause (7) on the use of a designation other than chartered accountant, and with the Council's position on a member appearing on a platform or in a broadcast

items.scenario: A member in practice is invited to speak at a national conference organised by a Ministry. From the platform he introduces himself as a management expert; explains, in answer to a question from the floor about a change in the tax law, what the change does and why it matters; adds that his firm provides taxation and audit services at reasonable rates and that anyone in the hall is welcome to approach it; and, when several delegates ask him afterwards how to reach him, hands out business cards carrying the firm name and telephone number. A partner reviewing the episode says only one clause is in play, because everything the member did was aimed at one thing, getting work.

items.stem: What must the firm change before the site goes live?

options.text: The monthly email and the page naming clients — the site must run on a pull and not a push model and names of clients may not be given, while the colour, the articles and the contact details may all stay
options.why: The guidelines answer each of the four. There is no restriction on the colours used in the website. The site must be run on a pull model and not a push model so that a person who wishes to locate the firm has access only on a specific pull request, and none of the information may be circulated on the firm's own initiative or by email or by any other mode except on such a request — which is what a monthly mailing is. Names of clients and fees charged cannot be given, the sole exception being a disclosure a regulator requires, which on these facts does not exist. And members may include articles, professional information, bulletin boards and professional updates, while the addresses, telephone numbers and email addresses of the head office and branches are on the permitted list.
keywords: pull model and not a push model
names of clients and fees charged cannot be given

options.text: The monthly email, the page naming clients and the bright green, the colour being a catch device of the kind the Council bars along with monograms
options.misconception: carries the bar on monograms and catch words, which belongs to the Clause (7) write-up guidelines, across to the website guidelines
options.why: The bar on a monogram or any kind of catch word is a condition on the write-up a member may publish under the proviso to Clause (7). The website guidelines say something different and say it plainly: there is no restriction on the colours used in the website.

options.text: The page naming clients only, since emailing the firm's own material to its own contact list is not pushing it at strangers
options.misconception: reads the pull requirement as protecting only strangers, when the guideline bars circulating the content by email to anybody absent a specific request
options.why: The guideline turns on the request and not on the recipient. Nothing held on the site may leave it at the firm's own initiative — not by email, not by any other route — unless somebody has specifically pulled it. A contact list is not a set of requests.

options.text: The monthly email and the articles, the articles being professional attainments displayed to the public, while the client names may stay because they are a plain fact about work already done
options.misconception: forbids the articles the guidelines expressly permit and permits the client names they expressly forbid
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. The guidelines list articles, professional information, bulletin boards and professional updates among the things a site may carry, along with anything else of professional interest or of wider importance, and educational videos on professional topics are allowed too. Client names and the fees charged are the head the guidelines single out for a bar, with one narrow exception that has to be earned.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines: no restriction on the colours used, the websites to be run on a pull and not a push technology with nothing circulated except on a specific pull request, names of clients and fees charged not to be given, and the permission to include articles, professional information, bulletin boards and professional updates

items.scenario: A firm has built a website and asks its ethics partner to look at it before it goes live. The background is a very bright green throughout. The site is configured to email its contents to every address in the firm's contact list on the first of each month. A page headed "Who we work with" lists the names of the partners and, beside them, the names of the firm's six largest clients; no regulator anywhere requires the firm to disclose who its clients are. A second page carries articles the partners have written on recent notifications, and a third gives the firm's addresses, telephone numbers and email addresses. The ethics partner is told that the design studio has already been paid and that only genuine breaches will be changed.

items.stem: What does the firm have to do, and what should it have done at the outset?

options.text: Add the italicised statement naming the regulator and the page may stay, the statement being what makes such a disclosure permissible
options.misconception: reads the italicised statement as the whole of the condition, when it is one of several and cannot extend the period
options.why: The statement explains a disclosure that is otherwise permitted; it does not create the permission. The permission needs a live requirement, and it stops when the requirement stops however the page is labelled — a note naming a rule that no longer exists proves the point rather than curing it.

options.text: Nothing needs to change, a fact once lawfully published not becoming misconduct because a foreign rule was repealed
options.misconception: treats the permission as attaching to the information, when it attaches to the requirement and lapses with it
options.why: The permission is expressly time-bound: it runs only till such period as the member works under the purview of the regulator or the requirement is in force. Once the requirement goes the general bar returns, and what is left on the page is the names of clients on a chartered accountant's website.

options.text: Take the page down now, and it should never have appeared in that form — the exception runs only to the extent of the regulator's requirement and only while it is in force, and it requires a statement in italics immediately below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule requiring it
options.why: The exception is drawn narrowly and each limb of it is a condition. Client names and fees go up at all only because some regulator — set up by statute or not, sitting in India or abroad — demands it; then only to the extent of the requirement that regulator has laid down; and then till such period as the member stays answerable to it, or as long as the demand itself lasts. A firm that discloses must also print, in italics and immediately under the disclosure, that it is made because the named regulator, having jurisdiction in the named place, requires it under the named rule or directive. A heading the firm chose for itself is not that note, and on the day the demand lapsed the general bar returned.
keywords: only to the extent of the requirement

options.text: Take the page down, and it should never have appeared at all, the guidelines allowing no exception for a regulator outside India
options.misconception: confines the exception to Indian regulators, when the guideline says in terms in India or outside India
options.why: The exception reaches any regulator, set up by statute or not, sitting in India or anywhere beyond it. A foreign securities regulator is squarely inside. What failed here was the missing italicised note and the page left standing, not the country the regulator sits in.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines, note to the head on the nature of assignments handled: disclosure of names of clients or fees charged permissible only where required by a regulator in India or outside India, only to the extent of the requirement and only till it is in force, with the italicised statement below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule or directive

items.scenario: A firm audits entities in a country whose securities regulator requires every audit firm on its register to publish the names of its listed audit clients. The firm puts those four names on its own website under a heading it has chosen itself, "Our marquee engagements", with no note explaining why they appear. Two years later the regulator withdraws the requirement. The firm keeps the page up, because it has become the most visited part of the site and two prospective clients have said it was what persuaded them to call. A partner argues that the disclosure was lawful when it was made, that nothing on the page has changed, and that a fact which was properly published cannot become misconduct because a foreign rule was repealed.

items.stem: Which parts of what he has done are misconduct, and is the senior member right about the website?

options.text: The senior member is wrong about the website itself, which is permissible if it follows the Institute's guidelines — but the telephone canvassing, the posts and the tagging of thirty traders, and the naming of existing clients on the site are each misconduct
options.why: Creating a website is not non-compliance so long as the site keeps to what the Institute has laid down; the Council approved the posting of particulars on a website under this very clause and even permits the nature of the services rendered to appear, on a specific pull request. What breaks the guidelines is everything around it. Seeking clients through telephone calls to family and friends is soliciting by personal communication. Sharing the address across posts and stories and tagging thirty traders is soliciting people to visit the website, which the guidelines bar in terms — a firm may provide a link to its page on a social networking site but members should not solicit people to visit or like it. And mentioning clients' names on the site is prohibited outright, there being no regulator here requiring it.
keywords: Creating a website is not non-compliance

options.text: The senior member is right and everything including the website is misconduct, because a website offering a service for a fee is an advertisement of that service
options.misconception: treats the website itself as the wrong, when the Council has approved websites and regulated their content instead
options.why: The Council approved the posting of particulars on a website under this clause and set out what may appear and on what terms. A site that obeys the guidelines is not misconduct; this one does not obey them, which is a different sentence and a different remedy.

options.text: Only the tagging is misconduct, since telephoning people who already know you is not soliciting and a member may name clients whose work he has actually done
options.misconception: reads friendship as a defence to canvassing and treats a true statement about a client as permissible
options.why: The Council bars circulating letters to a small field of possible clients and bars personal canvassing, and family and friends in one trade are exactly such a field. On the second half, the guidelines say names of clients and fees charged cannot be given, and truth is not the test.

options.text: None of it is misconduct, because online stock certification is not an area exclusively reserved for chartered accountants and the tender guideline therefore does not apply
options.misconception: answers with the tender guideline, which governs responses to tenders and has nothing to do with pushing a website at people who did not ask
options.why: The tender guideline decides whether a member may answer somebody else's invitation. Nothing here was an invitation: the member went out to thirty people who had not asked, which is the clause's own language of soliciting directly or indirectly by any other means.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines: creating a website is permissible if in line with the guidelines, members shall not issue any circular or other material soliciting people to visit the website and shall not solicit visits or likes on a social networking page, and names of clients may not be mentioned

items.scenario: A newly qualified member sets up in practice and does four things in his first month. He telephones family and friends in the retail trade asking them to send him work. He builds a website offering online stock certification for traders with cash credit limits at banks. He posts the website address across his social media accounts and stories and tags thirty traders of his locality with the caption "Easy Online Stock Certification Services". And on the site itself he names the traders who have already engaged him, so that visitors can see the practice is real. A senior member tells him the whole exercise is misconduct because a chartered accountant may not have a website that offers a service for a fee.

items.stem: What has to change before the site goes live?

options.text: The services and the areas of experience must move behind a specific request and the banner must go; the name, year of establishment, addresses, photographs, the networking link and the client download facility may all stand as drawn
options.why: The permitted list carries a marker against particular heads. The name, the year of establishment and the addresses with telephone, fax and email are simply allowed, and display of a passport style photograph is permitted. But the nature of the services rendered and a partner's area of experience are among the heads the guidelines allow to be displayable only on specific pull request, which is exactly what the managing partner's instruction forbids. No advertisement in the nature of a banner or of any other nature is permitted on the website at all. A firm can provide a link to its page on a social networking site, so long as it does not solicit people to visit or like that page. And the guidelines expressly allow a document management facility with distinct log-in and password for clients to access copies of their own documents.
keywords: displayable only on specific pull request

options.text: The banner and the photographs must go, a photograph of a member on a public page being advertisement of the person rather than of the firm
options.misconception: forbids the photograph the guidelines expressly allow
options.why: The guidelines say in one line that display of a passport style photograph is permitted, and the module's own worked illustration is a firm whose website carried passport size photographs of all its partners and was held to comply.

options.text: The banner, the networking link and the client download facility must go, a firm being barred from operating on a social platform and from holding client documents on a public site
options.misconception: forbids two facilities the guidelines expressly permit, mistaking a permitted link and a password-protected area for outward publicity
options.why: The guidelines allow a firm to provide a link to its page on a social networking site, the bar being on soliciting people to visit or like it. They also allow chat rooms with the confidentiality protocol observed and a document management facility with distinct log-in and password so that clients may access copies of their documents. Neither reaches anybody who has not asked.

options.text: Only the banner has to go, everything else being factual information about the firm that the guidelines permit on the face of the site
options.misconception: reads the permitted list as flat, missing that several heads are permitted only against a specific request
options.why: The list is not flat. Four heads carry the qualification that they are displayable only on a specific pull request — the nature of the services rendered, areas of experience, the number of articled assistants and the nature of the assignments handled. Two of them are on this landing page, and the managing partner's instruction is the thing that has to give way.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines: the information that may be displayed, the heads displayable only on a specific pull request including the nature of services rendered and areas of experience, the permission for a passport style photograph, for a link to a social networking page without soliciting visits or likes and for a document management facility with distinct log-in and password, and the bar on any advertisement in the nature of a banner or otherwise

items.scenario: A firm is redesigning its site and brings the wireframe to its ethics partner. The landing page, visible to anyone who arrives, is to carry the firm name, the year of establishment, the head office and branch addresses with telephone and email, a passport style photograph of each partner, a list of the services the firm provides, the area of experience of each partner, a link to the firm's page on a professional networking site, and a rotating banner advertising an accounting software the firm resells. Behind a log-in, clients are to be able to download copies of their own documents. The managing partner's instruction is that nothing on the landing page may be hidden behind a click, because a visitor who has to ask for information will simply leave.

items.stem: Which of the four may stand?

options.text: The change of address and the classified advertisement in the Institute's newsletter may stand; the congratulation may not; and the retirement announcement may stand only if the sentence about the two hundred bank audits comes out
options.why: The Council permits a member to advertise changes in partnerships or the dissolution of a firm, or any change in the address of practice and telephone numbers, with the announcement limited to a bare statement of facts and with thought given to how widely the chosen newspaper circulates and how many times the notice runs — so the address notice is inside it and the retirement notice is inside it up to the point where it stops being a bare statement of facts. It also permits a classified advertisement in the journal or newsletter of the Institute for sharing professional work on an assignment basis, carrying the accountant's name, address, telephone, fax, email and social networking addresses. And it answers the first notice directly: a prominent advertisement carrying the member's photograph on the opening of his office amounts to soliciting professional work by advertisement directly or indirectly, and who paid for it does not change what reached the public.

options.text: Only the classified advertisement in the Institute's own newsletter may stand, the clause naming advertisement among the prohibited means and admitting no exception in the public press
options.misconception: keeps one exception and drops the others, when the Council's list of permitted announcements includes changes of partnership, dissolution, address and telephone number
options.why: There are three exceptions and two of them work in the public press: a request to another chartered accountant in practice, and an announcement of a change in partnership, a dissolution, or a change of address or telephone number limited to a bare statement of facts. The newsletter classified is the third, not the only one.

options.text: All four may stand, since a congratulation is placed by well-wishers rather than by the member, a retirement is a fact, and a firm's record of bank audits is true
options.misconception: lets the form of words and the truth of the claim decide, when what is asked is whether the member's practice has been advertised to the public
options.why: The advertisement put in was quite prominent and carried the member's photograph, and ICAI holds the member guilty on those facts — a greeting is a wrapper and what reached the public was the opening of a practice with a face attached. And the permitted announcement is limited to a bare statement of facts, which a count of past audits is not.

options.text: The congratulation and the retirement notice may stand as announcements of events in a practice, while the change of address may not because it invites the public to a new place of business
options.misconception: inverts the exception, refusing the one announcement the Council names first and allowing the two it does not
options.why: The change in the address of practice and the telephone number is named in the permission itself. It is the congratulation carrying a photograph that ICAI treats as soliciting, and the claim about two hundred bank audits that takes the retirement notice past a bare statement of facts.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — advertisement and note in the press: the general bar on advertising for or offering to undertake professional work and on circulating letters to a small field of possible clients, with the exceptions for a request to another chartered accountant, an announcement of a change in partnership, dissolution, address or telephone number limited to a bare statement of facts, and a classified advertisement in the Institute's journal or newsletter carrying only the permitted particulars

items.scenario: Three notices appear in the same local newspaper on the same morning. The first is a prominent quarter-page carrying a photograph of a member, congratulating him on the opening ceremony of his new office; it was placed and paid for by the member's brother-in-law. The second is three lines from a second firm stating that its office has moved to a new address and giving the new telephone number. The third, from a third firm, announces that a partner has retired and that the firm continues under the remaining four partners, and adds a sentence saying the firm has completed more than two hundred bank audits. The same morning a fourth firm places a classified advertisement in the Institute's own newsletter offering to share assignment work, giving only its name, address, telephone number and email.

items.stem: What is the position of each member?

options.text: Neither is at fault, since every statement in both cases was true and Clause (6) reaches only false or exaggerated claims
options.misconception: imports the truthfulness test from the Clause (7) write-up guidelines into the soliciting limb
options.why: Honesty and the absence of exaggerated claims are conditions on the write-up a member may publish under the proviso to Clause (7). Clause (6) does not ask whether the claim is true; it asks whether the member has put his practice in front of the public, and a true boast does that as effectively as a false one.

options.text: The author is at fault and the interviewee is not, because he did not himself say anything on air and cannot be responsible for what the presenter chose to read
options.misconception: looks for the member's own voice, when the clause reaches solicitation made indirectly and by any other means
options.why: The clause catches what is done indirectly and by any other means. The member supplied the material knowing what it contained, and the effect was the promotion of the firm's name and of his own standing. ICAI holds the member guilty under Clause (6) on precisely these facts.

options.text: The interviewee is at fault and the author is not, an author being entitled to describe his own experience so that a reader can judge whether to trust the book
options.misconception: allows a professional justification to override a rule the Council wrote for books specifically
options.why: The Council addressed books, articles and presentations directly and drew the line at the designation and the firm name. The reason the rule exists is that a book reaches the public, so a claim of attainment inside it does the work an advertisement would do.

options.text: Both are at fault on the same principle — a member may give the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of his firm but may not mention professional attainments, and handing over a note that is then read out is publicity procured indirectly
options.why: On the book, the Council's line is that a book, an article or a presentation may not carry any professional attainment of its author or of his firm, though it may show the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm — so the four sentences of assignments and recognition are the wrong. On the interview, ICAI's own answer is that handing over a bio-data which the chairperson reads out promotes the firm's name and the partner's recognition and cannot be approved; details given in an interview must not highlight professional attainments, must be given only in response to a specific question and must be of a factual nature only. Answering the later questions factually does not undo the note.
keywords: designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — publication of books, articles or presentations, where a member may indicate the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm but not any professional attainment, read with the head on giving public interviews requiring that details not highlight professional attainments and be given only in response to a specific question and of a factual nature

items.scenario: Two members are reviewed by the same ethics committee. The first published a book on indirect taxes; the author's note at the front gives his name, the name of his firm, the words Chartered Accountant, and four sentences describing the assignments he has handled and the recognition he has received in the field. The second attended a television interview about a change in company law, handed the presenter a note about his firm setting out its association with an international network and his own standing as an expert, and sat quietly while the presenter read the note out on air; he answered the questions that followed factually and named no client. Each member says the other is the one at fault: the author says he only stated true facts about his own career, and the interviewee says he did not himself say a word of what was read out.

items.stem: Which of the four may go ahead, and on what terms?

options.text: None may go ahead, since any newspaper announcement mentioning a firm of chartered accountants amounts to advertisement of the firm
options.misconception: overlooks the express exception the Council created for jubilee advertisements
options.why: The Council created that exception deliberately and named the occasions: silver, golden, diamond, platinum and centenary celebrations may be published in a newspaper or newsletter, considering the need for interpersonal socialisation among members through such occasions. Denying it reads the clause without the guideline.

options.text: The seminar advertisement, the invitations and the sponsorship may go ahead as professional and community activities, but the jubilee advertisement may not, because celebrating twenty-five years advertises the firm's standing
options.misconception: inverts the guideline, allowing the three things the Council restricts and disallowing the one it permits
options.why: It is the other way round in each limb. The jubilee advertisement is expressly permitted; advertising an event the firm organises is expressly not; an invitation carrying the firm name goes only to clients, relatives and friends; and a firm may not sponsor an event unless it is a Programme Organising Unit event with prior CPE approval.

options.text: All four may go ahead, a celebration being a social occasion rather than a pursuit of work
options.misconception: reads the celebration permission as covering everything done around the celebration, including an event advertisement, a mailing to strangers and a sponsorship
options.why: The permission is for the celebration advertisement itself. The Council states separately that a firm's own events may not be advertised, separately again that invitations carrying the firm name go only to clients, relatives and friends, and separately again that a firm may not sponsor an event except one run by a Programme Organising Unit of ICAI with CPE approval.

options.text: The jubilee advertisement may go ahead; the seminar advertisement may not, a firm being barred from advertising an event it organises; the invitations may go to clients, relatives and friends but not to the businesses in the estate; and the sponsorship may not, unless the event is conducted by a Programme Organising Unit of ICAI with the prior approval of the CPE Directorate
options.why: A practice's silver, golden, diamond, platinum or centenary celebrations may be announced in a newspaper or newsletter — the Council made that exception on purpose — while a seminar the firm puts on is caught by the neighbouring line: a member is not permitted to advertise the events organised by a firm. On invitations, the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm may be used in greeting cards and in invitations for marriages, religious ceremonies and the opening or inauguration of an office, provided the cards travel only to clients, relatives and friends of the member sending them. And a member or firm is not permitted to sponsor an event, though it may sponsor one conducted by a Programme Organising Unit of the ICAI with the prior approval of the CPE Directorate; a member sponsoring a corporate social responsibility activity may use his own name with the prefix CA, but the firm name and the CA logo are not permitted.
keywords: silver, golden, diamond, platinum or centenary celebrations
not permitted to advertise the events organised by a Firm
only to clients, relatives and friends

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the issue of greeting cards or invitations, permitted only to clients, relatives and friends of the members concerned; the advertisement for silver, golden, diamond, platinum or centenary celebrations permitted in a newspaper or newsletter while the events organised by a firm may not be advertised; and sponsoring activities, where a member or firm may sponsor only an event conducted by a Programme Organising Unit of the ICAI with the prior approval of the CPE Directorate

items.scenario: A firm completes twenty-five years and puts four proposals to its partners. The first is a newspaper advertisement announcing the firm's silver jubilee. The second is an advertisement in the same newspaper for the two-day seminar on valuation the firm is organising to mark the occasion. The third is a set of printed invitations to the jubilee dinner carrying the firm name and the words Chartered Accountants, to be sent to the firm's clients, to the partners' relatives and friends, and to every business in the industrial estate where the office stands. The fourth is a proposal that the firm sponsor a district athletics meet, its name and logo to appear on the banner behind the podium. A partner says all four are safe because the Council has expressly allowed jubilee publicity.

items.stem: What should the auditor do with the draft?

options.text: Take out the account of the six years and the two disagreements, a long tenure and a record of standing up to management being claims of attainment barred by Clause (7)
options.misconception: applies the attainments limb to the factual account of how the audit was conducted, which the Council expressly permits the representation to contain
options.why: The representation is meant to set out how the auditor acted independently and conscientiously through the term of office, so describing that term is its permitted core. The parts that fail are the ones aimed at the members' vote and at publicity, not the ones aimed at the record.

options.text: Take out the list of other audits and the closing appeal, and keep the account of how he acted and the statement of willingness to continue — the representation may not amount directly or indirectly to canvassing for his continuance nor be used to secure needless publicity
options.why: Being given the chance to speak to the members hands the auditor no prescriptive right or a lien to an audit — that is where the Council starts. Two things the letter must then not do: reach for publicity it has no need of, and work, openly or by hint, as canvassing or soliciting for his continuance in the chair. What it may do is say, with dignity and in plain terms, how he carried out the audit independently and conscientiously while he held office, and add — if he chooses — his willingness to continue were the members to reappoint him. So the roll-call of other listed audits is publicity and the closing appeal is canvassing, while the account of the six years and its two disagreements is the permitted core.
keywords: prescriptive right or a lien to an audit
canvassing or soliciting for his continuance

options.text: Take out the statement of willingness to continue as well, since asking to be reappointed is the plainest form of soliciting work there is
options.misconception: removes the one thing the Council expressly allows the representation to contain
options.why: The Council allows exactly that sentence: the outgoing auditor may say, if he wishes to, that he would carry on in the office should the shareholders vote him back. What is barred is the argument built to procure that vote, not the plain statement that he is willing.

options.text: Send it as drafted — a statutory right of representation cannot be cut down by a professional guideline, and the auditor may say whatever he considers relevant to the members' decision
options.misconception: treats the statutory right as unbounded, when the Council has set the manner in which a member may exercise it
options.why: The statute gives the opportunity; the clause governs how a member may use it, and the two sit together. The Council's answer is that the right carries no prescriptive claim to the audit and that the wording must not canvass, directly or indirectly, for the auditor's continuance.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the scope of the representation an auditor is entitled to make on removal, now section 140(4) of the Companies Act, 2013: no prescriptive right or lien to an audit, the wording not to amount directly or indirectly to canvassing or soliciting for his continuance nor to secure needless publicity, and the permitted indication of willingness to continue if reappointed

items.scenario: A company proposes to remove its auditor before the expiry of his term and the auditor is given the opportunity to make a representation to the members. His draft runs to three pages. It sets out how he conducted the audit independently and conscientiously through his six years of office and describes the two disagreements he had with management and how each was resolved. It states that he is willing to continue if the members reappoint him. It lists the four other listed companies whose audits he holds. And it closes by asking the members to consider that no other firm knows the company as well as his does and that a change now would cost the company dearly. His junior partner says none of it can be touched, because the right to make a representation is given by statute and a professional guideline cannot cut down a statutory right.

items.stem: What is the total tax the bank must deduct under section 194N for the year?

options.misconception: applies the ordinary position for a recipient who has filed, ignoring the separate rate structure the section sets for one who has not
options.why: A co-operative society that has filed its returns is charged 2 per cent only on what it draws above ₹3 crores, which is ₹50,00,000 here. This society has filed none of the three returns, so the lower floor and the two rates govern instead.

options.misconception: uses the ordinary ₹1 crore boundary between the two rates and misses the higher one the section gives a co-operative society
options.why: Switching to 5 per cent at ₹1 crore would produce this. A co-operative society keeps the 2 per cent rate until the year's cash withdrawals pass ₹3 crores, and only what is paid after that point is charged at the higher rate.

options.misconception: charges the whole of the withdrawals, treating ₹20 lakhs as a trigger the year has to cross rather than an amount that stays out of the charge
options.why: Taxing ₹3 crores at 2 per cent and ₹50,00,000 at 5 per cent gives this figure, and it leaves the first ₹20,00,000 inside the charge. The words the section uses are about the sum paid above ₹20 lakhs, so that slice never enters the computation at all.

For a non-filer the section starts biting above ₹20 lakhs, so the first withdrawal is charged on ₹1,60,00,000 at 2 per cent, giving ₹3,20,000. Because the recipient is a co-operative society, 2 per cent runs until the year's withdrawals reach ₹3 crores: the second withdrawal carries ₹1,20,00,000 at 2 per cent, or ₹2,40,000, and the ₹50,00,000 beyond ₹3 crores at 5 per cent, or ₹2,50,000. The three pieces add to ₹8,10,000.
keywords: until the year's withdrawals reach ₹3 crores

citation.ref: Section 194N with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: Bhoomi Growers Co-operative Society banks with a nationalised bank and has filed no return of income for any of the three assessment years whose filing dates had gone by before previous year 2025-26 began. It withdraws cash of ₹1,80,00,000 on 26 May 2025 and a further ₹1,70,00,000 on 14 November 2025 from that account, and makes no other cash withdrawal in the year. The society is not itself in the business of banking.

items.stem: What must the nationalised bank deduct, and what must the travel company collect?

options.text: The bank deducts nothing, and the travel company collects ₹1,30,000
options.why: A co-operative society carrying on the business of banking is one of the recipients the section leaves out, and the exclusion does not bend for a poor filing record, so no tax is deducted on the ₹2,40,00,000. The tour-package limb charges 5 per cent on the first ₹10,00,000 and 20 per cent above it, so ₹50,000 and ₹80,000 are collected, ₹1,30,000 in all.
keywords: one of the recipients the section leaves out
5 per cent on the first ₹10,00,000 and 20 per cent above it

options.text: The bank deducts nothing, and the travel company collects ₹20,000
options.misconception: carries the Liberalised Remittance Scheme pattern into the tour-package limb, where the first ₹10,00,000 is charged rather than left out
options.why: On a remittance under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme the collection runs on the amount in excess of ₹10,00,000, and 5 per cent of ₹4,00,000 would be ₹20,000. The tour-package limb is built the other way: nothing is excluded, and the first ₹10,00,000 is itself charged.

options.text: The bank deducts nothing, and the travel company collects ₹2,80,000
options.misconception: puts the higher rate across the whole payment instead of only the part above ₹10,00,000
options.why: Charging 20 per cent on all ₹14,00,000 gives this. The limb is written as two layers, and the first ₹10,00,000 stays at the lower rate however large the package is.

options.text: The bank deducts ₹4,40,000, and the travel company collects ₹1,30,000
options.misconception: applies the non-filer rates to a recipient the section's own exclusion list keeps outside it
options.why: The arithmetic on the second half is right and the first half never gets that far. The list of recipients outside the section is read before any rate is reached, and a co-operative society in the banking business is on it.

citation.ref: Section 194N with its provisos, read with Section 206C(1G)

items.scenario: Sahakar Co-operative Bank, a co-operative society carrying on the business of banking, has filed no return of income for any of the three assessment years whose filing dates had gone by before previous year 2025-26 began. During that year it withdraws ₹2,40,00,000 in cash from its own account with a nationalised bank. Separately, its manager Mr Devang pays a travel company ₹14,00,000 in the same year for an overseas tour programme package.

items.stem: On what basis is the profit of each of the three computed under section 43CB?

options.text: Percentage of completion for the road contract, evenly over the period for the maintenance contract, and on finishing for the due-diligence assignment
options.why: Percentage of completion is the general rule and the road contract has nothing to take it out. The maintenance contract is a service contract asking for an indeterminate number of acts over a stated period, which is the limb that spreads the profit evenly over that period. The due-diligence assignment ran 74 days, inside the ninety-day limit, so its profit is taken when the service is finished.
keywords: Percentage of completion is the general rule
indeterminate number of acts over a stated period

options.text: Percentage of completion for the road contract, on finishing for the maintenance contract, and evenly over the period for the due-diligence assignment
options.misconception: swaps the two service-contract limbs, matching the short contract to the spreading rule and the open-ended one to the finishing rule
options.why: The two limbs answer different problems. Spreading evenly is for work whose acts cannot be counted in advance; taking the profit on finishing is for work short enough that the year end is unlikely to cut through it.

options.text: Percentage of completion for the road contract and for the due-diligence assignment, and evenly over the period for the maintenance contract
options.misconception: treats ninety days as a length a contract must exceed before the finishing rule is available, when it marks the contracts short enough for it
options.why: The limit works downwards, not upwards. A service contract of ninety days or less takes its profit on completion, so 74 days is inside the exit rather than outside it.

options.text: Percentage of completion for all three, the section admitting no other method
options.misconception: reads section 43CB as one rule and misses the two exits it gives a service contract
options.why: The section names percentage of completion first and then carves out two service-contract cases. A firm that spread the 74-day assignment across two years on a completion percentage would be using a method the section takes away from it.

citation.ref: Section 43CB with its provisos

items.scenario: Aarambh Engineering has three live contracts in previous year 2025-26. A road-widening contract that runs from June 2024 to March 2027. A maintenance contract under which it attends to breakdowns at a client's plant whenever they happen, over the twelve months to March 2026, with no fixed number of visits. A due-diligence assignment that began on 1 December 2025, ran for 74 days and was finished on 12 February 2026.

items.stem: What does section 43CB do with the two amounts?

options.text: Contract revenue is ₹306 crores and the contract cost is reduced by ₹5 crores, the company having treated both correctly
options.misconception: makes both mistakes at once, deferring the amount held back and netting the incidental interest
options.why: Each half of the company's treatment fails a separate sentence of the same section. One sentence pulls the ₹11 crores into revenue and the other keeps the ₹5 crores out of the cost.

options.text: Contract revenue is ₹317 crores, and the ₹5 crores of interest may not be taken off the contract cost
options.why: The section settles both. Money the customer holds back is part of contract revenue when the percentage is applied, so the ₹11 crores goes in and the figure becomes ₹317 crores. Interest, dividend and capital gains earned on the side may not reduce the contract cost, so the cost stands at its full amount and the ₹5 crores is dealt with on its own.
keywords: Money the customer holds back is part of contract revenue
may not reduce the contract cost

options.text: Contract revenue is ₹317 crores, and the ₹5 crores of interest may be taken off the contract cost because it arose out of the contract
options.misconception: nets incidental income against cost on the reasoning that it came from the contract, which is the netting the section forbids
options.why: Where the money came from is not the test. The section names interest, dividend and capital gains and keeps all three out of the contract cost, however closely they are tied to the work.

options.text: Contract revenue is ₹306 crores, the ₹11 crores entering only in 2028, and the ₹5 crores of interest may not be taken off the contract cost
options.misconception: applies the ordinary test of when an amount becomes receivable to money held back, which the section brings into revenue regardless
options.why: Waiting for the defect liability period is what the accounts may do and not what the section allows. It says in terms that contract revenue includes the amount held back, so it is measured now and not in the year the customer releases it.

citation.ref: Section 43CB with its provisos

items.scenario: Setu Constructions computes contract revenue of ₹306 crores for previous year 2025-26 on the percentage of completion of a bridge contract. Its customer holds back ₹11 crores until the defect liability period ends in 2028, and the company has left that out of the ₹306 crores because it is not yet receivable. The company also earned ₹5 crores of interest on the short-term deposit of an unspent mobilisation advance, and has credited that ₹5 crores against its contract cost for the year.

items.stem: How much of the ₹22.40 crores is chargeable for assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: ₹6.80 crores, the balance falling due for tax in a later year
options.why: The section fixes the year of charge as the earlier of the year the lender takes the interest to its profit and loss account and the year the money actually arrives. The ₹6.80 crores arrived, so that year is this one, and where the account it was parked in sits does not change the fact of receipt. The ₹15.60 crores has met neither event and waits for whichever comes first.
keywords: the earlier of the year the lender takes the interest
the year the money actually arrives

options.text: ₹15.60 crores now, and the ₹6.80 crores when it reaches the profit and loss account
options.misconception: treats money sitting in an interest suspense account as not yet received, and then taxes the unreceived half on accrual
options.why: This gets both halves the wrong way round. Cash that has come in has been received whatever account it is entered in, and the half that has not come in and has not been booked is the half that waits.

options.text: Nothing, since no part of the ₹22.40 crores reached the profit and loss account
options.misconception: reads a credit to the profit and loss account as the only trigger, when actual receipt is an independent one
options.why: There are two events and either will do. Reading only the first would let a bank take money in cash and defer the tax for as long as it chose not to book it as income.

options.text: The whole ₹22.40 crores, the bank keeping its books on the mercantile basis
options.misconception: applies the accrual basis the section was written to displace for this class of interest
options.why: Accrual is exactly what this section takes away. Its whole purpose is that a bank should not be taxed on interest a doubtful borrower has not paid, so the accrual on its own brings nothing to charge.

citation.ref: Section 43D read with the categories of bad and doubtful debt prescribed under the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Kaveri Bank, a scheduled bank, has ₹22.40 crores of interest accruing during previous year 2025-26 on advances that the Reserve Bank's prudential norms classify as sub-standard and doubtful, and that fall within the categories the Income-tax Rules prescribe. No part of the ₹22.40 crores was taken to the bank's profit and loss account. Of it, ₹6.80 crores was actually received during the year and credited to an interest suspense account; the remaining ₹15.60 crores was neither received nor credited anywhere as income.

items.stem: Which of the three amounts is chargeable for assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: Only the ₹2 crores
options.misconception: extends the receipt basis to every advance a bank holds, when the section reaches only the prescribed bad and doubtful categories
options.why: A bank's ordinary lending is taxed as anybody else's business income is. Nothing suspends accrual on an advance that is being serviced, so the ₹9 crores is charged this year.

options.text: All three amounts
options.misconception: computes the bank's interest income entirely on accrual and leaves the section out
options.why: This is the position the section exists to change. Two of the three amounts sit in the categories it covers, and one of those two has not met either of the events that bring it to charge.

options.text: The ₹9 crores and the ₹2 crores
