options.why: The relief runs only to advances inside the prescribed categories of bad and doubtful debt, so the ₹9 crores on a performing advance stays on the ordinary accrual basis and is charged. The ₹2 crores is inside the relief, but the bank took it to its profit and loss account, and that is one of the two events that ends the wait. The ₹4 crores has met neither.
keywords: only to advances inside the prescribed categories
one of the two events that ends the wait

options.text: Only the ₹9 crores
options.misconception: treats a credit to the profit and loss account as too little without the cash, when the section charges on whichever event comes first
options.why: Booking the interest as income is the first event named, and it stands on its own. A bank that has told its own accounts the interest is earned cannot then say it is untaxed for want of the money.

citation.ref: Section 43D read with the categories of bad and doubtful debt prescribed under the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Narmada Bank, a scheduled bank, has three amounts of interest for previous year 2025-26. ₹4 crores accrued on an advance the Reserve Bank's norms classify as doubtful, not received and not booked as income. ₹9 crores accrued on an ordinary performing advance, not received and not booked as income. ₹2 crores on another doubtful advance, not received, but taken to the bank's profit and loss account during the year.

items.stem: What is deductible for the provision under section 36(1)(viia)?

options.text: ₹4.50 crores
options.why: A foreign bank is given 5 per cent of total income and nothing else, and the total income the ceiling is worked on is the figure before this deduction and before Chapter VI-A — ₹90 crores here. Five per cent of ₹90 crores is ₹4.50 crores, and the provision actually made in the accounts does not raise the ceiling.
keywords: before this deduction and before Chapter VI-A

options.text: ₹30 crores
options.misconception: allows the provision the accounts carry, treating the clause as approving the bank's own figure
options.why: The clause is a ceiling and not an approval. What the bank charged in its books is the most it can ever claim, and the statutory percentage is what it actually gets.

options.text: ₹4 crores
options.misconception: works the 5 per cent ceiling on income after Chapter VI-A, when the clause says the ceiling is computed before it
options.why: Five per cent of ₹80 crores gives this. The words of the clause put both this deduction and Chapter VI-A after the figure the percentage is applied to, so the ₹10 crores does not come off first.

options.text: ₹7.65 crores
options.misconception: gives a foreign bank the 8.5 per cent rate the clause reserves for an Indian scheduled or non-scheduled bank or a co-operative bank
options.why: Eight and a half per cent of ₹90 crores produces this. The clause sorts lenders into groups and puts a bank incorporated outside India in the 5 per cent group, alongside a public financial institution and a non-banking financial company.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(viia)

items.scenario: Helvetia Bank AG, incorporated in and resident of Switzerland, carries on banking in India through its Chennai branch. For previous year 2025-26 the branch's total income, worked out before any deduction for a provision for bad and doubtful debts and before Chapter VI-A, is ₹90 crores. Chapter VI-A deductions of ₹10 crores are claimed. The branch made a provision for bad and doubtful debts of ₹30 crores in its accounts, and it has no rural branch.

items.stem: How much of the ₹8.30 crores written off is deductible under section 36(1)(vii)?

options.text: ₹8.30 crores
options.misconception: allows the whole write-off, applying the ordinary bad-debt rule to a lender the proviso singles out
options.why: For an assessee outside clause (viia) the whole write-off would go. For one inside it the proviso exists precisely so that the same loss is not deducted twice, once as a provision and again as a write-off.

options.text: ₹3.10 crores
options.why: Debiting the provision account is what lets the write-off be considered at all. The proviso then allows only the part of the write-off standing above the credit balance in that account, so ₹8.30 crores less ₹5.20 crores leaves ₹3.10 crores. The rest has already had its deduction, as the provision.
keywords: only the part of the write-off standing above the credit balance

options.text: ₹1.90 crores
options.misconception: sets the write-off against the current year's clause (viia) claim instead of against the credit balance standing in the provision account
options.why: Deducting ₹6.40 crores from ₹8.30 crores produces this. The proviso names the credit balance in the account, which is ₹5.20 crores here; this year's claim is a separate deduction and is not the figure to subtract.

options.text: Nil
options.misconception: reads the debit to the provision account as the whole of the relief, so nothing further is deductible even where the write-off is the larger figure
options.why: The debit is a condition, not a ceiling. Where the loss written off runs past what the provision account holds, the excess is a real deduction that year and the proviso is what measures it.

citation.ref: Section 36(2)(v) read with the proviso and Explanation 2 to Section 36(1)(vii) and Section 36(1)(viia)

items.scenario: Anantha Bank, an Indian scheduled bank, had a credit balance of ₹5.20 crores on 1 April 2025 in the provision account it maintains under section 36(1)(viia). During previous year 2025-26 advances of ₹8.30 crores became irrecoverable and were written off by debiting that provision account, so nothing was charged to the profit and loss account for the write-off. The bank's deduction under section 36(1)(viia) for the year itself comes to ₹6.40 crores.

items.stem: Is the notice valid?

options.text: Yes — assessment year 2024-25 is a year in which Suryodaya was still in existence
options.misconception: fixes the existence of the assessee at the year being assessed rather than at the date the notice is issued
options.why: The year assessed and the date of the notice are different questions. The liability for 2024-25 survives and passes to Vardaan, which is why the officer may proceed against Vardaan; what he may not do is address the notice to a company that had gone.

options.text: Yes — Vardaan appeared and filed replies, so section 292BB stops it objecting now
options.misconception: stretches section 292BB from the manner of serving a notice to the question of who the notice was issued against
options.why: Section 292BB closes arguments about service — that a notice came late, went to the wrong address, or did not arrive. It says nothing about a notice properly served on a name that answers to nobody.

options.text: No — it was issued against a company that no longer existed and the officer had been told so, and Vardaan taking part afterwards does not mend it
options.why: Once the scheme took effect the amalgamating company was gone and could no longer be a person against whom an assessment is made. The officer had been told of the amalgamation before the notice went out, so the proceeding was bad from the start, and the Supreme Court has held that participation by the surviving company does not repair a defect of that kind.
keywords: could no longer be a person against whom an assessment is made

options.text: Yes — a wrong name is a defect in the notice and section 292B is written for exactly that
options.misconception: treats a notice aimed at a person who does not exist as a clerical slip in naming, which is the class section 292B covers
options.why: Section 292B saves a document whose mistake leaves it still doing its job. Naming a company that has ceased to exist is not a slip in describing the right assessee; it means there is no assessee before the officer at all.

citation.ref: Section 292B read with Section 148 and Principal CIT v. Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.

items.scenario: Suryodaya Renewables Ltd amalgamated into Vardaan Infra Ltd with effect from 1 April 2025 under a scheme the National Company Law Tribunal approved, and Vardaan wrote to the Assessing Officer in May 2025 telling him so. In August 2026 the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 for assessment year 2024-25 in the name of Suryodaya Renewables Ltd. Vardaan's officers attended the hearings that followed and filed the replies asked for.

items.stem: Which of the two assessments survives the company's objection?

options.text: Neither survives, service at a superseded address being a defect that goes to jurisdiction
options.misconception: treats improper service as fatal even where the assessee appeared, which is the objection section 292BB removes
options.why: Late or misdirected service is the very complaint the section was enacted to close off once the assessee has come and co-operated. The company got the notice, forwarded, and then argued the case.

options.text: The 2026-27 assessment survives, and the 2025-26 assessment does not
options.misconception: reasons from whether the company actually knew of the proceedings, so participation cures the missing notice while a misdirected one is treated as never properly issued
options.why: Knowledge is not the test on either side. The section works on the manner of service and not on what the assessee happened to find out, and a notice under section 143(2) is the step by which the officer takes jurisdiction rather than a way of informing anybody.

options.text: The 2025-26 assessment survives, and the 2026-27 assessment does not
options.why: A notice that went to the wrong address is a fault in the manner of service, and once the company appeared and co-operated section 292BB shuts that objection out. The other year has no notice to argue about, and the Supreme Court has held that this section cures infirmities in serving a notice and never the total absence of one, so the officer never took the jurisdiction the assessment needs.
keywords: a fault in the manner of service
never the total absence of one

options.text: Both survive, the company having taken part in each year's proceedings
options.misconception: reads participation as curing every failure connected with a notice, rather than only failures in how it was served
options.why: Participation is the condition the section attaches to one kind of cure. Where no notice was ever issued there is nothing for the fiction to work on, and attending hearings cannot supply it.

citation.ref: Section 292BB read with Section 143(2) and CIT v. Laxman Das Khandelwal

items.scenario: Rachana Metals Ltd is assessed under section 143(3) for two years running. For assessment year 2025-26 the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 143(2) but sent it to the company's old registered office, from which it was forwarded a fortnight later. For assessment year 2026-27 he issued no notice under section 143(2) at all. In both years the company's representatives attended every hearing and filed each reply that was asked for.

items.stem: Which legs of that trip need an e-way bill?

options.text: Neither leg, since no e-way bill is ever needed for a movement under fifty kilometres
options.misconception: borrows the fifty-kilometre relaxation, which only excuses filling in Part B on a hop to the transporter, and inflates it into a blanket exemption
options.why: Fifty kilometres appears elsewhere and does something much smaller. On an intra-State hop from the consignor to his transporter, or from the transporter on to the consignee, the conveyance details in Part B may be left out. The bill itself is still generated, and that relaxation has nothing to do with weighing.

options.text: Only the outward leg is exempt; the run back to the works needs one
options.misconception: reads the clause as covering the journey to the weighbridge and misses that it names the journey back in the same breath
options.why: The clause is written both ways round. It reaches goods moving out to be weighed and goods moving back afterwards, so splitting the trip in half gets the second half wrong.

options.text: Both legs, the consignment being worth more than fifty thousand rupees
options.misconception: treats the fifty-thousand value test as beating the list of exempt movements, when that list is written to override it
options.why: Value decides whether the ordinary rule bites. It does not reach a movement the rule has already lifted out, and the weighing trip is one of those — which is why the clause never asks what the goods are worth.

options.text: Neither leg, the exemption covering the run out to the weighbridge and the run back
options.why: Rule 138(14) puts the weighing trip outside the requirement altogether. Goods travelling from the consignor's own place of business to a weighbridge, and the same goods travelling back to that place of business, need no e-way bill where the distance is up to twenty kilometres and a delivery challan under rule 55 rides with them. Twelve kilometres sits inside that, and the return leg is written into the clause as plainly as the outward one.

citation.ref: Rule 138(14), read with rule 55 and the third proviso to rule 138(3)

items.scenario: Vishwas Alloys, registered in Maharashtra, sends a lorry load of billets worth ₹6,80,000 from its Pune works to a public weighbridge twelve kilometres away to have the load weighed, and brings the same billets straight back to the works afterwards. A delivery challan drawn under rule 55 travels with the vehicle on both legs. Nothing is being sold.

items.stem: Is the squad right?

options.text: Yes, and the goods and the vehicle are open to detention
options.why: The clause lifts a weighing trip out of the requirement only while the distance stays within twenty kilometres. Twenty-six is outside it, so the ordinary rule returns. The consignment is worth more than fifty thousand rupees, a bill was due before the vehicle moved, and moving without one exposes the goods and the conveyance to detention.

options.text: Yes, but only because a sale lay behind the weighing; a weighing with no sale behind it is exempt at any distance
options.misconception: reads the requirement as attaching to a supply, when it attaches to the movement of goods whether or not anything is sold
options.why: An e-way bill follows the movement of goods and not the sale. A stock transfer, a job-work despatch and a trip to be weighed all sit under the same rule, and whether there is a buyer at the far end changes nothing about the distance.

options.text: No, the exemption running to twenty-five kilometres, so twenty-six is an argument the officer will lose
options.misconception: remembers that there is a distance limit but not which one, which is the near miss this clause invites
options.why: The figure written into the clause is twenty kilometres. There is no twenty-five anywhere in it, and a limit set by a rule is not something a few extra kilometres can be argued past.

options.text: No, a delivery challan standing in for an e-way bill whenever goods move to be weighed
options.misconception: makes the delivery challan the whole of the exemption, when it is only one of the two conditions the clause sets
options.why: The challan is a condition of the exemption, not a substitute for the bill. Both conditions have to hold together and the distance one has failed here.

citation.ref: Rule 138(14), read with rule 55 and section 129 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: Sundar Castings, registered in Tamil Nadu, sends a consignment worth ₹9,40,000 from its Hosur foundry to a weighbridge twenty-six kilometres away, carrying a delivery challan drawn under rule 55 and no e-way bill. A roving squad stops the vehicle on the way and says the movement should have been covered by an e-way bill.

items.stem: What does rule 41A require?

options.text: Anvaya settles the split itself, the rule letting it transfer the balance wholly or partly
options.misconception: reads the freedom to send the whole or a part as a freedom to pick the ratio, when the ratio is fixed by the rule
options.why: Two different choices are being run together here. How much of the balance goes across is the transferor's to decide, and the proviso then settles how it is shared, in the ratio of the value of assets held. He cannot direct a figure that ratio does not produce.
keywords: ratio of the value of assets held

options.text: FORM GST ITC-02A within thirty days of the separate registration, shared on the value of assets each place holds, and the credit lands only once Rajkot accepts it on the portal
options.why: Rule 41A gives the transferor thirty days from obtaining the separate registration to furnish the details in FORM GST ITC-02A on the common portal. The share is worked out on the value of assets held at the time of registration. Acceptance by the newly registered person is the step that actually moves anything, because until the transferee accepts, nothing is credited to his electronic credit ledger.

options.text: FORM GST ITC-02 with a chartered accountant's certificate, the route a transfer of business takes
options.misconception: reaches for the form and the certificate rule 41 requires on a sale, merger or demerger, where a business changes hands
options.why: Rule 41 covers a change in the constitution of a business, and there a certificate from a practising chartered accountant or cost accountant supports the transfer. Splitting one's own registration inside a State is not a change of hands, and rule 41A gives it a form of its own with no certificate attached.

options.text: Nothing may cross; the balance stays at Surat and the depot opens with an empty ledger
options.misconception: treats a second registration in the same State as a stranger, when rule 41A exists precisely so that credit is not stranded
options.why: The whole purpose of rule 41A is that credit follows the assets rather than being trapped where it accumulated. Transferring is optional, not forbidden — the balance may go wholly, partly, or not at all.

citation.ref: Rule 41A, read with rule 41 and section 25 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: Anvaya Textiles holds one GST registration in Gujarat, with its Surat mill as principal place of business and its Rajkot depot as an additional place of business. In April it takes a separate registration for the Rajkot depot under section 25, and it wants to move part of the credit sitting in the Surat ledger across to it.

items.stem: How much credit may go across to the Nashik registration?

options.text: ₹5,00,000, with ₹10,00,000 left at Nagpur
options.misconception: apportions on the assets input tax credit was actually taken on, which is the base the explanation to rule 41A exists to rule out
options.why: That is ₹30,00,000 over ₹90,00,000 of credit-bearing assets, one third of the balance. It is the natural-looking base and it is the wrong one, and the explanation was written to close it off.

options.text: ₹9,00,000, with ₹6,00,000 left at Nagpur
options.misconception: turns the ratio round and hands the new place the share belonging to the assets that stayed behind
options.why: ₹9,00,000 is three fifths, which is what the Nagpur assets earn. The numerator is the transferee's asset value, so the depot takes two fifths and Nagpur keeps three fifths, not the other way about.

options.text: ₹7,50,000, with ₹7,50,000 left at Nagpur
options.misconception: divides the balance evenly, as though taking a separate registration partitioned the business down the middle
options.why: Nothing in rule 41A splits anything equally. The rule names one basis, a ratio of asset values, and here that ratio is nowhere near half and half.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, with ₹9,00,000 left at Nagpur
options.why: The proviso shares the balance in the ratio of the value of assets held, and the explanation says that means the entire assets of the business, whether or not credit was availed on them. So the ratio is ₹60,00,000 against ₹1,50,00,000, which is two fifths, and two fifths of ₹15,00,000 is ₹6,00,000.
keywords: ratio of the value of assets held
whether or not credit was availed

citation.ref: Proviso to rule 41A(1) with its explanation

items.scenario: When Bhavani Ceramics takes a separate registration in July for its Nashik depot, its existing Nagpur registration holds ₹15,00,000 of unused credit in the electronic credit ledger. Assets at Nagpur are worth ₹90,00,000, of which input tax credit was actually taken on assets worth ₹60,00,000. Assets at Nashik are worth ₹60,00,000, of which input tax credit was actually taken on assets worth ₹30,00,000.

items.stem: Which of these go into GSTR-1 invoice by invoice?

options.text: The sales to Kerala and Goa
options.misconception: reads the limit as one lakh and above, so an invoice sitting exactly on the figure gets swept in
options.why: The test is a value that exceeds a lakh, and ₹1,00,000 does not exceed ₹1,00,000. An invoice standing exactly on the figure belongs with the smaller ones in the summary.

options.text: Only the sale to the buyer in Kerala
options.why: An invoice raised on an unregistered buyer is reported on its own only where the supply is inter-State and the value exceeds one lakh rupees. Kerala is inter-State and ₹1,80,000 clears the limit. Goa is inter-State but ₹1,00,000 does not clear it, so that one belongs in the State-wise summary. The Karnataka sale is intra-State and goes into the rate-wise consolidated figure whatever it is worth.

options.text: The sales to Kerala and Karnataka
options.misconception: applies the value test to every consumer sale and forgets that it reaches only the ones that crossed a State line
options.why: Value alone does not settle it. A sale to a consumer inside the State goes in rate by rate however large the invoice, because the tax is already sitting in the State that will consume the goods and nothing has to be traced anywhere.

options.text: All three
options.misconception: carries across the rule for supplies to registered buyers, where every invoice is reported one at a time
options.why: That is the rule for a registered buyer, and the reason is credit — his claim has to be matched against the seller's return. An unregistered buyer claims nothing, so the detail is asked for only where revenue has to be routed to another State.

citation.ref: Section 37(1), read with rule 59(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: Kaveri Appliances is registered in Karnataka. In one month it makes three sales to buyers who are not registered under GST — ₹1,80,000 to a buyer in Kerala, ₹1,00,000 to a buyer in Goa, and ₹3,40,000 to a buyer in Karnataka. It has no other outward supplies that month.

items.stem: Which change, made on its own, would do it?

options.text: Tarang crossing five crore rupees of turnover and becoming liable to issue e-invoices
options.misconception: assumes e-invoicing pulls consumer sales into invoice-wise reporting, when it does not reach a supply to an unregistered person at all
options.why: E-invoicing was brought in for reporting supplies made to registered persons. What a firm past that turnover picks up on the consumer side is a dynamic quick response code on the invoice, which is about what the document must carry, not about how the return is filled in.

options.text: The supply being of a service rather than of goods
options.misconception: expects services to be reported differently from goods, when the rule turns on the buyer, the State line and the value alone
options.why: Three things are asked of a consumer sale — was the buyer registered, was a State line crossed, and did the value exceed a lakh. What was supplied is not one of them.

options.text: The customer being in West Bengal instead of Odisha
options.why: Only two things settle this and the value has already cleared one of them, since ₹1,20,000 exceeds one lakh rupees. What is missing is that a State line was crossed. Put the customer in another State and it becomes an inter-State supply to an unregistered person above the limit, which goes in invoice by invoice.

options.text: The invoice rising to ₹5,00,000, the customer staying in Odisha
options.misconception: believes a large enough invoice earns its own line whatever the State, when the value test never reaches a sale inside the State
options.why: A sale to a consumer inside the State is consolidated rate by rate however large it is. Raising the figure changes the consolidated total and changes nothing else.

citation.ref: Section 37(1), read with rule 59(1) and rule 48(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: Tarang Furnishings, registered in Odisha, raises an invoice of ₹1,20,000 on a customer in Odisha who is not registered under GST, and reports it inside the rate-wise consolidated figure in GSTR-1. Its accountant asks what would have to be different for that one invoice to have gone in on its own.

items.stem: Is the accountant right?

options.text: Yes — a buyer at the concessional rate is barred from the payment route, and the bar stands
options.misconception: states the position the omitted sub-rule created, which is still the sentence printed in material that went to press before October 2024
options.why: That was the law and it stopped being the law when the sub-rule was omitted. It is the commonest wrong answer here for a plain reason — it is still in print, and a book written earlier says exactly this.

options.text: No — the sub-rule that closed that road was omitted with effect from 8 October 2024
options.why: Sub-rule (10) of rule 96 was what stopped a person who had bought at the concessional rate from exporting on payment of integrated tax. Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8 October 2024 omitted it. Rathi may now ship under a letter of undertaking or bond without payment and claim back the unused credit, or ship on payment of integrated tax and claim a refund of that tax.

options.text: No, but Rathi must first give up the credit of the 0.1 per cent to use the payment route
options.misconception: invents a price for the route that was reopened, as though the credit and the payment option could not be held at once
options.why: Nothing was put in the sub-rule's place. Omitting it left no condition behind it, so there is no reversal to make and no election to file.

options.text: Yes, and worse — buying at 0.1 per cent costs Rathi the credit of that tax as well
options.misconception: treats a concessional rate as though it were an exemption, which would break the credit chain
options.why: A low rate is not an exemption. Tax was charged and tax was paid, so the buyer takes credit of it in the ordinary way. That was so well before the omission and the omission did not touch it.
keywords: low rate is not an exemption

citation.ref: Rule 96, sub-rule (10) omitted by Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8 October 2024, read with Notification No. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 23 October 2017

items.scenario: Rathi Exports buys steel fittings in 2026 from a manufacturer at the concessional rate of 0.1 per cent under the merchant-export notifications, meeting every condition they set, and ships them abroad. Its accountant, working from a book printed in 2023, tells the partners that the only road open is a letter of undertaking without payment of tax, and that exporting on payment of integrated tax would be a breach.

items.stem: What may each of them claim?

options.text: Meghna nothing, a concessional rate not making an inverted duty structure, and Vidur a refund of the integrated tax
options.misconception: reads the inverted structure as needing a notified rate difference on the same goods in and out, and misses that a concessional sale is treated as one
options.why: The rate Meghna charges on the way out is lower than the rates it bore on the way in, which is what an inverted structure is. A supplier selling to a merchant exporter at the concessional rate is named as eligible for that refund.
keywords: lower than the rates it bore

options.text: Meghna a refund of unused credit on the inverted duty structure, and Vidur a refund of the integrated tax he paid on the export
options.why: Two different refunds sit on the two sides of this sale. Meghna sells at 0.1 per cent while buying at ordinary rates, so credit piles up that it cannot use, and a supplier selling to a merchant exporter at the concessional rate is eligible for the refund given on an inverted duty structure. Vidur, since the omission of sub-rule (10) of rule 96, may ship on payment of integrated tax and claim a refund of the integrated tax he paid.

options.text: Vidur both — a refund of the integrated tax paid on the export and a refund of the 0.1 per cent his supplier charged him
options.misconception: counts the same tax twice, treating the concessional tax as its own refund rather than as credit that funds the payment on export
options.why: The 0.1 per cent is credit sitting in Vidur's ledger. It goes towards the integrated tax he pays on the export, and it is that integrated tax which comes back to him. Claiming the small tax separately would return it twice over.

options.text: Meghna the inverted-structure refund, and Vidur only an export without payment under a letter of undertaking with a refund of unused credit
options.misconception: keeps the restriction the omitted sub-rule imposed on the exporter, so it allows him one route where he now has two
options.why: The road that sub-rule closed is open again. Vidur may still choose the letter of undertaking, but he is no longer confined to it, and he took the payment route here.

citation.ref: Rule 96 after the omission of sub-rule (10), with rule 89(5) and clause (ii) of the first proviso to section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: Meghna Steels sells fittings to Vidur Traders, a merchant exporter, at 0.1 per cent under the merchant-export notifications, while Meghna's own inputs bear tax at the ordinary rates. Vidur exports the fittings in 2026 on payment of integrated tax.

items.stem: Which cost formula does Ind AS 2 NOT permit for inventories?

options.text: Specific identification
options.misconception: forbids the formula the standard actually REQUIRES for items that are not interchangeable
options.why: Specific identification is not merely permitted, it is required for inventories that are not ordinarily interchangeable and for goods produced and segregated for a particular project. It is the formula that fits a jeweller's individual stones or a shipbuilder's hulls. Last-in, first-out is the one that is out.

options.text: All four are permitted, the entity choosing whichever gives the fairest presentation
options.misconception: reads the cost formula as a free choice, when the standard names one it forbids outright
options.why: The choice is not free. Ind AS 2 removes last-in, first-out altogether, because in a period of rising prices it leaves the oldest and cheapest costs sitting in the balance sheet while charging the newest against revenue. What is left is first-in, first-out or weighted average for interchangeable items, and specific identification for those that are not.

options.text: Last-in, first-out
options.why: Last-in, first-out is not permitted. For inventories that are ordinarily interchangeable the choice is between first-in, first-out and weighted average cost, and the same formula must be used for all inventories of a similar nature and use. Items that are NOT ordinarily interchangeable, and goods produced and segregated for a particular project, are costed by specific identification instead.

options.text: Weighted average cost
options.misconception: names one of the two formulas the standard actually offers as the one it forbids
options.why: Weighted average cost is one of the two permitted formulas, alongside first-in, first-out. An entity may choose between them, and having chosen must apply the same formula consistently to all inventories of a similar nature and use. The formula the standard forbids is last-in, first-out.

citation.ref: para 23 to 25

items.stem: At what amount are the raw materials carried at the year end?

options.text: At ₹4.5 lakh, because replacement cost is the measure of net realisable value for raw materials
options.misconception: treats replacement cost as the measure in every case, when it is reached for only after the finished-product test fails
options.why: Replacement cost is not the measure of net realisable value for raw materials in every case. Ind AS 2 reaches for it only once the finished-product test has failed, and then only as the best available measure of what the materials are worth. While the finished products are expected to sell at or above cost, the materials stay at their own cost of ₹6 lakh.

options.text: At ₹6 lakh, with an impairment loss of ₹1.5 lakh recognised under Ind AS 36
options.misconception: reaches for the impairment standard, which does not apply to inventories at all
options.why: Ind AS 36 excludes inventories from its scope, because their write-down rule is Ind AS 2's own. And on that rule there is no loss to recognise anyway. The test is whether the finished products will still sell at or above cost, and they will, so the materials stand at ₹6 lakh and nothing goes to profit or loss.

options.text: At ₹4.5 lakh, because inventories are always carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value
options.misconception: applies the general rule to raw materials and misses the exception written beside it
options.why: The general rule is stated correctly and then applied to the one case the standard carves out of it. Inventories are carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value, but materials held for use in production are not written down below cost where the finished goods will still sell at or above cost. A fall in the price of an input is not by itself a loss — the loss only arrives if the output cannot cover its cost.
keywords: lower of cost and net realisable value

options.text: At ₹6 lakh, with no write-down
options.why: Inventories are carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value, but Ind AS 2 writes an exception for raw materials. They are not written down below cost while the finished products into which they will be incorporated are expected to sell at or above cost. That is the position here, so nothing is written down and the materials stay at ₹6 lakh. Replacement cost matters only once that test has failed.
keywords: lower of cost and net realisable value

citation.ref: para 32

items.scenario: A manufacturer holds raw materials that cost ₹6 lakh. Their replacement cost at the year end has fallen to ₹4.5 lakh. The finished products into which those materials will be incorporated are still expected to sell at or above their cost.

items.stem: How is the dividend dealt with in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: A liability of ₹50 lakh is recognised at 31 March 2026, because the dividend is paid out of that year's profits
options.misconception: attaches the liability to the year whose profits fund the dividend rather than to the date the obligation arose
options.why: Which year's profits pay for a dividend is not the question. The question is whether an obligation existed at the reporting date, and on 31 March 2026 none did — the board was still free not to declare. A liability recognised in the earlier year would report an obligation the company did not have.
keywords: obligation existed at the reporting date

options.text: Neither recognised nor disclosed, since the dividend belongs to the next reporting period
options.misconception: drops the disclosure along with the liability
options.why: Recognition and disclosure are two different questions and only the first is answered no. A dividend declared after the reporting period is a non-adjusting event of sufficient significance that the company discloses its nature and amount, so a reader of the March accounts learns that ₹50 lakh is on its way out.

options.text: No liability is recognised; the dividend is disclosed
options.why: An event after the reporting period is adjusted for only where it gives evidence of a condition that existed at the reporting date. At 31 March 2026 the board had not declared anything, so there was no obligation on that date and no liability to recognise. The declaration is a non-adjusting event and is disclosed instead. Ind AS 10 uses this very case as its worked example.

options.text: A liability of ₹50 lakh is recognised at 31 March 2026, because the declaration came before the financial statements were approved for issue
options.misconception: treats every event occurring before approval as an adjusting event
options.why: The approval date sets the WINDOW in which events after the reporting period are considered; it does not decide which of them adjust. Only an event evidencing a condition that existed at the reporting date adjusts the numbers. A declaration made on 15 May is a new condition, so it is disclosed and not adjusted.

citation.ref: para 3 and 12

items.scenario: A company's reporting date is 31 March 2026. Its board declared a final dividend of ₹50 lakh on 15 May 2026. The financial statements were approved for issue on 30 June 2026.

items.stem: What does the company do about the claim?

options.text: Recognise an asset and income of ₹30 lakh, since the inflow is probable
options.misconception: applies a provision's probable threshold to an asset, where the bar is set higher at virtually certain
options.why: Probable is the threshold for recognising a PROVISION, not for recognising an asset. Ind AS 37 is deliberately asymmetric — a likely outflow is provided for, while a likely inflow is only disclosed — because bringing in a gain that may never arrive overstates both profit and net assets. The bar for the asset is virtually certain.

options.text: Recognise nothing and disclose nothing, since a contingent asset is never recognised
options.misconception: reads the bar on recognition as a bar on disclosure too
options.why: The bar is on recognition alone. A contingent asset whose inflow is probable is disclosed, so that a reader knows a claim of ₹30 lakh is running even though no number has entered the statements. Silence would keep from the reader something the company itself thinks is more likely than not to arrive.

options.text: Recognise an asset of ₹30 lakh and defer the income until the cash is received
options.misconception: recognises the asset anyway and parks the credit, when the asset itself is what must not be recognised
options.why: Deferring the credit does not cure the problem, because the asset is the half that Ind AS 37 refuses. A contingent asset is not recognised at all until realisation is virtually certain, and until then the company discloses it. Putting ₹30 lakh on the balance sheet with the gain held back still asserts a resource the company may never receive.

options.text: Recognise nothing, and disclose the contingent asset
options.why: A contingent asset is never recognised, because recognising it could bring into the accounts income that may never be realised. Where the inflow is probable it is disclosed, and that is the position here. The asset is recognised only once realisation becomes virtually certain, at which point it has stopped being contingent.

citation.ref: para 33 to 35

items.scenario: A company is suing a supplier for defective goods. Its lawyers advise that an inflow of ₹30 lakh is probable, but not virtually certain, at the reporting date.

items.stem: How does A Ltd account for its holding in B Ltd?

options.text: The holding is an ordinary investment measured at fair value, since 25 per cent is well below half
options.misconception: treats half the votes as the only line that matters, and misses the twenty per cent line entirely
options.why: There are two lines, not one. Above half, control and consolidation; at twenty per cent and above, significant influence and the equity method. Falling short of half only rules out a subsidiary. Measuring the holding as an ordinary investment would show a value and a dividend where the equity method shows A Ltd's share of B Ltd's own profit.

options.text: Control is presumed, so B Ltd is consolidated line by line as a subsidiary
options.misconception: reads a quarter of the voting power as control, which is a different and much higher test
options.why: Twenty-five per cent raises a presumption of significant influence, not of control. Control needs power over the investee, exposure to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect them. Line-by-line consolidation would bring in the whole of B Ltd's assets and revenue when A Ltd is entitled to a quarter of its results.

options.text: There is no significant influence unless A Ltd also has a seat on B Ltd's board
options.misconception: turns evidence that can establish influence below the twenty per cent line into a requirement above it
options.why: Board representation is one of the things that can EVIDENCE significant influence where the holding is under twenty per cent — alongside participation in policy decisions, material transactions, interchange of personnel and essential technical dependence. It is not a condition that has to be met once the holding is twenty-five per cent, where influence is presumed until it is shown to be absent.

options.text: Significant influence is presumed, so B Ltd is an associate and is equity accounted
options.why: Holding twenty per cent or more of the voting power raises a presumption of significant influence — a say in an investee's financial and operating policy choices, short of controlling them outright. Rebutting that presumption needs a clear demonstration that influence is absent, and nothing here offers one. So B Ltd is an associate, equity accounted rather than consolidated.

citation.ref: para 5-6

items.scenario: A Ltd holds 25 per cent of the voting power of B Ltd. Nothing else about the relationship is unusual.

items.stem: Is the machine impaired, and at what amount does it stand?

options.text: Not impaired, and the machine is written up to ₹105 lakh
options.misconception: treats the recoverable amount as a new carrying amount, when it is only a ceiling test
options.why: Recoverable amount is a ceiling the carrying amount must not exceed; it is not a measurement basis. Under the cost model the machine stays at ₹100 lakh less further depreciation, and an asset is never written UP because value in use turned out to be higher. Writing it up would recognise a gain the company has not earned.

options.text: Impaired by ₹8 lakh, recoverable amount being ₹92 lakh
options.misconception: takes the lower of the two measures instead of the higher
options.why: This takes the lower of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. The standard takes the higher, because the company will do whichever is better for it — if keeping the machine is worth ₹105 lakh, it will not sell it for ₹92 lakh. Either measure on its own can clear an asset of impairment.
keywords: fair value less costs of disposal

options.text: Not impaired; recoverable amount is ₹105 lakh and the machine stays at ₹100 lakh
options.why: Between fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, recoverable amount takes whichever is larger — here that is ₹105 lakh. Impairment only bites once carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount, and ₹100 lakh sits below ₹105 lakh, not above it. So nothing is written down and the carrying amount stands unchanged.
keywords: fair value less costs of disposal

options.text: Impaired by ₹1.5 lakh, recoverable amount being the average of the two measures at ₹98.5 lakh
options.misconception: averages the two measures, when the standard picks one of them
options.why: Recoverable amount is not an average of anything. Between fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, it takes whichever is larger, because the company recovers the asset one way or the other, not half each way. The larger figure here is ₹105 lakh, so there is no impairment at all.
keywords: fair value less costs of disposal

citation.ref: para 6

items.scenario: A machine has a carrying amount of ₹100 lakh. Its fair value less costs of disposal is ₹92 lakh and its value in use is ₹105 lakh.

items.stem: Where does the ₹15 lakh increase go?

options.text: To other comprehensive income, and then reclassified to profit or loss when the land is sold
options.misconception: recycles the revaluation surplus on disposal, when it moves straight to retained earnings
options.why: The first half is right and the second half is the trap. A revaluation surplus never passes through profit or loss. On disposal it is transferred directly to retained earnings, a movement inside equity that the statement of changes in equity shows and the statement of profit and loss never sees.

options.text: To other comprehensive income, accumulating in equity as a revaluation surplus
options.why: An upward revaluation goes to other comprehensive income and accumulates in equity as a revaluation surplus. It passes through profit or loss only to the extent it reverses a decrease on the SAME asset that was charged to profit or loss earlier, and here there was no such decrease. So the whole ₹15 lakh sits in the revaluation surplus.

options.text: Nowhere, until the land is sold and the increase is realised
options.misconception: keeps the cost model's answer after the revaluation model has been adopted
options.why: Waiting for a sale is the COST model's answer. Once the revaluation model is adopted for a class of assets, the asset is carried at its revalued amount and the increase is recognised at once in other comprehensive income. Recognising nothing would leave the land at ₹80 lakh, which is not what the revaluation model says it is worth.

options.text: To profit or loss as a gain of ₹15 lakh
options.misconception: routes a first upward revaluation through profit or loss, which is only ever the reversal route
options.why: Profit or loss takes an upward revaluation only where it reverses a decrease on the same asset already charged there, and this is the first revaluation of this land. An unrealised increase in the value of land the company still holds is not a gain it has earned, which is why it is parked in other comprehensive income until it is realised.

citation.ref: para 39-40

items.scenario: A company carries land at its cost of ₹80 lakh and now adopts the revaluation model. The land is revalued to ₹95 lakh. There has been no earlier revaluation of this land and no earlier decrease charged to profit or loss.

items.stem: How is the ₹4 lakh of interest treated?

options.text: Capitalised, because interest on money borrowed to buy an item of property, plant and equipment is a directly attributable cost under Ind AS 16
options.misconception: reads Ind AS 16's directly attributable costs as taking in interest on any borrowing
options.why: Ind AS 16's directly attributable costs are things like site preparation, delivery, installation and testing. Interest reaches the cost of an asset only through Ind AS 23, and only where the asset is a qualifying asset. Since this machine is not one, the ₹4 lakh is a finance cost of the period.

options.text: Capitalised as part of the machine's cost, because the borrowing was taken specifically to buy that machine
options.misconception: makes the link between the loan and the asset the test, when the test is what kind of asset it is
options.why: A specific borrowing decides HOW MUCH is capitalised once an asset qualifies; it does not decide whether the asset qualifies. The gateway is the nature of the asset — does it necessarily take a substantial period of time to get ready. This one is ready in three weeks, so it is not a qualifying asset and nothing is capitalised.

options.text: Expensed, because the machine is not a qualifying asset
options.why: Capitalisation attaches only to a qualifying asset, and the test here is about timing rather than about how the machine was bought: getting it ready for use or sale must necessarily demand a SUBSTANTIAL PERIOD. Three weeks fails that test, so this machine is not a qualifying asset, whatever funded the purchase, and the ₹4 lakh is expensed.

options.text: Capitalised in the proportion the three weeks bears to the year, and expensed for the rest
options.misconception: prorates the interest, when the standard asks a yes-or-no question about the asset
options.why: There is nothing to prorate. Ind AS 23 asks whether the asset necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready, and the answer is either yes or no. Where the answer is no, as here, no part of the borrowing cost is capitalised and the whole ₹4 lakh is expensed as incurred.

citation.ref: para 8

items.scenario: A company borrows ₹200 lakh specifically to buy a standard machine, which is delivered and installed within three weeks and is then ready for use. Interest of ₹4 lakh is incurred on that borrowing during the year.

items.stem: Which of these are cash equivalents?

options.text: All three, since all can be turned into cash quickly
options.misconception: reads liquidity alone as the test and drops the condition about the risk of a change in value
options.why: Being easy to sell is only half of it. A cash equivalent must also be convertible to a known amount of cash with an insignificant risk of changes in value, which is what keeps out both the equity shares and the twelve-month deposit. Counting all three would let a fall in the share price show up as a fall in the company's cash.

options.text: The treasury bill and the equity shares, since the shares are to be sold within a month
options.misconception: uses how long the company means to hold an investment, when the test is what it will be worth
options.why: Intention is not the test. Equity investments are excluded from cash equivalents because what they will fetch is not a known amount of cash — the price can move between now and the sale, so the risk of a change in value is not insignificant. A treasury bill sixty days from maturity carries no such doubt.

options.text: The treasury bill alone
options.why: A cash equivalent is parked there to meet commitments falling due soon, not held as an investment, so it has to sit near enough to maturity that what it will fetch is already settled — the holder turns it into a known amount whenever he wants, and runs only an insignificant risk that the amount shifts on him. The working guide is a maturity of about three months or less, measured from the day it was bought. The sixty-day treasury bill fits. The twelve-month deposit is too far from maturity when acquired, and equity investments are excluded because their value is not known in advance.

options.text: The treasury bill and the twelve-month deposit, both being bank and government instruments
options.misconception: classifies by the form of the instrument rather than by its time to maturity from acquisition
options.why: What the instrument is issued by does not decide the question; how near maturity it was when acquired does. The guide is about three months from acquisition, and a twelve-month deposit is far outside it. It is an investment, and the cash movement on making it is an investing cash flow rather than a movement within cash equivalents.

citation.ref: para 7-8

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company holds three things — a treasury bill bought sixty days before its maturity, a fixed deposit made for a term of twelve months, and listed equity shares the company intends to sell next month.

items.stem: Is the segment separately reportable?

options.text: Yes, because its revenue is 12 per cent of combined revenue
options.why: The three quantitative thresholds are alternatives, not a set to be met together. A segment is separately reportable if it crosses ten per cent of combined revenue, or ten per cent of the greater of combined profits and combined losses, or ten per cent of combined assets. Revenue of ₹120 crore against ₹1,000 crore is 12 per cent, so the first threshold is crossed and the segment is reportable.

options.text: Only if the segments already reported do not cover seventy-five per cent of external revenue
options.misconception: reads the seventy-five per cent rule as a cap that can exclude a segment, when it is a floor that only ever adds
options.why: The seventy-five per cent rule works in one direction only. Where the reportable segments together fall short of seventy-five per cent of external revenue, more segments are added until they reach it. It never takes away a segment that has already crossed one of the ten per cent thresholds, and this one has.

options.text: No, because it fails two of the three tests
options.misconception: requires all three thresholds to be met, when crossing any one of them is enough
options.why: Failing two changes nothing, because the tests are alternatives. Crossing any one of the three ten per cent thresholds makes a segment separately reportable, and this one crosses the revenue threshold at 12 per cent. Requiring all three would hide a segment that is a large part of what the company sells.

options.text: No, because profit is the test that decides and its profit is only 4 per cent
options.misconception: elevates one of the three thresholds above the other two
options.why: Profit is one of three, not the one that decides. Revenue, profit or loss, and assets each carry their own ten per cent threshold, and a segment that crosses any of them is reportable. A segment can be a big seller and a thin earner, and Ind AS 108 still wants it shown separately.

citation.ref: para 13 and 15

items.scenario: One of a company's operating segments has revenue, internal and external together, of ₹120 crore against combined revenue of all segments of ₹1,000 crore. Its profit is 4 per cent of the combined profit of all segments reporting a profit, and its assets are 6 per cent of the combined assets of all operating segments.

items.stem: What may the lessee do?

options.text: Elect not to recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, and charge the payments as an expense over the lease term
options.why: A lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for every lease, with two elections out — short-term leases of twelve months or less containing no purchase option, and leases of low-value assets. A nine-month lease with no purchase option fits the first. The election is about RECOGNITION only; the contract is still a lease.

options.text: Nothing; a right-of-use asset and a lease liability must be recognised, since there is no relief below twelve months
options.misconception: denies an election the standard expressly gives
options.why: The relief exists and is the more commonly used of the two. A lease of twelve months or less with no purchase option may be kept off the balance sheet at the lessee's choice, with the payments recognised as an expense on a straight-line basis or another systematic basis. Nine months with no purchase option is squarely inside it.

options.text: Treat the contract as outside Ind AS 116 altogether, since a short lease is not a lease
options.misconception: turns a recognition exemption into a scope exclusion
options.why: The exemption is an election about recognition, not a statement that the contract is something other than a lease. Ind AS 116 still applies — the term, the disclosures and the definition all come from it — and the standard requires a lessee taking the exemption to disclose that fact and the expense charged.

options.text: Take the exemption only if the office is also a low-value asset
options.misconception: reads the two elections as one cumulative test, when either stands on its own
options.why: They are two separate elections and either is enough on its own. One turns on the lease term being twelve months or less with no purchase option; the other turns on the underlying asset being of low value. An office is not a low-value asset, and it does not need to be, because the short-term election answers this case.

citation.ref: para 5 and 6

items.scenario: A company takes an office on a nine-month lease. There is no option to buy the property and no option to extend the term.

items.stem: What kind of change is this, and how is it accounted for?

options.text: A change in accounting estimate, but recognised retrospectively so the earlier years' depreciation is corrected
options.misconception: classifies the change correctly and then applies the wrong treatment to it
options.why: The classification is right and the treatment is the opposite of the rule. A change in accounting estimate is recognised prospectively — in the period of the change and, where it affects them, in future periods. The remaining carrying amount is written off over the revised remaining life, and no earlier year is touched.

options.text: A change in accounting estimate, recognised prospectively in this period and future periods
options.why: Useful life is an estimate, not a policy — the measurement basis is the policy, and how long the asset will last is a judgement about the future that new information can revise. A change in accounting estimate is recognised prospectively, by adjusting the depreciation of the current and future periods. Comparatives are not restated, because the earlier figures were not wrong when they were made.

options.text: A change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively with the comparatives restated
options.misconception: treats a revised estimate as a change of policy, which carries the retrospective treatment
options.why: A policy is the basis of measurement chosen — cost or revaluation, for instance — and changing one is applied retrospectively. Useful life is not that. Ind AS 8 names depreciation method and useful life as estimates, and it adds that where the two are hard to tell apart the change is treated as a change in accounting estimate.

options.text: A prior period error, corrected by restating the earlier years' depreciation
options.misconception: reads a revised estimate as evidence that the earlier estimate was a mistake
options.why: An error is a misstatement arising from a failure to use, or a misuse of, information that was available when those statements were approved. Nothing here says the ten-year life was unsupportable at the time; fresh technical advice has arrived since. That is a change in accounting estimate, taken prospectively, and the earlier years stand.

citation.ref: para 19 and 36

items.scenario: A company has depreciated a machine over an assumed useful life of ten years. In the current year, on fresh technical advice, it revises the remaining useful life so that the machine will now be written off over a total of seven years.

items.stem: What is the net asset value per unit?

options.misconception: deducts the liabilities but leaves the fund's other assets out of the total
options.why: 512 less 20, over 5, gives ₹98.40 — the deduction is right and the ₹8 crore of other assets has gone missing. Everything the fund owns counts, not only its investments, so the total is ₹520 crore before liabilities and ₹500 crore after.

options.misconception: adds the liabilities to the assets instead of subtracting them
options.why: 540 over 5 gives ₹108, which treats a debt as though it were a resource. Liabilities and accrued expenses reduce what belongs to the unit holders, so the sign is minus. The correct total is ₹500 crore and the net asset value is ₹100.

options.misconception: divides the assets by the units without deducting the liabilities and accrued expenses
options.why: 520 over 5 gives ₹104, and it is what the fund would be worth if it owed nothing. The liabilities and accrued expenses of ₹20 crore are a claim ahead of the unit holders, so they come off before the division. Leaving them in overstates every unit by ₹4.

Net asset value per unit is the market value of the fund's investments plus its other assets, minus its liabilities and accrued expenses, divided by the units outstanding. That is 512 plus 8 less 20, or ₹500 crore, over 5 crore units, giving ₹100 a unit.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A scheme's investments have a market value of ₹512 crore. It holds other assets of ₹8 crore, and its liabilities and accrued expenses come to ₹20 crore. There are 5 crore units outstanding.

items.stem: What are the option's intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹8 and time value ₹20
options.misconception: computes both correctly and then swaps them over
options.why: The two numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. Intrinsic value is what the option is worth if exercised now, 250 less 230, or ₹20. Time value is the balance of the premium, ₹8. Reading it the other way says an option ₹20 in the money is worth only ₹8 today.

options.text: Intrinsic value nil and time value ₹28
options.misconception: applies the call's rule to a put, taking spot minus strike and flooring the negative at zero
options.why: Spot minus strike is the CALL's intrinsic value, and 230 less 250 is negative, which is how this reaches nil. For a put it is the other way round — strike minus spot — because a put holder sells at the strike and buys at the spot. The put is in the money by ₹20.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹20 and time value ₹8
options.why: A put's intrinsic value is the excess of the strike over the spot, so 250 less 230 is ₹20. The premium is intrinsic value plus time value, so whatever is left of the ₹28 after the ₹20 is time value, which is ₹8.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹28 and time value nil
options.misconception: treats the whole premium as intrinsic value, leaving nothing for the time still to run
options.why: The premium is ₹28 but the intrinsic value is only what could be captured by exercising today, which is 250 less 230, or ₹20. The remaining ₹8 is time value — what a buyer pays for the chance that the share falls further before expiry. Time value is nil only at expiry.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A put option on a share has a strike price of ₹250. The share trades at ₹230 and the put's premium is ₹28.

items.stem: Which risk does adding more securities to a portfolio NOT remove?

options.text: Unsystematic risk, the part specific to individual securities
options.misconception: names the risk diversification exists to remove as the one it cannot touch
options.why: Unsystematic risk is exactly what diversification does remove. It is company-specific — a strike, a lost contract, a product recall — and across enough holdings these events offset one another. The part that survives is systematic risk, and that is why the market pays a premium for bearing it and not for the other.

options.text: Systematic risk, the market-wide part that beta measures
options.why: Diversification removes unsystematic risk, the part specific to individual securities, because one company's bad news is offset by another's good news. What is left in a well-diversified portfolio is systematic risk — interest rates, inflation, the economy — which strikes every security at once. Beta measures it, and no number of holdings reduces it.

options.text: Neither, since risk is a matter of the individual securities chosen rather than of their number
options.misconception: denies the diversification effect entirely, when the number of holdings is what removes the specific risk
options.why: The number of holdings is precisely what does the work on one of the two kinds. Adding securities whose fortunes are not perfectly linked reduces unsystematic risk without reducing expected return, which is the nearest thing to a free lunch in finance. It leaves systematic risk untouched.

options.text: Both, since a large enough portfolio carries almost no risk at all
options.misconception: reads diversification as removing risk altogether rather than removing one kind of it
options.why: A portfolio of every share on the exchange is still exposed to the market falling. Diversification removes unsystematic risk and stops there; systematic risk is the floor it cannot go below. A portfolio with almost no risk at all is one holding treasury bills, not one holding a great many shares.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.stem: What does that figure say?

options.text: There is a 99 per cent chance the bank loses ₹40 lakh tomorrow
options.misconception: attaches the confidence level to the loss happening rather than to the loss not being exceeded
options.why: The confidence level runs the other way. Ninety-nine per cent is the probability that the loss will NOT exceed ₹40 lakh, leaving one per cent that it will. Reading it as a ninety-nine per cent chance of losing that much would make an ordinary trading day a catastrophe.

options.text: The bank cannot lose more than ₹40 lakh in a day
options.misconception: reads a confidence level as a hard ceiling on the loss
options.why: Ninety-nine per cent is a confidence level, not a guarantee. One day in a hundred is expected to breach the figure, and on such a day the loss can be several times ₹40 lakh, because Value at Risk says nothing about the size of the losses beyond it. That is the reason expected shortfall is reported beside it.

options.text: The bank expects to lose ₹40 lakh on an average day
options.misconception: reads a tail measure as an average, when it marks the edge of the distribution rather than its middle
options.why: ₹40 lakh is the edge of the distribution, not its middle. It is the loss that should be exceeded on only one day in a hundred, so on an ordinary day the outcome is nowhere near it and may well be a profit. An average daily loss is a different statistic entirely.

options.text: On about one trading day in a hundred the loss should exceed ₹40 lakh, and it says nothing about how large that loss would be
options.why: Value at Risk states the largest loss expected over a stated horizon at a stated confidence. Ninety-nine per cent confidence leaves one day in a hundred outside the figure, so on roughly one trading day in a hundred the loss should be more than ₹40 lakh. How much more is the measure's famous blind spot — it marks where the tail begins and is silent about what is in it.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A bank reports a one-day Value at Risk of ₹40 lakh at 99 per cent confidence on its trading book.

items.stem: What is the value of the share?

options.misconception: leaves growth out of the denominator while putting it into the dividend
options.why: 4.20 over 0.12 gives ₹35.00, which discounts a growing stream as though it were flat. Growth belongs in the denominator too — it reduces the effective discount rate to 0.07, because part of the return comes as the dividend rises rather than as cash today. Dropping it here nearly halves the value.

The model runs on next year's dividend, so 4 grown at 5 per cent is ₹4.20. Value is that dividend divided by the excess of the required return over the growth rate, or 4.20 over 0.12 less 0.05. That is 4.20 over 0.07, which is ₹60.00.

options.misconception: uses the dividend just paid instead of the one expected next year
options.why: 4.00 over 0.07 gives ₹57.14. The dividend of ₹4 has already been paid, so a buyer today does not receive it. The model discounts the dividends still to come, and the first of those is 4 grown at 5 per cent, or ₹4.20. Using the dividend just paid understates the share by ₹2.86.

options.misconception: adds the growth rate to the required return instead of subtracting it
options.why: 4.20 over 0.17 gives ₹24.71. The sign is wrong. Growth makes a share worth MORE, not less, so it comes off the required return in the denominator rather than being added to it. The correct denominator is 0.12 less 0.05.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company has just paid a dividend of ₹4 a share. Dividends are expected to grow at 5 per cent a year indefinitely and the required return on the share is 12 per cent.

items.stem: What return does CAPM require on the share?

options.text: 19.2 per cent
options.misconception: multiplies beta by the whole market return instead of by the market risk premium
options.why: 6 plus 1.2 times 11 gives 19.2 per cent, and it charges for the risk-free rate twice — once on its own and again inside the market return. Beta scales only the PREMIUM for bearing market risk, which is 11 less 6, or 5 per cent.

options.text: 11.0 per cent
options.misconception: takes the market's own expected return, ignoring that this share's beta is not one
options.why: 11 per cent is what CAPM requires of a share with a beta of exactly 1. This share has a beta of 1.2, so it moves more than the market does and investors want more for holding it. The extra is 0.2 times the 5 per cent market risk premium, or 1 per cent, taking the required return to 12.

options.text: 12.0 per cent
options.why: The required return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. The market risk premium is the market return less the risk-free rate, 11 less 6, or 5 per cent. So 6 plus 1.2 times 5 is 6 plus 6, which is 12.0 per cent.

options.text: 10.2 per cent
options.misconception: divides the market risk premium by beta instead of multiplying by it
options.why: 6 plus 5 over 1.2 gives about 10.2 per cent, which makes a riskier share look like it needs LESS return than the market. Beta multiplies the market risk premium — a beta above one raises the required return, a beta below one lowers it.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: The risk-free rate is 6 per cent, the expected return on the market is 11 per cent, and a share has a beta of 1.2.

items.stem: What is the weighted average cost of capital?

options.text: 11.8 per cent
options.why: Debt's after-tax cost is 10 times 1 less 0.30, or 7 per cent, because the interest is deductible. The market-value weights are 600 over 1,000 and 400 over 1,000, so 0.6 and 0.4. The weighted average cost of capital is 0.6 times 15 plus 0.4 times 7, which is 9 plus 2.8, or 11.8 per cent.

options.text: 11.0 per cent
options.misconception: takes a simple average of the two costs, giving each source the same weight
options.why: 15 plus 7 over 2 gives 11.0 per cent. A simple average would only be right if the company had equal amounts of each. It has ₹600 lakh of equity against ₹400 lakh of debt, so the dearer source carries more of the weight. Weighting properly gives 11.8 per cent.

options.text: 13.0 per cent
options.misconception: uses debt's quoted pre-tax rate, ignoring the tax shield on interest
options.why: 0.6 times 15 plus 0.4 times 10 gives 13.0 per cent. Interest is deductible, so a rupee of interest costs the company only 70 paise once tax relief is counted. The after-tax cost of debt is 7 per cent, and using the pre-tax rate overstates the discount rate by 1.2 percentage points.

options.text: 10.2 per cent
options.misconception: applies each weight to the wrong source, costing the larger block at the cheaper rate
options.why: 0.4 times 15 plus 0.6 times 7 gives 10.2 per cent. The weights have been swapped, so the ₹600 lakh of equity is treated as the smaller block and the ₹400 lakh of debt as the larger. Each cost goes with its own market value — equity at 0.6, debt at 0.4.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company's equity has a market value of ₹600 lakh and costs 15 per cent. Its debt has a market value of ₹400 lakh and carries a pre-tax cost of 10 per cent. The tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What growth rate can it sustain from its own profits?

options.text: 10.8 per cent
options.why: Sustainable growth is the retention ratio times the return on equity. Paying out 40 per cent means retaining 60 per cent, so the retention ratio is 0.60. Multiplying by the 18 per cent return on equity gives 10.8 per cent — the money kept back, multiplied by what that kept-back money earns.

options.text: 18 per cent
options.misconception: reads the return on equity itself as the growth rate, forgetting that a dividend leaves the company
options.why: 18 per cent is what the equity earns, not what the company grows at. A firm grows at its return on equity only if it pays no dividend at all and reinvests every rupee. Paying out 40 per cent leaves 60 per cent to reinvest, so growth is 0.60 times 18, or 10.8 per cent.

options.text: 60 per cent
options.misconception: reports the retention ratio itself as the growth rate, with no reference to what the retained money earns
options.why: 60 per cent is the retention ratio, a share of profit rather than a rate of growth. Retained money grows the company only at the rate it earns, so the retention ratio has to be multiplied by the return on equity. 0.60 times 18 per cent is 10.8 per cent.

options.text: 7.2 per cent
options.misconception: uses the payout ratio in place of the retention ratio, so a generous dividend appears to fund growth
options.why: 0.40 times 18 gives 7.2 per cent, and it grows the company on the money it has just handed to shareholders. Only the profit RETAINED is available to invest, which is 60 per cent here. Using the payout ratio inverts the relationship — it would say the more a company pays out, the faster it grows.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company earns a return on equity of 18 per cent and pays out 40 per cent of its profit as dividend.

items.stem: What is its economic value added?

options.text: 16 per cent
options.misconception: answers with the return on capital, a rate, where the measure asked for is an amount of value
options.why: 240 over 1,500 is 16 per cent, the return on capital. It is a useful check — 16 per cent beats the 12 per cent weighted average cost of capital, so value has been added — but it is not the measure. Economic value added is stated in rupees, and it is the 4 per cent gap applied to ₹1,500 lakh, or ₹60 lakh.

options.text: ₹180 lakh
options.misconception: reports the capital charge as though it were the answer
options.why: ₹180 lakh is the capital charge, 1,500 times 12 per cent, not the value added. It is the amount that has to be SUBTRACTED from the ₹240 lakh of profit. What is left, ₹60 lakh, is the surplus over what the providers of capital required.

options.text: ₹240 lakh
options.misconception: reports the operating profit itself, never charging for the capital that produced it
options.why: ₹240 lakh is the net operating profit after tax before any charge for capital, and it is exactly the number economic value added exists to correct. Equity is not free — shareholders could have put ₹1,500 lakh elsewhere — so the ₹180 lakh cost of that capital comes off before anything is called value added.

options.text: ₹60 lakh
options.why: Economic value added is net operating profit after tax less a charge for all the capital that earned it. The capital charge is 1,500 times 12 per cent, or ₹180 lakh, so the value added is 240 less 180, which is ₹60 lakh. Positive, so the company earned more than its capital cost.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company earned net operating profit after tax of ₹240 lakh on capital employed of ₹1,500 lakh. Its weighted average cost of capital is 12 per cent.

items.stem: What are the fund's Sharpe and Treynor measures?

options.text: Sharpe 0.50 and Treynor 0.50
options.misconception: computes Treynor on total risk as well, so the two measures can never disagree
options.why: Using the standard deviation in both gives 0.50 twice, and it throws away the whole reason for having two measures. Treynor's denominator is beta, the systematic risk a diversified investor cannot escape. Where the two measures rank funds differently, the fund is carrying diversifiable risk the market does not pay for — and that signal disappears if both use the same denominator.

options.text: Sharpe 5.00 and Treynor 0.50
options.misconception: swaps the two denominators, dividing by beta for Sharpe and by standard deviation for Treynor
options.why: The excess return of 8 is right and the denominators are the wrong way round. Sharpe uses total risk, the standard deviation, so 8 over 16 is 0.50. Treynor uses systematic risk, the beta, so 8 over 1.6 is 5.00. The names go with the risk each one prices.

options.text: Sharpe 0.875 and Treynor 8.75
options.misconception: divides the raw return by the risk measure without first taking off the risk-free rate
options.why: 14 over 16 and 14 over 1.6 give these two. Both measures reward a fund for the return it earned ABOVE what a treasury bill would have paid, so the risk-free rate of 6 comes off the top first. Leaving it in credits the fund with a return anyone could have had without taking any risk.

options.text: Sharpe 0.50 and Treynor 5.00
options.why: Both measures start from the same excess return, 14 less the risk-free rate of 6, which is 8. Sharpe divides that by total risk, the standard deviation of 16, giving 0.50. Treynor divides the same 8 by systematic risk, the beta of 1.6, giving 5.00.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: A fund returned 14 per cent over the year. The risk-free rate was 6 per cent, the fund's standard deviation was 16 per cent and its beta was 1.6.

items.stem: What is its current yield, and how does it sit against the coupon rate?

options.text: 9 per cent, the same as the coupon rate
options.misconception: divides the coupon by face value, which simply restates the coupon rate
options.why: ₹9 over ₹100 of face value is 9 per cent, and it is the coupon rate rather than a yield. Nobody can buy this bond for ₹100 — the market asks ₹120 — so the return on money actually put in is ₹9 over ₹120, or 7.5 per cent. Current yield uses the price paid, not the face value.

options.text: 13.3 per cent
options.misconception: inverts the fraction, dividing the price by the coupon
options.why: 120 over 9 is 13.3, which is a number of years' purchase and not a yield at all. A yield is income over the money invested, so the coupon sits on top and the price underneath. ₹9 over ₹120 is 7.5 per cent.

options.text: 7.5 per cent, with the yield to maturity higher still
options.misconception: applies the below-par ordering to a bond trading above par, where the pull to redemption works the other way
options.why: The 7.5 per cent is right and the ordering is upside down. For a bond bought at ₹120 and redeemed at ₹100, the investor loses ₹20 of capital by maturity, so the yield to maturity is BELOW the current yield. Above par the order runs coupon rate, then current yield, then yield to maturity — the reverse of the discount-bond case.

options.text: 7.5 per cent, below the coupon rate of 9 per cent
options.why: Current yield is the annual coupon divided by the bond's MARKET PRICE, so ₹9 over ₹120 is 7.5 per cent. The bond trades above par, so an investor pays ₹120 to collect ₹9 a year, and the yield he actually earns on his money is below the coupon rate of 9 per cent printed on the paper.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond has a face value of ₹100 and a coupon rate of 9 per cent. It trades in the market at ₹120.

items.stem: Under interest rate parity, which currency stands at a forward discount?

options.text: The rupee, but at a forward premium, because a higher return makes a currency worth more forward
options.misconception: reverses the parity relation, treating the higher-yielding currency as the one that strengthens forward
options.why: It works the other way, and it has to. If the rupee paid 8 per cent AND strengthened forward, an investor could borrow dollars at 3 per cent, hold rupees, and sell the proceeds forward for a certain profit.
