The forward discount on the higher-interest currency is exactly what closes that gap.

options.text: The rupee, being the higher-interest currency, so the forward price of a dollar is above the spot
options.why: Under interest rate parity the currency with the higher interest rate stands at a forward discount, by the interest differential. The rupee rate is 8 per cent against 3 per cent, so the rupee is the higher-interest currency and it is the one at a forward discount. Quoting rupees per dollar, that means the forward rate is above the spot.

options.text: The rupee, because Indian inflation is higher than American inflation
options.misconception: answers with purchasing power parity, which works from inflation and predicts a future spot, not from interest rates
options.why: The conclusion is right and the reasoning belongs to a different relation. Purchasing power parity works from expected inflation and predicts a FUTURE SPOT rate. Interest rate parity works from interest rates and binds today's forward rate, and it is the one that answers this question. The scenario gives interest rates and no inflation figures at all.

options.text: Neither; the forward rate equals the spot rate, since parity means the two are the same
options.misconception: reads parity as equality of the rates rather than as the forward offsetting the interest differential
options.why: Parity does not mean the forward and the spot are equal. It means the forward is set so that the interest differential is exactly offset — borrow in one currency, deposit in the other, cover forward, and you end where you began. A forward equal to the spot would hand the dollar borrower a free 5 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year interest rates are 8 per cent in India and 3 per cent in the United States. The rupee-dollar spot rate is quoted as rupees per dollar.

items.stem: Is the partner right?

options.text: No — the auditor must obtain absolute assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement
options.misconception: overcorrects, replacing reasonable assurance with a level of assurance no audit can give
options.why: An audit is not capable of giving absolute assurance, which is why the standard sets the objective at reasonable assurance. The partner is wrong about the cost, not about the level of assurance.

options.text: Yes — the balance between benefit and cost is an inherent limitation of an audit, so cost alone justifies dropping the procedure
options.misconception: reads a limitation the standard describes as a permission the standard grants
options.why: The standard names the balance between benefit and cost to explain why an audit gives reasonable rather than absolute assurance. Naming a limitation is not granting a licence, and the same standard says so in the next breath.

options.text: No — where no alternative procedure exists, what it costs in time or money cannot on its own excuse leaving it out
options.why: The balance between benefit and cost is listed by SA 200 as an inherent limitation of an audit, and the same standard then shuts the door the partner wants: difficulty, time or cost is never on its own a reason to drop a procedure when there is no alternative to it, nor a reason to rest on evidence that is less than persuasive. High assurance comes from obtaining SAAE, not from what the work is priced at.

options.text: Yes, provided the partner documents the fee constraint in the audit file as the reason for the omission
options.misconception: treats documentation as a cure for an omission the standard does not permit
options.why: Writing down a reason does not make the reason good. Documenting an omission the standard does not permit records the breach; it does not authorise it.

citation.ref: the inherent limitations of an audit — timeliness of financial reporting and the balance between benefit and cost, read with the objective of obtaining reasonable assurance

items.scenario: A procedure on a material balance would take the team four extra days and the fee is already thin. There is no other procedure that would give evidence about the same assertion. The engagement partner says the standard recognises a balance between benefit and cost, so the procedure can be dropped.

items.stem: Before an engagement is accepted, SA 210 asks the auditor to get management to agree that it acknowledges, and understands, that three things are its own responsibility. Which three?

options.text: For the preparation of the financial statements; for the design of the audit programme; and for the fee being adequate to the scope of the work
options.misconception: hands management the auditor's own responsibility for designing the audit
options.why: Designing the audit is the auditor's work and can never be management's acknowledgement. Handing it over would make the auditor the reviewer of a programme the client wrote, and the fee is a matter of contract, not a precondition.

options.text: For the preparation of the financial statements; for internal control; and for accepting the auditor's opinion in whatever form it is finally expressed
options.misconception: asks management to bind itself in advance to the opinion, which is not a precondition but a limitation on the auditor
options.why: The opinion is formed at the end of the audit, on the evidence. Asking management to accept it in advance is not an acknowledgement of responsibility at all, and the third limb the standard actually requires is the access limb.
keywords: formed at the end of the audit

options.text: For preparing the financial statements under the applicable financial reporting framework; for such internal control as management determines is necessary to enable their preparation free from material misstatement; and to provide the auditor with access to all relevant information, any additional information he requests, and unrestricted access to persons within the entity
options.why: Those are the three limbs, in the standard's own order. The first fixes responsibility for the statements on management under the AFRF. The second fixes responsibility for such internal control as management determines is necessary. The third is the access limb — all relevant information, additional information the auditor requests, and unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence.
keywords: such internal control as management determines is necessary
unrestricted access to persons within the entity

options.text: For the preparation of the financial statements; for the detection of all frauds in the entity; and for the correctness of every accounting estimate
options.misconception: inflates management's acknowledgement into a guarantee no management could give
options.why: Management's responsibility is for prevention and detection of fraud, not for detecting all frauds, and an estimate is by nature uncertain. An acknowledgement drafted as a guarantee would be worthless as evidence.

citation.ref: para 6(b) — the three responsibilities management must acknowledge and understand for the preconditions for an audit to be present

items.stem: Which of these does SA 230 allow during the assembly of the final audit file?

options.text: The first three — a confirmation is evidence gathering rather than a conclusion, so it is administrative
options.misconception: splits procedure from conclusion and calls the procedure administrative
options.why: Performing a new audit procedure is the very thing the standard excludes, whether or not a conclusion follows from it. Evidence gathering after the report date is dealt with by the rule on additions to the file, which requires the reason, the date and the person to be documented.

options.text: The first two only — assembly is an administrative process that involves the performance of no new audit procedures and the drawing of no new conclusions
options.why: The assembly of the final audit file is an administrative process, and the standard says in terms that it does not involve the performance of new audit procedures or the drawing of new conclusions. Sorting, collating and cross-referencing working papers and signing off completion checklists are exactly the administrative changes it contemplates. A fresh confirmation and a rewritten conclusion are not administrative, and belong to the separate regime for documentation added after the date of the auditor's report.

options.text: None of them — nothing whatever may be touched once the auditor's report is dated
options.misconception: freezes the file at the report date and leaves the assembly period with nothing to do
options.why: The standard gives an assembly period and names the administrative changes that may be made in it. A rule that nothing may be touched would leave that period, and the examples in the standard, with no work to do.

options.text: All four — the file assembly period exists precisely so that outstanding work can be completed
options.misconception: treats the assembly window as extra time to finish the audit
options.why: The window is for putting the file in order, not for finishing the audit. The audit was complete on the date of the report; that is what allowed the report to be signed.
keywords: complete on the date of the report

citation.ref: the assembly of the final audit file as an administrative process, and the examples of administrative changes that may be made during it

items.scenario: Three weeks after the date of the auditor's report, and inside the file assembly period, a manager wants to make four changes to the audit file: sort and cross-reference the working papers, sign off the completion checklist, perform an additional confirmation procedure on a receivable that now looks doubtful, and rewrite the conclusion on that receivable.

items.stem: SA 240 says an auditor is likelier to miss a material misstatement caused by management fraud than one caused by employee fraud. Why?

options.text: Because management is frequently in a position to manipulate accounting records directly or indirectly, to present fraudulent financial information, or to override control procedures that otherwise appear to be operating effectively
options.why: The reason is position, not motive. Management is frequently in a position to manipulate accounting records directly or indirectly, to present fraudulent financial information, and to override control procedures that appear to be operating effectively — which is why the standard treats management override of controls as a risk present in every audit.

options.text: Because employee fraud is not a misstatement at all, being confined to misappropriation of assets
options.misconception: assumes misappropriation of assets cannot misstate the financial statements
options.why: Misappropriation of assets is one of the two types of fraud the standard is concerned with, precisely because it can cause a material misstatement — it is usually accompanied by false or misleading records concealing the theft.

options.text: Because management fraud is always larger in amount than employee fraud, so it crosses materiality more often
options.misconception: swaps a question about detection risk for a question about size
options.why: Size is not what the standard is talking about. The point is that the auditor is less likely to detect it, and that turns on management's position over the records and the controls, not on the rupees involved.

options.text: Because the auditor owes no duty to plan for management fraud, management being primarily responsible for prevention and detection
options.misconception: turns management's primary responsibility into an excuse for the auditor
options.why: Primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud does rest with management and those charged with governance, but that responsibility is theirs alongside the auditor's own duty to identify and assess the risks of material misstatement due to fraud.

citation.ref: para 7 — why fraud by management is likelier to escape the auditor's detection than fraud by an employee

items.stem: What does SA 260 (Revised) require of him?

options.text: To communicate those significant findings in writing to those charged with governance, and to include in the audit documentation the matters communicated orally and when and to whom they were communicated
options.why: The standard makes the form follow the judgment. Once the auditor's own professional judgment is that speaking would not be adequate, the significant findings from the audit go in writing to TCWG. Separately, where matters have been communicated orally, he shall include in the audit documentation the matters communicated and when and to whom they were communicated; where they were communicated in writing, he retains a copy.
keywords: when and to whom they were communicated

options.text: Nothing further — an oral communication at a meeting of the audit committee discharges the requirement in every case
options.misconception: ignores the auditor's own judgment on adequacy, which is what the standard turns on
options.why: The standard does not treat every oral communication as sufficient. It asks the auditor to judge adequacy, and where his judgment is that oral communication would not be adequate, writing is required.

options.text: To communicate the findings in writing to management instead, management being closer to the matters concerned
options.misconception: redirects to management a communication the standard directs at those charged with governance
options.why: Communicating with management does not relieve the auditor of communicating with those charged with governance. The two are different audiences with different responsibilities, and the standard keeps them apart.

options.text: To communicate every matter required by the standard in writing, oral communication never being permitted under SA 260 (Revised)
options.misconception: hardens a rule about significant findings into a bar on oral communication altogether
options.why: Oral communication is permitted, and much of the two-way communication the standard is built on happens that way. The written requirement attaches to significant findings where oral communication would not be adequate, and to independence for listed entities.

citation.ref: the communication process — the form of communication, the requirement to communicate significant findings in writing where oral communication would not be adequate, and the documentation of matters communicated orally

items.scenario: An engagement partner has communicated the significant findings from the audit to the audit committee at a meeting, orally, and judges that oral communication was not adequate in the circumstances.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) require instead?

options.text: A common engagement letter, but separate representation letters, management being asked to represent only on the areas each auditor audited
options.misconception: splits the representation letter along the work allocation, which the standard does not do
options.why: Management represents on the financial statements as a whole, not area by area. The standard asks for a common management representation letter for that reason.

options.text: A common engagement letter and a common management representation letter, and a work allocation document signed by all the joint auditors and communicated to those charged with governance
options.why: The standard requires the joint auditors to obtain a common engagement letter and a common management representation letter, so that the terms and the representations are the same for all of them. The division of work is not left informal either: the work allocation document is signed by all the joint auditors and communicated to TCWG, which is what makes each auditor's own allocation provable afterwards.

options.text: Nothing on any of these points — SA 299 (Revised) deals only with reporting, and planning is left to the joint auditors to arrange as they wish
options.misconception: confines the standard to its reporting paragraphs and ignores its planning requirements
options.why: The standard opens with planning: the audit plan and strategy are to be established by the joint auditors jointly, the division of audit areas and the common audit areas identified, and the allocation documented and communicated.

options.text: Separate engagement letters and separate representation letters, since a joint auditor answers only for the work that was allotted to him
options.misconception: reads the division of responsibility for audit work as a division of the engagement itself
options.why: Responsibility for allocated work is divided, but the engagement is one engagement over one set of financial statements. The standard therefore keeps the terms and the representations common even though the work is divided.

citation.ref: the requirement for a common engagement letter and a common management representation letter, and for the work allocation document to be signed by all the joint auditors and communicated to those charged with governance

items.scenario: Three firms are appointed joint auditors of a company. Each proposes to send its own engagement letter, obtain its own management representation letter, and keep the work allocation as an internal understanding between the three of them.

items.stem: In exercising judgment as to which of the assessed risks are significant risks, which of the following would SA 315 point to LEAST?

options.text: A risk of fraud
options.misconception: overlooks that whether the risk is a risk of fraud is the first matter the standard names
options.why: Whether the risk is a risk of fraud is the first of the matters the standard lists for this judgment, so it points strongly towards a significant risk rather than away from one.

options.text: A routine, non-complex transaction that is subject to systematic processing
options.why: Significant risks often relate to significant non-routine transactions or to matters of judgment, because both fall outside the ordinary run of processing. A routine, non-complex transaction that is subject to systematic processing is the opposite of that, and is the least likely of the four to give rise to a significant risk.

options.text: A significant transaction with a related party
options.misconception: treats a related party transaction as ordinary when the standard names it expressly
options.why: Whether the risk involves significant transactions with related parties is one of the named matters, which is why related party dealings attract special audit consideration.

options.text: A significant transaction that is outside the normal course of business for the entity, or otherwise appears unusual
options.misconception: reads an expressly named indicator as neutral
options.why: Whether the risk involves significant transactions that are outside the normal course of business, or that otherwise appear unusual, is another of the matters the standard names for this judgment.
keywords: outside the normal course of business

citation.ref: the matters the auditor considers in exercising judgment as to which of the assessed risks are significant risks

items.stem: What does SA 320 require the auditor to do?

options.text: Nothing — materiality for the financial statements as a whole governs every balance and disclosure without exception
options.misconception: treats one overall figure as the only materiality the standard allows
options.why: The standard expressly contemplates a lower materiality for particular items, precisely because a small misstatement in a sensitive disclosure can matter more to users than a large one elsewhere.

options.text: Reduce materiality for the financial statements as a whole to fifty thousand rupees, so that the sensitive disclosure is covered
options.misconception: drags the whole-statement figure down to the level of one sensitive item
options.why: Dropping the overall figure to the level of the most sensitive disclosure would multiply the work on every other balance for no gain. The standard's answer is a separate level for the particular item, not a new overall level.

options.text: Raise the matter with those charged with governance and let them fix the materiality level for the disclosure
options.misconception: hands a determination the standard gives the auditor to those charged with governance
options.why: Determining materiality is an exercise of the auditor's professional judgment. It is communicated where the standards require, but it is not set by the entity or by those charged with governance.

options.text: Determine a separate, lower materiality level to be applied to that particular class of transactions, account balance or disclosure
options.why: Where there are one or more particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures for which misstatements of lesser amounts than materiality for the financial statements as a whole could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users, the auditor shall also determine the materiality level to be applied to those particular items. He then sets performance materiality for them as well.

citation.ref: para 10 — materiality levels for particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures, read with the definition of performance materiality

items.scenario: Materiality for the financial statements as a whole has been set at forty lakh rupees. Directors' remuneration for the year is nine lakh rupees, and the auditor's view is that a misstatement of even fifty thousand rupees in that disclosure could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users, because the law requires it to be disclosed and users look at it closely.

items.stem: What does SA 330 say about the audit evidence to be obtained on the second engagement?

options.text: More persuasive audit evidence is required, because the higher the auditor's assessment of risk, the more persuasive the audit evidence he must obtain
options.why: The standard states the relation plainly: in designing the further audit procedures, the auditor shall obtain more persuasive audit evidence the higher his assessment of risk. That is achieved by changing the NTE of the procedures — their nature, timing and extent — for example by using a more reliable source or by increasing the sample.
keywords: the higher his assessment of risk

options.text: More evidence in quantity only, the standard being concerned with sufficiency rather than with the quality of what is obtained
options.misconception: reduces persuasiveness to sample size and drops the quality half of it
options.why: Persuasiveness has both halves in it. Obtaining more of a weak source does not make the evidence more persuasive, which is why the response to higher risk may be a change in the nature of the procedure rather than only in its extent.

options.text: The same evidence as on the first engagement, the standard requiring a consistent level of work across engagements
options.misconception: treats consistency of effort as the requirement, when the requirement is responsiveness to risk
options.why: The whole point of assessing risk is that the response varies with it. A level of work fixed in advance regardless of the assessment would make the risk assessment pointless.

options.text: Less evidence, because a high assessed risk means the auditor will qualify his opinion in any event
options.misconception: jumps from a high assessed risk straight to a modified opinion
options.why: A high assessed risk is a reason to do more work, not a conclusion that the statements are misstated. The opinion follows the evidence obtained; it does not replace the work of obtaining it.

citation.ref: para 7(b) — the auditor shall obtain more persuasive audit evidence the higher his assessment of risk

items.scenario: Two engagements are being planned. On the first, the risk of material misstatement in revenue is assessed as low. On the second, it is assessed as high.

items.stem: Which of the following does SA 450 require the audit documentation to include?

options.text: Only the misstatements that management refused to correct, corrected ones having left no trace in the financial statements
options.misconception: documents the argument rather than the population, losing the aggregate
options.why: The standard asks for all misstatements accumulated during the audit and whether they have been corrected. Dropping the corrected ones would hide how much was found, which is part of how the auditor evaluates the audit itself.

options.text: The performance materiality figure, which is the threshold below which misstatements need not be accumulated
options.misconception: puts performance materiality where the clearly trivial threshold belongs
options.why: Performance materiality is a planning figure used to set the extent of procedures. The accumulation threshold is clearly trivial, a much smaller amount, and it is that amount the documentation must record.

options.text: The amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial; all misstatements accumulated during the audit and whether they have been corrected; and the auditor's conclusion on whether uncorrected misstatements are material, with the basis for that conclusion
options.why: Those are the three documentation requirements of the standard, and they map onto its three jobs. The amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial records the accumulation threshold. All misstatements accumulated during the audit and whether they have been corrected records what was found. The auditor's conclusion on whether uncorrected misstatements are material, individually or in aggregate, and the basis for that conclusion, records the judgment made at the end.

options.text: Only the auditor's final conclusion, the working papers behind it being a matter for the firm's own quality control policies
options.misconception: leaves the conclusion standing without the record that supports it
options.why: A conclusion with no record of the threshold used or the misstatements found cannot be re-performed or reviewed. The standard names all three items for that reason.

citation.ref: the documentation requirement — the amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial, the misstatements accumulated during the audit, and the auditor's conclusion on uncorrected misstatements

items.stem: Does that answer the problem?

options.text: Yes — sufficiency is the measure of quantity, so a larger sample makes the evidence sufficient and therefore appropriate
options.misconception: treats sufficiency as producing appropriateness, when the two are separate measures
options.why: Sufficiency measures quantity and appropriateness measures quality. Making evidence sufficient does not make it appropriate; a large quantity of unreliable evidence is still unreliable.

options.text: No — audit evidence generated internally by the entity can never be used, whatever its quality
options.misconception: converts a point about relative reliability into an absolute bar on internal evidence
options.why: Internal evidence is used in every audit, and its reliability rises where the entity's related controls are effective. The problem here is the specific doubt about these photocopies, not a general bar.

options.text: No — merely obtaining more audit evidence does not compensate for its poor quality
options.why: Sufficiency and appropriateness are interrelated but they are not interchangeable. Merely obtaining more audit evidence does not compensate for its poor quality, so doubling a sample of a source whose reliability is in doubt gives more of the same doubt. The response to a quality problem is a change in the nature of the procedure — a more reliable source — not in its extent alone.

options.text: Yes, provided the manager documents in the file that the sample was doubled because of the doubt about reliability
options.misconception: substitutes a note about the problem for a response to it
options.why: Recording the doubt is not resolving it. The file would then show that the auditor knew the source was doubtful and did nothing about the doubt except count more of it.

citation.ref: the interrelationship between the sufficiency and the appropriateness of audit evidence — more evidence does not compensate for poor quality

items.scenario: A team's only evidence over a material expense is a set of photocopied internal vouchers whose reliability the manager doubts. He proposes to double the sample, from forty vouchers to eighty, and to conclude on that basis.

items.stem: When the auditor attends the physical inventory counting, SA 501 requires him to do four things. Which set is right?

options.text: Evaluate management's instructions, observe the count, inspect the inventory, and value the closing stock at net realisable value
options.misconception: adds a valuation step to a requirement aimed at existence and condition
options.why: Attendance under this requirement is directed at the existence and condition of inventory. Valuation is tested by separate procedures, and is not one of the four things attendance itself is for.

options.text: Count the entire inventory himself, agree it to the ledger, sign the count sheets and take custody of them until the audit is complete
options.misconception: makes the auditor the counter, when the count is management's procedure and the auditor's job is to test it
options.why: The count is management's, and the auditor attends to observe and test it. A full count by the auditor would substitute his work for management's responsibility and still tell him nothing about how the entity's own count procedures operate.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the inventory exists and is in good condition, attendance being one way of doing that
options.misconception: replaces a required procedure with a representation
options.why: A written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it covers. Where inventory is material, attendance is the procedure and the representation cannot stand in for it.

options.text: Evaluate the instructions and procedures management has laid down for recording and controlling the count; observe the performance of management's count procedures; inspect the inventory; and perform test counts
options.why: Those four are the standard's own list for attendance. He evaluates management's instructions and procedures, observes the performance of management's count procedures, inspects the inventory — which is how obsolete or damaged items are identified — and performs test counts, tracing items from the physical inventory to management's count records and from those records back to the floor.

citation.ref: para 4(a) — attendance at physical inventory counting, unless impracticable, and the four things the auditor does while attending

items.stem: Why does SA 505 treat negative confirmations as providing less persuasive audit evidence than positive confirmations?

options.text: Because a failure to receive a response does not explicitly indicate that the intended confirming party received the request, or that he verified the accuracy of the information in it
options.why: Silence is the whole of a negative confirmation's evidence, and silence is ambiguous. A failure to receive a response does not explicitly indicate that the intended confirming party received the request, nor that he verified the accuracy of the information in it — the letter may never have arrived, or may have been ignored. That is why the standard bars negative confirmations as the sole substantive procedure unless every one of its conditions is met.

options.text: Because negative confirmations may be used only where the population is small and made up of large individual balances
options.misconception: reverses the population condition the standard actually sets
options.why: The standard points the other way: one of its conditions is that the population comprises a large number of small, homogeneous account balances, transactions or conditions.

options.text: Because a negative confirmation is a response from the entity itself rather than from a third party
options.misconception: confuses who sends the reply, which is a third party in both forms of confirmation
options.why: Both forms of confirmation are direct written responses to the auditor from a third party. What differs is only whether the party is asked to reply in every case or only on disagreement.

options.text: Because the auditor may not perform alternative procedures where a negative confirmation is used
options.misconception: invents a bar on alternative procedures that the standard does not impose
options.why: Nothing in the standard prevents alternative procedures. The weakness of the negative form lies in what a non-response proves, not in what the auditor is allowed to do next.

citation.ref: the characteristics of negative confirmation requests and the conditions for using them as the sole substantive audit procedure

items.stem: What does SA 570 (Revised) require of the auditor's report?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" drawing attention to the absence of the note
options.misconception: uses the section built for adequate disclosure where there is no disclosure to point at
options.why: That section exists to draw attention to a disclosure management has actually made. With no note in the financial statements there is nothing for it to refer to, and the deficiency is a misstatement rather than an emphasis.
keywords: a disclosure management has actually made

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, the auditor being unable to satisfy himself about the outcome of the uncertainty
options.misconception: treats an inherent uncertainty about the future as an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: A disclaimer is for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Here the auditor has the evidence — he knows the uncertainty exists and that it has not been disclosed — so the problem is a misstatement, not a limitation on scope.

options.text: A qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate, and a statement in the Basis for Qualified or Basis for Adverse Opinion section that a material uncertainty exists — one casting significant doubt on whether the entity can continue as a going concern
options.why: Where adequate disclosure about the material uncertainty is not made, the standard requires a qualified or adverse opinion, as appropriate, and the Basis for Qualified or Basis for Adverse Opinion section must then say that a material uncertainty exists — one casting significant doubt on whether the entity can continue as a going concern. The missing disclosure is a misstatement of the financial statements, so it is the opinion that moves.

options.text: An adverse opinion in every case, because a going concern uncertainty is by nature pervasive
options.misconception: fixes the modification at adverse and removes the auditor's judgment on pervasiveness
options.why: The standard leaves the choice between qualified and adverse to the auditor's judgment on whether the effects are pervasive. Treating every such case as adverse would collapse two modifications into one.

citation.ref: para 23 — the auditor's report where adequate disclosure about a material uncertainty is not made in the financial statements

items.scenario: The going concern basis is appropriate, but a material uncertainty exists — there is real doubt about whether the company can carry on as a going concern. Management refuses to make any disclosure about it in the notes.

items.stem: What does SA 580 require instead?

options.text: Covering only the last quarter is acceptable, since the current management cannot represent about a period before it took charge
options.misconception: lets a change of management shrink the period the representations cover
options.why: Current management is responsible for the financial statements as a whole, whatever period it personally supervised. The standard says in terms that this fact does not diminish its responsibilities, and the requirement still applies.

options.text: Neither point matters, because written representations are not audit evidence at all
options.misconception: denies representations the status of evidence, when the standard makes them necessary evidence
options.why: Written representations are audit evidence, and necessary evidence at that. What they are not is sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about the matters they cover.

options.text: The letter must carry a date as close to the audit report as the work allows and never later than it, and must cover every financial statement and period that report deals with
options.why: Both halves of the proposal are wrong. On timing, the written representations must be dated as close to the signing as the work allows and plainly not after, the date of the auditor's report, because written representations are necessary audit evidence and a report cannot be dated before the evidence behind it exists. On coverage, the representations must reach all the financial statements and periods that report deals with; a change of management does not diminish responsibility for the financial statements as a whole.
keywords: not after, the date of the auditor's report
all the financial statements and periods

options.text: Dating one week after the report is acceptable, provided the partner records the reason in the audit file
options.misconception: allows evidence to be obtained after the report it supports, with a note in place of the rule
options.why: The report is dated once the auditor has obtained the evidence on which the opinion rests. A representation obtained afterwards was not evidence for that opinion, and no file note can change the order of the two dates.
keywords: the order of the two dates

citation.ref: para 14 — the date of the written representations and the period or periods they must cover

items.scenario: An engagement partner proposes to date the management representation letter one week after the date of his audit report, and to have it cover only the last quarter of the year, that being the period in which the current management took charge.

items.stem: What does SA 600 require the principal auditor to do?

options.text: Nothing — having stated the division of responsibility in his report, the principal auditor is insulated from the other auditor's findings
options.misconception: reads the division of responsibility as immunity from what the other auditor actually found
options.why: The division of responsibility governs responsibility for the other auditor's work. It does not stop the principal auditor from having to evaluate what that work found, because the component's numbers are inside the statements he is reporting on.

options.text: Re-audit the component's inventory himself, the other auditor's qualification having destroyed the reliability of his work
options.misconception: treats a modified report as evidence that the other auditor's work was defective
options.why: A qualification is the other auditor reporting properly on what he found, not a failure of his work. Nothing about it requires the principal auditor to repeat the audit of the component.

options.text: Modify his own report in every case, a qualification anywhere in the group carrying through automatically
options.misconception: makes the carry-through automatic and removes the judgment on significance
options.why: The standard asks for a judgment on nature and significance in relation to the financial statements being reported on. An automatic carry-through would qualify a group opinion for a matter trivial at that level.
keywords: a judgment on nature and significance

options.text: Weigh the modification's nature and significance against the financial statements he is himself reporting on, decide whether his own report must be modified too, and document how he dealt with it
options.why: Where the other auditor issues a modified report, the principal auditor weighs that modification's nature and significance against the financial statements of the entity he is himself reporting on, and asks whether it forces a modification of his own report. He also documents how he has dealt with the qualification in framing his report. A component qualification that is immaterial to the whole may leave his own opinion untouched; one that is not, will not.
keywords: a modification of his own report
documents how he has dealt with

citation.ref: the principal auditor's reporting considerations where the other auditor issues a modified report, and the related documentation requirement

items.scenario: The auditor of a component sends the principal auditor a report carrying a qualification on the component's inventory valuation. The principal auditor's assistant says the qualification is the other auditor's business alone and can simply be filed.

items.stem: Which of the following must the Opinion section of the auditor's report contain under SA 700 (Revised)?

options.text: A description of management's responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements
options.misconception: moves the responsibilities section into the opinion
options.why: Management's responsibilities have their own section further down the report. The Opinion section identifies what was audited and states the opinion; it does not describe anyone's responsibilities.

options.text: A description of the key audit matters determined for the current period
options.misconception: folds the Key Audit Matters section into the Opinion section
options.why: Key audit matters are communicated in their own section, placed after the Basis for Opinion section. They are not a substitute for the opinion and are not part of it.
keywords: not a substitute for the opinion

options.text: Identification of the entity whose financial statements have been audited, a statement that they have been audited, identification of the title of each statement comprising them, reference to the notes including the summary of significant accounting policies, and the date of or period covered by each statement
options.why: Those five are what the Opinion section must do before it states the opinion itself. It must identify the entity whose financial statements have been audited, state that the financial statements have been audited, identify the title of each statement making them up, point the reader at the notes including the summary of significant accounting policies, then specify the date of or period covered by each statement.
keywords: the notes including the summary of significant accounting policies
the date of or period covered

options.text: A statement that the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and that the auditor is independent of the entity
options.misconception: puts into the Opinion section two statements that belong to the Basis for Opinion section
options.why: Both of those belong to the Basis for Opinion section, which directly follows the Opinion section. Keeping them apart is what lets a reader see the opinion first and the reasons for it immediately after.

citation.ref: para 24 — the contents of the Opinion section of the auditor's report

items.stem: Does he communicate them in his report?

options.text: No — the auditor is prohibited from communicating key audit matters when he disclaims an opinion, unless he is required by law or regulation to do so
options.why: The prohibition is express. Where the auditor disclaims an opinion, he shall not communicate key audit matters unless he is required by law or regulation to do so. Reporting matters as having been of most significance would suggest the financial statements are more credible than a disclaimer allows, which is the opposite of what a disclaimer says.
keywords: unless he is required by law or regulation

options.text: No — key audit matters are never reported by any auditor once the opinion is modified in any way
options.misconception: extends a prohibition attached to a disclaimer to every modified opinion
options.why: A qualified or adverse opinion does not stop key audit matters being communicated; the prohibition attaches to a disclaimer of opinion alone.

options.text: Yes — the entity is listed, and key audit matters are required in every audit of a listed entity without exception
options.misconception: applies the listed-entity rule as if nothing could displace it
options.why: The listed-entity requirement is the general rule, and the disclaimer case is the express exception to it. A rule with a stated exception is not a rule without exception.

options.text: Yes, because key audit matters are how the auditor explains why he could not obtain the evidence
options.misconception: uses the key audit matters section to do the work of the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section
options.why: The reasons for a disclaimer belong in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section. Key audit matters are not a substitute for a modification required by SA 705 (Revised) and never carry the explanation for one.

citation.ref: the prohibition on communicating key audit matters where the auditor disclaims an opinion, unless required by law or regulation

items.scenario: An auditor of a listed company concludes that he cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on several material matters and disclaims an opinion. He has three matters he had intended to report as key audit matters, and no law or regulation requires him to communicate them.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require the Opinion section of his report to be headed, and what wording does it take?

options.text: Headed "Qualified Opinion", stating that except for the possible effects of the matters described, the financial statements present a true and fair view
options.misconception: uses the qualified wording where the effects are pervasive, and uses the possible-effects form where evidence was obtained
options.why: A qualification is for misstatements that are material but not pervasive, and "except for the possible effects" is the form used where the auditor was unable to obtain evidence. Neither fits a case where the evidence was obtained and the effects are pervasive.

options.text: Headed "Adverse Opinion", stating that because of the significance of the matters set out in the Basis for Adverse Opinion section, the financial statements do not present a true and fair view or do not give a true and fair view
options.why: Each modification carries its own heading and its own form of words. For an adverse opinion the section is headed "Adverse Opinion" and states that, because of the significance of the matters set out in the Basis for Adverse Opinion section, the financial statements do not present a true and fair view or do not give a true and fair view in accordance with the AFRF. The basis section immediately below takes the matching heading.
keywords: because of the significance of the matters
do not present a true and fair view

options.text: Headed "Disclaimer of Opinion", stating that the auditor does not express an opinion on the financial statements
options.misconception: uses the disclaimer, which belongs to an inability to obtain evidence, where the evidence was obtained
options.why: A disclaimer is for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence whose possible effects are material and pervasive. Here the auditor obtained his evidence and knows the statements are misstated, so he must say so.

options.text: Headed "Opinion", with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the misstatements
options.misconception: uses an emphasis paragraph in place of the modification the circumstances require
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph points at something already appropriately presented or disclosed in the statements themselves, and it is never a substitute for the modified opinion SA 705 (Revised) requires.

citation.ref: the form and content of the report when the opinion is modified — the heading and wording of the Opinion section for an adverse opinion and the matching Basis for Adverse Opinion section

items.scenario: An auditor has obtained the evidence he needs and concludes that misstatements in the financial statements are both material and pervasive.

items.stem: Under SA 706 (Revised), an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is NOT a substitute for which of the following?

options.text: Communication with those charged with governance under SA 260 (Revised)
options.misconception: names a communication the standard actually requires alongside an emphasis paragraph, not one it could replace
options.why: Where the auditor expects to include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph he must communicate that expectation and the proposed wording to those charged with governance. The two go together; the paragraph was never offered as a substitute for that communication.

options.text: Disclosures required by the applicable financial reporting framework, reporting under SA 570 (Revised) where a material uncertainty related to going concern exists, and a modified opinion required by SA 705 (Revised)
options.why: The standard names all three. An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not a substitute for disclosures the AFRF requires management to make, nor for the reporting SA 570 (Revised) requires where a material uncertainty related to going concern exists, nor for a modified opinion where the circumstances of SA 705 (Revised) apply. Each of those is a requirement in its own right, and an emphasis paragraph adds to them rather than replacing any of them.
keywords: material uncertainty related to going concern

options.text: The auditor's responsibilities section of the report
options.misconception: picks a standing section of every report that no paragraph was ever proposed to replace
options.why: The auditor's responsibilities section appears in every report as a matter of course. Nothing in the standard suggests an emphasis paragraph could stand in for it, so it is not one of the three the standard is guarding against.
keywords: the three the standard is guarding against

options.text: The audit documentation supporting the matter emphasised
options.misconception: confuses what appears in the report with what is kept in the file
options.why: Documentation is kept in the audit file and is never something a paragraph in the report could replace. The three substitutions the standard warns against are all things that would otherwise appear in the report or in the financial statements.

citation.ref: an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not a substitute for disclosures required by the framework, for reporting under SA 570 (Revised), or for a modified opinion under SA 705 (Revised)

items.stem: What does SA 720 (Revised) require the auditor's report to do?

options.text: Describe the uncorrected material misstatement of the other information in the Other Information section of the report, the opinion on the financial statements being unaffected
options.why: Where the auditor concludes that an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information exists, he describes it in the Other Information section of his report. The financial statements are not misstated here, so the opinion on the financial statements is unaffected — which is exactly why the standard gives the other information a section of its own rather than routing it through the opinion.

options.text: Add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the inconsistency
options.misconception: uses an emphasis paragraph for a matter that is not appropriately presented anywhere
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph draws the eye to something already appropriately presented, or disclosed, where the statements themselves put it. An uncorrected misstatement in the other information is neither appropriately presented nor inside the financial statements.

options.text: Say nothing in the report, the other information being outside the scope of the audit
options.misconception: treats other information as beyond the report because it is beyond the opinion
options.why: The other information is not audited, but the standard gives the auditor duties to read it, to consider it, and to report on it in a section of its own. Silence is not one of the available responses once he has concluded a material misstatement exists.

options.text: Qualify the opinion on the financial statements, a material inconsistency being a misstatement in the report as a whole
options.misconception: modifies an opinion on the financial statements for a defect in a document outside them
options.why: The opinion covers the financial statements. Here the statements are right and the directors' report is wrong, so a qualification would say something untrue about what was audited.

citation.ref: reporting where the auditor concludes that an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information exists — the Other Information section of the auditor's report

items.scenario: The directors' report contains a figure that is materially inconsistent with the audited financial statements. The auditor has discussed it with management and with those charged with governance, and the directors' report has still not been corrected. The financial statements themselves are not misstated.

items.stem: What is the firm's position?

options.text: The firm must hand over the papers, but only after the retention period has run out
options.misconception: turns a retention floor into a date on which ownership passes to the client
options.why: The retention period is a minimum for how long the firm keeps the documentation. Its expiry does not transfer ownership to anybody, and the papers remain the firm's afterwards.

options.text: The working papers must be destroyed once handed over, so the firm should refuse on that ground alone
options.misconception: reaches the right refusal by a wrong route, inventing a destruction rule
options.why: Nothing requires destruction on handing over, and destruction is exactly what the retention requirement forbids during the retention period. The reason for refusing is ownership, not any obligation to destroy.

options.text: The working papers belong to the client, the audit having been carried out on its behalf and at its cost
options.misconception: reads payment for an engagement as ownership of the auditor's own record of it
options.why: The client pays for an opinion, not for the auditor's record of how he reached it. If the papers belonged to the client the firm could not keep them for its retention period or produce them on a review.

options.text: The working papers are the property of the firm, which may at its discretion make portions or extracts available to the client, provided disclosure does not undermine the independence or the validity of the audit process
options.why: Ownership does not follow the fee. Engagement documentation is the property of the firm, and the firm may at its discretion make portions of it, or extracts from it, available to the client, provided the disclosure does not undermine the independence or the validity of the audit process. Handing over the file on demand would also cut across the firm's duty to retain the documentation for its retention period.

citation.ref: ownership of engagement documentation and its retention, read with the documentation requirements of SA 230

items.scenario: A client whose audit finished two years ago writes demanding that the firm hand over the full set of audit working papers, on the footing that the client paid for the audit and the papers relate to its own records.

items.stem: Has the requirement under Clause 8 been met?

options.text: Yes — the obligation is to attempt communication, and posting a letter is an attempt
options.misconception: converts a duty to communicate into a duty to try
options.why: The clause is about accepting a position previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him. A duty framed around communication is not discharged by an attempt nobody can prove.

options.text: No — the communication must be made after accepting the appointment, and this one was made before
options.misconception: reverses the timing, which the clause fixes at before acceptance
options.why: The communication comes before acceptance, not after. Timing is the one thing this member got right; his difficulty is proof of delivery.

options.text: Yes — the clause requires the communication to be in writing, and an ordinary letter is in writing
options.misconception: stops at the form of the communication and ignores the proof of its delivery
options.why: Writing is necessary but it is not the end of the requirement. Where delivery cannot be shown, the member has no answer to a complaint that the communication never happened.

options.text: No — the communication should be by registered post with acknowledgement due, or by hand against a written acknowledgement, so that positive evidence of delivery is available
options.why: Clause 8 requires communication in writing with the previous auditor, and the Council's guidance goes to how that is proved: the communication should be by registered post with acknowledgement due, or delivered by hand against a written acknowledgement, so that positive evidence of delivery is available. A photocopy of an ordinary letter proves that it was written, not that it reached anybody.
keywords: by hand against a written acknowledgement

citation.ref: Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule, read with the Council's guidance that communication with the previous auditor be by registered post with acknowledgement due or by hand against a written acknowledgement

items.scenario: A chartered accountant posts an ordinary letter to the previous auditor before accepting an appointment. He keeps a photocopy of the letter but has no proof that it was ever delivered. The previous auditor later says he received nothing.

items.stem: Clause 7 of Part I of the First Schedule bars a member in practice from using any designation or expression other than "Chartered Accountant" on professional documents, visiting cards, letterheads or signboards. What does it allow?

options.text: Any professional qualification obtained abroad, foreign bodies being outside the Council's reach
options.misconception: assumes a foreign qualification escapes the clause because the body is foreign
options.why: The test is not where the body sits but whether it is an institution recognised by the Central Government or by the Council. An unrecognised body's title falls outside the exception wherever it is based.

options.text: A degree from a university established by law in India, or one the Central Government recognises, and a title indicating membership of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India or of another body the Central Government or the Council recognises
options.why: The clause carries its own exception, and it is narrow. A member may use a degree of a university established by law in India — or one that carries recognition from the Central Government. He may equally use a title indicating membership of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. The same goes for a body other than the Institute, so long as it is one already recognised by the Central Government, or one the Council may yet come to recognise. Anything outside that exception is the designation the clause forbids.
keywords: a degree of a university established by law in India

options.text: Any designation the member has in fact earned, the clause being aimed only at false claims
options.misconception: reads the clause as a rule against untruth, when it is a rule about which designations may appear
options.why: The clause is not confined to false claims. A designation may be perfectly true and still fall outside the exception, and using it is misconduct all the same.

options.text: A description of the member's areas of specialisation, provided it is accurate
options.misconception: treats a description of expertise as a permitted designation
options.why: A description of expertise or specialisation is not a degree or a title of membership, so it does not enter the exception at all. Setting out one's specialisation in this way has been held to be misconduct.
keywords: not a degree or a title of membership

citation.ref: Clause 7 of Part I of the First Schedule — the designations and expressions a member in practice may use, and the exception for degrees and titles of membership

items.stem: May he be appointed?

options.text: Yes, provided his employer gives written consent to the appointment
options.misconception: treats a statutory disqualification as something an employer can waive
options.why: A disqualification under section 141 is imposed by statute on the auditor. No employer's consent can remove it, because the provision is there to protect the company being audited, not the employer.

options.text: No — section 141(3)(g) disqualifies a person who is in full time employment elsewhere, and that limb bites regardless of how many audits he holds
options.why: The clause has two limbs and they are independent. The first disqualifies a person who is in full time employment elsewhere; the second disqualifies a person or partner of a firm holding appointment as auditor of more than the specified number of companies. He fails on the first limb, so the count of his audits never arises.

options.text: Yes — a private company is excluded from the specified number, so no disqualification can arise on this appointment
options.misconception: uses an exclusion built for the counting limb to answer a question under the employment limb
options.why: Private companies below the prescribed paid-up capital are left out of the count, but that exclusion belongs to the counting limb. It says nothing about a person disqualified for being in full time employment elsewhere.

options.text: Yes — he holds no audits at all, so he is nowhere near the ceiling of twenty companies
options.misconception: applies the counting limb and misses the employment limb sitting beside it
options.why: The ceiling is only the second half of the clause. A person in full time employment elsewhere is disqualified by the first half whatever his count of audits is.

citation.ref: section 141(3)(g) — disqualification of a person in full time employment elsewhere, and of a person or partner of a firm holding appointment as auditor of more than the specified number of companies

items.scenario: A chartered accountant holds a certificate of practice and is also employed full time as the finance manager of a manufacturing company. He holds no company audits at all. A private company offers to appoint him as its statutory auditor.

items.stem: May he be appointed?

options.text: No — a person convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud is not eligible for appointment as auditor for ten years from the date of the conviction
options.why: Section 141(3) closes the door for a fixed period rather than for the length of the sentence. A person who has been convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud is not eligible for appointment as an auditor of any company for a period of ten years from the date of such conviction. Four years having passed, six remain.
keywords: convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud
ten years from the date of such conviction

options.text: Yes, provided the conviction is disclosed to the members before the appointment is made
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a statutory ineligibility
options.why: Eligibility under section 141 is not something the members can vote around. A disclosed disqualification is still a disqualification, and an appointment made in the teeth of it is void.

options.text: No — but the bar is permanent, a person once convicted of fraud never being eligible again
options.misconception: hardens a ten-year bar into a lifetime one
options.why: The statute fixes the period at ten years from the date of conviction. Reading it as permanent would rewrite a period the section states in terms.
keywords: ten years from the date of conviction

options.text: Yes — the sentence has been served, so the disqualification has spent itself
options.misconception: ties the disqualification to the sentence, when the section ties it to the date of conviction
options.why: The period runs from the date of the conviction, not from the end of the sentence. Serving a sentence discharges the punishment; it does not restart eligibility under the Companies Act.

citation.ref: section 141(3)(h) — a person convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud is not eligible for appointment as auditor for ten years from the date of conviction

items.scenario: A chartered accountant was convicted by a court four years ago of an offence involving fraud. He has since served his sentence and is otherwise in good standing. A company proposes to appoint him as its statutory auditor.

items.stem: What does section 143(12) with its rules require of him?

options.text: Report the matter to the audit committee within two days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of the fraud with a description, the approximate amount involved and the parties involved — with no report to the Central Government
options.why: The section splits at the prescribed amount. Below it, the auditor reports to the audit committee, or to the Board where the company has no audit committee, within two days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of the fraud with a description, the approximate amount involved and the parties involved. Only frauds at or above the prescribed amount travel to the Central Government.
keywords: the nature of the fraud with a description

options.text: Report nothing, since the amount is below the prescribed threshold and the section is therefore not engaged
options.misconception: reads the threshold as switching the duty off rather than switching the recipient
options.why: The threshold decides who is told, not whether anybody is told. A fraud below it still goes to the audit committee or the Board, and its details are disclosed in the Board's report.

options.text: Report the matter to the audit committee only after the company has completed its own investigation and confirmed the fraud
options.misconception: waits for proof, when the duty is triggered by the auditor's reason to believe
options.why: The duty is triggered when the auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud is being or has been committed. Waiting for the company to confirm it would put the timing of the report in the hands of the people it may concern.
keywords: in the hands of the people it may concern

options.text: Report the matter to the Central Government in the prescribed form, every suspected fraud being reportable to it
options.misconception: sends every fraud to the Central Government and loses the threshold the section is built around
options.why: The route to the Central Government is reserved for frauds involving the prescribed amount or more. A fraud below it is reported inside the company, which is what makes the threshold do any work.

citation.ref: section 143(12) read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 — reporting a fraud involving less than the prescribed amount to the audit committee or the Board within two days

items.scenario: An auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving an amount below the prescribed threshold is being committed against the company by its employees. The company has an audit committee.

items.stem: How is this reported under clause 3(vii) of CARO 2020?

options.text: Not at all, because the amount has not become finally payable while the company's letter is pending
options.misconception: suspends the dues' payability on the strength of a letter
options.why: A demand does not stop being payable because the company has asked for it to be reconsidered. Only a stay or an order changes what is payable, and there is neither here.
keywords: asked for it to be reconsidered

options.text: Under the disputed dues limb, with the amount and the forum shown as the assessing officer
options.misconception: treats a letter to the department as a proceeding, and the assessing officer as a forum
options.why: The disputed limb asks for the forum where the dispute is pending, which presupposes a proceeding before an appellate authority or a court. The officer who raised the demand is not a forum before which it is being contested.
keywords: the forum where the dispute is pending

options.text: Under both limbs, the amount being at once undisputed and the subject of a representation
options.misconception: reports one amount twice by treating the two limbs as overlapping
options.why: The two limbs are alternatives: an amount is either not deposited though undisputed, or not deposited on account of a dispute. Reporting the same demand under both would double-count it.

options.text: Under the undisputed dues limb, because a mere representation to the department is not a dispute for the purposes of the clause
options.why: The clause splits statutory dues into those not deposited though undisputed and those not deposited on account of a dispute. A mere representation to the concerned department is not a dispute — a dispute contemplates proceedings before an appellate authority or a court. So the demand is an undisputed due, and it is reported under that limb if it has been outstanding for more than six months from the date it became payable.

citation.ref: clause 3(vii)(a) and clause 3(vii)(b) — undisputed statutory dues in arrears for more than six months, and dues not deposited on account of a dispute with the amount and the forum

items.scenario: A company has not deposited an income-tax demand of eighteen lakh rupees. It has written a letter to the assessing officer asking him to reconsider the demand. No appeal has been filed before any appellate authority and no stay has been obtained.

items.stem: What does section 143(6) require?

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General has no time limit, and may comment at any time before the next annual general meeting
options.misconception: removes a period the section states expressly
options.why: The section fixes the window at sixty days from the date of receipt of the audit report. Leaving it open until the next annual general meeting would rewrite a period the statute states.
keywords: sixty days from the date of receipt

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General may replace the auditor's report with one of his own
options.misconception: turns a power to comment upon or supplement into a power to substitute
options.why: The power is to comment upon or supplement the audit report, which leaves the auditor's report standing. A supplementary comment sits alongside the report; it does not take its place.

options.text: The auditor sends a copy of his report to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, who has a right to conduct a supplementary audit and to comment upon or supplement the report within sixty days of receiving it
options.why: The report does not stop with the company. The auditor sends a copy to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, who within sixty days from the date of receipt of the audit report has a right to conduct a supplementary audit of the financial statements by such persons as he may authorise, and to comment upon or supplement the audit report.

options.text: The report goes only to the members of the company, the Comptroller and Auditor-General's role having ended when he appointed the auditor
options.misconception: treats the appointment power as the whole of the Comptroller and Auditor-General's role
options.why: Appointment is one power and supplementary audit is another. The section gives the Comptroller and Auditor-General a role after the report is signed as well as before the auditor is appointed.

citation.ref: section 143(6) — the auditor's report on a government company is sent to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, who may conduct a supplementary audit and comment upon or supplement the report within sixty days of receipt

items.scenario: The statutory auditor of a government company has signed his audit report. His assistant asks what happens to the report next.

items.stem: Who may be appointed internal auditor under section 138 with Rule 13?

options.text: Only a chartered accountant in practice, internal audit being an attest function reserved to the profession
options.misconception: reserves to chartered accountants in practice a role the rule opens to others
options.why: Internal audit under this section is not an attest function reserved to practising chartered accountants. The rule names the cost accountant and any other professional the Board decides on alongside the chartered accountant.

options.text: Anyone the Board chooses, the rule leaving the qualification entirely to the Board's discretion
options.misconception: reads the Board's discretion as covering the whole appointment rather than the residual category
options.why: The Board's discretion operates within a named list: chartered accountant, cost accountant, or such other professional as the Board decides. The last category still requires a professional, not simply anyone.

options.text: Only a person who is not an employee of the company, independence being a condition of the appointment
options.misconception: imports an independence bar the rule expressly declines to impose
options.why: On this very point the rule says he may or may not be an employee of the company. An employee is therefore eligible, whatever separate view the audit committee may take on how the function should be positioned.
keywords: may or may not be an employee

options.text: A chartered accountant, a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board — and he may or may not be an employee of the company
options.why: The rule is wider than the secretary thinks on both counts. Three kinds of person may hold the post: a chartered accountant, a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board. What the post covers is internal audit of what the company does and how it runs. And the rule says in terms that he may or may not be an employee of the company, so an insider is not excluded.
keywords: a chartered accountant, a cost accountant
such other professional as may be decided by the Board
may or may not be an employee

citation.ref: section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — who may be appointed internal auditor, and that he may or may not be an employee of the company

items.scenario: A company that is required to appoint an internal auditor wants to appoint its own general manager of finance, who is a cost accountant, to the role. The company secretary says only an outside chartered accountant may be appointed.

items.stem: The auditor has obtained the evidence he needs and concludes that the financial statements contain a misstatement whose effects are material but not pervasive. Which opinion does SA 705 (Revised) require?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion
options.misconception: applies the no-evidence branch of SA 705 to a misstatement the auditor has already measured
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion belongs to the other branch of SA 705 (Revised) — an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence whose possible effects could be both material and pervasive. Here the evidence was obtained and the misstatement is known.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: An adverse opinion
options.misconception: drops the second half of the test and treats any material misstatement as pervasive
options.why: An adverse opinion is for misstatements that are both material and pervasive. Dropping the second word leaves SA 705 (Revised) with one modification where it has three, and turns every qualification into an adverse opinion.

options.text: A qualified opinion
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) pairs each condition with one opinion. Where the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence and concludes that misstatements are material but not pervasive, he expresses a qualified opinion. Pervasive describes effects that are not confined to specific elements of the financial statements, or that represent a substantial proportion of them, or that are fundamental to users' understanding — and none of that is claimed here, so the modification stops at a qualification.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: uses an emphasis paragraph in place of a modification
options.why: SA 706 (Revised) allows an Emphasis of Matter paragraph only for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and says it is not a substitute for a modification. An uncorrected material misstatement is not a disclosure to emphasise.
keywords: not a substitute for a modification

citation.ref: para 5, 7(a)

items.stem: What does the clearly trivial threshold in SA 450 require him to do?

options.text: Report it to those charged with governance immediately, without adding it to the list
options.misconception: skips the accumulation that the later communication is built from
options.why: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance at the end of the audit, and that communication is built out of the accumulation. Reporting one item straight away replaces a list with an anecdote.

options.text: Leave it out, ₹6,000 being far below the ₹90 lakh materiality
options.misconception: treats the clearly trivial threshold as if it were materiality
options.why: Materiality decides at the end whether the financial statements are misstated. The clearly trivial threshold decides at the start what goes on the list at all, and it is set well below materiality, so an amount can be nowhere near materiality and still have to be accumulated.

options.text: Leave it out if the engagement partner records his agreement in the file
options.misconception: turns a test about the item into an approval given by a person
options.why: No approval converts an item into a clearly trivial one. The test is about the amount and its nature, judged beyond any reasonable doubt, and a signature does not remove the doubt the senior already has.

options.text: Accumulate it — where there is any uncertainty about whether an item is clearly trivial, it is treated as not clearly trivial
options.why: Clearly trivial is not a smaller word for immaterial. SA 450 has the auditor accumulate every misstatement identified during the audit other than those that are clearly trivial, and clearly trivial catches only amounts that are inconsequential in size and in nature, individually and in aggregate, beyond any reasonable doubt. The senior's uncertainty is itself the answer: where there is any doubt, the auditor accumulates the item.
keywords: inconsequential in size and in nature

citation.ref: The clearly trivial threshold

items.scenario: A senior finds a difference of ₹6,000 and is not sure whether it is inconsequential in nature, because it arises on a related party balance. Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is ₹90 lakh.
