options.text: No, because a listed company can never carry forward a business loss
options.misconception: reaches the right conclusion on a reason that is false
options.why: A listed company carries forward its business losses under section 72 like anybody else. What saves the set-off here is that section 79 does not apply to it.

options.text: Yes, unless the shares were sold on a recognised stock exchange
options.misconception: invents an exchange-based exception inside a section that never applies here
options.why: Section 79 carries no exception for trades done on an exchange. The company is outside the section altogether, because the public are substantially interested in it.

options.text: Yes, because more than half the shares changed hands, which is what section 79 tests
options.misconception: applies the continuity test to a company the section does not reach
options.why: The test in section 79 does bite on a change beyond the permitted level, but only for a closely held company. The gate is the kind of company first and the extent of the change second.

citation.ref: Section 79(1) read with Section 2(18)

items.scenario: Sagar Ports Ltd is listed on a recognised stock exchange and is a company in which the public are substantially interested. Over previous year 2025-26 more than eighty per cent of its shares changed hands on the exchange. It carries forward a business loss from an earlier year.

items.stem: Is that rent clubbed with Mr Ghosh's income?

options.text: No, but only because the shop is let out rather than used by her
options.misconception: makes the use of the asset the test
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) does not ask what the spouse does with the asset. Rent, business profit or interest would all be clubbed had the transfer been without adequate consideration.

options.text: Yes, because they were married at the time of the transfer
options.misconception: takes the subsisting marriage as sufficient by itself
options.why: The marriage must subsist, which it does, but that only opens the clause. It is the consideration that decides the case, and it was adequate.

options.text: No, because the transfer was for adequate consideration
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) clubs income from an asset transferred to the spouse only where the transfer was made otherwise than for adequate consideration. A sale at the full market price, paid from the wife's own money, is adequate consideration, so the rent is her income alone.

options.text: Yes, income from any asset received from a spouse is clubbed
options.misconception: drops the consideration condition and clubs on the relationship alone
options.why: The relationship is one condition and the absence of adequate consideration is another. Both sit in section 64(1)(iv) and both must hold before any clubbing starts.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv)

items.scenario: Mr Ghosh sold a shop to his wife on 1 April 2025 at its full market price of ₹40,00,000, which she paid from her own savings. She let the shop out and earned ₹3,00,000 of rent in previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: What must the Assessing Officer do before requiring that statement?

options.text: Direct a special audit under section 142(2A) first
options.misconception: makes one power a precondition of the other
options.why: The two powers are independent. A special audit is directed where the accounts are complex or the interests of revenue require it, and it is not a step on the way to asking for a statement of assets.

options.text: Obtain the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner
options.misconception: raises the approving authority above the one the proviso names
options.why: The higher approval belongs to a direction for special audit under section 142(2A). The statement of assets and liabilities needs the Joint Commissioner and nobody above him.

options.text: Nothing, the power under section 142(1) is his alone to exercise
options.misconception: treats every limb of section 142(1) as unsupervised
options.why: The notice calling for a return, or for accounts and documents, needs no approval. The statement of assets and liabilities outside the books is the one limb that carries a proviso requiring approval.

options.text: Obtain the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner
options.why: Section 142(1)(iii) lets the Assessing Officer call for a statement of all assets and liabilities of the assessee, whether included in the accounts or not, and the proviso to section 142(1) requires the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner before he asks for assets and liabilities not included in the accounts.
keywords: previous approval of the Joint Commissioner

citation.ref: Section 142(1)(iii) with the proviso to Section 142(1)

items.scenario: While assessing Mr Rane, the Assessing Officer wants a statement of all his assets and liabilities, including several that are not entered in the books of the business.

items.stem: As income of which previous year does section 68 charge that sum?

options.text: Previous year 2025-26, the year in which the sum was found credited in the books
options.why: Section 68 takes any sum found credited in the books an assessee keeps for a year and, where he gives no account of where it came from or gives one the officer cannot accept, charges it as income of the assessee of that previous year. The credit entry dates the charge, so previous year 2025-26 it is.
keywords: income of the assessee of that previous year

options.text: The previous year in which the money was actually earned, if that can be traced
options.misconception: looks for the real source when the section applies because there is none
options.why: Section 68 operates precisely where no satisfactory explanation of the nature and source is offered. Were the source traceable there would be nothing for the section to do.

options.text: No year at all, because an unexplained credit is added to capital rather than to income
options.misconception: treats an unexplained credit as a balance-sheet item
options.why: Section 68 exists to convert exactly such a credit into income. Left sitting in the capital account it would escape tax altogether, which is what the section prevents.

options.text: The previous year in which the Assessing Officer discovers the credit
options.misconception: dates the charge by the discovery rather than by the entry
options.why: Discovery may come years afterwards, and section 68 does not follow it. The section fixes the year by the entry standing in the books.

citation.ref: Section 68

items.scenario: During the assessment of Mr Wagh for previous year 2025-26 the Assessing Officer finds ₹15,00,000 credited in his books on 12 September 2025 with no name against it. Mr Wagh offers no explanation of where the money came from.

items.stem: Which of the four is an eligible assessee entitled to the Dispute Resolution Panel route?

options.text: All four, because every draft order carries a right to object
options.misconception: treats the draft order procedure as open to every assessee
options.why: Section 144C is not a general appeal route. A draft order is issued only to an eligible assessee, and the definition in section 144C(15)(b) is a narrow one.

options.text: Only (i), the Indian company whose variation comes from the Transfer Pricing Officer's order
options.why: Section 144C(15)(b) draws the definition of an eligible assessee round two groups. The first is a person whose proposed variation comes about as a consequence of the order of the Transfer Pricing Officer. The second is any non-resident not being a company or any foreign company. The Indian company in (i) is inside the first limb, while the other three are residents with variations of a purely domestic kind and fall outside both.
keywords: as a consequence of the order of the Transfer Pricing Officer
non-resident not being a company or any foreign company

options.text: Only (ii), (iii) and (iv), because a transfer pricing matter goes straight to the Commissioner (Appeals)
options.misconception: reverses the definition and sends the one qualifying case elsewhere
options.why: The transfer pricing case is the paradigm case for section 144C rather than the exception. It is the three domestic variations that have no route to the Panel.

options.text: Only (i) and (iv), because both of them are companies
options.misconception: makes being a company the test when residence and the source of the variation are
options.why: Being a company helps only where the company is a foreign one. A resident company with a domestic disallowance is not an eligible assessee.

citation.ref: Section 144C(15)(b) read with Section 144C(1)

items.scenario: Four assessees each face a proposed variation. (i) An Indian company, where the variation arises from an order of the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA(3). (ii) A resident individual, with a domestic disallowance. (iii) A resident partnership firm, with a cash credit addition. (iv) A resident company, with a disallowance under section 14A.

items.stem: May the Commissioner (Appeals) do that?

options.text: No, he may only confirm or annul, never enhance
options.misconception: understates the clause by dropping two of the four powers
options.why: Enhancement is expressly among his powers, and so is reduction. What section 251(2) adds is that no enhancement may be made without a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against it.

options.text: No, he may confirm, reduce, enhance or annul the assessment, and no longer set it aside
options.why: Section 251(1)(a) lists what the Commissioner (Appeals) may do with an order of assessment — confirm, reduce, enhance or annul it. The power to set aside the assessment and refer the case back was taken out of the clause, so an appeal has to be decided rather than returned.

options.text: Yes, setting the assessment aside and remanding it is the ordinary course on an incomplete record
options.misconception: applies the Tribunal's remand practice to the first appellate authority
options.why: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal can restore a matter for fresh consideration, and that is where the practice comes from. Section 251(1)(a) no longer gives the Commissioner (Appeals) the same power.

options.text: Yes, provided he records his reasons in writing
options.misconception: treats a reasons requirement as a substitute for the power itself
options.why: Reasons are required for whatever he does decide, under section 250(6). They cannot create a power that the clause has removed.

citation.ref: Section 251(1)(a) read with Section 251(2)

items.scenario: Hearing an appeal against an assessment, the Commissioner (Appeals) forms the view that the Assessing Officer investigated too little, and wants to send the matter back to him for a fresh assessment.

items.stem: Against which figure does section 270A measure the under-reported income?

options.text: Nil, because a scrutiny assessment always measures under-reporting from zero
options.misconception: treats a scrutiny assessment as though no return had been filed
options.why: A nil benchmark belongs to the case where no return was furnished at all, which section 270A(2)(b) deals with separately. Here a return was filed and processed.

options.text: ₹95,00,000, the income assessed, because that is what the penalty is charged on
options.misconception: confuses the assessed income with the amount of the under-reporting
options.why: The assessed income is one side of the comparison rather than the answer to it. Under-reported income is the difference between the assessed figure and the benchmark.

options.text: ₹85,00,000, the income determined in the section 143(1)(a) intimation
options.why: Where a return has been furnished and processed, section 270A(2)(a) treats a person as having under-reported his income if the income assessed is greater than the income determined in the intimation under section 143(1)(a). The benchmark is therefore the processed figure of ₹85,00,000 rather than the figure the company itself returned.

options.text: ₹80,00,000, the income shown in the return as filed
options.misconception: uses the returned figure where the Act names the processed one
options.why: The returned figure is the starting point for processing, not the benchmark for the penalty. Once an intimation under section 143(1)(a) exists, clause (a) of section 270A(2) points at the income determined in it.

citation.ref: Section 270A(2)(a) read with Section 270A(3)

items.scenario: Bhatia Ltd filed its return for assessment year 2026-27 showing income of ₹80,00,000. On processing under section 143(1)(a) the income was determined at ₹85,00,000. On scrutiny the Assessing Officer assessed the income at ₹95,00,000.

items.stem: Does that spending count as application of income under section 11?

options.text: No, but the shortfall may be accumulated under section 11(2) and spent in Nairobi later
options.misconception: uses the accumulation route to reach a purpose the section does not allow
options.why: Accumulation under section 11(2) defers application; it does not widen what counts as application. Money accumulated must still be spent on charitable purposes in India when the time comes.

options.text: Yes, because the trust is registered under section 12AB
options.misconception: treats registration as the whole of the exemption
options.why: Registration under section 12AB opens the door to sections 11 and 12. It does not answer the separate question whether a particular spending is application in India.

options.text: Yes, the school is charitable and section 11 does not care where the money is spent
options.misconception: drops the two words "in India" from the exemption
options.why: The words are part of the condition rather than a description of it. A purpose that is charitable in the abstract does not satisfy the clause if it is pursued outside India.

options.text: No, because section 11(1)(a) exempts income applied to charitable purposes in India
options.why: Section 11(1)(a) exempts income derived from property held under trust to the extent it is applied to charitable or religious purposes in India. Spending abroad falls outside those words, and Section 11(1)(c) allows the Board to direct otherwise only in named cases. With no direction, the school in Nairobi is not application.
keywords: applied to charitable or religious purposes in India

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(a) read with Section 11(1)(c)

items.scenario: A charitable trust registered under section 12AB earns ₹1,00,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 and spends ₹90,00,000 of it running a school in Nairobi. The Board has given no direction of any kind about this trust.

items.stem: What must it furnish on account of section 115JB, over and above its return?

options.text: A report from an accountant, but only where it also claims credit under section 115JAA
options.misconception: ties the report to the credit instead of to the charge
options.why: The report follows the application of section 115JB itself. Credit under section 115JAA is a later and separate matter and does not decide whether the report is due.

options.text: A report from an accountant saying that book profit has been worked out as the section requires
options.why: Section 115JB(4) makes every company the section reaches furnish a report from an accountant — the Explanation to section 288(2) says who counts as one — and what that report has to say is that book profit has been computed in accordance with what this section lays down. It is in the prescribed form and goes in by the due date for the return.
keywords: book profit has been computed in accordance with

options.text: A certificate from the Registrar of Companies that the accounts are in order
options.misconception: looks to company law for a certificate that the tax section asks an accountant for
options.why: The Registrar registers accounts and certifies nothing about book profit. Section 115JB(4) names an accountant within the meaning of the Explanation to section 288(2).

options.text: Nothing extra, because the audited accounts under the Companies Act already cover it
options.misconception: assumes the statutory audit discharges the section's own reporting duty
options.why: The audited accounts are the raw material from which book profit is worked out. Section 115JB(4) asks separately for a report certifying that the computation follows the section.

citation.ref: Section 115JB(4) read with the Explanation to Section 288(2)

items.scenario: Meghna Alloys Ltd is a domestic company that has not opted for section 115BAA. Its liability worked out under section 115JB exceeds its ordinary liability, so it will pay tax on book profit for assessment year 2026-27.

items.stem: Can she be made to pay it?

options.text: No, a direct demand on her is barred to the extent tax was deducted at source
options.why: Section 205 shuts the department's road to the deductee. Where tax is deductible at source, a person from whose income it was actually taken shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself for so much as was deducted. Failure to deposit is the deductor's own default, pursued under section 201, and the bar operates whether or not the money ever reached the government.
keywords: shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself

options.text: Yes, unless she produces proof that the employer deposited the money
options.misconception: puts the burden of the deductor's compliance on the deductee
options.why: What the deductee has to show is that tax was deducted from her income, which the certificate and her salary slips establish. What happened after that is between the department and the employer.

options.text: Yes, because credit under section 199 follows the deposit, so nothing was paid on her behalf
options.misconception: reads section 199 as the only provision in play and misses the bar
options.why: Section 199 governs whose payment the deducted tax is treated as. Section 205 stands beside it and stops the demand against the very person from whose income the tax was taken.

options.text: No, but only if she first files an application before the Assessing Officer
options.misconception: turns a statutory bar into a relief that has to be applied for
options.why: The bar is written into the Act rather than granted on request. It applies of its own force once the deduction from her income is shown.

citation.ref: Section 205 read with Section 199(1) and Section 201(1)

items.scenario: Ms Kamath's employer deducted ₹1,20,000 of tax from her salary during previous year 2025-26 and gave her the certificate of deduction, but never deposited the money with the Central Government. The department raises a demand on her for that ₹1,20,000.

items.stem: Can it withdraw the option?

options.text: Yes, once, in the way an individual may return to the old regime
options.misconception: borrows a one-time re-entry rule that belongs to a different section
options.why: A route back exists for an individual or Hindu undivided family under section 115BAC. Section 115BAA gives a company no equivalent.

options.text: Yes, it may opt out in any year simply by not making the claim in its return
options.misconception: treats the option as an annual election
options.why: Some concessional regimes are chosen year by year. Section 115BAA is not one of them, and silence in a later return does not undo the choice already made.

options.text: No, the option once exercised cannot be withdrawn for that or for any other previous year
options.why: Section 115BAA(5) provides that the option once exercised for any previous year cannot subsequently be withdrawn for the same or for any other previous year. The choice is made once and binds every year that follows, so a later turn in the arithmetic is no ground to return.

options.text: No, but it may withdraw with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner
options.misconception: invents an approval route into an unconditional bar
options.why: Section 115BAA(5) admits of no approval and no exception. There is no officer who can let the company back out of it.

citation.ref: Section 115BAA(5)

items.scenario: Trilok Cements Ltd exercised the option under section 115BAA for assessment year 2024-25. For assessment year 2026-27 it works out that the ordinary rates, taken with the deductions it gave up, would now cost it less, and it wants to go back.

items.stem: Is that certificate by itself enough to claim the treaty benefit?

options.text: Yes, because a certificate from the treaty partner's own authority is conclusive
options.misconception: treats the certificate as settling every question the treaty raises
options.why: The certificate proves residence. It says nothing about beneficial ownership, about the nature of the income, or about the particulars the prescribed form asks for.

options.text: Yes, section 90(4) names the certificate and asks for nothing else
options.misconception: stops at sub-section (4) and misses the sub-section that follows it
options.why: Sub-section (4) states the condition and sub-section (5) adds to it. Both sit inside section 90 and both have to be met.

options.text: No, because the certificate must instead come from the Indian tax authority
options.misconception: sends the applicant to the wrong government for the certificate
options.why: A tax residency certificate comes from the government of the country of which the person claims to be a resident. Singapore is the right source; what is missing is the further information.

options.text: No, the prescribed further documents and information must also be provided
options.why: Section 90(4) makes the tax residency certificate a necessary condition, and Section 90(5) adds that the assessee shall also provide such other documents and information as may be prescribed. Rule 21AB prescribes Form 10F for the particulars the certificate does not carry, so the certificate alone does not finish the job.
keywords: such other documents and information as may be prescribed

citation.ref: Section 90(5) read with Section 90(4) and Rule 21AB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Solaris Pte Ltd, a Singapore company, wants the benefit of the India-Singapore treaty on a payment received from an Indian customer. It has obtained a tax residency certificate from the Singapore tax authority.

items.stem: What becomes of the ₹3,00,00,000 disallowed?

options.text: It is lost, because a disallowance under section 94B is final
options.misconception: treats the limitation as a permanent denial rather than a deferral
options.why: Section 94B limits the interest deduction of a year; it does not extinguish the expenditure. Sub-section (4) is the carry-forward that makes it a rule about timing.

options.text: It is carried forward for eight assessment years and allowed against business profits of those years
options.why: Section 94B(4) does not throw the excess interest away. It travels forward across the eight assessment years immediately succeeding whichever year it was worked out in, and in each of them it may be set against profits and gains of any business or profession the company runs, subject to the same ceiling.
keywords: profits and gains of any business or profession

options.text: It is carried forward indefinitely until business profits absorb it
options.misconception: gives the carry-forward no outer limit
options.why: The period is fixed at eight assessment years. Whatever is unabsorbed at the end of that run lapses, unlike unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2).

options.text: It is carried forward for eight assessment years and set off against any head of income
options.misconception: gets the period right and widens the head against which it may be used
options.why: Section 94B(4) allows the carried-forward interest against the profits and gains of a business or profession only. Salary, house property and capital gains are not available to absorb it.

citation.ref: Section 94B(4) read with Section 94B(1)

items.scenario: Nimbus Auto Ltd, an Indian company, is denied a deduction for ₹3,00,00,000 of interest in previous year 2025-26 under section 94B. Its business income for that year is small.

items.stem: Is the hire charge royalty under section 9(1)(vi)?

options.text: Yes, but only because the equipment was physically brought into India
options.misconception: adds a location condition that the clause does not carry
options.why: The clause asks whether the consideration is for the use or right to use the equipment, and does not make the machine's location its test. What sources the payment in India is the payer being an Indian resident using it for a business carried on here.

options.text: No, it is business income of the German company and taxable only through a permanent establishment
options.misconception: applies the permanent establishment threshold to income the Act sources separately
options.why: Royalty deemed to accrue in India under section 9(1)(vi) is charged whether or not there is a permanent establishment. The permanent establishment test governs business profits, which this is not.

options.text: No, royalty covers only intangible property such as patents and trademarks
options.misconception: limits royalty to intellectual property and misses the equipment clause
options.why: Patents, trademarks, designs and secret formulae are on the list, and so is equipment. The equipment clause was put there so that hire of a machine is royalty rather than business profit.

options.text: Yes, consideration for the use of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment is royalty
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) defines royalty through a list, and one entry on it, clause (iva), covers what is paid for use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, leaving out only amounts that fall under section 44BB. Testing equipment hired for a fee sits squarely inside that clause.
keywords: use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment

citation.ref: Clause (iva) of Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi)

items.scenario: Kavi Labs Ltd, an Indian company, pays a German company for the hire of specialised testing equipment, which the German company ships to India for the period of the hire. The German company has no permanent establishment in India, and the payment has nothing to do with prospecting for or extraction of mineral oils.

items.stem: Which of the four may use section 44AD?

options.text: Only (ii), (iii) and (iv), because only a profession is excluded
options.misconception: applies one of the three exclusions and drops the other two
options.why: Commission or brokerage income and an agency business are excluded alongside the professions. All three exclusions sit in the same sub-section.

options.text: Only (iii), the trader in steel tubing
options.why: Section 44AD(6) puts three kinds of person outside the section: a person carrying on a profession referred to in section 44AA(1), a person earning income in the nature of commission or brokerage, and a person carrying on an agency business. Architecture is one of those professions, and the commission agent and the agency are excluded by name, so only the trader is left.

options.text: Only (i) and (iii), because a profession is a business for this purpose
options.misconception: folds a profession into business when the Act keeps the two apart
options.why: A profession referred to in section 44AA(1) is expressly kept out of section 44AD, and architecture is one of those professions. Professionals have their own presumptive section in section 44ADA.

options.text: All four, because each is a resident within the turnover limit
options.misconception: treats residence and turnover as the only conditions
options.why: Residence and turnover are the entry conditions. Section 44AD then removes three named kinds of business and profession whatever the turnover happens to be.

citation.ref: Section 44AD(6) read with Section 44AA(1)

items.scenario: Four residents want to compute income under section 44AD for previous year 2025-26, and each is comfortably within the turnover limit. (i) A practising architect. (ii) A commission agent for a fertiliser company. (iii) A trader in steel tubing. (iv) An advertising agency working purely on agency commission.

items.stem: Does the importer charge GST on that sale out of the warehouse?

options.text: No — the sale is exempt under a notification, so the importer must reverse the credit attributable to it
options.misconception: calls an excluded transaction exempt and then applies the reversal rule that follows an exempt supply
options.why: Paragraph 8 does not exempt the transaction; it keeps it outside supply entirely. Only an exempt supply drags in a reversal of credit, and there is no exempt supply here.

options.text: No — goods still lying in the warehouse, sold before anyone clears them for home consumption, are neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services
options.why: Paragraph 8(a) of Schedule III lifts these warehoused goods out of the scope of supply altogether when they change hands before clearance for home consumption. The tax on these goods is collected once, as integrated tax on the import, and it is collected from the Pune buyer when he files his bill of entry. Nothing is charged on the warehouse sale itself.

options.text: Yes — GST is payable when the Pune buyer files his bill of entry, and the importer must pay it at that point
options.misconception: mixes the collection of integrated tax at import with a liability on the warehouse sale
options.why: The person who files the bill of entry pays the integrated tax on the import, and that person is the Pune buyer. The importer owes nothing, because his sale is not a supply.

options.text: Yes — it is an inter-State supply of goods and integrated tax is payable on the sale value
options.misconception: treats a sale made inside the customs barrier as an ordinary supply
options.why: The goods have not been cleared for home consumption, so the transaction never reaches the charging section at all. Charging it here would tax the same import twice.

citation.ref: Section 7(2)(a) read with paragraph 8(a) of Schedule III

items.scenario: A consignment of machine parts lands at Nhava Sheva and is deposited in a customs bonded warehouse. Before any bill of entry for home consumption is filed, the importer sells the whole lot to a buyer in Pune, who then files the bill of entry himself and pays the customs duty.

items.stem: Is that handover a supply?

options.text: No — nothing was received for the press, and section 7 requires consideration before anything is a supply
options.misconception: stops at the general rule in section 7(1)(a) and never reaches Schedule I
options.why: Section 7(1)(c) pulls in the activities listed in Schedule I precisely because they are made without a price being paid. Reading consideration as an absolute requirement would leave the whole Schedule with nothing to do.

options.text: Yes, but only because the scrap dealer and the firm are related persons
options.misconception: reaches the right answer through the related-person entry rather than the entry that applies
options.why: The related-person entry is a separate paragraph and needs a relationship the facts do not give. This transfer is caught by the business-assets paragraph standing on its own.

options.text: Yes — a permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which input tax credit has been availed is a supply even though nothing was received for it
options.why: Paragraph 1 of Schedule I makes a permanent transfer or disposal of business assets a supply where input tax credit has been availed on those assets, and it does so without consideration. The press meets both limbs: the credit was taken, and the transfer is permanent.
keywords: permanent transfer or disposal of business assets
input tax credit has been availed

options.text: No — the press is scrap by the time it moves, and scrap is not a business asset
options.misconception: lets the condition of the asset decide whether it was a business asset
options.why: The paragraph asks whether the thing was a business asset on which credit was availed, not what it is worth on the day it leaves. A scrapped machine that carried credit is still inside the paragraph.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(c) read with paragraph 1 of Schedule I

items.scenario: A registered printing firm bought a colour press three years ago and took the full input tax credit on it. The press has now been scrapped and handed over to a scrap dealer free of charge. Nothing was received for it and nothing is due.

items.stem: At what rate is the hamper taxed?

options.text: At the rate of that one item in the hamper which attracts the highest rate of tax, the whole price taking that rate
options.why: Because the four are separately available and not naturally bundled, this is a mixed supply. Section 8(b) treats a mixed supply as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax, so one rate is applied to the entire price.

options.text: At the rate of the item with the largest value in the hamper, that item being the principal supply
options.misconception: applies the principal-supply test of a composite supply to a bundle that is not naturally bundled
options.why: A principal supply exists only inside a composite supply, where the items are naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business. Value alone does not create one.

options.text: At the lowest rate among the four, the customer having paid one consolidated price
options.misconception: inverts the rule in section 8(b)
options.why: The section names the highest rate, not the lowest. It is drafted that way so that a bundle cannot be used to carry a high-rate item out at a low-rate item's cost.

options.text: Each item at its own rate, the shop splitting the price between the four in proportion to their separate selling prices
options.misconception: splits a single supply that the law expressly taxes as one
options.why: Section 8 exists to stop that split. Once the four go out for a single price as one supply, they are taxed as one supply.

citation.ref: Section 8(b) read with section 2(74)

items.scenario: A stationery shop sells a festive hamper for a single price of two thousand rupees. It holds a diary, a pen stand, a box of chocolates and a table clock. Each of the four is sold separately in the shop as well, and they do not go together in the ordinary course of the trade.

items.stem: Must he take registration?

options.text: No — the farmer-producer company is registered, and the agent is covered by its registration
options.misconception: treats a principal's registration as covering the agent who supplies for him
options.why: Registration is granted person by person. An agent who supplies in his own name is a separate person with his own liability, which is exactly why section 24 names him.

options.text: No — his own turnover is nine lakh rupees, below the threshold in section 22
options.misconception: applies section 22 without noticing that section 24 overrides it
options.why: Section 24 begins with a non-obstante clause aimed at section 22(1). Wherever one of its clauses fits, the threshold never gets a chance to operate.

options.text: Yes — a person who makes a taxable supply of goods on behalf of another taxable person as an agent must register whatever his own turnover
options.why: Section 24(vii) puts persons who make a taxable supply of goods or services on behalf of other taxable persons, whether as an agent or otherwise, into compulsory registration, and section 24 opens by overriding the threshold in section 22(1). His own commission is therefore beside the point.
keywords: on behalf of other taxable persons

options.text: Yes, but only because grapes are agricultural produce and every dealer in them must register
options.misconception: invents a rule keyed to the commodity being sold
options.why: No clause of section 24 turns on what is being sold. What catches him is the capacity in which he sells — for somebody else.

citation.ref: Section 24(vii) read with section 22(1)

items.scenario: A commission agent in Nashik sells grapes in the mandi for a registered farmer-producer company, raising the invoices on the buyers in his own name. His own commission income for the year is nine lakh rupees, comfortably below any threshold.

items.stem: Does the four lakh rupees of reverse-charge freight enter his aggregate turnover?

options.text: Yes — tax was actually paid on it, and everything he paid tax on counts in his turnover
options.misconception: measures turnover by tax paid rather than by supplies made
options.why: Turnover is built out of what a person supplies, not out of what he buys. Tax he paid as a recipient never becomes his own turnover.

options.text: No — the definition leaves out inward supplies where he himself pays the tax under reverse charge
options.why: Section 2(6) builds aggregate turnover out of taxable supplies, exempt supplies, exports and inter-State supplies made on the same permanent account number, and then takes back out the inward supplies on which he himself paid the tax under reverse charge. Freight bought in is an inward supply, so it stays out.

options.text: No, and for the same reason the six lakh rupees of exempt sales stays out as well
options.misconception: gets the reverse-charge exclusion right and then wrongly drops exempt supplies too
options.why: Exempt supplies are named among the things aggregate turnover includes. Only the inward reverse-charge value is taken out.

options.text: Yes, but only half of it, the other half being treated as an outward supply to himself
options.misconception: invents a proportion that no clause of the definition contains
options.why: The definition either takes an amount in or leaves it out. There is no fraction anywhere in section 2(6).

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

items.scenario: A registered trader's books for the year show taxable sales of twenty-eight lakh rupees and exempt sales of six lakh rupees. Separately, he bought four lakh rupees of freight from goods transport agencies and paid the tax on it himself under reverse charge.

items.stem: How does the IGST Act treat the Bengaluru office and the Singapore branch?

options.text: As distinct persons only if the Singapore branch takes a registration in India
options.misconception: carries the two-registrations test in section 25(4) over to a case the Explanation covers on its own
options.why: Section 25(4) makes distinct persons out of two registrations held on one permanent account number. The India-and-outside-India case does not depend on registration at all.

options.text: As one and the same person, the branch being part of the Bengaluru company and not separately incorporated
options.misconception: lets the corporate form decide a question the Explanation settles by location
options.why: The provision does not ask whether the branch is a separate company. A branch of the very same company is caught, which is the whole point of it.

options.text: As establishments of distinct persons, one being an establishment in India and the other an establishment outside India of the same person
options.why: Explanation 1 to section 8 of the IGST Act says that where a person has an establishment in India and any other establishment outside India, those establishments shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons. Registration is not what creates the split here; the two locations do.

options.text: As unrelated persons, so nothing passing between them can ever be a supply
options.misconception: goes to the opposite extreme and puts the branch outside the Act altogether
options.why: The consequence of being distinct persons is that dealings between them can be supplies. Treating them as unrelated would remove the very charge this Explanation supports.

citation.ref: Explanation 1 to section 8, read with section 25(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A software company registered in Bengaluru has a branch office in Singapore that does part of the development work on its Indian projects. The branch is not a separate company and is not registered anywhere in India, and nothing is invoiced between the two.

items.stem: Can the department demand that tax after the registration has gone?

options.text: No — the dues had to be determined before the date of cancellation for them to survive it
options.misconception: reads a determination deadline into section 29(3) that its words rule out
options.why: The sub-section keeps the dues alive whether or not they are determined before or after the cancellation. That phrase is there to close exactly this argument.

options.text: Yes, but only if the department first restores the registration under section 30
options.misconception: confuses revocation, which the taxpayer applies for, with the department's power to demand
options.why: Section 30 is a route by which the taxpayer may get a cancelled registration back. It is not a pre-condition to a demand.

options.text: No — he is no longer a registered person, so no demand can be raised against him
options.misconception: treats registration as the source of the liability rather than the machinery for collecting it
options.why: The charge falls on the supply, not on the registration certificate. Section 29(3) says so in terms so that this argument cannot be run.

options.text: Yes — cancellation does not affect his liability to pay tax and other dues for any period before the date of cancellation
options.why: Section 29(3) keeps the liability alive: cancellation of registration does not wipe out tax and other dues owed for any period prior to the date of cancellation, and it makes no difference whether those dues were worked out before that date or long after. December 2025 is such a period, so the notice stands.
keywords: prior to the date of cancellation

citation.ref: Section 29(3)

items.scenario: A trader's registration is cancelled with effect from 31 March 2026. In August 2026 the department finds that he had under-declared his output tax for the quarter ended December 2025, and issues him a notice for it.

items.stem: What is the time of supply of the service?

options.text: 12 June 2026, the date of the invoice, that being the earlier of the two competing dates
options.why: Where the invoice is issued within the period prescribed under section 31, section 13(2)(a) fixes the time of supply as the date of issue of the invoice or the date of receipt of payment, whichever is earlier. The invoice of 12 June comes before the payment of 28 July, so the invoice date governs.
keywords: date of issue of the invoice

options.text: 3 June 2026, the day the service was completed
options.misconception: applies the limb of section 13(2) that operates only when the invoice is late
options.why: The date of provision of the service becomes the trigger under clause (b) only where the invoice is not issued within the prescribed period. This invoice was in time, so clause (a) applies.

options.text: 12 July 2026, being thirty days from the completion of the service
options.misconception: converts the outer limit for issuing an invoice into the time of supply itself
options.why: Thirty days is the deadline within which the invoice must be issued, not a date on which anything is deemed to happen. An invoice issued earlier fixes an earlier time of supply.

options.text: 28 July 2026, the day the client paid
options.misconception: treats payment as the sole trigger for a service
options.why: Payment is one of two competing dates and it wins only when it comes first. Here it comes second by more than six weeks.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)(a) read with section 31(2)

items.scenario: An architect finishes a design on 3 June 2026 and issues his tax invoice on 12 June 2026, well within the period the rules allow for a service invoice. The client pays him on 28 July 2026.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the opinion?

options.text: Nowhere — with no address the supply falls outside section 12 and no place of supply can be fixed
options.misconception: reads a gap into a clause written precisely to close it
options.why: The second limb is residual and always produces an answer. That is why it points at the supplier.

options.text: The State in which the mobile number was issued, that being the only clue to where he lives
options.misconception: treats a telephone number as an address on record
options.why: An address on record means an address of the recipient held in the supplier's own records. A mobile prefix is not an address and the clause does not mention one.

options.text: Delhi — the location of the supplier, there being no address on record for the unregistered recipient
options.why: Section 12(2)(b) fixes the place of supply for an unregistered recipient at the address on record where such an address exists, and its second limb makes it the location of the supplier in every other case. With nothing on record, Delhi becomes the place of supply.

options.text: The place where the client actually used the opinion
options.misconception: imports a place-of-use test that section 12 does not apply to a general service
options.why: Section 12(2) works from the recipient's registration or his address, and failing both from the supplier's location. Where the advice is put to work never enters it.

citation.ref: Section 12(2)(b)

items.scenario: A consultancy registered in Delhi gives a one-off tax opinion to an individual who is not registered under GST. He gives no address, and the firm's records hold nothing but his name and a mobile number.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the architect's service?

options.text: Hyderabad — the villa stands outside India, so the recipient's own location fixes the place of supply
options.why: The proviso to section 12(3) deals with the case where the immovable property is located outside India, and it hands the question back to the buyer of the service: the location of the recipient is what counts. Both parties being in India keeps the case inside section 12, and the recipient sits in Hyderabad.
keywords: immovable property is located outside India

options.text: Colombo — a service relating directly to immovable property is supplied where the property stands, wherever that is
options.misconception: applies the main limb of section 12(3) and ignores the proviso sitting under it
options.why: The main limb does point at the property, but the proviso carves out property outside India and sends the place of supply to the recipient instead. A place of supply abroad would also leave section 12 with nothing to tax.

options.text: It falls to be decided under section 13, the property and the work both being connected with Sri Lanka
options.misconception: switches to section 13 although both parties are in India
options.why: Section 13 applies only where the supplier or the recipient is located outside India. Here neither is, so section 12 governs from start to finish.

options.text: Chennai — the architect's own location, the drawings having been prepared at his desk
options.misconception: falls back on the supplier's location, which section 12(3) never uses
options.why: Section 12(3) chooses between the property and the recipient. Where the work was physically done is not one of the choices.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 12(3)

items.scenario: An architect registered in Chennai designs a villa for a client registered in Hyderabad. The villa is to be built in Colombo, Sri Lanka. Both the architect and the client are in India.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the generator?

options.text: Odisha — the buyer's truck moved the goods, so the movement terminates for delivery in Odisha
options.misconception: applies clause (a) to a case where delivery had already been made
options.why: Clause (a) needs a supply involving movement that terminates in delivery to the recipient. Delivery here was complete at the shed, and everything after it is the buyer's own carriage.

options.text: Odisha — the buyer is registered there, and that is where the generator ends up
options.misconception: uses the buyer's registration, which section 10 does not turn on for goods
options.why: Section 10 works from the movement of the goods, not from where the recipient happens to hold a registration. What the buyer does with the machine afterwards is his own affair.

options.text: Kolkata, but the supply is inter-State because the two parties are registered in different States
options.misconception: decides inter-State against intra-State by comparing registrations instead of the supplier's location with the place of supply
options.why: Sections 7 and 8 of the IGST Act compare the location of the supplier with the place of supply. Both are Kolkata, so this is an intra-State supply.

options.text: Kolkata — nothing had to be moved, so the place of supply is wherever the goods stood when the buyer took delivery of them
options.why: Section 10(1)(c) is written for a sale that does not involve movement of goods at all — neither side has to carry them anywhere — and it settles the place of supply by asking one question: what was the location of the goods at the time of the delivery? Here that is the rented shed, and the generator stood in Kolkata when it was handed over.
keywords: does not involve movement of goods
location of the goods at the time of the delivery

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(c) read with section 8(1)

items.scenario: A Kolkata company owns a generator lying in a rented shed in Kolkata. It sells the generator to a buyer registered in Odisha, who comes to the shed, inspects it, takes delivery there and carries it away in his own truck. The seller arranges no movement at all.

items.stem: May he take the credit before that return is filed?

options.text: Yes, provided he files the return before the annual return for that year is furnished
options.misconception: confuses the outer time limit in section 16(4) with the conditions in section 16(2)
options.why: Section 16(4) sets the last date by which a credit may be taken. Section 16(2) sets what must be true before it may be taken at all, and both have to be satisfied.

options.text: No — furnishing the return under section 39 is itself one of the conditions in section 16(2)
options.why: Section 16(2)(d) requires that the recipient has furnished the return under section 39, and the four conditions in section 16(2) work together, not in the alternative — the invoice, the receipt of the goods, the tax having reached the Government, and the return. Three out of four is not enough.

options.text: No, because a credit can never be taken until the supplier has filed his own annual return
options.misconception: invents a condition tied to the supplier's annual return
options.why: What section 16(2)(c) asks of the supplier is that the tax has actually been paid to the Government. His annual return appears nowhere in the section.

options.text: Yes — the credit accrues the moment the supplier pays the tax, and the return only reports it
options.misconception: treats the return as a formality rather than as a condition
options.why: Clause (d) is drafted as a condition in the same breath as the invoice and the receipt of the goods. The Act does not rank one above another.

citation.ref: Section 16(2)(d)

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer holds a valid tax invoice dated March 2026, has received the goods, and the supplier has actually paid the tax to the Government. The manufacturer has not yet filed his own return for March.

items.stem: Is the input tax credit available on the two appliances?

options.text: No — goods used for personal consumption are blocked by clause (g) of section 17(5), whatever name is on the invoice
options.why: Section 17(5)(g) blocks input tax credit on goods or services or both used for personal consumption. The clause looks at the use, and the name on the bill does not change what a refrigerator and a television in a director's flat are used for.

options.text: Yes, because the managing director's residence counts as a place of business of the firm
options.misconception: converts a residence into a place of business in order to escape the block
options.why: Clause (g) turns on personal consumption, not on the address at which the goods sit. Things a person uses in his home life are consumed personally wherever they are installed.

options.text: No — these are gifts to an employee and clause (h) blocks the credit
options.misconception: reaches the right answer through the wrong clause
options.why: Nothing has been given away; the firm still owns both appliances. Clause (h) needs a gift or a free supply, and it is clause (g) that actually catches this.

options.text: Yes — the invoices are in the firm's name and the tax has been charged, which is all section 16 asks
options.misconception: stops at the section 16 conditions and never reaches the block in section 17(5)
options.why: Section 17(5) opens with a non-obstante clause aimed at section 16(1). Satisfying section 16 is where the enquiry starts, not where it finishes.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(g)

items.scenario: A registered consultancy buys a refrigerator and a television and installs them in the flat its managing director lives in. Both bills are in the firm's name and tax has been charged on them. The firm keeps ownership of both appliances.

items.stem: Must Maharashtra add that credit back for non-payment within 180 days?

options.text: Yes, but only the tax must be added back, not the amount attributable to the value
options.misconception: invents a split between value and tax that the proviso does not make
options.why: What the proviso adds back is an amount equal to the input tax credit availed. There is no separate treatment of the value anywhere in it.

options.text: No — for a supply made without consideration under Schedule I the value is treated as having been paid, so the 180-day rule never bites
options.why: The second proviso to section 16(2) makes a recipient who has not paid the supplier within 180 days add the credit back. The Explanation to that proviso says the value of such supplies shall be deemed to have been paid where the supply is made without consideration as specified in Schedule I, and a stock transfer between distinct persons is one of those.

options.text: Yes — the proviso reaches every inward supply on which credit was taken, and two hundred days have passed
options.misconception: applies the proviso without the Explanation attached to it
options.why: The proviso and its Explanation are read together. The Explanation exists to take out cases where there was never a price to pay in the first place.

options.text: No — the rule reaches only services, and this is a supply of goods
options.misconception: limits the proviso to services
options.why: The proviso reaches any supply of goods or services or both. What puts this stock transfer outside it is the absence of a price, not the fact that goods moved.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2) with its Explanation, read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A company transfers stock from its Gujarat registration to its own Maharashtra registration under a tax invoice. Nothing is paid between the two and nothing ever will be. Maharashtra took the credit on the tax charged. Two hundred days have gone by.

items.stem: Can the principal take input tax credit on the castings?

options.text: Yes, but only after the machined castings come back to Coimbatore
options.misconception: postpones a credit the proviso allows at once
options.why: The credit is available once the conditions in section 16 are met. What the return of the goods governs is the separate one-year clock, not the taking of the credit.

options.text: Yes — credit is allowed on inputs sent directly to the job worker's place of business without being received at the principal's own premises first
options.why: The proviso to section 19(2) keeps the principal's input tax credit intact on castings that a supplier has directly sent to a job worker, without being first brought anywhere near the principal's own gate. Delivery straight to Belagavi is the very case the proviso is written for.
keywords: directly sent to a job worker

options.text: No — section 16(2)(b) requires the recipient to have received the goods, and he never did
options.misconception: applies the receipt condition without the deemed-receipt rule that sits beside it
options.why: The Explanation to section 16(2)(b) treats goods delivered to another person on the recipient's direction as received by the recipient, and section 19 says the same thing again for job work.

options.text: No — the credit on goods sent for job work belongs to the job worker, who holds them
options.misconception: gives the credit to whoever physically holds the goods
options.why: The credit follows the person to whom the supply was made and who bore the tax. The job worker never bought the castings.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 19(2), read with the Explanation to section 16(2)(b)

items.scenario: A principal in Coimbatore orders castings from a foundry in Rajkot and asks the foundry to deliver them straight to his job worker in Belagavi, who will machine them. The castings never come to Coimbatore at all.

items.stem: Which ledger does the deposit go into, and what may it be used for?

options.text: The electronic cash ledger, from which it may go towards tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount
options.why: Section 49(1) says every deposit made by internet banking, card, national electronic funds transfer, real time gross settlement or over the counter shall be credited to the electronic cash ledger. Section 49(3) then lets that balance be used for payment towards tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount payable under the Act.

options.text: The electronic credit ledger, out of which the June liability will be discharged
options.misconception: swaps the two ledgers
options.why: The credit ledger holds input tax credit and nothing else. Money paid in by challan never enters it.

options.text: The electronic cash ledger, but it may be used for tax only and never for interest or a late fee
options.misconception: narrows the uses the section expressly allows
options.why: Section 49(3) names tax, interest, penalty, fee and any other amount. Interest and late fee can in fact be paid from nowhere else.

options.text: The electronic liability register, the amount being set off against June's tax the moment it is paid in
options.misconception: treats a deposit as an immediate payment of tax
options.why: The liability register records what is owed. A deposit sits in the cash ledger until it is applied against that liability, which happens when the return is filed.

citation.ref: Section 49(1) and section 49(3)

items.scenario: A registered person deposits five lakh rupees by challan on 20 July 2026, intending it for his output tax for June. His return for June has not yet been filed.

items.stem: By when must the tax invoice be issued?

options.text: Within thirty days of 9 September 2026
options.misconception: borrows the thirty-day window that the rules give for a service
options.why: Thirty days is the period allowed for an invoice on a supply of services. A supply of goods has no such window.

options.text: On or before the removal of the goods for delivery to the buyer
options.misconception: applies clause (a), which governs only a supply involving movement
options.why: Clause (a) speaks of removal because it is written for goods that have to travel. Nothing was removed here, so clause (b) is the one that applies.

options.text: On or before 9 September 2026, the day the goods were delivered or made available to the buyer
options.why: Section 31(1)(b) covers a supply that does not involve movement of goods and requires the invoice to be issued before or at the time of delivery of goods or making available thereof to the recipient. That day here is 9 September 2026.
keywords: delivery of goods or making available

options.text: At any time before the return for September is filed
options.misconception: ties the invoice to the return rather than to the supply
options.why: Section 31 fixes the invoice to an event in the supply itself. The date of the return has nothing to do with it.

citation.ref: Section 31(1)(b)

items.scenario: A dealer sells a transformer that is already lying at the buyer's own site, where it had been left after a trial run. Nothing has to be moved. The buyer accepts it on 9 September 2026 and the dealer hands over the papers that day.

items.stem: What document must he issue to put it right?

options.text: A credit note, the original invoice needing to be corrected
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the two documents
options.why: A credit note reduces the value or the tax on an earlier invoice. Nothing is being reduced here; more tax is being charged than the invoice showed.

options.text: A debit note, but only if it is issued by 30 November 2026
options.misconception: transplants the credit note time limit onto a debit note
options.why: The November limit in section 34(2) is attached to a credit note, because a credit note takes tax out of the Government's hands. A debit note puts tax in and carries no such deadline.

options.text: A debit note, which is the document for an invoice in which the taxable value or the tax charged is less than what was payable
options.why: Under section 34(3) it is the supplier who must put out a debit note whenever an invoice undercharges: the taxable value or tax charged on it turns out to be less than what the supply itself carried. A credit note runs the other way, for an overcharge.

options.text: A revised tax invoice in place of the May invoice
options.misconception: uses the revised invoice, which exists for an entirely different situation
options.why: A revised invoice covers supplies made between the effective date of registration and the date the certificate is issued. It is not a correction tool for a live invoice.

citation.ref: Section 34(3) read with section 34(2)

items.scenario: A supplier finds that his May 2026 invoice charged tax on a taxable value of four lakh rupees when the correct taxable value was four lakh sixty thousand. The tax charged is therefore short by the amount on sixty thousand rupees.

items.stem: From which date do the two years in section 54(1) run?

options.text: The end of the financial year in which the export took place
options.misconception: converts a date-based rule into a year-end rule
options.why: Section 54(1) counts two years from a relevant date, and every clause of the Explanation gives a date. None of them gives a financial year.

options.text: The date on which the shipping bill was filed
options.misconception: takes the start of the export formalities as the relevant date
options.why: The shipping bill is a document filed before departure, not the departure. The Explanation names the day the vessel goes.

options.text: 14 May 2026, the day the ship left India
options.why: Explanation 2(a)(i) to section 54 says that where goods are exported out of India by sea or air, the relevant date is the date on which the ship or the aircraft in which such goods are loaded leaves India. Two years run from that day.

options.text: The date on which the export proceeds are received in convertible foreign exchange
options.misconception: applies the relevant date written for an export of services to an export of goods
options.why: Receipt of payment is the relevant date where services are exported. Goods take the date the carrier leaves the country.

citation.ref: Section 54(1) with Explanation 2(a)(i)

items.scenario: An exporter ships goods by sea under a letter of undertaking, without paying integrated tax. The vessel leaves the Indian port on 14 May 2026. He wants to claim a refund of the unutilised input tax credit on that shipment.

items.stem: Does section 54(3) allow that second claim?

options.text: No — a supply made under a letter of undertaking is not a zero-rated supply at all
options.misconception: arrives at the right answer for a reason that is wrong
options.why: Export under a letter of undertaking is a zero-rated supply and is the ordinary route to a credit refund. What stops him here is the drawback he has already taken.

options.text: No — refund of unutilised credit is shut out where the supplier has availed drawback in respect of central tax
options.why: The third proviso to section 54(3) says no refund of unutilised input tax credit shall be allowed if the supplier of goods or services avails of drawback in respect of central tax, or claims refund of the integrated tax paid on such supply. Having taken drawback of the central tax, he is barred on the same exports.
keywords: refund of unutilised input tax credit
drawback in respect of central tax

options.text: Yes — a zero-rated supply is one of the two cases section 54(3) allows, and nothing else matters
options.misconception: reads the first proviso and stops before the ones that follow it
options.why: The first proviso opens the gate for zero-rated supplies and for an inverted rate structure. The provisos after it close that gate again in named situations, and drawback of central tax is one of them.

options.text: Yes, but only to the extent the credit exceeds the drawback already received
options.misconception: invents a set-off where the proviso lays down an outright bar
options.why: The proviso does not net one against the other or allow the excess. It denies the refund.

citation.ref: Third proviso to section 54(3)

items.scenario: A manufacturer exports goods without payment of integrated tax under a letter of undertaking. For the very same exports he has already claimed duty drawback of the central tax component. He now also files for refund of his unutilised input tax credit.

items.stem: What must the officer do first under section 61?

options.text: Inform the registered person of the discrepancy and seek his explanation, and take no further action if the explanation is found acceptable
options.why: Section 61(1) requires the proper officer to scrutinise the return, inform the registered person of the discrepancy noticed and seek his explanation. Section 61(2) then says that where the explanation is found acceptable, the person shall be informed and no further action shall be taken.

options.text: Issue a show cause notice raising a demand on the three lakh rupees straight away
options.misconception: jumps to the demand provisions and skips the step section 61 puts first
options.why: A demand can follow, but only where no satisfactory explanation is given within the period allowed or the person does not correct the return. The scrutiny step comes first.

options.text: Cancel the registration and then recover the amount
options.misconception: treats a scrutiny discrepancy as a ground for cancellation
options.why: The grounds for cancellation are listed in section 29 and a discrepancy noticed on scrutiny is not among them. What section 61 asks for is an explanation.

options.text: Pass a best judgement assessment order under section 62
options.misconception: reaches for section 62, which is written for a return that was never filed
options.why: Section 62 applies where a registered person fails to furnish the return even after a notice. Here both returns were filed and merely disagree with one another.

citation.ref: Section 61(1) and section 61(2)

items.scenario: An officer scrutinising a registered person's returns for July 2026 notices that the outward supplies declared in the statement of outward supplies exceed those in the monthly return by three lakh rupees. Both returns were filed on time.

items.stem: Can the appeal still be entertained?

options.text: No — the three months ran out on 4 August 2026 and the Appellate Authority cannot condone delay
options.misconception: reads the three-month period as absolute
options.why: Section 107(4) expressly gives the power to condone up to one further month. It has to be asked for and justified, but it exists.

options.text: Yes, and no reason need be given, delay being condoned as a matter of course once the appeal is filed
options.misconception: treats condonation as automatic rather than as a power to be exercised
options.why: The extra month is not a right. The Appellate Authority has to be satisfied of sufficient cause before it allows the appeal in.

options.text: Yes — the period is six months from the date of the order, so he is comfortably in time
options.misconception: takes the six months the Commissioner has for a revision application as the taxpayer's own period
options.why: Six months is the period in section 107(2) for the department to have an order examined. A taxpayer's own appeal runs on three months.

options.text: Yes, if he satisfies the Appellate Authority of sufficient cause — three months are allowed and a further month may be given
options.why: Section 107(1) gives three months from the date the order is communicated, so the ordinary last date is 4 August 2026. Section 107(4) then lets the Appellate Authority add a further period of one month, but only for an appellant who can show sufficient cause for having missed that date, and the second week of August falls inside the extra month.

citation.ref: Section 107(1) and section 107(4)

items.scenario: An adjudication order is communicated to a taxpayer on 4 May 2026. He intends to appeal to the Appellate Authority, but his consultant has been unwell and the papers will not be ready until the second week of August 2026.

items.stem: Can the assessable value be the transaction value under section 14(1)?

options.text: No — there is no sale and no price, so the value must be found under the valuation rules instead
options.why: Section 14(1) sets the value of an imported consignment at its transaction value — the price actually paid or payable, and only where the thing has genuinely been sold for export to India. Where nothing is sold and no price is paid or payable, that base does not exist and the value is worked out under the Customs Valuation Rules made under the section.

options.text: Yes — the figure written on the invoice for customs purposes is the transaction value
options.misconception: treats a figure declared on paper as a price
options.why: An amount put on an invoice for the customs officer's benefit is not a price paid or payable by anybody. Transaction value needs a real sale behind it.

options.text: Yes — a free supply is a sale at a nil price, so the transaction value is nil and no duty falls
options.misconception: converts the absence of a sale into a sale at zero
options.why: A gift is not a sale and the Act does not deem it to be one. The duty is worked out on a value arrived at under the rules.

options.text: No — and the officer may then fix whatever value he considers appropriate
options.misconception: replaces the valuation rules with the officer's discretion
options.why: The rules lay down an ordered ladder — identical goods, similar goods, deductive value, computed value and finally the residual method. Discretion is not one of the rungs.

citation.ref: Section 14(1), with the rules made under it — Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007

items.scenario: A machine tool maker abroad ships a demonstration lathe to its Indian distributor free of charge, to be shown at a trade fair and sent back afterwards. No price is paid or payable, and the invoice is marked "value for customs purposes only".

items.stem: Which of the three costs stays out of the value for customs purposes?

options.text: None of the three — every cost incurred before the goods reach the importer's factory is added
options.misconception: takes the factory rather than the port as the finishing line
options.why: The rule stops at the place of importation, which is the port here. What happens on Indian roads afterwards falls outside it.

options.text: The insurance, that being a cost of the buyer rather than a cost of the goods
options.misconception: leaves out a cost that rule 10(2) names in terms
options.why: Rule 10(2) names the cost of insurance alongside the cost of transport. Who pays it does not decide whether it is added.

options.text: All three, imports being valued at the free on board price of the goods
options.misconception: values an import on a free on board basis
options.why: Imports into India are valued on a landed basis, and rule 10(2) is what carries the free on board price up to that point. Only the leg after the place of importation is left out.

options.text: The inland freight from the port to Nashik, transport being added only up to the place of importation
options.why: Rule 10(2) adds the cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling of the imported goods to the place of importation, together with the cost of insurance. Carriage beyond the place of importation is not covered, so the ocean freight and the insurance come in and the run to Nashik does not.

citation.ref: Rule 10(2), Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, read with section 14(1)

items.scenario: Goods travel by sea from Hamburg to Nhava Sheva. The importer pays ocean freight of one lakh twenty thousand rupees and insurance of forty thousand rupees. He then pays a trucker thirty-five thousand rupees to carry the consignment from Nhava Sheva to his factory in Nashik.

items.stem: May he value the goods that way under rule 9?

options.text: No — rule 9 may be applied only by the Commissioner, not by an assessing officer
options.misconception: invents a rank requirement the rules do not carry
options.why: Nothing in the rules reserves rule 9 to a particular rank of officer. What sinks this valuation is the basis chosen for it.

options.text: Yes — rule 9 is the residual method and leaves the officer free to adopt any value he thinks reasonable
options.misconception: reads "residual" as meaning unfettered
options.why: Rule 9 is residual in the sense that it comes last, not in the sense that it has no rules. Its second sub-rule is a list of prohibitions.

options.text: No — the rule expressly forbids a value based on the price of goods in the domestic market of the country of exportation
options.why: Rule 9(1) requires the value to be arrived at by reasonable means consistent with the principles and general provisions of the rules, and rule 9(2) then lists the bases the value shall not rest on, including the price of goods in the domestic market of the country of exportation, a system of minimum customs values, and arbitrary or fictitious values.
keywords: domestic market of the country of exportation

options.text: Yes, provided he gives the importer a hearing before he adopts the figure
options.misconception: treats a procedural safeguard as curing a forbidden basis
options.why: A hearing does not make a barred basis lawful. The basis itself is out, whatever procedure is followed before adopting it.

citation.ref: Rule 9, Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007

items.scenario: An officer cannot value a consignment under any of the earlier rules and comes down to rule 9, the residual method. He proposes to adopt the price at which the same goods are sold in the exporting country's own home market.

items.stem: Does that eighty-five thousand rupees enter the assessable value?

options.text: Yes — the cost of containers and of packing, whether for labour or for materials, is added to the price
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) brings into the price, so far as the buyer bears them and the invoice does not already carry them, the cost of containers — a crate counts as part of the goods it holds for customs purposes — and the cost of packing, whether for labour or for materials.
keywords: whether for labour or for materials

options.text: No, because it is shown separately on the invoice instead of being built into the price
options.misconception: reads a separately shown cost as an excluded one
options.why: Rule 10(1) operates on costs that are not already included in the price. Showing an amount separately is what brings the rule into play, not what escapes it.

options.text: No — packing is a cost of getting the goods onto the ship, not a cost of the goods themselves
options.misconception: separates packing from the goods although the rule joins the two
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) names packing in terms and treats the container as one with the goods. It is not left to a view about which costs belong to what.

options.text: Yes, but only the cost of the crates; the packing labour is a service and stays out
options.misconception: splits the rule at the very point where its words refuse to split
options.why: The words are "whether for labour or for materials", put there to stop that division being made.

citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a), Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows the price of the machine parts and, listed separately below it, eighty-five thousand rupees for the wooden crates the parts were packed in and for the labour that packed them. The crates are not returnable.

items.stem: On what grounds may warehoused goods lawfully be taken out of a warehouse?

options.text: Only for home consumption, for export, for a move to another bonded warehouse, or as the Act otherwise allows
options.why: Section 71 shuts every door but four. Warehoused goods may leave only for home consumption, for export, for a removal to another warehouse, or on some other footing the Act or another law gives. Both of the importer's plans fit — a clearance for home consumption on payment of duty, and a removal to another warehouse under section 67.

options.text: On any ground the owner chooses, once he has executed the bond under section 59
options.misconception: treats the bond as a licence to deal with the goods at will
options.why: The bond secures the duty and the interest; it does not decide what may be done with the goods. Section 71 is the provision that lists the ways out.

options.text: Only for home consumption on payment of duty — a warehouse-to-warehouse move needs the goods to be cleared first
options.misconception: leaves out one of the routes section 71 expressly names
options.why: Removal to another warehouse is one of the routes in section 71, and it is carried out under section 67 without the duty being paid first.

options.text: Only for export, warehousing being a facility meant for goods that will leave India again
options.misconception: reads warehousing as an export facility alone
options.why: Warehousing defers the duty; it does not require the goods to be exported. Clearance for home consumption on payment of duty is the ordinary way they come out.

citation.ref: Section 71 read with sections 67 and 68

items.scenario: An importer has goods lying in a bonded warehouse. He has found a buyer in Pune who wants part of the lot for his own use, and he would like to move the rest to a bonded warehouse nearer that buyer.

items.stem: What has to be established first before drawback under section 74 can be claimed?

options.text: That the goods have not been used at all after importation
options.misconception: turns a factor that reduces the rate into an outright bar
options.why: Goods used after importation can still earn drawback, at a reduced rate prescribed by the rules. Use changes the amount, not the entitlement.
