options.why: Section 7(4) requires the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain the existence of a default within fourteen days of the receipt of the application. The proviso to section 7(5) then says the Adjudicating Authority shall, before rejecting an application under clause (b), give a notice to the applicant to rectify the defect in his application within seven days of the date of receipt of such notice. So neither the file nor the defect is left to sit.

options.text: To wait until the applicant completes the file, no period running against the Authority
options.misconception: leaves the Authority without a clock
options.why: Section 7(4) puts a period of fourteen days on the Authority itself, running from the receipt of the application.

options.text: To refer the application to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board for verification before admitting it
options.misconception: inserts a step the section does not contain
options.why: Section 7 routes the application from the creditor to the Adjudicating Authority. The Board proposes a name where none is offered; it does not vet the application.

citation.ref: Section 7(4) with the proviso to section 7(5)

items.scenario: A financial creditor files an application under section 7 against Thistlebank Ltd on 1 February 2026. The registry finds that one annexure is missing. The creditor is told the application will simply lie until he chooses to complete it.

items.stem: What does section 24 allow them?

options.text: Both may attend the meeting, and neither has any right to vote
options.why: Section 24(3) requires the resolution professional to give notice of each meeting to the members of the committee, to the members of the suspended Board of Directors or the partners of the corporate person, and to operational creditors whose aggregate dues reach the level the Code specifies. Section 24(4) then says the directors, partners and one representative of operational creditors may attend the meetings of the committee of creditors but shall not have any right to vote. Presence and voting are separated in terms.

options.text: Neither may attend, the committee's meetings being closed to everyone but financial creditors
options.misconception: shuts out people the section invites
options.why: Section 24(3) requires notice to go to them precisely so they can be present. The Code wants them in the room and out of the vote.

options.text: The operational creditor may attend and vote, while the suspended director may only attend
options.misconception: splits the sub-section unevenly
options.why: Section 24(4) names the directors, the partners and the representative of operational creditors in the same breath and denies the vote to all of them alike.

options.text: Both may attend and both may vote, notice under section 24(3) carrying a vote with it
options.misconception: reads a right to notice as a right to vote
options.why: Section 24(4) closes that door with the words that they shall not have any right to vote. The voting share belongs to the financial creditors on the committee.

citation.ref: Sections 24(3) and 24(4)

items.scenario: The resolution professional of Harefield Ltd calls a meeting of the committee of creditors. The suspended managing director asks to attend, and an operational creditor whose dues are large enough to qualify under the Code asks to attend as well. Both say that if they may sit in the room, they may vote.

items.stem: What does the liquidator do with that agreement?

options.text: He gives effect to it, a contract freely made between creditors binding the liquidation
options.misconception: lets private agreement override the statutory order
options.why: Section 53(2) is written to stop exactly that. An arrangement between equally ranking recipients that disrupts the order is disregarded.

options.text: He disregards it, and distributes to the two of them rateably as the order of priority requires
options.why: Section 53(2) says any contractual arrangement between recipients under section 53(1) with equal ranking, if disrupting the order of priority under that sub-section, shall be disregarded by the liquidator. The two creditors sit on the same rung, so their private agreement cannot reorder them, and the statutory sharing on that rung stands.

options.text: He gives effect to it only if the committee of creditors approved the agreement during the resolution process
options.misconception: revives the arrangement through a committee approval
options.why: Section 53(2) makes no exception for an approval by the committee. The disregard turns on equal ranking and disruption of the order, and nothing else.

options.text: He refers the agreement to the Adjudicating Authority for a ruling before distributing anything
options.misconception: turns a self-executing rule into a court application
options.why: The sub-section tells the liquidator himself to disregard the arrangement. No direction from the Authority is needed to do it.

citation.ref: Section 53(2)

items.scenario: Two unsecured financial creditors of Ravenhill Ltd, who rank on the same rung of the liquidation waterfall, signed an inter-creditor agreement years ago under which one of them is to be paid in full before the other receives anything. Both file their claims in the liquidation.

items.stem: Is he eligible to submit a resolution plan?

options.text: No — but only because he is a related party of the corporate debtor
options.misconception: reaches the right answer by the wrong clause
options.why: Nothing in the facts makes him a related party. What disqualifies him is the invoked and unpaid guarantee under clause (h).

options.text: Yes — a guarantee bars an applicant only after a decree has been passed against him on it
options.misconception: adds a decree the clause does not require
options.why: The clause turns on invocation and non-payment. It says nothing about a decree.

options.text: Yes — section 29A looks only at the applicant's own borrowings, and the default here belongs to another company
options.misconception: reads clause (h) as if it were about the applicant's own account
options.why: Clause (h) is written about a guarantee the applicant gave for somebody else's debt. That is the whole point of the clause.

options.text: No — a person whose guarantee in favour of a creditor of a corporate debtor under the Code has been invoked and remains unpaid is ineligible
options.why: Section 29A(h) makes a person ineligible to submit a resolution plan if he has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor in respect of a corporate debtor against which an application for insolvency resolution made by such creditor has been admitted under the Code, and such guarantee has been invoked by the creditor and remains unpaid in full or part. The clause looks at the invoked guarantee itself, not at whose borrowing it secured.

citation.ref: Section 29A(h)

items.scenario: A prospective resolution applicant for Coldharbour Ltd had guaranteed a loan taken by another company against which an application under the Code was admitted. The guarantee was invoked by the creditor and remains unpaid. The applicant says the default is that other company's, not his.

items.stem: What does Regulation 17(6)(a) require?

options.text: A board resolution is enough, the Regulations leaving directors' pay to the board
options.misconception: stops at the recommendation and drops the approval
options.why: The same sub-regulation carries both steps. The board recommends and the shareholders approve.

options.text: The board recommends the fees or compensation, and the shareholders must approve it in general meeting
options.why: Regulation 17(6)(a) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 says the board of directors shall recommend all fees or compensation, if any, paid to non-executive directors, including independent directors, and shall require approval of shareholders in general meeting. Disclosure in the annual report reports the payment; it does not authorise it.

options.text: Approval of the stock exchange before the payment is made
options.misconception: sends an internal approval to the exchange
options.why: Regulation 17(6)(a) asks for the shareholders' approval. The exchange receives disclosures; it does not sanction directors' pay.

options.text: Approval only where the payee is an independent director, an ordinary non-executive director being outside the sub-regulation
options.misconception: narrows the class the sub-regulation names
options.why: The sub-regulation covers non-executive directors and says "including independent directors", so independent directors are inside the class rather than the whole of it.

citation.source: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
citation.ref: Regulation 17(6)(a)

items.scenario: The board of Aldergate Ltd, a listed entity, resolves to pay its non-executive directors a commission for the year. The company secretary proposes to put the resolution in the board minutes and disclose the amounts in the annual report, without taking the matter to a general meeting.

items.stem: What does Regulation 33(1)(a) require?

options.text: Uniform practices across the periods, but the basis of accounting is free so long as it is disclosed
options.misconception: drops the accrual requirement and keeps only uniformity
options.why: The sub-regulation names accrual accounting policy in terms, alongside the requirement of uniform practices. Disclosure does not substitute for either.

options.text: Nothing on the basis of accounting — Regulation 33 fixes only the time limits for filing
options.misconception: reduces Regulation 33 to its clocks
options.why: The time limits sit in Regulation 33(3). Regulation 33(1) sets conditions on how the results are prepared before any of them is filed.

options.text: Accrual for the annual results only, quarterly results being permitted on any consistent basis
options.misconception: splits the requirement between annual and quarterly results
options.why: Regulation 33(1)(a) applies to the financial results the entity submits, which include the quarterly ones. It draws no distinction of that kind.

options.text: The results must be prepared on the basis of accrual accounting policy, and on uniform accounting practices adopted for all the periods
options.why: Regulation 33(1)(a) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 requires the financial results to be prepared on the basis of accrual accounting policy and to be in accordance with uniform accounting practices adopted for all the periods. Both halves are broken here: the first quarter is not on accrual, and the two quarters are not on the same practices.

citation.source: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
citation.ref: Regulation 33(1)(a)

items.scenario: A listed entity prepares its quarterly results on a cash basis for the first quarter, because collections were slow, and on an accrual basis for the second. The finance head says each quarter is a fresh start and the basis may be chosen to suit the period.

items.stem: What has the exporter got wrong under section 7 of the Act?

options.text: Nothing, so long as the whole of the money is eventually brought into India within the permitted period
options.misconception: treats realisation as the only obligation FEMA imposes on an exporter
options.why: Realisation is a separate duty under section 8 and the regulations made under it. Section 7 attaches its own duty at the point of export, to the declaration itself.

options.text: The declaration was not required at all, section 7 applying only to the export of services
options.misconception: inverts the two limbs of section 7
options.why: Section 7(1) addresses the exporter of goods. Services are dealt with separately in section 7(3), which does not displace the duty on goods.

options.text: The declaration furnished on export must contain true and correct material particulars, including the full export value
options.why: Section 7(1)(a) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 requires every exporter of goods to furnish to the specified authority a declaration in such form and in such manner as may be specified, containing true and correct material particulars, including the amount representing the full export value of the goods. Understating the invoice makes the declaration untrue at the moment it is furnished, and a later correction does not reach back to cure it.

options.text: Nothing under FEMA — an understated invoice is a customs valuation matter alone
options.misconception: assigns the whole question to another statute
options.why: Customs has its own valuation rules, and section 7 separately requires the FEMA declaration to state the full export value. Both apply to the same shipment.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

items.scenario: Wexley Exports Ltd ships a consignment of machine parts to a buyer in Rotterdam. The commercial team, keen to keep the paperwork light, records an invoice value well below the price actually agreed, intending to correct it when the money comes in. The shipment otherwise complies with every realisation requirement.

items.stem: What is his residential status under section 2(v) while he is away?

options.text: He becomes a person resident outside India from the day he leaves, any departure from India changing his status at once
options.misconception: treats physical departure as the whole of the test
options.why: The departure limb of section 2(v) works only where the person goes for employment, for business or vocation, or in circumstances showing an intention to stay away for an uncertain period. A short trip for a stated purpose is outside it.

options.text: He becomes a person resident outside India once he has been away for more than one hundred and eighty-two days in the current year
options.misconception: counts days in the current year rather than applying the purpose test
options.why: The day count in section 2(v) looks at the preceding financial year, and the purpose of the stay abroad then overrides it. Counting the current year's days is the Income-tax Act's method, not this one.

options.text: He remains a person resident in India, the purpose of his stay abroad showing no intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period
options.why: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 takes a person out of the class of a person resident in India when he goes out of or stays outside India for taking up employment outside India, for carrying on a business or vocation outside India, or for any other purpose in such circumstances as would indicate his intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period. Medical treatment for a fixed four months, with a job held open and a return ticket, is none of those, so his residence does not change.

options.text: His status depends on where his bank account is held, and redesignation itself changes it
options.misconception: lets a banking formality decide a statutory status
options.why: Section 2(v) fixes the status and the bank account follows from it. Redesignating an account does not move a person from one class to the other.

citation.ref: Section 2(v)

items.scenario: Mr Sen, who has lived and worked in Kolkata all his life, goes to Singapore on 5 May 2026 for a four-month course of medical treatment, with a return ticket and his job in India held open for him. His bank asks whether his accounts must be redesignated because he is now abroad.

items.stem: Is quorum met for transacting this item of business?

options.text: No — a nine-member board always needs a fixed quorum of two directors regardless of interest
options.misconception: miscalculates the quorum threshold itself as a flat number
options.why: Quorum is the higher of one-third of total strength or two — for nine directors that is three, not two. Getting the base threshold wrong does not land on the right answer for the wrong reason here, since the exclusion of the interested director is also needed.
keywords: Quorum is the higher of one-third of total strength or two
for nine directors that is three, not two

options.text: Yes — three directors are physically present, and quorum for a nine-member board is three
options.misconception: includes the interested director in the count for the very item he is interested in
options.why: The threshold of three is correct, but the interested director must be excluded when the board takes up a matter he is interested in, leaving only two — short of quorum.
keywords: The threshold of three is correct
the interested director must be excluded

options.text: No — quorum needs the higher of one-third of nine (three, rounded up) or two, phone-in assent does not count as presence, and the interested director drops out of the count for this item, leaving only two eligible directors
options.why: Section 174 fixes quorum by total strength, not by whoever answers the phone, and section 184(2) removes the interested director from the count on a matter he is interested in. Three present minus one interested leaves two — short of the three the board's size demands.
keywords: Section 174 fixes quorum by total strength
removes the interested director from the count

options.text: Yes — five directors have indicated participation, well past any quorum threshold
options.misconception: counts telephonic assent as attendance for quorum purposes
options.why: A phone call is not the participation the Act recognises for quorum; only physical presence or the prescribed video-conferencing route counts. The two calling in are not part of the count at all.
keywords: A phone call is not the participation the Act recognises
only physical presence or the prescribed video-conferencing route counts

citation.ref: Section 174

items.scenario: A private company's board has nine directors in total. At a meeting called to approve a large capital purchase, three directors are physically present and two more directors ring in by phone call, insisting the chairman count them as present. One of the three directors physically present holds a personal interest in the very purchase being discussed.

items.stem: Is the certificate correct?

options.text: No — the hundred-and-twenty-day cap runs from the start of the calendar year, not between meetings
options.misconception: measures the gap from a fixed calendar point instead of between consecutive meetings
options.why: The cap is on the interval between one meeting and the next, wherever in the year they fall — not on distance from New Year's Day.
keywords: The cap is on the interval between one meeting and the next
not on distance from New Year's Day

options.text: No — the gap between the February and June meetings runs to roughly a hundred and twenty-five days, breaching the cap between two consecutive meetings regardless of the total count
options.why: Section 173 tests two things together — at least four meetings a year, and no gap between consecutive meetings beyond one hundred and twenty days. Five meetings satisfies the first test and fails the second; failing either breaches the section.
keywords: at least four meetings a year

options.text: Yes — the company held five meetings against a minimum of four, so the section is satisfied
options.misconception: treats the meeting count alone as the whole test
options.why: Meeting the headcount does not cure an oversized gap between two of the meetings. Both conditions must hold at once.
keywords: does not cure an oversized gap
Both conditions must hold at once

options.text: Yes — the hundred-and-twenty-day cap binds only small companies and one person companies, not a full public company
options.misconception: reverses which class carries the relaxed norm
options.why: The relaxed norm — one meeting each half-year, ninety-day gap — is for one person companies, small companies, dormant companies and private start-ups. A public company of this kind sits under the general four-meetings, hundred-and-twenty-day rule.
keywords: one meeting each half-year, ninety-day gap
A public company of this kind sits under the general four-meetings

citation.ref: Section 173

items.scenario: A public company holds board meetings on 1 January, 20 February, 25 June, 1 November and 15 December of the same year — five meetings in all. The company secretary certifies compliance with section 173, noting five meetings exceeds the minimum of four.

items.stem: Is the board's resolution enough to make the sale valid?

options.text: No, but only an ordinary resolution — not a special resolution — is needed given the business purpose
options.misconception: understates which class of resolution the section demands
options.why: Section 180(1)(a) names a special resolution specifically. An ordinary resolution does not meet the bar regardless of how sound the business rationale is.
keywords: An ordinary resolution does not meet the bar

options.text: No — selling substantially the whole undertaking needs a special resolution of the shareholders obtained before the sale, not an after-the-fact intimation
options.why: Section 180(1)(a) puts this class of disposal outside ordinary board power. The board may negotiate and execute only after the shareholders have cleared it by special resolution — informing them afterward reverses the sequence the section requires.
keywords: puts this class of disposal outside ordinary board power
informing them afterward reverses the sequence

options.text: Yes, once shareholders are informed of the completed sale at the next general meeting
options.misconception: treats post-facto shareholder intimation as equivalent to prior approval
options.why: Section 180 conditions the board's power on shareholder approval before the act, not disclosure after it. A completed sale cannot be retrofitted into compliance.
keywords: shareholder approval before the act, not disclosure after it

options.text: Yes — running the business, including disposing of its units, is squarely within the board's general management power
options.misconception: treats the board's general management power as covering a section 180 restriction
options.why: Section 180 is precisely a carve-out from the board's general power for a defined list of major acts. Substantially the whole undertaking is on that list.
keywords: a carve-out from the board's general power
Substantially the whole undertaking is on that list

citation.ref: Section 180

items.scenario: A company's board, by an ordinary resolution passed at a properly convened meeting, sells a manufacturing unit that makes up eighty-two per cent of the company's total assets and seventy-five per cent of its turnover, to fund an unrelated real-estate purchase. Shareholders learn of the sale only after the sale deed is executed.

items.stem: Does the articles clause achieve what the company claims?

options.text: No — independent directors are outside rotation by law already, but at least two-thirds of the six remaining directors, rounded up, must still be liable to rotation regardless of what the articles say
options.why: Section 152(6) sets a statutory floor for the non-independent directors. Two-thirds of six is four; the articles can arrange which four rotate and when, but cannot excuse the board from having any rotational directors at all.
keywords: sets a statutory floor for the non-independent directors
cannot excuse the board from having any rotational directors

options.text: No — because two-thirds of the full board of nine, not of the six non-independent directors, must be rotational
options.misconception: applies the two-thirds fraction to the wrong base
options.why: The fraction runs against the directors capable of being rotational — the board minus its independent directors — not against total board strength.
keywords: the directors capable of being rotational

options.text: Yes — articles can validly disapply rotation for the whole board, since section 152 defers to what the articles provide
options.misconception: reads the articles as able to override the statutory two-thirds floor
options.why: The articles choose how the rotating group works, not whether it exists. The two-thirds requirement is not one the articles can contract out of.
keywords: how the rotating group works, not whether it exists
not one the articles can contract out of

options.text: No — because independent directors must also be counted in the two-thirds pool of rotational directors
options.misconception: includes independent directors in the pool subject to rotation
options.why: Independent directors are excluded from rotation altogether under the Act; the two-thirds test is applied only to the directors who are not independent.
keywords: Independent directors are excluded from rotation altogether
applied only to the directors who are not independent

citation.ref: Section 152(6)

items.scenario: A public company has nine directors — three independent directors and six others, including the managing director. Its articles state that no director shall be liable to retire by rotation, and the company treats this as a complete exemption from section 152.

items.stem: Has he satisfied section 184?

options.text: Yes — having disclosed his interest, he is then free to participate and vote on the contract
options.misconception: treats disclosure as converting the specific vote into a lawful one
options.why: Disclosure is the first half of the duty; abstention from discussion and voting on that contract is the second half. One does not substitute for the other.
keywords: abstention from discussion and voting on that contract
One does not substitute for the other

options.text: Yes — an annual disclosure made at the first board meeting of the year covers every contract that comes up later that year
options.misconception: conflates the standing annual disclosure with the separate item-specific duty to abstain
options.why: The annual disclosure records the existence of the interest; it does not clear him to take part when a contract touching that very interest is actually discussed.
keywords: records the existence of the interest
does not clear him to take part

options.text: No — because his twenty-five per cent holding falls below the shareholding percentage that triggers disclosure
options.misconception: invents a shareholding threshold that section 184 does not set
options.why: The disclosure duty attaches to any concern or interest, however small; there is no minimum-holding gate under section 184 that has to be crossed first.
keywords: attaches to any concern or interest, however small
there is no minimum-holding gate under section 184

options.text: No — disclosure does not license participation; he must not take part in the discussion or vote on this contract, and the duty to disclose arose regardless of any shareholding threshold
options.why: Section 184(1) requires disclosure of general interest; section 184(2) separately bars an interested director from discussing or voting on the specific contract. Disclosing and then voting satisfies neither purpose the split duty serves.
keywords: bars an interested director from discussing or voting
satisfies neither purpose the split duty serves

citation.ref: Section 184

items.scenario: A director of a public company holds twenty-five per cent of a private company that supplies raw material to the public company. At the board meeting where a new supply contract with that private company comes up, he discloses his interest verbally for the first time that financial year, then goes on to join the discussion and vote in favour, believing the disclosure itself is what the section required.

items.stem: Is the refusal correct under section 190?

options.text: Yes — employment terms are confidential personnel records outside members' inspection rights generally
options.misconception: treats the record as shielded HR confidentiality
options.why: Section 190 carves this specific record out of ordinary confidentiality and makes it an inspectable document by name.
keywords: carves this specific record out of ordinary confidentiality

options.text: No — the company must keep the managing director's contract of service, or a memorandum of its terms, open for inspection by members without charge at the registered office
options.why: Section 190 makes this a members' right, not a board-and-auditor privilege. The contract or its memorandum sits at the registered office precisely so any member can walk in and look.
keywords: makes this a members' right, not a board-and-auditor privilege

options.text: Yes — only the board and the statutory auditor have a right to see the managing director's contract terms
options.misconception: narrows the inspecting class to board and auditor, excluding members
options.why: The section names members as the inspecting class. Board and auditor access is a separate matter and does not exhaust the right the section creates.
keywords: names members as the inspecting class
does not exhaust the right the section creates

options.text: No, but only after the shareholder pays the prescribed inspection fee
options.misconception: invents a fee where the section requires free inspection
options.why: Section 190 requires inspection to be allowed without charge; a fee is not part of the right it grants.
keywords: inspection to be allowed without charge
a fee is not part of the right it grants

citation.ref: Section 190

items.scenario: A shareholder of a public company writes to the company secretary asking to inspect the managing director's employment contract at the registered office. The company secretary refuses, saying employment terms are private personnel records that only the board and the statutory auditor may see.

items.stem: Is the CFO's proposal compliant with section 129(3)?

options.text: Yes — a subsidiary audited separately need not also be folded into the consolidated statement
options.misconception: treats a standalone audit as a substitute for consolidation
options.why: The separate audit produces the subsidiary's own true-and-fair opinion; it says nothing about whether the holding company's consolidated picture is complete without it.
keywords: says nothing about whether the holding company's consolidated picture is complete

options.text: No — every subsidiary is consolidated, profitable or not, and the company must lay a complete consolidated financial statement before the annual general meeting in addition to the standalone statements
options.why: Section 129(3) attaches to the holding company the moment it has a subsidiary, and the consolidation follows the applicable accounting standards across all of them. Selecting which subsidiaries to fold in is not a choice the section leaves to management.
keywords: the moment it has a subsidiary
not a choice the section leaves to management

options.text: Yes — a company may consolidate whichever subsidiaries it considers material to group performance
options.misconception: treats consolidation scope as a management discretion
options.why: Materiality by profitability is not a filter the section recognises. The obligation runs to every subsidiary once the threshold of having one is crossed.
keywords: Materiality by profitability is not a filter

options.text: No — but consolidated financial statements are required only once a company has more than three subsidiaries
options.misconception: invents a numeric gate on the number of subsidiaries
options.why: The obligation is triggered by having one or more subsidiaries, not by crossing any particular count of them.
keywords: triggered by having one or more subsidiaries
not by crossing any particular count

citation.ref: Section 129(3)

items.scenario: A listed holding company has three subsidiaries, one of which is loss-making. The CFO proposes preparing only the standalone financial statements and consolidating the two profitable subsidiaries alone, on the ground that the loss-making one drags down group numbers and is separately audited in any case.

items.stem: Is this board's report compliant with section 134?

options.text: Yes — section 186 particulars belong in the notes to accounts, not the board's report, so their absence here is immaterial
options.misconception: relocates a board's-report requirement into the financial statements
options.why: Section 134(3) names the board's report as the place these particulars sit; the notes to accounts serving a different disclosure does not excuse the report's own omission.
keywords: names the board's report as the place these particulars sit
does not excuse the report's own omission

options.text: No — the director's responsibility statement and the section 186 particulars must actually appear in the report, and "available on request" does not stand in for inclusion
options.why: Section 134(3) lists these as matters the report states; making them available separately, on request, is not the same as annexing them to the report the members receive with the notice of the AGM.
keywords: lists these as matters the report states
is not the same as annexing them to the report

options.text: No, but only because the director's responsibility statement is missing — private and unlisted public companies need not disclose section 186 particulars in the report
options.misconception: exempts non-listed companies from a requirement that is not tied to listing status
options.why: Section 134(3) requires section 186 particulars in the board's report generally; nothing in the clause confines it to listed companies.
keywords: requires section 186 particulars in the board's report generally
nothing in the clause confines it to listed companies

options.text: Yes — "available on request" satisfies the section so long as the particulars exist somewhere in the company's records
options.misconception: treats availability on request as equivalent to mandatory inclusion
options.why: The section requires the report to state these particulars, not merely that they can be produced if asked for.
keywords: requires the report to state these particulars
not merely that they can be produced if asked for

citation.ref: Section 134(3)

items.scenario: An unlisted public company above the prescribed size lines files a board's report stating only the dividend recommended and the state of the company's affairs, adding a line that "other prescribed particulars are available on request from the company secretary." The director's responsibility statement and the particulars of loans and investments under section 186 are both absent from the report itself.

items.stem: What is wrong here, if anything?

options.text: Filing is late against the sixty-day window running from the AGM, and at ₹12 crore of paid-up capital the return must separately carry a practising company secretary's certificate in Form MGT-8
options.why: Section 92(4) counts the sixty days from the date the AGM is held, not from the financial year end, so 5 December is six days late. Rule 11(2) requires certification by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8 for a listed company or one with paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more or turnover of ₹50 crore or more; ₹12 crore of capital crosses the first of those on its own.
keywords: counts the sixty days from the date the AGM is held, not from the financial year end
crosses the first of those on its own

options.text: Nothing is wrong — turnover is only ₹30 crore, below the ₹50 crore line, so no practising company secretary's certificate is needed
options.misconception: treats the two size tests as cumulative when either one on its own triggers the certificate
options.why: Rule 11(2) reads "paid-up share capital of ten crore rupees or more or turnover of fifty crore rupees or more". They are alternatives. Falling short on turnover does not rescue a company that is over the capital line — and the late filing stands in any case.
keywords: Falling short on turnover does not rescue a company that is over the capital line
the late filing stands in any case

options.text: Filing is on time, since the sixty days run from the financial year end rather than from the AGM
options.misconception: measures the filing window from the wrong reference date
options.why: The clock in section 92(4) starts at the AGM — or, where none was held, at the date by which it should have been held, with a statement of the reasons — not at the financial year's close.
keywords: not at the financial year's close

options.text: The in-house certification is adequate at this company's size, and only the filing date is a problem
options.misconception: accepts in-house certification as satisfying the practising-CS requirement
options.why: The annual return is signed by the company secretary or a director under section 92(1); Form MGT-8 is a separate, outside certificate from a company secretary in practice, and the company's own officers cannot supply it in place of him.
keywords: Form MGT-8 is a separate, outside certificate
the company's own officers cannot supply it

citation.ref: Sections 92(2) and 92(4), read with Rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 (Form MGT-8)

items.scenario: An unlisted public company's annual general meeting for the year was held on 30 September. Its annual return is filed sixty-six days later, on 5 December. The company's paid-up share capital is ₹12 crore and its turnover ₹30 crore, but the return carries only an in-house certification from the company's own officers.

items.stem: Does this rights issue process comply with section 62?

options.text: No, but only because the offer period requirement is directory and best practice, not a binding minimum
options.misconception: treats the statutory minimum as merely advisory
options.why: Section 62(1)(a) fixes the fifteen-to-thirty-day window as a binding condition of the offer, not a discretionary target the board may shorten for convenience.
keywords: a binding condition of the offer
not a discretionary target the board may shorten

options.text: Yes — a shorter offer period is acceptable so long as every shareholder is notified on the same day
options.misconception: treats simultaneous notice as a substitute for the minimum offer period
options.why: Simultaneous notice answers a fairness concern about timing between shareholders; it does not shorten the fifteen-day floor the section itself sets.
keywords: does not shorten the fifteen-day floor
Simultaneous notice answers a fairness concern

options.text: No — the offer must stay open at least fifteen days, so a nine-day window falls short, and allotment cannot close out shareholders' renunciation rights before they are exercised or declined
options.why: Section 62(1)(a) sets the offer period at not less than fifteen and not more than thirty days, and preserves the right to renounce in favour of another person unless the articles exclude it. Rushing allotment defeats both protections at once.
keywords: the offer period at not less than fifteen
preserves the right to renounce in favour of another person

options.text: Yes — renunciation rights arise only where the articles expressly grant them, and these articles are silent
options.misconception: reverses the default position on renunciation
options.why: The right of renunciation is the default under section 62(1)(a) unless the articles exclude it — silence in the articles leaves the default right standing, not absent.
keywords: The right of renunciation is the default
silence in the articles leaves the default right standing

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(a)

items.scenario: A company sends rights issue offer letters to all its equity shareholders on 1 March, in the ratio of one new share for every five held, stating the offer closes on 10 March — nine days later — and that allotment will follow immediately on closure without waiting on any renunciation requests, "to save time."

items.stem: Is the finance team's view correct?

options.text: No — section 71(5) bars a prospectus for debentures unless a debenture trustee is appointed before the offer, with the trust deed executed within sixty days of allotment, and the issuer's own guarantee does not stand in for that independent office
options.why: Section 71(5) attaches to the kind of offer: a prospectus, or an invitation to the public or to more than five hundred members. A public issue on a prospectus is inside it whatever the amount. Rule 18(1)(c) fixes the timing at both ends. The trustee exists precisely because the issuer's own assurance is not an independent check on the issuer's own security — the trustee holds the charge and enforces it for debenture-holders who cannot negotiate individually.
keywords: attaches to the kind of offer
the issuer's own assurance is not an independent check

options.text: No, but only because a trustee is required for unsecured debentures, and this issue is secured
options.misconception: reverses which kind of issue needs closer independent protection
options.why: A secured issue still needs a trustee to hold and enforce that very security on debenture-holders' behalf. Security is not what triggers section 71(5), and unsecured issues do not sit outside it either.
keywords: A secured issue still needs a trustee
Security is not what triggers section 71(5)

options.text: Yes — the company's own guarantee is functionally equivalent to an independent trustee's protection
options.misconception: treats the issuer's self-guarantee as equivalent to an independent trustee
options.why: A guarantee from the very party debenture-holders need protection against cannot supply the independence the trustee requirement exists for.
keywords: from the very party debenture-holders need protection against
cannot supply the independence the trustee requirement exists for

options.text: Yes — the trustee requirement bites only above a prescribed rupee size of issue, and forty crore is below that line
options.misconception: reads a money threshold into a requirement that turns on the kind of offer
options.why: Section 71(5) names no rupee figure anywhere. It is the prospectus, or the invitation to the public or to more than five hundred members, that pulls the trustee in. A private placement to twenty identified investors of the same forty crore would sit outside the sub-section; this public issue does not.

citation.ref: Section 71(5), read with Rule 18(1)(c) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company plans a public issue, on a prospectus, of secured debentures worth forty crore rupees, to be listed. Its finance team argues no debenture trustee is needed because the issue already carries the company's own guarantee over its assets, which they consider sufficient security for subscribers.

items.stem: Which of these three steps can lawfully proceed during the moratorium?

options.text: Only the suit against the promoter under the personal guarantee
options.why: Section 14 bars suits against the corporate debtor and enforcement of security interests over its assets — the eviction suit and the pledge enforcement both fall inside that bar. The moratorium expressly does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee for the corporate debtor, so the promoter can still be sued personally.
keywords: bars suits against the corporate debtor and enforcement of security interests
does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee

options.text: All three, since the moratorium protects the company and everyone connected with its debts equally
options.misconception: extends the moratorium's protection to the personal guarantor
options.why: The moratorium protects the corporate debtor's assets and proceedings against it — it was never meant to let a personal guarantor hide behind the company's insolvency, and the Code says so directly.
keywords: protects the corporate debtor's assets and proceedings against it
never meant to let a personal guarantor hide behind the company's insolvency

options.text: The landlord's suit, since rent already accrued is a pre-existing right rather than a new claim
options.misconception: misreads the suit bar as applying only to fresh claims
options.why: Section 14 bars institution or continuation of suits against the corporate debtor without regard to when the underlying claim arose — an accrued but unenforced claim is exactly what the moratorium freezes.
keywords: without regard to when the underlying claim arose
an accrued but unenforced claim is exactly what the moratorium freezes

options.text: The pledge enforcement, since a pledge is a possessory security sitting outside the moratorium
options.misconception: invents a pledge exception to the security-enforcement bar
options.why: Section 14 bars enforcement of any security interest created by the corporate debtor, without carving out possessory forms such as a pledge.
keywords: bars enforcement of any security interest
without carving out possessory forms such as a pledge

citation.ref: Section 14

items.scenario: Three days after the Adjudicating Authority admits a corporate insolvency resolution application against a company, its landlord — owed six months' rent — files a civil suit for eviction and recovery, and a bank enforces a pledge it holds over the company's shares as security for a loan. Separately, the same bank sues the promoter, who had personally guaranteed the company's debt.

items.stem: Which statement about this timeline is correct?

options.text: The resolution carries, because a committee of creditors decides everything by a simple majority of fifty-one per cent of voting share
options.misconception: applies the section 21(8) default vote to a decision the Code has separately fixed
options.why: Fifty-one per cent under section 21(8) is the default for ordinary committee decisions. Extension of the process is one of the matters the Code takes out of that default — section 12(2) names sixty-six per cent, as do section 28(3) and section 30(4).
keywords: the default for ordinary committee decisions
one of the matters the Code takes out of that default

options.text: A second extension of sixty days is available so long as the total stays within three hundred and thirty days
options.misconception: reads the outer cap as a budget the committee may keep drawing extensions against
options.why: The three-hundred-and-thirty-day figure is a ceiling, not an entitlement. Section 12 permits one extension of up to ninety days and no more; the ceiling does not create a second one.
keywords: the ceiling does not create a second one

options.text: Time spent in litigation is excluded from the statutory clock, so the process has plenty of room and a second extension is unnecessary
options.misconception: treats litigation time as an exclusion when the 2019 amendment wrote it into the cap
options.why: The proviso to section 12(3) was inserted precisely to stop that argument. It requires completion within three hundred and thirty days "including any extension of the period of corporate insolvency resolution process granted under this section and the time taken in legal proceedings".
keywords: was inserted precisely to stop that argument
requires completion within three hundred and thirty days

options.text: The extension resolution fails at sixty per cent because section 12(2) needs sixty-six per cent of voting share, only one extension of up to ninety days is ever available, and the forty-five days lost in court sit inside the three-hundred-and-thirty-day outer limit rather than outside it
options.why: Section 12(2) fixes the committee's extension vote at sixty-six per cent, so a sixty per cent resolution does not carry. Section 12(1) and (2) allow a single extension of up to ninety days, not a series of them. The proviso to section 12(3) caps the process at three hundred and thirty days from the insolvency commencement date and says in terms that the time taken in legal proceedings relating to the process is counted within it.
keywords: fixes the committee's extension vote at sixty-six per cent
a single extension of up to ninety days, not a series of them
caps the process at three hundred and thirty days

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and the proviso to section 12(3)

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process against a steel company commences on 1 April 2026. On 10 September 2026 the committee of creditors, by a vote of sixty per cent of voting share, resolves to instruct the resolution professional to seek a ninety-day extension. A promoter's writ petition then keeps the process in court for forty-five days. In February 2027 the resolution professional proposes asking for a second extension of sixty days.

items.stem: How should the resolution professional have constituted the committee, and what happens to that claim?

options.text: All three are correctly on the committee, because a genuine financial debt supported by banking evidence carries voting rights whoever the lender is
options.misconception: treats proof of the debt as proof of the right to vote
options.why: Genuineness of the debt is what gets a creditor admitted. The proviso to section 21(2) then asks a different question — is this creditor a related party of the corporate debtor — and answers it against the promoter-owned lender regardless of how clean the money trail is.
keywords: Genuineness of the debt is what gets a creditor admitted
regardless of how clean the money trail is

options.text: The promoter-owned finance company is a related party under section 5(24) and the first proviso to section 21(2) denies it representation, participation and voting — but its ₹20 crore claim stands admitted as financial debt and is paid in its class, and Ind AS 24 still requires the relationship to be disclosed
options.why: The proviso to section 21(2) removes a related-party financial creditor from the committee's decision-making so insiders cannot steer the outcome. It says nothing about the debt itself, which remains admitted and shares in distribution. Ind AS 24's disclosure duty is a financial reporting duty and runs independently of who may vote.
keywords: removes a related-party financial creditor from the committee's decision-making
It says nothing about the debt itself
runs independently of who may vote

options.text: The finance company keeps its vote because "related party" for this purpose takes its meaning from section 2(76) of the Companies Act, which does not reach a promoter's separate company
options.misconception: borrows the Companies Act definition where the Code supplies its own, wider one
options.why: Section 5(24) of the Code has its own definition of related party, deliberately wider than section 2(76) of the Companies Act, and it is that definition the proviso to section 21(2) uses.
keywords: has its own definition of related party, deliberately wider
it is that definition the proviso to section 21(2) uses

options.text: The related-party finance company loses both its vote and its claim, so the ₹20 crore is extinguished on constitution of the committee
options.misconception: reads exclusion from the committee as extinguishment of the debt
options.why: Nothing in section 21 extinguishes a claim. Only a resolution plan approved under section 31, or a distribution under section 53 in liquidation, decides what a creditor is paid.
keywords: Nothing in section 21 extinguishes a claim
decides what a creditor is paid

citation.ref: Sections 5(24) and the first proviso to section 21(2), read with Ind AS 24

items.scenario: A corporate debtor's financial creditors are a bank owed ₹120 crore, a mutual fund owed ₹60 crore, and a non-banking finance company owed ₹20 crore that is wholly owned by the corporate debtor's promoter. The resolution professional admits all three claims, then constitutes the committee of creditors with all three as voting members, reasoning that the finance company's debt is a genuine financial debt fully supported by bank transfers. The corporate debtor's auditor separately asks whether the finance company must still appear in the related party note.

items.stem: How are the ₹100 crore applied?

options.text: ₹8 crore to costs, then the secured bank's ₹70 crore in full ahead of workmen because a secured creditor always outranks employees
options.misconception: keeps the secured creditor above workmen when section 53(1)(b) ranks them equally
options.why: Section 53(1)(b) puts workmen's dues for the twenty-four months and the debts of a secured creditor who relinquished security on the same rung, to be shared rateably. There is no priority between them.
keywords: There is no priority between them
on the same rung, to be shared rateably

options.text: ₹22 crore to workmen first as an overriding preferential payment under section 326 of the Companies Act, then ₹8 crore of costs, then the secured bank
options.misconception: applies the Companies Act preferential payments to a liquidation governed by the Code
options.why: Section 327(7) of the Companies Act says sections 326 and 327 do not apply in the event of liquidation under the Code. The waterfall in section 53 is the only order that operates, and it puts costs above everything.
keywords: The waterfall in section 53 is the only order that operates

options.text: ₹8 crore to costs first, then the remaining ₹92 crore shared rateably between the ₹22 crore of workmen's dues and the ₹70 crore of the relinquishing secured bank, which rank equally — leaving nothing for the other employees or the government, and section 326 has no application because section 327(7) shuts it out of an IBC liquidation
options.why: Section 53(1)(a) takes the process and liquidation costs in full. Clause (b) then puts workmen's dues for twenty-four months and a relinquishing secured creditor's debt on the same rung, sharing rateably — ₹92 crore against ₹92 crore of claims here, so that rung absorbs the lot. Employees other than workmen sit in clause (c) and government dues in clause (e), both below it. Section 327(7) of the Companies Act expressly disapplies sections 326 and 327 in a liquidation under the Code, which the Supreme Court upheld in Moser Baer Karamchari Union.
keywords: takes the process and liquidation costs in full
on the same rung, sharing rateably
expressly disapplies sections 326 and 327 in a liquidation under the Code

options.text: ₹8 crore to costs, then government dues of ₹15 crore as a Crown debt, then the rest down the waterfall
options.misconception: carries the old common-law priority of Crown debts into the Code's waterfall
options.why: Government dues sit in clause (e) of section 53(1), below workmen, below secured creditors who relinquished, below other employees and below unsecured financial creditors. The Code deliberately demoted them.

citation.ref: Section 53(1), read with section 327(7) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company goes into liquidation under the Code. Realisations are ₹100 crore. Liquidation and process costs are ₹8 crore. Workmen's dues for the twenty-four months before the liquidation commencement date are ₹22 crore. A secured bank owed ₹70 crore has relinquished its security into the liquidation estate. Employees other than workmen are owed ₹9 crore for the preceding twelve months, and government dues for the preceding two years are ₹15 crore. The workmen's union argues that section 326 of the Companies Act gives their dues an overriding priority ahead of everything, including the process costs.

items.stem: Is the promoter eligible to submit the resolution plan?

options.text: No — section 240A lifts only clauses (c) and (h) of section 29A for an MSME, so the non-performing asset and the invoked guarantee stop being disqualifications, but clause (b) on an undischarged insolvent stands and defeats him
options.why: Section 240A is a narrow window, not a general amnesty for MSME promoters. It names clauses (c) and (h) and nothing else. Every other limb of section 29A — including clause (b), an undischarged insolvent — continues to apply, and section 30(4) makes the committee check eligibility before it approves any plan.
keywords: a narrow window, not a general amnesty for MSME promoters
It names clauses (c) and (h) and nothing else
an undischarged insolvent — continues to apply

options.text: Yes — section 240A takes the whole of section 29A out of play for a corporate debtor that is an MSME
options.misconception: reads section 240A as switching off all of section 29A rather than two clauses
options.why: Section 240A is drafted by reference to clauses (c) and (h) specifically. Reading it as the whole section would let a convicted or disqualified applicant bid for any small enterprise, which is exactly what the section does not do.
keywords: drafted by reference to clauses (c) and (h) specifically
which is exactly what the section does not do

options.text: No — because the non-performing asset classification is more than one year old, which is itself a permanent bar for any resolution applicant
options.misconception: keeps clause (c) alive against an MSME promoter when section 240A removes it
options.why: Clause (c) is one of the two clauses section 240A switches off for an MSME. Ageing of the non-performing asset is what makes clause (c) bite in the ordinary case, and here that clause does not apply at all. The bar comes from clause (b).
keywords: one of the two clauses section 240A switches off

options.text: Yes — the committee of creditors may waive section 29A by a sixty-six per cent vote where the plan maximises value
options.misconception: treats an eligibility bar as something a supermajority can vote away
options.why: Section 29A is a statutory disqualification. Section 30(4) requires the committee to confirm eligibility before approving a plan; it gives the committee no power to excuse ineligibility at any voting percentage.
keywords: no power to excuse ineligibility at any voting percentage

citation.ref: Sections 29A(b), 29A(c), 29A(h), 30(4) and 240A

items.scenario: A corporate debtor is a registered small enterprise under the MSMED Act, 2006. Its promoter wants to submit a resolution plan. His personal account was classified as a non-performing asset three years before the insolvency commencement date, and a guarantee he gave to the company's bank was invoked and remains unpaid. He is also an undischarged insolvent in a separate personal bankruptcy that is still running. The committee of creditors is minded to accept his plan, relying on section 240A.

items.stem: Is the auditor right?

options.text: Yes on the second point only — the threshold is met, but a resolution professional takes over management in a pre-packaged process exactly as he does in a corporate insolvency resolution process
options.misconception: carries the section 17 displacement of the board into Chapter III-A
options.why: The pre-packaged process was built so that a small business is not paralysed by losing its own management. The board continues to run the company; the resolution professional supervises and reports rather than replacing it.
keywords: The board continues to run the company
supervises and reports rather than replacing it

options.text: No on both counts — the minimum default for a pre-packaged process is ten lakh rupees under S.O. 1543(E), so ₹40 lakh qualifies, and the pre-packaged process leaves management with the existing board under the supervision of a resolution professional
options.why: The second proviso to section 4 lets the Central Government notify a lower minimum for Chapter III-A, and S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021 fixed it at ten lakh rupees. Chapter III-A is a debtor-in-possession process: unlike a corporate insolvency resolution process under section 17, the board is not displaced. Eligibility, the sixty-six per cent approval of unrelated financial creditors and the base resolution plan are all satisfied here.
keywords: fixed it at ten lakh rupees

options.text: No — the threshold is met, but the approval needed is sixty-six per cent of all financial creditors including the related ones, so sixty-eight per cent of unrelated creditors is not the right test
options.misconception: counts related financial creditors into a threshold section 54A measures without them
options.why: Section 54A requires the approval of financial creditors of the corporate debtor who are not its related parties, representing not less than sixty-six per cent in value of the financial debt owed to such creditors. Related parties are excluded from both sides of the fraction, not added in.
keywords: Related parties are excluded from both sides of the fraction, not added in

options.text: Yes — one crore rupees is the minimum default for every process under the Code, so a ₹40 lakh default cannot start anything
options.misconception: applies the general section 4 threshold to Chapter III-A, missing the separate notification
options.why: One crore rupees is the notified minimum for an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process. The second proviso to section 4 provides for a separate, lower minimum for the pre-packaged process, and that minimum is ten lakh rupees.
keywords: the notified minimum for an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process
a separate, lower minimum for the pre-packaged process

citation.ref: Sections 54A and 54C, read with the second proviso to section 4 and notification S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021

items.scenario: A private company registered as a micro enterprise under the MSMED Act, 2006 has defaulted on ₹40 lakh owed to its bank. Its board wants to use the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process. Financial creditors who are unrelated to the company and hold sixty-eight per cent in value of the financial debt have given their approval, and the board has drawn up a base resolution plan. The company's auditor advises that the application cannot be made because ₹40 lakh is below the one crore rupee minimum default under section 4, and that the board will in any case be displaced the moment the process starts.

items.stem: What still has to be done, and by when?

options.text: Form FC-GPR must still be filed with the Reserve Bank not later than thirty days from the date of issue — by 20 July 2026 — because the return of allotment under section 42(8) and the FEMA report under Regulation 4(1) are separate filings to separate authorities
options.why: Section 42(8) required the return of allotment within fifteen days of the 20 June allotment, and 2 July meets it, unlocking the money under section 42(4). Regulation 4(1) of the FEM (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019 separately requires the issue to be reported in Form FC-GPR within thirty days of the date of issue. One filing never discharges the other, and Regulation 5 attaches a late submission fee to a delay.
keywords: reported in Form FC-GPR within thirty days of the date of issue
One filing never discharges the other

options.text: The return of allotment was itself late, because a private placement allotment must be reported to the Registrar within thirty days
options.misconception: applies the general thirty-day return of allotment to a private placement
options.why: Section 42(8) fixes fifteen days from the date of allotment for a private placement. Twenty June to 2 July is twelve days, so the filing was in time.
keywords: fixes fifteen days from the date of allotment for a private placement
so the filing was in time

options.text: Nothing further — the return of allotment filed with the Registrar is the statutory report of the issue, and the Reserve Bank draws on the Registrar's records
options.misconception: treats one regulator's filing as satisfying the other's
options.why: FEMA imposes its own reporting duty on the company in Form FC-GPR. The Reserve Bank does not take the Registrar's filing as its report, and no provision transmits one to the other.
keywords: does not take the Registrar's filing as its report
no provision transmits one to the other

options.text: Form FC-GPR is due within thirty days of the receipt of consideration, so the deadline was 4 June 2026 and the filing is already late
options.misconception: runs the FC-GPR clock from receipt of money instead of from the issue of shares
options.why: Regulation 4(1) runs the thirty days from the date of issue of the equity instruments. Receipt of consideration starts a different clock — the sixty days within which the shares must be issued.
keywords: runs the thirty days from the date of issue
Receipt of consideration starts a different clock

citation.ref: Regulation 4(1) of the FEM (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019, read with sections 42(4) and 42(8) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: An Indian private company issues equity shares on private placement to a Singapore investor under the automatic route. The consideration reaches its bank account on 5 May 2026. The board allots the shares on 20 June 2026. The company secretary files the return of allotment with the Registrar on 2 July 2026 and tells the board that this filing "closes the transaction", since the Registrar has been informed and the money can now be used.

items.stem: Is the reclassification correct?

options.text: Yes — classification is tested afresh on each reporting date, and at six per cent without control the holding is overseas portfolio investment
options.misconception: re-tests the classification each year instead of reading the Explanation to Rule 2(1)(q)
options.why: The Explanation exists precisely to stop annual re-testing. Classification is fixed at acquisition and stays fixed; dilution does not convert ODI into OPI.
keywords: exists precisely to stop annual re-testing
dilution does not convert ODI into OPI

options.text: Yes — and the change is immaterial in any case, since the same reporting applies to overseas direct investment and overseas portfolio investment
options.misconception: treats the two classifications as carrying identical obligations
options.why: The classifications carry different reporting, exit and end-use discipline. That is why the Rules bother to define them separately and why the Explanation locks the classification in place.
keywords: carry different reporting, exit and end-use discipline
the Explanation locks the classification in place

options.text: No — because the original investment was never overseas direct investment either, since ODI requires control and this company had none
options.misconception: makes control a necessary condition for ODI in a listed foreign entity
options.why: Control is one route into ODI, used for holdings below ten per cent. Ten per cent or more of a listed foreign entity's paid-up equity capital is ODI on the percentage alone.
keywords: Control is one route into ODI

options.text: No — an acquisition of ten per cent or more of a listed foreign entity is overseas direct investment under Rule 2(1)(q), and the Explanation to that rule keeps it overseas direct investment even after the holding falls below ten per cent or control is lost
options.why: Rule 2(1)(q) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 classifies an investment of ten per cent or more in the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity as overseas direct investment, with or without control. Its Explanation says in terms that such an investment continues to be treated as ODI even if it falls below ten per cent or the person loses control. Reporting obligations under Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022, including the Annual Performance Report, follow the classification and do not lapse with the percentage.
keywords: continues to be treated as ODI even if it falls below ten per cent
follow the classification and do not lapse with the percentage

citation.ref: Rules 2(1)(q) with its Explanation and 2(1)(s) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, read with Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022

items.scenario: An Indian manufacturing company subscribes to twelve per cent of the paid-up equity capital of a company listed on the Frankfurt exchange. It holds no board seat and exercises no control. Two years later the foreign company issues fresh shares to others and the Indian company's holding falls to six per cent. Its finance head proposes to reclassify the holding as overseas portfolio investment from that date and to stop filing the Annual Performance Report.

items.stem: Where is the consultant wrong?

options.text: On the officer only — ₹10 lakh was the old figure and ₹60 lakh is the current one, but a compounding order once passed closes the matter regardless of payment
options.misconception: treats the compounding order as the settlement instead of the payment
options.why: Compounding is admission plus payment. The 2024 Rules make the application void where the amount is not paid within fifteen days of the order, restoring the contravention to the penalty route under section 13.
keywords: make the application void where the amount is not paid within fifteen days

options.text: On both points — under the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024 an Assistant General Manager compounds a contravention below ₹60 lakh, so ₹45 lakh is within his powers, and the sum must be paid within fifteen days of the order or the application becomes void and FEMA applies as if it had never been made
options.why: The 2024 Rules, notified on 12 September 2024, superseded the 2000 Rules and raised the Assistant General Manager's limit from below ₹10 lakh to below ₹60 lakh. Payment within fifteen days of the compounding order is a condition of the compounding, not an administrative afterthought — miss it and the contravention revives under section 13.
keywords: raised the Assistant General Manager's limit from below ₹10 lakh to below ₹60 lakh
Payment within fifteen days of the compounding order is a condition of the compounding

options.text: Nowhere on the figures, but he has missed that a late FC-GPR is a contravention of clause (a) of section 3 and so cannot be compounded by the Reserve Bank at all
options.misconception: pushes an ordinary reporting default into the section 3(a) carve-out reserved for unauthorised dealing
options.why: Clause (a) of section 3 is about dealing in or transferring foreign exchange to or through an unauthorised person, and those contraventions go to the Directorate of Enforcement. A delayed FC-GPR is a reporting contravention the Reserve Bank compounds in the ordinary way.
keywords: those contraventions go to the Directorate of Enforcement
a reporting contravention the Reserve Bank compounds in the ordinary way

options.text: On the payment only — ₹10 lakh remains the Assistant General Manager's ceiling, so the application does have to go to a Deputy General Manager
options.misconception: applies the superseded 2000 Rules monetary limits
options.why: The ₹10 lakh figure comes from the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2000, which were superseded on 12 September 2024. Quoting it for a current application is quoting a repealed rule.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 15, read with the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024 (notified 12 September 2024)

items.scenario: An Indian company filed its Form FC-GPR eleven months late. The amount involved in the contravention is ₹45 lakh. It applies to the Reserve Bank to compound the contravention. Its consultant advises that the application must go to a Deputy General Manager because an Assistant General Manager can only compound contraventions below ₹10 lakh, and that once the compounding order is passed the matter is closed whether or not the company pays.

items.stem: What has gone wrong here?

options.text: Two things — the June sale took his traded value over ₹10 lakh in the same calendar quarter, so a disclosure to the company was due within two trading days under Regulation 7(2)(a), and the October purchase is a contra trade inside the six-month bar in clause 10 of Schedule B, so the profits are liable to be disgorged to the Investor Protection and Education Fund
options.why: Regulation 7(2)(a) aggregates the value traded in one transaction or a series over any calendar quarter, so ₹8 lakh and ₹4 lakh in the April-to-June quarter cross the ₹10 lakh line together. The company then had two trading days to notify the exchange under Regulation 7(2)(b). Clause 10 of Schedule B makes the code of conduct set a contra-trade period of not less than six months, and a purchase on 5 October is inside six months of a 20 June sale.
keywords: aggregates the value traded in one transaction or a series
two trading days to notify the exchange
a contra-trade period of not less than six months

options.text: Only the contra trade — the disclosure obligation runs from a financial year, not a calendar quarter, so his trades never had to be aggregated
options.misconception: substitutes the financial year for the calendar quarter the regulation names
options.why: Regulation 7(2)(a) names a calendar quarter. April to June is one quarter, and the two sales fall inside it.
keywords: the two sales fall inside it

options.text: Only the disclosure failure — the contra trade is permitted because he did not possess any unpublished price sensitive information when he bought back
options.misconception: treats absence of unpublished price sensitive information as curing a contra trade
options.why: The contra-trade restriction is a flat bar in the code of conduct on trading in the opposite direction within the period; it does not turn on whether he held unpublished price sensitive information at the time. That is a separate prohibition under Regulation 4.
keywords: a flat bar in the code of conduct on trading in the opposite direction
it does not turn on whether he held unpublished price sensitive information

options.text: Nothing — each transaction was below ₹10 lakh and the contra-trade restriction applies only to promoters and directors, not to designated persons generally
options.misconception: tests each trade in isolation and narrows the contra-trade bar to promoters and directors
options.why: Regulation 7(2)(a) says "in one transaction or a series of transactions over any calendar quarter", which is aggregation by design. Clause 10 of Schedule B is written for designated persons, the class this person falls in.

citation.ref: Regulations 7(2)(a) and 7(2)(b), and clause 10 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9

items.scenario: A designated person of a listed company sells shares worth ₹8 lakh on 10 April 2026 and a further ₹4 lakh on 20 June 2026. He makes no disclosure to the company, on the view that neither sale on its own crossed ₹10 lakh. On 5 October 2026 he buys the company's shares back at a lower price and books a gain. The compliance officer had given him no written relaxation.

items.stem: Is the merchant banker's advice correct?

options.text: No — the acquisition takes them past twenty-five per cent for the first time, which triggers an open offer under Regulation 3(1) for at least twenty-six per cent of the voting capital, and the public announcement is due on 12 August, the date of agreeing to acquire, with the detailed public statement within five working days
options.why: Regulation 3(2) is the creeping route and is open only to an acquirer already holding twenty-five per cent or more. At twenty-four per cent this acquirer is below that gate, so crossing twenty-five per cent falls under Regulation 3(1). Regulation 7(1) fixes the minimum offer size at twenty-six per cent, Regulation 13(1) fixes the public announcement at the date of agreeing to acquire, and Regulation 13(4) gives five working days for the detailed public statement.
keywords: open only to an acquirer already holding twenty-five per cent or more
fixes the minimum offer size at twenty-six per cent
the public announcement at the date of agreeing to acquire

options.text: No on the offer, but the announcement may indeed wait until the shares are transferred, since no acquisition has yet taken place
options.misconception: ties the public announcement to completion rather than to the agreement
options.why: Regulation 13(1) fixes the public announcement at the date of agreeing to acquire shares, voting rights or control. The agreement itself is the trigger; waiting for the transfer would leave the market uninformed for the whole gap.
keywords: The agreement itself is the trigger
would leave the market uninformed for the whole gap

options.text: No — an open offer is due, but for twenty-five per cent of the voting capital so that public shareholding is preserved
options.misconception: confuses the trigger percentage with the minimum offer size
options.why: Twenty-five per cent is the trigger under Regulation 3(1). The size of the offer is fixed separately by Regulation 7(1) at not less than twenty-six per cent of the voting capital.
keywords: Twenty-five per cent is the trigger
The size of the offer is fixed separately by Regulation 7(1)

options.text: Yes — a three per cent purchase is within the five per cent a financial year allows, so Regulation 3(2) covers it
options.misconception: applies the creeping acquisition route to an acquirer who has not yet reached 25 per cent
options.why: Regulation 3(2) opens only once the acquirer already holds twenty-five per cent or more but below the maximum permissible non-public shareholding. Below twenty-five per cent there is nothing to creep from — Regulation 3(1) governs the first crossing.
keywords: there is nothing to creep from

citation.source: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011

items.scenario: An acquirer and the persons acting in concert with him hold twenty-four per cent of the voting rights of a listed target company. On 12 August 2026 they sign a share purchase agreement to buy a further three per cent from a retiring promoter. Their merchant banker advises that no open offer is needed because the creeping acquisition route allows up to five per cent in a financial year, and that in any case the public announcement can wait until the shares are actually transferred.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The audit committee's approval is needed, but the whole audit committee approves it and the shareholder resolution can be carried by the related parties' own votes since they hold the majority
options.misconception: ignores the independent-directors-only rule and the abstention requirement
options.why: Regulation 23(2) confines approval to the independent directors on the audit committee, and Regulation 23(7) makes all related parties abstain from voting on the shareholder resolution. Both exist so the interested side cannot approve its own transaction.
keywords: confines approval to the independent directors on the audit committee
the interested side cannot approve its own transaction

options.text: Both are right — an ordinary-course, arm's length transaction is outside the approval machinery under section 188, and what needs no approval needs no disclosure
options.misconception: carries the section 188 arm's length exemption into LODR and then into Ind AS 24
options.why: The exemption belongs to section 188 and stops there. Regulation 23(2) requires audit committee approval for all related party transactions, and Ind AS 24 disclosure is independent of every approval regime.
keywords: The exemption belongs to section 188 and stops there

options.text: No approval is needed under either regime, because Regulation 23(5) exempts transactions in the ordinary course of business
options.misconception: mistakes the wholly-owned subsidiary carve-out for an ordinary-course exemption
