options.misconception: reads "deal with it as he considers necessary" as a duty to adopt
options.why: The statutory words leave the judgement with the company's auditor. SA 600 requires him to perform procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the other auditor's work is adequate for his purposes, and where it is not and he cannot do enough more, to qualify his opinion or disclaim it for a limitation on scope — none of which is possible if he is bound to copy out what he was sent.

citation.ref: Section 143(8) with Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, section 143(12) with Rule 13, and SA 600

items.scenario: An Indian listed company has a branch in Indonesia whose accounts are audited by a local firm appointed under section 139, and an Indian branch audited by the company's own auditor. The Indonesian branch auditor uncovers a fraud of about ₹3 crore committed by the branch manager, notes it in his report on the branch accounts and sends that report to the company's Board. The company's management then tells the statutory auditor that the branch report is final, that he must reproduce it in his own report, and that the fraud is now his alone to report because the branch auditor is not the auditor of the company.

items.stem: Were the two resolutions validly passed?

options.text: Both could in any case have been delegated to the managing director under the proviso to section 179(3), so the manner of passing them does not matter
options.misconception: reads the proviso as covering the whole of the section 179(3) list
options.why: The proviso permits delegation of three powers and no others — to borrow monies, to invest the funds of the company, and to grant loans or give guarantee or provide security in respect of loans. Approving the accounts and appointing a key managerial person are outside it, and a delegation the proviso does not allow is no delegation at all.

options.text: Neither was — approving the financial statement and the Board's report, and appointing a key managerial person, are both powers that section 179(3) with Rule 8 requires to be exercised by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Board, and section 175(1) forbids a resolution by circulation on any matter required to be placed before the Board at a meeting
options.why: Section 179(3) lists the powers the Board may exercise only by means of resolutions passed at meetings of the Board, and the approval of the financial statement and the Board's report is one of them. Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 prescribes further such powers under the last clause of that sub-section, among them the appointment or removal of key managerial personnel, which is what a chief financial officer is. Section 175(1) then says that no resolution shall be passed by circulation on any matter which is required by the Act or otherwise to be placed before the Board at a meeting, so signing an email round cannot carry either of them.

options.text: The accounts resolution was valid because section 134 requires only the Board's approval and does not mention a meeting, and only the chief financial officer's appointment fails
options.misconception: reads section 134 on its own and misses section 179(3)
options.why: Section 134(1) requires the financial statements to be approved by the Board of Directors and signed on its behalf, and it is section 179(3) that says how that approval is to be given — by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Board. The two sections are read together, and the second is the one that decides the manner.

options.text: Both were, because section 175 allows a resolution to be passed by circulation once it is approved by a majority of the directors entitled to vote on it
options.misconception: reads the machinery in section 175 and skips the bar at the front of it
options.why: Section 175 does permit a resolution by circulation approved by a majority of the directors entitled to vote, but only after its opening words have been satisfied: no resolution shall be passed by circulation on any matter which is required by the Act or otherwise to be placed before the Board at a meeting. Both of these matters are on that list.

citation.ref: Section 179(3) with its proviso and Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, read with section 175(1) and section 134(1)

items.scenario: The directors of a public company are scattered across three cities in the week the accounts are due. The company secretary circulates two draft resolutions by email — one approving the audited financial statements and the Board's report for the year, and one appointing a new chief financial officer — and records both as passed when a majority of the directors sign and return them.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The defect can be repaired by having the members ratify the arrangement at the next annual general meeting
options.misconception: overlooks the word "prior" in section 192(1)
options.why: Section 192(1) requires that prior approval for the arrangement be accorded by a resolution of the company in general meeting. An approval obtained after the arrangement has been entered into is not prior approval, and the consequence in section 192(3) attaches to an arrangement entered into in contravention of the section, not to one that stays uncorrected.

options.text: The arrangement is void from the beginning, so the shares issued to Mr R can be cancelled and no third party can take anything under it
options.misconception: reads "voidable at the instance of the company" as void
options.why: Section 192(3) makes the arrangement voidable at the instance of the company, and even that is taken away in two cases — where restitution of the money or other consideration is no longer possible and the company has been indemnified by another person for the loss, and where rights have been acquired bona fide for value and without notice of the contravention by any other person.

options.text: The arrangement needed prior approval by a resolution of the company in general meeting and, Mr R being a director of the holding company, a resolution in general meeting of the holding company too, with the value of the asset calculated by a registered valuer set out in the notice; the arm's-length and ordinary-course finding is irrelevant because section 192 carries no such carve-out; and as things stand the arrangement is voidable at the instance of the company
options.why: Section 192(1) forbids a company to enter into an arrangement by which it acquires assets for consideration other than cash from its own director unless prior approval is accorded by a resolution of the company in general meeting, and where that director is a director of the holding company, by a resolution in general meeting of the holding company as well. Section 192(2) requires the notice for that resolution to include the particulars of the arrangement along with the value of the assets involved, duly calculated by a registered valuer, so the finance team's own figure will not do. The fourth proviso to section 188 exempts a transaction in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis from that section only; section 192 has no value threshold and no such exemption anywhere in it. Section 192(3) then makes an arrangement entered into in contravention of the section voidable at the instance of the company.

options.text: Nothing more was needed, because a transaction in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis is outside the related party approval machinery altogether
options.misconception: treats section 192 as though it were a limb of section 188
options.why: The fourth proviso to section 188 carves out an ordinary-course arm's-length transaction from section 188 and from nothing else. Section 192 is a separate prohibition aimed at the kind of consideration rather than at the price, and a payment in shares instead of cash engages it whatever the price was and whatever business the company is in.

citation.ref: Sections 192(1), 192(2) and 192(3), read with the fourth proviso to section 188 and section 247

items.scenario: A logistics company buys and sells warehouses all the time. It acquires a warehouse from Mr R, its whole-time director, who is also a director of its holding company, and pays for it entirely by issuing equity shares to him. The audit committee satisfies itself that the price is on arm's length terms and that the purchase is in the company's ordinary course of business, and concludes on that footing that the fourth proviso to section 188 takes the transaction outside the related party machinery. The Board approves it at a meeting. The value of the warehouse was worked out by the company's own finance team, no resolution was put to any general meeting, and the holding company was merely informed.

items.stem: What is wrong with the appointment?

options.text: Nothing is wrong now, because section 196(5) provides that acts done before the general meeting's approval are not invalid, which cures the appointment itself
options.misconception: reads a saving of acts as a validation of the appointment
options.why: Section 196(5) saves the acts done by the person before the approval so that third parties dealing with the company are not prejudiced. It says nothing about the appointment, which still has to satisfy sections 196(1), 196(2), 196(3) and 196(4) on its own terms.

options.text: Only the age is a difficulty, and it is cured by an application to the Central Government for approval of the appointment of a person over seventy
options.misconception: reads the age proviso as a government route rather than a shareholder one
options.why: The Central Government's approval under section 196(4) is needed where the appointment is at variance with the conditions specified in Part I of Schedule V, which is a different question. The route past the age of seventy is in the proviso to section 196(3)(a) and it is a special resolution of the members, with the justification indicated in the explanatory statement annexed to the notice.

options.text: Four things — section 196(1) forbids a company to appoint or employ a managing director and a manager at the same time; section 196(2) allows a term of no more than five years at a time; the proviso to section 196(3)(a) requires a special resolution, with the justification set out in the explanatory statement, for a person who has attained the age of seventy; and section 196(4) requires a return in the prescribed form to be filed with the Registrar within sixty days of the appointment
options.why: Section 196(1) bars a company from having a managing director and a manager in office together, so the manager already there is itself a bar. Under section 196(2) any one appointment or re-appointment to the office of managing director, whole-time director or manager may run for no more than five years, which a seven-year term overshoots. Section 196(3)(a) disqualifies a person who has attained the age of seventy years, and its proviso lets the appointment be made only by passing a special resolution whose explanatory statement indicates the justification for appointing him — an ordinary resolution on a silent notice is neither. Section 196(4) then requires the filing of a return in the prescribed form with the Registrar within sixty days of the appointment.

options.text: The seven-year term is unobjectionable, because section 196(2) only forbids a re-appointment made earlier than one year before the expiry of the existing term
options.misconception: reads the second half of section 196(2) and drops the first
options.why: The sub-section contains two rules in one sentence. The first is that no appointment or re-appointment shall be for a term exceeding five years at a time; the second is that no re-appointment shall be made earlier than one year before the expiry of the term. Dropping the first leaves the cap on the length of the term unaccounted for.

citation.ref: Sections 196(1), 196(2), 196(3)(a) with its proviso, 196(4) and 196(5), read with Part I of Schedule V

items.scenario: A public company already employs a manager. At a Board meeting it approves the appointment of Mr K, aged seventy-two, as its managing director for a term of seven years on stated terms, and the appointment is then put to the members and carried as an ordinary resolution, the notice saying nothing about his age. Nothing is filed with the Registrar. Six months later the company secretary says the appointment is beyond challenge because Mr K has been functioning and section 196(5) protects everything he has done.

items.stem: What is wrong with what the Registrar has done?

options.text: Three things — section 206(3) required him to record his reasons in writing before issuing the notice for further books; section 209 lets him enter, search and seize only after obtaining an order from the Special Court, and only after allowing the company to take copies of or extracts from the books seized; and section 209(2) requires the seized books to be returned as soon as may be and in any case not later than one hundred and eighty days, subject only to their being called for again by an order in writing
options.why: Section 206(3) lets the Registrar call for further books, papers and explanations where the reply was not furnished or was inadequate or where the scrutiny shows an unsatisfactory state of affairs, but requires him to record his reasons in writing before issuing that notice. Section 209 is the only power to take anything away, and it is conditional twice over: he may enter, search and seize only after obtaining an order from the Special Court for the seizure, and only after allowing the company to take copies of or extracts from the books and papers being seized. Section 209(2) then requires the return of what was seized as soon as may be and in any case not later than one hundred and eighty days, with the books capable of being called for again for a further like period by an order in writing.

options.text: The seizure is lawful, because section 207(3) vests the Registrar with the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
options.misconception: reads a power of discovery and production as a power to seize
options.why: Section 207(3) gives him the powers of a civil court in respect of the discovery and production of books of account and other documents at a specified place and time, and of summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath. Compelling production is not the same as entering premises and taking documents away, which is what section 209 governs and conditions on an order of the Special Court.

options.text: He may keep the books for as long as the inquiry runs, since the Act sets no outer limit on documents held for an inquiry into fraud
options.misconception: ignores the return clocks the Chapter actually contains
options.why: There are two of them. Section 207(2) lets books required to be produced be kept in his custody for a period not exceeding one hundred and eighty days before they are returned, and section 209(2) imposes the same outer limit on books that have been seized, in each case with liberty to call for them again if they are needed.

options.text: Recording reasons under section 206(3) is a matter of internal record and can be done after the notice has gone out, so nothing turns on the order in which he did it
options.misconception: treats a pre-condition to the power as a filing formality
options.why: The sub-section says that before issuing the notice the Registrar shall record his reasons in writing. That order is the safeguard: the reasons are what a court later tests the exercise of the power against, and reasons composed after the notice was served are reasons for a decision already taken.

items.scenario: After scrutinising a company's filings the Registrar issues a written notice calling for an explanation, and the company sends back a partial reply. The Registrar then issues a second notice calling for further books and papers, without recording anything on his file about why. When the company delays, he arrives at the registered office with two officers, takes away the general ledger and the purchase files, refuses the accountant's request to photocopy them first, and says they will be returned whenever the inquiry finishes. He has obtained no order from any court.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The State agency may continue in parallel, since the bar in section 212(2) is confined to other investigating agencies of the Central Government
options.misconception: reads only half of the words in section 212(2)
options.why: The sub-section names both — no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government shall proceed with an investigation in a case assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office in respect of any offence under the Act, and where such an investigation has already been initiated it shall not be proceeded with further, the records being transferred to that Office.

options.text: The letter to the Ministry is the right route, because section 210 lets the Central Government order an investigation on a representation made to it by any person
options.misconception: borrows the representation limb from section 206(4) and puts it in section 210
options.why: A representation made by any person is a trigger for the Registrar's inquiry under section 206(4). Section 210(1) has three grounds and none of them is a letter from shareholders — a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208, an intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or the public interest.

options.text: The shareholders should have the company pass a special resolution that its affairs ought to be investigated, on which the Central Government would then be bound to order one
options.misconception: turns a discretionary ground into a duty and hands the remedy to the majority complained of
options.why: A special resolution under section 210(1)(b) is a ground on which the Central Government may order an investigation, not one on which it must; the only compulsion is in section 210(2), where a court or the Tribunal has ordered that the affairs ought to be investigated. It is also no remedy for a minority, since the resolution would have to be carried in a general meeting of the very company whose promoters are the complaint.

options.text: The shareholders' route is an application to the Tribunal under section 213, which their one-tenth of the total voting power satisfies, and if the Tribunal orders that the affairs ought to be investigated the Central Government then appoints the inspectors; the Registrar's section 208 report is a ground on which the Central Government may itself order an investigation under section 210(1) or assign it to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office; and once it is assigned, section 212(2) stops any other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government from proceeding
options.why: Section 213 puts the members' application before the Tribunal, on an application by not less than one hundred members or by members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in a company having a share capital; the Tribunal decides that there will be an investigation and the Central Government then appoints one or more competent persons as inspectors. Section 210(1) is the Central Government's own power and its first ground is the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208. Section 212(2) is written in terms that cover both — no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government shall proceed with an investigation in a case assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office in respect of any offence under the Act, and one already begun shall not be proceeded with further.

citation.ref: Sections 210(1), 210(2), 212(2) and 213, read with section 206(4) and section 208

items.scenario: Shareholders holding twelve per cent of the total voting power of an unlisted public company write to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs demanding an investigation into the diversion of funds by the promoters, and are told nothing for months. The Registrar has separately submitted a report under section 208 recommending a further investigation, and the Central Government has assigned the case to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office. Meanwhile a State economic offences wing, having received the same complaint, begins its own investigation into offences under the Companies Act. The shareholders' counsel advises that their letter is the correct route and that the State agency may run in parallel because section 212(2) only stops other central agencies.

items.stem: How should the petition be dealt with?

options.text: The company's reply is a complete answer, because a company with no assets cannot usefully be wound up and the Tribunal should dismiss the petition on that footing
options.misconception: contradicts the express words of section 273(2)
options.why: Section 273(2) says the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets of the company have been mortgaged for an amount equal to or in excess of those assets, or that the company has no assets. A winding up is not only a way of paying creditors; it also brings the company's affairs, and the conduct of those who ran it, under an officer of the Tribunal.

options.text: It succeeds on the six years of non-filing, since once a ground in section 271 is made out any creditor of the company may petition on it
options.misconception: reads the grounds in section 271 without the list of petitioners in section 272
options.why: The two sections do different jobs. Section 271 says on what grounds a company may be wound up; section 272(1) says who may present the petition, and it names the company, a contributory or contributories, the Registrar, a person authorised by the Central Government, and the Central or a State Government on the sovereignty ground. A ground made out by a person with no standing takes the petition nowhere.

options.text: It fails on the first ground, because inability to pay debts is no longer a ground in section 271 and the creditor's remedy is an application under section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; it fails on the second as well, because although six years of non-filing is a ground under section 271, a trade creditor is not one of the persons section 272 allows to petition; and the company's own answer is worth nothing, section 273(2) forbidding a refusal merely because it has no assets
options.why: Section 271 now carries five grounds — a special resolution of the company, conduct against the sovereignty and integrity of India and the like, fraudulent conduct or a fraudulent purpose on an application by the Registrar or a person authorised by the Central Government, a default in filing financial statements or annual returns for five consecutive financial years, and the just and equitable ground. Inability to pay debts was taken out when the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 rewrote Chapter XX, and the unpaid operational creditor's route is now an application under section 9 of that Code. Section 272(1) then lists who may petition — the company, a contributory, the Registrar, a person authorised by the Central Government, and the Central or a State Government on the sovereignty ground — and a trade creditor is not among them. Section 273(2) closes the company's answer: the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order merely because the assets have been mortgaged for an amount equal to or in excess of them, or because the company has no assets.

options.text: It succeeds on inability to pay debts, which survives inside section 271 as the just and equitable ground
options.misconception: rebadges a ground Parliament removed as the residual one
options.why: The just and equitable ground is about whether the substratum of the company has gone, whether it is a deadlocked quasi-partnership, and the like. Reading a plain failure to pay into it would put back the very jurisdiction the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 moved to sections 7 and 9, and would let a creditor bypass the Code's own machinery of demand notice, dispute and default.

citation.ref: Sections 271, 272(1) and 273(2), read with section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

items.scenario: A trade creditor is owed ₹2 crore by a private company which has admitted the debt and simply cannot pay. He presents a petition to the Tribunal for the winding up of the company on the ground that it is unable to pay its debts, and adds that the company has filed neither financial statements nor annual returns for the last six consecutive financial years. The company's shareholders have passed no resolution of any kind. In reply the company says only that it has no assets left at all, so a winding up order would serve no purpose.

items.stem: What has the company missed?

options.text: Three things — section 380(1) required the prescribed documents to be delivered to the Registrar for registration within thirty days of establishing the place of business; section 381 requires a balance sheet and profit and loss account of the Indian business, with the prescribed documents annexed, to be delivered to the Registrar, and Rule 5 requires those accounts to be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India; and because more than fifty per cent of its paid-up share capital is held by companies incorporated in India, section 379(2) requires it to comply with the Chapter and such other provisions as are prescribed as if it were a company incorporated in India
options.why: Section 380(1) gives a foreign company thirty days from the establishment of its place of business in India to deliver to the Registrar its constitutional documents, the address of its principal office, the list of its directors and secretary, the name of a person resident in India authorised to accept service, and the other prescribed particulars. Section 381 then requires it, in every calendar year, to make out a balance sheet and profit and loss account in the prescribed form with the prescribed documents annexed and to deliver a copy to the Registrar, and Rule 5 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014 requires those accounts to be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India or by a firm or limited liability partnership of practising chartered accountants. Section 379(2) adds the sting for this company: where not less than fifty per cent of the paid-up share capital is held by one or more citizens of India or by one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, whether singly or in the aggregate, it complies with the Chapter and such other provisions as may be prescribed as if it were an Indian company.

options.text: The Singapore auditors' report is sufficient for the accounts of the Indian business, since the company is incorporated in Singapore and audited there under Singapore law
options.misconception: overlooks the audit requirement in the Foreign Companies Rules
options.why: What section 381 asks for is not the company's global accounts but the accounts of its business in India, and Rule 5 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014 requires those to be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India or by a firm or limited liability partnership of practising chartered accountants.

options.text: Nothing, because a company incorporated outside India answers to the Reserve Bank for its Indian presence and the Companies Act reaches only companies incorporated in India
options.misconception: treats the exchange permission as the whole of the compliance
options.why: The two regulators answer different questions. The Foreign Exchange Management (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any Other Place of Business) Regulations, 2016 decide whether the office may exist; Chapter XXII of the Companies Act, 2013 decides what the Registrar must be told about it, and section 379(1) applies sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393 to all foreign companies.

options.text: Section 379(2) does not apply, because the fifty per cent limb speaks of citizens of India and the holders here are companies
options.misconception: reads only the first half of the clause
options.why: The clause covers holdings by one or more citizens of India, by one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, or by a combination of the two, whether singly or in the aggregate. Sixty per cent held by two Indian companies is squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Sections 379(1), 379(2), 380(1) and 381, read with Rules 4 and 5 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company incorporated in Singapore obtained the Reserve Bank's approval and opened a branch office in Mumbai on 5 January 2026, from which it has been trading since. Sixty per cent of its paid-up share capital is held by two companies incorporated in India. It has filed everything the Reserve Bank asks for and has delivered nothing at all to the Registrar of Companies, and the accounts of its Indian business for 2025-26 were audited by its Singapore auditors. Its Indian counsel says the Reserve Bank's approval is what governs its presence here and the Companies Act has no application to a company incorporated abroad.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The Indian chain does breach the restriction, because a wholly owned subsidiary is a subsidiary like any other and every layer below the company counts towards the two
options.misconception: applies the two-layer limit without the proviso that discounts a wholly owned layer
options.why: Explanation (d) to section 2(87) does make a layer mean a subsidiary or subsidiaries, but the count is done under Rule 2(1), whose second proviso removes one layer consisting of one or more wholly owned subsidiary or subsidiaries from the computation. On these facts that leaves two layers, which is what the Rule permits.

options.text: The wholly owned layer that is not counted for the restriction is also left out of the consolidated financial statements, since the Act treats it as though it were not there
options.misconception: carries a structural exclusion across into the accounts
options.why: The Rule discounts that layer for one purpose only — computing how deep the group may be. Section 129(3) requires the consolidation of all the subsidiaries and associate companies, and Ind AS 110 brings in every entity the parent controls. A subsidiary a group is allowed to have is not a subsidiary it may leave out of its accounts.

options.text: The Indian chain is within Rule 2(1), because one layer consisting of a wholly owned subsidiary is not taken into account, leaving two counted layers; the German company is protected by the proviso that saves the acquisition of a company incorporated outside India having subsidiaries beyond two layers as per the laws of that country; and none of it affects the accounts, section 129(3) and Ind AS 110 consolidating every entity the company controls, the wholly owned layer and the German chain included
options.why: Rule 2(1) of the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017 forbids more than two layers of subsidiaries, and its second proviso says that for computing the number of layers one layer consisting of one or more wholly owned subsidiary or subsidiaries shall not be taken into account — so A Limited drops out of the count and B and C are the two that remain. The first proviso says the Rule does not affect a company from acquiring a company incorporated outside India with subsidiaries beyond two layers as per the laws of that country. Section 129(3) is a separate question and asks nothing about layers: it requires a consolidated financial statement of the company and of all its subsidiaries and associates, and Ind AS 110 consolidates on control however far down the chain the control runs.

options.text: The German acquisition breaches the restriction and the chain beneath it has to be collapsed to two layers within the period allowed by the Rules
options.misconception: ignores the first proviso to Rule 2(1)
options.why: The first proviso to Rule 2(1) says in terms that the restriction shall not affect a company from acquiring a company incorporated outside India with subsidiaries beyond two layers as per the laws of that country. The proviso to section 186(1) carries the same carve-out for investment subsidiaries. Nothing has to be collapsed.

citation.ref: Rule 2(1) of the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017 with both its provisos and the proviso to section 2(87), read with the proviso to section 186(1), section 129(3) and Ind AS 110

items.scenario: An Indian manufacturing company — not a banking company, a non-banking financial company, an insurer or a Government company — holds the whole of the equity of A Limited, which holds eighty per cent of B Limited, which holds sixty per cent of C Limited. During the year it also acquires a company incorporated in Germany which, under German law, already carries four layers of subsidiaries beneath it. The group's new chief financial officer says the Indian chain is one layer too deep, that the German acquisition has to be unwound, and that since the wholly owned layer does not count for the restriction it also drops out of the consolidated financial statements.

items.stem: Can the application be filed?

options.text: No, because the powers of the board stand suspended under section 17(1), so the company has lost the right to bring proceedings until the process ends
options.misconception: confuses the suspension of the board's powers with the loss of the company's rights
options.why: Section 17(1) suspends the powers of the board and vests them in the insolvency professional; it does not take the company's rights away. Section 25(2)(b) then requires the resolution professional to represent and act on behalf of the corporate debtor with third parties and to exercise its rights for its benefit in judicial, quasi-judicial and arbitration proceedings.

options.text: Yes — Explanation II to section 11 says that nothing in the section shall prevent a corporate debtor covered by its clauses from initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process against another corporate debtor, the section barring a company from being taken into a fresh process of its own and not from recovering what it is owed
options.why: Section 11 lists the persons not entitled to make an application, and clause (a) does name a corporate debtor undergoing a corporate insolvency resolution process. Explanation II, inserted in 2020, says what the whole section is aimed at: nothing in it shall prevent a corporate debtor referred to in those clauses from initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process against another corporate debtor. The disability is about being put into a second process of its own, and a receivable owed to the company is an asset the professional is bound to pursue.

options.text: No, because section 11(a) disentitles a corporate debtor undergoing a resolution process from making any application under the Code while that process runs
options.misconception: reads clause (a) without the Explanation that governs it
options.why: Clause (a) is read with Explanation II, which was added precisely because the clause was being read this way. The Explanation says nothing in the section shall prevent such a corporate debtor from initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process against another corporate debtor.

options.text: No, and the company must in addition wait twelve months after its own process ends before it can apply against anybody
options.misconception: applies clause (b), which is about the company being taken into a fresh process itself
options.why: The twelve-month bar in clause (b) applies to a corporate debtor having completed a corporate insolvency resolution process in the twelve months preceding the application — that is, to an application made against it. It says nothing about an application the company makes against a different corporate debtor, which Explanation II expressly allows.

citation.ref: Section 11 with Explanations I and II, read with sections 17(1) and 25(2)(b)

items.scenario: A company is itself undergoing a corporate insolvency resolution process. One of its own customers, a separate company, has defaulted on a financial debt of ₹4 crore owed to it, well above the amount notified under section 4. The resolution professional wants to file an application under section 7 against that customer to recover it. A member of the suspended Board tells him that section 11(a) makes this impossible, because a corporate debtor undergoing a resolution process is not entitled to make an application under the Code.

items.stem: How do the two claims stand?

options.text: Both claims are gone, because the last date stated in the public announcement under section 15 is the cut-off and a claim submitted after it cannot be entertained
options.misconception: reads the announced date as a cut-off the Regulations do not make it
options.why: Section 15(1)(c) requires the announcement to state the last date for the submission of claims, as may be specified, and what is specified is Regulation 6, which sets it at fourteen days from the interim resolution professional's appointment. Regulation 12 then provides expressly for the creditor who missed it, allowing submission up to the ninetieth day of the insolvency commencement date.

options.text: Supplier P's claim must be taken on record, because Regulation 12 lets a creditor who missed the last date in the announcement submit his claim with proof up to the ninetieth day of the insolvency commencement date and 20 August is inside that; supplier Q's claim stands extinguished on the approval of the plan under section 31(1), and his suit cannot proceed
options.why: The last date stated under section 15(1)(c) is not the end of the road. Regulation 12 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 lets a creditor who fails to submit his claim within the time stipulated in the public announcement submit it to the interim resolution professional or the resolution professional on or before the ninetieth day of the insolvency commencement date, which for a commencement on 1 June 2026 runs to the end of August. Supplier Q is on the other side of a different line: section 31(1) makes an approved plan binding on the corporate debtor and all its creditors, and the Supreme Court in Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons Private Limited v Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited held that on approval all claims not part of the plan stand extinguished and no person may start a proceeding on such a claim.

options.text: Both claims survive, because section 3(6) defines a claim as a right to payment whether or not it is fixed, matured, disputed or undisputed, and nothing in the Code takes that right away
options.misconception: reads the width of the definition as immunity from the effect of an approved plan
options.why: The definition in section 3(6) is deliberately wide so that everything owed can be brought into the process. What happens to a claim that is not brought in is decided by section 31(1), which binds every creditor to the approved plan, and by Ghanashyam Mishra, which held that claims not forming part of the plan stand extinguished on its approval.

options.text: Supplier Q's claim survives because he was never served individually, a newspaper announcement being notice only to those who happen to read it
options.misconception: treats the section 15 public announcement as insufficient service
options.why: The Code chose a public announcement precisely because a corporate debtor's creditors cannot all be known at the outset. Regulation 6 requires publication in one English and one regional language newspaper with wide circulation at the location of the registered office and the principal office, on the corporate debtor's own website and on the website designated by the Board, and that announcement is the notice the statute contemplates.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)(c) and section 31(1), read with Regulations 6 and 12 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 and section 3(6)

items.scenario: An application against a company is admitted on 1 June 2026, which is therefore the insolvency commencement date. The interim resolution professional is appointed the same day and makes the public announcement on 4 June, stating 18 June 2026 as the last date for the submission of claims. Supplier P, owed ₹6 crore, misses that date and submits his claim with proof on 20 August 2026; the resolution professional refuses to look at it, saying the last date has gone. Supplier Q never submits a claim at all, and after the Adjudicating Authority approves a resolution plan on 5 December 2026 he files a civil suit against the company for his dues.

items.stem: What is the correct set of answers?

options.text: Section 20(1) settles the auditor's question, so the financial statements continue on the going concern basis whatever the company's circumstances are
options.misconception: reads a management duty as an accounting conclusion
options.why: The two uses of the same phrase point in different directions. Section 20(1) tells the professional what to try to achieve; Ind AS 1 asks whether management has a realistic alternative to liquidating the entity or ceasing to trade, and SA 570 requires the auditor to evaluate that assessment on the evidence. Admission into the process is a fact to be weighed in that evaluation, not an answer to it.

options.text: He cannot raise the interim finance until a committee of creditors has been constituted and has approved it by sixty-six per cent under section 28
options.misconception: applies the resolution professional's constraint to the interim resolution professional
options.why: Section 28 constrains the resolution professional, and section 25(2)(c) is what sends him there. The interim resolution professional acts before there is any committee to approve anything, and section 20(2)(c) gives him the authority in his own right, limited only by the proviso about encumbered property.

options.text: He must take custody of the subsidiary's warehouse as well, because the subsidiary is consolidated in the corporate debtor's financial statements and its assets are therefore the corporate debtor's
options.misconception: reads a consolidation boundary as a custody boundary
options.why: Consolidation under Ind AS 110 presents the group as one economic entity for reporting; it does not transfer the ownership of anything. The Explanation to section 18 says in terms that the assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor are not assets he takes control and custody of, and the subsidiary remains a separate corporate person with its own board.

options.text: The bailed machinery and the subsidiary's warehouse are both outside the assets he takes custody of, by the Explanation to section 18; he applies to the Adjudicating Authority under section 19 for directions against the suspended directors; he may raise the interim finance on his own authority under section 20(2)(c), there being no committee yet, but may create no security interest over encumbered property without the prior consent of the creditor secured over it; and section 20(1) is a management mandate, the going concern basis of the financial statements remaining a separate assessment under Ind AS 1 and SA 570
options.why: The Explanation to section 18 takes out of the word "assets" both assets owned by a third party in possession of the corporate debtor held under trust or under contractual arrangements including bailment, and the assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor. Section 19 obliges the personnel and promoters to extend all assistance and lets him apply to the Adjudicating Authority for directions where they do not. Section 20(2)(c) gives the interim resolution professional the authority to raise interim finance, with the proviso that no security interest be created over encumbered property without the prior consent of the creditor whose debt is secured over it. And section 20(1) tells him to manage the operations as a going concern, which is an instruction about how to run the company; whether the financial statements may be prepared on a going concern basis is decided under Ind AS 1 and tested by the auditor under SA 570.

citation.ref: Section 18(1) with its Explanation, sections 19 and 20(1) and 20(2)(c), read with section 28, Ind AS 1 and SA 570

items.scenario: On the day an application is admitted the interim resolution professional takes over a manufacturing company. Four things land on his desk in the first week. Machinery worth ₹9 crore sits on the factory floor under a bailment from a third party. A warehouse worth ₹30 crore is owned by the company's wholly owned Indian subsidiary. The suspended directors will not hand over the accounting records. And the plant needs ₹15 crore of interim finance to keep running, at a point when no committee of creditors has been constituted. The statutory auditor, who is finishing the previous year's audit, asks whether section 20(1) has settled the going concern question for him by requiring the company to be run as a going concern.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the three points?

options.text: He was right about the notice, because a person who cannot vote at a meeting has no entitlement to be called to it
options.misconception: reads section 24(4) as cancelling the notice section 24(3) requires
options.why: The two sub-sections do different things. Section 24(3) is the notice provision and it names the members of the suspended Board of Directors expressly; section 24(4) then says those directors, the partners and one representative of the operational creditors may attend but shall not have any right to vote. Attendance without a vote is exactly what the Code intends.

options.text: The replacement succeeded, since a decision at the first meeting is carried by a majority of the voting share present and voting
options.misconception: uses an ordinary majority where the Code sets a super-majority
options.why: Section 22(2) fixes the majority for this decision itself, and fixes it at not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors. The Code uses that figure for the decisions it treats as structural — appointing or replacing the professional under section 22(2), approving the acts listed in section 28, approving a plan under section 30(4) and resolving to liquidate under section 33(2).

options.text: The replacement failed, because section 22(2) requires not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors; section 24(3) requires notice of every meeting of the committee to be given to the members of the suspended Board of Directors even though section 24(4) gives them no vote; and interim finance was not his to raise alone, section 25(2)(c) making him raise it subject to the approval of the committee of creditors under section 28
options.why: Section 22(2) lets the committee, in its first meeting, resolve to appoint the interim resolution professional as the resolution professional or to replace him, by a majority vote of not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors; sixty per cent does not carry it. Section 24(3) requires notice of each meeting to the members of the committee, to the members of the suspended Board of Directors or the partners, and to operational creditors whose aggregate dues are not less than a tenth of the debt; section 24(4) then lets them attend without a vote, and Vijay Kumar Jain v Standard Chartered Bank held that a suspended director is entitled to the agenda and the resolution plans as well. Section 25(2)(c) requires the resolution professional to raise interim finance subject to the approval of the committee of creditors under section 28.

options.text: He was right about the interim finance, because section 23(2) gives the resolution professional the powers and duties of the interim resolution professional, including the section 20(2)(c) power
options.misconception: reads section 23(2) without the duty section that follows it
options.why: Section 23(2) does carry the powers across, and section 25(2)(c) then states his own duty in terms that answer this question — to raise interim finances subject to the approval of the committee of creditors under section 28. Section 28(4) makes an action taken without that approval void, so the general transfer of powers cannot be read as overriding the specific constraint.

citation.ref: Sections 22(2), 23(2), 24(3), 24(4) and 25(2)(c), read with sections 28(3) and 28(4)

items.scenario: At the first meeting of the committee of creditors, held on the sixth day after its constitution, financial creditors holding sixty per cent of the voting share vote to replace the interim resolution professional with someone else, and the minute records the resolution as carried. The professional who continues in office thereafter declines to send notice of later meetings to the members of the suspended Board, on the ground that they have no right to vote in them, and raises ₹40 crore of interim finance on his own signature, saying that section 23(2) gives him all the powers of the interim resolution professional.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The change of auditor is governed by sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act alone, the Code being silent about the auditors of a corporate debtor
options.misconception: overlooks clause (m) of section 28(1)
options.why: The Code is not silent. Section 28(1)(m) names the statutory auditors and the internal auditors in terms, and section 28(1) begins "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force", which is the phrase that decides the contest with the Companies Act machinery.

options.text: The sale to the managing director's brother's company is unobjectionable because it was at the market price and so on arm's length terms
options.misconception: imports section 188's arm's-length carve-out into a section that has none
options.why: The exemption for an ordinary-course transaction on an arm's length basis lives in the fourth proviso to section 188 of the Companies Act. Section 28(1)(f) says simply that the resolution professional shall not undertake any related party transaction without the prior approval of the committee — the price is not the test, the counterparty is.

options.text: The actions are voidable at the instance of the committee of creditors, which may ratify them at its next meeting if it is content with what was done
options.misconception: reads the word "void" in section 28(4) as voidable
options.why: Section 28(4) says that where an action under sub-section (1) is taken without seeking the approval of the committee in the manner required, such action shall be void. There is nobody at whose instance it stands or falls and nothing to ratify; the committee's remedy under section 28(5) is to report the professional to the Board for action against him.

options.text: All three needed the committee's prior approval by a vote of sixty-six per cent, because a change in the appointment or terms of contract of the statutory auditors, a related party transaction and a delegation of his authority to any other person are each on the section 28(1) list; and each of the three, taken without that approval, is void
options.why: Section 28(1) opens with a non obstante clause and names all three — clause (m) covers making changes in the appointment or terms of contract of the statutory auditors or internal auditors of the corporate debtor, clause (f) covers undertaking any related party transaction, and clause (h) covers delegating his authority to any other person. Section 28(2) requires him to convene a meeting and seek the committee's vote before taking any of them, and section 28(3) fixes the majority at sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors. Section 28(4) then says that an action taken without that approval shall be void, and section 28(5) lets the committee report him to the Board.

citation.ref: Sections 28(1)(f), 28(1)(h), 28(1)(m), 28(2), 28(3), 28(4) and 28(5), read with sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the fourth proviso to section 188 of that Act

items.scenario: Four months into a resolution process the resolution professional decides that the company's statutory auditor is too close to the old promoters. He obtains the auditor's resignation, appoints a new firm in the resulting vacancy, and treats the whole thing as a matter for sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act. In the same month he sells finished goods worth ₹12 crore, at the market price, to a company owned by a brother of the suspended managing director, and he delegates his day-to-day authority over the plant to a senior manager so that he can concentrate on the information memorandum. He takes none of the three to the committee of creditors, saying that section 17(1) has put the board's powers in him.

items.stem: What must the resolution professional tell him?

options.text: That the payment order is fatal, section 30(2)(a) requiring the plan to provide for the payment of the insolvency resolution process costs in priority to the payment of the other debts; that the general meetings are unnecessary, any shareholder approval required under the Companies Act for implementing the plan's actions being deemed given by the Explanation to section 30(2); and that the Competition Commission's approval cannot wait, because it has to be obtained before the committee of creditors approves the plan
options.why: Section 30(2)(a) requires the resolution professional to confirm that the plan provides for the payment of the insolvency resolution process costs in the manner specified by the Board in priority to the payment of the other debts of the corporate debtor, so a plan that pays those costs out of the residue fails at the examination stage and never reaches the committee. The Explanation to section 30(2) says that if any approval of shareholders is required under the Companies Act, 2013 or any other law for the implementation of the actions under the resolution plan, such approval shall be deemed to have been given and it shall not be a contravention of that Act or law — which covers the fresh issue, the capital reduction and the object clause together. The proviso to section 31(4) is the exception that is not deemed: where the plan contains a provision for a combination as referred to in section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002, the applicant shall obtain the approval of the Competition Commission of India prior to the approval of the plan by the committee of creditors.

options.text: That the Competition Commission's approval may indeed be taken within one year of the Adjudicating Authority's order, like every other approval any law requires
options.misconception: reads the body of section 31(4) and misses its proviso
options.why: The body of section 31(4) does give the resolution applicant one year from the Adjudicating Authority's approval, or the period provided in the relevant law if longer, to obtain the approvals any law requires. Its proviso then takes one approval out of that timetable and puts it earlier than everything else — the competition approval comes before the committee of creditors votes on the plan.

options.text: That the general meetings are indispensable, since a reduction of share capital and an alteration of the object clause each require a special resolution of the members under the Companies Act
options.misconception: overlooks the deeming in the Explanation to section 30(2)
options.why: They would be indispensable outside a resolution process. The Explanation to section 30(2) exists because a company in insolvency cannot realistically go back to the shareholders whose equity the plan is extinguishing, and it deems any such approval to have been given and puts the plan outside a contravention of the Act.

options.text: That the payment order is acceptable, because process costs rank first only in a liquidation under section 53 and a resolution plan is free to order its own payments
options.misconception: reads the waterfall as the only place the Code protects process costs
options.why: Section 53(1)(a) does put the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs at the head of the waterfall, and section 30(2)(a) imposes the same priority inside a resolution plan independently of it. The two work together, which is why a plan that leaves those costs to be paid out of the residue cannot be presented to the committee at all.

citation.ref: Sections 30(2)(a) and 30(2) with the Explanation to clause (e), and section 31(4) with its proviso, read with section 53(1)(a) of the Code and section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002

items.scenario: A resolution plan for a listed manufacturing company issues fresh equity to the applicant, writes the existing share capital down to nil and alters the object clause of the memorandum. The acquisition it effects is a combination as referred to in section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002. On the money, the plan pays the financial creditors first and pays the insolvency resolution process costs out of what is left. The applicant's covering note says he will convene general meetings for the capital reduction and the object clause once the Adjudicating Authority has approved the plan, and will apply to the Competition Commission of India within the year that section 31(4) allows for obtaining approvals.

items.stem: How do the two appeals stand?

options.text: The creditor is in time, because section 62 allows forty-five days for an appeal against an order approving a resolution plan
options.misconception: uses the Supreme Court limitation for an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal
options.why: Section 62 is the appeal from the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal to the Supreme Court, on a question of law, within forty-five days of receipt of the Appellate Tribunal's order and a further fifteen on sufficient cause. The appeal from the Adjudicating Authority to the Appellate Tribunal is section 61, and its clock is thirty days.

options.text: The creditor's ground is a good one, since a plan that pays him far less than the business is worth contravenes the law within section 61(3)(i)
options.misconception: dresses a complaint about commercial terms as a contravention of law
options.why: Section 61(3)(i) is about a plan whose contents offend some provision of law — a payment the Code forbids, a term a statute prohibits. The amount a dissenting financial creditor is offered is controlled instead by the statutory minimum in section 30(2)(b), and above that floor the distribution is the commercial wisdom of the committee, which is not open to judicial review.

options.text: Both appeals are in time, because appeals to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal are governed by one limitation of forty-five days with condonation, whatever the order below was passed under
options.misconception: assumes one forum means one limitation
options.why: The forum is common and the limitation is not. An appeal under the Code is governed by section 61(2) — thirty days, with a further fifteen at most — and an appeal under the Companies Act by section 421(3) — forty-five days, with a further forty-five. Section 61(1) opens with the words "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained under the Companies Act, 2013" for that reason.

options.text: The creditor's appeal is beyond saving on time — section 61(2) gives thirty days and its proviso a further fifteen at most, so forty-eight days is outside what the Appellate Tribunal can condone — and his complaint is in any case not on the closed list of grounds in section 61(3); the shareholder's appeal is inside the further period of forty-five days that the proviso to section 421(3) of the Companies Act allows, and may be entertained on sufficient cause
options.why: Section 61(2) requires an appeal to be filed within thirty days, and its proviso lets the Appellate Tribunal allow a further period which shall not exceed fifteen days on sufficient cause, so forty-five days is the outer edge and 20 September is the forty-eighth day. Section 61(3) then lists the only grounds on which an order approving a plan may be attacked — contravention of law, material irregularity by the resolution professional, the operational creditors not being paid in the manner specified, the process costs not being paid in priority, or non-compliance with any other criteria specified by the Board — and the commercial merits of the plan are on none of them, which is what K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel put beyond argument. The Companies Act runs a different clock before the same forum: section 421(3) gives forty-five days from the date the copy of the order was made available, with a further period not exceeding forty-five days on sufficient cause.

citation.ref: Sections 61(1), 61(2) with its proviso, 61(3) and 62 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and section 30(2)(b) of the Code

items.scenario: The Adjudicating Authority approves a resolution plan on 3 August 2026 and a dissenting financial creditor receives a copy of the order the same day. He instructs counsel on 20 September 2026 to appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, his complaint being that the committee of creditors accepted a plan paying him far less than he believes the business is worth. On the same day, a shareholder of an unrelated company instructs the same counsel to appeal to the same Appellate Tribunal against an order of the National Company Law Tribunal dated 3 August 2026 passed under section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, a copy of which was made available to him that day.

items.stem: Can the application be filed against this company?

options.text: No — section 3(7) excludes a financial service provider from the meaning of a corporate person, so a non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank is not a corporate debtor for Part II at all, and the route is section 227, under which such providers are dealt with under separate Rules on an application by the appropriate regulator
options.why: Section 3(7) defines a corporate person as a company, a limited liability partnership or any other person incorporated with limited liability under any law, but shall not include any financial service provider; and section 3(17) defines a financial service provider as a person engaged in the business of providing financial services in terms of an authorisation issued or a registration granted by a financial sector regulator. A registered non-banking financial company answers that description, so there is no corporate debtor for section 7 to operate on however plain the default. Section 227 is the route that exists instead: the Central Government, in consultation with the appropriate financial sector regulator, notifies such providers, and their proceedings are conducted under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers and Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2019 on an application made by that regulator.

options.text: Yes, because a debenture-holder is a financial creditor and section 7 lets a financial creditor apply where a default has occurred
options.misconception: tests the creditor and never tests the debtor
options.why: The section has two ends and both have to qualify. The applicant must be a financial creditor and the respondent must be a corporate debtor, which section 3(8) defines as a corporate person who owes a debt — and section 3(7) takes a financial service provider out of the meaning of a corporate person.

options.text: Yes, provided the default exceeds the minimum amount notified under section 4, which it plainly does
options.misconception: treats the monetary threshold as the only gate
options.why: Section 4 fixes the floor below which Part II does not apply; it does not decide who Part II applies to. That is settled by the definitions in section 3, under which a financial service provider is not a corporate person and therefore never a corporate debtor.

options.text: No, because money raised by issuing debentures is a claim on a security rather than a financial debt within section 5(8)
options.misconception: reads section 5(8) as excluding debentures, which it expressly includes
options.why: Section 5(8) defines financial debt as a debt along with interest disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and lists what it includes, among them any amount raised pursuant to the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument. The debenture money is a financial debt; the obstacle is at the other end of the application.

citation.ref: Sections 3(7), 3(8), 3(17), 5(8) and 227 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with section 4 and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers and Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2019

items.scenario: A non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank of India has defaulted on ₹50 crore of listed debentures, an amount far above the minimum notified under section 4. One of the debenture-holders wants to file an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 against it, pointing out that the debenture money was clearly disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money.

items.stem: What is Beta to Alpha under the Companies Act, 2013?

options.text: A subsidiary — twenty per cent of the voting power is the statutory line for control
options.misconception: reads the significant-influence line as the control line
options.why: Section 2(87) makes a subsidiary out of control of the composition of the Board of Directors or of more than one-half of the total voting power. Twenty-two per cent is nowhere near a half, and section 2(6) exists precisely for the holdings that stop short of it.

options.text: Neither — a shareholding with no agreement over business decisions creates no relationship under the Act
options.misconception: treats the agreement limb as the only route to significant influence
options.why: The Explanation to section 2(6) offers two routes and either one alone is enough: at least twenty per cent of the total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement. The first route asks for no agreement at all.

options.text: An associate company — twenty per cent of the voting power is significant influence, not control
options.why: Section 2(6) calls a company an associate company of another where that other has a significant influence over it but it is not a subsidiary, and the Explanation fixes significant influence at control of at least twenty per cent of the total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement. Twenty-two per cent clears that line. A subsidiary under section 2(87) needs control of the composition of the Board of Directors or of more than one-half of the total voting power, and Alpha has neither.

options.text: A joint venture, because the Act treats every twenty per cent holding as one
options.misconception: collapses the joint venture limb into the percentage test
options.why: A joint venture is a joint arrangement in which the parties have joint control and rights to the net assets of the arrangement. It is brought inside the words "associate company" by definition, but joint control has to be shown; a bare twenty-two per cent stake does not create it.

citation.ref: Section 2(6) with its Explanation, read with section 2(87)

items.scenario: Alpha Ltd holds 22 per cent of the total voting power in Beta Ltd. It has no agreement with Beta about how Beta's business decisions are taken, no right to appoint any of Beta's directors, and no other holding in it. Beta's finance head tells his board that Beta has become a subsidiary of Alpha.

items.stem: What does section 12 require of the company in its first month?

options.text: A registered office within one hundred and eighty days, the period the Act allows before business may commence
options.misconception: borrows section 10A's clock for a duty that runs on its own
options.why: Section 10A stops a company from commencing business until a declaration is filed within one hundred and eighty days of incorporation, and it answers a different question — whether the subscribers have paid for their shares. The registered office duty in section 12(1) is thirty days and applies whether or not any business has begun.

options.text: A registered office within thirty days of incorporation, with verification of it filed with the Registrar inside the same thirty days
options.why: Section 12(1) requires a company to have, within thirty days of its incorporation and at all times thereafter, a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications and notices addressed to it. Section 12(2) requires the company to furnish the Registrar with verification of that registered office within the same thirty days. Neither duty waits for a permanent office or for the first annual return.

options.text: Only the name board outside the place of business; the address is a matter for the Registrar's own records
options.misconception: keeps the display duty and drops the filing duty
options.why: Section 12(3) does require the name and the address of the registered office to be painted or affixed outside every place of business, in legible letters and in a local language as well. That is an addition to section 12(2), not a substitute for it.

options.text: Nothing until the first annual general meeting, when the office details go in with the annual return
options.misconception: pushes an incorporation-stage duty into the first annual filing
options.why: The annual return under section 92 reports the year that has gone. Section 12 is a standing obligation that starts running on the day the company is registered, and a company with no address to receive notices at is a company nobody can serve.

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and 12(3), read with section 10A

items.scenario: A private company is incorporated on 4 May 2026. Its promoter intends to work from a co-working desk for the first year, put up the company's name board only when a permanent office is taken, and give the Registrar the registered office details along with the first annual return.

items.stem: Has the special resolution been passed?

options.text: The question cannot be answered, because a special resolution has to be put to a poll and this was one
options.misconception: invents a voting mechanism that section 114 does not prescribe
options.why: Section 114 says nothing about how the votes are taken. A special resolution may be carried on a show of hands, on a poll or by electronic means; what it needs is the stated intention and the three-to-one margin on the votes actually cast.

options.text: Yes — a simple majority is enough once the notice has described the motion as a special resolution
options.misconception: treats the notice of intention as supplying the majority
options.why: The notice of intention is one of three conditions in section 114(2) and the easiest to satisfy. Calling a motion special does not lower what it has to poll; it only makes clear which threshold the meeting is being asked to clear.

options.text: Yes — more than seventy per cent of the votes cast were in favour
options.misconception: measures the majority against the votes cast instead of against the votes cast against
options.why: The test counts the votes against and multiplies them, which works out at seventy-five per cent of the votes cast. 5,400 out of the 7,300 cast is a little over seventy-three per cent, so the motion is short by the section's own arithmetic as well as by the ratio.

options.text: No — the votes in favour must be at least three times the votes against, and three times 1,900 is 5,700
options.why: Section 114(2) makes a resolution special only where the intention was specified in the notice, the notice required by the Act was duly given, and the votes cast in favour are not less than three times the number of votes cast against. Three times 1,900 comes to 5,700 and only 5,400 were cast in favour, so the motion falls short. It carries as an ordinary resolution, since the votes in favour exceed those against, and that is all it is.

citation.ref: Sections 114(1) and 114(2)

items.scenario: At a general meeting the notice of which stated the intention to propose the motion as a special resolution, a poll is taken. 5,400 votes are cast in favour and 1,900 against; the remaining members abstain.

items.stem: Was there a quorum under section 103?

options.text: Yes — fifty-three is comfortably above the fifteen the section asks for
options.misconception: counts proxies towards a quorum the section reserves for members in the room
options.why: A proxy may be lodged, inspected and voted on a poll, and still does nothing here. The quorum is a count of members personally present, which is why section 103 uses those two words and not "represented".

options.text: Yes — the quorum for any general meeting is five members, and twelve attended
options.misconception: applies the smallest slab to a company of every size
options.why: Five is the number only where the members are not more than one thousand. This register carries 1,240, which lands the company in the middle slab of fifteen; the slabs move with the size of the membership.

options.text: No — this company needed fifteen members present in person, and proxies do not count towards the quorum
options.why: Section 103(1)(a) fixes the quorum of a public company at five members personally present where the members are not more than one thousand, fifteen where they are more than one thousand but up to five thousand, and thirty where they exceed five thousand. With 1,240 members the number is fifteen. The words "personally present" leave proxies out of the count however many are validly lodged, so twelve is what the chairman actually had.

options.text: No — the company needed thirty members personally present
options.misconception: reads the slab meant for more than five thousand members
options.why: Thirty applies where the members exceed five thousand. At 1,240 the company is in the second slab, so the shortfall is real but the number the chairman needed was fifteen.

citation.ref: Sections 103(1)(a) and 103(2)

items.scenario: A public company with 1,240 members on its register calls a general meeting. Twelve members attend in person; forty-one others have lodged valid proxies. The chairman counts fifty-three and declares the meeting in order.

items.stem: When does each company's first financial year end?

options.text: Both on 31 March 2027, because a company's first financial year is always a full year
options.misconception: assumes a first accounting period of twelve months
options.why: Nothing in the definition asks for twelve months. Vega gets a first financial year of barely a quarter, and a company incorporated in late March gets one of a few days; the length follows the date of incorporation, not the other way round.

options.text: Vega on 31 March 2026 and Orion on 31 March 2027
options.why: Section 2(41) defines the financial year as the period ending on the 31st day of March every year, and where a company has been incorporated on or after the 1st day of January of a year, the period ending on the 31st day of March of the following year. Vega was incorporated on 20 December 2025, before that cut-off, so its first financial year runs a little over three months to 31 March 2026. Orion was incorporated on 12 February 2026, after it, so its first financial year runs to 31 March 2027.

options.text: Vega on 31 March 2027 and Orion on 31 March 2026
options.misconception: reverses the 1 January test
options.why: The extension belongs to the company incorporated on or after 1 January, which is Orion. Vega, incorporated in December, is on the ordinary footing and closes at the next 31 March.

options.text: Both on 31 March 2026, since every company in India closes its books on 31 March
options.misconception: applies the year end and drops the rule that fixes the first one
options.why: The 31 March close is only half of section 2(41). The other half moves the first year end forward by a whole year for a company incorporated on or after 1 January, so two companies incorporated seven weeks apart can close their first accounts a year apart.

citation.ref: Section 2(41)

items.scenario: A group incorporates two companies during one restructuring — Vega Ltd on 20 December 2025 and Orion Ltd on 12 February 2026. The group controller proposes to close the first accounts of both on 31 March 2026 so that the consolidation has a single cut-off.

items.stem: What is wrong with what the proxy holder did?

options.text: Nothing — a proxy stands in the member's shoes for every purpose of the meeting
options.misconception: treats the proxy as the member himself
options.why: A proxy is an agent for voting and for nothing else. Section 105 gives him the vote on a poll and expressly withholds the right to speak, so he cannot debate, move an amendment or be counted in the quorum.

options.text: All of it — a proxy has no right to speak, may not vote except on a poll, and may not act for more than fifty members
options.why: The first proviso to section 105(1) says a proxy shall not have the right to speak at the meeting and shall not be entitled to vote except on a poll, which disposes of both the request for the floor and the raised hand. The second proviso limits one person to acting as proxy on behalf of not more than fifty members and such number of shares as is prescribed, so sixty instruments break the cap on their own.

options.text: Only the sixty instruments; the ten per cent share ceiling in the rules is the real cap and fifty is guidance
options.misconception: demotes a number written into the section to a guideline
options.why: Fifty members is in section 105(1) itself and the share ceiling comes from the rules made under it. Both bind at once, and the fifty is not advisory merely because a second limit sits beside it.

options.text: Only the request to speak; on the voting he stands exactly where the member would
options.misconception: gives the proxy the member's vote on a show of hands
options.why: The proviso separates the two. A proxy's vote counts on a poll, where shares are counted, and not on a show of hands, where the meeting counts the members entitled to be there in their own right — which is why the raised hand is worth nothing.

citation.ref: Section 105(1) with its first and second provisos
