options.why: Section 47(1) is the clearance step — the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance for home consumption once satisfied that the goods are not prohibited and the duty and charges have been paid. It settles nothing about the classification and is not an assessment order.

citation.ref: Sections 17(1), 17(4) and 17(5), read with sections 46(1) and 47(1)

items.scenario: An importer files a bill of entry for home consumption, self-assessing the goods under a heading that carries a lower rate. The proper officer examines the goods, disagrees, and re-assesses them under a different heading. The importer does not accept the change and says so, but pays under protest so that the consignment can move.

items.stem: What follows?

options.text: Nothing can be recovered at all, the one-year period for a notice having expired
options.misconception: quotes the pre-2016 limitation of one year, which was replaced by two years for an ordinary short-levy
options.why: One year was the earlier period and it is no longer the law; an ordinary short-levy now carries two years from the relevant date. In any event the payment here was voluntary, so limitation never came into it.

options.text: He must also pay a penalty equal to fifteen per cent of the duty for the immunity to apply
options.misconception: imports the pre-notice penalty from a collusion case under section 28(5) into an ordinary short-levy under section 28(2)
options.why: The fifteen per cent penalty belongs to section 28(5), which deals with a case of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. An ordinary short-levy under section 28(1) needs only the duty and the interest.

options.text: A notice must still issue, since the period for a notice in a non-collusion case is two years and eighteen months is inside it
options.misconception: reads the limitation period as compelling a notice, when section 28(2) removes the need for one where the duty and interest are paid voluntarily
options.why: The two years in section 28(1)(a) is the outer limit for serving a notice, not an instruction to serve one. Where the duty and interest are paid voluntarily and the officer is informed, section 28(2) bars a notice for that amount.

options.text: The proper officer shall not serve a notice for the amount paid, though he may still proceed for any part found short paid
options.why: Section 28(2) lets the person pay the duty on his own ascertainment or on the officer's, with interest under section 28AA, and inform the proper officer in writing, and the proper officer shall not serve any notice in respect of the amount so paid. What survives is the officer's right to proceed for any amount found short paid beyond what was paid.

citation.ref: Sections 28(1)(a) and 28(2), read with sections 28(4), 28(5) and 28AA

items.scenario: An importer discovers, eighteen months after clearance, that a consignment was short-levied because of a clerical mistake in his own declaration. There was no collusion and nothing was suppressed. Before any notice reaches him he pays the differential duty with interest and writes to the proper officer telling him so.

items.stem: Which vessel may consume the imported stores without payment of duty?

options.text: The vessel sailing to Singapore, and only for fuel, spare parts being outside the meaning of stores
options.misconception: reads the definition of stores too narrowly, when section 2(38) includes spare parts and equipment expressly
options.why: Section 2(38) casts a wide net for stores — goods meant for use aboard a vessel or aircraft — and folds fuel, spare parts and any other article of equipment into that net, present or not for immediate fitting. Spare parts sit inside the definition on its own terms.

options.text: The vessel sailing to Singapore, being a foreign-going vessel; the coastal vessel's stores are dutiable in the ordinary way
options.why: Section 87 allows imported stores on board to be consumed without payment of duty while the vessel is a foreign-going vessel, and section 2(21) makes that one engaged in the carriage of goods or passengers between a port in India and a port outside India. A coastal vessel plying between two Indian ports is not one.

options.text: Both, since section 87 speaks of stores consumed on board and says nothing about the voyage
options.misconception: drops the foreign-going condition, which is the only thing section 87 turns on
options.why: Section 87 is conditional in its own words — the consumption is free of duty while the vessel or aircraft is a foreign-going one. Strip that condition out and the section says nothing at all about which stores it covers.

options.text: Neither, until the stores have been warehoused under section 85 and cleared for consumption
options.misconception: makes warehousing a precondition, when section 85 is an option for stores entered for warehousing rather than a step every ship must take
options.why: Section 85 lets imported goods entered for warehousing and intended for use as stores be warehoused without assessment to duty. It is a facility for stores that go into a warehouse, not a precondition to consuming stores already on board under section 87.

citation.ref: Section 87, read with sections 2(21), 2(38) and 85

items.scenario: A shipping company runs two vessels out of an Indian port. One carries cargo between that port and Singapore. The other carries cargo between that port and another Indian port and never leaves Indian waters. Imported fuel and provisions are taken on board both, and are consumed at sea.

items.stem: Does the explanation reach the supplies made before it was issued?

options.text: No — it operates only from the date of the second notification, like any other amendment
options.misconception: reads a section 11(3) explanation as an ordinary prospective amendment when the sub-section gives it always-was effect
options.why: An ordinary amending notification only works prospectively, from the day it is issued. Section 11(3) is written to do something else: once inserted within the one-year window, the explanation shall have effect from the very date the parent notification began, not from the date of the insertion itself. That reach-back is the reason the power carries a fenced time limit in the first place.

options.text: No — an exemption once granted can only be narrowed by withdrawing the notification and issuing a fresh one
options.misconception: denies a clarificatory power that section 11(3) expressly grants
options.why: Withdrawal and re-issue is one route, but it is not the only one. Section 11(3) gives a separate power to clarify the scope or applicability of an existing notification by inserting an explanation into it, and the department is entitled to use that power instead.

options.text: Yes — it was inserted within a year of the parent notification, so it takes effect as though it had been part of it from the start
options.why: Section 11(3) lets the Government insert an explanation into a notification issued under section 11(1), so long as it does so within one year of that notification's own date of issue. Once inserted inside that window, the change reads as if it had always been there — folded into the notification from its first day rather than starting fresh from the day of insertion. Eleven months sits inside that window, so the clarification reaches back to 1 April, the parent notification's own effective date.
keywords: as if it had always been

options.text: Yes, but only if a special order under section 11(2) is passed for this supplier
options.misconception: confuses the general notification power with the exceptional special-order power that operates case by case
options.why: Section 11(2) is a different tool from section 11(3). It lets the Government act supply by supply through a special order in each case, but that order has to rest on its own stated exceptional nature — it does nothing to unlock or extend an existing general notification. Section 11(3) calls for none of that; it only lets an explanation be added to a notification already in force.

citation.ref: Section 11(3), read with section 11(1)

items.scenario: A notification issued under section 11(1) exempts a described category of services with effect from 1 April. Eleven months later the Government issues a second notification inserting an explanation into the first one, saying the description was never meant to cover a particular sub-category. A supplier who treated that sub-category as exempt from April onwards is told he owes tax for the whole period.

items.stem: On which of the three must the company pay GST under reverse charge?

options.text: The sitting fees and the rent, since the recipient in both cases is a body corporate
options.misconception: treats a company recipient as the trigger, when the trigger is a service supplied by a person acting as a director
options.why: The recipient being a body corporate is a condition of entry 6, not the whole of it; the supply must also be made by a director acting as such. Renting out property he owns personally is not that, so the rent stays on the director and no reverse charge arises on the company.

options.text: All three, because each is a payment by a company to its own director
options.misconception: makes the identity of the payee the test when the notification asks in what capacity the service was supplied
options.why: Entry 6 asks what was supplied and in what capacity, not who was paid. Employment is outside supply altogether, and a letting made in the director's own right as a property owner is supplied in a capacity that is not that of a director, so two of the three payments fall outside the entry.

options.text: Only the sitting fees
options.why: The whole-time director's salary is not a supply at all — entry 1 of Schedule III puts services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment outside the scope of supply. The sitting fees are not employment income and fall inside entry 6 of Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), so the company pays under reverse charge in cash. The rent is supplied in the director's personal capacity as owner of the godown, not in his capacity as a director, so entry 6 does not reach it.

options.text: None, because a director is an employee of the company and employment is outside GST
options.misconception: extends the employment exclusion to a non-executive director who has no employment with the company
options.why: A whole-time director is an employee and an independent director is not. The employment exclusion covers the first and cannot be stretched to the second, whose sitting fees are paid for services rendered to the company otherwise than under a contract of employment.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entry 1 of Schedule III, and Circulars 140/10/2020-GST and 201/13/2023-GST

items.scenario: A private limited company makes three payments in a month. It pays a monthly salary to its whole-time director, booked as salary and subjected to tax deduction at source under section 192 of the Income-tax Act. It pays sitting fees to an independent director for attending board meetings, with deduction under section 194J. And it pays rent to another director for a godown he owns personally and has let to the company.

items.stem: Which of the three sales is a supply of services under paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II?

options.text: All three, because a builder selling flats is always supplying a construction service
options.misconception: reads paragraph 5(b) as taxing every sale by a builder rather than as a rule about when the money arrived
options.why: The trade of the seller is not the test. Paragraph 5(b) turns on when the consideration was received, and paragraph 5 of Schedule III keeps a completed building outside GST no matter who sells it.

options.text: None, because the sale of a building is outside GST under Schedule III
options.misconception: reads paragraph 5 of Schedule III without the opening words that make it subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II
options.why: Paragraph 5 of Schedule III is expressly made subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II. It keeps a completed building outside GST, and it surrenders to paragraph 5(b) wherever money came in before completion, which is exactly Flat 1.

options.text: Flat 1 alone
options.why: The carve-out in paragraph 5(b) applies only where the entire consideration has been received after the completion certificate or after first occupation, whichever is earlier. Flat 1 fails it because a booking amount came in before either event, and the whole value then becomes a supply of services. Flat 2 and Flat 3 both satisfy it — for Flat 3 the earlier of the two events was first occupation, and the entire consideration came after that.

options.text: Flats 1 and 3
options.misconception: treats the completion certificate as the only trigger and overlooks that first occupation can come earlier
options.why: The paragraph names two events and takes the earlier of them, and it is the completion certificate that is qualified by the words where required. For Flat 3 the building had already been first occupied when the money came in, so the exception is met and the sale is not a supply of services.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II, read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III

items.scenario: A builder sells three flats in one project. For Flat 1 the buyer paid a small booking amount before the competent authority issued the completion certificate and the rest afterwards. For Flat 2 the buyer paid the whole price after that certificate was issued. Flat 3 was bought by a family who paid the entire price after the building had been first occupied by earlier residents but before the certificate finally came through.

items.stem: Is the chain right about its counter invoices?

options.text: No, but nothing is needed either, since a customer who is unregistered can take no credit
options.misconception: reads the requirement backwards — it applies because the customer is unregistered, not despite it
options.why: Credit is not what the rule is about. The requirement attaches to an invoice issued to an unregistered customer, so the customer's inability to take credit is the reason the rule exists rather than a reason to skip it.

options.text: Yes — one scannable code on the invoice discharges both requirements
options.misconception: treats the electronic-invoicing code and the dynamic code as one obligation when they serve different purposes
options.why: They are two obligations in two different rules, aimed at two different readers. One lets anyone verify that an invoice was reported; the other lets a consumer pay. A code that does the first does not do the second.

options.text: No — a counter invoice needs a Dynamic Quick Response code carrying payment details, which is not what the Portal returns
options.why: The counter invoices go to an unregistered customer, and rule 46 requires such an invoice to bear a Dynamic Quick Response code — a payment instruction the customer can scan and pay with. The code the Portal returns with an Invoice Reference Number is static and identifies the invoice; it does nothing the dynamic code is there to do.

options.text: No — the chain must also report its counter invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal
options.misconception: extends rule 48(4) to business-to-consumer supplies, which it has never covered
options.why: Rule 48(4) covers supplies to a registered person, exports and supplies to a special economic zone. A business-to-consumer invoice is outside it and is never uploaded to the Invoice Registration Portal, which is precisely why the separate dynamic-code requirement exists.

citation.ref: Rule 46 (the Dynamic Quick Response code requirement) with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax, read with rule 48(4)

items.scenario: A retail chain is above the notified turnover for both electronic invoicing and the code requirement in rule 46. It reports its invoices to registered dealers to the Invoice Registration Portal and receives an Invoice Reference Number with the signed code the Portal returns. It then prints that same Portal-generated code on the counter invoices it hands to walk-in customers, saying an invoice bearing a scannable code satisfies the rule.

items.stem: Which of the two balances can he claim back as a refund?

options.text: Both balances, since section 49(6) covers the cash ledger and the credit ledger alike
options.misconception: reads section 49(6) as a right to a refund when it only routes the claim to section 54, which then restricts credit refunds
options.why: Section 49(6) does mention both ledgers, but it grants nothing by itself — it says the balance may be refunded in accordance with section 54. Section 54(3) is where the credit ledger is cut down to two cases, and neither of them fits a purely domestic supplier.

options.text: The credit ledger balance only, because money once paid into the cash ledger is tax already paid
options.misconception: treats a challan deposit as a payment of tax when it becomes tax only on being debited against a liability
options.why: A challan credits the cash ledger; it does not discharge anything. The amount becomes tax only when it is debited against a liability, and until then it is the taxpayer's money sitting on the portal.

options.text: Neither, because a balance in either ledger can only be set off against future liability
options.misconception: treats both ledgers as carry-forward accounts when the cash ledger holds the taxpayer's own money
options.why: Carrying forward is what happens to the credit balance, and it is a fair description of it. It is not true of the cash ledger, where the money is a deposit the taxpayer made and has never spent, and the proviso to section 54(1) exists to give it back.

options.text: The cash ledger balance only
options.why: Section 49(6) lets a balance be refunded in accordance with section 54, and the proviso to section 54(1) gives the electronic cash ledger balance its own route because that money is a deposit, not tax. The unutilised credit cannot follow it — section 54(3) allows a refund of credit only on zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax or under an inverted duty structure, and he has neither.

citation.ref: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1), read with section 54(3)

items.scenario: A trader over-deposited on a challan and has ₹4,20,000 sitting unused in his electronic cash ledger. He also has ₹6,00,000 of unutilised input tax credit in his electronic credit ledger. He makes only domestic taxable supplies, all at the same rate as the goods he buys, and he exports nothing.

items.stem: From which date does interest under section 56 run?

options.text: From 10 March 2026, the date of the appellate order
options.misconception: starts the clock at the order when both the main limb and the proviso start it at the receipt of an application
options.why: Neither limb of section 56 mentions the date of an order as a starting point. The main limb runs from the application under section 54(1) and the proviso from the application filed consequent to the order, so the date of the appellate order does no work here.
keywords: the application filed consequent to the order

options.text: No interest is payable, because the refund was never ordered by the proper officer under section 54(5)
options.misconception: overlooks the Explanation deeming an appellate order of refund to be an order under section 54(5)
options.why: The Explanation to section 56 deems an order of refund made by an appellate authority, the Tribunal or a court against an order of the proper officer to be an order passed under section 54(5). The refund is therefore ordered under that sub-section for the purposes of the section, and interest follows.

options.text: From the day after sixty days from 2 April 2026
options.why: The proviso to section 56 applies because the refund arises from an order that has attained finality, and it starts the clock at sixty days from the date of receipt of the application filed consequent to such order. That application is the one dated 2 April 2026, so interest runs from the day immediately after those sixty days until 20 August 2026, at the higher rate the proviso carries.

options.text: From sixty days after the original 2023 refund application
options.misconception: uses the first application when the proviso names the one filed after the order
options.why: The original application was rejected and the proviso does not revive it. It names the application filed consequent to the order that attained finality, and that is the 2026 application, not the 2023 one.
keywords: the application filed consequent to the order

citation.ref: Proviso to section 56 with the Explanation to section 56, read with sections 54(1) and 54(5)

items.scenario: A refund claim filed in 2023 was rejected. The Appellate Authority allowed it by an order dated 10 March 2026, and no further appeal was filed, so the order attained finality. The claimant filed a fresh refund application consequent to that order on 2 April 2026. The department actually paid on 20 August 2026.

items.stem: Which of the two steps was open to the Appellate Authority?

options.text: Both, because an appellate authority has all the powers of the authority whose order it is reviewing
options.misconception: assumes a general appellate power of remand that section 107(11) removes in terms
options.why: The powers of a first appellate authority under GST are the ones section 107(11) gives it, and that sub-section names three — confirming, modifying or annulling — and then takes away a fourth by barring a reference back. There is no residual power to fall back on.

options.text: Neither
options.why: Section 107(11) lets the Appellate Authority pass an order confirming, modifying or annulling the decision appealed against but expressly says it shall not refer the case back to the adjudicating authority, so the remand is outside its power and the contracts had to be examined in its own further inquiry. The first proviso then bars an order enhancing a penalty unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed order.

options.text: The remand, but not the enhancement
options.misconception: half-remembers the sub-section, keeping the bar in its first proviso and dropping the bar in its main limb
options.why: The bar on sending the case back sits in the main limb of section 107(11) itself, not in a proviso. Both steps fail, and for different reasons — one for want of power, the other for want of notice.

options.text: The enhancement, because no fresh tax was demanded and the proviso only protects against a demand of tax
options.misconception: reads the first proviso as covering tax alone when it names fee, penalty, fine in lieu of confiscation, refund and credit
options.why: The first proviso to section 107(11) reaches an order that enhances any fee or penalty, or a fine standing in place of confiscation; one that confiscates goods worth more than those already taken; and one reducing a refund or the input tax credit allowed. A penalty is squarely inside that list, and the second proviso is the one that deals with tax.

citation.ref: Section 107(11) with its first proviso

items.scenario: Hearing a taxpayer's first appeal, the Appellate Authority finds that the adjudicating authority never looked at a bundle of contracts the taxpayer had filed. It sends the matter back to that officer for a fresh order, and in the same order it raises the penalty from the figure the adjudicating authority had imposed, without putting the increase to the appellant.

items.stem: May he do so?

options.text: No — revision lies only where the order is prejudicial to the taxpayer, and this one favoured him
options.misconception: inverts the direction of section 108, which is written for orders prejudicial to the revenue
options.why: Section 108(1) opens the revisional power where an order works against revenue in the sense the section means by prejudicial to the interest of revenue. An exemption wrongly allowed is exactly that; a taxpayer aggrieved by an order goes in appeal instead.
keywords: prejudicial to the interest of revenue

options.text: Yes, and with no time limit, because the point is a fresh one the appeal never touched
options.misconception: takes the proviso's permission without the window it is given in
options.why: The proviso grants the power and fixes its outer limit in the same breath — one year from the appellate order or the three years in clause (b), whichever is later. A fresh point buys a longer window, not an unlimited one.

options.text: No — once an order has gone in appeal it is out of the revisional power altogether
options.misconception: applies clause (a) of section 108(2) without reading the proviso that qualifies it
options.why: That is what clause (a) says on its own, and the proviso immediately following it says otherwise for a point which has not been raised and decided in the appeal. Reading the clause without its proviso closes a door the section deliberately leaves open.

options.text: Yes, on the exemption point, within one year of the appellate order or three years of the original order, whichever is later
options.why: Clause (a) of section 108(2) bars revision of an order that has already gone up in appeal, but the first proviso carves out an exception: the Revisional Authority can still act on a point the appeal left untouched — one that has not been raised and decided there — as long as it moves before the expiry of one year from the date of the order in the appeal or the three years in clause (b), whichever is later. The exemption is such a point.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(a) and (b) with the first proviso to section 108(2), read with section 108(1)

items.scenario: A Deputy Commissioner passed an order in April 2024 covering two issues — the classification of a product and an exemption he allowed on a separate supply. The taxpayer appealed on classification alone, and the Appellate Authority decided that issue in November 2025. The Revisional Authority now wants to revise the same April 2024 order on the exemption, which was never argued in the appeal.

items.stem: Can the order still be rectified under section 161?

options.text: No — the first proviso puts an absolute stop at six months from the date of the order
options.misconception: reads the first proviso without the second one that immediately carves an exception out of it
options.why: The six-month limit is real, and the very next proviso says it shall not apply where the correction is of a clerical or arithmetical error. An absolute reading of the first proviso leaves the second with nothing to do.

options.text: Yes — the six-month limit does not apply to a purely arithmetical mistake
options.why: A wrong addition in the summary is an error apparent on the face of record, and the second proviso to section 161 removes the outer time limit whenever what is being fixed is nothing more than a clerical or arithmetical error traced to an accidental slip or omission. Eight months is therefore no obstacle.
keywords: apparent on the face of record

options.text: No — section 161 corrects a notice or a certificate, and a demand order has to be reopened under the demand provisions instead
options.misconception: narrows section 161 to notices when it names decisions and orders in the same breath
options.why: Section 161 applies to any decision, order, notice, certificate or other document. A demand order is squarely within it, and nothing in the section sends an arithmetical slip back through the demand machinery.

options.text: No — the taxpayer had only three months to bring the error to the authority's notice and that has long gone
options.misconception: treats the affected person's window as the only route when the authority may also act on its own motion
options.why: Three months is the window for the affected person to bring an error to notice, and it is not the limit on the power itself. The authority may rectify on its own motion, and the accountant pointing the mistake out is simply how it came to be noticed.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: A demand order sets out the computation correctly in its body but adds the figures wrongly in the summary at the end, so the amount demanded is higher than the working supports. The mistake comes to light eight months after the order was issued, when the taxpayer's accountant reconciles the file.

items.stem: Is his argument good under section 171?

options.text: No, and the amount he kept is recovered from him as a demand of tax under section 74A
options.misconception: treats profiteering as unpaid tax when the amount belongs to the recipient and follows its own machinery
options.why: The amount was never tax; it was the recipient's money, collected in a price that should have come down. The order returns it to the recipient with interest, or where he cannot be identified sends it to the Consumer Welfare Fund, and adds a penalty under section 171(3A).

options.text: No — the obligation is measured against the rate reduction itself, not against last quarter's price
options.why: Section 171(1) is triggered by two things only, a reduction in rate of tax and the benefit of input tax credit, and it requires each to be passed on by way of commensurate reduction in prices. Commensurate means matched to that benefit, so a cut funded by a cheaper input leaves the rate reduction still in his hands, and the amount kept is the profiteered amount.

options.text: Yes, because the National Anti-profiteering Authority no longer exists to examine such a case
options.misconception: confuses which body examines a case with whether the obligation in section 171(1) exists at all
options.why: The obligation in section 171(1) sits in the Act and does not depend on which body examines it. The examining authority has moved more than once, most recently to the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal, and a notified cut-off governs fresh requests, but none of that rewrites the duty to pass the benefit on.

options.text: Yes — the section looks at the net price the consumer actually pays, and that price has fallen
options.misconception: reads section 171 as a general price control when it is tied to two named benefits
options.why: Section 171 is not a price control and does not ask whether prices are lower in general. It asks whether the two named benefits reached the recipient, and a saving from some other cause answers a question the section never puts.

citation.ref: Sections 171(1), 171(2) with its proviso and 171(3A), with the Explanation to section 171

items.scenario: The GST rate on a manufacturer's product is reduced. In the same quarter his own raw material became cheaper, and he cut his selling price by an amount that reflects the raw material saving alone, keeping the tax reduction for himself. He argues that his price is lower than it was, so the consumer has been looked after and nothing more is owed.

items.stem: What does section 152 say about that?

options.text: The information could not be used in the proceedings without first giving the taxpayer a hearing
options.why: Section 152(1) has two prohibitions and the second is this one — information gathered under section 150 or section 151 cannot be put to use in any proceedings under this Act unless the person concerned is first given an opportunity of being heard. Lawful collection of the information does not carry lawful use with it.

options.text: Nothing — the bar covers information called for under section 151, not an information return under section 150
options.misconception: reads the bar as applying to one of the two sections when section 152 names both
options.why: Section 152(1) opens by naming information given for the purposes of section 150 or section 151. An information return filed by a third party is within the first of those, so the bar applies with full force.

options.text: Nothing — the information was lawfully obtained, so it may be used like any other material on record
options.misconception: treats lawful collection as lawful use when section 152 separates the two
options.why: Section 150 makes the collection lawful and section 152 then restricts what may be done with what was collected. The two sections do different jobs, and satisfying the first says nothing about the second.

options.text: Nothing — section 152 bars publishing such information, not using it in an assessment
options.misconception: reads the publication limb of section 152(1) and stops before the use limb that follows it
options.why: Publication is the first limb. The same sub-section goes on to bar use in any proceedings without a hearing, and it is that second limb the officer has walked past.

citation.ref: Section 152(1), read with sections 150 and 151

items.scenario: The department obtains a taxpayer's transaction figures from an information return a third party filed under section 150. Without putting those figures to the taxpayer or telling him where they came from, the officer relies on them to raise a demand.

items.stem: Must he register?

options.text: Yes, once his turnover crosses the section 22 threshold, since section 23 only helps a small supplier
options.misconception: treats section 23 as a turnover rule when it turns on what a person supplies, not how much
options.why: Section 23 says nothing about turnover. It relieves a person because of what he supplies — goods not liable to tax or wholly exempt — and a large dealer in exempt vegetables is as much within it as a small one.

options.text: No, but only if he first obtains a notification exempting him under section 23(2)
options.misconception: turns an automatic relief in section 23(1) into an application under the separate power in section 23(2)
options.why: Section 23(1) operates by itself and needs no order or application. Section 23(2) is a separate power for the Government to notify further categories, and it is not a condition of the relief the first sub-section already gives.

options.text: No — section 23 now overrides section 24, and he supplies nothing but exempt goods
options.why: Section 23(1)(a) covers a person engaged exclusively in supplying goods wholly exempt from tax, and the Finance Act, 2023 substituted the opening of the sub-section so that it applies notwithstanding section 22(1) or section 24, with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. The compulsory category for a person liable to pay tax under reverse charge therefore cannot pull him in.

options.text: Yes — section 24 opens with its own overriding words and prevails over section 23
options.misconception: applies the position as it stood before the 2023 substitution, when the two sections were argued against each other
options.why: That was the argument until the Finance Act, 2023 settled it by putting overriding words at the front of section 23(1) naming section 24 itself. After the substitution section 23 prevails, and because it was given retrospective effect the earlier position does not survive for past years either.

citation.ref: Section 23(1)(a) as substituted by the Finance Act, 2023 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, read with section 24

items.scenario: A trader deals only in fresh, unbranded and unpackaged vegetables, which are wholly exempt. He makes no other supply. He regularly hires a goods transport agency to move his produce, and tax on that freight is payable by the recipient under reverse charge. His consultant tells him that section 24 makes registration compulsory for a person liable to pay tax under reverse charge.

items.stem: Which of the four can he take in appeal to the Appellate Authority?

options.text: The demand order and the refund rejection
options.why: Section 121 says no appeal shall lie against four kinds of order, and two of the four grievances are on that list — an order passed under section 80, which is the instalments provision, and one covering the seizure or retention of books of account. The demand and the refund rejection determine liability and remain appealable under section 107(1).
keywords: seizure or retention of books of account

options.text: The demand order, the refund rejection and the retention of books, because retention hurts him most
options.misconception: measures appealability by how much an order hurts rather than by the list in section 121
options.why: Hardship is not the test. Section 121 puts on that same list any order over the seizure or retention of books, plus registers and other documents held the same way, and once a matter sits there the size of the grievance changes nothing. A writ remains available; an appeal does not.

options.text: All four, since section 107 lets any person aggrieved by any decision or order appeal
options.misconception: reads section 107(1) without section 121, which opens with words overriding every other provision
options.why: Section 107(1) is wide, and section 121 is written to cut into it — notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any provision of the Act, no appeal shall lie against the four matters it lists. The wide words in one section do not survive the overriding words in the other.

options.text: The demand order alone
options.misconception: assumes a refund rejection is an administrative decision when it determines a right to money
options.why: A refund rejection appears nowhere in section 121 and it decides whether the taxpayer gets his money, so it is appealable in the ordinary way. Only the instalments order and the retention of books are shut out.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (b) and (d), read with sections 80 and 107(1)

items.scenario: A registered person is unhappy with four things at once. A demand order under section 74A. An order refusing his request to pay that demand in instalments. An order retaining his seized books of account for longer than he thinks proper. And an order rejecting a refund claim.

items.stem: Is the officer right?

options.text: Yes — the bond runs with the warehousing period fixed under section 61 and cannot be released early
options.misconception: ties the bond to a calendar when section 73 ties it to the goods and the money
options.why: Section 61 fixes how long goods may remain warehoused; it says nothing about the life of the bond. Section 73 is the provision that ends the bond, and its two triggers are the goods being accounted for and the amounts due being paid.
keywords: how long goods may remain warehoused

options.text: No, and no order is needed either — the bond lapses of itself the moment the last of the goods leaves the warehouse
options.misconception: skips the proper officer's act of cancellation, which section 73 makes part of the discharge
options.why: The bond does not simply fall away. Section 73 requires the proper officer to cancel it as discharged in full and to deliver it on demand, so there is an act to be done and a document to be handed back.
keywords: cancel it as discharged in full

options.text: No — section 73 requires the bond to be cancelled and returned once the goods are accounted for and the money is paid
options.why: Section 73 ties the bond's release to two facts about the section 59 goods rather than to a date: every item has left the warehouse by a clearance, an export, a transfer, or is otherwise duly accounted for, and all amounts due against those goods have already reached the department. Once both facts hold, the officer's job is fixed rather than discretionary — the bond stands discharged in full and has to be handed back. Both facts hold here.

options.text: Yes — the bond also covers penalties and fines that may yet be found due, so it can never be given back
options.misconception: reads the bond's coverage as an open-ended liability when section 73 provides for its discharge in full
options.why: A section 59 bond does bind the importer to pay penalties and fines incurred in respect of those goods, and section 73 still provides for its cancellation once all amounts due on account of the goods have been paid. The coverage is wide; it is not perpetual.

citation.ref: Section 73, read with sections 59(1) and 71

items.scenario: An importer warehoused a consignment against a bond executed under section 59. He has since cleared part of the consignment for home consumption on payment of duty and exported the rest, and every amount due on the goods has been paid. He asks for his bond back. The officer says a warehousing bond stays alive until the warehousing period would have expired.

items.stem: What rate applies, and does interest run?

options.text: The rate in force on 20 July, and interest once the free period ended, since the goods were in a warehouse
options.misconception: treats storage in a warehouse building as warehousing, and applies section 15(1)(b) with section 61
options.why: Section 15(1)(b) and the interest in section 61 both apply to warehoused goods, and these are not warehoused goods however they are stored. It is the legal status the section confers, not the building, that decides.

options.text: The rate in force on 1 June, and no interest, because goods stored under section 49 are not warehoused goods
options.why: Section 49 says in terms that goods so stored shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods, so the warehousing chapter never engages. The goods were entered for home consumption, section 15(1)(a) fixes the rate by the date the bill of entry was presented, and the interest in section 61(2) attaches only to warehoused goods.
keywords: shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods

options.text: The rate in force on 1 June, but interest still runs, because the goods physically occupied a warehouse
options.misconception: keeps half of the warehousing consequences after correctly rejecting the other half
options.why: The same sentence produces both answers. Once the goods are not deemed to be warehoused goods, neither the rate rule for warehoused goods nor the interest that attaches to them can apply, and the importer pays only rent and charges for the storage.
keywords: not deemed to be warehoused goods

options.text: The rate in force on the date of entry inwards of the carrying vessel
options.misconception: applies the proviso to section 15(1)(a) about a bill of entry presented before arrival, which is not what happened
options.why: That proviso deems a bill of entry filed ahead of the vessel to have been presented on the date of entry inwards. Here the bill of entry was presented and assessed in the ordinary way after arrival, so the proviso has nothing to bite on.

citation.ref: Section 49, read with sections 15(1)(a), 15(1)(b) and 61(2)

items.scenario: An importer presented a bill of entry for home consumption on 1 June and was assessed. He could not arrange funds, and on his application the Deputy Commissioner permitted the goods to be stored in a public warehouse under section 49 pending clearance. He paid and took delivery on 20 July. Between the two dates the rate of basic customs duty went up, and he is told interest has also run because his goods sat in a warehouse.

items.stem: How should the Authority deal with the application?

options.text: It must allow it, because an advance ruling concerns goods yet to be imported and the pending appeal concerns a past import
options.misconception: reads the bar as being about the consignment when the proviso speaks of the question raised
options.why: An advance ruling does look forward, and that is why the applicant may apply at all. The bar is a separate filter and it is worded around the question raised in the application, which is identical in both matters.

options.text: It may allow it, and the ruling will then settle the pending appeal as well
options.misconception: gives the ruling a reach section 28J does not, extending it to a forum already seised of the matter
options.why: Section 28J makes a ruling binding on the applicant and on the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs and officers subordinate to him in respect of that applicant. An appellate forum already hearing the matter is not among them.

options.text: It must reject it straight away, without hearing the applicant, since the bar is absolute
options.misconception: skips the hearing the section requires before any rejection, however clear the ground
options.why: The ground is indeed mandatory, but the procedure is not summary. No application may be rejected without giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, and the order must record the reasons for the rejection.

options.text: It must not allow it — the bar looks at the question, and the same question is pending in his own case
options.why: The proviso to section 28-I(2) says the Authority shall not allow an application where the question raised in it is already pending in the applicant's case before any officer of customs, the Appellate Tribunal or any court. It is the question raised that the bar examines, not the consignment, so a fresh import does not escape it.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 28-I(2), read with sections 28-I(4), 28H(2) and 28J(1)

items.scenario: An importer is already in dispute about the classification of a particular machine — his appeal on an earlier consignment of the identical machine is pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). He now applies to the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings on the classification of the same machine for an import he plans next year, saying a future consignment is a different transaction from a past one.

items.stem: Is the manager right, and if not, when does duty fall?

options.text: He is wrong, but the duty was already paid when the shop imported the camera
options.misconception: confuses warehousing, which defers duty, with clearance for home consumption, which pays it
options.why: Depositing goods in a warehouse is precisely how an importer avoids paying at import. Duty on warehoused goods is paid later, on a bill of entry for home consumption presented under section 68, which is what the sale to the passenger brings about.

options.text: He is right — a duty-free shop is outside the customs frontiers of India
options.misconception: treats a bonded shop inside the terminal as foreign territory rather than as a warehouse under the Act
options.why: The shop stands on Indian soil and is licensed under the Customs Act. Being a bonded warehouse defers the duty on its stock; it does not put the premises outside India or outside the Act.

options.text: He is wrong — the camera was imported and warehoused, and duty falls when it is cleared for home consumption
options.why: A duty-free shop is a licensed warehouse and its stock is warehoused goods on which duty has been deferred, not remitted. Section 71 lets those goods leave only by a permitted route, and a sale to an arriving passenger takes the home-consumption route, so duty falls when the goods are cleared for home consumption under section 68.

options.text: He is wrong, and the duty is charged at the rate in force on the day the shop first imported the camera
options.misconception: applies section 15(1)(a) to goods cleared out of a warehouse, where section 15(1)(b) governs
options.why: For warehoused goods the rate is fixed by section 15(1)(b) — the date on which the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of them is presented under section 68 — so a rate change between the shop's import and the sale counts against the buyer.

citation.ref: Sections 68 and 71, read with section 15(1)(b)

items.scenario: A passenger landing at Delhi from abroad buys a camera at the arrival duty-free shop inside the terminal. The shop's manager assures him that no customs duty can ever arise on it, because the camera was never imported into India at all.

items.stem: Which of the two is added to the transaction value?

options.text: Both, since both are paid to the seller in connection with the imported goods
options.misconception: adds every payment made to the seller and ignores the two explanations that carve exclusions out of the clause
options.why: Payment to the seller is not by itself enough. The clause carries an explanation excluding charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India, and another excluding payments for the right to distribute or resell where they are not a condition of the sale for export to India.
keywords: a condition of the sale for export

options.text: The running royalty only
options.why: Rule 10(1)(c) reaches this kind of royalties and licence fees payment because it is tied to the imported goods and the buyer has no way to get the goods without paying it — that is what makes it a condition of the sale, regardless of how the supplier chooses to measure it against later domestic turnover. The lump sum falls outside the clause instead: an explanation strips out any charge paid purely for the right to reproduce the imported goods within India.

options.text: Neither, because a royalty measured on domestic sales relates to the finished product rather than to the imported goods
options.misconception: uses the measure of the royalty as the test in place of the condition-of-sale test the rule actually applies
options.why: How a royalty is computed does not decide the question. The rule asks whether it is related to the imported goods and whether the buyer is required to pay it as a condition of the sale, and here the supplier will not ship without it.

options.text: The lump sum only, because it is a fixed amount attributable to the goods while a running royalty is a post-import expense
options.misconception: inverts both limbs, adding the payment the explanation excludes and dropping the one the clause includes
options.why: The clause has no rule about fixed sums against running amounts. It includes a royalty paid as a condition of the sale whenever it falls due, and an explanation expressly keeps out charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India.
keywords: as a condition of the sale

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) with its explanations, read with section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: An Indian company imports machinery from a foreign supplier and makes two further payments to the same supplier. One is a running royalty on its domestic sales of the finished output, which the supply contract makes a precondition of shipment — the supplier will not ship until the royalty agreement is signed. The other is a lump sum for the right to reproduce the imported design in India. Neither is included in the invoice price.

items.stem: Is he right about the option?

options.text: No — for goods that are not prohibited the officer must offer the option, and the fine is capped
options.why: Section 125(1) gives the officer a discretion to offer a fine in lieu of confiscation where the import or export of the goods is prohibited, and obliges him to offer it in the case of any other goods. These goods are freely importable, so redemption had to be offered, and a proviso caps the fine at the market price of the goods less the duty chargeable on them.

options.text: No, but only because a mis-declaration of value is not a ground of confiscation in the first place
options.misconception: overlooks section 111(m), which reaches goods not corresponding in respect of value with the entry made
options.why: Section 111(m) covers goods which do not correspond in respect of value or in any other particular with the entry made under the Act, so the liability to confiscation stands. What fails is the refusal to offer redemption, not the confiscation itself.

options.text: No, and once the redemption fine is paid no duty is payable, the fine standing in place of it
options.misconception: ignores section 125(2), under which the owner is in addition liable to duty and charges on the goods
options.why: Section 125(2) says that where a fine is imposed the owner shall in addition be liable to any duty and charges payable in respect of the goods. Redemption buys the goods back; it does not extinguish the levy.

options.text: Yes — the option under section 125 is always at the adjudicating officer's discretion
options.misconception: reads the word may across the whole of section 125(1) when the sub-section uses may and shall for two different classes of goods
options.why: The sub-section splits into two. The discretion belongs to prohibited goods; for any other goods the officer shall give the option, and reading a single word across both halves erases the distinction the section is built on.

citation.ref: Section 125(1) with its proviso and section 125(2), read with section 111(m)

items.scenario: A consignment of freely importable goods is held liable to confiscation under section 111(m) because the declared particulars do not correspond in respect of value with the entry made. The adjudicating officer orders absolute confiscation and refuses to offer redemption, saying the option to pay a fine is his to give or withhold as he sees fit.

items.stem: Which cargo may lawfully be unloaded at that moment?

options.text: The aircraft's cargo, but not the vessel's
options.why: Section 31(1) bars the master of a vessel from permitting the unloading of imported goods until the proper officer has passed an order granting entry inwards, and that requirement is written for a vessel alone. Delivering the arrival manifest is a precondition of entry inwards under section 31(2), not a substitute for the order itself.

options.text: Both, once the goods are found to be mentioned in the manifest, entry inwards being needed only for loading export cargo
options.misconception: swaps entry inwards with entry outwards, which is the order a vessel needs before export goods are loaded
options.why: Mention in the manifest is a separate requirement under section 32 and it applies to every conveyance, but it does not replace entry inwards. The order needed before export goods are loaded on a vessel is entry outwards, a different order in a different section.

options.text: Neither, until entry inwards has been granted to each conveyance
options.misconception: extends a requirement written for vessels to aircraft, for which no entry inwards exists
options.why: Section 31 speaks throughout of the master of a vessel. There is no grant of entry inwards for an aircraft, so its cargo may be unloaded once the other conditions, including mention in the manifest, are satisfied.

options.text: Both, because the arrival manifest was delivered before arrival in each case
options.misconception: treats the manifest as the permission to unload when it is only the condition that lets the permission be given
options.why: Section 31(2) makes delivery of the manifest the thing that unlocks the officer's order; it does not make the manifest the order. Until entry inwards is granted, a vessel's cargo stays aboard.

citation.ref: Sections 31(1) and 31(2), read with sections 30(1) and 32

items.scenario: A vessel and an aircraft arrive at the same customs station on the same morning, both carrying imported cargo, and the arrival manifest for each was delivered before arrival. The ground handler begins unloading the aircraft at once. The shipping agent begins unloading the vessel at the same time, saying the manifest was filed and nothing more is needed.

items.stem: What is its aggregate turnover for the year?

options.text: ₹22 lakh
options.misconception: leaves exempt supplies out of aggregate turnover because no tax was charged on them
options.why: Exempt supplies are named in the definition and go in. A person whose sales are mostly exempt can be pushed over the registration line by them, which is the whole reason the definition says so in terms.

options.text: ₹31 lakh
options.why: Section 2(6) counts taxable supplies, exempt supplies, exports and same-PAN inter-State supplies on an all India basis. The value of inward supplies on which the person himself pays tax on a reverse charge basis is expressly taken out, and the taxes are taken out too, so the figure is ₹18 lakh plus ₹9 lakh plus ₹4 lakh.

options.text: ₹34.24 lakh
options.misconception: adds both the reverse-charge inward supplies and the tax charged on outward supplies
options.why: The definition ends by excluding central tax, State tax, Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess. Turnover is measured before the tax, and the inward supplies do not belong in it either.

options.text: ₹34 lakh
options.misconception: adds the inward supplies bearing reverse-charge tax, which the definition excludes
options.why: The ₹3 lakh of legal services is a purchase, not a supply the firm made. Section 2(6) excludes the value of inward supplies on which tax is payable on reverse charge basis precisely so that buying does not inflate turnover.

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

items.scenario: A firm holds one GST registration, in Karnataka, under a single Permanent Account Number. For the year its books show taxable outward supplies of ₹18 lakh, exempt outward supplies of ₹9 lakh, exports of ₹4 lakh, GST of ₹3.24 lakh charged on its outward supplies, and inward legal services of ₹3 lakh on which the firm itself paid tax under reverse charge.

items.stem: Which of these four was subsumed when GST came in?

options.text: Basic customs duty and the CGST and SGST, the integrated tax on imports having replaced the customs duty
options.misconception: reads the integrated tax charged at import as a replacement for basic customs duty rather than a levy sitting beside it
options.why: Integrated tax on an import is charged in addition to basic customs duty, not instead of it, and it is collected under the Customs Tariff Act as if it were a duty of customs. The customs duty was never subsumed.

options.text: Only the last — the other three were left standing
options.why: The 101st Constitution Amendment folded central excise, service tax, VAT and a family of State levies into one tax under Article 246A. It left basic customs duty on imports, stamp duty on instruments, and the State levies on alcoholic liquor for human consumption outside GST altogether, which is why all three are still being paid.

options.text: All four, GST being a comprehensive tax on every supply in the country
options.misconception: takes the word comprehensive literally and forgets the express carve-outs
options.why: Article 366(12A) itself excludes the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption from the definition of goods and services tax, and imports keep their own customs levy. The tax is broad, not universal.

options.text: Stamp duty and the CGST and SGST, stamp duty being a tax on a transaction
options.misconception: treats stamp duty as a transaction tax of the kind GST replaced
options.why: Stamp duty is a duty on the instrument — the deed itself — and it stayed with the States and the Union under their own entries. A lease attracting GST can attract stamp duty on the same document without any double taxation question arising.

citation.ref: Article 246A with Article 366(12A)

items.scenario: A manufacturer lists the levies it still pays alongside GST — basic customs duty on an imported machine, stamp duty on a lease deed for its warehouse, State excise on liquor bought for its guest house, and CGST and SGST on its input purchases.

items.stem: What is the legal effect of the Council's decision on that State?

options.text: It is a recommendation — it does not by itself bind the State legislature or Government
options.why: Article 279A makes the Council a constitutional body whose function is to make recommendations to the Union and the States. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals the Supreme Court held those recommendations carry persuasive value and are not binding, because Article 246A gives Parliament and the State legislatures simultaneous power to legislate on GST. The exemption takes effect in that State only when its own notification issues.

options.text: It binds every State from the moment it is carried by the prescribed majority
options.misconception: reads the weighted-voting machinery as making the outcome binding rather than as making it representative
options.why: The voting weights decide when the Council has taken a decision; they say nothing about whether that decision commands a legislature. The Court has held in terms that it does not.

options.text: It has no legal standing at all, the Council being an advisory committee outside the Constitution
options.misconception: swings past the recommendatory point into denying the Council its constitutional status
options.why: The Council is created by Article 279A itself and its recommendations are what the GST statutes repeatedly require the Government to act upon before notifying anything. Not binding is a long way from having no standing.

options.text: It binds the Centre but not the States, the Centre having voted for it
options.misconception: splits the binding force by who voted, when the Article makes no such distinction
options.why: Article 279A draws no line between the Union and the States on this. The recommendation is addressed to both and binds neither of its own force.

citation.ref: Article 279A(4) and 279A(9)

items.scenario: At a meeting of the GST Council a proposal to exempt a described service is carried by the prescribed weighted majority — on the figures given to the members, the Centre's vote weighs one third of the votes cast, the States' votes together weigh two thirds, and three fourths of the weighted votes present and voting are needed to carry a decision. One State afterwards declines to issue the matching State tax notification.

items.stem: Which of the two is exempt?

options.text: Neither, surgery being a taxable service in every case
options.misconception: forgets that health care services are exempt at all
options.why: Diagnosis, treatment and care for illness, injury, deformity, abnormality or pregnancy in a recognised system of medicine are squarely within the exemption. Most of what a hospital does bears no tax.

options.text: The reconstruction after the burn injury; the cosmetic reshaping is taxable
options.why: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt, but the definition takes out cosmetic or plastic surgery — except where it is undertaken to restore or reconstruct anatomy or functions of the body affected by congenital defects, developmental abnormalities, injury or trauma. A hand disfigured by fire is injury, so the reconstruction stays inside the exemption and the elective reshaping does not.

options.text: Both, provided the hospital charges no separate room rent
options.misconception: makes an unrelated billing detail the test of the exemption
options.why: Whether a room is billed separately has nothing to do with whether a procedure is cosmetic or reconstructive. The carve-out in the definition is about the purpose of the surgery.

options.text: Both, since everything performed inside a hospital is health care
options.misconception: attaches the exemption to the building rather than to the service being supplied
options.why: The exemption follows the service. A hospital's shop rentals, its canteen sales to visitors and its cosmetic work are all taxable in the same premises where its ward is exempt.

citation.ref: Entry 74, with the definition of health care services in paragraph 2 of the notification

items.scenario: A hospital performs two operations in one week. The first reshapes a patient's nose purely for appearance, at the patient's request. The second reconstructs a hand disfigured in a factory fire.

items.stem: How does the agency's GST position differ between the two contracts?

options.text: The school contract is exempt and the college contract is taxable
options.why: Entry 66 exempts services supplied to an educational institution by way of transportation, catering, security, cleaning or house-keeping only where the institution provides education up to higher secondary school or equivalent. A degree college is an educational institution for what it supplies to its own students, but the inward leg of the exemption does not reach it, so cleaning the college bears tax.

options.text: Both are exempt, the recipient being an educational institution in each case
options.misconception: reads clause (b) as covering every educational institution, ignoring the cut-down that limits it to schools
options.why: Being an educational institution is necessary and not sufficient. The clause that exempts bought-in services names the school level expressly, and a degree college falls outside that limb while remaining an educational institution for its own supplies.

options.text: The college contract is exempt and the school contract is not, degree courses being the recognised qualification
options.misconception: inverts the rule by assuming the higher qualification attracts the wider exemption
options.why: The exemption for bought-in services runs the other way and stops at school level. Recognition of a degree matters to whether the college is an educational institution at all, not to whether its cleaning contractor is exempt.

options.text: Both are taxable, house-keeping never being covered by an education exemption
options.misconception: denies the inward-services limb of entry 66 altogether
options.why: The entry lists security, cleaning and house-keeping performed in such institution among the services it exempts. The limit is which institutions, not which services.

citation.ref: Entry 66, clause (b), with the definition of educational institution in paragraph 2

items.scenario: A housekeeping agency signs two cleaning contracts. One is with a school teaching classes up to the twelfth standard. The other is with a private college awarding a degree recognised by law.

items.stem: How is each letting taxed?

options.text: Both are taxable, with the landlord charging GST once his rental receipts cross the registration threshold
options.misconception: leaves the liability with the supplier when the notified entry has moved it to the recipient
options.why: The family letting stays exempt whatever the landlord's receipts are, and on the company letting the tax is not the landlord's to charge — reverse charge takes it off him entirely.

options.text: The letting to the family is exempt; the letting to the company bears GST, which the company pays under reverse charge
options.why: Renting of a residential dwelling for use as residence is exempt except where the recipient is a registered person. Once the tenant is registered the supply leaves the exemption, and the notified entry puts the liability on the recipient under reverse charge — so the company pays in cash even though the landlord is unregistered and has nothing to do.

options.text: Both are exempt, the flat being used as a residence in each case
options.misconception: applies the old form of the entry, which turned only on the dwelling and the use
options.why: That was the position before the entry was amended. It now carries the words except where the recipient is a registered person, so the tenant's status decides it and the use alone no longer does.

options.text: The company's letting is exempt because a person actually lives in the flat, and the family's letting is taxable
options.misconception: keeps the use-as-residence test and inverts the outcome
options.why: The carve-out that survives on residence is narrow and covers a proprietor renting in his personal capacity for his own home. A company housing a director is renting on the account of its business.

citation.ref: Entry 12 as amended, with entry 5AA of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: An individual who is not registered under GST owns a flat and lets it in two successive years. In the first year the tenant is a salaried family that lives in it. In the second the tenant is a company registered under GST, which houses its managing director in the flat.

items.stem: Which receipts are exempt from GST?

options.text: Only the counselling receipts
options.why: The exemption is not for a charitable body but for charitable activities as the notification defines them — public health work including care or counselling of persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance, advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga, certain educational and skill programmes for named vulnerable groups, and preservation of environment. Coaching for a competitive examination is none of those, so the trust pays tax on it like anybody else.

options.text: Only the coaching receipts, education being a charitable purpose
options.misconception: imports the Income-tax Act's wider idea of a charitable purpose into a GST definition that is a closed list
options.why: The notification's list of charitable activities does not include education generally. Its educational limb is confined to programmes for abandoned or orphaned children, abused persons, prisoners and the elderly in rural areas.

options.text: Both, the trust's registration under section 12AB exempting everything it earns
options.misconception: treats registration under the Income-tax Act as an exemption from GST in itself
options.why: Registration qualifies the entity and is only the first of two conditions. What the entity supplies has to fall inside the defined list as well, and most trusts have receipts on both sides of that line.

options.text: Neither, GST having no exemption for a trust
options.misconception: denies entry 1 altogether
options.why: Entry 1 exists and exempts services by a 12AA or 12AB entity by way of charitable activities. The counselling described is squarely inside the public health limb of the definition.

citation.ref: Entry 1, with the definition of charitable activities in paragraph 2 of the notification

items.scenario: A charitable trust that holds registration under section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 has two streams of receipts. One is from counselling persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance. The other is from a fee-charging coaching class it runs for a competitive examination.

items.stem: What happens to the central and State tax already paid, and does interest run on the integrated tax?

options.text: It is lost, a payment under the wrong head not being a payment of tax at all
options.misconception: treats a misclassified payment as a nullity, which is the opposite of what the section provides
options.why: The section exists to prevent that outcome. It calls the amount taxes so paid and orders their refund, and it also protects the taxpayer from interest on the correct head.

options.text: It is refunded to him, and no interest is payable on the integrated tax
options.why: Section 77 says a registered person who paid central and State tax on a transaction he considered intra-State, which is subsequently held to be inter-State, shall be refunded the amount so paid, and shall not be required to pay any interest on the integrated tax. Section 19 of the IGST Act carries the mirror rule the other way. The money was with the exchequer all along; only the head was wrong.

options.text: It is adjusted against the integrated tax liability automatically, with no refund claim needed
options.misconception: assumes the ledgers move money between heads, when the section provides for a refund
options.why: There is no automatic transfer between the central, State and integrated tax heads. The section gives a refund of what was paid wrongly, and a refund is claimed.

options.text: It is refunded, but interest runs on the integrated tax from its original due date
options.misconception: applies the ordinary section 50 interest rule to a payment the statute expressly relieves
options.why: Section 50 would charge interest on a late payment of tax, and section 77 is the exception that displaces it for exactly this situation. The sub-section on interest is there precisely so this answer is wrong.

citation.ref: Section 77, read with section 19 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A supplier treated a supply as intra-State and paid central tax and State tax of ₹6 lakh in June 2025. In 2026 the department holds that the supply was inter-State. The supplier now pays integrated tax of ₹6 lakh on the same supply.

items.stem: Is the summons valid, and what does the transporter risk if he gives an untrue answer?

options.text: Valid — the power reaches any person whose evidence is thought necessary, and the inquiry is deemed judicial, so an untrue answer carries the consequences of giving false evidence
options.why: Section 70(1) lets the proper officer summon any person whose attendance he considers necessary either to give evidence or to produce a document, and it is not confined to the taxpayer under investigation. Section 70(2) deems every such inquiry a judicial proceeding, which is what puts a false statement inside the ordinary criminal law rather than the penalty provisions.

options.text: Invalid — a summons may be issued only to the registered person under investigation
options.misconception: narrows the words any person to the taxpayer whose affairs are being examined
options.why: The sub-section says any person, and investigations routinely summon suppliers, customers, transporters and bank officials against whom nothing is alleged. Being a witness is not being an accused.

options.text: Valid only after a show cause notice has first been served on the supplier
options.misconception: makes an inquiry power wait for the adjudication it is meant to precede
options.why: The power is exercisable in any inquiry, and an inquiry is what happens before a notice is framed. Requiring the notice first would make the section useless.

options.text: Valid, but the inquiry is administrative, so an untrue answer at worst attracts a general penalty
options.misconception: misses the deeming in section 70(2) and downgrades a criminal consequence to a penalty
options.why: Section 70(2) deems the inquiry a judicial proceeding for the penal provisions on false evidence. That deeming is the whole sanction behind a summons and is what makes a recorded statement worth taking.

citation.ref: Sections 70(1) and 70(2)

items.scenario: An officer investigating a supplier issues a summons to the supplier's transporter, requiring him to appear, give evidence about the consignments carried and produce his records. No proceeding of any kind is pending against the transporter himself.

items.stem: What penalty does section 122(1) fix on these facts?

options.text: Nothing under section 122; the residual penalty in section 125 applies instead
options.misconception: reaches for the residual penalty when the conduct is on the section 122 list
options.why: Section 125 applies only where no penalty is separately provided. Issuing an invoice without a supply is named in section 122(1), so the residual provision never comes into play.

options.misconception: takes the tax involved as the penalty and ignores the floor the sub-section sets beneath it
options.why: The fixed sum is a floor, not an alternative the officer may pass over. Where the tax is smaller, the fixed sum is what applies, which is how a small-value offence still costs something.

options.misconception: adds the two amounts when the sub-section asks which of them is higher
options.why: The words are whichever is higher, and they choose between the two figures. Nothing in the sub-section adds them together.

Section 122(1) sets one formula for all the specified offences it lists, issuing an invoice without a supply among them — the tax evaded or the credit wrongly availed, or the fixed sum the sub-section names, whichever is higher. With ₹7,000 of tax against a ₹10,000 fixed sum, the higher of the two is the fixed sum.

citation.ref: Section 122(1), read with section 125

items.scenario: A supplier issues an invoice without any actual supply of goods and takes input tax credit on it. The tax involved works out to ₹7,000. Take it as given that the fixed sum named in section 122(1) alongside the tax amount is ₹10,000.

items.stem: What is the position in June 2026?

options.text: It continues, and the taxpayer's only route out is to object to the Commissioner and offer a bank guarantee
options.misconception: treats the objection remedy available while the attachment runs as the only exit after it has expired
options.why: Rule 159(5) does give an objection route within seven days, and it matters during the year. It is beside the point once the year has run and the order has spent itself.

options.text: The attachment has already ceased by operation of law, one year having run from the date of the order
options.why: Section 83(1) permits a provisional attachment where proceedings are pending and the Commissioner is of the opinion, recorded in writing, that it is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. Section 83(2) then puts a life on that order: one year on from its date, the attachment lapses by itself. Nothing has to be applied for and no releasing order is needed.
keywords: protect the interest of the revenue

options.text: It was never valid, an audit under section 65 not being a proceeding that supports an attachment
options.misconception: denies the section one of the proceedings it expressly names as a trigger
options.why: Section 83 lists the chapters whose proceedings support an attachment and audit is among them. The defect here is age, not authority.

options.text: It continues until the audit concludes and a demand is determined
options.misconception: ties the life of the attachment to the proceedings rather than to the statutory year
options.why: Pending proceedings are what allow the attachment to be made in the first place. They do not extend it, because sub-section (2) fixes its life independently.

citation.ref: Sections 83(1) and 83(2)

items.scenario: During an audit under section 65, the Commissioner records in writing his opinion that attaching the taxpayer's bank account is necessary to protect the revenue, and passes an order under section 83 on 1 March 2025. In June 2026 the audit is still running, no demand has been raised, and the bank still refuses to operate the account.

items.stem: Whom may the department recover the ₹12 lakh from?

options.text: From either of them — the transferor and the transferee are jointly and severally liable for dues up to the date of transfer
options.why: Section 85 makes a taxable person transferring a business and the person to whom it is transferred jointly and severally liable, wholly or to the extent of the transfer, for tax, interest or penalty due up to the time of the transfer, whether determined before or after it. A private allocation of liabilities binds the two parties and not the department.
keywords: up to the time of the transfer
whether determined before or after it

options.text: Only from the seller, the liability being personal to the person who incurred it
options.misconception: treats tax liability as staying with the person who earned the income, which is what section 85 displaces
options.why: Chapter XVI exists to attach liability to people other than the original taxable person, and section 85 is its widest provision. A buyer of a business takes the pre-transfer dues with it.

options.text: Only from the buyer, who now owns the business the tax arose in
options.misconception: replaces joint and several liability with a transfer of the liability
options.why: The section makes both liable, not the buyer alone. The department may proceed against either or both, and the seller does not walk away by selling.
