options.text: No — the plan is complete, but a remark to investors naming neither centre nor date does not commit the company to anybody
options.why: The first condition is met: this is a detailed formal plan, right down to the approximate number of employees who will be paid off. The second is where it fails. What creates the obligation is having raised a valid expectation in those affected, and there are only two routes to it — starting to implement the plan, or announcing its main features to them in terms specific enough to be believed. A line about a programme covering part of the network, under review, with more to follow, names no centre and no date, and the people whose jobs and contracts are going were not told at all. Employees, customers and suppliers are the parties the standard has in mind, and none of them has been given anything to rely on.

options.text: Yes — the ₹9 crore is a reliable estimate and the outflow is probable, so the general test for a provision is satisfied
options.misconception: runs the general recognition test without the obligating event, which for a restructuring is defined by its own rule
options.why: A reliable estimate and a probable outflow are the second and third conditions for any provision, and the first is a present obligation arising from a past event. For a restructuring the standard says exactly what that past event is, and a board decision the company has told nobody about is not it. Two conditions out of three is none.

options.text: Yes — the plan meets every content requirement and a public statement was made before the year end
options.misconception: counts any public statement as the announcement, when what is said has to set out the main features specifically enough for those affected to believe them
options.why: Being public is not the test, and neither is the date. A statement binds the company only when it is detailed enough that the people it affects can act on it. This one could cover any part of the network, at any time, and expressly leaves the decision open, so nobody hearing it could plan around the closure of these two centres.

options.text: No, and none can arise until the employees have been served with formal notice, whatever else the company does
options.misconception: makes formal notice the only route, when starting to implement the plan does the same work without a word being said
options.why: Notice is one way and not the only one. Beginning to dismantle plant or selling the assets of the operation shows a commitment as plainly as any announcement does, and the standard treats either as enough. A company that quietly started stripping out one of the centres in March would have an obligation at 31 March with nothing in writing.

citation.ref: para 72(b), read with para 73

items.scenario: On 12 March 2026 a company's board approved shutting two of its four service centres. The plan names both centres, puts the cost at ₹9 crore, sets the timetable, and identifies the 240 or so employees who will be paid off, where they work and what they do. On 18 March the chief executive told an investor call that a cost programme covering part of the network was under review, with more to follow next quarter. Nothing was said to the staff of the two centres, to their customers or to their suppliers, and no asset was sold or dismantled, before 31 March 2026.

items.stem: Is a restructuring provision recognised at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes — the plan is detailed and it was announced to the employees and the unions before the year end, which is what the standard asks for
options.misconception: reads the announcement as sufficient on its own, without asking whether a plan starting two and a half years out could commit anybody
options.why: Both boxes look ticked and one of them is not. The announcement route works only where what is announced could reasonably make those affected believe the company is committed now. A move that cannot begin for two and a half years, with a yearly review written into it, announces an intention rather than a commitment, and the people told about it can see that as clearly as the board can.

options.text: Yes, at the present value of the ₹60 crore discounted over the period to October 2028
options.misconception: goes straight to measurement and discounting when no obligation exists to be measured
options.why: Discounting is right where a provision has been recognised and the money will go out much later, so the arithmetic here is not the error. The error is one step earlier. There is no present obligation at 31 March 2026, so there is nothing to discount, and a discounted figure for a liability that does not exist is still a liability that does not exist.

options.text: No — a move that cannot begin for two and a half years, and that the board will revisit every year, does not commit the company now
options.why: The plan clears the first condition easily; it is a detailed formal plan and it was put to everyone affected. It fails the second for a reason that is easy to walk past. For an announcement to bind, the work has to be planned to begin as soon as it can and to be finished inside a stretch of time short enough that big changes are unlikely. A start two and a half years away, with an annual review built into the plan itself, leaves the company room to change its mind — and says so out loud. So nothing here has raised a valid expectation of the kind the standard means, however complete the plan and however widely it was announced. The obligation will arise when the delay has shrunk or the work has begun.

options.text: No, and no obligation can arise before the new site is finished, since until then the move cannot begin
options.misconception: ties the obligation to the new site being ready, when what matters is whether the company has committed itself
options.why: Physical readiness is not the trigger. What the standard is looking for is a commitment the company can no longer realistically walk away from, and that can be created well before the first machine moves — by starting to implement the plan, or by announcing it once the timetable is close enough to be believed. Waiting for the new site would push recognition past the point at which the company was plainly committed.

citation.ref: para 72 and 74

items.scenario: On 5 March 2026 a company's board approved moving all its manufacturing from one state to another. The plan names both plants, puts the cost at ₹60 crore, and identifies the 900 employees who will be paid off, where they work and what they do. On 10 March it was put to the workforce and to the unions in full. The plan also says the move cannot start before October 2028, because the new site has to be built first, and that the board will review the whole thing every year until then.

items.stem: Which market does the company measure in, and on what comparison?

options.text: Market P, because a market that pays more must be the one with the greater volume and level of activity, and so the principal market
options.misconception: infers which market is principal from the price it quotes, when volume and level of activity settle it and the facts here say neither market wins on those
options.why: Price and depth are different things, and a thin market often quotes the better price for exactly that reason. The principal market is identified by where the asset trades most and most actively, tested afresh for each asset and each entity. Here the facts say the two markets are level on that measure, which is why the fallback is in play at all.

options.text: Market Q, because ₹585 a tonne is left there after both transaction costs and transport costs, against ₹575 in Market P
options.why: Fair value is measured in the principal market, the one where this commodity changes hands in the greatest volume and with the most activity, and that market must be used even if another one would leave the seller better off. Here neither market is that, so the second question is reached: which is the most advantageous market? That is the one leaving the seller with the largest amount once both the cost of doing the deal and the cost of getting the goods to the market are taken off. Market P leaves 640 − 40 − 25 = ₹575 a tonne and Market Q leaves 620 − 10 − 25 = ₹585, so Market Q is where the measurement is made, even though it quotes the lower price.

options.text: Market P, because after transport it leaves ₹615 a tonne against Market Q's ₹595
options.misconception: leaves transaction costs out of the comparison between markets; they are kept out of the fair value figure itself, not out of the test of which market is most advantageous
options.why: This mixes up two different rules that both concern transaction costs. Fair value is not reduced by them, because they belong to the transaction rather than to the asset, and two companies holding the same commodity in the same market must arrive at the same figure. But choosing between markets is a different question, and there the company is asking what it would end up with, so the costs of dealing count. Left out, they flip the answer.

options.text: Market P, because ₹640 a tonne is the higher price
options.misconception: compares the headline prices, when the choice between markets is made on what is left after the costs of dealing and of getting the goods there
options.why: Six hundred and forty is more than six hundred and twenty and that settles nothing. Market P charges ₹40 a tonne to deal, four times what Market Q charges, and once that is taken off the seller ends up worse off in the market with the better sticker price. The test asks what the company would actually be left holding.

citation.ref: para 16, with the meaning of the most advantageous market in Appendix A, read with para 25 and 26

items.scenario: A company holds 4,000 tonnes of a commodity at 31 March 2026 and can deal in two markets. The two are evenly matched in volume and in level of activity and the company trades in both, so neither is its principal market. Market P would pay ₹640 a tonne, with transaction costs of ₹40 a tonne and ₹25 a tonne to move the commodity there. Market Q would pay ₹620 a tonne, with transaction costs of ₹10 a tonne and ₹25 a tonne to move it there. Location is a characteristic of the commodity.

items.stem: What happens to the ₹18 crore in the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹5.4 crore goes to the non-controlling interests on the October sale, and the write-down moves nothing at all
options.why: Selling part of a subsidiary while keeping control is a partial disposal, and where the foreign operation sits inside a subsidiary the parent re-attributes the proportionate share of the accumulated exchange differences to the non-controlling interests rather than sending anything through profit or loss — 30 per cent of ₹18 crore, or ₹5.4 crore. The write-down is a different kind of event altogether. Reducing what a foreign operation is carried at, whether because it has made losses of its own or because the investor has recognised an impairment, is not a partial disposal, so nothing comes out of the reserve when it happens. Only a sale that costs the parent control would send the entire balance from equity to profit or loss, and neither event here does that.

options.text: ₹5.4 crore is reclassified to profit or loss on the October sale, and the write-down moves nothing
options.misconception: recycles the proportionate share through profit or loss on a partial disposal of a subsidiary where control is kept, when for a subsidiary it moves across within equity
options.why: The figure and the treatment of the write-down are both right, and the destination is wrong. Selling shares in a subsidiary while keeping control is a dealing between the parent and the other owners of the group's equity, and a dealing of that kind never touches profit or loss. The reserve moves sideways to the non-controlling interests. Reclassifying to profit or loss is what happens on any other partial disposal, an associate's for example, where there is no minority in the group's accounts to move it to.

options.text: The whole ₹18 crore is reclassified to profit or loss, the sale and the write-down together having reduced the parent's interest in the operation
options.misconception: reclassifies the full balance while control is retained, which the standard keeps for a disposal that costs the parent control
options.why: Emptying the reserve belongs to a disposal of the foreign operation, or to a partial disposal that loses control. The parent still holds 70 per cent and still consolidates, so the operation has not gone anywhere and neither has most of the reserve. Recycling all of it would put ₹18 crore of gain into a year in which the group sold under a third of a subsidiary and wrote down some goodwill.

options.text: ₹5.4 crore goes to the non-controlling interests on the October sale, and a share of the reserve is also reclassified to profit or loss on the write-down
options.misconception: treats an impairment write-down as if it reduced the parent's interest in the foreign operation, which it does not
options.why: The October half is right. The write-down half is the trap the standard closes by name: a reduction in what the operation is carried at, from its own losses or from an impairment, does not constitute a partial disposal, so no part of the reserve is recycled at the time of it. Nothing about the parent's ownership changed on 31 March — the same 70 per cent before and after — and it is a change in ownership that moves this reserve.

citation.ref: para 48, 48A, 48C and 48D

items.scenario: An Indian parent has owned the whole of a foreign subsidiary for years, and ₹18 crore of exchange differences on translating it stand as a credit in the foreign currency translation reserve. On 1 October 2025 the parent sold 30 per cent of the subsidiary to an outside investor and kept control. On 31 March 2026 an impairment review wrote the goodwill on that subsidiary down by ₹7 crore. The finance director wants a share of the reserve reclassified to profit or loss on the write-down as well.

items.stem: What amount does the company include in the transaction price for the service incentive?

options.text: ₹10.00 crore
options.misconception: includes the best possible outcome in full; the constraint on variable consideration can only hold an estimate down, never lift it to the highest amount
options.why: Ten crore is what the contract pays if everything goes right, and it has a three in ten chance of happening. An estimate is not a hope. The constraint the standard puts on variable consideration exists to keep revenue from being recognised and then reversed, so it works in one direction only, and no part of it turns an estimate into the best case.

options.text: ₹5.00 crore
options.misconception: takes the single most likely outcome, which suits a contract that can end only two ways and not one with a spread of outcomes
options.why: Five crore is the outcome with the highest single probability, at 0.50, and picking it throws away everything the company knows about the other two. The method that fits an amount spread across several outcomes is the one that uses all of them, and here that method and this one give different answers, which is precisely why the standard does not leave the choice open.

options.text: ₹7.50 crore
options.misconception: averages the two amounts the contract could actually pay and ignores the probabilities altogether
options.why: Five and ten average to seven and a half, and the arithmetic quietly drops both the possibility of nothing at all and the weights attached to each outcome. A probability weighting is what makes the figure a prediction rather than a midpoint, and an outcome with a one in five chance of paying nothing has to pull the estimate down.

options.text: ₹5.50 crore
options.why: The incentive can land anywhere across a spread of amounts and the company has a long run of similar contracts to read that spread from, so the expected value — each possible amount weighted by the chance of it happening — is the method that better predicts what the company will be entitled to: (0 × 0.20) + (5 × 0.50) + (10 × 0.30) = ₹5.50 crore. The depot fee is the other case. It has only two possible outcomes, ₹4 crore or nothing, so there the most likely amount predicts better and the estimate would be ₹4 crore rather than a weighted figure no outcome can deliver. The method is picked on the shape of each amount's outcomes, one amount at a time, not once for the whole contract.

citation.ref: para 53, read with para 54 and 55

items.scenario: A logistics company signs a two-year contract. Besides the fixed fee it will be paid a service incentive at the end of the second year, and its record across many similar contracts says the incentive will come to nothing with a probability of 0.20, ₹5 crore with a probability of 0.50 and ₹10 crore with a probability of 0.30. The same contract carries a separate one-off fee of ₹4 crore if a new depot opens by a fixed date and nothing if it does not, with no other outcome possible. On the facts it is highly probable that no significant reversal of revenue will arise on either amount.

items.stem: At what amount does the block enter investment property, and what is it carried at on 31 March 2027?

options.text: It enters at ₹9 crore and stands at ₹8.40 crore a year later
options.misconception: revalues the block on the transfer and then depreciates the revalued figure, mixing the fair value step with the cost model that follows
options.why: Spreading ₹9 crore over the fifteen years still to run gives ₹0.60 crore for the year and ₹8.40 crore at the end of it. The arithmetic is sound and the opening figure is not. A transfer is a change of label, not a measurement event, so there is no moment at which the ₹9 crore can get onto the books to be depreciated in the first place.

options.text: It enters at ₹6 crore and stands at ₹5.60 crore a year later
options.why: A property moves into the investment class when, and only when, its use changes, and the end of owner-occupation on 1 April 2026 is that change. What the move does not do is remeasure anything: transfers between the investment, owner-occupied and inventory classes do not change the carrying amount of the property, nor its cost for measurement or for disclosure, so the block enters investment property at ₹6 crore and the ₹3 crore of uplift is recognised nowhere. Afterwards the Indian text leaves exactly one policy open, which is the cost model for all of its investment property, and Ind AS 16 supplies the mechanics, so depreciation continues on the same ₹6 crore across the fifteen years still to run — ₹0.40 crore for the year, leaving ₹5.60 crore on 31 March 2027. The valuer has not wasted his time either, because an entity on this model still has to arrive at what the property would fetch, and that number is produced for the purpose of disclosure only.
keywords: do not change the carrying amount
cost model for all of its investment property
for the purpose of disclosure only

options.text: It enters at ₹6 crore and stands at ₹6 crore a year later
options.misconception: reads the cost model as freezing the carrying amount, when it is Ind AS 16's cost model and depreciation is part of it
options.why: The opening figure is right. Standing still for a year is not. Naming the cost model is not the same as saying nothing further happens to the number, because the model is Ind AS 16's, and under Ind AS 16 a building with a finite life is written down over that life whether a tenant is in it or the owner is. A property let out wears out at the same rate as one lived in.

options.text: It enters at ₹9 crore and stands at ₹9 crore a year later
options.misconception: applies the fair value model, under which an investment property is remeasured each year and not depreciated at all — a model the Indian standard does not carry
options.why: This is the international treatment and it is not the Indian one. Ind AS 40 gives an entity no choice of models, so a property cannot be brought in at a valuer's figure and then held there. Two things go wrong at once on these numbers: ₹3 crore of gain is reported that nobody realised, and a building with fifteen years of life left is carried for a year without being written down by anything.

citation.ref: para 57(c) and para 59, read with the measurement after recognition requirements

items.scenario: Nandini Ltd bought an office block on 1 April 2016 for ₹10 crore and ran its own head office from it. The block is depreciated on a straight line over 25 years with no residual value, so ₹4 crore of depreciation had accumulated by 31 March 2026. On 1 April 2026 the company moved its staff out and let the whole block to a tenant on an operating lease. A valuer put the block at ₹9 crore on that date. The company year end is 31 March.

items.stem: What is the impairment loss on the unit, and where does the first slice of it fall?

options.text: ₹150 lakh, of which goodwill absorbs ₹100 lakh and falls to nil, the rest going over the other three assets in proportion to what each is carried at
options.why: Recoverable amount comes first, and it is whichever is larger of the fair value less costs of disposal and the value it has in use — ₹445 lakh less ₹15 lakh of selling costs is ₹430 lakh, against ₹450 lakh from holding on, so ₹450 lakh is the figure. Carrying amount exceeds it, so an impairment loss of ₹150 lakh arises. Where it lands is not a matter of judgement either. The loss goes first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill sitting in the unit, so goodwill takes ₹100 lakh of it and falls to nil; only what survives that step is spread across the remaining assets pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount each one stands at. That leaves ₹50 lakh to go over ₹500 lakh of building, plant and patent.
keywords: fair value less costs of disposal and the value it has in use
first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill
pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount

options.text: ₹150 lakh, allocated ₹90 lakh to the building, ₹45 lakh to the plant and ₹15 lakh to the patent, leaving goodwill untouched
options.misconception: reverses the order, sparing goodwill until the identifiable assets have taken the loss
options.why: Spreading ₹150 lakh over the ₹500 lakh of identifiable assets gives these three figures and uses the loss up, so goodwill survives in full. That is the order the other way round. Goodwill is the asset with the least evidence behind it, which is why it takes the first blow and not the last; leaving it whole while writing a building down by ₹90 lakh reports the unit's most solid asset as its weakest.

options.text: ₹150 lakh, spread over all four assets in proportion to their carrying amounts, so goodwill takes ₹25 lakh
options.misconception: treats the allocation as one pro rata sum over every asset, when goodwill is written off first and in full before anything else is touched
options.why: One hundred and fifty times one hundred over six hundred gives ₹25 lakh to goodwill, and it leaves ₹75 lakh of goodwill standing on the balance sheet of a unit that has just been shown to be worth less than its book. Goodwill is written down before the other assets precisely because it has no recoverable amount of its own to defend, so it is the first thing to go rather than one claimant among four.

options.text: ₹170 lakh, of which goodwill absorbs ₹100 lakh
options.misconception: takes the lower of the two measures as the recoverable amount, when the standard asks for the higher of them
options.why: Four hundred and forty-five less fifteen is ₹430 lakh, and ₹600 lakh less ₹430 lakh is ₹170 lakh. The ordering step is right and the recoverable amount is not. An entity is not obliged to take the worse of the two routes open to it: if the unit is worth ₹450 lakh kept and ₹430 lakh sold, nobody would sell, so the unit is not impaired by more than the ₹150 lakh that keeping it leaves on the table.

citation.ref: the definition of recoverable amount, read with the order of allocation of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit

items.scenario: The Salem unit of a company is a cash-generating unit. At 31 March 2026 it carries goodwill of ₹100 lakh, a building of ₹300 lakh, plant of ₹150 lakh and a patent of ₹50 lakh, ₹600 lakh in all. An impairment indicator is present. The unit could be sold as it stands for ₹445 lakh, with ₹15 lakh of costs to get the sale done, and the cash it is expected to throw off in the years ahead has a present value of ₹450 lakh.

items.stem: What are the building, the plant and the patent carried at once the loss has been allocated in full?

options.text: Building ₹270 lakh, plant ₹135 lakh, patent ₹48 lakh
options.misconception: applies the floor and stops there, leaving the part of the loss it blocked with nowhere to go
options.why: The floor is found correctly and the patent rightly stops at ₹48 lakh. What is missing is the next sentence of the rule. Three assets here add to ₹453 lakh against a recoverable amount of ₹450 lakh, so ₹3 lakh of the loss has simply gone missing and the unit has not been written down to what it is worth. Whatever a floor blocks does not vanish; it moves on to the assets that still have room.

options.text: Building ₹268 lakh, plant ₹134 lakh, patent ₹48 lakh
options.why: In allocating an impairment loss the carrying amount of an individual asset shall not be reduced below the highest of three things — its fair value less costs of disposal, its value in use, and zero. For the patent those are ₹44 lakh, ₹48 lakh and nil, so ₹48 lakh is the floor and the patent can absorb only ₹2 lakh of the ₹5 lakh the pro rata step handed it. The ₹3 lakh that will not fit does not disappear; it is allocated over the other assets of the unit in proportion to what they are carried at, which puts ₹2 lakh more on the building and ₹1 lakh more on the plant. So the building ends at 300 − 30 − 2 = ₹268 lakh, the plant at 150 − 15 − 1 = ₹134 lakh and the patent at ₹48 lakh, and with goodwill gone the unit stands at ₹450 lakh.
keywords: shall not be reduced below the highest of
fair value less costs of disposal

options.text: Building ₹268.50 lakh, plant ₹133.50 lakh, patent ₹48 lakh
options.misconception: reallocates what the floor blocked in equal shares instead of in proportion to carrying amounts
options.why: The floor is applied correctly and the patent stops at ₹48 lakh. Splitting the ₹3 lakh released down the middle then puts ₹1.50 lakh on each of the building and the plant, which ignores that one of them is carried at twice the other. The second allocation follows the same rule as the first, so the ₹3 lakh goes 300 to 150, or ₹2 lakh and ₹1 lakh. The unit reaches ₹450 lakh either way, which is exactly why this one has to be caught on the rule rather than on the total.

options.text: Building ₹270 lakh, plant ₹135 lakh, patent ₹45 lakh
options.misconception: takes the patent's fair value less costs of disposal as its floor without asking which of the three candidates is the highest, and a floor of ₹44 lakh blocks nothing
options.why: Read this way the patent could go down to ₹44 lakh, its ₹5 lakh share only takes it to ₹45 lakh, nothing is blocked, and the pro rata figures stand untouched. The same answer comes out of never looking for a floor at all, which is what makes it the comfortable mistake. Three figures are compared and the largest wins, and the ₹48 lakh the patent will earn by being kept beats both the ₹44 lakh it would sell for and zero. Writing it to ₹45 lakh reports an asset at less than the company can get out of it either way.

citation.ref: the limit on allocating an impairment loss to an individual asset within a cash-generating unit, and the reallocation of what that limit blocks

items.scenario: A cash-generating unit carries goodwill of ₹100 lakh, a building of ₹300 lakh, plant of ₹150 lakh and a patent of ₹50 lakh. Its recoverable amount at 31 March 2026 is ₹450 lakh, so an impairment loss of ₹150 lakh arises; goodwill absorbs ₹100 lakh of it and falls to nil, and the pro rata step would put ₹30 lakh on the building, ₹15 lakh on the plant and ₹5 lakh on the patent. The patent alone can be measured on its own — it would fetch ₹44 lakh net of the legal costs of selling it, and the licence income it will earn if kept has a present value of ₹48 lakh. Neither the building nor the plant can be measured individually.

items.stem: Which of the two propositions is right, and what reaches profit or loss?

options.text: A sale has occurred, and of the ₹8,00,000 only ₹4,80,000 reaches profit or loss
options.why: Occupying the warehouse afterwards is not the test. Whether there has been a sale is settled by the Ind AS 115 requirements on when a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of an asset, and the leaseback in isolation does not preclude a sale, because what a lease moves is the right to control the use of the building for twelve years rather than the building. Had Hansa kept a substantive repurchase option the financier would never have obtained control and the whole arrangement would have been a financing transaction, but there is none, so a sale it is. The gain is then split rather than taken whole. The total gain is fair value ₹20,00,000 less the carrying amount ₹12,00,000, or ₹8,00,000; the slice standing for the right of use kept back is (8,00,000 / 20,00,000) × 8,00,000 = ₹3,20,000, and that slice is not recognised, because those rights never left. What is left, ₹4,80,000, is the gain on the rights that did pass to the financier.
keywords: in isolation does not preclude a sale

options.text: Neither — no sale has occurred, so the warehouse stays at ₹12,00,000, the ₹20,00,000 is a financial liability and no gain arises
options.misconception: reads continued occupation as proof that control never passed, when a lease hands over only the right to use an asset and not the asset itself
options.why: Using something is not owning it. The financier can sell the warehouse, mortgage it and keep whatever it is worth when the twelve years are up, none of which Hansa can now do, so control has plainly moved. Treating this as a loan would leave a warehouse on the books of a company that no longer owns it and would hide a real gain for twelve years.

options.text: A sale has occurred, and of the ₹8,00,000 only ₹3,20,000 reaches profit or loss
options.misconception: recognises the slice of gain that relates to the right of use kept back and holds the rest, which is the split the wrong way round
options.why: Both slices are computed correctly and then swapped. What is held back is the gain on the rights Hansa still has, because a company cannot report a profit on something it has not given up; what is recognised is the gain on the rights that went to the financier, which is ₹8,00,000 less ₹3,20,000. Recognising ₹3,20,000 reports a profit on the twelve years Hansa kept and reports nothing on the part it actually sold.

options.text: A sale has occurred and the whole ₹8,00,000 goes to profit or loss, the price being equal to fair value
options.misconception: treats a sale and leaseback like an outright sale, when part of the value of the asset has stayed with the seller in the form of the right to use it
options.why: A price at fair value settles that no adjustment for off-market terms is needed; it says nothing about how much gain is recognised. Hansa has not parted with the whole warehouse. It has parted with everything except twelve years of use, and no gain can be reported on rights the company still holds — those rights come across into the right-of-use asset instead.

citation.ref: sale and leaseback transactions — assessing whether the transfer is a sale, and the gain restricted to the rights transferred

items.scenario: Hansa Ltd sells a warehouse to a financier for ₹20,00,000 in cash, which is also the warehouse fair value that day, and takes it straight back on a twelve-year lease. The warehouse stood in Hansa's books at ₹12,00,000 immediately before the sale. The present value of the twelve years of rentals, at the rate implicit in the lease, is ₹8,00,000. There is no option to buy the warehouse back. Hansa's finance head says that since the company will be using the warehouse for twelve more years nothing has really been sold, and that if it has, the whole ₹8,00,000 belongs in this year's profit.

items.stem: At what amount is the restructuring provision recognised at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹9.00 crore
options.why: That an obligation exists settles nothing about its size. A restructuring provision holds only its direct expenditures, and those are the amounts necessarily entailed by the restructuring which are at the same time not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. Only the retrenchment compensation of ₹9.00 crore answers to both. Retraining and relocating the 60 workmen who stay on, marketing the Pune line and the new IT system are named as excluded and are charged as they arise, because they buy the company something in the years to come. The ₹1.20 crore of April trading is among the future operating losses that stay outside a provision unless they relate to an onerous contract, and none here does. And the ₹6.00 crore expected on the land is a gain on an expected disposal, not taken into account in measuring the provision even though the sale is part of the plan.
keywords: not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity
unless they relate to an onerous contract
not taken into account in measuring the provision

options.text: ₹15.50 crore
options.misconception: provides for every cost the announced plan names, treating the announcement as fixing the amount as well as creating the obligation
options.why: Nine plus two plus one and a half plus three is ₹15.50 crore, and it sweeps in three things the standard names as excluded by title. Retraining or relocating staff who continue with the company, marketing, and investment in new systems and distribution networks all relate to how the business will be run afterwards, so they are expenses of the years that get the benefit. Announcing a plan tells the world what the company intends; it does not turn every line of that plan into a liability at the year end.

options.text: ₹10.20 crore
options.misconception: provides for the trading losses the plant will run up before it shuts, when a loss from future trading is not a present obligation
options.why: Nine plus one and two tenths is ₹10.20 crore. The April losses are real and they are next year's. A provision is a present obligation at the reporting date, and a company that expects to trade at a loss for a month has no obligation to anybody for that loss — it can shut the plant tomorrow instead. Losses of this kind are provided for only where the contract producing them is itself onerous, and the scenario rules that out.

options.text: ₹3.00 crore
options.misconception: nets the gain expected on selling the land against the costs, when a gain on an expected disposal is left out of the measurement altogether
options.why: Nine less six is ₹3.00 crore, and it reports a company that has to find ₹9 crore as though it had to find three. The land has not been sold, and the gain on it, whenever it comes, will be recognised on its own account at that time. Setting an unrealised gain against a liability understates the liability and brings a profit forward, which is why the standard keeps the two apart even where the sale is part of the same plan.

citation.ref: a restructuring provision includes only direct expenditures, read with the costs excluded and with future operating losses and gains on expected disposals

items.scenario: Girnar Ltd will close its Nagpur plant. A detailed plan naming the plant, its 240 workmen, the amounts and a start date was approved on 10 March 2026, and letters went to the workmen and to customers on 15 March 2026, so a constructive obligation exists at the 31 March 2026 year end. The estimates are retrenchment compensation ₹9.00 crore; retraining and relocating the 60 workmen who move to the Pune plant ₹2.00 crore; marketing the Pune product line ₹1.50 crore; a new IT system at Pune ₹3.00 crore; operating losses of the Nagpur plant for April 2026 ₹1.20 crore; and an expected gain of ₹6.00 crore on selling the Nagpur land. No contract of the company is onerous.

items.stem: What does Girnar do about the supply contract and the material already in store?

options.text: Provide ₹18.20 lakh, being the ₹14 lakh on the contract and the ₹4.20 lakh the stock has lost
options.misconception: rolls a fall in the value of an asset the company already owns into a provision, when a loss on an asset is written off that asset
options.why: The two numbers are right and one of them is in the wrong place. A provision is a liability, and Girnar owes nobody anything for the 6,000 units it has already bought and holds. What has happened there is that an asset is worth less than its book, which is written off the asset itself. Putting it in the provision would carry the stock at ₹30 lakh it cannot realise and show a liability that does not exist.

options.text: Nothing for either, since the contract is still executory and the material has not been sold
options.misconception: applies the exclusion for executory contracts to a contract that has become onerous, which is the one case the standard pulls back in
options.why: A contract neither side has performed is normally outside this standard, and the exception is precisely a contract that has turned against the entity. Girnar is committed to paying ₹1,00,00,000 for material it can only turn into ₹86,00,000, and pretending that costs nothing until the units arrive would let a company keep every bad bargain off its balance sheet until the day it settles.

options.text: Provide ₹18 lakh, the amount the supplier will accept to let the company out
options.misconception: reads the way out of a contract as the only way out, without comparing it with what going through with the contract would cost
options.why: Eighteen lakh is one of the two figures to be compared, not the answer. Girnar can pay the supplier ₹18 lakh and walk away, or it can take the material and sell it on, which costs it ₹14 lakh net. Nobody pays ₹18 lakh to avoid a ₹14 lakh loss, so a provision of ₹18 lakh reports a company behaving worse than it will.

options.text: Provide ₹14 lakh on the contract, after first writing the 6,000 units in store down by ₹4.20 lakh
options.why: A contract is onerous where the unavoidable costs of meeting it run past the benefit it will bring, and this one does, so it is provided for — but two steps, in order. Any impairment loss on the assets used to fulfil that contract is recognised before the provision is set up, so the 6,000 units already in store come down from ₹500 to ₹430 each, a write-down of ₹4.20 lakh charged against the stock and not against a provision. The provision is then measured at the least net cost of exiting the contract, and that is the cheaper of the two ways out. Going through with the 20,000 units costs ₹1,00,00,000 and brings ₹86,00,000 back on resale, a net ₹14,00,000, against ₹18,00,000 to be released. The cheaper way out is ₹14 lakh, so ₹14 lakh is provided.

citation.ref: onerous contracts — the unavoidable costs, the least net cost of exiting, and the impairment step that comes first

items.scenario: The same closure leaves Girnar Ltd with a supply contract it cannot cancel. It must take 20,000 more units of a raw material at ₹500 a unit, and that material is used only at the plant being shut. The material can be resold to another buyer at ₹430 a unit. The supplier has offered to release Girnar from the contract for ₹18 lakh. Girnar also holds 6,000 units of the same material in store at Nagpur, carried at the ₹500 a unit it paid, which can now fetch only ₹430 a unit as well.

items.stem: What deferred tax asset may Rampur Alloys recognise on the unused tax losses?

options.text: Nothing at all, because a company with a history of recent losses cannot recognise a deferred tax asset on unused losses
options.misconception: hardens a stricter evidence test into an outright bar
options.why: The standard raises the bar for a loss-making company; it does not close the door. Taxable temporary differences that reverse in the right window are themselves future taxable amounts by construction, so they carry recognition without anyone having to believe a forecast, and Rampur has ₹12 crore of them. Refusing the whole asset understates the company by ₹3.00 crore for no reason the standard gives.

options.text: ₹7.50 crore
options.misconception: counts every taxable temporary difference without asking whether it reverses while the losses are still alive
options.why: Thirty crore at a quarter gives ₹7.50 crore, and it treats a reversal in the eleventh year as though it could be set against a loss that lapsed in the eighth. A taxable temporary difference helps only where it produces taxable profit at a time when the loss is still there to absorb it. Timing is part of the test and not a detail beside it.

options.text: ₹20.00 crore
options.misconception: recognises on the whole carried-forward loss because the law permits it to be carried forward at all
options.why: Eighty crore at a quarter gives ₹20.00 crore, and it books an asset for a saving that needs ₹80 crore of future profit to be worth anything. The right to carry a loss forward is a permission, not a benefit. What turns it into an asset is profit to set it against, and that is the very thing three loss-making years put in doubt.

options.text: ₹3.00 crore
options.why: Losses already on the books are themselves strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available, which is why the test tightens rather than relaxes for a company in this position. For a company with a history of recent losses, the asset is allowed only so far as it has taxable temporary differences that will throw up taxable amounts the losses can actually be set against before they lapse, or convincing other evidence that enough taxable profit is on its way. Of the ₹30 crore, only the ₹12 crore reversing in the fourth year does that work; the ₹18 crore reversing in the eleventh arrives after the losses have gone, so there is nothing left for it to soak up. A five-year plan resting on a product nobody has launched is a forecast of the same species as the two that have already failed. So the asset is 12 × 25% = ₹3.00 crore, and nothing is recognised on the other ₹68 crore.
keywords: strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available

citation.ref: recognition of a deferred tax asset on the carry forward of unused tax losses where the entity has a history of recent losses, and the tests for whether taxable profit will be available before the losses expire

items.scenario: Rampur Alloys Ltd has made a loss in each of the last three years and carries forward unused tax losses of ₹80 crore, which lapse at the end of the eighth year from now. Against the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity it has taxable temporary differences of ₹30 crore — ₹12 crore of them will reverse in the fourth year from now and the other ₹18 crore in the eleventh. The board's five-year plan shows a return to profit built on a product not yet launched. The tax rate is 25 per cent.

items.stem: What is the bond worth today?

options.text: ₹ 875.69, the three coupons discounted and the ₹ 1,000 redemption brought back from year four
options.misconception: takes the fourth year's flow to be the redemption alone and loses the fourth coupon, which is riding inside it
options.why: The holder is paid the fourth coupon on the same day he is repaid the principal, so the year four flow is ₹ 1,100, not ₹ 1,000. Discounting only the redemption drops ₹ 100 from the last year and understates the bond by ₹ 63.55, which is that coupon at the year four factor.

options.text: ₹ 1,000.00, since a bond redeemed at par is worth its face value
options.misconception: discounts at the coupon rate instead of the yield, which is the one case where price and face value agree
options.why: Discounting these same flows at 10 per cent does give ₹ 1,000, and that is the trap: price equals face value only when the coupon rate and the required yield are the same number. Here the market wants 12 per cent, so the discount rate is 12 per cent and the answer moves below par.
keywords: price equals face value only when the coupon rate and the required yield are the same number

options.text: ₹ 939.24, each year's flow brought back at the 12 per cent factor for that year
options.why: Take the present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 in years one to three and the final flow of ₹ 1,100 in year four, which is the fourth coupon together with the redemption: 89.29 + 79.72 + 71.18 + 699.05 = ₹ 939.24. The bond sells below its face value because the 10 per cent it pays is short of the 12 per cent the market is asking, and the discount is what closes that gap.
keywords: present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 in years one to three and the final flow of ₹ 1,100

options.text: ₹ 920.00, the face value less the 2 per cent shortfall in coupon for each of the four years
options.misconception: nets the yield gap off the face value year by year without discounting anything
options.why: Four years of a 2 per cent shortfall on ₹ 1,000 is ₹ 80, and taking that straight off par treats a rupee due in year four as worth a rupee today. Every shortfall has to be brought back at 12 per cent before it is subtracted, and doing that properly lands at ₹ 939.24.
keywords: treats a rupee due in year four as worth a rupee today

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation — bond value as the present value of the coupon and redemption flows

items.scenario: Sarayu Power Ltd has a bond outstanding with a face value of ₹ 1,000. It carries a coupon of 10 per cent payable once a year and matures in four years, when it is redeemed at par. Bonds of the same standing yield 12 per cent. The discount factors at 12 per cent are 0.8929 for year one, 0.7972 for year two, 0.7118 for year three and 0.6355 for year four.

items.stem: What should he make of the ₹ 960 quote?

options.text: It is dear by ₹ 84.31, against a value of ₹ 875.69
options.misconception: builds the benchmark by discounting the ₹ 1,000 redemption alone and leaving the fourth coupon out of the final year
options.why: ₹ 875.69 comes from discounting only three coupons and the bare redemption. The fourth coupon is paid on the redemption date, so year four brings ₹ 1,100 and the value is ₹ 939.24. The overpricing is real, but it is ₹ 20.76 and not ₹ 84.31.

options.text: It is dear by ₹ 20.76, so he should not buy at that price
options.why: Work out what the bond is worth to somebody wanting 12 per cent before looking at the quote. That is the present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 and the final flow of ₹ 1,100: 89.29 + 79.72 + 71.18 + 699.05 = ₹ 939.24. The market is asking ₹ 960 for it, which is ₹ 20.76 more, so a buyer at that price earns something under 12 per cent and the bond is not for him.
keywords: present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 and the final flow of ₹ 1,100

options.text: It is fairly priced, because ₹ 100 of coupon on a ₹ 960 quote is a 10.42 per cent return
options.misconception: judges the bond by its current yield, which counts the coupon and ignores the ₹ 40 of redemption gain still to come
options.why: 100 ÷ 960 is 10.42 per cent, and that is the current yield: the coupon measured against the price. It leaves out the ₹ 40 the holder picks up when ₹ 960 is repaid as ₹ 1,000. Counting both, the return at ₹ 960 is above 10.42 per cent and still short of the 12 per cent he wants, which is why ₹ 939.24 is where he would have to buy.

options.text: It is cheap by ₹ 40, because ₹ 960 is below the ₹ 1,000 he will be repaid
options.misconception: measures cheapness against the redemption value rather than against the present value at the yield he requires
options.why: Every bond yielding more than its coupon sells below par, so sitting under ₹ 1,000 says nothing on its own. The yardstick is what the flows are worth at the return he wants, and that is ₹ 939.24. Face value is what he collects in four years, not what those flows are worth today.
keywords: Every bond yielding more than its coupon sells below par

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation — comparing a market quotation with the present value at the required yield

items.scenario: The same Sarayu Power bond — face value ₹ 1,000, coupon 10 per cent paid once a year, four years to redemption at par, market yield 12 per cent, discount factors 0.8929, 0.7972, 0.7118 and 0.6355 — is quoted on the exchange at ₹ 960. A fund manager who wants a 12 per cent return is deciding whether to buy at that quote.

items.stem: What is the bond's Macaulay duration?

options.text: 3.47 years, weighting each year's present value by the year it falls in
options.why: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time before the promised money is back in his hands, so weight each year's present value by its year number and divide by the price. The numerator is 89.29 + 159.44 + 213.54 + 2,796.20 = ₹ 3,258.47, and 3,258.47 ÷ 939.24 = 3.47 years. It is short of the four years to redemption, and it must be for any bond paying a coupon, because some of the money arrives before the last day.
keywords: weight each year's present value by its year number

options.text: 3.26 years, dividing the time-weighted present values by the ₹ 1,000 face value
options.misconception: divides by face value instead of by the price, so the weights no longer add to one
options.why: The divisor has to be the same total the present values add up to, which is the price of ₹ 939.24. Dividing 3,258.47 by ₹ 1,000 instead makes the four weights sum to 0.94 rather than to 1, and every duration computed that way comes out too short.
keywords: The divisor has to be the same total the present values add up to

options.text: 3.57 years, weighting each year by the cash flow received in it
options.misconception: weights the years by the rupees received rather than by what those rupees are worth today
options.why: Weighting by the raw flows gives (100 + 200 + 300 + 4,400) ÷ 1,400 = 3.57 years, which treats ₹ 100 arriving in year four as the equal of ₹ 100 arriving in year one. Duration is built on present values precisely because those two rupees are not equal, and using them pulls the answer down to 3.47 years.
keywords: treats ₹ 100 arriving in year four as the equal of ₹ 100 arriving in year one

options.text: 2.50 years, the average of the four years the bond runs
options.misconception: gives each year equal billing when three quarters of the bond's value arrives in the last one
options.why: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4) ÷ 4 = 2.5 years would be right only if the four flows were equal. Year four carries ₹ 699.05 of the ₹ 939.24, about 74 per cent of the whole, so the weighted answer sits near four rather than near the middle, at 3.47 years.
keywords: would be right only if the four flows were equal

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation — Macaulay duration of a coupon bearing bond

items.scenario: Sarayu Power's bond has a face value of ₹ 1,000, pays a coupon of 10 per cent once a year and is redeemed at par in four years. At a yield of 12 per cent it is priced at ₹ 939.24, made up of present values of 89.29, 79.72, 71.18 and 699.05 for the four years in order.

items.stem: What is its modified duration?

options.text: 3.47, the same figure, because the coupon is annual
options.misconception: reads an annual coupon as meaning there is nothing to adjust, when the adjustment is for the yield and not for the frequency
options.why: An annual coupon fixes n at 1; it does not remove the divisor. The yield is still 12 per cent, so the figure is divided by 1.12 whatever n happens to be, and the two durations differ by that much. They are equal only at a yield of nil.
keywords: An annual coupon fixes n at 1

options.text: 3.15, dividing the Macaulay figure by one plus the 10 per cent coupon rate
options.misconception: puts the coupon rate in the divisor where the yield to maturity belongs
options.why: 3.4693 ÷ 1.10 = 3.15 uses the rate the bond pays. The divisor is built from the rate the market requires, which is 12 per cent here, so it is 1.12 and the answer is 3.10. The two rates are equal only for a bond priced at par, and this one is not.
keywords: The divisor is built from the rate the market requires

options.text: 3.10, the Macaulay figure adjusted for the yield
options.why: Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by (1 + YTM/n), where n is the number of times a year interest is compounded. The coupon here is annual, so n is 1 and the divisor is 1.12: 3.4693 ÷ 1.12 = 3.10. This is the figure that goes into a price change estimate, and it is smaller than the Macaulay figure for every bond with a yield above nought.
keywords: Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by (1 + YTM/n)

options.text: 3.89, the Macaulay figure grossed up by the yield
options.misconception: multiplies by one plus the yield instead of dividing, which makes the bond look more sensitive than it is
options.why: 3.4693 × 1.12 = 3.89 runs the adjustment backwards. The modified figure is always the smaller of the two, because dividing by a number above one shrinks it, and a bond cannot be made more rate sensitive by the arithmetic that adjusts for the yield.
keywords: The modified figure is always the smaller of the two

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation — modified duration and the adjustment for the yield

items.scenario: Sarayu Power's four year bond pays a coupon of 10 per cent once a year and yields 12 per cent. Its Macaulay duration works out at 3.4693 years.

items.stem: How many dollars does he borrow today, and at what rate?

options.text: US$ 5,00,000, borrowed at the 8 per cent United States borrowing rate
options.why: The company has a dollar receivable, so the hedge has to create the opposite position: it must borrow US dollars now, convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate, put the rupees on deposit at home, and let the customer's payment repay the dollar loan on the due date. Size the loan so that principal plus interest equals the receipt. Borrowing costs 8% per annum in the United States, which is 2% for three months, so US$ 5,10,000 ÷ 1.02 = US$ 5,00,000 is what he takes today.
keywords: convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate
principal plus interest equals the receipt

options.text: US$ 5,10,000, borrowed at the 8 per cent United States borrowing rate
options.misconception: borrows the receipt itself and forgets that the loan grows by its own interest before the receipt arrives
options.why: Borrowing the whole US$ 5,10,000 leaves US$ 5,20,200 to repay after three months at 2 per cent, and the customer is only paying US$ 5,10,000. The company would be US$ 10,200 short and would have to buy that at whatever the rate is then, which is the exposure the hedge was supposed to close.

options.text: US$ 4,98,778, borrowed at the 9 per cent Indian borrowing rate
options.misconception: applies the home borrowing rate to a foreign currency loan, when each leg carries the rate of its own money market
options.why: 9 per cent is the cost of borrowing rupees in India. This loan is in dollars and is taken in the United States, so it carries the United States borrowing rate of 8 per cent. The Indian rates come in on the other leg, where the converted rupees are placed on deposit.
keywords: This loan is in dollars and is taken in the United States

options.text: US$ 5,04,950, borrowed at the 4 per cent United States deposit rate
options.misconception: sizes a borrowing on the rate the company would earn as a lender rather than the rate it will be charged
options.why: 4 per cent is what a dollar deposit pays; it is not what a bank charges to lend. The loan runs at 8 per cent, which is 2 per cent for the quarter, so the divisor is 1.02 and not 1.01. Borrowing US$ 5,04,950 at 2 per cent means repaying US$ 5,15,050, so the wrong side of the quote leaves about US$ 5,050 of the loan for the company to find on the due date.
keywords: it is not what a bank charges to lend

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — money market hedging of a foreign currency receivable

items.scenario: Tapti Exports Ltd, an Indian company, will be paid US$ 5,10,000 by an American buyer in exactly three months. Spot is ₹ 83.00 per US$ and the three month forward is ₹ 83.60. Annual interest rates are 6 per cent on deposits and 9 per cent on borrowings in India, and 4 per cent on deposits and 8 per cent on borrowings in the United States. The treasurer decides to cover the receipt through the money market instead of the forward market. Ignore transaction costs and taxes.

items.stem: How many rupees does the company have in hand today, and at which rate?

options.text: ₹ 4,15,00,000, converting the borrowed dollars at spot
options.why: The borrowed dollars are sold immediately at the spot rate of ₹ 83.00, because the whole point of borrowing today is to turn the future receipt into rupees at a rate that is known now: US$ 5,00,000 × 83.00 = ₹ 4,15,00,000. From this moment the exchange rate can do what it likes; the company holds rupees and owes dollars that its customer will supply.

options.text: ₹ 4,26,36,000, the receipt taken at the forward rate
options.misconception: mixes the two covers, pricing the money market chain with the rate that belongs to the forward contract
options.why: ₹ 4,26,36,000 is what the forward contract produces, and it is the figure the money market hedge is eventually compared against. It is not a step inside the money market hedge, which uses spot on day one and the two interest rates thereafter.

options.text: ₹ 4,18,00,000, the borrowed dollars taken at the forward rate
options.misconception: uses a three month rate for a conversion that happens on day one
options.why: ₹ 83.60 is the price of a dollar delivered in three months. The dollars being sold here are in the company's account today, so they fetch today's price of ₹ 83.00. The interest earned on the rupees over the three months is what stands in for the difference between the two rates.
keywords: the price of a dollar delivered in three months

options.text: ₹ 4,23,30,000, converting the US$ 5,10,000 receipt
options.misconception: converts the money the customer will pay in three months, which the company does not hold and cannot sell today
options.why: The US$ 5,10,000 does not exist yet. What is available for conversion today is the loan the bank has just paid out, which is US$ 5,00,000. The receipt's job is to repay that loan on the due date, not to be sold now.
keywords: What is available for conversion today is the loan

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — the spot conversion leg of a money market hedge

items.scenario: Tapti Exports has borrowed US$ 5,00,000 in the United States for three months, an amount sized so that the loan with its interest is exactly settled by the US$ 5,10,000 its customer will pay on the due date. Spot is ₹ 83.00 per US$ and the three month forward is ₹ 83.60.

items.stem: What sum will the company hold on the due date?

options.text: ₹ 4,39,90,000, a full year of interest at 6 per cent
options.misconception: applies an annual rate to a three month period without scaling it
options.why: 6 per cent is quoted for a year and the money is only invested for a quarter of one, so a quarter of the rate applies. Charging the whole 6 per cent credits the company with nine months of interest it never earns.
keywords: credits the company with nine months of interest it never earns

options.text: ₹ 4,24,33,750, at the Indian borrowing rate for three months
options.misconception: pays the borrowing rate on money the company is lending, when the two sides of an Indian quote are 9 per cent and 6 per cent
options.why: 9 per cent is what a bank charges the company; 6 per cent is what it pays the company. A depositor receives the lower of the two, so the quarter's interest is 1.5 per cent and not 2.25 per cent. Taking the wrong side flatters the hedge by ₹ 3,11,250.
keywords: A depositor receives the lower of the two

options.text: ₹ 4,15,00,000, since the hedge is already complete once the rupees are in hand
options.misconception: stops the chain at the conversion and forgets that the rupees earn a return over the three months
options.why: The comparison is against a forward contract settling in three months, so the money market amount has to be carried to the same date. Rupees sitting from today until then earn the Indian deposit rate, and leaving that out understates the hedge by ₹ 6,22,500.
keywords: the money market amount has to be carried to the same date

options.text: ₹ 4,21,22,500, at the Indian deposit rate for three months
options.why: The rupees are placed on deposit in India at 6% p.a., which is 1.5% for three months, so ₹ 4,15,00,000 × 1.015 = ₹ 4,21,22,500 on the due date. That figure is fixed the day the hedge is put on: nothing the exchange rate does afterwards can change it, which is the whole point of the exercise.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — the home deposit leg of a money market hedge

items.scenario: Tapti Exports has sold its borrowed dollars at spot and holds ₹ 4,15,00,000 today. The rupees will sit in India for the three months until the customer pays. Indian rates are 6 per cent a year on deposits and 9 per cent a year on borrowings; United States rates are 4 per cent on deposits and 8 per cent on borrowings.

items.stem: Which cover should the company take, and by how much is it better?

options.text: The forward, by ₹ 11,36,000
options.misconception: compares the forward proceeds with the rupees raised on day one and forgets the deposit interest on the other side
options.why: ₹ 4,26,36,000 less ₹ 4,15,00,000 is ₹ 11,36,000, but ₹ 4,15,00,000 is a figure for today and the forward settles in three months. The money market amount on the due date is ₹ 4,21,22,500, and comparing two sums standing on the same date gives ₹ 5,13,500.
keywords: comparing two sums standing on the same date

options.text: The money market hedge, by ₹ 5,13,500, because manufacturing the rate beats paying a bank's forward margin
options.misconception: assumes the home made rate must beat the quoted one, when which is better depends entirely on the four rates and the forward quote
options.why: The two amounts are ₹ 4,26,36,000 on the forward against ₹ 4,21,22,500 through the money market, so the ₹ 5,13,500 runs the other way. A money market hedge wins when the quoted forward is priced meanly against the interest rates; here it is priced generously and the bank's number is the better one.

options.text: The forward, by ₹ 5,13,500
options.why: Under a forward contract the exporter sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60, giving 5,10,000 × 83.60 = ₹ 4,26,36,000. Set against the ₹ 4,21,22,500 the money market chain produces on the same day, the forward yields ₹ 5,13,500 more. Both cover the exposure completely, so the larger certain sum decides it and the company should take the forward contract.
keywords: sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60

options.text: Neither is better, because interest rate parity makes the two produce the same rupees
options.misconception: treats parity as a fact about the quoted forward, when it is a relationship the quote may depart from and here does
options.why: Parity would put the three month forward near ₹ 82.59, which is what the four interest rates manufacture. The bank is actually quoting ₹ 83.60. The gap between the two is exactly why the comparison has to be done with figures rather than assumed away.
keywords: Parity would put the three month forward near ₹ 82.59

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — money market hedge compared with forward cover

items.scenario: Tapti Exports has worked its money market hedge through and finds it will hold ₹ 4,21,22,500 on the day the customer pays. The alternative on the table is a three month forward at ₹ 83.60 per US$ on the whole receipt of US$ 5,10,000. Spot today is ₹ 83.00.

items.stem: What rate per US$ has the money market hedge actually secured?

options.misconception: quotes the bank's forward rate as though the money market chain had reproduced it, which it only would if parity held exactly
options.why: ₹ 83.60 is the rate on the cover the company did not take. The money market route builds its own rate out of the four interest rates and the spot, and here that comes to ₹ 82.59. The two agree only when the quoted forward sits exactly where the interest rates put it.
keywords: the rate on the cover the company did not take

options.misconception: reads the rate at which the conversion happened as the rate the hedge achieved, ignoring the interest on both legs
options.why: Spot is where the single conversion took place, and if that were the whole story the two interest rates would not matter. The company pays 2 per cent on dollars and earns 1.5 per cent on rupees over the quarter, and that half a per cent of leakage is what carries the effective rate below spot.
keywords: Spot is where the single conversion took place

options.why: Divide the rupees the company ends up with by the dollars the customer actually pays: 4,21,22,500 ÷ 5,10,000. The effective rate under the money market hedge is only ₹ 82.59 per US$, which is below both today's spot of ₹ 83.00 and the ₹ 83.60 on offer forward. Expressing a hedge as a rate is what makes two covers of the same exposure comparable in one line.
keywords: effective rate under the money market hedge is only ₹ 82.59

options.misconception: divides by the dollars borrowed rather than by the dollars the customer pays, so the interest on the loan is counted as a gain
options.why: 4,21,22,500 ÷ 5,00,000 gives ₹ 84.25, and it answers the wrong question. The company is covering a receipt of US$ 5,10,000, and it is that exposure the rate has to be measured against. The US$ 10,000 difference is the loan's interest, which the company never converts.
keywords: it is that exposure the rate has to be measured against

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — the effective rate secured by a money market hedge

items.scenario: Tapti Exports borrowed US$ 5,00,000, sold it at ₹ 83.00 and will hold ₹ 4,21,22,500 on the day its customer pays US$ 5,10,000. The finance head wants the hedge expressed as a rate per dollar so that he can set it beside the ₹ 83.60 the bank is quoting three months forward.

items.stem: What return should he expect on the portfolio?

options.text: 15.0 per cent, the average of the two expected returns
options.misconception: averages the two returns as though the money were split evenly, when the split is 40 to 60
options.why: (18 + 12) ÷ 2 = 15 per cent is the answer for an equal split. Here 60 paise of every rupee sits in the lower returning security, so the portfolio has to come out nearer 12 per cent than the halfway mark does.
keywords: is the answer for an equal split

options.text: 14.4 per cent
options.why: Portfolio return is the plain weighted average of the two returns, with each security's share of the money as its weight: (0.40 × 18%) + (0.60 × 12%) = 7.2% + 7.2% = 14.4%. Nothing about correlation enters here. Diversification works on the risk half of the problem and leaves the expected return exactly where the weights put it.
keywords: weighted average of the two returns

options.text: It cannot be found without using the plus 0.30 correlation
options.misconception: believes correlation changes the portfolio's return, when it only changes the spread of outcomes around that return
options.why: Correlation says how the two securities move in relation to each other, which is a statement about risk. Expected return adds up linearly whatever the correlation is, so 14.4 per cent holds at plus 0.30, at nil and at minus 1. Only the standard deviation moves.
keywords: Expected return adds up linearly whatever the correlation is

options.text: 15.6 per cent
options.misconception: puts the larger weight on the higher returning security, reversing which one holds 40 per cent
options.why: (0.60 × 18) + (0.40 × 12) = 15.6 per cent puts 60 per cent into P. The investor has 40 per cent in P and 60 per cent in Q, so the arithmetic runs the other way and lands at 14.4 per cent. The 1.2 percentage points between the two answers is the whole value of reading which weight belongs to which security.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management — expected return of a two security portfolio

items.scenario: An investor puts 40 per cent of his money into Security P, which is expected to return 18 per cent and has a standard deviation of 25 per cent, and 60 per cent into Security Q, which is expected to return 12 per cent and has a standard deviation of 15 per cent. The correlation coefficient between the two is plus 0.30.

items.stem: What has gone wrong, and what is the portfolio's standard deviation?

options.text: The second term is wrong — it should be 0.36 × 15 = 5.4, and the standard deviation is 12.63 per cent
options.misconception: puts the standard deviation into a variance formula where its square belongs
options.why: Every term in the variance formula is in squared units, so Q contributes its variance of 225 and not its standard deviation of 15. The square root is taken once, at the very end, on the total. 0.36 × 225 = 81 is correct as written, and swapping in 5.4 would give a total of 159.4 and a standard deviation of 12.63 per cent, understating the risk by more than two and a half percentage points.
keywords: Every term in the variance formula is in squared units

options.text: Nothing is wrong — 19 per cent is the portfolio's risk
options.misconception: accepts the weighted average of the two standard deviations as the portfolio's risk, which holds only at a correlation of plus one
options.why: 19 per cent is a real number in this problem, and it is the wrong one. It is the weighted average of 25 and 15, which the portfolio's risk equals only when the two securities move in lockstep. At a correlation of plus 0.30 they do not, and the answer falls to 15.33 per cent.
keywords: which the portfolio's risk equals only when the two securities move in lockstep

options.text: The cross term has lost the correlation coefficient — it should be 54, and the standard deviation is 15.33 per cent
options.why: The formula is portfolio variance = x1²σ1² + x2²σ2² + 2x1x2r12σ1σ2, and the analyst has dropped the r from the last term. His first two terms are right: 0.16 × 625 = 100 and 0.36 × 225 = 81. The cross term is 2 × 0.40 × 0.60 × 0.30 × 25 × 15 = 54, not 180. So portfolio variance = 100 + 81 + 54 = 235, and the square root of 235 = 15.33%. His own 19 per cent is not a random error either: it is exactly what the risk would be if the two were perfectly positively correlated, (0.40 × 25) + (0.60 × 15) = 19%. The 3.67 percentage points between the two figures are the reduction of portfolio risk through diversification, and leaving r out throws all of it away.
keywords: reduction of portfolio risk through diversification

options.text: The weights should not be squared — 0.40 × 625 = 250 and 0.60 × 225 = 135, and the standard deviation is 20.95 per cent
options.misconception: puts the weights into the variance formula unsquared, which they never are
options.why: Each security's own term carries its weight squared, because variance is measured in squared units and the weight has to be squared to match. 0.40 × 0.40 × 625 = 100 is right as it stands, and so is the second term. Unsquaring both gives 250 + 135 + 54 = 439 and a standard deviation of 20.95 per cent, which is further from the truth than the analyst's own answer. The fault in his working is further along, in the cross term.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management — variance of a two security portfolio and the correlation term

items.scenario: An analyst is finding the risk of a portfolio holding 40 per cent of Security P, whose standard deviation is 25 per cent, and 60 per cent of Security Q, whose standard deviation is 15 per cent. The correlation coefficient between them is plus 0.30. His working reads: first term 0.16 × 625 = 100; second term 0.36 × 225 = 81; cross term 2 × 0.40 × 0.60 × 25 × 15 = 180; variance 361; standard deviation 19 per cent.

items.stem: What is the cost of capital of the issue?

options.text: 10.20 per cent
options.why: Take the dividend growth model on net proceeds. The expected dividend is ₹ 9 × 1.08 = ₹ 9.72. Net proceeds per share are ₹ 450 less 2 per cent, which is ₹ 441. So the cost is 9.72 ÷ 441 + 0.08 = 0.0220 + 0.08 = 10.20 per cent. The number of shares behind each receipt does not enter this at all, because a cost of capital is a rate and the ratio cancels out of both halves of it.

options.text: 2.20 per cent
options.misconception: stops at the dividend yield on net proceeds and never adds the growth rate back
options.why: 9.72 ÷ 441 is 0.0220, and that is only the first half of the model. A shareholder buying in expects the dividend to grow at 8 per cent a year as well as to be paid, so the growth rate is added to the yield. Leaving it out understates what the company must earn by four fifths.
keywords: that is only the first half of the model

options.text: 10.04 per cent
options.misconception: uses the dividend just paid where the model asks for the dividend expected a year hence
options.why: 9 ÷ 441 + 0.08 puts last year's dividend over next year's price. The numerator has to be the dividend the buyer will actually receive, which is ₹ 9 grown by 8 per cent. Using the wrong one shaves 16 basis points off the cost, and the same slip on a larger dividend costs more.
keywords: puts last year's dividend over next year's price

options.text: 10.16 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the market price and forgets that 2 per cent of the proceeds never reaches the company
options.why: 9.72 ÷ 450 + 0.08 measures the cost against what the investor pays. The company only gets ₹ 441 of it, so that smaller sum is the base the return has to be earned on. Ignoring issue costs always makes a source of finance look cheaper than it is.
keywords: measures the cost against what the investor pays

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management — cost of capital of a depository receipt issue

items.scenario: Vindhya Motors Ltd plans a global depository receipt issue. Its shares trade at ₹ 450 in India, it has just paid a dividend of ₹ 9 a share which is expected to grow at 8 per cent a year, each receipt will stand for three shares, and issue costs will come to 2 per cent of the proceeds.

items.stem: What does the company actually receive from the issue?

options.text: ₹ 8.82 crore
options.misconception: prices one share for each receipt and loses two thirds of the issue
options.why: 2,00,000 × ₹ 441 counts one share to a receipt. Each receipt here stands for three, so the issue is 6,00,000 shares and the proceeds are three times as large. The ratio is the first thing to read in any depository receipt question, because every figure after it is multiplied by it.
keywords: counts one share to a receipt

options.text: ₹ 26.46 crore
options.why: Count the shares before pricing anything: 2,00,000 receipts × 3 shares is 6,00,000 shares. Each raises ₹ 450 less the 2 per cent that goes on the issue, which is ₹ 441. So 6,00,000 shares × ₹ 441 = ₹ 26.46 crore reaches the company. The gross of ₹ 27 crore is what investors part with; the difference is the cost of getting the issue away.

options.text: ₹ 27.00 crore
options.misconception: takes the gross amount investors pay as the amount the company gets, leaving issue costs out
options.why: 6,00,000 × ₹ 450 is what is subscribed. The bankers, lawyers and listing take 2 per cent of it before anything reaches the company, so ₹ 54 lakh comes off and ₹ 26.46 crore is left. The cost of capital is worked on the net figure for the same reason.

options.text: ₹ 27.54 crore
options.misconception: adds the 2 per cent to the price instead of deducting it, as though issue costs were charged on top to the investor
options.why: ₹ 450 × 1.02 = ₹ 459 would mean the issue was priced above the market and the extra handed to the company. Issue costs come out of the proceeds, not on top of the price, so the multiplier is 0.98 and the net price is ₹ 441.
keywords: Issue costs come out of the proceeds, not on top of the price

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management — net proceeds of a depository receipt issue

items.scenario: Vindhya Motors will issue 2,00,000 global depository receipts, each standing for three of its shares. The shares trade at ₹ 450 in India and the issue is priced off that. Issue costs are 2 per cent of the proceeds.

items.stem: What are the up and down factors, and what does the call pay in each state?

options.text: u is 1.25 and d is 0.80, and the call pays ₹ 40 on the up move and nothing on the down
options.why: Each factor is a future price over today's price, so u = 250/200 = 1.25 and d = 160/200 = 0.80. The payoffs are then read off the exercise price, and a call is never exercised at a loss, so Cu = Max (0, 250 − 210) = ₹ 40. At ₹ 160 the strike stands above the share, so the holder walks away and Cd is nil.

options.text: u is 1.19 and d is 0.76, and the call pays ₹ 40 on the up move and nothing on the down
options.misconception: builds the two factors on the exercise price instead of on the share price the tree starts from
options.why: 250 ÷ 210 is 1.19 and 160 ÷ 210 is 0.76, and both measure an outcome against the strike. The two factors describe how the share moves, so each is the future price over today's share price of ₹ 200. The exercise price enters once, at the payoff line, and never in the factors.
keywords: The two factors describe how the share moves

options.text: u is 1.25 and d is 0.80, and the call pays ₹ 50 on the up move and nothing on the down
options.misconception: measures the call's payoff from the price the share stands at today rather than from the exercise price
options.why: 250 less 200 is ₹ 50, and that is what the share gains, not what the call pays. A call pays whatever the share stands above the exercise price, which is 250 less 210. The ₹ 10 between the two answers is the option starting out of the money.
keywords: that is what the share gains, not what the call pays

options.text: u is 1.25 and d is 0.80, and the call pays ₹ 40 on the up move and costs ₹ 50 on the down
options.misconception: lets the call carry the loss on the down move, when its holder simply abandons a right he paid for
options.why: 160 less 210 is minus ₹ 50, and that is the loss on owning the share, not on owning the call. A call is a right and not an obligation, so at ₹ 160 the holder lets it lapse and the worst the option can do at expiry is nothing. That nought is what the Max of zero and the difference is there to enforce.
keywords: the worst the option can do at expiry is nothing

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — the one period tree, its factors and the payoff at each node

items.scenario: The share of Chenab Ltd trades at ₹ 200 today. Over the next year it will be worth either ₹ 250 or ₹ 160, and nothing in between. The risk free rate of interest is 8 per cent a year. A European call option on the share, exercisable in one year, has an exercise price of ₹ 210.

items.stem: What weight does the model put on the up move?
