options.why: The risk neutral probability is the weight under which the share itself grows at the risk free rate, and it comes out of the two factors and that rate: p = (r − d) ÷ (u − d), which here is (1.08 − 0.80) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80), so 0.28 ÷ 0.45 = 0.6222. Check it on the share rather than on the option — 250 × 0.6222 plus 160 × 0.3778 is ₹ 216, and ₹ 216 brought back at 1.08 is the ₹ 200 the share costs today.

options.misconception: measures the gap downward from the up factor, so the weight belonging to the fall is reported as the weight on the rise
options.why: (1.25 − 1.08) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80) is 0.17 ÷ 0.45, or 0.3778, which is the weight on the fall and not on the rise. The distance is measured up from the down factor, because how far the risk free growth stands above the worse outcome is what says how much weight the better one must carry.
keywords: which is the weight on the fall and not on the rise

options.misconception: stops at the numerator and never divides by the spread between the two factors
options.why: 0.28 is how far the growth factor of 1.08 stands above the down factor of 0.80, and it is only the top of the fraction. Dividing it by the whole spread of 0.45 is what turns a distance into a share of one, and a figure that has been divided by nothing cannot be a weight at all.
keywords: it is only the top of the fraction

options.text: minus 1.60
options.misconception: puts the 8 per cent rate itself into the formula where the growth factor of 1.08 belongs
options.why: (0.08 − 0.80) ÷ 0.45 gives minus 1.60. A negative weight is the signal that r in this formula is not the rate but one plus the rate — the factor money grows by over the period, which is 1.08 for a full year at 8 per cent.
keywords: A negative weight is the signal

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — the risk neutral weight from the two factors and the risk free growth factor

items.scenario: Chenab Ltd's share stands at ₹ 200 and in one year will be worth either ₹ 250 or ₹ 160. The up factor is therefore 1.25 and the down factor 0.80. The risk free rate is 8 per cent a year, so money grows over the year by a factor of 1.08.

items.stem: What is the call worth today?

options.why: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate. Under the risk neutral weights the option is expected to be worth (0.6222 × 40) + (0.3778 × 0) = ₹ 24.89 a year from now, and bringing that back one year, 24.89 ÷ 1.08 = ₹ 23.05, is what it is worth today.
keywords: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate

options.misconception: discounts the option's expected payoff at the cost of equity, when the position the model builds carries no risk to be paid for
options.why: 24.89 ÷ 1.15 is ₹ 21.64, and it charges the option 15 per cent. The argument behind this price is that a holding in the share and a written call can be combined into a position worth the same amount whichever way the share goes, and a certain amount is brought back at the risk free rate. A rate carrying a premium for risk has nothing to attach itself to here.
keywords: a certain amount is brought back at the risk free rate

options.misconception: prices the call on the up move alone, as though the ₹ 250 outcome were certain to arrive
options.why: 40 ÷ 1.08 is ₹ 37.04, and it pays today for a payoff of ₹ 40 that is not certain. More than a third of the weight sits on the ₹ 160 branch, where the option expires worthless, and that branch belongs in the average before anything is discounted.
keywords: a payoff of ₹ 40 that is not certain

options.misconception: hangs the up payoff on the weight belonging to the fall, so the branch that pays is given the smaller of the two weights
options.why: 0.3778 × 40 is ₹ 15.11, and 15.11 ÷ 1.08 is ₹ 13.99. But 0.3778 is the weight on ₹ 160, where the call pays nothing at all. The ₹ 40 belongs to the ₹ 250 branch and carries 0.6222 with it.
keywords: the weight on ₹ 160, where the call pays nothing at all

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation — the expected payoff under the risk neutral weights, discounted at the risk free rate

items.scenario: Chenab Ltd's share stands at ₹ 200 and will be worth either ₹ 250 or ₹ 160 in a year. A one year call struck at ₹ 210 therefore pays ₹ 40 on the up move and nothing on the down, and the risk neutral weight on the up move works out at 0.6222. The risk free rate is 8 per cent a year. Chenab's own cost of equity is 15 per cent.

items.stem: What is the present value of the cost of buying a van and selling it after one year?

options.why: Only two dates carry anything. The van is paid for today, and at the end of the first year ₹ 4,00,000 comes in from the sale while ₹ 1,50,000 has gone out on running it, so that year is ₹ 2,50,000 to the good. One-year cycle, then: −6,00,000 plus 0.909 × (4,00,000 − 1,50,000), which is −6,00,000 plus 2,27,250, a present value of cost of −₹ 3,72,750.
keywords: a present value of cost of −₹ 3,72,750

options.misconception: brings the sale proceeds back but leaves the year's running cost out of the cycle altogether
options.why: −6,00,000 plus 0.909 × 4,00,000 gives minus ₹ 2,36,400, and it counts the sale while forgetting that the van was driven for a year first. The ₹ 1,50,000 falls on the same day as the sale, so it is netted against the ₹ 4,00,000 before the factor is applied.
keywords: it counts the sale while forgetting that the van was driven for a year first

options.misconception: discounts the running cost but never brings the resale value into the cycle at all
options.why: −6,00,000 less 0.909 × 1,50,000 gives minus ₹ 7,36,350, and it treats the van as worthless after a year. It is sold for ₹ 4,00,000 at the very moment the cycle ends, and in a cycle this short that receipt is the largest single item in the sum.
keywords: it treats the van as worthless after a year

options.misconception: nets the three amounts against one another without discounting the two that fall a year away
options.why: ₹ 6,00,000 out today, ₹ 1,50,000 out and ₹ 4,00,000 in a year later, added up flat, gives minus ₹ 3,50,000. The running cost and the sale both fall at the end of the first year, and both have to be brought back at 0.909 before they meet an amount paid today.
keywords: both have to be brought back at 0.909

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — the present value of cost of one replacement cycle

items.scenario: Sutlej Logistics Ltd runs a fleet of delivery vans and replaces them one after another without a break. A van costs ₹ 6,00,000. It costs ₹ 1,50,000 to run in its first year, ₹ 2,00,000 in its second and ₹ 2,60,000 in its third. Sold at the end of its first year it fetches ₹ 4,00,000, at the end of the second ₹ 3,00,000 and at the end of the third ₹ 1,80,000. The cost of capital is 10 per cent and the present value factors are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751 for years one to three.

items.stem: What is the present value of the cost if each van is kept for two years?

options.misconception: discounts the second year's net amount at the cumulative two-year factor, which belongs to a sum arriving in both years rather than in one
options.why: 1,00,000 × 1.735 is ₹ 1,73,500, and it treats the second year's net amount as though it arrived twice, once in each year. A cumulative factor turns a level yearly amount into a present value. A single sum falling at the end of the second year meets the second year's own factor of 0.826 and nothing else.
keywords: it treats the second year's net amount as though it arrived twice

options.misconception: adds the four amounts as they stand, so a rupee spent two years out counts the same as one spent today
options.why: 6,00,000 plus 1,50,000 plus 2,00,000 less 3,00,000 is ₹ 6,50,000, and it lands within ₹ 3,750 of the right answer by luck rather than by method. The two running costs fall a year apart and the sale is two years away, so each meets its own factor before anything is added.
keywords: each meets its own factor before anything is added

options.misconception: discounts the second year's sale proceeds but leaves that year's running cost out of the netting
options.why: −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 plus 3,00,000 × 0.826 gives minus ₹ 4,88,550, and it collects the sale while forgetting the ₹ 2,00,000 the van cost to run in the year it was sold. Both fall at the end of the second year, so they are netted first and the net amount meets the factor.
keywords: the ₹ 2,00,000 the van cost to run in the year it was sold

options.why: The first year carries the running cost on its own, 1,50,000 × 0.909, which is ₹ 1,36,350 out. The second year carries a sale of ₹ 3,00,000 against running costs of ₹ 2,00,000. Two-year cycle, then: −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 plus (3,00,000 − 2,00,000) × 0.826, which is −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 plus 82,600, a present value of cost of −₹ 6,53,750.
keywords: a present value of cost of −₹ 6,53,750

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — netting the resale against the operating cost of the year of sale

items.scenario: Sutlej Logistics' vans cost ₹ 6,00,000 each and are replaced on a continuous cycle. Running costs are ₹ 1,50,000 in year one, ₹ 2,00,000 in year two and ₹ 2,60,000 in year three, and the resale values at the end of those years are ₹ 4,00,000, ₹ 3,00,000 and ₹ 1,80,000. The cost of capital is 10 per cent, the yearly present value factors are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751, and the cumulative factors are 0.909, 1.735 and 2.486.

items.stem: What is the present value of the cost if each van is kept for three years?

options.why: Running costs fall in all three years and the sale only at the close of the third, where it is netted against that year's running cost. Three-year cycle, then: −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 less 1,65,200 plus (1,80,000 − 2,60,000) × 0.751, which is −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 less 1,65,200 less 60,080, a present value of cost of −₹ 9,61,630. That last term subtracts rather than adds, because by its third year the van costs more to run than it fetches.
keywords: a present value of cost of −₹ 9,61,630

options.misconception: collects a resale in the second year as well as in the third, when a van can only be sold once
options.why: Adding 3,00,000 × 0.826 on top of the third year's figure sells the same van twice. The resale values for years one and two say what the van would fetch if the cycle ended there. In a three year cycle it does not end there, and the only money ever received for the van is the ₹ 1,80,000 at the close of the third year.

options.misconception: adds the outlay and the three running costs and takes the sale off, without discounting any of them
options.why: 6,00,000 plus 1,50,000 plus 2,00,000 plus 2,60,000 less 1,80,000 is ₹ 10,30,000 of undiscounted money. At 10 per cent a rupee due in the third year is worth about 75 paise, and putting every flow against its own factor brings the figure down to ₹ 9,61,630.
keywords: a rupee due in the third year is worth about 75 paise

options.misconception: nets nothing against the third year's sale, so the year the van costs most to run is the year whose running cost goes missing
options.why: −6,00,000 less 1,36,350 less 1,65,200 plus 1,80,000 × 0.751 gives minus ₹ 7,66,370, and it leaves out the ₹ 2,60,000 spent running the van in its third year. That is the largest of the three running costs and it falls on the very day of the sale.
keywords: it leaves out the ₹ 2,60,000 spent running the van in its third year

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — a replacement cycle where the operating cost overtakes the resale value

items.scenario: Sutlej Logistics' vans cost ₹ 6,00,000 each and are replaced on a continuous cycle. Running costs are ₹ 1,50,000, ₹ 2,00,000 and ₹ 2,60,000 in years one to three, and the resale values at the end of those years are ₹ 4,00,000, ₹ 3,00,000 and ₹ 1,80,000. The cost of capital is 10 per cent and the yearly present value factors are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751.

items.stem: What is the yearly charge each cycle works out at?

options.why: The three totals run for different lengths, so they cannot be set beside one another until each has become a yearly figure. Equivalent Annual Cost is the present value of cash outflow divided by the PVAF for that cycle, and so 3,72,750 ÷ 0.909 = ₹ 4,10,066; 6,53,750 ÷ 1.735 = ₹ 3,76,801; 9,61,630 ÷ 2.486 = ₹ 3,86,819.
keywords: present value of cash outflow divided by the PVAF

options.misconception: divides each total by the discount factor of the cycle's last year instead of by the cumulative factor covering all its years
options.why: The factors 0.826 and 0.751 discount one sum arriving on one date. What is wanted is the level yearly amount whose present value across the whole cycle equals the total, and only the cumulative factor does that job. The one year answer agrees under both readings, because 0.909 happens to be the cumulative factor as well as the first year's, and that is what lets this slip survive a spot check.
keywords: only the cumulative factor does that job

options.misconception: multiplies each total by the annuity factor when the conversion divides by it
options.why: A two year cycle cannot cost ₹ 11,34,256 a year when the whole of it costs ₹ 6,53,750. Multiplying runs the arithmetic backwards: an annuity factor turns a yearly amount into a present value, so coming back from a present value to a yearly amount means dividing by it.
keywords: an annuity factor turns a yearly amount into a present value

options.misconception: uses one annuity factor for all three cycles rather than each cycle's own
options.why: Dividing all three by 2.486 spreads a one year cycle over three years, which is the one thing this exercise exists to prevent. Each total is spread over the years it actually covers, which is why only the three year figure of ₹ 3,86,819 comes out right here.
keywords: Each total is spread over the years it actually covers

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — converting each cycle's present value of cost into a yearly amount

items.scenario: Sutlej Logistics' three replacement cycles for its vans come out at present values of cost of ₹ 3,72,750 over one year, ₹ 6,53,750 over two years and ₹ 9,61,630 over three. At 10 per cent the cumulative present value factors are 0.909 for one year, 1.735 for two years and 2.486 for three; the yearly factors are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751.

items.stem: How often should the vans be replaced?

options.text: Every year, because ₹ 3,72,750 is the smallest present value of cost of the three
options.misconception: reads the smallest total as the cheapest policy, when the one year total is small only because it buys one year of service
options.why: ₹ 3,72,750 buys twelve months of a van and ₹ 9,61,630 buys thirty-six. A total covering fewer years will nearly always look smaller, which is the whole reason the three are put on a yearly footing first. Per year the one year cycle is the dearest of the three, at ₹ 4,10,066.
keywords: A total covering fewer years will nearly always look smaller

options.text: Every year, because ₹ 1,50,000 is the lowest running cost of the three years
options.misconception: picks the cycle with the smallest running cost, leaving out the capital cost of buying a new van that often
options.why: Running costs do climb with age, from ₹ 1,50,000 to ₹ 2,60,000. But replacing every year also means paying ₹ 6,00,000 for a new van every year and losing ₹ 2,00,000 on the resale each time. Once both are counted, the yearly charge on the one year cycle is the highest of the three at ₹ 4,10,066.
keywords: losing ₹ 2,00,000 on the resale each time

options.text: Every three years, because the yearly charge keeps falling the longer a van is kept
options.misconception: assumes the yearly figure falls without limit as the cycle lengthens, when running costs climb and resale values drop as the van ages
options.why: The yearly charge falls from ₹ 4,10,066 to ₹ 3,76,801 and then turns and rises to ₹ 3,86,819. Spreading the purchase price over more years pushes it down; a van costing ₹ 2,60,000 to run in its third year and fetching only ₹ 1,80,000 pushes it back up. The lowest point sits in the middle, and only working all three cycles finds it.
keywords: The lowest point sits in the middle

options.text: Every two years
options.why: On a cycle that repeats without a break the yearly charge is the only comparable figure, and the lowest Equivalent Annual Cost is ₹ 3,76,801, so the vans should be replaced every two years. It beats the next best cycle by ₹ 10,018 a van a year, and the one year cycle by ₹ 33,265.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — choosing the cycle with the lowest equivalent annual cost

items.scenario: Sutlej Logistics' three replacement cycles come out at yearly charges of ₹ 4,10,066 for a one year cycle, ₹ 3,76,801 for two years and ₹ 3,86,819 for three. Their plain present values of cost were ₹ 3,72,750, ₹ 6,53,750 and ₹ 9,61,630 in the same order. A van costs ₹ 6,00,000 and fetches ₹ 4,00,000 when it is a year old.

items.stem: What is the company's net operating profit after tax for the year?

options.text: ₹ 700 lakh
options.misconception: stops at operating profit, when the measure is stated after the tax charged on that operating profit
options.why: ₹ 700 lakh is what operations earned before any tax at all. The measure is an after tax one, so 30 per cent of ₹ 700 lakh, or ₹ 210 lakh, comes off first, and the book entry that took no money out then goes back on, landing at ₹ 520 lakh.
keywords: what operations earned before any tax at all

options.text: ₹ 520 lakh
options.why: Begin at operating profit: EBIT is 2,000 − 800 − 500 = 700. Tax is charged on that and not on the profit left after interest, so ₹ 210 lakh comes off. Then add back the non-cash provision of ₹ 30 lakh, which was deducted in the accounts and paid to nobody, giving NOPAT of ₹ 520 lakh.

options.text: ₹ 450 lakh
options.misconception: charges tax on the profit left after interest, so the lenders' share of the return is treated as somebody else's income
options.why: 600 × 0.70 plus 30 is ₹ 450 lakh, and it takes the ₹ 100 lakh of interest out before tax. This figure is the return to everybody who financed the business, lenders included, so interest is not taken out of it. What the debt costs is charged later and in one place, inside the weighted average cost of capital.
keywords: interest is not taken out of it

options.text: ₹ 490 lakh
options.misconception: leaves the provision for doubtful debts inside operating cost, when nothing was actually paid out on it
options.why: 700 less 210 is ₹ 490 lakh, and it charges the year with a ₹ 30 lakh provision that took no money out of the business. It is a book entry, so it is put back to leave a figure that measures what operations actually produced. The same ₹ 30 lakh goes back on the capital side too, because the receivables in the balance sheet are shown after it.
keywords: a ₹ 30 lakh provision that took no money out of the business

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation — operating profit after tax, adjusted for non-cash charges

items.scenario: Godavari Industries Ltd's accounts for the year show, in ₹ lakh, revenue of 2,000, direct costs of 800 and selling, general and administrative expenses of 500. Sitting inside that ₹ 500 lakh is a provision for bad and doubtful debts of ₹ 30 lakh. Interest for the year is ₹ 100 lakh and the tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: On what amount of capital is the charge for capital levied?

options.text: ₹ 1,830 lakh
options.why: Two steps. Take total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600, which strips out the current liabilities and provisions the business pays nothing for and leaves ₹ 1,800 lakh. Then put back the non-cash adjustment of 30, the very provision that was added to the profit, which gives ₹ 1,830 lakh.
keywords: total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600

options.text: ₹ 1,300 lakh
options.misconception: counts the shareholders' funds alone and forgets that the borrowings are capital too and are paid for
options.why: 900 plus 400 is the equity side and nothing else. The ₹ 500 lakh of non-current borrowings is capital invested in the business, and it is charged for at the cost of debt. That is precisely why the rate applied here is a weighted average of two costs rather than one.
keywords: it is charged for at the cost of debt

options.text: ₹ 1,800 lakh
options.misconception: takes out the liabilities that bear no interest but never puts the non-cash provision back, so the two sides of the subtraction stop matching
options.why: ₹ 1,800 lakh is the right subtraction and one step short of the answer. The ₹ 30 lakh provision was added back to the profit, and the receivables it was taken off sit inside these assets, so it goes back here as well. Leaving it out sets a smaller capital base against a profit that has already been grossed up.
keywords: sets a smaller capital base against a profit that has already been grossed up

options.text: ₹ 2,400 lakh
options.misconception: charges the whole asset base, including the part suppliers and other trade creditors are funding for nothing
options.why: The ₹ 600 lakh of current liabilities and provisions is money the business is using and paying no interest on. Capital that costs nothing carries no charge, so it comes out of the base before the weighted average cost of capital is applied to what is left.
keywords: Capital that costs nothing carries no charge

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation — invested capital as total assets less the liabilities that bear no interest

items.scenario: Godavari Industries Ltd's balance sheet shows total assets of ₹ 2,400 lakh, funded by equity share capital of ₹ 900 lakh, reserves of ₹ 400 lakh, non-current borrowings of ₹ 500 lakh and current liabilities and provisions of ₹ 600 lakh. The trade receivables inside total assets are stated after a provision for bad and doubtful debts of ₹ 30 lakh, and that same ₹ 30 lakh has been added back in arriving at the year's operating profit after tax.

items.stem: What rate does the charge for capital apply?

options.text: 7.96 per cent
options.misconception: divides each source by total assets rather than by the funded capital, so the two weights add to about three quarters instead of to one
options.why: 1,300 and 500 taken over ₹ 2,400 lakh give weights of 0.54 and 0.21, which come to 0.75 and not to 1. The ₹ 600 lakh of current liabilities and provisions was removed from the base precisely because it costs nothing, so it is not in the denominator either. The weights are taken over the ₹ 1,800 lakh that equity and debt actually fund.
keywords: which come to 0.75 and not to 1

options.text: 12 per cent
options.misconception: prices the whole of the capital at the shareholders' required return, leaving the cheaper borrowed part out of the average
options.why: Debt is a little over a quarter of the ₹ 1,800 lakh and it costs 7 per cent once the tax relief on interest is counted, well under the 12 per cent the shareholders want. An average that ignores it overstates the rate by about 1.4 percentage points here, and a rate that is too high reports a company as destroying value when it is not.
keywords: An average that ignores it overstates the rate

options.text: 10.44 per cent
options.misconception: builds the weights on the capital base after the non-cash adjustment, when that adjustment belongs to the amount charged and not to the funding behind it
options.why: Dividing 1,300 and 500 by 1,830 makes the two weights add to 0.98 rather than to 1, because the extra ₹ 30 lakh has no source of funding standing behind it. The mix comes from the ₹ 1,800 lakh of equity and debt; the ₹ 1,830 lakh is what the resulting rate is then applied to.
keywords: makes the two weights add to 0.98 rather than to 1

options.text: 10.61 per cent
options.why: Weight each source by its share of the funded capital, which is equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800, and take the debt at what it costs after the tax it saves. That gives (1,300/1,800 × 12%) + (500/1,800 × 10% × 0.70), which is 8.67% + 1.94% = 10.61%.
keywords: equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation — the weighted average cost of the equity and debt funding the invested capital

items.scenario: Godavari Industries is funded by equity of ₹ 1,300 lakh — share capital of 900 and reserves of 400 — and non-current borrowings of ₹ 500 lakh, so ₹ 1,800 lakh in all once the ₹ 600 lakh of current liabilities and provisions has been stripped out of its ₹ 2,400 lakh of assets. Adding back a non-cash provision of ₹ 30 lakh takes the capital actually invested to ₹ 1,830 lakh. The cost of equity is 12 per cent, the cost of debt before tax is 10 per cent and the tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What is the company's economic value added for the year, and what does it say?

options.text: ₹ 300.40 lakh, and the operations paid for their capital and left a surplus
options.misconception: charges the whole capital at the shareholders' 12 per cent, so the borrowed part is priced as though it were equity
options.why: 1,830 × 12% is ₹ 219.60 lakh, and it charges every rupee at what the shareholders want. More than a quarter of that capital is borrowed and costs 7 per cent once the tax relief on interest is counted, so the true charge is ₹ 194.18 lakh and the surplus is ₹ 325.82 lakh.
keywords: it charges every rupee at what the shareholders want

options.text: ₹ 325.82 lakh, and the operations paid for their capital and left a surplus
options.why: Charge the capital first: capital charge = 1,830 × 10.61% = ₹ 194.18 lakh is what the providers of that capital required for the year. Take it off the operating profit after tax and EVA = 520 − 194.18 = ₹ 325.82 lakh. A positive EVA says the year's operations paid for every rupee of capital they used and left ₹ 325.82 lakh over.

options.text: ₹ 295.82 lakh, and the operations paid for their capital and left a surplus
options.misconception: adds the non-cash provision to the capital base but leaves it out of the profit, so one side of the subtraction is adjusted and the other is not
options.why: 490 less 194.18 is ₹ 295.82 lakh, and it starts from a profit still carrying the ₹ 30 lakh provision as though it were a cost. That same ₹ 30 lakh has already gone into the ₹ 1,830 lakh of capital. Whichever way the adjustment is made it is made on both sides, and the profit here is ₹ 520 lakh.
keywords: it is made on both sides

options.text: ₹ 329.00 lakh, and the operations paid for their capital and left a surplus
options.misconception: levies the charge on the ₹ 1,800 lakh the weights were built from rather than on the capital actually invested
options.why: 1,800 × 10.61% is ₹ 191.00 lakh, which leaves ₹ 329.00 lakh. But ₹ 1,800 lakh is only where the mix of funding came from. What is charged is the ₹ 1,830 lakh actually invested, because the profit it is set against was grossed up by the very same ₹ 30 lakh. The two sides have to be adjusted alike or the surplus comes out too large.
keywords: The two sides have to be adjusted alike

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation — the capital charge deducted from the adjusted operating profit after tax

items.scenario: Godavari Industries' operating profit after tax for the year is ₹ 520 lakh, after adding back a non-cash provision of ₹ 30 lakh. Its invested capital, after taking out the liabilities that bear no interest and adding back the same ₹ 30 lakh, is ₹ 1,830 lakh. Its weighted average cost of capital, weighted on the ₹ 1,800 lakh of equity and debt behind that capital, is 10.61 per cent.

items.stem: What must CA Prakash settle before he takes the engagement on?

options.text: Two things — that he has what the engagement needs by way of skill and experience, and that the yardstick Trisha will use to write the description is both fit for the purpose and visible to the forty distributors and their auditors, which benchmarks Trisha keeps to itself are not
options.why: Before accepting, the service auditor has to be satisfied that he possesses the capabilities and competence to carry out an engagement of this kind. Never having done one is a matter to answer by preparation, by staffing and by consultation, not an automatic bar. He must also be satisfied that the criteria the service organisation will apply in writing the description of its system are suitable and available to user entities and their auditors. In-house benchmarks kept inside Trisha fail the second half of that: an auditor at one of the forty distributors who cannot see the yardstick cannot tell what the description is asserting, and a report he cannot interpret is a report he cannot use.
keywords: suitable and available to user entities

options.text: He must decline outright, because an engagement of this kind may only be taken by a practitioner who has reported on a service organisation before
options.misconception: turns a requirement to have the skill and experience the work needs into a bar on anybody doing it for the first time
options.why: There is no first-engagement bar anywhere in the standard. What is asked is that the service auditor has the capabilities and competence for the work, which can be built by training, by bringing in someone who has done it, or by consultation. A rule that nobody may do this work for the first time would leave nobody able to do it at all.

options.text: Only his independence — capability follows from being a chartered accountant, and a yardstick a service organisation's own board has approved is by that fact a proper one
options.misconception: reads approval inside the service organisation as the test of suitability, when suitability is judged by whether user entities and their auditors can work with the criteria
options.why: Independence is necessary and it is not the whole of acceptance. Approval by the service organisation's board says who authorised the benchmarks. It does not say whether they are suitable for measuring a description of the system, and it says nothing at all about whether anyone outside the company can see them.

options.text: Nothing at this stage — competence is a matter for his own conscience, the yardstick is the service organisation's to choose, and naming it in the report is all that anybody needs
options.misconception: treats naming the criteria in the report as a substitute for the criteria being fit for purpose and visible before the engagement is taken on
options.why: Naming a yardstick tells a reader which one was used; it does not make it usable. The condition is settled before acceptance and it has two halves, and the second half is that the criteria are available to user entities and their auditors, so that the people relying on the report can see what the description was measured against.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — acceptance of an SAE 3402 engagement, the service auditor's own capability and the criteria for the description of the system

items.scenario: Trisha Systems runs warehouse management and customer invoicing for forty pharmaceutical distributors. It wants an assurance report on the design and operation of its controls for the year, and approaches CA Prakash, who has audited financial statements for twenty years and has never reported on a service organisation before. Trisha tells him it will write the description of its system against a set of in-house benchmarks its own board signed off, which it does not release outside the company, and that the distributors' auditors "can take the description as it stands".

items.stem: How should the service auditor answer that proposal?

options.text: Refuse the engagement altogether, because any limit a service organisation proposes on the scope makes an assurance report impossible
options.misconception: turns a condition about limits that leave a report useless into a bar on drawing any boundary at all
options.why: Every engagement has a boundary and the standard does not ask for one that has none. What it asks is that the boundary will not be so limited that little of use is left inside it for the group and the people who audit it. The answer here is to move the boundary, not to walk away from the work.

options.text: Accept it — paying statutory deductions across is the group's own legal duty, so controls over it can never be relevant to a report on the service organisation
options.misconception: confuses whose legal obligation the remittance is with whose controls actually perform it
options.why: The obligation is indeed the group's, which is exactly why it matters that the organisation it handed the work to performs it properly. A control is relevant to a user entity's financial reporting because of what it can cause to go wrong in those statements, not because of whose name is on the challan.
keywords: what it can cause to go wrong in those statements

options.text: Refuse the boundary — a description cut that narrow is of no real use to the group's own auditors, and money withheld from wages and paid over late lands in the group's financial statements as a charge it did not expect
options.why: Before accepting, the service auditor has to be satisfied that the boundary drawn round the engagement, and round the description of the system, will not be so limited that little of use is left inside it for the group and the people who audit it. Remittance is no side issue for a user entity. Amounts deducted from an employee's wages stay the employer's liability until they reach the authority, and paying them across late turns into interest and penalty in the employer's own books. Controls over remittance therefore bear directly on the user entity's financial reporting, and cutting them out is the very limitation this condition exists to catch.

options.text: Accept it — the description says plainly what it covers, and any user auditor who wants comfort on remittance can commission separate work
options.misconception: treats a boundary that is honestly stated as curing a boundary drawn so tight that the report cannot serve the people who read it
options.why: A stated boundary is honest and it does not answer the question the condition asks, which is whether what is left inside is still of use. Sending every user entity away to commission its own work on the part that was cut out defeats the reason a service organisation obtains one report for many readers in the first place.
keywords: whether what is left inside is still of use

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — acceptance of an SAE 3402 engagement, and the scope and description not being cut so narrow as to be useless to user entities

items.scenario: A service organisation computes the wages of a logistics group's eleven thousand employees and pays over the provident fund contributions and the tax deducted at source on the group's behalf. It has asked for an assurance report on its controls, and proposes to draw the boundary of the description of its system around wage computation only, leaving out everything to do with paying the deducted amounts across to the authorities, on the ground that remittance is "a compliance matter, not an accounting one".

items.stem: The team leader is asked why the audit cannot stop where the field team wants to stop. What is the answer?

options.text: It must stop — whether the scheme achieved anything is a question about the policy, and an auditor may not go behind a sanction of the executive
options.misconception: reads the bar on questioning policy as a bar on measuring whether the policy's own stated objective was reached
options.why: An auditor takes the policy as given. Measuring what it delivered is not questioning it: the objective the department set for itself is the yardstick, and the department supplied it. Asking whether that objective was met is the whole of effectiveness, and it is the one question this scheme most needs put to it.

options.text: Because what has been done so far answers only the two questions a compliance audit asks, and this audit has three further ones to put about the scheme itself
options.why: Tracing transactions to the manual and the sanction orders is compliance work. Its two concerns are regularity, meaning that what was done keeps to the formal criteria set by the laws, rules and agreements binding on the entity, and propriety, meaning that it also keeps to the general principles of sound financial management and to the conduct expected of a public official. A performance audit puts three more questions to the same scheme: economy, whether the resources were got in the right quantity and quality at the best price; efficiency, whether the output obtained was the most those inputs could have yielded; and effectiveness, whether the objective was actually met and the intended impact reached. Purifiers bought correctly and never switched on answer the first two questions well and the last three badly.

options.text: It cannot stop, but only because the uncommissioned purifiers are an asset carried at a value it will never earn, which is a matter for the financial audit to pick up
options.misconception: turns a failure of delivery into a valuation question, and loses the finding the legislature can act on
options.why: Whether the asset is carried at the right amount is a real question and it is a different one. A performance audit reports that a third of the purifiers never worked and asks why that happened, which is a finding somebody can do something about. A write-down would tidy the balance sheet and tell nobody anything.

options.text: It may stop — between them, the two concerns of a compliance audit exhaust what a government auditor is entitled to examine
options.misconception: treats compliance auditing's two concerns as the outer edge of government audit, when compliance is one aspect inside a performance audit rather than a substitute for it
options.why: Regularity and propriety are the concerns of compliance auditing, and when compliance work sits inside a performance audit it is one aspect of the examination rather than the end of it. Failing to comply can be the cause of a scheme's collapse, or the explanation for it, or its consequence, which is why the work already done feeds the performance audit instead of closing it.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the two concerns of compliance auditing and the three questions a performance audit puts

items.scenario: A State department installed water purifiers in village schools under a three-year scheme. The field team from the Comptroller and Auditor General's office has traced every purchase to the procurement manual and the sanction orders, found the tendering in order and the rates within the approved schedule, and wants to close the audit there. The school registers show that a third of the purifiers were never commissioned, and that the schools which did get a working one still buy drinking water in cans.

items.stem: What should the team do before it goes anywhere near the districts, and what does the missing target list mean?

options.text: Treat it as a compliance audit instead, because with no targets from the department the three questions of a performance audit cannot be measured at all
options.misconception: treats the entity's silence as making performance unmeasurable, when the yardstick can be derived from the scheme's own sanction and from comparable practice
options.why: A yardstick does not have to come from the audited entity. It can be derived from the sanction that created the scheme, from its guidelines, from comparable schemes elsewhere and from accepted good practice, and it is settled in the planning stage precisely so that a scheme with no stated targets can still be measured.

options.text: Go to the districts first — a performance audit is led by what the evidence shows, and fixing a yardstick in advance would prejudge the findings
options.misconception: confuses having a yardstick with having a conclusion, and leaves the team with no basis on which to call anything a shortfall
options.why: Audit criteria are the standard against which performance is measured, not the answer to the question. Without them there is nothing that makes a shortfall a shortfall, and the field work has no shape. Evidence gathered before anybody has decided what question it answers is the reason a design matrix exists at all.

options.text: Plan the audit first — build a picture of the mission from its own papers and from the legislature's, settle what the audit is for and how far it reaches, fix the yardstick, decide the approach and the questions, and set the whole design out on paper before any field work; and treat the absence of targets as a finding about the department rather than an obstacle
options.why: Planning a performance audit starts with understanding the entity and the programme, drawn from the entity's own files, from legislative material such as the reports of the Public Accounts Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings, from policy papers, from academic work, from earlier audits, from media coverage and from focus groups. Only then are the objectives and the scope defined, the audit criteria determined, the approach settled and the audit questions developed. The design is then written into an audit design matrix, which sets each objective beside its questions, its yardstick, the evidence needed and how that evidence will be gathered and analysed. And the missing targets are themselves reportable: fixing measurable objectives and performance indicators is the department's own responsibility, so the auditors say so rather than quietly inventing a yardstick on the department's behalf.

options.text: Ask the department to fix targets now and audit against those, since a performance audit cannot proceed where the entity set itself no measurable objectives
options.misconception: lets the entity's own failure to set objectives stop the audit, when that failure is one of the things the audit exists to report
options.why: Targets written after the event to satisfy an auditor measure nothing. Where the department fixed no measurable objectives and no performance indicators, that is reported as a finding about the department, and the audit still derives its yardstick from the sanction that created the scheme, from the scheme guidelines, from comparable schemes and from accepted practice.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — planning a performance audit, the sources for understanding the entity, the audit design matrix, and whose responsibility measurable objectives are

items.scenario: A performance audit of a State horticulture mission is about to begin. The team proposes to leave for the districts on Monday, collect subsidy files and vouchers, and work out afterwards what the audit is about. It has no written statement of what good performance by this mission would look like. When it asks the department for the mission's targets, it is told the department never fixed any.

items.stem: The manager reviews the file. What is missing?

options.text: Nearly all of it — being on the premises is where the work happens, not the work itself, and three of the four things the assistant went there to do were never done
options.why: Where inventory is material, attendance at physical counting is required and it means four things done on the spot. The auditor evaluates the instructions and procedures management has laid down for recording and controlling the count. He must observe the count as management's own teams carry it out, including the control over goods moving in and out while it runs. He must inspect the inventory itself, which is the only way ageing, damage and slow movement are seen at all. And he performs test counts of his own in both directions, from the floor to the records and from the records to the floor. Walking the aisles behind the stores manager and agreeing totals afterwards is none of the four; it tests the arithmetic on somebody else's sheets.

options.text: Nothing, because the count sheets were signed by the stores manager, and a signed record from the officer responsible is sufficient appropriate audit evidence about quantities
options.misconception: substitutes a management representation for procedures the auditor could have performed himself over a material balance
options.why: A record management prepared and signed is management's assertion. It does not become audit evidence through the seniority of the person who signed it, and a written representation cannot stand in place of procedures the auditor was able to perform.

options.text: Only the counting — he should have counted a sample himself; evaluating management's instructions belongs in the planning file and looking over the stock is work for whoever does the valuation
options.misconception: scatters the four procedures across other parts of the audit, when all four belong to the attendance itself
options.why: All four sit inside the attendance. Evaluating the instructions is done at the count, because that is where you find out whether they were followed, and looking over the stock while it is being counted is what surfaces the damaged and slow moving items. That feeds the valuation work rather than being replaced by it.

options.text: Nothing of substance — the assistant was there while counting was going on, which is what attendance means, and tying the sheets back to the ledger is the corroboration
options.misconception: reads attendance as physical presence, when it is the name for four particular procedures performed while the count is running
options.why: Presence is where the four procedures happen and it is not a substitute for them. An auditor who was in the building and did nothing has evidence that a count took place and none at all about whether the quantities carried in the financial statements exist.

citation.ref: Attendance at physical inventory counting where inventory is material to the financial statements

items.scenario: Inventory is material to a ceramics maker. The audit assistant is sent to the year end count at the main works. He arrives two hours after counting has begun, walks the aisles with the stores manager, is told which racks have been done, collects the completed count sheets at the end of the day, and back at the office agrees their totals to the stock ledger. His working paper records that attendance at the count was carried out.

items.stem: Which files may the reviewer take, and what is he looking at in them?

options.text: Everything on the list, since quality in a firm is one thing and the reviewer has to see how it works across the whole practice
options.misconception: extends the review from attestation work to every service the unit sells, when the framework is confined to attestation engagements
options.why: Quality across a whole practice is a good thing and it is not what this review is for. The review is confined to attestation services, and a reviewer ranging over tax and consultancy files would be examining work that nobody appointed him to examine.

options.text: Only the statutory audits, and he will form his own view on each opinion and report the ones he considers wrong
options.misconception: turns a review of the unit's systems into a second audit of the auditee, and reads a wrong opinion as the thing a reviewer reports
options.why: A second opinion on the auditee's accounts is not the reviewer's function, because the practice unit is the subject of the review and its clients are not. The reviewer reports on how the unit's systems behaved on the files he sampled, which is why a report can be qualified without anybody saying the accounts were wrong.
keywords: the practice unit is the subject of the review

options.text: Only the audits and the certifications, and he is examining how the firm runs that work rather than re-deciding any opinion it reached
options.why: Peer review is an examination and review of the systems and procedures a practice unit has put in place to secure the quality of its attestation services, judged against the technical, ethical and professional standards and any regulatory requirements that apply. Two things follow from that sentence. The income tax returns and the warehouse consultancy are outside the review, because they are not attestation work. And the review does not sit in judgment on whether an opinion was right; it asks whether the work behind the opinion was planned, performed, documented and reviewed the way the standards require.

options.text: Only the certifications, those being the engagements where the firm reports on somebody else's information; the statutory audits belong to the Quality Review Board instead
options.misconception: splits attestation work between two bodies, when a statutory audit sits squarely inside peer review
options.why: A statutory audit is attestation work and is squarely inside peer review. The Quality Review Board is a separate mechanism set up by the Central Government with its own remit, and the existence of a second body does not carve audits out of the first.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — what peer review examines and what it does not

items.scenario: A practice unit has been selected for peer review. The reviewer asks for a list of its engagements for the review period. The managing partner sends the whole client list — statutory audits, income tax return work, a consultancy assignment on warehouse layout and two certifications — says the reviewer may take any file he likes from it, and adds that he expects the review to end in a verdict on whether the firm's audit opinions were right.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The finance head is right — the line applies to what the auditor holds personally, and a relative's shares sit outside section 141 altogether
options.misconception: confines the securities test to the auditor in person, when the provision names the relative expressly
options.why: The provision reaches the person, that person's relative and that person's partner. A relative's holding is inside it, and the money line the Rules draw was written for exactly this case.

options.text: The partner is right — once a relative's holding crosses the line the disqualification is absolute, and the firm can never audit this company again
options.misconception: reads the corrective provision out of the Rules and turns a curable breach into a permanent bar
options.why: The Rules provide for correction. A holding brought back within the prescribed limit inside the period allowed removes the disqualification, and nothing makes the bar permanent. A lifetime bar over shares a sister inherited would be out of all proportion to what the provision is protecting, which is the auditor's independence in fact and in appearance.

options.text: The holding does not matter because the shares were inherited rather than bought, the disqualification being aimed at an auditor's family deliberately taking an interest
options.misconception: reads intention into a test that turns only on what is held and what it is worth
options.why: How the securities came to be held does not enter the test. What is asked is whether a relative holds securities in the company and whether their face value is over the line, and an inheritance answers both questions the same way a purchase would.

options.text: Neither of them is right — the holding does bar the appointment as things stand, but the Rules allow a period in which it can be brought back inside the line, and the bringing back has to actually happen
options.why: A person may not be appointed auditor where a relative holds securities of, or an interest in, the company whose face value exceeds the prescribed limit, which the Rules set at one lakh rupees. Two things follow. The test is face value and not market value, so a rise in the price of the shares does not by itself create a disqualification. And the Rules do not treat the breach as incurable: where a holding goes over the line, corrective action to bring it back within the limit may be taken inside the corrective window the Rules allow. What the finance head cannot do is leave it there, because the window is a period in which to act and not a period in which the breach does not count.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d)(i) read with Rule 10 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 — a relative's holding and the corrective action the Rules allow

items.scenario: CA Meera is proposed for reappointment as auditor of an unlisted public company. Her sister, who is a relative for the purposes of the Companies Act, has just inherited shares in that company whose face value is above the line the Rules draw. Meera's partner says the firm must decline at once and that the office is gone for good. The company's finance head says the shares can simply be sold and that nobody need mention any of it.

items.stem: What goes into the report under the lending clause?

options.text: All four — the clause reaches a guarantee given and security put up as well as money lent, and a payment that no bill will ever absorb and that has to come back in cash is a loan wearing a trade name
options.why: Clause 3(iii) is not confined to lending. It asks whether the company, during the year, granted a loan, made a payment that is an advance in the nature of a loan, stood as guarantor for anyone, or put up security for anyone; and where it did, the report gives the aggregate amount during the year together with the balance still outstanding at the year end, split between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and every other party on the other. So the corporate guarantee and the pledged deposits belong here as guarantees or security given for somebody else. The mobilisation sum belongs here too, because the Order's own heading covers loans and advances in the nature of loans, and an interest free payment that nothing will be set off against and that has to be returned as money is not a trade advance whatever the voucher calls it. Section 186 is the subject of a different clause, and answering that one does not answer this one.
keywords: advances in the nature of loans

options.text: The subsidiary loans only — the finance head is right that the clause is about loans, and money paid to a contractor under a contract is a trade advance whatever its terms
options.misconception: lets the label on a payment decide the clause, when the clause looks at what the payment actually is
options.why: A trade advance is one that a bill will absorb. Where nothing will ever be set off against it and the money has to come back as money, the label on the voucher has stopped describing the transaction, and the report says what the transaction is.

options.text: Nothing at all, because the company's principal business is not to give loans and the clause is lifted for such a company
options.misconception: reverses the Order's own carve-out, which lifts parts of the clause from a company whose principal business IS lending
options.why: The carve-out runs the other way. Parts of the clause are lifted from a company whose principal business is to give loans, because for such a company the answers would amount to its whole trading activity. A manufacturer sits squarely inside the clause.
keywords: principal business is to give loans

options.text: The subsidiary loans and the mobilisation sum only — a guarantee and a pledge are reported under the clause on section 186, and the same fact is not reported twice
options.misconception: treats the two clauses as alternatives, when one asks what the company put out and the other asks whether a section was complied with
options.why: The two clauses ask different questions and both of them are answered. One asks what the company gave out during the year and on what terms; the other asks whether the statutory limits and procedures governing loans, investments, guarantees and security were kept. A guarantee that complies with the section is still a guarantee that has to be reported.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)(a) — loans, advances in the nature of loans, guarantees and security, and the amounts to be stated

items.scenario: A company reportable under CARO 2020, whose principal business is not lending, did four things during the year. It gave a corporate guarantee for a bank facility taken by an associate. It pledged its own fixed deposits as security for a supplier's working capital line. It paid a large interest free mobilisation sum to a civil contractor which the contract does not set off against any bill and which the contractor has been asked to return in money. And it lent to two subsidiaries. The finance head's note to the auditor says the lending clause is about loans, so only the last of the four is reportable, and that the guarantee and the pledge belong to the clause on section 186 instead.

items.stem: For which of the three does each firm answer, and for which does only one?

options.text: Both firms answer for the first two; only D answers for the third
options.why: Joint and several responsibility attaches to audit work that was not divided at all and that every one of the firms carried out together; to decisions taken jointly at planning about the nature, timing and extent of procedures in areas held in common; and to a matter one of them puts in front of the others where they all agree what to do about it. The related party area was kept in common and its tests were agreed together, so it falls under the first two heads. The odd account was brought to everybody's notice and settled by agreement, so it falls under the third. Work validly allotted to one firm remains that firm's own, whether or not it also issues a separate report, so the careless receivable testing is D's alone.

options.text: Both firms answer for all three, because they put their names to one report on the whole of the financial statements
options.misconception: reads a common report as abolishing the division of work, when the division is exactly what the Standard preserves
options.why: A common report does not merge the work behind it. In respect of the work divided among them, each joint auditor is responsible only for what was allotted to him, and the heads of joint and several responsibility are the named exceptions to that rule rather than a rule that swallows it.
keywords: each joint auditor is responsible only for what was allotted

options.text: Only D answers, for all three, since the related party area and the odd account both sat in D's half of the ledger
options.misconception: allocates responsibility by where the balance sits rather than by how the work was divided and how the decisions were taken
options.why: Responsibility follows the allocation of work and the decisions taken, not the ledger. An area the firms agreed to keep in common is undivided work however the balances fall, and a decision the two firms reached together is a decision of both of them.

options.text: Both answer for the first only; the second is C's alone for having raised it, and the third is D's alone
options.misconception: penalises the joint auditor who spoke up, when raising a matter is precisely what brings it inside the joint head
options.why: Raising a matter is the act that puts it in front of all of them. Where one joint auditor brings something to the others' notice and they agree what to do, the agreement belongs to everybody. Penalising the one who spoke would make silence the safe course, which is the opposite of what the Standard is built to produce.

citation.ref: The matters for which all the joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible

items.scenario: Two firms, C and D, are joint auditors. The signed allocation gives purchases and payables to C and revenue and receivables to D. Three things then go wrong. At planning both firms sat together and settled how related party transactions, an area they agreed to keep in common, would be tested; the tests they agreed on were too narrow to catch a large sale routed through a director's firm. Separately, C noticed something odd in an account inside D's area, raised it at a joint meeting, both firms agreed no further work was needed, and it turned out to matter. Third, D's own testing of a receivable was plainly careless.

items.stem: Are the first two firms right?

options.text: No — presentation and disclosure of the financial statements, whether they meet the requirements of the relevant statutes, and whether the report itself complies, are matters every joint auditor answers for however the underlying work was split
options.why: Joint and several responsibility is not confined to work held in common. Alongside the audit work that is not divided and the decisions taken jointly, the Standard puts three matters that bind all the joint auditors whatever the allocation says: examining that the financial statements meet the requirements of the relevant statutes, the presentation and disclosure of those statements under the applicable framework, and ensuring that the audit report itself complies with the statutes, the Standards on Auditing and the other pronouncements of the Institute. A missing disclosure is squarely inside the second of those, so all three firms answer for it even though only one audited the division behind it.

options.text: No, but only the firm that signed the report first answers, that firm taking the lead responsibility for the document as a whole
options.misconception: invents a lead joint auditor, a rank the Standard does not create
options.why: There is no principal or lead joint auditor. The joint auditors are equal, the order of signature carries no meaning, and the matters that bind all of them bind each of them alike.
keywords: no principal or lead joint auditor

options.text: Yes — responsibility follows the allocation, and the division the note describes was allotted to the third firm alone
options.misconception: applies the rule for divided audit work to a matter the Standard lists as belonging to all the joint auditors regardless of the division
options.why: Responsibility follows the allocation for the audit work that was divided. Presentation and disclosure of the financial statements is not in that category: it is one of the matters listed as binding all the joint auditors, because the statements are one document and the members receive one set of them.
keywords: Presentation and disclosure of the financial statements

options.text: Yes, unless the first two firms actually read the note, in which case having seen it makes it a matter brought to their notice
options.misconception: makes a shared responsibility depend on whether the other firms happened to look, which would reward not looking
options.why: A matter brought to the notice of the joint auditors is a separate head and it is not the one in play here. Presentation and disclosure binds everybody whether or not anyone happened to read a particular note, and a rule that turned on who looked would reward looking away.
keywords: brought to the notice of the joint auditors

citation.ref: Joint and several responsibility for compliance with statutes, for presentation and disclosure, and for the audit report

items.scenario: Three firms audit a company jointly and have divided the work by division. After the report is signed it emerges that a disclosure the applicable framework requires was left out of a note, and that the note relates entirely to the division allotted to the third firm. The first two firms say the omission is the third firm's, since the underlying work was allotted to it and neither of them touched that division.

items.stem: Is that enough?

options.text: No — the board was right to appoint, but what the members must pass is a special resolution, since replacing an auditor before his term ends always needs one
options.misconception: imports the special resolution required to remove an auditor into a vacancy the auditor created by leaving of his own accord
options.why: A special resolution, with the Central Government's prior approval, is what removing an auditor before the expiry of his term requires. Nobody removed this auditor; he resigned. What the Act asks of the members afterwards is approval of the Board's appointment.

options.text: No — where the vacancy was caused by a resignation the board's appointment stands only if the members approve it at a meeting called within a fixed period, so a general meeting has to be convened now
options.why: A resignation leaves a casual vacancy in the office of auditor. In a company whose accounts are not audited by an auditor appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General, that vacancy is filled by the Board of Directors within thirty days. But where it was caused by a resignation the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting, convened within three months of the Board's recommendation. Waiting ten months for the annual general meeting misses that, and the point of the rule is that the members get to pass on an auditor who has come in because the last one walked out.
keywords: Board of Directors within thirty days
approved by the company at a general meeting

options.text: Yes — the board fills a casual vacancy, and the appointment runs to the next annual general meeting where the members deal with it in the ordinary way
options.misconception: applies the general rule for a casual vacancy to one caused by resignation, which the Act singles out for the members' approval
options.why: That is the position where the vacancy arose some other way. A vacancy caused by a resignation is singled out, and the members' approval has to be obtained at a general meeting inside a fixed period rather than whenever the next annual meeting happens to fall.

options.text: No — a vacancy caused by resignation can only be filled by the members, so the board's appointment is a nullity and the company has no auditor
options.misconception: reads the requirement of members' approval as meaning the Board has no power to appoint at all, which would leave the company unaudited for months
options.why: The Board does appoint, and it appoints quickly, so that the company is not left without an auditor while a general meeting is arranged. The members' approval sits on top of that appointment; it does not take the place of it.

citation.ref: Section 139(8) — a casual vacancy caused by the resignation of an auditor

items.scenario: The statutory auditor of an unlisted public company with no government shareholding resigns in the middle of the year. The board meets, appoints a replacement, and proposes to leave the matter there until the next annual general meeting, which is ten months away, saying the members can confirm the appointment then along with the ordinary reappointment business.

items.stem: Which of the three may go ahead?

options.text: All three, provided the audit committee approves each of them, since approval is what the section requires before any other service is rendered
options.misconception: reads audit committee approval as a gateway through the prohibited list, when it is the gate for the services that are not prohibited
options.why: Approval is the condition for the other services an auditor may render. It cannot let through the ones the section names, and a committee that purported to approve a financial system implementation would be approving something the Act has already refused.
keywords: the other services an auditor may render

options.text: Only the tax appeal — the bar reaches a service rendered through a partner acting on his own account and through an entity standing in that relationship to the firm, and neither control nor a shared name is needed to bring them in
options.why: Section 144 bars the listed services whether they are rendered directly or indirectly, and the Act says what that phrase means for a firm: the service is caught if it comes from the firm itself, from any partner of the firm, from the firm's parent, subsidiary or associate entity, from an entity in which the firm or a partner has significant influence or control, or from an entity trading on a name or brand the firm or a partner uses. So designing and installing a financial reporting system is caught through the associate entity limb on its own, without any question of control or of a shared name arising. Investment advice from a partner is caught through the partner limb, and taking the work in a personal capacity does not step outside it. Appearing in a tax appeal is not one of the listed services and may be taken with the approval the section requires.

options.text: The system work and the tax appeal — a partner acting on his own account is not the appointed auditor, and the section binds the appointed auditor
options.misconception: reads the bar as binding only the appointed firm, when the Act's definition of indirect rendering names the firm's partners expressly
options.why: The definition of rendering a service indirectly names any partner of the firm. A partner who takes the work on his own account is exactly the arrangement that wording exists to catch, and the audited company gets the same advice from the same person either way.

options.text: The partner's advice and the tax appeal — the associate is a separate legal person that the firm neither controls nor shares a name with, so it falls outside the section
options.misconception: treats control and a shared brand as the only routes into the bar, when a parent, subsidiary or associate entity is a route of its own
options.why: Control and a shared brand are two routes and they are not the only ones. A parent, subsidiary or associate entity stands as its own limb of the definition, so an entity in that relationship with the firm is inside the bar without any question of control arising at all.

citation.ref: Section 144 with its Explanation — what it means for a firm to render a service directly or indirectly

items.scenario: A firm is the statutory auditor of a listed company, and three arrangements are put to its audit committee for the year. An entity that is an associate of the audit firm, in which the firm holds a minority stake it does not control and which trades under a completely different name, is to build and install the company's new consolidation and financial reporting system. A partner of the audit firm, acting in his personal capacity and not through the firm, is to advise the company on where to park its surplus funds. And the firm itself is to appear for the company in a tax appeal.

items.stem: What does the service auditor tell him?

options.text: He can agree, because the description of the tests performed is what makes a report a type 2 report, and that description can be attached to work done at any level of assurance
options.misconception: treats the description of tests of controls as the thing that makes a report a type 2 report, when what makes it one is a reasonable assurance opinion on operating effectiveness across the period
options.why: The account of the tests and their results is part of a type 2 report and it is not what constitutes one. What constitutes one is an opinion, held to reasonable assurance, that controls tied to the stated control objectives ran effectively over the period the report names, supported by the service organisation's assertion in the same period form. Bolting a list of tests onto a lesser engagement produces a document that looks like the report and does not carry it.

options.text: He can agree and issue the result as a type 1 report instead, since a type 1 report is the lighter of the two and asks less of the service auditor
options.misconception: reads type 1 as a lower grade of assurance rather than as a report on a different subject matter fixed at a single date
options.why: The two reports are not a heavy version and a light version of one thing. Both are reasonable assurance reports, and what separates them is what is reported on and over what span — a type 1 report speaks about the description and the design of controls as at a stated date and says nothing about how they ran, while a type 2 report reaches operating effectiveness across a period. Choosing type 1 would give the eleven intermediaries' auditors nothing about the year at all.

options.text: He can agree, provided the report says on its face that only limited assurance was obtained, so that each of the eleven sets of auditors can decide for itself what to make of it
options.misconception: treats disclosing a lower grade of assurance as curing an engagement the standard does not offer at that grade
options.why: Telling a reader how little was done is honest and it does not create a form of engagement the standard has not provided. The service auditor's objectives are fixed at reasonable assurance, and a report reaching the eleven user auditors under this standard's name is understood by them to carry that. Labelling the shortfall shifts the problem to the reader instead of answering it.

options.text: There is no cheaper grade of assurance available here — the report he is asking for either carries the assurance the standard fixes for it or it is not that report at all
options.why: Under SAE 3402 the service auditor sets out to obtain reasonable assurance on three matters based on suitable criteria — that the service organisation's account of its system fairly presents that system as it was designed and put in place, that the controls attached to the stated control objectives were suitably designed, and, where the engagement reaches it, that those controls operated effectively so that the stated control objectives were met throughout the specified period. A type 2 report is the vehicle that carries the third of those. It comprises the description of the system, the service organisation's own written assertion, and an assurance report which conveys that reasonable assurance and sets out a description of the tests of controls performed and what they showed. A limited assurance engagement produces a negatively worded conclusion off far less work, and nothing in the standard offers it as a cheaper route to the same document.

citation.ref: Objectives of the service auditor and the contents of a type 1 and a type 2 report

items.scenario: Vaidehi Datacentres runs the billing and revenue-recording application for eleven insurance intermediaries. Their auditors have asked for a report covering the whole financial year, and for comfort that the controls actually worked across it rather than merely being well designed. Vaidehi's chief executive tells the service auditor he wants the work done "as a review rather than an audit" — less testing, a conclusion worded in the negative form, a smaller fee — and says the result can still be handed over as a type 2 report, because it will cover the year and some controls will have been tested.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way those three have been placed?

options.text: Nothing is wrong. Each item has been placed where the money for it sits, and an integrated report exists to show where the money went
options.misconception: reads the six capitals as headings for expenditure rather than as the stores of value a business draws on and changes
options.why: Following the money puts every capital under the financial one, which empties the framework of its point. The six are stores of value the organisation uses and affects over the short, medium and long term, and a training programme paid for in cash is an addition to human capital in the same way that a plant paid for in cash is an addition to manufactured capital.

options.text: The training and the workforce both belong under the capital the framework keeps for the organisation's own people, and the natural capital section reports only one of the two directions that capital runs in
options.why: Human capital is the people themselves — their skills and experience, what they are capable of, their motivation to improve things, and whether they can grasp the organisation's strategy and carry it out. Money laid out on training is counted in rupees, and what it builds is human capital rather than financial capital, which is the pool of funds the organisation has to work with, whether that pool came from borrowing, from shareholders, from grants or from its own operations. Staff are not equipment either, so they cannot sit under manufactured capital, which holds the production-oriented plant, buildings and infrastructure that people have built for the business to use. And natural capital runs both ways: it is an input the company draws on and it is also something the company's activities affect for better or for worse, so a section reporting water drawn and nothing about the quarry left behind reports half of it.

options.text: The training belongs under intellectual capital, since training is knowledge, and the workforce under social capital, since a workforce is a community
options.misconception: swaps human capital for the two capitals nearest to it, the organisation's own knowledge and its outside relationships, when the subject is the organisation's own people
options.why: Intellectual capital is what sits behind future earning power — research and development, innovation and the outside relationships that give a competitive edge. Social capital is the relationships and the trust an organisation builds with its community, its customers and its suppliers, and the social licence to operate that comes with them. Neither is the organisation's own staff, and human capital is the one that holds their skills, their capacity and their motivation.

options.text: Only the natural capital section is at fault — training spend is financial capital because it is spent from funds, and the workforce is manufactured capital because the plant cannot run without it
options.misconception: keeps people under two headings that describe money and machinery, leaving the framework with nowhere to report skills and motivation
options.why: That reading leaves the framework with no home for skills, capacity and motivation, which is exactly what human capital was put there to hold. Financial capital is the pool of funds available for use, not everything bought with it; manufactured capital is equipment, buildings and infrastructure, not the people who operate them.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Integrated Reporting and the six capitals, and what each of human, financial, manufactured and natural capital covers

items.scenario: A cement company publishes an integrated report on a voluntary basis. Under financial capital it shows the amount spent on its operator training academy, on the reasoning that the spend came out of the same pool of money as everything else. Under manufactured capital it shows the number of people on the payroll, on the reasoning that they are what makes the plant run. Its natural capital section reports the volume of water drawn from the borewells and nothing else. An assurance practitioner reads the draft before the board approves it.

items.stem: What does the partner do now?

options.text: Describe it. The test is significance in the audit, this matter was the most significant thing in it, and what is said to the audit committee is a separate obligation under a different standard
options.misconception: treats the population the auditor chooses from as incidental, when the selection begins inside what was communicated with those charged with governance
options.why: Significance is the second step and not the first.
