The standard has the auditor start inside a defined population and then rank within it, so a matter that never entered the population cannot be ranked out of it. The two obligations are also not independent of each other here — this is precisely the sort of finding the audit committee should have heard about while the audit was running.

options.text: Describe it, and add a sentence in the section recording that the matter was not discussed with the audit committee, so that the reader can weigh it for himself
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to disclose a gap in communication rather than closing it, which is not what the Key Audit Matters section is for
options.why: The section exists to tell a reader which matters were of most significance in the audit and how they were addressed, not to record what the auditor did or did not tell the committee. Disclosure is not a substitute for communication where communication is what was required, and a note of that kind would raise a question in the reader's mind that the report cannot then answer.

options.text: Leave it out and take the matter no further, because a matter outside what was communicated to the committee can never be a key audit matter
options.misconception: turns a rule about where the selection starts into a permanent bar, and leaves the auditor silent about a significant finding he owed those charged with governance
options.why: The rule fixes where the choosing begins; it does not put a matter beyond reach for ever. The answer to a significant finding that never reached the committee is to raise it with the committee, after which it stands in the population like everything else. Reading the rule as a bar rewards the failure to communicate by making it permanent.

options.text: He cannot lift it straight into the section. It goes to the audit committee first — which it should have done anyway — and only then can he weigh it against the rest of what was reported to them
options.why: SA 701 has the auditor begin from the matters communicated with those charged with governance and decide, out of that population, which ones called for significant auditor attention. From what survives, his own professional judgement picks the small number that were of most significance in the audit of the current period, and those are the ones the section describes. A matter that never reached the committee has not entered the population, and the cure is not silence but communication: a judgement that ran three weeks and settled the carrying amount of a large balance is the kind of significant finding those charged with governance are owed while there is still time to do something about it. Printing it in the report first would also have the committee reading about the audit's hardest question in a published document.
keywords: communicated with those charged with governance

citation.ref: Determining key audit matters — the population selected from and the auditor's judgement within it

items.scenario: Kanchan Alloys Limited is listed. During the audit the team spent three weeks on the carrying amount of a large slow-moving spares holding, which was the hardest single judgement of the year; it was settled between the manager and the finance head and never went to the audit committee, and the committee's minutes carry nothing about it. A revenue recognition question and a disputed tax demand were both taken to the committee in the normal course. At the drafting stage the engagement partner proposes to describe the spares holding in the Key Audit Matters section, on the ground that it was plainly the matter of most significance in the audit.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way the testing has been set up?

options.text: The wrong figure is driving the work. The lower working figure is what the risk assessment and the extent of testing are set against, and testing to the headline figure leaves the small misstatements free to add up behind it
options.why: Performance materiality is the amount the auditor fixes below materiality for the financial statements as a whole so as to bring down to an appropriately low level the chance that the uncorrected and undetected misstatements, taken together, end up over that headline figure. It is determined for a stated purpose — assessing where the risks of material misstatement lie, and settling the nature, timing and extent of the further audit procedures — so procedures designed against the headline number are designed against a figure that was never meant to size them. The senior's rule also mistakes what materiality says. An item below the headline figure is not harmless by that fact; it is the aggregate the auditor has to answer for at the end, and the whole reason for a lower working figure is that individually small errors can carry the accounts over the line between them.

options.text: Nothing is wrong. Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is the standard the accounts are judged against, so it is the right standard to design the testing against
options.misconception: uses the reporting threshold as the working threshold, which leaves no allowance for the misstatements the audit does not find
options.why: The reporting threshold and the working threshold do different jobs. If the work is sized at the reporting threshold there is no room left for what the procedures miss, and the auditor arrives at the end with a set of small uncorrected items and no basis for saying they do not add up to something that matters.

options.text: The senior should test to a figure lower than performance materiality on every balance, since performance materiality is itself only a planning estimate
options.misconception: replaces a determined figure with a vaguer instruction to be careful, when performance materiality is the determined figure the work is designed against
options.why: Performance materiality is not an estimate waiting to be improved on by caution. It is a figure the auditor determines and records, and the point of determining it is that the extent of testing then follows from it. An instruction to go lower still without saying how far replaces a decision with a mood.

options.text: The senior should have had the threshold approved by the audit committee before setting the samples
options.misconception: hands to the entity a judgement the standard leaves with the auditor
options.why: Materiality in both its forms is the auditor's own judgement, exercised on the users of the financial statements and on the risk of aggregation, and it is not for the entity to set or approve. Those charged with governance are told about significant findings; they do not fix the figure the audit is designed against.

citation.ref: para 9 and 11 — the definition of performance materiality and the purposes it is determined for

items.scenario: On the audit of a distribution company, the senior fixes the sample sizes for purchases testing and instructs the team to follow up any individual item above materiality for the financial statements as a whole and to let anything below it pass, "because by definition nothing under that figure can matter". Performance materiality was determined at the planning meeting and written on the front sheet of the file, and nothing done since has referred to it.

items.stem: What does the reviewer require to be put right?

options.text: Nothing. The file records materiality for the financial statements as a whole, which is the figure the opinion is given against; the rest are working numbers the team uses along the way
options.misconception: treats the working figures as scratch when the standard names each of them as part of the audit documentation
options.why: The standard names four things the documentation carries, and the headline figure is only the first of them. The others are not scratch: they are what the extent of every test was chosen against, so a file without them cannot show why the work was the size it was.

options.text: Only the February revision, since the figures it replaced no longer describe the audit that was performed
options.misconception: reads a later figure as replacing the record of the earlier one, when what has to be recorded is the revision itself
options.why: A revision is recorded as a revision, which means the file shows what the figure was, what it became and why it moved. Work done before the change was sized on the earlier figure, and a file showing only the final number cannot explain the sample sizes that sit in the first half of it.

options.text: Only performance materiality, the separate level for the remuneration disclosures being a matter of judgement rather than a determined figure
options.misconception: treats a level set for a particular class of disclosures as informal, when it is determined under the same requirement and recorded under the same one
options.why: A lower level set for particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures is determined in the same way as any other materiality figure and is recorded in the same place. Calling it a judgement rather than a figure does not take it out of the documentation requirement, and the remuneration disclosures were tested against it.

options.text: Three things are missing — the lower level set for the remuneration disclosures, the performance materiality figure itself, and the February revision with the amounts on either side of it
options.why: The audit documentation carries materiality for the financial statements as a whole; the level or levels fixed for particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures where any were fixed; performance materiality; and any revision of those amounts as the audit went on. Only the first of the four is in this file. A number kept on somebody's own machine has not been put into the audit documentation at all, and a decision taken in a meeting and never written down cannot be read afterwards by anyone who was not in the room — which is the point of the requirement, since these are the amounts the extent of every procedure was chosen against.

citation.ref: Documentation of materiality, performance materiality and any revision of them

items.scenario: A reviewer opens the completed file of a manufacturing audit. The materiality memorandum records one number, materiality for the financial statements as a whole, with the benchmark chosen and the percentage applied to it. A separate lower level had been set for the directors' remuneration disclosures, and materiality was raised in February when the draft results came in ahead of expectation; both were decided in team meetings and neither is written anywhere in the file. The performance materiality figure lives on a spreadsheet the senior keeps on his own laptop.

items.stem: Which of the two areas may be given to the internal auditors?

options.text: The cut-off matching only — a higher assessed risk does not by itself shut an area off, and what shuts this one off is the kind of judgement settling the allowance calls for
options.why: The revised standard keeps internal auditors providing direct assistance out of work that involves making significant judgements in the audit; out of areas of higher assessed risk of material misstatement where the judgement required is more than limited; and out of work the internal auditors themselves did and have already reported on internally. The qualifier in the middle of that list decides this case. Both areas are higher risk, so a manager who reads the rule as "higher risk means hands off" loses staff he could properly have used on the cut-off, where the work is matching three documents against each other. A manager who reads it as "testing is testing" makes the more dangerous mistake, because an expected credit loss allowance built on staging rules and forward-looking overlays is a judgement the auditor has to reach for himself and cannot supervise his way out of.
keywords: higher assessed risk of material misstatement

options.text: The expected credit loss work only, since a judgemental area is where a second pair of eyes helps most, while cut-off testing is the auditor's own responsibility
options.misconception: inverts the rule, handing across exactly the work the standard reserves to the external auditor
options.why: It is the other way round. A second opinion on a judgement is not what direct assistance is for; the internal auditors work under the external auditor's direction and are not independent of the entity whose estimate is in question. Cut-off testing is ordinary evidence gathering and is the part of this plan that could properly have been handed over.

options.text: Both, since objectivity and competence have been evaluated and the written agreements are in place, and those are the conditions the standard sets for direct assistance
options.misconception: reads the entry conditions as the whole of the rule and misses the work that stays closed however well those conditions are met
options.why: Evaluating objectivity and competence and taking the two written agreements are what open the door; they say nothing about which work may go through it. The revised standard closes certain work off entirely, and an estimate that turns on management's own staging choices is inside what it closes.

options.text: Neither, because both areas carry a higher assessed risk of material misstatement, and higher risk areas are closed to direct assistance
options.misconception: drops the qualifier about how much judgement the work calls for and treats every higher-risk area as barred
options.why: The standard does not close higher-risk areas outright. It closes those of them where the judgement required is more than limited, and matching a disbursement advice to a bank entry and an acknowledgement for a few days either side of the year end is not judgement of that order. Reading the bar too widely costs the audit staff it was entitled to use.

citation.ref: para 30 — work that may not be assigned to internal auditors providing direct assistance

items.scenario: On the audit of a listed non-banking finance company, the external auditor has assessed two areas as carrying a higher risk of material misstatement. The first is the allowance for expected credit losses on the loan book, where management picks the staging rules and adds forward-looking overlays of its own. The second is the cut-off of loan disbursements at the year end, where the work is to match the disbursement advice, the bank statement entry and the borrower's acknowledgement for the days either side of the balance sheet date. Objectivity and competence have been evaluated for two internal auditors and both written agreements are in place. The manager proposes to give them both areas as direct assistance, on the ground that each is testing and nothing more.

items.stem: Is that plan acceptable?

options.text: Yes, provided the firm reviews every working paper the internal auditors produce and re-performs a sample of each area
options.misconception: offers more review as a cure for the external auditor having performed too little of the audit himself
options.why: Review is already required and going behind a portion of the work to the underlying evidence is already required. Neither answers the question of how much of the audit the external auditor performed, and stacking review on top of an arrangement of this size is checking somebody else's audit rather than conducting one.

options.text: No, because internal auditors may not be used on more than one area of an audit at a time
options.misconception: invents a numerical limit the standard does not set, in place of the judgement it does require
options.why: There is no such count anywhere in the standard. What it asks for is a judgement about how much of the audit is left in the external auditor's own hands, and a rule of thumb about the number of areas would pass plans that fail that question and block plans that pass it.

options.text: Yes. No task on the plan is on the prohibited list, the evaluations are done and both written agreements are in place, so every condition the standard sets has been met
options.misconception: treats the task-by-task tests as the whole of the standard and never asks what the plan adds up to
options.why: Each condition is asked of a task, and there is a further question asked of the plan. Adding up permitted tasks can still produce an audit the external auditor has barely performed, and that is the outcome the aggregate evaluation exists to catch.

options.text: Not as it stands. Every task passes on its own, and the plan still has to be looked at as a whole, which is where it fails
options.why: The prohibitions are one control and they are not the only one. The external auditor also has to weigh the plan as a whole — how far he means to lean on the function's own work, set beside how many internal auditors he means to take as direct assistance and on what — and ask whether the two together still leave him sufficiently involved in the audit, since sole responsibility for the audit opinion stays his and is not shared out with the work. This plan clears every task-by-task test and fails that one. A firm whose own people touch nothing but the estimates and the report has put its name to an audit performed mostly by the entity's employees, and no amount of direction, supervision and review converts that back into its own work. The remedy is to do more of the audit directly, not to add another layer of review on top of it.
keywords: sole responsibility for the audit opinion

citation.ref: Evaluating in aggregate whether the external auditor remains sufficiently involved in the audit

items.scenario: A firm is short of qualified staff on a large manufacturing audit. It plans to use the internal audit function's own work on the inventory counts, the fixed asset verification and the compliance testing, and in addition to take six internal auditors as direct assistance for vouching, payables testing and the bank reconciliations. None of those tasks is on the prohibited list, objectivity and competence have been evaluated, and the written agreements have been obtained. Set out on paper, the plan leaves the firm's own people doing little beyond the significant estimates and the report itself.

items.stem: Is the file adequate under SA 230?

options.text: Yes, provided the engagement partner can explain the reasoning if he is asked about it afterwards
options.misconception: rests the adequacy of a file on somebody being available to speak for it
options.why: The requirement is written about a reader who was not there and who has nobody to ask. An explanation given later is not in the file, may not be available when it is wanted, and cannot be tested against what the file actually shows.

options.text: Yes. The study and the adjusted figure are the evidence the conclusion rests on, and gathering evidence is what a file is for
options.misconception: treats the documents collected as the whole of the documentation and leaves out the record of what the auditor made of them
options.why: Documents collected are one part of a file and the auditor's own reasoning is another. A study prepared by management is management's view; nothing in the file says what the auditor thought of it, why one adjustment answered the point, or how a fortnight of work reached that answer.

options.text: No, but only the consultation needs recording. The disagreement inside the team is an internal matter and does not belong on a client file
options.misconception: separates the consultation from the disagreement that prompted it, when both belong to the significant judgement the file has to show
options.why: The three views and the consultation are one episode, and the file has to show how the conclusion was reached rather than only that advice was taken. A record naming the consultation while hiding the difference of opinion that caused it leaves the reader with the smaller half of the story.

options.text: No. It shows the answer and not the question — what is missing is the record of the matter itself, of the conclusion reached on it, and of the judgements that produced that conclusion
options.why: Documentation has to be full enough for an experienced auditor with no previous connection with the audit to follow the nature, timing and extent of what was done, what came out of it and what evidence was obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions arrived at, together with the significant professional judgements made in arriving at them. One line saying the matter was concluded satisfactory tells such a reader nothing about why the arm's length question was hard, which views were held, what the technical partner was asked and what he answered, or why one adjustment settled the point and a larger one was not needed. The study and the figure are evidence; the reasoning is what the file is short of, and it is the third head of the requirement.
keywords: no previous connection with the audit

citation.ref: para 8 — form, content and extent of audit documentation

items.scenario: On the audit of a listed company, the team spent a fortnight on whether a large sale to a company owned by the managing director's brother was on arm's length terms. Three views were held inside the team, the engagement partner consulted the firm's technical partner, and the matter was closed by accepting management's transfer pricing study subject to one adjustment. The file carries the study, the adjusted figure, and a working paper headed "Related party sale — concluded satisfactory".

items.stem: Which of the three descriptions fits the reader SA 230 is written about?

options.text: None of the three. He is somebody with real audit experience who had nothing to do with this engagement, and he may come from inside the firm or from outside it
options.why: The standard describes an experienced auditor, whether internal or external to the firm, who has practical audit experience together with a reasonable understanding of how audits are conducted, of the Standards and of the legal and regulatory requirements that bind them, of the business environment the entity trades in, and of the auditing and financial reporting questions that belong to its industry. He must also have no previous connection with the audit, and that is what makes him a fair test of the file: he cannot supply from memory what the papers have failed to say. Rank inside the firm is not part of it, prior knowledge of the client is the opposite of it, and the qualification on its own does not reach it.
keywords: no previous connection with the audit

options.text: The third — any chartered accountant, since the qualification is the standard of competence the profession itself sets
options.misconception: substitutes a qualification for the description the standard actually gives, which is about audit experience and specific understandings
options.why: The qualification is not the description. What is asked for is practical audit experience together with a working understanding of how an audit is run, of the Standards and of the legal and regulatory requirements that apply, of the environment the entity trades in, and of the auditing and financial reporting questions that arise in its industry. A member with none of that experience does not answer the description.

options.text: The first — a partner of the same firm, since the standard is about whether the firm can stand behind the file
options.misconception: reads the notional reader as a rank inside the firm rather than as somebody who did not work on this audit
options.why: Seniority is not what the description turns on. What it turns on is that the person had nothing to do with this engagement, so that the file has to speak for itself, and a partner of the same firm may be as close to the audit as anybody on it.

options.text: The second — somebody who has audited this client before, since knowledge of the client is what makes a judgement about sufficiency possible
options.misconception: gives the notional reader prior knowledge of the very audit the file is supposed to convey to him
options.why: This turns the test inside out. The reader is defined by having no previous connection with the audit, precisely so that anything he needs has to be in the file rather than in his memory. A reader who already knows the client will fill gaps the file has left.
keywords: no previous connection with the audit

citation.ref: Definition of an experienced auditor

items.scenario: A firm's methodology says a file passes SA 230 if "a chartered accountant could follow it". The quality reviewer says the standard describes a particular kind of reader and the methodology has flattened him into anybody with the qualification. Three assistants offer descriptions. The first says the reader must be a partner of the same firm, because only a partner carries the responsibility the test is about. The second says he must be somebody who has audited this client before, because otherwise he cannot tell whether the work done was enough. The third says any chartered accountant will do, since they are all trained the same way.

items.stem: May the negative requests stand as the only substantive procedure on subscriber receivables?

options.text: Yes, provided the senior follows up every request that comes back unanswered with alternative procedures such as tracing subsequent receipts
options.misconception: borrows the treatment of non-responses to positive requests and offers it as a substitute for the conditions that let a negative request stand alone
options.why: Chasing non-responses belongs to positive confirmations, where a reply was expected and did not arrive. With a negative request no reply is expected at all, so there is no silence to follow up and no list of parties to chase. The plan would not be improved by that step, and the missing condition about the controls would still be missing.

options.text: No, and the population is not the reason. Three of the four conditions hold; what is missing is evidence about the controls, and a strategy that never tested them cannot produce it
options.why: A negative confirmation request may stand as the sole substantive procedure against an assessed risk at the assertion level only where four things hold at once — the assessed risk of material misstatement is low; the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence that the controls relevant to that assertion are operating effectively; the population is a large number of small, homogeneous balances; and a very low exception rate is expected, with nothing known to the auditor that would make recipients throw the request away. Nine thousand identical small subscriptions answer the third and fourth handsomely and the senior's own assessment answers the first. The second is missing, and the low assessment cannot fill it: a risk assessed as low without testing any control is a judgement about the controls rather than evidence about them. The reason the standard insists on it is that a negative request produces evidence only when somebody bothers to disagree, so silence is allowed to do the work only where the controls behind the balances have been shown to be running.
keywords: assessed risk of material misstatement is low

options.text: Yes. The risk was assessed as low, the population is large and made up of small identical balances, and a very low exception rate is expected, so the conditions are satisfied
options.misconception: counts three of the four conditions and leaves out the one about the controls
options.why: Three of them are satisfied and the fourth is not even attempted. The condition left out asks for evidence about how the controls relevant to the assertion actually ran, and an assessment of risk is not that evidence — it is the auditor's expectation, formed before any control was tested.

options.text: No, because a negative confirmation can never be the only substantive procedure on a receivables balance — positive requests must always be sent alongside them
options.misconception: turns a set of conditions into an outright prohibition, when the standard plainly allows negative requests to stand alone where all of them hold
options.why: The standard sets conditions rather than a ban, and a population of this shape is close to the case it had in mind. What stops this plan is one missing condition, and if the firm tested the billing and collection controls and found them working, the plan would stand.

citation.ref: para 15 — conditions for using negative confirmation requests as the sole substantive procedure

items.scenario: A cable television operator carries about nine thousand subscriber balances, each of a few hundred rupees, every one of them on the same monthly plan. The audit senior has assessed the risk of material misstatement on subscriber receivables as low. The strategy for the area is wholly substantive — no controls over billing or collection were tested, because testing them was judged to cost more than testing the balances. Nothing known to the team suggests that subscribers ignore post from the operator, and last year's exception rate on this population was negligible. The senior proposes to send negative confirmation requests to a sample of subscribers and to do nothing else on the balance.

items.stem: Which of the four may the firm take?

options.text: The turnover certificate and the appearance before the appellate authority only — the other two are on the list the section shuts out, and the committee's approval cannot open a door the section closes
options.why: Section 144 lets an auditor give a company other services only where the Board of Directors or the audit committee has approved them, and it then lifts several kinds of work out of that permission altogether — book keeping and accounting, internal audit, the design and implementation of any financial information system, actuarial services, advice on investments, investment banking, financial services farmed out to the auditor, management services, and anything further that may be prescribed. Valuing the gratuity and leave encashment liabilities is actuarial services, and it is the shape the section exists to stop, since the firm would end up auditing a figure it produced. Taking charge of purchase planning and vendor selection is management services, because the firm would be making the company's own operating decisions. Certifying turnover and appearing in a tax appeal are on neither list, so the committee's approval is enough for them.
keywords: design and implementation of any financial information system

options.text: All four, since the section governs what the auditor does for the holding company and the subsidiaries, and every one of these is work for the audited company itself
options.misconception: reverses the reach of the section, which starts at the audited company and extends outwards to its holding and subsidiary companies
options.why: The section starts with the company whose auditor the firm is and then reaches outwards, catching the same services rendered to that company's holding company and its subsidiaries as well. Reading it as applying only to the relatives of the audit client leaves the client itself unprotected, which is the opposite of what the provision does.

options.text: The turnover certificate, the tax appearance and the valuation of the two employee liabilities — the valuation is a computation the auditor is well placed to make and the committee has approved it
options.misconception: treats the audit committee's approval as able to authorise a service the section names, and reads competence as permission
options.why: Approval is the gate for the services that are not named. For the ones that are, no approval is available, and being the person best able to do the work is the reason it is barred rather than a reason to allow it — an auditor who computes a liability then has to audit his own arithmetic.

options.text: The tax appearance only. Certifying turnover for a bank is an assurance service the statutory auditor may not give the company alongside the audit
options.misconception: invents a bar on certification, which the section does not name and which auditors are appointed to perform elsewhere
options.why: Nothing in the section touches certification, and a statutory auditor certifying a figure drawn from books he has audited is ordinary work of the profession. The bar is a list, and reasoning by feel about what looks uncomfortable produces refusals the law does not require.

citation.ref: Section 144 — services an auditor of a company shall not render, and the approval route for the rest

items.scenario: Nirjala Ceramics Limited's audit committee asks the company's statutory auditors to take on four pieces of work for the company itself, each for a fee and each approved in principle by the committee at the same meeting. First, to compute the valuation of the gratuity and leave encashment liabilities that will go into the accounts the firm audits. Second, to run the company's purchase planning and vendor selection desk for a year while the post is vacant. Third, to certify the company's turnover for a bank. Fourth, to appear for the company before the income tax appellate authority in an old assessment matter.

items.stem: What does the firm have to do about that clause?

options.text: Rewrite it. The clause is defective on its face, and every listed audit run under it has been defective too, however careful the review turned out to be
options.why: For an audit of the financial statements of a listed entity the firm's policies must require an engagement quality control review, and that review is an objective evaluation, by somebody off the team, of the significant judgements the engagement team made and of the conclusions it drew when it framed the report. The review has to be completed before the report is dated. A policy that allows it to be finished seven days after signing can never produce a compliant engagement, so the clause is non-compliant on its face and the fault sits in the manual rather than in any one partner's diary. Withdrawing and reissuing is not the cure either — it is what a firm does when something has already gone wrong, and a policy cannot be built on the expectation of it.
keywords: the significant judgements the engagement team made
completed before the report is dated
the clause is non-compliant on its face

options.text: Amend it for listed clients only, since it is listing that brings the engagement quality control review in; for every other client the seven-day wording may stand
options.misconception: reads the timing rule as something listing switches on, when what listing decides is whether a review is required at all and never when it must be finished
options.why: Listing settles a different question. For an audit of the financial statements of a listed entity a review is mandatory, and for other engagements the firm sets its own criteria for which ones need one. But wherever a review is required — by the standard or by the firm's own criteria — it is the same review, and a review that lands after the report has been dated has arrived too late to do its work on any engagement at all.

options.text: Keep it, and add that where the reviewer objects within the seven days the firm will withdraw the report and issue a revised one, which gives the reviewer the same power he would have had before signature
options.misconception: treats withdrawal and reissue as equivalent to getting the report right the first time, when a report already in a lender's hands cannot be recalled from the people who have read it
options.why: A report that has been signed, dated and sent has been acted on. A revised one reaches the company; it does not reach everybody who has already read the first. The reviewer's leverage before signature is that nothing has gone out yet, and a promise to correct afterwards swaps a control for an apology.

options.text: Nothing. The requirement bites when the report leaves the firm, and the manual can fix its own internal milestones anywhere it likes so long as the reviewer sees the file before the client relies on it
options.misconception: treats signature and issue as two events the firm may space apart at will, so a report already signed and handed over is read as not yet issued
options.why: A signed report handed to the company has gone. Treating issue as a later moment the firm defines for itself would let any deadline be met by renaming the step that has already happened, and it is exactly the reading the requirement forecloses. The reviewer's work has to be finished while it can still change something, which is before the partner puts a date on the report.

citation.ref: Engagement quality control review mandatory for audits of the financial statements of listed entities, and its completion before the report is dated

items.scenario: A mid-sized firm is rewriting its audit manual ahead of a peer review. The clause governing listed clients reads: "Where the client is a listed entity, the engagement quality control review shall be completed within seven days of the signing of the audit report, and the reviewer's observations shall be recorded in the permanent file." The partner who drafted it explains the thinking. Nothing is being skipped: the review still happens on every listed audit, the reviewer still gets the whole file, and if he raises something serious the firm will withdraw the report and issue a corrected one. Putting the review after signature only means the team is not held up by one person's diary in the last week of a reporting season, and the clause is stricter than nothing, which is what the manual said before.

items.stem: Is Sanjeev eligible to act as the reviewer on this engagement?

options.text: No, but only because he has never acted as engagement partner on a listed audit. Had he been a partner throughout, his earlier work on this engagement would not have mattered
options.misconception: keeps the listed-entity standing requirement and drops the objectivity requirement, when both have to hold and the second is the one his history breaks
options.why: Both requirements are live and he fails both. The listed-entity requirement is real: the reviewer on such an audit needs experience and authority enough to act as the audit engagement partner on audits of listed entities, which eleven unlisted years do not supply. But even a partner of that standing could not review an engagement he had worked on, because participating in the engagement or making decisions for the team is what the objectivity requirement rules out.

options.text: Yes. Eligibility is tested when the reviewer is appointed, and on that date he is a partner of the firm and not a member of the engagement team
options.misconception: reads eligibility as a snapshot taken on the date of appointment, when what destroys objectivity is having done the work that is about to be reviewed
options.why: The date he stopped being a manager does not change what he did before it. The review exists to put somebody in front of the team's judgements who did not make them, and a man reading his own working papers supplies no distance at all. Testing the position only on the day of appointment would make the requirement satisfiable by a transfer.

options.text: No. He is not eligible on either limb — he worked on the very engagement he would be reviewing, and he does not have the standing a listed audit asks of a reviewer
options.why: Two things have to hold and neither does. Objectivity first: he was a member of the engagement team on this very audit, so he would be evaluating his own judgements, and participating in an engagement or making decisions for its team is what the reviewer must avoid. Being promoted in April does not undo the work he did up to March. Standing second: for an audit of the financial statements of a listed entity the reviewer must bring the technical expertise and authority the role calls for — experience and authority enough to have acted as the audit engagement partner on audits of listed entities — and eleven years of unlisted work is not that. So he is not eligible, and the firm needs another partner, another member of the Institute inside the firm, or a suitably qualified external person.
keywords: a member of the engagement team on this very audit
the technical expertise and authority the role calls for

options.text: Yes, provided he reviews only the parts of the engagement he did not personally work on, and a second reviewer is appointed for the rest
options.misconception: treats objectivity as something that can be divided area by area, when the review is of the engagement's significant judgements taken together
options.why: The review is an evaluation of the significant judgements of the engagement as a whole and of the conclusions drawn for the report, and those judgements do not come apart into the bits one man touched and the bits he did not. Splitting the role would also leave nobody looking at the engagement whole, which is the thing the review is for.

citation.ref: Eligibility of the engagement quality control reviewer, the additional standing required on an audit of a listed entity, and the objectivity requirement that rules out participation in the engagement

items.scenario: A firm needs an engagement quality control reviewer for the audit of a listed company for the year ended 31 March 2026. It proposes Sanjeev. He was the audit manager on this same engagement — he planned it, ran the fieldwork and signed off the working papers on the significant judgements — until he was admitted to the partnership on 1 April 2026 and handed the manager's role to somebody else. He has audited unlisted companies for eleven years and has never been the engagement partner on a listed audit. The engagement partner says both boxes are ticked: Sanjeev is a partner of the firm, which is the first thing the eligibility rule asks for, and he is no longer on the engagement team, which is the second.

items.stem: What does she tell the committee?

options.text: Both are government companies, so the Comptroller and Auditor General appoints the auditor of each, and his rights over the report follow from that
options.why: Section 2(45) turns on one test — a government holding of 51% or more of the paid-up capital — and the same clause carries a subsidiary of such a company into the class as well. Kaveri Power meets the test directly and Kaveri Renewables meets it through its parent. Whether the shares are listed has nothing to do with it. The consequence is that the statutory auditor of each is appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General under section 139(5) and not by the members at the annual general meeting, and that everything the section then gives him — directions on the manner of audit, a supplementary audit, a right to comment upon or supplement the report, a test audit — applies to both companies.
keywords: a government holding of 51% or more of the paid-up capital

options.text: Both are government companies, but the finance head is right about the appointment: the members appoint, and the Comptroller and Auditor General's role begins only once the signed report reaches him
options.misconception: keeps the definition and drops half its consequence, leaving the Comptroller and Auditor General with the supplementary-audit powers and not the appointment
options.why: The appointment is the first of the powers, not a separate matter. In a government company the auditor is appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General, who then directs the manner in which the accounts are to be audited; the supplementary audit and the right to comment come after the report and sit on top of that. Reading the section from the report backwards leaves out the half that shapes the audit before it starts.

options.text: Neither is, on these facts. A government company is one whose shares the Government holds and which is also listed, listing being what brings public accountability and the Comptroller and Auditor General with it
options.misconception: reads listing as the trigger for public sector audit, when listing is irrelevant to the definition and the accountability comes from the public money in the capital
options.why: Listing is beside the point. What brings the company inside the class is the proportion of its capital that public money has paid for, and a company whose shares are quoted nowhere is as much a government company as one that is quoted. Kaveri Power's shares being unlisted changes nothing about who appoints its auditor.

options.text: Kaveri Power is a government company and Kaveri Renewables is not, since the Government holds no share in the subsidiary and the test is about who holds the shares
options.misconception: stops at the direct-holding limb of the definition and drops the subsidiary limb the same clause carries
options.why: The definition does not stop at direct holding. It expressly carries a company that is a subsidiary of a government company into the same class, which is what stops a holding structure from taking a public-sector business outside the regime by one step. Kaveri Renewables is wholly owned by a government company and is therefore one itself.

citation.ref: Section 2(45) — government company, including a subsidiary of one; and section 139(5) — appointment of the auditor by the Comptroller and Auditor General

items.scenario: Kaveri Power Ltd is an unlisted company in which the Central Government holds 56 per cent of the paid-up share capital. It has one subsidiary, Kaveri Renewables Ltd, in which the Government holds nothing at all — every share is held by Kaveri Power. The group's finance head has put two proposals to the board. For Kaveri Power, the members should appoint the auditors at the annual general meeting, because in his reading the Comptroller and Auditor General audits public sector companies whose shares are listed and Kaveri Power's are not. For Kaveri Renewables, no question arises at all, because the Government owns no part of it and it is an ordinary company owned by another company. The audit committee asks its chartered accountant to comment before the board resolves anything.

items.stem: What does Meera do about the two events?

options.text: She works the matter through with management and then judges what the answers are worth, reading them against everything else the review has shown her
options.why: A review takes in the entity's ability to continue in business, and where the practitioner becomes aware of events raising significant doubt about going concern the standard sets out what follows. She must inquire of management about its plans for future actions, about the feasibility of those plans, and about whether management believes their outcome will improve the position. She must then evaluate the answers, asking whether they give a sufficient basis for the statements to stay on the going concern basis, or whether the statements are materially misstated or otherwise misleading about the company's ability to carry on. And she must weigh those answers against everything else she has learned during the review — including that the talks the managing director is relying on are the very thing he does not want disclosed.
keywords: inquire of management about its plans

options.text: She withdraws from the engagement. A doubt about the entity's survival is beyond what a review can settle, and continuing would lend her name to a question she has no way of answering
options.misconception: turns a procedure the standard prescribes into a reason to leave, when withdrawal answers a management-imposed limitation and not a difficult subject
options.why: Withdrawal is the answer to management blocking the work — a limitation imposed after acceptance, severe enough that a disclaimer looks likely, on an engagement no law requires. Nothing has been blocked here. A going concern doubt is a matter the standard tells the practitioner how to handle inside the review, so leaving would be walking away from work that has been laid out for her.

options.text: She leaves the conclusion unmodified and adds an Emphasis of Matter paragraph naming the loan recall and the lost contract, which puts the reader on notice without her having to reach a view
options.misconception: reads limited assurance as excusing the practitioner from reaching a view on a subject the standard puts inside a review
options.why: An emphasis paragraph draws attention to something already properly presented in the financial statements, and here nothing has been presented at all — the company does not want the refinancing talks mentioned. Pointing at a matter is not a substitute for working out whether the statements are misleading about it, which is the step the standard requires before any conclusion is reached.

options.text: She takes the written representation. In a limited assurance engagement management's own statement about the future is the evidence available, and asking for more than the representation turns the review into something it is not
options.misconception: treats a written representation as evidence in place of the inquiry and evaluation the standard sets out, when a representation is what management believes and not a test of whether the belief is sound
options.why: A representation records management's position; it does not examine it. The standard asks the practitioner to inquire into the plans and their feasibility and then to evaluate what he is told, which is a different activity from collecting a signature on the answer. Limited assurance describes the level of the conclusion, not permission to stop at what management says.

citation.ref: Going concern in a review — inquiry into management's plans and their feasibility, evaluation of the responses, and consideration of them against all other information obtained

items.scenario: Meera is reviewing the financial statements of a road logistics company under SRE 2400 (Revised) for a lender. Two things surface while she is working. The company's bank has recalled its term loan and given it ninety days to pay, and the customer that supplied two-fifths of last year's revenue has served notice terminating its contract. The managing director tells her that going concern is an audit question and this is not an audit; that a review is inquiry and analytical procedures and she has done both; and that if she wants comfort he will sign a written representation saying the company will continue in operation for the foreseeable future. He adds that the company is in talks with two other banks but would rather not put anything about that in the financial statements while the talks are live.

items.stem: What is the partner objecting to, and how should the report read?

options.text: The whole shape of the paragraph. A review does not produce an opinion at all, so both the assertion and the headings have to be rebuilt in the form the standard prescribes
options.why: The partner's point is that no review can end in an opinion. What Anjali has is limited assurance, obtained mainly through inquiry and analytical procedures, and it is reported in the negative form: nothing has come to her attention that causes her to believe the statements fail to give a true and fair view. Because the misstatement is material but not pervasive the conclusion is qualified, and the standard fixes how that is set out — the conclusion paragraph is headed "Qualified Conclusion", and immediately before it a separate paragraph headed "Basis for Qualified Conclusion" describes the matter that caused the modification. The conclusion itself then runs except for the effects of the matter described in that paragraph, nothing has come to her attention causing her to doubt the statements.
keywords: nothing has come to her attention
except for the effects of the matter described

options.text: The size of the modification. A misstatement management refuses to correct is a matter of substance, so the conclusion should be adverse rather than qualified
options.misconception: reads a refusal to correct as raising the severity of the modification, when severity is decided by whether the effects are pervasive and not by management's attitude
options.why: Whether management corrects a misstatement decides whether it is still there at the reporting date; it does not decide how far through the statements it reaches. An adverse conclusion is for effects that are both material and pervasive. This one is material and confined to a single line, so it is the qualified rung of the ladder.

options.text: Only the heading. The word "Opinion" should read "Conclusion"; with that changed the paragraph says what it needs to say
options.misconception: fixes the label and leaves the positive form underneath it, when what separates a review from an audit is that the practitioner never asserts the statements are right
options.why: Renaming the heading over a sentence that still begins "in our opinion, the statements give a true and fair view" changes nothing about what the sentence claims. A review is not built to support that claim. The form of words has to change with the heading, because the form is where the level of assurance actually lives.

options.text: The modification itself. Since the overstatement touches one line only, the conclusion should stay unmodified and the rental should be described in an Other Matter paragraph
options.misconception: treats a paragraph that describes a matter as an alternative to modifying, when a material misstatement requires the conclusion itself to change
options.why: A paragraph describing a matter is not a view about it. Where the practitioner determines the financial statements are materially misstated, the conclusion is modified — qualified here, adverse if the effects were pervasive — and no descriptive paragraph anywhere in the report does that job in its place. Being confined to one line is what makes the modification qualified rather than adverse; it is not a reason to have none.

citation.ref: The negative form of the conclusion on a review, and the headings and wording required when the conclusion is qualified for a material misstatement

items.scenario: Anjali has finished a review of a warehousing company's financial statements under SRE 2400 (Revised). One matter is unresolved. Rental income from a godown sold in December has been recognised for the whole year, an overstatement she considers material; it is confined to that one line and affects nothing else in the statements, and management will not correct it. Her draft report carries a paragraph headed "Opinion" which reads: "In our opinion, except for the rental income referred to above, the financial statements give a true and fair view." Her partner reads the draft and says the substance of it is right — material, not pervasive, therefore a qualification — but that the report as drafted could not be issued from this engagement at all.

items.stem: What does Girnar conclude about the transaction, and about the minority's share?

options.text: It is negative goodwill, so ₹8 crore is deducted rateably from the non-monetary assets acquired and only any remainder is a gain
options.misconception: carries forward the old treatment, under which an excess was allocated against the assets acquired before anything reached the accounts
options.why: Allocating an excess across the assets is how capital reserve used to be avoided; it is not the method here. Under Ind AS 103 the excess is recognised as a gain in its own right once the reassessment is done, and the assets stay at the amounts the acquisition-date measurement gave them. Reducing them would understate depreciation and the carrying amounts of everything acquired for as long as the assets are held.

options.text: It is a bargain purchase, and the whole of the gain belongs to Girnar with nothing going to the minority
options.why: Two separate questions, and the facts answer both. On the first, a bargain purchase arises where the value of the identifiable net assets acquired exceeds the consideration transferred taken together with the amount of any non-controlling interest — ₹128 crore against ₹90 crore of cash and ₹30 crore of minority — and the standard warns that this happens only in extremely rare circumstances, so the reason has to be visible in the facts before anyone believes the arithmetic. Here it is. The standard's own example of how a bargain arises is a forced sale — one where the seller is acting under compulsion — and lenders completing a transfer inside a tribunal's window is such a sale. On the second question, the gain is attributed to the acquirer, and there is no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders. The minority is brought in at its own measured amount and takes nothing further.

options.text: There is no gain. The valuer's ₹128 crore must be written down to ₹120 crore so that what was acquired equals what was given
options.misconception: treats a figure that produces an uncomfortable answer as evidence of a bad valuation, and balances the acquisition by moving the measured value of the assets
options.why: The identifiable assets and liabilities are measured on their own terms at the acquisition date, not adjusted to make an equation come out flat. Ind AS 103 does allow a bargain to arise and provides for the gain, which it would not need to do if the answer were always to write the assets down. What the standard asks for instead is a second look at the identification and the measurement before the gain is booked — a check, not a plug.

options.text: It is a bargain purchase, and 25 per cent of the gain is credited to the non-controlling interest as its share of the undervalued assets
options.misconception: treats the gain like a post-acquisition profit of the subsidiary, which is split between the two sets of owners, when it arises on the acquirer's own bargain
options.why: Post-acquisition profits are shared because both sets of owners own the company that earned them. This gain is not that. It measures how much less the acquirer paid than what it bought was worth, and only the acquirer paid anything. So the gain is attributed to the acquirer and there is no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders. Splitting it would credit the minority twice over — once when it is brought in at ₹30 crore, and again out of a bargain it did not strike.
keywords: no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders

citation.ref: Bargain purchase — the circumstances in which a gain arises, the forced sale example, and attribution of the gain wholly to the acquirer

items.scenario: Sabari Cements Ltd was put up for sale by its lenders, who had enforced a pledge over the promoter's shares and had to complete the transfer inside a ninety-day window set by the tribunal that approved the resolution. On 1 October 20X6 Girnar Ltd bought 75 per cent of the equity for cash of ₹90 crore. A qualified valuer measured the identifiable net assets acquired at ₹128 crore and the fair value of the 25 per cent non-controlling interest at ₹30 crore. Girnar's finance director says the arithmetic must be wrong somewhere, because a buyer does not simply receive ₹8 crore for turning up; and that if the figures do stand, the minority should be given its 25 per cent share of whatever gain there is, since the minority owns 25 per cent of the company that carried the undervalued assets.

items.stem: What has to be done before the gain is recognised?

options.text: Nothing further. An independent valuation obtained at arm's length is the evidence, and re-doing the work would only duplicate it
options.misconception: reads the reassessment as a second valuation, so an independent first valuation looks like it has already been done
options.why: The reassessment is not a re-valuation. It asks a different question — whether everything that should have been recognised was recognised, and whether the method used for each amount was the one the standard requires — and a valuer engaged to price the net assets was not asked either of those. A liability nobody handed him is not in his report, and it is exactly what turns a bargain into an ordinary purchase.

options.text: Look for the reason, and if none can be evidenced, recognise no gain at all and leave the difference to be sorted out later
options.misconception: treats the absence of clear evidence as a bar to recognising anything, when what it changes is only the route the gain takes into equity
options.why: Failing to find the reason does not make the excess disappear, and nothing in the standard leaves it unrecognised. What changes is the route. Where clear evidence of the underlying reasons does exist, the gain goes through other comprehensive income on the acquisition date and is accumulated in equity as capital reserve. Where it does not, the gain is recognised directly in equity as capital reserve instead — it never touches other comprehensive income and it is never left out of the accounts.

options.text: Establish why the bargain arose, then go back over what was identified and re-check how each amount was measured
options.why: The standard treats a bargain as improbable enough to be a warning sign, so it puts a gate in front of the gain. The acquirer first determines whether there is clear evidence of the underlying reasons for calling the combination a bargain purchase. If there is, it then reassesses whether it has correctly identified all of the assets acquired and every liability assumed, recognising anything that surfaces in that review; and it must review the procedures used to measure the identifiable assets and liabilities, the non-controlling interest, any equity interest it already held, and the consideration transferred. An unrecognised liability or an overstated asset is the commonest cause of an apparent bargain, and neither shows up in a valuation report that was never asked to look for it.
keywords: clear evidence of the underlying reasons
correctly identified all of the assets acquired
review the procedures used to measure

options.text: Obtain the seller's own books at the acquisition date and adopt those carrying amounts for anything the valuer measured differently
options.misconception: treats the acquiree's existing carrying amounts as the check on the acquirer's measurement, when the acquisition-date exercise deliberately departs from them
options.why: The acquiree's carrying amounts are what the acquisition accounting replaces. They are struck under the seller's own policies and carry its own history of depreciation and impairment, and they say nothing about whether the acquirer has identified everything it bought. Using them as the arbiter would defeat the purpose of measuring identifiable assets and liabilities afresh.

citation.ref: The reassessment required before a bargain purchase gain is recognised, and the two routes into capital reserve

items.scenario: On the Sabari Cements acquisition — 75 per cent for ₹90 crore in cash, identifiable net assets measured at ₹128 crore, the 25 per cent non-controlling interest at a fair value of ₹30 crore — Girnar's group controller has satisfied himself that the transfer really was forced and that the arithmetic holds. He proposes to put the gain through on the strength of the valuation report, which he describes as the work of an independent professional whom nobody at Girnar instructed on the answer. The audit committee asks whether anything else has to happen first.

items.stem: What are the two figures, and where does the gain go?

options.text: ₹8 crore, credited to profit or loss for the year, since it is a gain the acquirer has made on the acquisition date
options.misconception: applies the answer IFRS 3 gives, which is the difference this standard was deliberately written to create
options.why: Under IFRS 3 the gain is income of the year. Ind AS departs from that on purpose, because a gain recognised on the day of an acquisition, measured off valuations rather than off anything realised, is not the kind of number earnings should carry. So the gain is recognised in other comprehensive income, from where it is accumulated in equity as capital reserve, and it does not go to profit or loss at all. Getting this backwards is the standard trap in an Ind AS paper.
keywords: does not go to profit or loss

options.text: ₹8 crore on either basis. How the minority is measured changes the split of equity, not the acquirer's gain
options.misconception: treats the measurement choice for the non-controlling interest as a presentation matter inside equity, when the amount chosen sits on the same side of the comparison as the consideration
options.why: The minority's measured amount is one of the things the net assets are compared against, so changing it changes the answer. On the proportionate share of the identifiable net assets basis the minority comes in at ₹32 crore rather than ₹30 crore, the total against which the ₹128 crore is measured becomes ₹122 crore, and the gain is ₹6 crore. The higher the minority is carried, the smaller the bargain the acquirer is treated as having struck.
keywords: proportionate share of the identifiable net assets

options.text: ₹38 crore, being the ₹128 crore of net assets less the ₹90 crore of cash actually paid
options.misconception: compares the net assets with the cash alone and leaves the non-controlling interest out of the comparison altogether
options.why: The whole of the net assets is on one side of the comparison, so the whole of what was given for them has to be on the other — and 25 per cent of the company was not bought at all. Leaving the minority out treats ₹90 crore as having purchased ₹128 crore of assets, which would make a bargain out of every acquisition of a subsidiary that is not wholly owned.

options.text: ₹8 crore if the minority is carried at fair value, ₹6 crore if it is carried at its share of net assets — either way through other comprehensive income into capital reserve
options.why: With the non-controlling interest at fair value, what Girnar gave adds up to ₹90 crore of cash plus ₹30 crore, that is ₹120 crore, against identifiable net assets of ₹128 crore, so there is a gain of ₹8 crore. The alternative basis carries the minority at 25 per cent of ₹128 crore, ₹32 crore, which makes the comparison ₹122 crore against ₹128 crore. The choice is available combination by combination and it moves the gain, because a minority measured at fair value carries its share of goodwill and a minority measured on net assets does not. Whichever is chosen, the gain is recognised in other comprehensive income on the acquisition date and accumulated in equity as capital reserve.
keywords: accumulated in equity as capital reserve

citation.ref: Measuring the bargain purchase gain under both bases for the non-controlling interest, and its recognition in other comprehensive income

items.scenario: Girnar Ltd's reassessment on the Sabari Cements acquisition found nothing further to recognise and nothing measured wrongly, and the reason for the bargain is documented. Cash paid was ₹90 crore for 75 per cent; identifiable net assets are ₹128 crore; the fair value of the 25 per cent non-controlling interest is ₹30 crore. The board has not yet chosen how to measure the non-controlling interest for this combination, and asks what difference the choice makes to the gain and where the gain will appear.

items.stem: What is the interest charge for the year, and what is wrong with the accountant's approach?

options.text: ₹48,000 in profit or loss, with anything left over deferred and released over the average remaining service life of the members
options.misconception: reaches for the corridor approach, under which actuarial swings were smoothed into future periods
options.why: Smoothing is gone. Every actuarial difference is recognised in the year it arises, in full, and the balance sheet carries the deficit as it actually stands rather than a version of it that lags reality by several years. What the standard gives up in place of the corridor is not deferral but location: the amounts are recognised now, and recognised outside profit or loss.

options.text: ₹48,000, and the movement cannot all go to profit or loss because one of its three parts belongs elsewhere
options.why: Net interest on the net defined benefit liability is worked out by applying the discount rate to the opening net defined benefit liability. That opening figure is ₹40,00,000 less ₹34,00,000, which is ₹6,00,000, and 8 per cent of it is ₹48,000. What the figure measures is narrow and worth holding on to: the movement in the year that comes from the passage of time, and nothing else. Everything else that moved the deficit — the year's service, an amendment, the actuary changing his mind — is a different component with its own destination, which is why the total cannot be charged in one line.
keywords: net interest on the net defined benefit liability

options.text: ₹3,20,000, being 8 per cent of the obligation of ₹40,00,000
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross obligation and forgets that the fund earns interest income at the same rate, which the standard already nets off
options.why: Both sides unwind. The obligation grows by ₹3,20,000 and the plan assets earn interest income of ₹2,72,000 at the same discount rate, and the standard charges the difference rather than the gross figure. Charging ₹3,20,000 would double-count, because the ₹2,72,000 would then have to be credited somewhere and there is nowhere in profit or loss for it to go without reversing most of what was just charged.

options.text: ₹48,000, and the accountant is right — the whole movement is one cost and profit or loss is where a cost belongs
options.misconception: treats every movement in the net liability as an expense of the year, which is what the split of defined benefit cost into three components exists to prevent
options.why: Defined benefit cost is recognised in three named parts. Service cost, which is the current service cost, any past service cost and any gain or loss on settlement, is charged in profit or loss; net interest on the net liability is charged there too; and remeasurements of that same net liability are recognised in other comprehensive income instead. The third part is deliberately kept out of earnings, because a swing driven by a change in the discount rate says nothing about the year's trading and would drown what does.

citation.ref: The three components of defined benefit cost and where each is recognised, and the measurement of net interest

items.scenario: Trisala Metals Ltd runs a funded gratuity plan. At 1 April 20X5 the present value of the obligation is ₹40,00,000 and the fair value of the plan assets is ₹34,00,000. The discount rate on high quality corporate bonds is 8 per cent. There is no asset ceiling. The company's accountant has drafted the entries by taking the movement in the net liability over the year and putting the whole of it through profit or loss, on the ground that the pension deficit is one cost and dividing it up only confuses the reader.

items.stem: What is charged to profit or loss for the year?

options.text: ₹8,48,000, with the whole of the amendment falling into this year
options.why: Past service cost is what a plan amendment does to the present value of benefits already earned for service in earlier periods, and it is recognised as an expense at the earlier of two dates: when the amendment happens, and when the entity recognises any related restructuring costs or termination benefits. The amendment happened on 31 March 20X6, so the whole ₹2,00,000 falls in this year and is not spread over the years still to be served. The actuary's instinct is about the future; the cost is about the past, and it was created the day the promise changed.

options.text: ₹6,73,000, the amendment being taken evenly over the eight remaining years
options.misconception: matches the amendment against the future service the company hopes to buy with it, when what the amendment changed is the value of service already rendered
options.why: Nothing is bought with a past service cost, which is what makes it past. The benefit that went up relates to years the employees have already worked, so there is no future period for it to attach to, and the standard names the recognition date rather than leaving it to judgement. The charge is current service cost ₹6,00,000, plus past service cost ₹2,00,000, plus net interest ₹48,000, which is ₹8,48,000.

options.text: ₹6,48,000, with the ₹2,00,000 amendment taken to other comprehensive income as a remeasurement of the liability
options.misconception: treats anything that moves the obligation without cash changing hands as a remeasurement, when a plan amendment is the company's own decision and not an actuarial outcome
options.why: Remeasurements are the parts of the movement nobody chose: the actuary's experience adjustments, changes in his assumptions, and the fund performing differently from the discount rate. A plan amendment is none of those. The board decided to promise more, and the cost of that decision is service cost, which is charged in profit or loss along with the current service cost it sits beside.

options.text: ₹6,48,000 now, with the ₹2,00,000 recognised only when the improved benefits are actually paid out
options.misconception: waits for cash, when the obligation is measured on the promise rather than on the settlement
options.why: Gratuity accounting has never waited for payment; if it did, the whole obligation would be off the balance sheet until the first employee retired. The amendment increased what is owed for work already done, so it is an expense of the year in which it was made, and the payment years later simply settles a liability that has been carried since.

citation.ref: Recognition of past service cost on a plan amendment, and the amounts recognised in profit or loss for a defined benefit plan

items.scenario: Trisala Metals Ltd's gratuity plan opened the year with an obligation of ₹40,00,000 and plan assets of ₹34,00,000, discounted at 8 per cent. The current service cost for the year to 31 March 20X6 is ₹6,00,000 and net interest is ₹48,000. On 31 March 20X6, the last day of the year, the company amends the plan so that the benefit earned for service in earlier years rises by ₹2,00,000. The actuary suggests recognising that ₹2,00,000 over the eight years the workforce still has to serve, since it is those years the company expects to buy with it.

items.stem: What are the two remeasurement legs for the year?

options.text: An actuarial gain of ₹70,000 on the obligation, and a return of ₹4,00,000 on the plan assets
options.misconception: reads the growth in the fund as its return, when most of that growth is the contribution paid in and part of it has already been recognised inside net interest
options.why: The movement in a fund is not what it earned. Roll the assets forward the same way: ₹34,00,000 at the start, plus ₹2,72,000 of interest income at the discount rate, plus ₹5,00,000 contributed, less ₹3,00,000 paid out, comes to ₹38,72,000 against an actual ₹38,00,000, so there is a loss of ₹72,000. That figure is the return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest — the ₹2,72,000 has already gone through profit or loss inside the net interest line, and counting it again here would recognise it twice.
keywords: return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest

options.text: There are none. The actuary's closing figures are the measurement, so there is nothing left over to recognise
options.misconception: treats the actuary's balance as the whole answer, when the remeasurement is precisely the difference between that balance and what the year's known movements would have produced
options.why: The closing balances are where the exercise ends, not where it starts. The year's charge to profit or loss is built from service cost and net interest, and those figures do not by themselves get the opening balance to the closing one. What is left over is the remeasurement, and it has to be recognised somewhere or the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss will not agree.

options.text: An actuarial gain of ₹70,000 on the obligation, and a shortfall of ₹72,000 on the plan assets
options.why: Build each side up and compare it with what the actuary reports. The obligation: ₹40,00,000 at the start, plus ₹3,20,000 of interest, plus ₹6,00,000 of current service cost, plus the ₹2,00,000 amendment, less the ₹3,00,000 of benefits paid out, comes to ₹48,20,000. The reported figure is ₹47,50,000, so the obligation is ₹70,000 smaller than the arithmetic predicted and there is an actuarial gain of ₹70,000 — which is what experience adjustments and changes in actuarial assumptions have done to the estimate between one year end and the next.

options.text: An actuarial loss of ₹70,000 on the obligation, and a shortfall of ₹72,000 on the plan assets
options.misconception: gets the direction wrong, reading a reported obligation lower than the rolled-forward figure as bad news because the obligation itself is a liability
options.why: The sign follows the direction of the surprise, not the nature of the balance. The rolled-forward obligation was ₹48,20,000 and the actuary reports ₹47,50,000, so the company owes less than the model said it would — that is a gain. An actuarial loss on the obligation is the other case, where the reported figure comes in above the roll-forward.

citation.ref: Actuarial gains and losses, and the return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest, as the components of remeasurements

items.scenario: For the year to 31 March 20X6 Trisala Metals Ltd's gratuity plan opened with an obligation of ₹40,00,000 and plan assets of ₹34,00,000, discounted at 8 per cent. Current service cost was ₹6,00,000, the plan was amended on the last day of the year adding ₹2,00,000 of past service cost, benefits of ₹3,00,000 were paid out of the fund and the company contributed ₹5,00,000, both on the last day. The actuary reports the closing obligation at ₹47,50,000 and the closing fair value of the plan assets at ₹38,00,000. The finance manager notes that the fund grew by ₹4,00,000 over the year and proposes to report that as the return on the plan assets.

items.stem: What is recognised in other comprehensive income, and what becomes of it later?

options.text: A net loss of ₹2,000, and it is never brought back through profit or loss
options.why: The two legs are netted before anything is presented: the ₹70,000 actuarial gain on the obligation against the ₹72,000 shortfall on the assets leaves a loss of ₹2,000. Once it is there it stays out of earnings, because a remeasurement shall not be reclassified to profit or loss at any later date, although the company may move the amount within equity, for instance out of a separate reserve into retained earnings. The whole year then ties: the closing net liability is ₹47,50,000 less ₹38,00,000, or ₹9,50,000, which is the opening ₹6,00,000 plus the ₹8,48,000 charge plus the ₹2,000 loss less the ₹5,00,000 contributed.
keywords: shall not be reclassified to profit or loss

options.text: A net loss of ₹2,000, which is recycled to profit or loss as the benefits are paid out in later years
options.misconception: assumes every item routed through other comprehensive income eventually finds its way into earnings, which is true of some items and expressly not of this one
options.why: Recycling is item by item, not a general rule of the statement.
