A foreign operation's translation reserve and a cash flow hedge reserve do come back; remeasurements of a defined benefit plan are named as one of the items that do not. If they were recycled, the smoothing the corridor used to provide would return by a side door, with the same swings hitting earnings years after the event that caused them.

options.text: A net gain of ₹2,000, the gain on the obligation being the larger of the two figures
options.misconception: nets the two legs the wrong way round, treating a gain on the liability side as automatically dominant
options.why: ₹72,000 is larger than ₹70,000, so the net figure is a loss. The two legs are simply added with their own signs — a gain because the obligation came in below the roll-forward, a loss because the fund came in below its expected value — and there is no ordering between them.

options.text: Nothing. The two legs are equal and opposite in substance and cancel before presentation
options.misconception: treats near-equal amounts as offsetting exactly, when the closing net liability will not reconcile unless the ₹2,000 difference is recognised
options.why: They are not equal, and the ₹2,000 has work to do. Without it the opening net liability of ₹6,00,000, the ₹8,48,000 charge and the ₹5,00,000 contribution give ₹9,48,000, while the balance sheet has to show ₹9,50,000. The remeasurement is what closes that gap, which is why a reconciliation of the opening and closing net liability is the usual way of proving the year's figures.

citation.ref: Remeasurements recognised in other comprehensive income are not reclassified to profit or loss, and the reconciliation of the net defined benefit liability

items.scenario: Trisala Metals Ltd's gratuity plan for the year to 31 March 20X6 produced an actuarial gain of ₹70,000 on the obligation and a shortfall of ₹72,000 on the plan assets. The charge to profit or loss for the year was ₹8,48,000, the opening net liability was ₹6,00,000, and ₹5,00,000 was contributed to the fund. The closing obligation is ₹47,50,000 and the closing fair value of the plan assets is ₹38,00,000. A director asks what reaches other comprehensive income, and whether the group will get it back in a later year when the plan settles.

items.stem: What price and what fraction does Ind AS 33 make him use for the months before 1 July?

options.text: ₹40 a share, the price at which the rights were actually taken up
options.misconception: uses the subscription price as the ex-rights value, confusing what the shareholder paid with what a share is worth afterwards
options.why: What the subscriber paid is one input, not the answer. After the issue every share in the company is worth the same thing, and that figure has to fall between the ₹64 the old shares were worth and the ₹40 the new one cost. Using ₹40 would say the whole company repriced to the subscription price, which would treat almost the entire holding as a gift.

options.text: ₹60 a share, giving a fraction of 16/15
options.why: Work out what a share is worth the moment the rights have been taken up. Five shares held were worth ₹64 each, ₹320 in all, and the sixth arrives for ₹40, so six shares are worth ₹360 and the theoretical ex-rights fair value is ₹60 per share. The adjustment is the fair value immediately before the rights were exercised divided by that figure, ₹64 over ₹60, which is 16/15. It says the same thing as a bonus issue of one share for every fifteen held, and the months before 1 July are restated as though those free shares had been in issue all along.

options.text: No adjustment at all — the shares were issued for cash and are counted from the date the money came in
options.misconception: treats a rights issue as an ordinary issue for cash, which is how it is counted only when it is priced at or above market
options.why: A rights issue priced below the market hands existing holders part of their new shares for nothing, and that free part is a bonus element. Because a bonus issue gives no new resources to the company, the shares representing it are treated as having always been in issue, which is why the restatement runs back through the current year and every prior period presented. The manager's approach is right only where the fraction comes out below one — the market having fallen during the rights period — in which case the issue is treated as one made at full market price and nothing is restated.

options.text: ₹52 a share, giving a fraction of 16/13
options.misconception: averages the market price and the subscription price without weighting them by how many shares stand at each
options.why: A straight average of ₹64 and ₹40 would be right if the issue were one new share for every one held. It is one for five, so the ₹64 shares outnumber the ₹40 share five to one and the weighting has to say so. The calculation is the total value of the holding after the issue divided by the number of shares that make it up, which is ₹360 over six.

citation.ref: Theoretical ex-rights fair value per share and the fraction applied to the shares in issue before a rights issue

items.scenario: Kestrel Foods Ltd had 30,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in issue throughout the year ended 31 March 2025. On 1 July 2025 it made a rights issue of one share for every five held, at ₹40 a share, which was taken up in full. The market price immediately before the rights were exercised was ₹64. The finance manager intends to count the new shares from 1 July and leave the earlier months alone, on the ground that the company received cash for every share it issued and a shareholder who did not want his rights could have sold them.

items.stem: What are the two figures?

options.text: ₹3.60 for 2025-26, with the comparative restated to ₹3.00
options.why: Two steps, and the same fraction does both. For the current year the 30,00,000 shares standing before the issue are scaled by 16/15 to 32,00,000 and counted for the three months to 30 June, giving 8,00,000; the actual 36,00,000 shares are counted for the nine months after, giving 27,00,000; the weighted average is 35,00,000 shares and ₹1,26,00,000 over that is ₹3.60. For the comparative, the whole of last year is restated on 30,00,000 × 16/15, that is 32,00,000 shares, so ₹96,00,000 gives ₹3.00 and that figure is presented in place of the ₹3.20 first published. Both years then sit on the same footing, which is the only way the trend means anything.

options.text: ₹3.65 for 2025-26, with the ₹3.20 comparative left as published
options.misconception: time-weights the old and new share counts without adjusting for the bonus element, and treats last year's published figure as final
options.why: Time-weighting alone gives 30,00,000 for three months and 36,00,000 for nine, that is 34,50,000 shares and ₹3.65. It understates the denominator because it ignores the shares handed over for nothing, and it leaves the two years measured on different share bases, so the apparent rise from ₹3.20 is partly the free element rather than trading. Restating the comparative is not optional tidying; it is what makes the comparison honest.

options.text: ₹3.50 for 2025-26, with the ₹3.20 comparative left as published
options.misconception: divides the year's profit by the shares in issue at the year end rather than by a weighted average
options.why: The closing count is not the denominator. Shares that existed for nine months of the year cannot be counted as though they funded the whole of it, and 36,00,000 is what stood only after 1 July. The weighted average exists precisely so that each block of shares is counted for the part of the year it was actually in issue.

options.text: ₹3.60 for 2025-26, with the ₹3.20 comparative left as published because last year's accounts are approved and cannot be reopened
options.misconception: confuses restating a presented comparative with reopening approved accounts, which is not what a retrospective earnings per share adjustment does
options.why: Nothing is reopened. Last year's approved financial statements stand as they were; what changes is the comparative figure shown alongside this year's, and the adjustment runs through each prior period presented for exactly that reason. Leaving ₹3.20 next to ₹3.60 would report a rise of about 13 per cent when the like-for-like rise is 20 per cent.

citation.ref: Weighted average number of shares after a rights issue, and retrospective adjustment of earnings per share for prior periods presented

items.scenario: Kestrel Foods Ltd had 30,00,000 equity shares in issue throughout the year ended 31 March 2025 and reported basic earnings per share of ₹3.20 on a profit of ₹96,00,000. On 1 July 2025 it made a rights issue of one for five at ₹40, taken up in full, when the market price immediately before exercise was ₹64; the adjustment fraction is 16/15. Profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹1,26,00,000. The board is signing off the financial statements and wants the two earnings per share figures that will appear on the face of the statement of profit and loss.

items.stem: On the measure his books already use, how much has he retained, and is he right?

options.text: Retained profit is ₹6,000, being the margin he earned on the trading
options.misconception: reports the profit and forgets the drawings, when the concept measures what is left after distributions to the owner
options.why: The margin was ₹6,000 and so were the drawings. Capital maintenance compares the two ends of the year after excluding distributions to and contributions from owners, so money taken out cannot also be money retained. What he has kept is the difference between the two, which is nothing.

options.text: Retained profit is nil, and on that measure he is right — but only for as long as prices stand still
options.why: His books use financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units, which asks one question: does the money amount of net assets at the end beat the money amount at the beginning, once what the owner put in and took out is set aside. Sales of ₹18,000 less the ₹6,000 drawn leave closing equity of ₹12,000 against opening equity of ₹12,000, so the profit for the year was ₹6,000 and retained profit is nil. He can start again by buying 6,000 units at ₹2, and the cycle repeats — which is the answer this concept gives and the reason it stops being adequate the moment the purchase price moves.

options.text: He has lost ₹2,400, which is what the general rise in prices has cost him
options.misconception: gives the right answer under a different concept of capital, before the question has asked which concept is being used
options.why: That figure is the answer once opening capital is restated into closing prices, and it is a real answer to a real question — but a different one. The books here are kept in money at what was paid, and on that basis the general price level does not enter the calculation at all. Which number is right depends entirely on which capital the trader is trying to keep intact, and that has to be settled first.

options.text: Nothing can be said until the closing stock is valued, since the measurement of profit depends on it
options.misconception: looks for a stock figure out of habit, when the facts say every unit was sold
options.why: There is no closing stock; all 6,000 units went. What replaced them is cash, and the whole of the answer is in the two equity figures and the drawings. The interesting question here is not what the stock is worth but what the ₹12,000 of cash can now buy, and that is what the other concepts of capital go on to ask.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units and the determination of profit

items.scenario: A trader started on 1 January with ₹12,000, all of it held as 6,000 units of a single product bought at ₹2 each. During the year he sold every unit at ₹3 and withdrew ₹6,000 for himself. Prices generally rose over the year, and this product rose with them. He keeps his books in rupees at what he paid, as he always has, and tells his accountant that he made ₹6,000, took ₹6,000, and is therefore exactly where he started.

items.stem: Measured in purchasing power, what has he retained and what could he safely have drawn?

options.text: He has retained nothing, exactly as under the money measure, because he holds cash and cash does not change in amount
options.misconception: reasons from the number of rupees held rather than from what those rupees will buy, which is the distinction this concept exists to draw
options.why: The rupees have not changed; what they command has. ₹12,000 bought 6,000 units in January and buys 5,000 at ₹2.40 in December, and a concept built on purchasing power is measuring exactly that loss. The money measure and this one give different answers on identical facts, and that is the point of asking which capital is being maintained.

options.text: He is ₹6,000 short, and nothing at all should have been drawn
options.misconception: applies the specific price of the product where the question uses the general price level
options.why: That is the answer when the yardstick is what this particular product now costs — the physical concept — and it is the right answer to that question. Here the yardstick is the general price index, 100 to 120, so the opening capital is restated to ₹14,400 rather than to ₹15,000. The two concepts are asking different things: one about general purchasing power, the other about replacing the specific goods traded in.

options.text: He is ₹2,400 short, and ₹3,600 was the most he could safely have drawn
options.why: Measured in units of constant purchasing power, the opening capital is restated at closing prices before the comparison is made: ₹12,000 × 120/100 is ₹14,400. Closing equity is ₹12,000, so retained profit is negative ₹2,400 and he has drawn that much too much. The reasoning behind the restatement is that only the part of a price rise that beats the general rise counts as profit; the rest is a capital maintenance adjustment sitting in equity rather than income. Had he drawn ₹3,600 he would still hold the ₹14,400 needed to buy 6,000 units at ₹2.40.

options.text: He is ₹2,400 short, and that ₹2,400 is an expense of the year
options.misconception: puts the restatement of opening capital through income, when it is the yardstick being reset rather than a cost being incurred
options.why: Nothing was consumed. The ₹2,400 is the amount by which the opening capital had to be restated to be comparable with the closing figure, so it belongs in equity as a capital maintenance adjustment and not in the measurement of income. Running it through profit would double-count against a concept whose whole method is to move the starting line rather than to charge for having moved it.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Financial capital maintenance in units of constant purchasing power, and capital maintenance adjustments

items.scenario: The same trader began the year with ₹12,000, turned 6,000 units bought at ₹2 into ₹18,000 of sales at ₹3, and drew ₹6,000. Over the year the general price index rose from 100 to 120. His banker, who lends against the business, cares about whether the money left in it still commands what it used to. The trader wants to know how much he could have taken without eating into that.

items.stem: What has he retained on that footing, and how is the concept actually chosen?

options.text: He is ₹6,000 short, and the accounts must use the physical concept because it is the most conservative of the three
options.misconception: picks a concept for its strictness, when the choice follows the information needs of the people using the statements
options.why: Conservatism does not decide it. A financial concept of capital, meaning invested money or invested purchasing power, is adopted where the users are chiefly concerned with keeping nominal invested capital or its purchasing power intact; a physical concept, which is operating capability, where their main concern is the entity's productive capacity. The concept selected is the point of reference from which profit is measured, and it settles the measurement basis as well: the physical concept requires current cost, a value struck at each measurement date rather than at the date of purchase.

options.text: He has retained ₹6,000, since he sold at ₹3 what had cost him ₹2
options.misconception: measures the margin against what was paid rather than against what replacing the goods now costs
options.why: Historical cost is the wrong comparison once the question is whether he can trade again. The replacement price is ₹2.50, so the ₹1 margin per unit is really ₹0.50 of profit and ₹0.50 of holding the goods while their price moved — and under this concept even that ₹0.50 is a capital maintenance adjustment in equity, not income.

options.text: He is ₹6,000 short and should have drawn nothing; and the concept is chosen by asking who reads the accounts
options.why: Under physical capital maintenance a profit arises only if the physical productive capacity at the end of the period exceeds what it was at the beginning. Opening capital restated at the closing current cost is 6,000 units at ₹2.50, or ₹15,000; the cash left once the stock is stated at what it would now cost is ₹9,000; so retained profit is negative ₹6,000 and there should have been no drawings at all. The ₹9,000 he holds will buy 3,600 units, not 6,000.

options.text: Nothing arises under any concept until the higher price is realised by selling stock at ₹2.50
options.misconception: confuses when an item is recognised with which concept of capital is in use, which are separate questions
options.why: Recognition and the concept of capital are two different decisions. The concept fixes what has to be kept intact before anything counts as profit; recognition rules then say when an item enters the statements. Under the physical concept a price change on the assets is never profit, realised or not, so waiting for a sale does not convert it into one.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Physical capital maintenance, and the choice between the financial and physical concepts of capital and its link to the measurement basis

items.scenario: The same trader began with ₹12,000 as 6,000 units at ₹2, sold them all at ₹3 and drew ₹6,000. By the end of the year the product itself costs ₹2.50 a unit, so the specific price index for it stands at 125. He intends to stay in the same trade next year and wants to put the same 6,000 units back on his shelves. His accountant asks which concept of capital the accounts should be built on, and says the strictest one must be the right one.

items.stem: What do the revenue and asset tests actually give?

options.text: A and B clear both tests, and B clears the asset test standing exactly on the line
options.why: The revenue test looks at what a segment reports, which takes in sales to external customers and intersegment sales or transfers alike, and it compares that with the combined revenue, internal and external, of all the operating segments. That combined figure is 300 + 90 + 50 + 40 + 45 = ₹525 crore, so the line is ₹52.5 crore, and only A at 300 and B at 90 are above it. Eliminating internal sales would hide a segment that trades mainly inside the group, which is a segment the reader most wants to see. On assets, B is in: the test reads 10 per cent or more, so a segment sitting exactly on the line is inside it, not outside.

options.text: A and B clear the revenue test, but on assets only A clears
options.misconception: reads a threshold written as ten per cent or more as though it said more than ten per cent, so a segment landing exactly on the line is excluded
options.why: Combined assets are 300 + 40 + 20 + 30 + 10 = ₹400 crore, so the line is ₹40 crore and Segment B is on it. The test is expressed as 10 per cent or more, which puts the boundary case inside. A threshold of this kind is drawn to catch a segment of that size, and reading it the other way would make reportability turn on a rounding difference of a single rupee.

options.text: All five clear, since each is reviewed separately by the decision maker
options.misconception: treats identification as reportability, when being an operating segment is what makes a segment eligible to be tested rather than reportable
options.why: Being reviewed separately is what makes something an operating segment; the thresholds then sort those segments into the ones reported on their own and the ones combined. C, D and E fail the revenue line of ₹52.5 crore and the asset line of ₹40 crore, so nothing about the way management reviews them makes them separately reportable at this stage.

options.text: Only A clears the revenue test, B's ₹90 crore being under ten per cent of the group's ₹425 crore of external revenue
options.misconception: uses external revenue as the denominator for the ten per cent test, which is the base for the seventy-five per cent floor and not for the thresholds
options.why: Two different bases do two different jobs. The ten per cent test uses the revenue all the operating segments report between them, ₹525 crore here, because that is the population being sorted. External revenue, ₹425 crore, is the base for the floor that runs afterwards and asks whether enough of the entity has been covered. On the correct base the line is ₹52.5 crore and B is comfortably through it.

citation.ref: Quantitative thresholds — the revenue test including intersegment sales, and the assets test

items.scenario: Kalpa Foods Ltd has five operating segments, each reviewed separately by its chief operating decision maker. For 2025-26, in ₹ crore: Segment A revenue 300, of which 200 is external and 100 is sold to Segment B, assets 300. Segment B revenue 90, all external, assets 40. Segment C revenue 50, all external, assets 20. Segment D revenue 40, all external, assets 30. Segment E revenue 45, all external, assets 10. The group accountant is applying the revenue and asset tests. He proposes to compare each segment's revenue against the ₹425 crore the group sold to outsiders, since inter-segment sales are eliminated on consolidation and cannot be revenue; and to exclude Segment B on assets because ₹40 crore is not more than ten per cent of ₹400 crore.

items.stem: What does the profit or loss test give for Segment B?

options.text: B is not reportable. The line is ₹3.8 crore, ten per cent of the net result of ₹38 crore, and a loss is not a profit
options.misconception: nets the profits against the losses to get one denominator, when the standard deliberately keeps the two totals apart and takes the larger
options.why: Netting would make the line move with how well the profitable segments happened to offset the loss-making ones, and in a year where they cancelled it would produce a denominator of nothing. The standard therefore forms the two totals separately, ₹68 crore of profits and ₹30 crore of losses, and uses the larger. In any event B would clear a line of ₹3.8 crore several times over, because its result is measured at its absolute amount rather than treated as a nil profit.

options.text: B is reportable — its ₹30 crore loss is taken at its absolute amount against a line of ₹6.8 crore
options.why: The test compares a segment's reported result, in absolute amount, with whichever is the larger in absolute amount of two totals: the combined profit of all the segments that did not report a loss, and the combined loss of all the segments that did. Profits here are 60 + 5 + 2 + 1 = ₹68 crore and losses are ₹30 crore, so the greater of the two is ₹68 crore and the line is ₹6.8 crore. A at 60 and B at 30 both clear it. Losing money is not a disqualification — a segment losing on that scale is exactly what a reader of the accounts needs to be shown separately.

options.text: B is reportable, and so is C, whose ₹5 crore clears ten per cent of the ₹30 crore of losses
options.misconception: uses the smaller of the two totals as the denominator, when the standard names the greater in absolute amount
options.why: The rule takes the greater of the two totals in absolute amount, which is the ₹68 crore of combined profits, not the ₹30 crore of combined losses. That gives a line of ₹6.8 crore, and C's ₹5 crore falls short of it, as do D at 2 and E at 1. Choosing the smaller total would lower the bar every time one segment made a big loss, so more segments would be reported for a reason that has nothing to do with their own size.

options.text: B is not reportable, because the test looks only at the segments that returned a profit
options.misconception: reads the two totals as selecting which segments are tested, when they only decide which denominator is used
options.why: The two totals build the denominator. Every operating segment is then measured against the line that results, whichever way its own result went, and the standard says so by taking the segment's result in absolute amount. Testing only the profitable ones would let a division losing ₹30 crore vanish into an all other segments column, which is the outcome the rule is written to prevent.

citation.ref: Quantitative thresholds — the profit or loss test, absolute amounts and the greater of combined profits and combined losses

items.scenario: Kalpa Foods Ltd's five operating segments returned the following results for 2025-26, in ₹ crore: A a profit of 60, B a loss of 30, C a profit of 5, D a profit of 2, E a profit of 1. The chief financial officer says Segment B cannot be a reportable segment because it lost money, and that in any case the test should be run against the group's net result of ₹38 crore, which is what the shareholders actually see.

items.stem: Is he finished, and what happens to the rest?

options.text: No — C has to be brought in as well, and only D and E are then combined
options.why: One more test runs after the thresholds, and it is measured on external revenue. The entity's external revenue is 200 + 90 + 50 + 40 + 45 = ₹425 crore. A and B bring in ₹290 crore, which is 68.2 per cent, so the reportable segments carry less than 75 per cent of it and further operating segments must be identified as reportable, whether or not they meet any threshold, until the floor is reached. Adding C, the largest of the three left, takes reportable external revenue to ₹340 crore, which is 80 per cent, and the exercise stops there.

options.text: Yes — the three thresholds are the whole test, and anything failing all of them is combined
options.misconception: stops at the thresholds, missing the floor that exists precisely because the thresholds can leave most of an entity uncovered
options.why: The thresholds select segments; the floor then checks whether enough of the entity has been captured. An entity of twenty even-sized divisions would have no segment above ten per cent and would report nothing at all, which is the case the floor is there to catch. Here A and B leave nearly a third of external revenue outside the reported segments, and that is below the line.

options.text: No — C, D and E should be aggregated into a single reportable segment to carry the coverage up to 100 per cent
options.misconception: uses aggregation to solve a coverage shortfall, when segments may only be combined where they are economically alike
options.why: Aggregation is not a device for meeting the floor. Two or more operating segments may be combined only where doing so fits the core principle, they have similar economic characteristics, and they are alike in the nature of their products, their production processes, their customers, their distribution and any regulatory environment. Nothing in the facts says C, D and E are alike, and combining unlike businesses to reach a percentage would defeat the purpose of segment reporting.

options.text: No — D and E have to be brought in too, and each of the five shown separately
options.misconception: treats the floor as switching on separate reporting for every remaining segment, when only enough segments are added to reach it
options.why: Segments are added until the floor is met and no further. Adding C alone takes coverage to 80 per cent, so D and E stay out and are combined and disclosed in a single all other segments category, kept apart from the other reconciling items, with the sources of that revenue described. Kalpa may still show D or E on its own if management thinks the information would be useful to readers, but nothing compels it. And because C is reportable for the first time this year, the prior period's segment data presented for comparison is restated to show C separately, unless that information is not available and the cost of developing it would be excessive.

citation.ref: The seventy-five per cent of entity revenue floor, the all other segments category, and restatement of comparatives for a newly reportable segment

items.scenario: Kalpa Foods Ltd has applied the three thresholds and found that Segments A and B are reportable and that C, D and E meet none of them. External revenue for 2025-26, in ₹ crore, is A 200, B 90, C 50, D 40 and E 45. The comparative disclosures already published for 2024-25 show only A and B. The group accountant is ready to publish A and B on their own for 2025-26 as well, and to put the other three together.

items.stem: How is the instrument presented?

options.text: A liability for the ₹40 crore only, with the dividends shown in equity because a dividend can be paid only out of profits
options.misconception: treats the legal source of a dividend as making it discretionary, when the contract obliges the company to pay it and the availability of profits is a separate constraint
options.why: A restriction on the fund a payment can come out of is not the same as a right to withhold the payment. The company has promised the dividend each year, and the promise is cumulative, so a year of insufficient profits defers it rather than cancels it. Both legs of the instrument are obligations and both belong on the liability side.

options.text: Equity, because preference shares are share capital and the holders are members
options.misconception: classifies by legal form and by the register of members, when the standard classifies by the substance of the contractual arrangement
options.why: Company law and this standard are answering different questions. Ind AS 32 looks for a contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset, and it warns that such an obligation may be established indirectly through the terms and conditions of the instrument rather than stated in so many words. Redemption at a fixed amount on a fixed date is exactly that obligation, however the holder is described in the register.

options.text: A compound instrument, split between a liability for the redemption amount and equity for the dividend stream
options.misconception: reaches for a split because the instrument has two legs, when a split requires one of them to be a genuine equity residual
options.why: A compound instrument needs a component that really is equity — a conversion option, or interest the issuer may simply decline to pay. Here the dividend is mandatory, so both legs are obligations and there is no residual to carve out. Splitting would put part of a liability into equity and understate the company's borrowings.

options.text: A financial liability in its entirety, with the 11 per cent as finance cost
options.why: What the instrument is called does not decide where it sits. An instrument is a financial liability where it carries an obligation to hand over cash that the issuer cannot avoid, and it is equity only where the issuer holds an unconditional right to avoid parting with cash. Here the dividend is mandatory each year and the principal falls due on a set date, so both legs are obligations, neither can be side-stepped, and the instrument is a liability in its entirety. The dividend follows the classification and goes through finance cost, so it reduces profit rather than appearing below it as an appropriation.

citation.ref: The contractual obligation test, the unconditional right to avoid delivering cash, and redeemable preference shares with a mandatory dividend

items.scenario: Ratnagiri Ports Ltd has issued 11 per cent cumulative preference shares of ₹40 crore, redeemable at par at the end of seven years, the dividend being payable every year without any discretion to withhold it. The company secretary points out that the instrument is share capital under the Companies Act, that the holders are members and not creditors, and that the registrar's records show it as part of the issued capital. He proposes to present the ₹40 crore within equity and to take the dividend to retained earnings as an appropriation.

items.stem: What is the position on both points?

options.text: A liability in full, including the ₹30 crore principal, since an instrument cannot be split down the middle
options.misconception: refuses to separate components, when a compound instrument is precisely one that has to be
options.why: Splitting is the required answer where an instrument has both an obligation and a residual. The principal here can never be demanded back, so it fails the liability definition; presenting it as debt would overstate borrowings by ₹30 crore and understate equity by the same amount. The liability is the coupon stream and the residual is everything else.

options.text: Equity in full, since the principal is never repayable
options.misconception: reads the absence of a maturity date as the whole test, when a stream of payments the issuer cannot refuse is an obligation in itself
options.why: A promise to pay ₹2.7 crore every year forever is worth more than most finite loans, not less. The test is whether the issuer can avoid parting with cash, and here it cannot avoid the coupon in any year. So the coupon leg is a liability measured at the present value of that stream, and only what is left of the proceeds sits in equity as the perpetual principal.

options.text: The coupon leg is a liability whatever the maturity, and the clearance changes nothing
options.why: Take the instrument apart. A perpetual bond with a coupon the issuer cannot skip has two components: the mandatory interest, which is an obligation to deliver cash and therefore a financial liability, and the perpetual principal, which nobody can demand back and which is therefore the equity part. Having no repayment date does not save the instrument, because the coupon obligation stands on its own. On the regulator, a shortage of foreign currency or the need to get an outside approval before paying does not negate what the issuer is bound to deliver or what the holder is entitled to receive. The obligation exists from the day the bonds are issued.

options.text: A liability, but each coupon becomes an obligation only once the regulatory authority has cleared that particular remittance
options.misconception: treats an external approval as a condition of owing, when it is only an obstacle to paying
options.why: A clearance controls whether the money may move, not whether it is owed, and the need to obtain approval for a payment from a regulatory authority leaves the company just as bound as it was before. If an outside approval could postpone recognition, any borrower facing an exchange control or a court attachment would report itself as having no liability, while the holder kept every contractual right it started with. The obligation is measured and presented from inception; a delay in remitting is a matter for disclosure, not classification.

citation.ref: Perpetual instruments with mandatory interest, and the effect of an outside restriction on the ability to pay

items.scenario: Ratnagiri Ports Ltd has also issued ₹30 crore of perpetual bonds carrying a 9 per cent coupon payable every year, with no right to skip it and no date on which the principal is ever repayable. A number of the holders are outside India, and every coupon remittance to them needs the clearance of the exchange-control regulator before the money can leave. The treasurer argues that nothing is ever repayable so the whole ₹30 crore is equity, and that in any case a coupon the company is not free to remit cannot be an obligation until the regulator has cleared it.

items.stem: How are the two instruments presented?

options.text: Both are equity, since the company chooses in the first case and the board decides in the second
options.misconception: reads any choice available to the issuer as an unconditional right to avoid delivering cash, whatever the choice costs
options.why: A choice helps only if one of the branches lets the company keep its resources. Handing over a warehouse worth more than ₹20 crore is a worse outcome than paying the cash, so the option is no escape at all. The second instrument is nearer the mark: the board's discretion over the interest does keep that leg out of liabilities, but the ₹10 crore itself still falls due on a fixed date and no discretion touches it.

options.text: The first is equity and the second a liability in full, since one has an escape route and the other has a redemption date
options.misconception: classifies each instrument on the single feature that stands out, rather than testing every cash flow the instrument carries
options.why: Each cash flow is tested, not the headline. The first instrument's escape route leads to an asset worth more than the cash, so it is no escape; the second one's redemption is an obligation but its interest is not. The result is the opposite of the one proposed on both counts.

options.text: Both are financial liabilities in full
options.misconception: treats a debenture as debt from end to end, missing that a payment nobody can compel is a residual interest whatever the instrument is called
options.why: The name on the second instrument is doing the work here. Interest that the board may simply decline to declare is not an obligation, so that leg meets the definition of equity even though it sits inside something called a debenture — the same reasoning that puts a mandatory preference dividend into liabilities, run the other way.

options.text: The first is a financial liability; the second splits into a liability and an equity component
options.why: On the first, the only escape from paying cash is to settle a non-financial obligation, the warehouse, and its value is significantly higher than the cash amount — so a settlement alternative of that shape gives the company no real way out and the ₹20 crore is a liability. On the second, redemption of ₹10 crore on a fixed date is an obligation to deliver cash and is the liability component, while interest payable only if the board declares it is the equity component. The company measures the liability at the present value of the redemption amount and puts the residual of the proceeds in equity.

citation.ref: A settlement alternative that is a non-financial obligation, and the liability and equity components of a compound instrument

items.scenario: Two more instruments sit on Ratnagiri Ports Ltd's balance sheet. The first is ₹20 crore of preference shares redeemable after five years in cash or, at the company's own choice, by transferring a warehouse whose fair value is well above ₹20 crore. The second is ₹10 crore of debentures redeemable after ten years, on which 10 per cent interest is payable only if the board declares it. The chief financial officer proposes to treat both as equity: the first because the company can choose not to pay cash at all, the second because the interest is at the board's discretion.

items.stem: What is the consideration transferred, and where do the two promises sit?

options.text: ₹101 crore, with the share promise in equity and the cash promise as a financial liability
options.why: Consideration transferred is measured at acquisition-date fair value, and contingent consideration is part of it at its own acquisition-date fair value. So the figure is ₹80 crore plus ₹12 crore plus ₹9 crore, which is ₹101 crore, and goodwill is struck off that rather than off the cash actually handed over. The classification of each promise then follows the definitions in Ind AS 32: an obligation to be settled by issuing a fixed number of the acquirer's own shares carries no obligation to deliver cash and is equity, while the promise of ₹15 crore in cash is a financial liability.

options.text: ₹101 crore, with both promises recognised as financial liabilities because both are obligations of the acquirer
options.misconception: treats every contingent payment as a liability, when the settlement currency decides it and shares are not cash
options.why: Being an obligation is not enough; what matters is what has to be handed over to settle it. The share promise is settled by delivering a fixed number of the acquirer's own shares and nothing else, so it is classified as equity and never appears on the liability side. Only the cash promise obliges the company to part with a financial asset.

options.text: ₹107 crore, taking the cash promise at the ₹15 crore that may become payable
options.misconception: measures a contingent cash promise at the amount payable if the condition is met, rather than at its fair value on the acquisition date
options.why: ₹15 crore is what will be paid if the approval comes; ₹9 crore is what the promise was worth on 1 July 2025, once the chance of the approval and the time value of money are taken into account. The standard uses fair value at the acquisition date for every element of the consideration, and using the undiscounted maximum would overstate goodwill and pre-empt an outcome nobody yet knows.

options.text: ₹80 crore, the two promises being contingent and therefore disclosed until they become payable
options.misconception: treats contingent consideration like a contingent liability under Ind AS 37, which is disclosed until it becomes probable
options.why: A contingent liability of the acquiree and contingent consideration of the acquirer are different animals. Contingent consideration is part of what the acquirer agreed to pay, so it is recognised on day one at its fair value, uncertainty and all — the uncertainty is priced into that fair value rather than being a reason to wait. Leaving it out would understate both the consideration and goodwill by ₹21 crore.

citation.ref: Contingent consideration recognised at acquisition-date fair value, and its classification as a liability or as equity

items.scenario: Vaishali Biotech Ltd acquired the whole of Sumeru Labs Ltd on 1 July 2025 for cash of ₹80 crore, plus two further promises. The first is 10,00,000 of Vaishali's own equity shares, a fixed number, if Sumeru's revenue for 2025-26 exceeds ₹100 crore; it was worth ₹12 crore on 1 July 2025. The second is cash of ₹15 crore if a drug approval comes through by 30 June 2026; it was worth ₹9 crore on 1 July 2025. The finance controller proposes to measure goodwill off the ₹80 crore paid and to disclose the two promises in a note until they are settled.

items.stem: What goes into the accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹2 crore and ₹2 crore, both added to goodwill
options.misconception: treats every later change in contingent consideration as a correction to the price paid, so it goes back to the goodwill figure
options.why: Goodwill is measured once, on the acquisition date, off what the consideration was worth then. Later movements are about how the bet turned out, not about what was agreed, and running them through goodwill would leave a balance that drifts for years with every reassessment. Goodwill moves only for a measurement period adjustment, which is information about facts that already existed on the acquisition date.

options.text: Nothing for the shares, and a ₹2 crore charge to profit or loss for the cash
options.why: Contingent consideration classified as equity is not remeasured, so the move from ₹12 crore to ₹14 crore is ignored altogether, and when the shares are eventually issued the settlement is dealt with within equity. The cash-settled obligation is treated the other way: it is measured at fair value at each reporting date and the movement is recognised in profit or loss, so the rise from ₹9 crore to ₹11 crore is a ₹2 crore charge for the year. It is not a measurement period adjustment either, because it comes from events after the acquisition date — the approval drawing nearer — rather than from information about what was already true on 1 July 2025.

options.text: ₹2 crore to profit or loss for the cash, and ₹2 crore taken to equity for the shares
options.misconception: remeasures the equity-classified promise and simply routes the change through equity instead of profit, when the promise is not remeasured at all
options.why: The rule is not about where the change is posted; it is that no change is recognised. An obligation to be settled in a fixed number of the acquirer's own shares is fixed at its acquisition-date value and left there, whatever the shares later become worth, because settling it costs the company nothing it can measure in cash. Recognising ₹2 crore in equity would move one part of equity into another for no reason.

options.text: Nothing for either, since neither contingency has yet been resolved at 31 March 2026
options.misconception: waits for the outcome before recognising anything, when a liability measured at fair value moves as the odds move
options.why: The cash obligation is a financial liability carried at fair value, and fair value changes with the probability of the approval well before the approval arrives. Waiting would keep the liability at ₹9 crore while everyone concerned knows it is worth ₹11 crore. The shares are indeed left alone, but for a different reason — not because the outcome is unresolved, but because an equity-classified promise is never remeasured.

citation.ref: Subsequent measurement of contingent consideration — equity not remeasured, other contingent consideration at fair value through profit or loss

items.scenario: On the Sumeru Labs acquisition of 1 July 2025, Vaishali Biotech Ltd recognised the share-settled earn-out in equity at ₹12 crore and the cash-settled earn-out as a liability at ₹9 crore. At 31 March 2026 the revenue target is all but certain and the share obligation is worth ₹14 crore, while the drug approval has moved several steps closer and the cash obligation is worth ₹11 crore. The finance controller wants both increases taken to goodwill, on the ground that both relate to the price paid for Sumeru.

items.stem: How is each of the two corrections accounted for?

options.text: Neither against goodwill — both are charged to profit or loss for the year in which they were discovered
options.misconception: treats every late discovery as an event of the year it was found, which would leave the acquisition accounting permanently as first drafted
options.why: The measurement period exists because a fair value exercise cannot be finished the week a deal closes, and inside it the accounting is put right retrospectively rather than through the current year. So the patent adjustment goes back to the acquisition date. The tax demand does not reach profit or loss of 2026-27 either — it is corrected under Ind AS 8 by restating the earlier figures, which is not the same as charging the year in which somebody noticed.

options.text: The patent against goodwill; the tax demand as an expense of 2026-27, being a liability identified in that year
options.misconception: treats the date of discovery as the date the liability arose, when the obligation existed before the acquisition
options.why: The demand is for 2023-24 and the obligation existed on the acquisition date, so nothing about 2026-27 caused it. Charging it there would report a cost of running the business in a year in which the business did nothing to incur it. The correct route is a restatement under Ind AS 8, which puts the liability where it belongs and leaves goodwill alone because the measurement period had already closed.

options.text: The patent against goodwill; the tax demand as a prior period error
options.why: The patent is a measurement-period adjustment: the information concerns facts that existed at the acquisition date and it arrived inside a year of it, so the provisional figure is corrected as though the accounting had been completed on 1 July 2025 — the patent rises by ₹6 crore to ₹18 crore and goodwill comes down by ₹6 crore. The tax demand surfaced in September 2026, more than one year after the acquisition, and the measurement period cannot run beyond one year however much is still unknown. A change coming to light after it closes is not put against goodwill: it is dealt with as an error under Ind AS 8, and the ₹3 crore liability is recognised that way.

options.text: Both against goodwill, since both concern facts existing on 1 July 2025
options.misconception: applies the acquisition-date facts test on its own and misses the one-year window that runs alongside it
options.why: Two conditions have to hold together, not one. The information must be about facts that existed at the acquisition date, and it must arrive within the measurement period, which ends as soon as the acquirer has what it was looking for or learns that no more is obtainable, and in no case runs past a year. The patent meets both, so goodwill comes down by ₹6 crore. The tax demand meets only the first, and the window closed on 30 June 2026.

citation.ref: The measurement period, retrospective adjustment of provisional amounts, and the treatment of information arriving after it ends

items.scenario: Vaishali Biotech Ltd acquired Sumeru Labs Ltd on 1 July 2025 and recognised a Sumeru patent provisionally at ₹12 crore. In February 2026 the valuers finished their work and put the patent at ₹18 crore, on licensing terms that were already in place on 1 July 2025. In September 2026 a tax demand of ₹3 crore for 2023-24 came to light; the liability existed at the acquisition date and nobody had known of it. The chief financial officer wants both corrections taken against goodwill, since both concern things that were true on the day of the acquisition.

items.stem: What is the exchange ratio, and how many shares does Ambar issue?

options.text: 0.375 of an Ambar share for each Beta share, so 3,75,000 shares are issued
options.misconception: multiplies the ratio by the acquirer's own share count instead of by the shares of the company being bought out
options.why: 10,00,000 × 0.375 gives 3,75,000, but Ambar's own shareholders are not being paid anything — they keep the shares they already hold. The ratio is applied to the 4,00,000 shares that are being extinguished, because it is their holders who receive new paper.

options.text: 0.375 of an Ambar share for each Beta share, so 1,50,000 shares are issued
options.why: On a market price basis the ratio is the market price of the target ÷ market price of the acquirer, which is 45 ÷ 120 = 0.375. It says that a Beta share is worth 0.375 of an Ambar share at today's prices. Applying it to the shares being bought out, Ambar issues 1,50,000 new shares for Beta's 4,00,000, and that is the only new paper the merger creates.
keywords: market price of the target ÷ market price of the acquirer

options.text: 0.625 of an Ambar share for each Beta share, so 2,50,000 shares are issued
options.misconception: settles the ratio on relative earnings per share when the boards agreed to settle it on market prices
options.why: 5 ÷ 8 is 0.625, which is the ratio on relative earnings, and it is a real basis — but it is not the basis these two boards chose. A ratio has to name what it was struck on, because the market price basis carries the market's view of growth and risk while the earnings basis carries only last year's profit.

options.text: 2.67 Ambar shares for each Beta share, so 10,66,667 shares are issued
options.misconception: builds the ratio as the acquirer's price over the target's, so the dearer share is handed over 2.67 times for each cheaper one
options.why: 120 ÷ 45 is 2.67, and that is how many Beta shares one Ambar share is worth, not the reverse. The ratio always answers how much of the buyer's own paper one unit of what is being bought is worth, so the target's price sits on top. Written the other way round Ambar would hand over more than nine times the value of what it was buying.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — the exchange ratio on a market price basis

items.scenario: Ambar Ltd is buying Beta Ltd by an exchange of shares. Ambar has 10,00,000 equity shares, earnings per share of ₹ 8 and a market price of ₹ 120 a share. Beta has 4,00,000 equity shares, earnings per share of ₹ 5 and a market price of ₹ 45 a share. The two boards have agreed that the ratio will be settled on the current market prices, and no synergy gains are expected.

items.stem: What are the merged company's earnings, share count and earnings per share?

options.text: Earnings ₹ 80,00,000 over 11,50,000 shares, giving an EPS of ₹ 6.96
options.misconception: issues the shares but leaves the target's earnings out, so the acquirer pays and receives nothing
options.why: This is the mirror of the last one. The new shares dilute the bottom of the fraction while the top still holds only Ambar's ₹ 80,00,000, and the fall to ₹ 6.96 is entirely manufactured. Both halves of a merger move together: the paper goes out and the earnings come in.

options.text: Earnings ₹ 1,00,00,000 over 11,50,000 shares, giving an EPS of ₹ 8.70
options.why: Earnings first, from the two share counts and the two per share figures: (10,00,000 × 8) + (4,00,000 × 5) is 80,00,000 plus 20,00,000, so the merged company earns ₹ 1,00,00,000. Shares next, and only the new paper is added, so total shares after merger = 10,00,000 + 1,50,000 = 11,50,000. Divide one by the other and 1,00,00,000 ÷ 11,50,000 = ₹ 8.70.

options.text: Earnings ₹ 1,00,00,000 over 14,00,000 shares, giving an EPS of ₹ 7.14
options.misconception: carries the target's own 4,00,000 shares into the merged count instead of the 1,50,000 shares issued to replace them
options.why: Beta's 4,00,000 shares cease to exist on the merger; they are handed in and 1,50,000 Ambar shares are handed out. Counting them again would mean the same earnings are shared by paper that has already been cancelled, and it makes every share for share deal look dilutive whatever price was paid.

options.text: Earnings ₹ 1,00,00,000 over 10,00,000 shares, giving an EPS of ₹ 10.00
options.misconception: takes in the target's earnings but never issues the shares that bought them
options.why: The earnings arrive because the shares were issued. Adding Beta's ₹ 20,00,000 to the top of the fraction while leaving the bottom at Ambar's old count prices the deal as a gift, and the ₹ 10.00 it produces is the arithmetic of paying nothing at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — total earnings and total shares of the merged entity

items.scenario: Ambar Ltd has 10,00,000 equity shares and earnings per share of ₹ 8. Beta Ltd has 4,00,000 equity shares and earnings per share of ₹ 5. Ambar is absorbing Beta and will issue 1,50,000 new shares to Beta's shareholders. No synergy gains are expected, so the earnings of the merged company are simply the two companies' earnings added together.

items.stem: What has the deal done to each set of shareholders?

options.text: Neither side is affected, because there are no synergy gains and the total earnings are unchanged
options.misconception: treats the absence of synergy as the absence of any transfer, when the ratio alone decides how one unchanged pool of earnings is split
options.why: Total earnings are indeed unchanged at ₹ 1,00,00,000. That is exactly why the ratio matters: with nothing created, whatever one side gains the other must lose, and here the ₹ 0.70 Ambar picks up is the other face of the ₹ 1.74 Beta's holders give up. No synergy makes the deal a pure division, not a non event.

options.text: Both sides gain — Ambar's holders move from ₹ 8.00 to ₹ 8.70 and Beta's from ₹ 5.00 to ₹ 8.70
options.misconception: sets the target's old per share figure beside the merged per share figure without scaling it by the ratio, so a holder is credited with a whole new share for each old one
options.why: A Beta holder does not own an Ambar share; he owns 0.375 of one. The equivalent EPS after merger is what the merged company earns on the fraction he actually received, which is ₹ 3.26, and against ₹ 5.00 that is a fall of ₹ 1.74 per share. Reading the ₹ 8.70 straight makes every merger look good to both sides at once, which cannot be true where there are no synergies.

options.text: Ambar's holders gain ₹ 0.70 a share; Beta's holders lose ₹ 1.74 a share
options.why: For Ambar the comparison is straight, because its holders still hold one share each: the figure rises from ₹ 8.00 before merger to ₹ 8.70 after merger, an increase of ₹ 0.70 per share. Beta's holders cannot be compared that way, because each of their shares has become 0.375 of a share, so the earnings behind what they now hold are 8.70 × 0.375 = ₹ 3.26 against ₹ 5.00 before merger. The target's side carries the dilution at this ratio.
keywords: rises from ₹ 8.00 before merger to ₹ 8.70 after merger

options.text: Ambar's holders lose, because 1,50,000 new shares were issued and their stake is now smaller
options.misconception: reads dilution off the share count alone, when what decides it is whether the earnings bought in per new share exceed what those shares were already earning
options.why: Issuing shares dilutes only if the earnings arriving with them are thinner than the earnings already there. Beta's ₹ 20,00,000 arrived on 1,50,000 shares, which is ₹ 13.33 of earnings a share against Ambar's ₹ 8.00, so the new paper is richer than the old and Ambar's figure had to rise. A smaller fraction of a bigger pool is not automatically less.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — impact on the shareholders of each company and the equivalent EPS

items.scenario: Ambar Ltd earned ₹ 8.00 a share before the merger and Beta Ltd earned ₹ 5.00 a share. Beta's holders received 0.375 of an Ambar share for each share they held. The merged company earns ₹ 8.70 a share. There are no synergy gains.

items.stem: What is the highest ratio Ambar can offer?

options.text: Nil — any share Ambar issues must dilute its earnings per share
options.misconception: looks only at the shares going out and forgets that earnings come in with them
options.why: Dilution is a race between the two halves of the fraction. Beta brings ₹ 20,00,000 of earnings, so up to 2,50,000 shares can be issued against it before the per share figure is pulled below ₹ 8. Only the 2,50,001st share dilutes.

Work backwards from the figure that must be protected. To hold its EPS at ₹ 8 on combined earnings, the merged company may carry no more shares than 1,00,00,000 ÷ 8 = 12,50,000. Ambar already has 10,00,000, so at most 2,50,000 may be issued, and 2,50,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 0.625 is the ceiling. With no synergies that ceiling is also the ratio of the two earnings figures, 5 over 8, which is what a break even ratio means.

options.misconception: stops at the maximum total share count and reads it as the number of shares that may be issued, forgetting the shares already in existence
options.why: 12,50,000 ÷ 4,00,000 is 3.125, and it treats the whole permitted share count as new paper. Ambar's 10,00,000 shares are already outstanding and come out first; only what is left over can be offered. A ratio above one would also mean the buyer handing out more shares than the company it is buying ever had.

options.misconception: takes the ratio struck on market prices as an upper limit, when it is only the price agreed and sits well below the point where dilution starts
options.why: 0.375 is where the two boards began, not where the arithmetic stops. Between 0.375 and 0.625 Ambar's own earnings per share still rises above ₹ 8 — it is simply rising by less — so there is real room to negotiate, and knowing where the room ends is the whole point of the calculation.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — the maximum exchange ratio without dilution of EPS

items.scenario: Ambar Ltd earns ₹ 8 a share on 10,00,000 shares. It is absorbing Beta Ltd, which has 4,00,000 shares and earns ₹ 5 a share. Combined earnings will be ₹ 1,00,00,000, with no synergy gains. Beta's board is pressing for a better exchange ratio than the 0.375 struck on market prices, and Ambar's board will go as far as it can without its own earnings per share falling below the ₹ 8 it reports today.

items.stem: What has the analyst done wrong, and what should year one and year four show?

options.text: He should have inflated the flows to money terms and also brought the rate down to its real 6 per cent
options.misconception: corrects one side of the fraction and then corrects the other as well, so inflation is removed twice over
options.why: Each fix on its own restores the match. Doing both puts inflation into the numerator and takes it out of the denominator at the same time, and the project is flattered by the full inflation factor. The rule has one step, not two: choose which currency the appraisal is in and put both halves in it.

options.text: He should have added the 8 per cent inflation to the 14.48 per cent and discounted at 22.48 per cent
options.misconception: assumes a stated cost of capital is a real rate needing a premium bolted on, when the premium is normally already inside it
options.why: A company's published cost of capital is what investors actually demand in the money they are actually paid, so the compensation for inflation is already inside the 14.48 per cent. Adding 8 per cent again charges the project for inflation twice and would reject investments that create value.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; the plant earns ₹ 16,00,000 a year and the company's rate is 14.48 per cent, so it should be rejected
options.misconception: reads a cash flow and a discount rate as two independent inputs, when each of them is stated in a currency of its own and only matching currencies may be divided
options.why: Both numbers are correct on their own and cannot be used together. A rate that has been lifted to compensate for rising prices is asking to be applied to rupees that have themselves risen, and pairing it with rupees of today counts the erosion twice. Almost every project fails that pairing, which is why the mistake is dangerous rather than merely untidy.

options.text: He discounted flows stated in today's prices at a rate that already carries inflation; the money flows run ₹ 17,28,000 in year one to ₹ 21,76,782 in year four
options.why: A cost of capital of this kind contains a premium for anticipated inflation, because investors want the return they require in real terms plus the inflation they expect. So the 14.48 per cent is a money rate, and it can only be used on money flows. The ₹ 16,00,000 is priced in today's rupees, and discounting it at 14.48 per cent takes inflation out of the numerator while leaving it in the denominator, which is where his negative ₹ 3,83,563 comes from. Restated at 8 per cent a year the flows are ₹ 17,28,000, ₹ 18,66,240, ₹ 20,15,539 and ₹ 21,76,782.
keywords: contains a premium for anticipated inflation
the return they require in real terms

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — the inflation premium in the discount rate and the restatement of real flows

items.scenario: Ketaki Polymers Ltd is appraising a plant costing ₹ 50,00,000 that will produce a net operating cash flow of ₹ 16,00,000 a year for four years, estimated in today's prices. Inflation is expected at 8 per cent a year and will lift revenues and costs alike. The company's cost of capital is 14.48 per cent. An analyst discounts ₹ 16,00,000 a year at 14.48 per cent, gets a present value of ₹ 46,16,437, reports a negative net present value of ₹ 3,83,563 and recommends rejection. Ignore tax.

items.stem: What is the project's net present value?

options.misconception: discounts flows priced in today's rupees at a rate that already carries an inflation premium, so inflation is charged in the denominator and never credited in the numerator
options.why: This is the figure a mismatch produces, and it is the commonest wrong answer in the topic because both of its inputs are given in the question. The ₹ 16,00,000 has to be lifted to the rupees each year will actually bring in before a rate of 14.48 per cent may touch it, or else the rate has to be brought down to meet it.

options.misconception: takes the real rate as the money rate less inflation, when the two are linked by division rather than by subtraction
options.why: 14.48 less 8 is 6.48 per cent, whose four year factor of 3.4273 gives ₹ 54,83,728 and a net present value of ₹ 4,83,728. The subtraction is a rough approximation that drifts as soon as either figure is large, because the real return is earned on money that has itself been revalued. Dividing 1.1448 by 1.08 is the exact statement.

Discounting the four money flows at 14.48 per cent gives ₹ 15,09,434, ₹ 14,23,994, ₹ 13,43,391 and ₹ 12,67,350, a present value of ₹ 55,44,169, and less the outlay that is a net present value of ₹ 5,44,169. The other route reaches the same place: the real discount rate is one plus the money rate over one plus inflation, less one, so 1.1448 ÷ 1.08 − 1 is 6 per cent, and the four year annuity factor at 6 per cent is 3.4651, which on ₹ 16,00,000 gives ₹ 55,44,169 again.
keywords: the four year annuity factor at 6 per cent is 3.4651

options.misconception: inflates the cash flows and then discounts them at the real rate, so the inflation adjustment is made twice in the same direction
options.why: The money flows discounted at 6 per cent give ₹ 67,08,267 and an apparent surplus more than three times the true one. Once the flows have been restated in the rupees of each year, the rate that belongs beside them is the money rate. Six per cent is the rate for flows left in today's prices.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — NPV on the money route and on the real route

items.scenario: Ketaki Polymers Ltd's plant costs ₹ 50,00,000 and produces ₹ 16,00,000 a year for four years in today's prices. Inflation is 8 per cent a year and touches every flow alike. The cost of capital, which carries an inflation premium, is 14.48 per cent. The money flows are ₹ 17,28,000, ₹ 18,66,240, ₹ 20,15,539 and ₹ 21,76,782. Ignore tax.

items.stem: What should the finance head tell him?

options.text: The real route always gives the higher figure, because a smaller rate discounts away less
options.misconception: looks only at the denominator and forgets that the numerator was left in today's prices for the same reason
options.why: The real rate is smaller and so are the flows it is applied to, by the same factor, which is precisely why the two present values coincide. A rate can never be compared with another rate on its own; it is only ever half of a pair.

options.text: They must always agree, because inflation is one number and it cancels wherever it is put
options.misconception: promotes a result that holds under a condition into a rule that holds under none
options.why: The cancelling depends on every rupee in the appraisal carrying the same inflation factor, which is true of this plant and untrue of most. A manual written on the strength of one clean example will be applied to a project with a tax shield in it, and the real route will then quietly give the wrong number with nothing to flag it.

options.text: They agree only while every flow moves with prices at the one rate; two common features of a project break that, and there the money route is the one that works
options.why: The two routes match here because the real rate was derived from the money rate by the very factor the flows were inflated by, so the same adjustment cancels on both sides of the fraction. It stops cancelling the moment a flow refuses to inflate. A depreciation tax shield is computed on historical cost and stays the same number of rupees however prices move, and where selling prices and input costs are expected to rise at different rates each stream has to be inflated at its own. In both cases there is no single real rate that reproduces the answer.
keywords: selling prices and input costs are expected to rise at different rates

options.text: The real route is a classroom shortcut and only the money route is acceptable in a real appraisal
options.misconception: mistakes a legitimate second method for an approximation, when it is the money method restated
options.why: Both are exact. The real route is often the cleaner one to write out — a level flow becomes a single annuity factor instead of four separate compoundings — and it is the money route with the inflation factor divided out of both halves rather than multiplied into both.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions — depreciation charges and inflation, and separate inflation rates for revenue and cost

items.scenario: Ketaki Polymers Ltd's board has seen the same plant appraised twice — once on money flows at 14.48 per cent and once on real flows at 6 per cent — and both routes returned ₹ 5,44,169. A director asks whether the company can therefore drop one of the two workings from its appraisal manual and always use whichever is quicker.

items.stem: What are the three Sharpe ratios?

options.misconception: puts beta in the denominator, which computes Treynor and reports it under Sharpe's name
options.why: These are the Treynor figures. The two ratios share a numerator and part company only underneath, and the whole reason both exist is that the denominators mean different things — one charges for every wobble in the returns, the other only for the part that moves with the market.

options.misconception: writes the fraction upside down, so risk is divided by reward and the best fund shows the largest number
options.why: 24 ÷ 13 is 1.846. Inverted, the ranking also inverts, and a fund with almost no risk would score near zero and look worst. The measure is read as reward earned for each unit of risk carried, so reward is on top.

options.misconception: divides the whole return by the standard deviation and never deducts the risk free rate
options.why: 19 ÷ 24 is 0.792. What is being measured is the reward for taking risk, and the part of the return a saver could have had without taking any is not a reward for anything. Leaving it in flatters every fund by the same 6 per cent divided by its own risk, which is a different distortion for each one.

Sharpe is the risk premium per unit of total risk, so the risk free rate comes off the return first and the standard deviation goes underneath. P gives (19 − 6) ÷ 24 = 0.542, Q gives (16 − 6) ÷ 14 = 0.714 and R gives (13 − 6) ÷ 9 = 0.778. Higher is better, so the ranking is R, Q, P — the exact reverse of the newsletter's, because the newsletter never charged any of them for the risk that produced the return.
keywords: the risk premium per unit of total risk

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management — the Sharpe ratio as risk premium per unit of total risk

items.scenario: A family office holds three funds. Fund P is a pharmaceutical sector fund returning 19 per cent with a standard deviation of 24 per cent and a beta of 1.4. Fund Q is a diversified equity fund returning 16 per cent, standard deviation 14 per cent, beta 1.1. Fund R is a diversified large cap fund returning 13 per cent, standard deviation 9 per cent, beta 0.7. The risk free rate is 6 per cent. The office's newsletter ranks them P, Q, R on returns.

items.stem: What do the Treynor ratios say, and which measure should be used on which fund?

options.text: P 9.29 per cent, Q 9.09 per cent, R 10.00 per cent, and Treynor should be used on all three because beta is the more scientific measure
options.misconception: treats beta as a better measure in principle rather than as the right one only where the unsystematic part has already been diversified away
options.why: Beta is the right denominator when somebody else's diversification has already removed what beta cannot see. The family office holds P alone, so nothing has removed P's industry risk and nobody else is carrying it. A measure that ignores a risk the investor is actually bearing flatters the fund.

options.text: P 13.57, Q 14.55, R 18.57 — the order is R, Q, P, the same as Sharpe's
options.misconception: divides the whole return by beta instead of the excess return, which happens to preserve the Sharpe ordering and hides the flip
options.why: 19 ÷ 1.4 is 13.57. Dropping the risk free rate matters more here than under Sharpe, because it is the deduction that lets a low beta fund like R be compared with a high beta one at all. It also destroys the whole teaching point of the question, which is that the two measures can and do disagree.

options.text: The two measures cannot legitimately disagree, so one of the six figures must be wrong
options.misconception: expects two ratios with different denominators to rank alike always, when their usual agreement is a fact about diversified portfolios and not a rule of arithmetic
options.why: They agree in most real cases because most portfolios are close to fully diversified, and then total risk and systematic risk are nearly the same thing. A disagreement is information rather than an error: it is the signature of a portfolio carrying risk the market does not pay for, and P is exactly that.

options.text: P 9.29 per cent, Q 9.09 per cent, R 10.00 per cent — the order is R, P, Q, and Sharpe is the measure for P while Treynor suits Q and R
options.why: Treynor keeps the same numerator and puts beta underneath, on the view that risk which can be diversified away should not be paid for. P gives 13 ÷ 1.4 = 9.29 per cent, Q gives 10 ÷ 1.1 = 9.09 per cent and R gives 7 ÷ 0.7 = 10.00 per cent. P jumps over Q because most of P's 24 per cent of wobble is specific to one industry and beta never sees it. For a sector-specific fund that risk is real and the holder carries it, so total risk is the right charge; for the two diversified funds the specific part is already negligible and beta is the fairer denominator.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management — the Treynor ratio, and which measure suits a sector fund against a diversified fund

items.scenario: Fund P is a pharmaceutical sector fund: return 19 per cent, standard deviation 24 per cent, beta 1.4. Fund Q is a diversified equity fund: return 16 per cent, standard deviation 14 per cent, beta 1.1. Fund R is a diversified large cap fund: return 13 per cent, standard deviation 9 per cent, beta 0.7. The risk free rate is 6 per cent. On Sharpe the order is R, Q, P. The family office holds P on its own and holds Q and R inside a wide portfolio of many funds.

items.stem: What does Jensen's alpha say about the three managers, and about the newsletter?

options.text: Alphas cannot be compared here at all, because the three funds have different betas
options.misconception: turns a caution about comparing alphas across very different portfolios into a bar on computing them
options.why: The caution is real — alpha is at its most meaningful between portfolios of similar beta, and comparing a sector fund's alpha with a large cap fund's is comparing two different games. But each alpha still says something about its own fund against its own benchmark, and that is what answers the newsletter.

options.text: Alphas of 5, 2 and minus 1 per cent — P is far ahead and the newsletter is right
options.misconception: measures each fund against the market's 14 per cent instead of against a benchmark carrying that fund's own beta
options.why: 19 less 14 is 5, and it credits P with everything its extra beta was always going to deliver. The benchmark has to be built at the fund's own beta, because a fund running at 1.4 is expected to beat a flat market and a fund at 0.7 is expected to trail it. Comparing all three against one number rewards leverage and calls it skill.

options.text: Only P has a positive alpha, because only P beat the market's 14 per cent
options.misconception: reads beating the market as the test, when the test is beating what this fund's own market exposure entitled it to
options.why: R returned 13 per cent against a market at 14 and still added value, because with a beta of 0.7 it was only entitled to 11.6. Judging a defensive fund by the index it deliberately does not track is the same error as the newsletter's, one step further on.

options.text: Alphas of 1.8, 1.2 and 1.4 per cent — all three managers added something, and the newsletter is measuring the wrong thing
options.why: Alpha is the return a fund actually made less what a benchmark carrying the same beta would have earned, so it isolates what management added over the reward for simply bearing market risk. The benchmark is 6 plus beta times 8. P's is 17.2 and its alpha is 1.8 per cent; Q's is 14.8 and its alpha 1.2 per cent; R's is 11.6 and its alpha 1.4 per cent. Every one is a positive alpha, so all three beat their own benchmark, and P's 19 per cent is largely the 1.4 beta doing its work. A ranking on raw return pays P for the risk it took rather than for the skill it showed.
keywords: P's is 17.2 and its alpha is 1.8 per cent
R's is 11.6 and its alpha 1.4 per cent
Every one is a positive alpha

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management — Jensen's alpha against a benchmark of the same beta

items.scenario: Fund P returned 19 per cent with a beta of 1.4, Fund Q 16 per cent with a beta of 1.1 and Fund R 13 per cent with a beta of 0.7. The risk free rate was 6 per cent and the market returned 14 per cent. The family office's newsletter has ranked the three P, Q, R on returns and told readers that P is the best managed of the three.

items.stem: What is the banker's answer, and what does the ₹ 80 crore decide?

options.text: Never, and no cash moves at all — the FRA simply fixes the rate the lender must charge
options.misconception: sees that no principal moves and concludes that nothing moves, so the hedge is imagined to bind a third party who never signed it
options.why: The FRA cannot reach into Tapti's loan agreement; the lender will charge whatever the market charges in six months. The hedge works by paying Tapti a cash amount that cancels the extra interest, so cash certainly moves — it is only the principal that does not.

options.text: In six months, when the FRA matures and the banker lends the ₹ 80 crore at 8.40 per cent
options.misconception: reads an FRA as a committed loan at the agreed rate rather than as a contract on a rate
options.why: The banker has promised a price, not a facility. If Tapti cannot find a lender in six months it will have an FRA and no borrowing, and the FRA will still settle on whatever the reference rate turns out to be. That is why an FRA is bought alongside a borrowing arrangement and never instead of one.

options.text: Today, and Tapti returns it at the end of the three month period with interest at 8.40 per cent
options.misconception: treats an FRA like a swap of principal, when the sum named in it is a measuring stick and never moves
options.why: Nothing is exchanged at the start. The contract's whole cash effect is a single net figure at settlement, which is what makes it cheap to enter and what keeps it off the balance sheet. A contract that moved ₹ 80 crore twice would be a loan with extra steps.
