options.text: Never — the ₹ 80 crore only sizes the settlement, which is a single cash payment of the interest difference
options.why: An FRA fixes a rate, and it is not a source of money. It is an off balance sheet contract in which there is no transfer of principal: the ₹ 80 crore is notional principal, there to scale the payment and nothing else. What changes hands on the settlement date is one net amount, which the formula gives as N(RR − FR)(dtm/DY) divided by [1 + RR(dtm/DY)] — the differential on the notional for the contract period, brought back to present value. Tapti still has to raise its ₹ 80 crore from a lender in the ordinary way.
keywords: there is no transfer of principal

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management — features of a forward rate agreement and its settlement formula

items.scenario: Tapti Cements Ltd will need to borrow ₹ 80 crore for three months, starting six months from today, and fears rates will rise. It buys a 6 × 9 Forward Rate Agreement from its banker at 8.40 per cent a year on a notional principal of ₹ 80 crore. The treasurer's assistant asks the banker when the ₹ 80 crore will be credited to the company.

items.stem: What is the final settlement amount, and who pays whom?

options.text: The banker pays Tapti Cements ₹ 11,75,318
options.misconception: discounts the differential at the agreed forward rate instead of at the rate that has actually fixed
options.why: 12,00,000 ÷ 1.021 gives ₹ 11,75,318, using 8.40 per cent in the denominator. The money being handed over early can only be invested at the rate the market is actually paying now, which is the 9.00 per cent that has just been fixed, so that is the rate that carries it forward and therefore the rate that brings it back.

options.text: The banker pays Tapti Cements ₹ 11,73,594
options.why: Take the differential first: ₹ 80 crore × (9.00% − 8.40%) × 3/12 comes to ₹ 12,00,000, which is the extra interest the three months will now cost. Then discount it, because an FRA is settled at the beginning of the period and not at the end, and the rate used is the actual reference rate that has just fixed: 12,00,000 ÷ 1.0225 = ₹ 11,73,594. The reference rate finished above the agreed forward rate, so the banker as seller pays the buyer.
keywords: settled at the beginning of the period and not at the end

options.text: The banker pays Tapti Cements ₹ 12,00,000
options.misconception: hands over the raw interest differential and forgets that the money arrives three months before the interest it is compensating for is paid
options.why: ₹ 12,00,000 is what the extra interest will cost when the loan period ends. Receiving it at the start of that period is receiving it early, and Tapti can put it on deposit for the three months, so paying the full amount early would overcompensate. Dividing by 1.0225 is what takes the three months of value back out.

options.text: Tapti Cements pays the banker ₹ 11,73,594
options.misconception: settles the right amount on the wrong leg, so the buyer who was protected against a rise ends up paying for one
options.why: The whole purpose of buying the FRA was to be paid when rates rose above 8.40 per cent, and 9.00 per cent is that event. Where the reference rate finishes above the agreed forward rate the banker as seller pays the buyer; only a fall below it turns the payment round. Paying here would make the hedge a loss on both sides at once.
keywords: the banker as seller pays the buyer

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management — the settlement amount discounted at the post change actual rate

items.scenario: Tapti Cements Ltd has bought a 6 × 9 Forward Rate Agreement at 8.40 per cent a year on a notional principal of ₹ 80 crore, to cover a three month borrowing starting six months out. On the settlement date the three month reference rate fixes at 9.00 per cent a year. Take the FRA period as 3/12 of a year.

items.stem: What happens on settlement, and what has the FRA achieved overall?

options.text: The banker pays Tapti ₹ 11,77,048
options.misconception: keeps the payer from the rate rise case, so the company is paid for an event that helped it
options.why: Tapti will borrow at 7.80 per cent, which is cheaper than the rate it locked. Being paid on top of that would leave it better off than the 8.40 per cent it contracted for, and the seller would be handing over money in both states of the world. The payer is decided by which side of 8.40 per cent the fixing lands on, and here the reference rate is now below the agreed forward rate, so the buyer owes the seller.
keywords: the reference rate is now below the agreed forward rate

options.text: Tapti pays the banker ₹ 12,00,000
options.misconception: pays the undiscounted differential, ignoring that settlement falls at the start of the borrowing period
options.why: The direction is right and the timing is not. The payment is made three months before the interest it relates to would have been paid, so it is brought back at the reference rate that has just fixed. Here that is 7.80 per cent, giving a divisor of 1.0195 rather than the 1.0225 that a 9.00 per cent fixing would have produced.

options.text: Nothing is payable — the FRA pays out when rates rise and simply lapses when they fall, so Tapti borrows at 7.80 per cent and keeps the saving
options.misconception: reads an FRA as an option that can be abandoned, when it is a firm contract that settles in both directions
options.why: An option costs a premium precisely because it can be walked away from. An FRA costs nothing at the outset for the opposite reason: it binds both parties, and the buyer owes the seller whenever the reference rate finishes below the agreed forward rate. The company has hedged itself against the unfavourable change in interest rate, and the price of that protection is giving up the favourable one.
keywords: hedged itself against the unfavourable change in interest rate

options.text: Tapti pays the banker ₹ 11,77,048, and its borrowing cost is still 8.40 per cent
options.why: The differential is the same ₹ 12,00,000, because the gap between 7.80 and 8.40 per cent is again 0.60 per cent, and it is discounted at the rate that has fixed: 12,00,000 ÷ 1.0195 = ₹ 11,77,048, payable by Tapti Cements to the banker. The company now borrows at 7.80 per cent and pays this amount away, and the receipt or payment offsets the movement in the actual borrowing cost either way, so the effective borrowing rate is fixed at 8.40%. That is what was bought.
keywords: payable by Tapti Cements to the banker
offsets the movement in the actual borrowing cost
the effective borrowing rate is fixed at 8.40%

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management — settlement where the reference rate falls below the forward rate, and the purpose of the hedge

items.scenario: Tapti Cements Ltd holds a 6 × 9 Forward Rate Agreement bought at 8.40 per cent a year on a notional principal of ₹ 80 crore, against a three month borrowing starting six months out. Rates have moved the other way and on the settlement date the three month reference rate fixes at 7.80 per cent a year. The treasurer is asked whether the hedge has cost the company anything. Take the FRA period as 3/12 of a year.

items.stem: Where should the six month forward rate sit, and does parity hold?

options.text: At ₹ 82.38 — so parity does not hold and the quoted forward is too dear
options.misconception: reads the equation upside down, putting the foreign growth factor on top so the higher interest currency strengthens forward
options.why: 84 × 1.02 ÷ 1.04 gives ₹ 82.38 and says a dollar will cost fewer rupees in six months. It cannot: the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount, because otherwise a saver could take the higher rate and lock the exchange back at today's price. The rupee earns 8 per cent, so the rupee is the one that must fall forward.

options.text: At ₹ 87.23 — so parity does not hold and the quoted forward is far too cheap
options.misconception: puts the annual rates into the equation for a contract that runs only six months
options.why: 84 × 1.08 ÷ 1.04 gives ₹ 87.23, and it prices a full year of interest into a half year contract. Both rates have to be cut to the period of the forward before the ratio is taken, and doing it to only one of them would be worse still. The error more than doubles the apparent mispricing.

options.text: At ₹ 85.65 — so parity does not hold and the quoted forward is too cheap
options.why: Covered parity says the size of the forward premium or discount should equal the interest rate differential between the two countries, which written as an equation is F ÷ S = (1 + rD) ÷ (1 + rF), with each rate taken for the length of the contract. Six months of 8 per cent is 4 per cent and six months of 4 per cent is 2 per cent, so 84.00 × (1.04 ÷ 1.02) = ₹ 85.65. That stands against the quoted forward of ₹ 85.00, which makes forward dollars cheaper than parity requires, and the gap is a profit somebody can take without risk.
keywords: the forward premium or discount should equal the interest rate differential

options.text: At ₹ 85.68 — so parity does not hold, but only just
options.misconception: adds the differential to the spot rate instead of dividing the two growth factors, which is an approximation that drifts
options.why: 84 × 1.02 gives ₹ 85.68, treating the 2 per cent gap as something to be added on. Parity is a ratio: the rupees have to grow by 1.04 and the dollars by 1.02, and the forward rate is whatever makes the two paths end level. The approximation is close at small rates and wrong wherever an examiner puts large ones.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — the covered interest rate parity equation

items.scenario: The spot rate is ₹ 84.00 per US dollar. Interest rates are 8 per cent a year in India and 4 per cent a year in the United States. The market is quoting a six month forward rate of ₹ 85.00 per US dollar. There are no transaction costs.

items.stem: Which way does the arbitrage run, and what does it make?

options.text: Borrow dollars, invest rupees, cover forward — a gain of ₹ 66,000
options.why: Forward dollars are cheap, so the leg that has to be bought forward is the cheap one and the rupee route wins. The arbitrageur should borrow dollars, convert at spot, invest the rupees in India, and buy the dollars back forward. At 4 per cent a year, US$ 1,02,000 is repayable in six months. Convert at spot to ₹ 84,00,000 and invest at 8% per annum for six months to get ₹ 87,36,000. Buying US$ 1,02,000 forward at ₹ 85.00 costs ₹ 86,70,000, and what is left is a riskless arbitrage gain of ₹ 66,000.
keywords: borrow dollars, convert at spot, invest the rupees in India
US$ 1,02,000 is repayable in six months
Convert at spot to ₹ 84,00,000 and invest at 8% per annum for six months to get ₹ 87,36,000

options.text: Borrow rupees, invest dollars, sell the dollars forward — a gain of ₹ 66,000
options.misconception: goes to the currency with the higher interest rate without asking what the forward market charges to come back out of it
options.why: Run that way the arithmetic is the same size and the other sign. Borrow ₹ 84,00,000 at 8 per cent a year and ₹ 87,36,000 is repayable; buy US$ 1,00,000, earn 2 per cent to reach US$ 1,02,000, and sell it forward at ₹ 85.00 for ₹ 86,70,000 — a loss of ₹ 66,000. Which way an arbitrage runs is decided by where the quoted forward sits against parity, never by which interest rate is larger.

options.text: Borrow dollars, invest rupees, cover forward — a gain of ₹ 3,36,000
options.misconception: counts the Indian interest as the profit and forgets that the dollars borrowed have to be bought back
options.why: ₹ 87,36,000 less ₹ 84,00,000 is ₹ 3,36,000, and every rupee of it is spoken for: the position is short dollars and closing it costs ₹ 86,70,000. The profit on an arbitrage is what is left after every leg has been unwound, which is why all four legs have to be written out before any number is reported; here what survives is a riskless arbitrage gain of ₹ 66,000.
keywords: what survives is a riskless arbitrage gain of ₹ 66,000

options.text: There is no arbitrage, because a quoted forward rate always embeds the interest differential
options.misconception: assumes parity holds by construction, when whether it holds is the very thing the question asks
options.why: Parity is what an efficient market tends towards, not an identity the quote is built from. Here the quote is 65 paise below the parity rate, and the arbitrage exists exactly for as long as that gap does: arbitrageurs buying dollars forward to close their positions are themselves what pushes the forward rate back up to ₹ 85.65.
keywords: arbitrageurs buying dollars forward to close their positions

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management — covered interest arbitrage where parity does not hold

items.scenario: The spot rate is ₹ 84.00 per US dollar, six month forward ₹ 85.00. Interest rates are 8 per cent a year in India and 4 per cent a year in the United States. Parity would put the six month forward at ₹ 85.65, so the quoted forward is below it. An arbitrageur can borrow or lend freely in either currency, faces no transaction costs, and starts by borrowing US$ 1,00,000.

items.stem: What is the one day value at risk?

options.text: About ₹ 12.34 lakh
options.misconception: uses the 95 per cent multiplier while reporting the answer as a 99 per cent figure
options.why: ₹ 7.5 lakh × 1.645 is ₹ 12.34 lakh, which is the correct 95 per cent number under the wrong heading. The two figures differ by more than 40 per cent, and a committee that reads one believing it is the other is being told that a loss expected on one day in twenty is expected on one day in a hundred.

options.text: ₹ 7.5 lakh
options.misconception: reports the daily volatility itself as the value at risk, so no confidence level has been applied at all
options.why: ₹ 7.5 lakh is one standard deviation, and a move of that size or more happens on roughly a third of all days. A value at risk has to name a confidence level, and naming one is the same act as multiplying by its multiplier. Without it the figure answers no question anybody asked.

options.text: About ₹ 11.65 crore
options.misconception: multiplies the whole portfolio by the z-score instead of multiplying its volatility by it
options.why: ₹ 5 crore × 2.33 is ₹ 11.65 crore, which is more than twice the money the desk holds and therefore cannot be a loss it could suffer. The multiplier scales a standard deviation, so the portfolio has to be converted into its daily wobble first and the multiplier applied to that.

options.text: About ₹ 17.48 lakh
options.why: Value at risk is built out of three things — the horizon, the confidence level and the loss itself — and the working is the z-score for the chosen confidence level multiplied by the standard deviation. Put the volatility into rupees first: 1.5 per cent of ₹ 5 crore is ₹ 7.5 lakh a day. At 99 per cent the multiplier is 2.33, so ₹ 7.5 lakh × 2.33 is about ₹ 17.48 lakh. On about one trading day in a hundred the desk should lose more than that.
keywords: the z-score for the chosen confidence level multiplied by the standard deviation
1.5 per cent of ₹ 5 crore is ₹ 7.5 lakh a day

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — the components of value at risk and the z score on the standard deviation

items.scenario: The treasury of Corvid Capital holds an equity portfolio worth ₹ 5 crore whose daily return has a standard deviation of 1.5 per cent. Returns may be taken as normally distributed. The risk committee wants the one day figure at 99 per cent confidence, and the analyst is told that the area under the normal curve gives 2.33 at that level and 1.645 at 95 per cent.

items.stem: What is the ten day value at risk?

options.text: About ₹ 55.26 lakh
options.why: Over a longer horizon the standard deviation scales by the square root of the number of days, not by the number of days, because daily moves that are independent partly cancel one another rather than piling up. So ₹ 17.48 lakh × 3.162 is about ₹ 55.26 lakh, and the committee should expect a loss worse than that on roughly one trading fortnight in a hundred.
keywords: the standard deviation scales by the square root of the number of days

options.text: About ₹ 1.75 lakh
options.misconception: divides by the number of days instead of scaling up, so a longer horizon is reported as safer
options.why: Dividing turns a ten day figure into something smaller than the one day figure, which says the desk is safer the longer it is exposed. Averaging has its uses elsewhere; here the question is the size of a loss over a window, and a wider window can only hold a larger one.

options.text: About ₹ 17.48 lakh
options.misconception: treats the horizon as an input the number does not depend on, so a longer window reports the same risk
options.why: The horizon is one of the three things a value at risk is built from, and changing it must change the answer. A desk can lose more in ten days than in one for the plain reason that it has ten chances rather than one; a figure that ignored the window would be unusable for any limit.

options.text: About ₹ 174.75 lakh
options.misconception: multiplies the daily figure by the number of days, as though every day's worst case arrived together
options.why: Ten times ₹ 17.48 lakh assumes ten consecutive bad days of exactly the worst size, which is a far rarer event than a ten day loss at the same confidence. Independent daily moves add in variance, and variance is the square of the standard deviation, which is where the root comes from.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — value at risk over a longer horizon

items.scenario: Corvid Capital's one day value at risk on its ₹ 5 crore equity portfolio is about ₹ 17.48 lakh at 99 per cent confidence. The risk committee now wants the same figure over ten trading days, on the same assumption of normally distributed daily returns. Take the square root of ten as 3.162.

items.stem: What should the board do with the figures?

options.text: Drop the exercise, since a model resting on an assumption markets break cannot be relied on
options.misconception: discards a measure for a limitation it states openly, leaving the position measured by nothing at all
options.why: Every risk measure rests on assumptions; the useful question is whether this one is stated and understood. Dealing limits, performance comparison and treasury management all need some agreed number, and abandoning the only one on offer replaces a known approximation with no measurement.

options.text: Use them as the worst loss the desk can suffer, and size the capital buffer at ₹ 55.26 lakh
options.misconception: reads a confidence threshold as a ceiling, so the one day in a hundred that breaches it is treated as impossible
options.why: A 99 per cent figure is the point beyond which the worst 1 per cent of outcomes begins, and it says nothing whatever about how far into that tail a bad day travels. Sizing a buffer at exactly the threshold funds every day except the ones that matter.

options.text: Use them for limits, performance measurement and balance sheet management, and record what they do not say
options.why: The measure has a settled set of uses: it puts a number on the largest loss a position is likely to suffer, gives a benchmark against which a desk's performance can be judged, sets limits for front-office dealers in a treasury, guides which trades are worth doing, and serves asset-liability management in a bank. Its limits belong in the same note rather than instead of it — the figure assumes a normal distribution of returns, says nothing about how large the loss becomes on the days it is breached, and rests on a standard deviation measured in the past.
keywords: sets limits for front-office dealers in a treasury
serves asset-liability management in a bank
assumes a normal distribution of returns

options.text: Keep them for reporting but not for limits, because a number computed from past volatility cannot bind a future trade
options.misconception: accepts the figure where it is harmless and refuses it exactly where the module puts it to work
options.why: Setting limits for individual dealers is one of the uses the measure was built for, and it is the use that changes behaviour. Past volatility is the input to almost every forward looking risk number in finance; the answer to its staleness is to recompute it often, not to stop acting on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — applications of value at risk and the normality assumption

items.scenario: Corvid Capital's board has been given a one day value at risk of ₹ 17.48 lakh and a ten day figure of ₹ 55.26 lakh, both at 99 per cent. One director wants the numbers written into the dealing mandates. Another says the model assumes something about returns that markets do not honour, and that on that ground the whole exercise should be dropped.

items.stem: Whose cash flows should decide this investment, and why do the two differ?

options.text: Whichever of the two is higher, since a project a company would accept on either view is worth doing
options.misconception: turns a choice of viewpoint into a search for the answer that approves the project
options.why: The two views answer different questions and only one of them is the shareholders' — whether the money comes back. Taking the better of the two guarantees that no foreign project is ever rejected on the ground that its earnings are stuck abroad, which is the risk the second view exists to catch.

options.text: The project's — its local currency return beats local competitors, which is the test for a foreign investment
options.misconception: applies the local comparison test to a plant that exists to replace the parent's imports rather than to compete for local customers
options.why: The local comparison is a fair test where the parent's alternative was to buy shares in a local company instead. It is not a test at all where the plant's output goes back to the parent, because it has no local competitor doing the same job. And a return that cannot be brought home does not reach the people the board answers to.

options.text: The parent's — what is actually remitted, after host and home tax and after the exchange control holdback
options.why: Project and parent flows come apart for three reasons: tax rules, exchange controls, and the form the return takes. Royalties and management fees are a cost inside the project and a return to the parent, so the same rupee is subtracted in one statement and added in the other. Profits sent home are taxed once in the host country and again at home. And a plant built to replace imports is not really competing with local firms, so the local comparison that the local-currency figure passes is not the test the Indian shareholders care about. What funds their dividends is what reaches India.
keywords: tax rules, exchange controls, and the form the return takes
Royalties and management fees are a cost inside the project
taxed once in the host country and again at home

options.text: The parent's, counting in the subsidiary's own borrowings and repayments alongside the remittances, since all of it is cash that moves
options.misconception: folds financing flows in with operating flows, so a loan drawdown reads as a return the investment produced
options.why: Both operating and financial flows reach the parent and both matter, but they must not be mixed with one another when the question is what the investment earns. A drawdown swells the year it lands in and the repayment hollows out a later one, and neither has anything to do with whether the plant is worth building.
keywords: they must not be mixed with one another

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management — project against parent cash flows

items.scenario: Sarthak Auto Ltd, an Indian company, is appraising a plant in a South American country. The local team's net present value in local currency comfortably clears what local competitors earn. The parent will receive royalties and management fees, the host country deducts tax on dividends remitted, and exchange control rules will hold back part of each year's profits for at least three years. The plant will supply components Sarthak currently imports.

items.stem: How does the ₹ 40 crore enter the appraisal, and where does the political risk go?

options.text: It cuts the outlay to ₹ 110 crore, and the political risk is handled by adjusting the cash flows
options.why: Balances stranded abroad by exchange control are direct blocked funds. They are already the company's money and are worth little where they sit, so where the parent can release them into a project in that country they go to reduce the cost of the investment outlay and only ₹ 110 crore of fresh money leaves India. Local and withholding taxes on remittance block funds indirectly and come off what counts to the parent. As for the political risk, the sounder place for it is the numerator: the flows expected each year are turned into certainty equivalents rather than a premium being loaded onto one discount rate.
keywords: they go to reduce the cost of the investment outlay

options.text: It cuts the outlay to ₹ 110 crore, and the political risk is handled by raising the discount rate
options.misconception: buries political risk in a single loaded rate, which penalises the near years far more heavily than the distant ones it actually threatens
options.why: A higher rate compounds, so it takes most from the flows furthest away and least from the flows closest — the opposite shape to a political risk, which usually threatens a mature plant more than a half built one. Combining every risk into one rate also hides which risk is being priced. Adjusting the flows themselves keeps the two questions apart.

options.text: It is added to the project's inflows in year one, and the political risk is handled by adjusting the cash flows
options.misconception: counts a balance the company already owns as a return the new project generated
options.why: The ₹ 40 crore existed before this plant was thought of, so it cannot be a receipt from it. Its effect is on the cost side: it means less new money has to be committed. Putting it in as an inflow would also discount it, which is the wrong treatment for money available today.

options.text: It is written off, and the political risk is handled by adjusting the cash flows
options.misconception: treats money that cannot be remitted as money that has been lost, when it retains its full value for anything spent inside that country
options.why: Blocked is not gone. The restriction is on crossing a border, not on spending, and a rupee of blocked balance put into a plant in that country buys exactly as much plant as a fresh rupee sent from India. Writing it off would make the company keep sending new money while an idle balance earns nothing beside it.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management — direct and indirect blocked funds, and adjusting cash flows for political risk

items.scenario: Sarthak Auto Ltd already has ₹ 40 crore of earlier profits sitting in the same South American country which exchange control will not let it bring home. It is now appraising a new plant there costing ₹ 150 crore, and the host authorities will allow the ₹ 40 crore to be spent inside the country. The board also wants the political risk of the venture reflected somewhere in the numbers.

items.stem: What is the treasurer's answer?

options.text: Interest rate risk, identified from the company's own repayment schedule and its credit rating
options.misconception: looks inside the company for the early warning of a risk whose source is the market
options.why: The repayment schedule says how much exposure there is; it says nothing about whether the rate is about to move. Two different questions get different evidence, and the second one is answered by what the central bank and the wider economy are doing.

options.text: There is no interest rate risk on a floating rate loan; the exposure belongs to the fixed rate borrower
options.misconception: hears floating as meaning the rate simply tracks the market and therefore costs nothing
options.why: Both shapes carry risk in opposite directions. Floating hurts when rates rise, because the cost of the same loan goes up; fixed hurts when rates fall, because the borrower keeps paying yesterday's price. Neither is the safe one, which is why the choice is a judgement about where rates are headed.

options.text: Operational risk, because the treasury chose a floating rate when it could have fixed
options.misconception: files a movement that comes from outside the company as a failure of its own people or processes
options.why: Operational risk is about what goes wrong inside — a payment keyed wrongly, a control that was not run. Nothing inside Sahyadri moves the repo rate. Choosing floating over fixed is a decision taken in the face of an outside risk, and calling the risk operational afterwards points the review at the wrong people.

options.text: Interest rate risk, and it is read off the central bank's stance, the government's own actions, growth, published industrial figures, foreign investment flows and the stock market
options.why: Financial risk is the unexpected change in things like prices, exchange rates, credit standing and interest rates, and a rate that resets sits squarely inside it: a movement in rates moves the value of assets and liabilities, and a floating rate borrower pays more as soon as rates climb, while the company on a fixed rate is the one left overpaying when they fall. What tells a treasurer it is coming is outside the company — the monetary policy of the government, a government action such as demonetisation, the rate of economic growth, the release of industrial data, what foreign investors are doing and how the stock market is moving.
keywords: Financial risk is the unexpected change in things like prices
a floating rate borrower pays more as soon as rates climb
the monetary policy of the government

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — financial risk, interest rate risk and the parameters that identify it

items.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd carries a ₹ 200 crore loan on which the interest rate resets with the market. The board asks the treasurer which heading this belongs under and, more usefully, what it should be watching so that it knows the exposure is about to bite.

items.stem: What is the exposure, and is the member right?

options.text: Currency risk, and he has it backwards — an exporter gains when the rupee weakens
options.why: Currency risk is a movement in exchange rates changing the cash flows of anyone dealing across a border, and it cuts both ways rather than only against. Sahyadri sells abroad and is paid in euro, so it gains if the rupee depreciates and each euro converts into more, which is the exact reverse of an importer with a foreign currency bill to settle. What to watch is government action, the nominal interest rate working through interest rate parity, the inflation rate working through purchasing power parity, natural calamities, war or a coup, and a change of government.
keywords: it gains if the rupee depreciates
the nominal interest rate working through interest rate parity
the inflation rate working through purchasing power parity

options.text: Currency risk, and he is right — a stronger rupee makes the company's euro receivable worth more
options.misconception: reads a strong home currency as good for everyone, which is the importer's position and the exact reverse of the exporter's
options.why: A stronger rupee means each euro buys fewer rupees, so the same invoice collects less. The gain from a strong rupee belongs to the company that has to buy foreign currency to pay a bill. Which side of the trade a company is on decides the sign of every exchange rate move.

options.text: There is no real exposure, because 90 days is too short a window for exchange rates to move materially
options.misconception: mistakes a short horizon for a small one, when daily currency moves accumulate over three months
options.why: Ninety days is long enough for a central bank meeting, an inflation print and an election. Currency risk is measured by the size of the move times the size of the exposure, and on a large receivable a move of two or three per cent is already worth hedging.

options.text: Counter party risk, since the exposure is to a European buyer who may not pay
options.misconception: confuses the risk that a debtor fails with the risk that the money he pays is worth a different amount
options.why: Both risks sit on the same invoice and they are separate. Counter party risk is about whether the buyer honours the obligation at all; currency risk is about what the payment converts into if he does. A buyer of perfect standing still leaves the exposure to the rate entirely open.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — currency risk for an exporter and the parameters that identify it

items.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd exports to Europe and is owed euro receivables due in 90 days. The finance committee wants to know which risk this is and what it should be watching, and one member argues that a strong rupee would be good news for the company.

items.stem: How are the two classified, and what should have been done about the supplier?

options.text: The supplier is counter party risk, and the way to manage it is to insure the whole purchase ledger
options.misconception: reaches for one instrument and skips the checks that would have kept the exposure small in the first place
options.why: Insurance is on the list and it is the last item on it, because it pays after the loss rather than preventing it, and it is priced on the quality of the counterparties anyway. Checking who is being dealt with, keeping any one name inside a limit and acting quickly on the first missed call are what keep the claim from arising.

options.text: Both are liquidity risk, since in each case cash the company expected did not turn up when it was wanted
options.misconception: classifies by the symptom, which is cash arriving late, instead of by the cause, which is a party defaulting in one case and a timing gap in the other
options.why: They need different cures. The supplier problem is fixed before the money leaves, by checking who is being dealt with and capping how much rides on one name. The timing gap is fixed afterwards, by lining collections up against payments or arranging a facility to bridge them. One label would send both to the same desk.

options.text: Both are operational risk, because in each case somebody inside the company failed to do their job
options.misconception: reads an outside party's default as an internal control failure, which is the boundary between operational and financial risk
options.why: Operational risk is a people or process failure inside the company. A supplier who takes an advance and vanishes made his own decision, and a collection cycle a month longer than the payment cycle is a structural feature of the trade rather than a mistake by a clerk. Calling both operational buries a financial exposure in a training plan.

options.text: The supplier is counter party risk and the missed payments are liquidity risk; the answer to the first is a process, not a single instrument
options.why: Counter party risk is the non-honouring of an obligation by the other side, and it covers goods that never arrive against money already paid just as much as it covers a borrower who defaults; credit risk sits inside it. Liquidity risk is being unable to meet liabilities as they fall due, and it comes either from not generating enough cash or from a mismatch in the timing of cash flows, which is exactly a month long gap between collections and payments. What manages the first is a routine — due diligence before dealing, not over committing to any one group, knowing its exposure limits and reviewing them and the credit approval procedure regularly, moving fast at the first sign of default, and taking performance guarantees or insurance.
keywords: the non-honouring of an obligation by the other side
a mismatch in the timing of cash flows

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — counter party risk and liquidity risk, and the techniques for managing counter party risk

items.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd paid a large advance to a machinery supplier who has since stopped answering calls. Separately, its treasury has twice missed paying its own suppliers on the due date, not for want of profit but because collections arrive about a month after bills fall due. The board wants both filed correctly and wants to know what would have prevented the first one.

items.stem: What is this, and what should Sahyadri do?

options.text: Political risk — and it is lowered by putting more of the venture into local hands and local money
options.why: The signs are the recognised ones: a demand that residents be employed, a restriction on conversion of currency, talk that ends in expropriation of foreign assets, and prices fixed by the state. Sahyadri should first size the country risk, from published political rankings, the country's macro-economic condition, how popular and how stable the government is, and what its own embassy there advises. What lowers the exposure is having less of a foreign look about the venture — sourcing raw materials and labour locally, going in with a joint venture partner, local financing so that a seizure would hurt local lenders too, and negotiations settled before the money is committed.
keywords: a restriction on conversion of currency
talk that ends in expropriation of foreign assets
local financing so that a seizure would hurt local lenders too

options.text: Not a financial risk at all, so it belongs on the strategic register rather than the treasurer's map
options.misconception: excludes political risk from financial risk because it is not itself a movement in a price, missing the route by which it is included
options.why: It is not a financial risk in the direct sense, and it is still counted under that heading, because an unexpected political change abroad produces country risk and country risk ends in a financial loss. The qualification is the thing an examiner asks for by name: the answer is that it is included, and the marks are for saying by what route.

options.text: Political risk, and nothing can be done about it except buy political risk insurance
options.misconception: treats a government's decision as entirely outside the company's influence, when how local the venture looks is a choice the company makes
options.why: A government confiscates a foreign asset more readily than one that employs its people, borrows from its banks and has a domestic partner on the board. Insurance pays afterwards; the four mitigations change how likely the event is, which is worth more.

options.text: Currency risk, because the threat that matters is the one about converting the local money
options.misconception: reads the label off the word currency, when what moves here is a government decision rather than an exchange rate
options.why: Currency risk is the rate moving in a market. A rule that stops money being converted at all is a government act, and it arrives alongside labour rules and threats to ownership that no exchange rate explains. The cure is different too: a forward contract does nothing about a conversion ban.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management — political risk, its identification, assessment of country risk and mitigation

items.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd has built a plant in an African country under a new government. That government has begun insisting that resident labour be employed, and has hinted that turning its currency into anything else may soon be restricted. Officials have also spoken publicly about foreign owned assets. The board wants the exposure named and wants to know what would lower it.

items.stem: Which description of the framework is the one the plan rests on?

options.text: The Reserve Bank sorts these companies into four graded layers on their size, their activity and how risky they are judged to be, and what the audit must test follows from the layer
options.why: The Bank arranges non-banking financial companies in four layers — base, middle, upper and a top layer that is meant to stay empty — and a company's place is read from three things together rather than any one of them: how big it is, what it actually does, and its perceived riskiness. Regulatory intensity climbs with each step up, so capital, governance, exposure limits and disclosure all tighten as a company rises. That is why the layer is not paperwork: it fixes which requirements the company must meet, and therefore which ones the audit programme has to reach for. A heavier plan on an unchanged business is the right answer when the layer has been read for the first time.

options.text: The layers are a reporting convenience for the Reserve Bank's own returns; they describe companies, they do not impose anything, and the audit programme is unaffected
options.misconception: treats the arrangement as descriptive furniture rather than as the thing that selects which prudential requirements apply to the company
options.why: The arrangement is not a description of companies; it is how the requirements are allotted to them. Capital floors, concentration limits, governance standards and disclosure obligations are written layer by layer, so reading the layer is how you learn what the company owes. An audit that skips that reading tests requirements the company may not have and misses the ones it does.

options.text: Three layers — base, middle and upper — the fourth having been dropped before the framework took effect, so the manager's note overstates it
options.misconception: reads a layer that is deliberately kept empty as a layer that does not exist, and so misses what happens when the Reserve Bank decides a company has become a systemic risk on its own
options.why: A layer kept empty is still a layer. It is held in reserve for a company already at the top of the stack whose potential to move the system has grown, and a company placed there moves up from the layer below rather than arriving from nowhere. Calling it dropped removes the Reserve Bank's sharpest instrument from the picture.

options.text: There is a single prudential rulebook for every non-banking financial company, so the classification cannot justify a heavier programme; the manager should restore last year's plan
options.misconception: believes the scale-based framework left uniform regulation standing, when replacing a single rulebook with a graded one is the whole of what it did
options.why: Uniformity is the thing the framework was brought in to end. Before it, one set of prudential requirements sat over companies of wildly different size and reach; after it, the requirements are graded, and a company's grade decides which of them bind it. Restoring last year's plan would test the wrong rulebook.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation for NBFCs
citation.ref: The four-layer structure, the basis on which a company is placed in a layer, and the top layer being ordinarily unpopulated

items.scenario: Vaishnavi Finance Ltd is an investment and credit company. Nothing about its business has changed in two years: the same three lending products, the same branch network, the same board. Its audit committee has therefore stopped the incoming statutory auditor's plan at the door and asked why the programme for the coming year is materially heavier than the one signed off last time — more testing of capital, a fresh section on concentration of credit, and a governance walkthrough that did not exist before. The audit manager's covering note says the Reserve Bank no longer treats every non-banking financial company as one population, and that where a company falls in the Bank's arrangement decides how much of the prudential rulebook the audit has to reach. One committee member reads the note and objects that a classification is a classification: it may change what the company files, but it cannot change what an auditor tests. Another says he has seen three names for the arrangement and is not sure the top of it exists at all. The engagement partner has to settle the description before the plan can be approved.

items.stem: Where does the company sit, and what follows for the audit?

options.text: Nowhere in particular — a company that is not named in the Reserve Bank's published list has no layer, and its obligations are whatever its own registration certificate specifies
options.misconception: assumes only the layer that is published by name has any effect, so a company absent from that list reads as unplaced
options.why: Only one layer is populated by the Bank naming companies. The others are populated by the facts — what the company does and how big it is — and every registered company therefore has a layer whether or not any list mentions it. Absence from the published list tells you the company is not in the upper layer; it tells you nothing else.

options.text: At the bottom, as the chief financial officer says — refusing deposits is what keeps a company out of the heavier layers, and the resolution settles it
options.misconception: treats deposit-taking as the only door into a heavier layer, so a company that has closed that door reads as being at the bottom whatever its size
options.why: Taking deposits is one route up, not the only one. A company that has never accepted a rupee of public money can still be large enough to matter to the system, and the framework was built precisely so that size counts on its own. The board resolution answers a question nobody asked.

options.text: In the middle band — refusing deposits does not decide it, and the company's asset size has already carried it past the line that does
options.why: Not taking deposits does not put a company in the base layer. The base layer is for non-deposit-taking companies sitting BELOW the prescribed asset-size threshold, which stands at a thousand crore rupees; once a non-deposit-taking company reaches or passes that threshold it moves into the middle layer, where it sits alongside every deposit-taking company whatever the size of those. At 1,840 crore rupees Harivansh is over the line and has been for more than a year, so the middle layer's prudential requirements — on concentration of credit, on exposures, on governance — are the ones that bind it and the ones the audit has to test. The absence of deposits changes none of that, and the fee quoted on last year's scope is not a reason to test the wrong rulebook.

options.text: In the upper band, since its assets are past the thousand-crore line and that line is what lifts a company to the top of the stack
options.misconception: reads the asset threshold as the door to the upper layer, when the upper layer is entered only when the Reserve Bank identifies the company and names it
options.why: The asset threshold moves a company from the base layer to the middle layer. It does not carry it further. The upper layer holds the companies the Reserve Bank has itself identified as warranting heavier treatment, scored against its own parameters, and a company is in it because the Bank has said so — not because a number in its balance sheet has been crossed.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation for NBFCs
citation.ref: Composition of the base layer and the middle layer, and the asset-size threshold that separates them for a company that takes no deposits

items.scenario: Harivansh Credit Ltd is a non-banking financial company with total assets of 1,840 crore rupees as at 31 March 2026. It has never taken a public deposit, its certificate of registration says so on its face, and its board passed a resolution years ago never to accept one. The company is not named in the Reserve Bank's published list of upper layer companies. On that footing the chief financial officer has asked you to cut back the audit programme: he says the company is plainly at the bottom of the Reserve Bank's arrangement, because everything that makes a company more heavily regulated flows from taking the public's money, and this company has never touched it. He adds that the fee was quoted on last year's scope and that the extra work on concentration of credit and on the governance framework has no basis he can explain to the board. Your manager has already found that the company's asset size crossed a line during the previous year and has been above it ever since.

items.stem: What does the classification of the account have to be at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Non-performing, and therefore sub-standard, because the dues have run past the ninety-day line that the Reserve Bank's phased tightening had reached by this year end
options.why: The Reserve Bank moved the applicable companies down to a single harmonised norm by stages, and the last stage lands on the year end you are auditing: from 31 March 2026 an account is non-performing once the instalment or the interest has been overdue beyond ninety days. At 112 days this account is past that line, so it is non-performing, and an account newly non-performing enters the sub-standard class rather than any deeper one. The staged dates are a deadline for getting there, not a menu of steps a company may choose from; and a middle layer company was on the tighter of the two old norms in any case, so this account would have failed the test on the earlier reading too.

options.text: Standard, because the account is fully secured and a recovery meeting is fixed; classification follows the prospect of recovery
options.misconception: imports the value of the security into the classification decision, when security bears on how much has to be provided and not on whether the asset is performing
options.why: Security decides the size of the provision, not the class of the asset. An account stops performing when the money stops arriving, and a comfortable charge over collateral does not make an unpaid instalment paid. A meeting in the diary is a plan, and a plan is not a receipt.

options.text: Non-performing, and straight into the doubtful class, since the account has been unpaid for well over a quarter and the company has no plan for it
options.misconception: jumps a class, treating the length of the arrears as what fixes the category, when a newly non-performing asset serves a period in the sub-standard class before it can move on
options.why: Length of arrears decides WHEN an asset stops performing. What happens after that is a separate ladder, and an asset joins it at the top: it spends a stated period in the first class before it can drop into the next. Skipping that period over-provides this year and leaves the file unable to explain the movement next year.

options.text: Standard. The company's own written policy governs, it has been applied consistently, and consistency is what an auditor is there to check
options.misconception: treats an entity's accounting policy as the source of a classification rule that a regulator has fixed, so a policy applied consistently reads as a policy applied correctly
options.why: A classification norm set by the regulator is not something a company's policy note can hold open. Consistency answers a different question: it asks whether the entity applied its policy the same way twice, and it has nothing to say when the policy itself is out of date. A policy that has gone unchallenged for three audits has simply been wrong for three audits.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation for NBFCs; NBFC prudential norms
citation.ref: The glide path bringing the non-performing asset norm to more than ninety days overdue by 31 March 2026, and the sub-standard class as the first classification of a newly non-performing asset

items.scenario: You are auditing a middle layer non-banking financial company for the year ended 31 March 2026. One borrower's account shows the instalment and the interest both unpaid for 112 days as at that date. The account is carried in the books as a standard asset. The finance controller produces a note he wrote three years ago setting out the company's classification policy, which says an account is treated as non-performing when the dues have run six months, and points out that the note has been used without challenge in every audit since. He argues that the borrower has been a customer for eleven years, that the security is comfortably in excess of the outstanding, and that a recovery meeting is scheduled for next month. He also says that the Reserve Bank published a series of dates for tightening this and that the company is entitled to sit on whichever step of that series it likes until the last one arrives. The engagement partner wants the position on the file today.

items.stem: What do the two decisions have to become?

options.text: The provision comes into this year's accounts and the interest already credited on the account has to come back out of profit
options.why: Two consequences follow together and both fall in the year of the reclassification. The prescribed provision on a sub-standard asset has to be created now, because the balance sheet being signed is the one that carries the asset in its new class. And the interest already taken to profit on the account has to be reversed. Income recognition on a non-performing asset is permitted only on realisation, so accrual on this account stopped on the day it stopped performing, and everything booked on it before that day and never actually collected has to be taken back out. That the interest was contractually due, and that nobody knew at the time, changes neither half.

options.text: Neither. Interest is reversed only where the borrower has formally defaulted or the account has gone to recovery, and the provision waits on the outcome of the recovery meeting
options.misconception: makes the reversal wait for a formal event outside the accounts, when the classification of the asset is itself the trigger
options.why: Nothing is waiting on a formal declaration or on the result of a meeting. The trigger is the classification of the asset, which has already been settled, and both consequences run from that moment. A provision that waits on an outcome is a provision made after the risk it was meant to cover has resolved itself.

options.text: Both stand. The classification changed at the year end, so the provision belongs to next year and the interest recognised before the change was correctly recognised when it was made
options.misconception: treats the date of the reclassification as the date the asset began to fail, when the classification records a state the account was already in
options.why: The reclassification is not an event that happened on the last day of the year; it is a finding about a condition the account had already reached. Everything that follows from the condition follows in the year in which the condition existed, which is this one.

options.text: The provision comes into this year, but the interest may stay, because it was earned under the contract and the company has not waived its right to it
options.misconception: confuses a legal entitlement to interest with the right to carry it in profit, when the norm asks whether the money arrived and not whether it is owed
options.why: The company's right to the money is untouched, and it may still sue for it. What the norm governs is whether that entitlement may sit in the profit and loss account before it has turned into cash, and on a non-performing account it may not. Losing the credit is not losing the claim.

citation.source: NBFC prudential norms — income recognition and provisioning
citation.ref: Income on a non-performing asset recognised only when actually realised, reversal of income recognised earlier and remaining unrealised, and provisioning against a sub-standard asset

items.scenario: The account in the previous engagement has now been agreed as non-performing and the company has accepted that it belongs in the sub-standard class. The finance controller has redrafted the note to the accounts and brought you two decisions he has taken on the back of the reclassification. First, he proposes to create the provision in the coming year rather than this one, on the ground that the account only became sub-standard on the last day of the year and a provision made on the last day serves no purpose. Second, he proposes to leave in profit the interest that was credited on this account month by month through the first three quarters, when nobody yet knew the account would fail. That interest, he says, was properly earned under the contract and properly recognised under the accounting policy in force at the time; reversing it now would be rewriting history with hindsight. The amount is not trivial and the company's profit for the year is thin.

items.stem: What goes into your report, and on which figures?

options.text: Move the reference into an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which is the heading that tells a reader something is being drawn to his attention without any reservation attaching to it
options.misconception: chooses the paragraph that points at a matter disclosed in the statements, when what is being communicated is a fact about the audit rather than about the statements
options.why: One paragraph draws attention to something already disclosed in the financial statements; the other communicates something about the audit that is not in them. Who audited which component is not disclosed in the statements at all, so it belongs in the second, and putting it in the first tells the reader to go looking in the accounts for a note that does not exist.

options.text: Keep the reference but use the chief financial officer's figures, since the reader is holding the consolidated statements and should be given percentages he can trace to them
options.misconception: treats the disclosure as a reconciliation to the consolidated numbers, when its purpose is to size the audit work done by others
options.why: The percentages measure coverage, not composition. Netting out intra-group trading shrinks the components as they appear in the consolidated statements but does not shrink the work the other auditors did, so figures taken after the entries understate the very thing the paragraph exists to disclose.

options.text: Keep the reference and state how much of the group the other auditors covered, on the components' figures before the consolidation entries go through
options.why: Where the report refers to the audits done by others, it has to disclose the magnitude of the portion those auditors covered — either as aggregate amounts or as percentages of the total assets, the revenues and the cash flows of the components concerned — and those figures are taken before consolidation adjustments are put through, so that the reader sees how much work was done by whom rather than what survived the eliminations. The paragraph belongs in the Other Matter section, and the reference is not a qualification of your opinion: it is an indication of the divided responsibility between the parent's auditor and the auditors of the subsidiaries. The chief financial officer's netted figures answer a question the paragraph is not asking.

options.text: Drop the reference. A report that points at another auditor's work casts doubt on the numbers, and where you are satisfied with their reports there is nothing to point at
options.misconception: reads a reference to another auditor as an expression of doubt about the figures, when it is a statement about who did the work
options.why: The paragraph says nothing about whether the figures are right. It says who examined them. Removing it does not remove a doubt, because there was none; it removes the reader's only means of knowing how much of the group one firm actually looked at.

citation.source: Guidance on audit of consolidated financial statements; SA 706
citation.ref: Disclosure of the portion of the consolidated financial statements audited by other auditors, stated before consolidation adjustments, and the reference as an indication of divided responsibility

items.scenario: You are the auditor of the consolidated financial statements of a group with two subsidiaries audited by other firms. You have their reports, you are satisfied with them, and you intend to refer to their audits in your own report. The group's chief financial officer has read your draft and objects to it twice over. First, he says that a paragraph naming other auditors will be read by the group's bankers as a qualification, and asks you either to drop the reference or, if you must keep it, to move it under a heading that signals no reservation. Second, he has recalculated the percentages you propose to disclose. Yours are struck on the components' own figures; his are struck after the group's consolidation entries have gone through, which removes the intra-group trading and brings the subsidiaries' share of revenue down by nearly a third. He says his are the more useful figures because they are the ones that appear in the consolidated statements the reader is holding. The audit committee meets tomorrow and wants your position in writing.

items.stem: On what does acceptance actually turn?

options.text: Whether a regulator or a recognised standard-setter is behind the rules; if one is, the basis is presumed acceptable, and if none is, it cannot be accepted
options.misconception: takes the presumption that attaches to a framework laid down by a regulator or a recognised standard-setter and turns it into the only route to acceptability
options.why: The presumption is a shortcut, not a gate. Where a regulator has prescribed the reporting provisions, or a recognised body has set them through a transparent process, the auditor may take acceptability as read absent something pointing the other way. Where neither has, the question is not closed — it is simply asked directly, by examining the framework itself.

options.text: Whether the basis written into the agreement shows the qualities an acceptable basis normally shows, weighed for this engagement — which is a judgement, not a checklist
options.why: Statements drawn up on a lender's accounting rules are prepared under a special purpose framework, and the financial reporting provisions of a contract are one of the recognised examples of that. Whether such a framework may be accepted is settled by SA 210, which asks whether it exhibits the attributes that acceptable frameworks normally exhibit; and in a special purpose engagement how much each of those attributes matters is a matter of professional judgment rather than a fixed ranking. So the partner's objection is a factor to be weighed, not a bar. A framework that two parties settled between them, with very cautious estimates chosen to serve their own needs, can still be acceptable for the purpose those parties have.

options.text: The senior partner is right to decline. Neutrality is not one consideration among several; a basis of accounting that both parties admit is deliberately cautious cannot be an acceptable basis for an audit
options.misconception: treats neutrality as a condition every acceptable basis of accounting must satisfy, so any deliberately cautious basis reads as automatically unacceptable
options.why: Neutrality is one of the qualities an acceptable basis usually shows, and it carries more weight in some engagements than in others. Where the statements exist to tell one identified reader what he could recover, deliberate caution is the point of the exercise rather than a defect in it, and refusing on that ground alone would rule out a whole category of engagements the standard plainly contemplates.

options.text: Nothing, since the loan agreement is a binding contract; once the parties have written the accounting rules into it the auditor's job is to apply them as they stand
options.misconception: reads the contract as removing the auditor's own decision about acceptance, when the contract binds the parties and not the firm asked to report on the result
options.why: A contract binds the people who signed it. The firm asked to report has not signed it, and it has its own decision to make about whether the basis of accounting is one it can report on at all. Treating the agreement as self-executing gives away the judgement the standard requires and leaves the firm with no answer if the basis turns out to be incoherent.

citation.ref: Financial reporting provisions of a contract as a special purpose framework, and acceptability determined under SA 210 by the attributes normally exhibited by acceptable frameworks

items.scenario: Your firm is the statutory auditor of a company whose lender, under the loan agreement, requires a separate set of financial statements for the same year drawn up on the accounting rules written into that agreement. Those rules are markedly more cautious than the standards the company normally reports under: receivables have to be written down heavily once they age past a stated point, and a class of intangible assets that the general framework would carry has to be left out altogether. The lender's credit team and the company's finance director negotiated every one of those rules between them, and neither pretends they are the right way to show the company to the world; they were chosen because the lender wants a cautious view of what it could recover. You are asked to audit the statements. The senior partner's first reaction is to decline. His reasoning is that a basis of accounting the two parties agreed for their own purposes is by definition not neutral, that an audit report cannot be put on a set of numbers built on a biased basis, and that the firm should not lend its name to a document whose rules were bargained rather than set.

items.stem: What do you require before you can sign?

options.text: The inventory basis, yes; the tax entry, no — deferred tax on a consolidation entry would recognise a liability to nobody, since the elimination exists only in the group's own presentation
options.misconception: ties the tax entry to a present obligation to a tax authority, when what is being recognised is the future tax effect of a difference the elimination has created
options.why: Nothing is being owed to anybody today, and that is not what the entry records. Removing the profit from the stock leaves the group carrying the asset at one figure while the tax authorities recognise another, and the entry records the tax effect of closing that gap when the stock is eventually sold outside the group. A difference that exists only in the consolidated presentation still has a tax consequence when it unwinds.

options.text: Nothing on either. The eliminations are complete, no tax has actually fallen due on them, and the note discloses the difference in the subsidiary's basis openly
options.misconception: reads both departures as adequately handled because each has a stated reason, when one misunderstands what the tax entry is for and the other applies a route the group's own framework does not offer
options.why: A disclosed departure is still a departure. Neither reason survives the requirement it is answering: one confuses tax that is payable now with tax that has been deferred, and the other borrows a relief that belongs to a different framework from the one this group reports under.

options.text: The spreadsheet read and traced, a tax entry against the profit taken out of stock, and the subsidiary's inventory brought onto the parent's basis
options.why: Start with where the entries live. Consolidation adjustments are not in any company's ledger — the parent keeps them in memorandum records, and reviewing those records to verify the entries made is the auditor's own step, not something the eliminations being arithmetically clean can replace. Then the two gaps. Stripping unrealised profit out of stock leaves the carrying amount and the tax base apart, which is a temporary difference, so deferred tax has to be recorded on the elimination even though no tax authority is owed anything today. And the consolidated statements have to be drawn using uniform accounting policies for like transactions in similar circumstances: under Ind AS 110 the subsidiary's inventory must be adjusted onto the group's basis before it is consolidated. Disclosing the difference instead is a route the older standards allowed where harmonising was impracticable, and it is not open here.

options.text: The tax entry, yes; the inventory basis, no — impracticability is a recognised answer where rebuilding the records would be disproportionate, provided the fact is disclosed
options.misconception: carries the impracticability relief across from the earlier accounting standards into an Ind AS consolidation, where the relief is a disclosure route and not an exemption
options.why: The relief exists, and it belongs to a framework this group is not using. Where the older standards let a group disclose that different policies had been applied because harmonising was impracticable, the Ind AS route requires the component's figures to be adjusted so they conform to the group's policies. The effort involved is a reason to start early, not a reason not to do it.

citation.source: Guidance on audit of consolidated financial statements; Ind AS 110; Ind AS 12
citation.ref: Consolidation adjustments kept in memorandum records, deferred tax on temporary differences arising from elimination of unrealised intra-group profit, and uniform accounting policies required under Ind AS

items.scenario: You are completing the audit of a group's consolidated financial statements under Ind AS. The consolidation was done by two people in the parent's accounts team working from a spreadsheet nobody else has seen; the subsidiaries' own ledgers show none of it, because none of these entries was ever posted in any company's books. The spreadsheet shows the intra-group sales, the interest and the inter-company balances all knocked out cleanly. Two things are missing. There is no tax entry against the profit stripped out of the stock the parent bought from a subsidiary and still holds, and the head of accounts explains that no tax has become payable or receivable anywhere in the group as a result of a bookkeeping elimination, so there is nothing to record. And one subsidiary values its inventory on a different basis from the parent's; the group has left that alone and added a note saying so, on the ground that bringing the subsidiary onto the parent's basis would mean rebuilding four years of costing records and is not practicable. Both positions are argued clearly and neither is a slip.

items.stem: What do you require on each?

options.text: Neither is a problem. The impairment test is triggered by an indication and there is none, and the pre-acquisition months are immaterial on the group's numbers
options.misconception: applies the indication-driven impairment rule to consolidation goodwill, and treats a period that must be excluded as a materiality question
options.why: One of these is not a test that waits to be triggered, and the other is not a question of size. Bringing in months during which the group did not control the subsidiary puts results into the consolidated accounts that do not belong to the group at all, and no materiality threshold makes them the group's.

options.text: The profit and loss account, yes; the impairment test, no — goodwill recognised this year cannot yet have been impaired, since the price was struck at fair value only months ago
options.misconception: treats a recent acquisition price as evidence that no impairment can have arisen, when the test is required at the reporting date regardless of how recently the goodwill arose
options.why: A price struck at arm's length months ago is evidence about that date, not about this one. The test is owed at the reporting date whatever the goodwill's age, and a first-year acquisition is precisely where an optimistic price shows up first — which is why the requirement carries no grace period.

options.text: The impairment test, yes; the profit and loss account, no — a full year of the subsidiary's trading gives the reader a better basis for comparison with next year
options.misconception: prefers a comparable presentation to an accurate one, when the period consolidated is fixed by when control existed and not by what reads more usefully
options.why: Comparability is achieved by disclosure, not by consolidating a period the group did not own. Including trading from before control existed reports as the group's results something that was somebody else's, and the reader who wants the comparison is given it in a note rather than in the primary statement.

options.text: An impairment test on the goodwill for this year end, and the subsidiary's results restricted to the part of the year the group actually controlled it
options.why: Consolidation goodwill is carried at the value fixed when control was acquired — it is not written up and it is not amortised down — and it is tested for impairment at every balance sheet date, whether or not anything has gone visibly wrong. So the auditor asks whether the parent determined an impairment loss at all, what procedure it used and whether the amount is fair, and looks separately at intra-group losses for any sign of an impairment that should have been recognised. "The subsidiary has traded well" is an assertion, not the test. On the second point, the subsidiary's income and expenses go into the consolidated statements only from the date control was gained, measured on the amounts recognised at the acquisition, so the pre-acquisition months come out however small they are.

citation.source: Guidance on audit of consolidated financial statements
citation.ref: Consolidation goodwill carried at its acquisition-date value and tested for impairment at each balance sheet date, and the subsidiary's income and expenses consolidated only from the date control is obtained

items.scenario: A group acquired a subsidiary partway through the year and recognised goodwill on the consolidation. You are auditing the consolidated statements for that year. Two things in the file trouble you. The goodwill sits at the figure fixed on acquisition and the working papers carry no impairment work of any kind; when you ask, the group's controller says the subsidiary has traded well since the acquisition, that nothing has gone wrong, and that an impairment test is something you do when there is an indication and there is none. He adds that the goodwill has only been on the balance sheet for a matter of months. Separately, the consolidated profit and loss account includes the subsidiary's revenue and costs for the whole of the subsidiary's own financial year. The controller explains that this is simpler and that the pre-acquisition months are immaterial in any case, and offers to give you the split if you want to check the figure. The audit committee meets in four days.

items.stem: Is the point closed, and if not, what remains?

options.text: Closed. The gap is inside the permitted limit, and once a component's reporting date is permissible the statements as drawn may be used as they stand
options.misconception: treats the limit on the gap as the whole of the requirement, so a permissible gap reads as a finished point
options.why: The limit decides whether the December statements may be used at all. It says nothing about what has to be done with the two months that fall between the two dates, and a group that stops at the limit consolidates a picture that is already three months stale on facts it knows about.

options.text: Not closed, but for one reason only: the December statements cannot be used at all, and the group must obtain a special-purpose set drawn to 31 March
options.misconception: reads the requirement to align reporting dates as absolute, when it yields to impracticability inside a stated limit
options.why: The rule prefers a common date and accepts a different one where a common date cannot practicably be achieved, which is the case where local law fixes the component's year end. Demanding a second closing asks for something the subsidiary is not permitted to produce, and the framework already provides for that.

options.text: Not closed. The gap is permissible, but the two months between the dates still have to be worked, and the move in the reporting period since last year still has to be disclosed
options.why: A component should be drawn up to the parent's own reporting date, and where that is not practicable the difference is tolerated within limits — not more than three months where the consolidated statements are under Ind AS, against not more than six months under the earlier standards — so a December close against a March parent may be used. Using it does not end the work. The auditor reviews the component's results between its date and the parent's for significant transactions or events that took place in that window and therefore need to be reflected, and a settled claim and a plant sale are exactly that. Separately, the assumption of consistency requires him to consider whether the lengths of the reporting periods and the year-ends are the same from one period to the next, and where a component's period has moved with a material effect, the change and how it has been treated must be disclosed.

options.text: Not closed, but the answer is disclosure alone: a note describing the two events and the change of period, without adjusting the consolidated figures
options.misconception: offers a note in place of an adjustment, when events in the intervening window are to be reflected in the consolidated amounts and not merely narrated
options.why: Disclosure is the answer to the change in the reporting period. It is not the answer to the events themselves: the effect of significant transactions occurring between the two dates is to be given recognition in the consolidated figures, and a note describing a settlement the numbers do not carry leaves the reader with two inconsistent accounts of the same year.

citation.source: Guidance on audit of consolidated financial statements
citation.ref: Permitted difference between a component's reporting date and the parent's, adjustment for events between those dates, and disclosure of a change in a component's reporting period

items.scenario: A group reporting under Ind AS to a 31 March year end has one foreign subsidiary whose statements are drawn up to 31 December, because the law of the country it operates in fixes that date and will not allow a second closing. The group has used the December statements in the consolidation. Your manager has confirmed that the gap between the two dates is within what the framework permits and has marked the point closed on the file. Two further facts have since come out of the group's own board papers. The subsidiary settled a long-running claim in February for an amount that is material to the group, and it sold a plant in the same month. Neither appears anywhere in the consolidated figures or the notes. And this subsidiary was consolidated to a 31 March date last year, when a temporary exemption in its own jurisdiction allowed it; the change back to December is not mentioned in the consolidated statements at all. The engagement partner asks whether your manager's "closed" is right.

items.stem: What has to change in the notes?

options.text: The breakdown goes in, but the subsidiary-level notes may stay — a disclosure that was required in a separate statement can hardly be wrong in a consolidated one
