options.misconception: reasons from a note being required somewhere to its being permissible everywhere, when the consolidated statements have their own disclosure population
options.why: A note earns its place by being relevant to the statements it sits in. Requirements that attach to a subsidiary's own statements do not follow the subsidiary into the consolidation, and carrying them across buries the disclosures that are relevant under a much larger pile that is not.

options.text: The two subsidiary-level notes come out, and nothing else changes; the consolidated totals already give the reader everything the framework asks for
options.misconception: applies the restriction on repeating component disclosures but misses the schedule of per-component figures that the same framework separately requires
options.why: Taking the repeated notes out is half the answer. The framework does not stop at saying what the consolidated notes must not contain; it also names a table they must contain, showing what share of the group each company in it represents. A reader given only the totals cannot tell whether the group is one company with hangers-on or five of roughly equal weight.

options.text: Nothing has to come out and nothing has to go in. Consolidated notes are not restricted, more disclosure is never a defect, and the consolidated totals are what a reader of consolidated statements needs
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a one-way ratchet where more is always safe, when the consolidated notes are confined to what is relevant to the consolidation and separately owe a per-component breakdown
options.why: Both halves are wrong in opposite directions. The consolidated notes are not a place to reprint whatever the components disclosed, and the per-component figures the manager has left out are required by name — so the notes are simultaneously too full and too empty.

options.text: The two subsidiary-level notes come out, and a component-by-component breakdown of net assets, profit and other comprehensive income goes in
options.why: Two rules pull in opposite directions and both bind. Section 129(4) read with MCA Circular 39/2014 is that consolidated statements carry only the disclosures relevant to the consolidation and do not merely repeat what the separate statements being consolidated have already said — so the micro and small enterprises note and the source of the bonus issue come out. Then Schedule III's general instructions for consolidated statements say what has to go in, separately for the parent and each component: net assets as an amount and as a percentage of consolidated net assets, share in profit or loss as an amount and as a percentage, and other comprehensive income as an amount and as a percentage, with the consolidation adjustments either shown on a line of their own or folded into those figures.

citation.source: Section 129(4); MCA Circular 39/2014; Schedule III general instructions
citation.ref: Consolidated statements carrying only disclosures relevant to the consolidation, and the per-component information on net assets, share in profit or loss and other comprehensive income

items.scenario: The notes to a group's consolidated financial statements have been prepared by copying every note out of each subsidiary's own separate statements and running them together under one set of headings. They therefore include the disclosure of dues to micro and small enterprises made by one subsidiary, and a note explaining out of which reserve another subsidiary funded a bonus issue. The group's reporting manager is proud of this: he says nothing has been left out, that a reader who wants detail can find it, and that no auditor has ever objected to a company disclosing more than it had to. What the notes do not contain is any statement of how much of the group's net assets or profit each company in it accounts for; the manager says nobody has ever asked for that and that the consolidated totals are what matter. He has asked you to confirm the notes are acceptable so the accounts can go to the printer this week.

items.stem: How far does the restriction reach?

options.text: Not this far. The restriction governs services to the audited company, and a separately incorporated company with its own board and its own auditor is not that company
options.misconception: reads the restriction as naming a single company, when it names a group of relationships around the audited company
options.why: Separate incorporation is exactly the arrangement the restriction was written to see past. If the audited company alone were named, any prohibited service could be routed through a subsidiary in an afternoon, and the section would protect nothing.

options.text: This far and further. The restriction covers the audited company, the company above it and the company below it alike, so an engagement at the subsidiary is inside it
options.why: The section does not stop at the entity being audited. It bites on the listed services wherever they are rendered to the company, to its holding company or to its subsidiary, so an engagement taken at a wholly owned subsidiary is squarely within its reach and not outside it. That the subsidiary is a separate legal person with its own board and its own auditor changes nothing, because what the section names is the relationship between the companies rather than their legal personalities. Book-keeping and accounts preparation is one of the named services, so this is not a borderline engagement.

options.text: It can be lifted by approval. The parent's audit committee may approve the engagement in advance, which is the route the section provides for services of this kind
options.misconception: applies the approval route, which exists for services the section does not list, to one of the services it does
options.why: Approval works on the other services an auditor may provide — the ones the section leaves alone. It has no effect on the listed services, which are shut out whoever approves them; an audit committee cannot consent its way past a prohibition addressed to it as much as to the auditor.

options.text: It reaches upward but not downward — a service to the company that controls the audited company could taint the audit, but a service to a company the audited company controls cannot
options.misconception: invents a direction for the restriction, letting it run to a holding company but not to a subsidiary, when both are named on the same footing
options.why: Both directions are named and neither is qualified. Nor would the invented distinction survive a moment's thought: a subsidiary's books are consolidated into the audited company's own statements, so work done below is work the audit above will be examining.

citation.ref: Prohibited services extending to services rendered to the company, its holding company and its subsidiary company

items.scenario: Your firm is the statutory auditor of a listed company. The chief financial officer of that company's wholly owned subsidiary has approached your tax partner directly and offered the subsidiary's book-keeping and accounts preparation work, at a fee that would be one of the firm's larger engagements. He has thought about the objection before making the offer and has three answers ready. The subsidiary is a separate company incorporated in its own right, with its own registered office, its own board and its own auditor, and your firm has no engagement with it of any kind. The restriction, he says, is written about the auditor's relationship with the company it audits, and your firm does not audit this one. Nothing about the work would ever reach the parent's financial statements without passing through the subsidiary's own audit first. And in any event, he offers to put the engagement to the parent's audit committee for approval, which he is confident of obtaining. Your tax partner wants to know whether he can take the call.

items.stem: Is the engagement inside the prohibition, and on what?

options.text: Outside it. The two firms are separate legal entities with no common partners and no shared income; a shared brand is a marketing arrangement, not a relationship the section recognises
options.misconception: treats legal separateness and separate finances as the test, when the section names the use of a common name, trade mark or brand as one of the connections that make a service the auditor's own
options.why: Legal separateness is the ordinary condition of a network, so a test that turned on it would exempt every network engagement there has ever been. The section reaches a service rendered through an entity whose name, trade mark or brand the firm or its partners use, which is what a shared brand is.

options.text: Inside it on the service, but not on the person — the work is a listed service, so the subsidiary should not have taken it from anyone, but your firm has done nothing
options.misconception: separates the character of the service from the identity of the provider, when the prohibition is a rule about what the auditor may render and needs both limbs to bite
options.why: The section does not tell a company what services it may buy; it tells an auditor what he may render. So the character of the work only matters once it has been shown that the auditor rendered it, and the question of whether your firm did anything is the question rather than an afterthought to it.

options.text: Inside it, but curable — the network firm may withdraw and refund the fee before the audit report is signed, which restores the position
options.misconception: treats a prohibited service as a defect that unwinding can cure before signature, when the prohibition attaches to the rendering of the service and not to the state of affairs on the reporting date
options.why: The service was rendered. Refunding the fee returns the money and leaves the fact where it was, because what the section forbids is the doing of the work rather than the holding of the proceeds. Withdrawal may be part of what the firm decides to do next; it is not a cure for what has already happened.

options.text: Inside it on both limbs — a listed service, rendered by an entity trading under your own brand, to a company the section reaches
options.why: Two limbs of the same section close on this engagement together. The work is design and implementation of a financial information system, which is one of the services named in the list, and it was taken at a company the section reaches. And it was carried out by a firm trading under your own brand name, which is one of the connections through which a service counts as rendered indirectly by the auditor — the work is treated as your firm's own however the invoice was addressed and whoever banked the fee. A separate incorporation, a foreign address, an arm's-length fee and the ignorance of everyone at your firm break neither limb.
keywords: design and implementation of a financial information system

citation.ref: Design and implementation of a financial information system as a prohibited service, and services rendered through an entity whose name, trade mark or brand is used by the firm or its partners

items.scenario: Your firm audits a listed company. During the year a firm in another country engaged the audited company's subsidiary to design and put in its new financial reporting system, for a substantial fee. That firm is a separate legal entity, incorporated abroad, with partners none of whom has any connection with yours; it pays its own taxes, carries its own insurance, and your firm receives no part of its income. What it does share is the name: it belongs to the same international network and trades under the same brand, and its letterhead and its engagement letter carry that brand at the top. Nobody at your firm knew about the engagement until the subsidiary's audit file crossed your desk. Your managing partner takes the view that this cannot be a problem, since the two firms are strangers in law, the fee never touched your accounts, and the work was contracted and performed entirely outside India. He asks you to note the position and move on.

items.stem: Was the engagement one the firm could take?

options.text: Yes, and no approval was needed — approval belongs to the listed services, and a service that is not on the list may be taken as the firm chooses
options.misconception: inverts the approval requirement, attaching it to the services that are prohibited outright rather than to the ones that may be rendered
options.why: Approval attaches to the services that are open, not to the ones that are shut. A listed service cannot be approved into existence, and an unlisted one is not free of conditions merely because it is unlisted — the clearance is the condition on which it may be taken at all.

options.text: Yes. The work is not one of the named services, and it was cleared by the audit committee before it started, which is what the section requires for services outside the list
options.why: Certification of foreign remittances is not among the services the section shuts out, so it was never prohibited work, and the question is only whether it was properly cleared. Other services stay open to the firm on one condition: they must be cleared in advance, meaning approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee, whichever of the two the company has. The approval here was taken, minuted and obtained before the work began, which is when it has to be obtained rather than afterwards. The engagement is therefore permissible and there is nothing to hand back. What the manager has found is the section working as designed.
keywords: approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee

options.text: No, because certification of a matter the audit may later touch is self-review, and self-review is the principle the section rests on
options.misconception: substitutes the principle behind the section for the section itself, so any engagement that could be argued to involve self-review reads as prohibited
options.why: The principle explains why the list looks the way it does; it is not a second, wider list running alongside it. Applying it directly would make the enumerated services pointless, and it would leave nobody able to say in advance what is permitted — which is the opposite of what a list is for.

options.text: No. The firm is the statutory auditor, and an auditor may not take non-audit work from the company it audits; the manager is right that the work should be handed back
options.misconception: reads the section as a general bar on non-audit work, when it bars a named list and expressly contemplates other services being provided
options.why: The section does not shut the auditor out of everything but the audit. It names the services that are closed and, in the same breath, provides for other services being rendered, which would make no sense if the bar were general. Handing back permitted work on a misreading costs the client and the firm and protects nobody.

citation.ref: Other services permitted where approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee, and certification work not being among the enumerated prohibited services

items.scenario: Your firm audits a listed company. Early in the year the company asked the firm to certify its foreign remittances for tax purposes, a recurring piece of work of a kind your firm does for many clients. The engagement was put to the company's audit committee, minuted, and approved before any work began; the fee is modest beside the audit fee. A newly joined manager has now read the section on prohibited services for the first time and has raised an alarm: he says the firm has taken non-audit work from an audit client, that the list of forbidden services shows how seriously the legislature treats the risk, and that the safe course is to hand the certification back, refund the fee and record the whole thing as a lapse. He points out that the firm is the company's statutory auditor and that certifying something the firm may later have to audit is exactly the self-review the section exists to prevent. The engagement partner asks you to settle it before the audit committee's next meeting.

items.stem: How do you characterise this transaction, and what follows?

options.text: As a disclosure matter. What makes a related party transaction risky is concealment, and nothing has been concealed here — the sale is recorded and the relationship is in the notes
options.misconception: equates the risk with non-disclosure, so a fully disclosed transaction reads as one carrying no risk
options.why: Concealment is one risk; it is not the only one. A transaction can be recorded, disclosed and entirely visible and still have been entered into for a reason the accounts do not show, and that possibility is what the extra procedures exist to test. Openness about who bought the land says nothing about why it was sold.

options.text: As a transaction requiring closer work only if something else in the file suggests a problem — the terms alone are unusual but not, on their own, a risk conclusion
options.misconception: waits for corroboration before concluding on risk, when the characterisation itself carries the conclusion
options.why: The conclusion is reached at the characterisation, not after it. Once the transaction is significant, with a related party, and outside what the company normally does, the risk conclusion is already made — and waiting for something else to turn up first means the extra work is designed only after the reason for it has been found by accident.

options.text: As one more related party transaction. The relationship is what makes it one, the relationship is disclosed, and it takes its place in the same population as the routine purchases
options.misconception: sorts related party transactions by the relationship alone, so a one-off sale of an asset the company has never traded lands in the same population as recurring trading
options.why: The relationship tells you it is a related party transaction. It does not tell you which kind. A transaction the company has never done before, in an asset it does not deal in, is a different animal from recurring trade, and putting the two in one population means the first gets tested at the sampling rate the second earned.

options.text: As a significant transaction with a related party that falls outside what this company normally does, which by itself makes it a matter demanding the fullest attention
options.why: A significant related party transaction that lies outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk, and that conclusion follows from the characterisation rather than from anything later found in the file. This transaction is outside the normal course on its face: the company has never sold land, holds none for sale, and the buyer is a firm owned by a close relative of the managing director. Disclosure of the relationship answers a presentation question and does nothing to the risk, and the routine purchases the finance director points at are inside the normal course of business, which is precisely why they are not treated the same way.

citation.ref: A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business treated as giving rise to a significant risk

items.scenario: Three weeks before its year end, a manufacturing company sold a parcel of surplus land, carried in its books for years, to a firm owned by the managing director's son-in-law. The price is a little above book value. The money is payable over three years, without interest and without security. The company has never sold land before and holds no other property for sale. The sale is recorded in the books and the related party relationship is disclosed in the notes. The finance director puts the position to you briskly: the transaction is in the books, the relationship is disclosed, the price is above cost, and every related party transaction the company has ever entered into has been handled the same way — the routine purchases from a director's trading firm, for instance, which you have tested on sampling for four years without comment. He asks why this one should be treated differently from those, and says that if the answer is only that the buyer is a relative, then the disclosure has already dealt with it.

items.stem: What does the standard require you to do here?

options.text: The summary and the minute are enough. They give you the terms and the reason, both from the company's own records, and the agreement adds nothing you do not already have
options.misconception: accepts a management-prepared summary as equivalent to the document it summarises, when the requirement is to inspect the document itself
options.why: A summary is management's account of what a document says, prepared by the people whose transaction you are examining. The requirement is to look at the thing itself, precisely because what is left out of a summary is what you were looking for.

options.text: Obtain external confirmation from the buyer of the terms and the reason, which is more reliable than anything held inside the company
options.misconception: reaches for third-party confirmation as the strongest evidence, when the third party is the related party whose motive is in question
options.why: Confirmation is strong where the confirming party is independent. Here the counterparty is the very person the transaction runs to, so a confirmation from him is management's account arriving on different notepaper, and it carries the reliability of neither an external source nor an internal record.

options.text: Read the contracts themselves, and test the reason for the transaction against the possibility that it exists to misstate the accounts or cover a loss of assets
options.why: For an identified significant related party transaction outside the normal course of business the standard asks for two specific things. The underlying contracts or agreements are inspected — not summarised, not described — because the terms that matter in a transaction like this are the ones nobody puts in a covering note. And the business rationale, or its absence, is evaluated against a particular question: whether the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal a misappropriation of assets. That is a sharper test than asking whether the reason sounds plausible, and "the land was surplus and we wanted cash" has not been measured against it at all.
keywords: outside the normal course of business

options.text: Read the contracts, but take the board's minute on the reason — the commercial wisdom of a sale is management's affair and not something an auditor evaluates
options.misconception: reads the evaluation of business rationale as second-guessing a commercial decision, when it is a test aimed at fraud rather than at prudence
options.why: Nobody is asking whether the sale was a good idea. The evaluation asks something narrower and harder: whether the reason offered holds up, or whether the transaction exists to do something to the accounts. That is squarely an auditor's business, and a minute recording a conclusion is not evidence of the reasoning behind it.

citation.ref: Procedures for identified significant related party transactions outside the normal course of business — inspecting the underlying contracts and evaluating the business rationale

items.scenario: You have concluded that the land sale to the managing director's son-in-law's firm is a significant related party transaction outside the company's normal course of business. You now have to design the work. The company's group financial controller offers to save you time. He will give you a signed summary of the transaction on company letterhead setting out the parties, the date, the consideration and the payment terms, all agreed to the ledger, and he points out that this contains everything the contract contains. He would rather not produce the agreement itself, which he says is with the company's solicitors and contains commercially sensitive material about other properties. On the reason for the sale, he says the board minuted that the land was surplus and that the company wanted cash, which is reason enough, and that asking why a company sold something it did not need is not an auditor's business. Your manager thinks the summary and the minute together are sufficient.

items.stem: What is wrong with closing it there?

options.text: The representation closes the completeness question, so the remaining work is only on the terms of this one transaction
options.misconception: treats a written representation as discharging the matter it deals with, when it supports other evidence and never stands in place of it
options.why: A written representation that all related party relationships and transactions have been disclosed is a necessary part of the file and not a sufficient one. It does not by itself provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the completeness of related party relationships and transactions, because it is management's assurance about the very thing management would be concealing if anything were being concealed — so completeness stays open and the procedures aimed at it stay owed.
keywords: completeness of related party relationships and transactions

options.text: Nothing. The consideration exceeds the carrying amount, so the company is not out of pocket, and a signed board representation covers the completeness of what you have been told
options.misconception: reads a headline price above book value as an answer to the terms, and a representation as evidence of the matter it addresses
options.why: Two shortcuts, and both fail. A price is not the same thing as terms, and a representation is not the same thing as evidence. Together they produce a working paper that records what management said and tests nothing.

options.text: The headline price is not the terms. Three years of free unsecured credit is where the value has actually moved, and that is what has to be evaluated and reflected
options.why: Beyond reading the contract, the standard asks the auditor to evaluate whether the terms are consistent with management's explanations and whether the transaction has been appropriately accounted for and disclosed. The price clears the carrying amount by a margin; the interest-free unsecured credit runs for three years, and the value of money the company will not see until then, with no charge for waiting and nothing to fall back on if the buyer fails, is where the substance of the transaction sits. So the arithmetic on the sale price answers the smallest of the questions, and the working paper concludes on a test nobody performed.
keywords: terms are consistent with management's explanations

options.text: The representation is the problem — it has been signed by the board rather than by management, so it must be reissued before the file can be closed
options.misconception: turns a question about what a representation proves into a question about who signed it, which leaves the same shortcut in place under a different signature
options.why: Reissuing it over another signature would change nothing about what it is worth. The objection to relying on it is not that the wrong person signed but that the document cannot do the work being asked of it, and a correctly signed version of an insufficient thing is still insufficient.

citation.ref: Evaluating whether the terms of a related party transaction are consistent with management's explanations and whether it is properly accounted for and disclosed, and the limits of a written representation as evidence

items.scenario: You have read the agreement for the land sale. The consideration is a little above the carrying amount, and it is payable in equal instalments over thirty-six months, carrying no interest and secured on nothing. The managing director makes his case directly. The company has recovered more than the asset stood at in its books, so no loss has been suffered and no asset has been given away; the accounts show a small gain rather than a charge, and there is therefore nothing for an auditor to write about. He has also handed you a written representation, signed by the board, that all related party relationships and transactions have been disclosed to you, and he suggests that between the representation and the fact that the price beats book value, the matter is closed. Your manager agrees that the arithmetic is right — the sale price does exceed the carrying amount — and has drafted a working paper concluding that the transaction is appropriately recorded.

items.stem: May the firm put an unmodified opinion on the balance sheet?

options.text: Yes, on condition that the report on the balance sheet refers to the disclaimer in an Other Matter paragraph, so the lender is told of it
options.misconception: treats disclosure of the disclaimer as curing a contradiction, when a paragraph describing the first report does not make the second one capable of being given
options.why: Telling the reader about the disclaimer does not remove the contradiction; it documents it. Referring to a modification on the complete set can be the right thing to do where the second report may properly be issued at all, which is a question that has to be answered first — and here the answer is no.

options.text: Yes, provided the two reports are never published together and the lender undertakes in writing not to circulate the one it receives
options.misconception: applies the separate-publication condition, which belongs to a report on one element, to a report on a whole financial statement
options.why: That condition exists, and it belongs to a different case. Where the subject of the second report is one element inside the statements, keeping the two reports apart is one of the things that has to hold. Where the subject is a whole financial statement, no amount of keeping them apart helps, because the objection is not that a reader will see both.

options.text: No. A whole financial statement is treated as too large a part of the set for a clean opinion on it to stand beside a disclaimer on the set
options.why: One whole statement out of a set is treated as a major portion of that set, however small it looks beside the rest, so a single financial statement can never be carved out and reported on cleanly on its own. An unmodified opinion on the balance sheet alone would therefore contradict the disclaimer already given on those statements as a whole, and the prohibition holds even where the report carrying the opinion is not published together with the report carrying the disclaimer. A fresh engagement letter, a separate fee and a single recipient do not change what the firm would be saying: that it can see the balance sheet clearly while it cannot see the statements the balance sheet is part of.

options.text: Yes, because the evidence problem went to results rather than to balances; the disclaimer on the complete set does not describe the firm's position on the balance sheet
options.misconception: reasons from the source of the evidence problem to the scope of what may be opined on, when the rule is fixed by the size of the portion rather than by where the difficulty arose
options.why: Where the difficulty arose is not the test. The rule works on how much of the complete set the second report covers, and a whole financial statement is over the line whatever the reason the first report was disclaimed. There is one narrow situation in which a disclaimer on results can sit beside a clean view of the state of affairs, and it is reached inside a single report on the complete set, not by opening a second engagement.

citation.ref: No unmodified opinion on a single financial statement where the complete set carries an adverse opinion or a disclaimer, a single statement being deemed a major portion of the set

items.scenario: Your firm has disclaimed an opinion on a company's complete set of financial statements, because records for a plant that carries most of the company's operations were destroyed and could not be reconstructed. The company's lender has now asked your firm, under a wholly separate engagement with its own letter and its own fee, for an audit report on the balance sheet alone. The company's finance director argues the point carefully. The new engagement is separate in every respect; the report will go only to the lender and will never be published alongside the disclaimed report; the balance sheet is a single statement rather than the complete set; and the firm has in fact obtained good evidence for most of what is on it, since the destroyed records went to results rather than to balances. He offers to put in writing that the lender will not circulate the report. The engagement partner is inclined to accept, on the footing that a separate engagement stands on its own feet.

items.stem: May the firm give an unmodified opinion on the schedule, and on what conditions?

options.text: Yes, but only if nothing in law forbids it, the report is kept out of the document carrying the disclaimer, and the schedule is a small part of the set — and the secretary's proposal breaks the second
options.why: An unmodified opinion on a specific element can be given despite a disclaimer on the complete set, and it can be given only where three things hold together: law or regulation does not prohibit it; the opinion is expressed in a report that is not published together with the report containing the disclaimer; and the element does not constitute a major portion of the entity's complete set of financial statements. Nothing here forbids the report, and a small receivables schedule verified in full clears the third. But binding the two reports into one annual report is publishing them together, so the secretary's convenience would destroy the second condition — the firm may report, in its own separate report, and not in that volume.

options.text: Yes, without conditions. The firm has the evidence for the schedule, and having the evidence is what entitles an auditor to an opinion
options.misconception: treats sufficiency of evidence as the whole of the entitlement, when the standard adds conditions that have nothing to do with how much work was done
options.why: Evidence is necessary and it is not sufficient. The conditions do a different job: they stop a clean opinion being read as saying something about statements the firm could not opine on, and no quantity of work on the schedule answers that concern.

options.text: Yes, and the binding is a presentation matter — what the conditions protect is the substance of the two opinions, not which covers they sit between
options.misconception: reads the separate-publication condition as a formality about presentation, when it is one of the three substantive conditions and is broken by exactly this arrangement
options.why: Where the two reports appear is the condition, not a gloss on it. It is there so that a reader holding a clean opinion on one element is not simultaneously holding a disclaimer on the statements it came from, and binding both into one volume produces exactly the reader the condition exists to prevent.

options.text: No. The disclaimer on the complete set governs everything drawn out of those statements, and an element is drawn out of them
options.misconception: extends the rule about a whole financial statement to an element, when the standard treats the two differently
options.why: The standard does not treat the two the same way. A whole financial statement is barred outright because of how much of the set it represents; an element is allowed through, on conditions, precisely because it may be small enough that a clean view of it says nothing inconsistent about the rest.

citation.ref: The three conditions on an unmodified opinion on a specific element where the complete set carries an adverse opinion or a disclaimer

items.scenario: The same firm, holding the same disclaimer on the same complete set of financial statements, has a second request. A counterparty to a bank guarantee wants an audit report on the company's schedule of trade receivables. That schedule is a small part of the statements, it was verified in full during the audit, and nothing about the destroyed plant records touched it. The firm is satisfied it has the evidence. Two people in the firm reach opposite conclusions and both cite the same rule: one says a report on an element may be given despite the disclaimer, so the firm may issue it; the other says the disclaimer governs everything drawn out of the statements, so it may not. Meanwhile the company's secretary has proposed, as a convenience, that the receivables report be bound into the back of the annual report along with the disclaimed audit report, so that every recipient has one document. Nothing in law or regulation forbids the firm from reporting on the schedule.

items.stem: Does the report have to reach the contractors?

options.text: No. The report covers the reporting entity, and businesses the company neither owns nor controls fall outside the boundary of what it reports on
options.misconception: draws the reporting boundary at ownership and control, when the principles are written to run beyond the entity's own gate
options.why: Ownership is not where the boundary is drawn. The principles are framed around the impact of the business rather than the perimeter of the company, and an impact that has been contracted out is still the company's impact. Drawing the line at control would let any company report itself clean by outsourcing whatever it did not want to disclose.

options.text: Only where the company has a contractual right to inspect. Reporting on a third party's premises without a right of access would put unverified information into the report
options.misconception: makes the reporting obligation depend on a right of inspection, when the expectation is that the entity engages with its chain rather than that it already has power over it
options.why: The absence of a right of access describes a difficulty, not an exemption. The framework expects the company to work on its chain — to encourage, to respond when something is wrong, and to say what it has done — and a company that has no visibility at all is reporting something meaningful when it says so.

options.text: Yes. The principles run down the chain the company buys through, and the conditions at the dyeing units belong in the report
options.why: The principles do not stop at the company's own gate. The governing structure is expected to encourage the entities in its value chain to adopt the same principles; the company is expected to respond to outside entities that violate them, and suppliers, distributors and sub-contractors are named among the entities that may engage with the business; and the principle on well-being covers employees including those in the value chain. So the dyeing units' working conditions sit inside what the report has to cover, and a single line saying suppliers are expected to obey the law is not a disclosure of what is happening at them.

options.text: Only to the extent of the complaints. Two named contractors have been complained about, so those two are a disclosable incident and the rest of the chain is not in scope
options.misconception: treats disclosure of the chain as an incident-reporting duty triggered by complaints, when the chain is inside the scope of the principles whether or not anything has gone wrong
options.why: Complaints are not the trigger. The chain is inside the scope of the principles as a standing matter, so what the company does across it — what it asks of suppliers, how it checks, what it does when something is found — is reportable whether or not anyone has complained. Reporting only what has already surfaced tells the reader about the company's complaints process rather than about its supply chain.

citation.source: BRSR; National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct
citation.ref: The principles extending to the value chain — encouraging chain entities to adopt them, responding to violating suppliers and sub-contractors, and well-being of employees including those in the value chain

items.scenario: A listed textile company is preparing its sustainability report. Almost all of its dyeing is done by independent contractors: separate businesses, on their own premises, with their own workforces and their own licences, paid by the metre. The company has had complaints about conditions at two of them. Its sustainability head proposes to say nothing about any of this. His reasoning is that the report is a report on the company, that these are not the company's employees and not the company's factories, that the company has no legal power to direct how they run their businesses, and that reporting on somebody else's premises would be presenting information the company cannot verify. He offers, if pressed, to add a line saying the company expects its suppliers to comply with law. The board has asked the statutory auditor whether that will do.

items.stem: What does the audit team conclude about the company's controls?

options.text: It is a control deficiency for the letter of weakness to management, but not a material weakness, because no misstatement reached the accounts that were finally adopted
options.misconception: grades the weakness by the misstatement that got through rather than by what the missing control could have failed to stop
options.why: A gap is graded on what it makes possible, not on what happened to be caught this year. Grading it by the outcome would make the same missing control a minor deficiency in a year the auditor happens to test that population and a serious one in a year he does not, which turns the grade into a fact about the audit rather than about the company.

options.text: It is a material weakness in the company's internal financial controls, and it is reported as one whatever happened to the numbers afterwards
options.why: A material weakness is a deficiency, or several of them together, big enough that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the annual accounts will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis. Nothing in this company looks at post-year-end sales returns against despatches made before the year end, so a return of any size can sit unrecorded until somebody outside the company asks for it. That is the possibility the definition is about, and the correction proves it rather than curing it: the control did not stop the misstatement, the audit did.
keywords: prevented or detected on a timely basis

options.text: Report it inside the opinion on the financial statements as a key audit matter, which is where a matter of this significance belongs
options.misconception: folds the separate reporting on controls into the opinion on the financial statements, when the two are distinct statements in the same report
options.why: A key audit matter says what most occupied the auditor during the audit of the financial statements. It is not a substitute for the statement the law separately requires about the controls, which has its own opinion and its own basis. A reader given only the key audit matters would never learn that the system had a hole in it.

options.text: Nothing needs to be said. The financial statements are now free of the misstatement, so the reporting on controls follows the numbers and stays clean
options.misconception: reads the controls opinion as following the corrected figures, when it answers a question of its own about the system that produced them
options.why: The law makes the auditor answer two questions that the corrected figures do not touch: whether the company had an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to financial statements in place, and whether those controls were operating effectively through the year. Here the returns were neither prevented nor detected by anything the company runs. The audit team found them, which is evidence about the audit and not about the system.

citation.ref: the separate statement the auditor's report makes on the adequacy of a company's internal financial controls and on whether they operated effectively

items.scenario: Sundaram & Rao are the statutory auditors of a listed pharmaceutical company. Late in the audit the team traces despatches made in the last fortnight of March to the goods returned register for April and May, and finds that a large block of those despatches came back. The company had recognised all of them as revenue. The team then asks what control the company runs over returns received after the year end against despatches made before it, and the answer is that there is none: the sales system closes at the year end, returns are booked in the month they arrive, and nobody reconciles the two. Nothing in the company's own reviews had picked the point up. It surfaced because the audit team went looking. Management accepts the finding at once, reverses the revenue in full, and re-issues the draft accounts before they are adopted. The finance head then says the file can be closed: the numbers are right, the auditor's own testing found the point, and there is nothing left to say about controls.

items.stem: How does the audit team have to deal with the two points?

options.text: Accept the second. The controls are working now and a report speaks as at the date it is signed, so an unmodified opinion on the controls is the right one
options.misconception: reads the controls opinion as describing the system on the day the report is dated, rather than at the date the financial statements are drawn to
options.why: Adequacy and operating effectiveness are judged as at the balance sheet date, because that is the date the financial statements are drawn to and it is those statements the controls are being reported on for. A weakness existing on that date is reported even where it has been mended since, and an unmodified controls opinion given on the strength of a remediation two months later would tell the reader something about a month he did not ask about and nothing about the year he did.
keywords: as at the balance sheet date

options.text: Reject both, and modify the opinion on the financial statements too, because a controls failure of this size is a limitation on the audit
options.misconception: treats a controls failure as a scope limitation on the audit of the financial statements, when the auditor was able to do the work and did it
options.why: A scope limitation is the auditor being unable to get evidence. Here he got it: he went round the missing control and tested the transactions himself, which is what an auditor does when a system cannot be relied on. The controls opinion records that the system was not there. The opinion on the financial statements records what he found once he had done the work without it.

options.text: Accept the first. The company is under the borrowing limit, so the clause does not apply to it and the second point never arises
options.misconception: reads the exemption as a size test open to any company, when it is written only for certain private companies
options.why: The exemption from this clause is not a size test that anybody can pass. It is available to a private company, and then only where the company is one of a narrow group — one-person companies and small companies — or where its turnover and its aggregate borrowings both sit under the prescribed limits. This client is a listed public company, so it is outside the exemption whatever its borrowings are, and the limit being quoted is not a limit that reaches it.

options.text: Reject both. The opinion on controls is adverse and describes the weakness, while the opinion on the financial statements themselves can still be clean
options.why: Where a material weakness existed at the year end, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion on internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and sets out what the weakness was. The opinion on the financial statements is a separate judgement: if the related party transactions have in the end been identified, measured and disclosed properly, that opinion can be unmodified. Two opinions, two questions, and the clean one does not soften the adverse one sitting beside it.
keywords: adverse opinion on internal financial controls

citation.ref: who the exemption from reporting on internal financial controls is available to, and the reporting where a weakness existed at the year end

items.scenario: Ganeshan & Co are auditing a listed public company that makes industrial fasteners. Through the whole of the year under audit the company had no working process for identifying and approving transactions with related parties: the list of related parties was last updated two years earlier, and purchase orders on group entities went through the ordinary vendor route with nobody checking the counterparty against that list. The company built the missing process two months after the year end and it has run properly since. The chief financial officer makes two points. First, the company's borrowings from its banks are well under the limit written into the exemption, so the clause about controls does not reach it at all. Second, even if it does, the process is in place now and the report is being signed now, so there is nothing adverse to say.

items.stem: What does Bhatia & Sons require before it can report on this statement?

options.text: Report on it as it stands with a caveat that the results may not be achieved, which covers the reader for everything in the document
options.misconception: uses the general caveat about the outcome as a substitute for telling the reader what kind of assumption each number rests on
options.why: Every report on prospective financial information carries that caveat, so it distinguishes nothing inside the document. A reader told only that the future is uncertain still cannot tell which of these five years the company itself expects and which it has merely drawn.

options.text: The notes must say, assumption by assumption, which are best-estimate and which are hypothetical, because this statement is a mixture of the two
options.why: A forecast rests on best-estimate assumptions about events management expects to occur and actions it expects to take. A projection built on hypothetical assumptions describes events that are not necessarily expected at all — a second plant nobody has sanctioned, a duty the government has not granted. One statement may be a mixture of both, and where it is, the material assumptions have to be disclosed with a clear indication of which of them is which, because a lender reading a single undifferentiated list cannot tell the order book from the wish.
keywords: A forecast rests on best-estimate assumptions
A projection built on hypothetical assumptions
a clear indication of which of them is which

options.text: Split the document and examine only years one and two, since prospective information resting on hypothetical assumptions cannot be examined at all
options.misconception: thinks hypothetical assumptions put the information outside the standard, when the standard covers both and asks a different question of each
options.why: The standard is written for both kinds. Of a best-estimate assumption the auditor asks whether it is unreasonable. Of a hypothetical one he asks whether it fits the purpose the information was prepared for, and whether every implication of it has been carried through the numbers — a plant assumed into the sales line has to appear in the capital spending line as well.

options.text: Nothing on that point. The whole statement is headed a projection, which already tells a reader that none of it is expected to occur
options.misconception: takes one heading over the whole document as the indication the standard asks for, when the two kinds of assumption run side by side inside it
options.why: Calling all five years a projection is not a smaller mistake than calling all five a forecast; it is the same mistake pointing the other way. It tells the lender to discount the order book, which management does expect to convert, as heavily as it discounts a plant nobody has approved.

citation.ref: a forecast, a projection and a statement that mixes the two, and the disclosure of which assumptions are of which kind

items.scenario: Bhatia & Sons have been asked to examine a five-year statement of projected profits that a speciality chemicals company is putting in front of a consortium of lenders. Years one and two are built from the company's order book, its existing plant and the prices in contracts already running; the management team says these are what it expects to happen. Years three and four assume a new plant at a second site, which the board has not approved and for which no land has been bought. Year five assumes a change in customs duty that the company has asked the government for and not been given. The document that reached Bhatia & Sons is headed "Projected Financial Statements" throughout, sets the five years out in one continuous table, and describes all the assumptions together in a single list of notes without saying which of them is which.

items.stem: What does Bhatia & Sons say to the managing director?

options.text: Leave the word "achievability" alone. The report itself uses it, so the letter is only borrowing the auditor's own language
options.misconception: reads the report's caveat as a claim that the outcome was tested, when the caveat exists to say the opposite
options.why: The report carries appropriate caveats concerning the achievability of the results, and a caveat is a warning rather than a finding. Turning it round into "the auditors verified the achievability" takes the one sentence that limits the report and prints it as the report's conclusion.
keywords: caveats concerning the achievability of the results

options.text: The letter has to be rewritten, and the work is not arithmetic — there is evidence to gather about the assumptions themselves and about how the statement was built
options.why: Before he can report at all, the auditor needs enough evidence to say that management's best-estimate assumptions are not unreasonable and that its hypothetical ones fit the purpose the statement was drawn for; that the information is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions; that every material assumption is disclosed; and that it has been drawn on a basis consistent with the historical financial statements, using accounting principles the company actually applies. None of that is adding up a table.
keywords: properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions
on a basis consistent with the historical financial statements

options.text: Rewrite the letter but agree to the shorter report, since the opinion itself is short and everything around it is standard wording
options.misconception: treats the report's descriptive paragraphs as filler, when they are what tells the reader what was examined and on what basis
options.why: The paragraphs he wants cut are the ones that identify the information examined, say who is responsible for the assumptions, and set out the basis of the opinion. Take those away and the lender is left with a conclusion he cannot place against anything.

options.text: Leave the letter. "Certified" is how a lender reads any auditor's report anyway, and the firm's opinion does in substance say the numbers are right
options.misconception: treats an opinion on prospective information as a warranty of the outcome, when the evidence behind a future event is itself speculative
options.why: The evidence behind a projection is about things that have not happened, so it is speculative in a way that evidence about last year's despatches is not. An opinion on whether the results will actually come out cannot be given at all. A letter saying they were certified as correct is not a loose description of the report; it says the opposite of what the report says.

citation.ref: the evidence the auditor obtains about the assumptions and the preparation of prospective financial information, and the caveats the report carries

items.scenario: The speciality chemicals company redrafts its statement and now marks each assumption. Its managing director then sends Bhatia & Sons a draft of the covering letter he intends to circulate with it to the lenders. The letter says the projections have been examined and certified as correct by the company's auditors, that the auditors have verified the achievability of the numbers, and that the consortium may therefore treat the five-year cash flows as assured. He also asks the firm to shorten its report, because in his view its only job on this engagement is to check the arithmetic in the table.

items.stem: How does the partner deal with the two?

options.text: Ask again for the minutes in writing, and if they are still withheld, issue a report that expresses no conclusion and says why
options.why: Reading the minutes of the meetings of the board and its committees is one of the procedures a reviewer ordinarily performs, so withholding them is a limitation on scope imposed by management. The auditor's first move is to request its removal. If management holds its position, he cannot complete the review or express a conclusion; he then tells management and those charged with governance in writing why the review could not be completed, and because a listed company's results have to carry a review report he issues one that disclaims a conclusion and gives the reason.
keywords: a limitation on scope imposed by management

options.text: Accept the secretary's reason. Minutes about an unannounced acquisition are price sensitive, so a reviewer has no right to them and this is not a scope limitation at all
options.misconception: reads a good commercial reason for withholding a document as taking the document out of the scope of the engagement
options.why: Why management withholds something changes nothing about what the auditor could not see. Sensitivity is a reason to control who in the firm reads the minutes and how they are held. It is not a reason for the engagement to carry on as though the procedure had been done.

options.text: Issue an unmodified conclusion and add an other matter paragraph recording that the minutes were not made available to the team
options.misconception: treats an unexamined area as something a paragraph can disclose around, when the auditor has no conclusion to express in the first place
options.why: A paragraph describing a gap does not fill it. The reader is being handed a conclusion the auditor was not in a position to reach, with the reason it could not be reached printed underneath, and of the two the conclusion is what gets quoted.

options.text: Let the junior finish. Until the ledger is vouched and the confirmations are all back the team has no basis for anything, and the minutes can wait behind that
options.misconception: applies an audit's procedures and evidence threshold to a review, so the engagement looks unfinished when the work it actually calls for is done
options.why: A review of interim financial information is designed to bring the risk of an inappropriate conclusion down to a moderate level, not to the low level an audit works to. It is built from inquiries of the persons responsible for financial and accounting matters and from analytical and other review procedures, and it does not require tests of the accounting records — so confirmations, a stock count and vouching a ledger are audit procedures the junior was never asked for.
keywords: inquiries of the persons responsible for financial and accounting matters
does not require tests of the accounting records

citation.ref: the nature of a review of interim financial information, and the course the auditor takes when management limits his scope

items.scenario: Deshpande & Associates are reviewing the half-yearly results of a listed logistics company. Two things are on the partner's desk. The first is a memorandum from the junior in charge, who has sent external confirmations to forty of the company's debtors and to its three bankers, has attended a stock count at the largest depot, and reports that he has not finished vouching the freight cost ledger and wants two more weeks. The second is a note from the company secretary declining the team's request for the minutes of the board and audit committee meetings held during the half year, on the ground that the board discussed a possible acquisition and the minutes are commercially sensitive. The company publishes its results in eleven days and the stock exchange requires a review report with them.

items.stem: What does the firm do about the note and about the publication?

options.text: The disclosure is adequate, so the report needs no change; and the omission from the publication is the company's own compliance problem
options.misconception: treats adequate disclosure as removing the need to say anything, and treats the missing report as somebody else's failure
options.why: Adequate disclosure decides which way the report goes, not whether the report mentions the matter at all. And the omission is not somebody else's: the document tells the market the auditor reviewed the numbers, so the firm's name is being used to support figures nobody can read against what the firm actually said.

options.text: Give a qualified conclusion, because a recalled loan with no replacement facility is a matter the reader has to be warned about in the conclusion itself
options.misconception: reaches for a qualified conclusion whenever the matter is grave, when what decides it is whether the interim information tells the reader about it
options.why: The conclusion is modified when something is wrong with the information, not when something is wrong with the company. Here the information says what has happened. A conclusion qualified over a matter the company has properly disclosed would tell the reader the note is unreliable, which is not what the firm found.

options.text: Withdraw the review report and require the company to republish the results with it attached before doing anything else
options.misconception: assumes the auditor can compel a listed company to republish, and that pulling the report is the remedy
options.why: The firm cannot make the company reissue anything, and taking its report away leaves the market holding the sentence that says the numbers were reviewed with nothing to read against it. What the firm can do is take advice on its own position, tell those charged with governance, and decide whether it is willing to continue as auditor.

options.text: Add an emphasis of matter paragraph on the uncertainty, and on the publication take advice before deciding what to do, including whether to stay on for the annual audit
options.why: Where an event casts significant doubt on the entity carrying on in business and management has disclosed the material uncertainty adequately, the review report is modified by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph. Had the disclosure been inadequate it would instead have carried a qualified or adverse conclusion, referring specifically to that uncertainty. On the publication, the firm considers seeking legal advice on what to do next, and weighs resigning from the appointment to audit the annual financial statements. A review is an assurance engagement, so the report carries a UDIN like any other, and the one that was generated and never published is on record.
keywords: resigning from the appointment to audit the annual financial statements

citation.ref: going concern uncertainty inside a review report, and the auditor's course when management publishes without the report

items.scenario: Three days before the same logistics company is due to publish, its largest lender recalls a term loan and demands repayment inside three months. The company has no committed facility to replace it. Management adds a note to the interim financial information setting the recall out, saying negotiations are under way, and describing the uncertainty over the company's ability to carry on in business. Deshpande & Associates are satisfied the note is adequate. The engagement letter records management's agreement that any document saying the interim information has been reviewed will carry the review report with it. On the publication date the company puts the results out with a line saying they have been reviewed by its statutory auditors, and does not include the report.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way he proposes to report?

options.text: Only the draft. Combining the two reports is efficient and it puts everything the audit committee needs in one place
options.misconception: reads the two reports as two copies of the same information, when they answer different questions for different readers
options.why: The assignment report goes to the auditee — the people who run procurement — with copies to local and executive management, and its purpose is to get something fixed. The comprehensive report goes to the audit committee and covers a period rather than an assignment. Fold one into the other and procurement never receives a report addressed to it, while the committee receives one assignment's detail where it asked for a quarter's picture.

options.text: Nothing, so long as the facts are right. No format is laid down for an internal audit report, so how it is packaged is his own judgement
options.misconception: reads the absence of a prescribed format as an absence of requirements, when what is left to judgement is presentation and not the reporting structure
options.why: It is true that no particular format or list of contents is mandated, and that content is a matter of professional judgement exercised in consultation with the auditee. That is about how the report reads. It does not touch who has to see a draft before a report becomes final, or the structure the reporting itself takes.

options.text: Only the merging. A draft is a courtesy, and where a finding may be fraud the auditor should not be showing it to the department under review at all
options.misconception: runs the draft-sharing requirement together with the separate duty on suspected fraud, and drops the first because of the second
options.why: Two different rules are being confused. No report may be issued in final form without a written draft having reached the auditee first, and that holds here. Separately, an actual or suspected fraud is brought to management immediately rather than held for any report. The assignment report still carries its overview of the objectives, scope and approach, its statement that the work was done under the Standards on Internal Audit, an executive summary of the key observations and a summary of the corrective actions agreed — and the draft is how the auditee gets to answer them before they are fixed.
keywords: an executive summary of the key observations

options.text: Two things: procurement must see a written draft before the report is final, and the assignment report and the quarterly report are separate reports with different readers
options.why: Reporting of internal audit results runs in two stages. The first is a report at the end of a particular assignment, issued to the auditee with copies to local and executive management. The second is a periodic — normally quarterly — comprehensive report from the Chief Internal Auditor to the audit committee. Merging them takes the assignment report away from the people whose process it is about. And no report goes out in final form unless a written draft of it has already been shared with the auditee, so "there is no time" is not an answer: the draft is part of the procedure and not a courtesy.
keywords: a written draft of it has already been shared with the auditee

citation.ref: the two stages internal audit reporting runs in, and the written draft that must reach the auditee before a report is issued in final form

items.scenario: A listed cement company's Chief Internal Auditor has finished an assignment on the procurement function. His team found that three vendors were empanelled without the tender committee meeting at all, and that advances against two of those orders are still outstanding a year later. He is preparing to put the assignment report straight into the audit committee's papers for next week. The head of procurement has asked to see it first and has been told there is no time. The Chief Internal Auditor also plans to fold this assignment's findings into a single document that will double as his quarterly report to the audit committee, on the ground that the committee should not have to read the same facts twice.

items.stem: What does Rukmini change in that plan?

options.text: Get the file and rely on it. It is the work of a chartered accountant, and the firm closing down does not change what is written in the papers
options.misconception: treats a predecessor's papers as evidence in themselves, when what they are worth depends on who made them and under what independence
options.why: A working paper is only as good as the work behind it. The reason this firm closed is itself a finding about the quality and the independence of that work, and papers from a partner who signed reports on companies he had not visited are no substitute for her own procedures. She may read them. She may not lean on them.

options.text: She must also read last year's statements and the predecessor's report, test whether the same policies have been applied, and judge how far the old firm's file can be leaned on at all
options.why: Three things sit on top of the assistant's plan. She reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report for anything relevant to the opening figures. She evaluates whether the accounting policies behind those figures have been applied consistently this year and, where one has changed, whether the change is accounted for and disclosed. And where the prior period was audited, evidence about the openings is ordinarily obtained by reviewing the predecessor auditor's working papers — but what that is worth turns on the predecessor's professional competence and independence, which in this case is the whole question.
keywords: the predecessor's professional competence and independence

options.text: Do fresh procedures on the opening balances and leave the accounting policies alone, since a policy question belongs to the year the policy was chosen in
options.misconception: separates the opening balances from the policies that produced them, when the standard asks about both together
options.why: An opening figure carries a policy inside it. If last year's inventory was valued one way and this year's another, the two columns are not comparable and the movement between them is not the movement it looks like, whichever year the choice was made in.

options.text: Very little. The prior period was audited, and an auditor does not audit again a period somebody else has already reported on
options.misconception: reads the duty on opening balances as a duty to re-audit last year, and declines it, when what is owed is evidence about this year's figures
options.why: Nobody is asking her to report on last year. The question is about this year: whether the opening column carries misstatements that materially affect the current period's reported figures, and whether last year's closing figures reached that column correctly. Both are facts about the statements she is going to sign.
keywords: carries misstatements that materially affect the current period's reported figures

citation.source: SA 510 Initial Audit Engagements — Opening Balances
citation.ref: the evidence to obtain about opening balances, the consistency of accounting policies, and reliance on the predecessor auditor's work

items.scenario: CA Rukmini has been appointed auditor of a mid-sized garment exporter. The previous year was audited by another firm, which has since been wound up after its senior partner was found to have signed reports on companies he had never visited; that firm's papers are with a former employee who is willing to hand them over. Rukmini's assistant proposes a plan. Take the prior year's closing figures straight into the current year's opening column. Get the old firm's working papers on inventory and receivables. Treat the matter as closed on the ground that the balances were audited once already and re-auditing them is outside this engagement.

items.stem: How does the engagement partner set the committee's expectations?

options.text: It is the annual audit done more thoroughly — the same standards, a lower materiality and a bigger sample
options.misconception: treats an investigation as an audit with the dials turned up, when the two answer different questions under different standards
options.why: Turning the dials does not change the question. An audit is conducted with professional scepticism, neither assuming dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty on the part of the people running the company, and is built to reach reasonable assurance about the statements taken as a whole. An investigation is built to establish whether one particular thing happened, where the money went, and what can be proved about it. A larger sample of an audit is still an audit.
keywords: neither assuming dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty

options.text: Give the committee the opinion it has asked for and add a paragraph describing the findings, since an opinion is what a chartered accountant's report carries
options.misconception: assumes any report from an auditor must end in an opinion, when a forensic report ends in findings and the basis for them
options.why: The report says what was found and what each finding rests on. It carries no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion, so there is nothing in it to qualify and nothing for such a paragraph to sit beside. A committee handed an opinion would read the investigation as assurance about the accounts, which is not what it bought.
keywords: no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion

options.text: The assignment runs under a different set of standards, starts from a different position, and ends in something that is not an opinion
options.why: A forensic engagement is carried out under the Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards the Institute has issued, and not under the Standards on Auditing. What it produces is findings of fact about the suspected act, rather than assurance about a set of financial statements. The starting position differs too: an investigation begins from a hypothesis that the act described may have happened, and designs its procedures to test that hypothesis until it can be settled one way or the other.
keywords: the Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
findings of fact about the suspected act
a hypothesis that the act described may have happened

options.text: It is the same work under a different name, so the committee should simply widen the scope of next year's statutory audit instead of commissioning anything separate
options.misconception: puts the investigation inside a future audit, when an audit's timing and design cannot answer a question about an allegation already made
options.why: An audit is planned around risks of material misstatement in one set of statements for one period. It is not planned around one named person and two named contractors, and by next year the records, the people and the balances involved will all have moved. A question about a specific suspected act is answered by an assignment built for that question.

citation.ref: the framework a forensic engagement is conducted under, and how its objective and its starting mindset differ from those of an audit

items.scenario: A listed company's audit committee has received an anonymous letter naming a general manager in the projects division and alleging that site mobilisation advances were routed to two contractors he controls. The committee asks the statutory auditor's firm to take on a separate assignment to establish what happened. At the first meeting the engagement partner is asked how this work will differ from the audit the same firm does every year. The finance director, sitting in, says he expects the professional to start from the position that the general manager is innocent until the papers say otherwise, and to give the committee an opinion at the end saying whether the accounts were fairly stated in the light of whatever is found.

items.stem: Which of the three can the engagement partner accept?

options.text: None of the three. Each of them takes something away from the report the committee actually needs
options.why: The scope comes from the suspected act, not from an audit's materiality. The evidence has to keep the integrity of its source, which a scan routed through the suspected department does not. And a forensic report has no opinion in it to qualify: it sets out findings of fact, the basis on which each of them was reached, and the limitations on the work performed. A tribunal reads those, not a reservation attached to an opinion that was never expressed.
keywords: the limitations on the work performed

options.text: The materiality proposal only. Seventy trivial payments cannot change a finding, and time spent on them is time not spent on the three that matter
options.misconception: imports an audit's materiality into an investigation, where a pattern of small payments is often the thing being looked for
options.why: An audit materiality threshold scopes an audit and scopes nothing here. The scope is fixed by the suspected act and by the agreed terms of the engagement. A run of small payments to the same two counterparties is precisely the shape a diversion takes when somebody is keeping each one under a review limit, so cutting the seventy would remove the pattern and leave three transactions that may each look defensible on their own.
keywords: The scope is fixed by the suspected act
the agreed terms of the engagement

options.text: The scanning proposal only. A scan is a faithful copy of the document, and the originals are safer left where they are
options.misconception: treats a copy made by the department under suspicion as equivalent to evidence whose source has been kept intact
options.why: Evidence meant to stand up outside the company needs the integrity of its source preserved: originals, or forensically sound images of digital records, an unbroken chain of custody, and corroboration from people and systems independent of those suspected. A scan produced by the very department under investigation, and chosen by that department, is none of those. The working papers behind each finding are kept to litigation grade for the same reason.

options.text: The scanning and the opinion. Both are matters of form, and the committee is entitled to ask for its report in whatever shape it finds useful
options.misconception: treats the form of the evidence and the form of the report as presentation choices, when both decide whether the work can be used for the purpose it was bought for
options.why: The committee commissioned this to put a file before a tribunal. Copies handed over by the people under investigation, and a conclusion dressed up as an audit opinion, are the two things most likely to be taken apart there. Form here is not presentation. It is whether the work survives contact with its purpose.

citation.ref: what fixes the scope of a forensic assignment, the integrity of evidence intended for legal proceedings, and what the written report states
