items.scenario: The investigation into the projects division is under way, and three proposals reach the engagement partner in a single week. The finance director suggests the team apply the annual audit's materiality threshold and look only at the three largest advances, since about seventy smaller payments to the same two contractors are individually trivial. The company secretary offers to have the projects department scan the mobilisation files and email them across, which will be quicker than the team taking the originals away. And the audit committee's chairman, who wants to put the file before a tribunal if the allegations hold up, asks whether the report can end in a qualified opinion so that the tribunal can see the professional's reservations on the face of it.

items.stem: What does Devika settle with the investor before she starts?

options.text: That the engagement produces factual findings and no assurance, that its report is not an audit, and that its circulation is fixed before she starts
options.why: The work is an agreed-upon procedures engagement under SRS 4400. Devika performs the procedures the parties have agreed and reports what she found; the investor draws its own conclusion from those findings, and nothing in the engagement says the receivables are fairly stated. The instruction letter therefore has to be corrected before she accepts. The terms must record that the procedures do not constitute an audit or a review and that no assurance will be expressed, and they must fix the limitation on distribution of the report — which the plan to pass it to eleven other investors makes something to settle now rather than afterwards.
keywords: an agreed-upon procedures engagement under SRS 4400
the procedures do not constitute an audit or a review
the limitation on distribution of the report

options.text: That she will report only the exceptions she finds, so the investor is not buried in detail about the accounts that agreed
options.misconception: treats the report as a list of problems, when it has to describe the work done as well as what the work turned up
options.why: The report describes the procedures performed in enough detail for the reader to see the extent of the work, and then describes what was found, including sufficient detail of the errors and exceptions found. A report of exceptions alone leaves the reader unable to tell a clean circularisation of twenty customers from a circularisation of two.

options.text: That she must give up the internal audit role first, because she cannot report on receivables she has been reviewing all year
options.misconception: applies an assurance engagement's independence requirement to an engagement that expresses no assurance
options.why: Independence is not a requirement of an agreed-upon procedures engagement, so the internal audit role does not bar her from taking this on. What it does mean is that where the auditor is not independent, a statement to that effect goes into the report of factual findings. She keeps the role and discloses it.

options.text: That she will report the procedures and add a conclusion of her own on whether the receivables look collectable, since that is what the investor is really after
options.misconception: adds a conclusion to an engagement whose whole design is that the reader forms his own
options.why: The moment she says whether they look collectable she has expressed assurance, and the engagement was not built to carry it — she agreed a list of procedures, not a scope wide enough for a view. The investor gets what it asked for by reading the findings, or it buys a different engagement.

citation.ref: the terms agreed before an agreed-upon procedures engagement, and what the report of factual findings has to contain

items.scenario: An investor is buying a minority stake in a family-owned auto components company and has asked CA Devika to do a piece of work on its receivables: circularise the twenty largest customers, age the ledger at the balance sheet date, and check the ledger against the last three bank statements. Devika has been the company's internal auditor for four years. The investor's instruction letter says it wants the auditor's assurance that the receivables are fairly stated, and adds that it intends to send the resulting report to eleven other investors it is bringing into the round. Devika has not signed anything yet.

items.stem: What does the audit team do about the ageing statement the credit controller uses?

options.text: Test the ageing in its own right, and expect to have to, because the general IT controls behind it cannot be relied on
options.why: Two of the general IT control objectives have gone here. One man writing a change and moving it into the live system himself breaks the objective that development, testing and live running are kept apart and that somebody other than the developer puts a change in. Accounts still live for staff who left break the objective that the access of a terminated employee is taken away promptly. Where the general IT controls are not operating, the dependencies resting on them cannot be relied on either — so the ageing has to be tested directly for completeness and accuracy, and the balances behind it approached with substantive procedures rather than by leaning on the system.
keywords: the access of a terminated employee is taken away promptly
substantive procedures rather than by leaning on the system

options.text: Ask the IT manager to fix both problems and then rely on the ageing, since the controls will be working by the time the report is signed
options.misconception: reads a general IT control as something the year-end position settles, when what is being relied on is how the system behaved during the period audited
options.why: The ageing the credit controller used in August came out of the system as it stood in August. A fix made now says something about next year. If the team wants to rely on that report for this year, it has to test that report for this year.

options.text: Nothing special. Her review is the control, and a manual control is tested by re-performing what she did
options.misconception: tests the human step and takes the report it runs on as given, when the report is itself something the system produced
options.why: Her review is only as good as what she is reviewing. The ageing she works from is a system-generated report — one of the five ways IT gets into the financial information, alongside an automated control, a calculation, an interface and the security the system enforces — and if the report is wrong she will review the wrong thing very carefully.

options.text: Drop the reliance on the ageing and on the automated approval, but keep relying on the depreciation calculation, which is arithmetic and cannot be touched by an access problem
options.misconception: treats a calculation as immune because the arithmetic is simple, when the same change and access weaknesses reach the rates and the schedule behind it
options.why: The arithmetic is not the risk. The rates, the lives and the schedule sit in the same system, under the same change process one man runs alone, and a depreciation charge comes out wrong in exactly the same way whether the multiplication went astray or the life did.

citation.source: Digital Auditing and Assurance — IT dependencies and general IT controls
citation.ref: the five types of IT dependency, the general IT control objectives, and what follows for the audit when those controls cannot be relied on

items.scenario: Kulkarni & Bhide are auditing a retail chain that runs everything on one enterprise system, and four things came out of the walkthrough. Purchase orders above a limit are held by the system until a second approver releases them. Depreciation on the store fit-out is worked out by the system on a schedule nobody touches. Point-of-sale takings move nightly from the till software into the general ledger through an automated feed. And the credit controller does her monthly review of overdue accounts off an ageing statement the system prints for her. The IT manager then mentions two things in passing: he moves his own changes into the live system himself, because there are only two people in his team, and the login accounts of three staff who left in the autumn are still active because nobody told him they had gone.

items.stem: What does Harith do?

options.text: Propose the reclassification, and if he gets nowhere on either matter withdraw, telling management and those charged with governance the reason
options.why: On the classification, having read the compiled information against what he knows of the business and of the framework, he must propose the amendment needed for it not to be misleading. Where management declines or does not permit the amendment, he withdraws. On the missing invoices there is a second road to the same place, and if neither matter moves, both point at withdrawal. Whatever version does go out, he obtains an acknowledgement from management that it has taken responsibility for the final version of the compiled information.
keywords: management declines or does not permit the amendment

options.text: Deal with the classification as he says, but simply carry the purchase figure, since a compilation does not require him to verify anything
options.misconception: reads the absence of a duty to verify as an absence of any duty about the information he has been handed
options.why: It is true that a compilation does not require him to verify what he is given. It is not true that he may compile from nothing. Where the records, documents or explanations provided are incomplete or inaccurate, he brings that to management's attention and must request the additional or corrected information. If it never comes, so that the engagement cannot be finished, he must withdraw and inform management and those charged with governance of the reason.
keywords: request the additional or corrected information
inform management and those charged with governance

options.text: Refuse to sign but stay on the engagement, so the company has time to find the invoices and think again without a withdrawal on its record
options.misconception: treats staying on without issuing as a neutral middle course, when the answer to a refusal is withdrawal and the reason being told to those charged with governance
options.why: An engagement nobody has withdrawn from and nobody will finish leaves the company free to tell its bankers that the accounts are with its accountant. If withdrawal genuinely is not possible — a law or a contract that prevents it — the practitioner determines his professional and legal responsibilities in the circumstances, which is a decision he takes and records, not a position he drifts into.

options.text: Compile the information as instructed and put a note in his report describing both matters, since responsibility for the figures is management's
options.misconception: uses a note in the report as a way of issuing information he knows to be misleading, when the report is not a place to disclose around a refusal
options.why: Management's responsibility for the figures does not put the practitioner's name at their disposal. A note describing the misclassification would leave a misleading balance sheet in circulation with an explanation attached to it, which is a different thing from not issuing it.

citation.ref: proposing amendments, asking for information management has not provided, and withdrawing where either is refused

items.scenario: CA Harith is compiling the annual financial information of a family-run trading company for its bankers, and two things come up as he reads the draft he has produced. A sum shown under short-term advances is in fact a loan taken from a director and belongs among borrowings; where it sits, the working capital position reads far better than it is. And a block of purchases has no supporting invoices at all — the accountant says the files are with the proprietor's son, who is travelling, and that Harith should carry the figure as it stands. Harith raises both. The proprietor tells him the classification has been the same for six years and will not be changed, and that the invoices will turn up eventually.

items.stem: Which of the three can Harith agree to?

options.text: The second only. That paragraph is boilerplate, while the other two change what the report asserts and cannot be given
options.misconception: reads the limiting paragraph as filler because it is standard, when standard wording is how a reader knows which kind of report he has
options.why: The paragraph is standard because every compilation report needs it, not because nobody reads it. Take it out and the report starts to look like the other reports the bank receives from auditors, which is precisely the confusion the wording exists to prevent.

options.text: None of the three. Each one would make the report say something the engagement was never built to support
options.why: The report has to explain that because a compilation is not an assurance engagement he was not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of what management gave him, and that he accordingly expresses no audit opinion or review conclusion on it. The paragraph the proprietor wants removed is the one that tells the bank what it is holding, and the two additions he wants would contradict it. What Harith can offer instead is a clear description of what he did and of what management is responsible for.
keywords: not required to verify the accuracy or completeness
expresses no audit opinion or review conclusion

options.text: The first two. Having compiled the information he does know whether it is materially misstated, and the paragraph he objects to adds nothing a bank does not already assume
options.misconception: treats familiarity with the numbers as a basis for a statement about them, when the engagement gathered no evidence to support one
options.why: He read the information and he knows the business, and neither of those is evidence. He tested nothing, confirmed nothing and inspected nothing, because the engagement did not call for any of it — so a sentence saying the statements are free of material misstatement would rest on nothing more than the fact that nothing struck him as odd.

options.text: The third only. "In our opinion" is a form of words every accountant's report carries, and it commits him to no more than the rest of the report already says
options.misconception: reads the opinion formula as a convention rather than as the thing that turns a compilation report into an assurance report
options.why: Those three words are the whole difference. A reader who sees them takes the paragraph they introduce as a conclusion the professional stands behind. A compilation report is not a vehicle to express an opinion or a conclusion about the information, in any form at all, and a borrowed form of words is exactly how that line gets crossed.
keywords: not a vehicle to express an opinion

citation.ref: what the practitioner's report must state, and what it may not be used to express

items.scenario: The trading company relents on the classification, the invoices arrive, and Harith finishes the compilation. The proprietor now wants the report worded so that his bankers will take it seriously, and asks for three changes. That it say the statements are free of material misstatement. That it drop the paragraph about not verifying anything, because in his words it makes it sound as though the accountant did nothing. And that it end with the words "in our opinion", so the bank's credit committee has something to point at.

items.stem: What figure does the capital gains computation start from?

options.text: ₹86,00,000, because no money beyond the stated price passed between the parties
options.misconception: reads the section as a charge on unaccounted cash, so proof that nothing was hidden is thought to answer it
options.why: Section 50C is a valuation rule and not an allegation. It works on what the stamp authority thought the land was worth, whatever the parties actually did. The remedy for a seller who says the valuation is too high is a reference to a Valuation Officer under section 50C(2), not a plea that the price was honest.

Ten per cent above the price is ₹94,60,000. The stamp duty value of ₹97,00,000 exceeds 110% of the consideration received, so the tolerance never opens and section 50C(1) puts the valuation in as the full value of consideration for the transfer. The price actually paid then drops out of the working altogether. The tolerance is a gate rather than a ceiling: once it is crossed, the whole valuation comes in, not the part of it above the line.

options.text: ₹94,60,000, the deeming stopping at the tolerance line
options.misconception: treats the ten per cent margin as the highest figure that can be deemed, instead of the test that decides whether any deeming happens
options.why: The margin decides whether the section applies at all. It does not cap what the section then substitutes. Once the valuation is outside the margin, the substituted figure is the valuation itself, so the computation begins at ₹97,00,000 and not at the boundary that was crossed on the way.

options.text: ₹86,00,000, the difference between the two figures being under fifteen per cent
options.misconception: invents a wider tolerance than the section carries, so a gap the law treats as fatal is read as forgivable
options.why: The margin is fixed and it is ten per cent of what the seller received, not fifteen and not a figure the facts of a case make reasonable. Here the valuation is a little over twelve per cent above the price, which is outside the margin, and being outside it is the whole of the test.

citation.ref: Section 50C(1) with the proviso carrying the ten per cent tolerance

items.scenario: Mr Sethi sold a plot of land on 4 July 2025 for ₹86,00,000, the whole of it received by cheque. The sub-registrar valued the plot at ₹97,00,000 on the date of registration. There was no earlier agreement fixing the price and no part of the money had been paid before the sale. His accountant has begun the capital gains working on ₹86,00,000, saying that the gap between the two figures is small enough for the tolerance in the section to protect him.

items.stem: What long-term capital gain goes into her total income?

options.why: The figure that enters the head is worked out without indexation. From the deemed consideration of ₹1,04,00,000 come the ₹1,20,000 of brokerage, being expenditure incurred wholly in connection with the transfer, then the cost of acquisition of ₹21,00,000 and the cost of improvement of ₹5,00,000, leaving ₹76,80,000. Any benefit she may take from the indices belongs to the calculation of tax under section 112 and is not allowed to change the income that goes into the total.

options.misconception: puts the indexation option into the computation of the head income, when it belongs only to the tax calculation
options.why: The indices give ₹32,90,000 and ₹7,12,121 for the two costs and produce this figure, and the figure is not useless — it is the base on which twenty per cent may be charged if that works out cheaper for her. But the income shown under capital gains, and carried into gross total income, is the unindexed one.

options.misconception: allows the cost of acquisition but not the cost of improvement, as though only what was paid to buy the asset counts
options.why: Money spent on the asset after it was bought — levelling and walling here — is a capital improvement, and section 48 allows it as a separate deduction alongside what was paid to acquire the land. Leaving out ₹5,00,000 overstates the gain by that amount.

options.misconception: deducts the two costs but forgets the brokerage, treating a selling expense as something the section does not allow
options.why: Expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer is the first deduction section 48 allows, before either cost. Brokerage on the sale is the plainest example of it, so ₹1,20,000 comes out and the answer is ₹1,20,000 lower.

citation.ref: Section 48 read with section 50C(1); the proviso to section 112(1) for the option confined to the tax calculation

items.scenario: Mrs Dutta, a resident individual, sold a plot of land in October 2025. Section 50C has already been applied and the consideration to be taken is ₹1,04,00,000. She had bought the plot in F.Y. 2014-15 for ₹21,00,000 and had it levelled and walled in F.Y. 2016-17 at a cost of ₹5,00,000. She paid her broker ₹1,20,000 on the sale. The notified cost inflation indices are 240 for F.Y. 2014-15, 264 for F.Y. 2016-17 and 376 for F.Y. 2025-26.

items.stem: What is the arm's length band this dataset produces?

options.text: ₹117 to ₹125 a unit, interpolating between the entries at 2.8 and 5.2 places along the list
options.misconception: interpolates between two entries when the count comes out fractional, instead of moving up to the next whole position
options.why: 2.8 is not a whole number, and the definition says what to do about that without any arithmetic between two entries: take the lowest value that satisfies the test, which means moving the count up to the next whole position. Interpolating would put forward a price no comparable in the set ever charged.

options.text: ₹115 to ₹121 a unit, five of the eight values being close enough to 65 per cent
options.misconception: rounds the count down at the top of the band, so a figure short of the percentile is accepted as reaching it
options.why: The wording sets a floor and not a nearest neighbour: the top of the band is the lowest value for which at least 65% of the values in the set are equal to or below it. Five of eight is 62.5 per cent, which is short, so the count moves up to six and the sixth value, ₹124, is the top.

options.text: ₹106 to ₹136 a unit, the whole spread the comparables cover
options.misconception: reads the band as the full range of the data, so any price a single comparable charged is treated as defensible
options.why: The arm's length range is a narrow central band running from the thirty-fifth percentile to the sixty-fifth percentile, and it throws away the tails on purpose, because the extreme comparable is the one most likely to be doing something the tested party is not. Taking the whole spread would let almost any price through.

options.text: ₹115 to ₹124 a unit
options.why: Two things have to hold before a band is built at all, and both hold here: the method is one the sub-rule lets in — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus or transactional net margin — and the dataset has six or more entries. The bottom of the band is the thirty-fifth percentile, which is the lowest value such that at least 35% of the values in the set are equal to or below it. 35% of eight is 2.8, so three of the eight have to sit at or under the figure, and the third value, ₹115, is the lowest one that does. The same reasoning at 65% needs six of the eight, giving ₹124 at the top. The price of ₹100 is below the band, so it does not stand.
keywords: the lowest value such that at least 35% of the values in the set

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(4) and Rule 10CA(8)(a) and (b)

items.scenario: Helix Instruments Ltd sold 1,50,000 bearings to its associated enterprise abroad at ₹100 a unit in previous year 2025-26. The comparable uncontrolled price method is the most appropriate method and the Transfer Pricing Officer accepts it. The dataset built from comparable uncontrolled transactions has eight entries, which in ascending order are ₹106, ₹110, ₹115, ₹118, ₹121, ₹124, ₹130 and ₹136 a unit.

items.stem: What price does the company's income have to be computed at?

options.text: ₹122 a unit
options.why: ₹98 falls outside the range, so the price it actually charged cannot stand and the arm's length price is the median of the dataset. Half of ten is five, a whole number, which is the case the definition provides for separately: the median is then the arithmetic mean of the fifth value and the one immediately after it. The fifth is ₹120 and the sixth is ₹124, so the price is ₹122.
keywords: the arm's length price is the median of the dataset
arithmetic mean of the fifth value

options.text: ₹116 a unit
options.misconception: pulls the price to the nearer edge of the band, on the view that reaching the boundary is enough to be at arm's length
options.why: Nothing in the sub-rule moves a price to the boundary. Being inside the band saves the price the company charged; being outside it replaces that price with the median, which sits in the middle of the data and is deliberately harsher than the edge.

options.text: ₹98 a unit stands, the price lying inside the spread the comparables cover
options.misconception: measures the price against the full data rather than against the band built from it
options.why: The comparables run from ₹104 to ₹140 and ₹98 is not even inside that. But the test is not the spread in any event: it is the narrow band from the thirty-fifth to the sixty-fifth percentile, here ₹116 to ₹128, and a price below it is replaced.

options.text: ₹120 a unit
options.misconception: takes the value at the halfway count as the median without averaging it with the next one, which is exactly the step the whole-number case adds
options.why: ₹120 would be right if half of ten had come out fractional, because the count would then move up and stop at a single value. It came out at five exactly, and where the count is exact the definition asks for the mean of that value and its successor. Skipping the averaging costs ₹2 a unit across every one of the 1,50,000 units.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(6) read with Rule 10CA(8)(c)

items.scenario: Torrent Optics Ltd sold 1,50,000 optical modules to its associated enterprise at ₹98 a unit in previous year 2025-26. The comparable uncontrolled price method is the most appropriate method. The dataset has ten entries, in ascending order ₹104, ₹108, ₹112, ₹116, ₹120, ₹124, ₹128, ₹132, ₹136 and ₹140 a unit. The band works out at ₹116 to ₹128 a unit.

items.stem: What follows from the adjustment?

options.text: ₹36,00,000 goes into total income and the section 10AA deduction runs on it as it does on the rest of the unit's profit
options.misconception: keeps the profit-linked deduction on the enhanced income, on the view that a zone unit's profits are relieved whatever raises them
options.why: The deduction was earned by what the unit exported and billed. An addition made because the billing was too low is not export profit the assessee ever declared, and the proviso shuts the deduction out of it precisely so that a company cannot choose to underprice and keep the relief on the correction.

options.text: Nothing is added, the gap between ₹122 and ₹98 being inside the notified tolerance band
options.misconception: applies the tolerance band to a case decided on the range, when the band belongs to the arithmetic mean route the range displaces
options.why: The tolerance the Central Government notifies applies where the dataset has fewer than six entries or the method is one the range does not cover, so the price is compared with an arithmetic mean. Where a band has been built, there is no further margin — and a gap of about a quarter of the declared price would be far outside any margin in any event.

options.text: ₹36,00,000 goes into total income, and the excess money must be brought back from the associated enterprise or carry interest
options.misconception: treats a secondary adjustment as following automatically from every primary one, ignoring the floor below which it does not apply
options.why: Repatriation is what a secondary adjustment asks for, and it does not fire here, because the primary adjustment does not exceed ₹1 crore in the year. The obligation to bring the money back and the interest that runs if it is not brought back both wait on that floor being crossed.
keywords: primary adjustment does not exceed ₹1 crore

options.text: ₹36,00,000 goes into total income, carries no deduction, and brings no obligation to repatriate anything
options.why: The transfer pricing adjustment is the ₹24 a unit shortfall across 1,50,000 units, so ₹36,00,000 is added to the total income of the company for the year. On that enhanced part, no deduction under section 10AA or Chapter VI-A is allowed, so the zone unit's relief does not stretch over it and the whole of the addition is taxed. Repatriation is a separate question and does not arise on these figures.
keywords: no deduction under section 10AA or Chapter VI-A

citation.ref: Section 92C(3) and (4) with the first proviso, and section 92CE(1) with its proviso

items.scenario: Torrent Optics Ltd charged its associated enterprise ₹98 a unit on 1,50,000 optical modules and the arm's length price has been settled at ₹122 a unit on the median of a ten-entry dataset. The company runs a unit in a special economic zone and claims a deduction under section 10AA on its profits. Its finance head expects the enhanced profit to carry the same deduction, and separately expects to have to bring money back from the associated enterprise.

items.stem: What penalties can the Assessing Officer impose on him?

options.text: ₹8,000 under section 271D only
options.misconception: leaves the interest out of the repayment test, so a deposit of ₹19,000 is read as below the limit
options.why: The repayment provision does not look at the principal on its own. It measures the deposit with whatever interest is payable on it, and ₹19,000 with ₹2,000 is ₹21,000. Paying the interest in cash is what pushes an otherwise harmless repayment over.

options.text: Nothing, no single amount reaching ₹20,000
options.misconception: tests each transaction on its own, which is the reading both provisions were amended to close
options.why: Taking amounts one at a time is exactly how the limit used to be got round, and both provisions now say so in terms — one by adding the earlier unpaid loan, the other by adding the interest. Reading them transaction by transaction leaves neither with anything to do.

options.text: ₹22,000 under section 271D and ₹21,000 under section 271E
options.misconception: charges the penalty on the aggregate that crossed the line, when the penalty is measured by the loan actually taken in cash after it was crossed
options.why: The aggregation test and the penalty measure are two different sums. The ₹14,000 broke nothing when it was taken, because nothing was then outstanding. Only the June loan was taken with the line already crossed, so ₹8,000 is what the penalty equals. The ₹21,000 on the repayment side is right, because there the whole sum repaid is what the section measures.

options.text: ₹8,000 under section 271D and ₹21,000 under section 271E
options.why: On the taking side the section adds the new loan to whatever the same lender has already advanced and which is still unpaid, and it bites once the total is ₹20,000 or more. ₹14,000 outstanding plus a fresh ₹8,000 is ₹22,000, so the June loan is the one taken in contravention, and the penalty is equal to that loan alone. On the repaying side the deposit is measured together with the interest payable on it, which takes ₹19,000 past the same line, and the penalty there is equal to the whole amount repaid.

citation.ref: Section 269SS with section 271D, and section 269T with section 271E

items.scenario: Mr Barot wholesales cloth and has income chargeable to tax. On 6 May 2025 he took ₹14,000 in cash as a loan from a supplier he is friendly with. That loan was still outstanding when, on 19 June 2025, he took a further ₹8,000 in cash from the same man. Separately, on 3 March 2026 he repaid in cash a deposit of ₹19,000 that a neighbour had placed with him two years earlier, together with ₹2,000 of interest that had accrued on it. Neither counterparty is a bank, a society or a government body.

items.stem: Which of these receipts breaks section 269ST?

options.text: The two receipts from Mr Nadkarni, and the ₹5,00,000 she drew from her bank
options.misconception: treats a person's own bank withdrawal as a receipt the section reaches, because cash of that size has come into her hands
options.why: A cash withdrawal by a person from an account with a bank, a co-operative bank or a post office savings bank is excluded from section 269ST by notification. It is her own money moving from one of her pockets to another, and a rule that limited it would stop a trader taking out her own float.

options.text: The two receipts from Mr Nadkarni, and the ₹5,40,000 taken at the wedding
options.misconception: adds up what several people gave at a single event, when the limb about an event measures each payer separately
options.why: The third limb does speak of receipts relating to one occasion, and it is there to stop a single payer splitting one payment into instalments across the days of an event. It is not a rule that adds three relatives together. Three cousins are three payers, and none of them reached the limit.

options.text: None of them, no single payment reaching ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: reads the limit as applying to each payment, when the first limb is expressly about the aggregate in a day
options.why: A limit on single payments would be met by writing two receipts, which is why the first limb is written on the day's total from one person and the second on a single transaction however it is paid. The September pair fails the first of those.

options.text: Only the two receipts from Mr Nadkarni
options.why: The section counts what one payer hands over in aggregate from a person in a day, so ₹1,45,000 and ₹85,000 from Mr Nadkarni on 8 September come to ₹2,30,000 and take her past the ₹2,00,000 line. The penalty equals the receipt, and the only way out of it is to prove that there were good and sufficient reasons for the contravention. The wedding money is tested per person, and ₹1,80,000 from each cousin stays under the line.
keywords: in aggregate from a person in a day

citation.ref: Section 269ST(a) and (c) with section 271DA, and Notification No. 28/2017 dated 5 April 2017

items.scenario: Mrs Kamat runs a furniture showroom. On 8 September 2025 she took ₹1,45,000 in cash from Mr Nadkarni for a dining set and, later the same day, ₹85,000 in cash from him for two cabinets. At her daughter's wedding on 2 December 2025 three cousins each handed her ₹1,80,000 in cash as a gift. In January 2026 she withdrew ₹5,00,000 in cash from her own current account at her bank.

items.stem: How is the advance dealt with?

options.text: No penalty, because the money was returned
options.misconception: treats a refund as curing the contravention, when the contravention was complete on the day the cash was taken
options.why: The wrong is in the mode of taking, and it was finished the moment the notes changed hands. Returning the money later is no more an answer than returning stolen goods. He was at least right to refund by cheque, because a cash refund would have raised a second question under the repayment provision.

options.text: Penalties of ₹3,20,000 under section 271D and ₹3,20,000 under section 271DA
options.misconception: applies both cash provisions to one receipt, missing the carve-out that keeps them from overlapping
options.why: The later provision expressly leaves out transactions of the nature the earlier one deals with. That carve-out exists so a single receipt cannot be punished twice over, and a property advance is squarely inside it.

options.text: No penalty, because the sale fell through
options.misconception: makes the penalty depend on the transfer completing, when the definition says in terms that it does not
options.why: The definition was drafted with the failed sale in mind. If completion decided the matter, any cash advance could be kept outside the section by calling the deal off, and the money would have moved in cash all the same.

options.text: A penalty of ₹3,20,000 under section 271D, and nothing under section 271DA
options.why: Money receivable in relation to the transfer of immovable property is a specified sum, and the section catches it whether or not the transfer takes place. The failed sale and the refund change nothing, so the penalty equal to the advance stands. As for the other provision, it stands back from a transaction of the kind the first one already governs, so there is no second penalty on the same receipt.
keywords: whether or not the transfer takes place

citation.ref: Section 269SS with the definition of specified sum and section 271D; the exclusion in section 269ST for transactions of the nature referred to in section 269SS

items.scenario: Mr Ranade agreed to sell his warehouse and took ₹3,20,000 in cash from the intending buyer as an advance on 11 August 2025. In January 2026 the buyer's bank refused him a loan, the sale never went through, and Mr Ranade returned the whole advance by cheque. He says no penalty can arise, because he took no loan, no property changed hands and the money went back.

items.stem: What goes in the other three boxes?

options.text: Variation of not more than ₹50 lakh, income returned of not more than ₹10 lakh, and no search, survey or treaty information behind the order
options.misconception: swaps the two ceilings, putting the larger figure on the dispute and the smaller on the taxpayer
options.why: The larger figure describes the taxpayer the Chapter was built for — a small one — and the smaller figure describes the size of quarrel it is worth resolving without an appeal. Swapping them would open the route to a big taxpayer with a big dispute and close it to the small taxpayer it was written for.

options.text: Variation of not more than ₹10 lakh, income returned of not more than ₹50 lakh, and no search, survey or treaty information behind the order
options.why: Section 245MA lets an order through only when all three hold together. The variations proposed or made in it must not exceed ₹10 lakh in the aggregate. A return must have been furnished for that year and the total income in it must not exceed ₹50 lakh. And the order must not rest on a search or a requisition, on a survey, or on information received under an agreement with another country. One failure shuts the door, however modest the dispute looks.

options.text: Variation of not more than ₹10 lakh, the returned income and the origin of the order both being immaterial once the variation is small
options.misconception: reads the three conditions as alternatives, so clearing one is thought to be enough
options.why: The conditions are cumulative and each does different work. A taxpayer with ₹80 lakh of returned income and a ₹3 lakh dispute is outside, and so is one whose figures are both small but whose assessment was framed on what a survey turned up.

options.text: Variation of not more than ₹10 lakh, income returned of not more than ₹50 lakh, and no prosecution ever launched against the client under any law
options.misconception: pulls a condition about the person into the test that is applied to the order
options.why: There are two sets of conditions and they are tested separately. Detention orders and convictions under the smuggling, money-laundering and black money laws go to whether the person may apply at all. What the order itself has to clear is the two money ceilings and the bar on search, survey and treaty information.

citation.ref: Explanation (b) to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(ii)

items.scenario: A tax adviser is writing a one-page checklist for clients who ask whether they can go to a Dispute Resolution Committee instead of filing an appeal. She has four boxes on it: the order must be one of the kinds the Chapter names, the variation must be small, the income returned must be small, and the order must not have come out of certain kinds of enquiry. Only the first box is filled in.

items.stem: Which of them can apply?

options.text: All three, the ceilings being guidance the Committee can relax on a proper case
options.misconception: treats the conditions as discretionary, when they define what the Committee may look at
options.why: The Committee has discretion over what it does with an application once it is admitted — it may modify, or decline to modify, and it may waive a penalty. It has no power to admit an order the Chapter does not reach, because that would be deciding a dispute the legislature gave it no jurisdiction over.

options.text: None of the three
options.why: Each fails on a different limb. Mr Salvi's dispute is small but the income he returned, ₹65 lakh, is over the ceiling on returned income. Ms Farid is comfortably inside on returned income but her variation of ₹12 lakh is over the ceiling on the dispute. Dhruva Traders is inside both figures and still fails, because an order founded on a survey is outside the Chapter whatever the amounts are. To be eligible a taxpayer has to clear all three, not two of them.

options.text: Mr Salvi and Dhruva Traders
options.misconception: applies the ₹50 lakh ceiling to the size of the dispute instead of to the income the taxpayer returned
options.why: Reading it that way lets Mr Salvi through on a ₹4 lakh variation and shuts Ms Farid out on ₹12 lakh, which happens to be the right result for her and the wrong one for him. The two ceilings attach to two different figures, and the larger one attaches to the return.

options.text: Dhruva Traders only
options.misconception: reads the two money ceilings as the whole of the test and forgets the bar on how the order was arrived at
options.why: Its figures are the best of the three and that is what makes it the tempting answer. The third condition is not about size at all: where an assessment rests on a search, a requisition, a survey or information from a treaty partner, the Chapter is closed and the ordinary appeal is the only road.

citation.ref: Section 245MA conditions applied — the variation, the returned income and orders founded on search or survey

items.scenario: Three clients received orders for assessment year 2025-26 and each wants to go to a Dispute Resolution Committee. Mr Salvi returned ₹65 lakh and his order adds ₹4 lakh. Ms Farid returned ₹31 lakh and her order adds ₹12 lakh. Dhruva Traders returned ₹22 lakh and its order adds ₹3 lakh, but the order was framed on what a survey at the shop turned up. None of the three has been detained or prosecuted under any law.

items.stem: What does she file, and who decides it?

options.text: The prescribed form with a fee of ₹10,000, decided by a bench of two
options.misconception: scales the fee to a tribunal's and gives the body an even number of members
options.why: A four-figure fee would be a real deterrent on a dispute capped at ₹10 lakh. And a body of two could deadlock, which is why the composition is odd-numbered and the rule says decisions are taken by majority.

options.text: The prescribed form with no fee, decided by a single Commissioner of the region
options.misconception: assumes a route meant to be cheap and quick carries no fee and is heard by one officer
options.why: It is cheap, but not free, and the fee is the same whatever the dispute is worth. A single decision-maker is what an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) already gives; the point of this route is a small collegiate body, most of it drawn from outside the serving department.

options.text: The prescribed form with a fee of ₹1,000, decided by a committee of three sitting for the region and deciding by majority
options.why: Rule 44DAB gives the form and puts a fee of ₹1,000 on it, a small sum on purpose, because the Chapter was built for small disputes. The Committee is constituted for each Principal Chief Commissioner's region and has three members: two officers retired from the Indian Revenue Service who held the post of Commissioner or higher for five years or more, and one serving officer not below Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. They are appointed for three years and decide by majority.

options.text: The prescribed form with the fee, but the matter goes to the Dispute Resolution Panel of three Commissioners
options.misconception: confuses the Committee under this Chapter with the Panel that hears a draft order under section 144C
options.why: The Panel under section 144C is a body of three serving Commissioners and it hears draft orders for eligible assessees. This Committee is a different body with a different composition, and an assessee who has the choice takes one road or the other, not both.

citation.ref: Rules 44DAA and 44DAB — composition of the Committee and the application with its fee

items.scenario: Ms Priyanka has cleared every condition and has decided to take her dispute to a Dispute Resolution Committee rather than appeal. Her article clerk is preparing the papers and asks what has to go with the application and who will actually hear it.

items.stem: How much of what the accountant said is right?

options.text: The second point only
options.misconception: assumes the concessional corporate rate sweeps away the whole of Chapter VI-A
options.why: It sweeps away most of it, and that is why the mistake is so easy to make. The two that survive are the deduction for new employment and the deduction for inter-corporate dividend, and they survive because neither is a shelter for the company's own profit — one pays for jobs and the other stops the same dividend being taxed twice.

options.text: Neither point
options.why: The deduction is 30 per cent of the additional employee cost of the year, and the same amount is allowed again in each of three assessment years counting from the one in which the employment was given, so a single year's hiring is relieved three times over. It is also available irrespective of the regime under which the company pays tax: the concessional route computes income without Chapter VI-A relief, but it keeps this deduction and section 80M standing.

options.text: The first point only
options.misconception: reads the relief as a one-year benefit, so hiring in a year is thought to be rewarded once
options.why: A one-year relief would reward the act of hiring rather than the keeping on of the employee, which is what the provision is aimed at. What the section does require of the claimant is that section 44AB applies to him, that his gross total income includes business profits, and that the accountant's report goes in before the specified date.

options.text: Both points
options.misconception: gives up a deduction that costs nothing to keep, on two independent errors that happen to point the same way
options.why: Believing both costs the company the relief in the year of hiring and in the two years after it. The safe habit is to check the regime provision itself, which lists what it takes away by name, rather than to reason from the general idea that a lower rate must come at a price.

citation.ref: Section 80JJAA(1) and (2); section 115BAA(2)(i) preserving sections 80JJAA and 80M

items.scenario: Sanchi Foods Pvt Ltd, whose accounts fall to be audited, took on a large number of new regular employees during 2025-26 and its head count rose. It pays tax at the concessional corporate rate under section 115BAA. Its accountant tells the directors two things: that the relief for new employment is a one-year benefit taken in the year of hiring, and that in any case choosing the concessional rate has given up every Chapter VI-A deduction.

items.stem: Whose cost can the company count?

options.text: None of the four groups
options.misconception: applies the general 240-day test to a footwear maker, so joiners in November look short by three months
options.why: On the general test the November joiners would indeed fail, and that is the trap. The shorter count exists because apparel, footwear and leather work is seasonal, and a business that hires for a season would otherwise never qualify for anything.

options.text: The 20 line workers and the 15 packers
options.misconception: treats provident fund membership as the employer's arrangement rather than a condition attached to the employee
options.why: The condition is written on the employee — one who does not participate in the recognised fund is not an additional employee. The relief is aimed at formal jobs, and the fund membership is the test of formality the section chose.

options.text: The 20 line workers only
options.why: For a business making apparel, footwear or leather goods the service test is 150 days rather than 240, and the twenty who started on 1 November were there for 151 days, so they are in. The twelve designers are out, because emoluments of more than ₹25,000 a month put an employee outside the definition. The fifteen packers are out, because an employee who does not participate in the recognised provident fund is excluded by name. The eight loaders are out on the mode of payment: wages handed over otherwise than by account payee cheque, bank draft or a prescribed electronic mode are left out of the cost.

options.text: The 20 line workers and the 8 loaders
options.misconception: treats the cash payment as a question of allowability of the wage, when it goes to whether the wage enters the additional employee cost at all
options.why: Wages paid in cash may well be deductible in computing business profits. The point here is different: the cost on which this deduction is worked out excludes emoluments paid outside the banking modes, so paying the loaders in cash keeps them out of the count even though they are otherwise qualifying employees.

citation.ref: Section 80JJAA, Explanation — the definition of additional employee and its exclusions

items.scenario: Nirvaan Leathers Ltd makes leather footwear and its accounts are audited. Its head count rose over 2025-26. Among those taken on were 20 line workers at ₹19,000 a month who joined on 1 November 2025 and stayed to the year end; 12 designers at ₹27,000 a month who joined in April; 15 packers at ₹18,000 a month who joined in April and are not in the company's recognised provident fund; and 8 loaders at ₹20,000 a month who joined in April and are handed their wages in cash every week.

items.stem: What is the deduction for A.Y. 2026-27, and what becomes of the 30?

options.text: ₹1,45,20,000, the whole additional employee cost being the deduction
options.misconception: takes the cost itself as the deduction instead of the fraction of it the section allows
options.why: The cost is the base and not the relief. A full deduction of the wage bill would be double-counting, since those wages have already been debited in arriving at the business profit; this deduction is a bonus of 30 per cent on top of that.

options.text: ₹49,23,000, counting the January joiners as well
options.misconception: brings the short-served employees into the current year's cost instead of the next year's
options.why: Their three months at ₹21,000 comes to ₹18,90,000 and 30 per cent of it is ₹5,67,000, which is where this figure comes from. It belongs to a later year. The deeming provision moves the whole of their cost into the succeeding year rather than splitting it, so nothing of it is claimed now.

options.text: ₹43,56,000, and the 30 are lost for good
options.misconception: reads the day count as a permanent bar rather than a test applied afresh each year
options.why: The figure is right and the conclusion about the January joiners is not. Losing them permanently would mean an employer hiring in the last quarter got nothing for those people ever, which would push all hiring into the first half of the year for reasons that have nothing to do with the business.

options.text: ₹43,56,000, and the 30 are not lost
options.why: The cost is the emoluments paid to the qualifying additional employees for the year: 55 people at ₹24,000 a month for the eleven months from 1 May comes to ₹1,45,20,000, and 30 per cent of that is ₹43,56,000, which the company takes for this year and for the two years after it. The January joiners served fewer days than the section asks for, but an employee who serves short in one year and long enough in the next is deemed to have been employed in the succeeding year, so their cost starts its own three-year run from the next assessment year if they stay.
keywords: deemed to have been employed in the succeeding year

citation.ref: Section 80JJAA — computation of additional employee cost, and the deeming of employment in the succeeding year

items.scenario: Anhad Textiles Ltd makes apparel and its accounts are audited. Its head count rose over 2025-26. After the exclusions have been worked through, 55 of the new employees qualify: each joined on 1 May 2025 at ₹24,000 a month, is in the recognised provident fund and is paid by bank transfer. A further 30 employees joined on 1 January 2026 at ₹21,000 a month and were there for 90 days by the year end. They are all still on the rolls.

items.stem: What does Kavach owe, and when?

options.text: The notification, within twelve months of the end of the reporting accounting year
options.misconception: gives the notification the report's clock, so an earlier duty is put after the thing it exists to announce
options.why: The form is right and the date is not. A notification that arrived at the same time as the report would tell the authority nothing it was not about to receive anyway, which is why it runs on its own and earlier clock.

options.text: The country-by-country report itself, within twelve months of the year end
options.misconception: treats every constituent entity as a reporting entity, so the Indian subsidiary is thought to owe the report
options.why: The report is the parent's duty, and it falls on an Indian entity only in the narrow cases where the parent's country will not collect it or will not share it. What Kavach has to watch is the notification, which is due at least two months before the date the report falls due — an earlier deadline than the report's own, and the one most often missed.

options.text: Nothing, the parent having filed at home in a country that exchanges reports with India
options.misconception: reads the exchange arrangement as excusing every Indian obligation, when it excuses only the report
options.why: The exchange arrangement is exactly what takes the report off Kavach. It does not touch the notification, whose whole purpose is to tell the Indian authority which foreign filing to go looking for. Without it the authority does not know whose report to ask Country M for.

options.text: A notification naming the parent, given ahead of the date the report itself falls due
options.why: Reporting attaches to a group whose consolidated revenue for the year before the reporting year is above ₹6,400 crore, and ₹9,300 crore is above it, so the group is in. The report, Form 3CEAD, is filed by the parent or the alternate reporting entity within twelve months of the end of the reporting accounting year, and here that is done abroad. What an Indian constituent entity of a foreign-parented group owes instead is a notification in Form 3CEAC, saying whether it is itself the alternate reporting entity and, if not, who the parent or alternate reporting entity is and where it is resident.

citation.ref: Section 286(1), (2) and (7) read with Rule 10DB

items.scenario: Kavach Systems Pvt Ltd is the Indian subsidiary of a group whose parent is resident in Country M. The group's consolidated revenue for the year ended 31 December 2024 was ₹9,300 crore. The reporting accounting year ended on 31 December 2025. Country M requires country-by-country reports and has an arrangement with India for exchanging them, and the parent files its report there on time. Kavach's finance head believes that nothing at all is due from an Indian subsidiary in these circumstances.

items.stem: What do the two of them have to furnish?

options.text: Both file the country-by-country report in India, a foreign parent's filing not counting
options.misconception: assumes India collects the report from its own residents regardless of where the parent has filed
options.why: Collecting the same report in every country the group operates in is exactly what the exchange machinery was built to avoid. India takes it from the parent's own tax authority and only steps in when that authority will not require it or will not pass it on.

options.text: Neither files the country-by-country report; Kavach Systems furnishes the master file in full and Kavach Services furnishes only its first part
options.why: An Indian constituent entity has to file the report itself only where the parent's country does not require one, has no arrangement for the exchange of such reports with India, or has been found in systemic failure and the entity has been told of it; none of that is so here. Where more than one Indian entity would be liable, the group may put one forward for all of them by conveying the nomination in Form 3CEAE. The master file is a separate duty with its own two tests, which Kavach Systems meets and Kavach Services does not — but Part A of that form goes in from every constituent entity whether or not the tests are met.

options.text: Kavach Services may simply be nominated to furnish the master file for both, being the smaller of the two
options.misconception: treats a nomination as something the group can decide internally, forgetting the form and the notice period that make it effective
options.why: A designation for the master file works only if it is conveyed to the designated Joint Director in Form 3CEAB at least 30 days before the form itself is due. A nomination recorded only in the group's own papers leaves both entities in default, and the smallness of the nominee is beside the point.

options.text: Kavach Systems furnishes the master file in full and Kavach Services furnishes nothing at all
options.misconception: reads the two master file tests as excusing a small entity entirely, when they decide only how much of the form it fills
options.why: The tests decide who furnishes the detailed information — the group's structure, its intangibles, its financing arrangements. They do not decide who is on the register at all. The short first part of the form is how the department knows which Indian companies belong to which international group.

citation.ref: Section 286(4) and (5) with the proviso; Rule 10DA(2), (3) and (4)

items.scenario: Kavach Systems Pvt Ltd and Kavach Services Pvt Ltd are both resident in India and both belong to the same group, whose parent is resident in Country M and whose consolidated revenue is ₹9,300 crore. Country M requires country-by-country reports and shares them with India. Kavach Systems had international transactions of ₹73 crore in the year; Kavach Services had ₹9 crore, none of it touching intangible property.

items.stem: What does the penalty provision produce on these facts?

options.text: The higher day-rate for all 50 days, the delay having gone past a month
options.misconception: applies the escalated rate retrospectively to the whole delay once the month is crossed
options.why: The higher rate is charged for the period exceeding one month, not from the beginning because a month was eventually exceeded. The first thirty days remain priced at the lower rate however long the default afterwards runs.

options.text: One day-rate for the whole 50 days, and a fixed sum for the inaccuracy
options.misconception: flattens the two bands into one rate, so a long delay costs the same each day as a short one
options.why: The bands are stepped so that the cost of delay rises the longer it lasts, which is the usual shape of a penalty meant to bring a filing in rather than to punish a late one. Using the lower rate throughout understates the charge for every day past the first month.

options.text: The fixed sum for the inaccuracy alone, the day-rates being for a report never filed at all
options.misconception: reads the day-rates as a charge for non-filing, when they are a charge for the period of the failure however it ends
options.why: Failure to furnish covers furnishing late as well as not furnishing, and the day-rates run for the period the report was outstanding. A report handed in a year late would otherwise cost the same as one handed in a day late.

options.text: A day-rate for the first month, a higher day-rate for the days after that, and a separate fixed sum for the inaccuracy
options.why: The delay is charged in two bands: ₹5,000 for each day while the default has run for not more than a month, and ₹15,000 for each day of the period beyond a month, so a 50-day delay is priced at two different rates on either side of the thirtieth day. A default that carries on even after a penalty order has been served costs ₹50,000 a day from the date that order is served, which did not happen here. The inaccuracy is charged on its own at ₹5,00,000, because the company knew of it when it filed and did not tell the authority.

citation.ref: Section 271GB(1), (3) and (4)

items.scenario: Aurum Alloys Ltd was the entity in the group obliged to furnish the country-by-country report, and it filed 50 days after the due date. No penalty order had been served on it in the meantime. Some weeks later it accepted that one of the figures in the report was wrong, and that it had known the figure was wrong on the day it filed and had said nothing to the prescribed authority.

items.stem: What has to happen to the ₹5,00,000 in the computation for A.Y. 2026-27?

options.text: Leave it. The two sides fixed 60 days in writing and the statute defers to the period the parties agreed
options.misconception: reads the agreed period as binding on its own, without noticing that the statute puts a ceiling over any agreement the parties can reach
options.why: An agreement chooses the period only up to a limit somebody else set. A written bargain may name any date it likes so long as it falls inside the statutory ceiling; a clause saying 60 days is read down to that ceiling rather than obeyed. Where there is no written agreement at all the period is shorter still, 15 days, which is the clearest sign that the parties are not the ones setting it.

options.text: Leave it. The sum was paid before the due date for furnishing the return, which is the test section 43B applies to everything it covers
options.misconception: carries the first proviso to section 43B across to clause (h), where Parliament did not extend it, so any payment before the return date reads as rescuing the deduction
options.why: The escape route is real for the rest of section 43B and it stops short of clause (h). ICAI's own guidance on the tax audit clause says so in terms — the benefit of paying by the return date is not available for a sum covered by clause (h). For money owed to a small supplier the only date that counts is the one the MSMED Act fixes, and once that has gone by, paying early in the next year changes the year of the deduction and nothing else.

options.text: Add ₹5,00,000 back this year, and it is gone for good — a payment outside the statutory period is not deductible in any year
options.misconception: treats clause (h) as a confiscation rather than a postponement, so a late payment reads as losing the expense permanently
options.why: Section 43B moves a deduction; it does not cancel one. Every clause in the section works the same way — the sum waits until the year the money actually leaves and is allowed then. Confiscation is what section 36(1)(va) does to a late employees' contribution, and mixing the two rules costs a full mark in a five-item computation because the treatment of the two figures is different.

options.text: Add ₹5,00,000 back this year and claim it in the year ending 31st March 2027
options.why: Clause (h) suspends the deduction for a sum payable to a micro or small enterprise that is not settled inside the time limit section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006 sets, which is at most 45 days where the parties put their bargain in writing. The moulds were accepted on 20th January 2026, so the money was due by 6th March 2026 and was six weeks late. The expense stays in the accounts for the year ended 31st March 2026 and is added back in the computation, and the deduction arrives in the year of actual payment, which here is the year ending 31st March 2027.
keywords: a sum payable to a micro or small enterprise
the time limit section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006 sets, which is at most 45 days
the deduction arrives in the year of actual payment

citation.ref: Section 43B(h) read with section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006

items.scenario: Meghna Castings Pvt Ltd follows the mercantile system. It took delivery of moulds worth ₹5,00,000 from Tarika Engineering on 20th January 2026. Tarika is registered as a small enterprise, and the written supply agreement the two signed fixes payment within 60 days of acceptance. Meghna paid on 20th April 2026, which is well before 31st October 2026, the due date for filing its return for A.Y. 2026-27. The accountant has left the ₹5,00,000 in the profit and loss account and claimed it, on two grounds — the parties agreed 60 days between themselves, and in any event the money went out long before the return did.

items.stem: How much does Ambar Textiles add back under section 43B(h)?

options.why: Clause (h) names a micro or small enterprise and nobody else. The Vasudha dues fell due on 27th March 2026 under the 45-day ceiling and were still open on 31st March, so ₹2,40,000 is added back and waits for the year of payment. Konark is a medium enterprise, which the clause never reaches, so its ₹3,00,000 is deductible on accrual in the ordinary way and the length of the delay makes no difference to it — not even the absence of a written agreement, which shortens the clock only for a supplier the clause covers.
keywords: Clause (h) names a micro or small enterprise and nobody else
a medium enterprise, which the clause never reaches
deductible on accrual in the ordinary way

options.text: Nil. Nothing has been paid, so no year of actual payment has arrived and there is nothing to shift between years yet
options.misconception: reads the clause as switching on when a late payment is made, when what it does is withhold the deduction until one is
options.why: The clause does not wait for a payment before it bites. It denies the deduction in the year of accrual the moment the statutory period has run out unpaid, and it hands the deduction to whichever later year the money finally leaves in. A supplier who is never paid at all leaves the deduction permanently unclaimed rather than permanently allowed.

options.text: ₹5,40,000. Both suppliers are registered under the MSMED Act and both are unpaid at the year end, so both sums wait for payment
options.misconception: treats registration under the MSMED Act as the test, when the clause names only two of the Act's three sizes and leaves the third alone
options.why: Registration is not the gate; size is. The clause reaches a sum payable to a micro or small enterprise and goes no further, and the medium size was left outside on purpose. Reading registration as the trigger turns a rule aimed at protecting the smallest suppliers into a general rule about paying anybody late, which is not what it says.

options.text: ₹3,00,000. The Konark balance is the older of the two and has no written agreement covering it, so it is the one outside the time limit
options.misconception: works out which balance is furthest past its date before asking whether the clause covers that supplier at all
options.why: The order of the questions matters. Whether a supplier is inside the clause is settled first, by size, and only then does the clock get read. Konark is outside the clause, so the 15-day period that applies where there is no written agreement never comes into it, and the balance is allowed on accrual however long it stands.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h) — scope limited to micro and small enterprises

items.scenario: Ambar Textiles Pvt Ltd has two supplier balances open at 31st March 2026. ₹2,40,000 is owed to Vasudha Threads, registered as a small enterprise, whose goods were accepted on 10th February 2026 under a written agreement allowing 45 days. ₹3,00,000 is owed to Konark Dyes, registered as a medium enterprise, whose goods were accepted on 5th January 2026 under no written agreement at all. Neither has been paid. Both suppliers hold current registrations under the MSMED Act and both have said so on their invoices.

items.stem: What is his total income for A.Y. 2026-27, and what becomes of the rest of the loss?

options.text: ₹6,00,000. A house property loss never meets salary income; it waits for house property income from the first year onwards
options.misconception: applies the carry-forward rule, which really is confined to this head, to the year the loss arises as well, when the first year is the one year the inter-head window is open
options.why: The two years work differently and that is the whole design. In the year the loss arises it may cross heads, up to two lakh, and salary is not excluded from what it can meet. From the following year the carried loss is confined to this head. Treating year one like year two gives a total income two lakh too high and drops a mark and a half of a set-off question.

options.text: ₹4,00,000, with the balance carried forward for eight assessment years and set off thereafter against house property income only
options.why: A loss under this head goes against income under any other head only up to ₹2,00,000 in the year, so the salary of ₹6,00,000 is reduced by that much and no more, leaving a total income of ₹4,00,000. What the ceiling holds back is not lost: the balance ₹1,20,000 is carried forward under section 71B for eight assessment years, and from next year it can meet income under the head house property and nothing else. Filing on time is not a condition of this particular carry forward, though it is of most of the others.
keywords: against income under any other head only up to ₹2,00,000 in the year
the balance ₹1,20,000 is carried forward under section 71B for eight assessment years

options.text: ₹2,80,000. The whole ₹3,20,000 comes off the salary, because the two-lakh ceiling in this area applies to interest on a self-occupied house and this house is let out
options.misconception: confuses the two-lakh ceiling on interest for a self-occupied property with the two-lakh ceiling on setting a computed house property loss against another head
options.why: Two different two-lakh limits sit close together and only one of them is in play. The first caps a deduction while the loss is being computed, and it is confined to a self-occupied property; this flat is let out, so the loss of ₹3,20,000 is computed in full and that limit never appears. The second caps the next step entirely separately — how much of a loss, once computed, may be taken against income under any other head — and it applies whatever kind of property produced it.

options.text: ₹4,00,000, and the unabsorbed ₹1,20,000 lapses, because two lakh is the largest loss this head is allowed to produce in a year
options.misconception: reads the two-lakh figure as a ceiling on the loss itself rather than on how much of it may cross into another head
options.why: Nothing caps the loss. Interest, municipal taxes and the standard deduction are all taken in full and the head produces whatever it produces. The ceiling sits one step later, on the journey out of the head, and a journey blocked this year is postponed rather than cancelled — which is exactly why section 71B exists and gives it eight years to find house property income to meet.

citation.ref: Section 71(3A) and section 71B — the ₹2 lakh inter-head cap and the eight-year carry forward

items.scenario: Mr Devansh, a resident individual aged 38, has shifted out of the default tax regime for A.Y. 2026-27. His salary for the year, computed, is ₹6,00,000. He owns one flat, let out through the year, on which the municipal taxes and the interest on the housing loan together exceed the rent, giving a loss under the head income from house property of ₹3,20,000. He has no other income and filed his return within the time allowed. His accountant has set the whole ₹3,20,000 against the salary.

items.stem: What happens to the house property loss under the default tax regime?

options.text: None of the loss meets any other head, and nothing is carried forward — the total income is ₹6,00,000
options.why: Under the default tax regime a loss under the head house property is not allowed to be set off against income under any other head at all, so the salary of ₹6,00,000 stands as the total income and the two-lakh window is simply not there. Nor is there anything to keep for later: the unabsorbed loss could not be carried forward to the following assessment year. The whole ₹3,20,000 goes, and what decides that is the choice of regime rather than the size of the loss.
keywords: Under the default tax regime a loss under the head house property is not allowed to be set off
the unabsorbed loss could not be carried forward to the following assessment year

options.text: None of it meets any other head this year, but the whole ₹3,20,000 is carried forward for eight years and can be set off against house property income later
options.misconception: reads the closed inter-head route as a postponement, when the regime extinguishes the loss instead of storing it
options.why: A rule that blocks a set-off and a rule that kills a loss look alike in the year they operate and differ completely afterwards. Here both apply: the loss cannot cross heads and it cannot be carried either. A company or a firm, by contrast, keeps the two-lakh window and the eight-year carry forward whether or not it has opted into a concessional regime of its own, which is why the answer turns on who the assessee is.

options.text: ₹2,00,000 still comes off the salary as before, but the unabsorbed ₹1,20,000 cannot be carried forward
options.misconception: keeps the inter-head window open and closes only the carry forward, when the regime shuts both doors and not one
options.why: Half the rule is being remembered. If the window were open the answer would be a total income of ₹4,00,000 with a loss that dies at the year end; the real answer keeps the whole salary in charge. Carrying half a rule across is worse than carrying none, because the figure it produces looks like a considered one.

options.text: Nothing moves. The regime changes the rates and the deductions available; it does not touch the set-off rules
options.misconception: reads the default regime as a rate schedule with a shorter list of deductions, when it also closes the inter-head route for this particular loss
options.why: The regime reaches further than the rate card. Along with the deductions it withdraws, it changes what a loss under this head may do, and the change is not a reduction of the two-lakh window but the removal of it. Assuming the set-off rules travel unchanged between the two regimes is the single most expensive assumption in a set-off question, because it moves the total income rather than the tax on it.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC read with section 71B — no inter-head set-off and no carry forward of a house property loss under the default regime

items.scenario: Take Mr Devansh again — salary of ₹6,00,000 computed, one let-out flat producing a loss under the head income from house property of ₹3,20,000, nothing else — but this year he has not shifted out of anything. He is taxed under the default tax regime under section 115BAC(1A), which is where an individual sits unless he opts out. He wants to know whether the answer on the house property loss moves at all, and if so by how much.

items.stem: How much tax should Nandan Retail deduct on these purchases?

options.text: Nothing. The seller collects on this sale instead, and a buyer deducts only where the seller has not collected
options.misconception: still expects the mirror-image collection on a sale of goods, and treats the buyer's obligation as a fallback that switches off when the seller acts
options.why: The collection the option is waiting for was taken off the statute book with effect from 1st April 2025, so there is no seller-side charge on a sale of goods for the buyer's obligation to defer to. What used to be an overlap with a tie-breaker is now a single obligation resting on the buyer alone, and the scenario says as much when it records that no tax is collectible at source on the sale.

options.text: ₹7,500, being 0.1 per cent of the whole ₹75,00,000
options.misconception: reads this section the way section 194-IA works, where crossing the line brings the whole consideration into charge, when here only the excess is charged
options.why: Two sections in this chapter use a fifty-lakh line and they use it differently. On a purchase of immovable property, once the line is crossed the deduction runs on the entire amount. On a purchase of goods the threshold is carved out first and only what stands above it is charged. Knowing which of the two shapes a section has is worth as much as knowing its rate.

Two separate tests decide this and they measure different things. The buyer is sized first — a turnover above ten crore rupees in the preceding financial year makes Nandan a buyer for this section, and ₹12 crore clears that. Then the purchases from that one seller are measured against fifty lakh. Tax then runs on the excess: 0.1% on the amount exceeding ₹50 lakh, which is ₹25,00,000, giving ₹2,500 for the year. Deduction is at credit or payment, whichever comes first.
keywords: which is ₹25,00,000, giving ₹2,500 for the year

options.text: ₹25,000, being 1 per cent of the ₹25,00,000 that stands above fifty lakh
options.misconception: takes the excess as the base correctly and then borrows the one per cent rate from the property section, which shares the fifty-lakh line but not the rate
options.why: The base is right and the rate is not. A purchase of goods is charged at one tenth of one per cent, a tenth of the rate on a purchase of property, and the difference is deliberate — this section is a reporting mechanism over ordinary trade rather than a collection on a one-off transfer. A tenfold error here also flows into the thirty per cent disallowance if the shortfall is ever picked up.

citation.ref: Section 194Q(1) — a buyer with turnover above ₹10 crore, 0.1 per cent on purchases from a seller exceeding ₹50 lakh in the year

items.scenario: Nandan Retail Ltd had a turnover of ₹12 crore in the previous year 2024-25. During 2025-26 it bought goods worth ₹75,00,000 from one resident seller, Suvarna Traders, across eleven invoices, and paid for all of them in the same year. Suvarna holds no certificate for deduction at a lower rate and the sale is not one on which tax is collectible at source. The accountant has worked the deduction out at one tenth of one per cent of ₹75,00,000 and wants the entry approved.

items.stem: At what rate is the doubly taxed income relieved?

options.text: At 11.7 per cent, applied to her total income of ₹10,00,000 rather than to the foreign fees
options.misconception: gets the rate right and the base wrong, relieving income that was only ever taxed once
options.why: Relief answers double taxation, so it can only reach the slice that two countries taxed. The Indian income of ₹8,00,000 was never charged in Country Z and nothing about it is doubled. Applying the rate to the whole total income would wipe out the entire Indian tax on a foreign receipt of one fifth of the income.

options.text: At 15 per cent, the rate she actually bore in Country Z
