options.misconception: treats the relief as a refund of the foreign tax rather than a credit capped by what India itself charged, so the higher of the two rates is read as the measure
options.why: Relief is a deduction from the Indian tax and can never exceed what India charged on that slice of income. Here the rate of tax in Country Z is 15% — ₹30,000 on ₹2,00,000 — and the Indian rate is the lower of the two, so the excess above the Indian rate is simply lost: it is neither refunded nor carried to another year. Where the foreign rate is the lower one it is the foreign rate that applies, so the rule is not a preference for either country.
keywords: the rate of tax in Country Z is 15%

options.text: At 11.7 per cent, because that is the lower of the two rates
options.why: Both rates are averages and neither is a slab rate. The Indian rate is the Indian income-tax after cess but before any double taxation relief, divided by the total income: ₹1,17,000 on a total income of ₹10,00,000 gives 11.7%. The foreign rate is the tax actually paid there divided by the income assessed there, ₹30,000 on ₹2,00,000, which is fifteen per cent. The deduction is worked out on the doubly taxed income at whichever is the lower of the two rates, and here that is India's.
keywords: ₹1,17,000 on a total income of ₹10,00,000 gives 11.7%
at whichever is the lower of the two rates

options.text: At 20 per cent, the slab rate her foreign fees were taxed at in India
options.misconception: uses the rate the top slice of income actually bore instead of the average rate the definition prescribes, which is the commonest error in this computation
options.why: The foreign fees do sit in the twenty per cent slab, and that is exactly why the definition is written as a division rather than as a lookup. Spreading the whole Indian tax over the whole total income gives one rate for the year, well below the top slab, and using the slab instead would overstate the relief by more than half.

citation.ref: Explanation to section 91 — the Indian rate of tax and the rate of tax of the said country

items.scenario: Ms Anvi, a resident individual aged 45, has shifted out of the default tax regime for A.Y. 2026-27. Her income in India for the previous year 2025-26, after every deduction she is entitled to, is ₹8,00,000. She also earned professional fees of ₹2,00,000 for work carried out in Country Z, which has no agreement with India for the avoidance of double taxation, and paid income-tax of ₹30,000 on those fees there. Ignore surcharge. Her accountant is about to work the relief out at the rate her last rupee of Indian income bore.

items.stem: What is her tax payable in India for A.Y. 2026-27?

options.text: ₹1,10,400, relieving the ₹6,600 by which the Country Z tax exceeds the Indian tax on those fees
options.misconception: relieves the difference between the two taxes instead of the doubly taxed income at the lower rate, so the credit comes out at a quarter of its size
options.why: The excess is the part that is NOT relieved, not the part that is. The computation runs the other way round: take the income taxed twice, apply the lower of the two rates to it, and deduct the result. The ₹6,600 the option wants to relieve is exactly the amount the cap throws away.

options.text: ₹1,17,000. There is no relief at all, because relief from double taxation comes from an agreement and there is none with Country Z
options.misconception: thinks relief lives only in a treaty, when the unilateral provision exists precisely for countries India has no treaty with
options.why: The absence of an agreement is the condition for this relief rather than a bar to it. Where a treaty exists, relief is given under it; where none exists, the Act grants relief on its own, on the six conditions it lists. Reading a missing treaty as a missing remedy costs the whole of a six-mark question.

options.text: ₹87,000, being ₹1,17,000 less the ₹30,000 borne in Country Z
options.misconception: gives credit for the whole foreign tax, ignoring the cap that limits relief to what India charged on the same income
options.why: A pound-for-pound refund of foreign tax would leave India collecting less on the foreign income than on the domestic income, and no country writes its relief that way. The measure is the doubly taxed income at the lower of the two rates, which caps the credit at the Indian tax on that income. Anything the other country charged above that stays with the other country.

A resident is taxed on world income, so the foreign fees are inside the total income of ₹10,00,000 and the Indian tax on the whole comes to ₹1,17,000 with cess. The relief is then the doubly taxed income of ₹2,00,000 taken at the lower rate of 11.7 per cent, a deduction of ₹23,400. That leaves ₹93,600 to pay. The ₹6,600 of Country Z tax above the Indian rate is neither refunded nor carried forward — it is the price of earning in a country that taxes more heavily than India does.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) — deduction on the doubly taxed income at the Indian rate or the foreign rate, whichever is lower

items.scenario: The same facts as before. Ms Anvi is resident, outside the default tax regime, with Indian income of ₹8,00,000 after all deductions and professional fees of ₹2,00,000 from Country Z, on which ₹30,000 of income-tax was paid there. India has no agreement with Country Z. Ignore surcharge. Her Indian tax before any relief, on the whole of her income and including health and education cess, is ₹1,17,000.

items.stem: Who has to get accounts audited under section 44AB?

options.text: Both, because the relief to ₹10 crore is available only to companies and these are proprietary concerns
options.misconception: attaches the relief to the form of the entity when it attaches to how the receipts and payments moved
options.why: Nothing in the provision mentions the form of the assessee. It asks two questions about cash and takes the same answer from a proprietor, a firm and a company alike. The form of the entity does matter elsewhere in this area — a company is audited under its own law and so furnishes a different form — but not to which threshold applies.

options.text: Neither. Both turnovers are below ₹10 crore
options.misconception: treats ₹10 crore as the standing limit for a business, when it is a relief that has to be earned and the standing limit is ₹1 crore
options.why: The accountant has taken the relief as the rule. A business is measured against ₹1 crore unless it qualifies for the higher figure, and qualifying is about how the money moved rather than about how much of it there was. Somebody at ₹2 crore who takes a fifth of his receipts in cash needs an audit; somebody at ₹9 crore who banks everything does not.
keywords: A business is measured against ₹1 crore unless it qualifies for the higher figure

options.text: Vardhan Traders only, because his cash payments at 4 per cent are the nearer of the four figures to the line
options.misconception: compares the percentages with each other instead of comparing each with the five per cent limit, so the closest figure reads as the failing one
options.why: Being near a limit is not being over it. Each of the four percentages is measured against the same five per cent and nothing else, and a business either satisfies both of its own conditions or does not. Vardhan satisfies both with room to spare; the fact that one of his figures is higher than another of his figures decides nothing.

options.text: Kamla Stores only
options.why: The ordinary business limit is ₹1 crore, and the ₹10 crore figure is a relief that has to be earned. To earn it, aggregate cash receipts and aggregate cash payments must each stay within 5% of their own totals, and both conditions have to be met together. Vardhan's three and four per cent clear both, so ₹8.5 crore sits inside the raised limit and no audit is needed. Cash receipts at 6% of total receipts break the first condition, so Kamla loses the relief, is measured against ₹1 crore, and ₹9 crore is far past it. A cheque or draft that is not account payee counts as cash in both tests.
keywords: aggregate cash receipts and aggregate cash payments must each stay within 5% of their own totals
both conditions have to be met together
Cash receipts at 6% of total receipts break the first condition
the ₹10 crore figure is a relief that has to be earned

citation.ref: Section 44AB(a) proviso — the ten crore limit where cash receipts and cash payments are each within five per cent

items.scenario: Two proprietors ask about the previous year 2025-26. Vardhan Traders has a turnover of ₹8.5 crore, with cash receipts running at 3 per cent of total receipts and cash payments at 4 per cent of total payments. Kamla Stores has a turnover of ₹9 crore, with cash receipts at 6 per cent of total receipts and cash payments at 2 per cent of total payments. Neither declares income on a presumptive basis. Their common accountant has told them that since both are under ₹10 crore, neither needs an audit under section 44AB.

items.stem: Which of them must get accounts audited?

options.text: Dr Roshni only. Nakul's banking keeps him inside the relief, which is what the cash conditions are for
options.misconception: treats the cash conditions as an exemption from audit rather than as the way a higher ceiling is earned
options.why: Clean banking buys a bigger allowance, not an escape. It moves the line from one crore to ten and then stops; past ten crore the condition has nothing left to give and the audit follows from the size of the business alone. A trader banking every rupee of ₹40 crore is audited exactly like one who does not.

options.text: Neither. Each of Nakul's businesses is well under ₹10 crore, and Dr Roshni is nowhere near the ₹1 crore business limit
options.misconception: tests each business separately and then measures a profession against the limit written for a business
options.why: Two mistakes compound here. A person is measured once, on everything he carries on, rather than business by business; and a profession has a limit of its own that is a twentieth of the business one, so measuring a doctor against a business figure will always say no.

options.text: Both
options.why: Turnover from all businesses is aggregated for section 44AB, so Nakul is measured on ₹11 crore and not on ₹7 crore and ₹4 crore apart. That is above the ten crore ceiling, and above that ceiling an audit is required however clean the banking is — the cash tests can lift the limit as far as ten crore and can never lift it beyond. A profession is measured on its own line, where gross receipts in profession above ₹50 lakh bring the audit in, so ₹55 lakh does.
keywords: Turnover from all businesses is aggregated for section 44AB
measured on ₹11 crore and not on ₹7 crore and ₹4 crore apart
gross receipts in profession above ₹50 lakh bring the audit in

options.text: Nakul only. Professional receipts are never aggregated with anything and ₹55 lakh is below every limit in the section
options.misconception: applies the business threshold to a profession, which has its own and much lower one
options.why: The point about aggregation is right and the threshold used is wrong. Professional receipts are indeed measured on their own rather than being added to a business turnover, and they are measured against fifty lakh. Getting the first half right and the second half wrong reaches the same answer as knowing neither.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(a) — turnover of all businesses aggregated; section 44AB(b) — profession above fifty lakh

items.scenario: Nakul runs two proprietary businesses — a textile business with a turnover of ₹7 crore and a retail business with a turnover of ₹4 crore — and every receipt and payment in both goes through account-payee banking, with no cash at all. In the same building Dr Roshni, a physician, has gross professional receipts of ₹55 lakh for the year and banks everything too. Neither declares income on a presumptive basis. Both ask whether an audit under section 44AB is needed for the previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: Does Mr Sen need a tax audit for the previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Yes
options.why: Section 44AD(4) catches a person who declared under the presumptive scheme in an earlier year and then declares a lower profit in a later one, and from the year of that default he is shut out of the scheme for the five years that follow. Section 44AB(e) then requires an audit of anyone that provision applies to, once his total income is above the amount not chargeable to tax. Both limbs hold here, so the accounts must be audited and books kept as well.
keywords: Section 44AD(4) catches a person who declared under the presumptive scheme in an earlier year and then declares a lower profit

options.text: No, provided he goes back to declaring the presumptive percentage from next year
options.misconception: thinks the consequence can be undone by returning to the scheme, when the exclusion runs for five successive years from the year of default
options.why: He cannot go back. Once the lower profit is declared, the scheme is closed to him for the year of default and the five years after it, so the books and the audit follow him through all six rather than attaching to one year he can trade his way out of. That is what makes the decision to declare below the rate a six-year decision.

options.text: Yes, but only because his income is above the exemption limit — the earlier presumptive year makes no difference
options.misconception: keeps one of the two conditions and drops the one that brings him inside the clause at all, which would make every small trader above the exemption limit auditable
options.why: Income above the exemption limit is a condition, not a trigger. Millions of people are above it and are not audited. What brings Mr Sen inside is the combination — a person who used the scheme and then declared below it, whose income is also above the limit — and dropping the first half turns a narrow clause into a universal one.

options.text: No. Turnover of ₹90 lakh is below every threshold the section sets for a business
options.misconception: reads section 44AB as a turnover test and nothing else, missing the clause that catches somebody stepping out of the presumptive scheme
options.why: Turnover is the commonest door into the section and it is not the only one. Separate clauses catch a transporter declaring below the presumptive figure, a professional declaring below his, and a person who has left the scheme for small businesses after having used it. Each of those bites at turnovers far below a crore.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(e) read with section 44AD(4) — a person shut out of the presumptive scheme whose income exceeds the exemption limit

items.scenario: Mr Sen declared his business profits on a presumptive basis under section 44AD for the previous year 2024-25. For 2025-26 his turnover is ₹90 lakh and he wants to declare a profit of ₹4,50,000, which is five per cent of turnover and below the presumptive rate. His total income for the year is above the amount not chargeable to income-tax. He points out that ₹90 lakh is nowhere near ₹1 crore and asks his accountant to file without an audit.

items.stem: What is wrong with that note?

options.text: Only the book profit half. The slab surcharge still applies, because the slabs are set by the Finance Act and the section says nothing about them
options.misconception: separates where a rule is printed from what it does, when the flat rate is the surcharge prescribed for income taxed under this very section
options.why: Where a rule is printed decides nothing about which income it reaches. The Finance Act prescribes several surcharges and directs each at particular income; the one that follows the concessional company rate is a flat ten per cent with no threshold, which is why a company on this route never computes marginal relief. Both halves of the note are wrong, not one.

options.text: Both halves are wrong
options.why: A company that opts pays 22 per cent, and the surcharge is a flat 10 per cent with no threshold at all, so there is no slab to read and no marginal relief to compute — the size of the total income changes nothing. With cess at four per cent the effective rate is 25.168 per cent whatever the company earns. And minimum alternate tax does not apply to a company that has opted for section 115BAA, so there is no floor underneath the computation and nothing to compare it against.
keywords: A company that opts pays 22 per cent, and the surcharge is a flat 10 per cent
the effective rate is 25.168 per cent
minimum alternate tax does not apply to a company that has opted for section 115BAA

options.text: Only the surcharge half. The slabs go, but book profit tax still sets a floor
options.misconception: reads the book profit charge as something that applies to every company, rather than as a charge the Act switches off for a company that opts
options.why: Half of the note is being corrected. The surcharge point is right, and the floor is the half that also has to go — which matters far more, because a floor that does not exist cannot be compared against, and a company that keeps computing book profit under a concessional regime is doing arithmetic nobody will ever ask it for.

options.text: Nothing. Twenty-two per cent, surcharge from the slab table, cess, and a book profit floor underneath
options.misconception: keeps both the ordinary company surcharge slabs and the book profit floor, when opting replaces the first and removes the second
options.why: Opting changes more than the headline rate. The surcharge that goes with the concessional rate is a single figure prescribed for it rather than the slab table that applies to companies on the ordinary rates, and the book profit charge is switched off altogether for a company that has opted. Reading the note as correct would give a wrong tax and a comparison the company never has to make.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — 22 per cent, flat 10 per cent surcharge, 4 per cent cess, an effective 25.168 per cent; MAT not applicable

items.scenario: Suryatek Ltd, a domestic company, is weighing section 115BAA for A.Y. 2026-27. Its finance head has circulated a one-line note before the board meeting — "twenty-two per cent, plus whatever surcharge our total income lands on in the slab table, plus cess, and minimum alternate tax still sets a floor underneath it because book profit tax applies to every company." The company's total income is a little over ₹1 crore, so the slab table would give it the lower of the two company surcharge rates.

items.stem: Which of the four claims survive the option?

options.text: Sections 80JJAA and 80M survive; the other two go
options.why: Total income under this route is computed without the deduction under section 10AA for a unit in a special economic zone and without additional depreciation under section 32(1)(iia), and both go the moment the option is taken. Chapter VI-A goes with them, but the section names two survivors — section 80JJAA on new employment and section 80M on dividends received from another domestic company. Ordinary depreciation is not lost either, though a block entitled to more than forty per cent is restricted to forty.
keywords: without the deduction under section 10AA for a unit in a special economic zone
section 80JJAA on new employment and section 80M on dividends received

options.text: Section 10AA survives because it is an exemption rather than a Chapter VI-A deduction; the other three go
options.misconception: sorts the provisions by where they sit in the Act, when the section lists section 10AA by name alongside the others
options.why: Sitting outside Chapter VI-A saves nothing here. The special economic zone deduction is named individually in the list, first, ahead of the Chapter VI-A sentence, precisely so that its position in the Act cannot be argued about. And the deduction that would actually have survived on that reasoning, section 80JJAA, sits squarely inside Chapter VI-A.

options.text: Only section 80M survives, since the whole of Chapter VI-A goes
options.misconception: remembers correctly that Chapter VI-A is withdrawn and forgets that the withdrawal itself carries two named exceptions
options.why: The withdrawal of Chapter VI-A is written with its exceptions in the same breath, and there are two of them. Employment generation is kept on purpose, because withdrawing it would have penalised the exact behaviour the concessional rate was meant to encourage; the dividend deduction is kept because taxing the same dividend twice as it passes through a chain of companies is not what the rate change was about.

options.text: All four. The option withdraws profit-linked deductions, and none of these four is one
options.misconception: remembers that the withdrawn list is about incentives and assumes anything not obviously profit-linked survives, when the section works from a named list rather than from a category
options.why: The section does not sort deductions by type; it names them. The list runs from the special economic zone exemption through additional depreciation, the tea, coffee and rubber and site restoration deposits, the scientific research deductions, the investment-linked deduction and the agricultural extension and skill development deductions, and then withdraws Chapter VI-A with two exceptions. Reasoning by category will lose marks the list would have saved.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — deductions not available; Chapter VI-A other than sections 80JJAA and 80M; depreciation restricted to forty per cent

items.scenario: Aarav Instruments Ltd, a domestic company, has four claims in its computation for A.Y. 2026-27 — ₹1.2 crore under section 10AA for its unit in a special economic zone, additional depreciation of ₹0.6 crore on plant installed during the year, ₹0.4 crore under section 80JJAA for new employees taken on, and ₹0.3 crore under section 80M for dividends it received from another domestic company. The board wants to know which of the four it would still have if it opted for section 115BAA this year.

items.stem: Which route leaves Trisara Tools with less to pay for A.Y. 2026-27?

options.text: Section 115BAA, because book profit tax would otherwise apply and it is the higher charge in a year like this
options.misconception: reaches for the escape from book profit tax in a year the scenario has already said book profit tax is the lower charge, so the escape is worth nothing
options.why: Escaping a charge helps only when the charge would have bitten. Book profit tax is a floor, so it costs a company nothing in a year when the ordinary computation is already above it, which the scenario says it is. What the company actually loses by opting is the credit built up in earlier years when the floor did bite, and that is a cost of opting rather than a saving.

options.text: Either. The two come out within a few lakh of each other, so it is a matter of the board's preference
options.misconception: assumes a concessional rate and a widened base roughly cancel, without doing the arithmetic that shows a gap of about sixty-four lakh
options.why: They are not close. Adding ₹2.3 crore back to the base outweighs the five-point drop in the effective rate, and the ₹0.8 crore of credit falls away on top of that. A guess that two routes are near enough to choose between on preference is the one answer a comparison question cannot accept, because the whole question is the arithmetic.

options.text: Section 115BAA, because twenty-two per cent beats thirty
options.misconception: compares the two rates instead of the two tax bills, so neither the widened base nor the dead MAT credit ever enters the arithmetic
options.why: Opting rebuilds the base before the rate ever touches it. Total income of ₹11.3 crore, arrived at by adding back the ₹1.2 crore, the ₹0.6 crore and the ₹0.5 crore, taxed at 25.168 per cent, gives ₹2,84,39,840. Worse, the brought-forward depreciation is deemed to have been given effect to, so it is not merely blocked this year — it can never be claimed in any later year either. A rate comparison hides both effects, and both are larger than the eight-point gap in the rates.
keywords: the brought-forward depreciation is deemed to have been given effect to

options.text: The normal provisions, this year
options.why: Under the normal provisions tax at thirty per cent on ₹9 crore is ₹2,70,00,000; surcharge is at seven per cent because the total income is above ₹1 crore and not above ₹10 crore; and cess at four per cent brings the bill to ₹3,00,45,600. The brought-forward MAT credit of ₹0.8 crore is then set off against that, leaving ₹2,20,45,600 to find, which is about ₹64 lakh less than the concessional route costs. Under section 115BAA the MAT credit cannot be set off at all, so opting now would waste it as well.
keywords: cess at four per cent brings the bill to ₹3,00,45,600
the MAT credit cannot be set off at all

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — loss and depreciation attributable to the forgone deductions deemed given effect; MAT credit not available against income taxed under the section

items.scenario: Trisara Tools Ltd, a domestic company, has a total income of ₹9 crore for 2025-26 under the normal provisions. That figure is after a deduction of ₹1.2 crore under section 10AA, additional depreciation of ₹0.6 crore, ₹0.4 crore under section 80JJAA, ₹0.3 crore under section 80M, and the set-off of ₹0.5 crore of brought-forward unabsorbed additional depreciation. It carries forward minimum alternate tax credit of ₹0.8 crore, and its book profit tax for the year is lower than its tax under the normal provisions. The CFO wants to opt for section 115BAA now, because twenty-two per cent beats thirty.

items.stem: When may Trisara Tools exercise the option?

options.text: Only in a year in which it holds no brought-forward loss and no MAT credit, since the section bars the option while either is outstanding
options.misconception: turns a planning point into a statutory condition, when nothing stops an opting company from holding either — they are simply lost
options.why: Nothing bars the option. A company may opt with a MAT credit and a pile of unabsorbed depreciation on its books; the credit then has nothing to set against and the depreciation is treated as already given effect to, so both quietly disappear. That is a reason to wait, which is a different thing from a rule that makes waiting compulsory.

options.text: In any year, and it may return to the normal provisions afterwards if the arithmetic turns against it
options.misconception: reads a free choice of the year of entry as a free choice every year, when the first exercise closes the door behind it
options.why: Freedom about when is not freedom about whether. The company may wait as long as it likes, and the year it stops waiting is final for that year and every year after it. That is why the decision is worth modelling over several years rather than one — the comparison that matters is not this year's two bills but the whole run of them.

options.text: In any assessment year it chooses, but once only
options.why: There is no time limit inside section 115BAA for exercising the option, and that is what makes the sequencing legitimate: a company holding brought-forward losses, unabsorbed depreciation from the withdrawn deductions, or a MAT credit may postpone the option to a later assessment year and use them up first. Two things then bind it. Once exercised the option cannot be withdrawn for any later year, and a failure of the conditions in any previous year makes the option invalid for that assessment year and for every later one, with the rest of the Act applying as though it had never been exercised.
keywords: There is no time limit inside section 115BAA for exercising the option
may postpone the option to a later assessment year
makes the option invalid for that assessment year and for every later one

options.text: In the first assessment year only. The auditor is right, and the chance has gone
options.misconception: carries the first-year rule from the manufacturing company provision, where it is real, across to this one, where no timeline exists
options.why: The neighbouring concessional rate for new manufacturing companies does work that way — its option has to be taken in the very first year and cannot be taken later. This one has no such requirement, and the difference between the two is a standing examination point precisely because they are read side by side in the same table.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — no timeline for the option, exhaust MAT credit and losses first, and the consequence of failing the conditions

items.scenario: Having seen that the normal provisions cost it less this year, the board of Trisara Tools asks whether the chance to opt is now gone. Its auditor says the option had to be exercised in the first assessment year the company was assessed in, and that a company which lets that year pass is on the ordinary rates for life. The company still holds ₹0.8 crore of MAT credit and ₹0.5 crore of unabsorbed additional depreciation.

items.stem: May Mr Ranvir use section 44AD for this year?

options.text: Yes
options.why: He is an eligible assessee, being a resident individual who has claimed neither section 10AA nor a deduction under the "certain incomes" heading of Chapter VI-A, and retail trading is an eligible business, being no profession, no commission or brokerage, no agency and no goods carriage. The ordinary ceiling is ₹200 lakh, and the raised ceiling of ₹300 lakh applies where aggregate cash receipts do not exceed 5% of total turnover. Cash of ₹9,00,000 on ₹2,80,00,000 is 3.21 per cent, so the higher ceiling is his and ₹2.8 crore sits inside it.
keywords: He is an eligible assessee, being a resident individual
retail trading is an eligible business
aggregate cash receipts do not exceed 5% of total turnover

options.text: Yes, and the cash proportion is beside the point — the ceiling is a flat ₹3 crore for everybody
options.misconception: treats the raised ceiling as a straight increase rather than as one conditioned on how the money came in
options.why: The higher ceiling is earned, not given. A trader with the same ₹2.8 crore of turnover who took ₹40,00,000 of it in cash would be over the five per cent line, would fall back to the two-crore ceiling, and would be outside the scheme altogether. Since Mr Ranvir passes the test, the answer this option reaches is right and the reason is wrong, which in a written answer costs the mark.

options.text: No. A proprietor may use the section only up to ₹1 crore; above that a tax audit is compulsory and the scheme is not available
options.misconception: mixes the tax audit threshold with the presumptive ceiling, which are different numbers doing different jobs
options.why: The two limits belong to different provisions and point in opposite directions. One crore is where an audit starts for a business that has not qualified for the higher audit ceiling; the presumptive scheme has its own limit and declaring under it takes the audit requirement away rather than triggering one. Reading a threshold from one section into the other is the fastest way to lose both marks.

options.text: No. Two crore is the limit and ₹2.8 crore is above it
options.misconception: knows the two-crore figure and not the condition that lifts it, so a business that qualifies for the higher ceiling is turned away
options.why: Two crore is the ordinary ceiling and it is not the only one. A separate and higher ceiling applies to a business that takes almost nothing in cash, and the whole design is to keep the scheme available to larger traders who bank their receipts while keeping cash businesses out of it. Stopping at the lower figure gives the wrong answer to a very common examination fact pattern.

citation.ref: Section 44AD(1) with the raised turnover ceiling of ₹300 lakh where cash receipts stay within five per cent

items.scenario: Mr Ranvir is resident in India and runs a retail trading business as a proprietor. His turnover for the previous year 2025-26 is ₹2,80,00,000, of which ₹9,00,000 came in as cash and the rest by NEFT. He has claimed no deduction under section 10AA and none under the "certain incomes" heading of Chapter VI-A. He wants to declare his income on a presumptive basis under section 44AD. A friend has told him the section stops at ₹2 crore and he is a long way past it.

items.stem: What is the least Mr Ranvir may declare under section 44AD?

options.why: The presumptive figure is 8% of the cash turnover of ₹9,00,000, which is ₹72,000, plus 6% of ₹2,71,00,000 received through prescribed electronic modes on or before the due date under section 139(1), which is ₹16,26,000. That gives ₹16,98,000. Declaring a higher sum is always open to him and the section says so; declaring less is what brings books and an audit in.
keywords: 6% of ₹2,71,00,000 received through prescribed electronic modes

options.text: ₹16,26,000, being six per cent of the banked receipts — the cash slice is outside the scheme
options.misconception: drops the cash turnover out of the computation instead of taxing it at the higher rate, confusing the five per cent eligibility test with the base
options.why: Cash receipts do two different jobs in this section and only one of them is about eligibility. Whether they stay within five per cent decides which ceiling applies; once he is in, the whole turnover is taxed and the cash part simply carries the higher rate. Leaving it out would let a trader shrink his own base by taking more cash, which is the opposite of what the section is for.

options.text: ₹22,40,000, being eight per cent of the whole turnover — six per cent is a concession that has to be applied for
options.misconception: reads the lower rate as a relief to be claimed rather than the rate the section itself sets for receipts that arrive through banking channels
options.why: Nothing has to be applied for. The section fixes six per cent for the part of the turnover received by account payee cheque, bank draft, electronic clearing or another prescribed electronic mode, provided it arrives by the due date for the return, and eight per cent for the rest. Declaring eight per cent on everything overstates his income by more than five lakh and he would pay tax on it.

options.text: ₹16,80,000, being six per cent of the whole ₹2,80,00,000
options.misconception: applies the lower rate to the whole turnover because most of it was banked, when each rate applies to its own slice
options.why: The two rates split the turnover; they are not alternatives to choose between on the strength of a majority. Applying six per cent to money that arrived in cash understates the presumptive figure by two per cent of that slice, and the shortfall here is ₹18,000 — small in rupees and fatal in a computation question, because the examiner is marking the split rather than the total.

citation.ref: Section 44AD(1) and its proviso prescribing six per cent for receipts through prescribed electronic modes

items.scenario: Mr Ranvir qualifies for section 44AD. His turnover for 2025-26 is ₹2,80,00,000, made up of ₹9,00,000 received in cash and ₹2,71,00,000 received by NEFT, and every rupee of the NEFT receipts was in the bank before 31st July 2026, which is his due date under section 139(1). His actual profit, if he drew up accounts, would be about ₹19 lakh. He proposes to declare six per cent of the whole turnover, on the footing that almost all of it was banked.

items.stem: By how much does the net profit have to be increased for these four items?

options.text: ₹19,50,000 — all four go back, and the interest on tax goes with the tax
options.why: All four are on the list of increases. The first is income-tax paid or payable, and the provision made for it, and the Act says in its own Explanation that income-tax here carries interest, surcharge and cess with it, so the whole ₹9,00,000 goes back and not ₹8,00,000. The second is the amount carried to any reserves, whatever name the reserve is given, so a debenture redemption reserve is caught as surely as a general reserve. The third is a provision for diminution in the value of any asset, which is what a doubtful-debt provision is. The fourth is dividends paid or proposed, proposed being enough on its own. Nine plus five plus two and a half plus three is ₹19,50,000.
keywords: income-tax paid or payable, and the provision made for it
the amount carried to any reserves, whatever name the reserve is given
dividends paid or proposed, proposed being enough on its own

options.text: ₹18,50,000 — the ₹1,00,000 of interest on late payment of tax is a financing cost and stays where it is
options.misconception: splits interest away from the tax it was charged on, reading the add-back as covering only the tax itself
options.why: There is a definition sitting under the section for exactly this argument, and it goes the other way: income-tax here carries interest, surcharge and cess with it. Interest for paying late is charged under the Act on the tax, so it is part of the amount that goes back. Taking it out would let a company reduce its book profit by being slow to pay.
keywords: income-tax here carries interest, surcharge and cess with it

options.text: ₹17,00,000 — the ₹2,50,000 for doubtful debts is a provision for a liability the company can estimate, so it is ascertained and stays
options.misconception: files a doubtful-debt provision under the clause about provisions for liabilities, when it is not a liability at all but a write-down of an asset
options.why: A doubtful-debt provision is not a liability of any kind, ascertained or otherwise — it is money the company doubts it will collect, so it is a provision for diminution in the value of any asset, which is a clause of its own on the list of increases. The clause about unascertained liabilities is a different clause and it is not the one that catches this.
keywords: a provision for diminution in the value of any asset

options.text: ₹16,50,000 — a dividend only becomes a dividend when the members approve it, so nothing has been paid and nothing goes back
options.misconception: waits for the company-law event, when the clause names the proposal itself
options.why: The clause covers dividends paid or proposed. Proposing is the trigger, and the whole reason both words are there is that a company would otherwise reduce its book profit every year by proposing in March and paying in August. Approval in August 2026 changes nothing about the year ended 31 March 2026.

citation.ref: Section 115JB, Explanation 1 clauses (a), (b), (e) and (i), with Explanation 2 on what income-tax takes in

items.scenario: Kalinga Ceramics Ltd is a domestic company that does not draw up Ind AS accounts and has not opted for section 115BAA. Its statement of profit and loss for the year ended 31 March 2026 shows a net profit of ₹60,00,000 after debiting a provision for income-tax of ₹9,00,000 (which includes ₹1,00,000 of interest on tax paid late), a transfer of ₹5,00,000 to the debenture redemption reserve, a provision of ₹2,50,000 for doubtful debts, and a proposed dividend of ₹3,00,000 that the shareholders will only approve in August 2026. The finance manager is preparing the working for section 115JB and asks which of those four figures go back on to the profit.

items.stem: What is the net effect of these three figures on the book profit?

options.text: Nil, and nothing needs to be written down, because the two depreciation clauses and the reserve clause always come to zero
options.misconception: treats a cap as an identity, so it never notices the year in which the transfer out of the reserve is bigger than the revaluation depreciation
options.why: They come to zero only when the transfer out of the reserve is exactly the revaluation depreciation. Here the company took ₹2,50,000 out of the reserve against ₹2,00,000 of revaluation depreciation, and the extra ₹50,000 is a credit to the profit that the section leaves alone. A company that emptied its revaluation reserve in one year would otherwise reduce its book profit by the whole of it.

options.text: Minus ₹2,50,000 — the transfer out of the reserve is a book entry and the whole of it comes off, and the depreciation figures are left as the accounts show them
options.misconception: reads the reserve clause on its own and drops the two depreciation clauses, so the cap that the second one creates never appears
options.why: The deduction for a transfer out of the revaluation reserve is written against the revaluation depreciation, and the only way to know what that ceiling is is to run the two depreciation clauses first. Leaving them out removes the measure and lets the whole transfer through.

options.text: Nil, but only after all three are put through the working, and ₹50,000 of the reserve transfer stays inside the book profit
options.why: Three separate clauses run in order and the accountant reaches the right total by the wrong road. First, add back the whole depreciation debited for the year, ₹12,00,000. Then take out the depreciation other than on account of revaluation of assets, ₹10,00,000, which leaves the ₹2,00,000 of revaluation depreciation sitting in the profit. Then the sum withdrawn from the revaluation reserve, where the company has taken it through the statement of profit and loss, comes out — but only so far as it does not exceed the depreciation on revaluation of the same assets. That caps the deduction at ₹2,00,000, so ₹50,000 of the credit stays in the book profit and the arithmetic only looks like nil.
keywords: depreciation other than on account of revaluation of assets
does not exceed the depreciation on revaluation

options.text: Plus ₹2,00,000 — the revaluation depreciation stays added and the transfer out of the reserve is not deductible at all, being a movement within reserves
options.misconception: sees the transfer as a reserve movement rather than a credit to the profit, missing that it has already been taken through the statement of profit and loss
options.why: The clause only bites on an amount that has been credited to the statement of profit and loss, and here it has been. If the transfer had gone straight from one reserve to another it would never have touched the profit and there would be nothing to take out. The company put it through the profit, so the deduction is live, up to the ceiling.

citation.ref: Section 115JB, Explanation 1 clause (g) and the reductions at clauses (iia) and (iib)

items.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd revalued its factory building some years ago. For the year ended 31 March 2026 its statement of profit and loss carries a depreciation charge of ₹12,00,000, of which ₹2,00,000 is depreciation on the revalued portion of the building. In the same statement the company has credited ₹2,50,000 transferred out of the revaluation reserve. Its accountant proposes to leave all three figures alone, on the ground that they cancel each other out anyway.

items.stem: What does the company do with these three?

options.text: Take out ₹1,50,000 and ₹14,00,000, and add back ₹4,00,000
options.misconception: adds the brought forward loss to the unabsorbed depreciation instead of taking the smaller of them, and treats an actuarial estimate as an unascertained liability because it is an estimate
options.why: The clause pairs the two figures and gives the smaller one, which is how a company is stopped from taking the benefit of a book loss made up of things other than depreciation. And an estimate is not the same as an unascertained liability: the company knows it owes gratuity, and an actuary has measured it on a recognised basis, which is what makes the liability ascertained.

options.text: Take out ₹6,00,000 only, because agricultural income has already been left out of the total income under the Act and cannot come off twice
options.misconception: confuses the ordinary computation with the book-profit computation, when the two are separate bases and each has to be adjusted on its own
options.why: Book profit is struck from the accounts, and the accounts have taken the agricultural income in. Nothing in the ordinary computation reaches across, which is the whole design of a separate base, so the deduction for income to which section 10 applies has to be made here as well.

options.text: Take out ₹1,50,000 and ₹6,00,000, and leave the gratuity provision alone
options.why: Each goes a different way. Agricultural income is income to which section 10 applies, so it comes out of the book profit because it was credited to the statement of profit and loss. A gratuity provision on actuarial valuation is an ascertained liability, and only provisions for liabilities that are not ascertained go back on to the profit, so this one is left where the accounts put it. For the third, the deduction is the lower of brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation as the books show them, so it is ₹6,00,000 and not ₹8,00,000 and not the two added together.
keywords: agricultural income is income to which section 10 applies
a gratuity provision on actuarial valuation is an ascertained liability
the lower of brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation

options.text: Take out ₹1,50,000 and ₹8,00,000, taking the depreciation figure because depreciation is the more reliable of the two book numbers
options.misconception: picks the larger of the paired figures on a judgement about reliability, when the clause names the smaller one and leaves nothing to choose
options.why: There is nothing to weigh. The clause reads the two figures as they stand in the books and allows the lower of brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation, so with ₹6,00,000 against ₹8,00,000 the answer is ₹6,00,000 whichever of them looks more solid.

citation.ref: Section 115JB, Explanation 1 clause (c) and the reductions at clauses (ii) and (iii)

items.scenario: Nilgiri Estates Ltd, a domestic company, is working out its book profit for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three figures are in dispute. It has credited agricultural income of ₹1,50,000 to the statement of profit and loss. It has debited a provision of ₹4,00,000 for gratuity, worked out by an actuary on the usual valuation. Its books of account show a brought forward loss of ₹6,00,000 and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹8,00,000, both figures positive.

items.stem: How much has the trust got to apply to its objects this year?

options.why: The corpus money is out of the base altogether. A contribution made with a written direction that it form part of the corpus is exempt on its own footing, provided it goes into one of the investment modes the Act lists, which a scheduled bank deposit is. So the income the test runs on is ₹50,00,000 — the property income and the ordinary voluntary contributions, which the Act deems to be income derived from property held under trust. 85% of it, ₹42,50,000, has to be applied in India during the year, and the remaining 15%, ₹7,50,000, may be kept back with no further condition.
keywords: the income the test runs on is ₹50,00,000
85% of it, ₹42,50,000, has to be applied
the remaining 15%, ₹7,50,000, may be kept back

options.misconception: reads the rule as requiring the whole of the income to be spent, so the standing fifteen per cent disappears
options.why: The requirement is at least 85 per cent, not all of it. The remaining fifteen per cent may be kept without stating a purpose, filing anything, or fixing a period — the only thing asked of it is that it sits in one of the specified investment modes.

options.misconception: reads the base as the income from trust property only, forgetting that voluntary contributions without a direction are deemed to be income from that property
options.why: That is 85 per cent of ₹35,00,000 and it drops the ₹15,00,000 of ordinary voluntary contributions. Contributions received without any direction are deemed by the Act to be income derived from property held under trust, which is exactly what puts them into the base. Only the corpus direction takes a contribution out.

options.misconception: puts the corpus contribution into the base with everything else, so the trust is asked to spend money it was told to keep
options.why: That is 85 per cent of ₹58,00,000, and it treats ₹8,00,000 of corpus contributions as ordinary income. It is not: a contribution with a direction to the corpus is exempt so long as the money is invested in a mode section 11(5) lists, and the trust here did exactly that. Counting it in would force the trust to spend the very money the donor said to keep, and would then tax it for not doing so.
keywords: invested in a mode section 11(5) lists

citation.ref: Sections 11(1)(a), 11(1)(d) and 12 — what enters the base and the 85 per cent test

items.scenario: Anandvan Charitable Trust is registered under section 12AB and runs a children's home. For the previous year 2025-26 it received ₹35,00,000 from property held under the trust and ₹15,00,000 as voluntary contributions with no direction attached. It separately received ₹8,00,000 from a donor who wrote that the money was to form part of the corpus, and the trustees put that sum straight into a scheduled bank deposit. The treasurer has taken all three receipts into one total of ₹58,00,000 and is working out what the trust must spend this year.

items.stem: How much of the year's spending is application of income?

options.text: ₹20,00,000, with the ₹7,00,000 allowed instead as depreciation over the life of the block
options.misconception: tries to spread a capital outgoing the way a business would, when the outgoing has already been allowed in full as application
options.why: The cost is allowed once, in the year it is spent, as application. Claiming depreciation on the same asset afterwards would allow the same money twice, which is why the Act shuts that door expressly.

The distinction the treasurer has drawn is not one the exemption makes. Application counts whether it is revenue or capital in nature, so money spent putting up a building for the trust's own objects is applied just as surely as money spent running the home. So ₹27,00,000 is applied, not ₹20,00,000. The reason is that the test asks whether the income was used for the charitable purpose, and a classroom is that purpose in brick.
keywords: application counts whether it is revenue or capital in nature

options.text: ₹27,00,000, but only if the trustees pass a resolution before the year ends recording the block as a charitable application
options.misconception: invents a procedural condition; the conditions that do exist attach to accumulation and to particular kinds of payment, not to ordinary spending
options.why: Nothing has to be resolved or filed for ordinary spending on the objects. Conditions attach where money is being kept rather than spent, or where a payment has a defect of its own such as no tax deducted. Spending on the objects during the year needs no paperwork at all.

options.misconception: carries the accounting split between revenue and capital into a test that never made it, so building anything reads as saving rather than spending
options.why: Accounting keeps capital out of the income statement because the asset survives the year. The exemption asks a different question — was the income used for the objects — and a classroom built for the children's home answers it. On the treasurer's reading a trust could never build anything without failing the test.

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(a) — application of income, revenue or capital

items.scenario: During the previous year 2025-26 Anandvan Charitable Trust spent ₹20,00,000 on running its children's home and ₹7,00,000 on building a new classroom block on land it already owned. Its treasurer has written in the accounts that only the ₹20,00,000 counts towards the trust's spending obligation, because the classroom block is a capital asset and the money is still with the trust in another form.

items.stem: How much of the ₹8,00,000 is application of income for Anandvan?

options.misconception: treats any payment to a registered trust as application, since the money has reached charity either way
options.why: Where the money ends up is not the test. One Explanation cuts an ordinary inter-trust donation down to eighty-five per cent of itself, and another shuts out a contribution to another trust's corpus completely. Both were written because a chain of trusts passing money along could otherwise satisfy the spending test without anybody spending anything.

The two payments are treated differently and neither is treated as the auditor has treated it. For the ordinary donation the Act allows ₹5,10,000, being 85% of the ₹6,00,000 donated out of current-year income, and the remaining fifteen per cent is simply lost — the idea is that money passed on to another trust should not buy a full exemption twice over. For the second payment the ₹2,00,000 corpus donation is not application at all, by a separate Explanation that names contributions to another trust's corpus and excludes them outright.
keywords: ₹5,10,000, being 85% of the ₹6,00,000 donated out of current-year income
the ₹2,00,000 corpus donation is not application at all

options.misconception: allows the ordinary donation in full and excludes the corpus one, which was the position before the eighty-five per cent restriction was brought in
options.why: Excluding the corpus payment is right and allowing the other in full is not. Since the restriction was introduced, an inter-trust donation out of current-year income counts only to the extent of eighty-five per cent of what is paid, and the Board has said the same thing again in its own circular.

options.misconception: applies the eighty-five per cent cut to both payments, missing that the corpus donation is excluded outright rather than reduced
options.why: The eighty-five per cent rule is written for donations other than corpus donations. A corpus contribution to another trust is dealt with by its own Explanation, and that one does not reduce it — it says the payment is not application, so nothing of the ₹2,00,000 counts.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 and Explanation 4(iii) to section 11(1), with CBDT Circular No. 3/2024

items.scenario: Out of its income for the previous year 2025-26, Anandvan Charitable Trust gave ₹6,00,000 to Prerna Vidya Trust, which is also registered under section 12AB, as an ordinary donation towards its work. It gave a further ₹2,00,000 to the same trust with a written direction that the money form part of that trust's corpus. Anandvan's auditor has put the whole ₹8,00,000 down as application.

items.stem: How much of the ₹4,00,000 is application for the previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Nothing, because a payment on which tax was not deducted is not application at all
options.misconception: applies the whole-payment rule from a different provision; the section that is carried across disallows a proportion, not the lot
options.why: The provision brought across takes out thirty per cent of the payment, which is what it does to a business as well. There is a separate rule about payments in cash above a small limit which does take out the whole amount, but that is a different defect and this payment does not have it.

options.text: ₹2,80,000, and the ₹1,20,000 is gone for good
options.misconception: reads the disallowance as a penalty, when it only moves the application into a later year
options.why: It is a timing rule, not a forfeiture. The amount held back becomes application in the year the tax is deducted and paid, so a trust that puts the default right recovers the whole of it, just later.

options.misconception: keeps the business disallowance provisions inside the business chapter, when an Explanation to section 11(1) expressly carries them into the trust computation
options.why: They are carried across on purpose. Without that, a trust could pay contractors and consultants without deducting anything and still count every rupee as application, which would put it in a better position than a business making the same payment.

The auditor is wrong about the reach of those rules: an Explanation to section 11(1) pulls the tax-deduction disallowance across and applies it to a trust's spending. So 30% of the payment, ₹1,20,000, is not application this year, and the remaining ₹2,80,000 is. The loss is not permanent — the same Explanation gives the ₹1,20,000 back as application in the year the tax is finally deducted and paid over.
keywords: 30% of the payment, ₹1,20,000, is not application this year

citation.ref: Explanation 3 to section 11(1), applying section 40(a)(ia) to a trust's application

items.scenario: Anandvan Charitable Trust paid ₹4,00,000 during the previous year 2025-26 to a building contractor. Tax was deductible on the payment and the trust deducted none, and none has been paid over by the due date for its return. The trust has shown the whole ₹4,00,000 as application of income. Its auditor says the disallowance rules of the business chapter have nothing to do with a charitable trust.

items.stem: Is the ₹6,00,000 sheltered from tax for the assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: Yes, and there is no outer limit on when the hostel has to be built, so long as the money stays in the specified securities
options.misconception: keeps the shelter and drops the clock, when the period stated in the form is capped and the money falls into tax at the end of it
options.why: The form has to state a period and that period cannot exceed five years, and the trust has stated three. If the money is not spent on the stated purpose within it, the amount becomes income of the trust. The investment condition and the time condition are separate and both are live.

options.text: No. The two-month requirement is a condition of the accumulation and the trust has missed it
options.misconception: reads the earlier of two dates as the one that decides the shelter, when the provision that takes the shelter away names the later one
options.why: The two-month date exists so that the accumulation can be seen while the accounts are being audited, and it is stated as a requirement. What takes the exemption away is a different provision, and it is written against the due date for the return. Reading the earlier date as the operative one costs the trust an exemption the Act does not take from it.

options.text: No, because the return itself was filed before the due date rather than on it, so the sequence of filings is wrong
options.misconception: invents an order between the two filings; nothing requires the form and the return in any particular sequence, only that both are in by the due date
options.why: Both filings have the same deadline and neither has to follow the other. What matters is that the form and the return were each with the department on or before 31 October 2026, and both were.

options.text: Yes. The form is late against the two-month rule but in time against the rule that decides the shelter
options.why: Two lines run together here. Section 11(2) shelters income set apart for a stated purpose and invested in the specified modes, and the statement is asked for two months before the due date for the return, which would have meant 31 August 2026. But the provision that actually withdraws the shelter withdraws it where the form is not in by the due date itself, and the Board has said in as many words that accumulation is not to be refused so long as the form reaches it on or before that date. The form went in on 20 September, the return on 30 September, and the period stated cannot run beyond five years, which three does not.
keywords: section 11(2) shelters income set apart for a stated purpose
the statement is asked for two months before the due date
the period stated cannot run beyond five years

citation.ref: Section 11(2) with section 13(9) and CBDT Circular No. 6/2023 on the filing of Form 10

items.scenario: Anandvan Charitable Trust set apart ₹6,00,000 during the previous year 2025-26 to build a hostel, and put the money into government securities. It stated the purpose and a period of three years in Form 10, which it filed on 20 September 2026. The due date for its return under section 139(1) is 31 October 2026 and it filed the return on 30 September 2026. Its auditor says the accumulation has failed, because the form should have been in by 31 August.

items.stem: What rate applies for the assessment year 2026-27, and when does that band close?

options.text: Nothing, because the unit did not begin manufacturing by 31 March 2020 and so never qualified at all
options.misconception: applies the ordinary commencement cut-off and misses the extension written for units whose approval was in hand before it
options.why: The extension exists for exactly this unit: approval in hand before 31 March 2020, manufacture beginning after it. The company began on 1 September 2020, inside the extended date, so it qualifies.

options.text: Fifty per cent, and the deduction stops altogether after the assessment year 2029-30
options.misconception: treats the second band as the last one, when a third band of five years exists for a unit that creates and uses the reinvestment reserve
options.why: The second band closing is not the end of the section. A further five years are available, at up to fifty per cent of profit, to a unit that debits the amount to its profit and loss account, credits it to the reinvestment reserve and then uses that reserve as the section directs. What ends in 2029-30 is the deduction that asks for no reserve.

options.text: Fifty per cent, and the band closes with the assessment year 2029-30
options.why: The tax head has missed the relief that let this unit start at all. The ordinary cut-off is that manufacture must begin by the assessment year 2020-21; where the letter of approval was issued on or before 31 March 2020 and the unit could not start by then, the date to begin was pushed out to 31 March 2021, and a unit that starts inside that window is treated as having begun during the assessment year 2020-21. So the first year is 2020-21, the full-rate band runs to 2024-25, and A.Y. 2026-27 falls in the 50% band. That band closes with A.Y. 2029-30, after which any further deduction depends on creating and using the reinvestment reserve.

options.text: One hundred per cent, because the first of the five full-rate years is the assessment year 2021-22
options.misconception: dates the first year from when manufacture actually began, when the relief fixes the first year at 2020-21 for every unit that used it
options.why: The relief does two things and the tax head has taken only the first. It lets a unit approved by 31 March 2020 begin as late as 31 March 2021, and it deems that unit to have begun during the assessment year 2020-21. Without the second half, the extension would quietly hand an extra year of full-rate deduction to units that were late.

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1) and (2), read with the commencement date as extended for a unit whose letter of approval was in hand before 31 March 2020

items.scenario: Meghna Precision Ltd holds a letter of approval for a Special Economic Zone unit issued to it on 10 February 2020. Building work ran late and the unit only began manufacturing on 1 September 2020. The company has been claiming the deduction ever since and its tax head now says that because manufacturing began in the previous year 2020-21, the first year of the deduction is the assessment year 2021-22 and the full-rate band therefore runs one year longer than the auditors have assumed.

items.stem: How do the two lots enter export turnover?

options.text: Both count, because both were eventually received in convertible foreign exchange
options.misconception: reads the definition as being about the currency and the route, when it also carries a clock
options.why: The currency and the route are two of the conditions and the timing is the third. Money that comes in late in the right currency is still late, and the definition drops it from export turnover unless somebody with the power to extend the period has extended it.

options.text: Both count, but the ₹20,00,000 goes into export turnover of the year in which it was actually received
options.misconception: moves the receipt into a later year's turnover, when export turnover is a figure of the year of export and a late receipt simply falls out of it
options.why: Export turnover belongs to the year in which the goods were exported. A receipt that misses the window does not travel forward into another year's export turnover; it drops out, and the proportion for the year of export is worked out without it.

options.text: The second one counts and the first one does not
options.why: Export turnover takes in consideration received in India in convertible foreign exchange within six months from the end of the previous year, and that window closed on 30 September 2026. The ₹20,00,000 that missed it is excluded from export turnover. But the same definition lets the competent authority allow a longer period, and the Reserve Bank is that authority, so an extension by the competent authority keeps the later receipt in and the ₹15,00,000 counts even though it arrived in December.
keywords: received in India in convertible foreign exchange within six months
the ₹20,00,000 that missed it is excluded from export turnover
an extension by the competent authority keeps the later receipt in

options.text: Neither counts, because an extension can only be granted before the six months have run and this one was not
options.misconception: invents a deadline for the extension itself; the provision allows a further period without fixing when the permission has to be asked for
options.why: The wording allows the competent authority such further period as it may allow, and does not say when the request has to be made. The company here did apply and did get further time, which is what the definition asks for.

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1) proviso and clause (ia) of Explanation 1 — realisation in convertible foreign exchange within six months

items.scenario: An SEZ unit's export sales for the previous year 2025-26 include two unpaid lots. The first, ₹20,00,000, was still outstanding on 30 September 2026 and the money reached the company's Indian bank in convertible foreign exchange in November 2026; no extension was ever asked for. The second, ₹15,00,000, was the subject of an application to the Reserve Bank of India, which allowed the company further time, and the money came in convertible foreign exchange in December 2026.

items.stem: What deduction does the company get for the assessment year 2026-27?

options.misconception: treats the late return as a matter for interest and fee only, and treats the deduction as unlimited because the section computes it from the unit's own profit
options.why: Filing late does carry interest and a fee, and it carries this as well. And the deduction is not free-standing: an Explanation under the section says it comes out of the total income computed before the section is applied, and cannot be more than that total income.

options.text: ₹90,00,000, provided the company applies for condonation of the delay in filing the return
options.misconception: assumes a discretion to excuse the delay for this purpose, when the section makes the due date a flat condition of the deduction
options.why: The section attaches the deduction to a return furnished on or before the due date and provides no relaxation of its own. There is no discretion written into it for a late return, which is why the date is worth putting in the diary rather than arguing about afterwards.

options.misconception: applies the ceiling correctly and misses the filing condition, which is absolute and comes first
options.why: The ceiling is right and it never gets reached. The condition about filing is not a matter of degree: a return that goes in after the due date takes the deduction away entirely, so there is no figure left for the ceiling to cap.

options.text: Nothing at all
options.why: Two conditions had to be met and one of them was not. The report goes in one month before that date, and 25 September is inside that, so the report is fine. But a return after the due date means no deduction at all — the section says so in terms and gives the officer nothing to weigh. Even had the return been in time the company would not have got ₹90,00,000, because the deduction cannot exceed the total income worked out before section 10AA, which caps it at ₹70,00,000.
keywords: the report goes in one month before that date
a return after the due date means no deduction at all
the deduction cannot exceed the total income worked out before section 10AA

citation.ref: Section 10AA — the Explanation on the ceiling, and the report and return conditions read with section 44AB and section 139(1)

items.scenario: Meghna Precision Ltd works out its section 10AA deduction for the assessment year 2026-27 at ₹90,00,000. Its total income for the year, computed under the Act before this deduction is given effect to, is ₹70,00,000. The accountant's report certifying the claim was furnished on 25 September 2026. The due date for the company's return under section 139(1) is 31 October 2026 and the company, waiting for a subsidiary's figures, filed it on 5 November 2026.

items.stem: Who may go to the Board on this proposed licence?

options.text: Only Kirin Seiki, the chapter being written for non-residents
options.misconception: reads the chapter as belonging to non-residents alone, when one of its clauses is written for the resident who deals with one
options.why: The chapter is largely about a non-resident's liability, which is not the same as saying only a non-resident may ask. One clause exists so that the Indian party to the transaction can get the same certainty, because it is the one who has to withhold and it is the one the department comes to if the withholding is short.

options.text: Either of them, but under different clauses and about different things
options.why: Counsel is wrong. A non-resident may ask under section 245N(a)(i) about a transaction it has undertaken or proposes to undertake, which is Kirin Seiki's own question about its own receipts. Separately, the Indian payer may ask under section 245N(a)(ii) about the non-resident's tax liability arising out of a transaction the resident proposes to undertake with that non-resident — so Deccan Forgings can put the same question, but framed as the Japanese company's liability rather than its own.
keywords: a non-resident may ask under section 245N(a)(i)
the Indian payer may ask under section 245N(a)(ii)

options.text: Either of them, but Deccan Forgings only if it belongs to a class of residents the Central Government has notified
options.misconception: takes the notified-class requirement, which belongs to a resident asking about its own liability, and applies it to a resident asking about a non-resident's
options.why: The notified-class requirement sits on a different clause — the one that lets a resident ask about its own tax liability. Where the resident is asking about the tax liability of the non-resident it deals with, no notification is needed and any resident may apply.

options.text: Neither, because the licence has not been signed and the Board rules only on transactions already carried out
options.misconception: thinks a ruling is retrospective, when the whole design is that a question can be settled before the transaction happens
options.why: The clauses cover a transaction undertaken or proposed to be undertaken. Certainty before signing is the reason the machinery exists; a party that has already signed has lost most of the value of asking.

citation.ref: Section 245N(a) and section 245N(b) — the questions and the applicants

items.scenario: Kirin Seiki KK, resident in Japan, is negotiating to license a manufacturing process to Deccan Forgings Ltd, an Indian company, and wants to know before it signs whether what it receives will be taxable in India. Deccan Forgings has the same worry from the other end, because it will be the one withholding. Its counsel tells it that only the foreign party can go to the Board for Advance Rulings, and that an Indian company can do nothing but wait for the assessment.

items.stem: What does the application cost, and can the company pull it back?

options.text: ₹5,00,000, and no — once lodged, an application can only be disposed of by an order of the Board
options.misconception: assumes the Board's control over its own file, when the Act gives the applicant a short right to withdraw as of course
options.why: The Act gives the applicant a plain right to withdraw inside a short window, without asking anybody. After that window the file is the Board's, which is exactly why the window is worth knowing about.

options.text: ₹5,00,000, and yes, if it acts inside a month of having applied
options.why: The ₹10,000 in the Act is a floor, and the rules prescribe more by reference to the size of the transaction. For a non-resident applicant the fee is ₹5 lakh where the transaction is above ₹100 crore and not above ₹300 crore, which is where a ₹150 crore licence sits; below ₹100 crore it is ₹2 lakh and above ₹300 crore it is ₹10 lakh. As for pulling back, an application may be withdrawn within 30 days of the day it was made, and three weeks is inside that.
keywords: the fee is ₹5 lakh where the transaction is above ₹100 crore
an application may be withdrawn within 30 days of the day it was made

options.text: ₹10,000, and yes, at any time before the ruling is pronounced
options.misconception: takes the figure named in the section as the whole answer and treats withdrawal as open until the ruling comes
options.why: The ₹10,000 in the section is a floor, and the section then lets the rules ask for more; what the rules ask for on a transaction of this size is a great deal more. Withdrawal is not open-ended either — it is tied to a short window running from the date of the application, not to the progress of the case.

options.text: ₹10,00,000, and yes, within thirty days
options.misconception: reads the top fee band as applying to everything above ₹100 crore, when there is a middle band between ₹100 crore and ₹300 crore
options.why: There are three bands for an applicant of this kind, not two. ₹150 crore falls in the middle one, and the top band starts where the transaction goes past ₹300 crore.

citation.ref: Section 245Q(2) and (3) with Rule 44E — the fee bands and withdrawal

items.scenario: Kirin Seiki KK decides to apply. The licence it proposes is worth ₹150 crore over three years. Its Indian adviser has budgeted ₹10,000 for the fee, on the footing that the Act names that figure. Three weeks after lodging the application the company's board changes its mind about the whole arrangement and wants the application out of the way before the department starts asking questions.

items.stem: Which of the two questions can the Board take up?

options.text: Only Deccan Forgings' question
options.why: The Board refuses a question already pending before the Tribunal, and Kirin Seiki's is: the exception for a pending question is written for a resident of a class the Central Government has notified, and a Japanese company is not that. Deccan Forgings' question is a different matter. The Board does turn away a transaction designed on the face of it for avoidance, but a question specifically about an impermissible avoidance arrangement is carved out of that refusal — that route is section 245N(a)(iv) and it is open to a resident and a non-resident alike. And in either case no application is refused without an opportunity of being heard, with reasons written into the order; where one is allowed, the ruling comes within 6 months of the Board receiving it.
keywords: the Board refuses a question already pending before the Tribunal
a question specifically about an impermissible avoidance arrangement
no application is refused without an opportunity of being heard

options.text: Neither, and both applicants must wait for the Tribunal to decide the earlier appeal
options.misconception: lets one applicant's pending proceeding block another applicant's unrelated question
options.why: The bar is about the applicant's own question. Deccan Forgings is asking something the Tribunal is not being asked, about an arrangement that has not happened, and nothing about the earlier appeal touches it.

options.text: Only Kirin Seiki's question
options.misconception: has the bars the wrong way round, reading the avoidance bar as absolute and the pending bar as applying only to Indian proceedings the applicant is not party to
options.why: Both readings fail. The pending bar looks at whether the question is already before an income-tax authority, the Tribunal or a court, and it is squarely engaged where the applicant's own appeal raises it. And the avoidance bar has an express carve-out for somebody who comes and asks whether a proposed arrangement is impermissible, which is the honest use of the machinery rather than an abuse of it. Whichever way a given application goes, the applicant is heard before anything is turned away, and once one is admitted the ruling comes within 6 months of the day it reached the Board.

options.text: Both questions
options.misconception: treats the pending proceeding as no obstacle because the year and the amount are different, when it is the question that has to be new and not the assessment
options.why: What the bar looks at is the question raised in the application, not the year or the sum. The same taxability question on a smaller licence is the same question, and letting it through would put the Board and the Tribunal on the same point at the same time.

citation.ref: Section 245R(2) with section 245N(a)(iv) — when the Board must refuse an application, and the time limit for a ruling

items.scenario: Kirin Seiki KK's application asks whether its licence receipts are taxable in India. The identical question, on a smaller licence to the same Indian company, is already before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in the company's own appeal for an earlier year. Separately, Deccan Forgings Ltd wants to ask whether routing part of the payment through a subsidiary in a third country would be an impermissible avoidance arrangement. Its adviser says there is no point asking, since the Board turns away anything to do with avoidance.

items.stem: What is open to the company, and what is open to the department?

options.text: An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal first, and only then to the High Court on a question of law
options.misconception: assumes the ordinary two-tier appeal path, when the appeal against a ruling goes straight to the High Court
options.why: The Tribunal does not sit above the Board for Advance Rulings. The appeal is written to go straight to the High Court, which is what makes the sixty-day period worth watching — there is no intermediate forum to absorb a delay.

options.text: The company has an appeal to the High Court, and the department can ask the Board to set the older ruling aside
options.why: The ruling is not final in that sense. An appeal to the High Court goes in within sixty days of the ruling being communicated, and the High Court may allow a further thirty days for sufficient cause where the appellant was kept from filing in time.
