As for the older ruling, where the Board finds on the Commissioner's representation or otherwise that a ruling was got by fraud or by misstating the facts, a ruling obtained by fraud can be declared void ab initio, and the Act then applies to the applicant as though the ruling had never been given.
keywords: an appeal to the High Court goes in within sixty days
the High Court may allow a further thirty days
a ruling obtained by fraud can be declared void ab initio

options.text: Only a writ petition for the company, and nothing at all for the department once the ruling has been given
options.misconception: treats a ruling as unappealable, which it was under the older Authority, and forgets the power to undo one procured by fraud
options.why: A statutory appeal now lies to the High Court against a ruling, so the extraordinary remedy is not the only road. And a ruling procured by fraud or misstatement can be declared void from the beginning, which exists precisely so that the machinery cannot be used to launder a false set of facts.

options.text: An appeal to the High Court within one hundred and twenty days, and for the department, an appeal on the same footing
options.misconception: stretches the appeal period and assumes the two sides get the same route on the same terms
options.why: The period is sixty days from communication, with a further thirty available on sufficient cause and nothing beyond that. The department's appeal to the High Court is provided for separately and through a scheme, and the answer to a ruling obtained by fraud is not an appeal at all but an order declaring it void.

citation.ref: Section 245W — appeal to the High Court — and section 245T — a ruling void ab initio

items.scenario: The Board for Advance Rulings pronounces a ruling against Deccan Forgings Ltd and the company is told of it on 4 May 2026. Its counsel says a ruling is final by its nature and the only way to disturb it is a writ petition in the High Court. Separately the department believes that a ruling the Board gave to another applicant two years ago was obtained on facts that were misstated, and wants to know what can be done about it now.

items.stem: How much interest can he deduct for the assessment year 2026-27?

options.misconception: allows the certified interest in full, as for a let-out house, forgetting that the ceiling is what distinguishes a self-occupied one
options.why: Interest is allowed in full only against a let-out property, where there is rent to set it against. A self-occupied house has an annual value of nil, so the interest creates a loss out of nothing, and the ceiling is how the Act limits that.

The higher ceiling is available and the accountant has counted the five years from the wrong day. Interest on a loan for acquisition or construction is capped at ₹2,00,000 in all, for one or two self-occupied houses together, and two conditions attach to it: construction has to be finished within five years from the end of the year the money was borrowed, and the lender has to give a certificate of the interest. The money was borrowed in the financial year 2020-21, so the five years run to 31 March 2026, and December 2025 is inside it. The certificate is in hand. So ₹2,00,000 of the ₹2,80,000 is allowed and the annual value of the house is nil.
keywords: interest on a loan for acquisition or construction is capped at ₹2,00,000 in all
construction has to be finished within five years
the lender has to give a certificate of the interest

options.text: Nothing, because a house with a nil annual value has no income to deduct anything from
options.misconception: treats a nil annual value as closing the head, when the interest deduction is expressly allowed against it and produces a loss
options.why: The deduction is allowed against the nil value and produces a loss under the head, which is exactly what it is for. That loss can then be set against other income within the limit the Act sets for such a set-off.

options.misconception: counts the five years from the date the loan was taken instead of from the end of the financial year in which it was taken
options.why: The period is measured from the end of the financial year in which the capital was borrowed, not from the drawdown. Borrowing in June 2020 starts the clock on 31 March 2021 and it runs to 31 March 2026, so a house finished in December 2025 is comfortably inside. The ₹30,000 ceiling is what is left when a condition fails, and none has.

citation.ref: Sections 23(2) and 24(b) — nil annual value and the two interest ceilings for a self-occupied house

items.scenario: Mr Bhatia has opted out of the default regime. He borrowed in June 2020 to build a house for himself to live in, and the building was finished in December 2025. He moved in the same month and the house has been self-occupied since. His lender has given him a certificate showing ₹2,80,000 of interest for the year ended 31 March 2026. His accountant says the ceiling is ₹30,000 because construction dragged on for more than five calendar years from the date of the loan.

items.stem: What goes into his income for the assessment year 2026-27 on account of the ₹90,000?

options.text: ₹63,000, under income from house property
options.why: Ownership is not the test here. Section 25A taxes it in the year it is realised, owner or not — the Act says in terms that the amount is charged under this head whether or not the assessee is the owner of the property in that year, which is what stops a recovery escaping by the simple step of selling first. A flat thirty per cent comes off, leaving ₹63,000, and that is what enters the assessment year 2026-27.
keywords: section 25A taxes it in the year it is realised, owner or not
a flat thirty per cent comes off, leaving ₹63,000

options.text: ₹90,000, under income from other sources
options.misconception: sends the recovery to the residuary head because the house is gone, when the section fixes the head as house property
options.why: The section names the head, and it names house property. Putting it under the residuary head would lose the thirty per cent allowance, which is one practical reason the head matters rather than being a label.

options.text: ₹90,000, under income from house property
options.misconception: brings in the recovery gross, forgetting the standard deduction the section carries of its own
options.why: The section allows thirty per cent of the amount recovered, which stands in for the costs of getting it in. It is a separate allowance written into the same section, and it applies whether or not any property is still owned.

options.text: Nothing
options.misconception: reads ownership as a condition of the charge, when the section was written to hold the charge after ownership ends
options.why: The section exists for this exact situation. Rent written off in one year and recovered in another would otherwise be untaxable whenever the owner had sold in between, and the words about ownership are there to shut that off.

citation.ref: Section 25A — unrealised rent and arrears recovered later, and the thirty per cent deduction

items.scenario: A tenant left a house owned by Mr Bhatia in 2023 owing ₹90,000 of rent, which Mr Bhatia wrote off as unrealised in that year and which was allowed to him. He sold that house in 2024. In February 2026 the former tenant, whose circumstances have improved, sends him the whole ₹90,000. Mr Bhatia's accountant says nothing is taxable, because he no longer owns the property and there is no house left to tax the income against.

items.stem: Is 30 September 2026 in time, and if not what is left to the company?

options.text: It is in time, because time only starts to run when the company's counsel is in a position to advise on the order
options.misconception: ties the start of the period to the party's readiness rather than to communication of the order
options.why: The period runs from communication, which is an event the department can prove and the party can date. A counsel's diary may well be sufficient cause for condoning a delay; it does not stop the clock from starting.

options.text: It is in time, the period being three months from the date of the order
options.misconception: carries the period for an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) across to the Tribunal and starts it from the wrong event
options.why: The two stages have different clocks and different starting points. For the Tribunal the period is two months and it is measured from the end of the month in which the order reached the party, which is more generous at the start of a month and much less generous than three months overall.

options.text: It is out of time and nothing can be done, the Tribunal having no power to condone a delay in an appeal to it
options.misconception: assumes the time limit is absolute, when the section expressly gives the Tribunal power to admit a late appeal
options.why: The power to admit a late appeal is written into the same section, and it is available for an appeal by either side and for a cross-objection. What the company cannot do is treat it as automatic; it has to show what kept it.

options.text: It is out of time, but the Tribunal can still take the appeal if it is satisfied about the delay
options.why: The clock is short and it does not run from the date on the order. The appeal goes in within two months from the end of the month the order was communicated, so with communication in June the period runs from 30 June and here that is 31 August 2026. The 30th of September is a month late. The Tribunal may still admit it, because a late appeal is admitted only if the Tribunal is satisfied there was sufficient cause for not presenting it in time — which is a discretion the company has to persuade somebody to exercise, not a right it can rely on.
keywords: the appeal goes in within two months from the end of the month
a late appeal is admitted only if the Tribunal is satisfied there was sufficient cause

citation.ref: Sections 253(1), 253(3) and 253(5) — the appeal, the two months and the power to admit a late appeal

items.scenario: An order of the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowing Vardhan Ceramics Ltd's appeal was communicated to the company on 24 June 2026. The company's counsel is abroad until the autumn and the directors propose to lodge the appeal to the Appellate Tribunal on 30 September 2026, on the footing that an appeal is in time if it goes in within the same financial year.

items.stem: What does each side pay, and who files for the department?

options.text: ₹1,500 for the company, because the fee bands stop at ₹2,00,000 and the middle band is the highest one written
options.misconception: reads the table as ending at the middle band, so every large assessment falls back to it
options.why: The ₹1,500 band stops at a total income of ₹2,00,000, and there is a band above it — one per cent of the assessed income, subject to a maximum. A company assessed at crores is in that band, not the one below.
keywords: the ₹1,500 band stops at a total income of ₹2,00,000

options.text: ₹10,000 for the company, nothing for the department, and the Assessing Officer files
options.why: The accounts department has taken the rate and missed the cap. Above a total income of ₹2,00,000 the fee is 1 per cent of the assessed income, capped at ₹10,000, so a company assessed at ₹3.2 crore pays ₹10,000 and not ₹3,20,000. On the department's side the Principal Commissioner does not appeal himself — he can direct the Assessing Officer to, and a departmental appeal carries no fee.
keywords: the fee is 1 per cent of the assessed income, capped at ₹10,000
the Principal Commissioner does not appeal himself — he can direct the Assessing Officer to
a departmental appeal carries no fee

options.text: ₹3,20,000 for the company, nothing for the department, and the Principal Commissioner files in his own name
options.misconception: applies the one per cent rate without its ceiling and treats the Commissioner as the appellant
options.why: The one per cent has a maximum written beside it, and the maximum is what a large assessment reaches. And the section gives the Principal Commissioner a power to direct rather than a right to appeal; the appeal is the Assessing Officer's.

options.text: ₹10,000 for the company and ₹10,000 for the department, the fee being payable on any appeal to the Tribunal
options.misconception: assumes symmetry between the parties, when the section expressly relieves an appeal filed by the Assessing Officer on the Commissioner's direction
options.why: The fee table exempts an appeal filed by the Assessing Officer on the direction of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner against an order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The two sides are not on the same footing here, and the department's appeal costs it nothing.

citation.ref: Sections 253(2), 253(6) and 253(7) — the department's route and the fees

items.scenario: Vardhan Ceramics Ltd's total income as computed by the Assessing Officer is ₹3.2 crore. The company is budgeting for its appeal to the Appellate Tribunal and its accounts department has provided for a fee of ₹3,20,000, being one per cent of the assessed income. On the other side, the Principal Commissioner is unhappy with the part of the order that went against the department and intends to lodge an appeal himself, and has asked what that will cost.

items.stem: What can the company do about the grounds it lost on?

options.text: File a cross-objection at any time before the department's appeal is heard
options.misconception: treats the cross-objection as open until the hearing, when it carries a fixed period from the notice
options.why: The period runs from receipt of the notice and not to the hearing date. A late cross-objection is possible, but only on the same footing as a late appeal — the Tribunal has to be satisfied about the delay.

options.text: Put them in a memorandum of cross-objections, which has its own short clock running from the notice
options.why: Receiving notice of the other side's appeal opens a door that the company's own lapse had shut. A memorandum of cross-objections goes in within 30 days of the notice, against any part of the order, and the Tribunal disposes of it as though it were an appeal filed in time. So the grounds the company lost on come back before the Tribunal even though its own period has long gone, and the Tribunal can allow a late cross-objection for sufficient cause as well.
keywords: a memorandum of cross-objections goes in within 30 days of the notice
the Tribunal disposes of it as though it were an appeal filed in time

options.text: File its own appeal now, the department's appeal having reopened the two-month period
options.misconception: thinks the other side's appeal restarts the appellant's own clock, when it opens a different and shorter route instead
options.why: Nothing restarts the two months. What the notice starts is a separate thirty-day period for a cross-objection, and the two are different filings with different forms and different clocks.

options.text: Nothing — its own appeal period has gone and the cross-objection can only answer the department's grounds
options.misconception: reads a cross-objection as a defence to the appeal, when it may be directed against any part of the order
options.why: A cross-objection is not confined to answering what the other side has raised. The section lets it be filed against any part of the order, which is what makes it a second chance rather than a reply.

citation.ref: Sections 253(4) and 253(5) — the memorandum of cross-objections

items.scenario: Vardhan Ceramics Ltd let its own two months run out and did not appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) order. On 12 August 2026 it receives notice that the Assessing Officer, on the Principal Commissioner's direction, has appealed to the Tribunal against the part of the order that went in the company's favour. The company is advised that it can now only defend the department's appeal, and that the grounds it lost on are closed to it for good.

items.stem: On what terms can the Tribunal stay the demand?

options.text: On any terms the Tribunal thinks fit, including none, since a stay is a discretionary relief
options.misconception: treats the stay power as unfettered, when the section attaches a money condition and two outer periods to it
options.why: The discretion is real but it starts after the conditions are met. The section fixes a minimum deposit or security before a stay can be granted at all, so an applicant who offers nothing is asking for something the Tribunal has no power to give.

options.text: Against ₹18,00,000, and there is no limit on extensions so long as the company keeps applying and keeps the deposit in place
options.misconception: turns a capped total into a renewable one, so the ceiling never bites
options.why: Extensions are not unlimited. Each one has to be applied for and each has to satisfy the conditions, and the section then puts a ceiling on the aggregate of the original stay and every extension together.

options.text: Against ₹18,00,000, and for as long as the appeal takes, since the delay is the Tribunal's and not the company's
options.misconception: reads the outer period as elastic where the assessee is not at fault, when it is written as a fixed ceiling on the total
options.why: The deposit is right and the open-ended stay is not. The section sets a first period and a total that the extended stay cannot exceed, and it asks separately whether the delay is attributable to the assessee before any extension is given at all.

options.text: Only against ₹18,00,000 in money or security, for a first period of not more than 180 days, and never beyond 365 days in all
options.why: The Tribunal's power to stay is conditional and time-bound. A stay needs a deposit of not less than 20 per cent of the tax, interest, fee, penalty or other sum payable, or security of the same amount, so on ₹90 lakh that is ₹18 lakh and a stay on nothing paid is not something the Tribunal can grant. The first stay runs up to 180 days, and an extension has to be applied for, with the deposit condition still met; and the whole of it cannot go past 365 days, after which the stay is at an end.
keywords: a stay needs a deposit of not less than 20 per cent
the first stay runs up to 180 days
and the whole of it cannot go past 365 days

citation.ref: Section 254(2A) — stay of demand, the deposit and the outer periods

items.scenario: The demand still standing against Vardhan Ceramics Ltd after the Commissioner (Appeals) order is ₹90,00,000. With its appeal before the Tribunal the company applies for a stay of recovery and tells the Tribunal that it cannot pay anything at all, since paying would defeat the purpose of the appeal. It also asks the Tribunal to keep the stay in place until the appeal is finally decided, however long that takes.

items.stem: Is nothing deductible, and is the tax team's reason the right one?

options.text: Tax is deductible on the ₹2,40,000 discount, a discount being a benefit like any other
options.misconception: reads the section literally and ignores the clarification the Board issued under its own power to remove difficulties
options.why: On a literal reading a discount is a benefit, which is exactly why the Board addressed it. It clarified that a discount is a lesser realisation of the sale price rather than something conferred, and that no deduction is called for. The section itself gives the Board that power.

options.text: Tax is deductible on the ₹18,000 of samples but not on the discount
options.misconception: applies the section to every benefit however small, missing the floor written into its own proviso
options.why: The section has a floor of its own. Where the value, or the total value, of what is given to one resident in the financial year stays within twenty thousand rupees, nothing has to be deducted at all, and samples worth ₹18,000 are inside it.

options.text: Nothing is deductible, and the tax team is right that both are trade practice within the same relaxation
options.misconception: extends the discount relaxation to free samples, which the clarification that created it expressly declined to do
options.why: The relaxation was given because sales discounts, cash discounts and rebates are a smaller sale price rather than something handed over, so on those, no tax is required to be deducted. The same clarification then says the relief is not to be stretched to free samples, and lists incentives such as a car, a gold coin or a sponsored trip as things on which tax has to be deducted.
keywords: sales discounts, cash discounts and rebates
on those, no tax is required to be deducted

options.text: Nothing is deductible, but the two escape for different reasons and only one of them is trade practice
options.why: The conclusion is right and the reason covers only half of it. Free samples are a benefit and the Board said expressly that the relaxation for discounts does not reach them. What saves them is the floor: no tax is deductible on the samples, because the aggregate value given to that person for the year does not exceed ₹20,000, and ₹18,000 does not. Had the samples come to ₹22,000 the company would have had to deduct on the whole of it.
keywords: no tax is deductible on the samples
the aggregate value given to that person for the year does not exceed ₹20,000

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 194R(1) — the twenty-thousand floor — with the CBDT guidelines under section 194R(2) on discounts and free samples

items.scenario: Zephyr Appliances Ltd, whose turnover is ₹80 crore, did two things in the financial year 2025-26. It allowed a distributor a cash discount of ₹2,40,000 off the listed price. And it sent a dealer, Ms Nita, free product samples during the year worth ₹18,000 in all. The tax team proposes to deduct nothing on either, on the single ground that both are ordinary trade practice and the Board has said trade practice is outside the section.

items.stem: What does the company have to do before the keys change hands?

options.text: Satisfy itself that the tax on ₹9,00,000 has actually been paid, and only then release the car
options.why: The finance head has spotted the problem and drawn the wrong conclusion. The benefit is wholly in kind, so there is nothing to deduct from, and the proviso written for that situation moves the duty rather than removing it: before releasing the benefit the provider must ensure that the tax required to be deducted has been paid. In practice that means the ambassador puts the company in funds or pays it himself as advance tax, and the company checks it before the keys move. Ten per cent of ₹9,00,000 is ₹90,000.
keywords: the benefit is wholly in kind, so there is nothing to deduct from
ensure that the tax required to be deducted has been paid

options.text: Report the value in its return of tax deducted and leave the tax to the ambassador, since he is the person whose income it is
options.misconception: turns a collection duty into a reporting duty, when the section puts the collection on the provider
options.why: It is the ambassador's income and the collection is still the company's job. The whole design of the section is that the person handing over the benefit is the one who has to see the tax reach the government, because the recipient often never files anything against it.

options.text: Deduct ₹90,000 from the next commercial payment it happens to make to the ambassador, whenever that falls
options.misconception: postpones the obligation to a future payment, when the duty is fixed to the moment of release
options.why: The duty is tied to releasing the benefit, not to the next convenient payment. Waiting for one would leave the car gone and the tax unpaid, which is precisely the position the proviso is designed to prevent.

options.text: Nothing — with no cash payment there is no deduction to make
options.misconception: reads the section as needing a payment to withhold from, which is the very gap the first proviso was written to close
options.why: That reading is why benefits in kind went untaxed for years, and the section was written to end it. It applies to a benefit whether it is convertible into money or not, and the proviso tells the provider what to do when there is no cash: make sure the tax has been paid first.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 194R(1) — a benefit wholly in kind, or partly in kind where the cash is not enough

items.scenario: Zephyr Appliances Ltd has decided to give a resident brand ambassador a car worth ₹9,00,000 for a campaign he has finished. Nothing is being paid to him in money for it. The keys are ready to be handed over next week. The finance head's note says that section 194R cannot apply because there is no payment out of which anything could be withheld, and that the ambassador will simply pay tax on the car in his own return.

items.stem: Does Mr Sameer have to see that tax is paid on the ₹60,000?

options.text: No — his receipts are under ₹1 crore, so the exclusion applies whatever he does
options.misconception: reads one limit into the proviso where two are written, one for business and a lower one for a profession
options.why: The proviso sets a limit for each. A person carrying on a business gets the higher figure and a person carrying on a profession the lower one, which is the ordinary pattern wherever the Act draws this distinction. Reading only the higher figure lets most professionals out of a section plainly meant to catch them.

options.text: Yes — the figure his accountant has quoted is the wrong one for a profession
options.why: There are two figures in the proviso and the accountant has taken the one that does not apply. An individual or HUF is out where turnover from business does not exceed ₹1 crore, but for a profession the figure is ₹50 lakh, not ₹1 crore, and it is measured for the immediately preceding financial year. Mr Sameer's professional receipts for 2024-25 were ₹62,00,000, which is past the professional limit, so he is inside the section and the ₹60,000 benefit is above the twenty-thousand floor.
keywords: an individual or HUF is out where turnover from business does not exceed ₹1 crore
for a profession the figure is ₹50 lakh
it is measured for the immediately preceding financial year

options.text: No — the exclusion is measured on the receipts of the year in which the benefit is given, and those are not yet known
options.misconception: measures the exclusion against the current year, which would leave the person unable to know his duty at the time he has to act
options.why: The test looks to the financial year immediately before the one in which the benefit is provided, which is a figure already settled when the benefit is handed over. Measuring against the current year would make the duty unknowable until after the moment for performing it had passed.

options.text: No — the exclusion is written for a company and an individual is outside the section altogether
options.misconception: has the proviso backwards; it is the small individual or HUF that is let out, and everybody else who is in
options.why: The section applies to any person providing a benefit, companies and individuals alike. The proviso then carves out the small individual or HUF by reference to turnover or receipts, so being an individual is what lets a person into the exclusion rather than out of the section.

citation.ref: Third proviso to section 194R(1) — the turnover and gross receipts limits for an individual or HUF

items.scenario: Mr Sameer practises as an architect on his own account. His gross receipts from the profession were ₹62,00,000 in the financial year 2024-25. During the financial year 2025-26 he gave a resident consultant who had helped him win a competition a holiday package worth ₹60,000. His accountant says there is nothing to do, because the small-person exclusion in section 194R is set at ₹1 crore and Mr Sameer is well below it.

items.stem: Is the junior right that the officer is holding nothing he can act on?

options.text: Yes, though for a different reason: material produced inside the department is not information from an independent source, so he must first obtain something from a third party
options.misconception: reads a source test into the word information, when the statute settles the question by naming the categories and one of them is generated inside the department
options.why: The list does not sort material by who made it. Sitting next to the audit objection is a case flagged under the Board's own risk management strategy, which is as internal as anything can be, and material thrown up by a survey the department itself carried out. Requiring an outside source would leave two of the named categories with nothing to do, which is a strong sign the requirement is not there.

options.text: No. An objection saying the earlier assessment was not made as the Act requires is one of the things the statute itself names, and that is what the reopening machinery runs on
options.why: Section 147 gives the officer his power to assess or reassess income that has escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year, and he may set that machinery going only where he holds information which suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment. The Act then closes the argument by listing what qualifies, and an audit objection to the effect that the earlier assessment was not made in accordance with the Act sits on that list, beside a flag raised under the Board's risk management strategy, material shared under a treaty, and something a Tribunal or a court has directed. Whose desk the objection came from is not a question the list asks.
keywords: power to assess or reassess income that has escaped assessment
information which suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment
an audit objection to the effect that the earlier assessment was not made in accordance with the Act

options.text: Yes. Reopening on an audit objection is reopening on the same material the officer already saw, and that is a change of opinion
options.misconception: carries the older change-of-opinion argument into a scheme that now decides at the threshold by a statutory list rather than by reasons recorded and defended
options.why: The threshold question is no longer whether the officer has changed his mind. It is narrower and more mechanical: does he hold something the statute names. He does. Whether the objection is right on the merits is exactly what the firm gets to argue in its reply and what the officer has to deal with in the order that follows, and losing that argument later is a different thing from having nothing to start with now.

options.text: No, and he may send the section 148 notice this afternoon, an audit objection being a finding the department has already reached
options.misconception: treats holding information as the end of the pre-notice stage rather than the event that starts it
options.why: Holding the material lets him begin; it does not let him finish. Before any notice under section 148 he has to put the case to the firm, take its answer and pass an order on whether this is a fit case, with approval from above. Sending the notice first is the fault that loses the department the reassessment, and it is a separate fault from having nothing to reopen on.

citation.ref: Sections 147 and 148 — the power to assess or reassess escaped income, and the statutory list of what counts as information, which includes an audit objection

items.scenario: An internal audit party goes back over a completed assessment of Harshad Metals for assessment year 2022-23 and objects that a deduction was allowed which the Act does not permit on those facts. The Assessing Officer has nothing else in front of him: no search, no survey, no report from a reporting entity, no fresh document from anybody outside the department. He wants to reopen. His junior tells him not to bother, on the ground that an audit objection is only the department's own second opinion about the department's own order, and a second opinion cannot be a reason to reopen anyone.

items.stem: What is wrong with the plan as drafted?

options.text: Nothing, provided the firm is told orally what the objection says before it replies
options.misconception: treats being told about the material as equivalent to being given it, when the requirement attaches the material to the notice itself
options.why: A description of a document is not the document. The requirement is that the show-cause notice go out with the material attached, so that the firm answers what the department actually holds rather than a summary of it. An oral account also leaves nothing on the record for the order, or for anybody reading the file afterwards, to test the reply against.

options.text: Only the four days. The period is fixed by statute at thirty days and cannot be cut, and everything else in the plan is a matter of internal sequencing
options.misconception: invents a fixed reply period for a notice whose period the statute leaves to the officer, and treats the order of approval as housekeeping
options.why: The statute lets the assessee answer within such period as the notice specifies, so the length is the officer's to set and a short window is challenged on fairness rather than on a number. What is not his to arrange is the sequence: an approval that arrives after the order it was supposed to authorise is not a control at all, and the notice that followed rests on an order nobody sanctioned.

options.text: Nothing that matters, because the faceless information-gathering route would have removed all of it, and the same relaxation is available here once the objection is put on the department's system
options.misconception: reads the section 135A relaxation as a facility the officer can bring about by moving a document onto a system, rather than as a rule about where the material actually came from
options.why: The relaxation turns on the source, not on the storage. Section 148A does not apply where the officer has received the material under the scheme notified under section 135A, and in that case he goes straight to the section 148 notice — but even there he still needs the prior approval of the specified authority, so the whole pre-notice stage does not fall away. An internal audit objection did not arrive by that route, and uploading it later does not change where it came from.
keywords: Section 148A does not apply where the officer has received the material under the scheme notified under section 135A
he still needs the prior approval of the specified authority

options.text: Three things: the letter carries none of the material, the reply window is the officer's to fix but the material is not his to withhold, and the approval is being taken after the step it is meant to control
options.why: The pre-notice stage has a shape. First comes a show-cause notice asking the firm why a notice under section 148 should not be issued in its case, and that notice must be accompanied by the information the officer is going on — sending the demand without the material defeats the point of asking. The firm then replies within the period specified in the notice, which the officer does fix himself, so four days is his call and not a defect. Then, and only then, he passes the order deciding whether this is a fit case, and that order needs approval before it is passed, from the specified authority — an Additional Commissioner, an Additional Director, a Joint Commissioner or a Joint Director. Approving afterwards approves nothing.
keywords: a show-cause notice asking the firm why a notice under section 148 should not be issued
accompanied by the information the officer is going on
replies within the period specified in the notice
an Additional Commissioner, an Additional Director, a Joint Commissioner or a Joint Director

citation.ref: Section 148A read with sections 148, 151 and 135A — the show-cause notice with the material attached, the reply period, the order with prior approval, and the specified authority

items.scenario: The officer decides to reopen Harshad Metals. He drafts a one-line letter telling the firm that a notice will follow, gives it four days to say something, and encloses nothing with it because the objection is an internal document. He intends to pass his order on whether this is a fit case straight after the four days, and to put the file up to the Additional Commissioner for approval once the section 148 notice has gone out, so that the approval covers both steps at once. His junior asks whether any of this would still be needed had the material reached him instead through the notified faceless information-gathering scheme.

items.stem: Which of the two notices, if either, is out of time?

options.text: Neither
options.why: Two clocks run, and each has an ordinary length and a longer one. The show-cause notice gets three years from the end of the relevant assessment year, extended to five years where the escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more on the material the officer holds — ₹64,00,000 is, so its outer limit is 31 March 2028 and 20 May 2026 is well inside it. The section 148 notice gets three years and three months, extended to five years and three months only where the officer has in his hands books of account or other documents or evidence showing escaped income at that level. The ledgers and purchase files are exactly that, so its outer limit is 30 June 2028 and 12 August 2026 is inside that too.
keywords: three years from the end of the relevant assessment year
extended to five years where the escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more
The section 148 notice gets three years and three months
five years and three months only where the officer has in his hands books of account or other documents or evidence

options.text: The show-cause notice alone, because the five-year extension is available only to the section 148 notice and not to the stage before it
options.misconception: gives the extension to one clock only, when both carry one and the difference between them is three months rather than the availability of an extension
options.why: Both stages carry a longer window at the ₹50 lakh level. What differs is the trigger: for the show-cause notice it is enough that the material with the officer suggests income of that size, while for the section 148 notice he must actually hold books of account or other documents or evidence showing it. Here he does, so both stages are open.

options.text: The section 148 notice alone. The show-cause notice caught the longer window, but the notice itself had to go out within three years and three months, which ran out on 30 June 2026
options.misconception: reads the longer window on the section 148 notice as something only a search opens, so an ordinary information case is thought to stop at three years and three months
options.why: A search is not what opens it. What opens it is what the officer actually holds — books of account or other documents or evidence that show escaped income of ₹50 lakh or more — however those papers reached him, and here they are the firm's own ledgers produced in an earlier proceeding. That carries the outer limit to 30 June 2028, so the section 148 notice is in time.
keywords: so the section 148 notice is in time

options.text: Both. Once three years from the end of the assessment year have gone, the whole reassessment machinery closes, and the extensions apply only where a search or requisition has taken place
options.misconception: collapses two clocks of different lengths into one and ties both extensions to a search
options.why: The two limits are not the same length and never were: the show-cause notice runs on three years and the section 148 notice on three years and three months, the extra quarter being there because the order has to be passed in between. Neither extension mentions a search. Each turns on the size of the escaped income, and the section 148 one additionally on the officer actually holding the papers that show it.

citation.ref: Section 149(1) and section 149(2) — the two outer limits, and the different triggers for the extended window at each stage

items.scenario: Assessment year 2022-23, which ended on 31 March 2023. The Assessing Officer's material puts the escaped income at ₹64,00,000, and he has the firm's own ledgers and purchase files, seized from nobody and produced in an earlier proceeding, which show it. He serves the show-cause notice on 20 May 2026. After the reply and the order he issues the section 148 notice on 12 August 2026. The firm says both are dead: three years from the end of the assessment year ran out on 31 March 2026.

items.stem: On what figure does the penalty bite, and under which limb?

options.text: ₹18,00,000, as misreporting on the whole of it
options.misconception: treats every addition sustained in an assessment as one undifferentiated block, so a disclosed estimate is punished on the same terms as an unevidenced claim
options.why: The two additions are not the same animal. One is a difference of judgement about a number both sides estimated, with the company's own workings on the record; the other is a claim with nothing behind it. The statute separates them: the first is carved out of under-reported income altogether, and only the second reaches the list that carries the higher rate.

options.text: ₹12,00,000, but as ordinary under-reporting, since the officer has not alleged fraud
options.misconception: reads the misreporting limb as needing an allegation of dishonesty, when it is a list of situations and a claim without evidence is on it
options.why: Nothing in the provision asks the officer to allege or prove fraud. It gives six situations, and if the addition falls into one of them the higher rate follows. An expenditure claim with no evidence at all behind it is the third of the six. The company's answer to it is evidence, not an argument about the officer's state of mind.

options.text: ₹18,00,000, as under-reporting at the lower rate
options.misconception: gets the carve-out and the misreporting list the wrong way round, keeping the estimate in and treating the unevidenced claim as an ordinary difference
options.why: Both halves of that are wrong, and each on its own would change the answer. The estimated overhead comes out because the company estimated it lower itself and said so; the consultancy stays in and goes to the higher rate because an expense nobody can produce a single document for is named in the misreporting list. Charging the whole at the lower rate lets the fabricated half off and punishes the honest half.

options.text: ₹12,00,000, as misreporting
options.why: The starting figure is the assessed income less what was determined on processing, ₹18,00,000. From it comes out anything the statute keeps outside under-reported income, and one of those carve-outs fits the overhead exactly: where the company has itself estimated a lower amount of disallowance on the same issue, has included that amount in the computation of its income, and has disclosed all material facts about it, the addition made on a higher estimate is not counted. That leaves ₹12,00,000. The consultancy is a claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence, and that phrase is one of the listed cases of misreporting of income, so the harsher limb applies to it.
keywords: the assessed income less what was determined on processing, ₹18,00,000
has itself estimated a lower amount of disallowance on the same issue
has disclosed all material facts about it
a claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence, and that phrase is one of the listed cases of misreporting of income

citation.ref: Section 270A(3), section 270A(6)(iii) and section 270A(9)(iii) — the computation, the carve-out for a self-estimated disallowance disclosed in full, and the unevidenced expenditure claim as misreporting

items.scenario: Sarvesh Alloys Ltd was processed under section 143(1)(a) at ₹18,00,000 and assessed under section 143(3) at ₹36,00,000. Two additions make up the difference. ₹6,00,000 is an estimated disallowance of a shared overhead: the company had itself worked out a smaller disallowance on the very same overhead, put that figure into its computation, and set out in the notes how it had arrived at it; the officer simply took a higher estimate. ₹12,00,000 is a claim for consultancy the company has produced no agreement, no invoice and no correspondence for.

items.stem: What is the penalty, and does the immunity plan work?

options.text: ₹6,00,000, and the immunity plan works provided the three steps are completed in order
options.misconception: reads the immunity as a procedural reward for paying up and not appealing, when the misreporting limb is a bar the assessee cannot clear by conduct
options.why: The three steps are real and they are all necessary: the tax and interest paid within the time in the notice of demand, no appeal filed against the assessment, and an application made within one month from the end of the month, counted from when the order landed. But they are not sufficient. The officer is forbidden to grant immunity where the penalty proceeding was started on one of the misreporting grounds, and an unevidenced expenditure claim is one of them, so the company can do everything right and still be refused.
keywords: no appeal filed against the assessment
an application made within one month from the end of the month

options.text: ₹24,00,000, being two hundred per cent of the under-reported income itself
options.misconception: applies the rate to the income rather than to the tax on it
options.why: The rate runs on tax, not on income. The provision says so twice over: it fixes fifty per cent and two hundred per cent of the tax payable on under-reported income, and it then spends a whole sub-section explaining how that tax is worked out. Applying the rate to the income would make the penalty larger than the assessment in most cases, which is a good sign the base has been read wrongly.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, and the immunity plan does not work
options.misconception: charges fifty per cent on the misreporting case, taking the ordinary rate because the higher one is thought to need a separate finding
options.why: Fifty per cent is the rate for under-reporting that is not misreporting. Once the addition falls in the misreporting list the rate doubles to two hundred, on the same tax base. Nothing further has to be found or recorded to get there; the classification of the addition is what sets the rate.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, and the immunity plan does not work
options.why: The base is not the tax on ₹12,00,000 standing alone. Tax payable on under-reported income is a two-step subtraction: it is the tax on the under-reported income as increased by the income determined in the preceding order, less the tax on that earlier income by itself — ₹13,00,000 minus ₹10,00,000, which is ₹3,00,000. Where the under-reporting results from misreporting the penalty is 200% of that, so ₹6,00,000. The plan then fails for a reason that has nothing to do with how well it is executed: immunity under section 270AA cannot be granted where the penalty was initiated for misreporting, and this one was.
keywords: Tax payable on under-reported income is a two-step subtraction
the tax on the under-reported income as increased by the income determined in the preceding order
Where the under-reporting results from misreporting the penalty is 200%
immunity under section 270AA cannot be granted where the penalty was initiated for misreporting

citation.ref: Section 270A(8) and section 270A(10)(iii) read with section 270AA(1) to (3) — the two-step tax computation, the two hundred per cent rate, and the misreporting bar on immunity

items.scenario: Staying with Sarvesh Alloys. Under-reported income has been settled at ₹12,00,000, and it results from misreporting. Tax on the assessed income as a whole comes to ₹13,00,000; tax on the ₹18,00,000 determined in the earlier order comes to ₹10,00,000. The company's finance head wants to pay the demand within the time in the notice, file no appeal, apply promptly, and take immunity so that the penalty goes away.

items.stem: Is the auditor right that the continuity test fails?

options.text: Yes. The exception for a gift covers only a gift made to a spouse, and a transfer to a son is an ordinary change of hands
options.misconception: narrows the exception to one relative when the provision uses the general word, which reaches a lineal descendant
options.why: The wording is not limited to a spouse. It covers a gift to any relative of the shareholder making the gift, and a son is a lineal descendant of his father. Reading it down to a spouse would leave the commonest family transfer of all — a parent passing shares to a child — outside a relief that exists precisely for family transfers rather than for trading in losses.

options.text: Yes, because Chandan's sale of 30% to Deepa is itself a change of more than half the voting power in one transaction
options.misconception: tests the size of the shares that moved rather than the size of the block that stayed
options.why: The section never asks how much moved. It asks how much stayed in the same hands, and the two figures are not complements of each other once an exception takes one transfer out of the count. Thirty per cent changing hands is not more than half of anything, and even if it were, what decides the case is that 60% of the voting power is still held by people who held it in the loss year.

options.text: No, but for a different reason: the test is applied on the date the loss is set off rather than on the last day of the year, and by then the register may read differently again
options.misconception: invents a floating test date, when the provision fixes two specific closing days and compares them
options.why: There is no floating date. The comparison is between two fixed closing days — the last day of the year in which the loss was incurred, and the last day of the year in which it is to be set off — and what happens in between is irrelevant except where it changes the second register. A test that moved with the set-off would be unworkable, because a company does not know on any given day which year's income will absorb the loss.

options.text: No. The son's 10% is not counted as a change at all, so the continuing block is above the line
options.why: The test compares two closing days. Do the people carrying at least 51% of the voting power on the last day of the previous year include those who carried as much when the loss arose? Counted crudely the auditor is right — Anil and Bhavesh between them carry 50%, one short. But the restriction is expressly disapplied where the change in shareholding comes about through a transfer of shares by way of gift to a relative of the shareholder making it, and a son is a relative. Bhavesh's 10% therefore does not count as having moved, the continuing holding is 60%, and the test is met. Chandan's sale to Deepa is the kind of change the section is aimed at, and even after it enough continuity is left.
keywords: at least 51% of the voting power on the last day of the previous year
Anil and Bhavesh between them carry 50%
a transfer of shares by way of gift to a relative of the shareholder

citation.ref: Section 79(1) and section 79(3)(i) — the fifty-one per cent continuity test on the two closing days, and the disapplication for a gift to a relative

items.scenario: Vanaja Chemicals Pvt Ltd is closely held and is not an eligible start-up. Its brought-forward business loss was incurred in the year ended 31 March 2024, when Anil held 35%, Bhavesh 25%, Chandan 30% and Deepa 10%. During the year ended 31 March 2026 Bhavesh gave 10% to his son, and Chandan sold his whole 30% to Deepa. On 31 March 2026 the register reads Anil 35%, Bhavesh 15%, Bhavesh's son 10%, Deepa 40%. The auditor says the loss is dead: the only two people on the register today who were also on it in the loss year are Anil and Bhavesh, and 35 plus 15 is 50.

items.stem: What is the total income, and what is carried forward?

options.text: ₹2,00,000, with the depreciation carried forward in full
options.misconception: applies the late-return bar to the depreciation as well, so ₹4,00,000 sits unused while income remains chargeable
options.why: The filing condition is written against a list of losses, and unabsorbed depreciation is not on it — it is expressly outside, along with a carried-forward house property loss. So the late return costs the company its ₹6,00,000 business loss and nothing else. Refusing the depreciation as well leaves ₹2,00,000 taxed that the statute allows to be absorbed.

options.text: Nil, with ₹2,00,000 of business loss carried forward
options.misconception: follows the accountant and sets the depreciation off first, which changes which of the two survives into next year
options.why: Setting the depreciation off first leaves a business loss standing at the end of the year instead of depreciation, and the two are not interchangeable: a business loss dies after eight years and needs a business to set it against, while depreciation goes forward with no limit and is far more useful. That is precisely why the order is fixed by statute rather than left to the assessee, and following the accountant here would quietly swap the better carry-forward for the worse one: the ₹2,00,000 left over at the end of the year would be business loss rather than depreciation.
keywords: the ₹2,00,000 left over at the end of the year would be business loss rather than depreciation

options.text: Nil, with ₹6,00,000 of business loss and ₹2,00,000 of depreciation carried forward
options.misconception: keeps the lapsed loss alive on the reasoning that a late return delays a claim rather than destroying it
options.why: A late return of loss does not park the loss for later. The entitlement to carry forward depends on the loss having been determined on a return filed within the time allowed, and where it was not, there is nothing to carry. The company keeps its set-off within the year the loss arose, but the amount does not travel.

options.text: Nil, with ₹2,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation carried forward
options.why: Three separate rules run here. First, a business loss may be carried forward only if it was determined on a return of loss filed under section 139(3) within the time allowed, so the ₹6,00,000 business loss cannot be carried forward and simply lapses; the ₹18,00,000 was in time and survives. Second, that filing condition does not touch unabsorbed depreciation, which travels under its own provision, so the ₹4,00,000 is available despite the late return. Third, the order is fixed: brought-forward business loss is set off before unabsorbed depreciation, which is the opposite of the accountant's plan. ₹20,00,000 less ₹18,00,000 leaves ₹2,00,000, which the depreciation absorbs, so the total income is nil and ₹2,00,000 of depreciation remains to go forward with no time limit against it.
keywords: a return of loss filed under section 139(3) within the time allowed
the ₹6,00,000 business loss cannot be carried forward
brought-forward business loss is set off before unabsorbed depreciation

citation.ref: Section 80 read with section 139(3), the exclusion of section 32(2) depreciation from that condition, and section 72(2) on the order of set-off

items.scenario: Vanaja Chemicals clears the continuity test. It brings forward a business loss of ₹18,00,000 from assessment year 2024-25, whose return of loss went in on time; a business loss of ₹6,00,000 from assessment year 2025-26, whose return went in three weeks after the due date; and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹4,00,000 from that same late year. Its business income for assessment year 2026-27 before any set-off is ₹20,00,000. The accountant proposes to set off the depreciation first, on the ground that it has no time limit and should therefore be used while the year can absorb it.

items.stem: Which parts of the accountant's advice are wrong?

options.text: Neither part, but the wedding shares and the legacy are both taxable because they came from outside the family
options.misconception: reads the marriage and inheritance exclusions as narrower versions of the relative exclusion, when they turn on the occasion and the instrument rather than on the giver
options.why: Those two exclusions do not ask who gave. One asks about the occasion — property received on the occasion of the marriage of the individual herself, which is why a gift at a sibling's wedding would not qualify — and the other asks about the instrument, covering anything that comes under a will or on an intestacy. A college friend's wedding gift and a grandmother's legacy are both outside the charge.

options.text: The second part only — the uncle is a relative, but the cash escapes because each gift is under fifty thousand
options.misconception: applies the fifty thousand test gift by gift rather than to the year's aggregate from all non-relatives
options.why: The provision adds up the year before it applies the limit. Testing each receipt separately would make the threshold meaningless, because any sum could be split into instalments of forty-nine thousand. Once the year's total from non-relatives crosses the line the entire total is income, so ₹55,000 is charged and not ₹5,000.

options.text: Both parts
options.why: The threshold is applied to the year's total from all non-relatives, not to each gift, and once that total goes past fifty thousand the whole of it is charged rather than the excess — so the two gifts totalling ₹55,000 are taxable in full, and the accountant has the arithmetic exactly backwards. The flat is the other way round: the brother or sister of either parent is inside the definition of relative, so her father's brother is a relative and the flat is not taxable at whatever value. Neither of the other two receipts is chargeable either — property coming on the occasion of the marriage of the individual herself is excluded, and so is anything received under a will or by way of inheritance.
keywords: the two gifts totalling ₹55,000 are taxable in full
her father's brother is a relative and the flat is not taxable
anything received under a will or by way of inheritance

options.text: The first part only — the cash is taxable, but the uncle is correctly treated
options.misconception: keeps a sibling of a parent outside the relative list, treating relative as meaning only spouse, parents and children
options.why: The list is wider than the household. It reaches the individual's own brother or sister, the spouse's brother or sister, the brother or sister of either parent, every lineal ascendant and descendant of the individual and of the spouse, and the spouse of any of those. An uncle on the father's side is squarely inside it, and once a giver is a relative the value of what is given stops mattering.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)(a) and the first proviso — aggregation of money receipts against the fifty thousand threshold, the definition of relative, and the exclusions for marriage of the individual and for a will or inheritance

items.scenario: Ms Nandini receives four things during the year. Two friends give her cash of ₹30,000 and ₹25,000 on no particular occasion. Her father's brother transfers a flat to her for nothing. Shares worth ₹1,80,000 come to her from a college friend on the occasion of her own wedding. Her grandmother's will leaves her ₹2,00,000, paid out by the executor in March. Her accountant says the cash is safe because neither gift on its own crosses fifty thousand, and that the flat must be taxed at its stamp duty value because an uncle is not on the list of close family.

items.stem: What is chargeable, once the accountant's three propositions are tested?

options.text: ₹4,70,000 in all, but computed as ₹3,50,000 plus ₹65,000 plus ₹55,000 of cash already charged
options.misconception: adds the money already brought in under the cash limb a second time when totalling the property limbs
options.why: The figure is right and the working double counts. The year's total under this head is ₹4,70,000 — the ₹55,000 of cash, the ₹3,50,000 shortfall on the plot and the ₹65,000 of movables — so the cash is one of the three components and not an addition to a total that already contains it.
keywords: The year's total under this head is ₹4,70,000

options.text: Nothing on the plot, ₹65,000 on the painting and chain, and ₹3,00,000 on the car
options.misconception: reads the immovable property test as a flat ten per cent tolerance and assumes anything valuable is property
options.why: Two mistakes cancel out into a wrong answer. The tolerance is not a flat ten per cent — it is the greater of ten per cent and fifty thousand, and on a ₹20,00,000 price the ten per cent figure is the one that governs, which the shortfall still exceeds. And a motor car is not property for this clause at all; the definition names its categories and stops, which is why cars, furniture and machinery given away change nothing under this head.
keywords: a motor car is not property for this clause

options.text: ₹3,50,000 on the plot and ₹65,000 on the painting and chain, and nothing on the car
options.why: The plot fails the accountant's own test. The shortfall is charged where the stamp duty value beats the price by more than the higher of fifty thousand and 10% of the consideration — 10% of ₹20,00,000 is ₹2,00,000, the larger of the two figures, and the gap of ₹3,50,000 beats it, so ₹3,50,000 is chargeable. Movables are tested differently: it is the aggregate fair market value of everything received without consideration in the year that meets the fifty thousand line, not each article, so the painting and the chain go in together at ₹65,000. The car escapes because property here is a closed list — land or building, shares and securities, jewellery, bullion, archaeological collections, drawings, paintings, sculptures, any other work of art, and a virtual digital asset — and a motor car is on none of it. The year's charge under this head therefore comes to ₹4,70,000.
keywords: the higher of fifty thousand and 10% of the consideration
the aggregate fair market value of everything received without consideration
the painting and the chain go in together at ₹65,000

options.text: ₹3,50,000 on the plot and nothing else
options.misconception: tests each movable article against fifty thousand separately, the way the accountant does, instead of aggregating them
options.why: The movable test aggregates before it compares. A painting at ₹40,000 and a chain at ₹25,000 are each under the line and together over it, and the provision looks at the total for the year rather than at the articles one by one. Both are on the list of property — a painting by name, and the chain as jewellery — so ₹65,000 goes in.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)(b)(B) and (c)(i) read with the definition of property — the higher-of test for immovable property, aggregation of movables against fifty thousand, and the closed list that leaves a motor car out

items.scenario: Three more receipts in the same year for Ms Nandini. She buys a plot from an unrelated seller for ₹20,00,000 when its stamp duty value is ₹23,50,000. A neighbour gives her a painting worth ₹40,000 and a gold chain worth ₹25,000, both for nothing. Her employer's retiring director gives her his motor car, worth ₹3,00,000, as a leaving present. Her accountant proposes to charge nothing on the plot because the shortfall is under ten per cent of the price, to charge nothing on the painting and the chain because neither is worth fifty thousand on its own, and to charge the car in full.

items.stem: On what does the department's case that this is an impermissible arrangement rest?

options.text: On the purpose limb alone, the size of the tax saved being what makes an arrangement impermissible once the purpose is admitted
options.misconception: treats the purpose test as the whole provision, so any tax-driven choice becomes impermissible and ordinary planning disappears
options.why: Purpose alone would catch every deliberate choice a taxpayer makes, including the ones the statute intends to be available. That is why the provision pairs the purpose with a second, separate question about the shape of the arrangement itself: is it non-arm's length, does it abuse the Act, does it lack commercial substance, is it carried out in a way nobody would use for a genuine purpose. A real loan taken because interest is deductible fails the second question and is planning; this fails it and is not.

options.text: On neither limb, because the transfers into the subsidiaries were real transfers, legally effective and properly registered
options.misconception: reads commercial substance as legal validity, when the question is whether the arrangement changes anything in substance and not whether the steps are effective
options.why: Every step in these arrangements is legally effective; that is the point of them. The question is a different one — whether the arrangement has substance beyond its form, which is asked by looking at what actually changed for the parties. Here the ownership economics are untouched, the money ends up where it always would have, and no new activity was created. Legal validity is the starting assumption of the enquiry, not an answer to it.

options.text: On both limbs together — that a tax benefit is what the splitting was for, and that the arrangement carries two of the four tainted features
options.why: The provision needs two things at once, and neither on its own is enough. The first is that the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, of the arrangement is to obtain a tax benefit: splitting a holding into three slices of 8% three months before a sale, when the treaty line sits at 10%, is difficult to explain any other way. The second is that at least one of four features is present, and here two are. The subsidiaries change nothing about the investor's business risk or cash flow, which is the mark of an arrangement lacking commercial substance. And using a treaty's shareholding threshold by manufacturing shareholders is a misuse or abuse of it — the letter is followed and the purpose is not.
keywords: the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, of the arrangement is to obtain a tax benefit
change nothing about the investor's business risk or cash flow
a misuse or abuse of it

options.text: On the tainted-element limb alone, since a company with no staff and no premises is an artificial entity whatever it was set up for
options.misconception: drops the purpose limb, which would make every dormant or holding subsidiary in a group an impermissible arrangement
options.why: Groups hold shares through shell companies for many reasons that have nothing to do with tax — ring-fencing liability, satisfying a regulator, preparing a future sale. Emptiness on its own is not the test, or every holding structure in the country would be caught. It becomes a case only when the emptiness is paired with a purpose, and it is the timing here, three months before the sale and sized exactly to the treaty line, that supplies it.

citation.ref: Section 96(1) read with section 97 — the twin purpose and tainted-element tests, and lack of commercial substance and misuse or abuse as two of the four elements

items.scenario: A foreign investor holds 24% of an Indian company. The treaty between the two countries exempts a seller's capital gains from Indian tax where the seller has held less than 10% of the company. Three months before a sale the investor incorporates three wholly owned subsidiaries in the same country, transfers 8% into each, and sells through them. The subsidiaries have no staff, no offices and no other assets; the funds reach the investor the same week; the group's risk on the shareholding is what it always was. The investor says the subsidiaries are ordinary group companies and that choosing a treaty-friendly structure is planning.

items.stem: Do any of the three exclusions in the rules keep GAAR out?

options.text: The threshold exclusion alone, no single party having saved three crore
options.misconception: reads the three crore figure as a per-assessee limit, when the rule adds up every party to the same arrangement
options.why: The rule counts the arrangement, not the assessee. It asks what the arrangement produced in total for everybody in it during the year, which is why an avoidance scheme cannot be put out of reach by spreading the benefit across enough participants. Three parties saving just under two crore each is precisely the case the aggregation is there for.

options.text: None of the three
options.why: Each argument fails on the words of the rule. The threshold is not per party: the exclusion applies where the tax benefit arising in aggregate to all parties to the arrangement in the relevant year does not exceed ₹3 crore, and ₹1.9 crore plus ₹1.6 crore plus ₹1.5 crore is ₹5 crore. The grandfathering is not a general rule about old shareholdings either; it protects income from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017, and June 2022 is after it. And the protection counsel is reaching for belongs to a foreign institutional investor that has taken no treaty benefit and invested under the securities regulator's regime, which describes neither this investor nor what it is doing.
keywords: the tax benefit arising in aggregate to all parties to the arrangement

options.text: The grandfathering exclusion alone, the shares having been bought years before the arrangement was thought of
options.misconception: dates the grandfathering from when the shares were bought relative to the scheme, rather than against the fixed statutory date
options.why: The grandfathering has one date in it and it is a calendar date, not a gap. Investments made before 1 April 2017 are protected on their transfer; everything acquired afterwards is exposed however long it has been held. Buying in June 2022 and selling in 2026 is a four-year hold and still outside the protection.

options.text: The foreign investor exclusion alone, since the rules keep GAAR away from non-residents investing into India
options.misconception: turns a narrow carve-out for a regulated institutional investor into a general exemption for non-residents
options.why: There is no general exemption for non-residents; if there were, a chapter aimed largely at cross-border structuring would have almost nothing to do. The carve-out is for a foreign institutional investor that is an assessee, has taken no benefit under a treaty, and has invested in accordance with the securities regulator's framework. This investor is an ordinary company and its whole case is a treaty benefit, so it fails two of the three conditions outright.

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(a), (b) and (d) — the aggregate three crore threshold across all parties, the foreign institutional investor carve-out, and grandfathering by reference to 1 April 2017

items.scenario: Same splitting arrangement. The tax saved by the investor is ₹1.9 crore; the two other parties to the arrangement save ₹1.6 crore and ₹1.5 crore between them on connected transactions in the same year. The 24% holding was bought in June 2022. The investor is a company, not a foreign institutional investor, and holds no permission from any Indian regulator. Its counsel argues that GAAR is shut out three times over: no single party saves three crore, the shares were bought long before the sale, and a foreign investor is protected by the rules in any event.

items.stem: How does that stand up?

options.text: Both of counsel's points fail, but so does the officer's sequence — the objections have to be sought and the reference made before any of this
options.why: On the substance, counsel is wrong twice. Once an arrangement is declared impermissible the authorities may disregard the extra companies or treat two or more parties as one and the same person, so a single holder of 24% is what remains and the treaty's ten per cent line is passed; that is an express consequence and not a rewriting of anybody's register. And section 90(2A) settles the treaty argument by making the anti-avoidance chapter apply even where the treaty would be more beneficial, which is the whole reason the chapter is worth having. But the officer cannot start with a computation. He must first issue a written notice to the assessee seeking its objections under Rule 10UB(1), and only then make a reference to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under section 144BA(1).
keywords: treat two or more parties as one and the same person
a reference to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under section 144BA(1)

options.text: Counsel is right on the treaty point, so nothing else needs deciding — the more beneficial provision governs
options.misconception: applies the general rule that a treaty prevails where it is more favourable, without noticing the sub-section that carves the anti-avoidance chapter out of it
options.why: The general rule is real: where a treaty applies, the Act governs only to the extent it is more beneficial to the assessee. But that rule carries an express exception for the anti-avoidance chapter, which applies to an assessee even when it is not beneficial to him. Without that exception a treaty-based scheme would be immune from the very provision aimed at treaty-based schemes.

options.text: Counsel is right on the second point — the consequences reach the tax treatment of income and never the ownership of shares
options.misconception: reads the consequence provision as limited to recomputing income, when it expressly allows the structure itself to be looked through
options.why: The listed consequences go further than numbers. They allow a step or a whole arrangement to be disregarded, combined or recharacterised, an accommodating party to be ignored, connected persons to be deemed one person, and a corporate structure to be looked through altogether. None of that changes who owns what in company law; it decides how the transaction is taxed, which is all the chapter is doing.

options.text: The officer's sequence is right — the reference goes up first, and the assessee is heard by the Principal Commissioner rather than by him
options.misconception: puts the hearing entirely at the higher level, when the rules require the officer to seek objections before he refers the case at all
options.why: The assessee is heard twice, and the first hearing belongs to the officer. He has to put the proposed application of the chapter to the assessee in writing and take its objections before the file moves. Only after that does the reference go up, and the Commissioner's own process follows. Referring first would send up a case the assessee has never been asked about.

citation.ref: Section 98(1) and section 90(2A) read with Rule 10UB(1) and section 144BA(1) — the consequences available, the chapter's priority over a treaty, and the two steps that come before any reference

items.scenario: The Assessing Officer is satisfied that the splitting is an impermissible arrangement. He proposes to write to the investor next week with a computation charging the whole gain in India, and to put the file up to the Principal Commissioner afterwards if the investor argues. The investor's counsel replies on two fronts: that the treaty is more beneficial and therefore governs whatever the domestic chapter says, and that in any event the officer cannot rewrite a shareholding that three separate companies genuinely hold.

items.stem: Which of them is right, and what does the farm income actually do?

options.text: Neither. The exemption holds, but the farm income is used to fix the rate on the rest
options.why: Agricultural income stays exempt and is never itself taxed. What happens instead is partial integration, and it runs for an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons, a body of individuals or an artificial juridical person once two gates are passed: net agricultural income above ₹5,000, and non-agricultural income above the basic exemption limit, which under the default regime is ₹4,00,000 whatever the person's age. Both are passed here. The effect is only on the rate — the farm income pushes the other income into higher slabs and is then taken back out — and on these figures it costs Mr Devraj ₹55,000 more before cess than if it had been ignored, because tax on ₹15,00,000 standing alone would have been ₹1,05,000. A company, a firm, a limited liability partnership, a co-operative society or a local authority is outside the scheme entirely.
keywords: the basic exemption limit, which under the default regime is ₹4,00,000
the farm income pushes the other income into higher slabs

options.text: Neither, and the scheme would apply in the same way had Mr Devraj been a partnership firm on the same figures
options.misconception: extends a scheme written for slab-rate assessees to entities taxed at a flat rate, where a rate device has nothing to work on
options.why: Integration only makes sense where rates rise in slabs, because its whole mechanism is to push income up a slab table. A firm, a company, a limited liability partnership, a co-operative society and a local authority are named as outside it, and for a flat-rate assessee there would be nothing for the device to do even if they were not.

options.text: The colleague, since aggregation means the two amounts are taxed as one
options.misconception: reads the first step of the computation as the whole of it, missing the subtraction that follows
options.why: The first step does add the two together, which is where this reading comes from. But there is a second step that computes tax on the farm income plus the exemption limit and takes it away again. Stopping after step one taxes exempt income and produces a figure far above what the statute asks for.

options.text: The accountant, since an exempt receipt cannot enter a tax computation at all
options.misconception: treats exemption as removing the amount from every use, when it is removed from the charge and kept for measuring the rate
options.why: Exemption answers one question — is this amount taxed — and the answer stays no throughout. It does not answer a second question, which is at what rate the taxable income is charged. The scheme uses the farm income only for the second, and proves it by subtracting the tax attributable to it at the end, so not a rupee of agricultural income bears tax.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) read with the partial integration conditions and section 115BAC(1A) — the two gates, the assessees covered, and the rate-only effect

items.scenario: Mr Devraj is a resident individual of 44 taxed under the default regime. For the year he has non-agricultural income of ₹15,00,000 and net agricultural income of ₹4,00,000. His accountant says the farm income is exempt, so it plays no part in the computation and the tax is simply the tax on ₹15,00,000. A colleague says the exemption is gone and the whole ₹19,00,000 is taxable.

items.stem: What is the tax liability for the year?

options.misconception: ignores the farm income entirely and charges the non-agricultural income on its own, which is the accountant's error carried through to a number
options.why: That figure is tax of ₹1,05,000 on ₹15,00,000 with cess on top, which is what the liability would be if agricultural income never touched the computation. It does touch it, through the rate, and the difference between the two answers is exactly what integration is for — ₹55,000 of extra tax before cess, produced without taxing a rupee of farm income.
