keywords: tax of ₹1,05,000 on ₹15,00,000 with cess on top

options.misconception: stops after step one, charging the aggregate and adding cess without the second-step subtraction
options.why: Step one is a working figure, not the answer. Charging ₹1,80,000 and adding cess taxes the agricultural income at the full slab rates, which the exemption forbids. The subtraction in step two is what strips that tax back out, and leaving it out is the commonest way this computation goes wrong under exam conditions. The right sequence ends at ₹1,60,000, and cess of ₹6,400 then takes the liability to ₹1,66,400.
keywords: cess of ₹6,400 then takes the liability to ₹1,66,400

options.why: Three steps and then cess. Step one charges the aggregate of the two incomes, ₹19,00,000: nothing on the first four lakh, ₹20,000 at 5%, ₹40,000 at 10%, ₹60,000 at 15% and ₹60,000 at 20% on the last three lakh, giving ₹1,80,000. Step two charges the farm income added to the basic exemption limit, ₹8,00,000, which falls wholly in the five per cent band and gives ₹20,000. Step three subtracts the second from the first and leaves ₹1,60,000, and there is no surcharge. Health and education cess at 4% adds ₹6,400, so the liability is ₹1,66,400.
keywords: charges the aggregate of the two incomes, ₹19,00,000
the basic exemption limit, ₹8,00,000, which falls wholly in the five per cent band and gives ₹20,000
subtracts the second from the first and leaves ₹1,60,000

options.misconception: takes step two on the farm income alone instead of on the farm income plus the basic exemption limit
options.why: Step two is deliberately generous: it charges the agricultural income as though it sat on top of a full basic exemption, which is what makes the subtraction big enough to leave the farm income untaxed. Computing it on ₹4,00,000 alone gives nil under the default regime, subtracts too little, and leaves part of the exempt income bearing tax.

citation.ref: The three-step partial integration computation read with the section 115BAC(1A) slabs for A.Y. 2026-27 and health and education cess at four per cent

items.scenario: Mr Devraj's figures again — non-agricultural income ₹15,00,000, net agricultural income ₹4,00,000, default regime, age 44, no surcharge in point because total income is under ₹50 lakh. The default slabs charge nothing up to ₹4,00,000, then 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% on successive bands of ₹4,00,000 each. His assistant has produced four candidate figures for the final liability and cannot decide between them.

items.stem: What is the net worth, and is the CFO right about indexation?

options.text: ₹15 crore, and no indexation is available
options.misconception: builds net worth straight off the balance sheet, so self-generated goodwill is treated as an asset with a cost
options.why: Goodwill a company never paid for has no cost to bring into a cost computation, and the explanation says so by fixing its value at nil for this purpose. Writing it up in the books does not create one. The same treatment applies to an asset whose entire cost has already been deducted under section 35AD, and for the same reason.

options.text: ₹12 crore, and no indexation is available
options.why: Net worth is the aggregate value of the total assets less the liabilities as they stand in the books, and a revaluation is left out of account. Three of the assets are taken at a value the explanations fix rather than at the carrying amount: a depreciable asset comes in at its written down value, so plant enters at ₹9 crore and not ₹11 crore; goodwill the company generated itself rather than bought comes in at nil; and an asset whose whole cost has been allowed under section 35AD also comes in at nil. Everything else goes in at book value. So ₹9 crore of plant plus ₹6 crore of land plus ₹7 crore of current assets, less ₹10 crore of liabilities, is a net worth of ₹12 crore. That figure is treated as the cost of acquisition and of improvement, and the section says in terms that no indexation benefit is available on it. The CFO's ₹15 crore is his ₹12 crore plus the goodwill he should have dropped.
keywords: a depreciable asset comes in at its written down value
goodwill the company generated itself rather than bought comes in at nil

options.text: ₹12 crore, and indexation is available because the division was held since 2015
options.misconception: assumes indexation follows automatically from a long-term holding, when this section removes it expressly
options.why: A long holding decides that the gain is long-term; it does not decide how the cost is measured. Here the cost is a deemed figure — net worth — and the section states that no indexation benefit is available in relation to it. Indexing ₹12 crore from 2015 would cut the gain by several crore on a cost that was never actually incurred in 2015.

options.text: ₹14 crore, and no indexation is available
options.misconception: drops the goodwill correctly but keeps the plant at its revalued figure, which is the change in value the definition tells you to ignore
options.why: The revaluation is the one adjustment the definition names and excludes, and for a depreciable asset it goes further: the figure to use is the written down value of the block, arrived at under the depreciation provisions, whatever the books have been written up or down to. Taking plant at ₹11 crore inflates net worth by ₹2 crore and reduces the gain by the same amount.

citation.ref: Section 50B(2)(i) read with Explanations 1 and 2 to section 50B — net worth as deemed cost, written down value for depreciable assets, nil for self-generated goodwill and section 35AD assets, and no indexation

items.scenario: Meghna Ltd transfers its castings division, run since 2015, to an unrelated buyer for ₹42 crore, no value being put against any individual asset or liability in the agreement. The deed states ₹15 crore against the land solely so that stamp duty can be worked out. The division's books show plant at a written down value of ₹9 crore against a revalued figure of ₹11 crore, land at ₹6 crore, self-generated goodwill written up to ₹3 crore, current assets ₹7 crore and liabilities ₹10 crore. The CFO computes net worth at ₹15 crore and proposes to index it.

items.stem: What is the capital gain and its tax, and is the filing plan right?

options.text: ₹13 crore long-term, taxed at 12.5 per cent, and the report is in time
options.misconception: takes the rule's first branch as the deemed consideration because it is described as a fair market value, missing that the rule compares two branches and takes the higher
options.why: A figure produced by the first branch is a candidate, not the answer. Rule 11UAE sets out two computations and then says the fair market value is whichever is higher, which stops a seller from being taxed on less than it actually received simply because the undertaking's book assets are modest. Here the cash beats the asset-based figure by ₹17 crore, and using the lower one would understate the gain by exactly that.

options.text: ₹30 crore, but short-term, taxed at slab rates, because the plant inside the division was depreciable
options.misconception: carries the short-term deeming for depreciable assets into a slump sale, where the undertaking is treated as one asset
options.why: A slump sale taxes the undertaking as a single capital asset transferred for one lump sum, and the character of the gain is settled by how long the undertaking was held — more than 36 months makes it long-term, whatever sits inside it. The rule that turns a depreciable asset's gain short-term belongs to an itemised transfer out of a block, which is exactly what a slump sale is not.
keywords: a single capital asset transferred for one lump sum

options.text: ₹33 crore long-term, taxed at 12.5 per cent, and the report is already late
options.misconception: deducts the CFO's original ₹9 crore of net-worth liabilities rather than the net worth itself, mixing the two computations
options.why: Two different liability figures appear in this question and they do different jobs. Net worth uses the book liabilities of the undertaking, ₹10 crore, and produces the deemed cost of ₹12 crore. The rule's own computation uses a different figure, ₹9 crore, because it leaves out provisions for unascertained liabilities. Only the net worth is deducted from the consideration; the rule's liability figure has already done its work inside the first branch.

options.text: ₹30 crore long-term, taxed at 12.5 per cent, and the report is already late by November
options.why: The rule does not stop at its first branch. The deemed consideration is the higher of FMV1, built from the undertaking's own assets and liabilities, and FMV2, which is the fair market value of what the seller actually received. FMV2 here is the monetary consideration of ₹42 crore, which beats FMV1 of ₹25 crore, so ₹42 crore is the full value of consideration. Deducting the net worth of ₹12 crore leaves a long-term gain of ₹30 crore, the division having been held for more than 36 months, and the rate is 12.5 per cent without indexation, giving ₹3.75 crore before surcharge and cess. The accountant's report certifying net worth is due on or before the specified date, being 30 September of the assessment year and one month ahead of the return, so a November filing misses it.
keywords: the higher of FMV1, built from the undertaking's own assets and liabilities, and FMV2
the division having been held for more than 36 months
the rate is 12.5 per cent without indexation
due on or before the specified date, being 30 September of the assessment year

citation.ref: Section 50B(1) and (2)(ii) read with Rule 11UAE and section 50B(3) — the higher of FMV1 and FMV2 as deemed consideration, the 36-month test, the section 112 rate, and the accountant's report by the specified date

items.scenario: Meghna Ltd's castings division again. Net worth is ₹12 crore. The buyer pays ₹42 crore in cash and nothing else. Working the rule, the book value of the assets other than the land comes to ₹19 crore, the stamp duty value of the land is ₹15 crore, and the book liabilities after excluding provisions for unascertained liabilities are ₹9 crore, so the first branch of the rule gives ₹25 crore. The division was held for eleven years. The CFO proposes to take ₹25 crore as the consideration because the rule deems a fair market value, and to file the accountant's report with the return in November.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way Hemant proposes to revise?

options.text: Nothing, other than that a report may be revised only once, so he must check none was issued earlier
options.misconception: invents a cap on the number of revisions, when the rule places none and instead limits the grounds
options.why: There is no limit on how many times a report may be revised. What is limited is why — revision is for technical requirements or amendments in law rather than for second thoughts — and the practical guidance is to make every change needed at one time rather than in instalments. A later court ruling can properly produce a further revision even after that.

options.text: Only the UDIN — the earlier one may be reused, since it identifies the engagement rather than the document
options.misconception: reads the identifier as attaching to the audit as a whole rather than to each signed document
options.why: The number identifies a signed document at a moment in time, which is what makes it useful for checking that a report on a portal is the one the auditor actually signed. A revised report is a different document signed on a different date, so it takes a new one. Reusing September's would make two different reports carry the same identifier.

options.text: The whole plan, because a report once uploaded cannot be revised at all and the payment can only be dealt with in the return
options.misconception: treats the uploaded report as final, missing the express rule that allows revision where a later payment changes a disallowance
options.why: The rule anticipates this exact sequence: the report goes up, then a payment covered by section 40 or section 43B is made before the return is filed, and the disallowance the report computed is no longer right. Leaving the report standing and correcting only the return would put the auditor's certified figures at odds with the computation they were certified for. The deadline that does bind is the one on the first report, which had to go in by the specified date, 30 September of the assessment year, one month ahead of the return; it fixes when the original was due and says nothing against correcting it.
keywords: the specified date, 30 September of the assessment year

options.text: A revised report is not a fresh one — it has to point back at what it replaces, say why, and be signed today with a new number
options.why: The ground for revising is sound: a payment made after the report was furnished which necessitates recalculation of a disallowance under section 40 or section 43B is exactly the case the rule provides for, and the replacement has to reach the department before the relevant assessment year is out. What Hemant has wrong is the form of it. The revised report must carry the reference of the earlier report, state on its face that it is a revised report and give the reason for revision, and be signed on the current date with a new UDIN rather than the one generated in September. A clean form with no back reference is a second report rather than a revision, and it leaves two inconsistent reports on the record with nothing explaining the gap.
keywords: necessitates recalculation of a disallowance under section 40 or section 43B
must carry the reference of the earlier report
signed on the current date with a new UDIN

citation.ref: Rule 6G(3) read with section 44AB and the Guidance Note on Tax Audit — the ground for revision, the assessment-year deadline, the back reference, the reason for revision and a fresh UDIN

items.scenario: Ketki Foods Pvt Ltd is audited under the Companies Act. Its tax audit report went up in September 2026 with a disallowance computed on unpaid statutory dues. In October the company paid ₹30 lakh of those dues, before the return was due. Hemant, the tax auditor, agrees to revise. He proposes to upload a fresh report on a clean form with today's figures, saying that mentioning the earlier report would only invite questions, and to carry across the number he generated when he signed in September.

items.stem: How should the two penalties be worked out?

options.text: Nothing on the trader, since the illness is a complete answer, and ₹10,000 on Hemant
options.misconception: treats reasonable cause as something that operates by itself once the facts are stated, rather than as a defence the person has to establish
options.why: The relief is real but it is not automatic. The person has to prove the cause, and the officer decides whether what is proved explains the whole of the failure. An illness from August might explain missing September but has to be shown to explain the months after recovery as well, and whether another professional could have been instructed is part of that enquiry.

options.text: ₹1,50,000 on the trader and ₹1,50,000 on Hemant, the same penalty applying to whoever caused the default
options.misconception: reads the audit penalty as attaching to the person at fault, when it attaches to the person required to get the audit done
options.why: The audit penalty names the person required to get the accounts audited, and that is the trader whatever the reason for the failure. The accountant's exposure is a separate provision with its own trigger — incorrect information in something he signed — and its own figure of ₹10,000 for each report or certificate. Applying the trader's figure to him borrows a penalty from a provision that does not mention him.

options.text: ₹1,50,000 on the trader, open to a defence, and ₹10,000 on Hemant on the same terms
options.why: The penalty for not getting the accounts audited or not furnishing the report by the specified date is the lower of one-half per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts and ₹1,50,000. Half a per cent of ₹4 crore is ₹2,00,000, so the cap governs and the figure is ₹1,50,000, not the officer's. It is also not automatic: no penalty is imposed where the person proves reasonable cause for the failure, and a long illness of the only accountant instructed is a defence to be made out on the facts rather than asserted. Hemant is not immune either. Section 271J reaches an accountant, a merchant banker or a registered valuer who furnishes incorrect information in a report or certificate, at ₹10,000 for each such report or certificate, levied by the Assessing Officer or the appellate Commissioner who comes across it — and the same reasonable cause defence is open to him.
keywords: the lower of one-half per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts and ₹1,50,000
no penalty is imposed where the person proves reasonable cause for the failure
Section 271J reaches an accountant, a merchant banker or a registered valuer
at ₹10,000 for each such report or certificate

options.text: ₹2,00,000 on the trader as the officer proposes, and nothing on Hemant
options.misconception: applies the half per cent without the cap, and assumes a penalty can only fall on the assessee
options.why: The provision is a lower-of, so the percentage is a ceiling that the fixed figure overtakes as soon as turnover passes ₹3 crore. On ₹4 crore the fixed figure wins. And the Act reaches professionals directly for what they certify; being outside the assessment does not put an accountant outside every penalty in the Act.

citation.ref: Section 271B read with section 273B, and section 271J — the lower-of penalty for a missing tax audit report, the reasonable cause defence, and the accountant's liability for incorrect information

items.scenario: A sole trader with turnover of ₹4 crore never furnished a tax audit report for the year. His accountant of eleven years fell seriously ill in August and was in hospital until December, and no other professional was instructed. Separately, Hemant has furnished one certificate to the department carrying a figure that turns out to be incorrect. The officer proposes ₹2,00,000 on the trader, being half a per cent of turnover, and says nothing can be charged on Hemant because he is not the assessee.

items.stem: Which month does each of the two supplies belong to?

options.text: The first on 15 May and the second on 30 May, since tax on a service falls due when the money is received
options.misconception: reads GST on services as payable on receipt, when payment is only one of two competing dates and is usually the later one
options.why: Payment matters, but only as one arm of a comparison. Under forward charge the supplier accounts for the tax when the earlier event happens, and on both of these assignments the money was the later event. A supplier who waits for the money pays late on every job that is billed before it is paid.

options.text: Both belong to April — the first on 25 April and the second on 10 April
options.why: Section 31 gives a supplier thirty days from the day a service is finished in which to raise its bill, and section 13(2) treats that window as a fork. The first bill went out on 25 April, inside the window, so the earlier of bill and money governs and the time of supply is 25 April. The second went out on 20 May, outside it, so the late invoice is set aside and the other arm of the fork applies: the earlier of the date of provision of the service and the date of payment, which puts the time of supply at 10 April. Both belong to April, and on the second the tax was already overdue by the time anybody wrote the bill.
keywords: thirty days from the day a service is finished
the earlier of bill and money governs and the time of supply is 25 April
the late invoice is set aside
the earlier of the date of provision of the service and the date of payment, which puts the time of supply at 10 April

options.text: Both on 10 April, because the time of supply of a service is the day the service was provided
options.misconception: makes the date of provision the general rule, when it is the fallback that applies only where the invoice missed its window
options.why: The day the work was done is not the ordinary test at all. Where the bill was raised in time the section never reaches the provision date; it compares bill with money and takes whichever came first. Making provision the general rule would tax the first assignment on 10 April, a fortnight before anything was billed or paid.

options.text: The first on 25 April and the second on 20 May, since in each case it is the bill that fixes the tax point
options.misconception: treats a late invoice as still fixing the time of supply, when missing the window is the very thing that switches the test
options.why: A bill raised outside the window does not stop being a bill, but it loses its power to set the tax point. The section reaches for the invoice date only where the invoice was raised in time; once it was not, the law looks past it to the day the work was done. Reading the second bill as the tax point pushes an April liability into May and leaves April short.

citation.ref: Section 13(2) read with section 31 and rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017 — the two arms of the forward charge test for services

items.scenario: Nivedita & Co., a firm of consultants registered in Bengaluru, finished two assignments for the same client on 10 April 2026. It billed the first on 25 April and was paid for it on 15 May. It billed the second on 20 May and was paid on 30 May. Its accountant has put both supplies in the May return, on the footing that a supply is taxed when its bill goes out.

items.stem: What is the time of supply of the ₹50,000, and is the relief available?

options.text: The day in July on which the training is actually delivered
options.misconception: reads the time of supply as the day the service happens, which is only the fallback arm and only where the invoice window was missed
options.why: The day the work is done enters the test only when the bill was raised outside its window. Nothing here has missed a window yet; what has happened is that money came in first, and money received before both the bill and the work fixes the tax point on its own.

options.text: 1 June, and the relief the accountant is relying on does not reach a service
options.why: Money taken before a bill is raised fixes the time of supply for the amount taken, so the ₹50,000 is an advance received for a service and its time of supply is 1 June — the day it was entered in the books or credited to the bank, whichever came first. The relief the accountant has in mind was given by notification for goods and not for services, so a trainer holding a client's retainer through June has a June liability whatever the bill later says.
keywords: the ₹50,000 is an advance received for a service and its time of supply is 1 June
given by notification for goods and not for services
Money taken before a bill is raised fixes the time of supply for the amount taken

options.text: Nothing is due until the programme is delivered, because a retainer is a deposit rather than consideration
options.misconception: treats a retainer as a refundable deposit outside the charge, when it was taken against an identified service
options.why: A deposit is money the supplier may have to give back and which is not applied to any particular supply. This ₹50,000 was taken against a named programme for a named client and will be set against its price, so it is consideration received in advance and it carries a tax point of its own.

options.text: 31 July, the date of the invoice for the programme
options.misconception: treats the invoice as the only tax point a service can have, when money received first takes that place to the extent of the money
options.why: The invoice date wins only where it is the earlier of the two events. Here the client's money arrived seven weeks before any bill, so the comparison is settled before the invoice exists. Taxing on 31 July would let any supplier defer tax on a retainer simply by billing late.

citation.ref: Section 13(2) — advance received against a service — read with the notified relief for advances that is confined to goods

items.scenario: Rohan Tutorials, registered in Pune, takes ₹50,000 from a corporate client on 1 June 2026 as a retainer for a training programme to be delivered in July and billed on 31 July. The money is entered in Rohan's books and credited to its bank on the same day. Its accountant points to the relief that lets a supplier ignore money taken before the invoice, and proposes to show nothing in the June return.

items.stem: How is each of the two extra amounts timed?

options.text: Both on 20 August, the day the customer's money for the invoice was received
options.misconception: gathers every receipt from one customer to one date, when interest for delayed payment carries a tax point tied to its own receipt
options.why: Interest for late payment is not part of the payment for the invoice it relates to. It is an addition to value that arises later and is taxed on the day it comes in, which here is more than a month after the invoice was settled.

options.text: The ₹800 must be taxed on 20 August as an advance, and the ₹2,000 on 30 September
options.misconception: reads a small overpayment as an ordinary advance, missing that the proviso hands the supplier a choice on amounts up to a thousand rupees
options.why: Ordinarily money received ahead of the bill does fix the tax point, and that is why this proviso exists. It carves a narrow exception for small sums received over an invoiced amount so that a utility billing thousands of customers need not chase every stray rupee. Taxing on 20 August is not wrong in principle; it is simply not the only choice the supplier has.

options.text: The ₹2,000 goes into the return for the month of the bill it relates to, by revising that month's figures
options.misconception: relates the interest back to the supply that produced it, when the section fixes its time of supply at receipt precisely to avoid that
options.why: The whole reason interest has a rule of its own is that nobody knows at the time of the original supply whether it will ever be charged or paid. Fixing its time of supply at receipt keeps the earlier return alone, and reopening that return is exactly what the provision is designed to prevent.

options.text: The ₹800 may be timed to the bill raised for it, and the ₹2,000 is timed to the day it arrives
options.why: A supplier who receives up to ₹1,000 more than the amount billed is not forced to treat that money as an advance: the proviso gives the supplier an option to take instead the date of the invoice raised for the excess, which is what keeps small overpayments on utility bills out of the return in which they happen to land. The ₹2,000 is a different animal. Interest charged for late payment is an addition to the value of the supply, and its time of supply is the day the supplier receives it, 30 September.
keywords: receives up to ₹1,000 more than the amount billed
the proviso gives the supplier an option
its time of supply is the day the supplier receives it, 30 September

citation.ref: Proviso to section 13(2) on excess received up to one thousand rupees, and section 13(6) on interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment

items.scenario: Shreya Utilities bills a customer ₹1,00,000 on 5 August 2026. The customer pays ₹1,00,800 on 20 August — ₹800 more than the bill — and the extra is left to be set against the next month's bill. The same customer separately pays ₹2,000 of interest for having settled an earlier bill late, and that money reaches Shreya on 30 September.

items.stem: What rate does each of the two jobs carry?

options.text: Both carry the higher rate, because both jobs were done before the change
options.misconception: treats the date of supply as deciding the rate, when the section never uses the date of supply as the time of supply
options.why: The date of supply sorts a case into one of two groups; it is not itself the answer. Within each group the section then picks between the bill and the money. On the first job neither of those fell before the change, so nothing keeps the old rate alive on it.

options.text: The first carries the lower rate and the second carries the higher one
options.why: Section 14 overrides sections 12 and 13 whenever the rate moves, and it sorts a transaction by where the supply, the bill and the money each sit against the day of the change. Both jobs were done before it. On the first, bill and money both came afterwards, so the earlier of those two governs: the time of supply is 25 September and the new rate of 5 per cent applies. On the second, the bill went out before the change and only the money came after, so what fixes the timing is the date of the invoice, 15 September, and the old rate of 18 per cent applies even though the money arrived under the new one.
keywords: Section 14 overrides sections 12 and 13 whenever the rate moves
the time of supply is 25 September and the new rate of 5 per cent applies
what fixes the timing is the date of the invoice, 15 September, and the old rate of 18 per cent

options.text: The first carries the higher rate and the second the lower one, the other way round
options.misconception: swaps the two limbs, applying the invoice date where both events followed the change and the earlier-of test where only one did
options.why: The limb that names the invoice date is the one where the invoice itself preceded the change — that is the second job, not the first. The earlier-of test belongs to the case where both bill and money came afterwards, which is the first. Reversing them gets both rates wrong in one stroke.

options.text: Both carry the lower rate, as the software charged
options.misconception: fixes the rate by the date the money came in, when payment is only one of three markers and counts only when it falls on the same side as the bill
options.why: Money is one marker of three, and it decides the answer only in the combinations where the section says so. Here the second job has its bill on the old side of the change, and that is enough to keep the old rate on it whatever day the money arrived. Charging the customer less than the law asks leaves the supplier to fund the difference.

citation.ref: Section 14(a)(i) and 14(a)(ii) — supply before a change in the rate of tax, with the invoice and the payment falling on either side

items.scenario: The rate of tax on the service Ananya Diagnostics supplies fell from 18 per cent to 5 per cent with effect from 22 September 2025. Two jobs were both carried out on 10 September. The first was billed on 25 September and paid on 30 September. The second was billed on 15 September and paid on 30 September. Ananya's billing software charged the lower rate on both, on the ground that the money for both came in after the change.

items.stem: What is the time of supply of each of these two jobs?

options.text: 15 September for both, the date on which each was billed
options.misconception: applies the invoice date because the invoice came first, when the section asks which markers fall on which side of the change rather than which happened earliest
options.why: An early bill fixes the timing only in the combinations where the section says it does, and this is not one of them. Here the supply itself came after the change, so the bill sits alone on the old side and the law looks to the money instead. Treating the bill as decisive would let any supplier pre-empt a rate cut by invoicing early.

options.text: 10 October for both, the day the work was actually done
options.misconception: falls back on the date of supply, which sorts a case into a group but is never itself the time of supply under this section
options.why: Not one of the six combinations in the section ends with the date of supply as the answer. It is the fact that decides which pair of markers to compare, and the answer is always the bill, the money, or the earlier of the two.

options.text: 30 September for the third and 29 September for the fourth
options.why: Both jobs were supplied after the change and billed before it. Where that is the shape and the money follows the change, the marker that counts is the date of receipt of payment, so the third has a time of supply of 30 September and the early bill does not carry the old rate forward. The fourth looks as though it was paid on 18 September, but the proviso substitutes the credit in the bank account whenever that credit lands more than four working days after the day the rate changed. 29 September is well past that, so the payment is treated as received on 29 September and the same limb applies to it.
keywords: the marker that counts is the date of receipt of payment, so the third has a time of supply of 30 September
the credit in the bank account whenever that credit lands more than four working days after the day the rate changed
the payment is treated as received on 29 September

options.text: 30 September for the third and 18 September for the fourth
options.misconception: uses the ordinary meaning of receipt of payment for the fourth and misses the proviso that displaces it around a change in rate
options.why: Ordinarily the earlier of the books entry and the bank credit is the date of receipt, and 18 September would be right. Around a change in the rate that ordinary meaning gives way: where the bank credit comes well after the day of change, it is the bank credit that counts, and the books entry drops out.

citation.ref: Section 14(b)(i) — supply after a change in the rate of tax — with the proviso on credit in the bank account after four working days

items.scenario: The same rate change applies — 18 per cent down to 5 per cent from 22 September 2025. Two further jobs were both carried out on 10 October and both billed in advance on 15 September. The third job was paid for on 30 September. On the fourth the customer's money was entered in the supplier's books on 18 September but was credited to the supplier's bank only on 29 September. The supplier proposes to treat the fourth as paid on 18 September.

items.stem: Which of the two credits, if either, may Girija take?

options.text: Both, because each is used in the course of the company's taxable business
options.misconception: treats business use as the test, when the construction clauses apply precisely to property that is used in the business
options.why: Business use is what makes a credit arguable in the first place; it is never what rescues one from these clauses. Every office block a company builds for itself is used in its business, and the clause is written to catch exactly that. What decides the kiln is its character as plant and machinery, not the use it is put to.

options.text: Neither, because both amounts were capitalised
options.misconception: reads capitalisation as what triggers the bar, when it is what extends the bar to repairs and renovation rather than what creates it
options.why: Capitalisation matters at the other end of the rule. It is the test for whether work on an existing building counts as construction at all. It does not decide whether the thing built is plant and machinery, and a capitalised kiln is as much plant and machinery as an uncapitalised one would be.

options.text: Neither, as the accountant says
options.misconception: reads the works contract bar as absolute, missing that the clause itself excepts construction of plant and machinery
options.why: The clause does not say "every immovable property". It says immovable property other than plant and machinery, and the explanation to the section then tells you what falls inside that exception. Machinery anchored to the floor of a factory and used to make what the business sells is the paradigm case, not a borderline one.

options.text: The kiln's credit may be taken; the office block's may not
options.why: The bar on works contract services stops where the immovable property being built is plant and machinery, and the explanation to section 17 says what that covers — apparatus, equipment or machinery fixed to earth by foundation or by structural support and put to use in making outward supplies, while keeping land, buildings and other civil structures out of it. A kiln bolted to a concrete base answers that description, so the works contract for it escapes the bar and the credit is available. An office block is a building and nothing more, so the credit on it is blocked.
keywords: the works contract for it escapes the bar and the credit is available
apparatus, equipment or machinery fixed to earth by foundation or by structural support
An office block is a building and nothing more, so the credit on it is blocked

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) with the explanation to section 17 defining plant and machinery

items.scenario: Girija Ceramics engages a works contractor to bolt a new kiln to a concrete foundation inside its factory, and in the same month engages a second works contractor to put up a two-storey office block on the same plot. Both amounts are capitalised. Its accountant claims neither credit, reading section 17(5) as shutting out every works contract that ends in something immovable.

items.stem: What is the position on the two amounts?

options.text: Both credits are available, because repairs and additions to an existing building are not construction at all
options.misconception: reads construction as putting up something new, when the definition expressly reaches renovation and additions once they are capitalised
options.why: If construction meant only new building, a company could gut and rebuild a property floor by floor and claim every rupee. The definition closes that road by naming re-construction, renovation, additions, alterations and repairs, and then limiting itself to the capitalised part of them.

options.text: Neither credit is available, as the consultant advises
options.misconception: reads any spending on an immovable property as construction, ignoring the words that tie the extension to capitalisation
options.why: The extension of "construction" is not open-ended. It reaches repairs and renovation only so far as they are capitalised, which is a deliberate line: money that goes through the profit and loss account has not added to the property and is not treated as building it.

options.text: The roof is blocked and the mezzanine is available, because a repair restores the building while an addition creates a separate asset
options.misconception: inverts the test, treating the accounting treatment as beside the point when it is the very thing the clause turns on
options.why: The clause does not ask whether the work restored something or added something. It asks how much of the cost was capitalised to the immovable property, and on those facts the answer is all of the mezzanine and none of the roof.

options.text: The credit on the roof is available; the credit on the mezzanine is not
options.why: Construction, for both limbs of the bar, is widened to take in re-construction, renovation, additions, alterations and repairs, but only to the extent of capitalisation to the immovable property. A repair charged to the profit and loss account is not capitalised, so it never becomes construction for this purpose and the bar has nothing to bite on. The mezzanine is an addition that was capitalised, so it is construction and the credit on it is shut out.
keywords: but only to the extent of capitalisation to the immovable property
A repair charged to the profit and loss account is not capitalised

citation.ref: Explanation to section 17(5)(c) and (d) on what construction includes and the extent of capitalisation

items.scenario: Vidhi Foods spends two amounts on its factory building in one year: ₹25 lakh re-laying a leaking roof, which its auditors require to be charged to the profit and loss account, and ₹15 lakh adding a mezzanine floor, which is capitalised. Its consultant advises that section 17(5) blocks the credit on both, since both are work done on an immovable property.

items.stem: What are the free on board value and the freight to be added?

options.why: Everything spent to bring the goods to the point at which they leave the exporting country belongs in the free on board value, so the inland leg to Osaka airport and the handling there join the ex-factory price — US $9,000 plus $400 plus $100 gives an FOB value of US $9,500. The flight is then added as the cost of bringing the goods to the place of importation, but on an import by air where that cost is known the rule caps it at 20 per cent of the free on board value. Twenty per cent of US $9,500 is US $1,900, so US $1,100 of what the airline charged never enters the value at all.
keywords: gives an FOB value of US $9,500
the rule caps it at 20 per cent of the free on board value
Twenty per cent of US $9,500 is US $1,900

options.misconception: builds the free on board value correctly but then adds the real freight, forgetting that the ceiling on air imports applies even when the actual figure is known and documented
options.why: The ceiling is not a fallback for when the freight cannot be found. It is a limit that operates precisely where the cost IS ascertainable, and it exists because air freight on a small heavy consignment can dwarf the goods. A documented US $3,000 is admitted only so far as the ceiling allows.

options.misconception: applies the twenty per cent to the ex-factory price instead of to the free on board value the rule names
options.why: The ceiling is a proportion of the free on board value, and the free on board value here is US $9,500 rather than US $9,000. Taking twenty per cent of the ex-factory price understates the freight by US $100 and carries the same error into the duty.

options.text: US $9,000 and US $3,000, as the clerk has taken them
options.misconception: treats the ex-factory price as the free on board value and the actual air freight as always includible, missing both the pre-shipment costs and the ceiling
options.why: Two things are wrong at once. The ex-factory price is not the free on board value — the costs of getting the goods to the airport of loading and handling them there are part of delivering them to the point of export and go in. And on an air import the actual freight is not taken as it stands; it is admitted only up to a ceiling.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2) — cost of transport to the place of importation, and the proviso capping it at twenty per cent of the free on board value for goods imported by air

items.scenario: Tanvi Instruments imports a testing rig by air from Osaka. The exporter's ex-factory price is US $9,000. Tanvi paid US $400 to move the rig from the factory to Osaka airport and US $100 for handling it there. The airline charged US $3,000 for the flight to Delhi. The clerk preparing the bill of entry has taken US $9,000 as the free on board value and added the airline's US $3,000 in full.

items.stem: What is the assessable value?

options.misconception: leaves insurance out altogether because no policy exists, when an unascertainable insurance cost is supplied by the rule rather than dropped
options.why: The absence of a document is the trigger for the rule, not an excuse from it. Where the insurance cost cannot be ascertained, a figure is deemed at a fixed proportion of the free on board value, which is why the rule exists at all. Dropping it understates the value by US $106.875 and every duty computed on it.

options.misconception: carries the airline's actual charge into the value instead of the capped figure
options.why: The whole point of the air freight ceiling is that the real charge is not what enters the value. Using US $3,000 in place of US $1,900 adds more than ninety thousand rupees of value that the rule keeps out, and it does so on the one mode of transport for which the limit was written.

options.misconception: adds the post-arrival unloading and inland carriage into the value and converts at the RBI reference rate
options.why: Two errors compound here. The place of importation is where the goods are brought for clearance, so unloading at Delhi airport and the road leg to Jaipur both fall outside the value. And where the customs law gives a rate of exchange, it is the rate notified under that law that governs, not a banking reference rate quoted the same day.

Where the insurance cost cannot be established the rule supplies one: insurance at 1.125 per cent of the free on board value, which is US $106.875 on an FOB of US $9,500. Nothing spent once the goods have arrived goes in, so costs after the goods reach the Indian airport are excluded — that covers both the unloading there and the run to Jaipur, the one per cent notional loading having gone in 2017. What is left is US $9,500 plus $1,900 plus $106.875, or US $11,506.875, converted at the rate the CBIC notified and not the RBI reference rate, giving an assessable value of ₹9,66,578.
keywords: insurance at 1.125 per cent of the free on board value, which is US $106.875
costs after the goods reach the Indian airport are excluded
converted at the rate the CBIC notified and not the RBI reference rate

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2) proviso on insurance at 1.125 per cent of the free on board value, read with section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 on the rate of exchange

items.scenario: On the same import, Tanvi's free on board value is settled at US $9,500 and the freight to be added at US $1,900. No insurance document exists. Tanvi paid ₹5,000 for unloading at Delhi airport and ₹12,000 to truck the rig to its plant in Jaipur. On the day the bill of entry was presented the rate of exchange notified by the CBIC was ₹84 to the dollar and the RBI reference rate was ₹83.50. Tanvi's consultant wants to add the two rupee amounts and convert the total at ₹83.50.

items.stem: What can Aarti expect, and when?

options.text: Nothing until the final order, since a refund is sanctioned only once
options.misconception: does not know the provisional route exists, and treats every refund as a single sanction at the end of verification
options.why: Exporters would be financing the department for months if that were so, which is why the Act carves out zero-rated claims for early release. A provisional sanction and a final one are two orders on the same claim, and the first is due long before the second.

options.text: Most of the money on a provisional basis within a week of the acknowledgement, with the balance on the final order
options.why: A claim on account of zero-rated supplies carries a provisional route: the officer may release 90 per cent of the amount claimed ahead of the final settlement of the claim. The rule now ties that release to the system's own identification and evaluation of risk and requires the provisional order within seven days of the acknowledgement, so the bulk of an exporter's money is not made to wait on the invoice check at all. Only the remainder follows the final order.
keywords: the officer may release 90 per cent of the amount claimed ahead of the final settlement
requires the provisional order within seven days of the acknowledgement

options.text: The whole amount within seven days, since the rule fixes a seven-day clock on the claim
options.misconception: reads the seven-day clock as covering the entire claim, when it governs only a provisional release of a fixed proportion of it
options.why: The clock and the proportion are two different limits and both apply. Seven days is how long the officer has to make the provisional order; a fixed share of the claim is how much that order may release. The rest waits for verification, and there is a separate and longer limit for that.

options.text: Most of the money, but only after the officer has verified the documents supporting the claim
options.misconception: puts the provisional release after verification, which is the one thing it is designed to come before
options.why: A release that waited for verification would not be provisional at all — it would be the final order under another name. The sequence in the section is release first on a risk view, examine afterwards, settle at the end.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) read with rule 91(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted with effect from 1 October 2025

items.scenario: Aarti Exports files a refund claim in November 2026 for unutilised credit on garments exported under a letter of undertaking. It has completed Aadhaar authentication and supplies nothing on any restricted list. Its finance head has budgeted on receiving the whole amount only once the department has finished examining the invoices, which he expects to take some months.

items.stem: Which of the two gets a provisional release?

options.text: Bela only, because cotton yarn is on no restricted list
options.misconception: knows the list of goods but treats Aadhaar authentication as a registration formality rather than a condition of the provisional route
options.why: Clean goods are not enough. Authentication is written into the same notification as a condition of early release, so a claimant who has not done it is outside the provisional route no matter what it exports.

options.text: Harsh only, because it has completed the Aadhaar authentication
options.misconception: knows the authentication condition but not the separate list of goods whose suppliers are excluded whatever their authentication status
options.why: Authentication is one of two gates and passing it settles only half the question. The notification also names goods, and a supplier of one of them is outside the provisional route however complete its own compliance is.

options.text: Both, since the exclusion goes to the refund itself and not to the provisional stage
options.misconception: reads the notification as denying the refund altogether, when what it denies is only the early release
options.why: Nothing in the notification takes away the refund. Both claimants may still be paid in full; what they lose is the right to have most of it released before verification, which is a question of timing rather than of entitlement.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: The Government has notified two classes of person who are kept out of the provisional route altogether — anyone who has not completed Aadhaar authentication under rule 10B, and anyone supplying areca nuts, pan masala, tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes, or essential oils. Harsh is caught by what it exports and Bela by the authentication it has not done, so each claim goes only by the final order and neither sees money early.
keywords: anyone who has not completed Aadhaar authentication under rule 10B
anyone supplying areca nuts, pan masala, tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes, or essential oils
each claim goes only by the final order

citation.ref: Section 54(6) and the notification of 17 September 2025 listing the classes of registered person not allowed refund on a provisional basis

items.scenario: Two refund claims land on the same officer's desk in November 2026, both for unutilised credit on exports made under a letter of undertaking. Harsh Traders exports areca nuts and has completed Aadhaar authentication. Bela Overseas exports cotton yarn and has not completed Aadhaar authentication. Both ask when the provisional money will reach them.

items.stem: What is the answer to each question?

options.text: Two months counted from the day the claim was uploaded, whether or not the papers were complete, and no certificate is needed
options.misconception: starts the clock at upload, when the period runs from a complete application and the acknowledgement is what marks it
options.why: The period is tied to an application complete in all respects, and the acknowledgement is the document that records when that happened. A claim uploaded with papers missing has not started the clock, which is why the acknowledgement rather than the upload is the reference point.

options.text: Two months from a complete application, and no certificate is needed on this class of claim
options.why: The final order is to be made within sixty days of receipt of the application complete in all respects, counted from the date shown on the acknowledgement. On the second question, a refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax is one of the cases the Act pays straight to the applicant instead of routing it to the Consumer Welfare Fund, so Aarti does not have to show that the burden was not passed on and needs no certificate to that effect.
keywords: within sixty days of receipt of the application complete in all respects
instead of routing it to the Consumer Welfare Fund
does not have to show that the burden was not passed on

options.text: Three months from a complete application, and a certificate is needed because the claim is above ₹2 lakh
options.misconception: uses the wrong statutory clock and applies the unjust enrichment test to a claim the Act expressly takes out of it
options.why: Both halves are wrong. The Act sets a shorter period than three months for the refund order, and the ₹2 lakh threshold governs only claims on which the test of unjust enrichment runs at all. On a claim for unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies it never runs.

options.text: Two months from a complete application, but a certificate is still needed because the claim exceeds ₹2 lakh
options.misconception: applies the ₹2 lakh threshold as though it were general, missing that the test it belongs to does not reach this class of claim
options.why: The threshold decides only HOW a claimant proves the burden was not passed on — a self-declaration below it, a certificate above it. It never decides WHETHER he has to prove it. On a claim the Act lists as payable to the applicant, there is nothing to prove and no document to produce.

citation.ref: Section 54(7) on the time limit for the refund order and section 54(8)(b) on refunds paid to the applicant rather than credited to the Fund

items.scenario: Aarti Exports, whose claim is for unutilised credit on garments exported without payment of tax under a letter of undertaking, asks two further questions. How long has the department to decide the claim, and must Aarti produce a chartered accountant's certificate showing that it did not recover the tax from anybody, given that the claim is well above ₹2 lakh?

items.stem: For what amount is the bond written, and must there be one per consignment?

options.text: ₹6,00,000, the duty itself, with a fresh bond for every consignment
options.misconception: reads the bond as security for the duty alone, and does not know that a single approved bond can stand behind a year of imports
options.why: Three times the duty is the figure because the importer's exposure is not the duty alone — it can reach the duty, a penalty of the same size, and fine and interest on top of both. And a fresh bond per consignment is not required where a general bond is in place: against such a bond a running account is kept, debited as goods go into the warehouse and credited as they come out on payment of duty.
keywords: the importer's exposure is not the duty alone
a running account is kept, debited as goods go into the warehouse

options.text: ₹12,00,000, twice the duty, with a general bond permitted
options.misconception: remembers that the bond is a multiple of the duty but takes the wrong multiple
options.why: Twice the duty would cover the duty and a penalty of the same size and leave nothing for fine and interest, which is why the Act asks for three times rather than two. The general bond half of the answer is right; the amount is not.

options.text: ₹18,00,000, and a single bond approved for the year can cover every consignment in it
options.why: The bond under section 59 is written for three times the duty assessed, so on a duty of ₹6,00,000 it is a bond for ₹18,00,000, by which the importer binds itself to obey the Act in respect of those goods, to pay the duty and the interest on or before the date a demand notice names, and to pay any fine or penalty incurred. It need not be one per consignment either: the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner may approve a general bond covering everything the importer warehouses over a stated period, and security may be asked for on top of it.
keywords: approve a general bond covering everything the importer warehouses over a stated period

options.text: ₹18,00,000, but a separate bond is required for each consignment
options.misconception: has the multiple right and misses the general bond, so treats every consignment as needing its own instrument
options.why: The multiple is right and the second half is not. The Act allows a consignment bond or a general bond, and the general bond is the ordinary arrangement for a regular importer precisely so that paperwork does not have to be repeated every month.

citation.ref: Section 59 — the warehousing bond in a sum equal to thrice the duty assessed, and the general bond approved for a specified period

items.scenario: Vishal Imports files a bill of entry for warehousing on goods assessed to duty of ₹6,00,000. It expects to warehouse consignments of a similar kind every month for the coming year and asks whether it must execute a fresh paper each time. Its manager has assumed the bond will be written for the duty on the consignment.

items.stem: What can Vishal give up, and at what cost?

options.text: Neither, because duty attached to the goods when they were deposited in the warehouse
options.misconception: thinks the duty crystallises on deposit, when warehousing is what defers it and relinquishment before clearance ends the liability
options.why: Warehousing exists to postpone the duty until the goods are taken out for home consumption. That is why the window for giving up title runs until the clearance order and not until deposit — before the order there is no home consumption and no duty to pay.

options.text: Both lots, since giving up title is a right of the owner
options.misconception: treats relinquishment as unqualified, when the Act withholds it exactly where an offence is in the picture
options.why: If it were unqualified, an importer facing a mis-declaration case could abandon the evidence and the duty together. The Act blocks that: goods about which an offence appears to have been committed cannot be given up, and the investigation runs its course with the duty still standing.

options.text: The first lot, but duty is still payable on it and only the interest stops running
options.misconception: reads relinquishment as stopping the interest clock rather than as ending the duty liability itself
options.why: Relinquishment does more than stop interest. The Act says the owner shall not be liable to pay duty on goods he has relinquished, which is the whole reason an importer would use it. What he must still meet are the penalties payable on the goods.

options.text: The first lot only, on paying any penalties due on it, after which no duty is payable on it
options.why: The owner of warehoused goods may relinquish title to them at any moment before an order for clearance for home consumption is made, upon paying whatever penalties are payable in respect of the goods, and once he has done so he is not liable to duty on them. The door is shut on the second lot: the right is withheld where an offence appears to have been committed in respect of the goods, and a mis-declared description under investigation is exactly that case.
keywords: may relinquish title to them at any moment before an order for clearance for home consumption is made
the right is withheld where an offence appears to have been committed in respect of the goods

citation.ref: Proviso to section 68 — relinquishment of title to warehoused goods before an order for clearance for home consumption

items.scenario: Vishal Imports cannot sell one warehoused lot and would rather walk away from it than pay duty on it. No order for its clearance has been made and nothing improper is alleged about it. A second lot is under investigation because its description on the bill of entry appears to have been mis-declared, and Vishal would like to give that one up as well.

items.stem: What may the proper officer do about the two lots?

options.text: Cancel the bond and recover from whoever gave the security, before touching the goods
options.misconception: treats the bond as the only road to recovery, when the section gives the officer a direct demand against the owner and a power of sale
options.why: The bond is a backstop, not the first step. The section puts the demand on the owner and, on default, lets the officer sell goods in the warehouse to satisfy it. A bond is cancelled when the goods it covers have been accounted for, which is the opposite of this situation.

options.text: Wait for the quarter, since a demand of this kind has to be preceded by a show cause notice and an adjudication
options.misconception: imports the ordinary adjudication machinery into a section where the demand is immediate and the notice comes only before sale
options.why: The section is written for goods that have already gone wrong inside a bonded system, and it makes the demand payable at once. The only notice it requires is the one before the officer sells goods to recover, and that is a different step from a show cause notice on the demand itself.

options.text: Demand the whole duty with interest, fine and penalties at once, and on default sell enough of Vishal's warehoused goods after giving notice
options.why: Warehoused goods may leave only for home consumption, for export or for another warehouse — section 71 allows nothing else — and a removal outside those is one of the cases in section 72, as is a lot still in the warehouse once its permitted period has ended. In each of them the officer may demand the full duty together with the interest, fine and penalties payable on the goods, and the owner has to pay it forthwith rather than at a time that suits its cash flow. Where it does not, the officer may, after giving the owner notice, detain and sell as much of the owner's goods lying in the warehouse as will cover the amount.
keywords: the owner has to pay it forthwith
detain and sell as much of the owner's goods lying in the warehouse

options.text: Act on the removed lot only, since the other lot never left the warehouse
options.misconception: reads the section as being about physical removal alone, and misses the limb that catches goods still lying there after the period expires
options.why: Overstaying is a case in its own right. Goods left in a warehouse after the permitted period are treated no differently from goods taken out improperly, because in both the deferral the warehouse gave has come to an end without the duty being paid.

citation.ref: Section 71 on permitted removals and section 72 on goods improperly removed or not removed within the permitted period

items.scenario: Two more of Vishal's lots go wrong. Its staff move one out of the warehouse without any clearance having been given. The other is still sitting in the warehouse when the period it was permitted to remain there runs out. Vishal offers to pay the duty on both when its next quarter's collections come in.

items.stem: Is the appeal in time, and if not can it still be admitted?

options.text: It is out of time by twenty days, counted from the date the order was passed
options.misconception: starts the clock at signature rather than at communication, which shortens every appeal period by the time the order takes to arrive
options.why: An appellant cannot be expected to appeal an order he has not seen, which is why the period runs from communication. Counting from 20 March takes a week off the company's time and would have the same effect on every order the department is slow to serve.

options.text: It is in time, because the extra month is available as of right and the appeal was filed within four months
options.misconception: reads the further month as an extension of the limitation period rather than as a discretion that has to be asked for and justified
options.why: The further month is not added to the period; it is a window in which the Authority MAY admit an appeal that is already late. The appellant has to satisfy it that the delay had a good reason, and an appeal filed inside that window without an explanation can still be refused.

options.text: It is out of time and beyond saving, as counsel advises
options.misconception: treats the three-month period as absolute, missing the further month within which the Authority may condone a delay
options.why: The period is not a cliff. The Authority has a discretion to take a late appeal within one further month where it is satisfied the delay had sufficient cause, and thirteen days sits comfortably inside that. Advice that the right is lost gives up a remedy the statute provides.

options.text: It is out of time by thirteen days, but the Appellate Authority may still admit it on cause shown
options.why: The three months run from the day the order was communicated to the appellant, not the day it was signed, so the clock started on 27 March 2026 and ran out on 27 June 2026. An appeal lodged on 10 July is thirteen days past that. The section then gives the Appellate Authority a further one month within which it may admit a late appeal if it is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay, so what Suhani needs is an application explaining the thirteen days, not a fresh strategy.
keywords: the day the order was communicated to the appellant
the clock started on 27 March 2026 and ran out on 27 June 2026

citation.ref: Section 107(1) on three months from communication of the order and section 107(4) on condonation within a further month

items.scenario: An adjudication order against Suhani Chemicals, registered in Maharashtra, is passed on 20 March 2026 and communicated to the company on 27 March 2026. Suhani files its appeal to the Appellate Authority on 10 July 2026. Its counsel counts three months from the day the order was passed, tells the board the appeal is three weeks out of time, and advises that nothing can be done about it.

items.stem: What are the two pre-deposits?

options.text: ₹3,93,000 on the first appeal and ₹50,000 on the second
options.misconception: applies the ten per cent to disputed interest and penalty as well, when the sub-section confines that component to tax
options.why: The sub-section names the remaining amount of TAX in dispute. Disputed interest of ₹50,000 and disputed penalty of ₹80,000 attract no pre-deposit at all, which is why the figure stops at ₹3,80,000. Adding them in overpays by ₹13,000 and misstates the rule for every later appeal.

options.text: ₹3,80,000 and ₹50,000, but the department may go on recovering the balance while the appeal is pending
options.misconception: treats the pre-deposit as an admission fee, when paying it is what suspends recovery of everything still in dispute
options.why: The two figures are right and the consequence is not. Once the pre-deposit is paid, recovery of the balance of the demand in dispute is deemed stayed until the appeal is disposed of. That stay is the commercial reason to pay rather than to argue about paying.
keywords: recovery of the balance of the demand in dispute is deemed stayed

options.text: ₹4,10,000 on the first appeal and ₹2,00,000 on the second
options.misconception: applies the ten per cent to the whole tax rather than to the disputed remainder, and treats the e-way bill penalty as payable in full before an appeal
options.why: The ten per cent bites only on what is left in dispute after the admitted tax has been paid, so it is ten per cent of ₹5 lakh and not of ₹8 lakh. And the proviso on a section 129(3) order asks for a quarter of the penalty, not the whole of it; requiring the whole would make the appeal pointless.

options.text: ₹3,80,000 on the first appeal and ₹50,000 on the second
options.why: Two amounts go in before the first appeal can be filed. First, the whole of the tax, interest, fine, fee and penalty the appellant admits, which is ₹3,30,000 here. Second, ten per cent of the tax still in dispute, which is 10 per cent of ₹5 lakh, or ₹50,000. The two together make ₹3,80,000, and nothing at all is deposited against the disputed interest or the disputed penalty. The e-way bill order has its own proviso, which asks for a sum equal to 25 per cent of the penalty, ₹50,000 on a penalty of ₹2 lakh.
keywords: the whole of the tax, interest, fine, fee and penalty the appellant admits
ten per cent of the tax still in dispute, which is 10 per cent of ₹5 lakh
a sum equal to 25 per cent of the penalty, ₹50,000 on a penalty of ₹2 lakh

citation.ref: Section 107(6) — the admitted amount and ten per cent of the tax in dispute — with its proviso on an order under section 129(3)

items.scenario: The order against Suhani Chemicals confirms tax of ₹8 lakh, interest of ₹80,000 and penalty of ₹80,000. Suhani admits ₹3 lakh of the tax and ₹30,000 of the interest and disputes everything else. A separate order under section 129(3) imposes a penalty of ₹2 lakh for goods moved without an e-way bill, which Suhani also wants to appeal. It asks what it must pay before each appeal can be filed.

items.stem: Is counsel right about either of those two things?

options.text: Right about both, since one forum cannot apply two different sets of rules to the parties before it
options.misconception: assumes the two sides must be treated identically, when the Act deliberately gives them different routes, periods and conditions
options.why: Symmetry is not the design. The taxpayer files an appeal; the department files a review application after the Commissioner has examined the record. Different names, different periods, and a money condition on one side only.

options.text: Right about the three months, wrong about the deposit
options.misconception: applies the taxpayer's limitation period to the department, which has a longer one of its own
options.why: The department is given twice as long, because its route begins with the Commissioner calling for and examining a record rather than with a party who already knows he has lost. Reading three months into it would let orders become final that the section keeps open for six.

options.text: Right about the deposit, wrong about the three months
options.misconception: reads the pre-deposit as a condition of every appeal to the Authority rather than of an appeal by the person the demand runs against
options.why: A pre-deposit is a part-payment of a demand, and there is no demand against the department to part-pay. The sub-section is written around an appellant who admits some of an order and disputes the rest, and the revenue is in neither position.

options.text: Right about neither
options.why: The department's route is a review application rather than an ordinary appeal. The Commissioner may, on his own motion or on a request from his State counterpart, examine the record of an order an adjudicating authority has passed and direct a subordinate officer to apply to the Appellate Authority — and he has six months from the day the order was communicated in which to do it, not three. There is no pre-deposit at all on a departmental appeal, because the sub-section that requires one speaks of an appellant paying what he admits and a share of what he disputes, which describes a taxpayer and not the revenue.
keywords: The Commissioner may, on his own motion or on a request from his State counterpart
he has six months from the day the order was communicated
There is no pre-deposit at all on a departmental appeal

citation.ref: Section 107(2) — the Commissioner's direction to an officer to apply to the Appellate Authority within six months of communication

items.scenario: A different order of the same year goes in Suhani Chemicals' favour. The Commissioner is not content with it and wants it tested before the Appellate Authority. Suhani's counsel tells the board that the department must move within three months like any other appellant, and must put up ten per cent of the tax it is chasing before it can be heard.

items.stem: By when must each of the three invoices be issued?

options.text: 3 June for the goods and 10 July for both of the services
options.misconception: applies the thirty-day window to every service, missing the longer one the rule gives financial companies
options.why: The rule names insurers, banking companies, financial institutions and non-banking financial companies and gives them a longer period, because their charges are often computed only after a cycle closes. Setu is one of those, so its outside date is a fortnight later than the consultancy's.

options.text: 31 July for all three, as the accounts team plans
options.misconception: treats the invoice deadline as a billing convenience the supplier sets, when each of the three has a statutory outside date
options.why: A monthly billing run is an internal habit, not a legal window. Each of these three has its own outside date and the earliest of them, the goods, had passed nearly two months before the team's chosen day. Late invoicing on services also changes the time of supply, so the tax falls due earlier than the bill suggests.

options.text: 3 July for the goods, 10 July for the consultancy and 25 July for Setu
options.misconception: borrows the thirty-day service window for a supply of goods, when goods are tied to the moment of removal
options.why: Goods get no window at all where the supply involves movement. The invoice has to exist before or at removal, because it is the document that travels with the consignment. Thirty days is a rule for services and has nothing to say about a lorry leaving a factory.

options.text: 3 June for the goods, 10 July for the consultancy and 25 July for Setu
options.why: Goods that move to the buyer carry their invoice before or at the moment of removal, so the consignment sent out on 3 June had to be invoiced on or before 3 June. A service may be billed before or after it is given, but within the window rule 47 sets — thirty days from the day the service was supplied, which takes the consultancy finished on 10 June to 10 July. That window is forty-five days for an insurer, a banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company, so Setu's service finished the same day may be billed as late as 25 July.
keywords: the consignment sent out on 3 June had to be invoiced on or before 3 June
which takes the consultancy finished on 10 June to 10 July
so Setu's service finished the same day may be billed as late as 25 July

citation.ref: Section 31(1) and section 31(2) read with rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017 on the thirty-day and forty-five-day windows

items.scenario: Meghna Services and its group company Setu Finance, a non-banking financial company, are both registered in Karnataka. Meghna dispatches goods to a buyer on 3 June 2026, the sale involving movement of the goods. Meghna also completes a consultancy assignment on 10 June 2026. Setu completes a financing service for a different customer on the same 10 June. The shared accounts team plans to raise all three bills together on 31 July.

items.stem: What must Meghna do, and for how much?

options.text: Raise no invoice at all, as the clerk proposes
options.misconception: treats an incomplete contract as producing no supply, when the work already done is a supply that has already been made
options.why: The contract stopped; the two visits did not un-happen. Services actually rendered are a supply whether or not the agreement they were rendered under ran its course, and the section provides a trigger for exactly this case so that such supplies do not fall out of the system.

options.text: Raise an invoice for the two visits on the date the contract would have ended
options.misconception: keeps the original timetable, when cessation itself is the event that brings the invoice forward
options.why: The trigger is the cessation, not the calendar the contract once had. Holding the bill until a date that has lost its meaning defers the tax on work already done and leaves the customer without a document it needs for its own credit.

options.text: Raise an invoice on 20 June for all four visits and issue a credit note for the two not made
options.misconception: bills the contract rather than the supply, then tries to undo the overbilling with a document the situation does not call for
options.why: The section says the invoice is issued to the extent of the supply made before the cessation, so there is nothing to bill for the visits that never happened and nothing for a credit note to reverse. Billing high and crediting back also overstates the month's outward supply on the return.

options.text: Raise an invoice dated 20 June for the two visits made
options.why: Where a supply of services ceases under a contract before it is complete, the invoice falls due at the time the supply ceases and it covers only the supply made up to that moment. So the bill is dated 20 June, the day the customer pulled out, and it is written for the two visits actually made, ₹80,000, rather than for the four the contract had promised. Waiting for a completion that will never come leaves a supply already made unbilled and its tax unpaid.
keywords: Where a supply of services ceases under a contract before it is complete
So the bill is dated 20 June
it is written for the two visits actually made

citation.ref: Section 31(6) — invoice at the time a supply of services ceases under a contract, to the extent of the supply made before cessation

items.scenario: Meghna Services holds a maintenance contract for four quarterly visits at ₹40,000 a visit. The customer terminates the contract on 20 June 2026 after the second visit has been made. Meghna's billing clerk proposes to raise no invoice at all, since the contract never ran to completion, and to settle with the customer by credit note at the year end.

items.stem: By when must the invoice be issued?

options.text: By 5 July 2026, whether or not the buyer has decided
options.why: Goods taken on approval for sale or return, moved out before the supply happens, carry their invoice at whichever comes first of two moments — the supply itself, or six months from the day they were removed. Removal was on 5 January 2026, so the outside date is 5 July 2026 and it does not wait on anybody's decision. Until then the goods travel on a delivery challan rather than an invoice, which is what lets them move at all when there is as yet no supply to bill.
keywords: six months from the day they were removed
so the outside date is 5 July 2026
the goods travel on a delivery challan rather than an invoice

options.text: On 5 January 2026, because goods that move must be invoiced at removal
options.misconception: applies the ordinary removal rule to goods sent out before any supply has taken place
options.why: The removal rule assumes a sale that has already been agreed, where the movement IS the supply. Goods sent on approval move before anyone knows whether there will be a supply at all, which is why the section gives them a rule of their own and lets them travel on a challan.

options.text: Within thirty days of removal, by 4 February 2026
options.misconception: borrows the services window for a movement of goods sent on approval
