options.why: Thirty days is the window for billing a service after it is given. It has no application to goods, and least of all to goods whose supply has not yet happened. The period the section gives here is far longer, and it runs from removal rather than from any service being performed.

options.text: When the buyer accepts the machine, as the clerk says
options.misconception: reads the approval basis as postponing the invoice indefinitely, missing the outer limit the section imposes
options.why: Acceptance is one of the two triggers, and it is the one that usually comes first. The section adds a second so that a buyer's silence cannot keep a supply outside the tax net for ever, and on these facts the silence has now outlasted the limit.

citation.ref: Section 31(7) — goods sent or taken on approval for sale or return, invoiced at the supply or six months from removal, whichever is earlier

items.scenario: Meghna Services sends a machine to a prospective buyer on approval on 5 January 2026, moving it out of its premises without an invoice. On 30 June 2026 the buyer has still not decided whether to keep it. Meghna's clerk says no invoice is due until the buyer accepts, because until then there is no supply to bill.

items.stem: By when must the show cause notice and the order be issued?

options.text: Notice by 30 September 2027 and the order by 31 December 2027
options.why: For tax pertaining to periods up to 2023-24 there are two demand roads, and section 73 governs a shortfall with any cause other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression. Misreading a rate notification is such a cause. The order in that road must be passed within three years of the due date for that year's annual return, so by 31 December 2027. The notice has to reach the person at least three months before that outer date, which puts it at 30 September 2027 — two years and nine months from the same starting point.
keywords: tax pertaining to periods up to 2023-24
section 73 governs a shortfall with any cause other than fraud

options.text: Both the notice and the order by 31 December 2027, the three years covering the whole exercise
options.misconception: treats the three years as one deadline for everything, missing that the notice carries its own earlier date so that the person has time to answer it
options.why: The three years is the last date for the order alone. A notice must be served at least three months before it, and that gap is what gives the person a chance to reply and the officer time to weigh the reply. A notice served on the eve of the three-year date is out of time even though an order on that date would not be.

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2029 and the order by 31 December 2029, five years being the outer limit for any demand
options.misconception: reads the five-year clock as the ordinary one and the three-year clock as a concession, when it is the other way about
options.why: Five years is available only where fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is alleged and made out. A bona fide misreading of a rate is none of the three, so the shorter clock is the one that runs, and treating the longer one as normal would keep this company exposed for two years after its liability had already closed.

options.text: There is no date left, because the newer demand provision replaced both clocks and governs every notice issued after it came into force
options.misconception: dates the new provision by when the notice happens to be written rather than by the year the tax belongs to
options.why: The newer provision is switched on by the financial year the tax pertains to, not by the day an officer picks up the file. It governs the financial years 2024-25 onwards. A demand for 2023-24 stays where it always was, however late the department gets to it.

citation.ref: Section 73 with sub-sections (2), (10) and (12), read against section 74A

items.scenario: A departmental audit of a Nagpur alloy maker covers the financial year 2023-24. It finds that one product line was taxed at the wrong rate because the person in charge read the rate notification wrongly, and ₹8 lakh of tax was short paid. Nothing else is alleged — no false document, nothing withheld from the department, no false entry. The company filed its annual return for that year by its due date of 31 December 2024. The adjudicating officer, opening the file in 2027, wants to know how much time he still has.

items.stem: By when must the notice and the order on this second finding be issued?

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2029 and the order by 31 December 2029
options.why: Invoices with no goods behind them are not a mistake. They sit in the limb about fraud, wilful misstatement and suppression, so section 74 governs a 2023-24 demand of this kind. The order there may be passed up to five years from the due date of that year's annual return, which is 31 December 2029, and the notice must precede that outer date by at least six months, which puts it at 30 June 2029 — four years and six months from the same start.
keywords: section 74 governs a 2023-24 demand of this kind

options.text: Notice by 31 December 2029 and the order within one year after that
options.misconception: borrows the notice-then-order shape of the newer provision and reads the five years as the deadline for the notice
options.why: In this road the five years is the outer date for the ORDER, and the notice has to land six months before it. Making the five years the notice date would push the order into a sixth year, which the section does not allow at all.

options.text: Notice by 30 September 2027 and the order by 31 December 2027, the clock being the same whatever the conduct
options.misconception: treats limitation as a single rule about time, when for a year up to 2023-24 the conduct picks the section and the section fixes the clock
options.why: For those years the law runs two roads and the conduct chooses one. A shortfall with an innocent cause is on the three-year road; one built on invoices without goods is on the five-year road. Reading one clock for both would close the second kind of case two years early.

options.text: No notice is possible, because credit taken on invoices without goods is dealt with only by prosecution
options.misconception: assumes that a fraud with a criminal side has no civil demand road, when the two run alongside each other
options.why: A prosecution and a demand are separate proceedings. The tax, the interest and the penalty are still determined by an adjudication under the demand provisions, and the criminal case neither replaces that nor has to finish before it.

citation.ref: Section 74 with sub-sections (2), (10) and (12)

items.scenario: The same audit turns up a second thing in the same year, 2023-24. A run of purchase invoices carries tax the company took credit of, ₹12 lakh in all, and the goods described in them never moved. The address of the supplier who raised them is a vacant plot. The company's annual return for 2023-24 was due on 31 December 2024.

items.stem: What are his deadlines, and what can be done if the order is not ready?

options.text: Notice within four years and six months and order within five years, since suppression may yet be alleged
options.misconception: keeps the fraud clock alive for a year in which the section carrying it no longer applies
options.why: For 2024-25 onwards an allegation of suppression no longer moves the deadline. It moves the penalty, and only the penalty. Waiting on the longer clock would take the officer past the date his notice had to be served, and there is no way back from that.

options.text: Notice within forty-two months of 31 December 2025, order within twelve months of that notice, and that twelve months may be stretched by six months
options.why: From 2024-25 the same clock runs whether or not suppression is alleged, and only the penalty moves. The notice must go out within forty-two months from the due date for the annual return of that year. The order must then follow within twelve months from the date of the notice. Where the officer cannot manage that, the Commissioner, or an officer the Commissioner authorises who is senior to the proper officer and not below the rank of Joint Commissioner, may extend the period by up to six months — for reasons written down before the twelve months run out, not afterwards.
keywords: within forty-two months from the due date for the annual return
within twelve months from the date of the notice
may extend the period by up to six months

options.text: Notice within two years and nine months and order within three years, no fraud having been alleged
options.misconception: carries the old non-fraud clock into a year that the newer provision governs
options.why: That pair of dates belongs to demands for periods up to 2023-24. From 2024-25 one clock serves both kinds of case and it is longer than the old non-fraud one, so using the old dates would make an officer think he was out of time when he had months in hand.

options.text: The twelve months may be extended by the proper officer himself, for as long as the file needs
options.misconception: reads the extension as the adjudicating officer's own discretion, when it is a superior's decision with a written reason and a fixed ceiling
options.why: The extension is not the proper officer's to give himself. It comes from the Commissioner or from an officer the Commissioner authorises who is senior to him and at least a Joint Commissioner, it is capped at six months, and the reasons have to be recorded before the original period expires rather than once it has gone.

citation.ref: Section 74A(2) and section 74A(7) with its proviso

items.scenario: A shortfall of ₹18 lakh is found in the returns of a Hyderabad trader for the financial year 2024-25, whose annual return was due on 31 December 2025. The department has not decided whether it will allege suppression. The proper officer expects the file to be a heavy one and is worried that he will not have the order ready in time.

items.stem: May he issue that notice?

options.text: No — the section bars a notice altogether where the year's amount is under the floor it names
options.why: The demand provision for 2024-25 onwards carries a proviso that stops a notice altogether where the tax not paid, short paid or erroneously refunded, or the credit wrongly taken or used, comes to less than ₹1,000 in a financial year. ₹860 is under that line, so no notice may be served at all. The floor is read year by year on the amount for that year, not invoice by invoice.
keywords: less than ₹1,000 in a financial year

options.text: Yes, and he must, since there is no minimum anywhere in the demand provisions
options.misconception: assumes the demand machinery has no de minimis, when the current provision opens with one
options.why: The proviso sits in the first sub-section of the governing section, so it is reached before anything else in it. It is a bar on issuing the notice, not a discretion the officer exercises after weighing the amount.

options.text: Yes, because the floor is read against each notice, so several small notices are each below it
options.misconception: reads the floor against the document rather than against the financial year, which would let any amount be split under it
options.why: The section measures the amount for a financial year. Splitting one year's shortfall across several notices would put every demand in the country under the floor, which is exactly what reading it by the year prevents.

options.text: No, but only because the sum is too small to be worth the department's time
options.misconception: treats a statutory bar as an administrative convenience, so it would bend on a day the department felt strongly
options.why: Nothing here turns on how the department feels about the amount. The section forbids the notice, so an officer who issued one anyway would be issuing something with no power behind it, however keen he was.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 74A(1)

items.scenario: A scrutiny of a small Kochi trader's returns for the financial year 2025-26 finds that ₹860 of tax was short paid over the whole year — one invoice on which the wrong rate was applied. The officer drafts a show cause notice for the amount, on the footing that a shortfall is a shortfall whatever its size.

items.stem: What does each reading cost the company beyond the tax itself?

options.text: Interest only on the suppression reading, interest being part of what is charged for concealment
options.misconception: reads interest as a sanction that follows fault, when it follows the delay alone
options.why: Interest is charged because the Government was without its money for a period, whatever the reason it was without it. It runs from the day after the tax fell due until it is paid, and no finding about the taxpayer's state of mind switches it on or off.

options.text: Interest either way, and then either the ten per cent penalty or a penalty of the same size as the tax
options.why: Interest under section 50 attaches to the tax from the day after it fell due and does not wait on which reading wins — it is compensation for money held back, not a punishment for anything. The penalty is where the two readings part company. Where the cause is anything other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, it is fixed at 10 per cent of the tax due from the person or ₹10,000, whichever is higher. Where one of those three is made out, what is charged is a penalty equal to the tax due.
keywords: Interest under section 50 attaches to the tax
10 per cent of the tax due from the person or ₹10,000, whichever is higher
a penalty equal to the tax due

options.text: A penalty the size of the tax on either reading, the section having stopped distinguishing the two from 2024-25
options.misconception: takes the one clock the new provision gives both cases and assumes the penalty was flattened along with it
options.why: What the newer provision made common to both cases is the limitation period. The penalty is exactly where the two are still held apart, and it is the reason the difference between an innocent shortfall and a suppressed one still has to be pleaded and proved.

options.text: A flat ₹10,000 on the bona fide reading, that being the figure the section names
options.misconception: reads the fixed sum as the penalty, when it is a floor sitting under the percentage
options.why: The section names two amounts and charges the higher of them. On a demand of this size the percentage is far above the fixed sum, so the fixed sum does no work at all here; it bites only on a small demand where the percentage would come to less than it.

citation.ref: Section 74A(5) read with section 50

items.scenario: An adjudication for the financial year 2024-25 finds that a Ludhiana manufacturer short paid ₹12 lakh of tax. Two readings of the same facts are on the table — the department's, that the shortfall was suppressed, and the company's, that it was a bona fide error in the way its software picked the rate. Nothing has been paid yet.

items.stem: What does the timing of the payment change?

options.text: Paying inside the window cuts the penalty to fifteen per cent rather than removing it
options.misconception: carries the fraud ladder's reduced rates into a case where the section gives a clean escape instead
options.why: The stepped payments belong to the suppression limb, where a penalty is always paid and only its size moves. On a bona fide shortfall the section does something different in kind: it takes the penalty away altogether, and there is no reduced rate to fall back on because nothing is left to reduce.

options.text: Paying the tax with interest before the notice, or soon enough after it, wipes the penalty out; paying later leaves ₹1 lakh
options.why: On a shortfall whose cause is not fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, the section gives two ways out. If the person pays the tax with the interest on it, on his own working or the officer's, and tells the officer in writing before any notice is served, no notice is served at all. If the notice has already gone out, the same payment made within sixty days of it means no penalty is payable and the proceedings on that notice are treated as finished. Only where the money comes later than that does the penalty attach through the order — here ₹1 lakh, being 10 per cent of ₹10 lakh.
keywords: made within sixty days of it
₹1 lakh, being 10 per cent of ₹10 lakh

options.text: The window runs from the order, not from the notice, so the company has until sixty days after adjudication
options.misconception: moves the deadline to the end of the proceeding, which would leave the officer adjudicating a case the payment was meant to prevent
options.why: The escape is timed off the notice precisely so that the adjudication never has to happen. Reading it off the order would mean the officer writing an order in every case and then unwinding it, which is what the sixty days after the notice exists to avoid.

options.text: Nothing about the penalty; paying early only stops the interest running
options.misconception: assumes the penalty is fixed by the order whatever the taxpayer does, when this section makes early payment the whole answer
options.why: The penalty here is not fixed at the order and then discounted. On a bona fide shortfall the section removes it entirely where the tax and interest reach the Government early enough, and the officer then has nothing left to impose.

citation.ref: Section 74A(8) read with section 74A(5)(i)

items.scenario: A Bhopal company's scrutiny for 2024-25 shows ₹10 lakh of tax short paid. Its accountant accepts the figure and says there was nothing behind it beyond a wrong rate sitting in the accounting software, which the department does not dispute. A show cause notice was served on 1 August 2026. The company has the cash and wants to know what the date of payment changes.

items.stem: What is the penalty at each of those moments?

options.text: Fifteen per cent now, twenty-five per cent shortly after the notice, fifty per cent shortly after the order, and the whole tax after that
options.why: The suppression limb runs a ladder, and every rung is a real reduction on the full penalty. Paying the tax with interest and a penalty of 15 per cent of the tax before any notice is served — ₹1.5 lakh here — stops the notice being issued. Paying with 25 per cent, ₹2.5 lakh, within sixty days of the notice ends the proceedings on it. Paying with 50 per cent, ₹5 lakh, within sixty days of the order ends them at that stage instead. Miss all three and what stands is the full amount equal to the tax, ₹10 lakh.
keywords: a penalty of 15 per cent of the tax before any notice
with 25 per cent, ₹2.5 lakh, within sixty days of the notice
with 50 per cent, ₹5 lakh, within sixty days of the order
the full amount equal to the tax, ₹10 lakh

options.text: The ladder ends at the notice; once the order is passed nothing can be reduced
options.misconception: stops the ladder one rung early, missing that a further reduced rate is open for sixty days after the order
options.why: There is a rung after the order as well, and it is worth taking — half the tax rather than all of it. Believing the ladder ends at the notice would cost this company ₹5 lakh for no reason.

options.text: No penalty at all if the tax and interest are paid within sixty days of the notice
options.misconception: applies the bona fide escape to a suppression case, where the section never lets the penalty fall to nothing
options.why: A clean escape exists only where the cause of the shortfall is not fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression. Once suppression is made out the ladder is the only relief available, and its lowest rung still carries a charge.

options.text: Fifteen per cent at every stage up to the order, and the full penalty afterwards
options.misconception: flattens a ladder into one reduced rate, so there is no reason left to pay early rather than late
options.why: The rates rise as the proceeding goes on, and that rise is the point of the design — the earlier the money comes, the less is charged. One rate throughout would remove any reason to settle before the officer had done the work.

citation.ref: Section 74A(9)

items.scenario: The same ₹10 lakh shortfall for 2024-25, but on this version of the facts the notice alleges suppression and the company's counsel says the allegation will stick. The company would rather pay than fight, and wants to know what each moment of paying will cost it — now, after the notice, or after the order.

items.stem: What reaches the electronic credit ledger, and how much of that is common credit?

options.text: ₹1,25,000 reaches the ledger, that being the credit which is certainly allowable
options.misconception: confuses the amount that survives apportionment with the amount that is credited in the first place
options.why: The ledger is credited with everything except the three exclusions, and the apportionment then happens against that balance. Crediting only the certainly-allowable part would leave the rule nothing to work on and would deny the taxable share of the common credit outright.

options.text: ₹2,05,000 reaches the ledger, and ₹80,000 of it is common credit
options.why: Three amounts never enter the ledger at all — the ₹20,000 on things used exclusively for non-business purposes, the ₹60,000 on things used exclusively for effecting exempt supplies, and the ₹15,000 on outdoor catering, which is blocked by section 17(5). Taking that ₹95,000 off ₹3,00,000 leaves ₹2,05,000 credited to the electronic credit ledger. Out of that, the ₹1,25,000 tied to the shampoo comes out next and is allowed in full, so what is left to be apportioned is ₹80,000.
keywords: ₹2,05,000 credited to the electronic credit ledger

options.text: ₹2,05,000 reaches the ledger and the whole of it has to be apportioned
options.misconception: apportions credit that was already tied to the taxable line, which the rule allows in full and takes out first
options.why: The rule removes the input tax on inputs used exclusively for taxable supplies before any apportionment starts, and here that is ₹1,25,000. What is left is the common credit, ₹80,000, and only that figure goes into the ratio. Running the ratio over ₹2,05,000 would reverse part of a credit the unit is entitled to keep whole.

options.text: ₹2,85,000 reaches the ledger, only the household amount being kept out
options.misconception: treats a blocked credit and a credit tied to exempt output as things to be apportioned, when both are kept out of the ledger before that
options.why: Both are removed before the ledger is credited at all. A credit blocked by the list in section 17(5) is not available on any footing, and input tax tied only to exempt output is not available either, so neither is ever a candidate for apportionment.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1), clauses (a) to (h), read with section 17(5)

items.scenario: A Coimbatore unit makes a taxable herbal shampoo and an exempt unprocessed farm product in the same shed. For October its input tax comes to ₹3,00,000 in all. Of that, ₹20,000 is on things used only for the owner's household, ₹60,000 is on things used only for the exempt line, ₹15,000 is on outdoor catering for a staff function, and ₹1,25,000 is on inputs used only for the shampoo. The rest is electricity, packaging film and shed rent, all used for both lines.

items.stem: What are the two amounts the rule makes it work out for October?

options.text: ₹16,000 and ₹4,000, but both worked out on last year's ratio of exempt to total turnover
options.misconception: borrows the fallback ratio for an ordinary month, when an earlier period's figures are reached for only where the month has none
options.why: The monthly working uses the month's own exempt and total turnover. Values from an earlier period are used only where there is no turnover in the month at all or the figures are not available, and the annual recomputation later uses the year's own turnover rather than the previous year's.

options.text: ₹41,000 and ₹10,250, the ratio and the flat rate both being applied to the ledger balance
options.misconception: applies the ratio to the whole credit in the ledger instead of to the common credit alone
options.why: Both amounts bite on the common credit and on nothing wider. The credit already tied to taxable supplies was taken out a step earlier, and running the ratio over the ledger balance would reverse a slice of it a second time.

options.text: ₹16,000 and nothing more, the non-business input tax having already been removed
options.misconception: reads the flat five per cent as a second bite at input tax already excluded, when it is an assumed use of a different pool
options.why: The earlier removal took out input tax on things used only for non-business purposes. The flat percentage is about a different pool altogether — the common inputs, which the rule assumes serve non-business purposes to that extent whether or not any such use is shown. The two do not overlap.

options.text: ₹16,000 for the exempt share and ₹4,000 for the assumed non-business share
options.why: D1, the part of the common credit attributable to exempt supplies, is the month's exempt turnover divided by the month's total turnover in the State, applied to the common credit. Exempt ₹1 crore over total ₹5 crore is one-fifth, and one-fifth of ₹80,000 is ₹16,000. The other amount does not depend on turnover at all — D2 is a flat 5 per cent of the common credit, ₹4,000. Both are computed on the month's own turnover.
keywords: D1, the part of the common credit attributable to exempt supplies
D2 is a flat 5 per cent of the common credit, ₹4,000

citation.ref: Rule 42(1), clauses (i) and (j)

items.scenario: The same Coimbatore unit, the same October. The common credit left after the exclusive amounts have been taken out is ₹80,000. Its exempt turnover for October is ₹1 crore and its total turnover in the State for the month is ₹5 crore. Last year the exempt line was a much smaller part of the business.

items.stem: What credit does October carry, and what happens to these figures later?

options.text: ₹1,85,000 for October, and a shortfall found at the year end carries interest from the date of the September return
options.misconception: dates the interest from the day the annual working is done, which would make delay in doing it free
options.why: Interest on a shortfall found on the annual working runs from the first day of the succeeding financial year, not from the day somebody got round to the calculation. Dating it from the return would reward leaving the working until the last permitted moment.

options.text: ₹1,85,000 for October and nothing more, the monthly reversals being final once the returns are filed
options.misconception: treats twelve monthly ratios as the final answer, when the rule requires the year to be redone on the year's own figures
options.why: Each month's ratio is provisional and is taken on that month's turnover, which swings about as the mix of sales changes. The rule requires the whole year to be worked again on the year's turnover, and it fixes a date for doing it.

options.text: ₹1,85,000 for October, and the two amounts are worked out again on the year's own turnover before the September return
options.why: The two amounts come to ₹20,000 together, and the registered person must reverse D1 and D2 by adding that sum to his output tax for the month. The eligible part of the common credit is therefore ₹80,000 less ₹20,000, that is ₹60,000, and adding the ₹1,25,000 tied to the taxable line gives a credit of ₹1,85,000 for October. Both amounts are then recomputed for the whole financial year on the year's own turnover, before the due date for the return for September of the following year. A shortfall found on that working goes back with interest at 18 per cent running from 1 April of the succeeding year; an excess reversed during the year is taken back as credit through that same return.
keywords: reverse D1 and D2 by adding that sum to his output tax
recomputed for the whole financial year

options.text: ₹2,05,000 for October, the reversal being made in cash and leaving the credit untouched
options.misconception: counts the ledger balance as the month's credit while paying the reversal separately, which uses the same ₹20,000 twice
options.why: The reversal is made by adding the amount to the output tax of the month, so the money leaves either way and the credit is worth ₹20,000 less. Calling the ledger balance the month's credit and then paying the reversal on top of it counts the same sum in both directions.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1), clauses (k) to (m), and rule 42(2)

items.scenario: The same October. The exempt share of the common credit is ₹16,000 and the assumed non-business share is ₹4,000. The credit tied only to the taxable shampoo line is ₹1,25,000 and the common credit is ₹80,000. The owner asks what he may actually use this month and whether that is the end of it.

items.stem: Where is the place of supply of each job?

options.text: The Netherlands for both, the recipient being there and cross-border services following the recipient
options.misconception: applies the general rule to a case the specific performance clause has already taken out of it
options.why: The general rule governs only what the specific clauses do not reach. A service on goods the recipient had to make physically available is squarely inside one of them, so the general rule never gets its turn.

options.text: Chennai for both, the supplier being in Chennai and both jobs being done there
options.misconception: reads the place of supply as wherever the work happened to be carried out, when only one clause makes that matter
options.why: Where the work is done matters because one clause says it does, and that clause is about goods put into the supplier's hands. For anything outside it the starting point is the recipient's location, whatever desk the work was done at.

options.text: Chennai for both, because payment for both comes into a Chennai bank in foreign exchange
options.misconception: ties the place of supply to where the money lands, which no clause of the section does
options.why: Nothing in these provisions turns on the bank the payment reaches. Receipt in convertible foreign exchange is one of the conditions an export of services has to satisfy, and it plays no part at all in fixing where a supply happened.

options.text: Chennai for the pump work and the Netherlands for the layout review
options.why: The performance clause reaches services on goods required to be made physically available by the recipient — put into the hands of whoever is to work on them — and it fixes the supply at the place where the services are actually performed. The pump had to be handed over before the testing could start, so that job is inside the clause and its place of supply is Chennai. The layout review needs no goods in anybody's hands, so it never reaches the clause and falls back on the general provision, which fixes the supply at the location of the recipient — the Netherlands.
keywords: required to be made physically available by the recipient
where the services are actually performed

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a) read with section 13(2)

items.scenario: A Chennai engineering consultancy takes two jobs from the same Dutch client in one month. In the first, the client ships a pump to the Chennai workshop for testing and calibration; the pump has to be in the consultancy's hands for the work to happen at all. In the second, the consultancy is asked to review a plant layout and comment on it, working only from drawings sent by email — no goods come to India and none are needed.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of each of the three jobs?

options.text: Germany, Pune and Pune, the third being carried out by engineers sitting in India
options.misconception: applies the performance rule to remote work, when the proviso for it fixes the supply where the goods are
options.why: Work done from a remote location by electronic means has its own answer written into the clause — the supply sits where the goods were standing when the service was supplied. Where the engineer sat is not the test, and if it were, the proviso would have nothing to do.

options.text: Germany, Pune and Singapore, in that order
options.why: The turbine was temporarily imported into India for repair and sent out again after it without being put to any other use here, and a proviso lifts exactly that case out of the performance clause; the general rule then takes over and the supply sits at the recipient's location in Germany. The press was made physically available to the repairer inside India and worked on there, so the work was performed at the workshop in Pune and that is where its supply sits. The third job was done from a remote location by electronic means, and the other proviso puts that supply where the goods stood in Singapore.
keywords: temporarily imported into India for repair
the work was performed at the workshop in Pune

options.text: Germany, Germany and Singapore, a repair being taxed at the owner's location in every case
options.misconception: turns the temporary-import proviso into a general rule about owners, when it is a narrow carve-out with three conditions
options.why: The carve-out applies only where goods came into India for repair or some other treatment, went out again after it, and were put to no other use here. The Indian mill's press meets none of that, so its supply stays where the work on it was done.

options.text: Pune, Pune and Pune, all three having been carried out by one Pune workshop
options.misconception: reads "actually performed" as the supplier's own address and misses both provisos sitting under the clause
options.why: The clause looks at where the work happened rather than where the supplier lives, and two provisos then take cases away from it altogether — goods brought in briefly and sent back, and work done remotely by electronic means. Only one of these three jobs is left where the workshop stands.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a) with both its provisos, read with section 13(2)

items.scenario: A Pune repair company closes three jobs in one month. A turbine came in from its German owner, entered India only for the repair, and went back straight afterwards with nothing else done to it here. A press belonging to an Indian textile mill was carted to the Pune workshop and overhauled there. A packaging machine standing on a customer's floor in Singapore was re-programmed from Pune over a secure link, and nobody touched it.

items.stem: Where is the place of supply in each case, and is the yacht hire an import of service?

options.text: Pune for both, the recipient of the yacht hire being in India
options.misconception: applies the general rule to the yacht, when a short hire of a means of transport is one of the named exceptions to it
options.why: A hire of a means of transport for a month or less is expressly taken out of the general rule and sent to the supplier's location. Had this hire run past a month the general rule would come back and the answer would change, which is why the length of the hire is in the facts.

options.text: Vietnam for the commission and Dubai for the yacht hire
options.misconception: puts an intermediary's supply where his principal sits, when the clause fixes it at the intermediary's own location
options.why: The clause names the supplier of the intermediary service, and that is the Pune firm. Where its principal is established makes no difference; if it did, no Indian intermediary working for a foreign client would ever have an Indian place of supply, which is the opposite of what the clause was written to achieve.

options.text: Pune for the commission and Dubai for the yacht hire, but the hire is still an import of service because the supplier is outside India
options.misconception: treats a foreign supplier as enough to make an import, when the place of supply must also be in India
options.why: An import of service needs three things together — the supplier outside India, the recipient in India, and the place of supply in India. The third fails here, so the transaction is outside the charge however foreign the owner of the yacht happens to be.

options.text: Pune for the commission and Dubai for the yacht hire, so the hire is not an import of service
options.why: Three kinds of supply have their place of supply fixed at the location of the supplier of services — services by a bank or a financial institution to its account holders, intermediary services, and the hiring of a means of transport other than aircraft and vessels for up to a period of one month. Arranging a sale between two other people for a commission is an intermediary service and the supplier is in Pune, so that is where the supply sits. The yacht is hired for twenty days, inside a month, so its supply sits where its supplier is, in Dubai. An import of service needs the place of supply to be in India, and this one is not.
keywords: up to a period of one month
the location of the supplier of services

citation.ref: Section 13(8) read with section 2(11)

items.scenario: A Pune firm does two things in one quarter. For a commission from a seller in Vietnam it finds an Indian buyer for that seller's machinery and arranges the sale between them; it never owns the machinery and never takes delivery of it. Separately, an Indian company hires a yacht for twenty days from its owner in Dubai, and wants to know whether that hire is an import of service on which it must pay tax itself.

items.stem: What can he actually claim, and by when?

options.text: Only the credit that built up because his buying rate is above his selling rate, and within two years of the relevant date
options.why: Unutilised credit comes back in only two situations, and one of them is where credit builds up because the rate on what he buys is higher than the rate on what he sells — an inverted duty structure. Nil-rated and exempt output is outside that head, and so are the goods and services the Government has notified as excluded from it. Credit that piled up for any other reason, slow sales among them, simply stays in the ledger. The claim itself has to be made within two years of the relevant date.
keywords: higher than the rate on what he sells
within two years of the relevant date

options.text: The inverted credit and the credit on the exempt fabric too, no tax having been collected on either
options.misconception: reads an exempt output as an inverted one, when the head expressly excludes nil-rated and exempt supplies
options.why: This head is about a rate that is lower, not a rate that is absent. Credit tied to exempt output is not refunded here and is not even allowed into the ledger in the first place, so there is nothing to claim on that line.

options.text: Only the inverted portion, and there is no time limit, a refund of credit not being a refund of tax
options.misconception: assumes the two-year limitation reaches only tax paid in cash
options.why: The limitation runs on the refund application itself, whatever head it is made under. A claim for accumulated credit lodged after the two years is out of time in exactly the way a claim for excess tax paid would be.

options.text: The whole ledger balance in cash, there being no restriction on which accumulated credit may be refunded
options.misconception: reads a refund of unutilised credit as a general right to cash out the ledger, when the provision names the only two ways in
options.why: Credit is meant to be used against output tax, and a refund of it is an exception written for two named situations. A balance sitting in the ledger for any other reason waits there until output tax comes along to absorb it.

citation.ref: Section 54(3)(ii) read with section 54(1)

items.scenario: A Surat maker of a finished textile taxed at 5 per cent buys yarn and chemicals taxed at 18 per cent. Credit has piled up in his ledger month after month and he cannot use it against his own small output tax. He also sells a little exempt fabric on the side. His consultant tells him he may claim the whole ledger balance back in cash whenever he likes, since it is his money.

items.stem: What is his Net ITC, and what figure goes into the denominator of the formula's second part?

options.text: ₹4,50,000 and ₹4,90,000, every rupee of credit taken in the month counting somewhere
options.misconception: puts capital goods into a formula whose definition of inputs keeps them out
options.why: Capital goods are excluded from the meaning of inputs, and the credit on them is spread over the life of the asset rather than handed back in the month of purchase. Adding the machine would refund in one month a credit the law never treats as an input credit at all.

options.text: ₹3,60,000 in both places, one defined term serving the whole formula
options.misconception: assumes a single figure runs through both parts, when the second part deliberately uses a wider base
options.why: The second part is a subtraction meant to strip out the credit the person has already set against his own output tax, so it is measured against everything he availed — inputs and input services alike. Using the narrower figure there makes the subtraction too small and the refund too big.

options.text: ₹3,60,000 as Net ITC, and ₹4,00,000 in the second part's denominator
options.why: Net ITC in this formula means only the credit availed on inputs during the period, and inputs are goods other than capital goods, so the moulding machine is out of it and so are the input services. Net ITC is therefore ₹3,60,000. The second part of the formula divides by something else — the credit availed on inputs and input services, ₹4,00,000 — and the two figures look alike without being the same. Using one where the other belongs changes the refund.
keywords: Net ITC in this formula means only the credit availed on inputs
inputs are goods other than capital goods
the credit availed on inputs and input services, ₹4,00,000

options.text: ₹4,00,000 in both places, inputs and input services counting for each
options.misconception: reads Net ITC the way the zero-rated formula reads it, where input services do count
options.why: The two formulas use one name for two things. Under the zero-rated head the term takes in input services; under this head it does not, and the narrowing is deliberate, because the refund here exists to unwind an inversion in the tax on goods.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) read with section 2(59)

items.scenario: For March, a Salem manufacturer whose only output is a 5 per cent product made from 18 per cent inputs takes credit of ₹3,60,000 on inputs, ₹40,000 on input services such as freight and audit fees, and ₹90,000 on a moulding machine bought that month. He is filling in the refund formula for an inverted duty structure and finds that it asks him for two different credit figures.

items.stem: What is the turnover of the inverted rated supply, and what is the adjusted total turnover?

options.text: ₹40,00,000 in both places, every taxable outward supply counting as inverted once the ledger has a balance
options.misconception: decides what is an inverted rated supply from the state of the ledger rather than from the rates on the goods
options.why: Whether a supply is inverted rated is settled line by line, on the rate the goods carry against the rate their inputs carried. A balance sitting in the ledger says nothing about which line put it there.

The numerator uses only the supplies the inversion arises on, so the turnover of the inverted rated supply of goods is ₹30,00,000. The denominator is wider. Adjusted total turnover is the turnover in the State for the period, taking out the value of exempt supplies other than zero-rated ones — and the 18 per cent goods are neither exempt nor zero-rated, so they stay in and it comes to ₹40,00,000, even though no refund arises on that line at all. The commonest error is to put ₹30,00,000 in both places, which makes the ratio one.
keywords: the turnover of the inverted rated supply of goods is ₹30,00,000
Adjusted total turnover is the turnover in the State

options.text: ₹30,00,000 and ₹10,00,000, the denominator being the turnover that is not inverted
options.misconception: reads the word "adjusted" as a subtraction of the inverted line itself
options.why: What "adjusted" takes out is the value of exempt supplies other than zero-rated ones, and nothing else. The inverted line is part of the total turnover; it is not something removed from it.

options.text: ₹30,00,000 in both places, only the inverted line belonging in a formula about the inversion
options.misconception: matches the denominator to the numerator, which makes the ratio one and hands back the whole of Net ITC
options.why: The denominator is deliberately the wider figure, because its job is to apportion the credit between the output the inversion arises on and everything else. Setting the two equal removes the apportionment the formula exists to make.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) read with the meaning of adjusted total turnover in rule 89(4)

items.scenario: The same Salem manufacturer, the same month. His sales of the 5 per cent product come to ₹30,00,000 and he also sold other goods carrying 18 per cent worth ₹10,00,000, on which no inversion arises at all. He made no exempt supplies and no zero-rated ones. He is working out the two turnover figures the formula needs.

items.stem: What is the most the formula will let him have back?

options.text: ₹2,70,000, the second part being tax he has already paid rather than a reduction of the refund
options.misconception: stops at the proportion and treats the subtraction as somebody else's arithmetic
options.why: The subtraction is part of the formula, not a separate adjustment. It takes out the credit that has already done its work against his own output tax, so that the refund covers only what genuinely could not be used.

The first part is the turnover of the inverted rated supply multiplied by Net ITC and divided by adjusted total turnover — ₹30,00,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹40,00,000 — so the first part comes to ₹2,70,000. The formula then subtracts the tax payable on that inverted rated supply multiplied by Net ITC and divided by the credit availed on inputs and input services, which is ₹1,50,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹4,00,000, or ₹1,35,000. Taking the second away from the first leaves ₹1,35,000, and that is the maximum refund the rule allows.
keywords: that is the maximum refund the rule allows

options.text: ₹1,50,000, the wider credit figure serving as Net ITC in both parts
options.misconception: lets input services into the numerator, where only the credit on inputs belongs
options.why: Net ITC in this formula is the credit on inputs alone. Putting the wider figure into the first part inflates the proportion and, put into the second part as well, cancels the ratio there — two errors that happen to leave a tidy-looking number.

options.text: ₹4,05,000, the two parts being added together
options.misconception: adds a limb the formula subtracts, which would refund the same credit twice over
options.why: The second limb comes off the first. Adding it would hand back both the unusable credit and the credit already set against output tax, so the same rupees would be relieved twice.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5), the maximum refund formula in full

items.scenario: Everything the Salem manufacturer needs is now on one sheet. Turnover of the inverted rated supply of goods ₹30,00,000; adjusted total turnover ₹40,00,000; Net ITC ₹3,60,000; credit availed on inputs and input services ₹4,00,000; tax payable on the inverted rated supply for the month ₹1,50,000.

items.stem: How long may the goods remain, and can the period be extended?

options.text: Till 31 March 2027, and no extension is possible once that year has been used
options.misconception: reads the year as an absolute outer limit, when it is an ordinary period that a named officer may add to
options.why: The year is the ordinary period and the Act names the officer who may extend it. What is capped is the length of any one extension, not whether an extension may be granted at all.

options.text: Till 1 April 2027, counted from the day the goods physically entered the warehouse
options.misconception: starts the clock at the physical deposit, when it starts at the order permitting the deposit
options.why: The period is measured from the date of the order permitting removal of the goods for deposit, which is a date on record and ascertainable. The day a lorry actually arrives is not the reference point, and using it would make the period depend on the transporter's timekeeping.

options.text: Till 31 March 2027, and any extension granted must be a full year, perishables included
options.misconception: treats the one-year ceiling on an extension as a fixed entitlement to a year
options.why: A year is the most that may be granted at one time, not the amount that must be granted. Where the goods will not last that long the officer grants less, because warehousing goods past their life serves nobody and leaves the revenue holding something worthless.

options.text: Till 31 March 2027, and a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may add to it, a year at a time at most
options.why: For goods in a warehouse of this kind the period runs till the expiry of one year from the date of the order under section 60 permitting the deposit, so from 1 April 2026 it ends on 31 March 2027. The Principal Commissioner of Customs or the Commissioner of Customs may extend it, but by not more than one year at a time, and the extension actually granted is cut back where the goods have a shelf life shorter than that — which packaged food usually does.
keywords: one year from the date of the order under section 60
not more than one year at a time
a shelf life shorter than that

citation.ref: Section 61(1) and its proviso on extension, read with section 60

items.scenario: An importer's consignment of packaged food is deposited in a licensed public warehouse where no manufacture is allowed. The order permitting the deposit is made on 1 April 2026. In February 2027 the buyer he was holding the goods for backs out, and he asks the department how much longer they may stay and whether the time can be stretched.

items.stem: Is anything extra due, and how much?

options.text: Yes — 15 per cent for 32 days, worked out on the value of the consignment
options.misconception: applies the rate to the wrong principal, so the answer moves with the goods rather than with the duty
options.why: The interest is on the duty that was deferred, not on the value of the consignment. The value is what the duty is computed from; it is not itself the sum interest runs on, and using it would multiply the charge several times over.

options.text: No — the goods were cleared inside the one-year warehousing period
options.misconception: assumes the interest-free window and the warehousing period are one clock, so anything inside the period is free
options.why: The two clocks start together and stop at different times. The warehousing period says how long the goods may lawfully stay; the ninety days says how long they may stay for nothing. A clearance inside the period but past ninety days is perfectly lawful and carries interest all the same.

options.text: Yes — interest on the whole duty from 1 April 2026 to 31 July 2026
options.misconception: charges the first ninety days as well, when they are free
options.why: Interest is charged only for the time beyond ninety days from the order. Counting from the order itself would take away the free period the section grants, and on a short overstay that is most of the sum.

options.text: Yes — about ₹2,630 of interest
options.why: Clearing inside the warehousing period does not make the deferment free. Interest attaches to the deferred duty for every day the goods stay beyond ninety days from the section 60 order, and ninety days from 1 April 2026 run out on 29 June 2026. Interest therefore runs from 30 June to 31 July 2026, which is 32 days, at 15 per cent a year — the rate fixed by the notification issued under section 47. On ₹2,00,000 that comes to about ₹2,630.
keywords: beyond ninety days from the section 60 order

citation.ref: Section 61(2) read with section 60 and the rate notified under section 47

items.scenario: Daksh Traders' consignment is deposited under an order made on 1 April 2026. The duty deferred on it is ₹2,00,000. The goods are cleared for home consumption on 31 July 2026, comfortably inside the warehousing period. The firm's accountant says nothing extra is due, because the goods came out well before the period ran out.

items.stem: Is that interest payable?

options.text: Yes, but at half the rate, re-export being a mitigating circumstance
options.misconception: invents a discretion where the answer is arithmetic
options.why: There is no reduced rate for goods that leave the country. The reason nothing is charged is not leniency towards the exporter; it is that the sum the interest is computed on comes to nought.

options.text: No, but only because the Board has waived interest generally for re-exported goods
options.misconception: credits an administrative waiver with a result the section produces by itself
options.why: The Board does have a power to waive interest in individual cases or for a notified class of goods, and it is a separate thing altogether. Here nothing needs waiving, because the charge never arises in the first place.

options.text: Yes — interest runs on the overstay whatever becomes of the goods afterwards
options.misconception: treats interest as rent for time in the warehouse rather than as a charge on unpaid duty
options.why: Interest compensates the Government for money it was kept out of. Where no duty was ever owed, no money was kept back and there is nothing to compensate, so the length of the stay changes nothing at all.

options.text: No — with no duty payable there is no principal for interest to run on
options.why: Interest here is an accessory to the duty and is worked out on it, so it cannot stand on its own. Where warehoused goods are re-exported from the warehouse under section 69, no duty is payable on them at all, so the principal is nil and the interest is nil however long they sat there. The Supreme Court settled the point in Pratibha Processors, holding interest to be compensatory rather than penal, and the Board may in any case waive interest in individual cases.
keywords: Interest here is an accessory to the duty
re-exported from the warehouse under section 69
the Supreme Court settled the point in Pratibha Processors

citation.ref: Section 61(2) read with section 69, and Pratibha Processors v. Union of India

items.scenario: Ved Exports left a consignment in a warehouse for fourteen months, well past the free ninety days. It then took the whole lot out of the warehouse for export rather than for home consumption, so no duty was ever paid on it. The department now raises a demand for interest on the duty that would have been payable, on the ground that the goods plainly overstayed.

items.stem: What is the position on that order?

options.text: The order stands, the time limit being a direction to the officer rather than a limit on the demand
options.misconception: reads a limitation provision as internal housekeeping, when the Act attaches a stated consequence to missing the date
options.why: The Act does not leave the consequence to be argued about afterwards. It says in terms what happens once the date passes: the proceedings are over. A limit with a stated consequence written beside it is not advice to the officer.

options.text: The order stands for the tax, only the penalty falling away with the delay
options.misconception: splits an order that the provision treats as one thing
options.why: What is concluded is the adjudication proceeding itself, and the tax is determined by that proceeding just as the penalty is. Nothing in it survives to support a demand for the tax on its own.

options.text: Nothing can be demanded — the proceedings closed by themselves when the three years ran out
options.why: The Act makes these time limits real rather than advisory. Where an adjudication order is not issued within three years in a section 73 case, or within five years in a section 74 case, the adjudication proceedings are deemed to be concluded. That happened here on 31 December 2026, before the order was written, so the order made in April 2027 is of no effect and nothing can be recovered under it.
keywords: the adjudication proceedings are deemed to be concluded
not issued within three years in a section 73 case
the order made in April 2027 is of no effect

options.text: The order stands, provided the Commissioner condones the delay
options.misconception: borrows the extension machinery of the newer demand provision into a section that has none
options.why: Extension of an adjudication deadline by a superior officer belongs to the demand provision for 2024-25 onwards, and even there it has to be granted before the period expires. For an earlier year there is nothing to condone with; when the period ends the proceedings end with it.

citation.ref: Section 75(10) read with sections 73(10) and 74(10)

items.scenario: A notice for the financial year 2022-23 was served on a Kanpur company in time and on the non-fraud footing. The annual return for that year fell due on 31 December 2023, so the order had to be passed by 31 December 2026. The adjudicating officer, held up by a transfer, passed it on 20 April 2027. The order confirms ₹6 lakh of tax and the department now asks the company to pay up.

items.stem: What may the officer do about that ₹2.5 lakh?

options.text: Ask her to pay or explain, and on silence recover it without any show cause notice at all
options.why: Self-assessed tax shown in a return under section 39 that stays unpaid, and the interest on it, is recovered directly under section 79, and no notice under section 73 or 74 is needed for it. The expression takes in the tax on outward supplies furnished under section 37 that never reached the section 39 return, which is exactly this gap. Because such a gap can have an innocent cause, the officer first communicates it and asks for payment or an explanation within a stated time, and moves to recovery only where the person neither pays nor explains.
keywords: Self-assessed tax shown in a return

options.text: Recover it under the recovery provisions at once, with no communication first
options.misconception: reads the absence of a show cause notice as the absence of any step before recovery
options.why: The provision removes the adjudication, not the fairness. A gap between the two returns often has a harmless cause — a typing slip, or a supply reported late in one return whose tax was paid on time through the other — so a communication asking for payment or an explanation comes first, and recovery follows only on silence.

options.text: Issue a show cause notice and adjudicate it, since every demand starts with one
options.misconception: assumes adjudication is the only road to a demand, when tax the person has already admitted needs no determination
options.why: Adjudication exists to determine an amount that is in dispute. Here the trader has declared the liability herself, so there is nothing left to determine and the Act sends it straight to recovery.

options.text: Nothing until the annual return, where the two monthly returns are reconciled
options.misconception: postpones a live liability to a reconciliation, when the tax is already admitted and already overdue
options.why: The annual return is where differences are reported, not where the liability arises. The tax on these outward supplies fell due with the monthly return, and interest has been running on it since.

citation.ref: Section 75(12) read with sections 37, 39 and 79

items.scenario: A Ranchi trader's statement of outward supplies for a month shows tax of ₹4 lakh. Her summary return for the same month shows and pays ₹1.5 lakh, and nothing was said anywhere about the difference. The officer wants the ₹2.5 lakh and asks whether he must first put her on notice and adjudicate it.

items.stem: Can that second penalty be imposed?

options.text: Yes — section 122 is a separate code of offences carrying its own penalties
options.misconception: reads the two provisions as independent, when one of them expressly bars the other once it has been used
options.why: Section 122 is indeed a separate list, and that is precisely why the bar had to be written. It stops one short payment being charged twice by moving between the two provisions.

options.text: No, but only because the first order has become final
options.misconception: ties the bar to finality, when it applies from the moment the first penalty is imposed
options.why: The bar works on the imposition, not on the expiry of appeal time. A second penalty would be equally barred while the first order was still under appeal, and it would still be barred if the appeal reduced the first penalty.

options.text: No — a penalty already imposed in the demand order shuts out any other for the same act
options.why: Once the demand order itself has carried a penalty under section 73 or section 74, the Act allows no penalty for the same act or omission to be laid on that person anywhere else in it. The short payment is one act, it has already been penalised in the order, and a second penalty under section 122 cannot be added on top of it. What the officer is describing as two different things is one act looked at twice.
keywords: no penalty for the same act or omission
a second penalty under section 122 cannot be added

options.text: Yes, so long as the second penalty is for a different amount
options.misconception: reads the bar as being about the size of the second penalty rather than about the act it punishes
options.why: The bar is on a second penalty for the same act, whatever figure is put on it. Changing the amount does not turn one short payment into two acts.

citation.ref: Section 75(13) read with section 122

items.scenario: An order confirms ₹5 lakh of tax against a Vadodara company and imposes the penalty the demand section carries. A month later the same officer proposes a further penalty under section 122 on the same short payment, on the footing that the two provisions punish different things and the company should feel both.

items.stem: What can he do?

options.text: Nothing until the usual period is over, that period being fixed by the Act
options.misconception: reads the three months as an absolute entitlement, when the officer may shorten it on written reasons
options.why: The three months is the ordinary position and the Act itself provides the exception. What the exception costs the officer is a reason written down, which is what makes the shortened period reviewable later.

options.text: Shorten the period, but recovery is confined to the assets of the Rajasthan registration
options.misconception: treats each State registration as a separate debtor, when recovery reaches the same person's other registrations
options.why: Separate registrations of one entity are distinct persons for charging tax on supplies between them. They are not separate debtors for paying it, and recovery may be made from the defaulter's distinct persons in other States, so Gujarat is squarely within reach.

options.text: Require payment sooner than usual, with his reasons written down, and later reach the Gujarat registration as well
options.why: The ordinary rule is that an amount payable under an order is to be paid within three months from the date of service of the order. That period can be cut down, though: an officer who thinks a shorter one expedient in the interest of revenue may name it, so long as he writes his reasons down before he does. If the money still does not come, recovery runs through one or more modes — deducting it from money owed to the defaulter, detaining and selling its goods, requiring a third party who owes it money to pay the Government instead, and attaching and selling its property — and it may be made from its distinct persons registered in other States as well.
keywords: within three months from the date of service of the order
expedient in the interest of revenue
from its distinct persons registered in other States

options.text: Attach the property straight away, a risk to revenue letting recovery begin before any period has run
options.misconception: confuses the power to shorten the payment period with a power to skip it altogether
options.why: Even where the revenue looks at risk, what the officer does under these sections is fix a shorter period and record why. Recovery starts on default within that shorter period. A provisional attachment during proceedings is a different power in a different section, with its own conditions and its own limits.

citation.ref: Sections 78 and 79(1), read with section 25(4) and (5)

items.scenario: An order confirming ₹40 lakh is served on a Jaipur company on 10 May 2026. The officer has information that the company is shifting its stock out of Rajasthan and winding up there, and that it holds a second registration in Gujarat under the same permanent account number. He wants the money before the usual time is up, and he wants to know how far his reach goes if it does not come.

items.stem: Which of the two movements needs an e-way bill?

options.text: Only the fabric, an e-way bill going with a delivery challan rather than with a tax invoice
options.misconception: ties the bill to one kind of document, when it attaches to the movement and reads its value off whichever document covers it
options.why: The rule looks at the movement of goods and takes the figure from the invoice, the bill of supply or the delivery challan, whichever the consignment travels on. Which document is used changes where the number comes from, not whether a bill is needed.

options.text: The chairs do and the fabric does not
options.why: A bill is needed before a movement of goods whose consignment value exceeds ₹50,000, and consignment value is the figure shown in the invoice, the bill of supply or the delivery challan, including the tax charged on it. The chairs are ₹48,000 with 18 per cent added, so the consignment value is ₹56,640 and the movement is above the line. The fabric travels on a delivery challan with no tax on it, its consignment value is ₹48,000, and it stays inside ₹50,000 — and because the job worker is in the same State, the rule that ignores value for job work across a State border never reaches it.
keywords: including the tax charged on it

options.text: Both, job work always needing a bill whatever the value
options.misconception: applies the rule written for job work across a State border to a job worker inside the same State
options.why: The rule that removes the value floor is written for goods sent by a principal in one State or Union territory to a job worker in another. A despatch to a job worker down the road is on the ordinary footing and the threshold applies to it in the usual way.

options.text: Neither, both consignments being ₹48,000
options.misconception: reads the threshold against the taxable value, when consignment value takes in the tax charged on it
options.why: The figure for this rule is the amount on the document with the tax added, not the taxable value underneath it. Two consignments with the same taxable value can fall on opposite sides of the line depending on the rate they carry.

citation.ref: Rule 138(1) with the explanation on the meaning of consignment value

items.scenario: A Kanpur furniture dealer sends office chairs to a buyer in Gujarat. The invoice shows a taxable value of ₹48,000 with integrated tax at 18 per cent on top of it. On the same morning he sends fabric worth ₹48,000 on a delivery challan to a job worker in his own State, with no tax charged. His despatch clerk says neither movement needs an e-way bill, both being ₹48,000 jobs.

items.stem: How many of the three movements actually need one?

options.text: Only the jewellery, its value being far above the line
options.misconception: gets the exemption exactly backwards — value is the one thing that does not matter for these goods
options.why: The jewellery is the clearest of the three. Articles of that chapter are named among the goods for which no bill is required, and being worth ₹9 lakh rather than ₹9,000 makes no difference whatever to that.

options.text: Only the port movement, the other two being ordinary commercial despatches
options.misconception: picks out the customs-related movement as the obvious exception and misses that the list is longer than customs
options.why: The customs movement is on the list, but so are the goods themselves in one case and the mode of carriage in another. Reading the list as a customs concession would leave both of the other two wrongly inside the rule.

options.text: None of the three
options.why: Each of them sits in the list of things the rules put outside the requirement, and value has nothing to do with any of them. Jewellery, goldsmiths' and silversmiths' wares and other articles of Chapter 71 are on that list, other than imitation jewellery. Goods being moved by a non-motorised conveyance are on it, which covers the handcart. So are goods on their way from a customs port or airport to an inland container depot, or to a container freight station, where customs will clear them. States may also notify areas inside which movements need no bill at all.

options.text: All three, no exemption applying once the value is above ₹50,000
options.misconception: reads the threshold as the only gate, when a separate list takes named goods and named movements out altogether
options.why: The threshold decides when the rule bites on goods it covers. A different provision lists goods and movements the rule does not cover at all, and for those the value is beside the point.

citation.ref: Rule 138(14) with the annexure listing goods needing no e-way bill

items.scenario: A Jaipur jeweller has three movements on one day. Gold necklaces worth ₹9 lakh go by car to an exhibition in Delhi. A porter wheels ₹80,000 of showroom fittings across two streets on a handcart. And an imported consignment travels from Mundra port to an inland container depot for clearance by customs. The office manager sets about generating three e-way bills.

items.stem: Is the e-way bill in existence, and who completes it?

options.text: Not yet, and only the supplier can complete it — a transporter cannot generate a bill
options.misconception: assumes generation belongs to the supplier alone, when the rules put it on the transporter in exactly this situation
options.why: The rules expressly allow the registered person to leave generation to the road transporter, giving the transporter's details in place of the vehicle number. The transporter then raises the bill from the information already sitting on the portal.

options.text: Yes, and the transporter has nothing to do, the consignment being under ₹1 lakh
options.misconception: invents a second threshold, when above fifty thousand rupees there is only one line and it has been crossed
options.why: There is no ₹1 lakh step anywhere in this rule. The single line is ₹50,000 of consignment value, and at ₹90,000 the movement is inside the requirement in full, transport details and all.

options.text: Not yet — the transport half is missing, and the transporter supplies it and generates the bill
options.why: The form has two halves. Part A carries the parties, the place of delivery, the document, the value and the HSN, and the registered person causing the movement furnishes it. Part B carries the transport document number and the vehicle number, and it is furnished by the person actually moving the goods. Where the registered person does not generate the bill himself and hands the goods to a road transporter, he furnishes the transporter's details instead, and the transporter generates the e-way bill on the strength of what is already in Part A. The bill exists only once Part B has been entered.
keywords: Part A carries the parties, the place of delivery
Part B carries the transport document number
the transporter generates the e-way bill

options.text: Yes — the bill exists as soon as the first half is filled in, and the vehicle number is added afterwards for convenience
options.misconception: treats the transport half as a detail added to an existing bill, when the bill does not come into being without it
options.why: Filling in the first half alone produces a slip with a temporary number, which is a placeholder and not an e-way bill. The bill and its number come into existence only when the transport details go in.

citation.ref: Rule 138(1) to (3) with Form GST EWB-01, Part A and Part B

items.scenario: A registered supplier in Surat has a ₹90,000 consignment to send to Nagpur. On the portal he fills in the parties, the place of delivery, the invoice details, the value and the HSN, then hands the goods to a road transporter and does nothing further. He assumes the bill is now in existence and that the vehicle number can be added by anybody later.

items.stem: Can Girish pay under the composition scheme in Meghalaya this year?

options.text: Yes, once the Assam registration is surrendered, because the ceiling is tested State by State on the turnover earned in that State
options.misconception: measures the eligibility figure per registration when the section measures it per Permanent Account Number
options.why: Turnover in a State is a real idea in this scheme, but it is the base the tax is calculated on, not the gate that lets a person in. Eligibility is tested on the all-India figure for the Permanent Account Number, which is why a person with shops in four States cannot compound in the smallest of them. Surrendering the Assam registration would not rewrite the preceding year either — the test looks back at a year that has already happened.

options.text: No. The figure to test is ₹82,00,000, and in Meghalaya the ceiling is ₹75 lakh
options.why: The gate in section 10(1) is not the turnover of one registration. It is aggregate turnover of the preceding financial year on an all India basis for every registration held against the same Permanent Account Number, so ₹60,00,000 and ₹22,00,000 are added and the figure under test is ₹82,00,000. Meghalaya is one of the eight Special Category States where the limit is ₹75 lakh, and ₹82,00,000 is past it. The plan fails a second time over: where several registered persons share a Permanent Account Number, none of them may opt unless all of them do, so compounding in one State while filing ordinary returns in another was never open to him.
keywords: aggregate turnover of the preceding financial year on an all India basis
one of the eight Special Category States where the limit is ₹75 lakh

options.text: No, and for a plainer reason: a person holding more than one registration can never pay under the composition scheme at all
options.misconception: hardens the rule that registrations under one Permanent Account Number must opt together into a bar on holding more than one
options.why: Nothing in section 10 shuts out a person with registrations in several States. What the proviso says is that they move together — either all of them opt or none does. A manufacturer with units in three States, each well inside the limit and the all-India total inside it too, may compound in all three. Girish fails on the figure, not on the shape of his business.

options.text: Yes. ₹82,00,000 is inside the ₹1.5 crore that the notification allows, and it is the notified figure and not the one in the section that governs
options.misconception: takes the headline figure out of the notification and misses that the same notification sets a lower one for eight named States
options.why: The notification did two things in one breath. It lifted section 10(1)'s fifty lakh rupees to ₹1.5 crore for most of the country, and it set a shorter figure for eight States named in it. A dealer in Maharashtra, or for that matter in Assam, is right to ask whether he is within the ₹1.5 crore limit. A dealer registered in Meghalaya is asking the wrong question, because his State is in the shorter list. Reading the headline and stopping there loses the half of the notification that decides this case.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) with its provisos, read with the composition turnover limits notified under Notification No. 14/2019 CT dated 07.03.2019

items.scenario: Girish Hardware holds two GST registrations against one Permanent Account Number. The Meghalaya registration had a turnover of ₹60,00,000 in the preceding financial year and the Assam one had ₹22,00,000. Both sell goods only, neither makes an inter-State outward supply, and nothing either sells is outside the levy. Girish wants to pay under the composition scheme for goods on the Meghalaya registration this year and file ordinary returns in Assam. His accountant says the figure to test is the ₹60,00,000 earned in Meghalaya, and that it sits below every limit anyone quotes.

items.stem: What is the tax for the year, and what becomes of the accountant's other two proposals?

options.text: ₹70,000, and both of the other proposals are dropped
options.why: A manufacturer in the scheme pays one per cent of the turnover in State, including exempt supplies — half of it central tax and half State tax — because that expression is defined to take in exempt supplies made within the State, so the charge falls on ₹70,00,000 and not on ₹58,00,000. The other two proposals die on one sub-section between them: a person paying under this scheme neither may collect the tax from customers nor claim any input tax credit. The ₹70,000 comes out of Vasant's own margin, and the ₹9,000 on consumables is a cost of running the workshop rather than a credit against anything.
keywords: one per cent of the turnover in State, including exempt supplies
neither may collect the tax from customers nor claim any input tax credit

options.misconception: reaches for the restaurant rate, which belongs to a different clause of the same section
options.why: Five per cent is the effective rate for a supplier of restaurant service, and six per cent belongs to the separate scheme for suppliers of services other than restaurant service. A maker of steel shelving is in neither. His rate is one per cent, and the work in this question is which turnover that one per cent is applied to, not which rate it is.

options.text: ₹58,000, the exempt supplies falling outside the base, with the other two proposals dropped
options.misconception: applies the trader's computation base to a manufacturer, when the scheme uses two different bases and which one applies turns on what the person is
options.why: There are two bases here and they are not interchangeable. For a trader — "other suppliers" in the section — the charge falls on the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State, so for a trader the exempt supplies are left out of the base. A manufacturer is not in that clause. His base is turnover in State as the definition writes it, and that definition takes exempt supplies in. Borrowing the trader's base costs ₹12,000 of tax on these figures and more on a bigger exempt line.
keywords: the charge falls on the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State
for a trader the exempt supplies are left out of the base
