options.text: ₹70,000, shown on the invoice as one per cent so the customers bear it, and then reduced by the ₹9,000 of input tax
options.misconception: treats the composition amount as an ordinary tax that can be passed forward on an invoice and set off against credit
options.why: The scheme is a bargain and both halves of it bite. What the supplier gives up is the right to charge tax onward and the right to take credit on his inputs; what he gets is a small flat percentage and a light return. A composition supplier who prints tax on his invoice is collecting something he is not authorised to collect, and his buyer gets no credit for it in any event, because the document is not a tax invoice.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a) and 10(4), read with section 2(112) and explanation 2 to section 10 for turnover in State, and rule 7 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for the rates

items.scenario: Vasant Metals makes steel shelving, is registered in Gujarat and pays under the composition scheme for goods. Its turnover in the State for the year is ₹70,00,000, of which ₹12,00,000 is exempt supplies. The accountant proposes three things at once: leave the exempt ₹12,00,000 out of the computation, print "GST 1%" on the invoices so that the customers carry the cost, and set the ₹9,000 of input tax on the workshop's consumables against what is left.

items.stem: Is that split right?

options.text: No. The whole ₹90,00,000 is taxable, but as a supply of goods, a flat being property that is sold rather than a service that is performed
options.misconception: classifies by what changes hands at the end instead of by the entry in Schedule II that governs the activity
options.why: Schedule II exists precisely because the ordinary instinct about goods and services gives the wrong answer in cases like this one. It says what a listed activity is to be treated as, and for construction of a complex or building it says services. Getting the head right matters beyond tidiness: the time of supply, the rate and the credit rules that follow all run off that classification.

options.text: No, the other way about. None of it is taxable, because the sale was completed only after the certificate had been issued
options.misconception: dates the test at the moment the sale is completed instead of at the receipt of the consideration
options.why: The paragraph never asks when the deed was signed or when possession changed hands. It asks when the money came in, measured against the certificate or first occupation. A builder who takes bookings during construction and registers the conveyance a year after completion is inside the paragraph for the whole price, and a builder who sells a finished flat outright for cash is outside it. The date of the sale decides nothing here.

options.text: No. The whole ₹90,00,000 is consideration for a supply of services
options.why: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II treats the construction of a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer as a supply of services, and lets a transaction out of it only where the entire consideration has been received after the completion certificate or after first occupation, whichever comes first. The word doing the work is "entire". Here ₹27,00,000 was received while construction was running, which is enough to hold the whole transaction inside the paragraph, and the whole sale is a supply of services. The later instalment does not change character by arriving after the certificate; it is part of the price of the same supply.
keywords: a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer
the entire consideration has been received after the completion certificate
the whole sale is a supply of services

options.text: Yes. Each instalment is tested on its own date, so the money that came in before the certificate is taxed and the money that came after is not
options.misconception: reads the carve-out as splitting one price into a taxed part and an untaxed part, when it tests the whole consideration once
options.why: Splitting by instalment would make the tax on a flat depend on the builder's payment schedule, and two identical flats sold on identical terms would carry different tax because one buyer paid faster. The paragraph asks a single question about the whole price, and it is a question with only two answers: either every rupee came after the certificate or first occupation, or the transaction stays a supply of services. There is no third position in which some of it is out.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II

items.scenario: Sarita Constructions sells a flat in its Pune project for ₹90,00,000. The buyer pays ₹27,00,000 while the block is still going up, and the remaining ₹63,00,000 three weeks after the completion certificate is issued by the competent authority. The builder's clerk proposes to charge GST on the ₹27,00,000 and to treat the ₹63,00,000 as the sale of a finished flat, which he says is outside GST altogether.

items.stem: How should each be treated?

options.text: Both are outside GST, the certificate having been issued before either matter was settled
options.misconception: treats the certificate as a date after which nothing about the project can be taxed, instead of as the test applied to when the consideration was received
options.why: The certificate is not an amnesty. It fixes the moment against which each transaction's receipts are measured, and a receipt that came before it was taxable when it came. Read the other way, a builder could take deposits through two years of construction and wipe the tax on all of them by finishing the building — which is the outcome the paragraph is written to prevent.

options.text: Both are taxable, a builder selling flats supplying a construction service in every case until the project is closed
options.misconception: ignores the exception in paragraph 5(b) and the Schedule III entry sitting under it
options.why: There is a real category of sale that GST does not reach, and this is it. Where the entire consideration comes after the certificate or after first occupation, the builder is selling a finished building, which the law puts beside the sale of land as something that is neither goods nor services. Taxing flat 12 would tax a transaction Parliament put outside the levy.

options.text: Flat 12 is outside GST, and the tax on flat 19's ₹5,00,000 is simply reversed in the return as tax that was never due
options.misconception: unwinds a liability that had genuinely arisen instead of using the document the Act provides for reducing it
options.why: The distinction is not bookkeeping fussiness. Tax on the ₹5,00,000 was correctly charged when the money came in, and what has happened since is that the supply has been cancelled. The Act has one instrument for that — a credit note, which carries its own time limit and its own condition about the recipient's credit. Treating it as tax never due would let a liability disappear with nothing linking it to the original invoice.

options.text: Flat 12 is outside GST; the ₹5,00,000 on flat 19 was taxable when it was received, and the refund goes out under a credit note
options.why: Flat 12 answers the exception in paragraph 5(b) exactly — the entire consideration came after the certificate — which drops it into paragraph 5 of Schedule III, the sale of a completed building, and Schedule III activities are neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Flat 19 is a different animal. The ₹5,00,000 came in before completion, when the transaction was a supply of services, and tax fell due on it then. Cancelling afterwards does not reach back and unmake that: Meru issues a credit note under section 34 and adjusts its liability forward. What separates the two flats is when the money arrived, not when the paperwork closed.
keywords: the sale of a completed building
neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III and section 34

items.scenario: Two things happen at Meru Builders in the month after the completion certificate for its Nashik project is issued. Flat 12 is sold outright for ₹55,00,000, the buyer paying the whole price after the certificate. And the buyer of flat 19, who had booked it before the certificate and paid ₹5,00,000 then, cancels and asks for his money back. The accountant proposes to treat the two alike — neither taxable, because both were settled after the certificate was in hand.

items.stem: Where is each supply placed, and which tax does Meghna Events charge?

options.text: Goa, Jaipur and Colombo — each supply placed where its event was actually held
options.misconception: applies the venue rule to every recipient, which is the rule for admission to an event and not the rule for organising one
options.why: Two neighbouring sub-sections do different work. Admission to an event goes to the venue for everybody, because the person buying a ticket is consuming the event where it stands. Organising an event goes to the venue only where the recipient is unregistered; where he is registered the supply follows him, because the business receiving the service is consuming it at its own place. The clerk has applied the ticket-holder's rule to a business client, and it moves two of the three answers.

options.text: Rajasthan, Jaipur and Gujarat — central and State tax on the first two, integrated tax on the third
options.why: Organising an event, and the services around it, is a specific case, and it asks first whether the recipient is registered. Sundar Tools is, so the place of supply is Rajasthan, the location of the registered recipient, and Goa never enters the answer. The wedding client is not registered, so it is Jaipur, where the event is actually held, and his Mumbai home never enters it. Ratnam Polymers is registered, so the place of supply is Gujarat even though the event sits outside India — the fallback that sends a foreign event back to the recipient's location is written for the unregistered case, and a registered recipient never leaves his own location in the first place. With the supplier in Rajasthan, the first two supplies stay inside the State and the third crosses a line.
keywords: the place of supply is Rajasthan, the location of the registered recipient
it is Jaipur, where the event is actually held
the place of supply is Gujarat even though the event sits outside India

options.text: Rajasthan, Mumbai and Gujarat — each supply placed at the recipient's own location
options.misconception: treats an unregistered person's home address as his location for a specific case that names the venue instead
options.why: An unregistered recipient does have a location for the general rule, taken from the address on record. But this is not the general rule. For organisation of an event the section names the venue for an unregistered recipient in terms, and a specific case displaces the general one wherever it applies. Mumbai would matter if the same client had bought consultancy; it does not matter for the wedding.

options.text: Rajasthan, Jaipur and Rajasthan — the Colombo event coming back to the organiser, there being no place of supply outside India
options.misconception: sends an event held abroad back to the supplier's location, when the provision names the recipient's
options.why: The section does refuse to place a supply in Colombo, and for a good reason: this chapter places supplies where both parties are in India, and a Sri Lankan venue is no use to it. But what it falls back to is the recipient's location, not the supplier's. On these facts the recipient is registered anyway, so the answer was Gujarat from the start and the fallback is never reached.

citation.ref: Section 12(7)

items.scenario: Meghna Events is registered in Rajasthan and runs three jobs in one quarter. It organises a distributor meet at a resort in Goa for Sundar Tools, which is registered in Rajasthan. It organises a wedding at a hotel in Jaipur for a private individual who is not registered and lives in Mumbai. And it organises a dealer awards night in Colombo for Ratnam Polymers, which is registered in Gujarat. The billing clerk proposes to place every supply where the event was held.

items.stem: Where are the three transport services placed?

options.text: Haryana, Delhi and Tamil Nadu
options.why: Transportation of goods, mail and courier included, is put on the recipient rather than on the route. Supplied to a registered person, the place of supply is that person's own location, so Haryana takes the Coimbatore run even though no part of it touches Haryana. The student is not registered, so it is Delhi, where the goods are handed over for their transportation, and Nagpur is only where they stop. The export consignment is placed in Tamil Nadu for the same reason as the first, Konar Exports being registered there. The proviso that once sent a consignment leaving India to its foreign destination has been omitted, so a destination outside India no longer moves the answer while supplier and recipient are both here.
keywords: Supplied to a registered person, the place of supply is that person's own location, so Haryana
it is Delhi, where the goods are handed over for their transportation
The export consignment is placed in Tamil Nadu

options.text: Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and the Netherlands — each supply placed where the goods end their journey
options.misconception: places a transport service at the destination, which is what the section deliberately does not do
options.why: The destination is the one thing this sub-section never asks about. It reads the recipient's registration and, failing that, the point of handover — nothing else. Placing transport at its destination would also produce an answer no GST law can use in the third case, since Rotterdam is not a State or Union territory in which a supply can be placed.

options.text: Haryana, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu — the recipient's location where he is registered and the destination where he is not
options.misconception: gets the registered half of the rule and substitutes the destination for the handover point in the unregistered half
options.why: The unregistered half turns on where the goods are handed over for their transportation, which is the moment the transporter takes charge of them. For a parcel booked over a counter in Delhi that is Delhi, whatever address is written on it. The rule is built that way because the handover is a fact the transporter can see at the time he issues the document, whereas a destination can be changed in transit.

options.text: Delhi in all three, that being where the transporter is located
options.misconception: falls back to the supplier's location, which is the last resort in the general rule and has no place in a specific one
options.why: The supplier's location is reached only under the general rule, and only where the recipient is unregistered and no address is on record for him. Transportation of goods is a specific case with its own two-line answer, so the general rule is never consulted. The coincidence that Delhi is the right answer in the second case comes from the handover point, not from where Ashwa Carriers sits.

citation.ref: Section 12(8), the proviso to which stands omitted

items.scenario: Ashwa Carriers, registered in Delhi, moves three consignments in March. Goods go from its Delhi warehouse to Coimbatore for Vega Fittings, which is registered in Haryana. A parcel is booked over the counter in Delhi and carried to Nagpur for a student who is not registered. And a consignment is picked up in Chennai and carried to Rotterdam for Konar Exports, which is registered in Tamil Nadu. The billing clerk proposes to place each supply where the consignment ends up.

items.stem: Which of the two must register?

options.text: Pritam alone
options.why: Section 24 does open with persons making any inter-State taxable supply, but the Government has since handed the ordinary threshold back to two classes of them by notification — inter-State supplies of taxable services, and inter-State supplies of notified handicraft and hand-made goods. Nabin's lamps fall in the second, so he keeps the ₹20 lakh limit, ₹10 lakh in the four States named beside it, and stays off the register at ₹15,00,000. Nothing was restored for ordinary goods, so the Kolkata trader making inter-State supplies of ordinary goods must register before his first such sale, whatever ₹8,00,000 looks like next to a threshold.
keywords: the Kolkata trader making inter-State supplies of ordinary goods must register

options.text: Nabin alone
options.misconception: has the restoration the wrong way round, thinking the strict first-rupee rule survives for services and has been relaxed for goods
options.why: The relaxation covers inter-State supply of taxable services and inter-State supply of notified handicraft and hand-made goods; it is ordinary goods that keep the strict rule. A consultant in Pune selling ₹12,00,000 of advice into three States need not register, and a trader selling ₹8,00,000 of fittings into one State must. That is the shape a student has to hold, because it is counter-intuitive in exactly this way.

options.text: Neither, until each crosses ₹20 lakh
options.misconception: applies the restored threshold to every kind of inter-State supply of goods rather than to the notified classes only
options.why: The threshold was put back for a named list, and bathroom fittings are not on it. What makes this worth being careful about is that the person who gets it wrong does not register at all, and unregistered supply carries the tax, the interest and a penalty together once it is found.

options.text: Both of them
options.misconception: reads the opening words of section 24 without the notifications that have taken two classes of supplier back out of it
options.why: Section 24 as printed would put every craftsman selling one lamp across a State line on the register with monthly returns for life, and that is the outcome the notifications were issued to prevent. The list in the section is a starting point that has been cut back four times, and reading the section without them gets two of the six answers in this area wrong.

citation.ref: Section 24(i) read with Notification No. 10/2017-Integrated Tax and Notification No. 3/2018-Integrated Tax

items.scenario: Two people in Kolkata, each far below every threshold, ask whether they must register for 2026-27. Nabin makes brass lamps that are notified handicraft goods and sells ₹15,00,000 of them to buyers in Bihar and Odisha. Pritam trades in packaged bathroom fittings and sells ₹8,00,000 of them to buyers in Jharkhand. Their common accountant says section 24 puts anybody who crosses a State line on the register from the first rupee, so both must register.

items.stem: Which of the two must register?

options.text: Both of them
options.misconception: knows the inward-supply rule and misses the exemption written for the supplier on the other side of it
options.why: Without the exemption, every small provider of a service taxed in the recipient's hands would be registered for the sake of filing nil returns forever. The notification was issued to stop that, and it does its work through section 23, which is a route out of registration rather than a threshold inside it.

options.text: Neither, both being below ₹20 lakh
options.misconception: treats the threshold as the only question, when section 24 lists persons for whom turnover is beside the point
options.why: Turnover decides who must register only after the section 24 list has been read, because that list applies irrespective of turnover. Kishan is on it at ₹7,00,000. Suraksha is off it, but for a reason of its own rather than because ₹18,00,000 is a small figure.

options.text: Kishan alone
options.why: The two sit on opposite sides of one idea. A person liable to pay tax under reverse charge on his inward supplies must register whatever his turnover, and the advocate's fee puts Kishan there at ₹7,00,000 — the liability is his, and a person with a liability has to have a return to declare it in. Suraksha is the mirror image: everything it sells is taxed in the recipient's hands, and a supplier whose outward supplies are all taxed that way is exempted by section 23. One warning travels with that exemption — the notification does not reach a supplier of metal scrap, who is back on the ordinary rules however his tax is collected.
keywords: liable to pay tax under reverse charge on his inward supplies must register
a supplier whose outward supplies are all taxed that way is exempted by section 23
the notification does not reach a supplier of metal scrap

options.text: Suraksha alone
options.misconception: turns the rule round and registers the person whose supplies bear reverse charge instead of the person who has to pay it
options.why: Registration follows the liability, and under reverse charge the liability has moved to the recipient. Suraksha collects nothing and owes nothing on these supplies, which is exactly why an exemption was written for it; Kishan owes tax on a service he bought, which is exactly why no threshold protects him. Getting this pair round the wrong way leaves the person who owes money unregistered and puts the person who owes none on monthly returns.

citation.ref: Section 24(iii) read with section 9(3), and section 23(2) with Notification No. 5/2017- Central Tax dated 19 June 2017 as amended

items.scenario: Two unregistered businesses in Indore. Kishan Stationers turns over ₹7,00,000 a year and pays an advocate ₹40,000 for a recovery notice, the tax on which the law puts on Kishan as the recipient. Suraksha Guards supplies manpower security services to companies only, ₹18,00,000 in the year, and the whole tax on those supplies is payable by the companies that receive them. Both ask whether they can stay off the register.

items.stem: Must Sharada register?

options.text: Yes, because the relaxation is for services supplied through an operator and she is selling goods
options.misconception: stops at the first notification and does not reach the later one that extended the threshold to intra-State supplies of goods
options.why: The services notification came first and for a while that answer was right. A later one extended the same relief to a person making intra-State supplies of goods through an operator. The remaining line is not goods against services — it is inside the State against across a State line, and Sharada's candles never leave Madhya Pradesh.

options.text: No, because the operator's tax collection at source already accounts for the tax on her sales, so nothing is left for her to declare
options.misconception: mistakes collection at source for payment of the tax on the supply, when it is only money parked in the supplier's ledger against it
options.why: Collection at source is not the tax on the supply. It is a small percentage the operator holds back and pays over, which lands in the supplier's electronic cash ledger for him to use against his own liability once he is registered. It never discharges the liability by itself, and a supplier who has to register is not relieved of returns because the operator collected something. Sharada's answer is right, but not for this reason.

options.text: No. She may stay off the register while these facts hold
options.why: Section 24 does list a person supplying through an electronic commerce operator that collects tax at source, but that limb has been cut back twice by notification. The threshold was handed back first to a supplier of services through such an operator, and then to a person making intra-State supplies of goods through one. Sharada is in the second: her buyers are all in her own State, so she may stay unregistered while ₹18,00,000 is inside the ₹20 lakh limit that applies to a supplier of goods there. Sell one box across a State line and the answer flips, because the restoration is written for intra-State supply alone.
keywords: a person supplying through an electronic commerce operator that collects tax at source
a person making intra-State supplies of goods through one

options.text: Yes, from the first rupee, because she supplies through an operator that collects tax at source
options.misconception: reads the section 24 limb as it was first enacted and misses both notifications that have narrowed it
options.why: That was the position when the section was written, and it made a marketplace unreachable for anybody too small to run monthly returns. The Government has since put the threshold back for services through an operator and then for intra-State supply of goods through one, which between them cover most people selling from home. Reading the section without the notifications registers people the law has deliberately let alone.

citation.ref: Section 24(ix) read with Notification No. 65/2017-Central Tax and Notification No. 34/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

items.scenario: Sharada makes scented candles at home in Indore and sells ₹18,00,000 of them in the year. Every buyer is in Madhya Pradesh and every sale goes through a marketplace app that collects tax at source on what it pays her. Her cousin sells consultancy through the same app and has been told he need not register. Sharada assumes the opposite must apply to her, because section 24 names people who supply through such an operator.

items.stem: What is wrong with the broker's account?

options.text: Nothing — the broker has it right on all three
options.misconception: takes the margin of dumping as the duty and treats a notification as self-contained once issued
options.why: Three separate things are wrong with that. The lesser of the two margins governs the amount. The duty is additional to every other duty on the goods. And the section keeps the notification under Parliament's eye and hands the whole Customs Act machinery to the collection of it, so the date for the rate of duty, the assessment, a refund and an appeal all work here as they do on ordinary duty.

options.text: Only the ₹90 a kilogram
options.misconception: applies the lesser duty rule correctly and still treats the anti-dumping duty as a substitute for the ordinary duty on the goods
options.why: Getting the quantum right is the harder half and this answer gets it. What it then misses is that the duty is additional. An importer facing an anti-dumping duty pays it on top of basic customs duty and integrated tax, which is why the trade cost of a finding is far higher than the headline figure suggests, and why the finding is worth contesting.

options.text: Only the point about standing in place of the basic customs duty
options.misconception: reads the ceiling in the section as the amount, missing that India restricts the levy to the lower of the two margins
options.why: The section sets a ceiling, not a rate: a duty not exceeding the margin of dumping. What fixes the actual figure is the rule that the duty be no more than the amount adequate to remove the injury. Where the injury margin is the smaller of the two, as it is here, it is the injury margin that is levied, and the difference between ₹90 and ₹80 is ten rupees a kilogram on every consignment.

options.text: All three points are wrong
options.why: Take the amount first. The section allows a duty not exceeding the margin of dumping, which is normal value less export price, ₹520 less ₹430, so ₹90 a kilogram is the ceiling. But India is held to the lower of the margin of dumping and the injury margin, and here the duty is ₹80 a kilogram and not ₹90. It replaces nothing: an anti-dumping duty is charged in addition to any other duty already on the goods, basic customs duty included. And the notification is not the end of it — every notification issued under the section is laid before each House of Parliament, and the machinery of the Customs Act on the date for the rate of duty, on assessment, on refunds and on appeals runs on this duty as it does on any other.
keywords: the lower of the margin of dumping and the injury margin
the duty is ₹80 a kilogram and not ₹90
in addition to any other duty already on the goods
laid before each House of Parliament

citation.ref: Section 9A(1) with sub-sections (7) and (8), and the lesser duty rule

items.scenario: The designated authority reports on a solvent imported from one country: its normal value there is ₹520 a kilogram, its export price to India is ₹430 a kilogram, and ₹80 a kilogram would be enough to remove the injury to the Indian producers. A trader who imports the solvent into the domestic tariff area is told three things by his broker — that the duty will be ₹90 a kilogram, that it will stand in place of the basic customs duty on the goods, and that the notification is the end of the matter once it is signed.

items.stem: What does Chitra pay, and how far back can the duty be made to reach?

options.text: Duty on the 10 tonnes, and the department may indeed reopen the last two years of consignments
options.misconception: treats the power to levy retrospectively as open-ended, when it is fenced by three findings and by a fixed number of days
options.why: The section lets the duty be levied retrospectively only on findings it names — a history of dumping that caused injury, or an importer who knew or should have known that the exporter was dumping and that injury would follow, together with injury caused by massive dumping of the article in a relatively short time, enough to undermine what the duty is for. Even where all of that is made out, the duty cannot be made payable from a date more than ninety days before the notification. Two years of past consignments are out of reach.
keywords: lets the duty be levied retrospectively only on findings it names
massive dumping of the article in a relatively short time
more than ninety days before the notification

options.text: Duty on the 10 tonnes cleared into the domestic tariff area, and no further back than ninety days
options.why: An article imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit, or by a unit in a special economic zone, carries no anti-dumping duty unless the notification says otherwise, and this one is silent, so the 30 tonnes that went into exported goods bear none. The section then carves out its own exception for what comes back into the country's ordinary trade: where the article is cleared as such into the domestic tariff area, or used in goods that are, the duty is imposed on that portion at the rate that applied when it was imported. Retrospective reach is a separate power with conditions of its own and a hard ceiling, and two years is beyond it on any reading.
keywords: An article imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit
the duty is imposed on that portion at the rate that applied when it was imported

options.text: No duty at all, an export oriented unit standing outside the levy whatever it does with the goods
options.misconception: reads the non-applicability as absolute and misses the exception for goods brought into the domestic tariff area
options.why: If that were right, every importer facing an anti-dumping duty would route his goods through an export oriented unit and clear them inland. The section closes that door in its own words: goods cleared as such into the home market, or used in goods that are, bear the duty on that portion, at the rate that applied on import. The exemption follows the export, not the unit's badge.

options.text: Duty on all 40 tonnes, an anti-dumping duty following the goods and not the importer
options.misconception: treats the duty as attaching to the article at import in every case, missing the exemption written for export oriented and special economic zone units
options.why: The exemption is deliberate policy rather than an oversight. A unit that imports an input and sends it straight back out as part of an exported product has not injured any domestic producer, so the duty is not levied on it. What the section then guards against is the unit becoming a duty-free door into the home market, which is why the portion cleared inland is caught.

citation.ref: Section 9A, non-applicability to export oriented units and special economic zone units, read with section 9A(3) on retrospective levy

items.scenario: An anti-dumping duty of ₹80 a kilogram is notified on a solvent on 1 September 2026, and the notification says nothing about export oriented units. Chitra Polymers, a 100 per cent export oriented unit, imports 40 tonnes after that date: 30 tonnes go into goods it exports and 10 tonnes are cleared as such into the domestic tariff area. Its consultant adds that the department can go back over every consignment Chitra imported in the previous two years, dumping being what it is.

items.stem: What is the obligation, and has the works manager got it right?

options.text: ₹3,00,00,000 by 31 July 2032, and no — ordinary shipments do not count towards it
options.why: The scheme lets capital goods in at zero customs duty, and for physical exports free of integrated tax and compensation cess as well. What is asked back is an export obligation of six times the duties, taxes and cess saved, which on ₹50,00,000 of duty saved is ₹3 crore. It has to be met within six years from the date of issue of the authorisation, so 31 July 2032 and not the working life of the machine. And the works manager has the harder half wrong: the specific obligation sits on top of what the firm was doing anyway, and nine months of business as usual discharges none of it.
keywords: an export obligation of six times the duties, taxes and cess saved
which on ₹50,00,000 of duty saved is ₹3 crore
within six years from the date of issue of the authorisation

options.text: ₹2,50,00,000 by 31 July 2032, at five times the duty saved
options.misconception: recalls the multiple wrongly, which changes the answer by half a crore on these figures
options.why: The multiple is six, and it is applied to the duties, taxes and cess saved rather than to the value of the machine — two places a candidate loses the mark. On ₹50,00,000 saved the specific obligation is ₹3 crore, and the six-year clock starts on the date the authorisation is issued, not on the date the machine lands.

options.text: ₹3,00,00,000, with no date attached, so long as the press is in use
options.misconception: reads the export obligation as open-ended, when the scheme fixes both the amount and the period
options.why: An obligation with no end date would be no obligation. The period is six years from the date the authorisation was issued, and the authorisation holder reports against it annually; falling short brings back the duty saved on the unfulfilled portion, with interest. The working life of the machine has nothing to do with it.

options.text: ₹3,00,00,000 by 31 July 2032, and yes — every export of that product counts towards it
options.misconception: takes the specific obligation as the whole of the promise and misses the average that has to be maintained beside it
options.why: Beside the specific figure stands the average export obligation of ₹4 crore, worked out from exports of the same and similar products over the preceding three licensing years, and it has to be maintained every financial year until the obligation is completed. Only what goes out above that average counts towards the specific figure. A year of shipping the usual ₹4 crore therefore moves the ₹3 crore not at all, and a firm that reads it this way discovers the shortfall at the end, with duty and interest falling due together.
keywords: the average export obligation of ₹4 crore
maintained every financial year until the obligation is completed

citation.ref: Chapter 5, EPCG scheme — specific export obligation and average export obligation

items.scenario: Lakhan Forgings takes an EPCG authorisation on 1 August 2026 and imports a press on which the duties, taxes and cess saved come to ₹50,00,000. Its exports of the same product averaged ₹4,00,00,000 a year over the preceding three licensing years and it expects to keep exporting at about that level. The works manager reads the obligation as ₹3,00,00,000 of exports at any time in the working life of the press, and says the next nine months of ordinary shipments will cover it.

items.stem: What is the position on the three points?

options.text: Domestic sourcing is open and cuts the obligation to ₹2.25 crore; importing in 2029 is not possible; and the press cannot be sold until the discharge certificate is granted
options.why: Capital goods may be sourced from a domestic manufacturer against an invalidation letter or an advance release order, and the Indian supplier picks up deemed export benefits for it. On that route the specific export obligation is 25 per cent less, so ₹2.25 crore in place of ₹3 crore. The authorisation is valid for import for twenty-four months from its date of issue and cannot be revalidated, which puts 2029 out of reach. And the machine stays under the Actual User condition until the export obligation is completed and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate is granted, so shipping the goods is not by itself enough to free it for sale.
keywords: sourced from a domestic manufacturer against an invalidation letter
the specific export obligation is 25 per cent less, so ₹2.25 crore
valid for import for twenty-four months from its date of issue and cannot be revalidated
until the export obligation is completed and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate is granted

options.text: Domestic sourcing is open but leaves the obligation at ₹3 crore; the authorisation can be revalidated for 2029; and the press may be sold once the exports are shipped
options.misconception: knows the three doors exist and has the answer wrong at each of them
options.why: Each of the three has a specific answer and this option misses all three. Indigenous sourcing carries its own reward — a quarter off the specific obligation, because the machine was bought in India rather than imported. Revalidation is not permitted under this scheme at all, unlike some neighbouring authorisations where it is allowed once. And the Actual User condition runs to the discharge certificate, not to the last shipment.

options.text: Domestic sourcing is not open at all under this scheme; the import must be made within twenty-four months; and the press may not be sold before the certificate
options.misconception: treats EPCG as an import-only scheme, when the policy provides two named routes for buying the machine in India
options.why: The scheme's own words offer indigenous sourcing, and the policy would be working against itself if it did not: a scheme meant to build manufacturing capacity that pushed every buyer abroad would be a strange one. The two routes are an invalidation letter and an advance release order, the supplier gets deemed export benefits, and the buyer's obligation drops by a quarter.

options.text: Domestic sourcing cuts the obligation to ₹2.25 crore, and the other two questions do not arise once the machine is bought in India
options.misconception: assumes the validity period and the Actual User condition are import conditions that fall away on domestic sourcing
options.why: They do not fall away. The Actual User condition attaches to the capital goods under the authorisation however they were obtained, and it runs to the discharge certificate. The twenty-four month validity is the life of the authorisation itself, which is what the firm would need if it changed its mind and went abroad after all. Buying in India changes the size of the obligation and nothing else about the conditions.

citation.ref: Chapter 5, EPCG scheme — validity for import, Actual User condition and Export Obligation Discharge Certificate, and indigenous sourcing

items.scenario: The same authorisation, issued on 1 August 2026 with ₹50,00,000 of duty saved, is in hand. Before importing, Lakhan Forgings finds an Indian maker of the same press and wants to buy from him instead. It asks two further things: it has had a slow year and would rather import in 2029 if it goes abroad after all, and a customer has offered to buy the press outright once ₹3 crore of exports have been shipped.

items.stem: How much interest under section 50 does Tarun Textiles owe?

options.text: About ₹2,959, on the whole ₹2,00,000 paid in cash
options.misconception: counts money that had already been credited to the cash ledger before the due date and lay there until the return was filed
options.why: The proviso to the rule exists for exactly this ₹50,000. An amount credited to the electronic cash ledger on or before the due date, and lying there until it is debited when the late return is filed, is left out of the base — the money reached the Government on 14 July and it was never kept waiting. Counting it charges the taxpayer for a delay in filing a form rather than a delay in paying tax, and it costs him about ₹740 here.
keywords: is left out of the base

options.text: About ₹2,219
options.why: Where the supplies of a period are declared in that period's own return, the return goes in late, and no proceedings have begun, the rule charges interest only on the part of the tax paid by debiting the electronic cash ledger, for the days the return is late, at the notified 18 per cent. So the ₹3,00,000 met from credit bears none. The ₹50,000 that had been sitting in the cash ledger since before the due date is taken out of the base by the proviso, because the Government has had that money since 14 July. That leaves ₹1,50,000 running for the thirty days from 21 July to 19 August, which comes to about ₹2,219.
keywords: only on the part of the tax paid by debiting the electronic cash ledger

options.text: About ₹7,397, on the whole ₹5,00,000 of tax declared
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross liability, which was the position before the proviso was inserted and made effective from the beginning
options.why: Interest on the gross liability was the original reading and it was undone deliberately. Credit sitting in the electronic credit ledger is tax that has already reached the Government once, in the hands of the supplier who charged it, so charging interest on the portion met from credit would collect for a delay that never happened. Only the cash portion is late in any real sense.

options.text: Nothing, the whole liability having been paid before any notice was issued
options.misconception: treats interest as a consequence of being caught rather than as compensation running from the due date
options.why: Interest under this section is automatic and self-assessed — the words are that the person pays it on his own. It runs from the day after the tax was due and stops when the tax is paid, and no notice is needed to start it. Paying up before anyone asks avoids penalty and proceedings; it does not avoid interest.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 50(1) read with rule 88B(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017 and its proviso

items.scenario: Tarun Textiles, registered in Kerala, should have filed its return for June 2026 by 20 July 2026 and filed it on 19 August 2026. The return showed tax of ₹5,00,000, of which ₹3,00,000 was paid by debiting the credit ledger and ₹2,00,000 by debiting the cash ledger. Of that cash, ₹50,000 had been deposited into the cash ledger on 14 July 2026 and sat there untouched until the return was filed. No proceedings under section 73 or section 74 had been started.

items.stem: What interest actually runs under section 50(3)?

options.text: Nothing on either, both having been reversed before anybody asked about them
options.misconception: treats reversal as undoing the wrong, when reversal is what stops the clock rather than what erases it
options.why: Reversing is the right thing to do and it is exactly what the rule expects — it is the event that ends the interest period. But the interest for the stretch between use and reversal has already accrued, and voluntary reversal does not wipe it. What voluntary reversal does buy is the avoidance of penalty and proceedings, which is a different and larger saving.

options.text: Interest on both amounts, running from the date each credit was taken
options.misconception: starts the clock at availment, when the rule starts it at utilisation
options.why: Starting at availment would charge for a period in which the Government was out of pocket by nothing at all, and on these facts it would add months to the ₹1,00,000 and create a liability on the ₹40,000 out of nothing. The rule fixes the start date precisely, and it also says how to find it where the fall in the balance came about through a return rather than through a straight debit.

options.text: About ₹4,073 on the whole ₹1,40,000 for the same fifty-nine days
options.misconception: charges the availed-but-unused credit as though taking it were the same as using it
options.why: Taking credit and using it are two events and the section names the second. Credit that sits in the ledger has cost the Government nothing, because nothing has been paid out of it; credit that has been used has discharged a liability that should have been met in cash, and that is what interest compensates for. The test is mechanical — did the ledger balance ever fall below the wrongly availed figure — and here for the ₹40,000 it did not.

options.text: About ₹2,910 on the ₹1,00,000, and nothing on the ₹40,000
options.why: The sub-section charges interest on credit wrongly availed and utilised, and the rule runs the clock from the date the wrong credit was utilised to the date it was reversed — not from the date it was taken. That is 10 January to 10 March, fifty-nine days, and ₹1,00,000 at the notified 18 per cent over that stretch comes to about ₹2,910. The ₹40,000 never became utilised at all: the rule's own Explanation says wrongly availed credit counts as used only when the ledger balance falls below it, and only to the extent it falls. Credit taken but never used carries no interest.
keywords: from the date the wrong credit was utilised to the date it was reversed
Credit taken but never used carries no interest

citation.ref: Section 50(3) read with rule 88B(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017 and its Explanation

items.scenario: The same firm, on a different question. It had taken ₹1,00,000 of credit it was not entitled to, and the balance in its credit ledger fell below that figure on 10 January 2026 when it paid a liability; it reversed the ₹1,00,000 on 10 March 2026. It had also taken ₹40,000 of credit it was not entitled to, but the balance in the credit ledger never once fell below ₹40,000 before that was reversed too. The accountant proposes to pay interest on ₹1,40,000 from the day each credit was taken.

items.stem: What has actually happened, and what follows if the partner stays silent?

options.text: It is a best judgment assessment, and an appeal is the only way to disturb it
options.misconception: confuses a notice pointing out differences with the order an officer passes when a return has not been filed at all
options.why: A best judgment assessment is what follows a person who does not file a return even after being told to. Bhavika filed its returns; what the officer is doing is checking them and asking a question. The two live in different sections and lead to different places, and treating a question as an order wastes the one chance to answer it cheaply.

options.text: It is a scrutiny, and an unanswered notice does lapse, the section carrying no consequence for silence
options.misconception: reads the absence of an order at the end of scrutiny as an absence of consequence
options.why: The consequence is not in the notice; it is in what the officer may do next. No satisfactory explanation within the period, or an accepted discrepancy that is never corrected in the return, is the trigger for an audit, a special audit, an inspection or a demand. Silence does not end the matter — it decides which of those the officer reaches for.

options.text: It is a scrutiny of returns, there is nothing yet to appeal against, and silence opens the door to heavier proceedings
options.why: The section lets the officer scrutinise a return to verify that it is correct, inform the person of the discrepancies he finds, and seek an explanation within a period not longer than thirty days. If the explanation is acceptable the matter ends there and the person is told so. Scrutiny of returns ends in no assessment order of its own, so an appeal has nothing to bite on. Staying silent past that period, or giving an explanation the officer does not accept and then not correcting the return, lets him move to an audit, a special audit, an inspection, or a demand under section 73, 74 or 74A.
keywords: inform the person of the discrepancies he finds
within a period not longer than thirty days
Scrutiny of returns ends in no assessment order of its own

options.text: It is a demand, and the tax stated in the notice is now payable
options.misconception: treats a discrepancy pointed out during scrutiny as a determined liability
options.why: Nothing has been determined. A discrepancy is a difference the officer has spotted, and it may have an innocent answer that ends the enquiry in one letter. A demand is a separate proceeding with its own notice, its own hearing and its own order, and the whole point of scrutiny is to see whether one is needed.

citation.ref: Section 61 read with rule 99 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: Bhavika Traders receives a notice from the proper officer setting out differences between the figures in two of its returns and asking for an explanation. The partner reads it as an assessment order and wants to file an appeal against it. He also thinks that if he simply says nothing, an unanswered notice will lapse of its own accord.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The order was in time and the return withdraws it, and no late fee is due because the assessment order had already taken the place of the return
options.misconception: treats the assessment order as discharging the obligation to file, when the whole mechanism is built to get the return filed
options.why: The order is a lever, not a substitute. Everything about the withdrawal machinery is designed to make the person file the return that was missing, which is why the order disappears when he does. What survives the withdrawal is expressly named: interest on the tax and late fee for the delay, both of which run on the original default and are not washed away by it.

options.text: The order was in time, but seventy-five days is too late and the order now stands
options.misconception: knows the sixty-day rule and does not know that a second window was opened behind it
options.why: A single sixty-day window was the position for years, and it produced the odd result that a person sixty-one days late was worse off than one who never filed at all, because the assessed figure hardened against him. The second window fixes that: another sixty days, bought at ₹100 a day for the delay beyond the first sixty, with the same deemed withdrawal at the end of it.

options.text: The order was in time, and the late return still withdraws it on payment of an extra late fee
options.why: Time first. Where a registered person does not furnish a return even after a notice under section 46, the officer may assess the tax to the best of his judgment on the material he has, and the order must be issued within five years from the due date of the annual return for the year concerned. For 2023-24 that due date is 31 December 2024, so the department had up to 31 December 2029 and 5 May 2026 is comfortably inside it. On the second point, a valid return within sixty days of service makes the order deemed withdrawn, with interest and late fee still payable. Miss that window and the person may still file within a further sixty days on an additional late fee of ₹100 a day for the delay beyond the first sixty, and the order is deemed withdrawn just the same. Seventy-five days falls inside the second window.
keywords: assess the tax to the best of his judgment
the department had up to 31 December 2029
a valid return within sixty days of service makes the order deemed withdrawn
a further sixty days on an additional late fee of ₹100 a day

options.text: The order was out of time, three years being the limit for a best judgment assessment
options.misconception: borrows a three-year limit from the demand provisions and applies it to an assessment made for want of a return
options.why: Three years belongs to a different family of provisions. The limit here is five years, and it is counted from the due date of the annual return for the year the unpaid tax relates to, not from the tax period or from the notice. On 2023-24 that arithmetic lands on 31 December 2029, and an order served in May 2026 has years to spare.

citation.ref: Section 62(1) and section 62(2) with its proviso

items.scenario: Chirag Steels did not file its return for a month falling in the financial year 2023-24, even after a notice under section 46. A best judgment assessment order is served on it on 5 May 2026. The firm files a valid return for that month on 19 July 2026, seventy-five days later. Its adviser says two things — that the order was out of time anyway, and that a return filed after sixty days can do nothing for it.

items.stem: What is Dhruv's position on the order?

options.text: The order is valid as it stands, permission from a senior officer being needed only where the person assessed is unregistered
options.misconception: attaches the permission requirement to the status of the taxpayer rather than to the kind of assessment being made
options.why: The permission has nothing to do with whether the person is registered. It is the price of the short cut: an officer is being allowed to assess without the enquiry a demand would need, so a senior officer has to agree that the haste is justified. The provision for an unascertainable taxpayer, where the person in charge of the goods is deemed to be the taxable person, is a separate matter in the same section.

options.text: An appeal to the Appellate Authority is indeed the only road open to him
options.misconception: misses the withdrawal route the section builds in beside the ordinary appeal
options.why: An appeal is available, but it is the slow road and it is not the only one. The section gives the senior officer power to withdraw the order, on the taxpayer's application or on his own motion, and to send the matter to an ordinary demand instead. That is the route designed for an order passed in a hurry on partial material, which is what a summary assessment is by definition.

options.text: It needed the prior permission of the Additional or Joint Commissioner, and Dhruv may ask that officer to withdraw it
options.why: Summary assessment is a short cut and it is fenced at both ends. It may be used only where the officer has evidence that a person has incurred a liability and sufficient grounds to believe that delay in passing an order would adversely affect the interest of the revenue, and it needs the prior permission of the Additional or Joint Commissioner before it is passed. An order made without that permission is made without the authority the section gives. The way out is written into the same section and is quicker than an appeal: on an application made within thirty days of receiving the order, or on his own motion where he finds the order erroneous, the Additional or Joint Commissioner may withdraw it, and the liability is then worked out under the ordinary demand provisions.
keywords: would adversely affect the interest of the revenue
the prior permission of the Additional or Joint Commissioner
on an application made within thirty days of receiving the order

options.text: The order can be withdrawn, but only by the officer who passed it
options.misconception: puts the power to undo the order in the hands of the officer who made it, when the section gives it to the senior officer whose permission the order required
options.why: The section names the Additional or Joint Commissioner on both sides — permission before, withdrawal afterwards — and that symmetry is the point of it. Letting the officer who passed the order be the only one who could take it back would leave the taxpayer asking the author of a hurried order to change his mind, with nothing above him short of an appeal.

citation.ref: Section 64(1) and section 64(2)

items.scenario: An officer, holding a delivery challan and a statement showing that a consignment on the road carries tax nobody has paid, passes a summary assessment order on Dhruv Exports on 4 June 2026 and serves it the same day. He asked nobody before passing it. Dhruv wants the order gone and is told by a consultant that an appeal is his only road.

items.stem: What must the mill actually do about the two bills?

options.text: Pay tax on both bills under reverse charge, transport of goods by road being a notified service whoever raises the bill
options.misconception: reads the entry as attaching to the service, when what decides it is whether the agency has itself registered, opted to pay and declared it on the invoice
options.why: The entry is written round the agency's own choice, not round the cargo. An agency that has opted to pay tax itself on its transport services and issued an invoice charging 12 per cent, which is the rate open to an agency that wants credit on its own inputs, has taken the supply out of reverse charge altogether. Paying again on Q's bill would tax the same freight twice, and the mill would have no way to recover the second payment.
keywords: opted to pay tax itself on its transport services
12 per cent, which is the rate open to an agency that wants credit

options.text: Pay tax itself on Agency P's freight, but at 12 per cent, that being the rate the law fixes for the carriage of goods by road
options.misconception: attaches the higher rate to the service, when the two rates follow the agency's decision about credit on its own inputs
options.why: There are two rates and the agency picks which one it lives under. Where it takes no credit on the diesel and services it buys, the rate is the lower one; where it wants that credit it opts to pay the tax itself and charges the higher one. P has taken the first road, which is why its bill shows no tax, and the mill steps into that rate and not into Q's.
keywords: takes no credit on the diesel and services it buys

options.text: Pay tax itself on Agency P's freight at 5 per cent, and pay Agency Q's bill as it stands, tax included
options.why: Two different questions are being answered by the same entry. For categories notified by the Government on the Council's recommendation the supplier drops out and the recipient pays on reverse charge, and road freight to a registered person is one of them. But the entry stops where the agency has registered, has chosen to pay the tax on its own transport services and has said so on the invoice — which is what Q has done, so Q's bill is an ordinary bill and the mill simply pays it. P has done none of that, so the agency has not exercised the option to pay the tax itself and the mill is the person who pays. The rate is 5 per cent, made up of 2.5 per cent central tax and 2.5 per cent State tax, and that is the rate precisely because P takes no credit on what it buys.
keywords: categories notified by the Government on the Council's recommendation
the recipient pays on reverse charge
the agency has not exercised the option to pay the tax itself
5 per cent, made up of 2.5 per cent central tax and 2.5 per cent State tax

options.text: Pay nothing on either. The agency earned the freight and remains the person liable; the department must look to it, not to the mill
options.misconception: treats reverse charge as a collection difficulty for the department rather than a shift of the whole liability, with all its compliance, onto the recipient
options.why: Reverse charge does not leave the liability where it was and merely change who is chased for it. Once a category is notified, every provision of the Act then applies to him as if he were the person liable to pay tax — so the mill registers for it, assesses it, pays it and reports it, and a demand for unpaid tax on P's freight would be raised on the mill with interest. Waiting for the department to pursue P is waiting for something that will not happen.
keywords: every provision of the Act then applies to him as if he were the person liable to pay tax

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for goods transport agency services, and the two rates at which those services are taxed

items.scenario: A registered spinning mill in Gujarat receives two freight bills in one month from two different goods transport agencies. Agency P's bill for ₹2,00,000 shows no tax at all and carries a note that P takes no credit on the diesel, tyres and services it buys. Agency Q's bill for ₹1,40,000 charges tax at 12 per cent and carries a signed declaration that Q has registered, has opted to pay the tax itself on its transport services, and is charging accordingly. The mill's accountant proposes to pay nothing at all on either bill: freight is freight, he says, and if any tax is due on it the department can go to the agency that earned the money.

items.stem: What is the right treatment of the two bills?

options.text: The individual advocate's bill is the company's liability; the firm's bill should have carried tax charged by the firm
options.misconception: reads the entry as reaching only a natural person, so a partnership of advocates is treated as an ordinary supplier who must charge
options.why: The finance head has read half the entry. It is written to cover the same legal service however the practice is organised, which is why it names the sole practitioner, the senior advocate and the partnership in one breath. If the firm had charged tax the company would have paid twice: once on the invoice and once on its own reverse charge liability, which does not go away because somebody else collected.
keywords: written to cover the same legal service however the practice is organised

options.text: The company pays on both, but discharges them by debiting the credit ledger, the balance being ample
options.misconception: treats a reverse charge liability as output tax, when the credit ledger may settle output tax alone and a recipient's reverse charge liability is defined out of that word
options.why: The credit ledger has a narrow reach: it settles output tax and nothing else, and output tax is what a person owes on his own outward supplies. Tax he owes because a reverse charge moved somebody else's liability onto him is expressly outside that, so the money has to go in through the cash ledger. Nothing is lost by it — credit of it is taken afterwards, once the tax has been paid and the ordinary conditions on credit are met — but the cash goes out first.
keywords: it settles output tax and nothing else
credit of it is taken afterwards

options.text: Neither bill bears tax at all, legal services from an advocate being exempt
options.misconception: carries an exemption written for small recipients across to every recipient, when what it protects is a business entity whose turnover is below the registration threshold
options.why: There is an exemption in this area and it is about who received the service, not about who supplied it. It shelters a business entity whose turnover has not reached the point at which registration bites, and a company turning over ₹80 crore is a long way outside it. For everybody else the entry stands and the recipient pays.
keywords: a business entity whose turnover has not reached the point at which registration bites

options.text: The company pays on both bills, in cash, and takes the credit afterwards
options.why: The entry names an individual advocate, a senior advocate and a firm of advocates alike, so the form the supplier takes makes no difference to who pays. What the entry does turn on is the recipient: it reaches any business entity located in the taxable territory, and this company is one. It also covers advice and appearance equally, so the tribunal work is caught on the same footing as the contract opinion. Both bills are therefore the company's own liability, and reverse charge tax is paid in cash.
keywords: The entry names an individual advocate, a senior advocate and a firm of advocates alike
the form the supplier takes makes no difference to who pays
any business entity located in the taxable territory
reverse charge tax is paid in cash

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for legal services, and section 49(4) with section 2(82)

items.scenario: A private limited company in Pune with a turnover of ₹80 crore takes legal work from two quarters in one month. An individual advocate advises it on a supply contract and bills ₹1,20,000 with no tax shown. A firm of advocates appears for it before a tribunal and bills ₹95,000, also with no tax. The finance head accepts the first bill as the company's own liability but says the second must be a mistake: a firm, he argues, is a supplier like any other and ought to have charged tax on its invoice. He also proposes to settle whatever is due by debiting the credit ledger, which is comfortably in funds.

items.stem: What is his ceiling for services, and is he inside it?

options.text: The ceiling was ₹9,20,000, the two limbs of the proviso being added together, and he is well inside it
options.misconception: reads "whichever is higher" as an instruction to add the percentage limb and the money limb, when it is an instruction to take one of them
options.why: The accountant's reading would make the allowance grow with turnover and then add a flat five lakh on top of it, which is not what a "whichever is higher" test does. Such a test names two candidates and picks one. Here the two candidates are ₹4,20,000 and ₹5,00,000, and the answer is ₹5,00,000, not ₹9,20,000.
keywords: names two candidates and picks one

options.text: The ceiling was ₹4,20,000, ten per cent of the preceding year's turnover, and he is over it
options.misconception: stops at the percentage limb and never reaches the money limb, so a small dealer whose ten per cent is tiny is given a far smaller allowance than the proviso gives him
options.why: This gets the outcome right for the wrong reason, and the reason is what he will be marked on. The percentage limb is only one of two, and for a dealer of this size it is the smaller. Reading it as the ceiling would punish exactly the dealers the money limb was written to protect — the ones whose turnover is small enough that ten per cent of it comes to almost nothing.
keywords: The percentage limb is only one of two

options.text: There is no ceiling to worry about, fitting and repairing goods he has himself sold being part of the sale rather than a separate service
options.misconception: folds an after-sale service into the supply of goods, when work charged for separately is a supply of services in its own right
options.why: If the fitting were bundled into the price of the goods there would be one supply to value. He charges for it separately, so it is a supply of services he makes alongside his goods, and it is exactly the kind of thing the proviso was written to measure. Treating it as part of the sale would let any composition dealer take on unlimited service work by writing one invoice instead of two.
keywords: a supply of services he makes alongside his goods

options.text: The ceiling was ₹5,00,000 and he is over it
options.why: A composition dealer in goods may also supply services worth no more than ten per cent of turnover in the State for the year before, or five lakh rupees, whichever is higher. It is a choice between the two limbs, not a sum of them. Ten per cent of ₹42,00,000 is ₹4,20,000, five lakh rupees is the larger of the two, and so his ceiling for services is ₹5,00,000. The ₹5,20,000 he actually earned is above it, and the scheme is no longer his.
keywords: services worth no more than ten per cent of turnover in the State for the year before
or five lakh rupees, whichever is higher

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 10(1)

items.scenario: A hardware dealer in Rajasthan has paid tax under the composition levy for goods all through 2025-26. His aggregate turnover for that year was ₹42,00,000. Alongside the counter sales he charges separately for fitting and repairing what he sells, and that work brought in ₹5,20,000 in the same year. His accountant tells him the service side is comfortably within the law because the proviso allows ten per cent of turnover and five lakh rupees, and ₹5,20,000 is inside the two of them added together.

items.stem: What is open to her, and at what rate?

options.text: Nothing at all. A supplier of services is shut out of composition, and the only relief a service provider ever gets is the small allowance inside the scheme for goods
options.misconception: stops at the bar in section 10(2)(a) and never reaches the later scheme, which exists because of that bar rather than in spite of it
options.why: This was the law once and it is not the law now. The allowance inside the goods scheme lets a trader do a little service work on the side; it was never a route in for somebody whose whole business is service. The later sub-section is the route in, and reading only the bar means telling a client to pay full rates on ₹46,00,000 when she need not.
keywords: lets a trader do a little service work on the side

options.text: The scheme for suppliers of services, at three per cent
options.misconception: reads the figure in the central Act as the whole tax, when the State law charges the same again on the same turnover
options.why: Three per cent is the central half. The State levies its own tax at the same figure on the same turnover, so what actually leaves her bank is double the number printed in the central rule. Quoting the single-Act figure to a client understates her cost by half, and the marking scheme asks for the rate she pays.
keywords: Three per cent is the central half

options.text: The scheme for suppliers of services, at six per cent of turnover in the State
options.why: Two separate schemes are being confused. A person engaged in the supply of services is barred from the scheme for goods, and that bar is why her accountant is half right. But a second scheme was written for precisely the person the bar excludes: it is open where aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year is within fifty lakh rupees, and her ₹46,00,000 is. The rate on it is six per cent of turnover in the State, counting central and State tax together, and she meets the other conditions.
keywords: A person engaged in the supply of services is barred from the scheme for goods
aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year is within fifty lakh rupees
six per cent of turnover in the State

options.text: The same half a per cent the hardware dealers pay, composition being one scheme with one rate for whoever enters it
options.misconception: reads the composition levy as a single rate, when the rate follows the category the person falls in
options.why: The rate is a table, not a number. A manufacturer or an ordinary supplier of goods pays the lowest figure, a restaurant service pays the middle one, and a supplier of services under the separate scheme pays the highest. Copying a neighbour's rate is copying his category, and she is not in it.
keywords: The rate is a table, not a number

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(a) and section 10(2A) read with rule 7 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An interior designer in Rajasthan supplies no goods at all. Her aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year was ₹46,00,000, she makes no supply outside the State, and she sells nothing through an electronic commerce operator. She has watched the hardware dealers in her building pay a composition levy at half a per cent of turnover and wants the same treatment, and her accountant has told her flatly that composition is for traders and restaurants.

items.stem: What value may the head office adopt for the 500 pumps?

options.text: ₹8,000, the price the branch will actually get from its customers
options.misconception: values this supply at the price of a later and different supply made by somebody else
options.why: There are two supplies here and only one of them is being valued. What the branch charges its customers is the value of the branch's own outward supply, on which the branch will pay tax. The head office's supply is the earlier one, and the branch's selling price enters it only through the ninety per cent measure, which takes nine tenths of it precisely because it is not the same transaction.
keywords: the value of the branch's own outward supply

options.text: ₹7,000 a pump, or ₹7,200 if the head office chooses it
options.why: Two registrations under one PAN are distinct persons, and a supply between distinct persons in the course of business is a supply even without consideration under paragraph 2 of Schedule I — so the transaction has to be valued whatever the manager thinks. Rule 28(1) runs in order, and the first measure is available here: the open market value, here the ₹7,000 charged to unrelated dealers. Because the branch will sell the pumps on as they stand, a second measure is also offered — ninety per cent of the ₹8,000 the branch charges its own unrelated customers, that is ₹7,200 — and the option belongs to the supplier and is not compulsory.
keywords: a supply between distinct persons in the course of business is a supply even without consideration under paragraph 2 of Schedule I
the open market value, here the ₹7,000 charged to unrelated dealers
ninety per cent of the ₹8,000 the branch charges its own unrelated customers, that is ₹7,200
the option belongs to the supplier and is not compulsory

options.text: ₹7,200 and nothing else, the goods being meant for onward supply as they stand
options.misconception: reads the ninety per cent measure as a rule that displaces open market value whenever the goods move on unchanged, when it is an option offered to the supplier
options.why: The proviso says the value shall be that figure at the option of the supplier, which means the head office may take it and may equally leave it. Here it happens to be the higher of the two, so a supplier told it was compulsory would pay more tax than the law asks. Whether it is higher or lower than open market value is not the test; whose choice it is, is.
keywords: at the option of the supplier

options.text: ₹6,000, the value written on the invoice
options.misconception: reaches for the proviso that lets a declared value stand without checking the one condition it carries, which is the recipient's credit position
options.why: That proviso is real but it is conditional. Where the recipient is entitled to full input tax credit, the value declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value, and the reason is that whatever the supplier charges comes straight back as the recipient's credit, so the figure cannot cost the exchequer anything. This branch makes exempt supplies and cannot take full credit, so the ₹6,000 on this invoice is not the value, and understating it would leave real tax unpaid.
keywords: Where the recipient is entitled to full input tax credit, the value declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value
the ₹6,000 on this invoice is not the value

citation.ref: Rule 28(1)(a) to (c) with its first and second provisos, read with section 25(4) and paragraph 2 of Schedule I to the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A pump maker has its head office registered in Maharashtra and a branch registered in Karnataka under the same PAN. In June 2026 the head office sends 500 pumps to the branch and raises an invoice at ₹6,000 a pump. It sells the same pumps to unrelated dealers at ₹7,000. The branch will resell them unchanged to its own customers, none of whom is a related person, at ₹8,000. The branch also makes a large volume of exempt supplies of its own, so it is not entitled to full input tax credit. The head office's manager says the invoice settles it: the two registrations belong to one company, and what one writes on the other's invoice is nobody else's business.

items.stem: On what value does the holding company pay tax, if any?

options.text: Nothing. There was no consideration, so there was no supply to value
options.misconception: applies the general requirement of consideration to a transaction the law lists as a supply without it
options.why: Consideration is the general test and this is one of the listed exceptions to it: an activity between related persons in the course of business is a supply even where nothing is paid. That is the whole reason a valuation rule for guarantees had to be written at all — if the free ones fell out of the net there would be nothing to value.
keywords: a supply even where nothing is paid

options.text: The open market value of a comparable guarantee commission that a bank would have charged
options.misconception: works the general sequence for related-person supplies when a later sub-rule opens by overriding it and fixes the figure itself
options.why: The general sequence starts at open market value and only moves on when that cannot be found, and it is exactly the enquiry the guarantee rule was written to end. That rule begins by displacing what goes before it and then names its own figure, so no comparable has to be hunted for and none may be used instead.
keywords: begins by displacing what goes before it

options.text: ₹2,00,000, one per cent of the ₹2 crore the subsidiary actually drew
options.misconception: measures the service by the money the borrower took, when what the holding company supplied was the promise, whether or not the borrower drew on it
options.why: The thing supplied is the standing behind the loan, and the bank had the benefit of it over the whole ₹5 crore from the day it was given. Drawing less does not shrink the promise, and a rule keyed to drawdowns would let a guarantee for a large facility be valued at almost nothing by leaving the facility idle. The base is what was guaranteed.

A guarantee given to a bank for a related person is a supply of service even where nothing is charged for it, and it has a valuation rule of its own that overrides the general sequence. The value is one per cent a year of the sum guaranteed, or what was actually charged, whichever is higher. Nothing was charged, so the figure is one per cent of ₹5 crore, that is ₹5,00,000 for the year. What the rule measures is the amount guaranteed and not the amount the bank actually released.
keywords: one per cent a year of the sum guaranteed, or what was actually charged, whichever is higher
one per cent of ₹5 crore, that is ₹5,00,000 for the year
the amount guaranteed and not the amount the bank actually released

citation.ref: Rule 28(2), read with paragraph 2 of Schedule I to the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A holding company in Tamil Nadu gives a bank a guarantee for a loan of ₹5 crore sanctioned to its Indian subsidiary, and charges the subsidiary nothing for it. The guarantee runs for one year. By the end of that year the subsidiary has drawn only ₹2 crore of the sanctioned amount. The subsidiary makes a substantial volume of exempt supplies and is not entitled to full input tax credit. The holding company's accountant sees no supply at all: no money changed hands, and in any case the group is one economic unit.

items.stem: Is the accountant right?

options.text: Yes, and he should have registered from the day the fixed deposit was made, that being when he first supplied a service
