options.misconception: reads the liability as arising from the character of a supply rather than from a turnover figure crossing a stated line
options.why: Nothing in the section makes a single receipt a trigger. Registration bites when aggregate turnover in a financial year goes past the limit that applies, and until it does the composition of the turnover only decides which limit that is. Even on the accountant's own reading he would have been liable when the figure crossed ₹20 lakh, not on the day the deposit was opened.
keywords: Registration bites when aggregate turnover in a financial year goes past the limit that applies

options.text: No, and for a simpler reason: interest is not a supply at all, so it never enters the reckoning in the first place
options.misconception: treats interest as outside the definition of turnover, when it is an exempt supply that counts in the total and is forgiven only for the separate "exclusively in goods" test
options.why: The answer is right and the route is wrong, and the route is what the marks are for. Aggregate turnover takes in exempt supplies, so the ₹2 lakh sits inside his ₹37 lakh and would count towards any limit. The concession does something narrower: it stops that receipt from changing which limit he is measured against.
keywords: Aggregate turnover takes in exempt supplies

options.text: No. He is not liable to register
options.why: Both halves of the accountant's reasoning have to be tested and the second one fails. The interest is an exempt supply and it does go into the figure, so his aggregate turnover of ₹37 lakh, the interest included, and the limit that applies to him is ₹40 lakh. What the accountant misses is an explanation written for exactly this: interest on money lent or deposited does not stop a person being engaged exclusively in the supply of goods. So he keeps the higher limit, his figure is inside it, and he is not liable to be registered.
keywords: his aggregate turnover of ₹37 lakh, the interest included, and the limit that applies to him is ₹40 lakh
interest on money lent or deposited does not stop a person being engaged exclusively in the supply of goods
he is not liable to be registered

options.text: Yes. Any supply of services at all takes the higher limit away, so his limit is ₹20 lakh and he crossed it long ago
options.misconception: applies the "exclusively in goods" test without the explanation that forgives one kind of exempt financial receipt
options.why: The general position is the ordinary limit at ₹20 lakh, and ₹10 lakh for the four special category States, with a higher figure available only to a person dealing exclusively in goods. The accountant has that much right. But the law then says in terms that money returned on a deposit or a loan does not spoil the description, because otherwise every trader with a bank account would lose the higher limit and the concession would mean nothing.
keywords: the ordinary limit at ₹20 lakh, and ₹10 lakh for the four special category States

citation.ref: Section 2(6) and section 22(1) with its Explanation, read with Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax dated 7 March 2019

items.scenario: A trader in Uttar Pradesh sells taxable goods within the State and nothing else, and his sales for 2026-27 come to ₹35 lakh. He makes no supply across a State line. Separately he has ₹2 lakh of interest credited on fixed deposits with his bank during the same year. His accountant says the interest is an exempt supply of services, so he can no longer be described as dealing only in goods, the higher limit is gone, and he should have registered months ago.

items.stem: Which of the three is liable to be registered?

options.text: Rekha and Vivek. Priya deals mainly in goods and her ₹32 lakh is under ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: reads "exclusively in the supply of goods" as "mainly in goods", so a small line of taxable services is allowed to ride along
options.why: The word in the notification is exclusively, and it is doing real work. One rupee of taxable service supply puts a person outside the higher limit altogether — there is no proportion test and no de minimis. The only receipt that is forgiven is the exempt financial one, and repair charges are not that.
keywords: One rupee of taxable service supply puts a person outside the higher limit

options.text: All three
options.why: Three different limits are in play and the adviser has applied one of them to everybody. Manipur is one of the four special category States for section 22, so the limit there is ₹10 lakh and she is liable on ₹12 lakh. Telangana is one of the States the notification carves out of the ₹40 lakh limit, so the limit is ₹20 lakh and ₹30 lakh crosses it, even though Vivek deals only in goods. Priya keeps no higher limit either, because taxable repair services are neither goods nor the one exempt financial receipt the explanation forgives, and her aggregate turnover of ₹32 lakh exceeds ₹20 lakh.
keywords: Manipur is one of the four special category States for section 22, so the limit there is ₹10 lakh and she is liable
Telangana is one of the States the notification carves out of the ₹40 lakh limit
taxable repair services are neither goods nor the one exempt financial receipt the explanation forgives
her aggregate turnover of ₹32 lakh exceeds ₹20 lakh

options.text: None. Each is under ₹40 lakh and none of them crosses a State line
options.misconception: applies one figure to the whole country and treats the absence of inter-State supply as the only other question
options.why: Making no inter-State supply matters, but it only keeps them out of the compulsory registration that an inter-State supply of goods brings on from the first rupee. It says nothing about the threshold, which is read State by State and category by category. On the correct limits Rekha is over hers, Vivek is over his, and Priya is over hers.
keywords: read State by State and category by category

options.text: Only Rekha
options.misconception: treats the higher goods limit as available everywhere outside the four special category States, missing the separate list of States the notification itself carves out
options.why: There are two lists and they are not the same list. The four States with the lowest limit come from the section; the notification that gives the higher limit to a dealer in goods then withdraws it from a further group, which is why a trader in Telangana or Uttarakhand or Puducherry is measured against the middle figure however pure his goods business is. Learning only the first list produces exactly this answer.
keywords: the notification that gives the higher limit to a dealer in goods then withdraws it from a further group

citation.ref: First proviso to section 22(1) and its Explanation (iii), read with exception (c) in Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax dated 7 March 2019

items.scenario: Three traders ask the same question for 2026-27 and none of them supplies anything across a State line. Rekha, in Manipur, sells taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹12 lakh. Vivek, in Telangana, sells taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹30 lakh. Priya, in Maharashtra, sells ₹30 lakh of taxable goods within the State and also earns ₹2 lakh from taxable repair work she charges for separately. Their common adviser says only Rekha need worry, the other two being traders in goods under the ₹40 lakh mark.

items.stem: What is the surcharge, and on what is it computed?

options.text: ₹1,20,000, ten per cent of the basic duty and the safeguard duty taken together
options.misconception: reads the surcharge as riding on every duty of customs on the article, when three trade-remedy duties are lifted out of the base by name
options.why: The base is the duties levied and collected on the article together with sums other statutes charge as an addition to a duty of customs — and then three levies are taken back out of it. They are the ones aimed at unfair or surging imports rather than at revenue, and leaving them in would make a trade remedy carry a social charge on top. The clerk's arithmetic is sound; his base is not.
keywords: aimed at unfair or surging imports rather than at revenue

options.text: ₹40,000, ten per cent of the basic customs duty alone
options.why: Two figures have to be settled before the surcharge can be. Basic customs duty of ₹4,00,000, being 10 per cent of the assessable value, is payable; and the country's share of imports is above the 3 per cent below which section 8B leaves a developing country alone, so the safeguard duty of ₹8,00,000 is charged as well. The surcharge is then a percentage of a base from which safeguard duty, countervailing duty, anti-dumping duty and the surcharge itself are excluded, which leaves the basic duty on its own. Ten per cent of ₹4,00,000 means the surcharge is ₹40,000.
keywords: Basic customs duty of ₹4,00,000, being 10 per cent of the assessable value
the country's share of imports is above the 3 per cent below which section 8B leaves a developing country alone, so the safeguard duty of ₹8,00,000 is charged
safeguard duty, countervailing duty, anti-dumping duty and the surcharge itself are excluded

options.text: ₹40,000, but by a different route: no safeguard duty is chargeable at all, the goods having come from a developing country
options.misconception: takes the developing-country relief as unconditional, when it falls away once that country's share of imports of the article passes 3 per cent
options.why: The figure is right and the reasoning would cost ₹8,00,000. The relief for a developing country holds only while its share of imports of that article stays at or below 3 per cent; at 6 per cent this consignment is outside it and the safeguard duty is payable. It also matters beyond the surcharge, because the safeguard duty goes into the base on which integrated tax is charged even though it stays out of this one.
keywords: holds only while its share of imports of that article stays at or below 3 per cent

options.text: ₹4,00,000, ten per cent of the assessable value
options.misconception: treats the surcharge as a duty on the value of the goods, when it is a surcharge on duty and the value never enters it
options.why: The whole character of this levy is that it rides on other duties. The assessable value is where those duties are computed from; it is not where this one is computed from. The test that shows it clearly is an import on which the basic duty has been exempted altogether — the value is unchanged and the surcharge is nil, which could not happen if value were the base.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods, read with section 8B(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

items.scenario: An importer brings in a consignment of an industrial chemical from a developing country in December 2026. Its value assessed under section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 is ₹40,00,000. Basic customs duty on the article is 10 per cent. A safeguard duty of 20 per cent is in force on it, and imports of that article from that country run at 6 per cent of all imports of it into India. No compensation cess arises. The importer's clerk works the social welfare surcharge at ten per cent of the basic duty and the safeguard duty added together.

items.stem: What is the integrated tax, and how much of the total is recoverable?

options.text: ₹9,43,200 of integrated tax; only that is recoverable, out of ₹21,83,200 paid
options.why: Integrated tax on an import is not charged on the section 14 value. Section 3(8) builds the base out of that value together with every duty of customs on the article and every other sum a statute charges on it as an addition to such a duty, so the safeguard duty and the surcharge both go in: ₹40,00,000 plus ₹4,00,000 plus ₹8,00,000 plus ₹40,000, that is ₹52,40,000. At 18 per cent that comes to ₹9,43,200. So the total payable is ₹21,83,200, and only the integrated tax is input tax credit; the rest are costs the price has to carry.
keywords: Section 3(8) builds the base out of that value together with every duty of customs on the article
At 18 per cent that comes to ₹9,43,200
the total payable is ₹21,83,200, and only the integrated tax is input tax credit; the rest are costs

options.text: ₹9,43,200 of integrated tax, and the surcharge must be charged on that as well, adding ₹94,320
options.misconception: applies the surcharge to the integrated tax, when a notification exempts the surcharge on integrated tax and on compensation cess
options.why: The direction of travel is one way only. The integrated tax is computed on a base that includes the surcharge; the surcharge is not then computed on the integrated tax, because a notification takes the integrated tax and the compensation cess out of the surcharge altogether. Charging both ways round would compound one levy on the other.
keywords: a notification takes the integrated tax and the compensation cess out of the surcharge

options.text: ₹9,43,200 of integrated tax, and the whole ₹21,83,200 is recoverable, every tax on a business input being creditable
options.misconception: treats the basic customs duty, the safeguard duty and the surcharge as entering the GST credit chain, when only the integrated tax collected at the port does
options.why: Only one of the four levies collected at the port belongs to the GST system, and it is the only one the credit ledger will ever see. The basic duty, the safeguard duty and the surcharge are customs levies that end where they are paid, which is why an importer prices them into his cost and prices the integrated tax out of it.
keywords: Only one of the four levies collected at the port belongs to the GST system

options.text: ₹7,20,000 of integrated tax, charged on the assessable value, and that much is recoverable
options.misconception: carries the section 14 value straight across to the integrated tax, when the later sub-section builds a different base by adding the duties to it
options.why: If the tax were charged on the bare value, an imported article would bear less tax than the same article bought at home, where the price the buyer pays already carries the maker's costs. The base is built up on purpose so that the import lands at the same tax as a domestic supply of the same thing. Missing the build-up understates the tax by ₹2,23,200 here.
keywords: The base is built up on purpose

citation.ref: Sections 3(7) and 3(8), with Notification No. 13/2018-Customs dated 2 February 2018 and section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: The same consignment is cleared. The importer is registered under GST and will use the chemical in manufacture. Assessable value ₹40,00,000, basic customs duty ₹4,00,000, safeguard duty ₹8,00,000, social welfare surcharge ₹40,000, integrated tax on the chemical at 18 per cent, no compensation cess. His accountant proposes to take credit of the whole of what was paid at the port, on the footing that a tax on a business input is a tax on a business input.

items.stem: What is the position on the consultant's two objections?

options.text: The second objection is right. The fabric and the dye come in duty free; the furnace oil does not, since it is not in the finished shirt
options.misconception: reads "input" as only what survives into the finished article, when the scheme names consumables in a class of their own for exactly that reason
options.why: If survival in the product were the test, the second class would be empty and would not have been written. Fuel, oil and catalyst are listed because they are consumed rather than incorporated, and the cost of them is as much a cost of making the export as the fabric is. Leaving them dutiable would put the exporter's price up by the duty on the energy he burns.
keywords: they are consumed rather than incorporated

options.text: Both are wrong: it may hold the authorisation, and all three items may come in duty free
options.why: An authorisation may be issued to a manufacturer exporter or to a merchant exporter tied to a supporting manufacturer, and this house has named its manufacturer, so the first objection fails on the eligibility rule itself. The second fails because the scheme describes two separate classes of goods, not one. It covers inputs physically incorporated in the export product, with a normal allowance for wastage — the fabric and the dye — and it separately says that fuel, oil and catalyst consumed in the process of producing the export product come in duty free as well.
keywords: An authorisation may be issued to a manufacturer exporter or to a merchant exporter tied to a supporting manufacturer
inputs physically incorporated in the export product, with a normal allowance for wastage
fuel, oil and catalyst consumed in the process of producing the export product come in duty free as well

options.text: Both are wrong, and the spares the buyer wants shipped with the shirts may be brought in duty free without limit alongside them
options.misconception: extends the duty-free entitlement to spares without the cap the scheme puts on them
options.why: Spares that have to go out with the export product can indeed come in under the authorisation, but not without a ceiling: they are capped at ten per cent of the CIF value of the authorisation. Treating them as uncapped is how an authorisation gets over-utilised, and the shortfall is recovered as duty with interest afterwards.
keywords: capped at ten per cent of the CIF value of the authorisation

options.text: The first objection is right. A trading house that manufactures nothing cannot hold an authorisation, whoever sews for it
options.misconception: ties the scheme to the person who does the manufacturing, when the eligibility rule names the merchant exporter separately and asks only that a supporting manufacturer be tied to him
options.why: The scheme is aimed at exports, and a great deal of India's exporting is done by houses that sell abroad and have the work done for them. The rule therefore names two kinds of holder, and the condition on the second is not that he manufactures but that a manufacturer is tied to him and named. There is one narrow exception, for pharmaceutical products made through a non-infringing process, where only a manufacturer exporter may hold one.
keywords: the condition on the second is not that he manufactures but that a manufacturer is tied to him and named

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy — eligible applicants and eligible inputs under Advance Authorisation, and the limit on mandatory spares

items.scenario: A garment house holds a confirmed export order. It buys nothing and makes nothing itself: the sewing is done by a factory it has named in its application as its supporting manufacturer. It wants to bring in three things without duty — the fabric that becomes the shirt, the dye that goes into the fabric, and the furnace oil burnt in the dyeing plant. Its consultant tells it two things. The scheme, he says, is for manufacturer exporters, so a trading house cannot hold an authorisation at all; and in any case fuel is not an input, because none of it ends up in the shirt.

items.stem: What does the pricing need, and what will actually be charged at the port?

options.text: The value addition is comfortably met, being the margin measured against the export realisation rather than against the cost of the inputs
options.misconception: divides the margin by the wrong figure, which flatters every case and flatters the thin ones most
options.why: Measured against the ₹88 lakh of realisation the same ₹8 lakh margin reads as roughly 9 per cent, which is not the test either, and dividing by the larger number will always give the smaller percentage. The formula puts the cost of the covered inputs underneath, so what is being asked is how much value the exporter added to what he brought in. Getting the denominator wrong is how an authorisation is applied for that cannot be redeemed.
keywords: how much value the exporter added to what he brought in

options.text: The value addition is short of the minimum, so the order must be repriced or the input bill cut; the anti-dumping duty and the integrated tax are both spared
options.why: Value addition is measured as the excess of what is realised on the export over what the imported inputs cost, as a proportion of that cost. Here ₹88 lakh against ₹80 lakh is 10 per cent, and the minimum value addition to be achieved is 15 per cent, lower only for specified products such as petroleum products. On duties, the scheme is generous and precise: basic customs duty, the additional duty, education cess, safeguard duty and its transition product-specific counterpart, countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty are all spared, and imports under the scheme are exempt from the whole of the integrated tax and the compensation cess.
keywords: the minimum value addition to be achieved is 15 per cent, lower only for specified products such as petroleum products
countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty are all spared
imports under the scheme are exempt from the whole of the integrated tax and the compensation cess

options.text: The value addition is short, and the integrated tax is payable at the port and taken back as credit in the usual way
options.misconception: carries the ordinary import position into a scheme whose point is that the money never leaves in the first place
options.why: Paying and reclaiming is the ordinary route for an importer, and it is exactly what this scheme removes. An exporter's working capital is the thing it protects: money paid at the port and recovered months later through a return is money he did not have while the order was being made. The exemption from integrated tax is outright, not deferred.
keywords: money paid at the port and recovered months later through a return

options.text: The value addition is short, and the anti-dumping duty is payable, a trade remedy not being a duty the scheme can waive
options.misconception: assumes the trade-remedy duties sit outside the exemption, when the scheme names them and the exception runs the other way
options.why: The list of duties spared names the trade remedies expressly, which settles it for a physical export. The exception is narrower and points the other way: for certain specified deemed exports the anti-dumping, countervailing and safeguard duties are not spared. Knowing which side of that line an order sits on is the whole of the question.
keywords: for certain specified deemed exports the anti-dumping, countervailing and safeguard duties are not spared

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy — minimum value addition and the duties exempted under Advance Authorisation

items.scenario: The same garment house prices the order. The inputs it will import come to ₹80 lakh at CIF value, and the export it expects to realise comes to ₹88 lakh at FOB value. It claims no drawback on anything else. Two of the inputs worry it: one attracts an anti-dumping duty in force against the country it is buying from, and all of them would ordinarily bear integrated tax at the port, which its accountant expects to pay and then claim back as credit.

items.stem: What may he do?

options.text: Neither may be sold. The condition attaches to whatever the duty-free input becomes, as much as to the input itself
options.misconception: extends the transfer bar past where it stops, so goods the exporter has actually manufactured are locked up as well
options.why: The bar is on the authorisation and on the material imported under it, and it stops there. Once the export obligation is over, the holder is expressly left free to dispose of what he has manufactured out of the duty-free input — otherwise a manufacturer would be left holding finished stock he could never sell. There is a separate condition where credit was taken on the inputs of exported goods, and it restricts use rather than forbidding sale outright.
keywords: The bar is on the authorisation and on the material imported under it

options.text: Ask for one revalidation and import the balance; sell the shirts; keep the fabric
options.why: The authorisation is valid for import for twelve months from the date of issue, and may be revalidated for another twelve months once only, which covers his three-month delay with room to spare. On disposal the answer splits, and the split is the point: the authorisation and the material imported under it are not transferable even after the export obligation has been completed, so the fabric stays with him; but the holder may dispose of the product manufactured out of the duty-free input once the export obligation is completed, so the shirts may be sold.
keywords: The authorisation is valid for import for twelve months from the date of issue, and may be revalidated for another twelve months once only
the material imported under it are not transferable
not transferable even after the export obligation has been completed
the holder may dispose of the product manufactured out of the duty-free input once the export obligation is completed

options.text: Sell both the shirts and the fabric — the export obligation has been discharged and nothing survives it
options.misconception: reads the discharge of the export obligation as releasing everything, when the bar on transferring the imported material survives it by design
options.why: Discharge ends the obligation to export; it does not turn duty-free material into ordinary stock. If it did, an exporter could bring in more than he needed, ship the minimum, and sell the surplus in India duty free against domestic sellers who paid duty on theirs. That is precisely the trade the condition exists to stop, which is why it is written to outlive completion.
keywords: it does not turn duty-free material into ordinary stock

options.text: Ask for revalidation as often as he needs it, there being no cap while the export obligation is outstanding; sell both the shirts and the fabric
options.misconception: reads revalidation as renewable at will, when the Regional Authority may allow it for a further twelve months on one occasion only
options.why: Revalidation is a single further period, not a rolling one, and an exporter who plans on repeated extensions will find the authorisation dead with fabric still to come. There is one case where the clock is set differently, and it is not this one: where the supply is a deemed export, the validity is co-terminus with the contracted duration of the project, or twelve months, whichever is later.
keywords: co-terminus with the contracted duration of the project

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy and Chapter 4 of the Handbook of Procedures — validity, revalidation and the Actual User condition for an Advance Authorisation

items.scenario: An Advance Authorisation was issued to an exporter on 1 March 2026. By February 2027 he has imported only part of the fabric it covers, and his supplier abroad cannot ship the rest for another three months. The export obligation on what he has already made has been discharged in full. He asks three things: whether he can still bring in the balance of the fabric, how often he can go on asking for more time, and whether the finished shirts lying in his warehouse and the leftover fabric beside them can now both be sold in India.

items.stem: What does the accountant's split cost, and what should be done instead?

options.text: Nothing can be done. The order of utilisation is fixed by the rules and the accountant has no choice to make
options.misconception: reads the rule as fixing the split as well as the sequence, when what it fixes is only that integrated credit goes first and leaves the rest open
options.why: The rule does two things and only the first is compulsory. The integrated tax credit must be used fully first, and it goes against integrated tax before anything else; after that the remainder may go against central tax and State tax in any order. That freedom is the taxpayer's, and treating it as a fixed rule is how ₹70,000 of credit gets left on the ledger.
keywords: The integrated tax credit must be used fully first
the remainder may go against central tax and State tax in any order

options.text: Set the ₹60,000 of central tax credit against the State tax shortfall instead, which clears both heads without any cash at all
options.misconception: treats central and State credit as interchangeable once the integrated credit is gone, when the two never cross
options.why: This is the one move the system will not allow. Central tax credit is never used for State tax, and State tax credit is never used for central tax, because the two taxes belong to two governments and a credit taken from one cannot discharge a debt owed to the other. Whatever is left after the integrated credit runs out has to be paid in cash on the head that is short.
keywords: Central tax credit is never used for State tax, and State tax credit is never used for central tax

options.text: It costs ₹70,000 of credit that can never be used and ₹90,000 of cash; the balance should go ₹90,000 to central tax and ₹10,000 to State tax
options.why: After the integrated tax is settled there is ₹1,00,000 of integrated tax credit left after the integrated tax is paid, and where it lands decides the cash. Put ₹90,000 of it against central tax and ₹10,000 against State tax: the central head is then cleared by that ₹90,000 plus the ₹60,000 of central credit, and the State head takes ₹10,000 plus its own ₹1,20,000, leaving ₹20,000 to be paid in cash. The accountant's split would have stranded ₹70,000 of State tax credit and forced ₹90,000 of cash on the central tax head, because central credit can never be moved across to help.
keywords: ₹1,00,000 of integrated tax credit left after the integrated tax is paid
Put ₹90,000 of it against central tax and ₹10,000 against State tax
leaving ₹20,000 to be paid in cash
The accountant's split would have stranded ₹70,000 of State tax credit and forced ₹90,000 of cash on the central tax head

options.text: Hold the integrated tax credit back, pay the integrated tax in cash, and let the central and State credit clear their own heads first
options.misconception: ignores the section that lets central or State credit be used only after the integrated credit has been exhausted
options.why: The order is not a preference. Central or State credit may be used towards any tax only after the integrated tax credit has been used up, so holding the integrated credit back is not open to him. It would also make things worse rather than better: the two smaller balances cannot cover their own heads, so cash would go out on the integrated tax and again on both the others.
keywords: only after the integrated tax credit has been used up

citation.ref: Sections 49(5)(e) and (f), 49A and 49B read with rule 88A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: For October 2026 a steel trader registered in Karnataka owes integrated tax ₹2,00,000, central tax ₹1,50,000 and State tax ₹1,50,000. Its electronic credit ledger holds integrated tax credit ₹3,00,000, central tax credit ₹60,000 and State tax credit ₹1,20,000. Its accountant proposes to set the integrated tax credit against the integrated tax first, as he must, and then to put the whole of the balance against the State tax head, on the footing that the State tax bill is the one with the least credit sitting behind it. The trader wants to part with as little cash as possible.

items.stem: How much has to come out of the cash ledger?

options.why: There is a restriction that sits on top of the ordinary right to use credit. Rule 86B bites where the value of taxable supply, exempt and zero-rated supplies left out, exceeds ₹50 lakh in a month, and at ₹80 lakh this person is inside it. Once it applies, the credit ledger may then discharge no more than 99 per cent of the output tax liability. So one per cent of ₹5,00,000, that is ₹5,000, has to come out of the cash ledger, and the rest may come from credit.
keywords: Rule 86B bites where the value of taxable supply, exempt and zero-rated supplies left out, exceeds ₹50 lakh in a month
the credit ledger may then discharge no more than 99 per cent of the output tax liability
one per cent of ₹5,00,000, that is ₹5,000, has to come out of the cash ledger

options.text: Nothing. The restriction is aimed at credit that looks doubtful, and nobody doubts this credit
options.misconception: reads the rule as a judgement applied case by case, when it is a flat restriction with a closed list of exceptions that have nothing to do with how good the credit is
options.why: The rule asks no questions about the quality of the credit. It applies on a turnover test alone, and the way out of it is one of the named exceptions — income tax above ₹1 lakh paid in each of the last two years by the person or its directors or partners, a refund above ₹1 lakh of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies or an inverted rate structure, and a few more of that kind. This company answers to none of them.
keywords: income tax above ₹1 lakh paid in each of the last two years

options.text: Nothing, because the rule applies only where the monthly output tax itself is above ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: reads the ₹50 lakh test against the tax rather than against the value of the taxable supplies
options.why: Set against tax, the threshold would catch almost nobody — ₹50 lakh of monthly output tax implies a turnover in the hundreds of crores. It is set against the value of taxable supplies precisely so that it reaches ordinary mid-sized businesses, and this one is over it four times before the tax is even worked out.
keywords: set against the value of taxable supplies

options.text: ₹80,000, one per cent of the ₹80 lakh of taxable supplies
options.misconception: applies the one per cent to the turnover, when the turnover only decides whether the rule applies and the one per cent is read against the tax
options.why: Two different figures do two different jobs here. The value of taxable supply is the gate: above the line the rule applies, below it the rule does not. What the one per cent is then taken of is the output tax liability, which is ₹5,00,000. Reading the percentage against turnover would make the cash payment sixteen times what the rule asks.
keywords: The value of taxable supply is the gate

citation.ref: Rule 86B with its exceptions

items.scenario: A different registered person in the same State has taxable supplies of ₹80 lakh for the month, none of them exempt and none zero-rated, and a total output tax liability of ₹5,00,000. Its electronic credit ledger holds more than enough to cover the whole of it, and every rupee of that credit is properly availed and undisputed. Nobody in the company has paid income tax of over ₹1 lakh in either of the last two years, and it has never received a refund of unutilised credit. Its accountant proposes to settle the entire ₹5,00,000 out of the credit ledger and pay nothing in cash.

items.stem: Is the finance head right?

options.text: No, but the tax falls on the Singapore parent, which must take a registration in India and pay it
options.misconception: moves the liability to the foreign supplier, when for an import of services to a business the charge sits on the Indian recipient
options.why: Making an overseas company register here for every service it renders to an Indian group company would be unenforceable, which is why the charge on an imported business service is put on the recipient in India. There is one class of service where the foreign supplier does register — online services supplied to unregistered consumers — and this is not that.
keywords: the charge on an imported business service is put on the recipient in India

options.text: No, but only because the retailer is registered; an unregistered recipient of an imported business service would pay nothing
options.misconception: assumes registration is what brings the charge on, when receiving such a service is itself a ground for compulsory registration
options.why: Registration is a consequence here, not a condition. A person who has to pay tax under reverse charge is required to register whatever his turnover, so an unregistered business receiving this support would have to take registration and then pay — it would not escape. The only person genuinely outside is the individual receiving a service for private purposes.
keywords: A person who has to pay tax under reverse charge is required to register whatever his turnover

options.text: Yes. An import of services means a service bought for a price, and nothing was bought here
options.misconception: reads a price into the definition of an import of services, when the definition asks only about geography
options.why: The definition and the charge are two separate questions and he has collapsed them. Section 2(11) asks only where the supplier is, where the recipient is, and where the place of supply is — a price is nowhere in it. Whether the transaction is a supply is then answered elsewhere, and for a related party abroad it is answered by the schedule that dispenses with consideration.
keywords: Section 2(11) asks only where the supplier is, where the recipient is, and where the place of supply is

options.text: No. The support is a supply and the retailer must pay integrated tax on it
options.why: The provision he is relying on does need a price, but it is not the only route in. Paragraph 4 of Schedule I makes an import of services from a related person, or from another establishment of the same person outside India, a supply even without consideration where it is in the course or furtherance of business. A parent and its subsidiary are related persons and the systems support is plainly for the business, so the retailer pays integrated tax on it under reverse charge and takes credit where it is eligible. The value is found under rule 28, the two being related persons.
keywords: Paragraph 4 of Schedule I makes an import of services from a related person, or from another establishment of the same person outside India, a supply even without consideration
the retailer pays integrated tax on it under reverse charge and takes credit where it is eligible
The value is found under rule 28, the two being related persons

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(c) read with paragraph 4 of Schedule I, and section 2(11) of the IGST Act, 2017 with section 5(3)

items.scenario: A retailer registered in Delhi is a subsidiary of a company in Singapore. The Singapore parent runs the buying and inventory systems the Delhi business depends on, and provides that support free of charge: no invoice is raised, nothing is remitted, and nothing appears in either company's books. The retailer's finance head sees nothing to declare. Import of services, he says, is a supply only where it is made for a consideration, and here there is none.

items.stem: Who is liable to pay tax on the two sets of customers?

options.text: On the businesses, the Indian recipient; on the individuals, the overseas company, which must appoint somebody here to register and pay
options.why: The two sets are handled by two different mechanisms. Where the recipient is a registered business the tax is paid by that recipient on reverse charge, as with any imported business service. The individuals are different: a non-taxable online recipient is an unregistered person in the taxable territory receiving these services, and asking each of them to register would be absurd, so the foreign supplier itself is liable and takes a single registration under the simplified scheme. Counsel's point is the one the law answers last — with no presence and no representative in India it must appoint a person here to register and pay on its behalf.
keywords: where the recipient is a registered business the tax is paid by that recipient on reverse charge
a non-taxable online recipient is an unregistered person in the taxable territory receiving these services
the foreign supplier itself is liable and takes a single registration under the simplified scheme
with no presence and no representative in India it must appoint a person here to register and pay on its behalf

options.text: The overseas company for both sets, since the supplier is the same and the service is the same
options.misconception: lets the character of the service decide, when what decides is whether the recipient is registered and can account for the tax himself
options.why: The service being identical is not the test. The scheme that puts the liability on the overseas supplier is drawn round the recipient who cannot account for the tax, and a registered business can. Putting the business supplies on the supplier as well would make it collect tax that its customers were entitled to claim back anyway, and would deny the customer the clean credit trail reverse charge gives him.
keywords: drawn round the recipient who cannot account for the tax

options.text: Nothing is payable on the individuals. A service imported by a person for his own private use is outside the levy
options.misconception: carries the general rule about personal imports into the one class of service written specifically to reach them
options.why: The general rule is real — an individual buying a service from abroad for private purposes is ordinarily outside, because the charge on imported services is built round business use. Online services are the deliberate exception, and the reason is competitive rather than revenue: an Indian supplier of the same thing must charge tax, so leaving the overseas one untaxed would hand it an advantage on price.
keywords: an Indian supplier of the same thing must charge tax

options.text: The Indian recipients in both cases, reverse charge being the answer wherever the supplier is abroad
options.misconception: extends reverse charge to a consumer who cannot register, cannot file a return and has no way of paying
options.why: Reverse charge works because the recipient is inside the system already. A private subscriber is not: he has no registration, no return and no ledger, and a tax he could only pay by registering for a single subscription would go uncollected. That is the practical reason the liability was put on the supplier for this class of service, and why a separate simplified registration had to be created for it.
keywords: a tax he could only pay by registering for a single subscription

citation.ref: Section 14 read with sections 2(16) and 2(17), and the simplified registration scheme for a supplier of online services

items.scenario: A company incorporated abroad streams design software over the internet to customers in India, with no human intervention on any order. Some of its customers are GST-registered businesses that use the software in their work. Many more are individuals who subscribe at home for their own use and are not registered under GST. The company has no office, no branch and no representative in India, and its counsel says that settles it: there is nobody here for the department to register.

items.stem: How does the pack have to be billed?

options.text: Four lines on the invoice — the 899 rupees split in proportion to shelf prices, each share at the rate its own item carries
options.misconception: treats a single price as something the supplier may allocate across the items behind it, when section 8 exists to stop exactly that
options.why: There is one price and the customer cannot decline any part of what he is paying it for, so there is one supply to be rated. If a supplier could write his own split, the tax on a bundle would depend on which share of the price he chose to put against the higher-rated item, and two shops selling the identical box would pay different amounts. The Act answers a bundle by fixing one rate for the whole of it.

options.text: One rate of 12 per cent, because the pack is sold as a set and a set takes the rate of the goods that give it its essential character
options.misconception: imports the tariff rule for classifying a set under one heading into section 8, which asks a different question and gives a different answer
options.why: Classifying goods under a heading and taxing a bundle of separately identifiable supplies are two exercises. Section 8 does not look for an essential character; it asks whether the supplies are naturally bundled, and where they are not it fixes the rate of the highest-rated part on the whole price. Essential character would also have pointed at the cheapest possible answer here, which is the direction a rule of that shape always drifts.

options.text: One rate of 18 per cent on the whole 899 rupees
options.why: Ask first whether this is a composite supply, because a bundle can only be mixed once that has been ruled out. Each item here is capable of being supplied separately, and the shop does sell each one on its own every other month of the year; the four sit in a box because it is August, not because that trade sells them together in the ordinary course of business. So they are not naturally bundled. Several supplies made together for a single price which are not a composite supply are a mixed supply, and a mixed supply is taxed as a supply of whichever part attracts the highest rate of tax. The water bottle's rate governs the lot, so the whole 899 rupees bears GST at 18 per cent.
keywords: each item here is capable of being supplied separately
that trade sells them together in the ordinary course of business
whichever part attracts the highest rate of tax
the whole 899 rupees bears GST at 18 per cent

options.text: One rate of 12 per cent, the bag being the most valuable thing in the box and so the item that gives the pack its character
options.misconception: reaches for the predominant element of a composite supply without first asking whether the four items are naturally bundled at all
options.why: A predominant element is a composite supply's idea. There, the parts are naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business, one of them is the principal supply and the other parts are ancillary to that principal supply, so the rate follows the principal one. None of that has been established here. Four goods a shop sells separately all year do not become naturally bundled because somebody put them in a carton, and picking the dearest item and calling it principal skips the only test that decides which rule applies.
keywords: naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business
the other parts are ancillary to that principal supply

citation.ref: Section 8(b) read with the definitions of mixed supply and composite supply in sections 2(74) and 2(30)

items.scenario: Kalpana Stationers, registered in Pune, boxes up a back-to-school pack every August: a school bag, a geometry box, a steel water bottle and a set of crayons, sold together for one price of 899 rupees. All four sit on the shelves separately the rest of the year, each with its own price tag, and a customer buying the pack cannot swap any of them out. Take the rates as given: the bag, the geometry box and the crayons bear 12 per cent, and the water bottle bears 18 per cent. The billing clerk proposes to spread the 899 rupees across the four in proportion to their shelf prices and charge each share at its own rate.

items.stem: What rate does the 6,00,000 rupees bear?

options.text: 5 per cent on the flour, and nothing at all on the carriage and the insurance, which are Kesar Agro's own costs of getting the goods there
options.misconception: treats a cost the supplier absorbs as falling outside the supply, when it is inside the single price the buyer pays
options.why: Nothing here is being recovered separately, so there is nothing to leave out. The 6,00,000 rupees is the whole consideration for a single composite supply, and the carriage and the cover are part of what that consideration buys. Had the contract been ex-factory, with the buyer arranging and paying for the lorry himself, the answer would change — not because the cost vanished, but because the supply would have ended at the factory gate.

options.text: 18 per cent on the whole 6,00,000 rupees, since a bundle takes the highest rate among its parts
options.misconception: applies the mixed supply rule without first ruling out a composite supply, which is the step that decides which of the two rules governs
options.why: The highest rate answers a bundle that is not naturally bundled. This one is, so the other half of section 8 applies and the rate follows the principal supply. Notice what the mistake costs here: the two routes give 5 per cent and 18 per cent on the same invoice, so a habit of reaching for the highest rate is not a safe shortcut that happens to land right — it is a thirteen-point error on 6,00,000 rupees.

options.text: 5 per cent on the whole 6,00,000 rupees
options.why: Where a supplier agrees to deliver at the buyer's premises and arranges the transport and the insurance himself, the whole thing is one contract that arrives naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business — nobody buys flour delivered and then hires his own lorry for the same load. What the distributor is buying is the flour; the carriage and the cover exist to get it to him, so the flour is the predominant element and the two services are ancillary to it. A composite supply is treated as a supply of its principal supply, so the flour's rate carries the entire 6,00,000 rupees at 5 per cent.
keywords: naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business
the two services are ancillary to it
treated as a supply of its principal supply

options.text: 5 per cent on a flour element and 18 per cent on a freight and insurance element carved out of the price
options.misconception: splits one composite supply into its parts because the parts would carry different rates if they were bought on their own
options.why: The rate those services would bear if somebody bought them separately says nothing about a contract that never sells them separately. There is one price, one delivery obligation and one thing the distributor ordered. Carving out an element the invoice never charged would make the tax depend on how the bill was typed.

citation.ref: Section 8(a) read with the definitions of composite supply and principal supply in sections 2(30) and 2(90)

items.scenario: Kesar Agro, a registered supplier in Rajkot, sells 200 quintals of packed flour to a distributor in the same State for 6,00,000 rupees. The contract says delivery is at the distributor's godown, and Kesar Agro arranges the lorries and the transit insurance itself and charges nothing extra for either — the 6,00,000 rupees covers the lot. Take the rates as given: the flour bears 5 per cent, and carriage and transit insurance bought on their own each bear 18 per cent. Kesar Agro's accountant is unsure whether to carve a freight and insurance element out of the 6,00,000 rupees and tax it at the higher rate.

items.stem: Which of the two belongs in the return?

options.text: The 5,00,000 rupees only, the sofa escaping because 18,000 rupees is nowhere near the threshold at which GST bites
options.misconception: reaches the right answer through the registration threshold, which is a rule about aggregate turnover and not about whether a thing is a supply
options.why: The threshold decides who must register; it never decides whether a transaction is a supply. Reading it that way would mean the sofa becomes taxable the moment Bhaskar's turnover is large enough, which it does not — the sale is outside the charge whatever his turnover, because it was not made in the course or furtherance of his business.

options.text: Both, because he is a registered person and the money is real in each case
options.misconception: makes registration the test, when registration decides who accounts for tax and the scope of supply decides what there is to account for
options.why: Registration is a status a person holds; supply is something a transaction either is or is not. The section asks about the transaction and never about the seller's registration number. If it were otherwise, the same sofa would be taxable in a registered man's hands and free in his neighbour's, which is not a distinction the Act draws anywhere.

options.text: Both, because a disposal is one of the forms named in the section and the sofa was disposed of
options.misconception: takes the list of forms as sufficient by itself, without the two conditions the same clause attaches to every one of them
options.why: Disposal is indeed one of the named forms, and the naming is not the test. Each form on that list becomes a supply only when two further things hold: a consideration, and a person acting in the course or furtherance of his own business. Read without those two conditions the clause would tax a man for giving his old sofa away, which is the reading the conditions exist to prevent.

options.text: The 5,00,000 rupees only
options.why: Clause (a) casts its net wide and then draws it tight twice. It takes in all forms of supply of goods or services or both — a sale, a transfer, a barter, an exchange, a licence, a rental, a lease, a disposal — and the list is illustrative rather than closed. But it takes them in only where the supply is made, or agreed to be made, for a consideration, and by a person acting in the course or furtherance of business. Consideration and business are two limbs and both have to be satisfied. The dealer transaction is a sale for a consideration made in the course of the fan trade, so it is a supply. The sofa fetched a consideration too, but selling the furniture out of one's own drawing room is not in the course or furtherance of business, so the second limb fails and it stays outside GST altogether.
keywords: all forms of supply of goods or services or both
a sale for a consideration made in the course of the fan trade
consideration and business are two limbs and both have to be satisfied
not in the course or furtherance of business

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

items.scenario: Bhaskar runs a proprietary firm in Nashik that trades in industrial fans. In March he sells fans to a dealer for 5,00,000 rupees on sixty days' credit. In the same week he sells the sofa set out of his own drawing room to a neighbour for 18,000 rupees; the sofa was bought years ago out of his salary, never entered the firm's books, and no credit was ever taken on it. His accountant proposes to put both amounts into the March return, saying that once a man is registered everything he sells is taxable.

items.stem: What has the accountant got wrong?

options.text: Both entries — the van is a supply of 9,00,000 rupees, and letting the godown is a supply of services
options.why: Exchange is one of the forms the section names, and that settles the van. A part-exchange is not one net payment; it is two supplies going in opposite directions, the dealer supplying the new van and the bakery supplying the old one, with the 1,50,000 rupees knocked off the price standing as the consideration for the old van. So the dealer's supply is valued at 9,00,000 rupees, not at the cash it happened to collect. Lease is another of the named forms, and the second Schedule then settles what kind of supply it is: any lease or letting out of a building for business is a supply of services. There is no category called income from property sitting outside GST.
keywords: Exchange is one of the forms the section names
a part-exchange is not one net payment
any lease or letting out of a building for business is a supply of services

options.text: Neither. The van's value is what was received, and a lease of immovable property transfers an interest in land and so lies outside the scope of supply
options.misconception: treats a lease of a building as a transfer of land outside GST, which is the exact question the second Schedule was written to answer
options.why: Sale of land, and sale of a completed building, are kept out by the third Schedule. A lease is not a sale. Letting a building out for business is named on the services side of the second Schedule, and a transfer of tenancy rights against a premium has been held to sit squarely inside the scope of supply for the same reason.

options.text: Only the godown. The van entry is right, because a trade-in is a discount on the price and 7,50,000 rupees is what changed hands
options.misconception: reads a trade-in as a reduction in price, when the thing handed over is itself consideration in a form other than money
options.why: A discount is something the seller gives up. Here the dealer received a van worth 1,50,000 rupees, which is consideration in kind and not an amount forgone. Treating it as a discount would let any supplier shrink his taxable value by taking part of the price in goods, and it would also hide the bakery's own supply of the old van entirely.

options.text: Only the van. The godown lease is inside GST but it is a supply of goods, a building being a thing rather than a service
options.misconception: gets the taxability right and the classification wrong, when the whole function of the second Schedule is to fix which of the two it is
options.why: Whether a transaction is a supply and what kind of supply it is are two separate questions, and the second Schedule answers the second one. It puts any lease, tenancy, easement or licence to occupy land, and any letting out of a building for business, on the services side. The classification matters beyond tidiness: it decides the place of supply and the time of supply, which are answered by different rules for goods and for services.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a) read with paragraph 2 of Schedule II

items.scenario: Chetna Motors, a registered dealer in Coimbatore, does two things in April. It sells a new delivery van listed at 9,00,000 rupees to a bakery, taking the bakery's old van in at an agreed 1,50,000 rupees and collecting 7,50,000 rupees in cash for the balance. It also lets its own godown to a courier company on a three-year lease at 40,000 rupees a month. Its accountant records the van as a supply of 7,50,000 rupees and leaves the godown out altogether, calling the rent income from property.

items.stem: What is the taxable value?

options.text: 79,900 rupees
options.why: Start with the transaction value, which is the price actually paid or payable where the parties are unrelated and price is the sole consideration. A discount given before or at the time of supply comes out of it if it has been duly recorded in the invoice, and this one has, so 72,000 rupees is where the count begins rather than where it ends. Three amounts then go back in. The municipal levy is a charge under a law other than the GST laws and it is charged separately by the supplier, so it is included. Crating is an incidental expense charged by the supplier before delivery, so it is included. The laboratory fee was Dhruv's own contractual liability, the builder discharged it directly and it never entered the price, so it is included as well. That is 72,000 plus 1,800 plus 2,500 plus 3,600, or 79,900 rupees.
keywords: the transaction value, which is the price actually paid or payable
a discount given before or at the time of supply comes out of it if it has been duly recorded in the invoice
a charge under a law other than the GST laws and it is charged separately
crating is an incidental expense charged by the supplier before delivery

options.text: 72,000 rupees — the three add-ons are recoveries, not the price of the tiles
options.misconception: treats an amount as outside the value because it sits on a line of its own, when the section is written to catch precisely what is charged on a line of its own
options.why: Putting a charge on a separate line is the condition for including a non-GST tax, not the escape from it. Every one of the three is inside the value for a reason the Act names: the levy because it is a tax under another law charged separately, the crating because it is an incidental expense charged before delivery, the laboratory fee because it was the supplier's liability paid by the recipient and left out of the price.

options.text: 87,900 rupees
options.misconception: adds the discount back, treating a reduction the supplier chose to give as something that cannot come off the taxable value
options.why: A discount shown in the invoice at the time of supply is deducted, and the Act says so in terms. What is refused is a discount that fails the conditions — one given afterwards with no agreement behind it, or one the invoice never recorded. This one was recorded in the invoice, so the price the parties actually settled on is 72,000 rupees and the count starts there.

options.text: 76,300 rupees
options.misconception: stops at what the supplier billed, missing the clause that reaches an amount the supplier was liable for and the recipient paid to a third party
options.why: This adds the levy and the crating and leaves the laboratory fee out, because Dhruv never invoiced it. That is exactly the case the section anticipates: an amount the supplier was liable to pay in relation to the supply, incurred instead by the recipient and not included in the price, is added to the value. The test is who was contractually liable, not who wrote the cheque.

citation.ref: Sections 15(2)(a), 15(2)(b) and 15(2)(c) read with sections 15(1) and 15(3)(a)

items.scenario: Dhruv Ceramics, Rajkot, invoices a builder for tiles. The list price is 80,000 rupees, against which the invoice itself shows a quantity discount of 8,000 rupees. On separate lines the same invoice charges a municipal levy of 1,800 rupees and crating of 2,500 rupees. Under the contract Dhruv Ceramics had to obtain a laboratory test certificate for the batch; the builder paid the laboratory's 3,600 rupees directly and Dhruv Ceramics has not billed it. The two are unrelated and the price is the only consideration. Dhruv's accountant proposes a taxable value of 72,000 rupees.

items.stem: Which of the four bears GST?

options.text: None of the four
options.misconception: attaches the exemption to the establishment rather than to the service, so anything done under the hospital's roof reads as exempt
options.why: The entry exempts health care services by a clinical establishment, not everything a clinical establishment does. The status of the provider is one half of the test and the character of the service is the other. That is also why the entry has to carve out a room charged at more than five thousand rupees a day outside intensive care — a hospital supplies things that are not health care, and the Act taxes those.

options.text: The hair transplant alone
options.why: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt, and the term reaches diagnosis, treatment or care for an illness, an injury, a deformity, an abnormality or a pregnancy in any system of medicine this country recognises. It also reaches carrying the patient to the establishment and back in an ambulance, so both ambulance runs travel with the treatment and are exempt. Hair transplants and cosmetic or plastic surgery are pushed out of the definition, but not absolutely: an operation that rebuilds or reconstructs a part of the body wrecked by an injury, by trauma, by a defect present at birth or by a developmental abnormality is inside the exemption after all. The jaw was crushed in the accident, so rebuilding it is reconstruction after injury. The hair transplant answers to nothing on that list and is taxable.
keywords: carrying the patient to the establishment and back in an ambulance
an operation that rebuilds or reconstructs a part of the body wrecked by an injury
the hair transplant answers to nothing on that list and is taxable

options.text: The hair transplant and the two ambulance runs
options.misconception: reads an ambulance as transport rather than as health care, when the definition takes patient transport in expressly and a second limb of the same entry catches whatever the first does not
options.why: The definition includes carrying the patient to a clinical establishment and back, so an ambulance run by the hospital is part of the exempt health care itself. And the entry has a second limb covering the transport of a patient in an ambulance other than what the first limb already covers, so even an ambulance run by somebody who is not a clinical establishment is exempt. There is no gap between the two for a patient's journey to fall into.

options.text: The hair transplant and the reconstruction of the jaw
options.misconception: applies the exclusion for hair transplants and cosmetic or plastic surgery without reading the exception that immediately follows it
options.why: The exclusion is real but it is qualified in the same breath. Surgery done to put back anatomy or a bodily function that a congenital defect, a developmental abnormality, an injury or trauma took away stays inside health care. Repairing a cleft lip is ICAI's own illustration of it, and a jaw crushed in a road accident is the same case with a different cause. What is outside is surgery done for appearance where nothing was lost.

citation.ref: Entry 74 read with the definition of health care services and its exclusion for hair transplant and cosmetic or plastic surgery

items.scenario: Sanjeevani Hospital, a clinical establishment in Indore, bills four things in a month. A road accident victim is admitted and treated as an inpatient in a general ward. The hospital's own ambulance brought him in and later took him home. A surgeon at the hospital rebuilds the same patient's jaw, which was crushed in the accident. The following week the same surgeon does a hair transplant for a walk-in client. The accounts head proposes to exempt all four, on the ground that a clinical establishment renders health care and nothing else.

items.stem: Which of the four bears GST?

options.text: The hospital's employee policy alone
options.why: From 22 September 2025 entry 36D exempts health insurance business an insurer supplies to an insured where the insured is not a group, and the explanation reads that as a contract whose insured is an individual, or an individual together with that individual's family. Rohit's family contract is one of those. So is his own accident cover, because health insurance business is defined to reach sickness benefits, medical, surgical or hospital expense benefits, travel cover and personal accident cover. A group is defined as people who come together with a shared purpose or for a common economic activity other than taking insurance, and an employer-employee arrangement is named inside that definition, so the hospital's staff policy is a group policy and stays taxable. Entry 36E then exempts reinsurance of the services the insurance entries exempt, so the ceded share follows the family policy it came from.
keywords: where the insured is not a group
an individual together with that individual's family
travel cover and personal accident cover
an employer-employee arrangement is named inside that definition

options.text: All four
options.misconception: works from the position before 22 September 2025, when there was no exemption for life or health insurance business at all
options.why: That was right until 22 September 2025 and is wrong from that date. Three entries came in together: one for life insurance business, one for health insurance business, each of them where the insured is not a group, and a third for the reinsurance of either. A note written before they came in will get three of these four wrong in the same direction.

options.text: The hospital's employee policy and Rohit's personal accident cover
options.misconception: reads health insurance business narrowly as hospitalisation cover, and so pushes accident cover outside an exemption that names it
options.why: The definition inserted with the exemption is wider than hospital bills. It reaches sickness benefits, medical, surgical or hospital expense benefits whether the patient is admitted or not, travel cover and personal accident cover. Rohit's accident cover is squarely inside it, and he is an individual rather than a group, so it is exempt.

options.text: The hospital's employee policy and the reinsurance cession
options.misconception: asks who the reinsurer's counterparty is, when the entry exempts reinsurance by reference to the underlying service instead
options.why: The reinsurance entry does not look at the reinsurer's own customer. It exempts reinsurance of the very services the life and health insurance entries exempt, so the character of the underlying policy carries through to the cession. Rohit's family policy is exempt, and the reinsurance of it is exempt with it. Had the underlying been the employees' group policy, the cession would have followed that instead and borne tax.
keywords: exempts reinsurance of the very services the life and health insurance entries exempt

citation.ref: Entries 36D and 36E inserted with effect from 22.09.2025, read with the definitions of group and of health insurance business

items.scenario: Suraksha General Insurance issues four things in October 2025. The first is a health policy under one contract covering Rohit, his wife and their two children. The second is a personal accident cover on Rohit alone. The third is a health policy for the four hundred employees of Sanjeevani Hospital, the hospital being the master policyholder. The fourth is not a policy at all: Suraksha cedes thirty per cent of the risk on Rohit's family policy to a reinsurer. Its tax head has been working from a note written in 2024 and thinks all four bear GST.

items.stem: What is the position on each consignment?

options.text: No duty on the first, duty payable on the second, and the section 23(1) route is closed on both
options.why: Section 13 covers goods pilfered after unloading and before the proper officer has ordered them cleared for home consumption or deposited in a warehouse; on those the importer is not liable to pay the duty, unless the goods are afterwards restored to him, and the bill goes to the custodian in whose shed they sat. The first consignment fits: unloaded, cartons tampered with, unit pieces missing, nothing restored. The second does not, because the clock had already stopped. Pilferage after the order for clearance and before the goods physically move out leaves the duty leviable. And section 13 is the whole of the law on pilferage, so a refund claim under section 23(1) for pilfered goods is not permissible on either one.
keywords: goods pilfered after unloading and before the proper officer has ordered them cleared
the importer is not liable to pay the duty
pilferage after the order for clearance and before the goods physically move out leaves the duty leviable
a refund claim under section 23(1) for pilfered goods is not permissible

options.text: A refund under section 23(1) on both, since duty on goods he never received cannot be right
options.misconception: uses section 23 as a general relief for anything that goes missing, when it expressly puts pilferage outside itself
options.why: Section 23 remits duty on goods lost otherwise than by pilferage, or destroyed. The words otherwise than by pilferage are doing work: they send pilfered goods back to section 13 and shut the refund door. The two sections are not alternatives a claimant may pick between, and choosing the wrong one is how a valid claim on the first consignment gets thrown out on the papers.

options.text: Duty on both — on the second because it was cleared, and on the first because relief needs the goods to be restored to him
options.misconception: inverts the restoration proviso, reading it as the condition for relief when it is the condition that takes relief away
options.why: Restoration is the exception, not the requirement. The importer is not liable for duty on pilfered goods except where they are restored to him, because a man who gets his goods back has lost nothing. Nothing was restored on the first consignment, so the relief stands.

options.text: No duty on either, because in both cases the goods were out of his hands when they went
options.misconception: takes the reasoning behind section 13 for the rule itself, when the rule is fixed to the clearance order and not to who held the goods
options.why: The reason the section exists is that a man should not pay duty on goods he did not control. But it is written to a moment, not to a state of affairs: the pilferage has to fall after unloading and before the order for clearance or for warehousing. Once that order is made the relief stops, whoever was physically holding the cartons at the time.

citation.ref: Section 13 read with section 23(1)

items.scenario: Nishant imports two consignments of ceramic bearings, both landed at Chennai. On the first, customs officers find at examination that three cartons have been tampered with and unit pieces are missing; the goods are still in the custodian's shed and no order for clearance has been made. Nothing is restored to him. On the second, the proper officer had already passed the order for clearance for home consumption when, before the lorry pulled out of the port, a carton was found broken open and pieces gone. His consultant advises a refund claim under section 23(1) on both.

items.stem: What does he do on each of the three?

options.text: Relinquish title on the fire-damaged goods and claim remission on the corroded ones
options.misconception: swaps the two remedies, when remission answers goods that are gone and relinquishment answers goods that are there and unwanted
options.why: Relinquishment is a right the owner has before an order for clearance under section 47 or an order permitting deposit under section 60 has been made. The glass panels were already in the warehouse under such an order, so that route was shut on them — and there was nothing left to relinquish in any case. Remission answers a loss; relinquishment answers a refusal.

options.text: Nothing on the third. Once the duty is paid and the clearance order is made, the consignment is closed
options.misconception: treats payment as the end of the matter, when an importer who finds pilferage only at removal is given a way to prove it
options.why: Pilferage is normally caught when customs examine the goods. Where it only surfaces as the importer removes them, the order for clearance or for bonding has already gone through and the duty has already been paid, so the importer asks the steamer agents, or insurance surveyors, for a survey; their report is what the claim then rests on. The remission reaches him in the shape of a refund of the duty he has already paid.
keywords: the importer asks the steamer agents, or insurance surveyors, for a survey

options.text: Claim remission under section 23(1) on all three, every one being a loss before clearance
options.misconception: treats section 23 as covering any consignment that disappoints, when it excludes pilferage and says nothing about goods the owner simply will not take
options.why: Only the fire is a section 23(1) case. The third is pilferage, which the sub-section puts outside itself in its own words. The corroded container is not lost or destroyed at all — it is sitting there, intact and unwanted — and the answer to that is relinquishment, which is a different sub-section with a different cut-off and a different consequence.

options.text: Apply for remission on the fire, relinquish title on the corroded container, and get a survey done on the third
options.why: Section 23(1) works where imported goods have been lost otherwise than by pilferage, or destroyed, at any time before clearance for home consumption, a warehouse included; on proof to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner the duty is remitted, and duty already paid comes back as a refund once the remission order issues. The fire left nothing, so it is the total loss the section asks for — and unlike section 13, this relief has to be asked for and proved rather than simply happening. The corroded container is a different remedy: section 23(2) lets the owner relinquish his title at any time before an order for clearance under section 47 or an order permitting deposit under section 60, and once he does he is not liable to the duty; that door shuts only if an offence appears to have been committed. On the third, the clearance order and the payment both came first, so he asks for a survey and builds the claim on the report.
keywords: lost otherwise than by pilferage, or destroyed, at any time before clearance
it is the total loss the section asks for
section 23(2) lets the owner relinquish his title

citation.ref: Sections 23(1) and 23(2), read with section 13

items.scenario: Three more of Nishant's consignments go wrong. A container of glass panels already deposited in a bonded warehouse is destroyed by a warehouse fire and nothing is recoverable. A container of machine tools arrives so badly corroded that he wants nothing to do with it; no order for clearance for home consumption has been made and none permitting deposit in a warehouse, and no offence is alleged in respect of the goods. On a third he had already paid the duty and taken the clearance order, and only when his own staff opened the cases inside the port did he find unit pieces missing.

items.stem: What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: Nothing can be done at all, because no appeal was filed and revision needs an appellate order to attach to
options.misconception: reads revision as a step that follows an appeal, when it exists for the order nobody appealed
options.why: Revision is not an appellate stage. It is the department's route to an order that has gone unchallenged, which is why the section makes the Authority wait until the departmental appeal window has closed before he uses it. An order already taken in appeal is the one case where his power is shut out, not the one case where it opens.

options.text: The whole plan. Revision corrects an order that has gone against the taxpayer, and this one went in his favour
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the power, which is the department's own second look and opens only where an order hurts the revenue
options.why: It points the other way. The gate is an order prejudicial to the interest of revenue, so a demand wrongly dropped is precisely what revision is for. A taxpayer aggrieved by an order has his own remedy and goes in appeal; he does not ask the Revisional Authority to help him.

options.text: Nothing. The trader was heard once already and the section asks for no second hearing
options.misconception: treats the hearing before the adjudicating officer as discharging the Revisional Authority's own duty, when the two hearings are about different proposed orders
options.why: The hearing before the Deputy Commissioner was about the case the Deputy Commissioner was deciding. What is now proposed is a different order, on grounds the trader has never answered, made by an officer he has never appeared before. The section requires the notice and the hearing wherever the revision is likely to affect the person adversely, and nothing about an earlier hearing satisfies it.

options.text: The grounds and the stay are sound; passing the revised order without hearing the trader is not
options.why: The Revisional Authority may act on his own motion, on information that reaches him, or at the request of the State tax Commissioner, and he may call for the record of any proceeding.
