Where a subordinate officer's order is prejudicial to the interest of revenue and is illegal or improper, or was made with material facts left out of account, he may stay its operation, make whatever further enquiry he needs, and pass a just order, enhancing, modifying or annulling the original. Both grounds are made out here: invoices on the file were not taken into account and the notification was misread. But where the order he proposes will affect the person adversely, he must serve a notice and give him a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and raising a demand of eighteen lakh rupees is as adverse as an order gets.
keywords: prejudicial to the interest of revenue and is illegal or improper
material facts left out of account
a reasonable opportunity of being heard

citation.ref: Section 108(1)

items.scenario: A Deputy Commissioner's order of June 2025 dropped a demand of eighteen lakh rupees against a trader. Nobody appealed it. In March 2026 the Additional Commissioner, acting as Revisional Authority on information that reached him, calls for the record. He finds that a bundle of invoices sitting on the file was left entirely out of account, and that the exemption notification was read in a way its words do not bear. He proposes to stay the order at once and, the same week, pass a revised order raising the demand, taking the view that the trader was heard by the Deputy Commissioner and is owed nothing further.

items.stem: How is the time he has left worked out?

options.text: He has no time at all, because the order went in appeal and an appealed order cannot be revised
options.misconception: reads the appeal bar as absolute, without the proviso that qualifies it for a point the appeal never decided
options.why: The bar exists so that two authorities do not decide the same question twice, which is why it lifts on a question the appeal never reached. The refund limb was never argued and never decided, so nothing would be decided twice. That is the whole reason the proviso is there.

options.text: Three years from the original order and nothing else, the appeal and the stay both being irrelevant to an unappealed point
options.misconception: keeps the plain three-year ceiling and drops both the extension the appeal earns and the exclusion the stay earns
options.why: The appeal is what brings the alternative one-year limb into play at all, and it is expressed as whichever is later precisely so that a long appeal does not shorten the Authority's time. And a stay is not neutral: the section stops the three years for the period a court or the Tribunal has held him back, because time he was forbidden to use should not be counted against him.

options.text: One year from the appellate order or three years from the original, whichever is later, and the four months of the stay do not count against the three years
options.why: Two rules run together here. An order already taken in appeal is out of reach, except on a point that was not raised and decided in that appeal; on such a point the Authority may still move, so long as he does so before one year has run from the date of the appellate order or before the three years from the original order have run, whichever is later. The refund limb is such a point. Then the clock itself: any period during which a court or the Appellate Tribunal has stayed the making of the revision order is left out when the three years are computed, so the four months of the High Court's stay are added back to the end.
keywords: a point that was not raised and decided in that appeal
before one year has run from the date of the appellate order
any period during which a court or the Appellate Tribunal has stayed the making of the revision order

options.text: One year from the appellate order, full stop, the three-year limit having been replaced once an appeal was filed
options.misconception: treats the one-year limb as a substitute for the three years rather than as the later of two dates
options.why: The two limbs sit side by side and the later of them governs. Read as a replacement, an appeal decided quickly would cut the Authority's time down instead of extending it, and an appeal decided after three years would give him a fresh year he was never meant to have. Whichever is later is what keeps both from happening.

citation.ref: The first and second provisos to section 108(2), read with sections 108(2)(b) and 108(5)

items.scenario: A Joint Commissioner's order of 10 February 2024 decided two things against Vasant Alloys — a classification question and the rejection of a refund. The company appealed the classification alone, and the Appellate Authority allowed it on 30 September 2025. The Revisional Authority wants to revise the same February 2024 order on the refund limb, which the appeal never touched. He was ready to move in June 2025, but the High Court stayed the making of any revision order between 1 May 2025 and 31 August 2025. He now asks his office how much time he has left.

items.stem: What is the position on its credit and its refund?

options.text: It is zero-rated on both, and the refund is whatever balance is sitting in the credit ledger at the end of the quarter
options.misconception: reads the refund as the ledger's closing balance, when the rule apportions it against turnover
options.why: The refund is not what the ledger happens to show. Rule 89(4) works it out as a proportion: the net input tax credit is multiplied by the turnover of zero-rated supply of goods plus the turnover of zero-rated supply of services, and divided by adjusted total turnover. Credit that belongs to the domestic and exempt side of the business stays where it is and waits for output tax.
keywords: Rule 89(4) works it out as a proportion

options.text: Only the German services are zero-rated; the racks are an ordinary domestic supply unless the zone unit exports what it makes with them
options.misconception: adds a condition the definition does not carry, when what it asks is that the supply be for the unit's authorised operations
options.why: The definition puts a supply to a special economic zone developer or unit for authorised operations alongside an export, and stops there. It does not follow the goods any further. What does have to be checked is the authorised-operations limb itself, because not every supply into a zone qualifies — only what the zone unit is authorised to be doing.

options.text: The credit behind the zero-rated supplies has to be reversed with the exempt-supply credit, and only tax actually paid can ever be refunded
options.misconception: applies the exempt-supply reversal to a zero-rated supply, which the Act carves out in the very sentence that allows the credit
options.why: That is the difference between an exempt supply and a zero-rated one. Exempt output kills the credit behind it; zero-rated output does not, and the Act says so by allowing the credit notwithstanding that the supply may be exempt. A refund of unutilised credit is exactly a refund of tax somebody else paid and Ira never got to use, which is the whole mechanism.

options.text: Both supplies are zero-rated, the credit survives, and it may ship under a letter of undertaking and claim the unutilised credit back
options.why: Zero-rated supply means the export of goods or services, and a supply of goods or services for authorised operations to a special economic zone developer or unit. What the unit does with the racks afterwards is not part of the test. Credit of input tax may be taken for making zero-rated supplies notwithstanding that the supply is itself an exempt supply, subject only to the blocked-credit rule, so the credit is not lost the way it is on the exempt domestic sales. The first of the two roads out is to supply under a bond or letter of undertaking without payment of integrated tax and claim refund of the unutilised input tax credit under section 54, and that road is open to every registered person making a zero-rated supply.
keywords: a supply of goods or services for authorised operations to a special economic zone developer or unit
notwithstanding that the supply is itself an exempt supply
the credit is not lost the way it is on the exempt domestic sales
a bond or letter of undertaking without payment of integrated tax

citation.ref: Sections 16(1), 16(2) and 16(3), read with section 54 of the CGST Act, 2017 and rule 89(4)

items.scenario: Ira Technologies, registered in Karnataka, does three things in a quarter. It exports design services to a client in Germany. It supplies fabricated racks to a unit inside a special economic zone, for that unit's authorised operations. And it makes a run of exempt domestic supplies. Its consultant tells it two things: that the racks are zero-rated only if the special economic zone unit is itself an exporter, and that since a slice of the output is exempt the input tax credit behind the zero-rated supplies has to be reversed like any other exempt-supply credit. Ira is sitting on a large unutilised credit balance and wants the cash.

items.stem: Where does that leave Ira on the three?

options.text: The refund on the goods shipment must go back, but without interest, because the buyer's failure to pay is not Ira's fault
options.misconception: reads the deposit-back obligation as a penalty for fault, when the proviso attaches interest to the money regardless of who is to blame
options.why: The proviso does not ask whose fault it was. The refund was paid out against an export whose proceeds never came, so the money goes back with the interest section 50 carries, within thirty days of the foreign exchange time limit expiring. Fault is not the trigger; non-realisation is. What can help Ira is an extension of the remittance period, because the thirty days run from the end of the period as extended.

options.text: The pay-and-claim road is open only to a notified class; the refund on the unpaid shipment goes back with interest; and the unpaid services are not an export at all
options.why: Section 16(4) of the IGST Act is what changed the second road. On the Council's recommendation, and subject to conditions it lays down, the Government notifies a class of persons, or a class of goods or services, who may take it — paying integrated tax on a zero-rated supply and claiming back the tax so paid. Unless Ira is inside such a notification, the letter of undertaking is the road it has. On the unpaid shipment, the proviso to section 16(3) makes a supplier who took a refund and then failed to realise the sale proceeds deposit it back, with the interest section 50 of the CGST Act carries, within thirty days after the time limit the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 allows for receipt of the remittance has expired. The services are a different problem altogether: an export of services is not complete until the exporter has been paid in convertible foreign exchange — or, where the Reserve Bank permits it, in Indian rupees — so an unpaid service never became an export in the first place.
keywords: Section 16(4) of the IGST Act is what changed the second road
the Government notifies a class of persons, or a class of goods or services
within thirty days after the time limit the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 allows
the exporter has been paid in convertible foreign exchange

options.text: It may switch to paying integrated tax whenever it likes, the two routes being at the exporter's choice
options.misconception: works from the position before section 16(4) was recast, when either route was open to any exporter
options.why: That was the law and it is not any more. The recast sub-section turns the pay-and-claim route into a permission the Government hands out by notification, to a class of persons or for a class of goods or services, rather than a choice each exporter makes for himself. An exporter outside every such notification has one road, not two.

options.text: The unpaid design services still count as an export, and the refund on them simply stays with Ira
options.misconception: treats an export of services as complete on the invoice, when receipt of the payment is part of the definition itself
options.why: Export of goods and export of services are defined differently on purpose. Goods have to leave the country; services have to be paid for, in convertible foreign exchange or in rupees where the Reserve Bank allows it, before the supply answers the definition at all. An unpaid service is not a zero-rated supply whose refund is at risk — it is not a zero-rated supply.

citation.ref: Section 16(4) as amended, and the proviso to section 16(3), read with the definition of export of services in section 2(6)

items.scenario: Ira Technologies now wants the other road: pay integrated tax on its exports and claim the tax back, because the money returns faster than a credit refund does. Two other things are on its desk. A shipment of goods exported last year under a letter of undertaking has still not been paid for, and the time the foreign exchange law allows for the remittance has just run out; Ira took a refund on that shipment when it went. And a client abroad has not paid at all for a batch of design services invoiced eight months ago.

items.stem: Which date does Kalinga build its acquisition accounting on?

options.text: 1st September 20X1, when the shares were entered in Kalinga's name in the register
options.misconception: waits for legal title instead of asking when the buyer could start deciding things
options.why: Registration records a change that has already happened in substance. The standard asks when the acquirer became able to direct the acquiree, and Kalinga was directing Rukmini for nearly a month before the register was written up. If title fixed the date, a registrar's backlog would move a company's reported results.

options.text: 1st April 20X1, the date the agreement names for the business to pass
options.misconception: lets a date the parties chose in their own contract fix the accounting date
options.why: A date written into a share purchase agreement settles who keeps the profits earned in between and who bears the losses. It answers nothing about when the buyer became able to run the business, so an appointed date the parties chose does not fix the acquisition date. That word carries accounting weight in one place only — inside a scheme of arrangement sanctioned under section 232, where the Ministry's circular of August 2019 deems the scheme's own date to be the acquisition date and the date control transferred. There is no scheme here, so the general rule is the whole of the answer.
keywords: an appointed date the parties chose does not fix the acquisition date

options.text: 4th August 20X1, when its nominees took the majority of Rukmini's board
options.why: Ind AS 103 fixes one date by one test, and the acquisition date is the day on which the acquirer obtains control of the acquiree. Control under Ind AS 110 needs all three of power over the investee, exposure to variable returns from being involved with it, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. A majority of the board seats is what hands Kalinga the first, and it carries the third with it, so all three arrive together on 4th August and not before. Signing, clearing, paying and registering are steps arranged around that day; none of them is a substitute for it.
keywords: the acquisition date is the day on which the acquirer obtains control
power over the investee, exposure to variable returns from being involved with it

options.text: 20th August 20X1, when the consideration was paid
options.misconception: treats payment as the event that transfers control
options.why: Payment is one of the things measured on the acquisition date, not the thing that sets it. Businesses are paid for before control, after control and in instalments falling either side of it; on this reasoning an earn-out settled in year three would keep moving the date for years.

citation.ref: Paragraph 8, read with the definition of control in Ind AS 110

items.scenario: Kalinga Ceramics Limited agrees to buy 68 per cent of Rukmini Tiles Limited from its promoters. There is no scheme before any Tribunal; the shares are bought under a share purchase agreement signed on 12th May 20X1, which names 1st April 20X1 as the date from which the business is to be treated as Kalinga's between the parties. Competition clearance comes through on 28th July 20X1, and on 4th August 20X1 Kalinga's three nominees take their seats and hold the majority of Rukmini's board. The price is paid on 20th August 20X1 and the shares are registered in Kalinga's name on 1st September 20X1.

items.stem: How are the two later figures dealt with?

options.text: Neither, because a value settled after the reporting date is a change in estimate carried forward from the date it becomes known
options.misconception: sends acquisition-date information into prospective estimate accounting
options.why: A change in estimate is what you make when the underlying facts themselves have moved. Nothing moved here. The plot's soil and title, and the contract's worth, were what they were in November 20X1 and only the knowledge caught up, which the standard sends backwards rather than forwards.

options.text: The June 20X2 figure goes back through the acquisition accounting; the February 20X3 one is corrected as a prior period error
options.why: Where the accounting for a combination is unfinished at a reporting date the acquirer carries the numbers on a provisional footing, and as facts that already existed on the day control passed come to light, the provisional amounts recognised at the acquisition date are retrospectively adjusted, with the difference falling on goodwill. That window is not open indefinitely. The measurement period ends when the missing facts arrive or when the acquirer learns they will not, and in no case does it run on: it shall not exceed one year from the day control passed, which shuts Sahyadri's window on 31st October 20X2. June 20X2 is inside it. February 20X3 is fifteen months out, and a change made then to something already true in November 20X1 is an error corrected under Ind AS 8.
keywords: the provisional amounts recognised at the acquisition date are retrospectively adjusted
the measurement period ends when the missing facts arrive
it shall not exceed one year from the day control passed

options.text: Both go through goodwill, since both concern conditions that existed on the day control passed
options.misconception: keeps the first half of the test and drops the deadline that goes with it
options.why: Two things have to be true together: the fact must have existed when control passed, and the information about it must arrive inside the year that follows. Keep only the first and a goodwill figure could be reopened a decade later on an old fact freshly noticed, which is the outcome the one year limit exists to prevent.

options.text: The June 20X2 figure goes through goodwill and the February 20X3 one is taken to profit or loss as a fair value change
options.misconception: reports a late-found acquisition-date fact as though it were this year's event
options.why: Putting it through this year's profit says something happened this year, and nothing did. A fact that was true on the day control passed but is found after the window closes is a prior period error, corrected by restating the earlier figures rather than by a hit to the current result.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 45 and 46, read with Ind AS 8 on errors

items.scenario: Sahyadri Alloys Limited obtains control of a target on 1st November 20X1 and closes its books on 31st March. At 31st March 20X2 the value of a plot of land taken over is still unsettled and is carried at ₹40 crore pending a valuation. The valuation arrives in June 20X2 at ₹46 crore, resting on soil and title facts that were already true in November 20X1. In February 20X3 a second report arrives, this time saying that a customer contract taken over had been worth ₹9 crore more than was recognised, again on facts true in November 20X1. The controller proposes to put both differences through goodwill.

items.stem: How is the earn-out treated, on acquisition and now?

options.text: ₹8 crore formed part of the consideration on day one, and the ₹7 crore fall goes to profit or loss — goodwill is left alone
options.why: The acquisition-date fair value of contingent consideration is part of what the acquirer is treated as having paid, so the consideration transferred was ₹128 crore and not ₹120 crore. What happens afterwards depends on why the number moved, and missing a revenue target after the deal is not a measurement period adjustment: nothing new has been learned about the state of the business on the day control passed. An earn-out to be settled in cash is a liability, so it is remeasured to fair value at each reporting date and the change is taken to profit or loss.
keywords: the acquisition-date fair value of contingent consideration is part of what the acquirer is treated as having paid
missing a revenue target after the deal is not a measurement period adjustment
remeasured to fair value at each reporting date and the change is taken to profit or loss

options.text: Take the ₹7 crore off goodwill, the earn-out having been part of the price
options.misconception: reads every later movement in an earn-out as a measurement period adjustment
options.why: Goodwill moves only for information about what was already true when control passed — a valuation that lands late, an obligation nobody had found. A revenue target missed because trading since the deal has been poor is news about this year, and routing it through goodwill would let a bad year quietly improve the balance sheet instead of the profit.

options.text: Leave the earn-out out of the consideration until it is known whether the target is met, and recognise it only if it becomes payable
options.misconception: waits for the contingency to resolve instead of measuring the promise itself
options.why: The standard measures the promise, not the outcome. On the day control passed the seller held a right worth ₹8 crore and the buyer carried an obligation of the same size. Omitting both understates what the business cost and would show a windfall gain later if the target were missed.

options.text: Hold it at ₹8 crore until it is settled, because contingent consideration is not remeasured
options.misconception: applies the equity rule to a cash-settled earn-out
options.why: Not remeasuring belongs to contingent consideration classified as equity, where the acquirer will hand over a fixed number of its own shares and no obligation to pay cash exists. This promise is cash, so it is a liability and it is marked to fair value at every reporting date until it is discharged.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 39, 58 and the treatment of contingent consideration classified as equity

items.scenario: Neelambari Foods Limited buys a bakery business for ₹120 crore in cash and a promise of a further ₹20 crore in cash if the unit's revenue crosses a stated figure within two years. The fair value of that promise on the day control passed was ₹8 crore. At the next reporting date trading has been poor, the target now looks unlikely to be met, and the promise is worth ₹1 crore. The finance head proposes to take the ₹7 crore fall off goodwill.

items.stem: What must Vindhya be able to show its own shareholders?

options.text: That the combined value of ₹1,320 crore exceeds Vindhya's own ₹900 crore, which it plainly does
options.misconception: compares the combined value with the acquirer alone and forgets what was given up
options.why: Of course the combined firm is bigger — Vindhya has taken in a ₹300 crore business and given away ₹360 crore of itself to do it. The comparison that decides anything sets the combined value against both standalone values together, and then asks what was paid above the target's own worth.

options.text: That the gain from combining is bigger than what it paid over Alaknanda's own worth — ₹120 crore against ₹60 crore, leaving Vindhya ₹60 crore
options.why: Value is created only where the combined business beats the two companies added together, and the excess of the combined value over the two standalone values is the synergy — ₹1,320 crore less ₹1,200 crore, so ₹120 crore. Against it stands the cost of getting it, which is the premium paid over the target's own value: ₹360 crore of shares for a business worth ₹300 crore, so ₹60 crore. The net gain to the acquirer is the value of synergy reduced by that premium, which leaves Vindhya ₹60 crore. An exchange ratio decides how the gain is divided, not whether there is one, and a ratio defensible on every weight could have handed Alaknanda's holders the whole ₹120 crore.
keywords: the excess of the combined value over the two standalone values is the synergy
the premium paid over the target's own value
an exchange ratio decides how the gain is divided, not whether there is one

options.text: That the ratio was fixed by an independent valuer on accepted weights, which is what shows the terms are fair to Vindhya's shareholders
options.misconception: mistakes a defensible way of splitting a gain for proof that a gain exists
options.why: The valuer answers how much of the combined company each side's holders should end up owning. He is not asked, and does not answer, whether owning that share of the combined company leaves Vindhya's holders better off than owning all of what they had. Both questions can be answered honestly and come out in opposite directions.

options.text: That the ₹360 crore of shares is less than the ₹420 crore Alaknanda's holders would have had on a book value ratio
options.misconception: measures the deal against a worse deal instead of against not doing it
options.why: A price lower than one nobody offered proves nothing. The benchmark is the target's standalone value, because that is what Vindhya could have left alone, and every rupee paid above it has to be earned back out of the gain from combining.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 Advanced Financial Management
citation.ref: Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — gains from mergers or synergy

items.scenario: Vindhya Steel Limited is worth ₹900 crore standing alone and Alaknanda Forgings Limited ₹300 crore. The two boards agree the combined business will be worth ₹1,320 crore. Vindhya will issue its own shares worth ₹360 crore to Alaknanda's holders. Vindhya's directors point to the exchange ratio behind that figure, fixed by an independent valuer on weights of 50 per cent to earnings per share, 25 per cent to market price and 25 per cent to book value, and tell their own shareholders that a ratio arrived at so carefully is proof the deal creates value for them.

items.stem: What does the auditor owe before he can use that report as evidence?

options.text: Three things — test what the valuer brings to the job, find out what he actually did, and judge whether his assumptions and methods carry the assertion
options.why: A report is not audit evidence merely because an expert produced it. The valuer here was chosen and paid by the company, so his report is the work of a management's expert, and how far the auditor goes with it turns on how much that work matters to his own conclusion. He must evaluate the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert, from his qualifications, his earlier work and what others who have used him say. He must obtain an understanding of what the expert did. And he must judge the appropriateness of that expert's work for the assertion it supports, which reaches the assumptions and methods chosen and whether those are accepted in the expert's own field and fit for financial reporting.
keywords: his report is the work of a management's expert
evaluate the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert
judge the appropriateness of that expert's work for the assertion it supports

options.text: Nothing further — the firm is well known and holds a registration, which answers competence and objectivity together
options.misconception: reads a credential as the answer to both of the questions the standard asks
options.why: A registration says something about capability and nothing about independence on this engagement. Objectivity asks what could pull the expert towards the number management wants — who instructs him, how much of his income the company is, whether his fee moves with the answer — and none of that shows on a certificate.

options.text: Obtain a fresh valuation from an auditor's expert, because work done for management can never support the auditor's conclusion
options.misconception: rules the management's expert out instead of testing what he produced
options.why: The standard sets out how such work is to be used, not how it is to be refused. Engaging an expert of the auditor's own is one response where the first report cannot be relied on, and that is a decision reached after the evaluation rather than in place of it.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the directors that the fair values are appropriate, and file it with the report
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for the evaluation the auditor has to make himself
options.why: A representation is management telling the auditor what management thinks, and it never stands in for evidence he could obtain himself. Here the whole question is whether the figure management handed him can be relied on, and asking management to confirm it adds nothing to what he already has.

citation.ref: Information prepared using the work of a management's expert

items.scenario: Kalinga Ceramics has completed its purchase and its statutory auditor is auditing the allocation of the purchase price. The fair values of the plant and of a customer relationship intangible come from a valuation firm that Kalinga's own management chose, instructed and paid. The engagement partner proposes to put the valuer's report on the file, note that the firm is well known and holds a registered valuer number, and conclude that the fair values are supported.

items.stem: Is the going concern basis available to Purnima?

options.text: No, but what fails is the assessment period, so the cure is to shorten the period the assessment covers
options.misconception: reads the twelve-month horizon as a window an entity may trim to fit its own facts
options.why: Twelve months is a floor on how far management must look, not a distance it may cut back when the view is bad. An entity that cannot see itself continuing that far has answered the question rather than run out of road, and the answer changes the basis of preparation.

options.text: Yes — nothing removes the basis until the board resolves to wind up or to stop trading
options.misconception: reads the rule as needing a decision and leaves out the limb that needs none
options.why: Two of the three triggers are decisions and the third is a state of affairs. A company whose only site is going and which cannot replace it has lost the basis because of what is true, not because of what has been minuted, and waiting for a resolution keeps the numbers on a footing the company no longer has.

options.text: No — the basis goes when there is no way out, whether or not anybody has decided anything
options.why: Three situations take the basis away and only two of them are decisions. Statements are prepared on a going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate the entity, or intends to stop trading, or management has no realistic alternative to closing. Purnima is in the third: four months of lease, the site let to another party, and nothing to move to. The third limb bites with no resolution behind it, so the statements are not prepared on a going concern basis and the company discloses that fact, the basis it has used instead, and why it is no longer regarded as a going concern. The point also settles the horizon question, because management's assessment reaches at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period, and Purnima cannot see four.
keywords: management has no realistic alternative to closing
the statements are not prepared on a going concern basis
management's assessment reaches at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period

options.text: Yes, so long as the lease position is set out in a note and the auditor adds a material uncertainty paragraph
options.misconception: treats a note and an emphasis as a cure for the wrong basis of preparation
options.why: A material uncertainty paragraph is for a company that is still a going concern with serious doubt around it. Where the basis itself has gone, every number in the statements is measured on a footing that does not apply, and a note beside them does not put them right — the auditor is dealing with a misstatement, not with an uncertainty.

citation.source: Ind AS 1, Presentation of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Going concern — the three situations in which the basis is unavailable

items.scenario: Purnima Textiles Limited has one mill and nothing else. Its lease of the land runs out in four months; the owner, a State body, has refused to renew it and has already let the site to somebody else. The mill cannot be moved. There is no money to buy another site, no other business, and no buyer for the undertaking. The board has passed no resolution to wind up, and the managing director says that while the directors have taken no decision to close, the accounts for the year just ended go on the going concern basis with a note describing the lease position.

items.stem: What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: It treats a list of examples as a scoring sheet — three items present do not settle Tamasa, and no item present does not clear Saraswati
options.why: The examples are there to direct attention, not to be counted. Negative operating cash flows indicated by the historical or the forecast statements, adverse key ratios and an inability to comply with the terms of loan agreements are each on the list and Tamasa has all three — but the list is neither all-inclusive nor conclusive, and a facility renewed in writing for three years is exactly the mitigating fact that has to be weighed against them. Saraswati is the other direction: losing the customer that pays for nine tenths of the business is on no list and is plainly capable of casting significant doubt.
keywords: negative operating cash flows indicated by the historical or the forecast statements
an inability to comply with the terms of loan agreements
the list is neither all-inclusive nor conclusive

options.text: Nothing — the list is the standard's own, and applying it as written is what the auditor is asked to do
options.misconception: reads a list of examples as a test with a pass mark on it
options.why: The words around the list say what it is: events or conditions that may, singly or together, cast significant doubt. The word "may" is doing the work. An auditor counting items is not exercising the judgement he is asked for, and the counting goes wrong in both directions.

options.text: Only the Tamasa conclusion is wrong — a full order book and a renewed facility mean no doubt arises there at all
options.misconception: lets one mitigating fact cancel the indicators instead of being weighed against them
options.why: A renewed facility is real evidence and it belongs on the other side of the scale; it does not remove the scale. The auditor still has to ask whether the company can service that facility out of cash flows that are negative today, and whether a covenant already broken puts the renewal itself at risk.

options.text: Only the Saraswati conclusion is wrong — customer concentration is a business risk and belongs to risk assessment rather than going concern
options.misconception: files a fact by its label instead of asking what it does to the entity
options.why: Every going concern indicator is a business risk of some kind. The question is whether the event can cast significant doubt on the entity continuing, and losing nine tenths of the revenue plainly can, under whatever heading it was first noticed.

citation.source: Ind AS 1, Presentation of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Examples of events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the ability to continue as a going concern

items.scenario: Two audits are reviewed on the same morning. Tamasa Papers Limited has cash flows from operations that are negative in both its past statements and its forecasts, key ratios that look bad, and a covenant on its term loan that it has broken; its order book is full and its bank has renewed the facility in writing for three years. Saraswati Cables Limited shows not one of the listed indicators, but the single customer that brings it nine tenths of its revenue has gone into insolvency. The audit senior proposes to conclude that a material uncertainty exists at Tamasa because three items on the list are present, and that none exists at Saraswati because no item on the list is.

items.stem: Which of the three decisions can stand?

options.text: The third only — where management will not assess, a modification is the remedy and no further evidence is available
options.misconception: turns management's inaction straight into an opinion without asking for the assessment
options.why: Not having got round to an assessment and refusing to make one are different situations, and the auditor finds out which he is in by asking. If management then declines, a consequence follows — but it follows from a request made and refused, not from a step the auditor left out.

options.text: The first and second — a signed representation and a confirmed enforceable letter are both audit evidence, and only the third decision is premature
options.misconception: treats written documents as sufficient evidence because they are written
options.why: Both are evidence and neither is sufficient. The representation says what management intends, and its intention is the very thing in doubt; the letter says what the trust has promised, and the promise is worth what the trust is worth. Written evidence about a future action still has to be tested against what the facts permit.

options.text: None of them — the agreements still have to be read, the supporter's means still have to be assessed, and management is first asked to do its assessment
options.why: A representation letter is management's word about its own plans and is never enough on its own; it does not release the auditor from reading the terms the company has broken and working out what they now allow the lender to do. On the promise of support, confirming that the arrangement exists, is lawful and can be enforced is half the work, because the financial ability of the party promising the money has to be assessed too — a binding promise from somebody who cannot pay is worth nothing. And where management has not yet performed an assessment, the step called for is to request one; jumping to a modified opinion skips the evidence the auditor was meant to gather.
keywords: a representation letter is management's word about its own plans and is never enough on its own
the financial ability of the party promising the money has to be assessed
where management has not yet performed an assessment, the step called for is to request one

options.text: The second only — the trust's letter has been confirmed as existing, lawful and enforceable, which is what the procedure names
options.misconception: stops at existence and enforceability and drops the ability to actually provide the funds
options.why: The procedure has two halves in one sentence: confirm that the arrangement exists, is lawful and can be enforced, and assess whether the party can find the money. A family trust can sign anything. Whether ₹30 crore is within its reach is what decides whether the letter is evidence or paper.

citation.ref: Additional audit procedures when events or conditions casting significant doubt are identified

items.scenario: The auditor of Bhadra Rollers Limited has identified conditions casting significant doubt on the company continuing. The file records three decisions. First, the directors have signed a representation setting out their refinancing plans, so the team has not read the loan agreements the company has breached. Second, a letter from the promoter's family trust promising ₹30 crore of support has been checked and found genuine and enforceable, and the team has minuted that the trust's own means need not be looked into. Third, management has made no going concern assessment at all, and the team has decided to modify the opinion on that footing alone.

items.stem: What does the team have to do with the forecast and with the minute books?

options.text: Test what the forecast assumes against how the last one turned out, and read the minutes for what the company itself has recorded about its difficulties
options.why: A forecast is worth what its assumptions are worth, so the auditor evaluates the assumptions underlying the cash flow and profit forecasts and weighs them against the historical accuracy of this company's own forecasting and against conditions in the market now. A 22 per cent rise in charter rates is a claim to be tested against broker data, and last year's miss is direct evidence about the method that produced this one. Separately, he reads minutes of meetings of shareholders, of those charged with governance and of the relevant committees for references to financing difficulties. That is where the company's own account of its trouble is written down, and it is evidence rather than a secretarial formality.
keywords: the assumptions underlying the cash flow and profit forecasts
the historical accuracy of this company's own forecasting
minutes of meetings of shareholders, of those charged with governance and of the relevant committees

options.text: Check that the forecast adds up and is internally consistent, and leave the minute books to the secretarial team
options.misconception: audits the arithmetic of a forecast instead of what it assumes
options.why: The arithmetic in a forecast is rarely where it fails; the assumptions are. A model that foots perfectly on a 22 per cent rate rise nobody can support proves only that the spreadsheet works, and it is the rate rise that decides whether the company survives.

options.text: Ask management to confirm the assumptions in writing, that being the evidence available about a future event
options.misconception: turns something that looks untestable into a representation instead of testing it
options.why: A future event cannot be confirmed, but the basis for expecting it can be tested — past forecasting accuracy, published charter rates, brokers' valuations of the two vessels. Reaching for a representation where testing is open is how a weak forecast gets on to the file unchallenged.

options.text: Read the minutes only if the forecast turns out to be unsupportable, minutes being corroborative rather than primary
options.misconception: makes a required procedure conditional on how another one turns out
options.why: The minutes are read as part of the work rather than as a fallback, and they often carry the fact that changes the whole picture — a bank's refusal noted at a board meeting, a rescue plan the committee turned down. An auditor who opens them last learns it after he has already formed a view.

citation.ref: Evaluating management's plans, the cash flow forecast and the reading of minutes

items.scenario: Ratnagiri Marine Limited's management has produced a cash flow forecast showing recovery within eighteen months. It rests on charter rates rising 22 per cent and on two vessels being sold at prices set by an in-house estimate. Last year's forecast, prepared the same way by the same people, was missed by a wide margin. The audit team has the forecast. It also has the minute books of the board, of the audit committee and of the last general meeting, which it has not opened, on the view that minutes are a company law matter for the secretarial team.

items.stem: What does clause (xix) ask the auditor to say?

options.text: An opinion, formed from named inputs, about the liabilities the company carried at the balance sheet date over the year after it
options.why: The clause names what he reasons from and leaves nothing to be added: the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of the company's financial assets and of payment of its financial liabilities, the other information that travels with the financial statements, and his knowledge of what the Board and management plan. On that footing he says whether no material uncertainty exists at the date on which he signs about the company being capable of meeting the liabilities it carried at the balance sheet date, as they fall due, within a period of one year from the balance sheet date. Directors' assurances are not one of the named inputs; and the year is measured from the balance sheet date, not from his report, so his own next report has nothing to do with it.
keywords: the ageing and expected dates of realisation of the company's financial assets
no material uncertainty exists at the date on which he signs
within a period of one year from the balance sheet date

options.text: Nothing separate — a clean opinion on the financial statements already says no material uncertainty exists
options.misconception: treats the audit opinion as discharging a separate reporting clause
options.why: The two questions overlap without being the same. The opinion is on the financial statements as a whole; the clause asks a narrower question about meeting a defined set of liabilities over a defined year, off a defined list of inputs, and it has to be answered in its own words in the CARO report.

options.text: The same opinion, but running for a year from the date of the audit report, so a liability arising after the year end is inside it and one at the year end may be outside
options.misconception: shifts both ends of the window on to the report date
options.why: Two dates do different jobs here and swapping them changes the answer. The opinion is formed as at the report date; the liabilities looked at are those the company carried at the balance sheet date, and the twelve months are counted from that date as well.

options.text: A certificate that the company will be able to pay everything it owes, for which the directors' assurances are the natural basis
options.misconception: reads the clause as a promise about the future rather than an opinion at a date
options.why: The clause asks for an opinion held as at the date the report is signed, off a list of inputs that does not include what the Board has said. Read as a certificate it would put the auditor behind a promise about events nobody can control, and it would move the basis from ratios and ageing to management's own confidence.

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xix)

items.scenario: Harihar Alloys Limited's auditor is drafting his report under CARO 2020. The ratios are strained and ₹40 crore of receivables are more than two years old, but the Board has a plan to sell a division and the auditor is satisfied there is no material uncertainty. Under clause (xix) he proposes to write that, on the strength of the directors' assurances, the company will be able to meet all its liabilities as and when they fall due, and that this holds until his next report. The audit manager asks him to read the clause once more before the report goes out.

items.stem: Why is that not the exercise the firm has been engaged for?

options.text: An audit gives an opinion on statements already drawn up; this looks for what is not in them, and then restates the figure the price was built on
options.why: An audit is an independent examination of financial information ending in an opinion on it. Due diligence is an examination of the business a buyer is about to put money into, made to confirm all material facts before the buyer commits, and its stated objective is to look specifically for any hidden liabilities or over-valued assets — the very things an unmodified opinion would not have brought to the surface. What comes out of it feeds the price, because net worth is restated for the over-valuation and under-valuation it finds in the assets and the liabilities.
keywords: made to confirm all material facts before the buyer commits
look specifically for any hidden liabilities or over-valued assets
net worth is restated for the over-valuation and under-valuation it finds

options.text: The review is narrower than that — it covers the tax position, and the audited accounts settle everything else
options.misconception: mistakes the tax strand for the whole of the financial review
options.why: Tax due diligence is a separate strand, usually folded into the financial review because a company's tax position is part of its financial state. It sits beside the work on liabilities, assets and earnings rather than standing in for it.

options.text: It is the exercise, done properly — the accountant re-performs the audit on the same figures with more scepticism
options.misconception: treats due diligence as a second audit of the same statements
options.why: The two ask different questions. An audit asks whether the statements give a true and fair view of what they contain; the review asks what a buyer needs to know before paying, which reaches obligations the company has never recorded and assets carried at figures no purchaser would pay.

options.text: It is unnecessary altogether where the opinion is unmodified, since that means no material misstatement exists
options.misconception: reads an audit opinion as a warranty about the business itself
options.why: An unmodified opinion says the statements are free of material misstatement measured against the reporting framework. Show cause notices that have not become demands, comfort letters that are not guarantees, and an indemnity given on a business sold years ago can all be missing from the statements without any of them being a misstatement.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — the difference from audit, and the objective of the review

items.scenario: A buyer's finance director engages a firm of chartered accountants for a financial due diligence review of a target, then tells the partner that since the target's statutory audit for the year is complete and the opinion unmodified, the review can be limited to re-reading the audit file and confirming that the audited figures were the ones used to price the deal.

items.stem: How does the accountant classify and treat the three?

options.text: None of them, because an item the accounting standards do not require to be recognised cannot bear on the price
options.misconception: lets the recognition rules decide what a buyer ought to pay
options.why: Recognition answers what goes into the statements. The price answers what the business is worth to somebody who will inherit everything it carries, recorded or not. The whole reason for looking for hidden liabilities is that the two questions have different answers.

options.text: Only the show cause notices, the other two being exposures of other people rather than of the target
options.misconception: reads a comfort letter and an indemnity as somebody else's problem
options.why: A comfort letter is given because the bank wants somebody standing behind the borrower, and it is relied on in practice even though it falls short of a guarantee. An indemnity given on a sale is the target's own promise to the buyer of that business. Both can be called on against the company this buyer is about to own.

options.text: All three, but they are reported to the buyer without touching the price, none of them having crystallised
options.misconception: separates telling the buyer from pricing the deal, when the review exists to join them
options.why: The review is done in order to price the deal. An exposure that has not crystallised still has a size and a likelihood, and the buyer's response is a lower offer or an indemnity from the seller. Telling him and leaving the price alone hands him the information and none of the protection.

options.text: All three are liabilities hidden from the accounts, and all three come off the restated net worth whatever the books show
options.why: These are the standard examples of what the exercise exists to surface. A company may leave out show cause notices which have not matured into demands, and those can be material and important. Letters of comfort given to banks and financial institutions are not guarantees, so they may not be disclosed in the balance sheet at all. And where a business has been sold under an agreement to take over and indemnify its liabilities and contingent liabilities up to the transfer date, that too may be absent from the books. The finance head is right that they are not in the accounts and wrong that they are not the buyer's concern, because after the deal the buyer owns them.
keywords: show cause notices which have not matured into demands
letters of comfort given to banks and financial institutions are not guarantees
an agreement to take over and indemnify its liabilities and contingent liabilities

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence — hidden liabilities

items.scenario: The review of a target turns up three things that are nowhere in its balance sheet. Tax show cause notices for ₹18 crore have not become demands and are not carried as contingent liabilities. Letters have been given to two banks that lent to a subsidiary. And in a business sold three years ago the target agreed to take over and indemnify the liabilities and contingent liabilities of that business up to the date of transfer, with nothing about it in the books. The target's finance head says none of the three belongs in the accounts, and that none of them is the buyer's concern.

items.stem: How does the accountant deal with the three?

options.text: Only the investments, a fall in realisable value being measurable where the other two are matters of opinion
options.misconception: keeps the findings that are easy to quantify and drops the ones needing judgement
options.why: Difficulty of measurement is not a reason to accept the figure in the books. Ageing gives a defensible estimate on the receivables and a brand out of use has a straightforward answer. Dropping the hard items is how a review comes back with a comfortable number and no use.

options.text: The receivables and the investments, but not the brand — an intangible carried at cost comes down only when an impairment test says so
options.misconception: applies the seller's reporting framework where the question is what the buyer is getting
options.why: An impairment test decides what the seller's own statements ought to have said. The buyer is asking something else: what does he receive for the ₹6 crore of the price that sits against this brand. A brand withdrawn from use two years ago produces nothing for him, and whether the seller ran the test properly does not change that.

options.text: None of them, each having been accepted by the statutory auditor, so the accountant has no basis to disagree
options.misconception: treats the audit as having already answered the buyer's question
options.why: The auditor formed a view under the framework the seller reports on, using the seller's own assumptions about holding periods and revival plans. The buyer's accountant is not bound by those assumptions, and testing them is the reason he was engaged.

options.text: All three are assets carried above what they are worth, and the restated net worth falls by the shortfall on each — the brand being the one to look hardest at
options.why: The three sit on the standard list. Uncollected or uncollectable receivables belong on it; so do investments carried at cost though realisable value is much lower; and so do intangible assets of no value. Being legally due does not make a three-year-old debt collectable, an intention to hold does not restore a value that has gone, and a brand nobody uses earns nothing for the buyer. The accountant is told to pay particular attention to the valuation of intangibles, which is where the gap between the books and the truth is usually widest.
keywords: investments carried at cost though realisable value is much lower

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence — over-valued assets

items.scenario: The same review finds ₹9 crore of receivables more than three years old against which nothing has been done; long-held investments carried at their cost of ₹25 crore whose value if sold today is ₹6 crore; and a brand carried as an intangible at ₹6 crore which the company stopped using two years ago. The seller answers that the receivables are legally due, that the investments are held for the long term so market movements do not matter, and that the brand could always be revived.

items.stem: What do the findings do to the case for the deal?

options.text: They take ₹45 crore off the price, and once the price comes down the deal is exactly as attractive as it was
options.misconception: repairs the price and forgets that the expected gain came out of the same accounts
options.why: Cutting the price restores what is being paid over the target's own value, which is half the answer. The other half is that the ₹60 crore of expected gain was itself estimated from the target's reported earnings, and earnings carrying unrecorded exposures are not the earnings the combination inherits.

options.text: They cut Kalindi's standalone value, which widens what Meghna is paying over it, and ₹45 crore against a ₹60 crore gain leaves almost nothing
options.why: The price rested on net worth and on the trend of profitability, and underneath it sat an assumption that every contingent liability capable of touching the business had been recorded. That assumption has failed. Restating net worth downwards lowers the target's standalone value, and the premium is what the buyer pays over the target's standalone value — so an unchanged price over a smaller value is a larger premium. The net gain to the acquirer is the value of synergy less that premium, so ₹60 crore of expected gain against a premium that has just grown by ₹45 crore leaves Meghna about ₹15 crore where it believed it had ₹60 crore.
keywords: the price rested on net worth and on the trend of profitability
the premium is what the buyer pays over the target's standalone value
the net gain to the acquirer is the value of synergy less that premium

options.text: Nothing, because the ₹60 crore expected gain comfortably exceeds the ₹45 crore found
options.misconception: sets the findings against the gain and leaves out what is being paid over the target's value
options.why: The gain from combining has to cover what is paid above the target's own worth before anything reaches the buyer. The findings do not shrink the gain; they enlarge what is being paid over the value, and it is the remainder after that which the ₹45 crore eats into.

options.text: Nothing to the case — the findings are what the warranties and indemnities in the agreement are for
options.misconception: treats a contractual remedy as the equal of not overpaying in the first place
options.why: A warranty is a promise to argue about later, worth what the seller is still good for and what a court will award. It does not change what the business is worth today, and a buyer who pays the full price and keeps a claim has swapped a certain ₹45 crore for an uncertain one.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 Advanced Financial Management, read with Paper 3 on the objective of financial due diligence
citation.ref: Gains from mergers or synergy, and the restatement of net worth in a due diligence review

items.scenario: Meghna Retail Limited has agreed to pay ₹340 crore for Kalindi Stores Limited, a figure arrived at from Kalindi's net worth and the way its profits have moved over recent years. Meghna's board expects the combined business to be worth ₹60 crore more than the two apart. The due diligence review then finds ₹45 crore of unrecorded exposures and assets carried above their worth. Meghna's finance director says the price is agreed and the findings are a matter for the warranties in the agreement rather than for the number.

items.stem: Which partner is right?

options.text: The first partner — the exception for non-assurance work applies only where the firm does audit the client and the service sits outside the audit
options.misconception: inverts the class of client the Council's addition actually covers
options.why: The addition runs the other way. It covers non-assurance work done for clients the firm does not audit, which is where the pull on the member's independence is weakest. A fee moving with the result of non-audit work done for a company the firm also audits is the combination the clause is most anxious about.

options.text: Neither — the clause catches the fee on its face, and the answer then turns on whether this engagement is inside the permitted list
options.why: A member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct where he charges or accepts, for professional work, fees which are contingent upon the findings or results of that work, or which are based on a percentage of profits, except as permitted by a regulation made under the Act. One per cent of the price finally paid moves with what the review turns up, so the clause is engaged and the first partner is right that far. Regulation 192 is the permission the clause points to, and beside the receiver, the liquidator, the co-operative society auditor and the valuer in direct tax matters it lets the Council add engagements — and the Council has added non-assurance services to non-audit clients. Since the buyer is not audited by the firm, the question is whether this review sits inside that class.
keywords: fees which are contingent upon the findings or results of that work
Regulation 192 is the permission the clause points to
the Council has added non-assurance services to non-audit clients

options.text: The second partner — the basis of the fee is a commercial matter, and the client's agreement in writing settles it
options.misconception: treats the client's consent as the test the clause applies
options.why: The clause looks at how the fee is worked out, not at who agreed to it. Consent from the person paying is present in every one of these engagements and would empty the rule if it were the answer. Permission comes from a regulation made under the Act, not from a signature on an engagement letter.

options.text: Neither, but for a different reason — a due diligence review is not professional work within the clause, so the basis of the fee does not matter
options.misconception: reads the clause as reaching only audit and assurance engagements
options.why: The clause speaks of any professional work a member in practice undertakes, and a financial due diligence review by a chartered accountant in practice is squarely inside it. That is exactly why the answer has to be found in the permitted list rather than in the nature of the engagement.

citation.ref: Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants in practice is offered one per cent of the price finally paid, as its fee for a financial due diligence review carried out for a buyer who is not an audit client of the firm. One partner says the fee is plainly misconduct because it moves with the outcome of the work. Another says any percentage fee is fine so long as the client agrees to it in writing.

items.stem: How should the auditor answer the finance team's reading of the definition?

options.text: Accept it. The definition sets out the relationships it covers, and a relationship it does not name is outside the standard, however uncomfortable the facts look
options.misconception: reads an inclusive definition as an exhaustive one, so a relationship absent from the printed list is treated as excluded by the standard
options.why: A definition that names examples and a definition that draws a boundary are two different instruments, and this one is the first kind. Its opening words are a test — expected sway in dealings with the entity — and the names that follow are the obvious cases, not the only ones. Reading the names as the whole rule would let any relationship be taken outside the standard by the simple fact that nobody thought to print it, which is the reading the test exists to prevent.

options.text: Apply the Companies Act's list of relatives instead, since disclosure in the notes is a matter of company law
options.misconception: takes the definition from the statute rather than from the applicable financial reporting framework, which is what governs a disclosure question
options.why: Two regimes run over the same facts and they are asking different questions. The Act's list of relatives decides whether a contract needed approval and whether a director was interested in it. What goes into the notes to the accounts is decided by the framework the statements are prepared under, and that framework has its own definition with its own test. Borrowing one to answer the other produces a right answer to a question nobody asked.

options.text: Ask whether the daughter is financially dependent on the Chief Financial Officer, and treat the customer as unrelated if she is not
options.misconception: swaps the standard's test of expected influence for a test of financial dependence, which is only one of the named examples
options.why: Dependants are one line in the list, not the rule the list illustrates. A grown daughter who supports herself can still be somebody her father would deal differently for, and he can still be somebody she would deal differently for. Turning the whole definition into a means test both narrows it and makes it easy to defeat: the money moves, and the relationship stays exactly where it was.

options.text: Tell them the list is a set of examples rather than a boundary, and that the question on these facts is one of sway, not of whether a particular label is printed in the standard
options.why: The standard describes close members of the family of a person as those who may be expected to influence, or be influenced by, that person in their dealings with the entity, and only then gives a list — which it opens with the word "includes". A list that includes is a list with room left in it, so reading it as a closed set inverts what the definition does. The second half of the answer is who the Chief Financial Officer is: he sits inside key management personnel, which makes him a related party of the company in his own right. So the live question is not whether "son-in-law" appears anywhere. It is whether a daughter and the man she is married to are people whose dealings with this company he could sway, or who could sway him — and an ₹8 crore run of sales to a company one of them directs is the fact that puts the question.

citation.ref: Close members of the family of a person, and key management personnel as related parties

items.scenario: A robotics manufacturer's last-quarter sales include ₹8 crore to a customer incorporated six months earlier. An audit assistant finds that a director of that customer is married to the daughter of the manufacturer's Chief Financial Officer. The finance team produces the definition from the accounting standard and reads out the people it names — a spouse or domestic partner, children, parents, brothers and sisters, the partner's children and dependants — and points out that a daughter's husband is on none of those lines. On that footing they have made no disclosure and want the matter closed before the audit committee meets.

items.stem: What does the money having arrived actually settle?

options.text: Existence and valuation together, so all that is left is whether the relationship should be described in the notes
options.misconception: collapses several assertions into the one the payment happens to touch, and reduces the whole matter to a disclosure question
options.why: Assertions do not travel in a bundle. A receipt speaks to whether a balance was collectible; it says nothing about cut-off, about the rights the entity had, or about whether the revenue is properly recognised in this period. And treating what remains as a disclosure question assumes the transaction itself is sound, which is the proposition under examination. Disclosure is what follows a conclusion about the transaction, not a substitute for reaching one.

options.text: Nothing about the year under audit, because a receipt after 31st March is a subsequent event and belongs in next year's file
options.misconception: files a fraud risk indicator as a subsequent-events question, so the fact that most sharpens the risk is set aside as belonging to another period
options.why: The date the money landed is not being used as an event of the new year. It is being used as a fact about the old one: a customer that settled a very large balance in the first week after the year end, on a deal struck weeks earlier, in a period the auditor is already looking at hard. Evidence obtained after the balance sheet date about conditions existing at it is exactly what an auditor is meant to use, and pushing it into another file loses the one thing that made the pattern visible.

options.text: The occurrence of the sales. Payment is the strongest single piece of evidence that a transaction was real, so substantive work on this revenue can be scaled back
options.misconception: treats cash received as proof that the underlying sale occurred, when the payer may be part of the same arrangement as the seller
options.why: The strength of external evidence comes from its independence, and that is precisely what is in doubt here. Where the counterparty is connected to an officer of the entity, its payment is not an outside voice confirming the entity's records; it is one more record made by people on the same side. Money can be sent round a circle and come back as a receipt. What the auditor still needs is the movement of goods, the terms, and the reason the customer exists.

options.text: The recovery question and nothing beyond it — the risk the auditor is weighing is about whether the sales happened at all, and a payment from the same counterparty cannot answer that
options.why: Cash from a debtor is evidence that the debtor paid. It is not evidence that goods moved, that the deal was struck on ordinary terms or that the year in which the revenue was booked is the right one. A large sale in the closing quarter, to a company set up during the same year, settled just after the year end and traced to an officer of the entity, is an unusual transaction on every one of those counts, and the auditor has to carry it as a significant risk of material misstatement rather than as a receivable that has since cleared. What he is testing for is fraudulent financial reporting — revenue put into a year it does not belong to, with a buyer whose purpose may be to receive it — and money from that same buyer is part of the arrangement, not a check on it. It also reaches backwards: once management has described a relationship as a coincidence, the auditor has to reconsider the reliability of management's representations across the whole file rather than on this item alone.

citation.ref: Professional scepticism, significant unusual transactions, and reconsidering management's representations where a misstatement may be fraudulent

items.scenario: The same ₹8 crore of sales was booked in the last quarter to a company incorporated during the year, and the money arrived on 5th April, five days after the year end and a few days before the audit began. The Chief Financial Officer says the point is now academic: the debtor has paid, so there is nothing left in the balance sheet to test, and the audit team should move on to areas where money is still outstanding.

items.stem: What does the auditor have to do instead of accepting that representation?

options.text: Report the matter to the Board and suspend testing until the company's own inquiry has finished and reported
options.misconception: hands the auditor's own procedures to the entity, so the audit's conclusion ends up resting on an inquiry the auditor did not run
options.why: Telling those charged with governance is right and it is not enough, because it is not a substitute for anything. The entity's inquiry is management's work, run by people the finding may reach, and its outcome is one more piece of information for the auditor to evaluate rather than the answer he was going to look for himself. Stopping work while it runs also costs him the thing he most needs — the chance to test the dealings before anybody has had time to arrange them.

options.text: Take the representation. A written statement from the officer who knows the facts is audit evidence, and the auditor is entitled to rely on it where nothing contradicts it
options.misconception: treats a written representation as a substitute for evidence, when it is a supplement to evidence and never stands alone on a matter this material
options.why: Something already contradicts it. The person signing is the person the relationship runs through, and the entity has been asked to disclose the relationship and has declined. A representation carries weight where it confirms what other work has shown; it carries none where it is offered in place of that work on a matter the auditor has flagged as a risk. Accepting it here would mean the audit's conclusion on this transaction rests on the account of the person the transaction points at.

options.text: Test this transaction thoroughly and leave the rest of the related party work as planned, since the planning stage already covered related parties
options.misconception: leaves the planning-stage related party list standing after it has been shown to be wrong, so the risk of further undisclosed parties is never reassessed
options.why: The planning work produced a list, and the list has just failed. That failure is information about the list, not only about the one name missing from it: whatever process produced it either did not reach this relationship or was not told about it, and the same process produced every other name on it. Reconsidering the risk that other related parties remain undisclosed is a separate requirement precisely because the natural instinct is to fix the gap that was found and leave the rest where it was.

options.text: Work the relationship through the whole file — confirm it, tell the team, get every dealing with this counterparty out of management, test those dealings, and ask what else has been kept back
options.why: A previously unidentified related party sets off a sequence, and a representation is nowhere near the start of it. The auditor first determines whether the surrounding circumstances confirm that the relationship exists. He then passes the information round the engagement team, because whoever is on receivables and whoever is on revenue both need it. He asks management to identify every dealing the entity has had with the party thus surfaced, performs substantive procedures on those dealings rather than accepting a description of them, and reconsiders the risk that further related parties are still undisclosed — one that was hidden makes the rest of the list less trustworthy, not more. And where the failure to disclose appears intentional, he weighs what that says about the audit as a whole, which is a larger question than this transaction.

citation.ref: Identification of previously unidentified or undisclosed related party transactions, and the response where non-disclosure appears intentional

items.scenario: The relationship between the customer's director and the Chief Financial Officer's daughter is now established. Management refuses to describe it in the notes and says the sales were at arm's length. The engagement partner proposes a way through: take a written representation from the Chief Financial Officer that the pricing was at arm's length, file it, and finish the audit on schedule.

items.stem: What is still missing from the file?

options.text: Nothing, once the board note is on the file. A record made by the board is the board's approval, and the date it carries does not change what it records
options.misconception: reads a document created after the question was asked as evidence of a decision taken before it, so the timing that makes the approval meaningful is treated as a formality
options.why: The date is the whole of it. The approval the Act asks for is a control that operates before money is committed, and a note written eleven months later cannot have controlled anything. What it is evidence of is that the board has now been told. The auditor may well record it as such; what he may not do is treat it as the evidence that the transaction was authorised when the company entered into it.

options.text: Nothing, because ₹8 crore falls below the threshold at which shareholders must approve a related party contract, so no approval was required in the first place
options.misconception: reads a threshold that decides when shareholders must approve on top of the board as though it decided whether any approval was needed at all
options.why: The thresholds sit above the board's approval, not in place of it. Crossing one adds a shareholder resolution to what the board has already done; staying below it removes the shareholders' step and leaves the board's exactly where it was. Reading a threshold as a floor below which nothing is required would mean the smaller a related party contract is, the less the company has to decide about it, which is the reverse of how the section is built.

options.text: Nothing. A contract signed by an authorised signatory is itself the company's authorisation, and no separate record is needed where the signature is valid
options.misconception: treats the counterparty's own document as evidence of the company's internal authorisation, so the person who signed becomes the proof that he was allowed to
options.why: A signature answers who bound the company. Authorisation answers whether the company decided to be bound, and it is a different event with a different record: a decision taken by the body the law puts in charge of the decision, taken before the commitment. If the signature were its own authority, no approval requirement could ever be broken by a signed contract, which would empty the requirement out.

options.text: Evidence that the company authorised the deal, which neither document supplies — one is the bargain itself and the other was written after the auditor asked
options.why: Three things are required of the auditor on a significant transaction outside the normal course: inspect the underlying contract, evaluate the business rationale for the deal and whether its terms sit with what management has said about it, and obtain audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved. The third is the one this file cannot meet. A contract records what the two sides agreed; it says nothing about whether the company's own machinery let it agree.
