And a note minuted eleven months late, after the auditor raised the point, records that the question was asked rather than that the approval existed when the company bound itself. The Act wanted a resolution before the contract was entered into, and there was none.

citation.source: SA 550, Related Parties, read with the Companies Act, 2013
citation.ref: Significant related party transactions outside the entity's normal course of business, read with section 188

items.scenario: The ₹8 crore contract is a significant transaction outside the entity's normal course of business. The audit file holds the signed contract and a board note recording it, minuted three weeks after the audit team raised the point and eleven months after the contract was made. No resolution was passed before the company committed itself. Management says the signed contract is the approval and the note puts any doubt to rest.

items.stem: Where does the shareholding leave the engagement partner?

options.text: Out. The bar reaches the group and it reaches a father, and the holding is ten times the room the proviso leaves
options.why: A father is a relative for this purpose, so the second comfort fails at the first step. The disqualification bites where the auditor or his relative holds any security or interest — in the company, in a subsidiary of it, in its holding company or in an associate — so the first comfort fails too, and a subsidiary is named in the very list the partner is trying to escape by pointing at it. What the proviso leaves is narrow: a relative may hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000. Here the face value is ₹10 each on 1,00,000 shares, which is ₹10,00,000, ten times what is allowed. He is disqualified from being the auditor of this company, and going on with the engagement while disqualified is itself professional misconduct rather than a matter to be corrected quietly at the end.
keywords: his relative holds any security or interest

options.text: Unaffected, because the shares of an unlisted subsidiary trade at well under their face value, so the money at stake is trivial
options.misconception: measures the holding by what it would fetch, when the limit in the provision is written in face value and does not move with the market
options.why: The limit is expressed in face value, and face value is fixed by the share itself rather than by what anybody would pay for it. That is deliberate: a market-value test would make an auditor's eligibility rise and fall with the client's own results, which is the thing being guarded against. Here the arithmetic is done on the ₹10 printed on each share, and it gives ₹10,00,000 whatever the shares are worth today.

options.text: Unaffected, because the shares are in a subsidiary and the audit engagement is with the parent
options.misconception: reads the disqualification as covering only the company being audited, when it names the subsidiary, the holding company and associates as well
options.why: The bar was drafted with exactly this arrangement in mind. An auditor whose family holds shares one level down has the same interest in the group's reported results as one who holds them at the top, because the subsidiary's numbers are consolidated into what he is signing. That is why the provision does not stop at the company but walks the group — up to the holding company, down to the subsidiary, and across to associates.

options.text: Unaffected, because the shares are his father's. What a relative owns is the relative's business, and independence is tested on the auditor
options.misconception: drops the relative limb of the provision, so a holding only counts when it stands in the auditor's own name
options.why: If the rule stopped at the auditor's own name it could be met in an afternoon by moving the shares to a parent. The provision names the auditor, his partner and his relative for that reason, and the only concession it makes to relatives is a small ceiling on face value — which is itself an admission that the relative's holding counts, or there would be nothing to put a ceiling on.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d)(i) with its proviso, read with Rule 10 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, and Clause (9), Part I, First Schedule, Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: Midway through the same audit the engagement partner learns that his father holds 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in AutoBots Limited, a subsidiary of the company he is auditing. AutoBots has paid-up capital of ₹5 crore and the shares change hands at a fraction of their face value. His co-partner offers two comforts: the shares are in a subsidiary and not in the audit client, and they belong to his father rather than to him.

items.stem: Is a qualified opinion the right modification here?

options.text: Yes. Only the note is wrong — the revenue itself is recorded at the right amount in the right account — so the misstatement touches one disclosure and a qualification covers it
options.misconception: measures pervasiveness by how many figures move, when the test is whether the effects are confined and a disclosure failure can reach the statements as a whole
options.why: A missing related party disclosure is not a small fact about one note. It changes how a reader understands revenue, receivables and the terms the business was done on, and it does so for a transaction worth more than half the year's profit. The standard's test looks at where the effects reach, not at how many figures were retyped, and here they reach the statements as a whole together with the reliability of what management has said about them.

options.text: No — the effects are not held inside any one part of the statements, and the funding round is not a fact the auditor is allowed to weigh
options.why: Pervasiveness is not measured by how many lines change. It asks whether the effects are confined, and these are not: revenue at more than half of profit before tax is misstated in its description, the related party note is wrong, and the refusal itself casts doubt on the integrity of the people who prepared everything else in the file. Put together, the misstatements are material and pervasive, because their effects are not confined to specific elements, accounts or items of the financial statements. Where a misstatement is pervasive, a qualification is not strong enough to say what has happened, and the modification the standard calls for is an adverse opinion. What the report will do to a funding negotiation is not a matter the auditor may take into account at all, in either direction.

options.text: No modification at all. Set the facts out fully in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which tells the reader everything without overstating the auditor's position
options.misconception: treats a paragraph that describes a matter as a way of not modifying, when such a paragraph may only draw attention to something already properly presented
options.why: A paragraph of that kind is built on the premise that the statements are right and something in them deserves attention. It cannot be used where the statements are wrong, and using it there tells the reader that a matter is worth noticing while the opinion above it says everything is in order. Describing a misstatement in careful detail and then declining to modify is not a middle course; it is an unmodified opinion with a footnote.

options.text: No — a disclaimer, because management's refusal means the auditor cannot obtain the evidence he needs about the relationship
options.misconception: treats a refusal to disclose a known fact as an inability to obtain evidence, so a misstatement is reported as a scope limitation
options.why: Two different failures produce two different reports. A scope limitation is where the auditor does not know; a misstatement is where he knows and the statements say otherwise. Here he knows — the assistant found the relationship, the circumstances confirm it, and management has been told. Nothing is missing from his evidence. What is wrong is the financial statements, and a disclaimer would say the opposite of the truth about his own work.

citation.source: SA 705 (Revised), Modifications to the Opinion in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: The meaning of pervasive, and the choice between a qualified and an adverse opinion

items.scenario: Management will not disclose the relationship. The transaction is ₹8 crore of revenue against a profit before tax of ₹15 crore, and the refusal comes after the officer concerned called the relationship a coincidence. The engagement partner proposes a qualified opinion with a long Basis for Qualified Opinion paragraph setting out the facts, and mentions that a funding round the company is negotiating would not survive anything harsher.

items.stem: What does the timetable require him to do, and when?

options.text: Report to the Board within 45 days, which is the period the Rule gives the auditor for that first step
options.misconception: attaches the forty-five days to the auditor's own step, when that period is what the Board is given to answer in
options.why: The two periods belong to two different people. The auditor's step is measured in days and is meant to be almost immediate, because the value of the warning falls the longer it is held. The longer period is the entity's, to look into what it has been told and to answer. Swapping them gives the auditor six weeks of silence the Rule never gave him, and leaves the entity no time at all.

options.text: Complete the audit, then file one consolidated report covering every matter he has found, which is both clearer for the Government and fairer to the company
options.misconception: treats the fraud report as part of the audit report, so a duty with its own statutory clock is folded into the timetable of the audit
options.why: The report under this sub-section is a separate filing to a separate addressee, and it exists precisely because the audit report comes too late to be any use. A fraud left unreported until the accounts are signed has had months of cover, and the periods in the Rule are measured in days for that reason. Tidiness is not a consideration the Rule offers, and a consolidated letter at the end is a breach dressed as good practice.

options.text: Put it to the Board or Audit Committee within days, ask them for an answer inside a fixed period, and send the whole exchange on once their answer arrives
options.why: The Rule runs a clock that management has no power to stop. The matter goes to the Board or the Audit Committee at once and not later than 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, and the letter that carries it asks for their reply or observations within 45 days. What then travels to the Central Government is three documents together — his own report, whatever the Board or Committee said back, and his comments on what they said — and they must leave within 15 days of the reply reaching him. None of the three periods waits for the audit to close, which is why management's request cannot be met even if the company's inquiry is genuine.
keywords: not later than 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud

options.text: Send his report straight to the Central Government without going to the Board first, since the fraud is internal and the Board may be compromised
options.misconception: skips the step the Rule places first, confusing who must be asked for a reply with who the report is ultimately made to
options.why: The Board or Committee is asked, and the Government is reported to. Those are two roles and the Rule assigns them in that order, because what reaches the Government is meant to include the entity's answer and the auditor's view of that answer. Going straight past the first step deprives the Government of exactly the material the Rule was built to collect, and the Rule already provides for a Board that says nothing — it does not need the auditor to decide in advance that it will.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
citation.ref: Section 143(12) and Rule 13(1), manner of reporting to the Central Government

items.scenario: On 5th June the engagement partner of a listed company has reason to believe that a purchase manager routed ₹1.8 crore of purchases through a supplier he controls, at inflated rates. Management asks him to hold the matter until the audit is finished and then set everything out in one letter, arguing that the company's own inquiry is running and that early reporting would be premature.

items.stem: What does the auditor send to the Central Government now?

options.text: Nothing yet. The Committee has asked for time on a matter it is actively investigating, and a reasonable extension is within the auditor's discretion
options.misconception: reads the forty-five days as a minimum the entity may extend by asking, when it is the outer limit after which the auditor must file whatever has or has not arrived
options.why: The period is not the auditor's to give away, because it is not there for his convenience or the company's. It is the entity's one chance to put its side to the Government, and the Rule fixes how long that chance lasts so that an inquiry can never be used to keep a report from being filed. An auditor who grants a month has, in substance, rewritten the Rule for the benefit of the people the report is about.

options.text: A fresh letter to the Committee restarting the forty-five days, since the Committee has now confirmed it is looking into the matter
options.misconception: treats a period that runs once from the auditor's first letter as one that can be reset by writing again
options.why: The clock started when the matter was first put to the Board or Committee, and nothing in the Rule lets it be wound back. If a second letter could restart it, the report could be postponed indefinitely by correspondence, which would leave the Government dependent on the goodwill of the people being reported. The auditor writes once and then files.

options.text: His report alone. There is no reply to forward, so there is nothing to attach to it
options.misconception: drops the note that goes in place of the reply, so the filing loses the very fact that the entity was asked and stayed silent
options.why: What is attached is not the reply — there is none — but the account of the asking. It tells the Government what the auditor put to the Board or Committee, and when, and that nothing came back. Send the report on its own and the file reads as though the first step had never been taken, which is both untrue and the reading least favourable to the auditor who did take it.

options.text: His report, together with a covering document explaining that the Committee was written to and has not answered
options.why: Silence does not extend the period and it does not excuse the filing. The report goes to the Central Government on the same terms it would have gone on if a reply had come, and what goes with it in place of the reply is a note containing the details of the report already sent to the Board or the Audit Committee and drawing no reply or observations. That note is the point of the step: without it the Government would receive a report and have no way of telling whether the entity had been asked at all, and an entity that answers nothing would end up in a better position than one that answers badly.
keywords: a note containing the details of the report already sent

citation.ref: Rule 13(1), where no reply or observations are received within the stipulated period

items.scenario: The forty-five days have run out. The Audit Committee has acknowledged the auditor's letter and has said nothing else; its own inquiry into the purchase manager is still going on and its chairman asks for another month before it commits itself to anything in writing.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way the report is about to go out?

options.text: Nothing of substance. The Rule requires a report and this is one; the form and the method of sending are matters of practice rather than requirements
options.misconception: treats a prescribed form and a prescribed manner as administrative preferences, when both are written into the Rule and a report in another shape is not the report the Rule asks for
options.why: The Rule sets out the form, the addressee, the carriage, the letterhead, the seal and the membership number one after another because a report of this kind has to be capable of being authenticated. A signed sheet on plain paper arriving by e-mail can be neither traced to a member nor proved to have been sent, which is exactly the position an auditor least wants to be in if the company later says it was never told.

options.text: Nearly everything about its form, its addressee and its carriage — the Rule prescribes all three and none of them has been followed
options.why: The Rule leaves the auditor no choices here. The report is made as a statement in Form ADT-4, not as a letter of the auditor's own design. It goes out in a sealed cover addressed to the Secretary of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, carried by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due or, failing that, Speed Post, with an e-mail afterwards only to confirm that it went. And it sits on the auditor's own letterhead carrying his postal address, e-mail address and telephone or mobile number, signed with his seal and showing his membership number, so that the Ministry can tell at a glance which member is making the report and reach him about it.

options.text: Only the addressee. The Rule contemplates e-mail, so sending it electronically to the right office satisfies the manner of reporting
options.misconception: reads the confirmatory e-mail as an alternative way of sending the report, when it follows the posted report rather than replacing it
options.why: The e-mail exists to confirm that something was posted, which means there has to be a posting for it to confirm. Its job is to close the gap while the sealed cover is in transit, not to carry the report itself. An e-mail on its own leaves no sealed cover, no acknowledged delivery and nothing on the prescribed form, so all three of the Rule's requirements fail together while the auditor believes he has filed.

options.text: Only the delivery. The Registrar of Companies is the right office, since that is where the company's filings are made and where its records sit
options.misconception: sends the report to the office that holds the company's own filings rather than to the officer the Rule names
options.why: The Registrar receives what a company files about itself. This report is not the company's filing and is not for the company's file — it is an auditor telling the Government that an offence may have been committed, and the Rule names the officer it must reach. Routing it into the company's own records is the one destination that makes the confidentiality of the sealed cover pointless.

citation.ref: Rule 13, the form of the report and the manner in which it is sent

items.scenario: An assistant prepares the filing. He drafts it as a signed letter on plain paper, addresses it to the Registrar of Companies, and proposes to send it as an attachment to an e-mail so that it is on record the same day.

items.stem: What must still happen about the ₹6 lakh?

options.text: The auditor reports it, but the company need disclose it in the Board's Report only if it is material to the financial statements
options.misconception: puts a materiality filter on a disclosure the Rule requires for every fraud reported to the Committee or the Board, whatever its size
options.why: The disclosure is not there because the amount changes the accounts. It is there so that members are told what has been found inside the company and what has been done about it, and that is worth knowing at six lakh as much as at six crore. If materiality governed, the disclosure would disappear in exactly the cases the sub-crore route was written for, which are the small ones.

options.text: Nothing. The threshold decides whether a fraud has to be reported at all, and this one is well below it
options.misconception: reads the one crore line as the trigger for any reporting duty, when it only decides whether the report goes outside the company or stays within it
options.why: The threshold sorts frauds by destination. Above it, the matter leaves the company and reaches the Government; below it, it goes to the Committee or the Board and then into the Board's Report for members to read. A small fraud is still a fraud committed by an employee against the company, and the sub-section that catches it is the same one — it simply sends it somewhere nearer.

options.text: It goes to the Audit Committee, but at the end of the audit, as part of the auditor's communication on completion
options.misconception: files a duty with its own two-day period as an end-of-audit communication, so the timing that gives the report its value is lost
options.why: The two-day period applies to both routes, not only to the one that ends at the Government. It is there because a fraud reported while the books, the stock records and the people are all still in place can be acted on, and one reported months later usually cannot. Holding it for the completion memorandum turns a statutory report into a summary of history.

options.text: It stays inside the company and it still moves on a clock, and the company then has to say so in its own report to members
options.why: Falling below the level that sends a matter to the Government changes the addressee, not the duty. The auditor reports it to the Audit Committee constituted under section 177, or to the Board where the company has no such Committee, immediately and no later than two days of his knowledge, and he states three things: the nature of the fraud with a description of it, the approximate amount involved, and who was involved. The company then carries it forward into the Board's Report, where it must set out the nature with a description, the approximate amount involved, the parties involved where remedial action has not been taken, and the remedial actions it has taken. Dismissal is one of those remedial actions; it is a thing to disclose, not a reason for not disclosing.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
citation.ref: Section 143(12) and Rules 13(3) and 13(4)

items.scenario: The second matter in the same audit is smaller: a storekeeper took ₹6 lakh of scrap sale proceeds in cash and kept them. Management says that since the amount is nowhere near the level at which the Government has to be told, nothing needs to happen at all — the man has been dismissed and the loss is immaterial against the company's size.

items.stem: What does the Order require the auditor to state?

options.text: Only the ₹1.8 crore matter, since the Order follows the same threshold the Companies Act uses for reporting to the Government
options.misconception: imports the one crore line into a clause of the Order that carries no threshold at all
options.why: Two provisions, two purposes. The Act's threshold decides who gets told about a fraud and how quickly. The Order's clause is about what a reader of the audit report is told, and it was written without a figure in it because a reader's interest in knowing that fraud occurred does not begin at a crore. Borrowing the threshold across would quietly delete the smaller half of what the clause was meant to surface.

options.text: Only frauds the auditor found himself. A matter reported to him by the company is the company's disclosure to make, not his
options.misconception: narrows a clause that covers what was noticed or reported to the auditor down to what he detected on his own procedures
options.why: The clause deliberately reaches both. An auditor who only had to report his own discoveries could be kept quiet by a company that told him things first, and the reader would never learn of a fraud the company had itself uncovered. Whether the knowledge came from his testing or across the table from management, the answer to the question is the same.

options.text: Nothing, because the statement already filed with the Central Government discharges the auditor's reporting duty on the same facts
options.misconception: treats a filing made to the Government as satisfying a duty owed to the readers of the audit report, when the two reports have different audiences
options.why: A sealed cover to the Ministry is read by the Government. The audit report is read by members, lenders and anybody else who picks up the annual report, and it is the only one of the two they will ever see. One report cannot discharge the other because neither audience is reached by the other document, and treating the filing as enough would leave the people who rely on the accounts knowing nothing.

options.text: Both of them, because the Order asks a question of its own and the auditor's materiality is not what answers it
options.why: The clause is a question put to the auditor rather than a threshold he applies: has any fraud by the company or any fraud on the company been noticed, or been reported to him, at any time in the year under audit? Where the answer is yes, he states the nature and the amount involved. Nothing in it turns on how large the fraud was against the accounts, and nothing in it turns on which route the fraud took under the Companies Act — the two matters here answer the same question, and both belong in the answer. Materiality decides what the auditor tests and what he treats as a misstatement; it does not decide which questions in the Order he chooses to answer.
keywords: any fraud by the company or any fraud on the company
the nature and the amount involved

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xi), reporting on fraud noticed or reported during the year

items.scenario: Both matters have now been reported down their own routes. The draft audit report is being assembled and the section carrying the auditor's answers under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 says nothing about either of them. The manager who drafted it explains that ₹1.8 crore and ₹6 lakh are both below the materiality he set for the audit, so neither needed to be mentioned in the report itself.

items.stem: What is the position on the threat and on the cost auditor's question?

options.text: There is one penalty for non-compliance whatever the company, so the listing of this company makes no difference to what he faces
options.misconception: flattens a penalty the Act pitches at two levels, so the higher exposure that attaches to a listed company is missed
options.why: The Act sets two figures and picks between them by whether the company is listed, with the heavier one falling on the listed case because more people rely on those accounts. Reading it as a single figure understates the exposure by four fifths on exactly the audits where it matters most, and misstates a provision that is asked about precisely because it distinguishes.

options.text: The exposure runs the other way — reporting is protected and failing to report is what carries a penalty, and the cost auditor carries the same duty in his own work
options.why: The Act says in terms that no duty to which an auditor of a company is subject is regarded as having been contravened by reason of his making this report, provided he makes it in good faith. That covers the confidentiality clause, which cannot be pleaded against a statutory report honestly made. The risk sits at the other end: an auditor who does not comply is liable to a penalty of five lakh rupees where the company is listed and one lakh rupees in any other case. And the duty is not the statutory auditor's alone — it applies mutatis mutandis to the cost auditor and the secretarial auditor in the performance of their own duties, so the man working on the cost records has his own obligation and cannot hand it across.
keywords: a penalty of five lakh rupees
mutatis mutandis to the cost auditor and the secretarial auditor

options.text: The confidentiality clause binds him, because it was freely agreed and the Act does not say that a contract with the client is overridden
options.misconception: puts a term of an engagement letter above a statutory reporting duty, when the Act expressly protects the reporting against any duty the auditor is subject to
options.why: A clause in a letter cannot switch off a duty Parliament imposed, and this Act does not leave the point to be argued: it names the protection and gives it to reporting done honestly. If a confidentiality term could stop the report, every company would put one in, and a provision written to bring frauds out of companies would be defeated by the companies it was written about.

options.text: The protection applies only once the fraud is proved, so until then he is exposed and should have waited for the company's inquiry to finish
options.misconception: makes the protection depend on the outcome, when the standard the Act sets is the auditor's honesty at the time he reports
options.why: The duty is triggered by reason to believe, not by proof, and the protection is pitched to match it. If it only arrived once a fraud was established, no auditor could ever report safely at the moment reporting is useful, and every report would wait for a finding that may take years. What is asked of him is that he acts honestly on what he has, and that is the test the protection is written to.

citation.ref: Section 143(13), the penalty for non-compliance with section 143(12), and its application to the cost auditor and the secretarial auditor under sections 148 and 204

items.scenario: After the filing goes out the company writes to the auditor threatening to sue on the confidentiality clause in his engagement letter, and asking him to confirm that he acted at his own risk. In the same week the company's cost auditor, who has come across the inflated purchase rates in his own work on the cost records, asks whether any of this reaches him or whether he can leave it to the statutory auditor.

items.stem: How should the three be classified before anything is added up?

options.text: The ₹6 lakh as judgemental, because it rests on the auditor's own judgement rather than on anything found in the books
options.misconception: classifies by whose judgement was used, when the judgemental class is defined by management's estimates and policies that the auditor disagrees with
options.why: Judgemental points at management, not at the auditor. It covers differences arising from estimates management made that the auditor considers unreasonable, or from accounting policies it selected or applied in a way he considers inappropriate. The ₹6 lakh has nothing to do with any view management took: it is the arithmetic of carrying a sample result across the population it came from, which is what the projected class exists to name.

options.text: As three different kinds — one beyond argument, one arising out of management's estimate, and one that exists only because a sample was extended to the population behind it
options.why: The depreciation slip is a factual misstatement: the arithmetic is wrong and there is nothing to debate about it. The ₹5 lakh is a judgemental misstatement, because it comes out of an accounting estimate management made and the auditor regards as unreasonable — the same figure would be no misstatement at all if he thought the estimate defensible. The ₹6 lakh is a projected misstatement: it is the auditor's best estimate for the population, reached by extending what a sample showed to the part of the population nobody looked at, so no single invoice in the books is wrong by that amount. Naming them matters before totalling them, because the three carry different weights when the partner decides what to ask management to correct.

options.text: Two, not three. The inventory overstatement stops being a misstatement once management corrects it, so only the depreciation error and the projection survive
options.misconception: treats correction by management as removing an item from the accumulation, when what changes is only whether it remains uncorrected
options.why: A misstatement is classified when it is identified, and correction is a later fact about it rather than a way of un-finding it. It stays in the accumulation, and the file records both that it was found and that it was put right. Dropping corrected items would leave the auditor with no picture of how many misstatements the work threw up, which is one of the things that tells him whether the audit strategy needs revisiting.

options.text: All three as factual, since each of them is a definite figure that the audit work has produced and can be supported
options.misconception: reads "factual" as meaning quantified, when it means that no judgement is in dispute about whether the item is wrong
options.why: The word is not about whether a number exists; it is about whether anybody could reasonably disagree. A depreciation calculation is either right or wrong and no opinion enters it. An inventory valuation rests on assumptions two competent people can take different views on. And a projection is a figure the auditor built rather than found. Calling all three factual erases exactly the distinctions the classification was made to draw.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Factual, judgemental and projected misstatements

items.scenario: Three misstatements come out of one audit. A ₹1 lakh arithmetic error in the depreciation schedule. An inventory valuation the auditor considers unreasonable, which overstates inventory by ₹5 lakh. And a ₹60,000 error found in a sample of sales invoices drawn from a population of ₹1 crore, from which the auditor's best estimate of the error in the whole population is ₹6 lakh. A junior lists all three as errors, adds them to ₹12 lakh and takes the total to the partner.

items.stem: Can the invoice error be set aside on that ground?

options.text: Yes, entirely. The threshold was set to keep small items out of the accumulation, and everything that flows from a small item is small too
options.misconception: applies the clearly trivial threshold to the projection as well as to the item, so an error found in a sample carries nothing across to the population it came from
options.why: Size does not travel that way. One invoice out by ₹60,000 in a sample says something about every invoice in the population that was not looked at, and the arithmetic of saying it is what turns a small finding into a large estimate. If a projection inherited the size of the item it came from, sampling would tell an auditor nothing he did not already know about the invoices he actually opened.

options.text: No, and the objection goes further — the auditor had no business fixing the threshold himself, since the standard sets the level at which an item becomes too small to accumulate
options.misconception: treats the clearly trivial amount as prescribed, when it is determined by the auditor for the engagement in front of him
options.why: There is no printed figure to look up. The auditor sets the amount for each engagement, having regard to the size of the entity and the materiality he has already determined, and he records what he set. The fault here is not that he chose a number but that the manager is pointing it at the wrong figure, and answering a misapplication by denying that the number exists leaves the audit with no threshold at all.

options.text: Only the ₹60,000 gets accumulated, because that is the error the audit work actually found; a projection is a calculation and not a misstatement to be accumulated
options.misconception: accumulates what was seen and never what the sample implies about the untested remainder, so the population is treated as clean because nobody opened it
options.why: The purpose of drawing a sample is to say something about the whole, and refusing to carry the result across throws that away. The projection is the auditor's best estimate of the misstatement in the population, and it is evaluated with everything else when he asks whether the statements are materially misstated. Accumulating only the items physically inspected would make every audit's conclusion depend on how many invoices happened to be pulled.

options.text: The individual error can be, and what the sample says about the rest of the population cannot — those are two different figures and the threshold only speaks to one of them
options.why: The amount the auditor fixes is the amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial, and it is applied to a misstatement he has identified. The ₹60,000 invoice is one of those and sits below the line. But the projection of that error across the ₹1 crore population is not a misstatement he found; it is his estimate of what the untested remainder is carrying, and at ₹6 lakh it stands at eight times the threshold. Applying the threshold to it would mean a population error of any size could be dismissed so long as it was discovered one small invoice at a time, which is the opposite of what sampling is for.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: The amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial, and projected misstatements

items.scenario: The engagement partner fixed ₹75,000 as the amount below which misstatements would be treated as too small to accumulate. The sales invoice error found in the sample is ₹60,000, drawn from a population of ₹1 crore, and the projection to that population comes to ₹6 lakh. The manager proposes to drop the whole matter on the ground that the error actually found is under the threshold the partner himself set.

items.stem: What must the documentation carry that it does not carry now?

options.text: The threshold, but that belongs in the planning file with materiality rather than in the completion section, since it is set at the start
options.misconception: files a documentation requirement of the completion standard under planning, so the figure sits where nobody evaluating misstatements will look for it
options.why: Where a firm keeps the paper is its own business; what the standard asks is that the amount is documented as part of the record of misstatements, because that is the record it explains. The threshold is not an abstract planning number — it is the reason particular items are absent from the accumulation, and it has to be readable next to the accumulation it shaped.

options.text: Nothing more. Only uncorrected misstatements matter to the opinion, so a corrected one has no place in a file that supports the opinion
options.misconception: drops corrected misstatements from the accumulation, so the file shows how many faults survived and never how many the audit found
options.why: What the file records is the work, not only the residue of it. The number of misstatements the audit threw up is evidence about the entity's controls and about whether the audit strategy needed revisiting, and both of those questions are answered by items that were later corrected. Keeping only the survivors also makes a well-corrected audit indistinguishable from one that found nothing.

options.text: The threshold the partner fixed, every misstatement the audit turned up with a note of whether it was put right — the inventory one included — and the reasoning behind the conclusion, not only the conclusion
options.why: Three things belong in the file and two of them are missing. First, the figure the partner fixed as the point below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial, because without it nobody can tell what was deliberately left out of the accumulation. Second, all misstatements accumulated during the audit, and against each of them whether it was corrected — which takes in the inventory valuation, since the fact that management put it right is part of what the file is recording rather than a reason to leave it out. Third, whether the uncorrected ones are material — individually or in aggregate — with the basis for that conclusion set down beside it, because a conclusion with no reasoning under it cannot be reviewed by anyone.
keywords: all misstatements accumulated during the audit

options.text: Nothing more. The partner's conclusion is on the file, and a conclusion is what the standard asks for — the reasoning behind it is the partner's own thinking
options.misconception: records a conclusion without the basis for it, so the file states an answer nobody can check
options.why: A conclusion on materiality is a judgement, and a judgement recorded without its grounds cannot be reviewed, defended or repeated. The standard asks for both together for that reason. It is also the part most likely to be wanted years later, by a reviewer or a regulator asking not what the partner decided but why that decision was open to him on these figures.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Documentation requirements

items.scenario: The file is being closed. It lists the two misstatements management refused to correct and records the partner's conclusion that they are not material. Management corrected the inventory valuation, and the assistant has left that one out on the ground that a corrected misstatement no longer affects the statements. A reviewer asks whether the file is complete.

items.stem: What should be done with that line on the checklist?

options.text: Complete it in respect of the clearly trivial items, since those were not communicated and the reasons for leaving them out should be recorded
options.misconception: extends the communication requirement to items below the clearly trivial threshold, which are never accumulated and so were never identified misstatements to communicate
options.why: Items under the threshold do not enter the accumulation at all, which is the whole purpose of setting one. There is no decision not to communicate them, because they never reached the stage at which communication arises. What the file does record about them is the threshold itself, and that single figure is the documentation the standard wants on the subject.

options.text: Complete it. Anything the firm's own checklist calls for is part of the file, and a reviewer's question is not answered by saying the standard does not ask
options.misconception: treats a firm checklist as the source of the requirement, so a line drafted in error generates work and a document that misdescribes what happened
options.why: A checklist is a tool for meeting the standard and can be wrong about it, as this one is. The right response to a line that asks for something the standard does not want is to say so on the file, which also gets the checklist mended for the next engagement. Filling it in anyway produces a paper describing a decision that never took place, and that paper stays on the file long after the checklist is forgotten.

options.text: It falls away only because management corrected the inventory misstatement; had it refused, the justification would have been needed
options.misconception: makes the answer turn on whether management corrected the misstatements, when the requirement to communicate them exists either way and there is no decision to justify in either case
options.why: Correction and communication are separate steps and the second comes first. The auditor communicates what he has accumulated and asks for it to be put right; what management then does with the request is the next question. Since the communication is required whatever the answer turns out to be, no version of these facts produces a decision not to communicate that would need justifying.

options.text: Strike it out as not applicable and say why, because the standard leaves no such decision to be made and none was made here
options.why: There is no document to write because there is nothing to justify. The standard requires the auditor to communicate identified misstatements and to request their correction, and a requirement is not a choice, so a justification for not communicating identified misstatements is exactly the one thing the documentation does not have to contain. On these facts the point is doubly dead: the partner did communicate the misstatements to those charged with governance and did ask for them to be corrected. Signing the line off with an invented explanation would put a false record on a file, which is a worse outcome than a blank.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Communication of misstatements with those charged with governance, and the limits of the documentation requirement

items.scenario: The firm's completion checklist carries a line requiring the engagement partner to file a justification for any decision not to take identified misstatements to those charged with governance. On this audit he did take them, and asked for their correction. The junior wants to know what to put against the line so that the checklist can be signed off.

items.stem: Which body may review which of the two audits?

options.text: Both bodies may take up both audits, since the Board's remit runs to the services of every member of the Institute and both audits were done by members
options.misconception: reads the Board's jurisdiction over members as unlimited, when it is expressly cut back to the entities the Authority's rule does not reach
options.why: The Board's remit is described by the members it covers and then bounded by the entities it may look at, and the second half is the one being dropped here. Leaving it out would put two regulators over the same audit file with power to reach different conclusions about the same partner, which is the duplication the boundary was drawn to avoid.

options.text: The Authority may take both, because a firm that falls within its reach on one client is within it for everything that firm signs
options.misconception: attaches the jurisdiction to the firm rather than to the company audited, so one listed client would pull the firm's whole portfolio into the Authority's reach
options.why: The line is drawn by the entity, not by the auditor. What decides whether an audit falls to the Authority is the company whose accounts were audited and whether it is of the class the rule names, so the same firm can have one audit inside and another outside on the same day. Reading the jurisdiction as attaching to the firm would sweep every small unlisted client of a large firm into the Authority and leave the Board with almost nothing.

options.text: One each, and neither file is open to both — the listed audit goes to the statutory Authority and the unlisted one to the Board that takes what the Authority does not
options.why: Overseeing the quality of audit services of listed companies sits with the National Financial Reporting Authority, so the listed audit is the Authority's, and the misconduct alleged by the whistle-blower is the kind of matter it investigates under section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. The Quality Review Board reviews the services of members of the Institute as well, but its reach begins where the Authority's stops: it takes the entities left outside Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, together with whatever the Authority sends across to it. The unlisted company is one of those, so that audit is the Board's. The two do not sit over the same file, and preparing for both on each would be preparing for something the scheme does not allow.

options.text: Neither, until the Institute's own disciplinary machinery has finished, since a complaint against a member is first a matter for the Institute
options.misconception: makes both reviewers wait on the Institute, when neither body's power to review or investigate is conditioned on the Institute acting first
options.why: These are separate mechanisms with separate purposes, and none of them queues behind the others. The Authority may take up an audit within its class on its own, and the Board reviews the quality of services within its own class without anybody's leave. A rule that made every review wait for a disciplinary outcome would mean the slowest process set the pace for all of them.

citation.ref: Section 132(4), read with Rule 3 of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018, and the remit of the Quality Review Board

items.scenario: The same firm of twelve partners audits two companies. One is an unlisted public company that falls outside Rule 3 and has not been referred to the Quality Review Board by anybody. The other is listed, and a whistle-blower has complained that the firm failed to identify related parties and that almost all of its sales went to a party that was never disclosed. The firm's managing partner assumes both regulators can take up both audits and is preparing for two reviews on each file.

items.stem: What is wrong with the assistant's single sentence?

options.text: Only the ₹18 lakh is reportable, because money set aside for a project that is still running has not been left unspent at all
options.misconception: treats money earmarked for work in progress as already spent, so the limb written for exactly that money is read as having nothing to report
options.why: Unspent means not spent, whatever the intention behind it. The Order writes a second limb precisely because that money is still sitting there, and the auditor has to say where it now sits rather than assume the project will get to it.

options.text: Nothing is wrong. The clause asks only whether unspent corporate social responsibility money was transferred, and one sentence answers that for the whole of it
options.misconception: reads clause (xx) as one question about a total, when it is two questions about two amounts that go to two different places
options.why: The clause is lettered (a) and (b) for a reason. Money left over on work that was never an approved project leaves the company altogether. Money left over on approved work that is still running stays with the company for that work. A single sentence tells the reader that ₹27 lakh went to a government fund, and ₹9 lakh of it was never meant to go there.

options.text: The whole ₹27 lakh should have gone to the Schedule VII fund, so the sentence is right and the company is in default of ₹9 lakh
options.misconception: sends money earmarked for a live project to the fund built for money with no project behind it, and then reads the company's correct treatment as a default
options.why: The ₹9 lakh belongs to an ongoing project, and section 135(6) keeps it inside the company by sending it to a special account held for that project. Pushing it out to a Schedule VII fund would strip the project of the money meant to finish it. The company has not defaulted; the assistant has put two amounts in one place.

options.text: The clause is written in two lettered limbs because the two amounts have two different destinations and two different clocks, so they are reported separately and never added together
options.why: The Order splits the reporting because the law splits the money. For spending other than ongoing projects the auditor answers one question: did the leftover reach a Fund specified in Schedule VII, and did it get there inside six months of the expiry of the financial year? The second proviso to section 135(5) is what sends it there, and that is the ₹18 lakh. Adding the ₹9 lakh to it produces a sentence that is untrue of both amounts at once.
keywords: six months of the expiry of the financial year

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xx)(a) and paragraph 3(xx)(b), read with the second proviso to section 135(5) and with section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Neelkanth Foods Limited is well past the CSR gates and has a CSR committee that recommended a policy and an amount. At the year end ₹18 lakh of the required spend is left over on activities that were never approved as ongoing projects, and a further ₹9 lakh is left over on one ongoing project the Board approved two years ago and which is still running. The audit assistant drafts a single sentence for the annexure to the auditor's report: "Unspent corporate social responsibility of ₹27 lakh has been transferred by the company after the year end." The engagement partner hands it back and asks him to read the clause again.

items.stem: How should the notices be dealt with in the financial statements?

options.text: Say nothing until the proceedings are decided, and disclose in the year the outcome is known
options.misconception: reads an unknown outcome as a reason for silence, when that same unknown is the thing the reader is entitled to be warned about
options.why: Waiting for certainty defeats the purpose. By the time the outcome is known the reader who needed the warning has already lent, invested or bought on statements that hid it. What gets disclosed is the uncertainty itself — what the notices are, what they could cost, and why no amount has been recognised.

options.text: Disclose only if a reliable amount can be put on the exposure; otherwise nothing goes in
options.misconception: borrows the reliable-measurement test from the recognition rule and uses it to switch off disclosure as well
options.why: Reliable measurement decides whether an amount goes on the face of the accounts. It does not decide whether the reader is told. Where no figure can honestly be put on the matter, that fact is itself part of what is disclosed.

options.text: Provide for the maximum penalty the notices could produce, as the chief financial officer suggests
options.misconception: turns an unsettled claim into a present obligation, so an amount nobody can yet be required to pay is charged against this year's profit
options.why: A provision needs a present obligation, an outflow that is more likely than not, and an amount that can be estimated reliably. Here the company may owe nothing. Booking the worst case understates the year's profit and tells the reader the matter has already gone against the company when it has not been decided at all.

options.text: Disclosed, not recognised — they are a contingent liability, and the uncertainty is the reason to tell the reader rather than a reason to stay silent
options.why: The notices are a possible obligation. They arose from something that has already happened, and whether the company owes anything at all will only be settled by an event nobody inside the company controls. That is the definition of a contingent liability, which is disclosed and never put on the face of the accounts. The only escape is narrow: silence is allowed where the chance of money going out is remote, and nothing counsel has said makes it remote here.

citation.source: Ind AS 37, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
citation.ref: Definition of a contingent liability, and the requirement to disclose one unless an outflow of economic benefits is remote

items.scenario: During the same audit CA Meera learns that the Enforcement Directorate has issued show-cause notices to Neelkanth for several breaches of the foreign exchange law, and that regulatory action may follow. The company's counsel will not say which way it will go and will not rule out a payment. The Board has put nothing in the financial statements, on the view that a matter whose outcome nobody knows cannot honestly be reported. The chief financial officer offers the opposite: book a provision for the largest penalty the notices could carry, and be done with it.

items.stem: Which paragraph, if any, can carry it?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph, as the partner suggests, since the matter weighs heavily on how the statements should be read
options.misconception: uses the emphasis paragraph as a general noticeboard, when it may only point back at a disclosure the statements already carry
options.why: An emphasis paragraph has to cite where in the statements the matter is set out, because its whole job is to make the reader turn to a note he might otherwise skim past. With no note to point at there is nothing to emphasise, and writing one would put a fact into the report that the accounts themselves do not carry.

options.text: Nothing may be said at all, because an auditor who is not modifying his opinion has nothing left to communicate
options.misconception: reads any additional paragraph as a softer form of a modified opinion, so an unmodified opinion is taken to close off every other kind of communication
options.why: The additional paragraphs exist for exactly this — matters that do not change the opinion. The report says so on its face, because an emphasis paragraph has to state that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter it raises. Silence is not the price of a clean opinion.

options.text: The key audit matters section, which is where a matter of this weight belongs once the auditor decides the reader needs it
options.misconception: treats the key audit matters section as a place for anything important, when what goes there is settled by how much of the audit the matter took and not by the auditor's wish to mention it
options.why: Key audit matters are chosen from what was communicated to those charged with governance, and they are the ones that took most of the auditor's attention on this audit. CA Meera has already concluded this is not one of them. Putting it there anyway would misdescribe how the audit was actually run.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph, because the matter is nowhere in the statements for a paragraph to point back at
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph points at something the statements themselves already present or disclose properly, and it must give the reader a reference to where that disclosure sits. There is no such disclosure here, so that door is shut. An Other Matter paragraph is written for the opposite case — a matter other than those presented or disclosed, which the reader needs in order to follow the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or her report. That is where this belongs.
keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

citation.source: SA 706 (Revised), Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: Definitions of an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and of an Other Matter paragraph

items.scenario: The Board has still put nothing about the notices in the financial statements — no note, no figure, nothing in the accounting policies. CA Meera does not consider that the omission requires her to modify her opinion, and it is not one of the matters she has determined to be a key audit matter. She does think a reader of her report needs to know the proceedings exist. Her partner suggests an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, saying that is the standard place for something a reader must not miss.

items.stem: What has to be established before the paragraph may be used, and is the second partner right about the rest?

options.text: Nothing, and the paragraph is closed to her anyway, because SA 701 applies to this audit and everything an auditor communicates then becomes one of the matters that section must carry
options.misconception: reads SA 701's application to the audit as deciding which matters are key audit matters, when the standard decides only that they must be communicated and leaves the choice of them to the auditor's judgement
options.why: SA 701 applying settles that a section has to be written and that its contents come from what was discussed with those charged with governance. It does not sweep in everything the auditor mentions anywhere in his report. Whether this particular matter is one of them is her judgement to make and to have made, and that judgement is exactly what the second condition asks her to check.

options.text: Nothing has to be established, and the second partner is right — an additional paragraph is a recognised way of raising a matter without qualifying the opinion
options.misconception: treats an extra paragraph as a milder form of qualification, so a real disagreement about the accounts is answered with a comment instead of an opinion
options.why: A modified opinion says the statements are wrong or that the auditor could not satisfy himself. A paragraph elsewhere says the opinion stands and here is something else worth knowing. Using the second where the first is called for tells the reader the accounts passed, which is the one thing the auditor has concluded is untrue.

options.text: Only that the opinion is unmodified; the second partner is therefore wrong for that reason alone
options.misconception: collapses two separate conditions into one and drops the law-and-regulation test, so an auditor forbidden to mention a matter would still write about it
options.why: Getting to the right answer by the wrong route leaves the wrong rule in his head. There are two tests before the paragraph may be used, and the first of them is about what the law permits the auditor to say at all. Some sectors do restrain an auditor from referring to a regulator's correspondence, and in those the paragraph is simply not open to him.

options.text: Two things, neither of which may be assumed — and the second partner is wrong about the rest, because an extra paragraph is never a substitute for a modified opinion
options.why: The paragraph comes with conditions and is not simply at the auditor's disposal. It must not be prohibited by law or regulation, which is a question about the statute and the sector rather than about the auditor's judgement. And where SA 701 applies, as it does here, the matter must not already have been determined to be a key audit matter — one matter is not described twice in two places as though it were two. Each has to be established rather than presumed. The second partner is wrong about the rest: where the auditor concludes the opinion has to be modified, saying it gently somewhere else in the report does not do the job the opinion does.

citation.source: SA 706 (Revised), Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: Conditions for including an Other Matter paragraph in the auditor's report

items.scenario: CA Meera has settled on an Other Matter paragraph and asks her junior to draft it. He asks whether anything has to be established before it can be written, or whether the paragraph is simply the auditor's to use once she has decided a reader needs the matter. A second partner reading over his shoulder says there is nothing to establish — and adds that the paragraph is a handy device generally, because had the omission been serious enough to require a modified opinion, the same paragraph would have carried the message and spared the company a qualification. SA 701 applies to this audit.

items.stem: What has the junior left out?

options.text: The duty arises only once a proceeding has matured into a demand, and none of these has
options.misconception: adds a maturity condition the rule does not carry, so the year in which the reader most needs the warning is the year the report says nothing
options.why: The word the rule uses is pending. A matter that has not yet become a demand is exactly the kind it is aimed at, because it is the one a reader cannot see anywhere in the balance sheet. Waiting for the demand would make the comment worthless in the year it counted.

options.text: Under the rules prescribing other matters for the auditor's report, she must give her views and comments on whether the company disclosed what its proceedings could cost it
options.why: Section 143(3)(j) lets the rules add matters to the auditor's report, and Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 is where they are set out. Its first item puts a question about the company's own disclosure: has the company shown what impact, if any, its pending litigations carry for its financial position, and shown it in the statements themselves? She gives her views and comments on that. The proceedings therefore reach the reader by a second road, and this one is about what the company disclosed rather than about what the auditor added.

options.text: Nothing further. An Other Matter paragraph naming the proceedings tells the reader everything the second duty would have told him
options.misconception: treats the auditor's own comment as interchangeable with the company's disclosure, when the two duties point in opposite directions
options.why: One duty is the auditor speaking about something the accounts do not contain. The other asks him to report on whether the company itself told the reader what its proceedings could cost. A comment by the auditor is not a disclosure by the company, and a report carrying only the first leaves the second question unanswered.

options.text: The duty is the Board's, under the contents prescribed for its own report, so the auditor records the omission and goes no further
options.misconception: hands a duty the rules put on the auditor back to the Board, so the auditor's silence is read as correct because somebody else was silent first
options.why: The Board does carry a good deal in its own report. This one is put on the auditor and is answered in his report, in the part that carries the matters the rules prescribe. Where the company has said nothing, that is the thing he has to comment on, not a reason for him to say nothing either.

citation.ref: Rule 11(1), read with section 143(3)(j) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Neelkanth has the Enforcement Directorate notices and two older tax matters, none of them yet turned into a demand. The Board's report is silent about all three and so are the notes to the accounts. CA Meera's junior now says the report is complete: the Other Matter paragraph tells the reader the proceedings exist, so the audit has done its part. CA Meera tells him to read the rules prescribing what else her report has to carry before he calls it finished.

items.stem: For which periods, if any, did Tapi have to be consolidated?

options.text: For both years in part — from the date control was obtained in 20X1-20X2 up to the date it was lost on the sale in 20X2-20X3
options.why: The standard has no exemption for temporary control, and none for a subsidiary that cannot get funds out of its own country either. What it tracks is the fact of control and not the plan behind it: consolidation begins from the date the investor obtains control, and ceases when the investor loses control. Girnar had control from the purchase, so the group accounts take Tapi in from that date and carry it until the sale drops the holding to 31 per cent. Two sets of consolidated statements are wrong, not one.
keywords: begins from the date the investor obtains control
ceases when the investor loses control

options.text: Neither year. The finance director is right that a holding bought to be sold on is outside consolidation
options.misconception: reads an intention to sell as an exemption, when the standard asks whether control existed and never how long it was meant to last
options.why: An intention is not a fact about the reporting period, and it can change at any board meeting. If a plan to sell removed a subsidiary from the group accounts, every parent could keep an unwanted result out simply by saying it was looking for a buyer. Tapi's own statements being available separately does not answer it: the group's statements are a different document answering a different question.

options.text: 20X1-20X2 only. Once the shares went on the market in the following year the holding was no longer part of the group
options.misconception: treats the whole year of the sale as outside consolidation, when control was actually held for part of it
options.why: Losing control part way through a year does not undo the part of the year in which it was held. The group's results carry the subsidiary up to the date of disposal and stop there, which is why the second year's consolidated statements are wrong as well rather than merely different.

options.text: 20X2-20X3 only, because that is the year in which the shareholding finally settled at a stable figure
options.misconception: waits for a settled shareholding before consolidating, so the year in which control was actually obtained is left out of the group accounts altogether
options.why: Nothing in the standard waits for a shareholding to stop moving, and 31 per cent is not control in any event. The year of acquisition is the first year the group had a subsidiary, and leaving it out hides the acquisition itself from anybody reading the comparatives afterwards.

citation.ref: Paragraph 20, as applied in the ICAI Study Material on Group Audits

items.scenario: Girnar Holdings Limited bought 51 per cent of Tapi Metals Limited during 20X1-20X2, meaning from the start to sell the holding on once a buyer appeared. In 20X2-20X3 it sold 20 per cent, leaving it with 31 per cent and no control. It left Tapi out of its consolidated financial statements in both years. Its finance director explains that control was temporary throughout, that folding in a company you are about to sell tells the reader something that will not be true for long, and that in any event Tapi's own audited statements were available to anybody who wanted them.

items.stem: How many of the secretary's three proposals stand?

options.text: One — the layout is his to choose, since the consolidated set is prepared for information and no form is laid down for it
options.misconception: treats the consolidated statements as a management document, so their form is read as a matter of presentation the company settles for itself
options.why: The statute fixes the form by tying it to the company's own statements, and the rules made under it send the consolidation to Schedule III and the applicable accounting standards. A layout of the company's own design would make one group's consolidated statements uncomparable with the next one's, which is the whole reason a form is prescribed.

options.text: None of them
options.why: Section 129(3) reaches a company that has one or more subsidiaries, and the section carries the expression further, including an associate company and a joint venture, so the 30 per cent holding is not outside it. The consolidated set is then drawn in the same form and manner as the company's own statements, not in a layout the secretary designs. And a separate statement giving the salient features of each subsidiary's financial statement is attached in Form AOC-1; notes do not stand in for it. Section 129(4) then carries the rules on preparation, adoption and audit across to the consolidated statements too.
keywords: including an associate company and a joint venture

options.text: All three, because the consolidated statements are prepared for information and nothing about them is prescribed
options.misconception: treats the consolidated set as voluntary, so neither its scope, its form nor what is attached to it is read as fixed by anything
options.why: Section 129(4) settles that the other way. The provisions on preparing, adopting and auditing a holding company's own statements run across to the consolidated ones, so they are approved by the Board, audited and laid before the members like any other set. Nothing about them is optional.

options.text: One — the associate stays out, since consolidation is a duty about subsidiaries and an associate is by definition not one
options.misconception: reads the word subsidiary in the section as ordinary speech, when the section itself widens it
options.why: The word is not left to ordinary speech here. The section pulls an associate company and a joint venture in alongside a subsidiary, which is why a company holding no subsidiary at all but one associate still has consolidated statements to prepare. What differs is how each is brought in, not whether it is brought in.

citation.ref: Sections 129(3) and 129(4), read with the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: Girnar has a wholly owned subsidiary, a 60 per cent subsidiary and a 30 per cent associate. Its company secretary is working out what actually has to be produced this year and proposes three things. Consolidate the two subsidiaries only, because an associate is not a subsidiary. Present the consolidated set in a summary layout of the company's own design, because no format is prescribed for something that is not the statutory accounts. Leave out the subsidiary-wise statement, because the same details already appear in the notes.

items.stem: What does the sale bring back into the consolidation work, and why?

options.text: Every consolidation adjustment is recomputed from scratch each year, so the question does not arise
options.misconception: erases the distinction between the two families of adjustment, so work that a change in shareholding makes necessary is repeated in years when nothing changed
options.why: The distinction is what tells an auditor where to look. One family is driven by the transactions of the year being consolidated and is redone every year; the other is driven by the shareholding and is redone only when that shareholding first arises or later moves. Treating both alike wastes effort in a quiet year and hides the work in a year like this one.

options.text: Both of the adjustments made when the holding first arose, because a change in the shareholding is the second occasion on which they are made
options.why: Two of the adjustments are called permanent consolidation adjustments not because they are made once and never touched, but because they are made only on the first occasion and on any later occasion when the shareholding in a consolidated entity changes. The sale is such an occasion, so both come back: the determination of goodwill or capital reserve, and the amount of equity attributable to the non-controlling interests. The auditor pays particular attention to the pre-acquisition reserves and to how they were split between the parent and the minority, because that split is what both figures are built on.

options.text: Nothing. The junior is right that both figures belong to the date of acquisition and are settled once for all
options.misconception: reads permanent as meaning never revisited, when it means made only when the shareholding first arises and whenever it later changes
options.why: The word describes the kind of adjustment, not its immunity. These are the ones that do not recur every year merely because a year has passed — they recur when the thing they were built on moves. A sale of a fifth of the holding moves it, and leaving both figures untouched leaves the minority's share of the group misstated.

options.text: Only the non-controlling interests figure, since goodwill was fixed at acquisition and a disposal touches the minority's share alone
options.misconception: freezes goodwill at acquisition and revisits only the other side of the same calculation, so one half of a paired adjustment moves and the other does not
options.why: The two are computed off the same starting position — what the parent paid against its share of the acquired equity. A change in the shareholding changes that share, so it reaches both. Moving one and not the other leaves a consolidated balance sheet that does not add up in the way the reader assumes it does.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Group Audits — permanent consolidation adjustments

items.scenario: Girnar's sale of 20 per cent of Tapi has gone through. The audit junior lists the consolidation work for the year and puts down only this year's eliminations — the intra-group balances, the unrealised profits and the policy alignments. He explains that the goodwill on Tapi was worked out when the shares were bought and is a figure of that date, so a later sale cannot reach back and change it.

items.stem: Is the finance director right about the depreciation policy?

options.text: Yes. A component's accounting policy is settled by its own board and confirmed by its own auditor, and the group takes its figures as it finds them
options.misconception: treats a component's policy as settled for group purposes by the component auditor's acceptance of it, when that auditor was reporting on a different set of statements
options.why: The component auditor asked whether that company's own statements gave a true and fair view under the policy that company had chosen. That is a different question from whether two components measuring the same kind of asset two different ways can be added together. Adding them unadjusted produces a depreciation charge for the group that follows no policy at all.

options.text: No, but the fix is for the subsidiary to restate its own audited accounts on the parent's policy and reissue them
options.misconception: pushes a consolidation adjustment back into a component's statutory accounts, so a working-paper alignment is turned into a reissued audited set
options.why: The alignment lives in the consolidation working papers and changes nothing in the subsidiary's own statutory accounts, which remain correct under the policy that company adopted. Reissuing them would be a large, public and unnecessary act, and it would still not be what the group's statements need.

options.text: No. All four belong to the same family of adjustments, and the differing policy is dealt with in the consolidation like the rest
options.why: All four are current period consolidation adjustments — the ones made in the very period being consolidated, as against the ones a change in shareholding brings back. The management fee and the loans go because a group cannot charge or lend to itself. The unrealised intra-group profit goes because nothing has yet been sold outside the group, and the deferred tax on that elimination goes in beside it. The differing depreciation policy is dealt with by harmonising it, because a consolidated set has to speak with one accounting voice whatever each component does in its own books. Its own auditor accepting it says something about that company and nothing about the group.

options.text: Yes, though for a different reason — the parent holds only 60 per cent, so it cannot impose its own policy on that company
options.misconception: reads the extent of ownership as deciding whether a policy has to be aligned, when a subsidiary is consolidated in full however much of it the parent owns
options.why: A subsidiary is brought in line by line whether the parent holds 60 per cent or all of it; what the holding decides is how much of the result belongs to the minority, not whether the numbers are made comparable first. And nothing is imposed on the subsidiary at all — the alignment is made for the group's own statements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Group Audits — current period consolidation adjustments

items.scenario: Four things sit on Girnar's consolidation working papers. The parent charged both subsidiaries a management fee. One subsidiary sold goods to the other at a profit and the goods are still in the buyer's stock. There are loans running between group companies. And the 60 per cent subsidiary depreciates its plant on a different policy from the parent's. The finance director accepts the first three as consolidation work but says the fourth is not: a depreciation policy is the subsidiary's own affair, its board chose it, and its own auditor has already accepted it as appropriate.

items.stem: Which part of that plan survives?
