options.text: Reproducing the qualification survives, because a modification on a consolidated component must appear in the group report word for word
options.misconception: copies a component's modification into the group report without asking what it does to the group's own numbers, so a matter material to one company is treated as automatically material to the group
options.why: A qualification on a component is a fact the principal auditor has to weigh, not a sentence he inherits. What matters is the size of the matter against the group and what it does to the consolidated figures. It may call for a modification of the group opinion, and it may be immaterial there; either way the wording is his own.

options.text: Asking for nothing beyond the signed report survives, since anything further would be trespassing on another auditor's file
options.misconception: reads the component auditor's report as the whole of what may be asked of him, when confirmations about how he stands towards the company are obtained separately
options.why: What is sought is not his working papers but written confirmation on matters such as whether he is free of the company, whether he has kept to the code of ethics, and the information the consolidation itself needs. Those are questions about him and about the figures, and asking them is part of relying on his work rather than an intrusion into it.

options.text: The borrowed materiality survives, because the auditor closest to the company is the one best placed to fix it
options.misconception: treats a figure set for one company's own statements as fit for a much larger set, when materiality is a judgement about the readers of the statements being reported on
options.why: Closeness to the company is not the test. A figure large enough to matter to the readers of a subsidiary's own accounts may be lost in a group several times its size, and a figure that matters to the group may be far below what that auditor ever looked at. The judgement belongs to whoever is reporting on the consolidated statements.

options.text: None of the three
options.why: Materiality for a consolidated set is computed for the group as a whole, and that figure is what tests whether the consolidation adjustments are appropriate and whether further components should be scoped in. It is not borrowed upward from a component. The principal auditor also works out a materiality for each component and passes it to the component auditor where he thinks the consolidated true and fair view needs it, and he obtains confirmations on matters such as independence and the code of ethics. On the qualification, copying it across is not the answer either: he weighs it under the standard on using the work of another auditor and decides what it does to his own opinion.

citation.source: SA 600, Using the Work of Another Auditor
citation.ref: Materiality in the audit of consolidated financial statements, as set out in the ICAI Study Material on Group Audits

items.scenario: The auditor of Girnar's consolidated financial statements is planning. He proposes three things. Take the materiality figure the 60 per cent subsidiary's own auditor used, since that auditor knows his own company far better. Ask that auditor for nothing beyond his signed report, since the report is his conclusion and everything else is his working papers. And on the qualified opinion that auditor has given on the subsidiary's standalone statements, simply reproduce the same qualification in the consolidated report so that nothing is lost.

items.stem: What does the Order actually require on the consolidated set?

options.text: Only the clauses that can sensibly be answered on group figures, which is a judgement for the engagement partner
options.misconception: makes the scope of the Order a matter of professional judgement, when it is settled in the Order's own words and admits no picking
options.why: A judgement-based scope would give two auditors two different annexures on identical facts, and it would put the auditor in charge of deciding which questions he is asked. The Order names the one clause and leaves nothing to select from.

options.text: One clause only, and its subject is what the component companies' own auditors said in their own reports
options.why: The Order stands down on a consolidated set apart from a single clause: it does not apply to the auditor's report there except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3. So the fixed asset, statutory dues and corporate social responsibility clauses are never asked. What the surviving clause asks is narrow — whether the reports of the companies drawn into the consolidation carry any qualifications or adverse remarks from their own auditors, and, where they do, he names each such company and the paragraph numbers of its own report where the remark sits.

options.text: The whole Order, as the manager proposes, since the consolidated statements are audited under the same section as the standalone ones
options.misconception: reads the Order as following the section rather than the statements, so clauses written about one company's own records are asked of a set of numbers no single company keeps
options.why: Most of the clauses ask about things a company keeps — its title deeds, its physical verification, its dues, its records. A consolidated set is an arithmetic combination and keeps none of them, so answering those clauses against it would mean answering about nobody. The Order says so itself rather than leaving it to be worked out.

options.text: Nothing at all. The Order is switched off on consolidated statements, so the annexure is simply not attached
options.misconception: turns a rule with one exception into a blanket exemption, so the single clause that does survive is dropped along with the rest
options.why: Switching off all but one clause is not switching the Order off. The one that survives exists for a reason: the group report otherwise says nothing about the fact that three of the companies inside it were reported on with qualifications, which is exactly what a reader of the consolidated statements cannot see for himself.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2, on application to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements, and paragraph 3(xxi)

items.scenario: The engagement manager is drafting the annexure to the report on Girnar's consolidated financial statements. She proposes to run the whole Order over the consolidated numbers — fixed assets, inventory, loans, statutory dues, the corporate social responsibility clauses, all of it — on the ground that the consolidated statements are financial statements audited under the same section, so the same annexure follows.

items.stem: Is the Board's appointment good in law?

options.text: No, and the company must now apply to the Tribunal, since the Board's power has failed and only the Tribunal can fill the gap
options.misconception: reaches for the Tribunal because the Board's route has failed, when the Act names the sitting auditor as the one who simply carries on
options.why: There is no gap. The section is written so that a failed appointment leaves the previous auditor in office rather than leaving the company unaudited, which is precisely so that nobody has to go anywhere for an order. The company's next step is an appointment made properly, not an application.

options.text: No. Nothing had fallen vacant for the Board to fill, and the section says who carries on instead
options.why: The Board's power is real but it is a power to fill a casual vacancy, and somebody turning an appointment down never creates one — he never took the office, so nothing became empty. What the meeting produced is treated as a meeting at which nobody was appointed. The Act then answers that case directly: where at an annual general meeting no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, the existing auditor shall continue in office. CA Preeti's appointment is defective in law.
keywords: no auditor is appointed or re-appointed

options.text: Yes, but the appointment must also be approved by the members at a general meeting within three months
options.misconception: applies the resignation proviso to a case where nobody resigned, so an appointment the Board had no power to make is treated as one that members can put right
options.why: That approval is attached to a casual vacancy caused by an auditor resigning, which is a different event with different consequences for the members. Nobody resigned here. And an approval cannot cure an appointment the Board had no power to make in the first place.

options.text: Yes. The secretary is right that a refused appointment leaves the office empty and the Board fills it
options.misconception: reads a declined appointment as a vacancy in the office, when the office was never taken up and the person who held it before never left it
options.why: A vacancy needs somebody to have vacated. CA Nandan never sat in the chair, so it was never vacated, and the auditor who was there before the meeting has not been replaced by anybody. Reading it the other way would let a board choose its own auditor whenever its preferred candidate at the meeting simply declined.

citation.ref: Sections 139(8) and 139(10)

items.scenario: At the annual general meeting of Kalinga Alloys Limited, CA Nandan was appointed statutory auditor for 2025-26. A week later he wrote to the company declining the appointment. The Board met, recorded a casual vacancy in the office of auditor, appointed CA Preeti in his place, and she accepted. The company secretary is satisfied: the Board acted inside its thirty days, the office cannot be left empty, and the section expressly gives the Board this power.

items.stem: On how many counts, if any, has she committed professional misconduct?

options.text: One — failing to check the statutory requirements. The letter to the outgoing auditor is a courtesy rather than an obligation
options.misconception: treats the communication with the outgoing auditor as professional politeness, so a clause is read as an etiquette anybody may waive
options.why: Courtesy is not the reason for it. The letter exists so that the person about to take the work can learn why the change is happening, which may itself be a reason not to accept, and so that an auditor cannot be replaced quietly by a client who did not care for his questions. It is a clause, and it stands whether or not politeness was intended.

options.text: Two
options.why: The First Schedule does not ask whether she was dishonest or whether anybody lost money. The first count is complete on the fact alone: she took a seat previously held by another chartered accountant, and no letter reached him in writing before she did it. The second count is complete on the other omission: she took the appointment without first ascertaining from the company whether what the Act asks of such an appointment had been duly complied with. Being qualified answers neither of them.
keywords: previously held by another chartered accountant

options.text: Three — one for each of the three things she failed to do
options.misconception: counts omissions rather than clauses, so every professional lapse is treated as misconduct under the First Schedule and the boundary of that Schedule is never learnt
options.why: Two of the three are named in the Schedule and the third is not. Starting fieldwork without written terms is a departure from a standard on auditing and from her own firm's manual, and it may well be a poor way to run an engagement, but the First Schedule is a list and this is not on it. Counting the things she skipped gives three; reading the clauses gives two, and only the second count is the one being asked for.

options.text: One — the letter to the outgoing auditor, and nothing more
options.misconception: knows the communication rule and does not know that verifying the statutory position before accepting is a separate clause with its own consequence
options.why: Two different omissions are named in two different clauses because they protect two different things. One protects the auditor who is going and the incoming auditor's own knowledge of why the change is happening. The other protects the validity of the appointment she is about to rely on. Doing one of them is not doing the other.

citation.ref: Clauses (8) and (9) of Part I of the First Schedule

items.scenario: CA Preeti accepted the Kalinga appointment on the day it was offered. She wrote nothing to the auditor who had been in office. She did not ask the company whether the requirements governing an appointment of this kind had been met. And she put her team on the fieldwork without the written terms of engagement her own firm's manual asks for, treating that as an internal housekeeping step. Asked about all three later, she says she did nothing dishonest: the Board offered the work, she is qualified to take it, she is not disqualified in relation to this company, and nobody has lost anything.

items.stem: What is the answer to the colleague's argument?

options.text: The person who loses if the appointment is bad is the auditor, which is why the clause puts the check on her
options.why: The reason is practical rather than formal. It is obligatory on the incoming auditor to satisfy herself that her own appointment followed the procedure the law lays down, because nobody else has any reason to. Months afterwards a shareholder, or the auditor who has just gone, is free to challenge the validity of what was done — and the person then holding an audit that was never validly conferred, with the fees taken and the report already issued, is her. CA Preeti has taken on exactly that risk.

options.text: He is right in substance, because a written confirmation from the company that all requirements were met discharges the auditor
options.misconception: swaps the member's own check for an assurance given by the client, so a promise from the people whose procedure is in question stands in for looking at it
options.why: The clause asks her to ascertain, and that is her act rather than theirs. A line in the engagement letter records that she asked; it does not record that she looked. The notice, the resolution and the register are all things she can read for herself, so the answer belongs on her file and not in somebody else's promise.

options.text: He is right except for listed companies, where the checks are heavier and the clause bites
options.misconception: invents a listing or size filter for a clause that carries none, so most appointments are read as outside a rule that covers all of them
options.why: The clause is written about accepting an appointment as auditor of a company and stops there. A small private company's appointment can be just as defective, and its shareholders just as willing to say so afterwards. Nothing in the clause turns on how big the client is.

options.text: The colleague is right. A defect in the company's own procedure is the company's problem and the auditor answers for her audit alone
options.misconception: separates the appointment from the audit, when an audit conducted under an appointment that falls is an audit the auditor cannot stand behind
options.why: The audit does not survive the appointment. If the appointment goes, the report was signed by somebody who was not the auditor, and everything done under it is open to question — the fees, the access to the records, the report itself. That is not the company's problem alone by any reading.

citation.ref: Clause (9) of Part I of the First Schedule, as explained in the ICAI Study Material on Professional Ethics

items.scenario: A colleague of CA Preeti's argues that the second of the two clauses adds nothing in practice. The company's own officers know whether the paperwork was in order, he says; if it was not, that is the company's failure and not the auditor's; and no auditor can be expected to audit the process by which he was appointed before he has even been appointed.

items.stem: What was CA Preeti required to do about that letter?

options.text: Nothing, because the resignation was in the previous year and the requirement runs only where the outgoing auditor leaves during the year she is appointed for
options.misconception: attaches a timing condition the guideline does not carry, so the letter goes unread whenever a resignation is a few months old
options.why: The guideline is about a change of auditor and says nothing about how recent the resignation was. The reasons a man gave for walking away from this company do not stop being relevant because a year end has gone by, and they are as likely to be about the company as about him.

options.text: Ask the outgoing auditor for a copy, since it is his letter and he is the one she has to communicate with anyway
options.misconception: sends her to the wrong holder of the letter, so a duty owed to one office is discharged by writing to another
options.why: The letter was written to the Board, so the Board is where a copy is sought. Her separate duty to write to the auditor who is going comes from a different source and answers a different question, and doing that one does not do this one.

options.text: Go to the Board for a copy before she accepted, and weigh what it said in deciding whether to accept at all
options.why: The guidelines put this on her and not on the company. An auditor who resigns and considers that there are professional reasons behind it which the Board ought to hear writes to the Board setting them out and copies the Institute. Before accepting appointment the incoming auditor has to go to the Board, obtain a copy of that letter and weigh what is in it. CA Preeti did neither. The Ethical Standards Board reviews communications of this kind and reports to the Council where it considers that necessary.

options.text: Nothing. The letter reached the Board and the Institute, so everybody entitled to it had it
options.misconception: reads the copy to the Institute as discharging the whole guideline, when the guideline exists so that the person about to take the work reads the letter before taking it
options.why: The Institute's copy is a record, and the Board's copy tells the people who already know. Neither of them is the person about to walk into the job. The whole point of the arrangement is that the incoming auditor learns why the last one left while he can still decline, which is why the duty to fetch it sits on him.

citation.source: Guidelines of the Ethical Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on removal and resignation of auditors
citation.ref: Paragraph A of the guidelines, as set out in the ICAI Study Material on Professional Ethics

items.scenario: The auditor who held office at Kalinga before all this had resigned in the previous year. He took the view that there were matters behind the resignation which the Board ought to be told about, wrote to the Board setting them out, and sent a copy of that letter to the Institute. Nobody mentioned any of this to CA Preeti when she was offered the work, and she did not ask. She now says that since the letter went to the Board and to the Institute, both of the people it was meant for had it.

items.stem: What does the standard require of her on the opening balances?

options.text: Five things, because a prior period audited by somebody else is exactly the situation the standard is written for
options.why: This is an initial audit engagement, and the definition covers a prior period audited by a predecessor auditor and not only one that was never audited at all. So the opening figures are hers to work on. She reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor's report; she determines whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward; she determines whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies; she obtains evidence on whether those policies were consistently applied and, where they were changed, whether the change has been properly accounted for, presented and disclosed; and she performs audit procedures on the opening balances themselves. The inventory policy sits squarely inside the last two.

options.text: She need only take a written representation from management that the opening balances are correct
options.misconception: swaps evidence for an assurance given by the people whose figures are in question, so the weakest source is used where the standard names procedures
options.why: A representation is evidence about what management says, not about what the inventory was worth. It has its place alongside other work and never in place of it, and here the very thing in doubt — the missing supporting records — is what management would be asserting about.

options.text: She must audit the whole of the previous year again, since she cannot rely on work she did not do
options.misconception: reads the duty on opening balances as a full re-performance of the predecessor's audit, so a defined piece of work becomes an unbounded one
options.why: The standard asks about the opening balances and the policies behind them, not about every transaction of a year she is not reporting on. Re-auditing the whole period would cost the company a second audit, delay the current one, and still not be what is being asked for.

options.text: Nothing beyond agreeing the figures to last year's audited statements. The assistant is right that a clean report on them is enough
options.misconception: treats a predecessor's opinion as audit evidence for the current auditor, when that opinion was given to other readers about a different period's statements
options.why: Another auditor's conclusion is not her evidence. She was not there for his work, does not know what he tested or what he accepted, and cannot answer for it. And the opening figures are inside this year's statements — a wrong opening inventory is a wrong cost of sales for the year she is reporting on.

citation.source: SA 510, Initial Audit Engagements — Opening Balances
citation.ref: Definition of an initial audit engagement, and the audit procedures on opening balances and on the consistency of accounting policies

items.scenario: CA Preeti begins the audit of 2025-26. The previous year was audited by the auditor who has now gone, and his report on it was unmodified. She finds that the closing inventory of that year was valued on a policy the company has since changed, and that the records supporting part of it are missing. Her assistant says the opening figures are not their problem: they were audited by somebody else who gave a clean report on them, so they can be taken as given and this year's work started from there.

items.stem: What does each of the two situations lead to?

options.text: Both lead to a disclaimer, since in both cases she cannot say the opening balances are right
options.misconception: treats every problem with opening balances as a limitation on scope, when a policy the company refuses to correct is a disagreement and not a gap in evidence
options.why: A disclaimer says the auditor could not form an opinion. On the policy she has formed one — she knows exactly what is wrong and can say so. Disclaiming there would hide a definite finding behind a claim of ignorance, and the reader would never learn what the auditor actually concluded.

options.text: Two different answers — one is a shortage of evidence and the other is a disagreement about the accounts
options.why: The standard separates them because they are different failures. Where she cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about the opening balances, what is missing is evidence, and she expresses a qualified opinion or disclaims an opinion depending on how much of the picture the gap reaches. Where the fault is in the accounts themselves — the opening balances hold a misstatement that is not properly presented or disclosed, or a policy was not applied consistently and the change was not properly dealt with — the opinion is qualified or adverse. Missing records point one way and an accounting policy the company will not correct points the other.
keywords: qualified opinion or disclaims an opinion

options.text: Both lead to a qualification, which is the proportionate answer where a single year's opening figures are involved
options.misconception: settles on the middle answer for both, so neither how far the missing evidence reaches nor how pervasive the misstatement is gets weighed at all
options.why: A qualification says the rest of the statements are fine. Whether that is true depends on how much of them the problem touches, and the standard makes the auditor ask that in both directions — evidence missing over a wide enough area calls for a disclaimer, and a misstatement pervasive enough calls for an adverse opinion. Choosing the middle answer in advance skips the question.

options.text: Neither touches the opinion. Both are put in an Other Matter paragraph so that the reader is told without the company being qualified
options.misconception: uses an additional paragraph to carry matters the auditor has concluded bear on his opinion, so the report reads clean while the auditor's own conclusion says otherwise
options.why: An additional paragraph never carries a matter that affects the opinion. Where evidence is missing or the accounts are wrong, the opinion is where the auditor says so; a paragraph elsewhere in the report would tell the reader the audit came out clean when the auditor has decided it did not.

citation.source: SA 510, Initial Audit Engagements — Opening Balances
citation.ref: Audit conclusions and reporting on opening balances

items.scenario: Two things have gone wrong for CA Preeti at Kalinga. The records supporting part of the previous year's closing inventory cannot be found, the predecessor's working papers are not open to her, and the stock itself has long since been sold. Separately, management accepts that the inventory valuation policy was changed but refuses to account for the change or disclose it, and will not amend the statements. She has to decide what her report says about each.

items.stem: What from these two deposits goes into Mr. Devrath's total income?

options.text: ₹49,200 — both figures, since the money for both came from the gift
options.misconception: follows the money instead of the asset, so income earned on income that was already clubbed gets clubbed a second time
options.why: The clause reaches the income arising from the asset that was transferred, and it stops there. Once the ₹48,000 has been taxed in the husband's hands it is her money to invest, the recurring deposit is her own asset rather than his gift, and what it earns is hers. Following the money instead would club every later reinvestment for ever, which is not what the words say.
keywords: the income arising from the asset that was transferred

options.why: Affection is not consideration, so the fixed deposit is an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration and what that asset earns belongs to the transferor. Eight per cent on ₹6,00,000 for the whole year is ₹48,000 of fixed deposit interest, and that is what is clubbed. The recurring deposit is a second and different asset: she bought it with income that had already been taxed in his hands, so what it earns is income on income, one step beyond what the clause reaches, and the ₹1,200 is not clubbed.
keywords: an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration

options.text: Nothing, because a gift between husband and wife is not taxed at all
options.misconception: mixes up two separate questions — whether the gift is taxed when it is received, and who is taxed on what the gifted asset earns afterwards
options.why: Both things are true at once and they do not touch each other. The gift is not income in her hands, because a receipt from a relative is left outside section 56(2)(x). Clubbing asks a different question about every year that follows: who pays tax on what the gifted asset earns. That answer comes from section 64(1)(iv) and it is the husband.
keywords: a receipt from a relative is left outside section 56(2)(x)

options.text: ₹1,200 only, because the fixed deposit stands in her name and is hers
options.misconception: reads the name on the deposit as the answer, when the clause works on where the money that bought the asset came from
options.why: Whose name is on the deposit decides nothing. The clause looks at where the asset came from, and this deposit was funded entirely by a transfer from her husband for no consideration. That makes the interest on it his to be taxed on and makes the recurring deposit's earnings hers, which is this answer turned exactly around.
keywords: the clause looks at where the asset came from

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv), with the rule that income arising to the spouse on accumulated clubbed income is not itself clubbed

items.scenario: Mr. Devrath gifted ₹6,00,000 to his wife, Mrs. Ila, on 1 April 2025. She put the whole of it into a bank fixed deposit in her own name at 8 per cent a year, and it stayed there untouched for the full year. Out of the interest the bank credited to her, she took ₹24,000 and opened a recurring deposit, also in her own name, which had earned ₹1,200 by 31 March 2026. The gift was made out of nothing but affection and no money or property came back the other way. Their return preparer has both figures in front of him and has to decide what, if anything, from these two deposits belongs in Mr. Devrath's total income for A.Y. 2026-27.

items.stem: How much of the boutique's profit goes into Mr. Devrath's total income?

options.why: Where transferred money is put into a business the clause reaches a proportion of the profit rather than all of it or none of it. The proportion is the value of the investment made out of the transfer set against the total investment in the business, both measured on the first day of the previous year. Four lakh against sixteen lakh is one-fourth of the profit, and one-fourth of ₹3,20,000 is ₹80,000, which is what is included in his income.
keywords: ₹80,000, which is what is included in his income
the total investment in the business

options.text: Nothing, because the profit was earned by her own effort in her own shop
options.misconception: reads the wife's personal effort as taking the profit outside the clause, when the exception for a person's own effort belongs to the minor child provision and not to this one
options.why: The let-out for income earned by a person's own effort sits in the provision about a minor child, and there is no such let-out for a spouse. Once money goes in without consideration the proportionate income comes back to the transferor, whoever did the work in the shop.
keywords: the proportionate income comes back to the transferor

options.text: ₹1,06,667, being one-third, comparing the gift with her own capital
options.misconception: puts the gifted money against the wife's existing capital instead of against the total capital, so the fraction is built on the wrong denominator
options.why: The denominator is the whole of the money in the business, which is her ₹12,00,000 plus the ₹4,00,000 that came in, ₹16,00,000 in all — not the ₹12,00,000 she started the day with. Comparing the gift with the old capital gives four against twelve, and the rule asks for four against sixteen.
keywords: her ₹12,00,000 plus the ₹4,00,000 that came in, ₹16,00,000 in all

options.text: ₹3,20,000, the whole profit, because the gift is what let the shop trade
options.misconception: treats any contribution of capital as making the whole business the transferor's, when the clause is written as a proportion for exactly that reason
options.why: Her own ₹12,00,000 was in the boutique before the gift arrived and her own work runs it. That is why the rule reaches only so much of the profit as the transferred money accounts for, and no more. Taking the whole ₹3,20,000 would tax the husband on a business that is three quarters hers.
keywords: reaches only so much of the profit as the transferred money accounts for

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv), the rule for a transferred asset invested by the spouse in a business

items.scenario: Mr. Devrath gifted ₹4,00,000 to his wife, Mrs. Ila, on 1 April 2025, which is the first day of the previous year, and asked nothing in return. She put the whole of it into her boutique as extra capital the same day. Her own capital in the boutique on that day stood at ₹12,00,000 and she has run the shop herself for nine years. The boutique earned a profit of ₹3,20,000 for the year ended 31 March 2026. Their return preparer accepts that the gift brings section 64(1)(iv) into play and now has to fix the amount.

items.stem: What is her income from the transfer, and at what rate does it bear tax?

options.text: ₹1,92,000, taxed at 30 per cent, the brokerage being a cost of the sale
options.misconception: carries over the capital gains habit of deducting expenditure incurred wholly in connection with the transfer, which this section deliberately withholds
options.why: Under the capital gains sections the cost of a transfer does come off, and breaking that habit is much of what this provision is for. It allows the price paid for the asset and nothing else — no expenditure, no allowance, under any provision of the Act. Brokerage is expenditure however tightly it is tied to the sale, so the ₹8,000 stays in.
keywords: no expenditure, no allowance, under any provision of the Act

options.text: ₹2,00,000, taxed at 30 per cent
options.why: One thing only may be taken off the consideration, and it is the cost of acquisition. Five lakh less the three lakh she paid for the asset leaves ₹2,00,000 of income from the transfer. The brokerage and the subscription are both expenditure, and the section shuts out a deduction for any expenditure or allowance under any provision of the Act, so neither comes off. That income is then taxed at 30% under section 115BBH, plus cess, whatever slab her salary falls in.

options.text: ₹2,00,000, taxed at her slab rate, since she is salaried and not a trader
options.misconception: thinks the special rate depends on the taxpayer dealing in these assets as a business, when the rate follows the asset and not the person
options.why: Nothing in the section looks at who the taxpayer is or what else she does. Where a total income includes income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, that income bears the special rate, and a salaried person and a full-time trader are treated alike. The meaning of transfer is applied to the asset whether or not it is a capital asset in her hands.
keywords: that income bears the special rate

options.text: ₹1,88,000, taxed at 30 per cent, both charges coming off
options.misconception: reads the restriction as shutting out only costs that are loosely connected, when it shuts out every cost except the price paid for the asset
options.why: This treats the bar as a test of how closely a cost is connected to the sale, and there is no such test in the words. The subscription and the brokerage fail together for one reason: they are not the cost of acquisition. Nothing here asks whether a cost was necessary, reasonable or tied to the transaction.
keywords: they are not the cost of acquisition

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(1) and (2)

items.scenario: Ms. Sanaya, a salaried resident with no business income, bought a crypto-asset for ₹3,00,000 in 2024 and sold it on an Indian exchange during the previous year 2025-26. The exchange credited her ₹5,00,000 and separately charged brokerage of ₹8,000, which its contract note shows as a line of its own. She also paid ₹4,000 during the year for a chart-reading subscription she used to decide when to sell. Her accountant is preparing the computation and is unsure how much of the two charges comes off.

items.stem: What can she do with the shortfall on the token?

options.text: Set it against the ₹3,00,000 of interest, the token not being a capital asset
options.misconception: thinks the bar depends on the asset being a capital asset, when the section applies whether it is one or not
options.why: Whether the token was a capital asset in her hands changes nothing. The meaning of transfer is applied to a virtual digital asset whether it is a capital asset or not, and the bar on set-off sits in the same section and travels with it. Calling the token stock-in-trade opens no door here.
keywords: whether it is a capital asset or not

options.text: None of the three
options.why: A non-fungible token is itself a virtual digital asset, so the ₹40,000 shortfall is a loss on the transfer of one. The section refuses a set-off against income computed under any provision of this Act, and because the words are that wide they take in the crypto gain as much as the interest. The same section refuses to let such a loss travel into a later year at all. So the ₹40,000 loss cannot be set off anywhere and it is not carried forward either.
keywords: the ₹40,000 loss cannot be set off anywhere
it is not carried forward either

options.text: Set it against the ₹2,00,000 crypto gain, leaving ₹1,60,000 taxable
options.misconception: assumes a loss can always meet a gain of the same kind, when this section blocks a set-off against income computed under any provision at all
options.why: Same-kind set-off is the ordinary rule and this section takes it away. It does not merely say the loss cannot go against other income; it says it cannot go against income computed under any provision of this Act, and a gain on another virtual digital asset is computed under a provision of this Act like everything else. One asset's loss cannot shelter another's gain.
keywords: it cannot go against income computed under any provision of this Act

options.text: Carry it forward eight years against a future gain on these assets
options.misconception: borrows the eight-year carry-forward that capital losses get, when this section refuses carry-forward outright
options.why: Eight years is the capital loss rule and it has no work to do here. A loss on a virtual digital asset is not carried forward at all, so there is nothing waiting in a later year and nothing to set it against when the next gain comes.
keywords: a loss on a virtual digital asset is not carried forward at all

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(2) and (3)

items.scenario: In the same year Ms. Sanaya sold a non-fungible token she had bought for ₹1,00,000, receiving ₹60,000 for it. Her gain for the year on a separate crypto-asset is ₹2,00,000, and she has ₹3,00,000 of interest income. She would like the shortfall on the token used somewhere and has asked her accountant whether it can go against the crypto gain, against the interest, or forward into next year.

items.stem: What do the two receipts add to her income for the year?

options.text: ₹70,000 and ₹90,000, both taxed at 30 per cent
options.misconception: sends a receipt of a virtual digital asset to the special 30 per cent charge, when that charge is on income from a transfer and she has received rather than transferred
options.why: The special rate falls on income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and she has transferred nothing — she has received. What comes in as a gift is charged as income from other sources at the rates that apply to the rest of her income. The special rate would come into it only later, on the day she sells what she was given.
keywords: income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and she has transferred nothing

options.text: ₹70,000 from the friend, nothing from the brother
options.why: A virtual digital asset was brought inside what property for section 56(2)(x) means, so one received for nothing is treated like any other property received for nothing. The test runs on the aggregate fair market value on the date of receipt, and ₹70,000 is past the ₹50,000 the clause allows, so the whole ₹70,000 is her income from other sources rather than the excess over fifty thousand. The brother's ₹90,000 is larger and is still nothing, because a receipt from a relative is left out of the clause and a brother is one.
keywords: the whole ₹70,000 is her income from other sources
a receipt from a relative is left out of the clause

options.text: ₹20,000 from the friend, nothing from the brother
options.misconception: reads the fifty thousand as a slice that is always free of tax, when it is a gate that lets the whole receipt in once it is crossed
options.why: Fifty thousand is a gate and not an allowance. Where property comes in without consideration and the aggregate crosses it, the aggregate fair market value is what is charged — the whole of it, not the top slice. A difference is charged only where there was a consideration and the shortfall is being measured, and here there was none.
keywords: the aggregate fair market value is what is charged

options.text: Nothing from either, these assets not being property for the clause
options.misconception: works from the older closed list of what the clause covers and misses the amendment that put a virtual digital asset inside the meaning of property
options.why: The list was widened for exactly this receipt. A virtual digital asset was added to what property means for the clause, so a gift of one is caught the same way as a gift of shares or jewellery. Working from the old list is how a receipt of this kind quietly stays out of a return.
keywords: a virtual digital asset was added to what property means for the clause

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x), read with the amendment bringing a virtual digital asset within the meaning of property

items.scenario: During the same year a friend transferred crypto-assets to Ms. Sanaya and asked nothing for them; their aggregate fair market value on the day she received them was ₹70,000. Two months later her brother did the same with crypto-assets worth ₹90,000. She has sold neither lot and both are sitting in her wallet on 31 March 2026. Her accountant is working out what, if anything, either receipt adds to her income for the year.

items.stem: When did the deduction fall due, and how much was it?

options.text: ₹2,000 in April 2026, when the money actually moved to him
options.misconception: reads a credit to the account of the resident as needing an account in the payee's own name, which is the reading the deeming rule was written to shut out
options.why: That reading is the one the section names and closes. Where the consideration goes to any account in the books of the person liable to pay, that entry counts, whether the ledger is a suspense account or an account by any other name. Otherwise a payer could hold every deduction back simply by parking the money on its own books until the next year.
keywords: whether the ledger is a suspense account or an account by any other name

options.text: Nothing, because the exchange is not buying the asset for itself
options.misconception: looks for a buyer, when the section fixes the duty on whoever is responsible for paying the resident
options.why: The section never names a buyer. It puts the duty on any person responsible for paying a resident a sum by way of consideration for the transfer of a virtual digital asset, which is a wider description and catches an exchange that settles the trade. Who ends the day owning the asset decides nothing about who deducts.
keywords: any person responsible for paying a resident

options.text: ₹2,000, but only if his receipts from the exchange pass ₹50,000 for the year
options.misconception: applies the specified person's threshold to a company payer, when a company sits in the other row of the table at ten thousand
options.why: Fifty thousand is the figure for a specified person, meaning an individual or a Hindu undivided family with small enough business receipts or none at all. An exchange is a company and belongs in the other row, where the threshold is ten thousand of aggregate consideration in the financial year. ₹2,00,000 is past either figure, so nothing here turns on the threshold.
keywords: ten thousand of aggregate consideration in the financial year

options.text: ₹2,000 in March 2026
options.why: Tax comes off on the credit of the consideration to his account or on payment of it by any mode, whichever is earlier, and here a credit came first. Nor does the section let a payer choose its way out of that by picking which account it credits: a credit to any account in the payer's own books is deemed to be a credit to the payee's account. One per cent of ₹2,00,000 is ₹2,000, and it was deductible in March 2026.
keywords: the credit of the consideration to his account
deemed to be a credit to the payee's account
₹2,000, and it was deductible in March 2026

citation.ref: Section 194S(1), with the rule deeming a credit to any account in the payer's books, including a suspense account, to be a credit to the payee

items.scenario: Meghdoot Exchange Ltd bought a crypto-asset from Mr. Iqbal, a resident, for ₹2,00,000. On 18 March 2026 it put the whole ₹2,00,000 into an account in its own books called "pending settlements" and told him the money would reach his bank on 7 April 2026, which it did. Its finance team has entered the deduction in the April quarter, on the ground that nothing left the company and nothing reached him in March.

items.stem: What should each of the two payers have done?

options.text: Both deduct on every payment from the first rupee
options.misconception: treats the thresholds as if they fell away once a payer is inside the section, when they decide whether the section bites at all
options.why: The thresholds are not a concession that a payer loses by crossing them; they decide whether any deduction is required in the first place. Zenith's July payment of ₹9,000 was below its figure at the time it was made and carried no duty, and reading the section otherwise would put every small trade inside it.
keywords: they decide whether any deduction is required in the first place

options.text: Dev deducts in June; Zenith deducts nothing in July but must deduct in November
options.why: Dev is a specified person — an individual with no income under the business head — so nothing comes off until his aggregate consideration in the financial year passes ₹50,000. His single payment is past it, so he deducts ₹800, one per cent of the ₹80,000, in June. Zenith is not a specified person, so its figure is ₹10,000 of aggregate consideration in the year. July's ₹9,000 alone sat inside it; November takes the aggregate to ₹13,000 and the duty to deduct at one per cent arrives with that payment.
keywords: aggregate consideration in the financial year

options.text: Neither deducts, both amounts being under ₹1,00,000
options.misconception: invents a single round threshold for the section, when there are two figures and which one applies depends on who is paying
options.why: There is no such figure anywhere in the provision. Two thresholds sit in a table, ₹50,000 and ₹10,000, and the row a payer falls in is settled by what the payer is rather than by how large the payment looks. Both of these payers are past their own figure.
keywords: two thresholds sit in a table, ₹50,000 and ₹10,000

options.text: Dev deducts nothing, since he is salaried and cannot be asked to run a deduction account
options.misconception: reads a specified person as somebody outside the section, when the label only raises the threshold and leaves the duty standing above it
options.why: Being a specified person does not take a payer out. It moves the figure up to ₹50,000 and gives him a gentler remittance timetable, and above that figure the duty is the same as anyone else's. An individual with only salary income who pays ₹80,000 for a crypto-asset is squarely inside the section.
keywords: it moves the figure up to ₹50,000

citation.ref: Section 194S and the table of thresholds for a specified person and for any other payer

items.scenario: Two payers bought crypto-assets from residents during 2025-26. Mr. Dev is a salaried employee with nothing at all chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession; he paid Ms. Rhea ₹80,000 in June for a cryptocurrency, and that was the only sum he paid her in the year. Zenith Ltd, a trading company, paid a resident dealer ₹9,000 in July and ₹4,000 in November for tokens. Neither payer has deducted anything so far, and both say the sums are too small to bother with.

items.stem: What has to happen before the swap is settled?

options.text: Each side has to satisfy itself that the tax on the transfer it is paying for has already been paid
options.why: A swap is the case the section writes about in terms. Where the consideration is wholly in kind, or is another virtual digital asset with no part in cash, there is no money out of which to take anything, so the duty changes shape rather than disappearing: the person responsible for paying must, before releasing the consideration, be satisfied that the tax due on that transfer has been paid. Here each side is paying the other in kind, so each must see that one per cent of ₹3,00,000 has gone in first.
keywords: the consideration is wholly in kind
one per cent of ₹3,00,000 has gone in first

options.text: Nothing, because with no cash there is nothing to deduct from
options.misconception: reads a deduction as needing a flow of money, when the absence of cash is the trigger for the special rule rather than an escape from it
options.why: No cash is what brings the special rule into play. The section anticipates a transfer settled entirely in assets and answers it by turning the duty into a check made before the asset moves. Reading it the other way would leave every barter outside the provision, which is the hole these words were written to close.
keywords: turning the duty into a check made before the asset moves

options.text: Only the side receiving the more valuable asset need do anything
options.misconception: looks for a single payer in a two-sided exchange, when each side is paying the other and each carries the duty
options.why: An exchange has no single payer. Each side hands over an asset as the consideration for the other, so each is a person responsible for paying consideration for a transfer, and the duty falls on both. Which asset is worth more settles nothing about who has to act.
keywords: each is a person responsible for paying consideration for a transfer

options.text: Take one per cent out of the asset and hand over the other ninety-nine
options.misconception: tries to carve the deduction out of the asset itself, when the rule asks for the tax to be paid in money before the consideration is released
options.why: The section does not split the asset. It asks the payer to be satisfied that the tax required to be deducted has already been paid on that consideration and then to release the whole of it. Slicing a token is not a payment of tax, and there is nobody the slice could be handed to.
keywords: the tax required to be deducted has already been paid

citation.ref: Section 194S, the rule for consideration wholly in kind or in exchange of another virtual digital asset

items.scenario: Ms. Tara, a resident, has agreed to swap one cryptocurrency worth ₹3,00,000 for another of the same value held by a resident counterparty. No money is to change hands either way and both of them are individuals with no business income. The settlement is set for next week. Their common adviser has been told by both sides that nothing needs doing, since neither is paying the other anything.

items.stem: What should the licensee do with the auditor's letter?

options.text: Accept it if the company also files the prescribed particulars
options.misconception: treats the prescribed particulars as an alternative to the certificate, when they are an addition to it and neither stands in for the other
options.why: The particulars are asked for in addition to the certificate and not instead of it. One provision makes the certificate the gateway to relief; a separate one asks for the extra papers the rules name to go alongside it. Filing the second while missing the first leaves the gateway shut.
keywords: in addition to the certificate and not instead of it

options.text: Accept it, since the section asks for proof of residence and this proves it better
options.misconception: reads the requirement as a standard of evidence to be satisfied any convincing way, when it names one issuer and admits no substitute
options.why: The provision was written because third-country residents were claiming benefits that were never meant for them, and a self-chosen document is exactly what it was aimed at. So it does not ask the payer to weigh evidence; it asks for a paper from one source and treats that source as the whole of the test.
keywords: it asks for a paper from one source

options.text: Treat the treaty rate as unavailable until the government certificate arrives
options.why: The relief under an agreement is allowed to a non-resident only where a certificate of its residence, obtained from the Government of that country or specified territory, is furnished. The condition is about who issued the paper, not about how convincing it reads: an auditor's letter is not a certificate from the Government, however well documented, and the tax office being slow is not an exception the section contains. Until the certificate is in hand the deduction runs at the rate the Act gives.
keywords: an auditor's letter is not a certificate from the Government
obtained from the Government of that country or specified territory

options.text: Accept it, because a certificate would in any case have to carry prescribed particulars on its face and this one does
options.misconception: thinks a government certificate is only good if it contains prescribed particulars, when the certificate is proof of residence with no condition at all about its contents
options.why: A certificate issued by the foreign Government is proof of residence without any further condition about what it must contain. That is the opposite of the reasoning here, and it also explains why the separate particulars exist: whatever the certificate happens to say is enough on its own, and anything already in it need not be repeated.
keywords: proof of residence without any further condition about what it must contain

citation.ref: Sections 90(4) and 90A(4)

items.scenario: Helvet AG, a Swiss company, has received royalty from an Indian licensee and wants the treaty rate applied at source. It has sent the licensee a signed letter from its own statutory auditors in Zurich confirming that it is resident in Switzerland for tax purposes and has filed Swiss returns for six years. Its finance director says the cantonal tax office takes months to issue anything and that an auditor's confirmation is stronger evidence anyway. The licensee's tax head has to settle the deduction this week.

items.stem: What still has to be obtained from Helvet AG?

options.text: A fresh certificate carrying all the prescribed particulars on its face
options.misconception: asks the foreign government to redraft its own certificate, when the requirement is that the assessee supply the missing particulars separately
options.why: No Indian provision can tell a foreign tax office what to print. The certificate is taken as it comes, and the gap is filled by the assessee furnishing the particulars itself. Sending it back for redrafting asks for something the section never demands and delays the relief for nothing.
keywords: the gap is filled by the assessee furnishing the particulars itself

options.text: All five particulars, including the period, since the list is filed as a whole
options.misconception: files the list mechanically, missing the express relief from repeating anything the certificate already contains
options.why: The requirement carries its own let-out: the assessee need not provide any part of the information that is already contained in the certificate. The dates are on this certificate, so the period is covered, and asking for it again is work that the provision expressly says is unnecessary.

options.text: Its status, its country of incorporation, its foreign tax number and its address there
options.why: Alongside the certificate the assessee has to provide the prescribed documents and information, and there are five of them: its status, its nationality or country of incorporation, its tax identification number in the country of residence or a unique identifying number where there is none, the period for which the residential status in the certificate applies, and its address there during that period. This certificate already carries the dates, so that one need not be repeated; the other four have still to come, and the company must keep documents that substantiate them if an officer asks.
keywords: its tax identification number in the country of residence
the period for which the residential status in the certificate applies
its address there during that period

options.text: Nothing further, the certificate being conclusive proof of residence
options.misconception: reads the certificate's conclusiveness on residence as answering every requirement, when a separate provision asks for particulars beyond it
options.why: The certificate settles residence and settles nothing else. A separate sub-section asks the taxpayer for the extra papers the rules name before a treaty benefit can be claimed, and that list has already been drawn up. Conclusive on one question does not mean sufficient on all of them.
keywords: a separate sub-section asks the taxpayer for the extra papers the rules name

citation.ref: Sections 90(5) and 90A(5), with the particulars notified by the Central Board of Direct Taxes

items.scenario: Helvet AG has now sent a certificate from the Swiss federal tax administration. It names the company, says it is resident in Switzerland, and gives the dates the statement covers. Nothing else appears on it. The Indian licensee's tax head remembers that something more has to be filed but cannot recall what, and wants to ask the company for only what is genuinely still outstanding rather than for everything twice.

items.stem: Where does each half of the answer come from?

options.text: The treaty governs both, since it prevails wherever it applies
options.misconception: reads a treaty as a complete code that displaces the Act altogether, when it prevails only where it actually says something
options.why: A treaty prevails on the questions it answers and on no others. Where it contains no provision on a matter, there is nothing to prevail over the Act and the Act runs. Treating silence as an answer would leave the royalty with a rate and no way of measuring what the rate applies to.
keywords: a treaty prevails on the questions it answers and on no others

options.text: The Act governs both, the treaty rate applying only if the Act is silent
options.misconception: turns the rule of preference upside down, applying the Act first and the treaty as a residue
options.why: The order runs the other way. Where the agreement speaks to a matter it is the specific provision and the Act's general words give way; the Act steps in only where the agreement says nothing. The rate is exactly a matter the agreement speaks to.
keywords: the Act steps in only where the agreement says nothing

options.text: One route or the other has to be chosen for the whole item, so the company must take the Act's arithmetic with the Act's rate
options.misconception: treats the more-beneficial choice as a single election covering everything, when it is made provision by provision
options.why: There is no all-or-nothing election here. The Act's own words allow the agreement to apply to the extent it is more beneficial, and that is measured provision against provision rather than package against package. Forcing the whole item down one road would take away a benefit the section deliberately gives.

options.text: The treaty caps the rate; the Act supplies the computation; and the two may be taken from different places
options.why: A specific provision of the agreement prevails over the general provisions of the Act, but where the agreement is silent the Act applies. An agreement generally does no more than share out taxing rights between the residence state and the source state, and the computation mechanism is usually not in it, so the figure is arrived at under domestic law while the rate is capped by the treaty. The taxpayer may lean on whichever provisions are more beneficial to him, either the treaty route or the domestic law route, and the choice is made item by item, which is why the two answers can come from two sources.
keywords: a specific provision of the agreement prevails over the general provisions
the computation mechanism is usually not in it
either the treaty route or the domestic law route

citation.ref: Section 90(2), with Circular No. 333 of 1982 on a specific provision of an agreement prevailing over the general provisions of the Act

items.scenario: The treaty between India and Helvet AG's country caps the tax on royalty at a rate lower than the one in the Act, but says nothing at all about how the royalty is to be worked out. The Act has its own rules for arriving at the figure, and on this contract they produce a smaller amount than the accounts show. The licensee's tax head wants one consistent answer: if the treaty governs the rate, does the treaty also govern the arithmetic, and can the company take the rate from one place and the arithmetic from the other?

items.stem: What is wrong with the filing, and can the company withdraw?

options.text: A fee of ₹10 lakh, the transaction being above ₹100 crore
options.misconception: reads the scale as two bands with one cut at ₹100 crore and misses the middle band
options.why: There are three bands, not two. ₹10 lakh is the top band and it begins above ₹300 crore. A transaction of ₹250 crore is past ₹100 crore and short of ₹300 crore, which is the middle band. Overpaying is not a safe way to be wrong about a scale the client has to fund.
keywords: ₹10 lakh is the top band and it begins above ₹300 crore

options.text: Four copies, a fee of ₹5 lakh and proof of its payment; and yes, it can still withdraw
options.why: The application goes in quadruplicate, not as a single copy. On the money, ₹10,000 is only the least that can be payable — the rules may fix a bigger figure and the bigger one wins — and a scale has been fixed by the size of the transaction for an applicant of this kind — ₹2 lakh up to ₹100 crore, ₹5 lakh above ₹100 crore but not above ₹300 crore, and ₹10 lakh beyond that. A ₹250 crore transaction sits in the middle band, so ₹5 lakh is payable and proof of the payment travels with the application. On the change of mind, an applicant may withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application, and ten days is inside that.
keywords: in quadruplicate, not as a single copy
withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application

options.text: Nothing is wrong; the Board can take its own copies, and nothing can be withdrawn once it is filed
options.misconception: treats the number of copies and the withdrawal window as office practice, when the section fixes both
options.why: Both sit in the statute. The application shall be made in quadruplicate, and a right to withdraw exists but it is time-boxed — within 30 days from the date of the application and not afterwards. Reading either as administration is how an application is rejected on its face, and how a company finds itself tied to a question it no longer wants answered.
keywords: a right to withdraw exists but it is time-boxed

options.text: The fee is ₹10,000, that being the figure the section itself names
options.misconception: reads the figure in the section as the whole answer and misses that it is a floor with a prescribed scale sitting above it
options.why: The section names that sum as a floor and lets the rules put a larger one above it, and the prescribed scale is what makes the difference. ₹10,000 is the fee only for an applicant who falls outside the scale altogether; for a non-resident asking about its own transaction the scale is banded by the amount involved, and ₹250 crore is nowhere near the bottom of it.
keywords: the prescribed scale is what makes the difference

citation.ref: Section 245Q(1), (2) and (3), with Rule 44E

items.scenario: Norvale Ltd, a non-resident, proposes a transaction of ₹250 crore with an Indian company and wants the tax position settled before it signs. Its counsel has filed a single copy of the application with a fee of ₹10,000 and no receipt attached, saying the Act names ₹10,000 and that one application is one application. Ten days after the filing the board changes its mind about the structure and asks whether it can get out.

items.stem: How should the Board's handling of the application be described?

options.text: Unsound, because the only grounds for refusing are avoidance and a valuation question
options.misconception: remembers two of the three grounds and drops the first
options.why: There are three grounds and a pending proceeding is the first of them. The other two are that the question involves the determination of the fair market value of any property, and that it relates to a transaction designed prima facie for avoidance of income-tax, each with its own narrow exception. Forgetting the first is how an application gets filed on a question that is already being fought elsewhere.
keywords: the determination of the fair market value of any property

options.text: Unsound throughout, the pending proceeding being somebody else's assessment
options.misconception: reads the bar as personal to the applicant, when the words reach a question pending anywhere and not only one pending against the applicant
options.why: The bar is on the question, not on the person. Where the question raised in the application is already pending, that is enough, and the section does not add that it must be pending in the applicant's own case. The same facts sitting inside the counterparty's assessment are exactly what the words describe.
keywords: the bar is on the question, not on the person

options.text: The subject matter was a bar, but the order refusing it cannot stand
options.why: Two things sit on opposite sides here. The Board shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before any income-tax authority, the Tribunal or a court, so the subject matter is a bar and this question cannot be ruled on. But the applicant must be given an opportunity to speak before any refusal, the reason for rejection has to appear in the order, and a copy of the order goes to the applicant and to the Commissioner. Skipping the hearing spoils the order even though the conclusion it reached was the right one.
keywords: already pending before any income-tax authority
given an opportunity to speak before any refusal
the reason for rejection has to appear in the order

options.text: Sound throughout, since a pending question leaves nothing to be heard about
options.misconception: reads the bar as making a hearing pointless, when the requirement to hear runs before any rejection whatever the ground
options.why: The requirement carries no qualification. It does not say an applicant must be heard where the ground is arguable; it says no application is to be rejected without giving him a hearing first. Part of what a hearing is for is to let the applicant show that the question pending elsewhere is not in truth the same question, and nobody can know that without asking.
keywords: no application is to be rejected without giving him a hearing first

citation.ref: Section 245R(2) and its provisos

items.scenario: Norvale Ltd files afresh. The question it asks turns on the same facts that are already before an Assessing Officer in a section 143(3) proceeding of its Indian counterparty. The Board sends a copy to the Commissioner, calls for the records, and then passes an order refusing the application. The order runs to one sentence, gives no ground, and Norvale was never called in before it was made.

items.stem: What can the Board do now?

options.text: Nothing, the department's only route having been an appeal within sixty days of the ruling
options.misconception: treats the appeal as the only route, when a separate section answers a ruling obtained on facts that were not true
options.why: An appeal tests whether a ruling is right on the facts it was given. This is a different complaint altogether — that the facts were not what they were said to be — and the Act answers it with a power to set the ruling aside from the beginning. That power carries no sixty-day window.
keywords: a power to set the ruling aside from the beginning

options.text: Declare the ruling void from the day it was made
options.why: Where the Board finds, on a representation made to it by the Commissioner or otherwise, that a ruling has been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, it may by order declare that ruling void ab initio. What follows is not that the ruling stops working from today: the Act applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, and the stretch between the ruling and the order is left out of the reckoning. A copy of the order goes to the applicant and the Commissioner.
keywords: declare that ruling void ab initio
obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts
as if the ruling had never been made

options.text: Nothing without proof of fraud in a court, or the company's own admission
options.misconception: imports a criminal standard of proof, when the section works on the Board's own finding after a representation or otherwise
options.why: The finding is the Board's to make, and it may act on a representation by the Commissioner or otherwise, which takes in what it notices for itself. The words also name misrepresentation of facts beside fraud, and a misdescription can be perfectly innocent. Neither a conviction nor an admission is needed before the order is made.
keywords: it may act on a representation by the Commissioner or otherwise

options.text: Withdraw the ruling for the future, leaving the two years alone
options.misconception: reads a declaration that a ruling is void as a withdrawal taking effect from today, when the phrase means the ruling is treated as never having existed
options.why: Void from the beginning is the whole point of the words. The Act then applies to the applicant as though no ruling had ever been pronounced, and that reaches the two years behind as much as the years ahead. Leaving the past alone would let a misdescription buy two years of certainty at no cost.
keywords: void from the beginning is the whole point of the words

citation.ref: Section 245T

items.scenario: On a later application Norvale Ltd obtained a ruling in its favour and has relied on it for two years. The Commissioner now writes to the Board saying that a term of the contract was described to it in a way the signed contract does not bear out, and that the ruling rests on that description. Norvale answers that a ruling once pronounced binds everyone and that the only route open to the department was an appeal, which it did not take.

items.stem: Where does the appeal go, and by when must it be filed?

options.text: The Appellate Tribunal, within sixty days
options.misconception: routes the challenge through the ordinary appellate ladder, when this section sends it straight to the High Court
options.why: The ordinary ladder has no part in this. The section names one forum and it is the High Court, which is much of why an advance ruling settles a question quickly — there is nothing standing between the Board and a constitutional court. Filing before the Tribunal would burn the sixty days and leave nothing behind.
keywords: the section names one forum and it is the High Court

options.text: Nowhere — only a ruling can be appealed against, and this is an order about a ruling
options.misconception: reads the appeal as lying against rulings alone, when the words cover a ruling pronounced or an order passed by the Board
options.why: The right is given against a ruling pronounced or an order passed by the Board, and a declaration that a ruling is void is such an order. Reading it as covering rulings alone would leave the sharpest thing the Board can do with no route of challenge at all.
keywords: a ruling pronounced or an order passed by the Board

options.text: The High Court, within sixty days of the date the order bears, and no extension is possible
options.misconception: starts the clock at signature and treats the period as absolute, when it runs from communication and can be extended for sufficient cause
options.why: Two things are wrong at once. Time runs from the communication of the ruling or order and not from the day it was signed, which matters when an order sits in a registry for a fortnight. And the period is not absolute: a further thirty days is open where the appellant shows he was prevented by sufficient cause.
keywords: time runs from the communication of the ruling or order

options.text: The High Court, within sixty days of communication, with a further thirty days available for good reason
options.why: An applicant aggrieved by a ruling pronounced or an order passed by the Board may appeal to the High Court, and there is no tier in between. It has to be filed within sixty days from the date the ruling or order was communicated, in the prescribed form and manner. Where the High Court is satisfied on an application by the appellant that he was prevented by sufficient cause from filing inside that time, it may grant a further thirty days — a discretion to be asked for, not an extension to be assumed.
keywords: may appeal to the High Court
within sixty days from the date the ruling or order was communicated
it may grant a further thirty days

citation.ref: Section 245W(1)

items.scenario: The Board has declared Norvale Ltd's ruling void. The order was signed on 20 March 2026 and reached the company on 3 April 2026. Norvale wants to challenge it. Its counsel is out of the country until late June and the papers cannot realistically be settled before then. The company asks where the challenge goes, from when the time runs, and what happens if it is late.

items.stem: Do these facts bring section 94(8) into play?

options.text: No, because he bought before the bonus was ever announced
options.misconception: adds a test of intention or foreknowledge that the sub-section does not contain
options.why: The clause measures dates and holdings and nothing else. It asks when the purchase was made against the record date, whether the extra units came free, when the original units went, and whether the free ones are still held. There is no room in it for what the buyer knew or meant, and that is what makes it a specific rule rather than a judgement.
keywords: it asks when the purchase was made against the record date

options.text: Yes — every condition the sub-section sets is satisfied
options.why: The clause is built out of three facts and each of them is here. He bought the units within three months before the record date, 1 May being inside three months of 20 June. He was allotted further units without any payment on the strength of holding them on that date. And he sold the original units within nine months after the record date, 10 December sitting well inside a window that closes on 20 March 2026, while continuing to hold the bonus units. What he knew when he bought is not one of the three.
keywords: within three months before the record date
within nine months after the record date
while continuing to hold the bonus units

options.text: No, because he has kept the bonus units and so has stripped nothing
options.misconception: reverses the third condition, reading continued holding as a defence when it is one of the things that must be true for the clause to bite
options.why: Continuing to hold the bonus units is a condition of the clause, not an escape from it. The mischief has exactly this shape: sell the original units at a loss, keep the free ones, and use the loss elsewhere. Had he sold the bonus units as well, the sub-section would not be looking at him.
keywords: continuing to hold the bonus units is a condition of the clause

options.text: No, because the nine months runs from the day he bought the units
options.misconception: measures both windows from the purchase, when one runs backwards from the record date and the other forwards from it
options.why: The record date is the fixed point and both windows are measured against it. Three months looks backwards from it to the purchase and nine months looks forwards from it to the sale. Running the nine months from 1 May would close the window in February 2026 and would answer a question the sub-section never asks.
keywords: the record date is the fixed point and both windows are measured against it

citation.ref: Section 94(8), clauses (a), (b) and (c)

items.scenario: Mr. Rohan bought 10,000 units of an equity-oriented mutual fund on 1 May 2025 at ₹40 a unit. The fund announced a bonus of one unit for every unit held and fixed 20 June 2025 as the record date; Rohan was allotted 10,000 bonus units and paid nothing for them. On 10 December 2025 he sold the original 10,000 units at ₹22 a unit and he still holds every one of the bonus units. His broker tells him the bonus stripping provision only catches somebody who buys after a bonus has been announced.

items.stem: What happens to the shortfall of ₹1,80,000?

options.text: It is added to the cost of the original units, so it simply disappears
options.misconception: puts the ignored amount back into the asset that was sold, when it attaches to the units still held
options.why: It attaches to the units he kept, which are the bonus ones. The original units are gone, and adding anything to their cost would cancel the loss and leave nothing to recover later. The clause moves the amount to the asset that still has a future, and that is what makes the recovery possible at all.
keywords: it attaches to the units he kept

options.text: It is left out this year and follows the bonus units instead
options.why: Two consequences run together. First, the ₹1,80,000 loss is ignored in computing his income chargeable to tax, so it cannot meet the share gains or anything else this year. Second, the amount so ignored is deemed to be the cost of acquisition of the bonus units he still holds. Nothing is destroyed by the sub-section: the amount moves across and comes back to him when those units are sold, which makes this a deferral rather than a penalty.
keywords: the cost of acquisition of the bonus units

options.text: It is disallowed and lost for good
options.misconception: stops at the first consequence and misses the second, which puts the ignored amount into the cost of the units still held
options.why: The clause has a second limb and it is the one that matters to him. The amount ignored is deemed to be the cost of purchase of the additional units, so it is not written off — it sits inside the cost of what he holds and cuts the gain when he sells. Treating it as lost overstates the tax on that later sale.
keywords: the amount ignored is deemed to be the cost of purchase of the additional units

options.text: It is allowed, but only against long-term capital gains
options.misconception: treats the loss as merely restricted in where it may go, when the clause takes it out of the computation altogether
options.why: There is no restricted set-off here. The loss is ignored for the purpose of computing income chargeable to tax, which puts it outside the set-off rules rather than inside them with conditions attached.
