Nothing in the clause looks at whether the gain it might have met was long term or short.
keywords: the loss is ignored for the purpose of computing income chargeable to tax

citation.ref: Section 94(8), sub-clauses (i) and (ii)

items.scenario: On the same facts Rohan paid ₹4,00,000 for the original 10,000 units and received ₹2,20,000 when he sold them, a shortfall of ₹1,80,000. He has long-term gains of ₹6,00,000 on shares this year and his return preparer has set the shortfall against them. The 10,000 bonus units are still in his folio and were allotted to him free.

items.stem: What is different on these facts?

options.text: Still caught, because he continues to hold all the bonus units
options.misconception: treats any one of the three conditions as enough on its own, when all three have to hold together
options.why: The three conditions are cumulative and holding the bonus units is only one of them. Once the sale falls outside the nine months the chain breaks, and a broken chain is not mended by the fact that one link is still there. That is what makes the window a real planning point rather than a formality.

options.text: The loss is allowed, but only against a future gain on the bonus units
options.misconception: invents a ring-fence around the bonus units, when a loss the clause does not touch is governed by the ordinary set-off rules
options.why: Once the clause is out of the way there is nothing special about this loss. It goes into the ordinary rules for setting off capital losses, which do not care where the gain it meets comes from beyond the usual short-term and long-term distinction. A ring-fence of that kind exists nowhere in the Act.
keywords: it goes into the ordinary rules for setting off capital losses

options.text: The loss is allowed now, and the ₹1,80,000 still goes into the bonus units
options.misconception: keeps the second consequence after the clause has stopped applying, when both consequences hang on the same three conditions
options.why: The cost transfer is part of the same clause and is switched on by the same three conditions. Once the sale is outside the window there is nothing to ignore, and so nothing to add anywhere. Taking the loss now and a higher cost later would give him the benefit twice over.
keywords: the cost transfer is part of the same clause

options.text: The sub-section does not apply, and the bonus units keep a nil cost
options.why: Nine months from 20 June 2025 end on 20 March 2026, so a sale on 15 April 2026 falls outside nine months and the third condition is not met. With one condition missing the clause does not apply at all, so the loss is allowed in the ordinary way and set off under the normal rules. Nothing moves across to the bonus units either — they keep the nil cost a bonus allotment carries.
keywords: the loss is allowed in the ordinary way

citation.ref: Section 94(8), clause (c) and the nine-month window

items.scenario: Rohan's adviser reruns the same facts with one change. The purchase on 1 May 2025 and the bonus record date of 20 June 2025 stay as they were, and he still holds all 10,000 bonus units, but the original units are sold on 15 April 2026 instead of in December. The shortfall on them is the same ₹1,80,000 and he has capital gains elsewhere to absorb it.

items.stem: Which parts of what has happened stand, and which do not?

options.text: Everything stands, approval and a hearing being matters of office practice
options.misconception: reads the approval and the hearing as internal housekeeping, when both are written into the sub-section as conditions of a valid direction
options.why: Both sit in the statute and both bind. The power is given to be used with the previous approval of a named senior authority, and the assessee is to be heard before the direction is made. A direction issued without them is not merely irregular; it is a direction the officer had no power to give in the first place.
keywords: a direction issued without them is not merely irregular

options.text: Nothing stands, accounts audited under the Companies Act being closed to him
options.misconception: reads a statutory audit as answering the officer's need, when the section expressly allows a direction even where the accounts have been audited elsewhere
options.why: The section says the opposite in terms. It lets the officer call for this audit on books audited under any other law for the time being in force, and on books nobody has audited at all. A statutory audit answers a different question from the one he is asking, and the company's argument fails on the words themselves.
keywords: audited under any other law for the time being in force

options.text: Nothing stands, since complexity alone cannot justify it and the revenue's interest has no place in the test
options.misconception: drops the interests of the revenue out of the list, when it is one of the things the officer is required to have regard to
options.why: The interests of the revenue sit in the list beside complexity, volume, doubts about correctness, multiplicity and the specialised nature of the business, and the officer weighs them together. Complexity was never meant to stand alone, and taking the revenue's interest out would leave the power without the very thing that makes it worth using.
keywords: the interests of the revenue sit in the list beside complexity

options.text: The ground for the direction is good; the way it was issued is not
options.why: The ground is sound. He may direct a special audit having regard to the nature and complexity of the accounts, their volume, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions and the specialised nature of the business, taken with the interests of the revenue, and a diamond trade with thousands of consignment entries sits squarely inside that. He is right about the company's argument too. But two steps were skipped and each is a condition: the previous approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and an opportunity of being heard given to the company before the direction goes out.
keywords: the nature and complexity of the accounts
an opportunity of being heard given to the company
the previous approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner

citation.ref: Section 142(2A), with the proviso requiring an opportunity of being heard

items.scenario: During the scrutiny of Ratnadeep Gems Ltd, a diamond trader with several thousand consignment and job-work entries a year, the Assessing Officer forms the view that the books cannot be read without help. He signs a direction under section 142(2A) the same afternoon and posts it. He has taken no approval from anybody above him and has not called the company in. The company writes back that its accounts were audited under the Companies Act only two months ago, so no further audit can be ordered at all.

items.stem: Do the extensions stand, and from when is the period counted?

options.text: Both stand, because only extensions the officer gives on his own motion count towards the limit
options.misconception: splits extensions by who asked for them, when the ceiling covers the aggregate however each extension came about
options.why: The section allows both kinds — the officer may extend on his own motion or on an application made by the assessee — and then puts a single ceiling over the total of everything. Who asked changes nothing about the count. Splitting them would let an assessee buy unlimited time simply by asking rather than waiting.
keywords: a single ceiling over the total of everything

options.text: Both extensions stand, each having been granted for a reason the officer accepted
options.misconception: reads the requirement of a good and sufficient reason as the only control, when a hard outer limit sits behind it
options.why: Reasons control each extension; the ceiling controls the total. The words say the aggregate of the period originally fixed and the periods so extended shall not exceed 180 days in any case, and the phrase "in any case" leaves no room for a reason good enough to break it. Both controls have to be satisfied at the same time.
keywords: the aggregate of the period originally fixed and the periods so extended

options.text: The second cannot stand, and time runs from 20 May 2025, the date on the direction
options.misconception: starts the clock at signature, when the section starts it at receipt by the assessee
options.why: Receipt is the trigger and it is in the sub-section for a reason: a company cannot begin an audit it has not been told about. Counting from the date the order bears would shorten the period by however long the post took, and that is precisely the unfairness the words remove.

options.text: The second extension cannot stand, and time runs from 1 June 2025
options.why: Extensions as such are perfectly proper: the officer may extend on his own motion or on the assessee's application for good and sufficient reason. What he may not do is let the original period and all the extensions together run beyond 180 days in any case, and 200 days is past it. The clock also starts where the section puts it — the 180 days are counted from the date on which the assessee receives the direction, not from the day the officer signed it, so it started on 1 June.
keywords: the date on which the assessee receives the direction

citation.ref: Section 142(2C) and its proviso

items.scenario: A direction for a special audit, this time properly approved and preceded by a hearing, was signed on 20 May 2025 and reached Ratnadeep Gems Ltd on 1 June 2025. It fixed 60 days for the report. The accountant asked for more time twice, and the officer extended it once by 60 days and again by 80, which takes the total to 200 days. Each extension was asked for in writing and each request set out a reason the officer accepted.

items.stem: Who fixes this bill, who pays it, and within what limits?

options.text: The accountant and the company may agree any rate, the guidelines being advice
options.misconception: reads the hourly floor and ceiling as guidance to be negotiated around, when they are the prescribed limits inside which the authority must fix the amount
options.why: The authority determines the amount in accordance with the prescribed guidelines, and the two figures live in those guidelines. They are not a suggestion. In any case there is nothing here for the company to agree to, because the company is not the payer.
keywords: the authority determines the amount in accordance with the prescribed guidelines

options.text: The company pays, its own accounts having made the audit necessary
options.misconception: treats the cost as a consequence of the assessee's record-keeping, when the statute puts it on the exchequer whatever the reason for the audit
options.why: Whose fault the complexity was is not the test. The sub-section says the expenses so determined shall be paid by the Central Government and stops there, and it says so because a power the revenue chooses to use should not be funded by the person it is used against. That is also part of what keeps the power from being used lightly.
keywords: the expenses so determined shall be paid by the Central Government

options.text: The Assessing Officer fixes the fee, having ordered the audit
options.misconception: leaves the fee with the officer who ordered the audit, when the statute puts it with the senior authority whose approval the direction itself needed
options.why: The determination is not the Assessing Officer's to make. It belongs to the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner — the same rank whose previous approval the direction needed. Keeping the officer away from the money is part of what makes the nomination and the payment independent of the assessment he is making.
keywords: it belongs to the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner

options.text: The senior authority fixes it inside an hourly floor and ceiling, and the Central Government pays
options.why: The company should not be paying at all. The expenses of and incidental to the special audit, the accountant's remuneration among them, are determined by the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under the prescribed guidelines, and once determined they are paid by the Central Government. The guidelines set a floor and a ceiling on the hourly rate: not less than ₹3,750 at the bottom, not more than ₹7,500 at the top, counted across the hours the direction allowed for. ₹9,000 an hour is above the ceiling, and the bill should never have come to the company.

citation.ref: Section 142(2D), read with Rule 14B

items.scenario: The special audit of Ratnadeep Gems Ltd is finished. The accountant's bill is for 240 hours at ₹9,000 an hour and he has sent it to the company. The Assessing Officer tells the company to settle it directly and to treat the cost as part of the price of its own record-keeping. The finance head has already put the amount in her forecast and wants to know whether any of this is right.

items.stem: What must happen on the first file, and what may happen on the second?

options.text: No separate hearing is needed, since Ratnadeep will read the findings in the order itself
options.misconception: treats sight of the finished order as the hearing, when the section requires the material to be put to the assessee before it is used
options.why: Seeing a conclusion after it has been reached is not an opportunity to answer it. The requirement is that the material proposed to be used be put to the assessee first, so that whatever is wrong in it can be met while the outcome can still change. An order that arrives with the findings already inside it comes too late to be answered.
keywords: the material proposed to be used be put to the assessee first

options.text: The hearing on material gathered is required in every case, with no exception
options.misconception: states the rule without its exception, when the section lifts the requirement where the assessment is a best judgement one
options.why: There is one carve-out and it matters here. Where the assessment is in the nature of a best judgement assessment, it is not obligatory for the officer to give an opportunity of being heard on the material before passing the order. The exception is narrow, and stating the rule flat would be wrong in the very case the second company has created.
keywords: it is not obligatory for the officer to give an opportunity of being heard on the material

options.text: Sundar Alloys faces a penalty only, a best judgement being for a missing return
options.misconception: reads best judgement as reserved for a missing return, when a failure to comply with a valid direction is itself one of its triggers
options.why: Failure to get the audit done is expressly one of the situations in which a best judgement assessment follows, and it stands alongside penalty rather than instead of it. Reading best judgement as available only where no return was filed would leave a company free to defeat the audit power by doing nothing at all.
keywords: failure to get the audit done is expressly one of the situations

options.text: The findings must be put to Ratnadeep first; Sundar Alloys can be assessed to the officer's best judgement
options.why: Before using anything the audit turned up, the officer has to give the company an opportunity of being heard on any material gathered on the basis of the audit which he proposes to use in the assessment. The one exception is where the assessment is itself a best judgement assessment. And that is what the second company has invited: where an assessee directed to get the audit done fails to do so, the officer may make a best judgement assessment under section 144, besides imposing penalty and taking such other steps as the law allows.
keywords: any material gathered on the basis of the audit
a best judgement assessment under section 144

citation.ref: Section 142(3) on material gathered, with section 144 on the consequence of a failure to comply

items.scenario: The special audit report on Ratnadeep Gems Ltd comes in and the Assessing Officer proposes to rest two paragraphs of his assessment order on findings it contains. He has not shown those findings to the company and intends the order to be the first the company hears of them. In another file in the same charge, Sundar Alloys Ltd was given a valid direction months ago and has simply produced nothing at all.

items.stem: Which Actions is India committed to, and what holds the commitment in place?

options.text: Four — Actions 3, 5, 6 and 13, controlled foreign company rules included
options.misconception: promotes controlled foreign company rules into the minimum standards and drops the dispute resolution standard to make room
options.why: Controlled foreign company rules are the clearest example of the other side of the line, and the standard that gets pushed out when they are let in is the one on dispute resolution. That standard exists because a state which will not resolve disputes exports the cost of its own rules on to everybody else, and it is the fourth of the four.
keywords: the standard that gets pushed out when they are let in is the one on dispute resolution

options.text: None in any binding sense, since only an Act of Parliament binds India
options.misconception: mistakes the absence of a supranational legislature for the absence of a commitment, and misses the review by other members that gives the minimum standards their force
options.why: It is quite true that only Parliament can change Indian tax law, and that is exactly why these four are enforced by peer review rather than by a court. A member commits to implementing them and to participating in the peer review of each, and the review is what makes non-implementation visible to everybody else. Calling that nothing is how a group ends up surprised by a filing obligation.
keywords: participating in the peer review of each

options.text: All fifteen, membership of the Inclusive Framework covering the package
options.misconception: reads membership as a commitment to the whole package, when the package deliberately carries three different grades of commitment
options.why: The measures come in three grades: new minimum standards that every state is to implement, revisions of standards that already existed and that not every participant has endorsed, and best practices, which are optional recommendations. Only the first grade binds. Reading the fifteen as one block makes an optional recommendation look like law and leads a group to plan around rules nobody has enacted.
keywords: new minimum standards that every state is to implement

options.text: Four of them, each watched by the other members
options.why: Four of the fifteen are minimum standards and a member of the Inclusive Framework commits to all four — Action 5 on harmful tax practices, Action 6 on treaty abuse, Action 13 on country-by-country reporting, and Action 14 on making dispute resolution more effective. Nothing forces a state's hand from outside, so the commitment is held another way: each of the four is reviewed by the other members, which is what makes a failure to implement visible.
keywords: Action 14 on making dispute resolution more effective

citation.ref: The explanatory statement on the three grades of commitment, and the four minimum standards

items.scenario: The treasury head of an Indian group that is setting up holding and financing companies abroad has read that India belongs to the Inclusive Framework on BEPS. She wants to know which of the fifteen Action Plans India is actually bound to put in place before she commits to a structure, and what "bound" can mean when the organisation behind the project cannot pass a law in any country.

items.stem: What is India's position on controlled foreign company rules?

options.text: It does not matter, the general anti-avoidance rule doing the same work
options.misconception: treats a general anti-avoidance rule as a substitute for a specific regime, when the two ask different questions
options.why: A general rule asks whether an arrangement lacks commercial substance and was entered into mainly for a tax benefit. A controlled foreign company regime asks a flat question about attributing a foreign subsidiary's income to its parent, whatever the reason for the structure. Neither does the other's work, which is why states that want the second write it separately.
keywords: a controlled foreign company regime asks a flat question about attributing

options.text: It must enact them, this being one of the four minimum standards
options.misconception: promotes a best practice into a minimum standard, which is the confusion the three grades of commitment exist to prevent
options.why: The four standards are on harmful tax practices, treaty abuse, country-by-country reporting and dispute resolution. Controlled foreign company rules are not among them, and the report says as much in terms. A group that plans on the footing that India must legislate here is planning around a law that does not exist.
keywords: Controlled foreign company rules are not among them

options.text: It is free to enact them or not, and it has not
options.why: The final report on Action 3 does not propose a minimum standard for controlled foreign company regimes. It offers a set of building blocks for an effective regime as a best practice, which is an optional recommendation, and the reason it went no further was a fundamental disagreement about whether such a regime should be used to protect other states' tax bases. So this is not a minimum standard, India is free either way, and it has not legislated.

options.text: It need not, because the project dropped the subject
options.misconception: reads the absence of a standard as the absence of work, when a full report exists and its recommendations are open to any state that wants them
options.why: The subject was worked on and reported on at length; what it did not produce was a binding standard. The building blocks are there and a state may take them up whole or in part whenever it chooses. Saying the subject was dropped would leave a group unready for the day India does legislate.

citation.ref: Action 3 final report on controlled foreign company rules

items.scenario: The same treasury head has been told that the BEPS project dealt with controlled foreign companies, and she wants to know whether India has to bring in rules of that kind before the group's foreign holding company can be relied on. Her worry is that a structure she signs off now will be overtaken by an obligation India has already accepted.

items.stem: What must a treaty contain to meet that standard?

options.text: A Principal Purpose Test in every treaty, that being the only accepted rule
options.misconception: reads one of the three permitted routes as the only one, when the standard leaves the choice of route to the states
options.why: The test standing alone is one of the three and it is the most common in practice, but it is not the only road. A limitation rule with the test beside it, or a limitation rule with a conduit financing mechanism attached, meet the standard just as well. The standard is about the level of protection reached, not about a single form of words.
keywords: The standard is about the level of protection reached

options.text: Only the statement of intention; which rule to use is a best practice
options.misconception: keeps the preamble and demotes the operative rule, when both halves belong to the same minimum standard
options.why: A statement of intention with nothing behind it decides no case. The standard has two halves and both of them are required — the express statement of what the states mean, and one of the three operative rules that lets a tax authority actually refuse the benefit. Demoting the second leaves the first as decoration.
keywords: both of them are required — the express statement of what the states mean

options.text: Nothing in the treaty; India's own anti-avoidance law is enough
options.misconception: sends a treaty-level standard to domestic law, when the commitment is about what the treaty itself contains
options.why: The commitment is about the text of the agreement. A state's own anti-avoidance rule may well reach the same arrangement, but the standard asks for protection written into the agreement so that both states are bound by it and a taxpayer can read it. Domestic law alone leaves the treaty looking like an open door.
keywords: the standard asks for protection written into the agreement

options.text: A statement of what the states intend, and one of three operative rules
options.why: Two things together. The treaty must carry an express statement that the states mean to eliminate double taxation without opening a way to no tax at all, or to a cut rate, through evasion or avoidance, treaty shopping included. It must then adopt one of three: a Limitation of Benefits rule combined with a Principal Purpose Test, the Principal Purpose Test on its own, or a Limitation of Benefits rule supplemented by a mechanism dealing with conduit financing arrangements. Which of the three is for the two states to settle.
keywords: a Limitation of Benefits rule combined with a Principal Purpose Test
a mechanism dealing with conduit financing arrangements

citation.ref: Action 6 minimum standard on preventing treaty abuse

items.scenario: The group's proposed holding company abroad would receive Indian dividends and pass most of them straight on to its own parent in a third country. The treasury head has been told the treaty may not be available to it, and that the treaty itself now has to carry protection of a particular kind. She wants to know what a treaty has to contain before India will regard it as meeting the standard on treaty shopping.

items.stem: What are export turnover and total turnover for the fraction?

options.why: Export turnover counts only what reached India in convertible foreign exchange inside six months from the end of the previous year, so the ₹20,00,000 that arrived in November without an extension drops out and ₹3,00,00,000 is left. Freight and insurance for delivery outside India are then taken out by the definition itself, leaving ₹2,90,00,000 of export turnover. Following the Supreme Court, the Board has settled that the same freight and insurance come out of total turnover as well, so ₹5,00,00,000 less ₹10,00,000 gives ₹4,90,00,000 of total turnover. The late receipt is not taken out below the line — only the freight and insurance are.
keywords: come out of total turnover as well

options.misconception: reads the exclusion out of the definition of export turnover alone and misses the clarification that carries the same sum into the denominator
options.why: The definition does sit in export turnover only, which is why the point was fought for years. It was settled the other way. One component of total turnover is export turnover, so a sum taken out of the numerator has to come out of the denominator too, or the fraction understates the export share. Leaving the whole ₹5,00,00,000 below the line costs the company deduction it is entitled to.
keywords: One component of total turnover is export turnover

options.misconception: reads the six-month rule as being about the currency the money came in rather than about when it arrived
options.why: The definition asks for two things at once. The consideration must be received in India in convertible foreign exchange, and it must be received inside six months from the end of the previous year, or inside such further period as the competent authority allows. The November money meets the first and fails the second, and nobody extended the time, so it stays out.
keywords: received inside six months from the end of the previous year

options.misconception: takes the freight out of the denominator but leaves it in the numerator, when the definition removes it from export turnover first
options.why: The exclusion begins in the meaning of export turnover, and freight, telecommunication charges and insurance for getting the goods to a buyer abroad are outside what that phrase covers. Whether the customer was billed for them separately makes no difference. The clarification then carries the same sum into total turnover; it never moves it there instead.
keywords: freight, telecommunication charges and insurance for getting the goods to a buyer abroad

citation.ref: Section 10AA, Explanation 1 on the meaning of export turnover, with Circular No. 4/2018 on excluding the same sum from total turnover

items.scenario: Vega Exports Ltd runs a unit in a Special Economic Zone. For the previous year 2025-26 its total turnover is ₹5,00,00,000, of which the accounts show export turnover of ₹3,20,00,000 and domestic sales of ₹1,80,00,000. Of the export figure, ₹3,00,00,000 came into India in convertible foreign exchange by 30 September 2026 and ₹20,00,000 only in November 2026, with nobody having extended the time. The export figure also includes ₹10,00,000 of freight and insurance attributable to delivering the goods outside India. The accountant has to settle the two turnovers before the fraction can be worked.

items.stem: What is the deduction for A.Y. 2026-27?

options.misconception: reads the life of the deduction as a single stretch at one rate, when the first five years and the next five carry different rates
options.why: The relief runs for fifteen years in all but not at one rate throughout. The first five assessment years carry the whole of the export profits, the next five carry half, and the last five carry half again against a reserve. A unit that began in 2019-20 is past the first five by the time A.Y. 2026-27 comes round.
keywords: The first five assessment years carry the whole of the export profits

options.misconception: leaves the freight inside the denominator while taking it out of the numerator, which shrinks the export share and the deduction with it
options.why: Using ₹5,00,00,000 below the line while ₹2,90,00,000 sits above it compares two figures measured on different rules. The same freight and insurance have to come out of both, and once they do the export share rises and so does the deduction. The gap between this answer and the right one is close to half a lakh of relief.
keywords: The same freight and insurance have to come out of both

options.misconception: applies the percentage to the whole profit of the unit instead of to the export profits worked out through the fraction
options.why: The percentage bites on export profits and not on the unit's whole profit. The fraction comes first, and it is there because a unit may sell at home as well as abroad — only the export share earns the deduction. Half of ₹80,00,000 would give relief on the domestic sales too.

Export profits are the unit's profits in the proportion export turnover bears to total turnover — ₹80,00,000 times ₹2,90,00,000 divided by ₹4,90,00,000, which comes to ₹47,34,694 of export profits. The unit began in the previous year 2019-20, so A.Y. 2020-21 was its first year and the five years at the full rate ended with A.Y. 2024-25. A.Y. 2026-27 falls in the next band, where the deduction is half, so ₹23,67,347 is the amount. It sits comfortably inside the total income of ₹1,10,00,000 worked out before the deduction.

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1) and (7), with the second band of five assessment years at fifty per cent

items.scenario: Vega Exports Ltd's unit began manufacturing on 1 October 2019 under a letter of approval issued that year. Its profits for the previous year 2025-26 are ₹80,00,000. Export turnover for the fraction has been settled at ₹2,90,00,000 and total turnover at ₹4,90,00,000. The company's total income for the year, computed before any deduction under this section, is ₹1,10,00,000. The accountant has to put a figure in the return.

items.stem: Under what provision does her relief come, and what has to be true for it?

options.text: Unilateral relief under section 91, on six conditions that must all hold
options.why: There is no treaty, so there is nothing for section 90 to work on and relief comes under section 91 instead. Its conditions all have to hold together: she is resident in India in the previous year the income is taxable in, the income accrued or arose to her outside India, it is not deemed to accrue or arise in India, it was subjected to income-tax in Country Z in her own hands, she has paid that tax there, and the two countries have signed nothing with each other, so there is no agreement for relief from double taxation. The deduction that follows is on the doubly taxed income at the Indian rate or the foreign rate, whichever is lower.
keywords: there is no agreement for relief from double taxation
she has paid that tax there

options.text: Neither, because relief needs an agreement and there is none
options.misconception: reads relief as available only by agreement, missing the provision the Act carries for countries India has no treaty with
options.why: India grants relief on its own for income taxed in a country it has no agreement with. Nothing has to be negotiated for it and no certificate from the other government opens it. What is needed is that the income bore tax there in her hands and that she actually paid it. Without the provision, income earned in most of the world would be taxed twice over.
keywords: India grants relief on its own

options.text: Section 91, but only where the foreign tax was deducted at source
options.misconception: adds a condition about how the foreign tax was collected, when the provision asks only that it was charged on the assessee and paid
options.why: How the money reached the foreign treasury is not one of the conditions. What the section asks is that the income was subjected to income-tax in that country in the assessee's own hands and that the tax on it has been paid. A payment on self-assessment counts every bit as much as a deduction at source.
keywords: subjected to income-tax in that country in the assessee's own hands

options.text: Section 90, which is where every credit for foreign tax is claimed
options.misconception: treats section 90 as the general credit provision, when it works only where an agreement exists and unilateral relief is a separate section
options.why: Section 90 gives effect to an agreement, and where there is none there is nothing to give effect to. Unilateral relief is a separate provision written for exactly this gap, and the two differ in more than their number — an agreement can settle which state may tax what, while unilateral relief does no more than reduce the Indian tax on income that has borne tax twice.
keywords: Unilateral relief is a separate provision written for exactly this gap

citation.ref: Section 91(1) and its conditions, with Rule 128 on credit for tax paid in a country outside India

items.scenario: Ms. Anvi was resident in India throughout the previous year 2025-26. She earned professional fees of ₹2,00,000 for work she carried out in Country Z, and Country Z charged her income-tax of ₹30,000 on it, which she paid there. India has no agreement with Country Z for the avoidance of double taxation. Her adviser has opened the return at the schedule for treaty relief and started filling it in.

items.stem: On what amount, and at what rate, does the Act charge Verity?

options.text: 35% of ₹38,00,000, the rate a foreign company pays on business profits
options.misconception: reaches for the ordinary company rate, forgetting that a special rate in Chapter XII displaces it for the income it names
options.why: The ordinary rate applies to what is left after the specially rated income is taken out. It does not apply to the fee itself. Verity has no permanent establishment and no fixed place of profession here, so there is no business income of a foreign company to rate in the first place — only a receipt that Chapter XII names and prices at 20% of what came in.

options.text: 10% of ₹50,00,000, which is the rate section 115A carries for a non-resident
options.misconception: carries across a concessional rate the section sets for interest on foreign-currency borrowing and applies it to a technical fee
options.why: Section 115A prices several receipts and they are not priced alike. Interest on certain foreign-currency loans and rupee bonds is rated at 4%, 5% or 9%; royalty and technical fees are rated at 20%. Ten per cent is a treaty figure in many agreements, and Verity's country has no treaty with India, so there is nothing here to bring that rate in.

options.text: 20% of ₹50,00,000, with nothing taken off for what it spent
options.why: Chapter XII carries its own rate for this receipt. Where a foreign company's total income includes fees for technical services paid by an Indian concern under an agreement with it, and the receipt is not income of the kind section 44DA deals with, the charge is 20% of the gross amount. The word gross is doing the work: there is no deduction for expenditure or allowance, because sections 28 to 44C and section 57 are all shut against this income. So the ₹12,00,000 of cost never enters the working and the tax is ₹10,00,000.
keywords: fees for technical services paid by an Indian concern
the charge is 20% of the gross amount
there is no deduction for expenditure or allowance

options.text: 20% of ₹38,00,000, the cost of earning the fee coming off first
options.misconception: treats a special rate under Chapter XII as though it sat on net income the way a rate under a normal head does
options.why: Netting is exactly what the section forbids. A rate under Chapter XII is fixed to a gross receipt so that a non-resident with no presence here need not be put to a computation at all, and the price of that simplicity is that spending is ignored. Allowing the ₹12,00,000 would let the same receipt be taxed twice over on two different bases depending on who drew the working.

citation.ref: Section 115A(1)(b) with the bar in section 115A(3) on deductions under sections 28 to 44C and section 57

items.scenario: Brightpath Analytics Ltd, an Indian company, paid ₹50,00,000 during P.Y. 2025-26 to Verity Data Pte Ltd for technical services rendered under an agreement Verity made with Brightpath. Verity is incorporated in and resident of a country that has no agreement with India for the avoidance of double taxation. It has no office, branch or fixed place of profession here and nobody in India works for it. Verity's own accounts show ₹12,00,000 of travel, salary and software cost incurred to earn the fee, and its consultant has filed a computation showing ₹38,00,000 of income and asks Brightpath to deduct on that.

items.stem: Which rate should Meridian actually deduct at?

options.text: 30%, the higher of the two rates, since the Act's rate is a floor
options.misconception: turns the more-beneficial test upside down and reads the Act as setting a minimum the treaty may only add to
options.why: There is no adding up and no floor. The two rates are alternatives and the assessee takes the better of them; the Act supplies the rate only where it is the kinder of the pair. Thirty per cent is neither of the two figures on the table.

options.text: 20% now, with Larsvik free to claim the difference back when it files a return
options.misconception: treats the beneficial rate as a refund entitlement rather than the rate the deductor is obliged to apply
options.why: The comparison is made when the tax is deducted, not a year later. A payer who deducts at a rate the assessee is not liable to has over-deducted, and forcing a non-resident with no other Indian income to file a return purely to recover the excess is the compliance burden the beneficial-rate rule exists to avoid.

options.text: 20%, because a statute passed by Parliament outranks an agreement with another country
options.misconception: reads the treaty as subordinate law, when the Act itself is what gives the treaty its footing and tells the assessee to take whichever is kinder
options.why: The treaty does not have to outrank the Act, because the Act stands aside for it by its own terms. Section 90 is the provision Parliament passed, and what it says is that the agreement's terms govern an assessee they cover wherever they are kinder than the Act. Applying 20% here would be disobeying the Act, not upholding it.

options.text: 10%, the rate in the agreement
options.why: Section 90(2) settles the contest without needing a refund claim. Where India has entered into an agreement with another country, the Act applies to an assessee covered by it only to the extent the Act is more beneficial to the assessee. Twenty per cent is not more beneficial than ten, so the Act's rate stands aside and the treaty rate of 10% is the one Meridian deducts at. Nothing is postponed to a refund; the choice is made at the moment of deduction.
keywords: only to the extent the Act is more beneficial to the assessee
the treaty rate of 10% is the one Meridian deducts at

citation.ref: Section 90(2) read with the rate for fees for technical services in section 115A(1)(b)

items.scenario: Meridian Foundry Ltd is about to pay ₹60,00,000 to Larsvik AB for technical services. Larsvik is resident in a country whose agreement with India puts fees for technical services at 10% of the gross amount, and it has given Meridian a residence certificate from that country's tax administration together with the particulars India prescribes. Meridian's tax cell says the agreement is only an agreement, that section 115A is the law passed by Parliament, and that it will therefore deduct at 20% and leave Larsvik to claim a refund.

items.stem: What must Aurum produce before Kestrel may use the agreement's rate?

options.text: The certificate on its own; Form 10F is only for individuals
options.misconception: reads the particulars as a personal-status form, when they are asked of every assessee claiming under an agreement and are excused only so far as the certificate already carries them
options.why: The particulars are asked of any assessee claiming under an agreement, company or not — one of them is the country of incorporation, which only an entity has. The one relaxation is narrower than this: an assessee need not repeat a particular that the certificate itself already contains. Aurum has produced no certificate, so nothing has been supplied and nothing can be excused.

options.text: A residence certificate issued by that country's own government, plus the prescribed particulars
options.why: Section 90(4) makes relief under an agreement conditional on the assessee obtaining a Tax Residency Certificate from the Government of that country, declaring its residence there. Section 90(5) then asks for prescribed particulars — status, nationality or country of incorporation, the tax identification number abroad, the period the certificate covers and the address abroad for that period. Those are the particulars set out in Form 10F. An auditor is not a government, so the letter is not the certificate the section asks for, whatever it says.
keywords: a Tax Residency Certificate from the Government of that country
the particulars set out in Form 10F

options.text: An Indian Permanent Account Number, which is the only thing the Act insists on
options.misconception: swaps the PAN requirement, which is about the rate for want of a number, for the residence proof that unlocks the treaty
options.why: Two different requirements are being run together. A Permanent Account Number goes to whether a higher deduction rate is forced for want of a number. Residence proof goes to whether the agreement applies at all. Aurum could hold a PAN and still get no relief without the certificate, and it can get relief with the certificate and no PAN.

options.text: Nothing more — a certificate from the payee's auditors proves residence just as well
options.misconception: treats residence as a matter of evidence the payer may weigh, when the section names one issuer and accepts no substitute
options.why: The section is not asking Kestrel to be satisfied. It names who must issue the document, and that is the other country's government, because only a tax administration can say that it treats the company as its resident for its own tax. An auditor can say where a company keeps its office; it cannot say who is entitled to tax it.

citation.ref: Sections 90(4) and 90(5) with Rule 21AB and the particulars in Form 10F

items.scenario: Kestrel Interiors Ltd is asked by Aurum Design GmbH to deduct at the 8% rate its country's agreement with India sets for technical fees. Aurum has sent a letter on its statutory auditors' paper confirming that Aurum is incorporated and managed in that country and pays tax there, along with a copy of its incorporation certificate. It has filed nothing with the Indian portal. Kestrel's finance head is satisfied by the auditors' letter and is ready to deduct at 8%.

items.stem: How much tax must Solstice deduct under section 195?

options.text: ₹8,00,000, but only after the Assessing Officer certifies the lower rate under section 197
options.misconception: makes the payer wait for an officer's certificate to apply a rate the treaty already fixes
options.why: A section 197 certificate is for deducting at a rate lower than the one the law otherwise requires. Here the law itself requires 10%, because the Act applies only so far as it is kinder than the agreement. Nothing has to be certified before Solstice may do what the statute already tells it to do, and the amount is unchanged either way.

options.text: Nothing, because the residence certificate exempts the payment from deduction
options.misconception: reads a residence certificate as an exemption certificate, when all it proves is which country's agreement applies
options.why: The certificate answers "whose treaty is this?" and nothing else. The treaty here does not exempt the fee — it prices it at 10%. A payment is relieved from deduction only by a certificate obtained under section 195(2) or section 197, which is a different document obtained from the Indian Assessing Officer for that purpose.

options.text: ₹16,00,000, because without a Permanent Account Number the higher rate is automatic
options.misconception: applies the no-PAN rate as an unconditional 20%, without asking whether the relaxation for non-residents has been earned
options.why: The higher rate is not automatic for a non-resident who has done what the relaxation asks. Its whole purpose is that a foreign company with no Indian income other than this fee has no reason to hold an Indian number, and it earns the relief by identifying itself another way — which this company has done, item by item. Deducting ₹16,00,000 would take twice the tax the two countries agreed India could take.

Rule 37BC relaxes section 206AA for a non-corporate non-resident or a foreign company with no Permanent Account Number receiving interest, royalty, technical fees, dividend or consideration for a capital asset, so long as it hands the payer its name, e-mail address, contact number, address abroad, residence certificate and tax identification number. All six are on the table here. Beyond that, a rate forced for want of a number cannot override the treaty in any case, because the agreement fixes what India may charge. So the treaty rate stands and tax deductible works out at ₹8,00,000.
keywords: a rate forced for want of a number cannot override the treaty

citation.ref: Section 195 with section 206AA and Rule 37BC, read against the agreement's rate under section 90(2)

items.scenario: Solstice Systems Ltd owes ₹80,00,000 to a foreign company for technical services performed wholly from abroad under an agreement with Solstice. The foreign company has no permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India. The agreement between the two countries puts technical fees at 10% of the gross amount, and the foreign company has furnished a residence certificate from its government, the particulars India prescribes, and its name, e-mail address, contact number, address in its own country and the tax identification number it is registered under there. It has never applied for a Permanent Account Number. Solstice's payroll system has queued the payment for deduction at 20%.

items.stem: How should this fee be computed and charged?

options.text: At 20% of the gross fee, with a deduction for the Indian costs of earning it
options.misconception: takes the rate from one provision and the deductions from the other, making a third rule that is in neither
options.why: The two provisions are a pair and each is complete. One gives a flat rate on a gross receipt and allows nothing; the other gives ordinary computation with real deductions at ordinary rates. Taking the rate from the first and the deductions from the second produces a charge the Act nowhere authorises.

options.text: At 20% of the gross fee, since that is the rate the Act sets for a technical fee
options.misconception: applies the flat rate without asking the one question that decides which of the two provisions governs
options.why: The flat rate is written to exclude exactly this case: it charges technical fees other than income of the kind section 44DA deals with. Where the contract belongs to an Indian establishment, the fee is that kind of income, and applying the gross rate would tax ₹9,00,00,000 as though the Pune office and its ₹5,50,00,000 of cost did not exist.

options.text: Under the presumptive scheme for services connected with the extraction of mineral oil
options.misconception: reaches for a presumptive provision because the payer is a marine business, when that scheme is expressly displaced for income falling under section 44DA
options.why: That presumptive scheme is for services or facilities supplied in connection with the prospecting for or extraction of mineral oil, which shipbuilding work is not. It is also shut out in terms for income covered by section 44DA, so even a business that could otherwise use it cannot use it for a fee its Indian establishment earned.

options.text: As business profits at the ordinary rates, with books and an audit
options.why: The fork is whether the contract the fee is paid under is effectively connected with a permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India, and here it plainly is: the Pune office made the contract, performs it and bears its cost. That takes the fee out of the flat 20% and into section 44DA, where it is computed under Profits and gains of business or profession and taxed at the normal rates, with the ₹5,50,00,000 allowed so far as it was spent wholly and exclusively for the Indian establishment. Section 44DA also makes books of account and audit compulsory, with the report furnished by the specified date.
keywords: effectively connected with a permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India
computed under Profits and gains of business or profession and taxed at the normal rates
section 44DA also makes books of account and audit compulsory

citation.ref: Section 44DA(1) and (2), with the exclusion in section 115A(1)(b) and the bar on section 44BB in section 44DA(3)

items.scenario: Halden Marine AS, a foreign company, keeps an engineering office in Pune with fourteen of its own engineers on its payroll. That office negotiated and signed the technical services contract with an Indian shipyard, its engineers perform every hour of the work the contract calls for, and every rupee of cost of performing it is booked there. The fee for P.Y. 2025-26 is ₹9,00,00,000 and Halden's Indian costs of earning it are ₹5,50,00,000. Halden's adviser has prepared a return charging 20% on the gross fee and keeping no books in India.

items.stem: What is the Nagpur officer required to do?

options.text: Hand everything over within 30 days of the first day of the search
options.misconception: mixes up the period with the thirty days that limit retention after an assessment, and starts the clock at the wrong end of the search
options.why: Two different numbers are being run together. Thirty days is the outer edge of retention after the assessments for the relevant years are complete, which is a much later stage. The handover period is sixty days, and it runs from the last authorisation being executed — the end of the search, not its opening day. A search over four premises could otherwise have its clock started before the later premises were even entered.

options.text: Hand over the books but keep the cash and gold, which are assets rather than documents
options.misconception: splits the sub-section into documents and valuables, when it names money, bullion and jewellery alongside the books in the same breath
options.why: The sub-section lists books of account or other documents and any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing, all going the same way. There is no document-and-asset divide in it. The cash and the gold go to Indore with the ledgers.

options.text: Hand everything to the Indore Assessing Officer within 60 days of 14 August 2026
options.why: Where the authorised officer has no jurisdiction over the person searched, section 132(9A) requires the books, documents, money, bullion, jewellery and other valuables to go to the Assessing Officer who does have it, and the outer limit is 60 days from the day the last of the authorisations for search was executed. The Act says when that day is: for a search it is the conclusion of the search as recorded in the last panchnama, which here is 14 August 2026. Once the handover is made, the retention decisions under sub-sections (8) and (9) belong to the Indore officer, not to Nagpur.
keywords: section 132(9A) requires the books, documents, money, bullion, jewellery and other valuables to go to the Assessing Officer
the outer limit is 60 days from the day the last of the authorisations for search was executed
the conclusion of the search as recorded in the last panchnama

options.text: Keep the seized material and exercise the retention powers himself, since he made the seizure
options.misconception: reads the power to seize as carrying the power to retain, when the Act separates the two and moves the second to the officer who will assess
options.why: The officer who seizes and the officer who assesses are deliberately split where they are not the same person. Retention decisions turn on what the assessment needs, and only the Assessing Officer with jurisdiction can know that. Holding the material past the sixty days and deciding on it in November would be exercising a power that has moved to Indore.

citation.ref: Section 132(9A) with Explanation 1 to section 132 on when the last authorisation is executed

items.scenario: A search under section 132 on Kanchan Textiles was carried out by an authorised officer of the Investigation wing at Nagpur. Kanchan is assessed at Indore and the Nagpur officer exercises no jurisdiction over it. The search ran over four premises and the last panchnama was drawn on 14 August 2026. Ledgers, ₹22 lakh in cash and a quantity of gold were seized. The Nagpur officer intends to hold all of it while he works through the ledgers, and to decide himself, in November, whether they should be kept longer.

items.stem: What is the position on the attachment?

options.text: It can be made within the window, but the approval must come from a Director or above, and it dies after six months
options.why: Section 132(9B) lets the authorised officer attach property provisionally during the search or within sixty days of the last authorisation being executed, so day forty is inside the window. Two conditions ride on it: reasons recorded in writing, which he has, and the prior approval of a Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director. A Joint Commissioner is not on that list, so this approval will not do. Section 132(9C) then fixes the life of the order — the attachment ceases to have effect six months from the date it was made.
keywords: section 132(9B) lets the authorised officer attach property provisionally
during the search or within sixty days of the last authorisation being executed
the attachment ceases to have effect six months from the date it was made

options.text: It can be made and lasts indefinitely, since the officer has recorded his reasons
options.misconception: treats recorded reasons as the only condition, when they are one of three and the shortest of the three is the clock
options.why: Reasons in writing are necessary and are nowhere near sufficient. The approval has to come from the right rank, the order has to fall inside the sixty-day window, and the attachment expires by force of the Act after six months. An attachment with no end would be a recovery order made before anybody had been assessed.

options.text: It holds until the assessment for the searched years is completed
options.misconception: ties a provisional attachment to the assessment it protects, when the Act gives it a fixed life of its own regardless of where the assessment has got to
options.why: The attachment is provisional and it is timed by the calendar, not by the progress of the assessment. Six months from the date of the order and it lapses, whether or not the assessment is anywhere near finished. That is the safeguard for an owner whose property is tied up before any demand exists.

options.text: It cannot be made at all now, because the power ends when the search ends
options.misconception: assumes a power exercisable during a search is exercisable only during it, missing the window the sub-section adds afterwards
options.why: The sub-section deliberately reaches past the search, because the reason to attach often appears only when the seized material has been read. It covers the search itself and then a further sixty days, counted from the execution of the last authorisation, so day forty is comfortably inside.

citation.ref: Sections 132(9B) and 132(9C)

items.scenario: Forty days after the last authorisation in the Kanchan Textiles search was executed, the authorised officer wants to tie up a godown the firm owns, because he expects a large demand and has heard the godown is being marketed. He has written down why he thinks it necessary and has obtained the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner in his wing. He asks how long the attachment will hold once the order is passed.

items.stem: What is wrong with the officer's plan?

options.text: Only the timing; any competent valuer may be used
options.misconception: reads the sub-section as naming a deadline but leaving the choice of valuer open, when it names the recipient just as tightly
options.why: The recipient is named as tightly as the clock. It is a Valuation Officer under section 142A, or somebody approved at Chief Commissioner or Director General level in the prescribed way. Experience of working for the department is not approval, and a valuation that decides how much tax a person owes cannot rest on an informal choice made in the same market as the seizure.

options.text: Only the choice of valuer; the reference may be made at any time before the assessment
options.misconception: assumes a step that feeds an assessment may be taken any time before it, when this one has its own short window measured from the search
options.why: The window is measured from the search, not from the assessment. Sixty days from the last authorisation being executed is the outer limit for making the reference, which is why the Act also gives the valuer his own sixty days to report — the pair are designed to get a value early rather than at leisure.

options.text: Both the person and the timing — the reference has a named recipient and a sixty-day window that has passed
options.why: Section 132(9D) is the sub-section that allows the reference, and it is specific about both. The reference goes to a Valuation Officer referred to in section 142A, or to a person, entity or registered valuer approved by a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General or Director General. A jeweller who has done work before but holds no approval is neither. And the reference itself may be made only during the search or within 60 days of the last authorisation being executed, so on day seventy the door has shut. Where a reference is validly made, the valuer must report within 60 days of receiving it.
keywords: section 132(9D) is the sub-section that allows the reference
the reference goes to a Valuation Officer referred to in section 142A
only during the search or within 60 days of the last authorisation being executed

options.text: Nothing; valuing seized property is part of the ordinary power to seize
options.misconception: treats valuation as incidental to seizure, when the Act had to add a sub-section to permit it and hedged that sub-section with limits
options.why: If it were incidental there would have been no need for a sub-section, and the sub-section exists precisely because a valuation binds a person and so needs a named valuer and a fixed clock. Reading it as an ordinary incident of seizure would erase both limits at once.

citation.ref: Section 132(9D) read with section 142A

items.scenario: Seventy days after the last authorisation in a search was executed, the authorised officer still holds the seized gold and wants a value put on it before the assessment is framed. He proposes to send it to a jeweller in the same market who has valued items for the department before but holds no departmental approval, and to ask for a figure whenever the jeweller can manage it.

items.stem: Where does the proprietor stand?

options.text: The team had to leave at 8 p.m., so anything found afterwards is bad
options.misconception: reads the restriction on the hour of entry as a restriction on the whole operation, so a lawful survey would end mid-count
options.why: Only the moment of entry is timed. Nothing in the section puts a stop on the work once it has begun, and a rule that did would make every survey of a large business impossible — the team would be counting stock against the clock and would have to walk out mid-inventory the moment the shutters came down.

options.text: Entry was bad because it was inside business hours; a survey must be after closing so as not to disturb trade
options.misconception: inverts the rule, assuming the protection is for the business's trading rather than a limit on when officers may arrive
options.why: The rule runs the other way for business premises: the authority may enter only while the place is open. Entering a shut shop would mean nobody there to give facilities, no proprietor or employee attending to the business, and no way to check cash or stock against what is being traded.

options.text: The entry was in time and the team may carry on past closing
options.why: The Act fixes when an authority may go in, not when it must come out. For a place where a business or profession is carried on, entry is permitted during the hours at which the place is open for the conduct of business, and 7.30 p.m. is inside 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Once entry is lawful the survey may continue after the place shuts, and the module illustrates exactly that with premises open until 11 p.m. and a survey entered at 10 p.m. So the 1 a.m. work stands and so does everything found in it.
keywords: entry is permitted during the hours at which the place is open for the conduct of business
once entry is lawful the survey may continue after the place shuts

options.text: Entry was bad because a place of business may be entered only between sunrise and sunset
options.misconception: applies the sunrise-to-sunset rule, which is for places other than business premises, to the business premises themselves
options.why: Sunrise to sunset is the rule for any other place — a home, a godown, a relative's premises — reached because the person says his books or stock are kept there. A place where the business itself is carried on is governed by its own trading hours, which is why a restaurant or a press open in the evening can be surveyed in the evening.

citation.ref: Section 133A(2), with the illustration in the module on continuing beyond closing time

items.scenario: A printing works trades from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. A survey team enters at 7.30 p.m., begins inspecting the job registers, and is still working at 1 a.m. The proprietor says the team had no business entering half an hour before he shut and that in any event it had to leave when the shutters came down at eight, and he asks his accountant whether anything found after 8 p.m. can be used.

items.stem: What may the team do about the godown?

options.text: It may be entered after sunset, since the restriction applies only to a residence
options.misconception: narrows the other-place rule to dwellings, when it covers every place that is not a place of business
options.why: The section does not single out a home. It divides places into those where the business or profession is carried on and everything else, and everything else takes the daylight rule — a warehouse, a relative's premises, a locked store. The brother's godown falls squarely on that side.

options.text: It may be entered at any hour, because the survey at the shop had already begun lawfully
options.misconception: carries a lawful entry at one place across to a different place, when each place is tested on its own kind and its own clock
options.why: Each place is tested separately. The shop was entered lawfully during its trading hours; that says nothing about the godown, which is not a place of business and so carries the daylight restriction. A survey that had begun at noon would face the same limit at the second address.

options.text: It may be surveyed on the proprietor's word, but not after sunset
options.why: The power reaches beyond business premises, and it does not care whose premises they are or whether any trade goes on there. It extends to any other place in which the person states that his books of account, documents, cash, stock or other valuables relating to the business are kept — so the brother's godown is within reach on the proprietor's own statement, and no separate authority for it is needed. But the timing rule changes with the kind of place: anywhere other than a place of business may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset. Eight o'clock, an hour after sunset, is outside it, and the team must go in daylight.
keywords: any other place in which the person states that his books of account, documents, cash, stock or other valuables relating to the business are kept
anywhere other than a place of business may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset

options.text: It cannot be surveyed at all, because the survey power stops at the taxpayer's own business premises
options.misconception: reads the power as tied to premises where business is carried on, missing the extension that follows the records to wherever the person says they are
options.why: If that were so, records could be put beyond reach by keeping them anywhere else, and the section is drafted to stop exactly that. The extension is triggered by the person's own statement about where the books are, and it does not matter whose premises they sit on or whether any business happens there.

citation.ref: Section 133A(1), last part, with the timing rule in section 133A(2)

items.scenario: During a survey at a hardware wholesaler at 6 p.m., the proprietor tells the team that the stock register and the purchase files are not on the premises at all — they are kept at his brother's godown two streets away, which is not a place where the wholesaler carries on any business. The team wants to go there straight away and reach it at about 8 p.m., an hour after sunset.

items.stem: Where does the Assessing Officer stand today?

options.text: The impounding was properly made, but the holding has run past its limit
options.why: The section allows an authority to impound and retain books or documents it has inspected, on one condition — recording reasons for doing so — and the officer has done that. What he has missed is the outer edge. Books may not be held beyond 15 days, leaving holidays out of the count, without the approval of a senior officer: a Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, a Principal Director General or Director General, a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, or a Principal Director or Director. Twenty working days with nobody's approval is five days past the line, and his own view of it is not what the Act asks for.
keywords: impound and retain books or documents it has inspected
on one condition — recording reasons for doing so
not be held beyond 15 days, leaving holidays out of the count, without the approval of a senior officer

options.text: He may hold them for such period as he thinks fit, which is what the section says
options.misconception: reads the opening words of the clause and stops before the proviso that puts a fortnight and an approval on top of them
options.why: Those words are there, and the very next sentence cuts them down. The discretion is real only inside fifteen days; past that it needs a senior officer's approval, and the reason is obvious — a business without its ledgers cannot invoice, pay or file, so an indefinite hold on one officer's say-so would be a penalty imposed without any finding.

options.text: He is inside the limit, because twenty working days is under fifteen days once holidays are excluded
options.misconception: excludes holidays a second time from a count that was already given in working days
options.why: Holidays come out once. Twenty working days already has them out, so it is twenty days for this purpose and not fewer. Taking them out again would let a fifteen-day limit stretch to three weeks or more depending on where the calendar fell.

options.text: The impounding itself was bad, because a survey team cannot take books at all
options.misconception: confuses impounding on survey with seizure on search, which is the power a survey genuinely does not have
options.why: Seizing assets is what a survey cannot do. Impounding books and documents it has inspected is expressly allowed, and it is how a survey preserves what it has seen. The two are different acts on different things, and the distinction between search and survey turns on it.

citation.ref: Section 133A(3)(b) with its proviso on retention beyond fifteen days

items.scenario: A survey team impounded a builder's site ledgers, writing in the file why it wanted to hold them. It is now the twentieth working day since, no holidays have fallen in between, and the ledgers are still in the Assessing Officer's cupboard. He proposes to keep them until the assessment is framed next year and has told his inspector he sees no reason to trouble anybody about it.

items.stem: Which of the four was beyond the team's power?

options.text: Marking and copying the registers, because the originals were not impounded first
options.misconception: invents a sequence, assuming a lesser power depends on a greater one having been used
options.why: Marking and copying stand on their own and need nothing to come before them. They exist so that a register cannot be quietly swapped afterwards, which is a reason to use them whether or not anything is impounded at all.

options.text: Carrying the cash away
options.why: Three of the four are named powers. An authority on survey may place marks of identification on books it has inspected and take extracts and copies; it may make an inventory of any cash, stock or valuables it has checked; and it may record the statement of any person where that may be useful or relevant to a proceeding under the Act. The fourth is barred in terms: no income-tax authority may remove, or cause to be removed, any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place it has entered. Safe custody is not an exception, because the section names no exception at all.
keywords: it may make an inventory of any cash, stock or valuables it has checked
it may record the statement of any person where that may be useful or relevant
no income-tax authority may remove, or cause to be removed, any cash, stock or other valuable article

options.text: Recording the manager's answers, since only the proprietor may be examined on survey
options.misconception: limits the statement power to the taxpayer, when the section reaches whoever is attending to the business at that time and place
options.why: The section reaches the proprietor, a trustee, an employee or any other person attending to or helping in the business at that time and place. A shift manager is squarely one of those, and often the only person who can explain what the registers show.

options.text: Listing the cash and stock, which is a seizure by another name
options.misconception: treats making an inventory as taking possession, when one is a written record and the other is removal
options.why: An inventory is a list. It changes nothing about who holds the money or the goods, which stay exactly where they were, and it is expressly permitted. Removal is the different act, and it is the one thing on this list the Act forbids.

citation.ref: Section 133A(3)(a), (c) and (d) with the prohibition in section 133A(4)

items.scenario: In the course of a survey at a jewellery showroom the team does four things: it puts identification marks on the sale registers it has looked through and takes copies of two of them; it lists the cash in the till and the stock on the shelves; it takes down the shift manager's answers in writing and has him sign them; and it puts ₹5,00,000 of the counter cash into an envelope and carries it to the office, telling the proprietor it will be safer there until the position is clear.

items.stem: What is wrong with the team's actions, and what can it do about the controller?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; a survey is a survey and carries the same powers whatever it is for
options.misconception: assumes one set of powers across both kinds of survey, when the Act cuts two of them away from the TDS version
options.why: The two are not the same survey. The general one exists to find undisclosed income, so it can hold books and count cash. The verification one exists to check whether tax was deducted from payments already in the books, which needs reading and asking and nothing more, so the Act takes the other two powers away.

options.text: Nothing can be done about the refusal without a fresh warrant from a higher authority
options.misconception: assumes obstruction needs a new authorisation, when the section itself lends the authority the powers of a civil court
options.why: No fresh warrant is needed. The section lends the surveying authority the powers under section 131(1) for the purpose of enforcing compliance, so it can summon, compel attendance and require production on the strength of the survey it is already conducting.

options.text: The impounding and the cash list are outside this kind of survey; the refusal can be met with the powers a civil court has
options.why: A survey under section 133A(2A) is the narrow one, run only to verify deduction or collection at source. It allows entry after sunrise and before sunset to inspect books and to require information, and the Act then says in terms that an authority acting under that sub-section shall not impound or retain books it has inspected, nor make an inventory of cash, stock or valuables. Both of those were done here. As for the controller, where a person refuses or evades giving facilities, furnishing information or having a statement recorded, the authority may use all the powers vested in it under section 131(1) — the court-like powers of discovery, enforcing attendance and compelling production.
keywords: a survey under section 133A(2A) is the narrow one, run only to verify deduction or collection at source
shall not impound or retain books it has inspected, nor make an inventory of cash, stock or valuables
the authority may use all the powers vested in it under section 131(1)

options.text: Only the cash list was wrong; books may always be impounded once inspected
options.misconception: keeps the impounding power because it feels central to any survey, when the restriction removes both powers in the same sentence
options.why: The restriction names them together and removes them together. Impounding is as much outside a verification survey as counting the safe is, and both ledgers must go back.

citation.ref: Section 133A(2A) with the restriction in the proviso to section 133A(3) and the power in section 133A(6)

items.scenario: A team enters a company's head office at 10 a.m. to check whether tax has been deducted and collected on the expenses in its books. It inspects the expense ledgers, then impounds two of them and makes a list of the cash lying in the office safe. The finance controller declines to answer any question, declines to produce the vendor files and declines to have anything he says written down.

items.stem: How much of Ostara's profit may India tax under the agreement?

options.text: All ₹54 crore, because a business connection exists and that is the Act's own test
options.misconception: applies the domestic test to an assessee entitled to a narrower treaty test, ignoring the choice section 90(2) gives
options.why: The domestic test applies only where it is the kinder of the two, and here it is not. Business connection is deliberately wider than a fixed place of business, which is why an enterprise from a treaty country is taxed on the narrower footing. The Assessing Officer's test would tax sales that never touched an Indian establishment.

options.text: Nothing, because an agreement always keeps business profits in the enterprise's home country
options.misconception: reads the article as an exemption for business profits, when it is a threshold that a fixed place in India crosses
options.why: The article does not exempt; it sets a threshold. Once there is a permanent establishment the source country taxes what belongs to it, and a branch with staff, a showroom and a workshop crosses that line comfortably. It is the profit not attributable to the branch that escapes, not all of it.

options.text: Half of ₹54 crore, the profit being split between the two countries
options.misconception: reaches for a share-out, when the article allocates by attribution to the establishment rather than by any fixed proportion
options.why: There is no fixed share in the article. What is taxed is the profit attributable to the permanent establishment, worked out on what that establishment actually did — its functions, the assets it used and the risks it carried. Here that exercise gives ₹14 crore, not an arbitrary half.

options.text: Only the ₹14 crore the branch earned
options.why: The Act and the agreement ask different questions and Ostara may take whichever answer is kinder. Under the Act a non-resident's business profits are taxed through a business connection under section 9(1)(i), and that net is the wider of the two. Under the agreement business profits are taxable in India only where there is a permanent establishment — a fixed place of business through which an enterprise carries on its business, wholly or in part, which the branch plainly is — and then only so much of the profit as is attributable to that establishment. The direct sales pass through no fixed place here, so ₹40 crore of them stays out.
keywords: a fixed place of business through which an enterprise carries on its business
