taxed through a business connection under section 9(1)(i)
only so much of the profit as is attributable to that establishment

citation.source: OECD Model Convention as adopted in India's agreements
citation.ref: Article 5(1) and Article 7, with section 92F(iiia) and section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Ostara Srl, resident in a country with which India has an agreement modelled on the OECD article, sells packaging machinery to Indian buyers. It runs a branch in Coimbatore with its own staff, showroom and service workshop, and the branch earns ₹14 crore of profit. Ostara also sells ₹40 crore worth of the same machines directly from its home office to Indian buyers who order online, with the branch playing no part. The Assessing Officer says Ostara has a business connection in India and so the whole ₹54 crore is taxable here.

items.stem: Is the Mumbai office a permanent establishment?

options.text: No, because the Reserve Bank has not permitted business there, and that alone settles it
options.misconception: hands the tax question to the banking regulator, when the permission is one fact among several and not a rule of tax law
options.why: The permission was one of the facts the Court weighed, not the test. A regulator's licence says what a company is allowed to do; whether a permanent establishment exists turns on what it actually did. An office that carried on the business in breach of its permission could still be a permanent establishment.

options.text: Yes, because the office handles the company's money, which is the heart of what it does
options.misconception: measures importance by the subject matter handled rather than by whether the income-earning transaction happens there
options.why: What matters is where the earning transaction takes place, not what the parcel contains. The customer is signed up abroad, the fee is charged abroad and the obligation is incurred abroad; India sees only the delivery. Handling money is what a courier does too, and that does not make a courier a permanent establishment.

options.text: Yes, because a staffed office at a fixed address is on the article's own list of examples
options.misconception: reads the list of places in the article as settling the matter, when every entry on it still has to satisfy the test in the opening paragraph
options.why: The list illustrates; it does not decide. A place of management, a branch, an office and the rest count only where the enterprise's business is carried on through them, and the exclusion for preparatory or auxiliary work sits over the whole list. An office that only prints and posts is not carrying on the remittance business.

options.text: No — the work is the tail end of a transaction completed abroad
options.why: This is the fact pattern in Union of India v. UAE Exchange Centre, where the Supreme Court held that a liaison office doing remittance work of exactly this kind is not a permanent establishment. The contract with the remitter is made abroad, the money changes hands abroad, and what Mumbai does is download the details, print and dispatch. The Reserve Bank had not permitted primary business activity there. Even if the office's activities were treated as business activities, the Court held they were of a preparatory or auxiliary character, which the article keeps outside the definition.
keywords: Union of India v. UAE Exchange Centre
they were of a preparatory or auxiliary character

citation.source: Union of India v. UAE Exchange Centre (2020) 425 ITR 30 (SC)
citation.ref: Article 5(1) with the preparatory or auxiliary exclusion in the article

items.scenario: Gulf Remit LLC, resident abroad, keeps a liaison office in Mumbai. Workers abroad hand their money to Gulf Remit there; the Mumbai office logs into the company's servers abroad, pulls down the list of who is to be paid and how much, prints the drafts and posts them by courier to the beneficiaries. The Reserve Bank's permission for the office is limited to liaison work and does not allow it to carry on the company's own business in India. The Assessing Officer says a staffed office that handles the company's core money flow must be a permanent establishment.

items.stem: Is the Delhi project office a permanent establishment?

options.text: Yes, because an office is expressly named in the article as a permanent establishment
options.misconception: reads a listed example as self-executing, missing that each example must still satisfy the opening definition
options.why: Naming an office as an example does not make every office one. The list is read subject to the definition it illustrates, so an office qualifies only where the enterprise's business is carried on through it. Otherwise every representative desk in the country would be a permanent establishment.

options.text: No, because only two people worked there and a permanent establishment needs a larger staff
options.misconception: makes headcount the test, when the Court looked at what the two people were qualified and paid to do
options.why: There is no minimum staff anywhere in the article. Two engineers doing the enterprise's core design work would have made the office a permanent establishment; twenty clerks passing letters would not. The Court's point was about the character of the work, not the size of the payroll.

options.text: Yes, because the office was opened for this contract and the contract is being performed in India
options.misconception: attaches the establishment to the project rather than asking what the office itself does
options.why: The question is about the office, not the project. Where the platform is built matters to other articles; this one asks whether the enterprise carries on its business through the fixed place. Design and fabrication happened abroad and Delhi passed letters, so the business did not run through Delhi.

options.text: No, because none of the enterprise's real work passes through it
options.why: This is DIT v. Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd. The Supreme Court held that a project office set up only as an auxiliary office to pass communications between the customer and the enterprise, incurring no expenditure on executing the contract and staffed by two people not qualified to do any core activity, is not a fixed place of business through which the core business of the enterprise is carried on. A fixed address in India is the starting point of the test and not the end of it.
keywords: DIT v. Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd
not a fixed place of business through which the core business of the enterprise is carried on

citation.source: DIT (International Taxation) v. Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd, Supreme Court
citation.ref: Article 5(1) — a fixed place counts only where the enterprise's core business runs through it

items.scenario: Kore Shipbuilders, resident abroad, won a turnkey contract from an Indian public sector customer for an offshore platform. It opened a project office in Delhi with two employees, an administrator and a coordinator, neither of them an engineer or a designer. Every rupee of design, fabrication and installation cost was incurred outside India and none of it was booked to the Delhi office, whose work was passing letters and drawings between the customer and the head office. The Assessing Officer says a project office opened for this very contract is a fixed place of business and so a permanent establishment.

items.stem: What is the position of the two enterprises?

options.text: Neither does, because no contract is signed at an Indian place of business
options.misconception: treats the place of signature as the test, which is the arrangement the agency limb of the article exists to catch
options.why: Signing abroad is precisely the arrangement the article's agency limb was written for. If the place of signature settled it, any enterprise could sell through India and post the contracts home for signature. What counts is where the business is actually carried on and who has the authority in fact.

options.text: Only Vento does; an agent with no premises cannot create a permanent establishment
options.misconception: insists on a fixed place for every permanent establishment, missing that the agency limb creates one without any premises at all
options.why: The agency limb needs no premises. That is its whole point: an enterprise that would have had a permanent establishment if it had opened an office should not escape by using a person instead. Mr Rane's authority to bind Aster does the work that a fixed place would otherwise have done.

options.text: Only Aster does; a liaison office can never amount to a permanent establishment
options.misconception: reads liaison office as a category that is safe by its name rather than by what its people do
options.why: The label on the door decides nothing. A liaison office that downloads details and posts drafts is outside; one that finds customers, sets prices and secures orders is inside. Two offices with the same name and the same signboard can fall on opposite sides.

options.text: Both have a permanent establishment in India
options.why: Vento's office has stopped being auxiliary. An office that finds new buyers, runs the marketing, settles the price, argues the commercial terms and secures orders is doing the selling business itself, and one doing all that forms a permanent establishment however the paperwork is signed elsewhere. Aster has the other kind. A non-resident who trades through an agent other than an independent agent — one who habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts in its name, or regularly delivers goods, or habitually secures orders for it — has a permanent establishment here, and the profits attributable to what the agent does are taxable in India. Mr Rane works for Aster alone and signed forty-one times, so he is neither independent nor occasional.
keywords: settles the price, argues the commercial terms and secures orders
an agent other than an independent agent
habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts in its name

citation.source: OECD Model Convention as adopted in India's agreements
citation.ref: Article 5(5) on a dependent agent, with the preparatory or auxiliary exclusion in Article 5(4)

items.scenario: Two more enterprises ask the same question. Vento GmbH's Indian liaison office finds new buyers, runs the marketing, settles price and delivery terms with them, argues the commercial points and passes finished orders to Germany, where the head office signs. Aster Inc has no Indian premises at all, but Mr Rane, who works for Aster alone and for nobody else, signed forty-one supply contracts in Aster's name in India last year on his own signature and arranged delivery from a rented store.

items.stem: Does the interest limitation apply to Cobalt this year?

options.text: No, because the section applies only to a foreign company's Indian branch and not to an Indian company
options.misconception: keeps half the class of borrowers and drops the other half, when both are named side by side
options.why: Both are named. An Indian company and the Indian permanent establishment of a foreign company are the two borrowers the section reaches, and Cobalt is the first of them. It escapes this year on the amount, not on what it is.

options.text: Yes, because the total interest of ₹1,55,00,000 is over ₹1 crore
options.misconception: adds unrelated third-party interest into a threshold the section measures only on associated-enterprise debt
options.why: The threshold is not a total interest bill. It is measured on interest in respect of debt issued by a non-resident associated enterprise, because that is the only borrowing the section is worried about. Ordinary bank borrowing from an unconnected Indian lender shifts no profit out of India and does not push a company over the line.

options.text: Yes, because the borrower is a company and any interest to a shareholder holding over half the shares is caught
options.misconception: reads the section as a shareholder-loan rule with no money threshold, when the threshold is one of its stated conditions
options.why: Being an associated enterprise is necessary and it is not enough. The section carries a money gate as well, and it is there so that small borrowings are not put through an EBITDA computation every year. Below ₹1 crore of associated-enterprise interest the section simply does not engage, whatever the shareholding.

options.text: No — the interest to the parent has not crossed the money threshold
options.why: Section 94B is aimed at an Indian company, or the Indian permanent establishment of a foreign company, that pays interest on debt issued by a non-resident associated enterprise. Both of those fit Cobalt. What does not fit is the third condition: the section applies only where that interest exceeds ₹1 crore, and ₹85,00,000 is under the line. The bank interest does not help the department, because the ₹1 crore is measured on the associated-enterprise borrowing, not on everything the company pays. So nothing is disallowed and the ₹25,00,000 comes back.
keywords: an Indian company, or the Indian permanent establishment of a foreign company
pays interest on debt issued by a non-resident associated enterprise
the section applies only where that interest exceeds ₹1 crore

citation.ref: Section 94B(1), with the exclusions in section 94B(1A) and (3)

items.scenario: Cobalt Tooling Ltd, an Indian company that makes press dies, paid ₹85,00,000 of interest during P.Y. 2025-26 on a loan from its Netherlands parent, which holds 90% of its shares. It paid a further ₹70,00,000 of interest to an Indian bank on an unconnected working-capital limit. Its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for the year were ₹2,00,00,000. The finance controller has read that interest to a foreign parent is capped at 30% of that figure and has provisionally disallowed ₹25,00,000.

items.stem: What actually becomes of the ₹1,20,00,000?

options.text: It is carried forward and may be set against any head of income in a later year
options.misconception: widens the set-off beyond the head the interest was disallowed under
options.why: The set-off is confined to income under Profits and gains of business or profession, and it is capped by that year's maximum allowable interest as well. Letting it reach house property or capital gains would give back through the side door what the section took at the front.

options.text: It is lost, a disallowance under this section being final
options.misconception: treats the limitation as a permanent denial rather than a deferral, which is what the carry-forward provision was written to prevent
options.why: The section limits interest to the profits of a year, and profits move about. Denying the deduction for ever would tax a company on a cost it genuinely bore merely because one year's earnings were low, so the Act lets it wait for a year with room instead.

options.text: It is carried forward without limit until there is room to absorb it
options.misconception: keeps the carry-forward but drops the number of years the Act puts on it
options.why: There is an outer edge and it is eight assessment years after the year of disallowance. Interest still unabsorbed at the end of them goes. The limit is what stops a company building an interest pool it can draw on for ever.

options.text: It is carried forward and set off against business income as headroom appears
options.why: Nothing is lost. Interest disallowed by the section is carried forward for up to eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year in which the disallowance was first made, and is claimed against income under Profits and gains of business or profession in a later year, but only so far as that year has room under its own ceiling. So ₹90,00,000 comes in for A.Y. 2026-27 and ₹30,00,000 waits for the following years, and the auditor's permanent difference is a timing difference.
keywords: Interest disallowed by the section is carried forward
for up to eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year in which the disallowance was first made

citation.ref: Section 94B(4)

items.scenario: Cobalt Tooling Ltd had ₹1,20,00,000 of interest disallowed under the interest limitation in A.Y. 2025-26. Its earnings have recovered and in A.Y. 2026-27 its own interest for the year sits ₹90,00,000 below the ceiling the section allows. Its auditor has written the ₹1,20,00,000 off as a permanent difference on the footing that a disallowance is final.

items.stem: Is Country D low-taxed, and what percentage does the top-up run at?

options.text: Yes, and the top-up runs at 15%, the minimum rate itself
options.misconception: charges the minimum rate as though nothing had been paid, instead of charging the gap between it and what was paid
options.why: The top-up brings the burden up to the minimum; it does not start again from nothing. Country D has already taken 12%, so only the three points that are missing are added. Charging the full 15% on top would tax the profit at 27%.

options.text: It has to be tested entity by entity, and only the entity below 15% is topped up
options.misconception: computes the rate per company, when the rules blend a jurisdiction's profits, losses and taxes before testing it
options.why: The test is jurisdictional. All the profits, losses and covered taxes of the group's entities in one country are blended and one rate is struck for the country, which is why the two entities' figures were added before dividing. Testing each company would produce a different answer whenever a group split its activities between two local subsidiaries.

options.text: The tax head is right — deduct the carve-out first, which makes the rate 15% and leaves nothing to top up
options.misconception: applies the substance carve-out to the denominator of the rate test, when the rules apply it only to the base the percentage is charged on
options.why: Order matters here and the rules fix it. The rate is computed on the jurisdiction's Net GloBE Income, undiminished; the carve-out is subtracted afterwards to give the excess profit. Doing it the tax head's way would let a jurisdiction with heavy payroll and plant test itself out of the rules altogether, which is the opposite of what a carve-out for substance is for.

options.text: Yes — the rate is 12% and the top-up percentage is 3%
options.why: The rate test is taxes over income before any carve-out: €3,000,000 divided by €25,000,000 gives an effective tax rate of 12% for the jurisdiction, which is below the minimum rate of 15%, so Country D is low-taxed and its entities are low-taxed constituent entities. The percentage is then the shortfall — minimum rate less effective tax rate, giving a Top-up Tax Percentage of 3%. The carve-out has no part in either step; it comes in afterwards, to shrink the base the 3% is charged on.
keywords: an effective tax rate of 12% for the jurisdiction
which is below the minimum rate of 15%
giving a Top-up Tax Percentage of 3%

citation.ref: Chapter 5, effective tax rate and top-up tax percentage, with the substance-based income exclusion

items.scenario: An in-scope group has two constituent entities in Country D. For the fiscal year their combined Net GloBE Income is €25,000,000 and their combined adjusted covered taxes are €3,000,000. The substance-based carve-out worked from payroll and tangible assets in Country D comes to €5,000,000. The group's tax head proposes to test Country D by taking the income after the carve-out, €20,000,000, against the €3,000,000 of taxes.

items.stem: Where is the top-up tax collected in each of the two years?

options.text: From the parent in the first year, and from the subsidiaries in A and B in the second
options.why: The rules run in a fixed order. Country C could have taken it first with a domestic minimum top-up tax and has not. Next in line, the Income Inclusion Rule charges the ultimate parent entity on its allocable share of the low-taxed subsidiary's top-up tax, which is what happens in the first year. When Country X repeals, the Undertaxed Profits Rule is the backstop: it denies deductions to, or makes an equivalent adjustment for, group entities in countries that have adopted the rules, so Countries A and B pick up what is left uncollected. The treasurer's year never arrives.
keywords: the Income Inclusion Rule charges the ultimate parent entity on its allocable share
the Undertaxed Profits Rule is the backstop

options.text: Nowhere in the second year, since a rule a country has repealed cannot be applied to its companies
options.misconception: reads the repeal as ending the group's exposure, when the backstop is applied by other countries to their own group entities
options.why: Nobody applies anything to Country X's companies. The other countries apply their own law to the group entities sitting inside them, and that is how the design survives a jurisdiction opting out. The revenue moves, rather than disappearing.

options.text: From the low-taxed subsidiary in Country C in both years, since that is where the profit is
options.misconception: assumes the country with the profit always collects, when it collects only if it has enacted a domestic minimum top-up tax
options.why: Country C gets first refusal and has not taken it. The domestic minimum top-up tax exists so that a low-tax jurisdiction can keep the revenue rather than hand it to a parent's country, but it only works if that jurisdiction has put it into its own law. Without it, the charge moves up the chain.

options.text: From the subsidiaries in Countries A and B in both years, the backstop applying whenever a jurisdiction is low-taxed
options.misconception: puts the backstop first, when it is written to catch only what the earlier rules leave uncollected
options.why: A backstop by definition waits. In the first year Country X charges the parent, so nothing is left over and the subsidiaries in A and B are not touched. Applying the backstop straight away would tax the same profit twice.

citation.ref: Chapter 2, income inclusion rule and undertaxed profits rule, with the rule order and the qualified domestic minimum top-up tax

items.scenario: A group's low-taxed subsidiary sits in Country C, which has not brought in a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax. The ultimate parent is in Country X. In one year Country X has the GloBE rules in its own law; in the next it repeals them, while the group's other subsidiaries in Countries A and B still have them. The group treasurer says that if neither Country C nor Country X charges the top-up, nobody can.

items.stem: How many of the adviser's three statements are right?

options.text: Only the second
options.misconception: reads scope as depending on local enactment, when it is set by the group's own size in its parent's consolidated accounts
options.why: Scope is decided by the consolidated revenue in the ultimate parent's financial statements, measured over the preceding four years. A country that has not enacted anything simply collects nothing itself; the group stays in scope and another country's rules reach its entities there.

options.text: Only the first
options.misconception: treats an agreed international standard as binding law on every member, when members agreed only to be consistent if they adopt
options.why: Nothing obliges a member to legislate. What was agreed is that a jurisdiction choosing to implement will do so in line with the agreed outcomes, so that the rules interlock instead of double-taxing. That is a different promise, and it is the reason the backstop rule exists at all — it would be pointless if adoption were compulsory.

options.text: None of them
options.why: Take them in turn. Adoption is a common approach, not an obligation — a jurisdiction need not bring the rules in, but one that does has agreed to do it consistently with the agreed outcomes, and other members' rules still reach the group's entities. Scope is set by size, not by who has enacted what: the rules apply to groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the parent's accounts in two of the four preceding years, and EUR 900 million clears it. And the 15 per cent global minimum tax is tested jurisdiction by jurisdiction on each country's effective tax rate, which is the whole reason a group with a high worldwide rate can still owe a top-up in one country.
keywords: Adoption is a common approach, not an obligation
consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the parent's accounts
the 15 per cent global minimum tax is tested jurisdiction by jurisdiction

options.text: Only the third
options.misconception: blends the group's tax bill globally, when the rules are built on a separate rate for each jurisdiction
options.why: Blending is jurisdictional, not global. All the group's profits, losses and covered taxes in one country are put together and a rate is struck for that country. A global average would let tax paid at a high rate in one country wash out a near-zero rate in another, which is exactly what the design sets out to stop.

citation.ref: GloBE Model Rules, scope and the common approach, with the 15 per cent minimum rate

items.scenario: A group with consolidated revenue of EUR 900 million in each of the last four years operates in eleven countries. Its adviser tells the board three things: that every country in the Inclusive Framework is obliged to enact the minimum tax rules, that a country which has not enacted them takes the group out of scope there, and that the minimum is tested on the group's worldwide tax bill rather than country by country.

items.stem: Does the subject-to-tax rule reach these two payments?

options.text: No, because 70 per cent is short of the control the rule requires
options.misconception: assumes connection needs near-total ownership, when the threshold sits just above half and de facto control counts on its own
options.why: The line is more than 50 per cent of the interests, held directly or indirectly, and a relationship of de facto control counts even without that. Seventy per cent through a common holding company is comfortably over, and the payer and payee need not own each other at all — being held by the same parent is enough.

options.text: Only the royalties; a guarantee fee is not a payment the rule covers
options.misconception: shortens the list of covered payments to the familiar two, when it names several more including this one
options.why: Guarantee and financing fees are named on the list in their own right, and so are payments for distribution rights, insurance and reinsurance premiums, rentals of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment and payments for services. The list is deliberately wide because a group that could only shift interest and royalties would simply relabel the payment.

options.text: Yes, both of them
options.why: Three conditions and all three are met. Covered payments include royalties and guarantee or financing fees as well as interest, distribution rights, insurance premiums, equipment rentals and services, so both payments are within the list. The payer and the payees are connected persons, meaning more than 50 per cent ownership held directly or indirectly, or de facto control — 70 per cent through a common holder is over the line. And the rate test looks at the nominal corporate rate in the receiving country, which must be under 9 per cent; Country R's headline 6 per cent is under it, so what the recipients paid after their own reliefs does not enter the question.
keywords: Covered payments include royalties and guarantee or financing fees
connected persons, meaning more than 50 per cent ownership held directly or indirectly, or de facto control
the nominal corporate rate in the receiving country, which must be under 9 per cent

options.text: No, because the recipients paid no tax at all, so there is no rate to compare
options.misconception: uses the tax actually borne as the comparator, when the rule was built on the statutory rate to keep the test simple and predictable
options.why: The comparator is the nominal rate the receiving country applies to that kind of income, not the bill after each company's own reliefs. Using the actual burden would need a full computation of a foreign company under foreign law before a payment could be made, which is precisely the work the rule was designed to avoid.

citation.ref: Subject-to-tax rule — covered payments, connected persons and the 9 per cent nominal rate test

items.scenario: Sarani Ltd is resident in a developing country whose per-head national income is well inside the World Bank line, and its treaty with Country R follows the model. In one year it pays Country R group companies ₹34 crore of royalties for a trademark licence and ₹9 crore of fees for a parent guarantee on its bank borrowing. Country R's headline corporate rate on such receipts is 6 per cent, although the recipients pay nothing after their own reliefs. The two Country R companies and Sarani are 70 per cent owned by the same holding company. Sarani's adviser says the rule can only be about interest, and that in any event what matters is the tax the recipients actually paid.

items.stem: Is the tax director right about the order and about how the rule takes effect?

options.text: Wrong on the order, right that a domestic statute is needed first
options.misconception: treats every new charge as needing home legislation, missing that this one operates by changing what the treaty allows
options.why: What was blocking the source country was its own treaty, which had given the taxing right away. The rule works by putting that right back, so the instrument that has to change is the treaty — through the multilateral instrument, or a bilateral amendment on a developing member's request.

options.text: Right on both, since the minimum tax rules are in force and the treaty rule is only a proposal
options.misconception: reads the treaty rule as aspirational, when it is a defined rule with an agreed place in the order and a named route into treaties
options.why: It is a settled part of Pillar Two with its own minimum rate of 9 per cent, its own list of covered payments and its own place ahead of the other half in the order. What varies is which pairs of countries have put it into their treaty yet, and that is a question about one treaty rather than about whether the rule exists.

options.text: Right on the order, wrong on the domestic law
options.misconception: keeps the minimum tax rules first because they are the better known half of Pillar Two, when the agreed order puts the treaty rule ahead of them
options.why: The order is the opposite of the intuition. The treaty rule was put first deliberately, because it exists for developing source countries and would be worth little if a parent's jurisdiction could take the same profit first. Running the minimum tax rules first would leave the source country collecting whatever happened to be left.

options.text: Wrong on both — the source country's claim comes first, and the rule enters through the treaty
options.why: The rule order settles the first point the other way. The subject-to-tax rule works in priority to the GloBE rules, so the source country may tax back the taxing rights it gave up under the treaty before the minimum tax is worked out, and what it takes is then part of the picture the minimum tax looks at. On the second, this is a treaty rule and not a domestic one: members bring it in by signing the multilateral instrument, or by amending a particular treaty bilaterally where a developing member asks for it.
keywords: The subject-to-tax rule works in priority to the GloBE rules
the source country may tax back the taxing rights it gave up under the treaty

citation.ref: Rule order — subject-to-tax rule ahead of the GloBE rules, and implementation by multilateral instrument or bilateral amendment

items.scenario: The same group's tax director accepts that the payments out of Sarani's country are within the subject-to-tax rule, but argues that the source country must wait: the minimum tax rules apply first, and once the group's position under them is settled there will be nothing left for the source country to take. He adds that the source country could not charge anything anyway until its parliament passes a domestic law of its own.

items.stem: What is the position on the ₹15,80,000?

options.text: Taxable only to the extent the premium exceeded the permitted share — the rest of the maturity proceeds stays exempt
options.misconception: treats the premium condition as a proportionate cap that shaves the exemption, when breaking it removes the exemption from the whole sum
options.why: There is no proportion in the clause. The premium condition is a gate: either the policy passes it in every year of its term and the whole sum stays outside total income, or it fails and the whole sum comes in. Splitting the receipt in the ratio of the excess premium is arithmetic the section never asks for.

options.text: Not exempt, because the premium payable for a year exceeds the share of the sum assured the clause allows for a policy of this vintage
options.why: For a policy issued on or after 1 April 2013 the exemption falls away if the premium payable for any year during the term exceeds 10 per cent of the actual capital sum assured. Here the premium is ₹1,20,000 is 12 per cent of the sum assured of ₹10,00,000, so the condition is broken in every year of the term and not merely in one. The relaxed limit of 15 per cent is available only where the life insured is a person with a disability under section 80U or has an ailment specified under section 80DDB, and neither applies. The whole receipt therefore enters his total income; nothing about it is apportioned.
keywords: the premium payable for any year during the term exceeds 10 per cent of the actual capital sum assured
the premium is ₹1,20,000 is 12 per cent of the sum assured

options.text: Exempt, because the premium of ₹1,20,000 is below the 15 per cent of sum assured that the clause allows
options.misconception: applies the 15 per cent relaxation, which the clause gives only where the insured is a person with a disability or a specified ailment, to a policyholder in good health
options.why: The 15 per cent figure is real but it is not general. It is the relaxed limit where the life insured is a person with a disability or a severe disability of the kind section 80U describes, or a person suffering from an ailment specified for section 80DDB. Mr Ramanan is neither, so his limit is the ordinary one. His nephew's remark is advice about somebody else's policy.

options.text: Exempt in full, because a sum received under a life insurance policy including the bonus allocated on it is outside total income and there is no premium test
options.misconception: remembers the opening words of the clause and stops there, missing that the exemption has carried a premium condition for every policy issued since 2003
options.why: The clause does begin by putting the sum outside total income, and for a policy issued before April 2003 that would be the end of it. Every issue date since has carried a condition on the premium — twenty per cent of the sum assured for policies issued between 2003 and 2012, ten per cent for those issued from April 2013 — and reading only the opening words is how a taxable receipt gets left out of a return.

citation.ref: Section 10(10D) and its provisos as they apply to policies issued on or after 1 April 2013, read with sections 80U and 80DDB

items.scenario: Mr Ramanan took an endowment policy from a domestic insurer in August 2015. The policy names a sum assured of ₹10,00,000 and the premium has been ₹1,20,000 every year since. It matured this year and the insurer paid him ₹15,80,000, deducting nothing. He has brought the cheque and the policy document to you and says the amount goes nowhere in his return, because a life insurance payout is exempt and always has been. He is in good health and has never claimed a deduction for a disability or for treatment of a specified ailment. His nephew, who took a similar policy in 2019 with a premium of 14 per cent of the sum assured, has told him that anything under 15 per cent is safe. You have to tell Mr Ramanan what to put in the return.

items.stem: How is Ms Bhagyalakshmi's ₹9,40,000 treated?

options.text: Inside total income, because the premium crosses the rupee ceiling that applies to a market-linked policy of this vintage
options.why: Beyond the share-of-sum-assured test, exemption is also lost on a unit linked policy issued on or after 1 February 2021 where the premium payable exceeds ₹2,50,000 for any previous year during the term. Her premium is ₹2,80,000 every year, so the ceiling is crossed every year. Her colleague is right about his own policy for a reason that does not help her: the ceiling is not applied to a policy issued by an IFSC insurance office. Hers came from a domestic insurer. What follows is not a charge under residuary income either — where this exemption is unavailable, section 45(1B) brings the receipt in as a capital gain of the year it was received.
keywords: a unit linked policy issued on or after 1 February 2021
the premium payable exceeds ₹2,50,000 for any previous year during the term
a policy issued by an IFSC insurance office

options.text: Outside total income, since the premium is under a tenth of the sum assured and that is the only test the clause sets
options.misconception: knows the share-of-sum-assured test and does not know that a market-linked policy issued from February 2021 carries a second, absolute ceiling on the premium as well
options.why: Passing the share test is necessary and it is not sufficient. From February 2021 a second condition sits beside it for this kind of policy, expressed as a plain rupee ceiling rather than as a share, and a policy has to clear both. Her premium clears the first and not the second.

options.text: Inside total income, and charged under income from other sources as a receipt the Act does not classify elsewhere
options.misconception: gets the exemption right and the head wrong, sweeping into residuary income a receipt the Act sends expressly to capital gains
options.why: The head is not left to the residue. Where a receipt on a market-linked policy falls outside this exemption, the Act deems the profit on it to be a capital gain of the previous year of receipt, and the amount allocated by way of bonus is part of what is charged. Putting it under other sources changes the computation and the rate.

options.text: Outside total income, because the rupee ceiling on premiums begins only with policies issued from April 2023
options.misconception: takes the date and the amount that belong to ordinary life policies and applies them to a market-linked one, which got its own ceiling two years earlier
options.why: Two ceilings were brought in, two years apart, and they are easy to swap. The ₹5,00,000 ceiling from April 2023 governs life policies other than market-linked ones. The market-linked policy got its own ceiling from February 2021, at a lower figure, and hers was issued after that date.

citation.ref: Section 10(10D) as it applies to unit linked policies issued on or after 1 February 2021, with the IFSC carve-out, read with section 45(1B)

items.scenario: Ms Bhagyalakshmi bought a market-linked policy from an Indian insurer in March 2022. Its sum assured is ₹30,00,000 and the annual premium is ₹2,80,000, which she has paid every year. The policy has both an insurance component and an investment component linked to units, and she surrendered it this year for ₹9,40,000 including the bonus allocated on it. She has worked out that the premium is 9.33 per cent of the sum assured, comfortably under a tenth, and has written to you that the receipt is therefore outside her total income. A colleague of hers holds an almost identical policy taken from an insurance office set up in the International Financial Services Centre at GIFT City and has been told his receipt is safe.

items.stem: What should she do?

options.text: Claim the exemption for the policy with the smaller premium, since the clause saves the cheaper policy
options.misconception: believes the statute picks the policy, when it hands the choice to the assessee and any set within the ceiling qualifies
options.why: Nothing in the clause prefers a smaller premium. It fixes a ceiling and leaves the selection to the person holding the policies, which is why the answer here is the larger receipt rather than the smaller premium. Reading a rule of selection into it costs her ₹21,00,000 of exemption for no reason.

options.text: Claim the exemption for one of the two, choosing the one that pays her more, and bring the other receipt into total income
options.why: Each policy passes the share-of-sum-assured test on its own, so the rupee ceiling decides. Where premiums are payable on more than one such policy, the aggregate of the premiums payable is what is measured, and hers is ₹5,40,000 for the year. Because that aggregate exceeds ₹5,00,000 the exemption is confined to those policies whose aggregate premium does not exceed ₹5,00,000, at the option of the assessee. Either policy alone qualifies — ₹3,00,000 or ₹2,40,000 — and both together do not. The choice is hers and the sensible one is the ₹52,00,000 receipt, so the ₹31,00,000 comes into total income.
keywords: the aggregate of the premiums payable is what is measured
those policies whose aggregate premium does not exceed ₹5,00,000, at the option of the assessee

options.text: Bring both receipts in, because the premiums added together cross the ceiling and the clause then fails all of them
options.misconception: gets the aggregation right and then reads the consequence as total loss, when the clause deliberately preserves the exemption for a set of policies within the ceiling
options.why: Aggregation is not extinction. Having added the premiums and found them over the line, the clause does not stop; it goes on to keep the exemption alive for whichever of those policies have premiums that stay within the ceiling. Losing both is a harsher outcome than the words produce.

options.text: Leave both receipts out, since each policy's own premium is below the ceiling
options.misconception: reads the ceiling policy by policy, which is right until a person holds more than one such policy, at which point the clause tests the premiums together
options.why: The broker's reading is the ordinary one and it stops working the moment a second policy of the same kind appears. Where premiums are payable on more than one such policy, the clause looks at their total for a year, not at each in turn — and hers total more than the ceiling.

citation.ref: Section 10(10D) as it applies to life insurance policies other than unit linked policies issued on or after 1 April 2023, and the aggregation of premiums on more than one such policy

items.scenario: Mrs Kalpana holds two endowment policies, neither of them market-linked, both taken out from a domestic insurer in June 2023. The first has a sum assured of ₹40,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹3,00,000; the second a sum assured of ₹30,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹2,40,000. Both premiums are well under a tenth of their own sums assured. Both policies mature in the same year: the first pays her ₹52,00,000 and the second ₹31,00,000. Her broker has told her the rupee ceiling is tested one policy at a time, so that with ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,40,000 neither policy is anywhere near it. She wants to know what to write in her return.

items.stem: Which of the three is right to leave out of total income?

options.text: None of them, because the father's policy failed the premium test in every year of its term
options.misconception: applies the premium test to a death claim, which is the one receipt the clause lifts out of every premium condition it sets
options.why: The premium tests govern maturity and surrender, not death. Applying them to a death claim would mean a family that insured a life heavily loses the exemption at the worst moment, which is the opposite of what the clause does; it says in terms that the premium conditions do not apply to a sum received on a death.

options.text: The father's death claim only
options.why: A sum paid out on the death of the person insured is exempt irrespective of what premium was payable, and none of the tests — the 10, 15 or 20 per cent of sum assured, or the ₹2,50,000 and ₹5,00,000 ceilings — applies to it. That is why the 18 per cent premium on the father's policy does not matter. The other two receipts are excluded from this exemption by name rather than by any premium test: a sum received under a keyman insurance policy is not exempt, and a policy stays a keyman policy even after it has been assigned to the keyman himself, so the firm's cheque is taxable. And a sum received under section 80DD(3), where the disabled dependant for whom the deposit was made dies before the depositor, is deemed the depositor's income of the year of receipt.
keywords: the death of the person insured is exempt irrespective of what premium was payable
a sum received under a keyman insurance policy is not exempt

options.text: The death claim and the disability scheme receipt, because both arose on a death
options.misconception: reads the death of the dependant as the same event as the death of the person insured, when the scheme receipt is charged precisely because the dependant died first
options.why: Two deaths, two different consequences. The exemption for a death claim is about the life insured under the policy. The scheme for a disabled dependant works the other way round — the deposit was made for the dependant, and his dying before the depositor is the very event that brings the amount back as the depositor's income.

options.text: The death claim and the firm's policy on the works manager, since he has retired and the policy was assigned to him
options.misconception: thinks assignment turns a keyman policy into an ordinary one, when the clause says such a policy keeps its character with or without consideration for the assignment
options.why: Assignment is the argument this exclusion was written to defeat. The definition takes in a policy assigned to any person during its term, with or without consideration, so the works manager's retirement and the transfer into his own name change nothing. The receipt is taxable in the hands of whoever gets it.

citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — the death exclusion from the premium conditions, Explanation 1 defining a keyman insurance policy, and the exclusion of sums received under section 80DD(3)

items.scenario: Three cheques reached the Venkataraman family this year and all three are described on their counterfoils as insurance receipts. The first is a claim settled after Mr Venkataraman's father died; his policy, taken in 2016, had an annual premium of 18 per cent of its sum assured. The second came to the family firm on a policy it had taken years ago on the life of its works manager, who has since retired and to whom the policy was assigned before he left. The third is the amount standing to the credit of a scheme with an insurer, which the family had subscribed to for a dependent brother with a severe disability and which fell in because the brother died before the depositor. The accountant has put all three outside total income on the footing that they are life insurance money.

items.stem: What do you tell the finance head about India's right to tax the fee?

options.text: India may tax the fee under its domestic law, subject to a ceiling rate on the gross amount that the two countries fixed between them
options.why: Article 12A of the UN Model says that fees for technical services may be taxed in the residence state without saying they are taxable there alone, and then gives the state in which the fees arise the right to tax them under its own law. Where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other state, that tax is held to a maximum rate on the gross amount of the fees, and the figure is settled by bilateral negotiation rather than written into the Model. The OECD Model has no article corresponding to it, which is why the counsel's reasoning would have been sound on a treaty drawn on that Model. India pioneered the idea and has had it in the Act since 1976.
keywords: a maximum rate on the gross amount of the fees
The OECD Model has no article corresponding to it

options.text: The counsel is right — without a permanent establishment the fee is business profits and only the residence state may tax it
options.misconception: reasons from the business profits article alone and misses that a separate fees article, where the treaty has one, gives the source state a right that does not depend on a permanent establishment
options.why: That reasoning holds where the only articles in play are the ones on business profits and permanent establishments. It fails where the treaty carries a separate article on fees for technical services, because that article gives the state where the fees arise a taxing right of its own and asks nothing about a fixed place of business.

options.text: The article makes the fee taxable in the residence state exclusively, the same as the OECD Model's treatment of royalties
options.misconception: reads a permissive taxing right in the residence state as an exclusive one, which is the difference the article was drafted to make
options.why: The wording is deliberate. It says the fees may be taxed in the residence state and stops short of saying they are taxable there only, and that omission is the whole point of the article. Reading in the word "only" would hand the source state nothing and make the second paragraph pointless.

options.text: India may tax the whole fee under its domestic law with no ceiling, because the article defers entirely to domestic law
options.misconception: reads the source state's right as unlimited, missing the second half of the paragraph, which caps the tax on the gross amount where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other state
options.why: The article grants the right and limits it in the same breath. Where the person beneficially entitled to the fee lives in the treaty partner, a ceiling bites at once: what the source state collects may not run past the agreed percentage of the gross sum. Withholding at the full domestic rate on a beneficially owned fee overcharges the payee and invites a refund claim.

citation.ref: Article 12A paragraphs 1 and 2, and the absence of a corresponding article in the OECD Model

items.scenario: An Indian manufacturer pays a design consultancy resident in a treaty partner state ₹1.4 crore for engineering advice worked up for its plant. The consultancy has no office, no employees and no equipment in India, and its counsel has written to the manufacturer saying that in the absence of a permanent establishment the fee is taxable in the consultancy's home state alone, so nothing should be withheld. The treaty in question was negotiated on the United Nations Model and contains a separate article on fees for technical services with a rate written into it. The manufacturer's finance head asks you whether the counsel's letter is a complete answer.

items.stem: How should the two invoices be treated?

options.text: Both are fees for technical services, since both are services rendered by an enterprise resident abroad
options.misconception: treats the article as covering services in general, when it reaches only three named kinds and asks what was actually applied to the customer's own situation
options.why: The article is not a charge on services at large. It names managerial, technical and consultancy services, and the tests it uses look at what was brought to bear for that customer. A fee earned by running every customer's transactions through the same pipe answers none of them.

options.text: Neither is a fee for technical services, because a bank supplies financial services rather than technical ones
options.misconception: decides the question by the payee's industry, when the article looks at what was done for the payer and expressly reaches a financial institution's advisory work
options.why: Nothing turns on the label over the door. A financial institution's fees are within the article where its people use knowledge, skill and expertise to give research, analysis or advice to a specific client on that client's circumstances. Deciding by industry would exempt the advisory arm of a bank and tax the identical advice from a consultancy.

options.text: The study is a fee for technical services and the card processing is not
options.why: Fees for technical services are defined as payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, with payments to an employee, for teaching in or by an educational institution, and by an individual for personal use kept out. Technical carries the sense of specialised knowledge, skill or expertise brought to bear on a particular art, science or profession, and consultancy the sense of advice of a specialised nature. The economists' study is research, analysis and advice worked up for one client's own circumstances, so it is within the article. Card settlement is a non-specialised payment and transmission service which applies no specialised knowledge on behalf of any particular client, and it is outside.
keywords: payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services
specialised knowledge, skill or expertise brought to bear on a particular art
a non-specialised payment and transmission service

options.text: The card processing is a fee for technical services because it runs on proprietary technology, and the study is ordinary advice
options.misconception: hears "technical" as meaning technological and inverts the test, which asks whether specialised expertise was applied for this client rather than whether machinery was involved
options.why: Sophisticated equipment on the supplier's side is not what the word reaches. The question is whether specialised knowledge was applied on behalf of this particular client, and a settlement network applies the same process to everybody. The study is the opposite: it exists only because of one client's contracts.

citation.ref: Article 12A — the definition of fees for technical services, its exclusions, and the illustration distinguishing client-specific advice from non-specialised transaction services

items.scenario: A bank resident in a treaty partner state sends an Indian retailer two invoices in the same quarter. The first is for a study its economists prepared on the retailer's own currency exposure, sitting with the retailer's treasurer over three weeks and recommending a hedging structure built around the retailer's contracts. The second is for processing the retailer's card settlements — a fee per transaction, run on the bank's network, with no person at the bank looking at any particular transaction. The retailer's tax head proposes to withhold on both under the treaty's article on fees for technical services, reasoning that both are services supplied by a bank abroad and the article does not distinguish.

items.stem: Is the adviser right that the treaty gives India nothing here?

options.text: Yes — without a permanent establishment the subscription income is business profits taxable only in the company's home state
options.misconception: applies the permanent establishment rule to a treaty that has since acquired an article written precisely for businesses with no presence in the market country
options.why: That was the whole difficulty the newer article was drafted to answer. Digitalisation lets a business earn substantially in a market country with no fixed place there and no employee concluding contracts, and the article gives the source state a taxing right that does not wait for a permanent establishment.

options.text: No — but only because the subscriptions are royalties for the use of copyright in films and music
options.misconception: reaches the right destination by the wrong article; a subscriber watching a film is paying for a service, not acquiring the right to use the copyright
options.why: The royalty article is about payments for the use of, or the right to use, a copyright. A viewer who streams a film buys access, not the right to exploit the work. The distinction matters because the two articles carry different definitions and different negotiated ceilings, and the newer article stands aside only where a payment genuinely is a royalty.

options.text: No — the treaty preserves India's right to tax income from automated digital services, and these subscriptions are within it
options.why: Article 12B was added to the UN Model in its 2021 update to keep the taxing rights of the state from which payments for automated digital services are made, and there is nothing answering to it in the OECD Model. An automated digital service is one provided over the internet or another electronic network requiring minimal human involvement from the provider, and the indicator is the ability to serve new users through the same basic processes without a matching rise in cost. Paragraph 6 lists what may qualify, digital content services among them, and film and music subscriptions delivered from a licensed catalogue are exactly that. The source state's tax is capped at a share of the gross payments settled by negotiation.
keywords: Article 12B was added to the UN Model in its 2021 update
requiring minimal human involvement from the provider

options.text: Yes — the article exists but reaches only online advertising and the supply of user data, which is not what this company sells
options.misconception: reads paragraph 6's list as the definition, when the definition is in paragraph 5 and the list only indicates what may fall within it
options.why: The list is illustrative and it is longer than two entries: it runs to online advertising, supply of user data, search engines, intermediation platforms, social media, digital content, online gaming, cloud computing and standardised online teaching. Even so, a service qualifies by meeting the definition, not by appearing on the list.

citation.ref: Article 12B paragraphs 1, 2, 5 and 6, added in the 2021 update, with no corresponding article in the OECD Model

items.scenario: A company resident in a treaty partner state sells film and music subscriptions to Indian viewers over its own website. It has no premises, staff or servers in India. Its catalogue is licensed once and then served to every subscriber from the same library; adding a hundred thousand Indian subscribers next quarter would need no extra people at the company. India's treaty with that state follows the United Nations Model and was updated after 2021. The company's adviser says that with no permanent establishment and no advice given to anybody, nothing in the treaty lets India tax the subscription income, and that a country wanting to tax it would have to legislate a levy of its own.

items.stem: Which article governs, and why?

options.text: Neither — with no permanent establishment in India the group is taxable at home alone
options.misconception: carries the permanent establishment requirement into articles that do not have one, which is the difference between the two Models on both royalties and the newer services articles
options.why: The royalties and fees articles of the UN Model give the source state a right that does not turn on a fixed place of business at all. The permanent establishment test belongs to business profits, and reading it across would empty three articles of content.

options.text: The royalties article, because a payment for the use of a patented process is a royalty and the newer article gives way to it
options.why: Paragraph 7 provides that the automated digital services article does not apply where the payments underlying the income qualify as a royalty, or as fees for technical services, under Article 12 or Article 12A. A payment for the use of a patented process is a royalty on the definition both Models share, so Article 12 governs and the withholding follows its negotiated ceiling. The second half of the director's letter also fails: the treaty was drawn on the UN Model, so what the OECD Model would have produced is beside the point, and under the UN Model the source state may tax a royalty as well as the residence state.
keywords: the payments underlying the income qualify as a royalty
the treaty was drawn on the UN Model

options.text: The automated digital services article, since the delivery is automated and needs no human involvement from the group
options.misconception: decides by how the payment is delivered, when the newer article steps aside for a payment that already answers to the royalty or fees article
options.why: Delivery is not the test of priority. However automated the portal, the payment is made for the use of a patented process, and the newer article contains an express instruction to stand back where that is so. Ranking the articles by the delivery channel would let any licensor move its income to a different rate by putting a login screen in front of it.

options.text: Whichever of the two articles produces the lower tax, since a treaty is read in the taxpayer's favour
options.misconception: invents a rule of choice; the articles are ordered by an express provision, and nothing lets a payer pick between them
options.why: There is no menu. The priority between these articles is written into the newer one, and a payment that is a royalty is taxed as a royalty whatever rate that produces. A treaty is read to relieve double taxation, not to let either side select the cheaper article after the fact.

citation.ref: Article 12B paragraph 7, read with Article 12 and Article 12A of the UN Model

items.scenario: The same treaty partner state is home to a chemicals group that licenses a patented process to an Indian manufacturer. The licence is delivered through the group's online portal: the manufacturer logs in, downloads the process parameters and gets automatic updates, and nobody at the group touches the account from one year to the next. The group's tax director argues two things in one letter — that the payment is for an automated digital service and so belongs under the newer article at its negotiated rate, and that in any event the OECD Model would give India nothing, so the lower of the two outcomes should be applied. The manufacturer's controller asks which article governs the withholding.

items.stem: What is charged, and at what rate?

options.text: The whole ₹12,00,000 of unrecorded donations is charged at 30 per cent
options.misconception: charges every anonymous donation and misses the exemption limit that was introduced to keep small collections out of the charge
options.why: Only the excess over an exemption limit is charged. The limit exists so that a trust taking small unrecorded sums at a counter is not taxed on all of them, and ignoring it here overstates the charge by five lakh rupees of donations.

options.text: ₹7,00,000 is charged at 30 per cent and the rest is dealt with as ordinary income of the trust
options.why: An anonymous donation is a voluntary contribution where the trust keeps no record of the giver's name and address and the other prescribed particulars. Such donations are charged at 30%, but only so far as they exceed an exemption limit, and that limit is the higher of 5% of the total donations received and ₹1,00,000. Five per cent of ₹1,00,00,000 is ₹5,00,000, which beats one lakh, so ₹12,00,000 less ₹5,00,000 leaves ₹7,00,000 charged at 30%, a tax of ₹2,10,000 before surcharge and cess. The remaining ₹5,00,000 is treated like any other donation and forms part of the income to which section 11 applies, so the application and accumulation tests are worked on the total income after taking out the part charged at the flat rate.
keywords: the higher of 5% of the total donations received and ₹1,00,000
The remaining ₹5,00,000 is treated like any other donation
forms part of the income to which section 11 applies

options.text: Nothing is charged on the donations, because a trust registered under section 12AB is assessed on its application of income and not on its receipts
options.misconception: treats registration as an answer to this charge, when the section is written to reach registered trusts and the exemption provisions are switched off for the part it taxes
options.why: Registration is what brings the trust within the regime, not what takes it out of this charge. The Act says in terms that the exemption provisions do not apply to an anonymous donation on which tax is payable under this section, so the receipt is charged whatever the trust's registration says.

options.text: ₹11,00,000 is charged at 30 per cent, being the unrecorded donations less the one lakh the section allows
options.misconception: takes ₹1,00,000 as the exemption limit rather than as the floor, and so never compares it with five per cent of the total donations
options.why: One lakh is one of two candidates, not the limit. The limit is whichever of the two is larger, and on total donations of a crore the percentage leg gives five lakh. Taking the fixed figure every time overcharges any trust whose donations run past twenty lakh rupees.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(1) and (3) — the rate, the exemption limit and the meaning of an anonymous donation — read with section 13(7)

items.scenario: Sharada Vidya Nidhi is a charitable trust registered under section 12AB, running a library and a scholarship scheme. Its receipts book for the year shows donations of ₹1,00,00,000 in all. Of those, ₹12,00,000 came in through collection boxes and by cash at the counter with no name or address written down for the giver and no other particulars recorded. The rest are receipted to named donors. The trust has applied ₹80,00,000 of its income during the year on its objects. Its treasurer has prepared the return on the footing that registration under section 12AB puts every donation received outside the charge, and the trustees want the position checked before it is filed.

items.stem: What should the two trusts actually provide for?

options.text: Neither provides anything, because both trusts have religious objects
options.misconception: stretches the exclusion for a wholly religious trust to cover a trust that is religious and charitable together, which the section deals with separately and does charge in one case
options.why: The exclusion is written for a trust established wholly for religious purposes, and the word doing the work is the one that means entirely. A trust that also runs a school is dealt with by the next limb, which charges anonymous donations directed to that school. Reading the two limbs as one would make the second limb dead words.

options.text: The temple trust provides nothing; the mixed trust provides on all ₹6,00,000 because it is not wholly religious
options.misconception: gets the exclusion right and then charges the mixed trust on everything, missing that only donations with a specific direction to a named kind of institution are caught
options.why: Failing the wholly religious test does not put every rupee into charge. For a trust that is religious and charitable together, the section picks out anonymous donations given with a direction for its educational or medical institutions and leaves its other anonymous receipts alone. The general shrine collections stay out.

options.text: The temple trust provides nothing; the mixed trust provides on the ₹2,00,000 directed to its school
options.why: A trust established wholly for religious purposes is outside section 115BBC, so the temple's ₹4,00,000 is not charged at 30% and its hundi box is left alone — which is why an unidentified offering at a shrine has never been a taxable event. The charge reaches a trust created for religious and charitable purposes together only where the anonymous donation carries a specific direction that it is for a university or other educational institution, or a hospital or other medical institution, run by that trust. The envelopes marked for the school building fund answer that description; the general shrine collections do not.
keywords: A trust established wholly for religious purposes is outside section 115BBC
a specific direction that it is for a university or other educational institution

options.text: Both should provide on the whole of their anonymous collections, since the section looks at the donation and not at the trust
options.misconception: reads the charge as attaching to a kind of receipt, when the section begins by asking what the trust was established for and excludes one kind of trust outright
options.why: The section starts with the recipient. A trust established wholly for religious purposes is outside it altogether, and a partly religious and partly charitable trust is inside it only for a narrow class of directed donations. Charging both trusts on everything ignores the two gates the section opens with.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(2) — the exclusion of a trust established wholly for religious purposes and the treatment of a wholly religious and charitable trust

items.scenario: Two clients bring the same question on the same morning. The first is a temple trust whose objects, as its deed records them, are the maintenance and worship of the deity and nothing else; its hundi collections this year came to ₹4,00,000 and no giver is identified. The second is a trust whose objects are religious and charitable together: it maintains a shrine and also runs a secondary school. Its anonymous collections were ₹6,00,000, of which ₹2,00,000 came in envelopes marked for the school building fund and the rest into the general shrine box. Both treasurers have read that anonymous donations attract a flat thirty per cent and both have provided for the tax.

items.stem: How is each firm's profit split?

options.text: Both profits are agricultural in full, because in each case the crop was grown by the seller on its own land
options.misconception: stops at the growing and ignores the manufacturing that follows it, when the rules exist precisely because one profit has two origins
options.why: Growing your own crop is what brings these rules into play, not what settles the answer. Once the seller also manufactures, the profit is part farm and part factory, and each rule fixes the share by a set percentage rather than by anybody's accounts.

options.text: Assam Leaf, ₹8,00,000 business; Malabar Beans, ₹4,00,000 business
options.why: Rule 8 applies where the assessee grows the tea leaves and manufactures the tea in India, and it makes 40% of the profit business income — ₹8,00,000 of Assam Leaf's ₹20,00,000, with the other sixty per cent agricultural. Rule 7B splits coffee, and it does so in two ways. Where the seller has grown, cured, roasted and ground the coffee in India, with or without chicory or other flavouring, the same 40% is business income, so ₹4,00,000 of Malabar Beans' ₹10,00,000 is charged and the rest is agricultural. The two arrive at the same share by different routes, and it is the processing done after the field that earns the higher business share for coffee.
keywords: Rule 8 applies where the assessee grows the tea leaves and manufactures the tea in India, and it makes 40% of the profit business income
grown, cured, roasted and ground the coffee in India

options.text: Assam Leaf, ₹8,00,000 business; Malabar Beans, ₹2,50,000 business
options.misconception: applies the twenty-five per cent split, which belongs to coffee that is only cured, to coffee the seller has also roasted and ground
options.why: The coffee rule has two rates and the work done decides which one. A quarter is business income where the seller grows and cures the coffee and no more. Roasting and grinding are factory operations, and once the seller does them the business share rises.

options.text: Assam Leaf, ₹12,00,000 business; Malabar Beans, ₹6,00,000 business
options.misconception: has the right percentages and puts them the wrong way round, giving the larger share to the factory when the rules give it to the field
options.why: The larger share of these profits is agricultural in both cases. The rules were written to keep the bulk of a grower's profit outside the charge, so the business share is the smaller of the two, and inverting them roughly doubles the tax.

citation.ref: Rule 8 for tea and Rule 7B for coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground by the seller in India

items.scenario: Two firms come to you with the same accounts problem. Assam Leaf grows tea on its own estate in Assam and manufactures the finished tea in its own factory; its profit on the sale of that tea for the year is ₹20,00,000. Malabar Beans grows coffee on its estate, and then cures, roasts and grinds it before selling it, mixing in chicory for one of its blends; its profit on the sale is ₹10,00,000. Both firms have put the whole of their profit into the return as agricultural income on the ground that everything started in their own fields, and both have been asked by the Assessing Officer to justify it. Neither has any income from any other source.

items.stem: Where is the accountant wrong?

options.text: Only on the treatment of the exempt half — one split does cover both, since both proprietors grow and process their own crop
options.misconception: reads the rules as one rule for growers who process, when there is a separate percentage for rubber, for tea and for each stage of coffee
options.why: There is no single grower-processor rule. Rubber, tea and the two stages of coffee each carry their own percentage, and they run from a quarter to two fifths. Applying one figure across the board gets one of the two files wrong by definition.

options.text: On both counts — the shares differ by crop, and the exempt half still has to be declared for the rate
options.why: Coffee that is grown and cured by the seller in India and no more is split 25% business income and 75% agricultural, so Wayanad Estates has ₹1,00,000 of business income and ₹3,00,000 exempt. Rule 7A covers centrifuged latex, cenex, crepes and block rubber made from the field latex of rubber plants the seller grew in India, and it makes 35% of the profit business income, ₹2,80,000 here, leaving ₹5.2 lakh as agricultural income. So the shares are not the same and the less the grower does after the field the larger his exempt share. On the second point, the agricultural part is exempt under section 10(1), but for an individual whose net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 it is taken into account for partial integration once the other income passes the basic exemption limit — the exemption survives, the rate does not.
keywords: Wayanad Estates has ₹1,00,000 of business income
Rule 7A covers centrifuged latex, cenex, crepes and block rubber
it makes 35% of the profit business income, ₹2,80,000 here, leaving ₹5.2 lakh as agricultural income

options.text: Only on the split — the shares differ by crop, but the agricultural half can indeed be left out of the return and forgotten
options.misconception: gets the percentages right and then treats an exempt receipt as an invisible one, when net agricultural income above five thousand rupees is read back in to fix the rate on the rest
options.why: Leaving it out of the computation of total income is right; forgetting it is not. For an individual with net agricultural income above ₹5,000 and other income over the basic exemption limit, the farm income is brought back for the limited purpose of setting the rate on the taxable income.

options.text: On the split only, and the other way round — the rubber profit is wholly agricultural because latex comes straight from the tree
options.misconception: treats processing latex into block rubber as part of growing, when the rule names those very products and charges more than a third of the profit as business income
options.why: The rule names centrifuged latex, cenex, crepes and technically specified block rubber, which is a list of manufactured products. A rule that had to name them would be pointless if making them counted as farming, and it charges a larger business share than either coffee stage or tea does.

citation.ref: Rule 7B for coffee grown and cured by the seller in India and Rule 7A for rubber, read with section 10(1)

items.scenario: Wayanad Estates grows coffee in India and cures it, and sells it at that stage to a roaster; it does no roasting or grinding itself. Its profit on the year's sales is ₹4,00,000. Kottayam Rubber grows rubber in India and processes the field latex from its own plants into centrifuged latex and block rubber, which it sells; its profit is ₹8,00,000. Both are proprietary concerns of individuals with no other business. The accountant handling both files has applied one split to both, on the reasoning that a grower who processes his own crop is in the same position whatever the crop, and has also told each proprietor that the farm half of the profit can be left out of the return entirely and forgotten.

items.stem: What is the gross annual value?

options.text: ₹4,20,000, being the fair rent, which is the highest of the four figures on the file
options.misconception: arrives at the right number by taking the largest figure on the page, which gives the wrong answer the moment the standard rent is above the actual rent
options.why: The figure is right and the route is not, and the route is what is being marked. Two of these figures are compared, one restricts the result and the fourth is compared with what is left. Take the largest of the four on a property where the tenant pays below the fair rent and the answer comes out too high.

options.text: ₹4,20,000, the rent actually received, because it is higher than the expected rent
options.why: The computation runs in two steps. The expected rent is the higher of the fair rent and the municipal value — ₹4,20,000 against ₹3,60,000 — but it is then restricted to the standard rent of ₹3,90,000, so the expected rent is ₹3,90,000. The gross annual value is then the higher of that expected rent and the rent actually received or receivable during the year, which is ₹4,20,000. The standard rent has done its work at the first step and has nothing to say at the second.
keywords: restricted to the standard rent of ₹3,90,000
the higher of that expected rent and the rent actually received or receivable during the year, which is ₹4,20,000

options.text: ₹3,90,000, because the standard rent caps what the property can be taxed on
options.misconception: treats the standard rent as a ceiling on the gross annual value, when it caps only the expected rent and never the rent the tenant actually paid
options.why: The standard rent does cap something, and it is the expected rent. It does not cap the rent actually received. Where the tenant has in fact paid more, that higher figure is what the owner is taxed on, and the accountant's note reads the restriction one step too far along the computation.

options.text: ₹3,60,000, the municipal value, since that is what the authority has assessed the property at
options.misconception: picks the municipal value alone, when it is only one of the two figures compared to arrive at the expected rent and the lower of them here
options.why: The municipal value is a candidate, not the answer. It is compared with the fair rent and the higher of the two is taken, before any question of the standard rent or the actual rent arises. Starting and stopping at the municipal figure understates the annual value by sixty thousand rupees.
