citation.ref: Section 23(1) — expected rent as the higher of fair rent and municipal value restricted to standard rent, and gross annual value as the higher of expected rent and actual rent

items.scenario: A flat in a rent-controlled locality was let for the whole year. Four figures sit in the file: the municipal authority values it at ₹3,60,000 a year, comparable flats in the building fetch ₹4,20,000 a year, the rent control authority has fixed ₹3,90,000 a year for it, and the tenant actually paid ₹4,20,000 during the year with nothing in arrears. The owner's accountant has taken ₹3,90,000 as the gross annual value, writing in his note that a landlord cannot be taxed on more than the law permits him to charge. The owner has asked you to confirm the figure before the return goes in.

items.stem: What is the income from this property, computed correctly?

options.text: A loss of ₹32,000, taking thirty per cent of the gross annual value before the municipal tax
options.misconception: reverses the order, applying the thirty per cent to the gross annual value instead of to the net annual value that remains after municipal tax
options.why: The order is fixed and it matters by twelve thousand rupees here. Municipal tax paid by the owner during the year is taken off the gross annual value first, and the statutory deduction is a share of what is left. Applying it to the gross figure inflates the deduction every time.

options.text: A loss of ₹4,000, deducting the municipal tax twice — once from the gross annual value and again as an expense
options.misconception: treats municipal tax as both a step in arriving at the net annual value and a separate outgoing, when the thirty per cent is the only deduction allowed for expenses
options.why: Municipal tax is deducted once. After it, the only deductions from the net annual value are the flat thirty per cent and the interest on borrowed capital, and the thirty per cent stands in for repairs, collection and everything else, whatever the owner actually spent.

options.text: A loss of ₹44,000
options.why: Municipal tax comes off first, because the net annual value is the gross annual value less the tax actually paid by the owner during the year: ₹4,20,000 less ₹40,000 makes the net annual value ₹3,80,000. The statutory deduction is thirty per cent of that net figure, not of the gross, which is ₹1,14,000. Interest on borrowed capital is allowed in full on a property that is let out, so the whole ₹3,10,000 goes. That leaves ₹3,80,000 less ₹1,14,000 less ₹3,10,000, a loss of ₹44,000. The owner's two-lakh figure belongs to a self-occupied property and has no application here.
keywords: thirty per cent of that net figure, not of the gross, which is ₹1,14,000

options.text: Income of ₹66,000, since interest on a housing loan stops at ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: carries the two-lakh interest ceiling, which belongs to a self-occupied property, onto a property that has been let out for the whole year
options.why: The ceiling is real and it is in the wrong place. On a let-out property the interest on borrowed capital is deductible in full, and the two-lakh limit applies where the property is self-occupied. Capping the interest here turns a genuine loss into an income and costs the owner the set-off.

citation.ref: Section 23(1) for net annual value and section 24(a) and (b) for the thirty per cent deduction and interest on borrowed capital

items.scenario: The same flat's gross annual value has been settled at ₹4,20,000. The owner paid the municipal corporation ₹40,000 of property tax during the year, and paid ₹3,10,000 of interest on the loan he took to buy the flat, for which the lender has given him a certificate. He has drawn up the computation himself: he has taken thirty per cent of ₹4,20,000 as the statutory deduction, then subtracted the municipal tax, and then stopped the interest at ₹2,00,000 because that, he says, is the figure the Act allows on a housing loan. He has arrived at a small positive income and wants it checked.

items.stem: Is the tax head's reasoning sound on this treaty?

options.text: Yes — with no place at the enterprise's disposal there is no permanent establishment, whatever the number of days
options.misconception: applies the fixed-place rule as though it were the only route to a permanent establishment on this Model, which carries a separate route measured in days
options.why: The fixed-place rule is one route and, on the Model this treaty follows, not the only one. A second route asks how long people have been in the country furnishing services and does not ask what premises they used, so the absence of a place at the enterprise's disposal does not end the enquiry.

options.text: No — but only because a supervisory activity of more than six months on a project site is itself a permanent establishment
options.misconception: reaches for the construction and supervisory limb, which needs a building site or an installation project, and applies it to advisory work with no such project
options.why: That limb exists and it is about something else. It covers a building site, an assembly or installation project and supervisory activity connected with one, and shortens the OECD Model's twelve months to six. Advice on an upgrade with no site of the enterprise's own falls under the services limb, which is measured in days rather than months.

options.text: No — the presence of the engineers can itself create a permanent establishment on this Model once it passes a threshold in days
options.why: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model creates a Service PE where an enterprise furnishes services, consultancy services included, through employees or other personnel it has engaged for the purpose, and those activities continue in the country for periods adding up to more than 183 days in any twelve-month period beginning or ending in the fiscal year. Two hundred days of engineers passes that, so a permanent establishment exists and the profits attributable to it are taxable in India. The reasoning would have been sound on an OECD Model treaty, because there is no Service PE clause in that Model and the presence would then have to be tested under the general principles of Article 5(1).
keywords: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model creates a Service PE

options.text: Yes on this treaty, though the answer would be different on an OECD Model treaty, which does contain a services test
options.misconception: has the two Models the wrong way round; the services route is the UN Model's addition and is what the OECD Model lacks
options.why: The Model that carries the services route is the UN Model, and the OECD Model is the one without it. Getting the pair round the wrong way reverses the answer in every question of this shape, because the whole point of the difference is that the UN Model gives the source state more.

citation.ref: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model and the absence of a corresponding clause in the OECD Model, read with Article 5(1)

items.scenario: An engineering company resident in a treaty partner state has been advising an Indian refinery on a plant upgrade. It has no office, workshop or warehouse in India. Its engineers fly in and out and work from the refinery's own site meeting rooms, which the refinery allots to whoever needs them on the day; over the twelve months to March their days in India add up to 200. The Indian refinery's tax head says that because the company has nothing at its own disposal in India, there is no fixed place of business and therefore no permanent establishment, and that the days spent are beside the point. The treaty was negotiated on the United Nations Model.

items.stem: What has to be done before the tickets are handed over?

options.text: Tax of ₹17,500 has to be paid, since a benefit in kind is charged at half the ordinary rate
options.misconception: invents a concessional rate for benefits in kind; the section sets one rate and the form of the benefit changes only who must see the tax paid
options.why: There is one rate in the section and nothing in it turns on whether the benefit came as money or as tickets. What the form changes is the mechanism — a deduction where there is cash, an assurance that the tax has been paid where there is not. Halving the rate is a valuation argument the section does not offer.

options.text: Nothing beyond the voucher — with no cash paid to the dealer there is no sum from which tax could be withheld
options.misconception: thinks the duty needs a payment to deduct from, when the section is written for benefits in kind and puts the duty of ensuring the tax is paid on the provider
options.why: The absence of cash is the situation the section was drafted for. Where the benefit is wholly in kind, the provider has to ensure that the tax due on it has been paid before releasing the benefit, rather than deducting from a payment that never happens. Handing over the tickets first is what breaks the section.

options.text: Tax of ₹33,000 has to be paid, computed on the value above the ₹20,000 the section leaves out
options.misconception: reads the ₹20,000 figure as an exempt slice carved out of every benefit, when it is a threshold that decides whether the section applies at all
options.why: The twenty thousand is a gate, not an allowance. Below it for the year, nothing is deducted; above it, the tax is worked out on the whole value of the benefit. Treating it as a slice to be subtracted understates the tax on every benefit that crosses the line.

options.text: Tax of ₹35,000 has to have been paid on the benefit before the tickets are released
options.why: A foreign trip given to a dealer is a benefit or perquisite arising from the dealer's business, so the section applies, and the manufacturer's turnover is far above the one-crore line that keeps a small individual or Hindu undivided family out. Tax is deductible at 10% of its value, which on a trip costing ₹3,50,000 comes to ₹35,000. Because the benefit is wholly in kind there is no payment to deduct from, so the manufacturer must ensure the tax has been paid before the benefit is released. The value taken is the whole ₹3,50,000, not the part above any threshold.
keywords: Tax is deductible at 10% of its value
on a trip costing ₹3,50,000 comes to ₹35,000

citation.ref: Section 194R(1) with its first proviso for benefits wholly in kind and its second proviso for the ₹20,000 and turnover thresholds

items.scenario: A pump manufacturer with a turnover of ₹90 crore runs an annual incentive for its dealers. Its best dealer this year, a resident firm, has won a trip to Singapore for two; the manufacturer has paid the tour operator ₹3,50,000 and holds the invoice. The tickets are issued and the trip is a fortnight away. The dealer has given the manufacturer nothing in return beyond having bought pumps, and no cash is changing hands. The manufacturer's accounts head has raised a voucher for ₹3,50,000 as sales promotion and asked whether anything else needs doing before the tickets go out, adding that with no payment being made there is nothing to withhold from and nothing to compute.

items.stem: Can the application be made?

options.text: No — the order rests on a survey, which puts it outside the scheme whatever the amounts
options.why: Her order is a specified order: an order of assessment is one of the kinds listed, and it was not made on the Dispute Resolution Panel's directions. The money tests are met as well, because the aggregate sum of the variations proposed or made must not exceed ₹10 lakh and hers is ₹9,40,000, and the return must have been furnished with a total income that does not exceed ₹50 lakh and hers showed ₹44,00,000. The third condition is the one that fails. Three origins shut the door: a search under section 132, a requisition under section 132A, an order founded on a survey carried out under section 133A, and equally anything the department learnt through one of the agreements sections 90 and 90A provide for. The day at her premises was a survey, so the road is an appeal and not the Committee.
keywords: Her order is a specified order
the aggregate sum of the variations proposed or made must not exceed ₹10 lakh
a total income that does not exceed ₹50 lakh
on a survey carried out under section 133A

options.text: Yes — the variation and the returned income are both within the limits, which is what the scheme asks
options.misconception: reads the two money limits as the whole of the test and misses the third condition, which asks where the order came from rather than how large it is
options.why: Three conditions have to be met together and the adviser has checked two. The third asks what the order is based on, and it is the one that decides this file. An application that satisfies the money tests can still be turned away at the door on the origin of the order.

options.text: Yes — the survey affects only whether the Committee can waive the penalty, not whether it can take the case
options.misconception: puts the survey exclusion at the wrong stage, treating it as a limit on the Committee's relief when it is a condition on the order before any application is admitted
options.why: The exclusion sits at the door, not at the end. It is written into the description of the order the scheme will look at, so an order resting on a survey never becomes the subject of an application. The Committee's powers to reduce or waive a penalty and to grant immunity are a separate question that only arises for cases it has taken.

options.text: No — an assessment order is not a specified order at all; only an intimation after processing a return can go to the Committee
options.misconception: reads the list of specified orders far too narrowly, when it runs to five kinds of order and an assessment order is one of them
options.why: The list is wider than that. It takes in a draft order in an eligible assessee's case, an intimation after processing a return or a statement where the adjustments are objected to, an order of assessment or reassessment other than one made on the Dispute Resolution Panel's directions, a rectification that enhances the assessment or reduces the loss, and an order treating a person as an assessee in default. Her order is squarely within it.

citation.ref: Section 245MA and Explanation (a) — the kinds of specified order and the three conditions on the order, read with Rule 44DAD

items.scenario: Ms Nandita received an assessment order in July making additions of ₹9,40,000 to the income she had returned. Her return for that year had shown a total income of ₹44,00,000. The order was made after the department spent a day at her business premises in the previous November, checking her stock register and impounding two books under section 133A. There was no search at her house or her office and nothing was seized under section 132. Her adviser has drafted an application to the Dispute Resolution Committee, writing in his covering letter that both money tests are comfortably met and that the Committee is therefore the quickest road, quicker than an appeal. She asks you to sign the application off.

items.stem: On what footing, if any, does a business connection arise for Meridian Cloud Inc?

options.text: On the payments limb, but only if the company also has a permanent establishment in India under the treaty
options.misconception: collapses the domestic deeming rule into the treaty test, so a question asked under the Act is answered out of the treaty
options.why: Two separate questions are being run together. Whether a business connection exists is decided by the Act, and it is decided here on the payments. What the treaty then does is limit India's right to tax the profits, and that is a second step taken afterwards, on the treaty's own terms.

options.text: On neither limb, because a digital business is tested only on its users and 1,20,000 is under 3 lakh
options.misconception: treats the user count as the only limb that can apply to an online business, so a payments test that is already satisfied is never reached
options.why: Nothing in the clause sorts non-residents by the kind of business they run and then applies one limb to each. Both limbs apply to everybody, and the money limb is the one this company fails. Reading the two as alternatives for different trades would let a large paid business escape by keeping its user numbers down.

options.text: On the payments limb alone
options.why: Significant economic presence of a non-resident is itself a business connection in India, and it has two limbs that stand apart. The first counts money: aggregate payments from dealings in goods, services or property with persons in India exceeding ₹2 crore in the previous year. ₹2,35,00,000 is past that line, so this limb is satisfied on its own. The second counts people — systematic and continuous soliciting of business, or interaction with at least 3 lakh users in India — and 1,20,000 falls well short. Either limb by itself is enough, so the company has a business connection here on the money even though the user test fails.
keywords: significant economic presence of a non-resident is itself a business connection in India
exceeding ₹2 crore in the previous year
at least 3 lakh users in India

options.text: On neither limb, because the company has no office or place of business in India
options.misconception: reads a physical presence test into a rule written for businesses that reach customers without one
options.why: The clause sets that argument aside in terms. The transactions count even where the agreement was made outside India, even where the company keeps no residence or place of business here, and even where it renders no services here. A nexus rule designed for a company that sells over a wire would be empty if an office were the test.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i)

items.scenario: Meridian Cloud Inc is incorporated in Country P and has no office, no employee and no agent in India. In previous year 2025-26 Indian customers paid it ₹2,35,00,000 for software subscriptions. Its free trial application was used by 1,20,000 people in India during the same year. Its Indian tax adviser has written that nothing arises in India because the company has no presence here.

items.stem: Is the first limb of significant economic presence satisfied?

options.text: No, because the first limb needs the non-resident to have a server or other equipment in India
options.misconception: puts a physical nexus back into a test built to work without one
options.why: Equipment in India would raise a different question altogether — a fixed place, and with it the older business connection tests and the treaty's permanent establishment. This limb asks only what was received and from whom. It was written because the equipment tests were producing nothing against companies that need no equipment here.

options.text: No, because a licence delivered over the internet is not goods, services or property
options.misconception: reads "property" as tangible property and misses that the clause names the download expressly
options.why: The argument would have force if the clause stopped at the three words. It does not: it goes on to name the download of data or software as one of the things it covers, which is the case the drafter had in front of him. A clause that named the very transaction and then excluded it would say nothing.

options.text: Yes, but only the payments received after the ₹2 crore mark was passed are within the limb
options.misconception: treats the threshold as a slab, so only the excess is thought to count
options.why: The ₹2 crore is a gate, not a slab. Once the year's aggregate is past it the limb is satisfied for the whole year, and every payment in that year's transactions is inside it. What the section limits afterwards is how much income is attributed to India, which is a separate calculation and not a haircut on the count that opened the gate.

options.text: Yes, and the counsel's objection is answered by the clause itself
options.why: The clause covers what a non-resident does with any person in India in respect of goods, services or property, and it says in terms that this takes in the provision of download of data or software in India. What is then counted is the aggregate of payments arising from those transactions during the previous year, and ₹2,30,00,000 crosses ₹2 crore. Where the servers sit and whether anybody is employed here are not part of the count.
keywords: the provision of download of data or software in India
the aggregate of payments arising from those transactions during the previous year

citation.ref: Explanation 2A(a) to section 9(1)(i)

items.scenario: Halcyon Systems LLC, resident in Country Q, licenses design software to Indian architects. They download it from servers outside India and pay by card. Receipts from Indian customers in previous year 2025-26 were ₹2,30,00,000. Halcyon has no server, no employee and no agent in India. Its counsel argues that a download is not a dealing in goods, services or property, so the first limb cannot even be counted.

items.stem: Does significant economic presence arise for Bluecrest Media Ltd?

options.text: No, because users only count if each of them pays something
options.misconception: adds a payment condition to a limb whose whole condition is a number of people
options.why: The limb sets a headcount and stops. Adding a payment test to it would fold the second limb back into the first and leave the section with one condition instead of two.

options.text: Yes, because the advertisers' payments are treated as arising from India
options.misconception: reaches the right answer through the wrong limb, by re-routing foreign advertising money into the payments test
options.why: The conclusion is right and the route is not, which matters because the route is what he would have to write. Money billed to advertisers outside India is not an aggregate of payments from persons in India, so the first limb stays at nil. What carries the case is the headcount.

options.text: No, because with nothing received from India the aggregate is nil and neither limb is met
options.misconception: reads both limbs as counting money, so a service given away free is thought to be outside the rule altogether
options.why: Only the first limb counts payments. If a nil receipt answered both, a company could put itself outside the rule by charging Indian users nothing and billing its advertisers elsewhere, which is the business model the second limb was written for.

options.text: Yes, on the user limb
options.why: The two limbs are independent and only one of them counts money. The second is systematic and continuous soliciting of business, or interaction with users in India, and its condition is a headcount of at least 3 lakh users in India. 4,10,000 clears it. The second limb turns on users, not on payments, so a free application with nothing received from India is squarely inside it. A nil figure on the money limb says nothing at all about this one.
keywords: a headcount of at least 3 lakh users in India
the second limb turns on users, not on payments

citation.ref: Explanation 2A(b) to section 9(1)(i)

items.scenario: Bluecrest Media Ltd, resident in Country R, runs a social application that costs Indian users nothing. 4,10,000 people in India used it every month through previous year 2025-26. All of Bluecrest's advertising revenue is billed to advertisers outside India and no rupee was received from anybody in India. Its adviser has closed the file on the ground that the aggregate of payments is nil.

items.stem: Which of Norvent's two activities gives it significant economic presence in India?

options.text: Both do, since both are dealings with persons in India well above ₹2 crore
options.misconception: adds the export buying into the aggregate and misses the carve-out written for exactly that activity
options.why: The aggregate is not simply everything a non-resident does that touches India. Buying here only in order to ship out is named and taken out, because a purchasing operation earns nothing in India — the profit is made where the goods are sold. Counting it would tax an exporter's cost.

options.text: Neither does, because every contract was signed abroad and there is no place of business here
options.misconception: relies on the two facts the clause says in terms make no difference
options.why: Both facts are true and both are listed as irrelevant. The clause was drafted against exactly this reasoning, so an answer built on it is answering the older business connection tests rather than this one.

options.text: The sensor sales do; the cotton buying does not
options.why: Three answers do not help the company on the sensors, because the clause sets all three aside: it makes no difference that the agreement was entered outside India, that the company has no residence or place of business in India, or that it renders no services here. The cotton is a different matter. Where a non-resident's activity in India goes no further than the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export, the activities do not constitute significant economic presence, so the buying stays outside however large the figure is.
keywords: no residence or place of business in India
the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export
the activities do not constitute significant economic presence

options.text: The cotton buying does and the sensor sales do not, because only the buying happens physically in India
options.misconception: looks for the activity carried on inside the country, which is the old nexus instinct rather than this test
options.why: This inverts the section twice over. The limb that is met is met by money received from persons in India, which is the sensors; and the one activity physically carried on here is the very one that is carved out. Physical presence is neither necessary nor sufficient.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i), the three set-asides and the proviso on purchase for export

items.scenario: Norvent Trading GmbH, resident in Country S, does two things touching India. It sells industrial sensors to Indian factories under contracts signed in Frankfurt, receiving ₹6,40,00,000 in previous year 2025-26; it keeps no office here and sends nobody. Separately, a buying agent purchases raw cotton in India on Norvent's account, ₹9,00,00,000 worth in the same year, every bale of which is shipped out and none of which is sold in India.

items.stem: What can India actually tax, and what does the treaty do to it?

options.text: Only the income traced to the Indian transactions, and even that yields to the treaty where the treaty is better
options.why: Where a business connection is established by significant economic presence, only so much of the income as is attributable to those transactions or activities is deemed to accrue or arise in India, so the worldwide figure is not the base. Then the second step: an assessee may take whichever of the Act and the treaty suits him, and the treaty applies where more beneficial. The treaty taxes business profits in the source State only through a permanent establishment, and significant economic presence is a rule of the Act that does not by itself make a permanent establishment. A company with nothing on the ground here can end up paying nothing under the treaty although the Act reaches it.
keywords: attributable to those transactions or activities
does not by itself make a permanent establishment

options.text: Nothing at all, because a treaty always overrides the Act
options.misconception: turns a rule that lets the assessee take the better of the two into a blanket override
options.why: The Act applies to the extent it is more beneficial to the assessee, which is a comparison made provision by provision and not a rule that the treaty wins. On these facts the treaty does happen to be better, but the answer has to be reached by comparing, because on other facts the Act is the kinder of the two and then the Act is what applies.

options.text: Only the Indian income, and the treaty cannot help, because significant economic presence is itself a permanent establishment
options.misconception: treats a domestic nexus rule as if it had written itself into the treaty
options.why: The Act cannot amend a treaty by defining a term of its own. Permanent establishment means what the treaty says it means — broadly a fixed place of business or a dependent agent — and a company with neither does not acquire one because Indian law has invented a separate nexus. That is the whole reason the second step is worth taking.

options.text: The whole worldwide income, because a business connection makes the non-resident taxable here on everything it earns
options.misconception: confuses a source rule with residence, so a deeming provision is read as turning the company into an Indian assessee
options.why: A business connection decides that some income is Indian in source. It does not change where the company is resident, and only a resident is taxed on worldwide income. The section itself says how much comes in, and it is the part traced to the Indian dealings.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) read with section 90(2)

items.scenario: Kestrel Analytics Inc, resident in Country T, has significant economic presence in India. Its Indian subscription receipts in previous year 2025-26 were ₹5,80,00,000 out of a worldwide ₹94,00,00,000. It has no office, employee or agent in India. India has a comprehensive treaty with Country T in the Model Convention's terms. Kestrel's Indian adviser has begun computing Indian tax on the whole worldwide figure.

items.stem: How much, if anything, is deemed dividend in Mr Arjun's hands?

options.text: Nil, because the advance carries interest at a commercial rate and has to be repaid
options.misconception: treats a loan that looks commercial as outside the clause, when the clause looks at who was paid and out of what
options.why: Commercial terms are not one of the three exceptions the clause allows. It catches the payment when it is made, on the footing that a shareholder is taking the company's profits in a form that is not called a dividend. Interest and a repayment date change the bargain, not the character the clause gives the payment.

options.text: ₹18,00,000, the whole of the accumulated profits
options.misconception: reads accumulated profits as the amount deemed rather than as the ceiling on it
options.why: Accumulated profits are a roof, not a floor and not a figure. If the advance had been ₹25,00,000, ₹18,00,000 would have been deemed dividend and the rest would not. Here the advance is the smaller of the two, so the advance is the answer.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, being 15 per cent of the advance
options.misconception: apportions the payment to the shareholding, as though the deeming were a share of the money rather than the money
options.why: The shareholding decides whether the clause applies at all. It does not decide how much. Once the holder is at or above the gate, what is deemed dividend is the sum advanced, limited only by accumulated profits.

A closely held company that lends to a shareholder who is the beneficial owner of shares carrying at least 10 per cent of the voting power pays a deemed dividend, and the ceiling on it is what the company possesses by way of accumulated profits. Mr Arjun at 15 per cent is inside the class, and the whole ₹10,00,000 advanced is within accumulated profits of ₹18,00,000, so all of it is deemed dividend and taxable as income from other sources. That leaves ₹8,00,000 of accumulated profits standing against anything the company pays out later in the year.
keywords: beneficial owner of shares carrying at least 10 per cent of the voting power
the whole ₹10,00,000 advanced is within accumulated profits

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e), first limb

items.scenario: Zenith Fabrics (P) Ltd is closely held: the public are not substantially interested in it. On 12 April 2025 it advanced ₹10,00,000 to Mr Arjun, who is the beneficial owner of shares carrying 15 per cent of its voting power. Its accumulated profits on that date stood at ₹18,00,000. The advance carries interest at the bank's own lending rate and is repayable in three years. Mr Arjun has shown nothing for it in his return.

items.stem: Is anything deemed dividend, and in whose hands?

options.text: ₹6,00,000, in the firm's hands
options.misconception: taxes whoever received the money, rather than the shareholder whose interest brought the clause into play
options.why: The clause names the shareholder as the person whose relationship with both sides makes the payment a dividend, and a dividend is the shareholder's income. Charging the firm would tax the borrower on a loan it has to repay.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, being 25 per cent of the loan
options.misconception: apportions to the share of income, when that share is a gate the shareholder is either through or not
options.why: Twenty per cent is the line that decides whether the concern limb applies. Above it, the payment to the concern is caught in full, subject only to accumulated profits. Below it, nothing is caught. There is no proportion in between.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, in Mr Arjun's hands
options.why: The clause reaches a payment to a concern — a firm, an HUF, an association, a body of individuals or a company — in which such a shareholder is a member or partner and has a substantial interest, meaning at least 20 per cent of the income of the concern. Mr Arjun is at 25 per cent, so the ₹6,00,000 lent to the firm is deemed dividend, and it is charged on the shareholder through whom the clause reached the firm rather than on the firm. It sits inside the ₹8,00,000 of accumulated profits then standing, which leaves ₹2,00,000.
keywords: has a substantial interest, meaning at least 20 per cent of the income of the concern
the ₹6,00,000 lent to the firm is deemed dividend

options.text: Nil, because the firm holds no shares and so is not a shareholder
options.misconception: reads the clause as reaching only shareholders, when the second limb exists precisely to catch money routed through a concern
options.why: The accountant is describing the loophole rather than the law. A shareholder who wanted the company's profits could simply have them lent to his firm, so the clause was widened to payments to a concern in which he is a member and holds a substantial interest. The firm's own shareholding is not part of the test.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e), payment to a concern in which the shareholder has a substantial interest

items.scenario: On 20 July 2025 Zenith Fabrics (P) Ltd lent ₹6,00,000 to Sundar & Co, a partnership firm. Mr Arjun, who holds shares carrying 15 per cent of Zenith's voting power as beneficial owner, is a partner in Sundar & Co and is entitled to 25 per cent of the firm's income. Zenith's accumulated profits still standing at that date were ₹8,00,000. The firm's accountant has told the Assessing Officer that the firm holds no shares in Zenith, so the clause cannot reach it.

items.stem: Which of the three answers keeps any part of the ₹10,00,000 out of section 2(22)(e)?

options.text: All three together, since taken as a whole they show an ordinary commercial dealing
options.misconception: bundles three separate defences into an impression, where the clause asks three separate questions and answers two of them against the company
options.why: Each answer has to stand on its own footing. Repayment is expressly said to make no difference, the money-lending exception fails its second condition, and only the set-off does anything — and it does it for ₹4,00,000, not for the whole. Adding weak points together does not make a strong one.

options.text: The first, since the money was back with the company inside the same previous year
options.misconception: reads the deeming as a test of whether the shareholder ended the year richer, instead of a charge fixed at the moment the payment was made
options.why: Subsequent repayment of the advance, or the charging of interest at the market rate, makes no difference to whether the clause applied when the money went out. The charge attaches on payment. If it did not, every such advance could be undone by a cheque in March, and the clause would reach only the careless.
keywords: subsequent repayment of the advance, or the charging of interest at the market rate, makes no difference

options.text: The third, and only as far as the ₹4,00,000 goes
options.why: Where a loan has already been treated as dividend and the company afterwards declares a dividend to all its shareholders, an amount declared and set off against that earlier borrowing is not treated as dividend a second time. So the ₹4,00,000 is adjusted and the remaining ₹6,00,000 of the original advance stays deemed dividend. It is a rule against double taxation of the same money, not an escape from the clause.
keywords: an amount declared and set off against that earlier borrowing

options.text: The second, this being a loan in the ordinary course of the company's business
options.misconception: takes the first exception without its second half — money-lending must be a substantial part of the business, not something the company does now and then
options.why: The exception has two conditions and both must hold. There has to be a loan made in the ordinary course of business, and lending money must be a substantial part of what the company does. Two obliging customers do not make a fabric maker a money-lender, so the exception is not open on these facts.
keywords: a loan made in the ordinary course of business

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e), exceptions, and the position on subsequent repayment

items.scenario: The Assessing Officer proposes to treat the ₹10,00,000 advanced by Zenith Fabrics (P) Ltd to Mr Arjun as deemed dividend. Three answers are put to him. First, the advance was repaid in full on 5 March 2026 and bore interest at the market rate throughout. Second, Zenith occasionally lends small sums to two long-standing customers, which is said to make this a loan in the course of its business. Third, in February 2026 Zenith declared a dividend of ₹4,00,000 to all its shareholders and set Mr Arjun's share of it against the outstanding advance.

items.stem: Is the ₹5,00,000 deemed dividend in Ms Priya's hands?

options.text: No, but only because the loan is smaller than the ₹8,00,000 of accumulated profits
options.misconception: right answer, wrong gate — the accumulated profits ceiling matters only for somebody already inside the class
options.why: The reason decides what he writes and what he does next time. Accumulated profits limit how much is deemed for a shareholder the clause has caught. Ms Priya is not caught at all, so the ceiling is never reached. On the same facts with profits of ₹2,00,000, this reasoning would give the wrong answer.

options.text: Yes, to the extent of 8 per cent of ₹5,00,000
options.misconception: apportions to the holding, when the holding is a gate that is either passed or not
options.why: There is no proportion anywhere in the clause. Below ten per cent nothing is deemed; at or above it the whole payment is deemed, up to accumulated profits. An answer of ₹40,000 comes from a rule the section does not contain.

options.text: No
options.why: The gate is a holding and not a position. The clause reaches a shareholder who is the beneficial owner of shares carrying at least ten per cent of the voting power, and Ms Priya at 8 per cent is under it, so the loan is not deemed dividend in her hands whatever the accumulated profits are. Being the finance director does not bring her in; nor would holding the shares for somebody else, because what the clause asks for is beneficial ownership.
keywords: Ms Priya at 8 per cent is under it
the loan is not deemed dividend in her hands

options.text: Yes, because she is an officer of the company and the money came out of accumulated profits
options.misconception: substitutes influence over the company for the shareholding the clause actually names
options.why: Control and shareholding are different things and the clause picked one of them. An officer with no shares takes a loan as an employee, and other provisions deal with that. Reading influence into the clause would make it turn on an assessment of who really runs the company, which is not a line a section can be applied along.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e), the ten per cent beneficial ownership test

items.scenario: Zenith Fabrics (P) Ltd also lent ₹5,00,000 to Ms Priya, its finance director, who is the beneficial owner of shares carrying 8 per cent of its voting power. Accumulated profits at the date of the loan were ₹8,00,000. The Assessing Officer proposes to charge the loan as deemed dividend, saying that she runs the company's money and that the profits were plainly there to pay it out of.

items.stem: What is Mr Rahul exposed to under section 276CC, and what has to be established?

options.text: Nothing, because prosecution needs a notice under section 148 and only one under section 142(1)(i) was issued
options.misconception: narrows the section to one of the three returns it names
options.why: The section names three: the return required under section 139(1), the return called for by a notice under section 142(1)(i), and the one under section 148. A failure on any of them is the offence, and here two of the three are on the facts.

options.text: Rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years with fine, the failure having to be shown as deliberate
options.why: Section 276CC punishes a wilful failure to furnish a return in due time — a return required under section 139(1), or called for by a notice under section 142(1)(i) or section 148. Wilfulness is an ingredient of the offence, which is why the diary matters; section 278E then makes the court presume that state of mind and leaves the accused to prove he did not have it. Where the tax that would have been evaded exceeds ₹25 lakh the band is six months to seven years with fine, and below that it is three months to two years with fine. ₹38,00,000 puts him in the higher band.
keywords: a wilful failure to furnish a return in due time
the tax that would have been evaded exceeds ₹25 lakh
six months to seven years with fine

options.text: Rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years with fine, whether or not the failure was deliberate
options.misconception: drops the mental element, which is an ingredient of the charge even though the burden on it is reversed
options.why: The band is right and the reason is not. Wilfulness has to be there for the offence to exist. What section 278E changes is who has to prove it: the court presumes the culpable mental state and the accused may prove its absence. A presumption that can be answered is not the same as an ingredient that has been removed.

options.text: Imprisonment of three months to two years with fine, that being the band for not filing a return
options.misconception: takes the lower band as the general one and misses that the amount of tax decides which band applies
options.why: There are two bands and the tax that would have been evaded chooses between them. The lower one is the residual case. On ₹38,00,000 the case is not residual, and quoting the softer band would understate the exposure by five years.

citation.ref: Section 276CC read with section 278E

items.scenario: Mr Rahul, a builder, did not furnish his return for assessment year 2025-26 by the due date and did not furnish it after a notice under section 142(1)(i) either. The assessment brought out tax of ₹38,00,000 that would have gone unpaid had the omission not come to light. His office diary, seized during a survey, records him telling his accountant twice to hold the return back until the survey blew over.

items.stem: Can the prosecution be launched?

options.text: Yes, because the bar has a ceiling and tax of ₹31,00,000 is above it
options.misconception: attaches the ₹25 lakh figure, or some ceiling, to the date bar, when the only ceiling in the section belongs to a different escape
options.why: Two different reliefs are being mixed. The date bar sets no limit on the tax at all. The only monetary condition in the section belongs to the other escape, the one for a person other than a company whose net tax is not more than ₹10,000. And ₹25 lakh is not a ceiling on any relief — it chooses between the two punishment bands.

options.text: Yes, because the bar is only for a return furnished inside the assessment year and that time has gone
options.misconception: reads one limb of the bar and stops, missing the updated return limb sitting beside it
options.why: The bar has two limbs joined by "or". Losing the first does not decide the case, because the second is written for exactly the person who has already lost it. An assessee who comes forward late and pays is the person the updated return machinery was built for.

options.text: No, because the additional income-tax paid on the updated return is a compounding of the offence
options.misconception: confuses paying an updated return's extra charge with compounding, which is a separate application to the Principal Commissioner under section 279(2)
options.why: The outcome is right and the mechanism is invented. An updated return bars the prosecution because the section says so. Compounding is a different route altogether, taken by application to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and it is what an assessee reaches for when no bar is available to him.

options.text: No, the updated return closes it
options.why: The section carries its own bar and it is a date, not an amount. No prosecution lies where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year in which it was due, and it lies just as little where an updated return is furnished within the time allowed by section 139(8A). Ms Esha missed the first door and walked through the second, so the size of the tax never comes into it. Fee for late filing, interest and the additional income-tax on an updated return are separate charges and still run.
keywords: furnished before the expiry of the assessment year
an updated return is furnished within the time allowed by section 139(8A)

citation.ref: Proviso to section 276CC, the return and updated return limbs

items.scenario: Ms Esha did not furnish her return for assessment year 2025-26 at all, and 31 March 2026 went by with nothing filed. In June 2027 she furnished an updated return for that year within the period section 139(8A) allows, paying the tax and the additional income-tax that goes with it. Tax finally determined for the year: ₹31,00,000. The Assessing Officer proposes to prosecute her, pointing out that the tax is well above ₹25 lakh and that she let the assessment year run out.

items.stem: Which of the two can be prosecuted under section 276CC?

options.text: Neither, since both figures are under ₹10,000
options.misconception: reads the ₹10,000 as a general threshold below which nobody is prosecuted, and misses who the relief is written for
options.why: The figure is real and the class is half the rule. A company is left out on purpose, because a company that does not file is not a small assessee who lost track of a deadline. Reading the limb without its opening words turns a targeted relief into a general one.

options.text: Gagan Ltd only
options.why: The second escape is an amount, and it is not open to everybody. Where the tax payable by a person other than a company — worked out on the income determined on regular assessment, less advance tax and self-assessment tax paid before the assessment year ended and any tax deducted or collected at source — is not more than ₹10,000, no prosecution lies. Mr Farhan's ₹9,000 is inside it. Gagan Ltd's ₹9,500 is smaller still and does it no good at all, because the relief is written for persons other than a company.
keywords: the tax payable by a person other than a company
is not more than ₹10,000, no prosecution lies

options.text: Both, because the ₹10,000 relief needs a return to have been furnished and neither furnished one
options.misconception: mixes the two escapes — the date bar needs a return, the amount bar does not
options.why: The date bar works because a return went in, late but inside the year or as an updated return. The amount escape works on a figure produced by the assessment itself and asks for no return at all. Requiring one would leave the second limb with nothing to do.

options.text: Mr Farhan only, because a company cannot be guilty of a wilful failure
options.misconception: thinks a company is outside prosecution altogether, when the Act reaches the company and its principal officer
options.why: Companies are prosecuted under this Act, and the person in charge is dealt with alongside. The answer also inverts the facts: it is Mr Farhan who has an escape and the company that has none.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 276CC, the ₹10,000 limb for a person other than a company

items.scenario: Mr Farhan, an individual, and Gagan Ltd both failed to furnish returns for assessment year 2025-26 and neither filed at any time. On regular assessment Mr Farhan's tax came to ₹47,000, against which he had paid advance tax and self-assessment tax of ₹30,000 before the assessment year ended and had suffered ₹8,000 of tax deducted at source, leaving ₹9,000. The same working for Gagan Ltd leaves ₹9,500. The Assessing Officer is deciding whom to proceed against.

items.stem: In whose hands does the rent fall, and at what figure?

options.text: ₹1,68,000, clubbed half with each parent
options.misconception: splits the income between the parents, where the section names one of them
options.why: The section picks the parent whose total income is greater, and it picks only one. Splitting would let a family move income to whichever side had room, which is what a clubbing provision exists to stop.

options.text: ₹1,68,000, assessed in Diya's own hands and not clubbed
options.misconception: assumes marriage takes a minor out of clubbing, when clubbing is expressly attracted for a minor married daughter
options.why: Marriage matters to section 27(i) and to nothing else here. Section 64(1A) clubs the income of a minor child, and the module states in terms that this holds for a minor married daughter too. The accountant's rule of thumb is the one thing the two provisions do not share.

options.text: ₹1,68,000, clubbed with Mr Sen
options.why: Two rules pull opposite ways here and the marriage decides between them. Where a house property goes without consideration to a minor child other than a married daughter, section 27(i) makes the transferor the deemed owner, the rent is his own income and clubbing never begins. Diya is a married daughter, so that route is shut. The property income is computed in her hands — ₹2,40,000 less the 30 per cent standard deduction, ₹1,68,000 — and then clubbed under section 64(1A) with the parent whose total income is greater. Clubbing is expressly attracted for a minor married daughter; it is only the deemed ownership route that leaves her out.
keywords: a minor child other than a married daughter
section 27(i) makes the transferor the deemed owner
₹2,40,000 less the 30 per cent standard deduction, ₹1,68,000

options.text: ₹2,40,000, taxed as Mr Sen's own income because he is the deemed owner
options.misconception: applies section 27(i) to a married daughter, whom that provision leaves out, and then forgets the standard deduction as well
options.why: Section 27(i) names a minor child other than a married daughter, so it does not reach Diya at all. The answer is wrong twice over: even where the deeming does apply, the income is still house property income and the 30 per cent deduction still comes off, so ₹2,40,000 would never be the figure.

citation.ref: Sections 64(1A) and 27(i), with section 24(a)

items.scenario: Mr Sen transferred a let-out flat to his daughter Diya in April 2025 without consideration. Diya turned 17 in January 2025 and married in March 2025. Rent for previous year 2025-26 was ₹2,40,000 and no municipal taxes were paid. Mr Sen's total income before any clubbing is higher than his wife's, and both of them have shifted out of the default tax regime. Mr Sen's accountant has shown the rent nowhere, saying a married daughter's income is her own.

items.stem: With whom is the ₹40,000 clubbed for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: With the father, unless the Assessing Officer moves it after hearing the mother
options.why: A minor's income goes into the income of the parent whose total income is greater, and that choice is made once. Having been clubbed with the father, the interest of ₹40,000 continues to be clubbed with him in later years even though the mother has now overtaken him. The only thing that moves it is the Assessing Officer being satisfied that a change is necessary, and he must give the other parent an opportunity of being heard before he decides. Nobody has asked him, so nothing has moved.
keywords: the parent whose total income is greater
the interest of ₹40,000 continues to be clubbed with him

options.text: With the grandmother, the deposit having come out of her gift
options.misconception: follows the money to its source, when section 64(1A) clubs a minor's income whoever provided the funds
options.why: Where the money came from matters under other clubbing provisions, notably those about transfers to a spouse or a son's wife. The minor's rule does not ask. It clubs the child's income with a parent whatever the underlying funds were, which is why a grandparent's gift does not park the income outside the family's returns.

options.text: With the mother, her total income now being the greater of the two
options.misconception: re-runs the comparison every year, when the section fixes the parent once and moves it only by an officer's order
options.why: The comparison decides where the income first lands. After that the section says it goes on being clubbed with that same parent. A yearly re-test would let a family shift a child's income between two returns by arranging which parent earned more, which is the opposite of what clubbing is for.

options.text: With the father, and it cannot be moved at all once it has been fixed
options.misconception: hardens the continuity rule into a bar, missing the Assessing Officer's power to change it
options.why: The answer is right and the reason overstates the rule by one step. Continuity is the default, not a lock. The Assessing Officer may club the income with the other parent if he is satisfied it is necessary, and the safeguard is that he hears that other parent first.

citation.ref: Section 64(1A) and its provisos on which parent

items.scenario: Aarav, aged 11, earns bank interest of ₹40,000 on a deposit made out of a gift from his grandmother. In earlier years the interest was clubbed with his father, whose total income was then the higher of the two. In previous year 2025-26 his mother's total income before clubbing is ₹22,00,000 and his father's is ₹19,00,000. The parents are living together and have made no application to anybody.

items.stem: How much of Ira's ₹97,000 is clubbed with her father?

options.text: ₹97,000, since a minor's income is clubbed whatever its source
options.misconception: applies the general rule without the exception written into the same sub-section
options.why: The general rule is right and it has an exception standing next to it, written so that a child who actually works for money is taxed on it herself. Ignoring it would club the earnings of a young performer with a parent who had nothing to do with them.

options.text: ₹22,000, but with whichever parent maintains her
options.misconception: uses the rule for parents whose marriage does not subsist, which decides the parent only in that case
options.why: Maintenance decides the parent where the marriage does not subsist. Where the parents are together, the test is which of them has the greater total income. Both rules exist and picking the wrong one gives the right figure in the wrong return.

Income a minor earns from manual work, or from any activity involving her skill, talent or specialised knowledge or experience, is left out of clubbing altogether, so the ₹75,000 of performance fees is assessed in Ira's own hands. What the exclusion does not cover is what the money afterwards earns. Interest of ₹22,000 on the deposit comes from the deposit and not from her playing, so it is clubbed with the parent whose total income is greater, and the ₹1,500 exemption then comes off it.
keywords: any activity involving her skill, talent or specialised knowledge or experience
the ₹75,000 of performance fees is assessed in Ira's own hands

options.text: Nothing, because all of it traces back to her own performing
options.misconception: extends the skill exclusion to what the earnings later produce, when it covers only the income from the activity itself
options.why: The exclusion looks at how the income arose, not at where the capital behind it came from. Once the fees are banked, the interest arises from a deposit, and a deposit earns the same interest whoever filled it. Tracing would let a minor's whole investment income out of clubbing after one paid performance.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 64(1A) on manual work and skill, with section 10(32)

items.scenario: Ira, aged 15, earned ₹75,000 in previous year 2025-26 playing the tabla at ticketed concerts. The fees were paid into a bank deposit in her name, which earned interest of ₹22,000 during the same year. Her father's total income before clubbing is higher than her mother's and both have shifted out of the default regime. Her father proposes to leave the whole ₹97,000 out of his return.

items.stem: Is the revision order good?

options.text: No, and the hearing was defective too, a revision needing the Assessing Officer to be heard as well
options.misconception: adds a party the section does not name, and in doing so loses the defect that is actually there
options.why: The section gives the hearing to the assessee. The Assessing Officer is not heard against his own order; he is the source of the record, and he is where an enquiry would naturally go. Running the two together hides the real fault, which is that no enquiry was made at all.

options.text: No, because the hearing is only half of what the section asks of him
options.why: Section 263(1) lets him revise an order of the Assessing Officer, or of the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA, where that order is both erroneous and, in that very respect, damaging to the Revenue. Two things fence the power and the company got one of them. He must give the assessee an opportunity of being heard, which happened; and he acts after making an enquiry that he considers necessary, which did not. Reading an order and forming a view is not an enquiry — it is the very thing an enquiry is there to test. So the order is bad however sound his view of the deduction, and the exercise begins again properly rather than the error becoming unrevisable.
keywords: after making an enquiry that he considers necessary

options.text: Yes, the company having been heard, which is what the section requires before he acts
options.misconception: treats the hearing as the whole of the procedure and drops the enquiry standing beside it in the same sentence
options.why: Neither step is written as a substitute for the other. The hearing protects the assessee; the enquiry is what gives the Commissioner something to be satisfied on besides his own reading of a file. A revision built on no material and no questions is an opinion about an opinion, and the assessee has no way to answer it.

options.text: Yes, an enquiry being unnecessary where the error is plain on the face of the record
options.misconception: makes one of two conditions optional on a ground the section does not contain
options.why: How obvious an error looks is not a test the section knows, and it is exactly the kind of judgement an enquiry exists to check. The Assessing Officer may hold material that explains the claim entirely. Nobody asked him for it, which is how a plain error stays plain.

citation.ref: Section 263(1)

items.scenario: The Principal Commissioner reads an assessment order on Vireo Ltd and forms the view that a deduction was wrongly allowed. He issues a show-cause notice, hears the company's counsel at length, and then signs an order under section 263 setting the assessment aside and directing a fresh one. He called for nothing from the Assessing Officer, put no question to anybody and looked at no material beyond the order in front of him. The company says the order still cannot stand.

items.stem: Does the "two possible views" answer keep the order out of section 263?

options.text: No, because the section itself treats orders of this kind as erroneous
options.why: The "two possible views" answer works where the officer looked and then chose. This file is not that. The section carries its own list of orders treated as erroneous and prejudicial without further argument: one passed without making inquiries or verification which the circumstances called for; one that allows any relief without inquiring into the claim; one out of line with a direction or instruction the CBDT has issued under section 119; and one that ignores a decision prejudicial to the assessee handed down by the jurisdictional High Court or by the Supreme Court. Two of those fit, and once a limb is met the order is erroneous by force of the section whatever view the officer says he took.
keywords: without making inquiries or verification which the circumstances called for
allows any relief without inquiring into the claim
a decision prejudicial to the assessee handed down by the jurisdictional High Court

options.text: No, and the order is void from the start, so no fresh assessment is needed
options.misconception: confuses a revisable order with a nullity
options.why: Section 263 sets an order aside and sends the matter back; it does not make the order a nothing. The distinction has teeth: a fresh assessment has to be made, and the deduction gets examined on its merits rather than disappearing along with the order.

options.text: No, but only on the unexamined claim; a High Court ruling binds him only where it is in the assessee's own case
options.misconception: reads the fourth limb too narrowly — it covers a decision in the case of the assessee or of any other person
options.why: The limb covers a decision of the jurisdictional High Court, or of the Supreme Court, and it does not matter whose case it was given in — the assessee's own or somebody else's. A ruling on the same point against another company is squarely inside it, and confining it to the assessee's own case would let an officer ignore settled law until sued about it.

options.text: Yes, because where two views are possible an order taking one of them cannot be erroneous
options.misconception: takes a rule made for a considered choice and applies it to an order where no choice was made
options.why: The proposition is sound in its own place. It protects an officer who examined a claim and formed a view. It has nothing to say about an officer who examined nothing, because there was no second view for him to have rejected.

citation.ref: Explanation to section 263(1) on orders deemed erroneous and prejudicial

items.scenario: Corvus Ltd's assessment allowed a deduction of ₹3,20,00,000 on a one-line claim. The file shows no query raised and no document called for on it. The same order also went against a ruling of the jurisdictional High Court in another company's case, a ruling that runs against the assessee on the identical point. The Assessing Officer's note says two views were possible on the deduction and he took one of them.

items.stem: Can the Principal Commissioner revise the order?

options.text: No, because on appeal the whole order merges in the appellate order
options.misconception: applies the doctrine of merger to the entire order, when the section confines it to what the appeal actually decided
options.why: Merger is real but it is limited to the matters the appellate authority considered and decided. If it swallowed the whole order, an assessee could put every issue out of reach by appealing on the smallest one, and the section was written to say so expressly.

options.text: Yes, on the section 80-IA issue but not on the section 14A one
options.why: An appeal does not put a whole order beyond revision. Where an order has been the subject-matter of an appeal, the revision power extends to matters not considered and decided in that appeal. The section 14A disallowance is before the Commissioner (Appeals) and must be left alone; the section 80-IA deduction has not been considered or decided by anybody, so it is still open to him. A pending appeal on an unrelated issue is no bar.
keywords: matters not considered and decided in that appeal

options.text: Yes, on both issues, the section giving him the whole order
options.misconception: overshoots the other way, ignoring the matters the appellate authority has already taken up
options.why: The power reaches only what the appeal has not considered and decided. Revising an issue that is live before the Commissioner (Appeals) would put two authorities on the same point at the same time, which is what the limitation is there to prevent.

options.text: No, not until the appeal is disposed of, and then only on what is left
options.misconception: turns a limit on subject-matter into a limit on timing
options.why: The section says nothing about waiting. Waiting would also be dangerous, because the revision clock runs from the end of the financial year in which the order under revision was passed and an appeal can easily outlast it. The right course is to act now on the untouched issue.

citation.ref: Explanation 1(c) to section 263(1)

items.scenario: Egret Ltd's assessment order is before the Commissioner (Appeals) on one issue, a disallowance under section 14A. The Principal Commissioner now proposes to revise the same order on a different issue altogether, a deduction under section 80-IA that the appeal does not mention. Egret says the order is before an appellate authority and is therefore beyond his reach.

items.stem: By when must the revision order be passed?

options.text: There is no limit, because the order is being set aside for a fresh assessment
options.misconception: confuses the revision order's own deadline with the time the Assessing Officer then gets
options.why: Two clocks are in play and this answer looks at the second. The revision order itself has to be made inside the two years. The fresh assessment that follows has its own separate time limit, and it never rescues a revision order made too late.

options.text: 31 March 2027
options.why: No revision order may be made after the expiry of two years from the end of the financial year — and the year that counts is the one in which the order sought to be revised was passed, not the year the Commissioner took up the file or issued his notice. The assessment order is dated 20.12.2024, which falls in F.Y. 2024-25, so the two years run out on 31 March 2027. The notice date changes nothing except how much of the two years is left to finish in, and here that is barely ten weeks.
keywords: two years from the end of the financial year
the order sought to be revised was passed

options.text: 31 December 2026, two years from the date of the order itself
options.misconception: measures from the order's date rather than from the end of its financial year
options.why: The period runs from the end of the financial year in which the order was passed, which moves the finishing line to a 31 March. Measuring from the date itself here would cost the Revenue three months and the wrong answer at a moment when only weeks are left.

options.text: 31 March 2029, two years from the end of the year in which the notice was issued
options.misconception: starts the clock at the Commissioner's own step, which is the one date the section does not use
options.why: A limitation that ran from the revising authority's own notice would be no limitation at all, because he chooses when to issue it. The section anchors the period to the order under revision so that an assessment cannot be reopened indefinitely.

citation.ref: Section 263(2)

items.scenario: The assessment order the Principal Commissioner wants to revise was passed by the Assessing Officer on 20.12.2024. He issued his notice under section 263 on 14 January 2027. His office has told him the clock runs from the end of the financial year in which the notice went out, so he has until March 2029.

items.stem: What does Article 4 do with a man both countries treat as resident?

options.text: Domestic law wins, so India taxes him as a resident and the treaty adds nothing
options.misconception: skips paragraph 2 altogether, which exists precisely because both domestic laws are right
options.why: If domestic law settled it, both countries would tax him on his worldwide income and the double taxation would stand. Paragraph 2 is the step that stops that, and reaching for section 6 alone leaves out the whole of the relief.

options.text: He is a resident of neither State for the treaty, so it does not apply to him
options.misconception: treats dual residence as disqualifying, when the treaty is written to resolve it
options.why: The article assumes that dual residence will happen and supplies the answer. Treating it as a bar would take the treaty away from exactly the people most likely to be taxed twice, which is who it is for.

options.text: He elects the State he would rather be treated as resident of
options.misconception: reads a mechanical ladder as an option, which would let the treaty be planned instead of applied
options.why: Every step is a question of fact, answered on the same facts by either country's revenue. A choice would let a person move his treaty residence by writing a letter, and the allocation of taxing rights that the rest of the treaty depends on would follow him.

options.text: Paragraph 2 deems him a resident of one State for the treaty, by a fixed order of tests
options.why: Paragraph 1 sends each State to its own law, so a person can be a resident of both — India by his stay, Country Y by his domicile — and both readings are correct at the same time. Paragraph 2 is the tie-breaker. It does not cancel either country's domestic law; it decides which State the treaty will treat him as resident of, and it works down a fixed order — permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, and then mutual agreement between the two governments. There is no election anywhere in it.

citation.source: OECD and UN Model Tax Conventions
citation.ref: Article 4, paragraphs 1 and 2

items.scenario: Mr Varun was in India for 194 days in previous year 2025-26 and is a resident under section 6. Country Y also taxes him on his worldwide income, because he is domiciled there under its own law. India and Country Y have a comprehensive treaty in the Model Convention's terms. His adviser has told him he must pick one of the two countries and file there.

items.stem: Which State does the tie-breaker deem him a resident of, and at which step does it stop?

options.text: India, at the centre of vital interests
options.why: The first step asks whether he has a permanent home available to him, and it settles nothing: the owned Mumbai flat and the leased apartment are each a home kept available to him, so he has one in both States. The same clause then moves on — where there is a home in both, the State that wins is the one with which his personal and economic relations are closer, which the article calls the centre of vital interests. Family, investments, bank accounts and social ties in India against a salary from Country Y put the balance clearly on the Indian side, so he is a resident only of India and the ladder stops there. Habitual abode is never reached.
keywords: a permanent home available to him
he has one in both States
his personal and economic relations are closer
he is a resident only of India

options.text: Country Y, at the permanent home step, since the lease is where he actually sleeps on working days
options.misconception: reads permanent home as the place he spends most nights, when the test asks what is available to him and both homes are
options.why: Availability is the test, not use. A flat kept ready for him all year is available whether he sleeps in it or not, and the article deals with the man who has two by moving on rather than by counting nights. Counting nights belongs to habitual abode, two rungs further down, and it is never reached here.

options.text: Country Y, at the centre of vital interests, because that is where his income is earned
options.misconception: weighs only the economic half of a test that says personal and economic together
options.why: The clause names personal and economic relations in the same breath. Family, home life and social ties count alongside where the salary is paid, and on these facts everything except the salary points one way. Taking the economic side alone would make the test a question of where a person works.

options.text: Nothing is settled until habitual abode is tested, both States having a real claim
options.misconception: carries on down a ladder that has already produced an answer
options.why: The ladder is sequential and it stops at the first rung that decides. Habitual abode is reached only where the centre of vital interests cannot be determined, or where he has a permanent home in neither State. Here the second rung answered the question, so the rest of the article is not applied.

citation.source: OECD and UN Model Tax Conventions
citation.ref: Article 4, paragraph 2(a) and 2(b)

items.scenario: Mr Varun owns a flat in Mumbai that is kept ready for him all year and holds a three-year lease on an apartment in Country Y. His wife and children live in Mumbai; his bank accounts, shares and other house property are in India and so is his family and social life. His employment income comes from Country Y, where he stays alone on working days, and one salary account is held there.

items.stem: Is the provisional attachment good?

options.text: No, the approval having come five days after the thing it was meant to authorise
options.why: Section 281B lets the Assessing Officer attach property provisionally while an assessment, or a reassessment of income which has escaped assessment, is pending, and it sets three conditions. The attachment must be made by an order in writing, which it was. He must be of the opinion that it is necessary for protecting the interests of the revenue, which he recorded. And it needs the prior approval of a Commissioner, a Principal Commissioner, a Chief Commissioner, a Principal Chief Commissioner, a Director, a Principal Director, a Director General or a Principal Director General — prior meaning before the attachment and not five days after it. Wednesday's signature cannot authorise Friday's act.
keywords: the prior approval of a Commissioner
necessary for protecting the interests of the revenue

options.text: No, because a fixed deposit is not property that section 281B reaches
options.misconception: narrows "any property of the assessee" with nothing in the section to support it
options.why: The section says any property of the assessee, and a deposit is among the easiest things to move, which is the mischief it addresses. Fixing on the kind of asset also misses the defect that is really there — one the same officer could cure tomorrow by taking the approval first.

options.text: Yes, the approval having been obtained, the section not saying when it must be taken
options.misconception: reads "prior" out of the requirement, which is the whole of what the second signature is for
options.why: An approval taken after a taxpayer's money is already frozen does not approve; it ratifies. The point of a second and senior officer is that somebody weighs the case before the property goes, and a protection of that kind cannot be supplied afterwards. The word in the section is the condition.

options.text: Yes, the written order and the recorded opinion being what the section asks for, the approval is internal
options.misconception: treats the approval as departmental housekeeping rather than a condition of the power itself
options.why: It sits in the same sentence as the power, so without it the officer simply does not have the power. Treating it as internal would let an attachment stand on one officer's fear of what might happen, which is the thing the requirement was put there to stop.

citation.ref: Section 281B(1)

items.scenario: A reassessment of income which has escaped assessment is pending against Mr Iqbal. Fearing the money will move, the Assessing Officer passes a written order on a Friday attaching a fixed deposit of ₹1,40,00,000, records in that order why he thinks the revenue is at risk, and serves it on the bank the same evening. He puts the file up to the Principal Commissioner the following Wednesday, who signs the approval that day. Mr Iqbal challenges what has been done.

items.stem: What must the officer do on 4 August 2026, and what follows as January 2027 comes on?

options.text: Revoke the attachment within 15 days, and invoke the guarantee if it is not renewed fifteen days before it expires
options.why: The guarantee has to come from a scheduled bank and be worth at least what the attached property would fetch in the open market, or enough to protect the revenue. Where no reference goes to the Valuation Officer, the revocation order is due within 15 days of receiving the guarantee; the 45-day limit belongs to cases where a reference is made, and the Valuation Officer himself reports within 30 days. The far end matters as much. If the assessee neither renews the guarantee nor furnishes a new one for an equal amount fifteen days before it expires, the officer shall invoke the guarantee in the interests of the revenue. Letting it lapse is not a passive act.
keywords: the revocation order is due within 15 days
the officer shall invoke the guarantee in the interests of the revenue

options.text: He need not revoke at all, a guarantee being an offer the officer may accept or refuse
options.misconception: reads a duty as a discretion
options.why: The section says the officer shall revoke where a qualifying guarantee is furnished. His judgement goes into whether the guarantee is worth enough, and once he has accepted that, the revocation follows. A power to refuse would leave an assessee paying for a guarantee and still holding an attached property.

options.text: Revoke within 30 days, that being the period the section works to
options.misconception: borrows the Valuation Officer's own reporting period and uses it as the revocation clock
options.why: Thirty days is how long the Valuation Officer has to estimate the fair market value and report. It is a step inside the longer route, not a deadline for the officer's own order. Three separate periods sit in this provision and each belongs to a different actor.

options.text: Revoke within 45 days, and do nothing about renewal until the guarantee has actually lapsed
options.misconception: takes the longer clock, which belongs to a case where a valuation reference was made, and treats a lapse as something to react to afterwards
options.why: The two periods are alternatives and the reference decides between them. No reference was made here, so 15 days applies.
