And the section acts before the expiry, not after: the duty to invoke arises when the assessee has failed to renew fifteen days ahead, precisely so the revenue is not left holding an expired piece of paper.

citation.ref: Section 281B(3) to (7)

items.scenario: A property of Mr Iqbal's is under a valid provisional attachment. On 4 August 2026 he hands the Assessing Officer a guarantee from a scheduled bank for an amount the officer accepts as enough to keep the revenue safe, and the officer makes no reference to the Valuation Officer. The guarantee runs out on 31 January 2027. Mr Iqbal has done nothing about renewing it and says the bank will simply tell him when it expires.

items.stem: What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since Form 3CD carries both the report and the particulars
options.misconception: collapses the report and the statement of particulars into a single document
options.why: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars and it is annexed to a report, never a report on its own. Filing 3CD alone would leave the audit opinion unsigned, and it would still not answer the date, which is wrong in this plan whatever forms are used.

options.text: Only the forms; the report may be furnished right up to the due date of the return
options.misconception: uses the return's due date as the audit's, when the audit runs a month ahead of it
options.why: The two dates were deliberately separated so that the return can be prepared on a finished audit rather than beside one. Working to 31 October also leaves no room at all if anything in the audit throws up a question, which is the situation the earlier date is meant to prevent.

options.text: The date is a month late and the two clients need different forms
options.why: The audit has to be completed and the report furnished before one month prior to the due date under section 139(1), so a signature on 31 October is a month too late; the date to work to is 30 September 2026. The forms then turn on who else audits the accounts. Where another law already requires an audit, that report goes in together with a further report from an accountant in Form 3CA. Where no other law requires it, the accountant furnishes Form 3CB. The particulars themselves go in Form 3CD in either case, prescribed under Rule 6G. So the LLP takes 3CA, Mr Kunal takes 3CB, and both take 3CD.
keywords: before one month prior to the due date
a further report from an accountant in Form 3CA
the particulars themselves go in Form 3CD

options.text: Only the date; Form 3CB serves for anybody audited under section 44AB
options.misconception: treats 3CB as the general form, when it is the one for accounts no other law audits
options.why: Form 3CB carries the accountant's own opinion on accounts nobody else has audited. Where a statutory audit already exists, that report is furnished and the accountant adds a further report in Form 3CA instead, so that the same accounts are not opined on twice from scratch.

citation.ref: Section 44AB with Rule 6G and Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD

items.scenario: Two clients need a tax audit for previous year 2025-26. Meridian Traders LLP has its accounts audited under the law governing limited liability partnerships. Mr Kunal's proprietary business is audited under no other law at all. The due date for both returns under section 139(1) is 31 October 2026. The article clerk has diarised both audit reports for signature on 31 October and proposes to use the same form for both.

items.stem: What is the most the penalty can be, and is there an answer to it?

options.text: ₹4,50,000, since half a per cent of turnover is the measure and the ₹1,50,000 cap is only for a profession
options.misconception: invents a limit on the cap, which applies to a business and a profession alike
options.why: The section sets two figures and takes the lower of them for everybody. On a large turnover the fixed figure is always the smaller, which is the whole point of having it — the penalty for one missing audit does not scale with the size of the business.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, and reasonable cause is no answer once the failure is admitted
options.misconception: reads section 273B out of the Act; it operates on failures that did happen
options.why: Section 273B only ever applies where the failure occurred, because otherwise there would be no penalty to lift. It asks why. A cause outside the proprietor's control for most of the year is exactly what it was written for, and the officer has to consider it.

options.text: Nil, because no penalty can follow where the books were with another agency
options.misconception: assumes the cause instead of proving it, and treats the relief as automatic
options.why: The relief is not automatic. Section 273B puts it on the assessee to prove reasonable cause, and until that is established the penalty is live. He would also have to explain the months after September 2026, when the books were back.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, and the seizure may answer it altogether
options.why: Section 271B fixes the penalty for failing to get accounts audited at one-half per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts, or ₹1,50,000, whichever is less. Half a per cent of ₹9,00,00,000 is ₹4,50,000, so the cap bites and the exposure is ₹1,50,000 rather than the officer's figure. Beyond that, section 273B says no penalty is leviable under section 271B if the assessee proves there was reasonable cause for the failure, and books held by another agency for most of the year is the kind of cause that has to be heard on evidence rather than assumed either way.
keywords: Half a per cent of ₹9,00,00,000 is ₹4,50,000
section 273B says no penalty is leviable under section 271B

citation.ref: Sections 271B and 273B

items.scenario: Sarita Foods, a proprietary business with turnover of ₹9,00,00,000 in previous year 2025-26, was required to get its accounts audited under section 44AB and did not. The Assessing Officer proposes a penalty of ₹4,50,000, being half a per cent of turnover. The proprietor's books and vouchers were seized by another agency in June 2025 and returned only in September 2026, and he has said so in writing.

items.stem: What is the value of the press once the rule 10(1) additions are made, before any transport or insurance is added?

options.misconception: adds the Pune drawings as well, reading the clause as covering design work of any kind rather than design work done outside India
options.why: The clause on buyer-supplied services is deliberately narrow on this point: it reaches engineering, development, art work, design work and plans undertaken outside India. Work done in India by an Indian consultant is left where it is, and the ₹1,50,000 stays out even though the drawings were just as necessary to the press as the German ones.
keywords: work done in India by an Indian consultant is left where it is

options.misconception: treats the licence fee and the resale share as post-import charges, when the first is a term of the sale itself and the second is measured on the imported goods
options.why: Both go in. A licence fee the buyer has to pay as a condition of sale of the goods being valued is added, so the ₹3,00,000 belongs in the price — and it stays there even though the patented process is run after the press has landed, which the clause says in terms. Separately, whatever share of the proceeds of a later resale, disposal or use of the goods reaches the seller is added by the clause that follows, so the ₹2,00,000 goes in too.
keywords: a licence fee the buyer has to pay as a condition of sale of the goods being valued is added, so the ₹3,00,000 belongs in the price
whatever share of the proceeds of a later resale, disposal or use of the goods reaches the seller is added

options.why: Six of the seven payments belong in the price and one does not. The ₹80,000 paid to the seller's own agent is a selling commission and is added, the clause reaching commissions and brokerage generally. Drawings made elsewhere than in India and needed to build the machine are added, so the German ₹2,00,000 goes in while the Pune ₹1,50,000 does not. Tools and moulds the buyer hands over free of charge for use in making the goods are added at their ₹60,000 value. The licence fee and the resale share are both caught by their own clauses. Adding ₹80,000, ₹2,00,000, ₹60,000, ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000 to ₹50,00,000 brings the price to ₹58,40,000.
keywords: the ₹80,000 paid to the seller's own agent is a selling commission and is added
drawings made elsewhere than in India and needed to build the machine are added
moulds the buyer hands over free of charge for use in making the goods are added at their ₹60,000 value

options.misconception: treats every commission alike, when the clause that adds commissions carries one carve-out and this payment falls squarely inside it
options.why: A fee an importer pays to an agent for representing him in buying the goods is a buying commission, and buying commission is the one commission the clause leaves out, so it is not added. Vasudha engaged that agent for itself and got a service of its own out of him; the seller got nothing. Bringing the ₹1,00,000 in overstates the price by exactly the amount the rule was written to keep out.
keywords: a fee an importer pays to an agent for representing him in buying the goods is a buying commission
buying commission is the one commission the clause leaves out, so it is not added

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)(i) with the note on buying commissions, rule 10(1)(b)(ii) and (iv), rule 10(1)(c) and rule 10(1)(d)

items.scenario: Vasudha Polymers imports a moulding press from Germany at a price of ₹50,00,000. Alongside the price it also paid or bore: ₹1,00,000 to an agent it engaged itself, to find a maker and negotiate for it; ₹80,000 to an agent who works for the German seller, which the contract made Vasudha pay; ₹2,00,000 billed separately for drawings prepared at the seller's own drawing office in Germany, without which the press could not have been built; ₹1,50,000 for drawings prepared by a consultant in Pune; ₹3,00,000 to the seller for the right to run the seller's patented process on the press, the seller having refused to ship until that licence was signed; ₹2,00,000 being two per cent of what Vasudha earns reselling the mouldings, which the contract requires it to hand the seller; and moulds Vasudha bought in India for ₹60,000 and shipped to the seller at no charge, to be used in building the press.

items.stem: What is the assessable value?

options.misconception: adds the freight and drops the insurance, treating insurance as the buyer's own arrangement rather than part of the cost of landing the goods
options.why: Insurance to the place of importation is added by its own clause of rule 10(2), on the same footing as transport. It is never simply left out: where it is documented the documented premium is added, and where it cannot be ascertained the fallback percentage is added instead.
keywords: insurance to the place of importation is added by its own clause of rule 10(2)

options.why: Rule 10(2) adds the cost of transport to the place of importation and the cost of insurance. Where those costs are ascertained and evidenced they go into the value as they stand, and here both are: a carrier's invoice and a policy are exactly what ascertains them. So ₹58,40,000 plus ₹2,50,000 plus ₹40,000, and the assessable value comes to ₹61,30,000. The percentages the clerk wants are fallbacks and nothing more.
keywords: where those costs are ascertained and evidenced they go into the value as they stand

options.misconception: reads the percentages in the provisos as the rule and the actual figures as the exception, when it is the other way about
options.why: The twenty per cent and the 1.125 per cent are fallbacks for a cost that cannot be ascertained, and each proviso says so on its face. Using them where the importer has produced the carrier's invoice and the policy inflates the value by more than nine lakh rupees and taxes him on money nobody spent.
keywords: the twenty per cent and the 1.125 per cent are fallbacks for a cost that cannot be ascertained

options.misconception: accepts the documented freight but still applies the notional percentage to insurance, as though insurance alone were always taken at the prescribed rate
options.why: A premium evidenced by the policy is ascertainable, so the 1.125 per cent fallback does not apply to it. The two clauses are tested the same way and independently of each other: whichever cost is proved is taken as proved, and only a cost that cannot be worked out is replaced by a percentage.
keywords: a premium evidenced by the policy is ascertainable, so the 1.125 per cent fallback does not apply to it

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2) with the provisos on the twenty per cent and 1.125 per cent fallbacks

items.scenario: An importer's rule 10(1) additions have been settled and the price of an imported press stands at ₹58,40,000 free on board. The goods came by sea. The importer produces the shipping line's invoice for the ocean freight it actually paid, ₹2,50,000, and the marine policy showing the premium it actually paid, ₹40,000. The clerk making out the bill of entry puts both papers aside and proposes to add twenty per cent of the price for transport and 1.125 per cent for insurance, saying those are the figures the rule lays down.

items.stem: What enters the value of the consignment?

options.text: Both the ₹10,000 and the ₹8,000
options.misconception: applies the price-linked test and stops there, missing that the clause carves out what governments pay however tightly it is tied to price
options.why: Price linkage is only the first half of the test. The second half asks who paid, and a payment from the Centre or a State is taken out even when it is calculated on the price to the last rupee. Reading the clause without its exclusion taxes the buyer's price and the Government's help at the same rate.
keywords: a payment from the Centre or a State is taken out even when it is calculated on the price

options.text: The State Government's ₹8,000 only
options.misconception: has the carve-out backwards, taking a government payment as the one the law is anxious about and a private one as harmless
options.why: The law is the other way round. It leaves government support out precisely so that a scheme meant to bring a price down is not taxed back up, and it brings private price-linked support in because that is ordinary consideration reaching the supplier by another route.
keywords: it leaves government support out precisely so that a scheme meant to bring a price down is not taxed back up

options.text: The association's ₹10,000 only
options.why: A subsidy comes into the value only when it is directly linked to the price, and both of these are, being worked out on the rate itself. But the exclusion is drawn by who pays, not by how the payment is calculated, and it reaches what the Central Government and the State Governments pay. So the association's ₹10,000 goes into the value and the State Government's ₹8,000 stays out. The Explanation settles whose value moves: the subsidy is added in the hands of the supplier who receives it, which is Meghna.
keywords: a subsidy comes into the value only when it is directly linked to the price
the association's ₹10,000 goes into the value
the subsidy is added in the hands of the supplier who receives it

options.text: Neither
options.misconception: treats a subsidy as third-party money outside the price altogether, which is the very reading the clause was written to close
options.why: The clause exists because the buyer pays less than the supply is worth whenever somebody else tops the supplier up. If money that is tied to the price could be kept out simply because it came from a third party, a supplier could move any part of his price onto a friendly payer and tax it nowhere. Money tied to the price is not kept out of the value simply because a third party paid it.
keywords: money tied to the price is not kept out of the value simply because a third party paid it

citation.ref: Section 15(2)(e) with the Explanation to section 15(2)

items.scenario: Meghna Papers, registered in Assam, sells notebooks to retailers. A paper trade association pays it ₹10,000 on every consignment sold at the association's recommended rate, the payment worked out on that rate itself. The State Government separately pays it ₹8,000 a consignment under a schools promotion scheme, also worked out on the rate. Its accountant leaves both out of the value, saying a subsidy is somebody else's money and never part of what the buyer pays.

items.stem: What is the value of the July supply, and what becomes of the ₹1,500?

options.text: ₹1,14,000, and the ₹1,500 joins the value of the same supply when it is received in September
options.why: The starting point is the transaction value, the price actually paid or payable, the two being unrelated and money the only consideration. A discount given at or before the supply is left out where it has been recorded in the invoice, so five per cent comes off and the price is ₹95,000. To that go the ₹2,000 cess, charged separately under a law other than the GST laws; the ₹3,000 crating, an incidental expense; the ₹4,000 Kalindi was liable to pay and the buyer bore instead; and the ₹10,000 price-linked subsidy from a body that is not a government. The value of the July supply is ₹1,14,000. Interest for delayed payment is part of the value of that same supply, and it is brought to tax when it is received, in September.
keywords: the starting point is the transaction value, the price actually paid or payable
a discount given at or before the supply is left out where it has been recorded in the invoice, so five per cent comes off and the price is ₹95,000
the value of the July supply is ₹1,14,000
interest for delayed payment is part of the value of that same supply

options.text: ₹1,14,000, and the ₹1,500 is a financing charge outside the value
options.misconception: gets the July figure right but treats a late-payment charge as a cost of credit rather than as an addition to the price of the goods
options.why: The clause names interest, late fee and penalty for delayed payment of the consideration and puts all three inside the value. It is not a separate supply of financing and it does not carry a rate of its own — it takes the rate of the tiles, because it is part of what the tiles were worth. What is special about it is only the timing.
keywords: the clause names interest, late fee and penalty for delayed payment of the consideration and puts all three inside the value

options.text: ₹1,10,000, the ₹4,000 staying out
options.misconception: reads the freight as the buyer's own cost because he paid it, missing that the contract had made it the supplier's to pay
options.why: What decides it is who was liable, not who wrote the cheque. Any amount the supplier was liable to pay in relation to the supply, which the recipient has incurred instead and which is not in the price, is added. Had the contract left the freight on the buyer from the start, nothing would go in — the ₹4,000 enters only because Kalindi owed it.
keywords: any amount the supplier was liable to pay in relation to the supply, which the recipient has incurred instead and which is not in the price, is added

options.text: ₹1,19,000, the discount not coming off
options.misconception: thinks a trade discount is a commercial arrangement between the parties rather than something the value provision itself excludes
options.why: A discount given at or before the time of supply is excluded outright, and the only condition is that it has been duly recorded in the invoice for that supply. Nothing more is asked of it — no prior agreement, no invoice-wise linkage, no reversal by the buyer. Those conditions belong to the other limb, which is for a discount given after the supply has been made.
keywords: a discount given at or before the time of supply is excluded outright

citation.ref: Section 15(1), section 15(2)(a) to (e) and section 15(3)(a), with the time of supply for interest under section 12

items.scenario: Kalindi Tiles, registered in Gujarat, invoices an unrelated buyer in July 2026 and takes nothing but money for the tiles. The list price is ₹1,00,000 and the invoice itself shows a trade discount of five per cent. On separate lines the same invoice charges a municipal cess of ₹2,000 levied under a State law and ₹3,000 for the special crating the buyer asked for. Under the contract Kalindi had to pay the transporter ₹4,000, but the buyer paid the transporter directly and that ₹4,000 is nowhere in the price. A trade body pays Kalindi ₹10,000 a consignment, worked out on the price. The buyer settles late, and in September 2026 Kalindi collects ₹1,500 from it for the delay.

items.stem: On which of the six does Bhramar itself have to pay the tax?

options.text: All six
options.misconception: reads the notified categories as covering whole trades, missing that three of the six carry a condition about who the supplier is
options.why: Three of the six entries end in an exception, and each exception is about the supplier rather than the service. A company running omnibuses answers for its own rides. A hotel or a guest house or a house-keeper or a delivery service that is itself liable to be registered answers for its own supplies. Sweeping all six onto the platform makes it pay tax that the law leaves with people who are already inside the system.
keywords: three of the six entries end in an exception, and each exception is about the supplier rather than the service

options.text: The cab rides, the one-bus owner's rides, the guest house rooms and the parcel deliveries
options.why: Where a service is notified, the operator pays the tax as if it were the supplier, and six categories are notified. The first is passenger transport by motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle, radio-taxi or any other motor vehicle except an omnibus, which takes in the cab rides. An omnibus has an entry of its own, and it falls away only where the person supplying through the operator is a company — so the one-bus owner is in and Nilgiri Travels is not, and Nilgiri pays on its own rides. Accommodation and local delivery are both notified, save where the supplier is himself liable for registration under section 22(1), which is why the guest house is in and the registered hotel chain is not.
keywords: the operator pays the tax as if it were the supplier
any other motor vehicle except an omnibus
it falls away only where the person supplying through the operator is a company
accommodation and local delivery are both notified, save where the supplier is himself liable for registration under section 22(1)

options.text: The cab rides only
options.misconception: works off the chapter body's list of five and never reaches the entry added from 22 September 2025
options.why: The list has grown. Accommodation, house-keeping and restaurant service have been notified for years, an omnibus entry was added with its company carve-out, and local delivery became the sixth category from 22 September 2025. A platform that pays only on cab rides is three entries behind and is short-paying on the rooms and the parcels.
keywords: local delivery became the sixth category from 22 September 2025

options.text: The cab rides, both omnibus operators' rides, the guest house rooms and the parcel deliveries
options.misconception: gets the accommodation carve-out right but misses the parallel one on omnibus rides, which turns on the supplier being a company rather than on his being registered
options.why: The two exceptions are not the same test. Accommodation, house-keeping and local delivery drop out where the supplier is liable for registration; omnibus rides drop out where the supplier is a company, registered or not. Nilgiri Travels is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, so its rides are its own to pay for and the platform collects tax at source on them instead.
keywords: omnibus rides drop out where the supplier is a company, registered or not

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-CT (R) as it stands from 22 September 2025, and section 22(1)

items.scenario: Bhramar Ltd runs an app in Karnataka and collects the money for everything booked through it. In October 2025, all of it within the State, the app carried six streams: cab rides by individual drivers; rides in an omnibus run by Nilgiri Travels Private Limited; rides in an omnibus run by a man who owns the one bus and whose takings are far below every registration threshold; rooms in a guest house whose owner is below every registration threshold; rooms of a hotel chain whose turnover is many times the threshold and which is registered; and parcels carried across the city by riders whose earnings are below every registration threshold. Bhramar's compliance head proposes to leave the tax on all six with the people who actually supplied, and to collect tax at source on all six.

items.stem: What is the base for the month's collection at source, and how much must be collected?

options.misconception: brings the deemed-supplier services into the base as well, running both machineries over the same rupees
options.why: The two regimes are exclusive by design. On a notified service the operator is already paying the whole tax as though it had made the supply, and there is no supplier's liability left for a collection at source to sit against. The definition says so in terms by excluding those services from the aggregate, so the ₹33 lakh is outside the base.
keywords: on a notified service the operator is already paying the whole tax as though it had made the supply, and there is no supplier's liability left for a collection at source to sit against

options.misconception: counts only the registered sellers' goods, treating a composition dealer, a hotel and a bus company as if the collection reached ordinary goods sellers alone
options.why: The base is drawn by whether a supply is taxable and made through the platform by a registered person, not by what kind of business the supplier runs. A composition dealer's goods, a registered hotel's rooms and a company's omnibus rides are all taxable supplies routed through the operator and outside the deemed-supplier list, so all three belong in the base.
keywords: the base is drawn by whether a supply is taxable and made through the platform by a registered person

options.misconception: takes the gross value of the month's supplies, forgetting that the word in the provision is the NET value
options.why: Returns are deducted, and they are deducted supplier by supplier within the same month. That is what makes the net value is ₹2,20,00,000 rather than the gross ₹2,40,00,000. Where a supplier's returns run past his supplies in a month the figure for him is treated as nil and never as a minus, and it is not carried into a later month either.
keywords: that is what makes the net value is ₹2,20,00,000 rather than the gross ₹2,40,00,000
where a supplier's returns run past his supplies in a month the figure for him is treated as nil and never as a minus

options.why: The base is the net value of taxable supplies: everything taxable that registered persons supplied through the platform in the month, the services on which the operator itself pays being left out, less the value of what was returned to those suppliers in the same month. So ₹2 crore less the ₹20 lakh returned, plus the composition dealer's ₹5,00,000, the hotel chain's ₹30,00,000 and the omnibus company's ₹5,00,000. On an intra-State supply the notified rate is 0.25 per cent of central tax alongside 0.25 per cent of State tax, half a per cent in all, which gives ₹1,10,000 — being CGST ₹55,000 and SGST ₹55,000.
keywords: the base is the net value of taxable supplies
less the value of what was returned to those suppliers in the same month
the notified rate is 0.25 per cent of central tax alongside 0.25 per cent of State tax
which gives ₹1,10,000 — being CGST ₹55,000 and SGST ₹55,000

citation.ref: Section 52(1) with its Explanation defining net value of taxable supplies, and the notified rate of 0.25 per cent central tax with 0.25 per cent State tax

items.scenario: An operator's October 2025 figures, every supply intra-State in Karnataka and every payment collected by the operator. Registered sellers supplied goods worth ₹2 crore through the platform, of which ₹20 lakh worth came back to those same sellers in the month. A composition dealer supplied goods worth ₹5,00,000 through it. A registered hotel chain supplied rooms worth ₹30,00,000. A company running omnibuses supplied rides worth ₹5,00,000. Four further streams — cab rides ₹20 lakh, an individual's omnibus rides ₹3 lakh, an unregistered guest house's rooms ₹4 lakh and unregistered riders' local delivery ₹6 lakh, ₹33 lakh together — are ones on which the operator itself pays the tax as the deemed supplier.

items.stem: Which set of answers is right?

options.text: Twenty days after the month for both; the annual statement by 30 September after the year; a rectification any time within three years; and thirty days for the notice
options.misconception: borrows the ordinary return calendar, where twenty days and 30 September do belong, and applies it to a collection statement that runs on its own dates
options.why: None of those dates is this statement's. Twenty days is a monthly return's clock, not a collector's. The three-year figure is the outer limit for filing the statement at all, which is a different question from how long an error may be corrected. And the answer to the officer's notice has a shorter clock than thirty days.
keywords: the three-year figure is the outer limit for filing the statement at all, which is a different question from how long an error may be corrected

options.text: Ten days after the month for the money, the statement going in with the annual one; and thirty days for the notice
options.misconception: separates the payment from the statement, when the section puts both on the same ten-day clock, and stretches the notice reply to a month
options.why: The payment and the monthly statement are due together, and the platform cannot in fact file the statement until the whole collected amount has been discharged. The notice is on a shorter clock still: an officer not below the rank of Deputy Commissioner may call for the volume of supplies made through the platform or the stock the suppliers hold, and the operator must furnish it within fifteen working days, with a general penalty waiting if he does not.
keywords: the operator must furnish it within fifteen working days

options.text: Ten days after the month for both; the annual statement by 31 December; a rectification at any time before the notice of any audit; and fifteen working days for the notice
options.misconception: gets three of the four right but reads the self-correction window as open until somebody comes looking, rather than closing on a date
options.why: The right to put an omission right is narrow twice over. It is only for a discrepancy the operator finds on his own, so anything thrown up by a scrutiny, an audit, an inspection or an enforcement proceeding is outside it altogether. And even for what he does find himself the door shuts on a fixed date rather than on an event.
keywords: it is only for a discrepancy the operator finds on his own

options.text: Ten days after the month for the money and for the statement; the annual statement by 31 December after the year; a rectification no later than 30 November after the year or the annual statement, whichever comes first; and fifteen working days for the notice
options.why: The amount collected reaches the Government within ten days after the end of the month, and the monthly statement in Form GSTR-8 runs on the very same clock. The annual statement is due by 31 December following the financial year. An omission the operator finds himself may be put right in a later month's statement with interest, but no later than 30 November following the financial year or the day the annual statement is filed, whichever falls earlier. The Deputy Commissioner's notice is answered within fifteen working days.
keywords: the amount collected reaches the Government within ten days after the end of the month
the monthly statement in Form GSTR-8 runs on the very same clock
the annual statement is due by 31 December following the financial year
no later than 30 November following the financial year or the day the annual statement is filed

citation.ref: Section 52(3), (4), (5) and (12) read with rule 67, and section 47 for the statement

items.scenario: An operator has collected tax at source for October 2025. Its finance team wants four dates settled before the month closes: when the money must reach the Government and when the monthly statement is due; when the annual statement for the year is due; how late an omission in the October statement may still be put right; and how long the operator has to answer a notice from an officer not below the rank of Deputy Commissioner asking what stock its suppliers are holding.

items.stem: What must the operator actually do?

options.text: Refuse the Tamil Nadu listing, stop collecting on his in-State sales too, and collect on the reverse charge supply
options.misconception: has both halves inverted — dropping the collection where it is required and making one where the supplier owes nothing
options.why: The in-State sales are exactly what the notification tells the operator to collect on. And on a supply where the recipient is liable, the supplier has no tax to pay, so collecting a slice of it at source takes money from a person against a liability that does not exist and leaves it stranded in his cash ledger.
keywords: on a supply where the recipient is liable, the supplier has no tax to pay

options.text: Open the listing and collect nothing from him, a composition taxpayer being outside the collection at source
options.misconception: treats the flat composition rate as a substitute for every other machinery, when the special procedure exists precisely because a composition dealer may sell goods on a platform
options.why: There is no exemption from collection at source for a composition supplier of goods. The very fact that a special procedure had to be written for him shows he is inside it: the notification tells the operator to collect on his goods and to declare them, and it adds a restriction on top rather than lifting one.
keywords: the notification tells the operator to collect on his goods and to declare them

options.text: Open the Tamil Nadu listing and collect at source on those sales as well
options.misconception: thinks the operator's job is to collect on whatever the dealer sells, when the platform is required to prevent one class of sale outright
options.why: A composition supplier cannot make an outward supply across a State boundary at all, so there is nothing for the operator to collect on — the sale should never have happened. The obligation put on the platform is a preventive one: it must build the check into the system rather than let the sale through and account for it afterwards.
keywords: a composition supplier cannot make an outward supply across a State boundary at all

options.text: Refuse the Tamil Nadu listing, collect at source on the dealer's in-State sales and report them; collect nothing on the reverse charge supply or on the imported goods
options.why: A composition taxpayer may sell goods through an operator, though not services, and the special procedure notified under section 148 by Notification No. 36/2023-CT binds the operator on three counts: it must not allow an inter-State supply of goods through it by such a person, it collects tax at source on the goods he does sell, and it declares those supplies in Form GSTR-8. The platform therefore has to carry the check that stops a Tamil Nadu buyer. Separately, nothing is collected where the recipient pays on reverse charge, because there is no supplier's liability to secure, and nothing on imported goods, which the Customs Act deals with.
keywords: the special procedure notified under section 148 by Notification No. 36/2023-CT binds the operator
it must not allow an inter-State supply of goods through it by such a person
nothing is collected where the recipient pays on reverse charge

citation.ref: Section 52(1) read with section 10(2)(d) and the special procedure under section 148 in Notification No. 36/2023-CT dated 4 August 2023

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Karnataka sells goods through an operator's platform. He asks the operator to open his listings to buyers in Tamil Nadu, and to stop collecting anything at source from him because a composition taxpayer pays a flat rate on his own turnover anyway. In the same month the platform also carries a supply on which the buyer, not the seller, is the one who pays the tax, and it handles goods a buyer is bringing in from abroad.

items.stem: What does the simplified route give it, and what does it cost?

options.text: Registration in seven working days after a physical verification, Aadhaar only shortening the paperwork
options.misconception: keeps the site visit in the picture, when the whole point of the route is that a successful Aadhaar authentication replaces it
options.why: The authentication is what stands in for the visit. Where the person opts for it and completes it, the portal grants the registration without anybody going to the premises, and it does so on a three-working-day clock rather than the longer one that applies where verification is needed.
keywords: where the person opts for it and completes it, the portal grants the registration without anybody going to the premises

options.text: Registration in three working days, and the restriction also stops a branch in another State from being registered
options.misconception: reads the restriction as one registration per PAN across the country, when it is counted State by State
options.why: The limit is one registration per State or Union territory, and each State is looked at on its own. A person on this route in Telangana may take a registration in another State as well, and may take it under this route too if the figures there also stay inside the ceiling.
keywords: the limit is one registration per State or Union territory, and each State is looked at on its own

options.text: Registration in three working days, and the warehouse may still be registered separately under rule 11
options.misconception: takes the route as pure speed with nothing surrendered, missing that it overrides the rule allowing separate registrations inside a State
options.why: The restriction is the price of the route and it is written into it. The one-per-State limit overrides the separate registrations for multiple places of business that rule 11 would otherwise permit. A person who needs those separate registrations has to come in by the ordinary door instead.
keywords: the one-per-State limit overrides the separate registrations for multiple places of business that rule 11 would otherwise permit

options.text: Registration in three working days with no visit — but the warehouse cannot have a registration of its own
options.why: Once the Aadhaar number is authenticated, registration is granted electronically by the common portal within three working days of the application, and there is no physical verification of the premises. What is given up is the freedom rule 11 otherwise allows: under this option there may be only one registration per State or Union territory against the same PAN, so the Telangana warehouse cannot be registered apart from the shop. Anantha has to choose between speed and separate registrations within the State.
keywords: registration is granted electronically by the common portal within three working days of the application
there may be only one registration per State or Union territory against the same PAN

citation.ref: Rule 14A, in force from 1 November 2025, read with rule 8, rule 10(1) and rule 11

items.scenario: Anantha Traders applies for registration in Telangana in December 2025. Its monthly output tax on sales to registered dealers will be about ₹1.6 lakh and it has opted for and completed Aadhaar authentication. It also runs a warehouse elsewhere in Telangana that it wants registered separately from the shop, and it is bracing for an officer to visit both before anything is granted.

items.stem: What must the firm do, and will it get through as things stand?

options.text: Apply to cancel this registration and take a fresh one
options.misconception: confuses coming off an option with ending the registration itself, and would surrender a live registration to do it
options.why: Withdrawal is from the option, not from the register. The registration survives it — the same number, the same effective date — and only the restriction and the ceiling fall away. Cancelling and re-registering would break the trail of returns and start the whole verification again for no purpose.
keywords: withdrawal is from the option, not from the register

options.text: File the withdrawal application — one tax period's return is the whole condition, and it is met
options.misconception: reads the one-tax-period requirement as the entire test and misses the second half, which asks for everything that has fallen due
options.why: The condition has two limbs joined together, not one. A single return proves the person has actually started filing; the rest of the requirement is that nothing due since registration is outstanding. A firm two returns behind fails the second limb even though it clears the first.
keywords: the rest of the requirement is that nothing due since registration is outstanding

options.text: File an application for withdrawal — and it will not be allowed yet, the two missing returns standing in the way
options.why: Leaving the option is a formal step: the person files an application for withdrawal, and it is allowed only on two conditions. He must have furnished the return for at least one tax period AND every return that fell due from the effective date of registration to the date of the application — so one return out of three is not enough. And no cancellation proceedings under section 29 may have been begun against him. Any change in the particulars given at registration also has to be amended before the application goes in.
keywords: the person files an application for withdrawal, and it is allowed only on two conditions
he must have furnished the return for at least one tax period
no cancellation proceedings under section 29 may have been begun against him

options.text: Nothing — the ceiling is a test for getting in and does not bind afterwards
options.misconception: treats the ₹2.5 lakh figure as an entry qualification, when it is the standing condition of staying on the route
options.why: The ceiling governs while the person is on the route, which is why there is a way out of it at all and why outgrowing it is the ordinary reason for leaving. A person who simply starts declaring more without coming off the option is declaring something the option does not let him declare.
keywords: the ceiling governs while the person is on the route, which is why there is a way out of it at all

citation.ref: Rule 14A on withdrawal, read with section 29

items.scenario: A firm has been on the simplified route for five months and its monthly output tax on sales to registered dealers is about to cross the ceiling. It has filed the return for its first tax period; two further returns that fell due since have not gone in. Nobody has begun anything against it. Its adviser says it can simply start declaring the larger figure from next month and sort the paperwork later.

items.stem: From when may the first firm declare the larger figure, and what becomes of the second firm's application?

options.text: From 1 May 2026, the month the ceiling was first crossed; the second firm's application is deemed approved once the period passes
options.misconception: backdates the relief to when the business actually outgrew the option, which is the one thing the rule says cannot be done
options.why: Backdating is refused in terms: the firm cannot raise its output tax liability beyond the limit for any period before the first day of the month following the order. The consequence is real and worth seeing — a firm that crosses the ceiling and is slow to apply spends those months unable to declare what it actually owes.
keywords: the firm cannot raise its output tax liability beyond the limit for any period before the first day of the month following the order

options.text: From 1 July 2026; the second firm's application is deemed approved, the cancellation being a separate matter
options.misconception: gets the date right but keeps the deemed approval alive, when the rule switches it off for exactly this situation
options.why: The two are not separate matters. The rule disapplies the deemed approval where cancellation proceedings have been begun after the withdrawal application and are pending, so silence from the officer cannot be read as consent. Without that, a person facing cancellation could leave the option by simply waiting out the clock.
keywords: the rule disapplies the deemed approval where cancellation proceedings have been begun after the withdrawal application

options.text: From 12 June 2026, the date of the order; the second firm's application waits until the cancellation proceedings end
options.misconception: starts the larger figure on the day of the order rather than on the first day of the month after it, and treats a pending cancellation as a pause instead of a refusal
options.why: The rule does not run from the order but from the month after it, so a part-month is never split. And a pending cancellation is not a delay for the withdrawal application to wait out — the application goes, because the officer is not going to release somebody from an option while he is considering taking the registration away altogether.
keywords: the rule does not run from the order but from the month after it, so a part-month is never split

options.text: From 1 July 2026, and nothing earlier; the second firm's application is rejected and no deemed approval saves it
options.why: After the order allowing withdrawal, the firm may declare output tax on supplies made to registered persons above ₹2.5 lakh from the first day of the succeeding month after the order, and it may not raise the figure for any period before that — so May and June stay inside the ceiling and 1 July 2026 is the start. Where cancellation proceedings are begun after a withdrawal application is filed and are still pending, the application is rejected, and the deemed approval under rule 9(5) does not apply to it.
keywords: the firm may declare output tax on supplies made to registered persons above ₹2.5 lakh from the first day of the succeeding month after the order
the application is rejected, and the deemed approval under rule 9(5) does not apply to it

citation.ref: Rule 14A on the effect of the withdrawal order, read with rule 9(5)

items.scenario: A proper officer allows one firm's withdrawal from the simplified route by an order dated 12 June 2026. That firm's output tax on supplies to registered dealers had already run above the ceiling in May and will again in June. A second firm's withdrawal application is still pending when the officer starts cancellation proceedings against it, and its accountant is counting on the application being treated as approved once the usual period runs out.

items.stem: What can Tanmayi do for those two buyers, and what happens afterwards?

options.text: Nothing before the quarterly statement — a quarterly filer reports once a quarter and that is the whole of it
options.misconception: reads quarterly filing as a wall between a supplier and his buyer's credit, which is the problem the facility was built to solve
options.why: Without the facility a buyer purchasing from a quarterly filer would have to wait to the end of the quarter for his credit, purely because of how often his supplier files. That delay is the reason the facility exists, and telling a buyer to wait when the supplier could have furnished the invoice is a choice, not a rule.
keywords: a buyer purchasing from a quarterly filer would have to wait to the end of the quarter for his credit

options.text: Furnish just those two through the Invoice Furnishing Facility by the 13th of November; they reach the buyers' October statements and are not repeated with the quarter
options.why: The facility is open for the first two months of the quarter and is an option, not an obligation — a quarterly filer may ignore it and report everything once a quarter instead. Tanmayi may pick out the two invoices those buyers need and furnish them up to the 13th of November, leaving the other ten for the quarterly statement. Invoices furnished this way appear in the recipient's Form GSTR-2A and Form GSTR-2B for that month, so the two buyers take their credit in October, and they are not furnished again in the quarterly statement.
keywords: the facility is open for the first two months of the quarter and is an option, not an obligation
furnish them up to the 13th of November
appear in the recipient's Form GSTR-2A and Form GSTR-2B for that month
they are not furnished again in the quarterly statement

options.text: Furnish the two by the 13th of November and furnish them again with the other ten in the quarterly statement
options.misconception: treats the facility as a preview of the quarterly statement rather than as a furnishing that stands on its own
options.why: What has gone through the facility in the first two months is not reported a second time. Repeating it would double the outward supplies on the record and hand the buyer a second copy of a credit he has already taken, which the reconciliation would then have to unpick.
keywords: what has gone through the facility in the first two months is not reported a second time

options.text: Furnish all twelve by the 11th of November, the facility being all or nothing for the month
options.misconception: borrows the monthly filer's 11th and assumes the whole month must go through together, when the supplier chooses which invoices to send
options.why: The 11th is the monthly filer's date; a quarterly filer's dates are the 13th. And the choice is invoice by invoice — the supplier furnishes such of the details as he considers necessary, which is exactly what lets Tanmayi help two buyers without touching the other ten.
keywords: the choice is invoice by invoice — the supplier furnishes such of the details as he considers necessary

citation.ref: Rule 59(2) and rule 59(3), with the quarterly time limit for Form GSTR-1

items.scenario: Tanmayi Ceramics, registered in Gujarat and inside the quarterly return scheme, issues twelve invoices to registered buyers in October 2026. Two of those buyers want their invoices to reach their own October statements so they can take the credit that month rather than waiting. Tanmayi's accountant says nothing can be done before the quarterly statement, and that anything furnished early would have to be furnished all over again with the quarter.

items.stem: How much of the ₹70 lakh can go through the facility and by when, and what does the missed October cost?

options.text: Nothing at all — a month once missed shuts the facility for the whole quarter, and the ₹70 lakh waits
options.misconception: treats skipping one month as forfeiting the facility, when each month stands on its own
options.why: Each of the first two months is a separate window, opening on the first of the following month and closing on the 13th. Missing October's window has no effect on November's. The only thing skipping a month does is push those invoices into the quarterly statement.
keywords: each of the first two months is a separate window, opening on the first of the following month and closing on the 13th

options.text: All ₹70 lakh by the 13th of December, the ceiling being for the quarter rather than for each month; and a late fee for October
options.misconception: pools the ceiling across the quarter, when it is measured separately in each of the two months
options.why: The ceiling is applied in each of the first two months on its own, so an unused October allowance does not roll into November. That is what leaves ₹20 lakh over here, and it is why a supplier with lumpy months plans which invoices go through the facility rather than assuming they all will.
keywords: the ceiling is applied in each of the first two months on its own, so an unused October allowance does not roll into November

options.text: Up to ₹50 lakh by the 13th of December, and a late fee of ₹200 a day for October
options.misconception: gets the ceiling right but charges the late fee that belongs to a return, when the facility is not one
options.why: A late fee is the price of a return furnished late. This is not a return, it is optional, and after the 13th it simply closes rather than becoming overdue — there is nothing left to be late with. A supplier who skips it pays nothing and reports everything in the quarterly statement instead.
keywords: after the 13th it simply closes rather than becoming overdue

options.text: Up to ₹50 lakh by the 13th of December, the rest waiting for the quarterly statement; and nothing for October
options.why: The facility carries a ceiling of ₹50 lakh of invoices in each of the first two months of the quarter, so November's ₹70 lakh cannot all go through it. Up to ₹50 lakh may be furnished by the 13th of December and the remaining ₹20 lakh waits for the quarterly statement, which for the October-December quarter is due by the 13th of January. October costs nothing: there is no late fee for not using the facility, because it is not a return and it cannot be filed late at all.
keywords: the facility carries a ceiling of ₹50 lakh of invoices in each of the first two months of the quarter
up to ₹50 lakh may be furnished by the 13th of December
there is no late fee for not using the facility, because it is not a return

citation.ref: Rule 59(2) with the ₹50 lakh monthly ceiling, read with section 47

items.scenario: A quarterly filer in Gujarat issues invoices worth ₹70 lakh to registered buyers in November 2026 and wants as much of that credit as possible in the buyers' hands in November itself. It also let October go by without using the facility at all, and its accountant is bracing for a late fee on the October omission.

items.stem: Which of the three objections holds?

options.text: None of the three
options.misconception: waves the notice period away as a formality, when it is a fixed period counted in working days and it has not been met
options.why: Fifteen working days is a real period and it is counted in working days rather than in calendar days, so it is longer than three weeks in practice. Nine calendar days between the notice and the visit does not come close, and the answer is to move the visit rather than to argue that the period does not matter.
keywords: fifteen working days is a real period and it is counted in working days rather than in calendar days

options.text: All three
options.misconception: reads a departmental audit as needing the taxpayer's cooperation on every term, when only the notice period is the taxpayer's protection
options.why: The section gives the registered person one guarantee about the start of an audit and it is the notice period. What the audit covers and where it is conducted are the Commissioner's to decide, and the person is instead required to help — to make the records available, to answer what is asked, and to let the work finish on time.
keywords: the section gives the registered person one guarantee about the start of an audit and it is the notice period

options.text: Only the objection about the notice
options.why: Two of the three are wrong on the face of the section. The period may be a financial year, a part of one, or several years together, so taking 2024-25 and 2025-26 in one exercise is ordinary. And the audit may be done in the officer's own office, or at the registered person's place of business, so the visit is the department's choice and not the company's. The notice objection is good: the notice must be issued not less than fifteen working days before the audit is conducted, and 1 July to 10 July is nowhere near that once weekends and holidays are taken out.
keywords: the period may be a financial year, a part of one, or several years together
the audit may be done in the officer's own office, or at the registered person's place of business
the notice must be issued not less than fifteen working days before the audit is conducted

options.text: Only the objection to the visit
options.misconception: confuses this audit with the desk exercise of scrutinising returns, which does happen from the officer's own office
options.why: Scrutiny of returns is the desk exercise; an audit under this section is expressly allowed at the person's premises, which is the whole reason the date of institution at the place of business is one of the two candidates for when the audit is treated as having commenced.
keywords: an audit under this section is expressly allowed at the person's premises

citation.ref: Section 65(1), (2) and (3) read with rule 101(2)

items.scenario: A Commissioner in Kerala decides to audit a food processor for the two financial years 2024-25 and 2025-26 together. The notice goes out on 1 July 2026 and the team plans to start at the company's factory on 10 July 2026. The company objects on three grounds: that the department cannot take two years in one exercise, that it cannot come to the factory at all and must work from its own office, and that in any event it has not been given enough notice.

items.stem: From whom may each amount be recovered, and how much from each person?

options.text: Jointly and severally, but only for dues determined before the partition and the dissolution
options.misconception: adds a condition about when the amount was determined, which both sub-sections expressly rule out
options.why: Both sub-sections say the liability holds whether the tax was determined before the event and remained unpaid or is determined after it. Any other reading would reward speed — divide the family or dissolve the firm before the department finishes its assessment and the money would be gone.
keywords: the liability holds whether the tax was determined before the event and remained unpaid or is determined after it

options.text: From nobody — both taxable persons ceased to exist before the amounts were determined
options.misconception: treats the end of the taxable person as the end of the dues, which is precisely the gap these provisions were written to close
options.why: These sections exist because a taxable person can be dissolved or divided while its tax cannot. They say in terms that it makes no difference whether the amount was determined before the event and left unpaid or determined after it, so a family cannot partition its way out and a firm cannot dissolve its way out.
keywords: it makes no difference whether the amount was determined before the event and left unpaid or determined after it

options.text: The whole ₹2 lakh from any member or group of members, and the whole ₹6 lakh from any former partner
options.why: On partition of the property of a Hindu undivided family or an association of persons, each member or group of members is jointly and severally liable for the dues up to the time of the partition. On dissolution of a firm, every person who was a partner is liable in the same way for the dues up to the time of the dissolution. Joint and several means the whole amount may be taken from any one of them, who then settles with the others himself, and it does not matter that the amounts were determined months after the event.
keywords: each member or group of members is jointly and severally liable for the dues up to the time of the partition
on dissolution of a firm, every person who was a partner is liable in the same way
the whole amount may be taken from any one of them

options.text: Each member and each former partner for his own share only
options.misconception: reads joint and several liability as a division of the debt, when it is the opposite — each person answers for all of it
options.why: A share-wise liability would leave the department chasing every member separately and losing whatever any one of them could not pay. Joint and several liability puts that risk on the members and partners rather than on the revenue: each is answerable for the whole, and the settling-up between them is their own affair.
keywords: each is answerable for the whole, and the settling-up between them is their own affair

citation.ref: Section 93(2) and section 93(3)

items.scenario: Two events in one district. A Hindu undivided family that ran a registered trading business partitioned its property in September 2025, and ₹2 lakh of tax up to that date was determined only in March 2026. A firm was dissolved in October 2025 owing ₹6 lakh, determined in February 2026. The eldest coparcener says nothing can be recovered because neither the family nor the firm exists any more, and one former partner says he can be asked for his profit share of the ₹6 lakh and not a rupee beyond it.

items.stem: On whom is the tax levied, and from whom is it recovered?

options.text: On the aunt but not on the receiver, a court-appointed receiver answering to the court rather than to the department
options.misconception: splits the two situations, when there are two sections in identical terms and the second exists precisely to cover court appointees
options.why: The second section names the Court of Wards, the Administrator General, the Official Trustee and any receiver or manager appointed by or under an order of a court, including anybody who in fact manages the business whatever he is called. Being answerable to a court is no answer to the department.
keywords: the Official Trustee and any receiver or manager appointed by or under an order of a court

options.text: On nobody until the minor is of age and the estate is released to the trader
options.misconception: treats incapacity as a suspension of the tax, when the provisions exist to make sure a running business is taxed while it runs
options.why: The business is trading and making supplies now, and the tax on those supplies falls now. Suspending it would leave a business operating outside the tax for as long as the incapacity or the minority lasts, which is exactly the outcome these sections are written to prevent.
keywords: the business is trading and making supplies now, and the tax on those supplies falls now

options.text: On the minor and on the incapacitated trader personally, the aunt and the receiver being no more than agents
options.misconception: keeps the liability on the beneficial owner, missing that the section moves both the levy and the recovery onto the person actually running the business
options.why: The words are that the tax shall be levied upon and be recoverable from the guardian, trustee, agent or receiver. It is not merely a collection mechanism laid over somebody else's liability — the person running the business is the one assessed, which is what makes the section work against a minor who cannot be assessed at all.
keywords: the person running the business is the one assessed

options.text: On the aunt and on the receiver, each answering as the person whose business it is would have answered
options.why: Where a business is carried on by a guardian, a trustee or an agent for a minor or another incapacitated person, the tax, interest and penalty are levied upon and recovered from whoever is running it. And the measure is fixed: it is recovered in like manner and to the same extent as it would have been from the minor himself, as if he were a major conducting the business. The next section says the same thing about an estate under the control of a Court of Wards, an Administrator General, an Official Trustee, or a receiver or manager appointed by a court.
keywords: where a business is carried on by a guardian, a trustee or an agent for a minor
it is recovered in like manner and to the same extent as it would have been from the minor himself
an estate under the control of a Court of Wards, an Administrator General, an Official Trustee, or a receiver or manager appointed by a court

citation.ref: Section 91 and section 92

items.scenario: A minor owns a registered trading business that his aunt runs on his behalf and for his benefit, taking nothing for herself. In the same town a court has appointed a receiver over the estate of a trader who can no longer manage his own affairs, and the receiver keeps that business going. Tax falls due on both businesses. The department is told it must wait — from the aunt, until the boy is of age, and from the receiver, until the court releases the estate.

items.stem: Who answers for the dues of the earlier period?

options.text: The young man and the beneficiary
options.why: Where the taxable person is a guardian running a ward's business for him, or a trustee running one under a trust for a beneficiary, and the guardianship or trust is terminated, the ward or the beneficiary becomes liable for the tax, interest or penalty due from that taxable person. The liability follows the business to the person it was being run for. Every part of the section gives way to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
keywords: the guardianship or trust is terminated, the ward or the beneficiary becomes liable for the tax, interest or penalty due from that taxable person
every part of the section gives way to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

options.text: Nobody — the liability ends with the arrangement
options.misconception: assumes a debt attached to an office disappears when the office does, when the section says exactly where it goes instead
options.why: Nothing in this chapter lets a liability evaporate because an arrangement ended. Each section names the person it moves to — a transferee, a director, a partner, a member, a legal representative — and on the end of a guardianship or a trust it names the ward or the beneficiary.
keywords: each section names the person it moves to — a transferee, a director, a partner, a member, a legal representative

options.text: The ward and the beneficiary, but only for dues determined before the termination
options.misconception: imports a cut-off by date of determination that this sub-section, like its neighbours, does not carry
options.why: The sub-section speaks of the tax, interest or penalty due from the taxable person, not of what had been quantified by the day the arrangement ended. A determination made afterwards for an earlier period is still a due of that period, and it lands on the ward or the beneficiary in the same way.
keywords: a determination made afterwards for an earlier period is still a due of that period

options.text: The former guardian and the former trustee, the liability having attached to them when the tax fell due
options.misconception: is right about who was liable during the arrangement and wrong about what termination does, which is to move the liability on
options.why: While the arrangement ran, the guardian and the trustee were indeed the persons assessed. Termination is the event the section is about, and what it does is shift the liability to the person the business was being run for. That is fair to the guardian, who was answering for somebody else's business and takes nothing out of it.
keywords: shift the liability to the person the business was being run for

citation.ref: Section 93(4) with the opening words of section 93

items.scenario: Two arrangements end in the same month. A guardianship over a minor's business ends in March when the boy comes of age, and a trust under which a trustee ran a business for a beneficiary is wound up the same month. Tax, interest and penalty are outstanding for the period before each ended. The former guardian and the former trustee both say their liability ended with their office, and the young man says he never ran the business and cannot be asked for anything.

items.stem: Can he enter either place, and what must be in his hands first?

options.text: He may walk into the godown on his own, an inspection of one's own assessee being routine, but needs authorisation for the transporter
options.misconception: treats a visit to one's own assessee as administration rather than a statutory power, when the authorisation is the source of the power for every place the section names
options.why: The section does not grade the places it reaches. The same authorisation is what opens the assessee's godown and the transporter's yard, and without it neither is open. An officer who walks in on his own has not carried out an inspection under the Act at all, and what he finds is exposed to exactly that argument.

options.text: He may enter both places once he writes the tip-off into his file, a recorded suspicion being the reason the section asks for
options.misconception: equates writing a suspicion down with holding a belief, when recording changes the paper and not the material behind it
options.why: Recording a thing does not raise it. The standard sits above mere suspicion and below evidence in hand: knowledge of facts that would make a reasonable person, knowing those same facts, draw the same conclusion. An anonymous rival's word, with no stock statement and no return checked against it, is the same suspicion after it is written down as it was before.

options.text: Neither, until an officer senior enough authorises him in writing, and that officer may sign only on a belief resting on material
options.why: The power to inspect is not put in the hands of the officer who wants to use it. It takes a written authorisation from an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner, and that officer may sign only where he has reasons to believe that the taxable person has hidden a supply or hidden stock, taken credit beyond what he is entitled to, or broken the Act to escape tax — or that a transporter, or the keeper of a warehouse or godown, is holding goods on which tax has escaped. On that one authorisation the proper officer may inspect the trader's own place of business and the transporter's premises alike. A rival's tip-off, standing alone, is a suspicion, and the threshold is higher than that: it asks what a reasonable person would conclude from the material actually in hand.
keywords: an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner
he has reasons to believe that the taxable person has hidden a supply
the proper officer may inspect the trader's own place of business

options.text: Nothing may be entered without a warrant from a magistrate, the criminal procedure code governing all searches
options.misconception: brings the criminal procedure in at the wrong stage — it shapes how a search is conducted, not who may authorise entry
options.why: The criminal procedure code is picked up for the manner of a search and a seizure, so far as it can apply. Who may authorise entry is settled inside the tax Act itself, and the officer it names is a Joint Commissioner or above, not a magistrate.

citation.ref: Section 67(1)

items.scenario: A range officer in Panipat has been told by a rival trader that Manthan Textiles is holding far more cloth in its godown than its returns account for, and that the transporter who moves its bales is warehousing some of it off the books. He wants to walk into the godown and into the transporter's yard, look at the stock and go through the registers. He has the tip-off and nothing else on file, and no paper from anybody senior to him.

items.stem: What may the officers do about the three things they have found?

options.text: Nothing may be seized until an order of confiscation has been passed, seizure being the step that follows confiscation
options.misconception: runs the sequence backwards, when what the section needs is that the goods are liable to confiscation, not that they have been confiscated
options.why: Liability to confiscation is a condition for seizure, not a finished order. If the order had to come first there would be nothing left to seize by the time it arrived, and the goods would be gone. The confiscation proceeding runs afterwards, on the goods already held.

options.text: The almirah stays shut without the occupant's consent, and his refusal ends the search there
options.misconception: makes the person being searched the gatekeeper of the search, which would leave the power to whoever is willing to co-operate
options.why: A power that stopped at a locked door would protect the one trader who bothered to lock it. Where access to a room, an almirah or a box is denied and there is reason to think goods, accounts or documents are concealed inside, the officer may break it open.

options.text: Seize the unregistered cloth and the notes, break the almirah open, and order that what cannot be carried away is not to be moved
options.why: Search and seizure turn on the same officer having reasons to believe that goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things that in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to a proceeding under the Act, are secreted in any place. Cloth kept out of the stock register is goods of the first kind, because failing to account for goods on which tax is due is one of the listed grounds of confiscation, and the delivery notes are things of the second. Where it is not practicable to seize a thing, the officer may instead direct the owner or custodian not to remove it or part with it without his permission. And where access is refused he may break open a door or an almirah, and he may seal the premises.
keywords: goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things
he may break open a door or an almirah, and he may seal the premises

options.text: The cloth on the loom must be left entirely alone, seizure being the only power the section gives over goods
options.misconception: reads the section as all or nothing, missing the detention direction written for goods that cannot practicably be taken away
options.why: The section anticipates exactly this. Where the goods cannot sensibly be lifted, the officer leaves them where they are and puts the owner or custodian under a direction not to move them or part with them without his permission. The goods stay put and stay reachable.

citation.ref: Section 67(2) and (4), read with section 130

items.scenario: The authorisation is signed and the officers go in. In a locked room at the back they find bales of cloth that appear in no stock register, and a bundle of delivery notes. The man in charge of the room will not open a steel almirah standing in it. Some of the cloth is already loaded on a loom and cannot be carried away.

items.stem: What can the trader get back, and on what terms?

options.text: It must wait out the six months; provisional release is open only for goods that would perish
options.misconception: confuses the relief given to the trader with the power given to the Government to dispose of perishable goods early
options.why: Provisional release is not limited by what the goods are. Any seized goods go back provisionally against a bond and security, or against payment of the tax, interest and penalty. The perishable and hazardous rule is a different thing entirely: it lets the department sell such goods off soon after seizure rather than watch them rot.

options.text: Paying the tax, the interest and the penalty closes the case as well as freeing the goods
options.misconception: reads a payment made to get goods released as a settlement of the liability, when it only substitutes money for the goods
options.why: Paying to release is a way of getting the stock back on the shelf. It does not stand in for an adjudication, does not stop a notice, and does not fix what is finally owed. The demand and the penalty are still determined in the ordinary way.

options.text: The six months can be extended for as long as the investigation runs, so nothing goes back yet
options.misconception: reads the extension as open-ended, when the section caps it at one further period of the same length
options.why: The extension is bounded twice over. It takes sufficient cause, and it buys at most six more months. Once that outer year has passed with no notice, the goods go back whatever stage the investigation has reached.

options.text: It can have them out now against security, and in any case the goods go back to it, no notice having come inside the statutory window
options.why: Two different reliefs run at once. The first is immediate: seized goods are released provisionally on the person executing a bond and furnishing security in the prescribed amount, or on his paying the tax, the interest and the penalty that apply. The second is a clock on the department. Where no notice about the seized goods is issued within six months of the seizure, the goods are returned to the person from whose possession they were taken. That period can be stretched by the proper officer for sufficient cause, but by no more than a further six months, and stretching it takes an act of his — silence does not extend anything.
keywords: on the person executing a bond and furnishing security in the prescribed amount
no notice about the seized goods is issued within six months of the seizure
the goods are returned to the person from whose possession they were taken

citation.ref: Section 67(6) and (7)

items.scenario: The cloth was seized on 10 May 2026. Manthan Textiles has its wedding season coming and needs the stock on its shelves now. By 20 December 2026 the department has issued no notice at all about the seized goods, and has not recorded anything extending its own time.

items.stem: What is the trader entitled to ask for?

options.text: The department may hold the books until the appeal against any demand is finally over
options.misconception: reads retention as running with the dispute, when it runs with the need to examine the record
options.why: Retention is measured by necessity, not by how long the litigation lasts. Once the examination and the proceedings no longer need a document it goes back, and a document not relied on in the case goes back within thirty days of the notice.

options.text: No copies at all — seized records are evidence and cannot be handled by the person they were taken from
options.misconception: treats the right to copies as a favour that would spoil the evidence, when the section gives it and guards it by requiring an officer to be present
options.why: The books are that trader's own accounting record and he still has returns to file from them. The section resolves the tension by allowing copies rather than the books, in an officer's presence, at a place and time the officer picks. Only a real risk to the investigation displaces it.

options.text: Copies of the books, taken in front of an officer at a place and time the officer names, and the return of the books once they are no longer needed
options.why: The person out of whose custody documents or books were taken is entitled to make copies of them, or to take extracts, in the presence of an authorised officer, at the place and time the proper officer indicates.
