That entitlement gives way in one case only: where in the officer's opinion the copying would prejudicially affect the investigation. The books themselves are retained only so long as necessary for their examination and for the proceedings, and where they are not relied on in the case they go back within thirty days of the show cause notice. As for how the premises were gone through, the search and the seizure follow, so far as they can, the procedure the criminal procedure code lays down for a search.
keywords: entitled to make copies of them, or to take extracts, in the presence of an authorised officer
retained only so long as necessary for their examination
the procedure the criminal procedure code lays down for a search

options.text: Copies only after the show cause notice is served, since until then there is nothing for him to answer
options.misconception: ties the right to copies to the stage of the case, when the section ties it to the seizure
options.why: The entitlement arises on the seizure, not on the notice. That is the point of it — the trader has to keep filing returns and running the business through the months before any notice, and he cannot do that out of books he no longer holds.

citation.ref: Section 67(5), (10) and (11)

items.scenario: The ledgers went with the officers. Manthan's accountant has a return to file next week and the figures he needs are in those books. He asks for them back and is told the department will hold them until the case is over. He also asks under what procedure his premises were gone through.

items.stem: On what does the classification turn?

options.text: On the words of the headings read with the notes of their own section or chapter; the titles decide nothing and the other chapter's note cannot be borrowed
options.why: Every classification starts at the first rule and goes no further if that rule settles it. The titles carried by a section, a chapter or a sub-chapter are given for ease of reference and no more, and they carry no legal force. What decides the matter is the terms of the headings together with any relative section or chapter notes, and the later rules are reached only where those headings and notes do not themselves require otherwise. A note belongs to the section or chapter it is printed in, so a note out of one chapter cannot be used to read the entries of another.
keywords: the titles carried by a section, a chapter or a sub-chapter are given for ease of reference and no more
the terms of the headings together with any relative section or chapter notes

options.text: On rules 2 to 6 applied in order, the first rule being the residual one used when the others fail
options.misconception: inverts the ladder, treating the opening rule as a last resort when it is the first test and usually the last
options.why: The order runs the other way. The matter is tested first against the headings and their notes, and only where that leaves it unsettled do the later rules come in. Most goods never leave the first rule at all.

options.text: On the note in the other chapter, since both chapters deal with the same material and the notes must be read together
options.misconception: reads chapter notes as general law running across the tariff, when each is drafted for the entries beneath it
options.why: A note is written to control the entries under it and is measured against those entries alone. Reading a note across chapters would let a definition drawn for one trade decide a dispute in another, and the rule shuts that door in terms.

options.text: On the chapter title, that being the tariff's own description of what the chapter is for
options.misconception: takes the title as the tariff speaking, when the tariff itself says the titles are there only to help a reader find his way
options.why: A title is a signpost. It tells a reader roughly where to look and it settles nothing when he gets there. Two goods that answer the same title can end up in different headings, and a good that answers no title can still be caught by the words of a heading.

citation.ref: Rule 1 of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: An importer of a plastic fitting argues before the appraiser that its goods belong in a particular chapter because that chapter's title describes them well, and backs the reading with a note printed at the head of a different chapter that deals with the same material. The appraiser points instead to the words of the competing heading itself and to a note of the chapter that heading sits in.

items.stem: How is each consignment classified?

options.text: The forgings are gear wheels already, being destined for nothing else
options.misconception: classifies by where the goods are headed rather than by the state they are presented in
options.why: Intended use does not do this work. What matters is the condition at presentation, and steel that still needs turning, grinding and heat treatment has not reached the character of a gear wheel. It is classified as what it is on the day it lands.

options.text: The crates as motor cars; the forgings not as gear wheels
options.why: A reference in a heading to an article is taken to reach that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that as presented it has the essential character of the finished one, and it is taken to reach the finished article as well when that article is presented unassembled or disassembled. A car in crates is a car on both counts, in the same way that railway coaches shipped without their seats are still railway coaches. The forgings fail from the other side. Only goods needing minor adjustment are treated as carrying the character of the finished article; goods still to be turned, ground or heat treated are not, and they stay where their own state puts them.
keywords: as presented it has the essential character of the finished one
the finished article as well when that article is presented unassembled

options.text: The cars go to parts headings because the seats are missing, so what arrives is not a complete car
options.misconception: treats any missing component as fatal, when the rule allows for the incomplete and asks only what character the goods carry
options.why: The rule reaches the incomplete article in terms. A car without seats is still recognisably a car and nothing else can be made of it, so it keeps its heading. Seats are fitted at the far end and their absence changes nothing about what the goods are.

options.text: Both go to the parts headings, neither being a working article at the moment of import
options.misconception: classifies by what will work on the day of import, when the rule is written precisely to reach goods that do not yet work
options.why: If working order were the test the rule would have nothing to do. It exists so that a machine shipped in pieces is not turned into a bag of parts by the packing. The question is not whether the goods run but whether, as they stand, they carry the character of the finished thing.

citation.ref: Rule 2(a) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: Two consignments reach the same appraiser. The first is a run of motor cars shipped knocked down, each crate holding one car's body, engine and wheels but no seats, needing only bolting together at the far end. The second is a lot of steel forgings that will one day be gear wheels, but that still have to be turned, ground and heat treated before they are.

items.stem: Where do the two consignments go?

options.text: Each to the heading of whichever ingredient weighs more in the blend
options.misconception: jumps to weighing ingredients, which is the later essential-character test, before asking whether the heading already covers the blend
options.why: The question of which component gives the goods their character arises only after two or more headings genuinely compete. Here the heading for the named material already reaches the mixture, so the matter is settled before any weighing starts.

options.text: To the coffee heading and to the natural rubber heading; blending has not moved either of them
options.why: A reference in a heading to a material or a substance is taken to include mixtures or combinations of that material with other materials, and a reference to goods of a given material is taken to include goods made wholly or partly of it. So the heading for coffee carries coffee blended with chicory, and the heading for natural rubber carries a compound of natural and synthetic rubber. The rule stops short of one thing: where the blending leaves the goods prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, it does not choose between them but hands the question on to the next rule.
keywords: include mixtures or combinations of that material with other materials
goods made wholly or partly of it

options.text: The blend goes to the chicory heading, coffee mixed with anything else no longer answering the description of coffee
options.misconception: treats the addition of a second material as displacing the first, when the rule keeps the goods with the material the heading names
options.why: The rule works the other way round. A reference to coffee takes in coffee mixed with chicory; it does not surrender the goods to the added ingredient. On the same footing natural rubber keeps a compound of natural and synthetic rubber.

options.text: To a residual heading for mixed products, neither blend being the pure substance the heading names
options.misconception: reads a heading naming a material as naming it in a pure state, when the rule expressly extends it to combinations
options.why: Very few traded goods are pure and the tariff does not pretend otherwise. A heading for a material reaches mixtures containing it, which is why coffee stays coffee. Falling to a residual entry would make the blending of a small quantity of anything a way of leaving the heading behind.

citation.ref: Rule 2(b) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: An importer brings in coffee that has been blended with chicory, and in the same week a compound of natural rubber and synthetic rubber. There is a heading for coffee and a heading for natural rubber, and neither heading says a word about blends. The appraiser asks whether the blending has taken either product out of its heading.

items.stem: Under which heading are the shavers classified, and why?

options.text: Heading 8509, being the earlier of the two competing entries in numerical order
options.misconception: reaches for the numerical tie-breaker without asking first whether one heading is more specific, and reaches for it the wrong way round
options.why: Numerical order is the last of the three tie-breakers and it comes into play only when specificity and essential character have both failed. Here specificity settles it at the first step. And when numerical order does apply, the heading standing last is the one that takes the goods, not the first.

options.text: Whichever heading carries the lower rate, an importer being entitled to the more favourable of two entries that both fit
options.misconception: imports a rule of favourable construction into classification, where the tariff describes goods rather than offering choices
options.why: Rate has no part in placing goods. The interpretative rules ask what the goods are and where the tariff describes them; what duty follows is a consequence of the answer, not an input to it.

options.text: Heading 8510, that entry naming these very goods where the other names a family they belong to
options.why: When two headings each fit the goods, the first tie-breaker is preference for the entry that gives the most specific description over one that describes more generally. Heading 8509 names a whole family — domestic appliances of an electro-mechanical kind with a motor of their own — into which a shaver falls along with many other things. Heading 8510 names shavers and hair clippers with self-contained motors, which is this product and very little else. So the goods are classified under 8510. Nowhere in the interpretative rules is the importer offered whichever of two headings carries the cheaper rate.
keywords: preference for the entry that gives the most specific description
so the goods are classified under 8510

options.text: Heading 8509, since it is the entry the importer chose and both headings fit the goods on their words
options.misconception: treats a genuine overlap as leaving the choice with the declarant, when the rules settle the overlap themselves
options.why: An overlap is what the rules are for. Where two headings both fit, the more specific one takes the goods, and the declaration made on the bill of entry does not decide it. Self-assessment lets the importer state a classification; it does not let him pick one.

citation.ref: Rule 3(a) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: Vardhan Imports enters a consignment of electric shavers under heading 8509, which covers electro-mechanical domestic appliances with self-contained electric motors. The appraiser points to heading 8510, which covers shavers and hair clippers with self-contained electric motors. The goods answer the words of both. Vardhan says the rate under 8509 is the lower of the two and it is entitled to the lower.

items.stem: How is the vehicle classified?

options.text: Under whichever heading the importer declares, both being available on these facts
options.misconception: reads an even contest as a free choice, when the rules exist precisely to close an even contest
options.why: A tie is not an option. The rule that closes it is arbitrary on purpose, so that two appraisers looking at the same vehicle reach the same heading. Leaving it to the declaration would make the rate depend on who filled in the form.

options.text: Under heading 8703, a vehicle that can carry people being a passenger vehicle first
options.misconception: resolves an even contest by preferring one use, when the facts already say the two uses are equally supported
options.why: The premise of this rule is that the contest is even. Once the appraiser has found that neither description fits better and that no component gives the goods their character, preferring one use is simply picking. The tariff supplies a rule so that nobody has to.

options.text: Under heading 8704, that entry standing later than the other among the two that fit equally
options.why: Two tie-breakers have already failed here — neither heading is the more specific, and no material or component gives the vehicle its character. The third is mechanical: among the headings that merit consideration equally, the goods go to the one standing last in numerical order. Heading 8704 comes after 8703, so the vehicle is classified under heading 8704. That is how the Tribunal decided it in Mahindra and Mahindra, and the Supreme Court left the decision standing.
keywords: among the headings that merit consideration equally, the goods go to the one standing last in numerical order
so the vehicle is classified under heading 8704

options.text: Under a residual heading, since neither of the two competing entries can be preferred
options.misconception: treats an unresolved contest as no fit at all, when both headings fit and the question is only which of them takes the goods
options.why: A residual entry is for goods no heading describes. These goods are described twice over, which is the opposite problem. The ladder ends by choosing between the two, and it does not send well-described goods to a residual entry.

citation.ref: Rule 3(c) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule, with Mahindra and Mahindra

items.scenario: A vehicle is presented that on its design carries people as readily as it carries goods. Heading 8703 covers motor cars and other vehicles principally designed to carry persons; heading 8704 covers motor vehicles for the transport of goods. Neither heading is more specific than the other for this vehicle, and no single component can be said to give it its character.

items.stem: How is the film classified, and is the sub-heading comparison sound?

options.text: Under 3925 30 00 as nearest to a plastic blind; and no, the two sub-headings he compared do not stand on the same footing
options.why: When the earlier rules have all failed to place goods, they go to the heading covering whatever goods these are most akin to. This film is no builder's ware, but the entry covering builders' wares of plastic not elsewhere specified takes in shutters, blinds and similar articles, and a film that cuts glare on a window is nearest to a plastic blind. Once the heading is fixed the sub-heading is settled by its own rule, and that rule works on one condition: only sub-headings at the same level are comparable. A one-dash entry cannot be weighed against a two-dash entry, and neither can entries taken from two different headings.
keywords: the heading covering whatever goods these are most akin to
only sub-headings at the same level are comparable

options.text: It goes to the akin heading, and the sub-heading comparison is sound because both entries are inside chapter 39
options.misconception: reads sameness of chapter as sameness of level, when level is a question of how deep an entry sits under its own heading
options.why: Sharing a chapter proves nothing about level. Sub-headings are compared only against others at the same depth within the same heading, which is why a one-dash entry is weighed against another one-dash entry and not against something sitting under it.

options.text: It cannot be classified at all, no heading naming it and no note reaching it
options.misconception: assumes the tariff can run out of answers, when it carries a rule for exactly the goods it does not name
options.why: The tariff is closed by design. Goods it does not name are placed with the goods they most resemble, so an unnamed article still gets a heading and a rate. A gap would make the levy unworkable for every new product.

options.text: The akin rule should have been tried first, being the simplest test on an unnamed product
options.misconception: moves the akin rule up the ladder, when it is reached only after the earlier rules have all failed
options.why: Resemblance is the last resort, not the first. Starting there would let a rough likeness override the words of a heading and a chapter note that between them might have placed the goods precisely. Its whole point is that everything else has already been tried.

citation.ref: Rules 4 and 6 of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: Vardhan also imports a plastic film pasted on car windows to cut sun glare. No entry in the tariff names it, and the first three rules have been worked through without placing it. Heading 3925 30 00 covers builders' wares of plastic not elsewhere specified, including shutters, blinds and similar articles. Having reached that heading the appraiser then weighs a one-dash sub-heading under it against a two-dash sub-heading under a different heading.

items.stem: What is the position on the three things Vikram raises?

options.text: Vikram's own case can be met by an amending notification like any other, a special order being reserved for defence and diplomatic imports
options.misconception: confuses the instrument with the beneficiary, when the difference is general relief by notification against relief for one case by order
options.why: A notification exempts a described class of goods generally. Relieving one importer is done by an order made for his case, and the order has to set out the exceptional circumstances that justify it. Who the beneficiary happens to be does not choose the instrument; how wide the relief is does.

options.text: A condition may fall after clearance; one importer alone is relieved only by an order made for his case; the ₹90 is not collected; and the clarification does reach back
options.why: The general power lets the Central Government exempt goods of any description from the whole or a part of the duty by notification, where it is satisfied that doing so is necessary in the public interest, and the exemption may be absolute or tied to conditions that fall due before clearance or after it — so the condition Vikram must meet afterwards is perfectly regular. Relief for a single importer is a different power altogether: the Act allows it by special order in each case, and only in circumstances of an exceptional nature that the order itself must state. On the small consignment nothing is collected at all, because no duty is collected where the amount leviable is ₹100 or less. And a clarification issued within one year of the notification has retrospective effect, so it governs clearances already made.
keywords: where it is satisfied that doing so is necessary in the public interest
the Act allows it by special order in each case
no duty is collected where the amount leviable is ₹100 or less
a clarification issued within one year of the notification has retrospective effect

options.text: The ₹90 is payable, there being no amount below which customs duty is left uncollected
options.misconception: assumes every rupee assessed is collected, missing the small-amount rule that stops collection outright
options.why: Collecting ninety rupees costs more than ninety rupees. The Act says so in effect by stopping collection where the duty leviable comes to a hundred rupees or less, and the stop is on collection rather than on the levy.

options.text: The condition is bad in law — a customs exemption must be satisfied at clearance or not claimed at all
options.misconception: reads an exemption as something tested once at the gate, when the section allows conditions falling on either side of clearance
options.why: Many exemptions exist precisely to be tested afterwards — an end-use condition cannot be verified while the goods sit on the dock. The section says in terms that a condition may be one to be fulfilled before clearance or after it, and an end-use scheme would be impossible if it did not.

citation.ref: Section 25(1), 25(2) and 25(2A)

items.scenario: Vikram Polymers imports a resin that a general notification exempts, on a condition the importer has to satisfy after the goods are cleared. Its factory flooded and it cannot satisfy the condition, so it writes to the Ministry asking to be relieved in its own case alone. On one small consignment the duty works out at ₹90. Eight months after the notification issued, the Government put out a clarification narrowing one word in it, and Vikram says a clarification cannot reach clearances already made.

items.stem: Until when does each of the two hold good?

options.text: It runs for exactly two years and dies on 15 September 2026, so the 2027 import misses it by longer than it thinks
options.misconception: counts two years and stops there, missing that the life is then carried forward to the following 31st of March
options.why: The two-year count is not the end of the sum. The exemption survives to the 31st March that comes next after the two years run out, which on these facts buys another six and a half months. Getting this wrong in the shorter direction costs a claim that was still good.

options.text: It runs until the Government withdraws it, the fixed life belonging to unconditional exemptions
options.misconception: puts the sunset on the wrong kind of exemption, when it is the conditional one that carries a life and the unconditional one that does not
options.why: The life attaches to exemptions granted subject to conditions. An absolute exemption carries no such clock and stands until it is modified or rescinded. Reading it backwards would leave a trader claiming a lapsed benefit for years.

options.text: Both die on the same date, every exemption being on one clock
options.misconception: assumes the sunset is universal, when a named list of exemptions is carved out of it
options.why: Several classes are deliberately left off the clock, because they rest on commitments the Government cannot let expire every couple of years — treaty obligations, constitutional privileges and the export promotion schemes among them. A trade policy benefit runs on its own scheme's terms.

options.text: The notification lapses on 31 March 2027, so the 2027 import misses it; the Foreign Trade Policy benefit is not on that clock at all
options.why: A conditional exemption, unless the notification says otherwise or it is varied or rescinded, runs to the 31st March that comes next after two years counted from the grant or the last variation. Count two years from 15 September 2024 and you reach 15 September 2026; the first 31st March after that is 31 March 2027, so the notification lapses on 31 March 2027 and an import in the middle of that year is too late. The life does not reach every conditional exemption: it is kept off a multilateral or bilateral trade agreement, obligations under international agreements including United Nations agencies and diplomats, privileges of constitutional authorities, schemes under the Foreign Trade Policy, Central Government schemes running longer than two years, re-imports, temporary imports, gifts and personal baggage, and any duty other than the basic customs duty, integrated tax included.
keywords: runs to the 31st March that comes next after two years counted from the grant
so the notification lapses on 31 March 2027
schemes under the Foreign Trade Policy

citation.ref: Section 25(4A)

items.scenario: Bharat Alloys relies on a conditional exemption notification issued on 15 September 2024, which names no end date of its own and has never been varied or rescinded. It is planning an import against that notification in the middle of 2027. Separately it draws a benefit under a Foreign Trade Policy scheme and its finance head assumes both die on the same day.

items.stem: On what date does the liability arise, and in which year does it fall?

options.text: 15 March 2026, so the tax belonged to 2025-26 and the return it went into is the wrong one
options.why: Where the supplier of the service is an associated enterprise sitting outside India, the ordinary reverse charge test is displaced by a proviso of its own. The sixty-day outer date drops out and only two dates compete: the date of payment, and the date of entry in the recipient's books of account, whichever of the two is earlier. Rudra's books carry the fee on 15 March 2026 and the money goes out on 30 June 2026, so the time of supply is 15 March 2026 and the liability falls in 2025-26. The invoice date does nothing at all in this proviso.
keywords: the supplier of the service is an associated enterprise sitting outside India
the date of entry in the recipient's books of account, whichever of the two is earlier
so the time of supply is 15 March 2026 and the liability falls in 2025-26

options.text: 1 April 2026, the invoice date, so 2026-27 is right after all
options.misconception: takes the invoice as the anchor, when the proviso for a supplier abroad in the same group does not name the invoice at all
options.why: The invoice is the anchor in the ordinary case, where the count of days runs from it. In this proviso it is simply absent. A group company can raise its invoice whenever it likes, and letting that date govern would hand the year of taxation to the overseas parent.

options.text: 31 May 2026, being the day after sixty days from the invoice
options.misconception: keeps the sixty-day outer limb, which the associated enterprise proviso removes altogether
options.why: The sixty-day date belongs to the ordinary reverse charge rule for services. For a service from an associated enterprise abroad the proviso replaces that test rather than adding to it, so no count of days from the invoice arises.

options.text: 30 June 2026, the day the money went out, so 2026-27
options.misconception: reads the proviso as a payment rule, missing that the books entry is the other of the two dates and here the earlier one
options.why: Payment is one of the two dates, not the only one. The proviso takes whichever of payment and the books entry comes first, and the fee was in the books three and a half months before the money moved.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 13(3)

items.scenario: Rudra Metals in Jharkhand takes management support from its parent in Singapore, which is an associated enterprise. The fee is written into Rudra's books on 15 March 2026. The parent's invoice is dated 1 April 2026 and the money leaves Rudra's bank on 30 June 2026. Rudra's finance head has put the reverse charge tax into the return for 2026-27, on the footing that the invoice is dated in that year.

items.stem: What is the time of supply of each?

options.text: 5 May for the goods and 1 July for the services
options.why: Goods and services run on different lists. For goods the law takes the earliest of three dates — the day the goods are received, the day the payment is entered in the recipient's books or debited from his bank account whichever comes first, and the day immediately following thirty days from the supplier's invoice. Those work out at 5 May, 20 June and 31 May, and the goods reach the buyer on 5 May, which is the earliest of the three. For services the receipt limb drops away and the outer date is stretched: the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice. Those are 10 August and 1 July, so the time of supply of the security services is 1 July — the tax fell due in July although nothing was paid until August.
keywords: the day immediately following thirty days from the supplier's invoice
the goods reach the buyer on 5 May, which is the earliest of the three
the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice
so the time of supply of the security services is 1 July

options.text: 20 June for the goods and 10 August for the services, payment being what triggers a reverse charge
options.misconception: treats reverse charge as a pay-then-tax scheme, when payment is only one of the competing dates and often not the earliest
options.why: If payment governed, a buyer could put off the tax simply by putting off the supplier. That is why both lists carry an outer date measured from the invoice, and why the goods list also counts the day the goods arrive. Payment wins only when it happens to come first.

options.text: 5 May for the goods and 30 June for the services
options.misconception: stops counting on the sixtieth day, when the section names the day immediately following it
options.why: Sixty days from 1 May ends on 30 June, and the date the section fixes is the one after that, which is 1 July. The same shape holds on the goods side, where thirty days from 1 May ends on 31 May. The extra day is written into both limbs and it is a favourite place to lose a mark.

options.text: 5 May for the goods and 10 August for the services, since tax cannot be due before the supplier has been paid
options.misconception: reads the outer date as a concession the buyer may ignore, when it is a ceiling that fixes the liability whether or not payment has moved
options.why: The outer date exists to stop exactly this. Once sixty days have run from the invoice the liability crystallises, and the buyer pays the tax out of its own pocket in July even though it settles the firm's bill in August. Waiting for the payment would leave the tax hostage to the buyer's own credit terms.

citation.ref: Sections 12(3) and 13(3)

items.scenario: Rudra Metals has two more inward supplies in 2026 on which it pays under reverse charge. The first is a consignment of goods of a notified kind from a registered supplier: the supplier's invoice is dated 1 May, the goods arrive on 5 May, the payment is entered in Rudra's books on 20 June and debited from its bank on 22 June. The second is security services from a firm: the invoice is dated 1 May and Rudra pays on 10 August.

items.stem: For how many days is this e-way bill valid?

options.text: Eleven days, the last 150 kilometres being too short to earn a day
options.misconception: rounds the leftover distance down, when the rule counts a part block as a whole one
options.why: The words that decide it are "or part thereof". Any distance left over after the whole blocks, however short, earns its own day. Rounding it away would leave a consignment travelling on an expired bill on the last leg of its journey.

options.text: A hundred and eighteen days, on the twenty-kilometre scale
options.misconception: applies the scale written for over-dimensional and part-by-ship shipments to ordinary road cargo
options.why: The tighter scale exists because those loads crawl. It is reserved for over-dimensional cargo and for a multimodal shipment with at least one leg by ship. Ordinary cargo on a highway runs on the 200-kilometre scale, and putting it on the other one would hand a truck four months for a four-day journey.

options.text: Twelve days
options.why: Ordinary cargo — anything that is neither over-dimensional nor a multimodal shipment with a leg by ship — earns one day for the first 200 kilometres and one more day for every 200 kilometres or part thereof after that. Take the first 200 off 2,350 and 2,150 kilometres are left. Divide those by 200 and you get ten whole blocks with 150 kilometres over, and a part block counts as a whole one, so eleven further days are earned. One plus eleven is twelve days in all for the 2,350 kilometre run.
keywords: one day for the first 200 kilometres and one more day for every 200 kilometres or part thereof
one plus eleven is twelve days in all for the 2,350 kilometre run

options.text: Thirteen days
options.misconception: counts the whole distance in blocks and then adds the first day again, paying twice for the opening 200 kilometres
options.why: The first 200 kilometres are the first day, not an extra one. Either take 200 off and count the remainder in blocks, or count the whole distance in blocks and add nothing — both give twelve. Doing both adds a day the rule does not give.

items.scenario: Chetan Logistics is moving ordinary cargo by road from Ludhiana to Bengaluru, 2,350 kilometres. It is not over-dimensional and no leg of the journey is by ship. The transporter enters the vehicle details in Part B at 10 a.m. on 1 November 2026 and wants to know how many days he has before the bill runs out.

items.stem: How long is each of the two e-way bills valid?

options.text: Five days for the transformer and thirty-six days for the container
options.misconception: adds a part block where the distance divides exactly, paying for a remainder that does not exist
options.why: The extra day is for a part block, and 680 kilometres leaves no part when divided by twenty. Thirty-four blocks give thirty-four days, and the opening block gives one, so the count stops at thirty-five. The rounding rule only ever works upward on a genuine remainder.

options.text: Five days for the transformer and thirty-five days for the container
options.why: Both consignments are on the tighter scale — over-dimensional cargo, and a multimodal shipment in which at least one leg is by ship, each get one day up to 20 kilometres and one further day for every 20 kilometres or part after that. The transformer's 90 is 20 plus 70; seventy divided by twenty gives three whole blocks and a remainder, and the remainder counts, so four more days on top of the first make the transformer's bill run five days. The container's 700 is 20 plus 680; six hundred and eighty divides by twenty exactly thirty-four times, so thirty-four more days on top of the first make the container's bill run thirty-five days.
keywords: one day up to 20 kilometres and one further day for every 20 kilometres or part after that
four more days on top of the first make the transformer's bill run five days
thirty-four more days on top of the first make the container's bill run thirty-five days

options.text: Five days for the transformer and four days for the container, most of whose journey is by road
options.misconception: makes the tighter scale depend on how much of the trip is by ship, when a single leg by ship is enough to bring the whole shipment onto it
options.why: The test is not a proportion. A consignment moving by more than one mode, any single leg of it carried by ship, goes on the tighter scale for the whole distance, however short the sea leg is, because it is the transfer and the sailing that eat the days.

options.text: Four days for the transformer and thirty-four days for the container
options.misconception: forgets that the opening block earns a day of its own before the counting of further blocks starts
options.why: The scale has two limbs and both pay. The first up to twenty kilometres earns one day, and each twenty kilometres or part after that earns one more. Dropping the opening day leaves every bill a day short, which is the day the goods are actually loaded.

items.scenario: Two more consignments leave the same depot. One is a transformer that travels as a single indivisible unit exceeding the dimensional limits set under the motor vehicle rules, moving 90 kilometres. The other is a container going 700 kilometres in all, part of it by road to a port and the rest by ship.

items.stem: When did the clock start, and how is a day counted?

options.text: It restarted on 3 November, the new vehicle entry generating the validity afresh
options.misconception: reads every Part B entry as a fresh generation, which would let a transporter renew a bill indefinitely by changing trucks
options.why: Only the first entry in Part B counts. Later ones record where the goods have got to and change nothing about how long the bill lasts — otherwise the validity period would be worth nothing, since a swap at a depot would buy a new one every time.

options.text: It started at 10 a.m. on 1 November 2026 and did not restart on 3 November; and a day closes at midnight, not at ten the next morning
options.why: The validity runs from the relevant date, which is the date and time the e-way bill was generated — and generation here means the first entry made in Part B, the moment the vehicle number or the transport document number goes in. Filling Part A does nothing to the clock, and a later change of vehicle does not restart it, however many times Part B is updated. Nor is a day twenty-four hours from that moment. The first day closes at midnight at the end of the day immediately following the date of generation, and each day after it closes at the next midnight.
keywords: the validity runs from the relevant date, which is the date and time the e-way bill was generated
the first day closes at midnight at the end of the day immediately following the date of generation

options.text: It started on Friday 30 October, when the consignor filled Part A and gave up the goods
options.misconception: starts the clock at the document rather than at the movement, when Part A can be filled days before anything moves
options.why: Part A is the invoice side of the bill and carries no vehicle. A consignor may fill it and wait for a transporter, and if the clock ran from then a bill could expire before the truck arrived. The count starts when the vehicle goes in.

options.text: Each day is twenty-four hours from the moment of generation, so the first day ended at 10 a.m. on 2 November
options.misconception: counts in clock hours when the rule counts in calendar days ending at midnight
options.why: Counting in hours would give two bills generated ten minutes apart on either side of midnight almost identical lives. The rule instead ends the first day at midnight at the close of the day after generation, so a bill made at four minutes past midnight and one made at two minutes to midnight on the same date expire together.

citation.ref: Explanation 1 and Explanation 2 to rule 138(10)

items.scenario: The consignor filled Part A on Friday 30 October 2026 and handed the goods over. The transporter put the vehicle number into Part B at 10 a.m. on Sunday 1 November 2026 and started the run. On 3 November the truck was changed at a depot and the new vehicle's number was entered. The clerk says the clock restarted on 3 November, and reckons each day as twenty-four hours from ten in the morning.

items.stem: What is open to him now?

options.text: Only the Commissioner can extend a validity period, and only by notification for a class of goods
options.misconception: takes one of the two extension powers as the only one, when the other sits with the transporter on the road
options.why: The Commissioner's power is real and it is general — a notification, on the Council's recommendation, extending validity for named categories of goods. It is no use to a truck stopped at night, which is why the rule also gives the transporter a power he can use himself.

options.text: He must generate a fresh e-way bill against the same invoice, expiry having ended the first one for good
options.misconception: treats expiry as final, when the rule provides a way of carrying the same bill on through a breakdown
options.why: A second bill against one invoice puts the same consignment on the portal twice and leaves the first movement unexplained. The rule answers the breakdown directly by letting the existing bill be extended, with the reason recorded on it, so one document covers one journey.

options.text: He may extend the same bill himself, within a short window that is still open, after entering the new vehicle and writing out the reason
options.why: Goods are not to move on a bill that has run out, and as a rule the validity cannot be extended at all. There are two exceptions and only one of them belongs to the transporter. Where a consignment cannot reach its destination inside the validity because of an exceptional circumstance such as a natural calamity, a law and order problem, a trans-shipment delay or an accident to the conveyance, the transporter carrying it at the time of expiry may extend the validity himself, updating Part B where the vehicle has changed and setting out the reason in detail. The window is narrow: the extension may be made within eight hours from the time the bill expired, so at five in the morning he still has it.
keywords: an exceptional circumstance such as a natural calamity, a law and order problem, a trans-shipment delay or an accident to the conveyance
the extension may be made within eight hours from the time the bill expired

options.text: He may extend at any time before the goods are delivered, the reason being genuine
options.misconception: reads the power as open-ended because the cause is good, missing that it closes a fixed number of hours after expiry
options.why: A genuine reason opens the power; it does not keep it open. The extension has to be made inside the short window that starts when the bill expires, and a transporter who waits until morning to think about it has let it close.

citation.ref: Third and fourth provisos to rule 138(10)

items.scenario: The Bengaluru-bound truck broke an axle 200 kilometres short and stood at the roadside all night. The bill's validity ran out at midnight. It is now five in the morning, a replacement vehicle has arrived, and the transporter who is carrying the consignment asks what he may do.

items.stem: Which importers may defer, and is the consultant right about Sahyadri?

options.text: Any importer holding an import-export code may defer, the facility being open to the trade generally
options.misconception: reads a widened class as a general entitlement, when each of the three classes is defined and entry to the new one is by approval
options.why: An import-export code is the minimum for importing at all and could not be the test for deferring duty; the deferment is credit from the Government and it is given to named classes. The new class has its own list of tests and an approval at the end of it.

options.text: Three classes may, and the consultant is out of date — a manufacturer approved by the Board's own directorate is now one of them, though only for a limited run of years
options.why: The Act lets the Central Government permit a class of importers to pay import duty after clearance instead of before it, and the Government has named three classes. Two are long standing: importers certified under the Authorised Economic Operator programme as AEO Tier-Two, with Tier-Three alongside them, and Authorised Public Undertakings. The third opened on 1 April 2026 — the Eligible Manufacturer Importer, a manufacturer importer approved by the Directorate of International Customs under the Board — so a manufacturer with no Authorised Economic Operator standing is not shut out any more. That third class is time-limited in a way the other two are not: it is permitted to defer only up to 31 March 2028.
keywords: certified under the Authorised Economic Operator programme as AEO Tier-Two
the Eligible Manufacturer Importer, a manufacturer importer approved by the Directorate of International Customs
it is permitted to defer only up to 31 March 2028

options.text: Only the two Authorised Economic Operator tiers may defer, the facility being a certification benefit
options.misconception: states the position as it stood before April 2026, when a third class was added that needs no certification at all
options.why: That was right until the new class opened. It is a real change of policy: the deferment is no longer a reward for certification alone but is open to a manufacturer who satisfies a list of tests directly, approved by a directorate rather than by the certification programme.

options.text: The new class, once approved, may defer for as long as it keeps its approval
options.misconception: misses that the permission for the new class carries an end date of its own, separate from the approval
options.why: The notification permits the new class only up to a stated date, so the approval and the permission expire on different terms. An importer planning its cash flow off this facility has to know the outer date as well as the approval, or it will budget for years it does not have.

citation.ref: Section 47(1), with the notification of 1 February 2026 effective from 1 April 2026

items.scenario: Sahyadri Motors, a manufacturer that imports its own components, has never held an Authorised Economic Operator certificate of any tier. In April 2026 it asks its consultant whether it can take delivery of its imports first and pay the duty afterwards, and is told that this is an Authorised Economic Operator benefit and nothing else.

items.stem: Can Sahyadri be approved, and what would a company with AEO Tier-One do?

options.text: No — the ₹40 crore is spread over three registrations and the turnover test has to be met by each registration on its own
options.misconception: applies the turnover test registration by registration, when it is measured across every registration under one permanent account number
options.why: The test is written at the level of the person, not the registration. A manufacturer with plants in three States would otherwise be worse off than the same business run from one, which is the opposite of what a size test is for.

options.text: Yes on every test; and an existing Tier-One entity that met the same tests could apply on the same footing
options.why: The tests are a list and Sahyadri clears each of them. It must import and manufacture, or else send its inputs or machinery out to a job worker without paying tax on them. It must hold a valid import-export code. It must have filed at least 25 import or export documents in the financial year before the application, a figure relaxed to ten for a micro, small or medium enterprise. It must hold at least one live GST registration showing manufacturing as the nature of its business, and a turnover across every registration under the same permanent account number of more than 5 crore in the last financial year. It must have been in business for two financial years, have filed all GST returns due, and carry a clean record. Last, it must produce a chartered accountant's certificate of solvency for the two years before the application. Never having been certified is no bar at all, and a Tier-One entity that meets the same list may apply too.
keywords: filed at least 25 import or export documents in the financial year before the application
a turnover across every registration under the same permanent account number of more than 5 crore
a chartered accountant's certificate of solvency for the two years before the application

options.text: No — the facility runs on Authorised Economic Operator certification and Sahyadri has none
options.misconception: keeps reading the deferment as a certification benefit after a class was created that is entered by direct approval
options.why: The new class was created for exactly this importer: a manufacturer that meets the tests but never went through the certification programme. Certification remains one road in; it is no longer the only one.

options.text: Yes, and the solvency certificate can be produced later if the department asks for it
options.misconception: treats the accountant's certificate as evidence to be produced on demand, when furnishing it is one of the conditions of eligibility
options.why: The certificate is part of the application, not an answer to a query. The whole facility is the Government carrying an importer's duty for weeks, so proof that the importer was solvent in each of the two preceding years goes in at the front.

citation.ref: Section 47(1), with the notification of 1 February 2026 and the circular of 28 February 2026

items.scenario: Sahyadri Motors makes its own vehicles, holds a valid import-export code, filed 60 import documents last financial year, has three GST registrations under one permanent account number showing manufacturing as its business with ₹40 crore of turnover between them, has traded for four years, has no GST return outstanding, has never had tax collected and not deposited and has no arrest, conviction or pending prosecution against it. It holds a chartered accountant's certificate that it was financially sound in each of the two years before it applies. It has never been an Authorised Economic Operator.

items.stem: When is the duty on each of the four bills of entry due?

options.text: The bill of the 4th on the 16th of that month, and the bill of the 19th on the 1st of the following month
options.misconception: uses the half-month table that the chapter body still prints, which was replaced in March 2026
options.why: That was the position until the amendment. The two halves of an ordinary month now share a single due date on the 1st of the month after, which is the change most likely to be missed, because the older table is still sitting in the printed material.

options.text: Two dates, not four — the pair in the ordinary month share one, and both March bills share another
options.why: The rule used to split every month in half, with the first fortnight falling due on the 16th of the same month. From March 2026 the halves were merged. A bill of entry returned for payment on any day of a month other than March, from the 1st to the last day of it, now carries duty due on the 1st day of the following month, so the bills of the 4th and the 19th share one due date. March is its own case and both halves of it fall together: a bill returned on any day from the 1st to the 31st of March is due on 31 March, so the bills of the 9th and the 24th are both due on 31 March 2027. Every one of these periods is reckoned excluding holidays.
keywords: now carries duty due on the 1st day of the following month, so the bills of the 4th and the 19th share one due date
a bill returned on any day from the 1st to the 31st of March is due on 31 March

options.text: The bill of 9 March on 16 March, and the bill of 24 March on 31 March
options.misconception: carries the same superseded half-month split into March, where both halves now land on the last day of the year
options.why: March is treated as one block ending on the 31st, because the year closes there and no duty of that year may be carried into the next. Both March bills therefore fall due on 31 March, and a mid-March date belongs to the old table.

options.text: All four on the 1st of the following month, March being no different from any other month
options.misconception: carries the ordinary rule into March, missing that the deferment cannot cross the end of the financial year
options.why: Applying the ordinary rule to March would push the duty into April and into the next financial year, which is the one thing the deferment is not allowed to do. March is written as a separate row for that reason and both of its halves fall on the 31st.

citation.ref: Rule 4 of the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016 as amended with effect from 1 March 2026

items.scenario: Sahyadri is approved and starts deferring. In one ordinary month its bills of entry are returned for payment on the 4th and on the 19th. In March 2027 two more are returned, on the 9th and on the 24th. Its accounts clerk is working from a textbook printed before March 2026 and has diarised four separate due dates.

items.stem: What happens to the facility, and what covers the undeclared consignment?

options.text: Nothing happens until there have been three defaults in three months
options.misconception: counts the threshold as three when the rule bites on a default more than once inside three consecutive months
options.why: The trigger is the second default inside the window, not the third. A facility that let an importer miss twice a quarter without consequence would be no discipline at all, given the size of the sums being carried.

options.text: The facility stops until the duty and the interest are cleared in full; the differential duty was due in a day; and the undeclared goods were never inside it
options.why: The facility is conditional throughout. Duty not paid by its due date carries interest until it is paid. Where an importer defaults more than once in three consecutive months, the deferment is withdrawn and stays withdrawn until the duty together with the interest is paid in full. Beyond that, deferment continues only for an importer who has paid each bill of entry by its due date and has paid any differential duty thrown up by a reassessment, with interest, within one day excluding holidays — so waiting for month end forfeits it. And some goods were never covered at all: goods which have not been assessed, or which the importer has not declared in the entry.
keywords: where an importer defaults more than once in three consecutive months, the deferment is withdrawn
goods which have not been assessed, or which the importer has not declared in the entry

options.text: The undeclared consignment simply rides along on the deferment with the rest of that bill of entry
options.misconception: treats the deferment as attaching to the bill of entry, when it attaches to goods that have actually been assessed and declared
options.why: The deferment postpones payment of a duty that has been worked out on a declaration. Goods nobody declared have no assessed duty to postpone, and letting them ride would turn the facility into cover for the very thing the examination caught.

options.text: Once withdrawn the facility is gone for good and cannot be regained
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal as permanent, when it lasts only until the arrears and the interest are cleared
options.why: The withdrawal is a lever, not a punishment. It lifts when the duty and the interest are paid in full, which is exactly what it was designed to bring about.

citation.ref: Section 47(2) with rules 5 and 6 of the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016

items.scenario: In a bad quarter Sahyadri misses its due date twice inside three months. In the same quarter a reassessment on one bill of entry throws up differential duty, which Sahyadri intends to settle at the end of the month, and an examination finds a consignment in another bill that was never declared in the entry at all.

items.stem: What can Eshan do about the six weeks, and by when must it do it?

options.text: Nothing can be done — the buyers lost the credit when the invoices went out without a registration number
options.misconception: treats a delay in the department's own certificate as the buyer's loss, which is the outcome the section exists to prevent
options.why: The gap is caused by the time the department takes to issue the certificate, and the section is there so that nobody pays for it. The revised invoices restore the credit for the whole period from the effective date.

options.text: It has until 1 May 2026, one month from the date its registration took effect
options.misconception: counts the month from the effective date, when it runs from the day the certificate was issued
options.why: Counting from the effective date would give a window that had often closed before the certificate arrived, which is the opposite of the relief intended. The month starts on the day the certificate is issued, so it always opens after the person knows he is registered.

options.text: Bill the period again on the document the Act provides for it, and do so by 15 June 2026
options.why: The Act has a document for exactly this gap. A registered person may, within one month from the date on which his registration certificate was issued, put out a revised invoice against every invoice he issued in the stretch beginning on the effective date of registration and ending on the day the certificate was issued to him. Eshan's certificate came on 15 May 2026, so the last day for the revised invoices is 15 June 2026, and they cover everything billed from 1 April 2026 onwards. Once they are issued the buyers hold documents that carry tax and can take credit on them.
keywords: put out a revised invoice against every invoice he issued in the stretch
within one month from the date on which his registration certificate was issued
so the last day for the revised invoices is 15 June 2026

options.text: It should raise credit notes against the old invoices and fresh invoices in their place
options.misconception: reaches for the credit note, which adjusts a supply already invoiced with tax, where the problem is invoices that carried no tax at all
options.why: A credit note reduces the value or the tax on a supply already documented under the Act. These invoices were issued before the certificate existed and carried nothing to reduce. The Act supplies a different document for the gap, and using it keeps one clean trail from the effective date.

citation.ref: Section 31(3)(a) with rule 53

items.scenario: Eshan Foods became liable to register on 1 April 2026 and applied in time, but its registration certificate was only issued on 15 May 2026, with effect from 1 April. Through those six weeks it went on billing its wholesale buyers on ordinary invoices carrying no tax and no registration number, and those buyers are now telling it they have no credit for the period.

items.stem: Which of Eshan's invoices actually have to go up on the portal?

options.text: The wholesale invoices and the exports; the counter bills do not, and the accountant is doing work the rule has not asked for
options.why: A notified class of persons has to make its invoices a different way: the particulars go up to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an Invoice Reference Number, and an invoice made any other way is not treated as an invoice at all. The class is a registered person whose aggregate turnover in any preceding financial year counting from 2017-18 has gone past 5 crore, and at ₹9 crore Eshan is well inside it. What the obligation bites on is supplies made to registered persons and exports. Sales to a walk-in customer are business-to-consumer and have not been brought in yet, so the counter bills stay off the portal.
keywords: the particulars go up to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an Invoice Reference Number
aggregate turnover in any preceding financial year counting from 2017-18 has gone past 5 crore
sales to a walk-in customer are business-to-consumer and have not been brought in yet

options.text: None of them, since the test looks at the current year's turnover and 2025-26 has not been assessed
options.misconception: reads the trigger as the running year's turnover, when it is any preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards
options.why: The test looks backwards deliberately, so that a business knows on the first day of a year whether it is in. And it reaches back to 2017-18, so one crossing in any earlier year enrols the person for good even if turnover later falls.

options.text: Only the exports, an e-invoice being a document for cross-border supplies
options.misconception: associates the portal with export documentation, when supplies to registered persons at home are the bulk of what it covers
options.why: Exports are inside the obligation but they are not what it is for. The purpose is to have business-to-business invoices reported at the moment they are made, so that the credit the buyer claims and the liability the seller reports come from one record.

options.text: Every invoice it issues, the test being about the person and not about who is being supplied
options.misconception: reads the turnover test as the whole rule, when the turnover decides who is in the class and the kind of supply decides which invoices go up
options.why: Two questions have to be answered, not one. Turnover puts the person inside the net; after that the obligation attaches to supplies to registered persons and to exports. Uploading counter bills as well adds work at the till and puts consumer data on the portal for no statutory reason.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) with the notification of 21 March 2020 as amended

items.scenario: Eshan Foods turned over ₹9 crore in 2025-26. It sells to registered wholesale dealers, it exports a little, and it runs a counter where members of the public walk in and buy packets. Its accountant has begun uploading every invoice the business issues, counter bills included, and complains that the counter takes twenty minutes longer each evening.

items.stem: Who has to report what on the portal?

options.text: The haulier must report, only banks and insurers being outside the obligation
options.misconception: shortens the exemption list to the financial trades, when it also names transport, entertainment and government
options.why: The list is longer than it looks. Alongside insurers and banking companies it carries goods transport agencies moving goods by road, suppliers of passenger transport, multiplex operators and Government departments and local authorities.

options.text: The zone unit must report, since the group's turnover is past the figure and turnover is what decides
options.misconception: lets turnover override a named exemption, when the list is written to stand whatever the turnover
options.why: The exemptions say in terms that these persons need not report even where their turnover has crossed the figure; they file a declaration to that effect instead. Note also which way round the zone exemption runs — the unit is out, the developer is in.

options.text: The advocate firm reports its invoice even though Eshan pays the tax; the zone unit, the distributor's documents and the haulier are all out
options.why: Being outside the charge and being outside the reporting obligation are two different questions. Where a notified supplier raises an invoice for a supply on which the recipient pays under reverse charge, the invoice still has to be reported, so the advocate firm at ₹8 crore reports it although Eshan discharges the tax. The exemptions, by contrast, are a named list that turnover does not defeat: a special economic zone unit — the unit, and not the developer — an insurer, a bank, a financial institution of any kind with a non-banking finance company counted in, a goods transport agency carrying goods by road, a supplier of passenger transportation service, a multiplex, and a Government department or local authority. The documents an Input Service Distributor issues are outside it too.
keywords: a special economic zone unit — the unit, and not the developer
the documents an Input Service Distributor issues are outside it too
the recipient pays under reverse charge, the invoice still has to be reported

options.text: The advocate firm need not report, the tax on those services being Eshan's to pay
options.misconception: assumes the reporting follows whoever pays the tax, when it follows whoever issues the invoice
options.why: The obligation sits on the person making the invoice. A notified supplier reports what it issues, and the fact that the buyer will account for the tax changes nothing about that. This is the finance head's reasoning and it is exactly backwards.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) with the notification of 21 March 2020 as amended

items.scenario: Legal services are supplied to Eshan by an advocate firm turning over ₹8 crore, and Eshan pays the tax on them itself. Eshan's group also has a unit inside a special economic zone and a registration as an Input Service Distributor, and it buys road haulage from a goods transport agency. The finance head reasons that where the recipient pays the tax the supplier has nothing to report, and that anybody over the turnover figure must report everything.

items.stem: Is the amendment good?

options.text: Bad, because six months had already run — the clock starts when the application for the ruling was filed
options.misconception: starts the clock at the wrong end, at the application rather than at the order sought to be rectified
options.why: The six months run from the date of the order that is being rectified. Counting from the application would make the window shrink with every month the Authority itself took, and could close it before the order was even pronounced.

options.text: Bad, because only the applicant may ask for a rectification and this came from the officer
options.misconception: reads the power as available on the applicant's motion alone, when the section names three sources and the Authority's own besides
options.why: The mistake may be spotted by the Authority itself, by the applicant, or by the concerned or jurisdictional officer. A rectification is about the record, not about whose interest it serves, and an officer may point out a mistake that costs the applicant money.

options.text: Good — putting right what the record already shows takes nothing away from anybody, so no hearing arises
options.misconception: treats every rectification alike, missing that the two directions that hurt the applicant carry a hearing of their own
options.why: Most rectifications are neutral and need no hearing. Two are not: one that raises the tax, and one that reduces the credit. In both the applicant is entitled to be heard first, because what looks like a clerical correction can carry a substantive change inside it.

options.text: It was made in time but it is bad all the same, because of how it was made
options.why: Either Authority may go back into its own order to put right a mistake apparent from the record — on its own motion, or on the mistake being pointed out by the applicant or by the concerned or jurisdictional officer — so long as six months from the date of that order have not run out. 5 July 2026 is inside six months of 10 February 2026, so the power was still alive on the day it was used. It was used wrongly nonetheless: where the rectification would have the effect of enhancing the tax liability, or of shrinking the credit he may take, the applicant must be heard before the order is passed. Amending the same afternoon, with nobody heard, is bad on that ground alone.
keywords: so long as six months from the date of that order have not run out
the applicant must be heard before the order is passed
the rectification would have the effect of enhancing the tax liability

citation.ref: Section 102

items.scenario: The Authority for Advance Ruling pronounced a ruling in Zeta Ltd's favour on 10 February 2026. On 5 July 2026 the jurisdictional officer writes in pointing to a mistake on the face of the record whose correction would raise Zeta's tax. The Authority amends the ruling the same afternoon. Zeta hears about it when the amended order reaches it in the post.

items.stem: Is either of them on safe ground?

options.text: Zeta is on safe ground — a ruling with no expiry date runs until it is withdrawn
options.misconception: treats silence about duration as permanence, when the Chapter ties the life of a ruling to the state of affairs behind it
options.why: Nothing has to be withdrawn. The ruling was an answer given on a particular law and a particular set of facts, and it lapses of itself when those move. Waiting for a withdrawal that nobody has to issue is how an applicant ends up carrying years of wrong returns.

options.text: Neither. The competitor was never covered, and Zeta's own cover ended when the entry it rested on was rewritten
options.why: A ruling under this Chapter is a private answer and not a precedent. It binds only the applicant who sought it and the concerned or jurisdictional officer in his case, which is why it does not reach a similarly placed taxable person in the same State. Nor does the applicant's own protection last for ever merely because no end date was written on it. The Chapter fixes no period at all: the ruling holds while the law, the facts and the circumstances that supported it stay as they were, and a notification rewriting the entry it turned on is a change of exactly that kind.
keywords: it binds only the applicant who sought it and the concerned or jurisdictional officer
the ruling holds while the law, the facts and the circumstances that supported it stay as they were

options.text: Both are wrong for one reason: the ruling expired on its first anniversary
options.misconception: invents a fixed life where the Chapter deliberately fixes none
options.why: There is no anniversary in the Chapter. A ruling could hold for ten years if nothing behind it moved, and could be worthless in six months if the law changed. Fixing an arbitrary life would make it useless for long-term planning, which is what it is for.

options.text: The competitor is on safe ground — the Authority is a State body, so its rulings settle the point for the State
options.misconception: reads the Authority as a tribunal laying down law for its territory, when it answers one applicant's question
options.why: The machinery is there to give one taxpayer certainty before he acts, not to build a body of law. Another trader may find the reasoning persuasive and may apply for a ruling of its own on its own facts, but it cannot stand behind somebody else's.

citation.ref: Section 103

items.scenario: Zeta's ruling stands and names no date on which it stops. A competitor in the same State, on facts it says are identical, starts applying the ruling in its own returns. Two years later a rate notification rewrites the very entry the ruling turned on, and Zeta goes on applying the ruling because it was never withdrawn.

items.stem: What must the Authority do first, and what follows from its order?

options.text: Nothing can be done now — six months from the ruling have long passed
options.misconception: borrows the rectification clock, when the power to declare a ruling void carries no period of its own
options.why: Two different powers are in play. Putting right a mistake on the record has a six-month window. Declaring a ruling void for fraud or suppression has none, because the fraud is usually discovered long afterwards, and a time bar would reward hiding the document well enough.

options.text: Hear Zeta before it makes the order; and once made, the Act applies as though the ruling had never been given
options.why: The power arises where the Authority or the Appellate Authority finds that the ruling was obtained by fraud, by suppression of material facts or by misrepresentation of facts, and a contract held back from the application is a suppressed material fact. But the order can be made only after the applicant has been given a hearing, so the Authority cannot declare first and listen afterwards. Once the order is made the ruling is void from the beginning and every provision of the Act applies to the applicant as though it had never been made, except that the stretch running from the ruling to the order declaring it void is left out when limitation is counted. A copy of the order goes to the applicant and to the officers.
keywords: obtained by fraud, by suppression of material facts or by misrepresentation of facts
the order can be made only after the applicant has been given a hearing

options.text: Declare it void at once — the suppression is established on the face of the contract
options.misconception: reads a strong case as removing the need to hear the other side, when the section attaches the hearing to the power itself
options.why: A document that looks decisive can have an answer. The applicant may say the contract was disclosed elsewhere, or that it did not bear on the question asked. The section makes the hearing a condition of the power, so an order made without one falls whatever the contract shows.

options.text: It may void the ruling, but only with effect from the date of its own order
options.misconception: reads the voiding as prospective, when the whole point is that the ruling is treated as never having been made
options.why: A ruling obtained by suppression protected the applicant for years it was never entitled to. Voiding it only from today would leave that protection intact for the past, which is where the money is. The statute instead wipes it out from the beginning and lets the demands run for the whole period.

citation.ref: Section 104

items.scenario: In October the jurisdictional officer produces a contract that Zeta held back when it applied for the ruling, and which would have changed the question the Authority was answering. The Authority is satisfied on the face of it and proposes to declare the ruling void and to let the department raise demands for the whole stretch since it was given.

items.stem: Is counsel right?

options.text: Right about the ledgers and wrong about the accountant — a person can be summoned but private books cannot be called for
options.misconception: splits a list that the section gives whole, treating books as beyond reach when compelling their production is named in it
options.why: The production of books of account and other records is one of the named powers, sitting beside the power to enforce attendance. The two go together: a witness with no documents in front of him can rarely settle a question about what a contract did.

options.text: Wrong, and the Authority is a civil court for every purpose of the criminal procedure code
options.misconception: overshoots — the deeming is written for one section of that code and is expressly withheld for one of its chapters
options.why: The Authority is deemed a civil court for the section dealing with prosecutions for offences against public justice, and is expressly not treated as one for the chapter on the provisions as to bail and the conduct of trials. The deeming is narrow and worth reading exactly.

options.text: No. Both the accountant and the ledgers can be required, the Authority holding a court's powers for that purpose
options.why: Both the Authority and the Appellate Authority are vested with the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure for a named set of things. It may order discovery and inspection. It may issue a commission. It is given the job of enforcing the attendance of a person and examining him on oath, and it is capable of compelling the production of books of account and other records. So the accountant can be made to come and the ledgers can be called for. Each is further deemed to be a civil court for the purpose of section 195 of the criminal procedure code, a proceeding before either is a judicial proceeding for the Penal Code, and each regulates its own procedure.
keywords: vested with the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure
enforcing the attendance of a person and examining him on oath
compelling the production of books of account and other records

options.text: Yes — it may invite the accountant and ask for the ledgers, but it has no power to compel either
options.misconception: reads an authority that answers questions as one without teeth, when the Chapter arms it with the compulsion a court has
options.why: An authority that can be ignored could not find the facts it needs, and it is deciding matters with tax consequences for years. The Chapter therefore gives it the court's powers to summon a person, put him on oath and call for records.

citation.ref: Sections 105 and 106

items.scenario: In the same proceeding the Authority calls Zeta's accountant to appear and answer on oath, and calls for the ledgers behind the suppressed contract. Zeta's counsel says an Authority for Advance Ruling is an advisory body set up to answer questions, that it may request but not require, and that neither the accountant nor the ledgers need come.

items.stem: Is the consultant right on either of the two?

options.text: Right on the first and wrong on the second — the sale at sea carries GST because title passed in India, and the in-bond sale is ignored for reversal
options.misconception: gets both halves the wrong way round, taxing the transaction that is out and ignoring the value that is in
options.why: It is the sale at sea that is untaxed and the in-bond sale whose value nonetheless counts for reversal. Reversing the pair costs tax on a transaction that bears none and leaves common credit unreversed that should have been.

options.text: Wrong on the first and right on the second — neither sale is taxed, but only one of them counts when credit is reversed
options.why: Both purchases sit in the Schedule that lists things treated as the supply of neither goods nor services. A sale made by endorsing the documents of title after the goods have left the foreign port and before they are cleared for home consumption falls in paragraph 8(b), so no GST is charged on the sale at sea itself; integrated tax comes only at clearance, and it is worked on the price paid by the last buyer, the one who files the bill of entry. The sale of warehoused goods before clearance is outside GST too, under paragraph 8(a). The two part company on credit: the value of the in-bond sale is counted as an exempt supply for the reversal worked under rules 42 and 43, and the value of a sale at sea is not.
keywords: falls in paragraph 8(b), so no GST is charged on the sale at sea itself
it is worked on the price paid by the last buyer, the one who files the bill of entry
the sale of warehoused goods before clearance is outside GST too, under paragraph 8(a)
counted as an exempt supply for the reversal worked under rules 42 and 43

options.text: Wrong on both — neither sale is a supply, so neither can enter a reversal calculation
options.misconception: assumes that being outside the levy is enough to be invisible for credit reversal, when one of these two is written into the reversal base by name
options.why: The reversal base is defined by its own explanation and it deliberately pulls one of these in.
