The value of a sale of warehoused goods before clearance counts as an exempt supply for that purpose, while the value of a sale at sea does not — a distinction with real money behind it for a trader doing both.

options.text: Right on both — a sale between two Indian parties is a supply wherever the goods happen to be floating
options.misconception: fixes the tax by where the parties are, when the Schedule takes the transaction out on the footing that the goods have not yet entered the country's tax net
options.why: Both parties being here does not make an import taxable twice. The goods are taxed once, at clearance, on the price the last buyer paid, and every sale up the chain before that is put outside the levy so that a chain of five endorsements does not carry five taxes.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 8(a) and 8(b) of Schedule III, with the explanation to section 17(3) and rules 42 and 43

items.scenario: Kunal Retail in Delhi buys an imported consignment from another importer by endorsement of the bill of lading while the ship is still at sea, and separately buys a lot lying in a customs bonded warehouse before anybody has cleared it. Its consultant advises that the seller of the first lot should have charged GST on the sale, and that the value of the second must be treated as an exempt supply when Kunal works out how much common credit to reverse.

items.stem: Whose arrest may be authorised here, and by whom?

options.text: Only the Pune firm's partners; the Surat firm is under the money line and there is no other road to an arrest
options.misconception: reads the money line as the whole of the gate, so the second-offence limb never gets read at all
options.why: The threshold is the ordinary gate and it is not the only one. The section reaches an offence punishable under either of the first two clauses, and separately an offence committed again by somebody already convicted. The Surat proprietor is in the second category, so the ₹1.4 crore does not save him. Reading only the first sentence of the section lets a repeat offender out on an arithmetic point.

options.text: Neither, until a criminal court has taken cognizance, arrest under this Act being available only once a complaint has been filed
options.misconception: puts arrest after prosecution, when the Act allows it during the investigation and asks for the Commissioner's sanction only at the prosecution stage
options.why: The two approvals sit at different moments. The Commissioner authorises an arrest while the investigation is running, on his reasons to believe; the Commissioner's previous sanction is what a prosecution needs before a complaint goes to court. Waiting for the court would make the arrest power useless in the only situation it exists for.

options.text: Both, but only the Commissioner may authorise either
options.why: An arrest under section 69 rests on one officer and one state of mind: the Commissioner must hold reasons to believe the person guilty of the offence before he authorises anyone to make it. On the money, the clauses the section reaches begin at an amount of tax exceeding 2 crore, which the Pune firm's credit is. The Surat firm sits below that line and would be out of reach but for the last limb of the section, because a repeat offence carries no monetary floor at all — a person convicted once and offending again may be arrested whatever the amount.
keywords: the Commissioner must hold reasons to believe the person guilty of the offence
an amount of tax exceeding 2 crore
a repeat offence carries no monetary floor at all

options.text: Both, and the Joint Commissioner who ran the investigations may sign the authorisations himself
options.misconception: treats the arrest power as travelling with the investigation, the way an inspection or a search authorisation does
options.why: Inspection and search are authorised by an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner, and that is where the confusion starts. Arrest is not in that family. The Act names the Commissioner and nobody else, and an authorisation signed by the officer running the case is bad however strong the file is. The rank is a safeguard, not a formality.

citation.ref: Section 69(1) read with section 132(1) clauses (a) to (d) and section 132(2)

items.scenario: Two investigations in one commissionerate close on the same day. The first is into a Pune firm that took credit of ₹2.4 crore on invoices for goods that never moved. The second is into a Surat firm that suppressed sales and evaded ₹1.4 crore; its proprietor was convicted three years ago, under the same Act, for suppressing sales in an earlier year. The Joint Commissioner who ran both investigations wants both sets of partners arrested and proposes to sign the authorisations himself.

items.stem: What must be done with each of the two?

options.text: Both may be released on bail by the Assistant Commissioner, the money limit going only to whether an arrest could be authorised at all
options.misconception: uses the arrest threshold to answer a bail question, when the Act sets two different figures for two different purposes
options.why: There are two figures and they do different work. The lower one decides whether an arrest may be authorised at all. The higher one decides whether the offence is cognizable and non-bailable once the arrest has happened. Collapsing them into one number hands departmental bail to somebody the Act says only a magistrate may release.

options.text: Both must be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours, and no departmental officer may bail either of them
options.misconception: reads every arrest under the Act as cognizable, when the Act makes only the largest band so
options.why: Being arrested and being held on a cognizable charge are two different things. The Act makes only the top band cognizable and non-bailable and leaves everything else non-cognizable and bailable. On the second man's figure a departmental officer not only may grant bail, he is the person the Act expects to do it, exercising the powers an officer in charge of a police station has.

options.text: The first may be held while the investigation is completed, the twenty-four hours running from the day the complaint is filed in court
options.misconception: starts the twenty-four hours at the wrong event, so the safeguard that exists to limit custody stops limiting anything
options.why: The clock runs from the arrest, not from any later step. It is a safeguard on the custody itself, which is why the section pairs it with telling the person in writing why he has been arrested. Reading it as running from the complaint would let the department hold somebody for as long as the investigation took.

options.text: The first must be told the grounds in writing and taken before a magistrate; the second the Assistant Commissioner may release on bail himself
options.why: The dividing line is a money line and it is not the arrest line. Where the tax evaded, the credit wrongly availed or the refund wrongly taken exceeds 5 crore the offence is cognizable and non-bailable, so the first man must be informed in writing of the grounds of his arrest and produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of the arrest, and only the magistrate can then consider bail. Every other offence under the Act is non-cognizable and bailable, and there the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner may release the person on bail himself.
keywords: the credit wrongly availed or the refund wrongly taken exceeds 5 crore
produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of the arrest
the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner may release the person on bail

citation.ref: Section 69(2) and 69(3) read with section 132(4) and section 132(5)

items.scenario: Two people are arrested on the same morning under authorisations the Commissioner signed. One is charged with availing credit of ₹6.2 crore on invoices with no supply behind them. The other is charged with evading ₹2.8 crore by keeping supplies off the books. Both are brought to the same office and the Assistant Commissioner on duty asks what he must now do with each of them before the day is out.

items.stem: What is the longest term of imprisonment each of the three can be given?

options.text: Five years, five years and three years, a second and every later offence carrying five years whatever the amount
options.misconception: borrows the repeat-offender rule for three first offences, and then shifts every band up one
options.why: The five-years-whatever-the-amount rule is real, and it is for a person convicted under the section who is convicted again. None of these three has been convicted before, so each is placed by his own amount. The repeat rule is the answer to a different question, asked of a different person.

options.text: Five years, three years and one year
options.why: Section 132 sets bands and the band is fixed by the amount, not by how bad the conduct sounds. Where the amount goes past ₹5 crore the offence may be punished with imprisonment up to five years and with fine. Where it is above ₹2 crore and does not go past ₹5 crore the term is up to three years and fine. The third band is narrower than the other two: it belongs only to the limb about invoices issued without any supply, and between ₹1 crore and ₹2 crore that limb carries up to one year and fine. For the first two bands the term also cannot fall below six months unless the judgment records special and adequate reasons.
keywords: punished with imprisonment up to five years and with fine
does not go past ₹5 crore the term is up to three years and fine
that limb carries up to one year and fine

options.text: Five years, three years, and nothing for the third — an amount below ₹2 crore is not an offence
options.misconception: applies the general ₹2 crore floor to the invoice limb, which has a band of its own starting lower
options.why: The ₹2 crore line is the floor for the ordinary bands. It is not a floor on the whole section. One limb — issuing an invoice or bill without any supply behind it and taking the benefit — is punishable from ₹1 crore upwards, and that is the limb the third accused is in. Reading the ₹2 crore as universal wipes out the band Parliament wrote for exactly this conduct.

options.text: Five years each, the maximum being the same in every case and the amount going only to what the judge actually awards
options.misconception: treats the amount as a sentencing factor when the Act makes it the thing that selects the maximum
options.why: Five years is the ceiling for the top band and for a second offence, not a general ceiling. The section ties each maximum to a money band, so the amount decides which ceiling applies before any question of sentencing arises. On this reading a ₹1.6 crore case would carry the same exposure as a ₹7 crore one.

citation.ref: Section 132(1) clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) read with section 132(2) and 132(3)

items.scenario: Three prosecutions are decided in one sessions court. In the first, ₹7 crore of tax was evaded by suppressing supplies. In the second, ₹3.1 crore of credit was wrongly availed. In the third, invoices were issued for supplies that were never made and the benefit of ₹1.6 crore was kept. None of the three accused has been convicted under the Act before.

items.stem: Who may compound, and what will it cost?

options.text: Only the third, and the amount is the whole of the tax involved
options.misconception: takes the ceiling of the band for the amount itself, so the Commissioner appears to have no discretion at all
options.why: The section gives a floor and a ceiling and leaves the working out to the rules, which set the amount by reference to the clause the offence falls in and the band it is punishable under. Treating the ceiling as the price would make every compounding cost the same and would remove the reason for applying at all in a small case.

options.text: All three, once each has paid the tax, interest and penalty, compounding being open whether or not prosecution has begun
options.misconception: reads the payment condition as the only condition, and never reaches the list of people the section refuses outright
options.why: Both halves of that sentence are true and they are not the whole test. The section carries its own list of people it does not apply to, and two of these three are on it: a person accused of committing an offence under section 132(1)(b), which is the limb about invoices issued with no supply behind them, and a person convicted for an offence under this Act by a court. Paying up does not lift either bar.
keywords: a person accused of committing an offence under section 132(1)(b)
a person convicted for an offence under this Act by a court

options.text: The first and the third, but not the second — only an actual conviction bars compounding
options.misconception: treats the bar as needing a conviction, when being accused under one particular clause is enough on its own
options.why: Conviction is one bar and it is not the only one. Another entry on the same list turns on being accused, not convicted, and it names one clause only — the invoice-without-supply limb. That is why the first applicant is refused while his case is still only an accusation. The list also shuts out somebody who has already been allowed to compound once for the listed clauses.

options.text: Only the third, and the amount is set within a statutory band worked out on the tax involved
options.why: Compounding is open before or after a prosecution starts, so the launch does not shut any of them out by itself. What shuts two of them out is the list in the section. The price for the one who is left is not at large: the compounding amount is not less than 25 per cent of the tax involved and not more than 100 per cent of that tax, and the application cannot be allowed at all until the tax, interest and penalty have been paid — which the third has done. Once the amount is paid, no further proceedings for the same offence may be started and any criminal proceedings already begun stand abated.
keywords: the compounding amount is not less than 25 per cent of the tax involved
and not more than 100 per cent of that tax
no further proceedings for the same offence may be started

citation.ref: Section 138(1), (2) and (3) read with rule 162 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: Three people apply to the Commissioner to compound. The first is accused of issuing invoices without any supply behind them so that his buyers could take credit. The second was convicted by a court last year of an offence under this Act. The third suppressed supplies in one year, has since paid the tax, the interest and the penalty in full, and has never applied to compound before. Prosecution has been launched against all three.

items.stem: How does the law treat the two masters?

options.text: The first is excused and has done what the excuse requires; the second has broken the rule
options.why: The general rule is a place rule: a vessel entering India from outside may call only at a customs port, and an aircraft only at a customs airport, unless the Board permits somewhere else — and that binds the first call after arrival and any later call while she still carries passengers or cargo brought in her. The one way out is that she was driven in by accident, stress of weather or some other cause she could not avoid, and it is not a free pass: the arrival has to be reported to the nearest customs officer or officer in charge of a police station, nothing may be unloaded without permission, and nobody may leave the vicinity. The first master has done all three. The second had no compulsion at all, and convenience is not one.
keywords: may call only at a customs port, and an aircraft only at a customs airport
driven in by accident, stress of weather or some other cause she could not avoid

options.text: Both are excused, the rule reaching only cargo that is actually landed
options.misconception: reads the section as a rule about unloading, when it is a rule about where the conveyance itself may go
options.why: The prohibition bites on the calling and the landing, not on the cargo coming off. That is deliberate: a conveyance sitting at an unapproved place with imported goods aboard is the situation the section exists to prevent, and a contravention operates as a presumption against the person in charge that he meant to bring goods in unlawfully.

options.text: The first is excused and need do nothing further, the emergency lifting customs control for as long as it lasts
options.misconception: treats the excuse as suspending the whole of the customs control rather than substituting a reporting duty for the place rule
options.why: The excuse replaces one obligation with three. Nothing about being blown off course lets goods come ashore unwatched; that is precisely when the risk is highest. Goods may be moved and people may leave only where health, safety or the preservation of life or property requires it, and the master must follow whatever directions the officer gives about the goods.

options.text: Neither is excused; the section admits no exception and both masters are liable
options.misconception: knows the prohibition and not the exception written into the same section for a conveyance in trouble
options.why: There is an exception and it is narrow on purpose. A master who is forced off his course by weather or an accident cannot be made to choose between his ship and the customs law. What the law asks of him instead is that he reports at once and keeps the cargo where it is until an officer says otherwise.

citation.ref: Section 29(1) and 29(2)

items.scenario: Two ships arrive off the same stretch of coast. The first is driven by a cyclone into a small fishing harbour that is not a customs port; her master anchors there, tells the nearest police station what has happened, and keeps everything aboard. The second, in calm weather and with cargo and passengers aboard, calls at the same harbour because it is nearer her buyer's godown than the customs port is. The Board has permitted neither call.

items.stem: What follows for each person in charge?

options.text: Both are late, and each faces a penalty
options.why: The two conveyances are on different clocks and both were missed. For a vehicle the document is an import report and it is due within twelve hours after its arrival at the customs station, so Wednesday morning is well outside. For a vessel or an aircraft it is an arrival manifest or import manifest and it goes in electronically before the conveyance arrives, so an hour after berthing is already too late. Where the document is not delivered in time and the proper officer is not satisfied there was sufficient cause, the person in charge is liable to a penalty up to 50,000.
keywords: an import report and it is due within twelve hours after its arrival
the person in charge is liable to a penalty up to 50,000

options.text: Neither is late — filing before unloading starts is what the section asks for
options.misconception: takes unloading as the deadline because that is when the manifest first gets used, when the section names arrival instead
options.why: The manifest is what the department reads before the conveyance gets here, so it can decide what to look at and be ready to supervise. Tying it to unloading would defeat that; and for a vehicle the section fixes a number of hours after arrival, which has nothing to do with when anything comes off.

options.text: Only the vehicle's is late; a vessel's manifest may be delivered at any time up to the grant of entry inwards
options.misconception: confuses the manifest with the thing that waits on it, so the deadline slides to whenever the vessel happens to be given entry inwards
options.why: Entry inwards is granted after the manifest has been delivered, or after a valid reason for not delivering it has been accepted. That makes the manifest the earlier event, not the later one. Reading the deadline off entry inwards would let a vessel set her own filing date by asking for entry inwards late.

options.text: Both are late, and the documents can no longer be accepted at all, so the goods stay where they are
options.misconception: treats lateness as making the document incapable of being received, rather than as attracting a penalty
options.why: A late manifest or import report may still be accepted by the proper officer on grounds he finds justified, and an incorrect or incomplete one may be amended or supplemented where there is no fraudulent intention. What lateness produces is a money consequence, not a dead end; treating it as a dead end would strand cargo for a filing slip.

citation.ref: Section 30(1) and 30(2) read with section 30(3)

items.scenario: Two consignments reach two customs stations on the same Monday. One comes by truck across a land border, and the person in charge files his document on Wednesday morning with no explanation for the gap. The other comes by sea, and the steamer agent files the vessel's document an hour after she has berthed, again with nothing said about the timing. The proper officer at each station is not satisfied that there was any sufficient cause.

items.stem: What may be landed now?

options.text: Everything except the machine tools
options.why: The bar on unloading before entry inwards is granted does not cover the whole ship. A passenger's own luggage, and a crew member's, and mail bags and animals sit outside it, and so do perishable goods and hazardous goods — the things that spoil, suffer or endanger if they are left waiting on a piece of paper. The suitcases, the post, the horses and the chilled fish are all in that list. The machine tools are ordinary cargo and they wait. Note also that the bar is written for vessels and not for aircraft or vehicles at all.
keywords: mail bags and animals sit outside it
and so do perishable goods and hazardous goods

options.text: Everything, entry inwards mattering only where duty is payable on the cargo
options.misconception: treats the order as a revenue formality, when it is the moment the department says it is ready to supervise the unloading
options.why: Entry inwards is not about who owes duty. It is the officer's acknowledgement that the department has the manifest and is ready to watch the cargo come off and assess it. Its date also fixes the rate of duty where a bill of entry was filed in advance, so it is not a piece of bookkeeping.

options.text: Only the passenger's baggage
options.misconception: remembers the first item on the list of exceptions and stops there
options.why: Baggage is the exception people remember because passengers are visible. The list is longer, and each of the others is on it for a reason of its own — post has its own regime, and animals, perishables and hazardous goods cannot safely be held.

options.text: Nothing at all until the officer has made his order
options.misconception: reads the bar as absolute, when the section carries its own list of things it does not touch
options.why: An absolute bar would mean livestock standing in a hold and fish spoiling because a manifest entry was queried. The section names the exceptions for that reason. Everything else does wait, so the instinct is right about the machine tools and wrong about the rest.

citation.ref: Section 31(1), 31(2) and 31(3) read with sections 32, 33 and 34

items.scenario: A vessel berths at a customs port and the proper officer has not yet made any order about her, a query on her manifest still being open. Waiting to come off are a passenger's suitcases, sacks of overseas post, two racehorses, a reefer container of chilled fish and a container of machine tools. The shipping agent asks what he may land while the query is open.

items.stem: Where do the two dates leave him?

options.text: Both are fine — a bill of entry may go in at any time before the goods are cleared, and as early as the importer likes
options.misconception: treats the bill of entry as a step in a queue rather than a document with a deadline at each end
options.why: The document is what the department assesses on, so it is wanted before the goods get here, not whenever the importer is ready. There is an advance window and it is measured against the expected arrival, so a filing months ahead has no arrival to be measured against.

options.text: The filing is late, and the goods must now be sold under the procedure for goods nobody clears
options.misconception: jumps from a late bill of entry to the uncleared-goods machinery, which runs on a different clock and a different event
options.why: Two different clocks are being mixed. Late presentation of a bill of entry costs the prescribed charges. The sale machinery is reached only when goods have sat unloaded for thirty days without being cleared for home consumption or warehoused, and here the importer filed on the third day.

options.text: The filing is late, and March would have been too early
options.why: The window has two ends. At the near end, the bill of entry is due before the close of the day preceding the day the vessel arrives at the station where the goods are to be cleared or warehoused, holidays counted in — so 9 May, not 12 May. The Board may prescribe a different limit for some cases but never later than the end of the day of arrival, so 12 May is outside on any view, and where the proper officer finds no sufficient cause the importer pays the prescribed charges for late presentation. At the far end, it may be lodged up to thirty days before the expected arrival and no earlier, which puts the earliest date at 10 April.
keywords: before the close of the day preceding the day the vessel arrives
lodged up to thirty days before the expected arrival and no earlier
the importer pays the prescribed charges for late presentation

options.text: The filing is in time, being within thirty days, and March would have been in time too
options.misconception: reads the thirty days as an outer limit running after arrival, when it is an advance window running before it
options.why: The thirty days runs backwards from the expected arrival, not forwards from it. Read the other way it would give an importer a month's grace after the ship berthed and would make the day-before deadline meaningless. That misreading also makes March look permissible, and it is not — March is more than thirty days before 10 May.

citation.ref: Section 46(3) with its provisos

items.scenario: An importer's vessel is expected at a customs port on 10 May and does berth on 10 May. He files his bill of entry for home consumption on 12 May and has nothing to say about why it went in then. He also asks his consultant whether he could instead have lodged it in the third week of March, when the goods were shipped, and got the whole thing out of the way early.

items.stem: Which of them owes interest, and how is the rate arrived at?

options.text: Neither; interest runs only against an importer on the deferred-payment scheme who misses his due date
options.misconception: reads the interest as attaching to the deferred-payment scheme, when the section carries three payment dates and interest backs all of them
options.why: Deferred payment is one of three limbs, not the only one that can be missed. The section fixes a date for self-assessment, a date for a returned bill of entry and a date under the deferred-payment rules, and interest answers a failure to pay in time under any of them.

options.text: The second only, and the rate sits inside a band the Central Government fixes within
options.why: The first importer is on the self-assessment limb, where the duty falls due on the date the bill of entry is presented, and he paid on that date. The second is on the assessment limb, where the duty is payable within one day, excluding holidays, of the bill of entry being returned to him — a Friday return with a closed weekend makes Monday the last day, so Wednesday is two days late. Interest then runs on what he did not pay, at a rate the Central Government fixes that is not below 10 per cent and not exceeding 36 per cent a year. The Board may waive it in the public interest, and that is a separate power from fixing it.
keywords: the duty is payable within one day, excluding holidays
not below 10 per cent and not exceeding 36 per cent a year

options.text: The second only, and the Board fixes whatever rate it thinks fit
options.misconception: gives the rate-fixing to the body that holds the waiver power, and drops the statutory band along with it
options.why: Two different bodies do two different things here. The Central Government fixes the rate and can only fix it inside the band the section sets. The Board's power is to waive interest in the public interest — a relief in a particular situation, not a licence to set the rate.

options.text: Both, the first importer's duty falling due only when the clearance order is made
options.misconception: reads the order permitting clearance as the thing that creates the payment obligation, when it is the thing that follows payment
options.why: The order permitting clearance for home consumption comes after the officer is satisfied the goods are not prohibited and the duty and charges have been paid. So payment precedes the order rather than waiting on it, and for a self-assessing importer the date is the date the bill of entry was presented.

citation.ref: Section 47(1) and 47(2) read with section 17

items.scenario: Two importers at one port. The first self-assesses and pays on the day he presents his bill of entry. The second's bill of entry is reassessed by the proper officer and returned to him for payment on a Friday; he pays on the following Wednesday, and the only closed days in between were the Saturday and the Sunday. Neither is on the deferred-payment scheme.

items.stem: What is open to each of them?

options.text: Neither — goods can only be disposed of after confiscation proceedings
options.misconception: confuses disposal of goods nobody has cleared with disposal of goods held to be offending
options.why: Confiscation follows a finding that something was done wrong. Nothing has been done wrong here; the importer is simply stuck. That is why the Act gives a commercial answer — sale by the custodian on notice — rather than a penal one.

options.text: The custodian may sell, and the importer may ask for the goods to be put into a public warehouse instead
options.why: Once thirty days have passed without the goods being cleared for home consumption or removed for warehousing, and the proper officer has allowed no further time, the custodian may sell them by auction — but only once the department has approved that sale and the importer has been told it is coming, so it is not something he does on his own. Animals, foodstuffs and hazardous goods may go sooner. The importer's answer is to satisfy the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner that he cannot clear within a reasonable time and have the goods stored in a public warehouse for thirty days, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner by thirty days at a time; the goods do not become warehoused goods and the warehousing chapter does not touch them.
keywords: the custodian may sell them by auction
extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner by thirty days at a time

options.text: The importer may put them in a public warehouse, and they then become warehoused goods with the warehousing period and interest running
options.misconception: treats storage pending clearance as ordinary warehousing because the goods go into a warehouse
options.why: The section says in terms that goods deposited this way are not warehoused goods for the purposes of the Act, so the warehousing chapter and its periods and interest do not apply. That is the whole point of the facility: somewhere to keep goods while a hold-up is sorted out, not entry into the bonding system.

options.text: The custodian may sell at once and on his own, the thirty days having run
options.misconception: reads the thirty days as the only condition on the sale, and drops the two protections that sit beside it
options.why: Time passing is what opens the door; it is not the whole procedure. The department has to approve the sale and the importer has to be given notice, because the goods are still his until they are sold and he may yet be able to clear them.

citation.ref: Section 48 read with section 49

items.scenario: A consignment of machine parts is unloaded and then sits. The importer is waiting on a clearance from another government department and has neither entered the goods for home consumption nor for warehousing. Thirty-five days have gone by. The custodian wants the shed space and the importer wants somewhere lawful to put the goods until his clearance comes through.

items.stem: Which of the four is an educational institution for the purposes of entry 66?

options.text: The school, the college, and the training institute for its electrician course only
options.why: The definition has three limbs and each of the four bodies has to be put against them. Pre-school and schooling to higher secondary or its equivalent is the first, and the school is in it. The second is education forming part of a curriculum for a qualification recognised by any law in force, and an AICTE-recognised degree is exactly that. The third is an approved vocational education course, which for an industrial training institute means a designated trade notified under the Apprentices Act — so the electrician course qualifies and the self-designed one does not. A coaching centre training people for a job leads to no qualification recognised by law, so it is not an educational institution however it styles itself.
keywords: a curriculum for a qualification recognised by any law in force
a designated trade notified under the Apprentices Act
a coaching centre training people for a job leads to no qualification recognised by law

options.text: The school and the training institute for both its courses, the college's degree being conferred by a university rather than by the college itself
options.misconception: asks who grants the qualification instead of whether the curriculum leads to one the law recognises, and then treats every course an affiliated institute runs as approved
options.why: The limb looks at the curriculum and the recognition, not at whose name is on the certificate; a college delivering an AICTE-recognised programme is in. And affiliation is not enough on its own for the training institute — the course itself has to be in a notified trade, which one of these two is not.

options.text: The school and the college only
options.misconception: stops at the two familiar limbs and never reaches the vocational one
options.why: There is a third limb and it is the one that carries industrial training institutes. It is narrow: the course has to be an approved vocational education course, which for a private institute means a trade the Central Government has notified, or a modular employable skill course approved by the national council. On this reading the electrician course would be taxed, and it is not.

options.text: All four, each of them teaching somebody something
options.misconception: reads the exemption as being about teaching in general, when it turns on a closed definition with three limbs
options.why: Teaching is not the test. The definition asks what the education leads to — a school stage, a qualification the law recognises, or a notified trade — and an institution that meets none of the three is outside entry 66 whatever it calls itself. Otherwise every tuition class in the country would be exempt.

citation.ref: Entry 66 read with the definitions of educational institution and approved vocational education course in paragraph 2

items.scenario: A trust runs four things under one registration. A school teaching to the twelfth standard. A college whose engineering degree is recognised by the All India Council for Technical Education. A centre coaching candidates for a bank recruitment test, which awards its own certificate at the end. And a private industrial training institute affiliated to the National Council for Vocational Education and Training, running an electrician course that the Central Government has notified under the Apprentices Act, 1961 and a mobile-repair course the institute designed itself.

items.stem: Which of the six bills carry GST?

options.text: None of the six, the trust being a charitable trust running the lot
options.misconception: reads the exemption as belonging to the person who owns the activity rather than to the activity itself
options.why: Entry 66 says nothing about who runs the institution. It asks what the institution provides, so one trust can hold two exempt units and two taxable ones at the same time. A trust's charitable character is a different exemption with its own conditions and it does not reach coaching.

options.text: The coaching fees and the mobile-repair fees
options.why: Entry 66 exempts what an educational institution supplies to its own students, faculty and staff, so the school fees, the college fees and the electrician-course fees are all out of tax. A separate item covers conducting an entrance examination against an entrance fee, and it extends to a private training institute in respect of its notified trades, so the college's entrance test fee is exempt too. What is left is the two supplies made by bodies that are not educational institutions for this purpose at all, and the coaching fees and the mobile-repair fees are taxable.
keywords: supplies to its own students, faculty and staff
conducting an entrance examination against an entrance fee
the coaching fees and the mobile-repair fees are taxable

options.text: The coaching fees only
options.misconception: treats the whole training institute as exempt because one of its courses is, when the entry follows the course and not the body
options.why: The institute is an educational institution only in respect of the notified trade. A course it designed for itself is not an approved vocational education course, so the fees for it are taxed even though the same institute's electrician fees are not. The exemption attaches course by course.

options.text: The coaching fees, the mobile-repair fees and the entrance test fee, an examination not being education
options.misconception: assumes only teaching is exempt, and misses the separate item that covers conducting an entrance examination
options.why: Conducting an entrance examination was not covered by the original entry and an item was added for it, so it now stands on its own footing. It is not being treated as teaching; it is separately exempt, and the consideration it names is the entrance fee.

citation.ref: Entry 66 items (a) and (aa)

items.scenario: In one month the same trust raises six sets of bills on the people it teaches: school fees, college fees, the fee for the college's own entrance test, coaching fees, fees for the training institute's electrician course and fees for its mobile-repair course. The accountant wants to know which of the six he must charge GST on.

items.stem: Which of those six bills carry GST?

options.text: The college's bus and canteen bills but not its guarding bill, guarding not being one of the listed services
options.misconception: half-remembers the list and drops the item that is on it
options.why: Security is on the list, alongside cleaning and housekeeping, and it is worded as being performed in the institution. Leaving it off would give a college an exemption on guarding that a school gets and the college does not — the list runs the other way about.

options.text: All three of the college's, and none of the school's
options.why: The inward limb of entry 66 is the one with a ceiling on it. Transport of students, faculty and staff is exempt when supplied to an institution whose education stops at higher secondary school or its equivalent, pre-school included, and so is catering, including a mid-day meal scheme the government sponsors, and so is security, cleaning or housekeeping performed inside the institution. Past that level none of the three is exempt, so the college's bus, canteen and guarding bills all carry tax while the school's identical bills do not.
keywords: catering, including a mid-day meal scheme the government sponsors
security, cleaning or housekeeping performed inside the institution

options.text: None of the six, the recipient being an educational institution in every case
options.misconception: reads the inward limb as reaching every educational institution, the way the output limb does
options.why: The two limbs are drawn differently on purpose. What an institution supplies to its own students is exempt at every level. What is supplied to it is exempt only up to higher secondary, so a degree college pays tax on the same bus and the same lunch that a school does not.

options.text: All six, an exemption for inward services being available only to a government institution
options.misconception: adds a public-ownership condition the entry does not carry
options.why: Nothing in the inward limb turns on who owns the school. A private school teaching to the twelfth standard gets the transport, catering and security exemption in the same way a government one does. The condition is the level taught, not the ownership.

citation.ref: Entry 66 item (b) sub-items (i), (ii) and (iii) with the proviso limiting them to pre-school and school education up to higher secondary

items.scenario: Three outside contractors bill the same trust in one month. A bus operator carries pupils and teachers to the school and students and lecturers to the college. A caterer runs the school kitchen, where a state-sponsored mid-day meal is served, and separately runs the college canteen. A guarding agency posts staff at both campuses.

items.stem: How is each subscription taxed?

options.text: The college's is exempt and the school's is taxable
options.why: The supply of online educational journals or periodicals to an educational institution is exempt, but not where the institution provides pre-school or school education up to higher secondary or its equivalent, or an approved vocational course. So this limb is the mirror image of the transport and catering limb: those stop at higher secondary and this one starts above it. A school library's subscription is taxed and a degree college library's is not.
keywords: supply of online educational journals or periodicals to an educational institution is exempt
but not where the institution provides pre-school or school education up to higher secondary or its equivalent

options.text: The school's is exempt and the college's is taxable
options.misconception: applies the transport and catering rule, which caps the exemption at higher secondary, to a limb the notification writes the other way round
options.why: This is the natural guess and it is exactly inverted. Transport, catering and security are for the school and stop below the college. Journals are withheld from the school and available to the college. The two rules sit in the same entry and point in opposite directions, which is what makes this examinable.

options.text: Both are exempt, the recipient being an educational institution in each case
options.misconception: treats every item in the inward list as reaching every educational institution
options.why: Each sub-item of the inward limb carries its own condition. Two of them are capped at higher secondary; this one is expressly withheld from institutions at that level and from approved vocational courses. Being an educational institution is the entry point, not the answer.

options.text: Both are taxable, an online subscription being a supply of information rather than an education service
options.misconception: asks what kind of service it is, when the entry names the supply directly
options.why: The list does not require the inward supply to be an education service — transport and catering plainly are not. The entry names online educational journals or periodicals in terms, so the only question left is which institution is receiving them.

citation.ref: Entry 66 item (b) sub-item (v) with the proviso excluding pre-school, school education up to higher secondary and approved vocational courses

items.scenario: A publisher sells the same annual subscription to online academic journals twice over to the same trust: once for the school library and once for the college library. The invoices are identical apart from the delivery address.

items.stem: Which of the agency's three bills carry GST?

options.text: All three, admission processing being a business support service outside entry 66 altogether
options.misconception: classifies the agency's work by what it is called commercially instead of reading the sub-item that names it
options.why: The inward list names services relating to admission to, or conduct of examination by, the institution, and that is what the agency does. How the agency describes its own line of business does not move it out of a sub-item written for it.

options.text: Only the mobile-repair one
options.why: Unlike transport, catering and security, services relating to admission to or conduct of examination by an educational institution are exempt however high the institution teaches, so the college's bill is exempt without more. A private ITI is an educational institution only in respect of a designated trade, and for those trades the exemption reaches both the services supplied to it and its own entrance examination fee. For any other trade GST is payable on the services by and to the institute, so the third bill is taxed.
keywords: services relating to admission to or conduct of examination by an educational institution
A private ITI is an educational institution only in respect of a designated trade

options.text: The two training institute bills
options.misconception: treats a private industrial training institute as never being an educational institution
options.why: A private institute is one for the trades the Central Government has notified, and for those trades the admission and examination services supplied to it are exempt in the same way as the college's. Only the course outside the notified list is taxed, so one of these two bills is exempt.

options.text: None of the three
options.misconception: extends the exemption from the notified trades to everything the institute runs
options.why: The exemption follows the course. On a trade that is not notified the institute is not an educational institution at all for this entry, and the services supplied to it are taxed like services to any other business. A single institute can be on both sides of the line at once.

citation.ref: Entry 66 item (b) sub-item (iv) read with Circular No. 55/29/2018 GST dated 09.08.2018

items.scenario: An outside agency does the same work for three clients: it takes in and processes admission applications and runs the sitting of the examination. Its clients are the trust's degree college, the training institute's electrician course notified under the Apprentices Act, and the same institute's self-designed mobile-repair course.

items.stem: Is the fresh claim out of time?

options.text: No — the first filing stops limitation for good, and time never runs again on that claim
options.misconception: treats the first filing as ending limitation rather than as pausing it for a measured stretch
options.why: What is protected is a defined period with two ends: the day of filing and the day the deficiencies were communicated. After that the clock starts running again, so a claimant who takes months to gather his documents can still go out of time. The pause is not a stop.

options.text: Yes — a fresh application is a fresh application, and it has to be inside the original two years
options.misconception: reads the requirement to file again as wiping out the first filing, when the rule that requires it also protects the time it cost
options.why: The requirement and the protection are in the same sub-rule. Without the exclusion the department could run a claim out of time by sitting on it and then asking for a document, which is the opposite of what a deficiency memo is for.

options.text: No, but the excluded stretch runs to the day the fresh claim is filed, so everything after the memo is protected too
options.misconception: takes the wrong end of the excluded period, and hands the claimant time he spent himself
options.why: The exclusion ends when the officer tells him what is wrong. From that moment the delay is his own, and the rule does not cover it. Reading it to the date of the fresh claim would give an indefinite extension to anybody who received one memo.

options.text: No — the days the claim spent with the officer do not count against him
options.why: Once a deficiency memo goes out the claimant does not amend the old application, he files a fresh one, and the rule that says so also protects him from the delay it causes. The period from the date the claim was filed to the date the deficiencies were communicated is excluded from the two years for the fresh claim. Here that is twenty-four days added back, and three weeks of his window were still unused when he first filed, so he is inside it.
keywords: Once a deficiency memo goes out the claimant
to the date the deficiencies were communicated is excluded from the two years

citation.ref: Proviso to rule 90(3) read with section 54(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter files a refund claim with three weeks of his two years still to run. Twenty-four days later the proper officer sends him a form listing documents that are missing and requiring him to file again once he has put them right. By the time he has assembled them the two years, counted straight through, have gone.

items.stem: From what day do the two years run in each of the three?

options.text: The land consignment from the date of the shipping bill, the service from the day the work finished, and the post from the day the exporter handed the parcel over
options.misconception: picks the exporter's own act in each case instead of the event the Explanation names
options.why: Each of these is the exporter doing something, and each is one step away from the statutory event: a shipping bill is filed before the frontier is crossed, completing a service is not being paid for it, and handing a parcel in is not the Post Office despatching it abroad. The Explanation picks events the department can verify.

options.text: The frontier crossing, the day the money came in, and the day the Post Office sent them out
options.why: Explanation 2 fixes the relevant date by the ground of the claim, so three grounds give three starting days and none of them is the invoice date. For goods exported by land it is the date on which the goods pass the frontier. For a service exported where the supply was completed before the money came, it is the date of receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange, or in rupees where the Reserve Bank permits it — and the other way about, where the payment came first, it is the date of the invoice. For goods exported by post it is the date on which the Post Office concerned despatched them to a place outside India.
keywords: it is the date on which the goods pass the frontier
it is the date of receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange

options.text: All three from the invoice date, that being when the export was recorded
options.misconception: uses one date for every claim because the accounts use one date, when the Explanation gives a different starting event to each ground
options.why: The invoice date is the answer to exactly one case in the table — export of services where the payment was received in advance of the invoice. Used across the board it starts the clock too early on a land export and, on a service paid late, before the exporter even knew he had a claim.

options.text: All three from the end of the financial year in which the export took place
options.misconception: borrows the year-end convention from filing deadlines elsewhere in the Act
options.why: Nothing in the refund provision runs on a financial year. The Explanation names a physical or commercial event for each ground — a frontier crossed, money received, a parcel despatched — and two years run from that event.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 to section 54, entries 1 and 4

items.scenario: An exporter has three unrelated claims to file in one quarter. One consignment went by truck across a land border to a neighbouring country. One was a consultancy for an Irish client, finished and invoiced well before the fee arrived from Dublin. One consignment went out through the Post Office to Canada. His accountant has entered the invoice date against all three.

items.stem: What may he issue, and how many documents does he need?

options.text: Three credit notes, one for each invoice, a note being tied to the invoice it corrects
options.misconception: reads the credit note as a mirror of a single invoice, when the section allows one against several
options.why: The section is written the other way about: it starts from several tax invoices already issued and lets the supplier answer the lot with one credit note, or with as many as he wants. A single consolidated note against several invoices is expressly contemplated.

options.text: Credit notes for the first two, and nothing under this section for the third, a quality complaint being a matter between the parties
options.misconception: treats deficiency as a contractual argument, when the section names it as a ground of its own
options.why: Goods or services found to be deficient is written into the sub-section alongside an excess charge and a return. It is there because the value actually supplied is less than the invoice said, which is a tax question and not only a commercial one.

options.text: A debit note for the first and credit notes for the other two
options.misconception: picks the document by who is out of pocket rather than by whether the invoice charged too much or too little
options.why: A debit note is for the opposite case — where the value or tax in the invoice is less than what was payable and the supplier has to charge more. Here the first invoice charged too much, which is the leading ground for a credit note. Getting this the wrong way round makes the supplier collect a second time on an over-charge.

options.text: One credit note covering all three invoices
options.why: All three situations are grounds in the same sub-section. The first is where the taxable value or tax charged in the invoice exceeds the value or tax payable on the supply. The second is where the goods are returned by the recipient. The third is where the goods or services are found to be deficient. And the section is not fussy about the paperwork: one or more credit notes may answer several invoices of the same financial year, so one document can settle all three — the number of documents is his choice, not the section's.
keywords: the taxable value or tax charged in the invoice exceeds the value or tax payable
where the goods are returned by the recipient
one or more credit notes may answer several invoices of the same financial year

citation.ref: Section 34(1)

items.scenario: A supplier's three February invoices to one buyer each went wrong in a different way. On the first the rate was keyed a slab too high, so more tax was charged than the supply bore. On the second the buyer sent a quarter of the consignment back. On the third the buyer says the goods that arrived were below the specification. The supplier would rather put all three right with one document than issue three.

items.stem: Which of the two reductions in output tax survives?

options.text: Both, because the annual return can be revised and the earlier date therefore fixes nothing
options.misconception: treats the annual return as reopenable, so the earlier of the two dates never bites
options.why: The limb turns on the date the annual return was furnished, which is a past event and does not move. Reading it as provisional would make the second limb useless and give every supplier the November date whatever he had already filed.

options.text: Only the August one
options.why: A credit note goes into the return of the month it is issued in, and the output tax liability is then reduced — but only if it is issued inside the outer limit, which has two candidate dates and takes whichever falls first. One is the 30th of November following the end of the financial year in which the supply was made, which for a February 2026 supply is 30 November 2026. The other is the date the relevant annual return is actually furnished, which here was 15 October 2026. Filing the annual return early pulled the shutter down early, so the November note is out of time for tax even though November had not ended.
keywords: the output tax liability is then reduced
the 30th of November following the end of the financial year
the date the relevant annual return is actually furnished

options.text: Both — 30 November had not passed when the second note was issued
options.misconception: reads the November date as the deadline and never applies the second limb that can arrive sooner
options.why: The section gives two dates and takes the earlier of them. The November date is only the answer where the annual return has not yet gone in. Once it has, the year is closed for this purpose, and that is the point of having the second limb at all.

options.text: Neither — a credit note against a February supply has to be issued inside the same financial year
options.misconception: reads the reference to a financial year in sub-section (1) as a deadline, when it describes the supplies a note may cover
options.why: The financial year in the first sub-section describes what a note may be raised against — supplies made in a financial year. The deadline is in the next sub-section and it deliberately runs past the year end, which is why an August note on a February supply is good.

citation.ref: Section 34(2)

items.scenario: A supplier made the supplies in question in February 2026. He issued one credit note against them in August 2026 and declared it in his August return. He filed his annual return for that financial year on 15 October 2026. He then issued a second credit note against the same supplies on 20 November 2026 and declared it in his November return.

items.stem: Can he reduce his output tax?

options.text: Yes, provided the distributor reverses the input tax credit it took on the original invoice
options.misconception: reads credit reversal by the immediate buyer as the whole condition, when the proviso asks who finally bore the tax
options.why: Reversal by the recipient is how the mechanism works when the proviso does not apply, and it is not an answer to the proviso. The question the proviso asks is whether the burden was handed further down the chain. Here it was, and the distributor's own credit position does not reach the customers who actually paid.

options.text: No, and he cannot give the price reduction either, since the section blocks the adjustment
options.misconception: reads a bar on the tax adjustment as a bar on the commercial arrangement behind it
options.why: The Act governs the tax, not the bargain. Two businesses may settle a price however they like, and a document recording that settlement without touching tax is unaffected by section 34. What the proviso stops is the supplier recovering tax from the government that somebody else has already paid him.

options.text: Yes — the proviso is about refund claims under section 54, not about credit notes
options.misconception: borrows the unjust-enrichment idea from the refund provisions and assumes it lives only there
options.why: The same principle appears twice in the Act because it can be defeated twice. The credit note route has its own proviso sitting in section 34 itself, and it does its work at the moment the supplier tries to reduce his liability, without any refund claim being made at all.

options.text: No, but he can still give the money back
options.why: The proviso to the same sub-section allows no reduction in the supplier's output tax liability where the incidence of tax and interest on the supply has been passed on to any other person. That is what has happened: the distributor recovered the tax from its own customers, so giving the supplier his tax back would leave the money with the distributor rather than with whoever bore it. Being inside the time limit does not help, because this is a separate condition. What is still open is a commercial credit note, which returns the price without any tax adjustment on either side.
keywords: where the incidence of tax and interest on the supply has been passed on
allows no reduction in the supplier's output tax liability
a commercial credit note, which returns the price without any tax adjustment

citation.ref: Proviso to section 34(2)

items.scenario: A supplier agrees, months after the event, to knock ten per cent off an old invoice because the goods underperformed. His buyer is a distributor who has already sold every unit on to its own customers at the full price and charged them tax on that full price. The supplier is inside the time limit and wants to take the tax back on the ten per cent.

items.stem: How are these treated while the vessel is in India?

options.text: Only the fuel and the lifejackets are stores; the shaft is a spare that will be fitted later and is ordinary imported cargo
options.misconception: reads the definition as covering only what is in use now, when it says the opposite in so many words
options.why: The definition was written to catch this argument. It names spare parts and other articles of equipment and adds that it does not matter whether they are for immediate fitting. A shaft carried for a future repair is a store, not cargo, and treating it as cargo would put duty on the ship's own equipment.

options.text: All four are stores; three may stay aboard duty-free and the oil may be transferred with permission
options.why: Stores means goods for use in a vessel or aircraft, and the definition says in terms that it takes in fuel, spare parts and other articles of equipment whether or not they are for immediate fitting — so an uncrated propeller shaft for a later voyage counts, and so do lifejackets. A vehicle's supplies are outside the definition altogether. Section 86 then does two things: imported stores may remain on board without payment of duty while the vessel is in India, and with the proper officer's permission they may be transferred to another vessel or aircraft as stores for consumption there.
keywords: whether or not they are for immediate fitting
imported stores may remain on board without payment of duty while the vessel is in India

options.text: They may stay aboard only until the vessel's cargo has been discharged, after which duty falls on whatever is left
options.misconception: attaches the duty-free period to the cargo operation instead of to the vessel's status
options.why: Nothing in section 86 turns on discharging cargo. Stores may remain on board without duty while the vessel is in India, and what ends the duty-free consumption is the vessel ceasing to be foreign-going, not her holds being emptied.

options.text: All four are stores, but nothing may be moved to another vessel without first paying duty and re-exporting
options.misconception: treats a transfer between two ships as an import followed by an export, when the section provides for it directly
options.why: Section 86 allows the transfer as such, on the proper officer's permission, for consumption on the receiving vessel or aircraft. Nothing is cleared for home consumption and no duty falls due, which is the whole convenience the section exists to give.

citation.ref: Section 2(38) read with section 86

items.scenario: A vessel arrives in India carrying, besides her cargo, drums of fuel, a crated propeller shaft that will not be fitted on this voyage, a consignment of lifejackets, and a pallet of engine oil that her owner wants moved across to a sister vessel berthed alongside for use on that ship's voyage. The master asks what he may leave where it is and what he may move.

items.stem: What duty position does that day create?

options.text: Duty becomes chargeable on what is still aboard, assessed off the store list in the manifest
options.why: Section 87 lets imported stores on board be consumed without payment of duty during the period the vessel is a foreign-going vessel, and that period runs from her first Indian port of arrival to her final Indian port of departure for somewhere outside India. Converting to a coastal run at Chennai ends it. From that day the ordinary law of levy applies, so import duty is chargeable on the unconsumed stores then on board, and the store list filed as part of the arrival manifest is the basic document for working the assessment out.
keywords: during the period the vessel is a foreign-going vessel
import duty is chargeable on the unconsumed stores then on board

options.text: Duty becomes chargeable on the whole of the stores that were brought in, including what was already burned at sea
options.misconception: charges duty on everything landed rather than on what survives the change of status
options.why: What was consumed while she was still foreign-going was lawfully consumed without duty and nothing reopens it. The charge falls on what is on board when the character changes, which is why the store list matters — it is the starting point from which consumption is deducted.

options.text: Nothing changes; the stores came in on a foreign-going vessel and keep that character for as long as they last
options.misconception: fixes the position at the moment of arrival, when the section describes a period that can end
options.why: The exemption is written as running during a period, not as a status the goods acquire on arrival. When the vessel stops being foreign-going the period stops, and stores consumed on a purely Indian run are consumed inside India like anything else.

options.text: Duty becomes chargeable, but only when she next goes foreign again and the stores are re-exported
options.misconception: defers the charge to a later voyage, when the event the section names has already happened
options.why: The taxable event is the vessel ceasing to be foreign-going with stores still aboard. Waiting for a future foreign voyage would mean the stores are burned duty-free on the coastal run, which is exactly what the section stops.

citation.ref: Section 87 read with the definition of foreign-going vessel in section 2(21)

items.scenario: A vessel reaches Kochi from Dubai with fuel and provisions aboard that were shipped abroad. She works cargo at Kochi and Chennai, and at Chennai her owners put her on a run between two Indian ports for the next six months before she goes foreign again. A quantity of the fuel and provisions is still aboard on the day the coastal run starts.

items.stem: On what does the officer settle the quantity?

options.text: On the value of the goods, anything under the prescribed money limit going aboard free
options.misconception: expects a money threshold, when the section works on quantity measured against the voyage
options.why: There is no money limit in this section. The test is physical — how big the ship is, how many people are aboard and how long she will be at sea — because the mischief being guarded against is quantity, not value.

options.text: On whatever the master orders, the vessel being the best judge of her own needs
options.misconception: hands the quantity to the person receiving the benefit, when the section gives the determination to the officer
options.why: The section says the quantity is such as the proper officer may determine. Leaving it to the master would turn a duty-free stores facility into a duty-free export channel, which is why the statute names the three things he has to weigh.

options.text: On what the ship can be expected to need for the voyage she is about to make
options.why: Indian-made goods put aboard a ship or a plane going foreign, to be used there as her stores, leave the country with no export duty on them, but only in such quantities as the proper officer determines — and the section tells him what to weigh: the size of the vessel, how many passengers and crew she carries, and the length of the voyage or journey she is about to depart on. The measure is the estimated requirement of that voyage, so a year's supply is outside it. And the benefit runs only while she is a foreign-going vessel.
keywords: the size of the vessel, how many passengers and crew she carries
the length of the voyage or journey she is about to depart on

options.text: On the estimated requirement, and the benefit continues after she starts running between Indian ports
options.misconception: gets the measure right and drops the condition that the vessel must be foreign-going
options.why: The estimate is right and the second half is not. The exemption is for stores on a foreign-going vessel. Once she is on a coastal run she is not one, and Indian goods put aboard her are supplied inside India in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Section 89

items.scenario: A chandler is asked to put Indian-grown rice, vegetables and drinking water aboard a vessel that is about to leave an Indian port for Singapore. He asks for the whole of a year's requirement to go aboard duty-free while the paperwork is open, and the proper officer says he will settle the quantity himself.

items.stem: How is each of the three dealt with?

options.text: The provisions go into the warehouse unassessed; the oil earns back all the duty and the tinned food earns back nearly all of it
options.why: Section 85 is a deliberate departure from ordinary warehousing, where goods are assessed on entry: where the importer declares that goods entered for warehousing are to be supplied as stores to vessels or aircraft with no import duty paid, the proper officer may permit them to be warehoused without being assessed to duty. Section 88 then carries the drawback chapter across to stores, and the rate splits: for fuel and lubricating oil taken aboard a foreign-going aircraft the drawback is the whole of the duty paid, against 98 per cent for other imported goods re-exported. Section 90 gives the same whole-duty treatment for stores for a ship of the Indian Navy.
keywords: permit them to be warehoused without being assessed to duty
the drawback is the whole of the duty paid
against 98 per cent for other imported goods re-exported

options.text: The provisions go in unassessed, and both the oil and the tinned food earn back the whole of the duty
options.misconception: extends the fuel-and-lubricant rate to every store put aboard, and loses the distinction the sections draw
options.why: The whole-duty drawback is written for fuel and lubricating oil taken on board a foreign-going aircraft, and for naval stores. Everything else re-exported goes on the ordinary drawback rate, which holds back a small part of the duty. The split is the examinable point.

options.text: All three are assessed in the ordinary way, with a refund once the goods are actually put aboard
options.misconception: assumes assessment always happens on warehousing and that relief can only come later as a refund
options.why: That is the ordinary rule and section 85 is the exception to it. Assessing stores that everybody knows are going straight back out, and then unwinding it, is work with no revenue in it, so the section lets the assessment be skipped on the importer's declaration.

options.text: The provisions cannot be warehoused at all, stores being outside the warehousing system
options.misconception: reads the special treatment of stores as excluding them from warehousing, when the section exists precisely to let them in
options.why: Keeping ships' stores in a bonded warehouse until a vessel calls for them is the arrangement section 85 was written to allow. What is disapplied is the assessment on entry, not the warehousing.

citation.ref: Sections 85, 88 and 90 read with sections 69 and 74

items.scenario: A chandler enters imported provisions for warehousing and declares that they will go aboard foreign-going vessels as stores with no duty paid on them. Separately he has duty-paid imported lubricating oil that he puts aboard a foreign-going aircraft, and duty-paid imported tinned food that he puts aboard the same aircraft. He asks what each of the three costs him.

items.stem: By when must the press be back with him or supplied from the job worker's premises?

options.text: 30 June 2027, but counted from the day the job worker received the press rather than the day it left the factory
options.misconception: applies the proviso written for goods sent straight to the job worker to goods that went out from the principal's own place
options.why: There is a proviso that starts the clock at receipt, and it is for capital goods sent directly to the job worker without first coming to the principal's place of business. This press went out from the factory, so the ordinary rule applies and the clock runs from despatch.

options.text: There is no date at all — capital goods sent for job work carry no time limit, only inputs do
options.misconception: over-reads the narrow carve-out for moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools into a rule about all capital goods
options.why: The carve-out is real and it is a list of four things: moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures, and tools. Everything else in the capital goods category, a press included, is on the three-year clock. The scenario rules the list out for exactly this reason.

options.text: 30 June 2025
options.misconception: applies the input clock to capital goods, so a machine is treated like the material it works on
options.why: One year is the period for inputs. Capital goods are on a longer clock because a machine may reasonably sit at a job worker's for years doing the work it was sent for. Using the shorter period would deem a supply of a press that is being used exactly as intended.

options.text: 30 June 2027
options.why: Capital goods sent out for job work carry a three-year clock, against one year for inputs, and it starts on the day they were sent out — so a press sent on 1 July 2024 must be received back or supplied from the job worker's premises by 30 June 2027. If that date passes with the press still there, the despatch is deemed a supply by the principal to the job worker made on the day the press went out, and the tax carries interest from that day.
keywords: a press sent on 1 July 2024 must be received back or supplied from the job worker's premises by 30 June 2027

citation.ref: Section 19(6) with its proviso and section 143(7)

items.scenario: A principal sent a hydraulic press from his own factory to a job worker on 1 July 2024, without payment of tax, for a job that keeps being put off. The press is capital goods and it is not a mould, a die, a jig, a fixture or a tool. His auditor, going through the job-work register in 2026, asks him for the date by which the press has to be dealt with.

items.stem: How is each of the three movements treated?

options.text: The principal must declare the shed as an additional place of business before shipping anything from it, whoever the job worker is
options.misconception: applies the declaration requirement across the board and misses the two situations in which it drops away
options.why: The declaration is the general requirement and it has two exceptions: where the job worker is registered, and where the principal deals in goods the Commissioner has notified. The first applies here, so the shipment can go ahead as things stand.

options.text: The return is not a supply at all — it is the same goods coming home, and tax has already been paid on the deemed supply
options.misconception: treats the deemed supply as settling the whole transaction, when it has already changed who owns the goods for tax purposes
options.why: The deeming treats the goods as having been supplied to the job worker on the day they went out. Once that has happened they are his, so sending them back is a movement in the other direction and a supply in its own right. He pays on it if he is liable to be registered, and he is.

options.text: The offcuts must come back to the principal and be supplied by him, the scrap belonging to the person who owned the material
options.misconception: reads the principal's route as the only one, when the section gives it as the fallback for an unregistered job worker
options.why: The provision names both routes and picks between them by registration. A registered job worker may send the scrap out from his own premises on payment of tax; it is only where he is unregistered that the principal has to do it. Hauling scrap back to the factory to sell it is exactly the waste the rule avoids.

options.text: The return is the job worker's supply, he may sell the offcuts himself, and the direct shipment needs no declaration
options.why: Once the period has run and the deeming has bitten, goods sent back afterwards are a supply by the job worker to the principal, and he pays tax on it because he is registered — that is over and above his job-work charges. Waste and scrap generated during the job work goes out on payment of tax from the job worker's own premises where he holds a registration, and from the principal's premises where he does not. And the principal may supply from that shed without declaring it as an additional place of business in two cases, one of which is that the job worker is registered under section 25.
keywords: goods sent back afterwards are a supply by the job worker to the principal
Waste and scrap generated during the job work
without declaring it as an additional place of business
the job worker is registered under section 25

citation.ref: Section 143(1) with its proviso, section 143(5) and section 19(3)

items.scenario: Inputs a principal sent out went past their period without coming back and the principal has already accounted for the deemed supply. Three things then happen. The job worker, who holds a registration of his own, sends the finished parts back. He also has a heap of offcuts from the same job that a local dealer will buy. And the principal has a customer who wants finished goods shipped straight from the job worker's shed, which the principal has never named on his own registration certificate.

items.stem: Goods or services?

options.text: Services, but only where the canteen is run by an outside contractor rather than by the factory itself
options.misconception: reads the classification as depending on who runs the kitchen, when the entry looks only at what is supplied
options.why: The entry describes a supply, not an arrangement. Whether the factory runs the canteen or engages somebody to run it may change who the supplier is and who the recipient is, and it does not change what the supply is.

options.text: A composite supply whose principal supply is the food, so it takes the rate the food would carry as goods
options.misconception: runs the natural-bundling analysis on a supply the Schedule has already classified, and lands on the wrong side
options.why: The Schedule lists this under composite supplies and then says what the whole of it is — services. There is no principal-supply exercise left to do, which is the difference between a deeming entry and the general composite supply rule.

options.text: Services
options.why: Schedule II settles it by deeming rather than by argument.
