Food or any other article for human consumption, or any drink, supplied by way of or as part of a service is treated as a supply of services — and it is listed among the composite supplies that the Schedule classifies whole. That is why a restaurant is never a supply of goods under GST however the bill is made up. What the ingredients cost does not enter into it, any more than it does for a works contract in the same paragraph.
keywords: Food or any other article for human consumption
is treated as a supply of services

options.text: Goods, because what changes hands is a tangible thing the worker takes and eats
options.misconception: classifies by what physically passes, which is the test the Schedule was written to displace
options.why: If physical transfer decided it, every restaurant in the country would be supplying goods and the rate, the time of supply and the place of supply would all move. The Schedule exists to stop that argument being available, and it names this exact supply.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6 of Schedule II read with section 7(1A)

items.scenario: A factory runs a canteen for its workers and charges them for their meals. The food is cooked on the premises and served at tables there; nothing is sold packed to take away, and the ingredients are the largest part of what a meal costs the factory. The accountant proposes to treat the canteen takings as a supply of goods because what the worker receives is a plate of food.

items.stem: Is he right that nothing else moves?

options.text: Yes — where the percentage is the same the classification is only a label
options.misconception: treats classification as a rate question alone, so everything downstream of it is invisible
options.why: The rate is the most visible consequence and it is not the only one. Two separate machineries hang off the same answer, and both of them can change the return even where the percentage does not move at all.

options.text: No — two other things are worked out under different sets of rules
options.why: Three things follow from the classification and only one of them is neutralised by the tariff happening to agree. The classification is what fixes the rate the supply bears in the first place, and a coincidence at today's rates is not the same as the question not arising. Beyond that, the time of supply runs on one section for goods and another for services, so the month the liability falls in can change. And the place of supply has its own separate rules for the two, which decides whether the tax is central and state tax or integrated tax — a change the return cannot absorb quietly.
keywords: the classification is what fixes the rate the supply bears
the time of supply runs on one section for goods and another for services
the place of supply has its own separate rules for the two

options.text: No, but only the place of supply moves; the time of supply runs on the invoice and payment dates in both cases
options.misconception: notices that both timing rules mention invoices and payments and concludes they are the same rule
options.why: Both rules use those events and they combine them differently, and the goods rule has its own features that the services rule does not share. Assuming they coincide is how a liability lands in the wrong month after a re-characterisation.

options.text: No, but the only thing that moves is the invoicing deadline; time and place of supply follow what the contract says
options.misconception: thinks the parties can fix the time and place of supply between themselves
options.why: Neither is left to the contract. Each is worked out under statutory rules that differ for goods and for services, and a contract cannot choose which set applies. What the parties agree affects the facts those rules are applied to, not the rules.

citation.ref: Section 7 read with Schedule II, sections 12 and 13, and sections 10 and 12 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A company has been treating a contract as a supply of goods. On audit the officer re-characterises it as a supply of services. The tariff happens to put both at the same percentage, and the finance head says that settles it — the tax is the same either way and nothing else in the return has to move.

items.stem: Which of the two can section 161 reach?

options.text: Neither, section 161 reaching only a notice or a certificate and not an order
options.misconception: reads the list of documents too narrowly and leaves out the one the section names first
options.why: The list is deliberately wide — a decision, an order, a notice, a certificate or any other document — and it is exercised by whichever authority issued the thing. An order is squarely inside it.

options.text: Both, an error being an error however it arose
options.misconception: reads the section as reaching any mistake, when it reaches only one that shows on the record without argument
options.why: The qualifying words do the work. If a point has to be argued before you can see that it is wrong, it is not apparent from the record, and rectification would become a way of re-hearing the case in front of the officer who decided it. That is what the appeal machinery is for.

options.text: Only the totalling
options.why: Section 161 lets any authority that passed or issued a decision, order, notice, certificate or other document rectify an error apparent on the face of the record in it, and it overrides the rest of the Act except section 160. A total that does not match the figures above it is apparent from the record itself — nothing outside the document is needed to see it. The other complaint is not: where a point of law is debatable, and two High Courts taking opposite views make it so, choosing one side of it is not an error that shows on the face of the record. That one belongs in an appeal.
keywords: rectify an error apparent on the face of the record
where a point of law is debatable, and two High Courts taking opposite views make it so

options.text: Only the point of law; an arithmetical slip has to be put right by passing a fresh order
options.misconception: inverts the test, sending the clearest case out of the section and the arguable one into it
options.why: An arithmetical slip is the paradigm case for this section, and it is treated so kindly that the ordinary time limit does not even apply to it. A debatable point of law is the paradigm case for an appeal. This answer swaps the two.

citation.ref: Section 161

items.scenario: One order carries two complaints. The figures set out in its body do not add up to the total demanded in its summary. And it decides a question of construction on which two High Courts have taken opposite views, choosing the view against the taxpayer without saying why. The taxpayer asks the same authority to put both right under section 161.

items.stem: Was the officer right that nothing could be done?

options.text: No, and there is no time limit on rectification at all, an error being correctable whenever it is found
options.misconception: generalises the exception for a clerical slip into the whole rule
options.why: There is a limit and it is six months, with one carve-out. The carve-out is narrow on purpose: it covers a slip in writing or in arithmetic, not a substantive error that happens to be obvious. Without the limit an order would never become final.

options.text: Yes — once three months have gone the order stands as it is
options.misconception: reads the taxpayer's window as the only route into the section, so the authority's own power disappears with it
options.why: The three months limits one of the three routes. It says nothing about the authority's own motion, which has a longer period, and nothing about the separate treatment of a clerical slip. Reading it as a general cut-off leaves an admitted arithmetical error standing.

options.text: No — his own application was late, but that does not exhaust the section
options.why: The section names three ways in. The authority may act on its own motion, or on a GST officer bringing the error to its notice, or on the affected person doing so within three months from the date of issue of the document. A letter on 20 August about a 10 April order is outside the third, so he cannot compel a rectification on his own application. But the officer may still act on his own motion, and there the limit is six months from the issue of the order, which here runs to 10 October 2026. Separately, a purely clerical or arithmetical error arising from an accidental slip or omission may be corrected even after that, so the November letter is not out of time either.
keywords: person doing so within three months from the date of issue of the document
the limit is six months from the issue of the order
clerical or arithmetical error arising from an accidental slip or omission

options.text: No, and his own application is in time, the three months running from when he discovered the mistake
options.misconception: starts the taxpayer's period at discovery, which is the rule in some limitation statutes and not in this section
options.why: The section fixes the start at the date the document was issued, not at the date anybody noticed. A discovery rule would make the period open-ended, which is exactly what a short window on an administrative correction is meant to avoid.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: An order was issued on 10 April 2026. The person it was made against wrote to the authority on 20 August 2026 pointing out that the figures in it had been totalled wrongly. The officer replied that nothing could now be done. In November the same person wrote again about a transposed digit in the same order.

items.stem: Where do the two arguments leave him?

options.text: The order falls — a notice citing the wrong section is no notice at all
options.misconception: treats a defect in a document as fatal in itself, without asking whether it did the document any harm
options.why: The saving section exists for this argument. What matters is whether the proceeding, taken as a whole, did what the Act requires. A wrong number on a notice whose contents told him the case, and which he answered, changed nothing about his ability to defend himself.

options.text: The order stands only if the department issues a corrected notice now and starts the adjudication again
options.misconception: asks for the defect to be cured prospectively, when the section says the proceeding was never invalid
options.why: The section does not cure a defect, it declares that the defect does not invalidate. There is nothing to redo. Re-issuing the notice would also raise a limitation problem that the saving provision is designed to avoid.

options.text: Neither works
options.why: Two sections close both doors. Under the first, an assessment, adjudication, notice, summons or other proceeding is not invalid merely for a mistake, defect or omission where in substance and effect it conforms to what the Act intends and requires — and a notice that told him exactly what the case against him was does conform. The same section adds that service cannot be questioned by a person who has already acted on it, or who did not question it at the earliest proceedings; he answered on the merits, so both limbs catch him. As for the suit, no civil court has jurisdiction over a question arising from anything done under the Act, and appeals to the High Court and Supreme Court are the exception to that, not a general saving.
keywords: where in substance and effect it conforms to what the Act intends and requires
service cannot be questioned by a person who has already acted on it
no civil court has jurisdiction over a question arising from anything done under the Act

options.text: The order stands, but the civil suit lies, the bar reaching only suits for recovery of tax
options.misconception: narrows the bar on civil courts to one kind of suit, when it is written around the subject matter instead
options.why: The bar is drawn by reference to the question, not the relief. Anything done, or meant to be done, under the Act puts the whole of the dispute beyond a civil court, because the Act supplies its own machinery for appeals and revision.

citation.ref: Section 160 read with section 162

items.scenario: A show cause notice quoted the wrong section number in its heading. The person it went to understood perfectly well what was being alleged, answered it on the merits, argued the case out and lost. He now wants the order set aside because of the wrong number, and says that if the tax authorities will not undo it he will file a civil suit.

items.stem: What is the penalty on him under section 122(1)?

options.text: A flat ₹10,000, that being the penalty the section fixes
options.misconception: reads the ten thousand as the penalty when it is only the floor the penalty cannot fall below
options.why: The ten thousand is the smaller of two limbs and it decides the answer only when the tax involved is smaller still. Here the money he holds is thirty times that, and paying the floor would let him keep the rest of his customers' money for the price of a fine.

options.text: Nothing under this section, because it reaches only a person who is on the register
options.misconception: treats registration as the gate to the whole of section 122, when only sub-section (2) is written that way
options.why: Sub-section (2) is the one confined to a registered person. Sub-section (1) speaks of a taxable person, which turns on whether the supplies are taxable and not on whether a form was filed. Read the other way, the man who never registered would end up better placed than the man who did.

options.text: The whole amount he took from his customers
options.why: Two of the twenty-one offences in the list catch him — collecting an amount as tax and failing to hand it over within three months of the due date, and collecting tax in a way the Act does not permit. Every offence in that list is priced the same way, at ₹10,000 or the tax evaded or not paid, whichever is higher, so the answer here is the ₹3 lakh he took from his customers. His argument about the register fails because a person whose supplies are taxable is a taxable person whether or not he has filled in the form, and failing to register is itself one of the offences in the same list.
keywords: ₹10,000 or the tax evaded or not paid, whichever is higher
the ₹3 lakh he took from his customers

options.text: The general penalty, since no penalty is separately provided for holding on to tax that has been collected
options.misconception: reaches for the residual penalty without first checking whether the conduct is already named in the list of offences
options.why: The general penalty exists for a contravention that has no penalty of its own. Holding on to collected tax is named in the list, so the residual provision never opens for it, and its ceiling of ₹25,000 would in any case be a small fraction of what he is sitting on.

citation.ref: Section 122(1) and the quantum clause closing sub-section (1)

items.scenario: A Kanpur hardware trader has never taken registration. Through 2026 he adds a line to every bill headed GST, and over the year ₹3 lakh reaches him that way from his customers. None of it goes to the Government, and the first of those collections fell due nine months before the department opens a file on him. When it does, he says the penalty section is written for a taxable person and he is not one, because he is not on the register.

items.stem: What is the exposure, and what would end it?

options.text: ₹40,000 under section 122(2) and a further ₹40,000 under section 73, because both provisions bite
options.misconception: stacks the penalty in the demand section on top of the penalty in the offences section for one and the same shortfall
options.why: One default does not carry two penalties. Where a demand is raised and the penalty is charged in that order, the Act shuts the door on any further penalty for the same act under any other provision, so the exposure is one figure and not two.

options.text: ₹4 lakh, the whole of the tax short paid
options.misconception: applies the fraud limb of sub-section (2) to conduct the department has already accepted was not fraud
options.why: The tax-equalling penalty is the second limb, and it opens only where fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is alleged and made out. Misreading a notification is none of those. Charging the fraud limb here would price a clerical slip the same as an invented invoice.

options.text: ₹10,000, because that is what the sub-section names first
options.misconception: takes the first figure in the clause as the answer instead of comparing the two the clause offers
options.why: The clause sets two candidates and awards the larger. The ten thousand wins only where a tenth of the tax comes to less than that, which means a shortfall under one lakh. Here the tenth is four times the floor.

options.text: ₹40,000 under section 122(2), with the demand running under section 73 and the penalty going away if it pays early enough
options.why: A registered person who has short paid for any reason other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is priced under the first limb of sub-section (2), at ₹10,000 or 10 per cent of the tax due, whichever is higher. Ten per cent of ₹4 lakh is ₹40,000, which is the higher of the two. For a year up to 2023-24 the demand for the tax itself runs under section 73, and that road has its own escape — pay the tax with interest before the notice is served, or within thirty days of it, and no penalty is payable under it.
keywords: ₹10,000 or 10 per cent of the tax due, whichever is higher
Ten per cent of ₹4 lakh is ₹40,000
the demand for the tax itself runs under section 73

citation.ref: Section 122(2)(a) read with sections 73(5), 73(8), 73(9) and 75(13)

items.scenario: A registered stationery wholesaler in Meerut short paid ₹4 lakh of tax for 2023-24 because its accountant read a rate notification the wrong way round. There is no false document, nothing withheld and no false entry — the department accepts all of that. It now wants to know the penalty it is exposed to, and under which provision the demand for the tax itself will come.

items.stem: On what footing, and for how much, can the consultant be penalised?

options.text: ₹25,000, the general penalty, since aiding a fraud has no penalty of its own
options.misconception: falls back on the residual penalty although a specific sub-section names this conduct and prices it
options.why: The residual provision opens only when nothing else covers the conduct. Two provisions cover it — the one for the beneficiary of a fake-invoice transaction and the one for a person who aids or abets a listed offence — so the residual ceiling never comes into it.

options.text: ₹10,000, because that is the floor and no tax was evaded by him personally
options.misconception: measures the penalty by the consultant's own tax rather than by the credit the transaction moved
options.why: The measure in this sub-section is the tax evaded or the credit availed of or passed on in the transaction, not anything on the beneficiary's own return. He may have no output tax at all and still answer for the whole of what the arrangement moved.

options.text: Nothing, because he is neither the supplier nor the person who took the credit
options.misconception: assumes a penalty can only reach a party to the supply, missing the sub-section written for the person behind it
options.why: If that were right, the man who designs the arrangement and takes a cut would be the only one it cannot touch. The sub-section exists because the beneficiary is often not on either invoice, and it fixes on two facts — that he gained from it, and that it happened at his instance.

options.text: ₹20 lakh under section 122(1A), on top of whatever the client pays
options.why: Sub-section (1A) was written for exactly this person. It reaches anyone who retains the benefit of a transaction falling in the fake-invoice, credit-without-goods or irregular-distribution clauses, and at whose instance the transaction is carried out. He arranged it and he was paid out of it, so both halves are met. The amount is not a slab and not a discretion — it is set at the tax evaded or the credit availed or passed on, so a penalty of ₹20 lakh, and it sits alongside the client's own exposure rather than replacing it.
keywords: retains the benefit of a transaction
at whose instance the transaction is carried out

citation.ref: Section 122(1A) read with clauses (i), (ii), (vii) and (ix) of section 122(1)

items.scenario: A tax consultant in Agra puts a client in touch with a paper firm, tells the client which invoices to ask for and how to book them, and the client takes ₹20 lakh of credit on goods that never moved. The consultant is paid a share of what the client saves. The client is being proceeded against. The consultant says he supplied nothing, took no credit and is not registered for any of this, so nothing can land on him.

items.stem: What should the chain put to the officer?

options.text: That the breach is minor because it was a single invoice out of thousands
options.misconception: measures minor by how often it happened instead of by the test the Explanation lays down
options.why: The Explanation does not count occurrences. It fixes on the amount of tax involved, and on whether the error is apparent on the face of the record. A single invoice carrying ₹6 lakh of tax would not be a minor breach, and a hundred small ones each under the line still would be.

options.text: That the penalty should be reduced, since the mistake was corrected promptly
options.misconception: argues about the size of a penalty that the section forbids altogether, and gives away the point
options.why: Prompt correction is a mitigating fact, and a voluntary disclosure before the officer finds the breach is one the Act tells him to weigh. But this breach clears the bar for no penalty at all, so arguing for a smaller one concedes that some is payable when none is.

options.text: That the residual penalty is a fixed ₹25,000, so the officer has no room to reduce it and the demand is bad
options.misconception: reads the ceiling as a fixed sum, which would put the penalty outside the general disciplines instead of inside them
options.why: The words are that it may extend to that figure, which makes it a ceiling and not a fixed amount. That matters in the opposite direction to the one this answer takes — the disciplines in section 126 are switched off only where the law fixes a penalty as a set sum or a set percentage, and a discretionary ceiling is neither.

options.text: That no penalty may be imposed at all, and that if any were, it would have to be measured against how grave the slip was
options.why: Section 126 forbids a penalty for a minor breach, for a procedural requirement, and for an omission or mistake in documentation that can be put right easily and carries neither fraudulent intent nor gross negligence. Its own Explanation settles both terms — a breach is minor where the tax involved is under ₹5,000, and a mistake is easily rectifiable where it is an error apparent on the face of the record. Both fit here. And the residual penalty, which may extend to ₹25,000, is a discretion and not a fixed sum, so the section's disciplines govern it and the amount must be commensurate with how grave the breach is.
keywords: a penalty for a minor breach
the residual penalty, which may extend to ₹25,000
commensurate with how grave the breach is

citation.ref: Section 126 with the Explanation to sub-section (1), read with section 125

items.scenario: A grocery chain in Varanasi files a return in which one recipient's GSTIN is typed with two digits transposed. The tax on that invoice is ₹3,000. The mistake is on the face of the return, the chain corrects it the same week the officer points it out, and there is no suggestion that anything was concealed. The officer proposes a penalty anyway and asks the chain to show why the residual provision should not apply.

items.stem: Which of the three is maintainable?

options.text: The first and the second
options.misconception: counts the buyer's year from the importer's payment rather than from the day the buyer bought the goods
options.why: A buyer who never dealt with customs cannot be expected to know when the importer paid, so his year is counted from his own purchase. Fourteen months after that purchase is outside it. Reading it from the importer's payment would sometimes help him and sometimes shut him out before he had even bought.

options.text: The first and the third
options.misconception: treats the small-amount rule as a matter the officer may waive rather than a bar in the section itself
options.why: The floor sits in a proviso to the same sub-section that creates the right, so it is not a threshold of convenience. Below it the refund is simply not made, whatever the merits, because the cost of processing would outrun the sum.

options.text: All three, since a protest keeps every claim alive
options.misconception: reads a protest as curing every defect in a claim instead of only removing the time limit
options.why: A protest does one thing — it takes away the one-year limit for the person who made it. It does not travel to somebody else's claim, and it does not lift the small-amount bar or the requirement to prove the burden was not handed on.

options.text: Only the first
options.why: The ordinary window is one year, and where it runs from depends on who is claiming. An importer counts it from the date of payment; a person other than the importer, from whom the duty was collected, counts it from the date he bought the goods, so the bearings buyer at fourteen months is late. Duty paid under protest has no time limit at all, so the dyes importer is in time however long it has been. The third claim fails on a different rule altogether — nothing is refunded where the amount claimed is less than ₹100.
keywords: The ordinary window is one year
Duty paid under protest has no time limit at all
the amount claimed is less than ₹100

citation.ref: Section 27(1) with its second and third provisos and the Explanation

items.scenario: Three refund claims land on one officer's desk. An importer of dyes paid duty two years ago and lodged its protest on the bill of entry at the time; it claims now. A trader who bought imported bearings from that importer, and bore the duty in the price, claims fourteen months after he bought them. A third importer claims ₹90 of duty overpaid last month.

items.stem: What do you tell him?

options.text: There is no limit, because the duty was self-assessed and the mistake was the importer's own
options.misconception: confuses the absence of a limit for duty paid under protest with the ordinary case
options.why: Only a protest recorded at the time takes the clock away. A self-assessment is not a protest — it is the importer's own assessment accepted as filed, and it starts the ordinary year running from payment like any other.

options.text: The last day is 30 November 2026, and the certificate has to be backed by documents because the law starts from the opposite assumption
options.why: An importer's year runs from the date of payment, so from 1 December 2025 the last day is 30 November 2026 and there is time. The claim has to carry documentary evidence, the invoices among it, showing both that the claimant paid the duty and that its incidence went no further. That is not a formality — section 28D presumes the burden was handed on to the buyer unless the contrary is proved, so the papers are there to knock down a presumption that starts against him.
keywords: section 28D presumes the burden was handed on to the buyer

options.text: The last day is 1 December 2026, and the certificate settles it
options.misconception: counts the year as ending on the anniversary of payment rather than the day before, and treats a certificate as proof rather than as one piece of evidence
options.why: A year from a date ends the day before the same date comes round again. And a certificate is an opinion about the accounts unless the accounts come with it; on its own it does not displace what the law assumes about who ended up paying.

options.text: The last day is 30 November 2026, and no evidence about the burden is needed because the goods have not been sold
options.misconception: assumes the presumption is switched off by the facts rather than by proof put before the officer
options.why: Whether the goods moved on is exactly what the officer cannot see, and the section makes him start from the assumption that they did and that the duty went with them. Unsold stock is a good answer, but it is an answer that has to be shown in the records, not asserted.

citation.ref: Section 27(1) and 27(1A) read with sections 28C and 28D

items.scenario: A ceramics importer paid duty on a self-assessed bill of entry on 1 December 2025. Its auditor spots in August 2026 that a quantity was keyed twice. The finance head is drafting the claim and asks two things — how long is left, and whether the auditor's certificate saying the excess was not recovered from anyone is enough on its own to get the money back.

items.stem: Is the officer right?

options.text: Yes — the bar was upheld by the Supreme Court and admits of no exceptions
options.misconception: remembers that the doctrine was upheld and forgets that the section itself carries a list of cases outside it
options.why: What the nine judges upheld was the doctrine and the machinery around it, not a rule without exceptions. The same sub-section that sends the money to the fund sets out seven situations in which it goes to the applicant, and they are part of the provision that was upheld.

options.text: No — an import by an individual for her own use is one of the listed exceptions, so the money is paid to her
options.why: Where an amount is found refundable the default is that it goes to the Consumer Welfare Fund, which is how the doctrine of unjust enrichment is worked into the Act — nobody should collect the duty twice, once from a buyer and once from the Government. But the sub-section lists the cases where the money goes to the applicant instead, and imports by an individual for his personal use is one of them. There is no buyer behind her to be protected, so the bar has nothing to bite on.
keywords: imports by an individual for his personal use

options.text: Yes, unless she produces evidence that she did not pass the duty on
options.misconception: applies the general evidence requirement to a case the section has already carved out on its face
options.why: The evidence requirement is how an importer or a buyer gets out from under the presumption. The exception for a personal import does not work that way — it turns on the character of the import itself, and asking her to prove a negative about buyers she never had would empty the exception.

options.text: No, because the duty was not paid under protest and the presumption therefore never arose
options.misconception: reads a protest as the thing that creates or removes the presumption about who bore the duty
options.why: A protest goes to time, not to burden. The Supreme Court has held in terms that the bar applies even where duty was paid under protest, and in the same case that an unchanged selling price does not by itself prove the incidence stayed with the importer.

citation.ref: Section 27(2) with clause (b) of its first proviso; Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India and CCE v. Allied Photographics India Ltd.

items.scenario: A retired violinist imported a single instrument for herself and paid ₹80,000 of duty, ₹30,000 more than was properly chargeable. She has not sold it and does not trade. The officer accepts the excess but proposes to send the money to the fund set up for the purpose, saying that the bar applies to everybody and that she has produced nothing to show she did not recover the duty from anyone.

items.stem: Where does the ₹1,50,000 go?

options.text: To the Consumer Welfare Fund, because the pricing shows the duty reached the buyers
options.why: The importer's own pricing method is the evidence against it — a selling price built on the duty actually paid carries that duty through to whoever bought the goods. Against that, a certificate cannot displace the presumption, because it speaks to the books and not to what the price was made of. So the sanction stands and the amount is credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund rather than paid over. The department does not simply keep the excess; it goes to the fund.
keywords: a certificate cannot displace the presumption
the amount is credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund

options.text: To the importer, because the certificate is the evidence the section asks for
options.misconception: treats a professional certificate as conclusive when the facts around it point the other way
options.why: The section asks for evidence, and a certificate is evidence that can be weighed and outweighed. Here it is contradicted by the way the price was constructed, and an officer who accepted it would be ignoring the one document that shows where the duty ended up.

options.text: To the importer, because an unchanged selling price after the import proves nothing was passed on
options.misconception: takes a steady price as proof that the burden stayed with the seller
options.why: The Supreme Court has held that an unchanged price does not by itself establish that the incidence was not passed on. A price can hold steady for a dozen reasons, and here the price was expressly built on the duty, so the argument runs backwards.

options.text: Nowhere — the claim fails and the department retains the money
options.misconception: confuses failing the unjust enrichment test with failing the refund claim itself
options.why: These are two separate questions. The first is whether the amount is refundable, and it is. The second is who receives it. Losing the second does not revive the department's right to money it should never have collected, which is precisely why the fund exists.

citation.ref: Section 27(2) read with section 28D and the Consumer Welfare Fund

items.scenario: An alloy importer overpaid ₹1,50,000 of duty and sold the whole consignment in the following month. Its price list for that lot was built up as landed cost plus the duty actually paid plus a fixed margin, and its chartered accountant has certified that the burden was retained. The department agrees the ₹1,50,000 was overpaid and passes an order sanctioning it.

items.stem: How much interest is payable, and from when?

options.text: Nothing, because the refund was paid within six months
options.misconception: borrows a six-month period from somewhere else in the customs machinery
options.why: The clock in this section is three months, and it runs from the date a complete application is received rather than from any order. Once it passes, interest is automatic; there is no second, longer grace.

options.text: ₹1,529, but only if the importer applies separately for interest
options.misconception: treats interest on a delayed refund as a claim of its own rather than as something the section attaches to the refund
options.why: The provision directs that interest be paid to the applicant once the three months are overrun. Nothing in it asks for a second application, and the arithmetic is the same whether the importer writes in or not.

options.text: ₹4,504, because interest runs from the date of the application
options.misconception: starts the interest on the day the claim was made instead of after the three months the department is given
options.why: The department is allowed three months to deal with a complete claim, and interest is the price of overrunning that, not of taking any time at all. Counting from the application would charge interest for a period in which nothing was yet overdue.

options.text: ₹1,529, for the 62 days beginning 21 December 2026
options.why: Interest runs where duty ordered to be refunded is not paid within three months of the date the complete application was received, and it runs from the day after those three months to the day of refund. Three months from 20 September 2026 ends on 20 December 2026, so the period is 21 December 2026 to 20 February 2027, which is 62 days. The notified rate is 6 per cent a year, inside the band of 5 to 30 per cent the Act allows, and ₹1,50,000 at that rate for 62 days is ₹1,529.
keywords: not paid within three months of the date the complete application was received
The notified rate is 6 per cent a year
₹1,50,000 at that rate for 62 days is ₹1,529

citation.ref: Section 27A read with Notification No. 75/2003-Customs (N.T.)

items.scenario: A machinery importer's refund application, complete in every respect, is acknowledged by the proper officer on 20 September 2026. The department accepts that the burden stayed with the importer, so the money is payable to it and not to the fund. The order is passed late and ₹1,50,000 reaches the importer on 20 February 2027. Its accountant wants the interest worked out.

items.stem: What should the importer be told to do?

options.text: File the refund claim, and let the refund officer decide the classification afresh
options.misconception: asks the refund officer to do the work of an appellate authority
options.why: A refund is closer to executing an order than to reviewing one. If a refund officer could re-open a classification, the appeal provisions would be optional, and two officers of equal rank would be free to disagree about the same consignment.

options.text: Get the bill of entry amended or reassessed first, because a refund claim is not a substitute for an appeal
options.why: Once an assessment stands, the duty is payable under it, and the officer deciding a refund cannot sit in appeal over an assessment another officer made. The Supreme Court said so in Priya Blue and later, in ITC Ltd, extended it to a self-assessed bill of entry — the importer's own assessment is still an assessment, and it has to be modified in appeal, within sixty days of the order, before any refund can follow. Put shortly, a refund claim is not a substitute for an appeal, so the route is amendment or reassessment first and the refund follows the modified assessment.
keywords: a refund claim is not a substitute for an appeal
extended it to a self-assessed bill of entry

options.text: File the refund claim, because a self-assessment is not an order and there is nothing to appeal
options.misconception: assumes that self-assessment leaves no order in existence, which is the very argument the Supreme Court rejected
options.why: That argument was put and turned down. A bill of entry the importer assessed is treated as an assessment for this purpose, so the appeal machinery is open to him and, being open, it is the road he has to take.

options.text: Do nothing, because the goods have been cleared and an assessment is final once clearance is given
options.misconception: treats clearance as closing every door, when the appeal road is open and timed
options.why: Clearance does not make an assessment unchallengeable. It can be taken in appeal, and the time to do that runs from the order, not from the day the goods left the docks.

citation.ref: Section 128; Priya Blue Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs and ITC Ltd. v. CCE

items.scenario: An importer of pumps filed its own bill of entry, classified the goods under a heading carrying a higher rate, and paid on that footing. The goods were cleared. Six weeks later a colleague points out that a lower heading fits. Nobody appealed anything. The importer files a refund claim for the difference and argues that since it assessed the goods itself there is no order of anybody else's to appeal against.

items.stem: What rate applies, and is the consultant right about the value?

options.text: 10 per cent, because the bill of entry went in before the notification
options.misconception: takes the day of presentation as the relevant day and ignores the entry inwards limb
options.why: Presentation is only one of the two candidates. A bill of entry may be lodged in advance of the ship arriving, and if that alone fixed the rate an importer could pick his rate by filing early. The section takes whichever of the two days falls later.

options.text: 15 per cent, and the value must be recomputed on the exchange rate of 5 March as well
options.misconception: carries the relevant date across from the rate to every other element of the assessment
options.why: The date this section fixes governs the rate and the tariff valuation and stops there. Valuation runs on its own provision, with its own rules about the rate of exchange, and it does not move because a duty notification did.

options.text: 15 per cent, and the value is untouched by any of this
options.why: For goods entered for home consumption there are two candidate days, the day the bill of entry is presented and the day the vessel is granted entry inwards, and the section takes whichever is later. Here that is 5 March, so the bill of entry is deemed presented on 5 March and the rate in force that day, 15 per cent, applies. The department's 10 per cent is wrong. The consultant is wrong too, for a different reason: this section settles only the rate of duty and the tariff valuation, and the value of the goods is fixed by section 14, which the notification does not touch.
keywords: the section takes whichever is later
so the bill of entry is deemed presented on 5 March
the rate in force that day, 15 per cent
the value of the goods is fixed by section 14

options.text: 10 per cent, because the vessel reached port on 3 March, before the notification took effect
options.misconception: uses the day the vessel physically arrived rather than the day entry inwards was granted
options.why: Arrival and entry inwards are different events. Entry inwards is the permission that lets unloading begin, and it is that grant, not the sighting of the ship, that the section names.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)(a) read with section 14

items.scenario: An importer of packaging machinery presents a bill of entry for home consumption on 1 March. The vessel touches port on 3 March and is granted entry inwards on 5 March. A notification effective 4 March lifts the rate on that machinery from 10 per cent to 15 per cent. The department assesses at 10 per cent. The importer's consultant says the department has it wrong, and that in any case the rise also changes the value on which duty is worked out.

items.stem: At what rate should the clearance be assessed?

options.text: 15 per cent, the rate when the into-bond bill of entry was filed
options.misconception: uses the warehousing document as the one that fixes the rate, when it only defers the duty
options.why: Warehousing postpones the duty; it does not settle it. That is the point of the separate limb — the liability crystallises when the goods come out for home consumption, and the rate is read on that day.

options.text: 7.5 per cent
options.why: Goods cleared out of a warehouse have their own limb in the section, and it names one day only — the day the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of those goods is presented. That is 25 June, when the exemption had already brought the rate to 7.5 per cent. The rate standing when the into-bond bill of entry went in is irrelevant to the assessment, so the department's 15 per cent is wrong.
keywords: the day the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of those goods is presented

options.text: The lower of the two rates, since an exemption cannot make an importer worse off
options.misconception: picks a rate on grounds of fairness rather than reading the day the section names
options.why: There is no choice in the provision. It happens to favour the importer here, and on a rise between warehousing and clearance the same rule would work against him. A rule that always gave the lower figure would be a different rule.

options.text: 15 per cent, because the rate is fixed when the vessel is granted entry inwards
options.misconception: applies the home-consumption limb, with its later-of-two-days test, to goods coming out of a warehouse
options.why: The later-of-two-days test belongs to goods entered for home consumption straight off the vessel. Once goods go into a warehouse the entry inwards date has done its work and the section switches to a single day.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)(b)

items.scenario: A chemicals importer warehoused a consignment on an into-bond bill of entry on 10 March, when the rate stood at 15 per cent. An exemption issued on 20 June brought the rate down to 7.5 per cent. The importer filed its ex-bond bill of entry for home consumption on 25 June and cleared the goods. The department assesses at 15 per cent, saying the goods entered the country when the rate was 15 per cent.

items.stem: How is the consignment assessed?

options.text: Duty on forty-eight cartons, with the loss falling on the person who held the goods
options.why: Where imported goods are pilfered after unloading and before the proper officer makes an order for clearance for home consumption or for deposit in a warehouse, the importer is not liable for the duty on them, unless the goods are later restored to him. The word pilfer means petty theft of unit articles rather than the loss of a whole package, and the three signs the claim needs are all here — tampering, a blank space for what is gone, and missing unit articles. The goods were in the custodian's charge, and the duty on what disappeared is his to pay.
keywords: The word pilfer means petty theft of unit articles
unless the goods are later restored to him
The goods were in the custodian's charge

options.text: Duty on all fifty cartons, with a refund to be claimed for the missing tools
options.misconception: routes a pilferage through the remission and refund machinery instead of the section that removes the liability outright
options.why: Where the loss is pilferage between unloading and the clearance order, that section applies and the remission provision does not. The liability never arises on the pilfered articles, so there is nothing to refund and no need to claim one.

options.text: No duty on the whole consignment, because the packages were tampered with
options.misconception: treats evidence of tampering as relieving the entire import rather than the articles actually taken
options.why: Relief attaches to what was pilfered, not to what sat beside it. Forty eight cartons arrived intact and are chargeable, and a rule that exempted a shipment because one carton was opened would invite exactly that.

options.text: Duty on all fifty cartons, because the importer cannot prove when the theft happened
options.misconception: puts the burden on the importer although the facts recorded at examination place the loss inside the protected window
options.why: The condition is that the pilferage occurred after unloading and before the order. It was found on examination, in the docks, with no order yet made, which places it inside that window. Had it been shown to have happened before unloading the section would not have opened.

citation.ref: Section 13 with the conditions and circumstances for a pilferage claim

items.scenario: Fifty cartons of hand tools are unloaded at a port and lie in the docks. When they are examined, before any order for clearance or for warehousing has been made, two cartons are open along one seam, and inside each there is an empty space where four boxed tools should sit. Nothing else is disturbed and no whole carton is missing. The importer asks not to be charged duty on what went missing.

items.stem: What must the importer do before that rate can be claimed?

options.text: Lodge details on the common portal once, obtain the number generated against them, and put up a bond covering the duty foregone
options.why: The rules for importing at a concessional rate against a specified end use apply wherever the benefit depends on the goods being used for manufacture, for an output service or for a specified end use. The importer files one-time prior information on the common portal — its own premises and its job worker, the goods, the notification, the end-use recipient and the ports it intends to use — and an identification number is generated against that filing. It then furnishes a continuity bond, with surety or security as the jurisdictional Deputy or Assistant Commissioner thinks fit, undertaking to pay the difference between the full duty and what it paid, with interest from the date of import, if the goods are not so used. Both the number and the bond are quoted on each bill of entry.
keywords: The importer files one-time prior information on the common portal
an identification number is generated against that filing
It then furnishes a continuity bond

options.text: Nothing beyond claiming the rate, since the notification carries its own conditions
options.misconception: reads the notification as self-executing and misses the separate rules that police the end use
options.why: A notification that turns on what happens to the goods after clearance needs a machinery to follow them, because customs loses sight of them at the gate. That machinery is the separate set of rules, and without the filing and the bond the concession is not available at all.

options.text: Move the job worker's part of the processing in-house, because goods under this scheme cannot leave the importer's premises
options.misconception: assumes the concession forbids job work, when the rules provide for it
options.why: Job work is contemplated. The job worker's name and address go into the very first filing, the goods travel to him under an invoice or an e-way bill, and the movement is recorded in the monthly statement.

options.text: Give an undertaking on each consignment and file a bond every time
options.misconception: treats the information and the bond as per-consignment when they are taken once and used repeatedly
options.why: The information is given once and updated when something changes, and the bond is a continuing one that is debited automatically as each bill of entry is cleared. Doing it per consignment is the burden the rules were rewritten to remove.

citation.ref: Rules 4 and 5 — importing at a concessional rate against an end use

items.scenario: A components importer wants the benefit of a notification whose lower rate is available only where the imported goods go into manufacture at its own works, with part of the processing done by a job worker in the next district. Its customs broker says the notification is enough on its own and that the lower rate can simply be claimed on the bill of entry.

items.stem: Can the Government act under section 8B, and with what?

options.text: Yes, but the only measure available is a duty
options.misconception: remembers the duty and forgets that the section was widened to a set of measures
options.why: A duty is one of three. A tariff-rate quota lets a stated quantity in at the ordinary rate and taxes the rest, and the section also leaves room for other prescribed measures, so the Government is not confined to price.

options.text: Yes, and no enquiry is needed once the industry shows a fall in output
options.misconception: treats the petition's evidence as the finding, skipping the enquiry the section requires
options.why: Satisfaction has to be reached on an enquiry. A fall in output can have many causes, and the enquiry is where the link between the imports and the injury is established rather than asserted.

options.text: No, because there is no allegation of dumping or of a subsidy
options.misconception: imports the tests for anti-dumping or countervailing duty into a provision that has neither
options.why: The three remedies answer three different complaints. This one answers a surge, however fairly priced, and it exists precisely for the case where nobody has done anything wrong but the domestic industry cannot absorb the volume.

options.text: Yes, on an enquiry, and it may impose a duty, a quota-linked rate or another prescribed measure
options.why: The section is triggered by two findings and only two — that the article is imported in increased quantities and under such conditions, and that this is causing or threatening to cause serious injury to the domestic industry. Nothing about pricing below home-market value or about a subsidy is needed, because those belong to the other two trade-remedy provisions. Once the enquiry supports both findings the Government may impose a safeguard duty, apply a tariff-rate quota, or take such other measure as it considers appropriate.
keywords: the article is imported in increased quantities and under such conditions
causing or threatening to cause serious injury to the domestic industry

citation.ref: Section 8B(1) with the definitions of serious injury and threat of serious injury

items.scenario: Domestic makers of a speciality glass petition the Central Government. Their case is that shipments of the article from abroad have climbed steeply over two years, that prices have been driven below their cost, and that two of the four Indian plants have stopped a shift. They do not allege that anybody is selling below their home-market price or is being subsidised. They ask for a duty and, if a duty will not do, for a cap on quantities.

items.stem: Against which sources may the measure be applied?

options.text: Against none of them, because the aggregate of all imports of the article is well over 9 per cent
options.misconception: applies the 9 per cent test to all imports instead of to the developing-country group
options.why: The aggregate that matters is the one built only from developing countries each below the individual share. Imports from a developed country never enter it, and the shelter it gives never extends to them.

options.text: Against every source, because the developing countries together are above the individual limit
options.misconception: adds the four shares and compares the total against the 3 per cent figure meant for a single country
options.why: The two figures do different jobs. Three per cent is measured country by country; the aggregate is measured against 9 per cent. Comparing a sum against the individual limit would make the exemption for small suppliers almost impossible to satisfy.

options.text: Against the developed country only
options.why: Two exemptions run for developing countries and both have to be cleared before a measure can reach one. The first spares an article from a developing country whose share of imports of that article does not exceed 3 per cent, and each of these four is under that line. The second spares developing countries each below that share where their imports taken together do not exceed 9 per cent — and the four here add up to 7 per cent, which is inside it. So none of the four can be measured against, while the developed country has no such shelter.
keywords: whose share of imports of that article does not exceed 3 per cent
taken together do not exceed 9 per cent
the four here add up to 7 per cent

options.text: Against the developed country and the country at 2.8 per cent
options.misconception: rounds a share that is under the line up to it, or reads the first exemption as excluding a country that is close to 3 per cent
options.why: The words are does not exceed. A share of 2.8 per cent does not exceed 3 per cent, so the first exemption covers it outright, and the second test is then about the group and not about the largest member of it.

citation.ref: Section 8B — exemptions for articles originating in developing countries

items.scenario: An enquiry into a surge of one article finds that imports come from five places. Four are notified developing countries, with shares of total imports of that article into India of 2.8 per cent, 2.2 per cent, 1.4 per cent and 0.6 per cent. The fifth is a developed country and supplies the rest. The enquiry establishes the surge and the injury.

items.stem: What can be done now, and for how long?

options.text: A provisional measure, for up to 200 days from its imposition, with the duty returned if the final finding is against injury
options.why: On a preliminary determination that the increased imports have caused or threatened serious injury, the Government may impose a provisional safeguard measure while the enquiry runs on. It may stay in force for not more than 200 days from the date it is imposed. If the final determination is that there was no injury and no threat of it, the duty already collected is refunded, so the risk of acting early sits with the exchequer and not with the importer.
keywords: the Government may impose a provisional safeguard measure
not more than 200 days from the date it is imposed
the duty already collected is refunded

options.text: A provisional measure for up to four years, the same as a final one
options.misconception: carries the duration of the final measure across to the provisional one
options.why: The two have separate clocks. Four years, extendable to a total of ten, belongs to a measure imposed after the enquiry. A measure imposed on a preliminary view is deliberately short, so that it cannot become a substitute for finishing the enquiry.

options.text: A provisional measure for up to 200 days, and the money is kept whatever the final finding says
options.misconception: gets the duration right and misses that the collection is conditional on the case being made out
options.why: The duty was levied on a view that had not yet been tested. If the finished enquiry finds no injury and no threat of it, the basis for having collected it disappears, and the section directs that it go back.

options.text: Nothing until the enquiry is finished, because a measure needs a final determination
options.misconception: reads the final determination as the only foundation for any measure
options.why: A provision for acting on a preliminary view exists because injury done while an enquiry runs cannot be undone afterwards. It is hedged — a short life and a refund if the case fails — but it is available.

citation.ref: Section 8B — provisional safeguard measures

items.scenario: An enquiry into a surge will take most of a year. On the material already gathered the authority records a preliminary view that the increase has caused serious injury, and the Central Government wants to act at once rather than watch the domestic industry through another two quarters. Its concern is what happens to the money collected if the finished enquiry goes the other way.

items.stem: How much of the import bears the safeguard duty?

options.text: Only the part that reaches the domestic tariff area, whether as it stands or inside finished goods
options.why: The measure does not apply to an article imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit or a special economic zone unit unless it is specifically made applicable to them. There are two exceptions to that shelter, and both are about goods coming into the home market — where the article is cleared as such into the domestic tariff area, and where it is used in goods that are so cleared. In those cases the measure reaches that portion which comes into the home market, at the rate that was leviable on it at import. The three quarters that leave the country as exports carry nothing.
keywords: imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit
the article is cleared as such into the domestic tariff area
the measure reaches that portion which comes into the home market

options.text: All of it, because the unit imported the article while a measure was in force
options.misconception: ignores the shelter for export oriented units entirely
options.why: A safeguard protects domestic producers from goods sold in India. An export oriented unit's imports that leave again as exports do not compete with them, so charging the whole import would tax an export.

options.text: Only the tenth sold on as it stands, because goods that go into manufacture lose their identity
options.misconception: reads the exception as reaching only the article in its original form
options.why: The clause names two situations, and the second is the article used in the manufacture of goods that are then cleared into the home market. If manufacture broke the link, an export oriented unit could sidestep every safeguard by processing the article before selling it here.

options.text: None of it, because the notification does not name export oriented units
options.misconception: stops at the shelter and misses the two exceptions written into the same clause
options.why: Silence in the notification means the measure was not specifically made applicable, which is only the first of three routes. The other two do not depend on the notification at all — they follow the goods into the domestic market.

citation.ref: Section 8B — imports by a 100% EOU or a unit in a special economic zone

items.scenario: A safeguard duty is in force on an article. A 100 per cent export oriented unit imports the same article. It keeps three quarters of what it imports for goods it exports, sells a tenth of it on, as it stands, into the domestic tariff area, and puts the rest into finished goods that are also sold into the domestic tariff area. The notification says nothing about export oriented units either way.

items.stem: Is the accountant right to hold the credit back?

options.text: Yes — the dyeing unit should take the credit, since it received the goods
options.misconception: gives the credit to the person who physically holds the goods rather than the person who bought them
options.why: The job worker never bought the fabric and the mill's invoice is not in its name. It is paid for a service, and it charges tax on that service. Credit follows the invoice and the ownership, not the address on the delivery.

options.text: No, but only if the goods are brought to the principal's works within the year
options.misconception: reads the direct-send provision as a concession conditional on a later visit to the principal's premises
options.why: Nothing requires the goods ever to reach the principal's premises. The section allows them to be supplied out straight from the job worker's place, and a rule sending them on a detour would defeat the reason the provision exists.

options.text: No — the section says in terms that the credit is available on a direct send
options.why: The general condition that a person must have received the goods is overridden here. The principal is entitled to take credit of input tax on inputs sent to a job worker, and the sub-section goes on to say that this is so even where the inputs are sent directly to the job worker without first being brought to his place of business. The same is written separately for capital goods. So the garment maker takes the credit on the mill's invoice in the ordinary way.
keywords: the inputs are sent directly to the job worker without first being brought to his place of business
the garment maker takes the credit on the mill's invoice

options.text: Yes — the credit can be taken only once the fabric comes back from the dyeing unit
options.misconception: delays the credit to the day the goods return, confusing the condition for taking credit with the clock for bringing goods back
options.why: The return clock and the credit are two different things. The credit is taken on the invoice; the clock decides what happens if the goods are not received back or supplied out in time. Waiting for the return would cost the principal working capital the section was written to protect.

citation.ref: Section 19(1) and 19(2), read with section 16(2)(b)

items.scenario: A registered garment maker buys grey fabric from a mill and asks the mill to deliver it straight to a dyeing unit that works for it. The fabric never enters the garment maker's own factory. Its accountant refuses to take the credit on the mill's invoice, saying the Act allows credit only to a person who has received the goods, and this company has not seen them.

items.stem: From what date does the one year run, and what happens when it ends?

options.text: From 10 April 2026, and on expiry the credit already taken has to be reversed
options.misconception: treats the consequence as a reversal of credit rather than a deemed outward supply
options.why: The credit is not disturbed. What the section does instead is treat the movement as a supply by the principal to the job worker, so the principal accounts for output tax on it. The two look similar on a cash flow and are quite different on a return.

options.text: From 6 April 2026, the date of despatch
options.misconception: uses the day the goods left the supplier, which is the rule for goods sent out by the principal itself
options.why: Sending out is the trigger only when the goods leave the principal's own premises. On a direct send the principal never had them, so the proviso moves the start to receipt by the job worker — which also protects the principal against a long transit it did not control.

options.text: From 10 April 2026, and on expiry the inputs count as supplied on the day they went out
options.why: Where the inputs go straight to the job worker, the proviso counts the one year from the date the job worker receives them, which is 10 April 2026 here, and not from anything the principal or its supplier did earlier. The three years for capital goods are counted the same way. If the year runs out with the goods neither received back nor supplied from the job worker's premises, the law then treats them as a supply the principal made to the job worker, dated back to the day they went out — so the tax is worked out on that earlier day, with interest running from it.
keywords: counts the one year from the date the job worker receives them
treats them as a supply the principal made to the job worker

options.text: From 10 April 2026, and on expiry the goods become the job worker's without any tax consequence
options.misconception: reads the deeming as transferring ownership rather than as fixing a tax point
options.why: The deeming is for tax only. Title is a matter for the contract between them, and the section says nothing about it — what it fixes is that a supply is treated as having happened, and when.

citation.ref: Section 19(3) with its proviso, and section 19(6) with its proviso

items.scenario: A registered garment maker's supplier despatched grey fabric to its dyeing unit on 6 April 2026. The dyeing unit signed for it on 10 April 2026. The fabric has still not come back or been supplied out from the dyeing unit's premises, and the finance team is working out when the position turns against the company.

items.stem: What must be filed, for what period, and by which date?

options.text: A tax invoice for each movement, since the goods left the registered premises
options.misconception: treats a job-work movement as a supply needing an invoice, when it moves on a different document
options.why: Sending goods for job work is not a supply, so no tax invoice is raised. The goods move under a delivery challan, prepared in triplicate and carrying the prescribed particulars, and it is those challans that the half-yearly form reports.
keywords: The goods move under a delivery challan, prepared in triplicate

options.text: Form GST ITC-04 once for 2026-27, by 25 April 2027
options.misconception: puts a principal above the turnover line on the annual cycle meant for smaller ones
options.why: The annual filing is for a principal whose previous year's turnover did not cross ₹5 crore. Above that the department wants the movement twice a year, so an annual return here would be late for the first six months by six months.

options.text: Nothing, because the goods came back inside the year and no supply took place
options.misconception: treats the reporting as triggered by a failure to return the goods
options.why: The form is a record of movement, not a confession. It is filed whether or not everything came back, and it is what tells the department that goods leaving the premises were job-work movements rather than sales.

options.text: Form GST ITC-04 for April to September 2026, by 25 October 2026
options.why: The challans for goods sent to a job worker and received back during a period are reported in Form GST ITC-04, filed by the twenty-fifth of the month after that period ends. Which period applies turns on the previous year's aggregate turnover — above ₹5 crore it is a half-year beginning on 1 April and on 1 October, and at or below that figure it is the whole financial year. At ₹9 crore this company is on the half-year, so the April to September challans go in by 25 October 2026. The form doubles as the intimation to the jurisdictional officer.
keywords: it is a half-year beginning on 1 April
the April to September challans go in by 25 October 2026

citation.ref: Rule 45(1) and 45(3) with its Explanation, read with rule 55

items.scenario: A registered garment maker in Tamil Nadu had an aggregate turnover of ₹9 crore in 2025-26. Between April and September 2026 it sent fabric out to two dyeing units several times and took most of it back. Its accountant has the movement papers in a file and is asking what has to be reported to the department about it, and by when.

items.stem: What is the right answer to the three?

options.text: The platform invoices, it answers as though it were the supplier, and on the foreign platform the person representing it here pays
options.why: Where a service is notified, the tax on supplies made through the operator is paid by the operator, and every provision of the Act then applies to it as if it were the supplier liable for paying the tax on that service. That single sentence carries the practical consequences — the invoice for such a service is issued by the operator and not by the driver behind it, and the operator answers for the return and the payment. Where the operator has no physical presence in the taxable territory, its representative there is liable, and where it has neither presence nor representative it must appoint someone here for the purpose.
keywords: as if it were the supplier liable for paying the tax
the invoice for such a service is issued by the operator

options.text: The foreign platform is outside the Act altogether, since it has no presence here
options.misconception: reads absence of a presence as absence of liability, ignoring the two provisos
options.why: Absence of a presence is exactly the case the provisos were written for. The liability lands on the person representing the operator here, and if there is nobody, the operator has to appoint one — so there is always somebody in the taxable territory to answer for it.

options.text: The platform pays, but only on goods sold through it as well as services
options.misconception: extends a provision confined to services to supplies of goods
options.why: The provision speaks of categories of services and nothing else. On goods sold through a platform the supplier remains liable, and the platform's duty is the separate one of collecting tax at source.

options.text: The driver invoices and the platform merely deposits the money on his behalf
options.misconception: treats the operator as a collecting agent rather than as the person the Act puts in the supplier's place
options.why: Collecting on someone's behalf is what tax collected at source is, and it is a different mechanism. Here the operator is not passing on somebody else's tax; the law has moved the liability, and the paperwork moves with it.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: A ride-hailing platform is told by its advisers that on notified services it must pay the tax itself. Its billing team asks three practical questions before the next release. Does the driver still raise the invoice? Does the platform have to hold a separate registration for these supplies as an agent? And what happens on a sister platform, run from abroad, with an office and staff in India but no presence of its own.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: Yes — the exception applies only where the company is also registered under GST
options.misconception: adds a registration condition the omnibus entry does not carry, by borrowing it from the entries that do
options.why: Two other entries are keyed to whether the supplier is liable to registration. This one is not. It turns on the supplier being a company incorporated under company law, and nothing else.

options.text: No — the platform pays on the individual's rides and the company pays on its own
options.why: Carrying passengers by an omnibus is a notified service, and an omnibus is a motor vehicle built or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which a 20-seater plainly is. But the entry carries an exception where the person supplying the service through the operator is a company. So the coach company pays the tax on its own rides, while the individual's rides fall on the platform. The vehicles being identical is beside the point; the entry sorts by who the supplier is.
keywords: built or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver
the person supplying the service through the operator is a company

options.text: Yes — the platform pays on both, because the service is the same
options.misconception: reads the entry as being about the vehicle alone and misses the exception written into the same line
options.why: The entry describes a service and then carves out one class of supplier from it. A company keeps its own books and files its own returns, so the reason for shifting the tax to the platform — a long tail of small suppliers — does not apply to it.

options.text: No — neither is notified, because a 20-seater is a maxicab and maxicabs are covered by the other entry
options.misconception: confuses the two vehicle definitions, which are separated by the passenger count
options.why: A maxicab carries more than six but not more than twelve passengers excluding the driver. Twenty seats is past that ceiling, so the vehicle is an omnibus and it is the omnibus entry, with its exception for a company, that governs.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017 CT (R) — omnibus entry and the definitions of omnibus, maxi cab and company

items.scenario: A platform lists intercity coach seats. Two operators supply them on identical 20-seater vehicles over the same route at the same fare. One is a private limited company; the other is an individual who owns three coaches. The platform's tax lead assumes that identical services must be treated identically and proposes to pay the tax on both.

items.stem: Is that split correct?

options.text: No — the platform pays on none of them, because a driver who is not registered cannot be taxed
options.misconception: reads the driver's lack of registration as a reason nothing is payable
options.why: The tax is on the supply, and the entry names the person who is to pay it. That is why the mechanism exists — thousands of drivers below the threshold would otherwise mean the service was never taxed at all.

options.text: Yes — a registered supplier always pays his own tax
options.misconception: assumes registration always brings the liability back to the supplier
options.why: Registration decides who files and who may take credit. It does not by itself decide who pays on a notified service, and on this entry the liability is on the platform whatever the driver's status.

options.text: Yes, but only for the two who were obliged to register, not the ones who registered voluntarily
options.misconception: invents a distinction between compulsory and voluntary registration that this entry does not draw
options.why: Where an entry does turn on registration it asks whether the supplier is liable to be registered, which is one test and not two. On this entry it asks nothing of the kind, so the distinction has nowhere to operate.

options.text: No — the platform pays on all of them
options.why: The entry for carrying passengers by a radio-taxi, a motorcab, a maxicab or a motorcycle is written without any exception at all. Unlike the entries for accommodation and for house-keeping, it does not ask whether the supplier is liable to registration, and unlike the omnibus entry it does not ask whether the supplier is a company. So the platform pays on every motorcab ride booked through it, whether or not the driver is registered or liable to be.
keywords: the platform pays on every motorcab ride booked through it
whether or not the driver is registered or liable to be

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017 CT (R) — passenger transport entry

items.scenario: The same platform also lists city cab rides. Its records show that most of the drivers on that fleet have a turnover far below any registration threshold and are not registered, a handful have registered voluntarily, and two have crossed the threshold and are registered because they had to be. The platform proposes to pay the tax only on rides by the unregistered drivers and to leave the registered ones to pay their own.

items.stem: On which of the two is the platform liable?

options.text: On the guest house only
options.why: House-keeping services such as plumbing and carpentry, and accommodation in hotels, guest houses and similar places, are both notified — but each entry stops where the supplier is liable to registration under section 22(1), that is, where aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh, or ₹10 lakh in a special category State. At ₹35 lakh the plumber is liable to registration, so the plumber pays the tax himself. The guest house at ₹12 lakh is not, so the platform pays on its rooms.
keywords: so the plumber pays the tax himself

options.text: On neither, because a person supplying through a platform must register in any case
options.misconception: applies the compulsory-registration rule for platform suppliers without its exception for notified services
options.why: That rule has its own carve-out. Where the operator is liable to pay the tax on a notified service, the supplier behind it keeps the benefit of the threshold, which is exactly why the guest house here is unregistered and lawfully so.

options.text: On the plumber only, because he is registered and can be traced
options.misconception: has the exception the right way round in shape and the wrong way round in effect
options.why: Being traceable is the reason the liability stays with him rather than moving to the platform. A supplier who must register files his own returns, so there is nothing for the mechanism to solve.

options.text: On both, because both services are in the notified list
options.misconception: reads the entries without the exception each of them carries
options.why: Being in the list is only half of it. These two entries were written to catch small suppliers who would otherwise stay outside the net, so each stops at the point where the supplier is large enough to be in the net on his own.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017 CT (R) — accommodation and house-keeping entries, read with sections 22(1) and 24(ix)

items.scenario: The same platform has a home-services tab and a stays tab. On the first, a plumber with a turnover of ₹35 lakh in a State with the ordinary threshold takes jobs through it. On the second, a guest house with a turnover of ₹12 lakh and no registration lists rooms. The platform's tax lead proposes to pay the tax on both, on the footing that both are notified services.
