items.stem: On which of the two restaurants does the platform pay the tax?

options.text: On both, because the hotel's restaurant is not at specified premises for this year
options.why: Restaurant service supplied through an operator is notified except where it is supplied from specified premises. What makes premises specified, for a financial year, is that hotel accommodation was supplied from them in the preceding financial year at a value above ₹7,500 for a unit for a day — or that a declaration was filed, either between 1 January and 31 March of the preceding year or within fifteen days of a registration acknowledgement. The test looks backwards at what was actually charged, not forwards at a new rate, and no declaration was filed. So neither restaurant is at specified premises and the platform pays on both.
keywords: except where it is supplied from specified premises
at a value above ₹7,500 for a unit for a day

options.text: On the standalone restaurant only, because the hotel could file a declaration at any time and be treated as specified
options.misconception: treats the declaration route as open all year, when both windows are fixed
options.why: Both declaration routes are timed. One runs from 1 January to 31 March of the preceding financial year, and the other has to be taken within fifteen days of the acknowledgement of a registration application. Outside those windows the backward-looking test is the only one left.

options.text: On neither, because a restaurant inside a hotel is never a notified supply
options.misconception: treats being inside a hotel as the test instead of what the rooms fetched
options.why: Plenty of hotels sell rooms well below the line, and their restaurants are squarely inside the notification. The address is not the test; the value of the accommodation is.

options.text: On the standalone restaurant only, because the hotel's tariff is now above the line
options.misconception: applies the current year's tariff, which is what the superseded definition turned on
options.why: The definition was rewritten so that the answer for a whole year is settled before the year begins, off what the previous year's bills actually showed. A rate card announced during the year cannot change the status of the restaurant beneath it mid-stream.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017 CT (R) — restaurant service entry, and the substituted definition of specified premises

items.scenario: A food-delivery platform lists two kitchens. One is a standalone neighbourhood restaurant. The other sits inside a hotel where, through the whole of the previous financial year, no room went for more than ₹6,000 a night, and the hotel has filed no declaration of any kind. The hotel has just raised its rack rate for the coming season to ₹9,000 a night and says that this takes its restaurant out of the platform's hands.

items.stem: How long does the company have, and from when?

options.text: Three months from communication, with three more available on cause shown
options.why: An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal lies within three months from the date on which the order is communicated to the person appealing, so the clock starts on 5 October 2026 and not on the day the order was signed. The Tribunal may admit an appeal after that, for a further period of up to three months, where it is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay. There is also a Removal of Difficulties Order which counts the three months from the later of communication and the day the President of the Tribunal enters office.
keywords: lies within three months from the date on which the order is communicated
satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay
the day the President of the Tribunal enters office

options.text: Sixty days from the order, which have gone
options.misconception: carries the time limit for the first appeal across to the appeal to the Tribunal
options.why: Sixty days, extendable by a month, is the window for going to the Appellate Authority against an adjudicating officer. The next rung up has a longer window, and the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: Three months, and no extension is possible whatever the reason
options.misconception: reads the period as absolute, missing the sub-section that lets the Tribunal admit a late appeal
options.why: The Tribunal has an express power to admit an appeal presented after the three months, for up to three months more, on being satisfied there was sufficient cause. It is not automatic, but it exists.

options.text: Three months from the date the order was signed
options.misconception: starts the clock at signature rather than at communication
options.why: A person cannot appeal against an order he has not seen. The section says communicated for that reason, and an order that sits in a file for a fortnight before it is served does not eat into the appellant's time.

citation.ref: Sections 112(1) and 112(6), read with the CGST (Ninth Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2019

items.scenario: A transport company in Haryana loses before the Appellate Authority. The order reaches it on 5 October 2026. Counsel is engaged late and the papers are only ready in the third week of December. A junior in the office says the appeal is hopeless because more than sixty days have gone by, and adds that in any case the clock started when the Appellate Authority signed the order in September.

items.stem: On what date is the appeal treated as filed?

options.text: 2 January 2027, the date of upload
options.why: The appeal goes up in Form GST APL-05 electronically, and a provisional acknowledgement issues at once in Part A of Form GST APL-02A. Where the order appealed against is not on the common portal the appellant has to upload a self-certified copy of it within seven days of filing, and if he does, the date of the provisional acknowledgement is the date of filing. Here the copy went up thirteen days later, so that rule does not apply and the date of filing becomes 2 January 2027, the day the copy was uploaded. The final acknowledgement then issues in Part B of the same form.
keywords: The appeal goes up in Form GST APL-05 electronically
upload a self-certified copy of it within seven days of filing
the date of filing becomes 2 January 2027

options.text: 27 December 2026, the last day of the seven-day window
options.misconception: treats the deadline as the filing date when it is missed
options.why: A missed deadline does not become the date of the act. The rule names two candidates only — the provisional acknowledgement or the actual upload — and where the window is overrun it is the actual upload that counts.

options.text: There is no valid appeal, because the seven days were missed
options.misconception: reads the seven-day rule as a condition of validity rather than as a rule about dating
options.why: Overrunning it costs the appellant the earlier date, and that is all. The appeal still stands, and whether it is in time is then judged against the later date.

options.text: 20 December 2026, the date of the provisional acknowledgement
options.misconception: takes the provisional acknowledgement as fixing the date in every case, when it does so only where the copy is uploaded in time
options.why: The provisional acknowledgement fixes the date in two situations — where the order was already on the portal, and where it was not but the copy went up inside the seven days. Neither is this one, so the date moves to the upload.

citation.ref: Rules 110 and 111 as amended with effect from 22 September 2025 — form of appeal and date of filing

items.scenario: The company files its appeal electronically on 20 December 2026 and a provisional acknowledgement issues the same day. The order it is appealing against was never put on the common portal, so a self-certified copy has to go up separately. The office uploads it on 2 January 2027. The company records 20 December 2026 in its file as the date of the appeal.

items.stem: Is it needed?

options.text: Yes — the delay runs from 20 December 2026, the day the appeal was first lodged
options.misconception: measures the delay from the first lodgement instead of from the date the appeal is treated as filed
options.why: There is only one filing date and the rules say which it is. Once the upload fixes it at 2 January 2027, that is the date every other question is answered against, including whether the appeal was in time.

options.text: No — the appeal is inside the ordinary three months as it is
options.why: Three months from 5 October 2026 runs to 5 January 2027, and the appeal now dates from 2 January 2027, three days inside it. Nothing has to be excused. The Tribunal's power to condone a delay of up to three further months is there for an appeal that lands after 5 January 2027, and an application asking it to be used invites a question about a delay that does not exist.
keywords: Three months from 5 October 2026 runs to 5 January 2027
power to condone a delay of up to three further months

options.text: Yes — any appeal filed in the second three months needs the delay excused
options.misconception: reads 2 January 2027 as falling in the extension period, which starts only after 5 January 2027
options.why: The first three months have not run out on 2 January. The extension period begins the day after they do, so an appeal on 2 January is an ordinary appeal and not a late one.

options.text: No — and if it had been late, the Tribunal would have had to admit it on the same facts
options.misconception: gets the outcome right and treats condonation as automatic
options.why: The right answer here is that nothing needs excusing. Had the appeal been late, the Tribunal would have had to be satisfied that there was sufficient cause, and slow paperwork is not sufficient cause merely because it is true.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) read with section 112(6)

items.scenario: The order was communicated on 5 October 2026 and the appeal now dates from 2 January 2027. The company's counsel is drafting an application asking the Tribunal to excuse the delay and setting out at length why the papers took so long. A colleague reading the draft asks whether the application is needed at all.

items.stem: Is the broker right on either count?

options.text: No on both — a power station is within the scheme, and the spares ride with it
options.why: The scheme reaches industrial plants, irrigation schemes, power projects, mining projects, projects for oil or mineral exploration and whatever else the Central Government notifies, so a thermal power station is squarely inside it. Spare parts, raw material and consumable stores may come in under the same heading up to 10 per cent of the value of the goods, and 8 per cent is within that. The whole point of the scheme is that a project made up of items at a dozen different rates is assessed at one consolidated rate instead of item by item.
keywords: irrigation schemes, power projects, mining projects
up to 10 per cent of the value of the goods

options.text: Right on both — the scheme is for the initial setting up of a manufacturing unit only
options.misconception: reads the scheme as confined to factories, missing the list of project types it names
options.why: The list is broader than manufacturing and names power projects in terms, alongside irrigation and mining. It also covers substantial expansion of a unit already running, not only a first setting up.

options.text: Right on the spares only — they must be assessed under their own headings
options.misconception: treats consumables and spares as outside the project because they are not the plant itself
options.why: They are allowed in under the same heading, within a ceiling set as a share of the value of the goods. Beyond that ceiling they do fall out, so the figure matters — but at 8 per cent nothing here does.

options.text: No, and because one consolidated rate applies, an exemption notification for any single item is lost
options.misconception: assumes the consolidated rate swallows every other concession
options.why: It does not. An individual exemption notification still applies to an item grouped under the heading, as the Supreme Court has held, so the scheme simplifies the assessment without taking away a benefit that would otherwise be available.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule — project imports

items.scenario: A company setting up a new thermal power station imports turbines, boilers, cables and control instruments in one consignment, each falling under a different heading with its own rate. In the same consignment are spare parts and consumable stores worth 8 per cent of the value of the goods. Its broker says the consolidated project rate is only for factories making goods, and that the spares must be assessed on their own headings in any event.

items.stem: How are the cases classified?

options.text: With the cameras
options.why: The rule names camera cases along with musical instrument cases, gun cases, drawing instrument cases, necklace cases and similar containers, and puts them with the article they hold where four things hold good — the container is specially shaped or fitted to contain that article, it is suitable for long-term use, it is presented with the article, and it is of a kind normally sold with it. All four are satisfied. Cost is not one of the tests; a case normally supplied with the goods is not classified separately however dear it is.
keywords: specially shaped or fitted to contain that article
it is suitable for long-term use

options.text: Separately, because a container is always classified on its own unless it is disposable
options.misconception: inverts the rule, which puts durable fitted cases with the goods and excludes only containers giving the whole its essential character
options.why: Durability is a reason to classify the case with the article, not against it — the rule asks in terms for a container suitable for long use. The exception it does carry is for a container that gives the whole its essential character, which a camera case does not.

options.text: With the cameras, but only if the case is worth less than the camera
options.misconception: invents a proportion test out of the same instinct about value
options.why: No such proportion appears in the rule. The four conditions are all it asks, and a case that meets them goes with the article whatever the split in value happens to be.

options.text: Separately as leather goods, because of their value
options.misconception: makes the value of the container the test, which the rule does not
options.why: The tests are about shape, durability, presentation and trade custom. A rule that turned on cost would make the classification of an identical case change from one shipment to the next as prices moved.

citation.ref: Rule 5(a) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: A trader imports cameras. Each arrives in a moulded leather case cut to the shape of that camera body, built to last as long as the camera, packed with it and sold with it as a set. The cases are expensive — nearly a fifth of the price of the set. The department wants to classify the cases separately as leather goods, saying their value is too large to be treated as packing.

items.stem: Are the cylinders classified with the gas?

options.text: Yes, because the deposit is refundable so the cylinders were never really sold
options.misconception: uses the commercial arrangement to decide a question the rule settles on the nature of the container
options.why: Whether the container is bought, hired or deposited against does not come into it. The rule looks at what the container is fit for, and a cylinder fit for repeated filling is outside the general limb whatever the invoice says.

options.text: Yes — they were presented with the gas and are the normal packing for it
options.misconception: applies the general limb and stops before the exception in the same rule
options.why: Both things the importer says are true, and they get it as far as the general limb. The exception then takes it back out again, because a container that will be used many times is closer to equipment than to packing.

options.text: No — they are classified separately
options.why: Packing materials and packing containers presented with the goods are normally classified with those goods where they are of a kind ordinarily used for packing them. But the rule carries its own exception, and it is that the provision does not apply where the packing material or container is clearly suitable for repetitive use. Returnable steel cylinders are built to be filled over and over, so they fall in the exception and are classified on their own.
keywords: container is clearly suitable for repetitive use

options.text: No, because the cylinders give the consignment its essential character
options.misconception: reaches the right answer by the wrong exception
options.why: There are two exceptions and this is the other one. The essential character exception is about a container so dominant that the whole takes its identity from it; here the consignment is gas, and it is repetitive use that decides the point.

citation.ref: Rule 5(b) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

items.scenario: The same trader imports industrial gas. It comes in heavy steel cylinders that go back to the supplier once empty and are filled again and again. The invoice shows the gas and a separate refundable deposit for the cylinders. The importer classifies the cylinders with the gas, saying they were presented with it and are the normal way that gas is packed.

items.stem: What do the dashes and the blank column mean?

options.text: The dashes show the level of the breakdown, and with no preferential rate notified the other column is the rate to use
options.why: A description preceded by one dash is a sub-classification of the article or group the heading covers. Two dashes mark a sub-classification of the one-dash description immediately above it, and three or four dashes go a level deeper still, under the description above them carrying one or two dashes. As for the columns, where no preferential rate has been notified for an entry the standard rate of duty applies, and the per cent sign means the duty is worked out at that percentage on the goods' value, which section 14 of the Customs Act defines.
keywords: is a sub-classification of the article or group the heading covers
the standard rate of duty applies

options.text: Two dashes mean a sub-classification of the heading itself, the same as one dash but printed differently
options.misconception: flattens the levels, losing the point that each level attaches to the description above it
options.why: One dash attaches to the heading; two dashes attach to the one-dash description immediately preceding. Reading them as the same would let goods be classified under a two-dash description whose parent description they do not answer.

options.text: The per cent sign means the duty is a percentage of the invoice price
options.misconception: takes the invoice figure as the base instead of the value the Act defines
options.why: The note points at the value the valuation section defines, and that value is built up under rules of its own. The invoice price is where it starts, not where it ends.

options.text: The dashes are a printing convention with no legal effect, and a blank column means no duty
options.misconception: treats the notes as typography and reads a blank preferential column as an exemption
options.why: The notes are part of the Schedule and they decide which description sits under which. A blank preferential column means no preferential rate has been notified for that entry, which sends you to the other column and not to nil.

citation.ref: General explanatory notes to the First Schedule

items.scenario: A junior in a customs broker's office is reading an entry in the First Schedule. Under one heading a description is preceded by a single dash, and under that sit two descriptions each preceded by two dashes. The column headed preferential rate is blank for the entry the goods fall under, and the standard rate column shows a figure with a per cent sign after it. He asks what he is looking at.

items.stem: Which clause catches which, and is the accountant right?

options.text: Neither is caught, because both structures serve the business
options.misconception: reads the business-purpose test into a clause that expressly overrides it
options.why: Business purpose is what makes credit available everywhere else, which is why this clause had to say that it applies even where the construction is for the business. Without those words the clause would hardly ever operate.

options.text: Clause (c) catches the first and clause (d) the second, so the accountant is wrong
options.why: The two clauses were written to close each other's gaps. Clause (c) shuts off credit on works contract services taken for constructing immovable property that is not plant and machinery, unless they feed a further supply of works contract service. Clause (d) shuts it off where a taxable person receives goods or services and puts them into constructing, on his own account, immovable property that is not plant or machinery — and it says in terms that it bites even where the construction is in the course or furtherance of business. Buying materials directly instead of hiring a contractor moves the cost from one clause to the other, not out of both.
keywords: constructing immovable property that is not plant and machinery
constructing, on his own account, immovable property that is not plant or machinery

options.text: Both are caught by clause (c), since a works contract and direct purchases come to the same thing
options.misconception: collapses the two clauses, which would leave the second with no work to do
options.why: The two are separate and their wording differs in a way that matters — one says plant and machinery, the other plant or machinery, and the Supreme Court has held those two expressions do not mean the same thing.

options.text: Clause (c) catches the first and nothing catches the second, so the accountant is right
options.misconception: reads the restriction as being about the contract used rather than about the building that results
options.why: If that were so, every developer would buy its own materials and escape. The second clause exists for exactly that route and is written around goods and services received directly rather than around a contract.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) with the Explanation on the meaning of construction

items.scenario: A developer incurs two costs in the same year. It engages a works contractor to put up its own head-office block, and capitalises what it pays. Separately it buys cement, steel and architect's services in its own name and uses them to raise a structure on its own land, without engaging any works contractor at all. Its accountant says the second is safe because the restriction is about works contract services and none was taken.

items.stem: How should the company answer him?

options.text: That any building let out on taxable rent is a plant, so the credit is always available
options.misconception: turns a fact-based test into a rule covering every let building
options.why: The Court said the answer depends on the business of the registered person and the part the building plays in it. Some let buildings will pass and some will not, and a company that asserts the rule without the facts will lose on the facts.

options.text: That the clause uses a different expression, and whether this building is a plant turns on what it does in the business
options.why: The Explanation defines plant and machinery. The clause the officer is applying says plant or machinery, and the Supreme Court in Safari Retreats held that the two expressions were chosen deliberately and cannot be given the same meaning, so the definition does not govern this clause at all. Whether a building is a plant is then a question of fact, answered by the functionality test — if the building is essential to the business of supplying the service of renting or leasing it, it can be a plant, and it drops out of the clause. A warehouse built for nothing but taxable letting meets that, so the credit on the cement, steel and architect is not blocked.
keywords: the Supreme Court in Safari Retreats
Whether a building is a plant is then a question of fact
the credit on the cement, steel and architect is not blocked

options.text: That the clauses are unconstitutional, so nothing in them can be applied
options.misconception: remembers that the clauses were challenged and forgets that the challenge failed
options.why: The same judgment upheld the validity of both clauses and of the section fixing the time limit for taking credit. The company wins on what the words mean, not on the words being struck down.

options.text: That the definition applies but a warehouse is apparatus fixed to earth and so within it
options.misconception: accepts the officer's premise and then argues inside a definition that excludes buildings in terms
options.why: That road is closed. The definition excludes land, buildings and other civil structures in so many words, so a warehouse can never be brought inside it. The answer has to be that the definition is not the one the clause uses.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(d); Chief Commissioner of CGST v. Safari Retreats Pvt. Ltd. (2024)

items.scenario: A company buys cement, steel and an architect's services on its own account and raises a warehouse. It carries on no other activity with that building — it is let out, the rent is taxable, and the building was put up for no purpose except to be let. The officer disallows the credit, reading the definition of plant and machinery in the Explanation, which excludes a building, and saying that settles it.

items.stem: What must he pay under section 129(1) to have the goods released?

options.text: Nothing yet, because the goods can only be released after the officer has passed his order
options.misconception: treats the order as the gateway to release, when release on payment or on security is available from the moment of detention
options.why: The order under section 129(3) fixes the penalty where the person disputes it or lets the clock run, and the section gives the officer seven days to issue a notice and seven more to pass that order. None of that stands between an owner and his lorry. He may pay the specified amount, or furnish security equal to it, and take the goods away at once — and on payment the proceedings on the notice are treated as finished.

options.text: ₹7,50,000, being the higher of 50 per cent of the value of the goods and 200 per cent of the tax
options.misconception: applies the limb for an owner who stays away to an owner standing at the check post
options.why: The higher of 50 per cent of the value of the goods and 200 per cent of the tax is the figure for taxable goods where the owner does not come forward at all. Coming forward is what buys the cheaper limb, and it is the only thing that separates the two. This owner came forward the next morning, so the harsher measure never engages, and applying it here would charge him ₹7,50,000 for a fault that costs ₹3,60,000. Note also which half of the table these figures come from: this lorry never left Madhya Pradesh, so the state limb governs. Had the consignment crossed a state line, the value share in that same comparison doubles to a hundred per cent and the tax it is weighed against is the integrated tax.
keywords: the higher of 50 per cent of the value of the goods and 200 per cent of the tax

options.text: ₹3,60,000, or security of the same amount instead of paying
options.why: Goods moved in contravention of the Act or the rules, the conveyance carrying them and the papers relating to both are liable to detention or seizure. Where the owner of taxable goods comes forward, the release figure is a penalty equal to 200 per cent of the tax payable on those goods. Twelve per cent of ₹15,00,000 means the tax payable on this consignment is ₹1,80,000, so the penalty is ₹3,60,000. He is not obliged to hand over cash — the goods and the lorry go out on a penalty of ₹3,60,000, or on security of that amount, whichever suits him.
keywords: a penalty equal to 200 per cent of the tax payable on those goods
the tax payable on this consignment is ₹1,80,000
the goods and the lorry go out on a penalty of ₹3,60,000

options.text: ₹1,80,000, the tax having to be paid over before the goods move
options.misconception: reads section 129 as a machinery for collecting the tax that was avoided, when it collects a penalty measured by that tax and leaves the tax itself where it was
options.why: Section 129 is not a demand. The tax on the supply is due under its own provisions whenever the supply is made, and detention does not advance or replace it. What the section asks for before the goods move is a penalty, and it uses the tax only as the yardstick for measuring that penalty. Paying ₹1,80,000 and calling it settled would leave the penalty untouched and the lorry where it is.

citation.ref: Section 129(1) with clause (a) and the proviso, on a movement inside one state

items.scenario: A lorry moving a consignment of taxable goods from Indore to Bhopal is stopped at a check post. The goods are worth ₹15,00,000 and the rate on them is 12 per cent. No e-way bill was generated and the driver carries no invoice. The proper officer serves an order of detention. The owner of the goods reaches the check post the next morning and says he will pay whatever is needed to get the lorry moving again.

items.stem: What penalty does section 129(1) fix for the crates?

options.text: ₹40,000, being 5 per cent of the value of the goods
options.misconception: reads the two figures as a percentage with a floor rather than a percentage with a ceiling, so it takes the larger of them
options.why: Both exempted-goods limbs are written as the LOWER of a percentage and a rupee figure. The rupee figure is a ceiling on what exempted goods can cost their owner, and taking ₹40,000 turns that protection into its opposite. The comparison is the whole of the arithmetic here, and it is the half a student skips when he has read the taxable-goods table first and carried its shape across.

options.text: ₹16,000, being 2 per cent of the value of the goods
options.misconception: applies the owner-comes-forward limb to an owner who cannot be found
options.why: Two per cent is the percentage in the limb that applies when the owner of exempted goods does come forward, and there it is compared with the same ₹25,000 ceiling. Nobody has come forward for these crates, so the 5 per cent limb is the one that runs. The two limbs differ only in the percentage — the ceiling is the same either way — which is why the first question to ask on exempted goods is who is standing in front of the officer.
keywords: the limb that applies when the owner of exempted goods does come forward

options.text: Nothing, because goods which bear no tax cannot bear a penalty measured by tax
options.misconception: assumes every section 129 penalty is measured by tax, so an exemption leaves nothing to multiply
options.why: That is true only of the taxable-goods limbs, which take 200 per cent of the tax. The exempted-goods limbs are measured on the VALUE of the goods and capped in rupees precisely because there is no tax to multiply. An exemption from tax is not an exemption from the documentation the Act requires for movement, and the crates travelled without any. One caution on the ceiling itself: ₹25,000 is what it stands at while the goods stay inside one state, and the percentages beside it are 2 and 5. Send the same crates across a state line and every one of those four numbers doubles — the ceiling becomes ₹50,000 and the percentages 4 and 10.

Exempted goods have their own two limbs and each of them is a cap, not a straight percentage. Where the owner stays away the figure is the lower of 5 per cent of the value of the goods and ₹25,000. Five per cent of ₹8,00,000 comes to ₹40,000, the cap is the smaller of the two numbers, and the release figure is therefore ₹25,000. Notice which way the comparison runs — on exempted goods a bigger consignment does not buy a bigger penalty once the ceiling is reached.
keywords: the lower of 5 per cent of the value of the goods and ₹25,000

citation.ref: Section 129(1), clauses (a) and (b), on exempted goods moving inside one state

items.scenario: In the same lorry sit two crates belonging to a second trader. What is in them is exempt from tax and worth ₹8,00,000. The address on the crates is a shop that closed a year ago and nobody answers the telephone number written on them. The officer has to fix a release figure for the crates as well.

items.stem: What does section 129 require of him between the detention and the order?

options.text: A notice within seven days and an order within thirty days of it, the longer period being for the reply
options.misconception: borrows a thirty-day answering period from the demand provisions, where it belongs, into a section that has none
options.why: Both periods here are seven days. The section deliberately runs a short pair of clocks because the goods are lying idle, and it buys the person's chance to answer through the hearing rather than through a long answering window. A thirty-day gap would leave a lorry standing for a month on an allegation nobody had yet decided.

options.text: An order first, and then a notice giving the person a chance to have it set aside
options.misconception: reverses the sequence, treating the hearing as an appeal against a figure already fixed rather than as the step that fixes it
options.why: The notice comes first and says what is proposed; the order comes second and decides it. Turning that round matters — a hearing after the amount is settled is a review of somebody's decision, while a hearing before it is what the section actually gives, a chance to stop the amount being fixed at all. The appeal against the order is a separate road with its own conditions.

options.text: A notice within seven days of the detention, then an order within seven days of serving it, and a hearing before he fixes the amount
options.why: Two clocks of seven days each run one after the other. The officer who detains the goods has seven days from the detention to issue a notice saying what penalty he says is payable, and seven days from the service of that notice to pass his order. Before he settles the amount he must give the person an opportunity of being heard, so the notice is a question and not a bill. If the person then pays, all proceedings on the notice are deemed concluded and the file is shut.
keywords: seven days from the detention to issue a notice
give the person an opportunity of being heard
all proceedings on the notice are deemed concluded

options.text: Nothing within any particular time, since the goods are already in his hands and the person can pay whenever he likes
options.misconception: reads detention as a holding power with no clock on the officer, forgetting that the goods stop earning the moment they stop moving
options.why: The clocks bind the officer, not the person, and that is the point of them. Goods sitting at a check post are goods nobody can sell, so the Act refuses to let the department take its time. Seven days to the notice and seven from its service to the order are outer limits on the department's side, and a person who is not given his hearing inside them has an order made without the thing the section says must precede it.

citation.ref: Section 129(3), (4) and (5)

items.scenario: A consignment is detained on 4 May 2026 and the transporter disputes that anything was wrong with the papers, so nobody pays anything. The officer wants to know what he has to do next, and by when, before he can recover the amount he thinks is due.

items.stem: What follows from his silence, and what does an appeal cost him?

options.text: The lorry can be sold along with the load, because both were detained together
options.misconception: treats the conveyance as part of the consignment, missing that a transporter who did not own the goods has his own way out
options.why: Both are liable to be sold once the fifteen days have gone, but the conveyance has a release valve the goods do not — the smaller of the penalty and ₹1 lakh. That exists because the person who owns the lorry is often not the person who mis-declared the load, and taking his lorry for somebody else's fault would be a penalty on the wrong person.

options.text: Nothing can be sold until the appeal period has run out, and the appeal itself costs him ten per cent of the penalty
options.misconception: carries the ordinary appeal pre-deposit of ten per cent of the tax in dispute across to a penalty order under section 129
options.why: The ordinary pre-deposit of ten per cent is calculated on the tax in dispute and belongs to the general appeal provision. An order under section 129(3) fixes a penalty and no tax, so the general rule has nothing to bite on; the law states its own figure for this order alone, a quarter of the penalty. And the fifteen days run from receipt of the order, not from the end of any appeal period.

options.text: He can simply file an appeal and the sale is stayed automatically with no payment at all
options.misconception: assumes filing an appeal freezes recovery, when it is the pre-deposit and not the filing that does it
options.why: The appeal is not admitted at all until the quarter is paid, so there is nothing on foot to stay. Filing a paper with no money behind it leaves the recovery running. That sequencing is what the pre-deposit is for — it stops an appeal being used as a way of standing still.

options.text: After fifteen days the load can be sold to recover the penalty; the lorry comes out for the penalty or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less; and an appeal needs a quarter of the penalty paid first
options.why: The Act gives fifteen days from the receipt of the order. Once they pass without payment, the goods or the conveyance become liable to be sold or otherwise disposed of under rule 144A to recover what is due, and a perishable or fast-depreciating load can have that period cut short. The lorry is treated separately and more kindly — a transporter gets it back on paying the penalty or ₹1 lakh, whichever is the smaller figure. And an appeal against an order of this kind is admitted only if 25 per cent of the penalty has already been paid.
keywords: fifteen days from the receipt of the order
sold or otherwise disposed of under rule 144A to recover what is due
only if 25 per cent of the penalty has already been paid

citation.ref: Section 129(6) with its proviso, read with rule 144A and the proviso to section 107(6)

items.scenario: The order fixing the penalty on that consignment is served on the transporter, who receives it on 20 May 2026 and does nothing about it. He is more worried about the lorry than the load — it is on hire to him and the owner wants it back. Six weeks later he decides to fight the order instead.

items.stem: What does section 171 catch here, and which body examines it?

options.text: Both the rate cut and the newly available credit; and the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal examines it
options.why: Section 171 puts the duty on the supplier and names two triggers, not one — a reduction in the rate of tax on a supply of goods or of services, and the benefit of input tax credit. Whichever of the two arises, the gain has to reach the buyer as a commensurate reduction in prices. Both of this chain's practices are therefore caught. The body that examines whether the gain actually reached the buyer is, since the Government empowered it in 2024, the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 109.
keywords: the gain has to reach the buyer as a commensurate reduction in prices
the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 109

options.text: Both, and the Competition Commission of India examines them
options.misconception: names the body that held this work for a stretch in the middle and has since handed it on
options.why: The work has moved twice. The National Anti-Profiteering Authority handled it from the start of the tax until November 2022; the Competition Commission of India took it over from December 2022 and held it until the end of September 2024; and the Principal Bench has had it since. Naming the middle holder in an answer written today gets the substance right and the forum wrong, which on a procedure question is most of the mark.
keywords: the Competition Commission of India took it over from December 2022

options.text: Neither, because a fall in the company's own costs is not a matter for the tax authorities
options.misconception: treats a rate cut and a fresh credit as ordinary cost savings, which they are not
options.why: A saving the company makes by buying cheaper or running leaner is indeed its own, and section 171 does not reach it. What the section reaches are two specific gains that come out of the tax system itself. Neither of the two things here is a cost saving — one is the State charging less tax and the other is the State giving back more credit — and both belong to the customer.

options.text: Only the rate cut, a credit the company chose to start taking being its own affair
options.misconception: reads the section as being about tax rates alone, when the credit limb is the reason the section was written
options.why: The two limbs stand side by side in the sub-section and the credit limb is if anything the older worry — the whole design of the tax was expected to free up credit, and the fear was that the freed-up money would stop at the seller. A supplier who begins claiming credit he could not claim before is better off by exactly that amount, and the section says that betterment belongs to his customer.

citation.ref: Section 171(1) and 171(2) with its Explanation

items.scenario: A chain of home-appliance shops keeps its shelf prices exactly where they were after the tax on two of its product lines was cut, and pockets the difference. Around the same time it starts taking credit on a class of inward supplies it had never claimed before, and again changes no price. A consumer group wants to know which of the two things it can complain about and to whom that complaint goes today.

items.stem: What will happen to the application?

options.text: It will be examined, because a sunset only stops the Authority passing fresh orders and not receiving fresh complaints
options.misconception: puts the cut-off at the wrong end of the process
options.why: It is the other way round. The notified date stops the Authority taking in requests; matters already before it are not swept away by it. Reading the cut-off as applying to orders would leave the Authority obliged to receive complaints it could never decide, which is not a state any provision is written to produce.

options.text: It will be examined only if the association is itself a buyer of the cement
options.misconception: invents a standing requirement and misses the bar that actually disposes of the application
options.why: Interested parties, which include consumer and trade bodies, could bring these matters while the provision was open, and standing was never the difficulty. The difficulty is the date. Answering on standing here would produce a careful analysis of the wrong question and score nothing, because the application fails before anybody looks at who filed it.

options.text: It will not be examined at all, whatever it shows
options.why: Section 171 carries a sunset clause which lets the Government notify a date after which the Authority shall not accept any request for examination. That date has been notified as 1 April 2025. A request for examination is the written application asking whether a credit or a rate cut has actually resulted in a lower price, which is exactly what this association is filing. Filed in October 2025 it is on the wrong side of the sunset, and the strength of the file does not come into it.
keywords: a sunset clause which lets the Government notify a date after which the Authority shall not accept any request for examination
That date has been notified as 1 April 2025

options.text: It will be examined, because the profiteering itself happened while the provision was fully alive
options.misconception: dates the bar by when the conduct occurred rather than by when the request is filed
options.why: The sunset is written against the ACCEPTANCE of a request, not against the conduct complained of. It shuts the door on new applications from the notified date onwards however old the conduct behind them, which is the whole point of a sunset — it lets a provision stop taking in new work while it finishes what it already has. A complaint about 2024 conduct filed in late 2025 is still a request made after the door closed.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 171(2)

items.scenario: A trade association has put together what it believes is a complete file showing that a cement dealer never passed on a rate reduction. Its papers are in order, the arithmetic is checked, and it proposes to file the written application in October 2025 asking for the matter to be examined.

items.stem: Which account of the route is right?

options.text: Straight to the Director General, the committees existing only to handle appeals against his report
options.misconception: treats the two committees as a review layer above the investigator rather than the filter that decides whether he is troubled at all
options.why: The committees sit before the investigation, not after it. Their job is to keep a full investigation — with its summonses and its production of documents — off a supplier's back until somebody has looked at the papers and thought there is something in them. A report of the Director General goes upward to the Authority, which decides; it does not go back to a committee.

options.text: To the Authority first, which then chooses whether to send it down for investigation
options.misconception: starts the route at the decision-maker, which would leave the Authority screening its own cases
options.why: The Authority is the body that finally determines whether profiteering happened and what is to be done about it, and it comes in at the end, on the Director General's report. Starting there would put the same body in charge of sifting and of judging. The Authority does have a hand in the timetable — the extensions at the committee and investigation stages are allowed by it — but that is not the same as receiving the complaint.

options.text: The same route, but the Director General has three months to investigate and no power to summon anyone
options.misconception: shortens the investigation clock and strips the investigator of the powers that make the stage work
options.why: Six months, extendable by three, is what the investigation gets, and the length is deliberate — proving that a price did not fall by the right amount means going through a supplier's costing over a period. The powers matter as much as the clock. Without the power to summon and to call for documents the investigation would depend on the supplier volunteering the figures that convict him.

options.text: The State-level Screening Committee, then the Standing Committee, then the Director General, then the Authority — with two months, two months and six months for the three working stages
options.why: A local application goes first to the State-level Screening Committee, which has two months from receiving it, extendable by one, to send it on with its recommendation. The Standing Committee, if it sees prima facie evidence, refers the matter to the Director General of Anti-Profiteering within two months, again extendable by one. The Director General then investigates and must finish within six months, extendable by a further three. He carries the powers of a civil court while doing it and the inquiry is deemed to be a judicial proceeding, which is why a summons from him is not a request.
keywords: A local application goes first to the State-level Screening Committee
must finish within six months, extendable by a further three
the inquiry is deemed to be a judicial proceeding

citation.ref: Rules 128, 129 and 133 read with section 171(2)

items.scenario: Take a complaint of local scope that was filed while requests were still being accepted. A trainee is asked to draw the route it will travel — who looks at it first, who investigates, how long each stage has, and what powers the investigator carries when he starts summoning people.

items.stem: What may the order direct, and what does delay cost?

options.text: Return to identified buyers only; whatever cannot be returned stays with the supplier
options.misconception: treats untraceable customers as a windfall for the person who overcharged them
options.why: That would leave the profit in the pocket of the person the order is against, and reward him most where his record-keeping is worst. The rules send the unclaimed part into the Consumer Welfare Funds instead, split between the Centre and the State, so the money at least goes back to consumers as a class even when it cannot go back to the individuals.

options.text: Return to identified buyers with interest, half of the untraceable amount into the Centre's Consumer Welfare Fund and half into the State's, and a further penalty if the money is not deposited in a month
options.why: The order may direct a reduction in prices and the return of the amount kept back, with interest at 18 per cent running from the date the higher amount was collected until the day it goes back. Where a buyer does not claim it or cannot be identified, the money is not kept by the supplier — 50 per cent of it goes with interest into the Consumer Welfare Fund of the Centre and the other 50 per cent into that of the State concerned. A penalty and cancellation of registration are also open to the Authority, and a person found to have profiteered pays a penalty of 10 per cent of the profiteered amount if it is not deposited within thirty days of the order.
keywords: interest at 18 per cent running from the date the higher amount was collected
50 per cent of it goes with interest into the Consumer Welfare Fund of the Centre
a penalty of 10 per cent of the profiteered amount
if it is not deposited within thirty days of the order

options.text: Interest at 18 per cent, but only from the date of the order, and no penalty as long as the principal is paid one day
options.misconception: starts the interest at the order and treats the deposit clock as advisory
options.why: Interest runs from the date the higher amount was collected, not from the date somebody noticed. Anything else would make holding on to the money free for as long as the investigation took. And the deposit clock has teeth — a month after the order, an unpaid profiteered amount attracts a penalty measured on that amount.

options.text: The whole unclaimed amount into the Centre's Consumer Welfare Fund
options.misconception: forgets that the tax has two halves and so does the fund the money lands in
options.why: There are two Consumer Welfare Funds, one of the Centre and one of the State or Union territory the order concerns, and the deposit is split evenly between them. That mirrors how the tax on the supply was shared in the first place. Putting it all in one is the same error as paying an entire liability under one head.

citation.ref: Section 171(3A) read with rule 133(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An order holds that a supplier kept back an amount that should have reached its customers. Most of those customers bought over the counter and cannot be traced from any record the supplier keeps. The supplier asks its accountant what the order can require of it and what happens if it simply does not pay.

items.stem: Was the order served?

options.text: Only if the department first tried and failed to serve it by hand, post and e-mail, since the portal is a last resort
options.misconception: borrows the sequencing that governs one mode and applies it to all of them
options.why: There is exactly one mode the Act keeps for the end of the queue — affixing the order at the place of business or on the officer's notice board, which is available only when none of the others is practicable. The rest, the portal included, may be used at once and in any order. Reading a queue into the whole list would make almost every service defective.

options.text: No, because service is complete only when the addressee actually receives the order and signs for it
options.misconception: reads service as a fact about the recipient rather than a set of acts by the sender that the Act deems to be service
options.why: If actual receipt were the test, a person could defeat every order by not opening his door. The Act instead lists acts the department may do and says when each of them counts. A communication is treated as served on the day it is tendered, published or affixed, and one sent by post is treated as received once the usual transit time has run. The person keeps the right to prove the contrary; he does not keep a right to say nothing.

options.text: No, because putting a document on the portal is a convenience and not a mode of service
options.misconception: treats the portal as a filing cabinet rather than one of the listed modes
options.why: Making the order available on the common portal is one of the modes the section lists, standing on the same footing as post or e-mail. It is not a courtesy copy. A registered person's portal login is the address the law expects him to watch, and an order sitting there is served whether or not he logs in.

options.text: Yes, twice over, and it is deemed to have reached the company after the time such post normally takes
options.why: The Act lists the ways an order may be served and any one of them is enough. Registered post, speed post or courier with acknowledgement due to the last known place of business or residence is one of them, and making the order available on the common portal is another, so the department used two. Where an order goes by registered or speed post it is deemed to have been received when the period normally taken by such post in transit expires, unless the person proves otherwise — and a missing acknowledgement card is not that proof.
keywords: Registered post, speed post or courier with acknowledgement due
making the order available on the common portal
the period normally taken by such post in transit

citation.ref: Section 169(1), (2) and (3)

items.scenario: A company says it never received a demand order and that the time for appealing it therefore cannot have started. The department's file shows the order was sent to the registered address by speed post and, on the same day, put up on the common portal against the company's login. The acknowledgement card has not come back.

items.stem: What is paid, and what is left alone?

options.text: ₹12,34,567 is paid, since a part of a rupee is always ignored
options.misconception: remembers only the dropping half of the rule and applies it to every amount
options.why: The rule cuts both ways and the fifty-paise mark is the hinge. Anything from fifty paise upward is rounded up to the next rupee and only what falls below it is ignored. Dropping every fraction would leave the Government short by a few paise on every return in the country, which is why the section was written with two limbs and not one.

options.text: ₹12,34,568 is paid; the invoices are left exactly as they are
options.why: The Act rounds tax, interest, penalty, fine, refund and any other sum payable or due under it to the nearest rupee. Where the part of a rupee is fifty paise or more it is raised to one rupee, and where it is less it is dropped. Seventy-two paise is the first case, so the consolidated payment is ₹12,34,568. The rounding reaches only the consolidated payment to the Government — a tax invoice is not rounded at all, so the paise stay on the invoices and only the total moves.
keywords: Where the part of a rupee is fifty paise or more it is raised to one rupee

options.text: Nothing is rounded, because the Act nowhere permits an approximate payment
options.misconception: treats rounding as an approximation the law would not tolerate, when the law prescribes it
options.why: Rounding here is not an approximation somebody chose — the Act directs it, so the rounded figure IS the amount payable. Paying ₹12,34,567.72 would be paying an amount the Act does not recognise. The provision exists precisely so that no challan in the country has to carry paise.

options.text: Each invoice is rounded first and the rounded figures are added
options.misconception: applies a rule about payments to the documents that lead up to them
options.why: The section speaks of sums payable or due under the Act, and a tax invoice is neither — it is a record of a supply. Rounding at the invoice level would also change the credit the buyer takes and would put his figures out of step with the seller's. Only the consolidated amount going to the Government is rounded.

citation.ref: Section 170

items.scenario: A firm's working for a month leaves a consolidated central tax liability of ₹12,34,567.72. Its invoices for the month, taken one by one, carry paise in them too. The accountant asks whether he should round each invoice and then add, or add and then round, and what figure goes into the payment challan.

items.stem: What duty is payable on those articles?

options.text: Duty on ₹15,000, being the excess over the general free allowance
options.misconception: runs personal effects through the money allowance instead of clearing them under the rule that comes first
options.why: The two clearances are separate and they run in order. Used personal effects go free under their own rule with no ceiling on them, and only then does the money allowance apply to what is left — new purchases, gifts, goods bought abroad. Netting the effects against the allowance would mean a passenger with a large but ordinary wardrobe paid duty on his own clothes.

options.text: None, but only because ₹90,000 is below the ₹1,00,000 ceiling on personal effects
options.misconception: invents a ceiling for a clearance the rule deliberately leaves open
options.why: There is no ceiling. The rule says the clearance is without limit, and reading a figure into it would turn a protection into a trap for the one passenger whose ordinary luggage happens to be valuable. What limits this clearance is the character of the articles — used, personal, needed for daily life or a travel souvenir — never their price.

options.text: None, and the general free allowance is not touched by them at all
options.why: Rule 3 clears a separate class of articles before any allowance is reached — travel souvenirs, and the used personal effects that the daily necessities of life call for, carried on the person or in bona fide baggage. That clearance is free of duty and, crucially, is given without any value limit, so the ₹90,000 figure decides nothing. The ₹75,000 allowance is for other articles and is still sitting there untouched. Personal effects now carry a wider sense as well — articles new or second-hand that a passenger might reasonably want for his own use on the journey, short of anything carried for trade.
keywords: the used personal effects that the daily necessities of life call for
is given without any value limit, so the ₹90,000 figure decides nothing

options.text: Duty on the camera alone, since it is not a daily necessity
options.misconception: reads the personal effects rule as covering only toiletries and clothing, missing that an article taken out of India and brought back is not an import at all
options.why: A camera the passenger already owned and took out with him is not something he has brought into the country in any real sense, and the rules deal with it twice over — it sits inside the widened idea of personal effects, and articles taken out earlier come back free on a declaration made at departure. Duty on a traveller's own long-owned possessions is not what the baggage rules are for.

citation.ref: Rule 3, read with Master Circular No. 4/2026-Customs dated 1 February 2026

items.scenario: A resident lands at Chennai from a three-week work trip. In his suitcase are the clothes he wore, the shaving kit and medicines he took with him, and a camera he has owned for years and carried out of India and back. Put together the officer values the lot at ₹90,000. Nothing in the bag appears in Annexure-I. He is told the general free allowance is ₹75,000 and starts working out the duty on the balance.

items.stem: How much of the couple's purchases is dutiable, and what does the tourist get?

options.text: ₹30,000 of hers is dutiable, none of his is, and the tourist has ₹25,000
options.why: A resident arriving otherwise than by land gets a general free allowance of ₹75,000 for articles outside Annexure-I, and the same ₹75,000 goes to a tourist of Indian origin and to a foreigner holding a valid visa that is not a tourist visa. The allowance is personal. One passenger's allowance cannot be pooled with another's, so her ₹1,05,000 takes her own ₹75,000 and leaves ₹30,000 dutiable, while his unused ₹35,000 helps nobody. A tourist of foreign origin is on a smaller footing and gets ₹25,000.
keywords: a general free allowance of ₹75,000 for articles outside Annexure-I
One passenger's allowance cannot be pooled with another's
A tourist of foreign origin is on a smaller footing and gets ₹25,000

options.text: Nothing of either, because a shortfall in one passenger's allowance may be transferred within a family with the officer's permission
options.misconception: imagines an official discretion to allow pooling, when the bar is absolute
options.why: No officer can permit it. The bar on pooling is stated flatly and no authority is given to relax it, which is the difference between this rule and the several places in the baggage rules where a Principal Commissioner may extend or relax something. Where the rules mean to allow a discretion they say so.

options.text: Nothing of either is dutiable, the couple having ₹1,50,000 between them
options.misconception: adds two allowances together for a family travelling as one
options.why: The rule refuses this in terms — the free allowance of one passenger may not be pooled with the free allowance of any other. It is written that way because the alternative invites a family to load one member's bag with everything expensive and count the rest of the family's heads against it. Relationship, one ticket and one address make no difference; the allowance follows the passenger.

options.text: ₹30,000 of hers is dutiable and the tourist also has ₹75,000, allowances being the same for everybody arriving by air
options.misconception: treats the allowance as a single figure for all arrivals, missing that the rule sets a lower one for a tourist of foreign origin
options.why: There are two figures, and which one a passenger gets turns on his class. Residents, tourists of Indian origin and foreigners on a long-stay visa other than a tourist visa are on ₹75,000. A tourist of foreign origin, who is here briefly and is not setting up a household, is on ₹25,000. Naming one figure for everyone loses half of what this rule says.

citation.ref: Rule 5

items.scenario: A husband and wife, both Indian residents, land together at Hyderabad from Singapore. She has bought articles outside Annexure-I worth ₹1,05,000; he has bought ₹40,000 worth. They travel on one ticket, live in one house and ask the officer to look at the two lots together. Standing behind them in the queue is a Japanese national on a tourist visa with articles worth ₹40,000.

items.stem: What is dutiable in his baggage?

options.misconception: puts the laptop inside the general free allowance, so the allowance is swallowed by it and everything else is charged
options.why: The laptop clearance is expressly in addition to the money allowance. Reading it as part of the allowance makes the concession worthless for anybody carrying a laptop worth more than ₹75,000, which is most laptops that are worth carrying. Add ₹85,000 and ₹1,10,000, subtract the allowance once, and you get ₹1,20,000 — an answer that has spent the allowance on something the rules had already cleared.

options.text: ₹35,000, but only if he is over 21, the laptop concession being for adults
options.misconception: guesses the age condition instead of reading it
options.why: The age written into the rule is 18, not 21, and the other condition is that the passenger is not a crew member. He is 29, so both are satisfied and the arithmetic is unaffected. Guessing a threshold that sits in the rule in plain figures is where marks go on a question of this kind.

A passenger of 18 years or more who is not a crew member may bring one new laptop, a notepad counting as one, free of duty in bona fide baggage, and that clearance sits on top of the general free allowance rather than inside it. So the ₹85,000 machine costs him nothing and leaves his ₹75,000 intact. The speakers and the tablet are ordinary new articles, they come to ₹1,10,000, and after the allowance the balance of ₹35,000 is dutiable.
keywords: may bring one new laptop, a notepad counting as one, free of duty
after the allowance the balance of ₹35,000 is dutiable

options.text: Nothing, because a laptop and its accessories all come in duty free
options.misconception: stretches the laptop concession into a class of goods rather than one named article
options.why: The concession is for one new laptop, notepad included, and stops there. Speakers and a tablet are not accessories to it in any sense the rule recognises — they are separate articles bought abroad and they meet the general free allowance like anything else. A second laptop would meet it too.

citation.ref: Rule 5, on the additional allowance for a laptop

items.scenario: A software engineer aged 29, an Indian resident, arrives at Bengaluru by air. He declares one new laptop bought abroad for ₹85,000, and a new pair of studio speakers and a new tablet bought abroad for ₹1,10,000 between them. None of it appears in Annexure-I. He is not a crew member.

items.stem: How much of the jewellery goes through free of duty?

options.text: 20 grams of his and 40 grams of hers
options.misconception: applies the female allowance on sex alone and skips the residence condition that comes before it
options.why: The residence test is a gate, and the two weights sit behind it. Only a passenger who has lived abroad for more than a year reaches the allowance at all; the split between 40 grams and 20 grams then decides how much of it he or she gets. A woman back after seven months is in the same position as a man back after seven months — no jewellery allowance whatever, though her ordinary money allowance is untouched.

options.text: 20 grams of his; none of hers
options.why: The jewellery allowance is given only to a resident or a tourist of Indian origin who has been residing abroad for more than one year, and it is then 40 grams if the passenger is female and 20 grams for any other passenger. He has been away twenty months, so he clears 20 grams and pays duty on the remaining 5 grams, which at ₹12,000 a gram makes ₹60,000 dutiable. His sister has been away seven months. She does not reach the qualifying period at all, so the fact that a female passenger would otherwise get 40 grams never comes into play and her whole 30 grams is dutiable.
keywords: who has been residing abroad for more than one year
it is then 40 grams if the passenger is female
he clears 20 grams and pays duty on the remaining 5 grams
which at ₹12,000 a gram makes ₹60,000 dutiable

options.text: All of his and all of hers, jewellery being used personal effects
options.misconception: folds newly bought jewellery into the personal effects clearance, which covers what a passenger already wore and used
options.why: Used personal jewellery a passenger already had and needs in daily life does travel as personal effects. Jewellery bought abroad on this trip is not that. The rules deal with it as a separate class with its own weight-based allowance, and beyond the allowance it bears duty. The word doing the work in the personal effects clearance is "used".

options.text: 25 grams of his, because the allowance is by value and his is below the limit
options.misconception: expects a rupee ceiling where the rule sets a weight
options.why: This allowance is written in grams and not in rupees, which is the unusual thing about it and the thing worth remembering. Two passengers carrying the same weight get the same clearance whether their gold is plain or heavily worked. Jewellery here means an article of adornment of gold, silver, platinum or another precious metal, studded or not.

citation.ref: Rule 6

items.scenario: A man who has been working in Muscat for twenty months returns to Kochi by air with 25 grams of gold jewellery bought there, valued at ₹12,000 a gram. His sister, who has been in Muscat for seven months on a short assignment, arrives on the same flight with 30 grams of gold jewellery bought there. Both are residents returning home.

items.stem: What duty do the two of them pay?

options.text: ₹33,250 and ₹73,500, at the rate in force on 20 June 2026
options.why: Baggage is exempt from integrated tax, compensation cess and the social welfare surcharge, and bears basic customs duty at 35 per cent on the value above the free allowances, so 35 per cent is the effective rate. His ₹1,70,000 less his ₹75,000 leaves ₹95,000, and 35 per cent of that is ₹33,250. His sister's clothes and gifts use up her whole allowance, and having been abroad only five months she has no jewellery allowance, so ₹2,10,000 is chargeable and 35 per cent of it is ₹73,500. The rate and the valuation are those in force on the day the declaration is made under section 77, so 20 June governs and the later change is irrelevant.
keywords: bears basic customs duty at 35 per cent on the value above the free allowances

options.text: ₹66,500 and ₹1,47,000, the rate for baggage being 70 per cent
options.misconception: applies the special rate that heading 9803 keeps for firearms and quantities of cartridges to ordinary baggage
options.why: The 70 per cent rate under heading 9803 is for firearms and for cartridges above 50, and even that heading does not reach motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages or tobacco. Ordinary declared articles — electronics, clothing, jewellery beyond an allowance — bear 35 per cent. Doubling the rate here doubles two answers that were otherwise right.
keywords: The 70 per cent rate under heading 9803 is for firearms and for cartridges above 50

options.text: ₹33,250 and ₹73,500, plus integrated tax and social welfare surcharge on each
options.misconception: stacks the ordinary import levies on top of the baggage rate, when baggage is exempt from them
options.why: The 35 per cent is the whole of it. Passenger baggage is exempt from integrated tax, from compensation cess and from the social welfare surcharge, which is why a single rate can be called the effective rate at all. Adding them would produce a figure no passenger has ever been asked for at a green channel.

options.text: ₹33,250 and ₹73,500, but at whatever rate is in force on 5 July 2026
options.misconception: fixes the rate at assessment or clearance, as for ordinary imported goods, instead of at the declaration
options.why: Baggage has its own relevant date and it is earlier than the one for a bill of entry. The rate of duty and the tariff valuation for baggage are those in force on the date the declaration under section 77 is made. That protects a passenger from a delay in the shed that is not his doing, and it is the single most likely thing to be tested about the rate.

citation.ref: Sections 77 and 78, read with Notification No. 26/2016-Customs as amended and heading 9803 of the Customs Tariff

items.scenario: A resident back from three years abroad lands at Delhi by air and files his baggage declaration under section 77 on 20 June 2026. He declares new electronics worth ₹1,70,000, none of it in Annexure-I, and nothing else chargeable. His sister on the same flight, back after five months abroad, declares new clothes and gifts worth exactly ₹75,000 and 35 grams of gold jewellery bought abroad worth ₹2,10,000. The baggage is held up and is actually assessed on 5 July 2026, and the Government alters the baggage rate with effect from 1 July 2026.

items.stem: What does section 15(3)(b) require?

options.text: Two things together — an agreement struck no later than the supply and tied to particular invoices, and the buyer having reversed the credit on the rebate
options.why: A discount given after a supply comes out of the value only when both conditions are satisfied and neither is enough on its own. The first is about timing and traceability — the discount must rest on an agreement struck at or before the time of such supply, and it must be specifically linked to the invoices it is set against, so that a rebate cannot be invented afterwards and spread across a year's trade. The second is about the other side of the transaction — the input tax credit attributable to the discount must have been reversed by the recipient, on the strength of the document the supplier issues. The scheme here meets the first; the second depends on what the dealers do.
keywords: the discount must rest on an agreement struck at or before the time of such supply
it must be specifically linked to the invoices it is set against
the input tax credit attributable to the discount must have been reversed by the recipient

options.text: Only that the rebate can be traced to particular invoices, a running course of dealing standing in for an agreement
options.misconception: lets a habit of giving year-end rebates take the place of the agreement the section asks for
options.why: Traceability is one half. The other is that the arrangement existed by the time the supply was made, so that the price the parties struck always carried the rebate inside it. A course of dealing is evidence that a supplier is generous, not evidence that this supply was priced with a discount already agreed. That is the distinction the timing condition draws.

options.text: Only that the scheme was in writing before the supplies, the reversal by the buyer being his own compliance problem
options.misconception: treats the two conditions as one, so a well-documented scheme is thought to settle the matter on the seller's side alone
options.why: The two conditions are joined and the section fails if either is missing. The reason the buyer's reversal is made the seller's problem is arithmetic — if the value falls and the buyer keeps the credit on the full value, the Government has paid out credit on tax that was never collected. Making the seller's relief wait on the buyer's reversal is how that hole is closed.

options.text: Nothing further, because a discount is by nature not part of the consideration
options.misconception: argues from what a discount is rather than from what the section allows
options.why: A discount given before or at the time of supply and shown on the invoice does come out of the value on that reasoning. A discount given afterwards does not, because the value was already fixed when the supply happened, and the section lets it be undone only on conditions. Reasoning from the nature of a discount skips the conditions and gets a whole limb of the provision wrong.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

items.scenario: A tyre maker runs a scheme under which dealers who cross a yearly volume earn a rebate, and the scheme is signed with each dealer before the year's first despatch. At the year end it works out each dealer's rebate, names the invoices it belongs to, and wants the rebate taken out of the value of those supplies. Its finance head asks what has to be true before that can be done.

items.stem: How does the supplier give effect to the rebate, and by when?

options.text: A debit note under section 34, since the dealer now owes less
options.misconception: picks the wrong one of the pair, reading the note from the direction the money moves rather than from whose liability changes
options.why: A debit note is issued when the value or the tax charged turns out to be too LOW and the supplier has more to pay. Here the value is coming down and the supplier's liability with it, which is a credit note. The pair is easy to reverse under exam pressure, and the safe test is to ask what happens to the supplier's output tax — down means credit note.

options.text: A credit note, but the outer date is the end of the financial year in which the note is issued
options.misconception: anchors the deadline to the note rather than to the year of the supply
options.why: The clock runs from the year of the SUPPLY, not the year of the note, which is what stops the deadline being reset simply by waiting. Count from the financial year in which the original supply was made, take 30 November after it, compare that with the date the annual return for that year is furnished, and the earlier of the two is the last day.

options.text: A credit note under section 34, declared in the return for the month it is issued and in any case by 30 November 2027 or the annual return, whichever comes first
options.why: The instrument is a credit note under section 34, covering the ₹40,000 and the tax on it, and it is what tells both sides and the department that the value has moved. The supplier declares it in the return for the month in which he issues it, and his output tax for that month falls accordingly. That declaration has an outer date, and the deadline is 30 November after the financial year of the supply closes, or the day the annual return for that year goes in, whichever falls first. December 2027 is past it, so a note issued then could not reduce the tax.
keywords: The instrument is a credit note under section 34
the deadline is 30 November after the financial year of the supply closes, or the day the annual return for that year goes in, whichever falls first

options.text: A credit note at any time, the outer date applying only to debit notes
options.misconception: remembers that one of the two documents has a cut-off and puts it on the wrong one
options.why: It is the credit note that carries the cut-off, and for a reason — a credit note takes money away from the exchequer, so the law will not let it be issued indefinitely against an old year. A debit note adds to the liability and nobody needs to be protected from it, so it has no such outer date.

citation.ref: Section 34(1) and 34(2) read with section 15(3)(b)(i)

items.scenario: The rebate on a dealer's 2026-27 purchases is settled in May 2027 and comes to ₹40,000 plus the tax on it. The agreement behind it was signed before the first supply of that year and names the invoices. The dealer has reversed the credit. The supplier's accountant wants to know what document to issue, and whether he can still do it in December 2027 if the work slips.

items.stem: How far can it go?

options.text: It cannot give the ₹20,000 at all without falling foul of the valuation rules
options.misconception: confuses being unable to reduce the tax with being unable to make the payment
