options.why: Nothing in the tax law stops a business from giving money back to a customer. What the law decides is whether the giving changes the value of the earlier supply, and here it does not. Refusing to pay would be answering a commercial question with a tax rule that was never about it.

options.text: It can issue a credit note under section 34 with tax on it, as long as the customer reverses the credit
options.misconception: thinks the buyer's reversal can cure a discount that failed the first condition
options.why: The two conditions are cumulative and the reversal answers only the second. A discount with no prior agreement fails at the first step, and nothing the buyer does afterwards puts it right. Asking the customer to reverse credit here would leave him worse off for no reason, since the supplier still cannot bring his own tax down.

options.text: It can hand over the ₹20,000 through a commercial credit note, but the tax on ₹8,00,000 stays paid
options.why: The first condition is not met — there was no agreement at or before the supply, and a goodwill gesture decided half a year later cannot be turned into one. So the discount cannot come out of the value, however genuine it is. What the supplier may still do is give the money, using a commercial credit note that carries no tax adjustment at all. The customer's credit is untouched, the supplier's output tax is untouched, and the ₹20,000 is simply a cost of keeping a customer.
keywords: there was no agreement at or before the supply
using a commercial credit note that carries no tax adjustment at all

options.text: It can reduce the value, because a discount linked to a specific invoice always qualifies
options.misconception: treats the linkage limb as the whole of the first condition and drops the timing limb
options.why: Linkage and timing are both inside the first condition and both have to hold. This gesture is perfectly well linked — everyone knows which delivery it is about — and still fails, because the arrangement did not exist when the supply was priced. That is exactly the case the timing words were written for.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)(i)

items.scenario: Six months after a supply of ₹8,00,000 the same supplier's board decides to let a long-standing customer off ₹20,000, because a delivery arrived late and cost the customer a sale. The decision is minuted at that meeting. Nothing about it appears in the dealer circular for the year, in the customer's contract, or in any paper written before the goods went out. The supplier wants its tax on the supply cut to match.

items.stem: Where does that leave the supplier?

options.text: It cannot reduce its output tax, even though its own paperwork is perfect
options.why: The second condition asks for something the supplier does not control. Until the credit attributable to the discount is reversed by the recipient, the condition in section 15(3)(b)(ii) is unmet, and the supplier cannot reduce its output tax liability by the credit note however good the agreement was. The reduction depends on the recipient acting, which is why suppliers write the reversal into the rebate agreement and hold the money until it is done.
keywords: the supplier cannot reduce its output tax liability by the credit note
Until the credit attributable to the discount is reversed by the recipient

options.text: It can reduce its output tax, the dealer's failure being the dealer's own exposure
options.misconception: splits the two sides, so each party answers only for its own returns
options.why: On this one point the law deliberately joins them. If the supplier's tax came down while the dealer's credit stayed up, the difference would be a permanent loss to the exchequer, and no penalty on the dealer recovers it. So the section makes the supplier's relief conditional on the dealer's act rather than merely penalising the dealer.

options.text: It can reduce its output tax because the credit note has already been issued and declared
options.misconception: treats issuing the document as the operative act
options.why: Issuing and declaring the note is the mechanism, not the entitlement. Both conditions still have to be met for the value to move, and a note sitting in a return does not make the recipient reverse anything. A supplier who has declared a note that turns out not to qualify has to undo the reduction.

options.text: It can reduce its output tax now and must add it back if the dealer never reverses
options.misconception: reads the condition as something that can be satisfied later, with an adjustment if it is not
options.why: The section states a condition, not a provisional entitlement. There is no mechanism for taking the reduction on trust and reversing it afterwards. The reduction is available when the reversal has happened and not before, which is a harder rule than it looks and is the point this marking scheme pays for.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)(ii) read with section 34(2)

items.scenario: A supplier's year-end rebate ticks every box on its own side. The agreement predates the supplies, the rebate is named against the invoices, and the credit note has gone out with tax on it. The dealer who received it has filed his returns for the period and has not reversed any credit; he says the rebate is a commercial matter between them and nothing to do with his returns.

items.stem: How is the integrated tax on imported goods levied and collected?

options.text: Under the Customs Tariff Act, but as a customs duty, so it is part of the cost of the goods
options.misconception: treats the collecting machinery as changing the character of the levy
options.why: Collecting a tax through the customs machinery does not turn it into a customs duty. It remains integrated tax, levied in addition to the customs duties, and that is what makes it creditable when a basic customs duty is not. The distinction decides real money on every bill of entry.

options.text: With the monthly return, the customs authorities collecting only the basic customs duty
options.misconception: stops at the charging provision and never reaches the proviso that moves the machinery
options.why: The charge and the machinery are two different questions, and this answer gets the charge right and never asks the second question. The proviso exists precisely so that one authority at one moment collects everything an import bears. Paying integrated tax on imports through a return would mean goods leaving the port before the tax on them was even computed.

options.text: On reverse charge by the importer, an overseas seller having no presence here
options.misconception: carries the treatment of imported SERVICES across to imported goods
options.why: Reverse charge is how imported services are taxed, because there is no port and nothing to intercept. Goods do cross a physical frontier and the customs machinery is already standing there, so the law uses it. Mixing the two is a common slip and it produces the wrong return, the wrong document and the wrong date.

options.text: At the port, under the Customs Tariff Act, at the moment customs duties fall due
options.why: The consultant has the first step right and the second wrong. Bringing goods into India is treated as a supply in the course of inter-State trade, so the charge is an integrated tax charge. But the proviso to section 5(1) takes the collection of it out of the ordinary machinery and puts it under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act. So it is levied and collected at the point when customs duties are levied under the Customs Act, on a value that Act determines, and it is paid at the port rather than through the monthly return.
keywords: treated as a supply in the course of inter-State trade
the proviso to section 5(1) takes the collection of it out of the ordinary machinery
puts it under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act

citation.ref: Section 7(2) and the proviso to section 5(1), read with section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

items.scenario: An importer in Pune is told by a consultant that because an import is an inter-State supply, the integrated tax on it should be paid with the monthly return like any other inter-State liability, and that customs has nothing to do with it. The company's own accountant thinks the tax is paid at the port. They ask which of them is right and under which provision.

items.stem: What value does the integrated tax go on?

options.text: ₹10,00,000, the assessable value being the value of the goods
options.misconception: uses the customs valuation figure for a levy that has its own valuation rule sitting on top of it
options.why: Section 14 answers what the goods are worth; section 3(8) answers what the integrated tax goes on, and the second builds on the first. The design is deliberate — the tax is meant to reach the landed cost of the article, duties included, so that an imported article and a domestic one bear a comparable charge. Stopping at ₹10,00,000 undercharges by the tax on the duties.

options.text: ₹11,00,000, the surcharge not entering the base because it is not a duty of customs
options.misconception: reads the second limb of the base as covering duties only, and drops the sums charged in the same manner as a duty
options.why: The limb is written wider than "duty" on purpose. Whatever some other law charges on the article, if it is added on top of the customs duty and gathered the same way, it goes into the base — and the social welfare surcharge is exactly that. Leaving it out costs ₹10,000 of base and ₹1,800 of tax on this consignment alone.

The accountant is a step short. The value for this purpose is fixed by section 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act and it is not the assessable value on its own — it is that value plus the duty of customs chargeable under section 12 and any other sum charged on the goods in the same manner as a customs duty. Ten per cent of ₹10,00,000 gives a basic customs duty of ₹1,00,000; the social welfare surcharge is 10 per cent of that duty, so ₹10,000. Adding the two to the assessable value gives an integrated tax base of ₹11,10,000.
keywords: fixed by section 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act
gives a basic customs duty of ₹1,00,000

options.text: ₹13,09,800, everything paid at the port going into the base
options.misconception: folds the integrated tax back into its own base
options.why: The base excludes the integrated tax itself and the compensation cess; nothing is taxed on itself. Circularity of that kind is why the sub-section names what goes in rather than saying "everything payable". Work the base out first, apply the rate to it once, and stop.

citation.ref: Section 3(8), read with the social welfare surcharge levied by section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018

items.scenario: A Maharashtra trader imports a consignment whose assessable value under section 14 of the Customs Act is ₹10,00,000. Basic customs duty on it is 10 per cent and the social welfare surcharge applies. The integrated tax rate on the goods is 18 per cent. The trader's accountant proposes to work the integrated tax out on ₹10,00,000.

items.stem: What is paid at the port in all?

options.text: ₹2,99,800, the surcharge being part of the integrated tax rather than an amount of its own
options.misconception: absorbs the surcharge into the tax it helped to compute
options.why: The surcharge does two separate jobs and only one of them is being remembered here. It enters the base on which the integrated tax is worked out, and it is also payable in its own right. Netting it away after using it once produces a challan ₹10,000 light.

options.text: ₹2,80,000, the integrated tax running on the assessable value
options.misconception: computes the tax on ₹10,00,000 and adds the duties afterwards
options.why: Eighteen per cent of ₹10,00,000 is ₹1,80,000, and adding the duties to that gives ₹2,90,000, not ₹2,80,000 — but the arithmetic hardly matters once the base is wrong. The base is the assessable value plus the duties, and the rate goes on the total, which is the whole teaching of section 3(8).

Eighteen per cent of ₹11,10,000 is an integrated tax of ₹1,99,800, and the clerk's second surcharge does not exist — the social welfare surcharge on integrated tax has been exempted, so it is charged on the basic customs duty and nowhere else. The three amounts are therefore ₹1,00,000 of basic customs duty, ₹10,000 of surcharge and ₹1,99,800 of integrated tax, which come to ₹3,09,800 in all at the port.
keywords: which come to ₹3,09,800 in all at the port

options.text: ₹3,29,780, the surcharge running on the integrated tax as well
options.misconception: applies the surcharge to every levy at the port instead of to the basic customs duty alone
options.why: The surcharge is capped at 10 per cent of the basic customs duty collected on the goods, and a separate exemption takes the integrated tax and the compensation cess out of its reach altogether. Charging it twice is the commonest arithmetic slip on this computation because the words "in addition to any other duties" invite it.

citation.ref: Section 3(7) read with Notification No. 13/2018-Customs dated 2 February 2018

items.scenario: The same consignment is now at the counter. The assessable value is ₹10,00,000, basic customs duty is ₹1,00,000, the social welfare surcharge is ₹10,000 and the integrated tax rate is 18 per cent on the base of ₹11,10,000. A clerk asks whether the surcharge has to be worked out a second time on the integrated tax before the challan is made.

items.stem: How much of it is creditable, and on what document?

options.text: ₹3,09,800, everything paid to the Government at the port
options.misconception: treats payment to the Government on a business input as the test for credit, instead of whether the amount is input tax
options.why: Credit is not a refund of everything a business pays the State. It runs only on taxes the definition of input tax names, and the customs duties are deliberately outside it — they are protective levies, not a tax on value added, and letting them through would undo their purpose. They go into the cost of the goods and are recovered, if at all, through the price.

options.text: ₹1,99,800 only, on the bill of entry
options.why: Only the integrated tax is input tax. Section 2(62) of the CGST Act defines input tax by naming the taxes it covers, and the integrated tax charged on the import of goods is one of them; the credit is then taken under section 16 on its ordinary conditions, and the document that carries it is the bill of entry rather than an invoice. The basic customs duty and the surcharge are outside that definition, so they are never creditable to anybody and simply form part of what the goods cost.
keywords: Section 2(62) of the CGST Act defines input tax
the document that carries it is the bill of entry
so they are never creditable to anybody

options.text: ₹2,09,800, the surcharge following the integrated tax it was computed alongside
options.misconception: lets the surcharge inherit the character of the tax it sits next to on the same document
options.why: Appearing on the same bill of entry decides nothing. The surcharge is a levy in the customs family, charged as an addition to a customs duty, and it is not among the taxes the definition of input tax lists. Its role in the integrated tax computation is to swell the base, which is the opposite of being creditable.

options.text: ₹1,99,800, but on the supplier's invoice, the bill of entry being only a customs document
options.misconception: looks for an invoice because that is the document credit usually rides on
options.why: The overseas seller's invoice is not a tax document under this Act and no Indian tax appears on it. The bill of entry is the prescribed document for credit of integrated tax paid on imported goods, which is why it must carry the importer's registration number. Filing the wrong document is how credit that was properly earned is lost.

citation.ref: Section 2(62) and section 16(2) read with rule 36(1)(d) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered trader has paid ₹1,00,000 of basic customs duty, ₹10,000 of social welfare surcharge and ₹1,99,800 of integrated tax on an import, and the goods are being used for its taxable business. Its accountant proposes to take the whole ₹3,09,800 into the credit ledger, on the footing that every one of the three was paid to the Government on a business input.

items.stem: What does section 60 let it do instead, and what does it have to give?

options.text: Ask for provisional payment, and no bond is needed once the officer has fixed a rate
options.misconception: reads the officer's order as replacing the security rather than as the thing the security backs
options.why: The order and the bond do different jobs. The order says what to pay meanwhile; the bond is the promise to make up the shortfall when the final figure arrives, and the security is what makes the promise worth having. Without them the department would be funding the difference for the whole period at no risk to the person who asked for the facility.

options.text: Nothing; the advice is right, and paying at the higher rate is the only safe course
options.misconception: treats over-payment as a costless precaution, when the section exists precisely to spare a business that cash
options.why: Paying at the higher rate ties up money for as long as the question takes and recovers it, if at all, through a refund claim with its own conditions and its own unjust-enrichment test. Section 60 gives a cheaper road — a formal permission to pay on a stated basis, so that the difference is settled once at the end rather than fought over as a refund.

options.text: Ask in writing for provisional payment; the officer answers within ninety days and takes a bond with security
options.why: A taxable person who cannot determine the value of a supply or the rate of tax on it may apply to the proper officer in writing, with his reasons and the papers behind them, for permission to pay tax provisionally. The officer may call for more, and must then pass his order within ninety days of receiving the request, fixing the rate or the value on which tax is to be paid meanwhile. The permission is conditional — the person executes a bond binding himself to pay the difference between what he pays provisionally and what is finally assessed, with such surety or security as the officer thinks fit.
keywords: may apply to the proper officer in writing, with his reasons
must then pass his order within ninety days of receiving the request
the person executes a bond binding himself to pay the difference

options.text: Ask orally at the range office, a written application being needed only where value rather than rate is in doubt
options.misconception: splits the two grounds and attaches the formality to only one of them
options.why: Both grounds — an unascertainable value and an unascertainable rate — go the same way, and the application is a written one in the prescribed form with the reasons stated. A telephone call leaves nothing for the officer to pass an order on and nothing for the person to rely on afterwards, which is the point of writing it down.

citation.ref: Section 60(1) and 60(2) read with rule 98 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A speciality chemicals maker cannot settle whether a new formulation falls in an entry taxed at one rate or in a neighbouring entry taxed at another, and the two rates are far apart. It does not want to under-pay and it does not want to over-pay for a year while the question is argued. It telephones the range office and is told to keep paying at the higher rate meanwhile.

items.stem: By when should the final order have come, and who may extend that?

options.text: By 1 December 2026; the Joint or Additional Commissioner may add six months and the Commissioner up to four years
options.why: The final assessment order runs on a clock of six months from the date the provisional assessment order was communicated, which here puts it at 1 December 2026. The clock can be stopped only by somebody senior and only with reasons recorded in writing — the Joint Commissioner or Additional Commissioner may extend it by a further period not exceeding six months, and beyond that the Commissioner may extend it by such period as he thinks fit, not exceeding four years. Nobody did either here, so February 2027 is late.
keywords: runs on a clock of six months from the date the provisional assessment order was communicated
which here puts it at 1 December 2026

options.text: There is no outer date, since the provisional payment continues until the dispute about the rate is settled
options.misconception: ties the finalisation to the resolution of the underlying doubt rather than to a clock
options.why: The section does not wait for certainty. It gives the officer six months from communication to finalise and lets seniors extend that within stated limits, whatever state the underlying question is in. A facility with no end date would leave a bond outstanding and a liability unquantified for years, which is what the four-year ceiling exists to prevent.

options.text: By 1 June 2027, a year being allowed for finalisation
options.misconception: rounds the period up to the familiar one-year figure instead of reading the six months the section gives
options.why: Six months is the base period and the extra six the Joint or Additional Commissioner can give is a separate act requiring recorded reasons, not an automatic second half. Treating the two as one year available by right removes the check the section builds in, which is that somebody senior has to look at the file and say why it is taking so long.

options.text: By 1 December 2026, and only the Commissioner may extend it, by six months
options.misconception: merges the two extending authorities into one and gives it the smaller of the two powers
options.why: There are two extensions and they are differently sized on purpose. The Joint or Additional Commissioner has the short one, six months. The Commissioner has the long one, as much as he thinks fit up to four years, for the case that is genuinely stuck behind litigation. Collapsing them loses the four-year outer limit, which is the figure most likely to be asked for.

citation.ref: Section 60(3)

items.scenario: A trader is allowed to pay provisionally and the order granting it is communicated to him on 1 June 2026. Nothing then happens for a long while. In February 2027 a new officer picks up the file, sees that no final assessment order has been passed, and asks whether he is out of time and who could have kept the file alive.

items.stem: How does interest run in each direction?

options.text: It pays no interest at all, because it paid the shortfall before the order was made
options.misconception: reads paying early as curing the delay, when the delay is measured from the original due date
options.why: The section says in terms that interest is payable whether the amount is paid before or after the final assessment order. The taxpayer had the use of the money from the original due date, and interest is the price of that use. Early payment is worth something — it stops the clock sooner — but it does not stop it having started.

options.text: Interest each way runs from the date of the final assessment order
options.misconception: takes the order as the event that creates both the liability and the refund, so both clocks start there
options.why: The two clocks start in different places and neither of them is the order. The tax was always due on its ordinary date and the provisional arrangement only postponed knowing how much; so interest on the shortfall reaches back to that ordinary date. The refund side starts from the application, because until somebody asks there is nothing for the department to be late about.

options.text: It pays interest from the day after the tax was originally due, early payment notwithstanding; it receives interest only for delay beyond sixty days from its refund application
options.why: On the paying side the interest runs at the section 50(1) rate from the day after the date the tax was originally due to be paid until the date it is actually paid, and it makes no difference whether the payment comes before or after the final order — paying early shortens the period but does not move its starting point. On the receiving side the taxpayer gets interest under section 56, and only for a period beyond sixty days from the date of the refund application, with the refund itself subject to section 54 and to unjust enrichment.
keywords: from the day after the date the tax was originally due to be paid
the taxpayer gets interest under section 56
only for a period beyond sixty days from the date of the refund application

options.text: It receives interest from the date of the refund application, with no waiting period
options.misconception: forgets the sixty-day window the department is given to process a refund before interest bites
options.why: Interest on a refund is compensation for delay, and a refund is not delayed on the day it is asked for. The law allows sixty days from the application, and only time beyond that carries interest. Claiming from day one overstates the entitlement and misses the figure the mark is for.

citation.ref: Section 60(4) and 60(5)

items.scenario: A final assessment order settles a taxpayer's position on both sides. For some months the finally assessed tax is higher than what was paid provisionally and the difference is due; for other months it is lower and money has to come back. The taxpayer paid the shortfall for the first set of months a fortnight before the final order was even signed, and filed its refund application for the second set on the day the order arrived.

items.stem: Which of them may take the credit, and on what test?

options.text: All three, because every one of the nine cars is bought for business
options.misconception: applies the general test of business use to a clause that overrides it
options.why: Business use is the ordinary condition for credit, and this clause exists to take certain things out of it however plainly they are used for business. Otherwise the block would never apply to anybody, since no business buys a car for fun. The three exceptions are the only way back in, and each of them describes what the vehicle is used FOR, not who bought it.

options.text: Only the dealership, a driving school's cars being used to teach rather than to supply anything
options.misconception: reads the exceptions as being about supplies of the vehicle itself and drops the training limb
options.why: Training on driving such motor vehicles is one of the three exceptions in its own right, and it is there because a driving school's car is its plant. The school does make a supply — of training — and the vehicle is the thing it is made with. Dropping this limb is the commonest way of losing half a mark on this clause.

options.text: None, because the exceptions apply only where the vehicle carries more than thirteen persons
options.misconception: confuses the seat test, which decides whether a vehicle is inside the block, with the exceptions, which decide when the block lifts
options.why: The two tests do different work. Seats decide whether the vehicle is an ineligible one at all — above thirteen it never was, so no exception is needed. The three exceptions are what rescue a vehicle that IS inside the seat limit. Merging them leaves a small car with no route to credit even when it is being sold or taught in.

options.text: The driving school and the dealership; the manufacturer may not
options.why: The block bites on motor vehicles for carrying persons with an approved seating capacity of not more than thirteen persons, the driver counted in, and it lifts in three named situations — a further supply of such motor vehicles, a taxable supply of transportation of passengers, and imparting training on driving them. A dealership's forecourt cars are held for a further supply of such vehicles and a driving school's cars are used for training, so both are outside the block. The manufacturer's cars are used for none of the three, so their credit is blocked however commercial the travel is.
keywords: an approved seating capacity of not more than thirteen persons
a taxable supply of transportation of passengers
a further supply of such motor vehicles

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

items.scenario: A driving school buys three cars to teach learners in, a dealership buys four cars to put on its forecourt, and a manufacturer buys two cars that its area managers use to visit customers. All nine are five-seaters. Each of the three businesses asks the same question about the tax on its purchase.

items.stem: On which of the four is the credit available?

options.text: All four, the chairman's car being used for the business of a transport operator
options.misconception: lets the buyer's line of business decide the question instead of the use the particular vehicle is put to
options.why: The exceptions look at what the vehicle does, not at what its owner does for a living. A tour operator's own staff car is used no differently from a manufacturer's, and it is blocked for the same reason. If the owner's trade decided it, every vehicle a transport company owned would be creditable, which is not what the clause says.

options.text: Only the seven-seater, the other three all being motor vehicles the clause blocks
options.misconception: treats every vehicle as caught by the clause unless an exception rescues it, forgetting that two of these were never inside it
options.why: Two separate gates come before the exceptions. A vehicle that carries goods is not a vehicle for the transportation of persons and the clause does not describe it. A vehicle above the seat limit is not an ineligible motor vehicle either. Only after those two questions are answered does one ask whether an exception applies, and by then the bus and the truck have already left the room.

options.text: The seven-seater and the bus only, a truck being a motor vehicle like any other
options.misconception: reads the clause as covering motor vehicles generally rather than motor vehicles for carrying persons
options.why: The words that matter are "for transportation of persons". A goods vehicle — a truck, a tipper, a dumper — is not within them, so its credit turns on nothing more than ordinary business use. Reading the clause as being about vehicles in general would block credit on the fleet of every haulier in the country.

options.text: All except the five-seater
options.why: Take them one at a time. The seven-seater is inside the seat limit but is used to carry passengers for hire, so credit is available on it under the transportation exception. The five-seater is inside the seat limit and is used for none of the three exceptions, so its credit is blocked. The twenty-six-seater bus is above thirteen seats, so it is not an ineligible motor vehicle at all and no exception is needed for it. The truck carries goods rather than persons, which puts it outside the clause altogether, and credit is available on it too.
keywords: so credit is available on it under the transportation exception
is used for none of the three exceptions, so its credit is blocked
The twenty-six-seater bus is above thirteen seats
The truck carries goods rather than persons

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a) applied to a mixed fleet

items.scenario: A tour operator in Mysuru bought four vehicles in one year — a seven-seater it hires out with a driver to customers, a five-seater that carries its chairman between his house and the office, a twenty-six-seater bus that brings its own staff to the depot each morning, and a truck that moves customers' luggage between hotels. It has the tax invoice for each.

items.stem: On which of the three is the credit allowed?

options.text: None, the exceptions in this clause applying only to somebody in the catering or insurance business
options.misconception: remembers the same-category door and forgets that a second one exists
options.why: There are two doors. Supplying the same category onward — a caterer buying catering, an insurer buying insurance — is one. Being obliged by law to provide the thing to employees is the other, and it is the one that saves the canteen here. Answering with only the first loses the case the facts were built around.

options.text: All three, since every one of them is a cost of employing people
options.misconception: treats staff welfare spending as a single class and assumes business purpose settles it
options.why: Being a genuine cost of employment is what makes these items deductible for income tax; it has nothing to do with this clause. The clause names them and blocks them, and it opens only for a supply of the same category onward or for a statutory obligation. Everything else, however reasonable, stays blocked.

options.text: The canteen and the health insurance, both being for the welfare of workers
options.misconception: extends the statutory-obligation door to anything that looks like the thing the statute requires
options.why: The door opens for what the law actually obliges the employer to provide, and it opens no wider. A policy the employer chose to buy is not something a law for the time being in force required of it, and the resemblance to a compulsory benefit does not help. The question to ask of each item is which enactment would be broken if it stopped.

options.text: The canteen only
options.why: Food and beverages, outdoor catering and health insurance are blocked unless one of two doors opens. The first is that the same category is used to make an outward taxable supply of that category, which is not the case anywhere here. The second is that the employer is obliged to provide it to its employees under a law for the time being in force. The canteen is run under exactly such a statutory obligation, so its credit is allowed. The outdoor catering for the family day is a kindness and not an obligation, and the health insurance is bought with no law requiring it, so both are blocked.
keywords: The canteen is run under exactly such a statutory obligation
The outdoor catering for the family day is a kindness and not an obligation
the health insurance is bought with no law requiring it

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(b) with its provisos

items.scenario: A factory with 400 workers runs a canteen on the premises because the labour law that applies to it requires an employer of that size to provide one. In the same year it pays a caterer to feed everybody at its annual family day, and it buys a medical policy for its shop-floor staff which no law obliges it to buy. All three suppliers have charged tax.

items.stem: What must the press do, and inside what time?

options.text: Return the goods to the supplier and claim drawback instead, which is the same money by a shorter road
options.misconception: reaches for drawback, not noticing that claiming it disqualifies the section 26A claim outright
options.why: One of the conditions of this refund is that the importer does not claim drawback under any other provision of the Act. The two are alternatives, not a choice of paperwork for one entitlement, and taking drawback shuts this door. Section 26A also requires the goods to be identified to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner as the very goods imported.

options.text: Export or destroy within six months of clearance, the same six months that govern the application
options.misconception: collapses the two clocks in section 26A into one
options.why: There are two separate periods and they measure different things. Thirty days from the clearance order is the time to dispose of the goods, extendable up to three months. Six months from the relevant date is the time to file the refund application, and the relevant date is fixed by which disposal route was taken. Using six months for both loses the tighter of the two.

options.text: Export it, relinquish title to it, or destroy it before the proper officer, all within thirty days of the clearance order and extendable by three months
options.why: Three routes are open and the importer picks one — export the goods, relinquish his title and abandon them to customs, or destroy them or render them commercially valueless in the presence of the proper officer. Whichever he picks must be done within thirty days from the date of the clearance order under section 47, and on sufficient cause the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may extend that period by up to three months. Scrapping the line in the yard with nobody watching satisfies none of the three, because the officer's presence is part of the condition.
keywords: must be done within thirty days from the date of the clearance order under section 47
may extend that period by up to three months
relinquish his title and abandon them to customs

options.text: Simply prove the defect and apply; what happens to the machine afterwards is its own affair
options.misconception: treats the defect as the whole of the entitlement, missing that the goods must leave the Indian market
options.why: A refund of import duty on goods that stay in the country and are used or sold would be a subsidy. The section is built so that the duty comes back only when the goods effectively un-import themselves — they go out again, they are given up to customs, or they are destroyed under supervision. The defect opens the door; disposing of the goods properly is what walks through it.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1)(b), (c) and (d) with the proviso

items.scenario: A printing press cleared an imported press line for home consumption on 3 March 2026 and found on its first production run that it could not hold the tolerances the contract specified. The supplier will not take it back and the press has no use for it. It wants the import duty back and its works manager suggests scrapping the line quietly in the yard and then applying.

items.stem: How long have they, and from when?

options.text: Six months from the relevant date for both, perishability going only to the amount refunded
options.misconception: treats the perishable bar as a discount rather than as a complete exclusion
options.why: It is an exclusion. Goods that are perishable or past their shelf life or recommended storage period are outside the section altogether, and nothing is refunded on them. The reason is that such goods lose their value with time whatever their quality, so a claim about them can never be shown to be about a defect at import.

options.text: Six months from a relevant date that differs with the route — and the fruit pulp gets nothing
options.why: The application goes in within six months from the relevant date, and the relevant date is not one day for everybody. Where the goods are exported it is the day the proper officer orders clearance and loading for export; where title is relinquished it is the day of relinquishment; where the goods are destroyed or rendered commercially valueless it is the day that happens. So the first importer counts from its loading order. The second gets nothing at all, because the refund is not allowed for perishable goods or goods past their shelf life or recommended storage period.
keywords: within six months from the relevant date
the refund is not allowed for perishable goods

options.text: One year from the relevant date, six months being the period for export duty refunds
options.misconception: swaps the period in this section for one remembered from elsewhere
options.why: Six months is the period on both roads — this section and the export duty refund in section 26 each give six months, though from different starting points. The one-year figure in this area belongs to something else entirely, the outer limit for re-importing goods on which export duty was paid.

options.text: Six months from the date the goods were cleared for home consumption, for both
options.misconception: anchors the application clock to the import rather than to the disposal
options.why: The clearance order starts the thirty-day disposal clock, not the refund application clock. The application clock starts when the disposal actually happens, because until then there is nothing to claim about. Counting from clearance would in some cases leave less time to apply than to act.

citation.ref: Section 26A(2) with its Explanation, and section 26A(3)

items.scenario: Two importers are in the same position on different goods. One shipped its defective consignment back out of India and holds the order permitting clearance and loading for export. The other could not sell or move a consignment of imported fruit pulp that turned out to be off specification and let it be destroyed. Both now want to know when their refund clock started and whether it runs at all.

items.stem: Can the export duty come back, and by when must the claim be lodged?

options.text: No, because export duty once paid is never refunded
options.misconception: assumes the finality of an export levy, missing the narrow provision written for rejected goods
options.why: The section exists for exactly this situation — goods that were exported, refused by the buyer and sent home. The policy is that a sale which never held should not leave an export duty behind it. The provision is narrow, and the "otherwise than by way of resale" condition is what keeps it that way.

options.text: Yes, and the claim must be in by 20 November 2026
options.why: Export duty is returned to whoever paid it, or to the person on whose behalf it was paid, on three conditions. The goods must come back to that person otherwise than by way of resale, which is satisfied here because the buyer returned them instead of selling them on. They must be re-imported within one year of the date of exportation, and January to May is inside that. And the claim must be lodged within six months of the day the proper officer passes the clearance order on the re-imported goods, which is 20 May 2026, so the last day is 20 November 2026.
keywords: come back to that person otherwise than by way of resale
re-imported within one year of the date of exportation
so the last day is 20 November 2026

options.text: Yes, but only if the goods are re-imported within six months of export
options.misconception: borrows the six-month claim period and uses it as the re-import window
options.why: Two different periods run here and it is worth keeping them apart. A year is allowed for the goods themselves to come back, which is generous because shipping and disputes take time. Six months is allowed for the paperwork once they have been cleared. Compressing the first into the second would kill claims the section means to allow.

options.text: Yes, and the claim must be in by 15 November 2026, six months from the re-import
options.misconception: counts from the day the goods arrived rather than from the day the officer cleared them
options.why: Arrival and clearance are different events and the section names the second. It is the order for clearance of the re-imported goods that starts the six months, which is sensible — the exporter cannot prove what came back until customs has looked at it. Five days is enough to lose a claim filed on the last day.

citation.ref: Section 26

items.scenario: An exporter shipped a consignment of brass fittings out of India in January 2026 and paid export duty on them. The overseas buyer rejected the lot and sent it straight back to the exporter rather than selling it on. The fittings were re-imported on 15 May 2026 and the proper officer passed his clearance order on them on 20 May 2026.

items.stem: What does the Authority do with the three questions?

options.text: The first two are taken up; the third is turned away, by an order giving reasons, and not before the contractor has been heard
options.why: All three sit inside the list of questions section 97(2) opens to an applicant — classification, whether a notification applies, time and value of a supply, admissibility of credit, liability to pay, whether registration is needed, and whether something the applicant does amounts to a supply. What stops the third is not its subject but its history: an application is not admitted where the question is already pending, or has been decided, in a proceeding in that applicant's own case, and an unanswered notice on the credit is such a proceeding. A rejection is made by a speaking order that gives its reasons, and it cannot be passed until the applicant has had a hearing.
keywords: the list of questions section 97(2) opens to an applicant
a speaking order that gives its reasons

options.text: All three are turned away, a pending notice on one question spoiling the whole application
options.misconception: attaches the bar to the applicant rather than to the question it is written about
options.why: The bar is written against the question, not against the person. Two of the three have no proceeding standing behind them and are taken up in the ordinary way; only the one already before an officer is turned away, and the contractor is not shut out of the forum altogether.

options.text: The credit question is turned away on the papers, an application barred on its face needing no hearing
options.misconception: treats a bar that looks obvious on the record as removing the right to be heard
options.why: The Authority passes its order admitting or rejecting only after hearing the applicant, and a rejection carries reasons of its own. A bar that looks plain to an officer may rest on facts the applicant can answer — that the earlier proceeding covers a different period, or a different question altogether — and the hearing is where that is said.

options.text: All three are taken up, admissibility of credit being one of the listed questions and a notice being no decision
options.misconception: reads the bar as reaching only a question already decided, when pending is a ground on its own
options.why: The words are pending or decided, and they are alternatives. A notice issued and not yet answered is a proceeding under way, which is all the bar asks for. Waiting until the officer has finished would defeat the object, which is to keep one question out of two forums at the same time.

citation.ref: Section 97(2) with the first proviso to section 98(2)

items.scenario: A Hyderabad infrastructure contractor puts three questions to the Authority for Advance Ruling in one application: how a product it makes is classified, whether a particular notification reaches a contract it has signed, and whether it may take credit on a class of inputs. Two months before it applied, its jurisdictional officer had issued it a notice about that very credit, and the notice has not yet been answered. The contractor expects a ruling on all three.

items.stem: What are the periods, the cost, and the effect of a divided bench?

options.text: Thirty days, the fee payable by whichever side appeals, and on a split the Authority's own ruling stands confirmed
options.misconception: treats a deadlocked bench as an affirmance, the way a divided appellate court is often treated elsewhere
options.why: An officer who appeals pays no fee at all; the fee is written for the applicant. And a deadlock is not treated as leaving the ruling standing: where the members differ it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on the question under appeal, so the original ruling does not survive the appeal either.

options.text: Thirty days from receipt, a further thirty on sufficient cause, a fee on the company alone and none on the officer, and on a split no ruling at all
options.why: The Authority itself must pronounce within ninety days of receipt of the application, and the Appellate Authority must decide an appeal within ninety days of its filing, so the clocks bind the forums as well as the parties. The party's own window runs from receipt of the ruling: thirty days as of right, and a further thirty where sufficient cause for the delay is shown, which is what counsel's absence would have to amount to. The fee is ₹10,000 under each Act and it falls on the applicant alone; an officer who appeals pays none. And where the two members differ, the appeal yields no advance ruling on the question, so the parties are left to argue the point in ordinary proceedings instead.
keywords: within ninety days of receipt of the application
thirty days as of right, and a further thirty where sufficient cause
₹10,000 under each Act and it falls on the applicant alone
where the two members differ, the appeal yields no advance ruling

options.text: Sixty days from the ruling in every case, one fee payable by whoever appeals, and a split sending the question back to the Authority
options.misconception: rolls the ordinary period and the extension into one automatic period, and invents a remand that the statute does not provide
options.why: Thirty days is the period. The further thirty has to be asked for and a sufficient cause shown, so a person who assumes sixty may find the sixtieth day is already too late. The fee is the applicant's alone. And a deadlock at the appellate level is the end of the road for that question — nothing goes back down, the Authority having already spoken.

options.text: Ninety days to appeal, matching the period the Authority itself gets, no fee on either side, and a split settled by a casting vote
options.misconception: borrows the forum's own ninety-day clock for the party's appeal and invents a casting vote for a two-member bench
options.why: Ninety days is what the Authority has to pronounce a ruling and what the Appellate Authority has to decide an appeal. The party's window is thirty days from receipt of the ruling. There is a fee and it is the applicant's. And the appellate bench has two members and no casting vote, which is precisely why the statute had to say what happens when they disagree.

citation.ref: Sections 98(6), 100(2) with its proviso, and 101(2) and (3)

items.scenario: A Pune machinery maker applied for an advance ruling on 4 January and had the ruling in its hands on 20 April. It reads against the company. Its counsel is abroad until the middle of June. The jurisdictional officer is unhappy with the same ruling and is asking his own office what an appeal would cost him. The company's finance head also wants to know what it is left with if the appellate bench cannot agree.

items.stem: What is the ruling worth in 2026, and what has the rival got out of it?

options.text: It survives both changes until the Authority formally recalls it, an order being needed before any ruling loses force
options.misconception: assumes a ruling can only be taken away by an order, confusing the fraud route with an ordinary lapse
options.why: An order is needed to declare a ruling void from the beginning where it was got by fraud, suppression or misrepresentation. Nothing of that kind is needed when the ground simply shifts. A ruling given on one notification and one formula does not speak to a different notification and a different formula, and no authority has to say so.

options.text: It runs five years from the day it was pronounced, so it protects the company until 2029 whatever has changed, and the rival may lean on it within the same State
options.misconception: gives a ruling a fixed life and reads a State-wide effect into a permission granted to one person
options.why: The Act fixes no life for a ruling. What it fixes is a condition — the ruling stands while the law, the facts and the circumstances it rested on stand. The State-wide idea comes from the Authority being constituted State by State, which settles where it sits, not whom its answers bind.

options.text: It no longer answers the company's question, and it never reached the rival at all
options.why: No fixed period is written into the Act; the ruling holds while the law, facts or circumstances behind it are unchanged, and here both halves have moved — the notification has been amended and an ingredient is different. Neither change needs an order to take the ruling away; it simply stops answering the question now being asked. As for the rival, the Act draws the circle tightly: a ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and that applicant's own officer. A competitor on the same facts gets nothing binding from it and must seek a ruling of its own, though it may still cite it for whatever persuasion it carries.
keywords: the ruling holds while the law, facts or circumstances behind it are unchanged
binds only the applicant who sought it
A competitor on the same facts gets nothing binding from it

options.text: The change of ingredient ends it but the amendment does not, a ruling speaking to the law as it stands from time to time
options.misconception: treats the ruling as a living statement of current law rather than an answer given on a fixed footing
options.why: The law, the facts and the circumstances are named side by side and none of the three is subordinate. A ruling is an answer to one question on one set of materials at one moment; when the provision behind it is amended the answer is no more reliable than it is when the product itself is changed.

citation.ref: Section 103(1) and 103(2)

items.scenario: A Nashik chemicals company obtained a ruling in 2024 that a preparation it makes falls under a particular heading. Since then the notification the ruling worked from has been amended, and the company has changed one ingredient of the preparation. A rival making much the same thing has been quoting that ruling to its own officer ever since it was published.

items.stem: Which of the exporter's three answers holds?

options.text: Only the second
options.why: A ruling obtained by fraud, by suppression of material facts or by misrepresentation of facts may be declared void from the beginning, and misrepresentation is a limb of its own — the department need not establish any design to deceive, only that a material fact was stated wrongly. So the first answer fails. But the order may be made only after hearing the applicant, so the second is a good answer and the department must put its case and listen to the reply before it does anything. The third is the exporter's worst point: once the ruling is treated as never made, the stretch between the ruling and the order setting it aside is left out of the counting, so the years that passed under the ruling have not run down the department's time.
keywords: by misrepresentation of facts may be declared void from the beginning
the order may be made only after hearing the applicant
the stretch between the ruling and the order setting it aside is left out of the counting

options.text: All three
options.misconception: reads the section as reaching only dishonesty, and reads the exclusion of the intervening period backwards
options.why: Three grounds are named and they are not the same thing: fraud, suppression of material facts, and misrepresentation of facts. A material fact stated wrongly falls in the third whether or not anybody meant harm. And the period between the ruling and the order is left out of the reckoning, which lengthens the department's reach rather than shortening it.

options.text: None, the order being one that may be passed on the record as it stands
options.misconception: treats a strong case on the merits as a reason to skip the hearing
options.why: The hearing does not depend on how weak the other side's case looks. The section allows the order to be made after hearing the applicant, so an order made without one is bad however clear the file seems. The exporter may have an answer — that the fact was immaterial, or that the department has misread it — and the hearing is where it goes.

options.text: Only the first, a misstatement leaving the ruling standing and the remedy being a fresh application on the correct facts
options.misconception: treats a wrong fact as something to be tidied up going forward rather than as a ground for undoing what was got by it
options.why: A fresh application would answer the question from now on and leave the benefit of the wrong fact exactly where it fell. That is what the void-from-the-beginning route exists to prevent: it removes the ruling from the start, and the Act then applies to the applicant as though it had never held one.

citation.ref: Section 104(1) with its proviso and Explanation

items.scenario: Two years after a ruling in its favour, a Ludhiana exporter is told by the department that a fact stated in its application was not true and that the department proposes to treat the ruling as never made. The exporter answers with three things: that the wrong fact was a slip and not a lie, that nobody has asked it for an explanation, and that whatever else happens the two years already gone cannot be reopened.

items.stem: How do the two applications stand?

options.text: Neither may proceed, ₹70 lakh being under a floor that admits of no exception
options.misconception: reads the investment floor as absolute, missing both the list it never applied to and the power to go under it
options.why: The floor comes with its exceptions written beside it — units already running, units in an electronics hardware, software or bio-technology park, and units in handicrafts, in agriculture and its allied lines, in information technology and services, in brass hardware and in handmade jewellery. Beyond that list a project may still be allowed in on a lower investment, case by case.

options.text: The running unit may apply to convert; the new project is under the floor and needs the one body that can let it in below
options.why: Only projects with a minimum investment of ₹1 crore in plant and machinery are considered for establishment as an EOU, and ₹70 lakh is under it, so the new promoter cannot walk in on the figure alone. The body that can let a project in below the line is the Board of Approval, which may allow establishment on a lower investment. The floor is written for establishment and is expressly not applied to units already running, so the Tiruppur firm's six years in the domestic tariff area help it rather than hinder it — an existing domestic unit may apply for conversion. What neither of them can assume is the home sales: a unit undertakes to export its entire production of goods and services, apart from the sales at home that the chapter separately permits.
keywords: a minimum investment of ₹1 crore in plant and machinery
the Board of Approval, which may allow establishment on a lower investment
undertakes to export its entire production of goods and services

options.text: The new project may proceed and the running unit may not, a domestic tariff area unit having to be wound up and started afresh
options.misconception: gets both halves the wrong way round and invents a bar on conversion
options.why: The chapter says in terms that existing domestic units may apply for conversion, and the investment floor is the one condition that does not reach a unit already running. It is the new project that the figure catches.

options.text: Both may proceed as they are, the figure being a guideline the Unit Approval Committee applies as it sees fit
options.misconception: turns a condition of establishment into advice, and gives the power to relax it to the wrong body
options.why: It is a condition, not advice, and the power to relax it is not the Committee's. An application for setting up a unit is considered by the Unit Approval Committee or by the Board of Approval as the case may be, but allowing a project in on a smaller investment is the Board's to do.

citation.ref: Chapter 6 — scope of the schemes, investment criteria and approvals

items.scenario: A Tiruppur firm has run a dyeing unit in the domestic tariff area for six years with plant and machinery of ₹70 lakh, and wants to convert it into an Export Oriented Unit. It also intends to go on supplying about a third of its output to garment makers down the road. A second promoter, with no existing unit, wants to set up a brand new EOU in the same line with the same ₹70 lakh of plant.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the machine and on the chemicals?

options.text: Both bear tax and the unit recovers it later, an EOU being a registered person like any other
options.misconception: collapses the scheme into ordinary GST and loses the duty-free import altogether
options.why: The duty-free import is the centre of the scheme and it is not a refund arrangement — nothing is paid on the way in. Only the home purchase carries tax, and even there the claim sits with the seller rather than with the unit.

options.text: The machine is free of duty once the Development Commissioner certifies the consignment, and the chemicals are free once the supplier holds a copy of the letter of permission
options.misconception: replaces the unit's own certification with a certificate per consignment, and treats a letter of permission as somebody else's tax exemption
options.why: Goods for the approved activity may be brought in on the unit's own certification, which is what replaced a certificate for each consignment. And a seller's tax position is not changed by holding the buyer's letter of permission; it is changed by the deemed export route, which the seller claims for itself.

options.text: The machine comes in free of duty on the unit's own certification and tied to export production; the chemicals bear GST, and it is the supplier who is put in funds
options.why: A unit may import, or take from the domestic tariff area, from a bonded warehouse or from an international exhibition held in India, the goods its approved activity needs, capital goods included, without basic customs duty, the additional duty under the Customs Tariff Act, integrated tax or compensation cess — and it may do so on a self-certification basis rather than waiting on an officer's view. The relief is held down by an actual user condition: the goods are the unit's to use for export production and not to pass on. Goods covered by GST bought at home are different. They go out on a tax invoice with GST and compensation cess, and the answer the scheme gives is on the seller's side — such a supply carries deemed export benefits, and the domestic supplier may claim the refund of that tax on the specified conditions.
keywords: it may do so on a self-certification basis
held down by an actual user condition
such a supply carries deemed export benefits

options.text: Both come in free of tax, the unit's exemption covering what it buys at home as much as what it imports
options.misconception: reads the exemption as attaching to the unit rather than to the import of goods that GST does not cover
options.why: What the chapter frees is the import, or the duty-free procurement, of goods outside GST. Goods covered by GST bought from the domestic tariff area leave the seller on a tax invoice with tax on it, and the scheme's answer to that is not exemption but a refund route on the seller's side.

citation.ref: Chapter 6 — entitlements of an EOU and supplies from the domestic tariff area

items.scenario: An Export Oriented Unit at Vapi is bringing in a coating line from Italy and buying its chemicals from a supplier in Gujarat. Its accountant expects both to reach the unit free of tax, and has already told the chemical supplier to raise a bill without GST on it.

items.stem: Where does the unit stand on the two questions?

options.text: Not in breach on the foreign exchange undertaking, and about two months left on the receivable
options.why: The undertaking is that the unit shall be a positive net foreign exchange earner, and the earnings are added up cumulatively in blocks of five years counted from the commencement of production, so a poor second year is answered by the rest of its own block instead of being judged on its own; the block can itself be extended in specified cases, and some sectors carry a higher value addition besides. The receivable is a separate condition — export proceeds are to be realised within nine months — so the seven-month-old bill has time on it, but not much.
keywords: the unit shall be a positive net foreign exchange earner
added up cumulatively in blocks of five years
export proceeds are to be realised within nine months

options.text: In breach on the foreign exchange undertaking but not on the receivable, a unit having to be positive from its first year of production
options.misconception: reads the starting point of the block as the start of a yearly test
options.why: Commencement of production is when the block starts running, not when an annual test begins. Nothing in the chapter asks a unit to be positive in its first year, and the whole point of a block is that the years inside it are added together.

options.text: In breach on neither, the requirement being only that exports beat imports by the time the letter of permission expires, with no limit on realisation
options.misconception: stretches the measuring block into the whole life of the unit and drops the realisation condition altogether
options.why: The measuring period is a block of five years, extendable in specified cases, not the unit's whole existence — the second block is a fresh reckoning and a unit cannot carry a deficit indefinitely. And realisation within the stated period is one of the scheme's conditions, not an afterthought.

options.text: In breach on both, the foreign exchange test being applied year by year and the proceeds being due in six months
options.misconception: reads the foreign exchange test annually and borrows a six-month realisation period from somewhere else
options.why: The test is cumulative over a block of five years from the commencement of production, which is exactly what lets a bad year sit beside good ones. And the period the chapter allows for realising export proceeds is nine months.

citation.ref: Chapter 6 — net foreign exchange earnings and other entitlements

items.scenario: An Export Oriented Unit making surgical instruments has just finished its second year of production. It exported heavily in year one and hardly at all in year two, and the payment for one large year-two shipment has been outstanding for seven months. Its finance head asks whether the unit has already broken something, and by when the money has to be in.

items.stem: What is wrong with the consultant's advice?

options.text: The transfer is right but the exit is wrong, since leaving needs the Board of Approval rather than the Development Commissioner
options.misconception: sends the exit to the body that approves establishment instead of the one that supervises the unit
options.why: The Board of Approval sits at the entrance — establishment, and a lower investment where it allows one. Opting out is with the approval of the Development Commissioner, or of the designated officer of the park scheme the unit belongs to. And the transfer half of the advice is wrong too, because it needs tax paid and intimation given first.

options.text: The exit is right but the transfer is wrong, goods being unable to move between units once one of them has decided to leave
options.misconception: invents a bar on inter-unit transfer and lets the penalty disappear
options.why: Transfers between units are allowed on the stated terms and nothing shuts them off because one unit is winding up. What the consultant has missed sits on the exit side, where an obligation not achieved attracts a penalty as well as the duties.

options.text: Nothing — a move between two units of the same scheme is internal to it, and exit is a matter of paying the duty on the closing stock
options.misconception: treats two separately approved units as one, and reads exit as a purely arithmetical settlement
options.why: Each unit is its own approval with its own undertaking, so a movement between them is a supply: taxed as one, and notified beforehand to both Development Commissioners and to customs. And exit is not arithmetic where an undertaking has been broken, because the failure carries its own consequence on top of the duty.

options.text: Both halves — the move is taxed and has to be notified in advance, and the exit carries more than duty because the undertaking was missed
options.why: A transfer of manufactured goods or capital goods from one such unit to another is allowed on payment of the applicable GST and compensation cess, with prior intimation to the Development Commissioners of the sending and the receiving units and to the customs authorities concerned; the receiving unit then treats what it took as imported goods when it later sells at home. Leaving is with the approval of the Development Commissioner, or of the designated officer where the unit sits in a technology park, and it is paid for — the excise and customs duties applicable on the goods in hand, and integrated, central, State or Union territory tax and compensation cess, under the industrial policy in force. And a unit that has not achieved its obligations is also liable to penalty at the time of exit, so the duty is the price of the goods and the penalty is the price of the broken undertaking.
keywords: with prior intimation to the Development Commissioners of the sending and the receiving units
Leaving is with the approval of the Development Commissioner
also liable to penalty at the time of exit

citation.ref: Chapter 6 — inter-unit transfer and exit from the scheme

items.scenario: An Export Oriented Unit has stopped exporting and wants out of the scheme. Before it goes it wants to move its finished stock and one machine to another such unit nearby. It has not met its foreign exchange undertaking. Its consultant says the goods can move on the unit's own paperwork and that leaving will cost nothing beyond the duty on what is in hand.

items.stem: Is the firm right to leave the ₹6,00,000 outside GST altogether?

options.text: No — a daily wage is payment for a service and the firm must account for tax on it as the recipient
options.misconception: treats the absence of a monthly salary and a payroll as the absence of employment
options.why: The entry looks at the relation, not at the pay cycle or the paperwork. A worker engaged by the firm and paid by it when the day ends is working under it, and a supply that never comes into existence cannot be taxed in anybody's hands.

options.text: Yes, but only because the workers are unregistered; a registered worker would have had to raise a tax invoice
options.misconception: makes registration the reason, when the reason is that there is no supply for anyone to invoice
options.why: Registration settles who pays the tax on a supply, not whether there is one. An employee's work for the employer is kept outside the meaning of supply, so no invoice arises whatever the worker's registration.

options.text: No — only wages under a written contract of employment are outside, and casual labour is a service bought in
options.misconception: adds a documentary condition that the entry does not carry
options.why: Nothing in the entry asks for a contract in writing. The Study Material takes the point the other way, giving casual workers engaged by a building contractor for his own contract, and by a security agency for its client's work, as people working in the course of employment.

options.text: Yes — daily-paid workers engaged by the firm are its employees for this purpose and what they give is outside the tax
options.why: The first entry of Schedule III takes the work an employee does for his employer, given in the course of or in relation to his employment, and puts it outside the charge altogether: neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Being paid at the end of a day rather than at the end of a month changes nothing there, because services given by a casual worker to an employer who pays wages on a daily basis are services given in the course of employment. So the ₹6,00,000 never becomes a supply at all, there is nothing on which the firm could be made to pay as recipient, and the figure does not enter its turnover either.
keywords: neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services
a casual worker to an employer who pays wages on a daily basis
services given in the course of employment

citation.ref: Paragraph 1 of Schedule III, with the Study Material's illustrations on casual workers

items.scenario: A Delhi consultancy firm engages ten casual workers directly through the year and pays each of them at the end of the day's work, ₹6,00,000 in all. There are no written contracts and none of the workers is registered. The firm's auditor says the ₹6,00,000 is payment for services bought in and should have been brought into the firm's GST records.

items.stem: Is either of the two the company's to pay tax on?

options.text: Both are taxable, a court fee being a fee for a service by a government body on which the company must pay under reverse charge
options.misconception: reads a court as another government body and reaches for reverse charge on its fee
options.why: Services by a court or Tribunal are not merely exempt; they are outside the meaning of supply, and nothing outside that meaning can be brought back in through reverse charge. Government services and court services are dealt with in different places for that very reason.

options.text: The sitting fees are taxable but the directors pay, being the suppliers, once their fees pass the registration threshold
options.misconception: applies the ordinary forward-charge rule to a supply the notification has moved to the recipient
options.why: Where a supply is notified for reverse charge the liability moves to the recipient by the notification itself, and the supplier's own registration position does not move it back. The company pays, and the directors' fees do not make them liable for the tax on this supply.

options.text: Both are outside GST, the court because it is a court and the directors because a director holds an office in the company
options.misconception: treats every director as an employee because of the office he holds
options.why: The office is not the test; employment is. A director who is not an employee supplies services to the company, and the notification putting those services on reverse charge exists for exactly that case. A whole-time director whose pay is treated and taxed as salary stands differently.

options.text: The court fees are outside GST; the sitting fees are taxable and the tax on them is the company's
options.why: What a court or Tribunal set up under any law in force does by way of service is listed in Schedule III, so the ₹80,000 attracts no tax in anybody's hands and the accountant is right about that half. The sitting fees are another matter. A non-executive director is not an employee of the company, so what he gives is not covered by the employment entry — he supplies services to it and those services are taxable. The tax on them is payable by the company as the recipient under reverse charge, so the fact that the directors raised no tax on their bills is what one would expect and settles nothing.
keywords: What a court or Tribunal set up under any law in force does
A non-executive director is not an employee of the company
payable by the company as the recipient under reverse charge

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule III, and section 9(3) with the notification on services by a director

items.scenario: A Delhi company paid ₹80,000 of court fees to a District Court in a recovery suit, and ₹4,00,000 of sitting fees to its two non-executive directors, neither of whom is on its payroll. Its accountant has left both out of the GST records because neither the court nor the directors charged any tax on their bills.

items.stem: What should he do about the Goa consignment?

options.text: Turn it down, or come out of the scheme — the Gujarat purchases were never the difficulty and this sale is
options.why: The condition is that the person is not engaged in making inter-State outward supplies of goods, and it is written about what leaves him, not about what reaches him. The bar is on outward supplies alone: buying goods from another State does not disqualify a composition supplier, and there is no restriction at all on his receiving inter-State inward supplies of goods or services. One consignment to Goa is an inter-State outward supply and its size changes nothing — he either declines the order or leaves the scheme and pays tax as an ordinary registered person from that day.
keywords: not engaged in making inter-State outward supplies of goods
The bar is on outward supplies alone
buying goods from another State does not disqualify a composition supplier

options.text: Send it, the ceiling being what matters and ₹40,000 leaving him far inside it
options.misconception: reduces the scheme to a turnover test and loses the conditions that sit beside it
options.why: Turnover is one condition among several. The bar on inter-State outward supplies stands on its own, and a person who breaches it is out of the scheme however modest his turnover.

options.text: Send it and charge integrated tax on that one consignment at the composition rate
options.misconception: imagines a composition rate that can be charged on a sale across a State border
options.why: A composition supplier does not collect tax from anyone — he pays out of his own pocket and issues a bill of supply. There is no inter-State version of the scheme, which is why the condition had to be written rather than a rate provided for it.

options.text: Send it, and stop buying from Gujarat instead, since it is the crossing of a State line that the scheme objects to
options.misconception: reverses the direction the condition points in
options.why: There is no restriction on a composition supplier receiving goods or services from another State, and cutting off his suppliers would cost him his business for nothing. The direction is the whole point: what goes out is what the condition looks at.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(c)

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Nagpur buys most of his stock from wholesalers in Gujarat and sells it across Maharashtra. In March a buyer in Goa asks him to send one consignment worth ₹40,000. His accountant tells him that since goods already cross a State border to reach him every month, one small consignment going the other way cannot matter.

items.stem: What has to happen instead, and from when?

options.text: He pays under the ordinary charge from 9 December, invoices from that day, tells the department within seven days and has thirty for his stock statement
options.why: The option lapses with effect from the day the ceiling is crossed — the day his aggregate turnover in the year exceeds the limit — so 9 December is the date and the year end does not come into it. From that day he is a person paying tax under the ordinary charging provision, and he must issue a tax invoice for every taxable supply he makes rather than a bill of supply. He has to file an intimation of withdrawal within seven days of the event, and he may furnish the statement of his stock of inputs, and of the inputs held in his semi-finished and finished goods on that date, within thirty days from the day the option went.
keywords: The option lapses with effect from the day the ceiling is crossed
his aggregate turnover in the year exceeds the limit
an intimation of withdrawal within seven days

options.text: He pays at the composition rate up to 9 December and at ordinary rates after it, but may go on issuing bills of supply until he files his intimation
options.misconception: ties the change of documents to the paperwork rather than to the event that caused it
