options.why: The documents change with the liability, not with the filing. From the day the option goes he is taxed under the ordinary charge, and every taxable supply he makes from that day needs a tax invoice. The intimation records what has already happened.

options.text: He is treated as a regular taxpayer from 1 December, the change taking effect from the start of the month in which the ceiling went
options.misconception: rounds the event to the beginning of a tax period
options.why: The provision names a day, and the day is the one on which the turnover crosses. Backdating to the first of the month would rewrite supplies that were correctly made under the scheme, and nothing asks for that.

options.text: He must apply to the proper officer, who fixes the date the option ends and may let it run to the year end
options.misconception: hands the officer a discretion the section does not give, and confuses a lapse with a denial
options.why: The lapse happens by itself when the condition fails; there is no application and no permission to wait for. An officer's order belongs to a different case — where the department seeks to deny the option for ineligibility or a contravention — and even there the date is tied to the event.

citation.ref: Section 10(3) read with rule 6 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore crosses the turnover ceiling on 9 December. His accountant plans to go on issuing bills of supply and paying at the composition rate until 31 March, and to start as a regular taxpayer from 1 April.

items.stem: Which account of the rebate and of the unpaid bill is right?

options.text: A percentage of the free-on-board value, issued as a scrip that may be set against anything payable on an import, integrated tax included
options.misconception: widens a credit written for one duty into a credit for everything payable at the port
options.why: The credit is confined to basic customs duty. Integrated tax paid at import comes back through the credit chain instead, and letting the scrip pay it would give the same tax back twice.

options.text: A percentage of the value invoiced to the buyer including freight and insurance, non-transferable, and usable only against the exporter's own imports
options.misconception: uses the delivered value rather than the value at the ship's side, and reads the scrip as personal to the exporter
options.why: The rate is applied on FOB value, which stops at the ship and leaves freight and insurance out. And the scrips are freely transferable — credits may be moved to other importers, which is what gives a scrip a market at all.

options.text: A notified percentage of the free-on-board value, issued as a transferable credit usable only against basic customs duty, and undone if the money never comes in
options.why: The rebate is granted at a notified rate expressed as a percentage of the FOB value of the exported item, with a value cap per unit where one has been fixed, and for some items as a fixed amount per unit instead. It comes as a transferable duty credit, an e-scrip held in an electronic ledger the Central Board keeps, and the credit may be used only to pay basic customs duty on imported goods, though the scrip itself can be passed to another importer. The claim does not wait on the money — the rebate is not dependent on realisation of the proceeds when it is issued — but it is deemed never to have been allowed if the sale proceeds are not received within the time the Foreign Exchange Management Act allows.
keywords: a notified rate expressed as a percentage of the FOB value
a transferable duty credit, an e-scrip held in an electronic ledger
deemed never to have been allowed if the sale proceeds are not received

options.text: A percentage of the free-on-board value, credited in cash to the exporter's bank account, and unaffected by whether the buyer pays
options.misconception: treats the scheme as a cash incentive and drops the realisation condition
options.why: The benefit is a duty credit in an electronic ledger and not money; its whole value lies in imports, the exporter's own or somebody else's. And failure to receive the proceeds within the time the foreign exchange law allows undoes the rebate altogether.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — form of rebate and sale proceeds

items.scenario: An exporter of leather goods has been credited under the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme for a shipment made in April 2026. It wants to know how the figure was arrived at, what it can do with the credit, and where it stands if the overseas buyer never pays.

items.stem: On which of the four does the rebate actually arise?

options.text: The shoes and the mineral, an export duty being exactly the kind of levy the scheme sets out to return
options.misconception: confuses a duty charged on the way out with the embedded burdens the scheme remits
options.why: What the scheme returns is the burden of duties, taxes and levies that stuck to the product while it was made and moved, and that nothing else gives back. An export duty is a charge the State means the exporter to bear, so a product carrying one is excluded rather than favoured.

options.text: The shoes and the supply into the zone, a supply to a zone unit being treated as an export
options.misconception: carries the GST treatment of a zone supply into a policy that names it as ineligible
options.why: A supply to a unit in a zone is zero-rated under the integrated tax law, which is a different question from whether this scheme pays on it. The chapter puts supplies from a domestic tariff area unit to such a unit on the ineligible list by name.

options.text: All four, the scheme being open to every export made from India
options.misconception: reads the scheme as a general export incentive rather than a remission of what stuck to the product
options.why: It gives back the taxes embedded in a product, and a long list of exports is kept out precisely because there is nothing embedded to give back, or because another route already does the work.

options.text: Only the shoes
options.why: The scheme pays on a product the exporter has made, and three separate entries on the ineligible list take out the rest. Goods that were imported and are exported again in the same form, or in substantially the same one, are excluded, which is what the untouched machine parts are. Supplies by a domestic tariff area unit to a special economic zone unit are excluded as well, so a sale into the zone earns nothing here whatever it earns elsewhere. And a product subject to export duty, or to a minimum export price, is out by name. The same list also carries transhipment exports, deemed exports, goods made in a warehouse operated under section 65 of the Customs Act, and exports for which no electronic documentation was generated.
keywords: exported again in the same form
Supplies by a domestic tariff area unit to a special economic zone unit
a product subject to export duty, or to a minimum export price

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — ineligible categories

items.scenario: A Kanpur exporter ships four lots in 2026: shoes it makes itself; a consignment of machine parts it imported last year and has not touched since; a supply to a unit inside a special economic zone; and a mineral on which export duty is payable. It has claimed the rebate on all four.

items.stem: What, if anything, does the scheme add?

options.text: It gives back the integrated tax on the export a second time, which is why it is claimed alongside the refund
options.misconception: reads the scheme as an extra layer over a tax that is already refunded
options.why: A tax refunded under another provision is outside the scheme by its own words. Integrated tax on an export comes back through the zero-rating route, and nothing here pays it again.

options.text: It gives back every tax the exporter pays, income tax on the export profit included
options.misconception: reads a remission of embedded indirect levies as a general refund of tax
options.why: The scheme is about duties, taxes and levies borne on the product — burdens that travel with the goods. A tax on the exporter's income is not borne on the product, and no part of it is remitted here.

options.text: Nothing, because a product that already carries a drawback claim is outside the scheme
options.misconception: turns a bar on paying the same duty twice into a bar on the exporter
options.why: What is kept out is the particular duty already given back, not the shipment and not the exporter. The remaining embedded levies are exactly what the scheme was built to reach.

options.text: It reaches the levies nothing else gives back, and nothing that has already been given back
options.why: The scheme rests on a plain idea, that taxes should not be exported. It gives back duties, taxes and levies at the Central, State and local level that are borne on the exported product and are not refunded under any other provision of law, and it takes in the prior stage cumulative indirect taxes on the goods and services used in making the product, and the levies on distributing it. The duty on the electricity that ran the looms and the tax on the fuel in the lorry are the kind of thing it is for. What it will not do is pay twice: the rebate is not available for a duty already exempted, remitted or credited, so the drawback and the integrated tax the exporter recovers stay outside the claim.
keywords: are not refunded under any other provision of law
not available for a duty already exempted, remitted or credited

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — objective

items.scenario: A textile exporter already recovers the integrated tax it pays on its exports, and takes a drawback of the customs duty on one imported input. Its consultant says the rebate claim under the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme may as well be dropped, because those two already cover everything the exporter pays.

items.stem: Where does its July 2026 export stand?

options.text: Outside it, a holder of such an authorisation having never been eligible
options.misconception: takes the position as it stood when the scheme began and assumes it has not moved since
options.why: The eligible class was widened twice. Authorisation holders, export oriented units and special economic zone units were let in for a period in 2024 and again from the middle of 2025, and the notifications that extended the scheme name them.

options.text: Outside it, the scheme having lapsed on 31 March 2026 with nothing to replace it
options.misconception: stops at the last extension it happens to have heard of
options.why: A further notification issued on 31 March 2026 carried the scheme on to 30 September 2026. A scheme that lives by extension has to be checked for the next notification before anybody says it has ended.

options.text: Inside it, but only for the part of the exporter's output not covered by the authorisation
options.misconception: splits an exporter's shipments where the notification includes a whole class of exporters
options.why: What was included is the class of exporter, not a fraction of its shipments. Nothing in the extension apportions a unit's exports between authorised and unauthorised production.

options.text: Inside the scheme on both counts
options.why: The scheme has run by a series of extensions rather than by one long life, and the exporter was told the right thing at the wrong moment. Holders of an Advance Authorisation, export oriented units and units in special economic zones were outside it at first; they were brought in for a stretch in 2024 running to 5 February 2025, and then again from 1 June 2025, and that later inclusion has not been withdrawn. As for the scheme itself, a notification of 30 September 2025 carried it to 31 March 2026 and a further one of 31 March 2026 carried it on to 30 September 2026, so an export made in July 2026 is inside the period as well as inside the eligible class.
keywords: brought in for a stretch in 2024 running to 5 February 2025, and then again from 1 June 2025
a further one of 31 March 2026 carried it on to 30 September 2026

citation.ref: DGFT Notification No. 35/2025 dated 30 September 2025 and Notification No. 74/2025-26 dated 31 March 2026, as carried in ICAI's Statutory Update for November 2026

items.scenario: A Ludhiana exporter holds an Advance Authorisation and exports under it in July 2026. It has been told twice, once in 2024 and again early in 2025, that a holder of such an authorisation is outside the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme, and it is no longer sure the scheme is even running.

items.stem: Which of the four supplies are deemed exports?

options.text: Only the supply to the export oriented unit, the two authorisations being customs schemes with no effect under GST
options.misconception: treats the foreign trade schemes as belonging only to customs
options.why: The notification names both authorisations expressly and defines each by reference to the Foreign Trade Policy. That is how a policy scheme is given a consequence under the tax law.

options.text: All four, since every one of them ends in an export
options.misconception: makes the eventual destination of the goods the test instead of the notified category
options.why: A deemed export is not a finding about where goods end up; it is a listed category. Goods sold to a customer that exports are an ordinary supply, and that customer's own export is dealt with on its own terms.

options.text: The first three, and the machine goes out untaxed because capital goods against such an authorisation are zero-rated
options.misconception: reads a deemed export as zero-rated, when the tax is charged first and refunded afterwards
options.why: Deemed exports are not zero rated. Every one of the notified supplies bears tax and cannot go under a bond or a letter of undertaking; the relief comes later, as a refund of the tax that was paid.

options.text: The first three; the last is an ordinary domestic supply
options.why: The notification made under section 147 names four categories and no more: goods supplied by a registered person against an Advance Authorisation; capital goods supplied against an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation; goods supplied to an export oriented unit; and gold supplied by a bank or a specified public sector undertaking against an Advance Authorisation. The pump maker's first three buyers each sit in one of them. The fourth does not, because the list turns on the buyer's authorisation or status and not on what the buyer means to do with the goods — a customer that exports most of its output is still an ordinary recipient, and the supply to it is taxed like any other.
keywords: The notification made under section 147 names four categories and no more
goods supplied by a registered person against an Advance Authorisation
goods supplied to an export oriented unit

citation.ref: Section 147 with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017

items.scenario: A Coimbatore pump maker supplies in 2026 to four buyers: a manufacturer holding an Advance Authorisation; a company holding an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation, to which it sends a machine; an export oriented unit; and an ordinary domestic customer which happens to export most of what it makes.

items.stem: Is the accountant right to treat the two consignments alike?

options.text: No — the zone supply is the deemed export and the supply to the export oriented unit is the zero-rated one
options.misconception: swaps the two treatments over
options.why: It is the supply to the export oriented unit that the notification lists as a deemed export. Zero rating belongs to exports and to supplies to a zone developer or unit for authorised operations, so it is the zone consignment that carries it.

options.text: No — one is a deemed export on which tax must be charged, and only the other may go under the undertaking
options.why: The two look alike and are governed differently. A supply to an export oriented unit is a deemed export: the goods are made in India, they do not leave India and they are paid for in rupees or in convertible foreign exchange, and such a supply is not zero-rated — tax has to be charged and paid on it and a refund of that tax claimed afterwards. A supply to a special economic zone unit for its authorised operations is a zero-rated supply under the integrated tax law, and a zero-rated supply may be made under a letter of undertaking without payment of tax, with the credit still available. So the undertaking covers the second consignment and not the first.
keywords: they do not leave India and they are paid for in rupees or in convertible foreign exchange
such a supply is not zero-rated — tax has to be charged and paid on it
A supply to a special economic zone unit for its authorised operations is a zero-rated supply

options.text: Yes — both are deemed exports, the buyer being a unit set up for export in each case
options.misconception: puts a zone unit into a list of categories it is not on
options.why: The four notified categories name an export oriented unit and do not name a unit in a special economic zone. The zone supply is dealt with by the integrated tax law as a zero-rated supply, which is a stronger relief reached by a different road.

options.text: Yes — both may go under the letter of undertaking, a refund being available on either footing in the end
options.misconception: treats the letter of undertaking as a shortcut wherever a refund would eventually be due
options.why: A letter of undertaking belongs to a zero-rated supply. A deemed export cannot be made under one at all: the tax is charged, paid and then claimed back, so skipping the payment leaves the supply short paid rather than merely early.

citation.ref: Section 147 and section 2(39), with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A Vadodara valve maker sends identical valves in one month to an export oriented unit in Gujarat and to a unit inside a special economic zone, for that unit's authorised operations. Its accountant proposes to treat the two alike and to send both out under the company's letter of undertaking without charging tax.

items.stem: Who can claim the refund on these facts?

options.text: Both, each for its own share, the tax having passed through both hands
options.misconception: divides one refund between two claimants
options.why: There is one payment of tax and one refund of it. The undertakings the rules ask for exist to make sure only one of the two asks, which is why a claim by the supplier depends on the recipient standing back.

options.text: The supplier alone, being the person who bore the tax and paid it to the government
options.misconception: assumes the person who paid the tax over is the only person who may ask for it back
options.why: The rules open the claim to the recipient as well, and on a deemed export it is the recipient that bore the tax in the price. Which of the two may claim turns on whether the recipient has taken the credit, not on who wrote the cheque to the treasury.

options.text: Neither, a credit once taken by the recipient extinguishing any refund of that tax
options.misconception: treats the recipient's credit as killing the refund rather than as the thing it reverses to make its claim
options.why: The credit the recipient takes on a deemed export is what it debits to make its own claim, so taking it is a step on the road to the refund rather than a bar to it. What the credit rules out is the supplier's claim.

options.text: The unit, because the road open to the supplier depends on the unit standing back and it has not
options.why: A refund of the tax paid on a deemed export may be applied for by the supplier or by the recipient, and the rules choose between them by a condition. The supplier may claim only where the recipient has not availed the credit on the supply and gives an undertaking that the supplier may claim it. Here the unit has taken the credit, so that door is shut. The recipient's own claim survives: it debits an amount equal to the refund from its electronic credit ledger and undertakes that it is claiming only on the invoices it has listed. For either of them the relevant date is the date on which the return covering the supply is furnished.
keywords: applied for by the supplier or by the recipient
The supplier may claim only where the recipient has not availed the credit
the date on which the return covering the supply is furnished

citation.ref: Rule 89(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017 with its proviso on deemed exports, and Explanation 2(b) to section 54

items.scenario: A Rajkot supplier charged and paid tax on a consignment of castings sent to an export oriented unit. Both the supplier and the unit now want the refund of that tax. The unit has already taken credit of the tax in its own returns.

items.stem: What is the correct treatment of the sale to the trading house?

options.text: A taxable domestic supply at the concessional rate, with the credit kept, provided the buyer meets what the notification asks of it
options.why: GST has no special provision for an export made through a third party. What it has is a pair of notifications letting a registered supplier bill such a buyer at a concessional rate of 0.1 per cent — half a point of central tax and half of State tax on a supply inside a State, and 0.1 per cent of integrated tax across one — with the supplier keeping its credit and claiming refund of what is left unused. It is neither a deemed export nor an export in the manufacturer's hands; the trading house makes the export. The concessional rate comes with conditions the buyer must meet: the supply goes on a tax invoice, the buyer must be registered with an Export Promotion Council, must put the supplier's registration number and invoice number in its shipping bill, and must export the goods within ninety days of that invoice. And there is no such form under GST — the transaction between the two is a supply and is taxed.
keywords: a concessional rate of 0.1 per cent
The concessional rate comes with conditions the buyer must meet
must export the goods within ninety days of that invoice

options.text: A deemed export, on which tax is charged at the full rate and refunded afterwards
options.misconception: files a sale to a trading house among the notified deemed export categories
options.why: The four notified categories are supplies against an Advance Authorisation, capital goods against an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation, supplies to an export oriented unit, and gold against an Advance Authorisation. A trading house that will export is none of them, and what it brings its seller is a low rate rather than a refund of a full one.

options.text: A supply on which no tax is payable, the buyer giving a declaration in place of the old form
options.misconception: carries a superseded procedure into GST
options.why: There is no provision under GST for buying without tax on a form of that kind, and the point has been clarified in terms. The transaction between a manufacturer and such a buyer is a supply, and the concession is a low rate rather than a nil one.

options.text: An export in the manufacturer's own hands, which may go under its letter of undertaking without tax
options.misconception: treats the buyer's eventual export as the seller's export
options.why: The person who exports is the one who takes the goods out of India under a shipping bill in its own name. The manufacturer has made a domestic sale, and its buyer's intention does not make that sale zero-rated.

citation.ref: Notification Nos. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and 41/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) dated 23 October 2017

items.scenario: An Ahmedabad manufacturer is asked by a trading house to bill it at the concessional rate for goods the trading house will itself ship abroad. The manufacturer's accountant thinks this must be a deemed export, and that the goods can go out without tax on the kind of form that was used before GST.

items.stem: Is anything due on that movement?

options.text: No — nothing was received for the goods, and a supply needs consideration
options.misconception: applies the general definition and misses the list of exceptions written beside it
options.why: Consideration is what the general definition asks for. Schedule I is the list of things that are supplies without it, and a movement between two registrations of one person is on that list.

options.text: Yes — it is a supply and needs a tax invoice, even though nothing was received for it
options.why: Two registrations held by the same person in two States are distinct persons for this Act, so what looks like an internal movement is a supply between two people. Schedule I brings a supply between distinct persons made in the course or furtherance of business inside the charge even without consideration, and a stock transfer for onward sale is plainly in the course of business. So integrated tax is payable on the movement, a tax invoice has to be raised rather than a challan alone, and the Karnataka registration takes credit of that tax.
keywords: Two registrations held by the same person in two States are distinct persons
a supply between distinct persons made in the course or furtherance of business
inside the charge even without consideration

options.text: Yes, but only when the branch sells the goods, the tax being due on the eventual selling price
options.misconception: defers the charge to the outward sale and loses the transfer altogether
options.why: There are two supplies here and not one. The transfer is taxed when it happens, on the value the valuation rules give a supply between distinct persons, and the branch's later sale is taxed separately with credit for the first.

options.text: No — the two units are one legal person, and a person cannot supply anything to himself
options.misconception: reasons from company law where the tax law has made a rule of its own
options.why: The Act makes the two establishments distinct persons for its own purposes, precisely so that a movement across a State line carries tax and the credit lands where the goods will be sold. Company law does not settle it.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule I read with section 25(4)

items.scenario: A company registered in Maharashtra sends finished goods worth ₹8,00,000 from its Pune works to its own branch in Karnataka, which holds a registration of its own, for the branch to sell. Nothing is charged and no money moves. The accountant has raised a delivery challan and left it there.

items.stem: Whose gifts, if anyone's, are caught?

options.text: Only the retiring employee's
options.why: An employer and its employee are related persons, so a gift from one to the other would be a supply although nothing came back for it. The proviso is what saves most of this: a gift that stops short of fifty thousand rupees in value in a financial year is not treated as a supply. The line is drawn employee by employee and year by year, so a ₹35,000 watch on its own leaves every one of the forty below it. The employee who was also given ₹22,000 in the same year is taken past ₹50,000, and the shelter the proviso gives runs out in his case; the other thirty-nine are untouched.
keywords: An employer and its employee are related persons
a gift that stops short of fifty thousand rupees in value in a financial year

options.text: Only the ₹22,000 gift is caught, a second gift in the same year being a supply whatever its size
options.misconception: treats the first gift as having spent the shelter entirely, when the test is the year's total for that employee
options.why: What is measured is the value of the gifts to that employee in the financial year taken together, not how many there were. Had the second gift been ₹10,000 the year's total would still have been under the line and nothing would have been caught at all.

options.text: Nobody's, a gift not being a supply where nothing is received for it
options.misconception: forgets that the employer and employee relation puts gifts inside Schedule I to begin with
options.why: Related persons are covered by Schedule I whether or not anything is paid, and an employer and its employee are related. The reason most staff gifts escape is the proviso and its figure, not the absence of a price.

options.text: All forty are caught, the company having given away far more than fifty thousand rupees in the year
options.misconception: adds the gifts up across the workforce instead of reading the line one employee at a time
options.why: The proviso is written about gifts by an employer to an employee, so it is applied employee by employee. Forty gifts of ₹35,000 are forty gifts below the line, and what the company spent in total is beside the point.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule I and its proviso

items.scenario: A company gives each of its forty employees a watch costing ₹35,000 at Diwali. In February, in the same financial year, it gives one of those forty a further gift costing ₹22,000 on his retirement. The accountant has kept all of it out of the GST records on the footing that gifts to staff are not supplies.

items.stem: Does anything arise on that advice?

options.text: No — no consideration passed, so nothing has been supplied
options.misconception: applies the general definition to a case the Schedule has deliberately taken out of it
options.why: Schedule I lists the transactions that are supplies without consideration, and this is the fourth of them. It was put there because a group could otherwise move services across the border free of tax simply by not charging for them.

options.text: Yes — it is a supply in the subsidiary's hands and the tax on it is the subsidiary's to pay
options.why: The fourth paragraph of Schedule I reaches the import of services from a related person abroad: where a person takes services from someone related to it, or from an establishment of its own outside India, in the course or furtherance of its business, that is a supply even though nothing is paid. A holding company and its subsidiary are related, and advice used in running the subsidiary's business is plainly for the business, so the absence of an invoice and of a payment does not take it out. Tax on an imported service is payable by the recipient in India under reverse charge, and the value is arrived at under the valuation rules rather than from a price nobody set.
keywords: the import of services from a related person abroad
that is a supply even though nothing is paid
payable by the recipient in India under reverse charge

options.text: Yes, but the holding company must register in India and pay, being the supplier
options.misconception: puts the liability on a supplier who is outside the country
options.why: Tax on the import of a service is payable by the recipient in India under reverse charge. That is the whole reason the charge is written that way — a foreign supplier is outside the reach of the Act and the Indian recipient is not.

options.text: Yes, but only if the subsidiary pays for the advice later, the charge arising when the money moves
options.misconception: waits for a payment that the entry says is not needed
options.why: The entry catches the import whether or not anything is paid, which is what marks it off from an ordinary import of services. Waiting for a payment that may never come would leave the supply untaxed for good.

citation.ref: Paragraph 4 of Schedule I read with section 5(3) of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary takes management advice from its holding company in Singapore through the year and is charged nothing for it. It uses the advice in running its own business. Seeing no invoice and no payment, its accountant has recorded nothing.

items.stem: What must the officer establish, and whose approval does he need?

options.text: He must obtain the Commissioner's approval, after which the dealer nominates the accountant, since the dealer will be paying
options.misconception: gives both the choice of accountant and the cost to the person being audited
options.why: The accountant is nominated by the Commissioner and named in the direction. The expenses, the accountant's remuneration included, are determined and paid by the Commissioner as well, so neither the choice nor the cost falls on the person audited.

options.text: He must show that the dealer's own auditor has refused to certify the accounts
options.misconception: makes the special audit a fallback for a statutory audit that has failed
options.why: Nothing of the kind is asked for. The section works off the officer's own opinion about value or credit, and it applies whether or not the accounts have been audited by anybody else.

options.text: He must weigh the difficulty of the case against what the revenue stands to lose, form his opinion on value or credit, and get the Commissioner's approval first
options.why: The power belongs to an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner and may be used at any stage of scrutiny, inquiry, investigation or other proceedings. What he does first is weigh the nature and complexity of the case against what the revenue stands to lose, and on that footing form the opinion that value has not been declared correctly, or that the credit availed sits outside the normal limits for the trade. Only then, and only with the prior approval of the Commissioner, may he direct the person to get its records examined and audited by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant whom the Commissioner nominates.
keywords: weigh the nature and complexity of the case against what the revenue stands to lose
the credit availed sits outside the normal limits for the trade
only with the prior approval of the Commissioner

options.text: Nothing beyond his own opinion, the section leaving the decision to the officer conducting the inquiry
options.misconception: reads a power given to an officer as one he may exercise on his own
options.why: Two things stand in the way. He must form the opinion on the stated grounds and not on a general unease, and he must have the Commissioner's prior approval before the direction goes out. Both exist because the direction puts a stranger into a person's books.

citation.ref: Section 66(1)

items.scenario: An inquiry into a Delhi electronics dealer has been running three months. The Deputy Commissioner conducting it has an eleven-volume file turning on contracts he cannot follow, believes the declared values are wrong, and finds the credit taken far above what the trade usually takes. He wants an outside accountant to go through the books and asks what he must satisfy himself of first.

items.stem: How do the company's two objections stand?

options.text: Both hold, and in any case the department may act on the report without hearing the company, an audit report being evidence in itself
options.misconception: adds a third error, that a report may be used without being put to the person it is about
options.why: Neither objection stands, and the third point is wrong as well. Before any material gathered in the special audit is used against the person in a proceeding, it has to be given an opportunity of being heard on it.

options.text: The second holds, the person audited paying, as it does for every other audit of its own books
options.misconception: carries the ordinary rule about who pays an auditor into a direction made by the department
options.why: This audit is the department's, done by its nominee for its own purposes. Its cost, remuneration included, is settled and borne by the Commissioner, and his determination of the amount is not open to argument.

options.text: The first holds, an audit already done under another law barring a second one over the same books
options.misconception: reads the earlier audits as having covered this ground already
options.why: The section says the opposite in terms — it has effect even where the accounts have been audited under any other provision or any other law. An audit under the companies law asks whether the accounts show a true and fair view; this one asks whether value was declared correctly and credit taken within normal limits.

options.text: Neither holds — the direction may be given anyway, and the cost is not the company's
options.why: The special audit may be directed notwithstanding that the person's accounts have already been audited under any other provision of this Act or under any other law in force, so last year's departmental audit and the audit under the companies law are both beside the point — they answered different questions. On the fee, the whole cost of the examination and audit, the accountant's remuneration included, is determined and paid by the Commissioner, and that determination is final. What the company does get is a hearing: it must be given an opportunity of being heard on any material gathered in the audit that the department proposes to use against it.
keywords: directed notwithstanding that the person's accounts have already been audited
under any other provision of this Act or under any other law in force
determined and paid by the Commissioner, and that determination is final

items.scenario: A Delhi company has been directed to get its records examined and audited by an accountant the Commissioner nominated. It raises two objections: that its accounts were audited by the department last year and again under the companies law, and that it will not be paying a stranger's fees.

items.stem: Can it file either now, and what happens to the tax?

options.text: Both can be filed on paying the late fee, a late fee being what the Act charges for a delayed filing
options.misconception: treats the late fee as the price of filing late, with no outer date at all
options.why: A late fee is what a person pays for filing between the due date and the bar. After three years there is nothing to pay a fee on, because the Act stops the filing being made, and no payment reopens it.

options.text: Neither can be filed, on two different dates nine days apart, and the tax is still owed
options.why: Each filing carries its own three-year bar running from its own due date, so the two doors shut on different days: the statement of outward supplies for April 2023 could be furnished up to 11 May 2026 and the return up to 20 May 2026. September 2026 is past both and neither can be furnished at all. The money in hand is beside the point, because what stands in the way is not an unpaid late fee but the bar itself. What does not go away is the liability: the tax remains payable and recoverable, and a demand may still be raised for it. The filings are closed while the debt stays open.
keywords: could be furnished up to 11 May 2026 and the return up to 20 May 2026
The filings are closed while the debt stays open

options.text: Both are barred, and the tax with them, a liability that cannot be reported being one that cannot be collected
options.misconception: reads the end of the filing window as the end of the liability
options.why: The bar is on furnishing the document, not on the demand. The tax for April 2023 stays payable, and the department's own time limits for raising a demand run on their own footing.

options.text: The return is barred but the statement of outward supplies is not, the three-year limit having been written for returns alone
options.misconception: knows one of the four provisions and assumes it stands alone
options.why: The Finance Act, 2023 put the same outer limit on four filings at once — the statement of outward supplies, the return, the annual return and the operator's statement. Each runs three years from its own due date, which is why two documents for one month close nine days apart.

citation.ref: Sections 37(5) and 39(11), inserted by the Finance Act, 2023

items.scenario: A Kanpur trader files monthly. In September 2026 it discovers that neither its statement of outward supplies nor its monthly return for April 2023 was ever filed. The two were due on 11 May 2023 and 20 May 2023. It has the tax and the late fee ready and wants to file both today.

items.stem: What does it actually have to file, and by when?

options.text: Only 2025-26's, and by 31 March 2027, the annual return following the accounts
options.misconception: borrows a year-end date from the accounts timetable
options.why: The date in the section is 31 December of the following financial year, and it does not move with anybody's audit or accounts timetable.

options.text: Both years' returns, by 31 December 2026, the notification relieving only the late fee
options.misconception: reads a notification exempting a class of persons from the return as a relief from its penalty
options.why: The notification exempts the person from furnishing the return for that year at all. A relief from late fee would leave the obligation standing and merely make it cheaper to be late.

options.text: Neither, the turnover in 2024-25 having been under the line and the exemption once earned holding for the next year too
options.misconception: treats the exemption as a status attaching to the person rather than a test applied year by year
options.why: The exemption is tested each year on that year's own aggregate turnover. A person under the line in one year and over it in the next is exempt for the first and must file for the second.

options.text: Only 2025-26's, and by 31 December 2026, so March 2027 would be late
options.why: The annual return for a financial year is due by 31 December of the year following it, so the one for 2025-26 falls due on 31 December 2026 and filing in March 2027 would be late whatever else were true. The other year is not due at all. The Commissioner may exempt a class of persons from the annual return by notification, and for 2024-25 onwards a registered person whose aggregate turnover in the year is up to ₹2 crore has been exempted from filing it for that year. That leaves this person exempt for 2024-25 at ₹1.6 crore and outside the exemption for 2025-26 at ₹2.9 crore.
keywords: due by 31 December of the year following it
aggregate turnover in the year is up to ₹2 crore

citation.ref: Section 44(1) read with Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025

items.scenario: A registered person's aggregate turnover was ₹1.6 crore in 2024-25 and ₹2.9 crore in 2025-26. Its consultant has told it to file the annual return for both years, and to do the two together in March 2027 to save a trip.

items.stem: What does the audit team put to the company about the year that has just closed?

options.text: Nothing, because the unit came in on budget, which is itself the evidence that the goodwill holds its value
options.misconception: treats a budget being met as a substitute for measuring recoverable amount
options.why: Meeting a budget says the year came out roughly as management planned. The test asks a different question — what the unit is worth today set against what it is carried at — and a budget built on the same forecasts that would support value in use cannot answer it. There is one place the standard lets an earlier answer stand in for this year's work and it is narrow: the most recent detailed calculation may be reused only where the unit is essentially the same collection of assets and liabilities, that earlier figure cleared the carrying amount by a substantial margin, and a shortfall now is remote. A budget met is none of the three.

options.text: Nothing — the manual matches the standard, which asks for a test only where something points to a loss of value
options.misconception: reads the indicator-driven test as the whole requirement and drops the annual one
options.why: That is the rule for an ordinary asset carried at cost, where the entity looks at each reporting date for signs of impairment and measures only if it finds one. Goodwill is deliberately outside it. Goodwill throws off no cash flows of its own and cannot be sold apart from the business, so the standard does not wait for a signal before asking what it is worth. Keep only the trigger and the goodwill's first bad year is found by the same managers whose unit it is.

options.text: A test was owed in 20X3-20X4 whatever the business heads said, so a year of the goodwill has gone unexamined
options.why: Goodwill bought in a business combination is one of the few things a company must put through an impairment test at least annually, and that duty stands irrespective of whether there is any indication that its value has fallen. A quiet year is not an exemption from the test; it is the ordinary year the annual rule was written for. Alongside it the unit is tested again whenever there is an indication that the unit may be impaired, so a bad year adds a test rather than replacing one. A manual that tests on a trigger alone has kept the second duty and thrown the first away, and 20X3-20X4 has closed with the goodwill unmeasured.
keywords: put through an impairment test at least annually
irrespective of whether there is any indication that its value has fallen
tested again whenever there is an indication that the unit may be impaired

options.text: Nothing this year; the omission is made good by testing twice next year, once for each period
options.misconception: thinks a missed annual test can be caught up by a later one
options.why: A test run next year measures next year's unit on next year's estimates. It cannot say what the unit was worth at the end of a year that has already closed, and it is that closed year's balance sheet which carried the goodwill at ₹90 crore. Doubling up later has the appearance of catching up while leaving the earlier figure resting on a measurement nobody ever made.

citation.ref: Annual impairment test of a cash-generating unit to which goodwill has been allocated

items.scenario: Girnar Logistics Limited reports under Ind AS and carries goodwill of ₹90 crore allocated to its Cold Chain cash-generating unit from a business combination three years ago. The company's accounting manual says the unit is put through an impairment test in any year in which the business heads report a concern about it, and in no other year. In 20X3-20X4 the business heads reported nothing, the unit came in on budget, and no test was carried out. The audit team is finishing its work on the unit and the manual is in front of it.

items.stem: How does the audit team answer that at the 31 March 20X6 year end?

options.text: The fixed date discharges one duty and not the other; the January events call for the unit to be looked at again at the year end
options.why: Girnar has met the floor and stopped there. A unit carrying goodwill is tested at least annually, and it is tested again whenever there is an indication that the unit may be impaired — two duties standing side by side, and the second does not sleep because the first has been discharged. Fixing the annual test to one date each year is what the standard permits, and the reason for fixing it is to stop the yearly measurement being moved about to suit the answer. It was never a statement that nothing between two test dates matters. So a customer worth a fifth of the revenue leaving, and a depot closing, are looked at on their own facts at the reporting date, and a fixed annual test date does not answer for an event later in the year.
keywords: tested at least annually, and it is tested again whenever there is an indication that the unit may be impaired
a fixed annual test date does not answer for an event later in the year

options.text: The test date must now be moved to 31 March, and from this year on the annual test is performed at the year end
options.misconception: fixes an interim problem by changing the policy instead of doing the work now
options.why: Nothing requires the annual test to sit at the reporting date, and moving it is not the answer to what happened in January. Changing the date also costs something: the point of holding it steady is comparability year on year, and a company that shifts it after bad news invites the question whether the shift was chosen for the answer it produced. The work owed here is an additional test now, not a rescheduled one.

options.text: Nothing at the year end; the January events are disclosed in the notes and taken into the 30 June 20X6 test
options.misconception: treats disclosure as an alternative to measuring
options.why: A note saying a large customer has gone does not tell a reader what the unit is now worth, and the balance sheet it sits behind still carries the goodwill at a figure measured before any of it happened. Disclosure runs alongside measurement in this standard; it has never been offered as a substitute for it.

options.text: The finance head is right — the annual test was performed on the correct date, and the standard asks for one test a year
options.misconception: reads the fixed date as a ceiling on how often the unit is tested
options.why: One test a year is the minimum and the date is fixed so that the minimum cannot be shopped around. Neither of those makes the yearly test the only one. Read that way, a company whose worst news always broke in the eight months after its test date would never measure the damage until the following year, which is the outcome the second duty exists to prevent.

citation.ref: Timing of the annual impairment test and the further test required on an indication of impairment

items.scenario: Girnar's manual is rewritten and the Cold Chain unit is now tested every 30 June, the same date each year, which is when the planning cycle produces the forecasts the test uses. The 30 June 20X5 test showed the unit comfortably clear. In January 20X6 the customer that took a fifth of the unit's revenue moved its business to a competitor and the unit's depot in the east was shut. The finance head tells the audit team that the year's test is done and properly dated, and that the next one falls due on 30 June 20X6.

items.stem: What does the audit partner accept?

options.text: Nothing comes back, because the earlier loss fell first on goodwill and that settles the whole unit
options.misconception: spreads the goodwill bar across every asset sitting in the same unit
options.why: The bar is written for goodwill and reaches nothing else. The plant is carrying ₹8 crore of the earlier loss, and the standard requires that to be revisited once the estimates behind recoverable amount have changed. Refusing on the goodwill's account would leave the plant standing below a figure the company can now show it is worth, which is the mirror of the fault the finance director is being stopped from committing.

options.text: The ₹14 crore on goodwill may be written back provided the company discloses in a note that it has done so
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a way of buying a treatment the standard refuses
options.why: A note explaining a figure does not make the figure permissible, and there is no disclosure anywhere that unlocks this one. What would be going back on the balance sheet is not the purchased goodwill at all. It is the value the present management has built since the write-down, and that has no place there however fully the notes describe it.

options.text: The whole ₹22 crore comes back, because the unit's recoverable amount now supports the full amount
options.misconception: settles the question on the unit as one figure and forgets that one asset inside it is excluded
options.why: A write-back is worked out asset by asset inside the unit, never on the unit as a single number. Even for the assets that may take one, the ceiling is not the unit's recoverable amount — it is what each asset would be carried at today, net of depreciation, had the earlier loss never been recognised at all. Goodwill then takes none of it, and an amount that no other asset in the unit can absorb is simply not recognised anywhere.

options.text: The ₹8 crore on the plant may come back, held to its own ceiling; the ₹14 crore on goodwill may not come back at all
options.why: The two halves of this write-down are not governed alike. For an asset other than goodwill the entity looks at each reporting date for signs that an earlier loss has shrunk or gone, and writes it back where the estimates behind recoverable amount have genuinely moved — held to the carrying amount, net of depreciation, the asset would have shown had the loss never been recognised. Goodwill is carved out of all of that: an impairment loss once recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period, whatever the unit goes on to earn. The reason is not nervousness about volatility. A later rise in what the goodwill is worth is far more likely to be goodwill the business has built for itself since, and internally generated goodwill is not something a company may put on its balance sheet under any heading.
keywords: an impairment loss once recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period
internally generated goodwill is not something a company may put on its balance sheet

citation.ref: Prohibition on reversing an impairment loss recognised for goodwill, and the ceiling on reversal for other assets

items.scenario: Anantara Diagnostics Limited recognised an impairment loss of ₹22 crore in 20X2-20X3 on the cash-generating unit that runs its imaging centres. ₹14 crore of it fell on goodwill from an earlier acquisition and ₹8 crore on the unit's plant. In 20X4-20X5 the unit wins back the hospital contract it had lost, its recoverable amount is now well above what the unit is carried at, and the finance director proposes to write back the whole ₹22 crore, goodwill included, on the ground that the reason for the write-down has gone away. The audit partner has the proposal in front of her.

items.stem: Which of the two is put right by restating a comparative, and on what reasoning?

options.text: Neither. Both are changes in accounting estimate, and both go to this year's profit or loss
options.misconception: sends information that existed all along into prospective estimate accounting
options.why: A change in estimate is what you make when the underlying facts themselves have moved. The building's facts did not move an inch; the report describing them was sitting in Vaitarna's own files while the accounts were being approved, which makes the difference an error and sends it backwards rather than forwards. The goodwill cannot come to this year's profit either, from any direction, because the one thing settled about a goodwill write-down is that it does not come back.

options.text: The goodwill only, because the building figure was right on the information the preparers themselves actually had
options.misconception: asks what the individual preparers knew instead of what the company held
options.why: The definition looks at information that was available, not at what happened to reach a particular desk. A report the company commissioned and had in hand is available to the company, and a breakdown in passing it along is precisely the failure those words are written to catch. Were ignorance inside an organisation a defence, the worse information travelled in a company the fewer errors it would be found to have.

options.text: Both. Each is a prior year figure that later information shows to have been wrong, so both comparatives are restated
options.misconception: turns any later change of view about a prior year into an error
options.why: What makes something an error is not that the figure looks wrong from here. It is that reliable information which existed and was available when those statements were approved for issue went unused. The valuation report was information of exactly that kind. A forecast made in good faith on what was known at the time is not, however the years since have turned out, and treating it as one would put every estimate in the accounts up for reopening whenever the future disagreed with it.

options.text: The building only. The goodwill write-down was not an error, and nothing reaches back to undo it
options.why: An error is an omission or a misstatement that comes of failing to use information which was available when those financial statements were approved for issue and could reasonably have been expected to have been taken into account. The valuation report fits that word for word — Vaitarna commissioned it, Vaitarna held it, nobody put it in front of the preparers, and the building went out ₹6 crore above what it supported. So a material prior period error is put right retrospectively, by restating the comparative amounts of the year it happened in, unless doing that is impracticable. The goodwill is a different animal altogether. The 20X3-20X4 forecasts were made on what was known then, and a good run since is fresh information rather than a fact anyone overlooked. Calling it an error is a route around a rule that has no route around it: an impairment loss once recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period.
keywords: a material prior period error is put right retrospectively, by restating the comparative amounts
an impairment loss once recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period

citation.source: Ind AS 8, Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors
citation.ref: Definition of a prior period error and its retrospective correction, read with Ind AS 36 on the reversal of an impairment loss recognised for goodwill

items.scenario: Vaitarna Ceramics Limited wrote the goodwill of its Tiles unit down by ₹18 crore in 20X3-20X4. In 20X5-20X6 the unit is earning ahead of every forecast, and the finance head proposes to restate the 20X3-20X4 comparative to take the write-down out, describing it in the draft note as the correction of an error because the forecasts relied on then have turned out to be too gloomy. Separately, the audit file shows that a valuation report on the unit's building, which Vaitarna had commissioned and held before the 20X4-20X5 accounts were approved for issue, never reached the team that prepared them, and that the building was carried ₹6 crore above what the report supported. Both matters go to the audit committee.

items.stem: How should the two advances stand?

options.text: Both are non-performing, each having been overdue beyond ninety days, and the guarantees go only to the provision required
options.misconception: applies the ninety-day rule to a Central Government guaranteed advance, when for that advance classification turns on repudiation of the guarantee on invocation
options.why: The ninety-day rule is where the analysis starts and not where it ends. The prudential norms carve out one exception, and it is narrow: a Central Government guaranteed facility is treated as non-performing only on repudiation of the guarantee when invoked. It is the State Government guaranteed advance that is caught by the ninety days.

options.text: Neither is non-performing, a guarantee of a government being the best security a bank can hold, so the classification and the interest both stand
options.misconception: reads a government guarantee as a substitute for a record of recovery, when the exception is confined to the Central Government and to classification alone
options.why: Nothing in the norms lets a guarantee replace the record of recovery for a State Government advance, and even for the Central Government advance the exception is confined to classification. Income is a separate question, and interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become non-performing is recognised only on realisation.

options.text: The State Government guaranteed advance is non-performing, and the Central Government guaranteed one is not yet — but the reason the guarantee has not been invoked must be obtained and reported, and on both advances the interest cannot be taken to income
options.why: The exception belongs to the Central Government alone and only for asset classification: a credit facility backed by a Central Government guarantee, though overdue, is treated as non-performing only when the Central Government repudiates its guarantee on invocation, and where the bank has not invoked it though the amount has been overdue for long, the reasoning is obtained and duly reported in the long form audit report. The exception does not apply to a State Government guaranteed advance, which is treated as non-performing if it remains overdue for more than 90 days. And for income recognition, whichever government stands behind it, interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become non-performing is not taken to income unless it is realised.

options.text: Both remain standard but the interest already accrued on both is reversed, income recognition and asset classification being governed by the same test
options.misconception: treats income recognition and asset classification as one rule, when the norms answer them separately and the State Government advance fails the classification test on its own
options.why: They are two rules and they can give different answers on the same advance, which is exactly what happens here. The State Government guaranteed advance fails the classification test because it has been overdue beyond ninety days, so reversing the interest and leaving it standard deals with half the problem.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — government guaranteed advances: interest not taken to income unless realised, a Central Government guaranteed facility treated as non-performing only when the guarantee is repudiated on invocation with the reasoning for non-invocation reported in the long form audit report, and a State Government guaranteed advance treated as non-performing if overdue for more than 90 days

items.scenario: Two advances at a branch on 31 March. The first is backed by a guarantee of the Central Government; the instalments have been overdue for two hundred days and the bank has not invoked the guarantee. The second is backed by a guarantee of a State Government and has been overdue for one hundred and forty days. The branch has kept both as standard and has taken the interest on both to income, on the footing that a sovereign guarantee removes the doubt about recovery.

items.stem: What does the asset classification require here?

options.text: The cash credit and the devolved letter of credit account, the term loan standing on its own because it is separately secured and separately serviced
options.misconception: allows separate security and separate servicing to save one facility, when borrower-wise classification takes no account of either
options.why: Borrower-wise classification does not ask how a facility is secured or how it has been served. Once the borrower is non-performing, every facility granted to him is treated as non-performing, and the term loan is not saved by its own conduct.

options.text: The cash credit and the term loan, but not the devolved letter of credit account, which is a non-fund exposure that crystallised and is dealt with under contingent liabilities
options.misconception: keeps a devolved letter of credit outside the borrower's principal account, when the norms bring that outstanding into it
options.why: The letter of credit stopped being a contingent liability the moment it devolved; what is left is money the bank has paid out and is owed. The norms say so directly — a debit arising out of devolvement kept in a separate account is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms.

options.text: Only the cash credit, since classification follows the conduct of each account and a term loan serviced on time is by definition a standard asset
options.misconception: classifies facility by facility, which is the approach the norms specifically direct the auditor to check against
options.why: That is facility-wise classification, and the norms name it as the thing to be guarded against: the auditor ensures that classification is borrower-wise, so once one facility is non-performing every facility granted to that borrower goes with it whatever its own conduct looks like.

options.text: All of it goes with the borrower — every facility granted to him is treated as non-performing, and the outstanding in the separate account carrying the devolved letter of credit is treated as part of his principal account for income recognition, asset classification and provisioning
options.why: The norms require the auditor to ensure that asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise, so all the facilities granted by a bank to a borrower have to be treated as non-performing and not merely the particular facility that has become irregular. And where debits arising out of devolvement of a letter of credit or of invoked guarantees are kept in a separate account, that outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the purpose of applying the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning — moving a debit into an account of its own does not take it outside the borrower's position.
keywords: devolvement of a letter of credit
part of the borrower's principal account

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise, so all facilities granted to a borrower are treated as non-performing, and a debit arising out of devolvement of a letter of credit or of invoked guarantees kept in a separate account is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for asset classification, income recognition and provisioning

items.scenario: One borrower at a branch holds three facilities. His cash credit account has been out of order for four months. His term loan is serviced to the day and nothing on it is overdue. A letter of credit opened for him devolved on the bank in January and the branch has parked that debit in a separate account of its own, outside the borrower's principal account, where it is still outstanding. The branch has classified the cash credit as non-performing and left the term loan and the devolved letter of credit account as standard.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the two questions?

options.text: The lead bank governs both — it holds the largest share, it sees the whole facility, and a member bank that departs from its certificate breaks the consortium arrangement
options.misconception: gives the lead bank the classification decision as well as the drawing power, when only the second is binding on members
options.why: Only one of the two is the lead bank's to settle. Its drawing power calculation and allocation bind the members; its view of whether the account performs does not, because each bank classifies the advance it has given by reference to its own experience of recovery.

options.text: Neither is settled until the consortium meets — classification and drawing power are both matters for the members acting together, and a bank acting alone on either is premature
options.misconception: turns both questions into joint decisions, when one is the lead bank's and the other is each member's own
options.why: Nothing is left to a meeting. The lead bank's drawing power calculation and allocation already bind the members, and the classification is each member bank's own to make on its own experience of recovery, which is why one bank in a consortium can hold an account as non-performing while another holds it as standard.

options.text: Your bank governs both — it carries its own credit risk on its own share, so it classifies on its own recovery and computes its own drawing power on the security available to it
options.misconception: extends the member bank's own judgement on classification to the drawing power, which the norms leave with the lead bank
options.why: The first half is right and the second is not. Drawing power in a consortium is computed and allocated once, by the lead bank, and that calculation and allocation are binding on the member banks; a member recomputing it for itself defeats the point of a common security pool.

options.text: Opposite answers — the classification is your bank's own to make on its own experience of recovery, so the account is non-performing and the interest reversed despite the lead bank's certificate; but the drawing power calculation and the allocation made by the lead bank are binding on the member banks, so the branch does not substitute its own
options.why: The two rules pull in different directions and both are in the norms. On classification, a consortium member grades what it lent by its own experience of recovery, weighed with whatever else that member can see; the credits over the last two quarters being short of the interest debited, the interest is reversed and the amount shown as a non-performing asset, and this is so despite the certificate of the lead bank classifying the account as performing. On drawing power the answer is the other way: in the case of consortium accounts, the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on member banks.
keywords: despite the certificate of the lead bank

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — consortium advances: the provision leaving classification with each member on its own recovery record whatever the lead bank has certified, read against the separate provision that fixes drawing power and its allocation with the lead bank and binds the members to it

items.scenario: Your bank is one of five in a consortium advancing to a large borrower, and it is not the lead bank. Over the last two quarters the credits in the borrower's account with your branch have come to less than the interest debited to it. The lead bank has issued a certificate classifying the account as performing across the consortium. Separately, the lead bank has computed the drawing power and allocated it among the member banks, and your branch manager thinks the computation was generous and wants to work out his own drawing power and restrict the borrower on that basis.

items.stem: What is wrong with the transaction and its accounting?

options.text: Only the two-year point — a contingent element is permissible where it is documented in the board-approved policy, and the treatment of the excess follows the accounting standards rather than the prudential norms
options.misconception: lets a board policy authorise what the norms forbid outright and lets the accounting standards displace the prudential treatment of the excess
options.why: The board's policy on procedures, valuation and delegation is one of the things the auditor examines, but it cannot authorise a contingent price, which the norms bar under any circumstances. And the treatment of the excess is settled by the norms themselves: it is not reversed, it is utilised against the shortfall on other sales.

options.text: All three — only an asset that has remained non-performing in the bank's books for at least two years may be sold; the sale has to be on a cash basis with the whole consideration received upfront and never at a contingent price; and where the sale is for more than the net book value the excess provision is not reversed but is kept to meet the shortfall on the sale of other non-performing financial assets
options.why: The auditor examines that only such a non-performing asset has been sold as has remained non-performing in the books of the bank for at least two years, so fourteen months fails at the threshold. He examines that the asset has been sold on a cash basis only — under no circumstances is a contingent price permitted where one bank sells such an account on to another, and every rupee of what is agreed must reach the seller upfront. Where the price beats net book value, the excess provision shall not be reversed; it stays put, ready to absorb a shortfall or a loss thrown up by some later sale of another non-performing financial asset. A write-back to the profit and loss account books a gain the norms do not let the bank take.
keywords: excess provision shall not be reversed

options.text: Only the contingent element — the two-year period is a guideline for the purchasing bank's due diligence, and a sale above net book value produces a real gain that belongs in the year it arises
options.misconception: treats the two-year holding condition as advisory and the excess as a distributable gain, when both are conditions the auditor examines
options.why: Both are conditions the auditor examines on the selling bank. The asset must have remained non-performing in its books for at least two years before it may be sold at all, and the excess over net book value is not a gain to be reported but a provision to be carried against the shortfall on other such sales.

options.text: Nothing, once the asset has been removed from the books on transfer and the sale was without recourse — those are the two tests, and both are met
options.misconception: stops at two of the conditions the auditor examines and reads them as the whole list
options.why: Removal from the books on transfer and a sale without recourse are two of the things examined, not all of them. The holding period of at least two years, the cash basis, the bar on buying back an asset the bank itself sold, and the treatment of a shortfall or an excess against net book value are each separately examined.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — sale of a non-performing asset by a bank: the asset must have remained non-performing in the books for at least two years, the sale is without recourse and on a cash basis only with the entire consideration received upfront and never at a contingent price, a shortfall against net book value is debited to the profit and loss account, and an excess is not reversed but utilised to meet the shortfall on the sale of other non-performing financial assets

items.scenario: A bank sold one of its non-performing assets to another bank during the year. Your file shows three things. The account had been classified as non-performing in the selling bank's books for fourteen months at the date of sale. The consideration was settled as a part payment now and a further amount payable only if the purchasing bank recovers above a stated figure. And the price exceeded the net book value of the asset, so the excess provision no longer needed has been written back to the profit and loss account for the year.

items.stem: What does the auditor verify on a purchase of non-performing assets?

options.text: That the assets were bought without recourse and removed from the seller's books — those being the seller's obligations, the purchasing bank's own work is confined to the price it paid
options.misconception: reads the conditions on the sale as the whole of the auditor's work and leaves the purchasing bank nothing to verify
options.why: The norms set out a separate list for the purchase side, and it is about what happens in the purchasing bank's books afterwards: provisioning by the classification status there, the adjustment of recoveries against acquisition cost first, and a 100 per cent risk weight for capital adequacy.

options.text: That any recovery is first adjusted against the acquisition cost with only the excess over that cost recognised as profit; that the asset purchased is subjected to the provisioning requirements appropriate to its classification status in the purchasing bank's own books; and that a 100 per cent risk weight has been assigned to non-performing assets purchased from other banks
options.why: All three of the bank's positions fail. Money coming in on a non-performing asset bought from another bank is first adjusted against its acquisition cost; profit appears only once collections have run past what was paid for the account. The purchased asset then attracts whatever provision matches its classification status in the books of the purchasing bank, so a discount at the price is no substitute for a provision. And for capital adequacy, banks assign 100 per cent risk weights to the non-performing assets purchased from other banks, whatever weight those accounts carried with the seller.
keywords: first adjusted against its acquisition cost
classification status in the books of the purchasing bank

options.text: That the discount to outstanding is reasonable and that the acquisition cost has been allocated across the individual accounts, the provision then following the classification the accounts carried with the seller
options.misconception: carries the seller's classification into the purchaser's books, when the provisioning follows the classification status in the purchasing bank's own books
options.why: The classification travels no further than the sale. The purchased asset is subjected to the provisioning requirements appropriate to its classification status in the books of the purchasing bank, which is a fresh question answered on the purchaser's own assessment.

options.text: That recoveries have been apportioned between principal and interest in the ratio the original loan documents provide, so that only the interest element is taken to the profit and loss account
options.misconception: applies an ordinary appropriation rule to a purchased non-performing asset, when the norms direct recoveries against the acquisition cost first
options.why: A purchased non-performing asset is not accounted on the original contract's appropriation. Recovery is first adjusted against the acquisition cost, and only what comes in above that cost is recognised as profit at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — purchase of non-performing assets: the purchased asset subjected to the provisioning requirements appropriate to its classification status in the books of the purchasing bank, recovery first adjusted against the acquisition cost with only the excess recognised as profit, and 100 per cent risk weights assigned for capital adequacy to non-performing assets purchased from other banks

items.scenario: The same bank has also bought a portfolio of non-performing assets from another bank at a discount to their outstanding. Three things are on the file. Recoveries received during the year have been taken to the profit and loss account in full as income. No provision has been carried against the purchased assets, on the view that they are already carried at the discounted acquisition cost. And for capital adequacy the bank has applied to them the risk weights that attached to those accounts in the selling bank's books.

items.stem: How many of the four proposals stand?

options.text: None of them — scope is the head of internal audit's call, and the Audit Committee of the Board has to approve it beforehand; the bank's own officers must be independent of the branch where the audit is conducted; an external concurrent auditor's tenure with the bank is generally not more than five years on a continuous basis; and no concurrent auditor may continue with a branch or business unit for more than three years
options.why: Each proposal fails a rule that exists for the same reason — a concurrent auditor who is close to what he audits stops being an early warning. What the work covers, and how much business and how many branches sit inside it, is the head of internal audit's call, signed off under due prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board — never a branch head's. Officers of the bank put on this work should be experienced, well trained and senior enough for it, and each of them must be independent of the branch whose books they examine. Tenure runs on two clocks.
