The Audit Committee of the Board sets how long an outside firm may serve, which generally shall not be more than five years on a continuous basis with that bank; and separately, one branch or business unit may not keep the same concurrent auditor for more than three years.
keywords: due prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board
not be more than five years on a continuous basis

options.text: Two — the branch-level scope and the use of the bank's own officers at their own branches are matters of internal organisation, while both the tenure limits are breached
options.misconception: treats scope-setting and the posting of the bank's own staff as internal housekeeping, when the norms fix both
options.why: Both are fixed. The scope and the coverage sit with the head of internal audit with the prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board, and the bank's own officials engaged on concurrent audit must be independent of the branch where the audit is conducted, which a man auditing his own branch cannot be.

options.text: Three — only the six-year continuous engagement fails, five years being the outer limit, and the four years at one branch is inside it because the branch limit runs with the branch and not with the firm
options.misconception: reads the three-year branch limit as attaching to something other than the auditor, so a firm can sit at one branch for as long as the bank likes
options.why: The three-year limit attaches to the concurrent auditor at a branch or business unit and it stands alongside the five-year limit with the bank as a whole, so four years at one branch fails on its own. And the scope and the staffing questions fail before either tenure question is reached.

options.text: All four — the choice between the bank's own staff and external auditors is the bank's, the Audit Committee sets the tenure, and where it has set none the general limits are only indicative
options.misconception: turns limits the Audit Committee applies into limits it may waive, and reads the whole arrangement as the bank's discretion
options.why: The choice between own staff and external auditors is indeed left to the bank, and that is the only part of the proposal that survives. The Audit Committee decides the tenure within the stated limits rather than instead of them, and the requirements on scope approval and on independence from the branch are not the bank's to waive.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — appointment of concurrent auditors and accountability: the provisions putting scope and coverage in the head of internal audit's hands subject to the Audit Committee approving beforehand, setting the experience, training, seniority and branch independence expected of a bank's own officers on the work, capping an outside firm's service with the bank at five continuous years as a general matter, and capping the same auditor's stay at one branch or business unit at three years

items.scenario: A bank is settling its concurrent audit arrangements for the coming year. The general manager proposes that the scope be fixed branch by branch by each branch head, that the bank use its own officers and post each of them to the branch where they normally work so that they know the business, that the external firm which has served the bank continuously for the last six years be continued, and that the same firm stay on at the large city branch it has covered for four years.

items.stem: What does the reporting system for concurrent audit actually require?

options.text: Everything goes into the quarterly review placed before the Audit Committee of the Board, which is the reporting channel the system provides, and the auditor keeps a dated note of when he found the fraud
options.misconception: makes the quarterly review the only channel, when major deficiencies and frauds are reported immediately and separately
options.why: The quarterly review is one of several channels and it is the slowest. Major deficiencies are highlighted in a special note and given immediately to the branch and the controlling offices, and a fraudulent transaction goes at once to the Inspection and Audit Department, the Chief Vigilance Officer and the branch managers concerned.

options.text: The fraudulent transactions go immediately to the Inspection and Audit Department at head office, to the Chief Vigilance Officer and to the branch managers concerned, except that the branch manager is not told where he is himself involved; the serious irregularity goes to the controlling or head office for immediate action while the minor ones are rectified in a timely manner; and a quarterly review of key features goes before the Audit Committee of the Board
options.why: The system is built so that nothing waits for a quarter and nothing routes through the person it is about. Whenever fraudulent transactions are detected they should immediately be reported to the Inspection and Audit Department at head office as also to the Chief Vigilance Officer and to the branch managers concerned, unless the branch manager is involved. Small irregularities the concurrent auditor raises are to be put right without delay; serious ones travel upward, to the controlling office or head office, for action taken at once. And a quarterly review setting out the key features thrown up by these audits goes before the Audit Committee of the Board, carrying zone-wise reporting of what was found and, once a year, an appraisal of how the system itself is working.
keywords: unless the branch manager is involved

options.text: The fraud goes to the branch manager first in every case, since he is the officer accountable for the branch, and it is for him to carry it to head office and to the Chief Vigilance Officer
options.misconception: routes the report through the branch manager without exception, when the requirement carves him out where he is himself involved
options.why: The branch managers concerned are among the people told, but the requirement carries its own exception for exactly this situation: the report goes to them unless the branch manager is involved. Routing it through the suspect is how the reporting line is defeated.

options.text: The fraud and the serious irregularity go to head office at once; the minor errors need no treatment at all, a concurrent audit being aimed at deficiencies that matter
options.misconception: discards minor irregularities, when the system requires them to be rectified in a timely manner rather than ignored
options.why: Minor irregularities are not dropped; they are to be rectified in a timely manner, which is a different instruction from either reporting them upward or letting them go. The difference between minor and serious decides where a finding goes, not whether it is dealt with.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — reporting systems for concurrent audit: major deficiencies highlighted in a special note and given immediately to the branch and controlling offices, a quarterly review of key features placed before the Audit Committee of the Board with zone-wise reporting and an annual appraisal, minor irregularities rectified in a timely manner and serious ones reported to the controlling or head offices for immediate action, and fraudulent transactions reported immediately to the Inspection and Audit Department at head office, to the Chief Vigilance Officer and to the branch managers concerned unless the branch manager is involved

items.scenario: Three weeks into the quarter a concurrent auditor finds a set of transactions he is satisfied are fraudulent, and the pattern points to the branch manager himself. He also has a serious irregularity in the sanction of an advance and a handful of small posting errors. The branch manager tells him to hold everything for the quarterly report, that anything about the branch goes out over the branch manager's own signature, and that small errors are not worth writing down at all.

items.stem: What is wrong with the draft?

options.text: Only the addressee — a regulator reading a report of contraventions is entitled to know what was found satisfactory, and the compliance paragraph is good practice
options.misconception: treats the bar on compliance statements as a matter of style, when the direction states it as the limit of the duty
options.why: It is not a matter of style. The direction says in terms that the duty is to report only the contraventions and that the report shall not contain any statement with respect to compliance, so a paragraph confirming compliance is outside what the auditor is asked to say.

options.text: Nothing — the report is the auditor's own document, and once the unfavourable statements are in it, how it is framed and where it is sent are matters of judgement
options.misconception: treats a prescribed exception report as a matter of the auditor's own framing, when the direction fixes its content and its addressee
options.why: Very little of it is left to judgement. The direction fixes what triggers the report, what it may contain, what it may not contain, and which office of the Reserve Bank receives it.

options.text: Only the compliance paragraph — the Reserve Bank's central office is the right addressee for a report about a company's fitness, and the regional office receives a copy
options.misconception: sends the exception report to the central office, when the direction names the Regional Office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision with jurisdiction over the registered office
options.why: The direction names its addressee, and the central office is not it. What receives the report is the Regional Office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision carrying jurisdiction over wherever the company keeps its registered office.

options.text: Both the addressee and the compliance paragraph — this report is filed with whichever Regional Office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision holds jurisdiction over the place the company is registered at, and the auditor's duty stops at the contraventions, with nothing set down either way about the provisions the company did keep
options.why: The directions fix both. An unfavourable or qualified statement on any specified matter, or a failure to keep Chapter III B of the Reserve Bank of India Act or the deposit and prudential directions, obliges the auditor to write those statements and that failure up and send the write-up to the Department of Non-Banking Supervision — to the Regional Office whose jurisdiction covers the place where the registered office of the company is located, never the central office. The same paragraph fixes the contents: report only the contraventions, and put down nothing whatever about the provisions the company did keep. A paragraph confirming that everything else is in order is precisely what is shut out.
keywords: registered office of the company is located

citation.source: Reserve Bank of India directions to auditors of non-banking financial companies
citation.ref: the direction creating the auditor's exception report — what sets it off (an unfavourable or qualified statement, or a failure to comply), which Reserve Bank office takes delivery of it (Non-Banking Supervision, at the Regional Office holding jurisdiction over where the company is registered), and the limit it puts on the contents (contraventions alone, and no statement about compliance)

items.scenario: You are the auditor of a non-banking financial company. Of the matters on which the Reserve Bank's directions require you to make a statement, two are unfavourable and the remainder are satisfactory. Your manager drafts the report to be sent to the regulator so that it sets out the two unfavourable statements and then, for completeness, records that the company has complied with everything else. He proposes to address it to the Reserve Bank's central office, on the view that a matter of this seriousness should not stop at a regional desk.

items.stem: What provision is required on the doubtful advance, and how is the standard asset provision presented?

options.text: ₹40 lakh — the whole of the part not covered by the realisable value of the security, the secured portion needing nothing while the security stands — and the presentation of the standard asset provision is a matter for Schedule III
options.misconception: stops at the unsecured limb and drops the age-based provision on the secured portion altogether
options.why: The age-based provision on the secured portion is additional to the 100 per cent on the unsecured part, not an alternative to it, and it is required precisely because security erodes while an account stays doubtful. The presentation of the standard asset provision is fixed by the prudential norms themselves.

options.text: ₹58 lakh — 100 per cent of the ₹40 lakh not covered by the realisable value of the security, plus 30 per cent of the ₹60 lakh secured portion, the asset having been doubtful for one to three years — and the standard asset provision is not netted from gross advances but shown separately as Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets
options.why: On a doubtful asset the provision has two limbs. One limb is a full 100 per cent charge on so much of the advance as is not covered by the realisable value of the security the company can validly fall back on — ₹40 lakh here. The other limb runs on the secured portion and rises with age: 20 per cent up to one year, 30 per cent for one to three years, 50 per cent past three. So the ₹60 lakh secured portion carries 30 per cent, being ₹18 lakh, and ₹58 lakh is due against the ₹24 lakh provided. As for standard assets, their provision stays out of any netting — gross advances are shown gross, and the provision sits on its own line in the balance sheet under the heading Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets.
keywords: not covered by the realisable value of the security
30 per cent for one to three years

options.text: ₹30 lakh — 50 per cent of the whole outstanding, the two-year age deciding a single percentage applied to the balance — and the standard asset provision is netted, since it is not reckoned for arriving at net non-performing assets
options.misconception: applies one percentage to the whole outstanding instead of splitting it between the unsecured part and the secured portion
options.why: The provision is never a single percentage of the outstanding. The part not covered by the realisable value of the security carries 100 per cent, and the age-based percentage applies to the secured portion alone. That the standard asset provision is not reckoned for arriving at net non-performing assets is a different point and does not make it a deduction from gross advances.

options.text: ₹64 lakh — 100 per cent of the unsecured ₹40 lakh plus 40 per cent of the secured ₹60 lakh, the one-to-three-year band carrying 40 per cent — and netting the standard asset provision against advances is right, a provision being a reduction of the asset
options.misconception: uses the bank slabs of 25, 40 and 100 per cent on a non-banking financial company, and nets a provision the norms require to be shown separately
options.why: Those are the bank slabs. For a non-banking financial company the secured portion of a doubtful asset carries 20 per cent up to one year, 30 per cent for one to three years and 50 per cent beyond three years. And the standard asset provision is presented separately as Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets rather than netted against advances.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — provisioning requirements: 100 per cent on whatever part of an advance the security's realisable value fails to cover, a further 20 per cent up to one year, 30 per cent for one to three years and 50 per cent beyond three years on the secured portion of a doubtful asset, and the direction that a standard asset provision be carried on its own line as Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets instead of netted off advances

items.scenario: A non-banking financial company's schedules show an advance of ₹100 lakh classified as doubtful, which has been in that category for two years; the realisable value of the security, assessed on a realistic basis, is ₹60 lakh, and the company has provided ₹24 lakh, being 40 per cent of the secured portion. Separately, the provision made against standard assets has been deducted from gross advances so that the balance sheet shows advances net of it.

items.stem: How many of the three statements are true?

options.text: All three — a company registered with the Reserve Bank is regulated on the same footing as a bank once it accepts deposits from the public
options.misconception: collapses the two regulatory regimes into one, when four named differences separate them however closely the company is supervised
options.why: Registration and close supervision do not make the two regimes one. Four differences are fixed and none of them turns on how well regulated the company is: demand deposits, the payment and settlement system, deposit insurance, and the priority sector.

options.text: None of them — a non-banking financial company cannot accept demand deposits although some may take term deposits; it sits outside the payment and settlement system, so no cheque can be drawn on it; the cover of the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation does not reach its depositors; and nothing obliges it to hold any minimum exposure to the priority sector
options.why: These are the standing differences between a bank and a non-banking financial company, and the marketing sheet gets all three wrong. Such a company cannot accept demand deposits, although some of them can take term deposits. They sit outside the payment and settlement system, so no cheque can be drawn on one of them. Cover from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation reaches a bank's depositors and not theirs. And no minimum exposure to the priority sector is asked of them at all.
keywords: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation
no minimum exposure to the priority sector

options.text: One — the deposit insurance statement is right, cover being available once the company holds a certificate of registration, while the cheque facility and the priority sector obligation are not
options.misconception: attaches deposit insurance to registration with the Reserve Bank, when the corporation's cover does not reach depositors of a non-banking financial company at all
options.why: Registration is what lets the company carry on business; it has nothing to do with deposit insurance. The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation's cover is not available to depositors of non-banking financial companies at all, which is the single sharpest difference from a bank deposit.

options.text: Two — a deposit-taking company may offer a chequable account and is inside the payment and settlement system, and only the insurance and the priority sector claims fail
options.misconception: reads the ability to accept deposits as an ability to accept demand deposits and to issue cheques
options.why: Accepting deposits and accepting demand deposits are different things. Some of these companies may accept term deposits; none may accept demand deposits, and they do not form part of the payment and settlement system, so no account with them can be operated by cheque.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — the four provisions separating such a company from a bank: demand deposits barred while term deposits are open to some, no place inside the payment and settlement system and so no cheque drawn on itself, no cover from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation for its depositors, and no floor on priority sector exposure

items.scenario: A depositor of a non-banking financial company you audit shows you the marketing sheet he was given. It tells him he may place money in an account he can draw on by cheque whenever he likes, that his money carries the same deposit insurance as a bank account, and that the company is required to lend a share of its book to the priority sector just as a bank is, which it offers as evidence of how closely it is regulated.

items.stem: What does section 27 and the Council's position on it require?

options.text: The temporary office requires a separate member in charge of its own, and the branch two hundred kilometres away is exempt from having one because it is beyond fifty kilometres from the municipal limits of the city where the first office is
options.misconception: inverts the fifty-kilometre rule, which is a condition of the exemption from a separate charge rather than a trigger for one
options.why: The distance works the other way. A second office may be without a separate member in charge where it is in the same premises, in the same city, or within a distance of fifty kilometres from the municipal limits of the city in which the first office is located — so an office two hundred kilometres away is precisely one that needs its own member in charge.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the temporary office so long as the Institute is told after it closes, and the branch is properly held because a member has been named as being in charge of it
options.misconception: makes the intimation a post-facto formality and treats naming a member in charge as satisfying the requirement
options.why: The intimation is due before the commencement of every winter, with a further intimation after closure, so telling the Institute afterwards is half of what is asked. And naming a member is not the requirement — the requirement is that he be actively associated with the office, which the 182-day test measures.

options.text: The temporary office is permitted for as long as the season requires, since the concession exists because the hill office cannot function in winter; only the name board and the letterhead are wrong, and ninety days at a branch is enough where the member is contactable throughout
options.misconception: reads the hill-area concession as open-ended and treats being contactable as active association
options.why: The concession carries a stated outer limit of three months in a year, and active association is a stated test rather than a matter of availability: residence at the place, or attendance at the office, for not less than 182 days in a year, or such other circumstances as the Executive Committee accepts.

options.text: The temporary office may run for a period not exceeding three months in a year, its name board must not be displayed at any other time, it must not be mentioned in letterheads, visiting cards or other documents as a place of business, and the Institute must be informed before the commencement of every winter and again when it closes — the regular office need not be closed; and a member is in charge of an office only where he is actively associated with it, which is deemed to exist if he resides at that place, or attends that office, for not less than 182 days in a year
options.why: The hill-area concession is a narrow one and every one of its conditions is being broken. A member or firm working out of a hill area may run a second office down in the plains, but for a stretch not exceeding three months in any one year; the regular office stays open and correspondence carries on from there; the firm's name board goes up at the plains office only across the months that office is allowed to work, and comes down otherwise; the temporary address may not appear as a place of business on a letterhead, on a visiting card or on anything else the firm issues; and before the commencement of every winter the Institute has to be told the date the office opens, and told again when it shuts. Separately, the requirement that a member be in charge of an office is satisfied only if he is actively associated with it, and that association is deemed to exist if he resides in the place where the office is situated for not less than 182 days in a year, or attends that office for not less than 182 days in a year.
keywords: before the commencement of every winter
not less than 182 days in a year

citation.ref: Section 27 and the Council's decisions on it — the hill-area concession permitting a temporary office in the plains for not more than three months in a year with the conditions on the name board, the letterhead and the intimation to the Institute before every winter, and the test of active association by residence or attendance for not less than 182 days in a year

items.scenario: A firm practising in a hill station opens an office in a city in the plains for four months of the year, keeps the name board of the firm up there all year round, prints the address on its letterheads as a place of business, and tells the Institute nothing about any of it; its regular hill office stays open throughout. Separately, the partner named as the member in charge of the firm's branch two hundred kilometres away lives elsewhere and attends that branch for about ninety days in the year.

items.stem: What does Chapter IX of the Council General Guidelines make of the offers?

options.text: The two management consultancy assignments are counted together, being payable to the statutory auditor and to an associate concern, and ₹55 lakh exceeds the ₹40 lakh statutory audit fee, so they cannot both be taken; the certification required to be done by the statutory auditors and the representation before an authority are excluded from other work altogether, as is an audit under any other statute
options.why: The guideline bars a member from accepting appointment as statutory auditor of a public sector undertaking, a Government company, a listed company or another public company with a turnover of ₹50 crore or more once the other work he takes on for that same company draws total remuneration above what the statutory audit itself pays. Fees for other work going to the statutory auditors and to their associate concerns are counted put together, and an associate concern reaches a partnership firm rendering such services in which a partner of the auditor firm, or a relative of one, is himself a partner. Other work covers management consultancy and every other professional service section 2(2)(iv) permits. Three things fall outside it, though: an audit some other statute demands, certification work required to be done by the statutory auditors, and any representation before an authority.
keywords: certification work required to be done by the statutory auditors

options.text: All four offers count towards the ceiling, so ₹75 lakh against a ₹40 lakh audit fee puts him well over, and none of them may be taken
options.misconception: sweeps in the two items the guideline expressly carves out of other work
options.why: Two of the four are carved out. Certification work required to be done by the statutory auditors and any representation before an authority are both excluded from the meaning of other work, and so is an audit under any other statute.

options.text: Only the ₹30 lakh assignment to Nanda's own firm counts, and being below the ₹40 lakh audit fee it may be accepted; what an independent firm in which a partner's wife is a partner earns is nothing to do with him
options.misconception: counts only the auditor's own fees, when the guideline aggregates the fees of the statutory auditor and his associate concerns
options.why: The guideline says in terms that the restriction applies in respect of fees for other work payable to the statutory auditors and their associate concerns put together, and it defines an associate concern to include a firm rendering such services in which a partner of the auditor firm or a relative is a partner.

options.text: The guideline does not reach this company at all, because the ₹50 crore turnover test applies to listed companies as it does to others and the restriction is aimed at unlisted public companies
options.misconception: reads a turnover test as an exclusion, when the company is well above ₹50 crore in any event
options.why: Whichever way the turnover qualifier is read, a listed company with a turnover of ₹300 crore is inside the guideline. The question the guideline then asks is only about the total remuneration for other work against the statutory audit fee.

citation.ref: Chapter IX — appointment as statutory auditor: the bar on accepting other work in regard to a public sector undertaking, Government company, listed company or other public company with a turnover of ₹50 crore or more once the total remuneration for it passes the statutory audit fee, the aggregation of fees payable to the statutory auditors and their associate concerns, and the three carve-outs — an audit some other statute demands, certification work required to be done by the statutory auditors, and any representation before an authority

items.scenario: CA Nanda is the statutory auditor of a listed company with a turnover of ₹300 crore. The audit fee for the year is ₹40 lakh. During the year the company offers his firm a management consultancy assignment for ₹30 lakh, and offers a further management consultancy assignment for ₹25 lakh to a partnership firm in which Nanda's partner's wife is a partner. It also asks him for a certification that the statutory auditors are required to give, for ₹12 lakh, and to appear for it before an appellate authority, for ₹8 lakh.

items.stem: How does Chapter VI of the Council General Guidelines count this?

options.text: The ceiling is sixty tax audit assignments per partner but a part-time practising partner is not taken into account, so the firm's collective limit is one hundred and eighty and two hundred exceeds it; the limit may be distributed between the partners in any manner whatsoever, so one partner signing them all is not itself the breach; the presumptive audits do not enter the count at all; and the head office and branches of one concern are one assignment
options.why: Four separate rules decide it. The ceiling stands at 60 tax audit assignments per partner in the firm, and a part-time practising partner is left out of that head count altogether, so three countable partners carry the firm to one hundred and eighty against the two hundred signed. Once the ceiling is worked out it may be split between the partners in any manner whatsoever, so the concentration in one man's hands is not itself the objection. Work done under sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE stays outside the reckoning entirely. And where one concern's head office and its branches are audited, the whole of that counts as one tax audit assignment.

options.text: The firm is inside the limit — four partners give two hundred and forty, the thirty presumptive audits and the four branch assignments both count towards it, and the total of two hundred and thirty-four is under
options.misconception: counts the part-time practising partner into the firm's ceiling and counts audits the guideline excludes from the reckoning
options.why: Two of the three steps are wrong in opposite directions. A part-time practising partner is not taken into account when reckoning the firm's tax audit assignments, and audits under sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE are not taken into account at all, so they cannot be added to the total either.

options.text: One partner may not sign more than sixty in any event, the ceiling being personal to each partner, so the firm is in breach the moment the sixty-first report was signed by him
options.misconception: reads the per-partner figure as a personal cap on signing, when the guideline lets the firm's aggregate be distributed between partners in any manner
options.why: The specified number is computed per partner but the resulting maximum may be distributed between the partners in any manner whatsoever — the Institute's own clarification is that one partner in a ten-partner firm may individually sign six hundred reports if the other nine sign none. What matters is the firm's aggregate.

options.text: Nothing is in breach — the guideline is a recommendation of the Council rather than a provision of the Act, and the audits under the presumptive sections make up the difference
options.misconception: treats a Council guideline as advisory, when contravening one is professional misconduct in its own right
options.why: Contravening any guideline issued by the Council is professional misconduct under Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule, so a guideline binds as firmly as a clause does. And the presumptive audits cannot make up a difference, because they do not enter the count.

citation.ref: Chapter VI — the ceiling on tax audits signed under section 44AB: 60 assignments per partner in a firm, the aggregate distributable between the partners in any manner whatsoever, audits under sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE excluded from the reckoning, the head office and branch offices of a concern regarded as one assignment, and a part-time practising partner not taken into account

items.scenario: A firm has four partners. One of them is a part-time practising partner. In the financial year just ended, one partner alone signed two hundred tax audit reports under section 44AB and no other partner signed any. The firm also completed thirty audits of assessees covered by the presumptive provisions in sections 44AD and 44AE, and it audited one concern's head office and its three branches, which it has counted as four assignments.

items.stem: How is the specified number of audit assignments counted here?

options.text: The number of partners is taken as it stands at the end of the financial year, so a partner admitted after acceptance enlarges the ceiling retrospectively and one who leaves reduces it
options.misconception: fixes the partner count at the year end, when the guideline fixes it at the date of acceptance of the assignment
options.why: The guideline fixes the date: how many partners the firm holds when it accepts the assignment is the figure that counts, so what happens to the partnership afterwards does not move the ceiling for an audit already accepted.

options.text: The ceiling belongs to the firm rather than to its partners, so thirty is the firm's limit whatever its size, and the exceptions for one person and dormant companies apply only to private companies
options.misconception: makes the ceiling a firm-level number and narrows the two exceptions to private companies
options.why: The specified number is construed as the specified number for every partner of the firm, so it scales with the countable partners. And the exception for one person companies and dormant companies is stated for audits whether in respect of private companies or other companies.

options.text: Thirty audit assignments per partner, with the partner in full-time employment elsewhere not counted, so the firm has one hundred and twenty; one person companies and dormant companies are excepted and do not enter the count; the head office and branches of one company are one assignment; the joint audit is taken into account; and the number of partners is taken as it stands on the date of acceptance
options.why: The ceiling stands at 30 audit assignments per partner in the firm; it covers private companies and every other company alike, and it excepts one person companies and dormant companies from the tally. A practising chartered accountant who holds full-time or part-time employment somewhere else drops out of the head count that fixes a firm's specified number, so four partners count here and not five. Where one firm audits a company's head office together with its branch offices, that is a single audit assignment, and one firm taking a branch or several branches of the same company likewise counts once. Audits accepted in combination with any other chartered accountant or firm do enter the count, so the joint audit tells. And the partner count used is the one standing on the date of acceptance of the assignment.
keywords: one person companies and dormant companies
in combination with any other chartered accountant

options.text: Thirty per partner across all five partners, giving one hundred and fifty, with the joint audit counted as half an assignment because responsibility is shared and each branch counted separately because each is a separate report
options.misconception: counts a partner in employment elsewhere, halves a joint audit and splits branch audits, none of which the guideline permits
options.why: Three errors in one. A partner in full-time employment elsewhere is not counted at all; an audit accepted in combination with another chartered accountant is taken into account whole; and the head office and branches of one company are one assignment however many reports are signed.

citation.ref: Chapter VIII — the specified number of audit assignments under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013: 30 assignments per partner with the exception of one person companies and dormant companies, audits accepted in combination with another chartered accountant taken into account, the head office and branch offices of a company regarded as one assignment, the number of partners taken on the date of acceptance, and a member in full-time or part-time employment elsewhere not counted

items.scenario: A firm has five partners on the date it is asked to accept a new company audit; one of them is in full-time employment with a bank and does not practise with the firm. Its register shows the audit of one company's head office and its four branches, all done by the firm; one audit accepted jointly with another firm; two one person companies; and three dormant companies.

items.stem: How do the Council's guidelines for the corporate form of practice answer him?

options.text: He must surrender his certificate of practice for the period, a whole-time office in a body corporate being an occupation for which the Council's general permission does not extend to a member holding one
options.misconception: treats the office as incompatible with practice, when the guidelines were made precisely to allow it alongside a full-time certificate
options.why: The guidelines exist to permit exactly this. The member retains a full-time certificate of practice, is regarded as being in full-time practice, and continues his attest work and his training of assistants.

options.text: He keeps a full-time certificate of practice and is regarded as being in full-time practice, so he continues attest functions in his individual or firm capacity and may train articled assistants; there is no restriction on the quantum of the equity held by him individually or with relatives; but the company's name must be approved by the Institute and the company registered with it, no audit practice may be carried on in corporate form, and it must not accept the internal audit or such other assignments prohibited for the statutory auditor firm
options.why: The Council opened this door itself: a practising member may serve as Managing Director, Whole-time Director or Manager where the body corporate does nothing but management consultancy and the other services section 2(2)(iv) permits. He keeps a full-time certificate of practice, counts as being in full-time practice, carries on attest work in whatever individual, proprietary or partnership capacity he practises in, and may still train articled and audit assistants. There is no restriction on the quantum of the equity holding — his own, or his and his relatives' taken together. What the guidelines do fix is the rest. The Institute approves the consultancy company's name and registers the company; no audit practice can be done in corporate form; and once he or his firm signs as statutory auditor of an entity, that company may take neither internal audit nor book-keeping nor anything else prohibited for the statutory auditor firm.
keywords: no restriction on the quantum of the equity holding
no audit practice can be done in corporate form
prohibited for the statutory auditor firm

options.text: He may take the office and hold any amount of equity, and the company may take the internal audit, the company being a separate person from the firm that signs the audit report
options.misconception: uses the company's separate legal personality to take work the statutory auditor firm could not take
options.why: The ethical compliance conditions shut that door in terms. Once the practitioner himself, or his sole proprietorship, or his partnership firm signs as statutory auditor of an entity, the consultancy company is barred from that entity's internal audit, from its book-keeping, and from any other professional assignment prohibited for the statutory auditor firm.

options.text: He may take the office but the company may also carry on audit practice in corporate form once it is registered with the Institute, registration being what makes the practice regular
options.misconception: reads registration with the Institute as authority to audit in corporate form, which the guidelines rule out expressly
options.why: Registration goes to the name and the standing of the consultancy company and nothing more. The guidelines clarify on abundant caution that no audit practice can be done in corporate form; what is permitted in corporate form is the consultancy practice previously done in individual or firm status.

citation.ref: Chapter XVII — guidelines for the corporate form of practice: the permission for a member to serve as Managing Director, Whole-time Director or Manager where the body corporate does nothing but management consultancy and the other services section 2(2)(iv) allows, the retention of a full-time certificate of practice with no cap on the equity he or his relatives may hold, the Institute's approval of the name and registration of the company, the bar on audit practice in corporate form, and the ethical compliance conditions on assignments prohibited for the statutory auditor firm

items.scenario: A member in practice wants to become the Managing Director of a company that he and his wife will wholly own, which will render only management consultancy and other services permitted by the Council. He asks four things: whether he must surrender his certificate of practice, whether he may still train articled assistants, whether his shareholding must be kept below some proportion, and whether the company may accept the internal audit of an entity where his own firm is the statutory auditor.

items.stem: Which of the five survive section 7?

options.text: Only the membership of the recognised foreign institute — every other entry is a designation or description other than chartered accountant, and the clause admits nothing else
options.misconception: reads the clause as admitting nothing but institute memberships, when the letters of a cost accountancy body and an empanelment as Registered Valuer are both permitted
options.why: The clause is narrow but it is not that narrow. The letters A.C.M.A. or F.C.M.A. may be used after the name by a member of that Institute, and an empanelment as an Insolvency Professional or a Registered Valuer may be mentioned on the visiting card and letter head.

options.text: The Cost Accountant designation, the letters F.C.M.A. and the directorship — the first two going together as one qualification and the third being a matter of public record in any event
options.misconception: lets the letters carry the designation with them and treats a publicly recorded office as free to mention
options.why: The two are deliberately separated: a member cannot designate himself a Cost Accountant though he may use the letters after his name. And a directorship is not free to mention because it is on a public record; members who are directors in companies are not permitted to mention those positions on professional documents.

options.text: The letters F.C.M.A., the membership of the recognised foreign institute, and the mention of being a Registered Valuer — but he may not designate himself a Cost Accountant, may not use the initials CPA, and may not mention his directorship
options.why: Three stand and three fall, and the line is not intuitive. The designation Cost Accountant is closed to him, yet the letters A.C.M.A. or F.C.M.A. may follow his name once he belongs to that Institute. Membership of an overseas accountancy institute may be mentioned where the Council has recognised the body, whether by a memorandum of understanding or by a mutual recognition agreement. Empanelment as an Insolvency Professional or a Registered Valuer may go on the visiting card and the letter head. Against those, a chartered accountant may not put on his professional stationery that he is an Income-tax Consultant, a Cost Accountant, a Company Secretary, a Cost Consultant or a Management Consultant; members are not permitted to use the initials CPA; and a member who sits on a company's board, belongs to a political party or holds office in a club or a similar body may not mention any of those positions.
keywords: not permitted to use the initials CPA

options.text: All except the initials CPA — the others are true statements of fact about the member's qualifications and offices, and a statement of fact cannot be an advertisement
options.misconception: treats truth as the test, when section 7 governs which descriptions may be used at all whether or not they are true
options.why: Truth is not the test. The member genuinely is a fellow of the cost accountancy institute and genuinely is a director, and he may still not designate himself a Cost Accountant or mention the directorship — section 7 governs which descriptions may be used, not whether they are accurate.

citation.ref: Section 7, with the Council's decisions on it — a member may use the letters A.C.M.A. or F.C.M.A. though he may not designate himself a Cost Accountant, may mention membership of a foreign institute of accountancy recognised by the Council through a memorandum of understanding or mutual recognition agreement, and may mention an empanelment as Insolvency Professional or Registered Valuer on his visiting card and letter head, while he may not describe himself as an Income-tax Consultant, Cost Accountant, Company Secretary, Cost Consultant or Management Consultant, may not use the initials CPA, and may not mention a directorship or a position in a political party, club or other organisation

items.scenario: A member in practice submits his new stationery for review. His visiting card describes him as a Cost Accountant, of which institute he is a fellow, and adds the letters F.C.M.A. after his name. It carries the initials CPA. It mentions his membership of an institute of accountancy abroad with which the Council has a memorandum of understanding. It records that he is empanelled as a Registered Valuer. And it names him as a director of a company on whose board he sits.

items.stem: What do the requirements say about the three?

options.text: None can be used as things stand — the reviewer must be a partner, another person in the firm who is a member of the Institute, a suitably qualified external person or a team drawn from those; on a listed audit he must besides carry experience and authority enough to serve as engagement partner on listed work; and where consultations become significant and objectivity cannot be held, somebody else inside the firm or a suitably qualified external person takes over one of the two roles, the reviewing or the consulting
options.why: The three fail on three different requirements. Eligibility is a closed list — a partner, somebody else inside the firm who is a member of the Institute, a suitably qualified external person, or a team drawn from those — so an employee outside the Institute is out. A listed audit narrows it further: the reviewer needs experience and authority to act as an audit engagement partner where the financial statements are a listed entity's, which the outside partner has never had. And consultation is permitted so that it does not by itself cost the reviewer his objectivity; but once the consultations grow significant in nature and extent, team and reviewer alike have to work at keeping that objectivity, and if they cannot, somebody else — inside the firm, or a suitably qualified external person — steps into one of the two roles, the reviewing or the consulting.
keywords: experience and authority to act as an audit engagement partner

options.text: The partner of the other firm is the only proper choice, an external reviewer being independent of the engagement in a way nobody inside the firm can be
options.misconception: treats externality as the qualification, when a listed-entity review needs experience and authority to act as an engagement partner on listed audits
options.why: A suitably qualified external person is one of the permitted choices, but a listed audit asks something more of whoever reviews it: experience and authority to act as an audit engagement partner where the entity is listed. This partner has never audited one.

options.text: The firm's own partner may act, since consultation by the engagement partner is expressly permitted and permitted consultation cannot damage the objectivity it is allowed to create
options.misconception: reads the permission to consult as unlimited, when the requirement turns on whether the consultations have become significant
options.why: The permission is there so that consultation does not by itself disqualify a reviewer, and it stops where the nature and extent of the consultations become significant. At that point objectivity has to be maintained by both sides, and where it cannot be, the roles are reassigned.

options.text: The senior employee may act — membership of the Institute goes to who may sign a report and not to who may review one, and the firm's own quality control system is what qualifies him
options.misconception: separates the reviewer's eligibility from membership of the Institute, which the requirement states directly
options.why: The requirement names it: another person in the firm acting as reviewer should be a member of the Institute. The firm's system does not supply the qualification.

citation.ref: the engagement quality control reviewer — who may be one (a partner, another member of the Institute inside the firm, a suitably qualified external person, or a team drawn from those), the further standing a listed audit asks of him (experience and authority to act as an audit engagement partner where the entity is listed), and the reassignment of either the reviewing or the consulting role to somebody else where significant consultations make objectivity impossible to hold

items.scenario: A firm has to put an engagement quality control reviewer on the audit of a listed company. Three names are proposed. A senior employee of the firm who is not a member of the Institute. A partner of another firm who has the capabilities and competence to act as an engagement partner but has never audited a listed entity. And a partner of this firm who has the standing for listed work but whom the engagement partner has consulted at length, week after week, on the very judgements the review will cover.

items.stem: What does SQC 1 require?

options.text: The report should only be issued after the difference is resolved; and where the reviewer's recommendations are not accepted by the engagement partner and the matter is not resolved to the reviewer's satisfaction, it is resolved by following the firm's established procedures, such as consulting another practitioner or firm, or a professional or regulatory body
options.why: Differences of opinion may arise within the engagement team, with those consulted, and between the engagement partner and the engagement quality control reviewer, and the rule is the same for all of them: the report should only be issued after resolution of such differences. Where the engagement partner turns down what the reviewer recommends and the reviewer is still not satisfied, the firm's established procedures settle it — taking the question, say, to another practitioner or firm, or a professional or regulatory body. That the engagement partner carries responsibility for the opinion does not let him sign over an unresolved difference.
keywords: another practitioner or firm, or a professional or regulatory body

options.text: A memorandum on file recording the reviewer's dissent is enough, because documentation of a difference of opinion is what the firm's system exists to capture
options.misconception: substitutes documenting the disagreement for resolving it, when the report may not be issued until it is resolved
options.why: Documentation is required as well, but it is not the answer to the question. The report should only be issued after resolution of the difference, so a memorandum recording that the difference is still open is a record that the report should not yet have been signed.

options.text: The reviewer's recommendations must be implemented, an unresolved difference at the review stage being resolved in favour of the reviewer by default
options.misconception: gives the reviewer a casting vote, when the requirement is a route to resolution rather than a rule about who wins
options.why: The requirement does not decide who is right. It routes the unresolved matter through the firm's established procedures — consultation with another practitioner or firm, or with a professional or regulatory body — and holds the report until that produces an answer.

options.text: The engagement partner's view prevails, the reviewer's role being to review rather than to decide and the responsibility for the opinion resting with the partner
options.misconception: turns the reviewer's lack of decision-making power into a rule that the partner may sign over his objection
options.why: The reviewer indeed does not make decisions for the engagement team, and the review does not reduce the engagement partner's responsibilities. Neither proposition permits a report to be issued while a difference between the two is unresolved.

citation.ref: differences of opinion — within the engagement team, with those consulted and between the engagement partner and the engagement quality control reviewer, with the report issued only after resolution and an unresolved difference taken through the firm's established procedures such as consulting another practitioner or firm or a professional or regulatory body

items.scenario: The engagement quality control reviewer has identified two issues and recommended changes. The engagement partner does not accept either recommendation, and after two meetings the reviewer remains dissatisfied. The client's lender wants the signed report tomorrow. The manager proposes to sign, put a memorandum on file recording the reviewer's dissent, and treat the reviewer's role as advisory because responsibility for the opinion is the engagement partner's alone.

items.stem: What do the engagement partner's leadership responsibilities require of him?

options.text: He must document the messages he gave the team, the leadership element being satisfied by a record that the tone was set rather than by the tone itself
options.misconception: converts a requirement about conduct into a documentation requirement
options.why: What is required is the conduct: actions and appropriate messages that emphasise the named matters. A record of having said the wrong things is not the discharge of the responsibility.

options.text: Nothing at the opening meeting — the leadership element belongs to the firm under SQC 1, and the engagement partner's own duties begin with the direction, supervision and review of the work
options.misconception: moves leadership responsibility on an engagement up to the firm, when the engagement partner carries it for each engagement
options.why: The firm carries leadership responsibility for quality within the firm, and the engagement partner separately takes responsibility for overall quality on each audit engagement, of which the messages he gives the team are the named means.

options.text: Only the remark about the junior — the deadline and the instruction on what to escalate are matters of engagement management on which the standard is silent
options.misconception: reads the deadline and escalation instructions as neutral management, when both cut against named elements of the leadership responsibility
options.why: Both are covered. Making the deadline the measure of a good job runs against the emphasis that quality is essential, and telling the team to bring nothing but numbers runs against the ability to raise concerns and against complying with the firm's policies and procedures.

options.text: His actions and his messages to the team must emphasise that quality is essential in performing audit engagements, the importance of performing work that complies with professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements, of complying with the firm's quality control policies and procedures, of the team's ability to raise concerns without fear of reprisals, and of issuing auditor's reports that are appropriate in the circumstances
options.why: Leadership responsibility for quality is the first of the engagement partner's responsibilities and it is discharged in what he does and says to the team, not in the review at the end. His actions and appropriate messages must emphasise the fact that quality is essential in performing audit engagements; the importance to audit quality of performing work that complies with professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements, of complying with the firm's quality control policies and procedures, of the team being able to raise concerns without fear of reprisals, and of issuing auditor's reports that are appropriate in the circumstances. Each of the three things he said cuts against one of those.
keywords: quality is essential in performing audit engagements

citation.ref: leadership responsibilities for quality on audits — the engagement partner's actions and appropriate messages emphasising that quality is essential, the importance of complying with professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements and with the firm's quality control policies and procedures, the room a team must have to raise concerns without fear of reprisals, and the issuing of auditor's reports that are appropriate in the circumstances

items.scenario: At the opening meeting of an audit the engagement partner tells the team three things. The reporting deadline is the measure of a good job. Nothing is to be brought to him that is not a number he has asked for. And he refers to a junior on last year's engagement who raised a concern about a client estimate as having made the file look bad. He then leaves the team to it, saying his own work begins at the final review.

items.stem: What is the materiality computed for the group actually used for?

options.text: To assess the appropriateness of the consolidation adjustments, permanent and current period, made by management in preparing the consolidated financial statements, and to determine whether a component's financial statements are material to the group so that further components are scoped in and the work of other auditors used — and the principal auditor separately obtains confirmations from component auditors on matters such as independence and compliance with the code of ethics and the information required for the consolidation and the disclosures
options.why: Group materiality has two named uses and the manager has taken neither. It is used to assess the appropriateness of the consolidation adjustments — the permanent ones and this period's alike — which management has put through in drawing up the consolidated financial statements. And the parent auditor can use the materiality computed at group level to determine whether a component's financial statements are material to the group, and so whether additional components should be scoped in and the work of other auditors used. Alongside that, the principal auditor obtains certain confirmations from component auditors, such as independence, compliance with the code of ethics, and the information required for the consolidation and the disclosure requirements.
keywords: assess the appropriateness of the consolidation adjustments

options.text: To set the component materiality for every component and nothing else, group materiality being an input to the component auditors' work rather than to the parent auditor's own
options.misconception: reduces group materiality to a figure passed downward, when its two named uses are the parent auditor's own
options.why: Communicating a materiality to a component auditor is one thing the principal auditor does where he believes it is required for a true and fair view on the consolidated statements. It is not what group materiality is for: it is used on the consolidation adjustments and on the scoping decision, both of which are the parent auditor's own work.

options.text: To be compared with each component auditor's own materiality, the lower of the two governing the group audit so that nothing material to a component escapes the consolidated statements
options.misconception: builds the group materiality out of the component auditors' figures, which are computed on a standalone basis for a different opinion
options.why: A component's materiality is computed component-wise on a standalone basis for the purpose of an opinion on that component's own financial statements. It is a figure for a different opinion, and taking the lower of the two does not turn it into the group's.

options.text: To decide whether the consolidated financial statements as a whole are materially misstated at the reporting stage, the adjustments themselves being management's arithmetic and outside the auditor's materiality judgement
options.misconception: treats the consolidation adjustments as arithmetic rather than as the thing group materiality is used to assess
options.why: The adjustments are precisely what group materiality is used on. Permanent adjustments turn on goodwill or capital reserve and the amount attributable to non-controlling interests, and current period adjustments on eliminations, deferred tax and harmonisation of policies — none of it is mere arithmetic.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: materiality in the audit of consolidated financial statements — computed for the group as a whole, used to assess the appropriateness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments made by management and to determine whether a component's financial statements are material to the group so that additional components are scoped in, with confirmations obtained from component auditors on independence, the code of ethics and the information required for the consolidation and disclosures

items.scenario: You have computed materiality for the group as a whole. Your manager proposes to use it only to size the samples on the parent's own balances; to accept the parent management's permanent and current period consolidation adjustments as given, since they are arithmetic rather than judgement; to decide which components to scope in by revenue share alone without reference to any materiality; and to put the component auditors' reports on file without asking those auditors anything.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Both may be consolidated as drawn, the limits of six months and three months applying to the preparation of the components' own financial statements rather than to their use in a consolidation
options.misconception: attaches the limits to the components' own reporting obligations, when they govern the difference permitted in a consolidation
options.why: The limits are stated for the consolidation itself. Whatever a component owes its own members by way of reporting, the gap tolerated when it is consolidated stops at six months under AS and at three months under Ind AS.

options.text: The 30 September component cannot be consolidated on those statements at all, the difference between reporting dates not being permitted to exceed three months under Ind AS and six months under AS; and the 31 December component's figures require adjustments for the effects of significant transactions or other events occurring between its date and the parent's
options.why: Same-date drawing is the rule: a component goes into the consolidation on figures made up as at the parent's own reporting date. Where that cannot practicably be done and the component's date differs, its figures have to be adjusted for whatever significant transactions or other events fell in between the two dates. And a ceiling sits over the whole arrangement — the gap may not be more than six months where AS governs, and it shrinks to three months in the case of financial statements under Ind AS. So a six-month gap in an Ind AS group is outside what is permitted, however carefully the figures are adjusted.
keywords: not be more than six months
three months in the case of financial statements under Ind AS

options.text: Both may be consolidated as drawn, provided the difference in reporting dates and its effect are disclosed, disclosure being the remedy the framework gives for a difference of this kind
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a substitute for the adjustments and for the outer limit on the gap
options.why: Disclosure has its own place — where the reporting periods of components have changed with a material effect, the entity discloses the change and the manner of its treatment. It does not stand in for the adjustments for intervening transactions, and it cannot widen a gap the framework caps at three months under Ind AS.

options.text: Neither may be consolidated on those statements, every component having to be drawn to the parent's own reporting date without exception
options.misconception: reads the same-date requirement as absolute, when the framework permits a difference where the same date is not practicable
options.why: The requirement is that the statements should be drawn to the same reporting date, with an allowance where that is not practicable. A three-month difference under Ind AS is inside what is allowed, provided the intervening significant transactions and events are adjusted for.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: components with differing reporting dates — statements drawn to the same reporting date as the parent where practicable, adjustments for the effects of significant transactions or other events occurring between the dates where it is not, the difference in any case not more than six months for financial statements under AS and three months under Ind AS, and disclosure of a change in a component's reporting period having a material effect

items.scenario: A parent reporting under Ind AS has a 31 March year end. One component cannot practicably draw its financial statements to that date and draws them to 31 December. Another draws them to 30 September. The consolidation senior proposes to take both sets of figures into the consolidation as they stand, on the footing that a difference in year ends is a presentation matter and that the components' own auditors have reported on the statements as drawn.

items.stem: What does the auditor have to consider?

options.text: Nothing beyond the shareholding — control for the purposes of consolidation is a question of voting rights, and an investor below one half consolidates only where a shareholders' agreement gives it further votes
options.misconception: makes voting rights the whole of the control question, when de facto control is expressly to be considered
options.why: De facto control is considered precisely because voting rights do not answer the question. It is defined by the practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally, and it does not depend on an agreement conferring extra votes.

options.text: De facto control — a shareholder whose votes stop well short of half nonetheless carrying the practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally — and, separately, the off balance sheet entities which sometimes do not qualify as subsidiaries but to which the parent has transferred the risks of business ventures
options.why: Identifying the components is not settled by counting votes. Control can be de facto: an investor holding short of a voting majority still has the practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally; that possibility has to be weighed while the auditor satisfies himself that every component is in. He must look as well at off balance sheet entities, which often fall short of the subsidiary definition and yet may be where the parent has parked the risks of one business venture or another. A dispersed shareholding that has never acted together, and six years of nominating a board majority, are exactly the facts the first of those two is aimed at.
keywords: practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally

options.text: The composition of the board alone, which decides control, so the auditor's work is confined to counting the parent's nominees against the total number of directors
options.misconception: reduces de facto control to an arithmetic test on board seats, when it turns on the practical ability to direct the relevant activities
options.why: The board's composition is evidence and not the test. What is being asked is whether the investor has the practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally, which is judged on the whole picture including how dispersed the other holdings are and how they have in fact been voted.

options.text: Only the vehicle to which the risks were transferred, that being a matter of substance, while a forty per cent holding is a matter of form settled by the register of members
options.misconception: applies substance to the off balance sheet vehicle and form to the shareholding, when both are questions of substance
options.why: Both are questions of substance and they are raised side by side. The off balance sheet entity is one of them; de facto control over the forty per cent held entity is the other, and it is answered on the practical ability to direct that entity's relevant activities.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: identifying the components of a group — de facto control, where a holding short of a voting majority still carries the practical ability to direct the relevant activities unilaterally, and off balance sheet entities, which often fall outside the subsidiary definition and yet hold risks of business ventures the parent has moved across to them

items.scenario: A parent holds shares carrying forty per cent of the voting rights in an entity. The rest is spread among several thousand small holders who have never voted together on anything. For six years the parent has nominated four of the seven directors and every board resolution has gone its way. The parent has also transferred the risks of two business ventures to a vehicle that does not meet the definition of a subsidiary. Management's view is that neither entity is a component, because voting rights below one half cannot amount to control.

items.stem: How is the work actually ordered and classified?

options.text: Tax due diligence must be reported separately in every case, being a separate exercise, and it is the one discipline that cannot be folded into the financial work
options.misconception: reads the separateness of the tax exercise as a bar on its being reported inside the financial work
options.why: It is a separate exercise and it is nevertheless generally included in the financial due diligence, because the tax position is an integral component of the financial status of the company.

options.text: The order is a matter of convenience — the exercises are independent disciplines and the buyer may take them in whichever sequence suits the deal timetable
options.misconception: treats the sequence as free, when financial due diligence is to follow the completion of commercial due diligence
options.why: One ordering is stated. Financial due diligence should be performed after the completion of commercial due diligence, because what the financial numbers have to be tested against is the commercial and strategic case the acquirer has formed.

options.text: There are three exercises — commercial, financial and legal — and matters such as personnel and the environment are covered inside the commercial work rather than separately
options.misconception: shortens the classification to three, when personnel, information systems and environmental due diligence are separately named
options.why: The classification names seven: commercial or operational, financial, tax, information systems, legal, environmental and personnel. Personnel due diligence has its own purpose — asking whether the staffing rules the target already runs on will sit comfortably with what the restructuring needs, or can be reshaped until they do.

options.text: Financial due diligence is performed after the completion of commercial or operational due diligence; the tax exercise stands on its own footing and yet, because what it measures runs right through a company's financial standing, its findings usually ride inside the financial work; and the remaining discipline-wise exercises are information systems, legal, environmental and personnel due diligence
options.why: Due diligence is sub-classified into discipline-wise exercises and two of them have a fixed relationship. Commercial or operational due diligence is generally performed by the acquiring enterprise and involves an evaluation from commercial, strategic and operational perspectives — whether the proposed merger would create operational synergies, for instance. Financial due diligence, the analysis of the books of account and other information on financial matters, should be performed after the completion of commercial due diligence. Tax stands as its own exercise; being an integral component of the financial status a buyer is measuring, it usually rides inside the financial work rather than standing apart. The others are information systems, legal, environmental and personnel due diligence.
keywords: after the completion of commercial due diligence
integral component of the financial status
information systems, legal, environmental and personnel

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — the classification of due diligence into commercial or operational, financial, tax, information systems, legal, environmental and personnel, with financial due diligence performed after the completion of commercial due diligence and tax due diligence generally included within it

items.scenario: A buyer's team is planning the work on a target. It intends to start with the books of account and the financial records, to run a separate tax exercise that will be reported apart from everything else, and to treat the commercial and strategic assessment as something the business development team can do afterwards if there is time.

items.stem: What do the six have in common in a due diligence?

options.text: They are all matters for the warranties and indemnities rather than for the price, since an asset carried too high is a question of accounting policy on which the seller has given a representation
options.misconception: pushes valuation questions into the warranties, when over-valued assets bear directly on the price the buyer pays
options.why: Over-valued assets go to the price, because the buyer is paying for a net asset position that does not exist. Warranties and indemnities are how a contingent or disputed exposure is allocated between the parties, which is a different problem.

options.text: They are all over-valued assets — the head under which a financial due diligence collects uncollectable receivables, obsolete or slow-moving inventories, litigated assets and property, investments carried at cost though the realisable value is much lower, infructuous project or deferred revenue expenditure, and group company balances under reconciliation
options.why: A due diligence is looking for two things the audited balance sheet does not tell the buyer: hidden liabilities and over-valued assets, and all six fall under the second. The head collects uncollected or uncollectable receivables; obsolete, slow or non-moving inventories or inventories valued above net realisable value, including large stocks of packing materials carrying the company's name; underused or obsolete plant and machinery and assets impaired by a fall in market value; assets carried at more than current market value through capitalisation of what is really revenue expenditure; litigated assets and property; investments carried at cost though the realisable value is much lower; investments carrying a very low rate of return; infructuous project expenditure or deferred revenue expenditure; and group company balances under reconciliation. That an audit report is unqualified says nothing about any of them, the audit having answered a different question.

options.text: They are all hidden liabilities, the head under which a due diligence collects exposures the balance sheet does not carry, and each of the six reduces the net worth the buyer is paying for
options.misconception: files carrying values that are too high under the head for liabilities that are missing altogether
options.why: Both heads reduce the net worth, which is why they are easy to swap, and they are separate. Hidden liabilities are exposures the statements do not carry at all — show cause notices not yet matured into demands, letters of comfort, future lease liabilities, unresolved labour litigation, an agreement to buy back shares at a stated price. These six are assets carried at more than they are worth.

options.text: Only three of them qualify — the receivables, the packing material and the abandoned project — the litigated land, the investments and the group balance being disputes rather than valuations
options.misconception: excludes litigated and unreconciled items from the over-valued assets head, which names all three
options.why: The head names litigated assets and property, investments carried at cost though the realisable value is much lower, and group company balances under reconciliation, each in its own right. A dispute about an asset is one of the reasons its carrying value cannot be relied on.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — over-valued assets in a financial due diligence: uncollected or uncollectable receivables, obsolete and slow-moving inventories or inventories above net realisable value, underused or obsolete plant and machinery, assets carried above current market value through capitalisation of revenue expenditure, litigated assets and property, investments carried at cost though the realisable value is much lower, investments carrying a very low return, infructuous project or deferred revenue expenditure, and group company balances under reconciliation

items.scenario: A financial due diligence on a manufacturer turns up six things in the balance sheet. Receivables from a customer now in liquidation. A very large stock of printed packing material carrying the target's own name. A plot of land under litigation. Investments carried at cost whose realisable value is a small fraction of it. A deferred revenue expenditure balance for a project abandoned three years ago. And a group company balance that has been under reconciliation for two years.
