The seller says all six are supported by an unqualified audit report and none of them is a liability.

items.stem: What does the reporting of prior audit issues require?

options.text: He should re-perform the original testing on all eleven issues and report fresh findings, the previous year's report having been superseded by this year's work
options.misconception: replaces the monitoring of prior issues with a fresh audit, when the standard asks for tracking and evaluation of the corrective action
options.why: Monitoring and reporting here means the periodic tracking of issues raised during prior audits and the evaluation of the corrective actions the auditee has taken, reporting open and pending matters to management and those charged with governance. Re-auditing everything answers a different question and loses the trail on what was promised.

options.text: An Action Taken Report carrying a reference to the previous audit report containing the reported issues, the implementation action agreed by management with its target implementation date, the status of the action taken classified as implemented or not implemented, the residual risk and rating for any unimplemented action, findings not implemented for a long period, and any critical finding requiring immediate action — and where no action is taken within a reasonable time he draws management's attention to it and ascertains the reasons where his recommendations have not been implemented
options.why: Closing out prior audit issues is the Chief Internal Auditor's to watch, and to watch continuously: he sees the agreed action plans through on time, and what he puts up is usually an Action Taken Report on the earlier audits. Such a report carries a pointer back to the report the issues came from; the action management agreed to, with its target implementation date; the state of that action, marked implemented or not; the residual risk and rating carried by anything left undone; findings that have sat unimplemented a long while; and any critical finding needing immediate action. Where nothing has been done within a reasonable time he should draw management's attention to it, and where his suggestions or recommendations have gone unacted upon he should find out why.

options.text: He should implement the four open items himself, having identified them and knowing what is needed, and report them closed
options.misconception: has the internal auditor take over the action plans, which would put him in charge of the controls he audits
options.why: The responsibility to implement the action plans remains with the management. An internal auditor who implements them is auditing his own work the next time round.

options.text: A count of open and closed issues is enough, the responsibility to implement the action plans resting with management, so the status of each is management's report to make and not the internal auditor's
options.misconception: uses management's ownership of the action plans to shrink the internal auditor's monitoring duty to a headcount
options.why: The responsibility to implement does rest with management, and the responsibility to monitor the closure of prior audit issues rests with the Chief Internal Auditor. What that monitoring produces is the Action Taken Report with its named contents, not a count.

citation.ref: Monitoring and Reporting of Prior Audit Issues — the Chief Internal Auditor's responsibility for monitoring the closure of prior audit issues, the contents of a typical Action Taken Report, and the requirement to draw management's attention where no follow-up action is taken within a reasonable time and to ascertain the reasons where recommendations have not been implemented

items.scenario: The audit committee asks the Chief Internal Auditor what became of last year's findings. He proposes to answer with one line: four of eleven remain open. Two of those four have had no action of any kind for eighteen months. On a third, management considered his recommendation and decided against it, and he has not asked why.

items.stem: What are they?

options.text: The detection and prevention of fraud, which is the purpose for which an internal audit function is established and the reason the external auditor looks at its work
options.misconception: substitutes one thing an internal audit function may find for the six named objectives of the function
options.why: Fraud may come out of internal audit work, and the prevention and detection of fraud is the responsibility of management and those charged with governance rather than the object of the function. The six named objectives are wider and none of them is framed that way.

options.text: Whatever the terms of the engagement provide, the scope being a matter for the appointing authority alone with no standard content
options.misconception: treats the scope as wholly contractual, when it has a named indicative content whatever the engagement adds
options.why: The scope and objective of internal audit do turn on how large the entity is, how it is put together and what its management asks of the function. Even so there is an indicative list of objectives and scope, of which monitoring of internal controls, examination of financial and operating information, review of operating activities, review of compliance with laws and regulations, risk management and governance are the six.

options.text: Examination of financial and operating information and monitoring of internal controls only — risk management and governance being the board's responsibilities and so outside the function's scope
options.misconception: excludes risk management and governance from the scope of the function because they are the board's responsibilities
options.why: Both are named inside the scope. That risk management and governance are the board's responsibilities is why the internal audit function evaluates them and reports on them; the definition of internal audit is framed around enhancing governance in the first place.

options.text: Monitoring of internal controls; examination of financial and operating information; review of operating activities; review of compliance with laws and regulations; risk management; and governance — internal auditing being not confined to financial transactions
options.why: Independent assurance is what an internal audit function supplies — on how well internal controls and risk-management processes are working — so that governance improves and the organisation reaches what it set out to reach. It is not confined to financial transactions: it includes review of operational activities, the underlying internal controls, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The objectives and scope of the internal audit function may include monitoring of internal controls, examination of financial and operating information, review of operating activities, review of compliance with laws and regulations, risk management, and governance. A function doing only what the junior describes would be one whose scope is narrow, which is a finding about that function rather than a statement about what internal audit is.
keywords: review of compliance with laws and regulations

citation.ref: the objectives and scope of an internal audit function — monitoring of internal controls, examination of financial and operating information, review of operating activities, review of compliance with laws and regulations, risk management and governance, internal auditing not being confined to financial transactions

items.scenario: A junior on the external audit team reads the internal audit charter and reports back that the function does nothing but vouch payments and reconcile the bank accounts, so there can be nothing in its work worth the external auditor's attention. The engagement partner asks him what the objectives and scope of an internal audit function are said to include.

items.stem: What is the detection risk the model gives, and what does it mean for the work?

options.text: 40 per cent — the detection risk is the combined inherent and control risk, since that is the risk the substantive procedures are designed to address
options.misconception: names the risk of material misstatement as the detection risk, when they are different risks and one belongs to the entity while the other belongs to the auditor
options.why: 40 per cent is the risk of material misstatement, which is inherent risk multiplied by control risk. It exists before the audit begins and the auditor cannot change it. Detection risk is the risk that he will not detect a misstatement that exists, and it is the only one of the three he controls.

options.text: 5 per cent — the acceptable detection risk is the audit risk the firm has fixed, the other two being matters for the entity rather than for the audit plan
options.misconception: sets detection risk equal to audit risk, which would make the assessment of inherent and control risk change nothing about the audit
options.why: If detection risk equalled audit risk the assessments would be decorative: the same substantive work would follow whether the risk of material misstatement was 40 per cent or 4 per cent. The whole point of the model is that the assessed risk of material misstatement decides how much detection risk is left over.

options.text: 12.5 per cent — audit risk is inherent risk multiplied by control risk multiplied by detection risk, so detection risk is 5 per cent divided by the 40 per cent risk of material misstatement, and the lower the figure the more persuasive the evidence the substantive procedures must produce
options.why: Audit risk is expressed as the product of the three: AR equals IR multiplied by CR multiplied by DR. Inherent risk and control risk together are the risk of material misstatement, here 80 per cent of 50 per cent, which is 40 per cent. Detection risk is then the audit risk divided by that figure, 5 per cent over 40 per cent, which is 12.5 per cent. The acceptable level of detection risk for a given level of audit risk bears an inverse relationship to the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level, so a high assessed risk squeezes detection risk down and the auditor must obtain more persuasive audit evidence.

options.text: 2 per cent — the three risks are multiplied together, so detection risk is 5 per cent of the 40 per cent risk of material misstatement
options.misconception: multiplies the audit risk by the risk of material misstatement, when the model treats audit risk as the product and detection risk as the unknown to be solved for
options.why: The multiplication runs the other way. Audit risk is the product of all three, so the two the auditor has assessed go into the denominator and the one he controls comes out: 5 per cent divided by 40 per cent, not 5 per cent of it.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — audit risk expressed as the product of inherent risk, control risk and detection risk, the risk of material misstatement as inherent risk multiplied by control risk, and the inverse relationship between the acceptable detection risk and the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level

items.scenario: A firm's audit methodology fixes the audit risk it is prepared to accept on every engagement at 5 per cent. On this engagement the team has assessed inherent risk on the revenue assertions at 80 per cent and control risk on the same assertions at 50 per cent. The manager now has to set the detection risk the substantive work must be planned to achieve.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two entries?

options.text: Only the detection risk entry — control risk may properly be assessed at nil where the controls have been tested and found to operate without exception, which is what the previous year's testing established
options.misconception: reads a clean test result as proof that control risk has been removed, when the inherent limitations of internal control keep it above zero whatever the testing shows
options.why: Testing can lower the assessed control risk; it cannot remove it. Some control risk will always exist because of the inherent limitations of any system of internal control, management override among them, and last year's result is in any event evidence about last year.

options.text: Neither — control risk and detection risk are both matters of the auditor's professional judgement, and a planning file records the judgement rather than a formula
options.misconception: treats the relationships between the three risks as a matter of judgement, when the model fixes them and only the assessments inside it are judgements
options.why: The assessments are judgements; the relationships are not. Audit risk is the product of the three risks, the risk of material misstatement is inherent risk multiplied by control risk, and the acceptable detection risk moves inversely to it. A judgement that breaks one of those is a mistake rather than a view.

options.text: Only the control risk entry — the detection risk entry is right, because a higher assessed risk of material misstatement means the entity carries more of the total audit risk and the auditor proportionately less
options.misconception: treats audit risk as a fixed quantity shared between the entity and the auditor, so that more of one leaves less of the other to worry about
options.why: Audit risk is not a quantity divided between them. It is the product of the risks, and the auditor holds it to an acceptably low level. When the risk of material misstatement rises the only term left to adjust is detection risk, and it has to fall.

options.text: Both — some control risk will always exist because every system of internal control has inherent limitations, so it can never be assessed at nil; and the acceptable detection risk moves inversely to the assessed risk of material misstatement, so raising the assessment lowers the detection risk the auditor may accept rather than raising it
options.why: The first entry states an impossibility. Some control risk will always exist because of the inherent limitations of any internal control system, so however well the controls tested, the risk they will fail to prevent or to detect and correct a material misstatement is not extinguished. The second entry inverts the relationship. The acceptable level of detection risk for a given level of audit risk bears an inverse relationship to the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level, so a risk raised from low to high leaves the auditor less detection risk to spend and obliges him to obtain more persuasive audit evidence.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — control risk always existing because of the inherent limitations of any internal control system, and the acceptable level of detection risk for a given level of audit risk bearing an inverse relationship to the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level

items.scenario: A partner reviewing a planning file finds two entries. The first records control risk on the purchases cycle as nil, on the ground that the company's controls were tested last year and found to work without a single exception. The second records that because the assessed risk of material misstatement on inventory valuation has been raised from low to high, the team will accept a correspondingly higher detection risk so that the timetable is not disturbed.

items.stem: How does SA 315 (Revised) actually divide the assertions?

options.text: Into three categories, but the allocation is by risk rather than by name — an assertion sits wherever the auditor has assessed the risk of material misstatement as significant
options.misconception: makes the categories a product of the risk assessment, when they are fixed definitions the risk assessment is then carried out against
options.why: The categories come first and the assessment is made against them. For each class of transactions, account balance and disclosure the auditor assesses the risk for each individual assertion, which he cannot do unless he already knows which assertions belong there.

options.text: Into three categories carrying the same four assertions in each — existence, completeness, accuracy and valuation — the category deciding only what the assertion is asked about
options.misconception: makes the three categories a single list applied three times, which is the assistant's own error restated
options.why: The lists differ in length and in content. Transactions and events carry five, and cut-off and occurrence appear there and nowhere else in that form; balances carry four including rights and obligations; presentation and disclosure carry four including classification and understandability.

options.text: Into two categories only — assertions about classes of transactions and assertions about account balances, presentation and disclosure being a matter of the applicable financial reporting framework rather than of assertions
options.misconception: drops the third category, when presentation and disclosure carries four assertions of its own that the auditor assesses like any other
options.why: There are three. Presentation and disclosure has its own four assertions — occurrence and rights and obligations, completeness, classification and understandability, and accuracy and valuation — and a disclosure can be misstated in each of those ways without any balance being wrong.

options.text: Into three categories that do not carry the same names — five for classes of transactions and events for the period, being occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut-off and classification; four for account balances at the period end, being existence, rights and obligations, completeness, and valuation and allocation; and four for presentation and disclosure, being occurrence and rights and obligations, completeness, classification and understandability, and accuracy and valuation
options.why: The three categories are named separately and their assertions are not interchangeable. Cut-off belongs to transactions and events, because it asks whether a transaction was recorded in the correct accounting period; existence belongs to balances, because it asks whether an asset, liability or equity interest is there at all; and understandability belongs to presentation and disclosure, because it asks whether the financial information is appropriately presented and described and whether the disclosures are clearly expressed. Completeness is the one word that appears in all three, and it means something different in each.
keywords: Cut-off belongs to transactions and events
understandability belongs to presentation and disclosure

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — how assertions are grouped into three categories, which assertions are named in each of them, and what the auditor uses the grouping for

items.scenario: An article assistant is tabulating the assertions his senior has assessed. He has put cut-off under account balances, existence under classes of transactions, and understandability under account balances, and he has written that each of the three categories carries the same four assertions under different names.

items.stem: How does SA 315 (Revised) have the two risks assessed and answered?

options.text: Both are assertion level risks — every risk ultimately shows up in some assertion, so both are answered by procedures on the balances affected, which is what extending the inventory sample does
options.misconception: collapses the two levels into one, leaving no room for the overall responses that a pervasive risk requires
options.why: A pervasive risk affects many assertions and cannot be answered by procedures on one of them. That is why the Standard separates the two levels: the overall financial statement level risk gets an overall response, and extending one sample leaves the rest of the statements exactly where they were.

options.text: Both are overall financial statement level risks, an incompetent preparer and an unsaleable product line each going to the reliability of the statements as a whole
options.misconception: raises a risk identified with one balance and one assertion to the pervasive level, which would leave the assertion level assessment with nothing in it
options.why: The inventory problem is identified with a particular balance and a particular assertion — the valuation and allocation of that inventory — and nothing about it spreads across the statements. Treating a specific risk as pervasive gives up the precision the assertion level assessment exists to provide.

options.text: Neither is a risk of material misstatement until a misstatement has been found — competence and obsolescence are matters for the management letter, and the risk assessment records only identified errors
options.misconception: waits for a misstatement before recognising a risk, when the assessment is of what could go wrong rather than of what has been found to have gone wrong
options.why: The assessment relates identified risks to what can go wrong at the assertion level and considers the likelihood of misstatement, including the possibility of multiple misstatements. It is made before the substantive work and is what directs it.

options.text: The accountant's incompetence is a risk at the overall financial statement level, because the errors it produces will not be confined to one balance or to one assertion, and it calls for an overall response; the obsolescent inventory is a risk at the assertion level, identified with the valuation and allocation assertion on that balance, and it is answered by procedures directed at that assertion
options.why: Risks are assessed at two levels and the level decides the response. A risk at the overall financial statement level relates pervasively to the financial statements as a whole and potentially affects many assertions — an incompetent accountant will produce errors across balances, transaction streams and disclosures, and across completeness, accuracy, existence and valuation alike. A risk at the assertion level attaches to a particular class of transactions, account balance or disclosure, and an assessment is made for each individual assertion, which is why the valuation risk on obsolescent inventory can be high in the same audit in which the valuation risk on payables is low.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the two levels at which risks of material misstatement get assessed, what makes a risk pervasive enough to touch the statements as a whole and many assertions with them, and why the other level is worked assertion by assertion inside a single class of transactions, balance or disclosure

items.scenario: Two findings on the same audit. The chief accountant has been promoted into a post he is not competent for and has been preparing the whole of the financial statements alone for eight months. Separately, the inventory of a discontinued product line is being carried at cost although it has not moved for two years. The manager proposes to answer both by extending the sample on inventory valuation.

items.stem: How does the module have an audit programme drawn up on a first appointment?

options.text: In one stage, completed before fieldwork begins, because a programme is a set of instructions to the assistants and instructions that change during the audit cannot control the work — and the programme may depart from the overall plan, being the more detailed of the two documents
options.misconception: treats the programme as fixed once issued and as free to override the plan, when it is built in stages and the plan governs it
options.why: Both halves fail. The details cannot be written until the internal and accounting procedures have been reviewed, because the deficiencies found there decide them. And the programme does not override the plan — the framework under the overall plan is strictly adhered to, and a necessary divergence is dealt with by modifying the plan first.

options.text: There is no set order — a typical audit programme is published for each industry and the auditor adopts the one for chemicals, adjusting it for the company's size
options.misconception: assumes a standard programme exists to be adopted, when procedures vary so widely with the entity that no typical programme can be drawn up
options.why: No two concerns match one another in the conditions they work under, in how they are organised, in the business they carry on, or in the state their books are kept in. Procedures therefore vary too widely for any typical audit programme to be drawn up at all, and the three stages are what replaces one.

options.text: In three stages — a broad outline first; the detail added once the accounting and internal procedures have been looked over, so that whatever deficiencies in the system of internal control that review exposes settle what the detail has to be; and the extent of the special first-time and opening balance procedures fixed once the detailed checking is finished — and where the programme needs a divergence from the overall plan, the plan is modified first and only then is the matter taken into the programme
options.why: The order exists because the middle stage depends on knowledge the firm does not yet have. A broad outline is drawn up to begin with; the details are filled in only after the internal and accounting procedures have been reviewed, so that the deficiencies in the system of internal control decide what is checked and how much; and the special procedures — independent verification of debtor and creditor balances, physical inspection of fixed assets, personal inspection of items of closing inventory and testing their values — are settled after the detailed checking is over. On the second question, the framework provided under the overall plan is to be strictly adhered to: if a divergence becomes necessary the overall plan is modified after due consideration, and only thereafter does the specific matter go into the programme.
keywords: deficiencies in the system of internal control

options.text: In two stages — an outline, then the details after the review of internal control — the special first-time procedures being unnecessary because a first-year audit is planned in the same way as any other
options.misconception: drops the third stage, when a first appointment carries opening balance and verification work that an established engagement does not
options.why: The third stage is the one a first appointment specifically needs. After the detailed checking procedure is over, the auditor determines the extent to which the special first-time and opening balance procedures must be applied — independent verification of balances, physical inspection of assets, personal inspection of stock items and testing their values.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — drawing up the audit programme in three stages on a first appointment, the rule that no typical audit programme can be drawn up, and the requirement that the framework provided under the overall plan be adhered to with the plan modified first where a divergence becomes necessary

items.scenario: A firm has been appointed for the first time to audit a chemicals company. The senior wants to hand the assistants a complete audit programme on day one, filled in down to the last procedure, before anyone has looked at the company's systems. He also finds that one area of the programme he has drafted needs work the overall audit strategy does not provide for, and proposes to put it in the programme and leave the strategy as it is.

items.stem: What does the module say about altering an audit programme?

options.text: All four are circumstances in which the programme has to be suitably altered during the audit — a substantial increase in the volume of turnover the procedures were designed for, a discovery that the internal control procedures were not as effective as assumed when the programme was framed, an extraordinary increase in book debts or in the value of stocks against the previous year, and a suspicion or information that assets have been misappropriated
options.why: The four are named. A programme designed for a certain volume of turnover has to be altered where the volume has substantially increased, as it does where there have been significant changes in the accounting organisation, procedures or personnel. It has to be altered again when the audit turns up controls that were not as effective as assumed when the programme was drawn. The same follows where book debts, or the value of stocks, show an extraordinary increase on last year's figures, and where the team comes to suspect — or is told outright — that company assets have been misappropriated. The plan and programme are reconsidered as the audit progresses; they are not worked through as issued.

options.text: Only where the client agrees, the programme being the basis on which the fee was quoted and the timetable agreed with management
options.misconception: makes the programme a matter for agreement with the client, when the auditor alone is responsible for the strategy, the plan and the programme
options.why: The auditor is responsible for establishing the audit strategy and the plan, and he may discuss elements of planning with management without compromising the effectiveness of the audit but cannot ask management to prepare them. What the programme must cover is not for the client to settle.

options.text: None during the audit — the programme is reviewed and modified at each subsequent engagement on the experience gained during previous audits, important changes in the business and the evaluation of internal control for the current year, which is where these four belong
options.misconception: confuses the review at the start of the next engagement with the alteration required in the middle of this one
options.why: Those three grounds are the review made at each subsequent engagement, and they are real. They are not a substitute for altering the programme during the audit, which the module deals with separately and illustrates with exactly these four circumstances.

options.text: Only the suspected misappropriation — a fraud indication forces the programme open, while volume, control effectiveness and the movement in balances are matters of extent that the existing sampling already absorbs
options.misconception: treats a change of volume or of control effectiveness as something the planned sample absorbs, when each is separately named as a ground for altering the programme
options.why: A sample designed for one volume of turnover does not absorb a threefold increase, and a programme built on an assumption about controls that turns out to be wrong is testing the wrong things. Each of the four is separately named, and none of them waits for the next audit.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the circumstances in which the audit programme has to be suitably altered during the audit, read with the grounds on which it is reviewed and modified at each subsequent engagement and the requirement that the plan and programme be reconsidered as the audit progresses

items.scenario: Four things happen during an audit that was programmed in April. Turnover for the year turns out to be nearly three times what the sampling in the programme was designed for. Compliance testing shows the authorisation controls over purchases were nothing like as effective as the programme assumed. Book debts have risen extraordinarily against last year. And a whisper reaches the team that a storekeeper has been removing finished goods. The engagement partner says the programme was approved and will be worked through as issued, with anything unusual noted for next year.

items.stem: What is wrong with that closing sentence?

options.text: It says the opposite of what the letter must say — the letter should clearly indicate that it discusses only the weaknesses that came to the auditor's attention as a result of his audit, and that his examination was not designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for management
options.why: The letter is a by-product of an audit of financial statements, not an assurance engagement on internal control. It lists the areas of weakness in the system and offers suggestions for improvement. Its own wording then has to make two things unmistakable: that the only weaknesses discussed are those the auditor noticed as a result of his audit, and that the work behind it had not been designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for anybody's purposes, management's included. A sentence certifying the rest of the system as adequate claims an opinion the auditor never formed and was never asked to form.
keywords: as a result of his audit
not been designed to determine the adequacy of internal control

options.text: The letter should not exist at all where the deficiencies are being reported to those charged with governance, one written communication about internal control being enough
options.misconception: makes the two communications alternatives, when significant deficiencies go in writing to those charged with governance and also to management at an appropriate level
options.why: They are not alternatives. Significant deficiencies go in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and in writing to management at an appropriate level of responsibility as well, unless it would be inappropriate to communicate directly with management in the circumstances.

options.text: The sentence is fine but the suggestions are not — a letter of weakness reports deficiencies and an auditor who suggests improvements has crossed into management consultancy
options.misconception: treats the suggestions as improper, when offering suggestions for improvement is part of what the letter is for
options.why: Offering suggestions is one of the things the letter does. It lists the areas of weakness in the system and offers suggestions for improvement, and the value of it as a reference document for revising the system depends on exactly that.

options.text: Nothing — the auditor has examined internal control in order to design his audit procedures, so he is in a position to say whether what he saw was adequate, and saying so is the service the letter provides
options.misconception: turns the understanding of internal control obtained for designing procedures into an opinion on the adequacy of the system
options.why: The audit included consideration of internal control in order to design audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances, and not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on its effectiveness. The letter has to say so; it cannot quietly do the opposite.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — what a letter of weakness sets out and the suggestions it carries, together with the disclaimer it has to include: the narrow origin of the weaknesses it names, and the purpose the auditor's examination was never built to serve

items.scenario: A draft letter of weakness lists eleven deficiencies and offers a suggestion against each. It then says that the firm has examined the company's internal control and is satisfied that, apart from the matters listed, the system is adequate for the company's needs. The partner is content, on the view that a client paying for a letter is entitled to know where it stands.

items.stem: How far does the letter actually carry him?

options.text: Only on the second — the letter forces the qualification, because a weakness the auditor has put in writing and the client has ignored is by that fact a significant deficiency requiring modification of the opinion
options.misconception: turns an uncorrected significant deficiency into an automatic modification, when the qualification is of the shortcomings in the accounts and is weighed for materiality and impact
options.why: A significant deficiency is communicated, not automatically reported in the opinion. What survives the letter is a narrower duty: to qualify over shortcomings in the accounts that were left uncorrected to his satisfaction, and he weighs how material the weaknesses are and what they do in deciding that.

options.text: Both ways — a weakness reported in writing and left uncorrected is management's failure, so the liability and the reporting question are both answered by the letter
options.misconception: reads the letter's protective effect as extending to the audit report, when the duty to qualify survives the letter entirely
options.why: The protection and the duty are separate. The letter may relieve the auditor of liability for a loss the client could have prevented; it does not relieve him of the duty to qualify where the defects have not been corrected to his satisfaction, weighing their materiality and impact.

options.text: Neither way — a letter of weakness is an internal courtesy with no legal significance, and the reporting question turns only on whether the defalcation is material to the financial statements
options.misconception: strips the letter of the protective value the module gives it, and reduces the reporting question to the size of the loss
options.why: The letter has real value: where a weak control later admits a large defalcation, or some comparable loss, it can cut down what the auditor is answerable for at law, and a reported case turned on exactly that. The reporting question is not only about the size of the loss either — it is about shortcomings in the accounts left uncorrected to the auditor's satisfaction.

options.text: On the first, a long way — the letter may serve to minimise legal liability, and in a reported case an auditor was acquitted of a charge of negligence over an employee's fraud because he had already informed the client of the unsatisfactory state of specific areas and suggested improvements that were not acted upon; on the second, nowhere — a letter, once written, still leaves the auditor bound to qualify his report over any shortcoming in the accounts that was left uncorrected to his satisfaction
options.why: The two questions have different answers and the module is explicit on both. Issuing a letter of weakness has great merit in relieving the auditor from liability when a serious fraud or loss lands that would probably never have happened had the client acted on the points he raised; a reported case acquitted an auditor of negligence over an employee's fraud on precisely that footing. The second question runs the other way. Having put the system's weaknesses to management in writing, he is not absolved of what is owed on the accounts themselves: a qualification is still due over any shortcoming left uncorrected to his satisfaction, judged on how material the weaknesses are and what they do.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the protective worth of a letter of weakness where a control gap later admits a large defalcation, the reported acquittal on a negligence charge that rested on one, and the countervailing rule that the letter buys no relief from qualifying the report over defects nobody put right

items.scenario: A firm issued a detailed letter of weakness in October naming the absence of any segregation between the officer who authorises payments and the officer who records them. Management did nothing about it. In February a defalcation of a material amount is discovered running through exactly that gap. The partner takes the view that the letter settles two things at once: the firm is protected from any allegation of negligence, and the audit report needs no qualification because the weakness was reported to management in writing.

items.stem: What does SA 570 (Revised) require once such events have been identified?

options.text: A written representation from management and those charged with governance about their plans for future action, which is the evidence the Standard specifies for a matter that depends on management's intentions
options.misconception: treats the written representation as the whole of the evidence, when representations never provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own
options.why: Requesting a written representation regarding management's plans for future actions is one named procedure among many. A representation standing alone is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the matter it speaks to. The plans still have to be evaluated for feasibility against loan terms, forecasts and the support arrangements.

options.text: Nothing further at this stage — the additional procedures are performed only once management has completed its own assessment, and until then the auditor's role is to wait for it
options.misconception: makes the auditor's work wait on management, when the Standard has him request the assessment where it has not been made and proceed with the other procedures
options.why: Where management has not yet performed an assessment, the auditor requests it — that is itself one of the additional procedures, and it does not suspend the others. It is not the auditor's responsibility to rectify a lack of analysis by management, and a lack of assessment may not prevent him from concluding.

options.text: Additional audit procedures, with mitigating factors weighed among them — going through the cash flow, profit and other forecasts with management; taking in whatever interim accounts are most recent; checking the loan documents for a covenant already broken; combing the minutes for any mention of trouble raising money; asking the entity's lawyers about outstanding litigation and claims; establishing that a promise of financial support is real, lawful and capable of enforcement and that the promisor could actually find the money; establishing what borrowing lines exist, on what terms and how far they stretch; running procedures over events after the reporting date; and testing what management intends to do next and whether it can be done at all
options.why: A written representation is one of the procedures, not a substitute for the rest of them. Once something has surfaced that throws real doubt over the entity's ability to carry on, enough evidence of the right kind has to be gathered to settle whether a material uncertainty exists, and it is gathered by running the further procedures with mitigating factors weighed among them. The restructuring puts the loan agreements and the borrowing facilities at the centre here, because their terms decide when repayment begins, and the forecast has to be examined rather than filed.

options.text: A separate section in the auditor's report headed Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern, the doubt having been identified, with the procedures then directed at the wording of the disclosure
options.misconception: jumps from identifying the events to the reporting consequence, skipping the work that decides whether a material uncertainty exists at all
options.why: The section comes later and only on a conclusion the auditor has not yet reached. Identifying events or conditions that may cast significant doubt is the trigger for the additional procedures; whether they amount to a material uncertainty is what those procedures decide.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — the further audit procedures, mitigating factors included, that follow once the auditor has spotted matters throwing real doubt over the entity's capacity to carry on as a going concern

items.scenario: A poultry company's sales have fallen from about ₹50 crore to about ₹10 crore in two years after repeated outbreaks of disease, a large part of its livestock has been lost, and its working capital facilities have been restructured with repayments starting next year. The auditor has identified events casting significant doubt on the ability to continue as a going concern. Her senior proposes to record the doubt in the file, obtain a written representation from the directors that the company is a going concern, and move on.

items.stem: What does the auditor do with the forecast, and with the delay?

options.text: Evaluate the forecast, but treat the delay in approval as an administrative matter — the date of approval is fixed by the board and the auditor has no standing to inquire into it
options.misconception: passes over a delay in approval, which the Standard treats as a matter to inquire into precisely because it may be a going concern symptom
options.why: The delay is named. If there is a delay in the approval of the financial statements after the date of the financial statements, the auditor inquires as to the reasons, and if he believes the delay may be related to the events or conditions relevant to the going concern assessment he performs the additional procedures and considers the effect on his conclusion.

options.text: Ask how dependable the forecast's input data is, given the way that data was produced, and whether the assumptions it rests on carry adequate support — testing each assumption against what is known, including the sanction letters for the repayment dates and the announced expenditure that has been left out; and inquire into the reasons for the delay in approval, performing the additional procedures and considering the effect on his conclusion if he believes the delay relates to the going concern events or conditions
options.why: Where the entity has prepared a cash flow forecast and the analysis of that forecast is a significant factor in considering the future outcome of the events or conditions, the work is in two named parts: evaluating the reliability of the underlying data generated to prepare it, and determining whether there is adequate support for the assumptions underlying it. Fresh batches with no fresh credit, longer supplier credit in a downturn, and announced expenditure missing from the forecast are three assumptions with no support on this file, and the loan agreements are the way to check when repayments actually begin. On the delay, where approval of the financial statements is late and the auditor believes it relates to the going concern assessment, he performs the additional procedures and considers the effect on his conclusion.

options.text: Recompute the forecast on the auditor's own assumptions and use his own figures as the benchmark, since management's assumptions are the very thing in doubt
options.misconception: has the auditor prepare a rival forecast, when his work is to test the support for management's assumptions rather than to substitute his own
options.why: It is not the auditor's responsibility to rectify a lack of analysis by management. He evaluates management's plans and the assumptions underlying management's forecast; building a competing forecast puts him in management's chair and answers nothing about the one he was given.

options.text: Accept the forecast as management's own document — a forecast is a projection of future events for which no audit evidence can exist, so the auditor records that it was obtained and reports on the disclosure instead
options.misconception: treats a forecast as unauditable, when the Standard directs the auditor at its data and its assumptions rather than at its outcome
options.why: The auditor is not asked to certify the outcome. He is asked to evaluate the reliability of the data used to build the forecast and whether the assumptions have adequate support, and an assumption contradicted by the bank's refusal of fresh facilities does not.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — where a cash flow forecast exists and its analysis weighs significantly, how dependable its input data is given the way that data was produced and whether its assumptions carry adequate support, read with the inquiry into a delay in approving the financial statements

items.scenario: The same company gives the auditor a cash flow forecast. It assumes fresh batches of livestock although the bankers have granted no fresh credit facilities, longer credit from feed suppliers although the company is visibly in difficulty, and no expenditure at all on the vaccination and veterinary programme management has announced or on the pollution complaints the neighbouring villagers have made. Separately, the approval of the financial statements has slipped by two months with no explanation.

items.stem: What does SA 600 have the auditor consider before accepting as principal auditor?

options.text: Four matters — the materiality of the portion of the financial information which he himself audits, his own degree of knowledge regarding the business of the components, the risk of material misstatement in the financial information of the components audited by the other auditors, and the performance of the additional procedures the Standard requires regarding those components, which may result in his having significant participation in that audit
options.why: Acceptance is a judgement about whether the firm can carry the opinion, and the Standard names what goes into it. A small portion audited by the principal auditor himself, little knowledge of the components' businesses, and a high risk of material misstatement in the parts audited by others all push the same way — towards additional procedures on those components, which is the fourth matter and which may leave the principal auditor with significant participation in an audit he thought he was only relying on.
keywords: portion audited by the principal auditor himself

options.text: Only whether he has the right to visit the components and examine their books, since without that right he cannot obtain evidence about them at all
options.misconception: makes a statutory right of visit a precondition of acceptance, when the right is exercised only where special circumstances make it essential
options.why: Where a statute confers such a right and the component already has an auditor of its own, the principal auditor may as a rule lean on that auditor's work instead of going, unless something out of the ordinary makes a visit or an examination essential. The right is a reserve power, not the basis on which the appointment is taken.

options.text: Only whether the other auditors are independent and professionally qualified — the principal auditor is entitled to rely on their work, so the components are their responsibility and not his at the acceptance stage
options.misconception: reduces acceptance to a check on the other auditors, when the four matters are about the principal auditor's own position
options.why: The four matters are about him, not them: how much he audits himself, how much he knows about the components' businesses, how risky the parts he does not audit are, and how much additional work those parts will need. Entitlement to rely on another auditor's work is a different rule and it comes later.

options.text: Whether the components together exceed a stated proportion of the consolidated figures, below which the appointment may be accepted without further inquiry
options.misconception: looks for a numerical threshold, when the Standard gives four matters to weigh and no proportion at which the question stops
options.why: There is no such proportion. The materiality of the portion the principal auditor audits is one of four matters to be considered together with his knowledge of the components' businesses, the risk of material misstatement in them and the additional procedures they will require.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — what weighs at acceptance as principal auditor: how material the slice he audits himself is, how well he knows the businesses the components carry on, what risk of material misstatement sits in the parts other auditors cover, and the extra procedures on those parts that may leave him significantly involved in that audit

items.scenario: A firm is offered the appointment as auditor of a group whose accounts consolidate eleven components. The firm would itself audit rather less than a fifth of the consolidated figures, knows nothing about the businesses of five of the components, and has been told that two of them operate in a sector with a history of large misstatements. A partner says the only question at acceptance is independence, since the work on the components belongs to their own auditors.

items.stem: How does SA 600 deal with the three?

options.text: Competence need not be considered for either foreign auditor, since each is appointed under his own country's law, and the limitation of procedures on the third component must be documented with its reasons like any other departure
options.misconception: exempts a foreign auditor from the competence consideration and removes the documentation exception the Standard actually grants
options.why: It is the other way round on both. Competence is precisely what has to be considered where the other auditor is not a member of the Institute, and the reasons for limiting the procedures need not be documented where quality control compliance has already been established on sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

options.text: None of their work may be used — a component whose auditor is not a member of the Institute, or is not professionally qualified at all, must be audited by the principal auditor himself
options.misconception: bars the use of an unqualified or non-member auditor's work outright, when the Standard answers it with a consideration of competence rather than a prohibition
options.why: The Standard does not prohibit it. It requires the principal auditor to consider the other auditor's professional competence in the context of the specific assignment where he is not a member of the Institute, and it contemplates in terms that the other auditor may be a person other than a professionally qualified auditor where the applicable law permits it.

options.text: All three are matters for the engagement letter rather than for the audit — the group's management chooses the component auditors, so the principal auditor records the position and reports on the consolidated figures as presented
options.misconception: hands the question to management, when the principal auditor remains responsible for his own opinion however the component auditors were chosen
options.why: Who appointed the component auditors does not change the principal auditor's position. He is responsible for the opinion on the financial information of the entity as a whole, and the Standard tells him what to consider about the auditors whose work he proposes to use.

options.text: The professional competence of the other auditor is to be considered in the context of the specific assignment where he is not a member of the Institute; a component's auditor may indeed be a person other than a professionally qualified auditor where the applicable law permits it, which does not by itself end the matter but goes to the same consideration of competence; and the principal auditor need not document the reasons for limiting his procedures where he has previously obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence that acceptable quality control policies and procedures are complied with in that auditor's practice
options.why: The three are separate rules and all three are in the Standard. Where the principal auditor proposes to lean on another auditor's work, and that auditor is not a member of the Institute, professional competence has to be weighed against what the specific assignment demands. The module's illustration of when that arises is the foreign component whose law allows a person other than a professionally qualified auditor to audit it. And the documentation duty carries its own exception: he need not document the reasons for limiting his procedures once he already holds sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the other auditor's practice runs on acceptable quality control policies and procedures.
keywords: not a member of the Institute
person other than a professionally qualified auditor
need not document the reasons for limiting

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — weighing an other auditor's professional competence where he falls outside the membership of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, the component audited by somebody carrying no professional qualification where local law allows it, and the exception that lifts the duty to write down why procedures were limited once quality control compliance has been established

items.scenario: Two of the group's components are abroad. One has an auditor who sits outside the membership of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India; the other is audited by somebody holding no professional qualification at all, which the local law permits. On evidence gathered earlier, the principal auditor has also satisfied himself that a third component's auditor runs a practice with acceptable quality control policies and procedures in place, and has limited his procedures there accordingly without writing down why.

items.stem: Does SA 620 require an expert here?

options.text: No — knowing little about a field outside accounting and auditing does not stop the auditor picking up enough of that field to carry the audit through without an auditor's expert, and the grounding may come from having audited entities that required such expertise, from education or professional development in the field, or from talking to auditors who have run similar engagements
options.why: The Standard's first question is whether an expert is needed, and it answers that an auditor who is not an expert may still obtain a sufficient understanding of the field to perform the audit without one. The three routes named are the three this manager has already taken. Such a discussion with other auditors is a different thing from consultation with an auditor's expert about a specific set of circumstances on the engagement, where the expert is given all the relevant facts so as to give informed advice on the particular matter.

options.text: Yes, unless management has itself used a management's expert, in which case the auditor uses that expert's work and needs none of his own
options.misconception: makes a management's expert a substitute for an auditor's expert, when management's use of one is a factor in the decision and never an answer to it
options.why: Whether management has used a management's expert is one of the considerations in deciding whether to use an auditor's expert, and it cuts both ways. It never removes the question, because information prepared using a management's expert has itself to be evaluated under SA 500.

options.text: No, but only because the swaps are plain — the moment any instrument is not plain the auditor loses the discretion, an expert being required wherever subjective and complex judgments arise
options.misconception: converts a factor that calls for more extensive procedures into a rule requiring an expert
options.why: Work relating to a significant matter involving subjective and complex judgments is one of the things that may suggest the need for different or more extensive procedures on an expert's work. It does not turn the decision whether to use an expert into a rule.

options.text: Yes — the valuation of complex financial instruments is one of the fields the Standard names, and where the subject matter falls in a named field an auditor's expert must be engaged
options.misconception: reads the list of fields as a list of mandatory triggers, when it illustrates where expertise may lie rather than where an expert must be appointed
options.why: The fields — valuation of complex financial instruments, actuarial calculation of liabilities, estimation of oil and gas reserves, interpretation of contracts, analysis of complex tax compliance issues — are examples of expertise other than accounting or auditing. They are not a list of engagements on which an expert is compulsory.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — determining the need for an auditor's expert: how an auditor lacking expertise in a relevant field can still get enough of a grip on it to carry the audit alone, through experience of auditing entities that demanded such expertise, education or professional development in the subject, or discussion with auditors who have run similar engagements

items.scenario: A manager is planning the audit of a company holding a portfolio of listed equity and plain interest rate swaps. He has audited four similar portfolios, has done a formal course on financial instruments, and has discussed the approach with the partner who ran a comparable engagement last year. He nonetheless proposes to appoint a valuation expert, on the view that SA 620 requires an expert wherever the subject matter lies outside accounting and auditing.

items.stem: What decides the nature, timing and extent of the auditor's procedures on an expert's work?

options.text: The expert's professional standing — where the expert belongs to a professional body with technical performance standards and ethical requirements, the auditor's procedures on his work may be confined to obtaining his report
options.misconception: lets membership of a professional body stand in for the auditor's own evaluation of the expert's work
options.why: Membership and technical performance standards are relevant to competence, capabilities and objectivity; they do not displace the evaluation of the work itself, and the auditor's sole responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by his use of an expert however well qualified.

options.text: Whether the expert is internal or external, and nothing else — an internal expert is covered by the firm's own quality control while an external expert is not, which settles the extent of the work in every case
options.misconception: reduces the five matters to one distinction, which would leave a familiar external expert on a routine matter treated exactly like an unknown one on a critical estimate
options.why: It is one of the factors and not the whole of it. On this engagement the expert is external and unknown and the matter is subjective and material and his work is integral to the audit — four separate reasons for more extensive procedures, of which the internal or external question is only one.

options.text: What kind of matter it is, what risk of material misstatement it carries, how much the audit as a whole rests on the expert's contribution, how well the auditor knows that expert's earlier work from having used it, and whether the expert falls inside the firm's quality control policies and procedures — and all four of the circumstances calling for more extensive procedures are present here: subjective and complex judgments, an expert not used before, work integral to the audit rather than advice on an individual matter, and an external expert outside the firm's quality control
options.why: The five matters are what the auditor considers in determining the nature, timing and extent of his procedures, and they are why the internal specialist used every year and this actuary cannot be reviewed alike. Four factors are separately named as calling for procedures that differ, or that go further, than they otherwise would, and every one of them is here: the work relates to a significant matter involving subjective and complex judgments; the auditor has not previously used that expert and has no prior knowledge of his competence, capabilities and objectivity; the expert is performing procedures integral to the audit rather than being consulted for advice on an individual matter; and he is an external expert and therefore not subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures.
keywords: nature, timing and extent of his procedures
not subject to the firm's quality control

options.text: Only how much the audit as a whole rests on the expert's contribution — the other matters go to whether to engage him rather than to what the auditor does about his work afterwards
options.misconception: keeps one of the five matters and assigns the rest to the engagement decision, when all five bear on the nature, timing and extent of the procedures
options.why: Significance is one of five. The nature of the matter, the risk of material misstatement in it, the auditor's knowledge of the expert's previous work and whether the expert falls inside the firm's quality control all bear on the same question, and the last two are exactly what separates a first-time external expert from a familiar internal one.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the matters the auditor considers in determining the nature, timing and extent of procedures on an auditor's expert's work, and the four factors that may suggest the need for different or more extensive procedures

items.scenario: A firm engages an external actuary it has never used before to value a defined benefit obligation that is the largest single estimate in the accounts and depends on subjective demographic assumptions. The actuary will not merely advise on a question put to him; he will perform procedures that form part of the audit itself. The engagement partner proposes the same review he applies to the internal specialist the firm uses every year, on the ground that both are experts and both have been engaged by the firm.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require here?

options.text: The inconsistent explanations may be left alone, since inquiry is the weakest form of audit evidence and the auditor should simply obtain a document instead
options.misconception: discards inconsistent responses because inquiry is weak evidence, when the inconsistency is itself something the Standard directs the auditor to investigate
options.why: The inconsistency is the finding. Where responses to inquiries of management or of those charged with governance are inconsistent, the auditor investigates the inconsistencies, and here the document that would replace the inquiry is the very thing in question.

options.text: The auditor must treat the challan as forged and report a suspected fraud, an altered document being conclusive of an intention to deceive
options.misconception: jumps from a document that may not be authentic to a conclusion of fraud, when what the Standard requires at this point is further investigation
options.why: What is required is to investigate further, not to conclude. The document may not be authentic or its terms may have been modified without disclosure — either possibility calls for work, and the conclusion comes after that work rather than instead of it.

options.text: Nothing further — an auditor is entitled to accept records and documents as genuine, and nine years of clean audits are the evidence on which that entitlement rests
options.misconception: reads the entitlement to accept documents as genuine as unconditional, when it stands only until there is reason to believe the contrary
options.why: The entitlement carries its own limit in the same sentence. It runs unless the auditor has reason to believe the contrary, and an altered date with an out-of-sequence serial number is such a reason. Past experience of honesty does not answer it; the Standard says skepticism is maintained notwithstanding that experience.

options.text: The auditor may accept records and documents as genuine unless he has reason to believe the contrary — and there is reason here, so where conditions identified during the audit cause him to believe a document may not be authentic or that terms in it have been modified and not disclosed, he investigates further; inconsistent responses to inquiries are themselves investigated; and the engagement team discussion happens notwithstanding the team's belief that management is honest and has integrity
options.why: The permission to take documents at face value is conditional and the condition has failed. The auditor may accept records and documents as genuine unless he has reason to believe the contrary. Where something the audit turns up gives him cause to doubt a document's authenticity, or to think its terms were altered and the alteration kept from him, he investigates further. Where management or those charged with governance answer his inquiries inconsistently, his duty is to investigate the inconsistencies. And skepticism is kept up right through the audit, on the footing that a fraudulent material misstatement could be sitting there however honest management has proved in the past — which is why the team discussion occurs notwithstanding the members' belief that they are honest.
keywords: unless he has reason to believe the contrary

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — maintaining professional skepticism throughout the audit notwithstanding past experience of the honesty and integrity of management and those charged with governance, accepting records and documents as genuine unless there is reason to believe the contrary, investigating further where a document may not be authentic or its terms modified, investigating inconsistent responses to inquiries, and holding the engagement team discussion notwithstanding the team's beliefs about management

items.scenario: An assistant produces a delivery challan whose date appears to have been altered and whose serial number is out of sequence with those around it. The finance head explains it one way and the storekeeper explains it another. The senior tells him to take the challan at face value, because the firm has audited this client for nine years and has never had a reason to doubt the directors, and to leave it out of the engagement team discussion for the same reason.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require once a misstatement may be fraud involving senior management?

options.text: Add it to the uncorrected misstatements and evaluate it at the end with the others — a misstatement below performance materiality cannot change the audit, whatever caused it
options.misconception: lets the amount decide, when the Standard's trigger is a misstatement whether material or not that may be the result of fraud involving management
options.why: The Standard says whether material or not in terms. A small misstatement that indicates management fraud is evidence about the whole audit, because an instance of fraud is unlikely to be an isolated occurrence and because the reliability of management's representations is now in question.

options.text: Go back over how the risks of material misstatement due to fraud were assessed, and over what that reassessment does to the nature, timing and extent of the audit procedures — the size of the misstatement being irrelevant to that requirement — and ask whether anything here points to employees, management or outsiders acting in concert, in weighing afresh how far the evidence already gathered can be relied on
options.why: The requirement is triggered by the character of the misstatement, not by its amount. A misstatement the auditor has found — whether material or not — that he has cause to think came out of fraud with management, senior management especially, mixed up in it sends him back to the risk assessment: he re-evaluates the fraud risks and works out what that reassessment does to the nature, timing and extent of his procedures. He must also ask whether anything in the circumstances points to possible collusion between employees, management or outsiders, in weighing afresh how far the evidence he already holds can be relied on — which is the point of the clerk who reports to the director.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement — a misstatement caused by fraud involving the finance director is an exceptional circumstance bringing the auditor's ability to continue into question
options.misconception: goes straight to withdrawal, which arises only on exceptional circumstances that bring the ability to continue into question and even then only after determining the responsibilities
options.why: Withdrawal is a separate and later question. Where exceptional circumstances do bring the ability to continue into question, the auditor first determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable, considers whether withdrawal is legally permitted, and if he withdraws discusses it with management and those charged with governance and determines whether there is a duty to report. Re-evaluating the risk assessment comes first and applies here.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the finance director explaining the credit note, and rely on it if the explanation is plausible
options.misconception: seeks the explanation from the person the suspicion is about and treats a representation as evidence of the very matter in doubt
options.why: Where the auditor has reason to believe a misstatement is fraud involving management, the reliability of management representations is one of the things he must reconsider, so a representation from the suspected person settles nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — evaluating audit evidence under SA 240 where a misstatement of any size looks as though fraud produced it with management mixed up in that fraud: the fresh look taken at the fraud risk assessment and at what it does to the nature, timing and extent of procedures, and the question of collusion between employees, management or outsiders

items.scenario: Late in the audit you find a single misstatement of ₹4 lakh, well below performance materiality. It arises from a credit note raised on the last day of the year by the finance director himself, backed by no supporting document, and passed for payment by a clerk who reports to him. You have reason to believe it is not an error. The manager proposes to add it to the schedule of uncorrected misstatements and carry on with the programme as planned.

items.stem: How does SA 240 deal with reporting outside the entity?

options.text: Confidentiality is absolute in both — an auditor may never disclose a client's affairs to a third party, and the remedy where governance will not act is to modify the opinion and resign
options.misconception: treats the duty of confidentiality as incapable of being overridden, when legal responsibilities may override it in some circumstances
options.why: The Standard says in terms that although the professional duty of confidentiality may preclude reporting, the auditor's legal responsibilities may override that duty in some circumstances. Treating it as absolute would mean a bank auditor could not perform the statutory duty the module names.

options.text: Both must be reported outside the entity in every case, a fraud being a matter of public interest that displaces the auditor's duty to the client
options.misconception: converts a duty that depends on the auditor's legal responsibilities into a general obligation to report every fraud externally
options.why: Nothing in the Standard makes external reporting automatic. The auditor determines whether he has a responsibility to report, and where he has none the duty of confidentiality is not displaced by the seriousness of what he has found.

options.text: The bank fraud is reportable and the trading company's is not, the difference being that a bank is regulated and an unlisted company is not
options.misconception: makes regulation of the entity the only route to an external report, missing the separate duty that arises where management and governance fail to act
options.why: There are two routes, not one. A statutory duty such as the bank auditor's is one; the other is a duty that arises in certain entities to report misstatements to the authorities once governance and management between them fail to take corrective action, which is exactly what has happened on the second engagement.

options.text: In each case the auditor works out whether somebody outside the entity has to be told of the fraud he has found or suspects — the professional duty of confidentiality may block that, but his obligations at law may cut across the duty, and a bank audit is the module's own example, the auditor there carrying a statutory duty to tell the supervisory authority when a fraud occurs; and in certain entities a duty to report misstatements to the authorities arises once governance and management alike will not act to put matters right
options.why: Confidentiality is the starting point and not the end of it. Having identified a fraud or come to suspect one, the auditor works out whether anybody outside the entity has to be told. His professional obligation to keep a client's information to himself may stand in the way of that; his obligations at law, though, may override the duty of confidentiality altogether, and banking is the example the module gives, the auditor there carrying a statutory duty to tell the Reserve Bank when a fraud occurs. The second engagement is the other named case: in certain entities a duty to report misstatements to the authorities arises once those charged with governance and management alike fail to take corrective action on what they have been told.
keywords: may override the duty of confidentiality

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — reporting to regulatory and enforcement authorities under SA 240: working out whether a fraud found or suspected has to be told to anybody outside the entity, the professional duty of confidentiality set against the legal obligations that can override it, with the bank auditor's statutory report of fraud to the Reserve Bank as the example, and the separate duty in certain entities to report misstatements once governance and management alike fail to take corrective action

items.scenario: Two engagements in the same firm. On the audit of a bank, the team establishes that a branch manager has been rolling over advances to conceal defaults. On the audit of an unlisted trading company, the team finds misstatements arising from a fraud, reports them to those charged with governance, and is told nothing will be done. In both cases the partner says the duty of confidentiality prevents the firm from telling anybody outside the company.

items.stem: Which of the five must be communicated to those charged with governance?

options.text: Only the two key audit matters — SA 701 requires key audit matters to be taken from the matters communicated to those charged with governance, so that is the only one where communication is a precondition
options.misconception: notices the SA 701 route into the report and mistakes it for the whole of SA 260's requirement
options.why: Key audit matters are indeed drawn from what was communicated, but SA 260 lists five circumstances and that is one of them. The other four carry the same communication requirement for the same reason.

options.text: None of them until the report is signed — communicating an expected modification before the audit is complete would compromise the auditor's independence by inviting management to negotiate the wording
options.misconception: treats advance communication as a threat to independence, when the Standard requires it and even suggests sharing a draft report
options.why: The Standard requires the communication in advance and the module suggests going further by providing a draft of the auditor's report to facilitate discussion of how the matters will be addressed. Communicating is not conceding, and the wording remains the auditor's.

options.text: Only the qualification and the going concern uncertainty — those two put the reader on notice of a problem, while key audit matters, an Emphasis of Matter and a comment on other information are presentational
