options.misconception: sorts the five by how bad they look rather than by whether they add information to the report, which is the test the Standard uses
options.why: The test is not severity. It is whether the auditor is required or considers it necessary to include additional information in the report, and key audit matters, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph and an uncorrected misstatement of the other information each do exactly that.

options.text: All five — the circumstances in which the auditor is required or may consider it necessary to include additional information in his report, and for which communication is required, are an expected modification under SA 705, a material uncertainty related to going concern under SA 570, key audit matters under SA 701, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph under SA 706, and an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information under SA 720 — and it may be useful to give them a draft of the report to facilitate a discussion of how the matters will be addressed
options.why: The list is closed and it has five entries, only one of which touches the opinion. The point of it is that anything which changes the report from its expected form and content is something those charged with governance were entitled to know about in advance, whether or not the opinion moves. The agreed terms of the engagement already refer to the expected form and content of the report, and this communication tells them where it will differ. Providing a draft of the auditor's report is the module's own suggestion for making that discussion work.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — the five situations that put something extra into the auditor's report and therefore have to be raised with those charged with governance beforehand: a modification expected under SA 705, going-concern material uncertainty under SA 570, key audit matters under SA 701, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph under SA 706, and other information left materially misstated under SA 720, together with the suggestion that a draft report be handed over

items.scenario: Five things are going to change the shape of this year's auditor's report. A qualification is expected on inventory valuation. A material uncertainty related to going concern will be reported. Two key audit matters will be described. An Emphasis of Matter paragraph will draw attention to a pending litigation note. And the annual report contains a statement about order book values that the auditor has concluded is a material misstatement of the other information and that management will not correct. The partner proposes to communicate only the qualification, since only that changes the opinion.

items.stem: What does SA 260 make of the three proposals?

options.text: The significant risks are properly omitted — they are the auditor's working judgement and communicating them before the work is done would prejudge the findings, which are communicated at the end
options.misconception: postpones the significant risks to the findings stage, when the Standard puts them in the overview of the planned scope and timing
options.why: They belong at the planning stage. What the auditor gives those charged with governance is an overview — the scope planned and the timing of it — and the significant risks he has identified are part of that overview, precisely so the recipients grasp why such matters call for special audit consideration.

options.text: Only the omission of the significant risks is wrong — handing over the detailed timings is candour rather than a fault, and letting the committee set the extent of testing is how oversight is exercised
options.misconception: keeps the requirement to communicate significant risks but ignores the predictability caution and the auditor's sole responsibility for the plan
options.why: Both of the other proposals fail on their own terms. Communicating the nature and timing of detailed audit procedures may reduce their effectiveness by making them too predictable, and the extent of substantive testing is part of the plan, which is the auditor's alone.

options.text: The overview of the planned scope and timing must name the significant risks he has identified, so leaving them out is wrong; scope and timing are communicated with care, lest the audit's effectiveness be compromised — a real danger when board members also run the company — because telling them the nature and timing of detailed procedures can make those procedures too predictable; and none of this shifts the sole responsibility for setting the overall audit strategy and the plan, which stays the auditor's, so the extent of testing is not the committee's to settle
options.why: The three proposals fail in three different ways. Naming the significant risks helps those charged with governance see why such matters need special audit consideration, and helps them oversee the financial reporting process, so the overview is exactly where they belong. Care is then owed the other way: the audit's effectiveness must not be compromised, and the danger is sharpest when board members are also running the company, as the managing director is here, since spelling out the nature and timing of detailed procedures can make them too predictable. And communication, helpful as it may be at the planning stage, leaves the sole responsibility where it was — setting the overall audit strategy and the plan, and with it the nature, timing and extent of the procedures needed for sufficient appropriate audit evidence, remains his.

options.text: All three are acceptable — a two-way communication is the point of SA 260, so the more the committee is told and the more it decides, the better the oversight
options.misconception: treats the two-way communication as unlimited, when the Standard warns against detail that makes procedures predictable and reserves the plan to the auditor
options.why: The Standard sets both a limit and a boundary. The limit is that care is necessary so as not to compromise the effectiveness of the audit; the boundary is that nothing communicated changes the auditor's sole responsibility for the strategy and the plan.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — what SA 260 says about telling those charged with governance the scope and timing planned for the audit: that the significant risks identified form part of it, that care is owed lest the audit's effectiveness be compromised, sharpest where board members also run the company, and that none of this shifts the sole responsibility for setting the overall audit strategy and the plan away from the auditor

items.scenario: At a meeting with an audit committee whose members include the managing director, an auditor is about to present his plan. He proposes to hand over the detailed programme with the dates of every surprise cash count and inventory visit, to omit the significant risks he has identified because naming them might alarm the members, and to invite the committee to settle the extent of the substantive testing on receivables.

items.stem: Where does the responsibility for that lapse lie under SA 299 (Revised)?

options.text: With all four jointly and severally — the area was not divided, and the Standard makes the joint auditors jointly and severally responsible for audit work that is not divided among them
options.misconception: stops at the general rule about undivided work and misses the narrowing that separates the agreed decision from its execution
options.why: That rule is real but it is qualified two paragraphs later. On the planning decisions for a common area the joint auditors answer for the appropriateness of what was agreed; the execution of the agreed procedures is the individual responsibility of the joint auditor who performed them.

options.text: With the lead or convening firm, which is responsible for the areas retained in common and for the quality of the work done in them
options.misconception: imports a lead auditor into a joint audit, which SA 299 does not create and which would displace both the joint and the individual responsibility
options.why: SA 299 knows no lead joint auditor. Responsibility is allocated by what was divided, what was agreed in common, and who executed the work, and there is no firm carrying the others.

options.text: With that firm alone — where the joint auditors have together settled, at planning, the nature, timing and extent of the procedures for an area held in common, what they all answer for is whether those decisions were appropriate; carrying the agreed procedures out properly falls on whichever joint auditor performed them
options.why: A common area is not a common excuse. Work left undivided and done by all of them binds the joint auditors jointly and severally, and so do the choices they made together while planning an area held in common. But the Standard then narrows that second limb: on such planning choices they answer only in respect of the appropriateness of what was settled about the nature, timing and extent of the procedures agreed between them, while performing those procedures properly is the individual responsibility of whichever joint auditor did the work. Nothing is wrong with the decision here; the execution failed.
keywords: only in respect of the appropriateness

options.text: With all four, but only if the work allocation document did not record who would perform the batch processing tests — the document being what fixes individual responsibility
options.misconception: makes the allocation document the only source of individual responsibility, when execution carries it whether or not the document names the performer
options.why: The allocation document divides the audit areas and is signed by all the joint auditors and communicated to those charged with governance, which avoids disputes about scope. It is not what makes the execution of an agreed procedure in a common area the responsibility of the auditor who performed it; the Standard does that directly.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — how SA 299 (Revised) splits responsibility in a joint audit between what was agreed together at planning for an undivided area, where all of them answer only for whether the agreed approach was appropriate, and the carrying out of that agreed work, which rests on the firm that actually performed it

items.scenario: Four firms audit a public sector bank jointly and have divided the work by zones. Information technology systems and controls was left undivided because of its nature, and all four agreed at planning what would be tested and how — general controls, application controls, controls over batch processing, back-up and data centre security. The testing of the batch processing controls was actually carried out by one firm's team and was done badly. That firm says the area was a common one, so the lapse is everybody's.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) require before the report is issued?

options.text: Communication of the modification only — an Emphasis of Matter paragraph does not modify the opinion, so there is nothing about it that those charged with governance need to be told in advance
options.misconception: limits the advance communication to matters that change the opinion, when the expectation of an Emphasis of Matter paragraph carries the same requirement
options.why: Both are named. Should an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, or an Other Matter paragraph, be in prospect, the joint auditors say so and give the wording they propose for it, exactly as they do for a modification.

options.text: Nothing beyond issuing a common audit report — the communication requirements about a modification belong to SA 705 and bind a sole auditor, a joint audit being governed by SA 299 alone
options.misconception: treats SA 299 as displacing the other Standards, when it repeats the requirement expressly so that it binds the joint auditors together
options.why: SA 299 carries the requirement itself, so that it is the joint auditors together who communicate the circumstances and the proposed wording, to ensure compliance with SA 705 and SA 706 respectively.

options.text: Those charged with governance must be told what circumstances have led to the modification the joint auditors expect, and what wording is proposed for it, so that SA 705 is complied with; they must likewise be told that an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is expected and what its proposed wording is, so that SA 706 is complied with — and before the report is finalised the joint auditors discuss their respective conclusions with one another
options.why: The Standard puts both communications on the joint auditors expressly. Expecting to modify the opinion, they must tell those charged with governance what circumstances brought the expected modification about, and the proposed wording for it. Expecting instead to add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, or an Other Matter paragraph, they must tell them that too, along with the proposed wording that paragraph will carry. And their report is not finalised until the joint auditors have talked their respective conclusions over between themselves — the conclusions that are going to make up the report's content.

options.text: A separate audit report from each firm — where a report will be modified, each joint auditor must express his own opinion so that the reader can see which firm stands behind the qualification
options.misconception: turns an agreed modification into a case for separate reports, when separate reports arise only from disagreement among the joint auditors
options.why: The joint auditors are required to issue a common audit report. Separate reports arise only where they are in disagreement about the opinion or about a matter to be covered by the report, and here all three agree.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — what SA 299 (Revised) makes the joint auditors tell those charged with governance before the report goes out: the circumstances behind a modification they expect and the wording proposed for it, so that SA 705 is met; the prospect of an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph and the wording proposed for that, so that SA 706 is met; read with the duty to talk their respective conclusions over among themselves before the report is finalised

items.scenario: Three joint auditors have agreed that the report will carry a qualification on revenue cut-off and an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to a note about a tax demand. One of them proposes that they simply issue the report as drafted, on the ground that those charged with governance will read the qualification and the paragraph when the report reaches them, and that showing them the wording beforehand invites an argument.

items.stem: What does SA 320 say about choosing a benchmark and the percentage applied to it?

options.text: Profit before tax is unusable on a loss-making entity, so revenue or gross profit is the benchmark here; the percentage cannot be carried across with it, since a rate laid on profit before tax from continuing operations would normally sit above one laid on total revenue; and for an entity that has custody of assets, assets may be the appropriate benchmark
options.why: Determining materiality involves professional judgement, and a percentage is applied to a chosen benchmark as a starting point. The choice of benchmark is affected by the elements of the financial statements, whether there are items on which users' attention tends to be focused, the nature of the entity and where it is in its life cycle together with its industry and economic environment, the ownership structure and the way the entity is financed, and the relative volatility of the benchmark. Where the entity has incurred losses, revenue or gross profit may be considered instead. The percentage then has to move with the benchmark, the two being tied together: a rate laid on profit before tax from continuing operations would normally be higher than one laid on total revenue. And where an entity has custody of assets, assets may be an appropriate benchmark.

options.text: Revenue is the benchmark, and the percentage applied to revenue will normally be higher than the one applied to profit before tax, revenue being the larger and therefore the safer figure
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between the percentage and the benchmark, which would set materiality far above anything the users of a loss-making company could tolerate
options.why: The relationship runs the other way. A rate laid on profit before tax from continuing operations would normally sit above one laid on total revenue, which is why switching benchmark without switching the percentage produces a materiality figure that means nothing.

options.text: Profit before tax stays as the benchmark whatever the result, materiality being about the entity's earning capacity, and the same percentage is applied to whichever figure is used since the percentage expresses the firm's tolerance for error
options.misconception: keeps one benchmark and one percentage for every entity, when the benchmark is chosen for the entity and the percentage moves with the benchmark
options.why: Neither half survives. The benchmark is chosen by reference to the entity, its life cycle, its industry, how it is financed and what its users look at, and a company with two loss years does not offer a usable profit figure. And the percentage is not a fixed tolerance carried between benchmarks — the rate laid on profit before tax from continuing operations sits above the rate that goes on total revenue.

options.text: Any benchmark may be used provided the same one is used consistently year on year, and for the depository the benchmark must be fee income, because assets held for clients are not the entity's own
options.misconception: makes consistency the governing rule and refuses assets as a benchmark for an entity that holds them for others
options.why: Consistency is not the test — the benchmark is revisited as the entity changes, and materiality itself may be revised during the audit on new information, a change in circumstances or a change in the auditor's understanding. And where an entity has custody of assets, assets may be an appropriate benchmark precisely because that is what its users are watching.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — how a benchmark is picked when materiality for the statements taken as a whole is being set, what factors bear on that choice, why the rate cannot travel unchanged from one benchmark to another (profit before tax from continuing operations carrying a higher one than total revenue), when losses push the auditor to revenue or gross profit instead, and when assets serve because the entity holds them for others

items.scenario: A construction company has made losses in each of the last two years. Revenue for the year is ₹800 crore, gross profit ₹24 crore and the loss before tax ₹6 crore. The manager proposes to keep profit before tax as the benchmark because the firm always uses it, and to apply to revenue, if he has to switch, the same percentage the firm applies to profit before tax. A second engagement in the same office is the audit of a depository that holds clients' assets but earns a small fee income.

items.stem: What does SA 402 give the user auditor to do at this point?

options.text: Nothing but obtain a Type 1 or Type 2 report — where no such report exists the user auditor cannot obtain evidence about controls he has no access to, and the scope limitation is real
options.misconception: treats the service auditor's report as the only source of understanding, when three other routes are named alongside it
options.why: The report is the first of four routes and the only one that depends on somebody else having already done the work. Contacting the service organisation through the user entity, visiting it and using another auditor are all available, and the absence of a report does not by itself create a scope limitation.

options.text: One or more of four things — obtain a Type 1 or Type 2 report if one is available; contact the service organisation, through the user entity, to obtain specific information; visit the service organisation and perform procedures that will provide the necessary information about the relevant controls; or use another auditor to perform such procedures at the service organisation
options.why: A disclaimer is what happens if the evidence cannot be obtained, not the first response to not having it yet. Where the user entity by itself cannot supply enough understanding, four routes open up and he may take one of them or several: obtaining a Type 1 or Type 2 report if available; contacting the service organisation through the user entity to obtain specific information; visiting the service organisation and performing procedures there; and using another auditor to perform those procedures on his behalf. Note the second route runs through the user entity rather than direct — the service organisation is the client's contractor, not the auditor's.

options.text: Write directly to the service organisation for its control documentation, the user auditor being entitled to deal with it as he would with any third party holding the entity's records
options.misconception: goes direct to the service organisation, when the Standard routes that contact through the user entity
options.why: The route is specified. The user auditor contacts the service organisation through the user entity to obtain specific information, because his engagement and his access both run through the client rather than through the client's contractor.

options.text: Assess the risks at the maximum and perform substantive procedures on payroll, an understanding of controls being needed only where the auditor intends to rely on them
options.misconception: skips the required understanding by assuming the worst, when the understanding is needed to identify and assess the risks at all rather than only to place reliance
options.why: The understanding is not optional. The user auditor obtains an understanding of how the user entity uses the services — their nature and significance, the nature and materiality of the transactions affected, the degree of interaction and the nature of the relationship — in order to provide a basis for identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement, which comes before any question of reliance.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: what the user auditor may do when the user entity cannot by itself give him enough understanding of the outsourced services — a Type 1 or Type 2 report where one exists, an approach to the service organisation made through the user entity, a visit there to carry out procedures himself, or another auditor engaged to carry them out for him

items.scenario: A company has outsourced its entire payroll to a service organisation. The user entity's own staff can describe what they send and what comes back but know nothing about the controls at the service organisation, and no service auditor's report exists. The user auditor concludes he has not obtained a sufficient understanding of the services and their effect on the user entity's internal control to assess the risks of material misstatement. His manager says the only remaining option is to disclaim.

items.stem: What does SA 402 require of him?

options.text: Nothing about the fraud, which is the service organisation's own affair and its own auditor's problem, and an unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph describing the limit of the work done
options.misconception: treats events at the service organisation as outside the audit, and uses a paragraph to describe a limitation instead of modifying for it
options.why: The Standard makes the inquiry a requirement precisely because a fraud or an uncorrected misstatement at the service organisation can affect the user entity's financial statements. And a limitation on obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence is answered by modifying the opinion, not by describing it in a paragraph beside an unmodified one.

options.text: Refer to the work of the service auditor in the report so that the reader can see where the limit lies, and issue an unmodified opinion
options.misconception: reaches for a reference to the service auditor's work as a way of explaining the position, when reference is barred in an unmodified report unless law or regulation requires it
options.why: A reference of that kind is barred. Where the opinion is unmodified, the service auditor's work goes unmentioned in the report unless some law or regulation says otherwise; and on the occasions when a reference is required, or helps a reader follow a modification, the report has to say in terms that mentioning it takes nothing away from the responsibility the user auditor bears for his own opinion.

options.text: Report the fraud at the service organisation to those charged with governance of the service organisation and obtain a written representation from it that no other matters exist, then proceed
options.misconception: directs the auditor at the service organisation's governance and at a representation from a party that is not his client
options.why: The inquiry is of the management of the user entity, which is his client, and the written representations in an audit come from that entity's management and those charged with governance. The service organisation's governance is not his reporting line.

options.text: Ask the user entity's own management two things — has the service organisation reported any fraud, any breach of law or regulation, or any misstatement left uncorrected that bears on these financial statements, and does the entity know of such a matter from any other source — then weigh what turns up against the nature, timing and extent of the rest of his work and against the conclusions he will reach; and modify the opinion under SA 705, sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the outsourced services being beyond his reach
options.why: Both halves are express requirements. The first is an inquiry: he inquires of management of the user entity — asking, in substance, two things — whether anything has come to the entity from the service organisation, or reached it any other way, about a fraud, about laws and regulations broken, or about uncorrected misstatements that bear on the statements he is auditing; and he then weighs what such matters do to the nature, timing and extent of his remaining procedures, to his conclusions and to his report. The second is the opinion: he modifies the opinion under SA 705, sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services the organisation provides being beyond his reach. An explanatory paragraph attached to an unmodified opinion does neither.
keywords: inquires of management of the user entity

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: the question the user auditor puts to his own client's management about fraud, breaches of law or regulation and misstatements left uncorrected at the service organisation, what he does with the answer, and the duty to modify under SA 705 when the outsourced services leave him without sufficient appropriate audit evidence — read with the bar on naming a service auditor's work in a report whose opinion is unmodified

items.scenario: A user auditor has learned informally that the service organisation processing the company's sales ledger wrote to the company during the year about a fraud by one of its own operators, and about misstatements it had not corrected. He has also been unable, after exhausting the available routes, to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services provided. He proposes to say nothing about the fraud, since it happened at the service organisation, and to issue an unmodified opinion with a paragraph explaining that part of the processing was outside his reach.

items.stem: What does SA 500 require of the two?

options.text: Only the confirmations need work — an ageing schedule comes from the accounting system that produced the financial statements, so testing it would be testing the same records twice
options.misconception: exempts entity-produced information from evaluation because it comes from the accounting records, which is the reason to test it rather than to trust it
options.why: The accounting records are the thing under audit. When information produced by the entity is used as audit evidence the auditor evaluates its reliability, completeness and accuracy, and an incomplete ageing schedule silently removes items from the population before the sample is drawn.

options.text: Evidence from an external source is not reliable merely because it is external — all responses carry some risk of interception, alteration or fraud whether they arrive on paper or electronically, and cancelled registrations with no fresh ones raise a real question whether the replies came from the intended parties; and information produced by the entity itself has to be evaluated for its reliability, completeness and accuracy before it is used as audit evidence
options.why: The two failures are the same failure at different ends. An external source does not settle reliability: circumstances can still exist that undercut evidence coming from outside the entity, and every reply carries some risk of interception, alteration or fraud — the medium, paper or electronic or anything else, makes no difference to that. What raises doubt is a reply that came in indirectly, or one that looks as though it was not sent by the originally intended confirming party, and businesses whose registrations were cancelled during the year are exactly that question. At the other end, where the auditor uses information produced by the entity he evaluates its reliability, completeness and accuracy, because a sample selected from an unverified schedule tests only what the schedule chose to show.

options.text: Both are acceptable — evidence from an external source is more reliable than evidence generated inside the entity, and an ageing schedule is a working paper rather than audit evidence, so neither needs further work
options.misconception: turns a general statement about relative reliability into a guarantee, and treats entity-produced information used to select a sample as though it were not evidence at all
options.why: External evidence is generally more reliable, which is not the same as reliable. And a schedule the auditor uses to select his sample is information produced by the entity being used as audit evidence, so its reliability, completeness and accuracy have to be evaluated.

options.text: Only the ageing schedule needs work — a confirmation is a direct written response from a third party, which is the most reliable form of audit evidence there is and cannot be improved on
options.misconception: treats the form of a confirmation as settling its reliability, when the question is whether the response actually came from the intended party
options.why: The form is not the point. If the auditor has doubt about the reliability of a response he obtains further audit evidence, and if he determines that a response is not reliable he evaluates the implications for his assessment of the risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and for the nature, timing and extent of other procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 500: why an outside source does not by itself make evidence reliable, the risk of interception, alteration or fraud that every reply carries whatever medium it comes in, the signs that a particular response should be doubted, and the separate duty to weigh how reliable, complete and accurate the entity's own information is before it is used as evidence

items.scenario: Two pieces of evidence go into the file without further work. The first is a set of confirmations that came back within a week from twenty-five creditors, all of whose registrations under the goods and services tax were cancelled during the year and none of whom has a fresh registration; the senior treats them as reliable because they came from outside the entity. The second is an ageing schedule of receivables printed by the company's own system, which the senior uses to select his sample; he has not checked it against anything.

items.stem: Who is right, and why?

options.text: The partner, because a five-year appointment creates a familiarity threat that can never be reduced to an acceptable level, so the work of this expert cannot be used at all
options.misconception: turns a threat into a disqualification, when the auditor evaluates the threats and the adequacy of the safeguards rather than ruling the expert out
options.why: The evaluation is of the threats and of whether the safeguards are adequate. Safeguards cannot eliminate all threats to an expert's objectivity, but the conclusion is a judgement about the evidence rather than an automatic exclusion of the expert.

options.text: The senior, but for a different reason — the evaluation of objectivity is required only for an auditor's expert under SA 620, a management's expert being management's responsibility
options.misconception: confines the objectivity evaluation to the auditor's own expert, when SA 500 requires it for a management's expert too
options.why: SA 500 requires it directly. Whenever a management's expert has had a hand in preparing something the auditor means to use as audit evidence, that expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity are evaluated, his work is understood, and its appropriateness as evidence for the assertion in question is evaluated too.

options.text: The partner — objectivity gets evaluated whether the entity employs the expert or engages him; a broad range of circumstances may threaten it, and since employment carries its own threat that never goes away, an expert on the payroll is not, as a rule, to be treated as any likelier to be objective than the rest of the staff, while for an engaged expert the auditor discusses the interests and relationships that may create threats — financial interests, business and personal relationships and the provision of other services — and evaluates whether the safeguards are adequate
options.why: Being engaged rather than employed changes the size of some threats, not the duty to look. A broad range of circumstances may threaten objectivity — self-interest, advocacy, familiarity, self-review and intimidation — and safeguards may be created by external structures such as the expert's profession or by his own work environment. Intimidation, for one, tends to weigh less on an expert the entity has engaged than on one it employs, and safeguards such as quality control policies may work better; but employment brings a threat that is always present, so an employed expert cannot ordinarily be regarded as more likely to be objective than other employees. Where the expert is engaged, it may be relevant to discuss with management and with him any interests and relationships creating threats — financial interests, business and personal relationships, the provision of other services — and to evaluate whether the safeguards are adequate.

options.text: The senior — an expert engaged by the entity is by definition independent of it, and the auditor's evaluation is confined to the expert's competence and capabilities
options.misconception: reads engagement as independence and drops objectivity from the three things the auditor evaluates
options.why: The auditor evaluates the competence, capabilities and objectivity of a management's expert, and objectivity is not established by the fact of engagement. An expert can be engaged and still carry a self-interest threat from five consecutive years of fees or from other services he provides.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 500: how the objectivity of a management's expert is evaluated, the range of circumstances that can threaten it and the safeguards coming from the expert's profession or his working environment, why an expert on the entity's payroll is not as a rule any likelier to be objective than the rest of its staff, and the interests and relationships to be discussed where the entity has engaged the expert instead

items.scenario: A mining company has engaged the same outside valuer for five years running to compute its environmental liabilities and site clean-up provisions, and describes him in its papers as an independent expert. The audit senior, having made inquiries of management, takes the view that because the valuer was engaged rather than employed and is called independent, his objectivity cannot be questioned and needs no evaluation. The audit partner disagrees.

items.stem: What is wrong with management's instructions?

options.text: Five things — the count should be supervised by a responsible officer not from the storage function, preferably from finance, with the storage in-charge present only to assist; inward and outward movement should not be allowed during the count because it distorts the result; the counting teams should be drawn from departments unconnected with storage, with counting and recording separated and serially numbered count sheets, distinctive marks or tags put on completed areas and each sheet signed by every team member; the paddy in silos should be measured with the strain gauges rather than assumed from silo capacity, since paddy may have been drawn from them; and work in progress should be estimated at each stage of production rather than for the plant as a whole
options.why: The first of the four things attendance is for is an evaluation — of the instructions management issued and of the procedures it set for recording and controlling what the count produces — and every one of these instructions fails it. A man supervising the count of the inventory he is responsible for is checking his own work. Movement of goods during a count is the classic way a quantity is counted twice or not at all. Teams drawn from the storage function have the same problem as the supervisor, and without distinctive marks nobody can show that an area was covered or covered once. Silo capacity is what the silo could hold, not what is in it. And work in progress estimated for the plant as a whole gives an inaccurate picture, because the stage of completion differs at each step.

options.text: Only the supervision — the officer responsible for storage must not supervise, but the rest is acceptable, and where the auditor doubts the result he performs additional test counts of his own
options.misconception: treats extra test counts as a cure for a badly designed count, when a test count checks the records against the count rather than repairing it
options.why: A test count traces items from the physical inventory to management's count records and back; it cannot repair a count in which goods moved, areas went unmarked and silos were estimated from capacity. The instructions are evaluated before the count, which is why the auditor reads them in advance.

options.text: Only the silos and the work in progress — those are measurement errors that produce wrong quantities, while supervision, movement of goods and the composition of the teams are matters of the company's internal organisation
options.misconception: separates measurement from control, when the control failures are what let a wrong quantity through unnoticed
options.why: The control failures are the reason a wrong quantity survives. A supervisor counting his own inventory, goods moving during the count and unmarked areas each produce quantities nobody can test afterwards, and they are named in the same evaluation as the silos and the work in progress.

options.text: Nothing — these are management's instructions and management is responsible for the count; the auditor observes the count, performs test counts and inspects the inventory, and the design of the count is not his to criticise
options.misconception: reduces attendance to observation, when evaluating management's instructions and procedures is one of the four things attendance is for
options.why: Attendance has four purposes and the first of them is evaluation: management's instructions, and the procedures it has set for recording and controlling what the physical inventory count produces, are both weighed. The other three — observing the count procedures being performed, inspecting the inventory and performing test counts — come after it.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501: the evaluation an auditor makes of what management has instructed and of the procedures set up to record and control what a physical inventory count produces — supervision by an officer outside the storage function, no inward or outward movement while the count runs, teams drawn from unconnected departments with counting kept separate from recording on serially numbered sheets, distinctive marks on areas already done and signed count sheets, silo quantities read off strain gauges rather than assumed from capacity, and work in progress estimated stage by stage through production

items.scenario: Before attending a rice mill's year end count, the auditor is given management's written instructions. The count is to be supervised by the officer responsible for storage. Receiving and despatch are to carry on as usual so that business is not interrupted. Counting is to be done by teams of three drawn from the storage staff, with no instruction about marking areas already counted or about signing the count sheets. Paddy in the steel silos is to be estimated from the capacity of each silo. Work in progress is to be estimated for the plant as a whole.

items.stem: What does SA 510 require about the opening inventory?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion — where the prior period was not audited at all, sufficient appropriate audit evidence about opening balances cannot be obtained and the limitation is absolute
options.misconception: treats an unaudited prior period as an automatic scope limitation, when the Standard sets out the procedures by which the evidence is obtained
options.why: A qualified opinion or a disclaimer follows only if the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances after performing the procedures. An initial audit engagement includes the case where the prior period financial statements were not audited, and the Standard tells him what to do about it.

options.text: A written representation from management that the opening inventory was correctly stated, that being the only evidence available for a period during which the firm was not the auditor
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for procedures, when representations never provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own
options.why: A representation on its own never amounts to sufficient appropriate audit evidence for the matter it covers. The three named procedures — the reconciliation from a current count, work on the valuation of the opening items, and work on gross profit and cut-off — are what produce the evidence.

options.text: Work done this period on the closing inventory balance says little about what was on hand when the period opened, so further procedures are needed — attend a count now and reconcile it back to the opening quantities, test how the opening items were valued, and test gross profit and cut-off
options.why: The auditor evaluates whether the procedures performed in the current period give evidence relevant to the opening balances or whether specific procedures are needed, and inventory is the case where they do not: what was done on the closing balance yields little audit evidence about what was on hand when the period began. Three further procedures are named for it. He attends a count in the current period, reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities. He works on how the opening items were valued. And he works on gross profit and cut-off.
keywords: reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities

options.text: Nothing more — the closing inventory, the purchases and the production records together fix the opening figure arithmetically, which is stronger evidence than any procedure on a count that has already happened
options.misconception: derives the opening balance from the closing one, when the current period's work on the closing balance gives little evidence about the opening quantities
options.why: The arithmetic assumes the very things under audit: that purchases and production were completely recorded and correctly cut off. That is why the Standard says the current period's procedures on the closing balance provide little audit evidence regarding the opening inventory and names three additional procedures instead.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510: why this period's work on the closing inventory balance yields little audit evidence about what was on hand when the period began, and the further procedures that can supply it — attending a count in the current period and reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities, testing how the opening items were valued, and testing gross profit and cut-off

items.scenario: A firm is appointed in July 2026 to audit a manufacturer for the year to 31 March 2027. The previous year was not audited at all and material inventories stood in the balance sheet at 31 March 2026. The manager plans to attend the count at 31 March 2027, and says that once the closing inventory is verified the opening figure follows from it, since the two are linked by the year's purchases and production records.

items.stem: What does SA 520 require when the closing analytical procedures show something new?

options.text: Note it for the following year — analytical procedures at the end of the audit are a review step, and reopening completed substantive work at that stage would mean the audit could never be concluded
options.misconception: treats the closing analytical procedures as incapable of changing the audit, when a previously unrecognised risk they reveal forces the assessment and the procedures to be revised
options.why: They are a review step that is also allowed to find things. Where they identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement the risk assessment is revised and the further planned procedures are modified, and an audit that cannot respond to that is an audit whose conclusion is known in advance.

options.text: Where the results identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement, SA 315 requires the auditor to revise his assessment of the risks of material misstatement and to modify the further planned audit procedures accordingly — procedures at this stage help him reach an overall conclusion on whether the statements sit consistently with what he understands of the entity, and they can resemble the ones used to assess risk in the first place
options.why: The manager has the purpose right and the consequence wrong. Analytical procedures designed and performed near the end of the audit are meant to check back against what the auditor concluded while working through the individual components and elements, and to help him draw reasonable conclusions on which the opinion can rest. But such procedures may throw up a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement, and where they do, SA 315 makes him revise his assessment of that risk and change the further procedures he had planned. Procedures at this stage can look similar to those that would be used as risk assessment procedures, which is exactly why they can find something new.
keywords: similar to those that would be used as risk assessment procedures

options.text: Treat the finding as an uncorrected misstatement and evaluate it with the others at the end, since at this stage of the audit there is no time left to perform further procedures
options.misconception: converts an identified risk into a misstatement, when nothing has yet been quantified and what is required is further work rather than an entry on a schedule
options.why: A relationship pointing to unrecorded sales is a risk, not a measured misstatement, and it cannot go on a schedule of uncorrected misstatements without an amount. What the Standard requires is that the assessment be revised and the further planned procedures modified.

options.text: Investigate the fluctuation by inquiring of management and obtain evidence relevant to their responses, and if the explanation is adequate no more is needed, the risk assessment being fixed at the planning stage
options.misconception: stops at the inquiry and treats the risk assessment as something settled at planning that later evidence cannot move
options.why: The inquiry is right as far as it goes and it is where the investigation starts. But the risk assessment is not fixed at planning: where the results identify a previously unrecognised risk, SA 315 requires it to be revised and the further planned procedures to be modified.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — SA 520: analytical procedures performed near the end of the audit that assist the auditor in forming an overall conclusion, the conclusions drawn from them verifying those formed during the audit of individual components, and the requirement that where their results identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement the auditor revise his assessment under SA 315 and modify the further planned audit procedures

items.scenario: The analytical procedures performed near the end of an audit, after all the substantive work is finished and the file is complete, throw up a relationship between freight cost and despatched volume that nobody noticed at planning and that points to a risk of unrecorded sales. The manager proposes to note it as a matter for next year's planning, on the ground that the procedures at this stage exist to confirm the conclusions already reached rather than to open new ones.

items.stem: What is wrong with what he has done?

options.text: Nothing — 120 items out of 4,000 is a sample, and projecting the misstatements found in a sample to the population is exactly what SA 530 requires for tests of details
options.misconception: treats any examination of part of a population as audit sampling, when sampling requires that every sampling unit have a chance of selection
options.why: Fewer than all the items is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Audit sampling requires that all the sampling units have a chance of selection, and an entry of ₹4 lakh posted in June had no chance of being picked here at all.

options.text: The selection — high value and key items may not be chosen deliberately, because deliberate selection destroys the randomness the Standard requires and biases the result
options.misconception: forbids the selective examination of specific items, when it is a legitimate way of obtaining audit evidence and only the projection is barred
options.why: Selecting specific items is legitimate and often efficient, and high value or key items and all items over a certain amount are the usual choices. What it cannot do is stand in for a conclusion about the whole population.

options.text: The projection — this is a selective examination of specific items rather than audit sampling, because the items were chosen for what they are and not so that every sampling unit had a chance of selection, so the results cannot be projected to the entire population and give no audit evidence about the remainder; and the approach is subject to non-sampling risk rather than to sampling risk
options.why: Audit sampling is the application of audit procedures to less than 100 per cent of the items within a population of audit relevance, done so that every sampling unit stands a chance of selection and the auditor gets a reasonable basis for a conclusion about the whole population. A selective examination of specific items is not that. It can be an efficient way of obtaining audit evidence and the items chosen here are sensibly chosen, but the results cannot be projected to the entire population and provide no audit evidence concerning the remainder of it. Such an approach is subject to non-sampling risk, which is the risk of the auditor reaching an erroneous conclusion for a reason unrelated to sampling — an inappropriate procedure, a misinterpretation of evidence, or a failure to recognise a misstatement or deviation.

options.text: The risk — an examination of specific items carries a higher sampling risk than a random sample of the same size, because the auditor's own judgement decides what is looked at
options.misconception: names the wrong risk, when a selective examination of specific items carries no sampling risk at all and carries non-sampling risk instead
options.why: Sampling risk is the risk that a conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion that testing the whole population would give, and it belongs to sampling. A selective examination of specific items is subject to non-sampling risk — an erroneous conclusion for a reason unrelated to sampling.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — the selective examination of specific items as a means of obtaining audit evidence: it does not constitute audit sampling, its results cannot be projected to the entire population and it provides no audit evidence concerning the remainder, and it is subject to non-sampling risk, read with the definition of audit sampling as the application of audit procedures to less than 100 per cent of the items such that all the sampling units have a chance of selection

items.scenario: Testing a population of 4,000 journal entries, an auditor picks every entry above ₹25 lakh, every entry posted on the last two days of the year, and every entry touching the litigation provision — 120 entries in all. He examines each one, finds three misstatements totalling ₹9 lakh, and projects that to the remaining 3,880 entries to arrive at his estimate of the misstatement in the population.

items.stem: How does SA 560 have the two events treated?

options.text: The dividend is adjusted because it will be approved and paid out of this year's profits, and the claim is disclosed because the amount was still uncertain at the year end
options.misconception: reverses the two, recognising a dividend for which no obligation existed at the reporting date and refusing to adjust a claim whose condition did exist then
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. No liability for the proposed dividend exists at the reporting date because there is no obligation to pay at that date, and the uncertainty about the claim at the year end is the very reason the later settlement is evidence about it.

options.text: The insurance claim is adjusted — it is an event providing evidence of a condition that existed at the date of the financial statements, and the settlement gives fresh information about an item already in them, so the ₹1 crore receivable is written down to the ₹45 lakh accepted; the proposed dividend is not adjusted but is disclosed in the notes, being an event providing evidence of a condition that arose after that date, with no obligation existing at the reporting date
options.why: The financial reporting frameworks identify two types of subsequent event and the treatment follows the type. The claim was lodged and outstanding at the year end and the later settlement provides evidence about a condition that existed then, giving fresh information about an item already included in the financial statements, so they are adjusted to reflect it. The dividend is the other type: the proposal came after the reporting period and no liability exists at the reporting date because there is no obligation to pay at that date, so it is not recognised and the auditor verifies instead that it is disclosed in the notes.
keywords: no obligation to pay at that date

options.text: Both are adjusted — each is a subsequent event of which the auditor has become aware before signing, and events known before the report date are reflected in the financial statements
options.misconception: adjusts for everything learned before the report date, when the adjusting type is defined by the date of the condition rather than by when the auditor learned of it
options.why: The dividing line is the date of the financial statements, not the date of the auditor's knowledge. An event providing evidence of a condition that arose after the date of the financial statements is disclosed rather than adjusted, however early the auditor hears of it.

options.text: Both are disclosed and neither is adjusted, as the manager proposes — both events occurred after the year end, and an amount fixed after the year end cannot be recognised in it
options.misconception: classifies by when the event happened instead of when the condition arose, which would leave every post-year-end settlement of a year-end balance unadjusted
options.why: Every subsequent event happens after the year end; that is what makes it subsequent. What divides them is whether the event gives evidence of a condition that existed at the date of the financial statements, and a settlement of a claim outstanding at that date does exactly that.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560: the split between a subsequent event that speaks to conditions already in place at the reporting date and one that speaks to conditions arising only afterwards, with an insurance claim outstanding at the year end and settled later adjusted as fresh information about something already in the statements, and a dividend proposed after the reporting period left to the notes because no obligation to pay existed at the reporting date

items.scenario: Two events reach an auditor before he signs, for a year ended 31 March. A claim of ₹1 crore against an insurer for stock damaged by flooding the previous September stands in the balance sheet as a receivable because it was unsettled at the year end; in April the surveyor recommended ₹45 lakh, the company consented, and ₹45 lakh was received on 15 May. Separately, on 17 April the board proposed a dividend of ₹1 crore, being ₹10 a share, which the general meeting is likely to approve months later. The manager proposes to disclose both in the notes and adjust neither.

items.stem: How does SA 610 (Revised) have the threats to their objectivity evaluated?

options.text: None of the three may be used for anything at all — an internal auditor is not independent of the entity, so direct assistance is available only where law or regulation expressly permits it
options.misconception: reads the internal auditors' lack of independence as a bar on direct assistance, when the Standard bars it only where there are significant threats to objectivity or insufficient competence
options.why: Internal auditors are indeed not independent of the entity, which is why the direction, supervision and review must recognise that. Direct assistance is prohibited only where law or regulation prohibits it, or where there are significant threats to the internal auditor's objectivity or he lacks sufficient competence for the proposed work.

options.text: The organisational status settles it — a function reporting to the audit committee rather than to management supports the objectivity of its auditors, and that is the test the Standard sets
options.misconception: makes the reporting line the whole of the objectivity question, when three further factors go to the individual and the particular work
options.why: Organisational status is one of the factors and it is about the function. Objectivity means being able to do the work proposed while keeping bias, any conflict of interest, and pressure brought by other people from overriding what the auditor's own professional judgment says — and a man testing the department he worked in for six years faces a threat no reporting line removes.

options.text: The organisational status of the function is one factor among several, and the others answer each of the three cases — whether the auditor is tied to the division or department whose work is being looked at; whether he has family or personal ties to somebody working in, or answerable for, that part of the entity; and whether he holds a financial interest of any size in the entity beyond pay on the terms his fellow employees of like seniority get — and the evaluation must include putting the question to the internal auditors themselves about interests and relationships that could create a threat
options.why: Reporting to the audit committee is the first factor and it goes to the function as a whole. The rest turn on the individual and on the particular job: association with the division — or the department — whose work is under audit, which is the first internal auditor's six years in purchases; family and personal relationships reaching somebody who works in, or answers for, that part of the entity, which is the second's brother-in-law; and significant financial interests held in the entity beyond pay on the terms his fellow employees of like seniority get, which is the third's shareholding. And the evaluation of threats to objectivity has to take in inquiry of the internal auditors themselves, about interests and relationships that could create a threat, so the external auditor puts the question rather than inferring the answer.

options.text: Only the financial interest disqualifies — a shareholding is measurable while a past posting and a family connection are matters of degree that the external auditor's own supervision can contain
options.misconception: keeps the one threat that can be quantified and treats supervision as a safeguard against the two that cannot
options.why: All three are named factors and none of them is answered by supervision. An internal auditor may not be used for direct assistance at all where the threats to his objectivity are significant, and how significant they are is settled before the work is handed over rather than managed afterwards.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — SA 610 (Revised): what bears on how real and how serious a threat to an internal auditor's objectivity is when he gives direct assistance — how far the function's place in the organisation, and the policies and procedures it works under, hold that objectivity up; family or personal ties to somebody working in, or answerable for, the part of the entity whose work is under audit; a link to the division or department that work belongs to; and a financial interest of any size in the entity beyond pay on the terms his fellow employees of like seniority get — together with the duty to put the question to the internal auditors themselves

items.scenario: An external auditor proposes to use three internal auditors to provide direct assistance. The first spent six years in the purchases department and is to be put on purchases testing. The second is the brother-in-law of the officer who authorises the payments he would be testing. The third holds shares in the company worth several times his annual salary, granted on terms not available to other employees at his level. The external auditor says the internal audit function reports to the audit committee, which settles the objectivity question for all three.

items.stem: May it?

options.text: No — where the law prescribes the wording the auditor is confined to what the law says, and a report in a prescribed form can never claim to have been made under the Standards on Auditing
options.misconception: reads a prescribed layout as cutting the report off from the Standards on Auditing altogether, when the standard provides expressly for the reference and states the condition on which it may be made
options.why: SA 700 (Revised) anticipates exactly this and gives the answer. It does not forbid the reference; it makes it conditional, and the condition is the list of minimum elements. A prescribed form that carries them may refer to the Standards on Auditing.

options.text: Yes, and no minimum applies — a report in the form the law prescribes complies with the Standards on Auditing by operation of the law that prescribed it
options.misconception: treats compliance with a prescribed layout as compliance with the Standards, when the reference to the Standards is conditional on the listed elements actually being present
options.why: The law settles what the report looks like; it does not settle what the report may claim. The claim to have audited in accordance with the Standards on Auditing is conditional, and the condition is that the thirteen elements are all there. A prescribed form missing one of them may not carry the reference.

options.text: Yes, but only once the Other Information section is added back, that section being one of the minimum elements the report must carry
options.misconception: puts the Other Information section among the minimum elements, when the list stops short of it and of two other sections the ordinary layout carries
options.why: It is not on the list. The minimum elements run from the title to the date and include nothing about other information, nothing about where the description of the auditor's responsibilities is located, and no separate section for other reporting responsibilities — which is why a prescribed form can be shorter than SA 700's own layout and still refer to the Standards.

options.text: Yes — a report whose layout or wording is prescribed by law or regulation may refer to the Standards on Auditing so long as it includes, at a minimum, each of the thirteen elements the standard lists, and an Other Information section, the location of the description of the auditor's responsibilities and the other reporting responsibilities section are not among them
options.why: The condition is a floor, not the whole of SA 700's own layout. Where a layout, or a wording, is forced on the auditor by a law or a regulation that applies to this entity, his report may refer to the Standards on Auditing only where it holds, at a minimum, each of thirteen elements — the title, the addressee, an Opinion section with a reference to the applicable financial reporting framework, an identification of the financial statements audited, the independence statement referring to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI, the sections addressing SA 570 and a Basis for Qualified or Adverse Opinion and SA 701 where each is applicable, a description of management's responsibilities with an identification of those responsible for oversight of the financial reporting process, a reference to the Standards on Auditing and to the law or regulation with a description of the auditor's responsibilities, the signature, the place and the date. Everything the regulator's form is missing sits outside that list.
keywords: Code of Ethics issued by ICAI

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): the condition on which a report whose layout, or wording, a law or regulation has fixed may still name the Standards on Auditing — the thirteen listed elements all being present in it as a floor

items.scenario: A regulator prescribes, word for word, the form of the auditor's report for the entities it supervises. The prescribed form carries a title, an addressee, an Opinion section naming the framework, an identification of the statements audited, the independence statement referring to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI, a description of management's responsibilities with the persons responsible for oversight named, a reference to the Standards on Auditing and to the regulator's own rules with a description of the auditor's responsibilities, the signature, the place and the date. It has no Other Information section, no paragraph on where the description of the auditor's responsibilities is located, and no separate section for other reporting responsibilities. The engagement partner wants to know whether the report may still say the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing.

items.stem: What does SA 700 (Revised) allow?

options.text: Not that — the report may refer to both only if there is no conflict between the two sets of requirements that would lead the auditor to form a different opinion, or not to include an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph that the Standards on Auditing require in the circumstances, and only if it carries at a minimum the same elements a prescribed report must carry; where the reference is made, the report clearly identifies both, including the jurisdiction of origin of the other standards
options.why: Dropping the paragraph is the conflict, so the dual reference fails on its own terms. Naming the Standards on Auditing alongside the International Standards on Auditing, or alongside another jurisdiction's standards, is open to him only where no conflict runs between them that would lead him to form a different opinion or not to include an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph that is required by the Standards on Auditing in the particular circumstances, and only if the report includes at a minimum each of the elements listed for a report prescribed by law or regulation. And when the report does refer to both, it clearly identifies them, including the jurisdiction of origin of the other auditing standards.
keywords: Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph

options.text: Refer to both with no condition at all — naming two sets of standards is a description of what was done, not a claim about either of them
options.misconception: reads the dual reference as a factual description, when the standard makes it conditional on the absence of conflict and on the minimum elements being present
options.why: It is a claim, and SA 700 (Revised) fences it with two conditions: no conflict of the kind described, and the minimum elements all present. A reference made without them tells the reader the report satisfies both sets of requirements when it satisfies only one.

options.text: Drop the paragraph and refer to both, with the explanatory sentence — a conflict that is disclosed to the reader is a conflict he can allow for
options.misconception: treats a disclosure of the conflict as curing it, when the condition for the dual reference is that no such conflict exists at all
options.why: The standard does not ask the auditor to explain the conflict; it asks whether there is one. A conflict that leads him not to include a paragraph the Standards on Auditing require is precisely the conflict named, and no sentence in the report makes the dual reference available once it exists.

options.text: Refer only to the other jurisdiction's standards, since the report is being prepared for the parent's group audit and those standards govern what it must contain
options.misconception: lets the reader of the report choose which standards the audit was conducted under, when the audit was conducted under both and the Standards on Auditing require the paragraph
options.why: The audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing as well, and dropping the reference does not drop the requirement. The paragraph is required in the circumstances by the Standards on Auditing, and an audit conducted under them includes it whatever else the report refers to.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): an auditor's report for an audit conducted in accordance with both the Standards on Auditing and the International Standards on Auditing or the auditing standards of another jurisdiction may refer to both only where no conflict would lead the auditor to a different opinion or to omitting a required Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, and only where the minimum elements are present, and it shall clearly identify both including the jurisdiction of origin of the other standards

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary of a foreign group is audited in accordance with the Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI and also the auditing standards of the parent's jurisdiction. A significant subsequent event has occurred which the Standards on Auditing require to be brought to users' attention in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph; the other jurisdiction's standards do not call for one, and the group reporting team has asked that the paragraph be dropped. The manager proposes to drop it and to have the report refer to both sets of standards, adding a sentence explaining that the other jurisdiction's standards do not require such a paragraph.

items.stem: How does SA 700 (Revised) treat the two?

options.text: The appendix is not covered and, management having refused, the auditor modifies his opinion because the presentation of the financial statements as a whole is now misleading
options.misconception: answers a presentation problem in the unaudited information with a modification of the opinion on the financial statements, when the standard answers it by identifying the information and explaining that it has not been audited
options.why: The defect is in how unaudited information is presented, not in the financial statements the opinion covers. SA 700 (Revised) gives the remedy: ask management to change the presentation, and on refusal identify the unaudited supplementary information and explain in the report that it has not been audited.

options.text: Both are covered by the opinion, since both are printed with the audited financial statements and a reader takes everything between the same covers as audited
options.misconception: extends the opinion to everything bound with the statements, when the standard provides for information that can be clearly differentiated and is not covered
options.why: The risk that a reader takes everything as audited is the reason for the differentiation requirement, not a reason to audit everything. Information that can be clearly differentiated from the financial statements is not covered by the opinion; what the standard requires is that the presentation make the difference visible.

options.text: Neither is covered by the opinion, both being outside what the framework requires, and the auditor states in his report that all supplementary information is unaudited
options.misconception: makes the framework's requirements the test, when the test is whether the information is an integral part of the financial statements by its nature or by how it is presented
options.why: Being outside the framework's requirements is what makes the information supplementary in the first place; it does not answer the question the standard asks next. Some supplementary information is an integral part of the statements by its nature or its presentation, and that information is covered by the opinion.

options.text: The reconciliation note is an integral part of the financial statements and is covered by the auditor's opinion; the appendix can be clearly differentiated, so it is not covered, and because management has refused to change how it is presented the auditor identifies the unaudited supplementary information and explains in his report that it has not been audited
options.why: The test is whether the supplementary information is nevertheless an integral part of the financial statements due to its nature or how it is presented. A note explaining or reconciling the extent of compliance with another framework, cross-referenced from the statements, is information that cannot be clearly differentiated from them, and where it is an integral part it shall be covered by the auditor's opinion. An additional profit and loss account presented as a separate schedule in an appendix is information that can be clearly differentiated; the auditor then evaluates whether it is presented in a way that sufficiently and clearly differentiates it, asks management to change the presentation where it is not, and where management refuses, identifies the information and explains in his report that it has not been audited.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): supplementary information that is an integral part of the financial statements shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, and where it is not an integral part but is not sufficiently and clearly differentiated the auditor asks management to change the presentation and, on refusal, identifies it and explains in his report that it has not been audited

items.scenario: Two things are printed with a company's audited financial statements and neither is required by the applicable framework. The first is a note that reconciles the extent to which the statements comply with another financial reporting framework, and it is cross-referenced from note 4. The second is an additional profit and loss account disclosing specific items of expenditure, presented as a separate schedule in an appendix, laid out in the same type and format as the statements with no marking to set it apart. Management refuses to change how the appendix is presented.

items.stem: Is he right under SA 700 (Revised)?

options.text: No, and the auditor must ask management to move the schedule into an appendix so that it can be clearly differentiated and left out of the opinion
options.misconception: treats the differentiation route as available for information that is an integral part of the financial statements, when that route is for information which is not
options.why: The two routes are alternatives and the first one is already closed. Asking management to change the presentation is what the standard requires for supplementary information that is not an integral part; a schedule the notes depend on is an integral part, and moving it does not change that.

options.text: No — the auditor evaluates whether the supplementary information is nevertheless an integral part of the financial statements due to its nature or how it is presented, and where it is, it shall be covered by his opinion; a schedule cross-referenced from the notes is covered, and a label cannot take it out
options.why: The label describes what management would like the schedule to be; the standard asks what it is. The auditor evaluates whether, in his professional judgement, supplementary information not required by the framework is nevertheless an integral part of the financial statements due to its nature or how it is presented, and when it is an integral part it shall be covered by the auditor's opinion. The module puts it plainly: a note, or a supplementary schedule, that the statements themselves have cross-referenced falls inside the opinion too.

options.text: Yes — information marked unaudited is by that fact outside the opinion, and the auditor's only duty is to check that the marking is prominent
options.misconception: lets a label decide the scope of the opinion, when the standard decides it on the nature of the information and how it is presented
options.why: If a label could decide it, any figure could be put beyond the opinion by heading it "unaudited", and the differentiation requirement would have nothing to do. Where the information is an integral part of the financial statements it is covered by the opinion whatever it is headed.

options.text: Yes, provided the auditor adds an Other Matter paragraph recording that the schedule is outside the scope of his opinion
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to move information out of an opinion the standard says covers it, rather than answering the question of whether it is an integral part
options.why: A paragraph cannot narrow an opinion the standard says extends to the information.
