The question is whether the schedule is an integral part of the financial statements, and a schedule the notes rely on and cross-refer to is one; the paragraph would tell the reader something untrue about the scope of the opinion.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): supplementary information that is an integral part of the financial statements due to its nature or how it is presented shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, the opinion covering notes or supplementary schedules cross-referenced from the financial statements

items.scenario: A company presents, within its financial statements, a schedule of key operating ratios headed "Unaudited — for information only". The schedule is cross-referenced from note 12, which relies on it to explain a movement in trade receivables. The finance director says the heading settles the matter and that the auditor's opinion cannot reach anything marked unaudited.

items.stem: What does SA 701 have the section say?

options.text: The section stays, and because the report already carries those two sections the paragraph excepts them by name — the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section — before saying that, beyond those, the auditor found no other key audit matters his report had to communicate
options.why: Both readings are half right. Where the auditor determines that there are no key audit matters to communicate, the report must still carry the section and say so — so deleting it is wrong. But a flat statement that there are no key audit matters would contradict the rest of the report, because a matter giving rise to a modification and a material uncertainty related to going concern are by their nature matters of most significance. The illustration in the module keeps the exception on the face of the sentence: the matter set out in the Basis for Qualified (Adverse) Opinion section, and the one set out under Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern, are excepted, and beyond them the auditor has determined there are no other key audit matters to communicate.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

options.text: Keep the section with the plain sentence that the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate, the two matters having their own sections and so being outside this one
options.misconception: says there are none at all in a report that carries two matters which are of most significance by their nature, so the sentence contradicts the rest of the report
options.why: They are outside the section and they are still of most significance in the audit, which is why the illustration keeps the word "other" in the sentence and names the sections the excepted matters sit in. Without the exception the report says on one page that nothing was of most significance and on another that the opinion is qualified.

options.text: Delete the section — a heading with nothing under it tells the reader less than no heading at all, and the two matters are already described elsewhere in the report
options.misconception: reads the requirement to communicate key audit matters as conditional on there being something to describe, when the section is required and carries a statement that there are none
options.why: The section is not conditional on its contents. Where the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate, the report must specifically mention that by carrying a Key Audit Matters paragraph which says so. A reader of a listed company's report expects the section and its absence is itself information.

options.text: Keep the section and describe the inventory misstatement and the going concern uncertainty in it as the key audit matters, they being the most significant matters in the audit
options.misconception: turns a cross-reference into a description, when the paragraph names those matters only to except them from a statement that there are no others
options.why: Naming them and describing them are different acts. Communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for expressing a modified opinion or for reporting under SA 570, so those two matters are reported in their own sections; the Key Audit Matters section refers to them and goes no further.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 701: where there are no key audit matters to communicate the report carries a Key Audit Matters paragraph saying so, and the module's illustration of that paragraph excepts by name the matter sitting in the modified-opinion basis section, and the one sitting under going concern, before saying no others were found for communication

items.scenario: The report on a listed company carries a Basis for Qualified Opinion section on an inventory misstatement and a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section. Nothing else in the audit required significant auditor attention. One manager wants the Key Audit Matters section deleted, since there is nothing left to put in it. Another wants it kept with a single sentence saying that the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate.

items.stem: What does SA 710 require in the report you are about to sign?

options.text: Your opinion refers to the current period only, comparatives never being covered by the opinion, so the earlier year is dealt with by a note in the accounts if management chooses
options.misconception: applies the corresponding figures rule to comparative financial statements, where the opinion refers to each period presented
options.why: That is the corresponding figures rule, and it is the other approach. The two differ in exactly this: for corresponding figures the opinion refers to the current period only, whereas for comparative financial statements it refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

options.text: Express the different opinion on the earlier period and put the reasons for the difference in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, the matter being fundamental to users' understanding
options.misconception: uses the paragraph reserved for a matter appropriately presented in the financial statements to carry the reasons for a change of opinion, which the standard places in an Other Matter paragraph
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph points at something the financial statements themselves already present, or disclose, appropriately. Why the auditor's opinion has changed is not in the financial statements at all; it is a matter relevant to users' understanding of the audit and of the report, and SA 710 names the Other Matter paragraph for it.

options.text: Reissue last year's report carrying the new opinion, and confine this year's report to this year, since an opinion is amended in the report that expressed it
options.misconception: reopens a completed engagement instead of expressing the changed opinion in the current report with its reasons in an Other Matter paragraph
options.why: SA 710 does not send the auditor back to the old report. The prior period is presented again in this year's financial statements and is covered by this year's opinion, so the different opinion is expressed here and the substantive reasons for it are disclosed in an Other Matter paragraph.

options.text: Because comparative financial statements are presented, your opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented, so a different opinion may be expressed on the earlier period now — and where the opinion on the prior period financial statements differs from the opinion you previously expressed on them, the substantive reasons for the different opinion are disclosed in an Other Matter paragraph in your report
options.why: Under the comparative financial statements approach the auditor's opinion refers to each period put on show, so the earlier year is not closed by last year's report — it is being reported on again. SA 710 then deals with the awkward case directly: when reporting on the current period's audit, if the auditor's opinion on the prior period financial statements differs from the opinion previously expressed, he shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph. The changed opinion goes in the opinion; the reasons for the change go in the paragraph.
keywords: differs from the opinion previously expressed

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 710: under the comparative approach every period put on show is one the auditor's opinion speaks to, and where the opinion on the prior period differs from the opinion previously expressed the substantive reasons for the difference are disclosed in an Other Matter paragraph

items.scenario: A company presents comparative financial statements for two years, both audited by you, and you expressed an unmodified opinion on the earlier year. Work on the current year has established that a warranty provision in the earlier year was materially understated on a basis you now accept was wrong, and the earlier year's figures as presented are unchanged. Your manager says the opinion you gave last year is final and this year's report can only deal with this year.

items.stem: What does SA 710 require you to do first?

options.text: Include an Other Matter paragraph stating that the prior period was audited by a predecessor auditor, the type of opinion he expressed and the date of his report, and leave the misstatement there
options.misconception: uses the paragraph that identifies a predecessor's report to carry a misstatement the standard deals with by informing management and the predecessor
options.why: That paragraph tells the reader who audited the prior period and what he concluded, which is a different job. A material misstatement in previously audited figures is reported to management with a request that the predecessor auditor be informed, and the paragraph does not stand in place of it.

options.text: Say nothing about the prior period — it was reported on by the predecessor auditor, and a successor does not go behind another member's report
options.misconception: treats the predecessor's report as closing the period, when the auditor reporting on comparative financial statements is expressing an opinion on that period as well
options.why: He is not going behind the report; he is expressing his own opinion on the same period, because with comparative financial statements the opinion refers to each period presented. Silence would leave him giving an opinion on figures he believes are materially misstated.

options.text: Qualify your opinion on the prior period at once, the opinion under comparative financial statements referring to each period presented
options.misconception: goes straight to the opinion, when the standard first requires management to be told and the predecessor auditor to be informed, and provides for the statements being amended instead
options.why: The opinion does reach the prior period, which is why the misstatement matters — but SA 710 does not have the auditor start there. He reports the matter to management and asks that the predecessor be informed, and where that leads to amended statements and a new report from the predecessor, he reports only on the current period.

options.text: Report the matter to the appropriate level of management and request that the predecessor auditor be informed — and if the prior period financial statements are then amended and the predecessor auditor agrees to issue a new report on them, report only on the current period
options.why: The standard puts two steps before the opinion. Where the auditor concludes that a material misstatement is present in previously audited figures of the financial statements, he should take the matter to management at the appropriate level and request that the predecessor auditor be informed. Should the prior years' statements then be amended and a new report issued on them by the predecessor auditor, the auditor shall report only on the current period. The route exists because the person who reported on those figures is the person who can put them right.
keywords: request that the predecessor auditor be informed
report only on the current period

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 710: where the auditor concludes that a material misstatement is present in previously audited figures he reports it to the appropriate level of management and requests that the predecessor auditor be informed, and where the prior period statements are amended and the predecessor issues a new report he reports only on the current period

items.scenario: You are in your first year with a company that presents comparative financial statements. The prior period was audited by a predecessor auditor who expressed an unmodified opinion. Your work establishes that a material misstatement exists in those previously audited figures and was never dealt with. A partner suggests you simply qualify your opinion on the prior period, since under this approach the opinion covers both years anyway.

items.stem: What else must that section contain?

options.text: The other statements, but they belong in the Responsibilities of Management and Auditor's Responsibilities sections rather than in a section of their own
options.misconception: scatters the required contents across other sections, when the standard requires a separate section headed Other Information carrying all of them
options.why: The standard requires a separate section with the heading Other Information, and it requires that section to include the statements. Spreading them elsewhere leaves the reader assembling from three places the one thing the section exists to tell him in one.

options.text: Four more things — a statement that management is responsible for the other information; an identification of what was obtained before the report's date and, for a listed entity, of what is expected after it; a line saying the opinion stops short of the other information, so no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion of any kind is given on it or will be; and an account of what the auditor must do with it — read it, consider it, report on it
options.why: The nothing-to-report sentence is the fifth of five contents, not the whole section. Five things go in. Management is responsible for the other information, and the section says so. The section then identifies whatever the auditor held before his report was dated and, in a listed entity, whatever is expected to be obtained once that date has passed. Third, the section says the opinion does not cover the other information, so on it he gives no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion of any sort, now or later. Fourth, it sets out his own duties over that information — to read it, to consider it, to report on it. Fifth, where something did reach him ahead of the report's date, the section either says he has nothing to report or spells out an uncorrected material misstatement he found in it.
keywords: management is responsible for the other information
does not cover the other information

options.text: The three other statements, but not the identification of information expected after the date of the report, which cannot be identified before it exists
options.misconception: reads the identification requirement as needing the document in hand, when for a listed entity the section identifies the other information expected to be obtained after the date of the report
options.why: The standard asks for the document to be identified, not read. In a listed entity the section names whatever is expected to reach the auditor once his report has been dated — which is why he settles first, in discussion with management, which documents will make up the annual report.

options.text: Nothing more — the conclusion is the point of the section, and the rest is standing wording that adds length without adding meaning
options.misconception: keeps the conclusion and drops the four elements that tell the reader what the conclusion is about and what it is worth
options.why: A reader who is told only that there is nothing to report does not know which documents were read, who is responsible for them, or that the opinion does not cover them. Each of the four is a separate requirement of the standard and each answers one of those questions.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 720 (Revised): the five contents of the Other Information section — who is responsible for that information; what was in hand before the report's date and, in a listed entity, what is awaited after it; that the opinion stops short of it; what the auditor's own duties over it are; and either nothing to report or an uncorrected material misstatement set out

items.scenario: The draft report on a listed company carries a section headed Other Information containing one sentence: that the auditor has read the other information and has nothing to report. The directors' report and the business responsibility statement were obtained before the date of the report; the shareholders' information section will only be available afterwards.

items.stem: What does SA 720 (Revised) allow?

options.text: Yes, but of them all only the line saying the opinion stops short of the other information is indispensable, the rest being detail
options.misconception: picks one statement out of the ordinary section and calls it the minimum, when the standard names three different elements for a prescribed wording
options.why: That statement belongs to the ordinary section's five contents and is not among the three the standard names here. The three for a prescribed wording are the identification of the other information obtained before the date of the report, the description of the auditor's responsibilities, and the explicit statement of the outcome of his work.

options.text: Yes — where law or regulation fixes the layout or the wording, three things are the floor for a report that still names the Standards on Auditing: what other information the auditor had in hand before his report was dated, what his duties over that information were, and, said outright, what came of the work he did on it
options.why: The prescribed wording carries all three, so the reference stands. SA 720 (Revised) writes a floor of its own for a prescribed form, and that floor is shorter than the ordinary section. It asks which other information the auditor held prior to the date his report bears; what his duties over that information were; and an explicit statement addressing the outcome his work on it reached. Management's responsibility, and the opinion stopping short of the other information, belong to the ordinary section and sit outside this minimum.

options.text: No condition arises — where the regulator has prescribed the wording, the report complies with the Standards on Auditing because the auditor has done what the law requires
options.misconception: treats obedience to the prescribed wording as compliance with the standard, when the reference to the Standards on Auditing is conditional on the three minimum elements
options.why: Following the prescribed wording settles what the auditor must write; it does not settle what he may claim about it. The reference to the Standards on Auditing is available only if the three minimum elements are present, and the auditor has to look for them.

options.text: No — a prescribed wording may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it carries everything the ordinary Other Information section carries, and two of the five are missing
options.misconception: reads the minimum for a prescribed wording as the full list required of the ordinary section, when the standard states a shorter list of three for this case
options.why: The standard writes a separate and shorter list for a prescribed wording, and it names three elements. Requiring the full five would leave no case in which a prescribed wording could ever refer to the Standards on Auditing, which is not what the provision is for.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 720 (Revised): where law or regulation requires the auditor to refer to other information using a specific layout or wording, the report may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it includes at a minimum an identification of the other information obtained prior to the date of the report, a description of the auditor's responsibilities with respect to it, and an explicit statement addressing the outcome of the auditor's work

items.scenario: A sectoral regulator prescribes the wording an auditor must use when referring to other information in his report on the entities it supervises. The prescribed wording identifies the documents obtained before the date of the report, describes the auditor's responsibilities in respect of them and states expressly what the outcome of his work on them was. It carries no statement that management is responsible for the other information and no statement that the opinion does not cover it. The partner asks whether the report can still refer to the Standards on Auditing.

items.stem: What does SA 800 require?

options.text: Determine materiality under SA 320 regardless — the existence of an agreed threshold does not relieve the auditor of that requirement — and in an audit of special purpose financial statements make the judgements about what is material by reference to the financial information needs of the intended users rather than of a wide range of users; and determine afresh the appropriate person to communicate with, because those responsible for oversight of the special purpose financial statements may not be those charged with governance responsible for the general purpose statements
options.why: Both of the manager's shortcuts are answered in terms. Management and the intended users may well have settled a figure below which misstatements found in the audit go uncorrected; a figure of that kind does not relieve the auditor of SA 320, under which he still fixes materiality for planning the work and for performing it. Second, a special purpose audit narrows whose needs count: what is material is weighed against the financial information needs of the intended users rather than against those of users at large. On the third point, SA 260 (Revised) has him settle who the appropriate persons are, and in an entity that also puts out a complete set of general purpose statements the people overseeing the special purpose ones may not be the same people.
keywords: financial information needs of the intended users
may not be the same people

options.text: Determine materiality under SA 320 on the common financial information needs of a wide range of users, since SA 320 is applied unchanged whatever the framework
options.misconception: applies SA 320 without the adjustment SA 800 makes to it, which is to base the judgements on the intended users rather than on users as a group
options.why: SA 320 applies, and SA 800 says how. The judgements about matters material to users are ordinarily based on the common financial information needs of users as a group; in an audit of special purpose financial statements they are based on the financial information needs of the intended users.

options.text: Determine materiality under SA 320, and communicate with the board audit committee as proposed, since those charged with governance of the entity are the same people whatever statements are being audited
options.misconception: assumes one governance body for both sets of statements, when the standard says those responsible for oversight of the special purpose financial statements may be different
options.why: Half the answer is right. The other half is what the standard warns against: where a complete set of general purpose statements is also prepared, whoever oversees the special purpose ones need not be the governance body sitting behind the general purpose set, so the appropriate person is settled afresh for this engagement.

options.text: Adopt the agreed threshold as materiality — the intended users are the only readers, and a threshold they have themselves agreed is by definition the level at which a misstatement would influence them
options.misconception: lets an agreement about which misstatements will be corrected settle the auditor's own materiality, which the standard says it does not
options.why: The threshold governs what will be corrected; materiality governs how the audit is planned and performed and how uncorrected misstatements are evaluated. The standard says so outright — a threshold of that kind leaves SA 320 exactly where it was, and materiality under it is still the auditor's to fix.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 800: materiality judgements based on the financial information needs of the intended users, an agreed correction threshold that does not relieve the auditor from determining materiality under SA 320, and the appropriate person to communicate with determined under SA 260 (Revised) where those overseeing the special purpose statements may not be those charged with governance for the general purpose ones

items.scenario: You are auditing financial statements prepared under the reporting clauses of a loan agreement between two companies. The borrower and the lender have agreed in the contract that misstatements below a stated figure identified during the audit will not be corrected. Your manager proposes to adopt that figure as the audit's materiality and to save time on the whole engagement, and to report significant findings to the same board audit committee that oversees the company's general purpose financial statements.

items.stem: What does SA 800 require of the report?

options.text: Nothing more — a note describing the basis of accounting, drawn attention to in the report, tells the reader everything about the framework that the standard asks for
options.misconception: treats the description of the basis of accounting as covering the purpose and the intended users, which the standard requires separately
options.why: The basis of accounting says how the statements were prepared. The standard also asks why and for whom: the report states the purpose behind them and, where that is needed, who they are for — or it sends the reader to a note holding as much.

options.text: Restrict the distribution of the report instead of describing its purpose — a report nobody else may use cannot be misused, so the description adds nothing
options.misconception: substitutes the restriction on distribution for the description of the purpose and the intended users, when the standard requires both and treats the restriction as an addition to the alert
options.why: The restriction is an addition to the alert, not a replacement for the description. The standard says that in addition to the alert the auditor may consider it appropriate to indicate that his report is intended solely for the specific users, and the report still describes the purpose for which the statements were prepared.

options.text: It shall set out the purpose for which the financial statements are prepared, with the intended users named where that is needed, or point to a note that carries it; management having had a choice of frameworks, the account of its responsibility shall reach its responsibility for deciding the framework it applied is acceptable in the circumstances; and the paragraph alerting readers may be widened to say the report is meant for those users alone, with the heading modified accordingly
options.why: Three separate requirements meet in this one report. First, a report on special purpose statements has to state the purpose for which the financial statements are prepared, with the intended users named where that is needed, unless a note in the statements already carries it and the report points there. Second, management having had a choice of frameworks, the account of its responsibility must reach further — to its responsibility for deciding that the framework it applied is acceptable in the circumstances. Third, where the auditor thinks it right to say his report is meant for those users alone, the alerting paragraph can be widened to take that in, with the heading modified accordingly.
keywords: purpose for which the financial statements are prepared

options.text: Put the purpose and the intended users in an Other Matter paragraph, which is where matters about the report rather than the financial statements belong
options.misconception: moves into a paragraph a description the standard makes part of the report's own account of the framework, and treats an addressable requirement as a matter of placement
options.why: The requirement is on the report as a whole and is met by describing the purpose and the intended users or by referring to a note that contains that information; it is not an Other Matter. What the standard does place in an added paragraph is the alert about the special purpose framework and, where used, the restriction on distribution or use.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 800: what a report on special purpose statements must add — the purpose behind them and, where that is needed, who they are for, or a pointer to a note holding as much; where management chose the framework, its responsibility for deciding the choice was acceptable; and an alerting paragraph that may be widened to restrict distribution or use, its heading changed to match

items.scenario: X Ltd's financial statements are prepared under the reporting provisions of its contract with Y Ltd. Management could have used one of two permitted frameworks and chose this one. Your draft report gives an unmodified opinion and draws attention to note A, which describes the basis of accounting. It does not say why the statements were prepared or who they are for, and the responsibilities paragraph says only that management is responsible for their preparation. You also want the report used by nobody but X Ltd and Y Ltd.

items.stem: What does SA 805 require him to settle before he accepts?

options.text: Nothing — an audit of one element by someone who does not audit the complete set is not permitted, because the two opinions would be given on the same records by different firms
options.misconception: turns a question about practicability into a prohibition, when the standard contemplates the engagement and asks only whether compliance with the SAs is practicable
options.why: SA 805 provides for exactly this engagement. It applies the requirement to comply with all relevant SAs irrespective of whether the auditor is also engaged on the complete set, and where he is not, it asks him to determine whether such an audit in accordance with the SAs is practicable — a question, not a bar.

options.text: Nothing beyond obtaining the other firm's audit file, from which he can take the understanding of the entity and the evidence about the quality of the accounting records
options.misconception: borrows another auditor's work in place of the understanding and evidence the standard says he will be without, when the requirement is to obtain his own
options.why: The gap the standard describes is a gap in his own knowledge and his own evidence. Reading another firm's file does not give him the grasp of the entity and of its internal control that comes of auditing the complete set, and what the accounting records give him may still have to be corroborated from somewhere else.

options.text: Nothing — he may accept and scale the Standards on Auditing down to the size of the element, adapting them as necessary being what the standard expressly permits
options.misconception: reads the instruction to adapt the SAs as necessary as permission to leave requirements out, when adaptation is about the circumstances of the engagement and not about the requirements
options.why: Adapting the SAs as necessary in the circumstances is how they are applied to an element; it is not a licence to drop them. That is why the standard asks a prior question — whether an audit in accordance with the SAs is practicable — and offers a different type of engagement as the answer where it is not.

options.text: Whether an audit of the element under the Standards on Auditing can be carried out at all — since the complete set is not his, his grasp of the entity, of its environment and of its internal control is thinner than the whole-set auditor's, nothing before him speaks to the general quality of the accounting records, what those records yield may have to be corroborated elsewhere, and a few SAs would put him to work disproportionate to the element; and should he conclude it may not be practicable, he can put to management whether some other type of engagement would
options.why: Every SA relevant to the audit binds him whether or not the complete set is also his, so the question is not which SAs he may drop but whether he can meet them. The complete set not being his, he settles first whether an audit of the element under the SAs is practicable, and the standard lists why it may not be. His grasp of the entity, of its environment and of its internal control is usually thinner than the whole-set auditor's. Nothing before him speaks to the general quality of the accounting records, or to the rest of the accounting information. What those records do yield may therefore have to be corroborated from somewhere else. And a few SAs would put him to work disproportionate to the element he is reporting on. Concluding that it may not be practicable, he can put to management whether some other type of engagement would serve better.
keywords: general quality of the accounting records

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 805: where the complete set is somebody else's engagement, the auditor settles first whether an audit of the one statement, or of the one element, under the SAs is practicable at all — the standard naming a thinner grasp of the entity and its internal control, nothing to show the general quality of the accounting records, a need to corroborate what those records give, and audit work certain SAs would make disproportionate

items.scenario: CA G is offered the audit of the trade payables balance of a company whose financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013 are audited by another firm. He has no other engagement with the company. He proposes to accept and to confine his work to circularising the suppliers and agreeing the balances to the ledger.

items.stem: What does SA 805 require?

options.text: The element can properly be considered in isolation, that being the point of an engagement on one element, so sales, cash and the allowance are outside the scope
options.misconception: reads the narrow subject of the engagement as a narrow field of work, when the standard says the interrelation of the items may require procedures beyond the element itself
options.why: The subject of the opinion is narrow; the work needed to support it is not necessarily. The individual statements and many of the elements, including their notes, are interrelated, so the auditor may not be able to consider the element in isolation and may need to perform procedures in relation to the interrelated items.

options.text: Materiality fixed for the specific element may be lower than the figure fixed for the complete set, and that reaches the nature, the timing and the extent of the procedures as well as the weighing of uncorrected misstatements; evidence from the audit of the complete set may be used, though the SAs still have the audit of the element planned and performed so that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind the opinion given on it; and the items hanging together as they do, work may be called for on the interrelated items
options.why: All three proposals are answered. Materiality settled for a specific element may be lower than the figure settled for the complete set, and where it is lower it reaches the nature, the timing and the extent of the procedures, and the weighing of uncorrected misstatements as well. Auditing an element alongside the complete set, he may well be able to lean on evidence gathered there, but the SAs have him plan and perform the audit of the element so that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind the opinion he gives on it. Finally, the statements and many of their elements, the related notes among them, hang together, so the element cannot always be looked at on its own and work may be called for on the interrelated items.

options.text: The complete set's materiality governs both engagements, one entity having one materiality, and the receivables work in the main audit is the evidence for both opinions
options.misconception: carries one materiality and one body of work across two engagements, when the standard says the element's materiality may be lower and requires evidence sufficient for the opinion on the element
options.why: Two opinions are being expressed and the second is on a much smaller subject, which is why the standard says the materiality determined for the element may be lower than that for the complete set. The evidence gathered in the main audit may be used, but it is not by itself the basis for the opinion on the element.

options.text: Evidence from the audit of the complete set cannot be used at all, each engagement standing on its own evidence, so the receivables work must be performed again for the element
options.misconception: separates the two engagements completely, when the standard expressly allows the auditor to use evidence obtained in the audit of the complete set
options.why: The standard says the opposite: when auditing an element in conjunction with the audit of the complete set, the auditor may be able to use audit evidence obtained in that audit. What it does not allow is stopping there, since the SAs still want sufficient appropriate audit evidence standing behind the opinion on the element.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 805: audit evidence obtained in the audit of the complete set may be used but the SAs require the audit of the element to be planned and performed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence for the opinion on it, procedures may be needed on interrelated items, and the materiality determined for the element may be lower than that determined for the complete set

items.scenario: You audit a company's complete set of financial statements and have also been engaged to audit its schedule of trade receivables. Your senior proposes to carry the materiality determined for the complete set across to the schedule, to rest the opinion on the schedule entirely on the receivables work already done in the main audit, and to look at the schedule on its own without touching sales, cash or the allowance for doubtful debts.

items.stem: What does SA 805 require?

options.text: Nothing follows — the standard speaks only to an adverse opinion or a disclaimer, so a qualified opinion on the complete set leaves the report on the schedule untouched
options.misconception: reads the rule about a contradictory unmodified opinion as the whole of the standard's treatment of a modification, when a qualified opinion and either paragraph each require the auditor to determine the effect on the report on the element
options.why: The adverse-or-disclaimer rule exists because an unmodified opinion would contradict it. A separate requirement runs ahead of it: where the report on the complete set is modified or carries an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, the auditor shall determine the effect on the report on the element and act where he deems it appropriate.

options.text: The opinion on the schedule must be qualified in the same terms, the two reports being drawn from the same accounting records and the same audit
options.misconception: makes the modification automatic, when the standard requires the auditor to determine the effect and to act only when he deems it appropriate
options.why: Nothing is carried across automatically. The auditor determines the effect that the modification may have on the report on the element, and modifies the opinion on the element or adds a paragraph when deemed appropriate — which on facts touching neither the schedule nor its measurement may mean a paragraph rather than a modification.

options.text: Determine the effect that the qualified opinion and the Emphasis of Matter may have on the report on the schedule and, when deemed appropriate, modify the opinion on the schedule or include an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph in that report — and even where the matters do not relate to the schedule, refer to the modification in an Other Matter paragraph if you judge it relevant to users' understanding of the audited element or of the related report
options.why: The contradiction rule is only one part of SA 805's treatment of a modification. Once the opinion on the complete set has been modified, or that report carries an Emphasis of Matter or an Other Matter paragraph, the auditor has to determine the effect it may work on the report on the single statement, or on the specific element, and, when deemed appropriate, to modify the opinion there or add a paragraph of the same kind. The standard then meets this very case: a modification, or either paragraph, that does not relate to the audited element can still be worth a reference in an Other Matter paragraph, where he judges it relevant to what users make of the element or of the report that goes with it.
keywords: does not relate to the audited element

options.text: A reference may be made only where the modification relates to the audited element; an unrelated matter has no place in a report on one schedule
options.misconception: excludes the very case the standard provides for, which is a modification that does not relate to the element but is still relevant to users' understanding of it or of the report
options.why: The standard names that case in terms. A modification, an Emphasis of Matter or an Other Matter paragraph may have nothing to do with the statement or the element under audit and still be worth a reference in an Other Matter paragraph, where he judges it relevant to what users make of the report.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 805: where the opinion on the complete set is modified or the report includes an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph the auditor shall determine the effect on the report on the single financial statement or specific element and, when deemed appropriate, modify the opinion or include such a paragraph, and he may refer to the modification in an Other Matter paragraph even where it does not relate to the audited element

items.scenario: You have qualified your opinion on a company's complete set of financial statements over a disputed tax provision, and your report also carries an Emphasis of Matter about a fire at a warehouse. You are separately engaged on, and about to report on, a schedule of net tangible assets. Neither the tax provision nor the fire touches that schedule. Your manager says the two reports are now unrelated, since the bar in SA 705 (Revised) bites only on an adverse opinion or a disclaimer.

items.stem: What does SA 810 require?

options.text: A qualified opinion on the summary financial statements, the aggregation of two segments being material but not pervasive to the summary as a whole
options.misconception: imports the audit modification grid into an opinion which asks only whether the summary is consistent with or a fair summary of the audited financial statements, and which the standard answers with an adverse opinion when it is not
options.why: The material-but-not-pervasive grid belongs to an opinion on financial statements. The opinion here answers one question only — is the summary consistent with what was audited, and a fair summary of it under the criteria applied — and where the answer is no and management will not change it, the standard prescribes an adverse opinion.

options.text: The unmodified consistency opinion, with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph describing the aggregation and its effect on the segment result
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to carry a defect that makes the summary not a fair summary, which the standard answers in the opinion itself
options.why: A paragraph beside a clean opinion says the summary is a fair summary and then explains why it is not. Where the summary is not a fair summary and management will not change it, the standard requires an adverse opinion on the summary financial statements.

options.text: An adverse opinion on the summary financial statements: they are no fair summary of what was audited, judged by the criteria applied, and management will not make the changes needed — and a similar restriction or alert must go into the report on the summary, because the report on the audited financial statements restricted distribution and alerted readers to the special purpose framework
options.why: The standard gives one answer for a summary that does not hold up, and it is not a qualification. Take a summary inconsistent in some material respect with what was audited, or one that is no fair summary of it under the criteria applied, where management will not make the changes needed: on that summary the auditor expresses an adverse opinion. Separately, if the report on the audited statements had its distribution or use restricted, or warned readers that those statements rest on a special purpose framework, then a similar restriction or alert goes into the report on the summary as well.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement, since a summary management refuses to correct cannot be reported on at all
options.misconception: leaves an engagement the standard tells the auditor how to finish, replacing a prescribed opinion with silence
options.why: The standard does not send the auditor away; it gives him the opinion to express. An adverse opinion on the summary tells the intended users exactly what withdrawal would leave them guessing at, which is that the summary is not a fair summary of the statements it claims to come from.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 810: an adverse opinion where the summary is inconsistent in some material respect with what was audited, or is no fair summary of it under the criteria applied, and management will not make the changes needed; and a similar restriction or alert in the report on the summary where the report on the audited statements restricted distribution or warned of a special purpose framework

items.scenario: You audited a company's financial statements under the accounting provisions of a regulator's framework; your report on them alerted readers to the special purpose framework and restricted its distribution to the regulator and the members. You are now reporting on summary financial statements derived from them. The summary aggregates two segments in a way that hides a loss in one of them, and management will not change it. The draft report on the summary says the summary is consistent in all material respects with the audited financial statements, and carries no alert or restriction of its own.

items.stem: What does the later date require the report on the summary financial statements to say?

options.text: Nothing — the auditor is not required to obtain additional evidence on the audited financial statements or to report on subsequent events, so the gap between the two dates has no reporting consequence
options.misconception: reads the rule that no additional evidence is required as removing the statement the standard requires precisely because the later date opens a gap
options.why: The two rules sit side by side and the second exists because of the first. The auditor need not go back over the audited financial statements, and for that reason the report on the summary must tell the reader that neither document reflects events after the date of the report on the audited financial statements.

options.text: That both documents — the summary and the audited statements behind it — do not reflect the effects of events falling after the date his report on those audited statements bears; and the introductory paragraph must also point to that report, give its date, say an unmodified opinion was expressed, and say the summary carries less by way of disclosure than the framework behind the audited statements requires, so that reading it is not a substitute for reading them
options.why: The colleague is right about the evidence and wrong about what follows from it. No fresh evidence on the audited statements is called for, and events after the date of his report on them need no reporting — which leaves a month in which something could have happened that neither document would show. So a report on the summary bearing the later date says as much: both sets of figures do not reflect the effects of events falling after the date his report on the audited statements bears. The introductory paragraph then points to that report, gives its date, records that an unmodified opinion was expressed, and says the summary carries less by way of disclosure than the framework behind the audited statements requires, so that reading it is not a substitute for reading them.
keywords: do not reflect the effects of events

options.text: That subsequent events to 15 July have been examined and their effects reported, the report on the summary being dated on that day
options.misconception: reads the later date as extending the subsequent events work, when the standard says no additional evidence on the audited financial statements is required and answers the gap with a statement instead
options.why: The date of a report is not a warranty that work was done up to it. Reporting on the summary once the audit is complete, he need gather no fresh evidence on the audited statements, and what happened after his report on them was dated is not his to report either.

options.text: Nothing, provided the report on the summary is dated 15 June to match the report on the audited financial statements and close the gap
options.misconception: back-dates a report to avoid a statement, when the report on the summary may be dated no earlier than the date the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate evidence on the summary
options.why: The date is not the auditor's to choose. The report on the summary financial statements is dated no earlier than the date on which he obtained sufficient appropriate evidence on which to base the opinion, including evidence that the summary has been prepared and that those with the recognised authority have taken responsibility for it, and no earlier than the date of the report on the audited financial statements.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 810: a report on the summary bearing a later date than the report on the audited statements says that both do not reflect the effects of events falling after that earlier date; the introductory paragraph points to that report, its date and the unmodified opinion, and says the summary carries less disclosure than the framework requires, so that reading it is not a substitute for reading the audited statements; and the report is dated no earlier than the later of the two dates

items.scenario: CA Madhur signed his report on a company's audited financial statements on 15 June, with an unmodified opinion. His report on the summary financial statements derived from them is dated 15 July. His draft identifies the summary statements, identifies the audited financial statements and expresses the consistency opinion. A colleague says the later date raises nothing, since no fresh evidence on the audited statements is called for and events after 15 June need no reporting.

items.stem: What does SA 810 require in each case?

options.text: In the first, ask management to put your report into the document, and failing that, settle on other steps and take them, so that management cannot go on inappropriately associating you with the summary printed there; in the second, satisfy yourself that you are named in the context of your report on the audited financial statements and that what is written does not give the impression that you reported on the summary itself, and if it does, ask management to change the wording or to drop the reference to you altogether
options.why: The standard covers association running in both directions. In the first case the entity means to say he has reported on a summary, prints the summary, and leaves his report out; he asks management to put the report in, and where management will not, he settles on other steps and takes them, so that management cannot go on inappropriately associating him with the summary printed in that document. In the second he audited the statements but was never engaged on the summary, and the entity means to name him and to say the summary figures come from statements he audited; there he must satisfy himself that the naming sits in the context of his report on the audited financial statements, and that what is written does not give the impression that the summary itself was reported on by him. If either fails, he asks management to change the wording or to drop the reference.

options.text: In both, withdraw the report on the audited financial statements, since the auditor cannot control how the entity refers to him
options.misconception: answers a misdescription by withdrawing an unrelated report, when the standard gives a graded set of steps ending in other appropriate actions
options.why: The report on the audited financial statements is not the problem and withdrawing it would take away information the users are entitled to. The standard asks for the report on the summary to be included, or for the statement to be changed or the reference removed, and failing those, for other appropriate actions.

options.text: In the first, issue a fresh report on the summary addressed to the readers of the booklet; in the second, accept an engagement on the summary so that the statement becomes accurate
options.misconception: reaches for a new engagement as the only remedy, when the standard's first step is to have the existing report included or the statement corrected
options.why: Engaging the auditor to report on the summary and including that report is offered by the standard as an alternative the entity may choose, not as the auditor's remedy. His steps are to request that the report be included, or that the statement be changed or the reference deleted, and then to carry out other appropriate actions.

options.text: In the first, nothing — the company may describe its own documents as it pleases, and the auditor's report exists whether or not it is reprinted; in the second, nothing either, since the statement is true
options.misconception: treats a true sentence about the auditor as harmless, when the standard is concerned with the impression the document leaves about what the auditor reported on
options.why: Each sentence may be true and still leave a reader believing the auditor gave an opinion he did not give. That is what the association requirements are for: the report goes in the document, or the reference is put in the context of the report actually given, or the reference goes.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 810: where the entity means to say he reported on a summary and leaves his report out of the document, he asks for it to be put in and otherwise takes steps so that management cannot go on inappropriately associating him with that summary; and where he was never engaged on the summary, he satisfies himself that any naming of him sits in the context of his report on the audited statements and does not give the impression that he reported on the summary

items.scenario: Two things reach you about the same client. In its investor booklet the company has printed a set of summary financial statements above the line "reported on by our auditors", and it does not intend to print your report on the summary. In a second document for a different year, in which you audited the financial statements but were never engaged on any summary, the company writes that the summary figures are derived from statements audited by you, in a way that reads as though you had reported on the summary itself.

items.stem: What does SRS 4400 require?

options.text: Accept without any restriction on distribution, since a report that must be laid before a public authority is a public document and the restriction adds nothing
options.misconception: removes a term the standard requires to be agreed, when the conflict between the agreed restriction and the law is the reason for not accepting at all
options.why: Dropping the term does not resolve the conflict; it hides it. The limitation on distribution is one of the matters to be agreed, and the standard's answer where that limitation would conflict with the legal requirements is that the auditor would not accept the engagement.

options.text: Accept — the matters to be agreed are guidance on good practice, and what actually binds the auditor is the list of contents the report of factual findings must carry
options.misconception: reads the matters to be agreed as advisory, when the standard states them as what must be agreed and attaches a refusal to one of them
options.why: The report's contents are one requirement and the terms are another. The standard sets out the matters to be agreed and then attaches a consequence to the fifth of them, which is that the auditor would not accept the engagement where the limitation on distribution conflicts with the legal requirements.

options.text: Accept, and add a sentence to the report recording that the restriction is subject to any statutory requirement to produce the report
options.misconception: drafts around a conflict the standard answers by refusing the engagement, leaving a restriction in the report that the law can override without the parties having agreed to it
options.why: A saving sentence leaves the parties agreeing to one thing and the law doing another, and the whole force of an agreed-upon procedures report is that the reader knows what was agreed. Where the limitation on distribution would conflict with the legal requirements, the auditor would not accept the engagement.

options.text: Do not accept the engagement — limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings are one of the five matters to be agreed, and where such a limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements the auditor would not accept the engagement; the other four are the nature of the engagement, and with it a warning that neither an audit nor a review is being done so that no assurance follows, the stated purpose, the identification of the financial information to which the procedures will be applied, and the nature, timing and extent of the specific procedures
options.why: The standard makes the agreement about distribution a condition of taking the work rather than a clause to be drafted around. Matters to be agreed run to limits on who may be given the report of factual findings, and where such a limit runs into conflict with the legal requirements, the auditor would not accept the engagement at all. That is the answer to a restriction the law will not allow: the work is declined, not taken on with a restriction nobody can honour.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the matters to be agreed, including limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings, and the requirement that the auditor would not accept the engagement where such a limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements

items.scenario: A bank and its borrower ask you to perform agreed-upon procedures on the borrower's stock statements. The draft terms restrict distribution of the report of factual findings to the two of them. A statute applying to the borrower requires any such report to be laid before a public authority, which the two parties do not want. The relationship manager suggests you accept and simply keep the restriction in the report.

items.stem: What does SRS 4400 require?

options.text: The report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority; an engagement letter should be sent documenting the key terms, listing the procedures to be performed as agreed between the parties and stating that distribution of the report would be restricted to the specified parties who have agreed to them; and the procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis, recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations
options.why: Each of the three assumptions is wrong. The report of factual findings goes, as a rule, to the appointing authority, and not to whichever officer happened to telephone. Client and auditor both gain from an engagement letter going out: it puts acceptance of the appointment beyond doubt and keeps misunderstanding away from the objectives and the scope, from how far his responsibilities run, and from the form the report will take; and it sets out the procedures agreed and says who alone may be given the report. And the procedures stop nowhere near inquiry alone — recomputation, comparison and other checks of clerical accuracy, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations all sit among what such an engagement may apply.

options.text: No engagement letter is needed for a non-assurance engagement, and the report may be addressed to whoever commissioned it, provided it says no assurance is expressed
options.misconception: reads the absence of assurance as an absence of formality, when the standard asks for an engagement letter and names the appointing authority as the ordinary addressee
options.why: The absence of assurance is exactly why the terms matter: a reader can only judge a report of factual findings if he knows what was agreed. The standard asks for an engagement letter documenting the key terms and names the appointing authority as the ordinary addressee.

options.text: The procedures in an agreed-upon procedures engagement are confined to inquiry and analytical work, examination of records and confirmation being audit procedures that would convert the engagement into an audit
options.misconception: confuses the procedures applied with the assurance given, when the standard's own list includes inspection and confirmations and the engagement still expresses no assurance
options.why: What separates the engagement from an audit is the absence of an opinion, not the absence of audit techniques — procedures of an audit nature are exactly what the parties settle on, and the factual findings are then reported. The listed procedures take in recomputation, comparison and other checks of clerical accuracy, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations.

options.text: An engagement letter is needed, but the listing of procedures belongs only in the report of factual findings; putting it in the letter commits the auditor before he has seen the records
options.misconception: keeps the letter and strips out the term that gives it its purpose, when the listing of the agreed procedures is one of the matters the standard puts in it
options.why: The letter is where the parties fix what will be done, which is the whole basis of the engagement. Among the matters it carries are a listing of the procedures to be performed as agreed between the parties, and a statement confining the report of factual findings to those parties who settled on the procedures in the first place.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority, the engagement letter includes a listing of the agreed procedures and a statement that distribution would be restricted to the specified parties, and the procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis, recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations

items.scenario: A company's finance head asks you over the telephone to perform agreed-upon procedures on its accounts payable and to address the report to him. No engagement letter is sent. Your assistant proposes to confine the work to inquiry of the accounts department and an analysis of the ageing, on the view that anything more would make the engagement an audit.

items.stem: How many of the three are right under SRS 4410?

options.text: Two — independence and quality control, both of which follow from the engagement being performed under a standard issued by the Institute
options.misconception: treats every standard of the Institute as carrying the independence requirements, when they do not apply to a non-assurance engagement unless law or regulation says otherwise
options.why: Quality control does follow, because SQC 1 reaches all Engagement Standards. Independence does not: no assurance being given, the independence requirements do not apply to a compilation engagement, though a law or a regulation may lay down rules of its own about independence or about disclosing it, and the relevant ethical requirements apply throughout.

options.text: One — the verification point, because a practitioner who puts his name to financial information must have satisfied himself that it is complete
options.misconception: reads the practitioner's name on the report as a warranty of the information, when the standard says the engagement does not require him to verify its accuracy or completeness
options.why: What his name is on is a statement that he compiled the information from what management provided, and the report says in terms that he is not required to verify its accuracy or completeness and does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion. Management retains responsibility for the financial information and for the basis on which it is prepared.

options.text: None — a compilation engagement gives no assurance; nobody asks the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over, or to gather evidence towards an audit opinion or a review conclusion; independence requirements do not apply, though a law or a regulation may lay down rules of its own about independence or about disclosing it, and the relevant ethical requirements do apply; and SQC 1 reaches a firm's compilation work because it reaches all Engagement Standards
options.why: Each statement fails on the face of the standard. Nobody asks the practitioner compiling financial information to verify the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over, nor to gather evidence towards an audit opinion or a review conclusion — so checking that every rupee of revenue has been booked forms no part of the work. No assurance being given, independence requirements do not apply, though a law or a regulation may lay down rules of its own about independence or about disclosing it; the relevant ethical requirements bind him throughout. And SQC 1 reaches all Engagement Standards, SRS 4410 among them, so it binds the firm on its compilation work as well.

options.text: All three — a member of the Institute performing professional work is bound by verification, independence and quality control alike
options.misconception: collapses three different regimes into one obligation of professional work, when the standard answers each of them separately for a compilation engagement
options.why: The standard separates them. Verification is not required at all; independence is not required unless law or regulation says so; quality control does apply, because SQC 1 reaches every Engagement Standard. Ethical requirements other than independence apply in every case.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: a compilation engagement gives no assurance and asks the practitioner neither to verify the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over nor to gather evidence towards an audit opinion or a review conclusion; independence requirements do not apply, though a law or a regulation may lay down rules of its own about it; and SQC 1 binds a firm on its compilation work because it reaches all Engagement Standards

items.scenario: Your firm has been engaged to compile the financial statements of a company from a draft trial balance for management's internal use. A team member says three things: that the firm must verify that all the revenue the company should have booked has in fact been booked; that the firm must be independent of the company; and that quality control standards do not reach an engagement of this kind.

items.stem: What does SRS 4410 require before the work begins?

options.text: Management's acknowledgement of responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of the records is the one term that must be settled first; the rest can be agreed as the work proceeds
options.misconception: picks one of management's responsibilities out of a list of terms the standard requires to be agreed before the engagement is accepted at all
options.why: That acknowledgement is one item inside one of the six terms. The practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed all of them, including the intended use and distribution of the information, the applicable framework, the objective and scope, his own responsibilities and the expected form and content of his report.

options.text: The practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed the terms with management, and with the engaging party where it is different, covering the intended use and distribution of the information and any restrictions on either, the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework, the objective and scope of the engagement, his own responsibilities including compliance with relevant ethical requirements, management's four responsibilities and the expected form and content of his report — and the agreed terms go into an engagement letter, or some other written agreement that will serve, prior to performing the engagement
options.why: Acceptance is barred until the terms are agreed, and the standard lists them. Who the information is meant for, how far it will travel, and what limits sit on either. Which financial reporting framework applies. What the compilation engagement is for and how far it reaches. What the practitioner himself is answerable for, the relevant ethical requirements among that. What management is answerable for — the financial information and its preparation and presentation under a framework fitting the intended use and users, such internal control as management judges necessary, the accuracy and completeness of the records, documents, explanations and other information handed over, and the judgments that preparing and presenting it calls for. And what the report will look like and hold. A second company being the engaging party, the terms are settled with it as well as with management, and they go into an engagement letter, or some other written agreement that will serve, prior to performing the engagement.
keywords: Acceptance is barred until the terms are agreed

options.text: An engagement letter is not required for a compilation engagement, which is a non-assurance service, so an exchange of emails at the end of the work is enough
options.misconception: drops a written agreement the standard requires before the work starts, on the ground that the engagement gives no assurance
options.why: The standard says the opposite, and says when: the agreed terms of engagement go into an engagement letter, or some other written agreement that will serve, before any of the work is performed. Non-assurance describes what the report says, not how the work is taken on.

options.text: The terms are agreed with management alone, the company paying the fee having no standing to settle the scope of work on another entity's financial information
options.misconception: leaves the engaging party out of the agreement, when the standard requires the terms to be agreed with management and the engaging party where the two are different
options.why: The standard names both. The terms are agreed with management, and the engaging party if different — which is exactly this case, where a second company in the group has engaged the firm to compile the client's information.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: the practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed the terms with management and the engaging party if different, covering the intended use and distribution and any restrictions, the applicable financial reporting framework, the objective and scope, the practitioner's responsibilities, management's responsibilities and the expected form and content of the report, recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable written agreement prior to performing the engagement

items.scenario: A company's chief financial officer asks your firm to start compiling the company's financial information at once, promising that the terms can be settled when the work is finished. He is willing to say now that management is responsible for the accuracy and completeness of the records it hands over. The information will be sent to a funding body under a grant contract, and a second company in the group, not the client, is paying your fee.

items.stem: What does SRS 4410 require?

options.text: Issue the report with a qualification describing the omitted expenditure, since the practitioner has read the information and can say what is wrong with it
options.misconception: modifies a report that expresses no opinion or conclusion capable of being modified, when the standard's remedy is an amendment and, failing that, withdrawal
options.why: There is nothing to qualify. His report is no vehicle for an opinion, and none for a conclusion either, on the financial information in any shape — so the standard gives him a different remedy: propose the amendments, and withdraw if they are declined.

options.text: Compile what management has provided and leave the disclosure to management, the financial information and its presentation being management's responsibility throughout
options.misconception: reads management's responsibility for the information as removing the practitioner's own requirement to propose amendments and to withdraw if they are declined
options.why: Management does keep responsibility for the financial information, and for the basis it rests on; that is why the practitioner proposes the amendments rather than imposing them. But the standard does not leave him there: if management declines, he withdraws from the engagement and tells management and those charged with governance why.

options.text: Issue the report and describe the omission in an explanatory paragraph, so that a reader is told what the compiled information does not show
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to carry a defect the standard requires to be amended or the engagement left, leaving misleading information in circulation with a note beside it
options.why: The paragraphs the report may carry are prescribed and none of them is for this. Where the compiled information is misleading and management will not amend it, the practitioner withdraws and tells management and those charged with governance why.

options.text: Propose the appropriate amendments to management, and where management declines them or will not let them be made, withdraw from the engagement, telling management and those charged with governance why you have gone — and where going is not open to you, settle what professional and legal responsibilities the circumstances carry
options.why: The standard makes the reading of the compiled information the last check, and gives that check teeth. Suppose he sees that the compiled information describes or refers to the applicable framework poorly, or needs amending if it is not to be materially misstated, or misleads for some other reason: he is to propose the appropriate amendments to management. Should management decline them, or refuse to let them be made, he must withdraw from the engagement, telling management and those charged with governance why he has gone; and where going is not open to him, he settles what professional and legal responsibilities the circumstances carry. Withdrawal follows on the same footing where the engagement cannot be finished because management never produced the records, documents, explanations or anything else asked for.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: where the practitioner becomes aware that the compiled financial information does not adequately describe the applicable framework, requires amendment not to be materially misstated, or is otherwise misleading, he proposes the appropriate amendments; where management declines he withdraws and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons; and where withdrawal is not possible he determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable

items.scenario: You are compiling a company's financial statements. Reading the compiled information before signing, you find that the expenditure on a new unit at Rourkela, paid out of a bank account maintained there, has not been shown under the appropriate heads, so the statements are misleading on the face of them. Management declines to make the amendment you propose. Earlier in the same engagement the company was slow to hand over the bank records and you had to ask twice before they came.

items.stem: What else must the practitioner's report contain?

options.text: A statement of negative assurance, that nothing has come to the practitioner's attention to suggest the compiled information is not prepared in accordance with the framework
options.misconception: puts a review conclusion into a compilation report, when the standard requires the report to say that no such conclusion is being expressed
options.why: Negative assurance is the language of a review under SRE 2400, which rests on inquiry and analytical procedures performed for that purpose. A compilation report has to say the opposite in terms: the practitioner does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on whether the information is prepared in accordance with the applicable framework.

options.text: The explanations about assurance, but not the special purpose paragraph — the framework is already identified in the report, and identifying it tells the reader all he needs about the basis used
options.misconception: treats identifying the framework as covering the purpose, the intended users and the warning about other uses, which the standard requires as a separate explanatory paragraph
options.why: Identifying the framework says which rules were followed. The explanatory paragraph says why the information was prepared, for whom, and that as a result it may not be suitable for other purposes — which is the thing a reader outside the intended group would otherwise get wrong.

options.text: Explanations that a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement, so verifying the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over is no part of the practitioner's work, and that accordingly nothing in the report is an audit opinion or a review conclusion about whether the applicable framework was followed — and, the framework here being a special purpose one, an explanatory paragraph giving the purpose for which the information is prepared and, where naming them is needed, the intended users, or pointing to a note that discloses it, and warning readers that information resting on such a framework may not be suitable for other purposes
options.why: Saying nothing about assurance is not the same as saying there is none.
