The report has to explain that a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement, so verifying the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over for the compilation is no part of the practitioner's work, and that accordingly nothing in it is an audit opinion or a review conclusion about whether the applicable framework was followed. And where the information rests on a special purpose framework, the report carries an explanatory paragraph: the purpose for which the information is prepared, the intended users where naming them is needed, or a pointer to a note disclosing as much, together with a warning to readers that information resting on such a framework may not be suitable for other purposes.
keywords: audit opinion or a review conclusion
may not be suitable for other purposes

options.text: Nothing — an important purpose of the report is to communicate the nature of the engagement, and naming the standard it was performed under does that in one line
options.misconception: treats the name of the standard as telling the reader what the engagement was worth, when the report is required to say in terms that no verification and no opinion or conclusion were given
options.why: A reader who does not know the standard learns nothing from its number. That is why the report spells the position out: verifying the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over is no part of the work, and neither an audit opinion nor a review conclusion is given on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: the report explains that a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement, so verifying the accuracy or completeness of what management hands over is no part of the work and neither an audit opinion nor a review conclusion is given; and where a special purpose framework is used, an explanatory paragraph gives the purpose and the intended users and warns that the information may not be suitable for other purposes

items.scenario: You have compiled financial information for a company on a basis of accounting set out in a grant contract, which is a special purpose framework, and management has acknowledged responsibility for the final version. Your draft report identifies the information and the framework, describes management's responsibilities and yours, and says the engagement was performed in accordance with SRS 4410. A colleague says nothing else is needed, since the report gives no opinion and there is nothing to explain.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require?

options.text: Accept — a review is an assurance engagement performed under a standard of the Institute, so it satisfies a statute that asks for the financial statements to be examined by a professional accountant
options.misconception: treats a review as interchangeable with an audit for a statutory purpose, when a law requiring an audit is the standard's own example of an engagement with no rational purpose
options.why: A review gives limited assurance in a negatively worded conclusion; an audit gives reasonable assurance in a positively worded opinion. Where the law requires the statements to be audited, the standard says there is no rational purpose for the review, and it is not for the practitioner to substitute one engagement for another.

options.text: Decline both points and stop there — where a review is inappropriate the practitioner withdraws from the relationship, recommending an alternative engagement being outside his role
options.misconception: stops at the refusal, when the standard expressly contemplates recommending another type of engagement where a review would not be appropriate
options.why: The standard goes on from the refusal. Where his preliminary understanding indicates that accepting a review would not be appropriate, the practitioner may consider recommending that another type of engagement be undertaken — an audit, or where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement, a compilation or other accounting services engagement.

options.text: Accept, and manage the difficulty by extending the procedures until they are equivalent to an audit and by expressing the conclusion in positive terms
options.misconception: converts a review into an audit by doing more work, when the level of assurance is a term of the engagement rather than a function of the effort
options.why: A review is a limited assurance engagement and its conclusion is negatively worded; more procedures do not turn it into a reasonable assurance engagement. If an audit is what the circumstances need, the standard has the practitioner recommend an audit, not perform one under a review engagement letter.

options.text: Unless required by law or regulation to do so, do not accept — there is no rational purpose for a review engagement where the engagement is intended to meet compliance requirements of a law or regulation that requires the financial statements to be audited, and a rational purpose may also be absent where the practitioner suspects association of his name with the financial statements in an inappropriate manner; where a review would not be appropriate he may recommend another type of engagement, an audit here, or where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement, a compilation or other accounting services engagement
options.why: The standard's first gate is whether the engagement has a rational purpose, and it names this exact case: a review taken on to satisfy the compliance demands of a law that itself requires the financial statements to be audited has no rational purpose at all. It names the second fact too — a rational purpose is unlikely where the practitioner suspects his name is being tied to the financial statements in an inappropriate manner. And where a review would not suit the circumstances, he may recommend another type of engagement: an audit where that fits better, or a compilation or other accounting services engagement where the circumstances rule an assurance engagement out.
keywords: requires the financial statements to be audited

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): a review engagement is not to be taken on, law or regulation apart, where the practitioner is not satisfied it has a rational purpose — there being none where the law requires the financial statements to be audited, and none likely where a significant scope limitation exists or where he suspects his name is being tied to the statements inappropriately; and where a review would not suit, he may recommend an audit, or a compilation or other accounting services engagement

items.scenario: A company whose financial statements a statute requires to be audited asks you, who are not its auditor, to review them instead and give a report the statute will accept. The directors say a review costs less and reaches the same place. Separately you notice that the company's prospectus draft names you in a way that suggests you stand behind the figures generally.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require now?

options.text: Continue and rely on inquiry of the finance department, a review being built primarily on inquiry and analytical procedures in any event
options.misconception: reads the ordinary shape of review procedures as making a restriction on access harmless, when the precondition is unrestricted access to the persons from whom the practitioner determines evidence is needed
options.why: A review is built primarily on inquiry, which is why who may be asked matters so much. The precondition is unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom the practitioner determines it necessary to obtain evidence, and a restriction on it is not cured by asking the people who remain.

options.text: Nothing follows from the preconditions, which are tested once before acceptance; from here the restriction is dealt with as a limitation on the evidence and answered in the conclusion
options.misconception: treats the preconditions as spent on acceptance, when the standard provides expressly for discovering after acceptance that one of them is not satisfied
options.why: The standard deals with the position after acceptance in its own paragraph. Where it comes to light, the engagement already taken on, that some precondition leaves the practitioner unsatisfied, he discusses the matter and determines whether it can be resolved, whether to continue, and whether and how to communicate it in his report.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management or those charged with governance and determine three things — whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and, if so, how to communicate the matter in your report — the precondition being management's agreement to give you every piece of information relevant to the statements, anything further you ask for, and free access to anybody in the entity from whom you judge evidence has to come
options.why: What the managing director has withdrawn is a precondition. Before accepting, the practitioner obtains management's agreement that it acknowledges and understands its responsibilities to provide him with access to all information relevant to the preparation of the financial statements, with additional information he may request, and with unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. Where it is discovered after acceptance that he is not satisfied as to any precondition, he shall discuss the matter with management or those charged with governance and shall determine whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and, if so, how to communicate the matter in his report.
keywords: whether the matter can be resolved
communicate the matter in his report

options.text: Withdraw at once — a precondition that fails after acceptance ends the engagement, there being nothing left to review
options.misconception: jumps to withdrawal, when the standard first has the practitioner discuss the matter and decide whether it can be resolved and whether to continue
options.why: Withdrawal may be where it ends, but the standard sets out the steps before it. He discusses the matter with management or those charged with governance and determines whether it can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue, and whether and how to communicate the matter in his report.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the preconditions include management's agreement to provide access to all relevant information, additional information requested and unrestricted access to persons within the entity, and where it is discovered after acceptance that a precondition is not satisfied the practitioner discusses the matter and determines whether it can be resolved, whether to continue with the engagement, and whether and how to communicate it in his report

items.scenario: You have accepted a review engagement. A month in, the managing director tells you that you may speak to the finance department only and to nobody else in the company, and that certain subsidiary records will not be made available. The engagement is not one that any law or regulation requires.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require on materiality?

options.text: No materiality is determined in a review, the conclusion being expressed in negative form on the financial statements as a whole rather than on individual amounts
options.misconception: reads a negatively worded conclusion as dispensing with a threshold, when the standard requires materiality to be determined and applied in designing the procedures
options.why: The conclusion is about whether the financial statements are materially misstated, so a threshold is unavoidable. A figure of materiality for the financial statements as a whole has to be fixed, then carried into the design of the procedures and into the weighing of what they yield.

options.text: Set materiality higher for a review, since fewer procedures are performed and a lower figure would demand work the engagement does not provide for
options.misconception: scales the measure of what matters to a reader by the amount of work being done, when the level of assurance changes the procedures and not the threshold
options.why: The threshold belongs to the reader of the financial statements, not to the engagement. What the practitioner judges material, taken across the financial statements as a whole, stands unchanged whether he is giving limited assurance or reasonable assurance.

options.text: Determine materiality for the financial statements as a whole and apply it in designing the procedures and in evaluating the results — what the practitioner judges material, taken across the financial statements as a whole, standing the same regardless of the level of assurance he obtains as the basis for his conclusion — and revise it once something surfaces during the review that would have led him to a different amount at the start
options.why: The standard closes the shortcut in one sentence: what the practitioner judges material, taken across the financial statements as a whole, stands the same regardless of the level of assurance he obtains as the basis for his conclusion. What the level of assurance changes is the procedures, not the threshold at which a misstatement would matter to a reader. So he fixes materiality for the financial statements as a whole, applies it both in designing the procedures and in weighing what they yield, and must revise it should something surface mid-review that would have led him to a different amount at the outset.
keywords: same regardless of the level of assurance

options.text: Determine materiality at the start and leave it there — revising it mid-engagement would change the basis on which procedures already performed were designed
options.misconception: fixes materiality against later information, when the standard requires revision where that information would have produced a different amount initially
options.why: The standard requires the revision precisely because the earlier figure was set without the information. Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is revised once something surfaces mid-review that would have led him to a different amount at the outset.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the practitioner determines materiality for the financial statements as a whole and applies it in designing procedures and evaluating results, his judgement about what is material being the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained, and he revises it on becoming aware of information that would have caused a different amount to be determined initially

items.scenario: Planning a review of a company's financial statements, your senior proposes to set materiality at twice the figure the company's auditors used for the annual audit, on the ground that a review gives limited assurance and fewer procedures are performed. Midway through the review a contingent liability comes to light which, had it been known at the start, would have led you to a lower figure.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require?

options.text: Accept the oral assurance and complete the review, written representations being a matter of form where the finance director has said the same thing
options.misconception: treats an oral assurance as equivalent to the written representation, when the refusal itself is what the standard says may signal that significant issues exist
options.why: Asking for the matter in writing rather than by word of mouth makes management think about it harder; a refusal to sign is itself a signal, warning the practitioner that a significant issue or two may be sitting there. That is why the refusal is dealt with and not accommodated.

options.text: Express a qualified conclusion, the missing representations being a limitation whose possible effects are material but not pervasive
options.misconception: answers a refusal of the representations about management's own responsibilities with a qualification, when the standard sends the practitioner to a disclaimer or to withdrawal
options.why: The two representations refused are the ones that underpin everything else — that management prepared the statements under the framework and that all transactions are recorded. The standard does not grade their absence; it requires a disclaimer of conclusion or withdrawal.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management and those charged with governance, re-evaluate the integrity of management and the effect this may have on the reliability of representations and evidence in general, and take appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the conclusion — and, the representations withheld being the ones about management's own responsibilities, disclaim a conclusion on those statements or withdraw from the engagement where the law allows him to go
options.why: The standard treats a refusal of these particular representations as going to the whole engagement rather than to one balance. Written representations asked for and not given send the practitioner first to a discussion with management and with those charged with governance; he then re-evaluates the integrity of management, weighs what the refusal does to the reliability of representations, oral or written, and of evidence at large, and takes such steps as are called for, among them settling what the refusal may do to the conclusion in his report. Beyond that, where what is withheld is management's acknowledgement of its own responsibilities — preparing the statements, recording every transaction — he must disclaim a conclusion on them, or withdraw from the engagement where the law permits him to go.

options.text: Treat it as a scope limitation confined to the items the representations covered and report on the rest of the financial statements
options.misconception: confines to particular items a refusal that goes to management's responsibility for the statements as a whole and to the recording of all transactions
options.why: These representations are not about particular items. They are that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the framework and that all transactions have been recorded and reflected in them, which is why their absence takes the conclusion on the statements as a whole with it.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): where management does not provide a requested written representation the practitioner discusses the matter, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and evidence, and takes appropriate actions, and he shall disclaim a conclusion or withdraw where management does not provide the required representations about its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements and the recording of all transactions

items.scenario: At the end of a review, management refuses to sign the representation that it has discharged its own responsibility — preparing the financial statements under the applicable framework, and recording every transaction and reflecting it in them. It offers instead an oral assurance from the finance director. Nothing in the engagement is required by law or regulation, and withdrawal is possible.

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require?

options.text: Request the removal of the limitation; management having refused, you are unable to complete the review and express a conclusion, and you put the reason why the review cannot be completed in writing, both to management at the right level and to those charged with governance — and, a report being required of you, disclaim a conclusion and give that same reason in the report, reporting also anything that makes you believe the interim financial information needs a material adjustment
options.why: Where management imposes a limitation on scope after the engagement is accepted, the auditor requests its removal. On a refusal he can neither finish the review nor give a conclusion, and the reason why the review cannot be completed goes in writing to management at the right level and to those charged with governance. He then looks to what law and regulation ask of him, a report among them; where one is required, he disclaims a conclusion and puts that same reason into the report itself. Anything that has come to his attention making him believe the interim financial information needs a material adjustment is communicated too.
keywords: reason why the review cannot be completed

options.text: Qualify the conclusion, indicating that except for the matter described in an explanatory paragraph the review was conducted in accordance with SRE 2410
options.misconception: uses the treatment reserved for a limitation arising from circumstances and clearly confined to specific matters that are not pervasive, on a limitation imposed by management
options.why: That route exists, and it is for a different limitation. It applies in rare circumstances where the limitation has some source other than management and touches only certain identified matters which, material though they are, do not pervade the statements. A limitation imposed by management is dealt with by requesting its removal and, where a report is required, disclaiming a conclusion.

options.text: Withdraw from the review without a report, an auditor who cannot complete his work having nothing to say
options.misconception: leaves the users with no report where the auditor is required to issue one and the standard tells him what it must contain
options.why: Where he is required to issue a report he issues one, and the standard fixes its content: he disclaims a conclusion and provides the reason why the review cannot be completed. What he may not do is stay silent about a limitation the reader would otherwise never see.

options.text: Nothing can be done now — the engagement should not have been accepted with such a limitation in prospect, so the position is a matter for the next engagement
options.misconception: applies the pre-acceptance rule to a limitation imposed after acceptance, when the standard deals with the two separately
options.why: The rule about not accepting applies where the auditor's preliminary knowledge indicates that he would be unable to complete the review because of a limitation management will impose. Where the limitation arrives after acceptance, the standard has him request its removal and then follow the steps that end in a disclaimer if a report is required.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: where management imposes a limitation on scope after acceptance the auditor requests its removal and, on refusal, is unable to complete the review, communicating in writing to management and those charged with governance the reason, and where he is required to issue a report he disclaims a conclusion and provides that reason in the report

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a listed company and are reviewing its quarterly interim financial information. After you accepted the engagement, management refused you access to the records of a material subsidiary. The listing regulations require you to issue a report on the quarterly results. A colleague suggests a conclusion qualified "except for" the subsidiary.

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require in each quarter?

options.text: A qualified conclusion in all three quarters, a material uncertainty about going concern being by its nature something the conclusion must be modified for
options.misconception: modifies the conclusion for an uncertainty that is adequately disclosed, when the standard answers adequate disclosure with an emphasis of matter paragraph
options.why: A disclosed uncertainty is information the reader has; there is nothing wrong with the interim information for the conclusion to be modified about. The standard answers it with an emphasis of matter paragraph and keeps the qualified or adverse conclusion for the case where the disclosure is not adequate.

options.text: An emphasis of matter paragraph in all three quarters, the auditor's job being to draw attention to the uncertainty however the company has dealt with it
options.misconception: uses the paragraph where the disclosure is inadequate, when a paragraph cannot supply a disclosure the interim information itself omits
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph draws attention to something the information says; it cannot stand in for something the information does not say. Where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, the auditor should express a qualified or adverse conclusion with specific reference to it.

options.text: Nothing in the first two quarters, going concern being assessed on annual financial statements, and a qualified conclusion in the third only when the annual audit comes round
options.misconception: defers going concern to the annual audit, when the standard deals with a material uncertainty coming to the auditor's attention during an interim review
options.why: The standard addresses going concern and significant uncertainties inside the interim review itself. A material uncertainty that comes to the auditor's attention as a result of inquiries or other review procedures is dealt with in the review report for that period, by paragraph or by conclusion depending on the disclosure.

options.text: First quarter, modify the review report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph; second quarter, modify the current report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty; third quarter, express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, the report pointing by specific reference to that uncertainty and the fact of its existence
options.why: The answer turns on the disclosure, not on the uncertainty. Where a material uncertainty comes to the auditor's attention and adequate disclosure is made in the interim financial information, he modifies the review report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph. Where he had already added such a paragraph to a prior audit or review report and the material uncertainty still exists with adequate disclosure made, he modifies the current period's report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty. And where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, he should express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, with specific reference in the report to the fact that there is such a material uncertainty.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: a material uncertainty about going concern adequately disclosed is met by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph, a continuing uncertainty adequately disclosed by adding a paragraph highlighting the continued material uncertainty, and an inadequately disclosed uncertainty by a qualified or adverse conclusion with specific reference to the material uncertainty

items.scenario: Reviewing a company's interim financial information, you find a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern. In the first quarter it is adequately disclosed in the interim information. In the second quarter the uncertainty is unchanged and adequately disclosed again, and your report for the first quarter had carried an emphasis of matter paragraph about it. In the third quarter the disclosure has been dropped from the interim information altogether.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require for each?

options.text: For the inadequate disclosure, express a qualified or adverse opinion, or withdraw from the engagement as appropriate; for the procedure that could not be applied, consider either withdrawal or a disclaimer of opinion describing the scope limitation in the report
options.why: The standard gives three different answers to three different failures and these are two of them. Where the auditor takes the view that the prospective financial information has not been presented and disclosed adequately — the highly sensitive assumption whose consequences go undisclosed is the module's own example — a qualified or adverse opinion should be expressed, or withdrawal from the engagement made as appropriate. Where conditions preclude application of a procedure he judged necessary, what he weighs instead is withdrawal, or else a disclaimer of the opinion, with the scope limitation described in the report.

options.text: A qualified opinion for both, each defect being material but capable of being described in the report
options.misconception: answers a scope limitation with a qualified opinion, when the standard's answer to conditions precluding necessary procedures is withdrawal or a disclaimer describing the limitation
options.why: The qualified opinion belongs on the disclosure side. Where conditions preclude the application of procedures the auditor considered necessary, what the standard has him consider is either withdrawal from the engagement or a disclaimer of the opinion describing the scope limitation in the report.

options.text: Neither is answered by an opinion — the report on prospective financial information carries negative assurance about the assumptions, and negative assurance cannot be qualified
options.misconception: forgets that the report also carries an opinion on whether the information is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions and presented in accordance with the framework
options.why: The report carries both. It states negative assurance as to whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, and separately it gives an opinion — has the prospective financial information been properly drawn up on those assumptions, and does its presentation follow the relevant financial reporting framework? It is that opinion which is qualified, made adverse or disclaimed.

options.text: An adverse opinion for both, setting out the reasons in the report, or withdrawal
options.misconception: applies the answer given for significant assumptions that do not provide a reasonable basis to a disclosure failure and to a scope limitation, which the standard answers differently
options.why: The adverse opinion is the answer to a third failure: significant assumptions that leave the prospective financial information with no reasonable basis under it. On these facts the assumptions are not unreasonable so far as they could be examined; a disclosure failure calls for a qualified or adverse opinion or withdrawal, and a scope limitation for withdrawal or a disclaimer.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3400: the reporting outcomes matched to what has gone wrong — presentation and disclosure that fall short, significant assumptions left without a reasonable basis, and conditions shutting out a procedure the auditor judged necessary

items.scenario: You are examining a company's five-year forecast. Two problems remain at the end of the work. The forecast turns on an assumption about a single customer's offtake which is highly sensitive, and the consequences of that sensitivity are not adequately disclosed. Separately, the company would not give you the capacity study on which the production assumption rests, so a procedure you considered necessary could not be applied. The assumptions themselves, so far as you could examine them, are not unreasonable.

items.stem: What does SAE 3402 require?

options.text: Test the controls over the year and give the opinion as asked — the written assertion is the service organisation's own document and does not limit what the service auditor may report on
options.misconception: treats the written assertion as background paperwork, when a type 2 report is built on an assertion covering the whole specified period and the service auditor reports on the matters asserted
options.why: The assertion is the second of the three components of the report, and the service auditor's objective is to obtain reasonable assurance about the matters asserted. An opinion on operating effectiveness throughout a period beside an assertion that speaks only as at a date would report on something nobody has asserted.

options.text: The assertion is a type 1 assertion and will not carry a type 2 report — a type 2 report comprises the description of the system, a written assertion with three limbs running throughout the specified period rather than two limbs at a date, being that the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented throughout the period, that the controls were suitably designed throughout the period and that they operated effectively throughout the period, and a service auditor's assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters, which also sets out the tests of controls performed and what those tests showed
options.why: The three components are the same in both reports and the difference sits inside the second of them. A type 1 report comprises the description of the system, a written assertion that the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented at the specified date and that the controls were suitably designed as at that date, and an assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters. A type 2 report comprises the description, an assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb that the controls operated effectively throughout it, and an assurance report that conveys reasonable assurance about those matters and carries, besides, a description of the tests of controls together with what those tests showed. The service auditor reports on the matters asserted, so an assertion pinned to a date cannot support an opinion covering a period.
keywords: description of the tests of controls

options.text: The only difference between the two is the description of the tests of controls, which may simply be attached to a type 1 report to make it a type 2
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to an attachment, when a type 1 report speaks as at a specified date on the description and the design and says nothing at all about operating effectiveness
options.why: A type 1 report speaks as at a specified date about the description and the suitability of the design, and it says in terms that the service auditor carried out nothing to test how the controls operated, so no opinion on their operating effectiveness is expressed. Attaching test results to it would contradict its own text.

options.text: Both report throughout a period; a type 1 report simply covers fewer of the control objectives than a type 2
options.misconception: makes the difference one of coverage, when it is one of a date against a period and of design against operating effectiveness
options.why: Coverage is not what separates them. A type 1 report covers the description and the design of controls as at a specified date; a type 2 report goes further, reaching the operating effectiveness of those controls throughout a specified period as well.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the three components of a type 1 and a type 2 report, the type 1 assertion speaking as at the specified date on the fair presentation of the description and the suitable design of controls and the type 2 assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb on operating effectiveness, the type 2 assurance report also including a description of the tests of controls and the results thereof

items.scenario: A payroll processing service organisation has asked you, as service auditor, for a type 2 report covering the year to 31 March. The written assertion it has drafted says that, based on suitable criteria, the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented as at 31 March and that the controls related to the stated control objectives were suitably designed as at that date. Its finance head asks you to test the controls over the whole year and to add your opinion on their operating effectiveness, leaving the assertion as it is.

items.stem: Which of the two is an engagement under SAE 3402?

options.text: Neither — the standard reaches a service organisation only where that organisation bears responsibility for the suitable design of its controls or is otherwise in a position to assert it, and it does not deal with engagements to report only on whether controls operated as described, nor with engagements confined to controls lying outside a service that bears on user entities' internal control over financial reporting, such as controls affecting production or quality control
options.why: Each request fails a different limb of the standard's own scope. SAE 3402 reaches a service organisation only where that organisation bears responsibility for the suitable design of its controls, or is otherwise able to make an assertion about it — which the bureau says it cannot. Nor does the standard deal with an engagement asking only whether the controls operated as described, which is exactly what the bureau has asked for. As for the manufacturer, controls over production scheduling and quality inspection are the standard's own illustration of controls falling outside a service that bears on user entities' internal control over financial reporting.

options.text: The manufacturer only, since it both designs and operates its own controls and can therefore make the assertion the standard requires
options.misconception: satisfies the design assertion and forgets the second limb, which excludes controls unrelated to user entities' financial reporting
options.why: Being able to assert the design is necessary and not sufficient. The standard does not deal with an engagement confined to controls that fall outside a service bearing on user entities' internal control over financial reporting, and production and quality control are its own examples of those.

options.text: The bureau only, since a report on whether controls operated as described is a report on operating effectiveness, which is what a type 2 report gives
options.misconception: equates a report only on whether controls operated as described with a type 2 report, when the standard excludes the first by name
options.why: They are not the same and the standard separates them expressly: an engagement whose whole question is whether a service organisation's controls ran the way somebody else described them is placed outside its scope by name. A type 2 report reaches operating effectiveness on top of a fairly presented description and a suitable design, all asserted by the service organisation.

options.text: Both — a service organisation is any third party providing services to user entities, and an assurance report on its controls is what the standard exists for
options.misconception: reads the definition of a service organisation as the whole of the standard's scope, when the scope also turns on the design assertion and on the controls being relevant to financial reporting
options.why: A service organisation is one whose services bear on user entities' internal control over financial reporting, and even then the standard applies only where that organisation is responsible for the suitable design of the controls or can assert it. Both limbs have to hold.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the two limbs of the standard's own scope — the service organisation's ability to assert the suitable design of its controls, and the controls having to bear on user entities' internal control over financial reporting — together with the engagements the standard places outside itself

items.scenario: Two requests reach your firm. A contract manufacturer wants an assurance report on the controls it operates over production scheduling and quality inspection for the companies it supplies. A data processing bureau wants a report only on whether the controls it runs operated as described to it by its parent, which designed them; the bureau will make no assertion about whether they were suitably designed.

items.stem: Does the Order apply to this company?

options.text: No — the borrowing test is failed but the company is still exempt, because two of the three money conditions are met and the exemption turns on the majority of them
options.misconception: reads the private company exemption as a test that can be passed on the balance of its conditions, when all of them must hold together
options.why: There is no balance to strike. The Order describes one class of private company, and it is a company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and has capital and reserves within ₹1 crore and borrowings within ₹1 crore and revenue within ₹10 crore. Fail one and the description no longer fits.

options.text: Yes — the borrowing test is failed. The exemption asks that borrowings from a bank or financial institution never top ₹1 crore at any point of time during the financial year, and ₹1.20 crore stood outstanding inside the year even though nothing did on 31 March
options.why: The three money tests are not all measured the same way, and this is the one that differs. Paid up capital and reserves and surplus are tested as on the balance sheet date, and ₹0.85 crore is inside the one crore rupees. Total revenue is tested for the financial year, and ₹8.40 crore is inside the ten crore rupees. But borrowings are tested at any point of time during the financial year, so the ₹1.20 crore drawn between June and November is what decides it, and repaying before the year end does not undo it. The exemption is conjunctive — every condition has to hold — so failing one puts the company inside the Order.
keywords: at any point of time during the financial year
as on the balance sheet date

options.text: No — every figure is below its limit on 31 March: ₹0.85 crore against ₹1 crore, nil borrowings against ₹1 crore, and ₹8.40 crore against ₹10 crore
options.misconception: measures all three tests at the balance sheet date, when the borrowing test is expressly measured at any point of time during the financial year
options.why: Only the first of the three is measured at the balance sheet date. The Order's words on borrowings are "at any point of time during the financial year", which is what catches a limit drawn and cleared inside the year, and the revenue test runs for the whole financial year as well.

options.text: Yes — but only because the total revenue of ₹8.40 crore is measured against a limit of ₹5 crore for a private limited company
options.misconception: uses the ₹5 crore working capital figure from clause 3(ii)(b) as the revenue limit in the applicability test
options.why: Five crore rupees is the working capital limit inside clause 3(ii)(b), which is one of the matters reported on once the Order applies. The revenue limit in the exemption is a total revenue not exceeding ten crore rupees during the financial year, which ₹8.40 crore is inside.

citation.ref: paragraph 1(2)(v) — the exempt private limited company: neither subsidiary nor holding company of any public company; its paid up capital together with reserves and surplus within one crore rupees on the balance sheet date; its bank and financial institution borrowings never above one crore rupees at any moment of the year; and its total revenue for the year within ten crore rupees

items.scenario: A private limited company, which is neither a subsidiary nor a holding company of any public company, closes its year on 31 March. Its paid up capital and reserves and surplus stand at ₹0.85 crore on that date. Its total revenue as disclosed in Schedule III, including revenue from discontinuing operations, is ₹8.40 crore. It had no borrowings at all on 31 March, but a cash credit limit of ₹1.20 crore was drawn from a bank between June and November and repaid in full before the year end. The audit manager has left the CARO annexure out of the report on the footing that all three figures are inside the limits at the balance sheet date.

items.stem: To which of the four does the Order apply?

options.text: The third and the fourth. The insurance company and the section 8 company are two of the five exempt classes; a Government company is not an exempt class at all; and the private company loses the exemption because it is a subsidiary of a public company, whatever its figures
options.why: The Order applies to every company including a foreign company and then exempts five classes: a banking company, an insurance company, a company licensed to operate under section 8, a One Person Company and a small company, and a private limited company meeting the stated conditions. An insurance company and a section 8 company are named outright. A Government company is nowhere in that list, so its size is beside the point. And the private company's exemption opens with the words "not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company", which this one is, so the ₹0.40 crore and the ₹6 crore never come into it.
keywords: not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company

options.text: The second, the third and the fourth. A section 8 company is a company like any other and the Order exempts only banking and insurance companies among special classes
options.misconception: shortens the exempt list to the two regulated financial classes, dropping the section 8 company, the One Person Company and the small company
options.why: The list has five entries, not two. A section 8 licensee under the Companies Act is named in it alongside the banking company and the insurance company, and so are a One Person Company and a small company.

options.text: None of them. A Government company is audited under directions issued by the Comptroller and Auditor General, and where those directions apply the Order does not
options.misconception: treats the C&AG's directions under section 143(5) as displacing the Order, when the two requirements sit on the same report
options.why: Directions under section 143(5) tell the auditor of a Government company how the audit is to be conducted and are reported on in his report; they do not take the company out of the Order. Paragraph 2 says every report made by the auditor under section 143 on a company to which the Order applies shall in addition contain the matters specified.

options.text: The third only. The fourth is inside every money limit — ₹0.40 crore against ₹1 crore, nil borrowings against ₹1 crore and ₹6 crore against ₹10 crore — so it is an exempt private company
options.misconception: applies the three money tests without the condition that opens the exemption, so a subsidiary of a public company is read as exempt on its figures
options.why: The figures are only reached if the company is one the exemption describes, and the description begins by excluding a subsidiary or holding company of a public company. Being inside all three limits does not help a company that fails the words before them.

citation.ref: paragraph 1 — the Order's reach over companies generally, foreign ones included on the clause (42) of section 2 meaning, and the five classes it lifts out: banking companies, insurers, section 8 licensees, the One Person Company with the small company, and the private limited company which is neither subsidiary nor holding company of any public company and which meets the stated conditions

items.scenario: A firm signs four audit reports this season. The first is an insurance company. The second holds a licence issued under section 8 of the Companies Act. The third is a Government company with revenue of ₹60 crore. The fourth is a private limited company which is the subsidiary of a public company, with paid up capital and reserves and surplus of ₹0.40 crore, no borrowings at any time in the year and total revenue of ₹6 crore. The article clerk proposes to attach the CARO annexure only to the third, on the view that the other three are all small or special enough to be outside it.

items.stem: What does paragraph 2 of the Order settle?

options.text: That the matters go into the report itself — paragraph 3's matters and paragraph 4's are added to whatever report the auditor makes under section 143 for a company the Order covers — and that the Order's reach takes in foreign companies too, on the clause (42) of section 2 meaning under the Companies Act
options.why: Paragraph 2 makes the Order an addition to the report under section 143 rather than a document of its own, so a separate note addressed elsewhere does not discharge it. And the reach of the Order is settled in paragraph 1, which covers companies generally, including a foreign company on the clause (42) of section 2 meaning; the five exempt classes are the only way out, and place of incorporation is not one of them.
keywords: an addition to the report under section 143
place of incorporation is not one of them

options.text: That the Order applies only to companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, a foreign company being governed by its own law of incorporation and reporting under Chapter XXII instead
options.misconception: reads the Order as confined to Indian incorporation, when paragraph 1 names a foreign company inside its scope
options.why: Paragraph 1 opens by reaching companies generally, a foreign company among them on the clause (42) of section 2 meaning. That definition is exactly the point of naming it, and it is a narrower set of exclusions than the auditor is imagining.

options.text: That the CARO answers are a separate report, which is why the Order calls them an annexure — they are signed separately and may be addressed to those charged with governance
options.misconception: reads the word annexure as making the Order's answers a distinct report, when paragraph 2 adds them to the report under section 143
options.why: What the answers are physically attached to is a matter of presentation. Paragraph 2 fixes the substance: the report made under section 143 shall in addition contain the matters specified, so they form part of that report and go to the same addressee.

options.text: That the Order applies to the auditor's report on the consolidated financial statements in full, so the same answers are repeated in both reports
options.misconception: drops the exception in paragraph 2, which confines the Order on a consolidated report to clause (xxi)
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the opposite in its second limb: on a report about consolidated financial statements the Order drops away, clause (xxi) of paragraph 3 alone excepted. Repeating the whole annexure there reports under clauses that do not apply to that report at all.

citation.ref: paragraph 2 — the matters of paragraphs 3 and 4 being added to whatever report the auditor makes under section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 for a company the Order covers, and the Order falling away on a report about consolidated financial statements save for clause (xxi) of paragraph 3 — read with paragraph 1 on the Order's reach over companies generally, foreign ones included

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies has an auditor who proposes to issue his CARO answers as a separate document, signed on the same day as the audit report but addressed to the board rather than to the members, on the view that the Order is a management reporting requirement and not part of the opinion. He also proposes to leave the Order out altogether for a foreign company he audits, on the view that an Order made under the Companies Act cannot reach a company incorporated abroad.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(vi) say?

options.text: That cost records are ones the Central Government has specified under section 148(1), and that the company has not in fact made or kept such accounts and records — with the basis for that unfavourable answer stated
options.why: The clause asks two questions in order. The first is whether maintenance of these records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148(1) — here it has. The second is whether the company then made and kept such accounts and records — here it did not. Whether a cost audit is required is a different question under the same section, and it is not what this clause states on. Because the answer is unfavourable, paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for it.
keywords: has been specified by the Central Government
a different question under the same section

options.text: That the company has not maintained cost records, and nothing more — the first limb is background and only the failure needs stating
options.misconception: answers only the second limb, when the clause asks the specification question in its own right and the basis for an unfavourable answer is separately required
options.why: A reader who is told only that records were not maintained does not know whether they were ever required. The clause asks whether maintenance has been specified by the Central Government under section 148(1) as its own question, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for the unfavourable answer that follows.

options.text: Nothing, correctly — the clause is about cost audit, and a company below the turnover threshold for a cost audit answers it as not applicable
options.misconception: reads clause 3(vi) as a question about cost audit, when it asks whether the maintenance of records has been specified and whether they have been maintained
options.why: Section 148 carries two separate powers, one to specify that cost records be kept and one to direct that they be audited, and the clause reaches only the first. A company can be well below any cost audit threshold and still be one for which cost records have been specified.

options.text: That the company has not maintained cost records, and that the audit opinion on the financial statements is qualified in consequence
options.misconception: turns an unfavourable answer inside the annexure into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The annexure and the opinion answer different questions. Paragraph 4(a) requires the basis for an unfavourable answer to be stated inside the Order; whether the opinion is modified is decided under SA 705 (Revised) on the evidence about the financial statements, and many unfavourable CARO answers sit beside an unmodified opinion.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company to which the Order applies makes a product for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records under sub-section (1) of section 148 of the Companies Act. The company keeps no cost records at all. It is below the turnover at which a cost audit would have to be conducted, and no cost auditor has been appointed. The audit manager answers clause 3(vi) with the words "not applicable, no cost audit is required".

items.stem: What does clause 3(vi) require here?

options.text: An affirmative answer on both limbs — the maintenance of cost records has been specified and such accounts and records have been so made and maintained — because the clause asks about the records and not about the cost audit
options.why: Clause 3(vi) puts two questions: has the Central Government specified, under section 148(1), that cost records be kept, and were such accounts and records then so made and maintained. Both are yes on these facts, so the answer is affirmative, and paragraph 4(a) is not engaged because the answer is neither unfavourable nor qualified. The failure to appoint a cost auditor is a non-compliance with a different limb of section 148, and putting it under this clause tells the reader that the records themselves were not kept, which is untrue.

options.text: An affirmative answer on the records, together with a statement under clause 3(vi) that the company has not appointed a cost auditor, since the reader of the annexure would otherwise be left unaware of it
options.misconception: adds material to a clause because a reader might want it, rather than because the clause asks for it
options.why: What a reader might find useful is not the test; the clause's words are. Clause 3(vi) asks two questions and both are about the records. A matter the Order does not ask about is not reported under a clause that asks about something else.

options.text: No answer at all — a clause answered in the affirmative is a clause with nothing to report, and the annexure carries only the exceptions
options.misconception: treats the annexure as exception reporting, when paragraph 3 requires a statement on each specified matter
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the auditor's report shall include a statement on the matters specified. Every clause that applies to the company is answered whichever way the answer falls, and an omitted clause tells the reader nothing about whether the question was asked.

options.text: An unfavourable answer, since section 148 has been contravened and the clause names section 148 in terms
options.misconception: reads the mention of section 148 as bringing everything in that section inside the clause, when the clause names only the specification of cost records under sub-section (1)
options.why: The clause names sub-section (1) of section 148, which is the power to specify that cost records be kept. It does not ask whether every requirement of the section has been met, and a company that has kept exactly the records specified has answered both limbs affirmatively.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi), read with paragraph 3 and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: Another company to which the Order applies is in a business for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records, and the company maintains them properly and completely. It was also required to have those records audited and has simply not appointed a cost auditor for the year. The audit senior proposes to answer clause 3(vi) by saying that the company has failed to comply with section 148, and to give the details of the missing cost audit in the annexure under that clause.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(viii) say?

options.text: That transactions absent from the books of account, ₹3.60 crore of them, were surrendered as income in the year's tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and that the previously unrecorded income was not then properly recorded in the books of account during the year — with the basis for that unfavourable answer stated
options.why: The clause has two limbs and a bare "Yes" answers only the first. Limb one: did any transaction the books never carried get surrendered, or disclosed as income, in the year's tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961? Limb two: was that previously unrecorded income then properly recorded in the books of account during the year? Paying the tax settles the position with the tax authority and does nothing about the books, so the second limb is unfavourable, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for that answer.
keywords: properly recorded in the books of account during the year

options.text: That the company surrendered ₹3.60 crore in a tax assessment during the year, which answers the clause, the treatment in the books being a matter for the accounting standards rather than for the Order
options.misconception: stops at the first limb, treating the recording of the income as outside the clause when the clause asks about it in terms
options.why: The clause reaches the books in terms. Its second limb wants to know whether income that was once unrecorded found its way properly into the ledgers inside the same year. That the accounting standards also have something to say about it does not remove the question from the Order.

options.text: That the company has surrendered ₹3.60 crore of unrecorded transactions and that a fraud of that amount has been noticed, which follows automatically from income being concealed
options.misconception: reads an affirmative answer under clause 3(viii) as itself establishing a fraud, when whether there was a fraud is decided separately
options.why: Clause 3(viii) reports a fact about unrecorded transactions surrendered in tax assessments and does not decide that a fraud occurred. Whether a fraud has been noticed or reported is answered under clause 3(xi), and reporting to the Central Government is governed by section 143(12) with Rule 13; an affirmative answer here can stand with no fraud reported at all.

options.text: Nothing under this clause — an amount surrendered in a tax assessment is a matter for clause 3(vii) on statutory dues, since it arises out of a tax proceeding
options.misconception: routes the answer to the statutory dues clause because tax is involved, when clause 3(vii) is about depositing dues and 3(viii) is about unrecorded transactions
options.why: Clause 3(vii) asks whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues and what is unpaid or disputed. Clause 3(viii) asks about transactions that were never in the books and were surrendered or disclosed as income in the tax assessments. They are different questions and this is the second one.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: During the year under audit a company surrendered ₹3.60 crore of sales that had never been entered in its books, as income in an assessment under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and paid the tax demanded. Nothing has been passed through the books of account, the management taking the view that the tax has been paid and the matter is closed. The audit manager's draft answers clause 3(viii) with the single word "Yes".

items.stem: What does clause 3(viii) require?

options.text: Only the ₹1.20 crore is inside the clause, and the answer is unfavourable, because the company had not recorded those transactions when they arose
options.misconception: reads the clause as asking whether the transactions were recorded when they occurred, when it asks whether the previously unrecorded income was recorded during the year
options.why: That the transactions were unrecorded is the premise of the clause, not its failing — the clause exists precisely for transactions that were never in the books. What it then asks is whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded during the year, and here it has.

options.text: Both amounts are reported, and the answer is unfavourable, because the ₹90 lakh is not in the books at the date the auditor signs his report
options.misconception: measures the clause at the date of the report instead of at the year, when both its limbs are expressed for the financial year under audit
options.why: The date of the report is not the period the clause covers. It asks about what was surrendered or disclosed during the year and what was recorded in the books during the year, so a surrender made after the year end belongs to the next year's answer.

options.text: Neither amount is reported, since income surrendered in a tax assessment and brought into the books is no longer unrecorded and the clause reaches only amounts still outside the books
options.misconception: confines the clause to unrecorded income that remains unrecorded, which would leave the second limb with nothing to answer
options.why: If the clause reached only amounts still outside the books, its second limb — asking whether income once unrecorded was properly brought into the books within the year — could never be answered in the affirmative. The clause asks about the surrender first and the recording second.

options.text: Only the ₹1.20 crore is inside the clause, and its answer is affirmative on both limbs — the transactions were surrendered as income during the year and the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year; the ₹90 lakh surrendered after the year end is not what the clause asks about
options.why: The clause is tied to the year twice over: the surrender must fall during the year, and so must the recording. Limb one looks at what the books never carried and was then surrendered, or disclosed as income, in the year's tax assessments; limb two at whether that once unrecorded income afterwards reached the ledgers properly, inside the same year. The ₹1.20 crore satisfies both, so the answer is affirmative and paragraph 4(a) is not engaged. The ₹90 lakh was surrendered after the year end, so it is outside the clause for the year under audit.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii)

items.scenario: A company has two matters on file at the year end. In an assessment completed in July of the year under audit it surrendered ₹1.20 crore of transactions that had not been in its books, and it passed the entries in the books in the same month, so the income now sits in the accounts. Separately, in May after the year end and before the audit report is signed, it surrendered a further ₹90 lakh in a fresh assessment. The audit senior proposes to report both amounts under clause 3(viii), and to answer the second limb "no" for both because the ₹90 lakh is not in the books.

items.stem: How do the three sub-clauses of clause 3(xii) come out?

options.text: Two are unfavourable — the ratio and the ten per cent — but the interest default is not reported, having been made good before the year end
options.misconception: reads the default sub-clause as reporting only defaults still outstanding, when it asks about a default for any period
options.why: The sub-clause reaches default in either direction — interest left unpaid, or the deposit itself not repaid — over any period at all. A default paid three months late is a default for a period, and the clause asks for the details of it.

options.text: None is unfavourable — the ratio of 1:20 permits deposits of twenty times Net Owned Funds, being ₹100 crore, and ₹110 crore is within the ten per cent tolerance the Nidhi Rules allow
options.misconception: turns the ten per cent unencumbered term deposit requirement into a tolerance on the deposit ratio
options.why: The ten per cent is a separate requirement about maintaining unencumbered term deposits to meet the liability; it is not a margin on the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio. The ratio allows ₹100 crore against ₹5 crore of Net Owned Funds, and ₹110 crore is outside it.

options.text: One is unfavourable — the ratio of 1:20 means Net Owned Funds must be at least one twentieth of deposits, so ₹5 crore against ₹110 crore fails; the ten per cent and the interest are matters for the Nidhi Rules and not for the Order
options.misconception: keeps the ratio and drops the other two sub-clauses, when all three are inside clause 3(xii)
options.why: Clause 3(xii) has three sub-clauses of its own, and the second names the ten per cent unencumbered term deposits specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014 while the third names any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment. That the Nidhi Rules are their source is why the clause cites them.

options.text: All three are unfavourable — deposits of ₹110 crore against Net Owned Funds of ₹5 crore exceed the ratio of 1:20, which allows ₹100 crore; unencumbered term deposits of 6 per cent fall short of the ten per cent required; and there was a default in payment of interest on deposits, which is reported for any period even though it has since been paid
options.why: Sub-clause (a) asks whether the Nidhi has complied with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20, so twenty times ₹5 crore is ₹100 crore and ₹110 crore breaches it. Sub-clause (b) turns on ten per cent unencumbered term deposits, that percentage being one the Nidhi Rules, 2014 fix, and 6 per cent falls under it. Sub-clause (c) asks after default — in paying interest on deposits, or in repaying them — over any period at all, and calls for the particulars: the words "for any period" catch a default that has since been made good. Each is answered separately, and each unfavourable answer carries paragraph 4(a) with it.
keywords: ten per cent unencumbered term deposits

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(a), (b) and (c), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A Nidhi company to which the Order applies has Net Owned Funds of ₹5 crore and deposits of ₹110 crore at the year end. Its unencumbered term deposits stand at 6 per cent, against the ten per cent the Nidhi Rules, 2014 require it to maintain. Interest on a group of deposits fell due in November and was paid in January, three months late. The audit manager proposes to answer clause 3(xii) with "the company is a Nidhi and has complied with the applicable requirements".

items.stem: What does clause 3(xii) require?

options.text: The first two sub-clauses are answered affirmatively, and the third is answered with the details of the default — the sub-clause reaches default in paying interest on deposits, or in repaying them, over any period at all, and calls for the particulars, without any threshold of amount or number
options.why: Each sub-clause is answered on its own facts, so two affirmative answers and one unfavourable answer is a perfectly ordinary shape for this clause. The third reaches default over any period at all — interest on deposits gone unpaid, or the deposit itself not repaid — and calls for the particulars. It sets no threshold of amount or number and does not ask whether a loss was caused, so a single late repayment is reported with the details, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for that answer.
keywords: no threshold of amount or number

options.text: All three are answered affirmatively, with a note that the auditor has applied a materiality threshold to the third sub-clause because a single depositor is immaterial to the financial statements as a whole
options.misconception: imports a financial statement materiality threshold into a clause that asks for the details of any default
options.why: Materiality for the financial statements decides what affects the opinion, not what the Order asks to be stated. The sub-clause asks about any default for any period and calls for the details, and an answer that filters it by materiality answers a different question.

options.text: All three are answered affirmatively — a repayment made a month late and before the year end is not a default, the deposit having been honoured in full
options.misconception: reads a default as failure to pay at all, when the sub-clause reaches a default in repayment for any period
options.why: The sub-clause is about timing as well as amount: a default in repayment for any period is what it names. A maturity paid a month after it fell due is a default for that month, whether or not the money was eventually paid in full.

options.text: The clause is answered affirmatively and the late repayment is reported instead under clause 3(v) on deposits, which is where a company's dealings with its depositors belong
options.misconception: moves a matter clause 3(xii) names expressly into the general deposits clause
options.why: Clause 3(xii) is the clause written for a Nidhi company, and its third sub-clause names a default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof in terms. A matter a clause asks about is answered under that clause.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(c), read with paragraph 3(xii)(a) and (b) and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A Nidhi company complies with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio and maintains unencumbered term deposits well above the ten per cent required. One depositor's maturity amount, due in August, was repaid in September after the depositor complained. The audit senior proposes to answer clause 3(xii) affirmatively and to say nothing about the late repayment, on the view that one depositor out of thousands is not material and no loss was caused.

items.stem: Which set is Rule 11?

options.text: The whole of CARO 2020, since Rule 11 is the rule under which the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order is made
options.misconception: attributes the Order to Rule 11, when the Order is made by the Central Government under section 143(11)
options.why: The Order is issued by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by section 143(11), after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority. Rule 11 sits under section 143(3)(j) and prescribes its own six matters.

options.text: The pending litigations, the provision for foreseeable losses on long term contracts and the delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund — the three the Rule originally carried, the later additions being recommendatory
options.misconception: stops at the Rule's three original matters and treats the funding chain, the dividend and the audit trail as optional
options.why: The Rule as it stands carries six matters, and the auditor's report shall include his views and comments on all of them. Nothing in it makes the representations on Intermediaries and Funding Parties, the compliance of the dividend with section 123 or the audit trail recommendatory.

options.text: The adequacy of internal financial controls and their operating effectiveness; whether any director is disqualified under section 164(2); and whether the financial statements comply with the accounting standards
options.misconception: lists three of the statements section 143(3) itself requires as though Rule 11 prescribed them
options.why: All three are in section 143(3) in their own clauses — internal financial controls in clause (i), the disqualification of a director in clause (g) and compliance with the accounting standards in clause (e). Rule 11 is what clause (j) reaches, and it prescribes a different six matters.

options.text: The impact of pending litigations on the financial position; provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts; delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund; the representations on funds advanced to Intermediaries and received from Funding Parties with the auditor's own statement on them; compliance of the dividend with section 123; and the accounting software's audit trail
options.why: Those six are what Rule 11 prescribes under clause (j) of section 143(3), which is the clause allowing other matters to be prescribed: the pending litigations, the provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts, any delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, the funding chain, the dividend under section 123, and the accounting software's audit trail. The internal financial controls statement the senior has already written is clause (i) of section 143(3) itself and not a Rule 11 matter, and CARO comes from section 143(11) and the Order made under it, so neither belongs in this list.

citation.ref: Rule 11, prescribing the other matters to be included in the auditor's report under clause (j) of sub-section (3) of section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: An audit senior is drafting the "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements" section for an unlisted public company. He has written paragraphs on the company's compliance with CARO 2020 and on the adequacy of internal financial controls, and asks which further matters Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 puts into the report.

items.stem: Is that enough under Rule 11?

options.text: No — the representations must also be given by the Ultimate Beneficiaries and the Funding Parties themselves, since they are the persons with knowledge of the understanding
options.misconception: extends the representation requirement to third parties, when the Rule asks about the management of the company under audit
options.why: The Rule speaks of what management has represented, to the best of what it knows and believes, and it excepts whatever the notes to the accounts already disclose. Nothing in it asks the auditor to obtain anything from an Intermediary, a Funding Party or an Ultimate Beneficiary.

options.text: Yes — the Rule asks whether the management has represented, and once the written representations are on file and reproduced, the requirement is discharged
options.misconception: reads the funding chain as two questions about management's representations, dropping the auditor's own sub-limb
options.why: Two of the three sub-limbs are about management's representations and the third is about the auditor. Leaving it out reports what the company said and nothing about whether the auditor did any work on it.

options.text: No — the Rule has a third sub-limb, under which the auditor states whether, based on such audit procedures as he has considered reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, anything has come to his notice that has caused him to believe that the two representations contain any material mis-statement
options.why: The funding chain in Rule 11 is written in three parts, and only the first two are about what management has represented — that no funds were advanced or loaned or invested in Intermediaries with the understanding that they would lend or invest in Ultimate Beneficiaries, and that no funds were received from Funding Parties with the understanding that the company would do the same. The third is the auditor's own, and it is what makes the requirement more than a transcription: he states that, on procedures he judged reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, no matter has reached his notice that would lead him to believe either representation carries a material mis-statement.
keywords: reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances

options.text: No — the auditor must certify that no funds were in fact advanced to any Ultimate Beneficiary through an Intermediary during the year
options.misconception: turns a statement that nothing has come to the auditor's notice into a positive certificate about the facts
options.why: The Rule does not ask for a certificate. It asks whether, based on procedures the auditor considered reasonable and appropriate, anything has come to his notice causing him to believe the representations contain a material mis-statement, which is a different and narrower statement than certifying what happened.

citation.ref: Rule 11(4)(i), (ii) and (iii) — the representation on funds advanced to Intermediaries, the representation on funds received from Funding Parties, and the auditor's own third statement: procedures he judged reasonable and appropriate, and whether any matter reached his notice suggesting either representation is materially mis-stated

items.scenario: A company has advanced funds during the year to two intermediary entities, one of them a foreign entity, and has received funds from a third. Management has given the auditor written representations in the terms Rule 11 requires. The audit manager proposes to reproduce those two representations in the report and stop there, saying that the Rule asks whether management has represented and management has represented.

items.stem: How does the Companies Act answer the three?

options.text: A penalty of twenty-five lakh rupees for a listed company and five lakh rupees for any other company; the provisions bind the statutory auditor alone; and confidentiality is preserved only where the fraud is ultimately established
options.misconception: raises both penalties, confines the duty to the statutory auditor and makes the good faith protection depend on the fraud being proved
options.why: The figures are five lakh rupees for a listed company and one lakh rupees for any other company. The duty reaches a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor as well.
