And section 143(13) protects reporting done in good faith, which is a test about the reporter's state of mind rather than about how the matter turns out.

options.text: No penalty at all where the fraud is below the prescribed amount and was reported to the audit committee; the reach to other auditors is a matter of professional guidance; and confidentiality is displaced only by an order of a court
options.misconception: reads the penalty as attaching only to the Central Government route and treats the extension to other auditors as guidance rather than statute
options.why: The penalty attaches to non-compliance with section 143(12), which covers the reporting of a fraud below the prescribed amount to the audit committee or the Board as much as the reporting of a larger one to the Central Government. The extension to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor is in the Act itself, and the protection in section 143(13) needs no court order.

options.text: A penalty of one lakh rupees whatever the company, the amount being fixed by the section rather than by the class of company; the provisions reach a cost auditor but not a secretarial auditor; and the good faith protection is a defence the auditor must plead
options.misconception: flattens a two-tier penalty into one figure and drops the secretarial auditor from a provision that names both
options.why: The penalty is two-tier and the tier is set by the class of company: five lakh rupees for a listed company, one lakh rupees for any other. And the provision names a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor together, by reference to section 148 and section 204.

options.text: A penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and one lakh rupees in the case of any other company; the fraud reporting provisions apply mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor performing their duties under sections 148 and 204; and under section 143(13) no duty to which the auditor is subject is regarded as contravened by reason of his reporting the matter if it is done in good faith
options.why: The three answers are in three separate places and each is stated in terms. Section 143(12) binds an auditor, a cost accountant and a company secretary in practice alike, and failing it costs five lakh rupees where the company is listed and one lakh rupees where it is not. Fraud reporting binds a cost auditor at his work under section 148, and a secretarial auditor at his under section 204, mutatis mutandis. And section 143(13) safeguards the act of reporting: an auditor who reports the matter in good faith contravenes no duty he is otherwise under.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) with Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, read with the application of the fraud reporting provisions mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor under sections 148 and 204, the penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and one lakh rupees in the case of any other company, and section 143(13) on reporting done in good faith

items.scenario: Three questions come up at a firm's training session. The statutory auditor of a listed company failed to report a fraud of ₹2 crore in the manner section 143(12) and Rule 13 require, and somebody asks what he is liable to. The cost auditor of an unlisted company found a fraud during his work under section 148 and believes the fraud reporting provisions are for statutory auditors only. And a third asks whether an auditor who reports a suspected fraud that later proves to be nothing has broken his duty of confidentiality to the client.

items.stem: What must the report state?

options.text: Both are problems — section 197(16) puts a statement into the report under section 143: is what the company pays its directors in step with that section, and has any director been paid beyond the ceiling it fixes? For auditors of public companies that statement goes under "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements"; and section 143(4) requires the reasons to be stated where any matter the report had to carry is answered in the negative or with a qualification
options.why: Section 197(16) came in with the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017. It asks the auditor to say whether what the company pays its directors squares with that section, whether any director has been paid beyond the ceiling it fixes, and whatever further particulars stand prescribed; ICAI's advisory places that statement, for auditors of public companies, under the section headed "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements". And section 143(4) is general: a matter the report was required to carry, once answered in the negative or with a qualification, brings the reasons with it — so a bare negative on the branch returns is half an answer.
keywords: Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements
answered in the negative or with a qualification

options.text: Only the remuneration is a problem — reasons under section 143(4) are required only where the audit opinion itself is modified, and this negative answer sits outside the opinion
options.misconception: attaches section 143(4) to a modified opinion, when it attaches to any matter required to be included in the report being answered in the negative or with a qualification
options.why: Section 143(4) is written about the matters required to be included in the audit report, not about the opinion. A negative answer on the branch returns is one of those matters, so the reasons are stated whether or not the opinion is modified.

options.text: Neither is a problem — remuneration is a matter for the company's own disclosures under section 197, and a negative answer under section 143(3) speaks for itself
options.misconception: leaves the remuneration statement to the company and treats a negative answer as needing no reasons
options.why: Section 197(16) puts the statement on the auditor and puts it in his report under section 143. And section 143(4) requires the reasons wherever a matter required to be in the report is answered in the negative or with a qualification, which is exactly what has happened on the branch returns.

options.text: Only the negative answer is a problem — the remuneration statement is required of auditors of listed companies alone, this being a governance disclosure
options.misconception: confines the section 197(16) statement to listed companies, when the advisory addresses auditors of public companies
options.why: Section 197(16) speaks of the auditor of the company, and ICAI's advisory addresses the placement of the statement for auditors of public companies. Nothing confines it to a listed company.

citation.ref: Section 197(16) — the auditor's statement in his report under section 143 on what directors are paid: whether it squares with that section, and whether any director has been paid beyond its ceiling — read with section 143(4), which calls for the reasons behind any negative or qualified answer to a matter the report had to carry

items.scenario: A public company's draft audit report says nothing at all about the remuneration paid to its directors. Separately, one of the statements required under section 143(3) is answered in the negative — proper returns adequate for the purposes of the audit were not received from two branches not visited by the auditor — and the draft records the negative answer without saying anything more. The engagement partner is asked whether either is a problem.

items.stem: How is the COSO framework actually built?

options.text: Seventeen principles across five components — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — each of which must be present and functioning for internal control to be effective, and three categories of objectives: operations, reporting and compliance
options.why: The framework, introduced in 1992, articulates seventeen principles representing the fundamental concepts associated with its five components, and the requirement is strict: the principles are relevant to every entity and must be present and functioning for a system of internal control to be effective. Its objectives are in three categories, and reporting is only one of them — operations objectives relate to the effectiveness and efficiency of operations including safeguarding assets against loss, reporting objectives to internal and external financial and non-financial reporting, and compliance objectives to compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

options.text: Five components and seventeen principles, but the controller is right about the scope — the framework is confined to internal control over financial reporting, which is why Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 was built on it
options.misconception: keeps the structure and narrows the objectives to financial reporting, dropping the operations and compliance categories
options.why: The framework lists three categories of objectives and reporting is one of them. That section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act is about internal control over financial reporting says something about that statute, not about the breadth of the framework.

options.text: Twenty criteria in four areas — purpose, commitment, capability, and monitoring and learning — with three categories of objectives
options.misconception: gives the CoCo framework's structure under the COSO name
options.why: Twenty criteria in those four areas is the Criteria of Control framework developed by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. COSO is seventeen principles across five components.

options.text: Thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives, in four domains
options.misconception: gives COBIT's structure under the COSO name
options.why: Thirty-four high-level processes and two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains is COBIT, created by ISACA for IT governance and management. It is an IT framework rather than a general internal control framework.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework: seventeen principles across the five components of control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication and monitoring, all of which must be present and functioning, and the three categories of operations, reporting and compliance objectives

items.scenario: A group's head office in India is being asked by its overseas parent to map its internal control documentation to the COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework. The finance controller tells the audit team that the framework is built on four components and about thirty principles, and that it deals with financial reporting objectives alone, so the group's operational and compliance controls fall outside the mapping.

items.stem: How many criteria or objectives does each carry, and in how many areas or domains?

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas; COBIT — thirty-four control objectives in two hundred and ten processes across four domains
options.misconception: swaps COBIT's processes and control objectives, so the smaller number becomes the larger
options.why: It is thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives, not the other way about. A framework with two hundred and ten processes carrying thirty-four objectives between them would have more processes than things to control.

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas, being purpose, commitment, capability, and monitoring and learning; COBIT — thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives across four domains — planning and organisation, then acquisition and implementation, then delivery and support, and finally monitoring and evaluation
options.why: The Criteria of Control framework includes twenty criteria for effective control in four areas of an organisation: purpose or direction, commitment or identity and values, capability or competence, and monitoring and learning or evolution, and each criterion is examined to identify the controls in place to address it. COBIT has thirty-four high-level processes that cover two hundred and ten control objectives, and those objectives fall into four domains: planning and organisation; then acquisition and implementation; then delivery and support; and finally monitoring and evaluation.
keywords: twenty criteria for effective control in four areas
two hundred and ten control objectives

options.text: CoCo — seventeen criteria in five areas; COBIT — twenty processes covering thirty-four control objectives in four domains
options.misconception: carries COSO's seventeen and five onto CoCo and inverts COBIT's two counts
options.why: Seventeen principles across five components belongs to COSO. CoCo is twenty criteria in four areas, and COBIT's thirty-four is the number of high-level processes while two hundred and ten is the number of control objectives they cover.

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas; COBIT — four high-level processes covering thirty-four control objectives in two hundred and ten activities
options.misconception: gets CoCo right and then reads COBIT's three numbers in the wrong order
options.why: The order of COBIT's numbers is the point of them: thirty-four high-level processes, two hundred and ten control objectives that those processes cover, and four domains they are categorised in.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the Criteria of Control framework of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants with twenty criteria in the four areas of purpose, commitment, capability and monitoring and learning, and COBIT with thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains

items.scenario: Two frameworks come up in the same meeting. One came from the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, meant to lift how an organisation performs and how it decides by strengthening control, risk management and governance, and it stresses that control involves the whole organisation but begins at the level of the individual employee. The other was created by ISACA for IT governance and management, and guides an organisation on how to use its applications, information, infrastructure and people.

items.stem: What do the two frameworks actually say?

options.text: The Turnbull Report is right as the adviser puts it, and section 404 requires the auditors to opine on internal control alone, the opinion on the financial statements being given separately under the auditing standards rather than as part of the same audit
options.misconception: splits the two section 404 opinions into separate engagements, when they are given as part of a single integrated audit
options.why: One integrated audit yields both opinions: an independent one on how effectively internal control over financial reporting is working, and the traditional one on the financial statements.

options.text: The Turnbull Report requires the review only from companies with no internal audit function, as the adviser says, but under section 404 the auditors do give two opinions
options.misconception: keeps the inversion of the Turnbull principle while correcting the Sarbanes-Oxley one
options.why: The two are separate principles in the guidance. Directors are to look yearly at how well internal control is working; and separately, a company holding no internal audit function is to ask itself now and then whether one is needed. The second does not qualify the first.

options.text: Turnbull puts an annual review of effectiveness on the directors — the whole group's internal control, and it reaches financial, operational and compliance controls together with risk management — and has them tell shareholders the review was done; a company holding no internal audit function is separately to ask itself, now and then, whether it needs one. Section 404 has the external auditors give two opinions inside one integrated audit: effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting, and the traditional opinion on the financial statements
options.why: Both halves of the adviser's account are inverted. Under the guidance the annual review of effectiveness belongs to the directors of every company, and it reaches every control there is — financial, operational and compliance controls alike, risk management with them. The internal audit function is a separate point: a company holding none is to ask itself, now and then, whether one is needed. And under the SEC rules and the PCAOB standard, management performs its own formal assessment and includes it in the annual report, while the external auditors give two opinions inside one integrated audit.

options.text: Both frameworks leave the review of effectiveness to management, the board's role being confined to receiving the report, and neither requires anything to be said to shareholders
options.misconception: moves the review off the board in both frameworks and drops the report to shareholders that Turnbull requires
options.why: The Turnbull principles put the review on the directors and require them to report to shareholders that they have conducted it. Under section 404 it is management that performs the formal assessment and includes it in the annual report, which is itself a report to shareholders.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the Turnbull Report's key principles, including the annual review of the effectiveness of the system of internal control covering financial, operational and compliance controls and risk management and the report to shareholders, and Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 with management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting and the two opinions given by the external auditors in a single integrated audit

items.scenario: A board is told two things by its adviser. First, that under the guidance the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales issued on the Combined Code, the directors need review the effectiveness of the system of internal control only where the company has no internal audit function, and that the review is confined to financial controls. Second, that under section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act the external auditor gives a single opinion covering the financial statements, management's assessment of internal control being enough on its own.

items.stem: What separates an internal control questionnaire from a check list?

options.text: The questionnaire is answered by the auditor and the check list by the client, the client being the one who knows whether a control was performed
options.misconception: reverses who answers each document
options.why: It is the other way round. Executives of the company, each in charge of his own area, are the ones meant to fill the questionnaire in, and the check list is a set of instructions or points for the auditor or his own staff.

options.text: Three things — the questionnaire runs to a great many detailed questions, while a check list stays at the main control objective for the area being reviewed; the questionnaire is usually answered by company executives while the check list is answered by the auditor or his staff; and a "No" in a questionnaire indicates a weakness but not its significance, whereas the check list calls for a specific statement wherever a weakness on its face might turn out to matter to the accounts taken as a whole
options.why: The two documents are built for different hands and different purposes, and the module draws the distinction in three parts. Volume and level: the questionnaire is detailed while the check list works at the level of the main control objective. Who answers: company executives in charge of the various areas fill the questionnaire, while the check list is for the auditor or his staff to follow, initial or answer. And what a negative answer carries: a "No" in a questionnaire flags a weakness without saying how much it matters, and the check list requires a specific statement wherever a weakness on its face might turn out to matter to the accounts taken as a whole.

options.text: The questionnaire evaluates the design of controls and the check list tests their operating effectiveness, so the second replaces tests of control
options.misconception: turns two recording and evaluation techniques into the audit procedures themselves
options.why: Both are techniques for evaluating and recording the system of internal control. Neither is a substitute for the tests of control through which the auditor obtains evidence about whether the controls operated effectively.

options.text: Nothing of substance — a check list in question form is a questionnaire, and the two are interchangeable so long as the same ground is covered
options.misconception: reads the similarity in form as an identity of purpose, when who answers and what a negative answer requires differ
options.why: A check list in question form does look like a questionnaire, which is why the distinction is drawn on other ground: who answers it, how detailed it is, and whether a negative answer must be followed by a specific statement about materiality.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the basic distinctions between an internal control questionnaire and a check list: the number and level of the questions, whether the company's executives or the auditor's staff answer them, and the specific statement a check list requires where an apparent weakness may prove to be material

items.scenario: An audit manager has sent the client's purchase department head a long list of detailed questions about the purchase cycle, to be answered Yes, No or Not applicable, and has separately given his own audit staff a shorter set of points to work through and initial as they test the same cycle. A trainee says the two documents are the same thing under different names.

items.stem: What is wrong with the firm's practice?

options.text: Only the questionnaire — a review conducted after the audit programme is settled is better evidence, because the team then knows what the substantive work found
options.misconception: values the review for what it confirms at the end, when its purpose is to decide the nature, timing and extent of the work in the first place
options.why: The review exists to let the auditor form an opinion on the reliance he may place on the system and to locate the areas of weakness, so that he can then settle the audit programme and fix the nature, timing and extent of his procedures. A review after the programme is settled cannot do either.

options.text: Only the timing — the questionnaire practice is sound, but the review must be completed before the audit programme is finalised in every case without exception
options.misconception: gets the timing right and makes it absolute, dropping the exception for small operations
options.why: The review is ordinarily a distinct phase before finalisation of the audit programme, and there is a stated exception: where the size of operations is rather small it may run alongside other audit procedures, the programme being adjusted afterwards.

options.text: Two things — in a continuing engagement it is good practice to issue a questionnaire irrespective of any change every third year, and a comprehensive review must be made at an interval of about three years where the auditor relies on his continuing knowledge; and the review of internal control should ordinarily be undertaken as a distinct phase before finalisation of the audit programme, the exception being where the size of operations is rather small
options.why: For the first year of an engagement a questionnaire is necessary, and for later years the auditor may ask the client to confirm whether the system has changed — but it is good practice in a continuing engagement to issue one every third year even where nothing has changed, which alerts the client to unnoticed changes and makes it more control-conscious. Separately, where the auditor leans on a continuing relationship and looks only at what changed in between, the whole system is still to be gone over afresh at an interval of about three years. And the review is ordinarily a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme, because its purpose is to shape the programme; only where the size of operations is rather small can it be undertaken in conjunction with other audit procedures.
keywords: an interval of about three years
before finalisation of the audit programme

options.text: Nothing — a questionnaire is required in the first year alone, and where the client confirms each year that nothing has changed the auditor has all the evidence about the system that he needs
options.misconception: treats the first-year questionnaire as the only one ever required, when a continuing engagement issues one every third year and comprehensively reviews the system at about that interval
options.why: The annual confirmation is the ordinary course, not the whole of it. A questionnaire every third year regardless of change, and a comprehensive review at an interval of about three years, exist precisely to catch the unnoticed and unspectacular changes a confirmation would not report.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the issue of an internal control questionnaire in the first year of an engagement and every third year in a continuing engagement, the comprehensive review of the system at an interval of about three years, and the review as a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme except where the size of operations is small

items.scenario: A firm has audited the same client for nine years. It issued an internal control questionnaire in the first year and has never issued one since, taking a written confirmation each year that the control system has not changed. It also reviews the internal controls at the end of the audit, after the audit programme has been settled, because that is when the team has most information. The client's operations are large and complex.

items.stem: What does an internal check system mean, and what does its effectiveness depend on?

options.text: It is the annual examination of the books by an independent person, and its effectiveness depends on the scope the management gives that person
options.misconception: describes internal audit, an independent appraisal function established within the organisation, rather than internal check
options.why: An independent appraisal function established within the organisation to examine and evaluate its activities, whose scope is determined by management, is internal audit. Internal check is not a separate examination at all — it is built into how the work is allocated and operates continuously as part of the routine.

options.text: It is the segregation of duties alone, and it is effective wherever two or more people are involved in a transaction, whatever their roles
options.misconception: reduces internal check to a headcount, dropping the requirement that one person's work be proved independently or made complementary to another's
options.why: Two people who each complete unrelated halves of a job prove nothing about each other's work. The system requires that the work of each person is either proved independently or made complementary to the work of another, which is a statement about how the duties relate rather than how many hands there are.

options.text: It is the arrangement of book-keeping and staff duties so that one hand alone cannot put a transaction through and record it in every one of its aspects, with the work of each person either proved independently or made complementary to another's — and its effectiveness depends on clarity of responsibility, division of work, standardisation and appraisal
options.why: Internal check is a built-in device in the organisation and job-allocation side of control: checks that sit on the day's transactions and run continuously as part of the ordinary routine. The point of arranging the work that way is caught in the phrase itself — no one person can carry through a transaction while also recording it in all its aspects — and the one man here does the opposite: he takes a transaction from invoice to bank reconciliation with no part of his work proved by anybody else. Its effectiveness rests on four things — clarity of responsibility, so that each person's responsibility is properly identified; division of work, segregated so that the flow is not interrupted and one person's work is complementary to another's, with rotation through the components of the job; standardisation of the accounting process by suitable policies; and appraisal, a periodic review of the chain of operations and workflow.
keywords: no one person can carry through a transaction

options.text: It is the set of controls the statutory auditor tests, and the proprietor is right that the statutory audit supplies the check where the company is too small to divide the work
options.misconception: treats the statutory audit as a substitute for internal check, when the scope of a statutory audit is limited by time and cost
options.why: The scope of a statutory audit is limited by both time and cost, which is why the existence of a system of internal check is increasingly recognised as essential for an audit to be effective, especially in a large organisation. The audit relies on internal check; it does not replace it.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the internal check system as an arrangement of book-keeping and staff duties under which one hand alone cannot both put a transaction through and record it, and the four considerations its effectiveness depends on: clarity of responsibility, division of work, standardisation and appraisal

items.scenario: A growing company has one accounts assistant who raises the sales invoice, posts it to the customer ledger, receives the cheque, banks it and prepares the bank reconciliation. The proprietor says this is efficient, that the man has been with him for years, and that the annual statutory audit is the check on him.

items.stem: Which of the general conditions of an internal check system are being broken?

options.text: None — a small company cannot divide duties as a large one can, and the conditions apply only where the organisation is large enough to permit an extensive division of responsibilities
options.misconception: reads an assumption behind the standard questionnaire as a limit on the conditions of internal check
options.why: That organisations permit an extensive division of duties and responsibilities is one of the basic assumptions behind a standardised internal control questionnaire, and it says that the larger the organisation the greater the scope for division. It is not a licence to drop compulsory leave, the separation of custody from the records, or a periodic review of delegated powers.

options.text: Two — the leave and the custody of the securities. The inventory count and the delegation of powers are matters of operational convenience for management rather than conditions of internal check
options.misconception: treats the count and the delegation as management's convenience, when both are named among the general conditions
options.why: Both are named. The conditions say that for inventory taking at the close of the year trading should if possible be suspended and the count done by staff belonging to several sections, and that financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously with the manner of their exercise reviewed periodically.

options.text: One — only the custody of the securities, since the other three are recommendations of good practice and carry no control significance
options.misconception: keeps the one condition with an obvious asset at the end of it and dismisses the rest
options.why: The general conditions are a single list and each entry is there for a reason. Uninterrupted leave, a custodian counting his own stores, and a delegation nobody has revisited in six years are each the kind of arrangement under which a loss goes unnoticed for years.

options.text: Four — leave is to be encouraged for every member of the staff, at least once in each year; whoever holds assets in physical custody is kept away from the books of account recording them; the year-end inventory count is taken with trading suspended where that can be managed, and by staff drawn from several sections; and financial and administrative powers are spread judiciously among different officers, with the way they are exercised looked at again periodically
options.why: Each of the three arrangements breaks a stated condition, and the inventory count breaks two. Compulsory leave exists so that a concealment which needs daily attention comes apart while its author is away. Custody of assets and access to the records of those assets are separated so that the man who can take a thing cannot also adjust the record of it. The count is done with trading suspended if possible and by staff from several sections rather than by the custodian himself. And delegated financial and administrative powers are reviewed periodically rather than settled once.
keywords: Custody of assets and access to the records

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the general conditions of an internal check system, including that complete control over any important part of the business rests with no single individual, that staff duties should be rotated, that every member of staff should be encouraged to take leave at least once a year, that persons having physical custody of assets must not have access to the books of account, that trading should if possible be suspended for the year-end inventory count which is done by staff of several sections, and that financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously and their exercise reviewed periodically

items.scenario: A company is writing down its internal check arrangements. Its cashier has taken no leave in four years and keeps the securities in the safe as well as the register recording them. The annual inventory count is done by the storekeeper who has custody of the stores, with trading continuing through the count so that despatches are not delayed. Financial powers were delegated to the branch heads six years ago and have not been looked at since.

items.stem: What is compliance audit concerned with?

options.text: Regularity alone — propriety belongs to propriety audit, which is a separate exercise the C&AG conducts under its own name
options.misconception: puts propriety wholly outside compliance auditing, when compliance auditing is concerned with it as one of its two limbs
options.why: Propriety audit is indeed a named exercise of its own, and that does not take propriety out of compliance auditing. Compliance auditing is concerned with regularity and with propriety, and the public sector context is why the second is equally pertinent.

options.text: Regularity and propriety both — regularity asking whether the subject matter holds to the formal criteria that laws, regulations and agreements throw up, and propriety asking whether the general principles of sound financial management, and the ethics expected of public officials, were observed; regularity is emphasised, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector
options.why: Compliance auditing has two concerns and the team leader has stopped at the first. Regularity asks whether the entity held to the formal criteria its laws, regulations and agreements throw up, and every purchase here satisfies it. Propriety asks after the general principles of sound financial management, and after how public officials are expected to conduct themselves; regularity carries the emphasis, while propriety stays equally pertinent, the public sector being a place where certain things are expected both of financial management and of the people running it. Equipment lying unused for two years is what a propriety concern looks like.

options.text: The economy, efficiency and effectiveness of the department's purchasing, which is what makes a stored asset reportable
options.misconception: reaches the right finding through performance audit's three questions, when the finding here comes from compliance auditing's own propriety limb
options.why: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness are the issues a performance audit addresses. A compliance audit reaches this finding through its own propriety limb — and when compliance auditing is conducted in combination with performance auditing, compliance is seen as one of the aspects of those three rather than the other way round.

options.text: Whether the financial statements of the department are free from material misstatement, which is what "in all material respects" means in the definition
options.misconception: reads compliance auditing as a financial audit because its definition uses the words in all material respects
options.why: The words describe the threshold, not the subject matter. What a compliance audit weighs is activities, financial transactions and information, and whether in all material respects they sit within the rules the entity is governed by; an opinion on financial statements is what financial audit is for.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance audit as an independent judgement on whether some subject matter squares with the criteria that apply to it, and its concern with regularity and with propriety, propriety being equally pertinent in the public sector context

items.scenario: A team is closing a compliance audit of a State department's purchase of medical equipment. Every purchase was made under a sanction issued by the competent authority, within the delegated financial powers, following the tender procedure the rules lay down. The team has also found that equipment worth several crores was bought two years before the building meant to house it was begun, and has been in storage since. The team leader says that since nothing broke a rule, the compliance audit has nothing to report.

items.stem: How is compliance auditing conducted?

options.text: Only as an individual compliance audit, since combining it with another type of audit would confuse two different sets of criteria and two different conclusions
options.misconception: makes the stand-alone compliance audit the only permitted form, when it is one of three
options.why: A separate individual compliance audit is one of the three ways, not the only one. The others are in relation with the audit of financial statements and in combination with performance auditing, and the criteria of each are stated for what they are.

options.text: Only alongside the audit of financial statements, compliance being a question about transactions and therefore inseparable from the accounts in which they are recorded
options.misconception: ties compliance auditing to the accounts, when its subject matter is activities and information as well as financial transactions
options.why: Compliance auditing assesses whether activities, financial transactions and information comply with the rules governing the entity, so much of its subject matter never reaches the accounts at all. It may be conducted separately or in combination with performance auditing.

options.text: In any of the three ways, but where it forms part of a performance audit the non-compliance is reported only if it caused the failure, a non-compliance that merely accompanies poor performance being outside the scope
options.misconception: narrows the relationship to causation, when a non-compliance may equally explain the state of the activities, or follow from it
options.why: The relationship is stated three ways round: a non-compliance may be the cause, or the explanation, or the consequence — whatever state the activities are in can sit in any of the three places. Requiring it to be the cause drops two of the three.

options.text: In one of three ways — in relation with the audit of financial statements, or separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing; and where it forms part of a performance audit, compliance ranks as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, a non-compliance standing as the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of whatever state the activities examined are in
options.why: Compliance auditing can sit inside a combined audit that carries other aspects too, and the three ways it is generally conducted are exactly those. Nothing has to be carved out here: inside a performance audit, compliance ranks as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness. A non-compliance can stand as the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of whatever state the activities under examination are in — which is precisely the relationship between works awarded without tender and works that failed.
keywords: one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness
the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance auditing conducted in relation with the audit of financial statements, separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing, where compliance ranks as one aspect among economy, efficiency and effectiveness

items.scenario: A performance audit of a State scheme for rural water supply finds that a third of the works were awarded without the tender process the scheme's own guidelines require, and that those works are the ones that have failed to deliver. The team is unsure whether the tendering failure belongs in the performance audit report at all, or must be carved out into a separate compliance audit, and whether a compliance audit can be run alongside a financial audit in the same engagement.

items.stem: What are the parts of the report?

options.text: Two — the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals and the introduction, the remaining material going to the Public Accounts Committee separately rather than into the report
options.misconception: routes two parts of the report to a committee, when the committees receive the report itself
options.why: The audit reports and annual accounts stand referred to the specialised committees; the committees are the readers rather than a separate destination for parts of the report. All four parts are in the report presented to Parliament.

options.text: Four — an introduction reviewing in general terms how Government companies, deemed Government companies and corporations have worked; what came of the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings; a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the C&AG's directions together with his comments on the accounts; and whatever significant audit results arose in the undertakings the Audit Board did not take up for appraisal
options.why: Both partners have one part each and are missing the other three. The report is presented to Parliament in several parts: a general review of working results, the results of the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings, a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the directions issued by the C&AG together with his comments on the accounts of the Government companies, and the significant results of audit of those undertakings not taken up for appraisal. The last of those is what answers the second partner: an undertaking the Audit Board did not appraise is still reported on.

options.text: One — the resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the C&AG's directions, the C&AG having no audit of his own to report on a Government company whose statutory audit is conducted by a firm
options.misconception: reduces the report to the compilation the first partner expects, when the C&AG conducts supplementary audit, test audit and comprehensive appraisals of his own
options.why: The resume of the company auditors' reports is one part of four, and it travels with the C&AG's own comments on the accounts. The other three parts are his own work: the general review, the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals, and the results of audit of the undertakings not appraised.

options.text: Four parts, but the significant results of audit of the undertakings not appraised by the Audit Board are given only where a statutory auditor has qualified his report on that undertaking
options.misconception: makes the fourth part conditional on a qualification, when it carries the significant results of audit of those undertakings whatever the statutory auditor said
options.why: The fourth part carries whatever significant audit results arose in the undertakings the Audit Board never took up for appraisal, and nothing conditions it on what the company's own auditor reported.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the parts of the C&AG's report on the audit of public sector undertakings presented to Parliament: the introduction with a general review of working results, the results of comprehensive appraisals conducted by the Audit Board, the resume of the company auditors' reports under the C&AG's directions with his comments, and the significant results of audit of undertakings not taken up for appraisal

items.scenario: A firm is reading the Comptroller and Auditor General's report on public sector undertakings for the first time and is trying to work out what it will contain. One partner expects it to be a compilation of the audit reports signed by the companies' own statutory auditors and nothing else. Another expects it to carry only the undertakings the Audit Board has appraised in depth, on the view that anything less than a full appraisal would not be worth reporting to Parliament.

items.stem: What is the position of the Audit Board?

options.text: The Audit Board's conclusions are final when signed, the enterprise's view being taken only after the report is laid before Parliament, when the committees call for it
options.misconception: postpones the enterprise's view to the committee stage, when the Board ascertains it before finalisation
options.why: The Board talks its findings and conclusions over with the enterprises' managements, and with the ministries and departments that control them, learning their view points before finalisation. What happens afterwards before the committees is a further stage, not the first hearing.

options.text: The Audit Board must confine itself to financial and accounting matters, technical questions being outside the Indian Audit and Accounts Department's competence and reserved to the enterprise's own management
options.misconception: accepts the objection about technical competence, when the Boards associate experts in the relevant disciplines with themselves for that purpose
options.why: That is exactly the problem the arrangement solves: the Audit Boards associate with themselves experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisals, which is what lets a comprehensive appraisal reach capacity utilisation, project formulation and the management of plant and machinery.

options.text: They have no separate legal entity, and they work under the C&AG's supervision and control, his reports carrying their appraisals; they associate with themselves experts in the disciplines the appraisal calls for; and before anything is finalised they talk their findings and conclusions over with the enterprises' managements, and with the ministries and departments that control them, to learn what those bodies think
options.why: The managing director is right about one thing and wrong about the consequences of it. The Audit Boards have no separate legal entity, which is why the Comptroller and Auditor General supervises and controls them, and why the results of their appraisals are incorporated in his reports rather than issued in their own name. His other two points are already met by how the Board works: it associates with itself experts in the disciplines the appraisals call for, and it talks its findings and conclusions over with the managements and with the controlling ministries and departments, learning their view points before finalisation.

options.text: The Audit Board is a statutory body constituted under the Act of 1971 that governs the C&AG's duties, powers and conditions of service, with a legal entity of its own, which is what gives its appraisals their standing
options.misconception: gives the Audit Board a legal personality it does not have
options.why: The Audit Boards have no separate legal entity. Their standing comes from the C&AG, under whose supervision and control they work and in whose reports their appraisals appear.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Audit Boards constituted for comprehensive audit appraisals, which associate experts in the relevant disciplines, discuss their findings with the managements and controlling ministries before finalisation, hold no separate legal entity of their own, and answer to the Comptroller and Auditor General for supervision and control

items.scenario: An Audit Board is appraising the working of a public sector fertiliser enterprise. Its draft findings are severe. The enterprise's managing director asks on what authority the Board acts, and says that a body constituted inside the audit department has no standing to appraise a company incorporated under the Companies Act, that its conclusions cannot be published without the enterprise being heard first, and that the technical judgements in the draft are beyond the competence of accountants.

items.stem: How did the requirement actually widen, and where does it stand now?

options.text: The top 100 in 2012 and the top 500 in 2015, which is where it still stands; the top 1,000 figure belongs to the Integrated Reporting recommendation, which is voluntary
options.misconception: stops the widening at the top 500 and attaches the top 1,000 to Integrated Reporting
options.why: The Integrated Reporting circular of 2017 advised the top 500 listed companies to adopt it on a voluntary basis from the financial year 2017-18. The top 1,000 is the reach of the business responsibility reporting requirement itself from December 2019, and it is not voluntary.

options.text: The top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation in 2012, the top 500 when the Business Responsibility Report became part of the Listing Regulations in 2015, and the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation with effect from 26 December 2019 — and reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23, disclosure having been voluntary in 2021-22
options.why: The requirement widened by rank three times and then changed form. In 2012 SEBI required the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation to file a Business Responsibility Report. In 2015 the BRR became part of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations and the top 500 listed companies by market capitalisation were required to file it. In 2019, by the fifth amendment and with effect from 26 December 2019, that annual-report obligation reached the thousand largest listed entities measured by market capitalisation. In 2021 SEBI introduced the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, and reporting under it is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23, disclosure having been voluntary in the financial year 2021-22. A company ranked about 800th is inside the top 1,000.

options.text: The top 1,000 listed entities, and reporting under BRSR has been mandatory since the financial year 2021-22, the year SEBI notified the new format
options.misconception: makes the year of notification the first mandatory year, when 2021-22 was the voluntary year
options.why: SEBI introduced the format in 2021 and the first mandatory year is 2022-23. Disclosure was voluntary in 2021-22, which is why a company that filed nothing for that year was not in default.

options.text: The top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, but reporting under BRSR is voluntary throughout, the format having been introduced in 2021 as a recommendation
options.misconception: gets the rank right and leaves the requirement voluntary, when it is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23
options.why: Reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23. The voluntary year was 2021-22, which is the only year in which disclosure was left to the company.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the widening of business responsibility reporting from the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation in 2012 to the top 500 in 2015 and the top 1,000 listed entities with effect from 26 December 2019, and the introduction of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report in 2021, mandatory from the financial year 2022-23 after a voluntary year in 2021-22

items.scenario: A listed company ranked about 800th by market capitalisation has never filed any sustainability report. Its company secretary tells the audit team that the reporting requirement has always been confined to the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation as SEBI first framed it in 2012, that nothing has changed since, and that in any event the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report is a voluntary format.

items.stem: How is the reporting questionnaire divided?

options.text: Three sections, but the essential indicators go in Section B and the leadership indicators in Section C, the first being about process and the second about performance
options.misconception: splits the essential and leadership indicators across two sections, when both classifications sit inside Section C
options.why: Section C classifies the key performance indicators into essential indicators, which are mandatory, and leadership indicators, which are voluntary. Both classes are principle-wise performance disclosures and both live in the same section.

options.text: Three sections — Section A, General Disclosures, with the details of the listed company, its products, services and operations, employee related details and its holding, subsidiary and associate companies; Section B, Management Process and disclosures, with the questions on policy and management processes, governance, leadership and oversight; and Section C, Principle-wise performance disclosures, where the key performance indicators are reported in alignment with the nine principles
options.why: The three sections are distinct and the company has run two of them together. Section A is general disclosures about the entity itself. Section B is management process and disclosures, holding the questions on policy and management processes, governance, leadership and oversight. Section C is principle-wise performance disclosures, and it is the only place the key performance indicators aligned to the nine principles belong. The division is what makes the report comparable across companies, sectors and years, which is the point of a standardised format.

options.text: Two sections — general disclosures and principle-wise performance disclosures — the management processes being reported inside the first as part of the description of the entity
options.misconception: folds Section B into Section A, when management process and disclosures is a section of its own
options.why: Management process and disclosures is Section B in its own right, holding the questions on policy and management processes, governance, leadership and oversight. What the entity is and how it is governed are answered in different sections.

options.text: Nine sections, one for each principle of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, with the general information about the entity distributed among them
options.misconception: turns the nine principles into the structure of the report, when they structure the disclosures within one section
options.why: The nine principles organise the key performance indicators within Section C. The report itself has three sections, and the details of the entity sit in Section A rather than being spread across the principles.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the three sections of the BRSR reporting questionnaire: Section A general disclosures, Section B management process and disclosures, and Section C principle-wise performance disclosures with key performance indicators aligned to the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct

items.scenario: A team is reviewing a company's first Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. The details of the listed entity, its products and services, its operations, its employee-related details and its holding, subsidiary and associate companies have been put in the same part of the report as the description of its policies, its governance and its board's oversight, and the key performance indicators reported against the nine principles have been split across both.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The requirement reaches the top 1,000 listed entities based on market capitalisation, so this company is outside it and using the format voluntarily does not bring it inside; and the BRSR is intended to have quantitative and standardised disclosures on ESG parameters so that companies, sectors and periods can be compared, which a narrative of the company's own cannot do
options.why: The obligation attaches by rank: it is the top 1,000 listed entities, ranked by market capitalisation, whose annual report must carry one, and a company outside that rank is not brought inside it by choosing to use the format. The reason for the format is comparability — quantitative and standardised disclosures on ESG parameters are what let companies, sectors and periods be set side by side — and the BRSR is expected to become the single means of disclosing sustainability related information in India, which is what a narrative in each company's own words prevents.

options.text: The company is inside the requirement, since BRSR reporting has been extended to all listed companies from the financial year 2022-23
options.misconception: reads the first mandatory year as an extension to every listed company, when the rank the requirement reaches was unchanged
options.why: The financial year 2022-23 is when reporting under BRSR became mandatory for those already within the requirement. SEBI has started with the top 1,000 listed companies, and the remaining listed companies are expected to follow rather than being inside it already.

options.text: The company is outside the requirement, and the reason for the format is to reduce the reporting burden by replacing several existing filings with one shorter document
options.misconception: explains a standardised quantitative format as a reduction of burden, when its stated purpose is comparability
options.why: The stated purpose is comparability across companies, sectors and time through quantitative and standardised disclosures. That it is expected to become the single means of disclosing sustainability information in India follows from that, and it is not a promise of a shorter document.

options.text: Any listed company that adopts the BRSR format becomes subject to the requirement in full from the year it first uses it, since the format and the obligation are the same thing
options.misconception: makes voluntary adoption of a format the trigger for a requirement that attaches by market capitalisation rank
options.why: What triggers the requirement is the entity's place among the top 1,000 listed entities based on market capitalisation. A format is a way of presenting disclosures, and using one does not change the rank the requirement is measured on.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the reach of the business responsibility and sustainability reporting requirement to the top 1,000 listed entities based on market capitalisation, and the purpose of the BRSR: quantitative and standardised disclosures on ESG parameters, so that companies, sectors and periods can be set side by side

items.scenario: A company ranked outside the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation wants to publish sustainability disclosures voluntarily and asks whether it may use the BRSR format, and whether doing so brings it inside SEBI's requirement. Its chairman also asks why SEBI moved from a narrative business responsibility report to this format at all, when the company already publishes a long sustainability narrative of its own.

items.stem: Which capitals do the three belong to?

options.text: Intellectual capital, social capital and financial capital respectively, the plant and the roads being capital expenditure funded from the pool of funds available to the organisation
options.misconception: classifies an asset by how it was paid for, when financial capital is the pool of funds itself
options.why: Financial capital is the pool of funds available to the organisation for producing goods or providing services, obtained through debt, equity or grants or generated by its own operations and investments. What the funds are spent on is a different capital, and infrastructure of this kind is manufactured capital.

options.text: Human capital, social capital and natural capital respectively
options.misconception: reads research and patents as the people who made them, and a water treatment plant as natural capital because its subject is water
options.why: Human capital is people's skills and experience, their capacity and motivation to innovate. The patents themselves are intellectual capital. And natural capital is an input to production which the organisation's activities also affect — water, land, minerals, forests, biodiversity — while a treatment plant built to handle it is infrastructure and so manufactured capital.

options.text: Intellectual capital, human capital and manufactured capital respectively
options.misconception: places a community programme under human capital, when human capital is about the organisation's own people
options.why: Human capital is the organisation's people — their skills, their capacity and motivation to innovate, their alignment with its governance framework and ethical values. Relationships with the communities around a plant, and the licence to operate they confer, are social capital.

options.text: Intellectual capital, social capital and manufactured capital respectively
options.why: Intellectual capital is the key element in an organisation's future earning potential, tied to investment in research and development, innovation, human resources and external relationships, and it is what determines competitive advantage — which is where a laboratory and four patents the competitors lack belong. Social capital is the institutions and relationships established within and between communities, stakeholder groups and networks, including common values, the trust and loyalty built with others, and the organisation's social licence to operate — which is the livelihood programme and the trust it has produced. Manufactured capital is the human-created, production-oriented equipment and tools available to the organisation, including buildings, equipment and infrastructure such as roads and water treatment plants.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the six capitals of Integrated Reporting: intellectual capital as the key element in future earning potential tied to research and development and innovation, social capital as the institutions and relationships within and between communities and stakeholder groups including the social licence to operate, and manufactured capital as the human-created production-oriented equipment and infrastructure including roads and water treatment plants

items.scenario: A company preparing an integrated report has three achievements it wants to place among the six capitals. It has built a research laboratory and registered four process patents that its competitors do not hold. It has taken its flagship livelihood programme from a few hundred families to several thousand, and reports that the trust this has built with the communities around its plants is what lets it operate there. And it has commissioned a water treatment plant and an internal road network at the same site.

items.stem: Which is a digital audit and which is auditing digitally?

options.text: The first is auditing digitally, because the auditor is working on digital systems; the second is a digital audit, because the audit itself has been digitised
options.misconception: swaps the two names, reading auditing digitally as auditing digital things
options.why: The phrase describes how the audit is conducted, not what it is conducted on. Auditing digitally is using technology to conduct an audit effectively and efficiently, which is the second engagement; the first, where assurance is placed on the effectiveness of the IT systems themselves, is the digital audit.

options.text: The first is a digital audit — placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems an organisation has implemented; the second is auditing digitally — using advancements in technology to conduct an audit that is effective and efficient
options.why: What separates them is where the technology sits. A digital audit sits on one side: placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems an organisation has implemented, so the systems are the subject matter and the output is assurance about them. Auditing digitally means using advancements in technology to conduct an audit that is effective and efficient, so the technology is the tool and the subject matter is whatever the audit was about anyway — a sampling tool selecting items by materiality, or a bot analysing statutory payment compliance, in an ordinary audit of financial statements.
keywords: placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems

options.text: Both are digital audits — any engagement in which technology is central is a digital audit, and the distinction is one of degree
options.misconception: makes the presence of technology the test, when the test is whether the IT systems are the subject matter or the tool
options.why: Technology is present in both and that is why it cannot be the test. In one the IT systems are what is being assured; in the other they are what the auditor uses to do work he would otherwise do by hand.

options.text: Neither — a digital audit is only an audit conducted entirely without the auditor attending the client's premises, which is what the second engagement will be
options.misconception: confuses a digital audit with a remote audit, which is about where the auditor is rather than what he assures
options.why: An audit conducted through online or electronic means, wholly or partly, is a remote or virtual audit, and that is a question about location. A digital audit is defined by its subject matter: assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems implemented in the organisation.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — a digital audit as placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems an organisation has implemented, and auditing digitally as using advancements in technology to conduct an audit that is effective and efficient

items.scenario: A firm takes on two engagements in the same month. In the first it is asked to review a manufacturer's technology-related controls, to identify gaps and risks in the IT systems the company has implemented and to say whether those systems are effective. In the second it is auditing a distributor's financial statements as it does every year, and this time it will use a sampling tool to select items from the sales population by reference to materiality and a bot to analyse compliance with statutory payments. The trainee's file calls both of them digital audits.

items.stem: Which considerations does this plan ignore?

options.text: Ensure the process works and is standardised before automating it, because bots do not easily adapt to process change; think people first and do not underestimate how difficult change is; treat automation as part of a broader digitalisation strategy rather than a stand-alone solution; and do not forget governance and data security in the risk framework
options.why: Each of those is one of the stated considerations and each is being broken here. Automating a process that differs across four plants and is being redesigned at two of them fails the instruction to ensure the process works and is standardised before automating, because bots do not easily adapt to process change. Telling nobody why fails the instruction to think people first and not underestimate that change is difficult. Sitting outside the technology roadmap fails the instruction that automation should be part of a broader digitalisation strategy and is not a stand-alone solution. And keeping it out of the risk framework is the one the module states as a warning in its own right: do not forget governance and data security.

options.text: None — the considerations are about choosing which processes to automate, and the board has chosen a repetitive high-volume cycle, which is the right target
options.misconception: reads the whole list as the single instruction to target the right processes
options.why: Targeting the right processes is one consideration among several, and choosing well does not answer the others: whether the process is stable and standardised, whether the people affected have been brought along, whether the work sits inside a wider strategy, and whether governance and data security are in the risk framework.

options.text: Only the standardisation point — the rest are matters of change management for the company rather than considerations an auditor is concerned with
options.misconception: separates change management from the considerations, when thinking people first is one of them
options.why: Thinking people first and not underestimating how difficult change is appears in the same list as the standardisation point, and for the same reason: an automation that the organisation has not absorbed does not produce the control it was built for.

options.text: Only the risk framework point — a robot that repeats an existing manual step introduces no new risk, so the other considerations do not arise
options.misconception: accepts the board's premise that automating a step changes nothing about it
options.why: The premise is what the considerations exist to correct. Automation introduces new challenges for the organisation, changes how transactions are initiated and processed, and requires the process to be standardised first, because a bot does not adapt to a process that is still moving.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the considerations and challenges of a digital audit: knowing the business benefits sought, thinking people first, targeting the right processes, ensuring the process works and is standardised before automating because bots do not easily adapt to process change, treating automation as part of a broader digitalisation strategy rather than a stand-alone solution, and keeping governance and data security in the risk framework

items.scenario: A company's board has approved a plan to automate its purchase-to-pay cycle with software robots inside three months. The process differs between the four plants and is being redesigned at two of them while the robots are built. Nobody has been told why the change is happening. The automation project sits outside the company's technology roadmap and outside its risk framework, on the view that a robot only repeats what a person was already doing.

items.stem: Which types of IT dependency are these?

options.text: An automated control, a calculation, an interface and a report — four of the five types, the fifth being security, which is segregation of duties and access restriction enabled by the IT environment
options.why: The five types of IT dependency are automated controls, reports, calculations, security and interfaces, and four of them are on this list. A refusal to accept a purchase order without a second approval is an automated control, designed into the IT environment to enforce a business rule. Depreciation computed by the system instead of a person is a calculation. Programmed logic transferring data from one IT system to another is an interface. And a system generated ageing listing used to select items for testing is a report. Security, the fifth, is the restriction of access to information and the separation of roles and responsibilities enabled by the IT environment.
keywords: automated controls, reports, calculations, security and interfaces

options.text: Only the automated control and the interface are IT dependencies. A calculation and a report are outputs of the system rather than dependencies, since the auditor can recompute or reperform them
options.misconception: excludes two of the five types on the ground that the auditor could check them by hand
options.why: Whether the auditor could recompute something does not decide whether the entity depends on IT to produce it. A dependency arises the moment the entity leans on IT anywhere along the life of a transaction — starting it off, approving it, writing it down, working it through, or reporting it and the rest of the financial data with it. Calculations and reports are two of the five named types.

options.text: All four are automated controls, since in each case the system rather than a person is doing the work
options.misconception: collapses the five types into one because a machine performs all of them
options.why: That a machine performs them is what makes them dependencies at all; it is not what distinguishes them. An automated control enforces a business rule, a calculation performs an accounting procedure, an interface transfers data between systems, and a report produces information — and each raises a different question for the audit.

options.text: An automated control, a calculation, an interface and a general IT control — a system generated report being part of the data centre and network operations controls
options.misconception: files a system generated report among the general IT controls, when reports are one of the five dependencies and general IT controls are management's response to them
options.why: Reports are one of the five types of IT dependency. General IT controls are the controls management implements to address the risks arising from those dependencies, grouped into access security, program change, and data centre and network operations; they are the response, not the dependency.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the five types of IT dependency: automated controls designed into the IT environment to enforce business rules, system generated reports, calculations performed by an IT system instead of a person, security including segregation of duties, and interfaces being programmed logic that transfers data from one IT system to another

items.scenario: Documenting a client's IT environment, an audit team lists four things. The system refuses a purchase order above a stated value unless a second approval is recorded. The system computes depreciation on every asset by applying the straight-line formula to its cost, residual value and useful life. Payroll data moves from the payroll sub-ledger into the general ledger through programmed logic each month. And the customer ageing listing the team will use to select debtors for confirmation is produced by the system.

items.stem: What are the three areas of general IT controls and their objectives, and what is the consequence?

options.text: The three areas are the same, but the objectives are operational rather than financial — general IT controls exist to keep the systems available, and their failure is a matter for management rather than for the audit
options.misconception: reads general IT controls as an availability concern, when each of the three objectives is expressed by reference to financial reporting objectives
options.why: Each of the three objectives is written by reference to meeting financial reporting objectives, which is exactly why the auditor scopes these controls into his testing where IT dependencies are identified.

options.text: Access security, program change and data centre and network operations — and where the controls are not operating effectively the auditor reports a material weakness to those charged with governance and continues to rely on the reports and calculations, having tested the underlying data
options.misconception: treats communication of the weakness as the whole response, when ineffective general IT controls leave the IT dependencies unrelied upon
options.why: Communicating the deficiency is a separate obligation and does not restore reliance. If the controls around the IT environment are not implemented or operating effectively, the general IT controls cannot be relied upon, and that reaches the IT dependencies which rest on them.

options.text: Access security, to ensure that access to programs and data is authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives; program change, to ensure that modified systems continue to meet financial reporting objectives; and data centre and network operations, to ensure that production systems are appropriately backed up to meet financial reporting objectives — and if the controls are not implemented or not operating effectively, the general IT controls cannot be relied on, which means the IT dependencies cannot be relied on either
options.why: The three groups map onto the three areas exactly. Removing a terminated user's access on a timely basis belongs to access security, whose objective is to ensure that access to programs and data is authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives. Segregated environments and changes tested and approved before migration belong to program change, whose objective is to ensure that modified systems continue to meet financial reporting objectives. Backups, restoration testing and batch job monitoring belong to data centre and network operations, whose objective is to ensure that production systems are appropriately backed up to meet financial reporting objectives. And the consequence is the reason for testing them at all: where the controls around the IT environment are not implemented or are not operating effectively, the general IT controls cannot be relied upon, and the IT dependencies they support cannot be relied upon either.

options.text: Access security, program change and data integrity — the third objective being to ensure that data is complete and accurate when it is entered, which is what backups and batch monitoring achieve
options.misconception: renames the third area after what it hopes for rather than what its controls do
options.why: The third area is data centre and network operations and its objective is to ensure that production systems are appropriately backed up to meet financial reporting objectives. Backups, restoration testing and batch job monitoring are about the operation and recoverability of the production environment rather than about validating data on entry.

citation.ref: Ch.
