Digital Auditing and Assurance — the three areas of general IT controls and their control objectives, being access security, program change, and data centre and network operations, and the consequence that where the controls around the IT environment are not implemented or not operating effectively the general IT controls and the IT dependencies resting on them cannot be relied upon

items.scenario: An audit team has identified several IT dependencies at a client and is scoping the general IT controls it will test. The controls it has listed are that a terminated employee's access is removed on a timely basis; that development, testing and production environments are kept separate and that changes are tested and approved before being migrated into production; and that data is backed up, that restoration testing is performed and that batch job schedules are monitored for failures. The manager asks which control objective each of the three groups is meant to meet, and what follows if the client's controls turn out not to be operating effectively.

items.stem: What are the risks arising from the use of IT?

options.text: Only risks that have already produced a misstatement in the financial statements, since a risk that has not affected the accounts is a matter for management
options.misconception: waits for a risk to become a misstatement before treating it as an audit matter
options.why: The auditor identifies the risks arising from the use of IT in order to decide which general IT controls to test and how far the IT dependencies can be relied on. A risk identified only after it has produced a misstatement has not been identified in time to do either.

options.text: Unauthorised access to data and unauthorised changes to applications — the two risks that involve somebody acting deliberately; the rest are operational failures rather than risks arising from the use of IT
options.misconception: confines the risks to deliberate acts, when failure to update, inappropriate manual intervention, downtime and compatibility are named risks too
options.why: Several of the named risks involve nobody acting deliberately at all: failure to make a necessary update, data loss or corruption, system downtime from hardware failure or power outage, and system integration and compatibility problems.

options.text: A list wider than unauthorised outside access — unauthorised access to data resulting in destruction or improper changes including the recording of unauthorised or non-existent transactions; IT personnel gaining access privileges beyond those necessary for their duties, breaking down segregation of duties; unauthorised changes to IT applications or to data in master files; failure to make necessary updates; inappropriate manual intervention; data loss or corruption; system downtime; and system integration and compatibility risks
options.why: Three of the four facts on the file are named risks in their own right. An IT administrator with rights beyond his duties is that named risk exactly — IT personnel who gain access privileges beyond those necessary for the duties assigned to them, so that segregation of duties breaks down. A deferred update is the failure to make necessary updates to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment. And two systems on different versions of the same software, with a patch never applied, is a compatibility risk, which arises where different versions are used or patches are not upgraded and which can produce bugs; where systems are integrated, a failure in one may also lead to widespread failure across the others.

options.text: The risks arising from the use of IT are the same as the risks a cyber attack presents, so the list is the list of attack types — malware, phishing, spoofing and the rest
options.misconception: substitutes the taxonomy of cyber attacks for the risks arising from the use of IT
options.why: Cyber risk is one source of risk and it has its own treatment. The risks arising from the use of IT are the wider list, and most of them — privileges beyond need, a missed update, an incompatible version, inappropriate manual intervention — involve no attacker at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the risks arising from the use of IT, including unauthorised access to data, IT personnel gaining access privileges beyond those necessary and breaking down segregation of duties, unauthorised changes to applications and to master file data, failure to make necessary updates, inappropriate manual intervention, data loss or corruption, system downtime, and system integration and compatibility risks

items.scenario: A client runs four separate IT systems that pass data between them, and two of them are on different versions of the same software because a patch was never applied to one. An IT administrator has rights well beyond what his duties need. A planned update to one application was deferred for a year. The finance controller says none of this is an audit matter, because the risks arising from the use of IT are limited to unauthorised access from outside the organisation.

items.stem: What do the considerations for a remote audit require?

options.text: The platform, timelines, data exchange mechanisms and access authorisations are agreed as part of planning; audit evidence is transferred through a document sharing platform whose access is sufficiently restricted and secured by encrypting the data sent across the network; the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees, and any screenshot of a document or record used as evidence should be previously authorised by the audited organisation; and access to the auditee's IT system should be through a virtual private network
options.why: Every one of the four proposals fails a stated requirement. Feasibility and planning include agreeing the audit timelines, the meeting platform to be used, the data exchange mechanisms and any access authorisation requests, which is not something left to each auditee's preference. Documentation for audit evidence is transferred through a document sharing platform, access to which is sufficiently restricted and secured by encrypting the data sent across the network, rather than by email attachments to individuals. Auditors should not take screenshots of auditees, and any screenshot of a document or record used as evidence should be previously authorised by the audited organisation. And where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system he should use a virtual private network, which creates a safe and encrypted online connection.

options.text: Nothing more than a documented assessment that a remote audit will be sufficient to achieve the audit objectives; once that assessment is made the mechanics are left to the team
options.misconception: keeps the risk assessment head and drops the two others, feasibility and planning and confidentiality, security and data protection
options.why: The assessment that a remote audit would be sufficient to achieve the audit objectives is one of three heads and it is made and documented for each audit involving the whole team and the audited organisation's representative. Feasibility and planning and confidentiality, security and data protection are the other two, and the mechanics are exactly what they govern.

options.text: That the audit be conducted onsite wherever the client's IT systems hold sensitive data, a remote audit being permissible only for documentation review
options.misconception: makes sensitive data a bar to remote auditing, when the module treats it as something the security and data protection requirements address
options.why: Remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed, and that is listed as one of the disadvantages to be assessed rather than as a rule confining remote audits to documentation review. Where access is given, it is secured — restricted platforms, encryption and a virtual private network.

options.text: Only the platform and the screenshots — how documents reach the team and how the auditor connects are matters of convenience once the client has agreed to give access
options.misconception: treats the transfer of evidence and the connection to the client's systems as convenience, when both are confidentiality, security and data protection requirements
options.why: Both sit under confidentiality, security and data protection. Access to the document sharing platform is sufficiently restricted and the data encrypted across the network, and access to the auditee's IT system is through a virtual private network so that unauthorised users cannot enter it.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the considerations for a remote audit under feasibility and planning, confidentiality, security and data protection, and risk assessment, including the document sharing platform with restricted access and encrypted data, the bar on taking screenshots of auditees and the prior authorisation of screenshots used as evidence, and the use of a virtual private network to access the auditee's IT system

items.scenario: A firm is planning to conduct most of a group audit remotely. The team proposes to run its interviews over whatever meeting platform each auditee prefers, to have documents emailed as attachments to whichever team member asks for them, to take screenshots of the auditees during the video sessions to evidence who was present, and to connect to the client's accounting system over the auditee's ordinary internet connection when direct access is granted.

items.stem: What has the manager left out?

options.text: That first-hand evidence cannot be obtained remotely, so everything gathered in a remote audit is second-hand and needs corroboration onsite
options.misconception: denies the very advantage the module names, that direct access lets the auditor take evidence straight from the IT system
options.why: One of the stated advantages is the opposite: the auditor can get first-hand evidence directly from the IT system where direct access is provided. What cannot be done remotely is physical verification of assets and stock taking.

options.text: That a remote audit widens the chance of doctored documents being put forward and of relevant information being left out, which may call for planning beyond the ordinary and for additional or different audit procedures; and that physical verification of assets and stock taking is not something that can be done remotely, quite apart from the loss of any ability to see the facility, the culture of the organisation and the body language of the auditees
options.why: The advantages the manager lists are real and they are stated alongside the disadvantages. The one with a consequence attached is that a remote audit widens the chance of doctored documents being put forward and of relevant information being left out, which may call for planning beyond the ordinary and for additional or different audit procedures — so keeping last year's programme unchanged is the precise thing a remote audit does not allow. And there are procedures a remote audit simply cannot reach: physical verification of assets and stock taking among them, which for an inventory-heavy manufacturer decides how much of the audit can be conducted this way.
keywords: physical verification of assets and stock taking

options.text: Nothing of substance — the disadvantages are about the auditor's comfort and about network quality, and neither affects the sufficiency of the evidence
options.misconception: reads the disadvantages as inconveniences, when two of them go directly to the evidence
options.why: Two go straight to the evidence: the increased opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information, and the impossibility of physical verification of assets and stock taking. Interrupted meetings and time zones are the inconveniences; these are not.

options.text: That a remote audit needs the client's written consent, without which the auditor must attend in person and the whole plan falls away
options.misconception: invents a consent requirement in place of the assessment the module actually requires
options.why: What is required is that the risks to achieving the audit objectives are identified, assessed and managed, and that the assessment of whether a remote audit would be sufficient to achieve those objectives is made and documented for each audit, involving the team and the audited organisation's representative.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the advantages and disadvantages of a remote audit, including the increased opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information which may call for additional planning and additional or different audit procedures, and the impossibility of performing physical verification of assets and stock taking remotely

items.scenario: A partner is deciding how much of next year's audit of an inventory-heavy manufacturer can be done remotely. His manager argues that a remote audit is strictly better: it costs less, the team is comfortable, evidence can be gathered over several weeks instead of in one concentrated visit, and specialists can be drawn from the firm's global network. He proposes to conduct the entire audit remotely and to keep the audit programme exactly as it was last year.

items.stem: Which of the three appointments can go ahead as proposed?

options.text: Firm B's, because the Reserve Bank's approval is what the law requires and the Board of any bank may then appoint
options.misconception: reads the Reserve Bank's approval as the appointment itself, when approval precedes an appointment that a banking company's shareholders make at the annual general meeting and a nationalised bank's Board makes
options.why: The Reserve Bank approves; it does not appoint. For a banking company the appointment is made at the annual general meeting of the shareholders, and the Board appoints only in a nationalised bank. Firm B's appointment by the Board of a private sector banking company is by the wrong body.

options.text: Firm C's, because the only disqualifications that matter are those in section 141 of the Companies Act and a spouse's default is not among them
options.misconception: treats section 141 as the whole of the eligibility test, when the Reserve Bank's declaration of indebtedness is an additional test that reaches family members
options.why: The declaration of indebtedness is expressly in addition to the declaration about the absence of the section 141 disqualifications, and it asks whether the auditor, the firm, its partners and their family members have been declared wilful defaulters. The partner's wife is a family member, and the declaration cannot be given.

options.text: None of them — Firm A cannot take a statutory audit while it holds an internal assignment in the bank in the same year, Firm B must be appointed at the annual general meeting of the shareholders and not by the Board, and Firm C's declaration of indebtedness covers family members declared wilful defaulters and sits alongside section 141, not inside it
options.why: Each proposal breaks one of the three initial considerations. A firm that holds an internal assignment with a bank in a given year may not, the Reserve Bank has said, take that same bank's statutory audit in that same year, so Firm A's revenue audit bars it. Shareholders appoint the auditor of a banking company, and they do it at the annual general meeting of the shareholders; a Board of Directors appoints only where the bank is a nationalised one. Approval by the Reserve Bank is needed either way, but approval is not appointment and does not stand in for the body that appoints. As for Firm C, the declaration of indebtedness that banks are advised to obtain is a written confirmation covering the auditor, the firm, its partners and their family members — none of them declared a wilful defaulter by any bank or financial institution. It sits alongside the separate declaration about section 141 disqualifications, so what section 141 leaves unsaid about a spouse does not help Firm C.
keywords: annual general meeting of the shareholders

options.text: Firm A's, because a revenue audit is not a concurrent audit and the bar applies only to firms doing concurrent audit of the same branch
options.misconception: narrows the same-year bar to concurrent audit, when it covers any internal assignment in the bank
options.why: The bar is on undertaking a statutory audit assignment while associated with internal assignments in the bank during the same year, and a revenue audit for the internal audit department is an internal assignment. Nothing confines it to concurrent audit or to the same branch.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — authority appointing the auditors: the annual general meeting for a banking company, the Board for a nationalised bank, the Reserve Bank's approval in either case; Stage I initial considerations: the declaration of indebtedness covering family members in addition to section 141, and internal assignments in the same year

items.scenario: Three firms are offered bank audits for 2025-26. Firm A is offered a statutory branch audit of a nationalised bank; during the same year it is carrying out a revenue audit assignment for the bank's internal audit department. Firm B is offered appointment as statutory central auditor of a private sector banking company; the bank's Board has resolved to appoint it and says the shareholders need not be troubled since the Reserve Bank has already given its approval. Firm C is offered a branch audit; the wife of one of its partners was declared a wilful defaulter by a financial institution two years ago, and the firm reasons that section 141 of the Companies Act says nothing about a partner's spouse.

items.stem: Which two items would she expect to find only in the central auditor's letter, and why?

options.text: Nothing — the two letters are identical because the Reserve Bank prescribes one format for every statutory auditor of a bank
options.misconception: assumes one prescribed letter, when the module sets out the branch letter as similar except for two items
options.why: The letters are on similar lines, not identical; the branch letter omits the particulars of other auditors and the statement of division of work because a single firm audits the branch.

options.text: The period of appointment and the declaration of indebtedness — because a branch appointment is for one year only and needs no declaration
options.misconception: invents a one-year branch tenure and exempts branch auditors from the declaration of indebtedness, which the Reserve Bank requires before appointing statutory central or branch auditors alike
options.why: The period of appointment is in both letters, and the declaration of indebtedness is obtained by the bank before appointing its statutory central or branch auditors. Neither distinguishes the two letters.

options.text: The particulars of the other central auditors and the statement of division of work among the joint auditors — because a statutory branch audit is carried out by a single firm, so there are no other auditors to name and no work to divide
options.why: The appointment letter of a statutory central auditor carries the period of appointment, the particulars of the other central auditors, the particulars of the previous auditors, the procedural requirements for accepting, a statement of the division of work and review and reporting responsibilities among the joint auditors in a nationalised bank, and the scope including special reports and certificates. A statutory branch auditor's letter is on similar lines except in regard to the particulars of other auditors and the statement of division of work, and the reason is structural: a statutory branch audit is carried out by a single firm, while most nationalised banks appoint four or more firms to act jointly as central auditors.

options.text: The particulars of the previous auditors and the scope of the assignment — because a branch auditor communicates with nobody and gives no certificates
options.misconception: drops the previous-auditor particulars and the scope from the branch letter, when both letters carry them and only the other-auditor particulars and the division of work are absent
options.why: The branch auditor's letter is on similar lines to the central auditor's except for the particulars of other auditors and the statement of division of work. The previous auditors and the scope are in both.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — contents of the appointment letter of statutory central auditors, and the branch auditor's letter on similar lines except for the particulars of other auditors and the statement of division of work, statutory branch audit being carried out by a single firm

items.scenario: A public sector bank has appointed five firms of chartered accountants as joint statutory central auditors and one firm for each of its audited branches. A newly qualified member of one branch audit firm compares her firm's appointment letter with the letter received by a central auditor and finds two items in the central auditor's letter that hers does not have. She also finds that her firm's letter, like the central auditor's, spells out the procedural requirements to be complied with in accepting the assignment and the period of appointment.

items.stem: What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: Nothing, provided the twelve Fridays are spread across the year and the branch auditors confirm the cash balances
options.misconception: treats the branch auditors' cash verification as curing the choice of dates, when the dates themselves must not be Fridays
options.why: The branch auditors do examine the cash balance on the selected dates, but the selection is the auditor's, on 12 odd dates not being Fridays, and the report goes to the Reserve Bank as well as the bank.

options.text: The dates must be 12 odd dates spread over different months of the fiscal year and not being Fridays, and the report is addressed to the Reserve Bank as well as to the bank's top management — the branch auditors are asked to verify the trial balances and examine the cash balance on the dates the central auditor selects
options.why: Statutory central auditors are asked by the Reserve Bank to check statutory liquidity ratio compliance on 12 odd dates, spread over different months of a fiscal year and not being Fridays; odd dates are chosen so that the position is tested on days the bank has not compiled for. Two addressees then receive that report — the Reserve Bank, and the bank's own top management. Weekly trial balances as on Fridays come up from the branch auditors for consolidation at head office, and on whichever dates the central auditor picks he asks those branch auditors to confirm that the relevant trial balances are correct and to examine the branch cash balance that day.

options.text: Only the addressee — twelve Fridays are the correct dates because the demand and time liabilities position is determined for every reporting Friday
options.misconception: takes the bank's own reporting Friday as the auditor's test date, when the Reserve Bank asks for odd dates that are expressly not Fridays
options.why: The position is compiled for every reporting Friday, which is exactly why the auditor's 12 dates are odd dates in different months not being Fridays. Testing the Fridays re-performs the bank's own compilation and misses the days in between.

options.text: Only the dates — any twelve dates will do provided they fall in different months, and the Audit Committee is the right addressee for every report of the statutory auditors
options.misconception: keeps the different-months rule but drops the not-Fridays rule and sends the report inside the bank only, when it goes to the top management and the Reserve Bank
options.why: The rule has two parts, different months and not Fridays, and the report is not an internal one: it reaches the Reserve Bank as well as the bank's own top management.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — compliance with CRR and SLR requirements: verification on 12 odd dates in different months of the fiscal year not being Fridays, the report to top management and the Reserve Bank, weekly Friday trial balances consolidated at head office, and the branch auditors' verification of the trial balances and cash balances on the selected dates

items.scenario: The statutory central auditors of a bank plan the verification of statutory liquidity ratio compliance for the year. A manager proposes to test the last Friday of each of the twelve months, since that is the reporting date the bank compiles its position for and the branch trial balances already exist for those days. He proposes to send the resulting report to the bank's Audit Committee only.

items.stem: How many of the four are correctly treated?

options.text: Two — the foreign borrowing is rightly netted, because inter-bank liabilities are netted against inter-bank assets, and the margins are rightly excluded
options.misconception: extends the netting allowed for the banking system in India to a bank abroad, when borrowings from abroad are liabilities to others and are taken at gross
options.why: The netting is permitted for liabilities towards the banking system in India against assets towards that system. A borrowing from a bank abroad is a liability to others and is considered at gross; the adverse balance in a Nostro mirror account is treated the same way.

options.text: Four — each treatment follows the guidelines on the composition of demand and time liabilities
options.misconception: accepts the compilation as it stands, when three of the four items go the other way under the Reserve Bank's list of exclusions and inclusions
options.why: Only the exclusion of margins for funded facilities is right. The refinance should be out, the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts should be in, and the foreign borrowing should be in at gross.

options.text: One — the margins in sundry deposits for funded facilities are rightly excluded; the NABARD refinance should be excluded, the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts should be included, and the foreign borrowing is a liability to others taken at gross, not netted
options.why: The items excluded from liabilities under the Reserve Bank's guidelines include paid-up capital, reserves, any credit balance in the profit and loss account, loans from the Reserve Bank, refinance from EXIM Bank, NHB, SIDBI and NABARD, part recoveries of debts considered bad and doubtful, and margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities — so item 4 is right and item 1 is wrong. The items included are the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts, so item 2 is wrong, and borrowings from abroad by banks in India, which are liabilities to others and are considered at gross, unlike liabilities towards the banking system in India, which may be netted against assets towards that system — so item 3 is wrong and the full ₹250 crore goes in.

options.text: Three — everything but the branch adjustment exclusion, since refinance is a borrowing and a borrowing is a liability
options.misconception: includes refinance from the term-lending institutions as an ordinary borrowing, when the guidelines exclude refinance from EXIM Bank, NHB, SIDBI and NABARD from the demand and time liabilities
options.why: Refinance from NABARD is in the list of exclusions alongside loans from the Reserve Bank, and the foreign borrowing is wrongly netted, so at most one item stands.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — computation of demand and time liabilities: the items excluded (capital, reserves, credit balance in profit and loss, loans from the Reserve Bank, refinance from EXIM Bank, NHB, SIDBI and NABARD, part recoveries of bad debts, margins in sundry deposits for funded facilities) and included (net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts, borrowings from abroad as liabilities to others at gross)

items.scenario: In examining the compilation of a bank's demand and time liabilities the auditor finds four items. (1) Refinance of ₹400 crore from NABARD has been included in liabilities. (2) The net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts has been excluded. (3) A borrowing of ₹250 crore from a bank abroad has been netted against a ₹90 crore balance the bank holds with that bank, and only ₹160 crore included. (4) Margins of ₹30 crore held in sundry deposits against funded facilities have been excluded.

items.stem: How do the three accounts stand?

options.text: All three are non-performing, since a stale stock statement, an excess over the limit and an unreviewed limit are each a breach of the terms of sanction
options.misconception: turns every deficiency into a non-performing classification, when the norms expressly refuse to classify an account as non-performing for deficiencies that are temporary
options.why: The norms distinguish a temporary deficiency from a non-performing account. Q's excess was temporary and the renewal fell due only in March; P's outstanding is irregular, not non-performing on that ground alone. Only R, unreviewed beyond 180 days, is non-performing.

options.text: P is irregular because its drawing power rests on a stock statement older than 3 months, Q is neither irregular nor non-performing because a temporary excess over the limit and a non-renewal on the due date are temporary deficiencies, and R is non-performing because its limit was not reviewed within 180 days of the due date
options.why: A bank should not classify an account as non-performing merely because of deficiencies that are temporary in nature, such as the non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, the balance outstanding exceeding the limit temporarily, or the non-renewal of limits on the due date — so Q's temporary deficiencies leave it regular. But the stock statements relied on for determining drawing power should not be older than 3 months, and the outstanding based on drawing power calculated from a stock statement older than 3 months is considered irregular — P's statement of 20 November is more than four months old on 31 March. And where a regular limit or an ad hoc one goes unreviewed for 180 days after its due date, or after the day the ad hoc sanction was given, the account is treated as non-performing — R's due date of 30 August leaves more than 180 days to 31 March, with no review at all.

options.text: P and Q are non-performing and R is regular, because R's sanctioned limit continues until it is formally cancelled
options.misconception: inverts the rules, treating temporary deficiencies as non-performing and an unreviewed limit as continuing, when the reverse holds
options.why: A limit does not run on unreviewed: 180 days from the due date without review makes R non-performing. Q's deficiencies are temporary and do not make it non-performing, and P's stale stock statement makes the outstanding irregular.

options.text: All three are regular — none has an overdue instalment or interest for more than 90 days, which is the only test of a non-performing advance
options.misconception: reduces the classification of a cash credit to the 90-day overdue test, when a limit not reviewed within 180 days of its due date makes the account non-performing without any overdue
options.why: The 90-day test is not the only road to a non-performing classification. An account whose limits are not reviewed within 180 days from the due date is treated as non-performing, and a drawing power computed from a stock statement older than 3 months makes the outstanding irregular.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — accounts with temporary deficiencies not classified as non-performing; stock statements for drawing power not older than 3 months, failing which the outstanding is irregular; limits not reviewed within 180 days from the due date or ad hoc sanction treated as non-performing

items.scenario: Three cash credit accounts at a branch on 31 March. Account P is within its sanctioned limit but the only stock statement on file is dated 20 November, and drawing power has been computed from it. Account Q exceeded its limit by a small amount for eleven days in March and was back within the limit by the month end; its limit fell due for renewal on 15 March and the renewal is pending. Account R's limit fell due for review on 30 August and no review, regular or ad hoc, has taken place since. The branch treats all three as standard and regular.

items.stem: What is the third list, and what is wrong with the two computations?

options.text: The third list is the special mention accounts; the mobilisation advance is an asset of the contractor and adds to drawing power, and each member bank computes its own drawing power on its own record of recovery
options.misconception: confuses the record-of-recovery rule for classifying consortium accounts with the drawing power rule, and adds the mobilisation advance when it must be reduced
options.why: Special mention accounts are a separate list. A mobilisation advance is money the contractor has already received against the work, so it is reduced, not added. And while each member bank classifies a consortium account on its own record of recovery, the drawing power calculation and allocation is the lead bank's and binds the members.

options.text: The third list is the accounts whose limits are unreviewed; only the consortium computation is wrong, because a mobilisation advance is not part of the security
options.misconception: treats the mobilisation advance as irrelevant because it is not security, when it is reduced from drawing power precisely because it is an advance received against the work in progress
options.why: The module requires the mobilisation advance to be reduced in calculating drawing power on a construction company's working capital limit, so that computation is wrong too. And the list the auditor asked for, advances slipping within 12 months of sanction, is the quick mortality list.

options.text: The third list is the quick or early mortality cases, advances slipping to non-performing within 12 months of sanction; the mobilisation advance received by the contractor must be reduced in calculating drawing power, and in a consortium the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on the member banks
options.why: The audit approach to advances directs the auditor to examine quick or early mortality accounts — any advance slipping to non-performing within 12 months of its sanction — as well as accounts adversely commented on by concurrent auditors or inspection and the restructured accounts. For working capital advances to companies in the construction business the drawing power needs careful calculation: the work in progress must be valued consistently and it must be ensured that the mobilisation advance received by the contractor is reduced while calculating drawing power. And in consortium accounts the drawing power calculation and allocation made by the lead bank is binding on the member banks, so the branch's own recomputation is out of place.

options.text: The third list is the accounts regularised near the balance sheet date; both computations are acceptable because drawing power is a matter for the sanctioning authority, not the auditor
options.misconception: hands drawing power to the sanctioning authority, when the auditor is directed to review whether drawing power is calculated on the basis of stock statements and net of margin
options.why: Reviewing the calculation of drawing power is part of evaluating the controls over advances, and the module's two specific cautions are the construction company's mobilisation advance and the lead bank's binding allocation. Accounts regularised near the balance sheet date are yet another list.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — substantive procedures on advances: accounts adversely commented upon, restructured accounts, and quick or early mortality cases slipping to non-performing within 12 months of sanction; drawing power for construction companies with the mobilisation advance reduced; the lead bank's drawing power calculation and allocation binding on consortium members

items.scenario: A branch auditor is selecting advances for detailed examination. The branch manager offers a list of accounts adversely commented on by the concurrent auditors and the Reserve Bank's inspection team, and a list of restructured accounts. The auditor also asks for a third list: every advance sanctioned during the year that has already slipped to non-performing. Among the large accounts he then looks at a construction company's working capital limit, where drawing power has been computed on the value of work in progress without reducing the mobilisation advance the company received from its principal, and a consortium account where the branch has recomputed drawing power on its own view of the stock and ignored the lead bank's allocation.

items.stem: What should the auditors say?

options.text: The ratio is 9.00 per cent and meets the minimum — off-balance-sheet items carry no capital charge until they crystallise into assets
options.misconception: keeps off-balance-sheet exposures out of the denominator, when the ratio is measured against risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items together
options.why: The formula names both risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items in the denominator; the risk-adjusted value of the off-balance-sheet items is part of what the capital must cover, whether or not anything has crystallised.

options.text: The ratio is 8.04 per cent, not 9.00 — the denominator is risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items together, ₹14,000 crore, so the bank is below the 9 per cent minimum the Reserve Bank requires on an ongoing basis, and the authentication cannot be given on the figure as computed
options.why: The capital to risk-weighted assets ratio is eligible total capital funds divided by risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items, multiplied by 100. Leaving the off-balance-sheet items out gives 1,125 divided by 12,500, or 9.00 per cent; including them gives 1,125 divided by 14,000, or 8.04 per cent, which is below the minimum of 9 per cent that the Reserve Bank requires banks to maintain on an ongoing basis. The authentication of the capital adequacy ratio is one of the certificates the statutory central auditors give, and it cannot be given on a ratio with the wrong denominator.

options.text: The ratio is 8.04 per cent but that is acceptable, because the minimum of 9 per cent is tested on the average of the year and not on the balance sheet date
options.misconception: makes the 9 per cent an annual average test, when the Reserve Bank requires the minimum to be maintained on an ongoing basis
options.why: The minimum of 9 per cent is to be maintained on an ongoing basis, so a shortfall on the balance sheet date is a shortfall. The ratio computed correctly is 8.04 per cent.

options.text: The ratio cannot be computed by the auditors at all — capital adequacy is a matter between the bank and the Reserve Bank and is not among the auditors' certificates
options.misconception: places the capital adequacy ratio outside the auditors' remit, when its authentication, with the disclosures and other ratios in the notes, is one of the certificates the statutory central auditors give
options.why: Authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, including its disclosure requirements and the other ratios reported in the notes to accounts, is expressly among the reports and certificates required of the statutory central auditors.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — capital adequacy: the CRAR formula with risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items in the denominator, the Reserve Bank's minimum of 9 per cent on an ongoing basis, and authentication of the capital adequacy ratio among the auditors' certificates

items.scenario: A bank's eligible total capital funds at 31 March are ₹1,125 crore. Its risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet are ₹12,500 crore and the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items is ₹1,500 crore. The finance head computes the capital to risk-weighted assets ratio as 9.00 per cent and reports that the bank exactly meets the Reserve Bank's minimum, and asks the statutory central auditors to authenticate it.

items.stem: How many of the trainee's four statements are correct?

options.text: Three — everything but the Basel III statement, which understates the accord
options.misconception: accepts the inverted tiers and the unweighted housing loan, when both are wrong on the module's own text and example
options.why: The Basel III statement is indeed wrong, but so are the other three: the tiers are inverted and the housing loan is weighted at 50 per cent, entering at ₹30 lakh.

options.text: Two — the statements on the tiers, since subordinated debt does rank ahead of equity on a winding up
options.misconception: reads capital quality from ranking on a winding up, when the tiers are ranked by availability to absorb losses as a going concern, which puts share capital and disclosed reserves first
options.why: Ranking ahead of shareholders on a winding up is what makes subordinated debt weaker as capital, not stronger: it is not fully available to cover losses while the bank trades. Tier I is the highest quality capital for that reason.

options.text: None — Tier I, share capital and disclosed reserves, is the highest quality capital because it is fully available to cover losses and Tier II has the lower loss absorption capacity; Basel III also covers stress testing and market liquidity risk and aims at shock absorption, risk management and governance, and transparency and disclosure; and a secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh carries a 50 per cent risk weight, so ₹60 lakh enters at ₹30 lakh
options.why: Capital is split for supervisory purposes into two tiers by quality. Share capital and disclosed reserves make up most of Tier I, which ranks highest in quality for one reason: it is fully available to cover losses, all of it. Tier II consists of certain reserves and certain types of subordinated debt, and its loss absorption capacity is lower. The trainee has the tiers the wrong way round, so the first two statements fall together. Basel III is the global standard on capital adequacy, stress testing and market liquidity risk, and three purposes sit behind it: a sector that can take the shock of financial or economic stress, better risk management and governance, and more transparency and disclosure. The module's own worked case takes a secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh at a 50 per cent risk weight, subject to conditions, so a loan of ₹60 lakh contributes ₹30 lakh to the denominator, not ₹60 lakh.

options.text: One — the housing loan statement, since loans enter the ratio at their book value and weighting applies only to investments
options.misconception: applies risk weights to investments alone, when every exposure including a housing loan is weighted before it enters the denominator
options.why: The denominator is risk-weighted assets, and the module's example is a housing loan: up to ₹75 lakh at 50 per cent, above at 75 per cent, commercial real estate at 100 per cent. The ₹60 lakh loan enters at ₹30 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — Basel III framework: standard on capital adequacy, stress testing and market liquidity risk with three aims; Tier I as share capital and disclosed reserves fully available to cover losses, Tier II with lower loss absorption capacity; the housing loan risk-weight example of ₹60 lakh entering at ₹30 lakh

items.scenario: A trainee's note on a bank's capital reads: "Tier II capital is the bank's highest quality capital because subordinated debt ranks ahead of shareholders; Tier I, being share capital and reserves, absorbs losses last. Basel III is concerned only with the amount of capital. A secured housing loan of ₹60 lakh enters the risk-weighted assets at ₹60 lakh."

items.stem: Which of the four call for a comment?

options.text: All four — a savings account is not opened for a business or professional concern, an account is inoperative only after no transactions for over two years, a deposit of ₹2 crore and above is a bulk deposit on which the correct bulk rate must have been offered, and interest on deposits is paid on the basis of 360 days in a year
options.why: Savings accounts are opened in the name of individuals, Hindu undivided families and some approved institutions, and are not opened for a business or professional concern, whose transactions run through current accounts; a firm of architects is a professional concern. A savings or current account is treated as inoperative or dormant if there are no transactions for over a period of two years, so twenty months is too early. Bulk deposits are ₹2 crore and above for scheduled commercial banks at present, and the auditor verifies that the correct rate of interest has been offered on them, which the retail card rate is not. And the auditor verifies that deposit interest was paid on a basis of 360 days to the year, never 365.

options.text: Only the first and third — the inoperative rule is one year and a 365-day year is the correct basis for interest
options.misconception: shortens the inoperative period to one year and takes the calendar year for deposit interest, when the rule is over two years and 360 days
options.why: An account is inoperative after no transactions for over two years, and interest on deposits is paid on the basis of 360 days in a year. Both of the trainee's other practices are wrong too.

options.text: None — each is a matter of the bank's commercial policy on which the auditor does not comment
options.misconception: treats the deposit rules as commercial policy, when each is an audit procedure the module directs on the deposits of a bank
options.why: The module's audit procedures on deposits direct each of these checks: the kind of customer a savings account may be opened for, the two-year inoperative rule, the bulk deposit rate and the 360-day interest basis.

options.text: Only the second and fourth — a firm may hold a savings account if all partners are individuals, and ₹3 crore is below the bulk threshold of ₹5 crore
options.misconception: lets a firm hold a savings account through its partners and misplaces the bulk deposit line, when savings accounts are not opened for business or professional concerns and bulk deposits start at ₹2 crore
options.why: The savings account is for individuals, Hindu undivided families and approved institutions, not for a business or professional concern however constituted. The bulk deposit line for scheduled commercial banks is ₹2 crore and above, so ₹3 crore is a bulk deposit.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — audit of deposits: savings accounts not opened for business or professional concerns, inoperative accounts after no transactions for over two years, the correct rate on bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above, and interest paid on the basis of 360 days in a year

items.scenario: A branch auditor notes four practices. (1) A savings account was opened during the year in the name of a partnership firm of architects. (2) A savings account with no transactions for twenty months has been flagged inoperative and frozen. (3) A term deposit of ₹3 crore from a company has been given the card rate for retail deposits. (4) Interest on term deposits is computed on a 365-day year.

items.stem: What should the auditor do about the two findings?

options.text: The March transactions go to the long form audit report only, not the main report; the NRO remittance is fine because NRO accounts, like NRE accounts, are freely repatriable
options.misconception: confines window-dressing to the long form audit report and equates NRO with NRE, when the module points to a qualification in the main audit report and NRO accounts are not repatriable except for current income
options.why: Window-dressing of the deposits and advances goes to the main audit report as a possible qualification, besides other reporting. The repatriability rule separates the two accounts: NRE repatriable, NRO not except for current income.

options.text: The March transactions should be reversed in the accounts by the auditor and the NRO remittance reported to the Reserve Bank as a fraud
options.misconception: has the auditor rewrite the books and treats a wrong remittance as a fraud, when the auditor reports and considers qualifying, and the NRO error is a breach of the repatriation rule rather than a fraud on the bank
options.why: The auditor does not pass entries; he considers a suitable qualification in the main report. The NRO remittance breaches the rule that such accounts are not repatriable except for current income, and is reported as such.

options.text: Neither needs action — the deposits were reversed after the year end so the position corrected itself, and a non-resident may repatriate his own money
options.misconception: reads the reversal after the year end as curing the balance sheet, when the reversal is what marks the transactions as window-dressing of the year-end figures
options.why: The transactions were reversed after the close of the year, which is the pattern the module describes as window-dressing; the year-end deposits and advances were inflated all the same. And an NRO account is not repatriable except for current income.

options.text: The March transactions are window-dressing that inflated both deposits and advances, and the auditor should consider a suitable qualification in the main audit report besides any other reporting; the NRO remittance is wrong because an NRO account is not repatriable except for current income subject to conditions, unlike an NRE account
options.why: This is the pattern the module works through. Overdrafts go out to customers as the balance sheet date nears; what was overdrawn comes straight back in as deposits; those deposits are then security for further advances; and once the year has closed the whole set is reversed. Both sides of the sheet are inflated, deposits and advances alike. Where that shape shows and window-dressing is the likely reading, a qualification in the main audit report is what the auditor must weigh up, beside whatever else he has to report. On the second finding, a balance in an NRE account may go abroad; a balance in an NRO account is not repatriable, current income aside and even then on conditions. The auditor checks credits, debits and repatriability against the Reserve Bank's guidelines.
keywords: qualification in the main audit report

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — deposits not to be inflated for presentation: overdrafts near the balance sheet date placed as deposits with further advances on their security, reversed after the year end, calling for a suitable qualification in the main audit report; NRE accounts repatriable and NRO accounts not repatriable except for current income

items.scenario: At a branch on 28 March, twelve current account customers were granted overdrafts they had not asked for, and on the same day each placed the overdrawn amount as a term deposit with the branch; three of them were then given fresh cash credit limits on the security of those deposits. The branch manager explains that the deposits were reversed on 3 April and that nothing was lost. The auditor also finds that an NRO account of a non-resident has been allowed to remit its entire closing balance abroad, the branch reasoning that all non-resident accounts are repatriable.

items.stem: Which items belong in the report to the Central Government, and where do the others go?

options.text: Items 1, 2, 3 and 4 — the adequacy of branch returns is a matter for the branch auditors and the committees' recommendations are a management matter
options.misconception: drops the adequacy of returns from the central auditors' report and treats the Ghosh and Jilani status as management's alone, when the report states the adequacy of returns and the auditors report on the committees' recommendations
options.why: The adequacy of the returns received from the offices and branches is one of the report's matters, and the status of compliance with the Ghosh and Jilani recommendations is one of the auditors' separate reports. The statutory liquidity ratio compliance is also a separate report, not a matter of the main one.

options.text: All six — the report to the Central Government is a single document carrying every matter the Reserve Bank asks the auditors to cover
options.misconception: folds the certificates into the statutory report, when the module separates the report's matters from the reports and certificates the terms of appointment require beside it
options.why: The report has its own listed matters. The statutory liquidity ratio report and the Ghosh and Jilani status report are separate documents required by the terms of appointment, like the long form audit report.

options.text: Items 1, 2, 4 and 5, together with whether any explanation called for was given and was satisfactory and any other matter for the Central Government's notice; items 3 and 6 are separate reports the terms of appointment require beside the main report and the long form audit report
options.why: Five things go into what a nationalised bank's auditor reports to the Central Government. Is the balance sheet a full and fair one, carrying every particular it needs and drawn up to exhibit a true and fair view? Does a true balance of profit or loss appear in the profit and loss account? Where explanation or information was called for, did it come, and was what came back satisfactory? Did the transactions of the bank he came across remain within the powers of that bank? And were the returns from its offices and branches adequate for him to audit on? Anything else he thinks the Central Government ought to be told of goes in beside these five. The report on compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements and the report on the status of compliance with the Ghosh Committee's recommendations on frauds and the Jilani Committee's on internal control are among the reports and certificates the terms of appointment require besides the audit report and the long form audit report.
keywords: within the powers of that bank

options.text: Items 1 and 2 only — the remaining four are matters for the long form audit report, which is where everything other than the opinion is said
options.misconception: pushes the powers-of-the-bank and adequacy-of-returns matters into the long form audit report, when both are among the matters the statutory report itself must state
options.why: Whether the transactions were within the powers of the bank and whether the branch returns were adequate are express matters of the report to the Central Government, as is whether explanations called for were given and satisfactory.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — auditor's report of a nationalised bank to the Central Government and its matters; the reports and certificates required by the terms of appointment beside the audit report and the long form audit report, including compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio and the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations

items.scenario: A partner drafting the statutory central auditors' report on a nationalised bank lists what it must say: (1) whether the balance sheet is a full and fair one exhibiting a true and fair view; (2) whether a true balance of profit or loss is shown by the profit and loss account; (3) whether the bank has complied with the statutory liquidity ratio on the dates tested; (4) whether the transactions of the bank that came to the auditors' notice were within the powers of the bank; (5) whether the returns from the branches were adequate for the audit; (6) the status of compliance with the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations.

items.stem: Which of the five are among the auditors' reports and certificates?

options.text: Two — only the internal financial controls report and the Bank Receipt forms certificate, the rest being for a nationalised bank alone
options.misconception: confines most certificates to nationalised banks, when the terms of appointment of public sector, private sector and foreign banks require them
options.why: The list comes from the terms on which auditors of banks in the public sector, banks in the private sector and foreign banks alike are appointed; a listed private sector bank gets the corporate governance certificate on top.

options.text: Four — everything but the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, which the director is right to say is the audit opinion itself
options.misconception: merges the prudential norms report into the opinion, when the module lists a report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines as a separate report
options.why: A report saying whether the Reserve Bank's guidelines were followed in recognising income, classifying assets and providing is in the list of reports and certificates. That the opinion also depends on the norms does not remove the separate report.

options.text: All five — each is listed among the reports and certificates the terms of appointment require, the corporate governance certificate applying to a bank listed on a stock exchange, and the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning is a separate report notwithstanding that the opinion also rests on them
options.why: The reports and certificates beside the audit report and the long form audit report include the report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting, the report saying whether the Reserve Bank's guidelines were followed in recognising income, classifying assets and providing, the report on any serious irregularity requiring immediate attention, the certificate on the custody of unused Bank Receipt forms and their utilisation, the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, the Ghosh and Jilani status report, the report on instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas, asset liability management, the certificate on corporate governance for banks listed on a stock exchange, and certification of claims of interest subsidies and subventions. The director's objection does not hold: the prudential norms report is listed as a separate report in its own right.

options.text: Three — the corporate governance certificate is for the company secretary and the rural credit-deposit ratio is a matter for the Reserve Bank's own inspection
options.misconception: reassigns two of the listed certificates to others, when the certificate on corporate governance for a listed bank and the report on adverse rural credit-deposit ratios are both among the auditors' certificates
options.why: Both are in the module's list: the certificate on corporate governance in case of banks listed on a stock exchange, and the report naming every instance where a rural credit-deposit ratio turns out adverse.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — reports and certificates required beside the audit report: internal financial controls, income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, serious irregularities, unused Bank Receipt forms, capital adequacy, Ghosh and Jilani, adverse rural credit-deposit ratio, asset liability management, corporate governance for a listed bank, and interest subsidy and subvention claims

items.scenario: A listed private sector bank asks its statutory central auditors which of the following it may expect from them beside the audit report: a report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting; a certificate on corporate governance; a report on instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas; a certificate on the custody and utilisation of unused Bank Receipt forms; and a report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines. A director says the last of these cannot be a separate report because it is already the substance of the audit opinion.

items.stem: What is the company's capital ratio, and does it meet the minimum?

options.text: 15 per cent — Tier I and Tier II together, ₹180 crore, against the aggregate of risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items, ₹1,200 crore; that exactly meets the minimum of 15 per cent, with no comfort above it
options.why: Every applicable non-banking financial company must hold its capital ratio — Tier I and Tier II taken together — at 15 per cent at the least, measured against its aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet plus the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items. The manager's 18 per cent divides ₹180 crore by the ₹1,000 crore on-balance-sheet figure alone; the ratio measured as the Directions require is ₹180 crore over ₹1,200 crore, which is 15 per cent, the minimum itself.

options.text: 18 per cent, and it meets the minimum — guarantees are contingent and enter the capital ratio only when invoked
options.misconception: leaves off-balance-sheet exposures out until they crystallise, when the Directions measure the ratio against the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items as well
options.why: The denominator is the aggregate of risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items. The guarantees enter now, at their risk-adjusted value, and the ratio is 15 per cent.

options.text: 12 per cent, below the minimum — only Tier I capital counts towards the ratio for a company that accepts no deposits
options.misconception: drops Tier II from the numerator, when the minimum capital ratio is defined as consisting of Tier I and Tier II capital
options.why: The ratio consists of Tier I and Tier II capital together, ₹180 crore, against ₹1,200 crore, which is 15 per cent and meets the minimum.

options.text: 15 per cent, but below the minimum, because a middle layer company must hold 18 per cent
options.misconception: invents a higher layer-based minimum, when the Directions set the minimum capital ratio at 15 per cent
options.why: The minimum under the Directions is 15 per cent of the aggregate risk-weighted exposures. At exactly 15 per cent the company meets it, though with nothing to spare.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — capital requirements: a minimum capital ratio of Tier I and Tier II capital of not less than 15 per cent of aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items

items.scenario: A non-banking financial company in the middle layer has Tier I capital of ₹120 crore and Tier II capital of ₹60 crore. Its risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet are ₹1,000 crore and the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items, mainly guarantees, is ₹200 crore. Its finance manager reports a capital ratio of 18 per cent and says the company is comfortably above the minimum.

items.stem: How should the two loans be classified?

options.text: X is doubtful and Y is standard, because restructuring is itself evidence of doubt and a missing security is a matter for provisioning, not classification
options.misconception: over-classifies the restructured loan and under-classifies the lost security, when the Directions place a restructured asset in sub-standard and a security-less threatened asset in loss
options.why: Restructuring puts an asset in sub-standard, not doubtful, for the year of performance. The non-availability of security with a threat to recovery is a classification rule making Y a loss asset, and the provisioning follows from that.

options.text: Both are standard — X because the borrower is performing and Y because nothing is overdue, an overdue being the only trigger for downgrading
options.misconception: makes an overdue the sole trigger of classification, when a restructured asset is sub-standard for a year of performance and a loss asset is defined by the threat to recovery, not by arrears
options.why: Neither the year of satisfactory performance nor the loss-asset definition turns on an overdue. X has not completed the year, and Y's security has gone.

options.text: X stays sub-standard, because a renegotiated or restructured asset remains sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance under the new terms and only nine months have run; Y is a loss asset, because an asset adversely affected by a threat of non-recoverability from the non-availability of security or a fraudulent act of the borrower is a loss asset whether or not it is overdue
options.why: An asset counts as sub-standard where interest or principal terms in the agreement were renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured once operations had begun, and it stays that way until one year of satisfactory performance has run under those new terms; nine months of performance do not complete the year. A loss asset means an asset identified as such by the company, by its internal or external auditor, or by the Reserve Bank on inspection, to the extent it has not been written off. It also means one adversely affected by a potential threat of non-recoverability — because the security has lost its value, because of the non-availability of security, or because of a fraudulent act or omission by the borrower. Disposing of the charged machinery is both the non-availability of security and a fraudulent act, and the absence of an overdue does not keep the loan standard.

options.text: X is standard, because restructuring with the borrower's consent is not a default; Y is sub-standard, since a loss asset must first pass through the doubtful category
options.misconception: treats classification as a ladder every asset must climb, when a loss asset is defined directly by the threat of non-recoverability and a restructured asset is expressly sub-standard for a year
options.why: The definitions are independent: an asset meeting the loss-asset definition is a loss asset without first being doubtful, and a restructured asset is sub-standard until one year of satisfactory performance has expired.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — asset classification: a renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured asset remains sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance; a loss asset as identified by the company, its auditor or the Reserve Bank, or as adversely affected by erosion or non-availability of security or a fraudulent act of the borrower

items.scenario: Two loans in a non-banking financial company's book on 31 March. Loan X was restructured on 1 July with a longer tenor and a lower rate, and the borrower has paid every restructured instalment for the nine months since; the company has moved it back to standard. Loan Y is not overdue, but the company's own inspection found that the machinery charged as security has been sold by the borrower and cannot be traced, and the company has left it as standard because no instalment has been missed.

items.stem: Which parts of the company's conduct comply with the Directions?

options.text: Everything but the late report — a short grace period for pending applications is reasonable and the renewal mandates are the depositors' consent
options.misconception: reads a grace period into "with immediate effect" and a standing mandate as consent, when the stop is immediate and the consent to renew must be express and voluntary at maturity
options.why: The stop on fresh deposits and renewals takes effect immediately on the downgrade, and a matured deposit is renewed only with the depositor's express and voluntary consent. The late report is only one of three failures.

options.text: Only letting the existing deposits run off to maturity — on the downgrade the company had to stop accepting fresh deposits and renewing existing ones with immediate effect, then within 15 working days report where it stood to whichever Regional Office of the Reserve Bank holds its registration, and renew no matured deposit without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor, which a standing mandate is not
options.why: In the event of downgrading of the credit rating below the minimum specified investment grade, an investment and credit company or a factor regularises the excess deposits by three steps: with immediate effect it stops accepting fresh public deposits and renewing existing deposits, all existing deposits run off to maturity, and within 15 working days it must report where it stands to whichever Regional Office of the Reserve Bank holds its registration. Accepting deposits for three more weeks breaks the first step, and 20 February is well beyond 15 working days from 10 January. And the Directions provide that no matured public deposit is renewed without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor, so a mandate signed at placement does not authorise the February renewals. Only the run-off to maturity is as the Directions require.

options.text: Everything — the company must regularise the excess in an orderly way and the Directions leave the method to its Board
options.misconception: leaves the method of regularisation to the Board, when the Directions prescribe the three steps and the 15 working day report
options.why: The method is prescribed: stop immediately, run off to maturity, report within 15 working days. The company departed from the first and third and renewed deposits it could not renew.

options.text: Nothing — even letting deposits run to maturity is wrong, because all public deposits must be repaid at once on a downgrade
options.misconception: turns the downgrade into an immediate repayment of all deposits, when the Directions have existing deposits run off to maturity
options.why: Existing deposits run off to maturity under the Directions; there is no immediate repayment. That step the company got right.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions on downgrade below the minimum investment grade: stop fresh deposits and renewals with immediate effect, existing deposits run off to maturity, report within 15 working days to the Regional Office, and no matured deposit renewed without express and voluntary consent

items.scenario: A deposit-taking investment and credit company's rating was downgraded below the minimum investment grade on 10 January. The company continued to accept fresh public deposits until 31 January "to let existing customers complete their applications", renewed deposits that matured in February on the footing that the depositors had signed automatic-renewal mandates when the deposits were placed, and wrote to the Reserve Bank's Regional Office on 20 February. The finance head says the excess over the permissible ceiling will be repaid as the deposits mature.

items.stem: Which of the four are reported as frauds under the classification?

options.text: Cases 1 and 2 — where no fraudulent intention is suspected or proved, a cash shortage is still a fraud if it exceeds ₹10,000, or if it exceeds ₹5,000 and was detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported by the person handling the cash; case 3 is under ₹5,000 and case 4 was reported on its occurrence
options.why: Cases of negligence and cash shortages are reported as fraud if the intention to cheat or defraud is suspected or proved. Where it is not, two cases are nevertheless treated as fraud and reported: cash shortages of more than ₹10,000, and cash shortages of more than ₹5,000 where management, the auditor or an inspecting officer found them and whoever was handling the cash had not reported them when they occurred. Case 1 exceeds ₹10,000 and is a fraud whoever reported it; case 2 exceeds ₹5,000, was found by the auditor and was not reported by the cashier; case 3 at ₹4,000 falls below the ₹5,000 line; case 4 at ₹8,000 is above ₹5,000 but was reported on its occurrence by the cashier, so it is not caught.

options.text: Case 2 only — a shortage reported by the cashier is by definition not a fraud, whatever its size
options.misconception: lets the cashier's own report clear any shortage, when a shortage above ₹10,000 is a fraud regardless of who reported it
options.why: The self-report matters only on the ₹5,000 line. Above ₹10,000 the shortage is treated as fraud whether or not the cashier reported it, so case 1 goes in with case 2.

options.text: None — without a suspected or proved intention to cheat, a cash shortage is negligence and is never reported as fraud
options.misconception: stops at the intention test, when the classification goes on to treat two kinds of unintended shortage as fraud on size and non-reporting
options.why: The Directions treat two classes of shortage as fraud even where fraudulent intention is not suspected or proved at the time of detection: above ₹10,000, and above ₹5,000 detected by others and unreported by the cash handler.

options.text: Cases 1, 2 and 4 — every shortage above ₹5,000 is a fraud, the self-report being relevant only below that line
options.misconception: applies the ₹5,000 line without its condition, when between ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 a shortage is a fraud only if detected by management, the auditor or an inspector and not reported by the cash handler
options.why: Case 4 is above ₹5,000 but was reported on its occurrence by the person handling the cash, and it does not exceed ₹10,000, so neither limb catches it.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Monitoring of Frauds Directions: negligence and cash shortages reported as fraud where intent is suspected or proved; otherwise cash shortages of more than ₹10,000, and of more than ₹5,000 if detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported by the person handling the cash

items.scenario: Four cash shortages at a non-banking financial company's branches during the year, in none of which any intention to cheat is suspected. (1) ₹12,000 short at a branch, reported by the cashier on the day. (2) ₹6,500 short, found by the internal auditor on a surprise count and never reported by the cashier. (3) ₹4,000 short, found by the branch manager and not reported by the cashier. (4) ₹8,000 short, reported by the cashier on the day it occurred. The company proposes to report only case 2 as a fraud.

items.stem: Who has committed an offence, and what does the Act say of each?

options.text: P, Q and R — Q too, because a member in employment who trains articled assistants is holding himself out as in practice without a certificate
options.misconception: reads the training of articled assistants by an employee as a false claim of practice, when the Act deems him in practice for that limited purpose
options.why: The Explanation to section 2(2) exists for Q. A member drawing a salary from a chartered accountant in practice, or from such a firm, is in practice for one purpose only — the training of articled assistants. He commits no offence.

options.text: P and R — setting up an establishment offering accounting services is practice though no client has been served, so P, a member without a certificate of practice, represents that he practises and offends section 24; R, not being a member, uses the designation and offends section 24; Q offends nothing, a salaried employee of a firm being deemed in practice for the limited purpose of training articled assistants
options.why: Practice does not wait for the first client. A member is in it once he is doing accountancy work, and equally once he merely holds himself out as ready to do it, whether or not anyone takes him up. Renting the office and putting the board up is therefore practice already, even though no client has been served. Section 24 reaches a member who holds no certificate of practice and yet gives out that he is practising, and it reaches anyone outside the membership who claims to be a member or writes the designation chartered accountant after his name; on first conviction the fine may extend to ₹1,000, and on a subsequent conviction to imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ₹5,000 or both. Q is within the Explanation to section 2(2). Where an associate or fellow draws a salary from a chartered accountant in practice, or from a firm of such accountants, one purpose alone puts him in practice: the training of articled assistants.

options.text: R only — P has served no client and so is not yet in practice, and Q cannot train articled assistants without a certificate of practice
options.misconception: waits for a client before treating an establishment as practice, and denies the Explanation that lets a salaried employee of a firm train articled assistants
options.why: Offering to render accounting services is practice; the establishment is enough. And the Explanation to section 2(2) deems Q in practice for the limited purpose of training articled assistants notwithstanding his employment.

options.text: P and R, but R's case goes to the Disciplinary Committee of the Institute, which alone punishes misuse of the designation
options.misconception: sends a non-member to the Institute's disciplinary machinery, when section 24 makes the misuse a criminal offence tried by a court with a fine and, on a second conviction, imprisonment
options.why: The Institute's Board of Discipline and Disciplinary Committee act on members. A person who is not a member and uses the designation is prosecuted under section 24, as in the module's case where a magistrate imposed a fine and, in default, rigorous imprisonment.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — section 2(2) and its Explanation on salaried employees training articled assistants; setting up an establishment as practice though no client is served; section 24 on a non-member using the designation and a member without a certificate representing that he practises, with the fine and imprisonment

items.scenario: Three people in one town. Mr. P, an associate member who holds no certificate of practice, has rented an office, put up a board offering accounting and audit services, and printed cards, though no client has yet walked in. Mr. Q, a fellow member, is a salaried employee of a firm of chartered accountants and trains two articled assistants registered under him. Mr. R, who failed the final examination, describes himself as a chartered accountant on his visiting cards and prepares accounts for shopkeepers for a fee.

items.stem: Which of the three is on the wrong side of the Act?

options.text: None — an LLP is a partnership and not a company, and both individual appointments are within practice
options.misconception: takes the LLP's own reading of section 25, when the section expressly brings in a limited liability partnership that has a company as a partner
options.why: For section 25 the term company includes a limited liability partnership which has a company as its partner. The LLP may not practise as chartered accountants and its officers knowingly a party are liable to the fines.

options.text: Sunita and the LLP — mediation is not among the roles Regulation 191 lists, so it needs the Council's specific permission
options.misconception: reads Regulation 191's list literally, when the Ethical Standards Board has read mediator as within arbitrator, which the regulation names
options.why: The Board's decision is that acting as a mediator in court is deemed covered within the meaning of arbitrator, which Regulation 191 permits to members in practice. No specific permission is needed.
