options.text: Only the LLP — a limited liability partnership with a company as a partner is a company for section 25 and may not practise as chartered accountants, and every director, manager, secretary or officer knowingly a party is liable to a fine up to ₹1,000 on first conviction and ₹5,000 after; Raj is deemed in practice under Regulation 191 as a secretary not employed on a salary-cum-full-time basis, and Sunita's mediation is within arbitrator, which Regulation 191 permits
options.why: Regulation 191, read with section 2(2)(iv), deems a member in practice where he acts in his professional capacity and neither personally nor as somebody's employee. It lists him as a receiver, a liquidator, a trustee, an executor, an administrator or an arbitrator, or an adviser or representative on costing, financial or taxation matters; it covers an appointment made by the Central Government, a State Government, a court or another legal authority; and it covers a secretary, unless he holds that post on a salary-cum-full-time basis — so Raj's appointment is within his practice. The Ethical Standards Board has decided that a member in practice can act as a mediator in court, mediation being deemed covered within arbitrator. Section 25 provides that no company, wherever incorporated, shall practise as chartered accountants, and for that section the term company includes any limited liability partnership which has a company as its partner; every director, manager, secretary and other officer knowingly a party to the contravention is punishable with a fine up to ₹1,000 on first conviction and up to ₹5,000 on any subsequent conviction.

options.text: Raj and the LLP — a member in practice may not hold the office of secretary of anybody, that being an occupation other than the profession
options.misconception: treats every secretaryship as another occupation under Clause 11, when Regulation 191 deems a member acting as secretary in his professional capacity to be in practice unless employed on a salary-cum-full-time basis
options.why: Regulation 191 names acting as a secretary among the things a member does in practice, with one carve-out: employment on a salary-cum-full-time basis. Raj's appointment is on a fee in his professional capacity and is within his practice.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Regulation 191 and the secretary not on a salary-cum-full-time basis, the Ethical Standards Board's decision on court mediators as within arbitrator, and section 25 on companies including a limited liability partnership with a company partner, with the fines on officers knowingly a party

items.scenario: CA Raj, in practice, is appointed by the Central Government as secretary to a metro project authority in his professional capacity, on a fee and not on a salary-cum-full-time basis. CA Sunita, in practice, is empanelled by a court as a mediator. Advisory Solutions LLP, whose partners are two chartered accountants and a private limited company, starts signing audit reports in the LLP's name; its company-partner's directors say an LLP is not a company and section 25 does not reach it.

items.stem: Which of the four is within the Council's permissions?

options.text: Arun and Charu — a Director Simplicitor draws no salary, so there is no conflict with the firm's audit, and the audit continues
options.misconception: reads the absence of remuneration as removing the auditor conflict, when the general permission for a Director Simplicitor is expressly withdrawn where the member or a partner is the company's auditor
options.why: The general permission to be a Director Simplicitor does not extend to a company in which the member or any of his partners is interested as auditor; the Council prohibits a member from auditing a company of which he is a director whether or not he holds a substantial interest.

options.text: Only Charu — a member may be a promoter or subscriber to the memorandum and be a Director Simplicitor of that company without permission; Arun's firm being Nila's auditor takes his directorship outside the general permission, Bela's signing of Registrar forms is a direct conflict of role, and Dev cannot hold the office of managing director where a relative holds a substantial interest of twenty per cent or more, so the Council will not grant it
options.why: A Director Simplicitor is an ordinary director who is not a managing or whole-time director, is required only at board meetings and is paid nothing but for attending them, and a member in practice is permitted generally to be one in any company including a board-managed company without specific permission — unless he or any of his partners is interested in the company as an auditor, which is Arun's position. The Council has also decided that a member may be a promoter or subscriber to the memorandum and articles of a company and be its Director Simplicitor without specific permission, which is Charu's. The Ethical Standards Board holds that a member in practice who is Director Simplicitor cannot sign the company's Registrar forms, as it is a direct conflict of role. And a member cannot accept and hold the office of managing or whole-time director if he, his partners or his relatives hold a substantial interest in the company; a brother is a relative, and shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power are a substantial interest.
keywords: interested in the company as an auditor

options.text: Charu and Dev — the substantial interest bar looks at the member's own holding, and Dev holds nothing
options.misconception: confines substantial interest to the member's own shares, when the twenty per cent is counted across the member, his relatives and the concerns in which they hold such an interest
options.why: A member is deemed to have a substantial interest where shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power are owned by him or by one or more of his relatives, and a brother is a relative. Dev cannot hold the office of managing director in that company.

options.text: Bela and Charu — signing statutory filings is a ministerial act any director may do, and it keeps the member within the Director Simplicitor role
options.misconception: treats the Registrar filings as within the Director Simplicitor role, when the Ethical Standards Board has decided that signing them is a direct conflict of role
options.why: The Board's decision is that a chartered accountant in practice who is a Director Simplicitor cannot sign the company's Registrar forms. A Director Simplicitor is required only at board meetings.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 11: the Director Simplicitor and the general permission withdrawn where the member or a partner is the auditor, the promoter or subscriber as Director Simplicitor, the Ethical Standards Board on signing Registrar forms, the managing director's office barred where relatives hold a substantial interest, relative and the twenty per cent voting test

items.scenario: Four members in practice. CA Arun is a director of Nila Ltd, attends only board meetings, draws sitting fees alone, and his firm is Nila's statutory auditor. CA Bela is a Director Simplicitor of Ravi Pvt Ltd and, being the only chartered accountant on the board, signs the company's annual filings with the Registrar of Companies. CA Charu subscribed to the memorandum of a new company as a promoter and sits on its board as an ordinary director without remuneration beyond sitting fees. CA Dev has been offered the office of managing director of a company in which his brother holds 24 per cent of the voting power, and has applied to the Council.

items.stem: Which of the six need the Council's specific and prior permission, and what else follows?

options.text: Items 2, 4 and 6 — being Karta of a trading business is engaging in business and always needs specific permission
options.misconception: treats the Karta of a family business as always outside the permissions, when the Council allows interest in a family business devolving by partition where the member takes no active part and invests only the family's funds
options.why: Interest in a family business concern, including interest devolving by inheritance, succession or partition, in whose management no active part is taken, is within the Council's resolutions; a Karta who invests only the family's funds and leaves the management alone is within the limit.

options.text: Items 2 and 6 need specific permission, and item 2 also costs her the attest functions because her teaching exceeds 25 hours a week; items 1 and 3 are generally permitted, item 4 is within the limit for a Karta investing family funds without active management, and item 5 needs no permission because equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity are outside Clause 11
options.why: The general resolution permits, without specific permission, part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute and the holding of public elective office such as a Member of Parliament or of a legislative assembly. Specific and prior approval from the Council is needed for a lectureship, part-time or full-time, on courses that do not relate to the Institute's own examinations, and for editing a journal that is not a professional one. Whichever permission applies, all such teaching taken together has a ceiling of 25 hours a week; a member above that ceiling cannot undertake attest functions, so at 28 hours she loses them. A member in practice engaged as Karta of a Hindu undivided family doing family business is within the limit prescribed by the Council if he makes investments from the funds of the family only, provided he is not actively engaged in the management. And members may transact in equity and currency derivatives in their personal capacity without the permission of the Council, though not in their professional capacity for clients.

options.text: Items 2, 5 and 6 — trading in derivatives is a business, and a member in practice must obtain permission before dealing in them at all
options.misconception: makes derivatives a business needing permission, when the module's answer is that equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity are not violative of Clause 11 and need no permission
options.why: Members in practice may engage in equity and currency derivative transactions in their personal capacity without the Council's permission; what they may not do is transact for clients in their professional capacity.

options.text: Items 1, 2 and 6 — any teaching for a fee is an occupation, and the Institute's own coaching is no exception
options.misconception: puts the Institute's coaching organisation on the same footing as an outside college, when part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute is in the general permission
options.why: The general resolution names part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute; it is lectureship for other courses and tutorship under other institutions that need specific permission.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 11: the general resolution (tutorship under the Institute's coaching organisation, public elective office), the specific resolution (lectureship for other courses, editorship of non-professional journals), the 25 teaching hours for attest functions, the Karta of a family business, and equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity

items.scenario: A member in practice lists six things she does or means to do: (1) teach part-time under the coaching organisation of the Institute; (2) take a full-time lectureship in a college for a commerce degree, which with her other teaching will take 28 hours a week; (3) sit as a Member of the Legislative Assembly; (4) act as Karta of her family's Hindu undivided family trading business that came to her on partition, investing only the family's funds and leaving the management to her brother; (5) buy and sell equity and currency derivatives in her own name; (6) edit a lifestyle magazine.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The sale of the goodwill of a deceased proprietor's firm to an eligible member is permitted and instalments are allowed where the agreement provides for them; the legal heir must obtain the Council's permission within a year of the death and the sale must be completed within that year, during which the firm name is kept in abeyance; Nair may then practise as a proprietor under the name Mehta & Co.
options.why: The Council considered under Clause 2 whether the goodwill of a proprietary concern of a chartered accountant can be sold after his death to another eligible member and permitted it, payments being allowed in instalments if the sale agreement contains such a provision. Where the proprietor died on or after 30 August 1998 the sale must be completed in all respects within a year of the death, the name of the firm is kept in abeyance — not removed — only up to one year from the death, and the Council's permission is for the deceased's legal heir to seek, within a year of the death. In the module's own illustration a widow selling her husband's practice with the right to use the firm name is in effect selling the goodwill, the act is permissible, and the buyer can continue to practise in that name as a proprietor.
keywords: within a year of the death

options.text: The sale is permitted, but the widow may continue to receive a share of the fees Nair earns under the name, since she is the legal representative
options.misconception: carries the partnership rule on a deceased partner's share across to a proprietorship, where there is no sharing of fees between the legal representative and the purchaser of the goodwill
options.why: In a proprietorship there is no sharing of fees between the legal representative of the single-member firm and the purchaser of the goodwill; the widow's entitlement is the price of the goodwill, in instalments if agreed.

options.text: The sale is permitted but the price must be paid in one sum, and the Institute need not be told until Nair applies to use the name
options.misconception: forbids instalments and lets the permission wait on the buyer, when instalments are allowed under the agreement and the legal heir must obtain the Council's permission within a year of the death
options.why: Payments may be made in instalments provided the sale agreement contains such a provision, and the Council's permission falls to the legal heir to seek, within a year of the death of the proprietor.

options.text: The sale is barred — a proprietor's goodwill dies with him, and a firm name can pass only to a partner
options.misconception: denies the Council's decision that the goodwill of a proprietary firm may be sold after the proprietor's death, which is exactly what the module's illustration permits
options.why: The goodwill of a proprietorship firm of a chartered accountant can be sold or transferred to another eligible member after the death of the proprietor, and the buyer may practise in the name as a proprietor.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule: sale of the goodwill of a proprietary firm after the proprietor's death, instalments under the agreement, the sale completed and the Council's permission obtained within a year of the death, the firm name kept in abeyance for a year, and Illustration 6 on the widow's sale with the firm name

items.scenario: CA Mehta, a sole proprietor practising as Mehta & Co., died on 5 May 2026. His widow proposes to sell the practice to CA Nair for ₹8 lakh, the price including the right to use the name Mehta & Co., payable in four half-yearly instalments under the agreement. She asks whether she must involve the Institute, and by when, and whether Nair can then practise as a proprietor under that name.

items.stem: How do the three stand under Clause 2 and the Council's decisions?

options.text: (3) is in time, because the year runs from the date the heir first approaches the Institute and not from the death
options.misconception: starts the one-year clock at the heir's approach, when the name is kept in abeyance up to one year from the death and a dispute extension needs information to the Institute within a year of the death
options.why: The clocks run from the death: the sale completed within a year of it, the Council's permission sought within a year of it, and the name in abeyance up to one year from it. The son has nothing to stand on after fifteen months of silence.

options.text: (1) and (2) are both misconduct, because a share can go to a legal representative only while at least one partner survives to earn it
options.misconception: reads the rule as needing a surviving partner, when the Council's decision applies equally where all partners die at the same time
options.why: The Council's decision on a deceased partner's share applies also where all the partners die at the same time, so the second firm's heirs take their share under the deed; it is the first firm, with no provision in its deed, that is in breach.

options.text: All three are permitted — a widow's share is a matter of goodwill among partners, and the Institute holds a deceased proprietor's name until a buyer appears
options.misconception: leaves the deceased partner's share to the partners' discretion and the firm name open-ended, when the share needs a provision in the deed and the name is held only one year
options.why: The share is permitted only under a provision of the partnership agreement, and the proprietorship name is kept in abeyance only up to one year from the death, the dispute extension needing a report to the Institute within that year.

options.text: (1) is misconduct, because a deceased partner's legal representative may receive a share of the firm only if the partnership agreement so provides; (2) is permitted, because the same rule applies where all the partners die at the same time and this deed provides for it; (3) is too late, because the firm name is kept in abeyance only up to one year from the death unless a dispute as to the heir was reported within that year
options.why: Under Clause 2, where there are two or more partners and one dies, the legal representative of the deceased partner can continue to receive a share of the firm only if the partnership agreement contains such a provision; paying the widow without one is sharing fees with a non-member. The same decision of the Council reaches the heirs where the partners of a firm all die at the same time, so the heirs under the second deed are within it. For a proprietorship, the name of the firm is kept in abeyance only up to a period of one year from the death of the proprietor, and it is only where there is a dispute as to the legal heir and the information is received by the Institute within a year of the death that the name is kept in abeyance till one year from the settlement of the dispute; the son, who reported nothing in fifteen months, has let the year run.
keywords: partnership agreement contains such a provision

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule: a deceased partner's legal representative receiving a share only under the partnership agreement, the decision applying where all partners die together, the proprietorship name kept in abeyance one year from death, and the extension where a dispute as to the heir is reported within a year

items.scenario: Three situations. (1) CA Iyer, a partner of a three-partner firm, died; the partnership deed says nothing about a deceased partner's share, but the surviving partners, out of regard, pay his widow one-fifth of the profits every year. (2) All three partners of another firm died in the same accident, and their heirs cite the deed, which provides for a deceased partner's family to receive a share for five years. (3) A sole proprietor died fifteen months ago; his son, who is not a chartered accountant, has not approached the Institute, and now asks that the firm name be held for a buyer he expects to find.

items.stem: Which of the four may he accept?

options.text: (1) and (3) — fees recovered progressively as the work is done make him indebted at no stage, and a bank's credit card is within the Board's decision where the outstanding beyond the credit period does not exceed ₹1,00,000; (2) is barred because a relative's indebtedness above ₹1,00,000 to a concern with no statutory limit is caught by Chapter X, and (4) is barred because the Board does not permit a member to audit a bank from which he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit
options.why: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines bars an appointment as auditor where the person taking it is indebted to the concern, or has stood guarantee or given security for somebody else's debt to it. It catches the member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm itself, and a relative of that member or partner. The line is whatever limit the statute fixes where there is one, and ₹1,00,000 everywhere else; a sister is a relative, the society has no statutory limit, and ₹1,50,000 exceeds the line. The Research Committee's opinion is that fees taken on a progressive basis, a part at a time as the work is done, leave the auditor indebted to the concern at no stage, so the advance is no bar. The Ethical Standards Board has decided that a member may hold the credit card of a bank he audits provided the outstanding does not exceed ₹1,00,000 beyond the prescribed credit period, and that a member is not permitted to accept the audit of a bank where he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit held there.

options.text: (1), (3) and (4) — a loan against his own fixed deposit is fully secured by the bank's own liability to him and is not indebtedness
options.misconception: nets the loan against the deposit, when the Board's decision is that a loan against a fixed deposit in the bank bars the audit of that bank
options.why: The Ethical Standards Board's decision is categorical: a member in practice is not permitted to accept the audit assignment of a bank where he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit held by him in that bank. The security does not save it.

options.text: (2) and (3) — Chapter X looks only at the member's own debts, and an advance of fees is a debt to the client that bars (1)
options.misconception: leaves relatives out of Chapter X and treats every fee advance as indebtedness, when the chapter names relatives and the progressive-fee opinion takes the advance out
options.why: Chapter X expressly extends to a relative of the member or partner, so the sister's ₹1,50,000 loan bars the society audit; and fees recovered progressively under the engagement terms do not make the auditor indebted at any stage.

options.text: (1) only — any dealing with a bank he audits, a credit card included, is a relationship the Board forbids
options.misconception: forbids the credit card outright, when the Board permits it within the indebtedness limit of ₹1,00,000 beyond the credit period
options.why: The Board allows a member to hold the credit card of a bank he audits, provided the outstanding balance does not exceed ₹1,00,000 beyond the prescribed credit period. At ₹80,000 the card is within the line.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Council General Guidelines Chapter X: indebtedness of the member, partner, firm or relative beyond ₹1,00,000 where no statute fixes a limit, the progressive-fee opinion of the Research Committee; Ethical Standards Board decisions on a bank's credit card within ₹1,00,000 and a loan against a fixed deposit

items.scenario: Four appointments offered to CA Om, in practice. (1) Tax audit of a partnership firm that has paid him ₹2,50,000 of fees in advance under an engagement letter providing for fees to be recovered progressively as parts of the work are done. (2) Audit of a co-operative society, governed by no statutory limit on indebtedness, from which his sister has an unsecured loan of ₹1,50,000. (3) Statutory audit of a bank whose credit card he holds, with ₹80,000 outstanding beyond the credit period. (4) Audit of another bank from which he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit he holds there.

items.stem: What must Wali do before accepting, and what of his own books?

options.text: He must obtain a copy of Vani's communication from the Board of Directors and consider it before accepting, and follow any direction of the Council or its committee not to accept in a case of unjustified removal; and he is in breach of Chapter V, which requires a member in practice to keep a cash book and a ledger for his practice whether or not section 44AA applies
options.why: Under the Ethical Standards Board's guidelines, an auditor who resigns or does not offer himself for reappointment sends a written communication of his professional reasons to the Board of Directors, copied to the Institute. The incoming auditor is then bound, before he accepts, to obtain a copy of that communication from the Board of Directors and to consider it. Chapter XI of the Council General Guidelines requires a member in practice to follow a direction given by the Council or an appropriate committee, to him as incoming auditor, not to accept the appointment in a case of unjustified removal of the earlier auditor. Chapter V requires a member in practice, or the firm of which he is a partner, to maintain proper books of account of the professional practice including a cash book and a ledger; and it makes no difference, the module's illustration holds, whether or not the Income-tax Act's section 44AA reaches him.

options.text: He may accept, because a resignation is not a removal and Chapter XI speaks only of removal; his books are a private matter
options.misconception: confines the Board's procedure to removals, when its guidelines expressly cover resignation and non-reappointment and place a duty on the incoming auditor in each
options.why: The Board's guidelines deal with an auditor who resigns, one who is not reappointed though willing, and removals by government and statutory authorities alike, and in each the incoming auditor must obtain and consider the communication. Chapter V makes the books a professional obligation.

options.text: He must obtain a no-objection certificate from Vani under Clause 8 and nothing more; his books are governed by the Income-tax Act alone
options.misconception: reduces the duty to a Clause 8 communication, when the Board's guidelines add the duty to obtain the outgoing auditor's written reasons from the Board of Directors, and misplaces the books rule in the Income-tax Act
options.why: Clause 8 communication stands on its own; the Board's guidelines require in addition that the incoming auditor obtain a copy of the communication of reasons from the Board of Directors and consider it. Chapter V, not section 44AA, requires his cash book and ledger.

options.text: The managing director's assurance is enough, because the Board's procedure binds the outgoing auditor only; and the Income-tax threshold settles his books
options.misconception: places the whole duty on the outgoing auditor and borrows the Income-tax threshold for the Council's books rule, when the incoming auditor must obtain and consider the communication and Chapter V applies regardless of section 44AA
options.why: The obligation to obtain a copy of the resignation communication from the Board of Directors and consider it is placed on the incoming auditor. And Chapter V's cash book and ledger are required of every member in practice whatever the Income-tax Act says.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board guidelines on resignation and non-reappointment with the incoming auditor's duty to obtain and consider the communication; Council General Guidelines Chapter XI on directions in unjustified removal and Chapter V on the cash book and ledger regardless of section 44AA

items.scenario: CA Vani resigned as auditor of Tarak Ltd after the board refused to correct a revenue recognition policy, and wrote to the board saying so, with a copy to the Institute. CA Wali is offered the appointment in her place; the managing director tells him the resignation was "personal" and that there is nothing to read. CA Wali also keeps no cash book or ledger for his own practice, reasoning that his receipts are below the limit at which section 44AA of the Income-tax Act requires books.

items.stem: What do the Council's self-regulatory measures say of the two proposals?

options.text: A statutory auditor firm of ten or more members should not conduct the branch audits, which should go to local firms of fewer than ten members, the exceptions being where the branch records are kept at the head office or significant operations are carried on at the branch; and associating a firm of fewer than five members as joint auditor of a large company is to be encouraged, so the senior firm should not object — the measures being recommendatory, with the Council expecting every member to implement them
options.why: A statutory audit firm of ten or more members should leave a company's branch audits to local firms below ten members, and nothing in that cuts into the statutory auditors' right of access to branch accounts under the Companies Act. Two situations relax it: branch accounting records kept at the head office, and significant operations of the company carried on at the branch office. Here the books are at the branches, so no exception applies. On a large company the Council would rather see a small practising firm — one of fewer than five members — brought in beside the senior firm as joint auditor, and a client who asks for exactly that should meet no objection from the senior firm. These measures are recommendatory, yet the Council looks to every member, without exception, to act on them.

options.text: Both proposals are prohibited outright, and a breach of either is professional misconduct under the Second Schedule
options.misconception: turns the recommendatory measures into a Schedule offence, when the module describes them as recommendatory measures the Council expects members to implement
options.why: The self-regulatory measures are recommendatory; the Council expects their implementation but the module does not put them in the Schedules. And the joint audit proposal is one the measures encourage, not prohibit.

options.text: The firm may audit the branches because the measures bind only firms of fewer than ten members, and the objection to the small joint auditor is sound
options.misconception: inverts the ten-member line and the joint audit measure, when it is the large firm that is asked to leave branch audits to local firms and not to object to a small joint auditor
options.why: The measure asks statutory auditors of ten or more members to leave branch audits to local firms of fewer than ten, and asks the senior firm not to object to a joint auditor of fewer than five members.

options.text: The firm may audit the branches under the head-office exception, since a statutory auditor always has access to branch accounts
options.misconception: reads the right of access as the exception, when the exception is for branch records actually maintained at the head office and the books here are at the branches
options.why: The right of access to branch accounts is preserved, but it is not the exception. The exception applies where the branch accounting records are maintained at the head office, and here they are kept at the branches.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recommended self-regulatory measures: branch audits by local firms of fewer than ten members with the head-office and significant-operations exceptions, joint audits with firms of fewer than five members, and the recommendatory nature of the measures

items.scenario: A firm of twelve partners is statutory auditor of a company with nine branches. The company proposes that the firm audit every branch itself, since the branch books are maintained at the branches. Separately, the company's board wants to add a three-partner firm as joint auditor; the twelve-partner firm objects that a firm that small should not sit beside it on a large company.

items.stem: Is the trainee right on either point?

options.text: No on both — the ratio excludes only typists and peons, so 22 count and four members suffice, and other fees need no disclosure of any kind
options.misconception: gets the arithmetic right by accident while keeping articled and audit assistants in the count, and drops the disclosure the Council recommends
options.why: Articled and audit assistants are expressly excluded along with typists and peons, so 12 count, not 22; and the Council recommends disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm.

options.text: Yes on both — the ratio is one member for every three non-qualified staff, and fees through another concern breach Clause 2 on sharing fees
options.misconception: misstates the ratio and reads the disclosure measure as a Clause 2 sharing bar, when the ratio is one to five and the measure asks only for disclosure of the payments
options.why: The measure is one member for every five non-qualified staff, and what the Council asks about payments received through a different firm of which the auditor is a partner or proprietor is disclosure as a good and healthy practice, not abstention.

options.text: No on the ratio and half-right on the fees — the ratio is at least one member for every five non-qualified staff excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work, so 12 count and four members exceed the required three; and the disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm is a good and healthy practice the Council recommends, not a legal bar
options.why: The Council's view is that a practising firm doing audit work should carry one member for every five non-qualified staff on its books — the count excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and anyone else not directly engaged in professional work of that kind. Of the 25, the 8 articled assistants, 2 audit assistants, 2 typists and the peon are excluded, leaving 12; 12 divided by five calls for three members, and the firm has four. On the fees, the Council has called it a good and healthy practice for an auditor to disclose what he was paid for other services rendered through a different firm, or firms, in which he is himself a partner or proprietor. That disclosure is recommended, and the partner should make it, but the trainee is wrong to call the fees unlawful on that ground.

options.text: Yes on the ratio — 25 staff need five members and the firm has four
options.misconception: counts every non-member employee, when articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work are excluded from the ratio
options.why: The 25 includes 13 excluded persons. The ratio is measured on the 12 non-qualified staff directly engaged in professional work, and four members are more than the three needed.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recommended self-regulatory measures: at least one member for every five non-qualified staff excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work; disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm as a good and healthy practice

items.scenario: A four-partner firm engaged in audit work employs 25 non-member staff: 8 articled assistants, 2 audit assistants, 2 typists, 1 peon and 12 semi-qualified audit staff. One partner also receives fees for tax consultancy to audit clients through a separate proprietary concern of his, and has never mentioned it to the firm's clients. A trainee says the firm breaches the staff ratio and that the separate fees are unlawful.

items.stem: How many of the six are permitted under the Board's decisions?

options.text: Five — everything but the messaging, since a trademark attorney's work is advice on intellectual property, which the Board calls routine professional work
options.misconception: merges advising on intellectual property rights with acting as a trademark or patent attorney, when the Board permits the first and forbids the second
options.why: The Board's decision draws the line inside the subject: acting as a trademark or patent attorney is not permitted, while professional advice in relation to intellectual property rights is routine professional work.

options.text: Four — the internal auditor may buy the shares, a member holding a certificate of practice may be on the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank, the firm may register on Udyog Aadhar, and a kiosk is permitted where the services are the professional activities of a practising chartered accountant; the messaging is not permitted, and a member may not act as a trademark or patent attorney though advice on intellectual property rights is routine professional work
options.why: The Board's decisions are that there is no prohibition for the internal auditor of a company to acquire or purchase its shares; that a practising member who holds a certificate of practice may join the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank, that role being similar to a Director Simplicitor's; that a firm may register itself on Udyog Aadhar; and that a kiosk run by a member in practice is open to him so long as what he offers over its counter stays inside the professional work the Act allows a practising chartered accountant to do, which filing tax returns and certifying does. Against these, messaging applications are closed to a member who would send messages making people aware of his practice and naming the services he provides, and a member in practice cannot act as a trademark or patent attorney, though professional advice on intellectual property rights is routine professional work and permissible.

options.text: Two — only the share purchase and the Udyog Aadhar registration; a co-operative bank board and a kiosk are business, and messaging a list is fine if the message is factual
options.misconception: rejects the co-operative bank board and the kiosk and accepts the messaging, the reverse of the Board's decisions on all three
options.why: The Board permits the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank and a kiosk providing professional services, and it does not permit messaging applications used to make people aware of a member's practice, factual or not.

options.text: Three — the share purchase, the Udyog Aadhar registration and the kiosk; an internal auditor may not, however, buy shares of a company he audits internally
options.misconception: contradicts itself on the shares and drops the co-operative bank board, when the Board finds no prohibition on the internal auditor's purchase and permits the Board of Management
options.why: There is no prohibition on an internal auditor acquiring the company's shares, and the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank is permitted, making four.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board decisions: messaging applications not permitted, the Board of Management of primary urban co-operative banks permitted, trademark and patent attorney not permitted but intellectual property advice routine, the internal auditor's share purchase, Udyog Aadhar registration, and kiosks for professional services

items.scenario: Six things members in practice propose. (1) Sending a message on a messaging application to a list of local businesses describing the firm's services. (2) An internal auditor of a listed company buying its shares on the exchange. (3) Sitting on the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank while holding a certificate of practice. (4) Acting as a trademark attorney for clients' brand registrations. (5) Registering the firm on the Udyog Aadhar portal of the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. (6) Running a kiosk in a mall offering tax return filing and certification.

items.stem: Which of the five can proceed as proposed?

options.text: Only Hema — a member in practice may be the authorised representative of a foreign company if he is not its auditor; Farah may hold either the audit or the monitoring agency, not both at once; Girish or his firm may not audit the joint venture of a company of which he is a non-executive director; Ishan may take e-return registration where it does not conflict with his employment but cannot certify the returns; and Jaya cannot exercise a lien over client records for non-payment of fees
options.why: The Board's decisions are that it is not permissible for a member or firm that is the statutory auditor of a bank to accept the assignment of agency for specialised monitoring of a customer of the same bank simultaneously, either assignment being open at one time; that a member in practice sitting as a non-executive director of a company must not take, himself or through a firm he is a partner in, the statutory audit of a joint venture of that company, since independence would be impacted; that a foreign company may name a member in practice as its authorised representative here, so long as that member is not its auditor; that e-return registration is open to a member in service where his employment obligation leaves room for it, though he cannot certify the return; and that a chartered accountant cannot exercise a lien over the client's documents or records for non-payment of his fees.

options.text: Hema and Jaya — a lien for unpaid fees is a general right of any professional over papers in his hands
options.misconception: imports the general lien of other professions, when the Board has decided that a chartered accountant cannot exercise a lien over client documents for non-payment of fees
options.why: The decision is specific: a chartered accountant cannot exercise lien over the client documents or records for non-payment of his fees. Jaya must return them.

options.text: Hema, Girish and Ishan — a joint venture is a separate company, and a member in service may certify returns he is registered to file
options.misconception: severs the joint venture from the director's company and lets a member in service certify, when the Board bars the joint venture audit for independence and limits the member in service to registration without certification
options.why: The Board's view is that auditing the joint venture of a company of which the member is a non-executive director would impact independence, and that a member in service may take e-return registration but cannot certify the return.

options.text: Hema and Farah — monitoring a borrower on the bank's behalf is work for the same client, not a conflicting one
options.misconception: sees the monitoring agency as part of the bank audit, when the Board treats the statutory audit of the bank and the monitoring of its customer as assignments a member may hold only one at a time
options.why: The Board does not permit the statutory auditor of a bank to accept the agency for specialised monitoring of a customer of the same bank simultaneously; the member can accept either of the assignments at one time.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board decisions: the statutory auditor of a bank and the agency for specialised monitoring of its customer, the non-executive director and the joint venture's audit, the authorised representative of a foreign company not its auditor, e-return registration by a member in service without certification, and no lien over client records

items.scenario: CA Farah, statutory auditor of a bank, is offered appointment as the agency for specialised monitoring of one of that bank's borrowers for the same period. CA Girish, a non-executive director of Hansa Ltd, is offered the statutory audit of Hansa's joint venture company. CA Hema is offered the role of authorised representative in India of a foreign company she does not audit. CA Ishan, in service, wants to register on the tax portal as an e-return intermediary and to certify the returns he files. CA Jaya has kept a former client's books and vouchers until her unpaid fees are settled.

items.stem: Which of the matters SQC 1 lists on the integrity of a client are engaged, and what must Meera's firm do if it still accepts?

options.text: Nearly all of them — signs pointing to money laundering or to other criminal conduct, why this firm is being sought and why the one before it is not being reappointed, who the principal owners are and what reputation they carry, a scope fenced in by the closed stock records, and a client pressing to hold the fee as low as it will go; accepting in spite of the issues obliges the firm to document how they were resolved
options.why: The integrity head of SQC 1 is a list of seven. Who the principal owners, the key management, the related parties and those charged with governance are, and what business reputation follows them. How the client runs and trades. Whether that group stretches accounting standards, and how it treats its internal control environment. Whether the fee is being pressed as low as it will possibly go. Whether the work is to be fenced in. Whether anything points to money laundering or to other criminal conduct. And what lies behind the approach to this firm and the non-reappointment of the previous one. The searches, the cash, the penny stocks, the complaint about the last auditor, the fee condition and the closed stock records each land on one of them. Acceptance remains open to the firm; what it then owes is a record of how those identified issues were resolved.

options.text: The searches and the fees, and the firm must decline — SQC 1 forbids accepting a client against whom any such indication exists
options.misconception: turns the integrity matters into an automatic bar, when SQC 1 has the firm consider them and, if it accepts despite identified issues, document how they were resolved
options.why: SQC 1 does not forbid acceptance. It has the firm weigh the matters up, and if it takes the work anyway with something already identified, write down how that was settled. The closed stock records are a further matter still — a scope fenced in.

options.text: Only the searches — a client's view of fees and of the previous auditor are commercial matters outside the quality control system
options.misconception: strips fees and the previous auditor out of the integrity matters, when SQC 1 names a client aggressively concerned with low fees and the reasons for non-reappointment of the previous firm
options.why: Both sit on the list. One entry asks whether the client is pressing to hold the fee as low as it will possibly go; another asks what lies behind the approach to this firm and the dropping of the one before it.

options.text: None yet — integrity is judged from the audit evidence once the engagement has begun, and acceptance turns only on whether the firm has the time and staff
options.misconception: postpones the integrity assessment to the fieldwork, when SQC 1 requires the information to be obtained before accepting a new client and lists integrity matters alongside capability
options.why: The firm obtains the information it considers necessary before accepting an engagement with a new client, and integrity is the first of the two heads it considers; capability, competence, time and resources is the second, not the only one.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 acceptance and continuance: the matters on the integrity of a client including money laundering, reasons for non-reappointment of the previous firm, fee pressure and scope limitation, and documenting how identified issues were resolved; Test Your Understanding 3

items.scenario: At a social function a businessman offers CA Meera the tax audits of his five family-owned firms at generous fees, complaining that his present auditor "asks too many questions". Over coffee a week later she learns that the Enforcement Directorate searched his premises a month ago and recovered a large sum in cash, and that the income-tax department has searched them over bogus capital gains on penny stocks. He adds that he does not want the audit fee to be "a rupee more than last year's" and that the stock records at two firms are "not for auditors".

items.stem: What do SQC 1's continuance and withdrawal policies require?

options.text: The manager's course — the continuance policies apply only at the annual renewal of the engagement, and mid-year information waits for it
options.misconception: confines continuance to the annual renewal, when the policies apply the moment the firm obtains information that would have caused it to decline
options.why: The trigger is obtaining information that would have caused the firm to decline the engagement if obtainable earlier, whenever it arrives; the policies then require consideration of reporting responsibilities and of withdrawal.

options.text: Neither course — the firm considers the professional and legal responsibilities that apply, including whether it must report to the person who made the appointment or to regulatory authorities, and the possibility of withdrawing from the engagement or from the client relationship too; if it withdraws it discusses the withdrawal and its reasons with management and those charged with governance, considers whether any requirement obliges it to remain or to report the withdrawal to regulators, and documents the significant issues, consultations and conclusions
options.why: A fact reaching the firm late which, had it surfaced in time, would have kept the firm out of the engagement altogether is what sets the continuance policies going. They send it back to the professional and legal duties in play: is whoever made the appointment entitled to be told, must regulatory authorities be told in certain instances, and is the answer to leave the engagement, to leave the client relationship along with it, or to stay. Going has steps of its own. What the firm may do is talked over at the right level of management and with those charged with governance; if leaving is right, the departure and the reasons for it are put to them as well; the firm asks whether any professional, regulatory or legal duty makes it remain in place, or makes it report its going and the reasons to a regulator; and it closes by documenting the significant issues, the consultations, the conclusions and the ground they stand on. A one-line letter skips the discussion, the reporting question and the record; the manager's view denies a withdrawal that the policies expressly contemplate.

options.text: The firm must withdraw, and must report the promoter to the regulator in every case — SQC 1 makes both mandatory
options.misconception: makes withdrawal and reporting automatic, when SQC 1 requires the firm to consider the possibility of withdrawing and whether a requirement to report exists
options.why: The policies require consideration of the possibility of withdrawal and of whether a professional, regulatory or legal requirement to report exists; neither is automatic, and a requirement to remain in place is itself among the things to consider.

options.text: The partner's course — a firm may withdraw whenever a client's integrity fails, and the less said the better for confidentiality
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as a private act, when the policies require discussion with management and those charged with governance, consideration of reporting to regulators, and documentation
options.why: Leaving is not a private act under SQC 1. It is talked through, with its reasons, at the right level of the client's management and with those charged with governance, the firm asks itself whether a regulator has to be told, and the issues and conclusions go on record.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 continuance where information would have caused the firm to decline: professional and legal responsibilities including reporting to the appointer or regulators, the possibility of withdrawal, and the four withdrawal policies on discussion, reasons, the requirement to remain or report, and documentation

items.scenario: Midway through the audit of a company, the firm learns that its promoter was convicted two years earlier of cheating investors in another venture, a fact the promoter concealed at the time of appointment and which would have led the firm to decline. The engagement partner wants to resign at once by a one-line letter and say nothing further to anyone. A senior manager says the firm cannot withdraw at all once appointed and must simply finish.

items.stem: What does SQC 1 say of the three?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — SQC 1 sets no fixed period for rotation and leaves confirmations to the firm's discretion
options.misconception: reads SQC 1 as silent on both points, when it fixes the confirmation at least annually and the listed-entity rotation at normally not more than seven years
options.why: SQC 1 fixes both. The written confirmation falls due at least once a year, from everyone obliged to be independent; and the engagement partner on a listed audit comes off after a set span that as a rule runs no longer than seven years.

options.text: The nine-year partner may continue if an engagement quality control review is done, since SQC 1 offers rotation and a quality control review as alternative safeguards
options.misconception: uses the general list of familiarity safeguards to override the specific rotation period for listed entities, when the seven-year rotation is the rule for those audits
options.why: Moving the senior people off, or putting an engagement quality control review over the work, are the examples SQC 1 gives of safeguards against familiarity in general. On a listed audit it goes past an example and fixes the outcome: the engagement partner comes off after a set span, as a rule no longer than seven years.

options.text: The confirmation must be obtained at least annually from everyone the Code obliges to be independent, not from partners alone every second year; on a listed entity the engagement partner comes off after a set span, as a rule not more than seven years, so nine is outside it; and the sole practitioner is right that the rotation rule excepts him, the quality safeguard for such a firm being a compulsory peer review
options.why: Two things are wrong with the confirmations — how often they are collected, and from whom. Written confirmation that the independence policies have been complied with falls due at least annually, and it falls due on everyone in the firm whom the Code obliges to be independent, not on the partners alone and not every other year. Familiarity weighs heaviest on the audit of a listed entity, and there the engagement partner comes off the job after a set span, as a rule not more than seven years; nine is past it. One case falls outside that: a listed audit run by a sole practitioner. Quality in such a firm is assured instead by a peer review that is compulsory, which also sees to it that proper reports come out of it.

options.text: Only the nine-year partner is wrong — confirmations from partners suffice because staff independence is the partners' responsibility, and a sole practitioner must rotate like anyone else by handing the client to another firm
options.misconception: narrows the confirmation to partners and denies the sole practitioner exception, when SQC 1 asks all personnel required to be independent and expressly excepts the sole practitioner
options.why: The confirmation comes from all firm personnel required to be independent under the Code, at least annually. And the rotation rule for listed entities carries an express exception for audits conducted by a sole practitioner, backed by mandatory peer review.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 ethical requirements: written confirmation of compliance with independence policies at least annually from all personnel required to be independent; rotation of the engagement partner on listed entities after normally not more than seven years, except a sole practitioner, whose firm is subject to mandatory peer review

items.scenario: A peer reviewer notes three things at a firm. It collects written confirmations of compliance with its independence policies from its partners every second year, and from no one else. The same partner has led the audit of a listed client for nine years. A sole practitioner in the same building has audited a listed company for eleven years and says his firm is outside the rotation rule.

items.stem: Which view matches SQC 1?

options.text: The second partner's — the firm sets criteria considering the nature of the engagement, including the extent of public interest, and the length of service of the senior personnel, with rotating the senior personnel or requiring an engagement quality control review as the example safeguards; and the manager is wrong, because all breaches of independence are promptly notified to the firm for appropriate action
options.why: Familiarity carries particular weight in SQC 1. Keep the same senior people on an assurance engagement year after year and the quality of what they produce can slip, so the firm writes down for itself when a safeguard becomes necessary. Two things bear on that judgement: what sort of engagement it is, and how far a matter of public interest is caught up in it; and the length of service those seniors already have behind them on the job. Two safeguards are offered as examples — move the seniors off, or set an engagement quality control review over the work. No single period is laid down for every engagement; the one fixed span in the standard is the rotation of the engagement partner on a listed entity. As for the junior's discovery, staff are to tell the firm at once of a situation or a relationship that threatens independence, and every breach of independence is promptly notified to the firm so that it can act on it. Nothing waits for the annual exercise.

options.text: The second partner's on the criteria, and the manager's on the breach, since the annual confirmation is the standard's mechanism for catching independence problems
options.misconception: makes the annual confirmation the only channel, when SQC 1 requires prompt notification of circumstances creating a threat and of all breaches, with the confirmation as an additional annual step
options.why: The annual written confirmation sits beside, not instead of, the requirement that personnel promptly notify the firm of threats and that all breaches of independence be promptly notified for appropriate action.

options.text: None — the familiarity threat is a matter for the Code of Ethics, and SQC 1 says nothing about it
options.misconception: pushes the familiarity threat out of SQC 1, when the standard lays special emphasis on it and prescribes criteria and safeguards
options.why: SQC 1 lays special emphasis on the familiarity threat, requires criteria for when safeguards are needed, and names rotation and an engagement quality control review as examples.

options.text: The first partner's — SQC 1 fixes three years for senior personnel and seven for the engagement partner on a listed entity
options.misconception: invents a three-year rule for senior personnel, when SQC 1 sets criteria by public interest and length of service and fixes a period only for the engagement partner on listed entities
options.why: There is no three-year rule. The firm determines the need for safeguards by criteria considering the nature of the engagement and the length of service; the seven-year figure belongs to the rotation of the engagement partner on listed entities.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 on the familiarity threat: criteria by the nature of the engagement including public interest and the length of service of senior personnel, rotation or an engagement quality control review as safeguards, and prompt notification of threats and breaches of independence to the firm

items.scenario: A firm is writing its criteria for when the familiarity threat needs a safeguard. One partner proposes a single rule: any senior person on any engagement for more than three years is moved off it. Another says the criteria should turn on what the engagement is and how long the person has served, with a choice of safeguards. A manager adds that a breach of independence discovered by a junior can wait for the year-end confirmation exercise.

items.stem: How many of the six matters SQC 1 requires monitoring to take into account does the firm fail?

options.text: One — the stale manual; the rest is the firm's choice of method, since SQC 1 fixes the objective of monitoring but not its means
options.misconception: leaves the means to the firm, when SQC 1 prescribes the periodic inspection of completed engagements, who carries the responsibility, and the handling of complaints
options.why: SQC 1 goes past the objective. It calls for finished work to be inspected from time to time, for the responsibility to sit with a partner or a person of standing enough for it, and for complaints and allegations to be handled whoever brings them.

options.text: At least four — the job of monitoring belongs with a partner, or another person inside the firm holding enough of the right experience and authority; finished files must be inspected from time to time, a selection of completed engagements at each pass, as part of judging whether the system was built and operated properly; complaints and allegations must be dealt with whoever raises them, insider or outsider; and shifts in professional standards must be carried through into the policies
options.why: Monitoring under SQC 1 runs continuously, as a weighing-up of the firm's whole quality control system, and periodically it reaches into finished work and inspects a selection of completed engagements. Six matters go into it. Whether the system was built properly and genuinely put into operation. Whether movements in professional standards, and in law and regulation, have been carried through into the policies. Whether the running of the monitoring has been handed to a partner, or to another person inside the firm holding enough of the right experience and authority. Whether complaints and allegations get dealt with — that the firm, or somebody it employs, fell short of professional standards or of what a regulator demands — no matter who brings them, from within or outside the firm. Whether staff who departed from the quality rules face remedial action. And whether anything is done where the rules are found wanting or are simply not complied with. An articled assistant's checklist, no file inspection in three years, an outsider's complaint filed unread and a manual left behind a revised standard fail the third, the first, the fourth and the second in turn.

options.text: Two — the stale manual and the uninspected files; a client's complaint is outside the system, and any staff member may run the checklist
options.misconception: excludes outside complaints and lets anyone monitor, when SQC 1 names complaints by a person within or outside the firm and requires a partner or person of sufficient experience and authority
options.why: A complaint from an outsider sits inside monitoring just as squarely as one from somebody on the staff, and running the process is a job for a partner, or for another person carrying enough of the right experience and authority.

options.text: None — monitoring under SQC 1 is an annual confirmation that the manual exists, which the firm does
options.misconception: reduces monitoring to a confirmation of the manual's existence, when SQC 1 requires evaluation of the system's design and operation with inspection of completed engagements
options.why: Monitoring is a continuing judgement on whether the policies bear on the work, go far enough, actually function and are followed, with finished files inspected from time to time, a selection of completed engagements at each pass. A checklist saying the manual exists is none of that.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 monitoring: periodic inspection of a selection of completed engagements, and the six factors — design and implementation, new developments, responsibility to a partner or person of sufficient experience and authority, complaints and allegations from within or outside the firm, remedial action, and action on deficiencies

items.scenario: A firm describes its monitoring of quality control. An articled assistant fills in a checklist each December confirming that the quality manual exists. No completed engagement file has been inspected in three years. A complaint from a client's audit committee that a manager had signed off work he had not reviewed was filed without inquiry because "clients are not part of the system". The manual has not been updated since a revised auditing standard took effect.

items.stem: Is he right about where his job ends?

options.text: No — monitoring under SQC 1 includes taking appropriate remedial action against personnel who did not conform to the quality control policies, and taking action when deficiencies in the design or operation of the policies and procedures, or non-compliance with the system, are identified; the manager's omissions call for the first and the unwritten consultation procedure for the second
options.why: Two of the six matters reach past the finding. One is remedial action, of a kind fitting the case, against a member of staff who has not held to the quality rules. The other is action where deficiencies in the design or operation of those rules come to light, or where the system is met with plain non-compliance. Finding and recording open monitoring; they do not close it. A manager who skipped a mandatory review on two listed audits has not held to the rules, and a consultation procedure that exists nowhere is a fault of design. Each calls for something to be done out of the monitoring process, whatever the human resources element separately does about performance evaluation.
keywords: deficiencies in the design or operation

options.text: No, because monitoring must be done by an external reviewer who alone can order action
options.misconception: hands monitoring to an outsider, when SQC 1 entrusts it to a partner or other persons with sufficient experience and authority in the firm
options.why: Monitoring stays inside the firm, in the hands of a partner or of others there carrying enough of the right experience and authority; outside review by the Peer Review Board is a different mechanism altogether.

options.text: Yes — monitoring tests whether the system works and reports the result; consequences for individuals and redesign of procedures are for the firm's leadership
options.misconception: splits finding from acting, when SQC 1's monitoring element expressly includes remedial action against personnel and action on deficiencies
options.why: SQC 1 places remedial action against non-conforming personnel and action on identified deficiencies inside the monitoring element itself, alongside the evaluation.

options.text: Yes on the manager, no on the procedure — personnel matters belong to human resources but the design of procedures is monitoring's to fix
options.misconception: keeps remedial action against personnel outside monitoring, when SQC 1 lists it among the matters monitoring must take into account
options.why: Acting on a member of staff who has not held to the quality rules is itself one of the six matters SQC 1 puts inside monitoring, sitting beside action on faults of design or of operation.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 monitoring: remedial action against personnel who did not conform, and action when deficiencies in the design or operation of the policies or non-compliance with the system are identified; responsibility to a partner or person of sufficient experience and authority

items.scenario: A firm's monitoring partner finds that a senior manager ignored the engagement quality control review step on two listed audits last year, and that the firm's consultation procedure was never written down, so nobody follows it. He records both findings and closes the file, reasoning that monitoring is a reporting exercise and that action on individuals belongs to the human resources element, not to monitoring.

items.stem: Who is right?

options.text: Firm B alone — unlisted companies are reviewed by the Peer Review Board and not by the Quality Review Board
options.misconception: confuses the Peer Review Board's review of a practice unit's systems with the Quality Review Board's review of audit quality of particular companies' auditors
options.why: Peer review examines a practice unit's systems and procedures for assurance services and is run by a Board constituted by the Council; the Quality Review Board, set up by the Central Government, reviews the quality of audit services for companies outside Rule 3, which is where Firm B's client sits.

options.text: Firm A — audit quality at a listed company is NFRA's ground, and what the Quality Review Board may look at is the rest: entities Rule 3 leaves out, together with whatever NFRA sends across to it; Firm B's unlisted company is outside Rule 3, so the Board may review it, and Firm C's insurance company is a Rule 3 entity that NFRA has referred, so the Board may review that too
options.why: Section 132(1) of the Companies Act is what sets NFRA up. Compliance with the accounting standards, and with the auditing standards, is its to watch over and to enforce; service quality is its to oversee under section 132(2); and section 132(4) lets it investigate the auditors of the classes of companies Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018 names — listed companies, insurers and banks among them. Audit quality at a listed company accordingly lies with NFRA. What is left to the Quality Review Board is everything Rule 3 does not reach, plus whatever NFRA refers across to it. So a listed company's auditor is NFRA's unless referred; an unlisted company Rule 3 never touched belongs to the Board; and a Rule 3 insurer arrives at the Board on the reference.

options.text: Nobody objects rightly — the Quality Review Board reviews every statutory auditor of a company on a risk-based approach, and NFRA only investigates after the Board reports
options.misconception: gives the Quality Review Board the whole field and makes NFRA its appeal body, when Rule 3 entities are NFRA's and the Board reviews only the rest and what NFRA refers
options.why: The risk-based selection is how the Board chooses among the auditors it may review; it does not extend the Board's reach to Rule 3 entities, whose auditors are overseen and investigated by NFRA directly.

options.text: Firm A and Firm C — an insurance company is a Rule 3 entity and stays with NFRA whatever NFRA says
options.misconception: ignores the reference route, when the Board may review entities referred to it by NFRA even though they are within Rule 3
options.why: The Board's remit covers entities other than those under Rule 3 and those referred to it by NFRA. A Rule 3 insurer referred by NFRA is within the second limb.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — mechanisms for review of quality control: NFRA under section 132 overseeing and investigating the auditors of Rule 3 companies including listed, insurance and banking companies; the Quality Review Board's review confined to entities outside Rule 3 and those referred to it by NFRA

items.scenario: Three auditors receive notices in the same month. Firm A, auditor of a listed company, is asked by the Quality Review Board to submit its audit files for a quality review of that audit. Firm B, auditor of a large unlisted private company that is not within Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, gets the same request from the Board. Firm C, auditor of an insurance company, is asked by the Quality Review Board for its files on a reference made to the Board by the National Financial Reporting Authority. Firm A objects that the Board has no jurisdiction over it.

items.stem: How many of the trainee's statements are correct?

options.text: One — the statement on the Quality Review Board, since it is the Institute's own body
options.misconception: swaps the parentage of the two Boards, when the Peer Review Board is the Council's and the Quality Review Board the Central Government's
options.why: The Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council; the Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government with members nominated by the Central Government and the Council. The trainee has them reversed.

options.text: None — the Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council and issues a peer review certificate only on an unqualified report, a qualified report bringing a follow-on review instead; the Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government with members nominated by it and the Council, its functions are to recommend to the Council, to review the quality of services and to guide members, and its reviews are done by technical reviewers it empanels from across the country; and NFRA's duties include monitoring and enforcing compliance with accounting and auditing standards and overseeing and suggesting measures for quality of service, with investigation under section 132(4) beside them
options.why: The Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council of the Institute; on completion of a review a peer review certificate is issued where the reviewer's report is unqualified, while on a qualified report the practice unit is told the certificate cannot be issued, with the reasons and the due date for a follow-on review decided by the Board. The Quality Review Board has been set up by the Central Government and consists of members nominated by the Central Government and the Council; its functions are to make recommendations to the Council on the quality of services provided by members, to review the quality of services including audit services, and to guide members to improve quality and adherence to statutory and regulatory requirements, and its reviews are carried out by technical reviewers empanelled by the Board on an engagement basis from across the country. NFRA carries two standing duties: compliance with the accounting standards, and with the auditing standards, is its to watch over and to enforce, and the service quality of the professions that deliver that compliance is its to oversee — and having overseen it, to suggest measures that would improve it. Investigation under section 132(4) of the auditors of certain classes of companies is a power sitting beside those duties, not the whole of them.

options.text: Two — the Peer Review Board does issue a certificate after every review, and NFRA does investigate
options.misconception: has the certificate issued on every review, when a qualified peer review report brings a refusal of the certificate and a follow-on review
options.why: A peer review certificate is issued in case of an unqualified report; on a qualified report the practice unit is informed that the certificate cannot be issued, with the reasons and the due date for a follow-on review. And NFRA's role is not confined to investigation.

options.text: One — the statement on NFRA, whose role under section 132 is investigation
options.misconception: reduces NFRA to an investigator, when section 132 gives it the duties of monitoring and enforcing compliance with standards and overseeing quality, with investigation as one power among them
options.why: NFRA's duties are to monitor and enforce compliance with accounting and auditing standards and to oversee the quality of service and suggest measures for improvement; investigation under section 132(4) is additional, not the limit.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — the Peer Review Board constituted by the Council with the peer review certificate on an unqualified report and a follow-on review on a qualified one; the Quality Review Board set up by the Central Government with nominated members, three functions and empanelled technical reviewers; NFRA's duties under section 132

items.scenario: A trainee's notes on the three review bodies read: "The Peer Review Board is set up by the Central Government and issues a certificate to every practice unit it reviews. The Quality Review Board is constituted by the Council of the Institute and its only function is to punish members for poor audits, using reviewers drawn from the Institute's staff. NFRA's duty is limited to investigating auditors after a complaint."

items.stem: Under which of Porter's five forces does the arrival of the household purifier belong?

options.text: Rivalry among existing firms — the water industry has become more crowded and volumes are being shared out
options.misconception: treats any fall in volume as evidence that competition inside the industry intensified
options.why: Rivalry counts the pressure the packaged water suppliers put on each other. Nothing in the facts says a competing jar supplier took Nirjhara's customers; the customers stopped buying jars. If the fall were rivalry, some rival's volume would have risen by what Nirjhara lost, and the whole industry's volume would not have shrunk.

options.text: The threat of new entrants — a new kind of supplier is now competing for the same customers
options.misconception: reads every new competitive threat as somebody entering this industry
options.why: Entry means a firm setting up to sell what this industry sells and taking a share of it. A purifier manufacturer sells appliances; it does not deliver jars, does not compete for shelf space against them and would not be affected by anything that raised the cost of bottling. Calling it entry points the board at entry barriers, which would not help.

options.text: The bargaining power of buyers — households have gained leverage over what they will pay for a jar
options.misconception: converts any loss of pricing power into buyer leverage
options.why: Buyer leverage is about the terms a customer can extract while still buying from the industry — switching cheaply between suppliers, buying in volume, knowing everybody's price. These households are not negotiating a better jar price; they have left the product. A discount aimed at buyer leverage would be spent on people who are no longer in the market.

options.text: The threat of substitutes — the purifier meets the same customer need from outside this industry
options.why: The threat of substitutes is the force that asks whether a customer can get the same job done by something that is not this industry's product at all. A household that treats its own municipal supply has stopped buying packaged water without buying it from a rival, so the pressure is coming from outside the industry rather than from inside it. The purifier maker never joined the packaged water business, so it is not a new entrant; it made the business unnecessary for that household.

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model — classifying an industry fact under the correct force

items.scenario: Nirjhara Springs sells packaged drinking water in twenty-litre jars to homes in three cities. Over two years the municipal supply in all three has become reliable enough to drink after treatment, and a cheap under-sink purifier has appeared in the market that most households can afford outright. Jar volumes fall by a fifth. Nirjhara's sales head reports to the board that the industry now faces a serious threat of new entrants, since the purifier makers have entered the drinking water business.

items.stem: How should the board treat the five forces reading in making this decision?
