options.text: As the wrong instrument, which should be dropped in favour of an internal review, because industry structure does not determine any single firm's profit
options.misconception: swings from treating structure as everything to treating it as nothing
options.why: It is true that structure does not fix one firm's profit. It does fix how much profit is available to compete for, which is exactly what a seven-year commitment is buying into. Dropping the industry reading would leave the board judging its own capabilities with no idea what they will be worth.

options.text: As inapplicable, since the model describes competition among firms already in an industry and Girija is committing new capacity rather than entering
options.misconception: confines the model to incumbents defending a position
options.why: The model is used just as often to test whether a position is worth taking as to describe one already held, and adding capacity is precisely a bet on the industry's future structure. Nothing in it restricts the reading to a firm that is standing still.

options.text: As a sufficient basis, since the five forces between them cover every source of competitive pressure on the company
options.misconception: mistakes a complete list of industry forces for a complete analysis of a decision
options.why: The five headings do cover the pressures that arise from the structure of an industry. They are silent on everything that is specific to this company — its costs, its capabilities, its people, its balance sheet — and on everything moving outside the industry's boundary. A decision resting on structure alone assumes Girija is an average firm in an average world for seven years.

options.text: As a starting point on industry structure, to be read alongside a scan of the wider environment and an honest look at what Girija itself owns
options.why: The model describes how profit is competed away in an industry, which is a real and necessary finding. It is a starting point and not the whole case, for two reasons the board can act on. It says nothing about what Girija itself owns that rivals do not, so it cannot explain why this company would earn more than the industry average — the firm's own activities and resources answer that. And it reads the industry as it stands, so changes moving through the wider environment over a seven-year payback have to be scanned separately.

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model — why the analysis is not used in isolation

items.scenario: Girija Ceramics is deciding whether to commit to a new sanitaryware plant that will take seven years to pay back. Its strategy team presents a five forces reading of the sanitaryware industry, concludes that the industry is moderately attractive, and recommends the commitment on that basis alone. A director asks whether anything else is needed before the board signs.

items.stem: Which primary activity of the value chain does the night shift's work belong to?

options.text: Service — setting aside packs whose seal has failed is quality assurance for the customer, which is after-sale work
options.misconception: reads any customer-protecting check as the after-sale service link
options.why: Service is what the firm does once the customer has the product — complaints, repairs, replacement, support. A seal checked before the carton leaves the bay is a control inside the outbound link. The same defect found by a shopkeeper a week later would be service, and the difference is when it is caught.

options.text: Outbound logistics — the goods are finished and are being held and moved towards the customer
options.why: The link a task belongs to is decided by where the goods stand and what is being done to them, not by the building the work happens in. These cartons have already been made and packed; nothing done on the night shift changes the product. Holding finished goods, matching them to orders and moving them out to whoever will receive them is outbound logistics, and it stays that link when it is performed on the factory premises.

options.text: Operations — the work is done inside the plant by plant employees, which is what operations means
options.misconception: sorts an activity by the department or the premises rather than by what happens to the goods
options.why: Operations is the link where inputs are converted, so that what comes out differs from what went in. The night shift converts nothing. Sorting by location would put the receiving dock, the canteen and the plant accounts office into operations too, and the chain would stop separating anything.

options.text: Inbound logistics — the shift is warehousing work, and warehousing is the receiving and storing link
options.misconception: treats all storage as one link, ignoring which end of the chain the stock sits at
options.why: A warehouse serves both ends of the business. Material waiting to be worked on sits at the front of the chain and finished goods waiting to be despatched sit at the back, and the same racking can hold both. What is being held here is output, so the link is the outbound one.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — matching an activity to a primary link

items.scenario: Ambika Snack Foods runs one factory. A night shift works in the despatch bay: it pulls finished cartons off the pallets the packing lines built during the day, checks each carton against the distributor orders for the next morning, sets aside any pack whose seal has failed, arranges the rest in the order the trucks will be unloaded on their routes, and loads them. The plant head describes this shift as part of operations because it happens inside the factory.

items.stem: What does this pattern tell the board about how the two costs should be judged?

options.text: The buying cost should be brought back down, because a support activity that exceeds its budget is not adding value to the product the customer pays for
options.misconception: treats support activities as overhead to be minimised rather than as work the primary links depend on
options.why: Support work is in the chain because the primary links cannot run without it, and the margin is what survives after all of it is paid for, not after the primary links alone. Cutting the specification back would return the scrap, the claims and the penalty, and every rupee of that would land in somebody else's budget.

options.text: It shows only that costs were moved between departments, so the total is unchanged and the exercise was accounting rather than strategy
options.misconception: assumes a cost that falls in one place must have risen by the same amount in another
options.why: Rework, scrapped material, warranty repairs and a delivery penalty are real outflows, not transfers. They disappeared rather than moving, and a linkage is valuable precisely because the amount removed downstream is larger than the amount added upstream.

options.text: The higher spend on buying and inspection is a linkage — money added in one activity that removed more cost from later ones, so the two must be judged together
options.why: Buying is a support activity that serves the whole chain, and incoming inspection sits at the front of it. The scrap, the warranty claims and the penalty all arose further down. Spending more in one place and taking more out of another is a linkage, and the only honest test is the effect on the chain as a whole. Judging the purchase manager on his own budget would restore the specification that was causing the later losses, and the saving would be reported as an improvement.

options.text: It shows the castings supplier was unreliable, so the firm should acquire a foundry and stop buying castings outside
options.misconception: jumps from a linkage inside the chain to owning another stage of it
options.why: Nothing in the facts says the supplier could not meet the tighter specification; the evidence is that it did, once the specification was written and the lots were checked. Acquiring a foundry answers a dependence the firm has just shown it does not have, and converts a purchase into fixed assets that then have to be kept busy.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — support activities, linkages and margin

items.scenario: Rewa Rail Components tightened the specification it buys castings against and added an inspection of every incoming lot. Buying costs and inspection costs both rose. Over the next year scrap on the machining lines fell sharply, warranty claims from two railway customers stopped, and a delivery penalty the firm had been paying was not levied. The purchase manager's budget is over, and he is being asked to bring buying costs back to where they were.

items.stem: Which of the two is a sustainable competitive advantage, and on what reasoning?

options.text: The discount — being the cheapest on the comparison lists is what buyers actually respond to, so it is the advantage the customer values
options.misconception: confuses being valued by the customer with being defensible against a competitor
options.why: Customer relevance is one test and it is passed here. It is not the only test. An advantage every rival can copy by making the same announcement stops being an advantage the moment one of them does, and the customer's regard transfers with the price.

options.text: The mining lease — a rival cannot buy the same thing, while the discount can be matched in a week
options.why: An advantage lasts only where a competitor with money and a year cannot obtain the same thing or something that does the same job for the buyer. Any producer can match a price; it costs a decision, not an asset, and doing so leaves both firms poorer and neither ahead. The lease is exclusive, is tied to a deposit that does not exist elsewhere within the haul radius, and runs long enough to shape the cost base, so the freight advantage it creates is one no rival can simply purchase.

options.text: Both — a firm that is cheapest today and holds a scarce input for twenty years has two advantages running at once
options.misconception: counts anything currently working as an advantage, without asking what stops it being copied
options.why: Being ahead today and holding an advantage are different claims. The list position is a result the firm is buying with margin and can hold only for as long as it pays; the lease is a position rivals cannot take. Counting both teaches the board to defend the one that cannot be defended.

options.text: Neither — an advantage in cement can only come from the brand, because cement from any producer is the same product
options.misconception: assumes a commodity leaves no room for advantage other than branding
options.why: Where the product is identical, the advantage moves into the cost of delivering it, and in cement that is largely freight. A deposit inside the haul radius is exactly the kind of advantage a commodity permits, and it is more durable than a brand claim on a bag of material buyers regard as interchangeable.

citation.ref: Competitive advantage — durability and the test of imitability

items.scenario: Marudhar Cement tells its lenders it holds two competitive advantages. The first is a launch discount that has taken it to the top of the price comparison lists in its region. The second is a mining lease it won in an auction over the only limestone deposit within three hundred kilometres of its grinding units, running for the next twenty years; every other producer in the region hauls limestone from beyond that radius.

items.stem: What is wrong with the board's reasoning?

options.text: It tests the wrong thing — cost is an outcome, and a competence is judged on customer relevance, difficulty of imitation and the breadth of markets it could open
options.why: Cost is an outcome, and it is the outcome a different strategy aims at; Prantik has chosen to win on turnaround and reporting quality rather than on price. The three questions that decide whether a capability is a core competence are whether it reaches something the customer values, whether a competitor would find it hard to imitate, and whether the same underlying skill opens a breadth of markets. The platform may well pass all three; the board has argued none of them.

options.text: The platform cannot be a core competence, because a competence has to be a skill held by people and a platform is a system the firm bought
options.misconception: rules out any competence with technology in it, instead of asking what was accumulated around it
options.why: It is right that a purchased asset on its own is rarely a competence. What decides it is whether the firm has built something around the asset that others cannot assemble — the rules, the validation, the interpretation, the people who improved it over years. That question has to be asked rather than answered by the presence of software.

options.text: Nothing — a capability that produces a lower cost per unit than every competitor is by definition a core competence
options.misconception: treats a cost advantage as itself a test of a core competence
options.why: A lower unit cost can come from an old plant, a cheap lease or a large order, none of which is knowledge the firm has accumulated. The tests ask what the capability is and whether anyone can copy it, not what number it produced last year.

options.text: The reasoning is sound but incomplete — the board should also confirm that the platform is unique to the firm, which is the fourth test
options.misconception: adds uniqueness as a separate test and leaves the cost argument standing
options.why: Uniqueness is not a fourth test sitting beside the others; it is what the imitation question is already asking, in the more useful form of how hard the thing would be to copy. Adding it changes nothing, and the cost argument the board actually made stays unexamined.

citation.ref: Core competency analysis — which parameters are tests of a core competency

items.scenario: Prantik Diagnostics runs pathology laboratories and has chosen to compete on turnaround and on the quality of its reporting rather than on price; its tests are priced above the local average and volumes are rising. Its board wants to name a core competence for the annual report and proposes its automated reporting platform, on the ground that it has brought the cost per test below the nearest competitor's.

items.stem: What is the strategic risk the board should be told about?

options.text: There is no strategic risk — covering the low end and the premium end at once widens the market served and spreads the firm's exposure
options.misconception: reads two positions as a hedge rather than as two operating models fighting over one cost base
options.why: Spreading exposure works where the two businesses are separately run and separately costed. Here they share the mill, the sales force and the overhead, so the range, changeovers and service the bespoke line needs land in the cost base the other half is promising to make the lowest in the market.

options.text: The risk is diversification — the bespoke line is a new business, and the board should be shown what the two businesses actually share
options.misconception: labels a second position in the same market as entry into a different business
options.why: Diversification means entering a business the firm is not in. Sonapur is selling home textiles in both halves, to the same kind of customer, through the same mill. The problem is not that the businesses are unrelated; it is that the two ways of competing are incompatible inside one cost structure.

options.text: The firm holds neither position — the bespoke half puts cost back into a base that has to be the lowest, and the cost-cutting half strips out what a premium buyer is paying for
options.why: The two ways of winning a broad market ask opposite things of the same operating model. Winning on price needs sameness, long runs and thin overhead; winning on difference needs variety, service and spending the buyer notices. Run through one mill, one sales force and one overhead, each half undoes the other: the firm ends with costs above whoever is truly cheapest and a proposition below whoever is truly better, and is beaten from both sides.

options.text: The risk is that the plan is a focus strategy applied to too broad a market, and it should be aimed at one segment instead
options.misconception: renames the plan as focus, which describes narrowing the market rather than holding two positions in it
options.why: A focus strategy takes one of the two ways of winning and points it at a single segment. This plan does not narrow anything — it aims at the whole market twice, in two incompatible ways. Choosing a segment would not resolve the contradiction; choosing a position would.

citation.ref: Generic competitive strategies — cost leadership against product differentiation

items.scenario: Sonapur Looms sells home textiles across the country. Its three-year plan has two halves. One cuts the range to four fabrics, runs them in long uninterrupted batches, closes the design studio and moves everything to one national distributor, to bring the price below every competitor. The other launches a bespoke line with a consultant who visits the customer's home, a two-week promise on custom sizes and a national advertising campaign. Both halves are to be run through the same mill, the same sales force and the same overhead.

items.stem: How should the board classify the move, and what must the note establish?

options.text: Related diversification — the two would be run by one board and financed from one balance sheet, which is the overlap that makes a move related
options.misconception: mistakes common ownership and shared capital for a shared activity
options.why: Shared money and shared management attention are exactly what an unrelated move has and all that it has; if they made a move related, no acquisition would ever be unrelated. The test looks for an operating activity the two businesses actually perform in common.

options.text: Backward integration — the acquisition takes the company into a stage of activity beyond its own, and integration is judged by whether it removes a dependence
options.misconception: calls any acquisition of a different kind of business an integration move
options.why: Integration means moving along this business's own chain — towards what supplies it or towards who sells to its customers. A hospital neither supplies a snack plant nor distributes its output, so it sits on no part of Ambika's chain and no dependence is being removed.

options.text: Unrelated diversification — nothing in the two chains of activities is shared, so the case must rest on Ambika being a better owner of the hospitals than whoever holds them now
options.why: A move is related only where a named activity is genuinely shared — a plant, a route to the customer, a technology, a brand the new buyer already relies on for that decision. Snack distribution to small shops and hospital operation share no such activity. That makes it unrelated diversification, and the argument has to change in kind: with no overlap to measure, the case rests on Ambika being a better owner than whoever holds them now, or on earnings that hold up when snacks do not.
keywords: a named activity is genuinely shared

options.text: Related diversification — both businesses sell to households and both rely on the company's name, which are the shared resources the classification asks for
options.misconception: accepts a category of customer as a shared activity
options.why: Serving households is a description of who pays, not of any work the two businesses do in common. Almost every consumer business shares it, which is why it cannot classify anything. A name that persuades a shopper to try a namkeen is not a name a family chooses a hospital on.

citation.ref: Related and unrelated diversification — classifying the move and what each has to prove

items.scenario: Ambika Snack Foods, a packaged snack maker with its own plant and a distributor network reaching small shops, proposes to acquire a chain of three hundred-bed hospitals. The note to the board calls the acquisition related diversification, on the ground that both businesses serve households, both depend on a trusted name, and both would be run by the same board.

items.stem: What should the board be told about the proposal?

options.text: It is horizontal integration, and the first question is whether the acquisition of competitors at the same stage would raise a competition-law objection
options.misconception: applies the sideways label, and its regulatory question, to a move up the chain
options.why: Horizontal means buying somebody doing the same work at the same stage — another refiner. Farms and a crushing unit are at an earlier stage and are not Halda's competitors, so no rival leaves the market. The competition question that follows a sideways move is not the one this proposal raises.

options.text: It is forward integration, since the company would be extending its control over more of the chain that ends with the shopper
options.misconception: treats any extension along the chain as movement towards the customer
options.why: Direction is decided by which way along the chain the firm moves. Farms and crushing sit before refining, so this is a move backward. Forward would mean taking on the distribution or the retailing that stands between Halda and the shopper — which is where the problem in these facts actually lies.

options.text: It is backward integration and it is the right answer, because owning the input takes cost out of the product and restores the margin the grocery chains are taking
options.misconception: reaches for integration whenever margin is thin, without asking which force is causing it
options.why: Naming the move is right and the conclusion is not. Owning the seed can only recover the margin the seed suppliers were earning, and the facts say that margin was not moving. The chains would go on renegotiating quarterly against a firm now carrying farms and a crushing plant it has to keep loaded.

options.text: It is backward integration, and it answers a dependence Halda does not have — the pressure named in the facts sits with the grocery chains, not with the seed suppliers
options.why: Acquiring farms and a crushing unit is a move towards what supplies the business, which is backward integration. That move buys control over an input the firm was dependent on others for. The facts describe the opposite: many small seed suppliers, steady prices, no shortage. The squeeze comes from four chains that hold Halda's route to the shopper and can move volume between suppliers for nothing. The proposal would add fixed assets and a plant to keep busy, and leave that untouched.

citation.ref: Backward, forward and horizontal integration — naming the move and testing what it answers

items.scenario: Halda Edible Oils refines and sells branded cooking oil. Its margin has been falling for six quarters. Its oilseed is bought from many small suppliers at prices that have been steady and it has never been short of seed. What has changed is at the other end: four large grocery chains now account for most of its volume, they carry their own label beside Halda's, they have moved buyers between them without paying anything to switch, and they renegotiate terms every quarter. The chief executive proposes acquiring oilseed farms and a crushing unit.

items.stem: Should the two structure this as a strategic alliance or as a joint venture, and why?

options.text: A joint venture — a separate company gives each partner freedom to run the plant its own way without shared decision-making
options.misconception: reads the joint venture as the looser arrangement, on the reasoning that a new company runs itself
options.why: It is the tighter of the two. Forming a company together means the assets, the people and the decisions move into one entity that both own and both govern, so neither can direct it alone. Independent running is what a contract preserves, and it is what this project cannot have.

options.text: A joint venture — one entity has to hold the licence and the assets, and both sides need a say in decisions neither can take alone
options.why: The choice turns on how much shared control the work needs. Here a single incorporated entity has to hold the licence and the assets, capital from both sides is locked in for four years, and each side depends on decisions the other makes about a shared process. A jointly owned company supplies the governance for exactly that: both own it, both sit on its board, and neither can move it alone.

options.text: A strategic alliance — the object is to obtain the German firm's process, and an alliance is the structure through which intellectual property is transferred
options.misconception: chooses the structure for access to technology, which either form can carry
options.why: Access to a process is a licensing term, and a licence can sit inside a contract or inside a jointly owned company equally well. It does not decide the structure. What decides it here is the licence in one entity's name, the locked-in capital and the shared operating decisions.

options.text: A strategic alliance — a contract is quicker to sign and cheaper to unwind if the plant does not work, and both sides keep their own assets
options.misconception: picks the structure by exit cost rather than by the control the work requires
options.why: Cheap exit is a real advantage of a contract and it is the wrong test here. A contract leaves each party deciding its own matters, which cannot work when one licensed entity must own the plant and each side depends on the other's day-to-day decisions. The ease of leaving is bought by giving up the governance the project needs.

citation.ref: Strategic alliance compared with a joint venture — shared ownership and control

items.scenario: Chandrakala Pharma and a German specialty chemicals maker plan to build one plant in India to produce an intermediate neither can make alone. Chandrakala brings the site, the approvals and the workforce; the German firm brings the process and the equipment. The regulator will licence the plant only to an entity incorporated in India whose owners are identified on the application. The plant will take four years to build, both sides are putting in capital, and each will depend day to day on decisions the other makes about the process and the output.

items.stem: What is wrong with the third measure?

options.text: Non-financial measures like a lounge count cannot be verified, so the process perspective should carry only measures that convert into rupees
options.misconception: rejects non-financial measures as such, which removes the reason the scorecard exists
options.why: The scorecard exists because the non-financial measures move first: time off the road and turnaround change before the accounts do. Restricting the process row to rupees would drop the two measures in this draft that are actually right.

options.text: It sits under the wrong heading — a lounge is what the passenger experiences, so the measure belongs under the customer perspective and should simply be moved
options.misconception: corrects the placement and leaves the deeper fault, that the measure suits a strategy the firm has not chosen
options.why: Moving it fixes a classification and keeps the problem. Utkal has chosen the lowest fare, so lounges are spending it has decided not to do; the measure would report on that spending just as misleadingly from the customer row as from the process row.

options.text: A measure has to come from the strategy the firm is running, and lounges track a premium position Utkal has not taken
options.why: The first two measures drive cost out of each coach and each run, which is what a lowest-fare operator is trying to do, so they are leading indicators of the money it will report. Lounges add cost the fare cannot carry and belong to a firm competing on experience. A measure has to come from the strategy the firm is running, or the scorecard reports faithfully on a plan the company never adopted.
keywords: the strategy the firm is running

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it — a scorecard is balanced when all four perspectives carry measures, and a lounge count is a legitimate internal process measure
options.misconception: reads balance as covering every heading rather than as choosing measures that fit the strategy
options.why: Balance means the four viewpoints are represented instead of the financial one standing alone. It has never meant that any initiative deserves a row. A full scorecard whose measures come from somewhere other than the strategy is a complete instrument pointed at the wrong target.

citation.ref: The balanced scorecard — choosing a measure that follows the strategy

items.scenario: Utkal Coach Lines runs intercity buses and competes on the lowest fare on every route it serves; its plan is built on standardised coaches, high occupancy and stripped-back overhead. Its draft balanced scorecard puts three measures under the internal process perspective: the average time a coach spends off the road for maintenance, the turnaround time between two runs, and the number of premium lounges opened at bus stations.

items.stem: Which of Porter's five forces has changed for Kadamba, when no new laboratory has opened?

options.text: The bargaining power of buyers — farmers can now demand lower rates, because they know a certificate has become easier to obtain
options.misconception: converts an incumbent's own pre-emptive price cut into leverage exercised by customers
options.why: Buyer leverage would mean the farmers pressing for terms and getting them. The facts run the other way: Kadamba cut its rates and offered the contracts without being asked. Customers gain from the change, and gaining from something is not the same as causing it. The pressure comes from the open door, and the farmers are its beneficiaries.

options.text: Rivalry among existing firms — the three licensed laboratories are competing harder, which is why rates have fallen
options.misconception: reads a price cut as evidence that the firms already inside are fighting each other
options.why: Rivalry counts the pressure the laboratories already in the district put on one another, and nothing in the facts says either of the other two changed a rate or chased Kadamba's customers. The cut is aimed at a laboratory that does not exist yet. Calling it rivalry would send Kadamba to study its two neighbours, when what changed is the door all three of them sit behind.

options.text: The bargaining power of suppliers — the equipment makers now sell to anyone, so they have gained leverage over the laboratories
options.misconception: reads an input becoming freely available as the supplier gaining power
options.why: A supplier has leverage when the buyer cannot readily go elsewhere and terms can be dictated to him. Equipment sold openly to whoever wants it is the picture of a supplier with little leverage rather than much. The open sale matters in these facts because it lowers the barrier to entry, and it says nothing about what the equipment makers can extract from Kadamba.

options.text: The threat of new entrants — the force measures how easily a firm could enter, so it presses on price before anybody does
options.why: The threat of new entrants asks how hard it is for a firm to set up and take a share, not how many have set up. Withdrawing the licence removed the barrier that was holding the district to three laboratories, and the equipment is on open sale, so entry is now a decision anybody can take. The rate cut and the lock-in contracts are what an incumbent does once the door is open, and they are the evidence that the pressure is already working. A force can press on price before anyone actually walks through.
keywords: how hard it is for a firm to set up

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model — the threat of potential entrants, read before an entrant arrives

items.scenario: Kadamba Assay Services runs a soil and water testing laboratory in a farming district. Until last year a state licence was needed before a laboratory could issue a test certificate, and only three laboratories in the district held one. That requirement has been withdrawn: any laboratory meeting a published equipment standard may now issue certificates, and the equipment is sold openly to whoever wants it. No new laboratory has opened. Kadamba has already cut its published rates and has begun offering annual contracts to its largest customers.

items.stem: What does the second half of a five forces analysis require the board to do with that table?

options.text: Say what the grading means for profit in this industry, then change Anantpur's own position against the force pressing hardest
options.why: A grading is a description, and the marks go to the answer that ends somewhere. Two conclusions are owed. The first is what the grading means for the industry's profit: where several forces press at once the margin leaks out of the industry, whichever firm holds the share. The second is about this firm, and it is the harder one — substitution presses hardest, so the board has to change Anantpur's own position against it by putting the network to work carrying what an electronic file cannot replace. Hoping a force weakens is not a plan.

options.text: Ask the banking association to slow the move to electronic filing, so that the force pressing hardest on the industry is reduced
options.misconception: answers a force by hoping it weakens rather than by changing the firm's position against it
options.why: The analysis names a pressure; the response it calls for is a change in what this firm does, because the force itself is somebody else's decision. Banks are moving to electronic filing because it is cheaper and faster for them, and no request from a supplier of the older method reverses that. The months spent asking are months not spent finding what the network can carry instead.

options.text: Nothing further — the table is the analysis, and grading each of the five forces is what the model asks for
options.misconception: mistakes a completed grading for a completed analysis
options.why: The five headings sort the pressure an industry is under, and sorting it is the first half of the work. No board can act on the word severe. The model is used to reach two findings, whether profit survives here and what this firm does about the force pressing hardest on it, and a table stopping before both has been filled in rather than used.

options.text: Conclude that the industry cannot be defended and put an exit to shareholders, since a severe substitute leaves no position worth holding
options.misconception: reads an unattractive industry as a verdict on this particular firm
options.why: The reading describes the structure of an industry. It does not say what this company owns or what else those assets could do, and firms earn well inside hostile industries for exactly that reason. An exit may be right in the end, and it would be a conclusion drawn from looking at Anantpur's own network, staff and customer relationships, not from the grading of the industry.

citation.ref: Porter's five forces model — from a graded industry to a decision the firm can act on

items.scenario: Anantpur Document Couriers carries physical files between bank branches and their regional offices. Its strategy team grades the five forces and hands the board a table: rivalry moderate, entry easy, supplier power low, buyer power high, and substitution severe, because the banks are moving to electronic filing and two of them have already stopped sending files from half their branches. The table ends there. The board asks what the analysis tells it to do.

items.stem: Which primary activity does the receiving clerk's work belong to?

options.text: Marketing and sales — matching what arrived against the client's schedule is how Vaidehi settles the scope of the job and its fee
options.misconception: assigns a physical handling step to the link that won the work, because one document is used in both
options.why: Finding buyers, quoting and closing the sale is marketing and sales, and at Vaidehi that happened before any carton was sent. The schedule is used twice, once to agree the job and once to check what came in, and the link is decided by what is being done at that moment, which here is receiving and verifying an input. A document appearing in two links does not merge them.

options.text: Operations — Vaidehi sells a service, so every step performed on a client's papers is part of delivering that service
options.misconception: collapses the whole chain into operations whenever the business has no physical product
options.why: Operations is the link where the input is converted, so that what leaves differs from what arrived. Scanning and indexing convert; counting and racking do not. If the absence of a physical product made everything operations, the sales call, the invoice and the courier back to the client would be operations too, and the firm would have one link and nothing left to compare.

options.text: Outbound logistics — the clerk is handling stored cartons, and storage is the link that holds goods until they move
options.misconception: treats all storage as one link, without asking which end of the chain the stock is sitting at
options.why: Storage happens at both ends. Papers waiting to be scanned are input held before the work; papers scanned and waiting to go back are output held after it. The same rack can hold both, so the rack decides nothing. What decides the link is the stage the material has reached.

options.text: Inbound logistics — the papers are the input, and they are being received, verified and held before any work is done on them
options.why: The five primary links exist in a service business as much as in a factory; what arrives and is held is a booking, a specimen or, here, a client's file. Nothing the clerk does changes the papers. Receiving them, checking them against the schedule and holding them until a bay is free is inbound logistics. Calling the whole service operations gives up the sorting altogether, and a chain that sorts nothing separates nothing.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — sorting a primary activity in a service business

items.scenario: Vaidehi Legal Process Services digitises and indexes case papers for law firms. Its receiving clerk opens the sealed cartons a client sends, counts the papers against the schedule enclosed with them, notes any file listed but not present, and puts the cartons into numbered racks where they wait until a scanning bay is free. The operations head says all of Vaidehi's work is operations, because the firm has no physical product and everything done to a client's papers is the service being sold.

items.stem: Which of the two may go to a contractor, and on what test?

options.text: Both — neither delivery nor installation converts an input, so both sit outside the links where the firm's value is actually created
options.misconception: treats outbound logistics and service as adding nothing, because the product was finished before them
options.why: Every primary link is in the chain because the product passes through it, and the customer is paying for a fitted kitchen rather than for a stack of modules. Installation is where that promise is kept or broken, and it is also the link feeding the design team. Deciding by whether an activity converts material would send the selling and the after-sale support out of the door as well.

options.text: The delivery fleet — the test is whether the firm holds an advantage in the link and whether a linkage runs through it, and only the crews hold both
options.why: A link where the firm has no advantage and no linkage worth keeping is a link somebody else can run. Delivery is such a link: the crates are the same, the roads are the same, and a carrier does it for less. The installation crews are not, because their reports are a linkage — work in one activity that removed cost from another, here the cutting the firm no longer does. Hand the crews out and the reports stop, quietly, and the on-site cutting comes back.

options.text: The installation crews — installation is support work rather than a primary link, and support work is the overhead a firm under margin pressure cuts first
options.misconception: calls a primary link support work, and then treats support work as overhead
options.why: Installation is the link through which the finished product reaches the customer, so it is primary and not support at all. Even were it support, that would not make it disposable: support work sits in the chain because the primary links cannot run without it, and the margin is what survives after every part of it is paid for. Cutting the crews removes the one link these facts show earning its keep twice over.

options.text: Neither — outsourcing gives up work the firm controls, and a contractor cannot be held to the standard an employee is held to
options.misconception: answers the outsourcing question with a general fear rather than by looking at the particular link
options.why: Standards are a matter of the contract and the supervision, and a road carrier moving crated modules can be held to a delivery window. The chain answers this case by case: what is the firm better at than the market, and where does money spent in one activity save more in another. Refusing every outsourcing keeps a delivery cost the facts show is avoidable.

citation.ref: Michael Porter's value chain — linkages, and reading an outsourcing decision off the chain

items.scenario: Devagiri Modular Kitchens designs, manufactures and fits kitchens in customers' homes. Under margin pressure it proposes to hand two things to contractors. The first is its delivery fleet, which carries finished modules to the customer's address; local road carriers quote less than the fleet costs and the modules travel in the same crates either way. The second is its installation crews, who report every site problem back to the design team; three changes made on those reports removed most of the on-site cutting the firm used to do.

items.stem: How should the board describe the coating method?

options.text: As a sustainable competitive advantage — two competitors have failed to copy it, and imitability is the test that decides whether an advantage lasts
options.misconception: stops at the imitation test and calls a resource an advantage before it has produced a single sale
options.why: Being uncopyable is what makes an advantage last once it exists; it does not bring one into being. An advantage exists when a customer picks this firm over the alternatives at a price that covers the cost of serving him, and here no customer is being asked to and the price is the same either way. What the board holds is a resource with the durability of an advantage and none of its effect.

options.text: As no advantage at all — a method that has produced no premium in fifteen years has been shown by the market not to matter
options.misconception: reads an absent result as proof the capability is worthless, when nothing was ever offered to the market
options.why: The market has not rejected the coating; it has never seen it. There is no separate price, no mention in the quotation and no reason for a buyer to ask about it. A verdict from buyers needs an offer first, and the honest description is that the test has not been run.

options.text: As a resource that is not yet an advantage — it survives the imitation test, but the firm is not arranged to turn it into a sale
options.why: Three questions decide an advantage and this method answers only one of them clearly. It is hard to copy: two rivals tried and failed, and the method was accumulated rather than bought. Whether buyers care is untested, because nobody has told them. And the firm is not arranged to use it — one price, one catalogue line, a sales force paid on units and a quotation with nowhere to record it. Until that changes the method earns nothing, and what is missing is organisation rather than a better claim.
keywords: organisation rather than a better claim

options.text: As a core competence rather than a competitive advantage, since it is know-how held across a team, and no further change is needed
options.misconception: relabels the capability and treats the naming as the work, leaving the same resource unsold
options.why: It may well be a core competence, being accumulated know-how spread across people rather than a purchased asset. That label answers a different question and changes nothing on the ground: the sales force is still paid on units and the quotation still has no line for a coating. Naming a capability correctly is not the same as arranging the business to earn from it.

citation.ref: Competitive advantage — a durable resource the organisation is not arranged to exploit

items.scenario: Suvarnarekha Optics has a lens-coating method built up over fifteen years across its process team and its testing bench; two rivals have tried to reproduce it and could not. Coated lenses sit in the same catalogue as the plain ones at the same price, the sales force is paid on units shipped, quotations carry no line for a coating, and the buyers at Suvarnarekha's customers have never been told the coating exists. The board wants to describe the method to its lenders as a sustainable competitive advantage.

items.stem: What does the core competence framework say about the board's conclusion?

options.text: It is a core competence, so Ponnani should raise its price to the engine maker for the remaining four years, while it still cannot be replaced
options.misconception: converts a finding about capability into a short-term pricing move and leaves the four years unused
options.why: The engine maker cannot switch quickly, so a higher price might hold for a while. It answers nothing about where this firm stands in five years, and it spends the goodwill of the one customer still buying. The framework points the other way: four years is the time available to prove the know-how in a second market, and a price rise does not use it.

options.text: It was never a core competence, because almost all output went to one customer and a competence has to serve many buyers
options.misconception: turns customer concentration into a fourth test, which is not one of the three
options.why: The three tests ask about relevance to the customer, difficulty of imitation, and the breadth of markets the capability could open. How many customers the firm sells to today is a fact about its order book. Concentration is a real risk and it belongs in a different conversation; here it is being used to settle a question about capability.

options.text: The competence is the fatigue-life know-how rather than the spring, so the breadth test asks which other markets that know-how could open
options.why: A core competence is a bundle of skills and know-how spread across parts of a company, and the valve spring is one product it happens to serve. Three questions decide whether a capability qualifies, and the third is breadth: could the same underlying skill carry the firm into products it does not sell today. That is precisely the question the board has skipped. Losing this customer removes a market; it does not remove the metallurgy and the test bench, and the board's work now is to find what else needs them.
keywords: spread across parts of a company
carry the firm into products it does not sell today

options.text: The board is right — a capability serving one product ends when that product ends, which is what makes it a product strength rather than a competence
options.misconception: identifies a capability with the single product it currently serves, which is what the breadth question exists to test
options.why: A capability attached to one product may indeed be a product strength, and the way to find out is to ask the breadth question rather than assume its answer. Springs are not the only components judged on fatigue life. If the know-how transfers it was a competence all along, and the board is about to write off the firm's most valuable thing on a definition it never tested.

citation.ref: Core competency analysis — the breadth test when the product a competence serves is ending

items.scenario: Ponnani Precision Springs makes valve springs for one diesel engine maker, which takes almost all of its output. The skill behind them is a metallurgy and fatigue-testing practice built across its metallurgists, its shop supervisors and its test bench over two decades, and the engine maker has never found a second source. That customer has now announced it will stop building diesel engines within four years. Ponnani's board concludes that its core competence is ending along with the engine.

items.stem: Which of the savings are consistent with the position Kaveripakkam has taken?

options.text: None of them — a firm competing on difference cannot cut cost without weakening its position, and should raise its price instead
options.misconception: reads differentiation as indifference to cost, and treats a price rise as the only lever a premium firm holds
options.why: Winning on difference requires the premium to stay above what the difference costs to provide, which makes cost a live question rather than an irrelevant one. Warehouse and print savings touch neither the estate nor the clearance. Raising the price instead asks the buyer to fund a freight arrangement he never asked for and cannot see.

options.text: The warehouses and the print runs — those cut cost the buyer never sees, while the blend and the panel are what the premium is paid for
options.why: Choosing to win on difference does not mean spending freely. It means carrying cost where the buyer notices the result and cutting it everywhere else. Warehousing and print runs sit outside what the buyer is paying for, so consolidating them takes cost out and leaves the position untouched. The blend and the tasting panel are the position: buyers said the estate and the clearance are why they pay twice the price, and removing either leaves a premium with nothing behind it.
keywords: carrying cost where the buyer notices
outside what the buyer is paying for
the blend and the tasting panel
a premium with nothing behind it

options.text: The blend and the print runs — moving to a common blend is what the lowest-cost producer does, and matching its cost base is how the pressure is relieved
options.misconception: imports the yardstick of a cost leader into a firm holding the opposite position
options.why: The cheapest producer blends because sameness is what its position needs, and it prices accordingly. Kaveripakkam prices at twice a blended pack. Copying one half of another position leaves it selling a blend at a premium, undercut by whoever is genuinely cheapest and passed over by whoever still names an estate.

options.text: All four — a cost is a cost, and a firm under margin pressure should take an even cut from every part of the business
options.misconception: cuts uniformly, which is the one method certain to remove whatever the position depends on
options.why: An even cut treats every rupee as the same rupee, and they are not the same: some spending is the reason the customer pays twice and some of it he never sees. Taking the same share out of the tasting panel as out of the warehouses saves the same money and dismantles the reason the price holds, which is the whole of what this firm has to sell.

citation.ref: Generic competitive strategies — which costs a differentiator may cut without losing its position

items.scenario: Kaveripakkam Speciality Teas sells single-estate tea at about twice the price of a blended pack. Every pack names the estate and the picking, and a tasting panel clears each lot before it is packed; buyers surveyed last year said those two things are why they pay the price. Costs have risen and the board wants savings. Four proposals are on the table: buy in tea for a common blend across estates, close two of five regional warehouses and consolidate freight, stop the tasting panel, and print the existing pack artwork in longer runs.

items.stem: How should the board treat the note?

options.text: As a move that must be refused — an unrelated acquisition carries a burden no board can discharge, so only related diversification is sound
options.misconception: turns a heavier burden of proof into a prohibition
options.why: Unrelated moves succeed where the buyer really is the better owner, bringing capital, discipline or management the business was short of. The burden is heavier because there is no overlap to measure, not because the answer is settled in advance. Refusing the whole category spares the board the argument it ought to be making the note produce.

options.text: As a related move after all — the bagasse would fire the hotels' boilers, which is a genuine shared input between the two businesses
options.misconception: converts a token overlap into a relatedness claim, without asking what the sharing is worth
options.why: A related move has to name the shared activity and say roughly what the sharing is worth, because an overlap nobody can size is a story rather than a saving. Boiler fuel is a small line in a hotel's costs and the bagasse has other buyers already. An overlap produced in a later paragraph, after the case was made on other grounds, decorates the argument instead of being it.

options.text: As a strong case — protecting the dividend against a bad cane year is what diversification is for, and steadier earnings are worth paying for
options.misconception: treats risk spreading as a benefit the company creates, when the shareholder can obtain it directly
options.why: Steadier group earnings are real, and the question is who they are worth something to. An investor holding a sugar mill because he wants exposure to sugar did not ask for a hotel, and one who wants both can hold both without the mill paying a premium for a business it has never run. That is why the smoothing argument is marked down rather than credited.

options.text: As an unrelated move resting on the weakest reason available — steadier earnings are something a shareholder can arrange far more cheaply
options.why: Sugar milling and hotel keeping share no operating activity, so this is unrelated diversification and the heavier burden of proof applies. The note rests on smoothing earnings, which is the argument investors mark down: a shareholder who wants both exposures buys both shares, and pays a broker rather than an acquisition premium for the privilege. What is missing is the claim that could carry the move, that Nallamala would be a better owner of these hotels than whoever holds them now.
keywords: a shareholder who wants both exposures

citation.ref: Related and unrelated diversification — the burden of proof an unrelated move carries

items.scenario: Nallamala Sugar Mills earns well in years when the cane crop is good and badly when it is not. It proposes to buy a chain of budget hotels. The board note gives one reason: hotel earnings do not move with the cane crop, so group earnings would be steadier and the dividend safer. A later paragraph adds that the mill's surplus bagasse could fire the hotels' boilers.

items.stem: What should the board be told first about the proposal?

options.text: It is horizontal integration, and because it takes rivals out of the market the competition question comes before the strategic one
options.why: Buying firms doing the same work at the same stage is horizontal integration, and it is the only one of the three directions that removes a competitor rather than a dependence. Two of four suppliers in one city leaving the market is a change in the market itself, so whether the combination is permitted is the question that has to be answered first; savings the board approves are worth nothing if the purchase cannot proceed. Control over the supply chain is not what this move buys.
keywords: removes a competitor rather than a dependence
the question that has to be answered first

options.text: It is backward integration, since the note's own reason is the saving on cement purchases, which is control over an input
options.misconception: names the direction from the reason given for the move rather than from the stage the acquired firms occupy
options.why: Direction is decided by where the acquired business sits on the chain. The two plants batch concrete, which is what Panchmahal does; neither of them makes cement. Buying more of the same stage may indeed improve the price paid for cement, because a larger buyer orders more, and that is a consequence of size rather than a move up the chain.

options.text: It is horizontal integration, and the test is the same as for any integration, namely whether the move removes a dependence the firm is under
options.misconception: applies the vertical test to a sideways move, which answers a different problem altogether
options.why: Naming the move is right and the test has been borrowed from the wrong direction. Buying a supplier or a channel is judged on whether the firm was dependent on it. Buying a competitor is judged on what removing that competitor does to the market, and on whether the combined operation is worth more than the two apart, which is why a regulator looks at it and usually does not look at the vertical moves.

options.text: It is forward integration, because the combined firm would serve more of the city's sites and so stands closer to the person who finally buys
options.misconception: reads a larger share of the same stage as movement towards the customer
options.why: Forward means taking on the stage that stands between the firm and the final buyer — the distributor, the branch, the site contractor. Panchmahal sells to sites now and would sell to sites afterwards. Serving more of them is a wider position at the same stage, and the chain has not been extended in either direction.

citation.ref: Horizontal integration — what follows from a sideways move, as against a vertical one

items.scenario: Panchmahal Ready-Mix Concrete runs three batching plants in one city and is one of four suppliers there. It proposes to buy the two smallest of the other three. Its note calls the purchase an integration that will give the company control over its supply chain, and asks the board to approve it on the strength of what the combined plants would save on cement purchases and truck movements.

items.stem: Which structure fits this work, and on what reasoning?

options.text: A joint venture — incorporating a company shows commitment and gives the arrangement a permanence a three-year contract cannot
options.misconception: picks the structure to signal seriousness rather than to supply the control the work needs
options.why: A separate company is the tighter of the two arrangements, because neither owner can move it alone, and that tightness is worth having when assets, capital and decisions genuinely have to be held in common. None of them do here. The chairman would be buying a board, a set of accounts and a shareholding to dispose of in three years, in exchange for a signal the obligations in a contract can carry by themselves.

options.text: A strategic alliance — a contract is quicker to sign and cheaper to unwind, and cost is what decides between the two forms
options.misconception: reaches the right structure by the wrong test, which fails the moment the work does need shared control
options.why: The conclusion happens to be right and the reasoning would mislead in the next case. A contract is cheaper, and that is not the question; a project needing one licensed entity with identified owners takes the more expensive form regardless of what it costs. The test is the control the work requires, and here it points at the cheaper structure by coincidence.

options.text: A joint venture — the two will be sharing revenue on each other's products, and revenue can only be divided through an entity both of them own
options.misconception: assumes a share of money requires shared ownership, when a contract can set the split
options.why: How money is divided is a term, and a contract states terms. A commission, a margin, a referral fee and a revenue share are written into agreements between separate companies every day. Nothing in these facts creates a common pool of income needing an owner; each side invoices its own customers at its own prices.

options.text: A strategic alliance — nothing here has to be owned or decided jointly, so a contract carries the whole of it
options.why: The structure follows how much shared control the work needs. Each side keeps its own assets and its own people, each quotes and invoices its own sales, no regulator wants an entity of its own, and neither depends on a decision the other takes day to day. A strategic alliance under a contract carries all of that and ends when the term does. Being taken seriously is a matter of what the agreement obliges each side to do, not of what has been incorporated.
keywords: how much shared control the work needs
each quotes and invoices its own sales
a strategic alliance under a contract

citation.ref: Strategic alliance compared with a joint venture — work that needs no shared control

items.scenario: Sringeri Solar installs rooftop solar systems, and a battery maker wants to work with it. Each would offer the other's product to its own customers for three years, quoting its own prices and invoicing its own sales. Neither would hold anything belonging to the other, the staff stay where they are, no approval is needed for either party to sell what the other makes, and either may walk away at the end of the term. Sringeri's chairman wants a jointly owned company incorporated anyway, so that both sides take the relationship seriously.

items.stem: What is the fault in the draft?

options.text: The fault is the number of measures — a perspective needs several before it can be relied on, and one measure to a row is too thin
options.misconception: invents a rule about how many measures a row carries, in place of the rule about what they measure
options.why: The instrument sets out what a company is trying to achieve under four headings and puts a measure against each aim, and a small number of well-chosen measures is what keeps a board reading it. Adding a second money figure to every row would double the draft and leave each of its faults exactly where it was. What is wrong here is what the measures are, not how many of them there are.

options.text: The fault is in the learning and growth row alone, and training spend per employee should be moved to the financial perspective where it belongs
options.misconception: corrects a placement and leaves the fault, which is that three rows report outcomes rather than what leads to them
options.why: Moving one measure tidies the table and changes nothing about what the table can tell the board. Revenue per customer and cost per batch would still be results, and the customer and process rows would still hold no measure that turns early. A scorecard whose measures are all outcomes is not repaired by rearranging which outcome sits in which row.

options.text: Every row holds a money figure, so the three perspectives that exist to move first have been filled with measures that move last
options.why: The last three perspectives are in the scorecard because they turn before the accounts do: a firm sees its skills, its cycle times and what its customers think change well before the effect reaches its results. Revenue per customer, cost per batch and training spend per employee are outcomes already in the ledger, so the draft reports four times over on what has happened and gives no early warning at all. A comparable unit is not the point of the instrument.

options.text: There is no fault — a scorecard is balanced when all four perspectives carry a measure, and one unit throughout makes the rows comparable
options.misconception: reads balance as filling every heading, and treats comparability as the purpose of the instrument
options.why: Balance means the four viewpoints are represented instead of the financial one standing alone, and a row filled with a financial measure has represented nothing new. Comparability is a convenience. The scorecard exists because the things that predict the results are not in the same unit as the results, and insisting on one unit is how this draft lost them.

citation.ref: The balanced scorecard — why the three non-financial perspectives exist

items.scenario: Tirthahalli Speciality Chemicals has drafted its first balanced scorecard. All four perspectives carry a measure: the financial row holds return on capital employed, the customer row holds revenue per customer, the internal process row holds cost per batch, and the learning and growth row holds training spend per employee. The finance director says the instrument is complete, because every perspective is filled and every measure is in rupees and can be set against last year's.

items.stem: Under which element of the McKinsey 7S framework does the bar-coded scanning routine belong?

options.text: Strategy, because the routine exists to deliver the one-day report the company competes on
options.misconception: reads anything done in service of a plan as being part of the plan
options.why: Everything a well-run company does is meant to serve its plan, so this test collapses six headings into one. Strategy is the plan for staying ahead of rivals, and here that plan is the promise of a report within a day — which the situation says was already the company's promise before the scanning existed. The routine is one of the means, and the model separates means from plan on purpose.

options.text: Systems, because it is a repeatable procedure that governs how the daily work is carried out
options.why: Systems are the routines and procedures by which the daily work actually gets done, and a scan at four fixed points with an alert on a missed one is precisely that. The sorting rule is to ask what kind of thing the fact is rather than which department introduced it. This one is a rule that runs every day without anybody deciding afresh, so it is a system rather than a plan, a reporting line or a capability.
keywords: routines and procedures by which the daily work actually gets done
what kind of thing the fact is
a rule that runs every day

options.text: Structure, because the arrangement is what makes the town centres and the city laboratory work as one
options.misconception: reads any arrangement that makes several sites act together as a question about reporting lines
options.why: Structure answers who reports to whom and where a decision may be taken, and the situation says plainly that the reporting lines were not touched. Coordination between sites can be achieved by a routine or by a reporting line, and these are different answers. Calling this structure would send the board looking for a manager to appoint when what it has built is a procedure.

options.text: Skills, because staff at every centre had to be taught to scan correctly before the arrangement could work
options.misconception: mistakes the training that a new routine requires for the routine itself
options.why: Almost every new procedure needs somebody taught to follow it, so this test would send nearly everything to skills and the heading would stop meaning anything. Skills is what the workforce is able to do. The scanning routine would still exist, still be written down and still raise alerts if the people operating it changed tomorrow, which is what shows it is not lodged in the people.

citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — placing one observed fact under a single element

items.scenario: Suvarna Diagnostics runs collection centres in small towns and promises a report within a day. Samples were going missing between the town centre and the city laboratory, and nobody could say where. Over the past year the company introduced a bar-coded routine under which every tube is scanned at four fixed points — when it is drawn, when it leaves the centre, when it reaches the laboratory and when the result is released — and a missing scan raises an alert at head office the same hour. Nothing else about the company changed. The reporting lines are as they were, the collection staff are the same people, and the promise made to patients is the one the company always made.

items.stem: Under which element of the McKinsey 7S framework does the supervisors' reluctance to stop a dryer belong?

options.text: Structure, because supervisors plainly do not have the authority to stop a dryer
options.misconception: reads a decision nobody is taking as a decision right that was never granted
options.why: The situation states the opposite — the rulebook gives the supervisor that authority and nobody disputes it. This is the commonest wrong placement in the framework, and it matters because the two findings have different repairs. If the right were missing, the repair would be to delegate it; the right is already delegated, so delegating it again would change nothing at all.

options.text: Shared values, because the company evidently values output more than the quality of what it ships
options.misconception: promotes one manager's conduct into a belief held by the whole organisation
options.why: Shared values are what the organisation believes it is for, and they show up in what everybody does rather than in what one person says on one shop floor. Here a written rule that protects quality is the company's stated position, and a single manager is working against it. That is a person out of step with the values, which is a different finding from values that are themselves wrong.

options.text: Style, because the right exists on paper and the manner of the person in charge is what stops anyone using it
options.why: Style is how those in charge behave and what the place feels like to work in, and this finding is entirely about conduct. The test that separates it from a reporting-line fault is whether the right to act was granted, and here the rulebook grants it in writing. A right that exists and is not used is a finding about the manner of the person in charge, not about where the authority sits.
keywords: whether the right to act was granted
a right that exists and is not used

options.text: Systems, because there is no procedure telling a supervisor when a dryer must be stopped
options.misconception: reads a behaviour that a written rule already covers as a missing procedure
options.why: A rule exists and it is written down, which is what a system is. Writing a second and more detailed one would not touch the reason the first is ignored. When a procedure is on the page and is not being followed, the fault has moved out of systems and into the people or the way they are led.

citation.source: ICAI Paper 6 Revision Test Paper, November 2026
citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — the suggested answer treating a centralised decision-making set-up and an autocratic leadership manner as findings under two separate elements

items.scenario: Ambika Seeds processes and grades seed at one plant. Its written rulebook says that a shift supervisor may stop a dryer on his own authority if he suspects the grain is being scorched, and nobody at the company disputes that the rule says so. In practice the dryers are never stopped. The plant head treats any stoppage as a personal failure by the supervisor on duty and says as much in front of the whole shift, so supervisors run damaged batches through rather than raise the matter. A visiting consultant is asked to place this finding.

items.stem: How should the consultants answer the managing director's two conditions?

options.text: Both conditions should be resisted — the seven carry equal weight, and the soft elements need the longest lead time, so they are the ones to begin on rather than to postpone
options.why: Hard and soft describe how visible an element is and how quickly it can be altered, not how much it matters. The seven carry equal weight, and the soft ones are slow precisely because they live in the people and move only as the people do — which makes a long lead time a reason to start early rather than a reason to defer. Shared values, not strategy, sits at the centre, because every other element is judged against what the company says it is for.
keywords: a long lead time a reason to start early
not strategy, sits at the centre

options.text: Neither condition matters much — the framework is a checklist for describing an organisation, so the order in which the seven are examined makes no difference to the findings
options.misconception: treats the model as a list to be filled in rather than as a test of whether the parts fit each other
options.why: If the model were a checklist, seven separate and correct descriptions would be a complete answer, and they are not. What earns the marks is naming which element is out of step with which other, and the order of work follows from that — the slowest element to move sets the timetable for the whole change.

options.text: The first condition should be resisted but the second accepted — strategy genuinely is the centre of the model, and the remaining six are worked out from it
options.misconception: puts strategy at the centre of the diagram, where shared values actually sit
options.why: Getting the weighting right and the centre wrong still produces the wrong order of work. Shared values occupy the middle because they are the standard the other six are measured against. Treating strategy as the centre invites a board to write a new plan and then expect structure, systems, staff, skills and style to fall in behind it, which is the exact failure the framework was built to expose.

options.text: Both conditions should be accepted — the framework separates hard from soft exactly so that a firm can fix what is documented and measurable before spending on culture
options.misconception: reads the hard and soft labels as a ranking of importance rather than as a statement about visibility and speed
options.why: The labels record that three elements are written down in plans, charts and manuals while four are not, which is a difference in how you find them and how fast you can move them. It has never been a difference in weight. A firm that alters its plan, its chart and its procedures and leaves the people, their capabilities and the beliefs of the place untouched has changed the half that shows.

citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — the digest's objective answer testing three contentions about the relative weight of hard and soft elements and about which element is central

items.scenario: Nandini Cold Chain has hired consultants to work through its operations with the 7S framework after a season of spoilage losses. At the opening meeting the managing director sets two conditions. He wants the three hard elements taken first, because they can be altered inside a quarter while the soft ones would take years, and he wants strategy treated as the element the other six follow from, since in his view everything a company does is downstream of its plan.

items.stem: What is the most useful thing a 7S reading gives this board?

options.text: That the hard elements have been dealt with properly, so the remaining trouble lies with the people and is a matter of execution rather than design
options.misconception: counts strategy and structure as the whole of the hard side and then blames the shortfall on staff
options.why: Systems is a hard element too, and the order-taking routine is a system that still holds a wholesale minimum. So the hard side was not dealt with either. Reading the rest as an execution failure by the people also misdescribes it — a driver who cannot be in two places at once and a salesman never taught to open a shop account are shortfalls in staff and skills, which are things the board provides, not things the people withheld.

options.text: That the plan was misjudged, since a year of trying has produced nothing and the wholesale arrangement worked for twenty years
options.misconception: reads the failure of a change as evidence that the change was wrong, when nothing around it was moved
options.why: Judging a plan by whether it landed assumes everything else was ready to carry it, and here three elements were left standing exactly as they were. The framework exists to stop this conclusion being reached too early — until the routine, the drivers and the selling capability have been moved to match the plan, nobody has yet found out whether the plan works.

options.text: That the elements which were never moved can be named exactly — the order-taking routine, the number of drivers and what the sales team is able to do — and that the plan cannot land until each is changed
options.why: The board altered strategy and structure and left systems, staff and skills where they were, so a plan aimed at hundreds of small shops is being run on a routine, a fleet and a selling capability built for eight large ones. Naming the elements which were never moved is the whole value of the reading, because each one names its own repair — drop the minimum order size, put more drivers on smaller rounds, and teach the sales team to open a shop account.
keywords: naming the elements which were never moved
each one names its own repair

options.text: That the elements should be ranked, the hard ones repaired first, and the soft ones left to settle behind them once the structure is right
options.misconception: treats the soft elements as consequences that follow automatically once the hard ones are correct
options.why: Nothing here settles by itself. A sales team that has only ever negotiated annual contracts will still be doing that next year unless somebody trains it, and the depot will still be short of drivers unless somebody hires them. The soft elements move slowest, so a repair sequence that leaves them until last guarantees the plan stays unlanded for another year.

citation.source: ICAI Paper 6 Revision Test Paper, November 2026
citation.ref: The McKinsey 7S framework — the suggested descriptive answer naming the misalignment between a firm's plan and the systems, staffing and capability left in place around it

items.scenario: Bhairavi Foods sold pickles to a handful of wholesale buyers for twenty years and has now decided to supply small neighbourhood shops directly instead. The board rewrote the plan and redrew the organisation chart, giving each district its own head. A year on, the change has not landed. The order-taking routine still refuses any order below a wholesale minimum, so most shops cannot place one. The depot has the same number of drivers it had when it served eight buyers and now has to reach hundreds of small addresses. The sales team knows how to negotiate an annual contract with a wholesaler and has never had to open an account with a shopkeeper. The board is being asked whether the new plan was a mistake.

items.stem: Under the Kano model, which sort of customer requirement does the repeated confirmation represent?

options.text: A performance requirement, since fewer confirmations plainly leave the customer happier and more of them leave the customer unhappier
options.misconception: treats a nuisance as a dial that can be turned down, when the right answer is that it should not be there at all
