options.why: Once the fabric is expected to bring in less than it costs to make — 660 against 765 — the yarn behind it comes down as well, and what the same yarn costs to buy in today is normally the best reading of what it is now worth. That is 430 a kilogram.
keywords: the yarn behind it comes down as well
what the same yarn costs to buy in today is normally the best reading of what it is now worth

options.text: At 310, what the yarn itself would fetch unspun.
options.misconception: measures a material held for use by what it would fetch if it were sold instead
options.why: What the yarn would fetch unspun is beside the point while it is held to be spun. A material can sit in the books above what it would fetch on its own and still be carried correctly, because the sale the mill is counting on is the fabric's and not the yarn's. 310 a kilogram is a price the mill is not going to take.
keywords: the sale the mill is counting on is the fabric's and not the yarn's
can sit in the books above what it would fetch on its own

options.text: At cost, 500.
options.misconception: leaves the yarn at cost even where the fabric it feeds is heading for a loss
options.why: A material held to be worked up is not taken below cost while the thing it will become is still expected to cover what that thing costs to make. A kilogram costs 500 to buy and 265 to spin, 765 altogether, against fabric proceeds of 660. A fall in the yarn's own price does not on its own reach the books.
keywords: not taken below cost while the thing it will become is still expected to cover what that thing costs to make
does not on its own reach the books

citation.ref: para 32

items.scenario: Neelambari Mills buys a yarn and spins it into fabric. At 31 March 2026 it holds 4,000 kilograms of the yarn, bought at 500 a kilogram. The same yarn now costs 430 a kilogram to buy in. Sold unspun, as it stands, it would fetch 310 a kilogram. Spinning one kilogram into fabric costs a further 265, and the fabric off a kilogram is expected to sell for 660 after the costs of selling it.

items.stem: What is basic earnings per share for the year to 31 March 2026?

options.text: 4.3 a share, the new shares counted from 1 October and no earlier.
options.why: Rights priced at or above the market — 117 against 90 — give nothing away, so the issue is shares sold for cash and the months before it are left as they were. The 4,80,000 new shares count from their own date, and earnings of 1,13,40,000 on that weighted average come to 4.3.
keywords: give nothing away, so the issue is shares sold for cash

options.text: 3.94 a share, the profit spread over the shares in issue at the year end.
options.misconception: divides by the shares in issue at the year end instead of a count weighted over the year
options.why: The closing count is not the denominator. Money that arrived on 1 October cannot have been earning through the six months before it, so shares are counted for the part of the year each block was actually in issue. Spreading 1,13,40,000 over all 28,80,000 shares for the whole year pushes the figure down to 3.94.
keywords: The closing count is not the denominator
counted for the part of the year each block was actually in issue

options.text: 4.39 a share, the months before the issue restated for the free element inside it.
options.misconception: restates the earlier months for a free element even where the rights were priced at or above the market and there is none to restate
options.why: Rights priced under the market hand the existing holders part of their new shares for nothing, and a part given away is treated as though it had always been in issue. The factor is the market price of 90 over the theoretical price once the rights are taken up, 94.5 here, which lifts the pre-issue months from 24,00,000 shares to 22,85,714. Earnings of 1,13,40,000 over a weighted average of 25,82,857 shares give 4.39.
keywords: hand the existing holders part of their new shares for nothing
a part given away is treated as though it had always been in issue

options.text: 4.73 a share, the profit spread over the shares in issue at the start of the year.
options.misconception: drops the new shares altogether and divides by the opening count
options.why: The opening count is not the denominator either. The 4,80,000 shares issued on 1 October were in issue for half the year and have to be counted for that half, so dropping them altogether flatters the figure to 4.73 on earnings of 1,13,40,000.
keywords: The opening count is not the denominator either
have to be counted for that half

citation.ref: para 26 and para 27(b), with Appendix A, para A2

items.scenario: Shubhankar Ltd had 24,00,000 equity shares in issue on 1 April 2025. On 1 October 2025 it offered its holders one new share for every 5 they held, at 117 a share, and the offer was taken up in full. The shares changed hands at 90 each in the market immediately before the rights were exercised. Profit for the year to 31 March 2026 attributable to the equity holders was 1,13,40,000.

items.stem: What deduction under section 10AA is available for A.Y. 2026-27?

options.text: Nothing — the third band of five years is reached only by creating a Special Economic Zone Re-investment Reserve, and none was created
options.misconception: applies the reserve condition of the third band to a year in the second band
options.why: The reserve is the condition for years eleven to fifteen. A.Y. 2026-27 is the unit's eighth year, in the 50% band, which carries no reserve condition at all.

options.text: 50% of ₹60,00,000, that is ₹30,00,000, because the whole profit of an SEZ unit is treated as derived from export
options.misconception: skips the apportionment, treating all of the unit's profit as export profit
options.why: Section 10AA(7) apportions: the export profits bear to the unit's profits the same proportion as export turnover bears to total turnover. A unit that sells ₹1,50,00,000 in the domestic market has profits that are not derived from export.

options.text: 100% of ₹37,50,000, because a unit that began before A.Y. 2020-21 remains in the full deduction band for as long as it exports
options.misconception: forgets that the 100% band is five years, not the life of the unit
options.why: The 100% band is five consecutive assessment years beginning with the year the unit begins; the next five are at 50%, and the five after that need a reserve. A unit that began in 2018-19 left the full band after A.Y. 2023-24.

options.text: 50% of ₹37,50,000, that is ₹18,75,000 — A.Y. 2026-27 is the eighth year of the unit, inside the second band of five years at 50%, and the export profits are the unit's profits in the ratio of export turnover to total turnover
options.why: The unit began in the previous year 2018-19, so A.Y. 2019-20 is its first year. The 100% band runs from A.Y. 2019-20 to A.Y. 2023-24 and the 50% band from A.Y. 2024-25 to A.Y. 2028-29; A.Y. 2026-27 sits in the second band of five years at 50%. Export profits, the unit's profits in the ratio of export turnover to total turnover, are ₹60,00,000 × ₹2,50,00,000 ÷ ₹4,00,00,000 = ₹37,50,000, and half of that is ₹18,75,000.
keywords: second band of five years at 50%
ratio of export turnover to total turnover

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1)(i) and (ii) — the 100% and 50% bands — and section 10AA(7), the export-turnover proportion

items.scenario: Orion Softech Ltd, which pays tax under the normal provisions of the Act, has a unit in a Special Economic Zone that began providing software services on 1 August 2018. For the previous year 2025-26 the unit's profits are ₹60,00,000, its total turnover ₹4,00,00,000 and its export turnover, all of it received in India in convertible foreign exchange by 30 September 2026, ₹2,50,00,000. No reserve has ever been created.

items.stem: What figures go into the section 10AA proportion?

options.text: Export turnover ₹2,63,00,000 and total turnover ₹4,88,00,000 — the late proceeds leave export turnover only, and the freight and insurance leave both
options.why: Export turnover means the consideration received in, or brought into, India in convertible foreign exchange within six months from the end of the previous year, so the ₹25,00,000 received in December 2026 is out of the numerator but remains part of the sales in the denominator. Freight and insurance attributable to delivery outside India are excluded from export turnover by Explanation 1, and by Circular 4/2018 the same amount is excluded from total turnover so that the proportion is like against like: ₹3,00,00,000 − ₹12,00,000 − ₹25,00,000 = ₹2,63,00,000 over ₹5,00,00,000 − ₹12,00,000 = ₹4,88,00,000.

options.text: Export turnover ₹3,00,00,000 and total turnover ₹5,00,00,000 — the accounts' figures are used as they stand
options.misconception: uses the book figures without applying the statutory definition
options.why: The accounts show sales; the section asks for consideration received in foreign exchange in time, net of freight, telecommunication and insurance for delivery abroad. Both adjustments change the proportion.

options.text: Export turnover ₹2,88,00,000 and total turnover ₹4,88,00,000 — the late proceeds still count, since the goods were exported in the year
options.misconception: treats export as the physical shipment rather than the receipt of foreign exchange in time
options.why: Receipt is what the definition turns on. The sale price has to land in India in convertible foreign exchange inside a six-month window that opens when the previous year closes, and only the competent authority can stretch that window. December 2026 is past 30 September 2026 and no extension was given, so ₹25,00,000 is not export turnover for this year.

options.text: Export turnover ₹2,63,00,000 and total turnover ₹5,00,00,000 — the exclusions in the definition of export turnover do not touch total turnover, which is not defined
options.misconception: reads the exclusions as one-sided, the position the Circular was issued to close
options.why: That was the revenue's argument, and the Supreme Court rejected it: what is excluded from export turnover on account of delivery abroad is excluded from total turnover too, and Circular 4/2018 directs officers to follow that. A one-sided exclusion would shrink the numerator alone and deny a deduction for profit that was in fact exported.

citation.ref: Explanation 1(ia) to section 10AA — export turnover, the six-month receipt rule and the exclusions — with CBDT Circular No. 4/2018 dated 14 August 2018 on excluding the same amounts from total turnover

items.scenario: An SEZ unit of a company shows export turnover of ₹3,00,00,000 in its accounts for the previous year 2025-26. That figure includes ₹12,00,000 of freight and insurance for delivering the goods to customers abroad, and ₹25,00,000 of sale proceeds that were received in India in convertible foreign exchange only in December 2026, with no extension from the Reserve Bank of India. Total turnover in the accounts is ₹5,00,00,000.

written.scenario: Saral Infra Ltd signs a road contract for a fixed price of ₹200 crore. Two further amounts are in the contract. First, an early-completion bonus of ₹20 crore, payable in full if the stretch is handed over by 31 December and nil otherwise; the project head assesses the chance of hitting that date at 70%. Second, a traffic-linked incentive that will pay nil, ₹5 crore or ₹10 crore with assessed probabilities of 20%, 50% and 30%; the payout turns on a count run by an independent authority in a corridor where the company has never built before, and the count will not be published for another three years.
written.question: Determine the amounts of variable consideration to be estimated, say which estimation method fits each and why, and state how the constraint applies to each.

points.text: Identify that both the bonus and the incentive are variable consideration, because the consideration promised in the contract includes amounts that vary with the occurrence or non-occurrence of a future event.

citation.ref: Determining the transaction price — variable consideration

points.text: State the two methods — the expected value, which weights every outcome in the range by its probability and adds the weighted figures, and the most likely amount, which is the single outcome carrying the highest chance. The choice is not a free choice; one method is picked because it predicts better, and the entity selects the method that better predicts the amount of consideration to which it will be entitled and applies one method consistently throughout the contract, though different types of variable consideration within a single contract may take different methods.

citation.ref: Para 53 — estimating the amount of variable consideration

points.text: Apply them. The bonus has only two possible outcomes, so the most likely amount is the better predictor and the estimate is ₹20 crore. The incentive has a range of outcomes that is neither binary nor concentrated on one value, so the expected value is the better predictor: (0 × 0.20) + (5 × 0.50) + (10 × 0.30) = ₹5.50 crore.

citation.ref: Para 53(a) and (b) — expected value and most likely amount

points.text: Apply the constraint. An estimate enters the transaction price only where, once the uncertainty later clears, it is highly probable that no significant reversal will follow in the revenue already booked. The incentive fails that test on three of the standard's own factors — the count sits outside the entity's influence, resolution of the uncertainty lies three years away, and the entity's experience with similar contracts is limited — so it is constrained to nil, while the ₹20 crore bonus is included.

citation.ref: Paras 56-58 — constraining estimates of variable consideration

points.text: Add that the transaction price is updated at the end of each reporting period, including the assessment of whether an estimate is still constrained, so a published traffic count in a later year brings the incentive into revenue then.

citation.ref: Reassessment of variable consideration

keywords: updated at the end of each reporting period

written.scenario: Three unrelated contracts at Auster Ltd. (a) A one-year contract to run a client's monthly payroll; if the client moved to another processor mid-year, that processor would not have to re-do the months already run. (b) Construction of a turbine hall on the customer's own land, where the customer takes title to the work in progress as it is built. (c) A survey vessel built to a naval buyer's specification, which contractual and practical restrictions prevent Auster from redirecting to any other customer, and where the contract gives Auster a right, enforceable at any time, to payment for the work completed to date including a reasonable margin.
written.question: State the criteria the standard sets for recognising revenue over time and say which one each contract meets.

points.text: State the rule first: revenue is recognised over time if any one of three criteria is met, and if none is met the performance obligation is satisfied at a point in time.

citation.ref: Para 35 — performance obligations satisfied over time

points.text: (a) Payroll — month by month, as Auster runs it, the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits it produces; the confirming test is that an incoming processor would have nothing to substantially re-perform for the months already run.

citation.ref: Para 35(a) — customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits

keywords: simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits

points.text: (b) Turbine hall — building on the customer's own land creates or enhances an asset, the work in progress, and title passes as it goes, so the customer controls it at every stage.

citation.ref: Para 35(b) — asset controlled by the customer as it is created

points.text: (c) Vessel — built to the naval buyer's specification and barred from redirection, the hull has no alternative use to Auster, which also holds an enforceable right to payment covering performance completed to date. Both halves of this criterion must hold; the specification alone would not be enough without the right to payment.

citation.ref: Para 35(c) — no alternative use and enforceable right to payment

written.scenario: Kaveri Ltd has used a building as its head office since it was bought for ₹10 crore. It is carried under the cost model of Ind AS 16 at ₹6 crore after ₹4 crore of accumulated depreciation. On 1 April 20X5 the company moves out and lets the whole building to a tenant under an operating lease. A valuer puts the fair value at that date at ₹9 crore. The finance head proposes to bring the building into investment property at ₹9 crore, route the ₹3 crore difference through other comprehensive income, and carry it at fair value every year after.
written.question: Advise on each part of the proposal, stating the amount at which the building enters investment property and how it is measured afterwards.

points.text: Confirm the reclassification itself. Nothing but a change in use moves a property into the investment class or out of it, and the standard lists the end of owner-occupation among its own evidence that one has happened. A change in management's intentions in isolation would not have been enough.

citation.ref: Transfers — evidence of a change in use

points.text: Reject the ₹9 crore. Moves across the investment, owner-occupied and inventory classes do not change the carrying amount already on the books, and leave cost untouched for measurement and for disclosure alike, so the building enters investment property at ₹6 crore.

citation.ref: Para 59 — transfers do not change carrying amount or cost

keywords: do not change the carrying amount

points.text: Reject the ₹3 crore to other comprehensive income. Nothing is remeasured on the transfer, so no gain arises; there is no revaluation surplus because the building was held under the cost model of Ind AS 16 and not the revaluation model.

citation.ref: Para 59 read with the Ind AS 16 cost model

points.text: Reject carrying it at fair value. The Indian text leaves one policy open: the cost model for all of its investment property, and Ind AS 16 governs how that measurement is carried out, so depreciation continues on the ₹6 crore carrying amount.

citation.ref: Measurement after recognition — cost model as the accounting policy

keywords: cost model for all of its investment property

points.text: Say what the ₹9 crore is for. Even on the cost model an entity must still arrive at what the property would fetch, and that figure is produced for the purpose of disclosure only.

citation.ref: Measurement after recognition — fair value measured for disclosure

keywords: for the purpose of disclosure only

written.scenario: The Salem unit of Devipur Ltd is a cash-generating unit. At 31 March 20X6 its carrying amounts, in ₹ lakh, are goodwill 100, building 300, plant 150 and a patent 50, a total of 600. An impairment indicator is present and the recoverable amount of the unit is assessed at ₹450 lakh. The patent could be sold on its own for ₹50 lakh with ₹2 lakh of legal costs. The recoverable amounts of the building and the plant cannot be determined individually because neither generates cash inflows that are largely independent.
written.question: Compute the impairment loss and allocate it, showing the carrying amount of each asset after the allocation.

points.text: Compute the loss. A unit's recoverable amount is set by whichever is higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and the value it has in use, and an impairment loss arises only where the carrying amount exceeds that figure. Here ₹600 lakh less ₹450 lakh gives an impairment loss of ₹150 lakh.

citation.ref: Recoverable amount and recognition of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit

keywords: higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and the value it has in use

points.text: State the order of allocation, which is where the marks sit: the loss goes first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill sitting in the unit, and only what survives that is spread over the unit's remaining assets pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount each of them holds. So goodwill absorbs ₹100 lakh and falls to nil.

citation.ref: Allocation of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit — order of allocation

keywords: first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill
pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount

points.text: Allocate the remaining ₹50 lakh over the other assets, whose carrying amounts total ₹500 lakh — building 50 × 300/500 = ₹30 lakh, plant 50 × 150/500 = ₹15 lakh, patent 50 × 50/500 = ₹5 lakh.

citation.ref: Allocation of an impairment loss pro rata to the other assets of the unit

points.text: Apply the floor. In allocating an impairment loss the carrying amount of an individual asset shall not be reduced below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal, its value in use, and zero. The patent's fair value less costs of disposal is 50 − 2 = ₹48 lakh, so it can absorb only ₹2 lakh of the ₹5 lakh.

citation.ref: Limit on allocation to an individual asset within a cash-generating unit

keywords: shall not be reduced below the highest of
fair value less costs of disposal

points.text: Reallocate the excess. The ₹3 lakh the patent cannot absorb is instead allocated pro rata to the other assets in the unit, in proportion to their carrying amounts — building 3 × 300/450 = ₹2 lakh, plant 3 × 150/450 = ₹1 lakh.

citation.ref: Reallocation of the unallocated portion of an impairment loss

keywords: allocated pro rata to the other assets

points.text: State the closing position. Goodwill nil, building 300 − 32 = ₹268 lakh, plant 150 − 16 = ₹134 lakh, patent ₹48 lakh, which totals ₹450 lakh and agrees with the recoverable amount of the unit.

citation.ref: Carrying amount of the unit after allocation of the impairment loss

written.scenario: Hansa Ltd sells its warehouse to Ferrum Leasing for cash of ₹20,00,000, which is also the fair value of the warehouse on that date. Immediately before the sale the warehouse is carried in Hansa's books at ₹12,00,000. On the same day Hansa takes the warehouse back on a lease for twelve years at annual rentals payable at each year end; the present value of those rentals, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease, is ₹8,00,000. There is no repurchase option and the transfer meets the requirements of Ind AS 115 for a performance obligation satisfied by transferring control. Hansa does not take the short-term or low-value exemption.
written.question: Show how Hansa Ltd, the seller-lessee, accounts for the transaction on the date of sale, including the journal entry.

points.text: Establish that a sale has occurred. Both parties apply the requirements of Ind AS 115 on when a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of an asset. The leaseback that stands in isolation does not preclude a sale — what the lease hands over is only the right to control the use of the asset; had there been a substantive repurchase option, no sale would have occurred and the whole transaction would have been a financing transaction.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback transactions — assessing whether the transfer is a sale

keywords: in isolation does not preclude a sale

points.text: Check the terms for off-market pricing. Because the consideration of ₹20,00,000 equals the fair value of the asset, no adjustment arises; a sale price below fair value would have been a prepayment of lease payments and one above fair value an additional financing provided by the buyer-lessor.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — adjustments for off-market terms

points.text: Measure the right-of-use asset by carrying forward a proportion of the previous carrying amount — the fraction that stands for the right of use retained, never the fraction sold away: (12,00,000 / 20,00,000) × 8,00,000 = ₹4,80,000. It is not measured at fair value and not at the full carrying amount.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — measurement of the right-of-use asset by the seller-lessee

keywords: proportion of the previous carrying amount

points.text: Split the gain. The total gain is fair value ₹20,00,000 less carrying amount ₹12,00,000 = ₹8,00,000, of which the portion relating to the right retained, (8,00,000 / 20,00,000) × 8,00,000 = ₹3,20,000, is not recognised because that right has not been transferred.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — gain restricted to the rights transferred

points.text: Recognise the slice of gain attaching to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor, and no more than that slice: 8,00,000 − 3,20,000 = ₹4,80,000.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — recognition of the gain on rights transferred

points.text: Give the entry: Cash Dr ₹20,00,000 and Right-of-use asset Dr ₹4,80,000; to Warehouse ₹12,00,000, to Lease liability ₹8,00,000 and to Gain on rights transferred ₹4,80,000. The underlying asset is derecognised in full and the leaseback is then accounted for as any other lease.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — seller-lessee accounting on the date of sale

written.scenario: On 20 February 20X6 the board of Girnar Ltd decided to close its Nagpur plant. A detailed plan approved on 10 March 20X6 names the plant, its 240 workmen, the amounts to be spent and a start date of 1 May 20X6. Letters went to the workmen and to customers on 15 March 20X6. The year end is 31 March 20X6. The estimates are: retrenchment compensation ₹9.00 crore; retraining and relocating 60 workmen who move to the Pune plant ₹2.00 crore; marketing the Pune product line ₹1.50 crore; a new IT system at Pune ₹3.00 crore; operating losses of the Nagpur plant for April 20X6 ₹1.20 crore; an expected gain of ₹6.00 crore on selling the Nagpur land. Separately, a non-cancellable contract obliges Girnar to buy 20,000 units of a raw material used only at Nagpur at ₹500 a unit; the material can be resold at ₹430 a unit, and the supplier will release Girnar for ₹18 lakh.
written.question: State whether a restructuring provision is required at 31 March 20X6 and compute the amount, giving your reason for including or excluding each item.

points.text: Set out the test. A constructive obligation to restructure arises only when the entity has a detailed formal plan identifying the business concerned, the principal locations affected, the staff who will be paid off on leaving — where they sit, what they do and the approximate number of employees involved — what will be spent and the timetable for putting the plan into effect, and has raised a valid expectation in those affected by starting to implement the plan or announcing its main features to them.

citation.ref: Para 72 — constructive obligation to restructure

points.text: Conclude that the obligation exists. The board decision of 20 February would not by itself have created an obligation, but the letters of 15 March communicated the plan before the end of the reporting period, so a provision is recognised at 31 March 20X6.

citation.ref: Board decision before the reporting date — announcement or implementation required

keywords: before the end of the reporting period

points.text: Measure it on direct expenditures only — those both necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. The retrenchment compensation of ₹9.00 crore meets both tests and goes in.

citation.ref: A restructuring provision includes only direct expenditures

keywords: not associated with the ongoing activities

points.text: Exclude the three costs the standard names. Retraining or relocating continuing staff ₹2.00 crore, marketing ₹1.50 crore and investment in new systems and distribution networks ₹3.00 crore all relate to the future conduct of the business and are recognised as they arise.

citation.ref: Costs excluded from a restructuring provision

points.text: Exclude the other two. Losses the entity can already identify from trading on until the restructuring date stay outside the provision — future operating losses are kept out unless they relate to an onerous contract — so ₹1.20 crore is out; and gains on the expected disposal of assets are not taken into account in measuring the provision even where the sale is part of the restructuring, so the ₹6.00 crore is not netted off.

citation.ref: Future operating losses and gains on expected disposal of assets

keywords: unless they relate to an onerous contract

points.text: Provide separately for the supply contract. It is onerous because the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations exceed the economic benefits expected to be received, and the unavoidable cost is the least net cost of exiting, being the lower of the cost of fulfilling it, ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹86,00,000 = ₹14 lakh, and the ₹18 lakh penalty for failing to fulfil it. So ₹14 lakh is provided, after first recognising any impairment loss on the assets used in fulfilling that contract.

citation.ref: Onerous contracts — measurement at the lower of fulfilment cost and penalty

written.scenario: Rampur Alloys Ltd has made losses in each of the last three years and carries forward unused tax losses of ₹80 crore. Against the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity it has taxable temporary differences of ₹30 crore that will reverse before the losses expire. The board's five-year plan shows a return to profit from next year, built on a new product yet to be launched. The tax rate is 25%.
written.question: Advise the amount of deferred tax asset that may be recognised and the disclosure that goes with it.

points.text: State the recognition rule. An entity books a deferred tax asset on the carry forward of unused tax losses only where it finds it probable that future taxable profit will be available for those losses to be set against.

citation.ref: Recognition of deferred tax assets for unused tax losses and unused tax credits

keywords: carry forward of unused tax losses
probable that future taxable profit will be available

points.text: Add the caution that decides this case. Losses already sitting unused are themselves strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available. An entity with a history of recent losses therefore recognises the asset only up to its sufficient taxable temporary differences, unless convincing other evidence shows enough taxable profit is coming.

citation.ref: History of recent losses — restriction on recognising a deferred tax asset

keywords: strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available

points.text: Apply it. The taxable temporary differences of ₹30 crore relate to the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity and reverse before expiry, so a deferred tax asset of 30 × 25% = ₹7.50 crore is recognised. A board plan resting on an unlaunched product is not convincing other evidence, so nothing is recognised on the balance of ₹50 crore.

citation.ref: Assessing whether taxable profit will be available against unused tax losses

points.text: Give the disclosure that goes with a recognition of this kind — state the amount of the deferred tax asset, then say separately what the nature of the evidence supporting its recognition was.

citation.ref: Para 82 — disclosure where recognition depends on future taxable profit

keywords: amount of the deferred tax asset
nature of the evidence supporting its recognition

points.text: Close with the reassessment. At the end of each reporting period the entity reassesses unrecognised deferred tax assets and recognises a previously unrecognised asset to the extent it has become probable that future taxable profits will allow it to be recovered.

citation.ref: Reassessment of unrecognised deferred tax assets at each reporting date

written.scenario: A competition regulator orders Vasant Ltd's owners to divest within 90 days. On 1 July 20X6 Arka Ltd acquires 75% of the equity of Vasant Ltd for cash of ₹90 crore. A qualified valuer measures the identifiable net assets acquired, in accordance with Ind AS 103, at ₹128 crore, and the fair value of the 25% non-controlling interest at ₹30 crore. Arka's board is minded to credit the difference to profit for the year and to show part of it as attributable to the non-controlling shareholders.
written.question: Compute the gain under both permitted measurement bases for non-controlling interest, state where it is recognised, and set out the steps Arka must take before recognising it.

points.text: Define the position. A bargain purchase arises in extremely rare circumstances where the value of the identifiable net assets acquired exceeds the consideration transferred plus the amount of any non-controlling interest, and a forced sale in which the seller is acting under compulsion — as here, a regulator's divestment order — is the standard's own example.

citation.ref: Bargain purchase — circumstances in which a gain arises

points.text: Set out the gate before recognition. Before any gain goes in, the acquirer asks whether clear evidence of the underlying reasons for a bargain exists at all; if it does, it goes back over the identification, checking it has correctly identified all of the assets acquired, every liability assumed alongside them, and must then review the procedures used to measure those identifiable assets and liabilities, the non-controlling interest, any previously held equity interest and the consideration transferred.

citation.ref: Reassessment required before recognising a gain on a bargain purchase

keywords: clear evidence of the underlying reasons
correctly identified all of the assets acquired
review the procedures used to measure

points.text: Compute with non-controlling interest at fair value: consideration ₹90 crore plus non-controlling interest ₹30 crore is ₹120 crore, against identifiable net assets of ₹128 crore, giving a gain of ₹8 crore.

citation.ref: Measurement of the gain where non-controlling interest is measured at fair value

points.text: Compute with non-controlling interest at its proportionate share of the identifiable net assets: 128 × 25% = ₹32 crore, so ₹90 crore plus ₹32 crore is ₹122 crore and the gain is ₹6 crore. The choice of basis is available for each business combination and changes the size of the gain.

citation.ref: Non-controlling interest measurement choice and its effect on the bargain purchase gain

keywords: proportionate share of the identifiable net assets

points.text: Correct the board on where it goes. Because clear evidence of the reason exists, the gain is recognised in other comprehensive income on the acquisition date and accumulated in equity as capital reserve. It does not go to profit or loss. Had no clear evidence existed, the gain would have been recognised directly in equity as capital reserve.

citation.ref: Recognition of a bargain purchase gain in OCI and accumulation as capital reserve

keywords: accumulated in equity as capital reserve
does not go to profit or loss

points.text: Correct the second error. The whole bargain purchase gain is attributed to the acquirer; the minority takes none of it, so there is no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders.

citation.ref: Attribution of the bargain purchase gain wholly to the acquirer

keywords: no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders

written.scenario: Malwa Ltd holds a subsidiary, an associate and a joint venture, and prepares consolidated financial statements as well as its own separate financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013. Its finance head proposes to carry the subsidiary at cost, the associate under the equity method and the joint venture at fair value through profit or loss, all of this in its own separate financial statements, and to credit an interim dividend declared by the subsidiary's board in March to the carrying amount of the investment.
written.question: State the measurement options Ind AS 27 permits in separate financial statements, comment on each part of the proposal, and give the reason India departed from IAS 27 here.

points.text: State the options. An entity shall account for investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures either at cost, or in accordance with Ind AS 109, and it shall apply the same accounting for each category of investments.

citation.ref: Para 10 — accounting for investments in separate financial statements

points.text: Reject the equity method for the associate. It is not one of the two options in Ind AS 27 and cannot be used in separate financial statements, whichever category the investment falls in.

citation.ref: Para 10 — the equity method is not available in separate financial statements

keywords: not one of the two options
cannot be used in separate financial statements

points.text: Give the reason for the carve-out from IAS 27, which permits the equity method: unlike cost and fair value, the equity method is not a measurement basis at all — it is a manner of consolidation — so permitting it here would produce inconsistent accounting as a matter of concept.

citation.ref: Appendix 1 — carve-out from IAS 27 on the equity method

points.text: Correct the dividend treatment. A dividend from a subsidiary, an associate or a joint venture is recognised in profit or loss in the separate financial statements when the entity's right to receive the dividend is established, not deducted from the carrying amount of the investment.

citation.ref: Recognition of dividends from subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures

keywords: right to receive the dividend is established

written.scenario: Nandan Ltd will present its first Ind AS financial statements for the year ending 31 March 20X6, with one year of comparative information. There is no change in its functional currency. Management wants to use fair value as deemed cost for two plants where valuations are available, previous GAAP carrying values for the rest of its property, plant and equipment because the old records are incomplete, and fair value for a let-out office block held as investment property. Its subsidiary wants to use fair value for all of its own plant in its standalone financial statements.
written.question: State the date of transition and advise on each of the four proposals.

points.text: Fix the date of transition, which is the beginning of the earliest period for which the entity presents full comparative information — 1 April 20X4 — and that is the date at which the opening Ind AS Balance Sheet is prepared.

citation.ref: Date of transition to Ind AS and the opening Ind AS Balance Sheet

points.text: Confirm the fair value option. On the transition date a first-time adopter may take any single item of property, plant and equipment at what it would then fetch, and carry that fair value as its deemed cost forward; the election is made on an item-by-item basis.

citation.ref: Para D5 — fair value as deemed cost for property, plant and equipment

keywords: fair value as its deemed cost

points.text: Refuse the mixture. The option to use previous GAAP carrying values as deemed cost has to be applied to all items of property, plant and equipment, so it cannot be taken for some assets while fair value is used for others; management must choose one route for the whole class.

citation.ref: Para D7AA — previous GAAP carrying value applied to all items

keywords: all items of property, plant and equipment
cannot be taken for some assets

points.text: Refuse fair value for the investment property. Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model, so the option of fair value as deemed cost is not available for investment property to a first-time adopter, though the previous GAAP carrying value option does extend to it.

citation.ref: Deemed cost for investment property read with Ind AS 40

points.text: Deal with the subsidiary. Nothing prevents different entities within a group from choosing different bases for their standalone financial statements, but in consolidated financial statements the entire group is treated as one reporting entity, so different bases may not be used there.

citation.ref: Deemed cost elections within a group for consolidated financial statements

keywords: different bases for their standalone financial statements

written.scenario: Sarvodaya Ltd runs a funded defined benefit gratuity plan. At 1 April 20X5 the present value of the obligation is ₹40,00,000 and the fair value of plan assets is ₹34,00,000. The discount rate on high quality corporate bonds is 8%. During the year the current service cost is ₹6,00,000, benefits of ₹3,00,000 are paid out of the fund and the company contributes ₹5,00,000, both on the last day of the year. On 31 March 20X6 the company amends the plan, raising the benefit for past service by ₹2,00,000. The actuary reports the closing obligation at ₹47,50,000 and the closing fair value of plan assets at ₹38,00,000. There is no asset ceiling.
written.question: Compute the amounts to be recognised in profit or loss and in other comprehensive income for the year, and reconcile the opening and closing net defined benefit liability.

points.text: Split the components first. Service cost, comprising current service cost, past service cost and any gain or loss on settlement, and net interest on the net defined benefit liability go to profit or loss; remeasurements of the net defined benefit liability go to other comprehensive income.

citation.ref: Components of defined benefit cost and where each is recognised

keywords: net interest on the net defined benefit liability

points.text: Compute net interest as the discount rate applied to the opening net defined benefit liability of 40,00,000 − 34,00,000 = ₹6,00,000, that is 8% × 6,00,000 = ₹48,000, which is the change during the period that arises from the passage of time.

citation.ref: Net interest on the net defined benefit liability (asset)

points.text: Charge the plan amendment in full. Past service cost measures how far a plan amendment shifts the present value of what is already owed for service rendered in earlier periods, and it is recognised as an expense at the earlier of the date the amendment occurs and the date related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised — so the whole ₹2,00,000 is expensed this year, not spread.

citation.ref: Recognition of past service cost on a plan amendment

points.text: Total the profit or loss charge: current service cost ₹6,00,000 plus past service cost ₹2,00,000 plus net interest ₹48,000 = ₹8,48,000.

citation.ref: Amounts recognised in profit or loss for a defined benefit plan

points.text: Roll the obligation forward to isolate the actuarial gain: 40,00,000 + interest 3,20,000 + 6,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹48,20,000 against the actuary's ₹47,50,000, an actuarial gain of ₹70,000 arising from experience adjustments or changes in actuarial assumptions.

citation.ref: Actuarial gains and losses as a component of remeasurements

points.text: Roll the plan assets forward: 34,00,000 + interest income 2,72,000 + contributions 5,00,000 − benefits 3,00,000 = ₹38,72,000 against the actual ₹38,00,000, so the return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest is a loss of ₹72,000.

citation.ref: Return on plan assets as a component of remeasurements

keywords: return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest

points.text: Close it out. The net remeasurement is a loss of ₹2,000 in other comprehensive income, which shall not be reclassified to profit or loss later on, though it may be transferred within equity; and the closing net liability of 47,50,000 − 38,00,000 = ₹9,50,000 agrees with 6,00,000 + 8,48,000 + 2,000 − 5,00,000.

citation.ref: Remeasurements recognised in OCI are not reclassified to profit or loss

keywords: shall not be reclassified to profit or loss

written.scenario: Tapti Ltd issues 5% convertible debentures at par for ₹50,00,000 on 1 April 20X5. Interest is payable annually in arrears. At the end of the third year the holder may either convert each debenture into a fixed number of Tapti's equity shares or take redemption at par. The market rate for an otherwise identical debenture without the conversion option is 10%. Discount factors at 10% are 0.9091, 0.8264 and 0.7513, and the three-year annuity factor is 2.4868.
written.question: Classify the instrument, explain how it is split on initial recognition, and compute the amount of each component.

points.text: Classify it. The instrument is a compound financial instrument because it contains both a liability component, being the contractual obligation to pay interest and to deliver cash on redemption, and an equity component, being the holder's option to convert into a fixed number of the issuer's own equity instruments.

citation.ref: Compound financial instruments — separate presentation of components

points.text: State the method. Measure the liability component first, as the present value of the contractual cash flows of interest and principal discounted at the rate the market would then have demanded on any similar liability that does not have an associated equity component, ignoring the possibility of exercise of the conversion option.

citation.ref: Para 31 — split accounting for a compound financial instrument

keywords: similar liability that does not have an associated equity component

points.text: Compute the liability. Present value of the principal is 50,00,000 × 0.7513 = ₹37,56,500 and present value of the interest of ₹2,50,000 a year is 2,50,000 × 2.4868 = ₹6,21,700, giving a liability component of ₹43,78,200.

citation.ref: Para 31 — measurement of the liability component at present value

points.text: Assign the equity component the residual: take the fair value of the instrument as a whole, deduct what was separately determined for the liability component, and what is left is 50,00,000 − 43,78,200 = ₹6,21,800. The two components always sum to the fair value of the instrument as a whole and no gain or loss arises from initially recognising the components separately.

written.scenario: Kaveri Exports Ltd, an Indian company, has shipped goods to a buyer in the United States and will receive US$ 5,10,000 exactly three months from today. The treasury desk has the following quotes and rates. Spot: ₹ 83.00 per US$. Three-month forward: ₹ 83.60 per US$. Annual interest rates — in India, deposit 6% and borrowing 9%; in the United States, deposit 4% and borrowing 8%. Ignore transaction costs, brokerage and taxes.
written.question: Show how a money market hedge would be put in place for this receipt, work out the rupee amount it produces on the due date, compare it with a three-month forward contract, and advise which cover the company should take.

points.text: Set out the direction first — the company has a dollar receivable, so a money market hedge means borrow US dollars now, convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate, and place the rupees on deposit in India, with the dollar receipt on the due date used to repay the dollar loan.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) — Money Market Hedging as an external technique

keywords: convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate

points.text: Size the dollar borrowing so that principal plus interest equals the receipt. The US borrowing rate is 8% p.a., which is 2% for three months, so the amount to borrow is US$ 5,10,000 ÷ 1.02 = US$ 5,00,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) read with the worked money market hedge in Test Your Knowledge

keywords: principal plus interest equals the receipt

points.text: Convert the borrowed dollars at the spot rate of ₹ 83.00 — US$ 5,00,000 × 83.00 = ₹ 4,15,00,000 available in rupees today.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 5.2 — spot quotation used for the immediate conversion leg

points.text: Place those rupees on deposit in India at 6% p.a., which is 1.5% for three months, giving ₹ 4,15,00,000 × 1.015 = ₹ 4,21,22,500 on the due date. This is the certain rupee amount under the money market hedge.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) — the deposit leg of the money market hedge

points.text: Value the alternative: under a forward contract the exporter sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60, giving 5,10,000 × 83.60 = ₹ 4,26,36,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 12 — Forward Contract

keywords: sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60

points.text: Conclude on the comparison: the forward yields ₹ 5,13,500 more (4,26,36,000 less 4,21,22,500), and the effective rate under the money market hedge is only ₹ 82.59 per US$ against ₹ 83.60 on the forward, so the company should take the forward contract.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

written.scenario: A bond of Narmada Power Ltd has a face value of ₹ 1,000, carries a coupon of 10% payable annually and matures in four years, when it is redeemed at par. The yield to maturity on comparable bonds is 12%. Use the following discount factors at 12%: year 1 — 0.8929, year 2 — 0.7972, year 3 — 0.7118, year 4 — 0.6355.
written.question: Compute the current price of the bond, its Macaulay duration and its modified duration, and estimate the change in the bond's price if the yield rises by 50 basis points.

points.text: Price the bond as the present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 and the final flow of ₹ 1,100 — 89.29 + 79.72 + 71.18 + 699.05 = ₹ 939.24.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8 — bond valuation as the present value of coupon and redemption flows

keywords: present value of the three coupons

points.text: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time within which the investor gets back the promised principal and the promised yield, so weight each year's present value by its year number — 89.29 + 159.44 + 213.54 + 2,796.20 = ₹ 3,258.47 — and divide by the price: 3,258.47 ÷ 939.24 = 3.47 years.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8(a) — Macaulay Duration

keywords: weight each year's present value by its year

points.text: Modified duration adjusts Macaulay duration for the yield, being Macaulay duration divided by (1 + YTM/n) — here 3.4693 ÷ 1.12 = 3.10, since the coupon is annual and n is 1.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8(b) — Modified Duration

points.text: Apply it to the yield move: the percentage price change is minus modified duration times the change in yield, so −3.10 × 0.50% = a fall of about 1.55%, which on ₹ 939.24 is a drop of ₹ 14.55 to roughly ₹ 924.69.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8 — duration as the measure of interest rate risk

keywords: minus modified duration times the change in yield

points.text: Add the standing relationships: a higher coupon rate lowers the duration, a higher yield-to-maturity lowers the duration, and a longer time to maturity raises it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8 — factors affecting a bond's duration

keywords: higher coupon rate lowers the duration
longer time to maturity raises it

written.scenario: The share of Chenab Ltd trades at ₹ 200 today. Over the next year the share is expected to be worth either ₹ 250 or ₹ 160, and nothing in between. The risk free rate of interest is 8% per annum. A European call option on the share with an exercise price of ₹ 210 expires in one year.
written.question: Using the binomial model, compute the fair value of the call option today and state the composition of the riskless hedge portfolio at the valuation date.

points.text: Set up the tree: the up factor u = 250/200 = 1.25 and the down factor d = 160/200 = 0.80, giving payoffs Cu = Max (0, 250 − 210) = ₹ 40 and Cd = Max (0, 160 − 210) = nil.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 — Binomial Model, construction of the price tree and terminal payoffs

points.text: Compute the risk neutral probability p = (r − d) ÷ (u − d) = (1.08 − 0.80) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80) = 0.28 ÷ 0.45 = 0.6222, so the probability of a fall is 1 − 0.6222 = 0.3778.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 read with Para 7.2 — Risk Neutral Method

points.text: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate — (0.6222 × 40) + (0.3778 × 0) = ₹ 24.89, and 24.89 ÷ 1.08 = ₹ 23.05 is the fair value of the call.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 — valuing the option by discounting the probability-weighted payoff

keywords: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate

points.text: State the hedge: delta = (Cu − Cd) ÷ (Su − Sd) = (40 − 0) ÷ (250 − 160) = 40/90 = 0.4444, so 0.4444 of a share is held for every one call option written.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation

written.scenario: Godavari Industries Ltd reports for the year (all figures in ₹ lakh) — revenue 2,000; direct costs 800; selling, general and administrative expenses 500, which include a provision for bad and doubtful debts of 30; interest 100. The tax rate is 30%. The balance sheet shows total assets of 2,400, made up on the funding side of equity share capital 900, reserves 400, non-current borrowings 500 and current liabilities and provisions 600. The trade receivables in total assets are already stated net of the same provision of 30. Pre-tax cost of debt is 10% and the cost of equity is 12%.
written.question: Compute the Economic Value Added of Godavari Industries Ltd for the year and say what the figure means.

points.text: Compute NOPAT — EBIT is 2,000 − 800 − 500 = 700; deduct tax at 30% on EBIT, 210; add back the non-cash provision for bad and doubtful debts of 30, giving NOPAT of ₹ 520 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step I — computation of NOPAT

points.text: Find the invested capital — total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600 gives 1,800, plus the same non-cash adjustment of 30, giving ₹ 1,830 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step II — finding out the Invested Capital

keywords: total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600

points.text: Compute the WACC on that capital — equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800, so (1,300/1,800 × 12%) + (500/1,800 × 10% × 0.70) = 8.67% + 1.94% = 10.61%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step III — compute the WACC

keywords: equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800

points.text: Finish it — capital charge = 1,830 × 10.61% = ₹ 194.18 lakh, so EVA = 520 − 194.18 = ₹ 325.82 lakh; a positive EVA means the company is producing value from the funds invested in it, over and above the cost of that capital.

written.scenario: Tapti Cements Ltd will need to borrow ₹ 80 crore for three months, starting six months from today. Fearing a rise in rates, it buys a 6 × 9 Forward Rate Agreement from its banker at 8.40% per annum on a notional principal of ₹ 80 crore. On the settlement date the three-month reference rate turns out to be (i) 9.00% per annum, and separately consider (ii) 7.80% per annum. Take the FRA period as 3/12 of a year.
written.question: Compute the final settlement amount in each case, state who pays whom, and explain what the company has achieved.

points.text: State the formula and the nature of the instrument — settlement is N(RR − FR)(dtm/DY) divided by [1 + RR(dtm/DY)], and the ₹ 80 crore is only notional principal because an FRA involves no transfer of principal and is settled in cash for the interest differential.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — Forward Rate Agreements, features and settlement formula

points.text: Case (i), reference rate 9.00% — the numerator is ₹ 80 crore × (9.00% − 8.40%) × 3/12 = ₹ 12,00,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — computation of the interest differential on the notional amount

points.text: Discount that differential at the actual reference rate, because an FRA is settled at the beginning of the period and not at the end — 12,00,000 ÷ [1 + 0.09 × 3/12] = 12,00,000 ÷ 1.0225 = ₹ 11,73,594, which the banker as seller pays to Tapti Cements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — the differential is discounted at the post-change actual rate

keywords: settled at the beginning of the period and not at the end

points.text: Case (ii), reference rate 7.80% — the reference rate is now below the agreed forward rate, so the buyer owes the seller: 12,00,000 ÷ [1 + 0.078 × 3/12] = 12,00,000 ÷ 1.0195 = ₹ 11,77,048 payable by Tapti Cements to the banker.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — if the Reference Rate is below the Forward Rate the buyer owes the seller

keywords: reference rate is now below the agreed forward rate
payable by Tapti Cements to the banker

points.text: Draw the conclusion — in both cases the FRA receipt or payment offsets the movement in the actual borrowing cost, so the effective borrowing rate is fixed at 8.40% and the company has hedged itself against the unfavourable change in interest rate.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — purpose of an FRA, protection from unfavourable changes to the interest rate

written.scenario: An investor is choosing between two securities. Security P has an expected return of 18% and a standard deviation of 25%. Security Q has an expected return of 12% and a standard deviation of 15%. The correlation coefficient between the returns of the two securities is +0.30. The investor places 40% of the funds in P and 60% in Q.
written.question: Compute the expected return and the standard deviation of this portfolio, and show how much risk the investor has removed by diversifying rather than holding the two in proportion.

points.text: Portfolio return is the plain weighted average of the two returns — (0.40 × 18%) + (0.60 × 12%) = 7.2% + 7.2% = 14.4%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4 — expected return of a portfolio as the weighted average of security returns

keywords: weighted average of the two returns

points.text: State the variance formula and work each term — portfolio variance = x1²σ1² + x2²σ2² + 2x1x2r12σ1σ2, giving 0.16 × 625 = 100, then 0.36 × 225 = 81, then 2 × 0.40 × 0.60 × 0.30 × 25 × 15 = 54.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.2 — portfolio variance of a two security portfolio

points.text: Add and take the root — portfolio variance = 100 + 81 + 54 = 235, so the portfolio standard deviation is the square root of 235 = 15.33%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.2 — portfolio standard deviation is the square root of the portfolio variance

points.text: Measure the benefit — had the two been perfectly positively correlated the standard deviation would be the weighted average, (0.40 × 25) + (0.60 × 15) = 19%, so the gap of 3.67 percentage points is the reduction of portfolio risk through diversification.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.3 and 4.4.3.1 — dilution of risk through diversification, and the perfectly positively correlated case

keywords: reduction of portfolio risk through diversification

written.scenario: Bhima Housing Finance Ltd has a book of home loans running to ₹ 900 crore. points.text: Creation of the pool of assets — the originator segregates assets backed by similar mortgages in terms of interest rate, risk, maturity and concentration, so that the pool is homogeneous.
