Adjusted total turnover is the turnover in the State excluding exempt supplies other than zero-rated ones, here ₹30,00,000 plus ₹10,00,000, that is ₹40,00,000, because the 18 per cent goods are part of the turnover even though no refund arises on them.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) read with rule 89(4)(E)

points.text: The formula is the turnover of inverted rated supply times Net ITC divided by adjusted total turnover, less the tax payable on the inverted rated supply times Net ITC divided by the credit availed on inputs and input services. That is ₹30,00,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹40,00,000, which is ₹2,70,000, less ₹1,50,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹4,00,000, which is ₹1,35,000. The maximum refund is ₹1,35,000.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) as substituted by Notification No. 14/2022-Central Tax dated 5 July 2022

written.scenario: Ishaan Exports, registered in Gujarat, exports under a letter of undertaking without payment of tax and claims refund of unutilised credit. One consignment was loaded on a vessel at Mundra on 10 March 2024 and the vessel left India on 14 March 2024. A second consignment went by road to Nepal and crossed the frontier on 20 March 2024. A software service was completed for a client in Ireland on 15 January 2024 and the payment arrived in convertible foreign exchange on 20 May 2024. On a fourth claim, filed on 1 February 2026, the officer issued a deficiency memo on 25 February 2026 asking for a fresh application.
written.question: State the relevant date and the last date for filing the refund claim in each of the first three cases, and explain how the deficiency memo affects the fourth.

points.text: A refund application is made before the expiry of two years from the relevant date, and Explanation 2 to section 54 fixes that date by the ground of the claim. For goods exported by sea or air it is the date on which the ship or aircraft in which the goods are loaded leaves India, so the first consignment's relevant date is 14 March 2024, not the loading date, and the claim may be filed up to 14 March 2026.

citation.ref: Section 54(1) and Explanation 2(a)(i) to section 54

points.text: For goods exported by land the relevant date is the date on which the goods pass the frontier, so for the Nepal consignment it is 20 March 2024 and the claim may be filed up to 20 March 2026.

citation.ref: Explanation 2(a)(ii) to section 54

points.text: For export of services where the supply was completed before the payment was received, the relevant date is the date of receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange, or in Indian rupees where the Reserve Bank permits it. The Irish service's relevant date is therefore 20 May 2024, not the completion date, and the claim may be filed up to 20 May 2026.

citation.ref: Explanation 2(c)(i) to section 54

points.text: Where the officer issues a deficiency memo requiring a fresh claim, the period from the date the claim was filed to the date the deficiencies were communicated is excluded from the two years. For the fourth claim the days from 1 February 2026 to 25 February 2026 do not count against Ishaan Exports when it files the fresh application.

citation.ref: Proviso to rule 90(3)

written.scenario: Two exporters file refund claims for unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies made under a letter of undertaking in November 2026. Kavya Textiles has completed Aadhaar authentication and exports garments. Pankaj Agro has not undergone Aadhaar authentication and exports areca nuts. Separately, Kavya Textiles asks whether it must prove that it did not pass the tax on to anyone, and how long the department has to decide its claim.
written.question: Explain the provisional refund available to each exporter after the changes effective 1 October 2025, the time limit for the final order, and whether the doctrine of unjust enrichment applies to these claims.

points.text: Section 54(6) lets the proper officer refund on a provisional basis 90 per cent of the amount claimed on account of zero-rated supplies, ahead of final settlement under section 54(5), except for categories of registered persons the Government notifies. Rule 91(2), as substituted with effect from 1 October 2025, ties the provisional sanction to the identification and evaluation of risk by the system and requires the order within seven days of the acknowledgement of the claim.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) read with rule 91(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025

points.text: The officer may, for reasons recorded in writing, decline the provisional route in a given case and proceed straight to the final order under rule 92; that order does not need revalidation. Kavya Textiles is otherwise inside the provisional route and can expect 90 per cent within seven days unless the officer records reasons not to.

citation.ref: Rule 91(2) as substituted with effect from 1 October 2025

points.text: Pankaj Agro is shut out twice over. Notification No. 14/2025-Central Tax, effective 1 October 2025, denies provisional refund to any person who has not undergone Aadhaar authentication under rule 10B, and to any person engaged in supplying areca nuts, pan masala, tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes, or essential oils. Its claim goes only by the final order.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) read with Notification No. 14/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025

points.text: The final order is made within sixty days of receipt of the complete application under section 54(7). Unjust enrichment does not apply: section 54(8)(b) directs that a refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, like one on an inverted duty structure, is paid to the applicant and not credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund, so Kavya Textiles need not show that the incidence was not passed on.

citation.ref: Section 54(7) and 54(8)(b)

written.scenario: Sanjeevani Hospital, a clinical establishment in Kerala, supplies in October 2026: inpatient treatment of a road-accident victim; reconstructive surgery on the same patient's face to restore its function after the injury; a hair-transplant procedure for another customer; and ambulance transport of patients to the hospital. Its group insurer, Surya Assurance, writes in the same month an individual health policy covering a self-employed person and her family; a group health policy for the hospital's own employees; and a personal accident cover for one individual. A reinsurer takes on part of the individual policy.
written.question: State, with reasons, which of these supplies are exempt from GST and which are taxable, taking account of the exemptions introduced with effect from 22 September 2025.

points.text: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt. The term covers, in any system of medicine India recognises, the diagnosis of a patient and the treatment or care given for an illness, an injury, a deformity, an abnormality or a pregnancy, and it takes in transport of that patient to a clinical establishment and back. So the inpatient treatment and the ambulance transport are both exempt.

citation.ref: Entry 74 with the definition of health care services in paragraph 2 of the notification

points.text: The definition excludes hair transplant and cosmetic or plastic surgery, except where such surgery is undertaken to restore or reconstruct anatomy or functions of the body affected by congenital defects, developmental abnormalities, injury or trauma. The reconstructive surgery after the accident is inside the exemption for that reason; the hair transplant is outside it and taxable.

citation.ref: Definition of health care services in paragraph 2 of the notification

points.text: From 22 September 2025, entry 36D exempts health insurance business wherever the insurer's cover runs to an insured that is not a group; the explanation reads that as a contract whose insured is an individual, or an individual together with that individual's family. Health insurance business is defined to cover sickness and medical expense benefits, travel cover and personal accident cover, so the individual family policy and the personal accident cover are both exempt.

citation.ref: Entry 36D and paragraph 2(zga), inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

points.text: A group is a set of persons who join together with a commonality of purpose or a common economic activity other than availing insurance, and expressly includes an employer-employee group. The hospital's employee policy is a group policy and stays taxable. Entry 36E exempts reinsurance of the services in entries 36C and 36D, so the reinsurer's share of the individual policy is exempt with it.

citation.ref: Entry 36E and paragraph 2(zfb), inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

written.scenario: Bhavya Chemicals imports a consignment of a chemical from a developing country in December 2026. Its assessable value under section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 is ₹40,00,000. Basic customs duty is 10 per cent. A safeguard duty of 20 per cent is in force on the article, and the share of imports of the article from that country is 6 per cent of total imports into India. The integrated tax rate on the chemical is 18 per cent. No compensation cess applies.
written.question: Compute the total customs duties and integrated tax payable, showing the base on which each is computed and explaining why the social welfare surcharge is computed as it is.

points.text: Basic customs duty is 10 per cent of the assessable value of ₹40,00,000, that is ₹4,00,000. The safeguard duty is chargeable because the exporting country's share of imports, 6 per cent, is above the 3 per cent below which section 8B leaves a developing country alone; it is 20 per cent of ₹40,00,000, that is ₹8,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with section 2 and section 8B(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

points.text: The social welfare surcharge is levied at 10 per cent on the aggregate of the duties of customs levied and collected under section 12 and any sum chargeable as an addition to such duty, but safeguard duty under section 8B, countervailing duty under section 9, anti-dumping duty under section 9A and the surcharge itself are excluded from that aggregate. So the surcharge is 10 per cent of the basic customs duty alone: ₹40,000, and not 10 per cent of ₹12,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 110(3) read with the exclusions in section 110(1)

points.text: Integrated tax under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act is levied on the value under section 3(8): the assessable value plus every duty of customs chargeable under section 12 and any sum chargeable in addition to it. The safeguard duty and the surcharge both go into that base. The base is ₹40,00,000 plus ₹4,00,000 plus ₹8,00,000 plus ₹40,000, that is ₹52,40,000, and the integrated tax at 18 per cent is ₹9,43,200. The surcharge is not levied on the integrated tax, that being exempted by Notification No. 13/2018-Customs.

citation.ref: Section 3(7) and 3(8), and Notification No. 13/2018-Customs dated 2 February 2018

points.text: Total payable is ₹4,00,000 plus ₹8,00,000 plus ₹40,000 plus ₹9,43,200, that is ₹21,83,200. Of this only the integrated tax of ₹9,43,200 is available as input tax credit to Bhavya Chemicals; basic customs duty, safeguard duty and the surcharge are costs.

citation.ref: Section 5(1) proviso, and section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with section 2(62)

written.scenario: A designated authority finds that a chemical is exported to India from a country at ₹400 a kilogram while its normal value in that country is ₹500 a kilogram, and that a duty of ₹80 a kilogram would be enough to remove the injury to the domestic industry. Three importers ask what this means for them: a trader in the domestic tariff area; a 100 per cent export oriented unit that uses the chemical to make goods it exports; and the same unit for a part of the chemical it clears as such into the domestic tariff area. The trader also asks whether the duty can reach consignments imported before the notification.
written.question: Explain how the anti-dumping duty is quantified under section 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and answer each of the three importers, including the question of retrospective levy.

points.text: Section 9A(1) permits an anti-dumping duty not exceeding the margin of dumping, which is the difference between the normal value and the export price: ₹500 less ₹400, that is ₹100 a kilogram. But the duty is restricted to the lower of the margin of dumping and the injury margin, the amount adequate to remove the injury to the domestic industry, so the duty is ₹80 a kilogram and not ₹100.

citation.ref: Section 9A(1) read with rule 4 of the Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and Collection of Anti-dumping Duty on Dumped Articles and for Determination of Injury) Rules, 1995

points.text: The trader in the domestic tariff area pays the ₹80 a kilogram on import, in addition to every other duty on the goods. The duty is collected under the Customs Act as if it were a duty of customs, so the provisions on the date for the rate of duty, assessment, refunds and appeals apply to it, and every notification under the section is laid before each House of Parliament.

citation.ref: Section 9A(7) and 9A(8)

points.text: The anti-dumping duty does not apply to articles imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit or a unit in a special economic zone unless the notification specifically makes it applicable to them. The unit's chemical used in goods it exports therefore bears no anti-dumping duty. The part cleared as such into the domestic tariff area is the exception the section itself carves out: the duty is imposed on that portion, at the rate applicable when it was imported into India.

citation.ref: Section 9A, non-applicability to export oriented units and special economic zone units

points.text: The duty can be levied retrospectively only under section 9A(3), where the Government finds a dumping history with injury behind it, or an importer who knew or had reason to know of the dumping and the harm it did, and that the injury is caused by massive dumping in a relatively short time likely to undermine the remedial effect of the duty. Even then the retrospective reach cannot go beyond ninety days before the date of the notification.

citation.ref: Section 9A(3)

written.scenario: Imports of an article into India have surged and the domestic industry seeks a safeguard measure. The imports come from four developing countries with shares of 2.5 per cent, 2 per cent, 1.5 per cent and 1 per cent of total imports, and from one developed country. The Central Government wants to act before the full enquiry ends. A 100 per cent export oriented unit also imports the article and clears part of it into the domestic tariff area.
written.question: Explain under section 8B of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 whether a safeguard measure can be applied to each source, what can be done before the enquiry ends, and how the export oriented unit is treated.

points.text: Section 8B lets the Central Government apply a safeguard measure where an article is imported in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic industry, and the measures are a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota or another prescribed measure.

citation.ref: Section 8B(1)

points.text: No measure is applied to an article originating in a developing country whose share of imports of the article does not exceed 3 per cent, and none to developing countries each below 3 per cent whose imports taken together do not exceed 9 per cent of total imports. Here each developing country is below 3 per cent and the four together are 7 per cent, within 9 per cent, so none of the four can be measured against; the developed country can be.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 8B(2)

points.text: On a preliminary determination that increased imports have caused or threatened serious injury, a provisional safeguard measure may be applied pending final determination, for not more than 200 days from the date of imposition. If the final determination finds no injury or threat, the provisional duty is refunded.

citation.ref: Section 8B, provisional safeguard measures

points.text: The measure does not apply to articles imported by a 100 per cent export oriented unit or a special economic zone unit unless it is specifically made applicable to them, or unless the article is cleared as such into the domestic tariff area or used in goods so cleared, in which case it applies to that portion as was leviable when it was imported.

citation.ref: Section 8B, articles imported by export oriented units and special economic zone units

written.scenario: Daksh Traders imports goods and, on 1 April 2026, the proper officer passes the order under section 60 permitting their deposit in a public warehouse; the duty assessed on the into-bond bill of entry is ₹2,00,000. It clears them for home consumption on 31 July 2026. A second importer, Aarohi Engineering, operates a warehouse where manufacturing is permitted under section 65 and deposits both machinery and raw material there. A third, Ved Exports, warehouses goods and later re-exports them from the warehouse without paying duty.
written.question: State the warehousing period and the interest, if any, payable by each of the three under section 61 of the Customs Act, 1962, computing the interest for Daksh Traders.

points.text: For goods other than those in a section 65 warehouse, the warehousing period runs till the expiry of one year from the date of the order under section 60 permitting deposit, and the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may extend it by not more than one year at a time, reducing the extension where the goods have a shorter shelf life. Daksh Traders' period therefore runs to 31 March 2027.

citation.ref: Section 61(1)(c) with its proviso

keywords: not more than one year at a time

points.text: Interest under section 61(2) is charged on the duty deferred where such goods remain in the warehouse beyond ninety days from the section 60 order, at the rate fixed under section 47, which is 15 per cent a year, till the date of payment. Ninety days from 1 April 2026 end on 29 June 2026, so interest runs from 30 June to 31 July 2026, 32 days: ₹2,00,000 at 15 per cent for 32 days, about ₹2,630.

citation.ref: Section 61(2) read with the rate notified under section 47(2)

points.text: In a warehouse where manufacture or other operations are permitted under section 65, the period for capital goods is till their clearance from the warehouse and for other goods till their consumption or clearance. No interest is chargeable for any of the time they remain warehoused, so Aarohi Engineering pays none on either the machinery or the raw material.

citation.ref: Section 61(1)(a) and (b) read with section 61(2)

points.text: Ved Exports pays no interest either. Interest is an accessory to the duty and is computed on it; where the goods are re-exported from the warehouse under section 69 no duty is payable, so the principal is nil and the interest is nil. The Supreme Court so held in Pratibha Processors, and the Board may in any case waive interest in individual cases.

citation.ref: Section 61(2) and section 69, as read in Pratibha Processors v. Union of India 1996 (88) ELT 12 (SC)

written.scenario: Hemant Imports files a bill of entry for warehousing on goods assessed to duty of ₹6,00,000 and asks what security it must give. It later finds it cannot sell the goods. One lot it wishes to give up without paying duty before any clearance order is made. A second lot is removed from the warehouse by its staff without any clearance. A third lot is still in the warehouse when its warehousing period expires. No offence is alleged in respect of the first lot.
written.question: Explain the bond Hemant Imports must execute under section 59 of the Customs Act, 1962, whether it may relinquish title to the first lot, and what the proper officer may do about the second and third lots under section 72.

points.text: Section 59(1) requires the importer to execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed, ₹18,00,000, binding itself to comply with the Act in respect of the goods, to pay on or before the date in a demand notice all duties and the interest under section 61(2), and to pay all penalties and fines incurred. The bond may be a consignment bond, or a general bond approved by the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner covering goods to be imported over a specified period; security may be required in addition.

Thrice the duty is the measure because the importer's exposure can reach the duty, a penalty equal to it, and fine and interest on top. A running account is kept against a general bond, debited as goods are warehoused and credited as they are cleared on payment of duty.

citation.ref: Section 59 read with regulations on the warehousing bond

points.text: The first lot may be given up. The proviso to section 68 lets the owner of warehoused goods relinquish title at any time before an order for clearance for home consumption is made, on payment of any penalties payable, and on relinquishment no duty is payable. The right is lost only where an offence appears to have been committed in respect of the goods, which is not alleged here.

citation.ref: Provisos to section 68

points.text: Section 71 forbids removal from a warehouse except for home consumption, export or transfer to another warehouse. The second lot, removed in contravention of section 71, and the third, not removed at the expiry of the period allowed under section 61, are both cases in section 72 where the proper officer may demand the full duty with interest, fine and penalties, to be paid forthwith. On default, after notice to the owner, the officer may detain and sell enough of the owner's goods in the warehouse to recover it.

citation.ref: Sections 71 and 72(1)(a), (b) and (d) with section 72(2)

written.scenario: Five consignments of Nilay Traders met different fates in 2026. The first was unloaded, and before the order for clearance some cartons were found tampered with and unit articles missing; nothing was recovered. The second was pilfered after the order for clearance for home consumption but before Nilay removed it from the customs area. The third was destroyed by fire in a public warehouse before clearance. The fourth Nilay decided not to take, and it wrote to the proper officer giving up its title before any clearance order. On the fifth, pilferage was noticed only when Nilay removed the goods, after the clearance order had been made and duty paid.
written.question: State, with reasons, the liability to duty in each case under sections 13 and 23 of the Customs Act, 1962, and the procedure open to Nilay Traders where duty has been paid.

points.text: Under section 13, goods pilfered after unloading — the pilferage falling before the proper officer has ordered them cleared for home consumption or sent into a warehouse — leave the importer not liable for duty on them, unless they are restored to him; the custodian under section 45 bears the duty instead. The first consignment shows the marks of pilferage, tampered packages with unit articles missing, and nothing was restored, so Nilay pays no duty on the missing articles.

citation.ref: Section 13 read with section 45(3)

points.text: Section 13 stops at the clearance order. Goods pilfered after the order for clearance is made but before they are actually removed are outside it, so duty on the second consignment is leviable. Section 13 is the only provision for pilferage, and a refund claim for pilfered goods under section 23(1) is not permissible.

citation.ref: Section 13 and section 23(1)

points.text: Section 23(1) covers goods lost, otherwise than by pilferage, or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption, including in a warehouse: on proof to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner the duty is remitted, and where it was already paid it comes back as a refund on the remission order. The fire in the warehouse is a total loss of the third consignment and earns remission. Unlike section 13, remission must be applied for and proved.

citation.ref: Section 23(1)

points.text: Section 23(2) lets the owner relinquish title to imported goods at any time before an order for clearance under section 47 or for deposit under section 60, and then no duty is payable, unless an offence appears to have been committed in respect of them. The fourth consignment is abandoned in time and bears no duty. On the fifth, the clearance order and the duty both precede the discovery, so Nilay obtains a survey report from the steamer agents or insurance surveyors and claims the remission as a refund of the duty paid on the pilfered articles.

citation.ref: Section 23(2), and section 13 as applied where pilferage is noticed on removal

written.scenario: Kirti Garments, a merchant exporter tied to a supporting manufacturer, wants to import fabric, dye and the fuel used in dyeing without duty against an export order. It asks which of these can come in duty-free, how much value it must add, what duties are spared, how long it has to import, and whether it can sell surplus imported fabric in India once the export order is completed.
written.question: Advise Kirti Garments on each point under the Advance Authorisation scheme of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023.

points.text: An Advance Authorisation may be issued to a manufacturer exporter or to a merchant exporter tied to a supporting manufacturer, so Kirti Garments is eligible. It allows duty-free import of inputs physically incorporated in the export product, with normal allowance for wastage, and of fuel, oil and catalyst consumed in producing it. The fabric and dye are incorporated inputs and the dyeing fuel is consumed in production, so all three qualify.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, Advance Authorisation — eligible applicants and eligible inputs

points.text: The authorisation is issued on standard input-output norms or self-declared norms, and the minimum value addition to be achieved is 15 per cent, lower only for specified products such as petroleum products. Imports under it come in free of basic customs duty and of the additional duty, of safeguard duty and its transition product-specific counterpart, of countervailing and anti-dumping duty, of education cess, and free in whole of integrated tax and compensation cess.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, Advance Authorisation — value addition and duties exempted, read with the customs exemption notification for the scheme

points.text: The authorisation is valid for import for twelve months from its date of issue, and may be revalidated for another twelve months once only. For supplies under deemed exports the validity is co-terminus with the contracted duration of the project or twelve months, whichever is later.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Handbook of Procedures, validity of an Advance Authorisation

points.text: No. The authorisation and the material imported under it are subject to the Actual User condition and are not transferable even after the export obligation is completed. Surplus fabric cannot be sold in India as such; it may be used only in the authorisation holder's own manufacture, and the scheme differs from a Duty Free Import Authorisation, which becomes transferable once the export obligation is fulfilled.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, Actual User condition for Advance Authorisation

written.scenario: Lakshya Auto Components, a manufacturer exporter, obtains an EPCG authorisation on 1 July 2026 and imports a machine on which the duties, taxes and cess saved come to ₹50 lakh. Its exports of the same product averaged ₹4 crore a year over the preceding three licensing years. It asks how much it must export and by when, whether it must keep exporting at its old level as well, how long it has to import, whether it can sell the machine, and what changes if it buys the machine from an Indian manufacturer instead.
written.question: Advise Lakshya Auto Components on each point under the Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023.

points.text: The scheme lets an exporter import capital goods for pre-production, production and post-production at zero customs duty, and for physical exports the import is also exempt from integrated tax and compensation cess. In return the holder takes on a specific export obligation of six times the duties, taxes and cess saved, to be fulfilled within six years from the date of issue of the authorisation: ₹3 crore of exports by 30 June 2032.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 of the Foreign Trade Policy, EPCG scheme and export obligation

points.text: Yes. The specific obligation is over and above the average export obligation, which is the average level of exports of the same and similar products in the preceding three licensing years, ₹4 crore a year here, and that average must be maintained every financial year until the obligation is completed. Only exports above the average count towards the ₹3 crore.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 of the Foreign Trade Policy, average export obligation

points.text: The authorisation is valid for import for twenty-four months from its date of issue and cannot be revalidated. The machine is under the Actual User condition until the export obligation is completed and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate is granted, so it cannot be sold before then.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 of the Foreign Trade Policy, validity and Actual User condition under EPCG

points.text: The machine may be sourced from a domestic manufacturer through an invalidation letter or an advance release order, and the domestic supplier then gets deemed export benefits. For indigenous sourcing the specific export obligation is 25 per cent less, so it would be ₹2.25 crore instead of ₹3 crore. If integrated tax and cess are paid in cash on an import and no input tax credit is taken, they are left out of the duty saved.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 of the Foreign Trade Policy, indigenous sourcing under EPCG

written.scenario: Manav Exports asks about the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme in 2026. It exports garments it manufactures, and it also re-exports some imported machinery parts in the same form, ships goods to a unit in a special economic zone, and exports a product subject to export duty. It holds an Advance Authorisation for part of its production. It wants to know what it gets, in what form, and whether the scheme is still running for its exports.
written.question: Explain the benefit under the scheme, the form it takes, which of Manav Exports' supplies are eligible, and the scheme's current period of operation.

points.text: The scheme refunds the duties, taxes and levies at Central, State and local level borne on an exported product that are not refunded under any other provision, including prior stage cumulative indirect taxes on inputs, on the principle that taxes should not be exported. It gives nothing for a duty already exempted, remitted or credited.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — objective

points.text: The rebate is at a notified percentage of the FOB value, with a value cap per unit where prescribed, or a fixed amount per unit. It is issued as a transferable duty credit e-scrip in an electronic ledger kept by the CBIC, usable only to pay basic customs duty on imports and freely transferable to other importers. It is not conditional on realisation of export proceeds at issue, but is deemed never to have been allowed if the proceeds are not received within the time the Foreign Exchange Management Act allows.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — form of rebate and sale proceeds

points.text: The manufactured garments are eligible. The three others are not: export of imported goods in the same or substantially the same form, supplies by a domestic tariff area unit to a special economic zone unit, and products subject to export duty or a minimum export price are all on the ineligible list, along with transhipment exports, deemed exports, goods made in a section 65 warehouse and exports without ICEGATE documentation.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 of the Foreign Trade Policy, RoDTEP — ineligible categories

points.text: The scheme runs by extension. Advance Authorisation holders, export oriented units and special economic zone units were brought in from 1 June 2025, so the authorisation is no bar. Notification No. 35/2025 dated 30 September 2025 extended the scheme for all of them to 31 March 2026, and Notification No. 74/2025-26 dated 31 March 2026 extended it again to 30 September 2026, so Manav's exports in 2026 are inside it.

citation.ref: DGFT Notification No. 35/2025 dated 30 September 2025 and Notification No. 74/2025-26 dated 31 March 2026, as carried in ICAI's Statutory Update for November 2026

written.scenario: Ojasvi Traders, registered in Maharashtra, imports goods with an assessable value of ₹10,00,000. Basic customs duty is 10 per cent, the social welfare surcharge applies, and the integrated tax rate is 18 per cent. Its accountant proposes to compute integrated tax on the assessable value alone and to take input tax credit of every amount paid at the port.
written.question: Explain under which law the integrated tax on the import is levied and on what value, compute the amounts payable, and state which of them Ojasvi Traders may take as credit.

points.text: Import of goods into India is treated as a supply in the course of inter-State trade by section 7(2) of the IGST Act, but the proviso to section 5(1) says the integrated tax on imported goods is levied and collected under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, at the point when customs duties are levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, on the value determined under the Customs Tariff Act.

citation.ref: Section 7(2) and the proviso to section 5(1), read with section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

points.text: The value under section 3(8) is the assessable value plus any duty of customs chargeable under section 12 and any sum chargeable in addition to it, so the accountant is wrong to use the assessable value alone. Basic customs duty is ₹1,00,000, the surcharge is 10 per cent of that, ₹10,000, and the integrated tax base is ₹11,10,000.

citation.ref: Section 3(8) read with section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018

points.text: Integrated tax at 18 per cent on ₹11,10,000 is ₹1,99,800, and no surcharge is levied on it. The total paid at the port is ₹1,00,000 plus ₹10,000 plus ₹1,99,800, that is ₹3,09,800.

citation.ref: Section 3(7) and Notification No. 13/2018-Customs dated 2 February 2018

points.text: Only the integrated tax of ₹1,99,800 is input tax within section 2(62) of the CGST Act and may be taken as credit under section 16, subject to its conditions and to possession of the bill of entry. The basic customs duty and the surcharge are not input tax and are never creditable; they are part of the cost of the goods.

citation.ref: Section 2(62)(a) and section 16(2) read with rule 36(1)(d) of the CGST Rules, 2017

written.scenario: Three shortfalls come to light at Yash Industries, registered in Gujarat, in 2026. First, ₹4 lakh of tax short paid for 2023-24 through a genuine classification error. Second, ₹6 lakh of input tax credit for 2023-24 taken on invoices for goods that were never received, which the officer treats as fraud. Third, ₹5 lakh of tax short paid for 2024-25, on which the officer has not yet decided whether to allege fraud. The due date for the annual return is 31 December following the financial year in each case.
written.question: Identify the section under which each demand is raised, and state the last date for issuing the show cause notice and for passing the order in each case, with reasons.

points.text: The first question is the period, not the conduct. For tax pertaining to financial years up to 2023-24, section 73 governs a shortfall for any reason other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, and section 74 governs the same shortfall where one of those is present. For 2024-25 onwards both give way to section 74A, which applies for any reason and keeps only the penalty different.

citation.ref: Sections 73(12), 74(12) and 74A(1), inserted and enacted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024

points.text: The classification error for 2023-24 is a section 73 case. The order must be passed within three years from the due date of the annual return for that year, 31 December 2024, so by 31 December 2027; and the notice must be issued at least three months before that, so by 30 September 2027, two years and nine months from the due date.

citation.ref: Section 73(2) and 73(10)

points.text: The invoices without goods for 2023-24 are a section 74 case, where the order must be passed within five years from the same due date, by 31 December 2029, and the notice at least six months before that, by 30 June 2029, four years and six months from the due date. The conduct decides the section, and the section decides the clock.

citation.ref: Section 74(2) and 74(10)

points.text: The 2024-25 shortfall is a section 74A case whether or not fraud is alleged. The notice must be issued within forty-two months from the due date of the annual return, 31 December 2025, so by 30 June 2029; the order within twelve months from the date of the notice, which the Commissioner or an officer not below Joint Commissioner may extend by up to six months for reasons recorded before the period expires. No notice at all is issued where the amount for the financial year is below ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 74A(1) proviso, 74A(2) and 74A(7)

written.scenario: Zoya Traders, registered in Delhi, short paid ₹10 lakh of tax for 2024-25. It asks what penalty it faces at each stage if the shortfall arose from a bona fide error, and what it faces if the officer establishes suppression of facts, in each of four situations: it pays before any notice; it pays within sixty days of the show cause notice; it pays within sixty days of the order; it pays later than that.
written.question: Set out the penalty at each stage under section 74A of the CGST Act, 2017 for both readings of the facts, with the interest position.

points.text: In every case the tax carries interest under section 50 from the day after it was due, whatever the penalty. Section 74A(5) fixes two penalties: for any reason other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, 10 per cent of the tax or ₹10,000, whichever is higher; for fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, a penalty equal to the tax.

citation.ref: Section 74A(5)

points.text: On the bona fide reading, section 74A(8) lets Zoya pay the tax with interest before the notice, or within sixty days of the notice, and in either case no penalty is payable and no notice, or no further proceedings, follow. Only if it pays later does the ₹1 lakh penalty, 10 per cent of ₹10 lakh, attach through the order.

citation.ref: Section 74A(8)

points.text: On the suppression reading, section 74A(9) runs a ladder: pay the tax and interest with a penalty of 15 per cent, ₹1.5 lakh, before the notice and no notice issues; pay with 25 per cent, ₹2.5 lakh, within sixty days of the notice and the proceedings conclude; pay with 50 per cent, ₹5 lakh, within sixty days of the order and they conclude; otherwise the full penalty equal to the tax, ₹10 lakh, stands.

citation.ref: Section 74A(9)

written.scenario: Four things happen to Ritika Enterprises, registered in Punjab, in 2026. An order under section 73 for 2022-23 is passed after the three-year limit has run out. Its statement of outward supplies for March shows ₹3 lakh more tax than the return it filed for the month, and it neither pays the difference nor replies to the officer's communication. A penalty is imposed on it under section 73, and the officer proposes a second penalty under section 122 for the same short payment. And on an order it does not dispute, it asks how long it has to pay and what happens if it does not.
written.question: Answer each under sections 75, 78 and 79 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Section 75(10) makes the time limits real: where the adjudication order is not issued within three years in a section 73 case or five years in a section 74 case, the proceedings are deemed to be concluded. The late order for 2022-23 is therefore of no effect and nothing can be demanded under it.

citation.ref: Section 75(10)

points.text: Under section 75(12), self-assessed tax shown in a return under section 39 that remains unpaid, and its interest, is recovered directly under section 79 without any notice under section 73 or 74; and self-assessed tax expressly includes tax on outward supplies furnished under section 37 but not included in the section 39 return. Because the difference may be a genuine reporting error, the officer first communicates it and asks for payment or an explanation, and proceeds under section 79 only where the person neither pays nor explains within the time given, which is Ritika's position.

citation.ref: Section 75(12) with its Explanation, read with Instruction No. 01/2022-GST dated 7 January 2022

points.text: Section 75(13) forbids the second penalty. Where a penalty is imposed under section 73 or 74, no penalty for the same act or omission is imposed on the same person under any other provision of the Act, so the section 122 penalty for the same short payment cannot be added.

citation.ref: Section 75(13)

points.text: Under section 78 any amount payable under an order must be paid within three months from the date of service of the order, and the officer may for reasons recorded in writing require payment sooner where it is expedient in the interest of revenue. On default, section 79 lets the officer recover by one or more modes: deducting the amount from money owed to the defaulter, detaining and selling its goods, requiring a third party who owes it money to pay the Government instead, and attaching and selling its property, and recovery may be made from its distinct persons in other States.

citation.ref: Section 78 with its proviso and section 79(1)(a) to (d) and 79(4)

written.scenario: An adjudication order against Neel Pharma, registered in Maharashtra, is passed on 20 March 2026 and communicated to it on 27 March 2026. It confirms tax of ₹8 lakh, interest of ₹80,000 and penalty of ₹80,000. Neel admits ₹3 lakh of the tax and ₹30,000 of the interest and wants to appeal the rest. It files the appeal on 10 July 2026. A separate order under section 129(3) imposes a penalty of ₹2 lakh for goods moved without an e-way bill, which Neel also wants to appeal. The department, for its part, wants to appeal a different order in Neel's favour.
written.question: Explain whether Neel Pharma's appeal is in time, compute the pre-deposit for each of its two appeals, state what the pre-deposit achieves, and contrast the department's position.

points.text: An appeal to the Appellate Authority lies within three months from the date the order is communicated, not the date it is passed, so the period runs from 27 March 2026 and ends on 27 June 2026. The appeal filed on 10 July is thirteen days late, but section 107(4) lets the Authority admit it within a further one month on being satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the delay.

citation.ref: Section 107(1) and 107(4)

points.text: Under section 107(6) the appeal is not filed unless Neel has paid, first, the full amount of tax, interest, fine, fee and penalty it admits, ₹3,30,000, and second, 10 per cent of the remaining tax in dispute, 10 per cent of ₹5 lakh, that is ₹50,000. The pre-deposit is ₹3,80,000; nothing is deposited against the disputed interest and penalty.

citation.ref: Section 107(6)(a) and (b)

points.text: The section 129(3) order is different: the proviso to section 107(6) requires a sum equal to 25 per cent of the penalty, ₹50,000, before that appeal is filed. On payment of the pre-deposit in either appeal, recovery of the balance of the disputed demand is deemed stayed until the appeal is disposed of.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 107(6) and section 107(7)

points.text: The department's appeal goes the other way. Under section 107(2) the Commissioner may, within six months of communication of the order, direct an officer to apply to the Appellate Authority against it, and there is no pre-deposit at all for a departmental appeal.

citation.ref: Section 107(2) and 107(3)

written.scenario: Om Logistics, registered in Haryana, loses before the Appellate Authority on 5 October 2026 in a matter involving tax of ₹30 lakh for three tax periods and a penalty of ₹12 lakh, on a question of fact. It files its appeal to the Appellate Tribunal electronically on 20 December 2026. The Appellate Authority's order was not uploaded on the common portal, and Om uploads a self-certified copy of it on 2 January 2027.
written.question: State the time limit for the appeal, the date on which it is treated as filed, and whether it can be heard by a single Member, under sections 109 and 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with the rules as amended from 22 September 2025.

points.text: Under section 112(1) the appeal lies within three months from the date the order is communicated, and section 112(6) lets the Tribunal admit it up to three months later on sufficient cause. An appeal filed on 20 December 2026 against an order of 5 October 2026 is within three months. The Removal of Difficulties Order counts the three months from the later of communication and the date the President enters office.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) and 112(6) read with the CGST (Ninth Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2019

points.text: The appeal is filed electronically in Form GST APL-05 and a provisional acknowledgement issues at once. Where the order appealed against is not on the common portal, the appellant uploads a self-certified copy within seven days of filing, and the date of the provisional acknowledgement is then the date of filing. Om uploaded the copy on 2 January 2027, more than seven days after 20 December, so the date of filing becomes 2 January 2027, the date of upload. The final acknowledgement follows in Part B of Form APL-02A.

citation.ref: Rule 110(1) and 110(4) as amended by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax with effect from 22 September 2025

points.text: Even on 2 January 2027 the appeal is inside the three months plus the further three months the Tribunal may condone, so it is not shut out; but Om must show sufficient cause for the part beyond 5 January 2027 only if the filing date fell after it, which it does not.

citation.ref: Section 112(6)

points.text: Section 109(8) lets a single Member hear an appeal, with the President's approval, where the tax or input tax credit involved, or the fine, fee or penalty determined, does not exceed ₹50 lakh and no question of law is involved. Rule 110A says the ₹50 lakh is reckoned cumulatively across all issues and all tax periods covered by the order. Om's matter is ₹30 lakh of tax, or ₹12 lakh of penalty, below the limit either way and on fact alone, so a single Member may hear it; otherwise one Judicial and one Technical Member sit together.

citation.ref: Section 109(8) read with rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017, inserted with effect from 22 September 2025

written.scenario: An adjudicating authority passes an order against Kabir Textiles, registered in Rajasthan, on 15 January 2026, communicated the same day, dropping a demand on one product and confirming it on another. Kabir appeals only the confirmed part and the Appellate Authority decides that appeal on 31 October 2026. The Revisional Authority believes the dropped demand was wrongly dropped. Separately, the adjudication order contains an arithmetical slip that overstates the confirmed demand by ₹40,000, which Kabir notices in February 2026.
written.question: Explain when and on what conditions the Revisional Authority may revise the order under section 108 of the CGST Act, 2017, and how Kabir has the arithmetical slip corrected under section 161.

points.text: Section 108(1) lets the Revisional Authority move by itself, on information reaching it, or at the State tax Commissioner's request. It calls for the record of a proceeding, and where a subordinate officer's order strikes it as both prejudicial to the interest of revenue and illegal or improper — or made with material facts left out of account — it may stay that order, hold an enquiry and pass a revised one, the person first having an opportunity of being heard.

citation.ref: Section 108(1)

keywords: prejudicial to the interest of revenue

points.text: Section 108(2) bars revision where the order has been subject to an appeal under section 107, 112, 117 or 118; where the six months for a departmental appeal under section 107(2) have not yet expired; or where more than three years have expired after the order. So the window opens on 16 July 2026 and closes on 15 January 2029.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(a) and (b)

points.text: The appeal does not close the door on the dropped demand. Where a point was not raised and decided in the appeal, the Revisional Authority may revise the order on that point before the expiry of one year from the date of the appellate order or three years from the original order, whichever is later: here 31 October 2027 or 15 January 2029, so by 15 January 2029. Time under a court's stay is excluded from the three years.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(c) with its proviso, and section 108(5)

points.text: Section 161 lets the authority that issued the order rectify an error apparent on the face of the record, on its own motion, on an officer's notice, or where the affected person brings it to notice within three months from the date of issue of the order. Kabir does so in February 2026, within time. No rectification is made after six months from the date of issue except a clerical or arithmetical error arising from an accidental slip, which this is; and a rectification that would increase liability requires a hearing.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its provisos

keywords: apparent on the face of the record

written.scenario: Sahil Stores, registered in Uttar Pradesh, discovers in September 2026 that it never filed its statement of outward supplies and its return for April 2023, due on 11 May 2023 and 20 May 2023. Its aggregate turnover was ₹1.8 crore in 2024-25 and ₹2.4 crore in 2025-26, and it asks whether it must file an annual return for either year.
written.question: Advise Sahil Stores on whether the April 2023 filings can still be made and on its annual return obligations for 2024-25 and 2025-26.

points.text: The Finance Act, 2023 put an outer limit on late returns. Section 37(5) bars furnishing the statement of outward supplies for a tax period after three years from its due date, and section 39(11) does the same for the return, with matching bars in section 44(2) for the annual return and section 52(15) for the operator's statement; the Government may extend the limit for a class of persons by notification.

citation.ref: Sections 37(5), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15), inserted by the Finance Act, 2023

points.text: Three years from 11 May 2023 ran out on 11 May 2026, and from 20 May 2023 on 20 May 2026. In September 2026 neither the statement nor the return for April 2023 can be furnished at all, late fee or not; the tax remains payable and recoverable, but the filings are closed.

citation.ref: Sections 37(5) and 39(11)

points.text: Section 44(1) requires an annual return for each financial year by 31 December following it, and lets the Commissioner exempt a class of persons by notification. Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax exempts, for 2024-25 onwards, a registered person whose aggregate turnover in the financial year is up to ₹2 crore from filing the annual return for that year. Sahil is exempt for 2024-25 at ₹1.8 crore and must file for 2025-26 at ₹2.4 crore, by 31 December 2026.

citation.ref: Section 44(1) read with Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025

written.scenario: Tara Ceramics, registered in Gujarat, has opted for the quarterly return scheme. In October 2026 it issues twelve invoices to registered buyers, and two of those buyers ask for their invoices to reach their statements in October itself so they can take credit that month. In November it issues invoices worth ₹70 lakh to registered buyers. It asks how and by when it furnishes each month's invoices and what the buyers will see.
written.question: Explain the Invoice Furnishing Facility and the quarterly statement of outward supplies available to Tara Ceramics under rule 59 of the CGST Rules, 2017, applying them to October and November.

points.text: A person in the quarterly return scheme furnishes its statement of outward supplies in Form GSTR-1 once a quarter, by the 13th of the month following the quarter, against the 11th of the following month for others. The Invoice Furnishing Facility is an option, not an obligation, for the first two months of the quarter, so that credit reaches recipients without waiting for the quarterly statement.

citation.ref: Rule 59(1) proviso and rule 59(2)

points.text: For October, Tara may furnish the two invoices those buyers need through the facility, up to the 13th of November, and leave the other ten for the quarterly statement. Invoices furnished through the facility appear in the recipients' Form GSTR-2A and GSTR-2B for that month, so the two buyers can take credit in October, and those invoices are not furnished again in the quarterly statement.

citation.ref: Rule 59(2) and 59(3)

points.text: The facility carries a ceiling of ₹50 lakh of invoices in each of the first two months of the quarter. November's ₹70 lakh cannot all go through it: up to ₹50 lakh may be furnished by the 13th of December, and the rest waits for the quarterly statement due by the 13th of January. December's invoices go only in the quarterly statement. There is no late fee for not using the facility, because it is not a return.

citation.ref: Rule 59(2) with the value limit, and rule 59(1)

written.scenario: For October 2026 Vikram Steels, registered in Karnataka, has output tax of ₹2,00,000 IGST, ₹1,50,000 CGST and ₹1,50,000 SGST. Its electronic credit ledger holds ₹3,00,000 of IGST credit, ₹60,000 of CGST credit and ₹1,20,000 of SGST credit. Its taxable turnover for the month is ₹80 lakh. It wants to pay the least possible in cash.
written.question: State the order in which the credit must be used under sections 49A and 49B of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 88A, compute the cash payable, and explain whether rule 86B affects the answer.

points.text: Section 49A says credit of central or State tax may be used against any tax only after the integrated tax credit has first been used fully. Rule 88A, made under section 49B, adds that integrated tax credit goes first against integrated tax, and the remainder against central tax and State tax in any order. Central tax credit is never used for State tax nor State tax credit for central tax.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5)(e) and (f), 49A and 49B read with rule 88A of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The ₹3,00,000 of IGST credit pays the ₹2,00,000 IGST liability first, leaving ₹1,00,000. Because the leftover may be split in any order, it is placed where the other credit is short: ₹90,000 against CGST, so that CGST credit of ₹60,000 clears the balance of that head, and ₹10,000 against SGST.

citation.ref: Rule 88A

points.text: SGST is then ₹1,50,000 less ₹10,000 of IGST credit less ₹1,20,000 of SGST credit, leaving ₹20,000 to be paid in cash. Every head is settled and the cash outgo is ₹20,000; putting the ₹1,00,000 against SGST instead would have stranded ₹70,000 of SGST credit and forced ₹90,000 of cash on CGST.

citation.ref: Section 49(4) and 49(5) read with rule 88A

points.text: Rule 86B bites on a registered person whose taxable supplies for a month, once exempt and zero-rated ones are left out, are worth above ₹50 lakh: the credit ledger may then discharge no more than 99 per cent of the output tax liability, so at least 1 per cent is paid in cash, unless one of the rule's exceptions applies. At ₹80 lakh Vikram is inside the rule. Its total output tax is ₹5,00,000, 1 per cent of which is ₹5,000, and its cash payment of ₹20,000 already exceeds that, so the rule changes nothing here.

citation.ref: Rule 86B

written.scenario: Anaya Traders, registered in Kerala, filed its return for March 2026, due on 20 April 2026, on 20 May 2026. The return showed tax of ₹5,00,000, of which ₹3,00,000 was paid by debiting the credit ledger and ₹2,00,000 by debiting the cash ledger; ₹50,000 of that cash had been deposited on 15 April 2026 and left lying in the cash ledger until the return was filed. Separately, it had wrongly availed ₹1,00,000 of credit that it utilised on 10 January 2026 and reversed on 10 March 2026, and another ₹40,000 wrongly availed that was never utilised. It also supplied goods worth ₹30 lakh, plus GST, to a State Government department in Kerala.
written.question: Compute the interest payable under section 50 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 88B, and state the tax the department deducts at source and when it would deduct nothing.

points.text: Where supplies of a tax period are declared in the return for that period and the return is filed late, the proviso to section 50(1) and rule 88B(1) charge interest only on the part of the tax paid by debiting the electronic cash ledger, for the delay in filing, at the notified 18 per cent. An amount credited to the cash ledger on or before the due date and lying there until it is debited on filing is left out of the base.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 50(1) read with rule 88B(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The ₹3,00,000 paid from credit bears no interest. Of the ₹2,00,000 paid from cash, the ₹50,000 deposited on 15 April and left there is excluded, so interest runs on ₹1,50,000 for the thirty days from 21 April to 20 May 2026: ₹1,50,000 at 18 per cent for thirty days, about ₹2,219.

citation.ref: Rule 88B(1) with its proviso

points.text: Section 50(3) charges interest on credit wrongly availed and utilised, at the notified 18 per cent, from the date of utilisation to the date of reversal under rule 88B(3). The ₹1,00,000 was utilised on 10 January and reversed on 10 March 2026, fifty-nine days, so the interest is about ₹2,910. The ₹40,000 that was availed but never utilised carries no interest: credit counts as utilised only when the ledger balance falls below the amount wrongly availed, and to that extent.

citation.ref: Section 50(3) read with rule 88B(3) and its Explanation

points.text: A State Government department is a deductor under section 51(1), and where the total value of supply under a contract exceeds ₹2.5 lakh it deducts 1 per cent as central tax and 1 per cent as State tax, 2 per cent in all, from the payment, on the value excluding the GST: ₹60,000 on ₹30 lakh, which Anaya sees in its electronic cash ledger. Nothing is deducted when the supplier's location, together with the place of supply, falls in one State while the deductor stands registered in a different one.

citation.ref: Section 51(1) with its proviso, read with section 20 of the IGST Act, 2017

written.scenario: Five movements begin at Bhairav Traders, registered in Punjab, in one week. Shoes worth ₹48,000 before GST at 18 per cent are sold and sent to a retailer in Gujarat. Cloth worth ₹48,000 is sent on a delivery challan to a job worker in Jalandhar, Punjab. Cloth worth ₹30,000 is sent on a delivery challan to a job worker in Himachal Pradesh. Gold jewellery worth ₹5 lakh is sent to a customer in Amritsar. Goods worth ₹90,000 are handed to a transporter for carriage by road, and Bhairav furnishes only the invoice details on the portal.
written.question: State for each movement whether an e-way bill is required under rule 138 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and who must generate it.

points.text: An e-way bill is required before the movement of goods of consignment value exceeding ₹50,000, whether the movement is in relation to a supply, for reasons other than supply, or an inward supply from an unregistered person. Consignment value is the value in the invoice, bill of supply or delivery challan, including the tax charged; for a movement other than supply it is the value on the delivery challan.

citation.ref: Rule 138(1) with its Explanation 2

points.text: The shoes need an e-way bill: ₹48,000 plus 18 per cent tax is ₹56,640, above the line. The cloth to Jalandhar does not: the movement is for job work, the challan value of ₹48,000 is the consignment value, and it is within ₹50,000. The cloth to Himachal Pradesh does: where a principal sends goods to a job worker in another State, the e-way bill is generated by the principal or a registered job worker irrespective of the value of the consignment.

citation.ref: Rule 138(1), third proviso to rule 138(1)

points.text: The jewellery needs none, whatever its value: jewellery, goldsmiths' and silversmiths' wares and other articles of Chapter 71, other than imitation jewellery, are among the goods for which no e-way bill is required, along with goods moved by a non-motorised conveyance, goods moved from a port or airport to an inland container depot for customs clearance, and movements within areas a State notifies.

citation.ref: Rule 138(14)(a) to (d) with the Annexure

points.text: For the ₹90,000 consignment the registered person causing the movement furnishes Part A, the parties, place of delivery, document, value and HSN; and Part B, the transport document and vehicle number, is furnished by the person transporting. Where the registered person does not generate the bill and hands the goods to a road transporter, he furnishes the transporter's details in Part B and the transporter generates the e-way bill on the basis of Part A. The bill exists only once Part B is entered.

written.scenario: Chetan Logistics carries three consignments. The first is ordinary cargo from Ludhiana to Bengaluru, 2,350 kilometres by road; the transporter enters the vehicle details in Part B at 10 a.m. on 1 November 2026. The second is an over-dimensional transformer moving 90 kilometres. The third is a container going by road to a port and then by ship, 700 kilometres in all. On the first, the truck breaks down and cannot reach Bengaluru within the validity period.
written.question: Compute the validity period of each e-way bill under rule 138(10) of the CGST Rules, 2017, state when it starts, and explain what Chetan Logistics can do about the breakdown.

points.text: For cargo other than over-dimensional cargo or a multimodal shipment with a leg by ship, the e-way bill is valid for one day up to 200 kilometres and one additional day for every 200 kilometres or part thereof after that. For 2,350 kilometres that is one day for the first 200 and eleven more for the remaining 2,150 kilometres, eleven parts of 200, so twelve days in all.

citation.ref: Rule 138(10), serial numbers 1 and 2 of the table

points.text: Over-dimensional cargo and a multimodal shipment in which at least one leg is by ship run on the tighter scale: one day up to 20 kilometres and one additional day for every 20 kilometres or part thereof. The transformer's 90 kilometres is one day for the first 20 and four more for the remaining 70, five days. The container's 700 kilometres is one day plus thirty-four, thirty-five days.

citation.ref: Rule 138(10), serial numbers 3 and 4 of the table

points.text: The period runs from the relevant date, which is the date and time the e-way bill is generated, that is when Part B is first entered, and a day, for this purpose, closes at midnight at the end of the day that follows that date. The first bill's clock starts at 10 a.m. on 1 November 2026.

citation.ref: Explanations 1 and 2 to rule 138(10)

points.text: Where a consignment cannot reach its destination within the validity period because of an exceptional circumstance such as a natural calamity, a law and order problem, trans-shipment delay or an accident to the conveyance, the transporter carrying it may extend the validity, giving the reason in detail, after updating Part B if needed. The extension may be made within eight hours from the time of expiry.

citation.ref: Proviso to rule 138(10)

written.scenario: Divya Enterprises, registered in Karnataka, has five events in 2026. It dispatches goods to a buyer on 3 June. It completes a consultancy service on 10 June. A bank it advises as a registered supplier of services completes a service on 10 June. A maintenance contract is terminated by the customer on 20 June after two of its four scheduled visits. Goods sent on approval on 5 January 2026 are still with the prospective buyer, undecided, on 30 June 2026.
written.question: State the last date by which a tax invoice must be issued in each case under section 31 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 47, and the extent of the invoice where the contract was terminated.

points.text: For goods, section 31(1) requires the invoice before or at the time of removal where the supply involves movement, and otherwise on delivery or making the goods available. The goods dispatched on 3 June are invoiced on or before 3 June, before or at removal.

citation.ref: Section 31(1)(a) and (b)

points.text: For services, section 31(2) allows the invoice before or after provision but within the period rule 47 prescribes: thirty days from the date of supply of the service, so the consultancy completed on 10 June is invoiced by 10 July. For an insurer, a banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company the period is forty-five days, so the bank's own service completed on 10 June may be invoiced by 25 July.

citation.ref: Section 31(2) read with rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Where a supply of services ceases under a contract before its completion, section 31(6) requires the invoice at the time the supply ceases, and only to the extent of the supply made before the cessation. The invoice is issued on 20 June for the two visits made, not for the four contracted.

citation.ref: Section 31(6)

points.text: Goods sent on approval for sale or return, removed before the supply happens, carry an invoice by whichever comes first: the moment of supply itself, or six months counted from the day they were removed. Removed on 5 January 2026 and still undecided, they must be invoiced by 5 July 2026 even if the buyer has not decided, and the goods move meanwhile on a delivery challan.

citation.ref: Section 31(7) read with rule 55(1)(c) of the CGST Rules, 2017

written.scenario: Eshan Foods, a registered manufacturer in Telangana with aggregate turnover of ₹9 crore in 2025-26, does the following in 2026. It sells exempt fresh produce to a wholesaler. It receives ₹2 lakh in advance for a supply of packaged foods. That supply is then cancelled and the advance refunded. It obtained its registration certificate on 15 May 2026 with effect from 1 April 2026, having issued ordinary invoices in between. It supplies goods to registered dealers, to walk-in consumers, and legal services are supplied to it by an advocate firm with turnover of ₹8 crore.
written.question: Name the document section 31(3) of the CGST Act, 2017 requires for each of the first four events, and explain which of the last three supplies must be reported as an e-invoice under rule 48(4).

points.text: A registered person supplying exempted goods or services, or paying tax under the composition levy, issues a bill of supply instead of a tax invoice, carrying no tax. On receipt of an advance he issues a receipt voucher; and where he then makes no supply and issues no invoice against that advance, he issues a refund voucher to the person who paid.

citation.ref: Section 31(3)(c), (d) and (e) read with rules 49, 50 and 51 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Within one month from the date of issue of the registration certificate, a registered person may issue a revised invoice against every invoice issued between the effective date of registration and the date the certificate was issued. Eshan may therefore issue revised invoices by 15 June 2026 for the supplies from 1 April to 15 May 2026, and its buyers then take credit on them.

citation.ref: Section 31(3)(a) read with rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Rule 48(4) requires a notified class of persons to prepare an e-invoice by uploading it on the Invoice Registration Portal and obtaining an Invoice Reference Number. The class is a registered person whose turnover, aggregated in any preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards, has gone past ₹5 crore; it bites on supplies to registered persons and on exports. At ₹9 crore Eshan is inside it: its supplies to registered dealers are e-invoiced and its supplies to walk-in consumers are not, business-to-consumer invoices not yet being covered.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) read with Notification No. 13/2020-Central Tax as amended

points.text: E-invoicing does not apply to a special economic zone unit, an insurer, a banking company or financial institution including a non-banking financial company, a goods transport agency, a supplier of passenger transportation service, a multiplex, a Government department, or to an Input Service Distributor's documents. It does apply where a notified supplier's invoice covers a supply on which the recipient pays under reverse charge, so the advocate firm at ₹8 crore must report its invoice to Eshan on the portal although Eshan pays the tax.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) with the exclusions in Notification No. 13/2020-Central Tax

written.scenario: Falguni Traders, registered in Gujarat, sold goods on three invoices in February 2026. In August 2026 the buyer returns a quarter of the goods on the first invoice, the second is found to have charged tax at 18 per cent where 5 per cent applied, and on the third the price is later reduced under a scheme the buyer has already passed on to its own customers. Falguni asks how to reduce its tax, by when, and whether one document can cover all three invoices.
written.question: Advise Falguni Traders under section 34 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Section 34(1) allows the supplier to issue a credit note where the taxable value or tax in an invoice exceeds what is payable, where the goods are returned by the recipient, or where the goods or services are found deficient. The returned quarter and the excess rate are both grounds. One or more credit notes may be issued for supplies made in a financial year, so a single credit note may cover the three February invoices together.

citation.ref: Section 34(1)

points.text: The credit note goes into the return of whichever month it is issued in, and the outer limit is the 30th of November that follows the financial year carrying that supply, or the day the annual return is actually furnished, whichever of the two falls first. For February 2026 supplies that is the return for August 2026, and in any event by 30 November 2026, and the output tax liability is then reduced.

citation.ref: Section 34(2)

points.text: The proviso to section 34(2) allows no reduction in output tax where the incidence of tax and interest on the supply has been passed on to any other person. On the third invoice the buyer has already passed the price and tax on to its customers, so Falguni cannot reduce its tax by a section 34 credit note; it may still give the price reduction by a commercial credit note without any tax adjustment.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 34(2)

written.scenario: Girish Forgings, registered in Maharashtra, sent steel blanks to a job worker on 1 May 2025 and a hydraulic press on 1 July 2024, both on delivery challans without tax, together with a set of dies. By 30 June 2026 the blanks are still with the job worker, who returns the finished parts only in September 2026. Girish also asks whether the job worker, who is registered, may sell the swarf and off-cuts the work generates, and whether Girish may sell finished parts to customers straight from the job worker's premises.
written.question: Explain the consequences under section 143 of the CGST Act, 2017 for the blanks, the press and the dies, and answer the two further questions.

points.text: Section 143 lets a registered principal send inputs or capital goods to a job worker without payment of tax, on condition that inputs are brought back or supplied from the job worker's premises within one year, and capital goods within three years, of being sent out. The Commissioner may on sufficient cause extend those periods by up to one year and two years respectively. Moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures and tools are outside the condition altogether, so the dies need never come back.

citation.ref: Section 143(1) with its provisos

points.text: The blanks were not returned within one year of 1 May 2025, so on 1 May 2026 the despatch is deemed a supply by Girish to the job worker on the day the blanks were sent out, 1 May 2025. Girish issues an invoice for it and declares the supply in the return for May 2026, the month in which the period expired, and pays interest from the original date of supply.

citation.ref: Section 143(3) read with rule 45(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The press sent on 1 July 2024 has until 30 June 2027, three years, and is within time; if it is not back by then the same deeming applies from 1 July 2024. When the job worker returns the finished parts in September 2026, after the period has run, the return is a supply by the job worker to Girish, taxable in the job worker's hands since he is registered.

citation.ref: Section 143(4)

points.text: Waste and scrap thrown up in the course of job work goes out on payment of tax: the job worker may supply it straight from his own premises where he is registered, and where he is not, the principal supplies it. Girish may supply finished goods to customers from the job worker's premises without bringing them back, on payment of tax, but only if it has declared that premises as an additional place of business or the job worker is registered, which he is.

citation.ref: Section 143(5) and the proviso to section 143(1)(b)

written.scenario: Harini Textiles, registered in Tamil Nadu with aggregate turnover of ₹12 crore in 2025-26, buys yarn from a mill and has it delivered straight to its job worker on 10 April 2026 without the yarn ever reaching Harini's factory. It asks whether it may take credit on the yarn, from when the one-year clock runs, what document covers the movement, and what it must file about the goods it sends for job work and when.
written.question: Answer under section 19 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 45 of the CGST Rules, 2017.

points.text: Section 19(1) and 19(2) let the principal take credit of input tax on inputs sent to a job worker, and expressly so even where the inputs are sent directly to the job worker's premises without first being brought to the principal's own place of business. Harini takes the credit on the yarn in the ordinary way on the mill's invoice.

citation.ref: Section 19(1) and 19(2)

points.text: Where the inputs go directly to the job worker, the one year within which they must be received back or supplied from the job worker's premises is counted from the date the job worker receives them, 10 April 2026, not from any despatch by Harini; the corresponding three years for capital goods run the same way. If the period passes, the inputs are deemed supplied by Harini to the job worker on the day they were sent out.

citation.ref: Section 19(3) with its Explanation

points.text: Goods sent for job work move under a delivery challan prepared in triplicate under rules 45 and 55, with the challan's details, and the challans for goods sent to and received from job workers in a period are reported in Form GST ITC-04 by the 25th of the month following the period. Because Harini's turnover exceeded ₹5 crore, the period is each half-year from 1 April and 1 October, so the April to September 2026 challans go in by 25 October 2026; a smaller principal files once a financial year. The form also serves as the intimation to the jurisdictional officer.

citation.ref: Rule 45(1) to 45(3) with the Explanation to rule 45(3), and rule 55

written.scenario: Ira Software, registered in Karnataka, exports services to clients abroad and also supplies software to a unit in a special economic zone for its authorised operations. It also makes exempt supplies in India. It asks whether its inputs' credit is lost on the exports as it would be on an exempt supply, what its two routes to a refund are, and what happens if a foreign client never pays.
written.question: Explain zero-rated supply under section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and answer Ira Software's three questions.

points.text: Zero-rated supply under section 16(1) means export of goods or services, and supply of goods or services for authorised operations to a special economic zone developer or unit. Both of Ira's supplies are zero-rated. Section 16(2) lets credit of input tax be taken for making zero-rated supplies notwithstanding that the supply may be an exempt supply, subject to section 17(5), so the credit is not lost as it would be on the exempt domestic supplies.

citation.ref: Section 16(1) and 16(2)

points.text: The first route is to supply without payment of integrated tax under a bond or letter of undertaking and claim refund of the unutilised input tax credit under section 54 of the CGST Act; that route is open to every registered person making zero-rated supplies. The refund is the rule 89(4) amount, computed on the turnover of zero-rated supplies against adjusted total turnover.

citation.ref: Section 16(3) read with section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017 and rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The second route, paying integrated tax on the zero-rated supply and claiming refund of the tax paid, is no longer open to everyone. Under section 16(4) it is available only to a class of persons the Government notifies, or for a class of goods or services it notifies, subject to the conditions it sets. Unless Ira is within a notification, it uses the letter of undertaking route.

citation.ref: Section 16(4) as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021

points.text: Where the proceeds of a zero-rated supply of goods are not realised, the proviso to section 16(3) requires the supplier to deposit the refund received, with interest under section 50 of the CGST Act, within thirty days after the expiry of the time the Foreign Exchange Management Act allows for receipt of the remittance. For services, the export itself is not complete unless payment is received in convertible foreign exchange or in rupees where the Reserve Bank permits, so an unpaid service is not an export at all.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 16(3), and section 2(6)(iv)

written.scenario: Jai Engineering, registered in Gujarat, supplies machines it makes in India to three buyers in 2026: a manufacturer holding an Advance Authorisation, an export oriented unit, and a merchant exporter who will export the machines within the period the notification allows. It also supplies components to a unit in a special economic zone. It asks which of these are exports, which are deemed exports, what tax applies to each, and who claims any refund.
