written.question: Advise Jai Engineering under section 147 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the notifications made under it, contrasting the treatment with zero-rated supply.

points.text: Deemed exports under section 147 are supplies of goods, notified by the Government, that are manufactured in India, do not leave India, and are paid for in rupees or in convertible foreign exchange. They are not zero-rated: the supplier charges tax on them and a refund of that tax is then claimed. The supply to the special economic zone unit for its authorised operations is different, being a zero-rated supply under section 16 of the IGST Act.

citation.ref: Section 147 and section 2(39), with section 16(1)(b) of the IGST Act, 2017

points.text: Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax notifies four categories: supply of goods by a registered person against an Advance Authorisation; supply of capital goods against an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation; supply of goods to an export oriented unit; and supply of gold by a bank or specified public sector undertaking against an Advance Authorisation. Jai's supplies to the authorisation holder and to the export oriented unit are both deemed exports.

citation.ref: Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017 under section 147

points.text: The refund of tax paid on a deemed export may be claimed by the supplier, or by the recipient where the supplier does not claim it, within two years of the relevant date, which is the date the return covering the supply is furnished. The merchant exporter's purchase is neither export nor deemed export in Jai's hands: it is a taxable domestic supply at the concessional rate of 0.1 per cent under the merchant-export notifications, with input tax credit retained, subject to the notification's conditions on export within the stated period; the merchant exporter then makes the export.

citation.ref: Third proviso to rule 89(1) and Explanation 2(b) to section 54; Notification No. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and 41/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate)

written.scenario: Four things happen around Kunal Retail, registered in Delhi, in 2026. It receives market research from a firm in the United States for a fee. Its holding company in Singapore provides it management support free of charge. Kunal's proprietor personally subscribes to a foreign streaming service for home use. Kunal buys imported goods from another importer by endorsement of the bill of lading while the ship is at sea, and separately buys goods lying in a customs bonded warehouse before they are cleared.
written.question: State the GST treatment of each, identifying who pays and under which provision.

points.text: Import of services under section 2(11) of the IGST Act is a supply where the supplier is outside India, the recipient is in India and the place of supply is in India. Section 7(1)(b) of the CGST Act makes import of services for a consideration a supply whether or not in the course of business. The market research is an import of services for business, and Kunal pays integrated tax on it under reverse charge and takes credit where eligible.

citation.ref: Section 2(11) and section 5(3) with Notification No. 10/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), read with section 7(1)(b) of the CGST Act, 2017

points.text: The support from the Singapore holding company is without consideration, which section 7(1)(b) alone would not reach. Paragraph 4 of Schedule I reaches it anyway: where a person imports services from a related person, or from another establishment of his own sited outside India, and does so in the course or furtherance of business, that is a supply even without consideration. Kunal therefore pays integrated tax on it under reverse charge, on the value under rule 28.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(c) read with paragraph 4 of Schedule I

points.text: The proprietor's personal streaming subscription is an online information and database access or retrieval service received by a non-taxable online recipient. The tax is not on him: the foreign supplier, or the person it appoints in India, registers under the simplified scheme and pays the integrated tax. An ordinary personal import of a service by an individual for private use, outside business, is otherwise not taxed in his hands.

citation.ref: Section 14 read with section 2(16) and 2(17)

points.text: Both purchases are outside GST by Schedule III. The high sea sale — title documents endorsed after despatch from the foreign port and before the goods are cleared for home consumption — counts as a supply of neither goods nor services under paragraph 8(b); integrated tax is levied only at clearance, on the last buyer who files the bill of entry, on the price he paid. The sale of warehoused goods before clearance is likewise outside GST under paragraph 8(a), but its value is counted as exempt supply for reversal under rules 42 and 43, which a high sea sale's value is not.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 8(a) and 8(b) of Schedule III, read with the Explanation to section 17(3)

written.scenario: Aarush Chemicals, registered in Gujarat, cannot decide whether a new product falls under an entry taxed at 5 per cent or one taxed at 18 per cent, and asks in May 2026 to pay tax provisionally. The provisional assessment order is communicated on 1 June 2026. On final assessment in 2027 the higher rate is upheld for part of the supplies and a lower value is accepted for others, so tax is due on some months and refundable on others.
written.question: Explain the procedure under section 60 of the CGST Act, 2017, the time within which the assessment must be finalised, and the interest position each way.

points.text: A taxable person who is unable to determine the value of a supply or the rate of tax applicable to it may request the proper officer in writing, giving reasons, for payment of tax on a provisional basis. The officer passes an order within ninety days of the request, allowing payment at the rate or on the value he specifies, and the person executes a bond, with such surety or security as the officer thinks fit, binding himself to pay the difference between the provisional and the finally assessed tax.

citation.ref: Section 60(1) and 60(2) read with rule 98 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The final assessment order must be passed within six months from the date of communication of the provisional assessment order, so by 1 December 2026 here. On sufficient cause and for reasons recorded in writing the Joint or Additional Commissioner may extend that by a further period not exceeding six months, and the Commissioner by such further period as he thinks fit not exceeding four years.

citation.ref: Section 60(3)

points.text: Where the final tax exceeds the provisional tax, Aarush pays the difference with interest at the section 50(1) rate from the day after the date the tax was originally due until the date of actual payment, whether it pays before or after the final order. Where the final tax is less, the excess is refunded under section 54 with interest under section 56 for any period beyond sixty days from the date of the refund application, subject to unjust enrichment.

citation.ref: Section 60(4) and 60(5)

written.scenario: Three registered persons in Rajasthan face three different assessments in 2026. Bhavika Traders receives a notice pointing out discrepancies between its returns. Chirag Steels has not filed its return for March 2024 despite a notice under section 46, and receives a best-judgment assessment order served on 1 August 2026. Dhruv Exports has an order passed on it under section 64 because the officer believed a delay would harm the revenue, and wants it withdrawn.
written.question: Explain the assessment each faces under sections 61, 62 and 64 of the CGST Act, 2017, the time within which each order may be passed, and what each person can do about it.

points.text: Bhavika's notice is a scrutiny under section 61. The officer scrutinises the return to verify its correctness and informs the person of discrepancies, seeking an explanation within a time not exceeding thirty days. An acceptable explanation ends the matter; where none is furnished within thirty days or the explanation is not accepted and no correction is made, the officer may go to audit, special audit, inspection or a demand under section 73 or 74. Scrutiny itself produces no assessment order.

citation.ref: Section 61 read with rule 99 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Chirag's order is a best-judgment assessment under section 62 of a registered person who failed to furnish a return after notice under section 46. The officer assesses to the best of his judgment on the material available, and the order must be issued within five years from the due date of the annual return for the financial year concerned, which for 2023-24 is 31 December 2024, so by 31 December 2029.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)

points.text: If Chirag furnishes a valid return within sixty days of service of the order, by 30 September 2026, the order is deemed withdrawn, though interest under section 50(1) and late fee under section 47 remain payable. If it misses that, it may still file within a further sixty days on paying an additional late fee of ₹100 a day for the delay beyond the first sixty, and the order is then deemed withdrawn likewise.

citation.ref: Section 62(2) with its proviso

points.text: Dhruv's is a summary assessment under section 64, made with the prior permission of the Additional or Joint Commissioner where the officer has evidence of a liability and believes delay would adversely affect the revenue. The Additional or Joint Commissioner may withdraw it on Dhruv's application made within thirty days of receipt of the order, or on his own motion where he finds it erroneous, and the liability is then determined under section 73 or 74 instead.

citation.ref: Section 64(1) and 64(2)

written.scenario: Esha Foods, registered in Kerala, receives a notice of audit under section 65 on 1 July 2026 for the two financial years 2024-25 and 2025-26. The officer asks for the records on 20 July 2026 and Esha makes them available on 25 July 2026. The audit team visits the premises on 1 August 2026. Esha asks how much notice it was entitled to, by when the audit must end, and what happens with the findings.
written.question: Answer under section 65 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017.

points.text: The Commissioner or an officer authorised by general or special order may audit any registered person for a financial year, part of one, or several years, at the person's place of business or in the office. The registered person is informed by notice not less than fifteen working days before the audit is conducted, so the notice of 1 July 2026 is in time for any date after mid-July.

citation.ref: Section 65(1) to 65(3) read with rule 101(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The audit is completed within three months from the date of its commencement, which is the later of the date the records called for are made available and the date the audit is actually instituted at the place of business. Here that is 1 August 2026, the visit, which is later than 25 July, so the audit must end by 1 November 2026. Where it cannot be completed in time the Commissioner may, for reasons recorded in writing, extend the period by a further period not exceeding six months.

citation.ref: Section 65(4) with its Explanation and proviso

points.text: Within thirty days of concluding the audit the officer informs Esha of the findings, the reasons for them, and its rights and obligations. Where the audit detects tax not paid or short paid, an erroneous refund or credit wrongly availed or utilised, the officer proceeds under section 73, 74 or 74A; the audit report is not itself a demand.

citation.ref: Section 65(6) and 65(7)

written.scenario: During an inquiry into Falak Electronics, registered in Delhi, the Assistant Commissioner forms the view that its declared values are not correct and its credit is far above the normal limits for its trade. He wants an outside professional to examine the books. Falak objects that it was audited under section 65 last year and asks who chooses the auditor, how long it takes, and who pays.
written.question: Explain the special audit under section 66 of the CGST Act, 2017 and answer Falak's objection and questions.

points.text: At any stage of scrutiny, inquiry, investigation or other proceedings, an officer of at least Assistant Commissioner rank may weigh the case's nature and complexity alongside what the revenue stands to lose, and form the view that value has been declared wrongly or that credit taken sits outside normal limits. He may then, with the prior approval of the Commissioner, direct the registered person to get its records examined and audited by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant the Commissioner has nominated.

citation.ref: Section 66(1)

points.text: The nominated professional submits a report, signed and certified, within ninety days to the Assistant Commissioner. On an application by Falak or the professional, or for any material and sufficient reason, the Assistant Commissioner may extend that by a further ninety days.

citation.ref: Section 66(2)

points.text: Falak's objection fails: the special audit may be directed notwithstanding that the accounts have been audited under any other provision of the Act or any other law, section 65 included. Falak is given an opportunity of being heard before any material gathered in the special audit is used against it in any proceedings.

citation.ref: Section 66(3) and 66(4)

points.text: The expenses of the examination and audit, including the remuneration of the chartered or cost accountant, are determined and paid by the Commissioner, and that determination is final. Where the audit detects a shortfall, the officer proceeds under section 73, 74 or 74A.

citation.ref: Section 66(5) and 66(6)

written.scenario: On 10 May 2026 officers of Central Tax enter the godown of Gaurav Traders, registered in Haryana, on an authorisation signed by a Joint Commissioner, and seize unaccounted goods and a set of ledgers. Gaurav asks on what basis the officers could enter, whether it can get the goods back to trade meanwhile, how long the department may keep what it seized, and whether it can have copies of the ledgers.
written.question: Answer under section 67 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Inspection under section 67(1) needs an officer not below Joint Commissioner who has reasons to believe that a taxable person has suppressed a transaction, claimed excess credit or contravened the Act to evade tax, or that a transporter or warehouse keeper is keeping goods that have escaped tax; he may then authorise any officer to inspect the place of business, and the transporter's or warehouse keeper's premises. Reasons to believe is the threshold, not mere suspicion.

citation.ref: Section 67(1)

points.text: Search and seizure under section 67(2) follow where the same officer has reasons to believe that goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things useful for or relevant to proceedings, are secreted in any place; he may search and seize them, or seal the premises where they cannot be seized. Goods that are not practicable to seize may be ordered not to be removed without permission.

citation.ref: Section 67(2) with its provisos

points.text: Gaurav may have the seized goods released provisionally on executing a bond and furnishing the prescribed security, or on payment of the applicable tax, interest and penalty. Where no notice is issued in respect of the seized goods within six months of the seizure, the goods are returned to the person from whom they were seized; the six months may be extended by the proper officer on sufficient cause for a further period not exceeding six months. Perishable or hazardous goods may be disposed of sooner under the notified procedure.

The person from whose custody documents are seized is entitled to make copies or take extracts in the presence of an officer, at such place and time as the officer indicates, except where doing so may prejudicially affect the investigation. Documents produced or seized may be retained only so long as necessary for their examination and for the proceedings, and the search and seizure are conducted as far as may be by the procedure of the criminal procedure law relating to search and seizure.

written.scenario: The Commissioner has reasons to believe that Harsh Metals, registered in Maharashtra, has taken credit of ₹6 crore on invoices for goods never supplied. A second firm, Ishita Traders, evaded ₹1.5 crore of tax by suppressing sales. Both ask whether their partners can be arrested, whether the offence is bailable, what punishment a court could impose, and whether the matter can be settled by compounding.
written.question: Answer under sections 69, 132 and 138 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Under section 69 the Commissioner may by order authorise an officer to make an arrest, provided he holds reasons to believe the person guilty of an offence under clauses (a) to (d) of section 132(1) that is punishable under clause (i) or (ii) of that sub-section, or under section 132(2) for a repeat offence. Those clauses reach an amount exceeding ₹2 crore, so Harsh's partners can be arrested and Ishita's, at ₹1.5 crore, cannot, unless the offence is a repeat.

citation.ref: Section 69(1) read with section 132(1)(i) and (ii) and 132(2)

points.text: Where the amount of tax evaded, credit wrongly availed or refund wrongly taken exceeds ₹5 crore the offence is cognizable and non-bailable: the arrested person is informed of the grounds of arrest in writing and produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours, and only a magistrate can grant bail. Every other offence is non-cognizable and bailable, and the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner may release the person on bail. Harsh's ₹6 crore is the first kind.

citation.ref: Section 69(2) and 69(3) read with section 132(4) and 132(5)

points.text: Section 132 punishes an amount above ₹5 crore with imprisonment up to five years and fine, an amount above ₹2 crore and up to ₹5 crore with up to three years and fine, and, only for issuing invoices without supply and retaining the benefit, an amount above ₹1 crore and up to ₹2 crore with up to one year and fine; a second offence carries up to five years whatever the amount. Imprisonment for the first two runs at least six months absent special and adequate reasons recorded in the judgment, and no prosecution lies without the Commissioner's previous sanction.

Compounding under section 138 is allowed before or after prosecution on payment of a compounding amount, not less than 25 per cent nor more than 100 per cent of the tax involved, and only after the tax, interest and penalty have been paid; it then bars further proceedings for the same offence and abates any prosecution. It is not open to a person accused of the fake-invoice offence in section 132(1)(b), so Harsh cannot compound; to a person already allowed to compound once for the listed clauses; or to a person convicted by a court. Ishita may apply.

citation.ref: Section 138(1) with its provisos, 138(2) and 138(3)

written.scenario: Four situations arise in Uttar Pradesh in 2026. Jatin, unregistered, collects ₹3 lakh as GST from customers and keeps it. Kavya Traders, registered, short paid ₹4 lakh of tax for 2023-24 through a bona fide error. Lalit, a consultant, arranged the fake invoices through which a client took ₹20 lakh of credit and was paid a fee out of it. Meera Stores filed a return with a clerical error in the recipient's GSTIN, involving tax of ₹3,000, and corrected it when told.
written.question: State the penalty exposure of each under sections 122, 125 and 126 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Collecting any amount as tax and failing to pay it to the Government beyond three months of the due date is one of the twenty-one offences in section 122(1), and so is collecting tax in contravention of the Act. The penalty is ₹10,000 or the amount of tax evaded or not paid, whichever is higher, so Jatin faces ₹3 lakh; being unregistered does not take him outside the section, which applies to a taxable person.

citation.ref: Section 122(1)(iii) and (iv) with the closing words of section 122(1)

points.text: Kavya falls under section 122(2): a registered person who short pays for any reason other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is liable to ₹10,000 or 10 per cent of the tax due, whichever is higher, so ₹40,000; had it been fraud the penalty would be ₹10,000 or the tax due, ₹4 lakh. For 2023-24 the demand itself runs under section 73, and paying before the notice or within thirty days of it removes the penalty under that section.

citation.ref: Section 122(2)(a) and (b)

points.text: Lalit is reached by section 122(1A): any person who retains the benefit of a transaction covered by the fake-invoice, credit-without-invoice or refund clauses of section 122(1), and at whose instance the transaction is conducted, is liable to a penalty equal to the tax evaded or the credit availed or passed on, so ₹20 lakh, quite apart from the client's own penalty.

citation.ref: Section 122(1A)

points.text: Meera's slip is a minor breach. Section 126 forbids any penalty for a minor breach, for a procedural requirement, or for an omission or mistake in documentation where the error can be put right easily and carries neither fraudulent intent nor gross negligence; a breach is minor where the tax involved is below ₹5,000, and a mistake is easily rectifiable where it is an error apparent on the face of record. The general penalty under section 125, up to ₹25,000 for a contravention with no penalty of its own, is discretionary and must be commensurate with the breach, and the disciplines of section 126 do not apply where the law fixes a penalty as a sum or a percentage.

citation.ref: Section 125 and section 126(1) with its Explanation, 126(2) and 126(6)

written.scenario: A truck carrying taxable goods worth ₹10 lakh, taxable at 18 per cent, belonging to Nakul Traders of Punjab is intercepted in Haryana on 5 March 2026 without an e-way bill and detained. In the same truck are exempted goods worth ₹6 lakh belonging to another trader who cannot be traced. Nakul comes forward to have its goods released; the other owner does not.
written.question: Compute the penalty for release of each lot under section 129 of the CGST Act, 2017, and set out the procedure and time limits that follow the detention.

points.text: Goods transported in contravention of the Act or rules, and the conveyance and documents, are liable to detention or seizure, and are released on payment of the section 129(1) penalty or on furnishing security of equal amount. Where the owner of taxable goods comes forward, the penalty is equal to 200 per cent of the tax payable. Tax on Nakul's goods is ₹1,80,000, so its penalty is ₹3,60,000; the goods may instead be released on security of that amount.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a) and 129(1)(c)

points.text: Where the owner does not come forward, the penalty on taxable goods is the higher of 50 per cent of the value and 200 per cent of the tax; for exempted goods it is the lower of 5 per cent of the value and ₹25,000 when the owner does not come forward, and the lower of 2 per cent and ₹25,000 when he does. The untraced trader's exempted goods worth ₹6 lakh therefore bear 5 per cent, ₹30,000, capped at ₹25,000, so ₹25,000.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a) and (b)

points.text: The officer detaining the goods issues a notice within seven days of the detention specifying the penalty, and passes an order within seven days from the service of that notice, after giving the person an opportunity of being heard. On payment of the penalty all proceedings on the notice are deemed concluded.

Where the penalty is not paid within fifteen days from receipt of the order, the goods or the conveyance are liable to be sold or disposed of under rule 144A to recover it, the conveyance being releasable on payment of the penalty or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less. An appeal against the order lies only on pre-deposit of 25 per cent of the penalty.

citation.ref: Section 129(6) with its proviso, read with the proviso to section 107(6)

written.scenario: Om Infra, registered in Telangana, wants certainty on whether a new arrangement with a client is a supply, on the classification of a product, and on whether it may take credit on certain inputs. On the credit question a show cause notice is already pending against it. It obtains a ruling on the first two questions, the jurisdictional officer disagrees with one, and a competitor asks whether it can rely on the ruling too. Om later learns that a fact it stated in the application was wrong.
written.question: Explain which questions can be brought, the route of appeal, on whom the ruling binds and for how long, and what follows from the wrong statement, under sections 97 to 104 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Advance ruling may be sought on the questions section 97(2) lists: classification of goods or services, applicability of a notification, time and value of supply, admissibility of input tax credit, liability to pay tax, the requirement to register, and whether an activity amounts to a supply. All three of Om's questions are within the list, but the Authority does not admit an application where the question is already pending or decided in any proceedings in the applicant's own case, so the credit question, on which a notice is pending, is rejected by a speaking order after a hearing.

citation.ref: Section 97(2) and the first proviso to section 98(2)

points.text: The Authority pronounces its ruling within ninety days of receipt of the application. The applicant, or the concerned or jurisdictional officer, may appeal to the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling within thirty days of receipt of the ruling, extendable by a further thirty days on sufficient cause, on a fee of ₹10,000 under each Act for the applicant and none for the officer; the Appellate Authority decides within ninety days of the appeal. Where its members differ, no advance ruling can be issued on that question.

citation.ref: Section 98(6), section 100(1) and (2) with its proviso, and section 101(2) and (3)

points.text: The ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and the concerned or jurisdictional officer in respect of that applicant; it does not bind the competitor or any other similarly placed person, who must seek its own. There is no fixed period: it binds until the law, facts or circumstances supporting the original ruling change.

citation.ref: Section 103(1) and 103(2)

points.text: Where the Authority or Appellate Authority finds that the ruling was obtained by fraud, suppression of material facts or misrepresentation of facts, it may, after hearing the applicant, declare the ruling void ab initio, and the Act then applies as if the ruling had never been made, excluding the period from the ruling to the order declaring it void. Om's wrong statement, if it was a misrepresentation of a material fact, exposes the ruling to that order.

citation.ref: Section 104(1) with its proviso and Explanation

written.scenario: Four events in Madhya Pradesh in 2026. Prakash sells his sole-proprietorship business as a going concern to Rohan on 1 April 2026 with ₹3 lakh of tax for 2025-26 still unpaid. Sanjay Pvt. Ltd. is wound up and a liquidator is appointed on 1 June 2026; ₹5 lakh of tax cannot be recovered from the company. Tarun retires from a partnership firm on 1 July 2026 and the firm tells the Commissioner on 15 September 2026. Uma carries on her minor nephew's business as his guardian.
written.question: State who is liable for the tax in each case, and to what extent, under sections 85, 88, 89, 90 and 91 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Where a taxable person parts with his business, whole or in part, whether by sale, by gift, by lease or otherwise, transferor and transferee stand jointly and severally liable — wholly, or so far as the transfer goes — for the tax, interest and penalty due up to the time of the transfer, whether that was settled before the transfer or after it. Prakash and Rohan are both liable for the ₹3 lakh, and Rohan is liable in the ordinary way for supplies made from 1 April 2026.

citation.ref: Section 85(1) and 85(2)

keywords: up to the time of the transfer

points.text: The liquidator must intimate his appointment to the Commissioner within thirty days, and the Commissioner, within three months of receiving that intimation, notifies him of the amount that would be sufficient to provide for the company's tax, interest and penalty. Where the amount cannot be recovered from a private company being wound up, every person who was a director during the period the tax was due is jointly and severally liable, unless he proves to the Commissioner's satisfaction that the non-recovery is not attributable to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part.

Section 89 makes the same rule for a private company that is not being wound up: where tax, interest or penalty cannot be recovered from it, every director during the period is jointly and severally liable, with the same defence, and the section is disapplied where the private company has since become a public company, except as to any personal penalty. Sanjay's directors answer for the ₹5 lakh unless they make out the defence.

citation.ref: Section 89(1) and 89(2)

points.text: The firm and each partner are jointly and severally liable for the firm's tax, interest and penalty, notwithstanding any contract to the contrary. A retiring partner is liable for dues up to the date of retirement, whether determined or not; but where the retirement is not intimated to the Commissioner within one month, his liability continues until the intimation is received. Tarun's intimation came on 15 September 2026, so he is liable for the firm's dues up to that date and not merely to 1 July. Uma, as guardian, is liable for the tax on the business as if the minor were a major conducting it himself.

citation.ref: Section 90 with its proviso, and section 91

written.scenario: Vardhan Imports files five bills of entry in one week and the appraiser questions the classification of each: (a) motor cars shipped in knocked-down form, without seats; (b) coffee blended with chicory; (c) electric shavers, which the importer entered under heading 8509 for electro-mechanical domestic appliances with a self-contained electric motor, although heading 8510 covers shavers and hair clippers with self-contained electric motors; (d) a vehicle that on its design is equally a vehicle for the transport of persons under heading 8703 and for the transport of goods under heading 8704; and (e) plastic film that is pasted on car windows to cut sun glare and finds no entry of its own in the tariff.
written.question: State which of the General Rules for Interpretation, in the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, decides each item, and how, and explain the order in which the rules are applied.

points.text: Rule 1 comes first and the rest follow only if it does not settle the matter. A section title, a chapter title, a sub-chapter title — each is there for ease of reference and carries no legal force. In law the classification follows instead from what the headings themselves say, together with any relative section or chapter notes; rules 2 to 6 come in only where those do not otherwise require. A note of one chapter cannot be applied to interpret the entries of another.

citation.ref: Rule 1 of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule

points.text: The knocked-down cars without seats are classified as motor cars under rule 2(a). A reference in a heading to an article includes that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that as presented it has the essential character of the complete article, and includes the complete article presented unassembled or disassembled. A car without seats is still a car, and railway coaches without seats are still railway coaches; only goods needing minor adjustments qualify, not goods still needing turning, grinding or heat treatment.

citation.ref: Rule 2(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation

points.text: Coffee blended with chicory stays within the heading for coffee under rule 2(b): a reference to a material or substance includes mixtures or combinations of that material with other materials, and a reference to goods of a given material includes goods consisting wholly or partly of it. The same rule sends natural rubber mixed with synthetic rubber to natural rubber. Where the mixture is prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, rule 2(b) hands the question to rule 3.

citation.ref: Rule 2(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation

points.text: The shavers go to heading 8510 under rule 3(a): the heading which provides the most specific description is preferred to a heading providing a more general description, and shavers with self-contained electric motors is more specific than electro-mechanical domestic appliances. Had rule 3(a) failed, rule 3(b) classifies mixtures, composite goods and retail sets by the material or component which gives them their essential character, which is why a lead pencil with an eraser at its end is a pencil.

citation.ref: Rules 3(a) and 3(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation

points.text: The vehicle equally classifiable under headings 8703 and 8704 goes to heading 8704 under rule 3(c): where rules 3(a) and 3(b) both fail to settle it, the goods fall to whichever of the competing headings stands last in numerical order, chosen from those that merit consideration equally. The Tribunal so held in Mahindra and Mahindra, and the Supreme Court maintained it.

citation.ref: Rule 3(c) of the General Rules for Interpretation; Mahindra and Mahindra v. CCE 1999 (109) ELT 739 (Tri.)

points.text: The sun-glare film, which no heading names, is classified under rule 4 with the goods to which it is most akin: heading 3925 30 00 covers builders' wares of plastic not elsewhere specified, including shutters, blinds and similar articles, and the film is most akin to plastic blinds. Rule 4 is reached only after rules 1 to 3 have failed, and rule 6 then settles the sub-heading, on the footing that only sub-headings at the same level are comparable.

citation.ref: Rules 4 and 6 of the General Rules for Interpretation

written.scenario: Meghdoot Power Ltd is setting up a new thermal power station and imports turbines, boilers, cables, control instruments, and spare parts and consumables worth 8 per cent of the value of the consignment, each item falling under a different heading with a different rate. In the same month its trading arm imports cameras, each in a fitted leather case that is sold with it, and industrial gas delivered in steel cylinders that are returned to the supplier for refilling.
written.question: Explain how the power station's imports are classified and assessed, and how rule 5 of the General Rules for Interpretation treats the camera cases and the gas cylinders. State what the dashes before a description in the First Schedule mean.

points.text: The power station's imports are project imports. The Indian tariff carries a Chapter 98 beyond the 97 chapters of the HSN, and heading 9801 groups all items of machinery, instruments, apparatus and appliances, components and raw materials required for the initial setting up of a unit, or for the substantial expansion of an existing unit, under one heading assessed at one consolidated rate of duty, irrespective of the nature of the goods and the classification each would otherwise carry.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule, read with the Project Imports Regulations, 1986

points.text: The scheme reaches an industrial plant, an irrigation scheme, power projects, mining work, oil or mineral exploration, and whatever else the Central Government notifies, so a thermal power station qualifies. Spare parts, raw material and consumable stores may be imported under the heading up to 10 per cent of the value of the goods, so the 8 per cent here rides with the project. An individual exemption notification still applies to an item grouped under the heading, as the Supreme Court has held.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule

points.text: The camera cases are classified with the cameras under rule 5(a). A case made for a camera, for a musical instrument, for a gun, for drawing instruments or for a necklace, and any similar container, goes with the article it holds when it is specially shaped or fitted to contain it, is suitable for long-term use, is presented with it and is of a kind normally sold with it. The rule does not apply to a container which gives the whole its essential character.

citation.ref: Rule 5(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation

points.text: The gas cylinders are classified separately. Rule 5(b) classifies packing materials and packing containers presented with the goods together with those goods when they are of a kind normally used for packing them, but the rule does not apply when the packing material or container is clearly suitable for repetitive use. Returnable steel cylinders are made for repetitive use, so they cannot be classified along with the gas.

citation.ref: Rule 5(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation

points.text: Under the general explanatory notes to the First Schedule, a description preceded by one dash is a sub-classification of the article or group covered by the heading; two dashes mark a sub-classification of the immediately preceding one-dash description; three or four dashes mark a sub-classification of the immediately preceding description carrying one or two dashes. A heading is a four-digit number, a sub-heading six digits, and a tariff item eight digits with the rate; the abbreviation "%" means duty at that percentage on the value under section 14 of the Customs Act, and where no preferential rate is notified the standard rate applies.

citation.ref: General explanatory notes and additional notes to the First Schedule

written.scenario: A vessel carrying a consignment of machine tools for Kritika Engineering, Pune, is expected at Nhava Sheva on 10 May 2026 and arrives that morning. The steamer agent files the arrival manifest electronically on 9 May and entry inwards is granted on 10 May. Kritika files its bill of entry for home consumption on 12 May, self-assesses the duty and pays it the same day. A second consignment of the same importer, which arrived on 1 April 2026, is still lying uncleared at the port on 5 May because the importer is short of funds.
written.question: Explain the duties of the person-in-charge on arrival, when Kritika should have presented its bill of entry and what the delay costs, when the duty was due, and what may happen to the uncleared consignment.

points.text: A vessel or aircraft entering India from outside may call or land, for the first time after arrival or while carrying passengers or cargo brought in it, only at a customs port or customs airport, unless the Board permits otherwise; the only excuse is being compelled by accident, stress of weather or other unavoidable cause, and then the arrival must be reported to the nearest customs or police officer and nothing unloaded without permission.

citation.ref: Section 29

points.text: The person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft delivers the arrival manifest or import manifest electronically before the arrival of the vessel or aircraft, and the person-in-charge of a vehicle delivers an import report within twelve hours after its arrival at the customs station. Where the manifest is not delivered in time without sufficient cause, the person-in-charge is liable to a penalty not exceeding ₹50,000. An incorrect or incomplete manifest may be amended or supplemented where there is no fraudulent intention.

citation.ref: Sections 30(1), 30(2) and 30(3)

points.text: Nothing may be unloaded from a vessel while her master lacks the proper officer's grant of entry inwards, and that grant waits on delivery of the arrival manifest or on a valid reason for the delay being accepted; this applies to vessels only, not to aircraft or vehicles, and does not apply to the unloading of baggage accompanying a passenger or crew member, mail bags, animals, perishable goods and hazardous goods. Goods may be unloaded only if mentioned in the manifest, at approved places, under the supervision of the proper officer.

citation.ref: Sections 31, 32, 33 and 34

points.text: The bill of entry goes in no later than the close of the day — holidays counted — immediately preceding the day on which the vessel, aircraft or vehicle bringing the goods reaches the customs station at which they are to be cleared for home consumption or warehoused, and may be lodged up to thirty days before the expected arrival; the Board may prescribe a later limit, not beyond the end of the day of arrival. Kritika's filing on 12 May is late, and unless the proper officer finds sufficient cause it pays the prescribed charges for late presentation. No bill of entry is needed for goods in transit or transhipment.

citation.ref: Section 46(3) with its provisos, read with the 2018 regulations on electronic filing of the bill of entry and paperless processing

points.text: The importer self-assesses the duty under section 17 and pays it on the date of presentation of the bill of entry, so Kritika's payment on 12 May was on time; where the bill of entry is returned for payment after assessment, reassessment or provisional assessment, the duty is paid within one day, excluding holidays, of its return; and a deferred-payment importer pays by the due date the rules specify. Duty not paid in time carries interest at a rate between 10 per cent and 36 per cent fixed by the Central Government, which the Board may waive in the public interest.

citation.ref: Sections 17(1), 47(1) and 47(2)

points.text: Goods not cleared for home consumption or warehousing within thirty days of unloading, or within such further time as the proper officer allows, or whose title has been relinquished, may be sold by the custodian by auction with the approval of the customs department and after notice to the importer; animals, foodstuffs and hazardous goods may be sold sooner. An importer who cannot clear within a reasonable time may instead apply under section 49 to store the goods in a public warehouse for up to thirty days, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner by thirty days at a time, without the goods becoming warehoused goods.

citation.ref: Sections 48 and 49

written.scenario: Sahyadri Motors Ltd, a manufacturer with a turnover of ₹40 crore, three GST registrations and an import-export code, filed 60 import documents in FY 2025-26 and has never been an Authorised Economic Operator. In April 2026 it asks whether it may pay import duty after clearance instead of before. Its bills of entry in a month are returned for payment on the 4th, the 19th and, in March 2027, on the 9th and the 24th.
written.question: State who may defer payment of import duty from 1 April 2026, whether Sahyadri qualifies, the due dates that apply to its four bills of entry, and what a default costs.

points.text: Section 47(1) lets the Central Government permit a class of importers to make deferred payment of import duty. Three classes are permitted: importers certified as AEO Tier-Two or AEO Tier-Three, Authorised Public Undertakings, and, with effect from 1 April 2026, the Eligible Manufacturer Importer, which is a manufacturer importer approved by the Directorate of International Customs; the third class is permitted to defer only up to 31 March 2028.

citation.ref: Section 47(1); Notification No. 12/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2026 read with Circular No. 8/2026-Customs

points.text: An Eligible Manufacturer Importer must be an importer and a manufacturer, or one that sends inputs or machinery to a job worker without paying tax on them; hold a valid IEC; have filed at least 25 import or export documents in the previous financial year, relaxed to 10 for an MSME; have at least one active GST registration showing manufacturing as the nature of business; have a combined turnover across all registrations under the same PAN above ₹5 crore in the last financial year; have been in business for at least two financial years; have filed all GST returns due; carry a clean record with no tax collected but not deposited, no arrest, conviction or pending prosecution under indirect tax law; and furnish a chartered accountant's certificate of solvency for the two preceding years. Sahyadri meets every test and may apply; an existing AEO-T1 entity meeting them may also apply.

citation.ref: Eligibility conditions for an Eligible Manufacturer Importer

points.text: Under rule 4 of the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016 as amended from 1 March 2026, duty on a bill of entry returned for payment on any day of a month other than March, from the 1st to the last day, is due on the 1st day of the following month; duty on a bill of entry returned on any day of March, from the 1st to the 31st, is due on 31 March. So the bills of entry of the 4th and the 19th are both due on the 1st of the following month, and the two March bills of the 9th and the 24th are both due on 31 March 2027, all periods excluding holidays.

citation.source: Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
citation.ref: Rule 4 as amended by Notification No. 13/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2026, effective 1 March 2026

points.text: The importer intimates its intention to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner having jurisdiction over the port and pays electronically. Duty not paid by the due date carries interest under section 47(2) until payment. If there is default more than once in three consecutive months the facility is withdrawn until the duty with interest is paid in full, and deferment continues only for an importer who paid each bill of entry by its due date and any differential duty on reassessment with interest within one day, excluding holidays. The facility never covers goods not assessed or not declared in the entry.

citation.source: Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
citation.ref: Rules 3, 5 and 6, read with section 47(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 and Circular No. 52/2016-Customs

written.scenario: Mr Rao, an Indian resident aged 45, returns to Delhi by air on 20 June 2026 after fourteen months of employment in Dubai, and declares: used clothing, a used phone and toiletries worth ₹90,000; a new camera and a new watch, bought abroad, worth ₹1,10,000 together; one new laptop worth ₹85,000; and 30 grams of gold jewellery bought abroad worth ₹1,80,000. His wife, who joined him only eight months ago, returns on the same flight with new perfumes and handbags worth ₹60,000 and 35 grams of gold jewellery bought abroad worth ₹2,10,000. Neither carries anything listed in Annexure-I. A colleague of Mr Rao arriving from Nepal by road the same week asks what allowance he has.
written.question: Compute the customs duty payable by Mr Rao and by his wife under the Baggage Rules, 2026, and answer the colleague. State the rate of duty and the date on which it is determined.

points.text: Under rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2026, which replaced the Baggage Rules, 2016 from 2 February 2026, every passenger including an infant clears free of duty, without any value limit, travel souvenirs together with such used personal effects as the daily necessities of life call for, leaving aside anything listed in Annexure-I. Personal effects now carries a wider sense: articles, new or second-hand, that a passenger might reasonably want for personal use on the journey, but nothing carried for commercial purposes. Mr Rao's clothing, phone and toiletries worth ₹90,000 are cleared free.

citation.ref: Rule 3, read with CBIC Master Circular No. 4/2026-Customs dated 1 February 2026

points.text: Rule 5 gives a general free allowance of ₹75,000 to a resident; to a tourist of Indian origin; and to a foreigner holding a valid visa which is not a tourist visa — each of them not an infant and arriving otherwise than by land — for articles outside Annexure-I carried on the person or in bona fide accompanied baggage; a tourist of foreign origin gets ₹25,000. The allowance of one passenger cannot be pooled with another's, so Mr Rao's ₹75,000 cannot absorb his wife's purchases and hers cannot absorb his. The old rule that a passenger from Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar got a smaller allowance is gone.

citation.ref: Rule 5

points.text: A passenger of 18 years or more, other than a crew member, may bring in bona fide baggage one new laptop, notepad included, without duty and on top of the general free allowance, so Mr Rao's laptop worth ₹85,000 is cleared free and does not eat into his ₹75,000. His camera and watch worth ₹1,10,000 exceed the allowance by ₹35,000, which is dutiable.

citation.ref: Rule 5

points.text: Rule 6 allows a resident or tourist of Indian origin who has resided abroad for more than one year duty-free clearance of jewellery up to 40 grams if brought by a female passenger and 20 grams if brought by any other passenger; jewellery means articles of adornment of gold, silver, platinum or other precious metals, studded or not. Mr Rao, abroad fourteen months, gets 20 grams free and pays duty on 10 grams, valued at ₹60,000. His wife has been abroad eight months, so she has no jewellery allowance at all: her 35 grams worth ₹2,10,000 is dutiable in full, and her perfumes and handbags of ₹60,000 sit inside her own ₹75,000 allowance.

citation.ref: Rule 6

points.text: Passenger baggage is exempt from IGST, compensation cess and social welfare surcharge, and basic customs duty at 35 per cent is levied on the value above the duty-free allowances, so the effective rate is 35 per cent; the rate and valuation are those in force on the date the baggage declaration is made under section 77, here 20 June 2026. Mr Rao pays 35 per cent of ₹95,000, that is ₹33,250; his wife pays 35 per cent of ₹2,10,000, that is ₹73,500. Firearms and cartridges above 50 are outside this rate and are charged at 70 per cent under heading 9803, which does not apply to motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages or tobacco.

citation.ref: Sections 77 and 78, read with Notification No. 26/2016-Customs as amended and heading 9803 of the Customs Tariff

points.text: A passenger who reaches India by land clears without duty nothing beyond used personal effects, and only such of them as the daily necessities of life call for; no general free allowance attaches to a land-border arrival, whatever the category of passenger. The colleague coming from Nepal by road therefore gets no ₹75,000 allowance, and anything new he carries is dutiable.

citation.ref: Rule 5, proviso on passengers arriving by land

written.scenario: MV Ocean Pearl, a foreign-going vessel, arrives at Mumbai from Singapore carrying cargo to be unloaded at Mumbai, cargo destined for Chennai that stays on board for the vessel's next call, and containers for Colombo that are landed at Mumbai and loaded on another ship. She carries imported fuel, provisions and spare parts. At Chennai she is chartered for three coastal voyages between Indian ports, and before that an Indian chandler supplies her with rice, fresh vegetables and bottled water made in India.
written.question: Distinguish transit from transhipment and state the duty position of each, and explain how the Customs Act treats the vessel's stores at each stage.

points.text: The Chennai cargo is in transit: it arrives in a conveyance, is shown in the arrival manifest as same-bottom cargo, and continues in the same conveyance to another customs station or a place outside India, passing without payment of duty. The Colombo containers are transhipped: they are landed and moved to a different conveyance, which needs a bill of transhipment, or a declaration for transhipment where an international treaty or bilateral agreement applies. In neither case is import duty collected, though the liability accrued on entry into territorial waters, and the difference lies in the continuity of the manifest record.

citation.ref: Sections 53, 54 and 55, read with section 2(24)

points.text: Stores are goods for use in a vessel or aircraft. Fuel counts, so do spare parts, and so does any other equipment article, whether or not it is meant for immediate fitting; a vehicle's supplies are outside the definition. Under section 86, imported stores may remain on board without payment of duty while the vessel is in India, and with the proper officer's permission may be transferred to another vessel or aircraft as stores for consumption there.

citation.ref: Sections 2(38) and 86

points.text: Under section 87, imported stores on board may be consumed without payment of duty during the period the vessel is a foreign-going vessel, which runs from the first Indian port of arrival to the final Indian port of departure for a destination outside India. When Ocean Pearl converts to coastal voyages at Chennai she ceases to be foreign-going, and import duty becomes chargeable on the unconsumed stores then on board, the stores list in the arrival manifest being the basic document for the assessment.

citation.ref: Section 87, read with section 2(21)

points.text: Under section 89, Indian-made goods wanted as stores aboard a foreign-going vessel leave the country free of export duty, in whatever quantity the proper officer settles after weighing the size of the vessel, how many passengers and crew she carries and the length of the voyage; the chandler's rice, vegetables and water go on board duty-free on that estimated requirement, but only while she is still foreign-going.

citation.ref: Section 89

points.text: Section 85 lets imported goods entered for warehousing be warehoused without being assessed to duty, where the importer declares that they will go to a vessel or an aircraft as stores and no duty will be paid on them. Section 88 applies section 69 and the drawback chapter to stores, so warehoused goods may be taken on board a foreign-going vessel without import duty, and duty-paid imported stores re-exported earn drawback under section 74; fuel and lubricating oil taken on board a foreign-going aircraft earn drawback of the whole of the duty, against the 98 per cent available on other goods. Under section 90 imported stores for a ship of the Indian Navy are consumed without duty and also earn drawback of the whole duty.

citation.ref: Sections 85, 88 and 90, read with sections 69 and 74

written.scenario: Nirvaan Metals imported 1,000 units of an alloy and paid duty of ₹4,00,000 on 1 December 2025 on a self-assessed bill of entry, against ₹2,50,000 properly payable, because the quantity was keyed in twice. It sold the entire lot in January 2026 at a price built up from cost plus the duty actually paid plus margin. It discovered the error in August 2026 and filed a complete refund application, acknowledged by the proper officer, on 20 September 2026, supported by its invoices and a chartered accountant's certificate. The department sanctioned ₹1,50,000 and paid it on 20 February 2027.
written.question: State who may claim a customs refund and within what time, whether Nirvaan's claim is in time, who receives the ₹1,50,000 and why, and the interest payable on it. Would the position differ if Nirvaan had first appealed against the assessment?

points.text: A refund of duty or interest may be claimed by the person who paid it or by the person who bore its incidence. An importer or exporter claims within one year from the date of payment; a person other than the importer from whom the duty was collected claims within one year from the date of purchase of the goods; where duty was exempted by a special order under section 25(2), the year runs from the date of the order; where the refund follows a judgment, decree or order of an appellate authority, Tribunal or court, from the date of that judgment; and where duty was paid provisionally under section 18, from the date of adjustment on final assessment or reassessment. Duty paid under protest has no time limit at all, and no refund is made if the amount claimed is less than ₹100.

citation.ref: Section 27(1) with its provisos and Explanation, and section 27(1B)

points.text: Nirvaan paid on 1 December 2025, so the year ran to 30 November 2026; its application of 20 September 2026 is in time. The application must carry documentary evidence, including the invoices referred to in section 28C, establishing that the duty was paid by the claimant and that its incidence has not been passed on to any other person, because section 28D presumes the opposite: every duty paid is taken to have reached the buyer's pocket, and it is for the claimant to prove otherwise.

citation.ref: Sections 27(1A), 28C and 28D

points.text: Where the amount is found refundable, section 27(2) directs it to the Consumer Welfare Fund, and it is paid to the applicant only in the listed cases: an importer or exporter who has not passed on the incidence; imports by an individual for personal use; a buyer who bore the duty and has not passed it on; export duty refundable under section 26; drawback under sections 74 and 75; a notified class of applicants; and duty paid in excess before the clearance order where the excess is evident from a self-assessed bill of entry or the duty payable appears in a reassessed bill of entry. This is the doctrine of unjust enrichment, upheld by nine judges in Mafatlal Industries, and the Supreme Court in Allied Photographics held that it applies even to duty paid under protest and that an unchanged price does not by itself prove the incidence was passed on.

citation.ref: Section 27(2) with its proviso; Mafatlal Industries Ltd v. UOI 1997 (89) ELT 247 (SC); CCE v. Allied Photographics 2004 (166) ELT 3 (SC)

points.text: Nirvaan priced its sales on the duty actually paid, so the excess ₹1,50,000 was recovered from its buyers and its own certificate cannot displace the presumption; the refund is sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund, not paid to Nirvaan. The department cannot simply keep the excess. Had the excess been paid before the clearance order and been evident from the self-assessed bill of entry itself, the last exception would have returned it to Nirvaan regardless of its pricing.

citation.ref: Section 27(2)(a) and (g)

points.text: Interest under section 27A runs where duty ordered to be refunded is not refunded within three months from the date of receipt of the complete application, from the day after those three months to the date of refund, at 6 per cent under Notification No. 75/2003-Customs (N.T.), the statutory band being 5 to 30 per cent. Had the ₹1,50,000 been payable to Nirvaan, the three months from 20 September 2026 would have ended on 20 December 2026 and interest would run for the 62 days from 21 December 2026 to 20 February 2027: ₹1,50,000 at 6 per cent for 62 days is ₹1,529. No interest is payable on deposits such as security for provisional release.

citation.ref: Section 27A read with Notification No. 75/2003-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2003

points.text: A refund claim is not a substitute for an appeal. Once an order of assessment stands, duty is payable under it, and the officer deciding a refund cannot sit in appeal over it; the Supreme Court so held in Priya Blue Industries and in ITC Ltd extended it to a self-assessed bill of entry, which must be modified in appeal under section 128, within sixty days of the order, before a refund can follow. Nirvaan's route is to seek amendment or reassessment of the bill of entry first, and the refund follows the modified assessment.

citation.ref: Section 27 read with section 128; Priya Blue Industries Ltd v. CCus 2004 (172) ELT 145 (SC); ITC Ltd v. CCE 2019 (368) ELT 216 (SC)

written.scenario: Tanish Precision imported a CNC machine and cleared it for home consumption on 10 April 2026, paying duty of ₹9,60,000. On trial runs, which were the only way to test it, the machine failed the tolerances written into the purchase contract. The supplier agreed to take it back. Tanish wants the duty back and asks how long it has and what it must do. Separately, in January 2026 it had exported a consignment of brass fittings on payment of export duty; the foreign buyer rejected them and returned them, not by resale, and they were re-imported on 15 May 2026 with the clearance order passed on 20 May 2026.
written.question: Explain the conditions and time limits for refund of the import duty on the machine under section 26A, and of the export duty on the fittings under section 26.

points.text: Section 26A refunds import duty paid on goods cleared for home consumption, so long as they can be easily identified and turn out to be defective, or else not in conformity with what the importer and the supplier had agreed as specifications. Nobody may have worked on them, repaired them or used them once imported — save for a use that was indispensable to bring the defect or the non-conformity to light; Tanish's trial runs were indispensable and do not defeat the claim.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1)(a)

points.text: The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner as the goods that were imported; the importer must not claim drawback under any other provision; and within thirty days of the clearance order under section 47 the importer must either export the goods, relinquish title and abandon them to customs, or destroy them or render them commercially valueless in the presence of the proper officer. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may on sufficient cause extend the thirty days by a period not exceeding three months. Tanish's clearance was on 10 April 2026, so the machine must be shipped back by 10 May 2026 unless extended, at the latest to 10 August 2026.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1)(b), (c) and (d) with the proviso

points.text: The application for refund is made within six months from the relevant date, which is the date of the order permitting clearance and loading for export under section 51 where the goods are exported, the date of relinquishment where title is relinquished, and the date of destruction where the goods are destroyed or rendered commercially valueless. No refund is allowed for perishable goods or goods past their shelf life or recommended storage period, nor for goods in respect of which an offence appears to have been committed.

citation.ref: Section 26A(2) with its Explanation and section 26A(3)

points.text: Section 26 gives the export duty back to whoever paid it, or to the person on whose behalf the payment was made, provided the goods come back to that person otherwise than by way of resale, return to India inside one year of the date they were exported, and the claim is lodged within six months of the day the proper officer passes the clearance order on the re-imported goods. The fittings exported in January 2026 and re-imported on 15 May 2026 are within the year, and the application must be made by 20 November 2026, six months from the clearance order of 20 May 2026.

citation.ref: Section 26

keywords: otherwise than by way of resale

written.scenario: When the rate of tax on a range of household appliances fell on 22 September 2025, Pranay Electronics kept its shelf prices unchanged and pocketed the difference, and separately began claiming input tax credit it had never taken before without cutting prices. A consumer body wants to complain in October 2025 and asks what will happen. The company also disputes a demand order which it says it never received: the department had sent it by speed post to the registered address and uploaded it on the common portal. Its tax for a month works out to ₹12,34,567.60.
written.question: Explain the obligation under section 171 and what an order against a profiteer contains, whether the consumer body's complaint will be examined at all, whether the demand order was validly served, and how the tax figure is rounded.

points.text: Section 171(1) puts a duty on the supplier: cut the rate of tax on a supply of goods or of services, or gain the benefit of input tax credit, and that gain must reach the recipient as a commensurate reduction in prices. Both of Pranay's practices are caught: the rate cut and the newly available credit are the two triggers, and a fall in its own costs would not have been one. The Authority which examines this is, since 1 October 2024 under Notification No. 18/2024-Central Tax, the Principal Bench of the GST Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 109; before that it was the National Anti-Profiteering Authority until November 2022 and the Competition Commission of India from 1 December 2022.

citation.ref: Sections 171(1) and 171(2) with its Explanation; Notification No. 18/2024-Central Tax dated 30 September 2024

points.text: The complaint will not be examined. Section 171 carries a sunset clause under which the Government may notify a date from which the Authority shall not accept any request for examination, and Notification No. 19/2024-Central Tax fixed that date as 1 April 2025. A request for examination is the written application asking whether credit or a rate cut has actually resulted in a commensurate reduction in price, and one filed in October 2025 is after the sunset, whatever the merits.

citation.ref: Section 171(2) proviso; Notification No. 19/2024-Central Tax dated 30 September 2024

points.text: Where a request was in time, the State-level Screening Committee examines a local application and forwards it with its recommendation to the Standing Committee within two months, extendable by one; the Standing Committee, on prima facie evidence, refers it to the Director General of Anti-Profiteering within two months, extendable by one; the DGAP investigates within six months, extendable by three, with the powers of a civil court, the inquiry being a judicial proceeding; and the Authority passes its order within six months of receiving the DGAP's report, after a hearing if asked for in writing.

citation.ref: Rules 128, 129 and 133, read with section 171(2)

points.text: Where profiteering is found, the Authority may order reduction in prices; return to the recipient of the amount not passed on with interest at 18 per cent from the date of collection of the higher amount until its return; where the recipient does not claim it or is not identifiable, deposit of 50 per cent of that amount with interest in the Consumer Welfare Fund of the Centre and 50 per cent in that of the State; a penalty; and cancellation of registration. Under section 171(3A) a person found to have profiteered pays a penalty of 10 per cent of the profiteered amount if it is not deposited within thirty days of the order. The order must be complied with immediately, failing which recovery follows.

citation.ref: Section 171(3A) with its Explanation, read with rule 133(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: The demand order was validly served. Section 169(1) permits service by giving or tendering it directly or by messenger or courier; by registered post, speed post or courier with acknowledgement due to the last known place of business or residence; by e-mail to the registered address; by making it available on the common portal; by publication in a newspaper circulating in the locality; and, only if none of these is practicable, by affixing it at the place of business or on the office notice board. Speed post and the portal are two of the listed modes; an order sent by registered or speed post is deemed received at the expiry of the period normally taken in transit unless the contrary is proved, and every communication is deemed served on the date it is tendered, published or affixed.

Under section 170 the amount of tax, interest, penalty, fine, refund or any other sum payable or due under the Act is rounded to the nearest rupee: a part of a rupee of fifty paise or more is increased to one rupee and a part of less than fifty paise is ignored. The rounding applies to the consolidated payment to the Government, not to individual tax invoices, so ₹12,34,567.60 is paid as ₹12,34,568.

citation.ref: Section 170

written.scenario: Two Surat firms approach you in April 2026. Kesari Trading buys embroidered fabric from local mills and exports it, and wants to become an Export Oriented Unit to import its packing machinery duty-free. Rangoli Textiles Pvt Ltd will set up a new dyeing and finishing unit with plant and machinery of ₹3.5 crore, importing the machinery, buying dyes from a Gujarat supplier, exporting most of the output, and selling some finished fabric at home. It asks what it gives up in return, how the foreign-exchange test is measured, and what leaving the scheme would cost.
written.question: Advise both firms on eligibility for the EOU scheme, the entitlements and obligations of an EOU, the net foreign exchange test, and exit from the scheme.

points.text: Kesari cannot be an EOU. A unit may be set up under the EOU, EHTP, STP or BTP schemes only where it undertakes to export its entire production, goods and services alike, apart from the sales into the domestic tariff area that are permitted; the schemes cover manufacture, which takes in repair, remaking, reconditioning and re-engineering, the rendering of services, the development of software, and agriculture with its allied activities. Trading units are not covered under these schemes, and a firm that only buys and exports is a trader.

citation.ref: Chapter 6, the scope of the EOU, EHTP, STP and BTP schemes

points.text: Rangoli qualifies on investment: only projects with a minimum investment of ₹1 crore in plant and machinery are considered for establishment as an EOU, and ₹3.5 crore clears it. The floor does not apply to existing units, to units in an EHTP, STP or BTP, or to an EOU working in any of these lines: handicrafts; agriculture, floriculture, aquaculture and animal husbandry; information technology and services; brass hardware; handmade jewellery. The Board of Approval may allow a lower investment. The application goes to the Unit Approval Committee or the Board of Approval, and an existing DTA unit may apply for conversion into an EOU.

citation.ref: Chapter 6, investment criteria and approvals for an EOU

points.text: An EOU may import, or procure from the domestic tariff area, from bonded warehouses or from an international exhibition held in India, all types of goods required for its activities, including capital goods, without payment of basic customs duty, the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, IGST and compensation cess, on a self-certification basis and subject to an actual user condition; the goods must be used for export production. Goods covered by GST bought from the DTA, such as Rangoli's dyes, are bought on payment of GST and compensation cess, and the DTA supplier earns deemed export benefits and may claim the refund of that GST subject to the conditions.

citation.ref: Chapter 6, entitlements of an EOU and supplies from the DTA

points.text: An EOU shall be a positive net foreign exchange earner, and the earnings are calculated cumulatively in blocks of five years starting from commencement of production, extendable in specified cases, with higher value addition required in certain sectors. Its other entitlements are exemption from industrial licensing for items reserved for micro and small enterprises, realisation of export proceeds within nine months, retention of 100 per cent of export earnings in an EEFC account, no bank guarantee at import or on job work in the DTA subject to conditions, and 100 per cent foreign direct investment through the automatic route.

citation.ref: Chapter 6, net foreign exchange earnings and other entitlements

points.text: The home sales are the exception, not the rule: every DTA sale is one that Chapter 6 permits on its own conditions, and finished goods may be sold in the DTA only if freely importable, on fulfilment of positive net foreign exchange, on payment of GST and compensation cess and reversal of the customs duties exempted on the inputs used, following the standard input output norms. Transfer of manufactured or capital goods to another EOU is allowed on payment of GST and cess with prior intimation to both Development Commissioners and customs, and the receiving unit treats them as imported goods when it later sells into the DTA.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6.07 and the inter-unit transfer provisions of Chapter 6

points.text: With the approval of the Development Commissioner, or the designated officer for an EHTP, STP or BTP, a unit may opt out of the scheme, and the exit is paid for: applicable excise and customs duties on the goods in hand, and IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST and compensation cess, all under the industrial policy in force; and a unit that has not achieved its obligations is also liable to penalty at the time of exit, the duty being the price of the goods and the penalty the price of the broken undertaking.

citation.ref: Chapter 6, exit from the scheme

written.scenario: Zapp Platforms Ltd, registered in Karnataka, runs an app through which, in October 2025, all within Karnataka, the following were supplied and paid for through the app: cab rides by individual drivers, ₹20 lakh; omnibus rides by Nilgiri Travels Pvt Ltd, a company, ₹5 lakh, and by an individual bus owner, ₹3 lakh; rooms of a guest house whose owner is not liable for registration, ₹4 lakh, and rooms of a registered hotel chain, ₹30 lakh; local delivery by riders who are not liable for registration, ₹6 lakh; goods sold by registered sellers, ₹2 crore, of which goods worth ₹20 lakh were returned in the month; and goods sold by a composition dealer, ₹5 lakh, who also asks Zapp to list his goods for buyers in Tamil Nadu.
written.question: Identify the supplies on which Zapp itself pays the tax under section 9(5), compute the tax it must collect at source under section 52 for October 2025, and state its compliance obligations and what it must refuse the composition dealer.

points.text: Under section 9(5) the Government may notify categories of services the tax on which, when supplied through an electronic commerce operator, is paid by the operator as if it were the supplier. Notification No. 17/2017-CT (R) as amended from 22 September 2025 lists six: passenger transport by radio-taxi, motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle or any motor vehicle except an omnibus; passenger transport by omnibus except where the supplier through the operator is a company; accommodation in hotels, inns, guest houses, clubs or campsites except where the supplier is liable for registration under section 22(1); house-keeping such as plumbing and carpentering with the same exception; restaurant service other than at specified premises; and local delivery with the same exception. An operator with no physical presence pays through its representative or a person it appoints.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with its provisos; Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended with effect from 22 September 2025

keywords: as if it were the supplier

points.text: Zapp pays the tax itself on the cab rides of ₹20 lakh, the individual's omnibus rides of ₹3 lakh, the unregistered guest house's rooms of ₹4 lakh and the riders' local delivery of ₹6 lakh. It does not pay on the omnibus rides of ₹5 lakh, because the supplier is a company and the company pays; nor on the registered hotel chain's ₹30 lakh, because that supplier is liable for registration under section 22(1); on both of those the ordinary charge stays with the supplier and Zapp collects tax at source instead.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) read with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entries (b), (c) and (f)

points.text: Under section 52 an operator that is not an agent must collect tax at source wherever it takes in the consideration for another supplier's sale, and the base is the net value of taxable supplies. The notified rate is 0.25 per cent CGST with 0.25 per cent SGST where the supply is intra-State, and 0.5 per cent IGST where it crosses a State. To find that base, add up the value of the month's taxable supplies of goods or services routed through the operator by every registered person, leaving out services notified under section 9(5), then take away the value of what was returned to those suppliers in the same month; the sum is done supplier by supplier, and a supplier whose returns run past his supplies counts as nil, never as a minus, that month or any later one.

citation.ref: Section 52(1) with its Explanation; Notification No. 52/2018-Central Tax as amended

points.text: Zapp's net value for October 2025 is the registered sellers' ₹2 crore less returns of ₹20 lakh, that is ₹1,80,00,000, plus the composition dealer's ₹5,00,000, plus the hotel chain's ₹30,00,000 and Nilgiri's omnibus rides of ₹5,00,000, which are taxable supplies through the operator outside section 9(5): ₹2,20,00,000 in all. Tax collected at source is 0.5 per cent of that, ₹1,10,000, being CGST ₹55,000 and SGST ₹55,000. The four section 9(5) supplies, ₹33 lakh together, are outside the net value because Zapp pays their tax itself.

citation.ref: Section 52(1) with its Explanation

points.text: Zapp must be registered as an operator under section 24(iv) for its section 9(5) supplies and under section 24(x) for collecting tax at source, applying in Form GST REG-07, and its sellers other than section 9(5) suppliers are registered under section 24(ix). The amount collected is paid to the Government within ten days after the end of the month, and a monthly statement in Form GSTR-8 goes in within ten days after the month; an annual statement is due before 31 December following the financial year; an omission in a statement may be rectified in a later month's statement with interest under section 50(1), but not after 30 November following the financial year or the annual statement, whichever is earlier. The supplier claims the amount reflected in the statement as credit in his electronic cash ledger, and an officer not below Deputy Commissioner may call for details of supplies or stock, to be furnished within fifteen working days.

A composition taxpayer may supply goods, but not services, through an operator, and the special procedure under section 148 in Notification No. 36/2023-CT binds Zapp: no composition supplier may be allowed to make an inter-State supply of goods over its platform, it collects tax at source on his goods, and it reports them in GSTR-8. Zapp must therefore refuse to list the dealer's goods for buyers in Tamil Nadu, and its platform must carry the check that blocks it. Tax is not collected at source on supplies taxed on reverse charge, nor on imports of goods, which fall under the Customs Act, nor on import of services.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(d) and section 148; Notification No. 36/2023-Central Tax dated 4 August 2023

written.scenario: Bharat Alloys imported four consignments at Kandla in 2026. First, 6,000 tonnes of scrap on which duty was paid after the clearance order; on taking delivery from the port, before the goods left, only 5,500 tonnes could be found and the port trust certified the shortfall. Second, 400 cartons of bearings from which 30 cartons had been broken open and emptied while in the custodian's charge, before any clearance order.
